conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 예약하다 becomes 예약할 수 있어요 ("can") and 예약할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 사진 찍다 means "to take a photo" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 사진 찍다 (sajin jjikda) = "to take a photo". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 사진 찍어요 plus one useful sentence like 사진 찍어 주세요 ("Please take a photo."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 사진 찍고 싶어요 for what you want, 사진 찍을 수 있어요 for what you can, 사진 못 찍어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help.

commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사진 찍다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사진 찍어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.shortExplanation: 당황하다 means "to be flustered" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.note: 완전 ('totally') is the everyday intensifier here; 갑자기 = 'all of a sudden'.

words.nuance: 당황하다 = to be momentarily flustered, thrown off, caught off guard — the perfect word for a 'my brain went blank' instant, NOT prolonged panic or dread. The Sino-Korean root is 唐慌: 唐 'abrupt/sudden' + 慌 'flurried, panicked', so it literally paints a sudden flurry of mind. Compare its neighbors: 긴장하다 (緊張) is the nervous tension you feel BEFORE an event (a held breath), while 당황하다 is the scramble in the MOMENT something unexpected hits. 놀라다 is plain 'be startled/surprised'; 당황하다 adds the 'and now I don't know what to do' confusion on top. The big English-speaker pitfall: don't say 당황돼 — unlike 걱정되다 or 긴장되다, 당황하다 already encodes the felt experience and is not normally built with 되다, so use 당황해 / 당황했어. Also keep the adjective 당황스럽다 ('the situation is bewildering') separate from the verb 당황하다 ('I got flustered').

Use 당황해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 당황돼 / 당황되다 — unlike 걱정되다 or 긴장되다, 당황하다 is not normally paired with 되다; use 당황해 / 당황했어 for the felt reaction.
Spacing the negative as 안 당황해 — because 당황 is a noun + 하다, the natural casual negative is 당황 안 해 (noun + 안 + 해).

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 당황하다 becomes 당황할 수 있어 ("can") and 당황할 거야 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 질투하다 means "to be jealous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to be jealous" in Korean is 질투하다 (jiltuhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 질투해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 질투하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 질투하는 거야? ("Are you jealous?") — then reshape the same stem into 질투하고 싶어 (desire), 질투할 수 있어 (ability), and 질투 못 해 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Teasing a partner or friend; playful tone is common.

examples.en: My boyfriend has a lot of female friends so I get a bit jealous.
examples.note: 남친 = 남자친구 (boyfriend), 여사친 = 여자 사람 친구 (female friend) — essential dating slang.

examples.romanization: chinguga naboda jaldwaeseo jiltuhaneun naega neomu sireo.
examples.en: I hate that I'm jealous of my friend doing better than me.
examples.note: 잘되다 = 'to go well / succeed'; 나보다 = 'than me'. Honest self-talk.

examples.ko: 걔 인스타 보면 가끔 질투 나.
examples.romanization: gyae inseuta bomyeon gakkeum jiltu na.

examples.note: 질투(가) 나다 is more natural than 질투하다 for a passing twinge; 걔 = 'that person (casual)'.

words.nuance: 질투하다 carries a sharp, possessive jealousy — the romantic or competitive sting of 'they have what I want and it bothers me'. The hanja is 嫉妬, where BOTH characters (嫉 and 妬) literally mean envy/jealousy, doubling the intensity. The crucial dividing line for English speakers: English 'jealous' is used loosely for mild envy, but Korean splits it. 부럽다 = harmless, friendly envy ('lucky you, I wish I had that') and is what you say ~90% of the time; saying 부러워 warms a conversation. 질투하다 / 질투 나다 is the bitter, edged version, and accusing a friend of 질투해 can genuinely sting. Also note register: to report the feeling, 질투(가) 나 ('I feel jealous') sounds more natural and less self-incriminating than the bald 질투해. Pitfall: never reach for 질투하다 when you just mean 'how nice for you' — that is 부럽다, full stop.

Use 질투해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 질투하다 where English 'jealous' only means envious — 'You went to Jeju? 부럽다!' not 질투해.
Saying 나는 너를 질투해 to mean light envy of a friend — to an actual friend this sounds accusatory; soften to 너 진짜 부럽다 or 질투 나려 그래.

words.shortExplanation: 포기하다 means "to give up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 포기하다 (pogihada) = "to give up". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 포기해요 plus one useful sentence like 포기하지 마 ("Don't give up"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 포기하고 싶어 for what you want, 포기할 수 있어 for what you can, 포기 못 해 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The standard motivational line — friends, coaches, dramas all use it.

examples.note: 진작에 = 'long ago / already'; 다이어트 포기 is a relatable running joke.

examples.ko: 집값 보고 서울에 집 사는 건 포기했어.
examples.romanization: jipgaps bogo seoure jip saneun geon pogihaesseo.
examples.en: After seeing the prices, I gave up on buying a place in Seoul.
examples.note: 집값 = housing prices; ~는 건 포기하다 = 'give up on doing'. A very real 20-30s concern.

examples.ko: 여기까지 왔는데 지금 포기하기엔 너무 아까워.
examples.romanization: yeogikkaji wanneunde jigeum pogihagien neomu akkawo.
examples.en: We've come this far — it'd be a waste to give up now.
examples.note: 아깝다 = 'too good to waste'; 여기까지 왔는데 = 'having come this far'.

words.nuance: 포기하다 = to give up, abandon, or relinquish a goal, plan, claim, or even a person. The hanja 抛棄 is vivid: 抛 'to throw/hurl away' + 棄 'to discard, abandon', so the image is hurling something aside and walking off — a decisive letting-go, not a gentle fade. Contrast 포기하다 (stop pursuing a goal entirely) with 그만두다 (stop/quit an ongoing activity — a job, a habit) and with 단념하다 (a more bookish 'resign oneself to abandoning hope'); in speech 포기하다 is the everyday choice. Grammar: it pairs with 을/를 (목표를 포기하다) or with 는 거 / 는 걸 (사는 걸 포기하다 = 'give up on buying'). Culturally the word is loaded: N포세대, the 'give-up generation', names young Koreans said to have surrendered dating, marriage, and kids to economic pressure. English-speaker pitfall: the negative is 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), NOT 안 포기해.

Use 포기해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spacing the negative wrong — it's 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), not 안 포기해.
Saying 일을 포기했어 to mean 'I quit my job' — for quitting an activity/job use 그만뒀어 (그만두다); 포기하다 is for giving up on a goal or outcome.

examples.en: This year I'm going to try taking on a marathon.

words.nuance: 도전하다 = to take something on, rise to a challenge, brave a new or daunting endeavor — overwhelmingly positive and aspirational (a job change, a new hobby, scary spicy food, a hard exam). Sincere promise to put in effort; softer and warmer than a firm guarantee.

examples.note: 늘리다 ('to improve/build up'); ~(으)려고 expresses purpose. Perfect learner sentence.

words.shortExplanation: 버티다 means "to hold out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 버티다 (beotida) = "to hold out". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 버텨요 plus one useful sentence like 조금만 더 버텨 ("Just hold on a little longer"). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Just hold on a little longer
usagePhrases.note: Gritty encouragement — survive the hard part; 조금만 더 = 'just a bit more'.

examples.en: I got through exam season running on coffee.
examples.note: ~(으)로 버티다 = 'get by on'; 시험 기간 = exam period. Universal student life.

examples.en: My boss was awful so I held out a year and then quit.
examples.note: 진상 = a nasty/awful person (slang); 퇴사하다 = 'to quit one's job'.

examples.en: Don't give up here — let's tough it out to the end.
examples.note: 끝까지 = 'to the very end'; pairs naturally with 포기하지 말다 in one breath.

words.nuance: 버티다 = to hold out, hang on, withstand, or scrape through a hard stretch — often financially or under pressure (a brutal job, no money, exam season). It is a pure native Korean verb (no hanja), and that street-level texture matters: 버티다 is grittier and more colloquial than its near-synonym 견디다. The line between them: 견디다 leans toward passively 'enduring/bearing' pain or hardship, while 버티다 adds an active 'dig-in-your-heels and refuse to collapse' stance — holding a position against a force. So young Koreans joke 월급날까지 버틴다 ('surviving till payday') and 일단 버텨 ('just hang in there for now'). Conjugation note: it's a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 버티 + 어 contracts to 버텨, and the past is 버티 + 었어 → 버텼어 (one syllable, not 버티었어). Pitfall: don't write the past as 버티었어 or 버텼써 — the correct spelling is 버텼어.

words.shortExplanation: 위로하다 means "to comfort" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 위로하다 (wirohada) means "to comfort". Start from the polite form 위로해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 위로하다. A strong first sentence is 위로해 줘서 고마워 ("Thanks for comforting me"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
~아/어 줘서 고마워 = 'thanks for (doing) for me'; very common.

examples.ko: 친구가 힘들 때 옆에서 위로해 줬어.
examples.romanization: chinguga himdeul ttae yeopeseo wirohae jwosseo.
examples.en: My friend comforted me when I was going through a hard time.
examples.note: 옆에서 ('by my side') + 위로해 주다 — the benefactive 주다 is almost always attached.

examples.ko: 말없이 안아주는 게 제일 큰 위로였어.
examples.romanization: mareopsi anajuneun ge jeil keun wiroyeosseo.
examples.en: Just being hugged without words was the biggest comfort.
examples.note: 위로 as a noun ('comfort'); 말없이 = 'without words', 안아주다 = 'to hug (someone)'.

examples.ko: 장례식에서 유가족을 어떻게 위로해야 할지 몰라서 그냥 손을 잡아 드렸어.
examples.romanization: jangnyesigeseo yugajogeul eotteoke wirohaeya halji mollaseo geunyang soneul jaba deuryeosseo.
examples.en: At the funeral I didn't know how to comfort the bereaved family, so I just held their hand.
examples.note: 유가족 = the bereaved family; ~해야 할지 몰라서 = 'not knowing how I should'. A weighty real moment.

words.nuance: 위로하다 = to comfort or console someone in pain, grief, or loss. The hanja 慰勞 is telling: 慰 'to soothe, console' + 勞 'toil, weariness', i.e. to soothe another's hardship — so the word carries real emotional weight and suits sorrow, bereavement, and exhaustion, not light cheering-up. In practice it almost always appears as 위로해 주다 (with the benefactive 주다, because comfort is something you GIVE someone) or as the noun 위로 (위로가 되다 'to be a comfort', 위로를 받다 'to be comforted'). Contrast it sharply with 응원하다: you 위로해 someone who is hurting or grieving, but you 응원해 someone facing a challenge ahead — comfort looks back at pain, cheering looks forward to a goal. The big English-speaker pitfall: dropping 주다. '나는 친구를 위로했어' is grammatical but sounds clinical and detached, like a report; the warm, natural sentence is 친구를 위로해 줬어.

Dropping the benefactive 주다 — 'I comforted my friend' is 친구를 위로해 줬어, not bare 친구를 위로했어 (which sounds clinical/detached).
Using 위로하다 to root for someone before a challenge — that's 응원하다; 위로하다 is for someone already hurting or grieving.

words.shortExplanation: 응원하다 means "to cheer on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to cheer on" in Korean is 응원하다 (eungwonhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 응원해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 응원하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 항상 응원할게 ("I'll always be rooting for you") — then reshape the same stem into 응원하고 싶어 (desire), 응원할 수 있어 (ability), and 응원 못 해 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.en: I'll always be rooting for you

examples.note: 잘되길 (= 잘되기를) 응원하다 = 'cheer for it to go well'; sweet, everyday support.

examples.en: I'm always on your side and rooting for you.

examples.ko: 손흥민 경기 있어서 친구들이랑 모여서 다 같이 응원했어.

examples.note: 응원하다 also = cheering for a sports team; 모이다 = 'to gather'. Football-watch culture.

words.nuance: 응원하다 = to cheer on, root for, and actively support — both literally (yelling for a sports team, 응원단 = a cheering squad) and emotionally (backing a friend's goals). The hanja 應援 says it well: 應 'to respond' + 援 'to aid, rescue', i.e. to answer someone's effort with support. The key contrast is with 위로하다: 응원하다 looks FORWARD and is upbeat — you cheer someone on toward a challenge or future ('you've got this!') — whereas 위로하다 looks BACK at pain to console it. So 응원해 / 응원할게 is lighter and brighter than 위로해. It often takes the benefactive 응원해 줘 when you ask others for support. usagePhrases.en: I have to make sure to eat / eat properly.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The classic caring sign-off to someone close; 잘 ('well/properly') almost always rides along.

examples.en: I always make sure to eat breakfast.
examples.note: Simplest frame: object + 챙겨 먹어요. 꼭 = 'without fail'.

examples.ko: 혼자 살면 끼니 챙겨 먹기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: honja salmyeon kkini chaenggyeo meokgi himdeureoyo.
examples.en: When you live alone, it's hard to eat proper meals.
examples.note: ~기 힘들다 = 'it's hard to ~'; 끼니 챙겨 먹기 is the relatable struggle of 자취 (living alone).

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 많아서 밥을 잘 못 챙겨 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri manaseo babeul jal mot chaenggyeo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I've been so busy lately I haven't been eating properly.
examples.note: Real-life excuse: 못 goes before the whole phrase (못 챙겨 먹다 = 'fail to manage to eat').

words.nuance: 챙겨 먹다 is a compound — 챙기다 ('to look after, gather up, pack') in its connective form (챙기 + 어 → 챙겨) plus 먹다 — so it literally means 'look-after-and-eat', i.e. make a point of eating instead of skipping. The dividing line from plain 먹다 is intention: 먹다 just reports that eating happens, while 챙겨 먹다 stresses the care of not missing a meal (끼니, 아침, 약, 영양제 all collocate). Its warmest use is 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 — a parent's or partner's way of saying 'take care of yourself', far more natural than the stiff textbook 식사를 잘 하세요. Watch the conjugation: it rides on 챙기다 (regular ㅣ-stem), so the 요-form is 챙겨 먹어요, never 챙기어 먹어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using bare 먹다 for the caring nuance — 밥 먹었어? only asks the fact, whereas 밥 잘 챙겨 먹고 있어? carries the affection.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙겨 먹다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨 먹어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying the stiff 식사를 잘 하세요 to show you care — for warmth Koreans say 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 / 끼니 잘 챙겨 먹어요.
Writing the polite form as 챙기어 먹어요 — 챙기다 is a regular ㅣ-stem, so 챙기 + 어 contracts to 챙겨, giving 챙겨 먹어요.
Misplacing 못 as 챙겨 못 먹어요 — the negation wraps the whole phrase: 못 챙겨 먹어요 ('can't manage to eat properly').

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 챙겨 먹다 becomes 챙겨 먹을 수 있어요 ("can") and 챙겨 먹을 거예요 ("will"). words.english: to submit/file (an application), to register a request
words.shortExplanation: 접수하다 means "to submit/file (an application), to register a request" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 접수하다 (jeopsuhada) means "to submit/file (an application), to register a request". Start from the polite form 접수해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 접수하다. A strong first sentence is 서류를 접수하다 ("to file/submit documents"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 접수하다 also becomes 접수하고 싶어요 (want), 접수할 수 있어요 (can), and 접수할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I submit/file (an application), to register a request.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not submit/file (an application), to register a request.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to submit/file (an application), to register a request.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can submit/file (an application), to register a request.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to submit/file (an application), to register a request.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Often used at a counter (창구) — you hand in paperwork and it formally enters the system.

examples.en: Please submit the application form on the first floor.
examples.note: Typical instruction at a 주민센터; 접수해 주세요 is the polite request form.

examples.en: It has to be filed by today for it to be processed.
examples.note: Notice the two-step pair: 접수 (intake) comes first, 처리 (processing) follows.

examples.en: I filed it online but the reference number isn't showing.
examples.note: Real help-desk situation; 접수번호 = the receipt/tracking number you get.

words.nuance: 접수하다 (接受하다, 接 'receive' + 受 'accept') means to formally lodge something so it enters an official system — an application, complaint, or request. The tricky part is that it works BOTH ways: from your side it is 'submit/file,' but from the staff's side it means 'to receive/accept,' which is why 접수 on a sign marks the intake counter, not the act of submitting. Compare 제출하다 ('to hand in/submit a single document') and 신청하다 ('to apply/request'): 제출하다 just stresses physically turning paper in, 신청하다 stresses the request itself, while 접수하다 stresses the moment it is officially logged. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the wrong member of the 접- family: 접수하다 (file a request) looks almost identical to 접속하다 (to log in / connect online), so learners type the wrong one constantly.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 접수하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 접수해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse 접수하다 (file/lodge a request) with 접속하다 (to log in / connect online) — same first syllable, unrelated meanings.
Saying 접수했어요 to mean 'they processed/finished it' is wrong; 접수 only means it was received and logged. Use 처리됐어요 for 'it was processed/done.'

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 접수하다 becomes 접수할 수 있어요 ("can") and 접수할 거예요 ("will"). words.english: to fill out/write up (a form or document)
words.shortExplanation: 작성하다 means "to fill out/write up (a form or document)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to fill out/write up (a form or document)" in Korean is 작성하다 (jakseonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 작성해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 작성하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 신청서를 작성하다 ("to fill out an application form") — then reshape the same stem into 작성하고 싶어요 (desire), 작성할 수 있어요 (ability), and 작성할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I fill out/write up (a form or document).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not fill out/write up (a form or document).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to fill out/write up (a form or document).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can fill out/write up (a form or document).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to fill out/write up (a form or document).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to fill out an application form
usagePhrases.note: The default verb for completing any form, contract, or report.

examples.en: Please fill in this box in Korean.
examples.note: 칸 = a single box/field on a form; very common counter instruction.

examples.ko: 계약서를 작성하기 전에 꼼꼼히 읽어 보세요.
examples.romanization: gyeyakseoreul jakseonghagi jeone kkomkkomhi ilgeo boseyo.
examples.en: Read it carefully before drawing up the contract.
examples.note: -기 전에 = 'before doing'; 계약서 = contract, key for housing/jobs.

examples.ko: 지원 동기를 어떻게 작성해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: jiwon donggireul eotteoke jakseonghaeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: I'm not sure how to write up my reason for applying.
examples.note: Real job-application worry; 지원 동기 = motivation/cover-letter section.

words.nuance: 작성하다 (作成하다, 作 'make' + 成 'complete') is the standard, slightly formal verb for filling out or composing a structured document — forms, contracts, reports, official emails. The sharp contrast is with 쓰다 ('to write'): 쓰다 is the broad physical act of writing anything (a love letter, a quick note, a single word), whereas 작성하다 implies there is a template, format, or official purpose you are completing. So '편지를 쓰다' (write a letter) is natural but '편지를 작성하다' sounds stiffly bureaucratic, while '보고서를 작성하다' (write up a report) is exactly right. It collocates with 신청서, 계약서, 보고서, 이력서, 양식. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 쓰다 everywhere because English 'write' covers both — at offices and work you should default to 작성하다 the moment a form or formal document is involved.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 작성하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 작성해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For a quick handwritten note use 쓰다; '메모를 작성하다' sounds overly stiff for something casual.
Don't say '작성하다' for creative writing like a poem or diary — that's 쓰다. 작성하다 needs a structured/official document.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 작성하다 becomes 작성할 수 있어요 ("can") and 작성할 거예요 ("will"). words.english: to be issued / to get issued (a document or card)
words.shortExplanation: 발급받다 means "to be issued / to get issued (a document or card)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 발급받다 (balgeupbatda) = "to be issued / to get issued (a document or card)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 발급받아요 plus one useful sentence like 증명서를 발급받다 ("to get a certificate issued"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 발급받고 싶어요 for what you want, 발급받을 수 있어요 for what you can, 발급받을 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.

usagePhrases.en: I be issued / to get issued (a document or card).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be issued / to get issued (a document or card).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be issued / to get issued (a document or card).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be issued / to get issued (a document or card).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be issued / to get issued (a document or card).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Used for any official document you receive: 등본, 증명서, 카드, 비자.

examples.en: Where do I go to get my alien registration card issued?
examples.note: -(으)려면 = 'in order to'; core task at 출입국 (immigration).

examples.en: You can also get a resident registration copy from a self-service kiosk.
examples.note: 무인발급기 = unmanned issuing machine, found in many public buildings.

examples.en: I lost my debit card so I got it reissued yesterday.
examples.note: Shows the very common 재발급받다; 체크카드 = debit card.

words.nuance: 발급받다 (發給받다: 發 'issue out' + 給 'give,' plus native 받다 'to receive') is a compound that bakes the direction into the verb — it is specifically YOU receiving an officially issued document. Its mirror is 발급하다, which is what the issuing office does, so the same event is 'office가 발급하다' / 'I가 발급받다.' For residents it is everywhere: ID cards, bank cards, certificates, visas, even certificates of employment. Near-synonyms: 받다 alone just means 'receive' (too generic for officialdom), and 떼다 is a casual colloquial verb Koreans use for pulling a certificate ('등본 한 통 떼다'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 받다 and saying 발급하다 about yourself; in English 'I issued my card' is impossible anyway, and Korean is equally strict — you 발급받다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발급받다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발급받아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't say 발급하다 about yourself — that's what the issuing office does. You 발급받다 (receive issuance).
Don't mix up the prefixes: 재발급 = reissue (lost item), but 발급 alone = first-time issue. Saying 재발급 for a brand-new card is wrong.

words.shortExplanation: 등록하다 means "to register / to enroll" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 등록하다 (deungnokhada) means "to register / to enroll". Start from the polite form 등록해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 등록하다. A strong first sentence is 회원으로 등록하다 ("to register as a member"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 등록하다 also becomes 등록하고 싶어요 (want), 등록할 수 있어요 (can), and 등록할 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not register / to enroll.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to register / to enroll.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to register / to enroll.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Note 으로 ('as'): you register in the capacity of a member.

examples.en: You have to register your fingerprint to enter.
examples.note: -아야 …할 수 있어요 = 'only if you do, you can'; biometric access.

examples.ko: 수강 신청은 다음 주에 등록하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: sugang sincheongeun daeum jue deungnokamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can register for the course next week.
examples.note: -(으)면 돼요 = 'it's enough to / you just need to'; 수강 신청 = course sign-up.

examples.en: I registered my new phone on the company system.
examples.note: Data-into-a-system sense; 에 marks where it's registered.

words.nuance: 등록하다 (登錄하다, 登 'enter/ascend' + 錄 'record') literally means 'to enter onto the record/register,' which is exactly its feel: putting a person, class, device, or data point onto an official list. The key contrast is with 가입하다 ('to join a service/club/insurance'): 가입하다 is about BECOMING A MEMBER of a body, while 등록하다 is about RECORDING something into a system — and they even take different particles (보험에 가입하다 vs. 시스템에 등록하다 / 회원으로 등록하다). Also distinguish 신청하다 ('apply/request'), which is the asking step before you are actually 등록된 (registered). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'register' and 'sign up' feel interchangeable, so learners say 등록하다 for subscribing to a streaming service where Koreans would say 가입하다. If the result is a membership, prefer 가입하다; if the result is your data on a list, use 등록하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 등록하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 등록해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
등록하다 vs 가입하다: 가입하다 is joining a service/club/insurance; 등록하다 is recording data or enrolling. Don't use 등록하다 for 'subscribe to a service.'
Watch the particle: 'register AS a member' is 회원으로 등록하다, not 회원을 등록하다.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

The crucial use for residents: visa, stay, contract, deadline.

examples.ko: 체류 기간을 연장하러 출입국에 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: cheryu giganeul yeonjanghareo churipguge gaya haeyo.
examples.en: I have to go to immigration to extend my period of stay.
examples.note: -(으)러 가다 = 'go in order to'; 체류 기간 = period of stay.

examples.ko: 도서관 책 대출을 한 번 더 연장할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: doseogwan chaek daechureul han beon deo yeonjanghal su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can extend the library book loan one more time.
examples.note: 대출 = loan/borrowing; 한 번 더 = one more time.

examples.ko: 마감을 이틀만 연장해 주시면 안 될까요?
examples.romanization: magameul iteulman yeonjanghae jusimyeon an doelkkayo?
examples.en: Could you possibly extend the deadline by just two days?
examples.note: -주시면 안 될까요? = very soft, deferential workplace request.

words.nuance: 연장하다 (延長하다, 延 'prolong' + 長 'long') means to make an existing time span longer — a visa, contract, loan, deadline, or operating hours. examples.note: 관리비 = building maintenance fee; standard for apartment dwellers.

examples.en: If you pay the fine within the deadline, you get a discount.

words.nuance: 납부하다 (納付하다, 納 'pay in/deliver' + 付 'hand over') is the formal verb for paying money OWED TO AN INSTITUTION — taxes, public utilities, insurance premiums, fines, tuition. words.shortExplanation: 처리하다 means "to process / to handle / to deal with" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not process / to handle / to deal with.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to process / to handle / to deal with.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can process / to handle / to deal with.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to process / to handle / to deal with.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Covers processing paperwork, requests, and getting things done.

examples.en: Once the application is received, it is processed within 3 days.
examples.note: Passive 처리되다 in official notices; pairs with 접수되다.

examples.en: I'll handle this issue.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 = speaker's promise; reassuring at work.

examples.ko: 고객 불만이 들어오면 바로 처리해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gogaek bulmani deureoomyeon baro cheorihaeya haeyo.
examples.en: When a customer complaint comes in, you have to deal with it immediately.
examples.note: 불만 = complaint; -아야 해요 = obligation.

words.nuance: 처리하다 (處理하다, 處 'manage/place' + 理 'put in order') is a workhorse meaning to process, handle, or take care of a task, request, or problem, and the passive 처리되다 ('be processed') saturates official status messages. The register is neutral-professional, ideal for office work and paperwork. Watch three near-neighbors: 해결하다 ('to solve/resolve') implies fully fixing a problem so it's gone, whereas 처리하다 can just mean 'deal with / move it along the pipeline' without a happy ending; 다루다 means 'to handle/treat' in the sense of how you manage a topic or object; and bare 하다 ('do') cannot stand in for 'take care of a matter.' The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that bare-하다 trap: 'I'll do this issue' translated literally as '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong — you must say 처리할게요. Reach for 처리하다 whenever English would say 'handle,' 'take care of,' or 'process.'

Use 처리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Learners overuse 하다 alone; '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong. Use 처리하다 to mean 'handle/take care of' a matter.
처리하다 (deal with/move along) isn't always 해결하다 (fully solve). If the issue is actually resolved, say 해결됐어요, not just 처리됐어요.

words.shortExplanation: 문의하다 means "to inquire / to ask (formally)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to inquire / to ask (formally)" in Korean is 문의하다 (munuihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 문의해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 문의하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 자세한 내용을 문의하다 ("to inquire about details") — then reshape the same stem into 문의하고 싶어요 (desire), 문의할 수 있어요 (ability), and 문의할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not inquire / to ask (formally).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to inquire / to ask (formally).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to inquire / to ask (formally).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Formal 'ask' for businesses, offices, customer service.

examples.en: For details, please inquire with the customer center.
examples.note: -(으)로 here = 'to' that contact point; standard closing line.

examples.en: I inquired with immigration about visa matters.
examples.note: ~ 관련해서 = 'regarding ~'; very relevant resident situation.

examples.en: I'd like to inquire whether a refund is possible.
examples.note: 문의드리다 = humble form to a business; -ㄴ데요 softens the request.

words.nuance: 문의하다 (問議하다, 問 'ask' + 議 'discuss/consult') is the formal, polite verb for making an inquiry to a business or institution — by phone, email, or in person — and it appears on every company's contact page. The sharp contrast is with 물어보다 ('to ask'), the everyday native verb you use with friends, classmates, or a stranger on the street; 물어보다 between you and a company sounds too casual, while 문의하다 between two friends sounds absurdly stiff, like saying 'I should like to make an inquiry' to your roommate. For extra deference to a business, the humble 문의드리다 ('I inquire (to you)') is common. Note the particle: the place you ask takes 에/에게/(으)로, not 을/를 (고객센터에 문의하다, not 고객센터를 문의하다). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'ask' is one word for every register, so learners either over-formalize among friends or under-formalize toward institutions; match 문의하다 to organizations and 물어보다 to people.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 문의하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 문의해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Use 물어보다 for asking a friend a question; 문의하다 is for organizations/services and sounds too formal between individuals.

usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

examples.en: After moving you must file a move-in report within 14 days.
examples.note: 전입신고 = move-in registration; a legal requirement for residents.

examples.en: I lost my card so I reported it lost right away.
examples.note: 바로 = right away; urgent, practical action.

examples.ko: 옆집에서 너무 시끄러워서 경찰에 신고할 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: yeopjibeseo neomu sikkeureowoseo gyeongchare singohal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: It was so loud next door I almost reported it to the police.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 = 'almost did'; everyday spoken nuance.

words.nuance: 신고하다 (申告하다, 申 'state/declare' + 告 'tell/announce') means to officially report or declare something TO AN AUTHORITY — a move (전입신고), a loss, an emergency, taxes (세금 신고), or wrongdoing — and it always points toward a government office or official channel (the authority takes 에). Three contrasts matter. 신청하다 ('apply/request') is the big look-alike trap: 신고 = NOTIFY/DECLARE a fact, 신청 = REQUEST/apply for something you want — you 전입신고 (declare your move) but 비자를 신청 (apply for a visa). 알리다 ('to inform/let know') is the general, non-official verb (친구에게 알리다, tell a friend). 고발하다/고소하다 are heavier legal terms (accuse/press charges) beyond ordinary reporting. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'report' is broad and friendly, so learners use 신고하다 to mean 'tell/report to my boss' — but to an individual that should be 보고하다 (report up a hierarchy) or 알리다, while 신고하다 is reserved for officialdom.

Use 신고해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse 신고하다 (report to authorities) with 신청하다 (apply for). 신고 = notify/declare; 신청 = request/apply.
Don't use 신고하다 for 'reporting to my manager' — that's 보고하다 or 알리다. 신고하다 implies a government/official channel.

Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 서명하다 also becomes 서명하고 싶어요 (want), 서명할 수 있어요 (can), and 서명할 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The signed surface takes 에: 서류에/계약서에 서명하다.

examples.en: Please check the contents and sign here.
examples.note: -고 = 'and then'; the surface 여기 takes 에.

examples.ko: 계약서에 서명하기 전에 다시 한번 읽어 봤어요.
examples.romanization: gyeyakseoe seomyeonghagi jeone dasi hanbeon ilgeo bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I read the contract once more before signing it.
examples.note: -기 전에 = before; smart habit for housing/job contracts.

examples.en: Is an electronic signature also legally recognized?
examples.note: 전자 서명 = e-signature; 인정되다 = be recognized/accepted.

words.nuance: 서명하다 (署名하다, 署 'sign/inscribe' + 名 'name') means to write your name on a document as a signature, and the surface you sign takes 에 (계약서에 서명하다). Two contrasts are essential. First, register: 사인하다 is a casual loanword (from English 'sign') that Koreans say constantly in speech — '여기 사인해 주세요' — but on formal/legal documents the proper written term is 서명; treat 서명하다 as the dignified twin of 사인하다. Second, and uniquely Korean: signing is not the only option, because Korea traditionally validates documents with a personal stamp called 도장, and the officially registered version is the 인감(도장). So a counter clerk may ask for either a 서명 or a 도장, and certain legal papers still prefer the stamp. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle plus assuming a signature is always enough: say 계약서에 서명하다 (not 계약서를 서명하다), and be ready to be asked for a 도장 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 서명하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 서명해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Particle error: it's 계약서에 서명하다 (sign ON the contract), not 계약서를 서명하다.
서명하다 (formal signing) vs 사인하다 (casual loanword): 사인하다 is fine in speech, but for official documents use 서명. Also don't confuse 사인(sign) with 싸인/사인 meaning an autograph — context decides.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 서명하다 becomes 서명할 수 있어요 ("can") and 서명할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 서명하다 means to write your name on a document as a signature, and the surface you sign takes 에 (계약서에 서명하다). Uniquely Korean: signing is not the only option, because Korea traditionally validates documents with a personal stamp called 도장, and the officially registered version is the 인감(도장). So a counter clerk may ask for either a 서명 or a 도장, and certain legal papers still prefer the stamp.
署名하다: 署 'sign/inscribe' + 名 'name.'

Register contrast: 사인하다 is a casual loanword (from English 'sign') that Koreans say constantly in speech — '여기 사인해 주세요' — but on formal/legal documents the proper written term is 서명; treat 서명하다 as the dignified twin of 사인하다.
The particle plus assuming a signature is always enough: say 계약서에 서명하다 (not 계약서를 서명하다), and be ready to be asked for a 도장 instead.

words.shortExplanation: 출력하다 means "to print out / to output" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to print out / to output" in Korean is 출력하다 (chullyeokhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 출력해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 출력하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 서류를 출력하다 ("to print out documents") — then reshape the same stem into 출력하고 싶어요 (desire), 출력할 수 있어요 (ability), and 출력할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not print out / to output.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to print out / to output.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can print out / to output.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to print out / to output.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The standard office/admin verb for printing files.

examples.en: Print out the registration copy and bring it.
examples.note: -아서 = do and then; 등본 = certified copy, a frequent admin request.

examples.en: You can print documents at convenience stores too.
examples.note: 도 = 'too/even'; Korean convenience stores have self-print kiosks.

examples.en: I saved the file as PDF and then printed it.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 다음에 = 'after doing'; everyday office workflow.

words.nuance: 출력하다 (出力하다, 出 'come out' + 力 'force/power') literally means 'output,' and in computing it broadly opposes 입력하다 (入力, 'input/type in'). In daily admin and office life, however, it almost always means specifically 'to print out' from a computer, and that is how you'll see it on kiosks and printer menus. The register contrast is with 프린트하다, the casual English-loan equivalent people say in conversation ('이거 프린트해 줘'); 출력하다 is the cleaner, more formal/technical choice for instructions and signage. Don't confuse it with 복사하다 ('to photocopy/copy'), which duplicates an existing physical page rather than rendering a digital file. The English-speaker pitfall is the in/out pair: 출력 (out) and 입력 (in) share the 력 base and look similar, so beginners mix up 'print/output' with 'type/input' — anchor it with 출 = 'exit/out,' the same 출 as in 출구 (exit).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 출력하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 출력해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse 출력하다 (print/output) with 입력하다 (input/type in). 출 = out, 입 = in.
출력하다 (print a digital file) isn't 복사하다 (photocopy an existing page). To duplicate paper on a copier, use 복사하다.

words.english: to sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan)
words.shortExplanation: 가입하다 means "to sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 가입하다 (gaiphada) = "to sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 가입해요 plus one useful sentence like 보험에 가입하다 ("to sign up for insurance"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 가입하고 싶어요 for what you want, 가입할 수 있어요 for what you can, 가입할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.

usagePhrases.en: I sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to sign up / to join / to enroll in (a service or plan).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Takes 에: you join 'into' a service or plan.

examples.en: I just signed up for a new phone plan.
examples.note: 에 marks what you join; 새로 = newly/just.

examples.ko: 이 앱은 가입하지 않아도 쓸 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: i aebeun gaipaji anado sseul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Can I use this app without signing up?
examples.note: -지 않아도 = 'even without doing'; avoids making an account.

examples.en: What documents do I need to enroll in health insurance?
examples.note: -(으)려면 = 'in order to'; 건강보험 = national health insurance.

words.nuance: 가입하다 (加入하다, 加 'add' + 入 'enter') literally means 'to add oneself in / enter into,' i.e. to BECOME A MEMBER OR SUBSCRIBER of a service, plan, club, or insurance — and it firmly takes the particle 에 (보험에 가입하다, the thing you enter into). The contrasts within this admin set are the crux. 등록하다 ('register/record data') puts information onto a list (지문을 등록하다), whereas 가입하다 makes you a member of a body; 신청하다 ('apply/request') is merely the asking step, which may precede actually being 가입된 (enrolled). 회원 가입 is the universal 'Sign Up' on Korean apps and sites. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because English says 'join the gym / join insurance' with a direct object, learners produce 보험을 가입하다, but Korean requires 에 — what you join takes 에, not 을/를. Anchor it as '들어가다(enter) INTO 에.'
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가입하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가입해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Use 에, not 을/를: it's 보험에 가입하다, not 보험을 가입하다. The thing you join takes 에.
가입하다 (become a member) vs 등록하다 (record data): for joining a service/plan use 가입하다; reserve 등록하다 for entering data like a fingerprint or device.

加入하다: 加 'add' + 入 'enter.'

The particle: because English says 'join the gym / join insurance' with a direct object, learners produce 보험을 가입하다, but Korean requires 에 — what you join takes 에, not 을/를. Anchor it as '들어가다(enter) INTO 에.'

words.shortExplanation: 다치다 means "to get hurt" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 다치다 (dachida) means "to get hurt". Start from the polite form 다쳐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 다치다. A strong first sentence is 어디 다쳤어요? ("Where did you get hurt?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 다치다 also becomes 다치고 싶어요 (want), 다칠 수 있어요 (can), and 다칠 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The first thing people ask if you limp in or hold an injured spot; 어디 = 'where (on the body)'.

examples.en: I hurt my hand.
examples.note: Simplest frame: body part + 을/를 + 다치다. The hurt body part is the object, not the subject.

examples.en: I hurt my knee while playing soccer.
examples.note: V-다가 = 'while doing X, (something happened)'; the most common way to set up how an injury occurred.

examples.ko: 넘어져서 손목을 좀 다쳤는데 병원 가야 할까요?
examples.romanization: neomeojyeoseo sonmogeul jom dachyeonneunde byeongwon gaya halkkayo?
examples.en: I fell and hurt my wrist a bit — should I go to the hospital?
examples.note: Real clinic-decision moment; 넘어지다 = to fall over, and naming 손목 (wrist) routes you to 정형외과 (orthopedics).

words.nuance: 다치다 is the everyday verb for getting physically injured — bumps, cuts, sprains, breaks — and crucially the injured body part takes 을/를, not 이/가 (무릎을 다쳤어요, not 무릎이). Although it translates as 'to hurt', it behaves like an intransitive 'to GET hurt' aimed at yourself, so you cannot use it to mean 'I hurt someone else' — that is 다치게 하다 or 상처를 입히다. The nearest neighbor is 아프다, and the dividing line matters: 다치다 is the one-time event of getting injured (넘어져서 다쳤어요), while 아프다 is the lingering pain or sickness that follows (지금도 아파요). It pairs habitually with 크게 다치다 (badly hurt), 살짝/조금 다치다 (slightly hurt), and 다친 데 (the injured spot). At a hospital, 다치다 plus the exact body part (발목, 허리, 손목) gets you to the right department fast.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 다쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 아프다 when you mean an injury — 아프다 is 'it hurts / I'm sick' (a state), but 다치다 is the act of getting injured (an event). Say '넘어져서 다쳤어요' for the injury, then '지금도 아파요' for the pain that remains.
Marking the body part with 이/가 — it's 무릎을 다쳤어요 (object 을), not 무릎이 다쳤어요. The body part is what you injure, so it takes 을/를.
Trying to say 'I hurt my friend' with 다치다 — 친구를 다쳤어요 is wrong because 다치다 is about getting hurt yourself. Use 친구를 다치게 했어요 ('I caused my friend to get hurt').

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 다치다 becomes 다칠 수 있어요 ("can") and 다칠 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 낫다 means "to heal / to get better" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to heal / to get better" in Korean is 낫다 (natda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 나아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 낫다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 빨리 나으세요 ("Get well soon") — then reshape the same stem into 낫고 싶어요 (desire), 나을 수 있어요 (ability), and 나을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not heal / to get better.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to heal / to get better.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can heal / to get better.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to heal / to get better.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
THE phrase to send a sick coworker or friend; the honorific 나으세요 is warmer and more polite than 빨리 나아요.

examples.en: My cold got better.
examples.note: Core pattern: the illness is the SUBJECT (감기가) — you don't heal something, the sickness heals on its own.

examples.en: I took the medicine and the cold got better quickly.
examples.note: ㅅ-irregular in action: 낫 + 았어요 → 나았어요 (the ㅅ drops). 금방 = 'in no time'. Don't write 낳았어요 (gave birth).

examples.ko: 푹 쉬면 곧 나을 거예요, 너무 무리하지 마세요.
examples.romanization: puk swimyeon gon naeul geoyeyo, neomu murihaji maseyo.
examples.en: If you rest well you'll soon get better, so don't overdo it.
examples.note: 푹 쉬다 = 'to rest fully'; the classic comforting send-off pairing 나을 거예요 with 무리하지 마세요.

words.nuance: 낫다 means an illness or wound heals, and it is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을, 나으세요) but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고, 낫지). It is intransitive — the cold or the cut is the subject (감기가 나았어요, 상처가 나았어요) — so you never 'heal something' with it; for that you'd use 치료하다 (to treat) or 고치다 (to cure/fix). The big trap for everyone, native and learner alike, is the homophone cluster: 낫다 'heal', 낳다 'give birth', and 났다 (from 나다, 'broke out/occurred') all sound like [낟따] but mean totally different things, so 나았어요 (got better) must never be spelled 낳았어요 (gave birth). Note 낫다 also has a second meaning, 'to be better/preferable' (이게 더 나아요 = this one's better), which shares the exact same conjugation. It collocates with 빨리/금방/곧 낫다 (heal fast/soon) and 다 낫다 (fully heal).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 낫다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 나아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the past as 낳았어요 (that means 'gave birth') instead of 나았어요 for 'got better'. The dictionary form is 낫다, not 낳다 — listen for the meaning, not just the sound.
Keeping the ㅅ before a vowel — it's 나아요/나았어요/나을, NOT 낫아요/낫았어요. The ㅅ only survives before consonants (낫습니다, 낫고).
Making it transitive like English 'heal it' — 감기를 나았어요 is wrong; the illness is the subject, so it's 감기가 나았어요. To 'cure' something actively, use 치료하다 or 고치다.
notes: ㅅ: memorize 나아 and 나아요 together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 낫다 becomes 나을 수 있어요 ("can") and 나을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 낫다 has an irregular stem (ㅅ). Memorize its polite form 나아요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

It collocates with 빨리/금방/곧 낫다 (heal fast/soon) and 다 낫다 (fully heal).
It is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을, 나으세요) but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고, 낫지).

words.shortExplanation: 삐다 means "to sprain" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 삐다 (ppida) = "to sprain". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 삐어요 plus one useful sentence like 발목 삐었어요 ("I sprained my ankle"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 삐고 싶어요 for what you want, 삘 수 있어요 for what you can, 삘 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The single most useful sprain phrase — say it at any 정형외과 or pharmacy; 발목 (ankle) is the default body part.

examples.en: I sprained my ankle.
examples.note: Bare-bones report; 삐다 almost always takes 발목 (ankle) or 손목 (wrist) as the object with 을/를.

examples.en: I sprained my ankle coming down the stairs.
examples.note: V-다가 sets up the mid-action accident; 내려오다 = to come down. A textbook way to explain how it happened.

examples.ko: 어제 발목을 삐었는데 오늘 더 부어서 병원에 가려고요.
examples.romanization: eoje balmogeul ppieonneunde oneul deo bueoseo byeongwone garyeogoyo.
examples.en: I sprained my ankle yesterday but it's more swollen today, so I'm going to the hospital.
examples.note: Real decision moment chaining 삐다 + 붓다 + clinic; -(으)려고요 = 'I intend to', softens the announcement.

words.nuance: 삐다 is the plain everyday verb for spraining a joint, overwhelmingly collocating with 발목 (ankle) and 손목 (wrist), with the joint as the object (발목을 삐다). Because a sprain is a sudden event you report after the fact, it lives most naturally in the past/result form 삐었어요 rather than the present. Mind the boundaries with its neighbors: 접질리다 also means to wrench/twist a joint and overlaps heavily, while the casual 삐끗하다 covers a milder 'tweak'; most importantly, 삐다 (a sprain — soft tissue) is NOT 부러지다 (a bone fracture), so a clinic needs to hear which one. There's no Sino-Korean root here — it's a native Korean word. For a doctor, 발목을 삐었어요 plus 부었어요 (it's swollen) communicates the whole problem; standard first-aid is to 얼음찜질하다 (ice it).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 삐다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 삐어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 삐다 (sprain a joint — soft tissue) with 부러지다 (to break/fracture a bone). A sprain is 발목을 삐었어요; a broken bone is 뼈가 부러졌어요. The treatment differs, so don't swap them at a clinic.
Using the present tense 삐어요 to report an injury that already happened — say 삐었어요 (past), since you're describing a completed event. Present 삐어요 sounds like a general 'one tends to sprain it'.
Marking the joint with 이/가 — it's 발목을 삐었어요 (object 을), not 발목이 삐었어요. You sprain the ankle, so it takes 을/를.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 삐다 becomes 삘 수 있어요 ("can") and 삘 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 삐다 is the plain everyday verb for spraining a joint, overwhelmingly collocating with 발목 (ankle) and 손목 (wrist), with the joint as the object (발목을 삐다). Because a sprain is a sudden event you report after the fact, it lives most naturally in the past/result form 삐었어요 rather than the present. For a doctor, 발목을 삐었어요 plus 부었어요 (it's swollen) communicates the whole problem; standard first-aid is to 얼음찜질하다 (ice it).

Mind the boundaries with its neighbors: 접질리다 also means to wrench/twist a joint and overlaps heavily, while the casual 삐끗하다 covers a milder 'tweak'; most importantly, 삐다 (a sprain — soft tissue) is NOT 부러지다 (a bone fracture), so a clinic needs to hear which one.
There's no Sino-Korean root here — it's a native Korean word.

words.shortExplanation: 긁다 means "to scratch" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 긁다 (geukda) means "to scratch". Start from the polite form 긁어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 긁다. A strong first sentence is 긁지 마세요 ("Don't scratch it"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 긁다 also becomes 긁고 싶어요 (want), 긁을 수 있어요 (can), and 긁을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
What the doctor says about a rash, bug bite, or healing wound; the most-heard form of this verb in a clinic.

examples.en: I scratched my back.
examples.note: Basic frame: the itchy spot or body part takes 을/를 — 등을 긁다, 팔을 긁다.

examples.en: I kept scratching the mosquito bite.
examples.note: 물린 데 = 'the bitten spot' (물리다 = to get bitten); 자꾸 = 'keep (doing)', very natural for an itch you can't leave alone.

examples.en: Even if it itches, you'll get a scar if you scratch, so hold back.
examples.note: Full real-life advice: 흉터가 남다 = 'a scar remains', 참다 = to endure; 가렵다 and 긁다 appear together as always.

words.nuance: 긁다 is the physical act of scratching with fingernails or an object, and the itchy spot or body part takes 을/를 (등을 긁다). Its inseparable partner is the adjective 가렵다 ('to be itchy'): 가려워서 긁어요 ('it itches so I scratch') is the default chain, and the key learner distinction is exactly this — 가렵다 is the SENSATION (a descriptive adjective, 'it itches'), while 긁다 is the ACTION you take in response (a verb, 'I scratch'). Don't confuse 긁다 with the look-alike 긋다 ('to draw a line / strike a match'), a different verb entirely. Beyond skin, 긁다 has lively idioms: 복권을 긁다 (scratch a lottery ticket), 카드를 긁다 (swipe/charge a card), and 신경을 긁다 ('to get on someone's nerves', literally 'scratch the nerves'). In a medical context the negative command 긁지 마세요 ('don't scratch') is what you'll hear most.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 긁다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 긁어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 긁다 (the action of scratching) with 가렵다 (the feeling of itching) — 가렵다 describes the sensation, 긁다 is what you do about it. '가려워서 긁었어요' uses both correctly: feeling first, action second.
Saying 가려워요 to mean 'I scratch' — 가렵다 is an adjective ('it's itchy'), so it cannot describe the action. Use 긁다 for scratching: 손으로 긁어요.
Confusing 긁다 with 긋다 ('to draw a line') because they look similar — they are unrelated verbs. Scratching an itch is always 긁다.

words.shortExplanation: 떨다 means "to shiver / to tremble" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to shiver / to tremble" in Korean is 떨다 (tteolda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 떨어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 떨다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 추워서 떨었어요 ("I was shivering because it was cold") — then reshape the same stem into 떨고 싶어요 (desire), 떨 수 있어요 (ability), and 떨 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not shiver / to tremble.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to shiver / to tremble.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to shiver / to tremble.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I was shivering because it was cold
usagePhrases.note: The standard way to say your body shook from cold; 추워서 = 'because it's cold', the most common trigger.

examples.en: I'm shivering because it's cold.
examples.note: Simplest form. 떨다 is the active verb for shaking your own body; the reason usually comes with -아서/-어서.

examples.ko: 면접 보기 전에 너무 긴장해서 손이 떨렸어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop bogi jeone neomu ginjanghaeseo soni tteollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was so nervous before the interview that my hands were shaking.
examples.note: Everyday nerves scenario; note the passive 떨리다 (손이 떨렸어요) for shaking you can't control — the natural choice here.

examples.ko: 열이 나고 몸이 으슬으슬 떨려서 병원에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: yeori nago momi euseureuseul tteollyeoseo byeongwone gasseoyo.
examples.en: I had a fever and my body was shivering with chills, so I went to the hospital.
examples.note: Real symptom report; 으슬으슬 = the shivery-chills mimetic, and 떨리다 conveys involuntary fever shakes.

words.nuance: 떨다 means to shake or shiver — from cold, fear, or nerves — and it is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ regularly drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings: formal 떱니다 (never 떨습니다 or 떨ㅂ니다), and 떠세요. The single most important thing for a learner is the active/passive split: 떨다 is active ('to shake [something / oneself]', and you can even 떨다 your leg as a habit — 다리를 떨다), but for involuntary body shaking Koreans overwhelmingly reach for the passive 떨리다 — 손이 떨려요 ('my hands are shaking') and 몸이 떨려요 are far more natural than the active 떨어요 here. Compare with neighbors: 흔들리다 is 'to sway/wobble' (a tree, a building), while 떨다/떨리다 is fine, fast trembling of the body. To sound native, glue on mimetic adverbs — 덜덜 (hard, cold/fear shiver) and 으슬으슬 (the chilly shiver of an oncoming fever). Note the unrelated idiom 엄살 떨다 / 수선 떨다, where 떨다 means 'to make a fuss'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떨다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떨어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Forgetting the ㄹ drops in the formal form — it's 떱니다, not 떨습니다 or 떨ㅂ니다. ㄹ-stems always lose the ㄹ before the ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ of an ending.

Using active 떨어요 for involuntary shaking — for hands or a body shaking on their own, the passive 떨려요 is the natural choice (손이 떨려요), not 손을 떨어요. Active 떨다 implies you're doing it (e.g., 다리를 떨다, jiggling your leg).
Confusing 떨다/떨리다 (fast body trembling) with 흔들리다 (to sway/wobble) — a shivering body is 떨려요, but a swaying tree or rocking boat is 흔들려요.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 떨어 and 떨어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 졸다 means "to doze off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 졸다 (jolda) = "to doze off". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 졸아요 plus one useful sentence like 회의 중에 졸았어요 ("I dozed off during the meeting"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 졸고 싶어요 for what you want, 졸 수 있어요 for what you can, 졸 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I dozed off during the meeting
usagePhrases.note: A relatable confession; 회의 중에 = 'in the middle of the meeting', the prototypical wrong place to nod off.

examples.en: I dozed off in class.
examples.note: Basic frame; 졸다 is intransitive and usually pinned to a place/time you shouldn't sleep (수업 시간에 = during class).

examples.ko: 점심 먹고 나서 자꾸 졸려서 결국 졸았어요.
examples.romanization: jeomsim meokgo naseo jakku jollyeoseo gyeolguk jorasseoyo.
examples.en: After lunch I kept getting sleepy and ended up dozing off.
examples.note: Shows the pair clearly: 졸리다 = 'to feel sleepy' (feeling) leads to 졸다 = 'to nod off' (act); 결국 = 'in the end'.

examples.ko: 지하철에서 깜빡 졸다가 내릴 역을 지나쳤어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo kkamppak joldaga naeril yeogeul jinachyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I dozed off for a moment on the subway and missed the stop I was supposed to get off at.
examples.note: Quintessential Seoul-commuter story; V-다가 = mid-action interruption, 지나치다 = to pass by/overshoot.

words.nuance: 졸다 means to nod off or drift into a light doze — typically somewhere you're not supposed to, like a meeting, class, or the subway — and it is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ: formal 좁니다 (not 졸습니다). The crucial learner distinction is between 졸다 and 졸리다: 졸리다 is the adjective-like state 'to feel sleepy' (졸려요 = 'I'm drowsy', the sensation), whereas 졸다 is the verb for actually drifting off (졸았어요 = 'I nodded off', the act). It's also distinct from 자다 ('to sleep' properly, lying down for real) — 졸다 is brief, upright, involuntary micro-sleep, while 자다 is full intentional sleep. There's no Sino-Korean root; it's native Korean. It collocates with 깜빡 졸다 (doze off for a second) and feeds the compound noun 졸음 ('drowsiness'), which builds 졸음운전 (drowsy driving), plastered on every Korean highway warning sign.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 졸다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 졸아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 졸려요 when you mean you actually nodded off — 졸리다 is the feeling 'I'm sleepy', but the act of dozing off is 졸다 (졸았어요). Don't report the nap with the sensation word.
Using 자다 for nodding off in a meeting — 자다 is real, intentional sleep lying down; the brief involuntary head-bob is 졸다. '회의 중에 잤어요' sounds like you full-on slept on purpose.
Forgetting the ㄹ drops in the formal form — it's 좁니다, not 졸습니다. ㄹ-stems lose the ㄹ before the ㅂ of -ㅂ니다.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 졸아 and 졸아요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 토하다 means "to vomit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 토하다 (tohada) means "to vomit". Start from the polite form 토해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 토하다. A strong first sentence is 토할 것 같아요 ("I feel like I'm going to throw up"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 토하다 also becomes 토하고 싶어요 (want), 토할 수 있어요 (can), and 토할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I feel like I'm going to throw up
usagePhrases.note: A crucial phrase for food poisoning, a hangover, or motion sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 것 같다 hedges 'I feel like I might'.

examples.en: I think I'm going to throw up.
examples.note: The bare warning you give while it's still coming on; learn this one cold for emergencies.

examples.en: I got carsick on the bus and almost threw up.
examples.note: 차멀미 = motion/car sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost did (but didn't)', a very common near-miss pattern.

examples.ko: 상한 걸 먹었는지 어젯밤부터 계속 토하고 설사도 해요.
examples.romanization: sanghan geol meogeonneunji eojetbambuteo gyesok tohago seolsado haeyo.
examples.en: I think I ate something spoiled — since last night I keep vomiting and have diarrhea too.
examples.note: Full food-poisoning report; 상하다 = to go bad, -았는지 = 'whether/maybe', 설사하다 = to have diarrhea. Clinic-ready.

words.nuance: 토하다 is the direct, neutral verb for vomiting (Sino-Korean 吐 'spit out/vomit' + 하다, so literally 'to do a 吐'), and it's perfectly fine to use at a clinic or pharmacy. While it's already on the way up, you hedge with 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I might throw up'). Mind the register and the synonyms: the everyday softer alternative is 게우다, and for mere nausea where nothing has come out yet, Koreans say 속이 안 좋다 ('my stomach is off') or 메스껍다 / 메슥거리다 ('to feel queasy') — these describe the queasy sensation, not the act, so don't say 토해요 unless you actually vomited. (There's also the very blunt slang 게워내다/'우웩'; 토하다 itself is the safe standard.) For a doctor, pairing 토하다 with 설사하다 (diarrhea) and 열이 나다 (fever) paints the classic 식중독 (food poisoning) picture. Note the object marker: what you throw up takes 을/를 (먹은 걸 다 토했어요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 토하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 토해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Overusing 토하다 for mild nausea — if you only feel queasy but haven't actually vomited, say 속이 안 좋아요 or 메스꺼워요, not 토해요. 토하다 means the vomiting actually happened.
Saying 토하고 싶어요 to mean 'I feel nauseous' — that literally means 'I want to vomit' (a desire), which sounds odd. Use 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I'm going to') for the urge.
Forgetting 토하다 is built on 하다 — the negative is 안 토해요 / 토하지 않아요 and the past is 토했어요, conjugating like every other 하다 verb (해요 → 토해요).

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.english: to be sick with / to suffer from
words.shortExplanation: 앓다 means "to be sick with / to suffer from" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to be sick with / to suffer from" in Korean is 앓다 (alta). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 앓아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 앓다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 며칠 동안 감기를 앓았어요 ("I was down with a cold for a few days") — then reshape the same stem into 앓고 싶어요 (desire), 앓을 수 있어요 (ability), and 앓을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I be sick with / to suffer from.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be sick with / to suffer from.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be sick with / to suffer from.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be sick with / to suffer from.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be sick with / to suffer from.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I was down with a cold for a few days
usagePhrases.note: 앓다 takes the illness as object (감기를); it sounds heavier and more drawn-out than just 아팠어요.

examples.en: I was sick with a cold.
examples.note: Core pattern: the illness is the OBJECT (감기를 앓다), unlike 아프다 which never takes an illness as object.

examples.ko: 독감을 심하게 앓아서 일주일 동안 회사를 못 갔어요.
examples.romanization: dokgameul simhage araseo iljuil dongan hoesareul mot gasseoyo.
examples.en: I had a bad case of the flu and couldn't go to work for a week.
examples.note: 독감 = influenza (worse than 감기); 심하게 = severely. The -아서 chains the heavy illness to its consequence.

examples.ko: 할머니께서는 오래 병을 앓으셨지만 끝까지 의연하셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeonikkeseoneun orae byeongeul areusyeotjiman kkeutkkaji uiyeonhasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My grandmother suffered from an illness for a long time but stayed composed to the end.
examples.note: Honorific -(으)시- for an elder (앓으셨다); 병을 앓다 = to suffer from a disease, a respectful, literary register.

words.nuance: 앓다 means to be laid low by, or suffer through, an illness over a stretch of time, and the defining grammar point is that it takes the sickness as a DIRECT OBJECT — 감기를 앓다, 독감을 앓다, 병을 앓다 — which is exactly where it parts ways with 아프다. The contrast is sharp: 아프다 is an adjective that just states something hurts or you're unwell (머리가 아파요, 몸이 아파요), whereas 앓다 is a verb meaning you actively 'go through' a named illness for a period. 앓다 also carries a heavier, more drawn-out, somewhat literary tone, so it readily extends to chronic disease and even emotional pain (마음의 병을 앓다 = 'to suffer a sickness of the heart'). The reduplicated 끙끙 앓다 paints someone groaning or quietly agonizing — over illness OR worries. Register-wise, in casual daily speech people far more often say 아팠어요; 앓다 sounds a notch more serious. It's native Korean (no hanja root). Note the modern slang 앓다 → '앓는 소리(를) 하다' meaning to whine/complain.

words.shortExplanation: 회복하다 means "to recover" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 회복하다 (hoebokhada) = "to recover". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 회복해요 plus one useful sentence like 건강을 회복했어요 ("I've recovered my health"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
건강을 회복하다 = to get one's health back; the standard collocation after illness or surgery.

examples.en: I recovered my health.
examples.note: Core pattern: 회복하다 is transitive — you recover SOMETHING (건강을/체력을/컨디션을), which takes 을/를.

examples.en: I'm recovering quickly after the surgery.
examples.note: 수술 후에 = after surgery; -고 있다 shows the recovery is ongoing. The clinical register fits a medical context.

examples.ko: 푹 쉬고 영양제도 챙겨 먹으면서 체력을 회복하려고 해요.
examples.romanization: puk swigo yeongyangjedo chaenggyeo meogeumyeonseo cheryeogeul hoebokaryeogo haeyo.

examples.note: Real recovery plan; 체력 = stamina, 챙겨 먹다 = to make a point of eating, -(으)려고 하다 = 'intend to'.

words.nuance: 회복하다 is the somewhat formal/clinical verb for recovering, built on Sino-Korean 回復 (回 'return' + 復 'restore', i.e. 'to return-and-restore'). It is transitive — you recover a thing you had lost, taking 을/를: 건강을 회복하다 (health), 체력을 회복하다 (stamina), 컨디션을 회복하다 (condition). When you want to say your body/condition recovered on its own without naming an object, use the passive 회복되다 (몸이 회복됐어요) rather than the active 몸이 회복했어요. Beyond the body, 회복하다 extends to non-medical comebacks — 신뢰를 회복하다 (restore trust), 경기가 회복되다 (the economy recovers). The bare noun 회복 (recovery) appears on hospital discharge papers.

words.shortExplanation: 삼키다 means "to swallow" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 삼키다 (samkida) means "to swallow". Start from the polite form 삼켜요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 삼키다. A strong first sentence is 약을 삼키기 힘들어요 ("It's hard to swallow the pills"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 삼키다 also becomes 삼키고 싶어요 (want), 삼킬 수 있어요 (can), and 삼킬 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: It's hard to swallow the pills
usagePhrases.note: Tell a pharmacist this and they may suggest smaller pills or syrup; V-기 힘들다 = 'hard to do'.

examples.en: I swallowed the medicine.
examples.note: Basic frame: what you swallow takes 을/를 — 약을/물을/음식을 삼키다.

examples.en: Swallow the tablet with water.
examples.note: 알약 = tablet/pill (vs 가루약 = powder medicine); the routine instruction for taking pills.

examples.ko: 목이 부어서 음식을 삼키기가 너무 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: mogi bueoseo eumsigeul samkigiga neomu himdeureoyo.
examples.en: My throat is swollen so it's really hard to swallow food.
examples.note: Ties 삼키다 to 붓다 (to swell); 삼키기(가) 힘들다 = 'hard to swallow', a key symptom phrase for a clinic visit.

words.nuance: 삼키다 is the verb for swallowing — food, drink, pills, or saliva — and what goes down takes 을/를 (약을 삼키다, 침을 삼키다). It's genuinely practical at a pharmacy or clinic: 약을 삼키기 힘들어요 ('hard to swallow pills') or 침 삼킬 때 목이 아파요 ('it hurts when I swallow') pinpoint throat problems precisely. The crucial sequence partner is 씹다 ('to chew'): you 씹다 first, then 삼키다 — '씹어서 삼켜요' puts them in order — so don't use one for the other. Distinguish it also from 마시다 ('to drink/gulp a liquid continuously'); 삼키다 is the single act of sending something down the throat. It's a native Korean word (no hanja). Figuratively, 삼키다 is rich and very common: 눈물을 삼키다 (swallow one's tears), 화를 삼키다 (swallow one's anger), 비명을 삼키다 (stifle a scream) — all meaning to hold an emotion back. Safety warnings use it too: 통째로 삼키지 마세요 ('don't swallow it whole').

words.shortExplanation: 고장나다 means "to break down / to malfunction" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to break down / to malfunction" in Korean is 고장나다 (gojangnada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 고장나요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 고장나다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 보일러가 고장났어요 ("The boiler broke down") — then reshape the same stem into 고장나고 싶다 (desire), 고장날 수 있어요 (ability), and 고장날 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not break down / to malfunction.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to break down / to malfunction.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can break down / to malfunction.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to break down / to malfunction.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The exact line to open a call to your 집주인 (landlord) about heating

examples.en: The AC broke down so it's really hot.
examples.note: 고장나서 = because it broke; the cause clause leads into the result

examples.en: I think the washing machine is broken.
examples.note: -ㄴ 것 같다 softens it to a guess, polite for first reporting a problem

examples.en: My phone suddenly broke.
examples.note: 갑자기 = suddenly, the natural adverb for an out-of-nowhere malfunction

words.nuance: 고장나다 is built from the Sino-Korean noun 고장 (故障, 'breakdown/fault') plus native 나다 ('to occur'), so it literally means 'a fault arises' — which is why it is intransitive: the machine breaks on its own and takes 이/가, never 을/를 (보일러가 고장났어요, not 보일러를). Use it for things with a mechanism — appliances, electronics, cars, elevators — not for soft objects that simply tear or wear out (옷이 찢어지다, 신발이 닳다). The near-synonym 망가지다 is broader and casual ('get wrecked/ruined') and can cover a smashed toy or a crumpled box, whereas 고장나다 specifically implies the function stopped working. The English-speaker trap: English lets a person 'break' something, but you cannot make 고장나다 transitive — to say a PERSON broke it, switch to 고장 내다 or 망가뜨리다 (동생이 리모컨을 고장 냈어요).

Saying 'X을/를 고장났어요' — 고장나다 takes 이/가, not 을/를, because the broken thing is the subject that the fault 'arose in', not an object you act on.
Using 고장나다 for a person breaking something on purpose — 'I broke the door' is 문을 고장 냈어요 or 문을 부쉈어요, since 고장나다 cannot take a doer.
Stretching it to torn clothes or a ripped bag — those are 찢어지다, not 고장나다, which needs a working mechanism to fail.
