words.shortExplanation: 수리하다 means "to repair / to fix" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 수리하다 (surihada) = "to repair / to fix". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 수리해요 plus one useful sentence like 수리해 주세요 ("Please fix it"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 수리하고 싶어요 for what you want, 수리할 수 있어요 for what you can, 수리할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not repair / to fix.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to repair / to fix.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I have to repair / to fix.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
What you say to a repair person or building manager (관리실)

examples.en: I need to get the boiler repaired.
examples.note: Object takes 을/를 here, unlike 고장나다 which takes 이/가

examples.en: How much does it cost to repair the fridge?
examples.note: -는 데 = the cost/effort of doing; the go-to frame for asking a quote

examples.en: They say the technician is coming to repair it tomorrow.
examples.note: 기사님 = service technician; -신대요 relays what the 관리실 told you

words.nuance: 수리하다 comes from 수리 (修理, 'mend-manage') and is the formal, on-the-invoice word for repair — you see it on signs, receipts, and in 수리비 (repair cost) and 수리 기사 (repair technician). Its everyday near-synonym 고치다 is native Korean and warmer: a friend 고쳐 줄게 ('I'll fix it for you'), but a service center 수리합니다. The dividing line is register and scale: 고치다 covers a quick DIY tweak or even fixing a habit (버릇을 고치다), while 수리하다 implies a professional working on machinery, a car, or a building, and it stays strictly physical. The English-speaker trap: 'fix' in English also means to fix a plan, a date, or a relationship — none of those take 수리하다. A relationship or a problem is 관계를 회복하다 / 문제를 해결하다, and setting a date is 날짜를 정하다, so reserve 수리하다 for objects that physically broke.

words.nuance: 설치하다 is from 설치 (設置, 'set up-place') and means putting equipment in and making it ready to run — air conditioners, shelves, a washing machine, CCTV — as well as installing software and apps. The dividing line against the plain native verb 놓다 ('put/place') is readiness: 놓다 just sets an object somewhere, while 설치하다 implies mounting, wiring, or configuring it into working order. Watch the sibling word 설정하다 (設定, 'configure'): you 설치 the app or the router first, then 설정 the options inside it — English 'set up' blurs these two, but Korean keeps them apart. The other English-speaker trap is 'uninstall': there is no 설치 취소; Koreans say 삭제하다 ('delete') or 지우다 for software and 철거하다/떼다 for physically removing fixtures, so don't try to negate 설치하다 to undo it.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 설치하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 설치해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 설치하다 (install) with 설정하다 (configure settings) — you 설치 the app, then 설정 the options; using one for the other reverses the order of the task.
Inventing 설치 취소 for 'uninstall' — that is not used; say 삭제하다/지우다 for apps or 철거하다 for physical fixtures.
Using 놓다 when you mean a real installation — 에어컨을 놓다 sounds like you just set the unit on the floor, not that it was mounted and wired to work.

words.nuance: 정리하다 is from 정리 (整理, 'arrange-manage') and means putting things into order so a space (or even a thought) looks settled and neat. Compare three neighbors learners blur: 치우다 emphasizes clearing things AWAY/out of sight, 청소하다 (淸掃) is removing dirt by sweeping/wiping/vacuuming, and 정리하다 is arranging what stays into proper order. So you can have a 정리된 (well-arranged) desk that is still dusty, because 정리 is about order, not cleanliness. A real strength of 정리하다 is that it also takes abstract objects: 생각을 정리하다 (collect your thoughts), 일정을 정리하다 (sort out a schedule), 관계를 정리하다 (end/wrap up a relationship). The English-speaker trap is mapping 'clean up' straight onto 정리하다 — if you mean wiping grime or mopping, that is 청소하다/닦다, not 정리하다.

Use 정리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 정리하다 when you mean removing dirt — wiping or mopping grime is 청소하다 or 닦다; 정리하다 is about arranging, not cleaning surfaces.
Confusing it with 치우다 — 정리하다 puts things in order in place, while 치우다 clears them away; '치워!' (get it out of here) is harsher than '정리해'.
Assuming it is physical-only — 정리하다 also covers 생각/일정/관계, so 'I need to sort out my schedule' is 일정을 정리해야 돼요, not a cleaning verb.

("Did you lock the door?"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 잠그고 싶어요 for what you want, 잠글 수 있어요 for what you can, 잠글 수 없어요 for what you can't. words.nuance: 잠그다 follows the ㅡ (으-탈락) irregular: the stem vowel 으 disappears before an 아/어 ending, and because the remaining stem vowel ㅏ is 'bright', it joins with 아 — so 잠그 + 아 → 잠가요 and 잠그 + 았 → 잠갔어요 (the 요-form is your anchor: hear 잠가요 and the past, negative, and request forms all fall out). Beyond doors and padlocks it is the standard verb for shutting off water taps and gas valves (수도/가스를 잠그다), which English splits into 'lock' vs 'turn off' but Korean unifies under one image of sealing something closed. Its opposites split too: 열다 (open a door) versus 풀다 (unlock/undo a lock or release). The English-speaker trap is the conjugation: learners regularize it to 잠궈요/잠궜어요, but those are non-standard — the 으 simply drops and ㅏ stays.

Use 잠가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 잠궈요/잠궜어요 — the correct forms are 잠가요/잠갔어요, because after the 으 drops the stem keeps ㅏ and takes the 아 ending, not 워.
Using 끄다 (switch off a device) for a water tap — a faucet or gas valve is 잠그다, while 끄다 is for lights, TVs, and powered machines.
Saying 문을 닫다 when you mean lock — 닫다 only shuts the door; to actually engage the lock you need 잠그다.
notes: eu: memorize 잠가 and 잠가요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 새다 means "to leak" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 새다 (saeda) means "to leak". Start from the polite form 새요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 새다. A strong first sentence is 물이 새요 ("Water is leaking"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 새다 also becomes 새고 싶다 (want), 샐 수 있어요 (can), and 샐 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

words.nuance: 새다 is intransitive — the liquid, gas, or light is the subject that escapes, so it always takes 이/가 (물이 새다, 가스가 새다, 불빛이 새다), never 을/를; nothing is leaking on purpose. Phonologically the stem vowel ㅐ does not add an extra vowel, it just fuses with the ending: 새 + 었 → 샜어요, 새 + 어요 → 새요. Be careful of the homophone 새다 meaning 'to stay up all night' (밤을 새다 / 밤새다) — that one takes the object 밤, while the leak sense never does, so the particle tells them apart. Compare 흐르다 ('to flow'), which describes liquid moving along a path normally (강물이 흐르다); 새다 specifically means escaping out through a crack, seam, or hole where it should not. The English-speaker trap is treating 'leak' as something you do to an object — in Korean the leaking substance is the grammatical subject.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 새다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 새요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 물을 새요 — leaks take 이/가 (물이 새요), never 을/를, because the leaking water is the subject, not a thing being acted on.
Mixing it up with 흘리다 ('spill/let flow') — you 흘리다 something on purpose or by accident, but a pipe 새다 on its own; 'the pipe is leaking' is 파이프에서 물이 새요.
Confusing the homophone — 밤을 새다 means staying up all night; a leak never takes 밤 or any object, so keep the particle 이/가.

words.nuance: 널다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-탈락) verb: the final ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, giving 넙니다 (formal), 너세요 (honorific request), and 너는 빨래 (the laundry being hung) — but it stays before vowel endings, so 너 + 어요 keeps it as 널어요. Its meaning is narrow and physical: spreading out WET laundry on a line, rack, or rail so it air-dries; the partner verb for taking the dry wash back down is 걷다 (빨래를 걷다). Don't confuse it with 말리다 ('to dry something'), which names the result/cause of drying (머리를 말리다 = dry your hair), or with 매달다 ('to hang up by suspending', like a picture or a sign) — 널다 implies laying cloth over something to dry, not hanging an object as decoration. The English-speaker trap is keeping the ㄹ in the formal/honorific forms by analogy with regular verbs.

Using 널다 to hang a picture or coat — that is 걸다 (그림을 걸다, 옷을 걸다); 널다 is specifically spreading wet laundry out to dry.
Mixing it with 말리다 — 말리다 is 'to dry (something)'; you 널어서 말리다, hang it out so that it dries, so the two verbs are not interchangeable.

words.nuance: 데우다 is the transitive 'warm something up' verb, used above all for food and drinks that are already cooked but went cold — leftover rice, soup, milk, a packed meal. Keep three look-alikes apart: 데우다 is the ACTION of heating, 따뜻하다 is an adjective for the resulting STATE ('it's warm'), and 덥다 is an adjective for the weather or your body feeling hot — so '국이 따뜻해요' (the soup is warm) is the result of '국을 데웠어요' (I heated the soup). For raising the food's heat further you choose by method: 끓이다 (boil), 굽다 (grill/roast), 볶다 (stir-fry), 요리하다 (cook generally); 데우다 only brings something back up to a comfortable temperature, it does not cook from raw. The big English-speaker trap is the near-homophone 데다 ('to get burned': 손을 데다 = I burned my hand) — drop one syllable and you change 'heat the food' into 'scald yourself'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 데우다 (heat food) with 데다 (get burned) — 손을 데다 means you burned your hand; the two differ by a single syllable so keep them straight.
Using 데우다 with an adjective slot — '음식이 데워요' is wrong for 'the food is warm'; the state is 음식이 따뜻해요, while 데우다 needs an object you heat (음식을 데워요).
Reaching for 데우다 to cook raw ingredients — raw meat or eggs are 굽다/끓이다/요리하다; 데우다 only reheats something already cooked.

words.nuance: 갈다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb (ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ: 갑니다, 가세요, 가는), and in the home sense it means swapping a used-up or worn part for a fresh one — bulbs, filters, batteries, wiper blades, bedsheets (이불을 갈다). words.nuance: 뽑다 means pulling something out from where it is set or embedded — a plug from an outlet, but also withdrawing cash from an ATM (돈을 뽑다), plucking a hair, pulling a weed, drawing a number in a lottery, or even selecting/recruiting a person (대표를 뽑다 = pick a representative). words.nuance: 꽂다 means inserting something so it stands or stays fixed in place — a plug into an outlet, a USB stick into a port, flowers into a vase, a book into a shelf (hence 책꽂이, 'bookshelf'). words.nuance: 전하다 (Sino-Korean 傳, 'transmit/hand down') means relaying something from a sender to a receiver: a message, regards, an item, news, or even a feeling, so the receiver takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께 while the thing passed takes 을/를. The nearest rival is 말하다, but 말하다 is you simply saying something yourself, whereas 전하다 stresses that you are the go-between carrying someone else's words or goods to a third party — '사장님이 잘했다고 전하래요' (the boss told me to tell you 'well done'). The big English-speaker trap is hearing 전 and thinking 전화하다 ('to make a phone call'): they share the 전 syllable but are unrelated, so '전해 주세요' is 'please relay it', not 'please call them'.

words.nuance: 알리다 is the causative of 알다 ('to know'), so literally 'to make (someone) know' — you give a piece of information to a person, who takes 에게/한테, while the fact taught takes 을/를. The form you will reach for ten times a day is 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'), used to ask for an address, a time, a price, or any update. The near-synonym 가르치다 also means 'let know', but 가르치다 leans toward teaching a skill or directions ('역으로 가는 길 좀 가르쳐 주세요'), while 알리다 is just transmitting a fact ('결과를 알려 주세요'). The classic learner error is using plain 알다: 알아요 means 'I know' (a state), and you cannot make a request with it — you must use the causative 알려 주세요 to mean 'inform me'. Beyond person-to-person, 알리다 also covers public announcing — '진실을 세상에 알리다' (reveal the truth to the world).

Use 알려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Do not say 알려 주세요 when you mean teaching a route or skill — that is closer to 가르쳐 주세요; 알려 주세요 is for transmitting a fact.

words.nuance: 설득하다 (Sino-Korean 說得, literally 'speak-and-gain', i.e. win someone over by talking) means to bring a reluctant person around to your view through reasoning, and crucially the person persuaded takes the object marker 을/를, not 에게 — 친구를 설득하다, never 친구에게 설득하다. Contrast it with 권하다 ('to recommend/urge'): 권하다 is gently offering a suggestion ('커피 한 잔 권하다'), whereas 설득하다 implies active back-and-forth against initial resistance, so it is stronger and more deliberate than just 말하다 or 권하다. The noun 설득 and adjective phrase 설득력이 있다 ('be persuasive') are common. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because English says 'persuade TO someone' feels wrong but learners still copy 에게 from verbs like 말하다, producing the ungrammatical 사람에게 설득하다. Also note 설득하다 is persuading someone to your side, not convincing yourself — for 'I'm convinced' you would say 납득이 됐어요.

Do not use 설득하다 for a light suggestion — that is 권하다; 설득하다 implies overcoming the other person's resistance.

words.nuance: 거절하다 (Sino-Korean 拒絶, 'block-and-sever') is the standard verb for declining a request, offer, or invitation, and the thing refused — 부탁, 제안, 초대 — takes 을/를. Compare it with the harsher 거부하다 (拒否, 'block-and-deny'): 거부하다 is a flat, often institutional rejection ('출석을 거부하다', 'refuse to comply'), while 거절하다 is the ordinary interpersonal 'no thanks'. Because directly refusing can feel rude in Korean social life, 거절하다 is habitually cushioned with 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), 정중하게 ('politely'), or 어렵겠어요 ('that would be difficult'); the bare verb can sound cold. A frequent English-speaker slip is reaching for 거절하다 to mean 'reject a person' romantically — that is 차다 (dump) or 까이다 (get rejected), not 거절하다, which targets the request, not the human. Also do not confuse it with 사양하다, a humble 'I'll pass' used to politely decline an offer of food or a gift.

words.nuance: 혼내다 means an older or higher-status person verbally disciplining someone beneath them — a parent a child, a teacher a pupil, a boss a junior — so the person scolded takes 을/를. The essential pair to learn is the active 혼내다 ('I scold') versus 혼나다 ('I get scolded'); '나 혼났어' ('I got chewed out') is something even adults say casually about a partner or boss. Distinguish it from 야단치다 (very close, slightly more old-fashioned/strong, often a parent shouting) and from 화내다, which is just 'to get angry / show anger' with no teaching aim — you can 화내다 at a stranger, but you only 혼내다 someone you have authority over. The English-speaker pitfall is direction: learners say '저는 부장님을 혼났어요' meaning to report being scolded, but that wrongly makes them the scolder; you must flip to 혼나다 — '부장님한테 혼났어요'. Keep 혼내다 (do the scolding) and 혼나다 (receive it) firmly apart.

words.shortExplanation: 따지다 means "to argue a point / call out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

words.nuance: 따지다 (native Korean, no hanja) has two distinct flavors that share the idea of 'pinning down the truth point by point'. One is confrontational: marching up to someone to demand an explanation for a wrong, where the person/place takes 에게/한테 and the tone is combative — you feel wronged and want answers ('왜 그랬냐고 따졌어'). The other is cool and analytical: scrutinizing or weighing details (조건을 따지다, 가격을 따지다, 손익을 따지다), often with 따져 보다. Compare 물어보다, which is a neutral 'ask a question' with no accusation — switching from 따지다 to 물어보다 instantly removes the hostility. The English-speaker pitfall is using 따지다 for ordinary curiosity: saying '선생님한테 따졌어요' when you merely asked a question sounds like you picked a fight with your teacher; for a polite query use 여쭤봤어요. Read the context to tell the confrontational sense from the analytical one.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 따지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 따져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
With a person, 따지다 sounds confrontational ('I called them out'); for a calm, non-accusatory question use 물어보다 / 여쭤보다.
Do not use it for trivial curiosity — '왜 늦었는지 따졌어요' implies you confronted them angrily, not that you simply wondered.

words.nuance: 우기다 (native Korean) means to keep insisting you are right even when you are probably wrong, so it always carries a negative, hard-headed tone — picture someone digging in past the point of reason. It is everyday spoken Korean among friends and family and reports the insistence using ~라고/다고 우기다 ('insist that…'). The key contrast is with the neutral 주장하다 (主張하다, 'to assert/claim'): 주장하다 is dignified and can be perfectly reasonable ('전문가들은 ~라고 주장한다'), whereas 우기다 paints the speaker as obstinate and likely mistaken — you would never use 우기다 in a formal report about your own well-founded position. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 우기다 as a plain synonym for 'insist': in English you can insist correctly and politely, but choosing 우기다 always smuggles in the judgment 'and you're being unreasonable', so for a calm, valid claim switch to 주장하다 or 강조하다.

Use 우겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
우기다 implies unreasonable, probably-wrong stubbornness; for a neutral or well-founded claim use 주장하다 instead.
Do not use 우기다 about your own reasonable position in formal speech — it makes you sound pig-headed; reserve it for genuinely stubborn insistence.

words.nuance: 떠들다 means making a loud, rowdy racket by talking, chattering, or carrying on, and it is almost always framed as something you should NOT do in a quiet place (library, classroom, late at night). Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㅂ and ㄴ and ㅅ endings (formal 떠듭니다, command 떠드세요) but stays before a vowel (떠들어요, 떠들었어요) — anchor this on the 요-form 떠들어요, which keeps the ㄹ. Contrast it with the neutral 이야기하다 / 수다 떨다 ('to chat'): 수다 떨다 is friendly gossip with no noise complaint, while 떠들다 specifically flags disruptive volume. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation: by false analogy with regular verbs people write 떠들습니다, but ㄹ drops before ㅂ, giving 떠듭니다; similarly the polite command is 떠드세요, not 떠들세요. Use 떠들다 when volume is the problem, not for ordinary conversation.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떠들다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떠들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Because it is a ㄹ-irregular, the formal form is 떠듭니다 and the command is 떠드세요 — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, never 떠들습니다.
떠들다 implies disruptive loudness; for ordinary friendly chatting use 이야기하다 or 수다 떨다 instead.
notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 떠들어 and 떠들어요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 떠들다 becomes 떠들 수 있어요 ("can") and 떠들 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 속이다 means "to deceive / trick" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 속이다 (sogi-da) means "to deceive / trick". Start from the polite form 속여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 속이다. A strong first sentence is 사람들을 속였어요. ("He deceived people."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 속이다 also becomes 속이고 싶어요 (want), 속일 수 있어요 (can), and 못 속여요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

words.nuance: 속이다 is the causative of 속다 ('to be fooled'), so literally 'to make (someone) be deceived' — to lead a person to believe something false, with the victim taking 을/를 and the falsified fact also often as object (나이를 속이다, 가격을 속이다). The companion verb 속다 / 속았어 ('I got fooled') is just as common in speech, and the two form an essential active/passive pair. Compare 거짓말하다 ('to tell a lie'): 거짓말하다 names the act of uttering a falsehood ('나한테 거짓말했어'), while 속이다 stresses the effect of successfully misleading someone — you can 거짓말하다 and fail, but 속이다 implies the deception landed. The English-speaker pitfall is direction, exactly as with 혼내다: learners say '제가 속였어요' to mean 'I got tricked', but that says you did the tricking; flip to the intransitive — '제가 속았어요' ('I was deceived'). Keep 속이다 (deceive someone) apart from 속다 (be deceived).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 속이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 속여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Use 속이다 when you trick someone and 속다 when you are the one fooled: '나 속았어' = 'I got tricked', not '나 속였어'.
Do not blur 속이다 with 거짓말하다: 거짓말하다 is uttering a lie, while 속이다 implies the lie actually misled the victim.

words.nuance: 놀리다 means making fun of someone, with the target taking 을/를 and the trait teased about taking (으)로 (외모로 놀리다, 사투리로 놀리다). Its emotional range is wide: from affectionate ribbing between close friends to genuinely hurtful mockery, so tone and relationship decide whether it lands as 장난 (a joke) or 상처 (a wound). Watch out for two look-alike traps. First, this 놀리다 (tease) is homonymous with a separate verb 놀리다 meaning 'to leave idle / keep unused' (손을 놀리다 'work the hands', 공장을 놀리다 'idle a factory') — same spelling, unrelated meaning, told apart only by context. Second, English speakers constantly mix 놀리다 (tease) with 놀다 (play, hang out); they share the 놀- root but '친구랑 놀았어요' is 'I hung out with a friend', whereas '친구를 놀렸어요' is 'I teased a friend'. The object particle differs too: 랑/하고 for 놀다 versus 을/를 for 놀리다.

To say what you tease someone about, use (으)로: '외모로 놀리다' (tease about looks), not 외모를 놀리다.

words.nuance: 털어놓다 is a compound of 털다 ('to shake/dust out', as you shake out a dusty cloth) plus 놓다 ('to set down'), giving the vivid image of shaking everything out of your chest and laying it on the table — i.e. unburdening worries, secrets, or true feelings you have bottled up, with the listener taking 에게/한테. Because the second element is 놓다, the present and past contract in speech (놓아요 becomes 놔요), giving 털어놔요 and 털어놨어요, while the formal keeps the full stem as 털어놓습니다. Compare 고백하다, which is confessing a specific fact or romantic feeling, whereas 털어놓다 is the broader emotional unburdening of accumulated 고민 to a confidant. The English-speaker pitfall is the contraction: learners over-regularize and write 털어놓았어요 / 털어놓아요, but natural speech is 털어놨어요 / 털어놔요 — and note the imperative drops back to 털어놓으세요 (no contraction before 으). Pair it with 고민, 속마음, 비밀.

Use 털어놔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
The 놓- base contracts in speech: say 털어놨어요 (past) and 털어놔요 (present), not the over-regular 털어놓았어요 / 털어놓아요.
Use 털어놓다 for unburdening accumulated worries to someone; for declaring a specific fact or romantic feeling, that is 고백하다.

words.nuance: 고백하다 (Sino-Korean 告白, literally 'tell-plainly', i.e. lay bare) most often means confessing romantic feelings — '좋아한다고 고백하다' — which in Korean dating culture, especially for people in their 20s-30s, is a defined, weighty moment that frequently marks the official start (사귀다) of a relationship; you 고백하다 first, and if accepted, you are now dating. It also covers admitting a hidden truth or fault, like a heartfelt confession of wrongdoing. The person confessed to takes 에게/한테. Contrast it with 사과하다 ('to apologize', 謝過, expressing regret for a wrong) and with 자백하다 ('to confess to a crime', as to police) — 고백하다 is the warm, personal baring of the heart, not a legal admission or an apology. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'confess' as one word: in English you 'confess your love' and 'confess to the crime' alike, but Korean reserves 고백하다 for heartfelt romantic/personal disclosure and uses 자백하다 for criminal confession; choosing 고백하다 with the police sounds oddly intimate.

For romantic confessions use 고백하다; 사과하다 means 'to apologize' (express regret for a wrong) and is a different act entirely.
Do not use 고백하다 for confessing a crime to authorities — that is 자백하다; 고백하다 is the warm, personal baring of feelings or a fault.

In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 구워요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 굽다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 고기를 굽다 ("to grill meat") — then reshape the same stem into 굽고 싶어요 (desire), 구울 수 있어요 (ability), and 구울 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to grill / to roast / to bake.

The default verb at Korean BBQ — at a 고깃집 you 고기를 구워 먹어요 (grill it on the table and eat it yourself).

examples.en: I'm baking bread.
examples.note: Simplest possible frame — note the form is 구워요, never 굽어요; the dictionary ㅂ is already gone.

examples.note: The constant question at the table. 구웠어요 is the ㅂ-irregular past — it is NOT 굽었어요.

examples.note: 구울게요 (ㅂ→우 + ㄹ게요) volunteers you for grill duty; said warmly to elders so they don't work.

words.nuance: 굽다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb: the dictionary ㅂ becomes 우 before any vowel ending, so the 요-form is 구워요 (not the textbook-looking 굽어요), past 구웠어요, future 구울 거예요 — memorize the 요-form and the rest follows. Meaning-wise it is dry-heat cooking with direct radiant heat: grilling meat, roasting, AND oven-baking bread all fall under this one word, which surprises English speakers who keep three separate verbs. Contrast it sharply with its kitchen neighbours: 굽다 uses no water and little-to-no oil (just the surface), whereas 볶다 tosses food in a little oil and 튀기다 submerges it in lots of oil. It is the single most useful cooking verb for a foreigner here because 구이 (grilled dishes) and Korean BBQ are everywhere. The classic learner trap is writing 굽어요/굽었어요 by analogy with regular verbs — say 구워요/구웠어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 굽다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 구워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it as a regular verb: 굽어요/굽었어요. It's ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ→우 gives 구워요/구웠어요.
Using 굽다 for boiling or deep-frying. Boiling a solid is 삶다, boiling a liquid is 끓이다, and deep-frying is 튀기다 — 굽다 is dry direct heat only.
Forgetting the ㅂ drops before consonant endings too in the future/modifier: it's 구울 거예요 and 구운 고기, not 굽을 거예요/굽은 고기.
notes: ㅂ: memorize 구워 and 구워요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 굽다 becomes 구울 수 있어요 ("can") and 구울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.english: to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil)
words.shortExplanation: 볶다 means "to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 볶다 (bokkda) = "to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 볶아요 plus one useful sentence like 김치를 볶다 ("to stir-fry kimchi"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 볶고 싶어요 for what you want, 볶을 수 있어요 for what you can, 볶을 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.en: I stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Stir-frying aged kimchi is a home staple (김치볶음밥, 볶음김치) — 볶다 implies tossing in a hot pan with a little oil.

examples.en: I'm stir-frying vegetables.
examples.note: Bare-bones frame; 볶아요 keeps the bright ㅏ vowel because the stem vowel ㅗ is bright — never 볶어요.

examples.en: I put in the rice and kimchi and stir-fried them together.
examples.note: The 김치볶음밥 move; 같이 볶다 = toss everything together. Past 볶았어요.

examples.en: Shall we coat the pan with oil and stir-fry the garlic first?
examples.note: 볶을까요? proposes a cooking step to whoever is cooking with you; …부터 = 'starting with'.

words.nuance: 볶다 is a regular verb and, because its stem vowel ㅗ is 'bright', it takes 아 endings: 볶아요, 볶았어요, never 볶어요. It means stir-frying or pan-frying in a SMALL amount of oil over high heat while constantly moving the food, so picture a wok-style toss. The dividing lines learners blur: 볶다 = a little oil + tossing; 튀기다 = a deep pool of oil + submerging (deep-fry); 부치다 = a thin film of oil for flat foods like 전/jeon; 굽다 = dry direct heat, no real oil. Tons of restaurant dish names freeze the noun form 볶음 onto the end (제육볶음 stir-fried pork, 낙지볶음 stir-fried octopus), so recognizing this verb lets you decode menus. The English pitfall is mapping every 'fry' to one word — English 'fry' splits in Korean into 볶다/튀기다/부치다, and choosing wrong changes the whole dish.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 볶다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 볶아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Translating English 'fry' as 볶다 when you mean deep-fry. Deep-frying in lots of oil is 튀기다; 볶다 is only a little oil with tossing.
Using 볶다 for pancake-style flat foods. Pan-frying 전/jeon or 부침개 is 부치다 (전을 부치다), not 볶다.
Writing 볶어요. The stem vowel is bright (ㅗ), so the ending is 아 → 볶아요/볶았어요.

words.shortExplanation: 삶다 means "to boil (food in water)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 삶다 (samda) means "to boil (food in water)". Start from the polite form 삶아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 삶다. A strong first sentence is 계란을 삶다 ("to boil an egg"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 삶다 also becomes 삶고 싶어요 (want), 삶을 수 있어요 (can), and 삶을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not boil (food in water).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to boil (food in water).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to boil (food in water).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
삶다 = cooking a SOLID food submerged in boiling water (eggs, noodles, potatoes), versus 끓이다 (boil a liquid / make soup).

examples.en: I'm boiling eggs.
examples.note: Simplest frame; 삶아요 keeps the bright ㅏ vowel — it is NOT 삶어요.

examples.en: I boiled the potatoes until soft.
examples.note: 푹 삶다 = boil thoroughly until tender, a very natural collocation. Past 삶았어요.

examples.ko: 국수 삶을게요, 양념장 좀 만들어 주세요.
examples.romanization: guksu salmeulgeyo, yangnyeomjang jom mandeureo juseyo.
examples.en: I'll boil the noodles, please make the sauce.
examples.note: 삶을게요 splits the kitchen tasks; …을게요 commits you to the noodle job.

words.nuance: 삶다 means to cook a solid food by fully submerging it in boiling water — eggs, noodles, potatoes, greens, even towels for sanitizing. The stem vowel ㅏ is bright, so endings take 아: 삶아요, 삶았어요 (never 삶어요), and the ㄻ batchim is pronounced [삼], giving [삼따]/[살마]. The crucial, constantly-confused boundary is 삶다 vs 끓이다: 삶다 = put a solid INTO water to cook the solid (계란을 삶다); 끓이다 = boil the LIQUID itself or make a brothy dish (물을 끓이다, 찌개를 끓이다). English 'boil' covers both, which is exactly why learners misfire — they say 계란을 끓이다 (literally 'bring the egg to a boil') when they mean 계란을 삶다. Compare also 데치다, which is only a quick few-second blanch, whereas 삶다 is full cooking-through.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 삶다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 삶아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 계란을 끓이다 for 'boil an egg'. Boiling a solid IN water is 삶다 → 계란을 삶다; 끓이다 is for boiling a liquid or making soup.
Writing 삶어요. The stem vowel is bright (ㅏ), so the ending is 아 → 삶아요/삶았어요.
Confusing it with 데치다. 삶다 cooks food fully through; 데치다 is only a brief blanch of a few seconds.

words.shortExplanation: 찌다 means "to steam" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to steam" in Korean is 찌다 (jjida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 쪄요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 찌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 만두를 찌다 ("to steam dumplings") — then reshape the same stem into 찌고 싶어요 (desire), 찔 수 있어요 (ability), and 찔 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
찐만두 (steamed mandu) vs 군만두 (pan-fried) — the verb on the menu tells you the cooking method.

examples.en: I'm steaming dumplings.
examples.note: Bare frame showing the contraction: 찌 + 어 → 쪄, never the spelled-out 찌어요.

examples.en: I lightly steamed the zucchini.
examples.note: 쪘어요 is the past (찌 + 었 → 쪘); 살짝 (lightly/briefly) pairs naturally with gentle steaming.

examples.en: Shall we steam rice cakes together?
examples.note: 찔까요? proposes steaming as the method; the stem is just 찌-, so the future modifier is 찔 (not 찌을).

words.nuance: 찌다 is a single-syllable ㅣ-stem verb, so ㅣ + 어 contracts to ㅕ: the 요-form is 쪄요 and the past is 쪘어요 — a spot where beginners wrongly write 찌어요/찌었어요. It means cooking with steam (hot vapor rising through 찜기), which keeps food moist and soft, and you'll meet it as the 찐- prefix on snacks (찐만두, 찐빵, 찐 고구마) and in the related dish-name suffix 찜 (갈비찜). Distinguish it from its wet-heat neighbours: 삶다 submerges the food in water, 끓이다 boils a liquid, but 찌다 keeps the food ABOVE the water in vapor. The sharpest pitfall, though, is the homonym: this 찌다 is spelled and conjugated identically to the 찌다 in 살이 찌다 ('to gain weight'), so 쪘어요 could mean 'I steamed it' or 'I gained weight' — only context and an object (만두를 쪘어요 vs 살이 쪘어요) tell them apart.

Forgetting the homonym: 쪘어요 with no object can read as 'gained weight' (살이 쪘어요). Keep the food object explicit — 만두를 쪘어요.
Treating 찌다 like 삶다/끓이다. Steaming keeps food above the water in vapor; it does not submerge it.

words.shortExplanation: 튀기다 means "to deep-fry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 튀기다 (twigida) = "to deep-fry". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 튀겨요 plus one useful sentence like 치킨을 튀기다 ("to deep-fry chicken"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
튀기다 = cook fully submerged in hot oil. The noun 튀김 then names dishes — 새우튀김, 야채튀김, 오징어튀김.

examples.en: I'm deep-frying shrimp.
examples.note: Simplest frame; the contracted form is 튀겨요, never the spelled-out 튀기어요.

examples.en: I deep-fried the shrimp until crispy.
examples.note: 바삭하게 = until crispy, the classic result phrase for 튀기다; past 튀겼어요.

examples.en: The oil is hot, so be careful when deep-frying.
examples.note: 튀길 때 = 'when deep-frying'; a natural safety reminder. …으니까 gives the reason.

words.nuance: 튀기다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb where ㅣ + 어 contracts to ㅕ, so it is 튀겨요/튀겼어요, not 튀기어요/튀기었어요. It specifically means cooking food fully submerged in plenty of hot oil — deep-frying — and the noun form 튀김 plasters menus and 분식 stalls (새우튀김, 오징어튀김, 모둠튀김), so the verb is worth learning just to order. The lines English speakers smear together: 튀기다 = a deep pool of oil, food submerged; 볶다 = a little oil, food tossed (stir-fry); 부치다 = a thin film of oil for flat foods (전/jeon); 굽다 = dry heat, essentially no oil. Because English 'fry' alone is ambiguous, learners over-use 튀기다 for anything cooked in a pan when they often mean 볶다 or 부치다. One more note: 튀기다 also means 'to bounce/flick' (공을 튀기다), but in daily food talk the deep-fry sense dominates.

Forgetting the future/modifier drops the 이: it's 튀길 거예요 and 튀긴 새우, not 튀기을 거예요/튀기은 새우.

words.english: to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)
words.shortExplanation: 끓이다 means "to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 끓이다 (kkeurida) means "to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)". Start from the polite form 끓여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 끓이다. A strong first sentence is 라면을 끓이다 ("to make ramyeon"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 끓이다 also becomes 끓이고 싶어요 (want), 끓일 수 있어요 (can), and 끓일 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The fixed phrase for cooking instant ramyeon. Koreans never say 라면을 만들다 for cooking it — it's always 끓이다.

examples.en: I'm making ramyeon.
examples.note: Bare everyday frame; the contracted form is 끓여요, never 끓이어요.

examples.en: I made soybean-paste stew.
examples.note: 끓이다 is THE verb for making any 찌개/국 — 만들다 sounds wrong here. Past 끓였어요.

examples.en: Shall I make you some ramyeon?
examples.note: 끓여 줄까요? offers to cook for someone — an extremely common, friendly line. …아/어 주다 = do it for you.

words.nuance: 끓이다 is the causative/transitive partner of 끓다 ('to be boiling'): you 끓이다 a liquid so that it 끓다. As a ㅣ-stem it contracts ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ, giving 끓여요/끓였어요 (not 끓이어요). Use it for boiling water and, crucially, for MAKING any brothy dish — 찌개, 국, 탕, 죽, and famously 라면 (라면을 끓이다 is frozen usage; never 라면을 만들다). The boundary learners must nail is 끓이다 vs 삶다: 끓이다 acts on the LIQUID or the dish (물을 끓이다, 김치찌개를 끓이다), while 삶다 acts on a SOLID dropped into water (계란을 삶다, 면을 삶다). English 'boil' flattens this distinction, so beginners say 라면을 삶다 or 계란을 끓이다 and sound off. Picture it this way: if the water is the point, 끓이다; if a solid going INTO the water is the point, 삶다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끓이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 끓여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 라면을 만들다 for cooking ramyeon. The set verb is 끓이다 → 라면을 끓이다.
Using 끓이다 to boil eggs or noodles. Boiling a solid in water is 삶다 → 계란을 삶다, 면을 삶다.
Writing 끓이어요/끓이었어요. The ㅣ-stem contracts: 끓이 + 어 → 끓여요, past 끓였어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끓이다 becomes 끓일 수 있어요 ("can") and 끓일 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: Use it for boiling water and, crucially, for MAKING any brothy dish — 찌개, 국, 탕, 죽, and famously 라면 (라면을 끓이다 is frozen usage; never 라면을 만들다).

The boundary learners must nail is 끓이다 vs 삶다: 끓이다 acts on the LIQUID or the dish (물을 끓이다, 김치찌개를 끓이다), while 삶다 acts on a SOLID dropped into water (계란을 삶다, 면을 삶다). Picture it this way: if the water is the point, 끓이다; if a solid going INTO the water is the point, 삶다.
끓이다 is the causative/transitive partner of 끓다 ('to be boiling'): you 끓이다 a liquid so that it 끓다.
As a ㅣ-stem it contracts ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ, giving 끓여요/끓였어요 (not 끓이어요).
English 'boil' flattens the distinction between 끓이다 and 삶다, so beginners say 라면을 삶다 or 계란을 끓이다 and sound off.

words.shortExplanation: 데치다 means "to blanch / to parboil (briefly)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to blanch / to parboil (briefly)" in Korean is 데치다 (dechida). The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not blanch / to parboil (briefly).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to blanch / to parboil (briefly).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to blanch / to parboil (briefly).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Step one of most 나물 side dishes: a quick dunk in boiling water, then drain and season (무치다).

examples.en: I'm blanching bean sprouts.
examples.note: Simplest frame; the contraction is 데쳐요 (데치 + 어 → 데쳐), never 데치어요.

examples.en: I quickly blanched the spinach.
examples.note: 데쳤어요 is the past; 살짝 (just briefly) is the signature partner for a short blanch.

examples.en: Shall I blanch the greens with you?
examples.note: 데칠까요? offers to do the blanching step; the stem drops 이 in the modifier → 데칠 (not 데치을).

words.nuance: 데치다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb (데쳐요/데쳤어요, ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ) meaning a quick blanch: dropping vegetables (or sometimes squid, bean sprouts) into already-boiling water for just a handful of seconds to soften them and set their color, then immediately draining. It is the gateway move of Korean 나물 banchan: 데치다 then 무치다 (season). words.english: to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)
words.shortExplanation: 무치다 means "to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 무치다 (muchida) = "to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)". usagePhrases.en: I season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The defining verb of Korean side dishes: mix blanched greens with 양념 by hand. The noun 무침 names dishes — 오이무침, 골뱅이무침.

examples.en: I'm seasoning the spinach.
examples.note: Bare frame; the contraction is 무쳐요 (무치 + 어 → 무쳐), never 무치어요.

examples.en: I dressed the spinach with sesame oil.
examples.note: 참기름에 무치다 is the quintessential namul finish; past 무쳤어요.

examples.en: Shall we blanch the bean sprouts and then season them?
examples.note: 데치다 + 무치다 = the standard banchan two-step; 무칠까요? proposes the dressing step.

words.nuance: 무치다 is the hands-on tossing that FINISHES most Korean banchan: you blanch (데치다) a vegetable, then 무치다 it with 양념 — sesame oil, garlic, soy or gochujang — until every strand is evenly coated, traditionally squeezing it 조물조물 by hand. As a ㅣ-stem it contracts to 무쳐요/무쳤어요. The noun 무침 labels a whole menu category of cold seasoned dishes (오이무침, 골뱅이무침, 무생채). The contrast learners MUST keep straight is 무치다 vs 비비다: 무치다 means DRESSING/coating a single ingredient with seasoning so it absorbs the flavor (a side dish), whereas 비비다 means STIRRING many components together into one mixed dish (비빔밥, 비빔국수). They feel similar in English ('mix/toss'), but a Korean would never say 밥을 무치다 for bibimbap or 나물을 비비다 for seasoned spinach. Anchor it: 무치다 = season one thing; 비비다 = stir everything together.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 무치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 무쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Using the wrong particle for the seasoning: it's 참기름에 무치다 (에 = with/in the seasoning), not 참기름을 무치다.

words.english: to slice / to cut (food, on a board)
words.shortExplanation: 썰다 means "to slice / to cut (food, on a board)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 썰다 (sseolda) means "to slice / to cut (food, on a board)". Start from the polite form 썰어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 썰다. A strong first sentence is 야채를 썰다 ("to slice vegetables"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 썰다 also becomes 썰고 싶어요 (want), 썰 수 있어요 (can), and 썰 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I slice / to cut (food, on a board).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not slice / to cut (food, on a board).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to slice / to cut (food, on a board).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can slice / to cut (food, on a board).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to slice / to cut (food, on a board).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
썰다 is the kitchen-specific 'cut' — slicing food on a board (도마). Far more natural than 자르다 for prepping food.

examples.en: I'm slicing onions.
examples.note: Bare frame; the ㄹ stays before the vowel ending → 썰어요, not 써요.

examples.en: I cut the meat into bite-sized pieces.
examples.note: 썰었어요 keeps the ㄹ before 었; 한입 크기로 = into bite-size. …(으)로 marks the resulting shape.

examples.en: Shall I slice the green onion?
examples.note: 썰까요? — the ㄹ DROPS before the ㄲ of 까, so it's 썰까 (not 썰을까).

words.nuance: 썰다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ vanishes before endings starting with ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ and before the ㄹ of -(으)ㄹ, giving 썹니다, 써세요, 썰 거예요, 썰까요? — but the ㄹ STAYS before vowel endings, so 썰어요/썰었어요. In the kitchen 썰다 is the natural verb for slicing food on a 도마 (cutting board), much more idiomatic than the general-purpose 자르다, which you'd use for cutting paper, hair, or a rope. The dividing line: 자르다 = cut/sever anything into pieces (broad); 썰다 = rhythmically slice food with a knife on a board (specific). Learn it bundled with the cutting adverbs you'll meet in every recipe — 얇게, 채 썰다 (julienne), 어슷하게, 송송, 깍둑썰다 — because Korean encodes the cut SHAPE in these adverbs rather than in the verb. The English-speaker trap is leaning on 자르다 for all cutting; for food prep, 썰다 is what sounds like a cook.

Adding 을 in the future/proposal. The ㄹ-stem just takes ㄹ: 썰 거예요, 썰까요? — not 썰을 거예요/썰을까요.

notes: ㄹ: memorize 썰어 and 썰어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 다지다 means "to mince / to finely chop" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to mince / to finely chop" in Korean is 다지다 (dajida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 다져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 다지다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 마늘을 다지다 ("to mince garlic") — then reshape the same stem into 다지고 싶어요 (desire), 다질 수 있어요 (ability), and 다질 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not mince / to finely chop.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to mince / to finely chop.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can mince / to finely chop.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

다진 마늘 (minced garlic) goes into nearly every Korean recipe; you can even buy it pre-minced at the mart.

examples.en: I'm mincing garlic.

examples.en: I finely minced the garlic and onion.
examples.note: 잘게 다지다 = mince finely; past 다졌어요. …이랑 = casual 'and'.

examples.en: Please mince some ginger too.
examples.note: 다져 주세요 asks for an ingredient to be minced; …도 = 'too/also'.

words.nuance: 다지다 means chopping something into very fine, near-uniform bits — distinctly finer than 썰다, often almost a paste. As a regular ㅣ-stem it contracts to 다져요/다졌어요. It shows up constantly as the past-attributive 다진 (다진 마늘, 다진 고기, 다진 파) on recipe cards and product labels, so it's worth recognizing even before you cook much — 다진 마늘 and ground meat (다진 고기) are pantry basics. The boundary with 썰다 is purely about FINENESS and motion: 썰다 is rhythmic slicing into visible pieces on a board, while 다지다 is repeated fine chopping until the pieces are tiny. Note the same verb has a vivid non-food sense, 'to firm up / consolidate' (기초를 다지다 'lay a firm foundation', 마음을 다지다 'steel one's resolve), but the kitchen meaning is what you'll use daily. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for the present-participle 다지는 when you want the finished 'minced' — Korean uses the past-attributive 다진 for that already-minced state.

words.shortExplanation: 비비다 means "to mix together (by stirring) / to rub" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 비비다 (bibida) = "to mix together (by stirring) / to rub". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 비벼요 plus one useful sentence like 밥을 비비다 ("to mix rice (into bibimbap)"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 비비고 싶어요 for what you want, 비빌 수 있어요 for what you can, 비빌 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.en: I mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to mix together (by stirring) / to rub.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
비비다 is the verb hiding inside 비빔밥 — you 밥을 비벼 먹어요, stirring rice with toppings and gochujang.

examples.en: I'm mixing the rice.
examples.note: Bare bibimbap frame; the contraction is 비벼요 (비비 + 어 → 비벼), never 비비어요.

examples.en: Add gochujang and mix it well before eating.
examples.note: 비벼서 드세요 = mix it, then eat — the standard table instruction. 잘 = well/thoroughly.

examples.en: Shall we mix the spicy noodles together?
examples.note: 비빌까요? proposes the mixing; note the near-pun of 비빔(국수) and the verb 비비다.

words.nuance: 비비다 means mixing by stirring and tossing many things together until evenly combined — it is literally the root of 비빔밥 and 비빔국수 (비빔 = the noun 'mixing'). As a regular ㅣ-stem it contracts to 비벼요/비볐어요. The contrast cooks must keep straight is 비비다 vs 무치다: 비비다 STIRS several components into one mixed dish (rice + toppings + sauce → bibimbap), whereas 무치다 DRESSES a single ingredient with seasoning so it soaks in (a side dish like 나물). English 'mix/toss' covers both, so beginners blur them — but 밥을 무치다 or 나물을 비비다 both sound wrong to a Korean. Beyond food, the same verb means physically rubbing two surfaces (눈을 비비다 'rub your eyes', 손을 비비다 'rub your hands', often in a pleading gesture), which is a handy everyday extension. Anchor it: at the table, 비비다 = stir it all together and eat.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비비다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 비벼요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 비비다 with 무치다. 비비다 = stir many things together (밥을 비비다); 무치다 = season/dress one ingredient (나물을 무치다).
Writing 비비어요/비비었어요. The ㅣ-stem contracts: 비비 + 어 → 비벼요, past 비볐어요.
Using the wrong particle for the sauce: it's 고추장에 비비다 (에 = with), not 고추장을 비비다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 비비다 becomes 비빌 수 있어요 ("can") and 비빌 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

Anchor it: at the table, 비비다 = stir it all together and eat.

As a regular ㅣ-stem it contracts to 비벼요/비볐어요.
English 'mix/toss' covers both 비비다 and 무치다, so beginners blur them.

words.english: to cool (something) down / to let cool
words.shortExplanation: 식히다 means "to cool (something) down / to let cool" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 식히다 (sikhida) means "to cool (something) down / to let cool". Start from the polite form 식혀요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 식히다. A strong first sentence is 국을 식히다 ("to cool the soup down"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 식히다 also becomes 식히고 싶어요 (want), 식힐 수 있어요 (can), and 식힐 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I cool (something) down / to let cool.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not cool (something) down / to let cool.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to cool (something) down / to let cool.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can cool (something) down / to let cool.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to cool (something) down / to let cool.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
식히다 is the causative of 식다 ('to cool off'): you 식히다 hot food so it 식다. Handy before serving kids or eating.

examples.en: Cool the soup down a bit.
examples.note: Bare frame; the contraction is 식혀요 (식히 + 어 → 식혀), never 식히어요. 좀 softens it to a request.

examples.en: I let the bread cool for a moment.
examples.note: 한 김 식히다 = let the heat off briefly; past 식혔어요.

examples.ko: 커피 너무 뜨거우니까 좀 식혀서 드세요.
examples.romanization: keopi neomu tteugeounikka jom sikyeoseo deuseyo.
examples.en: The coffee's too hot, so let it cool a bit before drinking.
examples.note: 식혀서 드세요 tells someone to let it cool first — caring and natural; …으니까 gives the reason.

words.nuance: 식히다 is the causative/transitive partner of intransitive 식다: 식다 means food cools off BY ITSELF (국이 식다 'the soup goes cold'), while 식히다 means YOU actively cool it — blowing on it, fanning it, leaving it out. The -히- is the causative infix, and as a ㅣ-stem it contracts to 식혀요/식혔어요. The key grammatical pitfall is transitivity: 식히다 takes an object (국을 식히다), whereas 식다 cannot, so '국을 식다' is ungrammatical — if there's a thing being cooled, you need 식히다. It's genuinely warm, useful table language: telling someone 식혀서 드세요 ('let it cool before eating') shows care. The other trap is the sound-alike 시키다, which means 'to order (food)' or 'to make someone do something' (숙제를 시키다); 식히다 and 시키다 are pronounced very similarly but are unrelated — 음식을 식히다 cools the food, 음식을 시키다 orders the food.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 식히다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 식혀요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using intransitive 식다 with an object. If you're cooling a thing, use the causative → 국을 식히다, not 국을 식다.
Confusing 식히다 with 시키다. 식히다 = cool something down; 시키다 = order food / make someone do something (음식을 시키다).
Writing 식히어요/식히었어요. The ㅣ-stem contracts: 식히 + 어 → 식혀요, past 식혔어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 식히다 becomes 식힐 수 있어요 ("can") and 식힐 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 식히다 means YOU actively cool food — blowing on it, fanning it, leaving it out. It's genuinely warm, useful table language: telling someone 식혀서 드세요 ('let it cool before eating') shows care.

The -히- is the causative infix that turns intransitive 식다 into transitive 식히다.

The trap is the sound-alike 시키다, which means 'to order (food)' or 'to make someone do something' (숙제를 시키다); 식히다 and 시키다 are pronounced very similarly but are unrelated — 음식을 식히다 cools the food, 음식을 시키다 orders the food.

words.shortExplanation: 옮기다 means "to move (something), to transfer" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to move (something), to transfer" in Korean is 옮기다 (omgida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 옮겨요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 옮기다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 책상 좀 저쪽으로 옮겨 주세요. ("Please move the desk over there.") — then reshape the same stem into 옮기고 싶어요 (desire), 옮길 수 있어요 (ability), and 옮길 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not move (something), to transfer.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to move (something), to transfer.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to move (something), to transfer.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Please move the desk over there.
usagePhrases.note: 옮기다 takes an object + a destination marked with -(으)로 ('toward'): 저쪽으로 옮기다.

examples.en: Please move the bags.
examples.note: The bare polite request — 짐을 옮기다 is the textbook object + verb pair for luggage.

examples.ko: 이사할 때 짐 옮기는 게 제일 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: isahal ttae jim olmgineun ge jeil himdeureoyo.
examples.en: When you move house, hauling the stuff is the hardest part.
examples.note: Note the division of labor: 이사하다 = move house (the whole event), 짐을 옮기다 = physically carry the boxes.

examples.ko: 무거우니까 우리 같이 저 소파를 옮길까요?
examples.romanization: mugeounikka uri gachi jeo sopareul olmgilkkayo?
examples.en: It's heavy, so shall we move that sofa together?
examples.note: Real-situation offer: 같이 + -(으)ㄹ까요? proposes doing the lifting as a team.

words.nuance: 옮기다 is the everyday transitive verb for relocating an object: you take hold of it and set it down in a new place, so it needs both an object (책상을) and usually a destination (저쪽으로). The sharpest contrast is with 움직이다, which means something stirs or budges where it is — 의자가 움직였어요 ('the chair shifted') versus 의자를 옮겼어요 ('I moved the chair to a new spot'). It also differs from 이사하다 (to move one's whole household) and from 나르다 (to ferry/haul loads back and forth, emphasizing the carrying labor). Koreans stretch 옮기다 figuratively to switching jobs (회사를 옮기다), seats (자리를 옮기다), schedules (일정을 옮기다), and even contagion (감기를 옮기다, 'pass on a cold'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using it intransitively like English 'move' in 'I'm moving next week' — for that you need 이사하다, because 옮기다 always demands the thing being moved.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 옮기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 옮겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't say bare 옮겨요 for 'I'm moving (house)' — 옮기다 is transitive and needs an object; for relocating your home use 이사해요.
Don't confuse it with 움직이다: 움직이다 = something budges/stirs on its own (차가 움직여요), while 옮기다 = YOU carry an object to a new place (차를 옮겨요).
Don't drop the destination particle: it's 저쪽으로 옮기다 ('-(으)로' = toward), not '저쪽 옮기다'.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 옮기다 becomes 옮길 수 있어요 ("can") and 옮길 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 끌다 means "to drag, to pull" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 끌다 (kkeulda) = "to drag, to pull". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 끌어요 plus one useful sentence like 의자를 끌지 말고 들어서 옮기세요. ("Don't drag the chair, lift it to move it."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 끌고 싶어요 for what you want, 끌 수 있어요 for what you can, 끌 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not drag, to pull.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to drag, to pull.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to drag, to pull.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Don't drag the chair, lift it to move it.
usagePhrases.note: 끌다 = drag along a surface; contrasted here with 들다 (lift) because dragging scratches and screeches.

examples.en: Pull the cord.
examples.note: Bare command with 줄을 끌다 = pull a rope/leash/string toward you along the ground.

examples.ko: 강아지가 산책할 때 자꾸 줄을 끌어요.
examples.romanization: gangajiga sanchaekal ttae jakku jureul kkeureoyo.
examples.en: My puppy keeps tugging the leash on walks.
examples.note: Everyday scene: 자꾸 ('keeps doing it') + 끌다 captures repeated tugging.

examples.ko: 발표를 너무 오래 끌어서 사람들이 지루해했어요.
examples.romanization: balpyoreul neomu orae kkeureoseo saramdeuri jiruhaehaesseoyo.
examples.en: The presentation dragged on so long that people got bored.
examples.note: Real-situation figurative use: 끌다 = drag out time, with the consequence (지루해하다) attached.

words.nuance: 끌다 covers two linked ideas: physically dragging something along a surface (a suitcase, a chair, a leash) and, figuratively, pulling something toward you — attention (관심을 끌다), popularity (인기를 끌다), or out in time (시간을 끌다). The near-synonym is 당기다, but the dividing line matters: 당기다 is a clean pull toward yourself in the air (문을 당기다 'pull the door'), while 끌다 implies dragging weight across the ground with friction. It is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ vanishes before consonant endings -ㅂ니다 and -(으)세요: 끕니다, 끄세요 — but it stays before vowels: 끌어요, 끌었어요. The dangerous trap for English speakers is the near-twin 끄다 ('to turn off', as in 불을 끄다); its imperative 꺼요/끄세요 sounds close to 끌다's forms, but they are entirely different verbs.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 끌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write the formal form as '끌습니다' — in a ㄹ-stem verb the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving 끕니다.
Don't mix up 끌다 (drag/pull) with 끄다 (turn off): 불을 꺼요 = 'turn off the light', 가방을 끌어요 = 'drag the bag'.
Don't use 끌다 for a crisp pull-toward-you with no friction (a door, a rope in the air) — that's 당기다; 끌다 implies dragging along the ground.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 끌어 and 끌어요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끌다 becomes 끌 수 있어요 ("can") and 끌 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 끌다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 끌어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.shortExplanation: 던지다 means "to throw" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 던지다 (deonjida) means "to throw". Start from the polite form 던져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 던지다. A strong first sentence is 쓰레기를 쓰레기통에 던졌어요. ("I threw the trash into the bin."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 던지다 also becomes 던지고 싶어요 (want), 던질 수 있어요 (can), and 던질 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I threw the trash into the bin.
usagePhrases.note: Destination takes 에: 쓰레기통에 던지다 = throw INTO the bin.

examples.en: Throw the ball.
examples.note: Bare command; 공을 던지다 is the core object + verb pair for throwing.

examples.en: Toss me the keys, please.
examples.note: Casual everyday request — 던져 주다 = throw it over to me through the air.

examples.en: The baseball player pitched the ball at 150 km/h.
examples.note: Real-situation use; in sports 던지다 is exactly 'to pitch/throw', here with a speed phrase.

words.nuance: 던지다 is the standard verb for throwing or tossing something through the air toward a spot, so the target naturally takes 에 (쓰레기통에 던지다). Its connotation is propulsion-through-air, which is why the key contrast is with 건네다 ('to hand over') and 주다 ('to give'): if you gently pass keys into someone's palm you 건네다 / 줘요, but if you lob them across the room you 던져요. Koreans extend it figuratively to 'putting something out there' — 질문을 던지다 (pose a question), 농담을 던지다 (crack a joke), 화두를 던지다 (raise a topic). A spelling point learners trip on is the past tense: 지 + 었 contracts to 졌, so it is 던졌어요, never the un-contracted '던지었어요'. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 던지다 whenever English says 'give/pass me X' — if there is no actual flight through the air, use 주다 or 건네다, because 던지다 can sound careless or even rude with fragile or respectful objects.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 던지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 던져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For handing something directly into someone's hand, don't use 던지다 (it implies hurling through the air) — use 주다 or 건네다.
The past tense contracts: write 던졌어요, not '던지었어요' (지 + 었 → 졌).
Don't drop the location particle for the target: it's 통에 던지다 ('에' = into/at), not '통을 던지다'.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 떨어뜨리다 means "to drop (something)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to drop (something)" in Korean is 떨어뜨리다 (tteoreotteurida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 떨어뜨려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 떨어뜨리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 휴대폰을 바닥에 떨어뜨렸어요. ("I dropped my phone on the floor.") — then reshape the same stem into 떨어뜨리고 싶어요 (desire), 떨어뜨릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 떨어뜨릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I dropped my phone on the floor.
usagePhrases.note: Landing spot takes 에: 바닥에 떨어뜨리다 = drop it onto the floor.

examples.en: I dropped the cup.
examples.note: Bare statement; the object marker 을/를 is essential since this verb is causative-transitive.

examples.en: I dropped the eggs and they all broke.
examples.note: -아서 links cause→result, pairing 떨어뜨리다 with 깨지다 ('break') for fragile things.

examples.ko: 지하철에서 지갑을 떨어뜨린 것 같은데 어떡하죠?
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo jigabeul tteoreotteurin geot gateunde eotteokajyo?
examples.en: I think I dropped my wallet on the subway — what should I do?
examples.note: Real-situation panic; -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 ('I think I...') softens an uncertain accident.

words.nuance: 떨어뜨리다 is the causative/transitive partner of 떨어지다 ('to fall'): you let something fall, usually by accident, so it always takes an object and often a landing point with 에 (바닥에 떨어뜨리다). The crucial contrast is with 흘리다 and 놓치다: 흘리다 is to drop/spill things little by little without noticing (동전을 흘리다 'lose coins along the way'), and 놓치다 is to lose your grip or miss catching something (공을 놓치다 'drop/miss the ball'), whereas 떨어뜨리다 squarely means you made one specific object fall to the ground. It also works figuratively — 점수를 떨어뜨리다 (lower a score), 고개를 떨어뜨리다 (drop one's head). Morphologically it is 떨어지다 + the causative suffix -뜨리-. Because the everyday meaning is an accident, the 'please don't' form (떨어뜨리지 마세요) is what you actually hear, far more than a positive command. Use 떨어뜨려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 떨어지다: 떨어지다 = something falls by itself (전화기가 떨어졌어요), while 떨어뜨리다 = YOU drop it (전화기를 떨어뜨렸어요).
Watch the spelling — the standard recommended form is 떨어뜨리다 (with 뜨); 떨어트리다 is also accepted but pick one and be consistent.
Don't use it for spilling/scattering things bit by bit unnoticed — that nuance is 흘리다 (동전을 흘리다), not 떨어뜨리다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 떨어뜨리다 becomes 떨어뜨릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 떨어뜨릴 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 피하다 means "to avoid, to dodge" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 피하다 (pihada) = "to avoid, to dodge". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 피해요 plus one useful sentence like 출퇴근 시간을 피해서 가세요. ("Go avoiding rush hour."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 피하고 싶어요 for what you want, 피할 수 있어요 for what you can, 피할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not avoid, to dodge.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to avoid, to dodge.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to avoid, to dodge.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
N을/를 피해서 = avoiding N; the single most useful daily pattern for dodging busy times.

examples.en: Let's avoid the crowded street.
examples.note: Simple plan; 길을 피해서 가다 = take a route that avoids it.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 자꾸 제 눈을 피해요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun jakku je nuneul pihaeyo.
examples.en: That person keeps avoiding eye contact with me.
examples.note: 눈을 피하다 = avoid someone's gaze — an idiom signaling guilt or discomfort.

examples.ko: 사고를 피하려면 차간 거리를 충분히 두고 운전하세요.
examples.romanization: sagoreul piharyeomyeon chagan georireul chungbunhi dugo unjeonhaseyo.
examples.en: To avoid an accident, drive keeping plenty of distance between cars.
examples.note: Real-situation safety advice; -(으)려면 = 'if you want to avoid', stating the condition.

words.nuance: 피하다 means to actively avoid, dodge, or steer clear of something — a person, a situation, bad weather, or a time of day — and the workhorse construction is N을/를 피해서 ('avoiding N'), perfect for dodging rush hour (출퇴근 시간을 피해서), crowds, or the heat. It is Sino-Korean: 避(피, 'avoid/evade') + 하다, literally 'to do avoidance', which is why it can feel slightly more deliberate than a casual sidestep. The key contrast is with 빠지다 and 거르다 (to skip/miss out on something, e.g. 회의에 빠지다 'skip the meeting', 식사를 거르다 'skip a meal') and with 막다 (to block something from happening to you): 피하다 is you moving yourself out of harm's way, not blocking it. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'avoid' onto 'skip an event' — saying 회의를 피했어요 to mean 'I skipped the meeting' actually implies you dodged it on purpose, which sounds evasive; for an innocent absence use 빠지다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 피하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 피해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 피하다 for innocently missing/skipping an event — that's 빠지다 or 거르다; 피하다 implies deliberately dodging.
It's transitive: include the thing avoided — 비를 피하다, 사람을 피하다, not bare 피하다.
Don't say '피하해요' — 하다 verbs contract to 해요, so the polite form is 피해요.

The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'avoid' onto 'skip an event' — saying 회의를 피했어요 to mean 'I skipped the meeting' actually implies you dodged it on purpose, which sounds evasive; for an innocent absence use 빠지다.

words.english: to turn over, to flip, to hand over
words.shortExplanation: 넘기다 means "to turn over, to flip, to hand over" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 넘기다 (neomgida) means "to turn over, to flip, to hand over". Start from the polite form 넘겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 넘기다. A strong first sentence is 다음 장으로 넘기세요. ("Turn to the next page."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 넘기다 also becomes 넘기고 싶어요 (want), 넘길 수 있어요 (can), and 넘길 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I turn over, to flip, to hand over.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not turn over, to flip, to hand over.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to turn over, to flip, to hand over.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can turn over, to flip, to hand over.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to turn over, to flip, to hand over.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
페이지/장을 넘기다 = turn a page; the destination uses -(으)로 (넘어가는 방향).

examples.en: Turn the page.
examples.note: Bare command; 페이지를 넘기다 is the core 'flip it over/past' meaning.

examples.en: I was busy so I just got lunch over with.
examples.note: Figurative 넘기다 = get past / make do with — here a meal rushed through.

examples.ko: 힘든 시기를 가족 덕분에 잘 넘겼어요.
examples.romanization: himdeun sigireul gajok deokbune jal neomgyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I got through the hard time okay thanks to my family.
examples.note: Real-situation use; 시기를 넘기다 = get past a period, with 덕분에 ('thanks to') giving credit.

words.nuance: 넘기다 is the causative/transitive partner of 넘다 ('to cross over a line/peak'): you make something go over or past, so it spans turning pages (장을 넘기다), swiping a screen (옆으로 넘기다), handing work or objects off to someone (담당자에게 넘기다), and getting through a tough stretch of time (시기를 넘기다, 고비를 넘기다). For literally placing an object into someone's hand the sharper word is 건네다, while 넘기다 carries the extra flavor of passing something on, off, or beyond — including offloading responsibility. Watch two look-alikes: 넘다 is intransitive ('cross over' — 선을 넘다), and 넘어지다 means 'to topple/trip and fall', which has nothing to do with handing over. When the recipient is a person, mark them with 에게/한테 (담당자에게 넘기다); when it is a page or screen, mark the direction with -(으)로 (다음 장으로 넘기다). The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 넘어지다 and 넘기다 as the same root and producing '넘어겼어요' — keep them separate.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 넘기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 넘겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 넘어지다 (to trip and fall over) — 넘기다 means to flip or hand something over, not to topple.
When handing something to a person, mark the recipient with 에게/한테: 담당자에게 넘기다, not '담당자를 넘기다'.
For carefully placing an object into someone's hand, 건네다 is more precise; 넘기다 stresses passing it on/off rather than the gentle handover.

The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 넘어지다 and 넘기다 as the same root and producing '넘어겼어요' — keep them separate.

words.shortExplanation: 들어올리다 means "to lift up, to raise" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to lift up, to raise" in Korean is 들어올리다 (deureoollida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 들어올려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 들어올리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 무거운 상자를 혼자 들어올렸어요. ("I lifted the heavy box by myself.") — then reshape the same stem into 들어올리고 싶어요 (desire), 들어올릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 들어올릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not lift up, to raise.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to lift up, to raise.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can lift up, to raise.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to lift up, to raise.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I lifted the heavy box by myself.
usagePhrases.note: 들어올리다 = raise something up off the ground with your hands; 혼자 ('alone') stresses the effort.

examples.en: Try raising your hand up.
examples.note: Simple body command; -아 보세요 ('try doing') softens it into an invitation.

examples.ko: 이 짐 좀 같이 들어올려 주실래요?
examples.romanization: i jim jom gachi deureoollyeo jusillaeyo?
examples.en: Could you help me lift this load together?
examples.note: Everyday polite request for help; -아 주실래요? is a warm, soft ask.

examples.ko: 바벨을 끝까지 들어올리지 못해서 다시 도전했어요.
examples.romanization: babereul kkeutkkaji deureoolliji motaeseo dasi dojeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't lift the barbell all the way up, so I tried again.
examples.note: Real-situation gym scene; 들어올리지 못하다 = fail to lift (ability-negation 못).

words.nuance: 들어올리다 is a compound of 들다 ('to hold/lift in the hand') + 올리다 ('to raise'), and the whole point of the compound is to foreground the UPWARD motion — getting a heavy box, a barbell, or a child up off a surface. The contrast with plain 들다 is the dividing line learners most need: 가방을 들다 just means to hold/carry a bag (it may already be in the air), whereas 가방을 들어올리다 specifically pictures the act of heaving it up. It also differs from 올리다 alone, which can raise something already in hand (선반에 올리다 'put it up on a shelf') without the lifting-from-below nuance. Collocations cluster around weight and effort: 번쩍 들어올리다 (hoist in one motion), 끝까지 들어올리다 (lift all the way up), 다리로 들어올리다 (lift with the legs). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using it as a blanket translation of 'lift/carry' — for simply toting a bag around, 들다 is far more natural, and reserving 들어올리다 for the genuine raising action keeps your Korean from sounding heavy-handed.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들어올리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어올려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't over-use it where plain 들다 works: 가방을 들다 ('carry a bag') is natural; 들어올리다 is for when the upward heave itself is the point.
Don't reach for 올리다 alone when you mean lifting from the ground up — 올리다 can mean 'place up on' (선반에 올리다); the 들어- adds the lifting-from-below sense.
Keep it as one word, 들어올리다 — the spaced form 들어 올리다 is also seen, but be consistent.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 들어올리다 becomes 들어올릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 들어올릴 거예요 ("will").
