words.english: to put down, to set down
words.shortExplanation: 내려놓다 means "to put down, to set down" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 내려놓다 (naeryeonota) = "to put down, to set down". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 내려놔요 plus one useful sentence like 짐을 여기에 내려놓으세요. ("Put your bags down here."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 내려놓고 싶어요 for what you want, 내려놓을 수 있어요 for what you can, 내려놓을 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I put down, to set down.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not put down, to set down.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to put down, to set down.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can put down, to set down.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to put down, to set down.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Landing spot takes 에: 여기에 내려놓다 = set it down right here.

examples.en: Put the bag down.
examples.note: Bare casual command; note the contraction 내려놓아 → 내려놔.

examples.en: If it's heavy, set it down and rest a moment.
examples.note: Everyday advice to someone struggling with a load.

examples.ko: 힘든 일은 다 잊고 마음을 좀 내려놓으세요.
examples.romanization: himdeun ireun da itgo maeumeul jom naeryeonoeuseyo.
examples.en: Forget the hard stuff and let your mind rest a little.
examples.note: Real-situation comfort; the figurative 마음을 내려놓다 = release stress, like 'putting down a burden'.

words.nuance: 내려놓다 combines 내리다 ('to bring down') + 놓다 ('to place'), so it means to lower something from your hands and set it on a surface — the natural opposite of 들어올리다. Its sharpest contrast is with bare 놓다 and 두다: 놓다 just means 'place/let go of' (책상에 놓다) and 두다 means 'leave/keep something somewhere' (그냥 둬요 'just leave it'), while 내려놓다 specifically adds the downward motion of unloading something you were holding up. Koreans use it with quiet beauty in the figurative sense 마음을 내려놓다 / 걱정을 내려놓다 — to let go of stress or attachment, exactly like the English 'put down a burden.' On conjugation: 놓 is a regular ㅎ-final stem, so before -아요 it contracts (내려놓아요 → 내려놔요, past 내려놨어요), but before -(으)세요 the ㅎ stays and you say 내려놓으세요. The English-speaker pitfall is producing '내려놔세요' by over-applying the contraction to the imperative — the polite command keeps the full stem: 내려놓으세요.

Use 내려놔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
The polite imperative is 내려놓으세요 (놓 keeps its full form before -(으)세요), not the over-contracted '내려놔세요'.
Don't substitute bare 놓다 or 두다 when you mean lowering something you held up — 내려놓다 adds the downward unloading motion that 놓다/두다 lack.
Mind the present-tense contraction: 내려놓아요 naturally becomes 내려놔요 (and past 내려놨어요).

words.english: to flip over, to turn inside out
words.shortExplanation: 뒤집다 means "to flip over, to turn inside out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

words.nuance: 뒤집다 means to turn something to its other side or inside out — flipping grilling meat (고기를 뒤집다), turning clothes for the wash (옷을 뒤집다), or, figuratively, overturning a situation, mood, or verdict (사건을 뒤집다). words.english: to lean on, to rely on
words.shortExplanation: 기대다 means "to lean on, to rely on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to lean on, to rely on" in Korean is 기대다 (gidaeda). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not lean on, to rely on.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to lean on, to rely on.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can lean on, to rely on.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to lean on, to rely on.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Don't lean on the wall, the paint comes off.
usagePhrases.note: N에 기대다 = lean against a surface; the particle is 에, not 을/를.

examples.en: Lean on the wall.
examples.note: Bare statement showing the core particle: 벽에 기대다, surface marked with 에.

examples.en: I was so tired I slept leaning against the window.
examples.note: Everyday commute scene; -아서 chains 'lean and (in that state) sleep'.

examples.ko: 힘들 때 언제든지 나한테 기대도 돼.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae eonjedeunji nahante gidaedo dwae.
examples.en: Whenever it's hard, you can always lean on me.
examples.note: Real-situation comfort in 반말; 기대도 돼 = 'you may lean on me', a warm offer of support.

words.nuance: 기대다 means to lean your body against something for physical support, and by natural extension to rely on or depend on someone emotionally. Particle choice is the heart of the word: surfaces take 에 (벽에 기대다, 창문에 기대다) and people take 에게/한테 (친구한테 기대다), or honorific 께 for elders (부모님께 기대다). The near-synonym for the figurative sense is 의지하다 ('to depend on for support'), which is a touch more serious and formal — 가족에게 의지하다 sounds weightier than the soft, warm 가족한테 기대다, and the latter still keeps the cozy image of literally leaning a shoulder. The standout English-speaker pitfall is the look-alike 기대하다 ('to expect / look forward to'): 기대돼요 means 'I'm looking forward to it' while 기대요 means 'I lean on it', and because their stems differ (기대다 vs 기대하다) mixing them up produces real confusion. Also keep the particle straight — it is 벽에 기대다, never '벽을 기대다'.

words.shortExplanation: 누르다 means "to press, to push (a button)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 누르다 (nureuda) = "to press, to push (a button)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 눌러요 plus one useful sentence like 몇 층 누르세요? ("Which floor should I press?"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 누르고 싶어요 for what you want, 누를 수 있어요 for what you can, 누를 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not press, to push (a button).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to press, to push (a button).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can press, to push (a button).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to press, to push (a button).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
층을 누르다 = press a floor button; the standard elevator question.

examples.en: Press the button.
examples.note: Bare command; 버튼을 누르다 is the core press-a-button pair.

examples.en: I pressed the close button in the elevator.
examples.note: Everyday scene; note the 르-irregular past 눌렀어요 (not '누르었어요').

examples.ko: 비밀번호를 누르고 별표를 누르면 문이 열려요.
examples.romanization: bimilbeonhoreul nureugo byeolpyoreul nureumyeon muni yeollyeoyo.
examples.en: Enter the PIN and press the star key, and the door opens.
examples.note: Real-situation door-lock instructions; chained 누르고 ('press and then') sequences the steps.

words.nuance: 누르다 is the go-to verb for pressing or pushing down — elevator buttons, doorbells, app icons, keypad keys, the 'like' button — and modern Korean life is so full of buttons that nailing it instantly sounds fluent. It is a textbook 르-irregular verb: before a vowel ending, the 르 transforms and an extra ㄹ appears, so the stem becomes 눌ㄹ-, giving 눌러요 and past 눌렀어요, while consonant endings stay regular (누릅니다, 누르고, 누르지 마세요). The meaning contrast to lock in is with 밀다 and 당기다: 누르다 is pressing DOWN on a surface or button, 밀다 is pushing a door/object away from you (문을 밀다 'push the door'), and 당기다 is pulling it toward you (문을 당기다) — so a door says 미세요/당기세요, never 누르세요, but a doorbell beside it says 누르세요. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: writing the un-irregular '누르어요' instead of 눌러요, and over-extending 'press/push' to doors, where Korean insists on 밀다 rather than 누르다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 누르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 눌러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
It's a 르-irregular: the polite form is 눌러요 (never '누르어요') and the past is 눌렀어요.
For pushing a door or object away (not pressing a button), use 밀다 — a door reads 미세요/당기세요, not '누르세요'.

words.english: to step aside, to get out of the way
words.shortExplanation: 비키다 means "to step aside, to get out of the way" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to step aside, to get out of the way.

usagePhrases.en: Sorry, could you step aside for a moment?
usagePhrases.note: 비켜 주시겠어요? = the most polite way to ask someone to move out of the way.

examples.en: Please move to the side a little.
examples.note: Simple polite request; 좀 + 주세요 keeps it gentle in a crowd.

examples.ko: 뒤에서 자전거가 와서 얼른 옆으로 비켰어요.
examples.romanization: dwieseo jajeongeoga waseo eolleun yeopeuro bikyeosseoyo.

examples.note: Everyday street scene; 얼른 ('quickly') captures the reflexive dodge.

examples.romanization: mun apeul makgo gyesyeoseo geureonde, jogeumman bikyeo jusigesseoyo?

words.nuance: 비키다 means to step aside or move your own body out of someone's way, which makes it intransitive — you shift yourself, you do not move an object. The polite requests 비켜 주세요 and 비켜 주시겠어요? are survival phrases for crowded subways, sidewalks, and elevator doors. Register caution is essential here: a bare, curt 비켜! is genuinely rude, the equivalent of barking 'Move it!' or 'Out of my way!', so unless you intend to be sharp you must cushion it with 주세요 or the very polite 주시겠어요. The contrast to fix is with 치우다 and 옮기다, which are transitive: if a box is blocking the hall, a person 비켜요 (steps aside) but you 치워요 / 옮겨요 the box (clear/move it). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'move out of the way' as transitive and trying to 비키다 an object, or — worse — using bare 비켜 with strangers and sounding aggressive without realizing it.

Bare 비켜! sounds aggressive (like 'Move it!') — in public always add 주세요 / 주시겠어요 to stay polite.
비키다 is intransitive (a person moves aside); to move an OBJECT out of the way, use 치우다 or 옮기다, not 비키다.
Mark the direction with -(으)로 for stepping aside: 옆으로 비키다, not '옆을 비키다'.

words.shortExplanation: 깨닫다 means "to realize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to realize" in Korean is 깨닫다 (kkaedatda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 깨달아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 깨닫다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 뒤늦게 깨달았어요 ("I realized too late") — then reshape the same stem into 깨닫고 싶어요 (desire), 깨달을 수 있어요 (ability), and 깨달을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
뒤늦게 = belatedly; the most common adverb with 깨닫다 when the realization lands after the fact

examples.en: I realized I'd left my wallet behind.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄴ 걸 깨닫다 = realize that you've done something; the single most useful frame for this verb

examples.ko: 한국에 살면서 매운 걸 잘 먹는다는 걸 깨달았어요.

examples.note: -는다는 걸 깨닫다 reports a realization about a present fact or habit, not a past action

examples.ko: 실수했다는 걸 그제야 깨닫고 바로 사과했어요.

words.nuance: 깨닫다 is a sudden dawning of understanding — the instant a fact or truth clicks into place, often something you feel you should have grasped sooner. Contrast it with 이해하다 (to comprehend), which is the gradual, effortful process of 'getting it'; 깨닫다 is the flash of insight that ends that process, and with 알다 (to know) which is the steady resulting state. It pairs habitually with 문득/뒤늦게/새삼 and the chunk V-(으)ㄴ 걸 깨닫다. The big English-speaker trap is the ㄷ irregular: in the 요-form the stem ㄷ turns to ㄹ before a vowel (깨달아요, 깨달았어요, 깨달으세요), but stays ㄷ before a consonant (깨닫고, 깨닫지). Learners overgeneralize and write 깨닫아요, which is simply wrong — anchor the whole verb on the correct 깨달아요.

Use 깨달아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

The ㄷ-irregular stem changes ㄷ to ㄹ before the vowel of -아요, so 깨닫 + 아요 becomes 깨달아요, never 깨닫아요.
깨달고 / 깨달지 (wrong) → 깨닫고 / 깨닫지
Before a consonant the ㄷ does NOT change. Many learners over-apply the ㄹ; keep ㄷ in 깨닫고, 깨닫지, 깨닫습니다.
Using 깨닫다 for slowly comprehending a lesson
For working through and understanding material use 이해하다; 깨닫다 is the sudden click, not the gradual grasp.
notes: ㄷ: memorize 깨달아 and 깨달아요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 깨닫다 becomes 깨달을 수 있어요 ("can") and 깨달을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 깨닫다 has an irregular stem (ㄷ). Memorize its polite form 깨달아요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 깨닫다 is a sudden dawning of understanding — the instant a fact or truth clicks into place, often something you feel you should have grasped sooner. It pairs habitually with 문득/뒤늦게/새삼 and the chunk V-(으)ㄴ 걸 깨닫다.

Contrast it with 이해하다 (to comprehend), which is the gradual, effortful process of 'getting it'; 깨닫다 is the flash of insight that ends that process. Contrast it too with 알다 (to know), which is the steady resulting state.

words.shortExplanation: 떠오르다 means "to come to mind" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 떠오르다 (tteooreuda) = "to come to mind". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 떠올라요 plus one useful sentence like 갑자기 떠올랐어요 ("It suddenly came to mind"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not come to mind.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to come to mind.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to come to mind.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
갑자기 = suddenly; for a memory or idea that pops up out of nowhere

examples.ko: 그 사람 이름이 갑자기 안 떠올라요.
examples.romanization: geu saram ireumi gapjagi an tteoollayo.
examples.en: That person's name suddenly won't come to me.
examples.note: 이름이 안 떠오르다 = a name won't surface; the natural way to say 'it's on the tip of my tongue'

examples.en: When I hear this song, my hometown comes to mind.
examples.note: N이/가 떠오르다 — whatever surfaces in your mind takes the subject marker, not 을/를

examples.en: A good idea came to me during the meeting.
examples.note: 떠올랐어요 shows the 르 irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ, so 떠오르 + 았 → 떠올랐

words.nuance: 떠오르다 literally means 'to float/rise up' (which is why it also describes the sun rising), and figuratively a thought, memory, name, or idea rises up into your mind on its own — it is intransitive, so the idea is the subject: 생각이 떠올라요. The crucial contrast is with its transitive twin 떠올리다 (to call something to mind on purpose): 떠오르다 happens TO you, 떠올리다 is something you DO. It also differs from 생각나다 (to come to mind), which is close but plainer and more about simple recall, whereas 떠오르다 has a vivid 'surfacing/floating up' image and fits fresh ideas. The English-speaker pitfall is particle choice: because 'I think of an idea' has an object in English, learners say 생각을 떠올라요, but the intransitive 떠오르다 demands 생각이 떠올라요. Watch the 르 irregular too: 떠오르 + 았 → 떠올랐어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떠오르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떠올라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
생각을 떠올라요 (wrong) → 생각이 떠올라요
떠오르다 is intransitive: the thought is the subject, so it takes 이/가. Use the transitive 떠올리다 if you want an 을/를 object.
떠오르았어요 (wrong) → 떠올랐어요
This is a 르-irregular verb. The 르 doubles to ㄹㄹ before -았/-어, giving 떠올랐어요, not 떠오르았어요.

떠오르다 = it surfaces by itself; 떠올리다 = you deliberately summon it. The particle (이 vs 을) tells you which one you need.
notes: 르: memorize 떠올라 and 떠올라요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 헷갈리다 means "to get confused" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 헷갈리다 (hetgallida) means "to get confused". Start from the polite form 헷갈려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 헷갈리다. A strong first sentence is 좀 헷갈려요 ("I'm a bit mixed up"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
the go-to phrase when two things blur together; softer and more specific than 모르겠어요

examples.en: I always mix up left and right.
examples.note: A랑 B가 헷갈리다 = mix up A and B; the two confusable things take 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: There were so many exits that I got turned around.
examples.note: 길이 헷갈리다 = lose track of the way; perfect for getting lost in a big station

examples.ko: 이 두 단어는 발음이 비슷해서 자꾸 헷갈려요.
examples.romanization: i du daneoneun bareumi biseutaeseo jakku hetgallyeoyo.
examples.en: These two words sound alike, so I keep confusing them.
examples.note: 자꾸 헷갈리다 = keep getting mixed up; 자꾸 stresses the repeated slip

words.nuance: 헷갈리다 is the everyday word for two or more things blurring together so you can't keep them straight — left vs. right, two similar names, which subway exit. The key contrast is with 모르겠다 (I don't know): with 모르겠다 you simply lack the information, but with 헷갈리다 you actually have it and are just getting two things crossed — you're tangled, not clueless. It's also lighter than 혼란스럽다 (to be in turmoil/disoriented), which is a heavier, almost emotional confusion. Grammatically it behaves like a feeling verb: both the experiencer (저는) and the confusing thing (이게/발음이) commonly take 이/가, and the confusable pair links with -랑/-하고. The main English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 모르겠어요 ('I don't know') when you really mean 'I keep getting these mixed up' — that's exactly 헷갈려요. Also beware the spelling: it is 헷, not 햇.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 헷갈리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 헷갈려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
햇갈리다 (wrong) → 헷갈리다
The first syllable is 헷 with ㅔ, not 햇 with ㅐ. This misspelling is extremely common even among natives, so fix it early.
Saying 모르겠어요 when you mean you're mixing two things up
모르겠어요 = you lack the knowledge; 헷갈려요 = you have it but keep crossing two similar items. They are not interchangeable.
왼쪽을 오른쪽을 헷갈려요 (wrong) → 왼쪽이랑 오른쪽이 헷갈려요
The confused items take 이/가 and are joined with -랑/-하고, not stacked with 을/를.

words.shortExplanation: 망설이다 means "to hesitate" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to hesitate" in Korean is 망설이다 (mangseorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 망설여요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 망설이다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 망설이지 마세요 ("Don't hesitate") — then reshape the same stem into 망설이고 싶어요 (desire), 망설일 수 있어요 (ability), and 망설일 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
encouraging someone to just go for it; very common in shops and pep talks

examples.en: I went back and forth for ages over whether to buy it.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ까 말까 망설이다 = waver between doing and not doing; the textbook indecision pattern

examples.en: I keep hesitating about whether to reach out.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ지 말지 망설이다 — another frame for dithering over a yes/no choice

examples.en: I dithered and ended up missing the chance.
examples.note: 망설이다가 = while hesitating (then something happens); 결국 = in the end

words.nuance: 망설이다 is to hesitate because you cannot commit to a choice — you waver, stall, and hold back at the threshold of acting. Its closest neighbor is 고민하다 (Sino-Korean 苦悶, 'bitter anguish'), but the dividing line is sharp: 고민하다 is the active mental labor of mulling a problem over, while 망설이다 is the stuck, hovering feeling right before you act, and it pairs constantly with -(으)ㄹ까 말까 (whether or not to). It also differs from 주저하다 (a stiffer, more written 'to be reluctant/hold back'); 망설이다 is the warmer, spoken everyday word. A useful collocation is 망설임 없이 (without hesitation) and 망설이다가 (hesitate, and as a result…). The English-speaker pitfall is using 망설이다 as a catch-all for 'worry' or 'think about it' — if you're chewing over a problem, that's 고민하다; 망설이다 specifically means you can't bring yourself to decide or move.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 망설이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 망설여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 망설이다 to mean general worrying/thinking it over
For mulling a problem use 고민하다. 망설이다 is specifically the inability to commit to an action, not broad worry.
살까 말까 고민할게요 vs 망설일게요 mixed up
If you're weighing pros and cons, 고민하다 fits; if you're frozen and can't act, 망설이다 fits. Don't treat them as identical.
망설리다 (wrong) → 망설이다
There is no extra ㄹ. The stem is 망설이-, giving 망설여요/망설였어요, not 망설려요.

words.shortExplanation: 판단하다 means "to judge" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 판단하다 (pandanhada) = "to judge". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 판단해요 plus one useful sentence like 스스로 판단하세요 ("Use your own judgment"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 판단하고 싶어요 for what you want, 판단할 수 있어요 for what you can, 판단할 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
스스로 = on one's own; common advice to let someone make the call themselves

examples.en: I'll decide based on how things look.
examples.note: N을/를 보고 판단하다 = judge after assessing N; the everyday 'let me see and decide' construction

examples.en: That's not for me to judge.
examples.note: 판단할 문제가 아니다 = not a matter for one to decide; a polite way to step back

examples.en: There isn't enough information, so it's hard to judge.
examples.note: 판단하기 어렵다 = hard to make a call; -기 어렵다 turns the verb into 'hard to ~'

words.nuance: 판단하다 (Sino-Korean 判斷, 'judge/decide' + 'sever' — literally to cut through and rule on something) means to assess a situation with reason and arrive at a conclusion; it is analytical, not emotional. The sharp contrast is with 결정하다 (決定, to decide on a choice): 판단하다 is the reasoning and weighing of evidence, and 결정하다 is the act of settling on the resulting option — you 판단 the facts, then make a 결정. It also differs from 평가하다 (評價, to evaluate/rate quality). Unlike English 'judge,' 판단하다 normally carries no 'being judgmental' overtone; to get that critical sense, Koreans add 함부로 판단하다 (judge rashly) or 겉모습만 보고 판단하다 (judge by looks alone). It collocates with 상황을 판단하다, 스스로 판단하다, and 판단하기 어렵다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 판단하다 where you simply chose between options (that's 결정하다), or importing the negative 'don't judge me' tone that the bare verb does not have.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 판단하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 판단해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 판단하다 when you mean settling on a choice → 결정하다
판단하다 is the reasoning/assessment; 결정하다 is locking in the decision that results. Say 메뉴를 결정했어요, not 메뉴를 판단했어요.
Assuming 판단하다 means 'be judgmental'
The plain verb is neutral and analytical. For the critical English sense, add 함부로 (rashly): 함부로 판단하지 마세요.
판단하다 with 에 instead of 을/를 for the object
It takes 을/를: 상황을 판단하다. Don't say 상황에 판단하다.

words.shortExplanation: 예상하다 means "to expect" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 예상하다 (yesanghada) means "to expect". Start from the polite form 예상해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 예상하다. A strong first sentence is 예상했던 대로예요 ("It's just as I expected"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 예상하다 also becomes 예상하고 싶어요 (want), 예상할 수 있어요 (can), and 예상할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
예상했던 대로 = as predicted; said when reality matches your forecast

examples.en: I expected traffic since it's the weekend.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다 = predict that something will happen; the standard 'forecast that' frame

examples.en: There were more people than I thought, so my prediction was off.
examples.note: 예상이 빗나가다 = a prediction misses; here 예상 is the subject with 이

examples.en: I'd more or less expected the result.
examples.note: 예상하고 있다 = to be anticipating (ongoing); 어느 정도 = to some degree

words.nuance: 예상하다 (Sino-Korean 豫想, 'beforehand' + 'think' — to think ahead) means to anticipate or predict an outcome from reasoning: what you calculate will happen. It is emotionally neutral, which is exactly where it splits from 기대하다 (期待, to look forward to / hope for): you can 예상하다 a bad result, but you would never 기대하다 one, because 기대 carries positive hope. It also differs from 예측하다 (豫測, to forecast), which is more technical/measured (weather, data, trends), whereas 예상하다 is the everyday 'I figured this would happen.' It collocates with -(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다, 예상보다, and 예상이 빗나가다. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'expect' covers both neutral prediction AND hopeful looking-forward; in Korean those split, so 'I'm expecting good news (hoping)' is 기대하고 있어요, while 'I expect it'll rain (forecast)' is 비가 올 거라고 예상해요. Picking the wrong one makes you sound oddly hopeful about bad outcomes.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 예상하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 예상해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 예상하다 when you mean hopeful anticipation → 기대하다
예상하다 is a neutral forecast; 기대하다 means you're hoping for / looking forward to it. 'I expect good news' = 기대하고 있어요.
예상해 instead of the natural 예상돼/예상이 가다 for 'it's expected'
When the outcome predicts itself, Korean often uses the passive 예상되다: 큰 변화가 예상돼요 (a big change is expected).
예상에 instead of 예상보다 for comparison
'Better than expected' is 예상보다 좋았어요, using 보다 (than), not 예상에.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 예상하다 becomes 예상할 수 있어요 ("can") and 예상할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 예상하다 means to anticipate or predict an outcome from reasoning: what you calculate will happen. It is emotionally neutral. It collocates with -(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다, 예상보다, and 예상이 빗나가다.

It also differs from 예측하다 (to forecast), which is more technical/measured (weather, data, trends), whereas 예상하다 is the everyday 'I figured this would happen.'

English 'expect' covers both neutral prediction AND hopeful looking-forward; in Korean those split, so 'I'm expecting good news (hoping)' is 기대하고 있어요, while 'I expect it'll rain (forecast)' is 비가 올 거라고 예상해요. Picking the wrong one makes you sound oddly hopeful about bad outcomes.

words.shortExplanation: 착각하다 means "to mistakenly think" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to mistakenly think" in Korean is 착각하다 (chakgakhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 착각해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 착각하다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
the polite, blame-free way to admit you misremembered or mixed something up

examples.en: I mistakenly thought today was Saturday.
examples.note: N인 줄 착각하다 = wrongly believe it's N; the key pattern for a false impression

examples.en: Sorry, I mistook you for someone else.
examples.note: A를 B로 착각하다 = mistake A for B; 으로/로 marks who you confused them with

examples.en: I thought the appointment was tomorrow, but I was mistaken.
examples.note: 착각이었어요 = it was a mix-up (noun form); a natural way to wrap up admitting an error

words.nuance: 착각하다 (Sino-Korean 錯覺, 'mistaken' + 'perception' — literally a misperception) means to hold a wrong belief or impression: you were sure of something — the date, a person's identity, what someone meant — that turned out to be false. The sharp line is against 실수하다 (失手, 'lose one's hand,' to slip up in action): 착각하다 is a wrong picture in your HEAD, while 실수하다 is a careless mistake in what you DO. It also differs from 오해하다 (誤解, to misunderstand), which is specifically misreading someone's words or intentions, whereas 착각 covers any mistaken impression including facts and identities. It collocates with N인 줄 착각하다, A를 B로 착각하다, and the noun 착각이었어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'I made a mistake' as 실수했어요 when you actually mis-thought something — if you got a fact wrong in your mind, it's 착각했어요, not 실수했어요. Memorize N인 줄 착각하다 as a fixed chunk.

Use 착각해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 실수하다 when you mean a wrong belief → 착각하다
실수하다 is a careless action-mistake; 착각하다 is thinking something false. 'I thought it was today (but wasn't)' = 착각했어요.
오해했어요 vs 착각했어요 mixed up
오해하다 is misreading a person's intent/words; 착각하다 is any mistaken impression, including plain facts. They overlap but aren't identical.
다른 사람을 착각했어요 (wrong) → 다른 사람으로 착각했어요
The mistaken identity takes 으로/로: A를 B로 착각하다. The 로 marks 'as B,' which the bare 을/를 can't express.

words.shortExplanation: 의심하다 means "to doubt" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 의심하다 (uisimhada) = "to doubt". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 의심해요 plus one useful sentence like 저를 의심하는 거예요? ("Are you doubting me?"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 의심하고 싶어요 for what you want, 의심할 수 있어요 for what you can, 의심할 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
a direct way to ask if someone suspects you; the person doubted takes 을/를

examples.en: At first I suspected it was a scam.
examples.note: N인 줄 알고 의심하다 = suspect it's N; very practical for spam calls and shady offers

examples.ko: 저는 그 사람 말을 의심하지 않아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu saram mareul uisimhaji anayo.
examples.en: I don't doubt what that person said.
examples.note: N을/를 의심하다 takes a direct object; here it's 말 (what was said)

examples.en: Don't doubt yourself so much.
examples.note: 자기 자신을 의심하다 = doubt oneself; a kind, encouraging thing to say

words.nuance: 의심하다 (Sino-Korean 疑心, 'doubt' + 'heart/mind' — a doubting heart) means to be suspicious of, or to doubt the truth, honesty, or safety of someone or something. It is transitive (object + 을/를) and runs from light skepticism about a claim to actively suspecting a person of wrongdoing. The contrast that matters: it is stronger and more pointed than simply being unsure (모르겠다 / 확실하지 않다) — 의심하다 means you positively suspect something is OFF, which is why aiming it at a person can sound accusatory (저를 의심해요? = 'You suspect me?'). It also differs from 믿지 않다 (to not believe), which is flat disbelief, whereas 의심하다 is the active, probing suspicion that something is wrong. It collocates with 눈을 의심하다 (doubt one's eyes), 의심할 여지가 없다, and 의심의 눈으로 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the object marker — because 의심하다 is transitive you must say 사람을 의심하다 (suspect a person), never 사람이 의심하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의심하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의심해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
사람이 의심하다 (wrong) → 사람을 의심하다
의심하다 is transitive, so the person or thing doubted takes 을/를. 사람이 의심하다 would mean 'the person suspects (someone).'

If you simply aren't sure, use 확실하지 않다 or 모르겠다. 의심하다 implies active suspicion that something is wrong, and can sound accusatory.

믿지 않다 = flatly not believing; 의심하다 = actively suspecting it's false or dishonest. Choose 의심하다 only when you mean real suspicion.

words.shortExplanation: 짐작하다 means "to guess" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 짐작하다 (jimjakhada) means "to guess". Start from the polite form 짐작해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 짐작하다. A strong first sentence is 대충 짐작이 가요 ("I can roughly guess"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 짐작하다 also becomes 짐작하고 싶어요 (want), 짐작할 수 있어요 (can), and 짐작할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
짐작이 가다 = to have a hunch; 대충 = roughly. A very natural fixed phrase

examples.ko: 표정만 봐도 무슨 일인지 짐작할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: pyojeongman bwado museun irinji jimjakal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can guess what's going on just from your face.
examples.note: N인지 짐작하다 = surmise what/whether N is; pairs with 만 봐도 (just by looking)

examples.en: I had a rough idea of the price.
examples.note: 짐작하고 있다 = to be surmising/assuming; 어느 정도 = to some degree

examples.en: I can't even begin to guess why they did that.
examples.note: 짐작도 안 가다 = can't even guess; the 도…안 form pushes it to 'not at all'

words.nuance: 짐작하다 is to make an educated guess — to infer or surmise something from limited clues rather than know it outright; you're reading the signs. The sharp contrast is with 찍다 (literally 'to stab/dot,' the slang for picking a multiple-choice answer at random): 짐작하다 is reasoned inference, 찍다 is a blind stab with no basis. It also differs from 추측하다 (Sino-Korean 推測, to conjecture), which is a touch more formal/logical, whereas 짐작하다 is the warm, everyday word and lives especially in the idiom 짐작이 가다 ('a guess comes to me' = I can imagine / I have a hunch), far more common in speech than the plain 짐작하다. It collocates with 대충 짐작이 가다, 짐작했던 대로, and the negative 짐작도 안 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 짐작하다 for a pure random guess on a quiz — that situation needs 찍다; reserve 짐작하다 for when you're actually inferring from evidence, and prefer 짐작이 가요 over 짐작해요 in conversation.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 짐작하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 짐작해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 짐작하다 for a random multiple-choice guess → 찍다
짐작하다 means inferring from clues. Picking an answer blind is 찍다: 모르는 문제는 그냥 찍었어요 (I just guessed on the ones I didn't know).
Overusing 짐작해요 where natives say 짐작이 가요
In speech the idiom 짐작이 가다 is far more natural for 'I can imagine / I have a hunch': 대충 짐작이 가요.
짐작하다 vs 추측하다 register
짐작하다 is the everyday spoken word; 추측하다 (推測) is more formal/logical (news, analysis). Don't sprinkle 추측하다 into casual chat.

words.shortExplanation: 떠올리다 means "to recall" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to recall" in Korean is 떠올리다 (tteoollida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 떠올려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 떠올리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 천천히 떠올려 보세요 ("Try to recall it slowly") — then reshape the same stem into 떠올리고 싶어요 (desire), 떠올릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 떠올릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
떠올려 보다 = try to bring to mind; a gentle prompt to jog someone's memory

examples.en: I tried to bring back the memory of that time.
examples.note: N을/를 떠올리다 = call N to mind on purpose; 기억을 떠올리다 = recall a memory

examples.ko: 이 사진을 보면 옛날 생각을 떠올리게 돼요.
examples.romanization: i sajineul bomyeon yennal saenggageul tteoollige dwaeyo.
examples.en: Looking at this photo makes me recall the old days.
examples.note: -게 되다 = end up doing; 생각을 떠올리다 = bring a thought to mind

examples.en: I struggled to recall that person's name.
examples.note: 떠올리려고 애쓰다 = strain to remember; 떠올리려고 = trying to bring it up

words.nuance: 떠올리다 is the transitive partner of 떠오르다 (it's the causative 'make it float up'): YOU deliberately call a memory, image, or idea to mind — 기억을 떠올리다 means you do the recalling, with the object marked 을/를. The all-important contrast is exactly with 떠오르다, where the thought surfaces on its own (기억이 떠올라요, marked 이/가): 떠올리다 = active effort, 떠오르다 = it happens to you, and the particle is your tell. It also differs from 기억하다 (記憶, plain 'to remember / retain in memory'): 떠올리다 is the vivid act of conjuring up an image or scene in the moment, while 기억하다 is the steady storage/retention of information. It collocates with 기억을/얼굴을/생각을 떠올리다 and 떠올려 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping it with 떠오르다 because English 'X comes to mind' and 'I bring X to mind' aren't clearly split — in Korean the particle decides: 생각을 떠올리다 (you recall) vs 생각이 떠오르다 (it pops up).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떠올리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떠올려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
생각이 떠올려요 (wrong) → 생각을 떠올려요 or 생각이 떠올라요
떠올리다 is transitive and needs 을/를. If you want 이/가, switch to the intransitive 떠오르다: 생각이 떠올라요.
Using 기억하다 for the vivid act of picturing something
기억하다 is steady retention ('I remember your name'); 떠올리다 is conjuring the image up now ('let me bring your face to mind').
떠올려지다 overused for 'comes to mind'
For something surfacing on its own, the natural verb is simply 떠오르다, not a passive of 떠올리다.

words.shortExplanation: 알아차리다 means "to notice" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 알아차리다 (aracharida) = "to notice". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 알아차려요 plus one useful sentence like 바로 알아차렸어요 ("I noticed right away"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 알아차리고 싶어요 for what you want, 알아차릴 수 있어요 for what you can, 알아차릴 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
바로 = immediately; for catching on the instant you sense something

examples.en: I quickly picked up that the mood was off.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄴ 걸 알아차리다 = notice that something is so; 금방 = in no time

examples.ko: 제가 실수한 걸 아무도 못 알아차렸어요.
examples.romanization: jega silsuhan geol amudo mot aracharyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Nobody noticed that I'd slipped up.
examples.note: 못 알아차리다 = didn't catch it; great for things that slip past people unnoticed

examples.en: Only then did I notice something had gone wrong.
examples.note: 그제야 알아차리다 = notice only at that point; -다는 걸 reports what you noticed

words.nuance: 알아차리다 (built from 알다 'know' + 차리다 'gather/pull together one's senses') is to notice or catch on — to suddenly become aware of something through perception: a shift in mood, a mistake, someone's hidden intention. It's about detection, not analysis; you sense it and it registers in an instant. The sharp contrast is with 깨닫다 (to realize a fact or truth, often deeper and more reflective): 알아차리다 is the quick 'oh, I noticed that,' while 깨닫다 is the weightier 'I came to understand.' It also outpaces plain 알다 (to know), which is the ongoing state of knowing, not the moment of catching on. It pairs with 눈치 (social awareness) — 눈치를 알아차리다 / 눈치채다 — and with 바로/금방 알아차리다 and 못 알아차리다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as plain 알다: 'I knew' is 알았어요, but 'I noticed/caught on' is specifically 알아차렸어요, the flash of detection rather than the steady knowing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 알아차리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 알아차려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 알다 (알았어요) for the moment of noticing → 알아차리다
알다 is the ongoing state of knowing; 알아차리다 is the instant of detecting. 'I caught on right away' = 바로 알아차렸어요.
알아차리다 vs 깨닫다 mixed up
알아차리다 = quick sensory noticing (the mood, a mistake); 깨닫다 = deeper realization of a truth. Don't use them interchangeably.
안 알아차렸어요 vs 못 알아차렸어요
For failing to notice, 못 (couldn't/didn't catch) is far more natural than 안: 아무도 못 알아차렸어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 알아차리다 becomes 알아차릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 알아차릴 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 알아차리다 is to notice or catch on — to suddenly become aware of something through perception: a shift in mood, a mistake, someone's hidden intention. Built from 알다 'know' + 차리다 'gather/pull together one's senses' — hence the sense of your awareness snapping into place.

words.shortExplanation: 되돌아보다 means "to look back on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 되돌아보다 (doedoraboda) means "to look back on". Start from the polite form 되돌아봐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 되돌아보다. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not look back on.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to look back on.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to look back on.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I looked back on the past year
usagePhrases.note: 지난 한 해 = the past year; a natural year-end reflection phrase

examples.ko: 한국에서 보낸 시간을 되돌아보면 정말 많이 변했어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseo bonaen siganeul doedorabomyeon jeongmal mani byeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Looking back on my time in Korea, I've changed a lot.
examples.note: N을/를 되돌아보면 = when you look back on N; -보면 sets up a reflective conclusion

examples.en: Whenever things get hard, I revisit how I felt at the start.
examples.note: 처음 마음을 되돌아보다 = return to your original intentions; -ㄹ 때마다 = every time

examples.ko: 실수를 되돌아보고 다음엔 더 잘하려고 해요.
examples.romanization: silsureul doedorabogo daeumen deo jalharyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I reflect on my mistakes and try to do better next time.
examples.note: 되돌아보고 = reflect and then; pairs with -(으)려고 하다 (intend to)

words.nuance: 되돌아보다 is to reflect on or look back over the past — your year, your choices, a relationship — usually to draw a lesson or feeling from it. The 되- prefix adds a 'back, again' nuance, so it's more reflective and complete than plain 돌아보다 (to turn and look around, which can be literal). It also differs from 반성하다 (反省, to self-reflect with remorse over a fault), which carries 'I did wrong and resolve to fix it'; 되돌아보다 is broader and gentler. It collocates with 지난 한 해를 되돌아보다, 삶을/지나온 길을 되돌아보다, and 되돌아볼 필요가 있다. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for physically turning your head to look behind — that's 돌아보다 or 뒤를 돌아보다; 되돌아보다 is overwhelmingly about reflecting on the past.

Use 되돌아봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 되돌아보다 for physically turning to look behind → 돌아보다
For literally glancing back over your shoulder, say 뒤를 돌아보다. 되돌아보다 is almost always figurative reflection on the past.
되돌아보다 vs 후회하다 confused
되돌아보다 is neutral review of the past; 후회하다 is specifically regretting it. You can 되돌아보다 happy memories, but you wouldn't 후회하다 them.

반성하다 (反省) implies remorse over a fault and resolve to improve; 되돌아보다 is broader, gentler reflection without the built-in guilt.

words.shortExplanation: 바뀌다 means "to change, to be switched" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to change, to be switched" in Korean is 바뀌다 (bakkwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 바뀌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 바뀌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요. ("The password changed.") — then reshape the same stem into 바뀌고 싶어요 (desire), 바뀔 수 있어요 (ability), and 바뀔 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not change, to be switched.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to change, to be switched.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can change, to be switched.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to change, to be switched.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
바뀌다 = something gets switched/replaced by something else. The thing that changes takes 이/가, never 을/를.

examples.en: The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
examples.note: Super common at work — schedules and times 'get changed' on you; note 3시로 with (으)로.

examples.en: Oh, the shop's name changed.
examples.note: ~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural the moment you spot a change.

examples.en: The plan might change again.
examples.note: 또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.

words.nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive twin of 바꾸다: the thing that changes is itself the subject (이/가) and nobody is named as the doer, so it covers things getting switched, replaced, or mixed up on their own. The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요) and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바뀌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바뀌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — '번호를 바뀌었어요' is wrong because 바뀌다 has no object. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요 or the past as 바꼈어요; the 바뀌- stem keeps its 위 and gives 바뀌어요 / 바뀌었어요.
Don't blur 바뀌다 and 변하다: 마음이 바뀌었어요 = I changed my mind (switched decisions), but 마음이 변했어요 = my feelings have transformed (e.g., fallen out of love).

The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.

words.shortExplanation: 달라지다 means "to become different, to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 달라지다 (dallajida) = "to become different, to change". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 달라져요 plus one useful sentence like 분위기가 완전히 달라졌어요. ("The atmosphere became completely different."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 달라지고 싶어요 for what you want, 달라질 수 있어요 for what you can, 달라질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not become different, to change.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to become different, to change.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can become different, to change.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to become different, to change.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (be different) + -아지다.

examples.en: Did you cut your hair? You look different.
examples.note: Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라지다 = the vibe/impression changed.

examples.en: Now that I've lived here, my thinking has changed a lot.
examples.note: Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.

examples.en: The rules will be different starting next year.
examples.note: Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.

words.nuance: 달라지다 spotlights the before-and-after gap: something is now clearly unlike how it used to be, which makes it the everyday verb for noticing change in a person's looks, mood, or a situation. It's the inchoative of the adjective 다르다 (to be different) — 다르 + -아지다 'become' — and that origin is the #1 pitfall: 다르다 states a static difference between two things (A는 B와 달라요 = A is different from B), while 달라지다 is the dynamic act of becoming different over time (분위기가 달라졌어요 = the mood changed). It overlaps with 변하다 and 바뀌다, but the dividing line is focus: 달라지다 = 'the result looks different now,' 변하다 = 'the inner nature transformed,' 바뀌다 = 'one thing got swapped for another.' Both 달라지다 and the thing changing take 이/가; the form 달라져요 comes from -지다 verbs taking 어 in the 요-form (지+어 → 져).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달라지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 다르다 — 다르다 is an adjective for a static difference (저는 형과 성격이 달라요), while 달라지다 is a verb for becoming different (성격이 달라졌어요).
It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요. To deliberately change something, use 바꾸다.
Don't say the present as 달라요 when you mean 'is changing'; 달라요 = 'is different (now)', 달라지고 있어요 = 'is becoming different'.

words.english: to increase, to grow, to stretch out
words.shortExplanation: 늘어나다 means "to increase, to grow, to stretch out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 늘어나다 (neureonada) means "to increase, to grow, to stretch out". Start from the polite form 늘어나요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 늘어나다. usagePhrases.en: I increase, to grow, to stretch out.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not increase, to grow, to stretch out.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to increase, to grow, to stretch out.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can increase, to grow, to stretch out.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to increase, to grow, to stretch out.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: My workload has grown a lot lately.
usagePhrases.note: 늘어나다 = an amount/number gets bigger. A touch more vivid and visual than plain 늘다.

examples.en: The foreign-resident population keeps growing.
examples.note: 점점 + 늘어나고 있어요 = 'is gradually increasing' — common in news and small talk.

examples.en: My card bill suddenly went up.
examples.note: Money talk: 지출이/요금이 늘어나다 (expenses/fees increase).

examples.en: If you practice, your vocabulary will naturally grow.
examples.note: Encouraging line about skills/knowledge increasing.

words.nuance: 늘어나다 means a quantity, number, or length gets bigger, and it feels more concrete and visual than its plainer synonym 늘다 — picture something physically stretching or a count climbing on a screen. The contrast worth memorizing: 늘다 vs 늘어나다 are near-interchangeable for amounts, but only 늘어나다 carries the physical 'stretch out and lose shape' meaning (니트가 늘어났어요), while only 늘다 is used for a skill improving (실력이 늘다, not 늘어나다). It's intransitive — the growing thing takes 이/가 — so if YOU increase something on purpose you must switch to the transitive 늘리다 (시간을 늘리다 = extend the time). The big English-speaker trap is treating 'increase' as transitive: 'I increased my savings' is 저축을 늘렸어요 with 늘리다, but 'my savings increased' is 저축이 늘어났어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 늘어나다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 늘어나요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't pair it with 을/를 as if it were transitive — say 일이 늘어났어요, not 일을 늘어났어요. Use 늘리다 when you actively increase something.
Don't use 늘어나다 for a skill getting better; that's 늘다: 한국어가 많이 늘었어요 (not 늘어났어요).
Don't confuse 늘어나다 (to increase) with 늘어서다 (to line up in a row) or 늘어지다 (to droop/sag); they look alike but mean different things.

words.english: to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle
words.shortExplanation: 줄어들다 means "to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle" in Korean is 줄어들다 (jureodeulda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 줄어들어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 줄어들다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 스트레스가 많이 줄어들었어요. ("My stress has gone down a lot.") — then reshape the same stem into 줄어들고 싶어요 (desire), 줄어들 수 있어요 (ability), and 줄어들 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I decrease, to shrink, to dwindle.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not decrease, to shrink, to dwindle.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can decrease, to shrink, to dwindle.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: My stress has gone down a lot.
usagePhrases.note: 줄어들다 = an amount/pressure gets smaller. More vivid and gradual-feeling than plain 줄다.

examples.en: Customers suddenly dropped off.
examples.note: Business small talk — 손님이/매출이 줄어들다.

examples.en: My weight is gradually going down.
examples.note: 조금씩 + 줄어들고 있어요 = 'is decreasing little by little'.

examples.ko: 월세 싼 데로 옮기면 부담이 줄어들 거예요.
examples.romanization: wolse ssan dero olmgimyeon budami jureodeul geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you move somewhere with cheaper rent, the burden will lessen.
examples.note: 옮기다 takes the place (데로), and 부담이 is what 줄어들다 acts on.

words.nuance: 줄어들다 means a quantity, size, or pressure shrinks, and it feels more vivid and gradual than its plainer synonym 줄다 — you can almost watch the number sliding down. It's the exact opposite of 늘어나다, and like that verb it pairs naturally with 점점/계속/조금씩 for a 'bit by bit' feel. 사라지다 = something is gone / no longer there. The lost thing takes 이/가.

words.nuance: 사라지다 means something stops being present — it's gone from sight or from existence — and it works for objects, people, places, and even feelings like worry or pain. words.english: to come up, to arise, to form, to get
words.shortExplanation: 생기다 means "to come up, to arise, to form, to get" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 생기다 (saenggida) means "to come up, to arise, to form, to get". Start from the polite form 생겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 생기다. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 생기다 also becomes 생기고 싶어요 (want), 생길 수 있어요 (can), and 생길 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.en: I come up, to arise, to form, to get.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not come up, to arise, to form, to get.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to come up, to arise, to form, to get.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

일이 생기다 = an errand/issue comes up — the #1 polite excuse for canceling plans.

examples.en: I got another pimple.
examples.note: For skin/body marks: 여드름이/멍이 생기다 ('a pimple/bruise forms').

examples.en: Did you get a boyfriend?
examples.note: Casual but super common — 애인이/여자친구가 생기다 = 'to get a partner'.

examples.en: If a problem comes up, contact me right away.
examples.note: 문제가 생기다 = a problem arises; the conditional 생기면 is everyday phrasing.

words.nuance: 생기다 covers a surprisingly wide range tied by one idea — something comes into being on its own: a thing appearing (가게가 생기다), an event or issue arising (일이/문제가 생기다), or a person 'getting' something they didn't have (돈이/시간이/애인이 생기다). The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that even when English says 'get,' 생기다 is intransitive, so what you acquire takes 이/가, not 을/를: 시간이 생겼어요, never 시간을 생겼어요. Contrast it with two relatives: 생기다 = something newly comes to exist, while 만들어지다 = something gets made/created by a process, and 받다 = you actively receive something handed to you (선물을 받다, with 을/를). Note too the unrelated second sense 'to look (a certain way)': 잘생기다 = good-looking, 못생기다 = plain — here 생기다 describes appearance, not appearance-into-existence.

Use 생겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't translate 'I got X' with 을/를 — it's 시간이 생겼어요 (I got time), not 시간을 생겼어요.
When canceling, '일이 생겼어요' is the natural set excuse; learners over-explain instead of using it.
Don't say 만들어요 when something just appears — 새 카페가 생겼어요 (a new cafe popped up), not 만들었어요 (which means somebody built it).

words.english: to break down, to get ruined
words.shortExplanation: 망가지다 means "to break down, to get ruined" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to break down, to get ruined" in Korean is 망가지다 (manggajida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 망가져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 망가지다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 우산이 바람에 망가졌어요. ("My umbrella got wrecked by the wind.") — then reshape the same stem into 망가지고 싶어요 (desire), 망가질 수 있어요 (ability), and 망가질 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I break down, to get ruined.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not break down, to get ruined.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to break down, to get ruined.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can break down, to get ruined.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to break down, to get ruined.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: My umbrella got wrecked by the wind.
usagePhrases.note: 망가지다 = something breaks and stops working / loses its shape. The broken thing takes 이/가; 바람에 = 'by the wind'.

examples.ko: 택배 상자가 다 망가진 채로 왔어요.
examples.romanization: taekbae sangjaga da manggajin chaero wasseoyo.
examples.en: The parcel box arrived completely wrecked.
examples.note: ~ㄴ 채로 = 'in a (ruined) state'; handy for complaints to delivery/sellers.

examples.en: My shoes got ruined from the rain.
examples.note: Everyday for clothes/shoes/bags getting damaged beyond use; 비(를) 맞다 = to get rained on.

examples.en: My diet plan totally fell apart.
examples.note: Figurative — plans, routines, or moods can 망가지다 ('get wrecked').

words.nuance: 망가지다 means something is damaged to the point it no longer works or holds its shape, and it's broader than its near-synonym 고장나다 — that word is specifically about machines/devices ceasing to function (시계가 고장났어요), whereas 망가지다 adds the nuance of physical wreckage and also stretches to objects, plans, health, and routines falling apart. So a phone that simply won't turn on is more naturally 고장났어요, but a phone with a smashed body is 망가졌어요. It's intransitive (the thing breaking takes 이/가); when a person ruins something on purpose or through carelessness, switch to the transitive 망가뜨리다 or the blunter 망치다 (계획을 망쳤어요 = I ruined the plan). The form 망가져요 follows the -지다 vowel rule (지 + 어 → 져). English speakers often try to say 'I broke it' with this verb — but you must use the transitive partner instead.

Use 망가져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 핸드폰이 망가졌어요 (the phone broke), but 핸드폰을 망가뜨렸어요 / 망쳤어요 when YOU broke it.
For a pure machine malfunction with no visible damage, 고장났어요 is more natural; reserve 망가지다 for real wreckage or 'falling apart'.
Don't use 망가지다 for brittle things shattering — a cup that smashes is 깨졌어요, not 망가졌어요.

words.english: to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart
words.shortExplanation: 무너지다 means "to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 무너지다 (muneojida) = "to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 무너져요 plus one useful sentence like 오래된 담이 무너졌어요. ("The old wall collapsed."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 무너지고 싶어요 for what you want, 무너질 수 있어요 for what you can, 무너질 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.en: I collapse, to crumble, to fall apart.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not collapse, to crumble, to fall apart.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart.

무너지다 = a structure caves in / crumbles down. The thing that collapses takes 이/가.

examples.en: The bridge collapsed in the heavy rain.
examples.note: Disaster/news context — 건물이/다리가 무너지다; 폭우로 = 'due to torrential rain'.

examples.en: Don't fall apart just because you lost once.
examples.note: 무너지지 마세요 = 'don't break down'; encouraging someone to stay strong.

examples.en: The trust collapsed in a single moment.
examples.note: 믿음이 무너지다 = trust crumbles; abstract things collapse too.

words.nuance: 무너지다 literally means a structure crumbles or caves in — a wall, a building, a bridge — but it's used just as often figuratively for emotions, plans, trust, or order collapsing, and among younger Koreans 멘탈이 무너지다 ('my mental collapsed') is everyday slang for breaking down under stress. The synonym to distinguish is 쓰러지다: both involve 'falling,' but 쓰러지다 means a person or upright thing topples over while staying intact (할머니가 쓰러지셨어요 = grandma collapsed/fainted), whereas 무너지다 means the thing breaks apart as it goes down. It's intransitive (the collapsing thing takes 이/가); to knock something down on purpose, use the transitive 무너뜨리다 (벽을 무너뜨리다). The 요-form is 무너져요 (지 + 어 → 져). One caution: the emotional 마음이 무너지다 is reserved for genuinely crushing moments, not mild letdowns.

Don't swap it with 쓰러지다 — a fainting person is 쓰러졌어요, not 무너졌어요; 무너지다 implies breaking apart, not just toppling.
Don't use 마음이 무너지다 for mild disappointment; it's strong, for heartbreak-level moments. For 'a bit let down' use 실망했어요.

A strong first sentence is 컵이 떨어져서 깨졌어요. ("The cup fell and broke."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 깨지다 also becomes 깨지고 싶어요 (want), 깨질 수 있어요 (can), and 깨질 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not break, to shatter, to fall through.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to break, to shatter, to fall through.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
깨지다 = a hard/brittle thing shatters or cracks. The broken thing takes 이/가.

examples.en: The eggs broke inside my bag.
examples.note: For brittle things — 유리가/접시가/계란이 깨지다.

examples.en: The world record was broken.
examples.note: 기록이 깨지다 = a record gets broken; a fixed sports/news collocation.

examples.en: The mood was suddenly ruined.
examples.note: 분위기가 깨지다 = the vibe/mood breaks — when one comment spoils the moment.

words.nuance: 깨지다 is the verb for hard, brittle things shattering or cracking — glass, dishes, phone screens, eggs — and the key is matching the verb to the material: it contrasts with 부러지다 (long, rigid things snapping: 팔이/연필이 부러지다) and 찢어지다 (paper or fabric tearing: 종이가/옷이 찢어지다). Figuratively it covers promises, deals, records, and moods 'breaking' (약속이/기록이/분위기가 깨지다), and in casual speech 둘이 깨졌어 means a couple split up. It's intransitive (the broken thing takes 이/가); to smash something yourself, use the transitive 깨다 (컵을 깼어요 = I broke the cup) — note the e/ae spelling difference, 깨다 vs 깨지다. The 요-form is 깨져요 (지 + 어 → 져). English speakers habitually say 'I broke the glass' with the intransitive form; you must use 깨다 when there's an agent.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 깨지다 as a complete polite sentence.

Don't use it transitively — say 유리가 깨졌어요 (the glass broke), but 유리를 깼어요 when YOU broke it (깨다).
Match the verb to the material: glass/ceramics 깨지다, sticks/bones 부러지다, paper/clothes 찢어지다.
Don't confuse the spellings — 깨다 (transitive, 'break/smash') vs 깨지다 (intransitive, 'get broken'); the 지 marks the passive-ish 'happens to it' meaning.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 깨지다 becomes 깨질 수 있어요 ("can") and 깨질 거예요 ("will"). words.english: to burst, to explode, to go off
words.shortExplanation: 터지다 means "to burst, to explode, to go off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: I do not burst, to explode, to go off.

터지다 = (signal) comes through. 와이파이/인터넷/데이터가 터지다 is the everyday way to say a signal works.

examples.en: It's a basement, so my phone has no signal.
examples.note: 폰이 안 터지다 = 'no reception' — essential for cafes, subways, basements.

examples.en: My blister popped and it hurts.
examples.note: For body stuff — 물집이/혈관이 터지다.

examples.en: I suddenly burst out laughing.
examples.note: 웃음이 터지다 = laughter erupts; you can't hold it in — a fixed, very natural phrase.

words.shortExplanation: 멎다 means "to stop, to cease (rain, bleeding)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 멎다 (meotda) = "to stop, to cease (rain, bleeding)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 멎어요 plus one useful sentence like 비가 멎었어요. ("The rain has stopped."). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not stop, to cease (rain, bleeding).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to stop, to cease (rain, bleeding).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can stop, to cease (rain, bleeding).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to stop, to cease (rain, bleeding).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
멎다 = a flowing/ongoing natural thing ceases on its own. The thing that stops takes 이/가.

examples.en: I'll head out once the snow stops.
examples.note: Conditional 멎으면 = 'once it stops' — natural for weather; note 멎으면 takes the 으 linker after the ㅈ-batchim.

examples.en: I was so startled my heart felt like it stopped.
examples.note: 심장이 멎다 = heart stops; the set phrase 멎는 줄 알았어요 = 'I thought it would stop'.

examples.en: The sound of rain stopped only after a long while.
examples.note: Slightly literary; 멎다 has a quieter, more natural feel than 멈추다.

words.nuance: 멎다 means something flowing or continuous comes to a halt by itself — rain, snow, wind, bleeding, a heartbeat, breath. So rain can be either 멎다 or 멈추다, but a car can only 멈추다, never 멎다. It's strictly intransitive and never takes an object; for stopping a vehicle or machine yourself you'd use 멈추다 or 세우다 (차를 세우다). One pronunciation note: the ㅈ-batchim means vowel endings add the 으/어 linker — hence 멎어요, 멎으면, 멎을 거예요.

Use 멎어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 멎다 for vehicles or machines — say 차가 멈췄어요 (the car stopped), not 차가 멎었어요.
It's intransitive, so don't add 을/를: 피가 멎었어요 (the bleeding stopped), not 피를 멎었어요. To stop something yourself, use 멈추다/세우다.

words.english: to continue, to be connected, to lead to
words.shortExplanation: 이어지다 means "to continue, to be connected, to lead to" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 이어지다 (ieojida) means "to continue, to be connected, to lead to". Start from the polite form 이어져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 이어지다. A strong first sentence is 이 길은 시장으로 이어져요. ("This road leads to the market."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 이어지다 also becomes 이어지고 싶어요 (want), 이어질 수 있어요 (can), and 이어질 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.en: I continue, to be connected, to lead to.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not continue, to be connected, to lead to.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to continue, to be connected, to lead to.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can continue, to be connected, to lead to.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to continue, to be connected, to lead to.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: This road leads to the market.
usagePhrases.note: 이어지다 = one thing connects/continues to another. Often with ~(으)로 (leads to) or ~까지 (continues until).

examples.en: The heat will continue into next week.
examples.note: Weather forecasts love this — 폭염이/장마가 이어지다; ~까지 marks how long it runs.

examples.en: The meeting dragged on until evening.
examples.note: 이어지다 = an event runs on longer than expected, without stopping.

examples.en: The accident led to major damage.
examples.note: ~(으)로 이어지다 for a cause leading to a (often serious) result.

words.nuance: 이어지다 means something continues without breaking, or one thing connects into another — a road leading somewhere (길이 ~로 이어지다), weather persisting (더위가 이어지다), a conversation flowing on, or a cause leading to a result (X로 이어지다). It's the intransitive partner of 잇다 (to connect/join), so when you actively link things you switch to 잇다 or the compound 이어 가다 (전통을 이어 가다 = to carry on a tradition). The synonym to weigh is 계속되다 (to continue): the two overlap for duration (회의가 이어지다/계속되다 are both fine), but only 이어지다 carries the spatial 'connects to / leads to' sense — a road 이어지다 to a place, never 계속되다 there. Use 이어져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 대화가 이어졌어요 (the conversation continued), but 대화를 이어 갔어요 when someone keeps it going (이어 가다).
For 'leads to a result,' use the particle (으)로: 노력이 성공으로 이어졌어요, not 성공에 이어졌어요.
Don't swap it with 계속되다 for spatial connection — a road that runs to the station is 역으로 이어져요, not 계속돼요.

words.english: to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)
words.shortExplanation: 두근거리다 means "to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)" in Korean is 두근거리다 (dugeungeorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 두근거려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 두근거리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 가슴이 두근거리다 ("for one's heart to pound") — then reshape the same stem into 두근거리고 싶어요 (desire), 두근거릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 두근거릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The default subject is 가슴(이) or 심장(이) — the heart, never the person. Say 가슴이 두근거려요, not 저는 두근거려요.

examples.en: My heart is going thump-thump.
examples.note: The simplest form: the mimetic 두근두근 + 하다. Kids and adults both say this.

examples.en: It's right before my presentation, so my heart is racing.
examples.note: 심장이 두근거리다 and 가슴이 두근거리다 are interchangeable; 가슴 sounds a touch softer and more everyday.

examples.ko: 내일 그 사람 만난다고 생각하니까 벌써 두근거려.
examples.romanization: naeil geu saram mannandago saenggakanikka beolsseo dugeungeoryeo.
examples.en: Just thinking about meeting them tomorrow, my heart's already fluttering.
examples.note: Casual 두근거려 to a close friend, with the subject 가슴 left unspoken because context makes it obvious.

words.nuance: 두근거리다 names the physical sensation of a pounding, fluttering heartbeat, built from the mimetic 두근 ('thump') + the repetitive-motion suffix -거리다, so its grammatical subject is 가슴/심장 and the person is marked with -은/는 or a cause phrase, never as the doer. It spans the whole range from giddy anticipation to dread, so Koreans lean on partners — 설레서 두근거리다 for good nerves, 긴장돼서 두근거리다 for bad — to pin down which. Its close cousin 떨리다 also means 'tremble/be nervous' but centres on shakiness rather than the heartbeat itself, and 설레다 names the emotion while 두근거리다 names the bodily symptom of it. The English-speaker trap is treating it like 'I'm excited' and saying 저는 두근거려요; let the heart be the subject (가슴이 두근거려요), or switch to 저는 설레요 when you mean the feeling.

Use 두근거려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 두근거려요 to mean 'I'm excited' — the heart is the subject, so use 가슴이 두근거려요 (or 저는 설레요 if you mean the feeling).
Imperative/propositive forms like 두근거리세요 are grammatically possible but sound odd in real life, since you can't really order someone's heart to pound.

words.english: to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)
words.shortExplanation: 그립다 means "to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 그립다 (geuripda) = "to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 그리워요 plus one useful sentence like 고향이 그립다 ("to miss one's hometown"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 그리워하고 싶어요 for what you want, 그리울 수 있어요 for what you can, 그리울 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
그립다 is an adjective, so what you miss takes -이/가, not -을/를: 고향이 그리워요, never 고향을 그리워요.

examples.en: I miss my hometown.
examples.note: The base pattern: the thing missed takes -이/가, and ㅂ-irregular 그립- + -어요 gives 그리워요.

examples.ko: 한국에 산 지 일 년 됐는데 가끔 엄마 음식이 그리워요.
examples.romanization: hanguge san ji il nyeon dwaenneunde gakkeum eomma eumsigi geuriwoyo.
examples.en: It's been a year living in Korea, and sometimes I miss my mom's cooking.
examples.note: Everyday expat use; you can long for food and places, not only people.

examples.en: I missed my friend so much that I made a video call.
examples.note: 그리워서 (because I missed) drives a real action. To say someone else actively misses, you'd switch to 그리워하다.

words.nuance: 그립다 is an adjective expressing your own felt longing, so the thing you miss is the subject (-이/가) and you cannot hang a direct object on it; to describe a third person missing something ('he misses home') Korean shifts to the verb 그리워하다, because Korean treats adjectives of feeling as reportable only from the inside. The sharp contrast to learn is 보고 싶다 vs 그립다: 보고 싶다 ('want to see') is the everyday, conversational way to say you miss a specific person and works fine for texting a friend, whereas 그립다 is more wistful, broader (it covers places, eras, tastes, not just faces), and reads as faintly literary. It's a ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ turns to 우 before vowel endings: 그립- + -어요 → 그리워요, past 그리웠어요. The classic English trap is the object particle — 'I miss my hometown' tempts you to say 고향을 그리워요, but the correct adjective frame is 고향이 그리워요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 그립다 as a complete polite sentence.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 그립다 becomes 그리울 수 있어요 ("can") and 그리울 거예요 ("will"). conjugationTips.body: 그립다 has an irregular stem (ㅂ). Memorize its polite form 그리워요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.english: to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed
words.shortExplanation: 부끄럽다 means "to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The textbook physical tell: 부끄러워서 + 얼굴이 빨개지다 ('face goes red') is the stock collocation.

examples.en: I'm a little shy.
examples.note: The base feeling about oneself; ㅂ-irregular 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요.

examples.ko: 사람들 앞에서 한국어로 말하는 게 아직 부끄러워요.
examples.romanization: saramdeul apeseo hangugeoro malhaneun ge ajik bukkeureowoyo.
examples.en: I'm still shy about speaking Korean in front of people.
examples.note: The cause (말하는 게) takes -이/가 because this is an adjective describing your own state.

examples.en: My younger sibling is shy around strangers.
examples.note: For someone else's shyness, switch to the verb 부끄러워하다, which can take an object (낯선 사람을).

words.nuance: 부끄럽다 covers both bashful shyness (meeting new people, being praised) and self-conscious embarrassment over a small slip, and it leans gentler, more inward and even endearing compared with 창피하다, which is sharper, louder, public mortification. The dividing line worth memorising: 부끄럽다 ≈ shy/quietly abashed and can sound cute, while 창피하다 ≈ 'I want to disappear' after a public blunder; a child hiding behind a parent is 부끄러워하는 것, not 창피해하는 것. words.english: to be embarrassing / to feel mortified
words.shortExplanation: 창피하다 means "to be embarrassing / to feel mortified" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to be embarrassing / to feel mortified" in Korean is 창피하다 (changpihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 창피해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 창피하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 창피해 죽겠다 ("to be dying of embarrassment") — then reshape the same stem into 창피해하고 싶어요 (desire), 창피할 수 있어요 (ability), and 창피할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs.
