usagePhrases.en: I be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
-아/어 죽겠다 ('dying of ~') is the go-to intensifier with feeling words; 창피해 죽겠어요 is extremely common.

examples.en: Ugh, this is so embarrassing.
examples.note: The blunt casual reaction. 하다-verb contracts: 창피하- + -아 → 창피해.

examples.en: Everyone was staring, so I was embarrassed.
examples.note: Past 창피했어요; the cause here is a public situation, which is typical of this word.

examples.ko: 그렇게 큰 소리로 말하면 내가 창피하잖아.
examples.romanization: geureoke keun soriro malhamyeon naega changpihajana.
examples.en: If you talk that loudly, you embarrass me.
examples.note: Used to tell someone they're embarrassing you; -잖아 adds a mild complaining, 'come on' tone.

words.nuance: 창피하다 is the stronger, more public sibling of 부끄럽다 — the 'I want the floor to swallow me' feeling after you trip in a crowd or get scolded openly — and it describes either your own mortification (저 창피해요) or the situation that causes it (창피한 상황). It is Sino-Korean: 창피 猖披, where 猖 means 'run wild/rampage' and 披 means 'spread open, be dishevelled,' the image being clothes worn so carelessly you're exposed, hence ashamed. words.english: to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous
words.shortExplanation: 황당하다 means "to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 황당하다 (hwangdanghada) = "to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 황당해요 plus one useful sentence like 황당한 일 ("an absurd / ridiculous incident"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 황당해하고 싶어요 for what you want, 황당할 수 있어요 for what you can, 황당할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
황당한 + noun describes the baffling thing itself: 황당한 일, 황당한 상황, 황당한 변명, 황당한 소문.

examples.en: This is honestly ridiculous.
examples.note: The base reaction. 하다-verb: 황당하- + -아요 → 황당해요.

examples.ko: 갑자기 예약이 취소됐다고 해서 너무 황당했어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi yeyagi chwisodwaetdago haeseo neomu hwangdanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: They suddenly said my reservation was canceled, so I was dumbfounded.
examples.note: Past 황당했어요; a very common customer-service mishap context.

examples.ko: 그 사람 변명이 너무 황당해서 웃음이 나왔어.
examples.romanization: geu saram byeonmyeongi neomu hwangdanghaeseo useumi nawasseo.
examples.en: His excuse was so absurd that I burst out laughing.
examples.note: 황당해서 (because it was absurd) leads to a reaction. Casual register with a friend.

words.nuance: 황당하다 captures the 'wait, what?' feeling when something is so unexpected or illogical that it leaves you stunned — a baffling excuse, an out-of-nowhere cancellation, an absurd demand — and it covers both the ridiculous thing itself (황당한 변명) and your reaction to it (너무 황당했어요). It is Sino-Korean: 황당 荒唐, where 荒 means 'wild/overgrown/desolate' and 唐 carries an old sense of 'boastful, rambling, far-fetched,' so the literal flavour is 'wildly preposterous.' The synonym to separate it from is 어이없다: 황당하다 leans toward 'bizarre/unbelievable, doesn't compute,' while 어이없다 adds exasperation or contempt ('so dumb it's almost offensive'); a UFO story is 황당하다, but a line-cutter is more 어이없다. Don't confuse it with the near-twin 당황하다 ('to panic/be flustered'), which is about losing your own composure, not judging something as absurd. As a 하다-adjective: 황당하- + -아요 → 황당해요, past 황당했어요. The English trap is translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies absurdity, not mere unexpectedness.

Use 황당해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies the thing was absurd or nonsensical, not just unexpected.
Confusing it with 당황하다 ('to be flustered/panicked'); 황당하다 judges the situation as absurd, while 당황하다 describes you losing composure.

words.shortExplanation: 어이없다 means "to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 어이없다 (eoieopda) means "to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless". usagePhrases.en: I be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless.

usagePhrases.en: I can be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The headword is a contraction of 어이가 없다; the 가 stays in careful speech and drops in fast speech: 어이없어.

examples.en: Wow, this is unbelievable.
examples.note: The everyday speechless reaction; the 가 of 어이가 없다 drops in casual speech.

examples.en: Someone cut in line, so I was totally flabbergasted.
examples.note: 없다-type adjective: 어이없- + -었어요 → 어이없었어요. Note -길래 = 'because (I saw/noticed).'

examples.ko: 그 말 듣고 너무 어이없어서 헛웃음이 나왔어.
examples.romanization: geu mal deutgo neomu eoieopseoseo heosuseumi nawasseo.
examples.en: After hearing that, I was so dumbfounded I let out a dry laugh.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 헛웃음 (a hollow, dry laugh). Casual register.

words.nuance: 어이없다 (full form 어이가 없다) is the punchy, everyday way Koreans react to something so absurd, unfair, or stupid that it stuns them into a speechless half-laugh — 어이 means roughly 'the wits/sense' you'd need to handle the situation, so 'lacking 어이' is being knocked clean out of your composure. Set beside 황당하다, it carries more exasperation or contempt: 황당하다 = 'this is bizarre/doesn't compute,' while 어이없다 = 'this is so dumb it almost offends me,' which is why it's what you mutter when someone cuts in line or hands you a nonsense excuse. It's a hair more casual than 황당하다 but still fine in polite speech (어이없어요); the truly rough register would be slang like 어처구니없다's blunt cousins or profanity. Because 없다 behaves like an adjective, a third party's reaction takes the verb 어이없어하다. The most common pitfalls are spelling and polarity: it is 어이없다 (the cute misspelling 어의없다 is wrong), and it is always negative — never use it for a pleasant surprise.

Use 어이없어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling or hearing it as 어의없다 — the word is 어이 (not 어의); standard spelling is 어이없다.
Using it for pleasant surprise; 어이없다 is always negative — bafflement mixed with annoyance.
Dropping into the plain adjective for someone else's reaction; a third person 'is dumbfounded' is 어이없어해요, using the -어하다 verb.

words.shortExplanation: 짜릿하다 means "to be thrilling / to feel an electric, tingling rush" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

짜릿한 + noun is the engine: 짜릿한 순간, 짜릿한 경기 (a nail-biter), 짜릿한 역전승 (a thrilling comeback win).

examples.en: Whoa, what a rush!
examples.note: The base exclamation. 하다-verb: 짜릿하- + -아 → 짜릿해.

examples.ko: 롤러코스터 탈 때 그 짜릿한 느낌이 좋아.

examples.note: Past 짜릿했어요; sports — especially a last-second turnaround — are the classic context.

words.nuance: 짜릿하다 originally describes a literal tingling, electric sensation — a mild shock, a cold splash, a limb that's gone numb — and extends to the metaphorical thrill of exhilarating moments like a comeback win, a thrill ride, or a daring success; it's overwhelmingly positive and high-adrenaline. words.english: to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close
words.shortExplanation: 섭섭하다 means "to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: I do not feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close.

usagePhrases.en: I want to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: please don't take it the wrong way
usagePhrases.note: A set phrase to reassure someone you didn't mean to slight them; 섭섭하게 생각하다 = 'to take it as a snub.'

examples.en: I'm a little hurt.
examples.note: The base feeling, kept soft with 조금. 하다-verb: 섭섭하- + -아요 → 섭섭해요.

examples.ko: 생일인데 연락도 안 해서 좀 섭섭했어요.
examples.romanization: saengirinde yeollakdo an haeseo jom seopseopaesseoyo.
examples.en: It was my birthday and you didn't even text, so I felt a bit hurt.

examples.en: Hearing you're already leaving makes me sad to see you go.
examples.note: The bittersweet-goodbye sense, not grievance at all. -네요 adds soft, freshly-felt emotion.

words.nuance: 섭섭하다 is a uniquely Korean shade of feeling: a gentle, wistful hurt or letdown when someone close doesn't meet your emotional expectations, or the bittersweet pang of parting. The near-synonym 서운하다 sits almost on top of it — most speakers use them interchangeably — with 섭섭하다 carrying a slightly older, warmer texture and 서운하다 feeling a touch softer and more current; both are far milder than anger, so they are wrong for 화나다 ('be angry') or 짜증나다 ('be annoyed/irritated'). As a 하다-adjective it contracts 섭섭하- + -아요 → 섭섭해요, and a third person's hurt takes the verb 섭섭해하다. The key English-speaker pitfall is treating it as anger or using it about strangers — it presumes a relationship close enough to have expectations in the first place.

Use 섭섭해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating it as anger; 섭섭하다 is tender disappointment, so 화나다/짜증나다 are wrong for this feeling.
Using it about strangers — it implies a relationship close enough to have expectations.
Reporting someone else's hurt with the plain adjective; a third person 'feels let down' is 섭섭해해요, using the -어하다 verb.

words.english: to be sick of / to get fed up with something
words.shortExplanation: 질리다 means "to be sick of / to get fed up with something" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 질리다 (jillida) means "to be sick of / to get fed up with something". Start from the polite form 질려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 질리다. A strong first sentence is 라면에 질리다 ("to be sick of ramen"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 질리다 also becomes 질리고 싶어요 (want), 질릴 수 있어요 (can), and 질릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I be sick of / to get fed up with something.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be sick of / to get fed up with something.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be sick of / to get fed up with something.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be sick of / to get fed up with something.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be sick of / to get fed up with something.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The source of your boredom takes -에 (most standard) or -이/가: 라면에 질렸어요 / 라면이 질렸어요.

examples.en: I'm sick of it now.
examples.note: The base 'fed up' statement; 이-stem 질리- + -었어요 → 질렸어요.

examples.ko: 매일 라면만 먹으니까 이제 진짜 질렸어요.
examples.romanization: maeil lamyeonman meogeunikka ije jinjja jillyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Eating only ramen every day, I'm really sick of it now.
examples.note: The source is marked with -에 (라면에) as the textbook choice; everyday over-saturation.

examples.ko: 그 말 듣고 겁에 질려서 아무 말도 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: geu mal deutgo geobe jillyeoseo amu maldo mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: Hearing that, I froze in fear and couldn't say a word.
examples.note: The other meaning entirely: 겁에 질리다 = paralyzed with fear. Context tells the two senses apart.

words.nuance: 질리다 is the everyday verb for being so over-saturated with something — a food, a routine, a song — that you can't stand a drop more of it, the 'I'm so done with this' feeling; for this sense you mark the source with -에 (most standard) or -이/가, and the partner phrases 질릴 만큼 / 질릴 정도 mean 'to the point of being fed up.' But it has a second, scarier life: 질리다 also means to turn pale or be paralyzed with fear, as in 겁에 질리다 ('frozen with terror') and 새파랗게 질리다 ('go deathly white'), so context decides which world you're in. Compared with 지겹다 ('tedious, dragging on and boring you'), 질리다 stresses saturation from too much of a thing rather than slow tedium, and unlike 싫증 나다 ('lose interest') it can hit a sharp 'can't take it' wall. The recurring English trap is the particle: 'I'm sick of ramen' tempts 라면을 질렸어요, but the correct marker is -에 (라면에 질렸어요) or -이/가, never -을/를.

Use 질려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the source with -을/를; use -에 (라면에 질렸어요) or -이/가.
Forgetting the second meaning — 겁에 질리다 / 얼굴이 질리다 means to go pale with fear, not 'be bored.'
Confusing it with 지겹다; 질리다 is saturation ('too much of it'), while 지겹다 is dragging tedium ('so boring it won't end').

words.english: to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation
words.shortExplanation: 설레다 means "to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation" in Korean is 설레다 (seolleda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 설레요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 설레다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 마음이 설레다 ("for one's heart to flutter") — then reshape the same stem into 설레고 싶어요 (desire), 설렐 수 있어요 (ability), and 설렐 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be excited / to feel one's heart flutter with anticipation.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The natural subject is 마음/가슴: 마음이 설레요. The cause comes via a -에/생각에 phrase, e.g. 여행 생각에 설레요.

examples.en: I'm so excited / my heart's all aflutter.
examples.note: The base feeling; 설레- + -어요 contracts to 설레요.

examples.ko: 내일 여행 가는 생각에 벌써 설레요.
examples.romanization: naeil yeohaeng ganeun saenggage beolsseo seolleyo.
examples.en: Just thinking about the trip tomorrow, I'm already giddy.
examples.note: The cause rides on 생각에 ('at the thought of'); note the standard form is 설레다, not 설레이다.

examples.en: It was a first date, so my heart was really fluttering.
examples.note: Past 설렜어요 (설레 + 었 → 설렜); one of the most-loved feeling words in K-dramas.

words.nuance: 설레다 is the warm, fluttery thrill of looking forward to something good — the butterflies before a date, a trip, or a fresh start — and it names the emotion itself, with 마음/가슴 as the typical subject. The contrast students need is 설레다 vs 긴장되다: both quicken the heart, but 설레다 is sweet, hopeful anticipation while 긴장되다 ('get nervous/tense') is anxious pressure, so a first date can be both 설레고 긴장돼요; meanwhile 두근거리다 names the bodily pounding that 설레다 produces. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that: copying the pretty but incorrect 설레임 from a caption, and mis-contracting the past as 설레었어요 instead of the natural 설렜어요.

words.english: to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement
words.shortExplanation: 들뜨다 means "to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 들뜨다 (deultteuda) = "to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 들떠요 plus one useful sentence like 마음이 들뜨다 ("for one's mood to lift / get giddy"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 들뜨고 싶어요 for what you want, 들뜰 수 있어요 for what you can, 들뜰 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be giddy / to get keyed up with restless excitement.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: for one's mood to lift / get giddy
usagePhrases.note: The subject is usually 마음/기분: 마음이 들떴어요 — a buzzy lift before something fun.

examples.en: My heart's already getting giddy.
examples.note: The base feeling; ㅡ-irregular 들뜨- + -어요 → 들떠요.

examples.en: Maybe because it's a long weekend, I felt giddy and restless.
examples.note: Past 들떴어요 (들뜨 + 었 → 들떴); the cause is often a holiday or event.

examples.en: Don't get too carried away — let's pack first.
examples.note: 들뜨지 말다 ('don't get over-excited'), a gentle reminder to stay grounded.

words.nuance: 들뜨다 is the bubbly, restless excitement that lifts your mood before something fun, literally formed from 들- ('rise up') + 뜨다 ('float'), so the image is your spirits floating up off the ground. That picture explains its faint undertone: you're so giddy you're a little distracted or unsettled, which is exactly why 너무 들뜨지 마 ('don't get carried away') is such a common caution. Against 설레다 (sweet, inward heart-fluttering anticipation), 들뜨다 is more buzzy, outward and hyped — and can shade slightly negative (over-excited, not thinking straight), whereas 설레다 stays purely lovely; it's also more restless than the simple high spirits of 신나다. It conjugates as a ㅡ-irregular: when a vowel ending follows, the ㅡ drops, so 들뜨- + -어 → 들떠 (요), past 들떴어요, and before -ㅂ니다 you get 들뜹니다. The English-speaker pitfalls are botching that ㅡ-drop (saying 들뜨어요 instead of 들떠요) and assuming it's purely positive when it can quietly imply 'overexcited.'

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 들뜨다 becomes 들뜰 수 있어요 ("can") and 들뜰 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 들뜨다 has an irregular stem (ㅡ). Memorize its polite form 들떠요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 들뜨다 is the bubbly, restless excitement that lifts your mood before something fun. Its faint undertone: you're so giddy you're a little distracted or unsettled, which is exactly why 너무 들뜨지 마 ('don't get carried away') is such a common caution.

Against 설레다 (sweet, inward heart-fluttering anticipation), 들뜨다 is more buzzy, outward and hyped — and can shade slightly negative (over-excited, not thinking straight), whereas 설레다 stays purely lovely. It's also more restless than the simple high spirits of 신나다.
Literally formed from 들- ('rise up') + 뜨다 ('float'), so the image is your spirits floating up off the ground.
It conjugates as a ㅡ-irregular: when a vowel ending follows, the ㅡ drops, so 들뜨- + -어 → 들떠(요), past 들떴어요, and before -ㅂ니다 you get 들뜹니다.
The English-speaker pitfalls are botching that ㅡ-drop (saying 들뜨어요 instead of 들떠요) and assuming it's purely positive when it can quietly imply 'overexcited.'

words.english: to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back
words.shortExplanation: 주눅들다 means "to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 주눅들다 (junukdeulda) means "to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back". Start from the polite form 주눅들어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 주눅들다. A strong first sentence is 주눅이 들다 ("for one's spirit to shrink (full form)"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 주눅들다 also becomes 주눅들고 싶어요 (want), 주눅들 수 있어요 (can), and 주눅들 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be intimidated / to feel cowed and shrink back.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: for one's spirit to shrink (full form)
usagePhrases.note: The compound comes from 주눅(이) 들다, so you'll also see the particle kept: 주눅이 들었어요.

examples.en: I get intimidated easily.
examples.note: The base statement about a tendency; 주눅들- + -어요 → 주눅들어요.

examples.ko: 한국어 실력이 부족해서 회의 때 자꾸 주눅들어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo sillyeogi bujokaeseo hoeui ttae jakku junukdeureoyo.
examples.en: My Korean isn't good enough, so I keep getting cowed in meetings.
examples.note: A very real expat workplace feeling; note formal 주눅듭니다 drops the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다.

examples.en: Don't shrink back — speak up confidently.
examples.note: 주눅들지 말다 paired with 당당하게 ('confidently'), the opposite attitude. A common pep-talk.

words.nuance: 주눅들다 (from 주눅(이) 들다, where 주눅 is the native noun for 'cowed timidity' and 들다 means 'to set in') means to feel so intimidated or self-conscious that you shrink back, lose your nerve, and can't assert yourself — a genuinely useful word for the expat experience of freezing up in Korean meetings or formal settings. Set it against 긴장하다 ('get nervous/tense'): 긴장하다 is momentary jitters before a test or speech and is neutral, whereas 주눅들다 is a deflating loss of confidence that makes you cower and stay small, often before someone or something more powerful; it's also more passive and lasting than a quick 당황하다 ('fluster'). It's built on 들다, so it follows the ㄹ-irregular pattern — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings, giving 주눅듭니다 (not 주눅들습니다) — while vowel endings keep it: 주눅들어요, past 주눅들었어요. The natural cure-words are 당당하다 ('be self-assured') and the encouragement 주눅들지 마. English-speaker pitfalls: keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다, and marking the cause with -을/를 instead of the correct -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 주눅들다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 주눅들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다 (saying 주눅들습니다) — the ㄹ drops: 주눅듭니다.
Marking the cause with -을/를; use -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
Equating it with plain 긴장하다; 주눅들다 is a deflating loss of confidence that makes you shrink, not just momentary nerves.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 주눅들어 and 주눅들어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 꺼내다 means "to take out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to take out" in Korean is 꺼내다 (kkeonaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 꺼내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 꺼내다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 가방에서 꺼내다 ("to take out of a bag") — then reshape the same stem into 꺼내고 싶어요 (desire), 꺼낼 수 있어요 (ability), and 꺼낼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to take out of a bag
usagePhrases.note: 에서 (out of) marks the enclosed space; this is the bread-and-butter pattern for 꺼내다

examples.en: Take your wallet out of the bag.
examples.note: casual command to a close friend; bare stem 꺼내 is the plainest form

examples.en: Can you take the side dishes out of the fridge?
examples.note: 줄래? is the soft favor-asking you use with a roommate or partner

examples.ko: 면접에서 그 질문을 꺼내실 줄은 몰랐어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseo geu jilmuneul kkeonaesil jureun mollasseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't expect them to bring up that question in the interview.
examples.note: real-situation figurative use: 꺼내시다 raises the topic, with honorific -시- for the interviewer

words.nuance: 꺼내다 is the default verb for taking something out of an enclosed space — a bag, pocket, fridge, drawer — so it almost always pairs with 에서 marking the place. The nearest rival is 빼다: the dividing line is that 빼다 is pulling out something fitted or stuck (a key from a lock, a tooth, a USB), while 꺼내다 is retrieving a freely-resting thing from inside. It's a plain native verb with no 한자, and the 내- piece carries an 'outward' feel (compare 내보내다 'send out'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 빼다 because 'take out' feels like 'pull out'; the second pitfall is the figurative 얘기를 꺼내다 ('bring up a topic') — learners try 가져오다 ('bring') here, but Korean specifically 'pulls the words out,' so 꺼내다 is required.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 꺼내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 꺼내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 빼다 to take a wallet out of a bag — 빼다 implies a fitted or stuck object you extract (열쇠를 빼다 'pull out a key'). For retrieving from open inner space, it must be 가방에서 지갑을 꺼내다.
Saying 얘기를 가져오다 to mean 'bring up a topic' — 가져오다 is physically fetching an object. To raise a subject you 'pull it out': 그 얘기 왜 꺼냈어? (Why did you bring that up?).
Forgetting the 에서 and using 에 — it is 가방에서 꺼내다 (out of), not 가방에 꺼내다; 에 would point to a destination, the wrong direction for 'taking out.'

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 꺼내다 becomes 꺼낼 수 있어요 ("can") and 꺼낼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 집다 means "to pick up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 집다 (jipda) = "to pick up". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 집어요 plus one useful sentence like 젓가락으로 집다 ("to pick up with chopsticks"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 집고 싶어요 for what you want, 집을 수 있어요 for what you can, 집을 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
(으)로 marks the tool; the prototypical 집다 scene is grasping food with chopsticks

examples.en: Pick that up for me.
examples.note: bare casual request; 집어 줘 is what you say when your hands are full

examples.en: Can I get tongs to pick up the meat?
examples.note: everyday Korean BBQ line; note 집게 (tongs) literally is 'the picking-up tool' from 집다

examples.ko: 마트에서 아무거나 집지 말고 유통기한부터 확인해.
examples.romanization: mateueseo amugeona jipji malgo yutonggihanbuteo hwaginhae.
examples.en: At the store, don't just grab whatever — check the expiration date first.
examples.note: real-situation 집다 = casually grabbing an item off a shelf, here in a negative -지 말다 command

words.nuance: 집다 means to pick up a small object with a precise pincer grasp — fingers, chopsticks, or tongs (집게, literally 'the picking tool,' comes straight from this verb). The contrast learners need is with 들다 (to lift/raise with the hand or arm) and 줍다 (to pick up off the ground something dropped): you 집어 a single fry, 들어 a heavy box, and 주워 a coin that fell. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The single biggest pitfall is conjugation: because it ends in ㅂ, English speakers over-apply the ㅂ-irregular and write 지워요, but 집다 is REGULAR — like its cousins 잡다 and 좁다 it keeps the ㅂ, so the 요-form is 집어요. A second trap is using 집다 for picking up off the floor; that situation wants 줍다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 집다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 집어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it as a ㅂ-irregular — the correct 요-form is 집어요, never 지워요. 집다, 잡다, 좁다 all keep their ㅂ, unlike true ㅂ-irregulars such as 돕다 → 도와요.
Using 집다 for picking trash up off the ground — that is 줍다 (쓰레기를 줍다). 집다 is a controlled fingertip grasp, not retrieving something that fell.
Confusing 집다 with 들다 for heavy or large things — you 집어 a coin but you must 들어 (lift) a suitcase; 집다 only works on small graspable objects.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 집다 becomes 집을 수 있어요 ("can") and 집을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

Because it ends in ㅂ, English speakers over-apply the ㅂ-irregular and write 지워요, but 집다 keeps the ㅂ like 잡다 and 좁다, giving 집어요.

words.shortExplanation: 두다 means "to put" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 두다 (duda) means "to put". Start from the polite form 둬요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 두다. A strong first sentence is 두고 오다 ("to leave (something) behind"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 두다 also becomes 두고 싶어요 (want), 둘 수 있어요 (can), and 둘 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
set it down and come away — 핸드폰 두고 왔어요 'I left my phone behind' is daily-essential

examples.en: Put it here.
examples.note: shortest casual form; note 두다 + 어 contracts the ㅜ to 둬, not 두요

examples.en: I put my umbrella here, where did it go?
examples.note: past 뒀어요 contracts from 두었어요; said when you can't find what you set down

examples.ko: 지갑을 집에 두고 나와서 다시 들어갔어요.
examples.romanization: jigabeul jibe dugo nawaseo dasi deureogasseoyo.
examples.en: I left my wallet at home, so I went back in.
examples.note: real-situation 두고 나오다 = leave behind by accident, one of the most useful expressions for residents

words.nuance: 두다 means to place something somewhere and leave it resting there — the emphasis falls on the resulting stationary state, not the motion of setting it down. That is exactly how it splits from 놓다, its nearest synonym: 놓다 stresses the physical act of letting go onto a surface, whereas 두다 stresses leaving it (and often abandoning or keeping it) in place. It is also hugely productive as an auxiliary, -어 두다 meaning 'do something and keep it that way' (예약해 뒀어요 'I went ahead and booked it'). It's a plain native verb with no 한자. The grammar pitfall: 두다 is a ㅜ-stem, so 두 + 어요 contracts to 둬요 — English speakers often write the wrong 두요. The usage pitfall is reaching for 놓다 or 넣다 in 'I left it at home' sentences, where Korean firmly uses 두고 오다/나오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 두다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 둬요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the polite form as 두요 — the ㅜ + 어 contraction is obligatory, so it must be 둬요 (or the full 두어요). The past is likewise 뒀어요, not 두었어요 in speech.
Saying 집에 놓고 왔어요 vs 두고 왔어요 carelessly — while 놓고 오다 exists, the idiomatic 'left it behind' that residents need is 두고 오다/나오다 (핸드폰 두고 왔어요).
Using 넣다 ('put in') when you mean leave-on-a-surface — 넣다 requires an inside (가방에 넣다). To leave a package at the door it is 문 앞에 두다, not 넣다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 두다 becomes 둘 수 있어요 ("can") and 둘 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 담다 means "to put into a container" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to put into a container" in Korean is 담다 (damda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 담아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 담다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 그릇에 담다 ("to put into a bowl/dish") — then reshape the same stem into 담고 싶어요 (desire), 담을 수 있어요 (ability), and 담을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not put into a container.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to put into a container.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can put into a container.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to put into a container.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
에 marks the container; plating food into serving dishes is the core scene

examples.en: Put some in here for me.
examples.note: casual; 담아 from 담 + 아요, a regular ㅏ-friendly stem

examples.en: I added it to the cart and paid later.
examples.note: everyday e-commerce: 장바구니에 담다 = add to cart, with -어 두다 'keep it there'

examples.ko: 남은 음식은 반찬통에 담아서 냉장고에 넣으세요.
examples.romanization: nameun eumsigeun banchantonge damaseo naengjanggoe neoeuseyo.
examples.en: Put the leftovers in a container and into the fridge.
examples.note: real kitchen instruction; notice 담다 fills the container, then 넣다 inserts it into the fridge

words.nuance: 담다 specifically means to load contents into a container — a bowl, box, bag, or shopping cart — so the focus is the container getting filled. Its nearest neighbor is 넣다 ('put in / insert'), and the line is clear: 넣다 emphasizes the inserting motion of one object into an opening (열쇠를 주머니에 넣다), while 담다 emphasizes filling a vessel with stuff, especially food or groceries. That is why every Korean shopping app labels its cart button 담기, and why plating is 그릇에 담다. It also has a warm figurative life — 마음을 담다 'put your heart in,' 정성을 담다 — which 넣다 cannot carry. It's a plain native verb, conjugating regularly (담 + 아요 = 담아요). Pitfall: English speakers default to 넣다 for bagging takeout, but natives say 봉투에 담아 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 담다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 담아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 넣다 at takeout/checkout — natives say 봉투에 담아 주세요 (load it into a bag). Reserve 넣다 for inserting a single thing into a slot or opening, not filling a container.
Saying 장바구니에 넣다 for 'add to cart' — the locked phrase online is 장바구니에 담다 (the button literally reads 담기). 넣다 sounds off here.
Trying 마음을 넣다 for 'put my heart into it' — the idiom is 마음을 담다 / 마음을 담아; 넣다 is too physical and is wrong for emotion or sincerity.

words.nuance: 끼우다 means to insert or wedge something snugly into a slot or gap so that it fits tightly — a SIM card into a tray, a cable into a port, a bookmark between pages, a ring onto a finger. words.nuance: 얹다 means to rest or lay something lightly on top of a surface — an egg on rice, a hand on a shoulder, a strawberry on a cake — so it pairs almost reflexively with 위에 ('on top of'). It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The signature pitfall is spelling, because of the ㄵ cluster: when you add a vowel the sound resyllabifies to [언저], so learners wrongly write 언어요 — but the ㅈ must stay, giving 얹어요, 얹었어요, 얹어 주세요. words.nuance: 감싸다 means to wrap something around an object so as to cover, cushion, or protect it — a towel around wet hair, bubble wrap around dishes, a blanket around your shivering body — and it carries a distinct flavor of enveloping and shielding. That protective nuance is what separates it from the plain 싸다 ('wrap/pack,' as in wrapping a gift or packing a lunch): the 감- prefix (from 감다 'wind/coil around') adds the 'all the way around, enveloping' feeling. Writing the past tense as 감싸았어요 — the ㅏ + 았 contracts fully to 감쌌어요.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: casual favor; 뜯 + 어 = 뜯어, a regular stem

words.nuance: 뜯다 means to tear, rip, or peel something open by pulling it apart — a snack bag, a delivery box, an envelope, a protective film — usually destructively and irreversibly. The contrast learners must hold is with 풀다 (to untie/undo, reversibly): you 풀어 a ribbon, a knot, or shoelaces and could re-tie them, but you 뜯어 sealed tape or a glued flap and there's no going back. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The headline pitfall is conjugation: because it ends in ㄷ, English speakers assume the ㄷ-irregular and write 뜰어요 — but 뜯다 is REGULAR (like 받다, 묻다 'bury', 믿다), so the ㄷ stays put: 뜯어요, 뜯었어요. Only true ㄷ-irregulars like 듣다 → 들어요 and 걷다 → 걸어요 change ㄷ to ㄹ.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 뜯다 as a complete polite sentence.

Using 풀다 to open sealed packaging — 풀다 is for undoing something tied or knotted (리본을 풀다). Sealed tape, bags, and boxes are 뜯다.
Saying 열다 ('open') for a snack bag or a vacuum-sealed packet — 열다 fits doors and lids; tearing into sealed packaging is 봉지를 뜯다.

Grow outward from one concrete line — 옷걸이에 걸다 ("to hang on a hanger") — then reshape the same stem into 걸고 싶어요 (desire), 걸 수 있어요 (ability), and 걸 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
에 marks where it hangs; the prototypical 'hang up a coat' scene

examples.en: Hang it here.
examples.note: casual; 걸 + 어 = 걸어요 in the present, the ㄹ survives before a vowel

examples.romanization: byeoge aekja jom georeo jul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Can you hang the picture frame on the wall?

words.nuance: 걸다 means to hang something on a hook, hanger, wall, or rail — a coat, a towel, a picture frame — and it stretches to latching a lock (자물쇠를 걸다) and, in a major separate sense, placing a phone call (전화를 걸다 'to call'). To take a hung thing back down you 내리다 or 떼다. The grammar story is the heart of this word: 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular, so the stem ㄹ DROPS before endings starting with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ — giving the formal 겁니다 (not 걸읍니다) and the future 걸 거예요 — yet the ㄹ stays before a vowel, keeping the present 걸어요. There's no 한자; it's native. Pitfall: English speakers force the formal as 걸읍니다 by analogy with regular verbs, and they may miss that 'make a call' in Korean is literally 'hang a call,' 전화를 걸다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 걸다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 걸어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.nuance: 쌓다 means to stack or pile things on top of one another — dishes, boxes, books — and it has a rich figurative life for accumulating things that build up over time: 경력을 쌓다 (build a career), 경험을 쌓다, 신뢰를 쌓다, 스트레스가 쌓이다. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

꽉 (tightly) is the habitual partner; said on buses/subways about the strap

examples.note: casual; 쥐 + 어 = 쥐어요 (often spoken 줘요), and 꽉 = tightly

examples.en: If you grip the pen too hard, your hand hurts.
examples.note: everyday; 쥐다 = clench the fist around something, with conditional -면

examples.romanization: jihacheol heundeullinikka sonjabi jal jwigo gyeseyo.

words.nuance: 쥐다 means to grip or clench — to close your hand firmly around something like a handle, a pen, or a strap, and it is the verb behind 주먹을 쥐다 'to make a fist.' What sets it apart from its neighbors is the whole-hand squeezing grasp: 집다 picks a small thing up with the fingertips (you 집어 a coin), and 잡다 is the broad 'catch/hold/grab' (you 잡아 a taxi, a hand, or a chance), but 쥐다 specifically clenches the fist tight around an object. It's a native verb, no 한자, and as a ㅟ-stem it conjugates 쥐 + 어 = 쥐어요 (colloquially heard as 줘요), with the formal 쥡니다. Pitfall: English speakers blur 쥐다 and 집다, but you 쥐어 a railing and 집어 a single fry.

words.shortExplanation: 대접하다 means "to treat / to host (with food)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to treat / to host (with food)" in Korean is 대접하다 (daejeophada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 대접해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 대접하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 제가 대접할게요 ("Let me treat you (to a meal)") — then reshape the same stem into 대접하고 싶어요 (desire), 대접할 수 있어요 (ability), and 대접 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I do not treat / to host (with food).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to treat / to host (with food).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can treat / to host (with food).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to treat / to host (with food).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Let me treat you (to a meal)
usagePhrases.note: Said when you want to pay and host; warmer and more formal than 제가 살게요, which is just 'I'll pay.'

examples.en: Today it's my treat.
examples.note: The everyday host line at a restaurant when you insist on paying; -ㄹ게요 signals a warm offer.

examples.en: I invited them over and hosted them with a Korean set meal.
examples.note: 한정식으로 대접하다 = host with N; the 으로 marks what you served. Implies real hosting effort.

examples.en: You shouldn't treat a customer like this.
examples.note: Shows the wider sense: 대접하다 also = how you treat people (service quality), not only feeding them.

words.nuance: 대접하다 is Sino-Korean (待接, 待 'receive/wait on' + 接 'meet/connect'), so its core is 'receiving someone and attending to them' — usually by serving food, but also by how respectfully you treat a person. The near-synonym is 사다 ('buy a meal'): 사다 just means you pay, while 대접하다 adds hosting, effort, and respect, typically toward an elder, a guest, or a client. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (대접해요, 대접했어요), and in the negative the 하다 splits off (대접 안 해요). The very common passive 대접받다 ('be treated/hosted') is as frequent as the active. English speakers wrongly stretch 대접하다 to tiny favors ('I'll get this coffee') — for casual treats say 제가 살게요 and reserve 대접하다 for proper hosting.

words.english: to help out / to lend a hand
words.shortExplanation: 거들다 means "to help out / to lend a hand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 거들다 (geodeulda) = "to help out / to lend a hand". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 거들어요 plus one useful sentence like 내가 거들어 줄게 ("I'll give you a hand"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 거들고 싶어요 for what you want, 거들 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 거들어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to help out / to lend a hand.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can help out / to lend a hand.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to help out / to lend a hand.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Offering to pitch in on a hands-on task like carrying, cooking, or cleaning up.

examples.en: Help your mom with the dishes a bit.
examples.note: 거들다 = chip in on a task someone is already doing, rather than doing the whole thing for them.

examples.en: I'll help out moving the boxes.
examples.note: 거들어 주다 = lend a hand for someone's benefit; very natural for moving day among friends.

examples.ko: 옆에서 말로만 거들지 말고 직접 좀 해.
examples.romanization: yeopeseo malloman geodeulji malgo jikjeop jom hae.

examples.note: Here 거들다 = add words/back someone up; 말로만 거들다 = 'help only with your mouth.'

words.nuance: 거들다 means to pitch in on a task that is already in progress — you are a secondary helper, not the main doer. The dividing line vs 돕다 (the general 'help') matters: 돕다 can be the primary act of helping or even rescuing, while 거들다 is lighter, side-by-side assistance ('lend a hand'), so you'd never 거들다 a drowning person. It also has a figurative sense, 말을 거들다 ('chime in, back someone up' in conversation). Crucially it is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 거듭니다 (never 거들습니다), but the ㄹ stays everywhere else (거들어요, 거들 거예요, 거들지 마세요). English speakers also tend to use it for serious help, where 돕다 is correct.

Use 거들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 거들습니다 — because of the ㄹ-irregular the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving 거듭니다.
Treating 거들다 as full-scale help or rescue ('please help me, I'm in trouble') — for serious help use 도와주세요/돕다; 거들다 is only light, secondary assistance.
Dropping the ㄹ where it should stay — the present is 거들어요, not 거어요; the ㄹ only disappears before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ.

words.shortExplanation: 양보하다 means "to yield / to give way" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 양보하다 also becomes 양보하고 싶어요 (want), 양보할 수 있어요 (can), and 양보 못 해요 (cannot). usagePhrases.en: I do not yield / to give way.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to yield / to give way.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can yield / to give way.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to yield / to give way.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: I'll give in this time.
examples.note: Everyday concession to keep harmony; 양보하다 here = back down, not literally hand something over.

examples.en: I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
examples.note: Classic 양보 scene; 께 is the honorific 'to' for the older person, raising the recipient.

words.nuance: 양보하다 is Sino-Korean (讓步, 讓 'yield/cede' + 步 'step' — literally 'yield a step'), and it covers both physical yielding (a seat, the right of way) and figurative conceding (backing down in an argument, letting someone have their way). The key contrast is with 포기하다 ('give up entirely'): 양보하다 means you give way to another person out of courtesy and could have kept it, whereas 포기하다 means you abandon a goal altogether. Culturally the nuance is positive — yielding is considerate, not weak — which is why you see the bare noun 양보 on subway signs and in driving etiquette (양보 운전). As a 하다-verb it's regular (양보해요), splitting in the negative (양보 안 해요). Don't confuse it with 포기하다 or with simply losing.

Don't confuse it with 포기하다 or with simply losing.

words.shortExplanation: 배웅하다 means "to see someone off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to see someone off" in Korean is 배웅하다 (baeunghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 배웅해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 배웅하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 배웅 안 나와도 돼 ("You don't have to come see me off") — then reshape the same stem into 배웅하고 싶어요 (desire), 배웅할 수 있어요 (ability), and 배웅 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not see someone off.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to see someone off.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to see someone off.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: You don't have to come see me off
usagePhrases.note: Politely telling a host not to walk you out; 나오다 = come out (to the door/gate).

examples.ko: 다음에 또 와, 하면서 배웅해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: daeume tto wa, hamyeonseo baeunghae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: They saw me off saying 'come again next time.'
examples.note: A natural parting scene after visiting someone's home; -아/어 주다 frames it as kindness done for you.

examples.ko: 친구가 떠나는 게 아쉬워서 역까지 배웅했어.
examples.romanization: chinguga tteonaneun ge aswiwoseo yeokkkaji baeunghaesseo.
examples.en: I was sad my friend was leaving, so I saw them off at the station.
examples.note: 역까지 배웅하다 = accompany a departing person as far as the station; 까지 marks the distance.

examples.ko: 할머니가 문 앞까지 나와서 배웅해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga mun apkkaji nawaseo baeunghae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandma came out to the door to see me off.
examples.note: Common Korean courtesy — older hosts walk guests out; -아/어 주시다 honors the kindness done for you.

words.nuance: 배웅하다 means to accompany someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, the station, or the airport — and it is the exact counterpart of 마중하다 ('to go meet someone arriving'). Keep that pair straight: 배웅 is for departures, 마중 is for arrivals, and learners constantly swap them. It differs from a plain goodbye (인사하다/잘 가) because it implies physically going part of the way with the person, which signals warmth and respect; declining a host's offer ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself a polite gesture. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (배웅해요, 배웅했어요) and splits in the negative (배웅 안 해요); the noun 배웅 also stands alone in 배웅 나가다 and 배웅 인사.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 배웅하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 배웅해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Swapping 배웅하다 (see off / departure) with 마중하다 (meet / arrival) — they are opposites; you 배웅하다 someone leaving and 마중하다 someone arriving.
Treating 배웅하다 as a mere verbal goodbye — it implies actually walking the person out or going part of the way, so just waving and saying 잘 가 is not yet 배웅.
Forcing an English 'see off' object pattern — it's 친구를 배웅하다 (person takes 을/를); don't add an extra 'off' particle or say 친구에게 배웅하다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 배웅하다 becomes 배웅할 수 있어요 ("can") and 배웅할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: To accompany someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, the station, or the airport. It implies physically going part of the way with the person, which signals warmth and respect; declining a host's offer ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself a polite gesture.

It is the exact counterpart of 마중하다 ('to go meet someone arriving'). Keep that pair straight: 배웅 is for departures, 마중 is for arrivals, and learners constantly swap them. It differs from a plain goodbye (인사하다/잘 가) because it involves going part of the way.
As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (배웅해요, 배웅했어요) and splits in the negative (배웅 안 해요); the noun 배웅 also stands alone in 배웅 나가다 and 배웅 인사.

words.shortExplanation: 맞이하다 means "to welcome / to greet (an arrival)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 맞이하다 (majihada) = "to welcome / to greet (an arrival)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 맞이해요 plus one useful sentence like 새해를 맞이해서 ("to welcome / on the occasion of the new year"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 맞이하고 싶어요 for what you want, 맞이할 수 있어요 for what you can, 맞이 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not welcome / to greet (an arrival).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to welcome / to greet (an arrival).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can welcome / to greet (an arrival).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to welcome / to greet (an arrival).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to welcome / on the occasion of the new year
usagePhrases.note: A very common set phrase opening greetings, sales, and announcements; N을/를 맞이해서 = 'to mark N.'

examples.en: The owner came out personally to welcome the guests.
examples.note: 맞이하다 = receive/greet an arrival; warmer and more formal than a plain 만나다 ('meet').

examples.en: To welcome the new year, my family ate rice-cake soup together.
examples.note: N을/를 맞이해서 = 'on the occasion of / to welcome N'; the fixed pattern for holidays and events.

examples.en: It feels strange to be about to enter my 30s.
examples.note: 맞이하다 also marks reaching a new life stage; here it frames turning thirty as something you 'greet.'

words.nuance: 맞이하다 means to welcome or receive, and it works in two registers: greeting an arriving person (손님을 맞이하다) and greeting an occasion or new phase (새해를/명절을/30대를 맞이하다). For people it overlaps with 마중하다 ('go out to meet an arrival') but sounds warmer and more formal and doesn't require going out to fetch them; against 만나다 ('meet'), 만나다 is a neutral two-way encounter, while 맞이하다 frames you as the host receiving someone. The everyday spoken cousin is 맞다 ('손님 맞을 준비'), but 맞이하다 is the clearer dictionary form. It is a regular 하다-verb (맞이해요, 맞이했어요), splitting in the negative (맞이 안 해요). Watch the look-alike 맞추다 ('fit/match/set'), an entirely different verb.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 맞이하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 맞이해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 맞이하다 (welcome/receive) with 맞추다 (fit/match/set) — they look similar but are unrelated verbs; 시간을 맞추다 ≠ 손님을 맞이하다.
Using 만나다 where 맞이하다 is meant — 만나다 is a neutral mutual 'meet,' but greeting an arriving guest as the host is 맞이하다.
Misattaching the occasion phrase — it's 새해를 맞이해서 (object 을/를), not 새해에 맞이해서; the event you welcome takes 을/를.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 맞이하다 becomes 맞이할 수 있어요 ("can") and 맞이할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: To welcome or receive, working in two registers: greeting an arriving person (손님을 맞이하다) and greeting an occasion or new phase (새해를/명절을/30대를 맞이하다).

words.english: to break / to violate (a rule or promise)
words.shortExplanation: 어기다 means "to break / to violate (a rule or promise)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 어기다 (eogida) means "to break / to violate (a rule or promise)". Start from the polite form 어겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 어기다. A strong first sentence is 약속을 어기다 ("to break a promise"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 어기다 also becomes 어기고 싶어요 (want), 어길 수 있어요 (can), and 못 어겨요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I break / to violate (a rule or promise).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not break / to violate (a rule or promise).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to break / to violate (a rule or promise).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can break / to violate (a rule or promise).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to break / to violate (a rule or promise).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The single most common collocation; failing to keep your word to someone.

examples.en: I broke my promise again, so my friend got angry.
examples.note: 약속을 어기다 is the go-to phrase for letting someone down by not keeping your word.

examples.en: It's dangerous to cross against the signal.
examples.note: 신호를 어기다 = ignore/run a traffic signal; -고 chains it to the next action (crossing).

examples.en: If you break company rules, there are penalties.
examples.note: 규정을 어기다 = violate regulations; 불이익 = disadvantage/penalty, a common workplace word.

words.nuance: 어기다 is the standard verb for breaking something intangible that you are bound to keep — a promise (약속), a rule (규칙), a law (법), a signal (신호), or an appointment. Its direct antonym is 지키다 ('keep/abide by'), and the cleanest way to learn it is as that opposite: you either 지키다 or 어기다 a 약속. The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that English 'break' covers both rules and physical objects, but 어기다 only works for the intangible — a broken cup or phone is 깨다/부수다/고장 내다, never 어기다. It is a regular verb (어겨요, 어겼어요, 어기지 마세요), and in practice the natural negative command is 어기지 마세요 rather than 지키지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 어겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 어기다 for breaking a physical object — for cups, phones, or windows use 깨다/부수다/고장 내다; 어기다 is only for promises, rules, laws, and signals.
Mixing it up with 지키다 — they are opposites; 약속을 어기다 = break a promise, 약속을 지키다 = keep one. Saying you 어기다 a promise you meant to keep reverses your meaning.
Translating 'I broke up with my friend' as 친구를 어기다 — that's nonsense in Korean; 어기다 never takes a person as object. Use 헤어지다/절교하다 for relationships.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 어기다 becomes 어길 수 있어요 ("can") and 어길 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: The standard verb for breaking something intangible that you are bound to keep — a promise (약속), a rule (규칙), a law (법), a signal (신호), or an appointment.
Its direct antonym is 지키다 ('keep/abide by'), and the cleanest way to learn it is as that opposite: you either 지키다 or 어기다 a 약속.
It is a regular verb (어겨요, 어겼어요, 어기지 마세요), and in practice the natural negative command is 어기지 마세요 rather than 지키지 마세요.
English 'break' covers both rules and physical objects, but 어기다 only works for the intangible — a broken cup or phone is 깨다/부수다/고장 내다, never 어기다.

words.english: to keep / to protect / to abide by
words.shortExplanation: 지키다 means "to keep / to protect / to abide by" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to keep / to protect / to abide by" in Korean is 지키다 (jikida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 지켜요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 지키다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I keep / to protect / to abide by.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not keep / to protect / to abide by.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to keep / to protect / to abide by.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can keep / to protect / to abide by.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to keep / to protect / to abide by.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Be sure to keep your promise
usagePhrases.note: The opposite of 약속을 어기다; pressing someone to follow through on their word.

examples.en: I always keep my promises no matter what.
examples.note: 약속을 지키다 = keep one's word; 무조건 = unconditionally/no matter what, stressing reliability.

examples.ko: 줄 설 때 순서 좀 지켜 주세요.
examples.romanization: jul seol ttae sunseo jom jikyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please follow the order when lining up.
examples.note: 순서를 지키다 = wait your turn / keep the order; -아/어 주세요 makes it a polite request.

examples.ko: 비밀 꼭 지켜 줄 수 있어?
examples.romanization: bimil kkok jikyeo jul su isseo?
examples.en: Can you definitely keep this a secret?
examples.note: 비밀을 지키다 = keep a secret; -아/어 주다 frames it as a favor done for the speaker.

words.nuance: 지키다 is a high-frequency verb covering three linked senses: keep (a promise, a secret, a time/appointment), abide by (rules, order, manners, distance), and protect/guard (a person, a home, a country). For promises and rules it is the direct antonym of 어기다, so learning the pair together fixes both. Against 보호하다 ('protect' — more formal/abstract, e.g. 환경을 보호하다), 지키다 is the everyday, hands-on 'guard/defend' and also carries the 'keep/abide by' meanings that 보호하다 lacks. The English idiom 'keep a promise' transfers, but 'keep' in the sense of physically retaining something is 가지다/두다, not 지키다. It is a regular verb (지켜요, 지켰어요); note that the literal negative 지키지 마세요 is rarely used — to tell someone not to break a rule you say 어기지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 지키다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 지켜요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 약속을 가지다 for 'keep a promise' — the verb is 지키다; 가지다 means to physically have/hold, so 약속을 가지다 is wrong.
Overextending 'keep' — 'keep the receipt / keep it in your bag' is 가지고 있다/두다, not 지키다; 지키다 is keep-a-promise/guard, not keep-an-object.
Using 지키지 마세요 to warn against rule-breaking — that literally means 'don't keep it'; the natural phrase is 어기지 마세요 ('don't break it').

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 지키다 becomes 지킬 수 있어요 ("can") and 지킬 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.english: to show kindness / to be generous
words.shortExplanation: 베풀다 means "to show kindness / to be generous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 베풀다 (bepulda) = "to show kindness / to be generous". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 베풀어요 plus one useful sentence like 은혜를 베풀다 ("to show kindness / do someone a great favor"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 베풀고 싶어요 for what you want, 베풀 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 베풀어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I show kindness / to be generous.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not show kindness / to be generous.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to show kindness / to be generous.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can show kindness / to be generous.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to show kindness / to be generous.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to show kindness / do someone a great favor
usagePhrases.note: 은혜/호의/친절을 베풀다 = bestow a kindness; slightly formal and heartfelt in tone.

examples.en: The boss is always generous to the employees.
examples.note: 잘 베풀다 = be generous/giving; 한테 marks the people who receive the kindness.

examples.ko: 어려울 때 도움을 베풀어 주셔서 감사해요.
examples.romanization: eoryeoul ttae doumeul bepureo jusyeoseo gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: Thank you for extending help when times were hard.
examples.note: 도움을 베풀다 = extend help; more elevated and grateful-sounding than plain 도와주다.

examples.en: They say what you give to others comes back to you.
examples.note: A common saying about generosity (karma-like); 만큼 = 'as much as,' linking giving and return.

words.nuance: 베풀다 means to give generously of yourself — kindness, help, hospitality, favors, even a feast — usually from a position of being able to give, which is why it suits a boss, an elder, or a benefactor. It is warmer and more elevated than the plain 주다 ('give'), and it pairs with abstract nouns (은혜, 호의, 친절, 인심, 도움) rather than concrete objects: 선물을 베풀다 sounds odd, while 친절을 베풀다 is natural. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 베풉니다 (never 베풀습니다), but the ㄹ stays elsewhere (베풀어요, 베풀 거예요, 베풀지 마세요). The biggest English-speaker trap is reaching for it as a generic 'give'; keep it for bestowing intangible kindness.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 베풀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 베풀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 베풀습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving 베풉니다.
Using 베풀다 with concrete gifts (선물을 베풀다 sounds unnatural) — pair it with abstract kindness like 친절/호의/도움; for physical objects use 주다/선물하다.
Treating it as neutral everyday 'give' — 베풀다 implies giving generously from a higher/able position; between equals for small things, plain 주다 or 도와주다 fits better.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 베풀어 and 베풀어요 together.

conjugationTips.body: 베풀다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 베풀어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.shortExplanation: 나누다 means "to share / to divide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

A strong first sentence is 반씩 나누자 ("Let's split it in half"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. examples.ko: 피자 한 판 시켜서 친구랑 나눠 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: pija han pan sikyeoseo chingurang nanwo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ordered a pizza and shared it with a friend.
examples.note: 나눠 먹다 = share food; 친구랑 marks the partner you split and ate it with.

examples.en: We split the bill evenly among the three of us.
examples.note: Splitting the check (n빵/더치페이); 나누다 is the verb for dividing the cost, 똑같이 = evenly.

examples.ko: 그 친구랑 고민을 나누면 마음이 편해져요.
examples.romanization: geu chingurang gomineul nanumyeon maeumi pyeonhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: Sharing my worries with that friend puts me at ease.
examples.note: 고민을 나누다 = share one's worries; shows 나누다 extends to feelings and talk, not just things.

words.nuance: 나누다 holds two linked ideas: to divide (split a bill, cut into portions, partition) and to share (food, feelings, conversation). It is a regular verb (나눠요, 나눴어요); for splitting a restaurant bill specifically, 나누다 and the slang n빵 both work. Contrast with 쪼개다 ('split/crack into pieces'), which is more physical and lacks the 'share with someone' warmth.

words.english: to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)
words.shortExplanation: 모시다 means "to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)" in Korean is 모시다 (mosida). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I have to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific).

usagePhrases.en: I live with (and look after) my parents

examples.en: I took my grandfather to the hospital.
examples.note: 모시고 가다 = the honorific of 데리고 가다, used when accompanying an elder you respect.

examples.en: I'll show the guest to their seat.
examples.note: A fixed service phrase; 모시다 elevates the customer, so it sounds polished and respectful.

examples.en: I drove the boss to the airport.
examples.note: 모셔다 드리다 = escort/drive someone respectfully all the way there; standard for superiors at work.

words.nuance: 모시다 is the suppletive honorific verb for accompanying, escorting, taking, or living with someone of higher status — parents, grandparents, bosses, clients, honored guests. It replaces the plain 데리고 가다/오다 (which is reserved for peers, children, and pets) whenever respect is owed, much as 잡수시다 replaces 먹다 or 주무시다 replaces 자다. You'll hear it constantly in two settings: service speech (손님을 모시겠습니다, 자리로 모시다) and family talk (부모님을 모시고 살다). It also has a ritual sense — 제사를 모시다 / 조상을 모시다 (to hold ancestral rites). It is a regular verb (모셔요, 모셨어요). The core pitfall for English speakers is status-blindness: using 데리고 가다 for an elder sounds rude, while using 모시다 for a friend or pet sounds absurdly over-deferential.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 모시다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 모셔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데리고 가다 for an elder, boss, or client — it sounds rude toward someone you should honor; switch to 모시고 가다.
Using 모시다 for friends, children, or pets — it is only for people you must respect; for equals or those below you use 데리다/데리고 가다.
Forgetting it's already honorific — you don't add another honorific to the object's verb redundantly; 모시고 가다 alone correctly raises the person, so 모시고 가시다 about your own action is off.

words.english: to recommend / to offer / to urge
words.shortExplanation: 권하다 means "to recommend / to offer / to urge" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 권하다 (gwonhada) = "to recommend / to offer / to urge". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 권해요 plus one useful sentence like 이거 한번 권해 드려요 ("I'd recommend trying this"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 권하고 싶어요 for what you want, 권할 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 권해요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.en: I recommend / to offer / to urge.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not recommend / to offer / to urge.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to recommend / to offer / to urge.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can recommend / to offer / to urge.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to recommend / to offer / to urge.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Suggesting a dish or product politely; -아/어 드리다 raises the act for the listener.

examples.en: The owner recommended this menu item to me.
examples.note: 권하다 = recommend/suggest, a touch more personal and formal than 추천하다, often said face-to-face.

examples.ko: 어른이 술을 권하시면 두 손으로 받아요.
examples.romanization: eoreuni sureul gwonhasimyeon du soneuro badayo.
examples.en: When an elder offers you a drink, receive it with both hands.
examples.note: Key etiquette: 두 손으로 받다 = receive with both hands; essential at any 회식 or family gathering.

examples.en: For your health, I'd like to urge you to quit smoking.
examples.note: 권하다 also = urge/advise a course of action; -고 싶다 softens it to a caring wish.

words.nuance: 권하다 is Sino-Korean (勸, 'urge/encourage') + 하다, and it spans a spectrum: recommending (a dish, a book), offering (food, a drink, a seat to someone), and urging/advising (a course of action like 금연). Against the neutral 추천하다 ('recommend' — often a product, a place, in writing or impersonally), 권하다 is more face-to-face and personal, and it carries the extra 'offer/press upon someone' meaning that 추천하다 lacks. In daily life its most culturally loaded use is 술을 권하다 — offering and sometimes insistently pressing drinks at a 회식 — where graceful refusal is its own social skill. It is a regular 하다-verb (권해요, 권했어요), and the negative can split (권 안 해요). The pitfall: don't assume 권하다 is always gentle; depending on context it can mean actively pushing something on someone.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 권하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 권해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Assuming 권하다 always means a soft suggestion — 술을 권하다 can mean actively pressing someone to drink, so read the social context before translating it as 'recommend.'
Swapping it for 추천하다 in every case — for an impersonal/written recommendation (a product, a tourist spot) 추천하다 fits; 권하다 leans personal and adds the 'offer/urge upon someone' sense.
Mishandling the recipient — it's 저한테 메뉴를 권하다 (person takes 한테/에게, thing takes 을/를); don't mark the person with 을/를.

words.shortExplanation: 사양하다 means "to politely decline" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 사양하다 (sayanghada) means "to politely decline". Start from the polite form 사양해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 사양하다. A strong first sentence is 사양하지 말고 드세요 ("Don't hold back, please eat"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 사양하다 also becomes 사양하고 싶어요 (want), 사양할 수 있어요 (can), and 사양 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
A host urging a guest not to be over-polite/decline — extremely common at the table.

examples.en: I'll accept the thought. I'll decline the gift.
examples.note: A polite gift refusal; 마음만 받다 = 'I'll just take the sentiment,' a standard softener before declining.

examples.ko: 한 잔 더 하라는 걸 정중히 사양했어요.
examples.romanization: han jan deo haraneun geol jeongjunghi sayanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: I politely declined another drink.
examples.note: 정중히 사양하다 = decline courteously; the go-to phrase for refusing drinks at 회식 gracefully.

examples.en: I'd rather pass on gatherings like this.
examples.note: 사양하다 softens a refusal of an invitation/event so it doesn't land like a flat rejection.

words.nuance: 사양하다 is Sino-Korean (辭讓, 辭 'decline/take leave' + 讓 'yield') and means to decline an offer — food, a drink, a gift, an invitation — courteously and somewhat formally. The sharp contrast is with 거절하다 ('reject/refuse'): 거절하다 is firm and can sound cold or final (거절당하다 = 'be rejected'), while 사양하다 is the soft, face-saving 'I'll pass, thank you,' typically for hospitality you appreciate but don't want to accept. Because Korean politeness often scripts a first, modest refusal, the host's fixed line 사양하지 말고 드세요 ('don't be shy, eat up') is something you'll hear constantly, and knowing how to 사양하다 gracefully is genuinely useful etiquette. It is a regular 하다-verb (사양해요, 사양했어요), splitting in the negative (사양 안 해요). Pitfall: using 거절하다 for a kind meal or gift sounds harsh.

Confusing it with 양보하다 — 사양하다 (辭讓) = decline an offer for yourself, while 양보하다 (讓步) = yield something to someone else; they share 讓 but aren't interchangeable.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to work (be on duty).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to work (be on duty).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
근무하다 takes the workplace with 에서 (the place where activity happens), never 에: 회사에서 근무해요.

examples.en: I work at a bank.
examples.note: Simplest self-introduction frame: 〈place〉에서 근무해요 — polished and resume-friendly.

examples.en: From what time to what time do you work?
examples.note: 부터…까지 frames a span; 근무하다 sounds more professional than 일하다 when asking a colleague's hours.

examples.ko: 다음 달부터 다른 지점에서 근무하게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: daeum dalbuteo dareun jijeomeseo geunmuhage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Starting next month I'll be working at a different branch.
examples.note: -게 됐어요 signals the transfer was decided by circumstance, not your own choice — humble and natural.

words.nuance: 근무하다 is the workplace word for 'to work / be on duty', focused on your employment and shift rather than the physical act of doing tasks. The hanja is 勤務 (勤 'diligence/service' + 務 'duty'), so it literally means 'serve one's duty' — that institutional flavor is why it dominates contracts, ID badges, and self-introductions. The sharp contrast is with 일하다: 일하다 is the everyday, hands-on 'do work' you say to friends, while 근무하다 is about being formally posted somewhere, so a soldier, a 9-to-5 office worker, or a clerk 근무한다 at a location. Habitual collocations are all fixed nouns: 주 5일 근무, 재택근무, 야간 근무, 근무 시간 (working hours), 근무 환경 (work environment). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the workplace takes 에서 (location of an activity), so it is 회사에서 근무해요, never 회사에 근무해요 or 회사를 근무해요. Also do not reach for 근무하다 to describe doing a single chore — that is 하다 or 일하다.

usagePhrases.note: The thing you are responsible for takes the object particle 을/를: 프로젝트를 담당해요.

examples.en: I'm in charge of this task.
examples.note: Bare, clear role statement; 을/를 on the task, 제가 to spotlight that it's you.

examples.en: Who is in charge of this matter?
examples.note: 이 건 = 'this case/matter', standard office wording for routing a question to the right person.

examples.note: -고 있습니다 = formal ongoing duty; right register for an email or a meeting.

words.nuance: 담당하다 means to officially be responsible for a specific task, client, or functional area at work. The hanja 擔當 is 擔 'to shoulder/carry' + 當 'to take on', so it literally pictures shouldering an assigned load — which is why it feels institutional and ongoing rather than a one-time effort. Compare it with its near-synonym 맡다: 맡다 is the warm, personal, often volunteered 'I'll take this on', whereas 담당하다 is the cool, official 'this is formally assigned to me', the version you put on a name card or org chart. The single most useful spin-off is the noun 담당자 ('the person in charge'), heard everywhere in offices and call centers (담당자분께 전달하겠습니다). Natural collocations: 업무를 담당하다, 마케팅을 담당하다, 담당 부서, 담당 구역. The key English-speaker pitfall is the particle — English 'in charge OF' tempts learners to use 에, but Korean treats the responsibility as a direct object, so it is 마케팅을 담당해요, never 마케팅에 담당해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 담당하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 담당해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Wrong particle: the thing you handle is a direct object — 마케팅을 담당해요, not 마케팅에 담당해요. English 'in charge of' misleads you toward 에.
Don't substitute 담당하다 for a casual 'I'll do it' among friends; it sounds like a formal job assignment. For volunteering warmly, 맡다 (제가 맡을게요) fits better.

words.shortExplanation: 맡다 means "to take charge of (be assigned)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 맡다 (matda) means "to take charge of (be assigned)". Start from the polite form 맡아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 맡다. A strong first sentence is 역할을 맡다 ("to take on a role"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 맡다 also becomes 맡고 싶어요 (want), 맡을 수 있어요 (can), and 맡을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.
