usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

역할(役割) 'role'; 맡다 collocates with roles, parts, and duties you personally accept.

examples.en: I'll take that on.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 = a willing commitment to the listener; sounds proactive and reliable.

examples.en: Assistant Manager Kim took charge of this event.
examples.note: Past 맡았어요 (stem ㅌ + 아) reports who got the assignment — note it is NOT 마랐어요.

examples.en: The department head entrusted me with that project.
examples.note: 맡기다 = causative 'hand over/entrust'; 저한테 marks the receiver — contrast with plain 맡다.

words.nuance: 맡다 is the everyday native-Korean verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part, even a saved seat. It feels more personal and active than the Sino-Korean 담당하다: where 담당하다 is the official 'assigned to me' on an org chart, 맡다 is the warm, often-volunteered 'I'll take this', so 제가 맡을게요 sounds team-friendly and proactive in a meeting. Crucial spelling and conjugation point: the stem ends in ㅌ, and it is a plain regular verb, NOT a ㄷ-irregular — so it stays 맡아요 / 맡았어요 / 맡을게요, and learners who mistakenly 'soften' the ㅌ to ㄹ (마라요, 마랐어요) are simply wrong. Its causative partner 맡기다 ('to entrust/hand over') flips the direction: you 맡다 a job yourself, but you 맡기다 it to someone else (저한테 맡기세요). Habitual collocations: 역할을 맡다, 책임을 맡다, 업무를 맡다, 자리를 맡다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 맡다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 맡아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Not a ㄷ-irregular: the stem is 맡- (ㅌ), so it conjugates 맡아요 / 맡았어요, never 마라요 / 마랐어요. Don't soften the ㅌ.
Don't confuse 맡다 (you take the task on) with its causative 맡기다 (you hand the task to someone else): 제가 맡을게요 vs. 저한테 맡기세요 are opposite directions.

words.shortExplanation: 보고하다 means "to report" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to report" in Korean is 보고하다 (bogohada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 보고해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 보고하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 팀장님께 보고하다 ("to report to the team leader") — then reshape the same stem into 보고하고 싶어요 (desire), 보고할 수 있어요 (ability), and 보고할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to report to the team leader
usagePhrases.note: The recipient (a superior) takes the honorific dative 께; 께 is the polite form of 에게/한테.

examples.en: I reported the results.
examples.note: Base pattern: 〈content〉을/를 보고하다. Clean and factual.

examples.en: If a problem comes up, please report it right away.
examples.note: 바로 = immediately; a very common instruction from a manager to staff.

examples.en: I'll report this directly to the manager myself.
examples.note: 보고드리겠습니다 = humble 보고드리다 + formal will; 께 marks the senior recipient.

words.nuance: 보고하다 is the formal verb for reporting information up a hierarchy — to a boss, a client, or headquarters. The hanja 報告 is 報 'to inform/requite' + 告 'to tell/announce', a doubled 'make known' that signals officialness. In Korea's hierarchy-conscious workplaces, 보고 (the report itself) is a weighty ritual, which is why you very often switch to the humble 보고드리다 when the listener outranks you. Grammar to nail: the recipient takes 께/에게(한테) and the content takes 을/를 (팀장님께 결과를 보고했어요). The decisive synonym contrast is with 말하다 / 알려주다: those are neutral 'tell / let know' for peers and friends, whereas 보고하다 frames the act as an upward, accountable report. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold — English 'report' covers casual gossip ('did you hear?'), but 보고하다 does NOT, so telling a friend news is 말하다/알려주다, not 보고하다; and learners forget to elevate to 보고드리다 when reporting to a senior.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보고하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보고해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 보고하다 for chatting with a friend or sharing gossip — English 'report/tell' is broader. For peers use 말하다 or 알려주다; 보고하다 is an official upward report.
When reporting to a superior, switch to the humble 보고드리다: 부장님께 보고드릴게요, not 부장님께 보고할게요 — plain 보고하다 to a senior can feel flat or even presumptuous.

words.shortExplanation: 진행하다 means "to proceed (carry out)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 진행하다 (jinhaenghada) = "to proceed (carry out)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 진행해요 plus one useful sentence like 계획대로 진행하다 ("to proceed as planned"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 진행하고 싶어요 for what you want, 진행할 수 있어요 for what you can, 진행할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
대로 = 'in accordance with'; 계획대로 / 예정대로 진행하다 are set business phrases.

examples.en: For now I'll proceed as planned.
examples.note: 일단 = 'for now / first off'; -(으)ㄹ게요 commits you to moving it forward.

examples.en: How far along is it now?
examples.note: Uses the passive 진행되다 — literally 'up to where has it progressed?', a standard status check.

examples.ko: 다음 단계를 진행하기 전에 한번 확인해 주세요.
examples.romanization: daeum dangyereul jinhaenghagi jeone hanbeon hwaginhae juseyo.
examples.en: Please double-check before we proceed to the next step.
examples.note: 단계 = stage; -기 전에 = 'before doing'. Active 진행하다 = you carry it forward.

words.nuance: 진행하다 means to push a task, process, project, or event forward — 'carry out / proceed with' — and it saturates Korean office life. The hanja 進行 is 進 'advance' + 行 'go/move', literally 'advance-and-go', a forward motion that fits a multi-step process. The single most important thing to master is the active/passive pair: active 진행하다 means YOU drive it (제가 진행할게요 'I'll move it forward'), while passive 진행되다 means it is underway by itself (잘 진행되고 있어요 'it's going well') — mixing these up is the classic learner error. A useful contrast is with 마치다/끝내다 (to finish): 진행하다 is about the ongoing middle of a process with stages, not the endpoint, so don't use it for completing a single discrete action. With events it gains a second sense, 'to host/run', giving 진행자 (MC). Habitual collocations: 계획대로 진행하다, 예정대로 진행되다, 진행 상황, 절차를 진행하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 진행하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 진행해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Keep active 진행하다 (you carry it out) separate from passive 진행되다 (it proceeds on its own): say 제가 진행할게요 for your action, 잘 진행되고 있어요 for the process. Learners wrongly say 잘 진행하고 있어요 to mean 'it's going well'.
Don't use 진행하다 for finishing one small action — it implies an ongoing, staged process. To complete a discrete task use 끝내다/마치다.

words.shortExplanation: 마치다 means "to finish (conclude)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 마치다 (machida) means "to finish (conclude)". Start from the polite form 마쳐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 마치다. A strong first sentence is 업무를 마치다 ("to finish one's work/duties"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 마치다 also becomes 마치고 싶어요 (want), 마칠 수 있어요 (can), and 마칠 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Transitive: the thing you conclude takes 을/를 — 업무를 / 일을 / 수업을 마치다.

examples.en: I finished all my work today.
examples.note: 다 = 'all'; past 마쳤어요 (ㅊ + ㅕ). Slightly formal, good for work or study.

examples.en: I'll take questions after I finish the presentation.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 뒤에 = 'after doing'; classic presentation phrasing.

examples.en: I successfully finished this quarter's report.
examples.note: 무사히 + 마치다 = brought a big task to a clean close; formal -습니다 for a report-out.

words.nuance: 마치다 means to finish or conclude something properly — your workday, a meeting, a report, a course of study. It is transitive (it takes an object: 일을 마치다) and carries a slightly formal, ceremonial 'bring to a proper close' flavor, which is exactly why public announcements use 마치겠습니다. Two contrasts a learner must hold apart. First, against 끝내다: both are transitive 'finish it', but 마치다 is more bookish and dignified (a meeting, a ceremony, a semester), while 끝내다 is the casual, hands-on 'get it done' of daily office chatter. Second, and the real pitfall, against 끝나다: 끝나다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it ends by itself') and takes no object, so 'the work ended' is 일이 끝났어요, never 일을 마쳤어요 unless you are the one actively concluding it. Conjugation: the stem 마치- + 어 contracts to 마쳐요 / 마쳤어요. Habitual collocations: 일을 마치다, 회의를 마치다, 학업을 마치다, 무사히 마치다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 마치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 마쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
마치다 is transitive and needs an object (일을 마치다). For 'it ended on its own' use the intransitive 끝나다 — 수업이 끝났어요, not 수업을 마쳤어요 (unless you yourself concluded it).
Don't reach for 마치다 in very casual coworker talk; it sounds formal/ceremonial. For 'let me just wrap this up', 끝내다 (이것만 끝내고 갈게요) is more natural.

First, against 끝내다: both are transitive 'finish it', but 마치다 is more bookish and dignified (a meeting, a ceremony, a semester), while 끝내다 is the casual, hands-on 'get it done' of daily office chatter. words.shortExplanation: 끝내다 means "to finish (wrap up)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to finish (wrap up)" in Korean is 끝내다 (kkeutnaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 끝내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 끝내다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 일을 끝내다 ("to get the work done") — then reshape the same stem into 끝내고 싶어요 (desire), 끝낼 수 있어요 (ability), and 끝낼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Transitive: 일을 / 숙제를 / 회의를 끝내다 — you actively bring it to an end.

examples.en: Let me just finish this and then go.
examples.note: 만 = 'just this'; -고 갈게요 chains 'finish, then leave'. Very natural daily phrase.

examples.en: I couldn't finish all the work.
examples.note: 못 + 끝내다 = 'couldn't manage to finish'; 다 = all. Past is 끝냈어요 (stem 끝내-).

examples.en: Can we wrap up the meeting within 30 minutes?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요 = 'do you think we can ~?'; practical scheduling question.

words.nuance: 끝내다 is the active, everyday verb for finishing or wrapping something up — you make it end. It is the transitive causative of 끝나다: the pair 끝내다 / 끝나다 is the cleanest minimal contrast in the whole 'finish' family, and getting it right is the core skill here. 끝내다 takes an object and means YOU end it (숙제를 끝냈어요 'I finished the homework'); 끝나다 is intransitive and means it ends by itself (수업이 끝났어요 'class ended'). Against 마치다, 끝내다 is the more casual, task-focused choice — perfect for daily office lines like 이것만 끝내고 갈게요 — whereas 마치다 is bookish and ceremonial. (Note 끝내다 also has a slang sense: 끝내주다 / 끝내준다 = 'awesome', literally 'it finishes you off'.) Conjugation is easy and regular: stem 끝내- gives past 끝냈어요. Habitual collocations: 일을 끝내다, 숙제를 끝내다, 빨리 끝내다, 오늘 안에 끝내다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끝내다 as a complete polite sentence.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끝내다 becomes 끝낼 수 있어요 ("can") and 끝낼 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 검토하다 means "to review (examine)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 검토하다 (geomtohada) = "to review (examine)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 검토해요 plus one useful sentence like 서류를 검토하다 ("to review documents"). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Could you review this proposal?
examples.note: -아/어 주시겠어요 = polite request; 좀 softens it. Standard for asking a colleague to check something.

examples.en: We're reviewing it internally.
examples.note: 검토 중 = 'under review'; a polished way to say 'no decision yet' without refusing.

words.nuance: 검토하다 means to review or examine something carefully — documents, proposals, plans, contracts — usually before approving or deciding. The hanja 檢討 is 檢 'inspect/examine' + 討 'investigate/discuss', a deliberate double 'scrutinize', which is why it sounds polished and weighty. The crucial synonym contrast is with 확인하다: 확인하다 is a quick 'check/confirm' a fact, a time, or a number, while 검토하다 implies sustained, careful inspection with judgment to follow — so confirming a meeting time is 확인하다, never 검토하다. words.shortExplanation: 야근하다 means "to work overtime (work late)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to work overtime (work late).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to work overtime (work late).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
야근 + 수당 'allowance'; the money you get for staying late — a frequent gripe topic.

examples.en: I'm working late again today.
examples.note: 오늘도 'again today' nails the weary office mood; present tense for a recurring reality.

examples.ko: 마감 때문에 이번 주 내내 야근했어요.
examples.romanization: magam ttaemune ibeon ju naenae yageunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I worked late all week because of the deadline.
examples.note: 때문에 = 'because of'; 내내 = 'the whole time/all through'. 마감 = deadline.

examples.note: -지 말고 = 'don't ~ but rather'; 들어가다 here = 'go home'. A caring thing to say to a coworker.

words.nuance: 야근하다 is the verb every Korean office worker knows: to stay and work into the evening, past regular hours. The hanja 夜勤 is 夜 'night' + 勤 'work/service' (the same 勤 as in 근무), literally 'night-work'. Its form is neutral, but in real use it almost always carries a tired, faintly complaining tone, because overtime is a charged feature of Korean work culture; the noun 야근 anchors a whole vocabulary of grievance — 야근 수당 (OT pay), 야근 잦아요 (lots of overtime), 칼퇴 (leaving right on time, the dream). The sharp boundary is against 야간근무: 야근 is staying late on an otherwise daytime job, whereas 야간근무 is a scheduled night shift (nurses, security, factory lines). Don't equate it with English 'overtime' as a contractual category either — that abstract concept is 초과근무 / 시간 외 근무. And for an all-nighter it escalates to 밤샘. Habitual collocations: 야근하다, 야근 수당, 야근이 잦다, 야근 안 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 야근하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 야근해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
야근하다 is not the contract concept 'overtime' — that's 초과근무 / 시간 외 근무. 야근 specifically = staying and working into the evening on a day job.
Don't use 야근하다 for a planned night shift; that's 야간근무. A nurse on rotation works 야간근무, not 야근.

words.shortExplanation: 퇴사하다 means "to resign (quit a job)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to resign (quit a job)" in Korean is 퇴사하다 (toesahada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 퇴사해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 퇴사하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 회사를 퇴사하다 ("to leave the company") — then reshape the same stem into 퇴사하고 싶어요 (desire), 퇴사할 수 있어요 (ability), and 퇴사할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not resign (quit a job).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to resign (quit a job).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to resign (quit a job).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Often just 퇴사하다 alone; if stated, the company can take 를 or appear with 에서.

examples.en: I'm leaving the company next month.
examples.note: Present tense for a fixed plan; 저 fronts 'as for me'. The standard way to announce it.

examples.en: Before resigning I have to hand over my work.
examples.note: -기 전에 = 'before doing'; 인수인계 is the obligatory pre-departure step.

examples.en: I heard Assistant Manager Kim resigned.
examples.note: -셨대요 = honorific 시 + reported -대요 'I heard that ~'; classic office grapevine.

words.nuance: 퇴사하다 means to leave your company — to resign or quit for good. The hanja 退社 is 退 'retreat/withdraw' + 社 'company', literally 'withdraw from the company', and it is the exact mirror of 입사하다 (入社, 'enter the company'), so the two are best memorized as a set. 퇴사 is a culturally loaded, much-discussed topic among younger Korean workers, traveling with 이직 (移職, changing jobs), 인수인계 (handover), and 퇴사 통보 (notice of resignation). The contrast with near-synonym 그만두다 ('quit/stop') is one of register: 그만두다 is plainer and broader (you can 그만두다 anything — a job, a hobby, smoking), while 퇴사하다 is the clean, specific corporate term for leaving employment. The big English-speaker pitfall is confusing 퇴사하다 with 퇴근하다: they look and sound alike but 퇴사하다 ENDS your employment, while 퇴근하다 just means going home at the end of a workday (its opposite is 출근하다). Habitual collocations: 퇴사하다, 퇴사 통보, 퇴사 사유, 퇴사 후.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 퇴사하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 퇴사해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't mix up 퇴사하다 (quit the company permanently) with 퇴근하다 (leave the office for the day). One ends your job; the other ends today's shift — 오늘 일찍 퇴근했어요 ≠ 퇴사했어요.
퇴사하다 vs 입사하다 direction: 퇴사(退) is leaving, 입사(入) is joining. Don't reverse them — 작년에 퇴사했어요 means you LEFT last year, not started.

words.shortExplanation: 입사하다 means "to join a company" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 입사하다 (ipsahada) = "to join a company". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 입사해요 plus one useful sentence like 회사에 입사하다 ("to join a company"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not join a company.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to join a company.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to join a company.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The company takes 에 (the destination you enter), NOT 을/를: 이 회사에 입사했어요.

examples.en: I joined this company last year.
examples.note: Note 에 on 회사 (destination), not 를. The base 'I joined ~' frame.

examples.en: When did you join the company?
examples.note: Honorific 하셨어요 to a coworker; a friendly, common get-to-know-you question.

examples.ko: 원하던 회사에 입사하게 돼서 정말 기뻐요.
examples.romanization: wonhadeon hoesae ipsahage dwaeseo jeongmal gippeoyo.
examples.en: I'm so happy I got into the company I wanted.
examples.note: 원하던 = 'that I'd wanted'; -게 돼서 = 'because it came to be that' — humble, gladdened tone.

words.nuance: 입사하다 means to join a company as an employee — your starting point in a job, the exact mirror image of 퇴사하다 (to leave). The hanja 入社 is 入 'enter' + 社 'company', literally 'enter the company', and because 入 is a verb of entering, the company you join takes the destination particle 에 (이 회사에 입사하다) — this is the number-one English-speaker pitfall, since English 'join the company' tempts you toward the object 를 (회사를 입사하다 is wrong). It anchors a cluster of new-employee vocabulary you'll hear daily: 신입 (new hire), 입사 동기 (people who joined the same year, a real social bond), 입사 지원 (job application), 입사 시험/면접 (entrance exam/interview). A subtle synonym note: 입사하다 specifically means entering a COMPANY, whereas 취직하다/취업하다 means 'to get employed / land a job' more generally, and 입학하다 (入學) is the parallel word for entering a SCHOOL — don't cross the 社/學 wires. Best learned paired with 퇴사하다 so you can narrate both ends of a job.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 입사하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 입사해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
The company takes 에 (destination), not 을/를: 회사에 입사했어요, never 회사를 입사했어요. English 'join the company' wrongly pulls you to a direct object.
Don't confuse 입사하다 (enter a company, 入社) with 입학하다 (enter a school, 入學). Starting university is 대학교에 입학했어요, not 입사했어요.

words.shortExplanation: 회의하다 means "to have a meeting" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 회의하다 (hoeuihada) means "to have a meeting". Start from the polite form 회의해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 회의하다. A strong first sentence is 팀이랑 회의하다 ("to have a meeting with the team"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to have a meeting.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to have a meeting.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to have a meeting with the team
usagePhrases.note: The people you meet with take (이)랑 / 와 / 과: 팀이랑 / 팀과 회의해요.

examples.en: I have a meeting with my team this afternoon.
examples.note: (이)랑 marks who you meet with; casual-polite 회의해요. Simple schedule statement.

examples.en: I'm in a meeting now, so I'll call later.
examples.note: 회의 중이라 = 'because I'm in a meeting'; uses the noun 회의, not the verb. Texted constantly.

examples.ko: 다 같이 모여서 한번 회의해 봅시다.
examples.romanization: da gachi moyeoseo hanbeon hoeuihae bopsida.
examples.en: Let's all get together and have a meeting.

words.nuance: 회의하다 means to hold or have a meeting — the daily texture of office life. The hanja 會議 is 會 'gather/assemble' + 議 'discuss/deliberate', literally 'gather-and-deliberate', which captures that it implies a real, purposeful, usually scheduled discussion rather than idle talk. In practice the bare noun 회의 surfaces even more than the verb: 회의 중이에요 (in a meeting), 회의 잡다 (set a meeting), 회의실 (meeting room), 회의록 (meeting minutes). Grammar to nail: co-participants take (이)랑/와/과 (팀이랑 회의해요), and the topic discussed often rides along with -에 대해(서) (그 문제에 대해 회의했어요). The decisive synonym contrast is with 얘기하다/이야기하다: those mean simply 'talk/chat', right for a two-minute hallway exchange, whereas 회의하다 frames it as a formal sit-down — so don't say 회의하다 for a quick chat (use 잠깐 얘기하다). Compare also 상의하다/논의하다 (to consult/deliberate on a matter), which stress the discussing more than the gathering.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 회의하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 회의해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For a casual quick chat, use 얘기하다 / 이야기하다 — 회의하다 implies a real, scheduled meeting, not a two-minute hallway talk (잠깐 얘기 좀 해요, not 잠깐 회의해요).
Co-participant particle: people you meet with take (이)랑 / 와 / 과, not 을/를 — 팀이랑 회의해요, not 팀을 회의해요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 회의하다 becomes 회의할 수 있어요 ("can") and 회의할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 회의하다 means to hold or have a meeting — the daily texture of office life. It implies a real, purposeful, usually scheduled discussion rather than idle talk. In practice the bare noun 회의 surfaces even more than the verb: 회의 중이에요 (in a meeting), 회의 잡다 (set a meeting), 회의실 (meeting room), 회의록 (meeting minutes). The hanja 會議 is 會 'gather/assemble' + 議 'discuss/deliberate', literally 'gather-and-deliberate', which captures that it implies a real, purposeful, usually scheduled discussion.

words.shortExplanation: 토라지다 means "to sulk (and turn away)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to sulk (and turn away)" in Korean is 토라지다 (torajida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 토라져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 토라지다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 여자친구가 또 토라졌어요. usagePhrases.en: My girlfriend got in a huff again.
usagePhrases.note: Classic relationship word — a partner gets quietly upset and goes cold.

examples.ko: 내가 농담한 걸 갖고 하루 종일 토라져 있었어.
examples.romanization: naega nongdamhan geol gatgo haru jongil torajyeo isseosseo.
examples.en: She sulked all day over a joke I made.
examples.note: 토라져 있다 = staying in the sulking state for a stretch of time.

examples.ko: 뭐 때문에 토라진 거야? 말을 해 줘야 알지.
examples.romanization: mwo ttaemune torajin geoya? mareul hae jwoya alji.
examples.en: What are you sulking about? You have to tell me so I know.
examples.note: A very natural thing to say to a sulking partner; 토라진 거야 reads the sulk as ongoing.

examples.ko: 선물 받고 금방 기분이 풀려서 더 이상 안 토라졌어요.
examples.romanization: seonmul batgo geumbang gibuni pullyeoseo deo isang an torajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: She got a gift and cheered up, so she stopped sulking.
examples.note: 기분이 풀리다 = the mood un-knots; the natural exit from 토라지다.

words.nuance: 토라지다 is the specific sulk where someone feels hurt or slighted and pointedly turns cold — going quiet, looking away, giving you the silent treatment. The dividing line versus its near-synonym 삐치다 matters: 삐치다 just names the hurt-and-pouty feeling, while 토라지다 foregrounds the visible turning-away and icy withdrawal, so it sounds a touch more serious and dramatic (단단히 토라지다 = sulk hard). It is far softer and more passive than 화내다, where the person openly shouts; a person who 토라지다 withdraws rather than explodes. Register is casual and affectionate, used overwhelmingly of couples, close friends, and children — you would not say a CEO 토라졌다 in a formal report. It collocates with 등을 돌리다, 입을 삐죽 내밀다, and the recovery phrase 기분이 풀리다. English-speaker pitfall: do not reach for 'angry' and translate it as 화나다 — that loses the whole 'silent, turned-away' core; also resist adding an object with 을/를, because 토라지다 is intransitive (you 토라지다 at a state, you don't 토라지다 something).

words.english: to get in a huff (and sulk)
words.shortExplanation: 삐치다 means "to get in a huff (and sulk)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: I get in a huff (and sulk).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not get in a huff (and sulk).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I have to get in a huff (and sulk).

examples.en: He got in a huff because I replied late.
examples.note: Texting culture — late replies genuinely make people 삐치다; -다고 gives the reason.

examples.ko: 삐친 거 아니야? 목소리가 왜 그래?
examples.romanization: ppichin geo aniya? moksoriga wae geurae?

examples.en: He gets in a huff easily and gets over it just as fast.
examples.note: Describing a personality that sulks quickly but holds no grudge; 풀리다 = the huff dissolves.

words.nuance: 삐치다 (very commonly spoken and spelled 삐지다) is the everyday word for getting into a sulky huff because your feelings were nicked — someone forgot you, replied late, left you out, or made a joke at your expense. The boundary versus 토라지다 is one of emphasis: 삐치다 spotlights the hurt-and-pouty internal state and is lighter, cuter, more childish, whereas 토라지다 adds the cold turning-away. It is far gentler than 화내다 (real anger) and is used constantly and affectionately among friends, siblings, and couples, often half-joking ('너 삐쳤어?'). It collocates with 금방 (삐쳤다 풀렸다 = huffed then got over it), the recovery verb 풀리다/풀어 주다, and 삐친 척 (pretend-sulking). English-speaker pitfall: learners overreach and translate any 'annoyed/angry' as 삐치다 — but 삐치다 is specifically the wounded-feelings pout, not general irritation (that's 짜증나다) and not shouting (that's 화내다). Also note it is intransitive: 나한테 삐쳤어, not 나를 삐쳤어.

Use 삐쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
삐지다 is the very common spoken variant; both are widely understood, but 삐치다 is the standard dictionary form, so prefer it in writing.
It's intransitive — say 친구가 삐쳤어요 / 나한테 삐쳤어요, never 친구를 삐쳤어요.
Past tense is 삐쳤어요 (삐치 + 었 → 삐쳐 + ㅆ). Don't write it as 삐쳣어요 or 삐쳤써요.

words.shortExplanation: 골내다 means "to get sulky-angry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 골내다 (gollaeda) means "to get sulky-angry". Start from the polite form 골내요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 골내다. A strong first sentence is 그만 좀 골내! ("Quit being sulky and grumpy!"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 골내다 also becomes 골내고 싶어요 (want), 골낼 수 있어요 (can), and 골낼 수 없어요 (cannot). Useful for choices and plans.

Requirement or obligation.
Reads as 'stop brooding in a sour mood'. Casual command.

examples.en: He's off by himself sulking because he lost the game.
examples.note: 골내다 = a moody, irritated sulk; pairs with 혼자 (alone).

examples.ko: 동생이 골낸 표정으로 방에 들어가 버렸어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi golnaen pyojeongeuro bange deureoga beoryeosseoyo.
examples.en: My younger sibling went into the room with a grumpy face.
examples.note: 골낸 표정 = a sullen, sulky expression; -아/어 버리다 adds the 'stormed off' feel.

examples.ko: 사소한 일로 골내지 말고 그냥 얘기해.
examples.romanization: sasohan illo golnaeji malgo geunyang yaegihae.
examples.en: Don't get all grumpy over a small thing — just talk it out.
examples.note: Encouraging communication instead of brooding.

words.nuance: 골내다 blends sulking with irritation — a grumpy, moody upset where someone broods, gives off a sour mood, and goes half-pouting, half-cross. On the spectrum it sits between 삐치다 (lighter, just hurt feelings) and 화내다 (open anger): grumpier and more visibly cross than 삐치다, but not the explosive shouting of 화내다. The word is built like 화내다: the noun 골 here means 'temper/sour mood' (as in 골이 났다 / 골이 잔뜩 났다), and 내다 means 'to put out/express', so 골내다 literally = 'to put out a sour temper'. Its intransitive partner is 골나다 ('to become grumpy'), exactly mirroring 화내다 / 화나다. It collocates with 혼자 (sulking alone), 골난 표정 (a sullen face), and ...한테 골내다 (be grumpy at someone). English-speaker pitfall: keep the 내다/나다 split straight — you 골내다 (actively show it) but you 골나다 (the mood arises in you); and don't confuse this 골 (temper) with the homographs 골 meaning 'brain' or the loanword 'goal'. It is colloquial, so it stays in casual speech, not formal writing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 골내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 골내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
골내다 (transitive, 'to put out grumpiness') vs 골나다 (intransitive, 'to become grumpy') — keep the 내/나 split exactly like 화내다 / 화나다. 'I got grumpy' = 골났어, but 'don't be grumpy at me' = 나한테 골내지 마.
Don't confuse this 골 (temper/sour mood) with the homographs 골 ('brain') or the loanword 골 ('goal') — only context tells them apart.
It's colloquial; in formal or written contexts prefer 화내다 or 짜증을 내다 instead of 골내다.

usagePhrases.en: I do not get irritated (and show it).

usagePhrases.en: I want to get irritated (and show it).

words.nuance: 짜증내다 is to outwardly express irritation or annoyance — snapping, a sharp tone, an exasperated huff or face. It is one of the most-used emotion verbs in daily Korean life: clearly negative and usually aimed at someone, yet lighter than full-blown 화내다 (real anger). The crucial contrast for learners is the 내다/나다 pair: 짜증나다 names the internal feeling that wells up ('나 짜증 나' = I'm annoyed / it's annoying me), while 짜증내다 names the outward act of taking it out on someone ('나한테 짜증 내지 마' = don't be snippy at me) — same root noun 짜증, different verb of expression vs arising, just like 화내다 / 화나다. It collocates with 한테 (the target), 자꾸 (repeatedly), 짜증 섞인 말투 (an irritated tone), and the noun can detach as 짜증을 내다. English-speaker pitfall: learners say 나 짜증내 to mean 'I'm annoyed', but that wrongly implies you're actively snapping at someone — use 짜증나 for the feeling. Also, the double ㅉ is a tense consonant romanized 'jj', not a plain 'j'.

words.shortExplanation: 떼쓰다 means "to throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: I do not throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: The kid is throwing a fit demanding I buy a toy.
usagePhrases.note: The textbook scene for 떼쓰다 — a child's nagging demand; note -아/어 달라고.

examples.ko: 마트에서 과자 사 달라고 바닥에 누워서 떼썼어요.
examples.romanization: mateueseo gwaja sa dallago badage nuwoseo ttesseosseoyo.
examples.en: He lay on the floor at the mart demanding snacks.
examples.note: 떼썼어요 = past (떼쓰 + 었, the ㅡ drops). Very vivid kid behavior.

examples.en: You can't keep throwing tantrums now that you're an adult.
examples.note: Playfully scolding adult stubbornness; -까지 = 'even to the point of'.

examples.ko: 아무리 떼써도 안 되는 건 안 돼.
examples.romanization: amuri ttesseodo an doeneun geon an dwae.
examples.en: No matter how much you whine for it, no means no.
examples.note: Firm boundary-setting language with kids; 아무리 ...아/어도 = no matter how.

words.nuance: 떼쓰다 is to insistently, unreasonably demand something — the whining, foot-stamping, floor-flopping, won't-take-no-for-an-answer behavior, prototypically a child but also said of adults acting childishly. It is built from the noun 떼 ('an unreasonable demand / a fit') plus 쓰다 ('to use/employ'), so it literally = 'to employ a fit'; the noun can stand alone as 떼를 쓰다, and the intensified 생떼를 쓰다 means an utterly baseless tantrum. Crucially it centers on stubborn demanding, not sadness or quiet sulking — that is the dividing line versus 보채다 (restless fretful whining/urging) and versus 삐치다 (wounded pouting). Conjugation follows the ㅡ-irregular: the stem 쓰- loses its ㅡ before -어, giving 써 / 써요 / 떼썼어요. It collocates almost obligatorily with -아/어 달라고 (떼쓰다) ('demand that something be done'). English-speaker pitfall: never write 떼쓰어요 — the ㅡ must drop to 떼써요; and watch the vowel, it is 떼 (ㅔ), not 때 (ㅐ).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떼쓰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떼써요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
쓰다 follows the ㅡ-irregular: stem 떼쓰- + 어 → 떼써, past 떼썼어요. Don't write 떼쓰어요.
It's 떼쓰다, not 때쓰다 — the first vowel is ㅔ (떼 = a fit / an unreasonable demand), not ㅐ.
떼쓰다 is stubborn demanding, not quiet sulking — don't use it where 삐치다 (hurt pout) or 보채다 (restless fussing) is meant.
notes: ㅡ: memorize 떼써 and 떼써요 together.

conjugationTips.body: 떼쓰다 has an irregular stem (ㅡ). Memorize its polite form 떼써요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.shortExplanation: 보채다 means "to fuss (and pester)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 보채다 (bochaeda) means "to fuss (and pester)". Start from the polite form 보채요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보채다. A strong first sentence is 아기가 배고픈지 계속 보채요. ("The baby keeps fussing — maybe it's hungry."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: The baby keeps fussing — maybe it's hungry.
usagePhrases.note: The core use: a baby crying and fretting for a need; 계속 = continuously.

examples.ko: 애가 밤새 보채서 한숨도 못 잤어요.
examples.romanization: aega bamsae bochaeseo hansumdo mot jasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby fussed all night so I didn't sleep a wink.
examples.note: 보채다 + 한숨도 못 자다 = a classic exhausted-parent line.

examples.ko: 빨리 가자고 옆에서 자꾸 보채니까 정신이 없어.
examples.romanization: ppalli gajago yeopeseo jakku bochaenikka jeongsini eopseo.
examples.en: He keeps pestering me to hurry, so I can't focus.
examples.note: 보채다 of an impatient adult nagging you to rush; -니까 gives the cause.

examples.en: What's so urgent that you keep pestering me?
examples.note: Pushing back on someone's impatient nagging.

words.nuance: 보채다 has two everyday senses that share one feel — restless, repeated fussing. First, a baby or young child fretting and crying for a need (hunger, sleep, wanting to be held: 안아 달라고 보채다). Second, a person impatiently pestering or nagging you to hurry up or give them something (빨리 가자고 보채다). The dividing line versus 떼쓰다 is the type of pressure: 떼쓰다 is a stubborn, specific, won't-budge demand ('buy me THAT toy'), whereas 보채다 leans toward restless, antsy whining and urging without a single fixed demand. It is also gentler and more sympathetic than 떼쓰다 — a fussing baby earns pity, a tantruming one earns a scolding. Conjugation: 보채- + 어 contracts (ㅐ + 어 → ㅐ) to 보채 / 보채요, past 보챘어요. It collocates with 밤새 보채다 (fuss all night), 계속/자꾸 보채다, and -아/어 달라고 보채다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 보채어요 — the vowels contract to 보채요; and don't stretch it to mean adult 'anger' — it is fussing/pestering, never shouting.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보채다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보채요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
보채 + 어 contracts to 보채 (보채요), past 보챘어요 — don't write 보채어요.
Mostly for babies or impatient pestering; it does not mean adult 'anger' — don't use it where 화내다 or 짜증내다 is meant.
For a stubborn, fixed demand ('I want THAT one'), use 떼쓰다; 보채다 is the looser, restless fussing.

words.shortExplanation: 달래다 means "to soothe (and calm down)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to soothe (and calm down)" in Korean is 달래다 (dallaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 달래요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 달래다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 우는 아이를 달래고 있어요. ("I'm soothing the crying child.") — then reshape the same stem into 달래고 싶어요 (desire), 달랠 수 있어요 (ability), and 달랠 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not soothe (and calm down).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to soothe (and calm down).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to soothe (and calm down).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The prototypical use — calming a crying kid.

examples.en: Even soothing him with candy didn't stop the crying.
examples.note: 달래도 = even though I soothe; pairs with 울음을 그치다 (stop crying).

examples.en: I broke a sweat trying to calm down the angry customer.
examples.note: Service-job reality; -느라 = in the course of (an effortful) doing.

examples.ko: 속상한 마음을 달래려고 매운 음식을 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: soksanghan maeumeul dallaeryeogo maeun eumsigeul meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ate spicy food to soothe my upset feelings.
examples.note: 마음을 달래다 = to comfort/soothe one's own heart; -려고 = in order to.

words.nuance: 달래다 is to soothe, comfort, or placate someone who is crying, upset, or angry — and, importantly, also to calm your own feelings (마음을 달래다 = comfort one's heart). It is the natural counterpart to 울다, 토라지다, 떼쓰다, 화나다: someone gets upset, and you 달래다 them back to calm. The tone is warm and caring. The dividing line versus 위로하다 (to console) is method and scope: 위로하다 consoles mainly with sympathetic words about a loss or sorrow, while 달래다 actively settles a present upset — by holding, coaxing, distracting, or placating — and works on anger and tantrums too, not just grief. Conjugation: 달래- + 어 contracts to 달래 / 달래요, past 달랬어요. It collocates with 우는 아이를 달래다, 화난 고객을 달래다, ...로 달래다 (소리로/사탕으로 달래다 = soothe with...), and 마음을 달래다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 달래어요 — the vowels contract to 달래요; and don't confuse the verb 달래다 with its exact homophone 달래, the wild chive eaten in spring — only context separates them.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달래다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달래요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
달래 + 어 contracts to 달래 (달래요), past 달랬어요 — never 달래어요.
달래다 (to soothe, transitive) takes 을/를: 아이를 달래다, 마음을 달래다 — don't drop the object marker.
The verb 달래다 is unrelated to the homophone 달래 (a wild chive); context makes it clear.

The dividing line versus 위로하다 (to console) is method and scope: 위로하다 consoles mainly with sympathetic words about a loss or sorrow, while 달래다 actively settles a present upset — by holding, coaxing, distracting, or placating — and works on anger and tantrums too, not just grief.

words.shortExplanation: 토닥이다 means "to pat (gently and comfortingly)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 토닥이다 (todagida) = "to pat (gently and comfortingly)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 토닥여요 plus one useful sentence like 등을 토닥여 줬어요. ("I gave their back a comforting pat."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 토닥이고 싶어요 for what you want, 토닥일 수 있어요 for what you can, 토닥일 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not pat (gently and comfortingly).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to pat (gently and comfortingly).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to pat (gently and comfortingly).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I gave their back a comforting pat.
usagePhrases.note: 토닥이다 + 주다 = pat someone to comfort them; the 주다 shows it's a kindness done for them.

examples.ko: 울지 말라고 아이 등을 토닥여 줬어요.
examples.romanization: ulji mallago ai deungeul todagyeo jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I patted the child's back, telling them not to cry.
examples.note: 토닥였어요 (past) = 토닥이 + 었; the ㅣ + 어 fuses to 여.

examples.en: He patted my shoulder, saying I'd worked hard.
examples.note: A very Korean gesture of recognition; -시- marks respect for the senior doing it.

examples.ko: 힘든 하루 끝에 스스로를 토닥여 주세요.
examples.romanization: himdeun haru kkeute seuseuroreul todagyeo juseyo.
examples.en: At the end of a hard day, give yourself a comforting pat.
examples.note: 스스로를 토닥이다 = self-comfort; gentle imperative with 주세요.

words.nuance: 토닥이다 is the soft, rhythmic comforting pat — on a back, shoulder, or head — that wordlessly says 'it's okay, you did well.' It is fundamentally a physical act of consolation, almost always paired with 주다 to show you are doing it for someone (등을 토닥여 주다). The word is the verb form of the mimetic adverb 토닥토닥 (the gentle pat-pat sound/motion), which is why it feels so tactile and warm. Its very close companion 다독이다 overlaps heavily, but the dividing line is focus: 토닥이다 stays on the literal, light patting motion, whereas 다독이다 leans into the emotional follow-through of reassuring and steadying a person back together. Conjugation is the 이다-stem pattern: 토닥이- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여, giving 토닥여 / 토닥여요, past 토닥였어요. It collocates with 등을/어깨를 토닥이다, 토닥여 주다, 위로하다, and 스스로를 토닥이다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 토닥이어요 — the stem-final ㅣ forces 여 → 토닥여요; and don't confuse the verb with the bare mimetic adverb 토닥토닥, even though they're family.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 토닥이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 토닥여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
이다-ending verb: 토닥이 + 어 → 토닥여 (the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여), past 토닥였어요. Don't write 토닥이어요.
It's a kindness toward someone, so it almost always takes 주다: 등을 토닥여 줬어요 — bare 토닥였어요 sounds incomplete in caring contexts.
Don't confuse the action verb 토닥이다 with the sound-symbolic adverb 토닥토닥 (the patting sound itself), though they are related.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 토닥이다 is the soft, rhythmic comforting pat — on a back, shoulder, or head — that wordlessly says 'it's okay, you did well.' It is fundamentally a physical act of consolation, almost always paired with 주다 to show you are doing it for someone (등을 토닥여 주다). It collocates with 등을/어깨를 토닥이다, 토닥여 주다, 위로하다, and 스스로를 토닥이다.

Its very close companion 다독이다 overlaps heavily, but the dividing line is focus: 토닥이다 stays on the literal, light patting motion, whereas 다독이다 leans into the emotional follow-through of reassuring and steadying a person back together.
The word is the verb form of the mimetic adverb 토닥토닥 (the gentle pat-pat sound/motion), which is why it feels so tactile and warm.
이다-stem pattern: 토닥이- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여, giving 토닥여 / 토닥여요, past 토닥였어요.
Don't write 토닥이어요 — the stem-final ㅣ forces 여 → 토닥여요. And don't confuse the verb with the bare mimetic adverb 토닥토닥, even though they're family.

words.shortExplanation: 다독이다 means "to comfort (by patting and reassuring)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 다독이다 (dadogida) means "to comfort (by patting and reassuring)". Start from the polite form 다독여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 다독이다. A strong first sentence is 힘들어하는 친구를 다독여 줬어요. ("I comforted and reassured my struggling friend."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 다독이다 also becomes 다독이고 싶어요 (want), 다독일 수 있어요 (can), and 다독일 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not comfort (by patting and reassuring).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to comfort (by patting and reassuring).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can comfort (by patting and reassuring).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to comfort (by patting and reassuring).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I comforted and reassured my struggling friend.
usagePhrases.note: 다독이다 = comfort + steady someone emotionally; often with 주다.

examples.ko: 실패한 후배를 다독이며 다시 해 보라고 했어요.
examples.romanization: silpaehan hubaereul dadogimyeo dasi hae borago haesseoyo.
examples.en: I reassured the junior who'd failed and told them to try again.
examples.note: 다독이며 = while comforting; the -으며 connective overlaps the two acts.

examples.ko: 엄마가 등을 다독여 주니까 마음이 놓였어요.
examples.romanization: eommaga deungeul dadogyeo junikka maeumi noyeosseoyo.
examples.en: When Mom patted my back reassuringly, I felt at ease.
examples.note: 다독여 주다 + 마음이 놓이다 = to feel relieved.

examples.en: I rallied the team members and revived the mood.
examples.note: 다독이다 can steady a group, not just one person; 분위기를 살리다 = revive the mood.

words.nuance: 다독이다 means to comfort and steady someone — gently patting while reassuring them so they settle, regroup, and feel supported. It is warmer and more emotionally loaded than the purely physical 토닥이다: where 토닥이다 highlights the literal pat-pat motion, 다독이다 carries the follow-through of 'pulling someone back together,' which is why it extends to rallying a group (팀을 다독여 분위기를 살리다) in a way 토닥이다 does not. Its true opposite is 다그치다 ('to press, push, urge harshly') — the same emotional axis pulled in reverse, which is why the pairing 다그치지 말고 다독여 주세요 ('don't pressure — reassure') is idiomatic. Conjugation is the 이다-stem pattern: 다독이- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여, giving 다독여 / 다독여요, past 다독였어요. It collocates with 다독여 주다, 다독이며 (위로하다), 마음이 놓이다, and 사기를/분위기를 살리다. words.shortExplanation: 격려하다 means "to encourage" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to encourage" in Korean is 격려하다 (gyeongnyeohada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 격려해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 격려하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 힘내라고 격려해 줬어요. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I encouraged them, saying 'hang in there.'
usagePhrases.note: 격려하다 + 주다 = encourage someone; slightly formal and warm.

examples.ko: 시험 떨어진 친구를 격려해 주고 싶었어요.
examples.romanization: siheom tteoreojin chingureul gyeongnyeohae jugo sipeosseoyo.
examples.en: I wanted to encourage my friend who failed the exam.
examples.note: Pairs with 떨어지다 (to fail); -아/어 주고 싶다 = want to do (for someone).

examples.en: The coach gave a speech encouraging the players.
examples.note: 격려하다 is the go-to verb for pep talks and speeches.

examples.ko: 힘든 시기에 격려해 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.
examples.romanization: himdeun sigie gyeongnyeohae jusyeoseo jeongmal gamsahaesseoyo.
examples.en: Thank you so much for encouraging me during a hard time.
examples.note: Polite gratitude; very natural in messages to mentors and seniors.

words.nuance: 격려하다 is to encourage or cheer someone on with words — a pep talk, a 'you can do it,' a supportive note during a hard stretch. It is Sino-Korean: 激勵 combines 激 ('rouse, stir up') and 勵 ('urge on, exhort'), literally 'to stir up and spur on,' which is why it sounds a notch more formal and elevated than its native-feeling cousins. The dividing line versus 응원하다 (應援, 'to root for/cheer') is tone and setting: 응원하다 is energetic supporter-style cheering (a fan 응원s a team), while 격려하다 is more dignified, verbal encouragement, fitting speeches, workplaces, mentors, and 격려의 말씀 (words of encouragement) at formal events; and unlike the physical comforting of 다독이다 / 토닥이다, 격려하다 works through words. words.shortExplanation: 야단치다 means "to scold (tell off)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 야단치다 (yadanchida) = "to scold (tell off)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 야단쳐요 plus one useful sentence like 엄마한테 야단맞았어요. ("I got told off by my mom."). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I got told off by my mom.
usagePhrases.note: Note the partner verb 야단맞다 = to get scolded (the receiving side); 한테 marks who from.

examples.en: The teacher scolded the students who were being noisy.
examples.note: 야단쳤어요 (past) = 야단치 + 었; the ㅣ + 어 fuses to 쳐.

examples.ko: 거짓말한 걸 알고 부모님이 크게 야단치셨어요.
examples.romanization: geojinmalhan geol algo bumonimi keuge yadanchisyeosseoyo.
examples.en: When they found out I lied, my parents scolded me a lot.
examples.note: 크게 야단치다 = to scold severely; -시- adds respect for the parents.

examples.en: It's better to gently reason with them than to scold.
examples.note: Contrasts 야단치다 with 타이르다 (to admonish gently); -기보다 = rather than.

words.nuance: 야단치다 is to scold or tell someone off — a parent, teacher, or boss reprimanding a child or junior for doing wrong. It is built from the noun 야단 ('a fuss, an uproar, a scolding') plus 치다 ('to strike/deliver'), so it literally = 'to deliver a scolding,' which is why the noun can detach as 야단을 치다 and the receiving side surfaces as 야단을 듣다 / 야단을 맞다. It is stronger and more authority-driven than plain 화내다 (simply being angry): 야단치다 implies a power gap (older/senior reprimanding younger) and a corrective purpose, not just venting emotion. Its gentler neighbor is 타이르다 ('to admonish and reason with calmly'), which is why 야단치기보다 타이르다 ('reason rather than scold') is a natural contrast. Conjugation: 야단치- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 쳐, giving 야단쳐 / 야단쳐요, past 야단쳤어요. It collocates with 크게 야단치다 (scold severely), 야단맞다/야단 듣다 (be scolded), and 혼나다 (get told off). 치다-ending: 야단치 + 어 → 야단쳐 (ㅣ+어 fuses to 쳐), past 야단쳤어요. Don't write 야단치어요.

It implies a senior-to-junior power gap; you don't 야단치다 your boss — between equals, 뭐라고 하다 or just 화내다 fits better.

words.shortExplanation: 비웃다 means "to sneer at (laugh at scornfully)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 비웃다 (biutda) means "to sneer at (laugh at scornfully)". Start from the polite form 비웃어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 비웃다. A strong first sentence is 내 꿈을 비웃지 마. ("Don't sneer at my dream."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 비웃다 also becomes 비웃고 싶어요 (want), 비웃을 수 있어요 (can), and 비웃을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not sneer at (laugh at scornfully).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to sneer at (laugh at scornfully).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can sneer at (laugh at scornfully).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to sneer at (laugh at scornfully).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
비웃다 takes a direct object (꿈을, 사람을) with 을/를; hurtful nuance.

examples.ko: 발음이 이상하다고 비웃을까 봐 말을 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: bareumi isanghadago biuseulkka bwa mareul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't speak up, afraid they'd laugh at my pronunciation.
examples.note: Very real fear for language learners; -을까 봐 = afraid that.

examples.ko: 남을 비웃는 사람은 결국 신뢰를 잃어요.
examples.romanization: nameul biunneun sarameun gyeolguk silloereul ireoyo.
examples.en: People who sneer at others end up losing trust.
examples.note: Moral-tone sentence; 남을 비웃다 = mock others.

examples.en: He scoffed and sneered at my plan.
examples.note: 콧방귀를 뀌다 (to scoff through the nose) pairs idiomatically with 비웃다.

words.nuance: 비웃다 is to laugh at someone scornfully — to mock, sneer, ridicule, and look down on them. It is a compound of the prefix 비- (Sino-Korean 非/卑, carrying a 'belittling, disparaging' force, as in 비하 'to demean' or 비방 'to slander') plus the native verb 웃다 ('to laugh'), so it is literally 'belittling laughter,' which is exactly what separates it from neutral 웃다. The dividing line versus 놀리다 ('to tease') is intent and warmth: 놀리다 can be light, affectionate teasing between friends ('I'm just teasing you'), whereas 비웃다 is contemptuous and genuinely hurtful, with the laugher looking down on the target. It collocates with 남을/실수를/꿈을 비웃다, 대놓고 비웃다 (sneer openly), and the idiom 콧방귀를 뀌며 비웃다 (scoff and sneer). Conjugation point: 웃다 keeps its ㅅ — it is NOT a ㅅ-irregular — so the forms are 비웃어요 / 비웃었어요 / 비웃을 거예요, with the ㅅ intact. English-speaker pitfall: never drop that ㅅ (비웃어요, not 비웄어요); and don't use 비웃다 for friendly ribbing — that's 놀리다 — or you will sound far harsher and meaner than you intend.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비웃다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 비웃어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
웃다 keeps its ㅅ (it is NOT a ㅅ-irregular): 비웃어요, 비웃었어요, 비웃을 거예요 — never 비웄어요 or 비우어요.
비웃다 is scornful and mean; for light, friendly teasing use 놀리다 instead, or you'll sound much harsher than intended.
It takes a direct object with 을/를 (사람을/실수를 비웃다), not 에게/한테 — don't say 나에게 비웃지 마, say 나를 비웃지 마.

words.shortExplanation: 벌다 means "to earn" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to earn" in Korean is 벌다 (beolda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 벌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 벌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 돈을 벌다 ("to earn money") — then reshape the same stem into 벌고 싶어요 (desire), 벌 수 있어요 (ability), and 벌 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
핵심 결합. 조사 을/를 은 회화에서 자주 생략돼 '돈 벌어요'로도 말해요

examples.en: I work and earn money.
examples.note: 가장 기본형. '-아서/어서'로 '일해서 → 그 결과 벌어요' 순서를 보여줘요

examples.ko: 요즘 부업으로 용돈 좀 벌고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum bueobeuro yongdon jom beolgo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days I'm earning some pocket money with a side gig.
examples.note: 일상 회화. '-고 있다'로 진행 중인 상태를 표현

examples.ko: 고생해서 번 돈이니까 함부로 쓰지 마.

words.nuance: 벌다 is the everyday verb for bringing in money or income through work — 돈을 벌다 is the core phrase, and 'making a living' is 먹고살다. The dividing line you must feel: 벌다 is acquiring income, 쓰다 is spending it, 모으다 is saving/accumulating it, so a salary you 벌어서 모아요 then 써요. Register is neutral and usable anywhere, but asking 얼마 벌어요? to a senior or new coworker is socially risky. Crucially 벌다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the final ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 and -ㄴ, giving the formal 법니다, yet it survives in 벌어요. The single biggest English-speaker trap is the past modifier — 'the money I earned' is 번 돈, never 벌은 돈, because ㄹ disappears before -ㄴ.

Use 벌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 벌은 돈 for 'earned money' — because ㄹ drops before -ㄴ, the correct past modifier is 번 돈.
Saying 법니다 wrong as 벌습니다 — a ㄹ-stem takes -ㅂ니다 (not -습니다) and the ㄹ drops, so the formal form is 법니다.
Using 만들다 ('make/create') for earning money — you don't 돈을 만들다 (that implies counterfeiting); you 돈을 벌다.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 벌어 and 벌어요 together.

conjugationTips.body: 벌다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 벌어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.nuance: 모으다 covers both saving money over time and gathering/pooling things or people together (돈, 동전, 사람, 자료, 회비). words.nuance: 아끼다 means to be sparing with a resource so as not to waste it — money, electricity, water, even time — and the set phrase 아껴 쓰다 ('use frugally') is one of the most common chunks in daily speech. Use 아껴요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the polite form as 아끼어요 instead of contracting ㅣ + 어 to 아껴요 (past 아꼈어요).
Saying 돈에 아끼다 with the wrong particle — the resource is a direct object, so it's 돈을 아끼다.

words.nuance: 낭비하다 means to waste or squander a resource — money, time, energy — and always carries a clearly negative tone, so unlike English 'spend' it can never be neutral. It is Sino-Korean: 浪費 literally 'reckless(浪) expense(費)', i.e. spending that flows away wastefully, paired with the verb 하다. The synonym boundary: 쓰다 is neutral 'to spend/use', 낭비하다 is 'to spend wastefully', and its opposites are 아끼다 / 절약하다 (be frugal). As a regular 하다 verb it gives 낭비해요, 낭비했어요, 낭비합니다.

Trying to use a polite command 낭비해 주세요 — you never politely ask someone to waste; use the prohibitive 낭비하지 마세요.
Treating 낭비하다 as a neutral 'spend' like English — it is always negative, so for ordinary spending use 쓰다, not 낭비하다.

words.nuance: 갚다 means to pay back what you owe — money (돈, 카드값, 대출, 빚) or, figuratively, a favor or kindness (은혜를 갚다, 신세를 갚다). Dropping the final consonant in spelling as 가파요 — keep it as 갚아요 even though it is pronounced [가파요].
Confusing 갚다 (pay back) with the noun 값 (price) — '값이 비싸다' (the price is high) has nothing to do with repaying.

words.nuance: 맡기다 means to entrust or hand something over into someone's care — money to a bank (돈을 은행에 맡기다 = deposit), bags to a counter, laundry to a shop, or a job to a person. It is the causative counterpart of 맡다 ('to take charge of, to keep'): you 맡겨 your money to the bank, and the bank 맡아 keeps it — same root, opposite direction, which is exactly where English speakers slip. For strictly financial deposits there is the formal 예금하다, but 맡기다 is the warm everyday word and also covers physical things and tasks, which 예금하다 cannot. It conjugates regularly, stem ㅣ + 어 contracting to 여: 맡기 + 어요 → 맡겨요, past 맡겼어요.

Confusing 맡기다 (entrust to others) with 맡다 (take charge oneself) — you 맡겨 your money to the bank; the bank 맡아 keeps it.
Marking the place with 에서 instead of 에 — deposit destination uses 은행에 맡기다, not 은행에서 맡기다.
Spelling the polite form as 맡기어요 — ㅣ + 어 contracts to 여, giving 맡겨요 (past 맡겼어요).

words.shortExplanation: 쳐다보다 means "to stare at / look up at" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to stare at / look up at" in Korean is 쳐다보다 (chyeodaboda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 쳐다봐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 쳐다보다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 빤히 쳐다보다 ("to stare openly / fixedly") — then reshape the same stem into 쳐다보고 싶어요 (desire), 쳐다볼 수 있어요 (ability), and 쳐다볼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I have to stare at / look up at.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
빤히 is the most natural adverb partner — a direct, unblinking stare

examples.en: The cat is looking at me

words.nuance: 쳐다보다 is built from 치어다(보다) ('look upward') fused with 보다, and that upward/fixed feel survives: it means to look directly and steadily at something, frequently raising your eyes (천장을, 하늘을 쳐다보다). The dividing line from plain 보다 is intensity and duration — 보다 is any neutral 'see/look', while 쳐다보다 is a held, pointed gaze. Against 바라보다 (a calm, fond, distant gaze) it is far less warm: aimed at a person it slides easily into the uncomfortable 'why are you staring at me' zone, so 왜 쳐다봐요? sounds mildly confrontational. It conjugates as a 보다-verb: 보 + -아 contracts to 봐, giving 쳐다봐요 / past 쳐다봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 쳐다보다 every time you'd say 'look at' — for watching TV, a movie, or a performance you want 보다, and forcing 쳐다보다 there sounds like you're glaring at the screen.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 쳐다보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 쳐다봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 쳐다보다 for casually watching TV or a movie — that situation is 보다. 영화를 쳐다봤어요 wrongly implies you sat glaring at the film; say 영화를 봤어요.
Marking the target with 에 instead of 를. It's 저를 쳐다봐요, not 저에 쳐다봐요 — 쳐다보다 takes a direct object with 을/를.
Assuming it always sounds rude. With 천장을/하늘을 쳐다보다 it is perfectly neutral; the negative tinge only appears when the object is a person.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 쳐다보다 becomes 쳐다볼 수 있어요 ("can") and 쳐다볼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: To look directly and steadily at something, frequently raising your eyes (천장을, 하늘을 쳐다보다). It is a held, pointed gaze rather than a neutral look.

words.shortExplanation: 바라보다 means "to gaze at / look at" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 바라보다 (baraboda) = "to gaze at / look at". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 바라봐요 plus one useful sentence like 창밖을 바라보다 ("to gaze out the window"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 바라보고 싶어요 for what you want, 바라볼 수 있어요 for what you can, 바라볼 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

examples.en: I gazed at the sky
examples.note: Basic past form; calm, contemplative single look

examples.en: Gazing at the Han River on the way home calms me down

examples.en: We are looking in the same direction
examples.note: Figurative use about shared values; -고 있다 for an ongoing stance

words.nuance: 바라보다 (from 바라- + 보다) is to look at something usually at some distance and with a calm, often emotional or contemplative feeling — scenery, a loved one's face, the future. The key contrast is with 쳐다보다: where 쳐다보다 is a pointed, sometimes prickly stare, 바라보다 is soft and almost never aggressive, which makes it the safe verb for looking fondly or wistfully at someone (사랑스럽게 바라보다). Against 보다 (any plain 'see/look'), 바라보다 adds emotional depth and the sense of holding your eyes on something across space. It also lives a second, figurative life — 같은 곳을 바라보다, 미래를 바라보다 — meaning to share a vision or face the future. It conjugates as a regular 보다-verb: 바라보 + -아 → 바라봐요, past 바라봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 바라보다 for reading fine print or inspecting an object up close; that nearness belongs to 살펴보다 or 보다, since 바라보다 implies looking across a gap, not scrutinizing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바라보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바라봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 바라보다 for reading small text or inspecting something up close. 계약서를 바라봤어요 sounds like you admired it from afar; for checking details say 살펴봤어요.
Confusing it with the homophone-feel of 바라다 ('to wish/hope'). 바라보다 (gaze) and 바라다 (hope) are different verbs — 행복을 바라요 = I wish for happiness, not 바라봐요.
Adding an aggressive adverb like 노려보듯 to 바라보다. The word's whole point is its gentle tone; pairing it with hostility contradicts it — use 노려보다 for an angry stare.

words.shortExplanation: 살펴보다 means "to look over / examine carefully" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 살펴보다 (salpyeoboda) means "to look over / examine carefully". Start from the polite form 살펴봐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 살펴보다. A strong first sentence is 꼼꼼히 살펴보다 ("to examine thoroughly"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 살펴보다 also becomes 살펴보고 싶어요 (want), 살펴볼 수 있어요 (can), and 살펴볼 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

examples.en: Let me look over the menu for a moment
examples.note: Polite -ㄹ게요 to a server; calm, attentive checking

examples.ko: 집을 계약하기 전에 옵션을 꼼꼼히 살펴보세요
examples.romanization: jibeul gyeyakagi jeone opsyeoneul kkomkkomhi salpyeoboseyo
examples.en: Before signing for the place, examine the options carefully
examples.note: 꼼꼼히 살펴보다 in a practical housing context

examples.ko: 증상을 좀 더 살펴보고 약을 드릴게요

words.nuance: 살펴보다 joins 살피다 ('to scan/watch attentively, take care') with 보다, so its core is attentive, careful looking — to review, inspect, or check something over until you understand it: documents, a room, symptoms, your surroundings. It is the everyday 'review/check over' verb and pairs habitually with 꼼꼼히 ('meticulously'). The sharp contrast is with 둘러보다: 둘러보다 is a relaxed sweep around a whole space, while 살펴보다 zooms in with intent to verify, so 가게를 둘러봤어요 (browsed the shop) and 가게를 살펴봤어요 (inspected/cased the shop) feel quite different. Versus 훑어보다 (a fast skim for the gist), 살펴보다 is slower and more thorough. As a 보다-verb it contracts 살펴보 + -아 → 살펴봐요, past 살펴봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'look over' in English can mean both 'skim' and 'scrutinize', but 살펴보다 only covers the careful end — if you mean a quick glance, use 훑어보다, not 살펴보다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 살펴보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 살펴봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing it with 둘러보다. 살펴보다 emphasizes careful inspection; 둘러보다 is a casual look-around. To a clerk, 그냥 둘러볼게요 means 'just browsing', whereas 살펴볼게요 implies you're scrutinizing the goods.
Using 살펴보다 when you only skimmed something. If you read fast for the gist, that's 훑어봤어요; 살펴봤어요 claims you went through it carefully.
Dropping the object particle in set advice. It's 주변을 살펴보세요, not 주변 살펴보세요 in careful speech — 살펴보다 governs a 을/를 object.

words.shortExplanation: 알아보다 means "to look into / recognize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to look into / recognize" in Korean is 알아보다 (araboda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 알아봐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 알아보다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 방법을 알아보다 ("to look into how to do something") — then reshape the same stem into 알아보고 싶어요 (desire), 알아볼 수 있어요 (ability), and 알아볼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: to look into how to do something
usagePhrases.note: The 'investigate/research' sense; super common life-admin phrase

examples.note: The go-to work/service line; -ㄹ게요 promises to check on it

words.nuance: 알아보다 fuses 알다 ('know') with 보다, and the two senses both fall out of 'look in order to know.' Sense 1 — investigate / look into / research (information, prices, options, procedures): 비자 연장 방법을 알아보다. This is one of the most useful verbs for living in Korea — 제가 알아볼게요 is how you tell someone you'll check on a matter. Sense 2 — recognize / make out (a face, handwriting, a thing): 글씨를 못 알아보겠어요. The crucial contrast is with plain 알다: 알다 is the static state 'to know', while 알아보다 is the active 'find out' or 'identify on sight' — you can 알다 a fact, but you 알아보다 to obtain it. It contracts as 알아보 + -아 → 알아봐요, past 알아봤어요; the recognition sense often appears negative as 못 알아보다. English-speaker pitfall: for 'recognize someone' don't use 알다 — 그 사람을 알아요 means you know them, while 그 사람을 알아봤어요 means you recognized them by sight.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 알아보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 알아봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 알다 for 'recognize'. 알다 is just 'to know'; to say you recognized someone on sight, use 알아보다 — 저를 알아봤어요, not 저를 알았어요.
Saying 찾다 when you mean to research options. 찾다 is 'to search for/find', but 'I'll look into it (and weigh the choices)' is 알아볼게요, not 찾을게요.
Forgetting 못 for the can't-recognize meaning. 'I couldn't recognize the handwriting' is 글씨를 못 알아봤어요; 안 알아봤어요 would mean you chose not to look into it.

words.english: to watch over / keep an eye on
words.shortExplanation: 지켜보다 means "to watch over / keep an eye on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 지켜보다 (jikyeoboda) = "to watch over / keep an eye on". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 지켜봐요 plus one useful sentence like 좀 더 지켜보다 ("to wait and see a bit longer"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 지켜보고 싶어요 for what you want, 지켜볼 수 있어요 for what you can, 지켜볼 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I watch over / keep an eye on.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not watch over / keep an eye on.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to watch over / keep an eye on.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can watch over / keep an eye on.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to watch over / keep an eye on.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to wait and see a bit longer
usagePhrases.note: The classic 'let's monitor before deciding' phrase

examples.en: I'll keep an eye on the bag
examples.note: Everyday favor; -ㄹ게요 offers to watch it

examples.en: Let's watch the condition for a few more days
examples.note: -읍시다 doctor's 'let's monitor it'; classic wait-and-see

examples.en: I'll watch the exchange rate a few days, then exchange money
examples.note: -다가 marks watching that leads into a later action

words.nuance: 지켜보다 combines 지키다 ('to guard/keep') with 보다, so unlike a one-off look it means to watch continuously over time — to monitor, keep an eye on, or 'wait and see.' That 지키다 root gives it a flavor of care or guardianship, which is why it dominates medical advice (며칠 더 지켜봅시다 = let's observe a few more days), parenting (아이를 지켜보다), and decisions you want to postpone until things develop (상황을 지켜보다). Contrast it with 쳐다보다 and 바라보다, which are momentary looks: 지켜보다 is durative — you keep looking across a stretch of time. It also differs from 살펴보다, which is a careful inspection at one moment rather than ongoing surveillance. With the helper -아 주다 it becomes warmly protective: 지켜봐 주다 = watch over someone for their sake. It contracts 지켜보 + -아 → 지켜봐요, past 지켜봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 지켜보다 for watching a show or game for fun — that single sitting is 보다; 지켜보다 implies vigilant, time-extended monitoring.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 지켜보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 지켜봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 지켜보다 for watching a movie or match for entertainment. That's 보다 — 경기를 봤어요. 경기를 지켜봤어요 implies tense, watchful monitoring of how it unfolds.
Treating it as a quick glance. 지켜보다 is durative; for an instant look use 쳐다보다 or 보다. 한 번 지켜봤어요 sounds odd because the verb implies sustained watching.
Dropping -아 주다 when you mean a favor. 'Please watch my seat' is most naturally 자리 좀 지켜봐 주세요; plain 지켜보세요 sounds like a cold instruction to surveil.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 지켜보다 becomes 지켜볼 수 있어요 ("can") and 지켜볼 거예요 ("will"). words.nuance: 둘러보다 is built from 두르다/둘러- ('to encircle, go around') plus 보다, so it literally means to send your eyes around a whole space — a store, a neighborhood, an exhibition — taking a broad, relaxed look. It is the natural verb for browsing: when a clerk asks 도와드릴까요?, the textbook reply is 그냥 둘러볼게요 or 둘러보는 거예요 ('I'm just looking'). The decisive contrast is with 들여다보다, its near-opposite: 둘러보다 is a wide sweep over many things, while 들여다보다 is a close peer into one thing, so 가게를 둘러보다 (browse the shop) vs 가방을 들여다보다 (peer into the bag). It also contrasts with 살펴보다, which adds careful scrutiny rather than a casual survey. As a 보다-verb it contracts 둘러보 + -아 → 둘러봐요, past 둘러봤어요. words.nuance: 들여다보다 comes from 들이다 ('to bring/let inward') in the -여다 form plus 보다 — literally 'look inward into' — so it means a close, leaning-in look into something: a container, a screen, or, figuratively, a problem. The defining feature is up-close, focused attention, usually with your head bent toward the object. The sharp contrast is with 둘러보다: 들여다보다 narrows onto one thing from near, while 둘러보다 sweeps broadly over a space — peering into a bag vs scanning a whole store. Against 살펴보다 (careful inspection that can be at normal distance), 들여다보다 adds the physical sense of bringing your eyes right up to or inside something. words.shortExplanation: 엿보다 means "to peek / spy on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 엿보다 (yeotboda) = "to peek / spy on". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 엿봐요 plus one useful sentence like 남의 것을 엿보다 ("to peek at someone else's things"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 엿보고 싶어요 for what you want, 엿볼 수 있어요 for what you can, 엿볼 수 없어요 for what you can't. words.nuance: 엿보다 uses the prefix 엿- ('secretly, on the sly') plus 보다, so its base meaning is to look at something furtively — peeking through a gap, spying, or sneaking a look at someone's private things. In its literal sense it almost always sounds sneaky or improper (남의 일기를 엿보다 = snoop in someone's diary), which sets it firmly apart from open looking verbs like 보다 or 바라보다. Two idiomatic extensions soften or neutralize it, though: 기회를 엿보다 ('watch for an opening', a normal strategic phrase) and ~을 엿볼 수 있다 ('offers a glimpse into', common in writing about an era, a culture, or someone's inner world). It contracts 엿보 + -아 → 엿봐요, past 엿봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 엿보다 just because English 'take a peek' sounds casual and harmless — in Korean the literal verb implies secrecy and intrusion, so for an innocent quick glance use 살짝 보다 or 힐끔 보다 instead.

Use 엿봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 엿보다 for an innocent quick look. It specifically implies secrecy/intrusion; for a harmless glance say 살짝 봤어요 or 힐끔 봤어요, not 엿봤어요.

words.nuance: 노려보다 derives from 노리다 ('to take aim at, target') plus 보다, and that 'taking aim' is exactly the feeling — to fix someone with an angry, hostile stare, i.e. to glare. It is strong and unambiguously negative, signaling irritation, threat, or a challenge, and pairs naturally with 눈을 부릅뜨고 ('eyes flung wide'). Compare the family: 보다 is neutral 'look', 쳐다보다 is an uncomfortable lingering stare, and 노려보다 is openly hostile — only the last carries real anger. A close casual synonym is 째려보다, which is more colloquial and often a quick, sharp dirty look, whereas 노려보다 can be a sustained, intense glare. Because 노리다 also means 'to covet/eye a target', 노려보다 occasionally edges toward 'eye something one is after', but its default is anger. It contracts 노려보 + -아 → 노려봐요, past 노려봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: never use 노려보다 where neutral English 'look at' would do — it always injects hostility, so for a plain look use 보다 and for an awkward stare use 쳐다보다.

words.nuance: 훑어보다 builds on 훑다 ('to strip/run along a surface', as in running a hand down a stalk) plus 보다, so it pictures the eyes sliding rapidly over a surface to grab the gist — skimming a menu, an article, a resume. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Listening in secretly; improper nuance

examples.en: You shouldn't listen in on someone's phone call
examples.note: -면 안 되다 forbids it; note ㄷ→ㄹ in 엿들으면

examples.ko: 카페에서 옆자리 얘기를 본의 아니게 엿들었어요

examples.en: At the cafe I unintentionally overheard the next table

words.nuance: 엿듣다 is the listening counterpart of 엿보다: the secret prefix 엿- plus 듣다 ('to hear/listen'), meaning to overhear or eavesdrop, normally on the sly. English-speaker pitfall (two of them): first, never write 엿듣어요 — that ignores the ㄷ-irregular; it must be 엿들어요. Second, don't assume 'overhear' is blameless and use it freely; the bare verb implies intrusion, so without 우연히 it can sound like you snooped on purpose.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

words.shortExplanation: 죽다 means "to die" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to die" in Korean is 죽다 (jukda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 죽어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 죽다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 배터리가 죽었어요 ("The battery died") — then reshape the same stem into 죽고 싶어요 (desire), 죽을 수 있어요 (ability), and 죽을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Just like English, 죽다 covers batteries and phones going dead — 배터리/핸드폰이 죽다.

examples.en: The flowers all died
examples.note: Plants and animals dying take 죽다 directly; the subject takes 이/가.

examples.en: I'm starving to death
examples.note: The most common spoken use: feeling + 죽겠어요 to dramatize, said casually among friends.

examples.note: Machines/devices losing power 'die' in Korean exactly as in English.

words.nuance: 죽다 is the plain, blunt word for 'to die', and that bluntness matters: Koreans almost never say it literally about a person they respect — there you use the honorific 돌아가시다 (literally 'to return/go back'), so 할아버지가 돌아가셨어요, never 죽었어요.
