As a regular consonant-stem verb it just adds 어요: 죽 + 어요 → 죽어요.

words.shortExplanation: 놀다 means "to play" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 놀다 (nolda) = "to play". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 놀아요 plus one useful sentence like 친구하고 놀아요 ("I hang out with friends"). Useful for choices and plans.

words.nuance: 놀다 spans a wide range English splits into different words: children 'playing', adults 'hanging out', and even 'goofing off / doing nothing productive' (그냥 집에서 놀았어요 = 'I just chilled at home'). A strong first sentence is 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? ("How long does it take?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 걸리다 also becomes 걸리고 싶어요 (want), 걸릴 수 있어요 (can), and 걸릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take (time) / to get caught.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to take (time) / to get caught.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can take (time) / to get caught.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to take (time) / to get caught.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
걸리다 with 시간 is THE way to ask about duration; the time, not you, is the subject.

examples.en: It takes an hour to get home
examples.note: Travel time: the duration is the subject — 한 시간이 걸려요.

examples.en: I caught a cold again
examples.note: A fixed expression every beginner needs; note the 에 particle.

examples.en: I was speeding and got caught by the police
examples.note: The 'get busted' sense, with the catcher marked by 한테.

words.nuance: 걸리다 is a high-frequency verb that fans out into three everyday senses learners meet fast: (1) time being needed — 시간이 걸리다; (2) catching an illness — 감기에 걸리다; and (3) getting caught/busted — 경찰한테 걸리다, 거짓말이 걸리다. examples.note: Everyday food/drink use; 에 marks what you put it into.

words.nuance: 넣다 means to put or insert something into a place or container, so it is a two-slot verb: it needs both the thing (을/를) and the destination (에) — 가방에 책을 넣어요. Mind the particle, too: the destination is 에 (the static location 'into'), not 에서 (which marks a source) — that 에 vs 에서 split is exactly what separates 넣다 ('put into', 에) from its opposite 빼다 ('take out from', 에서).

usagePhrases.en: I do not take out / to subtract.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to take out / to subtract.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can take out / to subtract.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to take out / to subtract.

examples.note: The idiom 살을 빼다 ('lose weight') with -려고 ('in order to').

words.nuance: 빼다 means to take something out, remove it, leave it off, or — in math — subtract, and it's the natural transitive opposite of 넣다 ('put in'). words.shortExplanation: 차다 means "to kick" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 차고 싶어요 for what you want, 찰 수 있어요 for what you can, 찰 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
차다 = kick, most often with 공 (a ball); what you kick takes 을/를.

examples.en: I kick the ball hard
examples.note: Most common with 공; 세게 ('hard') is a natural adverb partner.

examples.en: The child kicked a stone
examples.note: Simple past; note the contracted 찼어요 from the ㅏ stem.

examples.note: An invitation to play; 찰까요? proposes doing it together.

words.nuance: 차다 most commonly means to kick, taking a 을/를 object for what's kicked (공을 차다), and the instrument 'with the foot' takes 로 → 발로 차다. The thing to flag for learners is that 차다 is really three homophones sharing a spelling: (1) 'kick'; (2) 'be full / fill up' (방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 'the room filled with people'); and (3) 'wear' a watch or bracelet (시계를 차다) — context disambiguates, and as a beginner you should lock in 'kick' first. words.shortExplanation: 밟다 means "to step on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
밟다 = tread on something; what you step on takes 을/를.

examples.en: Sorry, I stepped on your foot
examples.note: Said after bumping someone in a crowd; pairs with 미안해요/죄송해요.

examples.en: I stepped on gum on the street
examples.note: Treading on something on the ground; the place takes 에서.

words.nuance: 밟다 means to step on or tread on something, taking a 을/를 object, and in daily life it shows up constantly in two settings: apologizing after stepping on someone in a crowd (발을 밟았어요 + 죄송해요) and driving, where you 밟다 the pedals — 액셀을 밟다 ('hit the gas'), 브레이크를 밟다 ('hit the brakes'). usagePhrases.en: I do not attend / to go around.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

다니다 = regularly go to a place like school/work; the place takes 에.

examples.en: I attend a Korean language academy
examples.note: Regular attendance at a school/academy; the institution takes 에.

words.nuance: 다니다 means to go to a place habitually — attend school, commute to a job, frequent the gym, keep going to a clinic — so it always implies repetition and an ongoing relationship, not a single trip; it also covers plain 'go about / get around' (밤에 혼자 다니지 마 'don't go around alone at night'). words.nuance: 세우다 is the transitive 'make (something) stand / bring to a stop', and it's the causative partner of 서다 ('to stand still / come to a stop, by itself'): 서다 is what a car does on its own, 세우다 is you stopping it. The transitivity pitfall is the one to drill: 세우다 takes a 을/를 object (차를 세우다 = 'stop the car'), while the intransitive 서다 doesn't (차가 섰어요 = 'the car stopped') — English uses 'stop' for both, so learners wrongly say 차가 세워요. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 비교하다 also becomes 비교하고 싶어요 (want), 비교할 수 있어요 (can), and 비교할 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The single most common collocation; Koreans 가격 비교 ('price comparison') before any purchase.

examples.en: I compare prices
examples.note: The plainest frame: object + 을/를 + 비교해요, an everyday shopping habit.

examples.ko: 사기 전에 두 제품을 비교해 봤어요
examples.romanization: sagi jeone du jepumeul bigyohae bwasseoyo
examples.en: Before buying, I compared the two products
examples.note: 사기 전에 ('before buying') + 비교해 봤어요 ('tried comparing') is exactly how a shopper talks.

examples.en: Please don't compare (your child) with others' children
examples.note: 남(의) ('other people's') + 와 + 비교하지 마세요 — a heartfelt request, the social side of this verb.

words.nuance: 비교하다 is the Sino-Korean verb 比較(비교, 'compare-contrast') + 하다, meaning to set two or more things side by side to weigh their differences. The thing(s) compared take 을/를, and the second item of a pair takes 와/과 (formal) or 하고/랑 (casual): A를 B와 비교하다. Being a 하다 verb it conjugates to 해요 (never 하요) and 했어요. Distinguish it from 대조하다 (對照, 'contrast'), which highlights opposites for academic effect, while 비교하다 is the neutral everyday word ('compare prices, compare two phones'). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners copy English 'compare A to B' and say 가격에 비교해요, but the object marker must be 을/를 — 가격을 비교해요. Note too the social weight of 비교당하다 ('to be compared', passive): Koreans dislike being measured against others, so 비교하지 마 ('stop comparing me') is emotionally loaded.

Use 비교해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 가격에 비교해요 with 에, copied from English 'compare to'. The thing compared is a direct object, so it must take 을/를: 가격을 비교해요.

words.shortExplanation: 선택하다 means "to choose" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to choose" in Korean is 선택하다 (seontaekhada). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object + 을/를 + 선택하다; 하나만 선택하세요 ('pick only one') is standard quiz/form wording.

examples.en: I chose the blue one
examples.note: Plain object frame: color + 을/를 + 선택했어요, e.g. picking a phone case.

examples.en: Please select your menu on the kiosk
examples.note: 에서 ('at/on') the kiosk + 선택해 주세요 — exactly what a café screen tells you.

examples.ko: 둘 다 좋아서 하나를 선택하기 어려워요
examples.romanization: dul da joaseo hanareul seontaekagi eoryeowoyo
examples.en: Both are good, so it's hard to pick one
examples.note: 선택하기 어렵다 ('hard to choose') turns the verb into a noun with -기.

words.nuance: 선택하다 is 選擇(선택, 'select-pick') + 하다 and means to pick a defined option from a presented set — menus, app settings, multiple-choice answers, life paths. Crucially, contrast it with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide'): 선택하다 is choosing one option among several that already exist, while 결정하다 is settling a matter or reaching a conclusion ('유학을 결정했어요' = decided to study abroad). As a 하다 verb it gives 선택해요 / 선택했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the 고르다 split: say 메뉴를 선택해요 with 을/를 (not 메뉴에), and don't force 선택하다 into casual chat where a native would simply say 골라요. Also, 'choose to do X' is not 선택하다 alone — Korean prefers ~기로 하다/결심하다.

words.shortExplanation: 결심하다 means "to decide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 결심하다 (gyeolsimhada) = "to decide". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 결심해요 plus one useful sentence like V-기로 결심하다 ("to resolve to do V"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The core grammar: 끊기로 결심했어요 ('resolved to quit'). The -기로 is almost obligatory.

examples.en: I resolved to learn Korean
examples.note: Textbook frame: V-기로 결심했어요, a goal you set for yourself.

examples.en: I firmly resolved to exercise from the new year
examples.note: 새해부터 ('from the new year') + 굳게 — a classic resolution sentence.

examples.en: After hesitating several times, I finally made up my mind
examples.note: 망설이다가 ('hesitating and then') + 결국 ('in the end') shows the inner struggle this verb implies.

words.nuance: 결심하다 is 決心(결심, 'decide-heart', literally 'fix the heart') + 하다, so it is not a neutral 'decide' but a determined, willpower-charged resolve — the New-Year-resolution verb. The indispensable pattern is V-기로 결심하다 ('make up one's mind to do V'): 담배를 끊기로 결심했어요. Contrast it sharply with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide-settle'): 결정하다 settles an external matter and can be about logistics or other people ('회의 날짜를 결정했어요' = decided the meeting date), whereas 결심하다 is always your own inner determination about your own action — you can't 결심하다 someone else's schedule. It is also stronger than casual 마음먹다, which feels homier. As a 하다 verb: 결심해요 / 결심했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping -기로 (saying 운동 결심했어요) and overusing 결심하다 for trivial choices; for 'I decided to have pasta tonight' Koreans just say 파스타 먹기로 했어요, reserving 결심하다 for serious resolve.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 결심하다 as a complete polite sentence.

words.shortExplanation: 기대하다 means "to expect" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 기대하다 (gidaehada) means "to expect". Start from the polite form 기대해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 기대하다. A strong first sentence is 여행을 기대하다 ("to look forward to a trip"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 기대하다 also becomes 기대하고 싶어요 (want), 기대할 수 있어요 (can), and 기대할 수 없어요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to look forward to a trip
usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 기대하다 for the happy-anticipation sense.

examples.en: I'm looking forward to the weekend
examples.note: Plain frame; the hopeful, positive flavor of the verb.

examples.en: I'm really excited for this movie
examples.note: 기대돼요 (from 기대되다) describes the feeling rising in you, no object needed.

examples.en: If you expect too much, you might be disappointed
examples.note: 기대하면 ('if you expect') + 실망하다 pairs hope with its risk.

words.nuance: 기대하다 is 期待(기대, 'period-await', i.e. 'await a hoped-for time') + 하다, and unlike English 'expect' it leans positive: it means to anticipate something good and look forward to it. The thing awaited takes 을/를 (여행을 기대해요). Its hugely common intransitive twin 기대되다/기대가 되다 ('to be exciting, to be looked forward to') describes the feeling welling up in you — 내일이 기대돼요 — and beginners must keep the two apart: you 기대하다 a thing, but a thing/situation 기대된다 to you. Contrast with 기다리다 ('wait'), which is just neutral temporal waiting with no hope ('버스를 기다려요'); and with 바라다 ('wish/hope') which is a desire without the sense of confident anticipation. As a 하다 verb: 기대해요 / 기대했어요. The pitfall: English speakers map 'expect' onto neutral or negative situations ('I expect rain', 'I expect you to be late') — Korean 기대하다 cannot carry that. For neutral prediction use 예상하다 (豫想); 기대하다 is only for things you hope will be good.

Use 기대해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 기대하다 for neutral or bad predictions like 'I expect it to rain'. That is 예상하다 (비가 올 것으로 예상해요). 기대하다 is positive anticipation only.

words.shortExplanation: 상상하다 means "to imagine" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to imagine" in Korean is 상상하다 (sangsanghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 상상해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 상상하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 미래를 상상하다 ("to imagine the future") — then reshape the same stem into 상상하고 싶어요 (desire), 상상할 수 있어요 (ability), and 상상할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object + 을/를 + 상상하다; the object is a scene/picture in the mind.

examples.en: I sometimes imagine traveling
examples.note: 가끔 ('sometimes') + object frame — a pleasant daydream.

examples.en: Try imagining how you'll be in 10 years
examples.note: 후의 모습 ('appearance after') + 상상해 보세요, a coaching-style prompt.

examples.ko: 그런 일이 생길 줄은 상상도 못 했어요
examples.romanization: geureon iri saenggil jureun sangsangdo mo taesseoyo
examples.en: I couldn't even imagine that would happen
examples.note: 상상도 못 하다 ('couldn't even imagine') is the natural way to express shock.

words.nuance: 상상하다 is 想像(상상, 'think-image', i.e. 'form a mental image') + 하다 — to picture in your mind something not present, from a fantasy to a hypothetical future. The thing imagined takes 을/를, and the gentle pattern 상상해 보세요 ('try to imagine') is far more natural than a bare command. Contrast it carefully with 생각하다 ('think'), which is broad reasoning, deliberation, or opinion, whereas 상상하다 specifically conjures a vivid image or scenario; '생각해 보세요' = think it over, but '상상해 보세요' = picture it. Also distinguish 공상하다 (空想, 'empty-imagine', daydreaming with a tinge of unreality) and 상상하다 (neutral, can be realistic planning). As a 하다 verb: 상상해요 / 상상했어요. The English-speaker pitfall: 'imagine that...' as a clause is handled with ~다고/는다고 상상하다 or just ~ㄴ/는 모습을 상상하다 (picture the scene), not a borrowed 'that' structure; and the very common 'I can't imagine' is idiomatically 상상도 못 하다 or 상상이 안 가다, not a literal 상상할 수 없다 in casual speech.

words.nuance: 받아들이다 is a native compound, 받다 ('receive') + 들이다 ('let in / take inward'), so it literally means 'receive and let inside' — to take something in and come to terms with it: a fact, a result, an apology, criticism, a proposal. usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

words.nuance: 마음먹다 is a vivid native idiom: 마음 ('heart/mind') + 먹다 ('eat'), literally 'to eat the mind' — to take a decision firmly inside you, i.e. make up your mind. Compare it with 결심하다: both mean 'resolve', but 마음먹다 is homier, more conversational and gut-level, while Sino-Korean 결심하다 is a touch more formal and goal-oriented — a New Year's 결심 looks better on a list, but a friend would say 나 운동하기로 마음먹었어. words.explanation: "to forget" in Korean is 잊어버리다 (ijeobeorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 잊어버려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 잊어버리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이름을 잊어버리다 ("to forget a name") — then reshape the same stem into 잊어버리고 싶어요 (desire), 잊어버릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 잊어버릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object + 을/를 + 잊어버리다; 약속을 잊어버리다 ('forget an appointment') is a common slip.

examples.en: I forgot the password
examples.note: Everyday frame; note the past 리 + 었 → 렸: 잊어버렸어요.

examples.en: It slipped my mind and I didn't bring an umbrella
examples.note: 깜빡 잊어버리고 ('forgetting in a flash, and...') chains to the consequence.

examples.en: Please forget all the bad memories
examples.note: 잊어버리세요 ('do forget') used kindly to help someone move on.

words.nuance: 잊어버리다 is the native compound 잊다 ('forget') + -어 버리다 (the auxiliary 버리다, 'throw away / do completely'), so it means to forget thoroughly, with the nuance that the memory is gone for good — often tinged with regret ('darn, it's gone'). Plain 잊다 states the bare fact of forgetting; 잊어버리다 adds finality and emotional color, which is why everyday speech overwhelmingly uses 잊어버리다. The object takes 을/를. Conjugation: the 리 stem contracts with 어 to 려, hence 잊어버려요 / 잊어버렸어요. The most dangerous English-speaker pitfall is the near-twin 잃어버리다 ('to lose a physical object'): 잊다 (forget, from the mind) vs 잃다 (lose, from your possession) differ by one jamo and one meaning — you 잊어버리다 a name but 잃어버리다 your wallet. Mixing them is the classic learner error. Also note: to tell someone 'don't forget', say 잊어버리지 마세요 or just 잊지 마세요; and writing the uncontracted 잊어버리었어요 is wrong — it must be 잊어버렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잊어버리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잊어버려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing it with 잃어버리다 ('lose an object'). You 잊어버리다 information (이름을 잊어버렸어요) but 잃어버리다 things (지갑을 잃어버렸어요). One jamo, totally different meaning.
Writing the uncontracted past 잊어버리었어요. The 리 + 었 contracts to 렸: 잊어버렸어요.
Thinking 잊다 and 잊어버리다 are fully interchangeable. 잊어버리다 adds 'completely/for good' and is the everyday choice; bare 잊다 is more neutral or literary.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 잊어버리다 becomes 잊어버릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 잊어버릴 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 생각나다 means "to come to mind" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 생각나다 (saenggangnada) = "to come to mind". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 생각나요 plus one useful sentence like 이름이 생각나다 ("a name comes to mind"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 생각나고 싶어요 for what you want, 생각날 수 있어요 for what you can, 생각날 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not come to mind.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to come to mind.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to come to mind.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The recalled thing takes 이/가, not 을/를: 단어가 생각나요.

examples.en: My hometown suddenly comes to mind
examples.note: 이/가 marks what surfaces in memory; the feeling arises on its own.

examples.en: I've got a good idea!
examples.note: 생각이 나다 split by 좋은 — the everyday 'I have an idea' exclamation.

examples.ko: 아무리 해도 그 단어가 생각나지 않아요
examples.romanization: amuri haedo geu daneoga saenggangnaji anayo
examples.en: No matter what, I just can't recall that word
examples.note: 아무리 해도 ('however much I try') + 생각나지 않다 = the tip-of-the-tongue feeling.

words.nuance: 생각나다 is 생각 ('thought') + 나다 ('arise / come out'), so it literally means 'a thought arises' — something comes to mind or you recall it spontaneously, without effort. This grammar is the heart of the word: because the memory surfaces by itself, the recalled thing is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (이름이 생각나요), not 을/를. Contrast it sharply with 생각하다 ('think'), which is volitional, active deliberation taking 을/를 (그 일을 생각해요 = I'm thinking about that): 생각하다 = you do the thinking; 생각나다 = a thought comes to you. Compare also 기억나다 ('a memory comes back', near-synonym, slightly more about stored memory) and 떠오르다 ('to float up', vivid for ideas/images suddenly emerging). 나다 is a regular verb: 생각나요 / 생각났어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the agency: learners translate 'I remember the name' as 이름을 생각나요 with an object, but Korean frames it as the name doing the surfacing — 이름이 생각나요. And 'I can't remember' is naturally the negative 생각이 안 나요 / 생각나지 않아요, not a 'can't' construction.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 생각나다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 생각나요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the recalled thing with 을/를: 이름을 생각나요. Because the memory arises on its own, it is the subject: 이름이 생각나요.
Confusing 생각나다 (a thought comes to you, involuntary) with 생각하다 (you actively think, volitional). 'I'm thinking about it' is 생각하고 있어요, not 생각나고 있어요.
Saying 생각할 수 없어요 for 'I can't remember'. The idiomatic form is the negative 생각이 안 나요 or 생각나지 않아요.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 생각나다 becomes 생각날 수 있어요 ("can") and 생각날 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 신경 쓰다 means "to care about" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 신경 쓰다 (singyeong sseuda) means "to care about". Start from the polite form 신경 써요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 신경 쓰다. A strong first sentence is 건강에 신경 쓰다 ("to look after one's health"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 신경 쓰다 also becomes 신경 쓰고 싶어요 (want), 신경 쓸 수 있어요 (can), and 신경 쓸 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
What you mind about takes 에: 외모에 신경 쓰다, 디테일에 신경 쓰다.

examples.en: I pay attention to how I dress
examples.note: 옷차림에 ('on one's outfit') + 신경 쓰다 — note the 에 particle.

examples.en: Don't let that kind of comment bother you
examples.note: 신경 쓰지 마세요 used to comfort someone who's hurt.

examples.ko: 다른 사람 눈치까지 신경 쓰느라 피곤해요
examples.romanization: dareun saram nunchikkaji singyeong sseuneura pigonhaeyo
examples.en: I'm tired from minding even other people's reactions
examples.note: 신경 쓰느라 ('busy minding, so...') links the caring to the exhaustion it causes.

words.nuance: 신경 쓰다 pairs the Sino-Korean noun 神經 (신경, 'nerve') with the verb 쓰다 ('use'), literally 'to use one's nerves' — to expend mental energy minding, caring about, or worrying over something. It spans neutral attention (디테일에 신경 쓰다 = pay attention to detail) and anxious preoccupation (남 눈치에 신경 쓰다 = fret over others' reactions). The object of concern takes 에 (or 에게/한테 for a person), not 을/를. Conjugation is a key trap: 쓰다 is a ㅡ-irregular, so the ㅡ drops before 어 — 쓰 + 어 → 써, giving 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요, never 신경 쓰어요. Contrast it with 걱정하다 ('worry'), which is pure anxiety about an outcome, whereas 신경 쓰다 is the act of devoting attention (which may or may not be worried); and with 관심 있다 ('be interested'), which is positive curiosity. The single most useful phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't worry about it / never mind'), heard constantly. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 을/를 (그 일을 신경 써요) — say 그 일에 신경 써요; and don't reach for 돌보다 ('physically take care of, tend') when you mean mental attention — '나는 외모에 신경 써' is care/attention, not nursing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 신경 쓰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 신경 써요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the concern with 을/를 (그것을 신경 써요). 신경 쓰다 takes 에: 그것에 신경 써요 (people: 그 사람에게 신경 써요).
Ignoring the ㅡ-irregular and writing 신경 쓰어요 / 신경 쓰었어요. The ㅡ drops: 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요.
Using 걱정하다 when you mean attentive minding. 신경 쓰다 = devote attention (possibly worried); 걱정하다 = be anxious about an outcome. 'I'm worried about the exam' is 시험이 걱정돼요.
notes: ㅡ: memorize 신경 써 and 신경 써요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 알아채다 means "to notice" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to notice" in Korean is 알아채다 (arachaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 알아채요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 알아채다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 분위기를 알아채다 ("to pick up on the mood") — then reshape the same stem into 알아채고 싶어요 (desire), 알아챌 수 있어요 (ability), and 알아챌 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to pick up on the mood
usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 알아채다; 변화를 알아채다 ('notice a change') is just as common.

examples.en: I noticed right away
examples.note: Plain frame; note the past 채 + 었 → 챘: 알아챘어요.

examples.en: Nobody noticed my mistake
examples.note: 못 알아채다 ('fail to notice') — 못 negates ability, here a lucky escape.

examples.en: Just from your expression, I caught that it was a lie
examples.note: ~ㄴ 걸 알아채다 ('notice that it is...') takes a whole clause as the object.

words.nuance: 알아채다 is the native compound 알다 ('know') + 채다 ('snatch / catch quickly'), so it means to suddenly catch on to or become aware of something — often something subtle, hidden, or not openly stated (a lie, a mood shift, a hint). The object takes 을/를, and a whole situation can be its object via ~ㄴ/는 걸 알아채다 (거짓말인 걸 알아챘어요). Conjugation: the 채 stem contracts with past 었 to 챘, giving 알아챘어요 (not 알아채었어요). Contrast it with 눈치채다, an almost identical everyday synonym focused on reading social cues; the two are largely interchangeable, though 눈치채다 leans toward interpersonal/atmospheric cues. Distinguish it from 알아보다 (알다 + 보다, 'look into'), which means to recognize someone/something or to investigate ('얼굴을 알아보다' = recognize a face; '가격을 알아보다' = look into a price) — a different verb, not 'notice'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'notice that X' must be packaged as ~ㄴ/는 걸 알아채다 or ~다는 걸 알아채다, not a borrowed 'that'-clause; and don't confuse the lookalike 알아보다 — to notice/catch on is 알아채다, while to recognize or check into is 알아보다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 알아채다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 알아채요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 알아채다 (notice/catch on, suddenly) with 알아보다 (recognize or look into). 'I recognized her face' is 얼굴을 알아봤어요, not 알아챘어요.
Writing the uncontracted past 알아채었어요. The 채 + 었 contracts to 챘: 알아챘어요.
Trying to attach an English 'that'-clause directly. 'I noticed that he lied' becomes 그가 거짓말한 걸 알아챘어요, using ~ㄴ 걸 to nominalize the clause.

words.shortExplanation: 들어오다 means "to come in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 들어오다 (deureooda) = "to come in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 들어와요 plus one useful sentence like 들어오세요 ("Please come in"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 들어오고 싶어요 for what you want, 들어올 수 있어요 for what you can, 들어올 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The standard polite invitation at a door; warmer than the bare command 들어와요.

examples.en: Come in, quick.
examples.note: Bare 들어와 (반말) to a close friend or family at the door.

examples.en: What time do you get home?
examples.note: Everyday register; 들어오다 is the natural verb for arriving home, not 오다.

examples.en: A lot of orders came in to the office earlier.
examples.note: Real-situation, figurative use: 주문이 들어오다 = orders come in (subject + 이/가).

words.nuance: 들어오다 combines 들다 (to enter) + 오다 (to come), so it is specifically 'to come IN toward where the speaker/hearer is'. The hard contrast for English speakers is its twin 들어가다 (들다 + 가다): both translate as 'go/come in', but Korean forces you to track viewpoint — choose 들어오다 only when the motion is toward your side, and 들어가다 when it moves away. In daily life 집에 들어오다 means 'get home' (not just 오다), and it also goes figurative for things arriving to you: 연락/전화/주문/돈이 들어오다, where the subject takes 이/가, never 를. Politeness ranges from the blunt 들어와 to the welcoming 들어오세요 you say to a guest. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 들어가요 the way English reuses 'come', and forgetting that 'inside here' wants 안으로/안에.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들어오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 들어가요 when you mean entering toward yourself — English 'come in' maps to 들어와요; 들어가다 moves away from you.
Marking incoming messages with 를: write 연락이 들어왔어요, not 연락을 들어왔어요 — this 들어오다 is intransitive.
Using 오다 alone for arriving home (집에 와요) when Koreans naturally say 집에 들어와요 for getting home for the day.

words.shortExplanation: 향하다 means "to head toward" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

words.nuance: 향하다 is Sino-Korean: 向 ('turn toward, face') + 하다, literally 'to do facing'. words.shortExplanation: 머물다 means "to stay" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: Simple; 며칠 (a few days) sits with no particle.

words.nuance: 머물다 means to stay or remain somewhere for a stretch of time — a hotel, a friend's house, a city — and figuratively for a feeling or gaze that lingers (마음에 머물다). The synonym boundary: 묵다 is the close cousin specifically for lodging overnight (호텔에서 묵다) and feels a touch more colloquial for 'put up at'; 있다 ('be/stay') is what casual travel talk actually uses — 호텔에 있어요 — while 머물다 sounds a bit more composed or written. words.shortExplanation: 다가오다 means "to come closer / to approach" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.en: I want to come closer / to approach.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

examples.note: Simple; 한테 marks me as the point it moved toward.

words.nuance: 다가오다 is 다가서다/다가- ('draw near') + 오다 (come), so it is 'to approach TOWARD the speaker' — a person, animal, or even a date getting closer. Versus the simpler 가까워지다 ('become close', often abstract like relationships), 다가오다 keeps a sense of active motion or a looming approach. A person you approach takes 한테/에게; when time or events are the subject they take 이/가 (시험이 다가와요) and the verb becomes the go-to way to say something is 'coming up'. It can also mean 'resonate' — 마음에 다가오다. The pitfall is mixing the come/go pair, plus marking the approaching event with 를 instead of 이/가.

examples.en: I slowly approached the cat.
examples.note: Simple; 한테 + 천천히 — moving toward the cat (away from me).

examples.en: Try reaching out to that person first.
examples.note: Everyday advice; -아 보다 (give it a try) + 먼저 (first).

words.nuance: 다가가다 is 다가- ('draw near') + 가다 (go), the 'going' counterpart of 다가오다: you move closer toward a target that sits away from the speaker. The whole difficulty for English speakers is that English 'approach' has no built-in direction, but Korean splits it by viewpoint — 다가가다 = I close in on it, 다가오다 = it closes in on me — so you must pick based on where 'here' is. examples.note: Simple; the everyday line a student says leaving the house.

examples.en: I'll just pop to the restroom.
examples.note: Everyday; the polite way to step away briefly and signal you'll return.

examples.ko: 부모님 댁에 다녀오느라 주말이 다 갔어요.

words.nuance: 다녀오다 is 다니다 ('go to and fro, frequent') + 오다 (come), fusing 'go AND come back' into one verb — so it is the natural choice whenever you leave somewhere but will return. It anchors two everyday home rituals: the person leaving says 다녀올게요 / 다녀오겠습니다, and whoever stays answers 다녀오세요 — a tiny exchange you will hear in every Korean household and drama. 에 marks the place; spotlights the very moment of crossing the threshold.

words.nuance: 들어서다 is 들다 (enter) + 서다 (stand/step), so its core image is 'to step across and stand inside' — it pinpoints the moment of crossing the threshold, not the journey of entering. The contrast English speakers need is with 들어가다/들어오다: those track direction (in-away vs in-toward), whereas 들어서다 freezes the instant your foot lands inside, which is why it pairs so often with -자/-니 ('the moment I stepped in …'). It is slightly more descriptive/literary, so for plain spoken 'go in / come in' a beginner should still reach for 들어가다 and 들어오다. It also has a strong figurative life in writing: 새 시대/국면/단계에 들어서다 = to enter a new era/phase/stage, and 건물이 들어서다 = a building 'goes up/comes to stand' on a site. Place takes 에, direction 으로. The pitfall is treating it as a free synonym of 들어가다 in casual speech, where it sounds oddly narrated.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들어서다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating 들어서다 as identical to 들어가다 — it stresses the act of stepping in, not the direction, and sounds literary in casual chat.
Forcing 를 on the place: it is 방에 들어서다, not 방을 들어서다 — the location takes 에 (or 으로 for direction).
Missing its idiomatic figurative use — 새 시대에 들어서다 (enter a new era) is standard; a flat 들어가다 there feels off.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 들어서다 becomes 들어설 수 있어요 ("can") and 들어설 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.english: to go over / to pass over
words.shortExplanation: 넘어가다 means "to go over / to pass over" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 넘어가다 (neomeogada) means "to go over / to pass over". Start from the polite form 넘어가요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 넘어가다. A strong first sentence is 다음으로 넘어가다 ("to move on to the next"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 넘어가다 also becomes 넘어가고 싶어요 (want), 넘어갈 수 있어요 (can), and 넘어갈 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

words.nuance: 넘어가다 is 넘다 (to cross/exceed) + 가다 (go): literally to go over something — a hill, wall, or ridge — to the other side, and figuratively to 'move on' to the next page, topic, or step (다음으로 넘어가다), which makes it a fixture in lessons and meetings. Watch three layers English speakers blur: the physical obstacle takes 를/을 (산을 넘어가다), the next item takes 으로/로 (다음으로 넘어가다), and the idiom 그냥 넘어가다 means to let something slide / overlook it. It also fixes the sunset image, 해가 넘어가다. The dangerous near-look-alike is 넘어지다 ('to fall over, topple') — one letter apart but a totally different action — and don't confuse it with the transitive 넘기다 ('to flip/hand over/get past'). For simply going somewhere, 가다 suffices; 넘어가다 specifically adds the 'over/across or onward' nuance. The pitfall is the 넘어가다/넘어지다 mix-up and choosing the wrong particle for obstacle vs next-step.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 넘어가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 넘어가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 넘어가다 (go over to the other side / move on) with 넘어지다 (to fall down, topple) — one syllable, opposite meaning.
Using the wrong particle: an obstacle takes 를/을 (산을 넘어가다) but the next step takes 으로 (다음으로 넘어가다).
Mixing it with transitive 넘기다 — you 페이지를 넘기다 (flip a page) but 다음 페이지로 넘어가다 (move on to the next page).

words.shortExplanation: 돌다 means "to turn / to go around" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to turn / to go around" in Korean is 돌다 (dolda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 돌아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 돌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 오른쪽으로 돌다 ("to turn right") — then reshape the same stem into 돌고 싶어요 (desire), 돌 수 있어요 (ability), and 돌 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to turn / to go around.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can turn / to go around.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to turn / to go around.

examples.en: I went around the track once.
examples.note: Everyday; 를 marks the loop's path, 한 바퀴 counts the lap.

examples.ko: 요즘 회사에 이상한 소문이 돌고 있어요.

words.nuance: 돌다 means to turn, spin, or go around, and intransitively to circulate (소문/돈/감기가 돌다 = rumors/money/a cold going around). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, which is the main hurdle: the ㄹ vanishes before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal is 돕니다 (not 돌습니다) and the polite 'please turn' for directions is 도세요 (not 돌으세요), while the 어-form is the regular 돌아요. The crucial pair English speakers must split is 돌다 vs 돌리다: 돌다 is intransitive (something turns/spins by itself — 팽이가 돌다, the wheel turns), whereas 돌리다 is transitive (you turn something — 핸들을 돌리다). Direction takes 으로 (오른쪽으로 돌다); a lap takes the counter 바퀴. The pitfall is regularizing the ㄹ-stem forms and using 돌다 where you actually act on an object, which needs 돌리다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the polite request as 돌으세요 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 도세요.
Saying 돌습니다 for the formal present — the ㄹ-stem rule removes the ㄹ, giving 돕니다.
Using 돌다 when you turn an object (핸들을 돌다) — that needs the transitive 돌리다 (핸들을 돌리다).
notes: ㄹ: memorize 돌아 and 돌아요 together.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.body: 돌다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 돌아요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.shortExplanation: 돌리다 means "to turn (something)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 돌리다 (dollida) = "to turn (something)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 돌려요 plus one useful sentence like 고개를 돌리다 ("to turn one's head"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 돌리고 싶어요 for what you want, 돌릴 수 있어요 for what you can, 돌릴 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
를 marks the thing turned (body part); 고개를 돌리다 = look/turn away.

examples.en: I turned my head to the left.
examples.note: Simple; 를 (object) + 으로 (direction) — you act on 고개.

examples.en: I ran the washing machine before bed.
examples.note: Everyday household phrase; 돌리다 = operate the machine.

examples.ko: 끝까지 설득해서 결국 그 사람 마음을 돌렸어요.
examples.romanization: kkeutkkaji seoldeukaeseo gyeolguk geu saram maeumeul dollyeosseoyo.

words.nuance: 돌리다 is the transitive partner of 돌다 (built with the causative -리-): you turn something — a handle, your head — or 'run' a machine like a washer or vacuum (세탁기를 돌리다). It is a regular 이-stem verb, so the 어-form is simply 돌려요 / 돌렸어요 with no ㄹ-drop drama, unlike its intransitive sibling 돌다. The clean rule English speakers need: if the thing turns by itself, use 돌다 (팽이가 돌아요); if you make something turn, use 돌리다 (팽이를 돌려요) — Korean splits self-turning vs turning-something the way English 'turn' does not. It also carries rich idioms: 마음을 돌리다 (change someone's mind / win them over), 고개를 돌리다 (turn away), 전화를 돌리다 (older: dial / route a call). The object always takes 를/을. The pitfall is reaching for 돌다 when an object is involved, and over-applying ㄹ-stem rules that simply don't apply here.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 돌다 (turn by itself) and 돌리다 (turn something) — the washer is 세탁기를 돌려요 because you operate it.
Dropping the object marker: it is 고개를 돌려요, not 고개 돌려요 — 돌리다 needs a 를/을 object.
Applying the ㄹ-stem drop here: 돌리다 is regular, so it is 돌립니다, never 돕니다 — that form belongs to 돌다.

words.english: to set out / to step forward
words.shortExplanation: 나서다 means "to set out / to step forward" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 나서다 (naseoda) means "to set out / to step forward". Start from the polite form 나서요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 나서다. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 나서다 also becomes 나서고 싶어요 (want), 나설 수 있어요 (can), and 나설 수 없어요 (cannot). words.nuance: 나서다 is 나다/나- ('come out') + 서다 (stand/step), giving two linked senses: to set out / head off (집을 나서다 = leave home to start your day; 길을 나서다 = hit the road) and to step forward — physically to the front, or figuratively to volunteer and take charge (문제 해결에 나서다 = step up to tackle a problem). The line versus plain 나가다 ('go out') matters: 나가다 just exits a space, while 나서다 carries the flavor of launching a journey or actively putting yourself forward, often with initiative or even pushiness — note 나서다 can imply meddling, as in 남의 일에 나서다 (butt into others' business). For leaving home, 집을 나서다 takes the object marker 를/을, where 나가다 would too but sounds plainer. Idioms like 발 벗고 나서다 (pitch in wholeheartedly) live here. The pitfall is treating it as a flat synonym of 나가다 and missing the 'take the initiative' nuance.

Use 나서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 나서다 (set out / step up) with 나가다 (just go out) — 나서다 implies beginning a journey or actively volunteering.
Using 에 for the place left: it is 집을 나서다 (를/을), not 집에 나서다.
Overusing 나서다 for 'help out' without noticing its 'put yourself forward' tone — 남의 일에 나서다 can sound like meddling.

examples.note: Real-situation; 눈이 마주치다 (subject + 이/가) + -아서 (so, as a result).

words.nuance: 마주치다 is 마주 ('facing, head-on') + 치다 ('strike'), literally 'to strike facing each other', i.e. to run/bump into someone or something unexpectedly, by chance. The person you encounter takes 를/을 (친구를 마주치다) or the comitative 와/과 (친구와 마주치다), and it is the fixed phrase for eye contact, 눈이 마주치다 — where the eyes are the subject with 이/가, a structure English speakers often get wrong by saying 눈을 마주쳤어요. The key contrast is with 만나다 ('to meet'): 만나다 covers planned, intended meetings (친구를 만나다 = meet up with a friend on purpose), while 마주치다 is strictly accidental and momentary, hence its frequent companion 우연히 (by chance). Compare also 부딪치다, the more physical 'collide/crash into' (사람과 부딪치다 = literally bump bodies). The pitfall is using 마주치다 for an arranged get-together, and mis-marking the eye-contact phrase with 를 instead of 이/가.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 마주치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 마주쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 마주치다 for a planned meet-up — that is 만나다; 마주치다 is always by chance.
Saying 눈을 마주쳤어요 for 'eyes met' — the set phrase makes 눈 the subject: 눈이 마주쳤어요.
Confusing it with 부딪치다 (physically collide) — 마주치다 is encountering/seeing, not crashing into someone.

words.shortExplanation: 데려오다 means "to bring (a person)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 데려오다 (deryeooda) = "to bring (a person)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 데려와요 plus one useful sentence like 친구를 데려오다 ("to bring a friend (here)"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 데려오고 싶어요 for what you want, 데려올 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 데려와요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The person is always marked with 를/을, never 와 'with'

examples.en: Bring your sibling.
examples.note: Bare casual command between close family

examples.en: I'll bring a friend to the party tomorrow.
examples.note: 를 marks the person, 에 marks the destination

examples.en: We brought the adopted puppy home from the shelter.
examples.note: Real-life adoption context; works for animals too

words.nuance: 데려오다 = 데리다 (to have someone in one's charge) + 오다 (to come), so it literally means 'come having someone with you' — to bring a living being TOWARD the speaker's side. The pair to learn against it is 데려가다 (take a person away from here) and 데리고 오다, which is the looser two-word version with the same meaning. The decisive split is animacy: people and animals take 데려오다/데려가다, but objects take 가져오다/가져가다 — Korean grammaticalizes 'living vs non-living' where English just says 'bring' for everything, and this is the number-one trap. Because 오다 is built in, the conjugation follows 오다: 와요/왔어요, giving 데려와요, 데려왔어요. It is neutral in register and extremely common in everyday speech: 아이를 데려오다, 친구를 데려오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데려오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데려와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 가방을 데려와요 for 'bring a bag' — 데려오다 is only for people/animals; an inanimate bag must be 가방을 가져와요.
Marking the person with 와/과 as in 친구와 데려와요 by copying English 'come WITH a friend' — the person is the object and takes 를/을: 친구를 데려와요.
Using 데려오다 when the movement is away from you (e.g. taking your kid to grandma's); that direction is 데려가다, not 데려오다.
notes: 오다 compound: memorize 데려와 and 데려와요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 데려다주다 means "to take (someone) somewhere" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 데려다주다 (deryeodajuda) means "to take (someone) somewhere". Start from the polite form 데려다줘요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 데려다주다. A strong first sentence is 집까지 데려다주다 ("to take (someone) all the way home"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 데려다주다 also becomes 데려다주고 싶어요 (want), 데려다줄 수 있어요 (can), and 못 데려다줘요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to take (someone) all the way home
usagePhrases.note: 까지 'as far as' marks the endpoint of the escort

examples.en: I'll take you there.
examples.note: Casual offer to a friend; 내가 stresses 'I'll do it'

examples.en: It's raining, so I'll take you home.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 까지 marks the endpoint

examples.ko: 아이를 매일 아침 학교에 데려다주고 회사에 가요.
examples.romanization: aireul maeil achim hakgyoe deryeodajugo hoesae gayo.
examples.en: I drop my child at school every morning and then go to work.
examples.note: Real routine; 데려다주고 chains to the next action

words.nuance: 데려다주다 stacks three pieces: 데리다 (have in charge) + -다(가) (do, then) + 주다 (give/do for someone), so it means 'escort a person to a place AND it's a favor for them'. Contrast it sharply with bare 데려가다 (take someone along), which is neutral about whose benefit it is — 데려다주다 always frames the trip as a kindness done for the passenger, exactly the nuance English 'give a ride / drop off' carries. The closest synonym 바래다주다 emphasizes accompanying/seeing off (often walking), while 데려다주다 emphasizes delivering them to the destination. For objects the parallel word is 가져다주다 (bring/fetch a thing for someone), so keep the people/thing split. Conjugation rides on 주다: 줘요/줬어요 → 데려다줘요, 데려다줬어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데려다주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데려다줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데려가다 to a friend you're kindly driving home — it loses the 'for your sake' warmth; 데려다주다 is the natural offer.
Saying 가져다주다 for a person ('데려다주다' vs '가져다주다'): 가져다주다 fetches an object, so use 데려다주다 for people.
Writing the request as 데려다 주세요 with a space and treating 주다 as separate is acceptable, but learners often drop 주다 entirely (데려다세요), which is ungrammatical — keep 주다.

words.shortExplanation: 찾아가다 means "to go visit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to go visit" in Korean is 찾아가다 (chajagada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 찾아가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 찾아가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 선생님을 찾아가다 ("to go (and seek out) the teacher") — then reshape the same stem into 찾아가고 싶어요 (desire), 찾아갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 찾아가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to go (and seek out) the teacher
usagePhrases.note: A person being visited takes 를/을

examples.en: I go visit grandma's place on the weekend.
examples.note: Everyday visit; 에 marks the destination

examples.en: If there's a problem, go to the office in person.
examples.note: 직접 + 로 = head there yourself to sort it out

examples.ko: 주소만 들고 처음 가는 동네를 물어물어 찾아갔어요.
examples.romanization: jusoman deulgo cheoeum ganeun dongnereul mureomureo chajagasseoyo.
examples.en: With only the address, I found my way to the unfamiliar neighborhood by asking around.
examples.note: Shows the 'seek out / track down' shade

words.nuance: 찾아가다 = 찾다 (to look for/seek) + -아 + 가다 (to go), literally 'go seeking', so it is not plain 가다 'go' — it adds the sense of actively going TO reach a specific person or hard-to-find place, away from the speaker. Its mirror image is 찾아오다 (someone comes seeking YOU), and the direction (가 = away, 와 = toward) is the whole contrast. Beside neutral 방문하다 (Sino-Korean 訪問, 'visit', stiff/formal, used in writing and news), 찾아가다 is the warm spoken word that implies effort and intention to meet. It also has a second concrete sense: 찾아가다 = to go and collect/claim something (e.g. 택배를 찾아가다 'pick up your parcel'). It rides on 가다: 가요/갔어요 → 찾아가요, 찾아갔어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 찾아가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 찾아가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 찾아오다 when YOU are the one travelling — 찾아오다 means the other person comes to you; if you go to them it's 찾아가다.
Substituting plain 가다 for an effortful visit and losing the 'seek out' nuance — 친구를 가요 is wrong/odd; say 친구를 찾아가요 or 친구한테 가요.
Forgetting the second meaning 'claim/pick up': students translate 택배 찾아가세요 as 'go visit the parcel'; it means 'come collect your parcel'.

words.shortExplanation: 들어주다 means "to grant (a request)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 들어주다 (deureojuda) = "to grant (a request)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 들어줘요 plus one useful sentence like 부탁을 들어주다 ("to grant a favor / say yes to a request"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to grant a favor / say yes to a request
usagePhrases.note: 부탁 is the most frequent object of this verb

examples.en: Just do me one favor.
examples.note: Casual; 하나만 'just one' softens the ask

examples.en: Thank you so much for granting my request.
examples.note: Honorific -주시- thanks a superior for saying yes

examples.ko: 아이의 부탁을 다 들어줄 수는 없지만 오늘은 들어줬어요.
examples.romanization: aiui butageul da deureojul suneun eopsjiman oneureun deureojwosseoyo.
examples.en: I can't grant the child's every request, but today I did.
examples.note: Real situation contrasting limits and an exception

words.nuance: 들어주다 = 듣다 (to hear/listen) + -어 + 주다 (do for someone), and crucially the ㄷ of 듣다 turns into ㄹ before a vowel (듣 → 들-), a regular ㄷ-irregular shift, giving 들어-. The 주다 adds 'as a favour for that person', so the whole verb means either (1) accept and fulfil a request/wish, or (2) listen attentively and supportively. Contrast it with plain 듣다, which is just neutral 'hear/listen' with no benefit attached — 음악을 들어요 'I listen to music' could never be 들어줘요 unless you mean you're doing it FOR someone. Its near-synonym 들어드리다 is the same verb made humble (드리다) for elders/customers. Habitual partners: 부탁을 들어주다, 소원을 들어주다, 이야기를 들어주다. Don't confuse it with 들다 'to lift/hold', a totally different verb.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들어주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 듣다 alone to mean 'grant my request' — 제 부탁을 들어요 sounds like 'I hear my favor'; granting is 부탁을 들어줘요.
Confusing 들어주다 (from 듣다, listen) with 들어주다 from 들다 (lift) for someone; for carrying a heavy thing for someone you'd say 들어 주다 (들다) — context and 짐 'load' vs 부탁 'request' disambiguate.
Forgetting the ㄷ→ㄹ change and writing 듣어줘요; the correct conjugated stem is 들어-, so 들어줘요.

words.shortExplanation: 챙기다 means "to take care of" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 챙기다 (chaenggida) means "to take care of". Start from the polite form 챙겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 챙기다. A strong first sentence is 짐을 챙기다 ("to pack/gather one's things"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 챙기다 also becomes 챙기고 싶어요 (want), 챙길 수 있어요 (can), and 못 챙겨요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take care of.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to take care of.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to take care of.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Grabbing the items you need before leaving

examples.en: Grab an umbrella!
examples.note: Bare casual reminder; object 우산 with no particle

examples.ko: 나갈 때 지갑이랑 열쇠를 꼭 챙기세요.
examples.romanization: nagal ttae jigabirang yeolsoereul kkok chaenggiseyo.
examples.en: Be sure to take your wallet and keys when you leave.
examples.note: 꼭 'without fail' + 챙기다 = don't forget to grab

examples.ko: 엄마가 매일 제 도시락을 챙겨 주시고 건강도 챙겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: eommaga maeil je dosirageul chaenggyeo jusigo geongangdo chaenggyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Mom packs my lunch every day and looks after my health too.
examples.note: Shows both senses: pack things AND care for a person

words.nuance: 챙기다 is one of the most useful 'caring' verbs in daily Korean, with a cluster of related senses: (1) gather/pack the things you need (짐을 챙기다), (2) make sure not to skip something, especially food (밥 챙겨 먹어 'make sure you eat'), and (3) look after a person attentively (동생 좀 챙겨 'keep an eye on your sibling'). Set it against 돌보다 (care for over time, like nursing a child or the sick): 챙기다 is quicker, more about 'making sure / not letting slip', while 돌보다 is sustained nurturing. It also contrasts with 챙겨 주다, where adding 주다 makes the care explicitly a favour for someone. The English trap is reaching for 들다 'lift' or 가지다 'have' when you mean 'grab/remember to bring' — that everyday act is 챙기다. Native warmth: 잘 챙겨 먹어요 is a standard way to say 'take care of yourself'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 들다 'to lift' for 'remember to bring an umbrella' — 우산을 들어요 means physically holding it up; 'grab/take it along' is 우산을 챙겨요.
Saying 밥을 먹어 to tell someone to take care of themselves, missing the nuance — Koreans say 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 ('make sure you eat'), where 챙기다 carries the care.
Treating 챙기다 as only 'pack objects' and never using it for people; 아이를 챙기다 / 동생을 챙기다 ('look after') is just as common.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 챙기다 becomes 챙길 수 있어요 ("can") and 챙길 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 챙기다 is one of the most useful 'caring' verbs in daily Korean, with a cluster of related senses: (1) gather/pack the things you need (짐을 챙기다), (2) make sure not to skip something, especially food (밥 챙겨 먹어 'make sure you eat'), and (3) look after a person attentively (동생 좀 챙겨 'keep an eye on your sibling'). Native warmth: 잘 챙겨 먹어요 is a standard way to say 'take care of yourself'.

Set it against 돌보다 (care for over time, like nursing a child or the sick): 챙기다 is quicker, more about 'making sure / not letting slip', while 돌보다 is sustained nurturing. It also contrasts with 챙겨 주다, where adding 주다 makes the care explicitly a favour for someone.
The English trap is reaching for 들다 'lift' or 가지다 'have' when you mean 'grab/remember to bring' — that everyday act is 챙기다.

words.shortExplanation: 바래다주다 means "to see (someone) off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to see (someone) off" in Korean is 바래다주다 (baraedajuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 바래다줘요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 바래다주다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 집까지 바래다주다 ("to walk/see (someone) all the way home") — then reshape the same stem into 바래다주고 싶어요 (desire), 바래다줄 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 바래다줘요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

words.nuance: 바래다주다 = 바래다 (an old verb meaning to accompany/see off) + 주다 (do as a favour), so it means walking or going along with someone partway to send them off kindly — a small act of care, warmer than just waving goodbye at the door. Compare it with its close neighbour 데려다주다: 데려다주다 stresses DELIVERING the person to a destination (often by car, you're the one in charge), whereas 바래다주다 stresses ACCOMPANYING/seeing off, traditionally on foot and out of courtesy. The dangerous look-alike is 바라다 'to wish/hope' (바라요 'I hope') and the spelling slips 바래요 — they are unrelated verbs, so keep them apart. The 주다 ending again frames the act as for the other person's benefit. Conjugation follows 주다: 바래다줘요, 바래다줬어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바래다주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바래다줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 바래다주다 (see someone off) with 바라다 (to wish); 'I hope you...' is 바라다, not 바래다주다.
Using 데려가다 for a courteous send-off home; 데려가다 just means 'take along' — the kind 'walk you home' nuance needs 바래다주다.
Dropping 주다 and saying 바래다 alone in modern speech — on its own 바래다 is dated; the living form is 바래다주다.

words.shortExplanation: 인사드리다 means "to greet (politely)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 인사드리다 (insadeurida) = "to greet (politely)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 인사드려요 plus one useful sentence like 선생님께 인사드리다 ("to (humbly) greet the teacher"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 인사드리고 싶어요 for what you want, 인사드릴 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 인사드려요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

words.nuance: 인사드리다 is the humble (겸양) counterpart of 인사하다, built from 인사 (Sino-Korean 人事, literally 'person-affair', meaning a greeting/bow) + 드리다, the humble version of 주다 'to give'. 드리다 lowers the SPEAKER to raise the listener, so you use 인사드리다 when greeting someone older or higher in status (a teacher, boss, in-laws), whereas neutral 인사하다 is for peers and juniors. The sharp contrast is direction of respect: 인사하다 is plain, 인사드리다 humbles yourself, and there is NO 인사받다-style humble for receiving. English has no grammatical humility, so learners either over-use it with friends (sounds stiff/odd) or under-use it with elders (sounds rude). Note the natural particle is 께 ('to', honorific), not 에게/한테, when naming the respected person.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 인사드리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 인사드려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 인사드리다 with close friends — it sounds overly formal/servile; among equals say 인사하다 (친구한테 인사했어).
Marking the respected person with 한테/에게 (선생님한테 인사드려요) instead of the honorific 께 — say 선생님께 인사드려요.
Assuming 인사 means only 'hello'; 인사 covers bows, greetings, and paying respects, so 인사드리다 can mean 'pay one's respects', not just 'say hi'.

words.shortExplanation: 도와드리다 means "to help (politely)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 도와드리다 (dowadeurida) means "to help (politely)". Start from the polite form 도와드려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 도와드리다. A strong first sentence is 무엇을 도와드릴까요? ("How may I help you?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 도와드리다 also becomes 도와드리고 싶어요 (want), 도와드릴 수 있어요 (can), and 못 도와드려요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

words.nuance: 도와드리다 is the humble form of 도와주다 ('help (as a favour)'), where 돕다 (to help) becomes 도와- by the ㅂ-irregular (돕 + 아 → 도와), and the helper-benefit 주다 is upgraded to its humble twin 드리다. So it literally means 'humbly do the favour of helping' — you lower yourself to help someone above you: a customer, elder, or guest. Contrast the three levels you must keep straight: 돕다 (bare dictionary 'help'), 도와주다 (help someone, neutral/friendly), 도와드리다 (help a superior, humble). English flattens all of these to 'help', so the pitfall is using 도와주다 with a customer (too casual for service) or, conversely, 도와드리다 with a buddy (oddly stiff). The phrase 무엇을 도와드릴까요? is the fixed, must-know service line. Conjugation follows 드리다: 도와드려요, 도와드렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 도와드리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 도와드려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 도와줄까요? to a customer or elder — it's too casual for service; the polite form is 도와드릴까요?.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular and writing 돕아드려요; 돕다 + 아 becomes 도와-, so it's 도와드려요.
Using 도와드리다 toward a younger friend; among peers 도와줄게 (도와주다) is natural and 도와드릴게 sounds over-formal.
notes: ㅂ irregular (돕다): memorize 도와드려 and 도와드려요 together.

The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

words.nuance: 부탁드리다 is the humble form of 부탁하다 ('to request a favour'), from 부탁 (Sino-Korean 付託, 'entrust/commit to') + 드리다, the humble 'give'. You use it to ask something of a superior, client, or anyone you want to treat with deference, while 부탁하다 is the neutral version for peers and 부탁해 the casual one for friends. The must-memorize fixed expression is 잘 부탁드립니다 / 잘 부탁드려요 — said when you begin a job, join a group, or ask for ongoing cooperation; it has no clean English equivalent ('please treat me well / I look forward to working with you'). The English pitfall is twofold: treating it as one literal 'please' (it's really 'I humbly entrust this favour to you'), and using plain 부탁하다 with a boss, which reads as too blunt. Particle: the person asked takes honorific 께. Conjugates on 드리다: 부탁드려요, 부탁드렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부탁드리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 부탁드려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 부탁하다 to a superior to sound polite — it's too plain; choose 부탁드리다 (부장님, 부탁드립니다).
Translating 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'please do well' and misusing it — it's a fixed social greeting meaning 'I look forward to your kind help'.
Saying 부탁드려 to a close friend; casually you'd say 부탁해 / 부탁 좀 들어줘, and 부탁드려 sounds stiff.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 사귀고 싶어요 for what you want, 사귈 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 사귀어요 for what you can't. Short everyday negative.

Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

words.nuance: 사귀다 covers BOTH platonic 'make friends' and romantic 'date / go out with', and only context (and the object) tells them apart: 친구를 사귀다 is befriending, 남자친구/여자친구를 사귀다 or just '두 사람이 사귀다' is dating. It contrasts with 만나다, which means 'meet/see' and is sometimes used loosely for dating too, but 사귀다 specifically marks an ongoing committed relationship, not a single meeting. The headline trap is spelling/conjugation: the stem ends in the vowel ㅟ, which does NOT contract in standard Korean, so the polite present is 사귀어요 — never the colloquial 사겨요 you'll hear spoken but mustn't write. The future/볼 forms do contract normally: 사귈 거예요, 사귈까요. Habitual partners: 친구를 사귀다, 오래 사귀다, 사귀자.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사귀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사귀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing or spelling the polite present as 사겨요 — the ㅟ stem doesn't contract; the correct written form is 사귀어요.
Using 만나다 when you mean a committed relationship — 만나다 can be a one-off meeting; for 'we're dating' say 사귀어요/사귀고 있어요.

Marking the partner with 와/과 like English 'date WITH' (친구와 사귀어요 is fine for 'with', but the simple object pattern 친구를 사귀어요 is the default) — learners drop the object particle and say 친구 사귀어, which is casual-only.

words.nuance: 친해지다 = 친하다 (to be close/friendly, with 친 from Sino-Korean 親 'intimate/familial') + -어지다, the 'become' suffix that turns an adjective into a change-of-state verb. So the built-in contrast is adjective vs verb: 친하다 describes the STATE of already being close (우리는 친해요 'we're close'), while 친해지다 describes the PROCESS of becoming close (우리 친해졌어요 'we've grown close'). English uses 'close' for both, so learners wrongly say 친했어요 ('we were close') when they mean 'we became close'. Because the partner is someone you grow close WITH, the particle is 와/과 (or 하고/랑), not the object 를. Conjugation follows 지다: 친해져요, 친해졌어요. Natural partners: 빨리/금방 친해지다, 친해지고 싶다.

examples.en: Those clothes really suit you.

examples.ko: 새 팀에 들어가서 사람들과 잘 어울리려고 노력했어요.

examples.note: Real situation blending 'mingle' and 'fit in'

words.nuance: 어울리다 runs on two everyday senses you choose by context: (1) with people (와/과) it means to mingle, socialize, get along — 친구들과 어울리다; (2) with things, clothes, or colors it means to match / suit / look good together — 옷이 잘 어울려요 'that outfit suits you'. For the matching sense, its synonym is 맞다 'to fit', but 맞다 is about correct size/fit while 어울리다 is about aesthetic harmony. English keeps 'hang out' and 'suit' in totally separate words, so the pitfall is not realizing one Korean verb does both — and that the compliment 'it suits you' is 어울려요, not 좋아 보여요. Note: the subject of the 'suit' sense is the clothing, with the person in 한테/에게.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어울리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 어울려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Marking the matching item with 를 (옷을 어울려요) — in the 'suit' sense the clothing is the subject: 옷이 어울려요.

words.shortExplanation: 헤어지다 means "to part" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 헤어지다 (heeojida) = "to part". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 헤어져요 plus one useful sentence like 친구와 헤어지다 ("to part from a friend"). Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: Casual; -자 = 'let's', simply splitting up to go home

examples.ko: 늦은 밤에 친구와 역 앞에서 헤어졌어요.
examples.romanization: neujeun bame chinguwa yeok apeseo heeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I parted from my friend in front of the station late at night.
examples.note: 와 marks the friend, 에서 the place

examples.en: We dated a long time but finally broke up last year.
examples.note: Romantic break-up; pairs naturally with 사귀다

words.nuance: 헤어지다 means two (or more) people who were together separating and going their own ways, and it doubles as THE standard word for a romantic break-up — 남자친구와 헤어졌어요 'I broke up with my boyfriend'. It is the natural antonym of 만나다 'to meet'. Keep it apart from 떠나다 'to leave (a place/person behind)', which focuses on one person departing a location, and from 헤매다 'to wander/be lost', a similar-looking but unrelated verb. The particle for the other person is 와/과 (or 하고/랑) 'with', NOT the object 를, because both sides separate mutually — a key difference from English transitive 'I left him'. Built on -어지다, it conjugates as 헤어져요, 헤어졌어요. The everyday goodbye sense (그럼 여기서 헤어져요) is gentle and common; only context or a partner like 남자친구 signals the break-up reading.

words.shortExplanation: 돌보다 means "to take care of" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 돌보다 (dolboda) means "to take care of". Start from the polite form 돌봐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 돌보다. A strong first sentence is 아이를 돌보다 ("to take care of a child"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 돌보다 also becomes 돌보고 싶어요 (want), 돌볼 수 있어요 (can), and 못 돌봐요 (cannot). usagePhrases.en: I do not take care of.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to take care of.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to take care of.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to take care of a child
usagePhrases.note: The cared-for one takes 를/을 (it's transitive)

examples.en: Look after your sibling for a bit.
examples.note: Casual command; 좀 softens the request

examples.romanization: jumare uri gangaji jom dolbwa juseyo.
examples.en: Please look after our puppy this weekend.

examples.ko: 할머니가 편찮으셔서 제가 돌봐 드리고 있어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga pyeonchaneusyeoseo jega dolbwa deurigo isseoyo.

examples.note: Humble 돌봐 드리다 for an elder; sustained caregiving

words.nuance: 돌보다 = 돌(아) + 보다 ('look around and watch over'), meaning to actively look after and nurture a person, child, patient, animal, or even plants over time — it carries responsibility and warmth, well beyond plain 보다 'to see/look'. Set it against 챙기다, which is quicker 'make sure / don't let slip' care (밥 챙겨 먹어), whereas 돌보다 is sustained nurturing (아기를 돌보다 'raise/tend a baby'). It also contrasts with the Sino-Korean 보살피다 (a near-synonym, slightly more literary/tender 'tend, look after'), and with 키우다 'to raise/bring up', which stresses growing/rearing rather than day-to-day care. The cared-for one is the direct object with 를/을. The English trap is reaching for 보다 alone ('watch the kids' → not 아이를 봐요 in writing, which can sound like merely 'see'); proper caregiving is 돌보다, and the warm request form is 돌봐 주세요. Conjugation follows 보다: 봐요/봤어요 → 돌봐요, 돌봤어요.

words.shortExplanation: 건네다 means "to hand over" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
건네주다 (= 건네다 + 주다) is the polite everyday way to ask someone to pass an object to a third person; the bare 건네세요 alone sounds oddly clinical.

examples.en: Pass me the water
examples.note: Casual 반말 between friends; 건네줘 = 건네 + 줘 drops politeness for someone close.

examples.en: I handed the book to my friend
examples.note: The particle 에게 marks the person who receives — this is the core sentence frame for 건네다.

examples.ko: 면접관이 서류를 받더니 조용히 명함을 건넸어요
examples.romanization: myeonjeopgwani seoryureul batdeoni joyonghi myeonghameul geonnesseoyo

examples.note: Real-situation, slightly formal narration; note 건네다 fits a composed, deliberate hand-over.

words.nuance: 건네다 is the verb for the deliberate, hand-to-hand act of passing a physical object to a person who is right next to you — money, a card, a cup. Compare it with 주다 (to give): 주다 only says ownership transfers and can happen at any distance, while 건네다 foregrounds the physical gesture of the hand reaching across the gap, so a server '건네준다' a menu but a company '준다' a bonus. In real speech it usually appears as 건네주다 (건네 + 주다) when you do it as a favor: 이거 건네주세요. Note the special idiom 말을 건네다 'to strike up a conversation', which English speakers wrongly read literally as 'hand over words'. Conjugation is easy because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 건네 + 어 contracts to plain 건네, so the 요-form is 건네요 (never 건네어요) and the past is 건넸어요 (never 건네었어요).

Use 건네요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write the past as 건네었어요 — a stem ending in ㅔ swallows the 어, so the correct contracted form is 건넸어요.
Don't reach for 건네다 when something is mailed or sent across a distance — that is 보내다; 건네다 needs the receiver to be within arm's reach.
Don't translate 'hand over words' literally; 말을 건네다 is an idiom for addressing/greeting someone, so use it whole rather than building it word by word.

words.explanation: 돌려주다 (dollyeojuda) = "to give back". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 돌려줘요 plus one useful sentence like 빌린 책 돌려주세요 ("Please give back the book you borrowed"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 돌려주고 싶어요 for what you want, 돌려줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 돌려줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Please give back the book you borrowed
usagePhrases.note: The default verb for returning anything borrowed; 빌린 + noun + 돌려주다 is the textbook pattern.

examples.en: I'll give the umbrella back tomorrow
examples.note: 반말 promise; -ㄹ게 commits the speaker to a future action for the listener's benefit.

examples.en: Who do I have to give this back to?
examples.note: Casual 한테 marks the person who should receive it back — the everyday spoken counterpart of 에게.

examples.en: The deposit is returned in full when you check out
examples.note: Real-situation honorific: to a customer you upgrade 돌려주다 → 돌려드리다 to raise the listener.

words.nuance: 돌려주다 is the compound 돌리다 (to turn / send back) + 주다 (to give), so it literally means 'turn it back and give it' — the standard word for returning a borrowed thing, money, or even a changed situation to its rightful place. Contrast it sharply with 갚다, which is narrower and means to settle a debt or repay an obligation (빚을 갚다, 은혜를 갚다); you 돌려주다 a borrowed umbrella but you 갚다 a loan, because 갚다 carries the sense of clearing what you owe, not just physically handing an item back. When the receiver outranks you, swap 주다 for the humble 드리다 → 돌려드리다 (보증금을 돌려드립니다). Because the verb ends in 주다, every form follows 주다 exactly: 줘 → 돌려줘, 줬어요 → 돌려줬어요, 주세요 → 돌려주세요 — there are no irregular surprises.
