Use 돌려줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 갚다 for handing back a borrowed object — 갚다 is for repaying money/debt or returning a favor; a borrowed book or umbrella takes 돌려주다.
Don't say 돌려주세요 to someone you must show deference to when you are the one returning it — to a boss or elder, use 돌려드릴게요 / 돌려드립니다.
Don't split it as 돌려 주다 thinking 주다 is a separate helper here — 돌려주다 is a settled single verb meaning 'give back', so keep it together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 돌려주다 becomes 돌려줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 돌려줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 돌려주다 is the standard word for returning a borrowed thing, money, or even a changed situation to its rightful place. When the receiver outranks you, swap 주다 for the humble 드리다 → 돌려드리다 (보증금을 돌려드립니다).

Contrast it sharply with 갚다, which is narrower and means to settle a debt or repay an obligation (빚을 갚다, 은혜를 갚다); you 돌려주다 a borrowed umbrella but you 갚다 a loan, because 갚다 carries the sense of clearing what you owe, not just physically handing an item back.
돌려주다 is the compound 돌리다 (to turn / send back) + 주다 (to give), so it literally means 'turn it back and give it'.
Because the verb ends in 주다, every form follows 주다 exactly: 줘 → 돌려줘, 줬어요 → 돌려줬어요, 주세요 → 돌려주세요 — there are no irregular surprises.

words.english: to look after / pack for someone
words.shortExplanation: 챙겨주다 means "to look after / pack for someone" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 챙겨주다 (chaenggyeojuda) means "to look after / pack for someone". Start from the polite form 챙겨줘요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 챙겨주다. A strong first sentence is 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 ("Make sure you eat properly"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 챙겨주다 also becomes 챙겨주고 싶어요 (want), 챙겨줄 수 있어요 (can), and 챙겨줄 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I look after / pack for someone.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not look after / pack for someone.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to look after / pack for someone.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can look after / pack for someone.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to look after / pack for someone.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
A warm parting line; 챙겨 먹다 means to look after your own meals, a hugely common caring phrase.

examples.en: Mom packed a lunchbox for me
examples.note: 반말 narration; the classic image of 챙겨주다 — a parent preparing your things out of care.

examples.en: Can you get the kid's supplies ready?
examples.note: -ㄹ래요 makes a soft request to do the caring task on someone's behalf.

examples.ko: 팀장님이 신입사원들을 하나하나 챙겨주셔서 다들 잘 적응했어요
examples.romanization: timjangnimi sinipsawondeureul hanahana chaenggyeojusyeoseo dadeul jal jeogeunghaesseoyo
examples.en: Because the team lead looked after each new hire personally, everyone settled in well
examples.note: Real-situation honorific 챙겨주시다 — here it means mentoring/taking care of people, not packing objects.

words.nuance: 챙겨주다 is 챙기다 (to gather up / see to what's needed) + 주다 (to give/do for), and it radiates warmth: you thoughtfully pull together someone's belongings, meals, or wellbeing because you care about them. The dividing line with the plain 주다 is the active 'seeing-to-it' nuance — 주다 merely transfers a thing, but 챙겨주다 implies you noticed what they'd need and took the trouble to prepare it, so Koreans use it about parents, partners, and caring seniors at work. It stretches figuratively too: 생일을 챙겨주다 (make a fuss of a birthday), 신입을 챙겨주다 (look out for a newcomer). The crucial pitfall: drop the 주 and 챙기다 alone means you do it for yourself (가방을 챙기다 = pack your own bag), so only 챙겨주다 expresses doing it for another. As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 챙겨줘요, 챙겨줬어요, 챙겨주세요, and the honorific 챙겨주세요/챙겨주셨어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙겨주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't drop the 주 when you mean caring for another person — 가방을 챙기다 = pack your own bag, whereas 가방을 챙겨주다 = pack it for someone else.
Don't read 챙겨주다 as only physical packing — 생일/건강/사람을 챙겨주다 means to look after a person or occasion, so 'pack' is the wrong gloss in those cases.
Don't confuse it with 챙기다's selfish reading 잇속을 챙기다 (look after one's own interests); adding 주다 flips the focus to the other person's benefit.

words.shortExplanation: 나르다 means "to carry / haul" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to carry / haul" in Korean is 나르다 (nareuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 날라요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 나르다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 짐을 나르다 ("to haul luggage") — then reshape the same stem into 나르고 싶어요 (desire), 나를 수 있어요 (ability), and 나를 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The headword collocation — 짐/상자/물건을 나르다, repeatedly transporting things from one spot to another.

examples.en: Carry this box over, please
examples.note: 반말 favor; 날라 줘 = 날라 (르 form) + 줘 asks a friend to haul it for you.

examples.en: We carried all the chairs over
examples.note: Past 날랐어요 shows the르 irregular doubling the ㄹ before 아.

examples.ko: 이삿날 친구들이 와서 짐을 차까지 같이 날라 줬어요
examples.romanization: isannal chingudeuri waseo jimeul chakkaji gachi nalla jwosseoyo
examples.en: On moving day my friends came and hauled the bags out to the car with me
examples.note: Real-situation; 나르다 fits the repeated trips of carrying load after load.

words.nuance: 나르다 means to physically transport objects — usually heavy or numerous, like boxes, furniture, bricks, or water — from one place to another, typically over repeated trips, so it conveys effortful hauling rather than a single act. Contrast it with 들다 (to lift / hold in the hand): 들다 is just raising or holding something, while 나르다 is the whole job of relocating things across a distance, so you 들다 a single chair to look at it but 나르다 a roomful of chairs to a truck. Note also 옮기다, which simply means 'to move (something) to another place' and can be one item or one move; 나르다 specifically evokes the laborious, back-and-forth carrying. The key conjugation point is that 나르다 is a 르-irregular: before 아/어 the 르 splits and the previous syllable gains a ㄹ patchim, so 나르 + 아 → 날라, giving 날라요 and past 날랐어요. Before a consonant the stem is untouched: 나르고, 나르지, 나릅니다, and the future/potential keep it too — 나를 거예요, 나를 수 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 나르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 날라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write 나르아요 / 나르었어요 — as a 르 irregular it becomes 날라요 and 날랐어요 with a doubled ㄹ.
Don't use 나르다 for lifting or holding one thing in your hand — that is 들다; 나르다 is transporting things across a distance, usually in repeated trips.
Don't confuse the future 나를 거예요 with the present — keep the bare stem 나를- before -ㄹ 거예요/-ㄹ 수 있어요 and only switch to 날라- before 아/어 endings.
notes: 르: memorize 날라 and 날라요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 가져다주다 means "to bring (to someone)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 가져다주다 (gajyeodajuda) = "to bring (to someone)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 가져다줘요 plus one useful sentence like 물 좀 가져다주세요 ("Please bring me some water"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 가져다주고 싶어요 for what you want, 가져다줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 가져다줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Standard restaurant/home request — fetch the thing and deliver it to me.

examples.en: Bring me the remote
examples.note: 반말 everyday request; the listener fetches it and brings it back to you.

examples.en: Can you take this book to my younger sibling?
examples.note: 에게 marks the receiver; -ㄹ래요 softens it into a friendly ask.

examples.en: I'll bring your drink to your table
examples.note: Real-situation service speech — to a customer it becomes the humble 가져다드리다.

words.nuance: 가져다주다 is built from 가지다 (to have/take) + the connective -다(가) + 주다 (to give), literally 'take it and then give it', i.e. go fetch something and bring it to a person. The sharp contrast to learn is direction: 가져다주다 brings the item TOWARD the receiver, whereas 가져가다 (take + go) carries it AWAY from here, and 가져오다 (take + come) just means bring it here without the 'for someone' nuance — so a server 가져다준다 your water (brings and hands it to you), but a customer 가져간다 the leftovers (takes them away). It also works abstractly: 행운을/변화를 가져다주다 'to bring luck/change'. When serving someone of higher status, raise the verb to 가져다드리다 (가져다드리겠습니다). As a 주다 compound all forms are regular and predictable: 가져다줘요, 가져다줬어요, 가져다주세요, honorific 가져다주세요/가져다주셨어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가져다주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가져다줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 가져가다 (take away from here) — 가져다주다 brings the item TO someone; 가져가다 carries it off in the opposite direction.
Don't drop the 주 and say 가져오다 when you mean doing it for a person — 가져오다 just means 'bring here', while 가져다주다 adds 'and give it to them'.
Don't keep plain 주다 when serving an elder or customer — politely it becomes 가져다드릴게요 / 가져다드리겠습니다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 가져다주다 becomes 가져다줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 가져다줄 거예요 ("will"). As a 주다 compound all forms are regular and predictable: 가져다줘요, 가져다줬어요, 가져다주세요, honorific 가져다주세요/가져다주셨어요.

words.english: to carry on one's shoulder / back
words.shortExplanation: 메다 means "to carry on one's shoulder / back" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 메다 (meda) means "to carry on one's shoulder / back". Start from the polite form 메요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 메다. A strong first sentence is 가방을 메다 ("to carry a bag (over the shoulder)"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 메다 also becomes 메고 싶어요 (want), 멜 수 있어요 (can), and 멜 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I carry on one's shoulder / back.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not carry on one's shoulder / back.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to carry on one's shoulder / back.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can carry on one's shoulder / back.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to carry on one's shoulder / back.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to carry a bag (over the shoulder)
usagePhrases.note: The defining collocation — 가방/배낭/책가방을 메다, anything worn by a strap on shoulder or back.

examples.en: Come with your bag on
examples.note: 반말; 메고 오다 tells someone to arrive wearing the bag.

examples.en: I carried a heavy backpack
examples.note: Past 멨어요 — the ㅔ stem contracts 메 + 었 down to 멨.

examples.ko: 등산 갈 때는 양쪽 어깨로 배낭을 메야 허리가 안 아파요
examples.romanization: deungsan gal ttaeneun yangjjok eokkaero baenangeul meya heoriga an apayo
examples.en: When hiking you should carry the backpack on both shoulders so your back doesn't hurt
examples.note: Real-situation advice; 메야 (메 + 어야) shows the obligation form of a ㅔ-stem verb.

words.nuance: 메다 means to carry something by slinging it on your shoulder or back with a strap — a backpack, a satchel, even a rifle. The dividing line you must keep clear is with 들다 (to carry in the hand): a handbag held in your fist is 들다, but the moment a strap goes over your shoulder it becomes 메다, so 가방을 들다 and 가방을 메다 picture two different postures. Also beware the homophone-ish 매다 'to tie/fasten' (넥타이를 매다, 신발끈을 매다) — same romanization, different spelling and meaning, and mixing them up is the number-one native-and-learner trip-up here. Conjugation is straightforward because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 메 + 어 contracts to plain 메, so the 요-form is 메요, the past is 멨어요, and the obligation form is 메야 해요 (never 메어요 / 메었어요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 메다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 메요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 들다 for a bag worn on the back — 들다 is hand-carrying; a shoulder or back bag with a strap takes 메다.
Don't spell it 매다 when you mean carrying — 매다 means to tie/fasten (넥타이를 매다); the strap-on-shoulder verb is 메다.
Don't write the past as 메었어요 — the ㅔ stem contracts, so it is 멨어요.

Conjugation is straightforward because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 메 + 어 contracts to plain 메, so the 요-form is 메요, the past is 멨어요, and the obligation form is 메야 해요 (never 메어요 / 메었어요).

words.shortExplanation: 업다 means "to carry on one's back (piggyback)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to carry on one's back (piggyback)" in Korean is 업다 (eopda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 업어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 업다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 아기를 업다 ("to carry a baby on one's back") — then reshape the same stem into 업고 싶어요 (desire), 업을 수 있어요 (ability), and 업을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not carry on one's back (piggyback).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to carry on one's back (piggyback).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can carry on one's back (piggyback).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to carry on one's back (piggyback).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to carry a baby on one's back
usagePhrases.note: The prototypical collocation — 업다 almost always pictures a baby or small child piggybacked.

examples.en: Shall I carry the baby on my back?
examples.note: 반말 offer; 업어 줘 = 업어 + 주- offers to piggyback for someone.

examples.en: Mom carried the child on her back
examples.note: Past 업었어요 — note the ㅂ stays, since 업다 is a regular verb, not ㅂ-irregular.

examples.ko: 다친 친구를 업고 한참을 걸어서 병원까지 갔어요
examples.romanization: dachin chingureul eopgo hanchameul georeoseo byeongwonkkaji gasseoyo
examples.en: I carried my injured friend on my back and walked a long way to the hospital
examples.note: Real-situation; 업고 가다 (piggyback + go) for helping someone who can't walk.

words.nuance: 업다 means to carry a person — almost always a baby, small child, or someone who can't walk — on your back, piggyback style, and it carries a tender, caregiving warmth (hence 업어 키우다 'to raise lovingly'). Distinguish it from 안다 'to hold in your arms / hug against your chest': a fussy infant facing you is 안다, but settled against your back it is 업다, two different holds. The pitfall that trips nearly every learner is the conjugation: 업다 looks like it should be a ㅂ-irregular (turning ㅂ into 우), but it is a perfectly regular consonant-stem verb, so the ㅂ stays put — 업 + 어 → 업어요, past 업었어요, potential 업을 수 있어요, polite command 업으세요. Saying 어워요 is wrong. Finally keep it apart from the look-alike 엎다 'to overturn / knock over' (그릇을 엎다), which is spelled with ㅍ and means something completely different.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 업다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 업어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't treat 업다 as a ㅂ irregular — it stays regular, so it is 업어요 (not 어워요) and 업었어요.
Don't use 안다 when the person is on your back — 안다 is holding in your arms against the chest; the back-carry is 업다.
Don't spell it 엎다 — that ㅍ verb means to overturn/tip over (그릇을 엎다), nothing to do with carrying a person.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 업다 becomes 업을 수 있어요 ("can") and 업을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 업다 means to carry a person — almost always a baby, small child, or someone who can't walk — on your back, piggyback style, and it carries a tender, caregiving warmth (hence 업어 키우다 'to raise lovingly').
Distinguish it from 안다 'to hold in your arms / hug against your chest': a fussy infant facing you is 안다, but settled against your back it is 업다, two different holds.

업다 looks like it should be a ㅂ-irregular (turning ㅂ into 우), but it is a perfectly regular consonant-stem verb, so the ㅂ stays put — 업 + 어 → 업어요, past 업었어요, potential 업을 수 있어요, polite command 업으세요. Saying 어워요 is wrong.
Keep it apart from the look-alike 엎다 'to overturn / knock over' (그릇을 엎다), which is spelled with ㅍ and means something completely different.

words.shortExplanation: 싣다 means "to load (onto a vehicle)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 싣다 (sitda) = "to load (onto a vehicle)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 실어요 plus one useful sentence like 짐을 차에 싣다 ("to load luggage into the car"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 싣고 싶어요 for what you want, 실을 수 있어요 for what you can, 실을 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not load (onto a vehicle).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to load (onto a vehicle).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to load (onto a vehicle).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to load luggage into the car
usagePhrases.note: The core frame — 물건/짐/화물을 (vehicle)에 싣다, putting cargo onto a means of transport.

examples.en: Load this into the car for me
examples.note: 반말 favor; 실어 줘 = 실어 (ㄷ→ㄹ form) + 줘 asks someone to load it for you.

examples.en: I loaded the boxes onto the truck
examples.note: Past 실었어요 — before the vowel the ㄷ has turned to ㄹ (ㄷ irregular).

examples.ko: 짐이 너무 많아서 한 번에 다 실을 수 없었어요
examples.romanization: jimi neomu manaseo han beone da sireul su eopseosseoyo
examples.en: There was so much luggage we couldn't load it all at once
examples.note: Real-situation; potential 실을 수 from the ㄷ-irregular stem before -ㄹ 수.

words.nuance: 싣다 means to load cargo, luggage, or goods ONTO a vehicle — a car, truck, ship, train, or plane — and it implies placing things on/in a means of transport, marked by 에 (트럭에 싣다). Contrast it with 담다 'to put into a container' (그릇에 담다, 가방에 담다): you 담다 rice into a bowl but you 싣다 boxes onto a truck, because 싣다 specifically targets transport, not ordinary containers. It also extends figuratively — 기사를 싣다 'to run an article', 마음을 실어 'putting one's heart into it'. The make-or-break point is that 싣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ changes to ㄹ, so 싣 + 어 → 실어요, past 실었어요, potential 실을 수 있어요, command 실으세요. Before a consonant the ㄷ is kept intact: 싣고, 싣지, 싣습니다. Mixing these two stems up is the classic error.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 싣다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 실어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write 싣어요 / 싣었어요 — as a ㄷ irregular the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel, giving 실어요 and 실었어요.
Don't keep ㄷ before -습니다's consonant turn into ㄹ — formal is 싣습니다 and 싣고/싣지 keep the ㄷ; only vowel endings switch to 실-.
Don't use 담다 for putting things onto a vehicle — 담다 is filling a container/bowl/bag, while loading onto a truck or car is 싣다.
notes: ㄷ: memorize 실어 and 실어요 together.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.body: 싣다 has an irregular stem (ㄷ). Memorize its polite form 실어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

words.shortExplanation: 나눠주다 means "to hand out / share out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 나눠주다 (nanwojuda) means "to hand out / share out". Start from the polite form 나눠줘요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 나눠주다. A strong first sentence is 간식을 나눠주다 ("to hand out snacks"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 나눠주다 also becomes 나눠주고 싶어요 (want), 나눠줄 수 있어요 (can), and 나눠줄 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not hand out / share out.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to hand out / share out.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can hand out / share out.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to hand out / share out.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The headword pattern — 간식/사탕/프린트를 나눠주다, giving one portion each to many people.

examples.en: Share out some candy
examples.note: 반말; 나눠줘 asks a friend to dole pieces out to the group.

examples.en: The teacher handed printouts to the students
examples.note: 에게 marks the recipients; the classic distribute-to-a-class scene.

examples.ko: 봉사자들이 길에서 따뜻한 국밥을 한 그릇씩 나눠줬어요
examples.romanization: bongsajadeuri gireseo ttatteutan gukbabeul han geureutssing nanwojwosseoyo
examples.en: The volunteers handed out a bowl of warm soup each on the street
examples.note: Real-situation; 씩 'each' underlines the one-portion-per-person sense of 나눠주다.

words.nuance: 나눠주다 is 나누다 (to divide / share / split) + 주다 (to give), so it means to break something into portions and hand one to each of several people — passing out snacks, handouts, or money to a group. The key contrast is with bare 나누다, which by itself only means 'to divide' or 'to share/have in common' (나누다 can also mean 대화를 나누다 'to share a conversation'); it lacks the explicit 'give it out to people' direction that the +주다 supplies, so 사탕을 나누다 sounds incomplete where 사탕을 나눠주다 is the natural 'hand the candy out'. Compare too 돌리다 (to pass/hand around, e.g. 떡을 돌리다 'distribute rice cakes to neighbors'), which overlaps but stresses circulating among a circle. The implied plurality of recipients is what separates 나눠주다 from one-to-one 건네다/주다. As a 주다 compound the conjugation is fully regular: 나눠줘요, 나눠줬어요, 나눠주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 나눠주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 나눠줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use bare 나누다 when you mean handing portions out — 나누다 alone is 'divide/share'; 나눠주다 adds the crucial 'give to each person'.
Don't use 나눠주다 for giving one whole thing to one person — its built-in nuance is dividing among several; for a single recipient use 주다 or 건네다.
Don't write 나눠 주다 as two loose words here — 나눠주다 is a settled verb meaning 'hand out / distribute', so keep it joined.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 나눠주다 becomes 나눠줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 나눠줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 나눠주다 means to break something into portions and hand one to each of several people — passing out snacks, handouts, or money to a group. The implied plurality of recipients is what separates 나눠주다 from one-to-one 건네다/주다.

나눠주다 is 나누다 (to divide / share / split) + 주다 (to give).
As a 주다 compound the conjugation is fully regular: 나눠줘요, 나눠줬어요, 나눠주세요.

words.shortExplanation: 내밀다 means "to hold out / stick out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to hold out / stick out" in Korean is 내밀다 (naemilda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 내밀어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 내밀다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 손을 내밀다 ("to hold out one's hand") — then reshape the same stem into 내밀고 싶어요 (desire), 내밀 수 있어요 (ability), and 내밀 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not hold out / stick out.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to hold out / stick out.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can hold out / stick out.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to hold out / stick out.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The core collocation — extend a hand for a shake, for help, or to receive something.

examples.en: Hold out your hand
examples.note: 반말; 내밀어 봐 = 내밀- + 어 봐 'try holding it out' — the ㄹ stays before the vowel 어.

examples.en: Don't stick your hand out the window
examples.note: Polite negative command; -지 마세요 keeps the full stem 내밀-.

examples.ko: 그가 첫인사로 명함을 내밀며 악수를 청했어요
examples.romanization: geuga cheosinsaro myeonghameul naemilmyeo aksureul cheonghaesseoyo
examples.en: He held out his business card as a first greeting and offered a handshake
examples.note: Real-situation; 내밀며 (내밀- + -며) describes presenting an object toward someone.

words.nuance: 내밀다 is 내- (out) + 밀다 (to push), literally 'to push outward', and it means to thrust or extend something forward — a hand, your head, your tongue, or an object you're presenting like a ticket or business card. The contrast to draw is with 내놓다 'to put out / set out' (음식을 내놓다, 의견을 내놓다): 내놓다 places or releases something out into the open, while 내밀다 specifically pushes it forward toward a person or through an opening, so you 손을 내밀다 (thrust your hand out to someone) but 쓰레기를 내놓다 (set the trash out). It carries a warm idiom, 도움의 손길을 내밀다 'to reach out a helping hand'. The conjugation pitfall is that 내밀다 is a ㄹ-stem verb where the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and ㅅ: hence formal 내밉니다 (not 내밀습니다) and polite command 내미세요 (not 내밀으세요). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 내밀어요, 내밀었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 내밀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 내밀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write the polite command as 내밀으세요 — a ㄹ-stem verb drops the ㄹ before ㅅ, so it is 내미세요.
Don't say 내밀습니다 for the formal present — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ-, giving 내밉니다.
Don't swap in 내놓다 when you mean thrusting toward someone — 내놓다 is 'set/put out into the open', while 내밀다 is pushing it forward at a person or out an opening.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 내밀어 and 내밀어요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 내밀다 becomes 내밀 수 있어요 ("can") and 내밀 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 전해주다 means "to pass on / deliver (to someone)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 전해주다 (jeonhaejuda) = "to pass on / deliver (to someone)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 전해줘요 plus one useful sentence like 이거 친구한테 전해주세요 ("Please pass this to my friend"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 전해주고 싶어요 for what you want, 전해줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 전해줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not pass on / deliver (to someone).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to pass on / deliver (to someone).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can pass on / deliver (to someone).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to pass on / deliver (to someone).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Please pass this to my friend
usagePhrases.note: The core favor pattern — relay an object or note to a third person on the speaker's behalf.

examples.en: Pass this to mom for me
examples.note: 반말; 전해줘 asks a family member to deliver it to a third person.

examples.en: I delivered this letter to the teacher
examples.note: 께 is the honorific of 에게, raising the recipient (the teacher) you handed it to.

examples.en: I'll be sure to relay the meeting results to the CEO
examples.note: Real-situation honorific — to a superior, 전해주다 becomes the humble 전해드리다.

words.nuance: 전해주다 is 전하다 (傳하다, 傳 'to transmit/convey') + 주다 (to give), so the Sino-Korean root literally means 'to pass something along and give it', i.e. to deliver an object, message, or feeling to someone — very often through a third person. It handles both physical things (a letter, a gift) and intangibles (안부를 전해줘요 'send my regards', 마음을 전해주다 'convey one's feelings'). The dividing line with 보내다 'to send' is distance and channel: 보내다 dispatches something across a gap (편지를 보내다 'mail a letter', 문자를 보내다 'send a text'), while 전해주다 emphasizes the item actually reaching and being handed to the recipient, frequently in person or via a go-between. To a superior, raise 주다 to the humble 드리다 → 전해드리다 (전해드리겠습니다), and use 께 for the honored recipient. As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 전해줘요, 전해줬어요, 전해주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 전해주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 전해줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 보내다 when you hand/relay something so it reaches a specific person — 보내다 is 'send (across a distance)'; 전해주다 stresses it being delivered to them, often via someone.
Don't keep plain 주다 when the recipient outranks you — use the humble 전해드리다 (전해드릴게요 / 전해드리겠습니다) and mark them with 께.
Don't say 전하다 alone in casual speech for doing someone a delivery favor — everyday Korean adds 주다, so 전해주세요, not bare 전하세요, sounds natural for 'please pass it on'.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 전해주다 becomes 전해줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 전해줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 전해주다 means to deliver an object, message, or feeling to someone — very often through a third person. It handles both physical things (a letter, a gift) and intangibles (안부를 전해줘요 'send my regards', 마음을 전해주다 'convey one's feelings'). To a superior, raise 주다 to the humble 드리다 → 전해드리다 (전해드리겠습니다), and use 께 for the honored recipient.

The dividing line with 보내다 'to send' is distance and channel: 보내다 dispatches something across a gap (편지를 보내다 'mail a letter', 문자를 보내다 'send a text'), while 전해주다 emphasizes the item actually reaching and being handed to the recipient, frequently in person or via a go-between.
전해주다 is 전하다 (傳하다, 傳 'to transmit/convey') + 주다 (to give), so the Sino-Korean root literally means 'to pass something along and give it'.
As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 전해줘요, 전해줬어요, 전해주세요.

words.shortExplanation: 세수하다 means "to wash one's face" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 세수하다 (sesuhada) means "to wash one's face". Start from the polite form 세수해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 세수하다. A strong first sentence is 아침에 세수해요 ("I wash my face in the morning"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 세수하다 also becomes 세수하고 싶어요 (want), 세수할 수 있어요 (can), and 세수할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not wash one's face.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to wash one's face.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to wash one's face.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I wash my face in the morning
usagePhrases.note: 아침에 marks the time 'in the morning'; 세수하다 means specifically the face, not the whole body.

examples.en: I get up and wash my face
examples.note: -아서 links 'get up' and 'wash' as one connected flow of waking up.

examples.en: I washed my face with cold water
examples.note: 찬물로 = 'with cold water'; many Koreans say cold water wakes them up.

examples.en: Hurry, wash your face and get to school
examples.note: -아야지 is a soft self-urging/nudging ending a parent uses to a child.

words.nuance: 세수하다 means specifically to wash your face (얼굴), built from the Sino-Korean noun 세수 (洗手, literally 'wash-hands', an old word that drifted to mean washing the face) plus 하다. Korean splits washing by body part, and this is the English-speaker pitfall: 씻다 is the broad 'wash (hands/body)', 샤워하다 is the whole body under water, and 감다 is reserved for hair — so '머리를 세수하다' or 'I'll wash (=shower) with 세수하다' are both wrong. Because it is a 하다 verb, the everyday form is just 세수해요, and the negative naturally splits the noun off as 세수 안 해요 rather than 안 세수해요. It collocates with 아침에, 찬물로/비누로, and chains with -고 into routines (세수하고 자요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 세수하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 세수해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 세수하다 for showering — it only covers the face; the whole body is 샤워하다 (or 씻다).
Don't put the negative as 안 세수해요; 하다-verbs split it as 세수 안 해요, which sounds far more natural.

words.shortExplanation: 감다 means "to wash (hair)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to wash (hair)" in Korean is 감다 (gamda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 감아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 감다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 머리를 감아요 ("I wash my hair") — then reshape the same stem into 감고 싶어요 (desire), 감을 수 있어요 (ability), and 감을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
머리를 is the fixed object; 감다 is the dedicated verb for hair.

examples.en: I washed my hair in the morning
examples.note: 감았어요 (감+았) is the past; a daily-routine statement.

examples.en: I wash my hair and dry it
examples.note: -고 chains it with 말리다 (to dry); the natural next step.

examples.en: I was too lazy today, so I didn't wash my hair
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; a very real-life confession.

words.nuance: 감다 is the body-part-specific verb for washing hair, and it almost always takes 머리 as its object (머리를 감다) — this part-by-part split is the core pitfall for English speakers, whose one verb 'wash' tempts them into 머리를 씻다, which Koreans don't say. Reserve 씻다 for hands/body, 세수하다 for the face, and 감다 for hair. Grammatically it is a regular consonant-stem verb, so 감 + 아요 → 감아요, past 감았어요, and the honorific request adds the linking 으: 감으세요. One trap to file away: an identical-looking homonym 감다 also means 'to close (the eyes)' (눈을 감다) and another 'to wind/wrap', so only context and the object (머리 vs 눈) tell them apart. It chains naturally as 머리를 감고 말리다.

Use 감아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't say 머리를 씻다 — hair takes 감다, not 씻다; 씻다 is for hands/body.
Don't drop the linking vowel in commands: it's 감으세요 (consonant stem + 으세요), not 감세요.

words.shortExplanation: 말리다 means "to dry (something)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 말리다 (mallida) = "to dry (something)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 말려요 plus one useful sentence like 머리를 말려요 ("I dry my hair"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 말리고 싶어요 for what you want, 말릴 수 있어요 for what you can, 말릴 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
머리를 = object; 말리다 is transitive 'make (it) dry'.

examples.en: I dry the towel in the sunlight
examples.note: 햇빛에 = 'in the sunlight'; 에 marks the location/medium.

examples.ko: 머리를 안 말리고 자면 감기 걸려요
examples.romanization: meorireul an malligo jamyeon gamgi geollyeoyo
examples.en: If you sleep without drying your hair, you'll catch a cold
examples.note: -고 자다 = 'sleep without doing'; a classic Korean caution.

examples.en: In the rainy season the laundry doesn't dry well
examples.note: Here 마르다 (intransitive 'dry up') is used — note the contrast with 말리다.

words.nuance: 말리다 means to dry something out — hair, laundry, wet shoes — and it is transitive, so it takes 을/를 for the thing you dry. Crucially distinguish it from its intransitive partner 마르다 ('become dry' by itself): YOU 빨래를 말리다 (you dry the laundry), but the laundry 빨래가 마르다 (the laundry dries) — picking the wrong one is the top pitfall, since English 'dry' is both. Grammatically 말리다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 말리 + 어 → 말려요, past 말렸어요 (never 말리어요). Beware a same-spelled homonym 말리다 meaning 'to stop / talk someone out of' (싸움을 말리다), so context decides; anchor the 'dry' sense first. It pairs with 드라이기로, 햇빛에, 밖에서, and chains after 감다 (머리 감고 말려요).

Don't confuse transitive 말리다 with intransitive 마르다 — you 빨래를 말리다, but 빨래가 마르다 (the laundry dries itself).
The polite form is 말려요 (말리 + 어), not 말리어요.

words.english: to apply / to put on (cream, etc.)
words.shortExplanation: 바르다 means "to apply / to put on (cream, etc.)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 바르다 (bareuda) means "to apply / to put on (cream, etc.)". Start from the polite form 발라요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 바르다. A strong first sentence is 로션을 발라요 ("I put on lotion"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 바르다 also becomes 바르고 싶어요 (want), 바를 수 있어요 (can), and 바를 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I apply / to put on (cream, etc.).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not apply / to put on (cream, etc.).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to apply / to put on (cream, etc.).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can apply / to put on (cream, etc.).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to apply / to put on (cream, etc.).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
로션을 = object; 바르다 = spread/apply onto skin or a surface.

examples.en: I wash my face and put on lotion
examples.note: -고 chains the steps; a basic morning skincare order.

examples.en: I spread jam on the bread
examples.note: 빵에 = 'onto the bread'; 바르다 also covers spreading food.

examples.en: Please spread the ointment evenly on the wound
examples.note: 골고루 = 'evenly'; -아 주세요 makes it a polite request to apply it.

words.nuance: 바르다 means to apply or spread a thin layer of something onto a surface — lotion, sunscreen, jam, ointment. The two-part frame is the thing applied + 을/를 and the surface + 에 (얼굴에 로션을 발라요), and getting that 에 right is a frequent pitfall: English 'put on my face' tempts 얼굴을 바르다, but the face is the surface (에), not the object. Distinguish it from neighbors: 칠하다 is to paint/coat a broad surface (벽을 칠하다 = paint a wall), and 묻히다 is to get/dab a substance onto something more loosely — 바르다 implies deliberate, spread-out application. Conjugation is the headline grammar point: 바르다 is 르-irregular, so before -아/어 the 르 drops and an extra ㄹ appears, giving 발라요 and past 발랐어요 — never 바르어요/바르었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Because it's 르-irregular, the past is 발랐어요, not 바르었어요 (and present 발라요, not 바르어요).
Don't mark the surface with 을/를 — it's 얼굴에 크림을 바르다 (surface takes 에), not 얼굴을 바르다.
notes: 르: memorize 발라 and 발라요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 빗다 means "to comb (hair)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빗어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빗다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 머리를 빗어요 ("I comb my hair") — then reshape the same stem into 빗고 싶어요 (desire), 빗을 수 있어요 (ability), and 빗을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
머리를 = object; 빗다 = comb/run a comb through the hair.

examples.en: I comb my hair in the morning
examples.note: 아침에 = 'in the morning'; part of getting ready.

examples.en: I combed my hair neatly
examples.note: 단정하게 = 'neatly, tidily'; 빗었어요 (빗+었) is the past.

examples.en: Please comb the tangled hair gently
examples.note: 엉킨 = 'tangled'; 살살 = 'gently', a careful instruction.

words.nuance: 빗다 means to comb or brush through your hair, taking 머리 as its object; the tool is the noun 빗 (a comb), so 빗으로 머리를 빗다 literally stacks 'comb with a comb'. Note the distinction from 빗기다 — the causative/transitive 'comb someone else's hair' (아이 머리를 빗기다), used when a parent grooms a child. Grammatically it is a regular consonant-stem verb: 빗 + 어요 → 빗어요, past 빗었어요, with the linking 으 in commands (빗으세요). It collocates with 단정하게, 곱게, 빗으로, and 아침에.

Use 빗어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

To comb SOMEONE ELSE'S hair (e.g. a child's), use the causative 빗기다, not plain 빗다.

words.shortExplanation: 깨우다 means "to wake (someone) up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 깨우다 (kkaeuda) = "to wake (someone) up". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 깨워요 plus one useful sentence like 아침에 동생을 깨워요 ("I wake my younger sibling in the morning"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 깨우고 싶어요 for what you want, 깨울 수 있어요 for what you can, 깨울 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I wake my younger sibling in the morning
usagePhrases.note: 동생을 = object; 깨우다 takes the person being woken.

examples.en: My mom woke me up
examples.note: 깨웠어요 (깨우+었→깨웠) is the past; someone waking you.

examples.en: Please don't wake the child
examples.note: -지 마세요 = polite prohibition; let the child sleep.

examples.ko: 내일 일찍 깨워 줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: naeil iljjik kkaewo jul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Can you wake me early tomorrow?
examples.note: 일찍 = 'early'; -아 줄 수 있어요? politely asks a favor.

words.nuance: 깨우다 is the transitive 'wake someone up', so it always takes a person as its object (저를 깨워요) — this is the pitfall, because English 'wake up' is both transitive and intransitive. 깨우다 is the causative of 깨다 ('wake up by oneself', as in 잠에서 깨다), and it contrasts with 일어나다 ('get up, rise from bed'): to say YOU woke and got out of bed, use 일어나다/깨다, and reserve 깨우다 for rousing another person. Conjugation: the stem ends in 우, so 우 + 어 contracts to 워, giving 깨워요 and past 깨웠어요. The set request 깨워 주세요 ('please wake me') is one of the most useful travel phrases. It collocates with 아침에, 일찍, 알람으로, and the person-object + 을/를.

Use 깨워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Use 깨우다 to wake SOMEONE ELSE; to say you yourself wake/get up, use 일어나다 or 깨다.
The contracted form is 깨워요 (깨우 + 어 → 깨워), not 깨우어요.

words.shortExplanation: 헹구다 means "to rinse" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 헹구다 (hengguda) means "to rinse". Start from the polite form 헹궈요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 헹구다. A strong first sentence is 그릇을 물로 헹궈요 ("I rinse the dish with water"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 헹구다 also becomes 헹구고 싶어요 (want), 헹굴 수 있어요 (can), and 헹굴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I rinse the dish with water
usagePhrases.note: 물로 = 'with water'; 헹구다 = rinse off with clean water.

examples.en: I wash the dishes and rinse them clean
examples.note: -고 chains it after 설거지하다; the natural finishing step.

examples.en: I rinsed the vegetables under running water
examples.note: 흐르는 물에 = 'under running water'; 헹궜어요 (헹구+었) is the past.

examples.en: You have to rinse out the shampoo well for healthy hair
examples.note: 충분히 = 'thoroughly'; -아야 = 'only if you ...', a real hair-care tip.

words.nuance: 헹구다 means to rinse something with clean water to flush off soap, dirt, or residue — dishes, vegetables, laundry, or your mouth. It is the final clean-water step that follows the actual washing, which is exactly its dividing line from 씻다: 씻다 is the broad 'wash (with soap/scrubbing)', while 헹구다 specifically removes what's left using plain water, so '비누로 헹구다' is odd — you 씻다 with soap, then 헹구다 with water. The object takes 을/를 and the water takes 에/로 (흐르는 물에 헹구다). Conjugation: the stem ends in 우, so 우 + 어 contracts to 궈, giving 헹궈요 and past 헹궜어요 — a common misspelling is 헹구어요/헹궈어요, both wrong. It chains after 설거지하다 and 씻다 and pairs with 흐르는 물에, 깨끗이, 충분히.

Use 헹궈요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
The contracted form is 헹궈요 (헹구 + 어 → 헹궈), not 헹구어요 or 헹궈어요.

words.shortExplanation: 사랑하다 means "to love" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to love" in Korean is 사랑하다 (saranghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 사랑해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 사랑하다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The person you love takes 을/를 (object marker), never 에 — 사랑하다 is a transitive verb that acts directly on a person.

examples.en: I love my family
examples.note: The neutral polite 해요 form — safe for almost any listener and the default for stating affection plainly.

examples.en: I love you
examples.note: 반말: 너를 ('you') plus bare 사랑해 marks intimacy, used only with a partner or someone very close.

examples.en: My parents loved each other their whole lives
examples.note: Honorific 시 (사랑하셨어요) raises the subject (parents), and 서로를 supplies the mutual object.

words.nuance: 사랑하다 is the weightiest love verb in Korean, covering romantic love, family love, and devotion to a cause; it is far heavier than English 'love you', which English speakers toss off to friends and even food. Use 사랑해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 사랑하다 becomes 사랑할 수 있어요 ("can") and 사랑할 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 미워하다 means "to hate" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 미워하다 (miwohada) = "to hate". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 미워해요 plus one useful sentence like 그 사람을 미워해요 ("I hate that person"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 미워하고 싶어요 for what you want, 미워할 수 있어요 for what you can, 미워할 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The target of hatred takes 을/를; 미워하다 attaches to a person, not an abstract thing.

examples.en: I don't hate anyone
examples.note: 아무도 ('nobody') must pair with the negative 하지 않아요 — Korean double-marks the negative.

examples.en: I hated my younger sibling for a while
examples.note: 한때 ('at one time') plus past 미워했어요 softens it into a feeling that has since passed.

examples.ko: 우리 이제 그만 서로 미워하지 마세요
examples.romanization: uri ije geuman seoro miwohaji maseyo
examples.en: Let's stop hating each other now
examples.note: 그만 ('stop / no more') with the polite 하지 마세요 is a gentle plea to end a feud.

words.nuance: 미워하다 means to actively feel hatred or resentment toward a person, and it is built from the adjective 밉다 ('to be hateful / detestable') by the regular pattern 밉다 → 미워 + 하다 (the ㅂ of 밉다 softens to 워). Because it is a 하다 verb, it contracts to 미워해요 / past 미워했어요 (not 미워하요), while keeping 하 in 미워할 거예요. Using 미워하다 for disliking a thing ('I hate kimchi') — things take 싫어하다; 미워하다 is for resenting people.
Writing 미워하요 instead of 미워해요 — as a 하다 verb it must contract 하 + 여 to 해.
Assuming 미워해 always means strong 'hate'; between close people it is often a light, sulky 'you meanie', so don't read it as literal hatred.

words.shortExplanation: 그리워하다 means "to miss" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 그리워하다 (geuriwohada) means "to miss". Start from the polite form 그리워해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 그리워하다. A strong first sentence is 고향을 그리워해요 ("I miss my hometown"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 그리워하다 also becomes 그리워하고 싶어요 (want), 그리워할 수 있어요 (can), and 그리워할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
A place or absent person takes 을/를 with the verb 그리워하다 (≠ the adjective 그립다, which takes 이/가).

examples.en: I miss Korean food
examples.note: Everyday line when living abroad; the food takes the object marker 을.

examples.en: He missed his old friends
examples.note: Third person + past 그리워했어요 — describing someone else's longing, which is exactly when 그리워하다 (not 그립다) is required.

examples.ko: 너무 그리워하지 마, 곧 만날 거야
examples.romanization: neomu geuriwohaji ma, gon mannal geoya
examples.en: Don't miss them too much, you'll meet soon
examples.note: 반말 comfort: 그리워하지 마 tells a friend not to pine.

words.nuance: 그리워하다 is the action verb 'to miss / long for / yearn after', formed from the adjective 그립다 ('to be missed') via 그립다 → 그리워 + 하다. The single most important point is the adjective-vs-verb split that trips up English speakers, who have only one word 'miss': use the adjective 그립다 for your own felt state, where the missed thing is the grammatical subject (고향이 그리워요 = lit. 'my hometown is missed-to-me' = I'm homesick), and use the verb 그리워하다 when you describe someone actively missing something, taking an 을/를 object (동생이 고향을 그리워해요). The other near-synonym is 보고 싶다 ('want to see / miss'): 보고 싶다 is light, common, and aimed at people you can still meet (엄마 보고 싶어), while 그리워하다 is more literary and wistful, often for what is gone, distant, or past — you 그리워하다 your childhood, not your friend across town. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 그리워해요 / past 그리워했어요 (never 그리워하요).

words.shortExplanation: 빌다 means "to pray" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to pray" in Korean is 빌다 (bilda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 소원을 빌어요 ("I make a wish") — then reshape the same stem into 빌고 싶어요 (desire), 빌 수 있어요 (ability), and 빌 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
소원을 빌다 ('wish a wish') is the set phrase for making a wish on a star, candle, or at New Year.

examples.en: I made a wish at New Year
examples.note: Past 빌었어요 — the stem 빌 keeps its ㄹ before the vowel ending 어.

examples.en: I pray for my family's health every day
examples.note: 건강을 빌다 ('pray for health') shows the 'pray for' sense aimed at a good outcome.

examples.ko: 시험 잘 보라고 행운을 빌어 줄게요
examples.romanization: siheom jal borago haenguneul bireo julgeyo
examples.en: I'll wish you luck on your exam
examples.note: 빌어 주다 ('wish on someone's behalf') + 줄게요 makes it a warm offer to a friend.

words.nuance: 빌다 spans three related senses — to pray, to make a wish, and to plead/beg — unified by the idea of earnestly asking a higher power or another person for something (소원을 빌다 = make a wish, 행운을 빌다 = wish luck, 용서를 빌다 = beg forgiveness, 잘못을 빌다 = apologize for a wrong). Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, and the rule is precise: the stem ㄹ drops only before endings starting with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, which is why the formal form is 빕니다 (not 빌습니다) and a noun-modifier is 비는; but before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, so the polite present is 빌어요 and the past is 빌었어요. A frequent pitfall is overusing the doubled future — it is 빌 거예요, with a single ㄹ, because the ㄹ does not double here. The biggest meaning trap is confusing 빌다 with 빌리다: in modern Korean 빌다 never means 'borrow' — that is exclusively 빌리다 (책을 빌리다 = borrow a book), so 'can I borrow this?' is 빌릴 수 있어요?, not 빌 수 있어요?. Use 빌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 빌습니다 — as a ㄹ-irregular the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, giving 빕니다.

words.shortExplanation: 키우다 means "to raise" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 키우다 (kiuda) = "to raise". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 키워요 plus one useful sentence like 강아지를 키워요 ("I have / raise a puppy"). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
키우다 is the default verb for keeping a pet — Korean 'has' a pet by 'raising' it, not by 가지다.

examples.en: I have (raise) a cat
examples.note: The everyday way to say you keep a pet — note the object marker 를 on the animal.

examples.en: My parents raised me
examples.note: 키워 주다 (did the raising for me) + honorific 시 → 키워 주셨어요, a respectful way to credit your parents.

examples.en: I want to grow the company bigger
examples.note: 키우다 + 크게 shows the 'make it grow' sense applied to a business.

words.nuance: 키우다 is the causative of 크다 ('to be big') — literally 'to make (something) grow / get bigger' — and it stretches across raising children, keeping pets, growing plants, and figuratively building skills, dreams, businesses, even bad habits (병을 키우다 = let an illness worsen). Conjugation is the 우-contraction, not an irregular: the stem 키우 ends in the vowel ㅜ, and ㅜ + 어 fuses into 워, so the casual form is 키워, polite 키워요, and past 키웠어요 (never 키우어요). Compared with its near-twin 기르다, the two overlap heavily for pets, plants, and children, but usage splits by habit: 키우다 is the more colloquial everyday choice for pets and for 'growing bigger' (실력을 키우다), while 기르다 sounds slightly more formal and is preferred for hair, beard, and nails (머리를 기르다, not 머리를 키우다). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 가지다 ('to have/own') for a pet because English says 'I have a dog' — Korean instead says 강아지를 키워요, since you raise the animal rather than possess it.

words.shortExplanation: 기르다 means "to grow" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.note: Note the casual present 길러 — the 르 doubles to ㄹㄹ before the vowel.

examples.en: My grandmother grows vegetables
examples.note: Honorific 께서 + 기르세요 raises the subject respectfully.

examples.ko: 어릴 때부터 좋은 습관을 길러야 해요
examples.romanization: eoril ttaebuteo joeun seupgwaneul gilleoya haeyo
examples.en: You should build good habits from a young age
examples.note: 기르다 in its 'cultivate' sense, with 야 해요 ('should').

words.shortExplanation: 낳다 means "to give birth" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
아기를 낳다 ('give birth to a baby') — the baby takes the object marker 를.

examples.en: My older sister gave birth to a daughter
examples.note: Past 낳았어요 — the stem ㅎ is kept and ㅏ + 았 attaches normally.

examples.en: The cat had five kittens
examples.note: 낳다 also covers animals; 마리 is the counter for animals.

examples.en: I want to have two children
examples.note: 낳고 싶어요 ('want to give birth') — 낳다 keeps its ㅎ before the consonant ending 고.

words.shortExplanation: 닮다 means "to resemble" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 닮다 (damda) = "to resemble". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 닮아요 plus one useful sentence like 엄마를 닮았어요 ("I take after my mom"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 닮고 싶어요 for what you want, 닮을 수 있어요 for what you can, 닮을 수 없어요 for what you can't. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The person you resemble takes 을/를, and Korean states it in the past 닮았어요 for a present fact.

examples.en: The baby looks a lot like the dad
examples.note: The go-to sentence about family resemblance, with 많이 ('a lot') and past 닮았어요.

examples.en: I take after my grandmother
examples.note: 닮다 covers both appearance and personality — context decides which.

examples.en: My personality really resembles my older brother's
examples.note: 형하고 닮다 ('resemble + with brother') — the partner of resemblance takes 하고.

words.nuance: 닮다 means to resemble or take after someone in looks or character, and its single most counter-intuitive feature for English speakers is tense: Korean overwhelmingly states a present resemblance in the PAST form 닮았어요, because the resembling is treated as a completed, settled state that holds now — so 엄마를 닮았어요 means 'I look like my mom (right now)', and saying present 닮아요 sounds oddly like an ongoing action and is rare. The grammar of the partners matters too: the person you take after takes the object marker 을/를 (아빠를 닮다), while two people who look alike are linked with 하고/와/과/랑 (형하고 닮다, 둘이 닮다). Distinguish it sharply from 같다 ('to be the same/identical'): 닮다 is partial likeness — a family resemblance — whereas 같다 claims sameness, so 'they look similar' is 닮았어요 but 'they're the same' is 같아요. It is a regular ㄻ-cluster verb (닮아요, 닮았어요, 닮습니다). A vivid native idiom for strong resemblance is 붕어빵처럼 닮았다, like two pastries from one mold.

Use 닮아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using the present 닮아요 for 'looks like' — Korean states a current resemblance in the past: 닮았어요.
Choosing 같다 ('be identical') when you mean only a resemblance — that is 닮다; 같다 claims they are the same.
Marking the person with 이/가 (엄마가 닮았어요 to mean 'I look like mom') — the one you resemble takes 을/를: 엄마를 닮았어요.

words.shortExplanation: 어울리다 means "to suit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 어울리다 (eoullida) means "to suit". Start from the polite form 어울려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 어울리다. A strong first sentence is 이 옷이 잘 어울려요 ("This outfit suits (you) well"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 어울리다 also becomes 어울리고 싶어요 (want), 어울릴 수 있어요 (can), and 어울릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
What looks good on you takes 이/가, not 을/를 — 옷이 어울려요, paired with 잘 ('well').

examples.en: That color really suits you
examples.note: A natural compliment; note 색이 (이/가), since the color is what suits.

examples.en: These shoes go well with the skirt
examples.note: Item + 하고 어울리다 = two things match each other.

examples.en: I quickly mixed in with the new coworkers
examples.note: Past 어울렸어요 in the 'get along / fit in' sense, with 금방 ('quickly').

words.nuance: 어울리다 carries two everyday meanings bound by one idea — 'to harmonize / fit together well': (1) to suit or look good on someone (이 옷이 잘 어울려요 = this suits you), and (2) to mingle, blend in, or get along with people (친구들하고 잘 어울려요). The particle pattern is the crux for English speakers, because English 'suits you' makes 'you' the object: in Korean the thing that suits is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (옷이 어울려요, never 옷을 어울려요), the person it suits is unmarked or takes 한테/에게, and a matching partner or group takes 하고/와/과 (치마하고 어울리다, 사람들하고 어울리다); a setting it fits takes 에 (분위기에 어울리다). Conjugation is the regular ㅣ-vowel contraction, not an irregular: 어울리 + 어 fuses to 어울려, giving polite 어울려요 and past 어울렸어요 (not 어울리어요). A useful contrast: 어울리다 ('look good / harmonize') vs 맞다 ('fit in size / be correct') — clothes that 어울리다 flatter you, clothes that 맞다 are the right size, and the two are not the same compliment.

Use 어울려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 을/를 for what suits you — say 옷이 어울려요 (이/가), never 옷을 어울려요; the flattering thing is the subject.
Writing 어울리어요 instead of the contracted 어울려요 — the stem-final ㅣ fuses with 어 to 려.
Confusing 어울리다 (look good / harmonize) with 맞다 (fit in size / be correct) — 'this suits you' is 어울려요, 'this fits (size)' is 맞아요.

words.shortExplanation: 분석하다 means "to analyze" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to analyze" in Korean is 분석하다 (bunseokhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 분석해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 분석하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 데이터를 분석하다 ("to analyze data") — then reshape the same stem into 분석하고 싶어요 (desire), 분석할 수 있어요 (ability), and 분석할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The textbook collocation; the thing studied takes 을/를, never 에.

examples.en: I analyze this chart
examples.note: Simplest object + 를 + 분석하다 frame; note the 하다→해요 contraction.

examples.en: Let's talk again after analyzing the results
examples.note: 분석한 후에 = 'after analyzing' shows the past-modifier -ㄴ before 후에.

examples.ko: 이 보고서는 시장 흐름을 아주 자세히 분석했어요
examples.romanization: i bogoseoneun sijang heureumeul aju jasehi bunseokaesseoyo
examples.en: This report analyzed the market trend in great detail
examples.note: Real report register: 자세히 + 분석했어요, the workhorse academic past tense.

words.nuance: 분석하다 means to analyze — to break a whole down into its parts (分 'divide' + 析 'split apart') so you can understand how it works: data, a cause, a problem, or a text. The hanja itself pictures cutting something open, which is why it always implies methodical dissection, not a casual glance. As a 하다 verb it must contract to 분석해요 (never 분석하요), and the object always takes 을/를. The pitfall for English speakers is register: in English you 'analyze' anything, but 분석하다 sounds clinical and academic, so for everyday 'let me look into it' Koreans reach for 살펴보다 (look over) or 알아보다 (check / find out). The near-synonym to watch is 분석하다 vs 분류하다: 분석하다 takes one thing apart to study it, while 분류하다 sorts many things into groups — analyzing a single survey vs classifying responses by age.

Use 분석해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 분석하요 — 하다 never stays as 하 before 요; it always contracts to 분석해요.
Saying 데이터에 분석해요. The thing analyzed is a direct object, so it must be 데이터를 분석해요.
Using 분석하다 for a quick everyday peek; for 'let me just look into it' 살펴볼게요 or 알아볼게요 sounds far more natural.

words.explanation: 평가하다 (pyeonggahada) = "to evaluate". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 평가해요 plus one useful sentence like 성과를 평가하다 ("to evaluate performance"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 평가하고 싶어요 for what you want, 평가할 수 있어요 for what you can, 평가할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Standard workplace frame: object + 를 + 평가하다 for appraisals.

examples.en: How do you rate that movie?
examples.note: 어떻게 평가해요? is the everyday way to ask for someone's assessment.

examples.en: The teacher evaluated the students' presentations
examples.note: Grading context; 발표를 평가했어요 with the plain past.

examples.en: Don't judge people only by their appearance
examples.note: 겉모습으로만 = 'by appearance alone'; 으로 marks the basis of judgment.

words.nuance: 평가하다 means to evaluate, assess, or rate the value of something — work, performance, art, or even a person (評 'judge/criticize' + 價 'price/value', literally 'to price-judge'). That 價 'value' core is why it feels measured and official, the word on report cards, performance reviews, and product reviews. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 평가해요. With 높게/좋게 평가하다 it means 'to think highly of', and 낮게 평가하다 means 'to underrate' — note these always need the ADVERB (높게), a spot English speakers trip on by reaching for 높은. The synonym line to hold is 평가하다 vs 판단하다: 평가하다 weighs worth on a scale (high/low, good/bad), while 판단하다 reaches a yes/no decision about a situation. Because 평가하다 can sound like you are sitting in judgment, Koreans soften it when appraising people directly, or switch to 판단하다.

Use 평가해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 평가하요 instead of the contracted 평가해요.
Saying 높은 평가해요 for 'rate highly' — it must be the adverb: 높게 평가해요.
Using 평가하다 to mean 'judge a person harshly' in casual talk; it sounds cold, so 판단하다 or a softened phrasing fits better.

words.shortExplanation: 증명하다 means "to prove" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 증명하다 (jeungmyeonghada) means "to prove". Start from the polite form 증명해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 증명하다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object + 를 + 증명하다 for establishing something is true.

examples.ko: 이 자료가 그 사실을 증명해 줘요
examples.romanization: i jaryoga geu sasireul jeungmyeonghae jwoyo
examples.en: This material proves that fact
examples.note: 증명해 주다 = 'serves as proof'; -아/어 주다 frames it as doing a favor.

examples.en: He proved his innocence to the end
examples.note: 결백을 증명했어요 — the courtroom collocation in the plain past.

examples.en: How can you prove that?
examples.note: 증명할 수 있어요 is the 'can' form, challenging someone to back a claim.

words.nuance: 증명하다 means to prove or demonstrate that something is true with evidence or logic — a fact, one's innocence, identity, or a theorem (證 'evidence/testimony' + 明 'make clear', literally 'make clear through evidence'). That 證 'evidence' root is the whole point: you cannot 증명하다 by merely asserting; you need proof, which is also why the noun 증명서 means an official certificate (재직증명서 = proof of employment). As a 하다 verb it contracts to 증명해요. The trap for English speakers is the verb pair 증명하다 vs 설명하다: in English 'prove' and 'explain' feel close, but 설명하다 just makes something understandable, while 증명하다 establishes it as TRUE. Likewise keep it apart from 보여주다 (to show / display): 보여주다 puts something in view; 증명하다 wins an argument with it.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 증명하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 증명해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 증명하요 instead of the contracted 증명해요.
Using 증명하다 when you only mean 'make clear' — that is 설명하다 (explain); 증명하다 demands evidence.
Confusing it with 보여주다 (to show): you 보여주다 a photo, but you 증명하다 the truth the photo supports.

words.shortExplanation: 주장하다 means "to argue / to claim" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to argue / to claim" in Korean is 주장하다 (jujanghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 주장해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 주장하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 의견을 주장하다 ("to assert an opinion") — then reshape the same stem into 주장하고 싶어요 (desire), 주장할 수 있어요 (ability), and 주장할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not argue / to claim.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to argue / to claim.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to argue / to claim.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Object + 를 + 주장하다 = to push a position you hold.

examples.en: I argue that I'm right
examples.note: -다고 주장하다 reports your own claim; 옳다고 from 옳다 (be right).

examples.en: Experts argue that the method is dangerous
examples.note: 위험하다고 — adjective + -다고, the news/academic reporting frame.

examples.en: Don't make claims without evidence
examples.note: 근거 없이 + 주장하지 마세요 warns against unsupported insistence.

words.nuance: 주장하다 means to argue, insist on, or claim a position you strongly believe and want others to accept (主 'main/master' + 張 'stretch/spread out', literally 'stretch out as one's main point'). That 主 'master/own' nuance is why it always carries personal conviction — you are pushing YOUR stance, not neutrally reporting. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 주장해요, and to report the content you claim you use the quotation frame -(ㄴ/는)다고 주장하다. The pitfall is 주장하다 vs 말하다: English speakers translate 'I said that...' with 주장하다, but 말하다 is neutral telling while 주장하다 implies you are taking a contested stand and defending it. Bonus: the noun 주장 also means 'team captain' in sports (the one who 'masters/leads'), so judge it by context.

Use 주장해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 주장하요 instead of the contracted 주장해요.
Using 주장하다 for a neutral 'I said' — that is 말하다; 주장하다 implies you are insisting on a contested point.
Dropping the quotation marker: claim THAT something is so needs -다고 주장하다, e.g. 위험하다고 주장하다, not 위험하다 주장하다.

words.shortExplanation: 강조하다 means "to emphasize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 강조하다 (gangjohada) = "to emphasize". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 강조해요 plus one useful sentence like 중요성을 강조하다 ("to emphasize the importance"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 강조하고 싶어요 for what you want, 강조할 수 있어요 for what you can, 강조할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The flagship collocation; 중요성 (importance) is the default object.

examples.en: I especially want to emphasize this point
examples.note: 이 점 (this point) + 강조하고 싶어요 — the speaker spotlighting one item.

examples.en: The teacher emphasized the importance of preparation
examples.note: 예습의 중요성을 강조했어요, the classic lecture-hall past tense.

examples.en: That person always emphasizes honesty
examples.note: 강조하세요 adds the honorific -시-; 정직 (honesty) as the value stressed.

words.nuance: 강조하다 means to emphasize, stress, or underline that something matters (強 'strong' + 調 'tone/tune', literally 'to set a strong tone'). That 強 'strong' element is why the word belongs to lectures, presentations, and persuasive writing — you are raising the volume on one point. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 강조해요, and the point stressed takes 을/를 (중요성을 강조하다), a spot where English speakers wrongly slip in 에. The synonym boundary to keep is 강조하다 vs 주장하다: 강조하다 turns up the weight of a point everyone may already accept ('this really matters'), whereas 주장하다 pushes a contested CLAIM others might reject. So a teacher 강조한다 that review is important, but a debater 주장한다 that a policy is wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 강조하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 강조해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 강조하요 instead of the contracted 강조해요.
Using 에 for the point emphasized — say 중요성을 강조해요, not 중요성에 강조해요.
Reaching for 강조하다 when you mean to push a debatable claim; that is 주장하다, while 강조하다 just amplifies a point.

words.shortExplanation: 제안하다 means "to propose / to suggest" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 제안하다 (jeanhada) means "to propose / to suggest". Start from the polite form 제안해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 제안하다. A strong first sentence is 방법을 제안하다 ("to propose a method"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 제안하다 also becomes 제안하고 싶어요 (want), 제안할 수 있어요 (can), and 제안할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not propose / to suggest.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to propose / to suggest.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to propose / to suggest.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Object + 를 + 제안하다 = to put forward a plan or idea.

examples.en: He proposed a good idea
examples.note: 아이디어를 제안했어요 — straightforward object in a work setting.

examples.en: I suggested we eat lunch together
examples.note: 먹자고 제안했어요 shows -자고 reporting a shared suggestion.

examples.en: Please propose a better solution
examples.note: 해결책 (solution) + 제안해 주세요, the polite request form.

words.nuance: 제안하다 means to propose or put forward a plan, idea, or course of action, usually in a formal or business setting (提 'lift/raise up' + 案 'plan/proposal', literally 'to raise a proposal'). The 提 'raise up' image fits a meeting where you formally table an idea. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 제안해요; to suggest doing something together you attach the propositive quotation -자고 제안하다 (먹자고 제안하다). The pitfall is 제안하다 vs 추천하다: English 'suggest' blurs them, but 제안하다 floats a NEW plan or course of action ('let's try this approach'), while 추천하다 recommends a specific known thing as good ('try this restaurant'). Because 제안하다 sounds formal, in casual chat Koreans drop it for V-자 or V-는 게 어때요?.

Use 제안해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 제안하요 instead of the contracted 제안해요.
Using 제안하다 to recommend a specific item (a film, a shop) — that is 추천하다; 제안하다 is for proposing a plan or action.
Forgetting the propositive marker for joint suggestions: 'let's meet' reported is 만나자고 제안하다, not 만나 제안하다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 제안하다 becomes 제안할 수 있어요 ("can") and 제안할 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 반대하다 means "to oppose" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to oppose" in Korean is 반대하다 (bandaehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 반대해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 반대하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 의견에 반대하다 ("to oppose an opinion") — then reshape the same stem into 반대하고 싶어요 (desire), 반대할 수 있어요 (ability), and 반대할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Critical particle: the thing opposed takes 에, NOT 을/를.

examples.en: I don't oppose that opinion
examples.note: 에 반대하다 in the negative; 그 의견에 marks what you're against.

examples.en: My parents opposed the marriage
examples.note: 결혼에 반대하셨어요 with honorific -시-; the classic family-drama line.

examples.en: Why do you oppose the plan?
examples.note: Asking someone's reason; 계획에 반대하세요 keeps the 에 particle.

words.nuance: 반대하다 means to oppose, object to, or be against something (反 'reverse/anti' + 對 'face/oppose', literally 'to face in the opposite direction'). The single most important thing for intermediate learners is the PARTICLE: the thing you oppose takes 에, never 을/를 — 의견에 반대하다, 계획에 반대하다. English 'oppose X' treats X as a direct object, so learners overwhelmingly write 의견을 반대해요, which is wrong. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 반대해요. Its clean antonym is 찬성하다 (to be in favor), which shares the same 에 frame. Keep it apart from 거부하다 (to refuse): 반대하다 is taking a stance against an idea in discussion, while 거부하다 is actively turning down a concrete request or offer.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 반대하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 반대해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 을/를 — the verb is intransitive here, so it must be 의견에 반대해요, not 의견을 반대해요.
Writing 반대하요 instead of the contracted 반대해요.
Mixing it with 거부하다 (refuse a request); 반대하다 is opposing a view, 거부하다 is rejecting a concrete offer.

words.english: to agree / to be in favor
