Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 찬성해요 plus one useful sentence like 의견에 찬성하다 ("to be in favor of an opinion"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 찬성하고 싶어요 for what you want, 찬성할 수 있어요 for what you can, 찬성할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I agree / to be in favor.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not agree / to be in favor.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to agree / to be in favor.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can agree / to be in favor.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to agree / to be in favor.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to be in favor of an opinion
usagePhrases.note: Like 반대하다, it takes 에: the thing supported is 에 찬성하다.

examples.en: I'm in favor of the plan
examples.note: 계획에 찬성해요 in a discussion; note the 에, parallel to 반대하다.

examples.en: Most people agreed with that opinion
examples.note: Reporting a vote or poll result; 의견에 찬성했어요.

examples.en: If you agree, please raise your hand
examples.note: 찬성하면 = 'if in favor', the show-of-hands voting context.

words.nuance: 찬성하다 means to agree with, approve of, or be in favor of a proposal or opinion, especially in a vote or formal discussion (贊 'approve/assist' + 成 'accomplish', literally 'to approve and help bring about'). Like its antonym 반대하다, the thing you support takes 에 — 의견에 찬성하다 — and English speakers must resist writing 의견을 찬성해요. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 찬성해요. The key synonym contrast is 찬성하다 vs 동의하다: 찬성하다 is voting YES on a proposal or motion ('all in favor'), while 동의하다 is agreeing with a person's point or feeling in conversation. Using 을/를 — it must be 제안에 찬성해요, not 제안을 찬성해요 (the particle is 에).
Writing 찬성하요 instead of the contracted 찬성해요.
Using 찬성하다 for 'I agree with you' in chat; that is 동의해요 or 맞아요 — 찬성하다 implies a formal vote on a motion.

words.shortExplanation: 거부하다 means "to refuse / to reject" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 거부하다 (geobuhada) means "to refuse / to reject". Start from the polite form 거부해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 거부하다. A strong first sentence is 제안을 거부하다 ("to reject a proposal"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 거부하다 also becomes 거부하고 싶어요 (want), 거부할 수 있어요 (can), and 거부할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not refuse / to reject.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to refuse / to reject.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to refuse / to reject.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
Object + 를 + 거부하다 = to turn down firmly. Note: 을/를, unlike 반대하다's 에.

examples.en: He refused the interview
examples.note: 인터뷰를 거부했어요 — a flat, firm refusal; object takes 를.

examples.en: The company flatly rejected his demands
examples.note: 요구를 단호히 거부했어요, the news-report register for firm rejection.

examples.en: Don't refuse a legitimate request
examples.note: 정당한 (legitimate) + 거부하지 마세요 urges against unfair refusal.

words.nuance: 거부하다 means to refuse, reject, or decline firmly — a proposal, request, demand, or order (拒 'ward off/resist' + 否 'no/deny', literally 'to ward off with a no'). Those hanja 'resist' + 'deny' make it strong and confrontational, the word for turning something down outright, often on principle. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 거부해요, and unlike 반대하다 the object takes 을/를 (요청을 거부하다). The pitfall is the synonym pair 거부하다 vs 거절하다: 거절하다 is the polite, softer 'decline' you use for an invitation or kind offer you'd rather not accept (제안을 정중히 거절했어요), whereas 거부하다 is a blunt, principled REFUSAL — a company 거부하다 demands, a witness 거부하다 to testify. Using 거부하다 when a friend invites you to dinner sounds harshly cold.

Use 거부해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 거부하요 instead of the contracted 거부해요.
Using 에 like with 반대하다 — 거부하다 takes a direct object: 요청을 거부해요, not 요청에 거부해요.
Using 거부하다 to politely turn down an invitation; that blunt tone offends — use 거절하다 for soft declines.

words.shortExplanation: 제공하다 means "to provide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to provide" in Korean is 제공하다 (jegonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 제공해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 제공하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 정보를 제공하다 ("to provide information") — then reshape the same stem into 제공하고 싶어요 (desire), 제공할 수 있어요 (ability), and 제공할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object + 를 + 제공하다; 정보 and 서비스 are the top objects.

examples.ko: 이 호텔은 무료 아침 식사를 제공해요
examples.romanization: i hotereun muryo achim siksareul jegonghaeyo
examples.en: This hotel provides free breakfast
examples.note: Service context; 아침 식사를 제공해요 on a hotel notice.

examples.en: The company provided lunch to the employees
examples.note: 직원들에게 ... 점심을 제공했어요 shows the 에게 recipient frame.

examples.en: Please provide detailed information
examples.note: 정보를 제공해 주세요, the polite request a customer makes.

words.nuance: 제공하다 means to provide, supply, or furnish something — information, services, food, resources — typically by an organization or in a formal context (提 'offer/raise up' + 供 'supply/offer', two 'give' hanja stacked for an official 'furnish'). Because both characters mean offering, the word feels institutional, the verb on hotel signs, contracts, and corporate notices. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 제공해요; the recipient takes 에게/한테 and the thing provided takes 을/를. The pitfall is register, not grammar: 제공하다 vs 주다. English 'give/provide' covers both, but 주다 is the warm everyday 'give' between people (친구가 선물을 줬어요), while 제공하다 is what a company or service does. Saying a friend 제공했어요 a gift sounds like a press release; use 줬어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 제공하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 제공해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 제공하요 instead of the contracted 제공해요.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 — it takes 에게/한테: 직원들에게 점심을 제공했어요.
Using 제공하다 for a friend giving you something; that stiff, corporate tone calls for 주다 instead.

words.shortExplanation: 포함하다 means "to include" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 포함하다 (pohamhada) = "to include". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 포함해요 plus one useful sentence like 세금을 포함하다 ("to include tax"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 포함하고 싶어요 for what you want, 포함할 수 있어요 for what you can, 포함할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Active frame: the whole includes the part, which takes 을/를.

examples.en: This price includes the shipping fee
examples.note: Active 포함하다: 가격(whole) includes 배송비(part), object takes 를.

examples.en: All costs are included
examples.note: Passive 포함되어 있어요 — the part is the subject and takes 이/가.

examples.en: Including me, there are five people
examples.note: 저를 포함해서 = 'including me', the handy counting set phrase.

words.nuance: 포함하다 means to include or contain something inside a larger whole (包 'wrap/envelop' + 含 'hold in the mouth/contain', literally 'to wrap and hold within'). The 'wrap around' image is why the bigger thing 포함하다 the smaller part. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 포함해요. The single most useful thing to learn is its passive partner 포함되다 (to be included), which flips the roles: active 가격이 세금을 포함해요 (price includes tax, part = object 을/를) vs passive 세금이 가격에 포함돼요 / 포함되어 있어요 (tax is included, part = subject 이/가). English speakers blur these and say 세금이 포함해요, which is wrong — if tax is the one being included, it must be the passive 포함되다. Also memorize the frozen phrase N을/를 포함해(서) = 'including N'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 포함하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 포함해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 포함하요 instead of the contracted 포함해요.
Saying 세금이 포함해요 — if the part is the subject, use the passive: 세금이 포함되어 있어요.
Forgetting that 'including me' is the set phrase 저를 포함해서, not a free word-for-word translation.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 포함하다 becomes 포함할 수 있어요 ("can") and 포함할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 구별하다 means "to distinguish" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 구별하다 (gubyeolhada) means "to distinguish". Start from the polite form 구별해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 구별하다. A strong first sentence is A와 B를 구별하다 ("to distinguish A from B"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 구별하다 also becomes 구별하고 싶어요 (want), 구별할 수 있어요 (can), and 구별할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The two compared join with 와/과 (or 하고), the whole takes 를.

examples.en: How do you tell these two apart?
examples.note: Asking the trick for two look-alikes; 이 둘은 ... 구별해요?

examples.en: I can't tell the twins apart well
examples.note: 구별하지 못해요 = the 'unable to' negative for lacking the skill.

examples.ko: 어른은 옳고 그름을 구별할 줄 알아야 해요
examples.romanization: eoreuneun olko geureumeul gubyeolhal jul araya haeyo
examples.en: An adult should know how to tell right from wrong
examples.note: 구별할 줄 알다 = 'know how to distinguish', a maturity expectation.

words.nuance: 구별하다 means to distinguish, differentiate, or tell apart two or more things by their differences (區 'divide/section' + 別 'separate/distinguish', literally 'to separate into distinct parts'). As a 하다 verb it contracts to 구별해요; the items compared join with 와/과 or 하고, and the whole takes 을/를 — 진짜와 가짜를 구별하다. The crucial synonym contrast is 구별하다 vs 구분하다 (both share 區): 구별하다 stresses perceiving the DIFFERENCE between similar things ('I can't tell the twins apart' — 구별 not possible), while 구분하다 stresses SORTING items into groups/categories ('separate the trash by type' — 쓰레기를 분리수거로 구분하다). English 'distinguish' leans toward 구별하다; if you mean 'divide into sections', reach for 구분하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 구별하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 구별해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 구별하요 instead of the contracted 구별해요.
Using 구별하다 when you mean to sort items into groups — that is 구분하다; 구별하다 is for telling similar things apart.
Marking only one item: distinguishing needs both, joined by 와/과 — 진짜와 가짜를 구별해요, not just 가짜를 구별해요.

words.shortExplanation: 비판하다 means "to criticize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to criticize" in Korean is 비판하다 (bipanhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 비판해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 비판하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 정책을 비판하다 ("to criticize a policy") — then reshape the same stem into 비판하고 싶어요 (desire), 비판할 수 있어요 (ability), and 비판할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object + 를 + 비판하다; abstract targets like 정책/결정 fit best.

examples.en: It's easy to criticize others
examples.note: 비판하기 nominalizes the verb; 남(others) as the target.

examples.en: The media criticized the decision harshly
examples.note: 결정을 강하게 비판했어요, the news-report register for public critique.

examples.en: Don't just criticize blindly; offer an alternative
examples.note: 무조건 + 비판하지 말고 contrasts empty criticism with proposing solutions.

words.nuance: 비판하다 means to criticize — to weigh something and point out its faults through reasoned judgment, as of a policy, idea, or work (批 'judge/comment on' + 判 'judge/decide', literally 'to judge and pass verdict'). Both hanja mean 'judge', which is why proper 비판 is analytical, not just venting. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 비판해요, object 을/를. The pitfall is the near-twin pair 비판하다 vs 비난하다 (they look almost alike): 비판하다 is reasoned CRITIQUE that can be constructive ('this policy has these flaws'), while 비난하다 (難 'blame/reproach') is purely negative personal BLAME or condemnation ('you're terrible'). English 'criticize' covers both, so learners wrongly use 비판하다 for a personal attack; if you mean to blame or condemn a person, that is 비난하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비판하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 비판해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 비판하요 instead of the contracted 비판해요.
Using 비판하다 to personally blame or insult someone — that is 비난하다; 비판하다 is reasoned, often constructive critique.
Marking the target with 에 — it takes 을/를: 정책을 비판해요, not 정책에 비판해요.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.english: to occur, to happen, to arise
words.shortExplanation: 발생하다 means "to occur, to happen, to arise" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 발생하다 (balsaenghada) = "to occur, to happen, to arise". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 발생해요 plus one useful sentence like 문제가 발생했어요. ("A problem occurred."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 발생하고 싶어요 for what you want, 발생할 수 있어요 for what you can, 발생할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I occur, to happen, to arise.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not occur, to happen, to arise.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to occur, to happen, to arise.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can occur, to happen, to arise.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to occur, to happen, to arise.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The thing that occurs always takes 이/가, never 을/를 — 발생하다 cannot take an object.

examples.en: Problems often occur here.
examples.note: Polite 발생해요 — note 하다 contracts 하 + 어 → 해, never 발생하요.

examples.en: An error occurred during payment.
examples.note: Formal 발생했습니다 is the exact wording you see on payment screens and system error pages.

examples.ko: 작은 실수가 큰 사고로 발생할 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: jageun silsuga keun sagoro balsaenghal sudo isseoyo.

words.nuance: 발생하다 (發生, 'issue-forth + arise') is the formal, written-leaning verb for an event, problem, or phenomenon coming into existence — accidents, errors, fires, costs, side effects, diseases. The everyday near-synonym is 생기다, and the dividing line is register and scale: 문제가 생겼어요 is what you say to a friend, while 문제가 발생했어요 belongs to news, reports, manuals, and official notices. Crucially it is intransitive — the thing that occurs takes 이/가, so you can never 'occur something' (no 발생하다 with 을/를). The classic English-speaker trap is translating 'cause a problem' as 문제를 발생하다; Korean instead says 문제가 발생하다 (a problem arises) or, for an agent making it happen, 문제를 일으키다. Remember 하다 contracts to 해요 — 발생하요 is a spelling error.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발생하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발생해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 문제가 발생했어요 (a problem occurred), not 문제를 발생했어요; for 'cause a problem' use 문제를 일으키다.
Writing 발생하요 instead of 발생해요 — every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 어 to 해, so the polite form is 발생해요.
Using it for tiny personal events sounds robotic — say 배가 고파졌어요, not 배고픔이 발생했어요; reserve 발생하다 for incidents, errors, and reports.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 발생하다 becomes 발생할 수 있어요 ("can") and 발생할 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 존재하다 means "to exist" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 존재하다 (jonjaehada) means "to exist". Start from the polite form 존재해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 존재하다. words.nuance: 존재하다 (存在, 'remain + be present') means 'to exist' in an abstract, weighty, or emphatic sense — common in writing, debate, philosophy, and serious topics. Its everyday near-synonym is 있다, and the line is sharp: for 'there is / I have' you must use 있다 (책이 있어요, 질문이 있어요), never 존재하다. Reach for 존재하다 only when you want to spotlight the very fact of something's existence — a method, a being, a problem — or to deny it categorically with 존재하지 않아요. It is intransitive, so the thing that exists takes 이/가 and there is no object. The big English-speaker pitfall is mapping every English 'exist/there is' onto 존재하다: 'there's a café nearby' is 근처에 카페가 있어요, and saying 카페가 존재해요 sounds comically grand. Don't replace everyday 있다 with 존재하다 — 'I have a question' is 질문이 있어요, not 질문이 존재해요; 'there's a store' is 가게가 있어요.

words.english: to develop, to advance, to progress
words.shortExplanation: 발전하다 means "to develop, to advance, to progress" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not develop, to advance, to progress.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to develop, to advance, to progress.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can develop, to advance, to progress.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to develop, to advance, to progress.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: Casual 발전했어 — for places and economies visibly growing over time.

examples.en: If you keep at it, your skills will improve.

examples.en: A small spat escalated into a big fight.
examples.note: Real-situation — 발전하다 can mean a situation escalates ~(으)로 into something bigger, often negative.

words.nuance: 발전하다 (發展, 'issue-forth + unfold/spread') means to move to a more advanced, mature, or larger stage — technology, economies, skills, companies, even relationships. It is normally intransitive (실력이 발전하다, 경제가 발전하다), and the 'into' target takes ~(으)로 (연인으로 발전하다 = develop into lovers). Its near-synonym 성장하다 ('grow') overlaps but leans biological/scale growth (아이가 성장하다 = a child grows up), whereas 발전하다 stresses qualitative advancement to a higher level. The number-one trap for learners is the look-alike 발견하다 (to discover) — one syllable apart and totally unrelated, so 신약을 발전하다 wrongly means 'develop a new drug' when you meant 발견하다 (discover). The second trap is using 발전하다 transitively; to actively develop something you need the causative 발전시키다 (기술을 발전시켰어요), never 기술을 발전했어요.

Use 발전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't mix up 발전하다 (develop/advance) with 발견하다 (discover) — one syllable apart, completely different meanings.
To say 'develop X' transitively, use the causative 발전시키다: 기술을 발전시켰어요, not 기술을 발전했어요.
Mark the 'into' goal with ~(으)로, not 을/를: 사업으로 발전했어요 (developed into a business), not 사업을 발전했어요.

words.english: to be improved, to be enhanced
words.shortExplanation: 향상되다 means "to be improved, to be enhanced" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 향상되다 (hyangsangdoeda) = "to be improved, to be enhanced". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 향상돼요 plus one useful sentence like 듣기 실력이 많이 향상됐어요. ("My listening skills have improved a lot."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 향상되고 싶어요 for what you want, 향상될 수 있어요 for what you can, 향상될 수 없어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not be improved, to be enhanced.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to be improved, to be enhanced.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can be improved, to be enhanced.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to be improved, to be enhanced.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: My listening skills have improved a lot.
usagePhrases.note: The thing that improves takes 이/가 — 향상되다 is intransitive (실력이/품질이 향상되다).

examples.en: Since I practice daily, my pronunciation got better.
examples.note: Casual 향상됐어 — classic study context: 발음이/문법이 향상되다.

examples.en: After the update, the speed greatly improved.
examples.note: Formal 향상됐습니다 fits product release notes and reviews.

examples.en: If you exercise regularly, your stamina will improve.
examples.note: Real-situation advice — 체력이 향상되다 is natural in health and fitness guidance.

words.nuance: 향상되다 (向上, 'turn-toward + up' + 되다) literally pictures something 'turning upward,' i.e. a skill, quality, or level rising and getting better. It is the intransitive, formal cousin of the everyday 좋아지다 (to get better): 실력이 좋아졌어요 is casual, while 실력이 향상됐어요 sounds polished and is what teachers, reviews, and reports use. Use it for measurable, ratable things — 실력, 품질, 성능, 효율, 체력, 삶의 질 — rather than moods or weather. The key English-speaker pitfall is the active/passive split: 향상되다 means something improved on its own, but if YOU improved it you must use the causative 향상시키다 (실력을 향상시켰어요), never 실력을 향상됐어요. Watch the spelling too: 되어요 contracts to 돼요 and the past is 향상됐어요 — 향상되요 and 향상됬어요 are both wrong.

Use 향상돼요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 실력이 향상됐어요 (skills improved), but 실력을 향상시켰어요 when YOU improved them (향상시키다).
Spell the polite form 향상돼요 and the past 향상됐어요 — not 향상되요 / 향상됬어요 (되 + 어 always contracts to 돼).
Don't apply it to feelings or weather — 'I feel better' is 기분이 좋아졌어요, not 기분이 향상됐어요; 향상되다 is for skills and measurable quality.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 향상되다 becomes 향상될 수 있어요 ("can") and 향상될 거예요 ("will"). words.nuance: 감소하다 (減少, 'reduce + few') is the formal, statistical verb for an amount or number going down, and it lives in a fixed pair with its opposite 증가하다 (增加, to increase) — the two appear together constantly in news, reports, and graphs. Its everyday near-synonyms are 줄다 and 줄어들다: a Korean tells a friend 손님이 줄었어요, but a report says 고객 수가 감소했습니다. The dividing line is purely register and context (numbers/data → 감소하다; daily talk → 줄다). It is intransitive (이/가), so the big pitfall for English speakers is trying to say 'reduce the cost' as 비용을 감소하다 — that is ungrammatical; to actively cut something you use the transitive 줄이다 (비용을 줄이다) or the causative 감소시키다. Reserve 감소하다 for things that go down on their own in a measured, formal frame.

Use 감소해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 비용이 감소했어요 (the cost decreased), but 비용을 줄였어요 when YOU cut it (줄이다).
In everyday talk 줄어들다 sounds far more natural — 살이 빠졌어요 / 손님이 줄었어요, not 감소했어요; save 감소하다 for statistics and formal contexts.
Don't confuse the 한자 pair — 감소하다 is decrease and 증가하다 is increase; mixing them in a report reverses your meaning entirely.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not form, to shape, to build up.

usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can form, to shape, to build up.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to form, to shape, to build up.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

examples.ko: 새로운 관계를 형성하는 데 시간이 걸려요.
examples.romanization: saeroun gwangyereul hyeongseonghaneun de sigani geollyeoyo.
examples.en: It takes time to form new relationships.
examples.note: 관계를 형성하다 = build a relationship; ~는 데 시간이 걸리다 = 'it takes time to.'

examples.note: For places or layers forming naturally, the intransitive 형성되다 is standard.

examples.note: Real-situation/formal — 의견이 모여 여론을 형성하다, common in essays about society.

words.nuance: 형성하다 (形成, 'shape/form + complete') means to form or build something up over time — a personality, a habit, a relationship, a group, a market, public opinion. Its everyday counterpart 만들다 ('make') is for concrete, physical objects (밥을 만들다 = make rice), whereas 형성하다 is reserved for gradual, structural, often intangible formation; saying 밥을 형성하다 is simply wrong. examples.note: Casual 구성해 — 두 명씩 (in twos); 조를 구성하다 = form teams/groups.

words.nuance: 적용하다 (適用, 'suitable + use') means to apply a rule, discount, theory, or method so it actually takes effect — the thing applied takes 을/를 and the target takes 에/에게 (새 규칙을 직원에게 적용하다). Transitive: the planned activity takes 을/를 — 조사를/교육을/정책을 실시하다. Formal register.

examples.en: I did my homework.
examples.note: For personal everyday tasks use plain 하다 — never 실시하다; 실시하다 is only for official, organized undertakings.

examples.en: The government implemented a new policy.
examples.note: Formal 실시했습니다 — 정책을 실시하다 is standard news and official phrasing.

examples.en: The company carries out health checkups every year.
examples.note: Real-situation/organizational — 검진을/점검을 실시하다 (conduct checkups/inspections).

words.nuance: 실시하다 (實施, 'actual + carry out') means to officially put a planned activity into effect — a survey, training, an exam, a policy, an inspection. It is formal and organizational, the language of governments, companies, and schools, not personal life. Its near-synonym 진행하다 (進行, to proceed with / run) overlaps but is broader and more neutral (회의를 진행하다 = run a meeting), whereas 실시하다 specifically frames the formal launch or enforcement of a scheme. It is transitive (을/를), and the passive 실시되다 ('is carried out / takes effect') is frequent in notices. The classic English-speaker pitfall is over-applying English 'do/carry out' to everyday actions: 'I did my homework' is 숙제를 했어요, and 숙제를 실시했어요 sounds absurdly bureaucratic — reserve 실시하다 for official, scheduled undertakings.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 실시하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 실시해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it for personal tasks — 'I did my homework' is 숙제를 했어요, not 숙제를 실시했어요; it's strictly for official, organized activities.
It's transitive — say 조사를 실시했어요; for 'was carried out' use the passive 실시되다 (조사가 실시됐어요).
Don't swap it freely with 진행하다 — 회의를 진행하다 (run a meeting) is neutral, while 실시하다 frames an official launch or enforcement (정책을 실시하다).

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 실시하다 becomes 실시할 수 있어요 ("can") and 실시할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.english: to solve, to resolve, to settle
words.shortExplanation: 해결하다 means "to solve, to resolve, to settle" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to solve, to resolve, to settle" in Korean is 해결하다 (haegyeolhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 해결해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 해결하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 문제를 빨리 해결해야 해요. ("We need to solve the problem quickly.") — then reshape the same stem into 해결하고 싶어요 (desire), 해결할 수 있어요 (ability), and 해결할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I solve, to resolve, to settle.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not solve, to resolve, to settle.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to solve, to resolve, to settle.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can solve, to resolve, to settle.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to solve, to resolve, to settle.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: We need to solve the problem quickly.
usagePhrases.note: Transitive — the problem takes 을/를; 문제를 해결하다 is the core collocation.

examples.en: I'll sort this out.
examples.note: Casual 해결할게 — the ~(으)ㄹ게 promise form, very natural for offering to handle something.

examples.ko: 이 앱으로 대부분의 문제를 해결할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i aebeuro daebubunui munjereul haegyeolhal su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can solve most problems with this app.
examples.note: 문제를 해결하다 + ~(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = 'can solve' — the everyday workhorse collocation.

examples.en: Both sides resolved the conflict through negotiation.
examples.note: Real-situation/formal — 갈등을 해결하다 covers disputes broadly, not just puzzles.

words.nuance: 해결하다 (解決, 'untie + decide/settle') is both the everyday and the formal verb for solving or settling a problem, conflict, or situation — its overwhelming partner is 문제 (문제를 해결하다). It is transitive (을/를), and its passive 해결되다 means a matter gets resolved or works out (문제가 해결됐어요). The key contrast English speakers need is with 풀다, which also translates as 'solve' but is literal-'untie' and applies to puzzles, math, riddles, and even stress or misunderstandings (수학 문제를 풀다, 오해를 풀다); 해결하다 covers real-life problems, disputes, and situations more broadly and abstractly. The usual pitfall is the active/passive mix: 'the problem was solved' is 문제가 해결됐어요 (passive 해결되다), not 문제가 해결했어요 — the active 해결하다 needs a solver and an object (제가 문제를 해결했어요).

Don't say 문제를 해결돼요 — 해결되다 is intransitive/passive and takes 이/가: 문제가 해결돼요.

words.english: to take up, to occupy, to account for
words.shortExplanation: 차지하다 means "to take up, to occupy, to account for" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 차지하다 (chajihada) = "to take up, to occupy, to account for". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 차지해요 plus one useful sentence like 식비가 생활비의 절반을 차지해요. ("Food costs take up half of my living expenses."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 차지하고 싶어요 for what you want, 차지할 수 있어요 for what you can, 차지할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I take up, to occupy, to account for.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take up, to occupy, to account for.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to take up, to occupy, to account for.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can take up, to occupy, to account for.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to take up, to occupy, to account for.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Food costs take up half of my living expenses.
usagePhrases.note: Transitive — the share taken takes 을/를; the whole it's part of takes ~의 (생활비의 절반을).

examples.en: The bag took up the whole spot.
examples.note: Casual 차지했어 — the literal 'take up space' sense, here a bag hogging a seat.

examples.en: Housing costs make up a large part of spending.
examples.note: 큰 부분을 차지하다 = account for a large share — common in budget talk.

examples.en: That singer took the number one spot on the music chart.
examples.note: Real-situation — 1위를 차지하다 for rankings and charts; here in formal news register.

words.nuance: 차지하다 (a native Korean verb, not Sino-Korean) carries two everyday senses: to take up a proportion or amount (식비가 절반을 차지하다 = food is half the cost) and to secure or win a position (1위를 차지하다 = take first place). It is transitive — the share or prize taken takes 을/를, and when you name the whole it belongs to, that whole takes ~의 (지출의 큰 부분을 차지하다). The first sense is the natural way to say 'X accounts for Y%' in budgets and statistics; the second is the chart/sports/competition sense. The key contrast English speakers miss is with 이기다 (to beat an opponent): 차지하다 is about securing the rank, share, or seat itself, not about defeating someone, so 1위를 차지하다 ('took first') is different from 상대를 이겼다 ('beat the opponent'). Don't confuse it either with 차치하다, a rare formal verb meaning 'to set aside (a topic).'
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 차지하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 차지해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
It's transitive — mark the share or rank with 을/를: 절반을 차지하다, 1위를 차지하다.
Don't confuse the 'win a rank' sense with 이기다 (to beat an opponent) — 차지하다 is about securing the position or share itself, not defeating someone.
When naming the whole, use ~의: 생활비의 절반을 차지하다 (take up half of the living costs), not 생활비를 절반 차지하다.

words.shortExplanation: 협력하다 means "to cooperate / to collaborate" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 협력하다 (hyeomnyeokhada) means "to cooperate / to collaborate". Start from the polite form 협력해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 협력하다. A strong first sentence is 서로 협력하다 ("to cooperate with each other"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 협력하다 also becomes 협력하고 싶어요 (want), 협력할 수 있어요 (can), and 협력 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not cooperate / to collaborate.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to cooperate / to collaborate.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to cooperate / to collaborate.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
서로 (each other) is the textbook partner word here; it frames cooperation as mutual, not one-sided.

examples.en: Let's cooperate together.
examples.note: Simple 요-form invitation; 같이 (together) makes the joint effort explicit between equals.

examples.ko: 두 회사가 협력해서 새 제품을 개발했어요.
examples.romanization: du hoesaga hyeomnyeokaeseo sae jepumeul gaebalhaesseoyo.
examples.en: The two companies collaborated to develop a new product.
examples.note: 협력해서 = 'by cooperating', chaining the joint effort to its result; very common in work and business talk.

examples.ko: 이번 프로젝트는 옆 팀과 긴밀히 협력해야 성공할 수 있습니다.
examples.romanization: ibeon peurojekteuneun yeop timgwa ginmilhi hyeomnyeokaeya seonggonghal su itseumnida.
examples.en: This project can only succeed if we cooperate closely with the next team.
examples.note: Real workplace register: partner marked with 과, 긴밀히 collocates, 협력해야 sets a condition for success.

words.nuance: 협력하다 (協力, literally '협 join forces + 력 strength') means two or more parties pooling effort toward a shared goal, so it fits teams, companies, departments, and governments rather than one friend doing you a casual favor. The dividing line to memorize: 돕다 / 도와주다 is one-directional help ('you help me'), while 협력하다 is mutual, goal-oriented teamwork ('we work together as partners'); 협조하다 is the close cousin meaning 'cooperate by going along with a request' (협조 부탁드립니다 = please cooperate with our request) and is softer and more procedural than the strategic 협력하다. The partner is marked with 와/과 or 하고 (옆 팀과 협력해요), it habitually pairs with 서로, 긴밀히, and 적극적으로, and the bare noun is everywhere: 국제 협력, 협력 업체, 협력 관계. Being a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly to 협력해요 / 협력했어요, and negatives usually split the noun off (협력 안 해요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 협력하다 whenever you'd say 'help' in English — for 'help me move this desk' you must say 도와주세요, never 협력해 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 협력하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 협력해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 협력하다 for a small one-off favor: 'help me carry this' is 이것 좀 도와주세요, not 협력해 주세요 — 협력하다 needs a joint, goal-directed effort, not single-person assistance.
Marking the partner with 에게/한테 (팀에게 협력해요). The co-worker takes 와/과 or 하고 because you act *with* them, not *toward* them: 옆 팀과 협력해요.
Confusing 협력하다 with 협조하다. When you simply comply with someone's request (filling in a form, following a procedure), say 협조해 주세요; reserve 협력하다 for strategic partnership.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 협력하다 becomes 협력할 수 있어요 ("can") and 협력할 거예요 ("will"). words.shortExplanation: 경쟁하다 means "to compete" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to compete" in Korean is 경쟁하다 (gyeongjaenghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 경쟁해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 경쟁하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 치열하게 경쟁하다 ("to compete fiercely") — then reshape the same stem into 경쟁하고 싶어요 (desire), 경쟁할 수 있어요 (ability), and 경쟁 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
치열하다 (fierce, cut-throat) is the signature adverb for 경쟁하다; describes tough, no-quarter rivalry.

examples.en: Let's compete to see who's faster.
examples.note: Light, playful use; 누가 ~지 sets up the thing being contested between two people.

examples.ko: 요즘 회사들이 가격으로 심하게 경쟁하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hoesadeuri gagyeogeuro simhage gyeongjaenghago isseoyo.
examples.en: These days companies are competing hard on price.
examples.note: (으)로 marks what they compete on; 경쟁하고 있다 (ongoing) frames it as a current, live situation.

examples.ko: 같은 자리를 두고 여러 명이 치열하게 경쟁했어요.
examples.romanization: gateun jarireul dugo yeoreo myeongi chiyeolhage gyeongjaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: Several people competed fiercely for the same position.
examples.note: Full real-life pattern: N을/를 두고 + 치열하게 + 경쟁하다, the way news reports describe a contest.

words.nuance: 경쟁하다 (競爭, '競 vie + 爭 contend') describes rivalry in which parties try to outdo one another for the same prize, market, or position, and its tone runs from neutral and sporty to tense and cut-throat depending on context. The boundary worth knowing: 경쟁하다 is contending against a rival, whereas 겨루다 is a more physical 'pit your skill/strength against' (used for matches and martial arts), and 다투다 leans toward quarreling or squabbling. Grammar is the trap zone here: the rival is marked with 와/과 (옆 가게와 경쟁해요), and what is at stake takes 을/를 두고, never a plain object on 경쟁 itself. It collocates with 치열하게, 심하게, and the set phrase 선의의 경쟁, and the noun saturates daily life: 경쟁률 (competition ratio), 입시 경쟁 (exam competition), 경쟁사 (a competitor), 경쟁력 (competitiveness). As a regular 하다-verb it gives 경쟁해요 / 경쟁했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 경쟁 like the English noun 'the competition' that you 'win' — Korean separates the act (경쟁) from the result, so you win 'in' the competition (경쟁에서 이기다), you don't 'beat the competition' as 경쟁을 이기다.

Use 경쟁해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 경쟁을 이겨요 for 'win the competition'. 경쟁 is the act of competing, not a contest you defeat, so use 경쟁에서 이기다 (win in the competition) instead.
Marking the rival with 을/를 (친구를 경쟁해요). The opponent takes 와/과: 친구와 경쟁해요 — you compete *with/against* them, so the comitative particle is required.
Reaching for 경쟁하다 for a one-off physical contest of strength or skill; for 'let's have a match / arm-wrestle' Koreans more often say 겨뤄요, reserving 경쟁하다 for sustained rivalry.

words.shortExplanation: 참여하다 means "to participate / to take part in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I have to participate / to take part in.

usagePhrases.en: to take part in an event
usagePhrases.note: 참여하다 takes 에 for the activity you join: 토론에 참여해요 = I take part in the discussion.

examples.en: I want to take part in that gathering too.
examples.note: Basic 에 marking plus 고 싶다; 참여하다 already implies you'll actually join in, not just watch.

examples.en: I actively took part in this volunteer activity.
examples.note: 적극적으로 collocates strongly; 참여하다 stresses hands-on involvement rather than mere attendance.

examples.ko: 회의에 참여는 했지만 의견은 한마디도 안 냈어요.

examples.en: I took part in the meeting but didn't say a single word.

words.nuance: 참여하다 (參與, '參 take part + 與 join in') means to actively take part in and contribute to an activity, event, or process, so its core is involvement, not physical presence. What you join is marked with 에 (행사에 참여하다), and it pairs habitually with 적극적으로 and the bare noun in 참여율 (participation rate), 시민 참여 (citizen participation), 참여형 (participatory). As a regular 하다-verb it is 참여해요 / 참여했어요. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to take responsibility to the very end
usagePhrases.note: 끝까지 (all the way to the end) is the signature partner; means seeing it through, not bailing out.

examples.en: I take responsibility for my own work.
examples.note: Clean 져요 form; shows the 지다 stem contracting and the matter (일) taken as object with 을 dropped.

examples.en: Who's going to take responsibility for this accident?
examples.note: 책임지다 + 을/를: 사고를 책임지다 = be answerable for the accident; future 거예요 presses for ownership.

examples.ko: 이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임지겠습니다.
examples.romanization: i ireun jega matasseunikka kkeutkkaji chaegimjigetseumnida.
examples.en: I took this on, so I'll take full responsibility to the end.
examples.note: Formal workplace pledge: 맡다 (take charge) sets it up, 책임지겠습니다 promises to own how it turns out.

words.nuance: 책임지다 is a compound of the Sino-Korean noun 책임 (責任, '責 duty + 任 charge') plus the native verb 지다 'to carry/bear', so it literally means 'to shoulder responsibility' — to take on and own the consequences of a mistake, a task, or even the care of a person. It is heavier and more accountable than 맡다 (to take charge of / be assigned): 맡다 is accepting a duty, while 책임지다 is promising to answer for the result, good or bad. It also reaches beyond fault into provision — 가족을 책임지다 means to support and care for one's family — so it overlaps emotionally with 돌보다 (to look after) in that nurturing sense. The matter takes 을/를, it collocates with 끝까지 and 확실히, and it lives in nouns like 책임감 (sense of responsibility) and 무책임 (irresponsibility). The conjugation pitfall is the key thing for English speakers: because the stem is 지다, you must contract it to 책임져요 / 책임졌어요 / 책임져 주세요 — never the literal *책임지어요 — and negatives split the noun off as 책임 안 져요.

Using 맡다 when the moment calls for accountability: 'I'll take responsibility for the result' is 결과를 책임질게요, not just 맡을게요 — 맡다 only says you'll handle it, not that you'll answer for how it ends.

words.english: to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)
words.shortExplanation: 의지하다 means "to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)" in Korean is 의지하다 (uijihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 의지해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 의지하다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
A person you lean on takes 에게/한테: 가족에게 / 친구한테 의지해요 — emotional, warm dependence.

examples.en: I rely on my older sister a lot.
examples.note: Casual 반말 with 한테; shows the everyday, intimate flavor of leaning on a close family member.

examples.ko: 힘들 때 친구에게 의지하면 마음이 편해져요.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae chinguege uijihamyeon maeumi pyeonhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: When times are hard, leaning on a friend makes you feel better.
examples.note: 에게 marks who you lean on; 의지하다 carries warm, trusting emotional dependence, not a transaction.

examples.en: Grandmother walks slowly, leaning on a cane.
examples.note: Physical sense with 에; 의지해서 chains the support to the action of walking.

words.nuance: 의지하다 (依支, '依 depend + 支 prop up') means to depend on or lean on someone or something for emotional, practical, or even physical support, and it almost always carries a warm, human feeling of trust rather than cold reliance. The boundary to learn: 의지하다 is leaning on someone for support and comfort, while 믿다 is believing in or trusting them, and 기대다 is the most physical/intimate 'lean against' (you can 어깨에 기대다 lean on a shoulder, and figuratively it sounds even tenderer). A crucial particle split: a person you rely on takes 에게/한테 (부모님께 의지해요), but an object you physically lean on takes 에 (벽에 의지하다). It collocates with 서로 and 많이, and the bare noun appears in 의지가 되다 (to be a source of support). The 하다-verb conjugates regularly to 의지해요 / 의지했어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) do not mark the person with 을/를 — English 'rely on someone' tempts a direct object, but Korean needs 에게/한테; and (2) the 'let's rely' (shallWe) form is unnatural, since relying isn't something two people propose doing in concert, so treat 의지할까요? as a real question ('shall I lean on you?'), not a casual suggestion.

Use 의지해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the person you rely on with 을/를 (부모님을 의지해요). The supporter takes 에게/한테/께: 부모님께 의지해요 — English 'rely on X' misleads you into a direct object.
Using 에 for a person or 에게 for an object. Split them: people take 에게/한테 (친구한테 의지해요), physical props take 에 (지팡이에 의지해요).
Confusing 의지하다 with 믿다. 'I trust you' is 너를 믿어, while 'I lean on you' is 너한테 의지해 — trusting and depending-for-support are different acts.

examples.en: I sincerely respect that person who always takes on challenges.

examples.note: 존경하게 되다 = 'come to respect', marking a shift in feeling triggered by witnessed behavior.

words.nuance: 존경하다 (尊敬, '尊 honor + 敬 revere') is deep respect and admiration for a person's character, achievements, or values — looking up to an elder, mentor, hero, or role model. Two boundaries matter. First, it is far stronger and more upward-looking than 좋아하다 (to like): you can like a singer's songs (좋아하다) yet 존경 a person only for who they are. Second, and the classic mix-up, 존경하다 vs 존중하다 (尊重): you 존경 a *person* you admire, but you 존중 someone's *choices, opinions, or rights* — 다른 사람의 의견을 존중하다 (respect others' opinions), never 존경. The admired person takes 을/를, the modifier 존경하는 is a common formal lead-in, and the passive 존경받다 ('be respected') is everywhere. As a regular 하다-verb it is 존경해요 / 존경했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'respect' covers both senses at once, so learners overuse 존경하다 for everyday courtesy ('respect the rules', 'respect your privacy') where Korean needs 존중하다 — 규칙을 존중하다, not 규칙을 존경하다.

examples.romanization: ppalgan sinhoreul musihago gireul geonneomyeon jeongmal wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: It's really dangerous to ignore a red light and cross.
examples.note: Disregard-a-rule sense; 무시하고 chains the flouting to its risky consequence.

examples.ko: 돈이 없다고 사람을 무시하면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: doni eopsdago sarameul musihamyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You shouldn't look down on people just because they have no money.
examples.note: The belittle sense, which is offensive; 무시당하다 (to be looked down on) is its common passive partner.

words.nuance: 무시하다 (無視, literally '無 without + 視 looking' — 'to not look at') carries two linked senses that context decides between: (1) to ignore or disregard something — a comment, a rule, a warning, a red light — and (2) to look down on, belittle, or disrespect a person, which is quite offensive. With an inanimate target it's the neutral first sense (신호를 무시하다 = disregard the signal); with a person it usually flips to the cutting second sense (사람을 무시하다 = treat them as inferior). Distinguish it from neighbors: 무시하다 (ignore by choice / belittle) is not 모르다 (genuinely not know) and not 외면하다 (deliberately turn one's face away, look away from a problem). The target takes 을/를, it pairs with 그냥, and the passive 무시당하다 ('be slighted') is everywhere in emotional talk. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 무시하다 just means the neutral English 'ignore' — aim it at a person and it commonly reads as 'look down on', so 나를 무시하지 마 is a forceful 'don't disrespect me', far heavier than 'don't ignore me'; if you only mean failing to notice, 무시하다 is the wrong verb entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 무시하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 무시해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Assuming 무시하다 always means a neutral 'ignore'. Aimed at a person it usually means 'look down on / disrespect', so 나를 무시하지 마 is a strong 'don't belittle me', not merely 'don't ignore me'.
Using 무시하다 for failing to notice something. 무시하다 is a deliberate disregard; if you simply didn't notice, say 못 봤어요 or 몰랐어요, not 무시했어요.
Marking the target with 에 (신호에 무시해요). What you ignore is a direct object: 신호를 무시해요, 사람을 무시해요 — always 을/를.

words.english: to discuss / to talk over (to decide)
words.shortExplanation: 의논하다 means "to discuss / to talk over (to decide)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to discuss / to talk over (to decide)" in Korean is 의논하다 (uinonhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 의논해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 의논하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 부모님과 의논하다 ("to talk it over with one's parents") — then reshape the same stem into 의논하고 싶어요 (desire), 의논할 수 있어요 (ability), and 의논 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I discuss / to talk over (to decide).
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not discuss / to talk over (to decide).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to discuss / to talk over (to decide).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can discuss / to talk over (to decide).
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to discuss / to talk over (to decide).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to talk it over with one's parents
usagePhrases.note: The person you consult takes 와/과 (or 하고): you discuss *with* them to reach a decision.

examples.en: Let's talk that over together.
examples.note: Simple 요-form invitation; 같이 marks it as a joint consultation, not a one-way report.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 부모님과 의논해 보고 결정할게요.
examples.romanization: i munjeneun bumonimgwa uinonhae bogo gyeoljeonghalgeyo.
examples.en: I'll talk this over with my parents before I decide.
examples.note: 와/과 marks who you consult; 의논해 보고 결정하다 shows the whole point is to reach a decision.

examples.en: I had a serious discussion with my teacher about my career path.
examples.note: Real-life pattern: 에 대해 (topic) + 와/과 (partner) + 진지하게 + 의논하다, the way you describe seeking advice.

words.nuance: 의논하다 (議論, '議 deliberate + 論 discuss') is to talk something over with someone in order to reach a decision or get advice, so its essence is practical, two-way consultation, not a formal contest of ideas. Hold three neighbors apart. 의논하다 / 상의하다 both mean 'consult to decide' (상의하다 sounds a touch more formal and businesslike), so they're near-twins. 토론하다 (debate) means weighing opposing sides on an issue — public, argumentative — which 의논하다 is not. And 대화하다 (converse) is just friendly chatting with no decision at stake. The crucial particles: the person you consult takes 와/과 or 하고 (친구와 의논해요), and the topic takes 에 대해 (진로에 대해 의논해요). It pairs with 같이, 진지하게, and lives in 의논 상대 (someone to talk things over with). As a 하다-verb it is 의논해요 / 의논했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'discuss it WITH my parents' tempts you toward a 'to' marker, but the consultation partner must take 와/과, never 에게/한테 — 의논하다 is mutual, not one-directional delivery.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의논하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의논해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the discussion partner with 에게/한테 (친구에게 의논해요). You talk things over *together*, so the partner takes 와/과 or 하고: 친구와 의논해요.
Using 의논하다 for a formal debate of opposing views; that is 토론하다. 의논하다 is consulting to decide, so a panel or classroom argument calls for 토론하다.
Treating 의논하다 as plain chatting. If there's no decision or advice at stake, 'let's talk' is 이야기해요 or 대화해요; 의논하다 specifically aims at settling something.

words.english: to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in
words.shortExplanation: 신뢰하다 means "to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 신뢰하다 (silloehada) = "to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 신뢰해요 plus one useful sentence like 서로 신뢰하다 ("to trust each other"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 신뢰하고 싶어요 for what you want, 신뢰할 수 있어요 for what you can, 신뢰 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: I trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The trusted person/thing takes 을/를; 서로 frames it as firm, mutual confidence between parties.

examples.en: I have confidence in that person.
examples.note: Plain 을/를 object; note this sounds firmer and more formal than the everyday 믿어요.

examples.ko: 저는 그 회사를 오래전부터 신뢰해 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu hoesareul oraejeonbuteo silloehae wasseoyo.
examples.en: I've trusted that company for a long time.
examples.note: 신뢰해 오다 (have been trusting) shows confidence built up over time, typical for brands and institutions.

examples.ko: 팀원들이 서로 신뢰해야 일이 잘 돼요.
examples.romanization: timwondeuri seoro silloehaeya iri jal dwaeyo.
examples.en: Team members have to trust one another for work to go well.
examples.note: Work register about reliability; 신뢰 here is reasoned, dependable confidence, not a fleeting hunch.

words.nuance: 신뢰하다 (信賴, '信 believe + 賴 rely') is firm, reasoned trust or confidence in a person, organization, or system, and it sounds notably more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust). The dividing line is register and grounds: you 신뢰 a colleague's competence, a company, a brand, or a system on the basis of a track record, whereas you 믿다 a friend, a rumor, a promise, or a religion more casually and on faith. (믿다 also covers 'believe that…', which 신뢰하다 never does.) The trusted target takes 을/를, and the noun 신뢰 collocates richly: 신뢰를 쌓다 (build trust), 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust), 신뢰 관계, 신뢰감. As a regular 하다-verb it is 신뢰해요 / 신뢰했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the 'big' word in casual speech: between close friends '나 믿지?' (you trust me, right?) is natural and warm, while 나 신뢰해? sounds stiff and oddly corporate — match 신뢰하다 to formal, reasoned, often written contexts and let 믿다 carry everyday emotional trust.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 신뢰하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 신뢰해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 신뢰하다 in very casual speech where 믿다 fits. Between friends '나 믿지?' is natural; 신뢰해? sounds stiff and businesslike, mismatched to an intimate register.
Using 신뢰하다 to mean 'believe that…'. For 'I believe he'll come' say 그가 올 거라고 믿어요; 신뢰하다 means trusting a person/thing, not believing a proposition.
Marking the trusted target with 에게/한테 (그 사람에게 신뢰해요). What you trust is a direct object: 그 사람을 신뢰해요 — always 을/를.

words.shortExplanation: 조언하다 means "to give advice / to counsel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 조언하다 (joeonhada) means "to give advice / to counsel". Start from the polite form 조언해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 조언하다. A strong first sentence is 후배에게 조언하다 ("to give advice to a junior"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 조언하다 also becomes 조언하고 싶어요 (want), 조언할 수 있어요 (can), and 조언 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not give advice / to counsel.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to give advice / to counsel.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can give advice / to counsel.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to give advice / to counsel.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to give advice to a junior
usagePhrases.note: The listener takes 에게/한테: 후배에게 / 친구한테 조언하다 — advice flows toward the receiver.

examples.en: I gave my friend honest advice.
examples.note: 에게 marks the receiver; 솔직하게 (honestly/frankly) is a natural adverb for candid counsel.

examples.ko: 전문가가 건강 관리에 대해 조언해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jeonmungaga geongang gwallie daehae joeonhae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: An expert gave advice about managing your health.
examples.note: N에 대해 조언해 주다: the 주다 helper frames it as a favor; sounds informed and slightly formal.

examples.ko: 제가 조언할 입장은 아니지만 한번 들어 보세요.
examples.romanization: jega joeonhal ipjangeun anijiman hanbeon deureo boseyo.
examples.en: I'm not really in a position to advise, but hear me out.
examples.note: 조언할 입장이 아니다 (not in a position to advise) is a humble hedge before offering an opinion.

words.nuance: 조언하다 (助言, '助 help + 言 words' — literally 'helping words') means to offer advice or counsel from knowledge or experience, and it sounds more thoughtful and a touch more formal than casually telling someone what to do. The key contrast is with 충고하다 (忠告): 조언 is helpful, supportive guidance you welcome, while 충고 carries a corrective, admonishing edge — closer to a warning or a talking-to ('너에게 충고하는데…' often precedes criticism), so they are not interchangeable in tone. It also differs from 추천하다 (recommend a specific thing) and 제안하다 (propose a course of action). Grammatically the listener takes 에게/한테 and the topic takes 에 대해; it lives as 조언해 주다 (give advice as a kindness) and the receiver's-side 조언을 구하다 (seek advice). As a 하다-verb it is 조언해요 / 조언했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the noun shape: English 'advise SOMEONE' tempts a direct object, but the person taught takes 에게/한테 (친구에게 조언해요), because what is actually 'given' is the 조언 itself — and note 조언 is uncountable-flavored, so 'a piece of advice' is 한마디 조언, not a pluralized form.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 조언하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 조언해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the advice-receiver with 을/를 (친구를 조언해요). The listener takes 에게/한테: 친구에게 조언해요 — the advice (조언) is what's given, not the person.

words.shortExplanation: 토론하다 means "to debate / to discuss (formally)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to debate / to discuss (formally)" in Korean is 토론하다 (toronhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 토론해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 토론하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 환경에 대해 토론하다 ("to debate about the environment") — then reshape the same stem into 토론하고 싶어요 (desire), 토론할 수 있어요 (ability), and 토론 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not debate / to discuss (formally).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to debate / to discuss (formally).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to debate / to discuss (formally).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The topic takes 에 대해 or (으)로: 그 주제로 / 환경에 대해 토론하다 = debate the issue from sides.

examples.en: Let's have a debate on that topic.
examples.note: Simple 요-form invite; (으)로 marks the topic, and 토론하다 implies weighing different sides, not chatting.

examples.en: The students debated about environmental issues.
examples.note: N에 대해 토론하다 = debate about N; presupposes presenting and weighing opposing arguments.

examples.en: Let's not fight emotionally — let's debate calmly.
examples.note: Contrasts 토론하다 (reasoned debate) with 싸우다 (quarrel); 토론 is meant to stay rational.

words.nuance: 토론하다 (討論, '討 examine + 論 argue') is to debate or discuss an issue formally, presenting and weighing different viewpoints, so it belongs to classrooms, panels, candidate debates, and structured meetings rather than casual chitchat. Place it among its neighbors: 토론하다 (argue a question from sides, often with opposing positions) is more confrontational and structured than 의논하다/상의하다 (talk something over together to decide), and entirely distinct from 대화하다 (just converse) and 싸우다 (quarrel) — a good 토론 stays reasoned even when heated. The topic takes 에 대해 or (으)로, it collocates with 열띤, 찬반, and 활발하게, and the noun appears in 토론회 (debate forum), 토론자 (debater), 끝장 토론 (a marathon, settle-it debate). As a regular 하다-verb it is 토론해요 / 토론했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'discuss' covers everything from a chat to a formal debate, so learners overuse 토론하다 for ordinary talk — if you just want to 'talk about' your weekend or 'chat' with a friend, say 이야기하다 or 대화하다; reserve 토론하다 for a genuine, argued exchange on an issue.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 토론하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 토론해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Useful for choices and plans.

words.nuance: 싫어하다 is the action verb 'to dislike / hate' and, like its opposite 좋아하다, takes the object marker 을/를: 벌레를 싫어해요. The verb describes a person's standing dislike, while 싫다 often voices an in-the-moment 'ugh, I don't want to'. The near-synonym to watch is 미워하다, which is 'to resent/hate a person' with an emotional, almost grudge-like color — you 미워하다 someone who hurt you, but you 싫어하다 cold weather or homework. words.shortExplanation: 알다 means "to know" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to know" in Korean is 알다 (alda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 알아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 알다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 저 사람을 알아요 ("I know that person") — then reshape the same stem into 알고 싶어요 (desire), 알 수 있어요 (ability), and 모르겠어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: 잘 알아요 = solid familiarity; object 를 on 식당

examples.en: Do you know what this word means?
examples.note: rising-intonation question; 뜻을 알다 'know the meaning'

words.nuance: 알다 means 'to know / be aware of / be acquainted with' and takes the object marker 을/를: 저 사람을 알아요. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and the honorific ㅅ, giving 압니다 (not 알습니다) and 아세요 (not 알으세요), but the ㄹ stays before vowel endings, so the everyday polite form is 알아요. words.shortExplanation: 모르다 means "to not know" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 모르다 (moreuda) = "to not know". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 몰라요 plus one useful sentence like 길을 몰라요 ("I don't know the way"). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

words.nuance: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know / be unaware of', the lexical opposite of 알다, and it likewise takes the object marker 을/를: 길을 몰라요. words.shortExplanation: 살다 means "to live" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

words.nuance: 살다 means 'to live' in two senses — to reside somewhere and to be alive — and is a ㄹ-irregular verb. The stem ㄹ disappears before ㅂ, ㄴ, and the honorific 시, producing 삽니다 (not 살읍니다), 사세요 (not 살으세요), and 사니까; before vowel endings the ㄹ stays, so the polite present is 살아요. For where you live, the default particle is the static-location 에: 서울에 살아요. Interestingly, because living is an activity carried out over time, the dynamic-location 에서 is also acceptable and common, especially with hopes and experiences (한국에서 살고 싶어요) — this is one of the few cases where both 에 and 에서 work with the same verb. Contrast 살다 with 거주하다 (居住하다, Sino-Korean 'to reside'), a stiff, formal/written word used on official forms (거주지 'place of residence'); in speech you always say 살다. conjugationTips.body: 살다 is a ㄹ-stem word. The ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings: 살다 → 삽니다 (formal), 사는 (describing a noun), 사세요 (honorific). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 살아요.

Interestingly, because living is an activity carried out over time, the dynamic-location 에서 is also acceptable and common, especially with hopes and experiences (한국에서 살고 싶어요) — this is one of the few cases where both 에 and 에서 work with the same verb.

The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄹ to say 살읍니다 instead of 삽니다, and reflexively choosing 에서 for every location when plain residence prefers 에.

words.shortExplanation: 만들다 means "to make" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to make" in Korean is 만들다 (mandeulda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 만들어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 만들다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 음식을 만들어요 ("I make food") — then reshape the same stem into 만들고 싶어요 (desire), 만들 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 만들어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

words.nuance: 만들다 means 'to make / create / build' something concrete or abstract (food, objects, plans, rules) and takes the object marker 을/를: 음식을 만들어요. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the stem ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and 시 — 만듭니다, 만드세요, 만드니까 — but the ㄹ stays before vowel endings, giving the polite present 만들어요 (never 만드러요) and the suggestion 만들까요. A key contrast is 만들다 vs 하다: both can translate as 'make/do', but 만들다 implies producing a tangible result that did not exist before (케이크를 만들다 'make a cake'), whereas 하다 is to perform an activity (요리를 하다 'do cooking'). Also distinguish 짓다 ('to build/construct' houses, and to compose names/poems, 집을 짓다) from 만들다, which is the broad everyday 'make'. The English-speaker pitfall is mishandling the irregular in both directions: dropping the ㄹ before a vowel (만드러요) or keeping it before a consonant (만들습니다 instead of 만듭니다).

Use 만들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Dropping the ㄹ before a vowel ending and writing 만드러요 — the ㄹ only drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/시, so the polite present is 만들어요.
Keeping the ㄹ before consonant endings (만들습니다) — as a ㄹ-irregular it must drop: 만듭니다, 만드세요.

notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 만들어 and 만들어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 배우다 means "to learn" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 배우다 (baeuda) = "to learn". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 배워요 plus one useful sentence like 한국어를 배워요 ("I learn Korean"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 배우고 싶어요 for what you want, 배울 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 배워요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
the subject/skill learned takes the object marker 을/를

examples.en: I learn Korean.
examples.note: two vowels contract: 배우 + 어요 → 배워요

examples.en: These days I'm learning guitar from a friend.
examples.note: source person takes 한테; 고 있다 = ongoing

examples.ko: 저는 운전을 배워서 회사에 차로 가고 싶어요.

examples.en: I want to learn to drive and go to work by car.
examples.note: real goal-linked sentence; 배워서 connects reason to plan

words.nuance: 배우다 means 'to learn / acquire a skill or subject' and takes the object marker 을/를: 한국어를 배워요. It is a regular verb, but the stem ends in the vowel 우, so when 어요 attaches the two vowels contract into 워 — 배우 + 어요 → 배워요 (not 배우어요), past 배웠어요. The natural partner verb is 가르치다 ('to teach'), the giving side of the same act; and the person you learn from takes 한테/에게서 (사람) — 선생님한테 배워요 — never the place particle 에서 for the source. Contrast 배우다 with 공부하다 (工夫하다, 'to study'): 공부하다 is the effort of studying (sitting down, reviewing, hitting the books), while 배우다 is the result of acquiring a skill or being taught it, often from someone. So you 공부하다 for an exam at your desk but 배우다 the piano from a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is writing the uncontracted 배우어요, and saying 학원에서 배우다 to mean 'learn from the academy' — 에서 marks where, while the human source must take 한테/에게서.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 배우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 배워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the uncontracted 배우어요 — the 우 + 어요 contracts, so the polite present is 배워요 (past 배웠어요).
Confusing 배우다 with 공부하다 — 공부하다 is the act of studying/reviewing; 배우다 is acquiring or being taught a skill. Use 시험공부를 해요 for exam prep, 피아노를 배워요 for taking lessons.
Marking the person you learn from with 에서 — a human source takes 한테/에게서: 선생님한테 배워요, not 선생님에서.

words.shortExplanation: 가르치다 means "to teach" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 가르치다 (gareuchida) means "to teach". Start from the polite form 가르쳐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 가르치다. A strong first sentence is 영어를 가르쳐요 ("I teach English"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 가르치다 also becomes 가르치고 싶어요 (want), 가르칠 수 있어요 (can), and 못 가르쳐요 (cannot). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: 치 + 어요 contracts to 쳐요

words.nuance: 가르치다 means 'to teach / instruct' and is the giving counterpart of 배우다 ('to learn'). It is a regular verb whose stem ends in 치, so 치 + 어요 contracts to 쳐요 — the polite present is 가르쳐요, past 가르쳤어요. Its argument structure is the classic give-pattern: the learner (recipient) takes 에게 or casual 한테, and the subject taught takes 을/를 — 학생들에게 영어를 가르쳐요. The single most important caution is the look-alike 가리키다 ('to point at / indicate', 시계를 가리키다 'point at the clock'): the two verbs sound close and even native speakers occasionally slip, but 가르치다 is teaching and 가리키다 is pointing — never swap them. Compare also with the honorific 가르침 ('teachings/guidance', a noun) and the polite request 가르쳐 주세요, which is how you say 'please show/tell me'. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing up 가르치다 with 가리키다, and forgetting that the person taught takes 에게/한테 (not 을/를), so 'teach the students' is 학생들에게 가르쳐요, with the lesson, not the student, as the 를-object.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가르치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가르쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 가르치다 (to teach) with the near-identical 가리키다 (to point at) — keep them apart: 한국어를 가르쳐요 vs 손가락으로 가리켜요.
Marking the learner with the object 를 (학생을 가르쳐요 to mean 'teach to the student') — the recipient takes 에게/한테: 학생에게 가르쳐요, and the lesson takes 를.

words.shortExplanation: 도와주다 means "to help" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to help" in Korean is 도와주다 (dowajuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 도와줘요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 도와주다 for study notes. words.nuance: 도와주다 means 'to help (for someone's benefit)' and is built from 돕다 ('to help') + 주다 ('to give'), so the 주다 already bakes in the warm sense of doing the help for another person. The base 돕다 is a ㅂ-irregular (돕 + 아요 → 도와요), which is why the compound surfaces as 도와- and the polite present is 도와줘요, past 도와줬어요. The person helped takes the object marker 을/를: 친구를 도와줘요. The most useful register fact is the request form: because 주다 is inside the verb, 'please help me' is simply 도와주세요 — adding a second giving verb to make 도와줘 주세요 is redundant and wrong. Contrast plain 돕다 (which feels more neutral/written, 어려운 이웃을 돕다 'help a struggling neighbor') with 도와주다 (the warm, conversational everyday form). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that double 주세요, plus marking the helped person with 에게 by analogy to 'give to' — but help is done to a person directly, so it is 저를 도와줘요, not 저에게 도와줘요.

words.shortExplanation: 시작하다 means "to start" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 시작하다 (sijakhada) = "to start". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 시작해요 plus one useful sentence like 일을 시작해요 ("I start work"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 시작하고 싶어요 for what you want, 시작할 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 시작해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
with an object (transitive) the thing started takes 을/를

examples.note: time at 에; intransitive, so 수업이

examples.note: real suggestion before an activity

words.nuance: 시작하다 means 'to start / begin' and is a Sino-Korean 하다 verb — 시작 (始作, literally 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do', i.e. 'set in motion') plus 하다. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly with 하다 → 해요: 시작해요 / 시작합니다 / 시작했어요. A point that trips learners is that 시작하다 works both transitively and intransitively: with a doer it takes an object (저는 일을 시작해요 'I start work', 을/를), and with no doer the thing simply begins and takes the subject marker (수업이 시작해요 'class starts', 이/가). Contrast it with the pure intransitive 시작되다 (始作되다, 'to be started/begin'), which is more formal and never takes an object — 회의가 시작됐어요 'the meeting began'. Its natural opposite is 끝나다 ('to end'). The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) conjugating the 하다 wrongly as 시작하요 instead of 시작해요, and (2) forcing an object onto the no-doer case (수업을 시작해요 when you simply mean class begins) — when nothing actively starts it, use 수업이 시작해요 or the passive 시작돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 시작하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 시작해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating the 하다 as 시작하요 — every 하다 verb becomes 해요, so it is 시작해요 (formal 시작합니다, past 시작했어요).
Forcing an object when there is no doer (수업을 시작해요 to mean 'class begins') — use the intransitive 수업이 시작해요, or 시작돼요.
Using the formal passive 시작되다 in casual speech where active 시작하다 fits — keep 시작되다 for announcements/writing (회의가 시작됩니다).

Contrast it with the pure intransitive 시작되다 (始作되다, 'to be started/begin'), which is more formal and never takes an object — 회의가 시작됐어요 'the meeting began'.
It is a Sino-Korean 하다 verb — 시작 (始作, literally 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do', i.e. 'set in motion') plus 하다.
As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly with 하다 → 해요: 시작해요 / 시작합니다 / 시작했어요.

The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) conjugating the 하다 wrongly as 시작하요 instead of 시작해요, and (2) forcing an object onto the no-doer case (수업을 시작해요 when you simply mean class begins) — when nothing actively starts it, use 수업이 시작해요 or the passive 시작돼요.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

words.nuance: 끝나다 means 'to end / be over / finish' as something that happens by itself — it is intransitive, so the thing that ends takes the subject marker 이/가: 수업이 끝나요, past 끝났어요 (끝나 + 았어요). The essential pairing is with its transitive twin 끝내다 ('to finish/end something'), used when a person actively brings an action to a close with an object: 저는 일을 끝내요 ('I finish the work', 을/를). This 끝나다 (happens) vs 끝내다 (someone does it) split mirrors 시작하다 family logic and is one of Korean's classic intransitive/transitive verb pairs (like 켜지다/켜다, 열리다/열다). The natural opposite is 시작하다 ('to begin'). A nuance of completion: 다 끝났어요 ('it's all done') is the everyday way to announce something is finished, and 끝 alone is an interjection meaning 'the end'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 끝나다 with an object — saying 일을 끝나요 by analogy to English 'I end the work' — when an actor finishes something it must be the transitive 일을 끝내요.

Using 끝나다 with an object (일을 끝나요) — 끝나다 is intransitive; when a person finishes something, use the transitive 끝내다: 일을 끝내요.
Marking the thing that ends with 을/를 (수업을 끝나요) — it takes the subject marker: 수업이 끝나요.

words.shortExplanation: 묻다 means "to ask" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

words.nuance: 묻다 means 'to ask (a question / inquire)' and takes the object marker 을/를 for the thing asked about: 길을 물어요. It is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the stem ㄷ changes to ㄹ, giving 물어요 and 물었어요 and 물을 거예요, but before consonant endings the ㄷ stays — 묻습니다, 묻고, 묻지 마세요. The person you ask takes 에게/한테, or honorific 께 for someone of higher status: 선생님께 물어요. In real speech Koreans far more often say 물어보다 ('ask and see', literally 묻다 + 보다), which sounds softer and more tentative than the bare, slightly abrupt 묻다 — so 물어보세요 ('please ask') is the natural request, not 물으세요. Two contrasts: do not confuse this 묻다 with the homograph 묻다 meaning 'to bury' (regular: 땅에 묻다), and distinguish 묻다 ('ask a question') from 부탁하다 ('to request a favor'). The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄷ before a vowel to say 묻어요 (which actually reads as the 'bury' verb) instead of the irregular 물어요.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 이사하고 싶어요 for what you want, 이사할 수 있어요 for what you can, 이사 못 해요 for what you can't.
