Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: I'm moving next month.
examples.note: Bare 이사해요 already implies changing homes; no extra object needed

examples.romanization: jibi jobaseo deo neolbeun goseuro isahago sipeoyo.

words.nuance: 이사하다 specifically means relocating your residence — changing the home you live in — built from Sino-Korean 移徙 (移 'shift', 徙 'relocate') plus 하다. Contrast it sharply with 옮기다, which is just physically moving an object from one spot to another (책상을 옮기다 'move the desk'); you never use 옮기다 for changing homes, and you never use 이사하다 for shifting furniture. It splits into 이사 가다 (move away, focus on departure) and 이사 오다 (move in, focus on arrival near the speaker). Being a 하다-verb, the negative wraps the noun: 이사 안 해요 / 이사 못 해요, NOT 안 이사해요. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating it like English 'move' as a transitive verb — Koreans don't say '집을 이사해요'; the home is implied, so just 이사해요 is complete.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이사하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이사해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 안 이사해요 — for 하다-compound verbs the negation goes inside, so the correct form is 이사 안 해요 (and 이사 못 해요 for inability).
Saying 집을 이사해요 by direct-translating 'move house' — 이사하다 already contains the idea of home, so the object is dropped; just say 이사해요.
Using 옮기다 for relocating yourself (e.g. 서울로 옮겼어요) — 옮기다 is only for moving objects; for changing residence use 서울로 이사했어요.

The biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating it like English 'move' as a transitive verb — Koreans don't say '집을 이사해요'; the home is implied, so just 이사해요 is complete.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

examples.note: -ㄹ까요 offers your own action; you're proposing to do the lending

examples.note: -ㄹ 수가 없다 with 가 adds an apologetic 'really can't' nuance

words.nuance: 빌려주다 is literally 빌려 (lend-and) + 주다 (give), so it means 'borrow-out to someone' — you give something for temporary use, expecting it back. The crucial contrast is with 빌리다, which is the SAME root from the other direction: 빌리다 = to borrow (you receive), 빌려주다 = to lend (you give). English speakers constantly swap these because casual English even uses 'borrow me your pen', but Korean keeps them strictly separate — 친구에게 책을 빌려줬어요 'I lent a book to my friend' vs 친구에게서 책을 빌렸어요 'I borrowed a book from my friend'. Watch the particles: the thing takes 를, the person you lend TO takes 에게/한테, whereas with 빌리다 the person you borrow FROM takes 에게서/한테서. The 주다 ending also carries a giving/favor feeling, so 빌려주다 sounds kind and helpful, which is why polite requests are simply 빌려주세요.

Use 빌려줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing direction: saying 친구한테 책을 빌렸어요 when you mean you GAVE the book — to lend you must use 빌려줬어요. 빌리다 = receive, 빌려주다 = give.
Marking the recipient with the wrong particle: with 빌려주다 the person takes 에게/한테 (to whom), not 에게서/한테서 (from whom, which belongs to 빌리다).
Dropping the 주다 and just saying 빌려요 to mean 'I lend' — 빌리다 by itself means 'borrow', so 'lend' needs the full 빌려주다.

words.shortExplanation: 버리다 means "to throw away" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to throw away" in Korean is 버리다 (beorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 버려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 버리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 쓰레기를 버리다 ("to throw away trash") — then reshape the same stem into 버리고 싶어요 (desire), 버릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 버려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Is it okay to throw this away?
examples.note: -아도 돼요 asks permission before discarding something

examples.en: I threw out all the clothes I don't wear.
examples.note: Topic 옷은 sets 'as for clothes'; 다 'all' shows total disposal

examples.en: It's still usable, so please don't throw it away.
examples.note: -ㄹ 만하다 'worth doing' justifies keeping it

words.nuance: 버리다 means to discard something as no longer wanted — to throw it out as trash or to abandon it. Don't confuse it with 던지다, which is to throw an object through the air toward a target (공을 던지다 'throw a ball'); 버리다 is about getting rid of, not about the flying motion. A second hugely important use is as an auxiliary verb -아/어 버리다, which colors the main verb with 'completely' or 'regrettably/finally': 잊어버리다 'forget (clean out of mind)', 가 버리다 '(someone) just left'. So a learner must read context: 버려요 alone = throw away, but 먹어 버려요 = eat it all up. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 던지다 whenever they see 'throw' — but 'throw away/out' in the disposal sense is always 버리다. Also note Korea's strict 분리수거 (recycling separation) culture, so 버리다 in daily life often pairs with sorting.

Use 버려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 던지다 for disposal (쓰레기를 던지다) — that means hurling the trash through the air; to dispose of it you must say 쓰레기를 버리다.
Misreading the auxiliary: hearing 다 써 버렸어요 as 'threw away while writing' — here 버리다 is auxiliary meaning 'used it all up'; the real main verb is 쓰다.
Forgetting that 버리다 also means 'abandon (a person)' (애인을 버리다) — so in emotional contexts it can sound harsh; don't use it lightly about people.

examples.en: My back hurts, so I can't pick it up.
examples.note: Inability 못 + irregular 주워요; bending down is the implied difficulty

words.nuance: 줍다 means to pick up something that is lying on the ground or floor, usually by bending down — typically things that fell or litter. It contrasts with 들다 'to lift/hold up' (which is about raising weight, no fallen-object implication) and with 집다 'to grab/pinch with fingers' (a precise small grasp, e.g. with chopsticks). Crucially 줍다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the ㅂ turns into a 우 sound, giving 주워, 주워요, 주웠어요, 주울 거예요 — but before a consonant ending the ㅂ stays, so the formal style is 줍습니다 (not 주웁니다) and 'don't' is 줍지 마세요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is regularizing it to 줍어요; that is wrong — say 주워요. Also note the place you pick it up FROM takes 에서 (바닥에서 주웠어요), since picking up is an action happening at a location.

Over-applying the irregular to consonant endings: saying 주웁니다 — before the consonant ㅅ the ㅂ is kept, so formal is 줍습니다.
Using 들다 (lift) for something on the floor: 바닥에서 동전을 들었어요 sounds off; for retrieving a fallen item use 줍다 → 주웠어요.
notes: ㅂ irregular: memorize 주워 and 주워요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 깨다 means "to break" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 깨다 (kkaeda) means "to break". Start from the polite form 깨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 깨다. A strong first sentence is 접시를 깨다 ("to break a plate"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 깨다 also becomes 깨고 싶어요 (want), 깰 수 있어요 (can), and 못 깨요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Object takes 를; brittle items (glass, dishes, eggs) are typical objects

examples.en: I was careful in case I'd break the cup.
examples.note: -ㄹ까 봐 'fearing that' — worrying about breaking it

examples.en: Crack the eggs and put them in the bowl.
examples.note: Cooking: 깨다 also covers cracking an eggshell open

examples.en: This is expensive, so please don't break it.
examples.note: -지 마세요 prohibition; 깨다 is transitive (you break it)

words.nuance: 깨다 (transitive) means to break a hard, brittle thing into pieces — glass, dishes, eggs — by impact. Distinguish it from 부수다, which is to smash/demolish a larger or sturdier structure (벽을 부수다 'break down a wall'), and from 깨지다, the intransitive partner: 내가 컵을 깼어요 'I broke the cup (I did it)' vs 컵이 깨졌어요 'the cup broke (it got broken)'. The same syllable 깨다 also means to wake up from sleep (잠을 깨다 / 잠에서 깨다), and figuratively to 'break' a record, silence, or atmosphere — so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is using 깨다 for things that don't shatter: tearing paper is 찢다, snapping a stick is 부러뜨리다, and breaking a machine so it stops working is 고장 내다 — not 깨다. Conjugation is regular: stem 깨- + 어 contracts to 깨, past 깼어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 깨다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 깨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing transitivity: saying 컵을 깨졌어요 — 깨지다 is intransitive ('the cup broke'), so with an object 을 you need the transitive 컵을 깼어요.
Using 깨다 for non-brittle breakage: 종이를 깼어요 for tearing paper is wrong — tearing is 찢다; a snapped stick is 부러뜨리다.
Saying 고장났어요 vs 깼어요 mix-up: a broken-down phone is 고장 났어요 (stopped working), not 깼어요, which implies you physically shattered it.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 흘리다 means "to spill" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to spill" in Korean is 흘리다 (heullida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 흘려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 흘리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 물을 흘리다 ("to spill water / let water drip") — then reshape the same stem into 흘리고 싶어요 (desire), 흘릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 흘려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to spill water / let water drip
usagePhrases.note: Object takes 를; small amounts dribbling out, often onto clothes

examples.en: Be careful not to spill the soup.
examples.note: -지 않게 'so as not to' + casual warning

examples.en: The kid keeps dropping rice (while eating).
examples.note: 자꾸 'repeatedly' + 흘려요; eating-spill sense

examples.en: I was so moved that I shed tears.
examples.note: Idiomatic 눈물을 흘리다 for crying; past 흘렸어요

words.nuance: 흘리다 is the transitive 'cause to flow/drip' — to let liquid or small grains escape and run out, usually a little at a time and by accident (옷에 국을 흘렸어요 'I dribbled soup on my clothes'). Two big contrasts: first, its intransitive partner is 흐르다 'to flow' (물이 흐르다 'water flows by itself') — don't say 흘러요 when YOU spilled it; you need 흘려요. Second, against 쏟다: 쏟다 is dumping a large amount out all at once (a whole cup tipping over), while 흘리다 is a gentler, trickling spill. Beyond liquids, 흘리다 is the idiomatic verb for bodily flow — 눈물을 흘리다 'shed tears', 땀을 흘리다 'sweat', 피를 흘리다 'bleed'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 흐르다/흘리다 confusion: English 'spill' is transitive, so map it to 흘리다 (or 쏟다 for big spills), never 흐르다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 흘리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 흘려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 물을 흘러요 when you spilled it — 흐르다 ('flow') is intransitive for liquid moving on its own; if you caused the spill, use the transitive 흘려요.
Using 흘리다 for a big sudden spill: knocking over a full glass is better said 쏟다 (쏟았어요) — 흘리다 implies a small, dribbling amount.
Forgetting the body-fluid idioms: trying to say 'cry' with 울다 only — to describe tears running down, Koreans say 눈물을 흘리다, and 땀을 흘리다 for sweating.

words.shortExplanation: 묶다 means "to tie" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 묶다 (mukda) = "to tie". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 묶어요 plus one useful sentence like 머리를 묶다 ("to tie one's hair (up)"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 묶고 싶어요 for what you want, 묶을 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 묶어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
묶다 is the go-to verb for tying hair into a ponytail; object 를

examples.en: Want me to tie your hair up?
examples.note: Casual offer -아 줄까; everyday between friends/family

examples.en: I tied the box up tightly with string.
examples.note: 단단히 'firmly' + means 끈으로; past 묶었어요

examples.ko: 택배 보내게 이 상자 좀 묶어 주세요.
examples.romanization: taekbae bonaege i sangja jom mukkeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please tie up this box so I can ship it.
examples.note: -게 'so that' links purpose to the request

words.nuance: 묶다 means to tie or bind things together with string, rope, or a band so they stay fastened — boxes, hair, shoelaces, bundles. Its natural antonym is 풀다 'to untie/undo'. Distinguish it from 매다, which specifically means to fasten by knotting around something (넥타이를 매다 'tie a necktie', 안전벨트를 매다 'fasten a seatbelt') — 매다 is about securing a band to/around the body, while 묶다 is the general 'bind together' for objects and hair. Note the binding material takes 으로: 끈으로 묶다 'tie with string'. Pronunciation is a trap: the ㄲ batchim before a vowel links, so 묶어요 sounds like [무꺼요], but you must spell it 묶어요, and the formal form is 묶습니다 [묵씀니다]. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 매다 for everything 'tie' — but for hair, boxes, and bundles, the correct verb is 묶다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 묶다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 묶어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling by ear: writing 무꺼요 because it sounds like [무꺼요] — the stem keeps its ㄲ, so it is written 묶어요.
Using 매다 for hair or boxes: 머리를 매다 / 박스를 매다 sounds wrong — 매다 is for neckties and seatbelts (fastening around); for hair and bundles use 묶다.
Forgetting the means particle: saying 끈을 묶어요 to mean 'tie WITH string' — the tool takes 으로, so it is 끈으로 묶어요 (끈을 묶어요 would mean 'tie the string itself').

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 풀다 means "to untie" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 풀다 (pulda) means "to untie". Start from the polite form 풀어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 풀다. A strong first sentence is 매듭을 풀다 ("to undo a knot"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 풀다 also becomes 풀고 싶어요 (want), 풀 수 있어요 (can), and 못 풀어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The prototypical 'untie'; opposite of 묶다

examples.en: Untie my shoelace for me.
examples.note: Casual favor 풀어 줘; literal untie sense

examples.en: Shall we solve this math problem together?
examples.note: -ㄹ까요 suggestion; 풀다 = solve, note ㄹ stays before 까

examples.ko: 주말에 여행 가서 스트레스 좀 풀고 와요.
examples.romanization: jumare yeohaeng gaseo seuteureseu jom pulgo wayo.
examples.en: Go on a trip this weekend and de-stress.
examples.note: 스트레스를 풀다 idiom; -고 오다 'do and come back'

words.nuance: 풀다 covers a wide web of meanings around 'undo/release': literally to untie or unfasten (매듭을 풀다 'undo a knot'), to solve a problem (문제를 풀다), to relieve stress or fatigue (스트레스를 풀다, 피로를 풀다), to unpack (짐을 풀다), and even to blow your nose (코를 풀다). Its literal antonym is 묶다 'to tie'. Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ disappears before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings, so the formal present is 풉니다 (not 풀습니다) and the prohibitive is 풀지 마세요 — but the ㄹ stays before vowels (풀어요) and before 까 (풀까요?). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, regularizing the irregular to 풀습니다; second, not realizing 풀다 is the everyday word for 'solve' a question — learners often hunt for a separate 'solve' verb, but 문제를 풀다 is exactly it.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 풀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 풀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 풀습니다 in formal style — 풀다 is a ㄹ-irregular, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ: the correct form is 풉니다.
Looking for another verb to mean 'solve': for solving a problem/quiz the natural verb IS 풀다 → 문제를 풀어요, not a separate word.
Over-dropping the ㄹ before vowels: writing 푸어요 — the ㄹ only drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ; before a vowel it stays, giving 풀어요.
notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 풀어 and 풀어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 접다 means "to fold" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to fold" in Korean is 접다 (jeopda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 접어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 접다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 빨래를 접다 ("to fold the laundry") — then reshape the same stem into 접고 싶어요 (desire), 접을 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 접어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Everyday chore collocation; object takes 를

examples.ko: 다 마른 빨래 좀 접어 줘.
examples.romanization: da mareun ppallae jom jeobeo jwo.
examples.en: Fold the dry laundry for me.
examples.note: Casual 접어 줘; chore request between housemates

examples.en: Fold the paper in half and make an airplane.
examples.note: -아서 'and then' links folding to the next step

examples.en: The rain stopped, so fold up your umbrella.
examples.note: -으니까 'since' gives the reason; 접으세요 polite command

words.nuance: 접다 means to fold something flat — cloth, paper, an umbrella — by bending it over onto itself, and by extension to close up a foldable object. Its natural antonyms are 펴다 'to unfold/spread flat' and 펼치다 'to open out/spread wide'. Distinguish 접다 from 구기다, which is to crumple/crease messily (종이를 구기다 'crumple paper into a ball') — 접다 is neat and deliberate, 구기다 is rumpling it up. Figuratively, 접다 means to give up or fold on a plan (꿈을 접다 'give up a dream', 사업을 접다 'fold a business'), much like English 'fold'. The result/shape takes 으로: 반으로 접다 'fold in half'. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation pronunciation — 접어요 links to [저버요] and the formal 접습니다 sounds like [접씀니다], but spelling stays 접어요/접습니다; also don't confuse neat folding (접다) with accidental crumpling (구기다).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 접다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 접어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 접다 (neatly fold) with 구기다 (crumple): 종이를 접었어요 means folded tidily; if you balled it up by accident that is 구겼어요.
Using the wrong particle for 'in half': saying 반을 접어요 — the resulting shape takes 으로, so it is 반으로 접어요.
Mixing up the antonym: to 'unfold/open out' the umbrella you need 펴다 (우산을 펴다), not a negated 접다.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The container takes 를, the contents take 으로: 병을 물로 채우다

examples.note: Casual 채워 줘; container 물통에 takes 에

Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to spill water (a lot, at once)
usagePhrases.note: Object takes 를; implies a sizable amount tipping out

examples.note: Casual exclamation 쏟았어; sudden accident

words.nuance: 쏟다 means to spill or pour out a sizable amount of liquid or contents all at once, usually by knocking something over — it feels stronger and more sudden than 흘리다, which is a small trickling spill (a few drops on your shirt). Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
치우다 = put things in order / clear away clutter; object 를

examples.ko: 밥 먹고 그릇 좀 치워 줘.
examples.romanization: bam meokgo geureut jom chiwo jwo.
examples.en: Clear away the dishes after eating.
examples.note: Casual 치워 줘; 'clear away' sense after a meal

examples.en: I tidied the room before the guests came.
examples.note: -기 전에 'before'; 치우다 = declutter/put in order

examples.en: Let's clear off the desk and study.
examples.note: 치우다 'clear off' a surface; -고 links to the next action

words.nuance: 치우다 means to tidy a space by clearing things away, putting them where they belong, or moving them out of the way — the focus is on removing clutter and restoring order (방을 치우다 'tidy the room', 책상을 치우다 'clear the desk'). So you 치우다 the toys (put them away) but 청소하다 the floor (mop it); a thorough clean often means doing both: 방을 치우고 청소해요. A second sense of 치우다 is simply to move/shove something out of the way (차 좀 치워 주세요 'please move your car'). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The default instrument: 손으로 (with the hand) is the most common partner phrase.

examples.note: 만지다 + 보다 = touch to check the texture; 한번 means 'go ahead and give it a try'.

examples.en: May I try touching the puppy?
examples.note: -아도 돼요? asks permission; the object 강아지 takes 를.

examples.ko: 페인트가 안 말라서 만지면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: peinteuga an mallaseo manjimyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: The paint is not dry, so you must not touch it.

words.nuance: 만지다 is the plain verb for touching something with your hand to feel its texture, temperature, or shape; the thing touched takes 을/를 (천을 만지다). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'touch' emotionally: 'that movie touched me' is NOT 만지다 but 감동받다 / 감동적이다 — 만지다 is strictly physical contact. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
잘 (well) is the habitual partner for visibility; opposite is 안 보이다.

examples.en: The sea is very visible from here.
examples.note: The thing seen takes 이/가 (바다가), not 을/를 — this is intransitive.

examples.en: Please show me your ticket.
examples.note: 보여 주다 = 'show'; here it IS transitive because of 주다, so 표를 takes 를.

examples.en: You look tired. Get some rest.
examples.note: Adjective stem 피곤하- + 보여요 = 'looks ~', a hugely common everyday use.

words.nuance: 보이다 is the passive/spontaneous counterpart of 보다 (to look): something enters your field of vision on its own, so the thing seen takes 이/가 (산이 보여요 = 'the mountain is visible'), NOT 을/를. The 요-form contracts 보이-+-어요 → 보여요 (past 보였어요). The sharp contrast learners need is 보이다 vs 보다: 보다 is an active choice ('I look at / watch'), 보이다 is involuntary ('it is seen / comes into view'). A second, very frequent meaning is 'to look/seem' — adjective stem + 보이다 (행복해 보여요 'you look happy'; 비싸 보여요 'it looks expensive'); here English 'looks' maps cleanly. Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Singing is heard from the next room.
examples.note: Source takes 에서 (옆방에서); the sound 노랫소리가 takes 가.

examples.en: The call is far, so I can't hear well.
examples.note: -아서 gives the cause; 안 들리다 is the standard 'can't hear you' on a call.

examples.en: That remark sounded a bit strange.
examples.note: Adverb 이상하게 + 들리다 = 'sounded ~', mirroring English 'sounds'.

words.nuance: 들리다 is the passive/spontaneous partner of 듣다 (to listen): a sound reaches your ears without effort, so what is heard takes 이/가 (음악이 들려요 = 'music is audible'), not 을/를. A second common sense is 'to sound (a certain way)': adverb + 들리다 (좋게 들려요 'sounds good'). With 주다 it means 'let/make someone hear' (노래를 들려 주다). Using 을/를 for the sound: 음악을 들려요 is wrong. 들리다 is intransitive, so 음악이 들려요. (Use 듣다 if you mean active 'I listen to music' = 음악을 들어요.)

words.shortExplanation: 가리키다 means "to point at" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 가리키다 (gariki-da) = "to point at". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 가리켜요 plus one useful sentence like 손가락으로 가리키다 ("to point with one's finger"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 가리키고 싶어요 for what you want, 가리킬 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 가리켜요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
손가락으로 (with the finger) is the instrument; also 손으로 (with the hand).

examples.en: Please point at that building with your hand.
examples.note: Instrument takes 으로 (손으로); target 건물을 takes 를.

examples.en: Don't point at people with your finger.
examples.note: -지 마세요 = polite prohibition; pointing at people is rude in Korea too.

examples.en: The clock pointed exactly to twelve.
examples.note: Inanimate subjects (clocks, needles) also use 가리키다 for 'indicate'.

words.nuance: 가리키다 means to indicate a direction, place, or thing — typically with a finger or hand — so the target takes 을/를 (저기를 가리키다 = 'point over there'). Mnemonic — 가리KIcida points (KI = 'key' you point with), 가르CHIcida teaches (the 르치 in the middle, like a 'lecture'). Mixing them yields comic errors: 학생을 가리켜요 literally 'I point at the student' instead of 학생을 가르쳐요 'I teach the student'. A second nuance: 가리키다 also covers inanimate 'indicating' — clock hands, arrows, a needle 'point to' something (바늘이 북쪽을 가리켜요). Use 가리켜요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.shortExplanation: 흔들다 means "to shake" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 흔들다 (heundeul-da) means "to shake". Start from the polite form 흔들어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 흔들다. A strong first sentence is 손을 흔들다 ("to wave one's hand"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 흔들다 also becomes 흔들고 싶어요 (want), 흔들 수 있어요 (can), and 못 흔들어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The idiom for waving hello/goodbye; 손을 흔들며 인사하다 'wave in greeting'.

examples.ko: 마시기 전에 병을 잘 흔들어 주세요.
examples.romanization: masigi jeone byeongeul jal heundeureo juseyo.
examples.en: Please shake the bottle well before drinking.
examples.note: 잘 흔들다 'shake well' is the fixed collocation on labels; 병을 takes 를.

examples.en: My friend waved from far away.
examples.note: 손을 흔들다 = 'wave the hand'; past 흔들었어요 keeps the ㄹ before a vowel.

examples.en: It's dangerous, so don't shake the ladder.
examples.note: -(으)니까 gives a reason; ㄹ drops before -지? No — 흔들지 keeps ㄹ (ㅈ is not ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ).

words.nuance: 흔들다 means to shake, wave, or rock something back and forth — a hand (손을 흔들다 'wave'), a head (고개를 흔들다 'shake one's head'), a bottle, a tree in the wind. It is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-탈락) verb: the stem ㄹ DROPS before the consonants ㅂ, ㄴ, ㅅ and before the noun-modifier ㄴ — hence 흔듭니다 (not 흔들습니다), 흔드세요, 흔드는 — but the ㄹ STAYS before a vowel, giving the regular 흔들어요 / 흔들었어요. The closest synonym is 떨다 'to tremble/shiver', but the line is who controls it: 흔들다 is transitive and deliberate ('I shake X'), while 떨다 is usually involuntary trembling (추워서 떨어요 'shiver from cold'). The English-speaker pitfall: a 'handshake' as a greeting is NOT 손을 흔들다 (that is waving) — to shake hands you say 악수하다 (握手, 'grasp-hand'). Also remember the ㄹ-drop only before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so 흔들지 마세요 and 흔들고 keep their ㄹ.

Keeping the ㄹ before ㅂ: 흔들습니다 is wrong. In a ㄹ-irregular verb the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 흔듭니다.
Using 손을 흔들다 to mean 'shake hands'. Waving is 손을 흔들다, but shaking hands in greeting is 악수하다 — different action entirely.
Dropping the ㄹ everywhere. Before a vowel it stays: the present is 흔들어요, not 흔어요; only ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ trigger the drop.
notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 흔들어 and 흔들어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 안다 means "to hug" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to hug" in Korean is 안다 (an-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 안아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 안다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 꼭 안다 ("to hug tightly") — then reshape the same stem into 안고 싶어요 (desire), 안을 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 안아요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
꼭 (firmly, tightly) is the emotional intensifier: 꼭 안아 주세요 'hold me tight'.

examples.en: The baby cried, so I held it tightly.
examples.note: 안아 주다 = hug for someone's benefit; 꼭 adds warmth/tightness.

examples.ko: 헤어질 때 친구를 한 번 안아요.
examples.romanization: heeojil ttae chingureul han beon anayo.
examples.en: I hug my friend once when we part.
examples.note: Hugging in greeting/parting; person takes 를, action is deliberate.

examples.en: I want to fall asleep holding the puppy.
examples.note: 품에 안다 = hold in the arms; -고 links to the next clause.

words.nuance: 안다 means to hold someone or something in your arms — a hug, cradling a baby, clasping a pet to your chest; the one embraced takes 을/를 (아기를 안다). Because the stem vowel is bright ㅏ (안-), the 요-form is 안아요 (past 안았어요) and the formal is 안습니다. The trap is the spelling twins: 안다 (hug) vs 알다 (know) vs the negative adverb 안. Watch 안 안아요 — the first 안 is 'not', the second is the verb stem, so the whole thing means 'I do not hug'. A useful synonym contrast is 안다 vs 껴안다 / 끌어안다: plain 안다 is neutral 'hold in arms', while 껴안다 (꼭 껴안다) and 끌어안다 stress a tighter, more enveloping embrace ('clutch, hug close'). The English-speaker pitfall: 'hug' as a casual social gesture is far less frequent in Korea than in the West, so 안다 most often appears with babies, family, romantic partners, or comfort — not as a default greeting between acquaintances; a bow or handshake (악수) is more typical.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 안다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 안아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 안다 (hug) with 알다 (know). 친구를 안아요 = 'I hug my friend'; 'I know my friend' is 친구를 알아요 — only the ㄴ vs ㄹ differs.
Mishandling negation. 'I don't hug' is 안 안아요 (adverb 안 + verb 안아요); writing a single 안아요 loses the negation, and 안안아요 with no space is incorrect.
Assuming 안다 works like a Western 'hug everyone hello'. Socially, default greetings are bows or 악수하다; reserve 안다 for close, affectionate, or comforting contexts.

words.shortExplanation: 밀다 means "to push" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 밀다 (mil-da) = "to push". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 밀어요 plus one useful sentence like 문을 밀다 ("to push a door"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 밀고 싶어요 for what you want, 밀 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 밀어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The classic door sign pair with 당기다 (pull): 미시오 'push' / 당기시오 'pull'.

examples.ko: 이 문은 당기지 말고 밀어 주세요.
examples.romanization: i muneun danggiji malgo mireo juseyo.
examples.en: Push this door, don't pull it.
examples.note: Directly contrasts 밀다 vs 당기다; -지 말고 = 'don't ~, instead'.

examples.en: Even when it's crowded, don't push.
examples.note: 밀지 마세요 keeps the ㄹ (ㅈ doesn't trigger the drop); subway-etiquette phrase.

examples.en: The load is heavy, so we have to push together.
examples.note: -아서 cause + -아야 해요 obligation; 밀어야 keeps ㄹ before a vowel.

words.nuance: 밀다 means to push — to apply force so something moves away from you (a door, a cart, a person in a crowd). It is a ㄹ-irregular: the stem ㄹ DROPS before ㅂ, ㄴ, ㅅ and the modifier ㄴ, so 밉니다 (not 밀습니다), 미세요, 미는 문 ('the door you push'); but it STAYS before a vowel, giving 밀어요 / 밀었어요. The obvious antonym is 당기다 'to pull', and the two define the universal Korean door signs 미시오 / 당기시오. A subtler synonym contrast is 밀다 vs 누르다: 밀다 moves an object across space ('push the cart'), whereas 누르다 presses straight down in place ('push/press a button' = 버튼을 누르다). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 'push a button' — never 버튼을 밀다, always 버튼을 누르다. Also note 밀다's idiomatic life: 면도하다 aside, 수염을 밀다 means 'shave off a beard', and 밀어주다 figuratively means 'to back/support someone'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 밀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 밀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 버튼을 밀다 for 'press a button'. Pressing down is 누르다 (버튼을 눌러요); 밀다 is for sliding/pushing an object across space.
Keeping the ㄹ before ㅂ: 밀습니다 is wrong. ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 밉니다.
Mixing up 밀다 (push) and 당기다 (pull) on door signs. 미시오 means push and 당기시오 means pull — reversing them sends people the wrong way.
notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 밀어 and 밀어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 당기다 means "to pull" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 당기다 (danggi-da) means "to pull". Start from the polite form 당겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 당기다. A strong first sentence is 문을 당기다 ("to pull a door"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 당기다 also becomes 당기고 싶어요 (want), 당길 수 있어요 (can), and 못 당겨요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Door-sign partner of 밀다: 당기시오 'pull'.

examples.ko: 이 문은 밀지 말고 당겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: i muneun milji malgo danggyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Pull this door, don't push it.
examples.note: Mirror of 밀다; 당겨 주세요 is the polite 'please pull'.

examples.en: I pull the chair forward a little.
examples.note: Direction 앞으로 (toward the front); object 의자를 takes 를.

examples.en: These days I keep craving spicy food.
examples.note: Idiomatic 당기다 = 'crave'; the food takes 이/가 (음식이 당겨요).

words.nuance: 당기다 means to pull — to draw something toward yourself (a door, a rope, a chair). Unlike its ㄹ-irregular antonym 밀다, 당기다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so the 요-form simply contracts 당기-+-어요 → 당겨요 (past 당겼어요, formal 당깁니다) with no ㄹ-drop. Its straight opposite is 밀다 'push', and together they label every Korean door (밀다 미시오 / 당기다 당기시오). A useful synonym contrast is 당기다 vs 끌다: 당기다 is a short pull toward you ('tug, draw'), while 끌다 is to drag something along the ground over distance (가방을 끌다 'drag a bag', 차를 끌다 'tow a car'). Watch a high-frequency idiom that surprises learners: 입맛이 당기다 / 음식이 당기다 means 'to crave food, feel an appetite' — the food is the subject (이/가), not the object. words.shortExplanation: 두드리다 means "to knock" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to knock" in Korean is 두드리다 (dudeuri-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 두드려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 두드리다 for study notes. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The prototypical use; 노크하다 (from English 'knock') is a casual synonym.

examples.en: Knock on the door first before going in.
examples.note: 두드리다 = repeated light striking to signal; 먼저 'first'.

examples.en: I lightly tapped my sleeping friend's shoulder.
examples.note: 어깨를 두드리다 = tap a shoulder; 살짝 'gently' suits the soft action.

examples.ko: 벨이 고장 났으니 문을 두드려 주세요.
examples.romanization: beri gojang nasseuni muneul dudeuryeo juseyo.
examples.en: The bell is broken, so please knock.
examples.note: -(으)니 gives a reason; 두드려 주세요 polite request.

words.nuance: 두드리다 means to strike a surface lightly and repeatedly — knock on a door, pat a shoulder or back, tap a keyboard — to make a sound or get attention. The key synonym contrast is force and repetition: 두드리다 is gentle, rhythmic tapping, whereas 치다 is a single firm strike ('hit, strike' — 공을 치다 'hit a ball') and 때리다 is to hit hard, usually a person, with a violent or punishing nuance (사람을 때리다 'beat someone'). So 어깨를 두드리다 comforts, but 어깨를 때리다 would mean to hit someone's shoulder hard. For doors specifically, casual speakers also borrow 노크하다 (from English 'knock'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 때리다 just because English 'knock' and 'hit' overlap — knocking on a door is always 두드리다 (or 노크하다), never 문을 때려요, which sounds like you are violently banging/attacking the door.

Use 두드려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 때리다 for knocking. 문을 때려요 means 'I beat/bang the door (violently)'; to knock politely say 문을 두드려요 or 노크해요.
Choosing 두드리다 for a single hard hit. A one-off strike is 치다 (공을 쳐요 'I hit the ball'); 두드리다 implies light, repeated tapping.
Marking the surface with 에: 문에 두드려요 is awkward. The thing struck is a direct object: 문을 두드려요.

words.shortExplanation: 막다 means "to block" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 막다 (mak-da) = "to block". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 막아요 plus one useful sentence like 길을 막다 ("to block a road/path"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 막고 싶어요 for what you want, 막을 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 막아요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Roads, entrances, exits: 길이 막히다 (passive) 'the road is jammed'.

examples.en: Don't block the entrance here.
examples.note: 막다 = obstruct a passage; -지 마세요 polite prohibition.

examples.en: I shut the window to block the cold wind.
examples.note: -(으)려고 'in order to'; 막다 here = keep out / shield against.

examples.en: There was an accident, so the police closed the road.
examples.note: 막다 = block off a road; contrast with 닫다 = shut a door.

words.nuance: 막다 means to block, obstruct, or stop something from passing — a road (길을 막다), an entrance, ears or nose (귀를 막다 'cover the ears') — and by extension to prevent or avert a problem (사고를 막다 'prevent an accident', 출혈을 막다 'stop the bleeding'). The 요-form is regular: bright ㅏ stem gives 막아요 (past 막았어요, formal 막습니다). The synonym contrast to nail is 막다 vs 닫다: 닫다 is to close a thing that has its own hinge or lid (문을 닫다 'close the door', 뚜껑을 닫다 'put the lid on'), while 막다 is to obstruct an opening or flow so nothing gets through (구멍을 막다 'plug a hole'). There is also a related passive 막히다 'to be blocked/jammed' (코가 막혔어요 'my nose is stuffed', 길이 막혀요 'traffic is jammed'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 닫다 for blocking a road — a road has no door to 'close', so it is 길을 막다, and traffic congestion is 길이 막히다, never 길이 닫혀요.

Using 닫다 to block a road. 길을 닫아요 is unnatural; obstructing a road is 길을 막아요, and 'traffic is jammed' is 길이 막혀요.

words.shortExplanation: 숨다 means "to hide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 숨다 (sum-da) means "to hide". Start from the polite form 숨어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 숨다. A strong first sentence is 뒤에 숨다 ("to hide behind"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 숨다 also becomes 숨고 싶어요 (want), 숨을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 숨어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Position word + 에: 문 뒤에 숨다 'hide behind the door'.

examples.ko: 놀랄 때 아이가 엄마 뒤로 숨어요.
examples.romanization: nollal ttae aiga eomma dwiro sumeoyo.
examples.en: When startled, the child hides behind mom.
examples.note: Direction 뒤로 (to behind) for the movement of hiding; subject is the hider.

examples.en: I ducked into a shop to escape the rain.
examples.note: 안으로 'into'; 숨다 here = duck/take cover, intransitive.

examples.en: It's dangerous here, so shall we hide over there?
examples.note: Place 저기에 (at over there); -(으)ㄹ까요? suggestion.

words.nuance: 숨다 is INTRANSITIVE 'to hide oneself' — you make yourself unseen, so the subject is the person hiding and the hiding place takes 에/뒤에/밑에 (책상 밑에 숨어요 'I hide under the desk'); there is no direct object. The 요-form is regular: 숨어요 (past 숨었어요, formal 숨습니다). The single most important contrast is 숨다 vs 숨기다: 숨다 = 'I hide (myself)' (intransitive), while the causative 숨기다 = 'I hide SOMETHING' (transitive, takes 을/를) — 돈을 숨기다 'hide money', 비밀을 숨기다 'conceal a secret'. English 'hide' is both, which is exactly why learners stumble. A near-synonym is 피하다 'to avoid/dodge', but 피하다 is to steer clear of something (사람을 피하다 'avoid a person'), whereas 숨다 is specifically to conceal your body from view. The English-speaker pitfall: 'I hid the key' must be 열쇠를 숨겼어요 (숨기다), NOT 열쇠를 숨었어요 — using 숨다 with an object is ungrammatical.

Use 숨어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Giving 숨다 a direct object. 'I hid the money' is 돈을 숨겼어요 (transitive 숨기다); 돈을 숨었어요 is wrong because 숨다 is intransitive.
Confusing 숨다 (hide oneself) with 숨기다 (hide a thing). 아이가 숨어요 = 'the child hides'; 아이를 숨겨요 = 'I hide the child away'.
Marking the hiding place with 를: 침대 밑을 숨어요 is wrong. Use 에 for the location: 침대 밑에 숨어요.

words.shortExplanation: 빠지다 means "to fall into" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to fall into" in Korean is 빠지다 (ppaji-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빠져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빠지다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 물에 빠지다 ("to fall into water / drown") — then reshape the same stem into 빠지고 싶어요 (desire), 빠질 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 빠져요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
물에 빠지다 is the set phrase; the place fallen into takes 에.

examples.ko: 조심하세요, 여기 구덩이에 빠질 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: josimhaseyo, yeogi gudeongie ppajil su isseoyo.
examples.en: Careful, you could fall into the pit here.
examples.note: Place takes 에 (구덩이에); -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = possibility/risk.

examples.en: My phone fell into the river and broke.
examples.note: 빠지다 = drop into; -아서 links cause to result.

examples.en: I'm totally hooked on that drama these days.
examples.note: Idiomatic 빠지다 = be absorbed/addicted; takes 에 (드라마에).

words.nuance: 빠지다 literally means to fall/drop into something — a hole, water, mud — by accident, with the place taking 에 (웅덩이에 빠지다 'fall into a puddle'). It is intransitive and spontaneous; the 요-form contracts 빠지-+-어요 → 빠져요 (past 빠졌어요). Beyond the literal sense it is enormously idiomatic, almost always with 에: 사랑에 빠지다 'fall in love', 게임에 빠지다 'get addicted to games', 살이 빠지다 'lose weight', and even 'be missing/left out' (명단에서 빠지다 'be dropped from the list'). The synonym contrast learners need is 빠지다 vs 넘어지다: 빠지다 is sinking/dropping DOWN INTO something, whereas 넘어지다 is toppling OVER, losing your balance on a flat surface (길에서 넘어지다 'fall over on the road'). The English-speaker pitfall: 'fall in love' tempts 를, but it is 사랑에 빠지다 with 에 (you fall INTO love); likewise weight loss is 살이 빠지다 (subject 이/가), never 살을 빠지다.

Use 빠져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 빠지다 (fall into) with 넘어지다 (fall over). Tripping on flat ground is 넘어졌어요; dropping into a hole/water is 빠졌어요.
Using 를 in idioms. 'Fall in love' is 사랑에 빠지다 and 'lose weight' is 살이 빠지다 — both use 에 or 이/가, never 사랑을/살을 빠지다.

words.shortExplanation: 갈아타다 means "to transfer" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 갈아타다 (garata-da) = "to transfer". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 갈아타요 plus one useful sentence like 지하철로 갈아타다 ("to transfer to the subway"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 갈아타고 싶어요 for what you want, 갈아탈 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 갈아타요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The new vehicle takes 로/으로, never 에서

examples.en: I transfer to the bus.
examples.note: Simplest frame: just the target vehicle + 로 + the verb

examples.en: Please transfer to line 2 at City Hall station.
examples.note: Everyday directions: 에서 marks where, 으로 marks which line

examples.ko: 환승하려면 다음 역에서 내려서 갈아타야 해요.
examples.romanization: hwanseungharyeomyeon daeum yeogeseo naeryeoseo garataya haeyo.
examples.en: To transfer you have to get off at the next station and change.
examples.note: Real situation: pairs 내리다 then 갈아타다, the natural commuting sequence

words.nuance: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin (換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride') printed on every subway sign and announcement: 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트'). The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서 — English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에. Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 갈아타다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 갈아타요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 지하철에 갈아타요 with 에. The destination vehicle is the thing you change INTO, so it needs directional 로/으로: 지하철로 갈아타요.
Using 타다 when you mean 'transfer': 버스를 타요 only means 'I board a bus', not 'I switch from another vehicle to the bus'. To express the switch you must use 갈아타다: 버스로 갈아타요.
Writing the polite form as 갈아타아요. 타다 already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges and disappears — the correct form is 갈아타요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 갈아타다 becomes 갈아탈 수 있어요 ("can") and 갈아탈 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.

The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin printed on every subway sign and announcement. 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트').
환승하다 is the Sino-Korean twin: 換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride'.
Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요.

The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서. English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에.

words.shortExplanation: 운전하다 means "to drive" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 운전하다 (unjeonha-da) means "to drive". Start from the polite form 운전해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 운전하다. A strong first sentence is 안전하게 운전하다 ("to drive safely"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 운전하다 also becomes 운전하고 싶어요 (want), 운전할 수 있어요 (can), and 운전 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
안전하게 is the default adverb in road-safety phrases

examples.en: I drive.
examples.note: Bare statement; 운전 + 해요, the 하다 verb contracting to 해요

examples.en: Please drive slowly at night.
examples.note: Everyday advice: adverb 천천히 sits right before the verb

examples.ko: 면허는 있는데 무서워서 아직 운전 못 해요.
examples.romanization: myeonheoneun inneunde museowoseo ajik unjeon mo taeyo.
examples.en: I have a license but I'm scared so I still can't drive.
examples.note: Real situation: shows the split negative 운전 + 못 + 해요

words.nuance: 운전하다 is Sino-Korean 운전 (運轉, 'move-turn', i.e. to keep a machine running) plus the light verb 하다, and it specifically means to operate a vehicle — primarily a car. Contrast it with 타다 'to ride/board', which is what a passenger does: the driver 운전해요 while everyone else just 타요. It is neutral in register and used by everyone, but the fixed compound 음주 운전 ('drinking driving') is the serious legal phrase you'll hear in warnings and news. Natural collocations include 안전 운전 (safe driving), 운전이 서툴다 (to be a clumsy driver), and 운전대를 잡다 (lit. 'grab the steering wheel' = to drive). Because it is a 하다 verb, the polite form is the irregular-looking but standard 운전해요 (하 + 여요 → 해요), and the negative and potential SPLIT the noun from 하다: 운전 안 해요, 운전 못 해요, never 안 운전해요. The English-speaker trap is exactly that splitting — and forgetting that the destination/route takes 까지 (집까지 운전해요) or 에서 for where the driving happens, since 운전하다 itself takes no direct object.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 운전하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 운전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Forming the negative as 안 운전해요. With 하다 compound verbs the 안/못 slips between the noun and 하다: 운전 안 해요, 운전 못 해요.
Using 운전하다 for being a passenger. If you merely rode in a car you 탔어요 (from 타다); 운전했어요 means YOU were behind the wheel.
Attaching a direct object like 차를 운전해요 in casual speech. While grammatically possible, Koreans normally just say 운전해요 and let context supply the car; over-marking 차를 sounds like a textbook.

words.shortExplanation: 주차하다 means "to park" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to park" in Korean is 주차하다 (juchaha-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 주차해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 주차하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 주차장에 주차하다 ("to park in the parking lot") — then reshape the same stem into 주차하고 싶어요 (desire), 주차할 수 있어요 (ability), and 주차 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to park in the parking lot
usagePhrases.note: 주차장 juchajang is the place; the spot itself takes 에

examples.en: I park here.
examples.note: Simplest: location 여기 + 에 marks where the car ends up

examples.en: I parked in the underground parking lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 지하 'underground' + 주차장, with past 했어요

examples.ko: 자리가 없어서 길에 잠깐 주차해도 돼요?
examples.romanization: jariga eopseoseo gire jamkkan juchahaedo dwaeyo?
examples.en: There's no space so may I park on the street for a moment?
examples.note: Real situation: asks permission with 해도 돼요 and the spot-marker 에

words.nuance: 주차하다 comes from Sino-Korean 주차 (駐車, 'halt-vehicle', i.e. to bring a car to a stop and leave it) plus 하다, so it means parking a vehicle, not stopping briefly to let someone out — that quick stop is 정차 (停車). Keep 주차하다 distinct from 세우다 ('to stand/stop something'): you can 차를 세우다 anywhere for a second, but 주차하다 implies leaving the car in a designated spot. Register is neutral and practical. The crucial particle point is that the resting place takes 에 (locative of where something settles), NOT 에서 (which marks where an action happens) — 주차장에 주차해요, never 주차장에서. Common collocations: 주차 금지 (no parking), 주차 요금 (parking fee), 주차 자리/공간 (a spot), 발레파킹 (valet). As a 하다 verb the negative and potential split the noun off: 주차 안 해요, 주차 못 해요. The English-speaker pitfall is the 에 vs 에서 choice and over-using a direct object — Koreans simply say 주차해요 and let context name the car.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 주차하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 주차해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the spot with 에서: 주차장에서 주차해요. Parking is about where the car comes to REST, so it takes 에: 주차장에 주차해요.
Confusing 주차하다 (park and leave) with 정차하다/세우다 (stop briefly). 'Pull over for a second to drop me off' is 잠깐 세워 주세요, not 주차해 주세요.
Saying 안 주차해요 for the negative. Split the compound: 주차 안 해요 (and 주차 못 해요 for the can-not).

words.shortExplanation: 막히다 means "to be blocked" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 막히다 (makhi-da) = "to be blocked". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 막혀요 plus one useful sentence like 길이 막히다 ("for the road to be congested"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 막히고 싶어요 for what you want, 막힐 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 막혀요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: for the road to be congested
usagePhrases.note: 길 + 이 막히다 is THE everyday way to say 'traffic is bad'

examples.en: The road is congested.
examples.note: Core frame: 길 takes subject 이, the verb is intransitive

examples.en: The road was very jammed because it was rush hour.
examples.note: Everyday: 퇴근 시간이라 'because it's leaving-work time' gives the cause

examples.ko: 지금 출발하면 차가 막혀서 두 시간 걸릴 거예요.
examples.romanization: jigeum chulbalhamyeon chaga makyeoseo du sigan geollil geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you leave now traffic will be bad and it'll take two hours.
examples.note: Real situation: 막혀서 chains cause to the 걸리다 'take time' result

words.nuance: 막히다 is the passive/intransitive partner of the transitive 막다 ('to block'): the -히- infix turns 'someone blocks X' into 'X gets blocked', so 막히다 is something that HAPPENS to a road, drain, or nose rather than something you do. For traffic this is the single most useful verb — 길이 막히다 / 차가 막히다 — and its opposite is 뚫리다 ('to open up/clear'), with 안 막히다 the everyday 'no traffic'. Do not confuse it with 막다 itself: 'I block the road' is 길을 막다, but 'the road is jammed' is 길이 막히다, and the particle flips from 을 to 이/가 accordingly. Register is plain and universal. Because the subject is a non-person, the polite/imperative-looking forms (막혀 주세요, 막힐까요?) are essentially never used about traffic. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as transitive: there is no 'I am blocked by traffic' with you as subject — Korean puts the ROAD in the subject slot (길이 막혀요), and you simply say 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 ('I was late because the road was jammed').
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 막히다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 막혀요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 막혀요 to mean 'I'm stuck in traffic'. 막히다 takes the ROAD as subject, not the person: 길이 막혀요, then 그래서 늦었어요.
Mixing up 막다 and 막히다. 길을 막다 = 'to block the road (actively)'; 길이 막히다 = 'the road is congested'. Watch the particle: 을 for the active verb, 이/가 for the passive one.
Using 막히다 for a person standing in your way. A person blocking you is 길을 막다 (they actively block) or 앞을 가로막다; 막히다 is reserved for roads, pipes, and noses.

words.shortExplanation: 넘어지다 means "to fall down" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 넘어지다 (neomeoji-da) means "to fall down". Start from the polite form 넘어져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 넘어지다. A strong first sentence is 길에서 넘어지다 ("to fall down on the street"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 넘어지다 also becomes 넘어지고 싶어요 (want), 넘어질 수 있어요 (can), and 못 넘어져요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: to fall down on the street
usagePhrases.note: Place of falling takes 에서, the action location

examples.en: The child fell down.
examples.note: Simplest: subject 이, past tense, no place needed

examples.en: I slipped on the icy road and fell down.
examples.note: Everyday: 미끄러지다 (cause) then 넘어지다 (result), the classic pair

examples.en: Grandmother fell on the stairs and went to the hospital.
examples.note: Real situation: honorific -시- on 넘어지셔서 and 가셨어요 for an elder

words.nuance: 넘어지다 means a standing person (or upright thing) loses balance and topples to the ground, built on 넘다 'to go over' + -어지다 'to come to be', literally 'to come to fall over'. The line to draw is against 떨어지다 ('to fall FROM a height / to drop'): a person on their feet 넘어지다, but a cup off a table or a leaf from a tree 떨어지다 — and against 쓰러지다, which is to collapse from illness/exhaustion (fainting) rather than from tripping. Register is plain and used for everyone. The place where you fall takes 에서 (action location), and the cause is usually chained with -어서: 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. Natural collocations: 넘어져서 무릎이 까지다 (scrape a knee falling), 넘어질 뻔하다 (almost fall), 넘어지지 않게 조심하다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 떨어지다 because English uses 'fall' for both — but 'I fell (down)' on flat ground is always 넘어지다; save 떨어지다 for dropping or falling off something.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 넘어지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 넘어져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 떨어지다 for tripping over on flat ground. A person who trips and goes down says 넘어졌어요; 떨어지다 is for falling FROM a height or an object dropping.
Using 넘어지다 for fainting/collapsing from illness. That is 쓰러지다 (더위 먹고 쓰러졌어요). 넘어지다 implies a trip or loss of footing, not a medical collapse.
Marking the place with 에 instead of 에서. Falling is an action that happens somewhere, so 계단에서 넘어졌어요 (with 에서), not 계단에 넘어졌어요.

words.shortExplanation: 부딪치다 means "to bump into" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to bump into" in Korean is 부딪치다 (budichi-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 부딪쳐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 부딪치다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 벽에 부딪치다 ("to bump into the wall") — then reshape the same stem into 부딪치고 싶어요 (desire), 부딪칠 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 부딪쳐요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
A fixed object you hit takes 에

examples.en: I bumped into the wall.
examples.note: Simplest: stationary 벽 takes 에, past tense

examples.en: I bumped my shoulder while rushing.
examples.note: Everyday: -다가 'while doing then', body part 어깨 takes 를

examples.ko: 지하철에서 모르는 사람과 부딪쳐서 죄송하다고 했어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo moreuneun saramgwa buditchyeoseo joesonghadago haesseoyo.
examples.en: I bumped into a stranger on the subway and said sorry.
examples.note: Real situation: 사람과 (mutual) + the social repair 죄송하다고 했어요

words.nuance: 부딪치다 means to strike or collide against something — a wall, a door, another person, or vehicle to vehicle. The particle does real work here: a stationary thing you hit takes 에 (문에 부딪치다), a body part you bang takes 을/를 (머리를 부딪치다), and a mutual collision with a moving party takes 과/와 (사람과 부딪치다). Beware the near-identical 부딪히다, which is the passive ('to be struck/run into by'): 차에 부딪히다 = 'to get hit by a car', so 부딪치다 vs 부딪히다 is the active-vs-passive divide, and learners constantly swap them. Do not confuse either with 만지다 ('to touch deliberately') — 부딪치다 is sudden and unintended impact. Register is plain. Collocations: 정면으로 부딪치다 (collide head-on), 세게 부딪치다 (hit hard), and figuratively 의견이 부딪치다 (opinions clash). The English-speaker pitfall is that 'bump into a friend' in English can simply mean 'run into = meet by chance' — that social sense is 우연히 만나다, NOT 부딪치다, which keeps its literal 'physical collision' meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부딪치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 부딪쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 부딪치다 for 'run into = happen to meet' a friend. That is 우연히 만나다; 부딪치다 only means a physical knock or collision.
Swapping 부딪치다 (active: I hit it) with 부딪히다 (passive: it hit me). 'I got hit by a car' is 차에 부딪혔어요; 'I bumped the wall' is 벽에 부딪쳤어요.

words.shortExplanation: 미끄러지다 means "to slip" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

words.nuance: 미끄러지다 is the VERB 'to slip / slide / lose footing', describing the motion of your foot or body sliding on a slick surface. It is plainly conjugated speech, fine in any everyday register, and softens to a gentle 서두르지 마세요 ('don't rush') when reassuring someone. The grammar heart of this word is that it is a 르 irregular: before a vowel ending the 르 sheds its ㅡ and an extra ㄹ appears, so 서두르 + 어요 → 서둘러요, and the past is 서둘렀어요 — anchor everything on 서둘러요. In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 헤매요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 헤매다 for study notes. words.nuance: 헤매다 means to wander about lost, roaming without finding your way — and by extension to flounder or struggle when you can't find a solution. The contrast to nail is against 산책하다 ('to take a stroll'), which is pleasant and purposeful: a 산책 is relaxing, but 헤매다 carries frustration and being lost. Don't confuse it with the similar-sounding 헤어지다 ('to break up / part ways') — totally different meaning. Register is plain and everyday. The place or route you wander through takes the object particle 을/를 (길을 헤매다), which surprises English speakers who expect a location particle like 에서 — but here the path is treated as the thing you traverse. As a verb stem ending in ㅐ, the vowel contractions are clean: 헤매 + 어요 → 헤매요, and the past 헤매 + 었어요 → 헤맸어요 (double ㅆ). Collocations: 길을 헤매다, 정신없이 헤매다 (wander in a daze), 헤매고 다니다 (roam around lost). words.nuance: 들르다 means to stop by / drop in somewhere briefly while on your way to another destination — the visit is short and incidental, not the main purpose of the trip. words.nuance: 지각하다 is Sino-Korean 지각 (遲刻, 'late-moment') + 하다, meaning specifically to arrive late to an appointed place like school, work, or a meeting — it is the institutional 'tardy', the kind a teacher or boss notes. words.nuance: 마중하다 is native Korean 마중 ('a going-out to receive an arriver') + 하다, meaning to go out and greet/pick up someone who is arriving — at a station, airport, or your door. words.nuance: 좋아지다 is the adjective 좋다 (good) plus -아지다, the pattern that turns a state-word into 'become that state', so it literally means 'come to be good' — a gradual drift from worse to better, not a fixed quality. The key contrast is 좋다 vs 좋아지다: 좋다 just says something IS good right now (기분이 좋아요 = I feel good), while 좋아지다 reports a CHANGE toward good (기분이 좋아졌어요 = I feel better than before). It is warm and neutral in register, fine in both 반말 and 존댓말, and shows up constantly with 몸(body), 기분(mood), 날씨(weather), 사이(relationship), and 실력(skill). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 좋다 when you really mean a transition — 'My Korean got better' is 좋아졌어요, never 좋았어요, because 좋았어요 just means 'it was good (in the past)'. Note too that 좋아지다 means 'come to like' when the subject is a person feeling (그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I came to like that person), so context decides between 'get better' and 'grow fond of'.

words.nuance: 변하다 is Sino-Korean: 變 (byeon, 'change, transform') + 하다, so it carries the feeling of something turning into a different state on its own, by nature or over time. The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 변하다 vs 바꾸다: 변하다 is intransitive — the thing changes by itself (날씨가 변해요 = the weather changes), while 바꾸다 is transitive — somebody deliberately swaps or replaces a thing (계획을 바꿔요 = I change the plan). A related pair is 변하다 vs 바뀌다 (the passive of 바꾸다): 바뀌다 implies an external switch (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = the traffic light switched), whereas 변하다 implies inner transformation (성격이 변했어요 = his personality changed). Register is neutral and everyday. The big pitfall is using 변하다 with a direct object — you cannot say *계획을 변해요 to mean 'I change the plan'; if there is an actor doing the changing, you need 바꾸다. 변하다 only ever describes the subject itself becoming different.

words.nuance: 늘다 means an amount, number, or ability grows bigger, and it is the everyday word for skills improving — 실력이 늘다 is THE phrase for 'getting better at something'. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the final ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, which is why the formal present is 늡니다 (not *늘습니다) — the ㄹ vanishes before -ㅂ니다. words.nuance: 줄다 is the exact opposite of 늘다 — it means an amount, number, or size gets smaller — and the two are learned as a pair (늘다/줄다). Like 늘다 it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving the formal 줍니다 (not *줄습니다). The crucial synonym contrast is 줄다 vs 줄이다: 줄다 is intransitive — the thing shrinks by itself (소리가 줄었어요 = the sound got quieter on its own), while 줄이다 is the causative — you deliberately reduce something (소리를 줄였어요 = I turned the sound down). Its formal report-style synonym is 감소하다 (Sino-Korean 減少, 'reduce-decrease'), used for statistics; 줄다 is the natural conversational word. words.nuance: 나아지다 is built from 낫다 ('to be better / to recover') plus -아지다 ('become'), so it specifically means coming UP from a bad or sick state — recovery and relief — which gives it a more emotional, hopeful color than the neutral 좋아지다. The contrast worth fixing: 좋아지다 simply moves from less-good to more-good (날씨가 좋아졌어요), while 나아지다 implies there was something WRONG that is now getting better — illness, a slump, a hard situation (몸이 나아졌어요, 형편이 나아졌어요). Because the root is 낫다 (a ㅅ-irregular: 낫다 → 나아), the spelling is 나아지다 with two ㅏ vowels and NO ㅅ. The classic English-speaker error is exactly that spelling: learners write *낫아지다, keeping the ㅅ, but the ㅅ of 낫다 drops between vowels, leaving 나아지다. Also note the bare root 낫다 alone already means 'get well' (감기가 나았어요 = my cold got better), so 낫다 and 나아지다 overlap for illness; 나아지다 just adds the gradual 'becoming' nuance and stretches to situations, not only bodies.

words.explanation: "to be nervous" in Korean is 긴장하다 (ginjanghada). words.nuance: 긴장하다 is Sino-Korean: 緊 (gin, 'tight') + 張 (jang, 'stretch') + 하다, literally 'to be tightly stretched' — a vivid image of nerves pulled taut before a big moment. It describes performance-type nerves (tests, interviews, stages, sports), the keyed-up tension you feel when stakes are high. The key contrast is 긴장하다 vs 무섭다 vs 걱정하다: 무섭다 is 'to be scared/afraid' of a threat (귀신이 무서워요 = ghosts are scary); 걱정하다 is 'to worry' about an outcome over time (시험이 걱정돼요 = I'm worried about the exam); but 긴장하다 is the immediate bodily tension of a high-pressure moment — your heart pounds, your shoulders stiffen. Note the very common passive-feel form 긴장되다 ('to get nervous', the feeling arising in you) — 긴장돼요 often sounds more natural than 긴장해요 for 'I feel nervous right now'. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping every 'nervous' to one word: 'I'm nervous about the future' is really worry (걱정), not 긴장; reserve 긴장하다 for that taut, just-before-it-happens tension.

Forming the negative as 안 긴장해요 — with 하다 verbs built on a noun, the 안 splits inside: 긴장 안 해요 is the natural negative.

words.shortExplanation: 안심하다 means "to feel relieved" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 안심하다 (ansimhada) = "to feel relieved". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 안심해요 plus one useful sentence like 이제 안심했어요 ("Now I feel relieved"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 안심하고 싶어요 for what you want, 안심할 수 있어요 for what you can, 안심 못 해요 for what you can't. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: Simple cause + relief, past tense

examples.ko: 아이가 집에 잘 도착해서 이제 안심해요
examples.romanization: aiga jibe jal dochakaeseo ije ansimhaeyo
examples.en: The child arrived home safely so now I'm at ease
examples.note: -아서 links the safe arrival to relief

words.nuance: 안심하다 is Sino-Korean: 安 (an, 'peace, safe') + 心 (sim, 'heart') + 하다, literally 'to make the heart peaceful' — that settling of the chest when a worry finally lifts. It is the natural pair-opposite of 걱정하다 (to worry): you 걱정하다 while the danger looms and 안심하다 once you know it's fine. The contrast you must keep clear is 안심하다 vs 안전하다, which look almost identical but differ by one syllable and one part of speech: 안심하다 is a VERB about a person's FEELING of relief (저는 안심했어요 = I felt relieved), while 안전하다 is an ADJECTIVE about a thing being SAFE (여기는 안전해요 = this place is safe). They share the 安 hanja, which is why beginners blur them. 안심하다 also commonly appears as 안심이 되다 ('to become reassured', feeling-driven) and in the warm imperative 안심하세요 ('rest assured'), which businesses and caretakers use a lot. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping in 안전하다 for the emotion — *저는 안전했어요 wrongly says 'I was safe', not 'I felt relieved'; relief is always 안심.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 안심하다 as a complete polite sentence.

Forming the negative as 안 안심해요 — split the 하다: 안심 안 해요. (The doubled 안 also just sounds wrong.)

words.nuance: 실망하다 is Sino-Korean: 失 (sil, 'lose') + 望 (mang, 'hope') + 하다, literally 'to lose hope' — the heart sinking when reality falls short of what you expected. That hanja root is the key to using it right: 실망 needs a prior expectation that wasn't met, so it's about LETDOWN, not plain sadness. The contrast English speakers must master is 실망하다 vs 슬프다: 슬프다 is 'to be sad' about a loss or sorrow with no expectation involved (강아지가 죽어서 슬퍼요 = I'm sad because my dog died), while 실망하다 specifically means a hope was dashed (성적에 실망했어요 = I'm disappointed by my grades). The defining grammar point is the particle: the thing that disappoints you takes 에 (결과에 실망했어요), and the PERSON who disappoints you takes 에게/한테 (그 사람에게 실망했어요 = I'm disappointed in that person). There's also a transitive partner 실망시키다 ('to disappoint someone', 부모님을 실망시켰어요 = I let my parents down). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 감동해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 감동하다 for study notes. words.nuance: 감동하다 is Sino-Korean: 感 (gam, 'feel') + 動 (dong, 'move') + 하다, literally 'to be moved by feeling' — the heart stirred deeply by kindness, beauty, art, or a touching story. The contrast to lock in is 감동하다 vs 감사하다: 감사하다 means 'to be grateful / thank' for something done for you (도와주셔서 감사합니다 = thank you for helping), a social acknowledgment; 감동하다 is the inner emotional swell of being touched, which may bring tears, not a thank-you. They share the 感 ('feel') hanja, which is why learners conflate them. A crucial usage note: Koreans very often say 감동받다 (감동 + 받다, 'to receive deep emotion') and 감동하다 almost interchangeably for 'I was touched' — 감동받았어요 is arguably the more frequent spoken form. The cause is marked with 에 (그 말에 감동했어요 = I was moved by those words). To describe the thing itself as moving, use the adjective 감동적이다 (감동적인 영화 = a moving film), not 감동하다, which is reserved for the person feeling. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 감사하다 ('thank you') when you really mean you were emotionally moved — the two feelings are different, and Koreans keep them apart.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 감동하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 감동해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.shortExplanation: 견디다 means "to bear" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Ability or possibility.

words.nuance: 견디다 means to withstand and hold out against something hard, painful, or long — hardship, heat, pain, loneliness, a tough stretch of life. words.shortExplanation: 걷다 means "to walk" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: 걸어서 'on foot' is the everyday answer to how you get somewhere

words.nuance: 걷다 means to walk on foot and is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요. The nearest relative is 산책하다 ('take a stroll'): 걷다 is the raw act of walking anywhere, while 산책하다 implies a leisurely walk for pleasure, so 'I walk to work' is 걸어서 출근해요, never 산책해서 출근해요. The trap for English speakers is that 걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that, and the path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에. words.shortExplanation: 뛰다 means "to run" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to run" in Korean is 뛰다 (ttwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 뛰어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 뛰다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 빨리 뛰어요 ("I run fast") — then reshape the same stem into 뛰고 싶어요 (desire), 뛸 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 뛰어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: everyday running/dashing about, not timed sport

words.nuance: 뛰다 is a regular verb whose stem ends in the vowel 위, so it simply adds 어 without contracting: 뛰어요, 뛰었어요. Before the formal ㅂ/ㄴ endings the stem shortens in the usual way to 뜁니다 and 뛸 거예요. Its key synonym is 달리다: 달리다 is the neutral, 'sporty' word for running over distance (마라톤을 달리다, 100미터를 달리다), while 뛰다 is the everyday word for dashing, rushing, or even jumping, so a child rushing across a room 뛰어다녀요 rather than 달려다녀요. Crucially 뛰다 also means 'to jump/leap' (제자리에서 뛰다 = jump in place; 심장이 뛰다 = the heart beats/pounds), so context decides between 'run' and 'jump'. The English-speaker pitfall is spelling: don't confuse 뛰다 (run) with 띄다 ('be visible / catch the eye', as in 눈에 띄다) — they sound close but are different verbs. Also note the polite-warning 뛰지 마세요 is the fixed phrase you'll see posted everywhere.

words.nuance: 서다 means to stand or, for vehicles, to come to a stop. Because the stem already ends in 어, the 요-ending merges instead of doubling: you get 서요 and the past 섰어요, never 서어요 or 서었어요. Watch the two sister verbs: 서다 is the plain state/result 'to be standing / take a standing position', while 일어서다 ('rise to one's feet') stresses the motion of getting up from sitting — so 'please stand up (from your seat)' is 일어서 주세요, but 'please stand here' is 여기 서 주세요. For vehicles 서다 overlaps with 멈추다 ('to halt'); 멈추다 is more general and can describe machines or actions stopping, while 서다 is the everyday word for a bus or car pulling up. Korean also has no separate verb for 'stand something up'; that meaning needs the causative 세우다.

words.nuance: 눕다 means to lie down and is a ㅂ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the ㅂ turns into a 우/워 sound, giving 누워요 and 누웠어요, while before a consonant the ㅂ stays, so the formal is 눕습니다 and you say 눕지 마세요, 눕고 싶어요. Don't confuse it with two neighbors: 눕다 is intransitive ('I lie down'), whereas the causative 눕히다 means 'lay someone/something down' (아기를 눕혀요 = lay the baby down), and 기대다 means 'to lean/recline' rather than fully lying flat. There's also a posture pair to keep straight: 눕다 (lie) vs 앉다 (sit) vs 서다 (stand). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'lie down' has no object but learners still want to add 를; in Korean the surface takes 에 (침대에 눕다), and reaching for 눕어요 by analogy with regular verbs is the classic error — it must be 누워요.

words.nuance: 들다 here means to lift or hold something up in your hand, and it is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so you get 듭니다, 드세요, and 드는 — but the ㄹ stays before a plain vowel, giving 들어요 and 들었어요. words.nuance: 놓다 means to set an object down onto a surface, and the place where you put it takes 에 (책상에 놓다 = put it on the desk). It's a regular verb, so the ㅎ stays in writing and you add 아: 놓아요, 놓았어요; in fast speech 놓아요 routinely contracts to 놔요 and 놓았어요 to 놨어요, but the full forms are clearer to learn first. The crucial contrast is with 넣다 ('put inside / insert'): 놓다 places something ON a surface, while 넣다 puts it INTO a container (가방에 넣다 = put it in the bag) — choosing the wrong one changes the meaning entirely. Compare too 두다 ('leave/keep something in a place', often longer-term: 여기 두세요 = leave it here). 놓다 also means 'to let go / release' (손을 놓다) and appears in helpful patterns like -아 놓다 ('do and leave it done', 켜 놓다 = leave it switched on). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'put' covers both 'on' and 'in', so learners overuse 놓다 where 넣다 is needed, and they mark the surface with 를 instead of the correct 에.
