words.nuance: 입다 is a regular verb (입어요, 입었어요, 입습니다) meaning to put on or wear clothing on the torso and legs — shirts, coats, dresses, trousers, uniforms. The thing English speakers must internalize is that Korean has no single verb for 'wear'; it splits the action by body part: 입다 for body clothes, 신다 for footwear (shoes, socks), 쓰다 for things on the head/face (hats, glasses), 끼다 for snug items (gloves, rings), 차다 for things you strap on (watch, belt), and 매다 for ties/scarves you knot. So 'wear shoes' is never 신발을 입다 — it must be 신발을 신다. A second nuance is aspect: 입다 is the action of putting on, while the resulting state 'be wearing' is 입고 있다 (티셔츠를 입고 있어요 = is wearing a T-shirt). The opposite, for taking off any of these, is the single verb 벗다. The pitfall is simply over-extending 입다 to cover everything 'wear' covers in English.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 입다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 입어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 입다 for shoes or socks — footwear takes 신다, so it must be 신발을 신어요, never 신발을 입어요.
Using 입다 for a hat or glasses — head/face items take 쓰다, so 'wear a hat' is 모자를 써요 and 'wear glasses' is 안경을 써요, not 입다.
Saying 옷을 입고 있어요 when you mean the action of getting dressed right now — 입고 있다 is ambiguous toward the state 'am wearing'; to stress the ongoing action of dressing, context or 입는 중이에요 is clearer.

words.nuance: 벗다 is the single, regular verb (벗어요, 벗었어요, 벗습니다) for taking off almost anything you wear — clothes, shoes, socks, a hat, glasses, gloves. This is the great convenience of Korean: the 'put on' side fragments into 입다/신다/쓰다/끼다/차다 by body part, but the 'take off' side collapses into just 벗다, so you don't have to match the item to a special remover. (Two small exceptions: accessories you fasten — a watch, a ring, a tie — are usually 풀다 'undo/untie' or 빼다 'pull out', so 시계를 풀다, 반지를 빼다 sound more natural than 벗다.) The everyday context is the Korean custom of removing shoes at the door: 신발을 벗고 들어오세요. The English-speaker pitfall is over-thinking it: learners who learned that shoes need 신다 sometimes invent a matching remover, but for taking off you simply use 벗다 for clothes, shoes, and hats alike. Don't say 안 신어요 to mean 'take off shoes' — that just means 'don't wear shoes'.

Using 안 + a wearing verb to mean 'take off' — 신발을 안 신어요 means 'I don't wear shoes', not 'I take off my shoes'; the action of removing is 신발을 벗어요.
Saying 시계를 벗다 for taking off a watch — a fastened watch is more naturally 시계를 풀다, and a ring is 반지를 빼다; 벗다 is for clothes, shoes, and hats.

words.nuance: 씻다 means to wash with water and, despite the tense-looking ㅅ, is a perfectly regular verb: the ㅅ stays in every form, giving 씻어요, 씻었어요, 씻습니다 (the ㅅ never drops the way it does in true ㅅ-irregular verbs like 짓다→지어요). It covers washing hands, face, body, and rinsing food. Korean, however, distributes 'wash/clean' across several verbs you must keep apart: 씻다 is for rinsing body parts and food; 감다 is reserved for washing hair (머리를 감다, never 머리를 씻다); 닦다 is 'wipe/scrub/polish' and is what you use for brushing teeth (이를 닦다) and wiping surfaces; and 빨다 is for washing laundry (빨래를 빨다), often replaced by 세탁하다 for machine washing 빨래하다. The whole-body version is 씻다 generically, or the Sino-Korean 샤워하다 'shower'. words.nuance: 신다 is the dedicated, regular verb (신어요, 신었어요, 신습니다) for putting on or wearing anything on the feet — shoes, sneakers, dress shoes, boots, socks, stockings. It exists because Korean assigns wearing verbs by body part rather than using one word like English 'wear': 입다 covers body clothes, 쓰다 the head and face, 끼다 snug items like gloves and rings, 차다 strapped items like watches, and 신다 specifically the feet. So 'wear sneakers' must be 운동화를 신다 and 'put on socks' is 양말을 신다 — using 입다 here is a clear error a native speaker would immediately notice. The matching state 'have on / be wearing' is 신고 있다 (장화를 신고 있어요 = is wearing boots), and the opposite is the all-purpose 벗다 (신발을 벗다). commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 신다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 신어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 신다 becomes 신을 수 있어요 ("can") and 신을 거예요 ("will"). words.nuance: 울다 means to cry and is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings starting with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so the formal present is 웁니다 (not 울습니다) and the honorific is 우세요; before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, giving 울어요 and 울었어요, and the future keeps it too in 울 거예요. The crier is the subject and takes 이/가 (아기가 울어요), unlike English where 'cry' can feel transitive. Its natural opposite is 웃다 (laugh), and its near-synonyms split by intensity and register: 눈물을 흘리다 ('shed tears', literally, more composed/quiet) describes tears running down without sobbing, while 흐느끼다 ('to sob') is heavier and more literary; plain 울다 is the everyday all-purpose word, often boosted by mimetics like 펑펑 울다 (bawl) or 엉엉 울다. Note 울다 also describes animals making their cry/call (새가 울다 = a bird sings/cries) and even a phone or alarm 'ringing/sounding'. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — writing 울습니다 by habit when the ㄹ must drop to 웁니다 — plus confusing 울다 with 웃다, which differ by a single jamo.

notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 울어 and 울어요 together.

words.shortExplanation: 켜다 means "to turn on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 켜다 (kyeoda) means "to turn on". Start from the polite form 켜요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 켜다. A strong first sentence is 불을 켜다 ("to turn on the light"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 켜다 also becomes 켜고 싶어요 (want), 켤 수 있어요 (can), and 못 켜요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Please turn on the light.
examples.note: Simple request; 좀 softens it to 'a little / would you'.

examples.en: The room was dark so I turned on the TV.
examples.note: Everyday cause-result; note the object particle 을 on 텔레비전.

examples.ko: 회의 시작하기 전에 빔프로젝터를 켜 놓을게요.

examples.en: I'll have the projector turned on before the meeting starts.
examples.note: Real situation; 켜 놓다 = turn on and leave it on ready.

words.nuance: 켜다 means to bring a device, screen, or flame to life by supplying power, and it is the exact opposite of 끄다 (to turn off) — the two are always taught as a pair. The dividing line English speakers miss is 켜다 vs 열다: 열다 is physically 'to open' (a door, a box, a lid), so you must never say 텔레비전을 열다 for switching a TV on — that sounds like prying the set apart. 켜다 also is not 틀다, which Koreans use casually for playing media or running water (음악을 틀다, 물을 틀다); 켜다 focuses on the power state itself. It is a plain native verb (no 한자), neutral in register and fine in both 불 켜 줘 to a friend and 불을 켜 주시겠어요? to a stranger. The biggest pitfall: English 'turn ON' tempts learners toward 돌리다 (to spin/turn) — but there is no rotating image here, so 돌리다 is wrong. Habitual collocations are 불을 켜다, 텔레비전·컴퓨터를 켜다, 에어컨·히터를 켜다, and 촛불을 켜다.

examples.en: Please turn off the light.
examples.note: Simple polite request with softening 좀.

examples.en: I turn off the light before sleeping.
examples.note: Everyday routine; -고 links two actions in sequence.

examples.ko: 회의 중에는 휴대폰을 꺼 두시기 바랍니다.

words.nuance: 끄다 is the direct opposite of 켜다 and means to cut the power to a device or to extinguish a flame, so the same verb that turns off a lamp also 'puts out' a fire (불을 끄다 covers both). The conjugation is the key trap: 끄다 is a ㅡ-dropping (으 불규칙) verb, so when you add 아/어, the bare ㅡ vowel disappears and the ㅓ of the ending takes over — giving 꺼요 and past 껐어요, never 끄어요. Register is neutral — 불 꺼 to a friend, 불을 꺼 주시겠어요? to a superior. A subtler point: to merely silence a phone, Koreans say 무음으로 하다 or 진동으로 하다, not 끄다, because 끄다 means the screen goes fully dark. The standard everyday phrase for brushing teeth — not 씻다; 양치(질)하다 is a synonym.

examples.en: I brush my teeth.
examples.note: Simple daily action; fixed collocation 이를 닦다.

examples.en: After eating, I wiped the table with a dishcloth.
examples.note: Everyday chore; 로 marks the tool 행주.

words.nuance: 닦다 is a hands-on cleaning verb that means to rub a surface to make it clean, dry, or shiny, and crucially it is the normal Korean word for brushing teeth — 이를 닦다 — even though English uses 'brush', not 'wipe'. The sharp contrast learners need is 닦다 vs 씻다: 씻다 means to wash with running water (손을 씻다, 얼굴을 씻다), so you 씻다 your hands but 닦다 your teeth, a table, or a window; mixing them up (이를 씻다) sounds odd to natives. 닦다 also differs from 청소하다, which is 'to clean a whole room/space' as a chore — you 청소하다 the house but 닦다 one specific surface. It is a plain native verb, neutral in register. Note the spelling: the stem ends in the double consonant ㄲ, so the present is 닦아요 (the ㄲ stays) and the formal is 닦습니다. Pitfall: do not import English 'clean' as one verb — Korean splits it into 닦다 (wipe/scrub a surface), 씻다 (wash with water), and 청소하다 (tidy a space). Saying 이를 씻다 for 'brush teeth' — 씻다 is to wash with water; teeth are brushed/wiped, so the correct phrase is 이를 닦다.
Using 청소하다 for wiping one surface — 청소하다 means to clean a whole space; for a single window or table use 닦다.
Spelling the present as 닦어요 — after the stem 닦, the ㅏ ending is used, giving 닦아요, not 닦어요.

It is neutral in register. Common collocations: 이를 닦다, 창문·바닥을 닦다, 눈물·땀을 닦다, 구두를 닦다.

The sharp contrast learners need is 닦다 vs 씻다: 씻다 means to wash with running water (손을 씻다, 얼굴을 씻다), so you 씻다 your hands but 닦다 your teeth, a table, or a window; mixing them up (이를 씻다) sounds odd to natives. 닦다 also differs from 청소하다, which is 'to clean a whole room/space' as a chore — you 청소하다 the house but 닦다 one specific surface.
Note the spelling: the stem ends in the double consonant ㄲ, so the present is 닦아요 (the ㄲ stays) and the formal is 닦습니다.
Do not import English 'clean' as one verb — Korean splits it into 닦다 (wipe/scrub a surface), 씻다 (wash with water), and 청소하다 (tidy a space).

words.shortExplanation: 팔다 means "to sell" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 팔다 (palda) means "to sell". Start from the polite form 팔아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 팔다. A strong first sentence is 표를 팔다 ("to sell tickets"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 팔다 also becomes 팔고 싶어요 (want), 팔 수 있어요 (can), and 못 팔아요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
For goods on offer; 여기서 표를 팔아요 = tickets are sold here.

examples.en: They sell tickets here.
examples.note: Simple statement of what's on offer.

examples.en: The convenience store sells umbrellas too.
examples.note: Everyday availability; 에서 marks the place of selling, 도 'also'.

examples.ko: 안 쓰는 옷을 중고로 싸게 팔았어요.
examples.romanization: an sseuneun oseul junggoro ssage parasseoyo.
examples.en: I sold clothes I don't use cheaply as secondhand.
examples.note: Real situation; 중고로 + 싸게 collocation.

words.nuance: 팔다 means to sell — to hand over goods in exchange for money — and it is the natural opposite of 사다 (to buy), so the two are learned as a pair. The conjugation is the headline feature: 팔다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ 탈락) verb, meaning the stem-final ㄹ drops out before endings beginning with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ. Use 팔아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 팔습니다 for the formal present — 팔다 is ㄹ-irregular, so ㄹ drops before -습니다 and the form becomes 팝니다.
Confusing 팔다 (to sell, active) with 팔리다 (to be sold / sell well) — say 책을 팔아요 to sell it, but 책이 잘 팔려요 for 'the book sells well'.

notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 팔아 and 팔아요 together.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 빌리다 means "to borrow" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to borrow" in Korean is 빌리다 (billida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빌려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빌리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 책을 빌리다 ("to borrow a book") — then reshape the same stem into 빌리고 싶어요 (desire), 빌릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 빌려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
도서관에서 책을 빌리다 — the source takes 에서 or 한테(서).

examples.en: Please lend me a pen.
examples.note: Simple request — note it's 빌려주다 (lend), what you say to the owner.

examples.en: I borrowed three books from the library.
examples.note: Everyday action; 에서 marks the source institution.

examples.ko: 보증금이 없어서 친구한테 돈을 좀 빌려야 했어요.
examples.romanization: bojeunggeumi eopseoseo chinguhante doneul jom billyeoya haesseoyo.
examples.en: I had no deposit so I had to borrow some money from a friend.
examples.note: Real situation; 한테 marks the person lender.

words.nuance: 빌리다 means to borrow — to take something with the understanding that you will return it (or, for money, repay it) — so it always implies a temporary, give-it-back relationship. The single biggest English-speaker trap is direction: 빌리다 is only 'borrow' (the thing comes TO you), while lending (giving it OUT to someone) is the separate verb 빌려주다, literally '빌리다 + 주다 (give)'. So '친구한테 책을 빌렸어요' = I borrowed a book from a friend, but '친구한테 책을 빌려줬어요' = I lent a book to a friend — the same 한테 changes meaning entirely depending on the verb. English 'borrow' and 'lend' are two words too, but learners reflexively use 빌리다 for both. The conjugation is regular (stem 빌리- + 어 → 빌려, past 빌렸어요). Watch the particles: the borrowed item takes 을/를, and the source takes 에서 for places (도서관에서) or 한테(서)/에게(서) for people. Register is neutral and native. Note also 빌리다 ≠ 임대하다/대여하다, the formal Sino-Korean for commercial renting (차를 대여하다). Common collocations: 책·돈·차를 빌리다, 도서관에서 빌리다, 빌려주다, 빌려 가다/오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 빌리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 빌려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 빌리다 to mean 'lend' — 빌리다 is only to borrow (it comes to you); to lend (give it out) you must say 빌려주다.
Marking the lender wrong — the person you borrow from takes 한테(서)/에게(서), as in 친구한테(서) 빌리다, not 친구를 빌리다.
Saying 빌려요 when you mean lending — to ask someone to lend you something, say 빌려주세요, not 빌리세요.

words.shortExplanation: 잡다 means "to grab" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 잡다 (japda) = "to grab". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 잡아요 plus one useful sentence like 손을 잡다 ("to hold hands"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 잡고 싶어요 for what you want, 잡을 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 잡아요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Physically grasp a hand; 손을 꼭 잡다 = hold tightly.

examples.en: Hold my hand.
examples.note: Simple physical action; fixed phrase 손을 잡다.

examples.en: It's hard to catch a taxi on the street.
examples.note: Everyday difficulty; -기가 어렵다 = it is hard to.

examples.en: We set the meeting date for next week.
examples.note: Real situation; figurative 날짜를 잡다 = fix a date.

words.nuance: 잡다 starts from the physical idea of closing your hand firmly around something — to grab, grasp, or hold — and from there fans out into many idioms Koreans use daily. The contrast to learn is 잡다 vs 들다: 들다 is to LIFT something up off a surface (가방을 들다 = pick up a bag), whereas 잡다 is to take HOLD of it without necessarily lifting (손잡이를 잡다 = grip the strap). It also differs from 쥐다, which is to clench in a fist (주먹을 쥐다); 잡다 is the broad everyday grip. Beyond the body, 잡다 means to CATCH (택시를 잡다 hail a cab, 도둑을 잡다 catch a thief, 물고기를 잡다 catch fish) and to SET/FIX a plan (약속을 잡다, 날짜를 잡다). The English pitfall is assuming 'grab' is purely physical and reaching for 가지다/들다 in the idioms — but 'catch a taxi' and 'set a date' both require 잡다 in Korean. It is a plain native verb, regular (잡아요, 잡았어요, formal 잡습니다), neutral register. Note the passive 잡히다 (be caught): 택시가 안 잡혀요. Common collocations: 손·손잡이를 잡다, 택시를 잡다, 약속·날짜를 잡다, 기회를 잡다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잡다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잡아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 들다 (to lift) when you mean grip — 가방을 들다 is to lift a bag, but to hold a strap or hand you say 잡다 (손잡이를 잡다).
Translating 'catch a taxi' literally with a different verb — Korean fixes this as 택시를 잡다; saying 택시를 받다/가지다 is wrong.

words.shortExplanation: 보내다 means "to send" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 보내다 (bonaeda) means "to send". Start from the polite form 보내요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보내다. A strong first sentence is 문자를 보내다 ("to send a text message"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 보내다 also becomes 보내고 싶어요 (want), 보낼 수 있어요 (can), and 못 보내요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
문자·메시지·이메일을 보내다; the recipient takes 에게/한테.

examples.en: I send a text to my friend.
examples.note: Simple action; 에게 marks the recipient.

examples.en: Please send me the address via KakaoTalk.
examples.note: Everyday request; 으로 marks the means/channel.

examples.en: I spent the vacation at my grandmother's in the countryside.
examples.note: Real situation; the 'spend time' sense of 보내다.

words.nuance: 보내다 means to send something or someone away from you toward another place or person — a message, a parcel, even a child to school — and it also carries the everyday idiom 시간을 보내다, 'to spend/pass time'. The sharp contrast is 보내다 vs 주다: 주다 (to give) is a face-to-face hand-over where giver and receiver are together, while 보내다 implies distance — the thing travels to reach the other person. So you 줘요 a gift you hand over now, but 보내요 a gift you mail; using 주다 for a text or parcel sounds like you are physically handing it across. The recipient particle is 에게/한테 (and honorific 께): 부모님께 보내다. For the 'spend time' sense, English speakers wrongly reach for 쓰다 (to use/spend money) — but time is 보내다, not 쓰다: 좋은 시간 보내세요! is the standard 'have a good time'. It is a plain native verb, regular (stem 보내- + 어 contracts to 보내, past 보냈어요), neutral register. The means/channel takes 으로 (이메일로, 택배로). Common collocations: 문자·이메일을 보내다, 소포·택배를 보내다, 시간·세월을 보내다, 사람을 보내다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 주다 for things sent over a distance — 주다 is a hand-to-hand give; for a text or parcel that travels, use 보내다 (소포를 보내다).
Saying 시간을 쓰다 for 'spend time' — 쓰다 is for spending money/using things; spending time is 시간을 보내다.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 — the person you send to takes 에게/한테/께 (친구에게 보내다), while the thing sent takes 을/를.

words.shortExplanation: 들어가다 means "to go in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to go in" in Korean is 들어가다 (deureogada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 들어가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 들어가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 방에 들어가다 ("to go into the room") — then reshape the same stem into 들어가고 싶어요 (desire), 들어갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 들어가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Enter an enclosed space; the place entered takes 에 or 안에.

examples.en: Go inside.
examples.note: Simple direction; 안으로 = toward the inside.

examples.en: It's cold, so let's go inside quickly.
examples.note: Everyday suggestion; -읍시다 'let's'.

examples.ko: 저는 보통 열한 시쯤 집에 들어가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun botong yeolhan sijjeum jibe deureogayo.
examples.en: I usually get home around eleven.
examples.note: Real routine; the 'get home' idiom of 들어가다.

words.nuance: 들어가다 combines 들다 (to enter) + 가다 (to go), so it literally means 'enter-and-go' — to move into an enclosed space in a direction AWAY from where the speaker stands. The crucial paired contrast is 들어가다 vs 들어오다: 들어오다 ('enter-and-come') is the same entering motion but TOWARD the speaker. So if you are inside a room and want someone to come in, you say 들어오세요 (come in), but if you are heading into a room over there, you 들어가요. English 'go in / come in' splits the same way, yet learners default to 들어가다 for both and tell a guest at their own door 들어가세요, which oddly means 'go away in / head on home'. Beyond the literal, 들어가다 idiomatically means to get home (집에 들어가다), to enter a school or job (대학·회사에 들어가다), and even 'to fit' (이 옷이 가방에 안 들어가요). It is a plain native compound, regular, neutral register. The destination takes 에 or 안에 (방에/방 안에 들어가다). Common collocations: 방·집에 들어가다, 학교·회사에 들어가다, 안으로 들어가다, 잘 안 들어가다(won't fit).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들어가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Telling a visitor at your door 들어가세요 — that means 'go on in (away from me) / head home'; to welcome them in toward you, say 들어오세요.
Using a 'to' particle like 으로 for the room — the space entered takes 에 (방에 들어가다); 으로 marks only a direction (안으로).
Forgetting the idioms — 'get home' is 집에 들어가다 and 'get into university' is 대학에 들어가다, not 집에 가다 / 대학에 가다 alone, which lose the 'enter' nuance.

structuredNuance.t: 들어가다 means to move into an enclosed space in a direction AWAY from where the speaker stands. Beyond the literal, 들어가다 idiomatically means to get home (집에 들어가다), to enter a school or job (대학·회사에 들어가다), and even 'to fit' (이 옷이 가방에 안 들어가요). It is neutral register. The destination takes 에 or 안에 (방에/방 안에 들어가다). Common collocations: 방·집에 들어가다, 학교·회사에 들어가다, 안으로 들어가다, 잘 안 들어가다(won't fit).

들어가다 combines 들다 (to enter) + 가다 (to go), so it literally means 'enter-and-go'. It is a plain native compound, regular.

words.shortExplanation: 나가다 means "to go out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 나가다 (nagada) = "to go out". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 나가요 plus one useful sentence like 밖에 나가다 ("to go outside"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Leave an inside space; 밖에/밖으로 나가다.

examples.en: I'm going outside.
examples.note: Simple action; 밖에 = to the outside.

examples.en: The weather's nice, so I'll step out for a bit.
examples.note: Everyday departure; 나갔다 오다 = go out and return.

examples.ko: 다음 주부터 새 회사에 나가기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: daeum jubuteo sae hoesae nagagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: I've decided to start going in to the new company next week.
examples.note: Real situation; 회사에 나가다 = report to work.

words.nuance: 나가다 is 나다/나- (to exit, come out) + 가다 (to go), literally 'exit-and-go' — to move from an inside space OUT, in a direction away from the speaker. It is the natural opposite of 들어가다 (go in). The paired contrast to master is 나가다 vs 나오다: 나오다 ('exit-and-come') is the same going-out motion but TOWARD the speaker, so if you are outside waiting and want someone to come out to you, you say 나오세요, whereas if you yourself are leaving a building, you 나가요. English 'go out / come out' divides identically, but learners often pick 나가다 regardless. Idiomatically 나가다 also means to go (in) to work or attend a regular gathering — 회사에 나가다, 동호회에 나가다 — and even 'to be broadcast/aired' for media. commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 나가다 as a complete polite sentence.

Saying 나가세요 to someone you want to come out to you — that tells them to leave away from you; to call them out toward you, say 나오세요.

words.shortExplanation: 올라가다 means "to go up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Move upward by stairs; the path takes 을/를 or 으로.

examples.en: I go up.
examples.note: Simple direction; 위로 = upward.

examples.en: Shall we go up to the rooftop by elevator?
examples.note: Everyday suggestion; 으로 marks the means, 까지 'all the way to'.

examples.en: Gas prices went up a lot this month.
examples.note: Real situation; the figurative 'rise' sense.

words.nuance: 올라가다 is 오르다/올라- (to rise, ascend) + 가다 (to go), literally 'rise-and-go' — to move UPWARD in a direction away from the speaker. Use 올라가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 올라가세요 to invite someone up to where you are — that sends them up away from you; to call them up toward you, say 올라오세요.
Using 올라가다 for movement toward the speaker — if the motion comes up to you, it must be 올라오다, not 올라가다.

words.shortExplanation: 내려가다 means "to go down" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to go down" in Korean is 내려가다 (naeryeogada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 내려가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 내려가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 계단을 내려가다 ("to go down the stairs") — then reshape the same stem into 내려가고 싶어요 (desire), 내려갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 내려가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Move downward by stairs; path takes 을/를 or 으로.

examples.en: I go down.
examples.note: Simple direction; 아래로 = downward.

examples.en: I have to go down the stairs carrying luggage.
examples.note: Everyday obligation; 을 marks the stairs as path.

examples.ko: 약을 먹고 나니까 열이 조금 내려갔어요.
examples.romanization: yageul meokgo nanikka yeori jogeum naeryeogasseoyo.
examples.en: After taking medicine, my fever went down a little.
examples.note: Real situation; the figurative 'drop' sense.

words.nuance: 내려가다 is 내리다/내려- (to descend, lower) + 가다 (to go), literally 'descend-and-go' — to move DOWNWARD in a direction away from the speaker. It is the exact opposite of 올라가다, and its toward-the-speaker partner is 내려오다 (come down). The contrast to lock in is 내려가다 vs 내려오다: standing downstairs and calling someone to join you, you say 내려오세요 (come down to me); heading down yourself, you 내려가요. words.shortExplanation: 돌아오다 means "to come back" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 돌아오다 (doraoda) = "to come back". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 돌아와요 plus one useful sentence like 집에 돌아오다 ("to come back home"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Return to a place toward the speaker; 에 marks the place.

examples.en: I come back home.
examples.note: Simple action; 에 marks the destination of return.

examples.en: I came back from a business trip yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday past; 에서 marks where you returned from.

examples.en: I'll come straight back home when work is done.
examples.note: Real situation; -을게요 promise to the listener.

words.nuance: 돌아오다 is 돌다/돌아- (to turn, circle back) + 오다 (to come), literally 'turn-and-come' — to come BACK to a place, in a direction TOWARD the speaker or the home base. Its mirror is 돌아가다 ('turn-and-go'), returning AWAY from the speaker, and this is the central trap: if you are at home and tell family you'll be back, you say 집에 돌아올게요 (I'll come back here), but speaking of returning to your faraway hometown you say 고향에 돌아가다 (go back there, away). English 'come back / go back' splits the same way, yet learners overuse 돌아오다. The destination of return takes 에 (집에 돌아오다), while the place you return FROM takes 에서 (여행에서 돌아오다). 돌아오다 also has the gentle idiom of things coming round again — 봄이 돌아오다 (spring returns), 기회가 돌아오다 (a chance comes back around). It is a plain native compound; the stem 돌아오- + 아 contracts to 돌아와, past 돌아왔어요, neutral register. Note 돌아오다 ≠ 다시 오다 exactly: 다시 오다 is just 'come again', while 돌아오다 implies returning to where you started. Common collocations: 집에 돌아오다, 여행·출장에서 돌아오다, 다시 돌아오다, 봄이 돌아오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌아오다 as a complete polite sentence.

Marking the origin with 을/를 — the place you return FROM takes 에서 (여행에서 돌아오다); the place you return TO takes 에 (집에 돌아오다).
Writing 돌아오아요 — the stem ends in 오, so 오 + 아 contracts to 와, giving 돌아와요 (past 돌아왔어요), never 돌아오아요.

words.shortExplanation: 생각하다 means "to think" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 생각하다 (saenggakada) means "to think". Start from the polite form 생각해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 생각하다. A strong first sentence is 저도 그렇게 생각해요. ("I think so too."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 생각하다 also becomes 생각하고 싶어요 (want), 생각할 수 있어요 (can), and 생각 못 해요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
그렇게 (like that) + 생각하다 is the everyday way to agree with an opinion.

examples.en: What are you thinking about?
examples.note: Casual 해; drop the object and Koreans understand 'about what'.

examples.en: I think this movie is fun.
examples.note: To report an opinion, attach -다고 to the plain form (재미있다 → 재미있다고).

examples.en: When I think of my family, I get strength.
examples.note: 생각하면 (when/if I think) + emotion — thinking 'of' a person, not just an idea.

words.nuance: 생각하다 (a native verb 생각 'thought' + 하다, not Sino-Korean) covers two jobs English splits apart: holding an opinion ('I think it's good') and mentally pondering or picturing ('I'm thinking about it / about you'). The near-synonym 믿다 means to believe with conviction, and 알다 means to know as fact; 생각하다 stays softer and more subjective, so use it for personal views. To report what you think, the partner pattern is -다고 생각하다 (좋다고 생각해요 = I think it's good); this is THE pitfall — English speakers say 생각해요 그것은 좋다 word-for-word, but Korean must embed the clause with -다고 before 생각하다. As a 하다 verb it splits in the negative (생각 안 해요, 생각 못 해요), and the polite stem is 생각해요, never 생각하어요.

Using 알다 (know) for an opinion, as in '좋은 영화라고 알아요.' 알다 is for facts you know; for a view use 생각하다 → 좋은 영화라고 생각해요.
Forming the negative as '안 생각해요.' Because 생각하다 is noun+하다, the 안 goes inside: 생각 안 해요.

words.shortExplanation: 느끼다 means "to feel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to feel" in Korean is 느끼다 (neukkida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 느껴요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 느끼다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 행복을 느껴요. ("I feel happiness.") — then reshape the same stem into 느끼고 싶어요 (desire), 느낄 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 느껴요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Emotion-noun + 을/를 + 느끼다; the feeling is the object, not an adjective.

examples.en: Are you cold? (lit. do you feel cold?)
examples.note: For bodily cold/hot Korean uses the adjective 춥다, NOT 느끼다 — a key boundary.

examples.en: I was moved by those words (lit. felt being moved).
examples.note: Past 느꼈어요; 감동을 느끼다 is a set collocation for being touched.

examples.en: I feel a lot of warmth/connection in Korea.
examples.note: 정 is an untranslatable Korean affection; 정을 느끼다 is how you say you sense it.

words.nuance: 느끼다 (a native verb, no 한자) means to become aware of something through the senses or the heart — an emotion (행복을 느끼다), a physical sensation (통증을 느끼다 = feel pain), or an abstract impression (차이·분위기를 느끼다). The contrast with 생각하다 is sharp: 느끼다 is what your body and heart register, 생각하다 is what your mind concludes. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-using it for states: 'I feel cold/sick/tired' in natural Korean is usually the plain adjective — 추워요, 아파요, 피곤해요 — not 추움을 느껴요. Reserve 느끼다 for when you're consciously naming the sensation as an object (감동을 느끼다, 책임감을 느끼다). Conjugation: the stem 느끼 + -어 contracts to 느껴 (느껴요, 느꼈어요), never the spelled-out 느끼어요.

Use 느껴요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying '나는 추움을 느껴요' for 'I feel cold.' Natural Korean uses the adjective directly: 추워요. 느끼다 here sounds like a clinical translation.
Writing 느끼어요 / 느끼었어요. The vowel stem contracts: 느껴요 / 느꼈어요.
Using 느끼다 for 'I feel that we should go.' That sense of 'feel = opinion' is 생각하다 in Korean: 가야 한다고 생각해요, not 느껴요.

words.shortExplanation: 기억하다 means "to remember" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 기억하다 (gieokada) = "to remember". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 기억해요 plus one useful sentence like 저를 기억해요? ("Do you remember me?"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 기억하고 싶어요 for what you want, 기억할 수 있어요 for what you can, 기억 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Person + 을/를 + 기억하다 to ask if someone recalls you.

examples.en: Do you remember my birthday?
examples.note: Casual 기억해; a common little relationship test.

examples.en: I still remember that day.
examples.note: 아직도 (still) + 기억하다 for a memory that lasts.

examples.en: Please be sure to remember the appointment.
examples.note: 기억해 주세요 asks someone to keep it in mind for your sake.

words.nuance: 기억하다 comes from the 한자 記憶 (記 'record' + 憶 'recollect'), literally 'record-and-recollect,' so it spans both keeping something in memory and calling it back up. The crucial contrast is with 외우다: 외우다 means to memorize by effort (study a list, learn lines), while 기억하다 is simply having or retrieving a memory — you 외우다 a phone number so you can later 기억하다 it. Its opposite is 잊다 (forget). A very natural alternative for spontaneous recall is the idiom 기억이 나다 ('a memory arises'): Koreans say 기억이 안 나요 far more than 기억 못 해요 for 'I can't recall it right now.' Pitfall for English speakers: don't use 기억하다 where English 'memorize' is meant (cramming for a test is 외우다), and remember it's a 하다 verb, so the negative is 기억 안 해요 / 기억 못 해요, with 안 inside.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 기억하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 기억해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 기억하다 for 'memorize this vocabulary.' Active memorization is 외우다: 이 단어를 외우세요, not 기억하세요.
Saying '기억 못 해요' for a name that just slipped your mind. Native speakers prefer the idiom 기억이 안 나요 ('it won't come to me') in that moment.
Confusing it with 생각나다. 생각나다 = something pops into mind / I just thought of it; 기억하다 = I hold it in memory. They overlap but aren't interchangeable in writing.

words.shortExplanation: 잊다 means "to forget" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 잊다 (itda) means "to forget". Start from the polite form 잊어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 잊다. A strong first sentence is 비밀번호를 잊었어요. ("I forgot the password."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 잊다 also becomes 잊고 싶어요 (want), 잊을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 잊어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Information + 을/를 + 잊다 when a fact drops out of memory.

examples.en: I forgot again!
examples.note: Casual past 잊었어; 또 (again) admits a habit.

examples.en: I want to forget bad memories quickly.
examples.note: 잊고 싶다 expresses the wish to let something go.

examples.en: I left my umbrella at the shop and just forgot about it.
examples.note: 두고 (leave behind) + 잊어버리다 — the umbrella stayed AND slipped my mind.

words.nuance: 잊다 (native verb) means something disappears from your memory — a password, a promise, a person. Its dead-opposite is 기억하다. The number-one English-speaker trap is the look-alike 잃다 'to lose (a physical object)': you 잃다 your wallet but 잊다 your password. They even sound close (잊다 [읻따] vs 잃다 [일타]), yet swapping them changes the meaning entirely. Koreans very often attach the auxiliary -어버리다 to make 잊어버리다, which adds a nuance of 'it's completely, irretrievably gone,' frequently with a tinge of relief or regret (다 잊어버렸어요). Note the consonant stem conjugates plainly: 잊어요, 잊었어요, and the formal is 잊습니다. For 'don't forget,' the fixed warning form is 잊지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잊다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잊어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 잃다 (lose an object) for forgetting information: '비밀번호를 잃었어요' is wrong for a forgotten password — use 잊었어요. Save 잃다 for losing your phone or keys.
Saying 'I forgot my umbrella at the shop' as 우산을 잊었어요 only. If you physically left it behind, Koreans say 우산을 (가게에) 두고 왔어요 or add 잊어버렸어요 — 잊다 alone covers the mind, not the leaving.
Treating 잊어버리다 as a separate, harder word. It's just 잊다 + -어버리다; use it freely for 'totally forgot.'

words.shortExplanation: 결정하다 means "to decide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to decide" in Korean is 결정하다 (gyeoljeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 결정해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 결정하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 메뉴를 결정했어요. ("I decided on the menu.") — then reshape the same stem into 결정하고 싶어요 (desire), 결정할 수 있어요 (ability), and 결정 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Thing chosen takes 을/를; 결정하다 = settle the matter.

examples.en: Did you decide what to eat?
examples.note: Casual; -ㄹ지 (what/whether) embeds the open question before 결정하다.

examples.ko: 여행 날짜를 아직 결정 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: yeohaeng naljjareul ajik gyeoljeong mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I still can't decide the travel date.
examples.note: 결정 못 하다 = unable to settle on it; 못 sits inside the 하다 verb.

examples.en: I decided to quit the company.
examples.note: Big life choice with -기로 결정하다; this is where 결정하다 outshines 정하다.

words.nuance: 결정하다 is built on the 한자 決定 (決 'resolve, cut through' + 定 'fix, settle'), so it literally means 'cut through and settle' — reaching a firm choice after deliberation. Three near-synonyms divide the space: 정하다 is the everyday, lighter 'set/decide' (그냥 정해요 = let's just settle it); 선택하다 (選擇) is 'select' from given options; 고르다 is the casual 'pick' (고르다 a fruit, a color). Use 결정하다 for consequential, considered decisions (a job, a move, a date) — for which thing to pick off a shelf, 고르다 or 선택하다 fits better. To decide to DO an action, the partner pattern is -기로 결정하다 (가기로 결정했어요); English speakers often forget the -기로 and say 결정했어요 가다. As a 하다 verb the negative splits: 결정 안 해요, 결정 못 해요. The heavier idiom 결정을 내리다 frames it as 'handing down' a decision.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 결정하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 결정해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 고르다 (pick) for a major life decision: '회사를 그만두는 것을 골랐어요' sounds like choosing off a menu. Say 그만두기로 결정했어요.
Forgetting -기로 when deciding to do something: '결정했어요 한국에 가다' is ungrammatical. Embed it: 한국에 가기로 결정했어요.
Forming the negative as 안 결정해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 결정 안 해요 (or 아직 결정 못 했어요 for 'haven't decided yet').

words.shortExplanation: 준비하다 means "to prepare" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 준비하다 (junbihada) = "to prepare". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 준비해요 plus one useful sentence like 저녁을 준비해요. ("I prepare dinner."). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Meal + 을/를 + 준비하다; getting food ready.

examples.en: Did you get the food ready?
examples.note: Casual; 밥 stands in for 'a meal' generally.

examples.en: I have to prepare for tomorrow's presentation.
examples.note: 준비해야 하다 expresses the obligation to get ready.

examples.en: Prepare the gift in advance (and keep it ready).
examples.note: 준비해 두다 = prepare and leave set; 미리 reinforces 'ahead of time.'

words.nuance: 준비하다 comes from 한자 準備 (準 'standard, level' + 備 'provide, equip'), literally 'get equipped to standard' — to ready things or yourself beforehand. It naturally collocates with events and outcomes: 시험을 준비하다, 여행을 준비하다, 저녁을 준비하다, 마음의 준비. Compare 마련하다 ('arrange/procure' funds or a place — 집을 마련하다) and 챙기다 ('gather up, pack' your own belongings — 여권 챙겼어? = did you grab your passport?); 준비하다 is the broad 'prepare,' while 챙기다 zooms in on not forgetting items. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'prepare FOR the exam' tempts 시험에 준비하다, but Korean treats the exam as a direct object — 시험을 준비하다. Also don't reach for 만들다 'make' when you only mean getting ready. As a 하다 verb, negate inside (준비 안 해요), and its passive 준비되다 ('be ready') is everywhere: 준비됐어요.

Wrong particle: '시험에 준비해요' for 'prepare for the exam.' Korean uses the object marker: 시험을 준비해요.
Using 만들다 (make) for getting ready: 'dinner is being prepared' is 저녁을 준비해요, not 저녁을 만들어요 unless you stress the cooking itself.
Saying '준비해요' to answer 'Are you ready?' The state 'I'm ready' is the passive 준비됐어요 / 준비됐어; 준비해요 means the act of preparing.

words.shortExplanation: 운동하다 means "to exercise" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

A strong first sentence is 매일 아침에 운동해요. ("I exercise every morning."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 운동하다 also becomes 운동하고 싶어요 (want), 운동할 수 있어요 (can), and 운동 못 해요 (cannot). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Time + 에 + 운동하다 for a routine.

examples.en: Are you working out these days?
examples.note: Casual check-in; 요즘 (lately) frames an ongoing habit.

examples.en: I want to exercise for my health.
examples.note: 건강을 위해서 (for the sake of health) + 운동하고 싶다.

examples.en: I can't exercise these days because I'm busy.
examples.note: Negative ability 운동 못 하다, with 못 inside the 하다 verb.

words.nuance: 운동하다 = 한자 運動 (運 'move, transport' + 動 'move') + 하다, literally 'movement-movement,' i.e. to physically exercise. The same noun 운동 also means a sports movement or a social campaign, but with 하다 it's working out. A key feature for learners: Korean builds most sports the same way — noun + 하다 (축구하다 play soccer, 수영하다 swim), though racket sports take 치다 'hit' instead (테니스 치다). The contrast with 놀다 ('play, hang out, have fun') matters: 놀다 is unstructured fun, 운동하다 is purposeful physical activity, so don't say 놀다 when you mean training. Natural collocations: 헬스장에서 운동하다, 건강을 위해 운동하다, 운동 부족. As a 하다 verb the negatives split — 운동 안 해요, 운동 못 해요 — and you can swap in 운동을 안 하다 with the object marker for a touch more emphasis.

Saying 안 운동해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 운동 안 해요 (or 운동을 안 해요).

words.shortExplanation: 사용하다 means "to use" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to use" in Korean is 사용하다 (sayonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 사용해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 사용하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이 앱을 자주 사용해요. ("I use this app often.") — then reshape the same stem into 사용하고 싶어요 (desire), 사용할 수 있어요 (ability), and 사용 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Tool + 을/를 + 사용하다; the thing used is the object.

examples.en: Can I use this?
examples.note: Very casual — here Koreans naturally swap in 쓰다, the everyday twin of 사용하다.

examples.en: You can use the wifi here.
examples.note: 사용할 수 있다 states availability or permission.

examples.en: May I use this restroom?
examples.note: -아도 돼요? asks permission; 사용하다 is polite and neutral for facilities.

words.nuance: 사용하다 is the 한자 使用 (使 'employ, make use of' + 用 'use') + 하다 — to put a tool, service, or facility to use. Its everyday native twin is 쓰다, which means the exact same 'use' but sounds more casual and conversational (이거 써도 돼? vs the more formal 이거 사용해도 돼요?). A third relative, 이용하다 (利用), leans toward using a service or system (지하철을 이용하다 = use the subway, 시설을 이용하다 = use the facilities). Rule of thumb: speech and casual notes → 쓰다; signs, manuals, and polite requests → 사용하다; services and transport → 이용하다. The pitfall is over-formalizing chat: a friend asks to borrow your pen and 사용해도 돼? sounds stiff — say 써도 돼? Also beware that 쓰다 is a homonym meaning 'write' and 'wear (on the head/face),' so context disambiguates. As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 사용 안 해요, 사용 못 해요.

Saying 안 사용해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 사용 안 해요. And for transport/services, 이용하다 often sounds more idiomatic (버스를 이용해요).

words.shortExplanation: 여행하다 means "to travel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 여행하다 (yeohaenghada) = "to travel". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 여행해요 plus one useful sentence like 혼자 여행해요. ("I travel alone."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 여행하고 싶어요 for what you want, 여행할 수 있어요 for what you can, 여행 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
혼자 (alone) + 여행하다 to describe travel style.

examples.en: Where are you traveling during the break?
examples.note: Casual; 어디 (where) + 여행하다.

examples.en: I'll travel to Europe next year.
examples.note: Destination + 으로 + 여행(을) 가다 — the go-to natural pattern.

examples.en: I like traveling by train.
examples.note: Means of transport + 로/으로; 여행하는 걸 좋아하다 states a preference.

words.nuance: 여행하다 is 한자 旅行 (旅 'journey, sojourn' + 行 'go') + 하다 — to travel, typically for leisure or sightseeing. Here's the natural-usage point most textbooks bury: Koreans far more often say 여행(을) 가다 'go on a trip' or 여행(을) 하다 with the noun split out than the bare verb 여행하다. A destination then takes 으로/로 ('toward') in 부산으로 여행 가다, or 을/를 when you 여행하다 a place you tour around (유럽을 여행하다). Compare 관광하다 (觀光, 'sightsee' — the tourist act of viewing attractions) and plain 가다 'go'; 여행하다 implies the whole trip, not a single going. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) saying just 가다 ('I went to Busan' = 부산에 갔어요) when you mean a vacation — add 여행; (2) attaching 에 to 여행하다 (제주도에 여행해요) — for the verb 여행하다 the place is the object (제주도를 여행해요), while with 가다 you use 으로/에. As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 여행 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 여행하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 여행해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using bare 가다 for a trip: '부산에 갔어요' just means you went there. For a vacation say 부산에 여행 갔어요 / 부산을 여행했어요.
Wrong particle with the verb: '제주도에 여행해요' is off — 여행하다 takes the place as object: 제주도를 여행해요. (With 가다 it's 제주도로/에 여행 가요.)
Saying 안 여행해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 여행 안 해요 — though 여행 안 가요 ('not going on a trip') is what Koreans more naturally say.

words.shortExplanation: 청소하다 means "to clean" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 청소하다 (cheongsohada) means "to clean". Start from the polite form 청소해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 청소하다. A strong first sentence is 방을 청소해요. ("I clean the room."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 청소하다 also becomes 청소하고 싶어요 (want), 청소할 수 있어요 (can), and 청소 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Space + 을/를 + 청소하다; cleaning a whole area.

examples.en: Clean your room, would you!
examples.note: Casual command with 좀 softening (or nagging) the order.

examples.en: Guests are coming, so I have to clean.
examples.note: -니까 (since) gives the reason; 청소해야 하다 = must clean.

examples.en: We clean the house together every weekend.
examples.note: 주말마다 (every weekend) + 청소하다 for a shared routine.

words.nuance: 청소하다 is 한자 淸掃 (淸 'clear, pure' + 掃 'sweep') + 하다 — literally 'sweep clean,' i.e. tidy up a room or space. The boundary with neighboring verbs is what trips learners: 씻다 = wash a body or food with water (손을 씻다, 과일을 씻다); 닦다 = wipe, scrub a surface, or polish (창문을 닦다, 이를 닦다 = brush teeth); 치우다 = clear away / put things in order (책상을 치우다). 청소하다 is the umbrella 'clean a space,' so you 청소하다 a room but 닦다 the table inside it and 씻다 your hands afterward. The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'clean' for all of these — saying 방을 씻어요 (washing the room with water) is unintentionally literal and odd; rooms are 청소해요. Natural partners: 방·집·화장실을 청소하다, 청소기를 돌리다, 대청소. As a 하다 verb the negative goes inside: 청소 안 해요, 청소 못 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 청소하다 as a complete polite sentence.

Using 씻다 (wash with water) for tidying a room: '방을 씻어요' literally means hosing the room down. A room is 방을 청소해요.
Using 청소하다 for wiping one surface or brushing teeth: the table is 닦아요, teeth are 이를 닦아요, not 청소해요. 청소하다 is for whole spaces.

words.shortExplanation: 노래하다 means "to sing" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to sing" in Korean is 노래하다 (noraehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 노래해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 노래하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 노래를 불러요. ("I sing a song.") — then reshape the same stem into 노래하고 싶어요 (desire), 노래할 수 있어요 (ability), and 노래 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The natural form: 노래를 부르다 (sing a song), preferred over bare 노래하다.

examples.en: Sing for me.
examples.note: Casual 불러 줘; Koreans say 노래(를) 부르다, not 노래하다, for singing a specific song.

examples.en: Shall we sing together?
examples.note: 노래할까요? proposes singing as a shared activity.

examples.ko: 저는 사람 앞에서 노래 못 해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun saram apeseo norae mo taeyo.
examples.en: I can't sing in front of people.
examples.note: Negative ability 노래 못 하다, with 못 inside the 하다 verb.

words.nuance: 노래하다 joins the native noun 노래 'a song' with 하다 to mean 'to sing,' but here's the catch that surprises learners: Koreans usually prefer 노래(를) 부르다 ('call out a song') for the act of singing, especially singing a particular song — 노래를 불러 주세요 sounds far more natural than 노래해 주세요. Bare 노래하다 leans poetic or general ('the birds are singing'), while 노래를 부르다 is the everyday choice at a 노래방 (karaoke room). For 'I'm a good singer,' the set phrase is 노래를 잘하다 (do songs well). Don't confuse it with 부르다 used alone, which also means 'to call (someone)' — context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'sing' one-to-one onto 노래하다 and never reaching for 부르다, which is what natives actually say. As a 하다 verb, the negative splits inside: 노래 안 해요, 노래 못 해요. Note 부르다 itself is a 르 irregular (불러요), separate from 노래하다's regular 하다 conjugation.

words.shortExplanation: 춤추다 means "to dance" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 춤추다 (chumchuda) = "to dance". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 춤춰요 plus one useful sentence like 음악에 맞춰 춤춰요. ("I dance to the music."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 춤추고 싶어요 for what you want, 춤출 수 있어요 for what you can, 춤 못 춰요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
음악에 맞춰 (in time with the music) + 춤추다.

examples.en: Wanna dance together?
examples.note: Casual invitation with -ㄹ래? — friendly, low-pressure.

examples.en: I want to dance with friends at the party.
examples.note: 친구들이랑 (casual 'with friends') + 춤추고 싶다.

examples.en: I can't dance when there are a lot of people.
examples.note: Negative ability; 춤 못 춰요 splits the noun off — note the 춰 contraction.

words.nuance: 춤추다 is a fused noun+verb: the noun 춤 'a dance' plus the native verb 추다 'to dance, perform (a dance).' Because 추다 already means 'dance,' the headword often un-fuses into 춤을 추다, especially when you add a modifier — 춤을 잘 추다 (dance well), 춤을 배우다 (learn to dance), 춤 실력 (dancing ability). Conjugation: the stem 추 + -어 contracts to 춰 (춰요, 춤췄어요, 춤출 거예요), and in the negative the noun separates so 안/못 land before the verb: 춤 안 춰요, 춤 못 춰요. Compare 노래하다, where the parallel and equally common form is 노래를 부르다 — both 'dance' and 'sing' prefer the noun + dedicated-verb construction over a plain 하다 verb.

Saying 춤해요 by analogy with 노래해요/운동해요. Dance has its own verb 추다 — say 춤춰요 or 춤을 춰요, never 춤하다.
Writing the contraction wrong: 춤추어요 / 춤추었어요 should be 춤춰요 / 춤췄어요 (추 + 어 → 춰).
Putting the negative outside as 안 춤춰요. Because it's noun+verb, split it: 춤 안 춰요 (and 춤 못 춰요 for can't).

words.shortExplanation: 대답하다 means "to answer" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 대답하다 (daedaphada) means "to answer". Start from the polite form 대답해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 대답하다. A strong first sentence is 질문에 대답하다 ("answer a question"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The thing answered takes 에, not 을: 질문에 대답해요, never 질문을 대답해요

examples.en: I answered, "Yes."
examples.note: Simple: the bare reply 네 plus 대답하다 — this is how you report what someone said back

examples.en: I answered the teacher's question right away.
examples.note: Everyday: note 질문에 (에, the question you reply TO) and 바로 = right away

examples.en: In the interview, don't panic — answer calmly.
examples.note: Real situation: 차분하게 대답하다 is the set phrase for composed, measured replies

words.nuance: 대답하다 is 對答(대답)하다, the hanja 對 'facing' + 答 'reply', so it literally means to 'reply facing' a question — you give a verbal response back to something someone asked. The key boundary is against 답하다 and 응답하다: 대답하다 is the everyday spoken word (a child 대답해요 when called), 답하다 is more clipped and written (편지에 답하다 'reply to a letter'), and 응답하다 is formal/technical (서버가 응답하다 'the server responds'). The single biggest English-speaker trap is the particle: in English you 'answer the question' (direct object), but in Korean the question is the target you reply toward, so it MUST be 질문에 대답하다 with 에 — 질문을 대답하다 sounds clearly wrong to natives. Also note this is a 하다 verb, so every form is regular: 대답 + 해요, and the negative cleanly splits the noun off as 대답 안 해요 / 대답 못 해요. Do not stretch it to phones (use 전화를 받다) or to 'responding to email,' which Koreans handle with 답장하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 대답하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 대답해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 질문을 대답해요 by copying English 'answer the question.' The question is what you reply toward, so use 에: 질문에 대답해요.
Using 대답하다 for answering the phone (전화를 대답해요). A ringing phone is 받다 — say 전화를 받아요.
Confusing 대답하다 (give an answer) with 질문하다 (pose a question) — they are opposite roles in a Q&A.

words.shortExplanation: 부탁하다 means "to ask a favor" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to ask a favor" in Korean is 부탁하다 (butakada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 부탁해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 부탁하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 잘 부탁합니다 ("I'm counting on you / nice to work with you") — then reshape the same stem into 부탁하고 싶어요 (desire), 부탁할 수 있어요 (ability), and 부탁 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not ask a favor.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to ask a favor.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to ask a favor.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I'm counting on you / nice to work with you
usagePhrases.note: The single most-used set phrase — said when starting a job, a class, or any relationship

examples.en: Take care of this for me, please.
examples.note: Simple: 좀 softens the ask between friends — banmal 부탁해 is casual but warm

examples.en: I was busy, so I asked my sibling to do the dishes.
examples.note: Everyday: the task (설거지를) + the person (동생에게) both appear

examples.ko: 부탁이 하나 있는데, 들어주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: butagi hana inneunde, deureojusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I have a favor to ask — could you grant it?
examples.note: Real situation: the polite framing 부탁이 있는데 sets up a request before stating it

words.nuance: 부탁하다 is 付託(부탁)하다, hanja 付 'hand over' + 託 'entrust', so the image is entrusting a task into someone's hands — you are asking them to do something FOR you, leaning on their goodwill. Contrast it sharply with 요청하다 and 시키다: 부탁하다 is personal and humble (you owe a thank-you), 요청하다 is formal/institutional (자료를 요청하다 'request documents'), and 시키다 is to MAKE/order someone do it from a position of authority — never use 시키다 with someone older or you sound bossy. The famous phrase 잘 부탁합니다 has no clean English equivalent; it pre-thanks someone for the cooperation you're about to receive and is near-mandatory in introductions. English speakers misfire two ways: they try to use 부탁하다 to order food or goods (that is 주문하다), and they attach the favor with the wrong particle — the person is 에게/한테, and the favor itself, if stated, is the object: 친구에게 부탁을 했어요. As a 하다 verb it is fully regular, negating as 부탁 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부탁하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 부탁해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 부탁하다 to order at a restaurant or shop (커피를 부탁해요). Ordering goods is 주문하다 — say 커피를 주문할게요.
Marking the person with 을/를 (친구를 부탁해요 meaning 'ask the friend'). The person asked is 에게/한테: 친구에게 부탁해요. (친구를 부탁해요 instead means 'please look after my friend.')
Swapping in 시키다 to be polite. 시키다 means to order/make someone do it and sounds bossy to elders; humble requests use 부탁하다.

words.shortExplanation: 약속하다 means "to promise" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 약속하다 (yaksokada) = "to promise". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 약속해요 plus one useful sentence like 친구와 약속하다 ("make plans with a friend"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 약속하고 싶어요 for what you want, 약속할 수 있어요 for what you can, 약속 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
와/하고 marks the other party; here 약속 means an appointment to meet

examples.en: I'll definitely come. I promise!
examples.note: Simple: standalone 약속해! as an emphatic vow between friends

examples.en: We promised to meet again next time.
examples.note: Everyday: -기로 약속하다 is the pattern for promising an action

examples.ko: 내일 두 시에 약속이 있어서 못 가요.
examples.romanization: naeil du sie yaksogi isseoseo mot gayo.
examples.en: I have an appointment at two tomorrow, so I can't go.
examples.note: Real situation: here the noun 약속 means a scheduled meet-up, not a vow

words.nuance: 약속하다 is 約束(약속)하다, hanja 約 'bind/pact' + 束 'tie up' — literally to 'bind and tie,' a vivid image of two people lashing their word together. The crucial thing for learners is that the noun 약속 carries TWO meanings that English splits: a 'promise' (a vow) and an 'appointment/plans' (a scheduled meeting). 친구와 약속이 있어요 means 'I have plans with a friend,' not 'I made a vow.' Contrast 약속하다 with 예약하다: 약속하다 is a person-to-person agreement to meet or to do something, while 예약하다 is to RESERVE a slot from a business (식당을 예약하다 'book a restaurant') — never say 식당을 약속하다. To promise an action, Koreans don't use the infinitive as in English ('promise to come'); they nominalize with -기로: 오기로 약속했어요. The verb honoring it is 지키다 (지키다, 'guard'), and breaking it is 어기다, so memorize 약속을 지키다/어기다 as a fixed pair. It is a regular 하다 verb (약속 + 해요), negating as 약속 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 약속하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 약속해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 약속하다 to reserve a table or hotel (식당을 약속해요). Booking a business slot is 예약하다 — say 식당을 예약했어요.
Copying English 'promise to come' as 오는 것을 약속해요. Korean nominalizes the action with -기로: 오기로 약속했어요.
Saying 약속을 지지 않다 or inventing a verb for 'break a promise.' Keep means 지키다, break means 어기다: 약속을 어겼어요.

words.shortExplanation: 소개하다 means "to introduce" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 소개하다 (sogaehada) means "to introduce". Start from the polite form 소개해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 소개하다. A strong first sentence is A를 B에게 소개하다 ("introduce A to B"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 소개하다 also becomes 소개하고 싶어요 (want), 소개할 수 있어요 (can), and 소개 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The person introduced is 을/를; the recipient is 에게/한테

examples.en: This is my friend. Let me introduce you.
examples.note: Simple: 소개할게요 (I'll introduce) used at the moment of presenting someone

examples.en: I introduced my boyfriend to my parents.
examples.note: Everyday: 을/를 for the person shown, 께 (honorific) for the parents who receive

examples.ko: 좋은 책 좀 소개해 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: joeun chaek jom sogaehae jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: Could you recommend a good book?
examples.note: Real situation: 소개하다 stretched to 'recommend' — common for books, shops, apps

words.nuance: 소개하다 is 紹介(소개)하다, hanja 紹 'connect/join' + 介 'go between', so the core sense is acting as a go-between who connects two parties — you present a person to someone else, or by extension present a place/product to an audience (recommend it). Watch the dual particle frame: the person or thing introduced takes 을/를, and the recipient takes 에게/한테 (honorific 께): 친구를 선생님께 소개했어요. Contrast 소개하다 with 추천하다: when recommending, 소개하다 means 'let me present/show you this option' (neutral introduction), while 추천하다 carries a stronger personal endorsement ('I vouch for it'). For introducing yourself, do not say 저를 소개해요 — Korean uses the set noun 자기소개를 하다. A culturally loaded offshoot is 소개팅 (소개 + meeting), being set up on a blind date by a mutual friend. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto 'meet' or 'greet': you 소개하다 (present) someone, but you 만나다 (meet) them and 인사하다 (greet) them — three different verbs. Regular 하다 verb: 소개 + 해요, negative 소개 안 해요.

Use 소개해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저를 소개할게요 for 'I'll introduce myself.' Use the fixed noun: 자기소개를 할게요 or 제 소개를 할게요.
Dropping the recipient particle or using 을/를 on both. The recipient is 에게/한테/께: 친구를 부모님께 소개했어요.
Confusing 소개하다 (present someone) with 만나다 (meet) or 인사하다 (greet) — introducing is not the same as meeting or saying hello.

words.shortExplanation: 설명하다 means "to explain" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to explain" in Korean is 설명하다 (seolmyeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 설명해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 설명하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이유를 설명하다 ("explain the reason") — then reshape the same stem into 설명하고 싶어요 (desire), 설명할 수 있어요 (ability), and 설명 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The thing explained takes 을/를: 이유를 설명해요

examples.en: How do I do this? Explain it to me.
examples.note: Simple: casual 설명해 줘 — asking a friend to walk you through something

examples.en: The teacher explained the grammar to us simply.
examples.note: Everyday: -아 주시다 shows the explaining was done as a favor by a senior

examples.en: Could you explain in detail why you were late?
examples.note: Real situation: -는지 embeds the question being explained; 자세히 = in detail

words.nuance: 설명하다 is 說明(설명)하다, hanja 說 'speak' + 明 'bright/clear', so it literally means to 'speak something into clarity' — you talk about a thing so the listener understands it. The dividing line against 설득하다 and 말하다 matters: 설명하다 is to make something UNDERSTOOD (neutral, informational), 설득하다 is to PERSUADE (change someone's mind), and 말하다 is just to 'say/tell' without the goal of clarifying. words.shortExplanation: 이야기하다 means "to talk" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
와/하고 marks the conversation partner; this is two-way chatting

examples.en: Let's talk later.
examples.note: Simple: contracted 얘기해 in banmal — exactly how friends actually speak

examples.en: I talked a lot with my family over the weekend.
examples.note: Everyday: 하고 = with; 많이 modifies the amount of talking

words.nuance: 이야기하다 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) built from the noun 이야기 'a story/talk' + 하다, so at heart it means to exchange talk — to chat, converse, or tell about something. So 친구와 이야기해요 feels friendly and chatty, while 대화해요 feels almost clinical. Massively important for sounding natural: in actual speech 이야기 contracts to 얘기 nearly every time — 얘기 좀 하자, 얘기해 줘. For talking ABOUT a topic, add -에 대해(서): 영화에 대해 이야기했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like one-shot 'tell me' — for a quick fact use 말해 줘, but for 'let's discuss / tell me the whole thing' use 이야기해 줘. It is a regular 하다 verb, negating as 이야기 안 해요.

Use 이야기해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.shortExplanation: 인사하다 means "to greet" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 인사하다 (insahada) means "to greet". Start from the polite form 인사해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 인사하다. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The person greeted takes 에게/한테/께: 선생님께 인사했어요

examples.en: I greeted them, saying "Hello."
examples.note: Simple: the greeting word 안녕하세요 reported with 인사하다

examples.en: The child greeted the adults politely.
examples.note: Everyday: 께 (honorific) + 공손히 (politely) — the respect register Korea expects

examples.ko: 이사 와서 옆집에 가서 인사하고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: isa waseo yeopjibe gaseo insahago wasseoyo.
examples.en: I moved in and went next door to introduce myself / pay my respects.
examples.note: Real situation: 인사하다 covers the courtesy visit to new neighbors

words.nuance: 인사하다 is 人事(인사)하다, hanja 人 'person' + 事 'affair' — literally 'the affairs between people,' which tells you it is broader than English 'greet': it covers saying hello, bowing, saying goodbye, and even paying one's formal respects. The person greeted takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께: 선생님께 인사했어요. Crucial cultural point baked into the verb: Korean greeting is physical and hierarchical — a younger person bows the head (고개를 숙이다) to an elder, and failing to 인사하다 first when meeting someone senior reads as rude. Contrast 인사하다 with 소개하다: greeting is the bow/hello you perform yourself, whereas introducing is presenting a third party. Note that the noun 인사 also means 'personnel/HR affairs' (인사부 = HR department) — same hanja, different sphere. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving out the bow-culture and treating it as a casual 'hi,' and also confusing it with the literal greeting words: 안녕하세요 is WHAT you say, 인사하다 is the act of greeting. It is a regular 하다 verb, negating as 인사 안 해요.

Use 인사해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the person with 을/를 (어른을 인사해요). Use 에게/한테/께: 어른께 인사해요.
Using 인사하다 to mean introducing someone else. To present a third person it's 소개하다; 인사하다 is the greeting itself.

words.shortExplanation: 사과하다 means "to apologize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to apologize" in Korean is 사과하다 (sagwahada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 사과해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 사과하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 친구에게 사과하다 ("apologize to a friend") — then reshape the same stem into 사과하고 싶어요 (desire), 사과할 수 있어요 (ability), and 사과 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The person wronged takes 에게/한테/께: 친구에게 사과했어요

examples.en: I'm sorry, I sincerely apologize.
examples.note: Simple: 사과할게 backs up the casual 미안해 with a fuller apology

examples.en: It was my mistake, so I apologized first.
examples.note: Everyday: -라서 gives the reason; 먼저 = first, taking the initiative

examples.note: Real situation: 공식적으로 (formally) + 습니다 — the register of a public apology

words.nuance: 사과하다 is 謝過(사과)하다, hanja 謝 'express thanks/apology' + 過 'fault/error', so it literally means to 'acknowledge one's fault' — you take responsibility for a mistake to the person you wronged, who is marked with 에게/한테 or honorific 께. The boundary against 미안하다 and 변명하다 is essential: 미안하다 is the adjective/feeling 'to be sorry' (an emotional state — 미안해요), while 사과하다 is the ACT of formally apologizing (you can 사과하다 even publicly or in writing); and 변명하다 is the opposite move, to 'make excuses.' So you might 사과하다 instead of merely feeling 미안하다. The cause of the apology attaches with -아서: 늦어서 사과했어요. A notorious trap is the homograph: 사과 also means 'apple' (native-Korean noun), so context disambiguates 사과를 했어요 'apologized' from 사과를 먹었어요 'ate an apple' — they share spelling but are unrelated words. words.shortExplanation: 초대하다 means "to invite" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 초대하다 (chodaehada) = "to invite". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 초대해요 plus one useful sentence like 친구를 집에 초대하다 ("invite a friend home"). Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Come to my birthday too. I'm inviting you!
examples.note: Simple: casual 초대할게 — the moment of inviting a friend

examples.en: I invited my coworkers to the housewarming.
examples.note: Everyday: the guests (동료들을) + the event (집들이에) in the standard frame

examples.en: We courteously invite you to our wedding.

words.nuance: 초대하다 is 招待(초대)하다, hanja 招 'beckon/summon' + 待 'receive/treat', so the image is beckoning someone over AND hosting them — inviting a guest to an event or your home with the intent to welcome and entertain them. The guest takes 을/를 and the event/place takes 에: 친구를 파티에 초대했어요. The sharp contrast is with 부르다: 초대하다 is a warm, planned invitation to a social occasion (you'll host them), whereas 부르다 is simply to 'call' someone over (call their name, summon them) with no hosting connotation — so 친구를 불렀어요 just means 'I called my friend over,' not 'I invited them to an event.' Using 부르다 where you mean a gracious invite sounds abrupt. Note the related noun 초대장 (invitation card) and the host's courtesy verb 모시다 for elevating an honored guest. The English-speaker pitfall is using 초대하다 for 'invite' in the loose sense of 'ask someone to come along casually' (that's closer to 같이 가자/오라고 하다), and forgetting that the EVENT is 에 while the guest is 을/를. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Well done! I praised them, saying they did great.
examples.note: Simple: -다고 reports the praising words

examples.en: The teacher praised my presentation.
examples.note: Everyday: 을/를 for what's praised, -아 주시다 marks it as kindness from a senior

examples.en: The more a child is praised, the better they do.
examples.note: Real situation: passive 칭찬을 받다 + -ㄹ수록 'the more...'

words.nuance: 칭찬하다 is 稱讚(칭찬)하다, hanja 稱 'state/declare' + 讚 'extol', so it means to openly declare someone's merit — to praise or commend a person for good work, effort, or behavior, with the person taking 을/를. The vital contrast is against 자랑하다: 칭찬하다 is praising SOMEONE ELSE for THEIR good qualities (외부를 향한 칭찬), whereas 자랑하다 is boasting about YOURSELF or your own things (자기 자랑). words.shortExplanation: 거짓말하다 means "to lie" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: Don't lie.
examples.note: Simple: blunt banmal prohibition — said when you catch someone fibbing

examples.en: My sibling lied to Mom.
examples.note: Everyday: 한테 (casual 'to') marks who was lied to

examples.ko: 그 사람은 눈 하나 깜짝 안 하고 거짓말해요.

words.nuance: 거짓말하다 is a native Korean compound: 거짓 'false' + 말 'speech/words' = 'false words,' plus 하다 — so it transparently means 'to do false-speech,' i.e. to tell a lie. Contrast it with 속이다 and 농담하다: 거짓말하다 is the act of stating an untruth (the words themselves are false), 속이다 is 'to deceive/trick' (to fool someone, broader than just words — you can 속이다 with actions), and 농담하다 is 'to joke,' which is harmless and not meant to be believed. Calling a joke a 거짓말 sounds like an accusation. A natural intensifier is 새빨간 거짓말 ('a bright-red lie' = a barefaced lie). The English-speaker pitfall is the reflex 'lie about something' — Korean doesn't take 'about' here; you simply 거짓말하다 and add context separately, or use 거짓말로 ... 하다. Also note English 'lie' looks intransitive but Korean often makes the lie an explicit object: 거짓말을 하다. It is a regular 하다 verb.

Using 속이다 and 거짓말하다 interchangeably. 거짓말하다 is about false words; 속이다 is to deceive/trick someone (possibly by actions).
Marking the listener with 을/를. The person lied to is 에게/한테: 친구한테 거짓말했어요, not 친구를 거짓말했어요.

usagePhrases.en: I do not ask a question.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to ask a question.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

examples.en: May I ask one question?
examples.note: Simple: the polite opener for raising a hand in class

words.nuance: 질문하다 is 質問(질문)하다, hanja 質 'inquire into substance' + 問 'ask', so it means to pose a question in order to obtain information — and the person asked takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께: 선생님께 질문했어요. The boundary against 묻다 is the one to nail: 질문하다 and 묻다 both mean 'ask,' but 질문하다 is the heavier Sino-Korean word for a deliberate, often public question (in class, a meeting, a Q&A), while 묻다 is the plain everyday verb for asking a quick thing ('let me ask you something' = 뭐 좀 물어볼게요). words.shortExplanation: 돌아가다 means "to go back" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 돌아가다 (doraga-da) means "to go back". Start from the polite form 돌아가요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 돌아가다. A strong first sentence is 집에 돌아가요 ("I go back home."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 돌아가다 also becomes 돌아가고 싶어요 (want), 돌아갈 수 있어요 (can), and 못 돌아가요 (cannot). Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Destination of return takes 에

examples.note: The 가 stem swallows the 아 ending, so it's 돌아가요, never 돌아가아요.

examples.en: I'm so tired I want to go back to the hotel.

words.nuance: 돌아가다 is literally 돌아(turn around) + 가다(go), so it paints you turning back and heading AWAY from the listener toward your origin — home, your country, a former state. The razor-sharp contrast is with 돌아오다(come back): direction is fixed by the speaker's standpoint, exactly like English go vs come, so a tourist phoning home says 한국에 돌아갈 거예요 (going back, away from here), but once landed says 집에 돌아왔어요 (came back). commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌아가다 as a complete polite sentence.

Writing 돌아가아요 by adding the full 아요 ending — the 가 stem already ends in ㅏ, so it contracts to 돌아가요.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: 출발 + 하다, and 하 + 아 always fuses to 해, giving 출발해요.
