words.nuance: 출발하다 is Sino-Korean 出發(출발: 出 go out + 發 set off/shoot) plus 하다, the crisp word for a journey or vehicle SETTING OFF from a starting line. Contrast it with 떠나다(leave): 출발하다 is neutral and logistical, fixed on the departure point and time (기차가 출발하다), so a station announcer uses it; 떠나다 carries the emotional weight of leaving something or someone behind. The starting place takes 에서 (부산에서 출발해요) and the time takes 에 (3시에 출발해요). Because it's a 하다 verb the stem 하 + 아 fuses to 해, so present is 출발해요 and the negative splits as 출발 안 해요. usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

examples.note: Arrival point 역 takes 에; 도착 + 하 + 았 → 도착했어요.

words.nuance: 도착하다 is Sino-Korean 到着(도착: 到 reach + 着 attach/touch down) plus 하다 — the moment of REACHING and touching a destination. Its mirror is 출발하다(depart), and the key is the particle: you arrive AT a place with 에 (호텔에 도착해요), whereas 출발하다 leaves FROM a place with 에서. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: I'm leaving tomorrow.
examples.note: 나 + 아 contracts, so it's 떠나요, never 떠나아요.

examples.en: I want to get away from the busy city for a while.
examples.note: The place left takes 를; 고 싶어요 adds the wish.

words.nuance: 떠나다 means to LEAVE a place, person, or situation behind, and unlike neutral 출발하다(depart) it carries feeling — separation, finality, the pull of moving on, which is why songs and goodbyes use it (곁을 떠나다 leave someone's side). words.shortExplanation: 멈추다 means "to stop" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to stop" in Korean is 멈추다 (meomchu-da). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Works for a vehicle halting on its own

examples.en: The car stopped all of a sudden.
examples.note: 추 + 어 fuses to 춰, so past is 멈췄어요.

examples.en: Please pull over briefly just ahead.
examples.note: 춰 주세요 politely asks the driver to halt.

examples.en: It's a red light, so we have to stop here.
examples.note: 니까 gives the reason; 야 해요 = must.

words.nuance: 멈추다 means coming to a HALT — ceasing motion that was underway — and it covers a person freezing, a car braking, the rain letting up, even a clock stopping (시계가 멈췄어요). The fine contrast is with 서다: 서다 emphasizes the final standing-still snapshot (차가 섰다), while 멈추다 highlights the act of arresting the movement; in daily speech they overlap heavily for vehicles. Keep it apart from 그만두다(quit), which abandons an activity or job permanently — you 멈추다 your steps but 그만두다 your job. It also has a transitive use, to stop something: 울음을 멈추다 (stop crying). Use 멈춰요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.shortExplanation: 움직이다 means "to move" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.note: 못 + 움직여요 expresses physical inability.

examples.en: Don't move while I take the photo.
examples.note: 지 마세요 asks someone to hold still.

examples.note: 조심히 = carefully; 야 해요 = must.

words.nuance: 움직이다 is the broad word for MOVING or shifting position, and its range is wide: your own body (몸을 움직이다), a crowd inching forward, an object that budges, even an abstract heart being moved (마음이 움직이다 = to be swayed). Contrast it with 이사하다(move house), the Sino-Korean 移徙 word reserved for relocating your home — English 'move' covers both, but Korean splits them, so 'I'm moving next month' is 이사해요, never 움직여요. It's a regular 이-stem verb: 이 + 어 fuses to 여, giving 움직여요 and 움직였어요. Pitfall: don't use it for changing residence.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 움직이다 as a complete polite sentence.

Writing 움직이어요 in full — the 이 stem plus 어 contracts to 여, so it's 움직여요 and past 움직였어요.

words.shortExplanation: 건너다 means "to cross" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The road crossed takes 을/를

examples.en: We cross the street here.
examples.note: 너 + 어 contracts, so it's 건너요, never 건너어요.

examples.en: You must cross when the light is green.

words.nuance: 건너다 means crossing FROM one side TO the other — a street, a river, a bridge, the sea — picturing the whole traverse from edge to edge. The road or water you cross takes the object particle 을/를 (길을 건너요), which surprises English speakers who expect 'across' to be adverbial. The sharp contrast is with 넘다(go over): 넘다 stresses surmounting a high obstacle or boundary, going OVER a mountain pass, a wall, even a limit (산을 넘다, 한계를 넘다), whereas 건너다 is the flat side-to-side passage of a road or river. Using 넘다 for crossing a flat street (길을 넘어요). 넘다 means going over a height or limit; an ordinary road or river is 건너다.
Writing 건너어요 with the full ending — the ㅓ-final stem contracts, so the present is 건너요 and the past is 건넜어요.

words.shortExplanation: 지나가다 means "to pass by" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: I pass in front of the bank.
usagePhrases.note: 앞을 지나가다 = pass in front of, with 을

examples.en: The bus just went by.
examples.note: 지나가 + 았 → 지나갔어요; 가 stem contracts.

examples.en: Excuse me, please let me through.
examples.note: 지나가 주세요 politely asks for room to pass.

examples.en: Go past this alley and you'll hit the market.
examples.note: 면 = if/when; handy for directions.

words.nuance: 지나가다 is 지나(pass) + 가다(go) — moving PAST a point and continuing on, AWAY from the listener, without stopping; a bus goes by, you slip past someone, a season passes (여름이 지나가다). Distinguish it from plain 지나다, which leans toward time ELAPSING (3년이 지났어요, three years passed) and is less about physical motion through space. Its pair 지나오다 adds the come-this-way direction. words.shortExplanation: 따라가다 means "to follow" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 따라가다 (ttaraga-da) = "to follow". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 따라가요 plus one useful sentence like 가이드를 따라가요 ("I follow the guide."). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: I'll just follow along.
examples.note: ㄹ게요 states your own intention to tag along.

examples.en: I don't know the way, so I have to follow the guide.
examples.note: Person followed takes 를; 야 해요 = must.

examples.en: My leg hurts, so I can't keep up.

words.nuance: 따라가다 is 따라(along/following) + 가다(go) — going ALONG behind someone or something, moving in the same direction AWAY from the listener; you trail a guide, tag after a friend, or figuratively 'keep up' (못 따라가요, can't keep pace). Its essential pair is 따라오다(come along/follow toward me): a leader walking ahead says 따라오세요 (follow me, toward where I'm going), but you describing yourself trailing them say 따라가요. The person or thing followed takes 을/를, not 에게 — a frequent English-speaker slip, since 'follow' feels like motion 'to' someone. Note 따라가다 is a 가다 compound, so despite the 라 it is NOT a 르-irregular; it conjugates regularly and 가 + 아 contracts to 가, giving 따라가요. It can also mean to copy/imitate (잘 따라 하다). Pitfall: don't mark the followed person with 에게.

Use 따라가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the person followed with 에게/한테 (친구에게 따라가요). The one you follow is a direct object: 친구를 따라가요.
Saying 따라오세요 when you mean to tell someone you'll go after them — from your viewpoint you move away, so it's 제가 따라갈게요; 따라오다 is for motion toward the speaker.
Over-applying 르 irregular logic to the 라 (expecting 따랄라 forms). 따라가다 is a compound of 가다 and conjugates regularly: 따라가요, 따라갔어요.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 따라가다 becomes 따라갈 수 있어요 ("can") and 따라갈 거예요 ("will"). The person followed takes 을/를, not 에게 — a frequent slip, since 'follow' feels like motion 'to' someone. Don't mark the followed person with 에게.

words.shortExplanation: 데려가다 means "to take a person" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 데려가다 (deryeoga-da) means "to take a person". Start from the polite form 데려가요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 데려가다. A strong first sentence is 아이를 데려가요 ("I take the child along."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 데려가다 also becomes 데려가고 싶어요 (want), 데려갈 수 있어요 (can), and 못 데려가요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take a person.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to take a person.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to take a person.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

examples.ko: 저도 그 식당에 좀 데려가 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeodo geu sikdange jom deryeoga juseyo.
examples.en: Please take me to that restaurant too.
examples.note: 데려가 주세요 asks to be brought along; 에 marks where.

examples.en: I take my child to school.
examples.note: Person 아이 takes 를, destination 학교 takes 에.

examples.en: I want to take my parents to the sea this weekend.
examples.note: 데려가다 for people; 가져가다 would be wrong here.

words.nuance: 데려가다 is 데리다(accompany) + 가다(go) — taking a PERSON or animal along with you, moving AWAY from the listener to another place; you take a child to school, a friend to a restaurant, a dog to the vet. The crucial split is animacy: 데려가다 is ONLY for living beings, while 가져가다 is for objects — English 'take' blurs them, so 'take the kids' is 아이들을 데려가요 but 'take the bags' is 가방을 가져가요. Its directional pair is 데려오다(bring a person toward me). For someone older or deserving respect, the politer 모시고 가다 is used instead of 데려가다 (할머니를 모시고 가요). The person takes 을/를 and the destination 에. As a 가다 compound it conjugates regularly (데려가요, 데려갔어요). Related 데려다주다 means to escort/drop someone off. Pitfall: never use 데려가다 for things.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데려가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데려가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데려가다 for objects (우산을 데려가요). Living beings use 데려가다; for an umbrella or any thing use 가져가다.

Picking 데려오다 when the motion is away from you — taking someone elsewhere from here is 데려가요; 데려오다 is bringing a person toward your location.

words.shortExplanation: 가져가다 means "to take a thing" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to take a thing" in Korean is 가져가다 (gajyeoga-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 가져가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 가져가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 우산을 가져가요 ("I take an umbrella.") — then reshape the same stem into 가져가고 싶어요 (desire), 가져갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 가져가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.en: It's raining, so I should take an umbrella.
examples.note: Thing 우산 takes 를; 야 해요 = must.

examples.en: Can I take the leftovers home?
examples.note: 도 돼요 politely asks permission.

words.nuance: 가져가다 is 가지다(have/hold) + 가다(go) — taking an OBJECT away with you to another place, moving AWAY from the listener; you take an umbrella, a passport, leftovers. The animacy split is the heart of it: 가져가다 is strictly for things, while 데려가다 is for people and animals — since English 'take' covers both, learners wrongly say 가져가다 about a child. Its directional pair is 가져오다(bring a thing toward me): leaving the house you 우산을 가져가요, but asking a waiter you say 메뉴판 가져와 주세요. The object takes 을/를 and the destination 에. As a 가다 compound it's regular: 가 + 아 contracts, giving 가져가요 and 가져갔어요. Casual speech often shortens 가지고 to 갖고, and 가지고 가다 = 가져가다. Pitfall: don't use it for people, and don't flip the direction with 가져오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가져가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가져가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 가져가다 for a person or pet (동생을 가져가요). Things use 가져가다; people and animals use 데려가다: 동생을 데려가요.
Choosing 가져오다 when the motion is away from you — carrying something off from here is 가져가요; 가져오다 brings a thing toward where you are.
Writing it long as 가지어 가요 — the contracted compound is 가져가다 (가져가요), and the casual variant is 갖고 가요.

words.shortExplanation: 가져오다 means "to bring a thing" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 가져오다 (gajyeoo-da) = "to bring a thing". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 가져와요 plus one useful sentence like 물 좀 가져와요 ("Bring some water."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 가져오고 싶어요 for what you want, 가져올 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 가져와요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

examples.note: 오 + 아 fuses to 와, so it's 가져와요, never 가져오아요.

examples.en: Could you bring the menu, please?
examples.note: 와 주세요 is the standard polite 'please bring' in a café.

examples.en: I'm worried because I didn't bring my passport.
examples.note: 안 가져오다 negates; 아서 gives the reason.

words.nuance: 가져오다 is 가지다(have/hold) + 오다(come) — bringing an OBJECT TOWARD the speaker's location, the mirror image of 가져가다(take away): here it points HERE, there it points away, exactly like English bring vs take keyed to where 'here' is. So in a restaurant you ask 메뉴판 가져와 주세요 (bring it to me), but leaving home you say 우산을 가져가요 (take it with me, away). The animacy rule still holds: things use 가져오다, whereas bringing a PERSON toward you is 데려오다 (아이를 데려와요). Figuratively it means to bring about (변화를 가져오다, bring about change). The object takes 을/를, often dropped in casual speech. As an 오다 compound it's regular and 오 + 아 fuses to 와, giving 가져와요 and 가져왔어요. Pitfall: don't aim the direction wrong with 가져가다, and don't use it for people.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가져오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가져와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 가져가다 when something should come toward you — asking a waiter for water is 물 가져와 주세요 (bring it here); 가져가다 would send it away.
Using 가져오다 for a person (친구를 가져왔어요). Bringing a living being toward you is 데려오다: 친구를 데려왔어요.
Writing 가져오아요 with the full ending — the 오 stem plus 아 fuses to 와, so the present is 가져와요 and the past is 가져왔어요.

words.shortExplanation: 이해하다 means "to understand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 이해하다 (ihaehada) means "to understand". Start from the polite form 이해해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 이해하다. A strong first sentence is 이해해요 ("I understand"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Warm reassuring reply, like 'I get it, it's okay'

examples.note: Object + 를 when YOU actively grasp something

words.nuance: 이해하다 is Sino-Korean: 理解 means 'untie/loosen (解) the logic (理)', so it pictures a tangled idea coming apart in your head — it covers both intellectual comprehension AND emotional sympathy ('I understand how you feel'). The dividing line versus 알다 is crucial: 알다 is to KNOW a fact ('I know his name', 이름을 알아요), while 이해하다 is to make sense of WHY or HOW something works. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (이해해요, past 이해했어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle in the negative: 'I don't understand' is almost always 이해가 안 돼요 (subject 가 + 되다, lit. 'understanding doesn't form'), not the literal 이해를 안 해요, which sounds like you're refusing to understand on purpose. Also resist translating 'understand my feelings' as 내 감정 — Koreans say 내 마음을 이해하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이해하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이해해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 알아요 when you mean 'I grasp/follow it' — 알다 is to know a fact, 이해하다 is to comprehend the reasoning; for 'I get why' use 이해해요.
Translating 'I don't understand' literally as 이해를 안 해요. That implies willful refusal. The natural form is 이해가 안 돼요 with 가, treating understanding as something that fails to occur.
Saying 내 감정을 이해해 주세요 for 'understand my feelings'. The idiomatic collocation is 마음 (heart): 내 마음을 이해해 주세요.

words.shortExplanation: 믿다 means "to believe" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

words.nuance: 믿다 is a single native word that spans two English verbs at once: to BELIEVE a fact/claim (그 말을 믿어요 'I believe that') and to TRUST a person (친구를 믿어요 'I trust my friend') — context, not a different word, tells them apart. The closest relatives are 믿음 (the noun, 'faith/trust') and the compound 신뢰하다 (信賴, the formal 'to have confidence in', used in business or writing); 믿다 is the warm, everyday spoken choice. Crucially, 믿다 keeps its ㄷ in the stem (믿어요, 믿었어요) — it is NOT a ㄷ-irregular like 듣다→들어요, so it never becomes *밀어요. Watch the homophone trap: that wrong *밀어요 collides head-on with the real verb 밀다 'to push' (밀어요), so one careless slip doesn't just misconjugate — it accidentally says 'push' instead of 'believe'. English 'believe in (a god/religion)' transfers fine: 신을 믿어요, 종교를 믿어요.

Use 믿어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it like a ㄷ-irregular and changing ㄷ→ㄹ: *밀어요. 믿다 is regular, so the stem ㄷ stays put — 믿어요, past 믿었어요. (듣다 does change: 듣다→들어요, but 믿다 does not.)
Confusing 믿다 (believe, 믿어요) with the look-alike 밀다 (push, 밀어요). They share a frame but are unrelated verbs — keep the ㄷ in 믿어요, or you literally say 'push'.
Using formal 신뢰하다 in casual speech with friends. Among friends, 너를 믿어 sounds natural; 너를 신뢰해 sounds like a corporate report.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 바라고 싶어요 for what you want, 바랄 수 있어요 for what you can, 바랄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.

examples.en: I hope for a good result
examples.note: Noun + 를; hoping for an outcome

examples.en: I hoped you'd recover soon
examples.note: Verb + 기를 바라다 = hope an action happens

examples.en: I hope things go well for you
examples.note: Casual; 잘되길 is 잘되기를 shortened in speech

words.nuance: 바라다 is to HOPE or WISH FOR something, especially good things for other people, which gives it a warmer, more selfless feel than 원하다 ('to want' for yourself). The sharp contrast learners need: 바라다 leans toward outcomes beyond your control that you wish would happen (평화를 바라요 'I hope for peace'), while 원하다 names a concrete desire you intend to get (돈을 원해요 'I want money'). Its signature grammar is verb-기를 바라다 ('I hope that ~ happens'): 합격하기를 바라요. THE famous pitfall: the present polite form is 바라요, but almost every Korean accidentally says/writes 바래요 — that 바래다 actually means 'to fade in color'! The textbook-correct form is 바라요 / past 바랐어요, even though 바래요 dominates casual texting. Don't confuse 바라다 (hope) with 바라보다 (to gaze at).

Use 바라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the polite form as 바래요. That belongs to 바래다 'to fade/discolor'. The standard form of 바라다 is 바라요, and the past is 바랐어요, not 바랬어요.
Using 바라다 for a selfish concrete want like 'I want this phone'. For tangible personal desires use 원하다 (이 폰을 원해요); 바라다 fits wishes for good outcomes, often for others.
Forgetting the 기를 frame for events: saying 빨리 낫고 바라요. The correct nominalizer is 낫기를 바라요 ('I hope you get well').

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

words.shortExplanation: 원하다 means "to want" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 원하다 (wonhada) means "to want". Start from the polite form 원해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 원하다. A strong first sentence is 뭘 원해요? ("What do you want?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 원하다 also becomes 원하고 싶어요 (want), 원할 수 있어요 (can), and 원할 수 없어요 (cannot). words.nuance: 원하다 is Sino-Korean (願 'wish/desire' + 하다) and means to WANT a thing or outcome — it takes a NOUN object (커피를 원해요 'I want coffee'). The critical contrast for English speakers is with -고 싶다: to want to DO an action, you cannot use 원하다, you must use the verb stem + 고 싶다 (가고 싶어요 'I want to go'), never 가는 것을 원해요, which sounds stiff and translated. Compared with 바라다 ('hope'), 원하다 is more direct, concrete, and self-centered — a desire you mean to fulfill, not a gentle wish. It also feels a touch more formal and forceful than 갖고 싶다 ('want to have'); a waiter or a contract uses 원하다. Pitfall: English 'I want to eat' tempts you to reach for 원하다, but the natural Korean is 먹고 싶어요. Reserve 원하다 for noun objects.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 원하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 원해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 원하다 to want an ACTION: 가는 것을 원해요 for 'I want to go'. Korean uses verb + 고 싶다 instead: 가고 싶어요.

words.shortExplanation: 걱정하다 means "to worry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to worry" in Korean is 걱정하다 (geokjeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 걱정해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 걱정하다 for study notes. examples.note: Person worried about + 를

words.nuance: 걱정하다 (걱정 = 'worry/anxiety' + 하다) is the everyday verb for being anxious or concerned about someone or something. Distinguish it sharply from 고민하다: 걱정하다 is feeling ANXIOUS about how things will turn out ('I'm worried about my grades'), whereas 고민하다 is actively DELIBERATING over a hard choice ('I'm agonizing over which job to take'). As a 하다-verb it splits in the negative — 걱정 안 해요 (separating the noun) or 걱정하지 않아요 — and the favor form 걱정해 주다 means 'to worry on someone's behalf', a kind gesture. The natural way to say 'I feel worried' is 걱정이 돼요 (걱정 + 이 + 되다), not 걱정을 해요, which sounds like deliberate worrying. The single most useful phrase in the whole language family is 걱정하지 마세요 ('don't worry') — memorize it. English 'I'm worried about you' is 네가 걱정돼 or 너를 걱정해, not 너에 대해 걱정해.

Use 걱정해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 걱정을 해요 for the feeling 'I'm worried'. Korean prefers 걱정이 돼요 (worry arises) for the spontaneous emotion.
Confusing 걱정하다 (anxious feeling) with 고민하다 (mulling over a decision). 'Worried about the result' = 결과를 걱정해요; 'agonizing over the choice' = 선택을 고민해요.
Over-attaching ~에 대해: 너에 대해 걱정해요. Natural Korean is 너를 걱정해요 or 네가 걱정돼요.

Short everyday negative.

Ability or possibility.

words.nuance: 놀라다 is to BE SURPRISED, STARTLED, or SHOCKED — a sudden involuntary reaction, so it lives mostly in the past tense (놀랐어요 'I was surprised') because by the time you speak, the jolt already happened. Although it ends in 라, it is NOT a 르-irregular like 빠르다→빨라요; it conjugates straightforwardly: 놀라 + 았어요 → 놀랐어요. The cause of the surprise takes the particle 에 (가격에 놀랐어요 'surprised at the price') or the connector -고 (듣고 놀랐어요 'heard and was surprised'). Distinguish it from 놀다 'to play' — one extra ㄹ-syllable apart but utterly different. Its constant companion is the mimetic word 깜짝 ('with a start'): 깜짝 놀랐어요 is the default phrase. To say something IS surprising/amazing, switch to the adjective 놀랍다 (놀라워요). English speakers wrongly mark the cause with 를; remember the trigger gets 에, not the object particle.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놀라다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놀라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the cause with 를: 가격을 놀랐어요. The thing that surprises you takes 에 — 가격에 놀랐어요 — because 놀라다 is intransitive.
Using the present 놀라요 for a past shock. Since surprise is instantaneous, use the past: 놀랐어요 ('I was surprised').
Mixing up 놀라다 (be surprised, 놀라요) with 놀다 (to play, 놀아요). To say something is amazing, use the adjective 놀랍다 → 놀라워요.

A strong first sentence is 주말을 즐겨요 ("I enjoy the weekend"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Ability or possibility.

words.nuance: 즐기다 means to ENJOY in the sense of actively savoring or relishing an activity — it is more deliberate and engaged than 좋아하다 ('to like'). The sharp distinction: 좋아하다 states a preference ('I like coffee', 커피를 좋아해요) and can apply to people you fancy, while 즐기다 means you actively partake in and take pleasure FROM something (커피를 즐겨요 'I enjoy/savor coffee', as a hobby or ritual). A very useful construction is 즐겨 + verb, meaning 'to habitually do X with pleasure': 즐겨 보다 ('enjoy watching, watch regularly'), 즐겨 듣다 ('enjoy listening to'). The biggest pitfall is English 'Enjoy your meal!' — do NOT say 식사를 즐기세요; the idiomatic phrase is 맛있게 드세요/잡수세요 ('eat deliciously'). Also note 즐기다 takes a noun object with 를, so 'enjoy reading' becomes 독서를 즐기다 or 책 읽는 걸 즐기다, not a bare verb.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 즐기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 즐겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 식사를 즐기세요 for 'Enjoy your meal'. The natural phrase is 맛있게 드세요 (or 맛있게 잡수세요 to elders); 즐기다 isn't used as a meal greeting.
Treating 즐기다 and 좋아하다 as identical. 좋아하다 = like/prefer (and is used for crushes); 즐기다 = actively savor an activity. 'I like you' is 좋아해요, never 즐겨요.
Attaching a bare verb: 읽다를 즐겨요. Nominalize first — 읽는 걸 즐겨요 or 독서를 즐겨요 ('enjoy reading').

words.shortExplanation: 후회하다 means "to regret" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to regret" in Korean is 후회하다 (huhoehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 후회해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 후회하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 후회 안 해요 ("I have no regrets") — then reshape the same stem into 후회하고 싶어요 (desire), 후회할 수 있어요 (ability), and 후회할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Firm, often defiant statement (noun split by 안)

examples.en: I regret that choice
examples.note: Object + 를; the thing you regret

examples.note: -아서 gives the reason for the regret

words.nuance: 후회하다 is Sino-Korean — 後悔 literally stacks 後 'after' + 悔 'regret/remorse', i.e. the regret that comes AFTER the deed — and names the painful wish that you had chosen differently. It typically points backward (그 결정을 후회해요 'I regret that decision') and frequently pairs with a reason clause in -아서/어서 or with a past-action nominalizer -(으)ㄴ 걸: 그렇게 말한 걸 후회해. Distinguish it from 아쉽다, which is a milder 'it's a shame / I wish it were a bit different' about things often outside your control, whereas 후회하다 carries genuine self-reproach over your own past action. Also separate it from 미안하다 ('to be sorry' TO someone) — 후회하다 is regret felt inside, not an apology directed at another person. Pitfall: 'I regret to inform you' has no 후회하다 equivalent; that polite-letter formula becomes 안타깝게도 or 죄송하지만. Keep the object with 를, and remember the negative splits as 후회 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 후회하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 후회해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 후회하다 as an apology to someone: 너한테 후회해. To apologize you need 미안하다/죄송하다 (미안해); 후회하다 is internal regret, not 'sorry to you'.
Confusing it with mild 아쉽다. 'It's a shame the trip ended' = 여행이 끝나서 아쉬워요; deep self-blame over your decision = 그 결정을 후회해요.
Saying 후회를 안 해요 awkwardly in speech — fine, but the more idiomatic split is 후회 안 해요, and 'I'll regret it' is 후회할 거예요, not 후회겠어요.

words.nuance: 화내다 literally combines 화 (火, Sino-Korean 'fire' = anger) + 내다 ('to put out, let out'), so it pictures LETTING THE FIRE OUT — to OUTWARDLY SHOW or express anger (raising your voice, scolding). The essential contrast is with 화나다 (화 + 나다 'to arise'): 화나다 is the anger RISING inside you, an involuntary feeling ('I'm angry / I got mad', 화났어요), while 화내다 is the active VENTING of it toward someone ('he got angry at me', 나한테 화냈어요). words.nuance: 무서워하다 is the VERB form built from the adjective 무섭다 ('scary/frightening') plus -어하다, the suffix that turns a feeling-adjective into 'to show/display that feeling'. Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
요리(料理) is the noun 'a dish/cuisine'; 하다 makes it a verb, which is why the negative splits as 요리(를) 안 해요

examples.en: Mom is cooking.
examples.note: Bare subject + verb — the simplest 요-form sentence, built on the stem 요리하 + 여요 → 요리해요

examples.en: On weekends I cook at home myself.
examples.note: 직접 ('in person, oneself') stresses that you do it yourself rather than buying or ordering

examples.en: I am tired today, so I can't cook.

words.nuance: 요리하다 (料理하다, 料 'handle/measure' + 理 'arrange/manage') means to actually prepare a dish — chopping, seasoning, applying heat — so it carries a sense of real cooking, not just touching the stove. Contrast it with 끓이다 ('boil', e.g. 라면을 끓이다 for instant noodles) and 데우다 ('reheat'): a Korean would say 라면을 끓여요, not 라면을 요리해요, because boiling ramyeon barely counts as 요리. words.shortExplanation: 고치다 means "to fix" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
고장 나다 = 'break down'; the broken thing is the object: 시계를 고쳐요

examples.en: I fix the watch.
examples.note: Plain object + verb; stem 고치 + 어요 → 고쳐요 (이+어 contracts to 여)

examples.en: I fixed the broken chair myself.
examples.note: 고장 난 is the past-modifier 'broken'; 고쳤어요 is the past tense

examples.en: Could you fix this bag for me?
examples.note: 좀 softens the request and 고쳐 주세요 asks someone to do it for your benefit

words.nuance: 고치다 is wonderfully broad: it repairs broken objects (자전거를 고치다), corrects mistakes (답을 고치다), reforms bad habits (버릇을 고치다), and even cures illness (병을 고치다) — the unifying idea is 'restore something faulty to a good state'. The sharp line to learn is 고치다 vs 바꾸다: 고치다 keeps the SAME thing and makes it work again, while 바꾸다 swaps it for a DIFFERENT one. If your phone is buggy, 핸드폰을 고쳐요 means repair this phone, but 핸드폰을 바꿔요 means get a new phone. Use 고쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

words.shortExplanation: 바꾸다 means "to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 바꾸다 (bakkuda) means "to change". Start from the polite form 바꿔요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 바꾸다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
for currency exchange Koreans say 돈을 바꾸다 / 환전하다; 달러로 바꿔요 ('change into dollars')

examples.en: I change my name.
examples.note: Simple object + verb; stem 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요 (ㅜ+어 contracts to 워)

examples.en: The size didn't fit, so I exchanged the clothes.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; the target size would take -(으)로

examples.en: Could you switch seats with me?
examples.note: Real request on a train/plane; 바꿔 주세요 asks the other person to do the swap

words.nuance: 바꾸다 means to replace one thing with another, or to alter something into a different state — money (돈을 바꾸다), seats (자리를 바꾸다), plans (계획을 바꾸다), even your mind (마음을 바꾸다). The dividing line from 고치다 is essential: 바꾸다 ends with a DIFFERENT thing, 고치다 keeps the SAME thing repaired. Returning a defective shirt for a new one is 옷을 바꾸다; mending the torn seam is 옷을 고치다. The destination of the change takes the particle -(으)로: 작은 걸로 바꿔 주세요 ('change it for the small one'). Note also 바뀌다, the intransitive twin: 바꾸다 is 'I change X' (transitive, takes 을/를), while 바뀌다 is 'X changes by itself' (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = 'the light changed') — mixing these up is a frequent error. Conjugation is regular: 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요, past 바꿨어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'change my mind' is 마음을 바꾸다, not 생각을 고치다, and 'change clothes (get dressed)' is 옷을 갈아입다, not 옷을 바꾸다.

Use 바꿔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 바꾸다 for repairing — fixing the same broken item is 고치다; 바꾸다 means swapping it for a different one.

words.shortExplanation: 그리다 means "to draw" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to draw" in Korean is 그리다 (geurida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 그려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 그리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 그림을 그리다 ("to draw a picture") — then reshape the same stem into 그리고 싶어요 (desire), 그릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 그려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
the cognate-object pattern: the noun 그림 ('picture') pairs with its verb 그리다 — 그림을 그려요

examples.en: I draw a picture.
examples.note: Core sentence; stem 그리 + 어요 → 그려요 (이+어 contracts to 여)

examples.en: The child drew a puppy.
examples.note: Past tense 그렸어요; the thing drawn takes -을/를

examples.en: Please draw a simple map here.
examples.note: 여기에 marks the surface with -에 ('onto here'); 그려 주세요 requests the favor

words.nuance: 그리다 means to draw or depict by hand — pictures, sketches, lines, maps (그림을 그리다, 약도를 그리다), and figuratively even to picture something in your mind (미래를 그리다, 'envision the future'). Keep it apart from 쓰다, which is 'to write' letters, words, and text: 글씨를 쓰다 vs 그림을 그리다 — Koreans firmly split writing from drawing, whereas English 'draw' and 'write' both involve a pen. Also distinguish 칠하다 ('to color in / paint a surface', 색을 칠하다) and 긋다 ('to rule a straight line', 줄을 긋다, a ㅅ-irregular). 그리다 itself is a regular 이-stem verb: 그리 + 어요 contracts to 그려요, past 그렸어요. Saying 그림을 쓰다 — the fixed pairing is 그림을 그리다 (cognate object); 쓰다 never collocates with 그림.

words.shortExplanation: 부르다 means "to call" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 부르다 (bureuda) = "to call". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 불러요 plus one useful sentence like 택시를 부르다 ("to call a taxi"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
부르다 = summon someone/something to come; 택시를 불러 주세요 ('please call a taxi')

examples.en: I call a taxi.
examples.note: 르-irregular in action: 부르 + 어요 drops ㅡ and doubles ㄹ → 불러요, never 부르어요

examples.ko: 사람이 안 와서 큰 소리로 불렀어요.
examples.romanization: sarami an waseo keun soriro bulleosseoyo.
examples.en: Nobody came, so I called out loudly.
examples.note: 큰 소리로 ('in a loud voice') uses -(으)로 for manner; past 불렀어요

examples.en: Shall we sing a song together?
examples.note: 부를까요? proposes singing; before 을 the stem stays 부르- (no doubling) → 부를

words.nuance: 부르다 chiefly means to call/summon someone to come (택시를 부르다, 친구를 부르다), to call out a name (이름을 부르다), and — a key idiom — to sing (노래를 부르다, the standard phrase, not 노래를 하다). Don't confuse it with 전화하다, which is 'to phone': 친구를 불러요 means call your friend over to where you are, while 친구한테 전화해요 means ring them up. It's a textbook 르-irregular: before an 아/어 ending the final ㅡ drops and an extra ㄹ appears, so 부르 + 어요 → 불러요 and past → 불렀어요, but before consonant endings it stays whole (부르고, 부를 거예요, 부릅니다). Two traps: first, learners say 부르어요 — wrong, it must be 불러요. Second, beware the homonym 부르다 'to be full' (배가 부르다), a completely different adjective; 배가 불러요 means 'I'm full', not 'the stomach calls'. Also note honorific contexts: to summon a superior you'd soften with 모시다 ('escort/bring respectfully') rather than bluntly 부르다.

Use 불러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 부르어요 — 부르다 is 르-irregular, so the 요-form is 불러요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles) and the past is 불렀어요.

words.shortExplanation: 고르다 means "to choose" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 고르다 (goreuda) means "to choose". Start from the polite form 골라요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 고르다. A strong first sentence is 선물을 고르다 ("to pick out a gift"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 고르다 also becomes 고르고 싶어요 (want), 고를 수 있어요 (can), and 못 골라요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
고르다 = pick one from several physical options; 선물을 골라요

examples.en: I choose clothes.
examples.note: 르-irregular: 고르 + 아요 drops ㅡ and doubles ㄹ → 골라요, never 고르아요

examples.en: I picked out pretty clothes at the store.
examples.note: 가게에서 uses -에서 for the place of action; past 골랐어요

examples.en: There are too many kinds, so I can't choose.
examples.note: 못 골라요 ('can't choose'); -아서 expresses the cause

words.nuance: 고르다 means to choose by picking one (or some) out of a concrete set of options laid before you — clothes on a rack, gifts in a shop, items on a menu. The fine line versus 선택하다 (選擇, a Sino-Korean synonym) is register and abstraction: 고르다 is everyday and hands-on ('grab that one'), while 선택하다 is more formal/written and fits weighty or abstract choices (진로를 선택하다, 'choose a career path'). It also differs from 정하다/결정하다 ('decide, settle'): you 골라요 among visible things, but you 정해요 a date or a plan. As a 르-irregular, before 아/어 the ㅡ drops and ㄹ doubles: 고르 + 아요 → 골라요, past 골랐어요; before consonants it's intact (고르고, 고를게요, 고릅니다). The headline pitfall is 고르아요 (wrong) for 골라요. Also, English 'choose to do something' (a course of action) is NOT 고르다 — say -기로 하다/결정하다; 고르다 needs a tangible thing as its object.

Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
머리를 잘라요 means cut your hair (often = get it cut at a salon)

examples.en: I cut the paper.
examples.note: 르-irregular: 자르 + 아요 drops ㅡ and doubles ㄹ → 잘라요, never 자르아요

words.shortExplanation: 정하다 means "to decide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 정하다 (jeonghada) = "to decide". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 정해요 plus one useful sentence like 날짜를 정하다 ("to set a date"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 정하고 싶어요 for what you want, 정할 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 정해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
정하다 fixes a concrete arrangement; 날짜를 정해요 ('let's decide the date')

examples.en: I set the time.
examples.note: Single 하다-verb (no separable noun), so it's regular: 정하 + 여요 → 정해요

examples.en: Let's decide our meeting time first.
examples.note: 먼저 ('first') sequences the action; 만날 is the future-modifier 'to meet'

examples.en: I haven't been able to decide my vacation dates yet.
examples.note: 아직 + past = 'not yet'; 못 정했어요 ('couldn't decide')

words.nuance: 정하다 (定하다, 定 'fix/settle') means to settle on and pin down a choice — a date, place, rule, or one's own mind — turning something open into something fixed. Its close synonym 결정하다 (決定, 'decide') leans more formal and weightier (회의에서 결정했어요, 'we decided in the meeting'), whereas 정하다 is the lighter everyday word for arranging plans (시간 정하자, 'let's set a time'). Don't confuse it with 고르다/선택하다 ('choose'): you 골라요 one item from several visible options, but you 정해요 an arrangement or commitment. Unlike the separable noun+하다 verbs (요리하다 → 요리 안 해요), here 정 is bound, so 안/못 go in FRONT: 안 정해요, 못 정해요 — saying 정 안 해요 is wrong. Conjugation: 정하 + 여요 → 정해요, past 정했어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'decide TO do something' is best rendered with -기로 하다 (가기로 했어요, 'decided to go'), not 정하다 alone; 정하다 wants a noun object like 날짜를/장소를.

Splitting it as 정 안 해요 — unlike 요리하다, the 정 in 정하다 is a bound Sino-root, so the negative is 안 정해요 and 못 정해요.
Using 정하다 for 'choose an item' — picking one of several is 고르다/선택하다; 정하다 is for settling an arrangement (date, place, plan).
Saying 가기를 정했어요 for 'I decided to go' — the natural form is 가기로 했어요 (-기로 하다); 정하다 takes a noun, not this clause.

words.shortExplanation: 신청하다 means "to apply for" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 신청하다 (sincheonghada) means "to apply for". Start from the polite form 신청해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 신청하다. A strong first sentence is 수업을 신청하다 ("to register for a class"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 신청하다 also becomes 신청하고 싶어요 (want), 신청할 수 있어요 (can), and 신청 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
신청하다 = formally sign up/apply via a form or system; 수업을 신청해요

examples.en: I register for a class.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound; the thing applied for takes -을/를, verb 신청해요

examples.en: I applied for the scholarship online.
examples.note: -(으)로 for the method; past 신청했어요

examples.ko: 기한이 지나서 지금은 신청 못 해요.
examples.romanization: gihani jinaseo jigeumeun sincheong mo taeyo.
examples.en: The deadline passed, so I can't apply now.
examples.note: 기한이 지나다 = 'deadline passes'; 못 splits as 신청 못 해요

words.nuance: 신청하다 (申請하다, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') means to formally apply, sign up, or put in a request through a proper channel — a class, a card, a scholarship, a subsidy — usually involving a form (신청서) or an online system. Distinguish it carefully from 부탁하다 ('ask a personal favor', 친구한테 부탁해요) and from 지원하다 (志願/支援): 지원하다 is 'apply' for a job or school admission (회사에 지원하다, 'apply to a company'), with a sense of volunteering yourself, whereas 신청하다 is 'apply for / request' a service, slot, or benefit that's offered. As a separable noun+하다 verb, 안/못 wedge before 하다: 신청 안 해요, 신청 못 해요. Conjugation is regular: 신청하 + 여요 → 신청해요, past 신청했어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 신청하다 for applying to a job/university — Koreans say 지원하다 there; and don't confuse the everyday 'ask someone to do me a favor' (부탁하다) with the institutional 신청하다.

Using 신청하다 for a job or college application — that's 지원하다 (회사에 지원해요); 신청하다 is for services, classes, cards, benefits.
Confusing it with 부탁하다 — asking a friend for a favor is 부탁하다; 신청하다 is a formal request through a system or form.
Saying 못 신청해요 — as a noun+하다 compound the negative is 신청 못 해요 / 신청 안 해요 (the split goes before 하다).

words.shortExplanation: 확인하다 means "to check" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 확인해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 확인하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이메일을 확인하다 ("to check email") — then reshape the same stem into 확인하고 싶어요 (desire), 확인할 수 있어요 (ability), and 확인 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
확인하다 = verify/confirm the content; 이메일을 확인해요

examples.en: I check my email.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요

examples.en: I have to check the time before leaving.
examples.note: -기 전에 ('before doing'); 확인해야 해요 expresses obligation

examples.en: Please check whether this address is correct.
examples.note: -는지 embeds the yes/no question; 확인해 주세요 requests the favor

words.nuance: 확인하다 (確認하다, 確 'certain/firm' + 認 'recognize') means to check, verify, or confirm that something is correct or true — facts, times, reservations, messages — making sure reality matches what you expect. The crucial contrast is with 찾다, which English 'check' can blur: 찾다 is 'to look FOR / search' something not yet located (열쇠를 찾다, 'look for the keys'), whereas 확인하다 is 'to verify' something you can already see (열쇠가 있는지 확인하다, 'check whether the keys are there'). It also differs from 알아보다 ('look into/inquire to find out', 가격을 알아보다). It's a regular noun+하다 verb: 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요, past 확인했어요, with 안/못 splitting before 하다 (확인 안 해요, 확인 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'check the box' or 'check off' is NOT 확인하다 — ticking a box is 체크하다/표시하다; and 'check out a book/check out (a hotel)' uses 빌리다 or 체크아웃하다, not 확인하다, which strictly means 'verify/confirm'.

Using 확인하다 for 'look for/search' — finding something lost is 찾다 (지갑을 찾다); 확인하다 verifies something you can already check.
Saying 확인하다 for 'check (tick) a box' — that's 체크하다/표시하다; 확인하다 means confirm/verify, not mark.
Splitting as 못 확인해요 — the standard negative for a noun+하다 verb is 확인 못 해요 / 확인 안 해요.

words.shortExplanation: 취소하다 means "to cancel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 취소하다 (chwisohada) = "to cancel". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 취소해요 plus one useful sentence like 예약을 취소하다 ("to cancel a reservation"). usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
취소하다 undoes a booking/order; 예약을 취소해요

examples.en: I cancel the reservation.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요

examples.en: Something came up, so I canceled the appointment.
examples.note: 일이 생기다 = 'something comes up'; -아서 gives the reason; past 취소했어요

examples.ko: 이미 결제해서 지금은 취소 못 해요.
examples.romanization: imi gyeoljehaeseo jigeumeun chwiso mo taeyo.
examples.en: I already paid, so I can't cancel now.
examples.note: 이미 ('already') + past reason; 못 splits as 취소 못 해요

words.nuance: 취소하다 (取消하다, 取 'take' + 消 'extinguish/erase') means to cancel — to call off or undo something already arranged: a reservation, an order, an appointment, a plan. The neat way to remember it: it's the natural opposite of 예약하다/신청하다 (book/apply). Distinguish it from 그만두다, which is 'to quit/stop' an ongoing activity or job (회사를 그만두다, 'quit the company'; 운동을 그만두다, 'stop exercising'): you 취소해요 a future arrangement, but you 그만둬요 something already in progress. It also differs from 미루다 ('postpone', 약속을 미루다, push the appointment later rather than scrap it) — canceling removes it, postponing reschedules it. As a noun+하다 verb it's regular: 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요, past 취소했어요, with 안/못 before 하다 (취소 안 해요, 취소 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'cancel my subscription / unsubscribe' is more often 해지하다 (解止, end a contract) than 취소하다, and don't use 취소하다 for 'quit a job' — that's 그만두다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 취소하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 취소해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 취소하다 becomes 취소할 수 있어요 ("can") and 취소할 거예요 ("will"). words.nuance: 출근하다 is Sino-Korean 出勤 — 出 'go out' + 勤 'duty/diligence' — so literally 'go out to your duty', i.e. physically travel to your workplace and start your shift. words.nuance: 퇴근하다 is Sino-Korean 退勤 — 退 'withdraw/retreat' + 勤 'duty' — literally 'withdraw from your duty', i.e. finish the workday and head home. It is the precise mirror of 출근하다 (出勤). words.shortExplanation: 졸업하다 means "to graduate" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: 졸업하다 (joreophada) = "to graduate". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 졸업해요 plus one useful sentence like 대학교를 졸업하다 ("to graduate (from) university"). Short everyday negative.

Ability or possibility.

words.nuance: 졸업하다 is Sino-Korean 卒業 — 卒 'finish/complete' + 業 'studies/work' — so 'complete one's studies' and receive a diploma. Its exact opposite is 입학하다 (入學, enter a school); a softer related word is 끝나다 'to end', but a course 끝나다, whereas a person 졸업하다. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'graduate FROM university' makes learners reach for 에서, but Korean treats the school as a direct OBJECT — 대학교를 졸업하다, never 대학교에서 졸업하다. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (졸업해요, 졸업했어요, formal 졸업합니다), and the negative/impossible forms split the noun (졸업 안 해요, 졸업 못 해요). Note Koreans very often state it in the past about themselves — 저 작년에 졸업했어요 — because graduating is a completed life event; the present 졸업해요 usually means a scheduled near-future ('I graduate this year').

words.nuance: 합격하다 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 合 'meet/match' + 格 'standard' — literally 'meet the standard', i.e. clear a cut-off and pass a test, interview, or admissions screen. Its opposite is 불합격하다 (不合格) or, much more colloquially, 떨어지다 'to fall/drop' (시험에 떨어졌어요 = I failed/flunked). Don't confuse 합격하다 with 통과하다 'to pass through': 통과하다 is moving past a checkpoint or a bill passing, while 합격하다 specifically means meeting a qualifying standard. words.nuance: 외우다 is a NATIVE Korean verb (no hanja), meaning to commit something to memory deliberately — to get it 'by heart' through effort. words.nuance: 복습하다 is Sino-Korean 復習 — 復 'again/repeat' + 習 'study' — literally 'study again', i.e. go back over material you've already learned to lock it in. words.nuance: 제출하다 is Sino-Korean 提出 — 提 'lift/raise up' + 出 'out' — so 'put forward, hand out', i.e. formally submit a document, application, or assignment to an authority. The opposite side of the transaction is 받다 'to receive'/접수하다 'to accept (a submission)'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'submit TO the office' tempts an English-style structure, but the destination simply takes 에 (사무실에 제출하다) and the document is a direct object (서류를 제출하다). conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 제출하다 becomes 제출할 수 있어요 ("can") and 제출할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: Formally submit a document, application, or assignment to an authority — 'put forward, hand out'. Its register is the key point: 제출하다 is the formal, official word, while everyday speech often just uses 내다 'to put out/hand in' — students say 숙제를 냈어요 casually but write 과제를 제출했습니다 formally.
The opposite side of the transaction is 받다 'to receive' / 접수하다 'to accept (a submission)'.
Sino-Korean 提出 — 提 'lift/raise up' + 出 'out' — so 'put forward, hand out'.

As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (제출해요, 제출했어요, formal 제출합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (제출 안 해요, 제출 못 해요). Pronunciation [제출하다] is straightforward, but watch the polite request form 제출해 주세요.
'submit TO the office' tempts an English-style structure, but the destination simply takes 에 (사무실에 제출하다) and the document is a direct object (서류를 제출하다).

words.shortExplanation: 참석하다 means "to attend" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
words.explanation: "to attend" in Korean is 참석하다 (chamseokada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 참석해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 참석하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 회의에 참석하다 ("to attend a meeting") — then reshape the same stem into 참석하고 싶어요 (desire), 참석할 수 있어요 (ability), and 참석 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

words.nuance: 참석하다 is Sino-Korean 參席 — 參 'take part' + 席 'seat' — literally 'take one's seat (and take part)', i.e. attend a formal event like a meeting, ceremony, or banquet. Its register is more formal than just 가다 'to go'; you 결혼식에 가요 casually but 결혼식에 참석합니다 in polite/written contexts. Distinguish it from its close cousin 참가하다 (參加, 'participate/enter'): 참석하다 emphasizes being PRESENT and seated at a gathering, while 참가하다 emphasizes actively TAKING PART (참가하다 fits a contest, race, or program — 대회에 참가하다). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'attend THE meeting' (object) drives learners to 회의를 참석하다, but Korean uses 에 — 회의에 참석하다 — because you 'join INTO' the event. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (참석해요, 참석했어요, formal 참석합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (참석 안 해요, 참석 못 해요).

Use 참석해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Using 참석하다 for a contest or competition — being present at a gathering is 참석하다, but actively competing/taking part is 참가하다: 대회에 참가하다.
Forming the negative as 안 참석해요 — split it: 참석 안 해요 (impossible = 참석 못 해요).

Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.

words.nuance: 취직하다 is Sino-Korean 就職 — 就 'take up/settle into' + 職 'a post/position' — literally 'take up a post', i.e. get hired and start a job. It nearly overlaps with 취업하다 (就業, 'take up work'): in daily speech they're interchangeable, but 취직 leans toward landing a specific job/post at a company, while 취업 is the broader 'entering employment' (you'll see 취업률 'employment rate', 취업 준비생 'job seeker'). Don't confuse 취직하다 with 일하다 'to work': 취직하다 is the one-time event of GETTING the job, while 일하다 is the ongoing doing of work — 좋은 데 취직해서 열심히 일해요 (I got a good job and work hard). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'get a job AT a company' makes learners write 회사를 취직하다, but the employer takes 에 — 회사에 취직하다. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (취직해요, 취직했어요, formal 취직합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (취직 안 해요, 취직 못 해요).

Saying 회사를 취직했어요 because English uses 'a company' as an object — the employer takes 에: 회사에 취직했어요.
Using 취직하다 for the act of working day-to-day — getting hired is 취직하다 (a one-time event), but doing the work is 일하다.
Forming the negative as 안 취직해요 — split the noun: 취직 안 해요 (impossible = 취직 못 해요).

extendedVocab.nuance: 오전 is the Sino-Korean clock label for the AM half of the day, literally 午前 'before noon' (午 = noon, 前 = before), and its mirror is 오후 午後 'after noon'. The key contrast learners blur is 오전 vs 아침: 아침 is the FELT early part of the day (sunrise to mid-morning, and also breakfast), while 오전 is the neutral clock span from midnight-ish to 12:00 used on schedules, tickets, and timetables. So you say 아침에 커피를 마셔요 (lived experience) but 오전 9시 출발 (a printed departure). It is more formal/factual than 아침 and pairs habitually with clock times (오전 9시), 회의/수업/근무, and 오전 중. The classic English-speaker pitfall is word order: AM attaches AFTER the number in English ('9 AM'), but in Korean the period leads, so it must be 오전 9시, never 9시 오전. Also do not reach for 오전 when you simply mean the breakfast-time feel of 'morning' — use 아침.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오전 시간이에요 when you mean the cozy early morning feel — that idea is 아침; 오전 is the neutral clock-span AM and sounds like a timetable.
Putting the period after the hour, e.g. 아홉 시 오전 — Korean fixes the order as 오전 아홉 시 (period first, then clock time).
Dropping 에 in 오전 회의 있어요 — to mark 'during the morning' you need 오전에 회의가 있어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 오후 is the Sino-Korean PM label, literally 午後 'after noon' (午 noon, 後 after), the exact counterpart of 오전 午前. It covers every PM hour from 12:00 until evening, where it hands off to 저녁. The contrast to watch is 오후 vs 저녁: 오후 is the neutral clock-PM you write on schedules (오후 3시 회의), while 저녁 is the lived early-evening AND the dinner meal; so a 6 p.m. plan can be 오후 6시 on a timetable but 저녁 when you talk about eating. 오후 collocates with clock times (오후 3시), 수업/회의/근무, and the fixed 오후 늦게 'late in the afternoon'. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is order: 'PM' follows the number in English but the period LEADS in Korean — say 오후 5시, never 5시 오후. A second trap is treating 오후 as a greeting-time word like 'good afternoon'; Korean has no clock-based greeting, so you still say 안녕하세요, not anything built on 오후.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 다섯 시 오후 — Korean order is period-then-time, so it must be 오후 다섯 시.
Using 오후 for an early-evening dinner plan — for the dinner-time feel switch to 저녁 (저녁 여섯 시), since 오후 is the neutral daytime-PM span.
Trying to greet someone with a phrase based on 오후 like English 'good afternoon' — Korean uses the all-purpose 안녕하세요 regardless of the hour.

extendedVocab.explanation: 아침 (achim) = "morning; also breakfast". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아침에 ("in the morning") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아침, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.note: basic: 아침에 = the time slot

extendedVocab.nuance: 아침 is a native Korean word that does double duty: the early part of the day (roughly sunrise to mid-morning) and the breakfast meal — the same way English 'morning' differs from the meal but Korean merges the breakfast sense into the time word. The grammar disambiguates: with 에 (아침에) it's the time, with 을 (아침을 먹다) it's the food. Contrast 아침 vs 오전: 아침 is the felt, lived early morning, while 오전 午前 is the neutral clock-AM you put on timetables — so 아침에 일어나요 (waking life) but 오전 9시 회의 (a scheduled item). Habitual partners: 아침에 일어나다/운동하다, 아침을 먹다/거르다 ('skip breakfast'), 아침 일찍, 매일 아침. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 오전 for the breakfast meal — 오전 is only the clock period and can never name food, so 'eat breakfast' must be 아침을 먹다, never 오전을 먹다. Also don't force 에 onto the meal sense: you eat 아침을, you don't 'eat at morning'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오전을 먹어요 for 'eat breakfast' — 오전 is only the clock-AM span; the meal is 아침, so it must be 아침을 먹어요.
Marking the breakfast meal with 에 (아침에 먹어요 meaning the food) — as a meal-object it needs 을: 아침을 먹어요. 아침에 먹어요 only means 'eat (something) in the morning'.
Assuming 아침 always equals clock-morning like 오전 — on schedules and tickets Koreans switch to 오전 9시; 아침 is the lived, informal morning.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 점심 means "lunch / noon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 점심 (jeomsim) means "lunch / noon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 점심을 먹어요 ("eat lunch"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 점심 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

time sense → 에
fixed compound (often written closed)
점심 modifies the noun directly

extendedVocab.nuance: 점심 is Sino-Korean, literally 點心 — 點 'a dot/spot' + 心 'heart/center', an old phrase for a small 'touch-the-heart' midday bite that came to mean both the noon-time and the lunch meal. Like 아침/저녁, grammar splits the senses: 점심을 먹다 (the meal) vs 점심에 (the time). Note the near-synonym 정오 正午 'exactly noon' is the precise clock point 12:00, while 점심 is the looser lunch-time/meal — you'd never say 정오를 먹다. Habitual partners: 점심을 먹다, 점심시간, 점심 약속, 점심 메뉴, and the ritual greeting 점심 먹었어요?. Two English-speaker pitfalls: (1) translating 'lunch break' word-for-word — Korean uses the set compound 점심시간, not 점심 휴식; (2) reading 점심 먹었어요? literally and giving a detailed menu report — like 'how's it going', it's mostly phatic, and 네, 먹었어요 is enough. Also remember the meal is an object (점심을 먹다), so don't say 점심에 먹다 when you mean eating the lunch itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 정오를 먹어요 for 'eat lunch' — 정오 is the clock instant 'noon (12:00)'; the meal is 점심, so use 점심을 먹어요.
Coining 점심 휴식 for 'lunch break' — the natural fixed word is 점심시간.
Answering 점심 먹었어요? with a long literal report — it's a routine greeting like 'how are you'; a simple 네, 먹었어요 fits.

extendedVocab.explanation: 요일 (yoil) means "day of the week". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무슨 요일 ("what day of the week"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. extendedVocab.nuance: 요일 is the Sino-Korean suffix that builds weekday names, 曜日 — 曜 'celestial body/light' + 日 'day', the same East-Asian system that names days after the sun, moon, and five elements: 일(日)요일 Sun, 월(月)요일 Moon, 화(火)요일 Fire/Mars, 수(水)요일 Water, 목(木)요일 Wood, 금(金)요일 Metal/Gold, 토(土)요일 Earth. By itself 요일 means 'day of the week' as a category. The key usage point is the question word: to ask which weekday you MUST use 무슨 요일이에요?, because 무슨 asks 'what kind/which of a known set'; 어느 요일 or 어떤 요일 sound unnatural here. Habitual partners: 무슨 요일, 요일마다, 요일별, 주말/평일 요일. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'which day → 어느', producing 어느 요일이에요?; Korean idiom locks this to 무슨 요일. Also, when you name a specific day for scheduling, the time particle is 에 (월요일에 가요), and 요일 stays attached to its element (no space inside 월요일).

Asking 어느 요일이에요? or 어떤 요일이에요? — the fixed natural question is 무슨 요일이에요?.
Forgetting 에 on a specific weekday in a schedule — 'I go on Monday' is 월요일에 가요, not 월요일 가요 for the time-when.
Splitting the word, e.g. 월 요일 — each weekday is one closed word: 월요일, 화요일, …

extendedVocab.nuance: 주말 is Sino-Korean, 週末 — 週 'week' + 末 'end', literally 'week-end', and its opposites are 평일 平日 'weekday' and 주중 週中 'midweek'. It refers to Saturday and Sunday as a block. The contrast worth noting is 주말 vs 휴일: 주말 is specifically the weekend, while 휴일 休日 is any day off including public holidays — so a Wednesday holiday is a 휴일 but not a 주말. Habitual partners: 주말에 쉬다/놀다, 이번/지난/다음 주말, 주말마다, 즐거운 주말, and the farewell 주말 잘 보내세요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners borrow 'at/on' loosely and write 주말에서, but 에서 marks a LOCATION or a source ('from'); the time-when always takes 에 → 주말에. A second subtlety: for 'this weekend' use 이번 주말 (이번 = the current instance), not 오늘 주말; and 다음 주말 'next weekend' vs 다음 주 주말 can differ, so keep 다음 주말 for the upcoming Sat–Sun.

Writing 주말에서 for 'on the weekend' — 에서 is for place/source; the time-when is 주말에.
Saying 오늘 주말 for 'this weekend' — use 이번 주말 (이번 marks the current weekend); 오늘 주말 mixes 'today' with 'weekend'.
Treating any day off as 주말 — a midweek public holiday is a 휴일, not a 주말 (which is strictly Sat–Sun).

extendedVocab.nuance: 어제 is a native deictic time word meaning 'yesterday', sitting in the set 그저께(엊그제) 'day before yesterday' – 어제 – 오늘 'today' – 내일 'tomorrow' – 모레 'day after tomorrow'. Its defining grammar quirk is that, like 오늘 and 내일, it normally takes NO 에: you say 어제 만났어요, never 어제에. (The particle reappears only when 어제 combines with a sub-period, e.g. 어제 아침에, where 에 attaches to 아침.) 어제 naturally pairs with past tense — 았어요/었어요 — so it's a reliable signal that the verb should be past. Habitual partners: 어제 아침/저녁, 어제부터, 어제 일 'yesterday's matter', 어제 본/한/간 + noun. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-marking with 에 by analogy to 'on' or to other time nouns like 주말에; bare 어제 is correct. A second trap is pairing 어제 with present or future tense; because it's firmly past, 어제 가요 is wrong — it must be 어제 갔어요.

Adding 에: 어제에 만났어요 — the bare time words 어제/오늘/내일 drop 에; say 어제 만났어요.
Using present/future with 어제 — 어제 갔어요 (past) is required, not 어제 가요.
Reaching for 그저께/엊그제 to mean plain 'yesterday' — those mean 'the day before yesterday'; simple yesterday is 어제.

extendedVocab.nuance: 개 is the Sino-Korean general counter for inanimate objects, 個/箇, the catch-all you use when no more specific counter fits (it won't do for people, animals, or flat/long things, which have their own counters). It REQUIRES native Korean numbers, and the first four plus 20 shorten before any counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (so 한 개, 두 개, 세 개, 네 개, 스무 개). Word order is fixed as noun + number + 개 (사과 세 개), unlike English 'three apples'. Habitual partners: 한 개에 (price per item), 몇 개, 여러 개 'several', 개수 'the count'. A second trap is English order: don't say 세 사과 개 or 개 세 사과; it's 사과 세 개. Note the contrast with 명/분 (people) and 마리 (animals): 개 is strictly for things.

extendedVocab.explanation: 가족 (gajok) means "family". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 가족 ("my family"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가족 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 (our) is the default possessive Koreans use even for 'my' family
literally 'family is many' — use 많다, not 크다, for member count
two nouns stacked directly, no 의 needed
과 is the bookish 'with'; 하고/랑 are the casual ones

examples.en: My family has four people.
examples.note: 명 is the counter for people; say the number + 명, not just the number

examples.en: I really love my family.
examples.note: 가족 takes the object particle 을 here because 사랑하다 acts on it

examples.note: 주말에는 fronts the time with 에 + 는 for 'as for weekends'

extendedVocab.nuance: 가족 is the Sino-Korean word 家族 ('house' 家 + 'clan/group' 族), so it names the whole family unit as a collective, never a single relative — for one member you must say 가족 한 명 or name the relationship (형, 누나). The near-synonym 식구 also means family but literally means 食口 'mouths to feed', stressing the people who live and eat under one roof, so 식구 feels warmer and more domestic ('우리 식구 다섯이에요') while 가족 is the neutral standard term that also covers relatives living apart. Register is neutral and safe in any setting. The big English-speaker trap is two-fold: 'big/small family' is 가족이 많다/적다 (many/few), never 가족이 크다 (that sounds like physically large bodies); and Koreans say 우리 가족 ('our family') where English forces 'my family', so the 우리 is idiomatic, not a mistake.

extendedVocab.explanation: "parents" is 부모님 (bumonim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 부모님 ("my parents"). Watch the particle attached to 부모님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 + the built-in honorific 님 = the polite default
use 계시다, the honorific of 있다, to match 님
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테, required by 님
댁 is the honorific of 집 (house)

examples.en: I live with my parents.
examples.note: 살다 (to live/reside) drops its ㄹ before some endings but keeps it in 살아요

examples.en: I call my parents every day.
examples.note: 드리다 is the humble form of 주다/하다 — you 'give' the call up to elders

examples.note: 계세요 (honorific 있어요) is obligatory because the subject is 부모님

extendedVocab.nuance: 부모님 is Sino-Korean 父母 ('father' 父 + 'mother' 母) plus the honorific suffix 님, so the respect is baked into the word itself and it is the everyday polite default — there is no need to add anything to make it courteous. The bare root 부모 exists but is abstract and institutional ('부모의 역할' the role of parents, '부모 교육' parenting education); aimed at a real person it sounds cold, so for your own or anyone's parents you say 부모님. Because 님 marks the referent as worthy of respect, every verb around it must climb to its honorific tier: 있다→계시다, 주다→드리다, 집→댁, 에게→께, and the topic/subject can even take 께서. The classic English-speaker pitfall is pairing 부모님 with plain verbs ('부모님이 있어요', '부모님한테 줬어요'); grammatically the words exist, but to a Korean ear it clashes like saying 'Her Majesty ate fast' — you must use 계세요 and 드렸어요/께.

Using plain 있어요/없어요 with 부모님 ('부모님이 있어요') — the honorific subject demands 계세요/안 계세요.

엄마 takes 가 as the thing-liked with 좋다
돕다 is ㅂ-irregular: 돕 + 아요 → 도와요
한테 is the casual dative that suits this intimate word

examples.note: 잘하다 = 잘 (well) + 하다, written as one word

examples.en: I really like my mom.
examples.note: 좋아하다 (verb, takes 를) acts on 엄마, unlike adjective 좋다 (takes 가)

examples.note: 주다 + 었어요 contracts to 줬어요; 한테 marks the recipient

Its formal counterpart is 어머니, the respectful word for polite or public settings (introducing her, speaking to in-laws, addressing a friend's mother as 어머니); think of the pair as a sliding scale, 엄마 (intimate) → 어머니 (formal/respectful). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 엄마 as a neutral all-purpose 'mother': calling a stranger's mother 엄마, or saying 엄마 to your boss when reporting on a parent, feels childish or over-familiar — switch up to 어머니 the moment the situation turns formal, just as English shifts from 'my mom' to 'my mother'.

examples.note: 다니다 means to attend/commute to regularly; pairs with 에

examples.note: 닮다 uses 를 + past 았어요; the resemblance is stated as completed

Using 아빠 in a formal context ('저희 아빠는 의사세요' to a stranger) — it sounds childish; use 아버지 for respectful or public speech.

examples.note: 명 counts people; one says 한 명, never 일 명

extendedVocab.nuance: 누나 is the word a MALE uses for an older sister, and like 형 it doubles as a warm address title a younger man uses for any older woman he is close to — an older female friend, senior student, or, famously, a beloved older woman ('누나' in K-pop). Its gendered partner is 언니, which a FEMALE uses for the very same older-sister relationship, so 누나 vs 언니 is split purely by who is speaking, and the word betrays the speaker's gender in a way English 'older sister' cannot. Register is casual but deferential: 누나 is itself a respectful address (you call her 누나, not her name) and you speak up to her with -요 forms. A very natural collocation is 도와주다 'help (as a favor)'. The headline English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나 and a woman 언니 for an older sister — swapping them is an immediate giveaway — and remember 누나 is also how a younger man fondly addresses an older woman, not only a sibling.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A female speaker using 누나 for her older sister — women say 언니; 누나 is strictly used by males.
Confusing 누나 (male→older sister) with 언니 (female→older sister) — the choice depends entirely on the SPEAKER's gender, not the sister's.
Addressing your older sister by her bare name rather than 누나 — Korean expects the kinship title 누나 for someone older.

extendedVocab.nuance: 오빠 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older brother, and it is the most socially loaded kinship term in Korean: a woman also calls a close older male friend, a senior, or especially a boyfriend 오빠, so '오빠' on its own can mean 'my big brother', 'my guy friend', or 'babe' depending on context — hence 친오빠 exists to specify the actual sibling. Its gendered counterpart is 형, used by a MALE for the same older-brother relationship, so 오빠 vs 형 splits by speaker, and the word instantly reveals the speaker is a woman. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 forms, and 오빠 is itself the address term (never his bare name). The major English-speaker pitfall is gender — a man must say 형, never 오빠 — and the cultural trap: because 오빠 also means 'boyfriend' in romantic use, calling a male friend 오빠 can imply flirtation, so learners should know the connotation before using it freely.

A male speaker using 오빠 for his older brother — men say 형; 오빠 is used only by females.

Saying 친오빠 when you mean a boyfriend — 친오빠 specifically means a blood older brother; for a boyfriend just say 남자친구.

extendedVocab.nuance: 언니 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older sister, and it extends warmly to any close older woman — an older female friend, a senior at school or work — and is also the friendly way younger women address a female shopkeeper or restaurant server ('언니, 여기요!'), so it ranges from blood sister to polite stranger. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 endings, and 언니 itself serves as the address (you say 언니, not her name). The chief English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나, never 언니, for an older sister; and don't be surprised to hear women call a saleswoman 언니 — it is friendly social lubricant, not a claim of kinship.

Thinking 언니 always means a relative — women also use 언니 to address an older female friend or even a shop assistant.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 동생 means "younger sibling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 동생 (dongsaeng) = "younger sibling". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 동생 ("my younger sibling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동생, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: works for a younger brother OR sister, any speaker
있다 'have'; 동생 ends in a consonant so it takes 이
남 (男 'male') specifies the sex of the sibling
여 (女 'female') specifies the sex of the sibling

examples.en: I have one younger sibling.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 동생 doesn't reveal the sex on its own

examples.en: I often take care of my younger sibling.
examples.note: 돌보다 'look after' → 돌봐요; 동생 takes object 을 here

examples.note: 키가 크다 = 'height is big' = tall; 남동생 makes the sex explicit

extendedVocab.nuance: 동생 (Sino-Korean 同生 'born of the same' parents) means a younger sibling and, unlike the older-sibling words, is NOT split by speaker gender and does NOT itself reveal whether the sibling is male or female — to specify you prepend 남 (男) for 남동생 'younger brother' or 여 (女) for 여동생 'younger sister'. It also extends to any younger person you are close to (a junior at work or school), mirroring how 형/오빠/누나/언니 work upward; the system is asymmetric — elders get gendered, speaker-dependent titles, while juniors share the one neutral 동생. Register: unlike the older-sibling titles, 동생 is NOT used as a direct address — you call a younger sibling by name, and 동생 is only how you refer to them. The key English-speaker pitfall is assuming 동생 means 'younger brother'; it is sex-neutral, so without 남/여 it could be either, and you should never address someone as '동생' the way you'd say '형' — call them by name instead.

Assuming 동생 means only 'younger brother' — it is sex-neutral; add 남 (남동생) or 여 (여동생) to specify, or it stays ambiguous.
Using 동생 as a direct address ('동생, 이리 와') — unlike 형/누나, you call a younger sibling by name, not by the word 동생.
Writing 일 명 / 이 명 to count siblings — people use native numbers with 명: 한 명, 두 명.

extendedVocab.explanation: 남편 (nampyeon) means "husband". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 남편 ("my husband"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 남편 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is idiomatic even for one's own husband

usagePhrases.en: I have a husband / I'm married
usagePhrases.note: 있다 'have'; a common way to say one is married
하고 is the casual 'with'; 과 is the formal version
분 raises it to honor another person's husband

examples.en: My husband is an office worker.
examples.note: 이에요 'is' after a consonant; 회사원 = company employee

examples.en: I travel with my husband.
examples.note: 여행을 가다 = to go on a trip; 하고 같이 = 'together with'

examples.en: My husband is really good at cooking.
examples.note: 잘하다 = be good at; 요리를 잘하다 = cook well

extendedVocab.nuance: 남편 (Sino-Korean 男便, lit. 'male side') is the standard, neutral word for 'husband', used for your own husband and, in plain speech, anyone's. To speak respectfully about ANOTHER person's husband you add the honorific counter 분 → 남편분 ('your husband'), much as 부모→부모님 climbs in politeness. Distinguish it sharply from 신랑 'groom/hubby', which literally means the bridegroom but is also used affectionately or by newlyweds for a husband, and from the blunt third-person 그 남자 — 남편 is the safe everyday choice. The decisive English-speaker pitfall is the boyfriend/husband line: 남편 means a legally married spouse only, so a girlfriend's partner is 남자친구, NOT 남편 — English casually says 'my man/my partner', but in Korean 남편 firmly implies marriage. Also, when honoring someone else's spouse, don't leave it as bare 남편; use 남편분 to stay polite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 남편 for a boyfriend ('제 남편이랑 데이트했어요' when not married) — 남편 means a married spouse; an unmarried partner is 남자친구.
Referring to a respected acquaintance's husband as just 남편 ('사장님 남편') — add the honorific and say 사장님 남편분.
Saying 남편를 instead of 남편을 — 남편 ends in a consonant, so the object particle is 을 (남편을).

extendedVocab.nuance: 아내 is the standard, slightly warm native word for one's own 'wife', the safe default in most speech. Its near-synonyms divide cleanly: 와이프 (from English 'wife') is very common in casual male conversation but too informal for formal writing; 부인 (夫人) is the POLITE word for ANOTHER man's wife ('사장님 부인') and sounds odd for your own; and 집사람/안사람 are older, humble self-references ('the person of the house') now fading and faintly old-fashioned. So the map is: 아내/와이프 = my wife (neutral/casual), 부인 = your wife (polite). The key English-speaker pitfall is the girlfriend/wife line: 아내 means a married spouse, so an unmarried partner is 여자친구, not 아내 — English 'my partner' blurs this, Korean does not. A second trap is calling your own wife 부인; reserve 부인 for politely referring to someone else's wife.

Calling your own wife 부인 ('제 부인은…') — 부인 is the polite word for ANOTHER man's wife; for your own say 아내 or 와이프.
Using 와이프 in formal writing or a speech — it's casual spoken slang; write 아내 in formal contexts.
