The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 'our' is idiomatic; can mean 'my kid'
있다 'have'; 아이 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
명 counts people; native number 두 + 명
키우다 'raise/bring up' takes the object 를

examples.en: I have one child.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 한 명 = one (person)

examples.en: My child goes to school.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination 학교 with the motion verb 가다

examples.en: I really love my child.
examples.note: 사랑하다 (verb) acts on 아이, which takes the object particle 를

extendedVocab.nuance: 아이 means 'child' in the broad sense — your own kid or any young person — and is routinely contracted to 애 in casual speech ('우리 애가…'), which is natural but a touch more colloquial. Pin down the age band against its neighbors: 아기 (or 애기) is a baby/infant who can't yet walk or talk; 아이/애 is a child roughly from toddler through pre-teen; 어린이 is the more formal, respectful 'child' used on signs and in institutions (어린이날 Children's Day, 어린이 보호구역 school zone); and 자녀 is the formal Sino-Korean word for one's offspring used on forms ('자녀가 몇 명이세요?'). So 아이 sits in the middle, neutral-casual. The main English-speaker pitfall is mixing 아이 with 아기: English 'kid/child/baby' overlap loosely, but calling a 10-year-old 아기 sounds like babying them, and calling a newborn 아이 understates how tiny they are — match the word to the age.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 아이 (child) with 아기 (baby) — 아기 is a pre-walking infant; a school-age kid is 아이, not 아기.
Using 아이 on a formal document or sign where 어린이/자녀 is expected ('아이 보호구역') — the public/formal word is 어린이 (어린이 보호구역).
Counting children with Sino numbers ('아이 이 명') — use native numbers with 명: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 머리 means "head; also hair" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 머리 (meori) means "head; also hair". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리가 아파요 ("my head hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 머리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the single most common '머리' complaint; 가 marks the body part
하다 sense of 'hair'; say this at a salon, not 머리카락을 자르다
감다 is the dedicated verb for hair only, never 씻다
fixed idiom 'good head' = clever; opposite is 머리가 나쁘다

examples.en: My head hurts.
examples.note: survival sentence; learn 가 + 아프다 as one chunk

examples.en: My hair is long.
examples.note: here 머리 = hair; the adjective 길다 forces the 'hair' reading

examples.en: I got a haircut and dyed it at the salon too.
examples.note: real situation; 자르다 + 염색하다 are the salon collocations

extendedVocab.nuance: 머리 covers both the head and the hair on it, and only context (the verb or adjective) tells them apart: 머리가 아프다 = head hurts, but 머리가 길다 / 머리를 감다 = hair. The strict word for a single strand is 머리카락, yet in speech Koreans almost always shorten it to 머리, so 'cut my hair' is 머리를 자르다, not 머리카락을 자르다. The pitfall for English speakers is the washing verb: hair takes 감다 (머리를 감다), never the 씻다 you use for hands or face, so 머리를 씻다 sounds childish or wrong. Also note 머리가 좋다/나쁘다 is a fixed idiom for being smart/dim, not a comment on hair quality, and the body part is always marked with 가 (머리가 아파요), not 을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 머리를 씻다 for washing hair — hair uses the special verb 감다, so the natural form is 머리를 감다.
Saying 머리카락을 자르다 at a salon — it is technically correct but stiff; native speakers just say 머리를 자르다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 귀 is the ear, and the key English-speaker pitfall is the verb of hearing. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the standard cold symptom, not just neck pain
fixed phrase; 마르다 is 르-irregular: 말라요
붓다 is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요

usagePhrases.en: to lose one's voice / be hoarse
usagePhrases.note: from shouting or a cold; 'the throat rests'

examples.en: My throat hurts.
examples.note: survival sentence; usually means sore throat from a cold

examples.en: Please give me some water, I'm thirsty.
examples.note: everyday; 목이 마르다 → 말라요 (르-irregular)

examples.note: real situation; 목이 쉬다 = go hoarse

extendedVocab.nuance: 목 covers both the neck and the throat, so 목이 아프다 most often means a sore throat from a cold, NOT neck pain — assuming it only means 'neck' is the main English-speaker pitfall (for true neck/shoulder stiffness Koreans more often say 목이 뻐근하다 or specify 목덜미). Thirst is the fixed phrase 목이 마르다 ('the throat dries'), where 마르다 is 르-irregular → 말라요, 말랐어요; do not invent 목이 건조하다. A swollen throat is 목이 붓다 (ㅅ-irregular → 부어요), the same swelling verb as 발이 붓다, and going hoarse is 목이 쉬다 (lit. 'the throat rests'). Idiomatically 목이 빠지게 기다리다 means to wait so eagerly your neck stretches out ('wait with bated breath'). A throat/neck symptom marks the part with 가 (목이 아파요).

Saying 목이 목말라요, doubling the word — the set phrase is simply 목이 말라요 (or colloquially just 목말라요).

extendedVocab.explanation: "a cold; illness" is 감기 (gamgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 감기에 걸리다 ("to catch a cold"). Watch the particle attached to 감기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 걸리다 takes 에, never 을/를
심하다 = severe; describes intensity
medicine is 먹다 (eat), not 마시다

usagePhrases.en: take care not to catch cold
usagePhrases.note: warm seasonal farewell

examples.en: I caught a cold.
examples.note: survival sentence; memorize 에 걸리다 as one unit

examples.en: Colds are going around these days.
examples.note: everyday; 유행이다 = be widespread/in fashion

examples.en: Take care not to catch a cold, the weather got cold.
examples.note: real situation; caring goodbye in winter

extendedVocab.nuance: 감기 (感氣, 'feeling/affecting + air/energy') is the Sino-Korean word for a common cold, the everyday illness with cough, runny nose, and sore throat — distinct from the heavier 독감 (毒感, 'poison-cold' = influenza/the flu), which is a serious, feverish illness, so don't call the flu just 감기. The critical grammar point is the particle: you 'catch' a cold with 감기에 걸리다, using 에, because 걸리다 ('get caught by/hung on') takes a location-like target — 감기를 걸리다 with 을 is the number-one English-speaker error. Cold medicine is taken with 먹다 (감기약을 먹다, lit. 'eat medicine'), never 마시다 ('drink'), even for liquid syrup. The phrase 감기 조심하세요 ('be careful of cold') is a warm, very common parting line when the weather turns cold, much like 'stay warm / don't catch a cold.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 감기를 걸리다 — 걸리다 requires the particle 에, so it is 감기에 걸리다.
Calling the flu 감기 — the flu is 독감 (a far more severe illness); 감기 is an ordinary cold.
Saying 감기약을 마시다 — medicine is 'eaten' in Korean, so use 감기약을 먹다 even for liquid medicine.

extendedVocab.explanation: 열 (yeol) = "fever". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 열이 나다 ("to have a fever") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 열, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase; 나다 lit. '(it) comes out'
높다, not 크다, for fever level
재다 = measure; with a thermometer
내리다 = come down, after medicine

examples.en: I have a fever.
examples.note: survival sentence; 열이 나다 is the core phrase

examples.en: My child has a high fever so I'm worried.
examples.note: everyday; 열이 높다, not 크다

examples.en: After taking medicine the fever went down a bit.

extendedVocab.nuance: 열 (熱, the hanja for 'heat') is a fever, and the must-learn collocation is 열이 나다, where 나다 literally means '(something) comes out/arises' — Korean conceives a fever as heat 'coming out' of the body, so you never say 열을 가지다 ('have/possess a fever'), a direct translation of English 'have' that sounds completely unnatural. You can also say 열이 있다 ('there is fever') as a calmer alternative. The level of a fever is described with 높다/낮다 (열이 높다 = high fever), not 크다/작다, and once treated, 열이 내리다 ('the fever comes down') is the natural way to say it subsides — paralleling how prices or temperature 내리다. To take someone's temperature is 열을 재다 (재다 = to measure), the same verb as 키를 재다 (measure height). Don't confuse this 열 with the homonym 열 meaning 'ten' (열 개 = ten items); context separates them.

Saying 열을 가지다 for having a fever — this English-style 'have' is unnatural; use 열이 나요 or 열이 있어요.
Describing a high fever as 열이 커요 — fever level uses 높다, so it is 열이 높아요.
Saying 열이 떨어지다 vs the idiom — while understandable, the standard expression for a fever subsiding is 열이 내리다.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 밥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I eat rice / I eat a meal
usagePhrases.note: object marker 을; the all-purpose word for having any meal
subject marker 이 spotlights the rice itself
drops the particle in casual speech; works as a friendly greeting
밥하다 = make rice/a meal, not 만들다

examples.en: I eat rice in the morning.
examples.note: simple daily routine with object 을

examples.en: If you're done eating, let's head out together.
examples.note: casual 반말; 밥 here = the whole meal, particle dropped

examples.romanization: siksa naogi jeone bapbuteo jom juseyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: 밥 literally is the bowl of cooked white rice, but by extension it is the default word for 'a meal' — which is why 밥 먹었어요? functions as a real greeting like 'how are you?', not a literal question about rice. The big English-speaker pitfall is hearing 밥 only as 'rice' and missing that 밥 먹자 means 'let's grab a bite', and that to a boss you must upgrade to 식사 to stay polite.

Greeting an elder with 밥 먹었어요? — too blunt; use the honorific 식사하셨어요? instead.

subject marker 이 to warn about temperature
하고 = and; the two together are the base of a Korean meal
끓이다 = boil/cook soup, the set verb here

examples.ko: 한국 사람은 밥에 국을 같이 먹어요.
examples.romanization: hanguk sarameun babe gugeul gachi meogeoyo.
examples.en: Koreans eat soup together with rice.
examples.note: simple cultural habit; 국 paired with 밥

examples.ko: 국이 좀 식었는데 다시 데워 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: gugi jom sigeonneunde dasi dewo deurilkkayo?

extendedVocab.nuance: 국 is a light, broth-based soup with plenty of liquid that you spoon up alongside rice at nearly every meal. The near-synonym to separate it from is 찌개: a 찌개 (jjigae) is thicker, saltier, more concentrated and simmered right in a communal pot (된장찌개, 김치찌개), whereas 국 (미역국, 콩나물국) is milder and served in your own bowl. There is also 탕, a heartier long-boiled soup-stew (갈비탕). The set verb is 끓이다(boil/make), and Koreans 먹다(eat) soup with a spoon. The classic English-speaker mistake is reaching for 마시다(drink) because in English we 'drink' or 'have' soup — in Korean you 먹다 국, and calling a thick 찌개 a 국 will sound off to a native ear.

Saying 국을 만들어요 — the natural verb is 국을 끓여요 (to boil).

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가 to describe the taste

usagePhrases.en: please give a bit more kimchi
usagePhrases.note: 반찬 refills are free; 좀 softens the request

examples.note: simple preference statement

extendedVocab.nuance: 김치 is salted, seasoned, lactic-acid-fermented vegetable — most often napa cabbage (배추김치) but also radish (깍두기), cucumber, and more — eaten as a 반찬(side dish), never as the main. The word to contrast is 반찬, the umbrella term for all the little shared side dishes: 김치 is one specific 반찬. The native-feeling verb is 담그다(to put up / ferment), and as it ages people say it 익다(ripens). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 김치 like a single countable food and giving it a main-course slot; another is using 만들다 — Koreans say 김치를 담그다. Note too that fresh, just-made kimchi (겉절이) and well-aged sour kimchi (묵은지) are different enough to have their own names.

Saying 김치를 만들어요 — the set verb is 김치를 담가요 (to ferment/put up).
Assuming all 김치 is cabbage — 깍두기 (radish) and 오이김치 (cucumber) are kimchi too; the word names the method, not one vegetable.

extendedVocab.explanation: 고기 (gogi) means "meat (esp. pork or beef)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고기를 먹어요 ("I eat meat"). Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가 to describe texture
-고 싶다 = want to; attaches to 먹다
굽다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 구워요; the verb for Korean BBQ

examples.en: I want to eat meat tonight.
examples.note: simple desire with -고 싶어요

examples.ko: 고기가 좀 질긴데 더 익혀 주세요.
examples.romanization: gogiga jom jilginde deo ikyeo juseyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: In everyday speech 고기 by default means red land meat — usually 돼지고기(pork) or 소고기(beef) — so 고기 먹으러 가자 implies a BBQ, not seafood. To be specific you compound the animal onto 고기: 닭고기(chicken), 소고기(beef), 돼지고기(pork). The words to contrast are 생선(fish as food) and 해산물(seafood), which Koreans do NOT file under 고기; chicken sits on the edge, so people usually say 닭고기 rather than bare 고기 for it. The set cooking verb is 굽다, a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 구워요/구웠어요 (not 'gubeoyo'). The English-speaker pitfall is the English umbrella sense of 'meat' that includes fish and poultry — in Korean, unmarked 고기 leans strongly toward pork/beef, and you should name the animal when you mean otherwise.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming bare 고기 covers fish or chicken — Koreans say 생선 for fish and usually 닭고기 for chicken; unmarked 고기 ≈ pork/beef.
Conjugating 굽다 as 'gubeoyo' regularly — it is ㅂ-irregular: 굽다 → 구워요, 구웠어요.
Using 고기 for seafood at a restaurant — order 회 (raw fish) or 해산물 (seafood); 고기 sets up the wrong dish.

structuredNuance.t: In everyday speech 고기 by default means red land meat — usually 돼지고기(pork) or 소고기(beef) — so 고기 먹으러 가자 implies a BBQ, not seafood. To be specific you compound the animal onto 고기: 닭고기(chicken), 소고기(beef), 돼지고기(pork).
The words to contrast are 생선(fish as food) and 해산물(seafood), which Koreans do NOT file under 고기; chicken sits on the edge, so people usually say 닭고기 rather than bare 고기 for it.

examples.en: I eat fish often.
examples.note: simple eating habit

examples.ko: 이 생선 진짜 싱싱한데 회로 드실래요?

examples.note: real-situation rule contrasting the two 'fish' words

extendedVocab.nuance: 생선 is 生鮮 — 生 'live/raw' + 鮮 'fresh' — literally 'fresh(-caught) thing', i.e. fish as FOOD, on the market stall or the dinner table. The essential contrast is 물고기, the live fish swimming in water (a pet goldfish, fish in a pond): same creature, but 물고기 is the animal and 생선 is the ingredient. Sliced raw for eating it becomes 회(sashimi), and dried fish is 건어물. 싱싱하다/신선하다(fresh) is its habitual partner adjective, and you 굽다(grill) or 조리다(braise) it. subject marker 가; 신선하다 = fresh
도 = also/too; 좀 softens the request
다듬다 = clean and trim produce before cooking

examples.en: I eat a lot of vegetables.
examples.note: simple healthy habit; mass noun, no plural ending

examples.ko: 고기만 말고 야채도 같이 싸 드세요.
examples.romanization: gogiman malgo yachaedo gachi ssa deuseyo.
examples.en: Don't just eat meat — wrap some vegetables with it too.
examples.note: everyday BBQ line; 쌈 culture, 도 adds vegetables

examples.ko: 메뉴에 채소 이름으로 적혀 있는데, 야채랑 같은 말이에요.
examples.romanization: menyue chaeso ireumeuro jeokyeo inneunde, yachaerang gateun marieyo.
examples.en: On the menu it's written as 채소, but that's the same word as 야채.
examples.note: real-situation note on the 야채 vs 채소 register

extendedVocab.nuance: 야채 means 'vegetables' as an uncountable mass — you never add a plural ending, even for a whole pile. Its near-twin is 채소(菜蔬): the two overlap almost completely, but 채소 is the more 'proper', Sino-Korean and slightly bookish term you'll see on menus, packaging, and nutrition labels, while 야채 is the everyday, conversational word (the 野 in 야채 is 'field', 菜 'vegetable'). For raw leaves you eat fresh, there's also 쌈채소/상추류. Habitual partners are 신선하다(fresh) and the prep verb 다듬다(trim). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: adding a plural like 'vegetables' (야채들 sounds wrong here), and over-using 야채 in formal writing where 채소 reads better. When unsure in writing, 채소 is the safe, neutral choice.

Using 야채 on a formal menu or label — 채소 is the expected, neutral term there.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 과일 means "fruit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 과일 (gwail) means "fruit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 과일을 먹어요 ("I eat fruit"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 과일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을; mass noun, no plural
subject marker 이; 달다 = sweet (ㄹ-stem)
깎다 = peel with a knife, the set verb for apples/pears
박스/상자 counter; you count by container, not by 'fruits'

examples.en: I eat fruit every day.
examples.note: simple daily habit; 과일 stays singular

examples.en: Shall I peel some fruit for dessert?
examples.note: everyday home line; 깎다 + 후식 (dessert) collocation

examples.ko: 선물용으로 과일 한 상자 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: seonmuryongeuro gwail han sangja pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: Please pack a box of fruit as a gift.
examples.note: real-situation line; 과일 counted by 상자, gift culture

extendedVocab.nuance: 과일 is the mass category 'fruit'; like English 'fruit' used generally, it takes no plural ending, and when you mean specific items you name them (사과 apple, 배 pear, 딸기 strawberry) and count with 개 or by container (한 상자). Note 과일 is native-Korean-feeling and general; the parallel formal/technical term you'll meet on labels is 과실(果實) or in compounds 과(果). Its signature partner verb is 깎다(to peel) — Koreans peel apples and pears for guests — and its taste adjectives are 달다(sweet) and 시다(sour). The English-speaker pitfall is forcing a plural (과일들 for 'fruits' is unnatural as a generic) and using 자르다(cut) where 깎다(peel) is expected; another is treating 과일 as a dessert by default — in Korea cut fruit is itself the classic 후식.

Pluralizing as 과일들 for generic 'fruits' — 과일 is a mass noun; keep it unmarked and name specific fruits when needed.
Saying 과일을 잘라요 for peeling an apple — the set verb is 깎다 (peel); 자르다 just means cut into pieces.
Counting fruit with the wrong unit — use 개 for pieces or 상자/박스 for boxes, not a plural of 과일.

extendedVocab.explanation: "apple" is 사과 (sagwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사과를 먹어요 ("I eat an apple"). Watch the particle attached to 사과 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가; 빨갛다 → 빨개요 (ㅎ-irregular)
깎다 = peel; apples are peeled before serving
개 counts items; numbers use native Korean 두

examples.en: I eat an apple every morning.
examples.note: simple daily habit; -마다 = every

examples.ko: 이 사과 좀 시지 않아요? 다른 거 주세요.
examples.romanization: i sagwa jom siji anayo? dareun geo juseyo.
examples.en: Isn't this apple a bit sour? Give me a different one.
examples.note: everyday market line; 시다 = sour

examples.ko: 사과 두 개 주세요. 아, 사과는 됐고 사과만 살게요.
examples.romanization: sagwa du gae juseyo. a, sagwaneun dwaetgo sagwaman salgeyo.
examples.en: Two apples, please. Oh — no need to apologize, I'll just buy the apples.
examples.note: real-situation pun showing 사과(apple) vs 사과(apology)

extendedVocab.nuance: 사과 the fruit is 沙果/砂果 ('sand fruit'), while the homophone 사과 'apology' is a different hanja, 謝過 ('thank/decline' + 'fault') — identical sound and spelling, separated only by context. At a fruit stall or table it unambiguously means the apple; with verbs like 하다/받다/드리다 (사과를 하다 'to apologize') it means the apology. As fruit its partners are 깎다(peel), 빨갛다(red, ㅎ-irregular → 빨개요), and tastes 달다/시다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the apple/apology mix-up, is the color verb: 빨갛다 is irregular, so 'the apple is red' is 사과가 빨개요, not 빨갛아요. Counting also trips learners — it's 사과 한 개/두 개 with native numbers, not Sino-Korean 일·이.

Confusing 사과 the fruit with 사과 = apology — context and the verb decide; 사과하다 = apologize, never 'to apple'.
Saying 사과가 빨갛아요 — 빨갛다 is ㅎ-irregular, so it becomes 사과가 빨개요.
Counting with Sino-Korean numbers (사과 이 개) — use native numbers with 개: 사과 두 개.

extendedVocab.explanation: 빵 (ppang) = "bread (and baked goods generally)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 빵을 먹어요 ("I eat bread") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빵, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을
subject marker 이; 부드럽다 → 부드러워요 (ㅂ-irregular)

usagePhrases.en: I buy it at the bakery
usagePhrases.note: 빵집 = 'bread house' = bakery; 에서 marks the place of the action
굽다 → 구워요; same verb as grilling/baking

examples.en: I eat bread in the morning.
examples.note: simple breakfast habit

examples.en: It's freshly baked bread, so it's still warm.
examples.note: everyday bakery line; 갓 구운 = freshly baked

examples.ko: 케이크도 빵집에서 파니까 빵 사러 갈 때 같이 보자.
examples.romanization: keikeudo ppangjibeseo panikka ppang sareo gal ttae gachi boja.
examples.en: They sell cake at the bakery too, so let's look when we go to buy bread.
examples.note: real-situation note that 빵/빵집 covers cakes and pastries

extendedVocab.nuance: 빵 is a broad word covering essentially all baked, leavened wheat goods — loaves, rolls, pastries, even cake-ish items — not just sliced sandwich bread; that's why a bakery is 빵집, literally 'bread house', and a pastry-loving person is a 빵순이/빵돌이. The word itself isn't Sino-Korean; it came via Portuguese pão through Japanese, which is why it's written in the native-feeling single syllable 빵. The contrast to keep straight is 케이크(cake) and 과자(cookies/snacks/crackers): 과자 is dry, crunchy snack food, NOT 빵. Habitual partners: 굽다(bake), 부드럽다(soft, ㅂ-irregular → 부드러워요), 바삭하다(crispy crust). The English-speaker pitfall is narrowing 빵 to 'loaf bread' and so being surprised that a croissant or 단팥빵 (red-bean bun) is also 빵 — and that you 'eat' (먹다) bread, never 'drink' it even when it's soft.

Calling cookies or crackers 빵 — dry, crunchy snacks are 과자, a separate category.
Conjugating 부드럽다 regularly as 부드럽어요 — it's ㅂ-irregular: 부드러워요.

usagePhrases.note: 마시다 = drink, the correct verb for any liquid
subject marker 가; 차갑다 → 차가워요 (ㅂ-irregular)
topic marker 는 marks milk as the contrasted topic
잔 counts glasses/cups of a drink

examples.en: I drink milk every day.
examples.note: simple daily habit; 마시다, not 먹다

examples.en: The milk smells a little off — it might have gone bad.
examples.note: everyday line; 상하다 = go bad/spoil

examples.ko: 커피에 넣게 우유 좀 데워 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: keopie neoke uyu jom dewo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you warm up some milk to put in the coffee?
examples.note: real-situation café request; 데우다 = warm up

extendedVocab.nuance: 우유 is 牛乳 — 牛 'cow' + 乳 'milk' — so it specifically means cow's milk; for other kinds you compound, e.g. 두유(豆乳, soy milk) or 분유(粉乳, powdered/baby formula). As a liquid it strictly takes 마시다(drink), not 먹다 — though, importantly, casual Korean does allow 먹다 for consuming food/drink generally (밥을 먹다, 약을 먹다), so you will hear 우유 먹어 to a child; still, the clean textbook verb is 마시다. The near-contrast is 요구르트(yogurt) and 치즈(cheese), which are 유제품(dairy) but not 우유. Habitual partners: 차갑다/시원하다(cold), 데우다(warm up), 상하다(spoil). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 먹다 from 'have milk', and forgetting the counter — milk is counted in 잔(glass) or 팩/병(carton/bottle), never with 개.

Using 먹어요 as the default for 우유 — the textbook verb is 마셔요 (drink); 먹다 is only loose/casual.
Counting milk with 개 — use 잔 (a glass), 팩 (a carton), or 병 (a bottle).
Assuming 우유 covers all milk — it's cow's milk; soy milk is 두유 and powdered/formula milk is 분유.

Watch the particle attached to 식당 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place where an action happens
에 marks the destination of movement
subject marker 이; 깔끔하다 = neat, clean
단골 = a place one frequents

examples.en: Let's eat lunch at this restaurant.
examples.note: simple line contrasting place-of-action 에서

examples.en: I'll go to that restaurant and grab a table first.
examples.note: everyday line; movement 에 then 가서

examples.ko: 회사 구내식당이 싸고 빨라서 점심은 거기서 해결해요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 식당 is 食堂 — 食 'eat' + 堂 'hall' — an 'eating hall', i.e. an ordinary, everyday place to have a meal: a neighborhood eatery, a noodle shop, or a 구내식당(cafeteria). The register contrast is 레스토랑, the loanword reserved for fancier, often Western, sit-down dining; you'd call a humble 백반집 a 식당, never a 레스토랑, and a candlelit Italian place a 레스토랑, not a plain 식당. The crucial grammar point is particle choice: use 에서 for an action done there (식당에서 먹어요 'eat AT the restaurant') but 에 for it as a destination (식당에 가요 'go TO the restaurant'). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 에/에서 split, since English 'at/to' don't map one-to-one; another is reaching for 레스토랑 as the default word for any restaurant when 식당 is the everyday term.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 에 instead of 에서 for an action — 식당에서 먹어요 (eat AT), but 식당에 가요 (go TO); the verb decides the particle.
Defaulting to 레스토랑 for any restaurant — everyday eateries are 식당; 레스토랑 implies an upscale/Western place.
Saying 식당으로 먹어요 — 으로 marks means/direction, not the location of an action; the location particle is 에서.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 메뉴 means "menu; a menu item / dish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 메뉴 (menyu) = "menu; a menu item / dish". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 메뉴를 봐요 ("I look at the menu") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 메뉴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 = look at; 봐요 in 요-form
메뉴판 = the physical menu card; 주세요 polite request

usagePhrases.en: there are many menu items / choices
usagePhrases.note: subject marker 가; here 메뉴 = the dishes available
메뉴 = a specific offered dish, not the list

examples.en: Please show me the menu.
examples.note: simple polite request at a restaurant

examples.ko: 여기 제일 잘 나가는 메뉴가 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: yeogi jeil jal naganeun menyuga mwoyeyo?
examples.en: What's the most popular dish here?
examples.note: everyday ordering line; 메뉴 = a dish, 잘 나가다 = sell well

examples.ko: 메뉴 정하기 전에 메뉴판부터 다시 볼까요?
examples.romanization: menyu jeonghagi jeone menyupanbuteo dasi bolkkayo?
examples.en: Before we decide on a dish, shall we look at the menu card again?
examples.note: real-situation line using both senses: dish vs physical menu

extendedVocab.nuance: 메뉴 (loanword from 'menu') carries two senses Koreans switch between freely: (1) the printed list of offerings, and (2) an individual dish/order — so 무슨 메뉴 먹을까? means 'which dish shall we get?', and 메뉴 정했어? means 'have you decided what to order?'. When you specifically mean the physical card you hand over, Koreans often say 메뉴판 (menu-board) to disambiguate. The dish sense overlaps with 음식(food in general) and 요리(a cooked dish), but 메뉴 frames it as a selectable option on offer. Common partners: 메뉴를 정하다/고르다(decide/choose a dish), 메뉴가 다양하다(varied), 오늘의 메뉴(today's special). The English-speaker pitfall is locking 메뉴 to the printed-list meaning only, then being confused by 이 집은 메뉴가 맛있어요 — which praises the dishes, not the paper.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 메뉴 only means the printed list — it also means an individual dish, e.g. 이 메뉴 맛있어요 = 'this dish is tasty'.
Asking for the physical card as just 메뉴 when clarity matters — say 메뉴판 (the menu board/card).
Pairing 메뉴 with 마시다/읽다 oddly — you 보다 (look at) a menu and 정하다/고르다 (decide/choose) a dish.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시장 means "traditional market" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 시장 (sijang) means "traditional market". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전통 시장 ("a traditional market"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 시장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The set phrase Koreans use to distinguish an old open-air market from a modern store; 전통 = 'tradition'.
에 marks the destination you move toward; pair it with movement verbs 가다/오다/다니다.
에서 marks where an action takes place; here the buying happens inside the market.
An idiom: 시장(을) 보다 literally 'see the market' but means to go shopping for groceries — note 보다, not 사다.

examples.en: The market is big.
examples.note: A bare description; subject particle 이 after a consonant. Start simple.

examples.en: Every weekend I buy fruit at the traditional market.
examples.note: 마다 = 'every'; 에서 because the buying happens at the market, not 에.

examples.ko: 시장에 가면 깎아 달라고 해 보세요.
examples.romanization: sijange gamyeon kkakka dallago hae boseyo.
examples.en: When you go to the market, try asking them to knock the price down.
examples.note: 깎다 = 'cut/discount the price' — real bargaining only happens at 시장, not at a fixed-price 마트.

extendedVocab.nuance: 시장 (市場, 'market-place/field') is an open traditional market: rows of small independent stalls selling produce, fish, side dishes and clothes, where prices are flexible and you can haggle. The dividing line from its near-synonym 마트 is atmosphere and pricing — 마트 is a single fixed-price corporate store, while 시장 is many vendors and bargaining (깎다) is normal. Don't confuse it with 장 alone (which in 장을 보다 / 장날 means the shopping or market-day event) or with the homophone 시장 (市長, 'mayor'); only context tells them apart. The classic English-speaker trap is the particle: you say 시장에 가요 for *going there* (에 = destination) but 시장에서 사요 for *buying there* (에서 = where the action happens), and English 'go shopping' becomes the fixed idiom 시장을 보다, using 보다 'see', never 사다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시장에서 가요 for 'I go to the market'. With the movement verb 가다 you need the destination particle 에 (시장에 가요); 에서 would wrongly mean an action performed *at* the market.
Translating 'go shopping' word-for-word as 시장을 사요. The fixed expression is 시장을 보다 ('see the market'); 사다 needs a specific object like 과일을 사요.
Mixing up 시장(市場, market) and 시장(市長, mayor) because they sound identical. They are different words; rely on context — 시장에 가다 = market, 시장님 = mayor.

structuredNuance.t: 시장 is an open traditional market: rows of small independent stalls selling produce, fish, side dishes and clothes, where prices are flexible and you can haggle.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마트 means "supermarket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "supermarket" is 마트 (mateu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 대형 마트 ("a large discount supermarket"). Watch the particle attached to 마트 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 대형 = 'large-scale'; the standard label for hypermarket chains like 이마트 or 홈플러스.
에 marks the destination; use with 가다/오다 when you mean heading there.

usagePhrases.en: I do the grocery shopping at the supermarket
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = where the action happens; 장(을) 보다 is the everyday idiom for 'grocery-shop'.
동네 = 'neighborhood'; a smaller local 마트, between a 대형 마트 and a corner 가게.

examples.en: The supermarket is close.
examples.note: Simple description; 가깝다 'to be near'. Note 가 after the vowel-final 마트.

examples.en: In the evening I bought milk and bread at the supermarket.
examples.note: 랑 = casual 'and' for listing items; 에서 because the buying is done there.

examples.ko: 주말에는 마트가 너무 붐벼서 평일에 장을 봐요.
examples.romanization: jumareneun mateuga neomu bumbyeoseo pyeongire jangeul bwayo.
examples.en: On weekends the supermarket is too crowded, so I shop on weekdays.
examples.note: 붐비다 'to be crowded'; ~아서/어서 gives the reason.

extendedVocab.nuance: 마트 is a clipped loanword from English 'mart', meaning a large modern self-service supermarket or discount store — typically a chain (이마트, 홈플러스, 롯데마트) with fixed prices, shopping carts and barcodes. The line against its synonyms is size and pricing: 시장 is many haggling stalls, a 가게 is a tiny single shop, a 편의점 is a small 24-hour store, while 마트 is a big one-stop store where you 장을 보다 ('do a grocery run'). Because it is borrowed, there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, English 'mart' is rare, so learners under-use this very common word and over-reach with 슈퍼마켓 (Koreans usually just say 마트 or the older 슈퍼); second, the particle split — 마트에 가요 for going there but 마트에서 사요 for buying there — and don't say 마트를 봐요; the grocery idiom attaches to 장, i.e. 장을 봐요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a tiny corner store a 마트. A small always-open shop is a 편의점 and a little independent store is a 가게; 마트 implies a large supermarket with carts and many aisles.
Saying 마트를 봐요 for 'I shop at the supermarket'. The shopping idiom is 장을 보다, so it is 마트에서 장을 봐요 — the object is 장, and the location takes 에서.
Defaulting to 슈퍼마켓 in every sentence. It is understood but stiff; natural speech uses 마트 (big store) or 슈퍼 (small local grocery).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 편의점 means "convenience store" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 편의점 (pyeonuijeom) = "convenience store". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 편의점 도시락 ("a convenience-store lunchbox") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 편의점, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 도시락 = packed meal; a cheap ready-to-eat box, a staple of Korean 편의점 culture.

usagePhrases.en: I go to the convenience store
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination with movement verbs 가다/오다.

usagePhrases.en: I buy (it) at the convenience store
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place of the action; the buying happens inside the store.
24시간 = 'open around the clock'; the defining feature of a 편의점.

examples.en: There are many convenience stores.
examples.note: Basic existence statement; 많다 'to be many'. 이 after a consonant.

examples.en: Late at night I bought ramen at the convenience store and ate it.
examples.note: 사 먹다 'buy and eat' is one chunk; 에서 marks where it happened.

examples.ko: 편의점에서 택배도 보내고 공과금도 낼 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: pyeonuijeomeseo taekbaedo bonaego gonggwageumdo nael su isseoyo.
examples.en: At the convenience store you can also send parcels and pay utility bills.
examples.note: ~을 수 있다 'can'; shows the real range of services beyond snacks.

extendedVocab.nuance: 편의점 (便宜店, 'convenience-store', 便宜 'convenient' + 店 'store') is the small, brightly lit, usually 24-hour chain store on every Korean corner — CU, GS25, 세븐일레븐, 이마트24. The contrast with its neighbors is scale and price: it is far smaller than a 마트, more expensive per item, but always open and packed with ready meals, drinks and services (parcel pickup, bill payment, ATM, cash withdrawal). It also differs from a plain 가게 in that 가게 is an independent mom-and-pop shop while 편의점 is a branded chain. Note the hanja 便宜: in Korean 편의 means 'convenience', though the same characters read 便宜 in Chinese mean 'cheap' — a false-friend trap if you know Chinese. The everyday English-speaker error is the destination/location particle (편의점에 가요 vs 편의점에서 사요) and assuming it only sells snacks; in Korea the 편의점 is a genuine errand hub.

Calling a big supermarket a 편의점. Size and price differ: a large multi-aisle store with carts is a 마트, while 편의점 is a small 24-hour corner store.
If you know Chinese, reading 편의(便宜) as 'cheap'. In Korean these characters mean 'convenience'; 편의점 is named for being handy, not for low prices (it is actually pricier than a 마트).
Saying 편의점에서 가요 for 'I go to the convenience store'. Movement to a place takes 에 (편의점에 가요); 에서 is only for an action done there, like 편의점에서 사요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 카페 means "cafe" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 카페 (kape) means "cafe". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조용한 카페 ("a quiet cafe"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 카페 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 조용하다 'to be quiet'; 조용한 카페 is a prized spot for studying or talking.
에 marks the destination you head to with 가다/오다.
에서 marks where the activity happens; people study and work in Korean cafes for hours.
투어 from 'tour'; visiting several trendy cafes in a day, a popular outing.

examples.en: The cafe is pretty.
examples.note: Simple description; 예쁘다 here praises the interior/atmosphere, a very common reason to pick a cafe.

examples.ko: 친구랑 카페에서 두 시간 동안 수다 떨었어요.
examples.romanization: chingurang kapeeseo du sigan dongan suda tteoreosseoyo.
examples.en: I chatted with a friend at the cafe for two hours.
examples.note: 동안 = 'for (a duration)'; 수다(를) 떨다 'to chat away' — cafes are social hubs.

examples.ko: 이 카페는 자리도 넓고 콘센트도 많아서 일하기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i kapeneun jarido neolbgo konsenteudo manaseo ilhagi joayo.
examples.en: This cafe has roomy seats and lots of outlets, so it's good for working.
examples.note: 콘센트 = power outlet; ~기 좋다 'good for ~ing' explains why Koreans 'cafe-work'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 카페 is a loanword (from French/English 'café') meaning a coffee shop — but in Korea it is as much a social and study space as a place to drink coffee; people sit for hours to chat, work on laptops, or go on a 카페 투어 of photogenic spots. The key contrast learners blur is 카페 vs 커피: 카페 is the *place*, 커피 is the *drink*, so '커피 마시러 카페에 가요' (go to the cafe to drink coffee). It overlaps with 커피숍 and the older 다방 (a dated tea-room), but 카페 is the modern default. Being borrowed, it has no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 카페/커피 mix-up, plus the particles — 카페에 가요 for going there but 카페에서 공부해요 for doing something there — and remember the purpose marker for 'to go drink coffee' is the verb stem + ~(으)러: 커피 마시러 카페에 가요.

Using 에 instead of 에서 for activities done inside: 카페에 공부해요 is wrong. An action performed at the cafe takes 에서 — 카페에서 공부해요.
Assuming a 카페 only sells coffee fast like a takeout stand. Korean cafes are sit-down social/study spaces; ordering one drink and staying for hours is normal and expected.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 은행 means "bank" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "bank" is 은행 (eunhaeng). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 은행 직원 ("a bank teller / bank employee"). Watch the particle attached to 은행 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 직원 = staff member; the person at the counter who handles your transaction.
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.

usagePhrases.en: I withdraw money at the bank
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = location of the action; note 돈을 찾다 'find money' = 'withdraw', an idiom.
계좌 (口座) = account; 계좌를 열다/만들다 'open an account', a first task for newcomers.

examples.en: The bank is far.
examples.note: Simple distance description; 멀다 'to be far'. 이 after a consonant.

examples.en: I opened a bankbook at the bank.
examples.note: 통장 = passbook/account; 에서 because the action is done at the bank.

examples.ko: 은행은 보통 네 시에 문을 닫으니까 일찍 가세요.
examples.romanization: eunhaengeun botong ne sie muneul dadeunikka iljjik gaseyo.
examples.en: Banks usually close at four, so go early.
examples.note: ~(으)니까 gives a reason for advice; 문을 닫다 'close (the doors)'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 은행 (銀行, literally 'silver-shop/row', 銀 'silver' + 行 'shop/business') is a bank handling savings, transfers, currency exchange and accounts — a critical first stop for newcomers needing a 계좌 (account) and 통장 (bankbook). Two things trip up English speakers. First, the verb for 'withdraw' is the idiom 돈을 찾다 — literally 'to find money' — not 빼다 or a literal 'withdraw'; conversely 'deposit' is 돈을 넣다 'put money in'. Second, watch the homophone-ish 은행(銀杏) meaning 'ginkgo (nut/tree)': written and pronounced almost the same, distinguished only by context (은행에 가다 = bank; 은행나무 = ginkgo tree). As always, 은행에 가요 marks the destination (에) while 은행에서 돈을 찾아요 marks where the action occurs (에서); the direct English calque 'I go at the bank' with 에서 is the classic slip.

Saying 돈을 빼요 or a literal 'withdraw' verb for taking money out. Korean uses the idiom 돈을 찾다 ('find money') for withdrawing, and 돈을 넣다 ('put money in') for depositing.
Writing 은행에서 가요 for 'I go to the bank'. Going to a place uses 에 (은행에 가요); 에서 marks an action done there, e.g. 은행에서 돈을 찾아요.
Confusing 은행(銀行, bank) with 은행(銀杏, ginkgo). They sound nearly identical; context decides — 은행 계좌 = bank account, but 은행나무 / 은행을 줍다 = ginkgo tree / picking up ginkgo nuts.

structuredNuance.t: 은행 is a bank handling savings, transfers, currency exchange and accounts — a critical first stop for newcomers needing a 계좌 (account) and 통장 (bankbook).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 공원 means "park" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 공원 (gongwon) = "park". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 넓은 공원 ("a spacious park") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넓다 'to be wide/spacious'; describes the open green area itself.
에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.

usagePhrases.en: I take a walk in the park
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = where the action happens; 산책(을) 하다 'to take a stroll' is the classic park activity.
벤치 from 'bench'; 벤치에 앉다 'sit on the bench' — note location 에 with the static verb 앉다.

examples.en: The park is spacious.
examples.note: Basic description; 넓다 'to be wide'. 이 after a consonant.

examples.en: Every evening I walk the dog in the park.
examples.note: 마다 'every'; 에서 because the walking happens in the park; 랑 'with' (casual).

examples.ko: 주말에는 공원에서 돗자리 깔고 도시락 먹는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: jumareneun gongwoneseo dotjari kkalgo dosirang meongneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: On weekends many people lay out a mat and eat lunchboxes in the park.
examples.note: 돗자리(를) 깔다 'spread a picnic mat' — a very Korean park scene; 에서 marks the location.

extendedVocab.nuance: 공원 (公園, 'public-garden', 公 'public' + 園 'garden') is a public green space for walking, exercise, picnics and rest — found in every Korean neighborhood, from small 근린공원 to huge ones like 한강공원 or 올림픽공원. The near-synonym to distinguish is 정원 (庭園), a private *garden* attached to a home or building: 공원 is open to everyone, 정원 is someone's own landscaped yard, so don't call a public park a 정원. It is also not 놀이공원 (an amusement park with rides) — that compound needs 놀이. The collocations are scenic: 공원에서 산책하다 (stroll), 운동하다 (exercise), 돗자리를 깔다 (spread a picnic mat). The English-speaker pitfall is again 공원에 가요 (destination, 에) versus 공원에서 산책해요 (action location, 에서); and the static verb 앉다 takes 에 — 벤치에 앉다 'sit on the bench', not 에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a private home garden a 공원. 공원 is a *public* green space; a private landscaped yard is a 정원 (庭園). The 公 in 공원 literally means 'public'.
Saying 공원에서 가요 for 'I go to the park'. Movement to the park needs 에 (공원에 가요); 에서 only marks an action carried out there, like 공원에서 운동해요.
Using 공원 to mean an amusement park. Rides-and-attractions parks are 놀이공원 (e.g. 에버랜드는 놀이공원이에요); a plain 공원 is just a green park.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 역 means "station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 역 (yeok) means "station". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지하철역 ("a subway station"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 역 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 지하철 'subway' + 역; the most common compound, since urban Koreans live by subway lines.
에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.
에서 = where the meeting happens; stations are the default Korean meeting point.
출구 (出口) = exit; Koreans navigate by exit number — '3번 출구에서 만나' ('meet at exit 3').

examples.en: The station is close.
examples.note: Simple description; 가깝다 'to be near'. A big plus when renting a room.

examples.en: I took the train at Seoul Station.
examples.note: 서울역 = Seoul Station; 에서 because boarding happens at the station; 타다 'to ride/board'.

examples.en: I'll come out of exit 3 and wait in front of the station.
examples.note: ~(으)로 나오다 'come out via'; 앞에서 'in front of' + 에서 marks the waiting spot.

extendedVocab.nuance: 역 (驛, 'relay station / post-horse stage') means a train or subway station and almost always attaches to a place or line name — 서울역, 강남역, 부산역. It is the everyday navigation anchor of Korean city life, with people meeting and giving directions by 출구 (exit) number. Distinguish it from 정류장 (停留場), which is a *bus stop* — buses stop at a 버스 정류장, not a 역, so don't mix them. The historical hanja 驛 refers to old relay-horse posts, now repurposed for rail. Beware two look-alikes: 역할 (役割, 'role') and the particle/adverb 역시 ('as expected') share the syllable 역 but are unrelated words. The reliable English-speaker error is particles: 역에 가요 for going to the station (에 = destination) but 역에서 만나요 / 기차를 타요 for an action at the station (에서); never say 역에서 가요 when you mean 'go there'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a bus stop a 역. Trains and subways stop at a 역, but buses stop at a 정류장 (버스 정류장). 'I'll wait at the bus stop' = 버스 정류장에서 기다릴게요, not 역에서.
Saying 역에서 가요 for 'I go to the station'. Going there takes 에 (역에 가요); 에서 is for an action done at the station, e.g. 역에서 만나요.
Confusing 역(驛, station) with 역할(役割, role). They share one syllable but are different words: 강남역 = Gangnam Station, but 역할이 중요해요 = 'the role is important'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 우체국 means "post office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "post office" is 우체국 (ucheguk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가까운 우체국 ("a nearby post office"). Watch the particle attached to 우체국 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 가깝다 'to be near'; handy when you need to mail something quickly.

usagePhrases.en: I go to the post office
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination with movement verbs.

usagePhrases.en: I mail it at the post office
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = where the action happens; 부치다 'to send/mail (a parcel or letter)'.
택배 (宅配) = home-delivery service; the post office's parcel-shipping option, often cheaper than private couriers.

examples.en: Where is the post office?
examples.note: Basic question with 어디 'where'; 이 after a consonant. Essential newcomer phrase.

examples.en: I mailed a parcel at the post office.
examples.note: 소포 'parcel' + 부치다 'to send'; 에서 marks where the sending was done.

examples.ko: 우체국에서 국제 택배 보내면 일주일쯤 걸려요.
examples.romanization: uchegugeseo gukje taekbae bonaemyeon iljuiljjeum geollyeoyo.
examples.en: If you send an international parcel from the post office, it takes about a week.
examples.note: ~(으)면 'if/when'; 걸리다 'to take (time)'; 쯤 'about'. Practical mailing info.

extendedVocab.nuance: 우체국 (郵遞局, 'mail-deliver-bureau': 郵 'post/mail' + 遞 'deliver/relay' + 局 'bureau/office') is the post office — it handles letters, parcels (소포), home-delivery 택배, and also some banking and bill payments through 우체국 (the postal bank). The verb you need is 부치다 'to send/mail', as in 편지를 부치다 / 소포를 부치다; be careful not to confuse it with the homophone 부치다 'to fry (a pancake)' or with 붙이다 'to stick/attach' — same sound, different spelling and meaning. Distinguish 우체국 from 은행: while the post office offers limited banking, money matters proper belong to a 은행, and parcels belong to the 우체국. The English-speaker pitfall is the usual particle pair — 우체국에 가요 (destination, 에) versus 우체국에서 부쳐요 (action location, 에서) — plus reaching for a literal 'send' verb instead of the idiomatic 부치다 for mail.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Going to a 은행 to send a parcel. Banking-proper is the 은행's job, but mailing letters and parcels (소포/택배) is done at the 우체국.
Confusing 부치다 (to mail) with 붙이다 (to stick/attach) — they sound the same. You 편지를 부치다 (mail a letter) but 우표를 붙이다 (stick on a stamp); the spelling and meaning differ.
Saying 우체국에서 가요 for 'I go to the post office'. Movement to the post office takes 에 (우체국에 가요); 에서 marks an action done there, like 우체국에서 소포를 부쳐요.

structuredNuance.t: 우체국 is the post office — it handles letters, parcels (소포), home-delivery 택배, and also some banking and bill payments through 우체국 (the postal bank). The verb you need is 부치다 'to send/mail', as in 편지를 부치다 / 소포를 부치다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 영화관 means "movie theater" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 영화관 (yeonghwagwan) = "movie theater". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가까운 영화관 ("a nearby movie theater") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 영화관, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 가깝다 'to be near'; useful when deciding where to catch a film.

usagePhrases.en: I go to the movie theater
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.

usagePhrases.en: I watch a movie at the theater
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = where the action happens; note 영화를 보다 'watch a movie', the verb is 보다 'see'.
매점 (賣店) = snack stand; where you buy 팝콘 and drinks before the show.

examples.en: The movie theater is big.
examples.note: Simple description; 크다 'to be big'. 이 after a consonant.

examples.en: On the weekend I watched a new movie at the theater.
examples.note: 에서 because the watching happens at the theater; 영화를 보다 'watch a movie'.

examples.ko: 요즘은 영화관에 안 가고 집에서 영화를 봐요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun yeonghwagwane an gago jibeseo yeonghwareul bwayo.
examples.en: These days I don't go to the theater; I watch movies at home.
examples.note: Contrast with ~고 'and'; shows 영화관 (the building) vs watching 영화 (the film) anywhere.

extendedVocab.nuance: 영화관 (映畵館, 'movie-hall': 映 'project/reflect' + 畵 'picture' + 館 'large building/hall') is the building where you watch films — the multiplexes CGV, 롯데시네마, 메가박스. The synonym 극장 (劇場, 'theater') historically means a stage/playhouse but is also used loosely for cinemas; 영화관 specifically means a *movie* theater, while 극장 can cover live-performance theaters too. The crucial contrast is 영화관 (the *place*/building) versus 영화 (the *film* itself): you 영화관에 가요 (go to the theater) to 영화를 봐요 (watch a movie), so don't say 영화에 가요. Note 영화를 보다 uses 보다 'see/watch', never 듣다 or a literal 'watch'. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this place-vs-thing mix and the particle pair: 영화관에 가요 for going (에 = destination) but 영화관에서 영화를 봐요 for the action inside (에서).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 영화에 가요 for 'I go to the movie theater'. 영화 is the film; the building is 영화관, so it is 영화관에 가요 (and you go there to 영화를 보다).
Saying 영화관에 영화를 봐요 with the wrong particle. An action done inside takes 에서 — 영화관에서 영화를 봐요; 에 here would only mark the destination of movement.
Forgetting the verb 보다 for films. 'Watch a movie' is 영화를 보다 ('see a movie'), not a literal 'watch' verb; you 영화관에서 영화를 봐요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 호텔 means "hotel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 호텔 (hotel) means "hotel". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 깨끗한 호텔 ("a clean hotel"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호텔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 깨끗하다 'to be clean'; a top concern when picking lodging.
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.
에서 = where the action happens; 자다 'to sleep' / 묵다 'to stay overnight'.
예약 (豫約) = booking; 예약(을) 하다 'to make a reservation', essential before a trip.

examples.en: The hotel is expensive.
examples.note: Simple description; 비싸다 'to be expensive'. 이 after a consonant.

examples.en: Yesterday I stayed one night at the hotel.
examples.note: 하룻밤 'one night'; 묵다 'to lodge/stay over', more precise than 자다 for travel.

examples.ko: 호텔이 역에서 가까워서 짐 들고 다니기 편했어요.
examples.romanization: hoteri yeogeseo gakkawoseo jim deulgo danigi pyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: The hotel was close to the station, so it was easy to get around with luggage.
examples.note: 역에서 가깝다 'close *from* the station' — note 에서 marks the reference point for distance.

extendedVocab.nuance: 호텔 is a loanword (from English 'hotel') meaning paid short-term lodging for travelers, from budget to luxury. For staying overnight the precise verb is 묵다 ('to lodge'), e.g. 호텔에서 묵다, though everyday speech also uses 자다 ('sleep'). Distinguish it from other Korean lodging: a 모텔 (motel) is a cheaper, often by-the-hour place; a 여관/여인숙 is an older budget inn; a 게스트하우스 is a hostel; a 펜션 is a self-catering holiday house — so 호텔 is the mid-to-upmarket option specifically. It is temporary paid lodging, never your own home (집). Being borrowed, it has no hanja. The English-speaker pitfalls are: using 집 for a hotel stay; forgetting 묵다 and over-relying on 자다; and the particles — note that with distance, 역에서 가까운 호텔 means 'a hotel *near* the station', where 에서 marks the point you measure *from*, while 호텔에 가요 (destination 에) and 호텔에서 자요 (action 에서) keep the usual split.

Calling your hotel stay 집. 호텔 is temporary paid lodging for travelers; 집 is your own home. 'I'm staying at a hotel' = 호텔에서 묵어요, not 집에서.
Using 자다 when 묵다 is more natural for travel lodging. 자다 just means 'sleep'; for staying overnight at accommodation, Koreans say 호텔에서 묵다 ('lodge at the hotel').
Saying 호텔에서 가까워요 to mean 'the hotel is close' on its own. 에서 here needs a reference point: 역에서 호텔이 가까워요 ('the hotel is close *from* the station'); without it, just say 호텔이 가까워요.

extendedVocab.explanation: "shop" is 가게 (gage). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 작은 가게 ("a small shop"). Watch the particle attached to 가게 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 작다 'to be small'; 가게 typically implies a modest, independent store.
에 marks the destination with movement verbs.
에서 = where the action happens; the buying is done in the shop.
꽃 'flower' + 가게; 가게 freely compounds with goods — 빵 가게 (bakery), 옷 가게 (clothing shop).

examples.en: The shop is small.
examples.note: Simple description; 작다 'to be small'. 가 after the vowel-final 가게.

examples.en: I bought milk at the shop in front of my house.
examples.note: 집 앞 'in front of the house'; 에서 marks where the buying happened.

examples.ko: 저 사장님이 가게를 삼십 년 동안 하셨어요.
examples.romanization: jeo sajangnimi gagereul samsim nyeon dongan hasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: That owner has run the shop for thirty years.
examples.note: 가게를 하다 'to run a shop'; 동안 'for (a period)'; honorific ~으셨 for the owner.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가게 is the general native-Korean word for a small shop or store — usually an independent, owner-run place, and it compounds freely with what it sells: 꽃 가게 (florist), 빵 가게 (bakery), 옷 가게 (clothes shop), 반찬 가게 (side-dish shop). The contrasts matter: a 가게 is smaller and more personal than a 마트 (big chain supermarket), and unlike a 편의점 it is an independent shop rather than a branded 24-hour chain. The verb 가게를 하다 / 가게를 차리다 means 'to run / open a shop'. Being a pure Korean word, it has no hanja (its more formal Sino-Korean cousin is 상점 商店). The English-speaker pitfalls: don't stretch 가게 to a huge store — that is a 마트 or 백화점 (department store); and keep the particle split, 가게에 가요 for going there (에) versus 가게에서 사요 for buying there (에서). English 'go to the shops' as a general outing maps better onto 장 보러 가다 or 쇼핑하러 가다, not a literal 가게에 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가게 for a large chain store or department store. 가게 is a small independent shop; a big supermarket is a 마트 and a department store is a 백화점.
Saying 가게에서 가요 for 'I go to the shop'. Movement to the shop takes 에 (가게에 가요); 에서 marks an action done there, e.g. 가게에서 빵을 사요.
Translating 'go shopping / go to the shops' as 가게에 가요. For a shopping outing Koreans say 쇼핑하러 가다 or 장 보러 가다; 가게에 가요 means going to one specific shop.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빌딩 means "building" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 빌딩 (bilding) = "building". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 높은 빌딩 ("a tall building") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빌딩, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 높다 'to be tall/high'; 빌딩 specifically implies a large, modern, multi-story structure.
에 marks the destination/goal with 들어가다 'to go in'.
에서 = where the action happens; offices inside take 에서 for activities.
숲 'forest'; a vivid set phrase for a dense cluster of tall buildings downtown.

examples.en: The building is tall.
examples.note: Simple description; 높다 'to be tall'. 이 after a consonant.

examples.en: I met my friend in that building.
examples.note: 에서 because the meeting (an action) took place inside the building.

examples.ko: 회사가 저 유리 빌딩 십오 층에 있어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaga jeo yuri bilding sibo cheunge isseoyo.
examples.en: My company is on the 15th floor of that glass building.
examples.note: 층 'floor'; 에 marks the static location 'on the floor' with 있다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빌딩 is a loanword (from English 'building') but narrower than English 'building': it means specifically a *large, modern, multi-story* structure — an office tower or commercial high-rise, as in 유리 빌딩 (glass tower) or the set phrase 빌딩 숲 ('a forest of buildings'). The contrast with synonyms is size and type: a small house is 집, never 빌딩; a general 'structure' is 건물 (建物), the broad Sino-Korean word that covers *any* building including small ones, while 빌딩 implies it is tall and imposing. So a two-story shop is a 건물, not a 빌딩. Being borrowed, it has no hanja (its umbrella term 건물 does: 建物 'build-thing'). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 빌딩 for every 'building' the way English does — default to 건물 for the neutral word — plus the particle split: 빌딩에 들어가요 / 십오 층에 있어요 (destination/static 에) versus 빌딩에서 일해요 (action inside, 에서).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 빌딩 as a catch-all for every 'building'. 빌딩 means a *tall modern* tower; the neutral word for any building (including small ones) is 건물. A small two-story shop is a 건물, not a 빌딩.
Calling a house a 빌딩. A home is 집; 빌딩 is a large multi-story commercial structure. 'I live in that building' for a residential block is better with 건물 or 아파트.
Saying 빌딩에서 들어가요 for 'I enter the building'. Entering (movement toward a goal) takes 에 with 들어가다 (빌딩에 들어가요); 에서 marks an action done inside, like 빌딩에서 일해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 방 means "room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 방 (bang) means "room". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 내 방 ("my room"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 방 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: casual possessive 내; the polite form is 제 방
subject 이; 좁다 is the natural opposite of 넓다 for rooms
static location takes 에 with 있다
action done inside a place takes 에서

examples.en: This is my room.
examples.note: 서술격 조사 이에요 after a consonant; introducing a space

examples.en: I play games with a friend in my room.
examples.note: action location 에서, not 에, because something is happening there

examples.en: The room is so small that there's only a bed.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 좁다 (cramped) vs 작다 (small in size)

extendedVocab.nuance: 방 is the Sino-Korean character 房 ('room, chamber') and is the all-purpose word for any enclosed room, and it builds dozens of everyday compounds: 안방 (master/main room), 공부방 (study room), 노래방 (singing room/karaoke), 찜질방 (Korean sauna room), and PC방 (internet cafe). The key contrast to fix in your head is 방 vs 집: 집 is the whole house/home, but 방 is just one room inside it, so 'I'm going home' must be 집에 가요, never 방에 가요. The grammar trap is the 에 vs 에서 split: merely being located in the room uses 에 (방에 있어요 = it's in the room), but any action carried out inside the room uses 에서 (방에서 공부해요 = I study in my room) — English 'in the room' blurs both, and overusing 에 for actions is the #1 beginner error. Collocations: 방을 치우다/정리하다 (tidy the room), 방이 좁다 (the room is cramped). Register is fully neutral, used by everyone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 방에서 있어요 for 'it's in the room.' Existence/location with 있다 takes 에 (방에 있어요); 에서 is only for actions performed there.
Translating 'I'm going home' as 방에 가요. 방 is a single room, not the home as a whole — use 집에 가요.
Pairing 작다 with rooms to mean 'cramped.' For a tight room Koreans prefer 방이 좁아요 (narrow/cramped); 작다 sounds like the room's dimensions are literally tiny.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 문 means "door" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "door" is 문 (mun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 문을 열다 ("to open the door"). Watch the particle attached to 문 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: transitive: the door is the object 을, you act on it
pair verb to 열다; both take 을
intransitive 열리다: subject 이, no agent
collocation for knocking rather than 치다

examples.en: Please close the door.
examples.note: 좀 softens the request; -아 주세요 = do it for me, politely

examples.en: The door closed by itself because of the wind.
examples.note: intransitive 닫히다 + 저절로 (on its own); no one closed it

examples.en: The delivery driver knocked on the door.
examples.note: 두드리다 is the set verb for knocking on a door

extendedVocab.nuance: 문 is the Sino-Korean 門 ('gate, door') and covers both interior doors and outer gates, feeding compounds like 정문 (main gate), 후문 (back gate), 대문 (front gate of a house), and even 창문 (window, lit. 'window-door'). The crucial grammar point for English speakers is the transitive/intransitive pair: 열다/닫다 are things YOU do to the door (문을 열어요 = I open it, object 을), whereas 열리다/닫히다 describe the door doing it on its own or in a resulting state (문이 열려요 = the door opens, subject 이). English uses 'open' for both, so learners wrongly say 문이 열어요; pick the verb by whether there's an actor. Also distinguish 문 (the physical door) from 입구 (entrance/way in) — 입구 is the opening/access point, 문 is the panel itself. Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 문이 열어요 to mean 'the door opens.' 열다 is transitive (needs someone opening); for the door opening on its own use the passive 문이 열려요.
Using 문을 쳐요 for knocking. Hitting (치다) sounds violent — knocking on a door is 문을 두드려요.
Confusing 문 and 입구. 입구 is the entrance/opening you walk through; 문 is the actual door. '정문 앞에서 만나요' (the main gate) ≠ '입구에서 만나요' (the entrance area).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 창문 means "window" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 창문 (changmun) = "window". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 창문을 열다 ("to open the window") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 창문, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object 을; same 열다/닫다 verbs as 문
pair verb; both transitive
spatial noun 밖 + 에 for the view beyond

usagePhrases.en: to come in through the window
usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the path/route in

examples.en: May I open the window?
examples.note: -아도 돼요 asks permission; 좀 softens it

examples.en: Sunlight comes in through the window.
examples.note: 으로 = the route/path the light travels

examples.en: It's snowing outside the window.
examples.note: 밖에 (outside) describes the scene beyond the glass

extendedVocab.nuance: 창문 is a compound of 창 (Sino-Korean 窓, 'window') + 문 (門, 'door'), literally 'window-door,' and it's the everyday spoken word; the bare 창 survives mainly in compounds and writing (유리창 'glass pane', 창가 'by the window', 차창 'car window') and sounds more literary alone. The big English-speaker trap is the particle: 'look through the window' uses 으로 to mark the route the gaze or light takes (창문으로 봐요), NOT 에 — English 'through' maps to directional 으로 here. Note 창문 takes the same transitive verbs as a door (열다/닫다), since it literally contains 문. Don't confuse 창문 with 거울 (mirror), which beginners sometimes mix up because both are flat glass surfaces on a wall. Register is fully neutral and used by all ages.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 창문에 하늘을 봐요 for 'I look at the sky through the window.' The window is the route, so use directional 창문으로 봐요; 에 would mark a static location.
Using bare 창 in casual speech, e.g. 창을 열어요. It sounds bookish — in conversation Koreans say 창문을 열어요.
Treating 창문 as opening intransitively: 창문이 열어요 is wrong. Use 창문이 열려요 (the window opens) for the passive, like 문.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 침대 means "bed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 침대 (chimdae) means "bed". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 침대에 눕다 ("to lie down on the bed"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 침대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to lie down on the bed
usagePhrases.note: destination/resting point 에 with 눕다
action (sleeping) inside takes 에서

usagePhrases.en: to get up out of bed
usagePhrases.note: starting point of the motion 에서
collocation: 정리하다, not 만들다

examples.ko: 저는 침대에서 안 자고 바닥에서 자요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun chimdaeeseo an jago badageseo jayo.
examples.en: I don't sleep in a bed, I sleep on the floor.
examples.note: contrast 에서…에서; many Koreans sleep on 이불 on the floor

examples.en: I was tired so I lay down on the bed.
examples.note: 눕다 → 누웠어요 (ㅂ-irregular past); 에 marks where you end up resting

examples.en: It's hard to get out of bed in the morning.
examples.note: 에서 = the point you rise from; -기 힘들다 = hard to do

extendedVocab.nuance: 침대 is Sino-Korean 寢臺 ('sleep-platform/stand') and specifically means a raised Western-style bed frame with a mattress; traditional Korean homes sleep on 이불 (bedding/duvet) laid on a warm 온돌 floor, so 침대 is not a universal given. The grammar trap is the 에 vs 에서 contrast tied to the verb: 눕다 (lie down) and 자다 vs the act — use 에 for reaching a resting position (침대에 누워요, you settle ONTO it) but 에서 for an activity carried out there (침대에서 자요, 침대에서 책을 읽어요). English 'on/in the bed' erases this. Contrast 침대 with 소파 (sofa) and 이불 (floor bedding): a foreigner saying '침대에서 자요' is fine, but describing Korean-style floor sleeping needs 바닥에서 자요 or 이불에서 자요. The set verb for making a bed is 침대를 정리하다, never 만들다 (which means to build one).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 침대에서 누워요 for 'I lie down on the bed.' 눕다 describes settling onto a spot, so it takes 에 (침대에 누워요); 에서 marks an ongoing action, not the resting destination.
Using 침대를 만들어요 to mean 'I make the bed.' 만들다 = construct/build. To tidy the bedding say 침대를 정리해요.
Assuming everyone uses a 침대. To describe floor sleeping on bedding, use 이불 or 바닥에서 자요, not 침대.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 의자 means "chair" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "chair" is 의자 (uija). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 의자에 앉다 ("to sit on the chair"). Watch the particle attached to 의자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: resting destination 에 with 앉다, never 에서

usagePhrases.en: to stand up from the chair
usagePhrases.note: starting point of the motion 에서
collocation 빼다 (pull out) for offering a seat
편하다 (comfortable) is the natural modifier

examples.en: Please have a seat on this chair.
examples.note: 앉다 + -으세요 honorific; 에 marks where you come to rest

examples.en: After the meeting I stood up from my chair.
examples.note: 에서 = the point you rise from; motion away

examples.en: This chair is plush and comfortable.
examples.note: 푹신하다 (soft/plush) + 편하다 collocate for seating

extendedVocab.nuance: 의자 is Sino-Korean 椅子 ('chair') and covers any seat with legs — dining chairs, office chairs (사무용 의자 or 사무 의자), folding chairs (접이식 의자). The single most common English-speaker error is the particle with 앉다: sitting DOWN is reaching a resting position, so it must be 의자에 앉아요 (에 = destination), not 의자에서 앉아요 — even though English 'sit ON the chair' tempts you toward a location particle. Compare with standing up, which is motion away and DOES take 에서: 의자에서 일어나요. Distinguish 의자 (chair, you sit on it) from 소파 (sofa/couch, plush multi-seat) and 책상 (desk) — beginners sometimes pair them loosely. The set phrase for offering someone a seat is 의자를 빼 드리다 (pull the chair out for them). Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의자에서 앉아요 for 'I sit on the chair.' 앉다 reaches a resting point, so it takes destination 에 (의자에 앉아요). Use 에서 only for leaving the chair (의자에서 일어나요).
Calling a sofa 의자. A plush multi-seat couch is 소파; 의자 is a single hard-ish chair.
Using 위에 redundantly: 의자 위에 앉아요 sounds odd for normal sitting. Just say 의자에 앉아요 — 위에 is for objects placed on top of the seat.

Distinguish 의자 (chair, you sit on it) from 소파 (sofa/couch, plush multi-seat) and 책상 (desk) — beginners sometimes pair them loosely.
의자 is Sino-Korean 椅子 ('chair').

extendedVocab.explanation: 책상 (chaeksang) = "desk". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 책상에서 공부하다 ("to study at the desk") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: action at the desk takes 에서
위 (top) + 에 for objects placed on it
collocation 정리하다 for clearing it
에 marks settling at the desk to work

examples.en: There's a laptop on the desk.
examples.note: 위에 = on top of; 있다 for existence

examples.ko: 조용한 카페보다 책상에서 더 잘 집중돼요.
examples.romanization: joyonghan kapeboda chaeksangeseo deo jal jipjungdwaeyo.
examples.en: I concentrate better at my desk than in a quiet cafe.
examples.note: 에서 = where the activity (focusing) happens; 보다 compares

examples.en: I tidied my desk neatly before the exam.
examples.note: 정리하다 + 깨끗이 (neatly); the set verb for clearing a desk

extendedVocab.nuance: 책상 literally combines 책 (book, 冊) + 상 (low table/stand, 床), i.e. a 'book-table' — a desk for studying or working, which is exactly why you must NOT use it for a dining table: that is 식탁 ('eating-table', 食卓). English 'table' lumps these together and causes the classic mistake of saying 책상 at a restaurant. The location particle splits the usual way: an action performed at the desk takes 에서 (책상에서 공부해요, 책상에서 일해요), while an object resting on its surface takes 위 + 에 (책상 위에 컵이 있어요). Also separate 책상 (a working desk) from 탁자 (a small side/coffee table) and 식탁 (dining table). The set verb for clearing/organizing a desk is 정리하다, not 청소하다 (청소 is more about cleaning floors/dirt). Register is neutral.

Calling a dining table 책상. A meal table is 식탁; 책상 is strictly a study/work desk. Saying 식당에서 책상에 앉아요 sounds wrong.
Using 에 for the activity: 책상에 공부해요 is incorrect. Studying is an action, so use 책상에서 공부해요. Reserve 에 for sitting down (책상에 앉아요).
Saying 책상을 청소해요 for tidying papers on it. To clear/organize the desktop use 책상을 정리해요; 청소 implies scrubbing dirt.
