extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 옷 means "clothes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 옷 (ot) means "clothes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 옷을 입다 ("to put on/wear clothes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 옷 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 입다 is the body-clothing verb; object 을
pair verb to 입다 for the torso/body
갈아입다 = change into other clothes
어울리다 collocation for looking good on you

examples.en: What should I wear today?
examples.note: 입다 + -ㄹ까요 (shall I/what shall); 옷 is implied, not stated

examples.en: I sweated so I changed my clothes.
examples.note: 갈아입다 → 갈아입었어요; -아서 gives the reason

examples.ko: 그 옷이 너한테 정말 잘 어울려.
examples.romanization: geu osi neohante jeongmal jal eoullyeo.
examples.en: Those clothes really suit you.
examples.note: 반말; 어울리다 = suit/look good on; 한테 = on/to you

extendedVocab.nuance: 옷 is a pure native Korean word (no hanja) meaning clothes/clothing for the body, and the verb you MUST pair it with is 입다 (to wear on the torso/body) — never 신다, which is reserved for footwear on the feet (신발을 신다), nor 쓰다 (hats/glasses) nor 끼다 (gloves/rings). English 'wear/put on' covers every garment with one verb, so this split is the central pitfall: 옷을 신어요 is a classic beginner error. To take clothes off is 벗다, to change them 갈아입다. For 'these clothes look good on you,' Korean says 옷이 잘 어울려요 (the clothes suit you), not a direct translation of 'you look good.' Note 옷 is treated as singular/uncountable grammatically (no plural needed): one outfit or a wardrobe full is still just 옷. The dressier counterpart 의상 (costume/attire, 衣裳) is for performances or formal contexts. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 옷을 신어요 to mean 'I wear clothes.' 신다 is only for footwear; clothing on the body takes 옷을 입어요.
Forcing a plural like 옷들을 입어요 for several garments. 옷 is uncountable here — 옷을 입어요 already covers any amount.
Translating 'you look good in that' word-for-word. Korean idiom is 그 옷이 잘 어울려요 (the clothes suit you), using 어울리다, not a literal 'you look good.'

extendedVocab.explanation: "shoes" is 신발 (sinbal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신발을 신다 ("to put on shoes"). Watch the particle attached to 신발 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 신다 is the footwear verb; object 을
벗다 for removing shoes/clothes; key at the entrance
갈아 신다 (change-wear) parallels 갈아입다 for clothes
맞다 (fit) collocation; 발에 = to the feet

examples.en: Please take your shoes off when you come in.
examples.note: -을 때 = when; removing shoes indoors is the norm in Korea

examples.ko: 새 신발이 발에 안 맞아서 불편해요.
examples.romanization: sae sinbari bare an majaseo bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The new shoes don't fit my feet so they're uncomfortable.
examples.note: 맞다 (fit) + -아서; 불편하다 (uncomfortable) for shoes

examples.ko: 운동하러 갈 때 운동화로 갈아 신어요.
examples.romanization: undonghareo gal ttae undonghwaro gara sineoyo.
examples.en: When I go exercise I change into sneakers.
examples.note: 갈아 신다 = swap shoes; 운동화 (sneakers) is a type of 신발

extendedVocab.nuance: 신발 is native Korean (built from the verb root 신- 'to wear on feet' + 발 'foot') and means footwear in general — 운동화 (sneakers), 구두 (dress shoes), 슬리퍼 (slippers) are all 신발. The verb it demands is 신다, used ONLY for things on the feet, which is the mirror-image trap to 옷: just as you can't say 옷을 신다, you can't say 신발을 입다. English 'put on' hides the distinction, so 신발을 입어요 is a frequent beginner slip. Removing shoes is 벗다 — and culturally this matters enormously, since you always take shoes off before entering a Korean home (집에 들어갈 때 신발을 벗어요). For fit, use 맞다 (신발이 발에 맞아요), not 맞추다 (which means to have something custom-made). Changing shoes is 갈아 신다, parallel to 갈아입다 for clothes. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 신발을 입어요 to mean 'I put on shoes.' 입다 is for body clothing; footwear takes 신발을 신어요.
Using 맞추다 for fit: 신발이 발에 맞춰요 is wrong. To say shoes fit, use 신발이 발에 맞아요 (맞다); 맞추다 means to custom-order them.
Forgetting the cultural verb 벗다 indoors. Saying you keep shoes on inside a home is unnatural — Koreans say 신발을 벗어요 at the door.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가방, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to carry a bag on the shoulder/back
usagePhrases.note: 메다 for backpacks/shoulder bags slung on you

usagePhrases.en: to carry a bag in the hand
usagePhrases.note: 들다 for hand-held bags; contrast with 메다
destination 에 with 넣다 (put in)
안 (inside) + 에 to specify the interior

examples.en: I put the book into the bag.
examples.note: 넣다 → 넣었어요; 에 marks where it goes in

examples.en: The bag is so heavy my shoulder hurts.
examples.note: 무겁다 (heavy, ㅂ-irregular) + -아서; common with 메다 bags

examples.en: Today I carried a backpack on my back and a laptop in my hand.
examples.note: 메다 (sling on) vs 들다 (hold in hand) — two carrying verbs

extendedVocab.nuance: 가방 is a loanword (originally from Japanese かばん, ultimately tied to Dutch/Chinese roots) and covers all bags — 책가방 (school bag), 백팩/배낭 (backpack), 핸드백 (handbag), 여행 가방 (suitcase/luggage). The interesting depth for English speakers is the TWO carrying verbs Korean forces you to choose between: 메다 (to sling on the shoulder or back, for backpacks and shoulder bags) versus 들다 (to hold/carry in the hand, for handbags and totes) — English 'carry' makes no such distinction, so saying 가방을 들어요 for a backpack you're actually wearing sounds off. For putting things inside, use 가방에 넣다 (넣다 = insert; destination 에); to specify the interior space say 가방 안에. Don't confuse 가방 with 주머니 (pocket) or 봉투/봉지 (paper/plastic bag from a store). Register is neutral and used by everyone.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가방을 들어요 for a backpack you wear on your back. A slung-on bag takes 메다 (가방을 메요); 들다 is only for hand-carried bags.
Saying 가방에 책이 들어요 for 'a book is in the bag.' Use 가방에 책이 있어요 (existence) or 가방 안에; 들다 here would mean 'to hold.'
Calling a store's plastic/paper carry bag a 가방. That's a 봉지 (plastic) or 봉투 (paper/envelope); 가방 is a reusable bag you own.

extendedVocab.explanation: 컴퓨터 (keompyuteo) means "computer". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 컴퓨터를 켜다 ("to turn on the computer"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 컴퓨터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 켜다 (switch on); object 을
pair verb 끄다 (switch off)
으로 marks the computer as the tool/means
느리다 (slow) collocation for performance

examples.en: One moment, let me turn on the computer.
examples.note: -ㄹ게요 = I'll (do it); 좀 softens; 켜다 for powering on

examples.en: These days my computer is so slow it's frustrating.
examples.note: 느리다 + -아서; 답답하다 (stifled/frustrated) about a slow PC

examples.en: I wrote the report on the computer.
examples.note: 으로 = by means of; 작성하다 (draft/write up) for documents

extendedVocab.nuance: 컴퓨터 is a loanword (English 'computer') and by default means a desktop or computers in general; a laptop is specifically 노트북 (lit. 'notebook,' a Konglish narrowing — note it does NOT mean a paper notebook, which is 공책), and a tablet is 태블릿. The English-speaker pitfall is the instrumental particle: when the computer is the TOOL you act through, use 으로 (컴퓨터로 일해요 = I work using the computer), not 에 — 'on the computer' in English tempts a location particle. But when an action happens AT the machine as a place, 에서 appears (컴퓨터에서 파일을 찾아요 = I look for a file on the computer). For power, the verbs are 켜다 (on) / 끄다 (off), the same pair used for lights and the TV. Don't confuse 컴퓨터 with 모니터 (the monitor screen) or 본체 (the tower/main unit). Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 컴퓨터에 일해요 for 'I work on the computer.' The computer is the means, so use 컴퓨터로 일해요 (으로 = by tool); 에 marks static location, not instrument.
Using 노트북 to mean a paper notebook. 노트북 = laptop; a writing notebook is 공책 or 노트.
Saying 컴퓨터를 열어요 to mean 'turn on the computer.' Powering on is 컴퓨터를 켜요 (켜다). 열다 (open) is for files/programs or doors, not booting up.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the phone as the means
충전하다 (charge) collocation; object 을
보다 for scrolling/checking the screen

usagePhrases.en: to set the phone to silent
usagePhrases.note: 무음으로 (to silent) + 하다

examples.en: My phone battery is dead.
examples.note: 배터리가 다 되다 = battery is used up; set phrase

examples.ko: 수업 중에는 휴대폰을 무음으로 해 주세요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 휴대폰 is Sino-Korean 携帶 ('carry/portable') + the loanword 폰 ('phone'), literally 'carry-phone,' and it's the standard term; in everyday speech Koreans equally say 핸드폰 (Konglish 'hand-phone') or just 폰, while 스마트폰 specifies a smartphone and 전화 alone usually means a landline or 'a phone call.' The English-speaker pitfall is again the instrumental: when the phone is the tool for an action use 으로 (휴대폰으로 전화해요, 휴대폰으로 찍어요), not 에 — 'on my phone' misleads you toward a location particle. Note 전화하다 already contains 'phone,' so you don't repeat it: say 전화해요, not 휴대폰을 전화해요; if you want to name the device, it's 휴대폰으로 전화해요. To charge is 충전하다, and a dead battery is 배터리가 다 됐어요 (set expression). Register is neutral; 폰 is the most casual.

extendedVocab.nuance: 열쇠 is a pure native Korean compound from the verb 열- ('to open') + 쇠 ('metal/iron'), literally an 'open-metal,' i.e. the metal thing that opens — a lovely transparent etymology, and its natural partner is 자물쇠 ('lock-metal,' a padlock/lock). It refers to a physical metal key; modern Korean homes mostly use a 도어록 (door lock keypad) or 번호키 (number/PIN key), so for an apartment you may hear 비밀번호 (passcode) rather than 열쇠. The English-speaker pitfall is the instrumental particle: a key is a TOOL, so 'open the door WITH a key' is 열쇠로 문을 열어요 (으로 = by means of), never 열쇠에. The verb for losing it is 잃어버리다 (lose irretrievably), and the handy verb 챙기다 means 'remember to take it with you.' Figuratively 열쇠 can also mean 'the key/solution' to a problem (문제의 열쇠), just like English. Register is neutral.

Using 잃다 vs 잃어버리다 carelessly. To say you lost (and can't find) the key, the natural form is 열쇠를 잃어버렸어요; plain 잃다 alone sounds incomplete in speech.
Calling a keypad lock a 열쇠. A PIN/keypad door lock is a 도어록 or 번호키, and its code is the 비밀번호 — 열쇠 is specifically a metal key.

extendedVocab.explanation: 날씨 (nalssi) means "weather". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 날씨가 좋아요 ("the weather is nice"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 날씨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

set phrase for cold easing off

extendedVocab.nuance: 날씨 is the pure-Korean word for the overall feel of the weather right now and is the single most common small-talk opener in Korea. Distinguish it from the Sino-Korean 기온(氣溫, 'air-temperature'), which is the measured number, and from 일기(日氣) / 기상(氣象), which are bookish words used in 일기예보 ('weather forecast'). You almost always pair 날씨 with the descriptive adjectives 좋다, 나쁘다, 춥다, 덥다, 맑다, 흐리다. The English-speaker pitfall is double: first, English says 'the weather IS cold' so learners reach for 이다, but Korean needs the adjective verb directly — 날씨가 추워요, never 날씨가 춥다이에요. Second, when stating a plain fact about the weather, default to the subject particle 가 (날씨가 좋아요), not the topic 는; 날씨는 좋아요 sounds like you are contrasting the weather against something else that is bad.

Saying 날씨가 춥다이에요, gluing 이에요 onto an adjective; 춥다 is already a full predicate, so the correct polite form is 날씨가 추워요.
Defaulting to 날씨는 좋아요 for a neutral statement; the contrast nuance of 는 implies 'the weather is fine (but something else isn't)', so neutral facts take 날씨가 좋아요.
Translating 'today's weather' as 오늘의 날씨 in speech; Koreans just say 오늘 날씨, dropping the possessive 의.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비 means "rain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "rain" is 비 (bi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비가 와요 ("it rains"). Watch the particle attached to 비 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: precipitation 'comes' with 오다

examples.note: describe current weather

examples.note: rain as 아서 reason

examples.note: negative future forecast

extendedVocab.nuance: Korean has no single verb meaning 'to rain'; instead precipitation 'arrives', so you say 비가 와요 (rain comes) using 오다. A more formal, written variant is 비가 내리다 ('rain falls'), favored in forecasts and lyrics, while 비가 오다 dominates everyday speech. To say rain stops, use the dedicated verb 그치다 (비가 그쳤어요), not 끝나다. Note 비 also forms many compounds: 소나기 (sudden shower), 장마 (the summer monsoon rains), 가랑비 (drizzle). The big English-speaker pitfall is inventing a verb: learners say 비가 해요 or 비해요 by analogy with English 'it rains', but 하다 never combines with 비 — the natural pairing is strictly 비가 오다 / 비가 내리다. A second trap is 비를 맞다 ('to take the rain on your body', i.e. get drenched), which uses 맞다, not 받다.

Saying 비가 해요 or 비해요 like English 'it rains'; 하다 never pairs with 비, so the natural form is 비가 와요.
Using 비를 받다 for getting caught in the rain; the idiom is 비를 맞다, since 맞다 means to take something on your body.
Saying 비가 끝났어요 for the rain stopping; the verb for precipitation letting up is 그치다, so it is 비가 그쳤어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 눈 means "snow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 눈 (nun) = "snow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 눈이 와요 ("it snows") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 눈, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: same 오다 verb as rain
add 많이 for heavy snowfall
a romantic seasonal word

examples.en: It snows a lot in winter.
examples.note: seasonal statement

examples.note: -고 linking two weather events

examples.note: snow leading to a result

extendedVocab.nuance: 눈 means snow and, like rain, it 'comes': 눈이 와요 with 오다 (or the loftier 눈이 내리다). The crucial thing for English speakers is that 눈 is a perfect homograph and homophone with 눈 'eye' — only context tells them apart, and pitch differs subtly in some regions but spelling is identical, so 눈이 와요 in a weather chat can only mean snow. Snow-specific compounds are rich and culturally loaded: 첫눈 (the first snowfall of the season, tied to romance), 함박눈 (big fluffy flakes), 눈사람 (snowman), 눈싸움 (snowball fight). The pitfall, again, is reaching for a verb: never 눈이 해요; snow only pairs with 오다 or 내리다. Also resist forcing the English mass-noun logic — you don't 'do' snow or 'make it snow', you simply say it comes.

Saying 눈이 해요 by analogy with 'it snows'; 하다 cannot take 눈, so use 눈이 와요 or the written 눈이 내려요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 바람 means "wind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 바람 (baram) means "wind". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 바람이 불어요 ("the wind blows"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 바람 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the dedicated verb 불다
세다 = forceful
pleasant wind
compound 찬 + 바람

examples.en: The wind is blowing hard today.
examples.note: describe a windy day

examples.note: wind as 아서 reason

examples.note: seasonal description

extendedVocab.nuance: 바람 is wind, and unlike rain or snow it does not 'come' — it 'blows', so the obligatory verb is 불다: 바람이 불어요. Describe its force with 세다 (강하다 in formal writing) and its pleasantness with 시원하다 or 선선하다. Watch a famous homonym trap: 바람 also means a romantic affair, as in 바람을 피우다 ('to cheat'), and 바람(이) 들다 can mean to be flighty; these are unrelated to weather but share the spelling, so context matters. The headline English-speaker pitfall is particle-verb mismatch: beginners copy the rain pattern and say 바람이 와요, but wind never takes 오다 — it is always 바람이 불다. A second subtle point: 'a strong wind' as a noun phrase is 센 바람 or 강한 바람, where the adjective comes before 바람, whereas to predicate it you say 바람이 세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 바람이 와요 by copying the rain pattern 비가 와요; wind 'blows', so it must be 바람이 불어요.
Describing strong wind as 바람이 커요; size adjective 크다 doesn't fit wind, use force adjective 세다 — 바람이 세요.
Saying 바람을 불어요 with an object particle; 바람 is the subject that blows, so it is 바람이 불어요.

extendedVocab.explanation: "sky" is 하늘 (haneul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 하늘이 맑아요 ("the sky is clear"). Watch the particle attached to 하늘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

examples.en: The sky is really clear today.
examples.note: nice-weather remark

extendedVocab.nuance: 하늘 is the pure-Korean word for the physical sky, and by extension 'heaven' in religious or poetic contexts (하느님 'God' literally contains it). It is one of the headword + 에 nouns: because the sky is a static location where things merely exist, you say 하늘에 구름이 있어요, never 하늘에서, since 에서 marks a place where an action happens. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 에 vs 에서 choice — 'a bird is flying IN the sky' becomes 하늘에서 새가 날아요 (action!), but 'there are clouds in the sky' stays 하늘에 (existence). A second trap is color: English keeps 'blue' fixed, but Korean 파랗다 is a ㅎ-irregular adjective, so 'the sky is blue' is 하늘이 파래요 (the ㅎ drops and a vowel shifts), not 파랗아요. Habitual collocations are 하늘이 맑다, 하늘이 흐리다, 하늘을 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 하늘에서 구름이 있어요 for clouds existing in the sky; existence takes 에, so it is 하늘에 구름이 있어요.
Conjugating the color as 하늘이 파랗아요; 파랗다 is ㅎ-irregular, so 'the sky is blue' is 하늘이 파래요.
Forcing English 'in the sky' as 하늘 안에; the sky is treated as a surface/location with plain 에, so say 하늘에.

extendedVocab.nuance: 구름 is the pure-Korean word for cloud, counted in 점 ('구름 한 점' = one wisp of cloud) and habitually described with 많다 (plentiful) or the verb 끼다 ('to settle in / gather'), as in 구름이 끼다 — the standard way to say 'it clouds over'. The dramatic 먹구름 (literally 'ink cloud') means a dark storm cloud. Distinguish 구름 from 안개 (fog/mist), which sits at ground level, and from 흐리다, the adjective for an overcast sky (흐려요), not a noun. The classic English-speaker pitfall is copying the rain template and saying 구름이 와요 — clouds do not 'come' the way rain does; they 끼다, 몰려오다, or simply 많다. Another subtle error is treating 흐리다 as if it were the cloud itself; 'it's cloudy/overcast' is 날씨가 흐려요 or 구름이 꼈어요, two different structures.

Using 구름 to mean ground-level fog; that is 안개, e.g. 안개가 꼈어요, while 구름 sits up in the sky.

extendedVocab.nuance: 색 is the Sino-Korean root 色 ('color'), and it appears both as a standalone noun and, more often in casual speech, expanded to 색깔 — the two are interchangeable, with 색깔 feeling slightly warmer and more spoken. As a suffix, 색 attaches to color stems to make full color nouns: 빨간색, 파란색, 노란색. There is also a fixed set of bare Sino-Korean color words — 녹색(綠色) green, 황색(黃色) yellow, 흑색(黑色) black — used in formal or technical registers. The English-speaker pitfall is the object particle: 좋아하다 ('to like') takes a direct object, so 'I like this color' must be 이 색을 좋아해요, with 을, even though English 'like' feels stative. Note too that 좋아하다 expresses a held preference, whereas 마음에 들다 ('it pleases me') is for a fresh, in-the-moment liking of one specific thing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the object particle and saying 밝은 색 좋아해요; 좋아하다 needs an object, so the natural form is 밝은 색을 좋아해요.
Using 좋아하다 to react to one item you just saw; for an on-the-spot 'I like this one' Koreans prefer 이 색이 마음에 들어요.
Treating 색깔 as more formal than 색; it is actually the more casual, conversational form, while bare 색 and Sino words like 녹색 lean formal.

extendedVocab.nuance: 파란색 ('the color blue') comes from the ㅎ-irregular 파랗다, whose modifier form is 파란 — so 'a blue sky' is 파란 하늘, while 'the sky is blue' as a predicate is 하늘이 파래요 (adjective) or 하늘이 파란색이에요 (noun). The English-speaker traps are therefore two: don't say 파란색 하늘 (drop 색 to get the natural 파란 하늘), and don't assume 파란 always equals English 'blue' — for grass or a traffic signal, 파란 can be what English calls green.

extendedVocab.nuance: 검은색 ('black') comes from the adjective 검다, giving the modifier 검은 — so 'black clothes' is 검은 옷, while 'it is black' is 검어요 or 검은색이에요. Unlike most colors here, 검다 is a regular adjective, so the modifier is straightforwardly 검은, not an irregular form. The Sino-Korean counterpart 흑색(黑色) and the loanword 블랙 appear in formal or fashion contexts. The English-speaker pitfall is the usual one: before a noun, native speech prefers 검은 옷 over the stiffer 검은색 옷, and 'I like black' needs the object particle — 검은색을 좋아해요, not 검은색 좋아해요.

Saying 검은색 옷 in casual speech; native speakers shorten it to 검은 옷 before the noun.
Dropping the object particle in 검은색 좋아해요; 좋아하다 needs an object, so say 검은색을 좋아해요.

usagePhrases.note: ㅡ in 쁘 drops, then 어요 attaches → 예뻐요

extendedVocab.nuance: 예쁘다 means pretty, lovely, or cute-attractive, and is the everyday compliment Koreans pay to things, people, scenery, even babies and handwriting. Its closest near-synonym is 아름답다, and the dividing line is register and scale: 예쁘다 is warm, casual, and personal ('cute and pretty'), while 아름답다 is grander, more literary and emotional ('beautiful, sublime') — a flower or a girl's outfit is 예뻐요, but a sunset or a symphony is 아름다워요. 귀엽다 leans 'adorable/charming', not just visually pretty. It habitually pairs with 정말/너무/참 (정말 예뻐요) and with 옷·얼굴·꽃·글씨. The English-speaker pitfall: do not write 예쁘어요 (forgetting the ㅡ drops), and remember the subject takes 이/가 (꽃이 예뻐요), because 예쁘다 is a descriptive adjective, not an action you do to an object.

extendedVocab.nuance: 멋있다 means cool, stylish, or impressively attractive — it admires a quality of taste, presence, or charisma, not mere prettiness. Built on 멋 ('style, flair, dash') + 있다 ('to have'), it literally says 'has flair', which is exactly why it conjugates as an 있다-type word: its present modifier is 멋있는 (like 재미있는, 맛있는), NOT 멋있은. Its near-identical twin is 멋지다, and the line is subtle: 멋있다 and 멋지다 are largely interchangeable ('cool/awesome'), but 멋지다 sounds a touch more exclamatory and is slightly more common in spontaneous praise (멋지다!), while 멋있다 can describe a steady, ongoing coolness. Contrast both with 예쁘다 (visually pretty) and 잘생기다 (good-looking of facial features) — a man with great style is 멋있어요 even if you wouldn't call him 예뻐요. It collocates with 사람·차·옷·모습·자세 and with intensifiers 정말/진짜/너무. The English-speaker pitfall: write 멋있는 not 멋있은 for the modifier, and never 멋있다 with 을/를 — the admired thing takes 이/가 (그 사람이 멋있어요).

Its near-identical twin is 멋지다, and the line is subtle: 멋있다 and 멋지다 are largely interchangeable ('cool/awesome'), but 멋지다 sounds a touch more exclamatory and is slightly more common in spontaneous praise (멋지다!), while 멋있다 can describe a steady, ongoing coolness. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 길다 means "long" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 길다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

ㄹ-irregular: final ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ (길 → 긴)
subject 길(road) marked with 이
길 + 게 → adverb 'lengthily/in a long way'

examples.en: This road is too long.
examples.note: 요-form 길어요; the ㄹ is kept because 어 is a vowel ending.

examples.en: I wore a long skirt.
examples.note: The modifier drops ㄹ before ㄴ, giving 긴 (not 길은) before 치마.

examples.en: The waiting time was long, so I got tired.
examples.note: 길어서 (요-form + 서) gives the reason 'because it was long'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 짧다 means "short" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 짧다 (jjalbda) means "short". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 짧아요 ("it is short"). regular modifier: stem + 은 (짧 → 짧은)
subject marked with 이/가
짧 + 게 → adverb 'short(ly)' with an action verb

examples.en: These pants are a bit short.
examples.note: 요-form 짧아요; vowel harmony picks 아요 because the stem vowel is ㅏ.

examples.en: I wrote one short piece of writing.
examples.note: Regular modifier 짧은 (stem + 은) before 글, since the stem ends in a consonant cluster.

examples.en: The vacation is short, so it's a shame.
examples.note: 짧아서 gives the reason 'because it's short'; pairs naturally with 아쉽다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빠르다 means "fast; quick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "fast; quick" is 빠르다 (ppareuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빨라요 ("it is fast"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

modifier is regular: stem + ㄴ (빠르 → 빠른)
subject marked with 이/가
빠르 + 게 → adverb 'quickly', common with motion verbs

examples.en: This train is really fast.
examples.note: 르-irregular in action: 빠르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ → 빨라요, never 빠르어요.

examples.en: I was glad to get a quick reply.
examples.note: The modifier 빠른 is regular (빠르 + ㄴ) and sits before 답장.

examples.en: Please come just a little faster.
examples.note: The set adverb 빨리 ('quickly') is the form you'll hear most in daily speech.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빠르다 means fast or quick — high in speed, whether a train, the internet, a reply, or a person's pace. Its conjugation is the classic 르-irregular: before an 아/어 ending the 르 splits into ㄹㄹ and the previous syllable gains a ㄹ batchim, so 빠르 + 아요 → 빨라요 (never 빠르어요 or 빠라요); the modifier 빠른, however, is perfectly regular. The crucial synonym contrast is 이르다 ('early in time'): 빠르다 is about SPEED (how fast something moves), while 이르다 is about TIMING (how early on the clock/calendar) — '버스가 빨라요' means the bus is fast, but '아직 일러요' means 'it's still early'. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 높다 means "high; tall" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 높다 (nopda) = "high; tall". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 높아요 ("it is high") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 높다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: last stem vowel ㅗ → 아요 by vowel harmony (높 → 높아요)
regular modifier: stem + 은 (높 → 높은)
subject marked with 이/가
높 + 게 → adverb 'high(ly)' with an action verb

examples.en: That mountain is very high.
examples.note: 요-form 높아요; the stem vowel ㅗ selects 아요, and the ㅍ links to give a '노파요' sound.

examples.en: I saw a tall building for the first time.
examples.note: The regular modifier 높은 (stem + 은) precedes 빌딩.

examples.en: The price was too high, so I didn't buy it.
examples.note: 높아서 marks the reason; note 가격이 높다 is the natural pairing for 'price is high'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 높다 means high or tall and also 'high in level' for abstractions — mountains and buildings (산이 높다, 빌딩이 높다), but also 가격이 높다 (price is high), 온도가 높다 (temperature is high), 소리가 높다 (pitch is high), and 가능성이 높다 (the likelihood is high). Conjugation is regular: vowel ㅗ takes 아요 (높아요), modifier is 높은. The key synonym boundary is with 크다 ('big/large') for people: a person's height is described with 키가 크다 (literally 'stature is big'), NOT 키가 높다 — 높다 is for objects rising from a base (a tower, a shelf), while a human's tallness is 키가 크다. Its opposites split too: 높다 ↔ 낮다 (low), but 크다 ↔ 작다 (small). It collocates with 산·건물·가격·온도·소리·확률·수준. English-speaker pitfall: 'a tall person' becomes 높은 사람 by direct translation, which sounds like 'a high-ranking/lofty person', not 'a tall one' — say 키가 큰 사람; reserve 높다 for things that stand high off the ground.

Using 높다 for a tall person (그 사람은 키가 높아요) — human height is 키가 크다: 키가 커요. 높다 is for objects rising from the ground.
Translating 'high price' word-for-word with 비싼 only — 'the price is high' is 가격이 높다, while 비싸다 describes the item itself (이 옷은 비싸요). Both are right but pattern differently.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 멀다 means "far" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

ㄹ-irregular: final ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ (멀 → 먼)
subject marked with 이/가
멀 → the set adverb 멀리 'far (away)', used with motion verbs

examples.en: My home is far from work.
examples.note: 요-form 멀어요; the reference point takes 에서 ('from'), as in 회사에서 멀다.

examples.en: I'm traveling to a faraway country.
examples.note: The modifier drops ㄹ before ㄴ → 먼 (not 멀은) before 나라.

examples.en: The station is far, so I take the bus.
examples.note: 멀어서 gives the reason 'because it's far'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 멀다 means far in distance (집이 멀다, 먼 길) and figuratively 'distant' in relationship or likelihood (사이가 멀어지다 = to grow apart; 거리가 멀다). It is the opposite of 가깝다 (near). Conjugation is ㄹ-irregular: the ㄹ stays before vowel endings (멀어요) but drops before the modifier ㄴ, so 'a far place' is 먼 곳, never 멀은 곳 — the same pattern as 길다→긴, 달다→단. The natural way to say the distance is FROM somewhere is with 에서: 여기에서 멀어요 ('it's far from here'). Note the set adverb is the irregular 멀리 ('far away', 멀리 가다), not 멀게. A subtle synonym point: for 'a remote/secluded place' Korean often prefers 외지다 or 외딴, while 멀다 is plain physical distance. It collocates with 집·학교·역·길·나라·거리·미래. English-speaker pitfalls: writing 멀은 for the modifier instead of 먼, and marking the reference with the wrong particle — say 회사에서 멀어요 (from work), not 회사에 멀어요.

Marking the reference point with 에 (회사에 멀어요) — 'far FROM X' uses 에서: 회사에서 멀어요.
Using 멀게 for 'far away' as an adverb — the idiomatic adverb is the irregular 멀리: 멀리 가다 (멀게 is grammatical but not what natives say for distance).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가깝다 means "close; near" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "close; near" is 가깝다 (gakkapda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가까워요 ("it is close"). Watch the particle attached to 가깝다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가까워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가깝 → 가까운)
subject marked with 이/가
the set adverb 가까이 'near/close', used with motion verbs

examples.en: The subway station is close.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular in action: 가깝 + 어요 → ㅂ turns to 우 → 가까워요, not 가깝아요.

examples.en: I met a close friend after a long time.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가까운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 친구; note 가까운 친구 = a close (intimate) friend.

examples.en: Work is close, so I commute on foot.
examples.note: 가까워서 gives the reason 'because it's close'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가깝다 means close or near in distance (집이 가깝다), and just as commonly 'close' in human relationships (가까운 사이 = an intimate relationship) and 'nearly equal' (백 명에 가깝다 = close to 100). It is the opposite of 멀다 (far). Its conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: the final ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel ending, so 가깝 + 어요 → 가까워요 and the modifier is 가까운 (never 가깝아요 or 가깝은) — the same shift as 무겁다→무거워, 어렵다→어려워. It collocates with 집·역·거리·사이·친구 and with the distance reference in 에서 (여기에서 가까워요). Using the adjective 가깝다 where a place noun is needed (가깝에 있어요) — for 'in the nearby area' use 근처: 근처에 있어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 깨끗하다 means "clean" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 깨끗하다 (kkaekkeutada) = "clean". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 깨끗해요 ("it is clean") shows how it actually behaves. 하다-modifier: 하 + ㄴ → 한 (깨끗하 → 깨끗한)
subject marked with 이/가
깨끗하 + 게 → adverb 'cleanly/spotlessly' with an action verb

examples.en: This bathroom is clean.
examples.note: 하다-pattern: 깨끗하 + 여요 contracts to 깨끗해요 (the standard 해요-form).

examples.en: I drink clean water.
examples.note: The 하다-modifier 깨끗한 (하 + ㄴ) precedes 물.

examples.en: I tidied the room cleanly.
examples.note: The set adverb 깨끗이 (note spelling: -이, sounds '깨끄시') is the idiomatic 'cleanly/thoroughly'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 깨끗하다 means clean — free of dirt (깨끗한 방), but also 'pure/clear' for water and air (깨끗한 물·공기), 'fair/honest' for conduct (깨끗한 정치 = clean politics), and 'fully/completely' as the adverb 깨끗이 (깨끗이 잊다 = to forget completely). extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무겁다 means "heavy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 무겁다 (mugeopda) means "heavy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무거워요 ("it is heavy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무겁다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 무거워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (무겁 → 무거운)
subject marked with 이/가
무겁 + 게 → adverb 'heavily', also for atmosphere/mood

examples.en: This bag is too heavy.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 무겁 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 무거워요, never 무겁어요.

examples.en: I moved a heavy box by myself.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 무거운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 상자.

examples.en: My eyelids are heavy, so I'm sleepy.
examples.note: 무거워서 gives the reason; 눈꺼풀이 무겁다 is the idiomatic 'eyelids feel heavy (sleepy)'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 무겁다 means heavy in weight (무거운 가방, 짐이 무겁다), and metaphorically 'weighty/grave' for moods, responsibilities, and the body when tired — 분위기가 무겁다 (the atmosphere is heavy/tense), 책임이 무겁다 (the responsibility is heavy), 몸이 무겁다 (one's body feels sluggish), 입이 무겁다 (literally 'heavy-mouthed' = tight-lipped, can keep a secret). It is the opposite of 가볍다 (light). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel ending, giving 무거워요 and the modifier 무거운 — the same shift as 가깝다→가까워, 춥다→추워. Be careful with 무겁다 vs 어렵다: both can render English 'heavy' figuratively, but 무겁다 is 'weighty/somber', whereas 어렵다 is 'difficult' — a heavy (hard) exam is 어려운 시험, not 무거운 시험. Using 무겁다 for a hard/difficult task (시험이 무거워요) — 'difficult' is 어렵다: 시험이 어려워요. 무겁다 is weight or somber mood, not difficulty.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가볍다 means "light (in weight)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "light (in weight)" is 가볍다 (gabyeopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가벼워요 ("it is light"). Watch the particle attached to 가볍다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가벼워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가볍 → 가벼운)
subject marked with 이/가
가볍 + 게 → adverb 'lightly/casually'

examples.en: This laptop is really light.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 가볍 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.

examples.en: I bought one light bag.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가벼운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 가방.

examples.en: Today my heart feels much lighter.
examples.note: 마음이 가볍다 = to feel relieved/unburdened — a common figurative use.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가볍다 means light in weight (가벼운 가방), and figuratively 'light' in many senses: 마음이 가볍다 (heart is light/relieved), 가벼운 감기 (a mild cold), 가벼운 농담 (a light joke), 가볍게 운동하다 (to exercise lightly), and even negatively 입이 가볍다 ('light-mouthed' = can't keep a secret, the exact opposite of 입이 무겁다). A synonym note: 가볍다 covers 'light/mild', but 'easy' (simple to do) is 쉽다, so 'an easy question' is 쉬운 문제, not 가벼운 문제 — though 가벼운 문제 can mean a 'minor/trivial' issue. Be careful too that 'light' as in brightness/color is 밝다 (밝은 색 = a light/bright color), not 가볍다. It collocates with 가방·노트북·옷·마음·발걸음·농담·감기. English-speaker pitfall: writing 가볍어요 instead of 가벼워요, and stretching 가볍다 to cover 'easy' (use 쉽다) or 'light-colored' (use 밝다).

Using 가볍다 for 'easy to do' (이 문제는 가벼워요 meaning simple) — 'easy' is 쉽다: 이 문제는 쉬워요. 가볍다 is weight or 'minor', not difficulty.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 새롭다 means "new" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 새롭다 (saeropda) = "new". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 새로워요 ("it is new/fresh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 새롭다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 새로워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (새롭 → 새로운)
subject marked with 이/가
새롭 + 게 → adverb 'newly/afresh'

examples.en: This restaurant is new.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular: 새롭 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 새로워요, not 새롭어요.

examples.en: I bought a new phone.
examples.note: The ㅂ-irregular modifier 새로운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 휴대폰 — the everyday way to say 'a new ~'.

examples.en: Seeing it again, that scenery feels fresh.
examples.note: Here 새롭다 means 'feels new/striking again', the emotional 'fresh' sense, not 'newly made'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 새롭다 means new in the sense of 'fresh, novel, renewed' — a new method, a fresh feeling, a renewed resolve (새로운 방법, 마음이 새롭다, 각오가 새롭다). Crucially it differs from the determiner 새 ('brand-new', placed directly before a noun): 새 (no conjugation) labels a physically new object — 새 차 (a brand-new car), 새 옷 (new clothes) — while 새롭다 is a full adjective expressing that something is novel or feels fresh, so '새 차' is a car just bought, but '느낌이 새로워요' means 'the feeling is fresh/novel'. Both translate as 'new', but you cannot say 새로운 차 to mean a factory-fresh car the way 새 차 does (새로운 차 leans 'a different/novel kind of car'). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, giving 새로워요 and the modifier 새로운 — the same shift as 가깝다→가까워, 무겁다→무거워. It collocates with 방법·기술·세상·마음·각오·디자인. Using 새로운 for a brand-new physical object where 새 fits better — 'new shoes (just bought)' is 새 신발, not 새로운 신발; 새 is the determiner for fresh-bought items.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 의사 means "doctor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 의사 (uisa) means "doctor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 의사 선생님 ("doctor (polite address)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 의사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: add 선생님 when speaking to or about a doctor respectfully
받다 'receive' is the verb that pairs with 진료, not 하다
goal/result takes 가/이, never 을/를
에서 marks the place where an action happens

examples.en: I am a doctor.
examples.note: plain self-introduction; 예요 attaches after the vowel-final 의사

examples.en: If you catch a cold, you go to the doctor.
examples.note: 한테 = casual 'to (a person)'; note 감기에 걸리다 'be caught by a cold'

examples.ko: 할머니께서는 마을에서 오래 환자를 보신 의사세요.
examples.romanization: halmeonikkeseoneun maeureseo orae hwanjareul bosin uisaseyo.
examples.en: Grandmother is a doctor who long looked after patients in the village.
examples.note: 환자를 보다 'see patients' is the idiom for a doctor practicing

extendedVocab.nuance: 의사 is Sino-Korean 醫師 ('medicine' 醫 + 'master/teacher' 師), so the word literally frames a doctor as a master of medicine — which is why Koreans almost reflexively append 선생님 (의사 선생님) when addressing or referring to one, the way English keeps 'Doctor' as a title. Saying bare 의사 to or about a specific physician can sound flat or even slightly disrespectful, like calling them 'the doc'. Distinguish 의사 (the licensed physician) from 의자 'chair', which differs by a single vowel and trips up beginners constantly, and from 환자 'patient' and 간호사 'nurse', the other people in the room. The natural verb is 환자를 보다 ('see patients') or 진료를 보다/받다, never the English-style '의사를 하다'; a doctor 의사가 되다 ('becomes' a doctor), with the goal marked by 가, not 을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의사님 by analogy with other -님 titles; Koreans actually say 의사 선생님, treating 선생님 itself as the honorific.
Writing 의사를 되고 싶어요 with 를; the thing you become takes 가/이, so it must be 의사가 되고 싶어요.
Confusing 의사 'doctor' with the near-identical 의자 'chair' — one wrong vowel changes the whole sentence.

extendedVocab.explanation: "nurse" is 간호사 (ganhosa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 간호사 선생님 ("nurse (polite address)"). usagePhrases.note: like doctors, nurses are addressed with 선생님 in clinics
the fixed verb is 놓다 'place', not 주다 'give'
resultative goal marked with 가

examples.en: I am a nurse.

extendedVocab.nuance: 간호사 is 看護師 ('watch over' 看 + 'protect' 護 + 'master' 師) — the picture is someone who watches over and protects the sick, a warmer image than the English 'nurse'. The crucial register point is that today 간호사 is fully gender-neutral and is the only respectful current term; the older 간호원 (with 員 'staff member') now sounds dated and faintly demeaning, much like 'stewardess' in English, so avoid it. Don't confuse 간호사 with 간병인, the paid caregiver who attends a patient's daily needs (eating, washing) but holds no nursing license. Beginners also overuse 주다 for injections — the locked collocation is 주사를 놓다 ('place a shot'), and you 'receive' one with 주사를 맞다, literally 'get hit by a shot'. As with all jobs ending in a vowel, the copula is 예요 (간호사예요), and one 간호사가 된다, not 를 된다.

Saying 주사를 주다 'give a shot' by translating English; the set phrase is 주사를 놓다, and the patient side is 주사를 맞다.
Mixing up 간호사 (licensed nurse) with 간병인 (unlicensed bedside caregiver).

extendedVocab.nuance: 경찰 is 警察 ('warn/be alert' 警 + 'inspect/observe' 察) — literally 'to watch alertly', capturing policing as vigilant observation. The word is flexible: by context it can mean the police force as an institution ('경찰이 수사 중이다', the police are investigating) or a single officer on the street, so to single out one human being unambiguously Koreans prefer 경찰관 (官 'official'). Saying 경찰예요 after a consonant; it must be 경찰이에요.
Using 경찰에게 신고하다 for reporting a crime; the institution-level idiom is 경찰에 신고하다 (에, not 에게).

extendedVocab.explanation: 요리사 (yorisa) means "cook". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 요리를 하다 ("cook / do the cooking"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요리사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the activity is 요리를 하다; the person is 요리사
에서 marks the workplace where cooking happens
goal of becoming marked with 가
만들다 'make' is the everyday verb for preparing dishes

examples.en: I am a cook.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 요리사

examples.en: The kimchi stew the cook made is really delicious.
examples.note: 만든 = past modifier of 만들다 describing the food

examples.ko: 제 꿈은 호텔에서 일하는 셰프가 되는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je kkumeun hotereseo ilhaneun syepeuga doeneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My dream is to become a chef working at a hotel.
examples.note: -는 거예요 nominalizes the goal; note 셰프 for a high-end chef

extendedVocab.nuance: 요리사 is 料理師 ('prepare/measure ingredients' 料 + 'arrange/manage' 理 + 'master' 師), so it frames cooking as the skilled craft of arranging ingredients. It refers to a professional who cooks for a living; the loanword 셰프 (chef) carries more prestige and a Western fine-dining flavor, while a traditional master cook may be called 조리사 (the term used on official culinary licenses) — overlapping but 조리사 sounds more institutional/cafeteria, 요리사 more general, 셰프 more upscale. The classic beginner slip is confusing the person 요리사 with the activity/dish 요리: '요리가 맛있어요' praises the food, '요리사가 친절해요' describes the person. Remember the activity is 요리를 하다 (do cooking), never '요리사를 하다'. Since the word ends in a vowel, it is 요리사예요, and one 요리사가 된다.

Confusing 요리사 (the cook) with 요리 (the cooking/dish): 요리를 하다 'to cook' vs 요리사가 되다 'to become a cook'.
Saying 요리사를 하다 for 'to cook'; the verb attaches to the activity 요리, so it is 요리를 하다.
Assuming 셰프 and 요리사 are identical; 셰프 specifically implies a Western-style or head chef, often at a hotel or fine restaurant.

extendedVocab.explanation: "singer" is 가수 (gasu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 노래를 부르다 ("sing a song"). object of liking takes 를
resultative goal marked with 가
서다 'stand'; 에 marks where one stands

examples.en: I am a singer.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel of 가수

examples.en: I really like that singer.
examples.note: 를 marks 가수 as the object of 좋아하다

examples.ko: 동생은 데뷔를 준비하는 연습생이라 아직 가수는 아니에요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengeun debwireul junbihaneun yeonseupsaengira ajik gasuneun anieyo.
examples.en: My sibling is a trainee preparing to debut, so not yet a singer.
examples.note: 연습생 'trainee'; -(이)라 'being, since'; 데뷔 'debut'

extendedVocab.nuance: 가수 is 歌手 ('song' 歌 + 'hand/skilled person' 手), a Sino-Korean pattern where 手 turns an art into the person who does it (compare 선수 'player', 가수 'singer'). It means a professional or recognized singer who performs for an audience; merely singing in the shower is 노래하다 or 노래를 부르다, and you would never call yourself a 가수 for that — claiming it implies you do it as a career, so Koreans distinguish a 가수 from a 연습생 (idol trainee not yet debuted) or someone who just '노래를 잘해요'. Note that the act of singing uses 부르다 ('노래를 부르다'), the very same verb as calling someone, which surprises learners. Saying 노래를 하다 and assuming it equals 부르다; the natural collocation for performing a song is 노래를 부르다.
Using 가수가 좋아해요 to mean 'I like the singer'; the singer is the object, so it must be 가수를 좋아해요.

나오다 'come out/appear'; 에 marks the work it appears in

examples.en: I am an actor.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 배우

examples.note: 연기를 잘하다 'be good at acting' is the set phrase

examples.ko: 이 드라마에는 유명한 배우들이 많이 나와요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 배우 is 俳優 (both 俳 and 優 historically meant 'performer/entertainer'), an old Sino-Korean compound that already covers actors of any gender in film, TV drama, and theater — so there is no need to mark gender, and the English loan 액터 is essentially never used in normal speech. The thing an actor does is 연기 'acting' (연기를 하다 / 연기를 잘하다), not '배우를 하다'; that 연기 vs 배우 split (craft vs person) mirrors 요리 vs 요리사 and trips learners up. The verb 나오다 ('come out') is the idiomatic way to say an actor 'appears in' a film or show. After the vowel, the copula is 배우예요, and one 배우가 된다.

Saying 배우를 하다 for 'to act'; the activity is 연기, so use 연기를 하다 or 연기를 잘하다.
Confusing 배우 (actor) with the wider 연예인 (any entertainer/celebrity), which also includes singers and comedians.

따다 'pick/win' is the verb for earning a medal
goal of becoming marked with 가

examples.en: I am an athlete.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel of 운동선수

examples.ko: 그 선수가 마지막에 골을 넣어서 이겼어요.
examples.romanization: geu seonsuga majimage goreul neoeoseo igyeosseoyo.

For a particular sport, swap in the sport name plus 선수: 축구 선수 (soccer), 야구 선수 (baseball), 수영 선수 (swimming); the bare 선수 is fine once context is clear ('그 선수가 빨라요'). Idiomatic partners include 메달을 따다 (win a medal) and 골을 넣다 (score a goal). Since the word ends in a vowel it is 운동선수예요, and one 운동선수가 된다, the goal marked by 가.

Calling a casual gym-goer a 운동선수; if they just exercise for health, say 운동을 해요, not 운동선수예요.
Saying 운동선수를 하다 for playing sports; the activity verb is 운동을 하다, and 선수 is the person.
Using 메달을 받다 'receive a medal' when the natural sporting idiom is 메달을 따다 'win a medal'.

Crucially, keep the legal-profession trio straight, since they share the 士/事 family but are different jobs: 변호사 (lawyer who represents you), 판사 (判事, the judge who decides), and 검사 (檢事, the prosecutor who charges); beginners frequently swap 변호사 and 판사. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기자 means "reporter" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기자 (gija) = "reporter". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기사를 쓰다 ("write an article") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기사 'news article' takes 쓰다; don't confuse with 기자 the person
취재 is the journalist's fieldwork; 하다 pairs with it
에서 marks the workplace
에게 marks the person questioned

examples.en: I am a reporter.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 기자

examples.en: The reporter asked the mayor a sharp question.
examples.note: 에게 marks 시장 as the person asked; 날카롭다 'sharp'

examples.ko: 선배는 십 년째 정치부에서 일하는 베테랑 기자예요.
examples.romanization: seonbaeneun sim nyeonjjae jeongchibueseo ilhaneun beterang gijayeyo.
examples.en: My senior is a veteran reporter who has worked the politics desk for ten years.
examples.note: -째 'for/into (a period)'; 정치부 'politics desk'

extendedVocab.nuance: 기자 is 記者 ('record/write down' 記 + 'person' 者), literally 'a person who records' — the 者 'person' suffix marks an agent (compare 학자 scholar, 독자 reader). It means a reporter/journalist who gathers and writes news; address one respectfully as 기자님. The pitfall is the near-homophone trap among 기자 (the reporter), 기사 (記事, the article they write — also 'driver' as in 택시 기사, a different word), and 작가 (作家, an author of books/scripts): you 기사를 쓰다 (write an article) but a 기자 is the human who does it, and a novelist is a 작가, not a 기자. Their core fieldwork verb is 취재하다 ('cover/gather news'), and they 인터뷰를 하다 (do interviews). Since 기자 ends in a vowel the copula is 기자예요, and questions to one take 에게/한테 (기자에게 질문하다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 기자 (the reporter) with 기사 (the article, or a driver); you write 기사를 쓰다, but the person is the 기자.
Confusing 기자 with 작가; a journalist is 기자, but a book/screenplay author is 작가.
Saying 기자를 질문하다; you ask to someone, so it is 기자에게/한테 질문하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 군인 means "soldier" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 군인 (gunin) means "soldier". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 나라를 지키다 ("protect the country"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 군인 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 지키다 'guard/protect'; the prototypical soldier's duty
군대 'the army (as an institution/service)'; 에 marks it
복무하다 is the formal verb for doing service; 으로 'as'
군 복무 is the standard phrase for the mandatory term

examples.en: I am a soldier.
examples.note: 이에요 after the consonant ending of 군인

examples.ko: 사촌 형은 지금 군대에서 군인으로 복무하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: sachon hyeongeun jigeum gundaeeseo gunineuro bongmuhago isseoyo.
examples.en: My cousin is now serving as a soldier in the military.
examples.note: 군대에서 'in the army'; -고 있다 'be (currently) doing'

examples.ko: 할아버지께서는 젊을 때 나라를 지킨 군인이셨어요.
examples.romanization: harabeojikkeseoneun jeolmeul ttae narareul jikin guninisyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandfather was a soldier who protected the country when he was young.
examples.note: -(으)셨- past honorific; 지킨 past modifier of 지키다

extendedVocab.nuance: 군인 is 軍人 ('army/military' 軍 + 'person' 人), the general word for any member of the armed forces. Distinguish three related terms learners blur: 군인 (a soldier, the person), 군대 (軍隊, the military as an institution or one's term of service — '군대에 가다' means to join up / do one's service), and 병사 (兵士, an enlisted rank specifically, more technical/military-register). In Korea, because of mandatory service, most young men 군대에 가다 and spend a stretch as a 군인, so '군 복무' (military service) is everyday vocabulary. The prototype verb is 나라를 지키다 ('protect the country'), and one serves 군인으로 복무하다 with the role-marking 으로. The critical grammar trap: 군인 ends in a consonant, so the copula is 이에요 (군인이에요) — never 군인예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 군인예요 after a consonant; it must be 군인이에요.
Confusing 군인 (a soldier, the person) with 군대 (the military institution / one's service term): '군대에 가요' = go do military service.
Using 군인을 가다 for 'join the army'; you go to the institution, so it is 군대에 가다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 농부 means "farmer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "farmer" is 농부 (nongbu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 농사를 짓다 ("farm / do farming"). Watch the particle attached to 농부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the activity is 농사 + 짓다, a fixed pair (literally 'build farming')
밭 'dry field'; 에서 marks where the work happens
키우다 'raise/grow' for crops and animals
시골 'rural area'; 에서 marks the place of living

examples.en: I am a farmer.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 농부

examples.ko: 농부가 아침 일찍 밭에 나가서 일해요.
examples.romanization: nongbuga achim iljjik bate nagaseo ilhaeyo.
examples.en: The farmer goes out to the field early in the morning and works.
examples.note: 나가다 'go out'; -아/어서 chains the actions

examples.ko: 할아버지는 평생 시골에서 농사를 지으신 농부세요.
examples.romanization: harabeojineun pyeongsaeng sigoreseo nongsareul jieusin nongbuseyo.
examples.en: Grandfather is a farmer who farmed in the countryside his whole life.
examples.note: 농사를 짓다 'to farm'; -(으)시- adds respect

extendedVocab.nuance: 농부 is 農夫 ('farming/agriculture' 農 + 'man/laborer' 夫), and that 夫 'man' element historically skews male, though in practice 농부 is used broadly today; a more neutral, modern alternative is 농민 (農民, 'farming people', common in news and policy) or the polite 농사꾼. The activity is 농사 ('farming'), joined by the irregular collocation 농사를 짓다 — literally 'to build/make farming', the same 짓다 used in 밥을 짓다 'cook rice' and 집을 짓다 'build a house'; never say '농부를 하다'. Keep the worker apart from the place and the work: 농부 (farmer) vs 농장 (the farm) vs 농사 (farming). Crops and livestock are 키우다 ('raise'). Since 농부 ends in a vowel, the copula is 농부예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 농부 (the farmer) with 농장 (the farm) or 농사 (farming): you 농사를 지어요 'do farming', but the person is the 농부.
Saying 농사를 하다; the locked verb is 농사를 짓다 (the same 짓다 as in 밥을 짓다).
Treating 농부 as strictly female-excluding when speaking generally; for a neutral or formal tone, 농민 is often preferred.

extendedVocab.explanation: 미용사 (miyongsa) = "hairdresser". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 머리를 자르다 ("cut hair") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 미용사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 머리 here = 'hair'; 자르다 'cut' is the everyday verb
에서 marks the workplace 미용실
파마 (from 'permanent') + 하다 for the styling service
goal of becoming marked with 가

examples.en: I am a hairdresser.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel of 미용사

examples.ko: 미용사가 제 머리를 예쁘게 잘라 줬어요.
examples.romanization: miyongsaga je meorireul yeppeuge jalla jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The hairdresser cut my hair nicely (for me).
examples.note: -아/어 주다 marks the service done for you; 예쁘게 'prettily'

examples.ko: 저 미용실 디자이너 선생님은 손님이 끊이지 않아요.
examples.romanization: jeo miyongsil dijaineo seonsaengnimeun sonnimi kkeuniji anayo.
examples.en: That salon's stylist never runs out of customers.
examples.note: 디자이너/선생님 are common in-salon address terms; 끊이지 않다 'never cease'

extendedVocab.nuance: 미용사 is 美容師 ('beauty' 美 + 'appearance/looks' 容 + 'master' 師) — literally a 'master of beautifying one's appearance', so it can cover hair, and historically skin/nails, though everyday use centers on hair. Don't confuse the worker with the workplace: the 미용사 works in a 미용실 (or the trendier loanword 헤어숍), so '미용실에 가요' means going to the salon, not the person. In real salons, customers and staff often address stylists as 디자이너(님) or 선생님 rather than the clinical-sounding 미용사, which is more of a job-category label; 미용사 vs 이발사 also matters — 이발사 is specifically a (traditionally men's) barber at a 이발소. The core verbs are 머리를 자르다 (cut hair) and 파마를 하다 (get a perm). After the vowel the copula is 미용사예요, and one 미용사가 된다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 미용사 (the worker) with 미용실 (the salon): '미용실에 가요' = go to the salon, while 미용사가 잘라요 = the hairdresser cuts.
Calling a traditional men's barber a 미용사; that role is 이발사, working at an 이발소.
Saying 머리를 깎다 for a haircut at a salon when 머리를 자르다 is the neutral choice (깎다 leans toward clippers/shaving very short).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교실 means "classroom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 교실 (gyosil) means "classroom". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교실에 ("to the classroom"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교실 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: destination 에: 교실에 가다 = go to the classroom
action-place 에서: 교실에서 공부하다
우리 here means 'my/our' group's room, very natural
넓다 = spacious; subject takes 이

examples.en: Where is the classroom?
examples.note: Simple location question; 이 marks the subject of 어디예요

examples.en: I chat with a friend in the classroom.
examples.note: 에서 = the place an action happens; 하고 = 'with'

examples.en: Class ended, so the students left the classroom.
examples.note: 나가다 takes 에서 (out from a place), never 에

extendedVocab.nuance: 교실 is Sino-Korean 教室 — 教 'teach' + 室 'room', literally 'teaching room', i.e. the single physical room where one class meets. The key contrast is 교실 vs 학교(學校 'school'): 학교 is the whole institution/campus, while 교실 is just one room inside it — so 'I'm at school' is 학교에 있어요, not 교실에 있어요 unless you literally mean the room. Also distinguish 교실 (the room) from 수업(授業, the lesson/class period that takes place in it). The everyday particle split is the trap for English speakers: use 에 when the room is a destination you move toward (교실에 들어가다 'enter the classroom'), but 에서 when you do an activity inside it (교실에서 발표하다 'present in the classroom'). English 'in the classroom' maps to 에서 only for actions; for static existence you say 교실에 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 학교 when you mean one room — 학교 is the whole school; the single room is 교실.
Using 에 for an action done inside (교실에 공부해요 ✗). An activity inside a place needs 에서: 교실에서 공부해요 ✓. Keep 에 only for going there or for 있다/없다.
Mapping English 'leave the classroom' to 교실에 나가다 ✗ — exiting a place uses 에서: 교실에서 나가다 ✓.

structuredNuance.t: 교실 is the single physical room where one class meets.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 숙제 means "homework" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "homework" is 숙제 (sukje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 숙제를 하다 ("do homework"). Watch the particle attached to 숙제 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The fixed verb is 하다, never 만들다; object takes 를
많다 = many/much; the amount is the subject, so 가
내다 = submit/turn in (also 제출하다, more formal)
Noun-noun compound; 숙제 takes the subject as a modifier

examples.en: Did you finish all your homework?
examples.note: Casual question; 다 = 'all/completely', a very common collocation with 하다

examples.en: Today there isn't much homework.
examples.note: 별로 + negative = 'not really/not much'; amount is the subject (가)

examples.en: I forgot the homework and didn't bring it.
examples.note: 깜빡하다 = 'absent-mindedly forget', the natural verb students use

extendedVocab.nuance: 숙제 is Sino-Korean 宿題 — 宿 'lodging/stay overnight' + 題 'topic/problem', literally a 'problem to take home overnight', i.e. work a teacher assigns to be done outside class. The verb is locked: Koreans say 숙제를 하다 'do homework', and 숙제를 내다 means a student turns it in (while a teacher 내다 a 숙제 means 'assign/set' it — context decides). Contrast 숙제 with 공부(工夫, 'study') and 과제(課題, 'assignment/coursework'): 공부하다 is the broad act of studying anything, whereas 숙제 is a specific assigned task, and 과제 is the more formal university word for a project or paper. The big English-speaker pitfall is translating 'do my homework' as 숙제를 만들다 'make homework' (✗ — that sounds like you created the assignment) or 숙제를 공부하다 (✗); the only natural pairing is 숙제를 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 숙제를 만들다 ('make homework') instead of 숙제를 하다 — 만들다 means create the task itself, not complete it.
Using 숙제를 공부하다 ✗. 공부하다 is general study; the set phrase to complete assigned work is 숙제를 하다.
Treating 숙제 as countable English plural and dropping the particle. You still need 를: 숙제를 했어요, not 숙제 했어요 in writing/formal speech.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시험 means "exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 시험 (siheom) = "exam". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험을 보다 ("take an exam") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시험, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed verb is 보다 (literally 'see'), never 하다
Existence/scheduling; the exam is the subject, so 이
붙다 'stick' = pass, 떨어지다 'fall' = fail; both take 에
기말(期末) = end of term; cf. 중간 시험 = midterm

examples.en: Is there an exam tomorrow?
examples.note: Casual; 있어요 used for a scheduled event existing

examples.en: I took the Korean exam yesterday.
examples.note: 봤어요 = past of 보다; the set phrase 시험을 보다

examples.en: I studied hard so I passed the exam.
examples.note: Pass = 시험에 붙다; note the particle is 에, not 를

extendedVocab.nuance: 시험 is Sino-Korean 試驗 — 試 'try/test' + 驗 'examine', literally 'a trial examination'. The collocation English speakers must memorize is 시험을 보다 — Koreans 'see' an exam, they do not 'do' it, so 시험을 하다 is wrong. Passing and failing are vivid metaphors with the particle 에: 시험에 붙다 (literally 'stick to the exam') = pass, 시험에 떨어지다 ('fall off the exam') = fail — note these take 에, not 을. extendedVocab.explanation: 수업 (sueop) means "class / lesson". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수업을 듣다 ("take / attend a class"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수업 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 듣다 'listen' is the set verb for attending a class
Scheduling; the class is the subject, so 이
늦다 takes 에 for the event you're late to
Subject-noun modifier; cf. 수학 수업 'math class'

examples.en: Do you have class today?
examples.note: Casual schedule check; 있어요 for a class existing on the timetable

examples.en: I usually attend class diligently.
examples.note: 수업을 듣다 = attend; 열심히 = 'diligently', a habitual collocation

examples.en: I'm sorry for being late to class.
examples.note: 늦다 + 에 marks the event; -아서 gives the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 수업 is Sino-Korean 授業 — 授 'give/confer' + 業 'work/study', literally 'conferring instruction', i.e. the lesson or class session itself (the activity and time period). The set verb is 수업을 듣다 'listen to a class' = attend/take it; from the teacher's side it is 수업을 하다 'give/teach a class'. Three near-neighbors confuse learners: 수업 (the lesson event) vs 교실(教室, the room it happens in) vs 과목(科目, the subject like 'math' or 'history') vs 강의(講義, a university lecture). So 'I have three classes today' = 수업 세 개, but 'I take three subjects' = 과목 세 개. The English-speaker pitfall is using 하다 to mean 'take a class' (수업을 하다 actually means 'to teach', which is what a professor does) — as a student you 듣다 a class. Also, 'go to class' is 수업에 가다 (event as destination with 에).

Confusing 수업 (lesson) with 교실 (room): you 'attend a 수업', but you 'sit in a 교실'.

extendedVocab.explanation: "notebook" is 공책 (gongchaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공책에 쓰다 ("write in a notebook"). Watch the particle attached to 공책 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Surface/destination of writing takes 에
Object takes 를; everyday shopping verb 사다
Counter is 권 (for bound paper goods), not 개
새 is a pre-noun modifier; no 의 needed

examples.en: Do you have a notebook?
examples.note: Simple possession question; 있어요 = have/exist

examples.en: I organize vocabulary in my notebook.
examples.note: 에 marks the writing surface; 정리하다 = 'tidy up/organize'

examples.en: Please give me just one notebook.
examples.note: 권 counts bound books; 만 = 'just/only'; 주세요 = polite request

extendedVocab.nuance: 공책 is Sino-Korean 空冊 — 空 'empty' + 冊 'book/volume', literally an 'empty book', i.e. a blank bound notebook for writing in. Because it is a 冊, it is counted with the unit 권 (공책 한 권), exactly like 책 'book' — counting it with 개 is the classic foreigner slip. In real life Koreans very often just say the English loanword 노트 (from 'note'); 공책 sounds slightly more textbook/childlike, while 노트 is the casual everyday choice, and a 'notebook computer' is 노트북 — don't confuse the three. Contrast 공책 (paper to write in) with 교과서(教科書, 'textbook' you read from) and 수첩(手帖, a small pocket planner/memo book). The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (use 권, not 개) and assuming 'notebook' must be 공책 — in conversation 노트 is more natural, and never let 노트북 slip in when you mean the paper kind.

Counting it with 개: 공책 한 개 ✗. Bound paper goods use 권: 공책 한 권 ✓.
Confusing 노트 (notebook) with 노트북 (laptop). 공책 = 노트; a laptop computer is 노트북.
Using 에서 for the writing surface: 공책에서 쓰다 ✗. Writing onto a surface takes 에: 공책에 쓰다 ✓.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 연필 means "pencil" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 연필 (yeonpil) = "pencil". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연필로 쓰다 ("write with a pencil") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연필, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument/tool takes 로/으로
깎다 = shave/sharpen, the set verb for pencils
Counter 자루 for long thin sticks (pens, brushes)
色 'color' + 연필; a common compound

examples.en: Please lend me a pencil.
examples.note: 좀 softens the request; 빌려주다 = lend (to me)

examples.ko: 저는 시험 볼 때 연필로 써요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun siheom bol ttae yeonpillo sseoyo.
examples.en: I write with a pencil when taking exams.
examples.note: 로 marks the tool; -ㄹ 때 = 'when ~ing'

examples.en: The pencil is blunt, so I need to sharpen it.
examples.note: 연필을 깎다 = sharpen; -아야 하다 = 'have to'

extendedVocab.nuance: 연필 is Sino-Korean 鉛筆 — 鉛 'lead' + 筆 'writing brush/pen', literally 'lead pen', the wooden graphite pencil. The instrument particle 로/으로 is essential: you write 연필로 ('with/by means of a pencil'), and the matching verb for upkeep is 연필을 깎다 'shave the pencil' = sharpen it. The counter 자루 is used for long slender objects (pens, pencils, brushes, even umbrellas) — 연필 한 자루 — so don't default to 개. Contrast the writing tools clearly: 연필 (pencil, erasable) vs 볼펜(ballpoint pen) vs 샤프(mechanical 'sharp' pencil) vs 펜(pen, general). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle — 'write with a pencil' must be 연필로, not 연필을 (학생이 연필을 써요 means 'uses a pencil' as an object, fine, but 'by means of' is 연필로); and English 'sharpen' tempts learners toward a 'make sharp' calque, when the idiomatic verb is the everyday 깎다 (the same verb used for peeling fruit).

Using 개 to count: 연필 한 개 sounds off; long thin items take 자루 — 연필 한 자루.
Saying 연필을 쓰다 when you mean 'write WITH a pencil' as the means — that needs the tool particle: 연필로 써요.
Confusing 연필 (pencil) with 볼펜 (pen). They are different tools; a ballpoint is 볼펜, a mechanical pencil is 샤프.

extendedVocab.explanation: 지우개 (jiugae) means "eraser". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지우개로 지우다 ("erase with an eraser"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 지우개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: Tool particle 로 + the verb 지우다 it derives from
Existence/possession; subject takes 가
빌리다 = borrow (from someone); object takes 를
Small everyday item often counted with native 하나/한 개

examples.en: Do you have an eraser?
examples.note: Quick classroom ask; 있어요 = have

examples.en: I write with a pencil and erase with an eraser.
examples.note: Parallel 로 ... 로 for two tools; 지우개로 지우다

examples.en: Could you lend me an eraser?
examples.note: -ㄹ 수 있다 = 'can'; a polite, softer request than 주세요

extendedVocab.nuance: 지우개 is a pure native-Korean word (not Sino-Korean): the verb stem 지우- 'to erase/remove' + the productive suffix -개 'a tool/instrument for ~ing'. That -개 pattern is worth learning because it builds many tool nouns the same way — 베다→베개 'pillow (cutting-rest tool)', 덮다→덮개 'cover', 따다→따개 'opener' — so 지우개 transparently means 'erasing-tool'. It pairs naturally with 연필 (you erase pencil, 연필로 쓴 것을 지우개로 지우다) and the tool particle is 로: 지우개로 지우다. Watch the verb/noun split: 지우다 is the verb 'to erase' and 지우개 is the object; a beginner who says 지우개해요 for 'I erase' is mixing them — the verb is 지워요. Korean erasers are often called 고무지우개 ('rubber eraser') when emphasizing material, and a whiteboard eraser is 칠판지우개.

Mixing the noun and its verb: saying 지우개하다 for 'to erase' ✗. The verb is 지우다 (지워요); 지우개 is only the object.
Dropping the tool particle: 지우개 지우다 ✗ in careful speech — use 로: 지우개로 지워요.
Calling it a 'rubber' by direct calque (고무 alone) — 고무 just means rubber; the eraser is 지우개 (or 고무지우개 if the material matters).

extendedVocab.explanation: "blackboard" is 칠판 (chilpan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 칠판에 쓰다 ("write on the board"). Watch the particle attached to 칠판 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Surface/destination takes 에
보다 'look at'; object takes 를
지우다 = wipe/erase the board
Position noun 앞; 칠판 앞에 서다 'stand in front of the board'

examples.en: Please look at the board.
examples.note: Teacher's instruction; 보세요 = polite imperative

examples.en: The teacher wrote the answer on the board.
examples.note: 에 marks the writing surface; 썼어요 past of 쓰다

examples.en: I couldn't see the board, so I moved forward.
examples.note: 보이다 'be visible' (≠ 보다); -아서 gives the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 칠판 is Sino-Korean 漆板 — 漆 'lacquer/black paint' + 板 'board/plank', literally a 'lacquered (black) board', the writing board at the front of a classroom. The two everyday actions split by particle: write ON it = 칠판에 쓰다 (surface destination with 에), but look AT it = 칠판을 보다 (object with 를). Many modern rooms have a white 화이트보드 (whiteboard, written with markers) instead of a chalk 칠판, but 칠판 still serves as the generic word for 'the board'. A subtle contrast English speakers miss: 보다 'look at' the board is intentional looking, whereas 보이다 'the board is/ isn't visible' is the spontaneous can-see verb — '칠판이 안 보여요' = 'I can't see the board', not '칠판을 안 봐요' ('I'm not looking at the board'). The pitfall is keeping the particles straight: 에 for writing on, 을 for looking at, and reaching for 보이다 (not 보다) when the issue is visibility.

Using 을 for writing on it: 칠판을 쓰다 ✗ (that sounds like 'use the board'). Writing onto a surface needs 에: 칠판에 쓰다.
Saying 칠판을 안 봐요 to mean 'I can't see the board'. That means 'I'm not looking at it'. For visibility use 보이다: 칠판이 안 보여요.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방학, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Time point/period takes 에: 방학에 여행하다
School 'goes on vacation'; 하다 here = the break begins
Season + 방학; cf. 겨울 방학 'winter break'
끝나다 = come to an end; subject takes 이

examples.en: When is the break?
examples.note: Simple schedule question; 이에요 = 'it is'

examples.en: I want to go to Korea during the break.
examples.note: 에 marks the time; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: I worked a part-time job during the break.
examples.note: 동안 = 'for the duration of'; a very common time collocation

extendedVocab.nuance: 방학 is Sino-Korean 放學 — 放 'release/let go' + 學 'studies', literally 'releasing (from) studies', i.e. the official school break between terms (summer/winter). The crucial contrast is 방학 vs 휴가(休暇, 'leave/holiday'): 방학 belongs to the school calendar and applies to students/teachers, while 휴가 is the time off a worker takes from a job — a salaried adult on vacation is 휴가 중, never 방학 중. Also distinguish 방학 (a scheduled school break) from 휴일(休日, a single day off / public holiday like a national holiday) and 연휴(連休, a string of consecutive holidays). Note 방학을 하다 means '(the school) goes on break / break starts', an event, not 'I take a vacation'. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a working adult's trip 방학 (it must be 휴가), and forgetting that 'during vacation' uses the time particle 에 (방학에) or the duration noun 동안 (방학 동안), not 에서.

Saying 방학에서 for 'during vacation' ✗. A time period takes 에 (방학에) or 동안 (방학 동안); 에서 is for places/actions.
Confusing 방학 (a multi-week term break) with 휴일 (a single day off) or 연휴 (a holiday stretch).

답하다 takes 에 for the question being answered
받다 = receive; what a speaker does at Q&A

examples.en: Any questions?
examples.note: Standard classroom check; 있어요 = exist/have

examples.en: I asked the teacher a question.
examples.note: 께 = honorific 'to' (for a teacher); 질문을 하다 = ask

examples.en: Good question. Let's think about it together.
examples.note: 좋은 질문 is a fixed compliment; -아 보다 = 'try ~ing'

extendedVocab.nuance: 질문 is Sino-Korean 質問 — 質 'substance/inquire into' + 問 'ask', literally 'to inquire and ask', i.e. a question put to someone. The set verb is 질문을 하다 (or the single verb 질문하다); the person you ask takes 에게/한테 (or honorific 께 for a teacher): 선생님께 질문을 하다. Its natural partner is 대답/답(答) — a 질문 is answered by a 대답. The big redundancy trap for English speakers is 질문을 물어보다 ✗: 물어보다 already means 'to ask', so this literally says 'ask a question-asking' — say either 질문을 하다 or just 물어보다, never both. Distinguish 질문 (a question seeking information/an answer) from 문제(問題, a 'problem' or exam item) — '3 questions on the test' are 문제 세 개, but 'I have a question for you' is 질문이 있어요. Note answering takes 에: 질문에 답하다, not 질문을 답하다.

Saying 질문을 물어보다 ✗ — 물어보다 already means 'ask', so it doubles up. Use 질문을 하다 OR 물어보다, not both.
Using 를 to answer: 질문을 답하다 ✗. 답하다 takes 에: 질문에 답하다 / 질문에 대답하다.
Using 질문 for an exam item. A test question/problem is 문제; 질문 is a question you ask a person for an answer.
