extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 신호등 means "traffic light" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 신호등 (sinhodeung) = "traffic light". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 빨간 신호등 ("red light") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 신호등, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 빨간 modifies it; the stop signal
바뀌다 = the color turns
지키다 = keep/observe the signal

usagePhrases.en: I stop in front of the light
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place of stopping

examples.en: The traffic light is red.
examples.note: Simple sentence; 색 names the color directly.

examples.en: Cross when the light turns green.
examples.note: Everyday: 면 (when/if) gives a condition; 초록불 = green light.

examples.ko: 신호등을 안 지키고 건너면 정말 위험해요.
examples.romanization: sinhodeungeul an jikigo geonneomyeon jeongmal wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: It's really dangerous to cross without obeying the lights.
examples.note: Real situation: 지키다 here = obey a rule, a key collocation for signals.

extendedVocab.nuance: 신호등 (信號燈, literally 'signal-lamp', 信號 = signal + 燈 = lamp) is the colored traffic light that controls cars and pedestrians at a crossing. Keep it apart from the bare word 신호, which means the 'signal' itself (you can 신호를 기다리다 'wait for the signal'), whereas 신호등 is the physical lamp unit. The individual colors get -불 ('light/fire'): 빨간불 red, 노란불 yellow, 초록불/파란불 green — and note Koreans often call the green light 파란불 ('blue light') for historical color reasons, which surprises English speakers. It collocates with 바뀌다 (change), 켜지다 (light up), 지키다 (obey), 빨간/초록 (red/green), and 건너다 (cross). The pitfall: 지키다 with 신호등 does not mean 'protect the light' as the dictionary gloss 'keep' might suggest — it means 'observe/obey' the signal, an idiom that doesn't transfer literally from English.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 신호등을 지키다 as 'protect the traffic light' — here 지키다 means 'obey/observe', so it means following the signal, not guarding it.
Confusing 신호 (the signal) with 신호등 (the lamp) — say 신호를 기다리다 'wait for the signal' but 신호등이 바뀌다 'the light changes'.
Assuming the green light is always 초록불 — Koreans commonly say 파란불 ('blue light') for go, so don't be thrown when 파란불 means green.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 횡단보도 means "crosswalk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 횡단보도 (hoengdanbodo) means "crosswalk". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 횡단보도를 건너요 ("I cross at the crosswalk"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 횡단보도 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 건너다 takes 을/를 for the thing crossed
에서 marks the place
existence with 가/이 + 없다
앞 = the spot just before it

examples.en: Please cross at the crosswalk.
examples.note: Simple instruction; 로 marks the route you cross by.

examples.en: I cross the crosswalk when the light is green.
examples.note: Everyday: 일 때 (when it is) sets the timing; pairs naturally with the green light.

examples.ko: 여기는 횡단보도가 멀어서 무단횡단하는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: yeogineun hoengdanbodoga meoreoseo mudanhoengdanhaneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: The crosswalk here is far, so many people jaywalk.
examples.note: Real situation: 무단횡단 = jaywalking, the opposite behavior.

extendedVocab.nuance: 횡단보도 (橫斷步道, literally 'cross-cut-walk-path': 橫斷 = cross over + 步道 = footpath) is the striped pedestrian crossing painted on the road. Its functional opposite is 무단횡단 (無斷橫斷, 'crossing without permission' = jaywalking), and the verb that pairs with it is 건너다 (cross), not 가다. Don't confuse 횡단보도 (the painted crossing) with 인도/보도 (the sidewalk you walk along) or 육교 (the pedestrian overpass). It collocates with 건너다 (cross), 기다리다 (wait), 신호등 (the light beside it), 초록불 (green light). The pitfall is the verb-and-particle pairing of 'cross': English 'cross the street' makes learners want 길에 건너요, but 건너다 takes the object marker — 길을 건너요 / 횡단보도를 건너요 — and when you mean 'by way of the crosswalk' you switch to 횡단보도로 건너요 with instrumental 로. A four-syllable Sino-Korean word, it is easy to misspell, so lock in 횡단보도.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 횡단보도에 건너요 — 건너다 takes the object marker, so it's 횡단보도를 건너요 (cross the crosswalk) or 횡단보도로 건너요 (cross by it).
Mixing up 횡단보도 (crosswalk) with 인도/보도 (sidewalk) — the crosswalk spans the road; the 인도 runs alongside it.
Using 가다 instead of 건너다 — to 'cross' you need 건너다; 가다 only means 'go', so 길을 건너다 not 길을 가다 for crossing over.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주차장 means "parking lot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "parking lot" is 주차장 (juchajang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주차장에 차를 세워요 ("I park the car in the lot"). Watch the particle attached to 주차장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I park the car in the lot
usagePhrases.note: 세우다 = bring to a stop/park

usagePhrases.en: I wait in the parking lot
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the activity place
넓다 describes its size
cost charged by time

examples.en: Where is the parking lot?
examples.note: Simple question; 가/이 marks the subject you're locating.

examples.en: I parked the car in the underground lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 에 marks the destination of parking; 지하 = underground.

examples.ko: 주말이라 백화점 주차장이 꽉 차서 한참 돌았어요.
examples.romanization: jumarira baekwajeom juchajangi kkwak chaseo hancham dorasseoyo.
examples.en: It's the weekend so the department-store lot was full and I circled for ages.
examples.note: Real situation: 꽉 차다 (be packed), 돌다 (circle looking for a spot).

extendedVocab.nuance: 주차장 (駐車場, literally 'park-car-place': 駐 = stay/park + 車 = car + 場 = ground/lot) is the lot or structure where cars are parked, sometimes free, sometimes charged by the hour. Distinguish it cleanly from the verb action 주차하다 ('to park') and from the related 場 words 정거장/정류장 (a vehicle stop) — they share the 'place' character 場 but mean very different sites, and learners blur 주차장 (cars sit) with 정거장 (vehicles pause). It collocates with 세우다 (pull in/park), 주차하다 (park), 요금 (fee), 넓다/좁다 (spacious/cramped), 지하/지상 (underground/above-ground), 만차/꽉 차다 (full). The pitfall is the directional particle: because it is a destination you 'go to', use 주차장에 가요 (static goal 에), NOT 주차장에서 가요 (에서 marks where action happens or a source) — a swap English speakers make constantly. Also park a car with 세우다 or 주차하다, not 만들다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 주차장에서 가요 to mean 'go to the parking lot' — going to a destination takes 에, so it's 주차장에 가요; 에서 marks where you do something or move out from.
Confusing 주차장 (where cars are parked) with 정거장 (where a bus/train stops) — both end in 場, but one is for parked cars, the other for boarding.
Saying 차를 주차장에 만들어요 for parking — to park you use 세우다 or 주차하다: 차를 주차장에 세워요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기름 means "gas / oil" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기름 (gireum) = "gas / oil". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기름을 넣어요 ("I put in gas") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기름, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = put in / fill up the tank
written solid; the cost of fuel
떨어지다 = run out / be used up
the proper word for kitchen oil

examples.en: There's no gas / oil.
examples.note: Simple existence sentence with 가/이 + 없다.

examples.en: I filled up the tank at the gas station.
examples.note: Everyday: 가득 = full; 주유소 = gas station, the place you 넣다 fuel.

examples.ko: 요즘 기름값이 너무 올라서 차를 잘 안 타게 돼요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gireumgapsi neomu ollaseo chareul jal an tage dwaeyo.
examples.en: Fuel prices have risen so much lately that I barely drive.
examples.note: Real situation: 기름값 (fuel price) + 오르다 (rise); a common complaint.

extendedVocab.nuance: 기름 is a native Korean word (no hanja) covering both car fuel and cooking/edible oil, so context decides whether it means gasoline or kitchen oil. The precise dividing lines: the formal/technical fuel word is 연료 (燃料, 'burn-material' = fuel in general) and the pump itself is 휘발유 (gasoline) or 경유 (diesel), while kitchen oil is properly 식용유 ('edible oil') or named by source (참기름 sesame oil, 올리브유 olive oil). So 기름 is the casual umbrella term; specialists narrow it down. It collocates with 넣다 (fill up), 값 (price → 기름값), 떨어지다 (run out), 가득 (full tank), 주유소 (gas station). The pitfall: don't say 기름을 채우다 by analogy with English 'fill up'; the idiomatic verb is 넣다 ('put in') — 기름을 넣다. And when you mean engine fuel specifically in formal contexts, English speakers reach for a loanword like 가솔린, but everyday Korean just says 기름.

Assuming 기름 only means car gasoline — it equally means cooking oil, so for the kitchen specify 식용유/참기름 to avoid 'I put gasoline in the pan'.
Saying 기름을 채워요 for 'fill up' — the natural verb is 넣다: 기름을 넣어요 (or 가득 넣다 to fill the tank).
Using a loanword like 가솔린 in casual speech — Koreans say 기름 for fuel at the pump; 가솔린/휘발유 sound technical or like a label.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 요금 means "fare / fee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 요금 (yogeum) means "fare / fee". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 요금을 내요 ("I pay the fare"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay a fee/fare
the metered charge
오르다 = rise
요금 covers utility charges too

examples.en: How much is the fare?
examples.note: Simple price question with 가/이 + 얼마.

examples.en: I paid the bus fare with a transit card.
examples.note: Everyday: 로 marks the means of payment; 내다 = pay.

examples.ko: 택시 요금이 기본요금보다 훨씬 많이 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: taeksi yogeumi gibonyogeumboda hwolssin mani nawasseoyo.
examples.en: The taxi fare came out much higher than the base fare.
examples.note: Real situation: 기본요금 (base fare), 나오다 (be tallied) — how charges 'come out'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 요금 (料金, literally 'charge-money': 料 = fee/materials + 金 = money) is the set, rate-based charge for using a service — a ride, phone line, utility, or hotel — fixed by a published tariff. Contrast it sharply with 값/가격 (the price of a physical thing you buy) and with 비용 (the broader 'cost/expense' you incur): you pay 요금 for a bus ride but 값/가격 for a bag, and you calculate total 비용 for a trip. Within transit it pairs as 버스/택시/지하철 요금 (fare), 기본요금 (base fare), 요금을 내다 (pay), 오르다/인상되다 (rise), 할인 (discount). The pitfall: English 'price' makes learners say 기차 값 for a fare, but a service charge is 요금 (기차 요금), and a ticket's price is 표 값 / 표 가격 — so the fare to ride and the price of the ticket are worded differently. Pay it with 내다, not 사다 (you don't 'buy' a fare).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기차 값 for a train fare — a service charge is 요금, so it's 기차 요금; reserve 값/가격 for the price of goods.
Using 사다 with 요금 — you 'pay' a fare with 내다 (요금을 내다), you don't 'buy' it; 사다 is for the ticket (표를 사다).
Confusing 요금 with 비용 — 요금 is the fixed rate for one service, while 비용 is overall cost/expense, so a whole trip's spending is 여행 비용, not 여행 요금.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정거장 means "stop / station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "stop / station" is 정거장 (jeonggeojang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정거장에서 내려요 ("I get off at the stop"). Watch the particle attached to 정거장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I get off at the stop
usagePhrases.note: 내리다 = get off, with 에서
the upcoming one on the route
counts distance along a line
에서 marks the waiting place

examples.en: I get off at the next stop.
examples.note: Everyday: 에서 + 내리다 is the fixed pattern for getting off.

examples.en: My place is three stops from here.
examples.note: Counting stops as a distance measure — a very common usage.

examples.en: The bus stop's location changed when it was moved.
examples.note: Real situation: 정거장 as a fixed point whose 위치 (location) can change.

extendedVocab.nuance: 정거장 (停車場, literally 'stop-car-place': 停 = halt + 車 = vehicle + 場 = ground) is a stop where a vehicle pauses to let people on and off, and it doubles as a counting unit ('two stops away'). The near-synonyms split by formality and mode: 정류장 (停留場) is the standard modern word for a bus stop (버스정류장), 정거장 sounds slightly older/literary and is also used loosely for stations, while a big rail/subway terminal is a 역 (驛, 'station'). So for a bus today most Koreans say 정류장; 역 is for trains/subway lines. It collocates with 내리다 (get off), 다음/이번 (next/this), 버스 (bus), counting 한/두/세 정거장. Two pitfalls: getting off uses 에서 + 내리다 (not 를), and English speakers blur the 場-words — keep 정거장/정류장 (a pause-and-board point) apart from 주차장 (a place cars are parked) and from 역 (a rail station building).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 정거장을 내려요 — 'get off at' takes 에서 with 내리다, so it's 정거장에서 내려요; 내리다 doesn't take the object marker for the place.
Confusing 정거장/정류장 (a stop) with 역 (a station) — use 역 for subway/train terminals (서울역) and 정류장 for a bus stop.
Mixing up 정거장 with 주차장 — both end in 場 but 정거장 is where a vehicle pauses to board, 주차장 is where cars are parked; don't swap them.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교통 means "traffic / transit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 교통 (gyotong) = "traffic / transit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교통이 복잡해요 ("traffic is heavy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 교통, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 복잡하다 = congested/complicated
buses + subway as a system
one card for fares
written solid; a road crash

examples.en: The traffic is heavy.
examples.note: Simple description; 복잡하다 is the go-to word for congestion.

examples.en: Public transit is really convenient in Seoul.
examples.note: Everyday: 대중교통 names the whole bus-and-subway system as a subject.

examples.ko: 출퇴근 시간에는 교통 체증이 심해서 지하철이 더 빨라요.
examples.romanization: chultoegeun siganeneun gyotong chejeungi simhaeseo jihacheori deo ppallayo.
examples.en: During rush hour the traffic jam is bad, so the subway is faster.
examples.note: Real situation: 교통 체증 (traffic jam), 출퇴근 (commute) — comparing modes.

extendedVocab.nuance: 교통 (交通, literally 'exchange-pass': 交 = cross/exchange + 通 = go through/communicate) is the broad abstract noun for the movement and flow of vehicles and people — the whole system of getting around, plus 'traffic' as in congestion. It is NOT a countable single vehicle: that is the pitfall — English 'a lot of traffic' is fine, but you can't use 교통 for 'a car' or 'a bus'; for those say 차/버스. Distinguish 교통 (the system/flow) from 교통수단 (交通手段, 'means of transport' = the specific modes) and from 길/도로 (the road itself). High-frequency compounds: 대중교통 (public transit), 교통카드 (transit card), 교통사고 (accident), 교통 체증/혼잡 (congestion), 교통편 (transport connection). When traffic is bad, Koreans say 교통이 복잡하다 or 길이 막히다 ('the road is blocked'); when it flows, 교통이 원활하다. Don't say 교통이 많다 for 'heavy traffic' — the natural adjective is 복잡하다 or 막히다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 교통 for a single vehicle — it means transit/traffic as a whole, not 'a car'; for one vehicle say 차, 버스, etc.
Saying 교통이 많아요 for 'heavy traffic' — the idiomatic phrasing is 교통이 복잡하다 or 길이 막히다; 많다 doesn't collocate here.
Confusing 교통 with 교통수단 — 교통 is the overall flow/system, while 교통수단 is the specific means (bus, subway, car), so 'which transport do you take?' is 무슨 교통수단, not 무슨 교통.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 인터넷 means "internet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 인터넷 (inteonet) means "internet". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 인터넷이 빨라요 ("the internet is fast"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 인터넷 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + descriptive 빠르다
fixed phrase 안 되다 = not working
instrument 으로, not 에
noun + noun compound, no particle

examples.en: The internet at our place is fast.
examples.note: topic 은 sets the scene, 이 marks the real subject 인터넷

examples.en: I buy train tickets on the internet.
examples.note: 으로 = the means/channel you act through

examples.ko: 인터넷이 안 돼서 일을 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: inteonesi an dwaeseo ireul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: The internet was down so I couldn't work.
examples.note: 안 되다 + 아서 chains the cause to the result

extendedVocab.nuance: 인터넷 is the plain loanword (from English 'internet') for the network itself, and 'to go online' is normally 인터넷을 하다 — Korean turns the bare noun into an activity with 하다 rather than coining a separate verb. Do not confuse it with 와이파이 (the local wireless signal you connect to) or 데이터 (your phone's mobile data plan): you can have 인터넷 through either. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you search 인터넷으로 (by means of the internet), never 인터넷에 — 에 would wrongly treat the internet as a static location. Also, when it stops working Koreans say 인터넷이 안 돼요 (it doesn't function), not 인터넷이 없어요, which would mean the service literally doesn't exist there.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 인터넷에 찾아요 for 'look it up online'. 에 marks a destination/location, but searching is done through a tool, so the instrument particle is required: 인터넷으로 찾아요.
Saying 인터넷을 빨라요 because English thinks of speed as something the internet 'has'. 빠르다 is a descriptive adjective, so its subject takes 이/가: 인터넷이 빨라요.
Using 인터넷이 없어요 when the connection drops. That means 'there is no internet (service) here'; for a temporary outage say 인터넷이 안 돼요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비밀번호 means "password" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "password" is 비밀번호 (bimilbeonho). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비밀번호를 입력해요 ("I enter the password"). Watch the particle attached to 비밀번호 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 + 입력하다 (type in)
casual 까먹다 in speech
subject 이 + 틀리다 (be incorrect)
object 을 + 바꾸다

examples.en: Please tell me the password.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 makes the request polite

examples.en: I forgot the password again.
examples.note: object 을; 까먹다 is casual for 잊어버리다

examples.en: This password is too easy.
examples.note: topic 는 contrasts this one against others

extendedVocab.nuance: 비밀번호 is Sino-Korean: 秘密 (비밀, 'secret') + 番號 (번호, 'number/code'), literally a 'secret number', so it naturally covers PINs and door-lock codes as well as login passwords. In casual speech almost everyone clips it to 비번, which is fine among friends but too slangy for a written form or a bank's formal prompt. The nearest neighbour is 암호 (暗號), which leans toward a cipher, secret signal, or military-style code; 비밀번호 is the ordinary everyday word you'll see on every signup screen. A common English-speaker slip is to assume you 'know' a password and reach for 알다, but for the action of typing it Korean prefers 입력하다 or 넣다 with the object marker: 비밀번호를 입력하다. When it's mistyped, say 비밀번호가 틀리다 (it's incorrect), not 비밀번호가 나쁘다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비밀번호가 입력해요 for entering it. 입력하다 is a transitive verb, so the password is its object: 비밀번호를 입력해요.
Treating 비밀번호 and 암호 as identical. 암호 suggests a cipher/secret signal; for an everyday account login the standard word is 비밀번호.
Saying 비밀번호가 안 맞아요 when you mean you forgot it. 안 맞다 = 'it doesn't match'; if you simply can't recall it, say 비밀번호를 까먹었어요/잊어버렸어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 앱 means "app" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 앱 (aep) = "app". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 앱을 깔아요 ("I install the app") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 앱, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: colloquial 깔다 for installing
object 을 + 지우다 (erase)
subject 이 + 꺼지다 (shut off)
noun compound, no particle

examples.ko: 이 앱으로 음식을 시킬 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i aebeuro eumsigeul sikil su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can order food with this app.
examples.note: 으로 = via the app; -ㄹ 수 있다 = can

examples.en: I want to install a new app.
examples.note: -고 싶다 expresses the speaker's wish

examples.en: The app suddenly closed.
examples.note: subject 이; 꺼지다 = shut off by itself

extendedVocab.nuance: 앱 is the clipped loanword from English 'app' and is now the default spoken word for a mobile application; the older borrowing 어플 (from 'application') still appears but sounds slightly dated, and the full 애플리케이션 is reserved for formal or technical writing. Note the gentle contrast with 프로그램, which Koreans tend to use for desktop/PC software, while 앱 implies the phone. For installing, the idiomatic everyday verb is 깔다 ('to lay down/spread'); 설치하다 (設置) is the more formal equivalent you'd read in a manual. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle pair: you open or install the app with 을/를 (앱을 열어요), but when it crashes on its own it becomes the subject with 이/가 — 앱이 꺼졌어요, because 꺼지다 is intransitive (it shuts off) versus 끄다 (you turn it off).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 앱이 열어요 for 'I open the app'. 열다 is transitive, so the app is the object: 앱을 열어요. (앱이 열려요 would mean 'the app opens (by itself)'.)
Calling a phone app 프로그램. Koreans reserve 프로그램 for PC software; for a smartphone app use 앱.
Using 설치하다 in casual chat. It's correct but stiff; friends say 앱을 깔다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 와이파이 is the loanword for local wireless internet (the spoken form follows the English 'Wi-Fi'), and the key distinction English speakers must hold is 와이파이 vs 데이터: 와이파이 is the free signal you join from a router, while 데이터 is your paid mobile-data allowance — running out of one doesn't affect the other. It also differs from 인터넷, the network as a whole; 와이파이 is just one way to reach it. The pitfall is the connection particle: you connect 와이파이에 (to the wifi, a destination) with 연결하다, not 와이파이로, because here the wifi is where you're attaching, not a tool you act through. And like other tech that simply stops responding, a dead signal is 와이파이가 안 돼요 (it won't function), not 와이파이가 없어요, which claims there's no network at all.

extendedVocab.nuance: 검색 is Sino-Korean: 檢 (검, 'inspect/examine') + 索 (색, 'search/seek out'), so it's the act of looking information up, especially online, and it readily becomes the verb 검색하다. usagePhrases.note: instrument 으로 + 쓰다
object 을 + 치다 (hit keys)
subject 이 + 편하다
noun compound, no particle

examples.en: I write text with the keyboard.
examples.note: 으로 = the tool; 글을 = the object written

examples.en: This keyboard is very comfortable.
examples.note: subject 이 with the adjective 편하다

examples.en: I bought a new keyboard.
examples.note: 새로 = newly (adverb); object 을

extendedVocab.nuance: 키보드 is the loanword for a computer or on-screen typing keyboard; note that a piano-style musical keyboard is also called 키보드, but the bank of keys themselves is 건반 and the Korean character layout is the 자판. 붇다 (ㄷ-irregular → 불어요) is the specific verb for noodles swelling and going soft if you wait too long; do not confuse it with 불다 'to blow'
봉지 'bag/packet' counts the sealed package; 개 also works informally
prefix-style compound: instant ramen in a cup you just add hot water to

examples.en: I like ramen.
examples.note: simple statement of preference with 을 marking the object

examples.ko: 밤에 라면을 끓여 먹으면 너무 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: bame ramyeoneul kkeuryeo meogeumyeon neomu masisseoyo.
examples.en: Ramen tastes so good when you cook and eat it at night.
examples.note: 끓여 먹다 'boil-and-eat' is the natural verb chain; note the late-night-snack culture

examples.ko: 면 다 붇기 전에 빨리 드세요.
examples.romanization: myeon da butgi jeone ppalli deuseyo.
examples.en: Eat quickly before the noodles get all soggy.
examples.note: real-table urgency; 면 = noodles, base verb 붇다 keeps ㄷ before the consonant ending 기 (붇기), 드세요 is the polite imperative

extendedVocab.nuance: 라면 to a Korean means the cheap instant noodle block you boil at home in a small pot (양은냄비), eaten with kimchi at midnight — it is comfort food and student food, not a restaurant meal. The crucial dividing line is 라면 vs 라멘: 라멘 is the Japanese-restaurant bowl with rich tonkotsu/miso broth and chashu, while 라면 is the supermarket packet (신라면, 진라면). The word came in from Japanese ラーメン (itself from Chinese 拉麵 'pulled noodles'), but in Korea it shifted to mean the instant version specifically. Register is fully casual and neutral — anyone says it. The collocation trap: you 끓이다 'boil' ramen, you do not 만들다 'make' it, and the noodles 붇다 'swell/go soggy' (ㄷ-irregular → 불어요/불었어요, but 붇기 before a consonant) rather than 'get wet' — note 붇다 is a different verb from 불다 'to blow'. English speakers also wrongly assume 라면 covers fancy ramen-shop noodles; for that you must say 라멘.

Using 라면 to mean the Japanese ramen-shop dish — that is 라멘. Mixing them up makes a Korean picture a supermarket packet, not a restaurant bowl.
Describing soggy noodles as 라면이 젖었어요 ('the ramen got wet') — the correct verb is 불었어요 (from the ㄷ-irregular base 붇다, not 불다 'to blow'), the specific word for noodles swelling and softening.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 김밥 means "gimbap; seaweed rice roll" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "gimbap; seaweed rice roll" is 김밥 (gimbap). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 김밥을 싸다 ("to roll/make gimbap"). usagePhrases.note: the verb is 싸다 'wrap', because you roll the rice and fillings in seaweed; not 만들다 for the rolling act
줄 'line/strip' is the proper counter for a whole long roll; one 줄 is cut into bite pieces
compound naming by filling: 참치 'tuna' + 김밥; menus list 야채김밥, 치즈김밥 the same way
the famous cheap chain; shows 김밥 as everyday fast food you grab on the go

examples.en: One roll of gimbap, please.
examples.note: ordering at a shop; note the counter 줄, never 개, for a whole roll

examples.ko: 소풍 갈 때 엄마가 김밥을 싸 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: sopung gal ttae eommaga gimbabeul ssa jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: When we went on a picnic, my mom rolled gimbap for us.
examples.note: 싸 주다 'roll for someone' + honorific 주셨어요; picnic-and-gimbap is a core memory

examples.ko: 김밥은 식어도 맛있어서 들고 다니기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gimbabeun sigeodo masisseoseo deulgo danigi joayo.
examples.en: Gimbap is tasty even cold, so it is great to carry around.
examples.note: real reasoning with -아서; explains why it is the go-to portable food

extendedVocab.nuance: 김밥 is steamed rice and fillings (egg, pickled radish, carrot, spinach, ham) rolled in dried laver and sliced into bite-size pieces — cheap, portable, the definitive picnic and lunchbox food. The name transparently combines 김 'dried laver/seaweed' + 밥 'rice', so a learner can decode it. Do not confuse it with Japanese 김초밥/마키(스시): gimbap rice is seasoned with sesame oil and salt, not vinegar, and the fillings are cooked, so it is its own dish, not 'Korean sushi' (Koreans dislike that label). Two collocation points trip up English speakers: you 싸다 'wrap/roll' gimbap (the rolling motion), not 만들다; and you count a whole roll with 줄 'strip', so '두 줄' = two rolls, while 개 would wrongly count individual slices. Register is casual and universal.

Counting whole rolls with 개 — 김밥 두 개 sounds like two single slices. Use 줄: 김밥 두 줄 = two rolls.
Calling it 'Korean sushi' or equating it with 초밥 — the rice uses sesame oil and salt (not vinegar) and the fillings are cooked, so it is a distinct dish; many Koreans find the sushi comparison off.
Saying 김밥을 만들어요 for the act of rolling — the idiomatic verb is 싸다 (싸요), as in 김밥을 싸요, because you are wrapping/rolling it.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비빔밥 means "bibimbap; mixed rice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 비빔밥 (bibimbap) = "bibimbap; mixed rice". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비빔밥을 비비다 ("to mix the bibimbap") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 비빔밥, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the matching verb 비비다 'mix/rub' shares the root of the noun; you stir everything before eating
고추장 is the signature sauce; 넣다 'put in' is how you add it before mixing
compound: 돌솥 'stone pot' + 비빔밥, served sizzling so the bottom rice crisps
그릇 'bowl' is the natural counter for served rice dishes

examples.en: I like bibimbap.
examples.note: plain preference; 을 marks the object

examples.en: Add the chili paste and mix it well before eating.
examples.note: real serving instruction; 비벼서 (from 비비다) + 드세요, the polite imperative

examples.ko: 채소가 많아서 비빔밥은 건강한 한 끼예요.
examples.romanization: chaesoga manaseo bibimbabeun geonganghan han kkiyeyo.
examples.en: Because it has lots of vegetables, bibimbap is a healthy meal.
examples.note: reasoning with -아서; 한 끼 'one meal' frames it as a full, balanced meal

extendedVocab.nuance: 비빔밥 is a bowl of warm rice topped with seasoned vegetables (나물), often an egg and a little meat, plus 고추장 chili paste, all stirred together right before eating. The name is pure native Korean and self-explaining: it is 비비다 'to mix/rub' turned into the noun 비빔 + 밥 'rice', literally 'mixed rice'. The whole point is the mixing, which sets up the key collocation 비비다 — you 비벼서 먹다 'mix-and-eat', and a learner who eats it in neat layers has missed the dish. Distinguish it from 덮밥 'rice topped with something' (a 덮밥 you eat as-is, scooping topping with rice; a 비빔밥 you must stir). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 섞다 'to mix' — 섞다 is for blending separate substances (mixing flour and water), but for stirring food in a bowl with utensils the idiomatic verb is 비비다. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Eating it in layers without stirring — by definition 비빔밥 must be 비벼서 (mixed) first; leaving it un-mixed defeats the dish and the name.
Using 섞다 instead of 비비다 ('비빔밥을 섞어요') — 섞다 is for combining separate ingredients; the in-bowl stirring of food is 비비다.
Forgetting the object particle in casual speech and over-correcting to 가/이 — it is 비빔밥을 먹어요/비벼요 (object 을), since the rice is what you act on.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 불고기 means "bulgogi; grilled marinated beef" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 불고기 (bulgogi) means "bulgogi; grilled marinated beef". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불고기를 재우다 ("to marinate the bulgogi"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 불고기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 재우다 'let it rest/soak' is the cooking term for marinating the beef in sauce before grilling
양념 'seasoning mix'; 불고기 is defined by its sweet 간장(soy) base, unlike spicy dishes
백반-style set: 불고기 with rice and side dishes at a restaurant
굽다 'grill/roast'; note it is a ㅂ-irregular, so 굽다 → 구워요

examples.en: I like bulgogi.
examples.note: simple preference; 를 marks the object after a vowel

examples.en: I want to eat bulgogi tonight.
examples.note: -고 싶다 'want to'; a very natural dinner wish

examples.ko: 불고기는 양념이 달아서 아이들도 잘 먹어요.
examples.romanization: bulgogineun yangnyeomi daraseo aideuldo jal meogeoyo.
examples.en: Bulgogi has a sweet marinade, so even kids eat it well.
examples.note: reasoning with -아서; explains why this mild, sweet meat is family-friendly

extendedVocab.nuance: 불고기 is thin slices of beef marinated in a sweet soy-sauce mix (간장, sugar, garlic, sesame oil, often pear or onion) and grilled or pan-cooked, giving a tender, sweet-savory result rather than charred plain meat. The name is native Korean and decodes literally as 불 'fire' + 고기 'meat', i.e. 'fire-meat'. The sharpest contrast is 불고기 vs 갈비/삼겹살: 갈비 is short rib (also marinated, on the bone), 삼겹살 is fatty pork belly grilled plain and dipped after, while 불고기 is sliced, pre-marinated, sweet. So 불고기 is not a generic word for 'grilled meat' — that broader idea is 구이 or 고기구이. Collocation note for English speakers: you 재우다 'marinate' (let it soak) the meat, and you 굽다 'grill' it (ㅂ-irregular: 구워요). The pitfall is assuming any Korean BBQ meat is 불고기; if it is unmarinated pork belly it is 삼겹살, not 불고기. Register is neutral, used by everyone.

Using 불고기 for any grilled meat — it specifically means thin, sweet-soy-marinated beef. Plain grilled pork belly is 삼겹살; ribs are 갈비.
Conjugating 굽다 'grill' as regular (구버요) — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct form is 구워요 (불고기를 구워요).
Calling the sauce 소스 — the marinade for Korean meat is 양념, and 불고기 is 양념 고기 (seasoned meat); 소스 sounds like a Western dipping sauce.

Watch the particle attached to 떡볶이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 인분 'portion per person'; street tteokbokki is sold by the serving, not by piece
맵다 'spicy' (ㅂ-irregular → 매워요); spiciness is its defining trait
compound by style: 국물 'broth' version with more sauce to drink/dip in
볶다 'stir-fry' is the root verb; the cakes are cooked down in the sauce

examples.en: I like tteokbokki.
examples.note: plain preference statement

examples.en: One serving of tteokbokki at the snack shop, please.
examples.note: real ordering; 분식집 = snack bar, counter 인분 for the serving

examples.ko: 떡볶이가 너무 매워서 물을 많이 마셨어요.
examples.romanization: tteokbokkiga neomu maewoseo mureul mani masyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The tteokbokki was so spicy that I drank a lot of water.
examples.note: cause-result with -아서; 맵다 → 매워서 (ㅂ-irregular)

extendedVocab.nuance: 떡볶이 is chewy cylindrical rice cakes (떡) simmered in a sweet-spicy 고추장 red sauce, the iconic 분식 (snack-shop) street food eaten by students after school. The name is native Korean: 떡 'rice cake' + 볶이 from 볶다 'to stir-fry', so literally 'stir-fried rice cakes' (even though it is now more simmered than fried). The key collocation is the adjective 맵다 'spicy', a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 매워요/매워서 — spiciness is the whole identity of the dish, so expecting it to be sweet-only is the beginner's surprise. It is counted by 인분 'serving per person', not by individual cakes. Contrast 떡볶이 with plain 떡 (rice cake), which can be a chewy sweet snack like 가래떡; 떡볶이 specifically means the saucy spicy dish. English-speaker pitfall: do not call it 'rice cake' alone in a food context — that suggests the unseasoned 떡 or even a Western rice cracker; the dish is always the full word 떡볶이. Register is casual and youthful.

Conjugating 맵다 as regular (맵어요) — it is ㅂ-irregular: 매워요 (떡볶이가 매워요).
Ordering by 개 ('떡볶이 두 개') — street tteokbokki is portioned, so use 인분: 떡볶이 이 인분 (two servings).

The key trait is the adjective 맵다 'spicy', a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 매워요/매워서 — spiciness is the whole identity of the dish, so expecting it to be sweet-only is the beginner's surprise. Do not call it 'rice cake' alone in a food context — that suggests the unseasoned 떡 or even a Western rice cracker; the dish is always the full word 떡볶이.

extendedVocab.nuance: 치킨 in Korea means deep-fried (or sauced) chicken that you order for delivery and share with friends or family over beer — a whole social ritual, not just a food. It is an English loanword (chicken), but its meaning narrowed: 치킨 = fried chicken the dish, while the live bird or raw meat is 닭 'chicken' / 닭고기 'chicken meat'. This is the central pitfall for English speakers: '닭/닭고기' for the ingredient, '치킨' only for the cooked fried dish — saying 치킨 for raw chicken in a recipe is wrong. Key collocations: you 시키다 'order' it (delivery culture), count it with 마리 (whole animal, so 한 마리 / 반 마리), and pair it as 치맥 (치킨+맥주). Contrast 후라이드(치킨) 'plain fried' vs 양념(치킨) 'sweet-spicy sauced' — the classic 'half-and-half' is 반반. Register is fully casual and ubiquitous.

Counting it with 개 — a whole order is one animal, so use 마리: 치킨 한 마리; a half order is 반 마리.
Saying 치킨을 만들어요 for ordering in — Koreans 시키다/주문하다 (order) chicken for delivery: 치킨 시켰어요 ('we ordered chicken').

usagePhrases.note: 빚다 'shape by hand' is the artisanal verb for folding dumplings (also used for 송편, pottery)

extendedVocab.nuance: 만두 are dough pockets filled with minced meat, tofu, vegetables, and glass noodles, which can be steamed (찐만두), pan-fried (군만두), or boiled in soup (물만두/만둣국) — one word covering all methods, so you prefix the style. It is Sino-Korean, written 饅頭 (literally 'steamed bun/stuffed head'), a word shared across East Asia. A learner should not equate it narrowly with Japanese 'gyoza': 교자(만두) is the thin-skinned pan-fried type, but 만두 is the broad category, including thick-skinned and soup versions. The grammar pitfall is the strongest one: Korean nouns are not pluralized, so 'dumplings' is still just 만두 (never 만두들 here) — you say 만두를 먹어요 for any number. The signature verb is 빚다 'to shape/fold by hand' (the same verb used for shaping 송편 rice cakes), which is more idiomatic than 만들다 for the folding craft. Register is neutral and everyday.

Adding a plural -들 because English says 'dumpling-s' — Korean nouns are number-neutral; 만두 already covers one or many: 만두를 먹어요.
Assuming 만두 = gyoza only — 교자 is the thin-skin fried subtype; 만두 is the umbrella term covering steamed, fried, and soup versions.

compound by ingredient: 전복 'abalone' + 죽; also 호박죽 pumpkin, 닭죽 chicken
그릇 'bowl' is the counter; porridge is served and eaten by the bowl

examples.en: I like porridge.
examples.note: plain preference statement

extendedVocab.nuance: 죽 is a soft, slow-simmered rice porridge eaten when you are sick, recovering, or want something gentle on the stomach — culturally it carries a strong 'comfort / convalescence / care' feeling, so bringing someone 죽 signals concern. It is Sino-Korean, written 粥 'congee/gruel'. Distinguish it along a thickness scale: 미음 is the thinnest (strained, for the very ill or babies), 죽 is the standard porridge, and 누룽지 is the toasted scorched-rice version — so 죽 is the middle, everyday term. The verb pitfall is double: first, although 죽 is liquidy, you 먹다 'eat' it (with a spoon), never 마시다 'drink' — Korean treats spoon-food as 'eaten'; second, the most idiomatic cooking verb is 쑤다 'to cook porridge', a special-purpose verb (죽을 쑤다), more precise than generic 끓이다. English speakers reaching for 'drink' because it is soupy will sound off. Register is neutral and warm.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 죽을 마셔요 ('drink the porridge') — you eat it with a spoon, so it must be 죽을 먹어요; Korean classifies spoon-eaten food as 먹다 regardless of how liquid it is.
Using 만들다 for cooking it — the precise idiomatic verb is 쑤다 (죽을 쑤다); 끓이다 'boil' is acceptable but 쑤다 is the natural choice.
Confusing it with 미음 — 미음 is the thin, strained gruel for the very sick or infants; standard porridge is 죽.

usagePhrases.note: 만들다 'make'; home cooks prepare several 반찬 ahead for the week

usagePhrases.en: please give me more side dishes
usagePhrases.note: the polite refill request; 반찬 are usually free and refillable at restaurants

가게 'shop'; ready-made 반찬 stores where busy people buy side dishes

examples.en: This place has a lot of side dishes.
examples.note: describing a restaurant's spread; 이 집 'this establishment'

examples.en: Please give me some more side dishes.

examples.en: Mom makes side dishes in advance on Sundays.
examples.note: 미리 'in advance'; the weekly batch-cooking routine

extendedVocab.nuance: 반찬 are the small shared side dishes — kimchi, seasoned vegetables (나물), braised items, pickles — set out alongside rice and soup at every Korean meal; they are communal, usually free at restaurants, and refillable on request. It is Sino-Korean, written 飯饌, literally 'rice (飯) + prepared food (饌)', i.e. dishes that accompany rice — the etymology itself tells you they are companions to 밥, not standalone mains. The core contrast is 반찬 vs 주요리/메인 (main dish): a 반찬 is never what you 'order' as your meal; it supports the rice. Within 반찬, 밑반찬 are the long-keeping fridge staples. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 반찬 like a Western 'side' you order individually (a side of fries) — in Korea they come automatically with the meal and you ask for more with 반찬 좀 더 주세요, you do not order them à la carte. Another subtlety: 반찬 is generally an uncountable category; you talk about 반찬이 많다/적다 (many/few). Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 반찬 as a main dish you order on its own — 반찬 (literally 'food that goes with rice') accompanies the meal; the main is 주요리/메인 or the specific dish name.
Expecting to pay per side or order them individually like Western 'sides' — in Korea they usually come free with the meal and you simply ask 반찬 좀 더 주세요 for refills.
Pluralizing as 반찬들 to mean 'side dishes' — 반찬 is a number-neutral category noun; use 반찬이 많아요 ('there are many side dishes').

extendedVocab.explanation: 간식 (gansik) means "snack". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 간식을 먹다 ("to have a snack"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 간식 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 'eat'; a light bite between meals to tide you over
시간 'time'; the set snack break, especially for children at school/home
-거리 'stuff/material for'; 간식거리 = snack items, things to nibble
으로 marks 'as/for' a snack; names what the snack is

examples.en: I like snacks.
examples.note: simple preference statement

examples.en: I'm hungry — shall we have a little snack?
examples.note: -는데 'since/and' background + -ㄹ까요 suggestion; everyday offer

extendedVocab.nuance: 간식 is a light snack eaten between meals to bridge hunger — fruit, rice cakes, cookies, bread — never a full meal in itself. It is Sino-Korean, written 間食, literally 'between (間) + eating (食)', i.e. 'eating in between', which pinpoints its meaning: food taken in the gap between regular meals. This sets up a precise three-way contrast you should master: 간식 = between-meal snack, 후식 (後食) = dessert right after a meal, 야식 (夜食) = late-night food. They are not interchangeable — fruit eaten at 3 p.m. is 간식, the same fruit eaten right after dinner is 후식, and fried chicken at midnight is 야식. The English-speaker pitfall is using 간식 for any non-main food including dessert; keep 간식 strictly for the between-meals bite and use 후식 for the end-of-meal sweet. Culturally, 간식 strongly evokes children's snack time. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 간식 to mean dessert after a meal — that is 후식 (literally 'after-food'). 간식 (literally 'between-food') is specifically the between-meals bite.
Calling a full meal 간식 because it is informal — 간식 is by definition light and supplementary; a proper meal is 식사/밥.
Confusing it with 야식 — late-night eating (after dinner, at night) is 야식 (夜食); 간식 is the daytime between-meals snack.

extendedVocab.nuance: 후식 is dessert — the sweet or finishing course eaten right after a meal, such as fruit, ice cream, tteok, or coffee. It is Sino-Korean, written 後食, literally 'after (後) + eating (食)', i.e. 'after-food', so the etymology directly encodes 'what you eat after the meal'. The key synonym pair is 후식 vs 디저트: they mean the same thing, but 후식 is the native Sino-Korean term that feels slightly more traditional/formal (a set-menu 'course' served as 후식), while 디저트 is the English loanword that dominates café culture and trendy sweets — you order 디저트 at a dessert café, but a Korean restaurant's set meal lists 후식. The sharp contrast to drill is 후식 (after-meal dessert) vs 간식 (間食, between-meals snack): an apple after lunch is 후식; an apple at 3 p.m. between meals is 간식. The English-speaker pitfall is lumping all sweet snacks as 'dessert/후식' — Korean separates the end-of-meal course (후식) from the between-meal nibble (간식). Register is neutral.

Assuming 후식 and 디저트 differ in meaning — they are synonyms; 후식 is the native term (more in set-meal/formal contexts), 디저트 the loanword (café/trendy contexts).
Saying 후식을 마셔요 for a coffee dessert and treating it oddly — even coffee 'as dessert' is framed with 으로: 후식으로 커피를 마셔요 (have coffee for dessert).

extendedVocab.nuance: 라떼 is a café latte — espresso with lots of steamed milk — and by extension flavored milk drinks like 녹차라떼 (green-tea latte) or 고구마라떼 (sweet-potato latte). usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다 (drink); 차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를, not 을
the verb for letting tea leaves steep; 차를 끓이다 is to boil it
counter 잔 for cups/glasses of liquid; the number 한 (one) comes before the counter

usagePhrases.en: to serve tea to a guest
usagePhrases.note: 대접하다 is a polite, hospitable verb for offering food or drink to someone

examples.en: I drink tea in the morning.
examples.note: Basic habit sentence; 마셔요 is the 요-form of 마시다, which contracts 마시+어요 to 마셔요.

examples.en: Shall I give you a cup of warm tea?
examples.note: 드릴까요 is the humble offering form; note 따뜻한 (warm) modifying the noun directly before 차.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸렸을 때는 따뜻한 유자차를 마시는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gamgie geollyeosseul ttaeneun ttatteutan yujachareul masineun ge joayo.
examples.en: When you catch a cold, it's good to drink warm citron tea.
examples.note: Real-life advice register; 유자차 (citron tea) shows how a flavor word attaches in front of 차.

extendedVocab.nuance: 차 (茶) is the Sino-Korean word for 'tea,' the brewed leaf or herbal drink, and because it is a beverage it must pair with 마시다 (to drink), never 먹다 (to eat) — though casual speakers do say 차를 먹다 colloquially, learners should default to 마시다. usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 주스 ends in a vowel, so 를 not 을
the fruit word goes directly in front; 사과 주스 (apple juice), 포도 주스 (grape juice)
짜다 means to press/squeeze; for fresh-squeezed juice you also hear 생주스 (fresh juice)
counter 잔 covers both cups and glasses of liquid in Korean

examples.en: The child likes juice.
examples.note: Simple preference; 좋아하다 takes 를 on its object, so 주스를 좋아해요.

examples.ko: 저는 아침마다 오렌지 주스를 한 잔 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun achimmada orenji juseureul han jan masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink a glass of orange juice every morning.
examples.note: 아침마다 = 'every morning' (마다 = each); the flavor word 오렌지 sits before 주스.

examples.ko: 여기 갓 짜낸 생주스가 정말 신선해요.
examples.romanization: yeogi gat jjanaen saengjuseuga jeongmal sinseonhaeyo.
examples.en: The freshly squeezed juice here is really fresh.
examples.note: Cafe register; 생주스 (fresh juice) contrasts with bottled 주스, and 갓 means 'just now / freshly.'

extendedVocab.nuance: 주스 is a direct loanword from English 'juice,' written in 한글 to fit Korean sounds (the English 'j' becomes ㅈ and the final cluster simplifies), and like all drinks it pairs with 마시다, not 먹다. counter 캔 (from English 'can') for canned drinks; use 한 병 for a bottle
톡 쏘다 is the set phrase for a sharp carbonated bite on the tongue

usagePhrases.en: to put ice in the cola
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination (into the cola); 넣다 = to put in

examples.en: Cola, please.
examples.note: Ordering minimal form; 주세요 (please give) is the everyday way to order at a counter.

examples.en: With pizza, cold cola really is the best.
examples.note: 에는 marks pairing ('with pizza'); 역시 = 'as expected / sure enough,' a very natural filler here.

examples.ko: 탄산 빠진 콜라는 맛이 없어서 안 마셔요.
examples.romanization: tansan ppajin kollaneun masi eopseoseo an masyeoyo.
examples.en: Flat cola tastes bad, so I don't drink it.
examples.note: Real-life complaint; 탄산 빠진 = 'with the fizz gone (flat),' and 안 마셔요 negates with 안.

extendedVocab.explanation: 맥주 (maekju) means "beer". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 맥주를 마셔요 ("I drink beer"). Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 맥주 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 counts glasses; a bottle is 한 병 and draft is 생맥주
따르다 (르 irregular: 따라요) is the verb for pouring a drink for someone
에 links the pairing; this combo is nicknamed 치맥 (치킨 + 맥주)

examples.en: How about a glass of beer?
examples.note: Casual invitation; 어때요? (how about?) is the standard way to suggest a drink.

examples.en: Draft beer is colder and fresher than bottled beer.
examples.note: Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 생맥주 (draft) vs 병맥주 (bottled) is a real distinction Koreans make.

examples.ko: 오늘 같은 날엔 치킨에 시원한 맥주 한잔 해야죠.
examples.romanization: oneul gateun naren chikine siwonhan maekju hanjan haeyajyo.
examples.en: On a day like today, you've gotta have chicken and a cold beer.
examples.note: Idiomatic 한잔 하다 ('have a drink'); 해야죠 = 'we really should,' a warm persuasive ending.

extendedVocab.nuance: 맥주 (麥酒) is Sino-Korean, literally 'barley(麥) + liquor(酒),' so the 한자 itself tells you it is a grain-based alcohol; as a beverage it takes 마시다, never 먹다 in careful speech. A core contrast for learners is 생맥주 vs 병맥주: 생 (raw/fresh) + 맥주 means draft beer on tap, while 병맥주 is bottled — bars list them separately, and 생맥주 is often shortened to 생맥. Do not confuse 맥주 (beer) with 술 (alcohol in general): 술 is the umbrella term, and 맥주, 소주, 와인 are all types of 술. The habitual collocation 치맥 (치킨 + 맥주, 'chicken and beer') is a cultural fixture, and 한잔 하다 ('have a drink/one round') is the social ritual phrase. English speakers often default to 먹다 because 'have a beer' feels like eating-and-drinking together, but the verb stays 마시다 (or the polite 드시다); also, when pouring for elders, use two hands and the verb 따르다, a 르-irregular that becomes 따라 줘요.

소주 is sold by the 병 (bottle); the shot glass serving is 한 잔
따르다 (르 irregular → 따라) + 주다 (do for someone); pouring for others is etiquette
에 links the food pairing; grilled 삼겹살 with 소주 is a classic combo

examples.en: One bottle of soju, please.
examples.note: Ordering form; soju comes by the bottle, so 한 병 is the natural count.

examples.ko: 어른께는 두 손으로 소주를 따라 드려야 해요.
examples.romanization: eoreunkkeneun du soneuro sojureul ttara deuryeoya haeyo.
examples.en: You must pour soju for elders with both hands.
examples.note: Etiquette sentence; 께 is the honorific 'to,' and 따라 드리다 is the humble 'pour for (a superior).'

examples.ko: 오랜만에 친구들이랑 소주 한잔하면서 회포를 풀었어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane chingudeurirang soju hanjanhamyeonseo hoeporeul pureosseoyo.
examples.en: I caught up with friends over soju after a long time.
examples.note: Social register; 한잔하다 ('have a drink') + 회포를 풀다 ('unburden / catch up') is very idiomatic.

extendedVocab.nuance: 소주 (燒酒) is Sino-Korean, literally 'burn(燒) + liquor(酒)' — a nod to its distilled origin — and as an alcoholic beverage it pairs with 마시다, never 먹다 in standard speech. It is Korea's most common spirit, clear and served chilled in small glasses, and the social rituals around it matter as much as the word: you pour for others (not yourself), use two hands toward elders, and turn your head slightly away when drinking before a senior. Contrast 소주 with 맥주 (beer) and the popular mix 소맥 (소주 + 맥주, a soju-beer bomb); all are 술 (alcohol). A learner pitfall is counting soju with 잔 only — while a single shot is 한 잔, you order it by the 병 (bottle), so '소주 한 병 주세요' is what you say to a server. Another trap is English speakers calling it 'soju wine' or assuming it's like sake; it is distilled and stronger than rice wine, and the verb of choice for pouring, 따르다, is a 르-irregular (따라요), not a regular verb.

Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 을 + 마시다; 와인 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so it takes 을 (not 를)
color word in front; white is 화이트 와인, sparkling is 스파클링 와인
따다 is to pop/open a sealed bottle; 와인을 따르다 is to pour it
잔 counts glasses; a bottle is 한 병

examples.en: Would you like a glass of wine?
examples.note: Polite invitation; 하실래요? is the honorific '~ㄹ래요?' offering form.

examples.ko: 이 레드 와인은 고기 요리랑 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: i redeu waineun gogi yorirang jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: This red wine goes well with meat dishes.
examples.note: Pairing language; 어울리다 ('to suit/match') + 랑 ('with') is how Koreans describe food-and-drink harmony.

examples.ko: 기념일이라서 분위기 좋은 곳에서 와인을 한 병 시켰어요.
examples.romanization: ginyeomiriraseo bunwigi joeun goseseo waineul han byeong sikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Since it was an anniversary, we ordered a bottle of wine at a nice place.
examples.note: Occasion register; 시키다 ('to order') and 한 병 (a bottle) fit a special-night context.

extendedVocab.nuance: 와인 is a loanword from English 'wine' (the 'w' sound becomes 와 and 'ine' becomes 인), carrying no 한자, and as a beverage it takes 마시다 rather than 먹다. Crucially for particles, 와인 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so unlike vowel-final drink words it takes 을 (와인을), not 를 — a detail English speakers routinely get wrong. Color and style words go in front loanword-style: 레드 와인 (red), 화이트 와인 (white), 로제 와인 (rosé), 스파클링 와인 (sparkling). A subtle near-synonym note: traditional Korean fruit/rice wines are 술 too but go by names like 막걸리 (rice wine) or 과실주 (fruit wine), so 와인 specifically signals the grape, Western-style drink. Natural collocations include 와인을 따다 (to uncork — note 따다, not 마시다, for opening) and 와인이 잘 어울리다 (the wine pairs well). The everyday counter is 잔 for a glass and 병 for a bottle; when ordering at a restaurant the verb 시키다 (to order) is common.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 를 after 와인: because 와인 ends in the consonant ㄴ, the object particle is 을 → 와인을 마셔요, not 와인를.
Saying 와인을 먹어요: wine is a drink, so use 마시다 → 와인을 마셔요.
Calling 막걸리 a kind of 와인: 와인 means grape/Western wine specifically; Korean rice wine is 막걸리, a different category of 술.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 녹차 means "green tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 녹차 (nokcha) means "green tea". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 녹차를 마셔요 ("I drink green tea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 녹차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 녹차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 counts cups of liquid; 한 (one) precedes the counter
우리다 is to steep leaves; over-steeping makes it 떫다 (astringent/bitter)
녹차 also flavors desserts; 녹차 라떼 (green tea latte) is another common one

examples.en: I like green tea more than coffee.
examples.note: Comparison with 보다 ('than') + 더 ('more'); a simple preference sentence.

examples.en: If you steep green tea too long, it turns astringent.
examples.note: Conditional ~면; 떫어지다 ('become astringent') teaches the real taste vocabulary for over-brewed tea.

examples.ko: 식사 후에 따뜻한 녹차 한 잔이면 속이 편해요.
examples.romanization: siksa hue ttatteutan nokcha han janimyeon sogi pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: A warm cup of green tea after a meal settles the stomach.
examples.note: Wellness register; 속이 편하다 ('the stomach is at ease') is the idiomatic digestive phrase.

extendedVocab.nuance: 녹차 (綠茶) is Sino-Korean, literally 'green(綠) + tea(茶),' so the 한자 transparently names the color and the drink; as a beverage it takes 마시다, never 먹다. It is a specific type within the broad 차 family, contrasting with 홍차 (紅茶, 'red tea' = black tea), 보리차 (barley tea), and 옥수수차 (corn tea); note the Korean naming logic differs from English, since what English calls 'black tea' is 홍차 ('red tea') in Korean, matching the East Asian convention. A flavor note worth knowing: green tea steeped too long becomes 떫다 (astringent/puckery), a taste word distinct from 쓰다 (bitter), and Koreans will say 떫어요 about over-brewed tea. 녹차 also works as a dessert flavor (녹차 아이스크림, 녹차 라떼), where it doubles as 말차/matcha-style flavoring. English speakers should avoid the 먹다 reflex and remember the verb for steeping is 우리다 (not 끓이다, which is to boil); the natural counter is 한 잔.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 녹차를 먹어요: green tea is a drink → 녹차를 마셔요 (먹다 is for solids).
Assuming 'black tea' is 검은차: in Korean it is 홍차 ('red tea'); 녹차 is green tea, and the color words follow the East Asian convention.
Describing over-steeped tea as 써요 (bitter) when you mean 떫어요 (astringent): green tea's harsh edge is 떫다, the puckery taste, not 쓰다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 생수 means "bottled water" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "bottled water" is 생수 (saengsu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 생수를 마셔요 ("I drink bottled water"). Watch the particle attached to 생수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 생수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
water is counted by the 병 (bottle); 한 통 for a large jug
sold at convenience stores (편의점); 사다 = to buy
통 counts large containers; 2리터 한 통 is a 2-liter jug

examples.en: I bought a bottle of water at the convenience store.
examples.note: Shopping past tense; 한 병 is the natural counter for a single bottle.

examples.ko: 수돗물 대신 생수를 마시는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: sudonmul daesin saengsureul masineun sarami manayo.
examples.en: Many people drink bottled water instead of tap water.
examples.note: Contrast with 대신 ('instead of'); pairs 생수 against 수돗물 (tap water).

examples.ko: 등산 갈 때는 생수를 넉넉히 챙겨 가세요.
examples.romanization: deungsan gal ttaeneun saengsureul neongneoki chaenggyeo gaseyo.
examples.en: When you go hiking, pack plenty of bottled water.
examples.note: Practical advice; 넉넉히 ('amply') + 챙겨 가다 ('pack and take along') is everyday usage.

extendedVocab.nuance: 생수 (生水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'raw(生) + water(水)' — 'raw' here means untreated/natural spring water sold in bottles — and as a drink it takes 마시다, not 먹다. The key contrast learners need is the three-way split among Korean 'water' words: 물 is the plain general word for water; 수돗물 (水道+물) is tap water from the faucet; and 생수 specifically means commercially bottled mineral/spring water. So you 'drink 물' generally, but you 'buy 생수' at a store. Another near term is 정수기 물 (water from a filter/purifier). The 生 in 생수 is the same 'raw/fresh' morpheme seen in 생맥주 (draft beer) and 생주스 (fresh juice). English speakers sometimes call all drinking water 생수, but if it came from the tap it is 수돗물, and if from a cooler it is 정수기 물. Natural collocations: 생수를 사다 (buy bottled water), counted as 한 병 (a bottle) or 한 통 (a big jug, e.g. 2리터).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 생수를 먹어요: water is a drink → 생수를 마셔요 (먹다 is reserved for solids, though 약을 먹다 'take medicine' is a fixed exception).
Using 생수 for tap water: 생수 is bottled/commercial water; faucet water is 수돗물. Don't say '생수로 손을 씻어요' for tap water.
Counting water with 개: a bottle is 한 병, a big jug is 한 통 — 개 is the wrong counter for bottled water.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 탄산수 means "sparkling water" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 탄산수 (tansansu) = "sparkling water". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 탄산수를 마셔요 ("I drink sparkling water") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 탄산수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 탄산수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
톡 쏘다 is the set phrase for a sharp carbonated tingle on the tongue

usagePhrases.en: to add lemon to the sparkling water
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks 'into'; a lemon slice (레몬 한 조각) is a common addition
counted by the 병 (bottle) or, in a glass, 한 잔

examples.en: Do you like sparkling water?
examples.note: Polite question; 좋아하세요? is the honorific of 좋아하다 for asking someone's taste.

examples.en: I drink sparkling water instead of cola.
examples.note: Health-conscious choice; 대신 ('instead of') sets 탄산수 against sugary 콜라.

examples.ko: 탄산수에 레몬 한 조각 넣으면 훨씬 상큼해요.
examples.romanization: tansansue remon han jogang neoeumyeon hwolssin sangkeumhaeyo.
examples.en: If you add a slice of lemon to sparkling water, it's much more refreshing.
examples.note: Conditional ~면; 상큼하다 ('zesty/refreshing') is the natural taste adjective here.

extendedVocab.nuance: 탄산수 (炭酸水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'carbonic-acid(炭酸) + water(水),' i.e. carbonated water; as a drink it takes 마시다, never 먹다. The 탄산 morpheme ('carbonation/fizz') is the same one in 탄산음료 (carbonated soft drinks), so 탄산수 is unflavored fizzy water while 탄산음료 is the broad category of sweet sodas like 콜라 and 사이다. Contrast 탄산수 with 생수 (still bottled water): the difference is purely the bubbles — 탄산수 has 탄산 (fizz), 생수 does not. When the bubbles go flat, Koreans say 탄산이 빠지다 ('the fizz escapes'), and the lively bite is described as 톡 쏘다. English speakers sometimes conflate 탄산수 with 사이다, but 사이다 is sweet lemon-lime soda, whereas 탄산수 is plain carbonated water with no sugar. A natural way to dress it up is 탄산수에 레몬을 넣다 (add lemon), and the standard counters are 한 병 (a bottle) or 한 잔 (a glass).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 탄산수를 먹어요: sparkling water is a drink → 탄산수를 마셔요.
Confusing 탄산수 with 사이다: 사이다 is sweet lemon-lime soda; 탄산수 is unsweetened carbonated water. Ask for 탄산수 if you want no sugar.
Describing flat sparkling water as 탄산수가 죽었어요 literally-translated from English 'dead': Koreans say 탄산이 빠졌어요 ('the fizz escaped').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 음료수 means "beverage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 음료수 (eumnyosu) means "beverage". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 음료수를 마셔요 ("I drink a beverage"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 음료수 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다; 음료수 ends in a vowel so it takes 를
잔 for a glass; canned is 한 캔, bottled is 한 병
코너 (from 'corner') labels a store aisle; 음료 코너 is the shortened form
시원하다 ('cool/refreshing') is the habitual adjective for chilled drinks

examples.en: What would you like to drink? Shall I get you a drink?
examples.note: Host offering; 드릴까요? is the humble 'shall I give,' standard when serving a guest.

examples.ko: 저는 단 음료수보다 물을 더 자주 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun dan eumnyosuboda mureul deo jaju masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink water more often than sweet drinks.
examples.note: Comparison with 보다 ('than'); 단 ('sweet') modifies 음료수 to mean sugary drinks.

examples.ko: 회의 전에 음료수 좀 준비해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: hoeui jeone eumnyosu jom junbihae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you prepare some drinks before the meeting?
examples.note: Workplace request; 준비해 주시겠어요? is a polite '~해 주시겠어요?' favor-asking form.

extendedVocab.nuance: 음료수 (飮料水) is Sino-Korean, literally 'drink(飮) + material(料) + water(水),' a transparent label meaning 'a beverage,' and naturally it pairs with 마시다, not 먹다. It is the umbrella term for non-alcoholic drinks — sodas, juices, sweet drinks — but in everyday speech it leans toward soft drinks/sodas rather than water, tea, or coffee; if you ask '음료수 드릴까요?' a host will usually reach for juice or a soda, not plain water. Note the near-synonym 음료 (飮料): 음료 is the slightly more formal/written 'beverage' (seen on menus and labels as 음료 코너), while 음료수 is the spoken everyday word. Both contrast with 술 (alcoholic drinks), which 음료수 excludes. A pitfall for English speakers: 'beverage' in English can include coffee or tea, but Korean 음료수 in casual use rarely covers 커피 or 차 — those are named directly. Habitual collocations include 시원한 음료수 (a cold drink) and 음료수 한 잔/캔/병, plus the store sign 음료 코너 (beverage aisle).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 음료수를 먹어요: a beverage is a drink → 음료수를 마셔요.
Using 음료수 to mean plain water: 음료수 implies sodas/sweet drinks; for water say 물 or 생수. '음료수 주세요' likely gets you a soft drink.
Treating 음료수 as including alcohol: it covers non-alcoholic drinks only; alcoholic ones are 술 (e.g., 맥주, 소주).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 얼음 means "ice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "ice" is 얼음 (eoreum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 얼음을 넣다 ("to put in ice"). Watch the particle attached to 얼음 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 얼음 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을; the verb is 넣다 (put in), not 마시다
녹다 ('to melt'); 얼음 takes subject 이 because it ends in a consonant
좀 ('a little/some') softens the request; 주세요 is the polite 'please give'
깨다 ('to break'); crushed ice for drinks is 잔얼음 or 분쇄 얼음

examples.en: Please put ice in the cola.
examples.note: Ordering request; 에 marks 'into the cola,' and 넣어 주세요 asks someone to add it for you.

examples.en: Since it's hot out, the ice melts quickly.
examples.note: Cause with ~니까; 금방 ('right away') + 녹다 ('melt') describes fast melting.

examples.ko: 아이스 아메리카노는 얼음을 가득 넣어야 제맛이에요.
examples.romanization: aiseu amerikanoneun eoreumeul gadeung neoeoya jemasieyo.
examples.en: Iced americano tastes right only when packed full of ice.
examples.note: Cafe register; 가득 ('full') + ~야 제맛이다 ('is only truly tasty when') is an idiomatic 'that's the way it should be.'

extendedVocab.nuance: 얼음 is a native Korean word (from the verb 얼다 'to freeze' + the noun-forming ending -음, literally 'the frozen thing'), so it carries no 한자, and unlike every drink in this set you do NOT 마시다 it — you put it in (넣다), it melts (녹다), or you crush it (깨다). This is the headline pitfall: English 'ice' in drinks tempts learners to treat it like a beverage, but 얼음 is a solid object, so 얼음을 마셔요 is wrong; instead you say 얼음을 넣어요 (put ice in) and then 마셔요 the drink itself. Grammatically, 얼음 ends in the consonant ㅁ, so it takes the subject particle 이 (얼음이 녹아요) and object particle 을 (얼음을 넣어요), not 가/를. 달다 ('to be sweet') is the signature taste; the ㄹ drops before some endings (단 식혜)

examples.en: Try a glass of sikhye.
examples.note: Offering; 드셔 보세요 ('please try [drinking]') uses honorific 드시다 + ~아 보다 'try doing.'

examples.ko: 식혜는 차갑게 해서 마셔야 더 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: sikyeneun chagapge haeseo masyeoya deo masisseoyo.
examples.en: Sikhye tastes better when you drink it chilled.
examples.note: Serving tip; 차갑게 해서 ('make it cold and then') + ~야 ('only if/must') explains the right way to serve it.

extendedVocab.nuance: 식혜 (食醯) is a traditional sweet rice beverage made by fermenting steamed rice with malt water (엿기름), leaving tender rice grains floating in a cool, sweet liquid; as a drink it takes 마시다, not 먹다 — though because of the floating rice some people half-jokingly 먹다 it. Note the 한자 (食 'food/eat' + 醯, an old character for fermented liquid) and the spelling: it is 식혜 with ㅖ, not to be confused with 식해 (食醢), a completely different fermented-fish side dish from the east coast — a near-homophone (sikhye vs sikhae) but a savory food, a classic native-speaker spelling trap too. The signature taste adjective is 달다 (sweet), and it is always served 차갑게 (cold), especially after sauna visits and at 명절 (holidays) like Chuseok and Lunar New Year. A near comparison: 식혜 vs 수정과 (수정과 is a darker cinnamon-ginger punch with dried persimmon) — both are traditional sweet drinks but taste entirely different. English speakers should default to 마시다 and remember the counter 한 잔; to make it is 만들다 (a ㄹ-irregular verb).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 바나나 means "banana" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 바나나 (banana) means "banana". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 바나나를 먹어요 ("I eat a banana"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 바나나 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the final vowel ㅏ
노랗다 becomes 노래요 (ㅎ-irregular)
개 is the all-purpose counter for items
compound: noun + noun, no particle between them

examples.en: A banana, please.
examples.note: bare noun + 주세요 is the simplest way to ask for something

examples.en: I eat a banana every morning.
examples.note: 마다 means 'every'; 를 marks the thing eaten

examples.en: The banana got too ripe so it turned brown.
examples.note: real kitchen complaint; -아서 links cause to result

extendedVocab.nuance: 바나나 is a loanword (from English 'banana') written in Hangul, and unlike English it carries no plural form — one banana and a whole bunch are both just 바나나, with quantity shown by a number plus the counter 개 (바나나 세 개). Koreans give every syllable equal length and a flat, even rhythm (ba-na-na), without the stressed first syllable English speakers instinctively add. Note the spelling difference: the fruit is 바나나, but a near-look-alike loanword 바나 does not exist, so don't shorten it. It pairs naturally with 익다 (to ripen), 까다 (to peel), and the compound 바나나 우유 (the beloved banana-flavored milk). The classic English-speaker trap is adding an English-style plural ('바나나들' for 'bananas') — 들 is grammatically possible but sounds unnatural for fruit you'd buy or eat, so leave the noun bare and let context or a counter carry the number.

Saying '바나나들을 먹어요' to mean 'I eat bananas' — Korean does not pluralize food nouns this way; 들 sounds forced. Use the bare noun: 바나나를 먹어요.
Stressing the first syllable like English BA-nana. Korean has no word stress; pronounce all three syllables evenly or you sound unnatural.
Writing the subject as '바나나는' when first introducing it in a sentence like 'the banana is yellow' — for a plain new fact use 바나나가 노래요; 는 adds a contrast nuance you may not intend.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 딸기 means "strawberry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "strawberry" is 딸기 (ttalgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 딸기를 먹어요 ("I eat strawberries"). Watch the particle attached to 딸기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the vowel 이
빨갛다 → 빨개요 (ㅎ-irregular adjective)
개 counts individual berries
flavor, not real fruit inside

examples.en: Do you like strawberries?
examples.note: drop the particle in casual speech: 딸기(를) 좋아해요

examples.en: These strawberries are really sweet and tasty.
examples.note: 달다 + 맛있다 linked with 고; 가 marks the topic being judged

examples.en: Strawberries are in season in spring so they're cheap.
examples.note: 제철 = peak season; -이라(서) gives the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 딸기 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean and not a loanword), so it never takes a plural ending — a single berry and a whole carton are both 딸기. It is strongly tied to spring (봄), the season when it is 제철 (at its peak), and it is the default 'pink/sweet' flavor in Korea: 딸기 우유, 딸기 아이스크림, 딸기 케이크 all mean the flavor, with no actual berries guaranteed. Don't confuse 딸기 with 산딸기 — 산딸기 (literally 'mountain strawberry') is a wild raspberry, a different fruit. The English-speaker pitfall here is double: first, pluralizing ('딸기들') which sounds unnatural for fruit; second, mishearing the tense double consonant ㄸ at the start — it is a hard, unaspirated 'tt', not a soft English 'd', so 딸기 (ttalgi) is not 달기. It collocates with 달다 (sweet), 빨갛다 (red), 따다 (to pick), and 씻다 (to wash).

Pronouncing 딸기 with a soft English 'd' (dalgi). The initial ㄸ is a tense consonant; say a tight, unaspirated 'tt' or the word sounds like a different one.
Using 딸기들 for 'strawberries'. Korean fruit nouns stay bare; the plural marker 들 is unnatural here. Say 딸기를 먹어요 for any amount.
Calling a raspberry 딸기. A wild raspberry is 산딸기 and a regular one is 라즈베리 — 딸기 alone always means the cultivated strawberry.

extendedVocab.explanation: 포도 (podo) = "grapes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 포도를 먹어요 ("I eat grapes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 포도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 after the vowel ㅗ
달다 → 달아요; 가 marks the subject
송이 counts clustered/blossom-like things
noun compound, no linking particle

examples.en: One bunch of grapes, please.
examples.note: 송이 is the natural counter, not 개

examples.ko: 이 포도가 씨가 없어서 먹기 편해요.
examples.romanization: i podoga ssiga eopseoseo meokgi pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: These grapes are seedless so they're easy to eat.
examples.note: 씨 = seed; -아서 gives the reason, 먹기 편하다 = easy to eat

examples.en: When autumn comes, grapes get really sweet.
examples.note: -아지다 shows a change of state (become sweet)

extendedVocab.nuance: 포도 is Sino-Korean, written 葡萄 (the two characters together simply name the fruit; neither is used alone in everyday Korean). It is grammatically a mass/group word, so it is never pluralized and a 'bunch' is counted with the counter 송이 (포도 한 송이), the same counter used for a cluster of flowers — using the all-purpose 개 here sounds childish or wrong. A single grape, if you must, is 포도 한 알 (알 = a small round unit, like a bead or pellet). Like 딸기, it doubles as a flavor word: 포도 주스, 포도 사탕, 포도 맛 candy. The English-speaker trap is treating 'grapes' as inherently plural and reaching for a plural marker, or saying 포도 한 개 — instead, learn the pair 송이 (bunch) and 알 (single grape). It collocates with 달다 (sweet), 시다 (sour), 씨 (seed/pip), and 따다 (to pick).

Counting grapes with 개 (포도 한 개). A cluster is 한 송이 and a single grape is 한 알; 개 is wrong for grapes.
Adding a plural like 포도들 because English 'grapes' is plural. 포도 is already a group noun — keep it bare.
Mixing up 송이 and 알: 송이 = a whole bunch, 알 = one individual grape. Asking for 포도 한 송이 at a store gets you a full bunch, not one grape.
