편한 is the adnominal of 편하다
subject marker 가; 편하다 = comfortable
paired footwear uses 켤레

examples.en: I wear sneakers.
examples.note: All footwear takes 신다 — never 입다, even for athletic shoes.

examples.ko: 발이 편한 운동화를 신고 많이 걸었어요.
examples.romanization: bari pyeonhan undonghwareul singo mani georeosseoyo.
examples.en: I walked a lot in comfortable sneakers.
examples.note: 발이 편하다 ('feet are comfortable') is the set phrase for comfy shoes.

examples.ko: 등산은 안 하지만 운동화가 편해서 자주 신어요.
examples.romanization: deungsaneun an hajiman undonghwaga pyeonhaeseo jaju sineoyo.
examples.en: I don't hike, but sneakers are comfy so I wear them often.
examples.note: Real situation: 신다 covers habitual wearing too; 자주 신다 = 'wear often'.

paired footwear uses 켤레

examples.en: I wear dress shoes.
examples.note: Formal leather shoes still take 신다, like every other shoe.

examples.ko: 발이 아파서 구두를 벗고 슬리퍼로 갈아 신었어요.
examples.romanization: bari apaseo gudureul beotgo seullipeoro gara sineosseoyo.
examples.en: My feet hurt so I took off the dress shoes and changed into slippers.
examples.note: 갈아 신다 ('change footwear') is the foot-specific 'change into' verb.

examples.ko: 정장에 맞춰 검은 구두를 신고 면접에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jeongjange matchwo geomeun gudureul singo myeonjeobe gasseoyo.
examples.en: I wore black dress shoes to match my suit for the interview.
examples.note: Real situation: 정장에 맞추다 ('match to a suit') shows 구두's formal register.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 청소 means "cleaning" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 청소 (cheongso) means "cleaning". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 청소를 하다 ("to do the cleaning"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 청소 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The default verb is 하다; 청소 is the object, so use 를.
Put the place right before 청소 with no particle: 방 청소, 화장실 청소.
대(大) 'big' + 청소 = a thorough top-to-bottom clean.
청소기 (cleaner machine) is 'vacuum'; you 돌리다 (spin/run) it, not 하다.

examples.en: I do the cleaning.
examples.note: Simple frame: 청소 + 를 + 해요 is the core pattern to memorize.

examples.en: I clean my room every weekend.
examples.note: Everyday: 청소하다 can take a direct object (방을) without saying 청소를.

examples.en: Cleaning is all done, so the house is sparkling.
examples.note: Real life: here 청소 is the subject with 가, and 끝나다 means it 'finished'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 청소 is Sino-Korean, 清掃 (清 'clear' + 掃 'sweep'), so its core sense is sweeping a space clean — floors, rooms, a car, a screen. Its everyday verb is 하다 (청소하다 / 청소를 하다). Do not confuse it with 정리 (整理), which is tidying/arranging objects into order: you 청소 the dust and grime off a surface, but you 정리 the scattered books on a desk; a messy-but-clean desk needs 정리, a dusty floor needs 청소. Register is neutral — kids and adults all say 청소해요. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'I clean' tempts learners to make 청소 the subject (청소가 해요 ✗), but 청소 is the thing being done, so it must be the OBJECT — 청소를 해요 (○). Also note 청소기 is the vacuum, and you 돌리다 it, never 청소를 하다 the machine itself.

청소가 해요. ✗ → 청소를 해요. ○
'Cleaning' is the action you perform, not the actor. With 하다 it is the object, so it takes 를, never 가.
Use 청소를 해요 or just 청소해요.
방을 정리해요 vs 방을 청소해요
Saying 청소 when you only put toys away is wrong — that is tidying. 청소 is for removing dirt/dust, 정리 is for arranging things.
Put-things-in-order = 정리; scrub/sweep dust = 청소.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빨래 means "laundry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "laundry" is 빨래 (ppallae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빨래를 하다 ("to do the laundry"). Watch the particle attached to 빨래 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The washing action; 빨래 is the object so it takes 를.
After washing you 널다 (spread out to dry) the wet clothes.
Dry clothes are 개다 (folded); note 개다, not 접다, for laundry.
Here 빨래 is the subject with 가; 마르다 = to dry out.

examples.en: I do the laundry today.
examples.note: Simple frame: 빨래 + 를 + 해요, the basic chore pattern.

examples.ko: 빨래가 많아서 세탁기를 두 번 돌렸어요.
examples.romanization: ppallaega manaseo setakgireul du beon dollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: There was a lot of laundry, so I ran the washer twice.
examples.note: Everyday: 빨래 as subject (가) + 많다; the machine 세탁기 you 돌리다.

examples.ko: 빨래를 다 널고 나서 커피 한잔하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: ppallaereul da neolgo naseo keopi hanjanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: After hanging all the laundry, I want a coffee.
examples.note: Real life: 널다 = hang to dry, and 고 나서 = 'after doing'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빨래 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) and is genuinely double-sided: it means both the ACTIVITY of washing clothes (빨래를 하다) and the physical LAUNDRY ITEMS themselves (빨래가 많다 'there's a lot of wash'). Its root is the verb 빨다 'to wash by hand/rub'. The near-synonym is 세탁 (洗濯), the stiffer Sino-Korean word you see on signs and machines — 세탁기 (washer), 세탁소 (dry-cleaner's), 세탁 코스; in casual home talk Koreans say 빨래, in formal/written contexts 세탁. The big pitfall for English speakers is treating 'do the laundry' as making something: 빨래를 만들다 (✗) is nonsense — laundry is washed, so it is 빨래를 하다. Second, the drying chore is 널다 (널어요), not 걸다; and folding finished laundry is 개다, not 접다. Choose the verb to the stage: 하다 → 널다 → 개다.

빨래를 만들어요. ✗ → 빨래를 해요. ○
'Make laundry' copies English literally; clothes are washed, not manufactured. The verb for the chore is 하다.
Use 빨래를 해요 or 빨래해요.
빨래를 걸어요. ✗ → 빨래를 널어요. ○
걸다 is hanging one item on a hook; spreading wet wash out to dry is its own verb, 널다.
Wet laundry to dry = 널다; fold dry laundry = 개다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 설거지 means "dish washing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

설거지 as subject with 가; 쌓이다 = to accumulate.
거리 = 'stuff/material for'; 설거지거리 = the dirty-dish workload.
당번 = person on rotation duty; common in homes and dorms.

examples.en: I wash the dishes.
examples.note: Simple frame: 설거지 + 를 + 해요, the whole-meal cleanup.

examples.en: Right after eating, I do the dishes.
examples.note: Everyday: 고 나서 'after'; 설거지하다 written solid is most natural here.

examples.ko: 설거지가 너무 많이 쌓여서 한숨이 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: seolgeojiga neomu mani ssayeoseo hansumi nawasseoyo.
examples.en: So many dishes piled up that I sighed.
examples.note: Real life: 설거지 as subject + 쌓이다; 한숨이 나오다 = a sigh comes out.

extendedVocab.nuance: 설거지 is a native Korean word for the specific chore of washing the dishes, pots, and utensils AFTER a meal — it bundles the whole task, not one plate. It always pairs with 하다 (설거지하다). The crucial contrast is with the verb 씻다 'to wash/rinse': you 씻다 an individual object or body part (사과를 씻다 'wash an apple', 손을 씻다 'wash hands'), but the household routine of clearing the table's dishes is the noun 설거지(를 하다). So '설거지를 씻다' (✗) sounds like washing the act itself. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that overlap — English uses 'wash the dishes', tempting 접시를 씻다, which is acceptable for literally rinsing plates, but the everyday CHORE Koreans name is 설거지하다. Note also it is one fixed word: don't break it into pieces. Common partners: 설거지가 쌓이다 (pile up), 설거지 당번 (dish duty).

설거지를 씻어요. ✗ → 설거지를 해요. ○
씻다 takes a concrete thing (hands, fruit, a plate). 설거지 is the named chore, so its verb is 하다.
Chore = 설거지를 해요; rinse one item = 접시를 씻다.
설거지를 만들어요. ✗ → 설거지를 해요. ○
Like other chores, you don't 'make' dish-washing. 하다 is the verb that activates the chore noun.
Always 설거지하다 for the action.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 요리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The action takes 하다; 요리 is the object with 를.
요리 as the finished dish; nationality goes in front with no particle.
요리법 (法 'method') is the native-style word; 레시피 is the loanword.
잘하다 'do well' fused; 요리를 잘해요 = a good cook.

examples.en: I cook.
examples.note: Simple frame: 요리 + 를 + 해요, the basic 'I cook' sentence.

examples.ko: 주말에 한국 요리를 만들어 보고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jumare hanguk yorireul mandeureo bogo sipeoyo.
examples.en: On weekends I want to try making Korean dishes.
examples.note: Everyday: here 요리 = the dish, so 만들다 'make' is fine; 아 보다 = 'try doing'.

examples.en: Mom's cooking is the most delicious in the world.
examples.note: Real life: 요리 as the result-food; 제일 = the most.

extendedVocab.nuance: 요리 is Sino-Korean, 料理 (料 'ingredients/measure' + 理 'manage/arrange'), literally 'managing ingredients', and it covers BOTH the act of cooking (요리를 하다) and the finished DISH/cuisine (한국 요리 'Korean cuisine', 엄마 요리 'mom's cooking'). Watch the verb split by meaning: for the ACTIVITY use 하다 (요리해요), but for producing a specific dish use 만들다 'make' (김치찌개를 만들어요). The near-synonym 음식 (飮食) means 'food' as a substance you eat or buy, while 요리 implies it was prepared/cooked with some skill — a bag of chips is 음식, not 요리. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 요리를 먹다 to mean 'I cook and eat': 요리를 먹다 actually means 'eat a dish', so for the act you need 요리를 하다. Also 요리사 (師 'master') is a professional chef. Common partners: 요리를 잘하다, 집밥 요리 (home-cooked food).

요리를 먹어요 (meaning 'I cook'). ✗ → 요리를 해요. ○
요리 is two-sided; 먹다 only fits the dish-meaning ('eat a dish'). For the act of cooking the verb is 하다.
Cook the action = 요리를 해요; eat the dish = 요리를 먹다.
이 요리는 음식이에요 misuse
음식 = food generally; 요리 = a prepared dish. Calling instant snacks 요리 overstates the effort.
Prepared/cooked = 요리; food in general = 음식.

structuredNuance.t: 요리 covers BOTH the act of cooking (요리를 하다) and the finished DISH/cuisine (한국 요리 'Korean cuisine', 엄마 요리 'mom's cooking'). Common partners: 요리를 잘하다, 집밥 요리 (home-cooked food).
The near-synonym 음식 (飮食) means 'food' as a substance you eat or buy, while 요리 implies it was prepared/cooked with some skill — a bag of chips is 음식, not 요리.
요리 is Sino-Korean, 料理 (料 'ingredients/measure' + 理 'manage/arrange'), literally 'managing ingredients'.
The pitfall is saying 요리를 먹다 to mean 'I cook and eat': 요리를 먹다 actually means 'eat a dish', so for the act you need 요리를 하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 쓰레기 means "trash" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "trash" is 쓰레기 (sseuregi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 쓰레기를 버리다 ("to throw away the trash"). Watch the particle attached to 쓰레기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The core verb is 버리다 (discard), with 쓰레기 as object 를.
통 = bin/container; 쓰레기통 is the can you throw trash into.
Korea sorts food waste separately; 음식물 (foodstuff) + 쓰레기.
분리수거 = sorted collection, the legally required recycling sort.

examples.en: I throw out the trash.
examples.note: Simple frame: 쓰레기 + 를 + 버리다, the key verb that is NOT 하다.

examples.en: Today is the day to take out food waste.
examples.note: Everyday: 버리는 날 = 'the day for throwing out'; food waste is its own category.

examples.ko: 쓰레기를 아무 데나 버리면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: sseuregireul amu dena beorimyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You mustn't throw trash just anywhere.
examples.note: Real life: 면 안 되다 = 'must not'; 아무 데나 = 'just any place'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 쓰레기 is a native Korean noun meaning garbage/waste, and unlike the chore nouns around it, its verb is NOT 하다 but 버리다 'to throw away/discard' (쓰레기를 버리다). The near-synonym 쓰레기 vs 폐기물 (廢棄物, formal 'waste matter') splits by register: 쓰레기 is the everyday spoken word, 폐기물 is industrial/legal (산업 폐기물 'industrial waste'). Used figuratively, 쓰레기 is also a harsh insult for a contemptible person ('that guy is 쓰레기' = scum), so be careful aiming it at people. The big English-speaker pitfall is overusing 하다: 쓰레기를 해요 (✗) is meaningless — trash is acted on with 버리다, or sorted with 분리수거하다. Second pitfall: 'take out the trash' should not become 쓰레기를 가지고 나가다 mechanically; the idiomatic phrase is just 쓰레기를 버리다 or 쓰레기를 내놓다 (put it out). 쓰레기를 해요. ✗ → 쓰레기를 버려요. ○
쓰레기 is not a 하다-chore; you discard it. The verb is 버리다.
Throw out = 쓰레기를 버리다; sort = 분리수거하다.
사람한테 함부로 쓰레기라고 하기
Literally 'trash', but as slang it means 'scumbag', a strong insult, so don't apply it to people lightly.
For objects only unless you truly mean the insult.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정리 means "tidying" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정리 (jeongni) = "tidying". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 정리를 하다 ("to tidy/organize") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 정리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The action takes 하다; 정리 is the object with 를.
정리하다 can take a direct object (방을) — arrange that space.
Fixed 4-syllable pair 整理整頓; emphasizes everything in its place.
정리 also works on abstractions — sorting ideas, plans, feelings.

examples.en: I tidy the desk.
examples.note: Simple frame: object + 정리하다 = put that thing in order.

examples.ko: 이사 가기 전에 짐을 정리하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: isa gagi jeone jimeul jeongnihago isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm sorting my stuff before moving.
examples.note: Everyday: 고 있다 = ongoing; 짐 = belongings/luggage to arrange.

examples.en: I'll summarize the meeting and email it.
examples.note: Real life: here 정리 = 'summarize/compile' information, a common office sense.

extendedVocab.nuance: 정리 is Sino-Korean, 整理 (整 'arrange/orderly' + 理 'manage'), meaning to put scattered things into order — and its scope is broad: physical stuff (책상을 정리하다 'tidy a desk'), abstract ideas (생각을 정리하다 'organize thoughts'), even finishing/winding up (관계를 정리하다 'end a relationship', 일을 정리하다 'wrap up affairs'). The verb is 하다. The sharp contrast is with 청소 (清掃): 정리 = arranging objects into their places; 청소 = removing dirt/dust by sweeping or wiping. A dusty but neat room needs 청소; a clean-floored but cluttered room needs 정리; Koreans often pair them — 청소하고 정리하다. The English-speaker pitfall is 정리를 만들다 (✗), copying 'make tidy'; the chore noun is activated by 하다 only. Also don't assume 정리 = mere cleaning — its summarize/conclude senses surprise learners, so 'I'll 정리 my notes' means compile/summarize them, not scrub them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
정리를 만들어요. ✗ → 정리를 해요. ○
'Make' doesn't apply; the chore/action noun pairs with 하다.
Always 정리하다 for the action.
방이 더러울 때 정리하다 vs 청소하다
If the floor is dirty, 정리 (arranging) doesn't help — you need 청소 (cleaning). Mixing them mislabels the task.
Arrange clutter = 정리; remove dirt = 청소.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 샤워 means "shower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 샤워 (syawo) means "shower". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 샤워를 하다 ("to take a shower"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 샤워 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The action takes 하다; 샤워 is the object with 를.
기 (器 'device') turns the loanword into the fixture: the showerhead/handset.

usagePhrases.en: a cold shower / shower with cold water
usagePhrases.note: Temperature goes in front, or the water as means with 로/으로.
고 나오다 = 'after doing, come out'; the natural post-shower phrase.

examples.en: I take a shower.
examples.note: Simple frame: 샤워 + 를 + 해요, even though 'shower' is a loanword it still needs 하다.

examples.en: Every morning I shower with warm water.
examples.note: Everyday: 로 marks the water as the means; 마다 = 'every'.

examples.ko: 운동하고 땀이 나서 얼른 샤워하러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: undonghago ttami naseo eolleun syawohareo gasseoyo.
examples.en: I sweated from exercise, so I quickly went to shower.
examples.note: Real life: 으러 가다 = 'go in order to'; 땀이 나다 = to sweat.

extendedVocab.nuance: 샤워 is a loanword from English 'shower', and like other action loanwords it Koreanizes by attaching 하다 (샤워하다 / 샤워를 하다) — it specifically means standing under running water. Contrast it with 목욕 (沐浴), which is soaking/bathing in a tub or at a bathhouse (목욕탕): a quick rinse standing up is 샤워, a long soak is 목욕. Both differ from 세수 (洗手), which is washing only the face. Register is fully neutral. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is dropping 하다 because 'shower' already feels like a verb in English — but 샤워 alone is just the noun; you must say 샤워하다, never use 샤워 bare as a verb. Second pitfall: choosing the wrong washing word — for the whole body standing up it's 샤워, not 씻다 broadly (though 씻다 'wash up' is a loose casual cover term) and not 세수 (face only). The water you use takes 로/으로: 찬물로 샤워하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
저는 샤워. (used as a verb) ✗ → 저는 샤워해요. ○
샤워 is a noun even though English 'shower' is a verb; standing alone it can't conjugate. It needs 하다.
Always 샤워하다 / 샤워를 하다.
샤워를 먹어요. ✗ → 샤워를 해요. ○
먹다 'eat' never fits washing; the activating verb for the chore noun is 하다.
Use 샤워해요; whole-body soak = 목욕하다.

extendedVocab.explanation: "washing face" is 세수 (sesu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 세수를 하다 ("to wash one's face"). Watch the particle attached to 세수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The action takes 하다; 세수 is the object with 를.
고 = 'and then'; the natural morning sequence after washing the face.
Idiom for a too-hasty, barely-there face wash, like a cat's lick.

usagePhrases.en: to wash the face with cold water
usagePhrases.note: The water takes 로; common to wake oneself up.

examples.en: I wash my face.
examples.note: Simple frame: 세수 + 를 + 해요; remember it's the FACE only.

examples.en: After waking, I wash my face first.
examples.note: Everyday: 부터 = 'starting with/first'; the first thing in the routine.

examples.ko: 어제는 피곤해서 세수도 안 하고 잤어요.
examples.romanization: eojeneun pigonhaeseo sesudo an hago jasseoyo.
examples.en: Yesterday I was so tired I slept without even washing my face.
examples.note: Real life: 도 안 하고 = 'without even doing'; 피곤하다 = tired.

extendedVocab.nuance: 세수 is Sino-Korean, 洗手 (洗 'wash' + 手 'hand'), and although it literally says 'wash hands', in modern usage it means washing the FACE (and hands) — the morning/evening face-wash, not the body. Its verb is 하다 (세수하다). Be careful with the three washing words: 세수 = face; 샤워 = whole-body standing rinse; 목욕 = soaking bath; and the plain verb 씻다 'wash' is the broad casual umbrella ('얼굴을 씻다' literally 'wash the face' is also said). Register is neutral and very everyday. The English-speaker pitfall comes straight from the hanja: learners read 洗手 and assume it means 'wash hands' for hygiene — but to say 'wash your hands' (before eating, after the toilet) Koreans use 손을 씻다, not 세수. Using 세수 for the whole body is also wrong (that's 샤워/목욕). A nice idiom to know: 고양이 세수, a 'cat wash', for splashing your face so quickly you barely cleaned it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
밥 먹기 전에 세수하세요 (meaning 'wash hands'). ✗ → 손을 씻으세요. ○
Despite the 手 'hand' hanja, 세수 = washing the face. Hand-washing for hygiene is 손을 씻다.
Hands = 손을 씻다; face routine = 세수하다.
세수로 몸을 씻어요. ✗ → 샤워해요 / 목욕해요. ○
세수 covers only the face, never the body. Whole-body washing is 샤워 (rinse) or 목욕 (soak).
Body = 샤워/목욕; face = 세수.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 양치 means "brushing teeth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 양치 (yangchi) = "brushing teeth". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 양치를 하다 / 양치질을 하다 ("to brush one's teeth") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 양치, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Both work; 양치질 is the fuller noun, both take 하다 with 를.
The default dental routine collocation; 고 = 'and then'.
양치 modifies the cup and tools used for brushing/rinsing.
가글(gargle) is the extra rinse step after 양치.

examples.en: I brush my teeth.
examples.note: Simple frame: 양치 + 를 + 해요; or just 양치해요.

examples.en: I always brush right after meals.
examples.note: Everyday: 고 나서 'after'; 꼭 = 'without fail'.

examples.ko: 자기 전에 양치하는 거 잊지 마세요.
examples.romanization: jagi jeone yangchihaneun geo itji maseyo.
examples.en: Don't forget to brush before bed.
examples.note: Real life: 는 거 nominalizes the action; 잊지 마세요 = 'don't forget'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 양치 (often the fuller 양치질) means brushing the teeth; it derives from hanja 養齒 (養 'nurture/care for' + 齒 'tooth') — 'caring for the teeth' — with the native suffix 질 (a 'doing of') giving 양치질. Its verb is 하다 (양치하다 / 양치질하다). The near-synonym 이를 닦다 'to scrub the teeth' (이 'tooth' + 닦다 'wipe/polish') is fully interchangeable in daily speech — 양치하다 = 이를 닦다 — though 닦다 highlights the scrubbing motion while 양치 names the routine including rinsing. Register is neutral; parents say it to kids constantly. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 솔질 or inventing 'teeth-brushing' literally; just use 양치하다 or 이를 닦다. Another trap is forgetting it's a noun: 양치 standing alone isn't a verb, so you must add 하다. And don't say 양치를 먹다 (✗) — 먹다 'eat' has no place in a brushing phrase. The toothbrush itself is 칫솔, the toothpaste 치약.

양치를 먹어요. ✗ → 양치를 해요. ○
먹다 doesn't belong to brushing; the chore noun is activated by 하다.
Use 양치해요 or 이를 닦아요.
이빨을 닦다 in polite speech
이빨 is a coarse/animal word for teeth; in normal/polite speech use 이 or 치아. So 이를 닦다, not 이빨을 닦다.
Polite: 양치하다 / 이를 닦다; avoid 이빨.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 산책 means "a walk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 산책 (sanchaek) means "a walk". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 산책을 하다 ("to take a walk"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 산책 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The activity takes 하다; 산책 is the object with 를.

usagePhrases.en: to go out for a walk
usagePhrases.note: 나가다 = go out; stresses leaving the house to stroll.
산책 as the noun event; 강아지 산책(을) 시키다 = walk the dog.
Place of the stroll takes 에서 (action location).

examples.en: I take a walk.
examples.note: Simple frame: 산책 + 를 + 해요, a leisurely stroll.

examples.ko: 저녁 먹고 동네 한 바퀴 산책해요.
examples.romanization: jeonyeong meokgo dongne han bakwi sanchaekaeyo.
examples.en: After dinner I stroll one loop around the neighborhood.
examples.note: Everyday: 한 바퀴 = 'one lap'; 동네 = neighborhood.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋아서 강아지랑 천천히 산책하고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga joaseo gangajirang cheoncheonhi sanchaekago wasseoyo.
examples.en: The weather was nice, so I went for a slow walk with my dog.
examples.note: Real life: 랑 = 'with' (casual); 고 오다 = 'go do and come back'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 산책 is Sino-Korean, 散策 (散 'scatter/disperse' + 策 'walking stick'), poetically 'wandering with a stick' — i.e. a relaxed, purpose-free stroll for pleasure or fresh air. Its verb is 하다 (산책하다 / 산책을 하다). The key contrast is with the plain verb 걷다 'to walk': 걷다 is the physical act of walking (to a destination, for transport, for exercise pace), while 산책 is the leisurely OUTING itself — you 산책하다 in a park to relax, but you 걷다 to the station because the bus didn't come. Also 산책 ≠ 등산 (登山 'climb a mountain', hiking). Register is neutral and pleasant. The English-speaker pitfall is 산책을 가다 (✗) modeled on 'go for a walk' — the chore/activity noun normally takes 하다, so use 산책하다; if you want the 'go out' nuance, say 산책(을) 나가다 or 산책하러 가다 'go in order to stroll'. Don't confuse it with simply 걷다 when the point is leisure.

산책을 가요. ✗ → 산책을 해요 / 산책하러 가요. ○
'Go for a walk' translated piece-by-piece is unnatural; the activity noun pairs with 하다, or use 하러 가다 for 'go to'.
Stroll = 산책하다; go to stroll = 산책하러 가다.
역까지 산책했어요 (meaning 'walked to the station'). ✗ → 역까지 걸어갔어요. ○
산책 is leisure, not getting somewhere. Walking to a destination is 걷다/걸어가다.
Leisure stroll = 산책; walk to a place = 걸어가다.

structuredNuance.t: 산책 is a relaxed, purpose-free stroll for pleasure or fresh air. Its verb is 하다 (산책하다 / 산책을 하다). Register is neutral and pleasant.

The key contrast is with the plain verb 걷다 'to walk': 걷다 is the physical act of walking (to a destination, for transport, for exercise pace), while 산책 is the leisurely OUTING itself — you 산책하다 in a park to relax, but you 걷다 to the station because the bus didn't come. Also 산책 ≠ 등산 (登山 'climb a mountain', hiking).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 휴식 means "rest" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "rest" is 휴식 (hyusik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 휴식을 취하다 ("to take a rest"). Watch the particle attached to 휴식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The idiomatic verb is 취하다 (take/assume), more than 하다: 휴식을 취하다.
휴식 modifies 시간; the scheduled break (class, work).
잠깐 = briefly; announced before a pause in meetings or workouts.
휴식 as subject with 이; pairs with 필요하다 'be needed'.

examples.en: I need rest.
examples.note: Simple frame: 휴식 + 이 + 필요해요; here it's the subject.

examples.ko: 회의 중간에 십 분 동안 휴식 시간을 가졌어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui junggane sip bun dongan hyusik siganeul gajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: We took a ten-minute break in the middle of the meeting.
examples.note: Everyday: 휴식 시간을 가지다 = 'have a break'; 동안 = 'for (duration)'.

examples.ko: 요즘 너무 무리해서 푹 휴식을 취하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum neomu murihaeseo pu kyusigeul chwihago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I've overdone it lately, so I want to rest fully.
examples.note: Real life: 휴식을 취하다 (formal 'take rest'); 푹 = thoroughly/deeply.

extendedVocab.nuance: 휴식 is Sino-Korean, 休息 (休 'rest' + 息 'breathe/pause'), 'resting and catching one's breath', a somewhat formal/written noun for taking a break. Its most idiomatic verb is 휴식을 취하다 'to take rest' (취하다 = take/assume), and 휴식하다 also exists, but in casual conversation Koreans far more often use the plain native verb 쉬다 'to rest' — '집에서 쉬어요' sounds natural where '집에서 휴식해요' sounds stiff. So the contrast is register: 휴식 = formal/signage/health-advice tone (충분한 휴식, 휴식 시간), 쉬다 = everyday speech. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 휴식 like a casual verb and overusing 휴식하다 in chat — prefer 쉬다 there. Also, because it's a noun, you cannot leave it bare for the action: pair it with 취하다/하다, or switch to 쉬다. Common collocations: 휴식 시간, 휴식을 취하다, 충분한 휴식, 잠깐 휴식.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
친구한테 '집에서 휴식해' (casual). △ → '집에서 쉬어'. ○
휴식하다 is stiff for casual talk; with friends the natural verb is 쉬다.
Casual rest = 쉬다; formal/written = 휴식(을 취하다).
저는 휴식. (noun used as a sentence) ✗ → 휴식을 취해요 / 쉬어요. ○
휴식 is a noun and can't stand as the predicate. Add 취하다/하다, or use 쉬다.
Use 휴식을 취하다 or 쉬다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 외출 means "going out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 외출 (oechul) = "going out". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 외출을 하다 ("to go out") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 외출, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The action takes 하다; 외출 is the object with 를.
준비 = preparation; 외출 준비(를) 하다 = prep before leaving.
중 (中 'in the middle of') marks the away status: 외출 중이에요.

usagePhrases.en: to not feel like going out
usagePhrases.note: 기 싫다 = 'hate to do'; common homebody phrase.

examples.en: I go out.
examples.note: Simple frame: 외출 + 를 + 해요; leaving the house.

examples.ko: 비가 와서 오늘은 외출 안 했어요.
examples.romanization: biga waseo oneureun oechul an haesseoyo.
examples.en: It rained, so I didn't go out today.
examples.note: Everyday: 안 + 했어요 negates; 와서 = 'because it came (rained)'.

examples.ko: 외출하기 전에 가스 불을 껐는지 꼭 확인하세요.
examples.romanization: oechulhagi jeone gaseu bureul kkeonneunji kko kwaginhaseyo.
examples.en: Before going out, be sure to check you turned off the gas.
examples.note: Real life: 기 전에 = 'before doing'; 는지 확인하다 = 'check whether'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 외출 is Sino-Korean, 外出 (外 'outside' + 出 'go out/exit'), 'going out of the house', and its verb is 하다 (외출하다 / 외출을 하다). It specifically means leaving home to go outside, often briefly. The near-synonym contrast: 외출 is leaving the HOUSE for a short while (외출 중 'stepped out'); 나가다 is the plain verb 'go out/exit' (any space); and 외박 (外泊) is the contrasting word for staying out OVERNIGHT (sleeping away from home) — useful so learners don't mix 외출 (out and back) with 외박 (out overnight). 외출 carries a slightly neutral-formal tone, common in notes ('외출 중입니다' 'I'm out'). The English-speaker pitfall is 외출을 가다 (✗), built from 'go out' — the activity noun takes 하다, so 외출하다; if you want a destination, name it with 가다 (시내에 가다 'go downtown') instead of forcing 외출 with 가다. Also remember it's a noun: don't use 외출 bare for the action. Collocations: 외출 준비, 외출 중, 외출 금지 (grounded/no-going-out).

외출을 가요. ✗ → 외출을 해요 / 외출해요. ○
'Go out' word-for-word doubles up; the activity noun pairs with 하다, not 가다.
Go out = 외출하다; to a place = (장소)에 가다.
밤새 친구 집에서 외출했어요 (meaning 'stayed over'). ✗ → 외박했어요. ○
외출 is out-and-back; sleeping away from home overnight is 외박.
Brief outing = 외출; overnight away = 외박.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 행복하다 means "happy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 행복하다 (haengbokada) means "happy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 행복해요 ("I am happy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 행복하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 conjugates to 해요, not 하요
modifier form 행복한 + noun
noun 행복 + 을, a set blessing
행복하게 turns it into an adverb 'happily'

examples.en: I am happy right now.
examples.note: plain 요-form 행복해요 stating your own state

examples.ko: 우리 가족은 작은 집에서도 행복하게 살아요.
examples.romanization: uri gajogeun jageun jibeseodo haengbokage sarayo.
examples.en: Our family lives happily even in a small house.
examples.note: 행복하게 as the adverb 'happily' modifying 살다

examples.ko: 오랜만에 친구를 다시 만나서 정말 행복했어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane chingureul dasi mannaseo jeongmal haengbokaesseoyo.
examples.en: I was really happy to meet my friend again after a long time.
examples.note: -아서 gives the cause, 행복했어요 is past tense

extendedVocab.nuance: 행복하다 is the deep, lasting 'happy' you feel about your life, family, or whole situation — closer to 'content/blessed' than a quick thrill. The Sino-Korean root is 幸福 (幸 good-fortune + 福 blessing), so it literally frames happiness as 'being blessed with good fortune', which is why it suits weddings, life reflections, and the standard blessing 행복하세요 ('be happy / may you be happy'). Contrast it with 기쁘다, which is a momentary gladness about one specific event (good news, a gift): you are 기쁘다 the instant you pass an exam, but 행복하다 about your life as a whole. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 행복해 → 행복해요 (never 행복하요), and the noun-modifying form is 행복한 사람. Biggest English-speaker trap: don't reach for 행복하다 every time you'd say 'happy' in English ('I'm happy you came', 'happy to help') — for those small, event-bound moments Korean uses 기쁘다 or 좋다, and overusing 행복하다 sounds melodramatic.

Saying 행복하요 — 하다 verbs/adjectives never just add 요 to 하. The vowel-contracted stem is 해, so it must be 행복해요.
Using 행복하다 for tiny moments like 'I'm happy you texted me' — that sounds overblown. For a specific small event Koreans say 기뻐요 or 좋아요; save 행복하다 for deep, whole-life happiness.
Treating it like an action verb and saying 행복하고 있어요 ('I am being happy'). It is a stative adjective; the present state is simply 행복해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 슬프다 means "sad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "sad" is 슬프다 (seulpeuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 슬퍼요 ("I am sad / it is sad"). Watch the particle attached to 슬프다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I am sad / it is sad
usagePhrases.note: ㅡ drops, 프 + 어요 → 퍼요
modifier form 슬픈 + noun
very common pairing with 소식
add -아하다 to describe someone else's sadness

examples.en: That story is really sad.
examples.note: 요-form 슬퍼요 describing a thing that evokes sadness

examples.en: When I listen to sad songs, tears come.
examples.note: modifier 슬픈 + noun, with -으면 'when/if'

examples.en: Everyone grieved because Grandmother passed away.
examples.note: 슬퍼하다 (not 슬퍼요) for a third person's visible grief

extendedVocab.nuance: 슬프다 is the core 'sad' for sorrow, loss, and touching/heartbreaking things — both 'I feel sad' and 'this is sad' (a sad movie, sad news). It is an adjective rooted in your own felt emotion, so for your own heart you say 슬퍼요, but to report that someone ELSE is sad Korean grammar prefers the derived verb 슬퍼하다 ('to act sad/grieve'): 동생이 슬퍼해요, not 동생이 슬퍼요 — this 형용사 → -아하다 → 동사 shift is a real adjective rule, the same as 좋다 → 좋아하다. Spelling-wise it is a ㅡ(으) irregular: drop the ㅡ before an ending starting with 어, so 슬프 + 어요 → 슬퍼요, and the modifier is 슬픈. Don't confuse 슬프다 with 우울하다 (憂鬱, 'depressed/gloomy'), which is a heavier, longer-lasting low mood rather than acute sorrow. Pitfall: writing 슬프어요 — the ㅡ must drop, giving 슬퍼요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 슬프어요 — 슬프다 is a ㅡ irregular, so the ㅡ disappears before -어요, producing 슬퍼요.
Saying 친구가 슬퍼요 to mean 'my friend is sad.' For another person's emotion use the verb 슬퍼하다 → 친구가 슬퍼해요; the bare adjective is reserved for your own feeling or for a thing that is sad.
Mixing up 슬프다 and 우울하다. 슬프다 is sorrow tied to an event (a sad film, a loss); 우울하다 is a heavier ongoing gloom. Don't say 슬프다 for clinical 'depressed.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기쁘다 means "glad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기쁘다 (gippeuda) = "glad". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기뻐요 ("I am glad") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기쁘다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㅡ drops, 쁘 + 어요 → 뻐요
the textbook collocation for happy news
note: greetings use 반갑다, not 기쁘다
-아하다 form for another person's joy

examples.en: I'm glad because I heard good news.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 기뻐요, tied to a specific event

examples.en: I was really glad that I passed the exam.
examples.note: past tense 기뻤어요 about one happy event

examples.en: My parents were glad too at the news of my passing.
examples.note: 기뻐하다 + honorific -시 for parents' visible joy

extendedVocab.nuance: 기쁘다 is gladness aimed at a SPECIFIC good event — good news, a success, a gift, a reunion — the spark of joy in the moment, not a settled state of life. This is exactly the line versus 행복하다: you are 기쁘다 the second you pass an exam, but 행복하다 about your life overall; reaching for 행복하다 for small wins sounds theatrical, while 기쁘다 fits them perfectly. Like 슬프다 it is a ㅡ irregular, so 기쁘 + 어요 → 기뻐요 (never 기쁘어요), modifier 기쁜. For another person's joy, shift to the verb 기뻐하다 (동생이 기뻐해요). A key English-speaker trap: 'glad/nice to meet you' is NOT 만나서 기뻐요 — Korean fixes that greeting as 만나서 반가워요 (from 반갑다), so save 기쁘다 for being glad about news and outcomes, not for the social 'nice to meet you.'

Saying 기쁘어요 — as a ㅡ irregular the ㅡ drops before -어요, giving 기뻐요.

Using 기쁘다 for deep life happiness ('I'm happy with my life' → 기뻐요?). That should be 행복해요; 기쁘다 is event-bound momentary gladness.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 화나다 means "angry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 화나다 (hwanada) means "angry". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 화나요 ("I get angry / I'm angry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 화나다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 stem → 나요 (no 하다 here)
past-modifier 화난 + noun
the full underlying phrase 화 + 가 + 나다
화 + 를 + 내다 = actively vent anger

examples.en: I get angry when I hear those words.
examples.note: -으니까 'because/when' + 화나요

examples.en: I got angry because my friend broke our promise.
examples.note: past 화났어요 with -아서 cause

examples.en: The boss got angry (vented) again.
examples.note: 화를 내다 + honorific 내셨어요 for actively showing anger

extendedVocab.nuance: 화나다 is anger that RISES in you in the moment — it is literally 화가 나다, where 화 (火, 'fire/wrath') is the anger and 나다 means 'to arise/come out', so the image is 'the fire comes up.' Because the verb is 나다, the form is 화나요 / 화났어요 — there is no 하다 here, so 화나해요 is wrong. Crucially, distinguish 화나다 from 화내다 (화를 내다): 화나다 is the inner feeling that arises ('I become/am angry'), while 화내다 is OUTWARDLY venting it at someone ('to get mad at / yell at'). So 나한테 화났어 = 'you're angry at me (you feel it)', but 나한테 화내지 마 = 'don't take your anger out on me.' Note also that the person you're angry at is marked with 한테/에게 (사람한테 화나다), which English 'angry at' doesn't visibly mark. For describing a face or person, the modifier is the past form 화난 (화난 표정). A blunter near-synonym is 짜증나다 ('to be irritated/annoyed'), a lighter, more peevish irritation than full 화.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 화나해요 — the verb is 나다 (to arise), not 하다, so it conjugates 화나요 / 화났어요. There is no 해 in it.
Confusing 화나다 and 화내다. 화나다 = the anger you feel inside; 화내다 (화를 내다) = outwardly venting/yelling. 'Don't be mad at me (outwardly)' is 화내지 마, not 화나지 마.
Forgetting the particle on the target: 'angry at my friend' is 친구한테 화나다, not 친구를 화나다. The person takes 한테/에게, never the object 를.

structuredNuance.t: 화나다 is anger that RISES in you in the moment. Crucially, distinguish 화나다 from 화내다 (화를 내다): 화나다 is the inner feeling that arises ('I become/am angry'), while 화내다 is OUTWARDLY venting it at someone ('to get mad at / yell at'). So 나한테 화났어 = 'you're angry at me (you feel it)', but 나한테 화내지 마 = 'don't take your anger out on me.'
A blunter near-synonym is 짜증나다 ('to be irritated/annoyed'), a lighter, more peevish irritation than full 화.
It is literally 화가 나다, where 화 (火, 'fire/wrath') is the anger and 나다 means 'to arise/come out', so the image is 'the fire comes up.'

modifier 피곤한 + noun
intensifier 너무 + 피곤하다, very common
noun 피곤 as accumulated tiredness

examples.note: 요-form 피곤해요 for your own bodily state

examples.note: -아서 cause + 너무 피곤해요

extendedVocab.nuance: 피곤하다 is physical/general tiredness — worn out, drained, exhausted — typically after work, study, travel, or poor sleep. It is Sino-Korean 疲困 (疲 weary + 困 exhausted), literally 'weary-exhausted', which is why it reads as bodily fatigue rather than sleepiness. Keep it apart from 졸리다 ('sleepy'): you can be 피곤하다 yet wide awake (drained but not nodding off), and 졸리다 is specifically wanting to sleep — don't swap them. It is also milder and more everyday than 지치다 ('to be worn out/burned out'), which implies you've reached your limit. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 피곤해요 (not 피곤하요). One common English-speaker slip: 피곤하다 normally describes a PERSON being tired; to call an activity 'tiring' you also use 피곤하다 (피곤한 일 = 'tiring work'), but to call a person 'tiresome/draining' Koreans say 피곤한 사람 — meaning 'a person who is exhausting to deal with', a nuance worth knowing so you don't misread it as 'a tired person.'

usagePhrases.note: ㅣ + 어요 contracts to 려요
modifier 졸린 + noun
noun 졸음 + 이 + 오다, a set phrase
-아서 죽겠다 = casual hyperbole 'so sleepy I could die'

examples.note: 요-form 졸려요 for your own drowsy state

examples.note: -고 나니까 'after doing ~, then' + 졸려요

examples.en: The class is boring, so I keep getting sleepy.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 자꾸 'repeatedly' + 졸려요

extendedVocab.nuance: 졸리다 is the specific feeling of drowsiness — your eyelids drooping, wanting to fall asleep — and it is the everyday way to say 'I'm sleepy.' Sharply separate it from 피곤하다 ('tired'): 피곤하다 is being physically drained (you can be exhausted yet alert), while 졸리다 is purely the urge to sleep, so after a heavy lunch you're 졸리다, but after a marathon you're 피곤하다. A closely related word is the noun 졸음 ('drowsiness'), used in 졸음이 오다 ('drowsiness comes') and 졸음운전 ('drowsy driving'). English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'I'm sleepy' as 졸려워요 by wrongly treating it like a ㅂ-irregular — 졸리다 is a plain ㅣ-stem, so it is 졸려요. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 배고프다 means "hungry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 배고프다 (baegopeuda) means "hungry". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 배고파요 ("I am hungry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 배고프다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅡ drops, 고프 + 아요 → 고파요
modifier 배고픈 + noun
the literal underlying form 배 + 가 + 고프다
-아 죽겠다 casual hyperbole 'so hungry I could die'

examples.en: I'm so hungry right now.
examples.note: 요-form 배고파요 for your own state

examples.en: I'm hungry because I skipped breakfast.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 배고파요

examples.en: I'm hungry, but all the restaurants are closed.
examples.note: -ㄴ데 'hungry, but/and' setting up the problem

extendedVocab.nuance: 배고프다 is the normal, everyday 'hungry' and is transparently a compound: 배 ('belly/stomach') + 고프다 ('to be empty/craving'), literally 'the stomach is empty' — which is why you'll also hear the spelled-out 배가 고프다 with the same meaning. The single bound word 고프다 is essentially only used with 배, so learn 배고프다 as a unit. Conjugation is the ㅡ irregular: drop the ㅡ before -아요, so 배고프 + 아요 → 배고파요 (note it takes 아, not 어, because the remaining vowel ㅗ is bright/positive); the modifier is 배고픈. Its natural opposite is 배부르다 ('to be full', a 르 irregular → 배불러요). English-speaker pitfalls: (1) writing 배고프아요 — the ㅡ must drop, giving 배고파요; (2) saying 나는 배고파요 in formal/polite company where 저는 is expected — 나는 is casual; (3) don't say 배고프다 to mean 'I want to eat that specific food' — that craving is 먹고 싶다, while 배고프다 is just the empty-stomach sensation.

Forgetting 고프다 only pairs with 배. You can't say 머리고프다 or use 고프다 alone for other hunger; the unit is 배고프다 (or 배가 고프다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목마르다 means "thirsty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "thirsty" is 목마르다 (mongmareuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 목말라요 ("I am thirsty"). Watch the particle attached to 목마르다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 르 irregular: 마르 + 아요 → 말라요
modifier 목마른 + noun
the literal underlying form 목 + 이 + 마르다
-아 죽겠다 casual hyperbole for intense thirst

examples.en: Please give me some water, I'm thirsty.
examples.note: 요-form 목말라요 plus a polite request

examples.en: I'm thirsty because the weather is hot.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 목말라요

examples.note: spelled-out 목이 마르다 with -고 나면 'after ~ing'

extendedVocab.nuance: 목마르다 means 'thirsty' and is literally 목 ('throat/neck') + 마르다 ('to dry up'), i.e. 'the throat goes dry' — you'll equally hear the unpacked 목이 마르다. The base verb 마르다 also means 'to dry' in general (빨래가 마르다 = 'the laundry dries') and even 'to be skinny' (몸이 말랐다), so context tells you which. The conjugation is the classic 르 irregular: before -아/어 the 르 doubles its ㄹ and the preceding syllable takes the added ㄹ, so 마르 + 아요 → 말라요, giving 목말라요 (modifier 목마른). Compare 모르다 → 몰라요 and 빠르다 → 빨라요 — same mechanism. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the #1 error is writing 목마르아요 as if it were regular — it must be 목말라요; (2) don't confuse it with 배고프다; thirst is 목마르다, hunger is 배고프다, and they are not interchangeable; (3) figuratively 목마르다 can mean 'to thirst/crave' (성공에 목마르다 = 'thirsty for success'), a nuance English shares, so that idiom does transfer.

Mixing up thirst and hunger. 목말라요 = thirsty (dry throat); 배고파요 = hungry (empty stomach). Don't use one for the other.
Treating 마르다 as only 'thirsty.' It also means 'to dry' (빨래가 마르다) and 'to be thin' (말랐다). For thirst you specifically need 목(이) 마르다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 심심하다 means "bored" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 심심하다 (simsimhada) = "bored". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 심심해요 ("I am bored") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 심심하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 심심한 + noun
-면 'if/when' + 심심하다, very common invite

usagePhrases.en: as a way to kill boredom
usagePhrases.note: fixed noun 심심풀이 'pastime' + 로

examples.en: I'm bored because I have nothing to do.
examples.note: -아서 cause + 심심해요

examples.ko: 주말에 심심하면 우리 집에 놀러 와.
examples.romanization: jumare simsimhamyeon uri jibe nolleo wa.
examples.en: If you're bored on the weekend, come hang out at my place.
examples.note: -면 'if bored' inviting someone, casual 반말

examples.en: I'm so bored being home alone.
examples.note: -으니까 'because/since' + 심심해요

extendedVocab.nuance: 심심하다 is the boredom you feel as a PERSON when you have nothing to do — restless, twiddling your thumbs, 'I'm bored.' This is the crucial contrast with 지루하다: 심심하다 describes the bored SUBJECT (a person with empty time → 나는 심심해), whereas 지루하다 describes a boring OBJECT/experience that drags (a dull movie or lecture → 영화가 지루해). So 'I'm bored' (nothing to do) is 심심해요, but 'this class is boring' is 이 수업이 지루해요 — swapping them is the classic learner error. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 심심해요 (not 심심하요). It pairs naturally with 심심하면 ~ ('if you're bored, ...') as a soft invitation, and with the fixed nouns 심심풀이 ('a pastime/something to kill time'). (Note: there is an unrelated homophone 심심하다 meaning 'bland/under-seasoned' for food, and a formal 심심한 사의 = 'deep gratitude' from 甚深; for emotions you only need the 'bored' sense.) Pitfall: English 'I'm bored OF this' tempts a 를/을, but 심심하다 takes no object — you simply say 심심해요.

Using 심심하다 for a boring thing. 'This movie is boring' is 영화가 지루해요, not 심심해요. 심심하다 = a person with nothing to do; 지루하다 = a tedious thing/experience.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무섭다 means "scary; afraid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 무섭다 (museopda) means "scary; afraid". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무서워요 ("it's scary / I'm scared"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무섭다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ irregular: 무섭 + 어요 → 무서워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier 무서운 + noun
the feared thing takes 이/가, not 을/를
-아하다 verb for a third person's fear

examples.en: This movie is so scary.
examples.note: 요-form 무서워요 describing a frightening thing

examples.en: I'm afraid of high places.
examples.note: 높은 곳이 — the feared thing marked with 이/가

examples.en: My little sibling is afraid of dark rooms.
examples.note: 무서워하다 + 을/를 for another person's fear

extendedVocab.nuance: 무섭다 covers both 'scary' (a thing is frightening: 무서운 영화) and 'afraid' (you feel fear: 개가 무서워요), and it carries a key grammar quirk shared by emotion adjectives like 좋다/싫다: the THING you fear is marked with 이/가, not the object 을/를 — so 'I'm afraid of dogs' is 개가 무서워요 (literally 'dogs are scary-to-me'), which trips up English speakers who expect 'fear' to take a direct object. When you switch to describing someone ELSE's fear, you must use the derived verb 무서워하다, and THEN the feared thing takes 을/를: 동생이 개를 무서워해요. Conjugation is the ㅂ irregular — ㅂ turns into 우 before a vowel — so 무섭 + 어요 → 무서워요 and the modifier is 무서운 (not 무섭은). Distinguish it from 무섭다's relatives: 두렵다 is a more literary, abstract dread (미래가 두렵다 = 'I dread the future'), while 무섭다 is the everyday, gut-level scary; and 겁나다 is a casual 'I'm freaked out.' Pitfall: never write 무섭어요 — the ㅂ must become 우.

Marking the feared thing with 을/를: 개를 무서워요. With the adjective 무섭다 the feared thing takes 이/가 → 개가 무서워요. (Only the verb 무서워하다 takes 을/를.)
Using 무섭다 directly for another person: 동생이 무서워요 to mean 'my sibling is scared.' That actually reads 'my sibling is scary (to me)!' For their fear use 동생이 무서워해요.

Conjugation is the ㅂ irregular — ㅂ turns into 우 before a vowel — so 무섭 + 어요 → 무서워요 and the modifier is 무서운 (not 무섭은).

Also never write 무섭어요 — the ㅂ must become 우.

extendedVocab.nuance: 즐겁다 is 'enjoyable/fun' centered on an ACTIVITY or shared time — a trip, a party, a class, time with friends — the pleasant feeling of doing something. It is the standard word in well-wishes like 즐거운 하루 보내세요 ('have a nice day') and 즐거운 여행 ('a pleasant trip'). Contrast it with 재미있다, its close cousin: 재미있다 leans toward 'interesting/amusing/funny' (a gripping book or a funny video can be 재미있다 even alone), while 즐겁다 emphasizes your overall enjoyment of a situation or time spent — a quiet family dinner is 즐겁다 more than 재미있다. Conjugation is the ㅂ irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel, so 즐겁 + 어요 → 즐거워요, and the modifier is 즐거운 (not 즐겁은). The adverb 즐겁게 ('enjoyably') is extremely common with verbs like 놀다/지내다. English-speaker pitfall: don't default to 재미있다 for every 'fun' — for 'have a good time' and pleasant shared occasions, Koreans reach for 즐겁다; and never write 즐겁어요 (the ㅂ must become 우).

Saying 즐겁어요 — as a ㅂ irregular, ㅂ becomes 우 before -어요, giving 즐거워요, with modifier 즐거운.
Always substituting 재미있다 for 'fun.' 재미있다 = interesting/amusing (even for a solo book/video); 즐겁다 = enjoyable shared time/activity. 'Have a good time' is 즐거운 시간 보내세요, not 재미있는 시간.
Forming the modifier as 즐겁은 여행. The ㅂ-irregular noun-modifier is 즐거운 → 즐거운 여행.

extendedVocab.nuance: 지루하다 is 'boring/tedious' for something that DRAGS — a long meeting, a dull movie, a slow lecture — the quality of an experience that wears your patience thin. This is the mirror image of 심심하다, and keeping them straight is one of the most useful distinctions in this set: 지루하다 describes the boring THING/experience (영화가 지루해 = 'the movie is boring'), while 심심하다 describes a bored PERSON with nothing to do (나는 심심해 = 'I'm bored'). So 'I'm bored' (idle) ≠ 'this is boring' (tedious) — the first is 심심해요, the second 지루해요. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 지루해요 (not 지루하요), modifier 지루한. A near-synonym is 따분하다, which is similar 'dull/tedious' with a slightly more listless, fed-up flavor; 지루하다 is the neutral default. English-speaker pitfall: because English uses one word 'boring/bored' for both the cause and the feeler, learners say 나는 지루해요 meaning 'I'm bored' — but that literally implies 'I am a boring thing.' For your own idle boredom say 심심해요; reserve 지루하다 for the tedious thing itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 지루하요 — 하다 contracts to 해, so it's 지루해요.
Saying 나는 지루해요 to mean 'I'm bored (nothing to do).' That reads as 'I am boring.' Use 심심해요 for a bored person; 지루하다 is for a tedious thing/experience.
Mixing 지루하다 and 심심하다 in general. Remember the pair: a dull movie/class = 지루하다 (it drags); a person with empty time = 심심하다 (idle).

extendedVocab.nuance: 덥다 is the ㅂ-irregular adjective for FELT air temperature being unpleasantly high — hot weather, a stuffy room, a sweaty body. The key English-speaker trap is that English 'hot' covers four different Korean words: use 덥다 ONLY for ambient air/weather. A hot object you touch is 뜨겁다 (뜨거운 커피, never 더운 커피), spicy food is 맵다, and pleasant warmth is 따뜻하다. Because it is ㅂ-irregular, the ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel: 덥다 → 더워요(polite) → 더운(modifier) → 더우니까(reason) → 더워서. Beginners constantly write 덥어요 or 덥은 by treating it as regular — that is the number-one error. It is neutral in register and used by everyone; the related noun is 더위 ('the heat'), and people say 더위를 먹다 to mean 'suffer heatstroke.'

Saying 덥은 날 or 덥어요 — 덥다 is ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ changes to 우: the correct forms are 더운 날 and 더워요.
Calling hot coffee or hot soup 덥다 (더운 커피). Objects that are hot to the touch take 뜨겁다 → 뜨거운 커피.
Using 덥다 for spicy food. 'This is too hot!' about chili means 매워요 (from 맵다), not 더워요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 춥다 is the ㅂ-irregular adjective for ambient air being unpleasantly cold — winter, a chilly room, a draft. The crucial contrast for English speakers is 춥다 vs 차갑다: 춥다 is how the WEATHER/AIR feels to your whole body, while 차갑다 is how a cold OBJECT feels to your hand (차가운 물 'cold water', 차가운 손 'cold hands'). Never say 추운 물 — water is 차갑다. As a ㅂ-irregular it conjugates 춥다 → 추워요 → 추운 → 추우니까 → 추워서, so writing 춥어요 or 춥은 (the regular pattern) is the classic beginner slip. It is register-neutral and universal. The matching noun is 추위, and 추위를 타다 means 'to be cold-sensitive,' the exact mirror of 더위를 타다.

Saying 추운 물 or 추운 손 for cold water or cold hands. A cold thing you touch is 차갑다 → 차가운 물, 차가운 손.
Confusing 춥다 with 차갑다 in feelings: a cold-hearted person is 차갑다 (차가운 사람), never 추운 사람.

extendedVocab.nuance: 따뜻하다 means pleasantly, comfortably warm and is overwhelmingly POSITIVE — that is what separates it from 덥다, which is the unpleasant 'too hot.' It stretches across three domains: weather (따뜻한 봄날), temperature of food/drink (따뜻한 국), and emotional warmth (따뜻한 사람, 따뜻한 말 'kind words'). The near-synonym 뜨겁다 is for things hot enough to burn, so 따뜻한 커피 is comfortably drinkable while 뜨거운 커피 is scalding — choosing wrong sounds odd. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates predictably: 따뜻하다 → 따뜻해요 (note 하 + 아 → 해), 따뜻한, 따뜻하게(adverb), 따뜻해서. The pitfall: learners write 따뜻하요 by forgetting that 하 + 여/아 contracts to 해. Register is neutral and the word is everywhere in everyday speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 따뜻하요 — every 하다-adjective contracts 하 + 아 into 해, so the polite form is 따뜻해요.
Using 따뜻하다 for very hot food/drink. Comfortably warm tea is 따뜻한 차; scalding coffee is 뜨거운 커피 (from 뜨겁다).
Treating it as a verb and asking 따뜻해요? to mean 'do you warm?' — it is a state adjective ('is warm'), so 따뜻해요? simply asks 'is it warm?'

In Korean the particle or ending next to 시원하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

extendedVocab.nuance: 시원하다 is the positive counterpart to 차갑다/춥다: it means PLEASANTLY cool and, by extension, refreshing or relieving. Its famous quirk for English speakers is that 시원하다 ≠ 'cold': a hot spicy soup is praised as 시원하다 (시원한 국물) because it clears your sinuses and settles your stomach, and a hot spring or a good back-scratch is also 시원하다. So unlike 차갑다 (purely low temperature), 시원하다 is about the refreshing SENSATION. It also covers emotional relief — 속이 시원하다 'I feel relieved/it's off my chest.' As a 하다-adjective: 시원하다 → 시원해요 → 시원한 → 시원하게 → 시원해서. The trap is writing 시원하요 (must contract to 시원해요) and assuming it always means 'cold' — temperature-cold drinks are better 차갑다/차가운. Register is neutral and conversational.

Writing 시원하요 — the 하다 contraction gives 시원해요.
Assuming 시원하다 means 'cold.' A genuinely cold drink is 차가운 음료; 시원하다 is the refreshing feeling, which even a hot soup can have.
Translating 속이 시원하다 literally as 'my stomach is cool.' It is an idiom meaning 'I feel relieved / that's satisfying.'

extendedVocab.nuance: 밝다 covers brightness of LIGHT (a sunlit room, a lit lamp), lightness of a COLOR (밝은 파랑 'light blue'), and figuratively a CHEERFUL personality (성격이 밝다). It is a regular adjective despite the ㄹㄱ cluster: 밝다 → 밝아요 (the 받침 keeps both consonants but the ㄱ pronounces as /k→g/), 밝은, 밝아서. A useful near-synonym is 환하다, which means brightly/glowingly lit and is more about a flood of light or a beaming smile (환한 미소), whereas 밝다 is the broad neutral word and the only one used for cheerful character or for clear eyesight/hearing (귀가 밝다 'sharp-eared'). Pitfall one: confusing the spelling with 밤 ('night') or 밥 ('rice') — 밝다 is bright. Pitfall two: pronouncing it; 밝다 sounds like [박따], and 밝아요 like [발가요], which trips learners up.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 밝다 (bright) with the noun 밤 (night) — they look related but 밝다 means bright/light, the opposite of dark.
Mispronouncing the conjugation: 밝아요 is read [발가요], not [발바요]; the ㄱ of the 받침 links to the following vowel.
Forgetting the figurative sense: 성격이 밝다 means 'cheerful,' so don't read it literally as 'the personality is bright/shiny.'

extendedVocab.nuance: 어둡다 is the exact opposite of 밝다 and, like 밝다, spans three layers: physical darkness (an unlit room, nighttime), dark COLOR tone (어두운 회색 'dark gray'), and a figurative GLOOMY mood or expression (표정이 어둡다, 분위기가 어둡다). Crucially it is ㅂ-IRREGULAR — 어둡다 → 어두워요 → 어두운 → 어두우니까 → 어두워서 — so the single most common beginner error is the regular-looking 어둡어요/어둡은. A near-synonym is 캄캄하다 ('pitch-dark'), which is far stronger: a room with no light at all is 캄캄하다, while 어둡다 is the general 'dark/dim.' One more nuance learners miss: 어둡다 can mean 'poorly informed' — 세상 물정에 어둡다 'naive about the world' or 길에 어둡다 'bad with directions,' mirroring how 밝다 means 'well-informed/sharp.' Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 어둡어요 or 어둡은 방 — 어둡다 is ㅂ-irregular, so use 어두워요 and 어두운 방.
Using 어둡다 for total blackness when you mean pitch-dark; for that, 캄캄하다 is stronger and more natural.
Missing the figurative range: 표정이 어둡다 means someone looks gloomy, not that their face is literally dark in color.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 시끄럽다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

adverb 시끄럽게 + 하다; what a teacher tells noisy kids to stop doing
literally 'the ears are noisy,' a vivid complaint about loudness

examples.en: It is noisy here.
examples.note: ㅂ-irregular polite form 시끄러워요, not 시끄럽어요

extendedVocab.nuance: 시끄럽다 means unpleasantly LOUD or noisy — places, sounds, machines, and people can all be 시끄럽다, and it is the direct opposite of 조용하다. It is ㅂ-IRREGULAR: 시끄럽다 → 시끄러워요 → 시끄러운 → 시끄러우니까 → 시끄러워서, so 시끄럽어요/시끄럽은 are the predictable beginner mistakes. Two register cautions: first, 시끄러워! barked at someone literally means 'shut up!' and is rude, so reserve it for very casual settings; politely you'd say 조금 시끄럽네요 or ask 조용히 해 주세요. Second, distinguish it from 떠들다, which is a VERB meaning 'to chatter/make a racket' (아이들이 떠들어요 'the kids are being rowdy') — 시끄럽다 describes the resulting state, 떠들다 the action. There is also a figurative 'a fuss/controversy is loud' use: 세상이 시끄럽다 'the world is in an uproar.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 시끄럽어요 or 시끄럽은 — because it is ㅂ-irregular, say 시끄러워요 and 시끄러운.
Telling an elder 시끄러워요 to mean 'please be quiet.' That sounds like 'you're being annoyingly loud / shut up'; use 조용히 해 주세요 instead.
Confusing the adjective 시끄럽다 with the verb 떠들다. People actively making noise 떠들다; the place/sound that results is 시끄럽다.

extendedVocab.explanation: "quiet" is 조용하다 (joyonghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조용한 곳 ("a quiet place"). Watch the particle attached to 조용하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

examples.note: real-situation use with 조용해지다 and -(으)니까

extendedVocab.nuance: 조용하다 is the opposite of 시끄럽다 and covers both a quiet PLACE/sound and a calm, reserved PERSONALITY (성격이 조용하다 = soft-spoken, low-key). As a 하다-adjective it conjugates regularly: 조용하다 → 조용해요 → 조용한 → 조용히(adverb, note the special 히 form) → 조용해서. The most useful distinction for English speakers is the adverb: 'be quiet!' is 조용히 해! (using 조용히), not 조용하게 — Koreans overwhelmingly use 조용히 here, so memorize it as a set phrase. The near-synonym 고요하다 is more literary/poetic and means a deep, serene stillness (고요한 밤 'a serene night'), whereas 조용하다 is the everyday neutral word you'd actually speak. Pitfall: writing 조용하요 instead of the contracted 조용해요, and reaching for 조용하게 when 조용히 is the natural adverb. Register is neutral and extremely common.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 조용하요 — the 하다 contraction yields 조용해요.
Saying 조용하게 해 for 'be quiet.' The idiomatic adverb is 조용히, so it should be 조용히 해 주세요.
Using 조용하다 of a person to imply they are boring; it neutrally means calm/reserved, and adding nuance like 'boring' needs a different word such as 재미없다.

extendedVocab.explanation: 넓다 (neolbda) = "wide, spacious". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 넓은 방 ("a spacious room") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

figurative: a 마음이 넓은 사람 is tolerant and forgiving

examples.note: 넓은 modifies 공원 in the noun-modifier shape

extendedVocab.nuance: 넓다 describes a wide AREA or surface — a room, a road, a field, a forehead — and is the opposite of 좁다. The essential contrast English speakers must learn is 넓다 vs 크다: 넓다 is two-dimensional spaciousness (floor area, breadth), while 크다 is overall bigness/size. A studio can be 작지만 넓다 ('small in size yet feels open'), and Koreans say 방이 넓다 for a roomy floor plan but 집이 크다 for a large house overall — mixing them sounds off. It is a regular adjective: 넓다 → 넓어요 (pronounced [널버요], the ㅂ of the ㄼ cluster surfaces), 넓은, 넓어서. Two famous idioms ride on it: 마음이 넓다 'broad-minded/generous' and 발이 넓다 'well-connected socially.' The pronunciation pitfall is that 넓다 is [널따] and 넓어요 is [널버요], not [넙어요]. Register is neutral and everyday.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 넓다 for height. A tall building is 높다 (높은 건물); 넓다 is only about horizontal width/area.
Swapping 넓다 and 크다: floor-area spaciousness is 넓다 (방이 넓다), while overall bigness is 크다 (집이 크다).
Mispronouncing the conjugation: 넓어요 is [널버요] — the hidden ㅂ in the ㄼ cluster is pronounced when a vowel follows.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 좁다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

figurative opposite of 마음이 넓다

extendedVocab.nuance: 좁다 is the opposite of 넓다 and means a narrow or cramped AREA — a small room, a tight alley, a narrow road. It is a regular adjective with a clean conjugation: 좁다 → 좁아요 → 좁은 → 좁아서. The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 넓다: keep 좁다 (cramped/narrow in area) separate from 짧다 (short in LENGTH). A short pencil is 짧다, never 좁다; a narrow corridor is 좁다, never 짧다. Likewise a small-in-size object is 작다, so 'a small room' meaning low floor area is 방이 좁다, while 'a small box' meaning little overall is 작은 상자. Figuratively, 마음이 좁다 ('narrow-minded, petty') and 속이 좁다 ('small-hearted, easily offended') are the negative counterparts to 넓다's generous idioms. Register is neutral. Because it ends in a simple 받침 ㅂ, there's no irregularity to trip over — the main risk is just mixing it up with 짧다 and 작다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 좁다 for short length. A short skirt or pencil is 짧다 (짧은 치마); 좁다 is only about narrowness of area/width.
Swapping 좁다 and 작다: a cramped (low-area) room is 방이 좁다, while a small-sized object is 작은 물건.
Reading 마음이 좁다 literally. It is an idiom meaning 'narrow-minded / petty,' not that someone's heart is physically small.

extendedVocab.nuance: 두껍다 describes a FLAT thing being thick — a book, a blanket, a wall, a coat, a slice — and is the opposite of 얇다. It is ㅂ-IRREGULAR: 두껍다 → 두꺼워요 → 두꺼운 → 두꺼우니까 → 두꺼워서, so the regular-looking 두껍어요/두껍은 are the standard beginner errors. The contrast every English speaker needs is 두껍다 vs 굵다: both translate as 'thick,' but 두껍다 is for flat/layered objects (두꺼운 책) while 굵다 is for ROUND/cylindrical things — a thick rope, a thick tree trunk, thick noodles, or thick fingers are 굵다 (굵은 밧줄, 굵은 면), and using 두껍다 there sounds wrong. So 'thick legs' is 다리가 굵다, not 두껍다. The noun is 두께 ('thickness'), and the idiom 낯이 두껍다 / 얼굴이 두껍다 means 'shameless, thick-skinned.' Register is neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 두껍어요 or 두껍은 책 — 두껍다 is ㅂ-irregular, so say 두꺼워요 and 두꺼운 책.
Using 두껍다 for round/cylindrical things. A thick rope, thick noodles, or thick legs are 굵다 (굵은 밧줄, 다리가 굵다), not 두껍다.

adverb 얇게 + 썰다, a common cooking instruction

examples.en: This paper is thin.
examples.note: regular polite form 얇아요 (얇- + 아요)

examples.en: I wore a thin shirt.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 자주 means "often" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 자주 (jaju) means "often". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자주 가요 ("I go often"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자주 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: sits right before the verb
frequency, repeated meetings
habitual eating
goes before the 안 of negation

examples.en: I eat kimchi often.
examples.note: Simple habit: 자주 sits directly before the verb 먹어요.

examples.en: These days I can't meet my friends often.
examples.note: Everyday: with 못, 자주 still comes first — 자주 못 만나요, not 못 자주.

examples.ko: 이 동네는 버스가 자주 안 와서 불편해요.
examples.romanization: i dongneneun beoseuga jaju an waseo bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: In this neighborhood the bus doesn't come often, so it's inconvenient.
examples.note: Real situation: 자주 안 와요 = 'comes rarely'; the adverb hugs the whole negated verb.

extendedVocab.nuance: 자주 means 'often / frequently' and describes how many TIMES an action repeats over a period — it answers 얼마나 자주 ('how often'), never how fast or how well. The frequency scale runs 항상(always) > 자주(often) > 가끔(sometimes) > 거의 안(hardly), and 자주 sits high but short of 'always'. Its natural opposite is 가끔; learners confuse 자주 with 빨리(quickly), but 자주 is about count of occurrences while 빨리 is about speed of one action — 빨리 먹어요 means 'eats fast', 자주 먹어요 means 'eats often'. Register-neutral, fine for everyone. The big English-speaker pitfall is word order: English lets you say 'I go there often' with the adverb last, but Korean glues 자주 immediately before the verb (자주 가요), and even before 안/못 in negatives (자주 안 가요).

Placing the adverb after 안 in negatives: 안 자주 와요 is wrong. The order is 자주 안 와요 ('doesn't come often').

extendedVocab.explanation: "sometimes" is 가끔 (gakkeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가끔 봐요 ("I see it sometimes"). Watch the particle attached to 가끔 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: low-frequency, before the verb

usagePhrases.en: I go once in a while
usagePhrases.note: occasional outing
spontaneous recollection
sporadic contact

examples.en: I sometimes eat ramyeon.
examples.note: Simple: 가끔 marks a low-frequency habit, sitting before 먹어요.

examples.en: On weekends I sometimes sleep in.
examples.note: Everyday: pairs naturally with 주말에는 to mean 'on some weekends, not all'.

examples.en: I'm busy, but every so often I call my parents.
examples.note: Real situation: 가끔은 (with 은) softly contrasts 'at least sometimes' against the busyness.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가끔 means 'sometimes / once in a while / occasionally' — clearly less frequent than 자주 but more than 거의 안(hardly ever): the scale is 항상 > 자주 > 가끔 > 거의 안 > 전혀 안. Its nearest rival is 때때로, which means the same but is more bookish/written; in everyday speech 가끔 is the natural choice, while 때때로 can sound like an essay. You can intensify it as 가끔씩 ('every now and then'), which feels even more sporadic and warm. Register-neutral and safe with anyone. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, word order — it must precede the verb (가끔 가요, not 가요 가끔); second, learners over-reach and use 가끔 for things that are actually frequent, so calibrate it as 'only occasionally', not 'fairly often'.

Putting it at the end like English 'I go sometimes': 가요 가끔 is wrong; say 가끔 가요.
Treating 가끔 and 자주 as interchangeable. 가끔 means it happens rarely; if it happens often, you must switch to 자주, or your listener will picture a much lower frequency.

extendedVocab.explanation: 항상 (hangsang) = "always". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 항상 웃어요 ("you always smile") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 항상, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 100% of the time, before the verb
habitual, no exceptions
standing emotional state
reliable repeated action

examples.en: My older sister always eats breakfast.
examples.note: Simple: 항상 = every single time, with no exception, before 먹어요.

examples.ko: 저는 항상 핸드폰을 손에 들고 다녀요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hangsang haendeuponeul sone deulgo danyeoyo.
examples.en: I always carry my phone in my hand.
examples.note: Everyday: 항상 stresses an unbroken habit; pairs well with 들고 다니다 ('carry around').

examples.en: Stay healthy and always be happy.
examples.note: Real situation: a warm blessing — here 늘 and 항상 are swapped freely; both mean 'always'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 항상 (Sino-Korean 恒常, 恒 'constant' + 常 'usual', literally 'constant-usual') means 'always / at all times', marking an action that holds without exception — far stronger than 보통(usually), which allows exceptions. Its near-synonym is 늘, a pure native word with the same meaning; the two are almost always interchangeable, though 늘 feels a touch softer and warmer (common in well-wishes) while 항상 sounds a hair more emphatic and is slightly more frequent in writing. Another cousin, 언제나, leans poetic/literary. All are register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 항상 to mean 'usually' — English 'always' is loose ('I'm always late-ish'), but Korean 항상 is literally 100%, so for a normal-but-not-absolute habit use 보통, and keep the word before the verb (항상 와요, not 와요 항상).

Using 항상 for something that is merely typical. 항상 = exactly every time; if there are exceptions you mean 보통('usually') instead.
Word-order slip: 와요 항상 copies English. Korean needs 항상 와요, adverb before verb.

extendedVocab.explanation: 보통 (botong) means "usually". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보통 가요 ("I usually go"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: general habit, allows exceptions
typical routine
default mode of doing
here 보통 works as a noun/modifier

examples.en: I usually get up at seven.
examples.note: Simple: 보통 = 'as a rule, with exceptions allowed', before 일어나요.

examples.en: I usually eat lunch near the office.
examples.note: Everyday: describes the default choice, not an absolute rule.

examples.ko: 보통은 안 그런데 오늘은 좀 피곤하네요.
examples.romanization: botongeun an geureonde oneureun jom pigonhaneyo.
examples.en: Usually I'm not like this, but today I'm a bit tired.
examples.note: Real situation: 보통은 (with 은) sets up a contrast — 'normally... but today...'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 보통 (Sino-Korean 普通, 普 'widespread' + 通 'common', literally 'widely-common') means 'usually / normally / ordinarily' and frames what happens as a rule WHILE leaving room for exceptions — that exception-tolerance is exactly what separates it from 항상(always, no exceptions). Uniquely among these adverbs, 보통 is also a noun/adjective meaning 'ordinary' (보통 사람 'an average person', 보통이에요 'it's so-so'), so context tells you which use is active. Register-neutral. extendedVocab.explanation: "early" is 일찍 (iljjik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일찍 자요 ("I sleep early"). ahead of the usual hour
arriving before time

examples.en: I usually sleep early.
examples.note: Simple: 일찍 = at an early hour, before 자요.

examples.en: Tomorrow I want to get up early.
examples.note: Everyday: 일찍 + 일어나다 is the standard 'wake up early' collocation.

examples.en: Worried about traffic, I left thirty minutes early.
examples.note: Real situation: 일찍 here means 'ahead of schedule', and 30분 일찍 = 'earlier by 30 min'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 일찍 means 'early' in the sense of an EARLY POINT IN TIME — early hour of the day or ahead of a schedule — and is the natural opposite of 늦게(late). Word order: 와요 일찍 mirrors English; Korean puts the adverb first — 일찍 와요.

usagePhrases.note: at a late hour
past the usual time
arriving behind time

examples.en: I went to bed too late yesterday.
examples.note: Simple: 늦게 = at a late hour, here intensified by 너무.

examples.en: On weekends I sleep in until late.
examples.note: Everyday: 늦게까지 ('until late') is a high-frequency collocation.

examples.en: The meeting ran long, so I worked late yesterday.
examples.note: Real situation: 늦게 describes finishing at a late hour, the opposite of 일찍 끝내다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 늦게 means 'late', i.e. at a LATE POINT IN TIME or behind schedule, and is the exact opposite of 일찍(early). extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 먼저 means "first" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 먼저 (meonjeo) means "first". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 먼저 가요 ("I'll go first / ahead"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 먼저 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: leaving before others

usagePhrases.en: please go ahead / do it first
usagePhrases.note: yielding politely
earlier in a sequence
taking the initiative

examples.en: I'll head off first.
examples.note: Simple: 먼저 = ahead of others in time/order, before 갈게요.

examples.en: Wash your hands first, then eat.
examples.note: Everyday: 먼저 marks step one of a sequence (먼저 A 하고 B).

examples.en: I'll be heading in/out first (leaving before you).
examples.note: Real situation: a polite set phrase to excuse yourself before colleagues — 'I'll go ahead.'

extendedVocab.nuance: 먼저 means 'first / beforehand / ahead (of others)' — it ranks one action or person EARLIER in a sequence or in time. The key contrast is 먼저 vs 처음: 먼저 is relative ('before the other thing/person', e.g. 먼저 가요 'go ahead of you'), while 처음 means 'the first time ever / the beginning' (처음 만나요 'meeting for the first time'). So 먼저 봤어요 = 'I saw it first (before you)', but 처음 봤어요 = 'I saw it for the first time'. 먼저 is also a courtesy word: 먼저 가세요 / 먼저 하세요 ('go ahead, you first') is everyday politeness, and 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 들어가겠습니다 softens leaving before others. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping every 'first' to one word — choose 먼저 for order-relative 'first/ahead', but 처음 for 'first-ever/at first', and keep 먼저 before the verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 처음 to mean 'go ahead of someone'. 처음 갈게요 sounds like 'I'll go for the first time'; to mean 'I'll go first (before you)' say 먼저 갈게요.
Conversely, using 먼저 for 'the first time'. 먼저 만나요 means 'meet first (before others)'; 'meet for the first time' is 처음 만나요.
Placing it after the verb. English 'you go first' tempts 가요 먼저; Korean order is 먼저 가요 (or politely 먼저 가세요).
