extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 벌써 means "already" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "already" is 벌써 (beolsseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌써 왔어요 ("you're here already?!"). Watch the particle attached to 벌써 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: sooner than expected
faster than thought
surprise at completion
time flew by

examples.en: Is it lunchtime already?
examples.note: Simple: 벌써 voices surprise that time passed fast.

examples.en: I've already finished that book.
examples.note: Everyday: with past tense + 다, 벌써 stresses 'done sooner than expected'.

examples.en: The snow has already melted. It must be spring.
examples.note: Real situation: 벌써 + the surprise-marker -네요 conveys mild astonishment.

extendedVocab.nuance: 벌써 means 'already', but its core flavor is SURPRISE that something happened sooner than you expected — 'wow, already?'. Compare its near-twin 이미: 이미 is the neutral 'already / by now' that simply reports a completed fact (이미 끝났어요 'it's already finished', stating it), whereas 벌써 adds the emotional jolt (벌써 끝났어요? 'it's done already?!'). So a flat report prefers 이미; an astonished reaction prefers 벌써. It naturally rides with past tense and with 다('all'), and often co-occurs with the exclamatory endings -네요/-군요. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't pair 벌써 with the future — English 'already' can sit oddly with plans, but 벌써 is about something that has ALREADY occurred, so it takes past/completed verbs (벌써 갔어요), not 벌써 갈 거예요. Use 곧/이미 곧 logic for 'soon' instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Attaching 벌써 to future actions: 벌써 갈 거예요 is wrong. 벌써 needs a completed event — 벌써 갔어요 ('already left').
Swapping in 벌써 where you only want a neutral report. To plainly state a fact, 이미 is better; 벌써 injects surprise you may not intend.
Word order: 끝났어요 벌써 follows English; Korean puts it first — 벌써 끝났어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아직 means "still; yet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 아직 (ajik) = "still; yet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아직 자요 ("they're still asleep") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아직, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ongoing state, before verb
아직 + negative = 'not yet'

usagePhrases.en: there's still a long way to go
usagePhrases.note: set phrase, 'not nearly done'
ongoing not-knowing

examples.en: I'm still a student.
examples.note: Simple: with a positive noun-sentence, 아직 = 'still'.

examples.en: I haven't eaten yet.
examples.note: Everyday: 아직 + 안/못 + past = 'not yet'; the most common pattern.

examples.en: Almost done? — No, not yet.
examples.note: Real situation: 아직 can stand alone as 아직이요 ('not yet') in reply.

extendedVocab.nuance: 아직 covers both 'still' and 'not yet', and which one surfaces depends on polarity: with a POSITIVE verb it means 'still' (아직 자요 'still sleeping'), and with a NEGATIVE verb it means 'not yet' (아직 안 잤어요 'haven't slept yet'). It is the natural counterpart to 벌써/이미 — 아직 안 끝났어요 ('not finished yet') is the mirror of 벌써 끝났어요 ('already finished'). It often rides with the ongoing form -고 있다 to stress an action in progress (아직 자고 있어요 'still sleeping right now') and shows up in fixed phrases like 아직 멀었어요 ('still a long way off'). Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the 아직/벌써 confusion and the negation logic: because English 'yet' lives in questions/negatives, learners forget that Korean 아직 itself flips meaning with the verb's polarity — pair 아직 with 안/못 to say 'not yet', and use it with a plain positive verb to say 'still'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 아직 with 벌써. 아직 안 왔어요 = 'hasn't come yet'; 벌써 왔어요 = 'already came'. They point in opposite directions.
Trying to say 'not yet' with a positive verb. 아직 먹었어요 reads as 'still ate' and is odd; you need the negative: 아직 안 먹었어요.
Adding -았/었- when the state still holds. For 'I'm still hungry' say 아직 배고파요 (present), not 아직 배고팠어요; the past tense would mean the hunger is already over, which contradicts 아직.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 또 means "again; also" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 또 (tto) means "again; also". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 또 와요 ("come again"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 또 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: repetition of the action
casual goodbye
exasperation at a repeat
unwanted recurrence

examples.en: Let's meet again tomorrow.
examples.note: Simple: 또 = 'one more time', a friendly repeat before 만나요.

examples.en: Late again? You were late yesterday too.
examples.note: Everyday: 또 here carries a tone of 'yet again', mild reproach.

examples.en: It was delicious. I'll come again next time!
examples.note: Real situation: 또 in a warm farewell; 또 올게요 / 또 봬요 are set goodbyes.

extendedVocab.nuance: 또 means 'again / once more', and by extension 'also/additionally'; it marks an action REPEATING. Its near-synonym is 다시, and the dividing line matters: 또 is a plain repetition or recurrence ('one more time', often emotional — delight in 또 봐요 or annoyance in 또?!), while 다시 leans toward 'again, properly / from the start / anew', as in redoing something (다시 하세요 'do it over (correctly)'). So 또 전화할게요 = 'I'll call again (next time)', but 다시 전화할게요 = 'I'll call back / try again'. 또 is the natural word in casual goodbyes (또 봐요, 또 만나요) and in venting (또 그래 'there you go again'). Register-neutral, very colloquial-friendly. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting every 'again' to one word — use 또 for casual recurrence/'see you again', 다시 for 'redo/anew', and keep it before the verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reaching for 다시 in a casual goodbye. 다시 봐요 is understandable but leans 'meet again (to pick things back up)'; the warm, idiomatic 'see you again' Koreans actually say is 또 봐요 / 또 만나요.
Using 또 when you mean 'do it over correctly'. 또 하세요 = 'do it one more time'; to mean 'redo it properly / from scratch' say 다시 하세요.
Word order: 와요 또 echoes English 'come again'; Korean puts the adverb first — 또 와요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 너무 means "too much" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "too much" is 너무 (neomu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 너무 비싸요 ("it's too expensive"). Watch the particle attached to 너무 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: excess, before adjective
너무 modifies the adverb 많이

usagePhrases.en: I love it / it's so good
usagePhrases.note: casual positive 'super'
너무 frozen into a verb

examples.en: These shoes are too small.
examples.note: Simple: classic 'excessive' use — 너무 + adjective = beyond the right amount.

examples.en: I drank too much coffee yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday: 너무 stacks onto 많이 ('a lot') to mean 'too much'.

examples.en: Wow, this cake is so delicious!
examples.note: Real situation: in casual speech 너무 flips positive, meaning 'so/really', not 'excessively'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 너무 literally means 'too / excessively' — past the appropriate point, usually a complaint (너무 비싸요 'too expensive', 너무 매워요 'too spicy'). The textbook contrast is 너무 vs 아주: 아주 is a neutral intensifier ('very', no judgment), while 너무 traditionally signals EXCESS (a problem). BUT in modern colloquial Korean, 너무 has drifted into a positive 'so/super' (너무 좋아요 'I love it', 너무 예뻐요 'so pretty') — so tone and context decide whether it's a complaint or enthusiasm. It also fossilizes into the verb 너무하다 ('to be too much / go overboard', e.g. 너무해요 'that's not fair'). Register: the positive sense is casual/spoken; in formal writing keep 너무 for genuine excess and use 매우/아주 for neutral emphasis. The English-speaker pitfall: don't assume 너무 is always negative like English 'too' — in speech 너무 좋다 is a compliment, and for plain neutral 'very' before an adjective, 아주/매우 is safer in formal contexts.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading every 너무 as the negative 'too'. 너무 좋아요 in conversation means 'I really love it', not 'I like it too much'.
Using 너무 for neutral 'very' in formal writing. There 너무 still implies excess; prefer 매우 or 아주 for plain emphasis.
Forgetting 너무하다 is a real verb. 너무해요 means 'that's too much / that's unfair', not a typo — it's 너무 used predicatively.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아주 means "very" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 아주 (aju) = "very". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아주 좋아요 ("it's very good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아주, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: neutral intensifier, before adjective
strengthens the verb
아주 + 많이 = 'very much'
아주 can even scale another adverb

examples.en: This bread is very tasty.
examples.note: Simple: 아주 = plain 'very', no nuance of excess, before 맛있어요.

examples.en: That person speaks Korean very well.
examples.note: Everyday: 아주 + 잘하다 cleanly means 'very well', a neutral compliment.

examples.en: This is a very important matter.
examples.note: Real situation: in writing/formal speech 아주 is the safe, judgment-free intensifier.

extendedVocab.nuance: 아주 means 'very / quite' — a NEUTRAL degree intensifier that simply turns the dial up without implying anything is excessive. That neutrality is the whole point of 아주 vs 너무: 너무 traditionally flags excess ('too much, a problem'), while 아주 just emphasizes (아주 비싸요 = 'very expensive' as a fact; 너무 비싸요 = 'too expensive', a complaint). Its close formal cousin is 매우, which means the same 'very' but sounds more written/bookish; in everyday speech 아주 (or casual 정말/진짜) is more natural, and 매우 shines in essays and news. 아주 sits before adjectives, descriptive verbs, and even other adverbs (아주 잘, 아주 많이). Register-neutral and safe with anyone, including formal contexts. The English-speaker pitfall is over-defaulting to 너무 for 'very' (because learners hear it constantly in casual speech) — when you want a clean, judgment-free 'very', especially in polite or written Korean, reach for 아주 or 매우.

Using 너무 when you want neutral 'very'. In careful speech/writing 너무 implies excess; for plain emphasis use 아주 (or 매우).
Thinking 아주 is only for negatives. It is fully neutral — 아주 좋아요 ('very good') is perfectly natural and positive.
Word order: 좋아요 아주 mirrors English; Korean places the intensifier first — 아주 좋아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 위 means "top, above" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 위 (wi) means "top, above". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 책상 위에 ("on the desk"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 위 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 위 + 에 marks the location
existence verb 있다
action place 에서 + verb

usagePhrases.en: I look up / look at the top
usagePhrases.note: direction object 를

examples.en: There is a computer on the desk.
examples.note: Basic frame: noun 위에 + 있다 says where a thing sits.

examples.en: The cat is sleeping on the roof.
examples.note: 에서 (not 에) because sleeping is an action happening up there.

examples.en: Raise your hands above your head.
examples.note: 위로 with 로 shows movement toward the top, used in real instructions.

extendedVocab.nuance: 위 (Sino-Korean would be 上, but 위 is native Korean) names the top surface of something or the space directly above it, and it must attach to a noun: 책상 위, 머리 위, never standing alone like English 'up'. The closest confusable is 위쪽: 위 points at the top itself or 'on top of', while 위쪽 means 'the upper side/upward direction' more loosely (방 위쪽이 더워요 = the upper part of the room is hotter). It is neutral in register and used by everyone, all day, for both physical position (책상 위) and abstract rank (위 사람 = a superior). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 위 like a preposition and dropping the noun, or saying 위에서 있어요 for simple existence — existence takes 에 (위에 있어요), and 에서 is reserved for an action done up there. Also do not confuse the noun 위 with 위 meaning 'stomach' (a different word, 한자 胃); context and the attached noun keep them apart.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 위에서 있어요 for 'it is on top' — existence uses 에 (위에 있어요); 에서 only marks where an action happens.
Dropping the noun and using 위 like English 'up' (위에 가요 to mean 'go up') — you need a noun (계단 위에 = on top of the stairs) or a motion verb like 올라가요.
Mixing up positional 위 with 위 = 'stomach' (위가 아파요 = my stomach hurts); the standalone meaning depends entirely on context.

extendedVocab.nuance: 아래 is the native Korean word for the area below or underneath something, and like all position nouns it clings to a noun: 책상 아래, 다리 아래. Its near-twin is 밑, and the boundary matters: 아래 is the broader 'below / lower area' (and can be abstract — 평균 아래 = below average), while 밑 leans more concrete and tactile, 'right underneath, the underside' (책상 밑에 = right under the desk, often where you'd reach with your hand), and 밑 sounds a touch more casual. 아래 also contrasts with 아래쪽 ('the lower side / downward direction', vaguer). extendedVocab.nuance: 앞 is the native Korean noun for the front side of a thing or the space directly ahead of it, and it attaches to a noun: 집 앞, 역 앞. Crucially, 앞 covers BOTH space ('in front of') and time ('ahead, upcoming') — 앞으로 means 'from now on / going forward', and 앞두다 means an event is just ahead. extendedVocab.nuance: 뒤 is the native Korean noun for the back side of something or the space behind it, and it attaches to a noun: 집 뒤, 건물 뒤. extendedVocab.nuance: 옆 is the native Korean noun for the side of a thing or the spot immediately beside it, and it attaches to a noun: 창문 옆, 은행 옆. It implies adjacency — right alongside, within touching or glancing distance — unlike 근처 ('in the vicinity', possibly some distance away) or 옆쪽 ('the side direction', vaguer). It also forms handy compounds: 옆집 (the house next door), 옆자리 (the seat beside you), 옆사람 (the person next to you). Register is neutral and very high-frequency in daily speech. The English-speaker traps: (1) 옆에서 있어요 for existence rather than 옆에 있어요; (2) reaching for 옆 when the thing is merely 'in the area' — that is 근처, while 옆 is strictly 'right next to'; and (3) forgetting the noun requirement, so 'sit beside me' is 제 옆에 앉으세요 (literally 'sit at my side'), not a bare preposition. Note 옆 is also written/pronounced carefully: the ㅍ batchim links to following vowels (옆에 sounds like '여페').

Using 옆 when you mean 'in the general area' — 옆 is strictly adjacent (right beside); for 'nearby' use 근처 (역 근처에).

extendedVocab.nuance: 안 is the native Korean noun for the inside or interior of an enclosed space, attaching to a noun: 가방 안, 방 안. Beyond physical interiors it marks LIMITS — 'within' a time or range: 한 시간 안에 (within an hour), 예산 안에서 (within budget). Two confusables matter. First, 속: both mean 'inside', but 속 implies being buried/immersed in a mass or depth (물속 = underwater, 마음속 = deep in one's heart, 가방 속 = down in the bag's contents), while 안 is the plainer 'inside the boundary' (방 안 = in the room). Second, the homograph 안 = 'not' (the negation adverb, 안 가요 = I don't go) — same syllable, totally different word, told apart by position (a negating 안 sits before a verb; the noun 안 follows a noun). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping 안 and using bare 에, so 가방에 넣어요 ('put it to/at the bag') instead of the clearer 가방 안에 넣어요 ('put it inside the bag'); (2) overusing 속 where plain 안 is natural; and (3) saying 안에서 있어요 for existence instead of 안에 있어요.

Confusing the noun 안 (inside) with the adverb 안 (not): 안 가요 means 'I don't go', while 방 안 means 'inside the room' — position before/after a verb tells you which.
Using 속 everywhere for 'inside' — 속 implies depth/immersion (마음속, 물속); for a plain enclosed space use 안 (방 안에).

Beware a crucial homograph: 밖에 also functions as a particle meaning 'only / nothing but', and it then REQUIRES a negative verb — 하나밖에 없어요 = 'there is only one' (literally 'outside of one, none'). You disambiguate by the verb: positional 밖에 takes a normal verb, particle 밖에 forces a negative (없어요/안). Contrast also with 바깥 (a near-synonym noun for 'outside/outdoors', slightly more concrete, as in 바깥 공기 = the outside air) and 밖쪽 ('the outer side', vaguer). Register is neutral. extendedVocab.nuance: 사이 is the native Korean noun for the space, gap, or interval between two things, attaching with the linking particle 와/과 to name both sides: 은행과 카페 사이, 너와 나 사이. It is wonderfully broad — physical gaps (건물 사이), time intervals (방학 사이에 = during the break), and crucially human RELATIONSHIPS (친구 사이 = the bond between friends; 사이가 좋다 = to be close). Compare it with 가운데/중간 ('the middle/center' of a single thing or group, not the gap between two distinct items): the chair in the center of the room is 방 가운데, but the shop wedged between the bank and cafe is 은행과 카페 사이. Register is neutral and idiomatic. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping the 와/과 that grammatically pairs the two sides, so 은행 카페 사이 sounds unfinished — say 은행과 카페 사이; (2) using 사이 for the center of one object where 가운데 belongs; and (3) missing the relationship meaning, so 우리 사이 ('our relationship') gets misread as a physical gap. Colloquially 사이 even contracts to 새 (밤새 = all through the night).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 근처 is a Sino-Korean noun (近處, 近 'near' + 處 'place') meaning the nearby area or vicinity surrounding a place; it attaches to a noun (집 근처) or to 이/그/저 (이 근처 = around here). Unlike the adjacency word 옆 ('right next to', touching distance), 근처 covers a looser radius — a few minutes' walk, the general neighborhood. Two near-synonyms to weigh: 근방 (近方) is a slightly more colloquial 'thereabouts', and 부근 (附近) is a more formal/written 'vicinity' (역 부근 sounds bookish); 근처 is the neutral everyday default. Compare also 가까이 (an adverb, 'nearby/closely', as in 가까이 오세요 = come closer) — 근처 is a place noun, 가까이 modifies a verb. Register: 근처 is comfortably conversational. extendedVocab.nuance: 가운데 is the native Korean noun for the middle or center point of a space, and figuratively 'among' a group; it attaches to a noun (방 가운데) and can mark selection (셋 가운데 하나 = one among three). extendedVocab.nuance: 운동 is Sino-Korean, 運動 ('move-motion'), and is the umbrella word for physical exercise; it normally appears as 운동하다 (운동을 해요). Crucially it is NOT counted or pluralized like English 'a workout' — you don't say 운동들 for several sessions; you say 운동을 자주 해요. The nearest relative is 스포츠 (a borrowed word for organized sports as a category, e.g. watching 스포츠 on TV), whereas 운동 is the act of exercising your own body, so '운동선수' = athlete but '스포츠 경기' = a sports match. The very same 運動 also means a social 'movement/campaign' (민주화 운동 the democracy movement), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') by analogy with 'make exercise' — Korean uses the light verb 하다; and remember the desire ending goes on the verb (운동하고 싶어요), never on the bare noun.

extendedVocab.nuance: 영화 is Sino-Korean, 映畵 ('project-picture'), literally a projected image, and it is the standard word for a movie/film. Don't confuse 영화 with 드라마: 드라마 is a serialized TV series, while 영화 is a self-contained cinema film, so a Korean TV soap is a 드라마, not a 영화. The cinema building is 영화관 (or the loanword 극장). The classic English-speaker pitfall is letting 'a movie' steer you to the generic counter 개 (영화 한 개 sounds wrong) — use 편; and don't calque 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가다, since you say 영화(를) 보러 가다, 'go in order to watch a movie'.

Saying 영화를 들어요 by mixing up senses — you don't 'listen to' a film; the verb is 보다, so 영화를 봐요.
Counting with 개 as in 영화 한 개 — films use the dedicated counter 편: 영화 한 편.
Translating 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가요 — Korean expresses purpose, so it is 영화를 보러 가요 ('go to watch a movie').

extendedVocab.explanation: 음악 (eumak) = "music". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 음악을 들어요 ("I listen to music") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 음악, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 듣다 'hear/listen' takes 을; note ㄷ→ㄹ in 들어요
좋다 is an adjective; subject marker 이
좋아하다 (verb) governs an object with 을
틀다 = switch on/play a track from a device

examples.en: I listen to music.
examples.note: bare habit, 듣다 → 들어요

examples.ko: 운동할 때 신나는 음악을 들으면 힘이 나요.
examples.romanization: undonghal ttae sinnaneun eumageul deureumyeon himi nayo.
examples.en: When I exercise, listening to upbeat music energizes me.
examples.note: 듣다 conditional 들으면; ㄷ-irregular

examples.ko: 카페에서 잔잔한 음악을 틀어 놓으니 분위기가 좋네요.
examples.romanization: kapeeseo janjanhan eumageul teureo noeuni bunwigiga jonneyo.
examples.en: With soft music playing in the café, the mood is nice.
examples.note: 틀어 놓다 = leave it playing in the background

extendedVocab.nuance: 음악 is Sino-Korean, 音樂 ('sound-pleasure/joy'), and is the general word for music. Its everyday partner verb is 듣다 ('hear/listen'), which is a ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel the ㄷ becomes ㄹ, so 듣 + 어요 → 들어요 and 듣 + 으면 → 들으면 — memorize this because beginners often write the wrong ❌들다. Distinguish 음악 from 노래: 노래 is a specific 'song' you can sing (with words and a tune), while 음악 is music as a whole, including instrumental pieces, so background café music is 음악, not 노래. Two near-verbs differ too — 듣다 is to receive sound, but 틀다 is to switch a track on from a device. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 ('watch') because you 'watch a music video' in English; for plain audio say 음악을 들어요, and avoid the false stem 들다 — the dictionary form is 듣다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 음악을 봐요 by analogy with watching videos — pure listening uses 듣다, so 음악을 들어요.
Writing the stem as 들다 and conjugating 들어요 from it — the base verb is the ㄷ-irregular 듣다; the ㄹ only appears before a vowel ending.
Using 만들다 for 'make/play music' on a device — to start a track you 틀다, e.g. 음악을 틀어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 노래 means "song" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 노래 (norae) means "song". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노래를 불러요 ("I sing a song"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노래 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 부르다 'to sing' (르-irregular) is the precise verb
듣다 → 들어요 for receiving the song
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 부르- → 부를 수 있어요
songs are counted with 곡, not 개

examples.en: I sing well.
examples.note: 부르다 → 불러요 (르-irregular doubling)

examples.ko: 친구 생일이라 다 같이 생일 노래를 불렀어요.
examples.romanization: chingu saengirira da gachi saengil noraereul bulleosseoyo.
examples.en: It was my friend's birthday, so we all sang the birthday song.
examples.note: past 불렀어요; 다 같이 = all together

examples.ko: 노래방에서 한 곡 부르고 나니까 스트레스가 풀렸어요.
examples.romanization: noraebangeseo han gok bureugo nanikka seuteureseuga pullyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After singing a song at the karaoke room, my stress melted away.
examples.note: 노래방 culture; counter 곡; -고 나니까

extendedVocab.nuance: 노래 is a native Korean word for a 'song' — a tune with lyrics you can perform — counted with the bound noun 곡 (노래 두 곡). The most natural verb is 부르다 ('to sing'), a 르-irregular: the stem doubles the ㄹ before a vowel, so 부르 + 어요 → 불러요 and 부르 + 었어요 → 불렀어요. The casual frame 노래를 하다 ('do a song') exists and means to sing, but 노래를 부르다 is more precise and common. Don't blur 노래 with 음악: 음악 is music in general (including instrumentals), while 노래 specifically has a singer and words. Karaoke is 노래방 ('song room'), a core social ritual. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 말하다 ('say/speak') because we 'say the words of a song' — singing is 부르다, never 말하다; and don't translate 'sing a song' twice over as ❌노래를 노래해요, which is redundant — just 노래를 불러요.

Saying 노래를 말해요 because the song 'has words' — speaking is 말하다, but singing is 부르다, so 노래를 불러요.
Forgetting the 르-irregular and writing 노래를 부러요 — the ㄹ doubles before a vowel: 부르 → 불러요.
Counting songs with 개 (노래 한 개) — the proper counter is 곡: 노래 한 곡.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 춤 means "dance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "dance" is 춤 (chum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 춤을 춰요 ("I dance"). Watch the particle attached to 춤 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: cognate verb 추다 'to dance' → 춰요
멋있다 'cool/impressive'; subject marker 이
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 추- → 출 수 있어요
배우다 'to learn' → 배워요

examples.en: I dance well.
examples.note: 추다 → 춰요 (우 + 어 contracts to 워)

examples.ko: 무대에서 아이돌처럼 춤을 추니까 다들 환호했어요.
examples.romanization: mudaeeseo aidolcheoreom chumeul chunikka dadeul hwanhohaesseoyo.
examples.en: When I danced like an idol on stage, everyone cheered.
examples.note: 춤을 추다 in action; -니까 sequence

examples.ko: 요즘 방송댄스 배우는데, 춤 동작이 생각보다 어려워요.
examples.romanization: yojeum bangsongdaenseu baeuneunde, chum dongjagi saenggakboda eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: I'm learning K-pop dance lately, and the moves are harder than I expected.
examples.note: 춤 + 동작 = dance move; -는데 background

extendedVocab.nuance: 춤 is a native noun for 'dance', and Korean uses a cognate-verb construction: the verb 추다 ('to dance') pairs only with 춤, giving 춤을 춰요 (추 + 어요 → 춰요, the 우+어 fuses to 워). This 'cognate object' pattern — noun and verb sharing a root — also appears in 잠을 자다 (sleep a sleep) and 꿈을 꾸다 (dream a dream), so learn it as a set. The dictionary form is 춤추다, written solid. The English-speaker pitfall is the reflex 춤을 해요 with the all-purpose light verb 하다 — that is unnatural for dance; you must use the specific verb 추다. Also, while 춤 covers dancing broadly, a single dance 'piece/move' is better called a 동작 (motion) or a specific genre (발레 ballet, 힙합 hip-hop), so don't try to count individual dances with 개. Note 멋있다 (cool) is the natural compliment, not 예쁘다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 춤을 해요 with the generic light verb — dance requires its cognate verb 추다, so 춤을 춰요.
Writing the contraction wrong as 추어요 left unfused — colloquial Korean contracts 추 + 어요 to 춰요.
Splitting the dictionary form as two words 춤 추다 in the lexicon sense — the verb 'to dance' is the single word 춤추다 (though 춤을 추다 as object+verb is fine).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그림 means "drawing; painting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그림 (geurim) = "drawing; painting". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그림을 그려요 ("I draw a picture") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그림, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: cognate verb 그리다 'to draw' → 그려요
예쁘다 (ㅡ-irregular) → 예뻐요; subject 이
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 on 그리- → 그릴 수 있어요
flat artworks are counted with 장 (sheets)

examples.en: I draw pictures.
examples.note: cognate pair 그림/그리다

examples.ko: 조카가 크레용으로 그림을 그려서 냉장고에 붙였어요.
examples.romanization: jokaga keureyongeuro geurimeul geuryeoseo naengjanggoe butyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My niece drew a picture with crayons, so I stuck it on the fridge.
examples.note: 그리다 → 그려서; everyday scene

examples.ko: 이 화가의 그림은 색감이 정말 예술이에요.
examples.romanization: i hwagaui geurimeun saekgami jeongmal yesurieyo.
examples.en: This painter's paintings have truly artistic colors.
examples.note: 화가 = painter; 그림 as fine-art painting

extendedVocab.nuance: 그림 is a native noun covering both a 'drawing' and a 'painting', formed from the verb 그리다 ('to draw/paint') — another cognate noun-verb pair, so 그림을 그리다 literally means 'draw a drawing'. A flat artwork is counted with 장 (sheets): 그림 한 장. Korean does not split 'draw' vs 'paint' lexically the way English does; 그리다 covers both pencil sketches and oil paintings, and you specify the medium (색연필로, 물감으로) if needed. The verb 그리다 also figuratively means to 'picture/long for' something (고향을 그리다, to yearn for home), but the everyday hobby sense is making art. The English-speaker pitfall is using 만들다 ('make') because we say 'make a drawing' — Korean uses the cognate verb 그리다, so say 그림을 그려요. Don't confuse 그림 with 사진 (a photograph): 그림 is hand-made art, 사진 is a photo you 찍다 ('take').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 그림을 만들어요 from 'make a picture' — drawing uses its cognate verb 그리다, so 그림을 그려요.
Using 그림 for a photograph — a photo is 사진 (taken with 찍다); 그림 is hand-drawn or painted art.
Counting with 개 (그림 한 개) — flat works on paper take 장: 그림 한 장.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 여행 means "travel; trip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 여행 (yeohaeng) means "travel; trip". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 여행을 가요 ("I go on a trip"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 여행 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 가다 'go'; the most idiomatic frame, 여행을 가다
light verb 하다 → 여행하다, more formal feel
-고 싶어요 on 가-; 를 on 여행
즐겁다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 즐거워요; subject 이

examples.en: I go on a trip during the vacation.
examples.note: 여행을 가다, time particle 에

examples.ko: 내년에 유럽으로 배낭여행을 떠나려고 돈을 모으고 있어요.
examples.romanization: naenyeone yureobeuro baenangyeohaengeul tteonaryeogo doneul moeugo isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm saving money to set off backpacking around Europe next year.
examples.note: 떠나다 = set off; 배낭여행 compound

examples.ko: 이번 제주도 여행 정말 좋았어, 다음엔 같이 가자.
examples.romanization: ibeon jejudo yeohaeng jeongmal joasseo, daeumen gachi gaja.
examples.en: This Jeju trip was really great; let's go together next time.
examples.note: casual 반말; 여행 as a concrete trip

extendedVocab.nuance: 여행 is Sino-Korean, 旅行 ('journey-go'), meaning travel or a trip. The single most natural verb is 가다 — 여행을 가다 ('go on a trip') — while 여행하다 (with light verb 하다) also works but feels a touch more formal/written. Distinguish 여행 from 출장: 출장 is a business trip you're sent on for work, whereas 여행 is travel for pleasure or sightseeing, so don't call a work assignment a 여행. A traveler is 여행자/여행객 and an overseas trip is 해외여행. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing 보다 ('see') because tourists 'go sightseeing' — to travel you 가다 or 하다, not 보다 (sightseeing specifically is 구경하다 or 관광하다). Also note destination takes (으)로/에 (제주도로 여행을 가다), and beginners often drop the particle on 여행 itself — keep 여행을 가다.

Saying 여행을 봐요 because travel involves 'seeing places' — the verb is 가다 (or 하다): 여행을 가요; sightseeing alone is 구경하다.
Calling a work trip 여행 — a business trip is 출장; 여행 is leisure travel.
Marking the destination with only 에 and no movement sense, e.g. 부산에 여행이에요 — say 부산으로/에 여행을 가요 to express going there.

Watch the particle attached to 독서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-noun + 하다; the standard frame 독서하다
topic-introducing 독서가 ...예요
좋아하다 governs the object 독서를
즐기다 'to enjoy' → 즐겨요, slightly literary

examples.en: I read before going to bed.
examples.note: 독서하다 for a tidy habit statement

examples.ko: 제 취미는 독서라서 주말마다 도서관에 가요.
examples.romanization: je chwimineun dokseoraseo jumalmada doseogwane gayo.
examples.en: My hobby is reading, so I go to the library every weekend.
examples.note: 독서 + 도서관 share the 書/도 imagery

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 바빠서 통 독서를 못 했네요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri bappaseo tong dokseoreul mo taenneyo.
examples.en: I've been so busy with work lately that I've hardly read at all.
examples.note: 통 + 못 했다 = hardly did; reflective tone

extendedVocab.nuance: 독서 is Sino-Korean, 讀書 ('read-book'), literally 'reading books', and it is a slightly formal, hobby-survey word — it's what you write when asked 취미가 뭐예요?, answering 독서예요. Because it already contains 書 ('book'), 독서 implies reading books specifically, so for casual everyday speech Koreans usually switch to the plain native verb phrase 책을 읽다 ('read a book') — 책 읽는 거 좋아해요 sounds far more natural in conversation than 독서를 좋아해요, which can feel stiff. It pairs with 하다 (독서하다), not 보다 ('watch'), even though English sometimes blurs 'read' and 'look at'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 (because you 'look at' a page) — reading text is 읽다, and the noun is 독서를 하다. extendedVocab.nuance: 취미 is Sino-Korean, 趣味 ('interest-taste'), and means a hobby or personal interest. extendedVocab.nuance: 낚시 is a native noun meaning fishing (with rod and hook) as a pastime, pairing with 가다 (낚시를 가다) or 하다 (낚시하다). Mark the spot with (으)로/에서: 바다로 낚시를 가다, 강에서 낚시하다.

Saying 낚시를 봐요 or other wrong verbs — pair 낚시 with 가다 or 하다: 낚시를 가요 / 낚시해요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 백화점 is Sino-Korean 百貨店, literally 'hundred-goods-store' (百 hundred + 貨 goods + 店 shop), a multi-floor flagship like Lotte or Shinsegae carrying brand clothing, cosmetics, and a food hall. The dividing line learners must feel is 백화점 vs 마트: a 마트 (대형마트, e.g. 이마트) is a warehouse-style discount store for groceries and household goods, while 백화점 is the upscale, salesclerk-served, higher-priced experience. A frequent English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because you 'shop AT' a store in English, beginners say 백화점에서 가요, but motion verbs like 가다/오다 require 에 (백화점에 가요); use 에서 only when an action happens there (백화점에서 옷을 봐요).

extendedVocab.nuance: 박물관 is Sino-Korean 博物館, literally 'broad-things-building' (博 broad + 物 things + 館 hall) — a place displaying historical relics, artifacts, and natural specimens so visitors learn about the past. extendedVocab.nuance: 미술관 is Sino-Korean 美術館, literally 'beauty-art-building' (美 beauty + 術 skill/art + 館 hall) — a building exhibiting paintings, sculpture, and fine art, frequently rotating special exhibitions (전시). Natural collocations: 전시를 보다/관람하다, 그림을 감상하다, 미술관 입장료, 특별전. extendedVocab.nuance: 교회 is Sino-Korean 敎會, literally 'teach-gather' (敎 teach + 會 assembly/meeting) — specifically a PROTESTANT Christian place of worship and its congregation, busiest on Sunday mornings. extendedVocab.nuance: 절 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) for a BUDDHIST temple, the mountainside complex where monks (스님) live and laypeople come to bow and pray quietly. extendedVocab.nuance: 경찰서 is Sino-Korean 警察署, literally 'guard-inspect-office' (警 alert/guard + 察 examine + 署 government bureau) — the police station where you report crimes, lost items, or accidents. extendedVocab.nuance: 소방서 is Sino-Korean 消防署, literally 'extinguish-defend-office' (消 extinguish + 防 prevent/defend + 署 government bureau) — the fire station where firefighters (소방관) and fire trucks (소방차) stand by for fires and rescues. The essential pairing every newcomer must memorize: in Korea you dial 119 for the 소방서 (fires AND ambulance/medical emergencies) but 112 for the 경찰서 (police). 에서 marks where the applying happens

examples.en: The embassy is far.
examples.note: Simple description; subject 이 + adjective 멀어요.

examples.note: 에서 marks the place of the action 받다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 대사관 is Sino-Korean 大使館, literally 'great-envoy-building' (大 great + 使 envoy/messenger + 館 hall) — your home country's main diplomatic mission abroad, which helps citizens with passports, visas, and emergencies. Two contrasts matter: 대사관 (embassy, the main mission, usually one per country in the capital Seoul) vs 영사관 (consulate, 領事館, a branch office in other cities handling consular services); and 대사 (the ambassador, a person) vs 대사관 (the building) — note 대사 is also a homonym for 'line/dialogue' in a script, so context matters. Register is neutral/official. Collocations: 대사관에 연락하다, 여권을 발급받다, 비자를 신청하다, 주한 미국 대사관 ('the US embassy in Korea'). extendedVocab.nuance: 한국 (韓國, 'Han nation') is the short, everyday name South Koreans use for their own country; the full official name is 대한민국 (大韓民國), which you mainly hear in formal contexts, news, and at sporting events ('대한민국!' chants). The key boundary for learners: 한국 by itself almost always means South Korea, NOT the whole peninsula — North Korea is 북한 (北韓, 'north Han') and you must never call it 한국. A second near-synonym is 우리나라 ('our country'), which Koreans use warmly when speaking among themselves to mean 'Korea' from an insider stance — but a foreigner saying 우리나라 sounds odd unless they identify as Korean, so as a learner stick with 한국. The particle trap: with movement verbs, 가다/오다 destinations take 에 (한국에 가요 = go to Korea), while origin and the location of an action take 에서 (한국에서 왔어요 = came from Korea; 한국에서 살아요 is also heard but residence more strictly prefers 한국에 살아요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한국에 왔어요 to mean 'I came FROM Korea' — 에 marks a destination, so this means 'I came TO Korea'; for origin use 한국에서 왔어요.
Calling North Korea 한국 — 한국 means South Korea only; North Korea is 북한, and conflating them can be politically sensitive.
Treating 한국 and 한국어 as interchangeable — 한국 is the country, 한국어 (or casually 한국말) is the Korean language; '한국을 공부해요' wrongly says you study the country instead of 한국어를 공부해요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 미국 (美國, literally 'beautiful country') is the standard Korean name for the United States, and crucially it does NOT come from the English sound 'America' — it is a Sino-Korean reading borrowed via Chinese, where 美 was chosen as a phonetic match for the 'me' in 'America' (the same character also means 'beautiful', so the name is a happy accident, not literal praise). 어느 = which (among a set); the standard question word for nations
나라 modifies 이름; the name of a country

usagePhrases.en: every country / from country to country
usagePhrases.note: 마다 = each/every; common in 나라마다 달라요 'differs by country'

In Korean the particle or ending next to 한국인 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 한국인 + 이에요; the copula for stating nationality
한국인 modifies 친구; a friend who is Korean
한국인 modifies 관광객; common in travel/news contexts
contrast term sharing the 人 suffix; 외국 + 인 = foreign person

examples.en: I am Korean.
examples.note: Simple nationality statement; 한국인 + 이에요

examples.en: That person is not Korean.
examples.note: Everyday negation; 이/가 아니다 = is not, 이 marks the subject of the negation

examples.ko: 회사에 한국인 동료가 세 명 있어요.
examples.romanization: hoesae hangugin dongnyoga se myeong isseoyo.
examples.en: There are three Korean colleagues at my company.
examples.note: Real-situation; 한국인 modifies 동료, 세 명 counts people

extendedVocab.nuance: 한국인 (韓國人, 'Korea-person') means 'a Korean person', built from 한국 + the Sino-Korean suffix 인 (人, 'person'). Its everyday near-synonym is 한국 사람, which means the same thing but feels warmer and more conversational, while 한국인 is slightly more formal and is the form you see in writing, documents, statistics, and news ('한국인 관광객', '재외 한국인'). Both are polite and acceptable — 한국인 is NOT more respectful, just a different register, so don't think you must use 한국인 to be polite. The key English-speaker pitfall is redundancy: because 인 already means 'person', you must NOT say '한국인 사람' — that doubles 'person-person'; choose either 한국인 OR 한국 사람, never both. A second pitfall is the copula: nationality uses 이에요/예요 attached directly (한국인이에요), and the negative is 한국인이 아니에요, with 이 marking the subject of 아니다.

Saying 한국인 사람 — 인 already means 'person', so this redundantly says 'Korean-person person'; use 한국인 or 한국 사람.
Thinking 한국인 is more polite than 한국 사람 — they're equally polite; 한국인 is just more formal/written register, not a respect upgrade.

extendedVocab.explanation: "world" is 세계 (segye). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전 세계 ("the whole world"). Watch the particle attached to 세계 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

세계 modifies 여행; traveling around the world
세계 modifies 최고; 'best in the world', common in praise/ads
세계 modifies 지도; a map of the world

examples.en: I want to travel the world.
examples.note: Simple; 세계 여행 as a noun phrase, 을 marks the object of 하다

examples.en: This song is famous all over the world.
examples.note: Everyday; 전 세계 = the whole world, 에서 marks the location of the state

examples.ko: 그 회사는 세계 시장에서 경쟁하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesaneun segye sijangeseo gyeongjaenghago isseoyo.
examples.en: That company competes in the world market.
examples.note: Real-situation; 세계 시장 = world market, 에서 marks the arena of the activity

extendedVocab.nuance: 세계 (世界, 'world-realm') means 'the world' as the whole earth and all its countries and peoples — a global, geographic scope. Its tricky near-synonym is 세상 (世上, 'world-above'), and the boundary matters: 세계 is the planet / international sphere (전 세계 'the whole world', 세계 지도 'world map', 세계 평화 'world peace'), whereas 세상 is 'the world' in the sense of human life, society, and 'how things are' (세상이 좋아졌어요 'the world/times have gotten better', 세상 물정 'the ways of the world'). So 'world map' is 세계 지도, never '세상 지도'; but '그런 세상에 살고 싶어요' (I want to live in such a world) uses 세상. The most useful collocation is 전 세계 ('the entire world'), where 전 (全) means 'all'. English speakers who learned 'world' as one word tend to overextend 세계 into the 세상 territory of 'life/society', so anchor it: 세계 = the globe and its nations; 세상 = the human world / life. Particle behavior is regular: 세계가 넓다 (the world is wide), 전 세계에서 (all over the world).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 세계 for 'the world' in the sense of life/society — 'the world has changed' (society/times) is 세상이 변했어요, not 세계; 세계 is the global/geographic world.
Saying 세상 지도 for 'world map' — the geographic compound is 세계 지도; 세상 is the human-life sense.

extendedVocab.explanation: 고향 (gohyang) = "hometown". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 고향이 어디예요? ("Where is your hometown?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고향, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 고향 + 이 + 어디예요; the standard way to ask someone's hometown
내려가다 ('go down') is idiomatic for returning to a hometown outside Seoul
고향 modifies 친구; a friend from where you grew up
고향 modifies 음식; the food of one's home region

examples.en: My hometown is Busan.
examples.note: Simple; 고향 + 은 topic, 이에요 copula naming the place

examples.en: I go to my hometown for the holidays.
examples.note: Everyday; 명절 = traditional holiday, 에 marks the destination

examples.en: I went down to my hometown after a long time and saw my parents.
examples.note: Real-situation; 내려가다 = go down (to one's hometown), 뵈다 = humble 'see/meet' for elders

extendedVocab.nuance: 고향 (故鄕, 'old village') means the place where you were born and grew up — the hanja combine 故 ('old/former') + 鄕 ('village/country home'), so it carries a built-in feeling of warmth, nostalgia, and roots, more emotional than the neutral English 'hometown'. It is NOT the same as 집 ('house/home, where you currently live') or 본가 ('one's parents' home'): you can live in Seoul (집은 서울) while your 고향 is Busan. A 고향 can be a city, a town, or a whole region, and it stays your 고향 even decades after you leave. A culturally important collocation is 고향에 내려가다 ('go DOWN to one's hometown') — because Seoul is the center, returning to a provincial hometown is idiomatically 'going down' (내려가다), and going back to Seoul is 올라가다 ('going up'), regardless of actual geography. English speakers often misuse 고향 for their current home or address; remember 고향 is specifically your place of origin and upbringing. The classic conversation opener is 고향이 어디예요? Particle behavior is regular: 고향에 가다 (go to), 고향에서 자라다 (grow up in).

Using 고향 to mean your current home — that's 집 (house/home you live in); 고향 is specifically where you were born and raised.
Saying 고향에 올라가요 for going to a provincial hometown — returning to a hometown outside Seoul is idiomatically 고향에 내려가다 ('go down').
Asking 고향이 뭐예요? — for a place you ask 고향이 어디예요? (where), since 뭐 (what) is for things, not locations.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 병 means "illness; disease" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 병 (byeong) means "illness; disease". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 병이 났어요 ("I got sick"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 병 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = the illness 'came out'; never use 받다 or 가지다 here
심하다, not 크다, describes how severe a condition is
고치다 is the casual verb for fixing illness or objects alike
걸리다 needs 에; this fixed phrase = 'got hooked by' a disease

examples.en: I'm relieved I didn't get sick.
examples.note: Simple: 병이 나다 ('fall ill'), negated as 안 나다; the most basic frame.

examples.en: Grandpa caught a serious disease, so he was hospitalized.
examples.note: Everyday: 큰 병 collocates with 걸리다 + 에, and 입원하다 = be admitted.

examples.ko: 이 병은 약으로 못 고치고 수술을 받아야 해요.
examples.romanization: i byeongeun yageuro mot gochigo susureul badaya haeyo.
examples.en: This disease can't be cured with medicine; you have to get surgery.
examples.note: Real-situation: contrasts 고치다(cure) with 수술을 받다(undergo surgery).

extendedVocab.nuance: 병 is the Sino-Korean word 病, the broad term for any illness from a cold to cancer; for a serious one Koreans add 큰 (큰 병) and for a minor one they often switch to 감기 or 몸살 instead. Two patterns split by particle: 병이 나다 (a disease 'breaks out,' using 나다 like 열이 나다 'run a fever') versus 병에 걸리다 ('get hooked by' a disease, requiring 에 exactly as 감기에 걸리다). The big English-speaker trap is forcing 'catch' into 받다 or 가지다 — Korean treats catching a disease as being snagged by it, so 병을 걸리다 (wrong particle) and 병을 받다 both sound broken; the disease is the thing you bump into, marked with 에. 병 is neutral in register and fine in both polite and casual speech, but when speaking about an elder's illness you raise the verb politely (병에 걸리셨어요).

Saying 병을 걸렸어요: 걸리다 demands the location/contact particle 에, so it must be 병에 걸렸어요.
Saying 병을 받았어요 by translating 'I caught a disease' literally: 받다 is for handing-over; use 병에 걸렸어요 or 병이 났어요.
Treating 병 like a countable thing you 'have' as in 병을 가지고 있어요: Koreans say 병이 있어요 (state of having an illness), not 가지다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주사 means "injection; shot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "injection; shot" is 주사 (jusa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주사를 맞아요 ("I get a shot"). Watch the particle attached to 주사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 맞다 (lit. 'be struck') is how the patient RECEIVES the injection
아프다 describes the painful sensation of the shot itself
놓다 is the action of the person ADMINISTERING it
무섭다 marks the feared thing with 가, not 를

examples.en: I don't want to get a shot.
examples.note: Simple: patient's side always pairs 주사 with 맞다.

examples.en: My cold was bad, so I got a shot at the clinic.
examples.note: Everyday: 주사 맞다 is the standard clinic experience after a 감기.

examples.ko: 간호사 선생님이 아이 팔에 주사를 놓아 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: ganhosa seonsaengnimi ai pare jusareul noa jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The nurse gave the child a shot in the arm.
examples.note: Real-situation: the giver uses 놓다, and -아 주시다 adds politeness for the nurse.

extendedVocab.nuance: 주사 is Sino-Korean 注射, literally 'pour (注) and shoot (射),' a vivid image of forcing fluid in through a needle. The crucial point is that the verb flips depending on who acts: the patient says 주사를 맞다 — and 맞다 literally means 'to be hit/struck,' the same verb as in 비를 맞다 (get rained on) or 매를 맞다 (get beaten), framing the shot as something done TO you — while the nurse who administers it says 주사를 놓다 ('lay/place' the shot). English speakers almost always reach for 받다 ('receive') because 'receive a shot' feels logical, but 주사를 받다 sounds unnatural; 받다 is reserved for treatment as a whole (치료를 받다), not the needle. Note 주사 covers the whole injection event, while the physical needle is 주삿바늘 and the syringe is 주사기.

Using 놓다 for yourself as the patient (주사를 놓았어요 meaning 'I got a shot'): 놓다 is the giver's verb; the patient says 맞았어요.
Saying 주사가 무서워해요 to mean 'I'm scared of shots': 무서워하다 needs a human subject; for the shot itself use 주사가 무서워요.

extendedVocab.explanation: 치료 (chiryo) = "treatment". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 치료를 받아요 ("I get treatment") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 = the patient RECEIVES the course of care
끝나다 (intransitive) means the process finished on its own
필요하다 marks what is needed with 가, not 를
시작하다 takes 를 for what you start

examples.en: Please get treatment quickly.
examples.note: Simple: patient + 치료를 받다, the core medical-care frame.

examples.ko: 3주 동안 병원에서 치료를 받고 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: 3ju dongan byeongwoneseo chiryoreul batgo mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I got treatment at the hospital for three weeks and improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 동안 (duration) + 치료를 받다 + 좋아지다 (get better).

examples.ko: 의사 선생님이 환자를 정성껏 치료해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: uisa seonsaengnimi hwanjareul jeongseongkkeot chiryohae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The doctor treated the patient with great care.
examples.note: Real-situation: the doctor's side uses the verb 치료하다, not 받다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 치료 is Sino-Korean 治療, where 治 means 'to govern/manage' and 療 means 'to heal,' together 'managing an illness back to health' — broader than a single procedure, it covers the whole healing process (medication, therapy, surgery as a package). Watch the actor split exactly as with 주사: the patient says 치료를 받다 ('receive treatment'), while the doctor says 환자를 치료하다 ('treat the patient'), so 받다 vs the 하다-verb tells you who is acting. The nearest neighbor is 진료 (診療, 'examine + heal'), which is narrower — 진료 is the consultation/seeing-the-doctor part (진료를 받다 = 'see a doctor'), whereas 치료 is the actual curing that follows. English speakers sometimes carry over the 'shot' verb and say 치료를 맞다; that is wrong — 맞다 belongs only to 주사. They also drop the particle in 치료가 필요하다, mistakenly saying 치료를 필요해요.

Saying 치료를 맞아요: 맞다 is only for 주사; treatment is 치료를 받아요.
Saying 치료를 필요해요: 필요하다 is an adjective taking 가, so it must be 치료가 필요해요.
Confusing 치료 with 진료: for just seeing the doctor say 진료를 받다; reserve 치료 for the actual cure.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 환자 means "patient" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 환자 (hwanja) means "patient". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환자가 많아요 ("there are many patients"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 많다 takes 가 for what is plentiful
보다 = a doctor examining; never 만나다 here

usagePhrases.en: I take care of a patient
usagePhrases.note: 돌보다 = look after, nurse a patient
회복하다 (回復) for getting well again

examples.en: There aren't many patients today.
examples.note: Simple: 환자가 + existence/quantity verb, the most basic frame.

examples.en: There were many patients in the ER, so I waited a long time.
examples.note: Everyday: 환자가 많다 + 기다리다 in a real hospital scene.

examples.ko: 의사 선생님이 입원 환자들을 한 명씩 봐요.
examples.romanization: uisa seonsaengnimi ibwon hwanjadeureul han myeongssik bwayo.
examples.en: The doctor sees the inpatients one by one.
examples.note: Real-situation: 환자를 보다 (examine) + 입원 환자 (inpatient) + 한 명씩.

extendedVocab.nuance: 환자 is Sino-Korean 患者, literally 患 'to suffer/afflict' + 者 'person,' i.e. 'a suffering person' — note that 者 is the same 'person' suffix in 기자(reporter) and 과학자(scientist), so the word is built on the idea of one afflicted by illness. The biggest pitfall is the verb for a doctor's exam: Korean says 환자를 보다, using 보다 ('look at') the way a doctor 'looks over' a case, NOT 만나다 ('meet'); 환자를 만나다 sounds like a casual social encounter, not a medical visit, so a doctor never says it about examining someone. Register-wise 환자 is a neutral clinical noun; when the patient is an elder you may add honorifics elsewhere in the sentence (보호자/분), but 환자 itself stays plain. A near term is 손님 — a pharmacy or clinic might call walk-ins 손님 (customers), but inside a hospital the sick person is specifically 환자.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의사가 환자를 만나요 to mean a doctor examines a patient: that sounds like a social meet-up; use 환자를 봐요.
Saying 환자를 가요 or 환자에 가요 confusing person with place: you go to 병원(hospital), and the doctor 환자를 봐요.
Adding wrong honorific verbs to 환자 reflexively (환자께서): 환자 is a neutral noun; honorifics attach by context, not automatically.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 체온 means "body temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "body temperature" is 체온 (cheon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 체온을 재요 ("I take (someone's) temperature"). Watch the particle attached to 체온 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 재다 = measure, the same verb as for height/length
높다 (high), not 크다 (big), for a reading
정상 (正常) = normal; ~이에요 after a consonant
확인하다 = verify the reading

examples.en: I take the temperature with a thermometer.
examples.note: Simple: instrument 체온계 + 체온을 재다, the core measuring frame.

examples.en: I had a fever, so I checked and my temperature was 38 degrees.
examples.note: Everyday: 재 보다 (try measuring) + ~도 for degrees Celsius.

examples.ko: 아기 체온이 갑자기 올라가서 병원에 데려갔어요.
examples.romanization: agi cheoni gapjagi ollagaseo byeongwone deryeogasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby's temperature suddenly went up, so I took them to the hospital.
examples.note: Real-situation: 체온이 올라가다 (rises) + 데려가다 (take a person).

extendedVocab.nuance: 체온 is Sino-Korean 體溫, literally 體 'body' + 溫 'warmth,' so it specifically means the warmth of the body, distinct from 온도 (溫度, 'temperature-degree'), which is the general word for any temperature — air, water, an oven. Use 체온 only for a person or animal's heat and 온도 for the room or weather; saying 방 체온 (room body-temperature) is wrong, it must be 방 온도. The verb is 재다 ('to measure'), the very same verb used for 키를 재다 (measure height) and 길이를 재다 (measure length), because temperature is a quantity you gauge, not something you 'look at' — so 체온을 보다 sounds off to natives. For a high or low reading Korean uses 높다/낮다, never 크다/작다 (big/small), which is the typical English-speaker slip. A closely related symptom word is 열 (fever): 열이 나다 means 'run a fever,' and you confirm it by 체온을 재다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 방 체온 for room temperature: 체온 is only for bodies; the room's temperature is 방 온도.
Saying 체온이 커요: a reading is 높다/낮다, so it must be 체온이 높아요.
Saying 체온을 봐요 instead of 재요: temperature is measured with an instrument, so the verb is 재다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 혈압 means "blood pressure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 혈압 (hyeorap) = "blood pressure". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 혈압을 재요 ("I take (someone's) blood pressure") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 혈압, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: 재다 = measure, same verb as 체온/키
높다, never 크다, for the reading
낮다 = low; common cause of dizziness
정상 (正常) = within normal range

examples.en: I take my blood pressure at home every day.
examples.note: Simple: habit + 혈압을 재다, the core measuring frame.

examples.ko: 우리 아버지는 혈압이 높아서 약을 드세요.
examples.romanization: uri abeojineun hyeorabi nopaseo yageul deuseyo.
examples.en: My father has high blood pressure, so he takes medicine.
examples.note: Everyday: 혈압이 높다 + 약을 드시다 (honorific 'take medicine').

examples.ko: 갑자기 일어나면 혈압이 떨어져서 어지러울 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi ireonamyeon hyeorabi tteoreojyeoseo eojireoul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you stand up suddenly, your blood pressure can drop and you may feel dizzy.
examples.note: Real-situation: 혈압이 떨어지다 (drops) + 어지럽다 (dizzy) + ~을 수 있다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 혈압 is Sino-Korean 血壓, literally 血 'blood' + 壓 'pressure,' a transparent compound naming the pressure of blood in the vessels. Like 체온, it is something you gauge, so the verb is 재다 ('measure') — the identical verb in 키를 재다 and 체온을 재다 — and high/low readings take 높다/낮다, the persistent English-speaker error being 크다/작다 (big/small), which are for physical size, not measured values. For movement of the reading, Korean uses 오르다/올라가다 (rises) and 떨어지다/내려가다 (drops), not 'go up/down' translated as 가다. Distinguish 혈압 from 맥박 (脈搏, pulse/heart rate): both are vital signs taken at the clinic, but 혈압 is the pressure number and 맥박 is the beats per minute. In casual talk people with chronic hypertension say 고혈압 (高血壓, 'high blood pressure' as a named condition), so 고혈압이 있어요 means 'I have hypertension,' a step beyond a one-time high reading.

Saying 혈압이 커요: a reading is described with 높다/낮다, so it must be 혈압이 높아요.
Saying 혈압을 봐요 instead of 재요: blood pressure is measured, so the verb is 재다.
Confusing 혈압 (pressure) with 맥박 (pulse): if you mean heart rate per minute, say 맥박, not 혈압.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상처 means "wound; cut" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 상처 (sangcheo) means "wound; cut". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상처가 났어요 ("I got a wound"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상처 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = a wound 'appeared'; physical injury
아프다 for the pain of the cut
낫다 (ㅅ-irregular) = heal/recover
소독하다 (消毒) = sterilize before bandaging

examples.en: I got a small cut on my finger.
examples.note: Simple: body part + 에 + 상처가 나다, the core 'get hurt' frame.

examples.ko: 넘어져서 무릎에 상처가 났는데 피가 났어요.
examples.romanization: neomeojyeoseo mureupe sangcheoga nanneunde piga nasseoyo.
examples.en: I fell and got a wound on my knee, and it bled.
examples.note: Everyday: 넘어지다(fall) + 상처가 나다 + 피가 나다 (bleed).

examples.ko: 연고를 바르고 며칠 지나니까 상처가 깨끗이 나았어요.
examples.romanization: yeongoreul bareugo myeochil jinanikka sangcheoga kkaekkeusi naasseoyo.
examples.en: I applied ointment, and after a few days the wound healed cleanly.
examples.note: Real-situation: 연고를 바르다(apply ointment) + 낫다 for healing.

extendedVocab.nuance: 상처 is Sino-Korean 傷處, literally 傷 'injure/wound' + 處 'place/spot,' i.e. 'the injured spot' on the body. Crucially, 상처 has a famous double life: physically it is a cut or wound (상처가 나다), but emotionally it means a hurt feeling, and there the collocation flips to 상처를 받다 ('receive a wound,' = be hurt) or 상처를 주다 ('give a wound,' = hurt someone). So a physical injury uses 나다 (it 'comes out'), while an emotional one uses 받다/주다 — mixing these is the classic trap: 상처를 받았어요 about a knee scrape sounds like your feelings were hurt, not your skin. For healing, use 낫다, an ㅅ-irregular verb that drops the ㅅ before a vowel (낫다 → 나아요, 나았어요), and it doubles as 'recover from illness' (감기가 나았어요). A near-synonym is 흉터 (scar) — 상처 is the fresh open wound, 흉터 is the lasting mark it leaves after it heals.

Saying 상처를 받았어요 about a physical cut: 받다 is for emotional hurt; a bodily wound is 상처가 났어요.
Conjugating 낫다 regularly as 낫아요: it is ㅅ-irregular, so the wound healed = 상처가 나았어요 (나아요).
Confusing 상처 with 흉터: the open wound is 상처; the scar left afterward is 흉터.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기침 means "cough" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cough" is 기침 (gichim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기침이 나요 ("a cough comes on"). Watch the particle attached to 기침 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = the cough 'comes out' involuntarily
하다 = perform the act of coughing
심하다 for a severe, persistent cough
멈추다 (intransitive) = it ceased

examples.en: My throat is itchy, so I keep coughing.
examples.note: Simple: cause 목이 간지럽다 + 기침이 나다, the involuntary frame.

examples.ko: 회의 중에 자꾸 기침을 해서 미안했어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui junge jakku gichimeul haeseo mianhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I kept coughing during the meeting, so I felt sorry.
examples.note: Everyday: 기침을 하다 (active) + 자꾸 (repeatedly) in a social setting.

examples.ko: 기침이 2주 넘게 안 멈추면 병원에 가 보세요.
examples.romanization: gichimi 2ju neomge an meomchumyeon byeongwone ga boseyo.
examples.en: If a cough doesn't stop for over two weeks, go see a doctor.
examples.note: Real-situation: 안 멈추다 + 가 보다 (go and see), giving health advice.

extendedVocab.nuance: 기침 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean), and it works in two equally natural patterns that differ subtly in viewpoint: 기침이 나다 frames the cough as something that 'comes out' on its own — built with 나다, the same verb in 열이 나다(run a fever), 콧물이 나다(runny nose), 재채기가 나다(sneeze) — stressing it's involuntary; whereas 기침을 하다 frames it as an action you perform, useful when you mean someone coughs deliberately or repeatedly. English speakers raised on 'have a cough' often try 기침을 가지다 ('possess a cough'), which is flatly wrong — Korean never 'has' a symptom with 가지다; symptoms either 나다 (come out) or you 하다 (do) them. Don't confuse 기침 with 재채기 (a sneeze): 기침 is a throat/chest cough, 재채기 is the explosive nose sneeze, and they are not interchangeable. For severity use 심하다 (기침이 심하다 = a bad cough), not 크다.

많다 for a heavy runny nose
닦다 = wipe away with a tissue
멈추다 = the discharge ceased

examples.note: Simple: cause 춥다 + 콧물이 나다, the core symptom frame.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸려서 콧물하고 기침이 같이 나요.
examples.romanization: gamgie geollyeoseo konmulhago gichimi gachi nayo.
examples.en: I caught a cold, so I have a runny nose and a cough together.
examples.note: Everyday: 콧물 + 기침 both with 나다, listed via 하고.

examples.ko: 휴지로 콧물을 닦고 손을 깨끗이 씻으세요.
examples.romanization: hyujiro konmureul dakgo soneul kkaekkeusi ssiseuseyo.
examples.en: Wipe your nose with a tissue and wash your hands well.
examples.note: Real-situation: 콧물을 닦다 (active wipe) + hygiene advice.

심하다 for a severe headache
나아지다 = improve (from 낫다)
두통약 = headache pill; 약을 먹다 idiom

examples.en: I've had a headache since yesterday.
examples.note: Simple: ~부터 (since) + 두통이 있다, the core 'have a headache' frame.

examples.ko: 스트레스 때문에 두통이 심해서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
examples.romanization: seuteureseu ttaemune dutongi simhaeseo iljjik toegeunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: My headache was bad from stress, so I left work early.
examples.note: Everyday: 때문에(because) + 두통이 심하다 + 퇴근하다 (leave work).

examples.ko: 두통약을 먹고 한숨 자고 나니까 좀 괜찮아졌어요.
examples.romanization: dutongyageul meokgo hansum jago nanikka jom gwaenchanajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I took a headache pill, slept a bit, and felt somewhat better.
examples.note: Real-situation: 두통약을 먹다 + 자고 나다 + 괜찮아지다 (get better).

extendedVocab.nuance: 두통 is Sino-Korean 頭痛, literally 頭 'head' + 痛 'ache/pain' — the same 痛 appears in 복통 (腹痛, stomachache) and 치통 (齒痛, toothache), so once you know 통 = 'ache' the whole pain family opens up. Both are correct, but to a friend 머리 아파 sounds natural and 두통이 있어 sounds slightly formal. The number-one English-speaker error is double-marking the pain: since 두통 already contains 痛 ('ache'), saying 두통이 아파요 literally means 'the headache hurts' — redundant and wrong; the noun takes 있다/심하다, not 아프다. 안 되다 = it doesn't happen; the standard 'upset stomach'
돕다 (ㅂ-irregular) = help; subject is a food/drink

examples.ko: 저는 우유를 마시면 소화가 잘 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun uyureul masimyeon sohwaga jal an dwaeyo.
examples.en: When I drink milk, I don't digest it well.
examples.note: Simple: condition + 소화가 안 되다, the core indigestion frame.

examples.ko: 급하게 먹으면 소화가 안 되니까 천천히 드세요.
examples.romanization: geupage meogeumyeon sohwaga an doenikka cheoncheonhi deuseyo.
examples.en: If you eat in a hurry you'll get indigestion, so please eat slowly.
examples.note: Everyday: 급하게(hastily) + 소화가 안 되다 + advice with 드세요.

examples.ko: 체했을 때는 소화제를 먹거나 손을 따 주면 좋아요.
examples.romanization: chehaesseul ttaeneun sohwajereul meokgeona soneul tta jumyeon joayo.
examples.en: When your stomach is upset, taking a digestive or pricking the finger helps.
examples.note: Real-situation: 체하다 (have indigestion) + 소화제 + folk remedy.

extendedVocab.nuance: 소화 is Sino-Korean 消化, literally 消 'dissolve/dissipate' + 化 'transform' — food being broken down and changed inside you. The governing verb is 되다 ('to become/happen'), so 소화가 되다 = 'digestion takes place' and 소화가 안 되다 = 'indigestion,' the everyday way to say your stomach is off. The big trap for English speakers is treating digestion as an action you do: 소화를 하다 or 소화를 못 하다 sounds unnatural, because Korean frames digestion as something that happens to/in you (되다), not something you actively perform — so 'I can't digest' is 소화가 안 돼요, never 소화를 못 해요. A close real-life synonym is the native verb 체하다, which is more acute: 소화가 안 되다 is general slow/poor digestion, while 체하다 means you got an actual blockage/upset stomach from eating, often suddenly. The medicine is 소화제 (消化劑, 'digestion-agent'), built with the same 劑 as 해열제 (fever reducer).

extendedVocab.explanation: 건강 (geongang) = "health". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 건강이 좋아요 ("my health is good") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다, not 높다, describes good health
나쁘다 for poor health
챙기다 = take care of, mind one's health
set farewell/blessing from 건강하다

examples.en: Health is the most important thing.
examples.note: Simple: 건강이 + adjective, the core 'health is X' frame.

examples.ko: 요즘 운동을 시작해서 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum undongeul sijakaeseo geongangi mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I started exercising lately, so my health has improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 운동을 시작하다 + 건강이 좋아지다 (improve).

examples.en: Grandma, please always stay healthy and live a long, long life.
examples.note: Real-situation: honorific 건강하시다 + 사세요 as a warm blessing.

extendedVocab.nuance: 건강 is Sino-Korean 健康, where 健 means 'sturdy/robust' and 康 means 'peaceful/well,' together the sound, robust state of body and mind. It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) — never 높다/낮다 (high/low), which is the typical English-influenced slip from 'high level of health' — and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy'). Its honorific imperative 건강하세요 is a beloved set phrase, a warm farewell/blessing meaning 'stay healthy,' especially said to elders and at New Year. A near-synonym is 컨디션 (a loanword from 'condition') — but 컨디션 is your day-to-day fitness/energy level (오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아 = 'I'm not feeling great today'), whereas 건강 is your overall, long-term state of wellness; don't swap them.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 봄 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: season takes time particle 에, never 에서
adjective 따뜻하다 in modifier form 따뜻한
subject with 이; 오다 → 와요
two nouns stack with no particle

examples.en: I like spring.
examples.note: 이/가 marks 봄 as the thing liked, not 을/를

examples.en: Cherry blossoms bloom in spring.
examples.note: 에 = time when; 피다 'bloom' → 펴요

examples.ko: 저는 추운 겨울보다 따뜻한 봄이 더 좋아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun chuun gyeoulboda ttatteutan bomi deo joayo.
examples.en: I prefer warm spring over cold winter.
examples.note: 보다 'than' + 더 'more' to compare seasons

extendedVocab.nuance: 봄 is the spring season, roughly March to May, the time of mild warmth (따뜻하다) and blossoms — 벚꽃 cherry blossoms above all. It is a pure native Korean word (no 한자), so unlike 춘하추동 it has no Sino reading you must memorize. The natural collocations are 봄이 오다 'spring comes', 봄이 되다 'it becomes spring', 봄 날씨 'spring weather', and 봄나물 'spring greens'. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you go 'in spring' with 봄에, never 봄에서 — 에서 marks the place an action happens, while 에 marks a point in time, and a season is a time. A second trap is treating 봄 like the subject of 'I like': Koreans say 봄이 좋아요 (spring is good-to-me) with 이/가, not 봄을 좋아요.

덥다 is ㅂ-irregular → modifier 더운
subject with 이, adjective 좋다
여름 + 방학, school break

examples.note: 덥다 ㅂ-irregular: 덥 + 어요 → 더워요

examples.romanization: yeoreumeneun biga jaju waseo usaneul gajigo danyeoyo.
examples.en: In summer it rains often so I carry an umbrella.
examples.note: 여름에는 sets the topic; 와서 'because it comes'

It is a native Korean word, so there is no 한자 to parse. extendedVocab.nuance: 계절 is the general word for 'season' (a time of year), the umbrella term under which 봄·여름·가을·겨울 sit. It is Sino-Korean, 季節 — 季 'season/quarter' + 節 'period, node' — so the four together are 사계절 (四季節), and you will constantly hear 사계절이 뚜렷하다 'the four seasons are clear-cut' as a point of pride about Korea. Do not confuse 계절 (a season of the year) with 시기 'a period/phase' or with the English loanword 시즌, which Koreans reserve for sports or TV ('시즌 2'); for the natural cycle of the year, 계절 is the only choice. Common partners: 계절이 바뀌다 'the season turns', 환절기 'the change-of-season period', 제철 'in-season (food)'. Pitfall: 'season' as in 'baseball season' is not 계절 — that is 시즌.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 날짜 means a calendar date — a specific day pinned to the month and year. It is a native-Korean compound built on 날 'day' (날 + the bound element -짜), so it is not Sino-Korean and has no hanja, even though the numbers you read inside a date (일·이·삼…) are Sino. Keep three look-alikes apart: 날짜 'date (which day of the month)' vs 요일 'day of the week (Monday…)' vs 날 'a day in general'. To ask a date Koreans say 며칠이에요?, and the answer uses Sino-Korean day numbers (오월 십오일 'May 15th'), not the native 하나·둘 set — that is the classic pitfall. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 생일 is 'birthday', Sino-Korean 生日 — 生 'birth/life' + 日 'day', literally 'birth-day'. The culturally loaded fact is that Koreans eat 미역국 (seaweed soup) on a birthday, because mothers traditionally ate it after giving birth. Register matters sharply here: for grandparents, bosses, or anyone you must honor, the polite word is the honorific 생신 (生辰), and the greeting upgrades to 생신 축하드립니다, not the casual 생일 축하해요 you'd say to a friend. The standard greeting is 생일 축하해요 / 생일 축하합니다, literally 'I celebrate (your) birthday' — note it is the verb 축하하다 plus the noun, not an adjective. Collocations: 생일 파티 'birthday party', 생일 선물 'birthday gift', 생일을 챙기다 'to make a fuss of someone's birthday'. Pitfall: don't say 생일 to or about an elder when respect is due — switch to 생신.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 휴일 is a non-working day — a day off or a holiday. It is Sino-Korean 休日, 休 'rest' + 日 'day', literally 'rest-day'. Watch the family of look-alikes built on 休: 휴일 'a day off (any non-work day)', 공휴일 (公休日) 'an official public holiday' marked red on the calendar, and 휴가 (休暇) 'leave/vacation you take from work', e.g. summer 여름휴가. The dividing line that trips English speakers: 휴일/공휴일 is a day that is officially free (a Sunday, 설날), whereas 휴가 is personal leave you request and spend, often traveling. So '연차 휴가' is paid leave, but New Year's Day is a 공휴일, not a 휴가. Collocations: 휴일을 보내다 'spend a day off', 황금연휴 'golden (long) holiday', 빨간 날 'a red day (holiday)' in casual speech. Pitfall: don't say 휴가 when you mean a calendar holiday everyone shares.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 새해 means 'the new year' — the turning of the year in general. It is a transparent native compound: 새 'new' + 해 'year/sun', so literally 'new year', and there is no hanja involved. extendedVocab.nuance: 설날 is the Korean Lunar New Year (음력설), the biggest holiday of the year, when families gather, eat 떡국 'rice-cake soup' (and adding a year of age is tied to eating it), and the young perform 세배, a deep New-Year bow to elders, often receiving 세뱃돈 'New Year money'. 설날 is native Korean (설 'New Year' + 날 'day'); often shortened to just 설. extendedVocab.nuance: 추석 is the autumn harvest festival, often glossed as 'Korean Thanksgiving', held on the 15th of the 8th lunar month under the full harvest moon (보름달). It is Sino-Korean 秋夕, 秋 'autumn' + 夕 'evening', literally 'autumn evening'; an older native name is 한가위. Families travel home, eat 송편 'half-moon rice cakes', and hold 차례, a rite honoring ancestors. Set it against 설날: both are the two great 명절 (festivals) with travel and ancestral rites, but 추석 is autumn's harvest thanks, 설날 is the lunar New Year — so calling 추석 a 'new year' is simply wrong. The Thanksgiving translation is a loose analogy, not an identity: there is no turkey and the date is lunar. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
