extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그릇 means "bowl" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그릇 (geureut) = "bowl". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그릇을 씻다 ("to wash a bowl") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그릇, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Pairs with 씻다 (rinse with water), the default verb for dishes — not 닦다.
그릇 is a productive suffix: 밥그릇 (rice), 국그릇 (soup), 개밥그릇 (dog's bowl).
Use the location particle 에 plus 담다 (to put food in) — the natural pair for filling a bowl.
그릇 is the typical thing you 깨다 (break/smash); 깨진 그릇 = a broken bowl.

examples.en: The bowl is pretty.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + descriptive adjective 예쁘다.

examples.en: Please serve the rice into a bowl.
examples.note: Everyday request: location 에 + 담다, the verb for putting food in.

examples.ko: 설거지할 때 깨지기 쉬운 그릇은 따로 씻으세요.
examples.romanization: seolgeojihal ttae kkaejigi swiun geureuseun ttaro ssiseuseyo.
examples.en: When you do the dishes, wash fragile bowls separately.
examples.note: Real situation: 깨지기 쉽다 (easy to break) modifying 그릇 in a kitchen instruction.

extendedVocab.nuance: 그릇 is the broad native-Korean word for a vessel that holds food — most often the deeper, rounded bowl that rice, soup, or 반찬 sit in, but it also works as the generic cover term for 'dishes/dishware' (그릇을 닦다 = do the dishes). The dividing line you must feel is 그릇 vs 접시: 그릇 is deep and holds something pourable or piled, while 접시 is the flat plate you lay food onto. Note the everyday verb is 씻다 (rinse), not the English-driven 닦다 (wipe) — 닦다 is for wiping a surface dry, not washing dishes. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you serve food 그릇에 담다 (into the bowl, location 에), so saying 그릇을 담다 is wrong because 담다 needs the destination, not the food, marked. Common collocations: 그릇을 씻다, 그릇에 담다, 그릇을 깨다, 밥그릇.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 그릇을 닦아요 for washing dishes. 닦다 means to wipe (a table, a window) — washing dishes with water is 그릇을 씻어요 / 설거지를 해요.
Don't say 밥을 그릇을 담아요. The bowl is the destination, so it takes 에: 밥을 그릇에 담아요. Marking the bowl with 을 makes the sentence ungrammatical.
Don't reach for 보울 (a borrowed 'bowl'). Korean uses the native 그릇; the loanword sounds unnatural for a normal eating bowl.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 접시 means "plate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 접시 (jeopsi) means "plate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 접시에 담다 ("to plate / put onto a plate"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 접시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to plate / put onto a plate
usagePhrases.note: Location 에 + 담다; food lands ON a flat 접시, so 에 is required, never 를.
Flat dishes are counted with 장 (sheet-counter) as well as 개; 종이 한 장 uses the same counter.
앞 (front) + 접시 = the small plate set in front of each diner to take shared food onto.
치우다 (clear away) is the natural verb for taking dirty 접시 off the table after a meal.

examples.en: The plate is dirty.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject 이 + adjective 더럽다.

examples.en: I arranged the fruit nicely on the plate.
examples.note: Everyday: location 에 + 담다 with the adverb 예쁘게.

examples.ko: 손님이 오시니까 앞접시도 함께 놓아 주세요.
examples.romanization: sonnimi osinikka apjeopsido hamkke noa juseyo.
examples.en: Since guests are coming, please also set out individual plates.
examples.note: Real situation: hosting context introducing 앞접시 and honorific 오시다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 접시 is a flat, shallow plate — the dish you LAY food onto (fruit, grilled meat, a slice of cake) rather than pour into. The contrast to lock in is 접시 vs 그릇: shape decides it, not the food itself. A flat dish is 접시 even for soup-adjacent food, while anything deep and rounded is 그릇. A useful sub-word is 앞접시, the small personal plate each diner pulls shared dishes onto — a normal part of Korean table manners. Because food sits ON the surface, the particle is 접시에 담다 / 접시에 놓다 (location 에); the classic English-speaker error is 접시를 담다, treating the plate as the object. Note plates can be counted with 장 (the sheet-counter, reflecting their flatness) as well as the all-purpose 개. Habitual collocations: 접시에 담다, 접시를 치우다, 접시를 깨다, 앞접시.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 과일을 접시를 담아요. The plate is where the fruit goes, so use 에: 과일을 접시에 담아요.
Don't assume soup goes on a 접시. Liquid or piled food needs the deeper 그릇; a flat 접시 is for things you lay flat, like meat or fruit.
Don't always default to 개 when counting. Flat plates are often counted with 장 — 접시 두 장 — which sounds more natural to many speakers.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 컵 means "cup" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cup" is 컵 (keop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 컵에 따르다 ("to pour into a cup"). Watch the particle attached to 컵 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Location 에 + 따르다 (pour); the liquid's destination is the cup, marked with 에.
컵 compounds freely: 종이컵 (paper), 머그컵 (mug), 텀블러 is separate but related.
When measuring a drink, the counter is 잔 (glass/cupful): 물 한 잔, 커피 두 잔.
헹구다 (rinse out) is the precise verb for quickly washing a drinking cup with water.

examples.en: The cup is clean.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 깨끗하다.

examples.en: Please pour water into the cup.
examples.note: Everyday request: destination 에 + 따르다 for pouring a drink.

examples.en: Since it's hot, I'll give it to you in a mug, not a paper cup.
examples.note: Real situation: contrasting 종이컵/머그컵 with 말고 (not ~ but) and honorific 드리다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 컵 is a loanword (from English 'cup') covering both cups and drinking glasses for any beverage — there is no everyday split between 'cup' and 'glass' the way English makes one; a glass tumbler and a coffee cup are both 컵 in normal speech, with 머그컵 (mug) and 종이컵 (paper cup) as specific compounds. Watch the difference between the OBJECT and the MEASURE: 컵 is the physical cup, but when you order or count a serving of a drink you switch to the counter 잔 — 커피 한 잔, not 커피 한 컵 in a café. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle with pouring: you pour a drink 컵에 따르다 (into the cup, location 에), so 컵을 따르다 is wrong. Also use 따르다 (pour) rather than the English-shaped 붓다, which sounds like dumping a large amount. Frequent collocations: 컵에 따르다, 컵을 헹구다, 종이컵, 머그컵.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't order 커피 한 컵 in a café. Servings of drinks use the counter 잔: 커피 한 잔. 컵 names the object, not the portion.
Don't say 물을 컵을 따라요. The cup is the destination of the pour, so it takes 에: 물을 컵에 따라요.
Don't worry about 'cup vs glass.' Korean 컵 covers both; you don't need a separate word for a drinking glass in everyday speech.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 숟가락 means "spoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 숟가락 (sutgarak) = "spoon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 숟가락으로 뜨다 ("to scoop with a spoon") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 숟가락, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 뜨다 (scoop up); the spoon is the tool, so 으로 is required.
숟가락 + 젓가락 together = 수저, the standard table-setting pair Koreans lay out.

usagePhrases.en: to set down / lay out a spoon
usagePhrases.note: 놓다 = set the spoon on the table; idiomatically 숟가락을 놓다 can also mean 'finish eating.'
밥 + 숟가락; also used figuratively for a mouthful, as in 한 숟가락만 더.

examples.en: There's no spoon.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + existence verb 없다.

examples.en: I scoop the soup with a spoon and eat it.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 뜨다, linked to 먹다 with -서.

examples.ko: 밥 다 먹었으면 숟가락 놓고 잠깐 쉬자.
examples.romanization: bap da meogeosseumyeon sutgarang noko jamkkan swija.
examples.en: If you're done eating, put down your spoon and rest a bit.
examples.note: Real situation: casual 반말 with the idiom 숟가락(을) 놓다 = stop eating.

extendedVocab.nuance: 숟가락 is the deep-bowled metal spoon at the heart of a Korean table — Koreans eat rice and especially soup/stew with it, unlike many cultures that treat the spoon as secondary to the fork. Pair it with the verb 뜨다 (to scoop up a liquid or rice), the precise partner verb. Crucially, 숟가락 + 젓가락 combine into 수저, the everyday word for the whole utensil set you lay out — if someone says 수저 놓아 줘, they mean set out both. A spelling trap: it's 숟가락 with ㄷ (a historical 술 'spoon' + 가락), even though 젓가락 takes ㅅ — learners often wrongly write 숫가락. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you eat 숟가락으로 (with a spoon, instrument 으로), never 숟가락에. Watch the idiom 숟가락을 놓다 — literally 'put down the spoon,' it commonly means to finish a meal. Collocations: 숟가락으로 뜨다, 숟가락을 놓다, 수저, 밥숟가락.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 숫가락. The correct spelling is 숟가락 with ㄷ; only 젓가락 uses ㅅ. They differ on purpose.
Don't say 숟가락에 먹어요. The spoon is the instrument, so it takes 으로: 숟가락으로 먹어요.
Don't take 숟가락을 놓다 literally every time. Beyond 'set the spoon down,' it idiomatically means 'finish eating,' so context matters.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 젓가락 means "chopsticks" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 젓가락 (jeotgarak) means "chopsticks". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 젓가락으로 집다 ("to pick up with chopsticks"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 젓가락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 집다 (grasp/pick up) — the precise verb for what chopsticks do.
Noun + 질 (doing-an-action) = handling chopsticks; 젓가락질이 서툴다 = clumsy with chopsticks.
나무 (wood) + 젓가락; the throwaway kind from a 분식집, vs everyday metal ones.
Paired utensils take the counter 벌 (set); 한 짝 = just one stick of the pair.

examples.en: Chopsticks are hard.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 어렵다.

examples.en: I pick up side dishes with chopsticks and eat them.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 집다, chained to 먹다 with -서.

examples.ko: 젓가락질이 아직 서툴러서 면이 자꾸 미끄러져요.
examples.romanization: jeotgarakjiri ajik seotulleoseo myeoni jakku mikkeureojyeoyo.
examples.en: My chopstick skill is still clumsy, so the noodles keep slipping.
examples.note: Real situation: 젓가락질 + 서투르다 (르-irregular), explaining a genuine struggle.

extendedVocab.nuance: 젓가락 is chopsticks — and Korean chopsticks are distinctively flat, heavy METAL ones, harder for beginners than the rounded wooden chopsticks of Japan or China. The partner verb is 집다 (to grasp/pick up), the action chopsticks perform; for noodles 면을 집다 is natural. A high-value derived word is 젓가락질, 'the skill/act of using chopsticks' (the 질 suffix = doing an action), so 젓가락질이 서툴다 = to be clumsy with chopsticks. Remember 젓가락 takes ㅅ while its partner 숟가락 takes ㄷ — don't cross them. Together they form 수저, the utensil set. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: the particle is 젓가락으로 (instrument 으로), not 젓가락에; and because the word is already plural in meaning, you don't pluralize it — to count, use 벌 for a pair (한 벌) or 짝 for a single stick. Collocations: 젓가락으로 집다, 젓가락질, 나무젓가락, 젓가락 한 벌.

Don't write 젇가락 or 저가락. The standard spelling is 젓가락 with ㅅ; pair it correctly against 숟가락 (ㄷ).
Don't say 젓가락에 먹어요. Chopsticks are the instrument: 젓가락으로 먹어요.
Don't count chopsticks with 개 as if singular. A usable pair is 한 벌; a single stick is 한 짝 — 개 sounds off for paired utensils.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 포크 means "fork" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "fork" is 포크 (pokeu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 포크로 찍다 ("to spear with a fork"). Watch the particle attached to 포크 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 찍다 (stab/spear) — the signature fork action for fruit or cake.
Loanword counted simply with 개/하나; 포크 하나 주세요 = please give me one fork.
In Western-dining contexts the knife is the loanword 나이프, paired with 포크 (vs native 칼).
일회용 (single-use) + 포크; the plastic kind handed out with takeout food.

examples.en: There's no fork.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + existence verb 없다.

examples.en: I spear the cake with a fork and eat it.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 찍다, the natural verb for forking cake.

examples.ko: 아이는 아직 젓가락이 서툴러서 포크로 먹는 게 편해요.
examples.romanization: aineun ajik jeotgaragi seotulleoseo pokeuro meongneun ge pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The child is still clumsy with chopsticks, so eating with a fork is easier.
examples.note: Real situation: contrasting 젓가락/포크 with the nominalizer -는 게.

extendedVocab.nuance: 포크 is a loanword (English 'fork') and in Korea is a SECONDARY, situational utensil — used for cake, fruit, salad, and Western food, while everyday rice and soup go with 숟가락 and 젓가락. Its natural partner verb is 찍다 (to stab/spear), as in 과일을 포크로 찍다; this 찍다 also means 'to stamp/take a photo,' so context disambiguates. Don't over-use 포크 — defaulting to a fork at a Korean meal of rice and 반찬 reads as foreign; reach for 젓가락 instead. Collocations: 포크로 찍다, 포크와 나이프, 일회용 포크, 포크 하나.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't pair 포크 with native 칼 in a table setting. Western place settings say 포크와 나이프; 칼 is the cooking knife.

In a Western place-setting the fork pairs with the loanword 나이프, whereas the all-purpose Korean kitchen knife is the native 칼 — so 포크와 나이프 (table setting) but 칼 (cooking).
The English-speaker pitfall is, as with all tools, the particle: 포크로 먹다 (instrument 으로), never 포크에. Collocations: 포크로 찍다, 포크와 나이프, 일회용 포크, 포크 하나.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 칼 means "knife" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 칼 (kal) = "knife". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 칼로 썰다 ("to slice with a knife") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 칼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 썰다 (slice into pieces) — the core knife action in cooking.

usagePhrases.en: the knife cuts well / is sharp
usagePhrases.note: Idiom: 들다 here means 'cuts well'; 안 든다 = it's dull. Not the 들다 'to hold.'
과도 (果刀, fruit-knife) is the small knife for peeling fruit, a specific type of 칼.
갈다 (grind/sharpen) is the verb for putting an edge back on a dull blade.

examples.en: The knife is sharp.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 날카롭다 (ㅂ-irregular).

examples.en: I slice the vegetables thinly with a knife.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 썰다 with the adverb 얇게.

examples.ko: 이 칼은 잘 안 드니까 한번 갈아야겠어요.
examples.romanization: i kareun jal an deunikka hanbeon garayagesseoyo.
examples.en: This knife doesn't cut well, so I'd better sharpen it.
examples.note: Real situation: the idiom 안 들다 (dull) + resolve ending -아야겠다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 칼 is the native, all-purpose Korean word for a knife — above all the kitchen knife, but the SAME word covers any blade: a pocketknife, a sword, a box cutter, all 칼. So unlike English, you don't switch words by type; you specify with a modifier (부엌칼 kitchen, 과도 fruit knife, 맥가이버 칼 Swiss-army). Two idioms are essential: 칼이 잘 들다 means 'the knife cuts well / is sharp' — here 들다 is NOT 'to hold' but 'to cut/take effect,' so 칼이 안 들어요 = it's dull; and 칼을 갈다 = to sharpen. The partner cutting verbs are 썰다 (slice into pieces) and 자르다 (cut through). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 칼로 썰다 (instrument 으로), never 칼에. Note that in a Western table setting the table knife is the loanword 나이프, not 칼. Collocations: 칼로 썰다, 칼이 들다, 칼을 갈다, 과도.

Don't say 칼에 잘라요. The knife is the instrument: 칼로 잘라요 / 칼로 썰어요.
Don't read 칼이 잘 들어요 as 'the knife holds well.' Here 들다 means 'cuts well / is sharp'; the opposite is 칼이 안 들어요 (dull).
Don't expect a different word for sword vs kitchen knife. Korean uses 칼 for both and adds a modifier (부엌칼, 과도) when the type matters.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 냄비 means "pot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 냄비 (naembi) means "pot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 냄비에 끓이다 ("to boil/cook in a pot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 냄비 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Location 에 + 끓이다; the cooking happens IN the pot, so 에 marks it, not 를.
받침 (support) — the mat you rest a hot 냄비 on so it doesn't burn the table.
Note: a rice/pressure cooker is 솥, a different (heavier, lidded) vessel from 냄비.

usagePhrases.en: for food to scorch onto the pot
usagePhrases.note: 눌어붙다 = stick-and-burn to the bottom; a common kitchen mishap with 냄비.

examples.en: The pot is hot.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular).

examples.ko: 라면은 작은 냄비에 끓이면 더 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: ramyeoneun jageun naembie kkeurimyeon deo masisseoyo.
examples.en: Ramen tastes better cooked in a small pot.
examples.note: Everyday: location 에 + 끓이다 with the conditional -면.

examples.ko: 냄비가 뜨거우니까 꼭 받침 위에 올려놓으세요.
examples.romanization: naembiga tteugeounikka kkok batchim wie ollyeonoeuseyo.
examples.en: Since the pot is hot, be sure to set it on a trivet.
examples.note: Real situation: reason -니까 + 냄비 받침 in a safety instruction.

extendedVocab.nuance: 냄비 is a relatively light cooking pot or saucepan — the everyday vessel for boiling soup, simmering 찌개, or making ramen. Two contrasts matter: 냄비 vs 솥 — 솥 is the heavier, deep, lidded cauldron/cooker (think 가마솥, 압력솥 for rice), so don't call a rice cooker a 냄비; and 냄비 vs 프라이팬 — the flat frying pan is its own loanword. The partner verb is 끓이다 (to boil/cook by boiling), and food that scorches onto the bottom 눌어붙다. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you cook 냄비에 끓이다 (location 에) — saying 냄비를 끓이다 literally means 'boil the pot itself,' which is wrong; the pot is where it happens, the food is the object (라면을 냄비에 끓이다). Culturally note 냄비 근성 ('a pot temperament') — a set phrase for quick-to-boil, quick-to-cool enthusiasm. Collocations: 냄비에 끓이다, 냄비 받침, 냄비가 눌어붙다, 냄비 뚜껑.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 냄비를 끓여요 to mean 'cook in the pot.' That reads as boiling the pot itself; say 냄비에 (라면을) 끓여요 — food is the object, the pot the location.
Don't call a rice cooker a 냄비. A deep lidded cooker is 솥 (압력솥, 전기밥솥); 냄비 is the lighter open saucepan.
Don't use 냄비 for a flat frying pan. That's 프라이팬 — different shape, different word.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 식탁 means "dining table" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "dining table" is 식탁 (siktak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식탁에서 먹다 ("to eat at the table"). Watch the particle attached to 식탁 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Action location 에서 + 먹다; an action happens AT the table, so 에서, not 에.
차리다 = lay out a meal/setting; 식탁을 차리다 / 밥상을 차리다 = prepare the table.
위 (top) pins location to the surface: 식탁 위에 그릇이 있다.
식탁 + 보 (cloth wrap) = the cloth spread over the dining table.

examples.en: The dining table is big.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 크다.

examples.en: The family sits around the table and eats.
examples.note: Everyday: 둘러앉다 (sit around) + the action verb 먹다.

examples.ko: 저녁 다 됐으니까 얼른 식탁 좀 차려 줄래?
examples.romanization: jeonyeok da dwaesseunikka eolleun siktak jom charyeo jullae?
examples.en: Dinner's ready, so could you set the table quickly?
examples.note: Real situation: casual request -어 줄래? with 식탁을 차리다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 식탁 is Sino-Korean, 食卓 — 食 'eat/food' + 卓 'table,' literally an 'eating-table,' i.e. the dining table. Distinguish it from 책상 (a desk, 冊床 'book-table' for study/work) and from 밥상, the lower, often portable meal-table (and by extension the whole spread of food) of more traditional dining — 밥상 emphasizes the laid meal, 식탁 the piece of furniture. The everyday verb is 식탁을 차리다 (set/lay the table). The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle: an ACTION done at the table uses 에서, so 식탁에서 밥을 먹다 — using 식탁에 먹다 is wrong because 에 marks static location/existence (식탁에 그릇이 있다), while 에서 marks where an action occurs. To pin something to the surface, add 위: 식탁 위에 놓다. Collocations: 식탁에서 먹다, 식탁을 차리다, 식탁 위, 식탁보.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 식탁에 밥을 먹어요. Eating is an action, so it needs 에서: 식탁에서 밥을 먹어요. Reserve 에 for existence: 식탁에 그릇이 있어요.
Don't confuse 식탁 with 책상. 식탁 (食卓) is for meals; 책상 (冊床) is the desk for studying or working.
Don't say 식탁을 만들어요 to mean 'set the table.' Use 차리다: 식탁을 차려요. 만들다 = build the furniture, not lay the meal.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주방 means "kitchen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주방 (jubang) = "kitchen". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 주방에서 요리하다 ("to cook in the kitchen") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주방, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Action location 에서 + 요리하다; cooking is an action, so 에서, not 에.
용품 (goods/supplies) — 주방 용품 = the pots, knives, and tools of a kitchen.
Real-estate/café term for a kitchen open to the dining area; 주방 takes many such modifiers.
주방 + 장 (長, head) = the chef in charge of a restaurant kitchen.

examples.en: The kitchen is spacious.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 넓다.

examples.en: Mom is making dinner in the kitchen.
examples.note: Everyday: action location 에서 + honorific progressive -고 계시다.

examples.ko: 식당 주방은 위생이 생명이라 늘 깨끗하게 관리해요.
examples.romanization: sikdang jubangeun wisaengi saengmyeongira neul kkaekkeutage gwallihaeyo.
examples.en: A restaurant kitchen lives or dies by hygiene, so it's always kept clean.
examples.note: Real situation: 주방 in a professional sense with 위생/관리하다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 주방 is Sino-Korean, 廚房 — 廚 'kitchen' + 房 'room,' literally the 'kitchen room.' The register contrast you should feel is 주방 vs 부엌: both name the cooking room, but 주방 is the slightly more formal, modern, and PROFESSIONAL-leaning word (a restaurant kitchen, kitchenware ads, 주방장 head chef, an apartment's '오픈 주방'), while 부엌 is the warm, homey native word for the kitchen at home — many speakers use them interchangeably for a home kitchen, but you'd never say a restaurant's 부엌 in a business context. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: cooking is an action, so 주방에서 요리하다 (action location 에서), not 주방에 요리하다 — 에 is only for existence (주방에 냉장고가 있다). Useful derivations: 주방 용품 (kitchenware), 주방장 (head chef). Collocations: 주방에서 요리하다, 주방 용품, 오픈 주방, 주방장.

Don't say 주방에 요리해요. Cooking is an action, so use 에서: 주방에서 요리해요. Keep 에 for existence: 주방에 냉장고가 있어요.
Don't treat 주방 and 부엌 as fully identical. For a home kitchen either works, but a restaurant's cooking area is 주방, not 부엌, in formal/business use.
Don't write the hanja-based word as if native. 주방 (廚房) is Sino-Korean; if you want the cozy home word, that's the native 부엌.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 도마 means "cutting board" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 도마 (doma) means "cutting board". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도마 위에서 썰다 ("to cut on the cutting board"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to cut on the cutting board
usagePhrases.note: 위 + action location 에서; you cut ON TOP of the board, so 위에서, not bare 에.

usagePhrases.en: to wipe the board with a cloth
usagePhrases.note: Here 닦다 (wipe) is right — wiping the board's surface, vs 씻다 for rinsing it.
나무 (wood) vs 플라스틱 도마 (plastic); material modifiers are common with 도마.

usagePhrases.en: the sound of chopping (on the board)
usagePhrases.note: 도마 소리 evokes the rhythmic knock of cooking; a vivid everyday collocation.

examples.en: The cutting board is clean.
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + adjective 깨끗하다.

examples.en: I slice the vegetables on the cutting board.
examples.note: Everyday: 도마 위에서 + 썰다, the standard chopping frame.

examples.ko: 고기랑 채소는 도마를 따로 써야 위생적이에요.
examples.romanization: gogirang chaesoneun domareul ttaro sseoya wisaengjeogieyo.
examples.en: It's more hygienic to use separate boards for meat and vegetables.
examples.note: Real situation: 따로 쓰다 (use separately) + 위생적이다 in a kitchen-safety tip.

extendedVocab.nuance: 도마 is the cutting board — the flat surface you set food on to chop with a 칼. There isn't a tricky near-synonym; the value is in the GRAMMAR and collocations. Because cutting happens on top of the board's surface, the natural frame is 도마 위에서 썰다 (위 'top' + action-location 에서) — bare 도마에 썰다 sounds incomplete, since 에 marks static existence, not where an action plays out. Note the two cleaning verbs split by sense: 도마를 씻다 = rinse it with water; 도마를 닦다 = wipe its surface — both valid, unlike with dishes where 닦다 was wrong. Korean kitchens commonly keep separate boards (고기용/채소용) for hygiene, so 도마를 따로 쓰다 is a natural phrase. Material modifiers abound: 나무 도마, 플라스틱 도마. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 위에서 and using 도마에, or marking the board as the object of 썰다. Collocations: 도마 위에서 썰다, 나무 도마, 도마를 씻다, 도마 소리.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 도마에 썰어요. Cutting happens on the surface, so use 도마 위에서 썰어요 — 위 + the action particle 에서.
Don't mark the board as the object of cutting: 도마를 썰어요 means 'cut the board.' The food is the object; the board is the place (도마 위에서).
Don't assume one cleaning verb. 도마를 씻다 = rinse with water, 도마를 닦다 = wipe the surface; choose by what you actually do.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 국자 means "ladle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "ladle" is 국자 (gukja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국자로 뜨다 ("to ladle/scoop with a ladle"). Watch the particle attached to 국자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Instrument 으로 + 뜨다 (scoop up liquid) — the exact partner verb for a ladle.

usagePhrases.en: to dish out with a ladle
usagePhrases.note: 푸다 (scoop and serve out) is also natural: 국을 국자로 퍼서 담다.
The chain 뜨다/푸다 → 그릇에 담다 is how you serve soup with 국자.
Counted simply with 개/하나; 국자 하나 주세요 = please give me a ladle.

examples.en: Where's the ladle?
examples.note: Simplest frame: subject 이 + location question 어디 있다.

examples.en: I ladle the stew and serve it into a bowl.
examples.note: Everyday: instrument 으로 + 뜨다, chained to 담다 with -서.

examples.ko: 국이 모자라면 국자로 더 퍼서 드세요.
examples.romanization: gugi mojaramyeon gukjaro deo peoseo deuseyo.
examples.en: If there isn't enough soup, ladle out more and help yourself.
examples.note: Real situation: conditional -면 + 푸다 (ㅜ-irregular) with honorific 드시다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 국자 is the long-handled ladle for serving soup or stew — native Korean, built transparently from 국 'soup' + 자 (a tool suffix seen in 주걱 'rice paddle' family of kitchen tools). Its dedicated partner verbs are 뜨다 (to scoop up a liquid) and 푸다 (to scoop-and-serve out), so a full serving action is 국을 국자로 떠서/퍼서 그릇에 담다. Don't confuse 국자 with 주걱, the flat rice paddle for scooping cooked rice — different shape, different food. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to brush one's teeth with a toothbrush
usagePhrases.note: 칫솔 ends in ㄹ, so the means particle is 로 (ㄹ behaves like a vowel here)
모(毛) = hair/bristle; 칫솔모가 부드럽다 = the bristles are soft
the routine action of swapping an old brush for a new one
counted with the general counter 개

examples.en: It's a new toothbrush.
examples.note: simple: 새 + noun = brand-new; here it just names the item

examples.en: Every morning I brush my teeth with a toothbrush.
examples.note: everyday: the full set phrase 칫솔로 이를 닦다; 마다 = every

examples.en: When the bristles splay out, you should swap in a new one.
examples.note: real-situation: 벌어지다 (to spread apart) is the natural verb for worn bristles

extendedVocab.nuance: 칫솔 names the BRUSH itself, and you must keep three related words apart: 칫솔 = the brush, 치약 = the paste, and 양치(질) = the whole act of brushing/rinsing the mouth. Don't say 칫솔을 닦아요 to mean brushing your teeth; that means cleaning the brush. Say 칫솔로 이를 닦아요.

usagePhrases.en: to brush one's teeth with toothpaste
usagePhrases.note: 치약 ends in ㄱ (consonant), so the means particle is 으로

usagePhrases.en: to put toothpaste on the toothbrush
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = to apply onto; the natural verb for loading the brush

헹구다 = to rinse with water; what you do after lathering

Don't write 샴푸으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 샴푸로.

usagePhrases.en: to look at oneself in the mirror
usagePhrases.note: 거울을 보다 = check your appearance, NOT stare at the glass

usagePhrases.en: to be reflected in the mirror
usagePhrases.note: 비치다 = to be reflected; 에 marks the surface showing the reflection
깨지다 = to break (for glass); a natural everyday event verb

Don't use 보이다 when you mean 'I look at myself' — 거울을 보다 is active (you look); 거울에 비치다/보이다 is the reflection appearing.

usagePhrases.note: 휴지 ends in a vowel → 로; 닦다 = to wipe clean

usagePhrases.en: to wash one's face at the sink
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place where the action happens; 세수 = washing the face

usagePhrases.en: to fill the bathtub with water
usagePhrases.note: 받다 here = to draw/collect water; 에 marks where the water goes

usagePhrases.en: to soak (one's body) in the tub
usagePhrases.note: 담그다 = to immerse/soak; the verb for sinking into hot water

usagePhrases.en: to take a bath in the tub
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = location of the activity; 목욕 = a soaking bath
반신(半身)욕 = soaking only the lower half; a common Korean tub habit

examples.en: The bathtub is big.
examples.note: simple: plain description with 크다, subject 가

extendedVocab.nuance: 욕조 is the soaking BATHTUB, and the contrast that matters is the activity word: a long soak in the 욕조 is 목욕(하다), whereas a quick standing rinse is 샤워(하다) — many Korean apartments have only a 샤워 stall with no 욕조 at all, so this is a real cultural distinction, not just vocabulary. Don't say 욕조를 채워요 in casual speech; the idiomatic phrase is 욕조에 물을 받아요.
Don't use 에 for the action of bathing; 'bathe in the tub' takes 에서 — 욕조에서 목욕해요.

Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to comb one's hair with a comb
usagePhrases.note: 빗 ends in a consonant → 으로; the noun 빗 and verb 빗다 share a root
the everyday action verb, even when using a brush
-어 넘기다 = to sweep/push back; styling direction
참빗 = closely set teeth; 얼레빗 = widely set teeth

examples.en: The comb is small.
examples.note: simple: plain description with 작다, subject 이

examples.en: In the morning I comb my hair with a comb.
examples.note: everyday: noun 빗 + verb 빗다 together; note the 으로 after a consonant

examples.ko: 엉킨 머리는 빗으로 천천히 빗어야 안 아파요.
examples.romanization: eongkin meorineun biseuro cheoncheonhi biseoya an apayo.
examples.en: Tangled hair you should comb slowly with a comb so it doesn't hurt.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빗 is a COMB, a native Korean word, and the neat thing learners must notice is that the noun 빗 and its action verb 빗다 (to comb) look and sound nearly identical — 빗으로 머리를 빗다 literally stacks 'comb-with hair comb,' which feels redundant in English but is perfectly natural in Korean. The near-synonym to separate is the tool type: 빗 is a flat comb, while a paddle/round HAIRBRUSH is 머리빗 or the loanword 브러시; in casual speech 빗 covers both, but a true brush is 브러시. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle after a consonant-final noun: it must be 빗으로, NOT 빗로 — and beginners often also drop the verb's irregularity, but 빗다 is regular (빗어요, 빗었어요). Don't say 머리를 솔질하다; the verb is simply 빗다.

Don't write 빗로 — 빗 ends in a consonant, so the means form is 빗으로.
Don't say 머리를 솔질해요 for combing; the verb is 빗다 — 머리를 빗어요.
Don't confuse the noun 빗 (comb) with 빚 (debt) — same sound, different spelling and meaning.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 면도기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 면도기 ends in a vowel → 로; 면도하다 = to shave (the action)
깎다 = to shave/trim; the verb pairing with 수염 (beard)
전기(電氣) + 면도기; the plug-in or rechargeable kind
날 = blade; the sharp part you replace when dull

examples.en: The razor is sharp.
examples.note: simple: state with 날카롭다, subject 가

examples.en: Every morning I shave with a razor.
examples.note: everyday: 면도기로 + 면도하다; 마다 = every

examples.note: real-situation: 무뎌지다 (become blunt) + 새것으로 바꾸다

extendedVocab.nuance: 면도기 is the shaving TOOL, and the hanja explains its whole family: 면(面) 'face' + 도(刀) 'blade/knife' = 면도 ('face-blading' = shaving), plus 기(器) 'device' = the razor itself. So 면도하다 means 'to shave' and 면도기 is the instrument. The contrast to keep clear is 면도기 (the device) vs 면도 (the act) vs 면도날 (the replaceable blade), and an electric one is 전기면도기. Its partner verbs are 면도하다 (shave) and, with 수염 (beard), 깎다 (수염을 깎다, 'cut/shave the beard'). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle plus a doubled object: you shave WITH the razor, so it's 면도기로 면도하다 (means 로, vowel-final); never 면도기를 면도하다, which would absurdly mean 'shave the razor.' Also 면도기 ends in a vowel, so it's 로, not 으로.

Don't say 면도기를 면도해요; you shave WITH it — 면도기로 면도해요 (or 면도기로 수염을 깎아요).
Don't write 면도기으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 면도기로.
Don't confuse 면도기 (the razor) with 면도 (the act of shaving); 'do a shave' is 면도하다, the tool is 면도기.

usagePhrases.en: to dry one's hair with a hair dryer
usagePhrases.note: 드라이기 ends in a vowel → 로; 말리다 = to dry (something), transitive

usagePhrases.en: to plug the dryer into the outlet
usagePhrases.note: 꽂다 = to plug/insert; 콘센트 = wall outlet
고장 나다 = to break/malfunction (for appliances)

examples.note: simple: state with 뜨겁다, subject 가

examples.en: After a shower I dry my hair with a hair dryer.
examples.note: everyday: 드라이기로 + 머리를 말리다; note transitive 말리다

Don't write 드라이기으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 드라이기로.

extendedVocab.explanation: 텔레비전 (tellebijeon) = "television". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 텔레비전을 봐요 ("I watch television") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: object 을 — the screen is what you watch
power on with 켜다, not 열다
power off with 끄다, the opposite of 켜다
subject 이 + descriptive adjective 크다

examples.en: I like television.
examples.note: simple: 을 marks the thing you like

examples.en: I watch TV while eating dinner.
examples.note: everyday: -(으)면서 'while' two actions at once

examples.ko: 드라마 보려고 텔레비전을 켰는데 정전이 됐어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 텔레비전 is the full English loanword (television), but in everyday conversation almost everyone shortens it to 티비(TV) — 티비 sounds normal in casual chat while 텔레비전 feels slightly more written or formal. The near-synonym to distinguish is the channel/broadcast itself: 텔레비전 is the physical set or the medium, whereas 방송 means the broadcast/program and 채널 is the channel you flip to. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb for 'turn on': you must use 켜다 (and 끄다 to turn off), never 열다 'open' — 텔레비전을 열어요 sounds like you are physically prying the box apart. Also remember it is the object of 보다, so it takes 을: 텔레비전을 봐요, not 텔레비전이 봐요.

Saying 텔레비전을 열어요 for turning it on. 열다 means to open a door or lid; an appliance is powered on with 켜다 — say 텔레비전을 켜요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 세탁기 is Sino-Korean, 洗濯機 literally 'wash(洗)-rinse(濯)-machine(機)', the standard word for a clothes washer. The key collocation an English speaker must memorize is 세탁기를 돌리다 — Koreans 'spin/turn' a washing machine (돌리다) rather than literally 'use' it; the 돌리다 image comes from the drum spinning, and the same verb runs a 청소기(vacuum) or 믹서. Do not say 세탁기를 해요 ('do the washer'), which sounds incomplete, nor 세탁기를 사용해요, which is grammatical but stiff and textbook-ish for daily speech. Distinguish 세탁기 (the appliance) from 빨래 (the laundry / the act of doing laundry) and 세탁 (the formal noun 'laundering', as on a 세탁소 dry-cleaner sign): you 빨래를 하다 'do the laundry' but 세탁기를 돌리다 'run the machine'.

Saying 세탁기를 해요 to mean 'run the washer'. 하다 'do' does not collocate here; the fixed verb is 돌리다 — say 세탁기를 돌려요.
Saying 세탁기에서 옷을 넣어요 when loading clothes. 에서 marks where an action happens or a source 'from'; putting something INTO the machine needs the destination 에 — 세탁기에 옷을 넣어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 청소기 is Sino-Korean, 淸掃機 'clean(淸)-sweep(掃)-machine(機)', and is itself the everyday short form of 진공청소기 (眞空, 'vacuum-cleaning machine'); in normal speech nobody says the full 진공청소기. Two particles compete and English speakers mix them up: use 으로 when the vacuum is the TOOL you clean with (청소기로 청소해요 'clean WITH the vacuum'), but 을 when the vacuum is the OBJECT you operate (청소기를 돌려요 'run the vacuum'). extendedVocab.nuance: 에어컨 is a clipped English loanword (air con(ditioner)) — Korean kept only the first half, which is why it looks shorter than the English source. For switching it on you have two natural verbs: 켜다 'turn on' (general, pairs with 끄다 'turn off') and the very colloquial 틀다 'put on/start running', which Koreans love for the AC, fan and radio (에어컨 좀 틀어 줘 'put the AC on for me'). The English-speaker pitfall is 열다 'open': 에어컨을 열어요 is wrong because you are not opening a door — power-driven machines are 켜다/끄다 or 틀다. Note 에어컨 is the cooling appliance; the heating equivalent is 난방 (or a 히터), and central building climate control is 냉난방, so do not stretch 에어컨 to mean 'heater'.

Using 에어컨 to mean a heater. 에어컨 only cools; for heating say 난방을 켜다 or 히터를 켜다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 선풍기 is Sino-Korean, 扇風機 'fan(扇)-wind(風)-machine(機)' — literally a machine that makes fan-wind — so the 기(機) ending matches 세탁기/청소기. The contrast learners need is with 부채, the hand-held folding fan you wave manually: 선풍기 is the electric standing/desk fan you plug in, 부채 is the non-electric one. The contrast English speakers must internalize is the IN/OUT particle pair: putting food IN uses the destination 에 (냉장고에 넣다), taking it OUT uses the source 에서 (냉장고에서 꺼내다) — many learners over-use 에서 for both. Distinguish the whole appliance 냉장고 (the fridge, chilled section) from the 냉동고/냉동실 'freezer (compartment)', built on 冷凍 'freeze' rather than 冷藏 'cold-store'; 김치냉장고 is the dedicated kimchi fridge found in most Korean homes.

Saying 냉장고에서 우유를 넣어요 for putting milk in. 에서 marks a source 'from'; to put something INTO the fridge you need the destination 에 — 냉장고에 우유를 넣어요.
Calling the freezer 냉장고. The chilled section is 냉장고/냉장실, but the freezer compartment is 냉동실 (冷凍 'freeze') — keep them separate.

extendedVocab.nuance: 소파 is the English loanword 'sofa', the Western-style upholstered couch for a living room; the everyday native alternative for a long bench-seat is rarely used, so 소파 is the default word. The sharp grammar point is 에 vs 에서 with this noun: use 에 for the END-POINT of a positioning verb — 소파에 앉다 'sit (down) on the sofa', 소파에 눕다 'lie on the sofa' — but 에서 when an ongoing ACTIVITY happens there — 소파에서 쉬다/책을 읽다 'rest / read on the sofa'. English 'on the sofa' hides this split, so learners wrongly say 소파에서 앉아요. A common collocation is 편한 소파 'a comfy sofa'; a sofa-bed is a 소파베드.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using 에 for an activity done on the sofa: 소파에 쉬어요 should be 소파에서 쉬어요, because resting is an ongoing action and its setting takes 에서.

extendedVocab.nuance: 옷장 combines native 옷 'clothes' + the bound morpheme -장 (from the hanja 欌, 'wooden cabinet/closet'), so it is a clothes-cabinet — the same -장 appears in 책장 'bookshelf' and 찬장 'cupboard'. object 을 + 닫다, opposite of 열다

usagePhrases.note: destination 에 (into the drawer)
relational noun 안 'inside' + 에

extendedVocab.nuance: 서랍 is a native Korean word (no hanja) for a single sliding drawer; a piece of furniture made of several stacked drawers is a 서랍장 'chest of drawers'. Unlike powered appliances, a drawer is genuinely opened and closed, so it correctly takes 열다 'open' / 닫다 'close' — the contrast to notice is 열다 (you actively open it) versus the passive 열리다 'be/get opened' used when it won't budge (서랍이 안 열려요 'the drawer won't open'). Saying 서랍에서 양말을 넣어요 for putting socks in. Into the drawer is the destination 에; 에서 means 'from' — say 서랍에 양말을 넣어요.

걷다 'gather/pull aside' (open them)
subject 이 + 있다
modifier 암막 'light-blocking'

examples.en: There is a curtain on the window.
examples.note: simple: 에 place + 있다

examples.note: everyday: 세다 'be strong' + -아서 reason, past

examples.note: real-situation: -기 전에 'before' + 고 listing two actions

extendedVocab.nuance: 커튼 is the English loanword 'curtain', the fabric window cover. The verb pitfall is severe: to close/draw curtains across a window the fixed verb is 치다 (커튼을 치다 'draw the curtains'), and to open them you 걷다 'gather aside' (커튼을 걷다) — note 치다 here means 'spread/draw across', the same 치다 as in 텐트를 치다 'pitch a tent', NOT 치다 'hit'. Do not say 커튼을 해요 'do the curtain', which is incomplete, and be careful that 열다/닫다 'open/close' sound less idiomatic than 걷다/치다 for curtains specifically. Distinguish 커튼 (cloth, on a window/stage) from 블라인드 'blinds' (the slatted kind): a thick light-blocking curtain is an 암막 커튼.

Saying 커튼을 해요 to draw them. 하다 doesn't collocate; the set verb is 치다 — say 커튼을 쳐요 to close them and 커튼을 걷어요 to open them.

extendedVocab.explanation: "bookshelf" is 책장 (chaekjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 책장이 있어요 ("there is a bookshelf"). Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: subject 이 + 있다

usagePhrases.en: I shelve it on the bookshelf
usagePhrases.note: 꽂다 'insert upright' (slot a book in), destination 에

usagePhrases.en: I pull it off the shelf
usagePhrases.note: source 에서 + 빼다 'pull out'
정리하다 'organize', object 을

examples.en: There is a bookshelf in the room.
examples.note: simple: 에 place + 있다

examples.en: I shelve the books I've finished on the bookcase.
examples.note: everyday: 다 읽다 'finish reading' modifier + 꽂다

examples.ko: 책장에 책이 너무 많아서 한 줄 더 쌓았어요.
examples.romanization: chaekjange chaegi neomu manaseo han jul deo ssaasseoyo.
examples.en: There were too many books on the shelf so I stacked another row.
examples.note: real-situation: -아서 reason + 쌓다 'pile up'

extendedVocab.nuance: 책장 combines 책 (冊 'book') + -장 (欌 'cabinet/case'), literally a book-cabinet, the same -장 as in 옷장 'wardrobe'. Watch a tricky homograph: 책장 also means 'a page/leaf of a book' (책장을 넘기다 'turn the page'), so context decides between 'bookshelf' and 'page'. The signature verb is 꽂다 'to slot/stand upright' for putting a book in (책을 책장에 꽂다) and 빼다/꺼내다 to take it out — 꽂다 captures sliding the spine into the row, far more natural than 넣다 here. Near-synonym: many people also say 책꽂이 (책+꽂이, from 꽂다) for a bookshelf, often a smaller open rack, whereas 책장 tends to be the larger cabinet-style unit. Into the shelf is 에, off the shelf is 에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using 넣다 for shelving books. 넣다 'put in' works for drawers, but standing a book upright on a shelf is 꽂다 — say 책을 꽂아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 과목 means "subject" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 과목 (gwamok) = "subject". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과목을 좋아해요 ("like a subject") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과목, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 좋아하다 takes the object marker 을/를, not 이/가
the verb 좋아하다 turns into the modifier 좋아하는 placed before the noun
with 많다 the noun takes the subject marker 이, never 을
두 Sino-Korean nouns stack bare with no particle between them

examples.en: I choose a subject.
examples.note: simple 를 + verb: 과목 is the thing you pick

examples.en: My favorite subject is music.
examples.note: 좋아하는 modifies 과목; 은 marks it as the topic of the sentence

examples.ko: 이번 학기에는 과목이 너무 많아서 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon hakgieneun gwamogi neomu manaseo himdeureoyo.
examples.en: This term there are so many subjects that it is hard.
examples.note: real complaint: 많아서 (so many, therefore) links the cause to 힘들다

extendedVocab.nuance: 과목 is a school subject as a field of study — math, science, music — the label on a curriculum, written 科目 (科 'branch/category' + 目 'item'), literally a 'category item'. Do not confuse it with 수업, which is the actual class period or lesson you sit through: you 'like a 과목' (the topic) but you 'have a 수업 at 3 o'clock' (the session). It also differs from 전공, the single 'major' you commit to at university — 과목 is any one of many courses. With descriptive adjectives like 많다 or 어렵다 it must take 이/가 (과목이 어려워요), but with 좋아하다/배우다 it takes 을/를; the English-speaker trap is forcing 'I like science' into 과목을 좋아하다 + a separate noun, when Koreans just name the subject directly (음악을 좋아해요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 과목을 많아요 by copying English 'I have many subjects' — 많다 is descriptive, so the subject takes 이: 과목이 많아요.
Using 과목 for the class hour, e.g. 과목이 세 시예요; the timetable slot is 수업, so say 수업이 세 시에 있어요.
Translating 'my major is...' as 제 과목은...; a university major is 전공, so it should be 제 전공은....

배우다 (to learn) takes the object marker 을
수학 + 시간 stack bare to mean the math lesson slot
잘하다 (do well) takes 을; this is the set phrase for a skill

examples.en: There is a lot of math homework.
examples.note: simple: 수학 modifies 숙제, and 많다 takes 이/가

examples.en: We learn math at school.
examples.note: 를 marks what we learn; 에서 marks the place

examples.ko: 저는 수학을 잘 못해서 학원에 다녀요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 수학 is the school subject mathematics, written 數學 (數 'number' + 學 'study') — literally the 'study of numbers'. The 學 ending is the standard Sino-Korean tag for an academic discipline, the same 학 in 과학, 역사학, 의학, so once you know it you can read whole subject names. Note the contrast between 수학 (the abstract discipline) and 산수, the simple 'arithmetic' little children do — adults studying equations always say 수학. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is the particle on the adjective: 'math is hard for me' feels like math is the object, but 어렵다/쉽다 are descriptive verbs, so math is the grammatical subject and takes 이 — 수학이 어려워요, never 수학을 어려워요. To express skill, use the fixed 수학을 잘하다/못하다 with 을, where the verb (not the adjective) governs the object marker.

Saying 수학을 어려워요 because English makes math the object; 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 수학이 어려워요.
Using 산수 (arithmetic) for the secondary-school subject; once it involves algebra say 수학.
Dropping 잘 and saying 수학을 해요 for 'I'm good at math'; you need 수학을 잘해요 to convey skill.

extendedVocab.explanation: "science" is 과학 (gwahak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 과학이 재미있어요 ("science is fun"). Watch the particle attached to 과학 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. 공부하다 takes the object marker 을
과학 modifies 선생님 with no particle between
과학 + 실험 stack to name the lab activity

examples.en: Science is fun.
examples.note: simple descriptive sentence: 이 marks 과학, 재미있다 follows

examples.en: We did an experiment in science class today.
examples.note: 과학 시간 = the lesson; 실험을 하다 is the set phrase

extendedVocab.nuance: 과학 is the school subject and the broad field of science, written 科學 (科 'branch/discipline' + 學 'study') — the 'study of disciplines', i.e. systematic knowledge. The same 과 appears in 과목 (subject) and 학과 (academic department), so the words cluster naturally. Keep 과학 (the field) separate from 과목 (any subject in general) — science is one 과목 among many; and from 기술, the 'technology/practical-skills' subject sometimes paired with it. Saying 과학을 재미있어요; 재미있다 is descriptive, so the subject takes 이: 과학이 재미있어요.

길다 is descriptive, so 역사 takes 가
country name 한국 modifies 역사 with no particle
좋아하다 takes the object marker 를

examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 를

examples.note: 한국 역사 is the topic (는); 길다 describes it

examples.ko: 역사 시험 때문에 어젯밤에 늦게까지 공부했어요.

Adding 의 in 한국의 역사 by reflex; natural everyday Korean stacks them bare as 한국 역사.

미술 + 시간 names the art lesson slot

examples.en: I like art (class).
examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 을

examples.en: We draw pictures in art class.
examples.note: 그림을 그리다 is the fixed verb-noun pair for drawing

examples.ko: 미술 시간에 만든 작품을 교실에 걸었어요.
examples.romanization: misul sigane mandeun jakpumeul gyosire georeosseoyo.
examples.en: We hung the work we made in art class on the wall.

extendedVocab.nuance: 미술 is the school subject of visual art — drawing, painting, making things — written 美術 (美 'beauty' + 術 'art/technique, skill'), literally the 'technique of beauty'. That same 술 'technique' appears in 기술 (technology) and 예술 (the arts), which helps you read related words. Crucially, 미술 is the subject/field, while 그림 is a concrete 'picture/drawing' you produce, and 예술 is 'the arts' in the grand sense (music, dance, literature too); a child does 미술 in school but creates a 그림. Using 미술 to mean a single picture; one drawing is 그림, while 미술 is the whole subject.
Confusing 미술 with 예술; 예술 is 'the arts' broadly (incl. music/dance), 미술 is specifically visual art.

extendedVocab.explanation: "PE" is 체육 (cheyuk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 체육을 좋아해요 ("like PE"). Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

체육 + 시간 names the gym-class slot
있다 (to exist) takes the subject marker 이
체육 + 복 (clothes) compound for gym clothes

examples.en: I like PE.
examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 을

examples.en: We played soccer in PE.
examples.note: 체육 시간 = the lesson; 축구를 하다 = play soccer

examples.ko: 내일 체육 시간에는 체육복을 꼭 가져와야 해요.
examples.romanization: naeil cheyuk siganeneun cheyukbogeul kkok gajyeowaya haeyo.
examples.en: Tomorrow for PE you must bring your gym clothes.

extendedVocab.nuance: 체육 is physical education, the school subject of exercise and sport, written 體育 (體 'body' + 育 'to raise, nurture'), literally 'raising/educating the body' — a neat mirror of 교육 (敎育, 'teaching-education'). Keep 체육 (the curriculum subject) distinct from 운동, the everyday word for 'exercise / a workout / sports' in general: you have a 체육 class at school but you go 운동(을) 하다 at the gym on weekends. The compound 체육복 ('PE + clothes') is the required gym uniform, and the venue is the 체육관 (gymnasium). With 있다 the noun takes 이/가 (체육 시간이 있어요), but with 좋아하다 it takes 을/를. Saying 체육을 있어요 for 'there's PE'; 있다 needs the subject marker: 체육 시간이 있어요.
Translating 'gym clothes' word-by-word; the fixed compound is 체육복, not 체육 옷.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 지리 means "geography" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 지리 (jiri) = "geography". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지리를 배워요 ("learn geography") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 지리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

지리 + 시간 names the geography lesson slot
country name 한국 modifies 지리 bare
공부하다 takes the object marker 를

examples.en: I learn geography.
examples.note: simple: 배우다 needs the object marker 를

examples.en: In geography we looked at a world map.
examples.note: note the near-twins: 지리 (the subject) vs 지도 (the map)

examples.ko: 저는 한국 지리는 잘 아는데 세계 지리는 어려워요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hanguk jirineun jal aneunde segye jirineun eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: I know Korean geography well but world geography is hard.
examples.note: real life: 는데 contrasts the two halves

extendedVocab.nuance: 지리 is geography, the subject about the earth's land, places, and features, written 地理 (地 'earth/ground' + 理 'principle, pattern'), literally 'the patterns of the land'. The 地 'earth' element ties it to 지도 (地圖, 'earth-map'), 지구 (地球, 'earth-globe'), and 지진 (地震, 'earth-quake'), so the cluster is learnable as a family. The trap pair is 지리 vs 지도: 지리 is the field of study (the knowledge), while 지도 is a physical map you hold or look at — in 지리 class you study a 지도. As a modifier, region names stack bare: 한국 지리, 세계 지리. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping in 지도 for the subject (지도를 배워요, 'learn the map'), or adding 의 (한국의 지리) where bare stacking is more natural.

Saying 지도를 배워요 to mean 'study geography'; 지도 is a map, so the subject is 지리를 배워요.
Adding 의 as in 한국의 지리 by reflex; natural Korean stacks it bare: 한국 지리.
Saying 지리를 어려워요; 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 지리가 어려워요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 성적 means "grades" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 성적 (seongjeok) means "grades". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성적이 좋아요 ("grades are good"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 성적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다 is descriptive, so 성적 takes 이
나오다 (come out) takes the subject marker 이
받다 (receive) takes the object marker 을
오르다 (rise) takes the subject marker 이

examples.en: My grades are good.
examples.note: simple descriptive: 좋다 takes the subject marker 이

examples.en: The grades come out next week.
examples.note: 성적이 나오다 = results are released/posted

examples.ko: 이번에 성적이 많이 올라서 부모님이 정말 기뻐하셨어요.
examples.romanization: ibeone seongjeogi mani ollaseo bumonimi jeongmal gippeohasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My grades went up a lot this time so my parents were really pleased.
examples.note: real life: 올라서 gives the reason; 기뻐하시다 (honorific) for parents

extendedVocab.nuance: 성적 means academic grades, marks, or results, written 成績 (成 'to accomplish, achieve' + 績 'achievement, merit'), literally 'accomplished achievements' — the outcome of your effort. Distinguish it from 점수, a single numeric 'score' on one test (시험 점수 90점), and from 시험, the 'exam' itself: you take a 시험, get a 점수 on it, and your overall 성적 reflects the term. Note the directional verbs that pair with it: 성적이 나오다 (results 'come out'/are released), 성적을 받다 (you 'receive' them), 성적이 오르다/떨어지다 (they rise/fall). The English-speaker pitfall is using 시험 where you mean the resulting grade ('my exam was good' → say 성적이 좋아요), and choosing the wrong particle: with descriptive 좋다 or motion 나오다/오르다 it's 이/가, only with 받다 is it 을/를.

Saying 시험이 좋아요 to mean 'my grades are good'; 시험 is the exam, the result is 성적, so say 성적이 좋아요.
Saying 성적을 좋아요 by treating grades as an object; 좋다 is descriptive, so use 성적이 좋아요.
Using 점수 for the whole term's standing; 점수 is one test's score, the cumulative record is 성적.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 학년 means "school year" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "school year" is 학년 (hangnyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 몇 학년이에요 ("what grade are you in"). Watch the particle attached to 학년 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

Sino-Korean number 일 + 학년 (note: 일 not 한)
올라가다 (go up) takes the subject marker 이
같은 (same) modifies 학년 directly

examples.en: I'm in first grade.
examples.note: Sino number 일 + 학년; 이에요 states the fact

examples.en: What grade is your sibling in now?
examples.note: 몇 학년 = 'which grade', the standard question

examples.ko: 내년에 삼 학년이 되면 공부가 더 어려워질 거예요.
examples.romanization: naenyeone sam hangnyeoni doemyeon gongbuga deo eoryeowojil geoyeyo.
examples.en: When I become a third-grader next year, studying will get harder.
examples.note: real life: 이 되면 = 'when (one) becomes', 어려워지다 = 'get harder'

extendedVocab.nuance: 학년 means a school grade or year level (1st year, 2nd year), written 學年 (學 'study' + 年 'year'), literally 'study-year'. Two things trip up English speakers. Second, keep 학년 (the grade/year you're in) separate from 학교 (the school building/institution) and from 학기 (學期, the 'semester/term' within a year): you're in 이 학년 at your 학교 during the spring 학기. To ask, use 몇 학년 ('which grade'). With 되다/올라가다 the noun takes 이/가 (삼 학년이 되다, 학년이 올라가다), and as a count noun before 이에요 you simply state 일 학년이에요.

Saying 한 학년이에요 for 'I'm in first grade'; grade levels use Sino numbers: 일 학년이에요.
Confusing 학년 with 학기; the year level is 학년, but a semester is 학기 (e.g. 이번 학기).
Asking 무슨 학년이에요?; the natural question word for a number is 몇, so say 몇 학년이에요?

extendedVocab.explanation: 전공 (jeongong) = "major". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전공이 뭐예요 ("what is your major") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전공, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

정하다 (decide) takes the object marker 을
바꾸다 (change) takes the object marker 을
전공 modifies 수업 to mean a course in one's major

examples.en: My major is Korean.
examples.note: 전공 + 은 marks the topic; 이에요/예요 states it

examples.en: What's your major?
examples.note: the everyday question to a university student

examples.note: real life: 에서...으로 = 'from...to', 바꾸다 = change

extendedVocab.nuance: 전공 is your academic major — the single specialized field you concentrate on at university — written 專攻 (專 'exclusive, sole' + 攻 'to attack, devote effort to'), literally 'to devote oneself exclusively', i.e. to specialize. It can also act as a verb with 하다: 한국어를 전공하다 ('to major in Korean'). The key contrast is 전공 vs 과목: a 과목 is any one of the many courses on your timetable, whereas 전공 is the one field you commit to — you take many 과목 but have one 전공. It also differs from 학과, the 'academic department' that houses the major. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a major 과목 (제 과목은..., wrong) and forgetting that with the verb form the field takes 을/를: not 한국어 전공해요 but 한국어를 전공해요; as a plain noun, though, 전공이 뭐예요 uses 이/가.

Saying 제 과목은 한국어예요 for 'my major is Korean'; a university major is 전공, so use 제 전공은 한국어예요.
Saying 한국어 전공해요 without a particle; the verb form needs 를: 한국어를 전공해요.
Confusing 전공 with 학과; 전공 is the field you study, 학과 is the department, e.g. 한국어학과.

The key contrast is 전공 vs 과목: a 과목 is any one of the many courses on your timetable, whereas 전공 is the one field you commit to — you take many 과목 but have one 전공. It also differs from 학과, the 'academic department' that houses the major.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 학원 means "private academy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 학원 (hagwon) means "private academy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 학원에 다녀요 ("attend an academy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 학원 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 다니다 (commute/attend) takes the destination marker 에
끝나다 (end) takes the subject marker 이
subject name 영어 modifies 학원 bare
끝나다 + 고 = 'after it ends', then do the next thing

examples.en: I go to an English academy.
examples.note: 학원에 다니다 = attend regularly; 에 marks where you go

examples.en: The academy lets out at nine.
examples.note: 끝나다 takes 이/가; 에 marks the clock time

examples.ko: 학교 끝나고 바로 학원에 가야 해서 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: hakgyo kkeunnago baro hagwone gaya haeseo neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: I have to go straight to the academy after school so I'm exhausted.
examples.note: real life: a very Korean routine; 가야 해서 gives the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 학원 is a private after-school academy (cram school) where students pay for extra lessons — English, math, piano, taekwondo — written 學院 (學 'study' + 院 'institution, hall'). The 院 'institution' element links it to 병원 (病院 hospital), 대학원 (大學院 graduate school), and 미용원/미장원, so the family is learnable. Sharply distinguish 학원 (a supplementary private institute) from 학교 (學校, the regular public/formal school) and from 대학원 (graduate school) — a child attends 학교 by day and 학원 in the evening. The verb of choice is 다니다, which implies habitual commuting/membership, with the 에 particle: 학원에 다니다 ('attend an academy regularly'), not the one-off 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 학교 for any place of learning, or marking the destination with 를 (학원를 다녀요, wrong) instead of 에.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a cram school 학교; the formal school is 학교, the private institute is 학원.
Saying 학원을 다녀요; the verb 다니다 takes the 에 particle for the place: 학원에 다녀요.
Using 가다 for habitual attendance; for ongoing enrollment Koreans say 다니다, e.g. 학원에 다녀요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 유학 means "studying abroad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "studying abroad" is 유학 (yuhak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 유학을 가요 ("go abroad to study"). Watch the particle attached to 유학 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 유학(을) 가다 is the set phrase; 가다 = go there
고 싶다 attaches to 가다 to express the wish
유학 + 생활 names the study-abroad lifestyle
유학(을) 오다 = come (here) to study, from the host's view

examples.en: I'm going to Japan to study abroad.
examples.note: 으로 marks the direction; 유학(을) 가다 is the fixed phrase

examples.en: My older sister went to America to study abroad.
examples.note: past 갔어요; the destination takes 으로/로

examples.ko: 몇 년 동안 유학을 다녀와서 한국어가 정말 유창해요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon dongan yuhageul danyeowaseo hangugeoga jeongmal yuchanghaeyo.
examples.en: Having spent a few years studying abroad, her Korean is really fluent.
examples.note: real life: 다녀오다 = 'go and come back', 유창하다 = fluent

extendedVocab.nuance: 유학 means going abroad to study, usually for a degree or a long course, written 留學 (留 'to stay, remain' + 學 'study'), literally 'to remain (somewhere) and study' — note the 留 'stay', which signals it's a sustained stay, not a quick visit. That 留 distinguishes it from 여행 (旅行 'travel'), a trip for leisure: you go on 여행 for a week but go on 유학 for years. It pairs with directional verbs and the destination particle 으로/로: 유학을 가다 (go away to study), 유학을 오다 (come to study, from the host country's angle), 유학을 다녀오다 (go and return). It can also be a verb: 미국에서 유학하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 여행 for academic study abroad, and marking the country with 에 instead of 으로/로 (일본에 유학을 가요 sounds off; say 일본으로 유학을 가요).

Using 여행 (a trip) for academic study abroad; a degree-length stay is 유학, e.g. 유학을 가다.
Saying 일본에 유학을 가요; the directional particle for a destination here is 으로/로: 일본으로 유학을 가요.
Saying 유학에 가요 instead of the set phrase; it's 유학을 가다 (or just 유학 가다), with 을 on 유학.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 얼굴 means "face" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 얼굴 (eolgul) = "face". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 얼굴이 예뻐요 ("the face is pretty") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 얼굴, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: describing looks; subject particle 이
빨갛다, a ㅎ-irregular, drops ㅎ before -아요
씻다 for water-washing, object particle 을
붓다 ㅅ-irregular → 부었어요 in past

examples.en: My older sister's face is really pretty.
examples.note: describing looks; possessive 언니 얼굴 needs no 의 in speech

examples.en: I get up in the morning and wash my face.
examples.note: note the verb 씻다, never 감다, takes the object 얼굴을

examples.en: I got so embarrassed that my face turned red.
examples.note: 빨개지다 = turn red; 이/가 marks the body part that changes

extendedVocab.nuance: 얼굴 is the whole human face — both its looks and its surface you wash — and is the everyday word with no formality issue; you use it equally with friends and elders. Its near-synonym 낯 (as in 낯이 익다 'the face looks familiar', 낯설다 'unfamiliar') is old-fashioned and survives mostly in set idioms, so for plain 'face' always reach for 얼굴. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers. First, hair on the head is 감다 (감다 = wash hair) but the FACE is 씻다, the same verb as for hands and dishes — never say 얼굴을 감다. Second, English 'big face' does not transfer: a flattering 'small face' is 얼굴이 작다 (a real Korean compliment about proportion), and you do not say 얼굴이 커요 to mean handsome. Color uses 빨갛다 (얼굴이 빨개요), and to feel for fever Koreans touch the 이마, not the whole 얼굴.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 얼굴을 감다 to mean 'wash my face' — 감다 is only for washing HAIR; the face takes 씻다, so it must be 얼굴을 씻어요.
Translating 'pretty face' as 얼굴이 이뻐다 with wrong spelling; the standard adjective is 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before -어요).
Using 얼굴이 커요 expecting it to sound flattering — in Korean a large face is unflattering; the compliment is 얼굴이 작다, 'small-faced'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 머리카락 means "hair strands" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 머리카락 (meorikarak) means "hair strands". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리카락이 길어요 ("the hair is long"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 머리카락 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 길다 describes length; 이 marks the subject
빠지다 = shed/fall out, intransitive, takes 이/가
자르다 르-irregular → 잘라요, object 을
까맣다 ㅎ-irregular → 까매요

examples.en: My hair is too long.
examples.note: describing length; 이 marks the strand as subject of 길다

examples.en: Lately a lot of my hair is falling out.
examples.note: 빠지다 is intransitive — the hair falls by itself, so use 이/가, not 을

examples.en: I got my hair cut short at the salon.
examples.note: 자르다 takes the object 을; 짧게 'short' is the adverb form of 짧다

extendedVocab.nuance: 머리카락 names the individual strands or the mass of hair as material, whereas 머리 is a slippery word that means both the head and, loosely, the hair growing on it. The dividing line: when you must be unambiguous that you mean the hair itself — counting it, shedding it, a strand on your food — choose 머리카락; for a haircut or hairstyle, casual 머리 is actually more common (머리 잘랐어 'I got a haircut'). One strand is 머리카락 한 올 (the counter 올 is for thread-like things). English speakers stumble two ways. First, English 'hair' is uncountable, but Korean lets you count strands, so 'a hair fell out' is 머리카락 한 올이 빠졌어요, not a plural. Second, hair falling out is 빠지다 (intransitive) — the hair leaves on its own — so it is 머리카락이 빠지다 with 이/가; learners wrongly force the object 을. And cutting is 자르다; 머리카락을 잘랐어요 means a trim, not amputation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 머리카락을 빠져요 with the object particle — 빠지다 is intransitive (the hair sheds itself), so it must be 머리카락이 빠져요.
Treating 머리 and 머리카락 as fully interchangeable; you cannot say 머리가 한 올 빠졌어요 for a single strand — counting strands needs 머리카락 한 올.
Mispronouncing/misspelling the verb as 자라요 (grow) when you mean 잘라요 (cut); 자르다 is a 르-irregular, so 'cut' becomes 잘라요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이마 means "forehead" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "forehead" is 이마 (ima). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이마가 넓어요 ("the forehead is wide"). Watch the particle attached to 이마 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 넓다 'wide/broad', not 크다; 이 marks the subject
뜨겁다 ㅂ-irregular → 뜨거워요, a fever sign
짚다 = press-check for fever, object 를
부딪히다 = get bumped, takes 를

examples.en: My forehead is a bit wide.
examples.note: 넓다 describes a broad surface — never 크다 for a forehead

examples.en: I have a fever so my forehead is hot.
examples.note: 뜨겁다 → 뜨거워요 (ㅂ-irregular); 나다 collocates with 열 for 'a fever comes'

examples.en: My mom felt my forehead to check.
examples.note: 짚다 is the precise verb for laying a hand to check temperature; 를 marks the spot

extendedVocab.nuance: 이마 is the forehead, the flat span above the eyebrows, and culturally it is the spot Koreans touch first to check a fever — so it collocates constantly with 열이 나다 ('a fever comes') and 뜨겁다 ('hot'). Two register-neutral verbs matter: to lay a palm on it to gauge temperature is 짚다 (이마를 짚다), and a wide forehead is 이마가 넓다. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is dimension: a forehead has area, not bulk, so 'a big forehead' must be 이마가 넓다 ('wide'), never 이마가 커요 ('big'), which sounds odd and almost comical to Koreans. A second trap is the fever verb — English 'I have a fever' becomes 열이 나다 (literally 'heat comes out'), so you say 열이 나서 이마가 뜨거워요, not the direct 열을 가지다. Note 뜨겁다 is ㅂ-irregular, giving 뜨거워요, and to feel hot to the touch you generally use 뜨겁다 for objects/skin, while 덥다 is for the weather/air.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이마가 커요 for a large forehead — area is described with 넓다, so the natural phrase is 이마가 넓어요.
Translating 'I have a fever' as 열을 가지고 있어요; Korean says 열이 나다, e.g. 열이 나서 이마가 뜨거워요.
Using 덥다 for a hot forehead — 덥다 is for ambient heat (weather); skin/objects that are hot to the touch take 뜨겁다, so 이마가 뜨거워요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 볼 means "cheek" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 볼 (bol) = "cheek". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 볼이 빨개요 ("my cheeks are red") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 볼, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 빨갛다 ㅎ-irregular → 빨개요; 이 marks the subject
통통하다 = plump (cute), gentle nuance
꼬집다 = pinch affectionately, object 을
뽀뽀하다 + location 에 for a peck

examples.en: The baby's cheeks are chubby.
examples.note: 통통하다 carries a warm, cute tone reserved for plumpness, not fat

examples.en: It was cold outside so my cheeks turned red.
examples.note: 빨개지다 'turn red'; cold weather reddens cheeks — a very common collocation

examples.en: Grandma gently pinched her grandchild's cheek.
examples.note: 꼬집다 = an affectionate pinch; 볼 (not 뺨) keeps it warm and loving

extendedVocab.nuance: 볼 is the soft, fleshy cheek and carries an inherently warm, tender tone — it is the word for chubby baby cheeks (볼이 통통하다), cold-reddened cheeks (볼이 빨개지다), and affectionate pinches (볼을 꼬집다). Its near-synonym 뺨 also means cheek but anatomically/coldly and, crucially, collocates with violence: 뺨을 때리다 / 뺨을 맞다 is 'to slap / be slapped across the face'. So the dividing line is emotional temperature: 볼 is gentle and intimate, 뺨 is clinical or harsh. For everyday loving or descriptive talk always pick 볼. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 뺨 as a neutral dictionary 'cheek' and accidentally importing the slapping connotation; a sentence like 아기 뺨이 통통해요 sounds jarring because 뺨 clashes with the cuteness. Also note color is 빨갛다 (볼이 빨개요), the ㅎ-irregular dropping ㅎ before -아요, and a kiss on the cheek attaches with location 에: 볼에 뽀뽀하다.

Using 뺨 as a neutral word for 'cheek' in affectionate contexts — 뺨 leans clinical and is tied to slapping (뺨을 때리다); for warm, everyday cheeks use 볼.
Writing 볼이 빨갛아요 — 빨갛다 is ㅎ-irregular, so before -아요 the ㅎ drops and the vowel contracts to 빨개요.
Attaching the wrong particle for a cheek kiss: it is 볼에 뽀뽀하다 (location 에), not 볼을 뽀뽀하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 턱 means "chin; jaw" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 턱 (teok) means "chin; jaw". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 턱이 아파요 ("my jaw hurts"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 턱 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
뾰족하다 = sharp/pointed shape

usagePhrases.en: I rest my chin (on my hand)
usagePhrases.note: 괴다 = prop up, object 을

usagePhrases.en: my jaw came out of joint
usagePhrases.note: 빠지다 here = get dislocated

examples.en: I chewed squid too much so my jaw hurts.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요 (ㅡ drops); jaw pain from chewing is 턱이 아프다

examples.ko: 손으로 턱을 괴고 멍하니 앉아 있었어요.
examples.romanization: soneuro teogeul goego meonghani anja isseosseoyo.
examples.en: I sat blankly resting my chin on my hand.
examples.note: 괴다 takes the object 턱을; this is the set pose 턱을 괴다

examples.en: That model has a pointy chin.
examples.note: 뾰족하다 describes a sharp V-line chin, a common beauty descriptor

extendedVocab.nuance: 턱 covers both the chin (the point of the lower face) and the jaw (the hinge), and context alone tells them apart — there is no separate everyday word for each, so 턱이 아프다 from chewing means the JAW, while 턱이 뾰족하다 describes the CHIN's shape. Key collocations: resting your chin on your hand is the fixed phrase 턱을 괴다 (괴다 = to prop), a sharp chin is 턱이 뾰족하다, and a dislocated jaw is 턱이 빠지다 (where 빠지다 means 'slip out of joint', the same verb used playfully in 턱이 빠지게 웃다 'to laugh one's jaw off'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting two distinct nouns and over-specifying — you do not need 'jawbone' vocabulary for daily life; 턱 does both jobs. A second trap is the verb for resting the chin: it is 괴다, not 놓다 or 대다, so 'I rest my chin on my hand' is 턱을 괴다. Note 아프다 is a ㅡ-stem (턱이 아파요), and the jaw 'coming out' uses intransitive 빠지다 with 이/가.

Assuming 턱 means only 'chin' and hunting for a separate 'jaw' word — 턱 covers both; 턱이 아파요 from chewing naturally means the jaw.
Saying 턱을 손에 놓다 / 대다 for resting the chin on a hand — the idiomatic verb is 괴다, so it is 턱을 괴다.
Using 턱을 빠졌어요 (object 을) for a dislocated jaw — 빠지다 is intransitive, so the jaw is the subject: 턱이 빠졌어요.
