extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 입금 means "deposit, paying money in" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 입금 (ipgeum) means "deposit, paying money in". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 입금하다 ("to deposit / pay money in"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 입금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 입금 + 하다; you 입금하다 into an account marked with 에
확인 (確認) — sellers ask for this to verify the money landed
무 (無) = without; paying into an account via ATM with no book

usagePhrases.en: for a deposit to go through
usagePhrases.note: 되다 is intransitive — money arrives on its own (입금됐어요)

examples.en: I just made the deposit.
examples.note: 방금 (just now) + the past tense is the quick 'it's done' line

examples.ko: 돈 보냈는데 입금 확인 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: don bonaenneunde ipgeum hwagin jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: I sent the money, so please confirm the deposit.
examples.note: exact phrase buyers say to sellers in online deals

examples.ko: 보증금은 계약하는 날 집주인 계좌로 입금하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: bojeunggeumeun gyeyakaneun nal jipjuin gyejwaro ipgeumhamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can pay the deposit into the landlord's account on the day you sign.
examples.note: real housing situation; 계좌로 입금하다 + ~면 되다 ('it's fine to')

extendedVocab.nuance: 입금 (入金, literally 'enter-money') is money going INTO an account, the exact opposite of 출금 (出金, 'exit-money') — picture the 入 character as funds stepping in. It takes 하다 when you do it, but note the key voice split: 입금하다 is what YOU actively do, while 입금되다 (intransitive) is what happens when money arrives on its own. Sellers and landlords constantly request 입금 확인 to verify your payment landed, and 무통장 입금 ('passbook-less deposit') is the normal ATM phrase for paying into someone's account. Collocations: 입금 확인, 무통장 입금, 보증금 입금. The English-speaker pitfall is direction (입금 in vs 출금 out) and, above all, saying 입금받다 — for money simply arriving the natural form is 입금되다 (입금됐어요), reserving 받다 for receiving a physical thing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reversing 입금 (money in) and 출금 (money out) — the 入 vs 出 hanja mark the direction.
Saying 입금받다 for money arriving; the natural intransitive is 입금되다 (입금됐어요).
Marking the account with 한테; an account takes 에/(으)로 — 계좌로 입금하다, not 계좌한테.

extendedVocab.explanation: "withdrawal, taking money out" is 출금 (chulgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 출금하다 ("to withdraw money"). 현금 (現金) = cash; the most common reason to 출금

usagePhrases.en: for a withdrawal to be blocked
usagePhrases.note: 안 되다 covers limits, fraud holds, or low balance

examples.en: I withdrew 50,000 won from the ATM.

extendedVocab.nuance: 출금 (出金, literally 'exit-money') is taking money OUT of an account, the natural pair to 입금 (入金, 'enter-money') — the 出 character even pictures funds leaving. It takes 하다, and the source account is marked with 에서 (통장에서 출금하다). It headlines every ATM screen and app menu. produce sold tied in a bundle is counted with 단, never 개

extendedVocab.nuance: 대파 is the thick, long, white-and-green scallion that anchors almost every Korean soup, stew, and stir-fry — the 대 means 'large', distinguishing it from the slim 쪽파 (small bunching onion) and the round-bulb 양파 (onion). English speakers reach for 'green onion' and assume one word covers all of them, but at a Korean market 대파, 쪽파, 양파, and 마늘쫑 are four different products in four different spots. The single biggest pitfall is the counter: 대파 is bundled and sold by the 단 (bunch), so '대파 한 단' is natural while '대파 한 개' sounds like you are pointing at one lonely stalk. It pairs habitually with 썰다/넣다 and especially the mimetic 송송 썰다 for chopping it into little rings dropped on top of a dish.

Saying 대파 한 개 — produce tied in a bundle takes 단, so it should be 대파 한 단; 개 makes it sound like a single odd stalk.
Using 대파 when you mean the round onion 양파 — they are different vegetables, and a 직역 of English 'onion' will not tell them apart.
Mixing up 대파 with the thin 쪽파; 쪽파 is for 파전/garnish, while 대파 is the workhorse for soups and stir-fries.

extendedVocab.nuance: 고춧가루 is the dried, ground red-chili powder that gives Korean food its signature red color and heat — literally 고추(chili) + 가루(powder). Do not confuse it with 고추장, the fermented red-chili paste: 가루 is dry and dusty, 장 is a thick sticky paste, and they are not interchangeable in a recipe. Compared with Western cayenne it is coarser and milder by volume, so Korean recipes pour it in by the 스푼. It collocates with 넣다 (stir in) and 뿌리다 (sprinkle on top), and its heat is described with 맵다.

Confusing 고춧가루 (dry powder) with 고추장 (thick fermented paste); they behave completely differently in cooking.
Pluralizing or counting it like a countable thing (고춧가루 한 개) — it is a powder, measured with 스푼/그램, e.g. 고춧가루 한 스푼.

usagePhrases.note: 두르다 = coat a pan by swirling oil around it
떨어지다 = run out / be used up (stock is gone)
에 marks the medium you fry IN

examples.en: Coat the pan with cooking oil.
examples.note: simple instruction; 두르다, not 넣다, for greasing a pan

examples.ko: 식용유가 다 떨어져서 사러 가야 해요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 식용유 is the everyday neutral frying oil (usually soybean or canola) — a Sino-Korean compound 食用油 meaning 'food-use oil', i.e. oil fit for eating, as opposed to industrial oil. The crucial contrast is with the aromatic finishing oils 참기름 (sesame) and 들기름 (perilla): 식용유 is the bland workhorse you cook IN, while 참기름/들기름 are fragrant seasonings you add at the END for flavor — never deep-fry in them. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb. In English you 'put oil in the pan', but Korean uses 두르다 (swirl/coat around) for greasing a pan: '식용유를 두르다' is natural, whereas '식용유를 넣다' sounds like you are pouring it into a soup. It collocates with 두르다 (coat), 튀기다 (deep-fry), and is counted by the 병.

Using 식용유 when you mean a flavoring oil like 참기름 — 식용유 is for cooking IN, not for the nutty finishing aroma.
Saying 식용유를 넣다 to mean greasing a pan — the idiomatic verb is 두르다 (swirl it around), so 식용유를 두르다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 들기름 is perilla-seed oil — 들(perilla/wild) + 기름(oil) — with a bold, nutty, earthy aroma that defines many 나물 (seasoned greens) and is brushed on 김 (laver). Its constant counterpart is 참기름, sesame oil (참 = 'true/genuine'): both are fragrant finishing oils, but 참기름 is lighter, sweeter, more universal, while 들기름 is heavier, grassier, and more regional/seasonal — a Korean cook chooses between them deliberately. Storing 들기름 at room temperature; it goes rancid quickly, so it should be refrigerated (냉장 보관).

extendedVocab.nuance: 깨소금 is toasted sesame seeds ground with a little salt — 깨(sesame) + 소금(salt) — used as a finishing seasoning scattered over 나물, 무침, and other 반찬. The flavor it gives is described by the very Korean word 고소하다 (toasty, nutty, oily-rich), a taste that has no neat English match; it is NOT 'savory' (감칠맛) and not 'salty' (짜다). Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, the name says 소금(salt), so learners assume it is mostly salt, but it is mostly sesame — its job is aroma, not saltiness. Second, timing: 깨소금 is a finishing touch added at the very end (마지막에), because grinding and heat dull the toasty smell. Note that in casual kitchen talk many Koreans also loosely call plain toasted whole sesame seeds 깨소금. It collocates with 뿌리다 and the mimetic 솔솔.

Assuming 깨소금 is basically salt because of the 소금 in the name — it is mostly toasted sesame; the point is aroma, not saltiness.
Adding it early in cooking; 깨소금 is a finishing garnish (마지막에 뿌리다), since heat kills the toasty 고소함.
Translating its taste as 'savory'; the right word is 고소하다 (nutty/toasty), which is distinct from 감칠맛 (umami-savory).

extendedVocab.nuance: 생강 is fresh ginger root, prized in Korean kitchens for killing the 비린내 (fishy/gamey smell) of meat and fish and for brewing 생강차 against colds. Its kick is best described by 알싸하다 (a sharp, tingling pungency) rather than 맵다 — 맵다 is the chili-heat of 고추, while ginger's bite is a different, almost numbing sharpness, so saying 생강이 매워요 sounds slightly off to natives. Because the flavor is so strong, recipes almost always pair it with 조금/조금만 (just a little) and the verb 다지다 (mince). It is usually peeled and minced, not sliced thick.

Describing ginger as 매워요 (chili-spicy); its sharp tingle is 알싸하다, a different sensation from 고추 heat.
Swapping 생강 (ginger) and 마늘 (garlic) when reading a marinade — they appear together (생강·마늘) but are different roots.
Adding too much because the flavor seems mild raw; recipes call for 조금만, as 생강 quickly overpowers a dish.

extendedVocab.nuance: 다시마 is dried kelp, the backbone of Korean soup stock, almost always steeped together with 멸치 (dried anchovies) to build 육수. Do not confuse it with 미역, the other common seaweed: 다시마 is thick, leathery, and used to MAKE broth (then removed), whereas 미역 is thin, slippery, and EATEN in 미역국 (birthday/postpartum seaweed soup). The make-or-break tip — and the spot beginners ruin broth — is timing: pull the 다시마 out right before the water boils (끓기 전에 건지다); boil it too long and the broth turns slimy, cloudy, and bitter. It is counted by the flat 장 (sheet), and collocates with 우리다 (steep), 건지다 (scoop out), and 국물/육수 (broth). The 'good broth' compliment that results is 시원하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 다시마 (kelp, for making broth) with 미역 (wakame, eaten in 미역국) — different seaweeds with different jobs.
Letting 다시마 boil; you should 건지다 it right before boiling (끓기 전에), or the broth becomes slimy and bitter.
Counting it with 개; flat sheets of kelp take 장, so 다시마 한 장.

extendedVocab.nuance: 육수 is the savory simmered stock at the base of soups, stews, and noodle dishes — Sino-Korean 肉水, literally 'meat-water', though in practice it is just as often drawn from 멸치 and 다시마, not only bones. The key contrast for learners is 육수 vs 국물: 육수 is the prepared stock you make on purpose as a base, while 국물 is simply 'the liquid in a dish' as served (the 국물 of your ramen, the 국물 of the kimchi). So you 육수를 내다 in advance, then ladle 국물 at the table. Two pitfalls: the 肉 character tempts English speakers to assume 육수 is always meat stock — it isn't. And the idiomatic verb is 내다/우리다 ('produce/steep' broth), not 만들다, so '육수를 내다' is what a cook says. Koreans judge a soup mainly by its 육수, praising it as 진하다 (rich) or 시원하다 (clean).

Treating 육수 and 국물 as the same word — 육수 is the stock you prepare as a base; 국물 is the liquid already in a finished dish.
Assuming 육수 must be meat stock because of 肉(육) — it is frequently anchovy/kelp stock; the word covers all simmered stocks.
Saying 육수를 만들다; the natural collocation is 육수를 내다 (or 우리다), the set verb for producing stock.

extendedVocab.nuance: 두부 is tofu, sold in firm pressed blocks counted with the special unit 모 ('두부 한 모', never 한 개). The contrast to internalize is 두부 vs 순두부: regular 두부 is firm enough to slice and pan-fry, while 순두부 ('pure/silken tofu') is barely-set custard eaten with a spoon in 순두부찌개 — calling silken tofu plain 두부 will confuse a Korean cook. Counting 두부 with 개 — a block of tofu takes the counter 모, so 두부 한 모.
Calling silken tofu 두부; the spoonable kind is 순두부, and mixing them up changes the dish entirely.

extendedVocab.nuance: 콩나물 are soybean sprouts — 콩(soybean) + 나물(edible greens) — the long ones with a yellow bean head, a dirt-cheap staple behind the side dish 콩나물무침 and the hangover soup 콩나물국. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, lumping both under 'bean sprouts' and grabbing the wrong one. Second, cooking time — the whole point is the 아삭한 (crunchy) texture, so you 살짝 삶다 (boil briefly); overboil and they go mushy (물러지다) and develop a beany 비린내. commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 콩나물 (soybean sprouts) with 숙주 (mung-bean sprouts) — different beans, different dishes; recipes name a specific one.
Overboiling them; the goal is 아삭함 (crunch), so 살짝 삶다, or they turn mushy (물러지다) and smell off.

extendedVocab.nuance: 노릇노릇 is a 의태어 (mimetic word) for the appetizing golden-brown surface of food fried, grilled, or toasted just right — built by reduplicating 노릇 from the color root 노랗다 (yellow). Unlike a neutral color word, it carries a built-in 'cooked to perfection, looks delicious' judgment, so it is almost always positive; its opposite outcome is 타다 (to burn), and you would never call burnt food 노릇노릇. It attaches to cooking verbs in two shapes — bare 노릇노릇 or the adverb 노릇노릇하게 — typically with 굽다, 부치다, 튀기다, 익다, and pairs naturally with texture mimetics like 바삭바삭 (crispy). The English-speaker pitfalls: spell it 노릇노릇 (not 노룻노룻), and don't stretch it to mean simply 'yellow' — 노릇노릇 is specifically the cooked golden of a surface, not the color of a lemon or a shirt.

Spelling it 노룻노룻 — the correct mimetic is 노릇노릇, tied to 노랗다.

usagePhrases.note: the default verb is 하다; spoken 요가하다 is fine, but never 운동하다
수업 = a class/lesson; 요가 클래스 (loanword) is interchangeable at studios
매트 is the fixed loanword for the mat; 깔개 (a Korean word for 'mat') is wrong here
-원(院) marks a small academy/clinic; same suffix as 학원, 병원

examples.en: I like yoga.
examples.note: the simplest frame: noun + 를 + 좋아하다, treating 요가 as a plain object

examples.ko: 저는 일주일에 두 번 요가를 해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun iljuire du beon yogareul haeyo.
examples.en: I do yoga twice a week.
examples.note: 일주일에 N 번 = N times per week; 에 marks the time-span the count happens within

examples.ko: 회사 근처에 요가원이 새로 생겼길래 등록했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesa geuncheoe yogawoni saero saenggyeotgillae deungnokaesseoyo.
examples.en: A yoga studio newly opened near my office, so I signed up.
examples.note: 생기다 = (a place) comes into being/opens; -길래 = 'since (I noticed)', a casual reason

The reflex error is treating it like exercise and saying 요가 운동을 하다 — that doubles 'exercise/do', so just use 요가를 하다 or, colloquially, 요가하다. Compare it with 스트레칭 (stretching): 요가 is a whole disciplined practice with poses (동작/자세) and breathing, while 스트레칭 is just loosening muscles, so they are not swappable. A studio is a 요가원 or 요가 스튜디오 — never 요가집, because the homey suffix -집 is for eateries and shops, not for a class venue. One session is a 요가 수업 / 요가 클래스, and the gear is a 요가 매트.

요가 운동을 해요. → 요가를 해요.

Drop 운동: 요가를 해요 / 요가해요.
요가집에 다녀요. → 요가원에 다녀요.
The suffix -집 means a shop or eatery (e.g. 빵집, 고깃집), so 요가집 sounds wrong for a class venue; studios use the academy suffix -원.
Use 요가원 or 요가 스튜디오.

기구(器具) = apparatus; contrasts with 매트 필라테스 done on a mat
등록하다(登錄) = to register; classes are sold as prepaid packages

examples.en: I do Pilates.
examples.note: the basic frame, naming the activity with the all-purpose verb 하다

examples.en: I'm doing Pilates these days to fix my posture.
examples.note: 다니다 = to attend regularly; -(으)려고 = 'in order to', stating your goal

examples.en: I bought a 10-session pass but I've already used it all.
examples.note: N회권(回券) = an N-session ticket; 끊다 = to buy (a ticketed pass), not 사다

The big learner trap is contrasting it with 요가: people will ask 매트(예요), 기구(예요)? — 매트 필라테스 is floor work, 기구 필라테스 uses the reformer machine, and 필라테스 generally targets core strength and posture (자세) whereas 요가 emphasizes flexibility and breathing, so don't call one the other. Say 회권(을) 끊다.
필테스를 해요. → 필라테스를 해요.
The correct transliteration keeps 라: 필라테스. Dropping it (필테스) or adding a vowel (파일라테스) are common spelling slips.
Spell it 필라테스, abbreviate 필테.

extendedVocab.explanation: 클라이밍 (keullaiming) = "(rock/sport) climbing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 클라이밍을 하다 ("to go climbing") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 클라이밍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: verb 하다; 클라이밍(을) 가다 ('go climbing') is just as common
실내(室內) = indoors; almost all city climbing is at indoor gyms
the short-wall, no-rope style most 20-30s actually do
-장(場) marks a sports venue/ground; cf. 운동장, 수영장

examples.en: I do climbing.
examples.note: the plain frame; 클라이밍 takes 하다 as its activity verb

examples.en: I go climbing with a friend every weekend.
examples.note: N마다 = every N; V-(으)러 가다 = go for the purpose of doing

examples.en: Is there somewhere that rents out climbing shoes at the gym?
examples.note: 암벽화(巖壁靴) = climbing shoes; 빌려주다 = to lend out (vs 빌리다 = to borrow)

extendedVocab.nuance: 클라이밍 is the English loanword 'climbing'; keep all four syllables — 클라밍 (dropping 이) is a frequent misspelling. The crucial distinction for an English speaker is 클라이밍 vs 등산(登山): 등산 is hiking/ascending an actual mountain on trails, while 클라이밍 is sport climbing up walls or rock faces — Koreans never mix them, so 'I went climbing this weekend' on a hiking trail should be 등산했어요. The trendy gym style is 볼더링 (bouldering: low walls, no rope, just 매트 below), done at an indoor 클라이밍장. Counter vocabulary that helps: 암벽화 (climbing shoes, which you can 빌리다) and 초크 (grip chalk). Beginners always confess 손에 힘이 없다 ('no grip strength').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
주말에 클라이밍 갔어요. (meaning a mountain hike) → 주말에 등산 갔어요.
등산 is trail hiking up a mountain; 클라이밍 is technical wall/rock climbing. Using 클라이밍 for a casual mountain walk misdescribes the activity.
Hiking a mountain = 등산; wall/rock climbing = 클라이밍.
클라밍을 해요. → 클라이밍을 해요.
The word transliterates 'climbing' with the 이 kept: 클라이밍. Omitting it is a spelling error.
Keep all syllables: 클라이밍.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 볼링 means "bowling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 볼링 (bolling) means "bowling". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 볼링을 치다 ("to bowl"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 볼링 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: use 치다 ('to strike'), the verb for ball/cue/racket games, not 하다
-장(場) = venue; a classic group hangout, often with 당구장 nearby
게임 is the counter for a round; you pay per 게임
-화(靴) = shoes (Sino-Korean); rent these at the counter

examples.en: I'm not very good at bowling.
examples.note: the simple frame; note 치다 as the verb and 못 + verb = 'can't (do well)'

examples.en: Want to go bowling later today?
examples.note: 이따가 = later (within today); -(으)ㄹ래? = casual 'shall we / want to?'

examples.en: How much is one game of bowling?
examples.note: N에 얼마예요? = how much per N; 에 distributes the price over each unit

extendedVocab.nuance: 볼링 is the loanword 'bowling', but the verb is the native 치다 ('to strike/hit'), shared with 당구를 치다, 테니스를 치다 and other implement-and-ball sports — saying 볼링을 하다 marks you as a foreigner. The mental model is: anything you strike with a hand/cue/racket takes 치다, whereas sports you run/play take 하다 (축구를 하다). A 볼링장 (-장 = venue) is a staple group outing and a softer alternative to a drinking 회식. You pay by the 게임 (the counter for a round), and you must swap into rented 볼링화 — the suffix -화(靴) is the Sino-Korean for 'footwear', the same one in 운동화 (sneakers) and 등산화 (hiking boots).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
볼링을 해요. → 볼링을 쳐요.
Implement-and-ball games collocate with 치다 ('strike'); 하다 is the generic 'do' and sounds unnatural for bowling.
Use 볼링을 치다.
운동화 신고 쳐도 돼요? → 볼링화로 갈아 신어야 해요.
Street/athletic shoes (운동화) damage and aren't allowed on the lane; you must change into rented 볼링화.
Rent and wear 볼링화 on the lane.

usagePhrases.note: verb 치다 ('strike'), like other cue/ball games; never 하다
-장(場) = venue; cheap and often open late into the night
the pocketed version; plain 당구 usually means pocketless carom
시간당(時間當) = per hour; the loser often covers the fee

examples.en: I can't play billiards.
examples.note: the basic frame; 못 쳐요 = 'can't play (well)', with the proper verb 치다

examples.en: I went to play billiards with friends.
examples.note: N(이)랑 = casual 'with'; V-(으)러 가다 = go in order to do

examples.en: Billiard halls usually charge by the hour.

extendedVocab.nuance: 당구(撞球) is Sino-Korean — 撞 'to strike' + 球 'ball', literally 'strike-ball' — and like other cue sports it takes the verb 치다, not 하다. 당구를 해요. → 당구를 쳐요.
Cue games collocate with 치다 ('strike'); 하다 is wrong for 당구 just as it is for 볼링.
Use 당구를 치다.
당구 = pool with pockets (assumed). → 포켓볼 for the pocketed game.
Plain 당구 in Korea defaults to pocketless carom (사구/쓰리쿠션); calling the six-pocket game 당구 without specifying confuses Koreans.
Say 포켓볼 when you mean pocket pool.

extendedVocab.explanation: 보드게임 (bodeugeim) = "board game". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보드게임을 하다 ("to play a board game") shows how it actually behaves. a pay-by-time cafe stocked with games; locals shorten it to 보드카페
룰 = rules (loanword); staff often explain the game for you
N이서 = '(as a group) of N'; 둘이서, 셋이서, 넷이서 …

examples.en: I like board games.
examples.note: the simple frame; 보드게임 is a plain object of 좋아하다

examples.en: The rules of this board game are a bit complicated.
examples.note: 복잡하다(複雜) = complicated, the descriptive verb here; 좀 softens the complaint

examples.ko: 넷이서 할 수 있는 보드게임 추천해 주세요.
examples.romanization: nesiseo hal su inneun bodeugeim chucheonhae juseyo.
examples.en: Please recommend a board game four people can play.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ 수 있는 = that can be done; 추천하다(推薦) = to recommend

Don't confuse the game with its parts: the physical board is a 게임판, while 보드게임 names the whole game, and 보드 alone can also mean a snowboard/skateboard, so keep the full 보드게임.

보드게임을 봐요. → 보드게임을 해요.

Use 보드게임을 하다.
우리 보드 하자. → 우리 보드게임 하자.
Bare 보드 is ambiguous (it can mean a snowboard/skateboard); say the full 보드게임 for the tabletop game.
Keep the full word 보드게임.

extendedVocab.explanation: 방탈출 (bangtalchul) means "escape room". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 방탈출을 하다 ("to do an escape room"). examples.en: I like escape rooms.
examples.note: the basic frame; 방탈출 as a plain object of 좋아하다

examples.ko: 우리 이번 주말에 방탈출 하러 갈까?
examples.romanization: uri ibeon jumare bangtalchul hareo galkka?
examples.en: Shall we go do an escape room this weekend?
examples.note: V-(으)러 가다 = go to do; -(으)ㄹ까? = soft 'shall we?' to a friend

examples.ko: 이 테마 너무 어려워서 결국 탈출 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: i tema neomu eoryeowoseo gyeolguk talchul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: This room was so hard we couldn't escape in the end.
examples.note: 결국(結局) = in the end; 탈출(脫出)하다 = to escape; -아서 gives the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 방탈출 is a transparent compound: 방 'room' + 탈출(脫出) 'escape/break-out' (脫 'shed/escape' + 出 'go out'), i.e. 'room escape'. Write it solid as 방탈출 (the set activity noun), not 방 탈출 with a space, and it's commonly clipped to 방탈. The verb is 하다 — the pitfall is English 'do an escape room' vs the false friend 보다: you never 방탈출을 보다 ('watch'), you 하다 (participate in) it. Inside, each scenario is a 테마 you book ahead; you can request a 힌트 when stuck, and the scary ones are 공포 테마. Don't confuse the noun 탈출 (the act of escaping, used in 탈출하다) with the venue word 방탈출 (the game itself). A staple group outing for young adults.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
방탈출을 봤어요. → 방탈출을 했어요.
It's a participatory game: you 하다 (do) it. 보다 ('watch') treats it like a show, which is wrong.
Use 방탈출을 하다.
방 탈출 하러 가자. → 방탈출 하러 가자.
As the name of the activity it is one set word, 방탈출 (or clipped 방탈); inserting a space reads as the literal phrase 'escape the room'.
Write it solid: 방탈출.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뮤지컬 means "musical (theater)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "musical (theater)" is 뮤지컬 (myujikeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 뮤지컬을 보다 ("to see a musical"). Watch the particle attached to 뮤지컬 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: performances take 보다 ('see/watch'), not 하다
공연(公演) = a live performance/show
예매(豫買) = advance ticket purchase, distinct from 예약 (reservation)
배우(俳優) = actor; fans choose shows by which performer is cast

examples.en: I like musicals.
examples.note: the simplest frame; 뮤지컬 as object of 좋아하다

examples.en: I saw a musical in Daehangno.
examples.note: 대학로 = Seoul's theater district; 편(編) is the counter for a work/show

examples.en: Weekend shows sell out fast.
examples.note: 매진(賣盡)되다 = to sell out (lit. 'selling exhausted'); 금방 = soon/quickly

extendedVocab.nuance: 뮤지컬 is the loanword 'musical', watched with the verb 보다 ('see'), like 영화를 보다 or 공연을 보다 — never 하다 unless you mean performing in it. The sharp contrast to learn is 뮤지컬 vs 연극(演劇): 연극 is a straight (spoken) play, while a 뮤지컬 is sung-through with songs and dance, so don't translate English 'play/theater' as 뮤지컬 by default. Korea has a huge scene centered on 대학로 (Daehangno) and big theaters, and fans pick shows by the 뮤지컬 배우 in the cast. The ticketing pitfall: use 예매하다 — 豫 'in advance' + 買 'buy' — for buying show tickets, NOT 예약하다 (豫約 'reserve'), which is for tables and rooms. Hot dates 매진되다 (sell out) quickly.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
뮤지컬을 예약했어요. → 뮤지컬을 예매했어요.
Tickets you buy in advance use 예매(豫買, 'pre-buy'); 예약(豫約, 'reserve') is for restaurants/hotels, not performance tickets.
Use 예매하다 for show tickets.
연극이랑 뮤지컬은 같은 거예요. → 뮤지컬은 노래로 하는 공연이에요.
연극 is a spoken play; a 뮤지컬 is sung-through with music and dance. Treating them as identical mislabels the genre.
Distinguish 연극 (play) from 뮤지컬 (musical).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 전시회 means "exhibition (art show)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 전시회 (jeonsihoe) = "exhibition (art show)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전시회에 가다 ("to go to an exhibition") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전시회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the standard outing phrase; 에 marks the destination
verb 보다, like other things you view/watch
-전(展) is the suffix for a themed show, shorter than -전시회
관람료(觀覽料) = viewing fee; many shows are 무료 (free)

examples.en: I see exhibitions often.
examples.note: the basic frame; 전시회 as object of 보다, with 자주 = 'often'

examples.ko: 주말에 친구랑 사진 전시회 보러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jumare chingurang sajin jeonsihoe boreo gasseoyo.
examples.en: I went to see a photo exhibition with a friend on the weekend.
examples.note: V-(으)러 가다 = go in order to see; a popular low-key date

examples.ko: 이 전시회는 무료라서 사람이 엄청 많아요.
examples.romanization: i jeonsihoeneun muryoraseo sarami eomcheong manayo.
examples.en: This exhibition is free, so there are a ton of people.
examples.note: 무료(無料) = free of charge; -라서 = 'because (it is)'; 엄청 = a ton (casual)

extendedVocab.nuance: 전시회 is Sino-Korean — 展示 'display/exhibit' (展 'spread out' + 示 'show') + 會 'gathering/event' — i.e. a (usually temporary) exhibition event you 보러 가다, a go-to casual outing or date for 20-30s, especially as a 사진전 (photo show) or 미술전 (art show), where -전(展) is the compact suffix. The key learner pitfall is 전시회 vs 미술관(美術館): a 전시회 is the *event* (it opens and closes on dates), whereas a 미술관 is the *building/museum* that houses it — don't say 전시회 when you mean the institution. On fees, art shows usually charge a 관람료 ('viewing fee'), not the generic 입장료 ('entry fee') used at amusement parks; look for 무료 shows, and many offer a 도슨트 (docent-guided tour).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
미술관에서 새 전시회가 생겼어요 (meaning the museum). → 전시회 is the event, 미술관 is the building.
전시회 names a temporary show with start/end dates; the permanent venue is a 미술관/갤러리. Swapping them confuses event with place.
Event = 전시회; building = 미술관/갤러리.
전시회 입장료가 얼마예요? → 전시회 관람료가 얼마예요?
For art/photo shows the fee is idiomatically 관람료 ('viewing fee'); 입장료 ('entry fee') fits theme parks and venues, not exhibitions.
Use 관람료 for exhibitions.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 노래방 means "noraebang, karaoke room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 노래방 (noraebang) means "noraebang, karaoke room". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노래방에 가다 ("to go to a karaoke room"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노래방 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to go to a karaoke room
usagePhrases.note: the standard outing phrase; the venue takes 가다
a pay-per-song booth, shortened to 코노; cheap and solo-friendly
곡(曲) = the counter for songs; 부르다 = to sing, not 하다
the free minutes staff add at the end if you ask

examples.en: I like karaoke rooms.
examples.note: the simple frame; the place 노래방 as object of 좋아하다

examples.en: Let's go to karaoke for round two!
examples.note: 2차(次) = the next stop on a night out; 로 marks 노래방 as the chosen next venue

examples.ko: 요즘은 혼자 코노 가서 스트레스 풀어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun honja kono gaseo seuteureseu pureoyo.
examples.en: These days I go to coin karaoke alone to de-stress.
examples.note: 스트레스(를) 풀다 = to relieve stress; 코노 = 코인 노래방

extendedVocab.nuance: 노래방 is a pure Korean compound: 노래 'song' + 방 'room' = 'song room', a private karaoke booth that is core Korean nightlife and the classic 2차 ('second round') after dinner or drinks. The big pitfall is calling it 가라오케 (karaoke): in Korea 가라오케 sounds dated or implies a pricey hostess bar with staff, so the everyday booth you rent with friends is always 노래방, and the cheap solo version is 코인 노래방 (코노). Verb-wise, you don't 하다 a song — you 부르다 ('sing') a 곡, where 곡(曲) is the proper counter (한 곡, 두 곡). A nice extra to know: you can plead 서비스 시간 넣어 주세요 to get free bonus minutes from staff.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
가라오케 가자. → 노래방 가자.
In Korea 가라오케 is dated or refers to a hostess bar; the standard friends'-night booth is a 노래방.
Use 노래방 (or 코노) for the ordinary karaoke room.
노래 한 곡 했어요. → 노래 한 곡 불렀어요.
Songs are sung with 부르다, not done with 하다; 곡 is the counter you pair with 부르다.
Use 노래를 부르다 / 한 곡 부르다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 찜질방 means "jjimjilbang, Korean sauna/spa" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "jjimjilbang, Korean sauna/spa" is 찜질방 (jjimjilbang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 찜질방에 가다 ("to go to a jjimjilbang"). Watch the particle attached to 찜질방 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the standard outing phrase; the venue takes 가다
the matching shirt-and-shorts set they hand you to wear
수면(睡眠) = sleep + 실(室) = room; you can stay overnight in many
the signature snack-bar drink, paired with 삶은 계란 (boiled eggs)

examples.en: I like jjimjilbang.
examples.note: the basic frame; the place as object of 좋아하다

examples.en: I went to a jjimjilbang on the weekend and rested deeply.
examples.note: 푹 쉬다 = to rest fully/deeply, the whole point of going; -아서 chains the two actions

examples.en: Is it okay to sleep at the jjimjilbang all night?
examples.note: 밤새 = all night long; V-아/어도 돼요? = 'is it okay to …?'

extendedVocab.nuance: 찜질방 is a Korean compound: 찜질 'applying heat/a hot compress' + 방 'room' — a 24-hour heated sauna/spa complex where you change into a 찜질복, sweat in heated 한증막 rooms, snack on 식혜 with 삶은 계란, and can even sleep over in a 수면실. The pitfall is treating it as a synonym of 목욕탕(沐浴湯): a 목욕탕 is a plain public bathhouse for washing/soaking in hot tubs, whereas a 찜질방 adds the dry heated 찜질 rooms, communal lounge areas, food, and overnight sleeping — much bigger in scope. Also note 찜질방 (the venue) vs 사우나 (a sauna, which may be just a sweat room inside a 목욕탕 or hotel). A cheap, very Korean way to relax or crash for the night.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
목욕탕에서 찜질하고 잘게요 (expecting a 찜질방). → 찜질방에 갈게요.
A 목욕탕 is a wash-and-soak bathhouse; the heated 찜질 rooms, lounge, food and overnight sleeping are features of a 찜질방.
Say 찜질방 when you want the sauna-spa complex.
제 옷 입고 들어가도 돼요? → 찜질복으로 갈아입어야 해요.
In the common areas you wear the provided matching 찜질복, not your own clothes.
Change into the 찜질복.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 동호회 means "hobby club, social/interest group" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 동호회 (donghohoe) = "hobby club, social/interest group". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 동호회에 가입하다 ("to join a club") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동호회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 가입하다(加入) = to sign up/join an organization; takes 에
any hobby + 동호회 names an adult interest group
정기(定期) = scheduled/regular; clubs gather on a set day
회비(會費) = the fee members chip in to run the group

examples.en: I joined a hiking club.
examples.note: the basic frame; 동호회 + 에 + 가입하다, the fixed 'join' pattern

examples.ko: 동호회 회비가 한 달에 만 원이에요.
examples.romanization: donghohoe hoebiga han dare man wonieyo.
examples.en: The club dues are 10,000 won a month.
examples.note: 한 달에 = per month; 회비 framed as a recurring monthly cost

examples.en: This club has a lot of working professionals.
examples.note: 직장인(職場人) = office worker/professional, a common club demographic

extendedVocab.nuance: 동호회(同好會) is Sino-Korean — 同 'same' + 好 'liking' + 會 'association', literally 'a society of people who like the same thing': an adult hobby/interest club (sports, photography, hiking) that is the main way working 20-30s meet people outside the office. The sharp contrast to learn is 동호회 vs 동아리: a 동아리 is a school/university circle for students, while adults join a 동호회, so don't use 동아리 for your office tennis group. Also distinguish the lasting, organized 동호회 from a one-off 모임 (a single get-together/meeting). Verb-wise you 가입하다 ('join/sign up', 加入) — not the literal 들어가다 ('go inside') — then pay 회비 (dues) and attend the 정기 모임.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
회사 동아리에 가입했어요 (an adult club). → 회사 동호회에 가입했어요.
동아리 is specifically a school/college circle; adult interest clubs are 동호회. Using 동아리 for a grown-ups' group sounds off.
Adults' club = 동호회; students' circle = 동아리.
동호회를 들어갔어요. → 동호회에 가입했어요.
Joining an organization uses 가입하다 with the particle 에; the literal 들어가다 ('enter a space') doesn't fit membership.
Use 동호회에 가입하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 보일러 means "boiler (home heating unit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 보일러 (boilleo) means "boiler (home heating unit)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보일러를 켜다 ("to turn on the boiler"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보일러 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: use 켜다/끄다 (on/off) like any appliance; 틀다 also works for 'crank it on'
고장 나다 is the set phrase for any machine failing; 나다 makes it intransitive
a real button (외출 = going out) that keeps pipes from freezing while saving gas
돌리다 (lit. 'make it spin/turn') is the idiomatic 'run an appliance' verb here

examples.en: I turn on the boiler.
examples.note: simple present; 켜다 = switch on, the most basic pairing

examples.ko: 겨울인데 보일러가 안 돼서 너무 추워요.
examples.romanization: gyeourinde boilleoga an dwaeseo neomu chuwoyo.
examples.en: It's winter and the boiler isn't working, so it's freezing.
examples.note: 안 되다 = 'not function'; ~아서 links cause to result

examples.ko: 집주인한테 보일러 좀 고쳐 달라고 연락했어요.
examples.romanization: jipjuinhante boilleo jom gochyeo dallago yeollakaesseoyo.
examples.en: I contacted the landlord asking them to please fix the boiler.
examples.note: real tenant move: ~한테 (to a person) + ~아 달라고 하다 (request a favor)

extendedVocab.nuance: 보일러 is a katakana-route loanword (from English 'boiler') but in a Korean home it means far more than the English word: one 보일러 heats BOTH the 온돌 floor and the hot-water supply, so when it dies you lose heat and hot showers at the same moment. Do not confuse it with 난방 (the heating itself, the warmth) or 히터 (a plug-in space heater) — 보일러 is the gas unit that produces 난방. The habitual verbs are 켜다/끄다 (on/off), 틀다 ('crank on'), and 돌리다 ('run it'), while a breakdown is always 고장 나다. The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 보일러가 죽었어요 ('the boiler died') as a direct translation of an English idiom; Koreans say 보일러가 고장 났어요 or 보일러가 안 돼요. Tenants report a dead 보일러 to the 집주인 (landlord) or 관리사무소 (management office) immediately, since no hot water is an emergency.

Mixing up 보일러 with 난방: 난방이 고장 났어요 sounds odd because 난방 is the abstract heating. The physical unit that broke is the 보일러, so 보일러가 고장 났어요 is what a repair person expects.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 = 'come into being'; the neutral verb for a problem showing up
발생하다 (occur) is the formal register you use when filing a 관리사무소 report
신고 = official report; 누수 신고를 하다 = lodge a leak complaint with management
흔적 = mark left behind (a water stain on the ceiling proving past leakage)

examples.en: Water is leaking from the ceiling.
examples.note: casual everyday phrasing: the verb 새다 (to leak), not the noun

examples.ko: 천장에서 물이 떨어져서 누수인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: cheonjangeseo muri tteoreojyeoseo nusuin geot gatayo.

examples.note: ~인 것 같다 = 'seems to be ~', a soft diagnosis

extendedVocab.nuance: 누수 is Sino-Korean: 漏水, literally 漏 'leak/seep' + 水 'water', i.e. 'leaking water'. Because it is a 한자어 noun it carries a formal, technical tone — it is the word you use when reporting damage to a 관리사무소, 집주인, or repair technician, and it appears on invoices and insurance forms. The dividing line you must learn: 누수 is a NOUN naming the phenomenon, whereas the everyday verb 'to leak' is 새다 (물이 새요). So a native speaker casually says 물이 새요 but writes 누수가 발생했습니다 on a report. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 누수 like a verb and producing 누수해요 — this does not exist; you must say 물이 새요 or 누수가 생겼어요. Also distinguish 누수 (water leaking) from its dangerous lookalike 누전 (漏電, electrical leakage/short circuit), and from 결로 (condensation), which looks like a leak but is just humidity beading on a cold surface. Establishing the source — 윗집 (upstairs) vs. building pipes — decides who pays.

Confusing 누수 (漏水, water leak) with 누전 (漏電, electrical short). They share 漏 'leak' but 누전 is electricity escaping and is a fire hazard; calling an electrician for 누수 or a plumber for 누전 sends the wrong person.
Calling condensation 누수: water beading on a cold window in winter is 결로, not 누수. Reporting 누수 when it's 결로 leads the landlord to look for a non-existent burst pipe.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 곰팡이 means "mold, mildew" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 곰팡이 (gompangi) = "mold, mildew". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 곰팡이가 피다 ("mold blooms/grows") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 곰팡이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the idiomatic verb: mold 'blossoms' like a flower — present 피어요, past 폈어요
슬다 is the native verb for mold/rust forming on a surface; common in speech
제거하다 (formal 'eliminate'); casually 곰팡이를 닦다 (wipe off) or 없애다
냄새 = smell; 곰팡이 냄새가 나다 = it smells musty, a tell-tale of hidden mold

examples.en: There's a lot of mold on the wall.
examples.note: location marked by 에; the simplest description

examples.en: During the rainy season, mold easily grows in the bathroom.
examples.note: 잘 + verb = 'easily/often'; 피어요 is from 피다 (to bloom), the verb mold takes

examples.ko: 곰팡이 때문에 벽지를 다 뜯어내고 새로 도배했어요.
examples.romanization: gompangi ttaemune byeokjireul da tteudeonaego saero dobaehaesseoyo.
examples.en: Because of the mold, I tore out all the wallpaper and re-papered.
examples.note: real consequence; ~때문에 (because of) + 뜯어내다 (rip out)

extendedVocab.nuance: 곰팡이 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) for mold/mildew, and it is a constant battle in Korean homes — in humid 욕실 (bathrooms), behind furniture pushed against cold exterior walls, and all through 장마 (the summer rainy season). The crucial collocation is the verb: mold 곰팡이가 피다, literally 'mold blooms', as if it were a flower (present 곰팡이가 피어요, past 곰팡이가 폈어요). A second native verb, 슬다 (곰팡이가 슬다 'mold sets in'), is also fully natural. The sharp pitfall for learners is the verb pair 피다 vs. 펴다: 피다 ('to bloom', intransitive) is what mold does, while 펴다 ('to unfold/spread out', transitive — you 펴 a blanket or an umbrella) is a different verb; never say 곰팡이를 펴다. Another mistake is translating 'mold grows' as 곰팡이가 자라요 — 자라다 is for living things like children or plants, so for mold Koreans say 폈어요 or 슬었어요. Do not confuse 곰팡이 with 먼지 (dust) or 때 (grime). Serious 곰팡이 is legitimate grounds to ask a 집주인 for repairs.

Confusing the verbs 피다 and 펴다: learners produce 곰팡이를 펴다. 펴다 means 'unfold/spread out' (you 펴 a blanket); mold uses the intransitive 피다, so it's 곰팡이가 피었어요/폈어요.
Saying 곰팡이가 자랐어요 ('the mold grew') by direct translation. 자라다 is for living organisms (children, plants). For everyday mold Koreans say 곰팡이가 폈어요 or 곰팡이가 슬었어요.
Mixing up 곰팡이 (mold) with 먼지 (dust) or 때 (grime). They are cleaned differently and described differently; black fuzzy growth on a damp wall is 곰팡이, a layer of fine particles is 먼지.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 환기 means "ventilation, airing out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 환기 (hwangi) means "ventilation, airing out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환기를 하다 ("to ventilate / air out"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 환기 + 하다 = the everyday verb: open the windows and let air through
시키다 (causative 'make it happen') — 환기를 시키다 stresses you actively cause airflow
잘 되다 = 'works well'; 환기가 잘 돼요 praises a room's airflow

usagePhrases.en: for a cross-breeze to blow through
usagePhrases.note: 맞바람 = cross-draft; opening windows on two sides so 맞바람이 쳐서 환기가 잘 돼요

examples.en: I air out the room.
examples.note: 환기 + 하다, the most basic form

examples.ko: 곰팡이가 안 생기게 매일 환기를 시켜요.
examples.romanization: gompangiga an saenggige maeil hwangireul sikyeoyo.
examples.en: I air it out every day so mold doesn't form.
examples.note: ~게 (so that) + causative 시키다; ties ventilation to mold prevention

examples.ko: 이 방은 창문이 작아서 환기가 잘 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: i bangeun changmuni jagaseo hwangiga jal an dwaeyo.
examples.en: This room has a small window, so it doesn't ventilate well.
examples.note: real flaw to flag when viewing a place; 잘 안 되다 = 'doesn't work well'

extendedVocab.nuance: 환기 is Sino-Korean: 換氣, literally 換 'change/exchange' + 氣 'air', i.e. 'changing out the air'. Koreans treat daily 환기 as serious housekeeping, because tightly sealed, well-insulated apartments trap cooking smells, CO2, and the moisture that breeds 곰팡이; you 환기 after cooking, after sleeping, and especially on dry winter days. The word takes BOTH 하다 and 시키다 — 환기하다 and 환기시키다 — and here they are effectively interchangeable, both meaning 'open up and let air through'; 시키다 just foregrounds that you are deliberately causing it. Distinguish 환기 sharply from 통풍 (通風), which is the passive property of air being able to pass through a space (a breezy room has good 통풍), whereas 환기 is the active act of refreshing the air. Also keep it apart from 난방 (heating) and 냉방 (cooling) — those change temperature, 환기 changes the air itself. The English-speaker pitfall: 환기 is a noun, so do not bolt it onto random verbs; pair it only with 하다/시키다, or describe airflow with 환기가 잘 되다/안 되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 환기 as if it were a verb stem with the wrong helper, e.g. 환기해 주세요 is fine but learners produce 환기 열어요. Say 환기를 하다/시키다, or 창문을 열어서 환기해요.
Confusing 환기 (actively refreshing the air) with 통풍 (a room's passive airflow/draftiness). A room 통풍이 잘 돼요 (is breezy); you yourself 환기를 시켜요 (air it out).
Mixing 환기 up with 난방 (heating) or 냉방 (cooling/AC). Opening a window for fresh air is 환기, not 냉방; 냉방 specifically means cooling with an air conditioner.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수도세 means "water bill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "water bill" is 수도세 (sudose). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 수도세를 내다 ("to pay the water bill"). Watch the particle attached to 수도세 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay (a fee/bill); the standard verb for any 공과금
나오다 (lit. 'comes out') is how Koreans say a bill is issued/lands
포함되다 = be included; the make-or-break rental question 'is it 포함이에요?'
요금 (料金, fee) is the technically correct word; on bills you see 상수도 요금

examples.en: I pay the water bill.
examples.note: object marker 를 + 내다, the core pairing

examples.en: Is the water bill included in the monthly rent?
examples.note: the essential question before signing; 포함되어 있다 = is included

examples.en: I got hit with a huge water bill because of a leak.
examples.note: real shock: 요금 폭탄을 맞다 = 'get hit by a bill bomb'

extendedVocab.nuance: 수도세 is one of the 공과금 (utility bills) tenants juggle, and it sits in a funny spot: it ends in 세 (稅, 'tax'), but a water charge is really a usage fee, so the textbook-correct term is 수도 요금 (水道料金) — 水道 'water-way/plumbing' + 料金 'fee'. In daily life, though, everyone says 수도세, just as they say 전기세 and 가스비. The verbs are register-defining: a bill 나오다 ('comes out', is issued) and you 내다 (pay) it — never 사다 (buy). The make-or-break rental question is whether it's 포함 (included) in the rent or paid separately. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers: first, do not buy a bill — 'pay the bill' is 수도세를 내다, and 'the bill was high' is 수도세가 많이 나왔어요, literally 'a lot came out'. Second, do not confuse 수도세 (the monetary bill) with 수돗물 (tap water, the actual H2O) — note the sai-siot ㅅ in 수돗물. The slang 요금 폭탄 ('bill bomb') describes a shockingly high bill, often traced to a hidden 누수.

Saying 수도세를 사요 ('I buy the water bill') because 'buy/pay' blur in the learner's head. Bills are paid: 수도세를 내요. They are issued: 수도세가 나왔어요.
Confusing 수도세 (the bill, the money) with 수돗물 (tap water itself). 수돗물을 마셔요 = 'I drink tap water'; 수도세를 내요 = 'I pay the water bill'.
Forcing 수도세가 높아요 from English 'the bill is high'. Korean idiom is 수도세가 많이 나왔어요 ('a lot came out') for an amount; 높다 fits temperatures and buildings, not a bill amount.

extendedVocab.explanation: 전기세 (jeongise) = "electricity bill". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전기세를 내다 ("to pay the electricity bill") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전기세, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay; the standard verb across all utility bills
나오다 = is issued; 많이 나오다 = comes out high
폭탄 (爆彈, bomb) = a shockingly high bill, the classic summer-AC complaint
요금 (料金, fee) is the accurate term; you see 전기 요금 on official KEPCO bills

examples.en: I pay the electricity bill.
examples.note: 를 + 내다, the base pattern

examples.en: I ran the AC a lot, so I'm scared of the electricity bill.
examples.note: 틀다 = crank on (an appliance); 무섭다 here = 'dreadful to think about'

examples.en: The electricity bill came out double last month's.
examples.note: comparison with 보다 (than) + 나/emphasis ('a whopping two times')

extendedVocab.nuance: 전기세 follows the same 세 (稅 'tax') vs. 요금 (料金 'fee') split as 수도세: the formally correct term is 전기 요금 (電氣料金), 電氣 'electricity' + 料金 'fee', because it is a usage charge, not a tax — yet 전기세 is what everyone actually says. What makes 전기세 special is Korea's 누진제 (累進制, progressive rate system): residential electricity is billed in escalating tiers, so heavy summer 에어컨 use can push you into a high bracket and spike the bill dramatically, which is why 전기세 폭탄 ('electricity bill bomb') is a fixed summer complaint. Verbs follow the bill pattern: it 나오다 (comes out/is issued) and you 내다 (pay) it. The pitfalls: first, do not confuse 전기세 (the bill, the money owed) with 전기 (電氣) itself, the electricity — 전기가 나갔어요 means 'the power went out', a totally different sentence from 전기세가 많이 나왔어요. Second, resist English 'high bill' as 전기세가 높아요; the idiom is 전기세가 많이 나왔어요. Unplugging unused 콘센트 (outlets) is the stereotypical 전기세-saving habit.

Saying 전기세가 높아요 from English 'the bill is high'. For a bill amount Koreans say 전기세가 많이 나왔어요. 높다 is reserved for height/temperature.
Assuming 세 means it is literally a tax and refusing to use 전기세. It is colloquially universal; just know the formal/written term is 전기 요금.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 = pay; note this one ends in 비 (費, expense), not 세
나오다 = is issued; 겨울에 많이 나오다 = comes out high in winter

usagePhrases.en: the gas bill is a burden
usagePhrases.note: 부담되다 = to weigh on you financially; a natural way to say a cost stings
도시가스 (都市gas, piped city gas) + 요금; the official term on the bill

examples.en: I pay the gas bill.
examples.note: 를 + 내다, the core pattern

examples.ko: 가스비 아끼려고 보일러를 외출 모드로 해 놔요.
examples.romanization: gaseubi akkiryeogo boilleoreul oechul modeuro hae nwayo.

examples.note: ~려고 (in order to) + 해 놓다 (do and leave it that way) — a money-saving habit

examples.ko: 이번 겨울은 가스비가 작년보다 더 비싸게 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon gyeoureun gaseubiga jangnyeonboda deo bissage nawasseoyo.
examples.en: This winter the gas bill came out more expensive than last year.
examples.note: real comparison; 보다 (than) + 비싸게 나오다

extendedVocab.explanation: "wallpapering" is 도배 (dobae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도배를 하다 ("to wallpaper (a place)"). Watch the particle attached to 도배 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 도배 + 하다 = the verb 'to do wallpapering'; the noun alone is not a verb
새로 = anew; the standard phrase for refreshing walls before move-in
비용 (費用, expense); a key negotiation figure with a landlord
the fixed pair Koreans name together when assessing or renovating a rental

examples.en: I had it freshly wallpapered.
examples.note: 새로 하다 = redo from new; the most common everyday use

examples.ko: 곰팡이 때문에 도배를 다시 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gompangi ttaemune dobaereul dasi haeya haeyo.
examples.en: Because of mold, I have to redo the wallpaper.
examples.note: ~때문에 (because of) + 다시 (again); mold is a classic trigger for re-papering

examples.ko: 집주인이 도배랑 장판을 새로 해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jipjuini dobaerang jangpaneul saero hae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The landlord redid the wallpaper and flooring for me.
examples.note: real perk: ~아 주다 (do a favor) + the 도배랑 장판 pair

extendedVocab.nuance: 도배 is Sino-Korean: 塗褙, literally 塗 'to coat/spread' + 褙 'to paper/back', i.e. the act of covering walls with 벽지 (wallpaper). Korea papers walls rather than painting them as the default finish, so 도배 is a routine event whenever someone moves in or prepares a unit to rent, and it is almost always spoken of as a pair with 장판 (the vinyl flooring): 도배랑 장판 새로 해 주세요 is a stock request to a 집주인. Stained or peeling 벽지 is a common reason a tenant negotiates for fresh 도배 before signing.

Using 도배 as a standalone verb: learners say 어제 도배 ('yesterday wallpaper'). It needs 하다: 어제 도배를 했어요.
Confusing 도배 (the act/service of papering) with 벽지 (the wallpaper material). You buy 벽지 and you do 도배; 벽지가 예뻐요 (the wallpaper is pretty) vs. 도배를 했어요 (I had it papered).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 장판 means "vinyl floor covering" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 장판 (jangpan) = "vinyl floor covering". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장판을 깔다 ("to lay the flooring") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장판, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 깔다 (to spread/lay down flat) is THE verb for flooring, mats, blankets
들뜨다 = to come unstuck and bulge; the most common 장판 defect
누렇다 (deep yellow) describes aged vinyl; grounds to ask for new 장판
the standard rental-checklist pair, named together for move-in renovation

examples.en: The floor covering is clean.
examples.note: simple description of condition with 깨끗하다

examples.en: When I turn on the boiler, the floor covering gets warm.
examples.note: ~면 (when/if) + 따뜻해지다 (become warm); the 온돌 effect on the vinyl

examples.en: The old flooring was yellowed, so I laid new one.
examples.note: real renovation; 누렇다 → 누래서 (because it's yellowed) + 깔다

extendedVocab.nuance: 장판 (often the full 장판지/壯版紙, 'thick-board paper', historically oil-treated floor paper) is the smooth vinyl sheet laid over the heated 온돌 floor in most Korean homes — it is what your bare feet touch and what warms up when the 보일러 runs. The signature collocation is the verb 깔다 ('to spread/lay flat'): you 장판을 깔다, the same verb you use to lay a mat or 이불 (bedding). Keep 장판 distinct from 바닥 (the floor structure itself, the ground you stand on) — 장판 is the covering ON the 바닥 — and from 마루 (wood-plank/parquet flooring) and 타일 (tile); 장판 specifically means the soft vinyl sheet. Like 도배, it is a fixed item on the rental checklist and is almost always paired with it: 도배랑 장판. Defects have set vocabulary worth knowing: 장판이 들뜨다 (lifts/bubbles up), 장판이 누렇다 (has yellowed with age), and water damage from 누수 soaking 장판 밑 (under the flooring). The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the wrong verb: flooring is laid (깔다), never 'worn' or 'put on' — avoid 장판을 입다 or 장판을 놓다; the correct phrase is 장판을 깔다.

Pairing 장판 with the wrong verb, e.g. 장판을 입다 (from 'put on'). Flooring is laid down: 장판을 깔다. 입다 is only for clothing.
Confusing 장판 (the vinyl covering) with 바닥 (the floor itself). 바닥이 차가워요 = the floor is cold; 장판을 새로 깔았어요 = I laid new vinyl flooring.
Calling all flooring 장판. Wood-plank flooring is 마루/원목마루 and tile is 타일; 장판 specifically means the soft vinyl sheet over 온돌.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 콘센트 means "electrical outlet, wall socket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 콘센트 (konsenteu) means "electrical outlet, wall socket". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 콘센트에 꽂다 ("to plug into the outlet"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 콘센트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 꽂다 (to insert/stick in) is the verb for putting a plug in
뽑다 (to pull out) is the opposite of 꽂다; the 전기세-saving move
부족하다 = to be insufficient; a stock complaint about older/small rooms
멀티탭 (multi-tap) extends one 콘센트 into many; what you buy when outlets are scarce

examples.en: Where is the outlet?
examples.note: asking location with 어디에 (at where); a daily-life question

examples.en: I plugged the phone charger into the outlet.
examples.note: 에 꽂다 = plug INTO; the destination-marking 에

examples.ko: 외출할 때 안 쓰는 콘센트는 다 뽑아 놔요.
examples.romanization: oechulhal ttae an sseuneun konsenteuneun da ppoba nwayo.
examples.en: When I go out, I unplug everything not in use.
examples.note: ~ㄹ 때 (when) + 뽑아 놓다 (unplug and leave it); a saving habit

extendedVocab.nuance: 콘센트 is a sneaky loanword: it comes via Japanese コンセント, itself a clipping of English 'concentric plug', so despite the spelling it has NOTHING to do with English 'consent' — it simply means the wall socket. You must keep three pieces separate: the 콘센트 is the socket in the wall; the 플러그 (plug) is on the end of the appliance cord; and the verbs are 꽂다 (to plug in/insert) and 뽑다 (to pull out/unplug). So 충전기를 콘센트에 꽂다 = 'plug the charger into the outlet'. The number of 콘센트 is a genuine concern in older or small Korean rooms, and the fix is a 멀티탭 (power strip, 'multi-tap'), another Konglish term. Unplugging idle devices at the 콘센트 is the classic 전기세-saving habit. Pitfalls for English speakers: first, never read 콘센트 as 'consent' — it is purely the outlet. Second, do not blur 콘센트 (the wall socket) with 플러그 (the cord's plug); 'plug it in' targets the 콘센트 (꽂다), while the thing you hold is the 플러그. Third, mind the verbs — you 꽂다/뽑다 a plug, you do not '열다/닫다' (open/close) an outlet.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 음식물쓰레기 means "food waste" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "food waste" is 음식물쓰레기 (eumsingmulsseuregi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 음식물쓰레기를 버리다 ("to throw out food waste"). Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 버리다 = to discard; the core verb, but it must go in the right bin
분리하다 (分離, to separate) from 일반쓰레기 and 재활용; legally required
봉투 = bag; you buy the official 음식물 전용 봉투 to dispose of it
냄새가 나다 = it stinks; the summer problem that forces frequent disposal

examples.en: I throw out the food waste.
examples.note: 를 + 버리다, the base pattern

examples.ko: 음식물쓰레기는 일반 쓰레기랑 따로 버려야 해요.
examples.romanization: eumsingmulsseuregineun ilban sseuregirang ttaro beoryeoya haeyo.
examples.en: Food waste has to be thrown out separately from regular trash.
examples.note: the key residency rule; ~랑 따로 (apart from) + ~아야 하다 (must)

examples.en: Our apartment disposes of food waste by card.
examples.note: real system: RFID smart bins; 카드로 (by card) marks the means

extendedVocab.nuance: 음식물쓰레기 is a transparent compound: 음식물 (飮食物, 'food/edibles') + 쓰레기 (native word for 'trash') — so literally 'food trash'. The thing every newcomer must internalize is that Korean law mandates separating garbage into at least three streams: 음식물쓰레기 (food waste), 일반쓰레기 (general non-recyclable trash), and 재활용 (recycling). 음식물쓰레기 goes only into designated bins — often weight-based RFID units in apartments where you tag a 카드 and dump it, or into official 음식물 전용 봉투 (yellow food-waste bags) elsewhere. Getting it wrong can mean a 과태료 (administrative fine) or an irritated 관리사무소, so it is a real survival skill. The verbs: you 버리다 (throw out) it and you 분리하다 / 분리수거하다 (sort it out for collection). Pitfalls: first, do not lump it with general trash — 음식물쓰레기 vs. 일반쓰레기 is a legal line, not a preference. Second, note what does NOT count as 음식물쓰레기 even though it came from food: large bones, eggshells, shellfish/clam shells, onion skins, and tea bags are 일반쓰레기, because the rule is roughly 'can livestock eat it?'. Getting that boundary wrong is the most common foreigner mistake.

데치다 = quick boil, then plunge into cold water to keep the green color

extendedVocab.nuance: 애호박 is the short, pale-green, tender Korean summer squash — softer, sweeter and thinner-skinned than the dark, firm Western zucchini, which Koreans call 주키니 or 돼지호박. The contrast that matters is 애호박 vs 호박: bare 호박 leans toward pumpkin/winter squash (think 호박죽, 단호박), so if you ask for 호박 at a mart you may not get the green stew squash you pictured — say 애호박 specifically. extendedVocab.nuance: 버섯 is the umbrella word 'mushroom', but in a real kitchen or market you almost always name the kind: 표고 (shiitake, deep aroma, meaty), 팽이 (enoki, thin white clusters), 새송이 (king oyster, thick stalk), 느타리 (oyster, frilly). Register is plain everyday vocabulary; the only social note is the BBQ ritual phrase. The single most useful collocation a resident learns is '상추 좀 더 주세요' — refills of 상추 are free at almost every 고깃집, so this one line earns its keep nightly. extendedVocab.nuance: 무 is the fat, white Korean radish (daikon) — milder, juicier and far bigger than the small red Western radish, and it's the backbone of 무국, 깍두기, 동치미, 무생채, and many soup stocks. Because a whole 무 is heavy, '반 개' (half) is a perfectly normal amount to ask for. The flavor word fused to it is 시원하다: when Koreans say a 무 broth is 시원해요, they do NOT mean cold — they mean clean, brisk, and refreshing on the palate, the same 시원하다 used to praise hot soup that clears your head. Register is plain everyday vocabulary. Natural collocations: 무를 썰다/채 썰다/넣다, 무국, 무생채, 깍두기, 뭇국(소고기뭇국). English-speaker pitfall: 'radish' summons the little crunchy red salad globe, which is the wrong picture entirely — 무 is a large white root used cooked or fermented; and the 시원하다 trap is real, so a learner who hears '시원한 국' must not picture a chilled soup. 무 is a native Korean word with no hanja.

Picturing the small red Western salad radish — 무 is the large white daikon used in soups, kimchi, and stews.
Reading 시원한 국 as 'a cold/cool soup' — for broth 시원하다 means a clean, refreshing flavor, and it's said even of piping-hot soup.
Counting it with 단 like a leafy green — the solid root takes 개 (한 개, 반 개), not 단.

extendedVocab.nuance: 멸치 is the dried anchovy, and the practical key is that it comes in sizes by purpose: big 국물용 (broth) anchovies for making stock, and tiny 볶음용 ones for the sweet-savory 멸치볶음 side dish — the suffix -용 ('for the use of') is what tells them apart on the package. A real resident tip: pull the dark gut (똥) out of large anchovies, or the broth goes bitter. English-speaker pitfall: don't picture the oily, salty anchovy fillets from a pizza — Korean 멸치 are whole dried fish, sweet snack-sized when small and broth-makers when large; and grabbing the little snack anchovies for stock, or boiling them too long, both produce a cloudy, bitter 육수.

Using tiny snack/볶음용 anchovies for stock instead of the large 국물용 — size is matched to purpose, and small ones won't give a clean broth.
Boiling the anchovies too long — long boiling makes the 육수 bitter and fishy; simmer briefly and strain them out.

extendedVocab.nuance: 돼지고기 is the everyday meat of Korea — cheaper than 소고기 (beef) and the heart of 삼겹살, 제육볶음, 김치찌개, and 보쌈. It's a transparent compound, 돼지 (pig) + 고기 (meat), and the whole 'animal + 고기' system is worth internalizing: 소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken, 양고기 lamb. The single most practical fact is the unit: at a 정육점 (butcher) or mart, meat is sold by the 근, and for meat one 근 = 600 g — so '한 근' is noticeably more than a Western pound. (Confusingly, for vegetables/fruit a 근 is often 375 g, but for meat assume 600 g.) Register is plain everyday vocabulary. You must also learn cut names — 삼겹살 (belly), 목살 (collar/neck), 앞다리살 (shoulder), 등심 (loin) — because the butcher needs the cut, not just 'pork'. Collocations: 돼지고기 한 근, 돼지고기를 볶다/굽다/삶다, 돼지고기 다짐육. English-speaker pitfall: English 'pork' hides the animal, so beginners reach for bare 고기 (meat) — but a butcher needs to hear 돼지고기 vs 소고기; and assuming 한 근 = 500 g (or a pound) gets the quantity wrong.

extendedVocab.nuance: 계란 is the everyday word for 'egg' and what you'll see on most cartons, menus and lips; 달걀 is the same thing in a slightly more 'proper'/native-flavored register (often preferred in writing and textbooks), so 계란 vs 달걀 is purely register — same egg, both correct. 계란 is in fact Sino-Korean, 鷄卵, literally 'chicken-egg' (鷄 chicken + 卵 egg), which is why it can feel a touch more clinical than the native 달걀; everyday speech leans 계란. Eggs are sold by the 판 (a tray of 30) in bulk or in smaller packs, and a single egg is counted with 알 (계란 한 알). Worth pairing: 노른자 (yolk), 흰자 (white), and the verbs 풀다 (whisk), 삶다 (boil), 부치다/프라이하다 (fry). Register is fully neutral. English-speaker pitfall: learners often treat 계란 and 달걀 as two different foods or worry which is 'correct' — relax, they're interchangeable; and the counter trips people up, since eggs aren't 개 — buy them by the 판 and count singles with 알. Also note the spoken 후라이 vs written 프라이 split for the fried egg.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 계란 and 달걀 are different things — they're the same egg; 계란 (Sino-Korean 鷄卵) is the everyday word, 달걀 the more 'proper'/written one.
Counting eggs with 개 ('계란 두 개') — singles take 알 (계란 한 알), and bulk is by the 판 (tray of 30).
Writing 후라이 because that's how it sounds — the spoken 계란후라이 is normal speech, but the standard spelling is 계란프라이.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 양배추 means "cabbage (head cabbage)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 양배추 (yangbaechu) = "cabbage (head cabbage)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 양배추 한 통 ("one head of cabbage") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the round cabbage is counted with 통 (whole-head counter)
반 통 = half; a common buy since a whole head is big
채 썰다 = to cut into thin strips for a coleslaw-style side
steamed cabbage leaves wrapped around rice/meat with 쌈장

examples.en: I want to buy just half a head of cabbage.
examples.note: graded simple: 반 통 + 만 'only'; -고 싶다 'want to'

examples.en: Pork cutlet comes with shredded cabbage on the side.
examples.note: everyday: 양배추 채 = the shredded cabbage; 같이 나오다 'comes together with'

examples.ko: 양배추를 푹 쪄서 쌈으로 싸 먹어요.
examples.romanization: yangbaechureul puk jjyeoseo ssameuro ssa meogeoyo.
examples.en: I steam the cabbage soft and eat it as wraps.
examples.note: real-situation: 푹 찌다 = steam thoroughly; 쌈으로 싸 먹다 chains the wrap idea

extendedVocab.nuance: 양배추 is the round, dense Western-style head cabbage — and the line to nail is 양배추 vs 배추: 양배추 is the spherical green cabbage for coleslaw, 양배추쌈, and 볶음, while 배추 (specifically 배추/배추 통배추) is the tall, loose-leafed napa cabbage that becomes 김치. They are different vegetables, and the 양- prefix marks the 'Western/foreign' import (compare 양파 onion, 양상추 iceberg). It's counted with 통 (한 통 = a whole head) and very commonly bought as 반 통, since a full head is heavy. Register is plain everyday vocabulary. The signature collocation every resident meets is 돈가스 + 양배추 채 (the shredded-cabbage side with pork cutlet), plus 양배추를 찌다/볶다/채 썰다 and 양배추쌈. English-speaker pitfall: English just says 'cabbage', collapsing two Korean vegetables, so a beginner may buy round 양배추 expecting to make kimchi (which needs 배추) — getting this wrong derails the recipe; and counting it with 개 instead of 통 sounds off. 양배추 is a native-plus-Sino blend in feel but treated as a plain everyday word; no hanja drill needed.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 양배추 (round head cabbage) with 배추 (tall napa cabbage) — kimchi needs 배추; 양배추 is for coleslaw, 쌈, and 볶음.
Counting it with 개 ('양배추 한 개') — the round head takes 통 (한 통, 반 통).
Assuming the 양- in 양배추/양상추 is just a fancy variant of 배추/상추 — 양- marks a distinct Western vegetable, not the same plant.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 보고서 means "report (written document)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 보고서 (bogoseo) means "report (written document)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보고서를 쓰다 ("to write a report"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보고서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쓰다 is the plain everyday verb coworkers use
작성하다 is the formal register for emails and notices
제출하다 is for officially handing it in
검토하다 is what a superior does to your draft

examples.en: What report is this?
examples.note: simple: 무슨 + noun asks 'what kind of'

examples.en: I have to submit the report by today.
examples.note: everyday: 까지 marks the deadline 'by'

examples.ko: 팀장님이 보고서를 다시 쓰래요. 주말에도 야근이에요.
examples.romanization: timjangnimi bogoseoreul dasi sseuraeyo. jumaredo yageunieyo.
examples.en: The team lead told me to rewrite the report. I'm working late even on the weekend.
examples.note: real situation: 쓰래요 is contracted 쓰라고 해요, reported command

extendedVocab.nuance: 보고서 is the standard word for any written work document, from a quick 주간 보고서 (weekly report) to a thick 출장 보고서 (trip report). It is Sino-Korean: 報告書, literally 'report-tell-document', where the 書 ending signals a formal written paper (compare 계획서 plan, 신청서 application form). The dividing line learners must feel is 보고서 (the paper you hand in) vs 발표 (the spoken presentation you give from it) vs 보고 (the act of reporting up): you 보고서를 작성해서 그걸로 발표해요. Register-wise 작성하다 belongs in formal/email speech while plain 쓰다 is fine between coworkers. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') because English says 'make a report' — in Korean 보고서를 만들다 sounds like physically constructing an object; a document is 쓰다 or 작성하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 보고서를 만들다 because English says 'make a report' — Korean treats a document as something you 쓰다/작성하다, not 만들다; 만들다 implies physically crafting an object
Confusing 보고서 (the written document) with 발표 (the spoken presentation) — you write a 보고서 and then give a 발표 about it
Writing 보고서 하다; the noun has no 하다 verb, so use 보고서를 쓰다 or, for the act of reporting, the separate verb 보고하다

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마감 means "deadline; closing (date)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "deadline; closing (date)" is 마감 (magam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마감이 언제예요? ("when is the deadline?"). Watch the particle attached to 마감 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the default way to ask the due date
지키다 literally 'protect/keep', the set partner verb
다가오다 paints it as nearing you

usagePhrases.en: to be chased by a deadline
usagePhrases.note: 쫓기다 'be chased', the idiom for crunch

examples.en: When's the deadline?
examples.note: simple: 언제 'when' + 예요

examples.en: This time I'll definitely meet the deadline.
examples.note: everyday: ㄹ게요 is a personal promise to the listener

examples.en: Chased by the deadline, I couldn't even eat lunch.
examples.note: real situation: 도 'even' + 못 'couldn't' stacks the hardship

extendedVocab.nuance: 마감 is a native Korean noun (from the verb 막다 'to block/close off') meaning the point at which something is sealed shut: a report's due date, an application cutoff, a shop's last order, even a magazine going to press. The near-synonym confusion is with 기한 and 데드라인: 기한 (期限) is the dry, official 'time limit/term' you see on documents (제출 기한), while 마감 feels more like the live moment things close, and 데드라인 is a borrowed buzzword. Its signature collocation is the idiom 마감에 쫓기다 (chased by the deadline), the universal way to describe last-minute panic. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'meet a deadline' onto 만나다 ('meet a person'): you do NOT 마감을 만나다 — you 마감을 지키다 (keep/protect it). Note 지키다 is the same verb used for keeping a promise (약속을 지키다), which is the right mental image.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 마감을 만나다 from English 'meet the deadline' — 만나다 is only for meeting people; the correct collocation is 마감을 지키다 ('protect/keep')
Defaulting to 데드라인 in formal writing — it sounds like office slang; written/official Korean prefers 마감 or 기한
Saying 마감했다 to mean you personally finished your task — 마감하다 means to close/wrap up an operation (a shop, an event); for finishing your own work use 끝냈어요 or 마감을 지켰어요

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 결재 means "approval; sign-off (by a superior)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 결재 (gyeoljae) = "approval; sign-off (by a superior)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결재를 받다 ("to get approval") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결재, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 'receive' — you, the junior, receive it
올리다 'send up', because it goes up the ladder
나다 'be issued', intransitive, it happens to you
who signs and in what order

examples.en: Did this get approved?
examples.note: simple: dropped 를 in casual speech, rising intonation = question

examples.en: I just submitted it for approval, so please take a look.
examples.note: everyday: 부탁드려요 is the polite 'I ask of you'

examples.ko: 부장님 결재가 아직 안 나서 진행을 못 하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim gyeoljaega ajik an naseo jinhaengeul mo tago isseoyo.
examples.en: The manager's sign-off hasn't come through yet, so I can't proceed.
examples.note: real situation: 아서 'because' chains the reason to the result

extendedVocab.nuance: 결재 is the formal sign-off a superior puts on a document or expenditure before it can proceed, today usually through groupware (전자결재). It is Sino-Korean 決裁, literally 'decide-judge' — a person with authority decides and cuts a ruling. The make-or-break point for everyone, Koreans included, is the homophone pair 결재 (approval) vs 결제 (決濟, payment) — pronounced almost identically but meaning sign-off vs paying money; mixing the spelling is the single most common Korean office typo, so a learner who gets it right looks sharp. Directionally, 결재 flows up: a junior 결재를 올리다/받다, while the boss 결재를 하다/내주다. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 결재를 하다 about yourself when you're the requester — you don't 'do' the approval, you 받다 (receive) it; only the approver does the 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 결제 — that homophone means paying money (카드 결제 'card payment'); the approval/sign-off word is 결재 (決裁)
Saying 결재를 하다 about yourself when you are the one asking — the approver 결재를 해 주다, but you the junior 결재를 받다/올리다
Treating 결재 as a casual 'okay' from a friend — it specifically means an authorized superior's formal sign-off, not everyday agreement (that's 동의 or just 좋아요)

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 거래처 means "client; business partner (company)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 거래처 (georaecheo) means "client; business partner (company)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 거래처에 가다 ("to go to a client's place"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 거래처 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to go to a client's place
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination you visit
관리하다 'maintain/look after' the account
와 'with', 미팅 is everyday office English
에 marks the party you reach out to

examples.en: There's a call from the client.
examples.note: simple: 에서 marks the source of the call

examples.en: That client always pays late.
examples.note: everyday: note 결제 'payment' here, not 결재

examples.ko: 새 거래처를 뚫어서 이번 분기 매출이 올랐어요.
examples.romanization: sae georaecheoreul ttureoseo ibeon bungi maechuri ollasseoyo.
examples.en: We landed a new account, so revenue rose this quarter.
examples.note: real situation: 뚫다 'break through' = win a new client, slangy and proud

extendedVocab.nuance: 거래처 means a company you do business with — depending on context a client, a vendor, or a supplier. It is built from native + Sino parts: 거래 (去來, 'go-come' = transactions/dealings) + 처 (處, 'place'), literally 'the place transactions happen', i.e. your business counterparty. The synonym line to hold: 거래처 is the B2B partner firm, 고객 (顧客) is a 'customer/client' broadly (can be an individual or a company), and 손님 is a face-to-face 'guest/customer' who walks in. A salesperson proudly says 거래처를 뚫다 (literally 'break through a client') to mean they won a new account. The English-speaker pitfall is calling an individual contact your 거래처 — the word denotes the company/account, not the person; for the person you'd say 거래처 담당자 (the contact at the client). Also don't downgrade a business partner to 손님, which sounds like a retail walk-in.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 손님 ('guest/walk-in customer') for a B2B partner firm — a business counterparty is a 거래처; 손님 sounds like someone entering a shop
Calling an individual person your 거래처 — the word means the company/account; the person is the 거래처 담당자 (the contact there)
Mixing 거래처 (your partner company) with 거래 (the transaction itself) — you visit a 거래처 to do a 거래
