extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어쩌면 means "maybe; possibly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "maybe; possibly" is 어쩌면 (eojjeomyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어쩌면 올지도 몰라요 ("maybe they'll come"). Watch the particle attached to 어쩌면 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: with -ㄹ지도 모르다
a tentative admission
a soft suggestion
a hedged outcome with -ㄹ 수도 있다

examples.ko: 어쩌면 이번 주말에 시간이 날 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: eojjeomyeon ibeon jumare sigani nal sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe I'll have some free time this weekend.
examples.note: 어쩌면 + -ㄹ 수도 있다 keeps the possibility open and uncommitted.

examples.ko: 어쩌면 우리 전에 만난 적 있을지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: eojjeomyeon uri jeone mannan jeok isseuljido mollayo.
examples.en: Maybe we've met somewhere before.
examples.note: 어쩌면 floats a half-formed hunch; -ㄹ지도 몰라요 is its natural partner ending.

examples.ko: 어쩌면 그 사람 말이 맞을지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: eojjeomyeon geu saram mari majeuljido mollayo.
examples.en: Maybe that person is right after all.
examples.note: Signals genuine openness to being wrong — a reconsidering 'maybe'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어쩌면 means 'maybe / possibly' and opens a genuine but uncertain possibility, often one the speaker had not fully considered until now — there's a reflective, 'come to think of it, perhaps...' flavor. It is grammatically drawn to the guessing endings -ㄹ지도 모르다 and -ㄹ 수도 있다, which carry the uncertainty through to the verb. Contrast it with 아마 ('probably'): 아마 is a fairly confident lean toward yes (아마 맞을 거예요 = it's probably right), while 어쩌면 is more open-ended and less committed, weighing a real but not-likely chance, and it can even introduce a surprising or contrary idea. (Note 어쩌면 also has a separate exclamatory use, '어쩌면 이렇게...!' = 'how on earth so...!', but the adverb of possibility is the core meaning here.) The English-speaker pitfall is treating 어쩌면 as confidently as 아마, or pairing it with a flat assertion — it needs a hedging ending, not a bare statement of fact.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 어쩌면 as confidently as 아마 (probably) — 아마 leans toward 'yes, likely' (아마 올 거예요), while 어쩌면 stays open and uncommitted ('maybe, who knows').
Pairing 어쩌면 with a flat assertion (어쩌면 비가 와요) — it needs a guessing ending: 어쩌면 비가 올지도 몰라요 / 올 수도 있어요.
Forgetting its reflective 'come to think of it' nuance — it often raises a possibility newly considered, not a settled prediction.

extendedVocab.english: as many as; no less than
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무려 means "as many as; no less than" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 무려 (muryeo) = "as many as; no less than". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 무려 백만 원 ("a whopping million won") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 무려, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: sits right before a number
emphasizes a large amount

usagePhrases.en: for no less than ten years
usagePhrases.note: before a duration
a striking comparison

examples.en: That bag costs a whopping three million won.
examples.note: 무려 right before the figure signals 'shockingly, that much'.

examples.en: I stood in line for a full two hours.
examples.note: 무려 ... -이나 doubles the emphasis on the surprisingly large quantity.

examples.ko: 이 영화를 무려 천만 명이 봤어요.
examples.romanization: i yeonghwareul muryeo cheonman myeongi bwasseoyo.
examples.en: No less than ten million people saw this movie.
examples.note: Pairs a big round number with 무려 to stress an impressive scale.

extendedVocab.nuance: 무려 goes directly before a number or quantity to stress that the amount is surprisingly, impressively large — 'a whopping', 'no less than', 'as many as' — broadcasting that the speaker finds the figure striking or hard to believe. It works ONLY with quantities (money, counts, durations, multiples), never with a general statement, and it loves to combine with the emphatic particle -이나/나 on the number (무려 두 시간이나). Contrast it with 약 (約, 'approximately / about'), which does the opposite job — softening a number into a rough estimate (약 백 명 = about a hundred); 무려 amplifies and dramatizes, 약 hedges and rounds. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving out the number (무려 비싸요 is wrong — say 무려 삼백만 원이에요), or confusing the amplifying 무려 with the estimating 약. If you want plain 'about', reach for 약 or 대략; if you want 'can you believe how much', that's 무려.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 무려 with no number after it — 무려 must front a quantity (무려 백만 원); 무려 비싸요 is wrong, say 무려 백만 원이에요 or just 정말 비싸요.
Confusing 무려 (amplifies: 'a whopping') with 약 (softens: 'about, approximately') — 약 백 명 = roughly 100, but 무려 백 명 = a whopping 100.
Treating 무려 as plain emphasis like 정말 for adjectives — 무려 specifically dramatizes a NUMBER, not a quality (not 무려 예뻐요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 심지어 means "even; on top of that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 심지어 (simjieo) means "even; on top of that". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 심지어 무료예요 ("it's even free"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 심지어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: tacks on a surprising bonus
an extreme example with 도
piling on a worse fact
escalates to the extreme case

examples.ko: 그 식당은 맛있고, 심지어 가격도 싸요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun masitgo, simjieo gagyeokdo ssayo.
examples.en: That restaurant is tasty, and on top of that it's cheap.
examples.note: 심지어 adds an extra, almost too-good point; note 도 on 가격.

examples.en: It was raining, and I didn't even have an umbrella.
examples.note: Escalates from bad to worse; 심지어 + 우산도 = 'didn't even have'.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 심지어 내 이름도 기억 못 해요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun simjieo nae ireumdo gieong mo taeyo.
examples.en: That person doesn't even remember my name.
examples.note: Pushes to an extreme case — of all things, not even the name.

extendedVocab.nuance: 심지어 introduces an extreme or surprising addition that pushes a point further than you'd expect — 'even', 'on top of that', 'and get this'. It escalates, whether the extra fact is good (맛있고, 심지어 싸다) or bad (춥고, 심지어 비까지 온다), and it characteristically triggers the particle 도 ('also/even') on the following item. Contrast it with 게다가 ('moreover / what's more'): 게다가 simply adds another point on the same level, fairly neutrally, while 심지어 signals that the next fact is the surprising, over-the-top extreme — the one that makes you raise your eyebrows. Compare also 조차/마저 (particles meaning 'even', stressing the least-expected case); 심지어 often works alongside them. The English-speaker pitfall is using 심지어 as a flat 'also' (that's 또/그리고) or swapping it for neutral 게다가, and forgetting the 도 that naturally follows — 심지어 사과도 안 했어요, not 심지어 사과 안 했어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 심지어 as a plain 'also/and' — that is 또/그리고; 심지어 specifically escalates to a SURPRISING, extreme addition.
Swapping it for neutral 게다가 (moreover) — 게다가 just adds another point, while 심지어 flags the most unexpected, eyebrow-raising one.
Dropping the 도 that usually follows — say 심지어 인사도 안 했어요 (even the greeting); leaving out 도 weakens the 'even' force.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 도저히 means "(cannot) possibly; no matter what" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "(cannot) possibly; no matter what" is 도저히 (dojeohi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 도저히 못 하겠어요 ("I just can't do it"). Watch the particle attached to 도저히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: always with a negative
strong refusal with 안

usagePhrases.en: I can't understand it at all
usagePhrases.note: with 이해가 안 되다
with -ㄹ 수 없다

examples.en: I can't figure out this problem no matter what.
examples.note: 도저히 + 모르겠어요 = total inability after real effort.

examples.en: It's so spicy I just can't eat it.
examples.note: 도저히 + 못 ...겠어요 conveys giving up despite trying.

examples.en: There's just no way I can make time.
examples.note: 도저히 + -ㄹ 수가 없다 = flat impossibility, however hard one tries.

extendedVocab.nuance: 도저히 means 'by no means / no matter how hard one tries', and it MUST be paired with a negative — 못, 안, 모르다, or -ㄹ 수 없다 — because its whole job is to intensify an impossibility reached after genuine effort: not just 'I can't', but 'I've tried and there is simply no way'. Without a negative the sentence is ungrammatical (도저히 할 수 있어요 is wrong). Contrast it with 절대 ('never / absolutely (not)'): 절대 can negate too, but it sounds like a firm vow or prohibition about will or principle (절대 안 해 = I absolutely won't, by choice), whereas 도저히 is about practical impossibility despite trying (도저히 못 해 = I genuinely can't manage it). It collocates with 도저히 ~ 수 없다, 도저히 못 ~겠다, 도저히 안 되다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 도저히 in a positive sentence, or reaching for it to mean a willful 'never' where 절대 fits better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도저히 in a positive sentence — it REQUIRES a negative (도저히 못 해요 / 안 돼요 / 이해가 안 돼요); 도저히 돼요 is ungrammatical.
Swapping it for 절대 (never, by will) — 절대 안 해 is a vow of refusal, while 도저히 못 해 is practical inability after trying; the nuance differs.
Forgetting the 'after real effort' meaning — 도저히 implies you genuinely tried and it's impossible, not a casual 'I don't feel like it'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 차라리 means "rather; would sooner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 차라리 (charari) = "rather; would sooner". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 차라리 안 가는 게 나아요 ("I'd rather not go") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 차라리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: with -는 게 낫다
preferring one option with -ㄹ래요
choosing the lesser hassle
comparing two bad options

examples.en: Rather than wait, walking would be faster.
examples.note: -느니 차라리 = 'rather than (doing X)' — the core comparison frame.

examples.ko: 복잡한 데 가느니 차라리 집에서 쉴래요.
examples.romanization: bokjapan de ganeuni charari jibeseo swillaeyo.
examples.en: I'd sooner rest at home than go somewhere crowded.
examples.note: Sets a disliked option (가느니) against the preferred-but-still-not-ideal one.

examples.ko: 택시비 낼 바엔 차라리 일찍 나올게요.
examples.romanization: taeksibi nael baen charari iljjing naolgeyo.
examples.en: Rather than pay for a taxi, I'll just leave early.
examples.note: -ㄹ 바엔 차라리 = 'if it comes to (X), I'd rather' — choosing the lesser cost.

extendedVocab.nuance: 차라리 picks the lesser of two undesirable options — 'I'd rather', 'I'd sooner', 'better to... instead' — when NEITHER choice is good and you're settling for the more bearable one. The tone is resigned, not enthusiastic: it's a grudging preference, often implying 'this still isn't great, but it beats the alternative'. It characteristically follows the patterns -느니 (차라리) and -ㄹ 바에(는)/-ㄹ 바엔 차라리, both meaning 'rather than doing X', which set up the worse option being rejected. Contrast it with a plain 더 좋다 ('like better'): 더 좋다 is a positive preference between two acceptable things, while 차라리 specifically chooses between two bad-ish things. The English-speaker pitfall is using 차라리 for an option you genuinely want and feel good about — that implies you're happy, which clashes with 차라리's 'lesser evil' resignation; and forgetting that it normally compares against a worse alternative, so it rarely stands alone without that contrast in mind.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 차라리 for an option you actually want and enjoy — it implies neither choice is good (차라리 굶을래 = I'd rather starve); for a happy preference use 더 좋다/더 낫다 plainly.
Forgetting it compares against a WORSE alternative — 차라리 normally answers an unspoken 'rather than that bad option', often with -느니 or -ㄹ 바엔.
Treating it as 'instead' for neutral swaps — '대신' handles plain substitution (커피 대신 차), while 차라리 carries the resigned 'lesser of two evils' choice.

structuredNuance.t: 차라리 picks the lesser of two undesirable options — 'I'd rather', 'I'd sooner', 'better to... instead' — when NEITHER choice is good and you're settling for the more bearable one. The tone is resigned, not enthusiastic: it's a grudging preference, often implying 'this still isn't great, but it beats the alternative'. It characteristically follows the patterns -느니 (차라리) and -ㄹ 바에(는)/-ㄹ 바엔 차라리, both meaning 'rather than doing X', which set up the worse option being rejected.
Contrast it with a plain 더 좋다 ('like better'): 더 좋다 is a positive preference between two acceptable things, while 차라리 specifically chooses between two bad-ish things.

The English-speaker pitfall is using 차라리 for an option you genuinely want and feel good about — that implies you're happy, which clashes with 차라리's 'lesser evil' resignation; and forgetting that it normally compares against a worse alternative, so it rarely stands alone without that contrast in mind.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 스킨 means "toner (skin)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 스킨 (seukin) means "toner (skin)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스킨 발랐어요? ("Did you put on toner?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스킨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 항상 바르다; 스킨 하다는 어색해요
두 단어를 붙여 말하면 한국의 기본 2단계 스킨케어를 가리켜요
올리브영 직원에게 하는 전형적인 부탁 표현
남성 라인은 보통 남성용·남자로 표시되고 올인원이 많아요

examples.en: After washing my face, I apply toner first.
examples.note: 부터 = '먼저, ~부터 시작해서'; 스킨 → 로션 순서를 강조해요

examples.ko: 이 스킨은 향이 거의 없어서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i seukineun hyangi geoui eopseoseo joayo.
examples.en: I like this toner because it has almost no scent.
examples.note: 거의 없다 = '거의 ~ 않다'; 무향이면 fragrance-free예요

examples.ko: 피부가 건성이라 자기 전에 스킨을 두 번 덧발라요.
examples.romanization: pibuga geonseongira jagi jeone seukineul du beon deotballayo.
examples.en: My skin is dry, so I layer toner twice before bed.
examples.note: 덧바르다 = 위에 한 번 더 바르다; 건성↔지성 짝으로 외우세요

extendedVocab.nuance: 한국어 '스킨'은 영어 skin(피부)이 아니라 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 토너를 가리키는 화장품 이름이에요. 같은 제품을 '토너'라고도 부르지만, 일상 대화에서는 거의 항상 '스킨'이라고 해요. 영어 단어를 그대로 가져온 콩글리시이기 때문에 영어권 학습자가 '피부'라는 뜻으로 오해하기 쉬운 대표적 함정이에요. 바르는 동작에는 반드시 '바르다'를 쓰고 '스킨 하다'나 '스킨 칠하다'는 어색해요. 보통 '스킨 로션 발랐어?'처럼 로션과 한 세트로 묶여 다니고, '향이 없다', '촉촉하다' 같은 표현과 자주 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
스킨을 '피부(skin)'라는 뜻으로 쓰는 것 — 신체 부위는 '피부'라고 해야 하고, '스킨'은 토너 제품이에요
'스킨 크림'이라고 묶어 부르는 것 — 그런 짝은 없고 기본 세트는 '스킨 + 로션'이에요
'스킨 하다'로 동사화하는 것 — 화장품을 바르는 동작은 '바르다'를 써서 '스킨 발라요'라고 해요

structuredNuance.t: 한국어 '스킨'은 영어 skin(피부)이 아니라 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 토너를 가리키는 화장품 이름이에요. 같은 제품을 '토너'라고도 부르지만, 일상 대화에서는 거의 항상 '스킨'이라고 해요. 보통 '스킨 로션 발랐어?'처럼 로션과 한 세트로 묶여 다니고, '향이 없다', '촉촉하다' 같은 표현과 자주 어울려요.
바르는 동작에는 반드시 '바르다'를 쓰고 '스킨 하다'나 '스킨 칠하다'는 어색해요.
영어 단어를 그대로 가져온 콩글리시이기 때문에 영어권 학습자가 '피부'라는 뜻으로 오해하기 쉬운 대표적 함정이에요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 로션 means "lotion, moisturizer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "lotion, moisturizer" is 로션 (rosyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 로션 발라요 ("I apply lotion"). Watch the particle attached to 로션 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 스킨 다음에 오는 두 번째 보습 단계
얼굴용은 그냥 로션, 몸은 바디로 구분해요
친구·룸메이트 사이의 반말 부탁
수분 = 촉촉함; 제품 라벨에 흔한 말이에요

examples.en: In winter you have to apply a lot of lotion.
examples.note: 건조한 한국 겨울에 아주 공감되는 문장이에요

examples.en: I like this lotion because it isn't sticky.
examples.note: 끈적거리다 = 끈끈하게 들러붙다; 로션 고를 때 핵심 포인트

examples.ko: 샤워하고 나서 다리에 바디로션을 듬뿍 발랐어요.
examples.romanization: syawohago naseo darie badirosyeoneul deumppuk ballasseoyo.
examples.en: After showering, I slathered body lotion on my legs.
examples.note: 듬뿍 = 아주 넉넉히; 바디로션은 몸 전용임을 보여줘요

extendedVocab.nuance: 로션은 스킨 다음에 발라 수분을 채우고 가두는 보습 단계예요. 가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '크림'인데, 로션은 묽고 가벼워 흡수가 빠르고, 크림은 더 되고 진해서 강한 보습이 필요할 때 써요. 또 하나 주의할 점은 그냥 '로션'은 얼굴용을 뜻하고, 몸에 바르는 건 반드시 '바디로션'이라고 한다는 거예요. 영어 lotion은 몸·얼굴을 안 가리지만 한국어에서는 '바디'를 붙이지 않으면 자동으로 얼굴용으로 받아들여요. 동사는 '바르다'이고, '끈적거리다', '흡수가 빠르다', '촉촉하다' 같은 말과 잘 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
로션과 크림을 같은 것으로 보는 것 — 크림이 더 진하고 무거우며, 로션은 가볍고 묽어요
몸에 바르는데 그냥 '로션'이라고만 하는 것 — 바디용은 '바디로션'이라고 해야 얼굴용과 구분돼요
'로션 칠하다'라고 하는 것 — 자연스러운 동사는 '바르다'예요

structuredNuance.t: 로션은 스킨 다음에 발라 수분을 채우고 가두는 보습 단계예요. '끈적거리다', '흡수가 빠르다', '촉촉하다' 같은 말과 잘 어울려요.
가장 헷갈리는 짝은 '크림'인데, 로션은 묽고 가벼워 흡수가 빠르고, 크림은 더 되고 진해서 강한 보습이 필요할 때 써요. 또 그냥 '로션'은 얼굴용을 뜻하고, 몸에 바르는 건 반드시 '바디로션'이라고 해요.
동사는 '바르다'를 써요.
영어 lotion은 몸·얼굴을 안 가리지만 한국어에서는 '바디'를 붙이지 않으면 자동으로 얼굴용으로 받아들여요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 선크림 means "sunscreen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 선크림 (seonkeurim) = "sunscreen". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 선크림 발랐어? ("Did you put on sunscreen?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 선크림, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 특히 여름에 아주 흔한 확인·잔소리 표현
꼭 = 빠짐없이; 조언할 때 써요
떨어지다 = 다 써서 없어지다
SPF는 '에스피에프'로 읽어요

examples.ko: 나가기 전에 선크림 바르는 거 잊지 마세요.
examples.romanization: nagagi jeone seonkeurim bareuneun geo itji maseyo.
examples.en: Don't forget to put on sunscreen before going out.
examples.note: 잊지 마세요 = '잊다'의 금지 명령형

examples.ko: 이 선크림은 백탁 현상이 없어서 데일리로 써요.
examples.romanization: i seonkeurimeun baekta kyeonsangi eopseoseo deilliro sseoyo.
examples.en: This sunscreen leaves no white cast, so I use it daily.
examples.note: 백탁 = 하얗게 뜨는 막; 선크림 후기에 꼭 나오는 말

examples.ko: 햇볕이 강한 날은 두세 시간마다 선크림을 덧발라요.
examples.romanization: haetbyeochi ganghan nareun duse siganmada seonkeurimeul deotballayo.
examples.en: On strong-sun days I reapply sunscreen every few hours.
examples.note: 덧바르다 = 위에 다시 바르다; 재도포를 뜻해요

extendedVocab.nuance: 선크림은 자외선을 막아 주는 제품으로, 영어 sunscreen에 한국어 '크림'을 붙여 만든 콩글리시 합성어예요. 한국에서는 여름뿐 아니라 사계절 내내 챙기는 필수품으로 여겨요. 비슷한 말로 '선블록(sunblock)'이 있지만 일상에서는 선크림이 압도적으로 흔하고, 영어처럼 'sunblock'을 말로 쓰면 살짝 번역투로 들려요. 표기에서 가장 자주 틀리는 부분이 첫 글자인데, 된소리 '썬'이 아니라 '선'이 표준이에요(브랜드명에만 '썬'을 써요). 고를 때는 'SPF가 높다', '백탁이 없다', '꾸덕하지 않다' 같은 표현으로 따지고, 동사는 '바르다·덧바르다'를 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'썬크림'처럼 된소리로 적는 것 — 표준 표기는 '선크림'이에요(상표가 아니면 '선'으로 써요)
말할 때 영어 'sunblock'을 쓰는 것 — 한국 사람은 거의 항상 '선크림'이라고 해요
한 번 바르고 끝낸다고 표현하는 것 — 실제로는 '덧바르다(재도포)'가 핵심이라 그 표현을 같이 익혀야 해요

structuredNuance.t: 선크림은 자외선을 막아 주는 제품이에요. 한국에서는 여름뿐 아니라 사계절 내내 챙기는 필수품으로 여겨요. 고를 때는 'SPF가 높다', '백탁이 없다', '꾸덕하지 않다' 같은 표현으로 따져요.
비슷한 말로 '선블록(sunblock)'이 있지만 일상에서는 선크림이 압도적으로 흔하고, 영어처럼 'sunblock'을 말로 쓰면 살짝 번역투로 들려요.
영어 sunscreen에 한국어 '크림'을 붙여 만든 콩글리시 합성어예요. 표기에서 가장 자주 틀리는 부분이 첫 글자인데, 된소리 '썬'이 아니라 '선'이 표준이에요(브랜드명에만 '썬'을 써요).
동사는 '바르다·덧바르다'를 써요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 파운데이션 means "foundation (makeup)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 파운데이션 (paundeisyeon) means "foundation (makeup)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 파운데이션 추천 ("foundation recommendation"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 파운데이션 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 검색어로도, 직원에게 하는 부탁으로도 흔해요
젊은 층이 아주 자주 쓰는 줄임말이에요
커버력 = 가리는 힘; 핵심 스펙이에요
펴 바르는 메이크업이라 동사는 바르다

examples.en: I prefer a natural foundation over high coverage.
examples.note: A보다 B = A보다 B를 더; 비교 조사 '보다'를 익혀요

examples.ko: 파데 색이 너무 밝아서 얼굴이 둥둥 떠요.
examples.romanization: pade saegi neomu balgaseo eolguri dungdung tteoyo.
examples.en: The foundation shade is too light, so my face looks washed out.
examples.note: (얼굴이) 뜨다 = 색이 안 맞아 따로 논다는 관용 표현

examples.ko: 여름엔 무겁지 않고 가벼운 파운데이션을 새로 샀어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen mugeopji anko gabyeoun paundeisyeoneul saero sasseoyo.
examples.en: For summer I bought a new lightweight foundation.
examples.note: 가볍다 = 발림·커버가 산뜻함; 계절별 선택을 보여줘요

extendedVocab.nuance: 파운데이션은 피부톤을 고르게 펴 발라 메이크업의 바탕을 만드는 베이스 화장품으로, 영어 foundation을 그대로 옮긴 외래어예요. 젊은 사람들은 거의 '파데'라고 줄여 말하니 둘 다 알아 두면 좋아요. 비슷한 베이스 제품인 'BB크림·쿠션'과 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 파운데이션은 액체·크림 타입으로 손이나 브러시로 펴 바르고, 쿠션은 퍼프에 묻혀 두드리는 휴대용 형태라는 점이 달라요. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 '칠하다(paint)'를 쓰는 것인데, 화장품은 '바르다'가 맞아요. 고를 때는 '커버력이 좋다', '호수(색번호)가 맞다', '들뜨지 않는다' 같은 표현과 함께 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'칠하다(to paint)'를 쓰는 것 — 파운데이션을 펴 바르는 동작은 '바르다'예요
자기 톤보다 너무 밝은 호수를 고르는 것 — 한국에서는 얼굴이 '둥둥 떠요'라고 표현하며 부자연스럽다고 봐요
파운데이션과 쿠션을 같은 말로 쓰는 것 — 쿠션은 퍼프로 두드리는 휴대형이라 따로 불러요

structuredNuance.t: 파운데이션은 피부톤을 고르게 펴 발라 메이크업의 바탕을 만드는 베이스 화장품이에요. 젊은 사람들은 거의 '파데'라고 줄여 말하니 둘 다 알아 두면 좋아요. 고를 때는 '커버력이 좋다', '호수(색번호)가 맞다', '들뜨지 않는다' 같은 표현과 함께 써요.
비슷한 베이스 제품인 'BB크림·쿠션'과 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 파운데이션은 액체·크림 타입으로 손이나 브러시로 펴 바르고, 쿠션은 퍼프에 묻혀 두드리는 휴대용 형태라는 점이 달라요.
영어 foundation을 그대로 옮긴 외래어예요.
펴 바르는 메이크업이라 동사는 '바르다'가 맞아요.
영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 '칠하다(paint)'를 쓰는 것인데, 화장품은 '바르다'가 맞아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 립스틱 means "lipstick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "lipstick" is 립스틱 (ripseutik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 립스틱 바르다 ("to put on lipstick"). Watch the particle attached to 립스틱 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 바르다
빨간 = 빨갛다의 관형형, '빨간색'도 가능
색 = 컬러; '무슨 색?'으로 물어요
지워지다 = 닦여 없어지다

examples.en: Today I put on red lipstick.
examples.note: 오늘의 메이크업을 설명하는 기본 문장

examples.ko: 이 립스틱은 잘 안 지워져서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i ripseutigeun jal an jiwojyeoseo joayo.
examples.en: I like this lipstick because it doesn't come off easily.
examples.note: 잘 안 ~지다 = 쉽게 ~되지 않다; 지속력을 칭찬해요

examples.ko: 밥 먹다가 컵에 립스틱이 묻어서 다시 발랐어요.
examples.romanization: bam meokdaga keobe ripseutigi mudeoseo dasi ballasseoyo.
examples.en: Lipstick rubbed onto my cup at lunch, so I reapplied.
examples.note: 묻다 = (색·얼룩이) 옮아 붙다; 자동사예요

extendedVocab.nuance: 립스틱은 입술에 색을 입히는 색조 화장품으로, 영어 lipstick을 그대로 가져온 외래어예요. 가장 자주 헷갈리는 짝이 '틴트'인데, 립스틱은 막대형으로 발색이 진하고 매트하거나 촉촉한 막을 입히는 느낌이라면, 틴트는 입술에 색이 '물드는(스며드는)' 가볍고 자연스러운 제형이에요. 그래서 '립스틱은 발랐다는 게 티 나고, 틴트는 자연스럽다'고 흔히 말해요. 동사는 '바르다'가 맞고 '칠하다'는 어색해요. 또 '묻다(색이 옮다)'는 자동사라 '컵에 립스틱이 묻었어요'처럼 색이 주어가 되는 점을 익혀 두면 좋아요. '발색이 좋다', '잘 안 지워진다', '색이 진하다' 같은 말과 자주 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
립스틱과 틴트를 같은 것으로 보는 것 — 틴트는 가볍게 물드는 타입, 립스틱은 진하고 막을 입히는 타입이에요
'립스틱 칠하다'라고 하는 것 — 자연스러운 동사는 '바르다'예요
'묻다'에 목적격 '을/를'을 붙여 '컵에 립스틱을 묻었어요'라고 하는 것 — '묻다'는 자동사라 색이 주어가 되어 '컵에 립스틱이 묻었어요'가 맞아요(일부러 묻힐 때만 타동사 '묻히다'를 써요)

structuredNuance.t: 립스틱은 입술에 색을 입히는 색조 화장품이에요. '발색이 좋다', '잘 안 지워진다', '색이 진하다' 같은 말과 자주 어울려요.
가장 자주 헷갈리는 짝이 '틴트'인데, 립스틱은 막대형으로 발색이 진하고 매트하거나 촉촉한 막을 입히는 느낌이라면, 틴트는 입술에 색이 '물드는(스며드는)' 가볍고 자연스러운 제형이에요. 그래서 '립스틱은 발랐다는 게 티 나고, 틴트는 자연스럽다'고 흔히 말해요.
영어 lipstick을 그대로 가져온 외래어예요.
동사는 '바르다'가 맞고 '칠하다'는 어색해요. 또 '묻다(색이 옮다)'는 자동사라 '컵에 립스틱이 묻었어요'처럼 색이 주어가 되는 점을 익혀 두면 좋아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마스카라 means "mascara" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 마스카라 (maseukara) = "mascara". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마스카라 하다 ("to do/apply mascara") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 마스카라, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 눈 화장은 하다·바르다 둘 다 자연스러워요
워터프루프 = 방수; 흔한 라벨이에요
번지다 = 경계를 넘어 퍼지다
물만으로는 안 지워져 클렌징이 필요해요

examples.en: I teared up, so my mascara smudged everywhere.
examples.note: 번지다 = 퍼져 흐르다; 자동사로 마스카라가 주어예요

examples.ko: 여름엔 땀에 강한 워터프루프 마스카라를 써요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen ttame ganghan woteopeurupeu maseukarareul sseoyo.
examples.en: In summer I use sweat-proof waterproof mascara.
examples.note: 에 강하다 = ~에 잘 견디다; 선택 이유를 말해요

examples.ko: 워터프루프는 클렌징 오일로 살살 녹여서 지워야 해요.
examples.romanization: woteopeurupeuneun keullenjing oillo salsal nogyeoseo jiwoya haeyo.
examples.en: Waterproof mascara needs to be melted off gently with cleansing oil.
examples.note: 살살 = 부드럽게; 제거 방법을 설명해요

extendedVocab.nuance: 마스카라는 속눈썹에 발라 길고 진하게 보이게 하는 눈 화장품으로, 영어 mascara를 옮긴 외래어예요. 비슷한 눈 화장품인 '아이라이너'와 헷갈리면 안 되는데, 마스카라는 속눈썹 자체에 바르는 것이고 아이라이너는 눈가에 선을 그리는 것이라 부위와 도구가 달라요. 동사는 '바르다'와 '하다'를 모두 쓸 수 있어요. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 부분은 '번지다'를 타동사로 오해하는 건데, '번지다'는 자동사라 '마스카라가 번졌어요'처럼 마스카라가 주어가 돼요. 또 워터프루프 타입은 물세수로 안 지워지므로 반드시 클렌징 제품으로 지워야 하고, 잘못 지우면 눈가에 번져 이른바 '판다 눈'이 된다고 표현해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
워터프루프 마스카라를 물·폼클렌저만으로 지우려는 것 — 오일 클렌징이 있어야 깨끗이 지워져요
마스카라(속눈썹)와 아이라이너(눈가 선)를 섞어 쓰는 것 — 부위가 다른 별개 제품이에요
'번지다'를 타동사로 쓰는 것 — '내가 마스카라를 번졌다'가 아니라 '마스카라가 번졌다'가 맞아요

structuredNuance.t: 마스카라는 속눈썹에 발라 길고 진하게 보이게 하는 눈 화장품이에요. 워터프루프 타입은 물세수로 안 지워지므로 반드시 클렌징 제품으로 지워야 하고, 잘못 지우면 눈가에 번져 이른바 '판다 눈'이 된다고 표현해요.
비슷한 눈 화장품인 '아이라이너'와 헷갈리면 안 되는데, 마스카라는 속눈썹 자체에 바르는 것이고 아이라이너는 눈가에 선을 그리는 것이라 부위와 도구가 달라요.
영어 mascara를 옮긴 외래어예요.
동사는 '바르다'와 '하다'를 모두 쓸 수 있어요. '번지다'는 자동사라 '마스카라가 번졌어요'처럼 마스카라가 주어가 돼요.
영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 부분은 '번지다'를 타동사로 오해하는 건데, '번지다'는 자동사라 '마스카라가 번졌어요'처럼 마스카라가 주어가 돼요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 클렌징 means "cleansing (makeup removal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 클렌징 (keullenjing) means "cleansing (makeup removal)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 클렌징 오일 ("cleansing oil"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 클렌징 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 오일 타입; 진한 화장에 잘 맞아요

usagePhrases.en: to do one's cleansing / remove makeup
usagePhrases.note: 하다를 붙이면 동사가 돼요
클렌징(1차) + 폼클렌저(2차)를 잇는 루틴
워터 타입; 순하고 빨라요

examples.ko: 화장을 진하게 했으면 클렌징을 꼼꼼히 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: hwajangeul jinhage haesseumyeon keullenjingeul kkomkkomhi haeya haeyo.
examples.en: If you wore heavy makeup, you have to cleanse thoroughly.
examples.note: 꼼꼼히 = 빈틈없이; -았/었으면 조건과 함께 써요

examples.ko: 저는 보통 클렌징 오일로 화장을 지워요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun botong keullenjing oillo hwajangeul jiwoyo.
examples.en: I usually remove my makeup with cleansing oil.
examples.note: (으)로 = 수단·도구 조사; 무엇으로 지우는지 표현

examples.ko: 클렌징을 건너뛰고 그냥 자면 다음 날 피부가 뒤집어져요.
examples.romanization: keullenjingeul geonneottwigo geunyang jamyeon daeum nal pibuga dwijibeojyeoyo.
examples.en: If I skip cleansing and just sleep, my skin breaks out the next day.
examples.note: 뒤집어지다 = 피부가 확 안 좋아지다(구어)

extendedVocab.nuance: 클렌징은 화장과 노폐물을 녹여 지우는 세안 단계를 통틀어 가리키는 외래어로, '클렌징 하다'처럼 '하다'를 붙여 동사로 써요. 핵심 구분은 그냥 물로 씻는 '세수'와의 차이예요. 세수는 물·비누로 얼굴을 씻는 일반 동작이고, 클렌징은 메이크업까지 전용 제품으로 '녹여서' 지운다는 점이 달라요. 그래서 물세수(물만으로 씻기)는 클렌징으로 치지 않아요. 오일·밤·워터 등 제형이 다양하고, 화장이 진한 날은 클렌징 후 폼클렌저로 한 번 더 씻는 '이중 세안'을 권해요. '꼼꼼히 하다', '화장을 지우다', '건너뛰다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
물세수(물만으로 씻기)를 클렌징으로 여기는 것 — 메이크업은 전용 클렌징 제품으로 녹여 지워야 해요
'클렌징'과 '세수'를 같은 말로 쓰는 것 — 세수는 기본 세안, 클렌징은 화장 제거 단계예요
클렌징을 영어 발음 'cleansing'으로만 떠올려 동사화를 빼먹는 것 — 한국어에서는 '클렌징 하다'로 써요

structuredNuance.t: 클렌징은 화장과 노폐물을 녹여 지우는 세안 단계를 통틀어 가리켜요. 오일·밤·워터 등 제형이 다양하고, 화장이 진한 날은 클렌징 후 폼클렌저로 한 번 더 씻는 '이중 세안'을 권해요. '꼼꼼히 하다', '화장을 지우다', '건너뛰다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
핵심 구분은 그냥 물로 씻는 '세수'와의 차이예요. 세수는 물·비누로 얼굴을 씻는 일반 동작이고, 클렌징은 메이크업까지 전용 제품으로 '녹여서' 지운다는 점이 달라요. 그래서 물세수(물만으로 씻기)는 클렌징으로 치지 않아요.
외래어(cleansing)예요.
'클렌징 하다'처럼 '하다'를 붙여 동사로 써요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 토너 means "toner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "toner" is 토너 (toneo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 토너 패드 ("toner pads"). Watch the particle attached to 토너 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 미리 적셔 둔 패드; 한국에서 아주 인기예요
각질을 부드럽게 정리해 주는 토너
스킨과 같은 단계, 동사는 바르다
진정 = 자극을 가라앉힘; 민감 피부용 라벨

examples.ko: 세안 후에 토너로 피부 결을 정돈해요.
examples.romanization: sean hue toneoro pibu gyeoreul jeongdonhaeyo.
examples.en: After washing, I smooth my skin's texture with toner.
examples.note: 결 = 표면 무늬·질감; 정돈하다 = 가지런히 하다

examples.en: Toner pads are really popular these days.
examples.note: 패드 타입은 최근 한국 뷰티 트렌드예요

examples.ko: 각질이 잘 일어나서 일주일에 두 번만 각질 토너를 써요.
examples.romanization: gakjiri jal ireonaseo iljuire du beonman gakjil toneoreul sseoyo.
examples.en: My skin flakes easily, so I use exfoliating toner only twice a week.
examples.note: 만 = 한정 조사; 과한 사용 주의를 보여줘요

extendedVocab.nuance: 토너는 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 제품으로, 사실상 '스킨'과 같은 단계를 가리키는 외래어(toner)예요. 둘의 분담을 알아 두면 좋은데, 일상 회화에서는 '스킨'이, 제품 설명·마케팅이나 기능을 강조할 때는 '토너'가 더 흔하게 쓰이는 느낌이에요. 그래서 같은 병을 두고 친구끼리는 '스킨 발랐어?'라고 하고, 광고에서는 '○○ 토너'라고 부르는 식이에요. 특히 '토너 패드', '각질 토너', '진정 토너'처럼 합성어로 자주 등장해요. 영어 화자가 두 단어를 다른 제품으로 오해하기 쉬운데 본질은 같은 단계라는 점이 핵심이고, 동사는 '바르다'를 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
토너와 스킨을 서로 다른 제품으로 생각하는 것 — 본질적으로 같은 첫 단계예요(이름·뉘앙스만 달라요)
각질 토너를 매일 쓰는 것 — 자주 쓰면 오히려 피부가 예민해질 수 있어요
토너에 '하다'를 붙여 '토너 하다'라고 하는 것 — 바르는 제품이라 '토너 바르다'가 맞아요

structuredNuance.t: 토너는 세안 후 가장 먼저 바르는 제품으로, 사실상 '스킨'과 같은 단계를 가리켜요. 특히 '토너 패드', '각질 토너', '진정 토너'처럼 합성어로 자주 등장해요.
'스킨'과의 분담을 알아 두면 좋은데, 일상 회화에서는 '스킨'이, 제품 설명·마케팅이나 기능을 강조할 때는 '토너'가 더 흔하게 쓰이는 느낌이에요. 그래서 같은 병을 두고 친구끼리는 '스킨 발랐어?'라고 하고, 광고에서는 '○○ 토너'라고 부르는 식이에요.
외래어(toner)예요.
동사는 '바르다'를 써요.
영어 화자가 토너와 스킨 두 단어를 다른 제품으로 오해하기 쉬운데, 본질은 같은 단계라는 점이 핵심이에요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 향수 means "perfume" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 향수 (hyangsu) = "perfume". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 향수 뿌리다 ("to spray perfume") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 향수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 바르다가 아니라 뿌리다예요
향 = 냄새·향기; '향이 좋다'처럼 써요
매장·온라인에서 흔한 요청
은은하다 = 진하지 않고 잔잔하다, 칭찬이에요

examples.en: Don't spray on too much perfume.
examples.note: 사무실·지하철 예절과 관련된 부탁

examples.ko: 이 향수는 향이 은은해서 부담이 없어요.
examples.romanization: i hyangsuneun hyangi euneunhaeseo budami eopseoyo.
examples.en: This perfume is subtle, so it isn't overpowering.
examples.note: 부담이 없다 = 거슬리지 않다; 향수 평에 흔해요

examples.ko: 면접 보러 갈 때는 향수를 안 뿌리는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop boreo gal ttaeneun hyangsureul an ppurineun ge joayo.
examples.en: It's better not to wear perfume when going to a job interview.
examples.note: 면접 = 면접 시험; 거주자에게 실용적인 조언

extendedVocab.nuance: 향수(香水)는 한자 그대로 '향기 향(香)' + '물 수(水)', 즉 '향기 나는 물'이라는 뜻의 한자어예요. 핵심 포인트는 동사인데, 향수는 분사형이라 '바르다'가 아니라 '뿌리다'와 함께 써요. 영어 'put on/wear perfume'을 직역해 '향수 바르다'라고 하면 어색하니 주의하세요. 비슷한 향 제품과도 구분되는데, 농도가 옅고 가벼운 건 보통 '향수' 안에서 오 드 뚜왈렛 등으로 나뉘고, 더 넓게는 '바디미스트'처럼 따로 부르는 제품도 있어요. 한국에서는 좁은 지하철·사무실을 의식해 '은은한' 향을 선호하는 분위기가 강하고, 너무 강하면 '향이 세다'며 다소 부정적으로 봐요. '향이 좋다·은은하다·오래간다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'향수 바르다'라고 하는 것 — 향수는 뿌리는 제품이라 동사 '뿌리다'를 써요
향을 너무 진하게 쓰는 것 — 한국의 사무실·대중교통 예절은 '은은한' 향을 선호해요
'향'과 '향수'를 섞어 쓰는 것 — '향'은 냄새 자체, '향수'는 그 향을 내는 제품이에요

structuredNuance.t: 향수는 '향기 나는 물'을 뜻해요. 한국에서는 좁은 지하철·사무실을 의식해 '은은한' 향을 선호하는 분위기가 강하고, 너무 강하면 '향이 세다'며 다소 부정적으로 봐요. '향이 좋다·은은하다·오래간다' 같은 표현과 잘 어울려요.
비슷한 향 제품과도 구분되는데, 농도가 옅고 가벼운 건 보통 '향수' 안에서 오 드 뚜왈렛 등으로 나뉘고, 더 넓게는 '바디미스트'처럼 따로 부르는 제품도 있어요.

핵심 포인트는 동사인데, 향수는 분사형이라 '바르다'가 아니라 '뿌리다'와 함께 써요.
영어 'put on/wear perfume'을 직역해 '향수 바르다'라고 하면 어색하니 주의하세요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매니큐어 means "nail polish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 매니큐어 (maenikyueo) means "nail polish". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 매니큐어 바르다 ("to apply nail polish"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 매니큐어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 동사는 바르다
리무버(remover)가 있어야 지워져요
색 = 컬러; 원하는 색을 골라요
젤네일은 더 오래가는 살롱 시술이에요

examples.en: I painted my nails at home over the weekend.
examples.note: 집에서 직접 하는 셀프 네일 상황

examples.en: My polish chipped, so I removed it with remover.
examples.note: 벗겨지다 = (막이) 떨어져 나가다; 자동사예요

examples.ko: 젤네일은 매니큐어보다 훨씬 오래가서 자주 안 해도 돼요.
examples.romanization: jelneireun maenikyueoboda hwolssin oraegaseo jaju an haedo dwaeyo.
examples.en: Gel lasts much longer than regular polish, so I redo it less often.
examples.note: 보다 = 비교 조사; 살롱 젤 vs 셀프 매니큐어 대비

extendedVocab.nuance: 한국어 '매니큐어'는 영어 manicure와 뜻이 어긋나는 대표적 함정 단어예요. 영어 manicure는 '손톱·손 관리 서비스 전체'를 뜻하지만, 한국어 매니큐어는 손톱에 바르는 색깔 있는 액체, 즉 영어로는 nail polish를 가리켜요. 그래서 손 관리 서비스를 말하려면 '네일(아트)', '네일 케어'라고 해야 해요. 더 오래가는 살롱 시술은 '젤네일'이라 따로 부르는데, 젤네일은 전용 램프에 굳혀 2~3주 가는 반면 매니큐어는 며칠이면 벗겨지는 차이가 있어요. 동사는 '바르다'이고, 지울 때는 '리무버'가 필요해요. '벗겨지다(막이 떨어지다)'는 자동사라 '매니큐어가 벗겨졌어요'처럼 매니큐어가 주어가 돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
매니큐어를 '손 관리 서비스(manicure)'라는 뜻으로 쓰는 것 — 한국어에서는 바르는 '네일 폴리시'를 뜻하고, 서비스는 '네일'이라고 해요
리무버 없이 매니큐어를 지우려는 것 — 전용 리무버가 있어야 지워져요
저절로 벗겨진 걸 말하면서 '매니큐어를 벗겨졌어요'처럼 '을/를'을 붙이는 것 — '벗겨지다'는 자동사라 '매니큐어가 벗겨졌어요'가 맞아요(내가 일부러 떼어 낼 때만 타동사 '벗기다'를 써요)

structuredNuance.t: 한국어 매니큐어는 손톱에 바르는 색깔 있는 액체, 즉 영어로는 nail polish를 가리켜요. 손 관리 서비스를 말하려면 '네일(아트)', '네일 케어'라고 해야 해요.
더 오래가는 살롱 시술은 '젤네일'이라 따로 부르는데, 젤네일은 전용 램프에 굳혀 2~3주 가는 반면 매니큐어는 며칠이면 벗겨지는 차이가 있어요.
동사는 '바르다'이고, 지울 때는 '리무버'가 필요해요. '벗겨지다(막이 떨어지다)'는 자동사라 '매니큐어가 벗겨졌어요'처럼 매니큐어가 주어가 돼요.
한국어 '매니큐어'는 영어 manicure와 뜻이 어긋나는 대표적 함정 단어예요. 영어 manicure는 '손톱·손 관리 서비스 전체'를 뜻하지만, 한국어에서는 바르는 액체(nail polish)를 가리켜요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 각질 means "dead skin, flaky skin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "dead skin, flaky skin" is 각질 (gakjil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 각질 제거 ("exfoliation (dead-skin removal)"). Watch the particle attached to 각질 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 제거 = 없앰; 흔한 제품·시술 이름
일어나다 = (살갗이) 들떠 일어나다
관리 = 꾸준히 돌봄
제거제 = 없애 주는 제품

examples.en: It's winter, so my face is getting flaky.
examples.note: 일어나다 = 살갗이 들뜨다; 자동사예요

examples.ko: 저는 일주일에 한 번만 각질을 제거해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun iljuire han beonman gakjireul jegeohaeyo.
examples.en: I exfoliate just once a week.
examples.note: 만 = 한정; 과하지 않게 한다는 뉘앙스

examples.ko: 각질이 많으면 화장이 잘 안 먹어서 들떠 보여요.
examples.romanization: gakjiri maneumyeon hwajangi jal an meogeoseo deultteo boyeoyo.
examples.en: With lots of dead skin, makeup doesn't take well and looks patchy.
examples.note: 화장이 안 먹다 = 화장이 잘 안 받다(관용구)

extendedVocab.nuance: 각질(角質)은 한자로 '뿔 각(角)' + '바탕 질(質)', 곧 피부 표면의 단단해진 죽은 세포층을 뜻하는 한자어로, 영어의 dead skin·keratin에 해당해요. 일상에서는 얼굴이나 몸에서 하얗게 들뜨거나 벗겨지는 살갗을 가리켜요. 헷갈리기 쉬운 피부 고민인 '여드름'과는 달라요 — 여드름은 모공이 막혀 생기는 뾰루지이고, 각질은 표면의 묵은 살갗이에요. 각질이 많으면 '화장이 안 먹는다(잘 받지 않는다)'는 관용 표현과 함께 자주 쓰여요. 동사 짝으로 '각질이 일어나다(들뜨다)'는 자동사라 각질이 주어가 되고, 없앨 때는 '각질을 제거하다'처럼 타동사로 써요. 다만 너무 자주 제거하면 피부가 오히려 예민해질 수 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
각질(묵은 살갗)과 여드름(뾰루지)을 같은 문제로 보는 것 — 원인과 관리법이 달라요
각질을 너무 자주 제거하는 것 — 피부 장벽이 약해져 오히려 예민해져요
'일어나다'를 사람 주어로 오해하는 것 — '각질이 일어나다'에서 일어나는 주체는 사람이 아니라 각질이에요

structuredNuance.t: 각질은 피부 표면의 단단해진 죽은 세포층으로, 영어의 dead skin·keratin에 해당해요. 일상에서는 얼굴이나 몸에서 하얗게 들뜨거나 벗겨지는 살갗을 가리켜요. 각질이 많으면 '화장이 안 먹는다(잘 받지 않는다)'는 관용 표현과 함께 자주 쓰여요. 다만 너무 자주 제거하면 피부가 오히려 예민해질 수 있어요.
헷갈리기 쉬운 피부 고민인 '여드름'과는 달라요 — 여드름은 모공이 막혀 생기는 뾰루지이고, 각질은 표면의 묵은 살갗이에요.
각질(角質)은 한자로 '뿔 각(角)' + '바탕 질(質)', 곧 피부 표면의 단단해진 죽은 세포층을 뜻하는 한자어예요.
동사 짝으로 '각질이 일어나다(들뜨다)'는 자동사라 각질이 주어가 되고, 없앨 때는 '각질을 제거하다'처럼 타동사로 써요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 화장솜 means "cotton pad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 화장솜 (hwajangsom) = "cotton pad". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 화장솜에 토너 묻히다 ("to dab toner on a cotton pad") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 화장솜, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to dab toner on a cotton pad
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = 적셔서 배게 하다(타동사)

usagePhrases.en: to wipe with a cotton pad
usagePhrases.note: 닦다 = 문질러 깨끗이 하다
단위는 장(얇고 납작한 것)
매니큐어 지울 때도 써요

examples.en: I soak a cotton pad with toner and wipe my face.
examples.note: 묻히다(타동사) + 닦다; 토너 사용법을 보여줘요

examples.ko: 매니큐어 지울 때 화장솜에 리무버를 적셔서 써요.
examples.romanization: maenikyueo jiul ttae hwajangsome rimubeoreul jeoksyeoseo sseoyo.
examples.en: When removing polish, I soak a cotton pad with remover.
examples.note: 적시다 = 액체에 젖게 하다; 묻히다와 비슷해요

examples.ko: 화장솜이 다 떨어져서 다이소에서 한 통 샀어요.
examples.romanization: hwajangsomi da tteoreojyeoseo daisoeseo han tong sasseoyo.
examples.en: I ran out of cotton pads, so I bought a tub at Daiso.
examples.note: 통 = 통째 용기 단위; 자취 생필품 느낌

extendedVocab.nuance: 화장솜은 '화장(化粧)' + 순우리말 '솜(cotton wool)'이 합쳐진 말로, 스킨이나 리무버를 묻혀 얼굴·손톱을 닦는 동그란 화장용 솜을 뜻해요. 발음이 비슷한 '화장지(化粧紙, 휴지·tissue)'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 화장솜은 액체를 머금는 두툼한 솜이고 화장지는 코를 풀거나 닦는 얇은 종이라 완전히 다른 물건이에요. 다이소·올리브영에서 싸게 사는 생필품이라 자취생이 자주 사요. 세는 단위로는 '개'가 아니라 얇고 납작한 것을 세는 '장'을 쓰는 게 자연스러워요. 자주 어울리는 동사는 '(토너를) 묻히다·적시다', '(얼굴을) 닦다'이고, '한 장 뽑다', '다 떨어지다' 같은 표현과도 함께 쓰여요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
화장솜을 '화장지(tissue)'나 '휴지'와 혼동하는 것 — 화장솜은 액체를 머금는 화장용 솜이에요
단위를 잘못 쓰는 것 — 화장솜은 '개'가 아니라 얇고 납작한 것을 세는 '장'으로 세요
'묻다'와 '묻히다'를 헷갈리는 것 — 솜에 토너를 적실 때는 타동사 '묻히다'를 써서 '토너를 묻혀요'라고 해요

structuredNuance.t: 화장솜은 스킨이나 리무버를 묻혀 얼굴·손톱을 닦는 동그란 화장용 솜이에요. 다이소·올리브영에서 싸게 사는 생필품이라 자취생이 자주 사요. 세는 단위로는 '개'가 아니라 얇고 납작한 것을 세는 '장'을 쓰는 게 자연스러워요. '한 장 뽑다', '다 떨어지다' 같은 표현과도 함께 쓰여요.
발음이 비슷한 '화장지(化粧紙, 휴지·tissue)'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 화장솜은 액체를 머금는 두툼한 솜이고 화장지는 코를 풀거나 닦는 얇은 종이라 완전히 다른 물건이에요.
화장솜은 '화장(化粧)' + 순우리말 '솜(cotton wool)'이 합쳐진 말이에요.
자주 어울리는 동사는 '(토너를) 묻히다·적시다', '(얼굴을) 닦다'예요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 니트 means "knit top / sweater" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 니트 (niteu) means "knit top / sweater". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 니트를 입다 ("to wear a knit top"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 니트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: any upper-body garment takes 입다, never 신다/쓰다
따갑다 (prickly) is the #1 wool complaint; don't say 가렵다, which is 'my skin itches'
clothing is counted with the counter 벌, not the generic 개
Koreans size up a sweater by thickness, so 얇다·두껍다 are the habitual adjectives

examples.en: It's a bit chilly today so I wore a knit.
examples.note: simplest frame: weather reason + 입다 in casual 해요체

examples.ko: 이 니트 목 부분이 따가운데 다른 색도 있어요?
examples.romanization: i niteu mok bubuni ttagaunde dareun saekdo isseoyo?
examples.en: The neck of this knit is itchy — do you have other colors too?
examples.note: real in-store line; 따갑다 describes the prickly wool sensation, not skin itch

examples.ko: 캐시미어 니트는 보풀이 잘 생겨서 손빨래해야 해요.
examples.romanization: kaesimieo niteuneun bopuri jal saenggyeoseo sonppallaehaeya haeyo.
examples.en: Cashmere knits pill easily so you have to hand-wash them.
examples.note: care talk: 보풀이 생기다 = to pill, 손빨래 = hand-wash

extendedVocab.nuance: 니트 comes from English 'knit', but in everyday Korean it has narrowed to mean one specific thing: a sweater-type pullover top, the fall/winter staple — NOT 'any knitted item' as in English. Its near-synonym 스웨터 exists but sounds slightly dated or textbook-ish; a real Korean shopper says 니트 far more often, and the two are interchangeable when they do appear. The dividing line worth knowing is 니트 (a finished sweater garment) versus 가디건 (an open-front knit you button up): both are knitwear, but 니트 closes over the head while 가디건 opens at the front. Register is fully neutral — you can say 니트 to anyone. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the verb: because you put it on the body you must use 입다, and saying 니트를 신다 (that's for shoes) or 쓰다 (hats/glasses) sounds badly wrong. Also resist the literal logic 'knit = anything knitted'; in Korean it is the garment, and the prickly complaint is 따갑다, distinct from 가렵다 (skin itching).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 니트를 신다 or 니트를 쓰다 — those verbs are for footwear and headwear; a sweater goes on the torso, so it must be 니트를 입다.
Assuming 니트 covers any knitted object (scarf, hat, blanket) like English 'knit' does — in daily Korean it specifically means a sweater-type top, so use 모자/목도리 for the others.
Describing the itch as 니트가 가려워요 — 가렵다 means your skin itches; the prickly-fabric feeling Koreans name is 따갑다, so say 니트가 따가워요.

Forgetting to specify 롱/숏 — Koreans almost always say which length, so just 패딩 주세요 sounds vague; say 롱패딩 / 숏패딩.
Using 신다 or 쓰다 because it's bulky outerwear — it still sits on the torso, so the verb is 입다.

The sharp near-synonym contrast is 후드티 (pullover, goes over the head) vs 후드집업 (the zip-up hooded jacket, 집업 from 'zip-up'): Koreans name these as two distinct products, so a learner who lumps them together will ask for the wrong rack. extendedVocab.nuance: 부츠 is straightforwardly English 'boots' and covers footwear rising above the ankle. The single most important thing for an English speaker is the verb: shoes and boots take 신다 (put on the feet), and 입다 — the verb for body clothing — is simply wrong here, a mistake learners make constantly because English uses one word 'wear' for everything. Korean also splits the counter: clothing is 벌 but footwear is 켤레 (a pair), so 부츠 한 켤레, never 부츠 한 개. Lengths get named — 발목 부츠 (ankle boots, also 앵클부츠) vs 롱부츠 (tall boots) — and winter shearling ones are 털부츠 (털 = fur). One more practical trap: Korean shoe sizes are millimeters (245 means 245 mm), so quote the number, not a US/EU size. Register is neutral; say 부츠 to anyone.

Giving a US/EU shoe size — Korean sizing is in mm, so 'size 8' means nothing in store; say the number like 245 or 250.

extendedVocab.nuance: 맨투맨 looks like English but is pure Konglish: it literally reads 'man-to-man', yet it means a crewneck sweatshirt — a round-necked, hood-less pullover. The decisive near-synonym contrast is 맨투맨 (no hood) vs 후드티 (hood added): they are the same body of garment differing only by the hood, and Koreans pick the word precisely, so mixing them up sends you to the wrong product. extendedVocab.nuance: 슬리퍼 (English 'slipper') in Korea covers open-backed slides worn both as indoor 실내화 and for quick neighborhood errands — broader than the cozy house-slipper the English word suggests. Culturally, the two-strap 삼선 슬리퍼 ('three-stripe slides') is practically a badge of the broke-but-comfy university/자취 (living-alone) student, so you'll hear it referenced affectionately. Register is casual. Bonus contrast: indoor 실내화 vs outdoor wearing is just context, same word.

Calling flip-flops 슬리퍼 — the toe-thong type is specifically 쪼리; reserve 슬리퍼 for open-backed slides.
Counting them 한 개 — footwear pairs are counted with 켤레, so 슬리퍼 한 켤레.

extendedVocab.nuance: 조끼 is a native Korean word (not a loanword) for a sleeveless top layer — it covers the torso while leaving the arms free. The near-synonym to know is the loanword 베스트 (from English 'vest'), which tends to be used for the dressy waistcoat in a suit, whereas plain 조끼 is the all-purpose everyday/outdoor sleeveless layer; both can mean 'vest', but a Korean reaches for 조끼 for the casual or padded kind. The hugely popular variant is 패딩 조끼 (puffer vest), a go-to for 환절기/간절기 (the changing seasons), and the arm-freedom makes 조끼 a favorite for hiking and outdoor work. The main contrast students confuse is 조끼 (sleeveless) vs 가디건 (sleeved open-front knit) — if it has sleeves it isn't a 조끼. Register is neutral. Use 입다, not 신다/쓰다; it's body clothing despite covering only the trunk.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 조끼 (sleeveless) with 가디건 (a sleeved open-front knit) — a vest has no sleeves, so the two are different garments.
Using 신다 or 쓰다 — it's worn on the torso, so the verb is 입다.
Assuming 조끼 always means a formal waistcoat — the dressy suit version is often called 베스트; plain 조끼 is the casual/padded all-rounder.

extendedVocab.nuance: 스카프 (English 'scarf') in Korean specifically means the LIGHT, decorative cloth — often silk — you tie around the neck, head, or even a bag handle, worn for style rather than warmth. The essential near-synonym contrast is 스카프 vs 목도리/머플러: 목도리 (native word) and 머플러 (from 'muffler') are the thick, warm winter neck-wraps, while 스카프 is the thin fashion piece — confusing them means wearing the wrong thing for the wrong purpose. The verb is its own pitfall: accessories like this take 하다 ('스카프를 하다') or 두르다 ('wrap'), and the body-clothing verb 입다 is wrong here, just as it would be for 모자 (which takes 쓰다). Because it's a thin flat sheet, the counter is 장, not the clothing counter 벌. Register is neutral. A current collocation: tying a 스카프 onto a 가방 (bag) is a popular styling trick.

Using 입다 for a scarf — neck accessories take 하다 or 두르다, so say 스카프를 하다 / 스카프를 두르다.
Counting it with the clothing counter 벌 — a thin flat cloth uses 장, so 스카프 한 장.

extendedVocab.nuance: 백팩 is English 'backpack' and names the two-shoulder bag carried on the back. The verb is the heart of the matter: bags worn on the shoulder or back take 메다, while 들다 means to carry by hand (a tote, a paper bag) and is wrong for a backpack — English's single 'carry' hides this, so 백팩을 들다 is a classic slip when you mean wearing it on your back. extendedVocab.nuance: 운동복 is a transparent Sino-Korean + native compound: 운동 (運動, 'exercise/movement') + 복 (服, 'clothing') = literally 'exercise-clothes', the umbrella term for activewear, both top and bottom. Because the hanja 복 means 'clothing/garment' generally, you'll meet it across many words (교복 school uniform, 한복 traditional dress, 수영복 swimsuit), which makes 운동복 easy to decode once you know the building block. The near-synonym to weigh is 트레이닝복 (from 'training'): that leans toward the matching tracksuit/sweats set (casually 츄리닝), while 운동복 spans gym, yoga, and running gear more broadly — overlapping but not identical. A subtle point for English speakers: 운동복 normally denotes a top-and-bottom SET, so it's counted 한 벌 and 'wear' is 입다, not 신다/쓰다. With athleisure now everywhere, people 평소에도 (even normally) wear 운동복, so it surfaces well beyond the gym. Register is neutral.

extendedVocab.explanation: 잔 (jan) means "glass; cup (counter for drinks)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 커피 한 잔 ("one cup of coffee"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday default: 잔 covers any served drink — coffee, tea, water, beer, soju.
Bar shorthand for another round; you'll hear this constantly while drinking together.
Written as ONE word, this is a verb meaning 'go have a (casual) drink', not literally one glass.
Spacing matters: number + space + 잔 (세 잔), never 세잔.

examples.en: One glass of water, please.
examples.note: Simplest form: [noun] + [native number] + 잔. The counter comes AFTER the number, before the verb.

examples.ko: 저는 하루에 커피를 세 잔씩 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun harue keopireul se janssing masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink three cups of coffee each day.
examples.note: Note 씩 ('each/per') after the counter — '세 잔씩' = three cups apiece per day, a natural habit phrase.

examples.ko: 딱 한 잔만 더 하고 갈게요.
examples.romanization: tta kan janman deo hago galgeyo.
examples.en: I'll have just one more drink and then go.
examples.note: Real bar line: 딱...만 = 'just exactly one', and 한 잔 하다 here means 'have a drink', not eat.

extendedVocab.nuance: 잔 is the counter for a serving of liquid held in a cup or glass — it counts the POURED drink, not the container itself. Its near-rivals are 병 (a whole bottle) and 컵 (the physical cup as an object), and the dividing line is what you're measuring: 맥주 한 병 is a full bottle, 맥주 한 잔 is one glass poured from it. The hanja is 盞 ('small cup'), though it feels fully native in use and always takes native-Korean numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean 일/이. Watch two traps: 한잔하다 written together is a VERB ('go for a drink') and is idiomatic, so don't read it as a literal count; and English 'a cup of coffee' tempts learners to reach for 컵, but the natural measure word for the drink itself is 잔.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 일 잔, 이 잔 with Sino-Korean numbers. Counters of servings take native numbers: 한 잔, 두 잔, 세 잔.
Using 잔 to count bottles. A sealed/whole bottle is 병 (맥주 두 병); 잔 is only the glass poured out.
Writing the drink-verb as two words '한 잔 하다' when you mean the idiom 'grab a drink' — the set verb is 한잔하다, one word.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 켤레 means "pair (counter for shoes, socks, gloves)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "pair (counter for shoes, socks, gloves)" is 켤레 (kyeolle). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신발 한 켤레 ("one pair of shoes"). Watch the particle attached to 켤레 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 켤레 counts things worn as a matching two-of-a-kind: shoes, socks, gloves.
Native numbers only: 한, 두, 세 켤레 — never 일 켤레.
The go-to question form when buying footwear or socks.
Gloves arrive as a set of two, so 켤레, not 개.

examples.en: I want to buy a pair of sneakers.
examples.note: Basic shape: [item] + 한 켤레. One 켤레 = the whole pair, both shoes together.

examples.en: Three pairs of socks are 5,000 won.
examples.note: Market pricing pattern: [quantity]에 [price]. 세 켤레에 = 'for three pairs'.

examples.ko: 등산하려고 두꺼운 양말 두 켤레를 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: deungsanharyeogo dukkeoun yangmal du kyeollereul chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I packed two pairs of thick socks to go hiking.
examples.note: 두 켤레를 marks the object; -려고 ('in order to') gives the purpose.

extendedVocab.nuance: 켤레 is the dedicated counter for items that come and are worn as a matched pair — shoes, sneakers, boots, socks, and gloves. The key conceptual point is that ONE 켤레 already means BOTH pieces together (the left and the right), so it functions like English 'a pair'; its near-synonym 짝, by contrast, isolates a SINGLE one of the two, as in 양말 한 짝 ('one sock' — implying its partner is missing). 켤레 is a native Korean word (no hanja) and always pairs with native numbers (한, 두, 세 켤레). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 because English counts 'a pair of shoes' as one set of objects — but footwear and hand/foot-wear that come in twos must take 켤레; another is calling a single lost shoe 한 켤레, when one of the pair is 한 짝.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting shoes with 개. 개 is the all-purpose counter for generic objects; matched footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레).
Saying 두 켤레 for one pair. A single pair (both shoes) is 한 켤레; 두 켤레 means two complete pairs.
Calling one sock 한 켤레. A lone single of the pair is 한 짝 (양말 한 짝); 켤레 always means both.

structuredNuance.t: 켤레 is the dedicated counter for items that come and are worn as a matched pair — shoes, sneakers, boots, socks, and gloves. The key conceptual point is that ONE 켤레 already means BOTH pieces together (the left and the right), so it functions like English 'a pair'. It always pairs with native numbers (한, 두, 세 켤레).
Its near-synonym 짝, by contrast, isolates a SINGLE one of the two, as in 양말 한 짝 ('one sock' — implying its partner is missing).
켤레 is a native Korean word (no hanja).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 벌 means "counter for sets of clothing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 벌 (beol) = "counter for sets of clothing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 옷 한 벌 ("one outfit/set of clothes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 벌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 벌 counts a complete garment or coordinated set: a suit, a dress, pajamas, hanbok.
A suit (jacket + trousers) counts as a single 벌 — one set.
Asks the count of garments or sets.
Native numbers go before 벌: 한, 두, 세 벌.

examples.en: I'm planning to buy a set of pajamas.
examples.note: Simple: [clothing] + 한 벌. Pajamas (top + bottom) are one 벌, not two.

examples.ko: 출근용 정장을 한 벌 새로 맞췄어요.
examples.romanization: chulgeunyong jeongjangeul han beol saero matchwosseoyo.
examples.en: I had a new work suit custom-made.
examples.note: 맞추다 = 'have tailor-made'; 출근용 = 'for commuting/work'. The whole suit = 한 벌.

examples.ko: 이번 여행에는 갈아입을 옷을 세 벌만 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeohaengeneun garaibeul oseul se beolman chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: For this trip I packed only three changes of clothes.
examples.note: 세 벌만 = 'just three sets'; 갈아입다 = 'to change clothes'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 벌 counts clothing as a COMPLETE garment or a coordinated outfit, so a suit, dress, hanbok, or pajama set is 한 벌 even though it physically has several pieces — the counter measures the whole worn unit, not the parts. Its near-synonyms split by what they measure: 벌 is the full set, while 장 counts a single flat piece (티셔츠 한 장 — one tee) and 개 is the casual generic count. 벌 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. The biggest English-speaker trap is logic-counting the pieces: a two-piece suit feels like 'two items', but the matching set is 한 벌, not 두 벌. A second trap is genre confusion — clothes are 벌, but the shoes that complete the look are 켤레, so don't say 신발 한 벌.

Counting a two-piece suit as 두 벌. The jacket-and-trousers set together is 한 벌 (one set).
Using 벌 for shoes. Footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레); clothing takes 벌.
Counting a single T-shirt as 한 벌 in casual speech. A flat single top is more naturally 티셔츠 한 장 or 한 개; 벌 leans toward full sets.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 권 means "counter for books and volumes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 권 (gwon) means "counter for books and volumes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 책 한 권 ("one book"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 권 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 권 counts bound things: books, notebooks, magazines, comic volumes.
Native numbers go before 권: 한, 두, 세 권.
The standard quantity question for anything bound.
Each volume of a series is counted separately as a 권.

examples.en: One notebook, please.
examples.note: Basic: [bound item] + 한 권. Notebooks count with 권 just like books.

examples.ko: 한 달에 책을 두 권 정도 읽어요.
examples.romanization: han dare chaegeul du gwon jeongdo ilgeoyo.
examples.en: I read about two books a month.
examples.note: 두 권 정도 = 'about two'; 정도 turns an exact count into an estimate.

examples.ko: 도서관에서 빌린 책 세 권을 오늘 반납해야 해요.
examples.romanization: doseogwaneseo billin chaek se gwoneul oneul bannapaeya haeyo.
examples.en: I have to return the three library books I borrowed today.
examples.note: 세 권을 marks the books as the object; 반납하다 = 'to return (borrowed items)'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 권 is the counter for anything BOUND into a spine — novels, textbooks, notebooks, magazines, and each separate volume of a multi-volume series. Its critical contrast is with 장, which counts a single loose SHEET: 종이 한 장 is one sheet of paper, but the whole bound book made of many sheets is 책 한 권. The hanja is 卷, originally 'a scroll/roll', which is why it now measures a complete bound work. It always takes native-Korean numbers and is among the most frequent counters when you talk about reading or studying. The classic English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to the all-purpose 개 ('책 두 개') because English just says 'two books' — but printed/bound works specifically take 권; a related slip is using 권 for a single page, when one page is 한 장.

Using 개 for books. 개 is for generic objects; bound books and volumes specifically take 권 (책 한 권).
Counting loose pages with 권. A single sheet/page is 장 (종이 한 장); the whole book is 권.
Counting a multi-volume set as 한 권 when you mean the whole series. Each volume is its own 권 (전 5권 = '5 volumes total').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 장 means "counter for flat/thin sheets (paper, tickets)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "counter for flat/thin sheets (paper, tickets)" is 장 (jang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 종이 한 장 ("one sheet of paper"). Watch the particle attached to 장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 장 counts flat, thin things: paper, tickets, photos, cards, banknotes.
Movie, concert, and transport tickets are counted with 장.
The quantity question for sheets, tickets, or photos.
Thin flat foods (김, a cheese slice) also use 장.

examples.en: Two movie tickets, please.
examples.note: Counter-window basic: [ticket] + 두 장 + 주세요. Tickets are flat, so 장.

examples.en: Could you give me just ten sheets of copy paper?
examples.note: 열 장만 = 'just ten sheets'; 만 caps the amount, and -시겠어요 makes it polite.

examples.ko: 가족사진을 한 장 인화하려고 사진관에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: gajoksajineul han jang inhwaharyeogo sajingwane gasseoyo.
examples.en: I went to a photo studio to print one family photo.
examples.note: 한 장 counts the photo; 인화하다 = 'to develop/print a photograph'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 장 counts flat, thin items — sheets of paper, tickets, photographs, banknotes, stickers, postcards, and even thin foods like a sheet of dried seaweed (김) or a slice of cheese. Its sharpest contrast is with 권: 장 is the single loose SHEET, whereas many sheets bound together become 책 한 권 (a book). The hanja is 張, meaning 'to stretch/spread out flat', which captures exactly the flatness it measures. It always takes native numbers and is one of the most-used counters in daily errands — at ticket counters, copy machines, and photo booths. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 (a generic count) for tickets and photos because English says 'two tickets'; the natural, expected counter is 장. A second trap is using 장 for a whole magazine or book, which is 권, since those are bound, not loose.

Counting a bound book with 장. 장 is a single sheet; a whole bound book is 권 (책 한 권).
Using 개 for tickets or photos. Flat items take 장 (표 두 장, 사진 한 장), not the generic 개.
Mixing up 장 with 잔 (a glass of drink). They are different words and counters — 종이 한 장 vs 커피 한 잔.

usagePhrases.note: 대 counts vehicles and machines: cars, bikes, phones, computers, ACs.
Native numbers go before 대: 한, 두, 세 대.
The quantity question for vehicles or appliances.
Home appliances and electronics count with 대.

examples.ko: 우리 집에 차가 한 대 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jibe chaga han dae isseoyo.
examples.en: There's one car in our household.
examples.note: Basic existence: [thing]이/가 한 대 있어요. 차가 한 대 있어요 = 'have one car'.

examples.en: There are as many as five computers in the office.
examples.note: 다섯 대나 — the 나 after the counter adds the surprised nuance 'as many as'.

examples.ko: 오래된 에어컨을 한 대 더 설치하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraedoen eeokeoneul han dae deo seolchihagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We decided to install one more old air conditioner.
examples.note: 한 대 더 = 'one more unit'; -기로 하다 = 'decide to'. Appliances take 대.

extendedVocab.nuance: 대 is the all-purpose counter for machines and vehicles — cars, motorcycles, bicycles, computers, phones, cameras, TVs, washing machines, and air conditioners — basically anything mechanical or electronic, so a resident reaches for it constantly when talking about appliances. The hanja is 臺 ('platform/stand'), historically the base a machine sat on, which is why it measures equipment. It contrasts with 채 (whole buildings) and 명 (people): the vehicle is 대, the people riding inside it are 명. It always takes native-Korean numbers. The main English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the generic 개 ('차 두 개') because English just says 'two cars'; machines and vehicles specifically take 대. A subtler trap is counting passengers with 대 — only the machine is 대, while the humans in it are counted with 명.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 for cars, computers, or appliances. Machines and vehicles specifically take 대 (차 한 대, 노트북 한 대).
Counting the people riding in a vehicle with 대. People are 명 (세 명); only the vehicle itself is 대.
Saying 일 대, 이 대 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 대, 두 대, 세 대.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 채 means "counter for houses and buildings" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 채 (chae) means "counter for houses and buildings". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 집 한 채 ("one house"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 채 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 채 counts whole houses and freestanding buildings.
Native numbers go before 채: 한, 두, 세 채.
The quantity question for houses or buildings.
채 is used when counting an apartment unit as an owned property.

examples.ko: 우리 동네에 집이 한 채 비어 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri dongnee jibi han chae bieo isseoyo.
examples.en: There's one empty house in our neighborhood.
examples.note: Basic: [building]이/가 한 채. 비어 있다 = 'be (standing) empty'.

examples.ko: 할머니는 시골에 집을 한 채 가지고 계세요.
examples.romanization: halmeonineun sigore jibeul han chae gajigo gyeseyo.
examples.en: My grandmother owns a house in the countryside.
examples.note: 한 채 counts the house; 계세요 is the honorific of 있다 ('has/owns'), respecting grandmother.

examples.ko: 이 일대에 새 아파트가 두 채나 들어섰어요.
examples.romanization: i ildaee sae apateuga du chaena deureoseosseoyo.
examples.en: As many as two new apartment buildings went up in this area.
examples.note: 두 채나 — 나 stresses the surprising number; 들어서다 = '(a building) goes up/is established'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 채 counts entire dwellings and sizeable standalone buildings — houses, traditional homes (한옥), and apartment buildings or units treated as whole properties — and it always refers to the STRUCTURE as a complete unit, not the rooms inside. Its near-synonym 동 is the counter used for numbered apartment BLOCKS in a complex (101동), while 채 counts the home as one property; rooms within, meanwhile, are 개 (방 두 개). 채 is a native Korean word (no hanja) and takes native numbers. You meet it most in real-estate talk and neighborhood descriptions. The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 ('집 두 개') because English says 'two houses'; whole buildings specifically take 채. Another trap is using 대 (the machine counter) for a building by analogy — buildings are never 대.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting rooms inside a home with 채. Individual rooms are 개 (방 한 개); the whole house/building is 채.
Using 대 for a building. 대 is for machines and vehicles; a house or building takes 채.
Defaulting to 개 for houses. A whole dwelling takes 채 (집 한 채), not the generic 개.

extendedVocab.english: counter for flowers and clustered fruit
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 송이 means "counter for flowers and clustered fruit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "counter for flowers and clustered fruit" is 송이 (songi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 장미 한 송이 ("one rose"). Watch the particle attached to 송이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 송이 counts a single blossom or a naturally clustered bunch.
Native numbers go before 송이: 한, 두, 세 송이.
Fruit that grows in clusters (grapes, bananas) is counted with 송이.
The quantity question for flowers or grape bunches.

examples.en: Just one rose, please.
examples.note: Flower-shop basic: [flower] + 한 송이. 만 = 'just', softening to a single bloom.

examples.en: One bunch of grapes is 10,000 won.
examples.note: 송이 counts the grape cluster; [quantity]에 [price] is fruit-stand pricing.

examples.ko: 졸업식 날 여자친구에게 꽃을 한 송이 건넸어요.
examples.romanization: joreopsing nal yeojachinguege kkocheul han songi geonnesseoyo.
examples.en: On graduation day I handed my girlfriend a single flower.
examples.note: 한 송이 counts the bloom; 건네다 = 'to hand over', and 에게 = 'to (a person)'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 송이 counts a single blossom on its stem or a naturally formed cluster of produce — one rose, one tulip, a bunch of grapes, a hand of bananas. Its essential contrast is with 다발: 송이 is ONE separate bloom or cluster, whereas 다발 is a tied BUNDLE of many (꽃 한 다발 = a bouquet, 꽃 한 송이 = a single flower). 송이 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It surfaces whenever you buy flowers or cluster-fruit. The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 ('장미 두 개') because English says 'two roses'; a flower naturally takes 송이. A subtler trap is calling a wrapped bouquet 한 송이 — a gift bouquet is 한 다발, while 송이 stays reserved for each individual stem or cluster.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 for a single flower. A bloom naturally takes 송이 (장미 한 송이), not the generic 개.
Calling a wrapped bouquet 한 송이. A bound bouquet is 한 다발; 송이 is one individual flower or cluster.
Counting loose individual grapes with 송이. The whole hanging cluster is 한 송이; single berries are 알 (포도 한 알).

extendedVocab.english: counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 줄 means "counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 줄 (jul) = "counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 김밥 한 줄 ("one roll of gimbap") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 줄, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 줄 counts long line-shaped things: a gimbap roll, a row, a line of text.
Native numbers go before 줄: 한, 두, 세 줄.

usagePhrases.en: to line up in a single row
usagePhrases.note: 한 줄로 + 서다 is a fixed phrase for forming one queue.
The quantity question for lines of text or rows.

examples.en: One roll of gimbap, please.
examples.note: Snack-shop basic: 김밥 + 한 줄. The whole uncut roll is 한 줄, not the slices.

examples.en: Please line up in a single line here.
examples.note: 한 줄로 = 'into one line'; the 로 marks the resulting arrangement. Common queue instruction.

examples.ko: 이 긴 글을 두 줄로 짧게 요약해 봤어요.
examples.romanization: i gin geureul du jullo jjalbge yoyakae bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I summarized this long text into two short lines.
examples.note: 두 줄로 = 'into two lines'; 줄 counts written lines as well as physical rows.

extendedVocab.nuance: 줄 counts things stretched out in a long line — a roll of gimbap (a long tube of rice and fillings), a row of seats, a queue of people, and lines of written text. Its everyday rivals split by shape: 줄 is the whole long line, but once gimbap is sliced, each round piece becomes 개 (김밥 한 개 = one slice). 줄 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers; note the set phrase 한 줄로 서다 ('stand in a single line'), heard constantly in queues. The English-speaker pitfall is counting cut gimbap pieces with 줄 — the uncut roll is 한 줄, individual slices are 개; another is using 개 for a row or queue when the natural counter is 줄.

Counting sliced gimbap pieces with 줄. The whole uncut roll is 한 줄; each cut slice is 개.
Using 개 for a queue or a row. A line of people or a row is 줄 (한 줄), not the generic 개.
Forgetting the 로 in the line-up phrase. The natural instruction is 한 줄로 서다 ('line up into one row'), with 로.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 마리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 마리 counts every kind of animal: pets, fish, birds, insects, livestock.
Native numbers go before 마리: 한, 두, 세 마리.
The quantity question for any creature.
A whole (cooked) chicken is counted with 마리 too.

examples.en: I want to raise one puppy.
examples.note: Basic: [animal] + 한 마리. 키우다 = 'to raise/keep (a pet)'.

examples.ko: 우리 집 어항에는 금붕어가 세 마리 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jip eohangeneun geumbungeoga se mari isseoyo.
examples.en: There are three goldfish in our fish tank.
examples.note: 세 마리 counts the fish; even tiny creatures take 마리, regardless of size.

examples.ko: 배고픈데 치킨 한 마리 시켜 먹을까요?
examples.romanization: baegopeunde chikin han mari sikyeo meogeulkkayo?
examples.en: I'm hungry — shall we order a whole chicken?
examples.note: 한 마리 counts the chicken; 시켜 먹다 = 'order in and eat'. Classic fried-chicken line.

extendedVocab.nuance: 마리 is the universal counter for animals — dogs, cats, fish, birds, insects, livestock, and even a whole cooked chicken or fish on the table. Crucially it is size-independent: the same word counts an ant (개미 한 마리) and an elephant (코끼리 한 마리). 마리 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. Its single most important contrast is with 명, the counter for PEOPLE: animals are 마리, humans are 명, and crossing that line matters socially. 마리 is also distinct from 분, the honorific people-counter. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 마리 for people because English says 'two' for both — but calling a person 한 마리 is insulting or mocking (treating them like an animal); always use 명 (or honorific 분) for humans. A second slip is the generic 개 for animals, which sounds wrong — creatures take 마리.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting people with 마리. People take 명 (or honorific 분); 마리 for a human is rude or mocking.
Using 개 for animals. Living creatures take 마리 (강아지 한 마리), not the generic object counter 개.
Saying 일 마리, 이 마리 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리, 세 마리.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 끼 means "counter for meals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "counter for meals" is 끼 (kki). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 하루 세 끼 ("three meals a day"). Watch the particle attached to 끼 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS: breakfast, lunch, dinner as sittings.
Native numbers go before 끼: 한, 두, 세 끼.
The quantity question for meal sittings.

usagePhrases.en: to make do with a quick meal
usagePhrases.note: 한 끼 + 때우다 is a set phrase for grabbing a quick bite to get by.

examples.en: I eat two meals a day.
examples.note: Basic habit: 하루에 [number] 끼 먹다. 끼 counts the sittings, not the dishes.

examples.ko: 오늘 너무 바빠서 한 끼밖에 못 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: oneul neomu bappaseo han kkibakke mon meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was so busy today I only ate one meal.
examples.note: 한 끼밖에 + 못 — 밖에 ('only') REQUIRES a negative verb, here 못 먹었어요.

examples.ko: 다이어트 중이라 저녁 한 끼는 가볍게 먹으려고 해요.
examples.romanization: daieoteu jungira jeonyeo kan kkineun gabyeopge meogeuryeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I'm dieting, so I try to eat one light dinner.
examples.note: 한 끼는 topic-marks the meal; -려고 하다 = 'try/intend to'. 중이라 = 'because I'm in the middle of'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS — one sitting of breakfast, lunch, or dinner is 한 끼 — so it measures the eating event, not the individual dishes on the table. This is its key contrast with 그릇 (a bowl/serving of food) and 개 (a single dish): 밥 한 끼 is one whole meal, while 밥 한 그릇 is one bowl of rice within it. 끼 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It's the natural way to talk about eating habits, skipping meals, and meal plans (하루 세 끼). Note the set phrase 한 끼 때우다 ('grab a quick bite to get by'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 끼 to count plates or dishes because English loosely says 'a meal' for food generally — but 끼 is the whole sitting; a single dish is 개 or 그릇. A second slip is Sino-Korean numbers (일 끼), when only native 한 끼, 두 끼 work.

Using Sino-Korean numbers like 일 끼, 삼 끼. Meal occasions take native numbers: 한 끼, 세 끼.
Pairing 밖에 ('only') with a positive verb. 한 끼밖에 demands a negative: 한 끼밖에 못 먹었어요, not 먹었어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 군데 means "counter for places/spots" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 군데 (gunde) = "counter for places/spots". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 한 군데 ("one place/spot") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 군데, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 군데 counts locations or spots: shops, sites, even sore spots on the body.
Native numbers go before 군데: 한, 두, 세 군데.
Extremely common: 몇 군데 = 'how many spots/places'.
여러 군데 = 'in several spots/places', for scattered locations or pains.

examples.ko: 여기 근처에 카페가 몇 군데 있어요?
examples.romanization: yeogi geuncheoe kapega myeot gunde isseoyo?
examples.en: How many cafés are there near here?
examples.note: Basic: [place] + 몇 군데. 군데 counts the locations being asked about.

examples.en: I even went to as many as three different hospitals.
examples.note: 세 군데나 — the 나 stresses 'as many as three'; 다니다 = 'go around/attend (repeatedly)'.

examples.en: I fell, so I ache in several spots on my body.
examples.note: 여러 군데 = 'in several places'; 군데 counts sore spots too, not just shops.

extendedVocab.nuance: 군데 counts locations or spots — shops you visited, apartments you toured, websites you checked, or places on the body that hurt — and it works equally for distinct establishments and for scattered points. Its near-synonym is 곳, which also means 'place', but 곳 is a fuller noun ('a place') and can stand alone or sound slightly more formal/written, whereas 군데 is specifically the conversational COUNTER you attach to a number (세 군데, 여러 군데). 군데 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It pairs constantly with 몇 군데 ('how many places') and 여러 군데 ('several places'). The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 for places because English says 'three places'; locations naturally take 군데 (or 곳). A separate, embarrassing trap is mixing 군데 (a spot) with the look-alike 군대 ('the military/army') — wholly different words.

Treating 곳 and 군데 as identical. 곳 is a standalone noun ('a place'); 군데 is the counter you put after a number.
