extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사고 means "accident" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사고 (sago) = "accident". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교통사고 ("traffic accident") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common compound; written as one solid word, 交通事故.
나다 is the intransitive 'occur' — nobody is blamed, it just happened.
내다 (transitive 'bring about') marks the subject as the one at fault.
現場 'present-spot' = the exact place it happened; police seal it off.

examples.en: There's an accident up ahead.
examples.note: Bare frame: 사고가 나다, the neutral 'an accident occurred', nobody blamed yet.

examples.en: I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
examples.note: 사고를 내다 openly admits fault; the 가/를 swap is the whole meaning.

examples.en: If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
examples.note: 112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance — memorize both.

extendedVocab.nuance: 사고 (事故, 'matter-incident') covers any sudden harmful event — car crashes, workplace mishaps, falls — and is the umbrella word a 교통사고 or 산업재해 sits under. The make-or-break contrast is purely grammatical and Koreans listen for it: 사고가 나다 (with 가) means the accident merely HAPPENED, assigning no blame, while 사고를 내다 (with 를) means the subject CAUSED it and is therefore liable — get the particle wrong and you may accidentally confess fault at the scene. Compare also 사건, which is an 'incident/case' in the investigative or criminal sense (a 살인 사건 is a murder CASE), whereas 사고 leans toward unintended mishap. Natural partners are 교통사고, 사고가 나다/내다, 사고 현장, and the everyday 접촉사고 (a minor fender-bender).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the 를 version admits liability and your insurer will treat it differently.
사고 is the EVENT, not the people; the injured person is a 피해자 and the at-fault driver a 가해자 — never call a person a 사고.
Don't reach for 사건 when you mean an everyday crash; 사건 implies a criminal/investigative 'case', while a road bump is a 사고 (or 접촉사고).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 합의 means "settlement / mutual agreement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 합의 (habui) means "settlement / mutual agreement". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 합의하다 ("to reach a settlement"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 합의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Used for accidents, disputes, and out-of-court deals between two parties.
金 'money' — the sum paid to settle, especially after an accident or assault.
書 'written document' that both sides sign to make the deal binding.
보다 here means 'work out/settle' — the colloquial verb of choice.

examples.en: I reached a settlement with the other party.
examples.note: 합의를 보다 is the everyday spoken phrasing; 상대방 = the other party.

examples.en: We agreed I'd receive one million won as a settlement.
examples.note: -기로 하다 marks the agreed-upon terms; 합의금 is the payout.

examples.en: We filled out the settlement agreement at the police station and the case wrapped up.
examples.note: 합의서 + 작성하다 is the set phrase; settling often closes a minor case.

extendedVocab.nuance: 합의 (合意, 'unite-intention', literally 'minds joined') is enormous in Korean accident and minor-crime culture: reaching 합의 with the victim — usually with 합의금 changing hands and a signed 합의서 — frequently reduces a sentence or makes the prosecutor drop the case entirely. The boundary learners blur is 합의 vs 동의: 합의 is a two-way deal where both parties negotiate and CONCEDE to a middle ground (often money, often legal), whereas 동의 is one-sided AGREEMENT that you accept someone's opinion or request ('I agree, that's fine'). It also differs from 약속, an everyday promise about plans. Register is formal-to-neutral, at home in police stations, insurance calls, and contracts. The English-speaker pitfall is using 합의했어요 for casually agreeing on dinner plans — that needs 동의했어요 or 그러기로 했어요; 합의 implies a negotiated, often compensated settlement.

합의 (a negotiated, usually compensated settlement) is not 동의 (agreeing with an opinion) — 'I agree with you' is 동의해요, never 합의해요.
Saying 합의했어요 implies the deal is final and concluded; if you're still bargaining, say 합의 중이에요 (we're in the middle of settling).
Don't use 합의 for casual plan-making ('let's agree to meet at six') — that's 약속하다 or 그러기로 하다; 합의 carries legal/financial weight.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 벌금 means "fine (criminal penalty)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "fine (criminal penalty)" is 벌금 (beolgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌금을 내다 ("to pay a fine"). Watch the particle attached to 벌금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 is the verb for paying penalties and fees; never 주다.
刑 'sentence' — a 벌금형 is a criminal sentence served by paying money rather than jail.
State the amount right after 벌금, no particle needed.
告知書 'notification document' = the official payment slip mailed to you.

examples.en: I paid a fine.
examples.note: Bare frame: 벌금을 내다; 내다 (not 주다) is the only natural verb for paying penalties.

examples.en: I got a heavy fine for drunk driving.
examples.note: -(으)로 gives the cause; 나오다 = (a charge) is issued/comes out.

examples.ko: 벌금 고지서가 집으로 와서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: beolgeum gojiseoga jibeuro waseo kkamjjang nollasseoyo.
examples.en: The fine notice came to my house and gave me a fright.
examples.note: 고지서 arrives by mail; -아서 links the surprise to receiving it.

extendedVocab.nuance: 벌금 (罰金, 'punishment-money') is a criminal-court fine imposed after a court finds you committed an actual offense, so it rides a completely different legal track from 과태료, the administrative penalty for petty rule-breaking. Koreans draw this line sharply: a 벌금 leaves a record that you were criminally penalized (a 벌금형 is literally a criminal sentence), while a 과태료 — like an illegal-parking charge — carries no such stain. The fixed verb is 벌금을 내다 ('pay'); the English-speaker trap is 벌금을 주다, which uses 'give' and makes it sound like you're handing over money as a gift or donation. Note too that 벌금 is the specific monetary penalty, whereas 처벌 is the broader concept of punishment (jail, suspension, fine) that a 벌금 is just one instance of. You'll most often hear it paired with 내다, 나오다 (it 'came out' = was issued), and 고지서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap 벌금 (criminal court fine) with 과태료 (administrative penalty like illegal parking) — a 벌금 means a court found you guilty, so the wrong word overstates the offense.
Use 벌금을 내다, not 벌금을 주다; 주다 ('give') makes it sound like a voluntary gift rather than a penalty you owe.
벌금 (a specific money fine) is not 처벌 (punishment in general); a 벌금 is one TYPE of 처벌, so don't treat the two as interchangeable.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 과태료 means "administrative fine (minor penalty)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 과태료 (gwataeryo) = "administrative fine (minor penalty)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과태료를 내다 ("to pay an administrative fine") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과태료, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Standard verb is 내다, the same as for any fee or penalty.
駐車 'parking'; the most common reason a city resident ever gets one.
賦課 'levy-charge' = the act of officially charging it to you.
The slip mailed to you stating the amount and deadline.

examples.en: I got hit with a fine.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 과태료가 나오다 = a fine is issued/comes out against you.

examples.en: I paid a fine for illegal parking.
examples.note: -(으)로 marks the cause; 과태료를 내다 is the set verb phrase.

examples.ko: 기한 안에 내면 과태료가 좀 깎여요.
examples.romanization: gihan ane naemyeon gwataeryoga jom kkakkyeoyo.
examples.en: If you pay within the deadline, the fine gets reduced a bit.
examples.note: Early payment usually earns a discount; 깎이다 = to be cut/reduced.

extendedVocab.nuance: 과태료 (過怠料, 'excess-negligence-fee') is a LIGHT administrative penalty for breaking minor non-criminal rules — illegal parking, a late 전입신고, missed reporting deadlines — and crucially it does NOT make you a criminal or leave a criminal record. That is the entire dividing line versus 벌금: a 벌금 is a court fine for an actual offense, whereas a 과태료 is just an administrative charge an office levies on you. Residents bump into 과태료 most often through parking tickets and late move-in registration, and many can be paid online with an early-payment discount. The verb is 과태료를 내다 (or it 나오다, 'comes out'). Two pitfalls: English speakers over-dramatize it by translating it as 'fine' and equating it with 벌금, and the spelling trips people up — it is 과태료 with 태 in the middle, NOT 과대료; the syllable is 怠 'negligence', not 大 'big'.

과태료 (administrative penalty) is not 벌금 (criminal court fine); confusing them makes a parking ticket sound like a criminal conviction.
It's 과태료, not 과대료 — the middle syllable is 태 (怠, negligence), and learners constantly misspell and mispronounce it as 대.
Don't say 과태료를 주다 ('give a fine'); like all penalties it takes 내다 (pay) or 나오다 (be issued).

extendedVocab.english: civil complaint / public petition or request
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 민원 means "civil complaint / public petition or request" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 민원 (minwon) means "civil complaint / public petition or request". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 민원을 넣다 ("to file a complaint/request"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 민원 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 'to put in' = to submit a 민원; also 민원을 제기하다 (more formal).
接受 'receive' = what the office does when it logs your 민원.
室 'room' = the desk/counter at a 구청 that handles public requests.
The online portal (it absorbed the old 민원24) where many 민원 are now filed.

examples.en: I filed a request at the community center.
examples.note: 민원을 넣다 is the everyday verb; 주민센터 is your local office.

examples.en: Lots of complaints come in about noise between floors.
examples.note: 들어오다 = (complaints) come in; 때문에 gives the cause.

examples.en: To lodge a civil complaint you need an ID.
examples.note: 민원을 제기하다 is the formal register; -(으)려면 = 'in order to'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 민원 (民願, 'people-wish') is any official request OR complaint a citizen submits to a public office — issuing a document, reporting a pothole, asking the 구청 to act — and it is the formal channel through which ordinary Koreans interact with bureaucracy. The key thing English speakers miss is its breadth: it is NOT only a 'complaint'. Contrast it with 불만, which is mere personal dissatisfaction or grumbling with no formal status; a 민원 is the official, logged, trackable submission, so context (a request vs a grievance) decides the tone. It is a neutral, administrative word, common in 민원실, 민원 접수, 민원 처리. The pitfall is the verb: say 민원을 넣다 or the formal 민원을 제기하다, never bare 민원을 하다, which sounds unfinished — 민원 needs a 'submit/raise' verb, not the generic 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
민원 (a formal request/complaint to a public office) is broader than 불만 (private dissatisfaction) — a 민원 is the official channel, not just venting.
Use 민원을 넣다 or 민원을 제기하다, not 민원을 하다, which sounds incomplete; 민원 pairs with submit/raise verbs.
Don't assume 민원 always means 'complaint' — it equally covers neutral requests like getting a certificate issued, so don't read hostility into it.

The pitfall is the verb: say 민원을 넣다 or the formal 민원을 제기하다, never bare 민원을 하다, which sounds unfinished — 민원 needs a 'submit/raise' verb, not the generic 하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 증명서 means "certificate / official proof document" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "certificate / official proof document" is 증명서 (jeungmyeongseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 재직증명서 ("certificate of employment"). Watch the particle attached to 증명서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 在職 'holding a post'; proves you work somewhere, needed for visas and loans.
떼다 literally 'detach/tear off' — the idiomatic verb for pulling an official copy.
發給 'issue-give' = official issuing; the word on kiosks and government sites.
所得 'income'; proof of earnings, often required for rent or a visa.

examples.en: I need to get one copy of a certificate.
examples.note: 통 is the counter for documents/letters; 떼다 = obtain a copy.

examples.ko: 증명서는 무인 발급기에서 뽑을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeungmyeongseoneun muin balgeupgieseo ppobeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can print certificates at the self-service kiosk.
examples.note: 무인 발급기 = unmanned issuing machine; 뽑다 = print/pull out.

examples.en: The bank asked for an income certificate, so I issued it on Gov24.
examples.note: -아서 links cause and action; 발급받다 = receive an official issuance.

extendedVocab.nuance: 증명서 (證明書, 'prove-clarify-document') is the catch-all suffix for official proof papers — 재직증명서, 소득증명서, 출입국사실증명서 — and the headword you attach a topic to. The detail that ambushes learners is the verb: Koreans say 증명서를 떼다, where 떼다 literally means 'to detach/tear off' (from the days of tearing a page off a register), so 'get a copy' is idiomatically 'detach a certificate'; the equally correct formal verb is 발급받다 ('receive an issuance'). Do NOT say 증명서를 만들다 ('make a certificate'), which implies you forged it yourself rather than having an authority issue it. Distinguish 증명서 from 신분증: a 증명서 PROVES a fact (your job, income), whereas a 신분증 is an ID CARD proving who you are — they are not interchangeable. Most 증명서 can now be pulled from a 무인 발급기 or 정부24 without queuing at a counter.

증명서 (a proof-of-fact document) is not 신분증 (an ID card) — don't use one when you mean the other; they serve different purposes.

Don't drop the topic prefix when a specific one is needed: a bank wants a 소득증명서 or 재직증명서, so bare 증명서 can be too vague at the counter.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목격자 means "witness (someone who saw an incident)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 목격자 (mokgyeokja) = "witness (someone who saw an incident)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 목격자를 찾다 ("to look for a witness") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 목격자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Seen on roadside posters: 목격자를 찾습니다 ('seeking witnesses').
陳述 'statement' = the account a witness gives to police.
Put the event before 목격자: 사고 목격자, 범행 목격자.
目擊 'eye-strike' = to see an event happen with your own eyes.

examples.en: Are you by any chance a witness?
examples.note: 혹시 softens a direct question to a stranger; -세요 is the polite 'are you ~?'

examples.en: There was a witness, so it was handled quickly.
examples.note: -아서 links cause and result; witnesses speed up claims and reports.

examples.ko: 제가 그 사고를 목격해서 진술하러 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jega geu sagoreul mokgyeokaeseo jinsulhareo wasseoyo.
examples.en: I witnessed that accident, so I came to give a statement.
examples.note: 목격하다 = to have seen it happen; pairs naturally with 진술하다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 목격자 (目擊者, 'eye-strike-person', the one who 'struck it with their eyes') is the eyewitness who actually SAW an incident — a key word around 교통사고 and crime, and you'll spot 목격자를 찾습니다 posters near accident spots. The role contrast to nail is 목격자 vs 피해자 vs 가해자: a 목격자 merely observed and was not harmed, a 피해자 is the one who suffered, and a 가해자 caused it — confusing them scrambles who police talk to and why. Register-wise the verb 목격하다 is markedly more formal than plain 봤어요 and signals you witnessed something report-worthy. That is also the pitfall: don't use 목격하다 for casually 'seeing' a friend or a movie — that is just 보다 or 만나다; reserve 목격하다 for accidents, crimes, and incidents serious enough to testify about.

목격자 (eyewitness) is not 피해자 (victim) — a witness saw the event but wasn't harmed, so don't swap the two when explaining your role.
목격하다 is for incidents and events only; for casually seeing a friend say 봤어요/만났어요 — 친구를 목격했어요 sounds absurd, as if you spotted them at a crime scene.
Don't say 목격자를 봤어요 to mean 'I witnessed it' — YOU are the 목격자; the verb you want is 목격했어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 피해자 means "victim (of an accident or crime)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 피해자 (pihaeja) means "victim (of an accident or crime)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 피해자 ("victim"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 피해자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 被害者 'suffer-harm-person' = the harmed party in an accident or crime.
加害者 'add-harm-person' = the one who caused it; learn the pair together.
입다 'to wear/sustain' is the fixed verb; the root noun is 피해.
補償 'make-good' = righting the harm, usually with money.

examples.en: I'm the victim of this accident.
examples.note: Core frame: 저는 ~의 피해자예요, establishing your role when reporting.

examples.en: The at-fault party says they'll handle it through insurance.
examples.note: Contrast 가해자 with 피해자; -(으)ㄴ대요 reports what they said.

examples.ko: 피해를 입은 만큼 보상을 받을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: pihaereul ibeun mankeum bosangeul badeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can get compensation in proportion to the harm suffered.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 만큼 = 'to the extent that'; pairs 피해 with 보상.

extendedVocab.nuance: 피해자 (被害者, where 被 marks the PASSIVE 'one who is harmed') always pairs with its mirror 가해자 (加害者, 'one who adds harm'); the 被 vs 加 character literally encodes who receives versus who inflicts, and knowing which you are shapes liability, insurance, and who owes whom. The base noun 피해 means 'damage/harm' and combines widely — 피해를 입다, 피해 보상, 재산 피해 — so master the noun and the family follows. It is standard, neutral legal vocabulary, not a dramatic word like English 'victim' can feel; Koreans use it matter-of-factly in reports. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb for suffering damage: it is the fixed collocation 피해를 입다 (using 입다, the same verb as 'to wear', here 'to sustain'); 피해를 받다 with the generic 'receive' is much less natural in this set pairing and marks you as a learner.

Don't mix 피해자 (the harmed party) with 가해자 (the at-fault party) — reversing them flips who is liable and who receives compensation.
Use 피해를 입다 for suffering damage; 피해를 받다 is unnatural in this fixed collocation, even though 받다 means 'receive'.
피해자 is neutral legal vocabulary — don't avoid it as too harsh; in a report calling yourself the 피해자 is simply stating your role, not melodrama.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 진술 means "statement / testimony (to police)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "statement / testimony (to police)" is 진술 (jinsul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 진술하다 ("to give a statement"). Watch the particle attached to 진술 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 陳述 'lay out-state' = to formally recount events to police or in court.
書 'document' = the paper that records your account, signed by you.
From the officer's side: the police 진술을 받다 from you.
A witness's formal account of what they saw.

examples.en: I stated it truthfully.
examples.note: 사실대로 = 'as it really is'; the cleanest frame for 진술하다.

examples.en: I wrote out a statement at the police station.
examples.note: 진술서 + 작성하다 is the set phrase for putting it in writing.

examples.en: I'd like to give my statement through an interpreter.
examples.note: A right worth knowing as a foreigner; -(으)ㄴ데요 softly opens the request.

extendedVocab.nuance: 진술 (陳述, 'lay-out and state') is your FORMAL account of what happened, given to police or written as a 진술서, and it carries far more weight than ordinary 말하다 because it can become evidence in a case. The contrast learners need is 진술 vs 설명: 설명 is a neutral 'explanation' you give anyone about anything, while 진술 is specifically a statement to authorities with legal consequences — use 진술 only in official contexts. As a foreign resident, remember you can request a 통역사 (interpreter) before you 진술하다; the police 진술을 받다 ('take' your statement) while you 진술하다 ('give' it). The nastiest pitfall is the near-homophone 진실 (眞實, 'truth'): 진술 (a statement, which may or may not be true) is NOT 진실 (the truth itself), and a 진술서 (statement document) is not a 진실서. One syllable, completely different word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
진술 (a formal statement to authorities) is heavier than 설명 (a casual explanation) — use 진술 only in police/legal contexts, not for explaining your weekend.
It's 진술, not 진실 (truth) — they sound nearly identical but a 진술 is your account (true or not), while 진실 is the actual truth; 진술서 ≠ 진실서.
Don't say 경찰이 진술했어요 when the police TOOK your statement — the officer 진술을 받다, the person being questioned 진술하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 처벌 means "punishment / legal penalty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 처벌 (cheobeol) = "punishment / legal penalty". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 처벌하다 ("to punish") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 처벌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 處罰 'handle-penalize'; subject is usually the law or authorities.
받다 marks YOU as the one penalized — the passive side.
水位 'water-level' used figuratively = the degree/level of the penalty.
刑事 'criminal' (as opposed to 민사, civil) punishment.

examples.en: Drunk driving is punished severely.
examples.note: 처벌받다 from the offender's side; 강하게 = severely/harshly.

examples.en: I stated that I don't want them punished.
examples.note: A real choice a victim can make to soften a minor case; -다고 reports your statement.

examples.en: Illegal parking is also subject to penalty.
examples.note: 처벌 대상이다 = 'to be a target/subject of punishment'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 처벌 (處罰, 'handle-and-penalize') is the legal PUNISHMENT itself — the whole category of sanctions, from a fine to imprisonment — and pairs with crimes and serious violations. The boundary with 벌금 is the one to fix: 벌금 is one specific FORM of 처벌 (a monetary court fine), whereas 처벌 is the umbrella concept that also includes jail (징역) and suspension, so they are part-and-whole, not synonyms. A culturally crucial phrase is 처벌을 원하지 않는다 ('I do not wish them punished'), which a 피해자 can state to soften or drop a minor case — tightly linked to 합의. The active/passive split is the grammar pitfall: use 처벌받다 (with 받다) when YOU are the one penalized, and 처벌하다 when the authority is doing the punishing; saying 처벌했어요 about yourself wrongly casts you as the punisher, not the punished.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 처벌했어요 about yourself when you mean you were punished — that makes you the one inflicting punishment; the correct form is 처벌받았어요.
처벌 (punishment in general) is not 벌금 (a specific fine) — a 벌금 is just one kind of 처벌, so don't use them as equals.
Don't confuse 형사 처벌 (criminal punishment) with 민사 (civil matters); 처벌 belongs to the criminal/penal side, while civil disputes seek compensation, not 처벌.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 반려견 means "companion dog (pet dog)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 반려견 (ballyeogyeon) means "companion dog (pet dog)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 반려견을 키우다 ("raise a companion dog"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반려견 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: '키우다' (to raise/rear) is the natural verb for having a pet, never '가지다' (to possess)
the particle '과/와' frames the dog as your companion on the walk, not an object you take
'동반(同伴)' = accompanying together; a fixed sign-word you see at pet-friendly venues
Koreans say '우리(our)' even for a personal pet, the same warm 'our' used in '우리 집, 우리 엄마'

examples.en: I raise one dog.
examples.note: everyday speech drops '반려견' for plain '강아지'; animals are counted with '마리'

examples.en: This cafe allows companion dogs.
examples.note: '동반이 가능하다' = accompaniment is possible — the polite venue phrasing on signs and websites

examples.en: Registering your companion dog is a legally set obligation.
examples.note: real-life: micro-chipping/registering a dog is mandatory in Korea, so this exact phrasing appears on official notices

extendedVocab.nuance: '반려견(伴侶犬)' is the warm, modern word for a pet dog, built from the hanja 반려(伴侶) 'companion/life-partner' + 견(犬) 'dog' — literally 'companion dog,' the very same 반려 used in 반려자 'one's spouse.' It has deliberately replaced the older near-synonym '애완견(愛玩犬),' where 애완(愛玩) means 'love-and-play-with,' i.e. treat as a cherished toy; the dividing line is respect — '애완견' frames the dog as a possession, '반려견' as family, so '애완견' now sounds dated and faintly callous in public or official use. Register-wise '반려견' is the polite/written form you use at vets, in signs, and in news; in casual chat Koreans almost always just say '강아지' regardless of the dog's age. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for '가지다(to have/own)' — you do not 'have' a dog in Korean, you 키우다 'raise' it, and you say 우리 강아지 'our dog' even when it is solely yours.

Saying '애완견': the 애완(愛玩 'love-toy') framing now sounds outdated and slightly disrespectful — use '반려견' in any polite or official context
Using '가지다(to have/own)' for owning a pet — Korean treats a pet as a living family member you 키우다(raise), so '강아지를 가지고 있어요' sounds like you own an object; say '강아지를 키워요'
Calling it '강아지' on an official form — there '반려견' is the expected register; '강아지' is purely conversational

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 반려묘 means "companion cat (pet cat)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "companion cat (pet cat)" is 반려묘 (ballyeomyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 반려묘를 입양하다 ("adopt a companion cat"). Watch the particle attached to 반려묘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: '입양하다(to adopt)' is the preferred, kinder verb over '사다(to buy)' in pet culture
cats, like all animals, are counted with the counter '마리', not '명' or '개'
literally 'cat's bathroom' — the everyday, non-clinical word for a litter box
'집사(執事 butler/steward)' is the affectionate self-label cat owners give themselves

examples.en: I like cats.
examples.note: simple level: in casual speech the word is plain '고양이', never '반려묘'

examples.en: Companion cats don't need to be walked.
examples.note: '산책을 시키다' = to make (a pet) take a walk — '시키다' adds the causative 'have it do'

examples.en: I call myself my companion cat's servant.
examples.note: real-life: the playful '집사' culture is huge online; '-라고 부르다' = to call (something) by a name

extendedVocab.nuance: '반려묘(伴侶猫)' pairs the hanja 반려(伴侶 'companion') with 묘(猫 'cat') and is the formal/written counterpart to '반려견,' carrying the same respectful 'family member' nuance; you meet it at vet clinics, pet shops, and on official notices. Its dated near-synonym is '애완묘(愛玩猫),' which (like '애완견') frames the cat as a plaything and now sounds cold — the dividing line is exactly the same respect gradient as 반려/애완. The key register fact English speakers miss: '반려묘' is essentially never used in everyday conversation, where '고양이' is the only natural word — saying '반려묘' to a friend sounds like you are reading a poster. Note the culture-bound collocation '집사(執事)': cat owners call themselves the cat's 'butler' because the cat is humorously cast as the master of the house, so '저는 집사예요' literally means 'I'm a butler' but really means 'I have a cat.' Don't translate English 'cat owner' as '고양이 주인' in friendly talk — '주인(owner)' sounds possessive; '집사' is the warm insider term.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사료 means "pet food (kibble/feed)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사료 (saryo) = "pet food (kibble/feed)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사료를 주다 ("give (pet) food") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사료, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: '주다(to give)' is the basic verb for feeding kibble; '먹이다' (feed) is the causative alternative
prefix the animal name directly — 강아지/고양이 사료 — to specify the food type
'바꾸다(to change/swap)' is used when changing brands or formulas
'습식(濕式 wet-type)' vs '건식(乾式 dry-type)' — the two standard product categories on packaging

examples.en: I give (it) food every day.
examples.note: simple level: '매일(every day)' + the core verb '주다'

examples.en: We're all out of cat food.
examples.note: '다 떨어지다' = to run out completely; '다' here means 'all gone', not 'fast'

examples.en: I recently switched to a small-kibble food.
examples.note: real-life shopping talk: '알갱이' = the individual pellet, '~로 바꾸다' = switch to ~

extendedVocab.nuance: '사료(飼料)' joins the hanja 사(飼 'to feed/rear') and 료(料 'material/stuff') — literally 'feeding-material' — and is the standard word for processed pet food, covering both dry kibble and wet pouches, as well as livestock feed; context alone tells you whether it's a cat or a cow. The crucial near-synonym contrast is '사료' vs '간식(間食)': '사료' is the daily staple meal, while '간식' (lit. 'between-meals food') is treats/snacks — calling a treat '사료' sounds wrong to a Korean ear. Another boundary is '사료' vs '음식(飮食)': '음식' is food for people, so using it for an animal's meal is a직역 trap; animals eat '사료,' people eat '음식.' Register is neutral and everyday. When shopping you'll constantly parse '건식 사료(dry)' versus '습식 사료(wet),' and you 사료를 주다/바꾸다, never 'have' food the way English does.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling pet treats '사료': treats are '간식(間食)', the daily meal is '사료' — they are different food categories, not interchangeable
Using '음식(飮食)' for pet food: '음식' is human food; an animal's processed meal is '사료'
Saying '사료를 가지다' to mean 'have food at home' — to feed, use '사료를 주다/먹이다'; '가지다' is just 'possess'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목줄 means "leash / collar" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 목줄 (mokjul) means "leash / collar". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목줄을 하다 ("put on a leash/collar"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목줄 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: '하다' is the casual, all-purpose verb for putting a leash on
'채우다(to fasten/buckle)' is more precise than '하다' — it pictures the clasp closing
'풀다(to undo/release)' is the natural opposite of 채우다
'착용(着用) 필수' = wearing-is-mandatory — the fixed phrasing on park signs

examples.en: My dog hates the leash.
examples.note: simple level: '싫어하다' = to dislike; topic '목줄을' takes object 을

examples.ko: 밖에 나갈 때는 꼭 목줄을 채워야 해요.
examples.romanization: bakke nagal ttaeneun kkong mokjureul chaewoya haeyo.
examples.en: When going outside you must fasten the leash.
examples.note: everyday rule: '-아야 해요' = have to; '채우다' is the natural verb for buckling it on

examples.en: In the park you can't let your dog off-leash.
examples.note: real-life: leashing in public is law in Korea; '-면 안 되다' = must not

extendedVocab.nuance: '목줄' is a pure-Korean compound of 목 'neck' + 줄 'rope/cord,' literally 'neck-rope,' and in everyday speech it loosely covers both the collar and the walking leash. The sharp near-synonym distinctions matter: the long walking line alone is often '리드줄' or just '줄'; a body harness worn across the chest (not the neck) is a completely different word, '하네스' or '가슴줄(chest-strap),' so calling a harness '목줄' is wrong. Also avoid the generic '끈(string/cord)' for a pet leash — '끈' is shoelace-level string, '목줄' is the specific pet item. The verb pair to lock in is 채우다(fasten on) ↔ 풀다(take off); '하다' works casually but '채우다/풀다' sound more native. Register is neutral and practical: because leashing in public is the law, the sign-phrase '목줄 착용 필수' is everywhere, and the English-speaker pitfall is saying '목줄을 입다(wear)' — clothing uses 입다, but a leash/collar is 채우다 or 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing '목줄(neck-rope)' with '하네스/가슴줄(chest harness)' — a body harness is not a 목줄; the words distinguish neck vs chest
Using generic '끈(string)' for a pet leash — '끈' is any cord/lace; the specific pet item is '목줄'
Saying '목줄을 입다(wear)' — 입다 is for clothing; a leash/collar is '채우다(fasten)' or casually '하다'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 예방접종 means "vaccination / preventive shot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "vaccination / preventive shot" is 예방접종 (yebangjeopjong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예방접종을 하다 ("get/do a vaccination"). Watch the particle attached to 예방접종 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: '하다' here means to carry out / receive the shot
'맞다(to be struck by)' is the idiomatic verb for getting any injection
'기록(記錄 record)' — vets keep one that boarding/grooming places ask for
'정기(定期 fixed-period)' = regular/scheduled, vs a one-off shot

examples.en: Today my dog got a shot.
examples.note: simple level: casual '주사(shot)' + '맞다'; the animal itself is the subject receiving it

examples.en: The rabies vaccination has to be given every year.
examples.note: everyday: '광견병(狂犬病)' = rabies; '맞히다' is the causative — you have your pet get it

examples.ko: 입소 전에 예방접종 기록을 보여 주세요.
examples.romanization: ipso jeone yebangjeopjong girogeul boyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please show the vaccination record before check-in.
examples.note: real-life: boarding facilities and groomers require this before admission

extendedVocab.nuance: '예방접종(豫防接種)' stacks the hanja 예방(豫防 'prevent in advance') + 접종(接種 'graft/inoculate'), literally 'preventive inoculation,' and is the full, mildly formal clinic term; in casual speech people shorten it to '접종' or just say '주사(注射 injection/shot).' The near-synonym line is scope: '예방접종' specifically means a preventive vaccine, whereas '주사' is any shot at all (including treatment injections), so they overlap but aren't identical. The signature English-speaker pitfall is the verb pair 맞다 vs 맞히다: '맞다' literally 'to be struck' is how Korean says 'receive an injection,' so the pet 주사를 맞다; when YOU take the pet to get the shot, you use the causative '맞히다' — 강아지에게 주사를 맞히다 'have the dog get a shot.' A second trap is the English instinct to 'take/get' or even 'eat' a vaccine: in Korean a shot is 맞다(received by needle), never 먹다(eat) — '백신을 먹다' is only correct for an oral vaccine, which is rare. Rabies (광견병) vaccination is legally mandatory and renewed yearly in Korea, so '매년 맞히다' is common.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up '맞다(the pet receives the shot)' with '맞히다(you have the pet get the shot)' — choose by who acts: the pet 맞다, the owner 맞히다
Saying '백신을 먹다(eat)' for an injected vaccine — shots are '맞다(received by needle)'; 먹다 only fits an oral dose
Using the long '예방접종' in casual talk where '주사' or '접종' is more natural, or vice versa on an official record

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 중성화 means "neutering / spaying" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 중성화 (jungseonghwa) = "neutering / spaying". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 중성화 수술 ("neutering surgery") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 중성화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: almost always paired with '수술(手術 surgery)' — the complete, natural form
'하다' for having the procedure done in general terms
'시키다' makes it causative (written solid) — you arrange it for the pet
'여부(與否 yes-or-no)' — the form-field word asked on adoption/boarding papers

examples.en: Our cat has been neutered.
examples.note: simple level: '중성화를 하다' as the basic done-state

examples.ko: 보호소에서 중성화 수술을 한 뒤에 입양 보내요.
examples.romanization: bohosoeseo jungseonghwa susureul han dwie ibyang bonaeyo.
examples.en: The shelter neuters them before adopting them out.
examples.note: everyday: '-ㄴ 뒤에' = after; '입양 보내다' = rehome

examples.en: They say neutering makes them calmer.
examples.note: real-life hearsay: '-다고 해요' = it is said that; '차분해지다' = become calm

extendedVocab.nuance: '중성화(中性化)' is built from 중성(中性 'neutral/neuter gender,' the same 중성 used in chemistry for 'neutral') + 화(化 '-ization/turning into'), so it literally means 'turning gender-neutral' and serves as the single umbrella term for both spaying females and neutering males — unlike English, everyday Korean does not split the two into separate words. It is almost always spoken as the fuller '중성화 수술(neutering surgery)'; bare '중성화' alone can sound clipped. A useful contrast: '중성화' is the elective desexing procedure, distinct from '불임(不姙 infertility),' which describes the resulting inability to reproduce, not the operation. The causative '중성화시키다' or '중성화를 하다' both work because the owner arranges what is done to the pet. Register is neutral-clinical; shelters and street-cat TNR (포획-중성화-방사) programs use this exact word, and 'TNR' itself is widely understood. The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for gendered terms like a 'spay' word — there isn't one; '중성화' covers both sexes, and dropping '수술' is the other common slip.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping '수술': bare '중성화' sounds incomplete — '중성화 수술' is the natural, full collocation Koreans actually say
Assuming separate male/female terms exist — '중성화' is one word for both spaying and neutering
Confusing '중성화(the procedure)' with '불임(the infertile state)' — you do the 수술, the result is 불임/번식 불가

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 입양 means "adoption (of a pet)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 입양 (ibyang) means "adoption (of a pet)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 입양을 하다 / 입양하다 ("adopt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 입양 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the general verb for adopting in (receiving) a pet or child
'보내다(to send off)' marks the giving side — you send the animal to a new home
common cause-driven collocation pairing 유기견 + 입양
Korea's well-known animal-welfare slogan; '사지 말고' = don't buy, instead...

examples.en: I adopted a cat.
examples.note: simple level: '입양하다' with the cat as object 을

examples.en: Adopt, don't shop.
examples.note: everyday slogan: the famous '사지 말고 입양하세요' on posters and campaigns

examples.ko: 새끼 고양이를 입양 보낼 곳을 찾고 있어요.
examples.romanization: saekki goyangireul ibyang bonael goseul chatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm looking for a home to adopt out the kittens.
examples.note: real-life: '입양 보낼 곳' = a place to send them; note the giving direction 보내다

extendedVocab.nuance: '입양(入養)' combines the hanja 입(入 'enter') + 양(養 'rear/nurture'), literally 'enter-to-be-raised,' and is the very same word used for adopting a child — applying it to pets deliberately signals the modern view that an animal joins the family rather than being purchased like goods. The decisive contrast for learners is direction, encoded by the helper verbs: '입양하다' (or 입양을 받다) means to adopt IN, i.e. you receive the pet, while '입양 보내다' means to adopt OUT, i.e. you give a pet away to a new home — same noun 입양, opposite flow set by 하다/받다 versus 보내다, and mixing these reverses your meaning. The other near-synonym tension is '입양하다' vs '사다(buy)': both can get you a pet, but '사다' frames it as a commercial transaction, which is exactly what the slogan '사지 말고 입양하세요(adopt, don't shop)' rejects; for shelter animals '입양' is the warmer, socially endorsed verb. Register is neutral and widely positive. The English pitfall is assuming 'adopt' is one-directional — in Korean you must pick the right helper to show whether the pet is coming to you or leaving you.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing direction: '입양하다' is RECEIVING a pet, '입양 보내다' is GIVING one away — the helper verb (하다/받다 vs 보내다) flips the meaning
Using '사다(buy)' for a shelter pet: it sounds like a purchase; '입양하다' is the kinder, expected verb (hence '사지 말고 입양하세요')
Saying '입양을 가다(go to adopt)' to mean you adopted — to receive a pet, the verb is '입양하다/입양을 받다', not 가다

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 유기견 means "abandoned/stray dog" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "abandoned/stray dog" is 유기견 (yugigyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 유기견을 구조하다 ("rescue an abandoned dog"). Watch the particle attached to 유기견 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: '구조하다(救助 to rescue)' — the verb for saving an animal in distress
'보호소(保護所 protection-place)' where rescued dogs are kept
frequently paired collocation; adopting an ex-stray carries positive weight
'출신(出身 originating from)' describes a dog's background, like 'graduated from'

examples.en: Our dog used to be a stray.
examples.note: simple level: '-이었어요' past tense for a former state ('was a...')

examples.en: I volunteer at an abandoned-dog shelter.
examples.note: everyday: '봉사활동(volunteer work)' is a very common collocation with 하다

examples.en: If you find a stray dog, report it.
examples.note: real-life: '발견하다' = discover/find; you can report to a shelter or a city hotline

extendedVocab.nuance: '유기견(遺棄犬)' is built from 유기(遺棄 'to abandon/desert,' the same 유기 in legal '유기죄 abandonment crime') + 견(犬 'dog'), so it specifically means a dog DESERTED BY ITS OWNER — a former pet now without a home. This is its key contrast with near-synonyms: '들개' is a feral/wild dog born and living on the streets (never owned), while '길고양이(street cat)' is the gentle everyday term for community cats; so '유기견' carries the extra meaning of betrayal/abandonment that '들개' lacks. The exact cat counterpart is '유기묘.' A spelling-look-alike pitfall for learners: the prefix 유기- here is 遺棄 'abandon' and is completely unrelated to '유기농(有機農 organic farming),' where 유기 is 有機 'organic' — same sound, different hanja, opposite topic. Register is neutral and the word appears constantly in animal-welfare contexts; adopting a '유기견' is socially praised in Korea, so phrases like '유기견 출신' (ex-stray background) are said with warmth, not stigma. The English-speaker trap is flattening 'stray' onto every loose dog — reserve '유기견' for abandoned ex-pets, not truly wild '들개.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing '유기견(abandoned by an owner)' with '들개(a truly feral dog born wild)' — 유기견 implies a former pet that was deserted
Misreading the 유기- prefix: it is 遺棄 'abandoned', NOT 有機 'organic' as in '유기농' — same sound, unrelated meaning
Using '유기견' for a stray cat — the cat words are '유기묘' (formal) or '길고양이' (everyday)

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 발톱 means "claw / (animal) nail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 발톱 (baltop) = "claw / (animal) nail". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 발톱을 깎다 ("trim the claws/nails") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 발톱, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: '깎다(to clip/shave off)' — the grooming verb for cutting them down
'갈다(to grind/file)' — what a cat does on a scratcher, not what you do with clippers
the cue that it's time for a trim; '길다' = to be long
one word from 깎다 + -이 (the tool suffix); compare '손톱깎이' for human nails

examples.en: The cat's claws are long.
examples.note: simple level: descriptive '길다'; the cue to trim

examples.en: I trim my dog's nails myself.
examples.note: everyday: '직접' = personally; '깎아 주다' = trim it (for the dog's benefit)

examples.en: The cat keeps sharpening its claws on the sofa.
examples.note: real-life: '자꾸' = repeatedly; why scratching posts ('스크래처') exist — note 갈다, not 깎다

extendedVocab.nuance: '발톱' is a pure-Korean compound of 발 'foot/paw' + 톱 'saw/serrated edge,' covering both a human's toenail and an animal's foot-claw with context deciding which. Its essential paired contrast is the body part '손톱' (손 'hand' + 톱) = fingernail/hand-claw versus '발톱' = the foot/paw nail; an animal walking on all fours has 발톱 on every paw, so calling them '손톱' is wrong. The trickier learner trap is the two grooming verbs that both attach to 발톱: '깎다' means YOU trim/clip them with clippers (a grooming act of removal), whereas '갈다' means the cat sharpens/grinds them on a surface (the cat's own act) — same noun, opposite agents and actions, so '발톱을 깎다' = you cut them, '발톱을 갈다' = the cat files them. Note also '갈다' is a homonym: here 'grind/sharpen,' but elsewhere 'replace' (배변패드를 갈다) — context separates them. Register is neutral everyday. Overgrown 발톱 can curl into the paw, so '발톱이 길면 다칠 수 있어요' is a common care reminder.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using '손톱(fingernail/hand-claw)' for an animal's paw claws — paws take '발톱' (발 'foot' + 톱)
Mixing up '깎다(you clip/trim them)' with '갈다(the cat sharpens/grinds them)' — different agents and actions on the same 발톱
Forgetting '갈다' is a homonym: 'sharpen' here but 'replace' elsewhere; let context (claws vs a pad) decide the meaning

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 털갈이 means "shedding (seasonal molt)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 털갈이 (teolgari) means "shedding (seasonal molt)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 털갈이를 하다 ("shed / molt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 털갈이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the noun takes '하다' to become the verb 'go through shedding'
'철' = (natural) season; spring and fall are the heavy ones
'심하다(to be severe/intense)' is the natural partner for heavy shedding
'시기(時期 period/time)' — interchangeable with '철' but slightly more neutral

examples.en: Lately a lot of hair is falling out.
examples.note: simple level: '털이 빠지다' = hair falls out, the observable sign of shedding

examples.ko: 털갈이할 때는 빗질을 자주 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: teolgarihal ttaeneun bitjireul jaju hae juseyo.
examples.en: During shedding, brush often.
examples.note: everyday care: '빗질' = brushing/combing; '-할 때' = when/during

examples.ko: 우리 고양이는 봄가을마다 털갈이가 정말 심해요.
examples.romanization: uri goyangineun bomgaeulmada teolgariga jeongmal simhaeyo.
examples.en: My cat sheds really heavily every spring and fall.
examples.note: real-life: '-마다' = every; long-haired breeds shed a lot seasonally

extendedVocab.nuance: '털갈이' is a pure-Korean compound of 털 'fur/hair' + 갈이 (from 갈다 'to replace/change,' nominalized), literally 'fur-changing,' and names the seasonal coat turnover when a pet sheds its old fur for a new layer; it peaks in spring and autumn, hence the common '봄/가을 털갈이 철.' The sharp near-synonym contrast learners need is '털갈이' vs '탈모(脫毛)': '털갈이' is the normal, healthy seasonal shed, whereas '탈모' (hanja 脫 'come off' + 毛 'hair') is hair LOSS/balding that signals a problem (illness, stress, skin disease) — so describing routine seasonal shedding as '탈모' wrongly implies your pet is sick. A grammar pitfall is the verb: because '갈이' already carries the 갈다 root as a fixed noun, you say '털갈이를 하다,' not '털을 갈다'; the compound is frozen. Also distinguish the everyday observation '털이 빠지다(hair falls out)' — that describes the symptom, while '털갈이' names the whole seasonal event. Register is neutral and conversational among pet owners, who reach for a '빗(brush)' and do extra '빗질' to manage the loose '빠진 털' during this period.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '털을 갈다': '갈이' is already the fixed nominal compound — the correct form is '털갈이를 하다', not a free '털을 갈다'
Confusing '털갈이(normal seasonal shedding)' with '탈모(脫毛, abnormal hair loss/balding)' — calling a healthy molt '탈모' implies illness
Mixing the symptom and the event: '털이 빠지다' describes hair falling out; '털갈이' names the whole seasonal coat change

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 동물병원 means "veterinary clinic (vet)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "veterinary clinic (vet)" is 동물병원 (dongmulbyeongwon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 동물병원에 가다 ("go to the vet"). Watch the particle attached to 동물병원 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the basic phrase; the destination takes '에' (location of arrival)
'데려가다(take a living being along)' — essential for animals/people
'가깝다(near)' modifying it — useful when searching a map app
'24시(twenty-four-hour)' = open around the clock, for emergencies

examples.en: Is there a vet clinic nearby?
examples.note: simple level: existence question '있어요?' — handy for a new resident

examples.en: My cat was sick so I took it to the vet.
examples.note: everyday: cause '-아서'; '데려가다' for living things, not '가져가다'

examples.en: If it's an emergency at night, find a 24-hour vet.
examples.note: real-life: '응급 상황' = emergency situation; '찾다' = look for/find

extendedVocab.nuance: '동물병원(動物病院)' is transparently 동물(動物 'animal') + 병원(病院 'hospital,' itself 병 'illness' + 원 'institution'), literally 'animal hospital,' and is the one standard word for any vet clinic, large or small — there is no separate casual term, so you use it with friends and on signs alike. Don't confuse the place with the person: '수의사(獸醫師 'beast-doctor')' is the veterinarian, while '동물병원' is where they work — so '수의사 병원' is not how Koreans name the clinic. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the take-verb: Korean strictly separates '데려가다' (take/bring a LIVING being along) from '가져가다' (carry an OBJECT), so you 강아지를 동물병원에 데려가다 — using '가져가다' for your pet treats it like luggage and sounds jarring (the same 데리다/가지다 split applies to people: you 데려가다 a friend, never 가져가다). Register is neutral. For overnight crises, larger cities have '24시 동물병원,' and the location particle is '에' (동물병원에 가다/데려가다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using '가져가다(carry an object)' instead of '데려가다(take a living being)' for your pet — animals and people are 데려가다, never 가져가다
Calling the clinic '수의사 병원': the place is '동물병원'; '수의사(獸醫師)' is the vet, the person who works there
Marking the destination with '에서' instead of '에': you 동물병원에 가다(go TO); '에서' would mean an action done AT the clinic

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 배변패드 means "pee pad / potty pad" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 배변패드 (baebyeonpaedeu) = "pee pad / potty pad". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 배변패드를 깔다 ("lay down a pee pad") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배변패드, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: '깔다(to spread/lay out flat)' — putting a fresh pad on the floor
'갈다(to replace)' — swapping out a soiled pad for a new one
'훈련(訓練 training)' — teaching a puppy to go on the pad

usagePhrases.en: have an accident off the pad
usagePhrases.note: '실수하다(to make a mistake)' — i.e. the dog goes in the wrong spot

examples.en: The dog goes nicely on the pee pad.
examples.note: simple level: '싸다' = to relieve oneself — casual but standard for pets; location takes 에

examples.en: You have to change the pee pad every day.
examples.note: everyday: '갈아 주다' = change it (for the pet's benefit); '-아야 하다' = have to

examples.en: It's not potty-pad trained yet.
examples.note: real-life: '훈련이 되다' = to be/get trained; '아직 안 됐다' = not done yet

extendedVocab.nuance: '배변패드' is a hybrid word: the Sino-Korean 배변(排便 'discharge-feces,' from 배 排 'expel' + 변 便 'excrement') plus the English loanword 패드(pad), literally 'elimination pad,' and it is the standard product name for the absorbent floor pads apartment-dwelling dog owners rely on indoors. The two verbs that pair with it must not be swapped: '깔다' = lay out a FRESH pad (spread it flat on the floor), while '갈다' = REPLACE a used one (the same 갈다 'replace' seen in 털갈이 and 사료를 갈다) — they name different steps in the routine, so '깔다' is setup and '갈다' is the daily swap. A meaning-boundary pitfall: don't say '기저귀(diaper),' which is worn ON the body — the floor product is '배변패드'; a wearable pet diaper would be '강아지 기저귀,' a different item. Register is everyday and practical. Because most Koreans live in apartments without yards, indoor '배변패드 훈련' is extremely common rather than relying on outdoor walks alone, and the blunt-but-normal pet verb '싸다(relieve itself)' is used freely here without sounding crude.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping '깔다(lay out a fresh pad)' and '갈다(replace a soiled pad)' — they are different steps: 깔다 sets it down, 갈다 swaps it out
Saying '기저귀(diaper)' for a floor pad: '기저귀' is worn on the body; the floor product is '배변패드'
Marking the spot with '를' instead of '에': the dog goes 배변패드에(on/at the pad); '배변패드를 싸다' is ungrammatical for the location

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 우정 means "friendship" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 우정 (ujeong) means "friendship". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우정이 깊다 ("the friendship is deep"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 우정 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 깊다 (deep) is the natural depth adjective; 우정이 깊어요 describes a close bond
쌓다 (to stack/pile up) frames friendship as built over time, not 만들다 (make)
진정한 (genuine) is the set modifier you hear in dramas, toasts, and graduation speeches
금이 가다 = a crack forms; idiom for a relationship that's been damaged but not fully broken

examples.en: Let's make our friendship never change, forever.
examples.note: 변치 말자 (let's not change) is a classic friendship-vow line; -자 is warm banmal 'let's'

examples.ko: 힘들 때 곁에 있어 주는 게 진짜 우정이죠.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae gyeote isseo juneun ge jinjja ujeongijyo.
examples.en: Being by your side when times are hard is real friendship.
examples.note: 곁에 있어 주다 = stay by one's side as a favor; -죠 adds a shared, reflective tone

examples.ko: 10년 우정인데 돈 문제로 이렇게 멀어질 줄 몰랐어.
examples.romanization: 10nyeon ujeonginde don munjero ireoke meoreojil jul mollasseo.
examples.en: We've been friends for 10 years; I never thought money would push us this far apart.
examples.note: 멀어지다 = grow distant; -ㄹ 줄 몰랐다 = didn't expect that it would, said in raw banmal

extendedVocab.nuance: 우정 (友情, 友 'friend' + 情 'feeling/affection') is the abstract bond of friendship itself, never the person — a friend is 친구, the relationship is 우정. The dividing line learners most need: don't say 우정 when you mean a buddy. Because 情 carries warm, weighty emotion, 우정 sounds sincere and long-term, reserved for meaningful bonds rather than casual acquaintances (those are just 아는 사이). You build it with 쌓다 (pile up) and describe it as 깊다 (deep) or 끈끈하다 (sticky-tight), and when it breaks you say 우정에 금이 가다. The big English-speaker pitfall is verbing it: 우정 cannot take 하다, so 'we friendship-ed' is impossible — say 친하게 지내다 (get along closely) for the action of being friends.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 우정 to mean 'a friend' (the person) — the person is 친구; 우정 is only the bond between friends
Saying 우정을 만들다 (make a friendship) — the idiomatic verbs are 쌓다 (build up) or 나누다 (share)
Attaching 하다 to it (우정하다 ✗) — for the action use 친하게 지내다; 우정 stays a pure noun

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 신뢰 means "trust" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "trust" is 신뢰 (silloe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신뢰가 가다 ("to feel trust toward someone"). Watch the particle attached to 신뢰 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 신뢰가 가다 (trust flows/comes) is the everyday way to say 'I find them trustworthy'
쌓다 (pile up) — trust is accumulated over repeated reliable actions, never made overnight
잃다 = lose; the result of a broken promise or a lie
무너지다 = crumble/collapse, a stronger total breakdown than just 잃다

examples.en: I trust that person.
examples.note: 신뢰하다 as a verb takes the person as object with 을/를, sounding considered and formal

examples.ko: 저 사람은 말한 건 꼭 지켜서 신뢰가 가.
examples.romanization: jeo sarameun malhan geon kkok jikyeoseo silloega ga.
examples.en: That person always keeps their word, so I trust them.
examples.note: 지키다 = keep (a promise); 신뢰가 가 is the natural banmal verdict on someone

examples.ko: 회사에서 신뢰를 쌓으려면 오랜 시간이 걸려요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo silloereul ssaeuryeomyeon oraen sigani geollyeoyo.
examples.en: Building trust at work takes a long time.
examples.note: -(으)려면 = if you want to; pairs with 쌓다 to stress trust as slow accumulation

extendedVocab.nuance: 신뢰 (信賴, 信 'believe' + 賴 'rely on') is trust as a reasoned, earned noun — more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust someone in the moment). The key contrast for learners is 신뢰 vs 믿음: 믿음 leans emotional or even religious (faith), while 신뢰 is confidence built on a track record, which is why it fits people, workplaces, and institutions alike. You say 신뢰가 가다 ('trust flows') when someone earns your confidence and 신뢰가 무너지다 when it shatters. Note that unlike 우정, 신뢰 does take 하다: 신뢰하다 means 'to trust (someone),' taking the person as a 을/를 object. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 믿다 in formal writing where Korean prefers the noun 신뢰 (e.g. 신뢰를 쌓다, not 믿음을 만들다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 신뢰 as only a noun — 신뢰하다 is a valid verb (저는 그를 신뢰해요); choose noun or verb by register
Confusing 신뢰 (earned, reasoned trust) with 믿음 (belief/faith), which is more emotional or religious
Saying 신뢰를 만들다 (make trust) — use 신뢰를 쌓다 (build up); trust is accumulated, not manufactured

extendedVocab.english: loyalty, sense of duty to people
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 의리 means "loyalty, sense of duty to people" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 의리 (uiri) = "loyalty, sense of duty to people". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 의리가 있다 ("to be loyal / have a sense of duty") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 의리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to be loyal / have a sense of duty
usagePhrases.note: 의리가 있다 is the standard way to praise that someone stands by their people
지키다 = uphold/guard; staying loyal through hard times rather than bailing

usagePhrases.en: to be disloyal / a fair-weather friend
usagePhrases.note: the bare 의리 없다 (dropping 가) is a very common spoken complaint

usagePhrases.en: to stick together out of loyalty
usagePhrases.note: 의리로 = on the basis of loyalty; habitually pairs with 뭉치다 (band together)

examples.en: I knew I could count on you — you're loyal.
examples.note: 너밖에 없다 = no one but you (for me); a warm banmal way to praise 의리

examples.ko: 야, 친구끼리 이러면 의리 없는 거지.
examples.romanization: ya, chingukkiri ireomyeon uiri eopsneun geoji.
examples.en: Hey, doing this to a friend is just disloyal.
examples.note: 친구끼리 = between friends; 없는 거지 turns it into a pointed accusation

examples.ko: 의리 때문에 손해 보면서도 끝까지 도와줬어요.
examples.romanization: uiri ttaemune sonhae bomyeonseodo kkeutkkaji dowajwosseoyo.
examples.en: I helped them to the very end out of loyalty, even taking a loss.
examples.note: 손해 보다 = take a loss; shows 의리 means staying loyal even when it costs you

extendedVocab.nuance: 의리 (義理, 義 'righteousness/duty' + 理 'principle') is a deeply Korean value: staying faithful to friends, family, or your crew even when it costs you, and repaying what you owe people emotionally. The sharp contrast learners must keep is 의리 vs 충성 (忠誠): 충성 is hierarchical allegiance to a company, country, or leader, whereas 의리 is horizontal, personal loyalty to people you share a bond with — so translating a soldier's 'loyalty' as 의리 is wrong. It saturates everyday friend talk ('의리 없냐?') and gangster/brotherhood films. In casual speech it very often appears bare without a particle (의리 있어, 의리 없어). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it to corporate 'loyalty'; 의리 is closer to ride-or-die faithfulness than to brand loyalty (that's 충성도).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 'loyalty to a company/country' as 의리 — that's 충성; 의리 is loyalty to people you have a bond with
Forgetting it's often used bare in speech: '의리 없어' is more natural than always '의리가 없어'
Confusing 의리 (faithfulness to people) with 정의 (justice) — they share the hanja 義 but mean different things

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 갈등 means "conflict, friction (between people)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 갈등 (galdeung) means "conflict, friction (between people)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 갈등이 생기다 ("for a conflict to arise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 갈등 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 (come into being) is the default verb for conflict starting up
겪다 = experience/undergo, used for difficult things you live through
풀다 (untie/loosen) is the natural 'resolve' verb — you loosen the knot, not win
common compound; also 부부 갈등 (marital), 노사 갈등 (labor-management)

examples.en: I've got some friction with a friend these days.
examples.note: -랑 = with (casual); 갈등이 있다 names tension without implying a shouting match

examples.ko: 갈등이 생기면 바로 대화로 푸는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: galdeungi saenggimyeon baro daehwaro puneun ge joayo.
examples.en: When conflict comes up, it's best to resolve it right away by talking.
examples.note: 대화로 풀다 = resolve through conversation; the instrumental 로 marks the means

examples.ko: 두 부서 사이의 갈등이 점점 깊어지고 있습니다.
examples.romanization: du buseo saiui galdeungi jeomjeom gipeojigo itseumnida.
examples.en: The conflict between the two departments is steadily deepening.
examples.note: 깊어지다 = grow deeper; -습니다 gives the formal workplace/report register

extendedVocab.nuance: 갈등 (葛藤) has a vivid literal origin: 葛 is kudzu vine and 藤 is wisteria vine — two vines twisting in opposite directions and tangling, the perfect image for clashing interests. It covers both interpersonal friction and inner dilemmas (내적 갈등), but in daily life it usually means tension between people. The contrast learners confuse: 갈등 vs 싸움 — 갈등 is the underlying, often quiet tension, while 싸움/다툼 is the open quarrel or fight; you can carry 갈등 for months without ever raising your voice. Because it's a knot of tangled vines, you 풀다 (untie) or 해결하다 (solve) it — never 이기다 (win). The English-speaker pitfall is using 갈등 for a single loud argument; that moment is 싸움, and 갈등 is the standing friction behind it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 갈등 for a loud argument — that moment is 싸움 or 다툼; 갈등 is the underlying tension behind it
Saying 갈등을 이기다 (win the conflict) — you 풀다 (untie) or 해결하다 (resolve) it; conflict isn't won
Forgetting it also covers inner conflict (내적 갈등); it's not only between people

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 오해 means "misunderstanding" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "misunderstanding" is 오해 (ohae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오해가 생기다 ("for a misunderstanding to arise"). Watch the particle attached to 오해 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 = arise; the standard collocation when wires get crossed
풀다 (untie) is exactly the verb you need when you apologize and explain
오해하다 is the verb form; 오해했어요 = I misunderstood / I got it wrong
오해하지 마 is an extremely common reassurance among friends defusing tension

examples.en: Ah, that's a misunderstanding.
examples.note: -예요 attaches after a vowel-final noun; the quickest way to flag a mix-up politely

examples.ko: 오해하지 마, 너 욕한 거 아니야.
examples.romanization: ohaehaji ma, neo yokan geo aniya.
examples.en: Don't get the wrong idea, I wasn't badmouthing you.
examples.note: 욕하다 = badmouth/curse; 오해하지 마 + 아니야 reassures a friend in banmal

examples.ko: 빨리 만나서 오해를 푸는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: ppalli mannaseo ohaereul puneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: We'd better meet soon and clear up the misunderstanding.
examples.note: -는 게 좋겠어요 = it'd be best to; a gentle suggestion to fix things in person

extendedVocab.nuance: 오해 (誤解, 誤 'mistake/wrong' + 解 'understand/untie') is reading a situation or someone's intent the wrong way. Its built-in hanja 解 ('untie') is why the fixing verb is 오해를 풀다 — you literally un-knot the wrong reading; never 오해를 고치다 (fix). The contrast learners need is 오해 vs 착각: 오해 is misreading another person or an external situation, while 착각 is a personal slip or delusion in your own head (e.g. 시간을 착각했어 'I had the time wrong'). The phrase 오해하지 마 ('don't misunderstand') is one of the most useful relationship lines you can own — it heads off conflict before it grows. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 오해 like English 'misunderstanding' that you 'fix' or 'solve'; in Korean you untie it (풀다), and you can also use the verb 오해하다 directly on a person (나를 오해했어).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오해를 고치다 (fix a misunderstanding) — the idiom is 오해를 풀다 (untie it)
Mixing up 오해 (misreading someone/something external) with 착각 (a slip or delusion in your own head)
Using 오해 for a factual error in a test or fact — that's 실수 or 틀리다, not 오해

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 험담 means "badmouthing, malicious gossip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 험담 (heomdam) = "badmouthing, malicious gossip". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 험담을 하다 ("to badmouth someone") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 험담, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb; the basic neutral form of the act of speaking ill

usagePhrases.en: to go on and on badmouthing
usagePhrases.note: 늘어놓다 = lay out at length; stresses nonstop trash-talk
뒤에서 = behind the back, the typical cowardly setting for 험담
남 = other people; 남 험담만 한다 = does nothing but talk others down

examples.ko: 남 험담은 안 하는 게 좋아.
examples.romanization: nam heomdameun an haneun ge joa.
examples.en: It's better not to badmouth others.
examples.note: 안 하는 게 좋아 = it's better not to; simple banmal advice with a moral tone

examples.ko: 걔는 맨날 뒤에서 동료 험담만 해.
examples.romanization: gyaeneun maennal dwieseo dongnyo heomdamman hae.
examples.en: She does nothing but badmouth coworkers behind their backs.
examples.note: 맨날 = every single day; 험담만 하다 = do only badmouthing, a banmal complaint

examples.ko: 험담은 결국 돌고 돌아 본인한테 돌아와요.
examples.romanization: heomdameun gyeolguk dolgo dora boninhante dorawayo.
examples.en: Badmouthing eventually goes around and comes back to you.
examples.note: 돌고 돌아 = going round and round; a proverb-like warning in polite speech

extendedVocab.nuance: 험담 (險談, 險 'steep/harsh/dangerous' + 談 'talk') is speaking ill of someone with a clearly cruel, malicious edge — the hanja literally paints 'harsh talk,' so it is never neutral. The contrast learners need: 험담 vs 뒷담화 vs 소문 — 험담 stresses the nasty content of the words, 뒷담화 stresses the behind-the-back act, and 소문 is a neutral rumor with no malice. So you can spread a 소문 by accident, but 험담 always carries ill will. It pairs with 하다, 늘어놓다, and the setting 뒤에서. The English-speaker pitfall is equating it with casual English 'gossip,' which can be playful; 험담 is stronger and always negative, so saying 험담은 안 좋아해요 actually signals good character rather than just disinterest in chit-chat (that lighter sense is 수다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 험담 for neutral chit-chat or rumors — light talk is 수다, a rumor is 소문; 험담 is always malicious
Treating 험담 as harmless 'gossip' — it implies real ill will, so it's heavier than English gossip
Confusing it with 뒷담화 — 험담 = the cruel words themselves, 뒷담화 = the behind-the-back act

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뒷담화 means "talking behind someone's back" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 뒷담화 (dwitdamhwa) means "talking behind someone's back". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 뒷담화를 하다 ("to talk behind someone's back"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뒷담화 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb; the everyday neutral form of the act
까다 = a slangy verb for dishing dirt; very colloquial among young people

usagePhrases.en: to catch wind that you were talked about
usagePhrases.note: 듣다 here = to hear that you were the subject of back-talk
대상 = object/target; who the group keeps gossiping about

examples.ko: 우리 뒷담화 같은 거 하지 말자.
examples.romanization: uri dwitdamhwa gateun geo haji malja.
examples.en: Let's not do stuff like talking behind people's backs.
examples.note: 같은 거 = stuff like; -자 makes it a soft group resolution in banmal

examples.ko: 내 뒷담화 한 거 다 들었거든?
examples.romanization: nae dwitdamhwa han geo da deureotgeodeun?
examples.en: I heard everything you said about me behind my back, okay?
examples.note: -거든 adds a pointed 'just so you know' jab; sharp banmal

examples.ko: 회식 자리에서 상사 뒷담화 까는 건 진짜 위험해요.
examples.romanization: hoesik jarieseo sangsa dwitdamhwa kkaneun geon jinjja wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: Trash-talking the boss at a company dinner is genuinely risky.
examples.note: 회식 = company dinner; 까다 is the slangy 'dish on,' fine in casual speech only

extendedVocab.nuance: 뒷담화 is a hybrid word: native Korean 뒤 'back' + the Sino-Korean 담화 (談話 'talk/discourse'), joined with a sai-siot ㅅ, literally 'back-talk.' It names the act of gossiping about someone who isn't present, focusing on the sneaky behind-the-back nature rather than purely cruel content. The contrast learners need: 뒷담화 vs 험담 — 뒷담화 is the behind-the-back act (the person could even praise you, though by default it's negative), while 험담 zeroes in on malicious words; 뒷담화 also feels a notch more casual and modern. Spelling it 뒷담하 or 뒤담화 — the correct form is 뒷담화 (뒤 + sai-siot ㅅ + 담화)
Using it for praise said behind someone's back — by default 뒷담화 is negative, so clarify if you mean otherwise
Using 까다 in formal or polite settings — 뒷담화 까다 is slang; with a superior use 뒷담화를 하다

extendedVocab.english: social awareness, ability to read the room
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 눈치 means "social awareness, ability to read the room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "social awareness, ability to read the room" is 눈치 (nunchi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 눈치가 빠르다 ("to be quick to read situations"). Watch the particle attached to 눈치 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be quick to read situations
usagePhrases.note: 빠르다 (fast) is the highest compliment — your social radar is sharp
없다 (lacking) = can't read the room at all; a genuine criticism

usagePhrases.en: to read someone's mood / walk on eggshells
usagePhrases.note: 보다 (watch) = checking how others feel, often a superior, before acting
채다 = to catch (on); 눈치챘어 = I noticed / I figured it out

examples.en: He's really quick to pick up on things.
examples.note: 눈치 빠르다 drops 가 in casual speech; the go-to banmal compliment for social sharpness

examples.ko: 저는 눈치가 없어서 분위기를 잘 못 읽어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun nunchiga eopseoseo bunwigireul jal mot ilgeoyo.
examples.en: I'm a bit clueless, so I don't read the mood well.
examples.note: 분위기를 읽다 = read the atmosphere; a humble self-description in polite speech

examples.ko: 사장님 눈치 보느라 일찍 못 가요.
examples.romanization: sajangnim nunchi boneura iljjing mot gayo.
examples.en: I can't leave early because I'm watching the boss's mood.
examples.note: -느라 = on account of (doing); 눈치 보다 toward a superior is classic office reality

extendedVocab.nuance: 눈치 is a native-Korean word (눈 'eye' + 치) and one of the most essential Korean social concepts: the radar for sensing what others feel and what's appropriate without being told. The distinctions learners trip on are between its set phrases: 눈치가 빠르다 ('quick eye') is high praise, 눈치가 없다 is a real social criticism, 눈치를 보다 means cautiously reading someone's mood (often a boss's, with a slightly self-conscious feel), and 눈치(를) 채다 means to catch on / notice something. So 보다 and 채다 are not interchangeable — one is ongoing wariness, the other is a moment of realization. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 눈치 to 'eyes' or vision because of 눈; it has nothing to do with eyesight and everything to do with social perceptiveness. Living in Korea you'll use and need this word daily.

Translating it as 'eyes' or eyesight because of 눈 — 눈치 is the social skill of reading people, not vision
Confusing 눈치를 보다 (cautiously read someone's mood) with 눈치를 채다 (notice/catch on to something)
Saying 눈치가 좋다 for 'quick-witted' — the set phrase is 눈치가 빠르다; 좋다 sounds off here
