extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 인연 means "a fateful connection, meant-to-be relationship" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 인연 (inyeon) = "a fateful connection, meant-to-be relationship". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 인연이 있다 ("to be fated to meet / have a connection") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 인연, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to be fated to meet / have a connection
usagePhrases.note: 있다 = there is; implies fate, not just acquaintance, brought you together

usagePhrases.en: for a connection to come about
usagePhrases.note: 닿다 = to reach/touch; poetic 'fate reached us and connected us'

usagePhrases.en: a good connection / good people to have met
usagePhrases.note: warm phrase for meaningful relationships worth keeping
끊다 = cut off; severing a relationship permanently

examples.en: I guess we're really meant to be.
examples.note: -나 봐 = I guess / it seems; a sweet, slightly flirty banmal line on a lucky coincidence

examples.en: I made a lot of good connections here.
examples.note: 만들다 is idiomatic with 인연; this is what you say when leaving a job or city

examples.en: I guess that person and I just weren't meant to be.
examples.note: -하고는 = with (contrastive); a reflective, gentle way to accept a falling-out or breakup

extendedVocab.nuance: 인연 (因緣, 因 'cause' + 緣 'condition/tie') is a Buddhist term — the idea that meetings happen because causes and conditions ripen, so some encounters feel destined. It carries a soft, almost spiritual warmth and applies to romance, friendships, mentors, even a chance encounter on a train. The contrast learners must keep is 인연 vs 관계: 관계 is any neutral relationship or connection (including official or logical ones), whereas 인연 specifically implies fate or destiny, so you can't swap them. '우리 인연인가 봐' is a sweet, slightly flirty line; cutting it off is 인연을 끊다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 인연 as a plain word for 'relationship'; that flattens its fated nuance — use 관계 for ordinary ties, and note you say 인연이 있다 / 인연이 닿다 rather than 인연을 만나다 (you don't 'meet a fate').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 인연 as a neutral word for any 'relationship' — that's 관계; 인연 carries fate/destiny
Saying 인연을 만나다 (meet a fate) — say 인연이 있다 / 인연이 닿다, or 인연을 만들다 for forming connections
Forcing it onto purely formal or business ties — those are 관계 or 거래 관계, not 인연

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 배신 means "betrayal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 배신 (baesin) means "betrayal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 배신을 당하다 ("to be betrayed"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 배신 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 당하다 = to have done to you; the passive everyday form when you're the victim
하다 verb; 네가 나를 배신했어 = you betrayed me, with you as the agent
-감 = sense/feeling; 배신감(이) 들다 = the betrayed feeling wells up
literally 'hit the back of the head'; vivid casual synonym for betraying

examples.ko: 어떻게 나한테 이럴 수가, 완전 배신이야.
examples.romanization: eotteoke nahante ireol suga, wanjeon baesiniya.
examples.en: How could you do this to me — this is total betrayal.
examples.note: 어떻게 ~수가 = how could (you); 배신이야 lands the emotional blow in banmal

examples.en: I never expected them to stab me in the back like that.
examples.note: 뒤통수(를) 치다 = backstab; -ㄹ 줄 몰랐다 = didn't expect that they would

examples.ko: 믿었던 친구한테 배신당해서 한동안 아무도 못 믿었어요.
examples.romanization: mideotdeon chinguhante baesindanghaeseo handongan amudo mon mideosseoyo.
examples.en: After being betrayed by a friend I trusted, I couldn't trust anyone for a while.
examples.note: 믿었던 = whom I had trusted; 배신당하다 makes you clearly the one betrayed

extendedVocab.nuance: 배신 (背信, 背 'turn one's back' + 信 'trust/faith') literally means turning your back on someone's trust — a heavy, emotional word for real broken loyalty, not a small letdown. The contrast learners need is 배신 vs 실망: 실망 is disappointment when someone falls short of your hopes, whereas 배신 is an active breaking of trust by someone you counted on, so a friend who forgets your birthday is 실망, but one who steals from you is 배신. Crucially for English speakers, voice matters: 배신하다 means you did the betraying, while 'I was betrayed' must be 배신을 당하다 / 배신당하다 — Korean won't let the active verb carry the passive sense. The vivid idiom 뒤통수(를) 치다 ('hit the back of the head') is the casual go-to for backstabbing, and 배신감 (the feeling) is used just as often as the act.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배신 for minor letdowns — it's strong, for genuinely broken trust; mild disappointment is 실망
Saying 배신했어 to mean 'I was betrayed' — that means you betrayed someone; use 배신당했어 for the passive
Forgetting 배신감 — to express the feeling, Koreans often say 배신감(이) 들다 rather than just 배신

extendedVocab.english: yielding, giving way, deferring to others
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 양보 means "yielding, giving way, deferring to others" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "yielding, giving way, deferring to others" is 양보 (yangbo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 양보하다 ("to yield / give way / defer"). Watch the particle attached to 양보 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb; the everyday form for graciously stepping aside
자리 = seat; the classic subway/bus courtesy, especially toward elders

usagePhrases.en: to meet halfway / each give a little
usagePhrases.note: 서로 = each other; the spirit of compromise in a disagreement

usagePhrases.en: give a little / cut me some slack
usagePhrases.note: a casual plea to be more flexible; banmal

examples.en: Go ahead first, I'll let you.
examples.note: 양보할게요 = I'll yield; -ㄹ게요 marks a polite on-the-spot offer to defer

examples.en: I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
examples.note: -께 = honorific 'to'; a daily act of courtesy that 양보 most strongly evokes

examples.ko: 둘 다 조금씩 양보하면 금방 해결될 거예요.
examples.romanization: dul da jogeumssik yangbohamyeon geumbang haegyeoldoel geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you each give a little, it'll be sorted out quickly.
examples.note: 조금씩 = little by little; 서로 양보하는 spirit applied to resolving conflict

extendedVocab.nuance: 양보 (讓步, 讓 'yield/concede' + 步 'step') literally means 'a yielding step' — stepping back so someone else can go first. It's the act of giving up your seat, your turn, or your preference for another's sake, and it's a prized social virtue in Korea, especially toward elders (자리를 양보하다 on the subway is everyday courtesy). The contrast learners must keep is 양보 vs 포기: 양보 is voluntarily and graciously ceding something to another person (it has a beneficiary), while 포기 is abandoning a goal or giving up entirely (no beneficiary, often defeat) — so 'I gave up my dream' is 포기, never 양보. It also covers traffic: 양보 운전 is courteous yielding right-of-way. The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing 'give up' into one word; in Korean, yielding to a person (양보) and quitting a goal (포기) are different verbs.

Confusing 양보 (graciously yielding to someone) with 포기 (giving up on a goal entirely) — different verbs
Using it only for seats — it also covers yielding your turn, your opinion, or right-of-way (양보 운전)
Saying 양보 to mean 'losing/being forced to give in' — 양보 is voluntary and gracious, not defeat

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 화해 means "reconciliation, making up" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 화해 (hwahae) = "reconciliation, making up". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 화해하다 ("to make up / reconcile") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 화해, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb; 우리 화해했어요 = we made up
친구하고 화해하다 = make up with a friend; the partner takes 와/과/하고

usagePhrases.en: to make up first / extend the olive branch
usagePhrases.note: 먼저 = first; being the bigger person who reaches out, seen as mature
손길 = a reaching hand/touch; the move toward making peace

examples.en: Let's stop fighting now and make up.
examples.note: 그만 싸우다 = stop fighting; -자 is a warm banmal 'let's' between close people

examples.en: I reached out first to make up.
examples.note: 먼저 화해하다 = be the first to reconcile; -려고 = intending to, with you taking the initiative

examples.en: After the marital spat, we sincerely reconciled.
examples.note: 부부 싸움 = couple's quarrel; 진심으로 = sincerely, stressing a real, heartfelt making-up

extendedVocab.nuance: 화해 (和解, 和 'harmony/peace' + 解 'untie/resolve') is making peace after a fight or falling-out — untying the harmony back together, restoring a damaged personal relationship. The verb 화해하다 is what you use with friends, partners, and family ('우리 화해하자'), and the partner is marked with 와/과/하고. The contrast learners need is 화해 vs 평화: 평화 (平和) is peace as a state — no war, calm, tranquility — whereas 화해 is the interpersonal act of two sides reconciling, so a peace treaty between nations leans 평화/평화 협정 while two friends making up is 화해. Being the one to reach out first, 먼저 화해하다, reads as mature and warm in Korean culture. The English-speaker pitfall is using 화해 for general 'peace' or applying 만들다 to it — just use the verb 화해하다 (or 화해를 하다), not 화해를 만들다.

Confusing 화해 (people reconciling) with 평화 (peace as a calm state / no war) — 화해 is interpersonal
Saying 화해를 만들다 (make a reconciliation) — use the verb 화해하다 or 화해를 하다
Dropping the partner particle — 'make up with a friend' is 친구와/하고 화해하다, not 친구를 화해하다

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 삼겹살 means "pork belly (grilled)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal) means "pork belly (grilled)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 삼겹살 2인분 주세요 ("Two servings of pork belly, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 삼겹살 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Two servings of pork belly, please
usagePhrases.note: Meat is ordered by 인분 (serving), never by piece — this is the core ordering phrase.

usagePhrases.en: Pork belly with a shot of soju
usagePhrases.note: 에 here marks the food you pair a drink with; the most iconic Korean food-and-drink combo.

usagePhrases.en: We grill and eat pork belly
usagePhrases.note: 굽다 → 구워 (ㅂ-irregular); you cook it yourself at the table-top grill.

usagePhrases.en: The fat renders right out, which is great
usagePhrases.note: 쫙 빠지다 is the set phrase Koreans use to praise well-grilled 삼겹살.

examples.en: Want to go eat pork belly?
examples.note: The everyday casual invite; 먹으러 가다 = go in order to eat.

examples.en: Is the pork belly fully cooked?
examples.note: 익다 = (food) to be cooked through; ask before you pick a piece off the grill.

examples.en: Pork belly only tastes right wrapped in a lettuce leaf.
examples.note: 쌈 = the lettuce/perilla wrap; -아야 제맛이다 = 'it's only truly good when…', a very natural food cliché.

extendedVocab.nuance: 삼겹살 literally breaks down as 삼(三, three) + 겹(layer) + 살(flesh) — 'three-layered meat' — naming the alternating stripes of fat and lean in pork belly, and it is the single most iconic Korean BBQ cut and a default casual group meal. Don't confuse it with 목살 (pork neck/collar, leaner) or 오겹살 (a five-layer belly cut with the skin on); waiters list these as separate menu lines. Register-wise the word itself is neutral, but the situation is firmly casual — friends, 회식 work dinners, late nights with soju — never a formal banquet. The pitfall for English speakers is the counter: 'a piece of pork belly' tempts you into 삼겹살 한 개, but you must order by 인분 (삼겹살 2인분), and you say 구워 먹다 (grill-and-eat) rather than the English 'have a barbecue,' because here you do the grilling yourself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 삼겹살 한 개 — meat is counted by 인분 (serving), so the correct order is 삼겹살 1인분 / 2인분.
Calling any grilled pork 삼겹살 — 삼겹살 is specifically the belly cut; 목살 (neck) and 항정살 (jowl) are different lines on the menu.
Using 만들다 ('make') for grilling at the table — Koreans say 삼겹살 구워 먹다 (grill and eat), not 삼겹살 만들다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 갈비 means "ribs (beef or pork)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "ribs (beef or pork)" is 갈비 (galbi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 돼지갈비 vs 소갈비 ("Pork ribs vs. beef ribs"). Watch the particle attached to 갈비 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 갈비 alone is ambiguous, so the species prefix 돼지/소 is almost always attached.
양념 = seasoning/marinade; -로 주세요 picks one option among several.
Grilled 갈비 is counted by 인분; ~이요 is the quick spoken order form.

usagePhrases.en: One bowl of rib soup, please
usagePhrases.note: 갈비탕 is a soup dish counted by 그릇 (bowl), not 인분 — a different format from grilled 갈비.

examples.en: This place is famous for its marinated ribs.
examples.note: 은/는 here flags 양념갈비 as the topic/specialty being contrasted.

examples.ko: 갈비는 좀 비싸지만 가끔 먹을 만해요.
examples.romanization: galbineun jom bissajiman gakkeum meogeul manhaeyo.
examples.en: Ribs are a bit pricey, but worth it once in a while.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 만하다 = 'worth doing'; beef 갈비 especially reads as a splurge.

examples.en: Shall we go for rib soup at lunch?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ까요? softly proposes a plan; 갈비탕 is a comforting everyday lunch.

extendedVocab.nuance: 갈비 means the rib cut, and it heads a whole family of dishes: grilled plain 생갈비, sweet-marinated 양념갈비, the braised 갈비찜, and the soup 갈비탕. The crucial ambiguity for a learner is species — 갈비 can be beef or pork, so Koreans say 소갈비 or 돼지갈비 to be clear, and at many casual BBQ joints an unqualified '갈비' defaults to the cheaper 돼지갈비, while 소갈비 reads as a costly, special-occasion meal. Note the cut sits next to 삼겹살 and 등심 as a grilling option but, unlike them, has a famous sweet marinade tradition (soy, sugar, pear, garlic). The English-speaker trap is treating 갈비 as automatically 'beef ribs' and then conflating the grilled cut with the soup: 갈비 is the rib itself, whereas 갈비탕 (-탕 = clear soup) is a boiled dish — ordering one expecting the other is a common mix-up.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 갈비 always means beef — at many BBQ spots an unmarked 갈비 defaults to pork (돼지갈비); specify 소갈비 for beef.
Treating 갈비 and 갈비탕 as the same thing — 갈비 is the grilled rib; 갈비탕 (-탕 soup) is a boiled broth dish.
Counting 갈비탕 by 인분 — soups are counted by 그릇 (bowl): 갈비탕 한 그릇, while grilled 갈비 uses 인분.

The English-speaker trap is treating 갈비 as automatically 'beef ribs' and then conflating the grilled cut with the soup: 갈비 is the rib itself, whereas 갈비탕 (-탕 = clear soup) is a boiled dish. Ordering one expecting the other is a common mix-up.

extendedVocab.explanation: 등심 (deungsim) = "sirloin / loin (cut of beef)". usagePhrases.note: A leaner premium beef cut at 소고기 (beef) restaurants, counted by 인분.
부드럽다 (ㅂ-irregular → 부드러워요) is the key praise word for a good cut.

usagePhrases.en: Between sirloin and tenderloin, which is better?
usagePhrases.note: N하고 N 중에 = 'among A and B'; the two cuts are constantly compared.

usagePhrases.en: I'll have the ribeye (marbled sirloin), please
usagePhrases.note: 꽃등심 = the marbled 'flower' upgrade of 등심, a prized higher-grade cut.

examples.en: At a beef restaurant, sirloin is the standard order.
examples.note: 기본 = the default/basic choice; -에서는 sets the location as the frame.

examples.en: Ribeye has good marbling, so it costs more.
examples.note: -아서 links cause→result; 마블링 (marbling) is the price driver for beef.

examples.en: If you overcook sirloin, it turns tough.
examples.note: 익히다 = to cook (transitive); 질겨지다 = to become chewy/tough — lean cuts dry out.

extendedVocab.nuance: 등심 is the loin/sirloin, the workhorse grilling cut at beef-focused restaurants — relatively lean yet tender, and the cut people mean by default when they say 'let's get 소고기.' It is a native Korean compound, 등 (back) + 심 (the core/inner flesh), not a Sino-Korean word, so don't go looking for a 한자 reading. The synonym boundary to nail is 등심 vs 안심: both are premium, but 등심 (sirloin, from the back) has a touch more fat and bite, while 안심 (tenderloin) is leaner and softer; menus list them side by side, and the marbled upgrade 꽃등심 ('flower sirloin' = ribeye) is the splurge tier above plain 등심. Collocations cluster around texture and grade: 등심이 부드럽다 (tender), 마블링이 좋다 (well-marbled), 질겨지다 (gets tough). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'sirloin/loin' loosely and ordering 등심 expecting cheap pork — it is almost always higher-priced beef — and overcooking it the way you might a steak, when Koreans grill these cuts only briefly to keep them 부드럽다.

Confusing 등심 (sirloin, slightly fattier, more bite) with 안심 (tenderloin, leaner and softer) — they are adjacent but distinct menu cuts.

Grilling 등심 long like a well-done steak — overcooking makes it 질겨지다 (tough); Koreans sear it briefly.

extendedVocab.explanation: 안심 (ansim) means "tenderloin (cut of meat)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 안심 스테이크로 주세요 ("I'll have the tenderloin steak"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 안심 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 안심 is the leanest, most tender cut and the classic steak choice; -로 picks the option.

usagePhrases.en: Tenderloin is more tender than sirloin
usagePhrases.note: N보다 = 'than N'; the standard comparison that defines 안심.
Counted by 인분 at beef restaurants, like other grilling cuts.
안심 exists for pork too and is the lean cut used in 돈가스 (cutlet).

examples.en: Tenderloin is low in fat, so it's clean and mild.
examples.note: 기름기 = fattiness; 담백하다 = mild, non-greasy — the signature flavor note for lean cuts.

examples.en: I ordered the steak as tenderloin.
examples.note: -(으)로 marks the material/choice the steak is made from.

examples.en: Because it was tenderloin, it was a bit pricier.
examples.note: N(이)라서 = 'because it is N'; 안심 is a premium lean cut.

extendedVocab.nuance: 안심 is the tenderloin — the leanest, softest muscle (it does little work), which is why it is the go-to for 스테이크 and why people praise it as 담백하다 (mild and clean, not greasy) and 부드럽다 (tender). The key contrast is 안심 vs 등심: counter to English intuition, the 'tenderloin' 안심 is the leaner one, while 등심 (sirloin) carries a bit more fat and chew — learners often guess the opposite. The headache here is the homonym: 안심 the cut is spelled identically to the verb 안심하다 (安心하다, 'to feel relieved / at ease', literally 'settle the heart'), so 안심하세요 means 'don't worry,' not anything about meat — only context (a menu vs. a conversation) disambiguates. Collocations: 안심 스테이크, 기름기가 적다, 담백하다. The pitfall is twofold — reading the meat 안심 as the feeling-relieved word, and assuming the 'tender' cut must be the fattier one when it is actually the leanest.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 안심 (tenderloin, the cut) with 안심하다 (安心 'to be relieved') — identical spelling, completely different meaning; only context tells them apart.
Assuming 안심 is fattier than 등심 — it is the opposite: 안심 (tenderloin) is the leaner, more 담백한 cut.
Describing 안심 as 느끼해요 (greasy) — lean cuts are 담백해요; 느끼하다 fits fatty foods, not tenderloin.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 닭다리 means "chicken leg / drumstick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "chicken leg / drumstick" is 닭다리 (dalkdari). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 닭다리 하나 주세요 ("Give me one chicken drumstick, please"). Watch the particle attached to 닭다리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Give me one chicken drumstick, please
usagePhrases.note: It's a discrete piece, so it's counted with 하나/개, not 인분.
살 = the flesh; 닭다리살 is the de-boned thigh/leg meat used in bowls and lunchboxes.

usagePhrases.en: Drumsticks are juicier than chicken breast
usagePhrases.note: 촉촉하다 = moist/juicy; the standard leg-vs-breast contrast.

usagePhrases.en: I go for the drumstick first
usagePhrases.note: N부터 = 'starting from N'; signals the leg is your favorite piece.

examples.ko: 치킨 시키면 저는 닭다리 먼저 먹어요.
examples.romanization: chikin sikimyeon jeoneun dalkdari meonjeo meogeoyo.
examples.en: When we order fried chicken, I eat the drumstick first.
examples.note: 시키다 = to order (food); 먼저 = first — the popular piece everyone reaches for.

examples.en: This is a lunchbox made with boneless chicken-leg meat.
examples.note: -(으)로 만들다 = 'made with'; 닭다리살 (de-boned) is common in 도시락.

examples.en: Kids usually like the drumsticks more.
examples.note: 보통 = usually; the leg is the easy-to-hold, kid-friendly piece.

extendedVocab.nuance: 닭다리 is a transparent compound, 닭(chicken) + 다리(leg), meaning the drumstick/leg — widely considered the juiciest, most flavorful part and often the most fought-over piece when a group shares 치킨 (fried chicken). The useful derived form is 닭다리살, the boneless leg/thigh meat (살 = flesh) that fills 도시락 lunchboxes and rice bowls; contrast it with 닭가슴살 (breast meat), the leaner, drier cut that dieters and gym-goers eat. Texture words pair naturally: 닭다리는 촉촉하다 (juicy/moist) versus 닭가슴살은 퍽퍽하다 (dry/mealy). The counting pitfall matters: because 닭다리 is one bone-in piece, count it with 개/하나 (닭다리 하나), never 인분, which is for table-grilled meat by the portion. A second English-speaker trap is treating leg and breast as interchangeable 'chicken' — Koreans care about the cut, so 닭다리 vs 닭가슴살 is a real menu-and-preference distinction, not a throwaway detail.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting 닭다리 with 인분 — it's a single piece, so use 개 or 하나 (닭다리 하나, 닭다리 두 개).
Treating 닭다리 (leg, juicy) and 닭가슴살 (breast, lean/dry) as the same 'chicken' — they differ a lot in fat and texture.
Saying 닭다리가 말랐어요 for 'the leg is dry' — use 퍽퍽하다 for dry meat; 마르다 means a body/object is thin or dried out.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 새우 means "shrimp / prawn" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 새우 (saeu) = "shrimp / prawn". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 새우 알레르기 있어요 ("I'm allergic to shrimp") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 새우, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: N 알레르기(가) 있다 = 'have an N allergy'; a safety-critical phrase when ordering.
튀김 = deep-fried dish; one of the most common 새우 preparations.
빼다 = to remove/omit; -아 주세요 politely requests it be taken out.

usagePhrases.en: Does this have shrimp in it?
usagePhrases.note: 들어가다 here = (an ingredient) to be included; the go-to question for allergies.

examples.en: Do you like shrimp?
examples.note: A simple everyday preference question with the bare noun.

examples.en: Does this fried rice have shrimp in it?
examples.note: 들어가다 asks whether an ingredient is inside — essential for checking allergens.

examples.ko: 새우 알레르기가 있어서 새우는 꼭 빼 주세요.
examples.romanization: saeu allereugiga isseoseo saeuneun kkok ppae juseyo.
examples.en: I have a shrimp allergy, so please be sure to leave the shrimp out.
examples.note: Chain allergy + 꼭(definitely) + 빼 주세요 to order safely in a real situation.

extendedVocab.nuance: 새우 (shrimp/prawn) is one of the most ubiquitous proteins in Korean cooking — fried as 새우튀김, in 볶음밥 (fried rice), in stews, in 깐쇼새우 — so the words around it are practical survival vocabulary, especially 새우 알레르기 있어요 and 새우 빼 주세요 for anyone with a shellfish allergy. Watch the verb 들어가다 ('to go in', here 'to be an ingredient'): 새우 들어가요? literally 'does shrimp go in?' is exactly how you ask whether a dish contains it. Keep 새우 distinct from neighboring shellfish — 게 (crab), 가재 (crayfish/lobster), 조개 (clam) — since 'seafood' in English blurs them but Korean menus name each. The big English-speaker pitfall is the omission phrase: learners reach for 새우 없어요 ('there's no shrimp') to mean 'I can't eat shrimp,' which only states a fact about availability; to make a request you must say 새우 빼 주세요 (remove the shrimp) or state the allergy outright.

Saying 새우 없어요 to mean 'I can't have shrimp' — that just means 'there is no shrimp'; request it with 새우 빼 주세요 or state 새우 알레르기 있어요.
Lumping 새우 with 게 (crab) or 가재 (crayfish) as one 'seafood' — Korean names each shellfish separately on menus.
Using 있다/없다 to ask if a dish contains shrimp — the natural verb is 들어가다: 새우 들어가요?

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 오징어 means "squid / cuttlefish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 오징어 (ojingeo) means "squid / cuttlefish". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오징어볶음 ("Spicy stir-fried squid"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오징어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 볶음 = stir-fry; a popular spicy dish eaten with rice.
질기다 = tough/chewy; squid turns rubbery when overcooked.
마르다 → 마른 (modifier); a classic 안주 (drinking snack) and beer companion.
Whole animals/seafood are counted with 마리, not 개.

examples.en: Do you like squid?
examples.note: Polite everyday preference question with -세요.

examples.ko: 오징어볶음은 밥이랑 같이 먹으면 진짜 맛있어요.
examples.romanization: ojingeobokkeumeun babirang gachi meogeumyeon jinjja masisseoyo.
examples.en: Spicy stir-fried squid is really good eaten with rice.
examples.note: N(이)랑 같이 = 'together with N'; a staple rice-pairing dish.

examples.en: If you cook squid too long, it gets rubbery.
examples.note: 익히다 = to cook (transitive); 질겨지다 = to turn tough — cook squid only briefly.

extendedVocab.nuance: 오징어 (squid) is a native everyday word that shows up across the menu: the spicy stir-fry 오징어볶음 eaten over rice, grilled 오징어구이, and especially the dried 마른 오징어, a quintessential 안주 (drinking snack) sold in every convenience store. The texture vocabulary is central — 질기다 (chewy/rubbery) and its change form 질겨지다 (to become tough) — because Koreans know squid must be cooked briefly or it turns rubbery, the opposite of beef which can simmer. The counting pitfall is real: a whole squid is 한 마리 (마리 counts animals and seafood), never 한 개. The other English-speaker trap is lumping cephalopods together: 오징어 (squid), 문어 (octopus), and 낙지 (small/long-arm octopus) are three distinct items with different dishes and prices, so calling all of them 'squid' will get you the wrong thing — for example 낙지볶음 and 오징어볶음 are separate menu lines.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting 오징어 with 개 — whole seafood takes 마리: 오징어 한 마리, 두 마리.
Calling 문어 (octopus) or 낙지 (small octopus) '오징어' — they are different animals and different dishes on the menu.
Using 딱딱하다 (hard, like a rock) for overcooked squid — the right word is 질기다 (chewy/rubbery).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 조개 means "clam / shellfish" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "clam / shellfish" is 조개 (jogae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조개구이 ("Grilled clams/shellfish"). Watch the particle attached to 조개 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 구이 = grilled dish; a popular seaside meal where you grill them at the table.
탕 = clear soup; clams give it a clean, savory broth.
Unopened clams during cooking are dead beforehand and shouldn't be eaten.

usagePhrases.en: The broth is clean and refreshing
usagePhrases.note: 시원하다 of soup = savory and clean-tasting, NOT temperature-cold.

examples.en: We had grilled clams at the seaside.
examples.note: -에서 marks the place of the action; 조개구이 is a classic coastal order.

examples.ko: 이 칼국수는 조개를 많이 넣어서 국물이 시원해요.
examples.romanization: i kalguksuneun jogaereul mani neoeoseo gungmuri siwonhaeyo.
examples.en: This noodle soup has lots of clams, so the broth is clean and savory.
examples.note: -아서 links cause→result; 시원하다 praises a clear, umami broth (not cold).

examples.ko: 조개는 모래가 있을 수 있으니까 잘 씻어요.
examples.romanization: jogaeneun moraega isseul su isseunikka jal ssiseoyo.
examples.en: Clams can have sand, so wash them well.
examples.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason; 해감 (purging sand) is a real prep step before cooking.

extendedVocab.nuance: 조개 is the general native word for clams and bivalve shellfish, and it heads dishes like 조개구이 (grilled clams) and 조개탕 (-탕, clear soup). Because it is a category word, when a recipe or menu needs a specific shellfish you switch to the precise name — 바지락 (manila clam), 홍합 (mussel), 가리비 (scallop), 꼬막 (cockle) — so calling all of them just 조개 can be too vague. The flavor cliché to internalize is 국물이 시원하다: with seafood broth, 시원하다 does NOT mean 'cold' but 'clean, brisk, savory' — a deeply Korean way to praise soup, and the classic English-speaker mistranslation. A second pitfall is the safety note baked into 조개가 안 열렸어요: an unopened clam after cooking should be discarded, and Koreans routinely 해감 (soak to purge sand) before cooking, so 모래 (sand) and 씻다 (wash) are common partner words.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 국물이 시원해요 as 'the broth is cold' — with seafood soup 시원하다 means clean, brisk, and savory, not low-temperature.
Using 조개 when the dish needs a specific shellfish — say 바지락 (manila clam), 홍합 (mussel), or 가리비 (scallop) by name.
Eating clams that 안 열렸어요 (didn't open) during cooking — those should be thrown out, not forced open.

Because it is a category word, when a recipe or menu needs a specific shellfish you switch to the precise name — 바지락 (manila clam), 홍합 (mussel), 가리비 (scallop), 꼬막 (cockle) — so calling all of them just 조개 can be too vague.
The classic English-speaker mistranslation is reading 국물이 시원하다 as 'the broth is cold' — with seafood soup it means clean, brisk, and savory, not low-temperature.

조림 = simmered in seasoned (often spicy) sauce, classically with radish (무).
비리다 = the specific fishy smell/taste of seafood, common with oily fish.
손 = a market counter meaning two fish sold as a set.

examples.en: Grilled mackerel often comes out at home-style set-meal places.
examples.note: 나오다 = (a dish) to be served/come out; 백반 meals frequently include 고등어구이.

examples.en: Braised mackerel is delicious simmered together with radish.
examples.note: N(이)랑 같이 = with N; 무 (radish) is the classic 조림 partner.

examples.ko: 고등어는 구울 때 냄새가 좀 나요.
examples.romanization: godeungeoneun guul ttae naemsaega jom nayo.
examples.en: Mackerel gives off a bit of a smell when grilling.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when ~ing'; 냄새가 나다 = a smell arises — oily fish are aromatic while cooking.

extendedVocab.nuance: 고등어 (mackerel) is an everyday, cheap, oily fish that anchors home cooking and 백반 (home-style set-meal) tables as 고등어구이 (grilled) or 고등어조림 (braised with radish). Assuming 고등어 한 손 = one fish — 손 is a counter meaning a pair (two fish) at the market.
Substituting a generic 생선 when a dish names 고등어 — mackerel's oily flavor differs from 갈치 (hairtail) or 삼치 (Spanish mackerel).

usagePhrases.note: 초밥 = vinegared-rice sushi; 연어 is one of the most popular toppings in Korea.
덮밥 = a bowl of rice covered with toppings; an easy everyday lunch.
회 = sliced raw fish; 연어회 is hugely popular, often all-you-can-eat (무한리필).
신선하다 = fresh; the key quality word for anything served raw.

examples.ko: 저는 회 중에서 연어를 제일 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hoe jungeseo yeoneoreul jeil joahaeyo.
examples.en: Among sashimi options, I like salmon the most.
examples.note: N 중에서 = 'among N'; 제일 = the most — 연어 is a top 회 pick.

examples.en: One salmon rice bowl and a miso soup, please.
examples.note: N 하나랑 N = 'one N and N'; a very common lunch order.

examples.en: Salmon is also delicious grilled.
examples.note: -아도 = 'even if / also'; 연어 works raw or cooked as 연어구이.

extendedVocab.nuance: 연어 (鰱魚, salmon) has surged in popularity in Korea, especially raw as 연어회 and 연어 초밥 and in 연어 덮밥 rice bowls, and it's a trendy, mild, fatty option that newcomers gravitate to before tackling more traditional fish. The contrast worth knowing is 연어 (salmon) vs 송어 (trout): they look similar and both appear raw, but they're different fish, and what budget all-you-can-eat 'salmon' spots serve is sometimes 송어 — so the names aren't interchangeable. Quality vocabulary centers on 신선하다 (fresh), essential since it's eaten raw. A cultural pitfall for English speakers: don't assume every traditional 횟집 (sashimi restaurant) features 연어 — long-established 횟집 often specialize in lean white fish like 광어 (flatfish) and 우럭 (rockfish), and 연어 is more a feature of modern, casual, or 무한리필 (all-you-can-eat) places. Also note 연어 is mild, so the 비리다 (fishy) complaint applies less to it than to oily fish like 고등어.

Confusing 연어 (salmon) with 송어 (trout) — they look alike and both appear raw, but they're different fish (some cheap buffets serve 송어).
Assuming every 횟집 serves 연어 — traditional sashimi houses often focus on white fish like 광어 (flatfish) and 우럭 (rockfish).
Calling raw salmon 초밥 — plain sliced raw salmon is 연어회; 초밥 specifically has the vinegared rice underneath.

extendedVocab.explanation: "grilled beef/pork intestines" is 곱창 (gopchang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 곱창 1인분 주세요 ("One serving of grilled intestines, please"). Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: One serving of grilled intestines, please
usagePhrases.note: Ordered by 인분 at a 곱창집; one serving is fairly small and pricey.

usagePhrases.en: Intestines with a shot of soju
usagePhrases.note: 에 pairs the food with the drink; a beloved late-night 술안주 combo.
곱창 = small intestine; 막창 (last stomach) and 대창 (large intestine) are distinct cuts.

usagePhrases.en: Fried rice at the end, please
usagePhrases.note: 볶음밥 fried in the leftover 곱창 pan is the traditional finish to the meal.

examples.en: How about grilled intestines and soju tonight?
examples.note: N 어때요? = 'how about N?'; 곱창 is a classic 술안주 (drinking food).

examples.en: People are pretty divided on grilled intestines.
examples.note: 호불호가 갈리다 = opinions split (love-it-or-hate-it); a very natural set phrase.

examples.ko: 곱창 다 먹고 마지막에 볶음밥 꼭 먹어요.
examples.romanization: gopchang da meokgo majimage bokkeumbap kkong meogeoyo.
examples.en: After finishing the intestines, we always get fried rice at the end.
examples.note: 다 먹다 = eat it all up; the pan-fried 볶음밥 finale is a must.

extendedVocab.nuance: 곱창 is grilled small intestine (most often beef, but 돼지곱창 / pork is common and cheaper), a beloved but polarizing 술안주 (drinking food) eaten late at night with soju, and the meal traditionally ends with 볶음밥 fried in the rich leftover-fat pan. The vocabulary Koreans attach to it is telling: it's a 호불호(가) 갈리는 음식 — a 'love-it-or-hate-it' food (호불호 好不好 = liking/disliking) — so that phrase is worth memorizing here. The crucial distinction is among offal cuts: 곱창 (small intestine, chewy with creamy filling), 대창 (large intestine, fattier, richer), and 막창 (the fourth stomach chamber, common in Daegu) are three different things with different textures and prices, not synonyms. Register is firmly casual and nighttime — you wouldn't propose 곱창 for a formal lunch. The English-speaker pitfall is treating all 'intestines/offal' as one item (and overlooking that an unqualified 곱창 may be pork), plus expecting it cheap — by weight 곱창 is often pricier than 삼겹살.

Lumping 곱창, 대창, and 막창 together — they are distinct offal cuts (small intestine / large intestine / fourth stomach) with different textures and prices.
Assuming 곱창 is always beef — pork 곱창 (돼지곱창) is common and noticeably cheaper, so the species is worth confirming.
Expecting 곱창 to be cheap because it's offal — per serving it's often pricier than 삼겹살; it's a treat, not a budget food.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 회 means "sliced raw fish (sashimi)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 회 (hoe) = "sliced raw fish (sashimi)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회 먹으러 가요 ("Let's go eat raw fish") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 회 = sliced raw fish, eaten at a 횟집; -(으)러 가다 = go in order to do.
모둠 = assorted; a mixed platter of several fish, great when undecided.
Sashimi is counted by 접시 (plate), reflecting how it's served.

usagePhrases.en: I'm not great with raw fish
usagePhrases.note: 잘 못 먹다 = can't really eat / am not good with — a soft, polite decline.

examples.en: Do you like sashimi?
examples.note: Polite preference question with -세요; a common ice-breaker by the coast.

examples.en: If you order the assorted platter, several kinds come out.
examples.note: 시키다 = to order; 나오다 = to be served — 모둠회 covers indecision.

examples.ko: 저는 익힌 게 좋아서 회는 잘 안 먹어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun ikin ge joaseo hoeneun jal an meogeoyo.
examples.en: I prefer cooked food, so I don't really eat raw fish.
examples.note: 익힌 거 = cooked thing; a natural, non-awkward way to opt out of 회.

extendedVocab.nuance: 회 (膾, sliced raw fish) is the centerpiece of Korean coastal dining, served at a 횟집 (sashimi restaurant) and typically shared as a 모둠회 (assorted) platter with banchan and a follow-up 매운탕 (spicy fish stew) made from the bones. The boundary that trips up English speakers is 회 vs 초밥 (sushi): 회 is JUST the sliced raw fish — no rice — whereas 초밥 is the vinegared-rice nigiri; so '연어회' is plain salmon slices while '연어 초밥' sits on rice. Korean overwhelmingly borrows Japanese 'sashimi/sushi' concepts but keeps its own words and rituals (eaten with 초장 chili-vinegar sauce or 쌈, lots of soju). Counting is by 접시 (plate), not 인분. Register: 회 먹으러 가요 is a casual, social, often celebratory or seaside-trip invitation. The other pitfall is the homonym field — 회 also lives inside 회사 (company), 회의 (meeting), 회식 (work dinner) — but standalone 회 in a food/restaurant context unambiguously means the raw fish; context, especially the word 횟집, makes it clear.

Confusing 회 (raw sliced fish, no rice) with 초밥 (sushi on vinegared rice) — 회 is the fish alone; 초밥 includes the rice.
Counting 회 by 인분 — sashimi is served and counted by 접시 (plate): 회 한 접시.
Reading standalone food-context 회 as 회사/회의 (company/meeting) — in a 횟집 it unambiguously means raw fish.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 폭염 means "heat wave" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 폭염 (pogyeom) means "heat wave". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 폭염이 계속되다 ("the heat wave continues"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 폭염 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: subject takes 이/가, verb 계속되다 not 오다
official top-level alert; 주의보 is the lighter advisory
에 marks the condition you brace against
fixed news collocation with 기록적이다

examples.en: It's a heat wave again today.
examples.note: simplest form: noun + 이에요 to state the weather

examples.en: Because of the heat wave it's hard to go outside.
examples.note: 폭염 때문에 = the heat wave as the cause of trouble

examples.ko: 폭염 경보가 내려서 야외 활동을 자제하라고 해요.
examples.romanization: pogyeom gyeongboga naeryeoseo yaoe hwaldongeul jajeharago haeyo.
examples.en: A heat wave warning was issued, so they're telling us to limit outdoor activity.
examples.note: 경보가 내리다 = a warning is issued; reacting to an official alert

extendedVocab.nuance: 폭염 is Sino-Korean, 暴炎 'violent + blaze', and means an extreme, dangerous spell of summer heat — the warning-level word you hear on the news and in the emergency text alerts (재난문자) that buzz your phone from late July. The dividing line from everyday 더위 is intensity and register: 더위 is the plain native noun for ordinary 'heat' you grumble about ('이 더위 좀 봐'), while 폭염 is official and severe, so you would not use 폭염 in light small talk. It naturally collocates with 경보/주의보 (warning/advisory), 계속되다, 기승을 부리다, and 기록적인. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is the verb: do not say 폭염이 와요 by analogy with 'a heat wave comes' — Koreans say 폭염이 계속돼요, 폭염이 심해요, or 폭염이 기승을 부려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 폭염 in casual small talk about a merely warm day — it is a severe, alert-level word, so for ordinary heat say 더위 or just 더워요.
Saying 폭염이 와요 ('the heat wave comes'), a direct translation of English. The natural verbs are 계속되다 (continues) or 심하다 (is severe): 폭염이 계속돼요.
Writing 폭염을 조심하세요 with the object particle. Use 폭염에 조심하세요 — 조심하다 takes 에 for the danger you watch out for.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 한파 means "cold wave" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cold wave" is 한파 (hanpa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한파가 몰려오다 ("a cold wave sweeps in"). Watch the particle attached to 한파 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 몰려오다 = surge in en masse, vivid news verb
top alert level; 한파 주의보 is the milder advisory
닥치다 = befall suddenly, set phrase for disasters
fixed collocation with 기록적이다

examples.en: Tomorrow there's a cold wave.
examples.note: simplest form: noun + 예요 to forecast

examples.en: The water pipes froze because of the cold wave.
examples.note: 한파 때문에 = cold wave as cause; 얼다 = to freeze

examples.ko: 한파가 닥쳐서 외출을 줄이는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: hanpaga dakchyeoseo oechureul jurineun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: A cold wave has hit, so it'd be better to go out less.
examples.note: 닥치다 collocation + advice with -는 게 좋다

extendedVocab.nuance: 한파 is Sino-Korean, 寒波 'cold + wave', literally a 'wave of cold', and is the winter twin of 폭염: a sudden, severe, alert-level cold snap announced on the news and by emergency text. The line against everyday 추위 is the same intensity gap as 폭염 vs 더위 — 추위 is the plain native noun for ordinary 'the cold' ('이 추위에 어딜 가'), while 한파 implies a sharp, warning-grade plunge that freezes pipes and disrupts transit. It collocates with 경보/주의보, 몰려오다, 닥치다, and 기승을 부리다. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: 'a cold front comes down' tempts 한파가 내려와요, but the idiomatic options are 한파가 와요, 한파가 닥쳐요, or 한파가 몰려와요 — and reserve 한파 for genuinely severe cold, not a slightly chilly afternoon.

Calling an ordinary chilly day a 한파. It is a severe, warning-level word — for everyday cold just say 추워요 or 추위.
Saying 한파가 내려요 ('the cold wave falls/comes down'), copying English. Use 한파가 와요, 한파가 닥쳐요, or 한파가 몰려와요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 천둥 is the native Korean word for thunder — the sound, the boom — and it is locked to the verb 치다 (천둥이 쳐요) or, for a longer rumble, 울리다. The key contrast every learner must nail is 천둥 vs 번개: 천둥 is what you HEAR (the crash), 번개 is what you SEE (the flash). They form the inseparable set phrase 천둥 번개, always in that order, the way English fixes 'thunder and lightning'. Saying 천둥이 와요, copying 'thunder comes'. Thunder 'strikes': the fixed verb is 치다 — 천둥이 쳐요.
Confusing 천둥 with 번개. 천둥 is the sound you hear; 번개 is the flash you see. They pair as 천둥 번개 but are not interchangeable.

extendedVocab.nuance: 서리 is the native word for frost — the thin white crystal coating that forms on cold autumn and early-winter mornings — and it pairs with the verb 내리다 ('to descend'), as Korean pictures frost as settling down from above (서리가 내려요). Distinguish it from neighbours: 얼음 is solid ice, 눈 is snow, 이슬 is dew (the same kind of overnight moisture but liquid, in warm weather) — 서리 is specifically dew that has frozen into white crystals. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: do not say 서리가 와요; frost 'descends' (내리다) or 'coats' a surface (끼다) — 창문에 서리가 꼈어요.

Confusing 서리 (frost, white crystals) with 얼음 (solid ice), 눈 (snow), or 이슬 (liquid dew). 서리 is frozen dew on cold mornings.
Saying 서리가 와요. The fixed verb is 내리다 (서리가 내려요), or 끼다 when it coats a surface like a window.
Forgetting 첫서리/된서리 as set words. The first frost is 첫서리 (not 첫 서리 loosely), a recognized seasonal milestone.

extendedVocab.nuance: 일교차 is Sino-Korean, 日較差 'day + compare + difference', i.e. the measured difference between the day's high and low temperature — a phrase Koreans use constantly in spring and autumn forecasts. examples.en: Tropical nights keep on, so I sleep with the AC on.
examples.note: -어서 cause; 켜고 자다 = sleep with it on

extendedVocab.nuance: 열대야 is Sino-Korean, 熱帶夜 'tropical-zone + night', and names a specific phenomenon: a summer night where the temperature never drops below 25°C, so the air stays oppressive and sleep is wretched. The contrast to draw is that 열대야 is strictly about the NIGHT not cooling down, whereas 폭염 is about extreme DAYTIME heat — a single hot spell can bring both, but they are not the same word. It is a fixture of Korean summer news and small talk, almost always glued to complaints about not sleeping (잠을 못 자다, 잠을 설치다) and running the 에어컨. It takes 계속되다 and 기승을 부리다, not 오다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 열대야 loosely for any hot day; it specifically means a hot, sleepless NIGHT, so a sweltering afternoon is 폭염 or just 더워요, not 열대야.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 열대야 for a hot daytime. It means specifically a hot, sleepless night (temperature staying above 25°C); a hot day is 폭염 or 더워요.
Saying 열대야가 와요. The natural verbs are 계속되다 (continues) or 기승을 부리다 (rages) — 열대야가 계속돼요.
Misspelling it. It is 열대야 (熱帶夜), not 열데야 or 열대얄 — three syllables, ending in 야.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 습도 means "humidity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "humidity" is 습도 (seupdo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 습도가 높다 ("the humidity is high"). Watch the particle attached to 습도 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: takes 높다/낮다, like a percentage reading
the opposite pole, also 낮다
끈적이다 = be sticky/clammy
compound, e.g. what a dehumidifier does

examples.en: The humidity is high today.
examples.note: simplest form: 높다 to read the level

examples.en: When the humidity is low, laundry dries fast.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if/when; everyday effect

examples.ko: 장마철에는 습도 때문에 곰팡이가 잘 생겨요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoreneun seupdo ttaemune gompangiga jal saenggyeoyo.
examples.en: In the rainy season, mold forms easily from the humidity.
examples.note: 습도 때문에 cause; 곰팡이가 생기다 = mold appears

extendedVocab.nuance: 습도 is Sino-Korean, 濕度 'moisture/damp + degree', i.e. the measured DEGREE of moisture in the air — a percentage reading, which is why, unlike most weather nouns, it takes 높다 (high) and 낮다 (low), exactly like a gauge. The -도 (度 'degree') ending is the same one in 온도 (temperature), 속도 (speed), 강도 (intensity), so anything ending in -도 is a measured level and pairs with 높다/낮다. Keep 습도 (humidity) apart from 온도 (temperature) and from 습기 (濕氣, the dampness/moisture you can feel or that clings to a wall) — 습도 is the number, 습기 is the felt damp. Koreans cite it constantly in muggy summers to explain why heat feels worse, tying into mold, laundry, and 제습기. The English-speaker pitfall is 습도가 많아요 — moisture feels like 'a lot', but a measured degree is high/low: 습도가 높아요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 습도가 많아요. As a measured degree it takes 높다/낮다, not 많다/적다 — say 습도가 높아요.
Confusing 습도 (humidity, the percentage) with 온도 (temperature). Both end in -도 and take 높다/낮다, but they measure different things.
Mixing 습도 with 습기. 습도 is the numerical humidity level; 습기 is the felt dampness/moisture (e.g. 벽에 습기가 차다, dampness builds on the wall).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 폭우 means "heavy rain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 폭우 (pogu) = "heavy rain". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 폭우가 쏟아지다 ("heavy rain pours down") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 폭우, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: vivid verb 쏟아지다, stronger than 내리다
alert term; 호우 경보 is the official wording
-로 cause; 침수되다 = be submerged
fixed news collocation

examples.en: Heavy rain is suddenly pouring down.
examples.note: simplest form: 갑자기 + the vivid 쏟아지다

examples.en: The subway stopped because of the heavy rain.
examples.note: 폭우 때문에 cause; 멈추다 = come to a halt

examples.ko: 폭우가 올 때는 지하 주차장을 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: poguga ol ttaeneun jiha juchajangeul josimhaseyo.
examples.en: When heavy rain comes, watch out for underground parking lots.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 = when; flood safety advice

extendedVocab.nuance: 폭우 is Sino-Korean, 暴雨 'violent + rain', a torrential downpour heavy enough to flood streets — the rain member of the 暴 family alongside 폭염 (暴炎), 폭설 (暴雪), all flagging sudden violence. The contrast scale runs 이슬비 (drizzle) → 비 (ordinary rain) → 소나기 (a brief sudden burst) → 폭우 (dangerous torrent); the meteorological office's own term is 호우 (豪雨). 폭우 loves the vivid verb 쏟아지다 ('to pour/gush down') and appears with 경보, 침수, 마비, 기록적인, so it carries danger and disruption. The English-speaker pitfall is flatness: 폭우가 와요 is grammatical but pale — for the intensity, say 폭우가 쏟아져요 — and don't stretch 폭우 over ordinary rain, where plain 비 is correct.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 폭우 for ordinary or light rain. It means a flooding torrent; for everyday rain say 비, and for a brief burst 소나기.
Saying 폭우가 와요 when you want to convey force. The natural collocation is the vivid 폭우가 쏟아져요.
Saying 폭우 때문에 침수됐어요 is fine, but the tight news phrasing for the cause is 폭우로 침수됐어요 with -로.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 건조기 means "clothes dryer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 건조기 (geonjogi) means "clothes dryer". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 의류 건조기 ("clothes dryer (full form)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 건조기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 의류(衣類) = clothing; the full form 의류 건조기 disambiguates from a food dehydrator, but in speech plain 건조기 is enough.
돌리다 (lit. 'spin/turn') is THE verb for any drum appliance — 세탁기 돌리다, 건조기 돌리다. Avoid 켜다 for a full cycle.
Particle 에 marks the destination; 빨래를 건조기에 넣다 = load the laundry into the dryer. Pairs with 꺼내다.
Particle 에서 marks the source you remove from; 꺼내다 (take out) is the natural opposite of 넣다.

examples.ko: 빨래 다 됐으면 건조기에 넣어 줘.
examples.romanization: ppallae da dwaesseumyeon geonjogie neoeo jwo.
examples.en: If the laundry's done, put it in the dryer.
examples.note: Teaches 다 되다 = 'to be finished/ready' (here, done washing); casual 줘 fits a roommate or partner.

examples.ko: 우리 집은 건조기가 없어서 빨래를 베란다에 널어요.
examples.romanization: uri jibeun geonjogiga eopseoseo ppallaereul berandae neoreoyo.
examples.en: We don't have a dryer, so we hang the laundry on the balcony.
examples.note: Teaches 널다 = 'hang out to dry,' the verb used instead of a dryer; 없어서 = 'because there isn't.'

examples.ko: 요즘 건조기는 옷감 안 상하게 저온으로 말려 줘서 인기가 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum geonjogineun otgam an sanghage jeooneuro mallyeo jwoseo ingiga manayo.
examples.en: These days dryers are popular because they dry on low heat so the fabric doesn't get damaged.
examples.note: Real selling-point register: 옷감(이) 상하다 = fabric gets ruined; 저온으로 말리다 = dry at low temperature.

extendedVocab.nuance: 건조기 = 乾燥機 ('dry-burn machine'), the 機 that 말리다(dries) things. 한국에서는 비교적 최근에야 보편화된 가전이라 아직 없는 집도 많아서, '건조기 있어요?'는 자취방·월세 집을 구할 때 실제로 자주 묻는 질문이에요. 비슷해 보이는 단어로 드라이기(머리 말리는 헤어드라이어)와 식품 건조기가 있는데, 일상 대화의 '건조기'는 거의 항상 의류 건조기를 뜻합니다. 영어 화자가 잘 빠지는 함정은 동사 선택이에요. 영어 'turn on the dryer'를 직역해 '건조기 켜다'라고 하면 전원만 넣은 느낌이라 어색하고, 한 통(load)을 돌려 말린다는 뜻은 반드시 '건조기 돌리다'로 표현합니다. 또 hair dryer를 '건조기'라고 부르면 큰 가전을 떠올리니 머리는 '드라이기'로 구분하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a hair dryer 건조기 — 건조기 is the big standing appliance for clothes; a hair dryer is 드라이기 (or 헤어드라이어). The two are not interchangeable.
Saying 건조기 켜다 for running a load — 켜다 only means 'flip the power on.' For drying a full load Koreans say 건조기 돌리다.
Treating 건조기 as automatically present in any home — in Korea it's a relatively new, often-absent appliance, so '건조기 있어요?' is a genuine question, not small talk.

structuredNuance.t: 옷을 말리는 큰 가전. 한국에서는 비교적 최근에야 보편화된 가전이라 아직 없는 집도 많아서, '건조기 있어요?'는 자취방·월세 집을 구할 때 실제로 자주 묻는 질문이에요.
건조기 = 乾燥機 ('dry-burn machine'), the 機 that 말리다(dries) things.

영어 화자가 잘 빠지는 함정은 동사 선택이에요. 영어 'turn on the dryer'를 직역해 '건조기 켜다'라고 하면 전원만 넣은 느낌이라 어색하고, 한 통(load)을 돌려 말린다는 뜻은 반드시 '건조기 돌리다'로 표현합니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가습기 means "humidifier" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "humidifier" is 가습기 (gaseupgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가습기 틀다 ("turn on the humidifier"). Watch the particle attached to 가습기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 틀다 is the go-to verb for devices that put out air/water/sound (가습기, 에어컨, 선풍기, 음악). More idiomatic here than 켜다.
물(을) 채우다 = fill with water; 채우다 (to fill) is the daily upkeep verb. Opposite of 비우다 (empty).
세척(洗滌) = washing/cleaning; 가습기 세척 is stressed heavily in Korea for hygiene reasons.
살균제(殺菌劑) = germ-killing agent; the word carries a heavy historical association in Korea (see nuance).

examples.en: It's so dry in winter that I sleep with the humidifier on.
examples.note: Teaches 건조하다 = 'to be dry' (air/skin), a stock winter complaint; 틀고 자다 = sleep with (it) on.

examples.ko: 가습기 물 좀 채워 줄래? 거의 다 떨어졌어.
examples.romanization: gaseupgi mul jom chaewo jullae? geoui da tteoreojyeosseo.
examples.en: Can you refill the humidifier? It's almost empty.
examples.note: Teaches 물이 떨어지다 = 'run out of water'; 줄래? is a soft casual request to a peer.

examples.ko: 가습기는 매일 안 씻으면 안에 물때하고 세균이 금방 껴요.
examples.romanization: gaseupgineun maeil an ssiseumyeon ane multtaehago segyuni geumbang kkyeoyo.
examples.en: If you don't wash the humidifier every day, scale and bacteria build up inside fast.
examples.note: Real-situation hygiene register: 물때(가) 끼다 = limescale builds up; reflects post-scandal caution.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가습기 = 加濕器, literally '加(add)-濕(moisture)-器(device)' — a device that ADDS humidity, the exact mirror image of 제습기(除濕器), which REMOVES it. 한국 아파트는 겨울 난방이 강해 공기가 매우 건조해지기 때문에 가습기가 거의 필수품이에요. 가장 큰 함정은 정반대 단어인 제습기와의 혼동입니다. 두 단어는 가운데 글자 加(더하다)와 除(없애다)만 다르니, 겨울엔 가습기(촉촉하게), 장마철엔 제습기(뽀송하게)로 외워 두세요. 동사도 주의: 영어 'turn on'을 그대로 '켜다'로 써도 틀리진 않지만, 물·바람을 내보내는 기기에는 '틀다'가 훨씬 자연스럽습니다. 끝으로 '가습기 살균제'는 과거 대규모 인명 피해를 낸 사건과 직결된 무거운 단어라, 한국인은 가습기 청결과 세척에 유난히 민감하다는 문화적 배경도 알아 두면 좋습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 가습기 (adds moisture, 加濕) with 제습기 (removes moisture, 除濕) — they are exact opposites. Use 가습기 in dry winter, 제습기 in humid summer/rainy season.
Saying 가습기 켜다 — not wrong, but 가습기 틀다 is the natural collocation because it puts out water vapor, like 에어컨/선풍기 틀다.
Mentioning 가습기 살균제 lightly — in Korea this phrase recalls a deadly disinfectant disaster, so it is sensitive, not casual product talk.

structuredNuance.t: 공기에 습기를 더하는 기기. 한국 아파트는 겨울 난방이 강해 공기가 매우 건조해지기 때문에 가습기가 거의 필수품이에요. 끝으로 '가습기 살균제'는 과거 대규모 인명 피해를 낸 사건과 직결된 무거운 단어라, 한국인은 가습기 청결과 세척에 유난히 민감하다는 문화적 배경도 알아 두면 좋습니다.
가습기 = 加濕器, literally '加(add)-濕(moisture)-器(device)' — a device that ADDS humidity, the exact mirror image of 제습기(除濕器), which REMOVES it.
가장 큰 함정은 정반대 단어인 제습기와의 혼동입니다. 두 단어는 가운데 글자 加(더하다)와 除(없애다)만 다르니, 겨울엔 가습기(촉촉하게), 장마철엔 제습기(뽀송하게)로 외워 두세요.
동사도 주의: 영어 'turn on'을 그대로 '켜다'로 써도 틀리진 않지만, 물·바람을 내보내는 기기에는 '틀다'가 훨씬 자연스럽습니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 공기청정기 means "air purifier" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 공기청정기 (gonggicheongjeonggi) = "air purifier". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공기청정기 틀다 ("turn on the air purifier") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공기청정기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 틀다 for an air-output device; 켜다 is also acceptable here. Casual short form: 공청기.
필터(를) 갈다 = replace the filter; 갈다 = swap out a consumable part (filters, batteries, blades).
미세먼지(微細-) = fine particulate dust; 심하다 = severe. The usual trigger for running the purifier.
돌리다 works too because a fan spins inside; 하루 종일 공기청정기 돌리다 = run it all day.

examples.ko: 미세먼지 심한 날엔 공기청정기를 하루 종일 틀어 놔요.
examples.romanization: misemeonji simhan naren gonggicheongjeonggireul haru jongil teureo nwayo.
examples.en: On days with bad fine dust, I leave the air purifier on all day.
examples.note: Teaches 틀어 놓다 = 'leave (it) turned on'; 하루 종일 = all day long.

examples.ko: 공기청정기 필터 갈 때 됐나 봐. 빨간불 들어왔어.
examples.romanization: gonggicheongjeonggi pilteo gal ttae dwaenna bwa. ppalganbul deureowasseo.
examples.en: Looks like it's time to change the filter. The red light came on.
examples.note: Teaches 빨간불(이) 들어오다 = 'the red light comes on'; ~ㄹ 때 되다 = 'time to do.'

examples.ko: 요즘은 미세먼지 농도 보고 자동으로 세기 조절되는 공기청정기가 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun misemeonji nongdo bogo jadongeuro segi jojeoldoeneun gonggicheongjeonggiga manayo.
examples.en: These days many purifiers auto-adjust their fan speed based on the dust level.
examples.note: Real product register: 농도 = concentration; 세기(가) 조절되다 = the strength is regulated automatically.

extendedVocab.nuance: 공기청정기 = 空氣(air)+淸淨(clean/purify)+器(device): the 器 that 淸淨하게(makes clean) the 空氣(air). 한국은 봄철 미세먼지·황사가 심해 공기청정기가 거의 생활필수품이 됐고, 자취하는 20-30대도 작은 모델 하나쯤 둡니다. 가장 흔한 혼동은 정수기(淨水器)와의 짝꿍 오류예요. 둘 다 '淸/淨'으로 깨끗하게 한다는 뜻이라 헷갈리지만, 공기청정기는 空氣(공기)를, 정수기는 水(물)를 다룹니다 — '청정/정수'의 글자 순서가 다른 것도 단서예요. 또 영어 화자는 'purifier'를 막연히 '청정기'라고만 부르기 쉬운데, 그러면 공기인지 물인지 모호하니 반드시 '공기'를 붙여 공기청정기(또는 캐주얼하게 공청기)라고 해야 통합니다. 동사는 공기를 내보낸다는 점에서 '틀다/돌리다'가 자연스럽고, 켜다도 무방합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 청정기 — it's ambiguous. Say 공기청정기 (or casual 공청기) so it's clear you mean an AIR purifier, not a water one.
Confusing 공기청정기 (air, 淸淨) with 정수기 (water, 淨水) — the 淸/淨 'clean' element overlaps, but one cleans air and the other cleans water.
Forgetting filter upkeep vocabulary — when the indicator turns red you say 필터 갈 때 됐다 (time to change the filter), using 갈다, not 바꾸다 for a routine consumable.

structuredNuance.t: 공기를 깨끗하게 거르는 기기. 한국은 봄철 미세먼지·황사가 심해 공기청정기가 거의 생활필수품이 됐고, 자취하는 20-30대도 작은 모델 하나쯤 둡니다. 동사는 공기를 내보낸다는 점에서 '틀다/돌리다'가 자연스럽고, 켜다도 무방합니다.
공기청정기 = 空氣(air)+淸淨(clean/purify)+器(device): the 器 that 淸淨하게(makes clean) the 空氣(air).
