extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 우편함 means "mailbox / letterbox" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "mailbox / letterbox" is 우편함 (upyeonham). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우편함을 확인하다 ("check the mailbox"). Watch the particle attached to 우편함 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 우편함 is the box at your building where incoming mail lands

usagePhrases.en: be slipped into / arrive in the mailbox
usagePhrases.note: 꽂히다 (passive) 'be stuck in' describes mail tucked into the slot
apartment lobbies have a wall of 공동 우편함, one slot per unit
many building 우편함 have a small dial/number lock

examples.en: A letter came in the mailbox.
examples.note: 오다 'come' is natural for mail arriving; 에 marks the location it landed in

examples.en: The maintenance-fee bill comes to the mailbox every month.
examples.note: 우편함으로 오다 '(come) by way of the mailbox' — 으로 marks the route/channel; 고지서 = bills

examples.ko: 등기우편은 우편함에 안 넣고 직접 받아야 해요.
examples.romanization: deunggiupyeoneun upyeonhame an neoko jikjeop badaya haeyo.
examples.en: Registered mail isn't left in the mailbox; you have to receive it in person.
examples.note: 등기 requires a signature, unlike regular mail; -지 않고 → 안 넣고 'without putting it in'

extendedVocab.nuance: 우편함 (郵便函, 郵便 'mail/post' + 函 'box/case') is the *incoming* mailbox where letters and official notices are delivered, usually a locked unit in an apartment lobby. The crucial contrast is 우편함 vs 우체통 (郵遞筒): the 우편함 is your private *receiving* box at home, while the red 우체통 on the street is the public *outgoing* box you drop letters into — confusing them is the classic learner slip because English 'mailbox' covers both directions. (And 우체국 is the post office building itself.) Note 函 means a case/box, distinct from 통 'cylinder/bin'. Habitual partners: 확인하다, 고지서, 등기우편, 공동 우편함, 비밀번호; mail 'comes' to it via 우편함으로 오다. Pitfall: check it regularly, because 고지서 (bills), tax notices, and government letters with deadlines arrive here — and don't expect 등기우편 (registered mail) in the box, since registered items need an in-person signature and are otherwise re-delivered (재배송).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 우편함 (your incoming home mailbox) with 우체통 (the red public postbox for outgoing letters); English 'mailbox' hides this in/out distinction.
Expecting 등기우편 to be left in the 우편함; registered mail requires an in-person handoff with a signature, or it is re-delivered.
Using 통 instead of 함: a home receiving box is 우편함 (函 'case'), while 우체통 (筒 'cylinder') is the street postbox — they are not interchangeable.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 관공서 means "government office / public agency" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 관공서 (gwangongseo) = "government office / public agency". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 관공서에 가다 ("go to a government office") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 관공서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 관공서 is the umbrella term for any public office (구청, 세무서, etc.)
업무 시간 (業務時間) usually weekdays 9 to 6, closed weekends and holidays
문을 닫다 'close (its) door' = be shut, esp. on 공휴일

usagePhrases.en: official paperwork from a public office
usagePhrases.note: documents issued or required by a 관공서

examples.en: Government offices are closed on weekends.
examples.note: 문을 닫다 'shut the door' = be closed; a basic, high-frequency fact for newcomers

examples.en: On public holidays all government offices are closed.
examples.note: 공휴일 (public holiday) closures catch newcomers off guard; 다 'all'

examples.en: Government offices only open on weekdays, so I run over during lunch.
examples.note: 평일에만 'only on weekdays'; 다녀오다 'go and come back' for a quick errand

extendedVocab.nuance: 관공서 (官公署, 官 'government/officialdom' + 公 'public' + 署 'bureau') is the general cover term for all government and public offices — the category that includes the 구청, 세무서, 동사무소, 보건소 and so on. The contrast to grasp is scope: 관공서 is the *umbrella word*, while 구청/세무서 are specific *instances* of it, so you use 관공서 when you mean 'public offices in general' (their hours, their closures) and the specific name when you mean one place. The practical knowledge baked into the word is the schedule: weekdays only, standard daytime hours (보통 9시–6시), and shut on 공휴일 — the set phrase being 관공서가 문을 닫다 ('the offices close their doors'). Habitual partners: 업무 시간, 공휴일, 휴무, 평일, 서류. Pitfall: English speakers assume offices keep bank-ATM-like evening or weekend access, but 관공서 generally close at 6 on weekdays and entirely on holidays — plan errands for a weekday morning, and use online services (정부24, 홈택스) when the office is shut.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 관공서 keep evening or weekend hours like a bank's ATM; they generally close at 6 on weekdays and are shut on weekends.
Trying to visit on a 공휴일 (public holiday); nearly all 관공서 문을 닫다 (are closed) and you'll need online services like 정부24 instead.
Using 관공서 when you mean one specific office; 관공서 is the umbrella category — for a particular errand name the actual office (구청, 세무서).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무척 means "very, really (strong, warm)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 무척 (mucheok) means "very, really (strong, warm)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무척 좋아요 ("I like it a lot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무척 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Warmer and more heartfelt than 아주; natural when talking about people or feelings
Adds genuine emotional weight; sounds sincere, not exaggerated
Works for weather and physical states; more expressive than a flat 아주
The -이나 suffix adds extra emphasis and a slightly literary, emotional tone

examples.en: That person is really kind.
examples.note: Simple subject + 무척 + adjective; notice 무척 sits right before the describing word

examples.en: Korean food really suits my taste.
examples.note: 입에 맞다 (lit. 'fit the mouth') is the set phrase for food agreeing with you

examples.en: I was really surprised to hear that news.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with emotion verbs like 놀라다, 기뻐하다, 슬퍼하다

extendedVocab.nuance: 무척 means 'very/really,' but unlike the neutral, almost clinical 아주, it carries a warm emotional undertone, so it gravitates toward feelings, people, and personal reactions rather than dry measurements. The dividing line with 아주: you would say 아주 정확하다 (very precise — a cool fact) but 무척 그립다 (miss someone terribly — a feeling). Register is soft and slightly literary, fully standard and never rude, so it works in heartfelt speech and writing alike; in fast texting younger Koreans swap in 너무 or 진짜. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for negation: English 'not very' does NOT become 무척 안 — Korean wants 그다지 안 or 별로 안 there, because 무척 only intensifies upward.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 무척 안 좋아요 for 'not very good' — 무척 only pushes a degree higher, so for 'not very' you need 별로 안 좋아요 or 그다지 좋지 않아요.
Treating 무척 as slang to avoid in polite settings; it is fully standard and soft/literary, so it never sounds rude or too casual even with a boss.
Forcing it onto cold technical facts (무척 정확하다); the emotional flavor clashes, and 아주/매우 정확하다 sounds far more natural there.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 굉장히 means "incredibly, extremely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "incredibly, extremely" is 굉장히 (goengjanghi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 굉장히 맛있어요 ("It's incredibly delicious"). Watch the particle attached to 굉장히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday strong intensifier, a clear notch above 아주
Loves words of size, scale, amount, or impressiveness
Expresses genuine surprise at a high degree
The base adjective stands alone: 우와, 굉장하다! = Wow, amazing!

examples.en: This bag is incredibly light.
examples.note: Simple form; 굉장히 directly modifies the adjective 가볍다

examples.en: I prepared incredibly hard for the interview.
examples.note: Here it stacks onto the adverb 열심히 to stress effort

examples.en: The subway is extremely crowded today.
examples.note: 붐비다 = to be crowded; a natural commuter remark with -네요 surprise

extendedVocab.nuance: 굉장히 is one of the most accessible STRONG intensifiers in everyday Korean and sounds natural in both casual chat and polite speech, even work emails. It comes from the hanja 宏壯 (굉장: 宏 'vast' + 壯 'magnificent') plus the adverbial -히, so at its root it paints something as grand or imposing — which is why it shines on scale and impressiveness (굉장히 크다/많다/대단하다). The synonym line: it overlaps with the breezier, more colloquial 엄청, but 굉장히 is a touch more composed and presentable, while 엄청 is punchier and more slang-leaning. Two English-speaker pitfalls: spelling (it is 굉장히 with 히, never 굉장이), and proportion — slapping 굉장히 on a trivial thing sounds like overstatement, where 꽤 or 좀 fits better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 굉장이 — the adverb is always 굉장히 (adjective stem 굉장 + -히); 굉장이 is simply a misspelling.
Overusing it on minor things (굉장히 for a tiny inconvenience); that reads as exaggeration, and 꽤 or 좀 would sound calmer and more natural.
Assuming the hanja meaning 'grand' lets it modify nouns like 상당한 does; 굉장히 is purely an adverb, so before a noun you must use the adjective form 굉장한 (굉장한 인기).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상당히 means "considerably, quite" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 상당히 (sangdanghi) = "considerably, quite". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 상당히 비싸요 ("It's quite expensive") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상당히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Measured and slightly formal; common in reviews and reports
Polished tone, good for feedback and workplace talk
Implies a notable, fact-like degree
Adnominal form 상당한: 상당한 시간 = a considerable amount of time

examples.en: This restaurant's prices are quite reasonable.
examples.note: Everyday-but-composed; 상당히 keeps the tone objective

examples.ko: 그 동네는 월세가 상당히 높은 편이에요.
examples.romanization: geu dongneneun wolsega sangdanghi nopeun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: Rents in that neighborhood are considerably high.
examples.note: -은 편이다 = 'tends to be,' softening the claim into a measured observation

examples.en: This project was considerably tricky.
examples.note: Sounds professional and controlled in a work debrief

extendedVocab.nuance: 상당히 marks a notable, MEASURED degree and carries a composed, semi-formal tone, so it lives in reviews, reports, and adult conversation. Its hanja 相當 (相 'mutual' + 當 'corresponding/befitting') literally means 'matching/befitting an amount' — i.e. 'amounting to a fair bit,' which is exactly why it feels objective, like you are reporting a fact rather than emoting. Synonym contrast: against the emotional 무척 or the casual 되게, 상당히 sounds understated and analytical; against 꽤 (also 'quite'), 상당히 is a touch stronger and more written-sounding. The key English-speaker pitfall is the adverb-vs-adnominal split: use 상당히 directly before a verb/adjective (상당히 어렵다), but switch to 상당한 directly before a noun (상당한 노력) — you cannot say 상당히 노력 as a noun phrase.

Confusing the adverb 상당히 with the adnominal 상당한; before a noun you must say 상당한 (상당한 시간/노력), not 상당히 시간.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 제법 means "fairly, quite (better than expected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 제법 (jebeop) means "fairly, quite (better than expected)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제법 잘하네요 ("You're pretty good (better than I expected)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 제법 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: You're pretty good (better than I expected)
usagePhrases.note: Carries mild, pleasant surprise
Notes that something has actually reached a real degree
Implies it exceeded low expectations
Stands alone as praise: 오, 제법인데? = Oh, not bad!

examples.en: Oh, you can actually cook pretty well!
examples.note: Casual 반말; 제법 carries the 'I didn't expect this' surprise

examples.en: It's gotten fairly chilly morning and evening.
examples.note: 쌀쌀하다 = chilly; classic autumn small talk with -아졌어요 'has become'

examples.ko: 이 식당, 가격은 싼데 맛은 제법이에요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang, gagyeogeun ssande maseun jebeobieyo.
examples.en: This place is cheap but the food is actually quite good.
examples.note: Shows the core nuance: the result beats the low price expectation

extendedVocab.nuance: 제법 means 'fairly/quite,' but its defining flavor is that something turned out BETTER or MORE than you expected, usually with a dash of admiration. That expectation gap is the whole point: 제법 잘하네요 is a warm compliment ('better than I thought!'), whereas a flat 잘하네요 is neutral praise, and a strong 아주 잘하네요 just rates a high level with no surprise. Synonym contrast: 꽤 also means 'quite/fairly' but is emotionally neutral about expectation, while 제법 specifically encodes 'pleasantly surprising.' Register is friendly and conversational. The English-speaker pitfall is social: because it implies 'I didn't expect you to be this good,' aiming 제법 at a clear expert or a respected senior can sound faintly patronizing — praise them with 정말/아주 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 제법 toward a clearly skilled senior or acknowledged expert; the 'surprisingly good' nuance reads as condescending — switch to 정말 잘하시네요.
Treating it as a plain synonym for 아주; 제법 specifically signals 'more/better than expected,' not just a high degree, so it cannot replace a neutral intensifier.
Applying it to things you always knew would be good (제법 맛있는 유명 맛집); with no surprise gap the word loses its point and sounds off.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 다소 means "somewhat, rather (formal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "somewhat, rather (formal)" is 다소 (daso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 다소 늦어질 수 있어요 ("It may be somewhat delayed"). Watch the particle attached to 다소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Formal softening tone for notices and emails
Politely understates a negative reaction
Common in reports and official announcements
Diplomatic way to express mild disappointment

examples.en: Today the wind will be somewhat strong.
examples.note: Pure weather-forecast register; the -겠습니다 ending matches the formal tone

examples.en: We apologize that the delivery is somewhat delayed.
examples.note: Standard wording in shop and delivery notices; softens the bad news

examples.ko: 설명이 다소 복잡하니 천천히 읽어 주세요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongi daso bokjapani cheoncheonhi ilgeo juseyo.
examples.en: The explanation is rather complex, so please read it slowly.
examples.note: A polite hedge inside instructions, lowering the alarm

extendedVocab.nuance: 다소 means 'somewhat / a little,' but it belongs squarely to FORMAL written and broadcast Korean — notices, weather reports, customer messages, official statements — not chatting with friends. Its hanja 多少 (多 'many' + 少 'few') literally pairs 'more-or-less,' giving it the cool, hedging feel of English 'somewhat,' and it gravitates to mildly negative partners (다소 지연/부족/아쉽다) to soften the blow politely. Synonym contrast: 다소 and 약간 both mean 'slightly,' but 약간 is everyday-neutral and 다소 is buttoned-up and bureaucratic; in casual speech Koreans simply say 좀 or 약간. The English-speaker pitfall is register mismatch and over-stacking: dropping 다소 into friendly chat sounds stiff, and because it means a SMALL-to-moderate degree, combining it with a strong word (다소 엄청) is self-contradictory.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 다소 in casual conversation with friends; it sounds oddly formal and newscaster-like — use 좀 or 약간 instead.
Pairing it with strong intensifiers (다소 엄청 / 다소 매우); 다소 caps the degree at small-to-moderate, so it contradicts a 'very' word.
Assuming it carries warmth like English 'a bit'; 다소 is detached and official, so for soft, friendly understatement 살짝 or 좀 fits better.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 살짝 means "slightly, lightly, just a touch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 살짝 (saljjak) = "slightly, lightly, just a touch". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 살짝 매워요 ("It's a little spicy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 살짝, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Very common for taste, temperature, and feelings
Cooking instruction: only briefly in hot water

usagePhrases.en: Please open the door just a bit
usagePhrases.note: Describes a small, gentle physical action
Softens an emotion in a cute, casual way

examples.en: The soup is slightly bland.
examples.note: 싱겁다 = bland; the simplest taste use, 살짝 + adjective

examples.en: Could you move over just a little here?
examples.note: 살짝 makes the request gentle and low-pressure for an action verb

examples.en: The price is a touch burdensome, honestly.
examples.note: 살짝 softens the complaint; -긴 하다 adds 'admittedly'

extendedVocab.nuance: 살짝 means 'slightly,' but with a light, gentle, often cute texture, and crucially it modifies ACTIONS as much as states — doing something briefly, softly, or by a small amount (살짝 만지다 'touch lightly,' 살짝 웃다 'smile faintly'). It is hugely common in casual speech and cooking. Synonym contrast with 약간: 약간 is the neutral, measurable 'a little' (약간 차이가 난다), whereas 살짝 is vivid, conversational, and tactile — 'just a touch,' often implying a quick, delicate motion. The big English-speaker pitfall is mentally filing it under 'somewhat' only and forgetting the action sense: English 'slightly' rarely describes how you do something, but 살짝 happily does (살짝 닫다 = close gently), so do not restrict it to adjectives. It also only ever means SMALL — never use it for big degrees.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 살짝 for large or serious degrees (살짝 위험해요 for a real danger); it only marks small, light amounts, so a true high degree needs 꽤/많이.
Forgetting it modifies actions, not just adjectives; 살짝 만지다 means 'touch lightly' and 살짝 열다 'open a crack' — it is not purely a 'somewhat' word.
Swapping in the formal 다소 in friendly chat to mean the same thing; 살짝 is warm and casual, while 다소 sounds like a press release.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 도무지 means "(not) at all, simply (can't)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 도무지 (domuji) means "(not) at all, simply (can't)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 도무지 모르겠어요 ("I simply have no idea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 도무지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Must pair with a negative; stresses total inability

usagePhrases.en: I just can't understand it at all
usagePhrases.note: 이해가 안 가다 = it doesn't make sense to me

usagePhrases.en: It just won't work no matter what
usagePhrases.note: Conveys frustration after repeated trying
잠이 안 오다 = sleep won't come

examples.en: I simply can't tell what this even means.
examples.note: Basic frame: 도무지 ... 모르겠다, the textbook 'can't grasp it' use

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 많아서 도무지 시간이 안 나요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri manaseo domuji sigani an nayo.
examples.en: I'm so busy lately that I just can't find any time.
examples.note: 시간이 나다 = to have time free; the 안 is what 도무지 leans on

examples.ko: 몇 번을 봐도 도무지 답을 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: myeot beoneul bwado domuji dabeul moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: No matter how many times I look, I just can't get the answer.
examples.note: 몇 번을 봐도 = 'however many times I look,' amplifying the helplessness

extendedVocab.nuance: 도무지 means 'not at all / simply (cannot)' and is a NEGATIVE-POLARITY adverb: it must be answered later in the sentence by a negative (안, 못, 모르다, -지 않다), and it adds a strong color of frustration and total impossibility, very often about failing to understand or grasp something. Synonym contrast: it is nearly interchangeable with 도저히, but 도저히 leans 'there is no way / it can't be done however hard I try' (도저히 못 참겠다), while 도무지 leans 'I simply can't make sense of it,' tilting toward confusion. Do NOT confuse it with the look-alike 도대체, which is an interrogative intensifier meaning 'what on earth?' (도대체 왜?) and questions rather than negates. The headline English-speaker pitfall: because English 'simply' can be positive, learners write 도무지 좋아요, which is impossible — 도무지 cannot appear in an affirmative sentence at all.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도무지 in a positive sentence (도무지 좋아요); it is negative-polarity and requires 안/못/모르다/-지 않다 to complete it.
Confusing it with 도대체 ('what on earth'); 도대체 questions or expresses exasperation (도대체 왜 그래요?), while 도무지 emphasizes flat inability.
Swapping it freely with 전혀; 전혀 is a neutral 'not at all' for any negated fact (전혀 안 맵다), whereas 도무지 specifically adds frustrated 'no matter what I do' inability.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 훨씬 means "much, far (more) — comparative" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "much, far (more) — comparative" is 훨씬 (hwolssin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 훨씬 더 좋아요 ("It's much better"). Watch the particle attached to 훨씬 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Almost always with a comparison; frequently sits before 더
Stresses a big gap between two things
버스보다 훨씬 빨라요 = much faster than the bus
낫다 → 나아요; common when comparing conditions or states

examples.en: This is far cheaper than that one.
examples.note: The bare A보다 B 훨씬 frame; 훨씬 marks how big the price gap is

examples.en: After taking the medicine, I feel much better.
examples.note: 괜찮아지다 = to get better; comparison is implied between before and after

examples.ko: 이 집이 전에 살던 곳보다 훨씬 넓어요.
examples.romanization: i jibi jeone saldeon gotboda hwolssin neolbeoyo.
examples.en: This place is far more spacious than where I lived before.
examples.note: 보다 names the thing compared; 훨씬 says the difference is large

extendedVocab.nuance: 훨씬 is the go-to word for emphasizing a LARGE gap in a comparison — 'much/far more' — and it implies the difference is significant, not slight. It pairs naturally with 더 (훨씬 더 빠르다) and with the 보다 comparative structure (택시보다 훨씬). The crucial contrast is with general intensifiers: 아주/너무 just rate one thing's degree on its own ('very fast'), but 훨씬 is inherently RELATIVE and needs a second thing to measure against ('much faster than X'). It also differs from 더 alone, which says merely 'more' with no claim about size, while 훨씬 insists the gap is big. The English-speaker pitfall: 'much better' tempts you to say 훨씬 좋아요 in isolation, but with no expressed or implied 'than what?' it sounds incomplete — Korean expects a comparison target, even if context supplies it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 훨씬 with no comparison at all (훨씬 좋아요 out of nowhere); it is comparative, so there must be an expressed or clearly implied 'than X.'
Replacing 아주/너무 with 훨씬 for a simple high degree; 훨씬 specifically means 'by a large margin more,' not a general 'very.'
Dropping 더 where the meaning is 'more' and expecting 훨씬 alone to carry it in subtle cases; 훨씬 더 is the safe, natural pairing for 'much more.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 되게 means "really, so (casual spoken)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 되게 (doege) = "really, so (casual spoken)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 되게 맛있어요 ("It's so good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 되게, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Super common in casual speech, like a spoken 'really'
Everyday complaint about distance or effort
Friendly compliment in relaxed conversation
Mainly spoken; in writing people prefer 정말/아주

examples.en: It's so hot today.
examples.note: The simplest pattern: 되게 + adjective in casual 해요-speech

examples.ko: 여기 분위기 되게 좋다, 자주 오자.
examples.romanization: yeogi bunwigi doege jota, jaju oja.
examples.en: This place has a really nice vibe, let's come often.
examples.note: 분위기 = vibe; pure 반말 among friends, where 되게 thrives

examples.en: The roads are really jammed today.
examples.note: 막히다 = to be congested; an everyday gripe with -네요

extendedVocab.nuance: 되게 is a very common CASUAL intensifier meaning 'really/so,' used almost exclusively in spoken Korean among friends, peers, and people you are comfortable with. It feels lively and effortless in conversation but looks out of place in formal writing or business email, where 아주, 매우, or 정말 belong. Synonym contrast: it sits right beside 엄청 and 진짜 as spoken boosters, but 되게 is the most conversational and a bit softer than the punchy 엄청; meaning-wise it just means 'very,' with none of the 'large amount' flavor 엄청 can carry. Two English-speaker pitfalls: spelling and register. Spelling — it is 되게 (from 되다), never 됬게 or 돼게, since 되 + 게 takes no extra ㅆ. Register — because it is so casual, using it in anything written or official instantly sounds too chatty.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 되게 in formal documents, emails, or reports, where it reads as too casual; use 매우/정말/아주 in those registers.
Spelling it 됬게 or 돼게; the correct form is 되게 (stem 되- + -게), with no doubled ㅆ and no 돼.
Assuming it means 'a lot/a ton' like 엄청 can for quantity; 되게 only intensifies a quality ('very'), so 되게 많이 is fine but 되게 alone won't carry 'a huge amount.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 엄청 means "super, a ton, tremendously" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 엄청 (eomcheong) means "super, a ton, tremendously". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 엄청 많아요 ("There's a ton"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 엄청 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Strong and casual; great for amounts and intensity alike
Common spoken intensifier across all ages
Adjective form: 효과가 엄청나요 = the effect is huge
Fuller adverb form: 엄청나게 노력했어요

examples.en: There are a ton of people.
examples.note: Quantity use; 엄청 + 많다 is the most natural high-amount pairing

examples.ko: 이번 시험 공부를 엄청 했는데 떨려요.
examples.romanization: ibeon siheom gongbureul eomcheong haenneunde tteollyeoyo.
examples.en: I studied a ton for this exam but I'm nervous.
examples.note: 떨리다 = to feel nervous/shaky; 엄청 here measures the effort

examples.en: The delivery came incredibly fast.
examples.note: 엄청 stacks onto the adverb 빨리; a classic food-delivery comment

extendedVocab.nuance: 엄청 is a punchy, casual way to say 'super / a ton,' and it is unusual among these adverbs in handling both QUANTITY (엄청 많다 'a ton') and INTENSITY (엄청 덥다 'super hot') with equal ease. Register is colloquial — extremely frequent in speech and texting across all ages, a step less formal than 굉장히 and far less formal than 매우/대단히. Synonym contrast: against 굉장히, 엄청 is breezier and more slang-flavored while 굉장히 sounds more presentable; against 되게, 엄청 hits harder and can carry the 'huge amount' sense that 되게 cannot. A handy feature is the adjective spin-off 엄청나다 ('to be tremendous') and its adverb 엄청나게, letting you say 효과가 엄청나요. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 한층 means "even more, a level more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "even more, a level more" is 한층 (hancheung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한층 더 좋아졌어요 ("It's gotten even better"). Watch the particle attached to 한층 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Often paired with 더; pictures stepping up one level
Common in product and service descriptions
Slightly formal; used for improvement and progress
Nice for relationships deepening one notch

examples.en: Now that it's spring, the days have gotten even warmer.
examples.note: 한층 + 더 implied; the 'one step up from before' feel is built in

examples.ko: 연습을 꾸준히 했더니 실력이 한층 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: yeonseubeul kkujunhi haetdeoni sillyeogi hancheung neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Since I practiced steadily, my skills improved even further.
examples.note: 한층 stresses a clear step up from an existing level

examples.en: Now that it's autumn, the foliage is even more beautiful.
examples.note: 단풍 = autumn leaves; the slightly literary tone suits 한층

extendedVocab.nuance: 한층 means 'even more / a level higher,' and it literally pictures improvement as climbing one more 층 (層, 'floor/story/layer') above an already-good state — that built-in 'from an existing baseline, step up one' is its core. Because of that, it almost always implies a POSITIVE upgrade and frequently appears as 한층 더 for extra force. Register is polished and a little written-sounding, so it suits reviews, product copy, and thoughtful speech more than rapid 반말. Synonym contrast: against plain 더 ('more,' no baseline assumption) 한층 insists there was already a good level you are now exceeding; against 훨씬 ('much more,' comparing two separate things by a big margin) 한층 is about one thing rising another step over its former self, and the rise can be modest. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 한층 for a first-time, baseline-less degree (it needs a prior state to step up from), and in casual chat a simple 더 or 훨씬 usually sounds more natural.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 한층 for a first-time degree with no prior baseline; it means going 'one level further' from an existing state, so without that earlier level it sounds wrong.
Treating it as fully casual; in chatty 반말 a plain 더 or 훨씬 sounds more natural, while 한층 leans formal and slightly literary.
Confusing it with 훨씬; 훨씬 compares two different things by a large margin (A보다 훨씬), whereas 한층 raises one thing a step above its own former state.

extendedVocab.explanation: 부쩍 (bujjeok) = "markedly, noticeably (more)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부쩍 늘었어요 ("It increased noticeably") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부쩍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Implies a sudden, visible rise over a short time
Common for sudden weather changes
Notes a marked change in someone's appearance
부쩍 자주 보이네요 = I see you around a lot more lately

examples.en: I've been noticeably more tired lately.
examples.note: 요즘 + 부쩍 is the textbook pairing for a recent, striking change

examples.ko: 환절기라 그런지 감기 환자가 부쩍 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgira geureonji gamgi hwanjaga bujjeong neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe because of the season change, cold patients have increased markedly.
examples.note: 환절기 = change of seasons; 늘다 is the change verb 부쩍 loves

examples.ko: 조카가 못 본 사이에 부쩍 컸어요.
examples.romanization: jokaga mot bon saie bujjeok keosseoyo.
examples.en: My niece/nephew has grown so much since I last saw them.
examples.note: 못 본 사이에 = 'while I wasn't seeing them'; stresses the jump you suddenly notice

extendedVocab.nuance: 부쩍 describes a MARKED, noticeable change that happened over a relatively short stretch — 'suddenly a lot more' — and it is a native Korean (non-Sino) word with a vivid, observational feel. Grammatically it craves VERBS OF CHANGE (늘다, 줄다, 커지다, 추워지다, 늙다) rather than static adjectives, and it pairs constantly with 요즘 to mean 'lately, and you can really tell.' The key synonym contrast is with 점점 and 차츰: those describe GRADUAL, step-by-step change ('more and more, slowly'), whereas 부쩍 stresses that the jump was striking and easy to notice, almost abrupt. The English-speaker pitfall: because English 'noticeably' attaches happily to adjectives ('noticeably pretty'), learners try 부쩍 예쁘다, which sounds odd — Korean wants the change form 부쩍 예뻐졌다 ('got noticeably prettier'), since 부쩍 is about movement to a new state, not a static quality.

Using 부쩍 with static adjectives (부쩍 예쁘다, 부쩍 크다); it needs verbs of change, so say 부쩍 예뻐졌다 or 부쩍 컸다.
Confusing it with the gradual 점점/차츰; those mean slow, steady change, while 부쩍 implies a sharp, noticeable jump in a short period.
Stretching it to long, slow trends; 부쩍 fits a recent, surprising surge (요즘 부쩍...), not a change spread evenly over many years.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 후련하다 means "relieved (after a burden lifts); refreshed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 후련하다 (huryeonhada) means "relieved (after a burden lifts); refreshed". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후련해요 ("I feel relieved"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후련하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective, so 하 + 여요 contracts to 해요 — the most common spoken form

usagePhrases.en: to feel a weight off one's chest
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; literally 'the insides feel clear' — say this after venting or finishing something
adverb form (하다→하게), e.g. 후련하게 울다 to have a good cleansing cry
-아/어지다 attaches to the 해 stem and shows the shift from heavy to light

examples.en: I'm relieved the exam is over.
examples.note: simple 해요 form; use it when a stressful thing is done, not just when you're happy

examples.ko: 할 말을 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련하네요.
examples.romanization: hal mareul da hago nanikka sogi huryeonhaneyo.
examples.en: Now that I've said everything I wanted to, I feel so relieved.
examples.note: -고 나니까 'now that I've finished ~' frames the classic after-venting context

examples.ko: 몇 년 묵은 고민을 털어놓고 나니까 가슴이 다 후련하더라고요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon mugeun gomineul teoreonoko nanikka gaseumi da huryeonhadeoragoyo.
examples.en: After finally pouring out a worry I'd carried for years, my chest felt completely clear.
examples.note: real-situation; 다 here is intensifier 'completely', and -더라고요 reports the felt experience

extendedVocab.nuance: 후련하다 names the clean, lightened sensation right after a burden or pent-up stress is released — finishing exams, finally venting, crying it out. Its near-synonym is 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broader word that also covers physical coolness (시원한 바람, a cool breeze) and refreshing drinks, while 후련하다 is reserved almost entirely for emotional/internal release, so '속이 후련하다' and '속이 시원하다' overlap but 바람이 후련하다 is wrong. It is NOT general happiness (기쁘다/행복하다) — it strictly presupposes something heavy was weighing on you and is now gone. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 후련해요 / 후련했어요 / 후련해서, and it collocates above all with 속이, 가슴이, and the adverb 후련하게. English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for it as a synonym of 'happy', but if there was no preceding pressure to discharge, a Korean ear hears it as odd — 'I'm 후련해' out of plain good cheer sounds like a non sequitur.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 후련하다 for plain happiness ('생일이라 후련해요') is wrong — it requires a preceding burden or stress that has just been lifted; for general joy use 기쁘다/행복하다.
Treating it as interchangeable with 시원하다 for physical coolness ('날씨가 후련해요') is wrong; 후련하다 is emotional/internal release only — say 시원하다 for a cool breeze or cold drink.
Saying '후련 있어요' (treating it like a noun) is wrong; it is an adjective, so conjugate it directly: 후련해요, 후련했어요.

extendedVocab.english: uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 찝찝하다 means "uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "uneasy; left with a bad/unresolved feeling" is 찝찝하다 (jjipjjipada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 찝찝해요 ("I feel uneasy about it"). Watch the particle attached to 찝찝하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective contracting to 해요 — common after an awkward or unresolved moment
뭔가 ('somehow/something') is the habitual partner adverb that triggers this word
attributive form (하다→한) modifying 기분/느낌
adverb form, e.g. 찝찝하게 헤어졌어요 we parted on an unsettled note

examples.en: Something just feels off.
examples.note: the bare, high-frequency form; 뭔가 sets up the vague unease

examples.en: I got an apology, but something still feels off.
examples.note: -는데 contrasts the apology with the lingering residue; use when a resolution doesn't fully satisfy

examples.ko: 계약서에 도장 찍긴 했는데 조건이 영 찝찝해서 다시 읽어 봤어요.
examples.romanization: gyeyakseoe dojang jjikgin haenneunde jogeoni yeong jjipjjipaeseo dasi ilgeo bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I did stamp the contract, but the terms left me so uneasy that I reread it.
examples.note: real-situation; 영 'utterly' + 찝찝해서 'because it felt off' gives the cause that drove an action

extendedVocab.nuance: 찝찝하다 is the nagging, not-quite-resolved discomfort that sticks to you — a conversation that ended badly, a decision you can't fully trust, even a slightly unclean feeling on your skin. Contrast it sharply with 불안하다: 불안하다 is forward-looking anxiety about what might happen, whereas 찝찝하다 is the backward-looking residue of something that already occurred and didn't settle cleanly. It is milder than 죄책감 (guilt) — more 'this won't sit right' than 'I did wrong'. It lives in casual speech and pairs constantly with 뭔가, 영, and 기분/느낌. Note the spelling: the standard dictionary form is 찜찜하다, but 찝찝하다 is the more emphatic, far more common everyday variant. English-speaker pitfall: learners map it to 'uncomfortable' and then misuse it for physical pain (a sore back is 아프다/불편하다, not 찝찝하다); 찝찝하다 is psychological/residual unease, or at most a faint 'icky, not-clean' feeling.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 불안하다 ('내일 시험이 찝찝해요') is wrong — for anxiety about a future event use 불안하다; 찝찝하다 is the lingering residue of something already past.
Using it in formal writing or a business report reads as too casual/slangy; in those registers prefer 꺼림칙하다 or 마음에 걸리다.
Applying it to physical pain ('허리가 찝찝해요') is wrong; for bodily discomfort say 불편하다 or 아프다 — 찝찝하다 is a mental/residual feeling (or a faint not-clean sensation).

extendedVocab.english: overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 벅차다 means "overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 벅차다 (beokchada) = "overwhelmed (with emotion); too much to handle". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 벅차요 ("it's overwhelming / I'm overcome") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 벅차다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; stem 벅차- already ends in ㅏ so it just adds 요 — context decides positive vs negative
set phrase; with 가슴이 it is the moved/overcome-by-joy sense
attributive form (차다→찬); common with 감동, 행복, 순간
adverb form, e.g. 벅차게 다가오다 to hit one overwhelmingly

examples.en: The work is a bit too much for me.
examples.note: simple form, practical sense: a load exceeds your capacity

examples.en: Getting my first paycheck, my heart just swells.
examples.note: the positive 'overcome with emotion' sense; 가슴이 is the tell

examples.ko: 혼자 부모님 병간호까지 하려니 솔직히 벅차서 동생한테 도움을 청했어요.
examples.romanization: honja bumonim byeongganhokkaji haryeoni soljiki beokchaseo dongsaenghante doumeul cheonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: Caring for my parents alone on top of everything was honestly too much, so I asked my younger sibling for help.
examples.note: real-situation; -려니 'when I try to' + 벅차서 gives the reason for an action

extendedVocab.nuance: 벅차다 carries two flavors that share one root idea — 'more than the vessel can hold'. One is the heart-swelling kind: overcome with joy, pride, or gratitude (가슴이 벅차다). The other is the practical kind: a workload or responsibility that exceeds your capacity (일이 벅차다). The 가슴이 + 벅차다 frame is almost always the warm, positive reading; a task as subject flips it to the stressful 'I can't cope' reading. Contrast it with 바쁘다: 바쁘다 only means you have a lot to do (busy), while 벅차다 says the amount is beyond what you can manage — you could be 안 바쁘다 yet still find one hard task 벅차다. Note 벅차다 is its own adjective, not a 하다-word, so the stem is 벅차- (벅차요, 벅찼어요, 벅차서, 벅찬). English-speaker pitfall: assuming it is always positive because of its frequent use in emotional moments — '일이 벅차다' is a genuine cry that something is too much.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 벅차다 is always positive is wrong — '이 일은 벅차요' means the task is overwhelming in a can't-cope, stressful way, not joyful.
Equating it with 바쁘다 ('요즘 벅차요' meaning merely 'busy') is imprecise; 바쁘다 = a lot to do, 벅차다 = the amount exceeds your capacity. Use 바쁘다 for ordinary busyness.
Writing 벅차해요 (adding -해요 as if it were a 하다-word) is wrong; the correct polite form is simply 벅차요.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 허전하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, for emotional emptiness

usagePhrases.en: to feel a void in one's heart
usagePhrases.note: set phrase for loneliness or loss; 마음이 is the default subject
attributive form (하다→한) modifying 마음/기분
adverb form, e.g. 집이 허전하게 느껴져요 the house feels empty

examples.en: Being alone, I feel a bit empty.
examples.note: simple form; the basic 'a void is here' use

examples.ko: 룸메이트가 이사 가니까 집이 너무 허전해요.
examples.romanization: rummeiteuga isa ganikka jibi neomu heojeonhaeyo.
examples.en: Now that my roommate moved out, the place feels so empty.
examples.note: the void left when someone is gone; subject can be a place, not just a person's heart

examples.ko: 20년 키운 강아지를 떠나보내고 나니 집안 곳곳이 허전해서 한동안 적응이 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: 20nyeon kiun gangajireul tteonabonaego nani jiban gotgosi heojeonhaeseo handongan jeogeungi an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: After saying goodbye to the dog I'd raised for 20 years, every corner of the house felt so empty that I couldn't adjust for a while.
examples.note: real-situation; 곳곳이 'in every corner' + 허전해서 conveys pervasive absence

extendedVocab.nuance: 허전하다 is the quiet, wistful emptiness left behind when something or someone familiar is missing — a friend moves away, a long routine ends, a pet passes, or you just feel a vague hollow. Contrast it with 외롭다: 외롭다 specifically means lonely/alone (a person without company), whereas 허전하다 is about a felt absence or void that can apply even in a crowd when something expected is gone — you can be surrounded by people and still 허전하다 because a particular presence is missing. It is gentler than 슬프다 (active sorrow); 허전하다 is hollowness, not crying. Notably it attaches not only to 마음/가슴 but to places (집이 허전하다) and even body parts (목이 허전하다 after a haircut, 손이 허전하다 without a ring). English-speaker pitfall: translating 'I miss you' as '당신이 허전해요' — that is wrong; 허전하다 describes the void you feel, not the act of missing a person. For 'I miss you' use 보고 싶어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating it with 슬프다 ('영화가 허전했어요' for a sad film) is wrong — 허전하다 is about absence/a hollow feeling, not tears or sorrow; use 슬프다 for active sadness.
Using 허전하다 to translate 'I miss you' ('네가 허전해' ) is wrong; that idea is 보고 싶어. 허전하다 names the void, not the missing.
Restricting it to people only is too narrow; remember it works for places and even a bare neck/finger (머리 자르니까 목이 허전해요).

extendedVocab.explanation: "reassured; reliable; pleasantly full" is 든든하다 (deundeunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 든든해요 ("I feel reassured / it's reassuring"). Watch the particle attached to 든든하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a very common compliment-adjacent word
set phrase; you feel backed-up and safe, 마음이 as subject
attributive form (하다→한); high praise for a friend or colleague
adverb form, e.g. 든든하게 먹다 to eat a hearty, filling meal

examples.en: Having you here, I feel reassured.
examples.note: casual 반말; warm thing to say to a close friend

examples.en: I had a hearty breakfast before heading out.
examples.note: the 'pleasantly full and fueled' sense; 든든하게 + 먹다 collocation

examples.ko: 보험까지 들어 두니 무슨 일이 생겨도 마음이 든든해서 발 뻗고 자게 돼요.
examples.romanization: boheomkkaji deureo duni museun iri saenggyeodo maeumi deundeunhaeseo bal ppeotgo jage dwaeyo.
examples.en: Now that I've even taken out insurance, I feel so secure that I can sleep soundly whatever happens.
examples.note: real-situation; the safety-net sense, with 발 뻗고 자다 'sleep with legs stretched = at ease'

extendedVocab.nuance: 든든하다 is the warm feeling of being backed up and secure — a dependable person at your side, a financial safety net, or a filling meal that fuels you for the day. Contrast it with 안심하다: 안심하다 is a verb meaning 'to feel relieved / set one's mind at ease' about a specific worry that has resolved, while 든든하다 is the standing, ongoing sense of having reliable support behind you (a backbone, not a resolved worry). Calling a person 든든하다 (그 사람 참 든든해요) is genuine praise for reliability. With food it means satisfyingly full and energized — more than 배부르다 (merely full): 든든하다 adds 'well-prepared, set up to go'. As a 하다-adjective it gives 든든해요 / 든든했어요 / 든든해서, and collocates with 마음이, 사람, and 든든하게 먹다. English-speaker pitfall: saying '저는 든든해요' to mean 'I am a reliable person' — Korean uses it for the reassurance you feel from something/someone, so frame it as 마음이 든든해요 or 그 사람이 든든해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배부르다 when you mean a hearty, fueling meal misses the nuance — 든든하게 먹다 implies being well-prepared and energized, not just 'no longer hungry'.

Saying '저는 든든한 사람이에요' to boast that you yourself are dependable sounds odd; let others call you 든든하다. Describe the feeling you give: '제가 있으면 든든하시죠?' is more natural, or just say 믿음직하다 of yourself sparingly.
Treating it as identical to 안심하다 is imprecise: 안심하다 (verb) = a worry resolved; 든든하다 (adjective) = ongoing backing/support behind you.

extendedVocab.english: light and unburdened; free of a load
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 홀가분하다 means "light and unburdened; free of a load" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 홀가분하다 (holgabunhada) = "light and unburdened; free of a load". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 홀가분해요 ("I feel unburdened") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 홀가분하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, said when a responsibility ends
set phrase; the weight-off-your-shoulders feeling
attributive form (하다→한) modifying 마음/기분
adverb form, e.g. 홀가분하게 떠나다 to leave unburdened

examples.en: Work's done, so I feel light and free.
examples.note: simple form; the relief of shedding a task

examples.ko: 짐 다 부치고 홀가분하게 여행 다녔어요.
examples.romanization: jim da buchigo holgabunhage yeohaeng danyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I shipped all my luggage and traveled light and carefree.
examples.note: literal lightness blending into emotional lightness; 홀가분하게 + 다니다

examples.ko: 오래 끌던 소송이 끝나니 어깨에 얹혔던 짐을 내려놓은 듯 홀가분하더라고요.
examples.romanization: orae kkeuldeon sosongi kkeunnani eokkaee eonjhyeotdeon jimeul naeryeonoeun deu tolgabunhadeoragoyo.
examples.en: When the long-dragging lawsuit ended, I felt as unburdened as if I'd set down a load on my shoulders.
examples.note: real-situation; the 듯 simile spells out the 'weight set down for good' core meaning

extendedVocab.nuance: 홀가분하다 is the buoyant lightness you feel after putting down a long-carried load — finishing a major project, paying off debt, ending an obligation. Contrast it carefully with its closest neighbor 후련하다: 후련하다 emphasizes the cathartic discharge of pent-up stress (the release), whereas 홀가분하다 emphasizes the resulting freedom and mobility (the lightness that remains) — after finally telling someone off you are 후련하다 (it came out), but after a years-long duty finally ends you are 홀가분하다 (you're free now). It implies a relatively lasting relief, not a fleeting one, and pairs above all with 마음이, 어깨, and 홀가분하게 떠나다/다니다. As a 하다-adjective: 홀가분해요 / 홀가분했어요 / 홀가분해서. English-speaker pitfall: using it for a momentary 'phew' — 홀가분하다 should mark a real burden that has been set down for good, so for a quick instant of relief 후련하다 or 다행이다 fits better.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for momentary relief ('버스 놓칠 뻔했다가 타서 홀가분해요') is wrong — that's 다행이다/후련하다; 홀가분하다 implies a lasting burden finally set down.
Treating it as identical to 후련하다 blurs a real line: 후련하다 = the cathartic release of stress; 홀가분하다 = the resulting freedom and lightness. Pick by which you mean.
Spelling or saying it 홀가뿐하다 / 홀가분 있어요 is wrong; it is the adjective 홀가분하다, conjugated 홀가분해요, 홀가분했어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 서먹하다 means "awkward/distant (between people not yet close)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 서먹하다 (seomeokada) means "awkward/distant (between people not yet close)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서먹해요 ("things feel awkward (between us)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서먹하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, describes the relationship's distance
reduplicated form that intensifies and softens the awkwardness, very common in speech
attributive form (하다→한); 사이 = the relationship between people
adverb form, e.g. 서먹하게 인사하다 to greet stiffly

examples.en: We're still a little distant with each other.
examples.note: simple form; states the relationship is not yet close

examples.en: We're on the same team, but it's still awkward between us.
examples.note: -지만 contrast frames not-yet-close coworkers

examples.ko: 10년 만에 만난 동창들과 처음엔 서먹했는데 술 한잔하니 금세 옛날로 돌아갔어요.
examples.romanization: 10nyeon mane mannan dongchangdeulgwa cheoeumen seomeokaenneunde sul hanjanhani geumse yennallo doragasseoyo.
examples.en: With classmates I met after 10 years it was awkward at first, but after a drink we quickly went back to the old days.
examples.note: real-situation; shows 서먹하다 as the dissolvable distance of a long gap

extendedVocab.nuance: 서먹하다 describes the awkward, not-yet-comfortable distance BETWEEN people who aren't close — new coworkers, friends after a long gap, two people after a quarrel. It is fundamentally relational. Contrast it with 어색하다 and 멋쩍다, the words learners confuse it with: 어색하다 covers awkwardness in general including situations and one's own self-consciousness (어색한 분위기, an awkward vibe; 어색한 미소, a forced smile), and 멋쩍다 is purely your own sheepish embarrassment — but 서먹하다 specifically names the coolness of a relationship, the gap of unfamiliarity between two parties. The reduplicated 서먹서먹하다 is idiomatic and a touch more vivid. As a 하다-adjective: 서먹해요 / 서먹했어요 / 서먹해서, and it pairs with 사이, 둘이, 분위기. English-speaker pitfall: using 서먹하다 for your own embarrassment ('칭찬받아서 서먹했어요') is wrong — that personal sheepishness is 멋쩍다/어색하다; 서먹하다 needs two parties and a relationship.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for self-conscious embarrassment ('실수해서 서먹했어요') is wrong — that's 어색하다/멋쩍다; 서먹하다 is the distance between two parties, not a feeling inside one person.
Saying you are 서먹하다 by yourself ('저 혼자 서먹해요') is wrong; it always needs a relationship — frame it as 둘이 서먹하다 or 사이가 서먹하다.
Confusing it with 낯설다 ('이 동네가 서먹해요') is wrong; for an unfamiliar place/thing use 낯설다, reserve 서먹하다 for the coolness between people.

extendedVocab.english: displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 못마땅하다 means "displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "displeased; not to one's liking; disapproving" is 못마땅하다 (monmattanghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 못마땅해요 ("I'm displeased / I disapprove"). Watch the particle attached to 못마땅하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, expresses disapproval of something
attributive form (하다→한); very common with 표정/얼굴/눈빛
set phrase; 여기다 = to regard/consider
adverb form, e.g. 못마땅하게 쳐다보다 to glare disapprovingly

examples.en: I'm not happy with that decision.
examples.note: casual 반말; the basic 'it doesn't sit right with me' use

examples.en: Mom had a disapproving look about my decision.
examples.note: the classic 못마땅한 표정 collocation; note the senior-reacts-to-junior pattern

examples.ko: 부장님은 신입의 복장이 영 못마땅하신지 회의 내내 인상을 쓰고 계셨어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimeun sinibui bokjangi yeong monmattanghasinji hoeui naenae insangeul sseugo gyesyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The manager, apparently quite displeased with the new hire's outfit, kept frowning throughout the meeting.
examples.note: real-situation; 못마땅하신지 'seemingly displeased' + honorific 시 shows third-person disapproval shown by face

extendedVocab.nuance: 못마땅하다 means something does not sit right with you — you disapprove of or find it unsatisfactory. The word transparently builds from 마땅하다 ('to be proper/fitting') negated by 못, so it literally reads 'not as it ought to be', which is exactly its flavor: a falling-short of your standard. It is typically shown through the face (못마땅한 표정/눈빛) rather than declared, and very often features a senior reacting to a junior's choice. Contrast it with 화나다: 화나다 is active anger that flares, whereas 못마땅하다 is quiet, simmering disapproval/dissatisfaction — you can be 못마땅하다 for days without ever being 화나다. Crucially, because it is an adjective of feeling, describing a THIRD person's displeasure requires 못마땅해하다 (부장님이 못마땅해하셨어요), not bare 못마땅하다. English-speaker pitfall: saying '엄마가 못마땅해요' to mean 'Mom is displeased' — that wrongly says 'I am displeased with Mom'; switch to 엄마가 못마땅해하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Describing someone else's displeasure with bare 못마땅하다 ('아빠가 못마땅해요') is wrong/ambiguous — Korean feeling-adjectives need -아/어하다 for third person: 아빠가 못마땅해하세요.
Confusing it with 화나다 ('너무 못마땅해서 소리쳤어요' for an outburst) overshoots; 못마땅하다 is quiet disapproval, not active anger. For flaring anger use 화나다.
Using it for disliking food/taste ('이 음식이 못마땅해요') is off; for plain dislike use 별로예요/마음에 안 들어요 — 못마땅하다 leans toward disapproving of conduct, choices, or attitudes.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 언짢다 means "displeased; in a sour/bad mood" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 언짢다 (eonjjanta) = "displeased; in a sour/bad mood". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 언짢아요 ("I'm displeased / I'm in a bad mood") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 언짢다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I'm displeased / I'm in a bad mood
usagePhrases.note: polite present; the ㅎ of the ㄶ batchim is silent, so it's pronounced [언짜나요]

usagePhrases.en: to be in a sour mood
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; 기분이 is the usual subject
attributive form (ㄶ stem + 은 → 언짢은); 기색 = a visible sign of a feeling
adverb form, e.g. 언짢게 듣다 to take something the wrong way

examples.en: That remark put me in a bit of a sour mood.
examples.note: simple past; reacting to something mildly offensive

examples.ko: 혹시 제 말 때문에 기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송해요.
examples.romanization: hoksi je mal ttaemune gibun eonjjaneusyeotdamyeon joesonghaeyo.
examples.en: If what I said happened to put you in a bad mood, I'm sorry.
examples.note: the very common polite apology frame 기분 언짢으셨다면

examples.ko: 사장님이 아침부터 무슨 일이 있으셨는지 종일 언짢은 기색이라 다들 눈치만 봤어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi achimbuteo museun iri isseusyeonneunji jongil eonjjaneun gisaegira dadeul nunchiman bwasseoyo.
examples.en: The boss had a displeased air all day as if something had happened in the morning, so everyone just read the room.
examples.note: real-situation; 언짢은 기색 + 눈치 보다 paints reading a superior's sour mood

extendedVocab.nuance: 언짢다 describes being in a displeased, slightly offended, sour mood — how you feel when something rubs you the wrong way but you're not full-blown angry. Contrast it with two neighbors: 못마땅하다 points outward at a specific thing you disapprove of (a choice, conduct), while 언짢다 points inward at your own soured emotional state/mood; and 화나다 is hot, flaring anger, whereas 언짢다 is a cooler, lower-grade displeasure. It appears constantly in courteous apologies — '기분 언짢으셨다면 죄송합니다' is a fixed politeness formula. Watch the pronunciation: the ㄶ batchim keeps its spelling but the ㅎ is not separately pronounced, so 언짢아요 sounds like [언짜나요] and 언짢다 like [언짠타]. English-speaker pitfall: respelling it phonetically as 언잖다 or 언짠다 because the ㅎ is inaudible — the correct spelling is always 언짢다 with ㄶ.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 언잖다 or 언짠다 is wrong — the standard spelling is 언짢다 with the ㄶ batchim, even though the ㅎ is not clearly heard.
Using it for real anger ('너무 언짢아서 소리쳤어요' for shouting) overshoots; 언짢다 is a soured mood or mild offense — for strong anger use 화나다.
Pointing it outward at a thing like 못마땅하다 ('그 결정이 언짢아요') is awkward; 언짢다 describes your mood (기분이 언짢다), while disapproval of the decision itself is 그 결정이 못마땅해요.

Respelling it phonetically as 언잖다 or 언짠다 because the ㅎ is inaudible is wrong — the correct spelling is always 언짢다 with ㄶ.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 흐뭇하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a gentle, satisfied warmth
attributive form (하다→한); very common with 미소/표정
set phrase; the prototypical action that goes with this feeling
adverb form modifying verbs like 보다, 웃다

examples.en: Hearing that news, I feel warm and pleased.
examples.note: simple form; quiet pleasure at a good outcome

examples.en: Watching the kids play, I feel so warm inside.
examples.note: the classic context: contentment watching others do well

examples.ko: 손주가 의젓하게 인사하는 모습을 할머니가 흐뭇한 미소로 바라보셨어요.
examples.romanization: sonjuga uijeotage insahaneun moseubeul halmeoniga heumutan misoro barabosyeosseoyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: 흐뭇하다 is a warm, gentle contentment — the soft, slightly proud satisfaction of seeing something turn out well, especially OTHERS doing well (kids at play, a junior succeeding, a grandchild behaving). Contrast it with 뿌듯하다 and 자랑스럽다, the words learners blur it with: 뿌듯하다 is the chest-filling pride you feel about your OWN achievement or close stake (시험에 붙어서 뿌듯해요), and 자랑스럽다 is 'proud (of)' often said outward; but 흐뭇하다 is the mellow, observing warmth of an onlooker pleased by a heartwarming scene, calmer and more tender than excited pride. Because it is often worn on the face, it pairs idiomatically with 미소, 표정, and 바라보다. As a 하다-adjective: 흐뭇해요 / 흐뭇했어요 / 흐뭇해서; for a third person's contentment use 흐뭇해하다 (부모님이 흐뭇해하셨어요). English-speaker pitfall: reaching for it about your own big win — '시험 붙어서 흐뭇해요' sounds detached; for personal achievement say 뿌듯하다.

Describing a third person's contentment with bare 흐뭇하다 ('할아버지가 흐뭇해요') is wrong; use 흐뭇해하다: 할아버지가 흐뭇해하셨어요.
Treating it as strong/excited happiness misreads the register; 흐뭇하다 is mellow and tender, so don't swap it for 신나다/너무 행복하다 when describing a thrill.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뭉클하다 means "deeply moved; choked up with emotion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "deeply moved; choked up with emotion" is 뭉클하다 (mungkeulhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 뭉클해요 ("I'm moved / it's touching"). Watch the particle attached to 뭉클하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective → 해요, a sudden welling of emotion
set phrase; the most common frame, 가슴이 as subject

usagePhrases.en: to get choked up (the nose tingles)
usagePhrases.note: vivid set phrase for that nearly-tearing-up moment
adverb form, e.g. 뭉클하게 다가오다 to hit one emotionally

examples.en: That scene was moving.
examples.note: simple past; the basic 'it touched me' use

examples.en: Reading my parents' letter, I got all choked up.
examples.note: the prototypical heartfelt context; 가슴이 뭉클하다

examples.ko: 참전 용사들이 서로 끌어안는 장면에서 나도 모르게 코끝이 뭉클해지더라고요.
examples.romanization: chamjeon yongsadeuri seoro kkeureoanneun jangmyeoneseo nado moreuge kokkeuchi mungkeulhaejideoragoyo.
examples.en: At the scene where the war veterans embraced, my nose tingled with tears before I knew it.
examples.note: real-situation; 코끝이 뭉클해지다 + 나도 모르게 'without realizing' captures the involuntary surge

extendedVocab.nuance: 뭉클하다 is the sudden lump-in-the-throat, heart-swelling rush of being deeply moved — a heartfelt letter, a reunion, a touching scene. The word is mimetic: 뭉클 evokes a soft mass welling up and pressing, so it captures the PHYSICAL sensation of emotion rising. Contrast it with 감동하다 (a verb, 'to be touched/impressed'): 감동하다 is the broader, more general statement that you were moved or impressed (even intellectually), whereas 뭉클하다 zeroes in on the warm, almost-teary bodily welling-up in a single instant — you can be 감동했어요 by an admirable feat without being 뭉클; 뭉클 needs the throat-tightening tenderness. It pairs idiomatically with 가슴이 and the very evocative 코끝이. As a 하다-adjective: 뭉클해요 / 뭉클했어요 / 뭉클해서. English-speaker pitfall: using it for cool intellectual admiration ('그 논문이 뭉클해요') is wrong — that is 인상적이다/감동적이다; 뭉클하다 is the momentary emotional, near-teary reaction, not 'impressive'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for intellectual admiration ('발표가 뭉클했어요' meaning 'impressive') is wrong — 뭉클하다 is the emotional, almost-teary welling-up; for 'impressive' use 인상적이다/감동적이다.
Treating it as a lasting state ('요즘 계속 뭉클해요') is off; it names a momentary surge in a touching instant that then passes, so it fits a specific moment, not an ongoing mood.
Blurring it with 감동하다 as if identical loses the nuance: 감동하다 (verb) is general 'moved/impressed'; 뭉클하다 (adjective) is the physical throat-tightening swell.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 멋쩍다 means "self-conscious; sheepish; awkwardly embarrassed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 멋쩍다 (meotjjeokda) = "self-conscious; sheepish; awkwardly embarrassed". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 멋쩍어요 ("I feel sheepish/awkward") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 멋쩍다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; stem 멋쩍- + 어요 (ㄱ batchim), for mild self-conscious embarrassment
attributive form (멋쩍- + 은); the signature collocation
set phrase for the awkward laugh you give when embarrassed
-아/어하다 form to describe someone else looking sheepish

examples.en: Getting praised makes me feel a bit sheepish.
examples.note: simple form; the classic trigger — praise you don't know how to take

examples.en: I had nothing to say, so I just laughed sheepishly.
examples.note: the awkward-laugh reflex; 멋쩍게 웃다 is the go-to collocation

examples.ko: 사람들 앞에서 발표하다 이름을 까먹어서 머리만 긁으며 멋쩍게 서 있었어요.
examples.romanization: saramdeul apeseo balpyohada ireumeul kkameogeoseo meoriman geulgeumyeo meotjjeokge seo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: I forgot the name mid-presentation in front of everyone and just stood there sheepishly scratching my head.
examples.note: real-situation; mild public embarrassment plus the head-scratch gesture, not deep shame

extendedVocab.nuance: 멋쩍다 is that mild, sheepish self-consciousness — being complimented, caught in a small slip, or left with nothing to say, so you give an awkward little laugh. Contrast it with 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: 부끄럽다 covers shyness or genuine shame, and 창피하다 is stronger 'embarrassing/mortifying' (a real loss of face), whereas 멋쩍다 is the lightest of the three — a momentary, almost endearing social awkwardness with no real shame, the feeling behind a bashful grin. Note it is NOT a 하다-adjective: the stem is 멋쩍- (멋쩍어요, 멋쩍었어요, 멋쩍어서, 멋쩍은), and the ㄱ batchim takes 어 not 해. It collocates above all with 웃음 and 웃다 (멋쩍은 웃음, 멋쩍게 웃다). English-speaker pitfall: confusing it with 서먹하다 — 멋쩍다 is your OWN in-the-moment sheepishness, while 서먹하다 is the distance BETWEEN two people, so they are not swappable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 멋적다 is wrong — the standard spelling is 멋쩍다 with ㅉ.
Conjugating it as a 하다-word ('멋쩍해요') is wrong; it is not 하다-based, so the correct forms are 멋쩍어요, 멋쩍었어요, 멋쩍어서.
Swapping it with 서먹하다 ('칭찬받아서 서먹했어요') is wrong; 멋쩍다 is your own sheepishness in the moment, whereas 서먹하다 is the distance between two people.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 안방 means "master bedroom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 안방 (anbang) means "master bedroom". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 안방 ("the master bedroom"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 안방 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 안 (inner) + 방 (room, 房); the biggest/main bedroom, traditionally the household head's room
차지하다 = to take/occupy; the natural verb when someone grabs the best room
an attached bathroom is a big selling point, so this phrase shows up in listings
the standard pair Koreans use to divide bedrooms among family or roommates

examples.en: This is the master bedroom.
examples.note: Pointing it out on a flat tour; 여기가 X-이에요 is the bare 'this is X' frame

examples.ko: 저는 안방 쓰고, 동생은 작은방 써요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun anbang sseugo, dongsaengeun jageunbang sseoyo.
examples.en: I use the master bedroom and my younger sibling uses the small room.
examples.note: 쓰다 ('use') is the everyday verb for occupying a room, not 살다

examples.ko: 집 보러 갔는데 안방이 생각보다 넓더라고요.
examples.romanization: jip boreo ganneunde anbangi saenggakboda neolbdeoragoyo.
examples.en: I went to see the place and the master bedroom was bigger than I'd expected.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports something you personally noticed on the spot, perfect for a viewing

extendedVocab.nuance: 안방 is literally 안 ('inner') + 방 ('room', from the hanja 房), so it points not to size first but to the 'innermost, main' bedroom — culturally the room of the household head, historically where the senior couple slept. The near-synonym trap is 큰방: 큰방 just means 'the big room' by floor area, while 안방 carries the 'master / main' status even in a flat where it isn't literally the largest. Don't confuse it with 거실 (the shared living room) — 안방 is private sleeping space. English speakers often over-extend it and call every bedroom 안방; only the one main room is 안방, the rest are 작은방 or plain 방. It pairs naturally with 안방 화장실 (en-suite) and the contrast set 안방 vs 작은방 when splitting rooms.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling any bedroom 안방. WHY: 안방 specifically means the one main/master room; the others are 작은방 or 방. FIX: reserve 안방 for the principal bedroom only.
Confusing 안방 with 거실 (living room). WHY: they look similar to a beginner but 안방 is a private bedroom while 거실 is the shared lounge. FIX: use 거실 for the open family area, 안방 for the couple's room.
Saying 큰방 when you mean the 'master' room. WHY: 큰방 only describes size, not status. FIX: use 안방 when you mean the main bedroom regardless of which is physically biggest.

extendedVocab.explanation: "utility room" is 다용도실 (dayongdosil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 다용도실 ("utility room"). Watch the particle attached to 다용도실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 다용도 多用途 ('many-use', i.e. multi-purpose) + 실 室 ('room'); the back room off the kitchen

usagePhrases.en: to keep (it) in the utility room
usagePhrases.note: 두다 = to keep/store; what you do with the washer, kimchi fridge, bulky stuff

usagePhrases.en: to have a separate utility room
usagePhrases.note: 따로 있다 = to exist separately; a common plus point in a listing
정리 整理 = sorting out; it clutters fast, so this is a recurring chore

examples.en: The washing machine is in the utility room.
examples.note: Basic location sentence; 에 marks where a thing sits

examples.en: We keep the kimchi fridge in the utility room.
examples.note: 두다 ('keep/store') is the habitual-storage verb, more natural here than 있다

examples.ko: 이 집은 다용도실이 따로 있어서 마음에 들어요.
examples.romanization: i jibeun dayongdosiri ttaro isseoseo maeume deureoyo.
examples.en: I like this place because it has a separate utility room.
examples.note: 다용도실이 따로 있다 is the set phrase house-hunters use as a selling point

extendedVocab.nuance: 다용도실 is a Sino-Korean compound: 다용도 多用途 literally 'many + use + purpose' = multi-purpose, plus 실 室 'room'. It's the small enclosed back space off the kitchen (often behind the 베란다) where the washing machine, 김치냉장고, cleaning supplies and recycling live — a near-universal feature of Korean apartments. The synonym to keep apart is 창고 倉庫 ('storehouse'): a 창고 is dead storage, while a 다용도실 is an active work-and-store space you use daily. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't assume laundry happens in the bathroom as in many Western homes — in Korea the washer lives in the 다용도실 (or 베란다); second, don't translate it as 'laundry room', because it does far more than laundry. It collocates with 세탁기, 김치냉장고, and 따로 있다.

Assuming laundry is done in the bathroom. WHY: Korean homes put the washer in the 다용도실 or 베란다, not the bathroom. FIX: locate the 세탁기 in the 다용도실.
Calling it 창고 (storehouse). WHY: 창고 is passive dead storage; 다용도실 is an active, in-home utility space. FIX: use 다용도실 for the working back room, 창고 for a true storeroom.
Rendering it 'laundry room'. WHY: it handles storage, the kimchi fridge and recycling too, not just laundry. FIX: say 'utility room' and let 세탁실 be the narrow 'laundry-only' term.

꽉 차다 = packed full; a constant complaint for shoe lovers

usagePhrases.en: on top of the shoe cabinet
usagePhrases.note: the flat top is a handy drop spot for keys, masks and deliveries

examples.en: Please put your shoes in the shoe cabinet.
examples.note: Polite request to a guest; 넣다 + 에 = 'put into' a place

examples.ko: 신발장이 꽉 차서 새 운동화 둘 데가 없어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 신발장 is 신발 ('shoes') + 장 (the native-reading of the hanja 欌, 'cabinet/wardrobe') — the same 장 you see in 옷장, 책장, 거실장, so once you learn it you can decode a whole family of furniture words. It sits at the 현관 (entryway) and is bound up with the absolute Korean rule that shoes come off the instant you step inside and go straight in. The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 신발 박스 / 신발 상자, but a 박스/상자 is a cardboard box you'd carry a single pair in — the built-in furniture piece is always 신발장. A second trap is thinking the shoe-removal is optional; saying 신발장에 넣어 주세요 to a guest is itself a polite way of signalling 'shoes off, please'. It collocates with 넣다, 꽉 차다, and 위에 올려 두다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it 신발 박스 or 신발 상자. WHY: 박스/상자 is a cardboard box, not the entryway furniture. FIX: use 신발장 for the built-in cabinet.
Walking in without using it. WHY: the cultural norm is shoes off and into the 신발장 at the door. FIX: take shoes off at the 현관 and place them in the 신발장.
Mixing up the 장 ('cabinet') in 신발장 with 장 ('market', 場/장). WHY: same syllable, different word. FIX: read the 장 in furniture words as 'cabinet' (欌), as in 옷장 and 책장.
