extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 깜짝 means "with a start; suddenly (startled)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 깜짝 (kkamjjak) means "with a start; suddenly (startled)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 깜짝 놀라다 ("to be startled / get a shock"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 깜짝 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to be startled / get a shock
usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing. 깜짝 almost always attaches to 놀라다 — treat them as one chunk.
A reflex exclamation when something startles you. Often stretched to 아이 깜짝이야 or 깜짝 놀랐잖아.
깜짝 + noun = 'surprise ~'. Also 깜짝 파티 (surprise party), 깜짝 방문 (surprise visit), 깜짝 발표 (surprise announcement).
Doubled 깜짝깜짝 means repeatedly flinching, e.g. from loud noises or being on edge.

examples.en: You startled me / I got a shock.
examples.note: The bare-minimum sentence; memorize 깜짝 놀라다 as one unit before anything else.

examples.en: You called me from behind so suddenly that I got startled.
examples.note: Note 불러서 (because you called) gives the cause; 깜짝 sits right before the verb it intensifies.

examples.ko: 뒤에서 친구가 '왁!' 하는 바람에 깜짝이야, 하고 소리를 질렀어요.
examples.romanization: dwieseo chinguga 'wak!' haneun barame kkamjjagiya, hago sorireul jilleosseoyo.
examples.en: My friend went 'Boo!' behind me, and I yelped 'You scared me!'
examples.note: Real-situation: 깜짝이야 used as the live spoken reaction inside a story (반말 narration).

extendedVocab.nuance: 깜짝 captures the split-second jolt of being startled, not a gradual surprise — it is the body's flinch the instant something pops up. Compare it with 갑자기 'suddenly': 갑자기 only marks that an event happened without warning (timing), while 깜짝 names the startle reaction itself, so they often appear together (갑자기 ~해서 깜짝 놀랐다). The dividing line vs 놀라다 alone is intensity-of-onset: 깜짝 forces the 'jump' reading. Its strongest collocation is 깜짝 놀라다, and the standalone 깜짝이야! is something you will say constantly. As a noun-modifier it means 'surprise ~' (깜짝 세일, 깜짝 방문). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 깜짝 as a verb: there is no 깜짝하다 — 깜짝 is an adverb and always needs 놀라다 (or another verb) behind it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 깜짝했어요 as if 깜짝 were a verb. 깜짝하다 is not a real word; you must say 깜짝 놀랐어요 — the adverb 깜짝 plus the verb 놀라다.
Using 깜짝 to mean 'suddenly' in a neutral sentence like '갑자기 비가 왔어요'. 깜짝 carries the startle/jump nuance, so for plain unexpected timing you need 갑자기, not 깜짝.
Reaching for 놀라운 (amazing/remarkable) when you mean the jolt. 놀랍다 describes something impressive; 깜짝 놀라다 is the physical flinch — don't swap them.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 두근두근 means "heart pounding (with excitement or nerves)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "heart pounding (with excitement or nerves)" is 두근두근 (dugeundugeun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가슴이 두근두근하다 ("one's heart goes thump-thump"). Watch the particle attached to 두근두근 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The textbook frame. The subject is 가슴 (chest/heart), and 두근두근 describes how it beats.
Pairs with 설레다 (to be thrilled) for positive anticipation — crushes, trips, first days.
Pairs with 떨리다 (to tremble/be nervous) for the anxious side — auditions, results, exams.
The single-action verb 두근거리다 is the more literary, write-it-down equivalent of 두근두근하다.

examples.en: My heart is pounding.
examples.note: The core sentence — note 가슴이 (heart, as subject) + 두근두근하다 as a descriptive verb.

examples.en: When I meet the person I like, my heart pounds.
examples.note: Everyday romantic context; 만나면 (when/if I meet) sets up the trigger for the flutter.

examples.en: It was my first day at work, so from the morning I was both fluttery and nervous.
examples.note: Real-situation: shows 두근두근 layered with 긴장되다, the mixed excited-anxious feeling a newcomer knows.

extendedVocab.nuance: 두근두근 is the sound-feeling of a fast heartbeat (의태어/의성어) and works for BOTH happy anticipation and anxious nerves — context and the partner verb decide which. The key contrast is with 긴장되다 'to be tense/nervous': 긴장되다 is flatly negative stress, whereas 두근두근 is warmer and bodily, often carrying 설렘 (sweet excitement), so a crush or a trip is 두근두근 but rarely just 긴장돼요. It is also distinct from 떨리다 (to physically tremble): 떨려요 can be visible shaking, while 두근두근 is specifically the heart's thumping. Use it adverbially (두근두근 떨려요) or as 두근두근하다. The pitfall for English speakers is mapping it to a pounding heart from physical exertion — after running, Koreans say 숨차다 or 헐떡거리다, not 두근두근, which is reserved for emotional racing. Also remember the subject is usually 가슴/심장, not 'I'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 반짝반짝 means "sparkling; twinkling; shiny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 반짝반짝 (banjjakbanjjak) = "sparkling; twinkling; shiny". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 반짝반짝 빛나다 ("to shine/sparkle brightly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 반짝반짝, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. usagePhrases.note: The core collocation, for stars, polished surfaces, jewelry, and eager eyes.
Descriptive verb form: 청소했더니 바닥이 반짝반짝해요 (after cleaning, the floor is sparkling).
Describes bright, eager eyes — a child's, or someone lit up with excitement.
Single 반짝 = a brief one-off flash, hence 반짝 세일 (a short, sudden sale) and 반짝 인기 (a brief fad).

examples.en: The stars are twinkling.
examples.note: The simplest frame — 반짝반짝 directly modifies 빛나다.

examples.en: After I finished the dishes, the bowls are sparkling clean.
examples.note: Everyday context; here 반짝반짝하다 works as a stand-alone descriptive verb, no 빛나다 needed.

examples.ko: 면접관 앞에서 아이가 눈을 반짝반짝하면서 자기 꿈을 이야기했어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeopgwan apeseo aiga nuneul banjjakbanjjakamyeonseo jagi kkumeul iyagihaesseoyo.
examples.en: In front of the interviewer, the child talked about her dream with sparkling, eager eyes.
examples.note: Real-situation: 눈이 반짝반짝 for the 'lit-up, eager' look rather than literal shine.

extendedVocab.nuance: 반짝반짝 evokes light bouncing off something repeatedly — stars, a just-mopped floor, jewelry, or wide eager eyes. It is famously the opening of the Korean 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' (반짝반짝 작은 별), so it instantly sounds storybook-warm. Two contrasts matter. First, single 반짝 means a brief, one-time flash (반짝 세일, 반짝 스타), whereas doubled 반짝반짝 means continuous glittering. Second, do not confuse it with 번쩍: 반짝 is small, cute, decorative sparkle, while 번쩍 (its 'big brother' with the heavier 어 vowel) is a sudden powerful flash — lightning 번쩍, or 정신이 번쩍 들다 'to snap wide awake'. Korean's vowel symbolism (bright ㅏ/ㅗ = small & cute, dark ㅓ/ㅜ = big & strong) is doing real work here. The English-speaker pitfall is using 반짝반짝 for steady brightness like a lamp; plain brightness is 밝다, and 반짝반짝 specifically requires the glitter/twinkle of reflected, intermittent light.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for steady, non-glittering brightness like a lit lamp or a bright room. Plain brightness is 밝다; 반짝반짝 requires sparkle/twinkle, not constant glow.
Mixing up 반짝 (small cute sparkle) with 번쩍 (a big sudden flash like lightning). The darker vowel in 번쩍 signals something larger and more startling.
Treating 반짝반짝 and single 반짝 as identical. Doubled = ongoing twinkling; single 반짝 = one brief flash, as in 반짝 세일 (flash sale).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주룩주룩 means "pouring (rain) steadily; streaming down" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주룩주룩 (jurukjuruk) means "pouring (rain) steadily; streaming down". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비가 주룩주룩 내리다 ("rain pours down steadily"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주룩주룩 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The default frame. 비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the full natural phrase for heavy streaming rain.
For tears running down the face in lines — pairs with 흐르다 (to flow).
For sweat streaming in the heat — 등에 땀이 주룩주룩 (sweat pouring down one's back).
Pairs with 쏟아지다 (to gush) to stress sheer volume of rain.

examples.en: It's pouring (rain).
examples.note: The base weather sentence; 내리다 is the most natural verb for falling rain.

examples.ko: 아침부터 비가 주룩주룩 내려서 우산을 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: achimbuteo biga jurukjurung naeryeoseo usaneul chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It's been pouring since morning, so I grabbed an umbrella.
examples.note: Everyday cause-effect: -아서 (because) links the rain to grabbing the umbrella.

examples.ko: 퇴근길에 갑자기 비가 주룩주룩 쏟아져서 옷이 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: toegeungire gapjagi biga jurukjuruk ssodajyeoseo osi da jeojeosseoyo.
examples.en: On the way home from work, rain suddenly poured down and my clothes got soaked.
examples.note: Real-situation: 주룩주룩 쏟아지다 emphasizing a heavy downpour that drenches you.

extendedVocab.nuance: 주룩주룩 describes liquid running down in steady, continuous streams — most often heavy rain, but equally tears and sweat. It is genuinely heavy and unbroken, which is what separates it from the soft drizzle words 부슬부슬 / 보슬보슬 (a fine misty rain you barely need an umbrella for). It also differs from 후두둑, the brief pattering of the first fat drops, and from 주르륵, a single quick run-down (one tear, water down a window); 주룩주룩 is the sustained, repeated version. The natural verb is 내리다 for rain and 흐르다 for tears/sweat. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 주룩주룩 with 오다 by analogy to 'rain comes' — 비가 주룩주룩 와요 is acceptable, but 내리다 sounds cleaner, and crucially you should NOT use 주룩주룩 for light rain at all. During Korea's 장마 (monsoon) season this is the word you'll see in every weather chat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for light rain or drizzle. A fine misty rain is 부슬부슬 / 보슬보슬; 주룩주룩 is genuinely heavy, streaming rain and sounds wrong for a sprinkle.
Defaulting to 비가 주룩주룩 와요. It is not wrong, but 비가 주룩주룩 내려요 is the more natural pairing native speakers prefer.
Pairing 주룩주룩 with snow. Snow doesn't 'stream down' — heavy snow is 펑펑 (눈이 펑펑 와요), so reserve 주룩주룩 for rain, tears, and sweat.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 펑펑 means "(crying) hard; (snowing) heavily; (spending) lavishly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "(crying) hard; (snowing) heavily; (spending) lavishly" is 펑펑 (peongpeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 펑펑 울다 ("to cry one's eyes out"). Watch the particle attached to 펑펑 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Very common: hard, body-shaking sobbing, not a few tears.
Big, fast snowfall in fat flakes. 눈이 펑펑 와요 / 펑펑 내려요.
To splurge / blow money freely, usually with a faintly disapproving tone.
Single 펑 is the actual burst sound — a balloon, a firework, a cork.

examples.en: I cried my eyes out.
examples.note: The base sentence; 펑펑 signals serious sobbing, far stronger than 조금 울었어요.

examples.ko: 밤새 눈이 펑펑 와서 길이 하얘졌어요.
examples.romanization: bamsae nuni peongpeong waseo giri hayaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It snowed heavily all night, so the roads turned white.
examples.note: Everyday weather; 펑펑 with 눈 specifically means thick, fast snowfall.

examples.ko: 월급 받자마자 돈을 펑펑 쓰더니 월말에 카드값 때문에 후회하더라고요.
examples.romanization: wolgeup batjamaja doneul peongpeong sseudeoni wolmare kadeugaps ttaemune huhoehadeoragoyo.
examples.en: She blew money the moment she got paid, then regretted it at month-end over the card bill.
examples.note: Real-situation: 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 with the disapproving 'splurge-then-regret' arc.

extendedVocab.nuance: 펑펑 has three everyday senses tied together by the image of something bursting out in abundance: crying hard (펑펑 울다), heavy snowfall (눈이 펑펑 와요), and splurging money (돈을 펑펑 쓰다). Context makes the meaning instantly clear, because each sense has a fixed partner verb (울다 / 오다·내리다 / 쓰다). Two contrasts to lock in. For crying, compare 엉엉 울다 (loud wailing, mouth open) — 펑펑 stresses the gushing flow of tears, 엉엉 the loud sound; both mean hard crying and often interchange. For snow, 펑펑 means big abundant flakes, unlike the rain word 주룩주룩, which never describes snow. The single 펑 is the literal 'pop/bang' of a burst (a vowel-darker, bigger cousin of 팡). The English-speaker pitfall is using 펑펑 for rain — heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 쏟아지다, and 펑펑 with weather means snow only.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 펑펑 for rain. Heavy rain is 주룩주룩 or 비가 쏟아지다; with weather, 펑펑 specifically means snow (눈이 펑펑).
Assuming 펑펑 울다 is mild crying. It means serious, hard sobbing — for just a couple of tears use 살짝 울다 or 눈물이 났어요.
Treating 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 as neutral 'spending'. It carries a wasteful/reckless tone; plain spending is just 돈을 쓰다, so don't use 펑펑 unless you mean to imply splurging.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 살금살금 means "stealthily; tiptoeing quietly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 살금살금 (salgeumsalgeum) = "stealthily; tiptoeing quietly". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 살금살금 걷다 ("to walk stealthily / tiptoe") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 살금살금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core usage: moving quietly on soft feet so as not to be noticed.
Approaching quietly, often to surprise someone or like a cat stalking prey.
Entering quietly, e.g. coming home late and not wanting to wake anyone.
Leaving a room/place without being noticed.

examples.en: I walked on tiptoe / I crept along.
examples.note: The base frame: 살금살금 directly modifies a verb of motion.

examples.ko: 아기가 자고 있어서 살금살금 걸어 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: agiga jago isseoseo salgeumsalgeum georeo nawasseoyo.
examples.en: The baby was sleeping, so I tiptoed out.
examples.note: Everyday considerate movement; -아서 gives the reason for being quiet.

examples.ko: 고양이가 참새를 향해 살금살금 다가가다가 결국 들켜서 참새가 날아가 버렸어요.
examples.romanization: goyangiga chamsaereul hyanghae salgeumsalgeum dagagadaga gyeolguk deulkyeoseo chamsaega naraga beoryeosseoyo.
examples.en: The cat crept toward the sparrow but got spotted in the end, and the sparrow flew off.
examples.note: Real-situation: stalking with 다가가다, the most natural verb for closing in quietly.

extendedVocab.nuance: 살금살금 describes moving deliberately and softly so you won't be heard or seen — tiptoeing past a sleeping roommate, a cat stalking a bird, sneaking home late. It carries a slightly playful, cautious feel and pairs with verbs of motion (걷다, 다가가다, 들어가다, 나오다). The sharp contrast to memorize is 슬금슬금: 슬금슬금 means edging away gradually and sheepishly, usually to dodge blame or slip out of a situation (혼날까 봐 슬금슬금 도망쳤다), so it foregrounds 'sneaking off to avoid something', while 살금살금 foregrounds 'quiet footsteps so as not to make noise'. It also differs from 슬며시/슬쩍, which mean doing something subtly or on the sly (slipping a note, a quiet smile) rather than literal quiet walking. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for fast quiet movement: stealthy-but-quick is 후다닥 or 잽싸게, whereas 살금살금 is inherently slow and careful.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 슬금슬금. 슬금슬금 implies edging away sheepishly to avoid blame; 살금살금 is about quiet, careful footsteps so as not to be heard.
Using it for fast quiet movement. Quick-and-quiet is 후다닥 / 잽싸게; 살금살금 is deliberately slow and tiptoeing.
Pairing it with non-motion verbs. 살금살금 needs a verb of moving (걷다, 다가가다); you can't say 살금살금 말하다 for whispering — that's 소곤소곤 / 속삭이다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 후다닥 means "hurriedly; in a quick dash" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 후다닥 (hudadak) means "hurriedly; in a quick dash". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후다닥 일어나다 ("to jump up quickly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후다닥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Springing up in a flustered burst, e.g. when you oversleep and bolt out of bed.

usagePhrases.en: to get ready in a rush
usagePhrases.note: Throwing yourself together fast and a little frantically.
Eating very fast, gulping it down before running off.
Running off suddenly, often half in a panic.

examples.en: I jumped up in a flash.
examples.note: The base frame: 후다닥 + a quick action verb.

examples.en: I overslept, so I got ready in a mad rush and left.
examples.note: Everyday morning scramble; -아서 links oversleeping to the frantic prep.

examples.ko: 바퀴벌레가 갑자기 나타나는 바람에 다들 비명을 지르며 후다닥 도망갔어요.
examples.romanization: bakwibeollega gapjagi natananeun barame dadeul bimyeongeul jireumyeo hudadak domanggasseoyo.
examples.en: A cockroach suddenly appeared, so everyone screamed and bolted.
examples.note: Real-situation: 후다닥 도망가다 for a sudden, slightly comic panic-dash.

extendedVocab.nuance: 후다닥 conveys doing something in a fast, slightly frantic burst — jumping up, scrambling to get ready, dashing off. The defining flavor is speed PLUS commotion or fluster, which is exactly what separates it from the neutral 빨리 'quickly' and from 잽싸게 'nimbly/deftly': 빨리 is plain speed and 잽싸게 implies smooth, skillful quickness, whereas 후다닥 implies a flustered scramble, often with noise or panic. It is also distinct from 허둥지둥, which stresses being flustered and disorganized (flailing, losing things in your haste); 후다닥 keeps the focus on the quick burst of action itself. Note 후다닥 has the heavy ㅜ/ㅏ vowels of a bigger, more energetic motion, versus the lighter 호다닥. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is pairing it with calm, careful, or slow actions — it clashes with 천천히 and with deliberate tasks, so use it only when there's a hurried, scrambling feel.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for calm, smooth speed. Efficient quickness is 빨리 or 잽싸게; 후다닥 implies a flustered, noisy scramble.
Pairing it with slow or careful actions. 후다닥 천천히 or 후다닥 + a meticulous task is contradictory — the word demands a hurried burst.
Confusing it with 허둥지둥. 허둥지둥 stresses panicky disorganization (flailing about); 후다닥 stresses the quick, sudden burst of the action.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빙글빙글 means "round and round; spinning" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "round and round; spinning" is 빙글빙글 (binggeulbinggeul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빙글빙글 돌다 ("to spin round and round"). Watch the particle attached to 빙글빙글 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: turning continuously in circles (intransitive).
The everyday way to say you feel dizzy: 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요.
Transitive: spinning an object, e.g. twirling a pen or a hula hoop.
Shorter 빙빙 is a near-synonym with a slightly faster, looser feel.

examples.en: The top spins round and round.
examples.note: The base frame: 빙글빙글 directly modifies 돌다.

examples.en: I stood up suddenly and my head started spinning.
examples.note: Everyday dizziness; -았더니 (did X, and as a result) links standing up to the dizzy spell.

examples.ko: 회전목마를 너무 오래 탔는지 내려서도 세상이 빙글빙글 도는 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: hoejeonmongmareul neomu orae tanneunji naeryeoseodo sesangi binggeulbinggeul doneun geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: Maybe I rode the carousel too long — even after getting off, the world seemed to spin.
examples.note: Real-situation: 빙글빙글 돌다 extended to a lingering whirling sensation.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빙글빙글 describes smooth, continuous rotation in place — a spinning top, a carousel, or a dizzy head whirling. For dizziness, 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요 is the natural everyday phrase you'd give a doctor or friend, and 어지러워요 (I'm dizzy) is its plain companion. The crucial contrast is with 데굴데굴: 빙글빙글 is rotating on the spot, while 데굴데굴 is a round object ROLLING ALONG the ground (a ball, a dropped tangerine) — same idea of turning, totally different path. Within the spinning family, the shorter 빙빙 is interchangeable in most cases but feels a touch quicker and is common in 빙빙 돌리다 / 빙빙 돌려 말하다 (to beat around the bush), whereas the darker-vowel 뱅뱅 suggests tighter, smaller circles. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is using 빙글빙글 for a single half-turn: one turn is just 돌다, and 빙글빙글 requires repeated, ongoing rotation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a single turn or half-turn. One turn is 돌다 by itself; 빙글빙글 implies continuous, repeated rotation.
Confusing it with 데굴데굴. 빙글빙글 is spinning in place; 데굴데굴 is rolling along the ground like a ball.

extendedVocab.explanation: 콜록콜록 (kollokkollok) = "cough-cough (sound of coughing)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 콜록콜록 기침하다 ("to cough repeatedly") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core pairing with 기침하다 (to cough); the two go together naturally.
Verb form for ongoing coughing fits, written as one word.
Light spoken form, often about a child. 아이가 콜록콜록해요.
Single 콜록 is one cough sound; doubling it = repeated coughing.

examples.en: I'm coughing (cough-cough).
examples.note: The base frame: 콜록콜록 directly modifies 기침하다.

examples.en: I caught a cold and coughed all night long.
examples.note: Everyday clinic/pharmacy line; 감기에 걸리다 (to catch a cold) is the standard collocation.

examples.ko: 옆자리 사람이 마스크도 안 쓰고 콜록콜록거려서 자리를 옮겼어요.
examples.romanization: yeopjari sarami maseukeudo an sseugo kollokkollokgeoryeoseo jarireul olmgyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The person next to me kept coughing without even a mask, so I moved seats.
examples.note: Real-situation: 콜록콜록거리다 in a slightly annoyed observation about someone else.

extendedVocab.nuance: 콜록콜록 is the onomatopoeia for repeated coughing and pairs naturally with 기침하다, or stands alone as 콜록콜록거리다 / 콜록콜록하다. It is the word you'll actually use to describe cold symptoms to a 약사 (pharmacist) or 의사 (doctor), alongside 기침이 나요 (I have a cough). A single dry cough is 콜록; the doubled form signals ongoing coughing fits. Two distinctions help. First, 콜록콜록 vs 쿨럭쿨럭: both exist, but the darker-vowel 쿨럭 suggests a deeper, heavier chest cough, while 콜록 is the lighter, standard form you should default to. Second, do not confuse coughing with sneezing — a sneeze is 에취 (the sound) or 재채기 (the noun/act), never 콜록콜록. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja; note that the related noun 기침 and verb 기침하다 are the clinical words, and 콜록콜록 is the vivid sound layered on top. extendedVocab.explanation: 쿨쿨 (kulkul) means "(sleeping) soundly; zzz". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 쿨쿨 자다 ("to sleep soundly / snooze away"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쿨쿨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: deep, sound sleep. 쿨쿨 almost always attaches to 자다.
Dropping into deep sleep (잠들다 = to fall asleep).
Progressive: someone is sound asleep right now.

usagePhrases.en: to snooze / breathe heavily in sleep
usagePhrases.note: Verb form, sometimes implying soft, audible sleeping breaths.

examples.en: (He) is sleeping soundly / zzz.
examples.note: The base frame: 쿨쿨 directly modifies 자다.

examples.en: On weekends I want to sleep in soundly until late.
examples.note: Everyday wish; -고 싶다 (want to) attaches to the verb after 쿨쿨.

examples.ko: 남편은 옆에서 아기가 우는데도 모르고 쿨쿨 자고 있더라고요.
examples.romanization: nampyeoneun yeopeseo agiga uneundedo moreugo kulkul jago itdeoragoyo.
examples.en: My husband was fast asleep, oblivious, even though the baby was crying right next to him.
examples.note: Real-situation: 쿨쿨 자다 with a fond-but-exasperated tone about dead-to-the-world sleep.

extendedVocab.nuance: 쿨쿨 is the cozy onomatopoeia for sleeping deeply and soundly — the Korean equivalent of 'zzz'. It pairs almost exclusively with 자다 / 잠들다 and carries a warm, slightly cute tone, so you'd use it for a tired roommate napping or a pet snoozing, not for a clinical sleep report (수면 / 숙면 are the formal words). Two contrasts sharpen it. First, 쿨쿨 means genuinely deep sleep, unlike 꾸벅꾸벅 졸다, which is nodding off / dozing while basically awake (on the subway, in a meeting). Second, do not equate it with snoring: heavy snoring is 드르렁드르렁 or the verb 코를 골다, whereas 쿨쿨 is peaceful, gentle sleeping — at most softly audible breathing, not a sawing snore. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 쿨쿨 to mean any kind of resting; for a quick nap-while-sitting you want 졸다, and for 'go to bed/sleep' in a neutral sense you simply use 자다 — 쿨쿨 specifically adds the 'out cold, sound asleep' picture.

Using it for dozing or nodding off while awake. A light doze is 꾸벅꾸벅 졸다; 쿨쿨 means genuinely deep, sound sleep.
Equating 쿨쿨 with snoring. Loud snoring is 드르렁드르렁 / 코를 골다; 쿨쿨 is peaceful sleeping, not a snore.
Using 쿨쿨 in a formal or medical context. For clinical 'sleep' use 자다 / 수면; 쿨쿨 is casual and a bit cute.

extendedVocab.explanation: "rolling (along the ground)" is 데굴데굴 (deguldegul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 데굴데굴 구르다 ("to roll along / tumble"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: a round thing rolling on the ground (구르다 = to roll).
Rolling off in a direction, away from you.

usagePhrases.en: to roll around on the floor
usagePhrases.note: Often used jokingly for laughing hard or writhing in pain on the floor.
Tense/emphatic variant 떼굴떼굴 for heavier, bigger, more forceful rolling.

examples.en: The ball is rolling away.
examples.note: The base frame: 데굴데굴 + 굴러가다 for a thing rolling off.

examples.en: The ball fell off the desk and rolled away.
examples.note: Everyday object mishap; -아서 chains 'fell off' to 'rolled away'.

examples.ko: 그 개그가 너무 웃겨서 다 같이 바닥에서 데굴데굴 굴렀어요.
examples.romanization: geu gaegeuga neomu utgyeoseo da gachi badageseo deguldegul gulleosseoyo.
examples.en: That joke was so funny we all rolled on the floor laughing.
examples.note: Real-situation: the idiomatic 'ROFL' use, 바닥에서 데굴데굴 구르다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 데굴데굴 describes a round object rolling along a surface — a ball, a dropped tangerine, a marble — and by extension a person 'rolling on the floor' laughing hard or doubled over in pain (바닥에서 데굴데굴 구르다, the Korean ROFL). The defining feature is travel along the ground, which is exactly the line against 빙글빙글: 빙글빙글 spins IN PLACE (a top, a dizzy head), while 데굴데굴 always moves the object ALONG. Size matters too: for tiny things rolling — a bead, a single tear, a marble down a slope — 또르르 is the natural choice, whereas 데굴데굴 fits ball-sized objects; and the tenser 떼굴떼굴 amps up the weight/force. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja, but notice the bright ㅔ/ㅜ vowels give it a rounder, friendlier feel than its heavier cousin 떼굴떼굴. The English-speaker pitfall is using 데굴데굴 for spinning in place; if nothing travels across the floor, you want 빙글빙글, not 데굴데굴.

Confusing it with 빙글빙글 (spinning in place). 데굴데굴 always involves a round thing moving along the ground.
Using it for tiny objects. For small things like beads or marbles rolling, 또르르 is more natural; 데굴데굴 fits ball-sized objects.
Forgetting the partner verb. 데굴데굴 needs 구르다 / 굴러가다; saying 데굴데굴 alone without the rolling verb sounds incomplete.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 두리번두리번 means "looking around (searchingly)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 두리번두리번 (duribeonduribeon) = "looking around (searchingly)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 두리번두리번 둘러보다 ("to look all around") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 두리번두리번, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Core collocation: scanning the surroundings (둘러보다 = to look around).
The 거리다 form, just as common as the doubled adverb in speech and writing.
Descriptive verb form: looking this way and that.
Pairs with 주위 / 사방 (surroundings, all directions).

examples.en: I looked all around.
examples.note: The base frame: 두리번두리번 + 둘러보다.

examples.en: I looked around the cafe searching for my friend.
examples.note: Everyday searching; -느라 (busy doing X) gives the reason for scanning.

examples.ko: 처음 와 본 동네라 출구가 어디인지 두리번거리다가 결국 지나가는 분께 길을 물었어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum wa bon dongnera chulguga eodiinji duribeongeoridaga gyeolguk jinaganeun bunkke gireul mureosseoyo.
examples.en: It was my first time in the area, so I looked around for the exit and finally asked a passerby for directions.
examples.note: Real-situation: 두리번거리다 for a lost newcomer getting their bearings.

extendedVocab.nuance: 두리번두리번 captures turning your head this way and that to take in your surroundings — searching for someone, getting your bearings when lost, or wide-eyed in a new place. It implies a slightly anxious or curious, restless scanning, and the 거리다 form 두리번거리다 is every bit as common as the doubled adverb. Two contrasts pin it down. Against a single glance: one quick look is 흘끗/힐끗 보다 or 쳐다보다, whereas 두리번두리번 is repeated looking in multiple directions. Against 기웃거리다 (기웃기웃): 기웃거리다 is craning to PEEK INTO a specific spot — a shop window, someone's doorway, often a bit nosy — while 두리번두리번 is broad, all-around scanning of open space. Being native onomatopoeia there is no hanja; note that the verb pair 둘러보다 'to look around' is the neutral action and 두리번두리번 adds the vivid restless-scanning picture. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for a single directed look; reserve 두리번두리번 for head-turning in several directions.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for a single glance. One look is 흘끗/힐끗 보다 or 쳐다보다; 두리번두리번 means repeated looking in multiple directions.
Confusing it with 기웃거리다 (peeking into a place). 두리번두리번 is broad all-around scanning; 기웃거리다 is craning to peek into one spot, often nosily.
Pairing it with a fixed-stare verb like 노려보다 (to glare). 두리번두리번 implies the eyes/head keep moving, so it clashes with steady-stare verbs.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 단순하다 means "to be simple, plain, uncomplicated" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 단순하다 (dansunhada) means "to be simple, plain, uncomplicated". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 디자인이 단순해요 ("The design is simple"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단순하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: praising a clean, minimal look; 하다-adjective, so 단순하 + 여요 → 단순해요
noun-modifying form is 단순한 + N, never 단순하는
단순한 = 'mere/plain', softening the error as not deep or malicious

usagePhrases.en: Don't think about it too simply
usagePhrases.note: 단순하게 = adverb; casual 반말 warning not to oversimplify

examples.en: This app's screen is simple.
examples.note: plain statement; 단순하다 praises an uncluttered interface

examples.ko: 저는 성격이 단순한 편이라 뒤끝이 없어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun seonggyeogi dansunhan pyeonira dwikkeuchi eopseoyo.
examples.en: I have a pretty simple personality, so I don't hold grudges.
examples.note: 단순한 + 편이다 = 'on the simple side'; describes an easygoing, low-drama nature, not low intelligence

examples.en: The cause was simpler than expected, so I fixed it quickly.
examples.note: 단순해서 = 아서/어서 reason; real troubleshooting reassurance

extendedVocab.nuance: 단순(單純) literally combines 單 'single' + 純 'pure', so the core image is 'one pure thing, nothing extra'. It means simple, plain, or uncomplicated in structure or design and is normally positive or neutral. The near-synonym to keep apart is 간단하다(簡單): 간단하다 stresses that a task is quick and brief to do (간단한 점심, 간단히 설명하다), while 단순하다 stresses that a thing's makeup is plain with few parts (단순한 구조). It is a 하다-adjective, so the 요-form is 단순해요 and the modifier is 단순한. Applied to a person, 단순하다 means easygoing and uncomplicated, NOT dumb. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the English insult 'he's simple' to mean stupid: 단순한 사람 actually sounds like a refreshingly drama-free person; for 'dumb' Koreans add words and say 머리가 단순하다 or 단순무식하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Swapping 간단하다 and 단순하다 freely. 간단한 식사 (a quick, light meal) cannot become 단순한 식사 without sounding odd, because 단순하다 describes plain structure, not brevity of effort. Use 간단하다 for quick/brief, 단순하다 for plain/uncomplicated.
Saying 단순한 사람 to call someone stupid. To a Korean ear it praises an easygoing, grudge-free personality. For 'dumb' you must say 머리가 단순하다 or 단순무식하다.
Conjugating it like a verb (단순하다고 생각하는 사람 is fine, but 단순하는 구조 is wrong). As an adjective the present modifier is 단순한, never 단순하는.

usagePhrases.note: 촘촘한 + N; the teeth sit very close with tiny gaps
촘촘하게 = adverb; habitual partner of 짜다(weave/knit)

figurative: a thorough plan with no loose gaps

examples.en: The mosquito net's holes are fine.
examples.note: plain description; tiny, evenly spaced gaps

examples.en: This knit is densely woven, so it's warm.
examples.note: 촘촘하게 짜이다 = passive 'to be woven tightly'; classic clothing comment

examples.ko: 계획을 너무 촘촘하게 세웠더니 쉴 틈이 없었어요.
examples.romanization: gyehoegeul neomu chomchomhage sewotdeoni swil teumi eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: I planned things so tightly that there was no room to rest.
examples.note: figurative; -았더니 reports the consequence of an over-detailed plan

extendedVocab.nuance: 촘촘하다 is a native Korean (고유어) word, often felt as the doubled 촘촘 'close-close', describing units packed very near each other with tiny, EVEN gaps: comb teeth, mesh, knit stitches, dotted print, or a finely detailed plan. Its tone is usually positive, carrying a sense of fineness and thoroughness. The synonym to contrast is 빽빽하다: 빽빽하다 stresses crowded fullness with no room to breathe and is often slightly negative (빽빽한 지하철), whereas 촘촘하다 stresses small regular spacing and craftsmanship (촘촘한 그물). The opposite is 성기다 / 듬성듬성하다 (sparse, gappy). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'dense' and landing on 빽빽하다 for everything: a fine-toothed comb or tightly knit fabric is 촘촘하다, not 빽빽하다, and big things crammed together (a packed train) are 빽빽하다, not 촘촘하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 촘촘하다 for large objects crowded together, e.g. 사람이 촘촘하다 for a packed crowd. People packed in are 빽빽하다; 촘촘하다 fits small repeated units like teeth, threads, stitches, dots.
Treating 촘촘하다 and 빽빽하다 as identical. 촘촘하다 = fine, even, often praised spacing; 빽빽하다 = crammed with no room, often a complaint. A tightly knit sweater is 촘촘한 니트, not 빽빽한 니트.
Pairing it with the wrong verb. The natural collocation is 촘촘하게 짜다/심다 (weave/plant densely); 촘촘하게 많다 is unnatural.

extendedVocab.explanation: 헐렁하다 (heolleonghada) = "to be loose, baggy, slack (clothing/fit)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 바지가 헐렁해요 ("The pants are baggy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 헐렁하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the fit is too loose around the body
헐렁한 + N; can be an intentional oversized style
헐렁하게 = adverb; a deliberate relaxed styling choice
non-clothing use for a fitting that has worked loose

examples.en: This T-shirt is a bit loose.
examples.note: plain fit comment while trying clothes on

examples.en: I lost weight, so my jeans got baggy.
examples.note: 헐렁해지다 = 'became loose'; -아지다 marks the change of state, not a permanent trait

examples.ko: 문고리가 헐렁해서 곧 빠질 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: mungoriga heolleonghaeseo got ppajil geot gatayo.
examples.en: The door handle is loose, so it looks like it'll fall off soon.
examples.note: 헐렁해서 = reason; shows the hardware sense beyond clothes

extendedVocab.nuance: 헐렁하다 is a native Korean word for loose, baggy, or slack — mainly clothes that hang away from the body, but also screws, handles, or fittings that have lost their grip. It is the opposite of 꽉 끼다 (skin-tight) and 빡빡하다 (stiff/resistant). The synonym worth separating is 넉넉하다: 넉넉한 옷 is pleasantly roomy with comfortable margin (a compliment), while 헐렁한 옷 leans toward too-loose, sloppy, or oversized. Figuratively 헐렁하다 can paint a person as lax and careless (성격이 헐렁하다 = laid-back to the point of unreliable). The big English-speaker pitfall is using 넓다 for loose clothing because English 'wide/loose' blur together: 넓다 means wide in AREA (a wide road, a wide room), so 바지가 넓다 sounds like the trousers cover a large floor area; loose FIT is 헐렁하다. Also remember 헐렁해지다 for 'became loose' — bare 헐렁했다 implies it was always baggy.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 넓다 for loose clothes (바지가 넓어요). 넓다 = wide in area; loose in fit = 헐렁하다. A baggy shirt is 헐렁한 셔츠, never 넓은 셔츠.
Dropping the change-of-state -아지다. Saying 청바지가 헐렁했다 to mean 'got loose' actually reads as 'the jeans were (always) baggy'; for 'became baggy' you need 헐렁해졌다.
Treating 헐렁하다 as a pure compliment. For a flattering 'nicely roomy' fit, Koreans prefer 넉넉하다; 헐렁하다 often implies it's looser than ideal.

extendedVocab.english: to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빡빡하다 means "to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 빡빡하다 (ppakppakada) means "to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일정이 빡빡해요 ("The schedule is tight"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 빡빡하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the most common figurative use: no spare time

usagePhrases.en: the door is stiff (hard to open)
usagePhrases.note: physical resistance when you push or slide it
빡빡한 + N; back-to-back with no breaks
barely enough money to cover everything

examples.en: The drawer is stiff, so it doesn't open well.
examples.note: physical sense; 빡빡해서 = reason for the resistance

examples.en: I have lots of meetings today, so my schedule is packed.
examples.note: the everyday office use; 일정이 빡빡하다 is a fixed collocation

examples.en: After paying rent, my living budget is tight.
examples.note: money sense; -고 나면 = 'once I've done'; very relatable for residents

extendedVocab.nuance: 빡빡하다 is a colloquial native word built on the tense, forceful sound 빡, and it splits into two everyday senses: physically tight and stiff (a drawer, screw, or door that RESISTS moving) and figuratively tight (a packed schedule or a barely-sufficient budget). In both, the core image is zero slack, no breathing room. The synonym to separate is 빠듯하다: 빠듯하다 leans on 'only just enough, cutting it close' (시간이 빠듯하다 = we'll barely make it), while 빡빡하다 adds a feeling of pressure, stiffness, and friction. Don't confuse it with the slang 빡세다, which means an activity is physically or mentally grueling/hardcore (운동이 빡세다), not 'tightly packed'. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'tight schedule' onto 좁다: 좁다 is narrow in physical SPACE (a narrow alley), so 일정이 좁다 is wrong; a tight schedule is 일정이 빡빡하다. Likewise a tight budget is 예산이 빡빡하다, not 예산이 좁다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 좁다 for a tight schedule or budget (일정이 좁아요 / 예산이 좁아요). 좁다 = narrow in space; tight in time/money = 빡빡하다 (or 빠듯하다).
Mixing up 빡빡하다 and 빡세다. 빡세다 (slang) = grueling/hardcore (알바가 빡세다); 빡빡하다 = tight with no slack (스케줄이 빡빡하다). They are not interchangeable.
Overusing it in very formal writing. 빡빡하다 is casual-to-neutral spoken Korean; in a stiff report you might prefer 빠듯하다 or 여유가 없다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매끄럽다 means "to be smooth, sleek, slick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be smooth, sleek, slick" is 매끄럽다 (maekkeureopda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 피부가 매끄러워요 ("The skin is smooth"). Watch the particle attached to 매끄럽다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular: 매끄럽 + 어요 → 매끄러워요
매끄러운 + N; ㅂ → 우 before the modifier 운
figurative: deal with something without friction or conflict
of an event or process running without hitches

examples.en: This paper has a smooth surface.
examples.note: plain touch description; note 매끄러워요, not 매끄럽어요

examples.en: After I put on lotion, my skin became smooth.
examples.note: 매끄러워지다 = change of state, still ㅂ-irregular; -았더니 reports the result

examples.en: I'm relieved the presentation ended smoothly.
examples.note: figurative: a polished, hitch-free flow; 매끄럽게 = adverb

extendedVocab.nuance: 매끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the ㅂ becomes 우/워, giving 매끄러워요, 매끄러운, 매끄러우니까, 매끄러워서 — memorize the 요-form 매끄러워요 and the rest follows. It means smooth and frictionless to the touch (skin, paper, fabric, a polished floor) and figuratively a process or speech that flows without awkward bumps. The crucial synonym contrast is 미끄럽다: both come from the same 'slip' family, but 매끄럽다 is the pleasant, sleek 'smooth to the touch' (a compliment for skin), while 미끄럽다 is the dangerous 'slippery, slip-prone' (a warning about a wet floor). Saying the bathroom floor is 매끄러워요 sounds like you admire its sleek finish; to warn someone they might slip you must say 미끄러워요. The English-speaker pitfall is the regular conjugation 매끄럽어요 — wrong; it must be 매끄러워요, because all ㅂ-irregular adjectives like 춥다→추워요 and 무겁다→무거워요 behave this way.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 매끄럽어요 / 매끄럽은. As a ㅂ-irregular it is 매끄러워요 and 매끄러운, exactly like 춥다 → 추워요 → 추운.
Confusing 매끄럽다 with 미끄럽다. 매끄럽다 = sleek/smooth to the touch (good); 미끄럽다 = slippery/slip-prone (danger). For 'careful, it's slippery' say 미끄러워요, not 매끄러워요.
Using it only for physical surfaces. 매끄럽다 also describes a smooth process or delivery — 일을 매끄럽게 처리하다, 발표가 매끄럽다.

extendedVocab.explanation: 거칠다 (geochilda) = "to be rough, coarse; (manner) harsh". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 손이 거칠어요 ("The hands are rough") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ㄹ-stem: 거칠 + 어요 → 거칠어요 (ㄹ kept before 어)
거친 + N; the ㄹ DROPS before ㄴ → 거친, not 거칠은

usagePhrases.en: the way of speaking is harsh
usagePhrases.note: figurative: blunt, rough manner of speech
거칠어지다 = change of state from smooth to rough

examples.en: This towel is a bit coarse.
examples.note: plain texture comment; not soft against the skin

examples.ko: 겨울이라 손이 거칠어져서 핸드크림을 자주 발라요.
examples.romanization: gyeourira soni geochireojyeoseo haendeukeurimeul jaju ballayo.
examples.en: It's winter, so my hands get rough and I use hand cream often.
examples.note: 거칠어지다 = becomes rough; -아서/어서 chains the reason

examples.ko: 그 사람은 말투가 거칠지만 마음은 따뜻해요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun maltuga geochiljiman maeumeun ttatteutaeyo.
examples.en: That person speaks harshly, but has a warm heart.
examples.note: figurative; -지만 contrasts the rough manner with the kind nature

extendedVocab.nuance: 거칠다 is a native ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) adjective meaning rough or coarse to the touch (skin, towels, unfinished surfaces) and, figuratively, harsh or rough in manner (말투가 거칠다, 운전이 거칠다, 숨이 거칠다). It is the antonym of 매끄럽다 and 부드럽다. The synonym to contrast is 까칠하다: 까칠하다 is a smaller, prickly roughness — slightly stubbly skin, OR a person who is touchy and prickly in temperament (성격이 까칠하다) — whereas 거칠다 is broader and rougher, covering coarse texture and genuinely harsh, wild behavior. The grammar pitfall English speakers hit is the ㄹ-stem rule: the ㄹ DROPS before ㄴ, so the present modifier is 거친 손, never 거칠은 손; but it STAYS before 어, giving 거칠어요. A second pitfall is limiting it to texture — in English 'rough' splits into many words, but 거칠다 naturally also covers harsh speech and aggressive, reckless driving (난폭운전).

Writing the modifier as 거칠은 (e.g. 거칠은 손). As a ㄹ-stem the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, so it must be 거친 손, like 길다 → 긴, 멀다 → 먼.
Limiting 거칠다 to physical texture. It also describes harsh speech (말투가 거칠다) and rough/aggressive driving (운전이 거칠다); ignoring these misses common usage.
Confusing 거칠다 with 까칠하다 for personality. 까칠하다 = touchy, prickly, hard to please; 거칠다 = harsh, wild, rough-mannered. They paint different characters.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 끈적하다 means "to be sticky, tacky, gooey" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 끈적하다 (kkeunjeokada) means "to be sticky, tacky, gooey". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 손이 끈적해요 ("My hands are sticky"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 끈적하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: typically after touching something sugary or sweaty
끈적한 + N; tacky residue underfoot
끈적하게 = adverb; partner of 남다(remain)
humid, clammy summer air clinging to the skin

examples.en: I spilled a drink, so the table is sticky.
examples.note: everyday cleanup scene; 끈적해서 also works for the reason

examples.en: In summer it's humid, so my body feels sticky.
examples.note: 끈적하다 for sweaty, clammy skin — a core Korean-summer word

examples.ko: 이 로션은 발라도 안 끈적해서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i rosyeoneun ballado an kkeunjeokaeseo joayo.
examples.en: This lotion isn't sticky even after applying, so it's nice.
examples.note: -아도 = 'even if'; a standard cosmetic-review point

extendedVocab.nuance: 끈적하다 (and its lively variants 끈적거리다, 끈적이다, 끈적끈적하다) is a native word for a sticky, tacky, clinging feel: spilled drinks drying on a table, sweat on a humid day, gooey residue, or honey on the fingers. For Korea's muggy summers it perfectly captures clammy skin and 끈적한 날씨. The doubled 끈적끈적하다 amps up to a heavier, syrupy stickiness. The key synonym contrast is with 미끄럽다 (slippery): they are near-opposites in physics — 끈적하다 GRIPS and clings so things stick together, while 미끄럽다 is frictionless so things slide apart. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing texture with taste: English 'sweet and sticky' bundles them, but in Korean 끈적하다 is purely the sticky TEXTURE, and 달다 is the sweet TASTE — a honey-coated table is 끈적하다, the honey itself is 달다. Figuratively 끈적한 시선/관계 can also mean an uncomfortably clingy gaze or relationship.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 끈적하다 with 미끄럽다. 끈적하다 clings and grips (sticky honey); 미끄럽다 slides away (slippery ice). They describe opposite surface behavior.
Using 달다 (sweet) when you mean the sticky feel. Texture = 끈적하다; taste = 달다. Don't say 이 바닥이 달아요 for a sticky floor.
Forgetting the colloquial -거리다/-이다 forms. In speech Koreans often say 손이 끈적거려요 / 끈적여요 for an ongoing sticky sensation; sticking only to 끈적하다 sounds a little flat.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빽빽하다 is a native word, felt through the tight, stuffed sound 빽, meaning crammed full with almost no gaps: a packed subway, a dense forest, lines of tiny text squeezed onto a page. Its emphasis is crowdedness and lack of room, and it often carries a slightly oppressive, uncomfortable tone. Contrast it carefully with 촘촘하다 and 복잡하다. Versus 촘촘하다: 촘촘하다 admires fine, even, deliberate spacing (a finely woven net), while 빽빽하다 just stresses 'stuffed full, no space' (a forest you can't walk through). Versus 복잡하다(複雜): 복잡하다 means complicated or chaotically busy in arrangement (복잡한 절차, 복잡한 길), whereas 빽빽하다 is specifically about physical density. The opposite is 한산하다 (deserted, sparse) or 듬성듬성하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using bare 많다 for a crowd: 사람이 많다 just says 'there are many people', while 빽빽하다 adds the crucial nuance of being packed in with no breathing space.

Confusing 빽빽하다 with 복잡하다. 복잡하다 = complicated/chaotic (복잡한 신청 절차); 빽빽하다 = physically densely packed (사람이 빽빽한 지하철). A crowded train is 빽빽하다; a confusing procedure is 복잡하다.
Using 많다 alone where you need density. 사람이 많아요 = 'there are lots of people'; for 'packed tight with no room' add 빽빽해요.
Applying 빽빽하다 to fine even spacing. A tightly knit fabric or fine-toothed comb is 촘촘하다; 빽빽하다 is for crowded fullness, not delicate spacing.

extendedVocab.english: to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 널찍하다 means "to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 널찍하다 (neoljjikada) = "to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방이 널찍해요 ("The room is spacious") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 널찍하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: pleasantly roomy, with a positive feel
널찍한 + N; sounds inviting and comfortable

usagePhrases.en: to settle into a roomy spot
usagePhrases.note: 널찍하게 = adverb; spreading out comfortably
easy to park because there's plenty of space

examples.en: This cafe has roomy seating.
examples.note: plain praise; a popular cafe-hunting criterion in Korea

examples.en: For a studio, the bathroom is quite spacious.
examples.note: N치고 = 'considering it's a ~'; a house-hunting compliment

examples.ko: 거실이 널찍해서 가구를 더 놓을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: geosiri neoljjikaeseo gagureul deo noeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: The living room is roomy, so I can fit more furniture.
examples.note: 널찍해서 = reason; -을 수 있다 shows the practical payoff

extendedVocab.nuance: 널찍하다 is a native word derived from 넓다 (wide) plus the suffix -찍하다, which adds a warm, satisfied 'pleasantly so' nuance — so it means not just wide but comfortably, generously roomy, almost always a compliment. The synonym to keep distinct is plain 넓다: 넓다 is the neutral, measurable 'wide/large in area' (운동장이 넓다), while 널찍하다 layers on the feeling that the space is enjoyably spacious and comfortable. You'd use 널찍하다 when house- or seat-hunting to say a place feels nice and open, not merely big. Its direct opposite is 비좁다 (cramped). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 넓다 for everything because English 'spacious' and 'wide' overlap: if you want the cozy, appreciative 'nice and roomy', 널찍하다 carries it, whereas 넓다 can sound flatly factual. Watch the spelling too — it is 널찍하다, not the common misspelling 넓직하다, even though it comes from 넓다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using plain 넓다 when you want the warm 'pleasantly roomy' nuance. 방이 넓어요 just states it's large; 방이 널찍해요 conveys it feels comfortably spacious — a nicer compliment when viewing a place.
Misspelling it as 넓직하다 because it derives from 넓다. The standard spelling is 널찍하다 (the ㄼ is not written out).
Applying it to abstract bigness. 널찍하다 is for physical, walk-around space (rooms, lots, seating); for a wide range of options or broad knowledge you'd use 넓다 (선택의 폭이 넓다), not 널찍하다.

extendedVocab.english: to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비좁다 means "to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 비좁다 (bijopda) means "to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 방이 비좁아요 ("The room is cramped"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 비좁다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: feels too small for what it's used for
비좁은 + N; barely room to pass
비좁게 = adverb; squeezed into too little space
uncomfortably tight, e.g. on a bus or plane

examples.en: The elevator is cramped.
examples.note: plain complaint; everyday apartment-building scene

examples.en: I have a lot of stuff, so the studio feels really cramped.
examples.note: 비좁다 stresses 'uncomfortably tight', stronger than plain 좁다

examples.en: The restaurant was so cramped I bumped into the person next to me.
examples.note: 비좁아서 = reason; concrete tight-space frustration

extendedVocab.nuance: 비좁다 is a native word: the intensifying prefix 비- attaches to 좁다 (narrow) and pushes it to 'so narrow it's uncomfortable', i.e. cramped. It is stronger and more clearly negative than plain 좁다, which can be a neutral statement of size (좁은 방 = a small room). Use 비좁다 for rooms stuffed with belongings, packed elevators, tight restaurant tables, or cramped seats. It is the direct antonym of 널찍하다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold. First, treating 비좁다 and 좁다 as identical: 좁다 just says 'narrow/small', while 비좁다 adds 'too tight for comfort', so a tiny but tidy room can be 좁다 yet only an over-stuffed, uncomfortable one is really 비좁다. Second, borrowing the English metaphor 'narrow-minded' onto this word: a narrow-minded person is 속이 좁다 / 마음이 좁다, never 비좁다 — 비좁다 is strictly about physical space.

Treating 비좁다 as identical to 좁다. 좁다 = narrow/small (can be neutral); 비좁다 = cramped, too tight to be comfortable. A cozy small room is 좁다; a suffocatingly packed one is 비좁다.
Using 비좁다 for a person being narrow-minded. That sense is 속이 좁다 or 마음이 좁다; 비좁다 only describes physical space.
Applying it to a narrow long shape that isn't uncomfortable. A slim margin or thin strip is 좁다; reserve 비좁다 for spaces that feel oppressively tight to be in.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 푹신하다 means "to be soft, fluffy, cushiony" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be soft, fluffy, cushiony" is 푹신하다 (puksinhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 침대가 푹신해요 ("The bed is soft/cushiony"). Watch the particle attached to 푹신하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: comfortable to sink into with a springy give
푹신한 + N; soft and inviting to sit on
doubled form intensifies to extra-soft and bouncy
soft sole that absorbs impact when walking

examples.en: The hotel pillow is fluffy.
examples.note: plain comfort comment; soft with pleasant give

examples.ko: 이 운동화는 밑창이 푹신해서 발이 편해요.
examples.romanization: i undonghwaneun mitchangi puksinhaeseo bari pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: These sneakers have a cushiony sole, so my feet are comfortable.
examples.note: 밑창(sole) + 푹신하다; -아서 chains the reason — a common shoe-shopping line

examples.ko: 새로 산 매트리스가 너무 푹신해서 허리가 좀 아파요.
examples.romanization: saero san maeteuriseuga neomu puksinhaeseo heoriga jom apayo.
examples.en: The new mattress is too soft, so my back hurts a bit.
examples.note: 너무 푹신하다 shows over-softness can be a downside, not always praise

extendedVocab.nuance: 푹신하다 (often doubled to 푹신푹신하다 for emphasis) is a native word built on the soft, sinking sound 푹, describing a soft, springy, cushiony feel with pleasant GIVE when you press it: beds, sofas, pillows, thick cushions, padded shoe soles, fluffy bread. Its opposite is 딱딱하다 (hard/firm). The synonym to separate is 부드럽다: 부드럽다 is smooth and gentle to the touch — about surface softness (부드러운 천, 부드러운 머릿결) — whereas 푹신하다 is about volumetric springiness, how something cushions and bounces back when compressed. A silk scarf is 부드럽다 (smooth) but not 푹신하다; a marshmallow pillow is both. For Koreans shopping for furniture, bedding, or shoes, 푹신하다 is a go-to comfort word. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'soft = always good': a mattress described as 너무 푹신하다 (too soft) is a complaint, because excessive softness lacks support and can hurt your back — Koreans often prefer something 적당히 단단한 (moderately firm).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 푹신하다 with 부드럽다. 부드럽다 = smooth/gentle to the touch (a soft fabric, smooth hair); 푹신하다 = springy and cushiony with give (a plush sofa). A smooth-but-firm leather seat is 부드럽다, not 푹신하다.
Assuming 푹신하다 is always positive. 너무 푹신한 매트리스 is a criticism — too soft, no support, sore back. Context decides whether it's praise.
Using it for a flat, firm surface. A thin yoga mat or hardwood floor is not 푹신하다; the word needs noticeable cushioning and bounce-back.

extendedVocab.english: to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 눅눅하다 means "to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 눅눅하다 (nungnukada) = "to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과자가 눅눅해요 ("The snack has gone soggy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 눅눅하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: lost its crispness after absorbing humidity
눅눅한 + N; not fully dried, still clammy
humid, clammy air that clings
눅눅해지다 = change of state from crisp/dry to damp

examples.en: The crackers have gone soggy.
examples.note: plain statement; the crunch is gone

examples.en: I didn't seal the snack bag, so it went soggy.
examples.note: 눅눅해지다 = 'became soggy'; -아서 chains the cause

examples.ko: 장마철엔 빨래가 눅눅해서 잘 안 말라요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren ppallaega nungnukaeseo jal an mallayo.
examples.en: During the rainy season, laundry stays damp and won't dry well.
examples.note: 장마철 context; 눅눅해서 = reason — a classic Korean monsoon problem

extendedVocab.nuance: 눅눅하다 is a native word for things that have absorbed moisture and turned damp, soggy, or limp: crackers and seaweed (김) that lost their crunch, laundry that stubbornly won't dry, a humid basement room, a 장마철 (rainy-season) apartment. It is essential vocabulary for Korea's sticky summers. Its opposite is the crisp/dry 바삭하다 (crispy) for food and 보송보송하다 (dry and fluffy) for textiles. The synonym English speakers most often confuse it with is 축축하다: 축축하다 is actively WET to the touch — there is visible or palpable water, like a wet towel or rain-soaked socks — whereas 눅눅하다 is the subtler, stale 'humidity-soaked, limp, no longer crisp' state where nothing is dripping but everything feels clammy and soft. A second pitfall is reaching for 젖다 (to get wet): soggy-from-humidity crackers are 눅눅해졌다, not 젖었다, because 젖다 implies they got splashed or soaked in liquid, not slowly softened by moist air.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 눅눅하다 with 축축하다. 축축하다 = wet/moist to the touch (a wet towel, damp socks); 눅눅하다 = damp-soggy and stale from humidity (limp crackers, a muggy room). Nothing drips when it's merely 눅눅하다.
Using 젖다 for soggy snacks. 젖다 = to get wet/soaked in liquid; humidity-softened food is 눅눅해지다, not 젖다. 과자가 젖었어요 sounds like water spilled on it.
Applying 눅눅하다 to pleasant softness. It is negative — limp, stale, clammy. A nice springy pillow is 푹신하다, never 눅눅하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 볼펜 means "ballpoint pen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 볼펜 (bolpen) means "ballpoint pen". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 볼펜 좀 빌려주세요 ("Lend me a pen, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 볼펜 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday request at a desk or counter; 좀 softens it into a polite favor

usagePhrases.en: Please write with a black pen
usagePhrases.note: Banks and offices often require 검은색 (black); 으로 marks the pen as the tool you write with
안 나오다 (won't come out) is THE idiom for a dead pen — the ink won't flow
Casual workplace ask; in speech Koreans drop the 이/가 subject marker after 볼펜

examples.en: Can I just borrow one pen?
examples.note: Simplest favor; 하나만 = just one, -아/어도 돼요? asks permission gently

examples.en: You can sign the document with a pen.
examples.note: Everyday bank/office line; -으면 됩니다 = 'it's fine if you ~', a soft instruction

examples.ko: 회의 때 쓸 볼펜이 한 자루도 없네요.
examples.romanization: hoeui ttae sseul bolpeni han jarudo eopsneyo.
examples.en: There isn't a single pen to use in the meeting.
examples.note: Real frustration; 자루 counts pens, and 한 자루도 없다 = not even one

extendedVocab.nuance: 볼펜 is a loanword shortened from English 'ball pen' and means specifically a ballpoint, the cheap everyday pen, whereas plain 펜 is the umbrella word for any pen and would also cover a 만년필 (fountain pen) or 사인펜 (felt-tip marker). Koreans default to 볼펜 for ordinary office pens and only switch to those other words when the type matters. The near-synonym 사인펜 is NOT a 'sign pen' for signing — it is a felt-tip; you sign with a 볼펜. Pair 볼펜 with 으로 to mean 'with a pen' (볼펜으로 쓰다), count it with the writing-implement counter 자루, and remember the English-speaker trap: a dead pen is 볼펜이 안 나와요 (the ink won't come out), not the literal 안 써져요, which sounds slightly off to natives.

Calling a felt-tip 사인펜 a signing pen by false-friend logic — 사인펜 is a marker; you actually sign with a 볼펜
Counting pens with the generic 개 in writing; the natural counter is 자루, as in 볼펜 한 자루

usagePhrases.note: 적어 두다 = write it down and keep it; the go-to phrase for taking a note for later

usagePhrases.en: Can you show me your notes?
usagePhrases.note: 필기 = handwritten class/meeting notes; -ㄹ래? is a casual peer request
권 is the book counter and the natural one for a bound notebook

extendedVocab.nuance: 노트 is a loanword from English 'note(book)' but in Korean it means the physical bound pad you write in, NOT an abstract 'note' or 'memo' (that idea is 메모). The dangerous near-homophone is 노트북, which to a Korean ear means a laptop computer 100% of the time, never a paper notebook — so the single syllable 북 completely changes the object. extendedVocab.nuance: 가위 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) and, crucially for English speakers, it is grammatically singular — Korean has no 'a pair of scissors' construction, so 가위 하나 / 가위 한 개 already means one whole pair, and you never pluralize it. (The very same word 가위 also names the folk 'sleep paralysis' demon in 가위에 눌리다, but as a stationery item it is simply scissors.) The big idiom trap is sharpness: Koreans say the blades 잘 들다 (cut well) or 안 들다 / 무디다 (don't cut / are dull), and they do NOT use the literal 날카롭다 ('sharp-edged') or 'not sharp' to mean a dull pair — 가위가 안 들어요 is how you complain. Pair it with 자르다 (cut) or the action noun 가위질 (가위 + the activity suffix 질, as in 걸레질, 부채질), and note the passive 잘리다 (종이가 잘 안 잘려요 = the paper won't cut).

extendedVocab.nuance: 메모지 is a hybrid: 메모 (a loanword from English 'memo') + 지 (紙, 'paper'), literally 'memo paper' — a small pad or loose sheets for quick jottings. extendedVocab.nuance: 미리 means doing something ahead of the relevant moment so you're ready when it arrives — its whole focus is the timing being early relative to a deadline or event. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing it with 우선 / 먼저 / 일단: 먼저 and 우선 mean 'first in a sequence or in priority' (do A before B), while 미리 means 'before the due time' (do it now so it's done early). 'I paid first' = 먼저 냈어요 (before others), but 'I paid in advance' = 미리 냈어요 (before the due date) — different ideas entirely. 미리 is native Korean, not Sino-Korean, and it glues onto preparation verbs: 미리 예약하다, 미리 준비하다, 미리 확인하다, 미리 알리다. Register is neutral and works in both polite and casual speech. Note the affectionate doubled 미리미리, which nags 'do it good and early.'

Using 미리 for 'firstly in a sequence': 미리 이거부터 해요 is odd; for ordering steps you want 우선/먼저 이거부터 해요. 미리 only means 'ahead of the due time.'
Dropping it where the early timing is the point: 예약했어요 alone just says 'I booked'; 미리 예약했어요 adds the crucial 'ahead of time' nuance.
Saying 미리 전에 (advance + before) as a redundant pair under the influence of English 'beforehand in advance'; 미리 already contains 'before,' so just 미리 준비했어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 우선 (優先, 優 'superior' + 先 'first') literally means 'take precedence,' so it marks what should come before everything else in importance, not merely in time. Compare 먼저 vs 우선: 먼저 is neutral sequence ('I'll go first / do this first'), while 우선 adds the flavor of priority and deliberate ranking ('first and foremost, before anything else'). Compare 우선 vs 일단: 일단 is 'for now, provisionally, then we'll see,' whereas 우선 ranks by importance. Compare 우선 vs 미리: 미리 is 'ahead of the deadline,' a totally different axis. The Sino-Korean root surfaces everywhere in daily life — 우선순위 (priority), 최우선 (top priority), 우선적으로 (preferentially) — so learning 우선 unlocks a whole word family. It pairs habitually with -부터 to pin the starting point. Register is neutral-to-formal and very common in workplace speech.

Forgetting 우선 strongly prefers -부터: bare 우선 이거 해요 is weaker than the natural 우선 이거부터 해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 일단 means "for now, first (before deciding the rest), once" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 일단 (ildan) = "for now, first (before deciding the rest), once". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 일단 ~하고 보다 ("just do ~ first and see") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: The signature pattern; 일단 해 보고 결정하자 = let's just try it and then decide
일단 밥부터 먹자 = let's just eat first, sort the rest out later
Tentative acknowledgment that leaves room to revisit
일단 시작하면 = once you actually get started

examples.en: Let's just sit down first and talk.
examples.note: Simple: 일단 settling one immediate step before the discussion

examples.ko: 고민은 나중에 하고 일단 신청서부터 내요.
examples.romanization: gomineun najunge hago ildan sincheongseobuteo naeyo.
examples.en: Worry about it later; for now, just submit the application first.
examples.note: Everyday: 일단 deferring the deciding while taking one provisional action

examples.ko: 집은 일단 계약했는데 이사 날짜는 아직 안 정했어요.
examples.romanization: jibeun ildan gyeyakaenneunde isa naljjaneun ajik an jeonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: I went ahead and signed for the place for now, but haven't set the move date yet.
examples.note: Real situation: 일단 = one thing settled provisionally while the rest stays open

extendedVocab.nuance: 일단 (一旦, 一 'one' + 旦 'daybreak/moment') means 'for the moment, as a first provisional move' — you commit to one step now and leave the rest to be sorted out later. The defining flavor is tentativeness, which is the sharp line against 우선 and 미리. 우선 ranks by importance ('this matters most, do it first'); 일단 just says 'let's do something for now and see' with no claim about priority. 미리 means 'ahead of the deadline'; 일단 has nothing to do with deadlines. Its signature construction is 일단 ~하고 보자 / ~하고 보다 ('just do X first and see how it goes'), pure spoken Korean for deferring decisions. A second sense is conditional 'once': 일단 시작하면 끝까지 해야죠 ('once you start, you should finish'). Register is casual-to-neutral and extremely high-frequency in everyday speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating it exactly with 우선: 일단 leans 'provisionally, for now,' while 우선 stresses priority/importance. 일단 해 보자 ≠ 우선 해 보자 in feel.
Expecting it to mean 'in advance': that nuance belongs to 미리, never 일단.
Missing the 'once' sense and over-translating: 일단 도착하면 연락해 means 'once you arrive, contact me,' not 'for now arrive.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 곧 means "soon, shortly, before long" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 곧 (got) means "soon, shortly, before long". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 곧 도착하다 ("to arrive soon"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 곧 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Classic 'on my way' text; 곧 도착해요 = I'll be there shortly
Announcing an event about to begin; 공연이 곧 시작합니다

usagePhrases.en: to end soon / be over shortly
usagePhrases.note: Reassurance; 거의 다 했어요, 곧 끝나요
Set adverb (esp. broadcasts/announcements): 곧이어 다음 순서입니다

examples.en: Spring is coming soon.
examples.note: Simple: 곧 + a near-future event, forward-looking only

examples.ko: 거의 다 왔어요, 곧 도착하니까 조금만 기다려요.
examples.romanization: geoui da wasseoyo, got dochakanikka jogeumman gidaryeoyo.
examples.en: I'm almost there; I'll arrive soon, so wait just a bit.
examples.note: Everyday: 곧 + 도착하다, the most relatable 'almost there' message

examples.ko: 탑승을 곧 시작하겠습니다. 잠시만 기다려 주십시오.
examples.romanization: tapseungeul got sijakagetseumnida. jamsiman gidaryeo jusipsio.
examples.en: Boarding will begin shortly. Please wait a moment.
examples.note: Real situation: 곧 in a formal announcement register at the airport/station

extendedVocab.nuance: 곧 means 'soon,' signaling that something will happen within a short time from the present. It strictly looks forward — 곧 can never describe the past. The key contrast is 곧 vs 금방: 금방 ('in a jiffy') is very casual and works both ways in time (it can even mean 'a moment ago' as in 금방 왔어요), while 곧 is cleaner, slightly more written/formal, and future-only, which is why station and airport announcements favor 곧. A second native-speaker pitfall is mixing 곧 (soon) with 이따가 (later today): 곧 means 'very shortly from now,' whereas 이따가 means 'later on, after some hours' — 곧 갈게요 ('I'm coming right away') is very different from 이따가 갈게요 ('I'll come by later'). 곧 is native Korean. The fixed compound 곧이어 ('coming up next') is worth memorizing as a unit.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 곧 for the recent past ('a moment ago'): that is 방금 / 금방, while 곧 is strictly future. 곧 도착했어요 is wrong; say 방금 도착했어요.
Confusing 곧 (soon) with 곳 (place): they look and sound similar but are unrelated — 곧 = soon, 곳 = a place/spot.
Swapping 곧 and 이따가: 곧 = right away/shortly; 이따가 = later (in a few hours). Don't say 곧 만나요 when you mean 'see you later today.'

extendedVocab.english: already (it's done and can't be changed)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이미 means "already (it's done and can't be changed)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "already (it's done and can't be changed)" is 이미 (imi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이미 끝나다 ("to be already over"). Watch the particle attached to 이미 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: States a finished, irreversible fact; 이미 끝난 일이에요 = it's a done deal
이미 늦었어요 = there's no point now, the moment has passed
이미 알고 있었어요 = I knew it beforehand, this is no news
이미 결정된 상태예요 = it's already (been) decided, fixed now

examples.en: I've already seen that movie.
examples.note: Simple: 이미 + completed action, a settled fact

examples.ko: 전화했을 때는 이미 가게가 문을 닫았더라고요.
examples.romanization: jeonhwahaesseul ttaeneun imi gagega muneul dadatdeoragoyo.
examples.en: By the time I called, the store had already closed.
examples.note: Everyday: 이미 with -더라고요 for a past-perfect 'it was already done' realization

examples.ko: 환불하려고 했는데 이미 배송이 시작돼서 취소가 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: hwanbulharyeogo haenneunde imi baesongi sijakdwaeseo chwisoga an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I tried to get a refund, but shipping had already started, so I couldn't cancel.
examples.note: Real situation: 이미 marking an irreversible point in a process

extendedVocab.nuance: 이미 means 'already,' emphasizing that an action or state is completed and now fixed — often colored by 'and there's no changing it now.' The sharp contrast every learner needs is 이미 vs 벌써. Both translate as 'already,' but 이미 is neutral and factual ('it is already done, that's just the situation'), while 벌써 adds emotional surprise that it happened so fast or so soon ('already?! that quick?'). 이미 끝났어요 = a calm statement of fact; 벌써 끝났어요?! = 'it's over already?!' with raised eyebrows. So choose 이미 when calmly noting that the moment/deadline has passed, and 벌써 when reacting to unexpected speed. 이미 is native Korean and is also future-blind: it only describes things already done, never things about to happen. It pairs naturally with completed clauses and with -더라고요, -았/었- past forms.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it freely with 벌써: 이미 is neutral about timing, while 벌써 carries 'so soon?!' surprise. Use 이미 for a flat fact, 벌써 for astonishment.
Using it for the future: 이미 only describes things already done. 'It'll already be finished by then' needs a future-perfect feel like 그때면 끝나 있을 거예요, not 이미 + future.
Forcing English word order: in English 'already' floats around, but Korean 이미 sits before the verb/predicate it modifies — 이미 다 먹었어요, not 다 먹었어요 이미.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아까 means "a little while ago, earlier (today)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 아까 (akka) = "a little while ago, earlier (today)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아까 말하다 ("to have said earlier") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아까, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 아까 말했잖아요 = I told you earlier (mild reminder)
아까부터 기다렸어요 = I've been waiting since earlier
아까 그 사람 = that person from before; refers back within today

usagePhrases.en: earlier in the day / this morning
usagePhrases.note: Pins 아까 to a rough part of today

examples.en: I ate a little while ago.
examples.note: Simple: 아까 placing an action in the recent past today

examples.ko: 아까 충전해 놨는데 벌써 배터리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: akka chungjeonhae nwanneunde beolsseo baeteoriga eopseoyo.
examples.en: I charged it earlier, but the battery's already dead.
examples.note: Everyday: 아까 contrasting an earlier action with the present state

examples.ko: 아까 회의 때 말씀하신 거 다시 한 번 설명해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: akka hoeui ttae malsseumhasin geo dasi han beon seolmyeonghae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you explain again what you mentioned earlier in the meeting?
examples.note: Real situation: 아까 + 때 referencing a specific earlier moment today, polite register

extendedVocab.nuance: 아까 refers to a short while earlier on the same day — broader than 'just now,' but always recent and never beyond today. The contrast learners most need is 아까 vs 방금: 방금 means literally seconds to a couple of minutes ago, while 아까 can stretch back a few hours (anywhere earlier today). 방금 도착했어요 = 'I arrived this second'; 아까 도착했어요 = 'I arrived a while ago (earlier today).' A second contrast is 아까 vs 전에: 전에 ('before / previously') is open-ended and can mean days, months, or years back, while 아까 is locked inside today. So use 아까 그거 ('that thing from earlier') only for something from the same day. 아까 is native Korean, casual-to-neutral in register, and combines productively with -부터 ('since earlier') and 그 + noun ('that ... from before').

Using it for yesterday or longer ago: 아까 stays within today's recent past. For further back use 어제 / 전에 / 지난번에.
Treating it the same as 방금: 방금 = seconds ago, 아까 = a broader 'earlier today.' Don't say 아까 도착했어요 if you literally just walked in — that's 방금.
Pairing 아까 with the future: it is past-only. 'A bit later' is 이따가, not 아까.
