extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 막 means "just (now), right as, recklessly/randomly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 막 (mak) means "just (now), right as, recklessly/randomly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지금 막 ("right this second"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 막 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Reinforces the 'just now' sense; 지금 막 도착했어요
막 나가려던 참이었어요 = I was just on the point of leaving
막 먹다 = eat mindlessly; 막 쓰다 = use/spend carelessly
이제 막 시작했어요 = we've only just started

examples.en: I just woke up (this second).
examples.note: Simple: 지금 막 + past for an action completed an instant ago

examples.en: Right as I was about to close the door, someone came running.
examples.note: Everyday: 막 + -려는데 marking the exact instant before another event

examples.en: When I'm stressed, I just end up eating mindlessly.
examples.note: Real situation: 막 in the 'recklessly, without restraint' sense

extendedVocab.nuance: 막 carries two everyday senses that context tells apart. (1) With a past tense or 참이다, it means 'just this very second' — even fresher and more immediate than 방금 — as in 지금 막 도착했어요 ('I arrived literally just now'). (2) In casual speech it also means doing something wildly, randomly, or without restraint, a shortening in feel of 마구: 막 먹다 (eat carelessly/a lot), 막 쓰다 (spend/use recklessly), 막 던지다 (throw all over the place). The pitfall for English speakers is hearing only the 'just' meaning and missing the 'recklessly' one, or vice versa — the following verb and tone decide it: 막 + past = time; 막 + ongoing careless action = manner. 막 is native Korean and very colloquial; the manner sense in particular sounds casual, so go easy on it in formal settings. It frequently teams up with 지금, 이제, and -려던 참이다 for the time reading.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the 'just now' 막 with the 'recklessly' 막: the meaning depends entirely on context and what verb follows. 막 먹었어요 with a time frame = 'just ate'; without one = 'ate mindlessly.'
Forgetting it usually leans on 지금 / 이제 or 참이다 for the time sense: bare 막 도착했어요 is fine, but 지금 막 / 이제 막 / 막 ~려던 참 sound more natural and unambiguous.
Using the careless 막 in polite/formal speech: 막 in the 'wildly' sense is colloquial and can sound crude — soften or avoid it when being formal.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 방금 means "just now, a moment ago (seconds)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "just now, a moment ago (seconds)" is 방금 (banggeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 방금 도착하다 ("to have just arrived"). usagePhrases.note: 방금 도착했어요 = I got here only seconds ago
방금 뭐라고 했어요? = asking to repeat what was said a second ago
Common variant emphasizing the very recent instant
방금까지 여기 있었어요 = it was right here until seconds ago

examples.en: I arrived just now.
examples.note: Simple: 방금 + past for an action seconds old

examples.en: The drink you just ordered is ready.
examples.note: Everyday: 방금 in a cafe, an order only moments old, polite -습니다 register

examples.ko: 방금까지 옆에 있었는데 잠깐 사이에 어디 갔지?
examples.romanization: banggeumkkaji yeope isseonneunde jamkkan saie eodi gatji?
examples.en: They were right beside me until just now; where'd they go in that instant?
examples.note: Real situation: 방금까지 emphasizing 'up until seconds ago'

extendedVocab.nuance: 방금 (方今, 方 'just/at the time' + 今 'now') is the tightest 'recent past' word, pointing to something that happened only seconds to a couple of minutes ago. The contrast learners need most is 방금 vs 아까: 방금 is 'this very moment past,' while 아까 stretches to 'earlier today' (potentially hours back). 방금 나갔어요 = 'they left seconds ago'; 아까 나갔어요 = 'they left a while ago.' Compare also 방금 vs 막: both can mean 'just now,' but 막 emphasizes the instantaneous edge ('right as it happened') and pairs with 지금/참이다, whereas 방금 is a standalone time word and a touch more neutral. Because of its Sino-Korean root, the variant 방금 전(에) ('just a moment before') is common. 방금 is strictly immediate past — never future. Register is neutral and fits both casual and polite speech, which is why staff use it (방금 주문하신…).

Stretching it to hours ago: for 'earlier today' use 아까. 방금 means only seconds to a couple minutes back.
Using it for the future: 방금 is strictly the immediate past, never 'in a moment' — that's 곧 / 이따가.
Over-distinguishing from 막 when they overlap: in many sentences 방금 도착했어요 and (지금) 막 도착했어요 are interchangeable, but pick 막 when you want the 'right as it happened' edge.

extendedVocab.english: in the meantime, all this while, during that time
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그동안 means "in the meantime, all this while, during that time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그동안 (geudongan) = "in the meantime, all this while, during that time". usagePhrases.en: to be thankful for everything up to now

examples.note: Real situation: 그동안 referring to an extended past saving period

extendedVocab.nuance: 그동안 (그 'that' + 동안 'duration/while') means 'during that time / all this while,' referring to a stretch of time spanning a known gap and usually leading up to now. It's the backbone of catching-up greetings (그동안 잘 지냈어요?) and farewell thanks (그동안 고마웠어요). The first pitfall is treating it as a single point: 그동안 is always a span, unlike 그때 ('at that time / that moment'). The second is direction — 그동안 vs 당분간: 그동안 looks back over time that has elapsed, while 당분간 ('for the time being') looks forward from now. So 'thanks for everything up to now' = 그동안 고마웠어요, but 'I'll rest for a while going forward' = 당분간 쉴게요. Grammatically 그동안 is flexible: it works as an adverb (그동안 바빴어요) and, with -의, as a noun modifier (그동안의 노력). Register is neutral and warm; the greeting use is everyday-polite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as a single point in time: 그동안 always refers to a span, not a moment like 그때. 'At that moment I was surprised' is 그때 놀랐어요, not 그동안.
Confusing it with 당분간 (for the time being, forward-looking): 그동안 looks back over elapsed time; 당분간 looks ahead.
Using it where you mean a specific past day: for 'the other day / last time' use 지난번 / 저번에, not 그동안.

extendedVocab.english: for the time being, for a while (from now)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 당분간 means "for the time being, for a while (from now)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 당분간 (dangbungan) means "for the time being, for a while (from now)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 당분간 쉬다 ("to rest for a while (going forward)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당분간 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to rest for a while (going forward)
usagePhrases.note: 당분간 쉬려고요 = I plan to take a break for the time being
당분간 못 만나요 = we can't meet for a while (a temporary inability)
당분간 외식 안 할 거예요 = I won't eat out for the time being

usagePhrases.en: for the time being at least
usagePhrases.note: Softens to 'at least for now'; implies it may change later

examples.en: I'll be busy for the time being.
examples.note: Simple: 당분간 + future, a temporary state ahead

examples.ko: 돈을 모아야 해서 당분간 여행은 안 가려고요.
examples.romanization: doneul moaya haeseo dangbungan yeohaengeun an garyeogoyo.
examples.en: I need to save money, so I'm not going to travel for the time being.
examples.note: Everyday: 당분간 + future restraint a budgeting resident relates to

examples.ko: 이직 준비 때문에 당분간 약속을 좀 줄이려고 해요.
examples.romanization: ijik junbi ttaemune dangbungan yaksogeul jom juriryeogo haeyo.
examples.en: Because I'm prepping for a job change, I'm going to cut back on plans for a while.
examples.note: Real situation: 당분간 marking a temporary phase ahead with -려고 해요

extendedVocab.nuance: 당분간 (當分間, roughly 當 'this present' + 分 'portion' + 間 'interval' — 'for this present interval') means 'for the time being': a limited stretch starting now and running into the near future, with a built-in implication that it's temporary and will change. The defining contrast is 당분간 vs 그동안: 당분간 points forward ('from now, for a while'), 그동안 points back over elapsed time. So 'I'll lie low for a while' = 당분간 조용히 지낼게요, but 'thanks for everything until now' = 그동안 고마웠어요. A second pitfall is using it for permanent states: 당분간 inherently signals 'this won't last forever.' It pairs naturally with future-plan endings (-(으)려고요, -ㄹ 거예요) and negatives of restraint (못, 안 ... -ㄹ 거예요), and it's often softened to 당분간은. Register is neutral and very common in everyday explanations of temporary plans.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 그동안: 당분간 points forward ('from now for a while'), while 그동안 points back over time that has passed.
Using it for permanent states: 당분간 implies the situation is temporary and expected to change. For 'forever / from now on for good' use 앞으로 (계속) / 영원히.
Pairing it with a plain past tense: since 당분간 looks forward, it wants future/intention forms — say 당분간 쉴 거예요 / 쉬려고요, not 당분간 쉬었어요.

extendedVocab.english: in that short time, in the blink of an eye (so fast)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그새 means "in that short time, in the blink of an eye (so fast)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "in that short time, in the blink of an eye (so fast)" is 그새 (geusae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그새 다 ~? ("did you ~ it all in that short time?"). Watch the particle attached to 그새 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: did you ~ it all in that short time?
usagePhrases.note: 그새 다 먹었어요? = you finished it all that fast?! (surprise)
그새 또 비가 오네요 = it's raining again already, in no time

usagePhrases.en: to forget in that short while
usagePhrases.note: 그새 잊어버렸어요 = it slipped my mind that quickly

usagePhrases.en: can't wait even that brief moment
usagePhrases.note: Noun use of 그새 (that short interval); 그새를 못 참고 = unable to wait even that bit

examples.en: They've grown so much in no time.
examples.note: Simple: 그새 + change, with built-in 'so fast!' surprise

examples.ko: 잠깐 화장실 다녀왔는데 그새 자리가 없어졌어요.
examples.romanization: jamkkan hwajangsil danyeowanneunde geusae jariga eopseojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I just popped to the restroom, and in that short time my seat was gone.
examples.note: Everyday: 그새 stressing how fast things changed in a brief absence

examples.ko: 분명히 여기 뒀는데 그새 어디 갔지?
examples.romanization: bunmyeonghi yeogi dwonneunde geusae eodi gatji?
examples.en: I clearly put it right here; where'd it go in that instant?
examples.note: Real situation: 그새 marking a baffling change over a brief moment

extendedVocab.nuance: 그새 is a contracted, set form of 그 사이 ('that interval/gap') and means 'in that short while' — almost always carrying a tone of surprise that so much changed in so little time. The contrast learners must keep straight is 그새 vs 그동안: 그동안 is a neutral, often longish stretch ('all this while'), while 그새 specifically flags a surprisingly short interval ('that quick?!'). 그동안 잘 지냈어요? is a calm catch-up; 그새 다 먹었어? is astonishment at speed. It can also work as a noun for that brief stretch itself (그새를 못 참다, 'can't even wait that little bit'). 그새 is native Korean and decidedly casual/spoken — great for reacting to quick changes among friends, less so in formal writing, where 그 사이에 / 그 짧은 사이에 reads better. Note the spelling: keep it as the single set word 그새 to carry the 'so fast!' nuance.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for long periods: 그새 specifically means a surprisingly short interval, not an extended stretch like 그동안.
Losing the surprise nuance by over-formalizing: in neutral writing 그 사이에 is fine, but the punchy 'so fast!' feeling lives in the set spoken form 그새.
Forgetting the noun use: 그새를 못 참다 ('can't wait even that brief moment') treats 그새 as the short interval itself — don't force it to be only an adverb.

extendedVocab.english: long ago, sooner (should have done it earlier)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 진작 means "long ago, sooner (should have done it earlier)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 진작 (jinjak) = "long ago, sooner (should have done it earlier)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 진작 ~ㄹ걸 ("should have ~ed sooner") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 진작, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 진작 할걸 = I should've done it long ago (self-regret)
진작 말했어야지 = you should've said so sooner (mild reproach)
Wishing the knowledge had come earlier
Emphatic variant; 진작에 했어야죠 = you really should've done it long ago

examples.en: You should've told me sooner.
examples.note: Simple: 진작 + -지 그랬어요, gentle 'why didn't you earlier' reproach

examples.ko: 이렇게 쉬운 걸 진작 할걸 그랬어요.
examples.romanization: ireoke swiun geol jinja kalgeol geuraesseoyo.
examples.en: I should have done something this easy long ago.
examples.note: Everyday: 진작 + -ㄹ걸 그랬다 expressing regret over delaying

examples.ko: 맛집인 줄 알았으면 진작 와 봤을 텐데.
examples.romanization: matjibin jul arasseumyeon jinjak wa bwasseul tende.
examples.en: If I'd known it was this good, I'd have come sooner.
examples.note: Real situation: 진작 in an -았/었을 텐데 hypothetical regret about timing

extendedVocab.nuance: 진작 means 'sooner / long ago,' but — and this is the whole point — it almost always carries regret or mild reproach that something wasn't done earlier than it actually was. It is not a neutral time word. The contrast learners must internalize is 진작 vs 전에 / 이미: 전에 ('before') and 이미 ('already') are neutral statements of fact, whereas 진작 is loaded with hindsight ('ah, if only it had been done earlier'). So 'I told you before' = 전에 말했어요 (neutral), but 'you should've told me sooner!' = 진작 말하지 (regretful). Because of this emotional core, 진작 habitually pairs with regret/counterfactual endings: -ㄹ걸 (그랬다), -았/었어야지, -았/었으면 ... -ㄹ 텐데. The emphatic variant 진작에 piles on the 'way earlier' feeling. 진작 is native-feeling, casual-to-neutral, and lands flat or even rude if you strip the regret framing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it as a neutral 'before' like 전에: 진작 always carries the 'should have, sooner' regret. For a plain factual 'before,' use 전에 / 미리.
Pairing it with plain statements instead of regret forms: it wants endings like -ㄹ걸, -았/었어야지, -았/었으면 ... -ㄹ 텐데. Bare 진작 했어요 sounds incomplete.
Confusing it with 미리 (in advance, neutral planning): 미리 예약했어요 = 'I booked ahead of time' (good planning); 진작 예약할걸 = 'I should've booked sooner' (regret). Different feelings entirely.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 고속버스 means "express (intercity) bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 고속버스 (gosokbeoseu) means "express (intercity) bus". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고속버스 타고 가요 ("I'm going by express bus"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고속버스 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 고속버스 + 타다 is the default frame; the means of transport you ride takes 을/를 or just 타고, never 으로 here
the building you depart from — 강남, 센트럴시티 등이 유명; buses use 터미널, never 역
우등(優等) = 'superior grade', 3 wide seats per row with more legroom and a higher fare; worth knowing when booking
예매(豫買) 'buy in advance' is the standard word for booking transport tickets ahead, usually on the 코버스 app

examples.en: The express bus is cheaper than the train.
examples.note: simple A보다 B comparison; 보다 attaches to the thing you measure against

examples.en: It's the weekend, so the express bus tickets are all sold out.
examples.note: 매진(賣盡)되다 = to sell out completely; book early on holidays

examples.ko: 우등으로 예매하면 자리가 넓어서 훨씬 편해요.
examples.romanization: udeungeuro yemaehamyeon jariga neolbeoseo hwolssin pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: If you book the premium one, the seats are wide so it's much more comfortable.
examples.note: 우등으로 uses 으로 'in the manner of'; this is why people pay extra

extendedVocab.nuance: 고속버스 (高速 'high-speed' + 버스) is the intercity coach that runs city-to-city on the expressway with few or no stops, so Koreans habitually weigh it against three rivals: the KTX (faster, pricier), the cheaper 무궁화호 train, and 시외버스, which makes more stops and reaches smaller towns. The dividing line you must keep straight is 고속버스 vs 시외버스 — 고속버스 means nonstop expressway travel between major cities and leaves from a 고속버스 터미널, while 시외버스 zig-zags through provincial towns from a different window. It is neutral everyday vocabulary anyone uses, collocating with 타다, 예매하다, 표/자리, and 우등. The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 고속버스역: buses board at a 터미널, and 역 belongs to trains and subways only; a second trap is reaching for 으로 ('by bus') when the natural pattern is simply 고속버스(를) 타다 or 타고 가다.

Confusing 고속버스 with 시외버스 — 고속버스 is nonstop expressway travel between major cities, while 시외버스 makes many stops and reaches smaller towns.
Forcing 고속버스로 가요 in casual speech — the idiomatic frame is 고속버스(를) 타고 가요; 으로 sounds stiff and textbook-ish here.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시외버스 means "intercity bus (with stops)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "intercity bus (with stops)" is 시외버스 (sioebeoseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시외버스 타다 ("to take an intercity bus"). Watch the particle attached to 시외버스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: used for trips to smaller cities or towns a 고속버스 doesn't reach
often shares a building with the 고속버스 terminal but has a separate ticket window
시간표 'time-table' = schedule; rural departures are sparse, so check it first
완행(緩行) 'slow-going' stops at many towns; its opposite is 직행(直行) 'direct'

examples.en: You get to that village by intercity bus.
examples.note: simple statement; the route a 고속버스 skips

examples.ko: 시외버스는 정류장에 자주 서서 시간이 더 걸려요.
examples.romanization: sioebeoseuneun jeongnyujange jaju seoseo sigani deo geollyeoyo.
examples.en: The intercity bus stops at stations often, so it takes more time.
examples.note: 서다 here = to stop/pull over; this is the trade-off vs 고속버스

examples.en: The last intercity bus is at 8, so we have to hurry.
examples.note: 막차 (last bus) is a survival word; rural lines end early in the evening

extendedVocab.nuance: 시외버스 (市外 'outside-the-city' + 버스) is the regional coach that covers shorter routes and makes multiple stops, so it reaches the provincial towns a 고속버스 deliberately skips. The synonym line learners must internalize is 시외버스 vs 고속버스: both are intercity buses, but 고속버스 means nonstop expressway runs between big cities, whereas 시외버스 threads through smaller places and is therefore slower — they even sell from different windows in the same terminal. Within 시외버스 there is a further split, 완행 (all-stops) vs 직행 (express/few-stops), so 직행 시외버스 can be nearly as quick as a 고속버스. It is plain, neutral vocabulary that collocates with 타다, 시간표, 막차, and 정류장. The big English-speaker pitfall is assuming buses run frequently the way they do in a city: rural 시외버스 lines may depart only a handful of times a day, so you must check the 시간표 and never count on a late return.

Treating 시외버스 and 고속버스 as interchangeable — they leave from different windows and serve different route types (provincial-with-stops vs nonstop-expressway).
Assuming frequent departures — rural 시외버스 lines may run only a few times a day, so always check the 시간표 and the 막차 time.

市外 'outside-the-city' + 버스 — the bus serving routes beyond the city limits.

done on the 코레일톡 (Korail Talk) app or at the station 매표소
특실(特室) 'special room' = first class, roomier; 일반실(一般室) = standard
자유석(自由席) = no assigned seat, cheaper; sit anywhere in the 자유석 cars, unlike 입석 (standing)

examples.en: I go from Seoul to Busan by KTX.
examples.note: with a named train/vehicle, 으로/로 'by means of' is natural here, unlike with 버스+타고

examples.ko: KTX 표가 비싸지만 빠르니까 자주 타요.

examples.ko: 주말에는 KTX 입석밖에 없을 때도 있어요.

Booking on the wrong app — KTX is Korail, so use 코레일톡, not the SRT app (SRT is a separate high-speed operator from 수서역).

usagePhrases.note: the small step-through automatic motorbike; very common among delivery riders
the ones zipping around with food; 배달(配達) = delivery
you need a 원동기 or 2종 소형 license depending on engine size
legally required; 헬멧 안 쓰면 단속(團束) 대상 (subject to a crackdown)

examples.en: That person rides a scooter.
examples.note: simple present habit; 타다 takes 을/를 for the vehicle you ride

examples.ko: 스쿠터는 좁은 골목도 잘 다녀서 편해요.
examples.romanization: seukuteoneun jobeun golmokdo jal danyeoseo pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: Scooters get through narrow alleys well, so they're convenient.
examples.note: 다니다 = to get around/move about; explains why they're popular for delivery

examples.ko: 비 올 때 스쿠터 타면 너무 위험해요.
examples.romanization: bi ol ttae seukuteo tamyeon neomu wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: Riding a scooter when it rains is really dangerous.
examples.note: 비(가) 오다 = to rain; a practical safety note residents make

extendedVocab.nuance: 스쿠터 (from English 'scooter') means specifically the small automatic step-through motorbike with a seat and a low floorboard — the workhorse of food-delivery riders — whereas 오토바이 is the umbrella word for any motorcycle, including big manual-gear bikes. That contrast, 스쿠터 vs 오토바이, is the one to lock in: every 스쿠터 is an 오토바이, but most Koreans say 오토바이 generically and 스쿠터 only for the little delivery-style one. Crucially, do not confuse it with 전동킥보드, the standing electric kick-scooter with no seat that English also calls a 'scooter' — same English word, totally different vehicle in Korean. It collocates with 타다, 배달, 면허, 헬멧. The classic English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 'scooter' overlap (kick-scooter ≠ 스쿠터); a second is assuming no licence is needed — even a small 스쿠터 legally requires at least a 원동기 licence.

Using 스쿠터 for an electric kick-scooter — that's a 전동킥보드; a 스쿠터 has a seat and a fuel engine.
Assuming no licence is needed — even small scooters require at least a 원동기 licence to ride legally.
Calling every motorbike a 스쿠터 — a large geared motorcycle is an 오토바이; 스쿠터 is just the small step-through kind.

Watch the particle attached to 트럭 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: 운전(運轉)하다 'operate/steer' is the standard verb for driving any vehicle
the small cargo truck everyone uses for moving; read '일 톤 트럭'
the truck a moving company brings; 이사(移徙) = moving house
대(臺) is the counter for vehicles and machines, never 개

examples.en: There's a truck over there.
examples.note: introduces the vehicle counter 대; 한 대 = one (vehicle)

examples.ko: 길에 트럭이 서 있어서 차가 막혀요.
examples.romanization: gire teureogi seo isseoseo chaga makyeoyo.
examples.en: A truck is parked on the road, so traffic is backed up.
examples.note: 서 있다 = to be standing/parked; 막히다 = (traffic) to be jammed

examples.ko: 과일 파는 트럭이 동네에 자주 와요.
examples.romanization: gwail paneun teureogi dongnee jaju wayo.
examples.en: A truck selling fruit often comes to the neighborhood.
examples.note: 파는 (from 팔다) modifies 트럭; the 트럭 행상 street-vendor scene

extendedVocab.nuance: 트럭 (from English 'truck') is everyday vocabulary mainly because of two very Korean sights: the 1톤 트럭 that families rent to move apartments, and the street vendors who sell fruit, vegetables, or fish straight off the back of one. There isn't a sharp single synonym, but note the register split — 트럭 is the ordinary spoken word, while 화물차(貨物車) 'cargo vehicle' is the more formal/official term you meet on road signs and in news. The counter is the trap that catches everyone: vehicles take 대 (트럭 한 대, 두 대), not the all-purpose 개, which would sound childish or wrong. It collocates with 운전하다, 빌리다, 1톤, 이사. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) counting with 개 instead of 대, and (2) pronouncing it like one clipped English syllable — Korean breaks the consonant cluster with an inserted ㅡ vowel, so it is two clear syllables, 트·럭.

Counting trucks with 개 — vehicles take the counter 대, so it must be 트럭 한 대, not 트럭 한 개.
Pronouncing it like the one-syllable English 'truck' — Korean inserts a ㅡ vowel, so it is two clearly articulated syllables, 트·럭, not a single clipped cluster.
Using 트럭 in a formal report where 화물차 is expected — 트럭 is casual; official/legal contexts prefer 화물차.

extendedVocab.explanation: 렌터카 (renteoka) = "rental car". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 렌터카 빌리다 ("to rent a car") shows how it actually behaves. 예약(豫約)하다 'book in advance', done online before a trip, especially for 제주도
보험(保險) = insurance; always ask about 자차(自車) collision coverage
반납(返納) 'give back' = return; mind the fuel and time rules

examples.en: When I go on a trip I rent a car.
examples.note: simple habit sentence; 빌리다 takes 을/를 for the thing rented

examples.ko: 렌터카 빌릴 때 면허증하고 신용카드가 필요해요.
examples.romanization: renteoka billil ttae myeonheojeunghago sinyongkadeuga piryohaeyo.
examples.en: When you rent a car you need your licence and a credit card.
examples.note: practical requirement; 하고 links two nouns in speech

examples.en: You have to return it with a full tank.
examples.note: 가득 채우다 = to fill up; the common 만(滿)탱크 return rule

extendedVocab.nuance: 렌터카 (from English 'rent-a-car') is the word residents reach for when a destination has weak public transport — above all 제주도, where almost every visitor rents. The boundary to keep clear is 렌터카 vs 카셰어링(car-sharing, e.g. 쏘카·그린카): a 렌터카 is a traditional desk-and-contract day-or-more rental, while 카셰어링 is the app-based by-the-minute/hour kind, so don't call a 쏘카 a 렌터카 in conversation. The main English-speaker pitfalls are (1) writing/saying 렌트카 instead of 렌터카, and (2) forgetting the paperwork: you normally need a credit card in your own name plus a valid licence (an international permit if your home licence isn't recognized), and you'll always be pushed to add 보험 at the counter.

Forgetting the rental requirements — you usually need a credit card in your own name plus a valid licence (an international permit if your home licence isn't accepted).

usagePhrases.note: Seoul's public bike-share; the name is deliberately cute/friendly
대여(貸與) = rental/checkout, done by app at a 대여소 (checkout point)
반납(返納) = return; you dock it at any 대여소 station
정기권(定期券) = a fixed-period pass (e.g. monthly), cheaper than paying per ride

examples.en: I ride a Ttareungi on weekends.
examples.note: simple habit; the brand name behaves like a normal object noun with 타다

examples.en: I get to the subway station quickly by Ttareungi.
examples.note: common last-mile use; 따릉이로 'by Ttareungi', 금방 = in no time

examples.en: You unlock the Ttareungi with the app.
examples.note: 잠금을 풀다 = to release the lock/unlock; how the system works

The contrast to hold is 따릉이 (the rental/share brand) vs 자전거 (any bicycle, including your own): all 따릉이 are 자전거, but you only call it 따릉이 when it's one of these app-unlocked share bikes. It collocates with 타다, 대여/반납, 정기권, and 앱. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) using 따릉이 for any bike — a personal bicycle is just 자전거 — and (2) assuming it exists nationwide, when outside Seoul you must look for the local equivalent.

Using 따릉이 for any bicycle — a personal bike is just 자전거; 따릉이 is the specific Seoul share brand.

Treating it as a generic word for 'public bike' — the generic term is 공공자전거; 따릉이 is a brand name.

usagePhrases.note: the standing share scooters from apps like 킥고잉, 씽씽
legally required; police run 단속(團束) crackdowns
you need at least a 원동기 licence to ride one legally
공유(共有) = shared; the app-based ones parked on sidewalks

examples.en: These days a lot of people ride electric kick-scooters.
examples.note: simple frequency statement with 많이; 타다 + 을/를

examples.ko: 전동킥보드는 헬멧을 안 쓰면 벌금을 내요.
examples.romanization: jeondongkikbodeuneun helmeseul an sseumyeon beolgeumeul naeyo.
examples.en: If you don't wear a helmet on a kick-scooter, you pay a fine.
examples.note: real rule since 2021; 벌금(罰金) = fine, 내다 = to pay

examples.en: I can get to work in ten minutes on a kick-scooter.
examples.note: 전동킥보드로 'by kick-scooter'; 십 분이면 = if it's (just) ten minutes

The sharp contrast to drill is 전동킥보드 vs 스쿠터: a 전동킥보드 is a standing board with no seat, whereas a 스쿠터 is a seated, usually petrol step-through motorbike — English blurs both as 'scooter', which is exactly why learners mix them up. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) calling it a 스쿠터 because of the shared English word, and (2) assuming it's rule-free — riding two-up, without a helmet, or without a licence can each draw a 벌금.

Confusing it with 스쿠터 — a 전동킥보드 is a standing electric board with no seat, not a seated motorbike.
Thinking it's rule-free — riding two people, with no helmet, or without a licence can all get you fined (벌금).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마을버스 means "village (neighborhood) bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 마을버스 (maeulbeoseu) = "village (neighborhood) bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마을버스 타다 ("to take the village bus") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: small green local buses that bridge gaps to the nearest subway station
정류장(停留場) 'stopping place' = bus stop; routes wind through the neighborhood
routes carry a district prefix plus a short number, like 종로11 or 강남07
환승(換乘) = transfer; you tap to transfer onward to the subway or a regular bus

examples.en: I take the village bus to my house.
examples.note: simple destination + 타다; 까지 marks the end point

examples.ko: 마을버스는 작아서 출근 시간에 사람이 꽉 차요.
examples.romanization: maeulbeoseuneun jagaseo chulgeun sigane sarami kkwak chayo.
examples.en: The village bus is small, so it's packed during commute hours.
examples.note: 꽉 차다 = to be packed full; 작아서 gives the reason

examples.en: Get off the subway and transfer to the village bus.
examples.note: 갈아타다 = to change/transfer vehicles; common spoken directions

extendedVocab.nuance: 마을버스 (마을 'village/neighborhood', native Korean, + 버스) is the small short-loop local bus that connects residential pockets — especially hilly ones away from main roads — to the nearest subway station or trunk bus line. The contrast to keep straight is 마을버스 vs 시내버스/광역버스: a 마을버스 only circles a small area as a feeder, a 시내버스 (city bus) runs longer routes across the city, and a 광역버스 connects cities, so don't expect a 마을버스 to take you far. Note 마을 is a pure-Korean word (not Sino-Korean), which is why it pairs warmly with the idea of a tight local community. It collocates with 타다, 정류장, 환승, 갈아타다, and route codes like 종로11. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) expecting it to travel a long distance, when it only feeds bigger lines, and (2) forgetting to tap your card — without the tap the 환승 (free-transfer) discount to the subway won't apply.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting it to travel far — a 마을버스 only loops the local area to feed bigger lines, unlike a 시내버스 or 광역버스.
Forgetting to tap for transfer — without tapping your transport card, the 환승 (free-transfer) discount onto the subway won't apply.
Calling any small bus a 마을버스 — the term is the official route category (green, district-numbered), not just 'a little bus'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 광역버스 means "wide-area (commuter) bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 광역버스 (gwangyeokbeoseu) means "wide-area (commuter) bus". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 광역버스 타다 ("to take the wide-area bus"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 광역버스 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: red express commuter buses linking Seoul with nearby cities like 수원, 일산
좌석(座席) = seat; these are seat-only and 입석 (standing) is restricted on them
노선(路線) = route/line; long commuter runs into the metro center
color-coded red, as opposed to blue (trunk) and green (local) city buses

examples.en: I go to work by wide-area bus.
examples.note: simple commute statement; 광역버스로 'by wide-area bus', 까지 = up to

examples.ko: 광역버스는 자리에 앉아서 갈 수 있어서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gwangyeokbeoseuneun jarie anjaseo gal su isseoseo joayo.
examples.en: The wide-area bus is nice because you can sit the whole way.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = can; the main appeal over a packed subway

examples.ko: 출근 시간에는 광역버스가 만석이라 한 대 보냈어요.
examples.romanization: chulgeun siganeneun gwangyeokbeoseuga manseogira han dae bonaesseoyo.
examples.en: At rush hour the wide-area bus was full, so I let one go by.
examples.note: 만석(滿席) = all seats taken; 한 대 보내다 = let one pass and wait

extendedVocab.nuance: 광역버스 (廣域 'wide area' + 버스) is the red long-haul commuter bus that links Seoul with surrounding 경기도 cities, engineered so suburban commuters can sit for the whole ride into the center. The contrast you must fix is 광역버스 vs 마을버스: 광역버스 spans long city-to-city commutes and is seat-oriented, while 마을버스 just circles one neighborhood as a feeder — opposite ends of the bus spectrum. Korea's buses are also color-coded, and 광역버스 is the 빨간 (red) one, versus blue trunk and green local buses, so locals will say '빨간 버스' to mean it. It collocates with 타다, 좌석, 노선, 만석, and the verb 출근하다 (commute to work). The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) mixing it up with 마을버스 (wrong scale entirely) and (2) expecting to stand: because seats are limited and standing is restricted, a 만석 bus means you simply wait for the next one rather than squeezing on.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing it up with 마을버스 — a 광역버스 covers long city-to-city commutes, while a 마을버스 only circles one neighborhood.
Expecting to stand on it — 광역버스 are largely seat-only with standing restricted, so when it's 만석 you wait for the next one.
Assuming all red buses are identical — color marks the category (red = 광역), but routes/노선 differ, so check the number.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 케이블카 means "cable car" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cable car" is 케이블카 (keibeulka). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 케이블카 타다 ("to ride a cable car"). Watch the particle attached to 케이블카 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the gondola hung from a cable, up mountains or to coastal viewpoints
왕복(往復) 'go-and-return' = round trip; the opposite is 편도(片道) one way
표(票) = ticket; you buy it at the lower station
the lower station; -는 곳 = 'the place where you do (it)'

examples.en: I ride the cable car on the mountain.
examples.note: simple location + 타다; 에서 marks where the action happens

examples.ko: 케이블카는 왕복으로 끊는 게 더 싸요.
examples.romanization: keibeulkaneun wangbogeuro kkeunhneun ge deo ssayo.
examples.en: Buying the cable car as a round trip is cheaper.
examples.note: 표를 끊다 = to buy a ticket (set idiom); 왕복으로 'as a round trip'

examples.ko: 바람이 너무 세서 케이블카 운행을 멈췄어요.
examples.romanization: barami neomu seseo keibeulka unhaengeul meomchwosseoyo.
examples.en: The wind was too strong, so they stopped running the cable car.
examples.note: 운행(運行)을 멈추다 = to suspend operation; weather closures happen

extendedVocab.nuance: 케이블카 (from English 'cable car') is leisure-and-tourism vocabulary — the gondola cabin that hangs from an overhead cable and carries you up 남산, 통영, or 여수 for the view, not for daily transport. The contrast to keep clear is by how it moves: a 케이블카 is suspended from a cable in the air, whereas a 모노레일 rides a single rail and a 트램 runs on tracks on the ground, so a ground-level car is not a 케이블카. Tickets pair it with the 왕복/편도 (round-trip / one-way) distinction, which directly affects price. It collocates with 타다, 왕복/편도, 표(를) 끊다, 야경, and 운행. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) calling a ground tram or funicular a 케이블카 (those are 트램/모노레일 — 케이블카 hangs in the air), and (2) buying two 편도 tickets when a single 왕복 ticket is cheaper for an up-and-back trip.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a ground tram or funicular a 케이블카 — that's a 트램 or 모노레일; a 케이블카 hangs from an overhead cable.
Buying two 편도 tickets when a 왕복 ticket is cheaper for a there-and-back trip.
Assuming it always runs — strong wind suspends 운행, so a cable-car plan can be canceled on the day.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 페리 means "ferry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 페리 (peri) = "ferry". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 페리 타다 ("to take a ferry") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 페리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the passenger/car ship to the islands; the formal term is 여객선(旅客船)
예매(豫買) = advance booking; popular island routes fill up
차량(車輛) = vehicle(s); the kind you can drive your car onto
터미널 = terminal; the port building you board from (also 여객터미널)

examples.en: I take a ferry when I go to the island.
examples.note: core use case stated simply; 섬 = island, 타다 + 을/를

examples.ko: 파도가 높아서 오늘 페리가 다 결항됐어요.
examples.romanization: padoga nopaseo oneul periga da gyeolhangdwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The waves are high, so all the ferries were canceled today.
examples.note: 결항(缺航)되다 = (a ship/flight) to be canceled; common in bad weather

examples.en: I loaded my car onto the ferry and went to Jeju.
examples.note: 싣다 (ㄷ-irregular: 싣고/실어) = to load cargo; the car-ferry option

extendedVocab.nuance: 페리 (from English 'ferry') is the everyday word for a passenger or car ship running point-to-point to Korea's islands; in formal notices and timetables you'll instead see the Sino-Korean 여객선(旅客船) 'traveler-guest ship', so 페리 ≈ 여객선 with 페리 being the casual term. The contrast to lock in is 페리 vs 유람선(遊覽船): a 페리 is transport that gets you from port A to island B, while a 유람선 is a sightseeing cruise that loops back to where it started — don't swap them. A practical companion word is 결항 (service cancellation), the thing you check before any island trip. It collocates with 타다, 예매, 차량, 터미널, and 결항. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) calling a tour boat a 페리 (that's a 유람선), and (2) not checking the weather: rough seas trigger 결항, so an island ferry plan can collapse at the last minute.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 페리 with a sightseeing cruise — a tour boat is a 유람선; a 페리 is point-to-point transport to a destination.
Not checking the weather — rough seas cause 결항 (cancellation), so an island ferry plan can fall through last minute.
Treating 페리 as too casual for documents — official schedules and signage use 여객선, the formal equivalent.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 변기 means "toilet (bowl)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 변기 (byeongi) means "toilet (bowl)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 변기 ("toilet bowl"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 변기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The porcelain fixture itself. The whole room is 화장실; only the bowl is 변기.
막히다 = to get blocked; the single most useful phrase for a renter to know.
물을 내리다 = to flush; 내리다 literally means 'bring/send down', i.e. let the water down.
Particle 에 marks the surface you sit on; 변기에 앉다, not 변기를 앉다.

examples.en: The toilet is clogged again.
examples.note: 또 = again; 막혔어요 is the past of 막히다, the go-to verb for a blocked toilet.

examples.en: Is it okay to throw the toilet paper in the toilet?
examples.note: 버리다 = to throw away; -아도 돼요? asks permission. A real question, since Korean plumbing usually handles 휴지.

examples.ko: 나오기 전에 변기 물 꼭 내리세요.
examples.romanization: naogi jeone byeongi mul kkong naeriseyo.
examples.en: Be sure to flush before you come out.
examples.note: 꼭 = without fail; in speech the object 을 in 물(을) 내리다 is commonly dropped.

extendedVocab.nuance: 변기(便器)는 한자로 '편할 편(便)·그릇 기(器)', 즉 '용변을 보는 그릇'이라는 뜻으로 화장실 안의 변기통 그 자체만 가리킵니다. 방 전체인 '화장실'과 헷갈리면 안 됩니다. 영어 화자는 'toilet'을 방과 변기에 둘 다 쓰지만, 한국어는 공간은 화장실, 기구는 변기로 또렷이 나눕니다. 가장 자주 쓰는 표현은 '변기가 막히다'와 '변기 물을 내리다'인데, 특히 자취나 월세 생활에서 수리를 부탁할 때 거의 필수입니다. 물을 흘려보내는 동작에 영어식으로 '누르다(press)'를 직역해 쓰지 말고, 한국어 관용 표현인 '물을 내리다'를 쓰는 것이 자연스럽습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the whole bathroom 변기 — the room is 화장실, the bowl is 변기. Saying 변기에 갔다 sounds like you climbed into the bowl; say 화장실에 갔다.
Saying 변기를 누르다 (a literal 'press the toilet') for flushing; the natural collocation is 변기 물을 내리다.
Using 를 for where you sit (변기를 앉다); the seat is a location, so it takes 에 → 변기에 앉다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 샤워기 means "showerhead / shower sprayer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "showerhead / shower sprayer" is 샤워기 (syawogi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 샤워기 ("showerhead / handheld shower"). Watch the particle attached to 샤워기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Most Korean bathrooms use a handheld 샤워기 on a hose, not a fixed overhead shower.

usagePhrases.en: to rinse off with the showerhead
usagePhrases.note: (으)로 marks the instrument; 헹구다 = to rinse off (with water).

usagePhrases.en: no water comes out of the showerhead
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the source the water comes out of; 물이 안 나오다 = water won't come out.
갈다 = to replace a part; filter showerheads (필터 샤워기) are very popular.

examples.en: The shower water suddenly turned cold.
examples.note: 차가워지다 = to become cold (차갑다 + -아지다); 보일러 trouble is a common culprit.

examples.en: I rinsed even the bathroom floor with the showerhead.
examples.note: 까지 = even/all the way to; 싹 = completely. A handheld 샤워기 doubles as a cleaning tool.

examples.en: The water pressure was weak, so I changed the showerhead.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 수압 = water pressure, 바꾸다 = to swap out.

extendedVocab.nuance: 샤워기는 '샤워(shower) + 기(器, 기구)'로, 물을 뿌리는 분사 기구 자체를 가리킵니다. 행위인 '샤워(샤워하다)'와 반드시 구분해야 합니다. 영어 화자가 가장 많이 저지르는 실수가 'I take a shower'를 떠올려 기구를 가리킬 때까지 그냥 '샤워'라고 하는 것인데, 손에 드는 그 물건은 '샤워기'입니다. 한국 욕실은 천장 고정형 대신 호스에 달린 손잡이형 샤워기가 대부분이라, 몸을 씻는 것은 물론 욕실 바닥이나 변기 주변을 헹구는 청소 도구로도 자주 씁니다. 수압이 약하거나 물때가 끼면 본체는 두고 '샤워기 헤드'만 갈아 끼우는 경우가 많아, 마트나 다이소에서 교체용 헤드를 흔히 팝니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 샤워기 (the sprayer/device) with 샤워 (the act of showering). 'I bought a 샤워' makes no sense; you buy a 샤워기.
Assuming a fixed overhead rain shower — in Korean homes it's almost always a handheld 샤워기 on a hose.
Saying 샤워기를 켜다/끄다 (turn the device on/off like an appliance); more natural is 물을 틀다/잠그다, since you control the water, not the head.

structuredNuance.t: 물을 뿌리는 분사 기구 자체를 가리킵니다. 행위인 '샤워(샤워하다)'와 반드시 구분해야 합니다. 한국 욕실은 천장 고정형 대신 호스에 달린 손잡이형 샤워기가 대부분이라, 몸을 씻는 것은 물론 욕실 바닥이나 변기 주변을 헹구는 청소 도구로도 자주 씁니다. 수압이 약하거나 물때가 끼면 본체는 두고 '샤워기 헤드'만 갈아 끼우는 경우가 많아, 마트나 다이소에서 교체용 헤드를 흔히 팝니다.
샤워기는 '샤워(shower) + 기(器, 기구)'로 이루어진 말입니다.
영어 화자가 가장 많이 저지르는 실수가 'I take a shower'를 떠올려 기구를 가리킬 때까지 그냥 '샤워'라고 하는 것인데, 손에 드는 그 물건은 '샤워기'입니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수도꼭지 means "faucet / tap" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 수도꼭지 (sudokkokji) = "faucet / tap". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수도꼭지 ("faucet, tap") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수도꼭지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The tap at a sink or basin; 수도 (水道, water supply) + 꼭지 (a native word for knob/spout).
잠그다 = to shut/close (also 'to lock'); the standard verb for closing a tap.
틀다 = to turn on running water or a machine; pairs with 잠그다 as its opposite.
물이 새다 = water leaks out; a frequent maintenance complaint in old apartments.

examples.en: Please turn off the tap while you brush your teeth.
examples.note: Note the conjugation: 잠그다 + -아 → 잠가 (the ㅡ drops). A common water-saving reminder.

examples.en: The faucet is dripping (water leaks drip-drip).
examples.note: 똑똑 is an onomatopoeia mimicking the dripping sound; 새요 from 새다.

examples.en: The cold-water tap is really stiff to turn.
examples.note: 뻑뻑하다 = stiff/hard to turn; 찬물 = cold water (vs. 더운물 hot water).

extendedVocab.nuance: 수도꼭지는 '수도(水道, 물이 다니는 길)'에 순우리말 '꼭지(끝에 튀어나온 손잡이·주둥이)'가 붙은 합성어로, 세면대나 싱크대에서 물을 틀고 잠그는 그 부분을 말합니다. 핵심은 동사 짝입니다. 가전제품은 켜다/끄다를 쓰지만 물은 '틀다(또는 열다)'와 '잠그다'를 쓰며, 영어 'turn off the tap'을 직역해 '수도꼭지를 끄다'라고 하면 어색합니다. 비슷한 말로 '수전(水栓)'이 있는데 이는 인테리어·설비 용어로 제품을 가리킬 때 쓰고, 일상 대화에서는 수도꼭지가 자연스럽습니다. 오래된 집에서는 물이 새거나(물이 새다) 손잡이가 뻑뻑해지는 일이 흔해 수리를 부탁할 때 자주 등장하는 단어입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 끄다 to turn off a tap — water is controlled with 잠그다 (close), not 끄다 (which is for fire/lights/appliances).
Forgetting the 으-irregular: 잠그다 becomes 잠가요/잠가서, not 잠궈요. (잠구다 is a common but nonstandard form.)
Mixing it up with 샤워기; 수도꼭지 is the basin/sink tap, while the shower sprayer is 샤워기.

structuredNuance.t: 세면대나 싱크대에서 물을 틀고 잠그는 그 부분을 말합니다. 오래된 집에서는 물이 새거나(물이 새다) 손잡이가 뻑뻑해지는 일이 흔해 수리를 부탁할 때 자주 등장하는 단어입니다.
비슷한 말로 '수전(水栓)'이 있는데 이는 인테리어·설비 용어로 제품을 가리킬 때 쓰고, 일상 대화에서는 수도꼭지가 자연스럽습니다.
수도꼭지는 '수도(水道, 물이 다니는 길)'에 순우리말 '꼭지(끝에 튀어나온 손잡이·주둥이)'가 붙은 합성어입니다.
핵심은 동사 짝입니다. 가전제품은 켜다/끄다를 쓰지만 물은 '틀다(또는 열다)'와 '잠그다'를 쓰며, 영어 'turn off the tap'을 직역해 '수도꼭지를 끄다'라고 하면 어색합니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 린스 means "(hair) conditioner / rinse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 린스 (rinseu) means "(hair) conditioner / rinse". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 린스 ("hair conditioner"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 린스 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Used after 샴푸; the textbook word is 컨디셔너, but in daily Korean 린스 is far more common.
린스(를) 하다 turns the noun into an action = to put on and use conditioner.
The usual order; -하고 here links two steps ('shampoo, and then conditioner').
떨어지다 here = to run out/be used up; a frequent shopping-list item.

examples.en: I always use conditioner too (not just shampoo).
examples.note: 까지 = even/all the way to, implying conditioner is the extra final step; 꼭 = without fail.

examples.en: If you don't rinse the conditioner out, your hair gets greasy and clumpy.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if; 떡지다 = (hair) to clump up and look greasy, like rice cake (떡).

examples.ko: 린스 다 떨어졌으니까 마트에서 사 와요.
examples.romanization: rinseu da tteoreojyeosseunikka mateueseo sa wayo.
examples.en: We're out of conditioner, so buy some at the store.
examples.note: 다 떨어지다 = to be completely out; -(으)니까 gives the reason for a request.

extendedVocab.nuance: 린스(rinse)는 영어에서 온 외래어지만 한국어에서는 의미가 좁아져 '샴푸 후에 바르는 헤어 컨디셔너'만을 뜻합니다. 여기에 영어 화자의 함정이 있습니다. 영어 rinse는 '물로 헹구다'라는 뜻이지만, 한국어 '린스'는 절대 '맹물로 헹굼'이 아니라 제품(컨디셔너) 자체를 가리킵니다. 헹구는 동작은 따로 '헹구다'를 씁니다. 비슷한 말 '컨디셔너', '트리트먼트'와 비교하면, 컨디셔너=린스로 거의 같고, 트리트먼트는 더 진하게 영양을 주는 집중 케어 제품이라는 차이가 있습니다. 사용 순서는 머리는 샴푸로 감고 → 린스를 바른 뒤 → 잘 헹구는 것이며, 덜 헹구면 머리가 '떡진다'고 표현하니 함께 알아 두면 자연스럽습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 린스 means a plain-water rinse (from English 'rinse') — in Korean it specifically means hair conditioner, a product.
Using it before 샴푸; the order is 샴푸 → 린스, never the reverse.
Confusing 린스 with 트리트먼트 — 트리트먼트 is a richer, deep-care treatment, not the everyday after-shampoo conditioner.

structuredNuance.t: 한국어에서는 의미가 좁아져 '샴푸 후에 바르는 헤어 컨디셔너'만을 뜻합니다. 사용 순서는 머리는 샴푸로 감고 → 린스를 바른 뒤 → 잘 헹구는 것이며, 덜 헹구면 머리가 '떡진다'고 표현하니 함께 알아 두면 자연스럽습니다.
비슷한 말 '컨디셔너', '트리트먼트'와 비교하면, 컨디셔너=린스로 거의 같고, 트리트먼트는 더 진하게 영양을 주는 집중 케어 제품이라는 차이가 있습니다.
린스(rinse)는 영어에서 온 외래어입니다.
영어 rinse는 '물로 헹구다'라는 뜻이지만, 한국어 '린스'는 절대 '맹물로 헹굼'이 아니라 제품(컨디셔너) 자체를 가리킵니다. 헹구는 동작은 따로 '헹구다'를 씁니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 바디워시 means "body wash / shower gel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "body wash / shower gel" is 바디워시 (badiwosi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바디워시 ("liquid body wash"). Watch the particle attached to 바디워시 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The liquid soap for the body; the solid bar version is 비누.
(으)로 marks the means; 씻다 = to wash (the body/an object).
짜다 = to squeeze out (from a tube/bottle); pump or squeeze bottles are standard.

usagePhrases.en: to put body wash on a shower puff
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = to apply/get something onto a surface; 샤워볼 = mesh shower puff.

examples.en: I use body wash instead of bar soap.
examples.note: 대신 = instead of; here it contrasts the liquid 바디워시 with solid 비누.

examples.en: I squeezed body wash onto the shower puff and made a lather.
examples.note: -아서 links two actions in sequence; 거품을 내다 = to work up a lather.

examples.en: This body wash has a subtle scent, so I like it.
examples.note: 은은하다 = subtle/faint (a positive word for a gentle scent), often used for 향 (scent).

extendedVocab.nuance: 바디워시(body wash)는 몸을 씻는 액체 비누로, '바디(body) + 워시(wash)'를 그대로 들여온 외래어입니다. 핵심 구분은 형태입니다. 고체는 '비누', 액체는 '바디워시'이며, 영어 화자가 둘 다 'soap'으로 묶어 생각해 액체 제품까지 '비누'라고 부르면 어색합니다. 또 하나, 영어 'shampoo'와 헷갈려 몸을 '샴푸로 씻는다'고 하면 안 됩니다. 한국어는 머리는 샴푸, 몸은 바디워시로 역할이 분명히 나뉩니다. 한국 2030 세대는 비누보다 바디워시를 선호하는 편이고, 보통 샤워볼이나 타월에 짜서 거품을 내 사용합니다. 향에 민감한 사람이 많아 '향이 은은하다/진하다' 같은 표현과 자주 함께 쓰입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 샴푸 for the body — 샴푸 is strictly for hair, 바디워시 is for the body.
Calling it 비누; 비누 is the solid bar, 바디워시 is the liquid. They are not interchangeable in Korean.
Saying 바디워시를 바르다 as the main verb; you 짜다 (squeeze out) and 거품을 내다 (lather), then 씻다 — 바르다 (smear on) fits lotion, not body wash.

structuredNuance.t: 몸을 씻는 액체 비누입니다. 한국 2030 세대는 비누보다 바디워시를 선호하는 편이고, 보통 샤워볼이나 타월에 짜서 거품을 내 사용합니다. 향에 민감한 사람이 많아 '향이 은은하다/진하다' 같은 표현과 자주 함께 쓰입니다.
핵심 구분은 형태입니다. 고체는 '비누', 액체는 '바디워시'입니다.
바디워시(body wash)는 '바디(body) + 워시(wash)'를 그대로 들여온 외래어입니다.
영어 화자가 고체와 액체를 둘 다 'soap'으로 묶어 생각해 액체 제품까지 '비누'라고 부르면 어색합니다. 또 영어 'shampoo'와 헷갈려 몸을 '샴푸로 씻는다'고 하면 안 됩니다. 한국어는 머리는 샴푸, 몸은 바디워시로 역할이 분명히 나뉩니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 배수구 means "drain (floor/sink drain)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 배수구 (baesugu) = "drain (floor/sink drain)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 배수구 ("drain hole") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배수구, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The drain in the bathroom floor or sink; everyday speech often says 하수구 instead.
막히다 = to clog up; the usual cause is hair (머리카락).
에서 marks the source; 냄새가 나다 = to give off a smell, a very common complaint.

usagePhrases.en: to pull hair out of the drain
usagePhrases.note: 빼다 = to remove/pull out; the routine fix for a slow drain.

examples.ko: 배수구에 머리카락이 껴서 물이 안 빠져요.
examples.romanization: baesugue meorikaragi kkyeoseo muri an ppajyeoyo.
examples.en: Hair is stuck in the drain, so the water won't go down.
examples.note: 끼다 = to get wedged/stuck; 물이 빠지다 = (the) water drains away.

examples.en: In summer, a smell comes up from the drain.
examples.note: 올라오다 = to come/rise up (toward you); common in older bathrooms.

examples.en: I opened the drain cover and cleaned it.
examples.note: 덮개 = cover/cap (from 덮다, to cover); -고 links the two actions.

extendedVocab.nuance: 배수구(排水口)는 한자로 '밀어낼 배(排)·물 수(水)·입 구(口)', 곧 '물을 밀어내 보내는 구멍'입니다. 욕실 바닥이나 세면대에서 물이 빠져나가는 그 구멍을 가리키며, 일상 대화에서는 비슷한 말 '하수구(下水口)'도 자주 씁니다. 굳이 나누자면 배수구는 집 안에서 물이 빠지는 구멍, 하수구는 그 물이 모여 흘러가는 바깥의 더 큰 하수 시설 쪽에 가깝지만, 일상에서는 거의 섞어 씁니다. 동사 짝이 영어와 달라 주의가 필요합니다. 물이 잘 빠질 때는 '물이 빠지다', 막힐 때는 '막히다'를 쓰며, 변기에서 쓰는 '물을 내리다'를 배수구에 그대로 가져다 쓰면 어색합니다. 머리카락이 껴서 물이 안 빠지거나(머리카락을 빼다) 여름에 냄새가 올라오는 일이 잦아 청소·수리 화제로 단골입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 물이 내려가다/물을 내리다 for a floor drain — for a drain the natural phrase is 물이 빠지다 (water drains away).
Confusing 배수구 (the drain that takes water away) with 수도꼭지 (the tap that supplies water). They are opposite ends of the plumbing.
Using 빠지다 transitively (물을 빠지다); 빠지다 is intransitive → 물이 빠지다, and you remove blockage with 머리카락을 빼다.

structuredNuance.t: 욕실 바닥이나 세면대에서 물이 빠져나가는 그 구멍을 가리킵니다. 머리카락이 껴서 물이 안 빠지거나(머리카락을 빼다) 여름에 냄새가 올라오는 일이 잦아 청소·수리 화제로 단골입니다.
일상 대화에서는 비슷한 말 '하수구(下水口)'도 자주 씁니다. 굳이 나누자면 배수구는 집 안에서 물이 빠지는 구멍, 하수구는 그 물이 모여 흘러가는 바깥의 더 큰 하수 시설 쪽에 가깝지만, 일상에서는 거의 섞어 씁니다.
배수구(排水口)는 한자로 '밀어낼 배(排)·물 수(水)·입 구(口)', 곧 '물을 밀어내 보내는 구멍'입니다.
동사 짝이 영어와 달라 주의가 필요합니다. 물이 잘 빠질 때는 '물이 빠지다', 막힐 때는 '막히다'를 쓰며, 변기에서 쓰는 '물을 내리다'를 배수구에 그대로 가져다 쓰면 어색합니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 변기솔 means "toilet brush" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 변기솔 (byeongisol) means "toilet brush". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 변기솔 ("toilet brush"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 변기솔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 변기 (toilet) + 솔 (a native word for brush); the brush for scrubbing the bowl.

usagePhrases.en: to scrub with a toilet brush
usagePhrases.note: (으)로 marks the tool; 닦다 = to scrub/wipe a surface clean.

usagePhrases.en: to clean the toilet with the brush
usagePhrases.note: 청소하다 = to clean (a space/object); pairs with 세제 (cleaning agent).
더럽다 = dirty; being a hygiene item, people replace it regularly.

examples.en: I put cleaner on the toilet brush and scrubbed hard.
examples.note: 박박 mimics vigorous scrubbing; 세제 = detergent/cleaner, 묻히다 = to apply onto.

examples.en: The toilet brush is kept hung up in the corner of the bathroom.
examples.note: 걸어 두다 = to leave (it) hanging; -아 두다 = to do and keep in that state.

examples.en: The toilet brush was too worn out, so I bought a new one.
examples.note: 낡다 = to be old/worn (of objects); 새로 = newly/anew (an adverb, not a noun).

extendedVocab.nuance: 변기솔은 '변기(便器)'에 순우리말 '솔(brush)'을 붙인 합성어로, 변기 안쪽을 문질러 닦는 솔을 말합니다. '변기 청소솔'이라고도 합니다. 솔과 비슷한 말로 '브러시'가 있지만, 화장실 청소 도구는 외래어 브러시보다 토박이말 '솔'을 붙인 변기솔이 훨씬 자연스럽습니다. 영어 화자가 주의할 점은 동사입니다. 표면을 문질러 닦는 행위는 '닦다(또는 문지르다)'이고, 물로 헹궈 씻는 '씻다'와는 다릅니다. 그래서 '변기솔로 변기를 씻다'보다 '변기솔로 변기를 닦다/청소하다'가 맞습니다. 보통 세제를 묻혀 박박 문질러 청소하며, 다이소 같은 곳에서 받침대와 세트로 쉽게 살 수 있고, 위생용품이라 낡으면 새것으로 교체하는 것이 일반적입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 칫솔 (toothbrush) for it, even jokingly — the toilet brush is specifically 변기솔.
Pairing it with 씻다 (to wash with water); for scrubbing a surface the natural verb is 닦다 or 문지르다.
Treating 새로 as a noun ('a 새로'); 새로 is an adverb meaning 'anew', so it's 새로 샀어요, while 'a new one' as a noun is 새것.

structuredNuance.t: 변기 안쪽을 문질러 닦는 솔을 말합니다. '변기 청소솔'이라고도 합니다. 보통 세제를 묻혀 박박 문질러 청소하며, 다이소 같은 곳에서 받침대와 세트로 쉽게 살 수 있고, 위생용품이라 낡으면 새것으로 교체하는 것이 일반적입니다.

변기솔은 '변기(便器)'에 순우리말 '솔(brush)'을 붙인 합성어입니다.
영어 화자가 주의할 점은 동사입니다. 표면을 문질러 닦는 행위는 '닦다(또는 문지르다)'이고, 물로 헹궈 씻는 '씻다'와는 다릅니다. 그래서 '변기솔로 변기를 씻다'보다 '변기솔로 변기를 닦다/청소하다'가 맞습니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 샤워커튼 means "shower curtain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "shower curtain" is 샤워커튼 (syawokeoteun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 샤워커튼 ("shower curtain"). Watch the particle attached to 샤워커튼 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Hung to keep water from splashing across the rest of the bathroom.
치다 here = to put up / draw a curtain across; the verb for closing curtains.

usagePhrases.en: to pull the shower curtain open
usagePhrases.note: 걷다 (here 'to draw back') = to gather/open a curtain; the opposite of 치다.

usagePhrases.en: mold grows on the shower curtain
usagePhrases.note: 곰팡이가 피다 = mold forms (피다, lit. 'to bloom'); very common in a damp bathroom.

examples.ko: 물 튀니까 샤워커튼 좀 쳐 줄래요?
examples.romanization: mul twinikka syawokeoteun jom chyeo jullaeyo?
examples.en: Water splashes, so could you draw the shower curtain?
examples.note: 튀다 = to splash; -아 줄래요? softly asks a favor. 치다 → 쳐 (draw it closed).

examples.en: Mold grew on the shower curtain, so I replaced it.
examples.note: 곰팡이가 피다 → 피어서; in speech this contracts to 펴서. 바꾸다 = to replace.

examples.ko: 한국 욕실은 보통 칸막이가 없어서 샤워커튼을 달아요.
examples.romanization: hanguk yoksireun botong kanmagiga eopseoseo syawokeoteuneul darayo.
examples.en: Korean bathrooms usually have no partition, so people hang a shower curtain.
examples.note: 칸막이 = partition; 달다 = to install/hang (a fixture).

extendedVocab.nuance: 샤워커튼은 '샤워(shower) + 커튼(curtain)'을 들여온 외래어로, 샤워할 때 물이 욕실 전체로 튀지 않게 막아 주는 커튼입니다. 영어 화자가 가장 헷갈리는 부분은 여닫는 동사입니다. 영어는 open/close로 끝나지만 한국어는 커튼을 칠 때 '치다(쳐서 닫다)', 열 때 '걷다(걷어서 열다)'를 쓰며, 문에 쓰는 '닫다/열다'를 커튼에 그대로 쓰면 어색합니다(특히 '커튼을 닫다'는 부자연스럽습니다). 또 그냥 '커튼'이라고만 하면 창문 커튼과 헷갈리니 욕실용은 '샤워커튼'으로 분명히 말하는 것이 좋습니다. 한국 욕실은 유리 칸막이(샤워부스)가 없는 집이 많아 샤워커튼을 다는 경우가 흔하고, 습기 때문에 곰팡이가 잘 피어서(말할 때는 흔히 '펴서') 자주 빨거나 교체하는 것이 좋습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 닫다 for a curtain — Koreans say 커튼을 치다 (draw closed) and 걷다 (draw open); 커튼을 닫다 sounds off.
Calling it just 커튼; without 샤워- it suggests a window curtain, so specify 샤워커튼 for the bathroom one.
Saying 곰팡이가 나다; the set phrase is 곰팡이가 피다 (lit. mold 'blooms'), and in careful writing keep 피다, not the casual 펴다.

structuredNuance.t: 샤워할 때 물이 욕실 전체로 튀지 않게 막아 주는 커튼입니다. 한국 욕실은 유리 칸막이(샤워부스)가 없는 집이 많아 샤워커튼을 다는 경우가 흔하고, 습기 때문에 곰팡이가 잘 피어서(말할 때는 흔히 '펴서') 자주 빨거나 교체하는 것이 좋습니다.
샤워커튼은 '샤워(shower) + 커튼(curtain)'을 들여온 외래어입니다.

영어 화자가 가장 헷갈리는 부분은 여닫는 동사입니다. 영어는 open/close로 끝나지만 한국어는 커튼을 칠 때 '치다(쳐서 닫다)', 열 때 '걷다(걷어서 열다)'를 쓰며, 문에 쓰는 '닫다/열다'를 커튼에 그대로 쓰면 어색합니다(특히 '커튼을 닫다'는 부자연스럽습니다). 또 그냥 '커튼'이라고만 하면 창문 커튼과 헷갈리니 욕실용은 '샤워커튼'으로 분명히 말하는 것이 좋습니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 욕실화 means "bathroom slippers" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 욕실화 (yoksilhwa) = "bathroom slippers". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 욕실화 ("bathroom slippers") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 욕실화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Rubber slippers worn only in the wet bathroom; 욕실 (浴室, bathroom) + 화 (靴, footwear).
신다 = to put on footwear (used for anything you wear on the feet).
갈아 신다 = to change footwear; you swap into them at the bathroom door.
미끄럽다 = slippery; worn-down soles make them a fall risk.

examples.en: Put on the bathroom slippers when you go into the bathroom.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 = when (doing); a standard house rule in many Korean homes.

examples.en: The soles of the bathroom slippers are worn, so I keep slipping.
examples.note: 닳다 = to wear down; 자꾸 = repeatedly; 미끄러지다 = to slip (the action).

examples.en: I bought a pair of bathroom slippers at Daiso.
examples.note: 켤레 = the counter for pairs of footwear (one 켤레 = one pair).

extendedVocab.nuance: 욕실화(浴室靴)는 한자로 '목욕할 욕(浴)·방 실(室)·신 화(靴)', 곧 '욕실에서 신는 신발'이라는 뜻입니다. 끝의 '-화(靴)'는 운동화, 실내화처럼 '신발'을 뜻하는 한자라 단어 구조를 알면 외우기 쉽습니다. 비슷한 말 '슬리퍼'와 비교하면, 슬리퍼는 마른 실내에서 신는 일반 실내화 전반을 가리키고, 욕실화는 물기 있는 욕실 전용 고무 슬리퍼라는 점이 다릅니다. 영어 화자가 주의할 두 가지: 첫째, 신발은 '입다'가 아니라 '신다'를 씁니다('욕실화를 입다'는 틀림). 둘째, 켤레가 세는 단위라 '욕실화 한 개'가 아니라 '한 켤레'라고 해야 자연스럽습니다. 한국 집에서는 욕실 문 앞에 두고 들어갈 때 갈아 신는 경우가 많고, 바닥이 닳으면 미끄러워 주기적으로 교체합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting them with 개 — footwear comes in pairs counted with 켤레 → 욕실화 한 켤레.
Using 입다 for slippers; anything worn on the feet takes 신다 (욕실화를 신다), never 입다.
Wearing 욕실화 around the dry living space; they are meant only for the wet bathroom floor.

structuredNuance.t: '욕실에서 신는 신발'이라는 뜻입니다. 한국 집에서는 욕실 문 앞에 두고 들어갈 때 갈아 신는 경우가 많고, 바닥이 닳으면 미끄러워 주기적으로 교체합니다.
비슷한 말 '슬리퍼'와 비교하면, 슬리퍼는 마른 실내에서 신는 일반 실내화 전반을 가리키고, 욕실화는 물기 있는 욕실 전용 고무 슬리퍼라는 점이 다릅니다.
욕실화(浴室靴)는 한자로 '목욕할 욕(浴)·방 실(室)·신 화(靴)'입니다. 끝의 '-화(靴)'는 운동화, 실내화처럼 '신발'을 뜻하는 한자라 단어 구조를 알면 외우기 쉽습니다.
영어 화자가 주의할 두 가지: 첫째, 신발은 '입다'가 아니라 '신다'를 씁니다('욕실화를 입다'는 틀림). 둘째, 켤레가 세는 단위라 '욕실화 한 개'가 아니라 '한 켤레'라고 해야 자연스럽습니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 면봉 means "cotton swab (Q-tip)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 면봉 (myeonbong) means "cotton swab (Q-tip)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 면봉 ("cotton swab"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 면봉 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The small cotton-tipped stick; 면 (綿, cotton) + 봉 (棒, stick/rod).

usagePhrases.en: to clean one's ears with a swab
usagePhrases.note: 귀를 파다 = lit. 'to dig the ears', the idiomatic phrase for cleaning them; its most common use.
통 = the tub/canister counter they're sold and stored in.

usagePhrases.en: to dab (liquid) onto a cotton swab
usagePhrases.note: 묻히다 = to get/apply (liquid, medicine) onto the tip.

examples.en: After a shower I clean my ears with a cotton swab.
examples.note: -고 here = and then; both 귀를 닦다 (wipe) and 귀를 파다 (dig out) work for ears.

examples.en: I dabbed disinfectant on a cotton swab and put it on the wound.
examples.note: 소독약 = disinfectant; 바르다 = to apply onto skin (르-irregular: 발랐어요).

examples.ko: 면봉 다 썼으니까 한 통 더 사야겠어요.
examples.romanization: myeonbong da sseosseunikka han tong deo sayagesseoyo.
examples.en: I'm out of cotton swabs, so I should buy another tub.
examples.note: 다 쓰다 = to use up; -아야겠다 = I'd better / I think I should.

extendedVocab.nuance: 면봉(綿棒)은 한자로 '솜 면(綿)·막대 봉(棒)', 곧 '솜이 달린 막대'라는 뜻으로 단어만 봐도 모양이 그려집니다. 영어 'Q-tip(상표명)'이나 'cotton swab'에 해당하는 일상어입니다. 비슷해 보이는 말과 꼭 구분하세요. '솜'은 뭉친 솜덩어리(cotton ball), '화장솜'은 화장 지울 때 쓰는 납작한 패드, '면봉'은 막대 끝에 솜이 달린 것입니다. 쓰임은 보통 샤워 후 귀를 닦거나(귀를 파다), 화장을 세밀하게 정리하거나, 상처에 약을 바를 때입니다. 세는 단위가 '한 통'이라는 점도 영어 화자가 놓치기 쉬운데, 보통 통 단위로 사서 욕실이나 화장대에 두고 씁니다. 참고로 한국에서는 귀 안쪽을 면봉으로 너무 깊이 파지 말라는 권고도 흔합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it only with 개 — a package is normally counted as 한 통 (a tub/canister).
Confusing 면봉 (cotton swab on a stick) with 솜 (a cotton ball) or 화장솜 (a flat cosmetic pad).
Saying 귀를 청소하다 too literally; the idiomatic phrase Koreans use is 귀를 파다 (or 귀를 닦다).

structuredNuance.t: '솜이 달린 막대'라는 뜻으로, 영어 'Q-tip(상표명)'이나 'cotton swab'에 해당하는 일상어입니다. 쓰임은 보통 샤워 후 귀를 닦거나(귀를 파다), 화장을 세밀하게 정리하거나, 상처에 약을 바를 때입니다. 보통 통 단위로 사서 욕실이나 화장대에 두고 씁니다. 참고로 한국에서는 귀 안쪽을 면봉으로 너무 깊이 파지 말라는 권고도 흔합니다.
비슷해 보이는 말과 꼭 구분하세요. '솜'은 뭉친 솜덩어리(cotton ball), '화장솜'은 화장 지울 때 쓰는 납작한 패드, '면봉'은 막대 끝에 솜이 달린 것입니다.
면봉(綿棒)은 한자로 '솜 면(綿)·막대 봉(棒)', 곧 '솜이 달린 막대'라는 뜻으로 단어만 봐도 모양이 그려집니다.
세는 단위가 '한 통'이라는 점도 영어 화자가 놓치기 쉬운데, 보통 통 단위로 사서 욕실이나 화장대에 두고 씁니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 욕실매트 means "bath mat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "bath mat" is 욕실매트 (yoksilmaeteu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 욕실매트 ("bath mat"). Watch the particle attached to 욕실매트 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The mat outside the shower that soaks up water from your feet; also called 발매트.

usagePhrases.en: to lay down the bath mat
usagePhrases.note: 깔다 = to spread/lay out flat on the floor (the verb for mats, rugs, bedding).
젖다 = to get wet/soaked; once soaked it needs drying out.
빨다 = to launder (cloth items); you can toss it in the washing machine.

examples.ko: 샤워하고 나오면 욕실매트가 발을 닦아 줘요.
examples.romanization: syawohago naomyeon yoksilmaeteuga bareul dakka jwoyo.
examples.en: When you step out of the shower, the bath mat dries your feet.
examples.note: -(으)면 = when/if; 발을 닦다 here = to dry the feet (닦다 covers both wipe and dry).

examples.en: If the bath mat stays damp, mold grows.
examples.note: 눅눅하다 = damp/clammy; 곰팡이가 피다 → 펴요 in speech (standard 피어요).

examples.en: I wash the bath mat once a week.
examples.note: 일주일에 한 번 = once a week; 에 marks frequency-per-period here.

extendedVocab.nuance: 욕실매트는 '욕실(浴室) + 매트(mat)'로, 샤워 후 욕실 밖이나 문 앞에 깔아 발의 물기를 닦는 매트입니다. 발에 닿는 용도라 순우리말식으로 '발매트'라고도 자주 부릅니다. 비슷한 말 '카펫/러그'와 헷갈리면 안 됩니다. 카펫·러그는 거실 등 마른 공간을 덮는 깔개이고, 욕실매트는 물기를 흡수하는 욕실 전용입니다. 동사 선택에서 영어 화자가 자주 막히는데, 바닥에 펼쳐 놓는 행위는 '놓다'가 아니라 '깔다'를 씁니다(이불, 돗자리, 매트 모두 깔다). 젖은 채 두면 눅눅해지고 곰팡이가 잘 피어서(말할 때는 흔히 '펴서') 자주 말리거나 세탁기에 '빨아' 줘야 하며, 미끄럼 방지가 되는 제품을 많이 씁니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it 카펫/러그 — those are dry-room rugs; the absorbent bathroom one is 욕실매트 (or 발매트).
Using 놓다 to put it down; a flat floor covering is laid with 깔다 (욕실매트를 깔다), not 놓다.
Saying 씻다 for washing the mat; cloth items are laundered with 빨다 (빨아요), while 씻다 is for the body or dishes.

structuredNuance.t: 샤워 후 욕실 밖이나 문 앞에 깔아 발의 물기를 닦는 매트입니다. 발에 닿는 용도라 순우리말식으로 '발매트'라고도 자주 부릅니다. 젖은 채 두면 눅눅해지고 곰팡이가 잘 피어서(말할 때는 흔히 '펴서') 자주 말리거나 세탁기에 '빨아' 줘야 하며, 미끄럼 방지가 되는 제품을 많이 씁니다.
비슷한 말 '카펫/러그'와 헷갈리면 안 됩니다. 카펫·러그는 거실 등 마른 공간을 덮는 깔개이고, 욕실매트는 물기를 흡수하는 욕실 전용입니다.
욕실매트는 '욕실(浴室) + 매트(mat)'로 이루어진 말입니다.
동사 선택에서 영어 화자가 자주 막히는데, 바닥에 펼쳐 놓는 행위는 '놓다'가 아니라 '깔다'를 씁니다(이불, 돗자리, 매트 모두 깔다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 때수건 means "exfoliating (scrub) towel / Italy towel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 때수건 (ttaesugeon) = "exfoliating (scrub) towel / Italy towel". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 때수건 ("scrubbing towel") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 때수건, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 때 (dead skin/grime) + 수건 (手巾, towel); the rough mitt for scrubbing skin, a Korean staple.
(때를) 밀다 = to push/scrub off dead skin; the signature verb for this item.
Done at the 목욕탕/찜질방 or at home; 때 = the rolled-off grime you can see.
까칠까칠하다 = rough-textured — which is exactly the point of it.

examples.en: At the bathhouse I scrubbed my back with the scrub towel.
examples.note: 등 = back; 밀다 → 밀었어요. A classic 목욕탕 (public bath) activity.

examples.ko: 때수건으로 너무 세게 밀면 피부가 따가워요.
examples.romanization: ttaesugeoneuro neomu sege milmyeon pibuga ttagawoyo.
examples.en: If you scrub too hard with the towel, your skin stings.
examples.note: 세게 = hard/forcefully (from 세다); 따갑다 = to sting/smart.

examples.ko: 외국인 친구한테 때수건 쓰는 법 알려 줬어요.
examples.romanization: oegugin chinguhante ttaesugeon sseuneun beop allyeo jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I taught my foreign friend how to use a scrub towel.
examples.note: -는 법 = how to/the way to; -한테 = to (a person). A genuinely Korean cultural item.

extendedVocab.nuance: 때수건은 순우리말 '때(피부에 쌓인 묵은 각질·때)'와 한자어 '수건(手巾, 손 수·수건 건)'이 합쳐진 말로, 까칠한 천으로 묵은 각질을 밀어내는 한국 목욕 문화의 상징입니다. 영어로는 흔히 'Italy towel'이라 부르는데, 핵심은 전용 동사 '밀다'입니다. 영어 화자는 수건이니 'wipe'를 떠올려 '닦다'를 쓰기 쉽지만, 때수건의 동작은 물기를 닦는 '닦다'가 아니라 힘주어 문질러 각질을 벗기는 '(때를) 밀다'입니다. 또 일반 '수건(타월)'과 달리 부드럽지 않고 일부러 까칠하게 만든 점이 다릅니다. 보통 목욕탕이나 찜질방에서, 또는 집에서 샤워할 때 쓰며, 너무 세게 밀면 피부가 상하거나 따가울 수 있어 외국인이라면 사용법과 적당한 세기를 알아 두면 좋습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 닦다 with it — the action is 때를 밀다 (to scrub/push off), not 닦다 (which is wiping water away).
Treating it like a soft 수건/타월; 때수건 is deliberately rough (까칠까칠) for exfoliating, not for drying off.
Saying 때를 빼다 or 때를 지우다; the fixed collocation for dead skin is 때를 밀다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 보라색 means "purple" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 보라색 (borasaek) means "purple". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 보라색 ("purple"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 보라색 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Standalone color noun; works as 'the purple one' in shops
Color noun directly modifies the next noun — no particle, no -ㄴ ending
연- (薄, 'thin/pale') prefix makes any color softer

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the purple one, please
usagePhrases.note: -(으)로 = 'in/by that color', the natural way to pick a color

examples.en: Purple is my favorite color.
examples.note: 색 + 을/를 좋아해요 names a favorite; note Korean makes 'purple' the object, not the subject

examples.en: Does this T-shirt also come in purple?
examples.note: -도 ('also') is the shopping reflex for asking about another color option

examples.ko: 보라색이랑 분홍색 중에 뭐가 더 나아요?
examples.romanization: borasaegirang bunhongsaek junge mwoga deo naayo?
examples.en: Between the purple and the pink, which is better?
examples.note: N이랑 N 중에 = 'among these listed', casual spoken comparison

extendedVocab.nuance: 보라색 is the general cover-word for the whole purple range. The 색 part is the Sino-Korean 色 ('color') glued onto the native root 보라, so almost every Korean color noun is '[root] + 색'. The dividing line with neighbours matters: 자주색 (紫朱色) leans into a deep reddish wine-purple, while 연보라색 is the pale lilac on cosmetics and stationery, and crucially 보라색 is NOT a shade of 파란색 (blue) — Korean treats purple and blue as fully separate basic colors, unlike the loose English habit of calling things 'blue-ish purple'. Register is neutral: 보라색 is fine in any setting. The classic English-speaker pitfall is grammar, not vocabulary: you do not say 보라색은 가방 ('purple-TOPIC bag'); the color noun sits bare right in front — 보라색 가방. Treat 보라색 like an adjective-noun in English ('purple bag') and just stack the two nouns.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding a particle or ending between color and noun, e.g. 보라색은 가방 or 보라색의 가방 — for a plain 'purple bag' the color noun attaches bare: 보라색 가방.
Filing 보라색 under 파란색 as if it were 'a kind of blue' — in Korean purple and blue are distinct basic colors, so 'bluish purple' must still be 보라색, not 파란색.
Over-using bare 보라 — dropping 색 happens in fast casual speech, but the safe, complete color noun a learner should default to is 보라색.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 분홍색 means "pink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "pink" is 분홍색 (bunhongsaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분홍색 ("pink"). Watch the particle attached to 분홍색 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Native-rooted standard word; the loanword 핑크 is equally common
Color noun stacks straight onto the noun it describes
연- (薄) = pale; opposite vibe from 형광 핑크 (neon pink)

usagePhrases.en: Got a color other than pink?
usagePhrases.note: N 말고 = 'not N (but something else)', asking for an alternative

examples.en: The cherry blossoms are pink, so they're really pretty.
examples.note: 이라서 = 'because it IS (a color)'; this -이라서 form is for nouns

examples.en: I painted my daughter's room pink.
examples.note: 색으로 칠하다 = 'paint (it) a color'; the -(으)로 marks the resulting color

examples.en: Red suits you better than pink.
examples.note: N보다 더 = comparison; 어울리다 = 'suits', a high-frequency clothing verb

extendedVocab.nuance: 분홍색 is the everyday word for pink and trades places freely with the English loanword 핑크, which sounds a touch trendier in fashion and beauty talk (립스틱 색, 네일). The first half 분홍 is itself Sino-Korean (粉紅, literally 'powder-red'), so the word's own history already says 'pinkish red' — which is exactly why the key boundary is with 빨간색 (red): pink is a separate color noun, not 'light red', and Koreans will not understand 연한 빨간색 as 'pink'. Tone-wise the word carries no built-in 'girly' baggage; the vibe comes from the shade — soft 연분홍색 vs loud 형광 핑크 (neon pink). The English-speaker pitfall is two-pronged: don't reach for 빨간색 to mean pink, and remember the 'because it is' reason form for a noun is N이라서 / N이어서 (분홍색이라서), never the verb-style 분홍색해서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling pink 빨간색 or 연한 빨간색 ('light red') — pink is its own color noun, 분홍색 (or 핑크), and 'light red' will not be read as pink.
Saying 분홍색이고 예뻐요 to mean 'it's pink so it's pretty' — the reason form for a noun is 분홍색이라서/이어서, while -이고 just lists ('it's pink AND pretty').
Treating 핑크 as slangy or wrong — it is fully standard in everyday and commercial Korean, so don't 'correct' it to 분홍색 in casual speech.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 회색 means "gray" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 회색 (hoesaek) = "gray". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회색 ("gray") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 회색, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday neutral; extremely common for clothing
Color + clothing item, a staple combo in real speech
진- (津) = deep/dark shade prefix
계열 (系列) = 'lineage of colors', used when matching outfits

examples.ko: 오늘 하늘이 회색이라 비 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: oneul haneuri hoesaegira bi ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: The sky is gray today, so it looks like it'll rain.
examples.note: 올 것 같아요 = 'looks like it will', a soft guess

examples.en: A gray suit is the safest choice.
examples.note: 무난하다 = 'safe/inoffensive', the go-to clothing compliment

examples.en: Which should I buy, gray or black?
examples.note: -ㄹ까요? asks the listener to weigh in on a decision

extendedVocab.nuance: 회색 is the default neutral of Korean wardrobes and interiors, so often it gets the praise 무난하다 ('safe, fail-proof, won't clash'). The 회 here is Sino-Korean 灰 ('ash'), so the word literally means 'ash-color' — a useful memory hook and a reminder that, like English, Korean stretches 회색 figuratively to an overcast mood or a dreary 'gray' day. Shades split into 연회색 (light gray) and 진회색 or the loanword 차콜 (charcoal). Two pitfalls hit English speakers. First, pronunciation: 회 is a single rounded 'hwe' syllable (close to 'hweh'), not 'hoe-ee' in two beats. Second, category: 회색 is its own neutral, NOT a kind of 흰색/하얀색 (white) — saying 밝은 흰색 won't mean 'light gray'; use 연회색.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Splitting 회 into two beats ('hoe-ee'); it's one rounded syllable, roughly 'hwe', so 회색 ≈ 'hwe-saek'.
Treating gray as 'light white' (밝은 흰색) — gray is the separate noun 회색, and a pale gray is 연회색, never a shade of 흰색.
Using 회색 for a person being 'gray/unwell' the English way — for a pale, sickly face Koreans say 안색이 안 좋다 ('complexion isn't good'), not 얼굴이 회색이에요.
