extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 갈색 means "brown" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 갈색 (galsaek) means "brown". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 갈색 ("brown"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 갈색 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: All-purpose brown: hair, leather, wood, coffee
The default way to describe brown hair
진- (津) = darker; the safe word for very dark brown hair (not 검은색)
밝은 ('bright/light') + color; common at the hair salon

examples.en: I dyed my hair brown.
examples.note: 색으로 염색하다 = 'dye (it) a color'; -(으)로 marks the new color

examples.ko: 갈색 구두가 이 바지랑 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: galsaek guduga i bajirang jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: Brown shoes go well with these pants.
examples.note: N(이)랑 잘 어울리다 = 'goes well with N'

examples.en: When you roast coffee beans, they turn brown.
examples.note: 색이 되다 = 'become/turn (a color)'; 색을 되다 is wrong

extendedVocab.nuance: 갈색 is your default, all-purpose brown for hair, leather, wood, and coffee. The 갈 is Sino-Korean 褐 ('brown, coarse cloth'), so it's literally 'brown-color', and it sits in the medium-to-dark band of the brown range. Know its two neighbours: 밤색 (栗色, 'chestnut-color') specifically names a warm reddish-brown loved for hair and shoes, and for pale tan tones people borrow 베이지(색) instead. The big English-speaker pitfalls are at the dark and light edges. At the dark end, very dark brown hair is 진갈색, not 검은색 (black) — Koreans hear those as different colors. At the light end, blonde is NOT 노란색 (yellow); it's 금발 (金髮, 'gold-hair') for the hair itself or 밝은 갈색 for dyed light-brown. Grammar-wise, use 갈색이 되다 ('become brown'), since 되다 takes the subject particle 이/가, not 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling very dark brown hair 검은색 — Korean separates 진갈색 (dark brown) from 검은색 (black); pick 진갈색 for dark-but-not-black hair.
Translating blonde as 노란색 (yellow) — natural Korean is 금발 (the hair) or 밝은 갈색 (a dyed light brown), never 노란색 머리.
Saying 갈색을 돼요 for 'turns brown' — 되다 ('become') takes 이/가, so it must be 갈색이 돼요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 남색 means "navy (deep blue)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "navy (deep blue)" is 남색 (namsaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 남색 ("navy / deep indigo-blue"). Watch the particle attached to 남색 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The dark end of blue; standard in suits and uniforms
Classic formal-wear color
네이비 swaps in freely in fashion contexts
계열 (系列) = color family, used when matching pieces

examples.en: A navy suit is a safe choice for an interview.
examples.note: N 때(는) = 'when it comes to (the occasion of) N'

examples.ko: 이 가방 검은색 말고 남색으로 살래요.
examples.romanization: i gabang geomeunsaeng malgo namsaegeuro sallaeyo.
examples.en: I'll buy this bag in navy, not black.
examples.note: N 말고 = 'not N (but ~)', swapping the chosen option

examples.en: Navy looks more composed than blue.
examples.note: 더 ~ 보여요 = 'looks more ~'; 차분하다 = calm/subdued

extendedVocab.nuance: 남색 is the deep, near-ink blue of school uniforms, business suits, and dark denim. The 남 is Sino-Korean 藍 ('indigo', the dye plant), so the word literally means 'indigo-color' — a good reminder that it lives at the DARK end of blue, the opposite pole from 하늘색 (sky blue). Against everyday 파란색 (a saturated mid-blue), 남색 reads as more formal and 차분하다 ('calm, composed'), which is exactly why it dominates uniforms and interview wear; younger shoppers often just say the loanword 네이비. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't merge 남색 with 파란색 — they are not interchangeable, and a navy suit described as 파란색 정장 will sound like a bright-blue suit. extendedVocab.nuance: 하늘색 is the soft, pale blue of a clear sky, and unlike most color words its first half is the native noun 하늘 ('sky'), not a Sino-Korean root — so it's literally 'sky-color', a perfect built-in mnemonic. Confusing the color noun with the sky itself — a clear sky is 하늘이 맑아요, not 하늘색이 맑아요 (that would be talking about the paint color being 'clear').

extendedVocab.explanation: 동그라미 (donggeurami) means "circle". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 동그라미 ("circle / round shape"). Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday native word for a circle (vs. formal 원)
그리다 = 'draw', the natural verb for shapes on paper

usagePhrases.en: to circle / mark with a circle
usagePhrases.note: 치다 here = 'put/strike a mark', a fixed collocation
On tests a 동그라미 means 'correct', the Korean 'O'

examples.en: Circle the correct answer.
examples.note: N에 동그라미를 치다 = 'put a circle ON N'; the surface takes 에

examples.en: The child drew a circle on the paper.
examples.note: 그리다 (draw) vs 치다 (mark): drawing a shape uses 그리다

examples.note: 가위표 ('scissor mark', X) is the partner of 동그라미

extendedVocab.nuance: 동그라미 is the warm, everyday native word for a circle (built on the adjective 동그랗다, 'round'), while 원 (圓, 'circle') is the formal/mathematical term you'd meet in geometry class — so a kid draws a 동그라미 but a textbook discusses 원의 넓이 ('the area of a circle'). The big cultural pitfall for English speakers is the GRADING SYSTEM: in Korea a 동그라미 (O) means 'correct' and an X (called 가위표 or 엑스) means 'wrong' — the O/X habit, not the American check-and-cross, so a circle here is never a neutral doodle but a clear 'yes/right'. Watch the two different verbs and particles: you 그리다 ('draw') a circle as a shape, but you 치다 ('mark') a circle onto an answer, and the thing you mark on takes 에 (정답에 동그라미를 치다).

Reaching for 원 in casual speech — for an ordinary round shape Koreans say 동그라미; save 원 for math/geometry.
Using 그리다 when you mean 'mark/circle an answer' — drawing the shape is 동그라미를 그리다, but circling a choice is 동그라미를 치다.
Reading a circle mark as neutral or as 'wrong' — in Korea 동그라미 (O) specifically means 'correct', and X (가위표) means 'wrong'.

모양 ('shape') attaches to the shape word
그리다 = 'draw'
On answers, 세모 = 'half right / maybe'

examples.note: 모양으로 자르다 = 'cut INTO a (shape)'; -(으)로 marks the resulting form

examples.note: N(이)라서 = 'because it IS (a noun)'

extendedVocab.nuance: 세모 is the friendly, kid-and-everyday word for a triangle, while 삼각형 (三角形, literally 'three-corner-shape') is reserved for math class and formal writing — the 모 in 세모/네모 is a native morpheme meaning 'corner/edge', so 세모 is intuitively 'three-corner'. Misreading a 세모 grading mark as 'wrong' — it signals 'partially right / borderline', between 동그라미 (correct) and X (wrong).

모양 = 'shape'

칸 = a cell on a form or grid

extendedVocab.nuance: 네모 is the casual native word that loosely covers BOTH squares and rectangles — like 세모, its 모 means 'corner', so 네모 is intuitively 'four-corner'. When you must be precise, the math terms split it: 정사각형 (正四角形, 'regular four-corner-shape') is a true square and 직사각형 (直四角形, 'right-angle four-corner-shape') is a rectangle. Also note 네모 칸 is the everyday term for a fill-in box on a form, so 'write it in the box' is 네모 칸에 쓰다, where the box takes 에 (or 안에 for 'inside').

Assuming 네모 means only a perfect square — colloquially it covers rectangles too; for a true square specify 정사각형, for a rectangle 직사각형.
Building 'square-shaped' as 네모적인 or 네모스러운 — the correct modifier comes from 네모나다, giving 네모난 (e.g. 네모난 상자).
Saying 네모를 쓰다 for 'fill in the box' — you write IN it: 네모 칸에 쓰다 (or 네모 칸 안에 쓰다).

extendedVocab.explanation: 줄무늬 (julmunui) means "stripes / striped pattern". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 줄무늬 ("stripes / striped pattern"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 줄무늬 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 줄 (line) + 무늬 (pattern)
Pattern noun stacks onto the clothing item
가로 = 'horizontal/sideways'
세로 = 'vertical/lengthwise'

examples.en: The striped T-shirt looks neat.
examples.note: 깔끔해 보이다 = 'looks tidy/clean'

examples.ko: 저는 무늬 없는 옷보다 줄무늬가 좋아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun munui eopsneun otboda julmunuiga joayo.
examples.en: I prefer striped clothes to plain ones.
examples.note: 무늬 없는 = 'patternless/plain'; N보다 N이 좋다 = prefer

extendedVocab.nuance: 줄무늬 is a transparent native compound: 줄 ('line/cord') + 무늬 ('pattern, decorative design'), so it's literally 'line-pattern'. The base 무늬 is the general word for ANY surface pattern, which is the key to a whole family — 체크무늬 (check), 물방울무늬 (polka dot), 꽃무늬 (floral), 줄무늬 (stripe) — and that's why dropping 무늬 changes the meaning: bare 줄 just means 'a line/string', not the patterned look, so a 'striped shirt' must be 줄무늬 셔츠, not 줄 셔츠. Koreans casually pin down direction with 가로 ('horizontal') vs 세로 ('vertical') when it matters for fashion. The standout English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation: 무늬 is pronounced like '무니' (the ㅢ after a consonant collapses to ㅣ), so 줄무늬 sounds like 'jul-mu-ni', never 'mu-nui'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 줄 for a striped pattern — bare 줄 means 'a line/string'; the pattern word needs 무늬, i.e. 줄무늬.
Pronouncing 무늬 as 'mu-nui' — after a consonant the ㅢ collapses to ㅣ, so it sounds like '무니' (줄무늬 ≈ 'jul-mu-ni').
Translating 'striped' with an adjective form like 줄무늬적인 — Korean just stacks the pattern noun: 줄무늬 셔츠.

extendedVocab.nuance: 체크무늬 is a hybrid word — the English loan 체크 ('check') plus native 무늬 ('pattern') — and it covers the whole checked family from fine gingham to tartan plaid (Korean doesn't split 'plaid' vs 'check' the way English does). It leans warm and casual, strongly tied to autumn/winter clothing (flannel shirts, mufflers) and cozy homeware (blankets, tablecloths). The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the 체크 homonym trap: 체크무늬 is the PATTERN, but 체크(하다) means 'to check/verify/tick' something entirely — so 이거 체크해 주세요 means 'please check (verify) this', never 'make this plaid'. Also, as with all pattern words, keep the 무늬: drop it and 체크 alone tilts toward the 'verify' meaning, so for the fabric look use the full 체크무늬 (or 체크 패턴).

examples.ko: 우산에 물방울무늬가 있어서 비 올 때 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: usane mulbangulmunuiga isseoseo bi ol ttae jal eoullyeoyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: 물방울무늬 is the textbook word for polka dots, literally 'water-drop pattern' (물방울 'water drop' + 무늬 'pattern'), since each round dot looks like a droplet. In casual speech, though, most Koreans say 땡땡이(무늬), an onomatopoeic nickname (originally from Japanese 点々 'dots'), so recognizing both registers matters: 물방울무늬 is the neutral/written form, 땡땡이무늬 the everyday spoken one. The pattern reads as retro and 귀엽다 ('cute'), popular on dresses, blouses, and umbrellas. Two English-speaker pitfalls: don't calque polka dots as 점무늬 ('dot-pattern') — it's understandable but not what people actually say; use 물방울무늬 or 땡땡이무늬. And keep the 무늬: bare 물방울 means a single literal water drop, so 'a polka-dot dress' is 물방울무늬 원피스, not 물방울 원피스.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calquing polka dots as 점무늬 ('dot-pattern') — it's understandable but unnatural; say 물방울무늬 or casual 땡땡이무늬.
Dropping 무늬 and saying only 물방울 — that means a single water drop, not the pattern; the pattern is 물방울무늬.
Treating 땡땡이무늬 as wrong or slangy-bad — it's the normal everyday spoken form, just less formal than 물방울무늬.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그러나 means "however, but (formal/written)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그러나 (geureona) means "however, but (formal/written)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그러나 문제가 있어요 ("However, there is a problem"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그러나 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sentence-initial contrast, more formal than 하지만
Pairs naturally with the plain written ending -다 in reports
Dramatic reversal in essays and narration
Marks an unexpected turn in a written account

examples.en: It's a good idea. However, there's no money.
examples.note: Simple two-sentence flip; 그러나 always opens the second sentence

examples.ko: 회사는 빠르게 성장했어요. 그러나 직원들은 더 힘들어졌어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaneun ppareuge seongjanghaesseoyo. geureona jigwondeureun deo himdeureojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The company grew fast. However, the employees had it harder.
examples.note: Report or news-style contrast between two facts

examples.ko: 여러 번 시도했지만 모두 실패했다. 그러나 그는 멈추지 않았다.
examples.romanization: yeoreo beon sidohaetjiman modu silpaehaetda. geureona geuneun meomchuji anatda.
examples.en: He tried many times but failed every time. However, he did not stop.
examples.note: Narrative register: note the bookish -다 ending matching 그러나's tone

extendedVocab.nuance: 그러나 means 'however' and is the formal, written-register cousin of 하지만 and 그렇지만. Its dividing line from those: 하지만 is the neutral all-purpose 'but' that works in speech and writing, while 그러나 feels distinctly literary and shows up in news articles, reports, essays, editorials, and official notices; in casual chat it sounds stiff, where 근데 or 하지만 fit far better. A second crucial point for English speakers: 그러나 almost always STARTS a fresh sentence and does not glue two clauses together inside one sentence. English 'but' can sit mid-sentence ('I tried, but I failed'), so learners wrongly write 시도했어요 그러나 실패했어요; correct Korean either puts 그러나 after a full stop or uses the clause-internal ending -지만 (시도했지만 실패했어요). Treat 그러나 as a heading-level pivot, not an inline conjunction.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it in casual speech where it sounds bookish; with friends say 근데 or 하지만 instead of 그러나
Gluing two clauses with it mid-sentence (시도했어요 그러나 실패했어요); 그러나 must start a new sentence, while -지만 attaches inside one (시도했지만 실패했어요)

extendedVocab.english: then, in that case, if so
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그러면 means "then, in that case, if so" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "then, in that case, if so" is 그러면 (geureomyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그러면 이렇게 해요 ("Then let's do it this way"). Watch the particle attached to 그러면 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Then let's do it this way
usagePhrases.note: Drawing a next step from what was just said

usagePhrases.en: In that case it won't do / you mustn't
usagePhrases.note: 그러면 안 되다 is a fixed 'that's not allowed' phrase
Settling a plan based on the prior point
Asking for the next move given the situation

examples.en: You're hungry? Then I'll make ramyeon.
examples.note: Simple condition-then-action; reacts to what the other person said

examples.ko: 이 서류가 필요해요. 그러면 먼저 주민센터에 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: i seoryuga piryohaeyo. geureomyeon meonjeo juminsenteoe gaya haeyo.
examples.en: You need this document. In that case, you have to go to the community center first.
examples.note: Chains a required step to a stated need

examples.en: Does everyone agree? Then I'll proceed as is.
examples.note: Shows the everyday contraction 그럼 in real conversation

extendedVocab.nuance: 그러면 means 'then / in that case' and links a conclusion or next step to a condition that was just stated, with the logic 'if that's the situation, then this.' It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + -면 ('if'), so literally it is 'if it is so' — keeping that origin in mind explains why it always reacts to a premise. In fast speech it contracts to 그럼, which is identical in meaning and is what you'll actually hear most of the time. The key contrast for learners is against 그리고: 그러면 responds to a CONDITION ('if so, then...'), whereas 그리고 simply lists the NEXT EVENT in time ('and then'). So 'I woke up and then ate' is 일어났어요. 그리고 먹었어요 — using 그러면 there is wrong because nothing is conditional. Note too that the lookalike 그러면서 ('while doing so') is a different word and not a contraction of this one.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 그리고; 그러면 means 'in that case (conditional)' and reacts to a premise, while 그리고 means 'and then (time sequence)'
Forgetting that the natural spoken contraction is 그럼, not the full 그러면, in everyday talk
Mixing it up with 그러면서 ('while/as one does that'); that is a separate connector, not a casual form of 그러면

extendedVocab.english: so, that's why, what I mean is
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그러니까 means "so, that's why, what I mean is" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그러니까 내 말이 ("Exactly, that's what I'm saying") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: 그러니까 내 말이 is a strong 'I totally agree' phrase

usagePhrases.en: That's why I told you to be careful
usagePhrases.note: Drawing an 'I-told-you-so' conclusion
Stating the logical takeaway as advice

usagePhrases.en: So, what do you mean by that?
usagePhrases.note: Filler-like use to reorganize or push a thought

examples.en: They say it'll rain. So bring an umbrella.
examples.note: Simple: derives a piece of advice from a fact

examples.ko: 주말엔 사람이 많아요. 그러니까 평일에 가는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: jumaren sarami manayo. geureonikka pyeongire ganeun ge naayo.
examples.en: Weekends are crowded. That's why going on a weekday is better.
examples.note: Gives the reasoning behind a recommendation

examples.ko: 그러니까 제 말은, 지금 결정하지 말자는 거예요.
examples.romanization: geureonikka je mareun, jigeum gyeoljeonghaji maljaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: What I mean is, let's not decide right now.
examples.note: 그러니까 제 말은 restates and clarifies your own point

extendedVocab.nuance: 그러니까 means 'so / that's why' and presents what follows as the reason-driven result of what came before. It comes from 그렇다 + -(으)니까 ('because it is so'), and that -니까 root is the key to its flavor: -니까 is the 'because' that naturally leads into commands, requests, and urging, which is exactly why 그러니까 pairs so well with advice (일찍 자요) and 'I-told-you-so' lines. This is the sharp dividing line from near-synonym 그래서: 그래서 (from 그렇다 + -아서) merely REPORTS a result neutrally ('so, as a result'), and crucially 그래서 cannot head a command, while 그러니까 actively REASONS and PERSUADES and happily does. Beyond logic, 그러니까 is a heavy conversational filler — 그러니까 내 말이 means 'exactly, that's my point!' (strong agreement), and a trailing 그러니까... works like English 'I mean...' when you restate yourself. English speakers who treat it as a plain synonym of 그래서 miss both the urging nuance and these idiomatic uses.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 그래서; 그러니까 reasons/urges and can introduce a command (그러니까 일찍 자요), while 그래서 only reports a result and cannot head an order
Missing the agreement idiom 그러니까 내 말이, which means 'exactly!' not a literal 'so my words'
Overusing it to start every sentence; as a filler it's fine in speech but looks sloppy if it opens written sentences repeatedly

extendedVocab.english: on top of that, moreover, what's more
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 게다가 means "on top of that, moreover, what's more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 게다가 (gedaga) means "on top of that, moreover, what's more". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 게다가 비싸요 ("And on top of that, it's expensive"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 게다가 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: And on top of that, it's expensive
usagePhrases.note: Piling on one more (often negative) point

usagePhrases.en: What's more, even the weather is bad
usagePhrases.note: 게다가 ~까지 stacks an extra burden

usagePhrases.en: On top of that, it's free
usagePhrases.note: Adding a further positive selling point

usagePhrases.en: Plus, the place is close too
usagePhrases.note: 게다가 ~도 tacks on another advantage

examples.en: This restaurant is tasty. On top of that, it's cheap.
examples.note: Simple: stacks a second perk in the same positive direction

examples.en: I worked overtime. On top of that, I even missed the last train.
examples.note: 게다가 ~까지 piling on a worse second misfortune

examples.ko: 방이 넓어요. 게다가 월세도 싸서 바로 계약했어요.
examples.romanization: bangi neolbeoyo. gedaga wolsedo ssaseo baro gyeyakaesseoyo.
examples.en: The room is spacious. Plus the rent is cheap too, so I signed right away.
examples.note: 게다가 ~도 reinforcing a decision with an added reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 게다가 means 'on top of that / moreover / what's more,' adding a second point that pushes in the SAME direction as the first — two good things or two bad things stacking up to intensify the overall impression. Its defining contrast is with neutral 그리고 ('and'): 그리고 simply lists items with no emotional slope ('A and B'), while 게다가 conveys 'and as if that weren't enough, also B,' so swapping in a flat 그리고 throws away the cumulative punch. It habitually teams up with the particles 까지 ('even') and 도 ('also') on the added item — 게다가 비까지 와요 ('and on top of that it's even raining'), 게다가 집도 가까워요 — and learning that 게다가 ... 까지/도 frame is the fastest way to sound natural. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 게다가 to add a CONTRASTING point ('it's expensive, however...'); 게다가 cannot pivot, so a contrast needs 하지만 or 그런데 instead.

Using it to add a contrasting point; 게다가 only stacks same-direction points, so a reversal needs 하지만 or 그런데
Swapping it for a neutral 그리고; 게다가 specifically means 'and what's more', adding cumulative emphasis, not just listing
Forgetting the partner particles; natural 게다가 sentences usually carry 까지 or 도 on the added element (게다가 날씨까지 안 좋아요)

extendedVocab.explanation: "therefore, accordingly, thus (formal)" is 따라서 (ttaraseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 따라서 결론은 ("Therefore, the conclusion is"). usagePhrases.note: Leads into a formal conclusion
Draws a formal consequence in a notice (with -ㅂ니다)
Common in official announcements

usagePhrases.en: Therefore, it may be subject to change
usagePhrases.note: Notice-style logical follow-up

examples.ko: 오늘은 휴일입니다. 따라서 은행은 문을 닫습니다.
examples.romanization: oneureun hyuirimnida. ttaraseo eunhaengeun muneul datseumnida.
examples.en: Today is a holiday. Therefore the bank is closed.
examples.note: Simple formal cause-effect, paired with -ㅂ니다 style

examples.en: The documents are incomplete. Accordingly, we cannot accept the application.
examples.note: Administrative, official register

examples.ko: 규정이 바뀌었습니다. 따라서 모두 다시 신청하셔야 합니다.
examples.romanization: gyujeongi bakkwieotseumnida. ttaraseo modu dasi sincheonghasyeoya hamnida.
examples.en: The rules have changed. Therefore, everyone must reapply.
examples.note: Announcing a required consequence in a notice

extendedVocab.nuance: 따라서 means 'therefore / accordingly / thus' and is the formal, logical 'so' of reports, public notices, instructions, contracts, and academic writing. It states a conclusion that follows STRICTLY and objectively from the prior statement, with a more official, impersonal tone than either 그래서 (plain spoken 'so') or 그러니까 (reasoning/urging 'so'). The dividing line: 그래서 and 그러니까 belong to everyday speech and can carry personal feeling or persuasion, whereas 따라서 is detached and rule-like, so in casual conversation it sounds like you're reading a press release. It pairs naturally with the formal -ㅂ니다 ending and with 다음과 같이 ('as follows'). The classic English-speaker trap is mixing this connector up with the homograph verb form 따라서 from 따르다 ('to follow') — as in 규칙을 따라서 ('following the rule'). The connector stands ALONE at the head of a sentence with no object; the verb form has something being followed in front of it.

Using it in casual chat where it sounds like an official notice; in speech use 그래서 or 그러니까 instead
Confusing it with the verb 따르다 ('to follow'): the connector 따라서 stands alone sentence-initially, while 규칙을 따라서 means 'following the rule'
Pairing it with the casual 요-ending; 따라서 belongs to the formal -ㅂ니다 register (따라서 주의가 필요합니다)

examples.romanization: wolgeubeun neureonan banmyeone ireun hwolssin manajyeosseoyo.

examples.note: Shows the bound form -ㄴ 반면에 joining the two sides in one sentence

extendedVocab.nuance: 반면에 means 'on the other hand / whereas / by contrast' and explicitly sets two distinct sides, options, or qualities against each other. It comes from the Sino-Korean noun 반면 (反面, literally 'opposite + face/side,' i.e. 'the reverse side') plus the location particle 에 — so its very composition is 'on the opposite side,' which is why it demands a clear A and a clear B to weigh. This is its dividing line from 그런데/근데: those handle a single-topic surprise or twist ('I went out, but it was closed'), whereas 반면에 is analytical and comparative, ideal for pros-and-cons and 'A is X, B is Y' contrasts. It also differs from 한편 in being a sharper head-to-head contrast rather than a loose scene-shift. Note it has two shapes: as a free adverb starting a sentence (반면에 단점도 있어요) and as a bound clause ending -는/은 반면에 attached to the previous verb/adjective (비싼 반면에 'while it's expensive'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping it onto a one-sided remark where there's no real B to contrast — without two sides, 반면에 has nothing to balance and sounds incomplete.

Using it for a single-situation surprise; that twist needs 그런데/근데, while 반면에 specifically compares two separate sides
Stating only one side; 반면에 needs a clear A and B, or the contrast has nothing to balance
Confusing the two forms; the standalone adverb is 반면에 (new sentence), but inside one sentence it attaches as -는/은 반면에 (비싼 반면에)

extendedVocab.nuance: 즉 means 'that is / in other words / namely' and introduces a RESTATEMENT or precise clarification of what you just said — never new information, only the same point re-expressed more sharply or simply. It is a single Sino-Korean syllable from the hanja 卽 ('namely, that is to say'), and that one-syllable crispness gives it a slightly formal, definitional ring that suits writing, explanations, legal/technical text, and definitions. The contrast to watch: do not confuse 즉 with 그리고 ('and'), which ADDS a separate item; 즉 re-explains, so if what follows is genuinely new content, 즉 is wrong. It overlaps heavily with 다시 말해 ('in other words'), but 즉 is terser and more bookish while 다시 말해 feels more conversational. Punctuation-wise it almost always takes a comma right after it (즉,) and pairs naturally with the nominalizing tails ...라는 거예요 / ...뜻이에요. In very casual chat it can feel clipped, where 그러니까 or 말하자면 sound friendlier.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it to add new information; 즉 only re-explains the same point, so anything genuinely new needs 그리고 instead
Overusing it in very casual speech; in chat 그러니까 or 말하자면 sound more natural than the bookish 즉
Dropping the comma; standard style writes 즉, with a comma before the restatement

extendedVocab.nuance: 다시 말해 literally breaks down as 다시 ('again') + 말해 (the connective form of 말하다, 'to speak'), so its bones say 'speaking again,' working exactly like English 'in other words.' It introduces a clearer, blunter, or more interpretive rephrasing of what you just said, and the fuller form 다시 말해서 is just as common and fully interchangeable. Its near-twin is 즉: both restate, but 다시 말해 is a touch more conversational and explanatory in feel, whereas 즉 is terser and more bookish — so when softly walking a listener through a confusing point, 다시 말해 sounds warmer. The pitfall for English speakers is the surface resemblance to the plain verb phrase 다시 말하다 meaning 'to say (it) again' i.e. to literally repeat the same words; 다시 말해 as a connector does NOT mean verbatim repetition — it signals a reworded explanation, the same idea recast, not the identical sentence said twice.

Adding brand-new information after it; like 즉, it must restate the same idea, just more clearly
Writing it as one word 다시말해; standard spacing keeps 다시 말해 (and 다시 말해서) as two words

examples.note: Introducing illustrative activities, here with 도 ... 도

extendedVocab.nuance: 예를 들어 means 'for example / for instance' and is the everyday way to introduce a concrete case of a general statement. It is built from the Sino-Korean noun 예 (例, 'example') plus the verb 들다 here meaning 'to raise/cite,' so it literally reads 'raising an example' — the same 들다 as in 손을 들다 ('raise one's hand'). Because it is genuinely a verb phrase, you can flex it: 예를 들어 볼게요 ('let me give an example'), 예를 들어서 (longer connective form), or 예를 들면 ('if one takes an example'), all natural and interchangeable. It works in every register, from chat to academic writing, which makes it one of the most reliable connectors for explaining yourself. The English-speaker pitfalls are two spelling traps: never close up the space (the standard is 예를 들어, not 예를들어), and never blend the variant endings into the non-word 예를 들어면 — the valid forms are 예를 들어 / 예를 들어서 / 예를 들면 only.

Writing it with no space as 예를들어; the standard spacing is 예를 들어 (and 예를 들어서)
Blending the endings into the incorrect 예를 들어면; the valid forms are 예를 들어, 예를 들어서, and 예를 들면
Pluralizing it like English 'examples'; Korean keeps the singular 예 here, e.g. 예를 들어, not 예들을 들어

Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그럼에도 불구하고 ("in spite of that, nevertheless"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그럼에도 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 그럼에도 불구하고 is the set, emphatic full form

usagePhrases.en: Even so, I didn't give up
usagePhrases.note: Pressing on despite an obstacle
Sticking to a decision against the odds

usagePhrases.en: Even so, the result was good
usagePhrases.note: An unexpected upside after difficulty

examples.en: It was hard. Even so, I finished it to the end.
examples.note: Simple: persistence despite a stated difficulty

examples.ko: 월급이 적어요. 그럼에도 이 일을 계속하는 이유가 있어요.
examples.romanization: wolgeubi jeogeoyo. geureomedo i ireul gyesokaneun iyuga isseoyo.
examples.en: The pay is low. Nevertheless, there's a reason I keep this job.
examples.note: Introduces a clause that defies expectation

extendedVocab.nuance: 그럼에도 means 'even so / nevertheless / despite that' and signals that what follows happens AGAINST the obstacle just mentioned. It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + the concessive ending -ㅁ에도 ('even though it is'), so structurally it is 'even though it is so.' It is most often heard in its set full form 그럼에도 불구하고 ('in spite of that' — 불구하고 from 不拘, 'not being bound by'), which adds gravity and is common in speeches, editorials, and formal writing. The dividing line to learn is against everyday 그래도: 그래도 is the casual, neutral 'still / even so' you use with friends, while 그럼에도 carries an elevated, determined, slightly dramatic tone — choosing 그럼에도 in a light chat sounds like you've suddenly switched to a TED talk. So the English-speaker pitfall is register mismatch: reach for 그래도 in conversation and reserve 그럼에도 (불구하고) for emphatic or written contexts. Also memorize the fixed spelling 불구하고 — not the common mishearing 불구하구.

Using it for light casual contrast where 그래도 fits; 그럼에도 sounds formal, weighty, and determined
Misspelling the set phrase as 그럼에도 불구하구; the correct form is 그럼에도 불구하고
Treating 불구하고 as optional filler; it specifically means 'in spite of (not bound by)', so 그럼에도 불구하고 is the deliberate emphatic form, not a redundancy

extendedVocab.english: meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 한편 means "meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part" is 한편 (hanpyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한편, 다른 곳에서는 ("Meanwhile, elsewhere"). usagePhrases.note: Shifting the scene to a parallel situation
한편으로는 introduces one of two mixed feelings

usagePhrases.en: At the same time, I was also worried
usagePhrases.note: Adding a coexisting, contrasting feeling

examples.romanization: hoesaneun chaeyongeul juryeosseoyo. hanpyeon eommuryangeun deo neureosseoyo.
examples.en: The company cut hiring. Meanwhile, the workload only grew.
examples.note: News-style topic shift to a parallel development

extendedVocab.nuance: 한편 means 'meanwhile / on the other hand / for one's part' and shifts attention to a PARALLEL or co-existing situation rather than flatly contradicting the first. It is Sino-Korean, 한 (一, 'one') + 편 (便/篇, 'side'), literally 'one side' — so it frames the next thing as 'one side of the picture,' which is why it can introduce a simultaneous scene, not just an opposite. In news writing, a bare 한편, ... is the standard way to switch topics ('In other news, ...'). Its near-synonym is 반면에, and the dividing line matters: 반면에 (反面, 'opposite side') is a SHARP head-to-head A-vs-B contrast for weighing pros and cons, whereas 한편 is looser and more reportorial, often just panning the camera to a parallel event or adding a coexisting angle. Its most useful conversational life is the doubled frame 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는 (또는 다른 한편으로는), meaning 'part of me... but part of me...,' for mixed feelings. The English pitfall is treating 한편 as a plain 'but'; it does not negate the first clause, it sets a second view beside it.

Treating it as a flat 'but'; 한편 sets a parallel or coexisting view beside the first, it doesn't contradict it (use 하지만 for negation)

Forgetting the mixed-feelings frame 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는, which is its most natural conversational use

examples.en: Everyone tried to stop me, but in the end I did it my way.
examples.note: Stresses the eventual result despite opposition, with -는데

extendedVocab.nuance: 결국 means 'in the end / eventually / after all' and sums up the FINAL outcome reached after a process, delay, or struggle. It is Sino-Korean, 결 (結, 'to conclude/tie up') + 국 (局, 'situation/end stage'), literally 'the concluding stage' — so it inherently looks back over a whole drawn-out affair to its settling point. The dividing line from near-synonym 드디어 is important: 드디어 celebrates a happy, long-awaited result with relief and excitement ('finally, at last!'), whereas 결국 is emotionally NEUTRAL and frequently tinged with resignation or a sense that the outcome was inevitable ('it came to this after all'). A second contrast English speakers stumble on: 결국 is NOT the 'finally/lastly' that orders items in a list — that ordinal sense ('firstly... finally...') is 마지막으로. 결국 is about how a story RESOLVED, not where an item sits in a sequence. It commonly follows a lead-in clause with -지만 or -는데 sketching the struggle, and the variant 결국엔 (with topic 은) adds extra weight to the final beat.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it for 드디어; 결국 is neutral or resigned ('after all'), while 드디어 carries relief and celebration ('finally, at last!')
Using it for ordinal 'finally/lastly' in a list; that sequencing sense is 마지막으로, not 결국
Expecting it to mean a positive result; 결국 often hints the outcome was inevitable or disappointing, so pair it with context that fits

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이온음료 means "sports drink, electrolyte drink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이온음료 (ioneumnyo) means "sports drink, electrolyte drink". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이온음료 ("sports drink"). usagePhrases.note: 포카리스웨트, 파워에이드 등이 대표 브랜드
편의점에서 주문할 때; 음료는 병/캔이라 보통 '하나'로 셈

usagePhrases.en: When you sweat, a sports drink is good
usagePhrases.note: 운동 후·아플 때 흔히 권하는 말; -으면 = '~하면'

usagePhrases.en: For a hangover it's gotta be a sports drink
usagePhrases.note: 숙취 宿醉 '묵은 취기'(밤새 남은 술기운); -지가 '당연하지' 하는 아는 척 어감을 더함

examples.en: I drank a sports drink after working out.
examples.note: -고 나서 = '~한 뒤에'; 동작 순서를 분명히 함

examples.ko: 몸살 났을 때 물보다 이온음료가 더 나아요.
examples.romanization: momsal nasseul ttae mulboda ioneumnyoga deo naayo.
examples.en: When you have body aches, a sports drink is better than water.
examples.note: 비교의 '보다'는 더 좋은 쪽 앞이 아니라 '물보다'처럼 기준 뒤에 붙음

examples.ko: 편의점에서 이온음료 한 병 사 왔어.
examples.romanization: pyeonuijeomeseo ioneumnyo han byeong sa wasseo.
examples.en: I grabbed a bottle of sports drink from the convenience store.
examples.note: 한 병 = 한 단위의 병; 반말 '사 왔어'는 친구 사이

extendedVocab.nuance: 이온음료(ion飮料, '이온+마실 거리')는 땀으로 빠진 전해질을 보충하는 스포츠 음료로 포카리스웨트가 대표격이다. 영어 화자는 보통 'Gatorade'라는 상표명으로 뭉뚱그리지만 한국에서는 운동뿐 아니라 숙취·몸살에도 일상적으로 마신다는 점이 다르다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃 단어는 에너지음료(핫식스·레드불)인데, 이온음료는 카페인이 거의 없고 '각성'이 아니라 '수분·전해질 보충'이 목적이라는 게 결정적 경계선이다. 또 비슷해 보이는 음료수는 '마시는 음료 전반'을 뜻하는 더 넓은 말이라, 이온음료가 음료수의 한 종류다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '이온음료를 마시다 / 이온음료 한 병', 그리고 '땀 흘리고 ~, 숙취엔 ~'. 영어식으로 'ion drink'라고 직역하면 한국에선 통해도 영어권에선 안 통하니, 영어로 옮길 땐 sports/electrolyte drink로 바꿔야 한다.

에너지음료(레드불·핫식스)와 혼동하면 안 됨 — 이온음료는 카페인으로 각성시키는 게 아니라 수분·전해질을 채우는 음료라 목적이 정반대다.
한 단어 '이온음료'로 쓴다. '이온 음료수'처럼 띄우거나 음료수를 덧붙이면 어색하다.
마실 때 동사는 '먹다'보다 '마시다'가 자연스럽다 — '이온음료를 마시다'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매실차 means "green plum tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "green plum tea" is 매실차 (maesilcha). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매실차 ("green plum tea"). usagePhrases.note: 매실청(매실 시럽)을 물에 타서 만든, 새콤달콤한 차
따뜻하게 = '따뜻한 상태로'; 가게에서 온도를 지정하는 표현

usagePhrases.ko: 소화 안 될 때 매실차 마셔
usagePhrases.romanization: sohwa an doel ttae maesilcha masyeo
usagePhrases.en: Drink plum tea when your digestion is off
usagePhrases.note: 매실은 소화에 좋다는 민간 통념; 반말 권유

usagePhrases.en: Plum tea is sweet and sour
usagePhrases.note: 새콤달콤 = 신맛+단맛이 어우러진 맛을 한 단어로

examples.en: My stomach was upset so I drank plum tea.
examples.note: 속 = 배 속·위장; -아서가 이유('속이 안 좋아서')를 이음

examples.en: This restaurant serves plum tea as a dessert drink.
examples.note: 후식(後食) '뒤에 먹는 것' = 디저트; 식당에서 흔함

examples.en: In summer I make plum tea cold (with the syrup).
examples.note: 타 먹다 = (가루·시럽을) 물에 풀어 마시다

extendedVocab.nuance: 매실차(梅實차, '매화나무 열매+차')는 매실청을 뜨거운 물이나 찬물에 타서 마시는 새콤달콤한 음료다. 영어 화자가 'tea'라는 말에 끌려 우려내는 허브티를 떠올리기 쉬운데, 매실차는 잎을 우리는 게 아니라 시럽을 희석한 것이라 본질이 다르다. 가장 가까운 이웃은 유자차로, 둘 다 '청(시럽)을 물에 타는 차'라는 점은 같지만 매실차는 새콤한 매실 맛에 소화제 이미지가 강하고 유자차는 달고 진한 감귤향에 감기 이미지가 강하다는 게 경계선이다. 재료인 매실 한 단어는 '열매' 자체를, 매실청은 '설탕에 절인 시럽'을, 매실차는 '그 시럽을 탄 음료'를 가리키므로 셋을 구분해야 한다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '매실차를 타다/마시다', '소화 안 될 때 ~', '후식으로 ~'. 푸짐한 식사 뒤 주인이 소화에 좋다며 내주기도 하고, 전통찻집 메뉴에서도 흔히 보인다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
매실(열매)과 매실차(음료)를 섞어 쓰면 안 됨 — 'I drank 매실'은 틀리고 마시는 것은 '매실차'다.
티백을 우리는 차로 오해하면 안 된다. 잎을 우린 게 아니라 시럽을 푼 것이라 단맛이 기본이다.
재료를 말할 땐 매실청(시럽), 마실 것을 말할 땐 매실차로 구별해서 써야 한다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 유자차 means "yuzu (citron) tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 유자차 (yujacha) = "yuzu (citron) tea". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 유자차 ("citron tea") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 유자차, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 유자청(유자 마멀레이드)을 뜨거운 물에 풀어 만든 차

usagePhrases.ko: 감기 기운 있을 때 유자차 마셔요
usagePhrases.romanization: gamgi giun isseul ttae yujacha masyeoyo
usagePhrases.en: Drink citron tea when you feel a cold coming on
usagePhrases.note: 감기 기운 = 감기 조짐; 비타민C가 많아 감기에 좋다는 통념
한 잔 = 컵·찻잔 단위; 따뜻한 음료는 보통 '잔'으로 셈

usagePhrases.en: Citron tea is good for a sore throat
usagePhrases.note: 목 = 목구멍; '목 아프다'는 인후통의 일상 표현

examples.en: My throat was scratchy so I made some citron tea.
examples.note: 칼칼하다 = 목이 까끌하고 따끔한 느낌

examples.en: In winter, warm citron tea is the best.
examples.note: 최고예요 = '제일 좋다'를 강조; 겨울 단골 음료

examples.ko: 마트에서 유자청 사면 집에서 유자차 만들 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: mateueseo yujacheong samyeon jibeseo yujacha mandeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you buy citron marmalade at the mart, you can make citron tea at home.
examples.note: 유자청 = 유자 마멀레이드/시럽; -으면 조건

extendedVocab.nuance: 유자차(柚子차, '유자 열매+차')는 유자청을 한 숟갈 떠서 뜨거운 물에 풀어 마시는, 걸쭉하고 단 겨울 음료다. 영어로 yuzu/citron tea라 하지만 잎을 우리는 차가 아니라 시럽·껍질을 물에 푼 것이라 컵 안에 유자 껍질 조각이 그대로 떠 있는 게 특징이다. 가장 가까운 이웃은 매실차로, 둘 다 '청을 물에 타는 차'지만 유자차는 달고 진한 감귤향에 감기·목 통증 이미지가, 매실차는 새콤한 맛에 소화 이미지가 강하다는 점이 갈린다. 또 재료인 유자청과 음료인 유자차를 구별해야 한다 — 냉장고에 유자청 한 병을 두고 떠 마시는 집이 많다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '유자차를 타다/마시다', '감기 기운 있을 때 ~', '목 아플 때 ~', '따뜻한 ~'. 추운 날 손을 녹이며 마시는 위안의 음료라는 정서가 단어에 배어 있다.

잎을 우린 차로 오해하면 안 됨 — 유자청(시럽·껍질)을 푼 것이라 컵 안에 껍질 건더기가 떠 있고 단맛이 기본이다.
헤드워드는 한 단어 '유자차'다. '유자 차'처럼 띄우면 어색하다.
재료는 유자청, 마실 것은 유자차로 구분 — '유자차를 사서 탄다'가 아니라 '유자청을 사서 유자차를 탄다'.

usagePhrases.note: 카페의 탄산 과일 음료: 레몬에이드, 자몽에이드, 청포도에이드
과일 이름+에이드로 종류를 말함; 자몽 = 그레이프프루트
탄산(炭酸) = 이산화탄소가 든 '거품/톡 쏘는' 성분

usagePhrases.en: I'll have an ade instead of coffee
usagePhrases.note: 말고 = '~이 아니라'; 비커피 음료를 고르는 흔한 표현

examples.en: The green-grape ade here is really good.

examples.en: When I go to a cafe, I only drink ade.
examples.note: -만 = '오직 ~만'; 커피를 안 마시는 사람의 말

extendedVocab.nuance: 에이드는 영어 접미사 '-ade(레몬에이드 등)'에서 온 외래어로, 카페에서 시럽과 탄산수를 섞어 얼음과 함께 내는 새콤달콤한 탄산 과일 음료를 통칭한다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 주스인데, 결정적 차이는 '탄산'이다 — 에이드는 톡 쏘는 거품이 있고 주스는 거품 없는 과즙 음료라, 탄산이 싫으면 에이드가 아니라 주스를 시켜야 한다. 또 모양이 비슷한 스무디와도 다르다: 스무디는 과일을 갈아 걸쭉한 반면 에이드는 맑은 탄산 음료다. 커피·차를 빼면 가장 인기 있는 선택지라, 커피를 못 마시는 사람이 카페에서 무난히 고르는 게 에이드다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '에이드를 시키다/마시다', '레몬·자몽·청포도+에이드', '시원한 ~'. 영어 화자가 'lemonade'를 떠올려 무탄산 레모네이드를 기대하면 어긋날 수 있는데, 한국 카페의 에이드는 대개 탄산이 든 점을 기억해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
철자는 그냥 '에이드'다 — '에이드음료'나 '에이드주스'처럼 군더더기를 붙이면 어색하다.
탄산 음료라는 점을 놓치면 안 됨 — 거품 없는 과일 음료를 원하면 에이드가 아니라 주스를 시켜야 한다.
영어 'lemonade' 감각으로 무탄산을 기대하면 안 된다 — 한국의 에이드는 보통 탄산이 들어간다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 스무디 means "smoothie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "smoothie" is 스무디 (seumudi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스무디 ("smoothie"). Watch the particle attached to 스무디 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 과일을 얼음과 갈아 만든 걸쭉한 카페 음료
하나요 = '하나 주세요'의 가벼운 줄임; 과일+스무디
갈다 = (믹서로) 갈다; -아서가 방법을 이음

usagePhrases.en: A smoothie and a frappuccino are different
usagePhrases.note: 랑 = '~와'; 스무디는 과일 베이스, 커피 없음

examples.ko: 과일 스무디 한 잔이면 아침 대신 돼요.
examples.romanization: gwail seumudi han janimyeon achim daesin dwaeyo.
examples.en: One fruit smoothie works as a breakfast replacement.
examples.note: 대신 되다 = 대체가 되다; -이면 조건

examples.en: The mango smoothie is the most popular here.
examples.note: 인기(人氣) '사람들의 좋아함' = 인기; 제일이 최상급

examples.en: The smoothie was so cold it gave me brain freeze.
examples.note: 머리가 띵하다 = 머리가 멍하게 얼얼하다(brain freeze)

extendedVocab.nuance: 스무디는 영어 smoothie를 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 과일을 얼음과 함께 믹서에 갈아 만든 걸쭉하고 차가운 음료다. 보통 과일 이름이 앞에 붙고(딸기 스무디, 망고 스무디) 띄어 쓰거나 붙여 써도 된다. 가장 헷갈리는 이웃은 셰이크인데, 스무디는 과일이 주재료이고 셰이크는 아이스크림·우유로 만든 더 진한 디저트 음료라는 점이 경계선이다. 또 모양은 비슷해도 커피를 간 음료는 스무디라 부르지 않고 프라푸치노·블렌디드라고 부르며, 맑은 탄산 과일 음료인 에이드와도 질감이 전혀 다르다. 카페에서 '건강한 느낌'으로 고르는 비커피 음료의 대표 격이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '스무디를 갈다/마시다', '딸기·망고+스무디', '한 잔'. 영어 화자가 'smoothie'를 부드러운 음료로 떠올려 우유 셰이크와 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 한국에서 스무디는 기본적으로 과일을 간 음료라는 점을 구분해야 한다.

커피를 간 블렌디드 음료를 스무디라 부르면 안 됨 — 그건 프라푸치노/블렌디드이고 스무디는 과일 베이스다.
고정 철자는 '스무디'다 — 체인 이름이 'Smoothie's'라 해도 '스무디스'라고 쓰지 않는다.
셰이크와 혼동 금물 — 셰이크는 아이스크림·우유 기반이라 스무디보다 훨씬 진하고 달다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 막걸리 means "makgeolli (Korean rice wine)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 막걸리 (makgeolli) = "makgeolli (Korean rice wine)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막걸리 ("makgeolli") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막걸리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 뽀얗고 살짝 탄산이 있는 발효 쌀 술, 약 6도
병(甁) 단위로 팖; 식당·주점에서 주문

usagePhrases.en: On rainy days it's makgeolli with green-onion pancake
usagePhrases.note: 막걸리에 파전 = 비 오는 날의 단골 조합; -지 어감
가라앉으니 흔든 뒤 따름; -아서가 순서를 이음

examples.ko: 전 부치는 날엔 꼭 막걸리를 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeon buchineun naren kkong makgeollireul masyeoyo.
examples.en: On days we make jeon (pancakes), we always drink makgeolli.
examples.note: 전(煎) = 기름에 부친 부침개; 꼭 = 반드시

examples.en: This makgeolli isn't sweet and tastes clean.
examples.note: 깔끔하다 = (뒷맛이) 개운하고 산뜻하다

examples.ko: 막걸리를 너무 많이 마시면 머리가 아파요.
examples.romanization: makgeollireul neomu mani masimyeon meoriga apayo.
examples.en: If you drink too much makgeolli, you get a headache.
examples.note: 막걸리 숙취에 대한 흔한 경고; -으면 조건

extendedVocab.nuance: 막걸리는 뽀얀 빛깔에 약한 탄산이 도는 6도가량의 발효 쌀 술로, 전통적으로 사발에 따라 마시고 비 오는 날 파전과 짝을 이루는 정서가 강하다. 같은 한국 술이라도 소주는 맑고 도수가 높은 증류주, 맥주는 톡 쏘는 곡물 술인 데 비해 막걸리는 탁하고 도수가 낮으며 푸근하고 서민적인 느낌이라는 점이 경계선이다. 비슷해 보이는 동동주는 막걸리의 위쪽 맑은 부분에 가깝지만 일반적으로 막걸리보다 덜 거르고 단맛이 더 도는 술로 구별된다. 병 속에서 앙금이 가라앉으므로 따르기 전에 흔들거나 저어야 끝까지 뽀얀 술이 나온다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '막걸리 한 병/한 사발', '막걸리에 파전', '막걸리를 흔들다/따르다'. 영어 화자가 'rice beer'로 옮기기 쉬운데 맥주처럼 끓여 발효한 술이 아니므로 표준 영어는 makgeolli 또는 rice wine이라는 점을 기억해야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
가볍게 탄산이 있고 앙금이 가라앉으니 흔들지 않으면 끝에 뿌연 찌꺼기만 따르게 된다 — 따르기 전에 흔들어야 한다.
'rice beer'로 직역하면 안 됨 — 끓여 만든 맥주가 아니라 발효 쌀 술이라, 영어로는 makgeolli/rice wine이 맞다.
단위는 병/사발이다 — 막걸리는 보통 병이나 사발로 세지 '잔'으로만 세지 않는다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 위스키 means "whiskey" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 위스키 (wiseuki) means "whiskey". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 위스키 ("whiskey"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 위스키 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 요즘 유행하는 하이볼의 기주(베이스 술)
한 잔 = 한 잔; 술을 권하는 표현

usagePhrases.en: I drink whiskey on the rocks
usagePhrases.note: 얼음에 = 얼음을 넣어 / 온더록스로

usagePhrases.en: Whiskey bars are popular these days
usagePhrases.note: 위스키 바 = 위스키 전문 바; 최근 유행

examples.en: Whiskey is strong so I drink it little by little.
examples.note: 독하다 = 도수가 높아 술기운이 세다; -아서가 이유

examples.en: If you mix whiskey with sparkling water, it becomes a highball.
examples.note: 타다 = (액체에) 섞다; -으면 조건, -이 되다 결과

examples.en: I got a bottle of whiskey as a gift.
examples.note: 선물로 = 선물 자격으로; 흔한 선물 품목

extendedVocab.nuance: 위스키는 영어 whiskey를 들여온 외래어로, 곡물을 증류해 오크통에 숙성한 독한 술이다. 최근 하이볼 열풍과 위스키 바 유행을 타고 한국에서 급격히 대중화되어, 스트레이트로, 얼음을 넣어(온더록스), 또는 탄산수를 타 하이볼로 마신다. 도수를 묘사할 때는 '독하다'가 자연스러운 짝이다 — 여기서 핵심 구분은 '독하다'와 '진하다'다: 술의 높은 알코올 도수에는 독하다를, 커피·국물 같은 맛의 농도에는 진하다를 쓰므로 위스키에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다가 맞다. 또 같은 양주라도 위스키는 곡물 증류주, 브랜디는 과일(포도) 증류주라는 점이 경계선이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '위스키 한 잔/한 병', '위스키를 마시다/타다', '얼음에/탄산수에'. 영어 화자가 'whiskey liquor'처럼 술을 한 번 더 붙이려 할 수 있는데, 위스키 자체가 술 이름이라 '위스키 술'은 군더더기다.

철자는 '위스키'다 — '위스키주'나 '위스끼'는 틀린 표기다.
'위스키 술'은 겹말이라 어색 — 위스키가 이미 술 이름이므로 술을 덧붙이지 않는다.
도수를 말할 땐 '독하다'를 쓴다 — '위스키가 진하다'는 맛 농도 표현이라 어색하고, 센 술기운은 '독하다'가 맞다.

영어 whiskey를 들여온 외래어다.
영어 화자가 'whiskey liquor'처럼 술을 한 번 더 붙이려 할 수 있는데, 위스키 자체가 술 이름이라 '위스키 술'은 군더더기다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아메리카노 means "americano (the default Korean coffee order)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "americano (the default Korean coffee order)" is 아메리카노 (amerikano). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아메리카노 ("americano"). Watch the particle attached to 아메리카노 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에스프레소+물; 한국에서 가장 많이 시키는 카페 음료
아이스 아메리카노 = 차가운 아메리카노, 국민 기본 메뉴
커피 주문 시 점원이 묻는 정해진 질문; 거 = 것
아아 = 아이스 아메리카노; 뜨아 = 뜨거운 아메리카노

examples.en: I drink an americano every morning.
examples.note: 매일 아침 = 날마다 아침; 일상 커피

examples.en: I drink only iced americanos even in winter.
examples.note: -에도 = '~인데도'; '얼어 죽어도 아이스' 정서

examples.en: Two americanos to go, please.
examples.note: 포장(包裝) '싸서 가져감' = 테이크아웃

extendedVocab.nuance: 아메리카노는 에스프레소에 뜨거운 물이나 얼음물을 더한 커피로, 한국 카페에서 압도적인 기본 주문이다. 특히 아이스 아메리카노는 한겨울에도 마시는 사람이 많아 '얼어 죽어도 아이스'라는 농담이 생겼고, 줄임말 아아(아이스)·뜨아(뜨거운)를 알면 현지인처럼 들린다. 핵심 구분은 막연한 '커피'와의 차이다 — 카페에서 그냥 '커피 주세요' 하면 어떤 음료인지 되묻게 되므로 아메리카노처럼 구체 메뉴로 말해야 하고, 그중 무난한 기본값이 아메리카노다. 또 라떼는 우유가 들어가 부드럽고 고소한 반면 아메리카노는 우유 없이 물로 희석해 깔끔하고 쌉쌀하다는 점이 경계선이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '아메리카노 한 잔/두 잔', '아이스/따뜻한 ~', '~ 포장해 주세요'. 주문하면 점원이 으레 '따뜻한 거요, 아이스요?'라고 물으니 이 질문에 답할 준비를 해 두면 좋다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
카페에서 그냥 '커피'만 달라고 하면 안 됨 — 구체 메뉴가 필요하고, 무난한 기본값은 아메리카노다.
아아는 '아이스 아메리카노'만 가리킨다 — 아무 아이스 커피나 아아라고 부르지 않는다.
라떼와 혼동 금물 — 우유가 들어가면 라떼이고, 물로만 희석한 것이 아메리카노다.

핵심 구분은 막연한 '커피'와의 차이다 — 카페에서 그냥 '커피 주세요' 하면 어떤 음료인지 되묻게 되므로 아메리카노처럼 구체 메뉴로 말해야 하고, 그중 무난한 기본값이 아메리카노다. 또 라떼는 우유가 들어가 부드럽고 고소한 반면 아메리카노는 우유 없이 물로 희석해 깔끔하고 쌉쌀하다는 점이 경계선이다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 생맥주 means "draft beer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 생맥주 (saengmaekju) = "draft beer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 생맥주 ("draft beer") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생맥주, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 흔히 '생맥'으로 줄임; 잔이나 피처 단위로 팖
잔 = 잔 단위; 주점에서 주문
오백 = 500cc 잔; 천 = 1000cc; 개로도 흔히 셈

usagePhrases.en: Shall we order a pitcher of draft?
usagePhrases.note: 피처 = 여럿이 나눠 마시는 큰 잔; -ㄹ까요? 제안

examples.en: With fried chicken, cold draft beer is the best.
examples.note: 치맥 = 치킨+맥주 문화; -엔 = '~에는'

examples.en: After work we went for a draft beer.
examples.note: 한잔하다 = 가볍게 술 한잔 마시다(붙여 씀)

examples.en: The draft here is cheaper than bottled beer.
examples.note: 병맥주 = 병에 든 맥주; 보다 = 비교 기준

extendedVocab.nuance: 생맥주(生麥酒, '날것의 보리 술')는 통에서 바로 따르는 드래프트 맥주로, 글자 그대로 가열·살균을 덜 한 '신선한' 맥주를 뜻한다. 한국 주점의 기본 술이며 특히 치킨과 짝지어 치맥 문화의 중심에 있다. 핵심 구분은 담는 방식이다 — 생맥주는 통에서 따르는 것, 병맥주는 병에 든 것, 캔맥주는 캔에 든 것이라 같은 맥주라도 서로 다른 말로 부른다. 크기는 오백(500cc)·천(1000cc)으로 부르고 여럿이 마실 땐 피처로 시키며, 입말에서는 '생맥'으로 줄여 쓰는 일이 아주 흔하다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '생맥주 한 잔/두 잔', '오백/천', '피처로', '치킨에 ~'. 영어 화자가 용량을 '500밀리리터'처럼 말하기 쉬운데, 주점에서는 '오백/천'이라고 해야 자연스럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
담는 방식으로 구분 — 통에서 따르면 생맥주, 병이면 병맥주, 캔이면 캔맥주이니 섞어 쓰면 안 된다.
크기를 주문할 땐 '오백/천'으로 말한다 — '500밀리리터'는 주점에서 어색하다.
마실 때는 '먹다'보다 '마시다'나 관용구 '한잔하다'가 자연스럽다 — '생맥주 한잔하다'.

structuredNuance.t: 통에서 바로 따르는 드래프트 맥주로, 글자 그대로 가열·살균을 덜 한 '신선한' 맥주를 뜻한다. 한국 주점의 기본 술이며 특히 치킨과 짝지어 치맥 문화의 중심에 있다. 크기는 오백(500cc)·천(1000cc)으로 부르고 여럿이 마실 땐 피처로 시키며, 입말에서는 '생맥'으로 줄여 쓰는 일이 아주 흔하다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '생맥주 한 잔/두 잔', '오백/천', '피처로', '치킨에 ~'.
핵심 구분은 담는 방식이다 — 생맥주는 통에서 따르는 것, 병맥주는 병에 든 것, 캔맥주는 캔에 든 것이라 같은 맥주라도 서로 다른 말로 부른다.
생맥주(生麥酒)는 '날것의 보리 술'로 이루어진 말이다.
영어 화자가 용량을 '500밀리리터'처럼 말하기 쉬운데, 주점에서는 '오백/천'이라고 해야 자연스럽다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 하이볼 means "highball (whiskey + soda)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 하이볼 (haibol) means "highball (whiskey + soda)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 하이볼 ("highball"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 하이볼 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 위스키+탄산수+얼음; 지금 매우 유행하는 술
한 잔 = 한 잔; 바·이자카야의 기본 주문
레몬 하이볼 = 레몬을 더한 변형; -로 선택

usagePhrases.en: A highball is low-proof so it's easy to drink
usagePhrases.note: 도수(度數) = 술의 알코올 세기; -아서 이유

examples.ko: 요즘 회식 때 하이볼 많이 마셔요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hoesik ttae haibol mani masyeoyo.
examples.en: These days we drink a lot of highballs at company dinners.
examples.note: 회식(會食) '모여서 먹음' = 회식; 소주를 일부 대체

examples.en: They sell canned highballs even at convenience stores.
examples.note: -에서도 = '~에서조차'; 캔으로 나온 즉석 버전

examples.en: Highballs are smoother than soju, so I like them.
examples.note: 부드럽다 = (목넘김이) 순하다; 보다 비교

extendedVocab.nuance: 하이볼은 영어 highball에서 온 외래어로, 위스키에 탄산수를 붓고 얼음을 넣어 만든 술이다. 도수가 낮고 청량해 이자카야·바는 물론 편의점 캔 음료로도 나오며, 요즘 한국에서 가장 유행하는 술 중 하나로 젊은 층이 소주 대신 고르는 경우가 많다. 핵심 구분은 술이냐 아니냐다 — 하이볼은 위스키가 든 '술'이고, 이름이 비슷해 보이는 에이드는 카페의 무알코올 탄산 과일 음료라 마시는 자리와 대상이 전혀 다르다. 또 같은 위스키 음료라도 위스키는 기주(원래 술), 하이볼은 그것을 탄산수로 희석한 칵테일이라는 점이 경계선이다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '하이볼 한 잔', '레몬 하이볼', '캔 하이볼', '하이볼을 마시다/타다'. 완전히 굳은 외래어이므로 '하이볼을'을 어색하게 '하이볼-어'처럼 끊어 발음하지 말고 자연스럽게 이어 읽으면 된다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
하이볼은 위스키가 든 술이다 — 무알코올 과일 탄산 음료인 에이드와 혼동하면 안 된다.
위스키와 하이볼을 같은 것으로 보면 안 됨 — 위스키는 원래 술, 하이볼은 탄산수로 희석한 칵테일이다.
완전한 외래어이니 '하이볼을'을 '하이볼-어'처럼 끊지 말고 자연스럽게 이어 발음한다.

structuredNuance.t: 위스키에 탄산수를 붓고 얼음을 넣어 만든 술이다. 도수가 낮고 청량해 이자카야·바는 물론 편의점 캔 음료로도 나오며, 요즘 한국에서 가장 유행하는 술 중 하나로 젊은 층이 소주 대신 고르는 경우가 많다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '하이볼 한 잔', '레몬 하이볼', '캔 하이볼', '하이볼을 마시다/타다'.
핵심 구분은 술이냐 아니냐다 — 하이볼은 위스키가 든 '술'이고, 이름이 비슷해 보이는 에이드는 카페의 무알코올 탄산 과일 음료라 마시는 자리와 대상이 전혀 다르다. 또 같은 위스키 음료라도 위스키는 기주(원래 술), 하이볼은 그것을 탄산수로 희석한 칵테일이라는 점이 경계선이다.
영어 highball에서 온 외래어다.
완전히 굳은 외래어이므로 '하이볼을'을 어색하게 '하이볼-어'처럼 끊어 발음하지 말고 자연스럽게 이어 읽으면 된다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 진하다 means "strong, rich, concentrated (of a drink/flavor)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "strong, rich, concentrated (of a drink/flavor)" is 진하다 (jinhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 진하다 ("to be strong/rich"). Watch the particle attached to 진하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 커피·차·국물·우유 등 농도가 짙은 맛
진하게 = 진한 상태로; 샷 추가 느낌을 요청
국물 = 탕·찌개의 액체; 맛의 농도에도 씀
진한+명사 = 진한 ___; 관형형

examples.en: I like strong coffee.
examples.note: 진한 = 진하다의 관형형(명사 앞 형태)

examples.ko: 이 녹차는 너무 진해서 좀 써요.
examples.romanization: i nokchaneun neomu jinhaeseo jom sseoyo.
examples.en: This green tea is so strong it's a bit bitter.
examples.note: -아서가 이유를 이음; 진하다→쓰다로 이어짐

examples.en: If you add less milk, it gets stronger.
examples.note: 진해지다 = 진하게 변하다; -으면 조건

extendedVocab.nuance: 진하다는 색·맛·농도가 짙다는 형용사로, 음료에 쓰면 진한 커피, 짙은 차, 우러난 국물, 고소한 우유처럼 '농도가 높은' 상태를 가리킨다. 형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '진한 커피'처럼 -ㄴ 관형형을, 부사처럼 쓸 땐 '진하게 해 주세요'를, 변화에는 '진해지다'를 쓴다. 가장 중요한 구분은 세 갈래다: ① 맛이 진한 데는 진하다를 쓰지 강하다(주로 힘·세기의 강함)는 쓰지 않고, ② 술의 높은 도수에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다를 쓰며, ③ 반대말은 묽고 약한 맛을 뜻하는 연하다다. 즉 진한 아메리카노↔연한 아메리카노, 독한 위스키(도수)↔진한 국물(맛 농도)로 갈래가 다르다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '진한 커피/라떼', '국물이 진하다', '진하게 (해 주세요)', '진해지다'. 영어 'strong'을 그대로 옮겨 술의 도수에까지 진하다를 쓰면 어색하니, 도수에는 독하다, 맛 농도에는 진하다로 갈라 써야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
맛이 진한 음료에는 진하다를 쓴다 — 강하다(힘·세기의 강함)는 맛 농도에 어색하다.
술의 높은 도수에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다 — 진하다는 도수가 아니라 맛의 농도를 가리킨다.
반대말은 연하다(묽다·약하다)다 — '안 진하다'보다 '연하다'가 자연스러운 짝이다.

structuredNuance.t: 색·맛·농도가 짙다는 형용사로, 음료에 쓰면 진한 커피, 짙은 차, 우러난 국물, 고소한 우유처럼 '농도가 높은' 상태를 가리킨다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '진한 커피/라떼', '국물이 진하다', '진하게 (해 주세요)', '진해지다'.
가장 중요한 구분은 세 갈래다: ① 맛이 진한 데는 진하다를 쓰지 강하다(주로 힘·세기의 강함)는 쓰지 않고, ② 술의 높은 도수에는 진하다가 아니라 독하다를 쓰며, ③ 반대말은 묽고 약한 맛을 뜻하는 연하다다. 즉 진한 아메리카노↔연한 아메리카노, 독한 위스키(도수)↔진한 국물(맛 농도)로 갈래가 다르다.
형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '진한 커피'처럼 -ㄴ 관형형을, 부사처럼 쓸 땐 '진하게 해 주세요'를, 변화에는 '진해지다'를 쓴다.
영어 'strong'을 그대로 옮겨 술의 도수에까지 진하다를 쓰면 어색하니, 도수에는 독하다, 맛 농도에는 진하다로 갈라 써야 한다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 미지근하다 means "to be lukewarm, tepid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 미지근하다 (mijigeunhada) = "to be lukewarm, tepid". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 미지근하다 ("to be lukewarm") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 미지근하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 뜨겁지도 차갑지도 않은; 음료에 대한 불평으로 자주 씀
얼음이 녹았을 때 흔히 하는 말
차갑지 않은 물을 원할 때(약 먹을 때 등) 유용
미지근해지다 = 미지근하게 변하다

examples.en: The beer is lukewarm so it tastes bad.
examples.note: -아서가 이유; 미지근한 맥주는 흔한 불평거리

examples.en: Take the medicine with lukewarm water.
examples.note: 이랑 = '~와 함께'; 약사·건강 조언에서 흔함

examples.en: The americano had cooled off and was lukewarm.
examples.note: 식다 = (음식·음료가) 차게 식다

extendedVocab.nuance: 미지근하다는 뜨겁지도 차갑지도 않은 '미적지근한' 온도를 뜻하는 형용사로, 뜨거워야 할 커피가 식었거나 차가워야 할 맥주가 미적지근해진 상태에 쓴다. 핵심 구분은 따뜻하다와의 차이다 — 따뜻하다는 마시기 좋게 기분 좋은 온기를 뜻하는 긍정어인 반면, 미지근하다는 마땅한 온도(뜨겁거나 차가워야 함)에 못 미친 상태라 대개 가벼운 불평의 어감을 띤다. 그래서 '커피가 따뜻해요'는 칭찬에 가깝지만 '커피가 미지근해요'는 식었다는 불만이다. 다만 약을 먹거나 속이 예민할 때 '미지근한 물'을 일부러 청하는 긍정적 쓰임도 있다. 형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '미지근한 물', 변화에는 '미지근해지다'를 쓴다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '물·커피·맥주가 미지근하다', '미지근한 물', '미지근해지다'. 액체·물건의 온도에 쓰는 말이라 날씨에는 어울리지 않으니, 포근한 날씨에는 미지근하다가 아니라 포근하다/따뜻하다를 써야 한다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
미지근하다(미적지근함)와 따뜻하다(기분 좋은 온기)는 다르다 — 뜨거워야 할 음료가 식은 건 따뜻하다가 아니라 미지근하다(불평)다.
날씨에는 쓰지 않는다 — 공기 온도가 아니라 주로 액체·물건에 쓰며, 포근한 날씨는 포근하다/따뜻하다다.
형용사이므로 명사 앞에서는 '미지근한 물'처럼 -ㄴ 관형형을 써야 한다 — '미지근 물'은 틀리다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 신기하다 means "amazing, fascinating, novel" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 신기하다 (singihada) means "amazing, fascinating, novel". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 신기하다 ("to be fascinating / amazing"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 신기하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: everyday word for 'wow, cool!' when something is new or surprising in a good way
adverbial 신기하다 + 게도; opens a sentence: 신기하게도 비가 딱 그쳤어 = amazingly the rain stopped right then
polite -네요 of fresh discovery; mild wonder at something you just learned or saw
신기한 (modifier) + 거(것); 신기한 거 봤어 = I saw something cool

examples.en: This flower is really cool.
examples.note: shortest 반말 form; just point and react, no object particle needed

examples.ko: 한국 지하철은 환승이 잘 돼 있어서 신기해요.
examples.romanization: hanguk jihacheoreun hwanseungi jal dwae isseoseo singihaeyo.
examples.en: The Korean subway transfers are so well-organized, it's amazing.
examples.note: -아서 reason + 신기해요; everyday remark foreigners share with Korean friends

examples.ko: 눈을 처음 봤을 때 너무 신기했어.
examples.romanization: nuneul cheoeum bwasseul ttae neomu singihaesseo.
examples.en: When I saw snow for the first time it was so amazing.
examples.note: past 신기했어 recalling a first experience; object 눈을 marks what amazed you

extendedVocab.nuance: 신기하다 is the go-to word for delighted, almost childlike wonder at something new, clever, or unexpected — a smart gadget, your first snow, a magic trick. The connotation is warm and positive. The Sino-Korean root is 神奇 (신기), literally 'divine + marvelous', so the feeling is that something is marvelously beyond the ordinary. The sharpest contrast is with 이상하다 ('weird/off'): both react to the unfamiliar, but 신기하다 is good-surprised ('cool!') while 이상하다 is bad-surprised ('something's wrong'). It also differs from 놀랍다 ('astonishing', more shock than charm). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like 'strange' — saying 신기하다 about a creepy noise sounds like you enjoyed it. As an adjective it never takes 를; you say 이게 신기해, not 이걸 신기해.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for creepy/bad weirdness ('a strange smell') — that negative 'weird' is 이상하다; 신기하다 is positive wonder, so it implies you liked it.
Writing the verbish 신기다 or conjugating 신기다 — the dictionary form keeps 하: 신기하다, 신기해요, 신기한.
Adding 를 as if it were a verb: 이걸 신기해(X). It is descriptive, so the thing that amazes you takes 이/가: 이게 신기해(O).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 황홀하다 means "enchanting, mesmerizing, blissful" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "enchanting, mesmerizing, blissful" is 황홀하다 (hwangholhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 황홀하다 ("to be enchanting / dazzling"). Watch the particle attached to 황홀하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: for a view, music, or moment so beautiful you almost lose yourself
반말, said softly while taking something gorgeous in
황홀한 (modifier) + noun; classic for sunsets, night views, 야경
황홀하다 + -ㄹ 정도로 = so beautiful that...; 황홀할 정도로 아름다웠어

examples.en: The sunset is truly mesmerizing.
examples.note: simple subject + 황홀해요; 노을(sunset) is the textbook trigger

examples.en: Walking the cherry blossom path, it was just breathtaking.
examples.note: -더라 reporting a vivid first-hand impression to a friend

examples.ko: 공연이 너무 황홀해서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
examples.romanization: gongyeoni neomu hwangholhaeseo sigan ganeun jul mollasseo.
examples.en: The show was so enchanting I lost track of time.
examples.note: -아서 cause chained to the set phrase 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어

extendedVocab.nuance: 황홀하다 describes beauty so intense it nearly sweeps you out of yourself — reserved for sunsets, night views, sublime music, a magical moment, never an everyday 'pretty'. The Sino-Korean 恍惚 (황홀) literally means 'dazed/entranced', so the word names the spellbound state of the viewer as much as the beauty itself, and it sounds literary and heightened. Contrast it with 아름답다 ('beautiful', the neutral aesthetic word) and 예쁘다 ('pretty', casual and small-scale): dropping 황홀하다 on a so-so cafe latte sounds theatrical. It also differs from 행복하다 ('happy'), which is general well-being, not being dazzled by beauty. The pitfall for English speakers is using it as a synonym for 'lovely/nice'; in Korean it implies near-overwhelm, so save it for genuinely stunning sights and pair it with 진짜/정말 or -할 정도로 for emphasis.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Overusing it for mildly nice things ('the coffee was 황홀해') — 황홀하다 implies almost overwhelming beauty; for ordinary nice use 좋다/예쁘다/멋지다.
Confusing it with 행복하다 (general happiness) — 황홀하다 is specifically about being entranced by beauty or a sublime moment, not everyday contentment.
Applying it to a person's looks bluntly ('너 황홀해') — it sounds odd/over-the-top about a person; for that use 예쁘다/멋지다, and reserve 황홀하다 for scenes and experiences.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아찔하다 means "dizzying, heart-stopping, scary-close" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 아찔하다 (ajjilhada) = "dizzying, heart-stopping, scary-close". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아찔하다 ("to be dizzying / heart-stopping") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아찔하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the rush when you almost got hurt or look down from a height
반말 reaction right after a near-miss
past tense, retelling a scary moment that already passed

usagePhrases.en: it's dizzying just to think about it
usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase 생각만 해도 + 아찔하다 = I shudder to imagine

examples.en: Looking down, I feel dizzy.
examples.note: bare 반말; height-induced vertigo in the moment

examples.en: A car cut in suddenly and it was really heart-stopping.
examples.note: -아서 cause + past; the near-accident-on-the-road use, extremely common

examples.en: I almost lost my wallet. That was scary-close.
examples.note: set frame 하마터면 …-ㄹ 뻔했어, then 아찔해 as the aftershock

extendedVocab.nuance: 아찔하다 captures the dizzy, stomach-dropping jolt of a near-miss or a dangerous height — the physical wave of 'whew, that was close'. It is at once literal vertigo and the split-second emotional shock of almost-disaster, which is why Koreans say it constantly after close calls in traffic. It is an onomatopoeic/mimetic adjective (from 아찔, the lurch of light-headedness), so there is no 한자. The key contrast is with 무섭다 ('scary'), which is steady, ongoing fear, whereas 아찔하다 is one instantaneous lurch; and with 짜릿하다 ('thrilling'), which is the pleasant tingle of excitement. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'dizzy = 어지럽다': 어지럽다 is plain medical dizziness (low blood sugar, spinning room), while 아찔하다 adds the danger/shock element. It habitually pairs with 하마터면…뻔하다 and 생각만 해도.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for ongoing fear ('I'm 아찔해 about the exam') — 아찔하다 is a momentary dizzy jolt; sustained fear is 무섭다/긴장되다.
Saying 아찔하다 for a happy thrill (a roller-coaster you enjoyed) — it implies danger or vertigo, not fun excitement; that pleasant rush is 짜릿하다.
Swapping in plain 어지럽다 for a near-miss — 어지럽다 is just physical dizziness; 아찔하다 carries the 'that was dangerously close' shock.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 섬뜩하다 means "creepy, chilling, eerie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 섬뜩하다 (seomtteukada) means "creepy, chilling, eerie". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 섬뜩하다 ("to be creepy / chilling"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 섬뜩하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the cold shiver when something is eerie or menacing
반말, reacting to a horror scene or unsettling sight
past tense, retelling an eerie moment after the fact
섬뜩한 (modifier) + noun; common with 느낌, 분위기, 눈빛

examples.en: That painting is kind of creepy.
examples.note: short 반말 + softener 좀; reacting to an unsettling image

examples.ko: 밤에 혼자 그 골목을 지나가는데 섬뜩했어.
examples.romanization: bame honja geu golmogeul jinaganeunde seomtteukaesseo.
examples.en: Walking through that alley alone at night was creepy.
examples.note: -는데 background + past; the lone-dark-alley scene

examples.en: That person's stare was really chilling.
examples.note: -더라 reporting a vivid impression of someone; 눈빛(gaze) is a stock partner

extendedVocab.nuance: 섬뜩하다 is the cold-spine, hair-raising creepiness of something eerie or sinister — a dark alley, an unsettling stare, a disturbing news story. It names the sudden chill that runs down your back, sharper and colder than the general fear of 무섭다. It is a native Korean mimetic word (from 섬뜩, the feel of a cold jolt), so there is no 한자. Compare it with three neighbors: 무섭다 ('scary', broad ongoing fear, even of exams); 소름 끼치다 ('to get goosebumps', very close and often interchangeable, focusing on the skin reaction); and 으스스하다 ('spooky/chilly', a milder ambient creepiness). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'creepy' loosely the way English does for a mildly off person ('he's a bit creepy'); in Korean that everyday 'off/sketchy' nuance is closer to 좀 이상하다, and 섬뜩하다 should be saved for a genuinely spine-chilling jolt. It pairs naturally with 눈빛, 분위기, 느낌, 사건.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for ordinary fear of, say, exams or a dog — 섬뜩하다 implies eerie, spine-chilling dread; everyday fear is 무섭다.
Confusing it with 신기하다 — 섬뜩하다 is negative and creepy; 신기하다 is positive fascination, the opposite reaction.
Calling a merely sketchy person 섬뜩하다 the way English says 'creepy guy' — that mild 'off' sense is 좀 이상하다; reserve 섬뜩하다 for a real chill.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 거북하다 means "uncomfortable, awkward, queasy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "uncomfortable, awkward, queasy" is 거북하다 (geobukada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 거북하다 ("to feel uncomfortable / queasy"). Watch the particle attached to 거북하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: covers both an awkward mood and an upset, heavy stomach

usagePhrases.en: to feel queasy in the stomach
usagePhrases.note: fixed collocation; 속(insides) + 이 + 거북하다 = bloated/uneasy stomach

usagePhrases.en: this feels awkward / my stomach's off
usagePhrases.note: 반말; meaning flips with context (people vs. 속이)
V-기 거북하다 pattern = uncomfortable/awkward to do something

examples.en: My stomach feels a bit off.
examples.note: the core stomach use; 속이 + 거북해, softened with 좀

examples.en: I overate, so my stomach feels queasy.
examples.note: -았더니 (I did X and as a result) + the 속이 거북하다 collocation

examples.en: Honestly, that question was awkward to answer.
examples.note: V-기 거북하다 (대답하기 거북하다) for a question you'd rather not field

extendedVocab.nuance: 거북하다 has two everyday lives: a queasy, heavy, ill-sitting stomach (속이 거북하다) and an awkward, uneasy social feeling (분위기가 거북하다, 마주치기 거북하다). Both share the core image of something not sitting right — physically or emotionally. The sharpest contrast is with 불편하다: 불편하다 covers broad 'inconvenient/uncomfortable', including practical inconvenience (불편한 의자 = an uncomfortable chair, 교통이 불편하다 = bad transit), whereas 거북하다 is the more inward, visceral 'this doesn't sit well with me' and is the natural word for an upset stomach. For a hard chair or bad transit you must use 불편하다, not 거북하다. It also overlaps with 어색하다 ('awkward, unfamiliar between people'), but 거북하다 adds a note of mild distaste or discomfort, not just unfamiliarity. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping all of 'uncomfortable' onto one word; remember 거북하다 for queasy stomachs and for situations you find off-putting, and 불편하다 for physical/practical discomfort.

Using it for physical inconvenience like a hard chair or far-away store — that is 불편하다; 거북하다 is queasy or socially ill-at-ease, not 'inconvenient'.
Forgetting the stomach sense — 속이 거북하다 is an extremely common natural collocation after a big meal; learners often only learn the 'awkward' meaning.
Using it for first-meeting shyness ('I felt 거북해 meeting new people') — pure unfamiliar awkwardness is 어색하다; 거북하다 implies it actively bothers you.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 야속하다 means "heartless (toward me), disappointing, cold" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 야속하다 (yasokada) = "heartless (toward me), disappointing, cold". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 야속하다 ("to feel let down by someone's coldness") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 야속하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to feel let down by someone's coldness
usagePhrases.note: soft resentment when someone you care about is unkind or distant
반말, gentle reproach to a close person
-더라 recalling a moment you personally felt slighted
야속한 (modifier) + noun; mild blame, not strong condemnation

examples.en: You're really being cold.
examples.note: bare 반말 reproach said straight to the person who let you down

examples.ko: 힘들 때 연락 한 번 없어서 좀 야속했어.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae yeolla kan beon eopseoseo jom yasokaesseo.
examples.en: You didn't reach out once when I was struggling, it felt cold.
examples.note: -아서 reason + softener 좀; classic complaint toward a friend

examples.en: Even the weather is being cruel — it's raining.
examples.note: playful extension to fate/circumstance with 야속하게 + 까지

extendedVocab.nuance: 야속하다 is the soft, wounded resentment you feel when someone close lets you down or seems cold — less anger than quiet hurt. It carries an implicit 'I expected warmth from you and didn't get it', so there is affection tucked underneath the complaint, and it is most natural toward family, close friends, a partner, or even personified fate/weather. The nearest synonym is 섭섭하다 ('hurt/let down'), and the dividing line matters: 섭섭하다 is the broad ache of disappointment ('I'm sad you forgot my birthday'), while 야속하다 specifically blames the other side's apparent heartlessness ('how could you be so cold to me'). It is gentler and more inward than 매정하다 ('cold-hearted', a flatter description of someone) and far softer than 화나다 ('angry'). The English-speaker pitfall is reading it as real anger or using it about strangers and institutions; with strangers there is no prior warmth to betray, so it rings false — use 차갑다/매정하다 instead, and save 야속하다 for people (or fate) you feel close enough to gently reproach.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for strangers or companies ('the bank was 야속해') — 야속하다 implies you expected kindness from a close relationship; for strangers use 차갑다/매정하다.
Treating it as strong anger — it is gentle, hurt reproach with affection underneath, not 화나다; raising your voice with 야속해 mismatches the tone.
Swapping it freely with 섭섭하다 — 섭섭하다 is general disappointment, while 야속하다 specifically points at the other person's coldness toward you.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정겹다 means "warm-hearted, cozy, full of affection" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정겹다 (jeonggyeopda) means "warm-hearted, cozy, full of affection". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정겹다 ("to be warm and heartfelt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정겹다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the cozy warmth of a homey scene or close relationship
반말; ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 정겹다 → 정겨워
정겨운 (ㅂ-irregular modifier) + noun; 정겹 + 은 → 정겨운
adverb form; 정겹게 인사하다 = greet warmly

examples.en: My neighborhood is really cozy and warm.
examples.note: shortest 반말; note the ㅂ-irregular 정겹다 → 정겨워, not 정겹어

examples.ko: 할머니 댁은 늘 정겨운 냄새가 나.
examples.romanization: halmeoni daegeun neul jeonggyeoun naemsaega na.
examples.en: Grandma's house always has a cozy, homey smell.
examples.note: 정겨운 (modifier) + 냄새; the ㅂ-irregular -은 form 정겨운

examples.en: We hadn't met in ages and they hugged me warmly.
examples.note: 정겹게 (adverb) + 안아주다; warmth expressed through an action

extendedVocab.nuance: 정겹다 carries the uniquely Korean feeling of 정(情) — deep, accumulated affectionate warmth between people — so it names the cozy, homey heart you get from a traditional market, an old neighborhood, or a close-knit gathering. The headword is 정(情, 'affection/bond') + 겹다 ('to be full of / overflowing with'), so it literally means 'brimming with 정'. It is about human warmth and connection, not mere physical comfort or temperature, which sets it apart from 따뜻하다 ('warm') — 따뜻하다 can be literal heat or a warm personality, while 정겹다 is specifically that 정-soaked, nostalgic homeyness, and it leans gentle and a touch literary. It also differs from 포근하다 ('soft, snug, cozy'), which is about physical/emotional softness rather than the people-bond of 정. Grammatically the trap is huge: 정겹다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so it becomes 정겨워(요), 정겨운, 정겨우니까 — never the regular 정겹어요/정겹은. English speakers also over-apply it to cute objects; it is about heartfelt human warmth, not cuteness (그건 귀여워, not 정겨워).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 정겹어요/정겹은 — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ turns to 우/워: 정겨워요, 정겨운, 정겨우면.
Using it for cute objects or animals — 정겹다 is heartfelt human/communal warmth (정), not cuteness; for cute use 귀엽다.
Reducing it to plain 'warm temperature' like 따뜻하다 — 정겹다 specifically means brimming with affectionate 정 and nostalgia, not literal or merely figurative warmth.
