extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 계정 means "account" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "account" is 계정 (gyejeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 계정 ("account"). Watch the particle attached to 계정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Your registered account on a service (Google, 네이버, Instagram); broader than 아이디
만들다 = to make; covers the whole account, more complete than 아이디를 만들다
삭제하다 = to delete (data); what you do to close an account permanently
정지되다 = to be suspended/frozen (passive); e.g. banned for spam

examples.en: I have two accounts.
examples.note: Simple counting with 개; 계정 is the subject marked 이

examples.en: I'll log in with my Google account.
examples.note: N으로 로그인하다 = log in with/via N; the everyday 'Sign in with Google'

examples.ko: 회사 계정이라 개인 메일은 못 봐요.
examples.romanization: hoesa gyejeongira gaein meireun mot bwayo.
examples.en: It's a work account, so I can't check personal mail.
examples.note: N이라(서) = because it's N; shows the work-vs-personal account distinction

extendedVocab.nuance: '계정'은 한자어 計定으로, 원래 회계에서 '셈을 정해 둔 항목'을 뜻하던 말이 온라인 '계정(account)'으로 확장됐어요. 아이디보다 큰 개념이라, 아이디·비밀번호·설정·데이터를 모두 포함하는 '계정' 전체를 가리켜요. 즉 아이디는 계정의 일부예요. 영어 'account'와 거의 1:1로 대응되지만, 영어의 'account'가 은행 계좌도 뜻하는 것과 달리 한국어는 은행은 '계좌(計座)', 온라인 서비스는 '계정(計定)'으로 단어를 나눠 써요. 발음이 비슷한 이 둘을 섞으면 '은행 계정 만들었어요'처럼 어색해지니, 돈은 계좌, 로그인은 계정으로 구분하세요. 동사는 '계정을 만들다/삭제하다'처럼 쓰고, 정지·해킹 같은 일을 당할 때는 '계정이 정지되다/털리다'처럼 피동으로 말해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 계정 (online account) with 계좌 (bank account). English 'account' covers both, but Korean splits them: money = 계좌, login = 계정.
계정 is broader than 아이디. A 계정 contains your 아이디, 비밀번호, and settings, so they aren't interchangeable.
When an account gets banned, say the passive 계정이 정지됐어요, not the active 계정을 정지했어요 (that would mean you suspended it).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 로그인 means "login, signing in" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 로그인 (rogeuin) = "login, signing in". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 로그인 ("login") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 로그인, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The noun for the act of signing in; from English 'login'
Add 하다 to make it a verb — the standard way Koreans verbify loanwords

usagePhrases.en: login won't work / can't log in
usagePhrases.note: 안 되다 = doesn't work (no fault implied); the classic complaint when a site fails
자동 = automatic; the 'remember me / keep me logged in' checkbox

examples.en: Log in here.
examples.note: Simple command: 로그인 + 하세요; note no object particle is needed

examples.en: I keep getting logged out.
examples.note: 풀리다 = to come undone; the natural way to say a session keeps dropping you

examples.en: I checked 'stay logged in'.
examples.note: 상태 유지 = keep status; the literal label of the stay-signed-in box

extendedVocab.nuance: '로그인'은 영어 'log in'을 그대로 들여온 외래어예요. 명사로 쓰다가 '하다'를 붙이면 '로그인하다'라는 동사가 되는데, 이렇게 외래어+하다로 동사를 만드는 건 한국어의 핵심 패턴이에요(클릭하다, 다운로드하다처럼요). 비슷한 말로 '접속하다'가 있는데, '접속(接續)'은 단순히 사이트에 '연결·접근'하는 것이고 '로그인'은 아이디·비밀번호를 넣어 '본인 확인 후 들어가는' 것이라 더 좁아요. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 동사로 써야 할 자리에 명사 '로그인'만 덜렁 쓰는 거예요. '나 로그인'이 아니라 '나 로그인했어'처럼 '하다'를 꼭 붙이세요. 한국 사이트는 본인인증 단계가 많아 로그인 절차가 영어권보다 복잡할 때가 많고, IT 도움을 청할 때 '로그인이 안 돼요'는 가장 많이 쓰는 문장 중 하나예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
To say 'I logged in', use 로그인했어요. Don't use the bare noun 로그인 as if it were a verb (로그인했다 needs 하다).
Don't overuse 접속하다 for 'log in'. 접속하다 just means connect/access; 로그인하다 means you entered credentials to authenticate.
The opposite is 로그아웃, not 로그오프 — 로그오프 is almost never used in Korea.

비슷한 말로 '접속하다'가 있는데, '접속(接續)'은 단순히 사이트에 '연결·접근'하는 것이고 '로그인'은 아이디·비밀번호를 넣어 '본인 확인 후 들어가는' 것이라 더 좁아요.
명사로 쓰다가 '하다'를 붙이면 '로그인하다'라는 동사가 되는데, 이렇게 외래어+하다로 동사를 만드는 건 한국어의 핵심 패턴이에요(클릭하다, 다운로드하다처럼요).
영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 동사로 써야 할 자리에 명사 '로그인'만 덜렁 쓰는 거예요. '나 로그인'이 아니라 '나 로그인했어'처럼 '하다'를 꼭 붙이세요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 로그아웃 means "logout, signing out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 로그아웃 (rogeuaut) means "logout, signing out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 로그아웃 ("logout"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 로그아웃 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The noun for the act of signing out; from English 'logout'
Add 하다 to verbify; pairs with 로그인하다 and implies you did it yourself
되다 = passive; used when the system signs you out automatically
자동 = automatic; the timed sign-out common on banking/government apps

examples.en: I logged out.
examples.note: Simple past with 하다; you performed the action yourself

examples.en: Always log out on shared computers.
examples.note: 꼭 ~하세요 = be sure to ~; the security reminder you see at a PC방

examples.en: It logs out automatically after a while.
examples.note: 일정 시간 = a set time; here the passive 로그아웃되다 shows the system did it

extendedVocab.nuance: '로그아웃'은 영어 'log out'에서 온 외래어로, 로그인의 반대예요. 계정에서 빠져나오는 것을 말하죠. 핵심은 '하다'와 '되다'의 구분이에요. 내가 직접 버튼을 눌러 나오면 능동의 '로그아웃하다', 보안 때문에 시스템이 나를 강제로 내보내면 피동의 '로그아웃되다'라고 해요. 영어는 'I got logged out'과 'I logged out'을 모두 'log out'으로 비슷하게 표현하지만, 한국어는 이 능동/피동을 동사 어미로 분명히 갈라서 말해야 자연스러워요. 또 '로그오프(log off)'라는 말은 한국에서 거의 안 쓰니 '로그아웃'으로 통일하세요. 한국 은행·관공서 사이트는 보안상 몇 분만 가만히 있어도 자동으로 로그아웃되는 경우가 많으니, 갑자기 풀려도 당황하지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Korea uses 로그아웃, not 로그오프 (log off). Stick with 로그아웃 in every register.
For the automatic version say the passive 로그아웃됐어요. Using 로그아웃했어요 wrongly implies you chose to sign out.
Don't say 로그아웃이 풀렸어요 — a session being dropped is itself 로그아웃되다; 풀리다 pairs with 로그인 (로그인이 풀리다).

structuredNuance.t: '로그아웃'은 영어 'log out'에서 온 외래어로, 로그인의 반대예요. 계정에서 빠져나오는 것을 말하죠. 한국 은행·관공서 사이트는 보안상 몇 분만 가만히 있어도 자동으로 로그아웃되는 경우가 많으니, 갑자기 풀려도 당황하지 마세요.
'로그오프(log off)'라는 말은 한국에서 거의 안 쓰니 '로그아웃'으로 통일하세요.
핵심은 '하다'와 '되다'의 구분이에요. 내가 직접 버튼을 눌러 나오면 능동의 '로그아웃하다', 보안 때문에 시스템이 나를 강제로 내보내면 피동의 '로그아웃되다'라고 해요.
영어는 'I got logged out'과 'I logged out'을 모두 'log out'으로 비슷하게 표현하지만, 한국어는 이 능동/피동을 동사 어미로 분명히 갈라서 말해야 자연스러워요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 회원가입 means "sign-up, membership registration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "sign-up, membership registration" is 회원가입 (hoewongaip). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 회원가입 ("sign-up"). Watch the particle attached to 회원가입 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 회원 (member) + 가입 (joining); registering as a member, the 'Sign up' button
Add 하다 to verbify; the full process of becoming a registered member
절차 = procedure/steps; Korean signups often have many
간편 = simple/easy; signing up via Kakao/Naver instead of a full form

examples.en: I signed up.
examples.note: Simple past with 하다; the whole account-creation done

examples.en: You have to sign up first before you can order.
examples.note: N부터 해야 = have to do N first; typical of Korean shopping sites

examples.en: You need phone verification when signing up.
examples.note: ~할 때 = when ~ing; 휴대폰 인증 is near-universal in Korea

extendedVocab.nuance: '회원가입'은 한자어 회원(會員, 'meeting-member' = member of a group) + 가입(加入, 'add-enter' = join)으로 이뤄진 말이에요. 글자 그대로 '회원으로 들어가 더해지는 것', 곧 멤버 등록이에요. 비슷해 보이는 '로그인'과는 시점이 달라요. '회원가입'은 처음 한 번 계정을 '만드는' 절차이고, '로그인'은 그 뒤로 매번 그 계정에 '들어가는' 행위예요. 영어로는 'sign up'과 'sign in'이 한 글자(up/in)만 달라 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 한국어는 단어 자체가 달라 오히려 구분이 쉬워요. 영어 화자가 자주 틀리는 건 어순으로, '가입회원'이라고 거꾸로 쓰면 틀린 말이 돼요(회원가입이 맞아요). 한국 사이트는 거의 다 회원가입을 해야 제대로 쓸 수 있고 본인인증·약관 동의 단계가 많아 번거로운데, 요즘은 카카오·네이버로 하는 '간편 가입'이 대세라 훨씬 빨라요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't reverse the order to 가입회원 — the correct compound is 회원가입 (member + join).
회원가입 is signing up (creating the account, done once); 로그인 is signing in afterward (done each visit). Don't confuse the two.
Say 회원가입했어요 for 'I signed up'; the bare noun 회원가입 can't stand in for the verb without 하다.

structuredNuance.t: 글자 그대로 '회원으로 들어가 더해지는 것', 곧 멤버 등록이에요. 한국 사이트는 거의 다 회원가입을 해야 제대로 쓸 수 있고 본인인증·약관 동의 단계가 많아 번거로운데, 요즘은 카카오·네이버로 하는 '간편 가입'이 대세라 훨씬 빨라요.
비슷해 보이는 '로그인'과는 시점이 달라요. '회원가입'은 처음 한 번 계정을 '만드는' 절차이고, '로그인'은 그 뒤로 매번 그 계정에 '들어가는' 행위예요.
'회원가입'은 한자어 회원(會員, 'meeting-member' = member of a group) + 가입(加入, 'add-enter' = join)으로 이뤄진 말이에요.
영어로는 'sign up'과 'sign in'이 한 글자(up/in)만 달라 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 한국어는 단어 자체가 달라 오히려 구분이 쉬워요. 영어 화자가 자주 틀리는 건 어순으로, '가입회원'이라고 거꾸로 쓰면 틀린 말이 돼요(회원가입이 맞아요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 즐겨찾기 means "bookmark, favorites" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 즐겨찾기 (jeulgyeochatgi) = "bookmark, favorites". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 즐겨찾기 ("bookmark/favorites") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 즐겨찾기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Native Korean: 즐겨 (enjoyably/often) + 찾기 (visiting); browser bookmarks
추가하다 = to add; the star/right-click menu action, note the 에 (destination)
등록하다 = to register; slightly more formal than 추가하다
목록 = list; your saved collection of sites

examples.en: This site is one of my bookmarks.
examples.note: Simple A는 B예요; 즐겨찾기 used as a plain noun

examples.ko: 자주 가는 사이트는 즐겨찾기에 추가해 두세요.
examples.romanization: jaju ganeun saiteuneun jeulgyeochatgie chugahae duseyo.
examples.en: Bookmark the sites you visit often.
examples.note: ~해 두다 = do ~ in advance for later; perfect for saving things

examples.en: I have too many bookmarks, so I can't find it.
examples.note: 못 찾겠다 = can't manage to find; a relatable clutter problem

extendedVocab.nuance: '즐겨찾기'는 영어 'bookmark/favorites'에 해당하는 순우리말이에요. '즐겨(즐기다에서 온, 자주·기꺼이)'와 '찾기(찾다의 명사형, 방문하기)'가 합쳐져 '자주 찾아가는 곳'이라는 뜻이 됐어요. 한국 브라우저 메뉴에는 거의 항상 '즐겨찾기'로 표시돼요. 영어식으로 '북마크'라고 해도 뜻은 통하지만, 메뉴 용어로는 '즐겨찾기'가 표준이니 익혀 두는 게 좋아요. 자주 헷갈리는 점 두 가지: 첫째, 띄어쓰기예요. 한 단어이므로 '즐겨 찾기'처럼 띄우면 안 돼요. 둘째, 조사예요. 영어 'add to favorites'의 to를 생각해 '즐겨찾기를 추가'라고 하기 쉬운데, 추가되는 '곳'을 가리키는 '에'를 써서 '즐겨찾기에 추가하다'가 맞아요. 동사처럼 쓸 때는 '하다'를 붙여 '그 글 즐겨찾기 해 놨어요'라고 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
즐겨찾기 is one word — don't split it as 즐겨 찾기 with a space.
Use the particle 에, not 를, for where you save it: 즐겨찾기에 추가하다 (add to favorites), not 즐겨찾기를 추가하다.
Although 북마크 is understood, Korean browser menus label it 즐겨찾기 — prefer the native term when reading the UI.

structuredNuance.t: '즐겨찾기'는 영어 'bookmark/favorites'에 해당하는 순우리말이에요. 한국 브라우저 메뉴에는 거의 항상 '즐겨찾기'로 표시돼요. 동사처럼 쓸 때는 '하다'를 붙여 '그 글 즐겨찾기 해 놨어요'라고 해요.
영어식으로 '북마크'라고 해도 뜻은 통하지만, 메뉴 용어로는 '즐겨찾기'가 표준이니 익혀 두는 게 좋아요.
'즐겨(즐기다에서 온, 자주·기꺼이)'와 '찾기(찾다의 명사형, 방문하기)'가 합쳐져 '자주 찾아가는 곳'이라는 뜻이 됐어요.
자주 헷갈리는 점 두 가지: 첫째, 띄어쓰기예요. 한 단어이므로 '즐겨 찾기'처럼 띄우면 안 돼요. 둘째, 조사예요. 영어 'add to favorites'의 to를 생각해 '즐겨찾기를 추가'라고 하기 쉬운데, 추가되는 '곳'을 가리키는 '에'를 써서 '즐겨찾기에 추가하다'가 맞아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 새로고침 means "refresh, reload" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 새로고침 (saerogochim) means "refresh, reload". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 새로고침 ("refresh"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 새로고침 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Native Korean: 새로 (anew) + 고침 (fixing/renewing); reloading a page
Add 하다 to verbify; reload the current page
안 되다 = doesn't work; when F5 does nothing
화면 = screen; the common full phrasing with object 을

examples.en: Try refreshing once.
examples.note: 한번 ~해 보세요 = give ~ a try; the gentlest piece of tech advice

examples.en: If the page doesn't load, refresh.
examples.note: 뜨다 = to come up/appear (of a page); conditional ~으면 + command

examples.en: It's the same no matter how much I refresh.
examples.note: 계속 ~해도 = even if I keep ~ing; venting that nothing changes

extendedVocab.nuance: '새로고침'은 페이지를 다시 불러오는 것을 뜻하는 순우리말이에요. '새로(newly, 부사)'와 '고침(고치다의 명사형, 고쳐 바꿈)'이 합쳐져 '새로 고쳐 바꿈'이라는 뜻이에요. 영어 'refresh'를 '리프레시'라고 외래어로 쓰는 일은 거의 없고, 화면이든 F5 키든 거의 항상 '새로고침'이라고 해요. 비슷한 말 '새로고침'과 '다시 불러오기(reload)'는 사실상 같은 동작을 가리키지만, 일상 대화와 브라우저 버튼에서는 '새로고침'이 압도적으로 흔해요. 주의할 점은 두 가지예요. 첫째, '새로고침'은 붙여 쓰는 한 단어라서 '새로 고침'처럼 띄우면 안 돼요. 둘째, 영어 화자는 'refresh'를 'fresh(신선한)'와 연결해 '신선하게 하다'로 오해하기 쉬운데, 여기서 '고침'은 '신선함'이 아니라 '고쳐 새로 함'이라는 뜻이에요. 동사로는 '하다'를 붙여 '새로고침했더니 장바구니가 비었어요'처럼 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
새로고침 is one word — don't write 새로 고침 with a space.
Don't say 리프레시 for refreshing a page; Koreans almost always use the native 새로고침.
It is not built from 신선하다 (fresh). The 고침 part means 'fix/renew', so don't translate it as 'make fresh'.

structuredNuance.t: '새로고침'은 페이지를 다시 불러오는 것을 뜻하는 순우리말이에요. 영어 'refresh'를 '리프레시'라고 외래어로 쓰는 일은 거의 없고, 화면이든 F5 키든 거의 항상 '새로고침'이라고 해요. 동사로는 '하다'를 붙여 '새로고침했더니 장바구니가 비었어요'처럼 써요.
비슷한 말 '새로고침'과 '다시 불러오기(reload)'는 사실상 같은 동작을 가리키지만, 일상 대화와 브라우저 버튼에서는 '새로고침'이 압도적으로 흔해요.
'새로(newly, 부사)'와 '고침(고치다의 명사형, 고쳐 바꿈)'이 합쳐져 '새로 고쳐 바꿈'이라는 뜻이에요.
주의할 점은 두 가지예요. 첫째, '새로고침'은 붙여 쓰는 한 단어라서 '새로 고침'처럼 띄우면 안 돼요. 둘째, 영어 화자는 'refresh'를 'fresh(신선한)'와 연결해 '신선하게 하다'로 오해하기 쉬운데, 여기서 '고침'은 '신선함'이 아니라 '고쳐 새로 함'이라는 뜻이에요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 다운로드 means "download" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "download" is 다운로드 (daullodeu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 다운로드 ("download"). Watch the particle attached to 다운로드 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: From English; saving a file from the internet to your device
Full form with 하다; in speech usually shortened to 다운받다
받다 = to receive; the everyday spoken form, very natural
안 되다 = doesn't work; when a file refuses to save

examples.en: Did you download this?
examples.note: 다운받다 = casual download; 받다 makes it sound natural in speech

examples.en: You have to download the app first.
examples.note: ~아야 되다 = have to ~; 먼저 marks the order of steps

examples.en: The download is slow because the internet is slow.
examples.note: 오래 걸리다 = to take a long time; written 다운로드 fits the explanatory tone

extendedVocab.nuance: '다운로드'는 영어 'download'를 그대로 옮긴 외래어로, 인터넷에서 내 기기로 파일을 '내려받는' 것을 뜻해요. 재미있는 점은 한국어가 영어의 down(아래)을 '받다(receive)'로 풀어 '다운받다'라는 반(半)외래어 동사를 만들어 쓴다는 거예요. 글·메뉴에서는 '다운로드(하다)'라고 정식으로 쓰지만, 말할 때는 '다운받다'나 더 줄여 '다운'이라고 하는 게 훨씬 자연스러워요. 예를 들어 '이거 다운받았어?'처럼요. 비슷한 말로 순우리말 '내려받다'가 있는데, 뜻은 똑같지만 공공기관 안내문 같은 격식 있는 글에서 주로 보이고 일상 회화에서는 잘 안 써요. 반대말은 '업로드/올리다'예요. 영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 회화에서까지 '다운로드하다'를 고집하는 것인데, 친구끼리는 '다운받다'가 훨씬 자연스럽게 들려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
In casual speech 다운받다 (or just 다운) is far more natural than the full 다운로드하다 — use 받다 with friends.
Don't confuse 다운로드 (saving onto your device) with 업로드 (sending a file out). They are opposite directions.
다운받다 already contains '받다 (receive)', so don't add another receiving verb — say 다운받았어, not 다운로드를 받았어.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 업로드 means "upload" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 업로드 (eomnodeu) = "upload". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 업로드 ("upload") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 업로드, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: From English; sending a file from your device out to the internet
Full form with 하다; sending up a photo, document, etc.
Native verb 'to put up'; the most natural way to say upload in speech
안 되다 = doesn't work; when a file won't go up

examples.en: I uploaded the photo.
examples.note: 올리다 = to put up; the everyday verb for posting/uploading

examples.en: You can just upload the file here.
examples.note: ~하면 돼요 = you just have to ~; note 에 marks the upload destination

examples.en: The file's too big, so it won't upload.
examples.note: 용량이 크다 = large file size; a frequent blocker

extendedVocab.nuance: '업로드'는 영어 'upload'에서 온 외래어로, 내 기기의 파일을 인터넷으로 '올려 보내는' 것을 뜻해요. 명사로 쓰고 '하다'를 붙여 '업로드하다'라는 동사를 만들 수 있지만, 일상 대화에서는 순우리말 '올리다'를 쓰는 게 훨씬 흔해요. '인스타에 사진 올렸어', '글 올렸어요'처럼요. 여기서 '업로드하다'와 '올리다'의 미묘한 차이를 알면 좋아요. '올리다'는 SNS·게시판에 글·사진을 '게시'한다는 느낌이 강하고, '업로드하다'는 서버·드라이브에 파일을 '전송'한다는 기술적 느낌이 더 강해요. 그래서 클라우드에 자료를 넣을 때는 '업로드하다'가, 인스타에 일상 사진을 공유할 때는 '올리다'가 더 어울려요. 반대말은 '다운로드/다운받다'예요. 영어 화자는 'upload'를 늘 '업로드하다'로 직역하기 쉬운데, 사진·글이라면 '올리다'가 한국어답게 들려요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
In everyday speech, prefer the native 올리다 over 업로드하다 for photos and posts (인스타에 올렸어, not 인스타에 업로드했어).
업로드 (sending up/out) and 다운로드 (bringing down/in) are opposites — don't swap them.
Use 에 for the place you upload to: 여기에 업로드하다 (upload here), not 여기를 업로드하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 캡처 means "screenshot, screen capture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 캡처 (kaepcheo) means "screenshot, screen capture". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 캡처 ("screenshot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 캡처 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: From English 'capture'; an image of your screen (standard spelling, not 캡쳐)
Add 하다 to verbify; capture what's on screen
화면 = screen; the fuller, clearer phrasing
~해서 보내다 = capture then send; the typical action chain

examples.en: I took a screenshot of this.
examples.note: Simple past with 하다; 캡처 functions as the verb stem

examples.en: I'll screenshot this and send it to you.
examples.note: ~해서 보내다 = do then send; the most common screenshot use

examples.en: The screenshot came out blurry.
examples.note: 흐릿하게 나오다 = to turn out blurry; an image-quality complaint

extendedVocab.nuance: '캡처'는 영어 'capture'에서 온 외래어로, 화면을 사진처럼 찍어 저장하는 것을 뜻해요. 정식 표기는 '캡처'이고, 사람들이 흔히 쓰는 '캡쳐'는 틀린 표기예요(외래어 표기법상 '쳐'가 아니라 '처'). 비슷한 말 '캡처'와 '스크린샷(screenshot)'은 둘 다 통하지만, 한국 일상에서는 '캡처'가 훨씬 입에 붙고 짧아서 더 자주 써요. 중요한 구분은 '캡처(screen capture)'와 '사진 찍다(take a real-world photo)'예요. 캡처는 휴대폰·컴퓨터 '화면 속 내용'을 그대로 저장하는 것이고, 카메라로 바깥 풍경을 담는 건 '사진(을) 찍다'예요. 영어 화자가 'take a screenshot'의 take를 생각해 '캡처를 찍다'라고 말하기 쉬운데, '캡처하다' 자체에 이미 '찍어 저장한다'는 뜻이 있어서 '찍다'를 또 붙일 필요가 없어요. 한국에서는 정보·증거를 공유할 때 캡처를 정말 많이 써요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Standard spelling is 캡처, not 캡쳐 — even though you'll see 캡쳐 everywhere online, write 캡처.
캡처 is capturing the screen's contents; don't confuse it with 사진 찍다 (taking a photo of the real world with a camera).
Don't say 캡처를 찍다. 캡처하다 already means 'take/save a screenshot', so adding 찍다 is redundant.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 첨부파일 means "attachment, attached file" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "attachment, attached file" is 첨부파일 (cheombupail). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 첨부파일 ("attachment"). Watch the particle attached to 첨부파일 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 첨부 (attaching) + 파일 (file); a file attached to an email/message
보내다 = to send; the basic email action
확인하다 = to check; what you ask a recipient to do
첨부하다 = to attach (the verb of the action), vs the noun 첨부파일

examples.en: I sent the attachment.
examples.note: Simple past with 보내다; 첨부파일 is the object

examples.en: The attachment won't open.
examples.note: 안 열리다 = won't open (intransitive); a frequent email problem

examples.en: I'll send it to you as an attachment.
examples.note: N으로 보내다 = send as/in the form of N; polite business phrasing

extendedVocab.nuance: '첨부파일'은 한자어 첨부(添附, '더해 붙이다')와 외래어 파일(file)이 합쳐진 말로, 이메일·메신저에 함께 딸려 보내는 파일을 뜻해요. 회사 생활에서 정말 자주 쓰는 단어예요. 핵심은 명사와 동사의 구분이에요. '첨부파일'은 붙여 보낸 '파일 그 자체(명사)'이고, 파일을 붙이는 '행위'는 '첨부하다(동사)'예요. 그래서 '파일을 첨부했어요(I attached the file)'와 '첨부파일을 보냈어요(I sent the attachment)'를 상황에 맞게 갈라 써야 해요. 비슷한 말로 그냥 '파일'이 있지만, '파일'은 모든 파일을 가리키는 넓은 말이고 '첨부파일'은 '메일·메시지에 붙여 보낸' 파일로 한정돼요. 영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 'attach a file'의 어순대로 '파일 첨부하다'에서 조사를 빠뜨리는 거예요. 목적어 조사 '을/를'을 넣어 '파일을 첨부하다'가 맞아요. '첨부파일 빠뜨렸어요(forgot the attachment)'는 직장에서 흔한 실수 표현이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
첨부파일 is the file itself (a noun); the action of attaching is 첨부하다 (a verb). Use 파일을 첨부하다 for the action, 첨부파일을 보내다 for the thing.
Don't drop the object particle: say 파일을 첨부하다, not 파일 첨부하다, when you mean the act of attaching.
Don't space the compound noun as 첨부 파일 in normal use; 첨부파일 is written as one word.

'첨부파일'은 한자어 첨부(添附, '더해 붙이다')와 외래어 파일(file)이 합쳐진 말이에요.
영어 화자가 자주 하는 실수는 'attach a file'의 어순대로 '파일 첨부하다'에서 조사를 빠뜨리는 거예요. 목적어 조사 '을/를'을 넣어 '파일을 첨부하다'가 맞아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 링크 means "link, URL" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 링크 (ringkeu) = "link, URL". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 링크 ("link") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 링크, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: From English; a clickable URL to a page/file (standard spelling, not 린크)
보내다 = to send; sharing a URL in chat
누르다 = to press; how Koreans usually say 'click', especially on mobile
복사하다 = to copy; the 'copy link' share option

examples.en: Please send me the link.
examples.note: Simple request: 보내다 + 주세요; the object particle 를 can drop in casual speech

examples.en: Nothing comes up even when I tap the link.
examples.note: 아무것도 안 뜨다 = nothing appears; a broken-link complaint using 누르다

examples.ko: 모르는 사람이 보낸 링크는 누르지 마세요.
examples.romanization: moreuneun sarami bonael lingkeuneun nureuji maseyo.
examples.en: Don't click links from people you don't know.
examples.note: 누르지 마세요 = don't press; basic phishing safety advice

extendedVocab.nuance: '링크'는 영어 'link'를 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 인터넷 주소(URL)나 누르면 다른 페이지로 가는 연결을 가리켜요. 표준 표기는 '링크'이고 '린크'는 틀려요. 한국어에서 흥미로운 점은 'click'을 옮기는 방식이에요. 컴퓨터 마우스 환경에서는 '클릭하다'도 쓰지만, 스마트폰이 일상인 한국에서는 손으로 '누르는' 동작이라 '누르다'를 훨씬 자주 써요. 그래서 '링크 클릭해 보세요'보다 '링크 눌러 보세요'가 더 자연스럽게 들려요. 비슷한 말로 '주소(URL)'가 있는데, '주소'는 'https://...' 같은 글자 형태의 인터넷 주소를 가리키고, '링크'는 그 주소를 담아 '누르면 이동하는' 연결 전체를 뜻해 약간 더 넓어요. 또 '링크를 걸다'라는 표현은 글이나 메시지에 링크를 삽입한다는 뜻으로 자주 써요. 모르는 사람이 보낸 링크는 피싱일 수 있으니 누르지 말라는 안전 안내도 자주 들어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
On mobile, Koreans say 링크를 누르다 (press/tap) far more than 클릭하다 (click) — 누르다 sounds more natural in speech.
Don't write 린크 — the standard spelling is 링크.
Don't equate 링크 exactly with 주소. 주소 is the text URL itself; 링크 is the clickable connection that carries you to it.

structuredNuance.t: '링크'는 영어 'link'를 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 인터넷 주소(URL)나 누르면 다른 페이지로 가는 연결을 가리켜요. 표준 표기는 '링크'이고 '린크'는 틀려요. 또 '링크를 걸다'라는 표현은 글이나 메시지에 링크를 삽입한다는 뜻으로 자주 써요. 모르는 사람이 보낸 링크는 피싱일 수 있으니 누르지 말라는 안전 안내도 자주 들어요.
비슷한 말로 '주소(URL)'가 있는데, '주소'는 'https://...' 같은 글자 형태의 인터넷 주소를 가리키고, '링크'는 그 주소를 담아 '누르면 이동하는' 연결 전체를 뜻해 약간 더 넓어요.
한국어에서 흥미로운 점은 'click'을 옮기는 방식이에요. 컴퓨터 마우스 환경에서는 '클릭하다'도 쓰지만, 스마트폰이 일상인 한국에서는 손으로 '누르는' 동작이라 '누르다'를 훨씬 자주 써요. 그래서 '링크 클릭해 보세요'보다 '링크 눌러 보세요'가 더 자연스럽게 들려요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 결혼식 means "wedding (ceremony)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 결혼식 (gyeolhonsik) means "wedding (ceremony)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 결혼식에 가다 ("go to a wedding"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 결혼식 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Take the particle 에 (destination/event), never 을 — you go TO the event
Set idiom for the couple having their ceremony; 올리다 (lit. 'raise/offer up') sounds more elevated than 하다
Add 場 (-장, 'place') for the building; 예식장 (禮式場) is the equally common synonym
You receive a 청첩장 (invitation); 초대받다 = 'be invited' in passive

examples.en: There's a wedding next week.
examples.note: Simple 있다 existence sentence — note 결혼식이, the subject marker, not 결혼식을

examples.en: There are so many weddings every weekend that it's a bit of a financial burden.
examples.note: 마다 = 'every'; weekend weddings + 축의금 are a real money pressure Koreans joke about

examples.ko: 부장님 딸 결혼식이라 회사 사람들이 다 같이 갔어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim ttal gyeolhonsigira hoesa saramdeuri da gachi gasseoyo.
examples.en: It was our manager's daughter's wedding, so everyone from the office went together.
examples.note: Shows the workplace-obligation register: attending a boss's family wedding is near-mandatory

extendedVocab.nuance: 결혼식 is the wedding CEREMONY (식 = 式 'ceremony/rite'), as opposed to 결혼 (結婚, 'tie + marry'), which is the marriage or the act of getting married — so 결혼했어요 means 'I got married,' while 결혼식에 갔어요 means 'I attended a wedding.' That 결혼/결혼식 split is the #1 trap for English speakers, since English 'wedding' blurs both. Compared with the everyday synonym 예식 (禮式, 'ceremony of courtesy'), 결혼식 is the plain default and 예식 sounds slightly more formal/venue-flavored (hence 예식장). The ceremony itself is famously short (30–60 minutes); the socially weighty part is the buffet meal afterward, which your cash gift 축의금 helps cover. Habitual collocations: 결혼식에 가다/참석하다, 결혼식을 올리다, 결혼식장. Take 에 for attendance — 결혼식을 가다 is a common particle error.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't confuse 결혼식 (the ceremony you attend) with 결혼 (the marriage): '결혼했어요' means YOU got married, so saying it when you only went to a friend's wedding wrongly announces your own marriage. Use 결혼식에 갔어요.
Avoid 결혼식을 가다 — 'go' targets a destination, so the natural particle is 에: 결혼식에 가다. The 을/를 here sounds like you're somehow 'doing' the wedding.
Don't say 결혼식을 하다 for the couple holding it; the idiomatic verb is 올리다 (결혼식을 올리다) or simply 결혼하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 장례식 means "funeral" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "funeral" is 장례식 (jangnyesik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 장례식에 가다 ("go to a funeral"). Watch the particle attached to 장례식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Particle 에 for attendance; you go to pay respects (조문하다)
장례식장 (場) is the building, often inside a hospital; 빈소 (殯所) is the specific mourning room
參席 'take part'; more formal than 가다, standard in workplace announcements
Said of the bereaved family holding it; drop 식 and use 치르다 ('go through / carry out')

examples.en: I wore black clothes to the funeral.
examples.note: Basic 입고 가다 ('wear and go'); dark, plain clothing is expected

examples.ko: 부장님 아버님 장례식이라 부서 사람들이 다 조문하러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim abeonim jangnyesigira buseo saramdeuri da jomunhareo gasseoyo.
examples.en: It was our manager's father's funeral, so the whole team went to pay respects.
examples.note: 조문하러 가다 = 'go in order to pay condolences'; teaches the -러 purpose ending in a real obligation context

examples.en: It was such sudden news that I rushed straight to the funeral hall.
examples.note: Real-situation register; 달려가다 ('run/rush to') conveys urgency and closeness to the bereaved

extendedVocab.nuance: 장례식 is a funeral — 葬 'bury' + 禮 'rite' + 式 'ceremony,' literally the 'burial-rite ceremony.' Distinguish it from the act-focused 장례 (葬禮, the funeral proceedings the family 치르다 'carries out') and from 조문/문상 (弔問/問喪), which is what a GUEST does — paying condolences. So the family 장례를 치르다, while you 장례식에 가서 조문하다. Korean funerals typically run three days at a 장례식장 frequently attached to a hospital, with the 빈소 (殯所, wake room) as the core space. Attending a colleague's or friend's family wake is a heavy social duty; you bring 조의금 in a plain white envelope and wear muted dark clothing. English speakers wrongly carry over 'congratulations'-type warmth — the funeral register is solemn and understated, and bright clothing or cheerful words badly misfire.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't say or bring anything 축하 (congratulatory): the correct sentiment is 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ('I humbly pray for the deceased's peace') or a quiet word of condolence. 축하 at a funeral is a severe register error.
Don't confuse the white-envelope 조의금 (funeral) with the wedding 축의금; using the wrong word or a colored envelope is a serious faux pas.
Don't mix up 장례식 (the ceremony/event) with 장례 (the family's act of holding it): a guest goes to the 장례식, but it's the family that 장례를 치르다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 돌잔치 means "first-birthday party (for a baby)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 돌잔치 (doljanchi) = "first-birthday party (for a baby)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 돌잔치를 하다 ("hold a first-birthday party") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 돌잔치, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Said of the parents throwing it; 하다 is natural here
Coworkers/friends with a baby invite you; implies a gift or cash
The highlight: the baby grabs an object said to foretell its future
答禮 'gift in return'; parents give guests 떡, towels, etc. in thanks

examples.en: My niece's first-birthday party is next month.
examples.note: Simple 있다 sentence; 돌잔치 takes the subject marker 가

examples.en: At the doljanchi the baby grabbed the microphone in the doljabi.
examples.note: 에서 marks the location of the action; guests cheer whichever object the baby picks

examples.ko: 요즘은 돌잔치를 작게 가족끼리만 하는 집도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun doljanchireul jakge gajokkkiriman haneun jipdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many families hold the doljanchi small, just among relatives.
examples.note: 끼리 = 'among (only)'; reflects the real shift from lavish halls to intimate gatherings

extendedVocab.nuance: 돌잔치 = 돌 (native Korean for a baby's first birthday) + 잔치 (native Korean for 'feast/celebration'), so unlike most life-event words here it is NOT Sino-Korean — there's no hanja. 돌 historically marked surviving the dangerous first year when infant mortality was high, which is why it's celebrated rather than treated like an ordinary 생일. Keep that contrast sharp: 돌잔치 is ONLY the first birthday; every later birthday is 생일, and the polite/honorific 생신 is for elders. The signature ritual is 돌잡이, where the baby grabs an object (money, thread, pencil, mic…) believed to predict its future. As a guest you give cash or a baby gift and may receive a 답례품 in return. Watch the spelling: 돌잔치 is one word, not 돌 잔치.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
돌잔치 is specifically the FIRST birthday — don't use it for a 5th or 30th birthday. Any ordinary birthday is 생일 (and 생신 for an elder).
Write it as one word, 돌잔치, not 돌 잔치 with a space; 잔치 ('feast') is fused onto 돌.
Don't call it 첫 번째 생일 파티 as a literal translation of 'first birthday party' — Koreans have the dedicated word 돌잔치, and the calque sounds foreign.

structuredNuance.t: 돌잔치 is a baby's first-birthday celebration. 돌 historically marked surviving the dangerous first year when infant mortality was high, which is why it's celebrated rather than treated like an ordinary 생일. The signature ritual is 돌잡이, where the baby grabs an object (money, thread, pencil, mic…) believed to predict its future. As a guest you give cash or a baby gift and may receive a 답례품 in return.
Keep the contrast sharp: 돌잔치 is ONLY the first birthday; every later birthday is 생일, and the polite/honorific 생신 is for elders.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 환갑 means "60th birthday (hwangap)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 환갑 (hwangap) means "60th birthday (hwangap)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환갑을 맞다 ("reach one's 60th birthday"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환갑 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 맞다 = 'greet/meet' a milestone date; 환갑을 맞이하다 is the fuller form
Add 잔치 ('feast'); the traditional celebration party
Use 시 honorific because it concerns an elder
進甲; the year after 환갑, sometimes also marked

examples.en: My father turns 60 this year.
examples.note: Honorific 이세요 because it's about a parent — never the plain 환갑이에요 for an elder

examples.ko: 예전에는 환갑잔치를 크게 했는데 요즘은 잘 안 해요.
examples.romanization: yejeoneneun hwangapjanchireul keuge haenneunde yojeumeun jal an haeyo.
examples.en: People used to hold big 60th banquets, but these days they often don't.
examples.note: -는데 sets up the past-vs-now contrast; longer lifespans made 60 less momentous

examples.ko: 할머니 환갑이라 온 가족이 호텔에서 식사를 했어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoni hwangabira on gajogi hotereseo siksareul haesseoyo.
examples.en: It was grandmother's 60th, so the whole family had a meal at a hotel.
examples.note: Real-situation use; shows the modern trend of a family meal/trip replacing a banquet

extendedVocab.nuance: 환갑 (還甲, 'return + sexagenary-cycle') literally means the 갑(甲) has come full circle: traditional Korea counts years on a 60-term zodiac cycle (干支), so turning 60 'returns' you to the cycle's start — hence also written 회갑 (回甲, 'revolve + cycle'), the more formal variant. Don't confuse it with the milestone above it, 칠순/고희 (70th, 古稀 'rare since old times'), or with 진갑 (進甲, the 61st). Because life expectancy was once short, reaching 환갑 was a rare achievement worthy of a big 환갑잔치; today, with people routinely living far longer, families more often mark it with a trip or gift than a banquet. Crucial register point: 환갑 always concerns an elder, so use honorifics — 환갑이세요, 환갑을 맞으셨어요 — and pair it with 생신 (not 생일) when naming the birthday itself.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Because it concerns an elder, use honorific forms: 환갑이세요 / 환갑이시다, not the plain 환갑이에요. Dropping the 시 honorific about a parent or grandparent sounds disrespectful.
Don't equate 환갑 with simply 'turning 60' in a Western sense — it's tied to the 60-year 干支 cycle and Korean age reckoning, so the cultural weight (and sometimes the exact year) differs.
Don't reach for 생일 when speaking of the elder's day; pair 환갑 with the honorific 생신 (e.g. 환갑 생신).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 청첩장 means "wedding invitation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "wedding invitation" is 청첩장 (cheongcheopjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 청첩장을 주다 / 받다 ("give / receive a wedding invitation"). Watch the particle attached to 청첩장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 implies a soft obligation to attend or send 축의금
Sent as a KakaoTalk link; now the default, bundling a map and account number
돌리다 ('send around') = casually handing them to friends and coworkers
文句 'phrasing'; the formal text announcing the couple and date

examples.en: I received a wedding invitation yesterday.
examples.note: Basic 받다 sentence; 청첩장 takes 을 as the object

examples.ko: 친구가 청첩장 주려고 일부러 만나자고 했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga cheongcheopjang juryeogo ilbureo mannajago haesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend asked to meet up on purpose just to give me the invitation.
examples.note: -(으)려고 = 'in order to'; handing a paper 청첩장 in person is a courteous gesture

examples.ko: 모바일 청첩장에 계좌번호랑 오시는 길이 다 들어 있더라고요.
examples.romanization: mobail cheongcheopjange gyejwabeonhorang osineun giri da deureo itdeoragoyo.
examples.en: The mobile invitation had the bank account number and directions all included.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a fresh discovery; reflects how digital invites bundle 축의금 transfer info

extendedVocab.nuance: 청첩장 (請牒狀) breaks down as 請 'request/invite' + 牒 'official note' + 狀 'document/letter' — a 'letter requesting your presence,' specifically for a WEDDING. Keep it apart from the general 초대장 (招待狀, any invitation card to a party/event): every 청첩장 is a 초대장, but you only call it 청첩장 for a wedding. Increasingly it arrives as a 모바일 청첩장, a KakaoTalk link that bundles a map, schedule, and the couple's bank account number for transferring 축의금. Receiving one carries a quiet obligation: you're expected either to attend or to send the cash gift, and ignoring a close friend's or coworker's 청첩장 can genuinely strain the relationship. Habitual verbs: 청첩장을 주다/받다/돌리다. The hanja is opaque even to many Koreans, so just learn it as a fixed word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't substitute 초대장 (general invitation card) for 청첩장: 초대장 covers any party/event, while 청첩장 is the wedding-specific term. Calling a wedding invite a 초대장 sounds slightly off.
Don't treat a received 청첩장 as optional info — from a close friend or coworker it's a soft social obligation; silence (no attendance and no 축의금) can damage the relationship.
Don't say 청첩장을 보내다 only for paper — these days 청첩장을 보내다 most often means sending the KakaoTalk 모바일 청첩장 link, so don't picture an envelope by default.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 축의금 means "congratulatory cash gift (at weddings)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 축의금 (chuguigeum) = "congratulatory cash gift (at weddings)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 축의금을 내다 ("give/pay the cash gift") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 축의금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 내다 ('hand in / pay') is the standard verb at the 접수처 (reception desk)
보내다 = transfer it to their account when you can't attend
封套 'envelope'; a white envelope you sign your name on at the desk
Common baseline amounts; closer relationships and elders give more

examples.en: I gave 50,000 won as the gift.
examples.note: (으)로 = 'as/by means of'; 5만 원 is the common baseline amount

examples.ko: 접수처에서 봉투에 이름 적고 축의금을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: jeopsucheoeseo bongtue ireum jeokgo chuguigeumeul naesseoyo.
examples.en: I wrote my name on the envelope at the reception desk and handed in the gift.
examples.note: You sign so the couple can record who gave what — teaches the desk routine

examples.ko: 결혼식에 못 가서 축의금만 계좌로 보냈어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsige mot gaseo chuguigeumman gyejwaro bonaesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't make the wedding, so I just sent the gift to their account.
examples.note: Real situation; -만 ('only') + 계좌로 ('by account') shows transfer is fully acceptable

extendedVocab.nuance: 축의금 (祝儀金) = 祝 'congratulate' + 儀 'ceremony/propriety' + 金 'money' — literally 'money for a congratulatory ceremony,' the cash you give at HAPPY events, above all weddings. Its exact mirror image is 조의금 (弔儀金, 'condolence-ceremony money') for funerals: same 儀金 ending, opposite first character (祝 'congratulate' vs 弔 'mourn'), and opposite occasions — confusing the two, or reusing the wrong envelope, is a real and embarrassing error. You place 축의금 in a WHITE envelope, sign it, and hand it in at the 접수처 (reception desk) so the couple can record who gave it. Amounts start around 50,000 won and rise with closeness, traditionally in odd denominations (5/7/10만). extendedVocab.explanation: 조용히 (joyonghi) means "quietly, calmly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조용히 해 주세요 ("please be quiet"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조용히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request for quiet in a library, cafe, or meeting; 해 주세요 softens it
Lower your voice so others aren't disturbed; contrast 작게 말하다 (low volume)
조용히 지내요 = I'm keeping a calm, low-key life these days
Casual and slightly sharp; 좀 here adds mild irritation, not politeness

examples.en: Be quiet, please.
examples.note: Blunt 반말 between close friends or to a noisy kid; 좀 nudges it toward a plea

examples.en: The baby's sleeping, so come in quietly.
examples.note: 조용히 attaches to the action verb 들어오다 — it modifies HOW you enter

examples.ko: 요즘은 그냥 집에서 조용히 쉬고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun geunyang jibeseo joyonghi swigo isseoyo.
examples.en: These days I'm just resting quietly at home.
examples.note: Here 조용히 = low-key / peacefully, not literal silence

extendedVocab.nuance: 조용히 is the adverb of the adjective 조용하다 and stretches from literal silence ('be quiet') to a calm, low-key MANNER of doing things ('live quietly, rest peacefully'), so it's far more useful in speech than the adjective alone. The dividing line with its neighbors matters: 작게 means low in VOLUME, 가만히 means without MOVING, and 몰래 means in SECRET — only 조용히 covers undisturbing quietness. It collocates with 하다, 말하다, 지내다, 들어오다. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as the adjective: you cannot say '조용히 사람' for 'a quiet person' — that needs the adjective form 조용한 사람, while 조용히 only modifies a verb. Also mind the spelling: it ends in 히, not 이.

Spelling it 조용이; the standard adverb form is 조용히 with 히 (the 이/히 choice is fixed per word and just has to be memorized).
Using 조용히 to mean 'secretly / on the sly' — that idea is 몰래 (몰래 나가다 = sneak out). 조용히 only means without noise or fuss.
Saying 조용히 사람 for 'a quiet person'; 조용히 modifies verbs only, so a noun needs the adjective 조용한 (조용한 사람).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 깨끗이 means "cleanly, thoroughly (clean)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cleanly, thoroughly (clean)" is 깨끗이 (kkaekkeusi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 깨끗이 씻다 ("to wash thoroughly"). Watch the particle attached to 깨끗이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing — hands, dishes, vegetables, fruit
Stresses cleaning all the way, leaving nothing dirty
For wiping a surface until no dirt or smudge remains
깨끗이 비웠어요 = I cleaned my plate / left nothing

examples.en: Wash your hands well.
examples.note: Bare everyday hygiene reminder; 깨끗이 tells you to wash THOROUGHLY, not just briefly

examples.ko: 이사 가기 전에 집을 깨끗이 치웠어요.
examples.romanization: isa gagi jeone jibeul kkaekkeusi chiwosseoyo.
examples.en: I cleaned the place up thoroughly before moving out.
examples.note: The move-out / deposit context where 깨끗이 = leave it spotless

examples.en: I've cleanly put the past behind me.
examples.note: Figurative: 깨끗이 잊다 = forget completely, with no residue of feeling

extendedVocab.nuance: 깨끗이 is the adverb of 깨끗하다 and crucially means doing something so the RESULT is clean and complete, not merely 'in a clean manner' — the focus is thoroughness. It's the natural partner of 씻다, 닦다, 청소하다, 치우다, and it extends figuratively to 깨끗이 잊다 (forget cleanly) or 깨끗이 인정하다 (admit it cleanly, with no excuses). Compare 깔끔하게, which describes a tidy, neat appearance/finish (깔끔하게 정리하다), whereas 깨끗이 emphasizes the absence of dirt or residue. The notorious trap is spelling: despite all its 히-ending siblings here, this word ends in 이 — 깨끗이, never 깨끗히. Roughly, when the stem ends in a ㅅ-type sound the adverb often takes 이.

Spelling it 깨끗히; the correct adverb is 깨끗이 with 이. This is one of the most common spelling errors even for native speakers.
Limiting it to physical surfaces — it also means finishing/resolving something completely, as in 깨끗이 잊다 or 깨끗이 포기하다 (give up cleanly).
Reaching for 깨끗이 when you mean a neat, stylish finish; that nuance is 깔끔하게 (깔끔하게 차려입다 = dress neatly), not 깨끗이.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가만히 means "still, motionless; just (leave be)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 가만히 (gamanhi) = "still, motionless; just (leave be)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가만히 있어 ("stay still / stay put") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가만히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Telling someone not to move or fidget; also 'stay out of it'
Asking someone to stop touching or meddling; 좀 adds exasperation

usagePhrases.en: now that I think it over quietly
usagePhrases.note: Sets up a reflective realization
Threat form; the same 가만히 turns menacing here

examples.en: Stay still.
examples.note: Bare command — to a wriggling child or someone about to make things worse

examples.ko: 가만히 좀 있어 봐, 내가 해 줄게.
examples.romanization: gamanhi jom isseo bwa, naega hae julge.
examples.en: Hold still a sec, I'll do it for you.
examples.note: Gentle 반말; 가만히 + 있다 = don't move, vs 가만히 + 두다 = don't touch

examples.en: Thinking it over quietly, I realized I'd messed up.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a realization you came to; 가만히 = calmly, taking a moment

extendedVocab.nuance: 가만히 carries two everyday senses that English splits apart: physically staying STILL (가만히 있어 = don't move) and letting something BE / not interfering (가만히 둬 = leave it alone). Note the meaning rides on the verb — 가만히 있다 is about your own body, 가만히 두다 is about not touching another thing. Don't confuse it with 조용히 (without noise): you can sit 가만히 yet keep talking. There's also a buried threat: 가만 안 둬 / 가만히 안 있을 거야 means 'I won't let this go,' so the same word can sound soothing or menacing purely by context. It frequently shortens to 가만 in speech (가만, 이게 뭐지? = 'wait, what's this?').

Translating it only as 'quietly'; 가만히 usually means 'without moving' or 'leave it be', not silence — that's 조용히.
Confusing 가만히 두다 (leave alone) with 가만히 있다 (stay still); the verb decides the meaning, so swapping them changes who/what is acting.
Missing the warning tone in 가만 안 둬 — beginners read it literally, but it's an idiom for 'you'll pay for this / I won't let it slide.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 꼼꼼히 means "thoroughly, meticulously" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 꼼꼼히 (kkomkkomhi) means "thoroughly, meticulously". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 꼼꼼히 확인하다 ("to check carefully"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 꼼꼼히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The most common pairing — documents, orders, contracts, bills
Reading every line and detail rather than skimming
Making sure absolutely nothing is left out
Weighing every detail before deciding or paying

examples.en: Look it over slowly and carefully.
examples.note: Bare advice; 꼼꼼히 pairs naturally with 천천히 — careful work isn't rushed

examples.ko: 짐을 꼼꼼히 챙겼는데도 우산을 두고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jimeul kkomkkomhi chaenggyeonneundedo usaneul dugo wasseoyo.
examples.en: Even though I packed carefully, I left my umbrella behind.
examples.note: -는데도 = even though; shows 꼼꼼히 = leaving nothing out

examples.en: The boss taught me the work thoroughly.
examples.note: A compliment — being called 꼼꼼하다 is high praise at a Korean workplace

extendedVocab.nuance: 꼼꼼히 is the adverb of 꼼꼼하다 and describes doing something with careful, detail-by-detail attention, never skipping or rushing. In Korea being 꼼꼼하다 is a strong virtue — it's a top answer when describing your work strengths in an interview. The fine line with 자세히 is the key thing for learners: 자세히 is about the DEPTH of detail covered (자세히 설명하다 = explain in full detail), while 꼼꼼히 is about the CAREFULNESS of the doer (꼼꼼히 확인하다 = check meticulously so nothing is missed). It naturally attaches to 확인하다, 읽다, 챙기다, 따지다, and it ends in 히. The pitfall is pairing it with speed: 꼼꼼히 is inherently unhurried, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 jars — thoroughness and haste pull against each other.

Spelling it 꼼꼼이; the standard adverb is 꼼꼼히 with 히.
Swapping it with 자세히 — 꼼꼼히 stresses the careful manner of the doer, 자세히 stresses the amount of detail, so '꼼꼼히 설명하다' sounds odd where '자세히 설명하다' is natural.
Combining it with speed words; 꼼꼼히 implies taking your time, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 하다 is self-contradictory.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 충분히 means "enough, sufficiently, plenty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "enough, sufficiently, plenty" is 충분히 (chungbunhi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 충분히 자다 ("to sleep enough"). Watch the particle attached to 충분히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 충분히 잤어요 = I slept plenty / got enough sleep
Reassuring someone you completely get it
Confirming something is well within reach
Sympathizing — 'anyone could react that way'

examples.en: There's plenty of time.
examples.note: Bare reassurance to take the pressure off; 충분히 = enough and to spare

examples.en: Cook the meat thoroughly before eating.
examples.note: 익히다 = cook through; here 충분히 = to a sufficient degree

examples.en: I completely understand how you feel.
examples.note: Warm, empathetic; spoken 충분히 softens into 'completely/totally'

extendedVocab.nuance: 충분히 comes from 充分 (充 'to fill' + 分 'portion/share', literally 'a full portion') and means a quantity or degree has been fully met — enough sleep, enough time, enough understanding. The key contrast for learners is with 완전히 (完全, 'complete'): 충분히 means 'enough for the purpose', not necessarily 100%, so 충분히 익히다 = cook it ENOUGH, while 완전히 익히다 = cook it ALL the way through. In conversation 충분히 also broadens into 'easily / readily' (충분히 그럴 수 있어요 = that could easily happen), which surprises learners expecting a literal amount. It's polite and supportive, which is why it floods comforting speech: 충분히 잘했어요, 충분히 이해해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 충분히 (sufficiently / enough) with 완전히 (completely / entirely); 충분히 means 'enough for the need', not 'totally'.
Forgetting the 'easily / readily' sense in 충분히 그럴 수 있어요 — it's not about a measured amount but about something being entirely plausible.
Over-translating it as 'a lot' (많이); 충분히 means it MEETS the need, whereas 많이 just means a large amount with no judgment of sufficiency.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 분명히 means "clearly, surely, definitely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 분명히 (bunmyeonghi) = "clearly, surely, definitely". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 분명히 말하다 ("to say clearly / state plainly") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 분명히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Making your point unmistakable, leaving no room for doubt
분명히 기억나요 = I remember it for certain
Insisting something is so, often against pushback
분명히 올 거예요 = they'll definitely come

examples.en: I definitely put it right here…
examples.note: Bare, half to yourself, when something's gone missing — the classic 분명히 moment

examples.en: Please tell me clearly from now on.
examples.note: 분명히 = unambiguously; a polite request for plain communication

examples.en: You clearly said it'd be done by yesterday.
examples.note: -잖아요 reminds the listener of a shared fact; 분명히 adds insistence

extendedVocab.nuance: 분명히 comes from 分明 (分 'divide' + 明 'bright/clear', i.e. 'distinctly clear') and links two senses: stating something plainly ('clearly say'), and asserting strong certainty ('surely, definitely'). The second floods spoken Korean, especially the exasperated 분명히 …했는데 ('I definitely did X, but…') when reality contradicts you. The sharp contrast to learn is with 확실히 (確實): 분명히 leans on the SPEAKER'S own conviction and memory ('I'm sure I did'), while 확실히 points to OBJECTIVE, checkable fact ('it's confirmed'). So 분명히 그 사람이었어 = I'm certain it was him; 확실히 그 사람이었어 leans toward 'it's been verified'. Because 분명히 voices real confidence, it clashes with a hedge — pair guesses with 아마 (probably) instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 분명히 and 확실히 as identical; 분명히 expresses your own subjective certainty, 확실히 reports objective, verifiable certainty.
Using 분명히 for a mere guess; it claims genuine confidence, so an unsure statement needs 아마 (아마 올 거예요 = they'll probably come).
Forgetting the plain 'clearly/distinctly' meaning — 분명히 말하다 is about clarity of statement, not just certainty.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 확실히 means "certainly, for sure, noticeably" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 확실히 (hwaksilhi) means "certainly, for sure, noticeably". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 확실히 알다 ("to know for sure"). Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 확실히 알아보고 알려줄게요 = I'll check for certain and let you know
Noting an obvious, observable difference
Pinning something down so there's no doubt later
One-word agreement: 확실히. = Definitely.

examples.en: After the medicine I'm noticeably better.
examples.note: Bare remark; here 확실히 = 'you can clearly tell' the difference

examples.ko: 이건 확실히 해 둬야 나중에 문제가 없어요.
examples.romanization: igeon hwaksilhi hae dwoya najunge munjega eopseoyo.
examples.en: We should settle this clearly so there's no problem later.
examples.note: 확실히 해 두다 = nail it down / make sure

examples.en: The new phone is definitely faster, I'll give it that.
examples.note: -긴 하다 concedes a point; 확실히 confirms an observed fact

extendedVocab.nuance: 확실히 comes from 確實 (確 'firm/certain' + 實 'real/solid', i.e. 'firmly real') and means 'certainly, for sure' — but its most useful everyday flavor is 'noticeably', when you can plainly OBSERVE a difference: 확실히 빠르다 (clearly faster), 확실히 낫다 (clearly better). Set against 분명히, the divide is subjective vs objective: 분명히 voices the speaker's inner conviction, whereas 확실히 points to verifiable, demonstrable fact. The fixed phrase 확실히 하다 / 확실히 해 두다 ('make it definite / settle it for sure') is everywhere at work and in agreements. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 'noticeably' reading — learners hear 확실히 다르다 as 'surely different' when a Korean means 'you can clearly SEE it's different.'

Treating 확실히 and 분명히 as interchangeable; 확실히 emphasizes objective, checkable certainty, 분명히 your personal conviction.
Overlooking the 'noticeably' sense — 확실히 다르다 / 확실히 좋아지다 means a difference you can plainly observe, not merely 'surely'.
Saying 확실히 사람 etc.; like all these -히 words it modifies a verb or adjective, never a noun directly (a noun needs 확실한).

Watch the particle attached to 간단히 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Giving a short, no-frills explanation
간단히 먹읍시다 = let's just eat something light
Connector that sets up a concise summary
Finishing without fuss or ceremony

examples.en: I just had gimbap for a quick lunch.
examples.note: 간단히 + 먹다 is THE phrase for a light, fast meal

examples.en: I'll keep the meeting short.
examples.note: A polite promise at work to not drag things out

examples.en: Simply put, the point is there isn't enough money.
examples.note: 간단히 말하면 = in short / to sum up

extendedVocab.nuance: 간단히 comes from 簡單 (簡 'brief/simple' + 單 'single', i.e. 'plain and single') and means doing something in a simple, brief, light way — a quick meal, a short explanation, a no-fuss finish. The crucial contrast is with 쉽게 (easily): 간단히 describes a small SCALE or effort, while 쉽게 describes low DIFFICULTY, so a task can be done 간단히 (quickly, lightly) yet still not be 쉽게 (it might be hard but short). The connector 간단히 말하면 ('in short') is a handy summarizing tool. The English-speaker trap is using it for a lavish meal or event — 간단히 inherently implies modest and light, so '간단히 잔치' (a simple feast) is a contradiction; for that you'd describe scale differently.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 간단히 (simply / lightly / briefly) with 쉽게 (easily); 간단히 is about small scale or low fuss, 쉽게 is about low difficulty.
Using 간단히 for a big, elaborate meal or event — it implies something light and quick, never a full spread.
Forgetting 간단히 먹다 is idiomatic for a fast, light meal; learners over-literally say 빨리 먹다 ('eat fast'), which is about speed, not lightness.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 자세히 means "in detail, closely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 자세히 (jasehi) = "in detail, closely". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 자세히 설명하다 ("to explain in detail") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 자세히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Asking for or giving a full, detailed explanation
Examining something up close and carefully
Researching all the details before deciding
Polite request for more specifics

examples.en: Tell me in a bit more detail.
examples.note: Bare 반말 request; 자세히 = with more specifics, not louder or faster

examples.en: I asked about the contract terms in detail.
examples.note: A smart move before signing anything in Korea

examples.en: When I looked closely, there was a scratch.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a discovery; 자세히 보다 = inspect up close

extendedVocab.nuance: 자세히 comes from 仔細 (仔 'careful' + 細 'fine/minute', i.e. 'down to the fine details') and means 'in detail / closely' — the natural opposite of 간단히. It pairs with 설명하다, 보다, 알아보다, 묻다 whenever you want full information rather than a quick gloss, and 자세히 설명해 주세요 is a survival phrase for getting specifics on contracts, services, and instructions in Korea. Two contrasts sharpen it: against 정확히 (正確, 'accurately'), 자세히 is about AMOUNT of detail while 정확히 is about CORRECTNESS — a long explanation can be 자세히 yet still wrong, hence not 정확히. And against 꼼꼼히, 자세히 describes the detail delivered, 꼼꼼히 the careful manner of the doer. It never describes a quantity of things, only thoroughness of explanation or observation.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 자세히 (in detail) with 정확히 (accurately / exactly); detailed is not the same as precise — you can explain at length yet inaccurately.
Using 자세히 about an amount of items; it describes thoroughness of explaining or looking, not how much there is (use 많이 for quantity).
Confusing it with 꼼꼼히; 자세히 설명하다 (give lots of detail) is natural, while 꼼꼼히 fits checking/handling (꼼꼼히 확인하다).

extendedVocab.explanation: 무심코 (musimko) means "absentmindedly, without thinking". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무심코 말하다 ("to say without thinking"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무심코 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Letting something slip with no intent
A careless comment, often unexpectedly hurtful
Tapping a button on autopilot
Something done without conscious thought

examples.en: It was just something I said without thinking.
examples.note: Bare apology/excuse; signals there was no bad intent

examples.en: I pressed the button without thinking, then canceled.
examples.note: -았다가 = did it, then reversed; 무심코 = on autopilot

examples.en: It was a thoughtless act, but it caused a misunderstanding.
examples.note: 오해를 사다 = to invite a misunderstanding

extendedVocab.nuance: 무심코 means doing or saying something absentmindedly, with no conscious intent, and it almost always sets up an UNINTENDED consequence — that's why it lives in apologies and reflections (무심코 한 말 = 'something I said without thinking'). It's built on 無心 (無 'without' + 心 'heart/mind', i.e. 'no mind/attention') plus the native suffix -코. The contrast to keep straight is the pair 무심코 vs 일부러 (on purpose): they're direct opposites, so 무심코 is your go-to when disclaiming intent. Don't confuse it with 무심하게, which means coldly/indifferently (a personality), whereas 무심코 means a one-off lapse of attention. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for anything planned — by definition 무심코 cannot describe a deliberate act.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 무심코 (without thinking) with 일부러 (on purpose); they are direct opposites, so they can't describe the same act.
Using 무심코 for a planned action; it specifically means there was no intention, so it clashes with anything deliberate.
Mixing it up with 무심하게 (coldly / indifferently) — 무심코 is a momentary lapse of attention, not a cold attitude.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 일부러 means "on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)" is 일부러 (ilbureo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일부러 그런 거 아니에요 ("I didn't do it on purpose"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I didn't do it on purpose
usagePhrases.note: The standard defense / apology after an accident
Going out of your way to see someone
Deliberately setting time aside for someone
Choosing not to do something on purpose

examples.en: I didn't do it on purpose.
examples.note: Bare, high-frequency apology; the #1 use of 일부러

examples.ko: 바쁠 텐데 일부러 와 줘서 고마워요.
examples.romanization: bappeul tende ilbureo wa jwoseo gomawoyo.
examples.en: Thanks for coming all this way even though you're busy.
examples.note: The warm 'went out of your way' sense — a sincere thank-you

examples.ko: 일부러 매운 걸 골랐어요, 스트레스 풀려고.
examples.romanization: ilbureo maeun geol gollasseoyo, seuteureseu pullyeogo.
examples.en: I picked something spicy on purpose, to relieve stress.
examples.note: Shows clear 'deliberately' intent toward a goal

extendedVocab.nuance: 일부러 (native Korean, no hanja) holds two everyday meanings English keeps apart: 'on purpose / intentionally', and 'going out of one's way / specially' to do a kindness. The first lives in apologies (일부러 그런 거 아니에요 = I didn't mean to), the second in thanks (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요 = thanks for making the special trip); both share the core of DELIBERATE effort, which makes it the opposite of 무심코. The contrast learners need is with 억지로 (reluctantly / by force): both involve doing something, but 일부러 is willing and intentional while 억지로 is against your will — 일부러 먹다 (eat on purpose, maybe for a reason) vs 억지로 먹다 (force yourself to eat). The pitfall is missing the warm 'special trip' reading and hearing only blame.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 일부러 (on purpose, willingly) with 억지로 (reluctantly / forcibly); intent is not the same as being forced — 억지로 means against your will.
Missing the warm 'going out of your way' sense, which is very common in thank-yous (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요).
Over-using it for routine choices; for a plain decision Koreans often just state the action, reserving 일부러 for genuinely deliberate or out-of-the-way acts.

extendedVocab.english: to one's heart's content, as much as you like
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마음껏 means "to one's heart's content, as much as you like" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 마음껏 (maeumkkeot) = "to one's heart's content, as much as you like". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마음껏 드세요 ("eat as much as you like") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 마음껏, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: eat as much as you like
usagePhrases.note: Gracious host phrase at a meal
Telling someone to have a great time without holding back

usagePhrases.en: to rest as much as you want
usagePhrases.note: Encouraging full, guilt-free rest
Inviting a totally free choice

examples.en: I made a lot, so please help yourself.
examples.note: 차리다 = set out food; warm 존댓말 hospitality

examples.en: The exam's over, so let's have all the fun we want today.
examples.note: 마음껏 놀다 = hang out / play with no restraint (반말)

examples.en: I rested as much as I wanted over the vacation.
examples.note: A satisfied way to describe a good, unhurried break

extendedVocab.nuance: 마음껏 means doing something fully and freely, to your heart's content, with no need to hold back — a generous, warm word that shines in hosting (마음껏 드세요) and in urging someone to enjoy or rest without restraint. It's 마음 ('heart/mind') + the native suffix -껏 ('to the very limit of'), the same -껏 you meet in 힘껏 (with all one's strength) and 정성껏 (with all one's care), so think of it as 'heart-to-the-max'. The contrast worth noting is with 실컷 (to one's fill / as much as one wants): the two overlap heavily, but 실컷 is more casual and often tied to satisfying an appetite or urge (실컷 자다 = sleep all you want), while 마음껏 sounds a touch warmer and more giving. The pitfall: it specifically means WITHOUT limits, so it clashes with any cap.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing it as two words 마음 껏; the suffix -껏 attaches directly to form one word, 마음껏.
Using 마음껏 where a limit applies — it means freely and without holding back, so it contradicts any restriction (e.g. 'pick one only').
Assuming 마음껏 and 실컷 are identical; they're close, but 실컷 is more casual and appetite-focused, while 마음껏 feels warmer and more generous.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 면 means "cotton (fabric)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 면 (myeon) means "cotton (fabric)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 면 100% ("100% cotton"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 면 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Reads exactly like this on a Korean clothing tag; spoken as '면 백 퍼센트'.
순(純, pure) + 면; the label word on bedding, towels, and baby clothes.
면 + item is the normal way to say what a thing is made of — no 으로 needed.
소재 = material/fabric; staff lean on this word when describing what clothes are made from.

examples.en: Is this cotton?
examples.note: The shortest, most useful tag-check question; 이거 + 명사 + 이에요? identifies a material.

examples.en: In summer cotton material is nice because it's cool.
examples.note: 시원하다 pairs naturally with breathable fabric; -아서 here gives the reason you like it.

examples.ko: 면 100%라서 빨면 좀 줄어들 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: myeon 100%raseo ppalmyeon jom jureodeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: It's 100% cotton, so it may shrink a bit when you wash it.
examples.note: 줄어들다 (shrink) is the real warning shop staff give about cotton; -라서 links the cause.

extendedVocab.nuance: 면 is the Sino-Korean word for cotton fabric (한자 綿, 'cotton/silk-floss'), and it papers Korean clothing, bedding, and towel tags. The near-synonym trap is 솜: 면 is the woven cloth you wear, while 솜 is the fluffy stuffing/batting packed inside a duvet or padded jacket — same raw fiber, totally different product, so a 솜이불 (stuffed quilt) is not a 면 garment. Register is neutral; everyone from shop staff to friends just says 면. The big English-speaker pitfall is the homophones: 면 also means 'noodles' (麵) and 'side/aspect' (面), so only the shopping-vs-food context separates them. Another trap is over-marking the material — beginners say 면으로 만든 티셔츠, but natural Korean is simply 면 티셔츠, sticking the material straight onto the noun.

Adding 으로 만든 every time (면으로 만든 바지). It is grammatical but heavy; native speech just says 면 바지, 면 티셔츠 with the material glued onto the noun.
Reading the tag homophone wrong: 면 on a menu is 'noodles' (麵), not cotton. Let the clothes-vs-food context tell you which 면 it is.

extendedVocab.explanation: "leather" is 가죽 (gajuk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 진짜 가죽 ("real / genuine leather"). Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: What you ask for when you don't want fake; 진짜 = real, the everyday opposite of 가짜.
인조(人造, man-made) + 가죽; the formal label term, more precise than the casual 가짜 가죽.
소(cow) + 가죽; the most common leather for bags and shoes, named by animal.
가죽 + item is the standard pattern for naming a leather thing.

examples.en: Is this real leather?
examples.note: The single most useful market question; 진짜 in front flags that you doubt it's genuine.

examples.ko: 가죽 제품은 비 오는 날 조심해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gajuk jepumeun bi oneun nal josimhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: You have to be careful with leather products on rainy days.
examples.note: 조심하다 + -아야 하다 gives practical 'you must' care advice you'll actually hear.

examples.en: For real leather, the price is awfully cheap, isn't it?
examples.note: N치고 = 'for / considering a N'; -ㄴ데요 softly voices polite suspicion about a too-good deal.

The synonym line that trips up English speakers is 피부 vs 가죽: both can translate as 'skin,' but 피부 is living human/animal skin and skincare, whereas 가죽 is the tanned material made from a hide — you have nice 피부, but you buy a 가죽 가방. Register is neutral; casual speech freely says 가짜 가죽 for fake, while labels prefer 인조가죽. Natural collocations are 진짜 가죽, 소가죽, 가죽 지갑/가방/구두, and the verb 가죽이 갈라지다 (the leather cracks). The pitfall: vendors at markets like Dongdaemun call PU/synthetic 가죽 loosely, so always confirm with 진짜 가죽이에요? before paying a leather price.

Assuming any item called 가죽 is genuine. Sellers apply 가죽 to PU/synthetic too, so pin it down with 진짜 가죽이에요? or look for the label word 인조가죽.
Saying 가죽으로 every time; for naming an item, native speech just compounds it: 가죽 지갑, 가죽 구두, 가죽 소파.

니트 (knit) + 울 to pin down the material of the sweater.

examples.en: Is this coat wool?
examples.note: Basic material check; 명사 + 이에요? is your all-purpose 'is this made of ___?' question.

examples.en: Wool is warm, but you mustn't machine-/water-wash it.
examples.note: -지만 contrasts the upside with the catch; 물세탁하면 안 되다 = washing with water is not allowed.

examples.ko: 울 스웨터는 드라이클리닝 맡기는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: ul seuweteoneun deuraikeullining matgineun ge joayo.
examples.en: It's best to take wool sweaters to the dry cleaner.
examples.note: 맡기다 = to entrust/drop off; V-는 게 좋다 = 'it's best to' for recommended care.

extendedVocab.nuance: 울 is the loanword for wool (straight from English 'wool'), and it dominates Korean winter-clothing tags. Its register-twin is 양모 (羊毛, literally 'sheep-hair'): same material, but 양모 is the bookish label word on care tags while 울 is what anyone says out loud — call a sweater 양모 니트 in conversation and it sounds like you read it off a box. A second contrast worth knowing is 캐시미어 (cashmere), a pricier, softer goat fiber often blended with 울; a tag reading 울 70 캐시미어 30 is a blend, which is why asking 울 몇 퍼센트예요? signals you know quality. The classic English-speaker pitfall is spelling/sound: 울 (wool) versus 월 (month, as in 1월) — one vowel apart and totally different, so don't write 월 코트.

Writing 월 (month) for 울 (wool). They look and sound close but 월 is the calendar word (예: 12월), while the fabric is 울. A '월 코트' makes no sense.
Calling 양모 in everyday conversation. 양모 (羊毛) is the formal label term; spoken Korean uses 울. Save 양모 for reading care tags.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 실크 means "silk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 실크 (silkeu) means "silk". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 실크 스카프 ("silk scarf"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 실크 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 실크 + item; scarves are the most common silk buy, often as a gift.
On the tag of nicer blouses and scarves; spoken '실크 백 퍼센트'.
Native term you meet around 한복 (hanbok) and traditional craft goods.
같다 (to be like) turns it into a texture description rather than the actual material.

examples.en: Is this scarf silk?
examples.note: Quick material check; the most natural opener before you ask the price or feel it.

examples.en: Since it's silk, only hand-washing is possible.
examples.note: -라서 gives the reason; 손세탁만 가능하다 = the standard care limit for delicate silk.

examples.ko: 선물용으로 실크 스카프 하나 살까 해요.
examples.romanization: seonmuryongeuro silkeu seukapeu hana salkka haeyo.
examples.en: I'm thinking of buying a silk scarf as a gift.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ까 하다 = 'thinking of doing'; 선물용 = for-gift purpose, a useful shopping word.

extendedVocab.nuance: 실크 is the everyday loanword for silk and rules modern speech and department-store tags. Its synonym is the native 비단, but the line is register and setting, not meaning: 비단 carries a traditional, almost literary flavor and lives around 한복, 보자기, and craft fairs, so saying 비단 스카프 at a glossy mall sounds quaint even though staff understand it — there they expect 실크. The texture that sells it is 부드럽다 (soft) and a smooth 촉감 (feel/touch), and a near-miss word is 새틴/satin, a weave that can be silk or polyester, so 실크 같다 ('silk-like') is how you hedge when you're unsure it's the real fiber. The pitfall for English speakers is care: 'silk' feels washable in English, but real 실크 almost always needs 손세탁 (hand washing) or dry cleaning, never a machine.

Saying 비단 in a modern department store. Staff get it, but 비단 (native, traditional) belongs with 한복 and crafts; for a mall blouse everyone says 실크.
Expecting to machine-wash 실크. Real silk needs 손세탁 or 드라이클리닝; tossing it in the washer ruins the fiber and the shine.
Confusing 실크 (the actual fiber) with 실크 같다 ('silky'). The 같다 form only describes texture — a 실크 같은 블라우스 may really be polyester.
