extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 골프 means "golf" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 골프 (golpeu) means "golf". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 골프 쳐요? ("Do you play golf?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 골프 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Golf also takes 치다; a common question among professionals and older colleagues.
스크린 골프 (indoor simulator golf) is hugely popular and affordable in Korea.

usagePhrases.en: I'm in the middle of learning golf
usagePhrases.note: -는 중이다 = 'in the process of'; golf lessons have spread to younger people.
골프장 = the course; 'going out to the course' = 필드 나가다.

examples.ko: 주말에 친구들이랑 스크린 골프 치러 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jumare chingudeurirang seukeurin golpeu chireo gasseoyo.
examples.en: On the weekend I went to play screen golf with friends.
examples.note: 치러 가다 = 'go in order to play (hit)'; 스크린 골프 is social and often paired with drinks.

examples.en: Golf is daunting to start because the equipment is expensive.
examples.note: 부담되다 = 'feel burdensome'; -기 turns 시작하다 into the noun 'starting'.

examples.ko: 부장님이 주말마다 골프 치러 필드 나가세요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimi jumalmada golpeu chireo pildeu nagaseyo.
examples.en: My boss goes out to the course to play golf every weekend.
examples.note: 필드 나가다 = 'go out to the real course'; -세요 is the honorific for the senior 부장님.

extendedVocab.nuance: 골프 is a loanword (no hanja), and like the other racket/club sports it takes 치다 ('to hit') — 골프를 치다, never 골프를 하다, because you strike the ball with a club. Socially it carries a slightly upscale, business-networking image, but 스크린 골프 (screen/simulator golf) has made it casual and accessible — a common night out with friends and coworkers. Two insider words English speakers should learn: the real outdoor course is called 필드 ('field'), and 필드 나가다 means 'go play on an actual course' (as opposed to the screen). In casual speech, plain 골프 치러 가자 often actually means 스크린 골프, so don't assume every mention implies an expensive outdoor round.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 골프 하다 instead of 골프 치다 — club-and-ball sports take 치다.
Assuming 골프 always means an expensive outdoor round — in casual speech it often means 스크린 골프.
Not knowing 필드 — Koreans call the real course 필드 and say 필드 나가다 for playing outdoors; 골프장 is the formal term.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 스키 means "skiing, ski" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "skiing, ski" is 스키 (seuki). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스키 탈 줄 알아요? ("Do you know how to ski?"). Watch the particle attached to 스키 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Do you know how to ski?
usagePhrases.note: Crucial verb: 스키는 타다 ('ride'), used for gear you stand on and ride.
타러 가다 = 'go in order to ride/do'; winter resort trips are common.
스키장 covers the whole resort; the major ones are in 강원도.
빌리다 = 'borrow/rent'; renting (대여) gear at the resort is normal for casual skiers.

examples.ko: 겨울에 강원도로 스키 타러 갈 거예요.
examples.romanization: gyeoure gangwondoro seuki tareo gal geoyeyo.
examples.en: This winter I'm going to Gangwon-do to ski.
examples.note: -로 marks direction toward 강원도; 타러 가다 = 'go to ski'.

examples.en: It was my first time skiing, so I rode the beginner course.
examples.note: 처음이라 = 'since it's the first time'; 초보자 코스 = 'beginner course'.

examples.ko: 스키 탈 때 넘어지면 진짜 아파요.
examples.romanization: seuki tal ttae neomeojimyeon jinjja apayo.
examples.en: When you fall while skiing, it really hurts.
examples.note: 넘어지다 = 'fall down'; -ㄹ 때 = 'when/while doing'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 스키 is a loanword (no hanja), and the verb is the whole lesson here: it takes 타다 ('to ride'), never 하다 — 스키를 타다. 타다 is the verb for anything you mount, board, or stand on to move (bus, bike, ski, skateboard), which is exactly why ski, snowboard, and skates all use it rather than 하다. Winter ski trips to 강원도 resorts are a popular group outing, often combined with 보드 (snowboarding) at the same place. The resort and slopes together are 스키장, and gear rental (대여/빌리다) is the norm for casual participants. The pitfall, besides 스키 하다, is conflating 스키 with 보드/스노보드 — they are different activities done at the same 스키장.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스키 하다 — the correct verb is 스키 타다 (you ride skis).
Confusing 스키 (skiing) with 보드/스노보드 (snowboarding) — different sports at the same 스키장.
Using 하다 for board sports too — snowboarding is also 보드(를) 타다, not 하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 스케이트 means "skating, ice skating" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 스케이트 (seukeiteu) = "skating, ice skating". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 스케이트 탈 줄 알아요? ("Can you skate?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 스케이트, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Like 스키, skating takes 타다, since you stand on the blades and ride.
타러 가자 = casual 'let's go to skate'; a popular winter date activity.
스케이트장 = the ice rink; seasonal outdoor rinks pop up in winter.
스케이트화 = the boots themselves (화 = 'footwear'); rented at the rink.

examples.en: In winter I went skating at an outdoor rink.
examples.note: 야외 = 'outdoor'; seasonal rinks at city plazas are popular dates.

examples.ko: 스케이트 처음 타는 사람은 벽 잡고 타요.
examples.romanization: seukeiteu cheoeum taneun sarameun byeok japgo tayo.
examples.en: First-timers skate while holding onto the wall.
examples.note: 벽 잡고 = 'gripping the wall'; -고 links the two simultaneous actions.

examples.ko: 김연아 덕분에 피겨 스케이트 인기가 많아졌어요.
examples.romanization: gimyeona deokbune pigyeo seukeiteu ingiga manajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to Kim Yu-na, figure skating became very popular.
examples.note: 피겨 스케이트 = 'figure skating'; 덕분에 marks the positive cause.

extendedVocab.nuance: 스케이트 is a loanword (no hanja) and, like 스키, takes 타다 ('to ride') — 스케이트를 타다 — because you stand on the blades and glide; 하다 is wrong. Korea has a strong skating culture thanks to short-track and figure stars like 김연아 (Kim Yu-na), and seasonal outdoor 스케이트장 are a classic winter date spot. The vocabulary to keep distinct trips up English speakers: 스케이트장 is the rink (place), while 스케이트화 is the boots (화 = footwear), and bare 스케이트 can mean the activity or loosely the gear. Also distinguish ice 스케이트 from 인라인/롤러 (inline/roller skating), which likewise take 타다 but happen on wheels, not ice.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스케이트 하다 instead of 스케이트 타다 — you ride skates, so it's 타다.
Mixing 스케이트장 (the rink) with 스케이트화 (the boots) — one is the place, one is the footwear.
Assuming 스케이트 means roller skating — that's 인라인/롤러; plain 스케이트 defaults to ice skating.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마라톤 means "marathon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 마라톤 (maraton) means "marathon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 마라톤 뛰어요? ("Do you run marathons?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 마라톤 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Marathons take the verb 뛰다 (to run); 달리다 also works.
대회(大會) = 'tournament/event'; weekend city marathons are common.
하프(half) 마라톤 — many beginners start here before a 풀코스 (full course).

usagePhrases.en: I signed up for a marathon
usagePhrases.note: 신청하다 = 'apply/register'; entries open online and fill up fast.

examples.ko: 이번 가을에 처음으로 하프 마라톤 뛰어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon gaeure cheoeumeuro hapeu maraton ttwieoyo.
examples.en: This fall I'm running my first half marathon.
examples.note: 처음으로 = 'for the first time'; the present tense here states a fixed near plan.

examples.en: If you finish the marathon, they give you a medal.
examples.note: 완주(完走)하다 = 'run the full course'; -면 = 'if/when', 줘요 has an unstated 'they'.

examples.ko: 요즘 러닝이 유행이라 마라톤 대회마다 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum neoningi yuhaengira maraton daehoemada sarami manayo.
examples.en: Running is trendy lately, so every marathon event is packed.
examples.note: 유행이라 = 'since it's a trend'; 마다 = 'every (single)'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 마라톤 is a loanword (no hanja) and fits the current 러닝 (running) boom among Koreans in their 20s-30s, where running crews and weekend 마라톤 대회 are genuinely trendy social scenes. The verb is 뛰다 or 달리다 ('to run') — not 하다; the fine distinction is that 뛰다 is the everyday word that also means 'jump/sprint', while 달리다 is a touch more squarely 'run/dash', and for marathons the two are interchangeable. Useful related words: 완주 (完走, 'complete the run') means finishing the full distance, and many start with a 하프 마라톤 before attempting the 풀코스. The pitfall for English speakers is assuming 마라톤 always means the full 42.195km; in casual use it loosely covers any race distance run at a 마라톤 대회.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 마라톤 하다 — natural Korean is 마라톤(을) 뛰다 or 마라톤(을) 달리다.
Assuming 마라톤 always means the full 42.195km — casually it can mean any race distance at a 마라톤 대회.
Forgetting 완주 — 'finishing' a marathon is 완주하다, a specific word, not just 끝내다 ('end it').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 경기 means "match, game (sporting event)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "match, game (sporting event)" is 경기 (gyeonggi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 경기 봤어요? ("Did you watch the game?"). Watch the particle attached to 경기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 경기 is the standard word for a sports match in any sport.
시작하다 = 'begin'; said the moment a match kicks off.
결과(結果) = 'result'; 경기 결과 is how you ask the final score/outcome.
있다 = 'there is'; a common check before planning to watch.

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 중요한 축구 경기가 있어요.
examples.romanization: oneul jeonyeoge jungyohan chukgu gyeonggiga isseoyo.
examples.en: There's an important soccer match this evening.
examples.note: Attach 경기 after the sport: 축구 경기, 야구 경기; 이/가 있다 = 'there is'.

examples.ko: 경기가 너무 박빙이라 끝까지 손에 땀을 쥐었어요.
examples.romanization: gyeonggiga neomu bakbingira kkeutkkaji sone ttameul jwieosseoyo.
examples.en: The game was so close I was on edge until the end.
examples.note: 박빙 = 'neck and neck'; 손에 땀을 쥐다 = idiom 'be on the edge of your seat'.

examples.en: The game was canceled today because of rain.
examples.note: 취소되다 = 'be canceled' (passive); 비 와서 = 'because it rained'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 경기 (競技, literally 'compete(競)-skill(技)', i.e. a contest of skill) is the all-purpose word for a sporting match and pairs with any sport (축구 경기, 야구 경기). The key contrast for English speakers is register: 경기 is the neutral, formal-friendly term for pro and broadcast sports, whereas the loanword 게임 fits casual pickup play — so defaulting to 게임 for a real match sounds off. A close synonym is 시합 (試合), which leans slightly toward 'contest/bout' and is common in spoken, head-to-head contexts; 경기 stays the safe neutral choice. The classic trap is the homophone: 경기 also means 'the economy' (경기가 안 좋다 = 'the economy is bad'), an unrelated word with different hanja (景氣) — only context tells them apart, but in a sports conversation 경기 is always the match.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Defaulting to 게임 for a pro match — use 경기 for real sporting events; 게임 implies casual play.
Treating 경기 and 시합 as totally separate — they overlap; 시합 just emphasizes the contest, 경기 is neutral.
Confusing 경기 (競技, sports match) with the homophone 경기 (景氣, the economy), as in 경기가 안 좋다 — different word, context disambiguates.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 심판 means "referee, umpire" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 심판 (simpan) = "referee, umpire". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 심판이 휘슬 불었어요 ("The referee blew the whistle") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 심판, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 휘슬(을) 불다 = 'blow the whistle'; signals a foul or stoppage.
판정(判定) = 'ruling/decision'; 심판 판정 often sparks fan complaints.
A heated shout at a bad call; 똑바로 = 'properly', 봐 is blunt 반말.
오심(誤審) = a refereeing error; a very common sports-news word.

examples.ko: 심판이 우리 팀한테만 불리하게 판정하는 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: simpani uri timhanteman bullihage panjeonghaneun geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: It felt like the ref was ruling unfairly against only our team.
examples.note: 한테만 = 'only against'; 불리하게 = 'disadvantageously'.

examples.en: Anyone can see that play was a wrong call.
examples.note: 누가 봐도 = 'no matter who looks / obviously'; 오심 = 'bad call'.

examples.ko: 요즘은 비디오 판독으로 심판 오심을 줄여요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun bidio pandogeuro simpan osimeul juryeoyo.
examples.en: These days they reduce referee errors with video review.
examples.note: 비디오 판독 = 'video review (VAR-style)'; -으로 = 'by means of'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 심판 (審判, literally 'examine(審)-judge(判)') is the referee/umpire across all sports, and it doubles as both the official (person) and the act of officiating. To follow sports talk you need its companions: 판정 (判定, 'ruling/decision'), 오심 (誤審, 'erroneous judgment' = a wrong call), and 비디오 판독 (video review), since fans endlessly grumble about 심판 판정. The whistle collocation is 휘슬을 불다. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not say 레퍼리 — the natural word is 심판, the loanword sounds out of place. Second, 심판 has a heavier non-sports sense of divine 'judgment' (최후의 심판 = 'the Last Judgment'); in a sports context it strictly means the on-field official, so context keeps the two apart.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 레퍼리 — Koreans say 심판, not the English loanword.
Confusing 심판 (referee) with the judgment/verdict sense (최후의 심판 'the Last Judgment') — in sports it's strictly the official.
Saying 심판 실수 for a bad call when the precise term exists — a misjudged call is 오심 (誤審), the standard sports-news word.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 망치 means "hammer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 망치 (mangchi) means "hammer". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 망치 ("hammer"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 망치 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday tool for driving nails; a basic item in any 공구함.

usagePhrases.en: to drive a nail in with a hammer
usagePhrases.note: 못을 박다 = drive a nail in; the tool takes the (으)로 particle, not 을/를.
Noun + 질 turns the tool into the activity; 망치질하다 = to hammer.
고무(rubber) + 망치; soft head for furniture so it leaves no marks.

examples.en: This is a hammer.
examples.note: Plain naming sentence; 망치 ends in a vowel so it takes 예요, not 이에요.

examples.ko: 벽에 액자 걸려고 망치로 못을 박았어요.
examples.romanization: byeoge aekja geollyeogo mangchiro moseul bagasseoyo.
examples.en: I hammered a nail into the wall to hang a frame.
examples.note: 걸려고 = in order to hang; the action verb is 박다, and 망치로 marks the instrument.

examples.ko: 고무망치는 가구 조립할 때 흠집 안 나서 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gomumangchineun gagu joripal ttae heumjip an naseo joayo.
examples.en: A rubber mallet is good for assembling furniture since it doesn't leave marks.
examples.note: 흠집(이) 나다 = a scratch forms; this is the register a Korean uses while doing IKEA-style assembly.

extendedVocab.nuance: 망치는 못이나 핀을 두드려 박을 때 쓰는 가장 기본적인 손공구입니다. 영어 'hammer'는 명사이자 동사이지만, 한국어 '망치'는 순수 명사라서 '망치하다'라는 동사는 없고, 반드시 '망치로 못을 박다(drive a nail with a hammer)'처럼 도구(으)로 + 동작 동사 구조로 풀어 써야 합니다. 이것이 영어 화자가 가장 자주 빠지는 직역 함정입니다. 두드리는 행위 자체는 '망치질'이라 하고, 비슷한 도구인 '망치(claw hammer)'와 '고무망치(rubber mallet)'는 머리 재질로 구분합니다. 흔히 '못을 박다, 망치질을 하다, 망치로 두드리다'처럼 어울려 쓰며, 도구를 나타낼 때 '망치를'이 아니라 '망치로'를 쓰는 점을 꼭 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 망치를 치다 or 망치하다 — Korean has no verb form of the tool; the natural phrase is 망치로 못을 박다 (drive the nail), with 망치 marked by 로.
Marking the hammer with 을/를 as if it were the object: 망치를 박다 is wrong. You drive the 못(nail) and the hammer is the instrument → 망치로.
Confusing 망치 (hammer) with 못 (nail); the hammer is what hits, the 못 is what gets hit.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 못 means "nail (for hammering)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "nail (for hammering)" is 못 (mot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 못 ("nail"). Watch the particle attached to 못 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The metal nail you hammer in; written the same as 못 'cannot' but a separate word.
박다 = drive/embed; the standard verb that pairs with 못, never 넣다.
빼다 = pull out; use pliers (펜치) or the claw of a hammer.
The dent or hole left in the wall; too many can mean a deposit deduction.

examples.en: There's a nail here.
examples.note: 못 ends in a consonant, so the subject form is 못이, not 못가.

examples.ko: 전셋집이라 못 박는 거 조심해야 돼요.
examples.romanization: jeonsetjibira mot bangneun geo josimhaeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: It's a jeonse place, so I have to be careful about hammering nails.
examples.note: Here 못 is the noun object of 박다; landlords may deduct from the deposit for wall damage.

examples.ko: 벽에 못 자국 남으면 보증금에서 깎일 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: byeoge mot jagung nameumyeon bojeunggeumeseo kkakkil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: If nail marks are left on the wall, it could be deducted from the deposit.
examples.note: 못 자국 = nail marks; 깎이다 = get docked — a real concern in Korean rentals.

extendedVocab.nuance: 못은 망치로 벽이나 나무에 두드려 박는 금속 핀입니다. 같은 도구류라도 '못'은 두드려서 고정하고 '나사(screw)'는 돌려서 고정한다는 점이 핵심 차이라, 못에는 '박다/빼다', 나사에는 '조이다/풀다'를 씁니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 'put a nail in'을 직역해 '못을 넣다'라고 하기 쉬운데, 못은 '넣다(put in)'가 아니라 '박다(drive in)'와 어울립니다. 둘째, 부정 부사 '못'(못 가요 = can't go)과 글자가 똑같아 헷갈리지만, 명사 못은 '못이, 못을'처럼 조사가 붙고 부사 못은 동사 앞에 홀로 옵니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '못을 박다, 못을 빼다, 못 자국, 못이 박히다(get driven in, 피동)'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up the noun 못 (nail) with the adverb 못 used for inability (못 해요 = can't do). The noun takes particles (못을), the adverb sits bare before a verb.
Using 넣다 from English 'put a nail in' — a nail is 박다 (driven in) with force, not just 넣다 (placed in).
Saying 못을 치다 for hammering a nail; the verb is 못을 박다 (the hammer does the 치다, the nail gets 박다).

같은 도구류라도 '못'은 두드려서 고정하고 '나사(screw)'는 돌려서 고정한다는 점이 핵심 차이라, 못에는 '박다/빼다', 나사에는 '조이다/풀다'를 씁니다.

영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 'put a nail in'을 직역해 '못을 넣다'라고 하기 쉬운데, 못은 '넣다(put in)'가 아니라 '박다(drive in)'와 어울립니다. 둘째, 부정 부사 '못'(못 가요 = can't go)과 글자가 똑같아 헷갈리지만, 명사 못은 '못이, 못을'처럼 조사가 붙고 부사 못은 동사 앞에 홀로 옵니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 드라이버 means "screwdriver" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 드라이버 (deuraibeo) = "screwdriver". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 드라이버 ("screwdriver") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 드라이버, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The hand tool for screws; the same loanword also means a golf 'driver', so context matters.
십자(十字) = cross-shaped; the type you need most often at home.
일자(一字) = straight-line shape; for slotted screws.

usagePhrases.en: to loosen a screw with a screwdriver
usagePhrases.note: 풀다 = loosen/undo; 조이다 = tighten — the verb pair to learn together.

examples.en: Please hand me the screwdriver.
examples.note: Simple request; 드라이버 ends in a vowel so 주세요 attaches cleanly with no extra particle needed in casual speech.

examples.ko: 콘센트 커버 갈려면 십자드라이버 있어야 돼요.
examples.romanization: konsenteu keobeo gallyeomyeon sipjadeuraibeo isseoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: To change the outlet cover, you need a Phillips screwdriver.
examples.note: 갈다 = replace; here 십자 specifies the cross head so the listener brings the right one.

examples.ko: 안경 나사 풀렸는데 정밀 드라이버 있어요?
examples.romanization: angyeong nasa pullyeonneunde jeongmil deuraibeo isseoyo?
examples.en: My glasses screw came loose — do you have a precision screwdriver?
examples.note: 정밀(精密) 드라이버 = the tiny screwdriver for glasses/electronics; note the polite 있어요? for asking to borrow.

extendedVocab.nuance: 드라이버는 나사를 돌려 풀고 조이는 손공구입니다. 이름 그대로 영어 'driver'를 빌린 외래어인데, 한국어에서는 같은 발음이 골프채 '드라이버'와 운전자 'driver(기사·드라이버)' 뜻으로도 쓰여서 철물점·공구 맥락이 아니면 오해할 수 있습니다. 영어로는 'screwdriver'지만 한국어에서는 'screw'에 해당하는 부분을 빼고 그냥 '드라이버'라고만 하므로, '스크루드라이버'라고 말하면 어색합니다. 머리 모양에 따라 '십자(十字, cross-shaped)드라이버=Phillips'와 '일자(一字, single-line)드라이버=flathead'로 나뉘고, 작은 것은 '정밀 드라이버'라 합니다. 늘 나사와 함께 '나사를 풀다(loosen)/조이다(tighten)' 동사를 짝지어 외우면 자연스럽습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 스크루드라이버 — Korean drops the 'screw' part; it is simply 드라이버. Saying the full English compound sounds unnatural.
Assuming 드라이버 always means a golf club or a chauffeur — at the hardware store or for repairs it means a screwdriver; context disambiguates.
Mixing up 십자(Phillips) and 일자(flat) heads when asking for one; the wrong head won't fit the screw slot.

이름 그대로 영어 'driver'를 빌린 외래어인데, 한국어에서는 같은 발음이 골프채 '드라이버'와 운전자 'driver(기사·드라이버)' 뜻으로도 쓰여서 철물점·공구 맥락이 아니면 오해할 수 있습니다.
영어로는 'screwdriver'지만 한국어에서는 'screw'에 해당하는 부분을 빼고 그냥 '드라이버'라고만 하므로, '스크루드라이버'라고 말하면 어색합니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 나사 means "screw" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 나사 (nasa) means "screw". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 나사 ("screw"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 나사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The threaded fastener you turn with a 드라이버, as opposed to a hammered 못.
조이다 = tighten; the key verb to memorize with 나사.
풀다 = loosen; the opposite of 조이다.

usagePhrases.en: for a screw to come loose / fall out
usagePhrases.note: Also a slang idiom: 나사(가) 빠졌다 = to be spaced out / off one's game.

examples.en: The screw is small.
examples.note: Basic description; 나사 ends in a vowel so the subject marker is 나사가.

examples.en: The chair was wobbly, so I retightened the screws.
examples.note: 흔들거리다 = wobble; 다시 조이다 = tighten again — the everyday fix for loose furniture.

examples.ko: 나사 하나 모자라서 가구 조립을 못 끝냈어요.
examples.romanization: nasa hana mojaraseo gagu joribeul mot kkeunnaesseoyo.
examples.en: I was one screw short, so I couldn't finish assembling the furniture.
examples.note: 모자라다 = be short of; a common frustration with flat-pack furniture (note 못 끝내다 = couldn't finish).

extendedVocab.nuance: 나사는 드라이버로 돌려 박아 고정하는 나선형 부품으로, 영어 'screw'에 해당합니다. 핵심 구분은 옆 단어 '못(nail)'입니다. 못은 망치로 두드려 박고 동사 '박다/빼다'와 쓰지만, 나사는 돌려서 고정하므로 '조이다(tighten)/풀다(loosen)'와 어울립니다. 따라서 영어 'put in a screw'를 '나사를 박다'로 직역하면 어색하고, '나사를 조이다'가 자연스럽습니다. 비슷한 부품으로 끝이 뾰족하지 않고 너트와 짝을 이루는 '볼트(bolt)'가 따로 있으니 혼동하지 마세요. 또 일상에서 '나사(가) 빠졌다'는 실제 나사가 풀렸다는 뜻 외에 '사람이 정신이 좀 없다·멍하다'는 농담조 관용구로도 자주 쓰입니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '나사를 조이다/풀다, 나사가 헐거워지다, 나사가 빠지다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 박다 for screws from English 'put in' — you 조이다/풀다 (turn) a 나사, you don't 박다 (drive) it like a nail.
Confusing 나사 (screw, turned in) with 못 (nail, hammered in); the fastening method decides the word.
Calling a bolt a 나사 in technical contexts — a 볼트(bolt) pairs with a nut and is distinct, though casual speech blurs them.

structuredNuance.t: 나사는 드라이버로 돌려 박아 고정하는 나선형 부품으로, 영어 'screw'에 해당합니다. 일상에서 '나사(가) 빠졌다'는 실제 나사가 풀렸다는 뜻 외에 '사람이 정신이 좀 없다·멍하다'는 농담조 관용구로도 자주 쓰입니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '나사를 조이다/풀다, 나사가 헐거워지다, 나사가 빠지다'입니다.
핵심 구분은 옆 단어 '못(nail)'입니다. 못은 망치로 두드려 박고 동사 '박다/빼다'와 쓰지만, 나사는 돌려서 고정하므로 '조이다(tighten)/풀다(loosen)'와 어울립니다. 비슷한 부품으로 끝이 뾰족하지 않고 너트와 짝을 이루는 '볼트(bolt)'가 따로 있으니 혼동하지 마세요.
영어 'put in a screw'를 '나사를 박다'로 직역하면 어색하고, '나사를 조이다'가 자연스럽습니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 줄자 means "tape measure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "tape measure" is 줄자 (julja). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 줄자 ("tape measure"). Watch the particle attached to 줄자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The retractable measuring tape; 줄(line/cord) + 자(ruler).

usagePhrases.en: to measure with a tape measure
usagePhrases.note: 재다 = measure; the verb that pairs with any measuring tool, marked by 로.
치수 = dimensions; what you check before buying furniture.
Set phrase for sizing a space: 가로(width, horizontal) 세로(length, vertical).

examples.en: Try measuring it with a tape measure.
examples.note: 재 보다 = give measuring a try; the tool takes 로 (줄자로), not 을.

examples.ko: 냉장고 들어갈 자리 줄자로 먼저 재 보세요.
examples.romanization: naengjanggo deureogal jari juljaro meonjeo jae boseyo.
examples.en: Measure the spot where the fridge will go with a tape measure first.
examples.note: 들어갈 자리 = the spot it'll fit into; 먼저 = first, stressing you measure before buying.

examples.ko: 이 책상 가로세로 좀 재 줄래? 새 방에 들어갈지 봐야 돼.
examples.romanization: i chaeksang garosero jom jae jullae? sae bange deureogalji bwaya dwae.
examples.en: Can you measure this desk's width and length? I need to see if it fits the new room.
examples.note: 들어갈지 = whether it'll fit; casual 재 줄래? asks a friend for the favor.

extendedVocab.nuance: 줄자는 둘둘 말리는 띠로 길이나 공간의 치수를 잴 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 이름은 '줄(line/cord)' + '자(ruler)'가 합쳐진 말이라, 빳빳한 막대 모양의 '자(straight ruler)'와 구분됩니다. 곧고 짧은 길이는 '자'로 재고, 가구·가전이 들어갈 큰 공간은 휘어지며 길게 늘어나는 '줄자'로 잽니다. 동사는 영어 'measure'에 해당하는 '재다'를 쓰는데, 영어 화자는 'see/check the length'를 직역해 '길이를 보다'라고 하기 쉽습니다. 길이는 '보다(look)'가 아니라 '재다(measure)'와 어울립니다. 공간을 잴 때는 '가로(width)세로(length)'를 함께 말하는 게 자연스럽고, 도구는 '줄자를'이 아니라 '줄자로 재다'처럼 (으)로로 표시합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '치수를 재다, 길이를 재다, 줄자로 재다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 자 alone for the flexible tape — a plain 자 is a rigid straight ruler; the retractable one is specifically 줄자.
Saying 길이를 보다 from English 'check the length' — you 재다 (measure) a length, you don't 보다 (look at) it.
Marking the tool with 을/를: 줄자를 재다 is wrong; the instrument takes 로 → 줄자로 재다.

structuredNuance.t: 줄자는 둘둘 말리는 띠로 길이나 공간의 치수를 잴 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 동사는 영어 'measure'에 해당하는 '재다'를 씁니다. 공간을 잴 때는 '가로(width)세로(length)'를 함께 말하는 게 자연스럽고, 도구는 '줄자를'이 아니라 '줄자로 재다'처럼 (으)로로 표시합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '치수를 재다, 길이를 재다, 줄자로 재다'입니다.
이름은 '줄(line/cord)' + '자(ruler)'가 합쳐진 말이라, 빳빳한 막대 모양의 '자(straight ruler)'와 구분됩니다. 곧고 짧은 길이는 '자'로 재고, 가구·가전이 들어갈 큰 공간은 휘어지며 길게 늘어나는 '줄자'로 잽니다.
영어 화자는 'see/check the length'를 직역해 '길이를 보다'라고 하기 쉽습니다. 길이는 '보다(look)'가 아니라 '재다(measure)'와 어울립니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사다리 means "ladder" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사다리 (sadari) = "ladder". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사다리 ("ladder") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사다리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: For reaching high places; a folding step ladder is common at home.
올라가다 = go up; 에 marks the thing you climb onto, not 를.
사다리 + 차(車, vehicle); the truck-mounted lift used on Korean moving days.
A popular way to decide who pays/loses by drawing ladder lines.

examples.en: The ladder is tall.
examples.note: Simple description; 사다리 ends in a vowel so the subject form is 사다리가.

examples.ko: 전등 갈아야 하는데 사다리 좀 잡아 줄래?
examples.romanization: jeondeung garaya haneunde sadari jom jaba jullae?
examples.en: I have to change the light — can you hold the ladder for me?
examples.note: 잡아 주다 = hold (for someone's safety); a very common everyday request.

examples.en: When moving, it was the 5th floor, so we called a ladder lift truck.
examples.note: 사다리차(를) 부르다 = call a ladder truck; reflects how high-floor Korean moves actually work.

extendedVocab.nuance: 사다리는 디딤대를 밟고 높은 곳에 올라갈 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 비슷해 보이는 '계단(stairs)'과 꼭 구분해야 하는데, 계단은 건물에 붙박이로 설치된 층계이고 사다리는 옮길 수 있는 도구라는 점이 다릅니다. 그래서 천장 전등을 갈 때는 '사다리에 올라가다'라고 하지 '계단에 올라가다'라고 하지 않습니다. 영어와 다른 점은 조사인데, 'climb up the ladder'를 직역해 '사다리를 올라가다'라고 하기 쉽지만, 올라가 닿는 대상은 '에/위에'로 표시해 '사다리에 올라가다'가 자연스럽습니다. 한국 생활에서는 이사 때 높은 층으로 짐을 올리는 '사다리차(ladder lift truck)'와, 커피 내기처럼 순서를 정하는 놀이 '사다리 타기'도 함께 알아 두면 좋습니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '사다리에 올라가다, 사다리를 놓다(set up), 사다리를 잡다(hold)'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계단 (stairs) for 사다리 — 계단 is built-in steps in a building; a portable ladder is 사다리.
Marking with 를: 사다리를 올라가다 from English 'climb the ladder' is awkward; the destination takes 에 → 사다리에 올라가다.
Forgetting 사다리차 on moving day — high-floor moves in Korea rely on the ladder lift truck, a distinct word.

structuredNuance.t: 사다리는 디딤대를 밟고 높은 곳에 올라갈 때 쓰는 도구입니다. 한국 생활에서는 이사 때 높은 층으로 짐을 올리는 '사다리차(ladder lift truck)'와, 커피 내기처럼 순서를 정하는 놀이 '사다리 타기'도 함께 알아 두면 좋습니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '사다리에 올라가다, 사다리를 놓다(set up), 사다리를 잡다(hold)'입니다.
비슷해 보이는 '계단(stairs)'과 꼭 구분해야 하는데, 계단은 건물에 붙박이로 설치된 층계이고 사다리는 옮길 수 있는 도구라는 점이 다릅니다. 그래서 천장 전등을 갈 때는 '사다리에 올라가다'라고 하지 '계단에 올라가다'라고 하지 않습니다.
영어와 다른 점은 조사인데, 'climb up the ladder'를 직역해 '사다리를 올라가다'라고 하기 쉽지만, 올라가 닿는 대상은 '에/위에'로 표시해 '사다리에 올라가다'가 자연스럽습니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 페인트 means "paint" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 페인트 (peinteu) means "paint". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 페인트 ("paint"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 페인트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Wall/furniture coating paint; a loanword from English 'paint'.
칠하다 = coat/apply; the standard verb with 페인트, not 그리다.
페인트 + 칠(漆, lacquer/coating); 페인트칠하다 = to do the painting.
묻다 = get smeared on; warn people about wet paint with this verb.

examples.en: The paint isn't dry yet.
examples.note: 마르다 → 말랐어요 (르-irregular: 르 doubles to ㄹㄹ); 아직 안 ~ = not yet.

examples.ko: 방 분위기 바꾸려고 한쪽 벽에 페인트 칠했어요.
examples.romanization: bang bunwigi bakkuryeogo hanjjok byeoge peinteu chilhaesseoyo.
examples.en: To change the room's mood, I painted one wall.
examples.note: 분위기 = mood/vibe; accent-wall DIY is popular, and 칠하다 is the verb, not 그리다.

examples.en: I bought a roller and masking tape to paint it myself.
examples.note: 셀프 = DIY/by oneself; 롤러 = paint roller — the real-situation register of a weekend project.

extendedVocab.nuance: 페인트는 벽이나 가구에 발라 색과 보호막을 입히는 도료로, 영어 'paint'를 그대로 빌린 외래어입니다. 가장 중요한 동사 구분은 '칠하다 vs 그리다'입니다. 한국어에서 '그리다(draw/paint a picture)'는 그림이나 형상을 그릴 때 쓰고, 벽을 색칠하는 것은 반드시 '칠하다(coat)'를 씁니다. 영어 'paint the wall'과 'paint a picture'가 같은 동사라서 영어 화자는 '벽을 그리다'라고 잘못 말하기 쉬운데, 벽에는 '페인트를 칠하다'가 맞습니다. 또 화장품이나 연고를 '바르다(apply/spread)'와 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 넓은 면을 도료로 덮는 작업은 '바르다'보다 '칠하다'가 자연스럽습니다. 행위 자체는 한자 漆(칠)이 붙은 '페인트칠'이라 하고, 옷에 묻으면 '페인트가 묻다'라고 합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '페인트를 칠하다, 페인트가 마르다, 페인트가 묻다, 셀프 페인트칠'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 벽을 그리다 from English 'paint the wall' — 그리다 is for drawing a picture; coating a wall is 페인트를 칠하다.
Using 바르다 by default — 바르다 fits creams/ointments on a small area; for walls the idiomatic verb is 칠하다.
Forgetting 마스킹테이프 to mask the edges; without it the paint lines come out messy (a practical, not grammatical, slip).

행위 자체는 한자 漆(칠)이 붙은 '페인트칠'이라 합니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 전동드릴 means "power drill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "power drill" is 전동드릴 (jeondongdeuril). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전동드릴 ("electric/power drill"). Watch the particle attached to 전동드릴 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 전동(電動) = motor-driven; for boring holes or driving screws fast.
구멍을 뚫다 = bore a hole through; the core phrase for drilling.
충전(充電) = recharge; the cordless kind most people buy now.
비트 = the swappable tip; you swap bits for screws vs. holes.

examples.en: This is a power drill.
examples.note: 전동드릴 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), so the copula is 이에요, not 예요.

examples.ko: 선반 달려고 전동드릴로 벽에 구멍 뚫었어요.
examples.romanization: seonban dallyeogo jeondongdeurillo byeoge gumeong ttureosseoyo.
examples.en: To put up a shelf, I drilled holes in the wall with a power drill.
examples.note: 달다 = mount/hang; 뚫다 = bore through, and the tool takes 로 → 전동드릴로.

examples.ko: 콘크리트 벽은 일반 드릴로는 안 뚫려요.
examples.romanization: konkeuriteu byeogeun ilban deurilloneun an ttulhnyeoyo.
examples.en: You can't drill into a concrete wall with a regular drill.
examples.note: 안 뚫리다 = won't bore through (passive); concrete needs a hammer drill — a real DIY caution.

extendedVocab.nuance: 전동드릴은 한자 電動(전동, 'electric-motion' = motor-driven)이 붙은 말로, 모터 힘으로 구멍을 뚫거나 나사를 빠르게 박는 전동 공구입니다. 사람이 손으로 돌리는 '수동 드릴'이나 '드라이버'와 달리 전기로 돌아간다는 점이 핵심이라, 가구를 자주 조립하면 작업 속도가 훨씬 빨라집니다. 영어 화자가 가장 잘 틀리는 부분은 동사입니다. 'drill a hole'을 직역하면 '구멍을 파다'가 떠오르지만, '파다(dig)'는 흙·땅을 팔 때 쓰고, 단단한 벽이나 나무를 관통해 구멍을 낼 때는 '뚫다(bore/pierce through)'를 씁니다. 그래서 '벽에 구멍을 뚫다'가 맞습니다. 요즘은 선 없는 '충전(充電) 드릴'이 대세이고, 용도에 따라 끝의 '드릴 비트(drill bit)'를 갈아 끼웁니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '구멍을 뚫다, 나사를 박다, 드릴로 뚫다, 비트를 끼우다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 구멍을 파다 from English 'drill a hole' — 파다 (dig) is for soil/ground; piercing a wall or wood is 구멍을 뚫다 (bore through).
Marking the tool with 을/를: 전동드릴을 뚫다 is wrong; the instrument takes 로 → 전동드릴로 뚫다.
Expecting a basic 전동드릴 to pierce concrete; concrete needs a 해머드릴/임팩트 드릴 (hammer/impact drill).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 케이블타이 means "cable tie / zip tie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 케이블타이 (keibeultai) = "cable tie / zip tie". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 케이블타이 ("cable tie / zip tie") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 케이블타이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Plastic strap for bundling cords; also called 케이블 타이 / 타이밴드.

usagePhrases.en: to bundle with a cable tie
usagePhrases.note: 묶다 = tie/bind; the verb that goes with it, marked by 로.
선 정리 = cable management, the main reason people buy these.

usagePhrases.en: to cut the cable tie off
usagePhrases.note: 자르다 = cut; once tightened a standard one only comes off by cutting.

examples.en: I bundled it with a cable tie.
examples.note: 묶다 → 묶었어요; the tool takes 로 (케이블타이로), the cords are the unstated object.

examples.ko: 책상 밑에 선 너무 지저분해서 케이블타이로 묶었어요.
examples.romanization: chaeksang mite seon neomu jijeobunhaeseo keibeultairo mukkeosseoyo.
examples.en: The cords under the desk were so messy that I bundled them with cable ties.
examples.note: 지저분하다 = messy; classic desk cable-management situation.

examples.ko: 케이블타이는 한 번 조이면 자르기 전엔 못 풀어요.
examples.romanization: keibeultaineun han beon joimyeon jareugi jeonen mot pureoyo.
examples.en: Once you tighten a zip tie, you can't undo it without cutting.
examples.note: 조이다 = tighten; 못 풀다 = can't undo — they're one-way unless you buy reusable ones.

extendedVocab.nuance: 케이블타이는 영어 'cable tie'를 그대로 빌린 외래어로, 어지러운 전선을 한데 묶어 정리하는 플라스틱 끈입니다. 한국에서는 '선 정리(cable management)'의 필수품으로, 책상 밑이나 TV 뒤 전선을 깔끔히 묶을 때 자주 씁니다. 묶는 도구라는 점에서 옆 단원의 '노끈(twine)'과 헷갈릴 수 있는데, 노끈은 풀었다 다시 묶을 수 있는 천·종이 끈이고, 케이블타이는 톱니로 한 방향만 조여지는 일회용 플라스틱이라 한 번 조이면 가위로 '잘라야(cut)' 풀린다는 점이 결정적으로 다릅니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 그냥 '끈/줄(string/cord)'이라고 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데 일방향 플라스틱 타이는 구체적으로 '케이블타이'입니다. 둘째, 다시 풀어 쓰려 하지만 일반 제품은 'reusable(재사용)' 표시가 없으면 잘라서만 제거됩니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '케이블타이로 묶다, 선을 정리하다, 케이블타이를 조이다/자르다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it just 끈/줄 (string/cord) — the one-way plastic tie is specifically 케이블타이; the generic word loses the meaning.
Marking the tool with 을/를: 케이블타이를 묶다 means tying the tie itself; you bundle cords with it → 케이블타이로 묶다.
Expecting to reuse a standard one; unless labeled 재사용(reusable), it must be cut (자르다) to release.

structuredNuance.t: 케이블타이는 영어 'cable tie'를 그대로 빌린 외래어로, 어지러운 전선을 한데 묶어 정리하는 플라스틱 끈입니다. 한국에서는 '선 정리(cable management)'의 필수품으로, 책상 밑이나 TV 뒤 전선을 깔끔히 묶을 때 자주 씁니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '케이블타이로 묶다, 선을 정리하다, 케이블타이를 조이다/자르다'입니다.
묶는 도구라는 점에서 옆 단원의 '노끈(twine)'과 헷갈릴 수 있는데, 노끈은 풀었다 다시 묶을 수 있는 천·종이 끈이고, 케이블타이는 톱니로 한 방향만 조여지는 일회용 플라스틱이라 한 번 조이면 가위로 '잘라야(cut)' 풀린다는 점이 결정적으로 다릅니다.
영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 그냥 '끈/줄(string/cord)'이라고 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데 일방향 플라스틱 타이는 구체적으로 '케이블타이'입니다. 둘째, 다시 풀어 쓰려 하지만 일반 제품은 'reusable(재사용)' 표시가 없으면 잘라서만 제거됩니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 손전등 means "flashlight / torch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 손전등 (sonjeondeung) means "flashlight / torch". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 손전등 ("flashlight"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 손전등 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 손(hand) + 전등(電燈, electric lamp); the casual loanword 후레쉬/플래시 is also common.
비추다 = shine/cast light onto; the verb that pairs with it.
켜다 = switch on; 끄다 = switch off — the on/off pair.
Most people just use the phone's built-in light day to day.

examples.en: I turn on the flashlight.
examples.note: 켜다 (turn on a light/device) is the verb for lights; its opposite is 끄다.

examples.ko: 어두운데 핸드폰 손전등 좀 켜 줄래?
examples.romanization: eoduunde haendeupon sonjeondeung jom kyeo jullae?
examples.en: It's dark — can you turn on your phone flashlight?
examples.note: Everyday request; the phone light is most people's default 손전등 these days.

examples.en: The power went out, so I found the breaker box with a flashlight.
examples.note: 정전(停電) = blackout; 두꺼비집 = breaker box (colloquial), and the tool takes 으로.

extendedVocab.nuance: 손전등은 한자 電燈(전등, 'electric lamp')에 '손(hand)'이 붙은 말로, 손에 들고 빛을 비추는 휴대용 조명입니다. 반드시 구분할 단어가 '전등'입니다. '전등'은 방이나 천장에 붙은 일반 조명(room/ceiling light)을 뜻하므로, 손에 드는 것은 '손'을 붙여 '손전등'이라 해야 합니다. 일상 회화에서는 외래어 '후레쉬(flash)'나 '플래시'를 더 자주 쓰고, 요즘은 대부분 휴대폰 내장 '손전등' 기능으로 해결합니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 동사입니다. 영어 'shine the light'를 직역할 때 비슷한 발음의 '비치다'를 쓰기 쉬운데, '비치다'는 빛이 저절로 비쳐 든다는 자동사(피동)이고, 내가 손전등으로 어딘가를 비출 때는 타동사 '비추다(shine onto)'를 써야 합니다. 또 불은 '켜다(turn on)/끄다(turn off)'와 짝을 이룹니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '손전등을 켜다/끄다, 손전등을 비추다, 손전등으로 비추다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 전등 alone — a plain 전등 is a room/ceiling lamp; the handheld one must be 손전등 (with 손).
Saying 손전등을 비치다 — 비치다 is intransitive (light shines through by itself); to aim a flashlight you use the transitive 비추다.
Marking the instrument with 을 instead of 으로: you light an area 손전등으로 (with the flashlight), not 손전등을.

structuredNuance.t: 손전등은 손에 들고 빛을 비추는 휴대용 조명입니다. 일상 회화에서는 외래어 '후레쉬(flash)'나 '플래시'를 더 자주 쓰고, 요즘은 대부분 휴대폰 내장 '손전등' 기능으로 해결합니다. 불은 '켜다(turn on)/끄다(turn off)'와 짝을 이룹니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '손전등을 켜다/끄다, 손전등을 비추다, 손전등으로 비추다'입니다.
반드시 구분할 단어가 '전등'입니다. '전등'은 방이나 천장에 붙은 일반 조명(room/ceiling light)을 뜻하므로, 손에 드는 것은 '손'을 붙여 '손전등'이라 해야 합니다.
손전등은 한자 電燈(전등, 'electric lamp')에 '손(hand)'이 붙은 말입니다.
영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 동사입니다. 영어 'shine the light'를 직역할 때 비슷한 발음의 '비치다'를 쓰기 쉬운데, '비치다'는 빛이 저절로 비쳐 든다는 자동사(피동)이고, 내가 손전등으로 어딘가를 비출 때는 타동사 '비추다(shine onto)'를 써야 합니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 공구함 means "toolbox" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "toolbox" is 공구함 (gongguham). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공구함 ("toolbox"). Watch the particle attached to 공구함 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 공구(工具, tools) + 함(函, case/box); where you keep your hand tools.
넣어 두다 = put away and store; the location takes 에.
A boxed set of basic tools; a handy single purchase for a new home.
The essentials: 망치, 드라이버, 줄자, 펜치 and the like.

examples.en: The toolbox is heavy.
examples.note: 공구함 ends in a consonant (ㅁ), so the subject marker is 공구함이.

examples.en: Put the screwdriver back in the toolbox.
examples.note: 다시 넣어 두다 = put it back and store it; 에 marks the destination, plain 둬 is casual.

examples.en: When I moved, I got myself a basic toolbox.
examples.note: 장만하다 = acquire/get (deliberately, for oneself); the natural verb for setting up a home.

extendedVocab.nuance: 공구함은 한자 工具(공구, 'work-tool')에 函(함, 'case/box')이 붙은 합성어로, 망치·드라이버·줄자 같은 손공구를 한데 모아 두는 상자입니다. 어휘 선택에서 두 가지를 구분하면 좋습니다. 첫째, 그릇이나 통은 한국어로 '상자/박스'라고 뭉뚱그리기 쉽지만, 공구 전용 케이스는 한자 '함(函)'을 쓴 '공구함'이 자연스럽습니다(같은 '함'이 '사물함=locker, 우편함=mailbox'에도 쓰입니다). 둘째, 영어 'tool'은 한국어에서 '공구(工具)'와 '도구(道具)' 둘로 나뉘는데, 망치·드릴 같은 철물·연장은 '공구'가 자연스럽고, '도구'는 더 넓게 '수단·기구'를 뜻해 'a tool for learning(학습 도구)'처럼 추상적으로도 씁니다. 그래서 철물점 맥락에서는 '도구함'보다 '공구함'이 맞습니다. 자취·이사 때 기본 '공구 세트'를 하나 '장만해' 두면 간단한 수리나 가구 조립을 직접 할 수 있어 편리합니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '공구함에 넣어 두다, 공구 세트를 장만하다, 기본 공구를 갖추다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 상자/박스 generically — those mean any box; the dedicated tool case uses the 함(函) suffix → 공구함.
Saying 도구함 for a hardware toolbox — for physical tools 공구(工具) is the natural word; 도구(道具) leans abstract/general.
Marking with 를: 공구함을 넣다 means putting the box itself somewhere; to store tools inside, the box takes 에 → 공구함에 넣다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 노끈 means "string / twine / cord" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 노끈 (nokkeun) = "string / twine / cord". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 노끈 ("string/twine") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 노끈, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Thin cord for tying things; thicker than thread, thinner than rope.
묶다 = tie/bind; the core verb with 노끈, marked by 로.
Common for bundling cardboard for 분리수거 (sorted recycling).
풀다 = undo/untie; the opposite of 묶다.

examples.en: I tied it with twine.
examples.note: 묶다 → 묶었어요; the twine is the instrument, so 노끈으로, with the object understood.

examples.en: Tie the newspapers with twine and put them out for recycling.
examples.note: 내놓다 = put out (for collection); a core chore in Korean apartment life.

examples.ko: 노끈이 약해서 무거운 거 묶으면 끊어져요.
examples.romanization: nokkeuni yakaeseo mugeoun geo mukkeumyeon kkeuneojyeoyo.
examples.en: The twine is weak, so it snaps if you tie heavy things.
examples.note: 끊어지다 = snap/break (intransitive); use stronger 밧줄 (rope) for heavy loads.

extendedVocab.nuance: 노끈은 물건을 묶을 때 쓰는 가는 끈으로, 굵기로 비슷한 말들을 가르는 게 핵심입니다. 바느질용 '실(thread)'보다는 굵고, 짐을 옮기거나 매는 '밧줄(rope)'보다는 가늘어서, 가벼운 물건을 묶기에 알맞습니다. 한국에서는 특히 종이박스나 신문지를 모아 '분리수거(sorted recycling)'로 내놓을 때 노끈으로 묶는 모습을 흔히 봅니다. 영어 화자가 잘 틀리는 점은 두 가지입니다. 첫째, 영어 'string'을 떠올려 바느질 '실'과 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 박스를 묶는 끈은 '실'이 아니라 '노끈'입니다. 둘째, 동사 짝을 헷갈리기 쉬운데, 묶는 것은 '묶다(tie/bind)', 푸는 것은 '풀다(untie)', 끈이 저절로 끊기는 것은 자동사 '끊어지다'를 씁니다. 무거운 것을 묶으면 끊어질 수 있으니 그럴 땐 더 튼튼한 '밧줄'을 쓰는 게 좋습니다. 자주 쓰는 짝은 '노끈으로 묶다, 박스를 묶다, 노끈을 풀다, 노끈이 끊어지다'입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 실 (thread) from English 'string' — 실 is fine sewing thread; bundling cord for boxes is 노끈.
Expecting 노끈 to hold heavy loads; for that you need a thicker 밧줄 (rope) — the words differ by thickness/strength.
Marking with 을/를: 노끈을 묶다 means tying the twine itself; you bind the box with twine → 노끈으로 (박스를) 묶다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 후텁지근하다 means "muggy, hot and humid (sticky)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 후텁지근하다 (huteopjigeunhada) means "muggy, hot and humid (sticky)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후텁지근하다 ("to be muggy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후텁지근하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Korean summer's sticky heat that clings to your skin; the go-to July–August complaint
polite present; say it when you step outside and the air feels like a wet towel
modifier -ㄴ attaches to the stem before a noun; describes the kind of day
-아/어서 reason form; natural lead-in to '에어컨 켰어요 (I turned on the AC)'

examples.en: It's a bit muggy today.
examples.note: the bare minimum small-talk line; -네요 reacts to what you feel right now

examples.ko: 장마철이라 그런지 방 안이 너무 후텁지근해요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheorira geureonji bang ani neomu huteopjigeunhaeyo.
examples.en: Maybe because it's monsoon season, the room is so muggy.
examples.note: 장마철 (rainy season) is the prime context; -(이)라 그런지 = 'maybe because'

examples.ko: 밖에 나가자마자 후텁지근해서 바로 다시 들어왔어.
examples.romanization: bakke nagajamaja huteopjigeunhaeseo baro dasi deureowasseo.
examples.en: The second I stepped outside it was so muggy I came right back in.
examples.note: casual 반말; -자마자 = 'the moment that', capturing the wall-of-humidity feeling

extendedVocab.nuance: 후텁지근하다 names heat AND humidity together — the heavy, steamy, clothes-sticking-to-skin air of a Korean summer night, not just a high number on the thermometer. The sharp contrast is with plain 덥다 (simply 'hot', could be dry desert heat) and with 무덥다 (also oppressive but a touch more formal/written); 후텁지근하다 is the spoken, sensory, slightly whiny word you use when the muggy air actually bothers you. It collocates with 날씨, 방 안, 공기, and especially 장마철. The English-speaker trap is reaching for it whenever it's 'hot' — if there's no stickiness, it must be 덥다, because the whole point of this word is the wet, suffocating quality. Also watch the spelling: standard is 후텁지근하다 (not 후덥지근하다), even though it relates to 덥다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for dry heat: a sunny but dry 28°C day is 덥다, not 후텁지근하다 — this word requires humidity, so reserve it for sticky, sweaty air.
Spelling it 후덥지근하다 by analogy with 덥다; the dictionary-standard form is 후텁지근하다 with ㅌ.
Saying '나는 후텁지근해요' to mean 'I feel hot/sweaty' — the subject is the air or the weather, not a person; for yourself say 덥다 or 땀나다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 쌀쌀하다 means "chilly, nippy (cool air)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "chilly, nippy (cool air)" is 쌀쌀하다 (ssalssalhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 쌀쌀하다 ("to be chilly"). Watch the particle attached to 쌀쌀하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the brisk cool of early morning or late autumn; not freezing, just jacket-weather
polite present; the default spring/fall weather small talk
modifier -ㄴ before a noun; also 쌀쌀한 바람 (a chilly wind)
set phrase for the daily temperature swing (일교차)

examples.en: It's a bit chilly today.
examples.note: the simplest version; 좀 softens it to 'a little'

examples.en: These days it's chilly morning and evening, so take a jacket.
examples.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason for advice; classic seasonal line you'll hear constantly

examples.en: With the wind blowing too, it's way chillier than I expected.
examples.note: -까지 ('even/on top of that') stacks the wind onto the cold; -네요 for in-the-moment reaction

extendedVocab.nuance: 쌀쌀하다 is a mild, brisk chill — the kind that makes you reach for a light jacket or cardigan, the signature feeling of spring mornings and autumn evenings. The dividing line you must learn: 쌀쌀하다 (cool, jacket weather) < 싸늘하다 (genuinely cold, often eerie) < 춥다 (cold, the all-purpose word) < 매섭다 (painfully biting winter cold). So if your teeth chatter, it's already past 쌀쌀하다. A second, equally common use is about people: 쌀쌀하다 / 쌀쌀맞다 / 쌀쌀하게 대하다 describe a cold, aloof, standoffish attitude — context (weather vs. a person) tells you which. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as 'cold'; it is deliberately understated, closer to 'a bit nippy', and overusing it for real cold sounds off.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for deep winter cold: when it actually hurts, switch to 춥다 or 매섭다 — 쌀쌀하다 only covers the mild, jacket-level chill.
Treating it as a synonym of 싸늘하다; 싸늘하다 is colder and can feel eerie/tense, whereas 쌀쌀하다 is just pleasantly brisk.
Forgetting the personality meaning: '그 사람 좀 쌀쌀해' means 'that person is a bit cold/distant', not that they feel cool to the touch.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 포근하다 means "mild and cozy (unusually warm)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 포근하다 (pogeunhada) = "mild and cozy (unusually warm)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 포근하다 ("to be mild/cozy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 포근하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: gently warm — a winter day milder than usual, or a soft, snug feeling
polite present; said with relief when winter cold eases
modifier -ㄴ before a noun; also 포근한 이불 (a cozy blanket)
날(이) + adjective is a very natural weather frame

examples.en: It's a bit mild today.
examples.note: the basic line; perfect when a cold spell suddenly softens

examples.en: Even though it's midwinter, the day's so mild I came out for a walk.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ데도 = 'even though'; the textbook context of a surprisingly warm winter day

examples.en: The blanket's so cozy I just can't get up.
examples.note: 반말; shows the 'soft & snug' object sense — 도저히 + 못 = 'no way can I'

extendedVocab.nuance: 포근하다 carries warmth wrapped in comfort — most often a winter day that turns out gentler than expected, or soft, snuggly things like 이불 (blankets), 옷, and a mother's hug. The key contrast is with 따뜻하다, which is the neutral, all-temperature 'warm'; 포근하다 adds emotion — you say it with relief, contentment, or affection, never about plain heat. It pairs with 날씨, 날, 이불, 분위기, 품 (embrace). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, do not use it for summer warmth or any strong heat — it is reserved for gentle, mild warmth, so a hot day is 덥다, never 포근하다. Second, do not limit it to weather: '이불이 포근하다' (the blanket is cozy) is just as natural and very common.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for hot weather: 포근하다 is gentle, mild warmth only — a sweltering summer day is 덥다/무덥다, and calling it 포근하다 sounds wrong.
Assuming it equals 따뜻하다: 따뜻하다 is the neutral 'warm', while 포근하다 always adds a cozy, emotionally positive feeling.
Limiting it to weather and missing the object use; '포근한 스웨터/이불' (a cozy sweater/blanket) is an everyday, natural collocation.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무덥다 means "sweltering, hot and stifling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 무덥다 (mudeopda) means "sweltering, hot and stifling". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무덥다 ("to be sweltering"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무덥다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: intense, oppressive, usually humid summer heat; ㅂ-irregular stem
polite present: 무덥 + 어요 → 무더워요 (ㅂ→우)
무더운 before a noun (ㅂ-irregular modifier)
the forecast staple: 무더위가 계속되다 (the heat wave continues)

examples.en: It's really sweltering today.
examples.note: the simple reaction line; 진짜 adds 'really'

examples.ko: 무더운 날에는 수분 섭취가 정말 중요해요.
examples.romanization: mudeoun nareneun subun seopchwiga jeongmal jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: On sweltering days, staying hydrated is really important.
examples.note: newscast-style advice; 무더운 날 = a sweltering day

examples.ko: 밤에도 안 식어서 무더운 열대야가 계속되고 있어요.
examples.romanization: bamedo an sigeoseo mudeoun yeoldaeyaga gyesokdoego isseoyo.
examples.en: It doesn't even cool down at night, so the sweltering tropical nights keep going.
examples.note: 열대야 ('tropical night') pairs naturally with 무덥다; -고 있다 for an ongoing stretch

extendedVocab.nuance: 무덥다 is heat with weight — heavy, stifling, energy-draining, almost always with humidity behind it, a clear step above plain 덥다. The 무- here is the intensifying/heavy 'mu-', so think 'heavily hot'. Contrast: 덥다 = neutral 'hot' (any hot), 무덥다 = oppressively, stiflingly hot, and the spoken/sensory cousin 후텁지근하다 leans on the sticky muggy feel while 무덥다 sounds a notch more standard and is the form used in forecasts and writing. Its noun 무더위 appears all over summer weather reports (무더위 특보, 무더위가 기승을 부리다). The two pitfalls: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — it is 무더워요/무더운/무더위, never 무덥어요/무덥은; (2) don't downgrade it to mild warmth — 무덥다 is reserved for genuinely draining heat, so a pleasantly warm day is 따뜻하다, not 무덥다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 무덥어요/무덥은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct forms are 무더워요 and 무더운.
Using it for mild or pleasant warmth: 무덥다 is intense, stifling heat — a nice warm day is 따뜻하다, and a merely hot day is 덥다.
Forgetting the high-frequency noun 무더위; in forecasts you'll hear 무더위가 계속되다/기승을 부리다 far more than the adjective.

structuredNuance.t: 무덥다 is heat with weight — heavy, stifling, energy-draining, almost always with humidity behind it, a clear step above plain 덥다. Its noun 무더위 appears all over summer weather reports (무더위 특보, 무더위가 기승을 부리다).

Contrast: 덥다 = neutral 'hot' (any hot), 무덥다 = oppressively, stiflingly hot, and the spoken/sensory cousin 후텁지근하다 leans on the sticky muggy feel while 무덥다 sounds a notch more standard and is the form used in forecasts and writing.

It is ㅂ-irregular — 무덥 + 어요 → 무더워요, modifier 무더운, noun 무더위, never 무덥어요/무덥은.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 선선하다 means "pleasantly cool, refreshing (air)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "pleasantly cool, refreshing (air)" is 선선하다 (seonseonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 선선하다 ("to be pleasantly cool"). Watch the particle attached to 선선하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: comfortable coolness, especially early autumn after the summer heat breaks
polite present; said with relief as the weather turns nice
선선한 most often pairs with 바람 (breeze) or 날씨/공기
-아/어지다 for the seasonal change: '날씨가 선선해졌어요'

examples.en: It's pleasantly cool now.
examples.note: the basic line; 이제 ('now') signals the season has turned

examples.ko: 아침 공기가 선선해서 산책하기 딱 좋아요.
examples.romanization: achim gonggiga seonseonhaeseo sanchaekagi ttak joayo.
examples.en: The morning air is so cool that it's just right for a walk.
examples.note: 딱 좋다 = 'just right'; -기 좋다 = 'good for ~ing'

examples.en: The heat has eased off and it's finally turned cool.
examples.note: 한풀 꺾이다 = '(heat) to die down', a very Korean expression; 드디어 = 'finally'

extendedVocab.nuance: 선선하다 is pleasant, refreshing coolness — the welcome relief when summer finally lets go and early autumn arrives, the temperature where you feel comfortable without a jacket. It is always positive, which is exactly the dividing line from its neighbors: 선선하다 (nice, comfortable cool) → 쌀쌀하다 (chilly enough to want a jacket) → 싸늘하다 (uncomfortably, sharply cold). So once you actually feel cold, you have left 선선하다 behind. It collocates with 바람, 날씨, 공기, 가을 and very often appears as 선선해지다 to mark the change of season, or with 한풀 꺾이다 (the heat dying down). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'cool' too literally and applying it to genuinely cold weather, or pairing it with ongoing summer heat — 선선하다 inherently implies the heat has already passed and what's left feels good.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it when it's actually cold: 선선하다 means comfortable, refreshing cool — if you need a jacket, that's 쌀쌀하다, not 선선하다.
Pairing it with peak summer: saying '여름이 선선해요' clashes, because 선선하다 implies the heat has already eased; use it for early autumn or cool evenings.
Confusing it with 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broad 'refreshing/cool' (drinks, AC, relief), while 선선하다 is specifically the pleasant coolness of the air/weather.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 화창하다 means "sunny and clear (bright, fine weather)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 화창하다 (hwachanghada) = "sunny and clear (bright, fine weather)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 화창하다 ("to be sunny and clear") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 화창하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: bright, beautiful blue-sky weather; the ideal day to go out
polite present; a cheerful weather report
화창한 + 날씨/봄날 are the typical pairings
standard weather-subject frame

examples.en: The weather's lovely and sunny today.
examples.note: the simple delighted reaction; note 날씨(가) often drops 가 in speech

examples.ko: 날씨가 화창해서 한강 가기 딱 좋아요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga hwachanghaeseo hangang gagi ttak joayo.
examples.en: The weather's so nice and sunny it's perfect for going to the Han River.
examples.note: -아서 reason + -기 좋다; 화창한 날 is when everyone heads to 한강

examples.ko: 내일은 미세먼지도 없고 하늘이 화창할 거래요.
examples.romanization: naeireun misemeonjido eopsgo haneuri hwachanghal georaeyo.
examples.en: They say tomorrow there'll be no fine dust and the sky will be clear and sunny.
examples.note: -(이)래요 reports a forecast; 미세먼지 (fine dust) is a real daily concern in Korea

extendedVocab.nuance: 화창하다 describes bright, clear, beautiful weather — sunny skies, fresh air, the kind of day that lifts your mood, classically a spring or autumn 'perfect day'. It is Sino-Korean: 和 (hwa, 'harmonious/gentle') + 暢 (chang, 'flowing freely/unobstructed'), so the image is of mild, freely bright, unblocked weather. The contrast to learn: 맑다 just means 'clear' (sky, water, even sound) and is purely about clarity, while 화창하다 adds warmth, brightness and a pleasant mood — a clear but bitterly cold winter sky is 맑다, not 화창하다. It pairs with 날씨, 봄날, 하늘, 가을. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use it merely for 'not raining' — cloudy-but-dry is not 화창하다; and it describes daytime brightness, so it doesn't fit a clear night sky (for that, 맑다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using it for 'just not raining': a gray, dry, overcast day is not 화창하다 — the word requires genuine bright, pleasant sunshine.
Treating it as identical to 맑다: 맑다 is plain clarity (it can be clear but freezing), whereas 화창하다 adds warm, cheerful brightness, so a cold clear day is 맑다.
Applying it to night: 화창하다 is about daytime brightness; a clear night sky is 하늘이 맑다, not 화창하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 습하다 means "humid, damp" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 습하다 (seupada) means "humid, damp". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 습하다 ("to be humid/damp"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 습하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: high moisture in the air; the defining feature of Korean summer and the rainy season
polite present; also said of a damp room or basement
습한 before a noun; also 습한 공기 (damp air)
습하다 + 덥다 is the classic Korean-summer combo

examples.en: It's a bit humid today.
examples.note: the bare small-talk line; you'll feel it before you see it

examples.ko: 장마철엔 너무 습해서 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
examples.romanization: jangmacheoren neomu seupaeseo ppallaega jal an mallayo.
examples.en: During the rainy season it's so humid the laundry won't dry well.
examples.note: a very real apartment-life problem; -아서 links cause to result

examples.ko: 방이 습한 것 같아서 제습기를 틀었어.
examples.romanization: bangi seupan geot gataseo jeseupgireul teureosseo.
examples.en: The room felt damp so I turned on the dehumidifier.
examples.note: 반말; 제습기 (dehumidifier) is a summer essential — -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 = 'seems'

extendedVocab.nuance: 습하다 is about moisture in the air, deliberately separate from temperature — you can have a 습한 but cool, clammy day (a damp basement, a rainy spring). It is Sino-Korean from 濕 ('wet/damp'), and its exact opposite is 건조하다 (dry, from 乾燥). In Korea it is the word behind summer misery: 빨래가 안 마르다 (laundry won't dry), 곰팡이 (mold), and the constant hum of the 제습기 (dehumidifier). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is collapsing it into 'hot': 습하다 means humid, not hot — they merely co-occur in summer, so a cool damp day is still 습하다, and a dry hot desert day is 덥다 but absolutely not 습하다. Keep the pair straight: 습하다 (humid) ↔ 건조하다 (dry), and pair 습하다 with 덥다 only when both are true.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing it with 덥다 ('hot'): 습하다 is purely about moisture, so you can be 습한데 안 더워요 (humid but not hot) — don't use it to mean heat.
Using it for dry conditions: the opposite of 습하다 is 건조하다, so a dry winter day is 건조하다, never 습하다.
Forgetting the indoor/room use: '방/지하실이 습하다' (the room/basement is damp) is just as common as talking about the weather.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 건조하다 means "dry (air, skin)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "dry (air, skin)" is 건조하다 (geonjohada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 건조하다 ("to be dry"). Watch the particle attached to 건조하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: low humidity in the air; the hallmark of Korean winter and spring
polite present; also used for dry skin (피부가 건조해요)
건조한 before a noun; also 건조한 공기/피부
a real fire-risk warning issued in dry seasons (건조주의보가 내려지다)

examples.en: It's so dry these days.
examples.note: the simple seasonal complaint, peak winter

examples.en: The weather's so dry my lips keep chapping.
examples.note: 트다 = (skin/lips) to chap; -아서 cause, -네요 reaction

examples.ko: 피부가 건조할 땐 자기 전에 보습 크림을 꼭 발라요.
examples.romanization: pibuga geonjohal ttaen jagi jeone boseup keurimeul kkok ballayo.
examples.en: When my skin is dry, I always put on moisturizer before bed.
examples.note: shows the skin use; -(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when', 꼭 = 'without fail'

extendedVocab.nuance: 건조하다 is the dryness of low-humidity air — the exact opposite of 습하다 — typical of Korean winter and the spring fire-warning season, when 가습기 (humidifiers) come out and 건조주의보 (dry-weather advisories) get issued. It is Sino-Korean: 乾 (geon, 'dry/heaven') + 燥 (jo, 'parched'), literally 'dried and parched'. Its range is wide: equally natural for skin (피부가 건조하다, 입술이 트다) and even for a person's manner or a piece of writing — 건조한 말투/문체 means a dry, flat, emotionless tone. The two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) don't mix it up with 습하다 — they are antonyms, 건조하다 = dry, 습하다 = humid; (2) don't box it into weather only, since 'my skin is dry' (피부가 건조해요) is one of its most everyday uses, and the metaphorical 'dry/dull' sense is common too.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing it up with 습하다: they are opposites — 건조하다 means dry (low humidity), 습하다 means humid, so don't swap them.
Limiting it to weather: 피부가 건조하다 (dry skin) and 입술이 건조하다/트다 (chapped lips) are extremely common, everyday uses.
Missing the figurative sense: 건조한 말투/분위기 means a dry, flat, unfeeling tone or mood — context tells you it's not about humidity.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매섭다 means "bitterly cold, biting (wind, cold)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 매섭다 (maeseopda) = "bitterly cold, biting (wind, cold)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매섭다 ("to be biting/fierce") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매섭다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: piercing winter cold or a sharp, cutting wind; ㅂ-irregular stem
polite present: 매섭 + 어요 → 매서워요 (ㅂ→우)
매서운 + 바람/추위 are the standard pairings
매섭게 (adverb) intensifies 춥다

examples.en: The wind is really biting today.
examples.note: the simple reaction; 진짜 adds force, -네요 reacts on the spot

examples.ko: 추위가 매서우니까 패딩 단단히 입고 나가세요.
examples.romanization: chuwiga maeseounikka paeding dandanhi ipgo nagaseyo.
examples.en: The cold is biting, so bundle up well in your padded coat before you go.
examples.note: -(으)니까 reason for advice; 패딩 (padded coat) is the Korean winter uniform

examples.ko: 한파에 칼바람까지 매섭게 불어서 귀가 다 얼었어.
examples.romanization: hanpae kalbaramkkaji maeseopge bureoseo gwiga da eoreosseo.
examples.en: On top of the cold wave, a knife-sharp wind blew bitterly and my ears froze solid.
examples.note: 반말; 칼바람 (knife wind) + 매섭다 is very natural, -까지 stacks the wind on the cold wave

extendedVocab.nuance: 매섭다 describes a fierce, piercing, almost painful quality — most often a biting winter wind or a sharp cold that hurts exposed skin, the harshest end of the cold scale (쌀쌀하다 → 싸늘하다 → 춥다 → 매섭다). Its core sense isn't temperature but 'cutting/severe', which is why it transfers to people: 매서운 눈빛 (a piercing, fierce stare), 매섭게 몰아붙이다 (to scold/press sharply). It collocates with 바람, 추위, 한파, 칼바람, 눈빛. Two things trip English speakers up: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — it is 매서워요/매서운/매섭게, never 매섭어요/매섭은; (2) don't use it for ordinary cold — 매섭다 is reserved for harsh, biting, painful cold or wind, so a merely cold day is 춥다 and a mildly chilly one is 쌀쌀하다, with 매섭다 saved for when the wind actually stings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 매섭어요/매섭은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct forms are 매서워요 and 매서운.
Using it for mild cold: 매섭다 is harsh, painful, biting cold — a normal cold day is 춥다, and a light chill is 쌀쌀하다.
Missing the figurative use: 매서운 눈빛/말투 means a fierce, sharp gaze or tone, reflecting the word's core sense of 'cutting/severe'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 따사롭다 means "warm and gentle (sunlight)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 따사롭다 (ttasaropda) means "warm and gentle (sunlight)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 따사롭다 ("to be warm and gentle"). usagePhrases.note: the soft, comforting warmth of sunshine; ㅂ-irregular stem
polite present: 따사롭 + 어요 → 따사로워요 (ㅂ→우)
the most common pairing: 햇살/햇볕 (sunshine)
the natural subject is sunlight, not air temperature

examples.en: The sunshine is so warm and gentle.
examples.note: the simple admiring line; 참 = 'truly', a soft intensifier

examples.ko: 봄 햇살이 따사로워서 벤치에 한참 앉아 있었어요.
examples.romanization: bom haetsari ttasarowoseo benchie hancham anja isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The spring sunshine was so gentle and warm that I sat on the bench for a long while.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 한참 = 'for a good while', the cozy basking feeling

examples.ko: 겨울인데도 창으로 따사로운 볕이 들어와서 마음까지 포근해졌어.
examples.romanization: gyeourindedo changeuro ttasaroun byeochi deureowaseo maeumkkaji pogeunhaejyeosseo.
examples.en: Even in winter, gentle sun came through the window and even my heart felt cozy.
examples.note: 반말; 볕이 들다 = 'sun shines in', -까지 extends the warmth to the heart

extendedVocab.nuance: 따사롭다 is the softer, more poetic cousin of 따뜻하다, used almost exclusively for sunlight (햇살, 햇볕, 볕) and, by extension, warm-hearted feelings (따사로운 미소, 따사로운 정). Where 따뜻하다 is the everyday, all-purpose 'warm' (warm water, a warm room, a warm person), 따사롭다 specifically evokes a gentle, soothing, slightly literary warmth and a peaceful mood — which is why you meet it in captions, lyrics, essays, and heartfelt speech far more than in plain weather chat. It collocates above all with 햇살/햇볕/볕, and with 미소, 정, 손길. Two pitfalls: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — 따사로워요/따사로운, never 따사롭어요/따사롭은; (2) don't use it for general air temperature or to describe how warm a room or drink is — for that you want 따뜻하다, because 따사롭다 is tied to the gentle warmth of sunshine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as 따사롭어요/따사롭은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so use 따사로워요 and 따사로운.
Using it for air temperature or objects: a warm room or warm coffee is 따뜻하다 — 따사롭다 is mainly for sunlight (and warm feelings), not general warmth.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 싸늘하다 means "cold and chilly (and often eerie/tense)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cold and chilly (and often eerie/tense)" is 싸늘하다 (ssaneulhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 싸늘하다 ("to be cold/chilly"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: a sharper, colder chill than 쌀쌀하다; air that's gone genuinely cold
polite present; said when the temperature has clearly dropped
싸늘한 + 공기/날씨; also 싸늘한 분위기 (a tense, frosty mood)
-아/어지다; weather or a mood suddenly going cold

examples.en: It's a bit cold at night.
examples.note: the simple line; the chill that comes after dark

examples.en: Once the sun set, the air suddenly turned cold.
examples.note: -(으)니까 cause-then-effect; -아지다 marks the change to cold

examples.en: One joke from me and the mood turned ice-cold.
examples.note: 반말; the very common figurative use — a frozen, awkward atmosphere after a flat joke

Placed on the cold scale it sits 쌀쌀하다 (mild, jacket weather) < 싸늘하다 (genuinely cold, often eerie) < 춥다/매섭다. But its most useful everyday life is figurative: 분위기가 싸늘하다 / 싸늘해지다 describes a room going awkwardly silent, frosty, or hostile — the classic case being right after someone tells a joke that bombs (썰렁하다 is the lighter 'lame/cringe' version; 싸늘하다 is the heavier 'frozen, hostile' one). It pairs with 공기, 날씨, 새벽, 시선, 반응, 분위기. The pitfalls: don't equate it with 쌀쌀하다 (싸늘하다 is colder and tenser), and don't miss the atmosphere meaning, which natives use constantly.

Missing the figurative 'cold atmosphere' use: 분위기/반응이 싸늘하다 (a frosty mood/reaction) is extremely common in daily conversation, not just weather.
Confusing it with 썰렁하다: after a bad joke, 썰렁하다 = 'lame/cringe', whereas 싸늘하다 = the heavier 'frozen, hostile' silence.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 푹푹 찌다 means "to be boiling/scorching (oppressively hot)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 푹푹 찌다 (pukpuk jjida) = "to be boiling/scorching (oppressively hot)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 푹푹 찌다 ("to be sweltering/boiling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 푹푹 찌다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: vivid idiom: heat so heavy the air feels steamed; standard spacing is 푹푹 찌다
polite present: 찌 + 어요 → 쪄요
찌는 (present modifier) before a noun
pairs with 더위 (heat) for peak-summer days

examples.en: It's totally boiling outside.
examples.note: the everyday exaggeration; 완전 ('totally') is casual intensifier slang

examples.ko: 에어컨 없이는 푹푹 찌는 여름을 도저히 못 버텨요.
examples.romanization: eeokeon eopsineun pukpuk jjineun yeoreumeul dojeohi mot beotyeoyo.
examples.en: Without AC, there's no way I can survive the sweltering summer.
examples.note: 버티다 = to endure; 찌는 modifies 여름, 도저히 + 못 = 'simply can't'

examples.en: Maybe because it's the dog days of summer, it's been sweltering since morning.
examples.note: 반말; 삼복더위 = the hottest stretch (복날), -아서 그런지 = 'maybe because'

extendedVocab.nuance: 푹푹 찌다 literally means '(the heat) steams you' — 찌다 is the verb 'to steam', and the mimetic 푹푹 paints heat pressing down in thick waves, so the whole phrase is an idiomatic, highly colloquial way to say it's brutally, oppressively hot. It outranks even 무덥다 in vividness and feeling, and unlike the other items here it is a verb phrase, not a single adjective, so it conjugates on 찌다 (쪄요, 찌는, 쪘어요). You'll hear it everywhere in a Korean heat wave, paired with 더위, 날씨, 여름. Two real pitfalls: (1) 찌다 is a homophone minefield — the same 찌다 means 'to gain weight' (살이 찌다) and 'to steam food' (만두를 찌다), so only the weather context (날씨/더위/밖) tells you it's 'sweltering'; (2) spacing — the standard written form keeps a space, 푹푹 찌다, not 푹푹찌다.

Confusing this 찌다 with 찌다 'to gain weight' (살이 찌다) or 'to steam food' (만두를 찌다); only the weather context makes it 'sweltering'.
Writing it as one word 푹푹찌다; the standard form spaces the mimetic adverb: 푹푹 찌다.
Treating it as an adjective and saying 푹푹 쪄서 날씨 → it's a verb phrase, so conjugate on 찌다 (푹푹 쪄요, 푹푹 찌는 날씨).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 친절하다 means "to be kind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 친절하다 (chinjeolhada) means "to be kind". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 친절해요 ("someone is kind"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 친절하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요, never 친절하요
modifier 친절한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
adverb 친절하게 + verb

examples.en: That person is kind.
examples.note: Plain 반말 친절해; drop 요 with close friends.

examples.en: The staff here is really kind.
examples.note: -들이 marks plural staff; 친절하다 describes how they treat customers.

examples.ko: 길을 몰랐는데 어떤 분이 친절하게 가르쳐 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: gireul mollanneunde eotteon buni chinjeolhage gareuchyeo jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't know the way, but someone kindly showed me.
examples.note: 친절하게 (adverb) + 주시다 honorific = a kind favor done for you.

extendedVocab.nuance: 친절하다 is 'kind' in the sense of warm, attentive, service-minded behavior toward others — the word you reach for about staff, neighbors, or strangers who go out of their way for you. It is Sino-Korean 親切 (친 'close/intimate' + 절 'earnest/keen'), literally 'intimately earnest'. Compare 착하다, which is about an inherently good, gentle heart (a moral quality), whereas 친절하다 is about outward considerate treatment in a given moment — a cold person can still be 친절한 at work. It also differs from 다정하다 (affectionate, emotionally close). It follows the regular 하다 conjugation, so 하다 becomes 해요 (친절해요), and the adverb 친절하게 ('kindly') pairs naturally with verbs like 가르쳐 주다 or 설명하다. The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 친절하요 (the 하 must fuse to 해), and don't use it for an object or food — 'kind' as in 'a kind gesture' is fine, but you can't call coffee 친절한.
