Saying 친절하요 — the 하다 ending must contract to 해요, so it is 친절해요, never 친절하요.
Using 친절하다 to mean 'good-hearted' in general (e.g. '그는 친절한 사람이라 거짓말을 안 해요'). For inner goodness use 착하다; 친절하다 specifically describes considerate outward behavior.
Treating it like a verb and saying 친절했다 to mean 'acted kindly once' while expecting a do-form — it is an adjective, so to say someone 'was kind to me' you often add the action: 친절하게 대해 줬어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 똑똑하다 means "to be smart" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be smart" is 똑똑하다 (ttokttokada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 똑똑해요 ("someone is smart"). Watch the particle attached to 똑똑하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 똑똑한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
머리(head) + 똑똑하다 collocation

examples.en: Our puppy is really smart.
examples.note: 반말 똑똑해; 똑똑하다 works for clever animals too.

examples.en: That student was smart from a young age.
examples.note: Past 똑똑했어요; -서부터 = 'starting from'.

examples.en: If you act smart(ly), you won't lose out.
examples.note: Adverb 똑똑하게 = 'cleverly/shrewdly', not just 'intelligently'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 똑똑하다 is native Korean (not Sino-Korean), and it means 'smart' in the everyday sense of being quick, sharp, and able to understand and judge well — equally natural for a bright child, a clever student, or a clever pet. The nearest rivals are 영리하다 (clever/shrewd, slightly more about cunning and cute cleverness, often for kids and animals) and 똑똑하다's bookish cousin 지능이 높다 ('high IQ'); 똑똑하다 is the warm spoken word, while 우수하다 (excellent) or 유능하다 (competent/capable) describe proven performance and ability at work rather than raw brains. The adverb 똑똑하게 can drift toward 'shrewdly, without being fooled', as in 똑똑하게 소비하다 ('shop smart'). It takes the regular 하다 conjugation (똑똑해요). The English-speaker pitfall: 'smart' in English also means stylish/well-dressed, but 똑똑하다 NEVER means fashionable — for that you need 멋있다 or 옷을 잘 입다 — and beginners often misfire by saying 똑똑하요 instead of the contracted 똑똑해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 똑똑하요 instead of 똑똑해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 똑똑하다 for 'smart' meaning well-dressed/sharp-looking (e.g. '오늘 정말 똑똑해 보여요' to mean a sharp outfit). That English sense doesn't transfer; use 멋있다 or 깔끔하다 for appearance.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 게으르다 means "to be lazy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 게으르다 (geeureuda) = "to be lazy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 게을러요 ("someone is lazy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 게으르다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 르 irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ
modifier 게으른 (regular)
subject takes 이/가
noun 게으름 + 피우다 set phrase

examples.en: I'm really lazy on weekends.
examples.note: 반말 게을러; 르 irregular gives 게을러.

examples.ko: 동생이 너무 게을러서 방 청소를 안 해요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi neomu geeulleoseo bang cheongsoreul an haeyo.
examples.en: My sibling is so lazy that they don't clean their room.
examples.note: 게을러서 (르 irregular + 서) = 'because lazy'.

examples.ko: 요즘 좀 게을러져서 운동을 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jom geeulleojyeoseo undongeul mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I've gotten a bit lazy lately so I couldn't work out.
examples.note: 게을러지다 = 'become lazy' (게으르다 + 어지다).

extendedVocab.nuance: 게으르다 means 'lazy/idle', describing someone who avoids effort and puts things off; it is native Korean (not Sino-Korean) and carries a clearly negative, faintly scolding tone, so it is something you say about yourself jokingly or about a close family member, but rarely to a senior's face. Its mirror opposite is 부지런하다 (diligent), and its near-neighbor 느리다 means 'slow' (about speed), which is different — a fast worker can still be 게으른 if they dodge work, and a 게으른 person isn't necessarily 느린. Conjugation is the key lesson: 게으르다 is a 르-irregular verb, so before 어요 the 르 doubles the ㄹ and the vowel becomes 어 → 게을러요 (the stem 게으르- → 게을러-); but the modifier and dictionary-style forms stay regular (게으른 사람, 게으릅니다). Watch the set noun phrase 게으름을 피우다 ('to slack off'). The English-speaker pitfall is conjugating it like a regular ㅡ-vowel verb and saying 게으러요 — you must apply the 르 rule to get 게을러요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 게으러요 — this is a 르 irregular, so the ㄹ doubles: the correct form is 게을러요.
Confusing it with 느리다. 게으르다 = unwilling to work (laziness); 느리다 = slow in speed. '동작이 게으르다' to mean physically slow is wrong; say 동작이 느리다.
Using 게으르다 bluntly about a boss or elder. It is judgmental; soften with humor about yourself (저 오늘 좀 게을렀어요) rather than labeling a superior.

extendedVocab.explanation: 부지런하다 (bujireonhada) means "to be diligent". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부지런해요 ("someone is diligent"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부지런하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 부지런한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
adverb 부지런히 + verb

examples.en: My mom is really diligent.
examples.note: 반말 부지런해; about a hardworking habit.

examples.en: Diligent people get up early in the morning.
examples.note: Modifier 부지런한 + 사람.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 부지런히 공부해서 시험에 붙었어요.
examples.romanization: geu chinguneun bujireonhi gongbuhaeseo siheome buteosseoyo.
examples.en: That friend studied diligently and passed the exam.
examples.note: Adverb 부지런히 = 'diligently/busily'; note the -히 form.

extendedVocab.nuance: 부지런하다 means 'diligent, industrious, hardworking by habit', the warm-praise opposite of 게으르다. The 부지런 part is native Korean (not a hanja compound), joined to 하다. The dividing line with near-synonyms matters: 성실하다 (Sino 誠實, 'sincere/faithful') praises a conscientious, reliable, earnest character — about attitude and trustworthiness — while 부지런하다 emphasizes physically keeping busy, not being idle, getting up early and getting things done; 열심히 하다 ('do hard') describes effort on a specific task in the moment, whereas 부지런하다 is a standing trait. The adverb is irregular in spelling — 부지런히 (not 부지런하게 in everyday use) — as in 부지런히 일하다. It conjugates regularly as a 하다 adjective (부지런해요). The English-speaker pitfall: 'diligent' in English often modifies effort on one job, so learners try to plug 부지런하다 into a single action ('I studied diligently') as a verb; for that, use the adverb 부지런히 + verb, and avoid the beginner error 부지런하요 (it must contract to 부지런해요).

examples.ko: 그 친구는 너무 솔직해서 가끔 상처를 줘요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 솔직하다 means 'honest, frank, candid' — speaking your real thoughts and feelings openly without hiding or sugar-coating. It is Sino-Korean 率直 (솔/率 'frank, straightforward' + 직/直 'straight'), literally 'frank and straight'. The crucial contrast is with 정직하다 (Sino 正直 'upright-straight'), which is moral honesty — not lying, not cheating, being truthful as an ethical quality; 솔직하다 is about emotional candor, saying what you really feel, even bluntly, so 솔직하다 can sometimes mean 'too blunt', while 정직하다 is unambiguously praise. The adverb 솔직히 ('honestly, to be frank') is one of the most common conversation openers in Korean (솔직히 말하면…). It follows the regular 하다 conjugation (솔직해요). English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 솔직하다 when you mean morally honest/trustworthy (use 정직하다), and never say 솔직하요 — it contracts to 솔직해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 솔직하요 instead of 솔직해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 솔직하다 for 'honest' in the moral sense of not stealing or not lying (e.g. '그는 돈에 솔직해요'). For ethical honesty use 정직하다; 솔직하다 is about openly expressing real feelings.
Forgetting the discourse adverb 솔직히. To say 'honestly speaking' Koreans say 솔직히 말해서 / 솔직히 말하면, not 솔직하게 말하면 in casual speech.

extendedVocab.explanation: 착하다 (chakada) = "to be nice". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 착해요 ("someone is nice") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 착하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 착한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
idiomatic: 'a kind price' = good value

examples.en: My classmate is good-natured.
examples.note: 반말 착해; describes a gentle heart.

examples.note: Modifier 착한; -께 honorific for adults.

examples.note: Idiom 가격이 착하다 = 'reasonably cheap'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 착하다 is native Korean and describes an inherently good, gentle, kind-hearted, obedient nature — the goodness is a character trait, a soft and well-meaning heart, often used of children, students, and pets. The key contrast is with 친절하다: 착하다 is about who someone IS inside (good-hearted, won't hurt you, does the right thing), while 친절하다 is about considerate outward treatment in a moment; a shop clerk can be 친절한 at work while a child is 착한 by nature. Note a cultural nuance: calling an adult 착하다 can faintly imply 'naive/pushover' or sound like praising a child, so among grown-ups it is gentle but mild praise. A very common modern idiom is 가격이 착하다 / 착한 가격 ('a kind price' = pleasantly cheap, good value). It conjugates regularly (착해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'nice' in English is a catch-all (nice weather, nice food), but 착하다 applies almost only to a person's (or animal's) moral character — you cannot say 날씨가 착해요 for 'nice weather' (use 좋다), and beginners must contract 착하 + 요 to 착해요, never 착하요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 착하요 instead of 착해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 착하다 as a general 'nice' for things, weather, or food (e.g. '날씨가 착해요'). 착하다 is about good-hearted character; for pleasant things use 좋다.
Praising a respected adult or boss with 착하다 expecting strong praise — it can sound like calling them a naive pushover or talking down to them. For an admirable adult, 좋은 분이에요 or 인품이 훌륭하다 is safer.

extendedVocab.explanation: 나쁘다 (nappeuda) means "to be bad". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 나빠요 ("something is bad"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 나쁘다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅡ drops before 아 → 나빠
modifier 나쁜 + noun
subject takes 이/가

usagePhrases.en: to be bad for the body

examples.en: I'm in a bit of a bad mood.
examples.note: 반말 나빠; 기분이 나쁘다 = mood is bad.

examples.en: Cigarettes are bad for your health.
examples.note: -에 나쁘다 = 'bad for'; note 에, not 을.

examples.note: Modifier 나쁜 + 소식; 들어서 = 'because heard'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 나쁘다 is native Korean and is the all-purpose opposite of 좋다, covering 'bad, poor, harmful, unpleasant' — bad weather, a bad mood, a bad habit, bad news, bad for your health. Near-synonyms split by domain: 나쁘다 is the broad evaluative 'bad', while 못되다 means 'wicked, ill-natured' (a morally bad, mean person, stronger and more accusatory), and 안 좋다 ('not good') is a softer, more polite way to say something is bad without the harsh punch of 나쁘다. The conjugation lesson is the ㅡ (으) drop: the stem 나쁘- loses its ㅡ before an ending starting with a vowel, and since the preceding vowel is the bright ㅏ, you add 아 → 나빠요 (past 나빴어요). Useful frame: X에 나쁘다 = 'bad for X' (몸에 나쁘다). English-speaker pitfalls: don't say 나쁘어요 — the ㅡ must drop to give 나빠요; and 'I feel bad' meaning sorry/guilty is NOT 기분이 나빠요 (that means you're in a bad/annoyed mood) — use 미안하다 for apology or 마음이 안 좋다 for feeling bad about something.

Saying 나쁘어요 instead of 나빠요 — 나쁘다 is a ㅡ-irregular: drop ㅡ and add 아 → 나빠요.
Translating English 'I feel bad (guilty/sorry)' as 기분이 나빠요. That means 'I'm in a bad/offended mood'. Use 미안해요 to apologize or 마음이 안 좋아요 to feel bad about something.
Using 나쁘다 for a morally wicked, malicious person and expecting full force — 나쁜 사람 is fine for 'bad person', but for 'mean/ill-natured' 못된 사람 is stronger and more precise.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이상하다 means "to be strange" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be strange" is 이상하다 (isanghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이상해요 ("something is strange"). Watch the particle attached to 이상하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 이상한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
좀 softens the judgment

examples.en: Something feels a bit off.
examples.note: 반말 이상해; 뭔가 = 'something'.

examples.en: The smell was off, so I didn't eat it.
examples.note: 이상해서 = 'because strange'; food going bad.

examples.ko: 오늘 그 사람 행동이 좀 이상했어요.
examples.romanization: oneul geu saram haengdongi jom isanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: That person's behavior was a bit strange today.
examples.note: Past 이상했어요; 행동이 이상하다 = odd behavior.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이상하다 means 'strange, odd, weird, off' — something that doesn't seem normal or feels not-right, from a funny smell to peculiar behavior to a glitchy phone. It is Sino-Korean 異常 (이/異 'different' + 상/常 'normal, usual'), literally 'departing from the usual', which captures the feel exactly: deviating from the expected. The nearest contrast is 신기하다 (Sino 神奇), which is 'strange' in the GOOD sense of fascinating, novel, wondrous — eyes-wide curiosity — whereas 이상하다 leans negative or uneasy ('that's weird/off'); also distinguish 이상하다 from 특이하다 ('distinctive, unusual' in a more neutral, noteworthy way). It conjugates regularly (이상해요). English-speaker pitfall: English 'strange' can be admiring ('a strange and beautiful film'), but if you mean wonderfully novel use 신기하다, not 이상하다 — and saying 음식이 이상해요 implies it has gone bad or tastes wrong, a real complaint. Don't say 이상하요; it contracts to 이상해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이상하요 instead of 이상해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 이상하다 to mean 'amazing/fascinatingly strange'. For wonder and novelty use 신기하다; 이상하다 signals something feels off, unsettling, or wrong.
Casually calling a person 이상한 사람 to mean 'an interesting eccentric'. To Koreans 이상한 사람 strongly implies 'a creepy/weird person', which is insulting; use 독특하다 or 특이하다 for a neutral 'unusual person'.

extendedVocab.explanation: 특별하다 (teukbyeolhada) = "to be special". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 특별해요 ("something is special") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 특별하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. extendedVocab.nuance: 특별하다 means 'special, particular, out of the ordinary' — a day, gift, person, or place that stands apart and carries extra value or meaning. It is Sino-Korean 特別 (특/特 'special, particular' + 별/別 'distinguish, separate'), literally 'specially set apart'. Watch the contrast with 특이하다 (Sino 特異, 'distinctive/peculiar'): 특별하다 = special and usually precious/valued (a special day, a special someone), while 특이하다 = unusual/peculiar in a more neutral or even slightly odd way (a peculiar habit); calling food 특이한 맛 means 'an unusual taste', not 'a wonderful taste'. Also note 특별하다 (adjective, 'is special') vs the adverb 특별히 ('specially, in particular'), which modifies verbs (특별히 신경 쓰다). It conjugates regularly (특별해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'special' in English can mean 'specialized/dedicated' (a special tool, special forces), but for that meaning Korean uses the prefix 특수 (특수 장비, 특수 부대), not 특별하다; and don't say 특별하요 — it must contract to 특별해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 중요하다 means "to be important" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 중요하다 (jungyohada) means "to be important". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 중요해요 ("something is important"). examples.note: 반말 중요해; 이거 = casual 'this'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 중요하다 means 'important, significant, crucial' — carrying weight, mattering a great deal. It is Sino-Korean 重要 (중/重 'heavy' + 요/要 'essential, vital'), a vivid literal image of 'heavy and essential', i.e. weighty and indispensable. The sharp contrast is with 필요하다 ('necessary/needed'): 중요하다 ranks how much something MATTERS in significance, while 필요하다 says something is REQUIRED to get a result — an exam can be 중요한 (it matters a lot) and a pencil 필요한 (you need it to take the test); they are not interchangeable. Also distinguish 소중하다 ('precious, dear'), which is emotional preciousness rather than functional weight. The collocation 중요하게 생각하다 / 중요하게 여기다 means 'to value, to prioritize'. It conjugates regularly (중요해요). English-speaker pitfall: learners blur 'important' and 'necessary' — for 'I need it' use 필요하다, reserving 중요하다 for 'it matters'; and never say 중요하요 (contract to 중요해요).

Saying 중요하요 instead of 중요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 중요하다 with 필요하다. 중요하다 = matters/significant; 필요하다 = needed/required. '연필이 중요해요' (the pencil is important) usually should be '연필이 필요해요' (I need a pencil).

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be necessary" is 필요하다 (piryohada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 필요해요 ("something is necessary"). modifier 필요한 + noun

examples.en: I need your help right now.
examples.note: 반말 필요해; the needed thing (도움) takes 이/가.

examples.ko: 이 일을 끝내려면 시간이 더 필요해요.
examples.romanization: i ireul kkeunnaeryeomyeon sigani deo piryohaeyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: 필요하다 means 'to be necessary / to be needed', and it is the standard Korean way to say 'I need something'. It is Sino-Korean 必要 (필/必 'must, inevitably' + 요/要 'essential'), literally 'must-have, essential'. The grammar is the heart of the lesson and the main pitfall: Korean treats the needed thing as the GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT with 이/가, not as an object — so 'I need money' is 돈이 필요해요 (lit. 'money is necessary'), and the person who needs it is marked 한테/에게 (저한테 돈이 필요해요), never 돈을 필요해요. Contrast 필요하다 with 중요하다 ('important/matters'): needed vs. significant. The pattern -(으)ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다 means 'there is/isn't a need to ~' (걱정할 필요 없어요). It conjugates regularly (필요해요). English-speaker pitfall: because English 'need' is a transitive verb taking an object, learners wrongly say 나는 물을 필요해요; the correct, natural Korean is 나는 물이 필요해요 — and don't say 필요하요 (contract to 필요해요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 물을 필요해요 with an object particle. 필요하다 takes the needed thing as the subject: say 물이 필요해요. Mark the needer with 한테/에게 (저한테 물이 필요해요).
Saying 필요하요 instead of 필요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 필요하다 with 중요하다. 필요하다 = required/needed to achieve something; 중요하다 = significant/matters. '시간이 중요해요' (time matters) and '시간이 필요해요' (I need time) say different things.

The grammar is the heart of the lesson: Korean treats the needed thing as the GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT with 이/가, not as an object — so 'I need money' is 돈이 필요해요 (lit. Sino-Korean 必要 (필/必 'must, inevitably' + 요/要 'essential'), literally 'must-have, essential'.
It conjugates regularly (필요해요); the contracted form is 필요해요, never 필요하요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비슷하다 means "to be similar" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 비슷하다 (biseutada) = "to be similar". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비슷해요 ("things are similar") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 비슷하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 → 해요
modifier 비슷한 + noun
subject takes 이/가
compare-target takes 와/과 or 랑

examples.en: The two of us have kind of similar personalities.
examples.note: 반말 비슷해; 둘이 = 'the two'.

examples.en: This bag is similar to that bag.
examples.note: -(이)랑 비슷하다 = 'similar to' (casual).

examples.ko: 맛이 비슷해서 두 개를 자꾸 헷갈려요.
examples.romanization: masi biseutaeseo du gaereul jakku hetgallyeoyo.
examples.en: The tastes are similar, so I keep mixing the two up.
examples.note: 비슷해서 = 'because similar'; 자꾸 = 'keep ~ing'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 비슷하다 means 'similar, alike, resembling' — two things that are close but not identical. It is native Korean (not a hanja word). The crucial contrast is with 같다 ('same/identical'): 비슷하다 says they RESEMBLE each other (close, comparable, but with differences), while 같다 says they are THE SAME; '가격이 비슷해요' = the prices are similar/comparable, but '가격이 같아요' = the prices are exactly the same — mixing these up changes the fact. Note the comparison particle: the thing you compare against takes 와/과 (formal) or 랑/이랑 (casual) plus 비슷하다 (A는 B와 비슷하다). Useful collocations: 성격이 비슷하다, 분위기가 비슷하다, 비슷한 또래 ('similar-aged peers'). It conjugates regularly (비슷해요). English-speaker pitfall: English says 'similar TO', so learners reach for 에/에게, but Korean uses 와/과/랑 — say 이거랑 비슷해요, not 이거에 비슷해요; and don't say 비슷하요 (contract to 비슷해요).

Saying 비슷하요 instead of 비슷해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빨갛다 means "to be red" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 빨갛다 (ppalgata) means "to be red". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사과가 빨개요 ("The apple is red"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 빨갛다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, not 을/를
빨간색 = the noun 'red color'
빨개지다 = become red, change of state
빨간 = the modifier that sits before a noun

examples.en: This apple is red
examples.note: the most basic 요-form: 빨갛다 → 빨개요

examples.en: The evening sky was dyed red
examples.note: 빨갛게 = the adverb 'redly', + 물들다 'to be dyed'

examples.en: I got embarrassed so my face turned red
examples.note: 빨개지다 captures the change, not just the state

extendedVocab.nuance: 빨갛다 is the vivid, pure 'red' of an apple, a stop light, or a blushing face. Among red words, contrast it with 붉다, which is the more literary, darker 'reddish/crimson' used for blood, sunsets, and emotion (붉은 노을), while 빨갛다 is the bright everyday red a child would point at. As an adjective it describes a STATE, so the thing that is red takes 이/가 (얼굴이 빨개요), never 을/를. The biggest trap for English speakers is the ㅎ-irregular: the stem-final ㅎ vanishes AND the vowel fuses, so it is never 빨갛아요 but 빨개요, and the noun-modifying form is 빨간 (빨간 사과), not 빨갛은. To say something 'turns red,' use 빨개지다, because 빨갛다 alone is a static quality, not a change. Note 빨간색 is the noun 'the color red.'

Using the modifier 빨갛은 사과 — drop the ㅎ for the modifier too: it is 빨간 사과.
Saying 사과를 빨개요 with 을/를 — a color is a state, so use 이/가: 사과가 빨개요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 파랗다 means "to be blue" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be blue" is 파랗다 (parata). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 하늘이 파래요 ("The sky is blue"). Watch the particle attached to 파랗다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the classic blue thing, state with 이/가
파란색 = the noun 'blue', sits before another noun
파랗게 = adverb 'bluely' + 칠하다 'paint'
새- prefix intensifies the shade

examples.en: The sky is blue today
examples.note: basic 요-form: 파랗다 → 파래요

examples.en: The sea is really blue, isn't it
examples.note: -네요 adds a tone of fresh observation

examples.en: My lips went blue (from cold/fear)
examples.note: 파랗게 질리다 is a set phrase for going pale/blue

extendedVocab.nuance: 파랗다 is the bright blue of a clear sky and the sea, and in Korean it famously also covers what English calls 'green' for traffic lights and fresh leaves (파란불 'the green light,' 파란 잔디 'green grass') — a real surprise for learners. The neighboring word 푸르다 is more poetic and leans 'verdant/azure,' used for 푸른 산 'green mountains' and 푸른 하늘 in songs, while 파랗다 is the plain everyday blue. Being an adjective, the blue thing takes 이/가 (하늘이 파래요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular is the key pitfall: never 파랗아요 but 파래요, and the modifier is 파란 (파란 바다), not 파랗은. Use 파래지다 for 'turn blue,' and 파란색 for the noun 'the color blue.'

Saying 파랗아요 — the ㅎ deletes and the vowel fuses, giving 파래요 as the polite form.
Forming the modifier as 파랗은 바다 — it must be 파란 바다 with the ㅎ dropped.
Assuming 파랗다 only means 'blue' — for a traffic 'go' light Koreans say 파란불, so it can map to English 'green.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 노랗다 means "to be yellow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 노랗다 (norata) = "to be yellow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 바나나가 노래요 ("The banana is yellow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 노랗다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a fruit
노란색 = noun 'yellow' before another noun
노랗게 = adverb + 익다 'ripen', a natural pair
샛- prefix intensifies the yellow

examples.en: This banana is yellow
examples.note: basic 요-form: 노랗다 → 노래요

examples.en: In autumn the ginkgo leaves turn yellow
examples.note: 노랗게 물들다 = 'be dyed yellow'

examples.en: After starving for days my vision went yellow (I felt faint)
examples.note: 눈앞이 노래지다 is an idiom for dizziness/despair

extendedVocab.nuance: 노랗다 is the cheerful pure yellow of a banana, a chick, or a school bus. Korean color adjectives like this come in a 'bright vs dark' vowel-harmony pair: 노랗다 (bright, with ㅗ/ㅏ) feels light and vivid, while its darker partner 누렇다 (with ㅜ/ㅓ) means a dull, dingy, faded yellow like old paper or unhealthy skin — choosing the wrong one changes the whole feeling. As an adjective it takes 이/가 on the yellow thing (잎이 노래요), not 을/를. Watch the ㅎ-irregular: it is 노래요, never 노랗아요, and the modifier is 노란 (노란 우산), not 노랗은. There is also a vivid set phrase 눈앞이 노래지다 'to feel faint/hopeless,' literally 'the front of the eyes turns yellow.' The noun is 노란색.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 노랗아요 — ㅎ drops and the vowel fuses to 노래요 for the polite form.
Writing the modifier as 노랗은 우산 — the correct modifier is 노란 우산.
Mixing up 노랗다 and 누렇다 — 노랗다 is bright/fresh yellow, 누렇다 is dull/sickly yellow, so they are not interchangeable.

extendedVocab.explanation: 까맣다 (kkamata) means "to be black". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 머리가 까매요 ("The hair is black"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 까맣다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing hair
까만색 = noun 'black' before another noun
까맣게 + 타다, a very common pair
idiom: 'forget blackly' = forget utterly

examples.en: The cat is black
examples.note: basic 요-form: 까맣다 → 까매요

examples.en: My face got tanned dark in summer
examples.note: 까맣게 타다 = 'get burnt/tanned black'

examples.en: I had completely forgotten the appointment
examples.note: 까맣게 잊다 = forget utterly, a fixed expression

extendedVocab.nuance: 까맣다 is everyday black — black hair, a black cat, a dark night sky, or skin tanned by the sun. It is the 'bright/casual' vowel-harmony partner of 꺼멓다 (darker, grimier black) and is closely related to the Sino-flavored noun 검은색; the near-synonym adjective 검다 is slightly more formal/neutral ('to be black/dark'), while 까맣다 sounds more vivid and conversational. As a state adjective the black thing takes 이/가 (머리가 까매요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular trap applies: it is 까매요, never 까맣아요, and the modifier is 까만 (까만 신발), not 까맣은. Korean also uses 까맣게 figuratively — 까맣게 잊다 'to forget completely' and 까맣게 타다 'to get a deep tan' — which do not translate word-for-word into English. The noun is 까만색 (or 검은색).

Saying 까맣아요 — the ㅎ-irregular gives 까매요 as the polite form.
Using the modifier 까맣은 신발 — it should be 까만 신발 with ㅎ dropped.
Translating 까맣게 잊다 literally as 'forget black' — it is an idiom meaning 'to forget completely.'

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be white" is 하얗다 (hayata). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 눈이 하얘요 ("The snow is white"). usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing snow
하얀색 = noun 'white' before another noun
하얗게 + 변하다, change of color
새- prefix = brilliant, spotless white

examples.en: This paper is white
examples.note: basic 요-form: 하얗다 → 하얘요

examples.en: It snowed and the whole world turned white
examples.note: 하얘지다 = the change 'become white'

examples.en: She was so shocked her face went white
examples.note: 하얗게 질리다 = go pale, a set phrase

extendedVocab.nuance: 하얗다 is bright, clean white — fresh snow, white paper, clouds, a crisp white shirt. It is the casual, vivid counterpart of the more neutral 희다 'to be white' (희다 sounds slightly bookish, e.g. 흰 눈 in writing), and the darker harmony partner 허옇다 means a dull, pale, washed-out white. As a state adjective the white thing takes 이/가 (눈이 하얘요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular is the core pitfall: it is 하얘요, never 하얗아요, and the noun-modifier is 하얀 (하얀 셔츠), not 하얗은 — though note the related stem 희다 gives the very common modifier 흰 (흰색, 흰 눈). extendedVocab.explanation: 동그랗다 (donggeurata) = "to be round". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 달이 동그래요 ("The moon is round") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a shape
동그란 = the modifier before a noun
동그랗게 뜨다, a vivid set phrase
the related noun built from the same root

examples.en: This mirror is round
examples.note: basic 요-form: 동그랗다 → 동그래요

examples.en: The child opened her eyes wide
examples.note: 동그랗게 뜨다 shows surprise

examples.en: Please shape the dough into rounds
examples.note: 동그랗게 빚다 = 'mold into a round shape'

extendedVocab.nuance: 동그랗다 describes a small, neat, circular roundness — a coin, a plate, the full moon, wide-open eyes. A favorite collocation is 눈을 동그랗게 뜨다 'to open the eyes wide (in surprise),' where 동그랗게 is the adverb form.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 귀엽다 means "to be cute" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 귀엽다 (gwiyeopda) means "to be cute". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 강아지가 귀여워요 ("The puppy is cute"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 귀엽다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing an animal
귀여운 = the modifier before a noun
귀엽게 = adverb form + 웃다
귀여워 + 죽겠다, a strong casual reaction

examples.en: This cat is cute
examples.note: basic 요-form via ㅂ-irregular: 귀엽다 → 귀여워요

examples.en: The baby is really cute(-looking)
examples.note: 귀엽게 생기다 = 'be cute in looks'

examples.ko: 강아지가 너무 귀여워서 계속 보게 돼요
examples.romanization: gangajiga neomu gwiyeowoseo gyesok boge dwaeyo
examples.en: The puppy is so cute I keep looking
examples.note: -아서 links 'cute' to the result

extendedVocab.nuance: 귀엽다 means 'cute, adorable, endearing' — the small-and-lovable charm of babies, animals, and round little objects, and it can also describe an older person's behavior as 'charmingly sweet.' Crucially it is NOT the same as 예쁘다 'pretty/beautiful': 귀엽다 is about lovable charm (a chubby puppy), while 예쁘다 is about visual prettiness (an elegant dress), so calling a grown adult only 귀엽다 can imply 'cute like a kid' rather than 'gorgeous.' As a state adjective the cute thing takes 이/가 (아기가 귀여워요), not 을/를. The grammar pitfall is the ㅂ-irregular: the stem-final ㅂ turns into 우/워 before a vowel, so it is 귀여워요, never 귀엽어요, and the modifier is 귀여운 (귀여운 인형), not 귀엽은. The past is 귀여웠어요. Beware: not every ㅂ word is irregular (좁다 → 좁아요), but 귀엽다 is.

Saying 귀엽어요 — 귀엽다 is ㅂ-irregular, so ㅂ becomes 워 and the polite form is 귀여워요.
Using the modifier 귀엽은 인형 — the ㅂ becomes 운, giving 귀여운 인형.
Calling an adult 귀여워요 to mean 'beautiful' — that conveys 'cute/endearing'; for 'pretty' use 예뻐요 instead.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 멋지다 means "to be cool" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be cool" is 멋지다 (meotjida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저 차가 멋져요 ("That car is cool"). Watch the particle attached to 멋지다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing an object
멋진 = the modifier before a noun
멋지게 = adverb form + 차려입다

usagePhrases.en: to be told one is cool
usagePhrases.note: 멋지다 + quotative, a common compliment

examples.en: This building is cool
examples.note: basic 요-form: 멋지다 → 멋져요

examples.en: You dressed really sharply today
examples.note: 멋지게 차려입다 = dress stylishly

examples.en: Behaving so maturely — that's really cool
examples.note: 멋지다 here praises character, not looks

extendedVocab.nuance: 멋지다 means 'cool, stylish, splendid, impressive,' praising not just looks but admirable style or character — a sharp outfit, a stunning view, or someone who acts with class. Built from the native noun 멋 'style/flair/taste,' it is warmer and more sincere than the English loanword 쿨하다, which means 'cool' in the sense of laid-back/unbothered, not 'awesome.' Compare also 멋있다, a near-twin: 멋있다 and 멋지다 are nearly interchangeable, with 멋지다 sounding a touch more exclamatory/admiring. As a state adjective the impressive thing takes 이/가 (경치가 멋져요), not 을/를. Although it ends in 지, it is a fully REGULAR adjective: the stem 멋지- + 어 contracts to 멋져요 (never 멋지어요). The pitfall is leaving it bare as 멋지요 — that drops the required 어, so always use 멋져요; the modifier is 멋진 (멋진 옷) and the past is 멋졌어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 멋지요 for the polite form — the stem needs 어, contracting to 멋져요.
Writing 멋지어요 in full — 지 + 어 contracts, so the natural form is 멋져요.
Using 쿨하다 to mean 'awesome' — 쿨하다 means 'laid-back/unbothered'; for 'cool/impressive' use 멋지다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 날씬하다 means "to be slim" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 날씬하다 (nalssinhada) = "to be slim". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 언니가 날씬해요 ("My older sister is slim") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 날씬하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a person
날씬한 = the modifier before a noun
날씬하게 = adverb + 보이다 'appear'
common body-part collocation

examples.en: That actor is slim
examples.note: basic 하다-form: 날씬하다 → 날씬해요

examples.en: I exercised so my legs got slimmer
examples.note: 날씬해지다 = the change 'become slim'

examples.ko: 이 옷을 입으면 더 날씬해 보여요
examples.romanization: i oseul ibeumyeon deo nalssinhae boyeoyo
examples.en: You look slimmer in these clothes
examples.note: 날씬해 보이다 = 'appear slim'

extendedVocab.nuance: 날씬하다 is a flattering 'slim, slender, trim' — a fit, attractive thinness people aspire to, often paired with 몸매 'figure' (날씬한 몸매). It is firmly positive, unlike the plain near-synonym 마르다 'to be thin,' which is neutral-to-negative and can imply 'skinny/scrawny' or even unhealthily underweight (너무 말랐어요 'too skinny'); so complimenting someone, choose 날씬하다, not 마르다. Note 마르다 is also a르-irregular verb-like form, whereas 날씬하다 is a clean 하다 adjective. As a state adjective the slim person/part takes 이/가 (다리가 날씬해요), not 을/를. The 하다 pitfall: never 날씬하요 — the 하다 ending becomes 해요 (하 + 여 → 해), so it is 날씬해요. The modifier is 날씬한 (날씬한 모델), the adverb 날씬하게, and 'get slimmer' is 날씬해지다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 날씬하요 — every 하다 adjective conjugates to 해요, so it is 날씬해요.
Using 마르다 as a compliment — 마르다 can sound 'too skinny'; for an admiring 'slim' use 날씬하다.
Marking the body part with 을/를 (다리를 날씬해요) — it is a state, so use 이/가: 다리가 날씬해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뚱뚱하다 means "to be fat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 뚱뚱하다 (ttungttunghada) means "to be fat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고양이가 뚱뚱해요 ("The cat is fat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뚱뚱하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, gentler on an animal
뚱뚱한 = the modifier before a noun
뚱뚱해 + 보이다, often a worry about clothes
뚱뚱한 + 체형, describing body type

examples.en: This penguin is fat
examples.note: basic 하다-form: 뚱뚱하다 → 뚱뚱해요

examples.en: I gained weight lately so I got a bit fat
examples.note: 뚱뚱해지다 = the change; 살이 찌다 = gain weight

examples.en: Will I look fat in these clothes?
examples.note: 뚱뚱해 보이다, a typical self-conscious question

extendedVocab.nuance: 뚱뚱하다 is the blunt, plain word for 'fat/chubby,' and like English 'fat' it is sensitive: said straight to or about a person it sounds rude, so Koreans soften it about people and use it freely only for animals or stuffed toys. For people, the polite alternatives are 통통하다 'pleasantly plump/chubby' (cute, kind) and the gentle euphemism 살이 좀 있다 'to have a bit of weight'; the opposite is 날씬하다 'slim.' Note 뚱뚱하다 describes the standing state, while the verb 살이 찌다 'to gain weight' describes the process. As a state adjective the heavy thing takes 이/가 (배가 뚱뚱해요), not 을/를. The 하다 trap: never 뚱뚱하요 — it conjugates to 뚱뚱해요. The modifier is 뚱뚱한 (뚱뚱한 강아지), the adverb 뚱뚱하게, and 'get fat' is 뚱뚱해지다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 뚱뚱하요 — the 하다 ending becomes 해요, so the polite form is 뚱뚱해요.
Calling a person 뚱뚱해요 to their face — it sounds harsh; soften with 통통하다 or 살이 좀 있다.
Confusing the state with the action — 뚱뚱하다 is 'to be fat,' but 'to gain weight' is the verb 살이 찌다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 건강하다 means "to be healthy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be healthy" is 건강하다 (geonganghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 할머니가 건강해요 ("My grandmother is healthy"). Watch the particle attached to 건강하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a person
건강한 = the modifier before a noun
건강하게 + 지내다, a warm farewell phrase

usagePhrases.en: to take care of one's health
usagePhrases.note: the noun 건강 + 챙기다

examples.en: My father is healthy
examples.note: basic 하다-form: 건강하다 → 건강해요

examples.en: I eat lots of vegetables so I got healthier
examples.note: 건강해지다 = the change 'become healthy'

examples.en: Stay healthy in the new year too
examples.note: 건강하게 지내세요 is a common well-wish

extendedVocab.nuance: 건강하다 means 'to be healthy, in good physical condition' — strong, well, free of illness — for a person, a body, or by extension healthy food and habits. It is Sino-Korean: 健康 (健 'sturdy/robust' + 康 'at ease/well'), literally 'robust and well,' which is why the noun 건강 'health' shows up everywhere (건강 검진 'health checkup,' 건강을 챙기다 'mind one's health'). Distinguish it from 튼튼하다 'sturdy/robust,' which stresses physical toughness and durability and also describes objects (튼튼한 책상 'a sturdy desk'), whereas 건강하다 is about wellness and is normally for living things. As a state adjective the healthy one takes 이/가 (몸이 건강해요), not 을/를. The 하다 pitfall: never 건강하요 — it becomes 건강해요. The modifier is 건강한 (건강한 습관), and 건강하게 지내세요 is a standard 'take care / be well' wish.

Saying 건강하요 — the 하다 ending conjugates to 해요, giving 건강해요.
Using 건강하다 for an object — for a sturdy thing like a desk use 튼튼하다; 건강하다 is for living bodies.
Saying 몸을 건강해요 with 을/를 — it is a state, so use 이/가: 몸이 건강해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어떻다 means "to be how" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어떻다 (eotteota) = "to be how". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 날씨가 어때요? ("How is the weather?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 어떻다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: asking about a state with 이/가
어떤 = the modifier 'what kind of'
어떻게 = the adverb 'how/in what way'
어떻게 해 contracted, a panicked reaction

examples.en: How's this outfit? / What do you think?
examples.note: 어때요 also means 'how about it?' to suggest

examples.en: How was the movie yesterday?
examples.note: past form: 어떻다 → 어땠어요

examples.en: How do you get to Seoul?
examples.note: 어떻게 = the adverb for asking the manner

extendedVocab.nuance: 어떻다 is the question-adjective 'to be how / to be what-like,' the root behind a whole family Koreans use constantly. Learn its three faces: 어때(요)? = 'How is it? / How about it?' (asking a state or making a soft suggestion — 이거 어때요?), 어떤 = the modifier 'what kind of' before a noun (어떤 음악 'what kind of music'), and 어떻게 = the adverb 'how / in what way' for asking method (어떻게 해요? 'how do you do it?'). Do not confuse 어떻다 with 어떡하다, the contraction of 어떻게 하다 'to do how,' which gives the very common cry 어떡해! 'what do I do?!' As an irregular ㅎ adjective, the polite/question form is 어때요, never 어떻아요, and the past is 어땠어요. The single most frequent learner error is choosing the wrong family member — using 어떤 where 어떻게 is needed, or vice versa.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 어떻아요 — 어떻다 is ㅎ-irregular, so the question form is 어때요 (past 어땠어요).
Mixing 어떤 and 어떻게 — 어떤 + noun = 'what kind of' (어떤 색), but 어떻게 + verb = 'how' (어떻게 가요).
Writing 어떻해 for 'what do I do' — the set phrase is 어떡해 (from 어떻게 해), not 어떻해.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 달다 means "to be sweet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 달다 (dalda) means "to be sweet". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 달콤하다 ("to be sweet and lovely"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 달다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: softer, more poetic cousin of 달다, used for desserts and even romance
the noun 단맛 (sweet + taste) is how you name the flavor itself
꿀처럼 is the go-to simile for intense sweetness

usagePhrases.en: to be tasty / to keep saying
usagePhrases.note: idiom: food is delicious, or a word is 'always on your lips'

examples.en: This candy is really sweet.
examples.note: plain statement with 정말 for emphasis; note the subject takes 이

examples.en: The strawberries were sweeter than expected, so I was surprised.
examples.note: -아서 links the taste to your reaction

examples.ko: 손님, 단거 좋아하시면 이 케이크 추천드려요.
examples.romanization: sonnim, dangeo joahasimyeon i keikeu chucheondeuryeoyo.
examples.en: If you like sweet things, sir, I recommend this cake.
examples.note: shop register: 단거 = 단 것 (sweet thing), 추천드리다 is humble

extendedVocab.nuance: 달다 is the basic word for sugary, honey-like sweetness, and the dividing line you must learn is 달다 vs 달콤하다: 달다 is the flat, factual report ('this is sweet, maybe too sweet'), while 달콤하다 adds a warm, pleasant, almost romantic glow ('sweet and lovely') and is preferred for desserts, perfume, even 달콤한 사랑. As an adjective 달다 takes 이/가 on the thing tasted (커피가 달아요), never 을/를. Watch the irregular conjugation: the stem ends in ㄹ, which drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ — so the formal form is 답니다 (not 달습니다) and the modifier is 단 (단 음식), yet 달아요 keeps the ㄹ. The English-speaker trap is twofold: do not write 다라요, and remember that to 'add sugar' uses a verb (설탕을 넣다), because English 'sweeten' has no one-word match here. 달다 also coexists with the unrelated verb 달다 meaning 'to hang/attach', so context decides.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '이 커피를 달아요' — 달다 is descriptive, so the tasted item is the subject with 이/가: 이 커피가 달아요.
Writing the polite form as 다라요; the correct contraction keeps the block as 달아요.
Using the formal 달습니다 — because of ㄹ-dropping it must be 답니다.

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be sour" is 시다 (sida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신맛이 나다 ("to taste sour"). usagePhrases.note: 신맛 (sour + taste) names the flavor; 나다 means the taste 'comes out'
vivid variant of 시다, hints at a slightly off or fermented sour smell too
the GOOD sour — bright and appetizing, as in 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour)
식초 (vinegar) is the benchmark for sharp sourness

examples.en: The lemon is too sour.
examples.note: basic taste report; 너무 = too (much)

examples.en: The kimchi has fermented, so it's a little sour.
examples.note: -아서 ties fermentation to the sourness; 익다 = to ripen/ferment

examples.ko: 이거 상했나 봐요, 우유에서 신맛이 나요.
examples.romanization: igeo sanghaenna bwayo, uyueseo sinmasi nayo.

examples.note: real situation: sour milk signals spoilage, using 신맛이 나다

extendedVocab.nuance: 시다 is the sharp, acidic taste of lemon, vinegar, or over-fermented kimchi, and the key contrast is 시다 vs 새콤하다: 시다 is neutral-to-negative (it can simply mean 'too sour' or even 'spoiled'), whereas 새콤하다 is always the pleasant, refreshing tang you want in 새콤달콤 sweet-and-sour dishes. 간 = the salt level of a dish; 간이 짜다/싱겁다 is how cooks judge food
adverb 짜게 + 먹다; doctors warn 짜게 먹지 마세요 (don't eat salty)
소금 (salt) as the obvious benchmark

examples.en: The soup is a bit salty.
examples.note: everyday complaint at the table; 좀 softens it

examples.ko: 라면을 끓일 때 스프를 다 넣으면 짜요.
examples.romanization: ramyeoneul kkeuril ttae seupeureul da neoeumyeon jjayo.
examples.en: If you add the whole seasoning packet when cooking ramen, it gets salty.
examples.note: -(으)면 condition → result

examples.ko: 사장님이 좀 짠 편이라 회식을 잘 안 사요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi jom jjan pyeonira hoesigeul jal an sayo.
examples.en: The boss is a bit stingy, so he rarely treats us to dinner.
examples.note: real-life slang: 짜다 = tightfisted, not about taste

extendedVocab.nuance: 짜다 means having a strong salt taste, and the practical contrast for cooking is 짜다 vs 간이 맞다: 짜다 says there is too much salt, while 간이 맞다 means the seasoning is just right (and 싱겁다 means too little). Second, 짜다 has a very common figurative meaning — 'stingy / tightfisted' — so 그 사람 진짜 짜 means 'that person is so cheap', nothing to do with food; English 'salty' meaning 'bitter/annoyed' does NOT transfer to Korean 짜다, so do not use it that way. Using 짜다 to mean emotionally 'salty/annoyed' as in English — in Korean that figurative sense is 'stingy', so the English idiom does not carry over.
Saying '이 국을 짜요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 짜요.

usagePhrases.note: the standard cook's verdict opposite 간이 짜다
맛이 + 싱겁다 reports a weak overall flavor
adverb 싱겁게 + 먹다; health-conscious eating
figurative: someone whose jokes or actions fall flat

examples.en: The soup is a bit bland.
examples.note: table comment; 좀 keeps it polite

examples.en: I didn't add salt, so the stew is bland.
examples.note: -아서 cause; pairs the missing salt with the result

examples.ko: 병원 밥은 싱겁게 나와서 처음엔 입에 안 맞았어요.
examples.romanization: byeongwon babeun singgeopge nawaseo cheoeumen ibe an majasseoyo.
examples.en: Hospital food comes lightly seasoned, so at first it didn't suit my taste.
examples.note: real situation with 싱겁게 and 입에 맞다

extendedVocab.nuance: 싱겁다 is the exact opposite of 짜다: it means a dish lacks salt or has too weak a flavor. The contrast to fix is 싱겁다 vs 담백하다 — both describe mild food, but 싱겁다 is a complaint ('underseasoned, needs salt') while 담백하다 is praise ('cleanly light, refreshing'); never mix them up when complimenting a cook. The bland thing takes 이/가 (국이 싱거워요). This is a ㅂ-irregular: before a vowel ending the ㅂ becomes 우, so 싱겁 + 어요 → 싱거워요, past 싱거웠어요, modifier 싱거운; the formal form keeps ㅂ as 싱겁습니다. The English-speaker trap is writing the regular 싱겁어요 — that form does not exist. Like several taste words it has a figurative use: a person or a story can be 싱겁다, meaning 'anticlimactic, a let-down', as in 그 영화 결말 좀 싱거웠어 ('the ending was a bit flat').

Writing 싱겁어요; because it is ㅂ-irregular the correct form is 싱거워요.
Calling underseasoned food 담백하다 to be polite — 담백하다 is praise, but if it truly lacks salt the honest word is 싱겁다.
Saying '이 국을 싱거워요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 싱거워요.

김 = steam; you often warn 뜨거우니까 김 조심하세요
adverb 뜨겁게 + 데우다 (warm up)
figurative: intense passion or public attention

examples.en: The coffee is still hot.
examples.note: everyday; 아직 = still

examples.ko: 방금 끓여서 국이 너무 뜨거워요, 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: banggeum kkeuryeoseo gugi neomu tteugeowoyo, josimhaseyo.
examples.en: I just boiled it, so the soup is very hot — be careful.
examples.note: -아서 cause + warning 조심하세요

examples.ko: 뜨거운 거 못 드시면 조금 식혀서 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: tteugeoun geo mot deusimyeon jogeum sikyeoseo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: If you can't handle hot things, I'll let it cool a bit before serving.
examples.note: service register: 드시다/드리다 honorifics with 식히다

extendedVocab.nuance: 뜨겁다 describes high temperature you feel by touch or in the mouth — hot soup, hot coffee — and the crucial contrast for English speakers is 뜨겁다 vs 맵다: English 'hot' covers both temperature and spice, but Korean splits them, so a fiery chili dish is 맵다 (spicy), never 뜨겁다. Use 뜨겁다 only for heat. The hot thing takes 이/가 (커피가 뜨거워요). It is a ㅂ-irregular verb: 뜨겁 + 어요 → 뜨거워요, past 뜨거웠어요, modifier 뜨거운 (뜨거운 물), but formal 뜨겁습니다 keeps the ㅂ. Avoid the made-up form 뜨겁어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 뜨겁다 for spicy food because English says 'hot' — spicy is 맵다; 뜨겁다 is only temperature.
Writing 뜨겁어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 뜨거워요.
Confusing 뜨겁다 (burning hot) with 따뜻하다 (comfortably warm) — they differ by intensity.

figurative: emotionally distant, unfriendly

examples.note: basic; 정말 emphasizes

Writing 차갑어요; the ㅂ-irregular polite form is 차가워요.

vivid idiom: 입에서 살살 녹아요 (melts in your mouth)

figurative: easygoing, mild-tempered

The contrast you need is 부드럽다 vs 말랑하다: 부드럽다 is broad and refined (smooth, mellow, gentle), while 말랑하다 specifically means squishy-springy to the touch like a marshmallow or 말랑한 젤리; for tender, melt-in-the-mouth food Koreans prefer 부드럽다. The soft thing takes 이/가 (빵이 부드러워요). It is ㅂ-irregular: 부드럽 + 어요 → 부드러워요, past 부드러웠어요, modifier 부드러운, but formal 부드럽습니다 keeps ㅂ. A useful opposite is 딱딱하다 (hard, stiff). Note the strong figurative range: 부드러운 사람 (a gentle person), 부드러운 말투 (a soft tone) — unlike English 'soft', this is a compliment about character, not weakness. Avoid the invalid form 부드럽어요.

Writing 부드럽어요; as a ㅂ-irregular it becomes 부드러워요.

Saying '이 빵을 부드러워요' — the food is the subject: 이 빵이 부드러워요.

examples.ko: 회의 분위기가 너무 딱딱해서 농담 한마디 했어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui bunwigiga neomu ttakttakaeseo nongdam hanmadi haesseoyo.
examples.en: The meeting felt so stiff that I cracked a joke.
examples.note: figurative use about atmosphere

extendedVocab.nuance: 딱딱하다 describes a stiff, unyielding hardness — stale bread, a hard chair, frozen-solid food. The contrast to know is 딱딱하다 vs 질기다: 딱딱하다 means rigid and crunchy-hard (it cracks), while 질기다 means tough and chewy (it stretches and resists your teeth, like overcooked squid or gristly meat) — beginners often say 딱딱하다 when they mean 질기다. As a description the hard thing takes 이/가 (과자가 딱딱해요). It follows the regular 하다 pattern: 딱딱하 + 여요 → 딱딱해요, past 딱딱했어요, modifier 딱딱한, formal 딱딱합니다. The opposite for food is 부드럽다. Figuratively 딱딱하다 means stiff or overly formal — 딱딱한 분위기 (a stiff atmosphere), 딱딱한 사람 (an inflexible person) — and the onomatopoeic doubling 딱딱 gives it that hard, knocking feel. Avoid the form 딱딱하요 (the 하다 ending is 해요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 딱딱하요; 하다-verbs end in 해요, so it is 딱딱해요.
Using 딱딱하다 for chewy/tough food — that is 질기다; 딱딱하다 is rigid and crunchy.
Saying '이 떡을 딱딱해요' — the food is the subject: 이 떡이 딱딱해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 신선하다 means "to be fresh" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 신선하다 (sinseonhada) = "to be fresh". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 신선한 재료 ("fresh ingredients") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 신선하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 재료 = ingredients; a staple cooking/marketing phrase
신선도 (freshness level, 度 = degree) is the measurable noun
adverb 신선하게 + 보관하다 (store)
figurative: a pleasantly surprising, novel impression

examples.en: This milk is fresh.
examples.note: basic; product freshness

examples.en: It came in this morning, so the fish is fresh.
examples.note: -아서 cause; market situation

examples.ko: 발상이 정말 신선하네요, 그런 생각은 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: balsangi jeongmal sinseonhaneyo, geureon saenggageun mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: What a fresh idea — I'd never have thought of that.
examples.note: figurative 신선하다 about ideas, with -네요 admiration

extendedVocab.nuance: 신선하다 is Sino-Korean from 新鮮 (新 'new' + 鮮 'fresh/clear'), and it means newly harvested, just-caught, not spoiled — most at home with produce, seafood, and dairy. The contrast to master is 신선하다 vs 싱싱하다: 신선하다 is the broad, slightly formal word (also used figuratively for ideas), while 싱싱하다 is the lively, native-Korean word that specifically evokes plump, vibrant, still-alive freshness — a fish flapping at the market is 싱싱하다 more than 신선하다. The fresh thing takes 이/가 (생선이 신선해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 신선해요, past 신선했어요, modifier 신선한, formal 신선합니다. The big English-speaker pitfall: 'fresh' in English also means cheeky/impertinent and cool weather — neither transfers; Korean 신선하다 is purely about freshness/novelty. For a refreshing breeze use 시원하다 instead. Figuratively 신선한 충격 means a pleasantly novel surprise.

Using 신선하다 to mean cheeky or to mean cool weather as English 'fresh' can — those senses don't exist in Korean.
Saying 신선하요; the 하다 ending is 해요, so it is 신선해요.
Choosing 신선하다 when you want the vivid 'plump and lively' image of market seafood — that's 싱싱하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 고소하다 means "to be nutty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 고소하다 (gosohada) means "to be nutty". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고소한 맛 ("a nutty, roasted flavor"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고소하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the core descriptor for sesame/nut taste
고소하다 describes aroma as well as taste
adverb 고소하게 + 볶다 (stir-fry/roast)
figurative slang: smug pleasure at someone's misfortune

examples.en: This bread has a nutty flavor.
examples.note: basic; 맛이 나다 for 'taste comes out'

examples.en: I drizzled a little sesame oil, so it's even nuttier.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 참기름 is the prototypical 고소한 oil

examples.en: It was kind of satisfying to see that annoying person get scolded.
examples.note: figurative/slang 고소하다 = schadenfreude, with -더라

extendedVocab.nuance: 고소하다 names a flavor English barely has a single word for: the warm, toasty, savory taste/aroma of roasted sesame, peanuts, perilla, nuts, and grains — think 참기름, 들기름, 콩가루. The contrast to learn is 고소하다 vs 구수하다: 고소하다 is the bright, light roasted-sesame note, while 구수하다 is a deeper, earthier roasted warmth (well-brewed 숭늉/누룽지, soybean paste 된장, barley tea) — they overlap but 구수하다 feels heartier and more rustic. There is no Sino-Korean root; it is native Korean. The tasty thing takes 이/가 (빵이 고소해요) or you say X에서 고소한 맛이 나다. Regular 하다 conjugation: 고소해요, past 고소했어요, modifier 고소한, formal 고소합니다. English-speaker pitfall: 'nutty' is only an approximation — do not restrict 고소하다 to literal nuts, and beware its common slang meaning 'serves you right / I'm secretly glad', a sense pure English 'nutty' never carries.

Limiting 고소하다 to literal nuts — it covers roasted sesame, oils, and grains, and even describes a savory aroma.
Saying 고소하요; as a 하다-adjective it is 고소해요.
Missing the slang sense: 고소하다 can mean smug satisfaction at someone's misfortune, not just flavor.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 느끼하다 means "to be greasy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be greasy" is 느끼하다 (neukkihada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 느끼한 음식 ("greasy/heavy food"). Watch the particle attached to 느끼하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the default modifier; fried or fatty dishes
속 (stomach) + 느끼하다: the heavy, sickly feeling
느끼함 (the greasiness) + 잡다; e.g. 김치가 느끼함을 잡아줘요
figurative: an over-the-top flirty or corny remark

examples.en: This pizza is a bit greasy.
examples.note: basic; 좀 softens the complaint

examples.ko: 기름진 고기를 많이 먹어서 속이 느끼해요.
examples.romanization: gireumjin gogireul mani meogeoseo sogi neukkihaeyo.
examples.en: I ate a lot of fatty meat, so I feel queasy.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 속이 느끼하다 = stomach feels heavy

examples.ko: 그 사람 자꾸 느끼한 말 해서 좀 부담스러웠어요.
examples.romanization: geu saram jakku neukkihan mal haeseo jom budamseureowosseoyo.
examples.en: He kept saying cheesy lines, so it felt a bit much.
examples.note: figurative 느끼하다 = corny/cringey, with 부담스럽다

extendedVocab.nuance: 느끼하다 describes the heavy, oily, cloying feeling of fatty food — pizza, cream pasta, deep-fried meat — and crucially also the queasy after-feeling in your stomach (속이 느끼하다). The contrast to fix is 느끼하다 vs 기름지다: 기름지다 neutrally states a dish is oily/rich (it can even be appetizing), while 느끼하다 carries the negative 'too rich, makes me want something to cut it' nuance — that's why Koreans say 느끼할 때 김치/콜라가 필요해. Its opposite is 담백하다 (cleanly light). The greasy thing takes 이/가 (피자가 느끼해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 느끼해요, past 느끼했어요, modifier 느끼한, formal 느끼합니다. Big English-speaker pitfall: 'greasy' is only half the meaning — 느끼하다 is also the standard way to call a person or their words 'cheesy / corny / smarmy' (느끼한 멘트, 느끼한 남자), so a slick flirt is 느끼하다, which surprises learners expecting only a food word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 느끼하다 as neutral 'oily' — for plain richness use 기름지다; 느끼하다 implies it's unpleasantly heavy.
Missing the figurative sense: 느끼한 멘트/남자 means cheesy or smarmy, a very common usage.
Saying 느끼하요; the 하다 form is 느끼해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 담백하다 means "to be light" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 담백하다 (dambaekada) = "to be light". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 담백한 맛 ("a clean, mild flavor") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 담백하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the praise phrase for non-greasy taste
기름기 (oiliness) + 없다; what makes food 담백하다
adverb 담백하게 + 조리하다 (cook/prepare)
figurative: plain-spoken, without affectation

examples.en: This tofu dish is light and clean.
examples.note: basic praise for mild food

examples.en: It's made without oil, so it's light and clean-tasting.
examples.note: -아서 cause; 담백하다 + 깔끔하다 pairing

examples.ko: 그 배우는 인터뷰에서 늘 담백하게 말해서 호감이에요.
examples.romanization: geu baeuneun inteobyueseo neul dambaekage malhaeseo hogamieyo.
examples.en: That actor always speaks plainly in interviews, which makes him likeable.
examples.note: figurative 담백하다 about a frank manner

extendedVocab.nuance: 담백하다 is Sino-Korean from 淡白 (淡 'thin/light in taste' + 白 'plain/white'), and it is the praise-word for food that tastes clean and mild without grease or heavy seasoning — white fish, tofu, chicken breast, clear broth. It is the deliberate opposite of 느끼하다 (cloyingly greasy). The contrast to master is 담백하다 vs 싱겁다: both describe non-strong flavor, but 담백하다 is a compliment ('refreshingly clean, light'), while 싱겁다 is a complaint ('underseasoned, needs salt') — so call good light food 담백하다, never 싱겁다. The food takes 이/가 (두부 요리가 담백해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 담백해요, past 담백했어요, modifier 담백한, formal 담백합니다. English-speaker pitfall: do not translate with plain 'light' as in low-calorie or pale-colored — 담백하다 is specifically about a clean, non-greasy taste. Figuratively it also praises a frank, unpretentious personality (담백한 사람).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 담백하다 (praise: clean and light) with 싱겁다 (complaint: underseasoned) — they are not interchangeable.
Translating 담백하다 as 'light' in the sense of low-calorie or pale — it means clean, non-greasy taste.
Saying 담백하요; the 하다 form is 담백해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매우 means "very" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 매우 (maeu) means "very". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 매우 좋아요. ("It is very good."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 매우 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sits directly in front of the adjective it boosts
Pairs naturally with formal 합니다-style endings

usagePhrases.en: It is a very important issue.
usagePhrases.note: Modifying an adjective inside a noun phrase (중요한)
Can boost an adverb like 빠르게, not only adjectives

examples.en: This book is very difficult.
examples.note: Basic: 매우 placed right before the adjective stem

examples.en: I was very disappointed with the meeting result.
examples.note: Everyday-formal: pairs with 합니다체 in a work setting

examples.ko: 조사 결과 안전성이 매우 높은 것으로 나타났습니다.
examples.romanization: josa gyeolgwa anjeonseongi maeu nopeun geoseuro natanatseumnida.
examples.en: The survey showed the safety level to be very high.
examples.note: Real situation: 매우 in a report/news register where 진짜 would feel wrong

extendedVocab.nuance: 매우 means 'very/highly' and signals a high degree, but it lives mostly in the written and formal-spoken register — reports, news, lectures, business email — so a Korean rarely blurts 매우 to a friend. Its nearest neighbors are 정말 and 너무: 정말 carries personal sincerity/surprise ('I really mean it'), 너무 originally meant 'excessively/too much' and now also means 'so' in casual speech, while 매우 is the cool, objective booster with no emotional color. It habitually pairs with 합니다-style endings and abstract adjectives (매우 중요하다, 매우 높다, 매우 만족하다). The English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for 매우 in chat because the textbook glossed it first, which sounds stiff and bookish — like writing 'most assuredly' to a buddy. Also, like all degree adverbs it goes BEFORE the word it modifies (매우 좋다), never after the verb the way English can append 'a lot'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 매우 to a close friend in casual chat — it sounds textbook-stiff; use 정말 or 진짜 instead (정말 좋아 / 진짜 좋아, not 매우 좋아).
Placing it after the predicate as in '좋아요 매우' by analogy with English 'good, very much'; Korean degree adverbs must precede the adjective: 매우 좋아요.
Using 매우 with a verb of quantity to mean 'a lot' (e.g. 매우 먹었어요 for 'ate a lot'); for amount use 많이, and reserve 매우 for adjectives/states.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정말 means "really" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "really" is 정말 (jeongmal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정말 맛있어요. ("It is really delicious."). Watch the particle attached to 정말 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Boosting an adjective with genuine feeling
Adds heartfelt sincerity to 고맙다
As a one-word reaction expressing surprise
Strengthens an apology to sound earnest

examples.en: I am really happy today.
examples.note: Basic: 정말 conveys 'I sincerely feel this'

examples.en: That movie was really sad.
examples.note: Everyday: spoken reaction to a shared experience

examples.en: Thank you so very much for coming despite being busy.
examples.note: Real situation: 정말 + 감사합니다 layers warmth onto a formal thank-you

extendedVocab.nuance: 정말 comes from the Sino-Korean 正(정, correct/true)+ 말(speech) — literally 'true words' — so at its core it asserts truth and sincerity, which is why it feels heartfelt rather than merely intensifying. Contrast with 진짜 ('real thing', 眞), which is the casual street twin and can sound slightly more exclamatory or skeptical; and with 너무, which stresses sheer degree ('so/too') without the truth-claim. So 정말 좋아요 = 'I genuinely like it' while 너무 좋아요 = 'I like it SO much.' It is the safe all-register intensifier — fine with both 해요체 and 합니다체 — and stacks beautifully on emotion words (정말 고맙다, 정말 미안하다, 정말 다행이다). As a standalone 정말? / 정말요? it means 'Really?!' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'really' is a one-size-fits-all booster, so learners pour 정말 into sentences that actually want 너무 for sheer degree (정말 추워요 just affirms 'it really is cold,' while 너무 추워요 conveys 'it's unbearably cold') — match the feeling, not just the word. A second trap is reaching for the punchier 진짜 in formal thanks or apologies where 정말 is the safer, more polished choice (정말 감사합니다, not 진짜 감사합니다 to a boss). Note the spelling: it is 정말, not 정말로 unless you deliberately add the adverbial -로 for extra emphasis.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 정말 where the emotion calls for 너무; 정말 just affirms truth ('it really is hot'), whereas 너무 더워요 carries the 'unbearably/so hot' intensity English speakers usually intend.
Saying 정말로 everywhere thinking it is the only correct form; bare 정말 is the normal adverb, and 정말로 is a heavier, more emphatic variant used sparingly.
Forcing English word order like '좋아요 정말'; place 정말 before the adjective or verb it intensifies: 정말 좋아요.

It is the safe all-register intensifier — fine with both 해요체 and 합니다체 — and stacks beautifully on emotion words (정말 고맙다, 정말 미안하다, 정말 다행이다). As a standalone 정말? / 정말요? it means 'Really?!'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 진짜 means "really" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 진짜 (jinjja) = "really". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 진짜 재미있어요. ("It is really fun.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 진짜, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Casual booster, very common among friends
One-word reaction of surprise or doubt
In 반말, questioning authenticity
Exclamation with the plain 다 ending

examples.en: This coffee is really hot.
examples.note: Basic: 진짜 before an adjective in friendly 해요체

examples.en: I was seriously so startled.
examples.note: Everyday 반말: 진짜 amps up a casual story

examples.ko: 그 가게 음식이 진짜 진짜 맛있어서 또 갔어.
examples.romanization: geu gage eumsigi jinjja jinjja masisseoseo tto gasseo.
examples.en: The food there was so so good that I went again.
examples.note: Real situation: doubling 진짜 for playful emphasis in speech

extendedVocab.nuance: 진짜 is built on the Sino-Korean 眞(진, true/genuine) + 짜 and literally names 'the real thing/genuine article,' so as a noun it means 'the real one' (가짜 = fake is its antonym) and as an adverb it became the everyday casual 'really.' Its near-twin is 정말 (正말, 'true words'): both mean 'really,' but 진짜 is more colloquial, more exclamatory, and slightly punchier, so friends and younger speakers prefer it, while 정말 sounds a touch more polished and works better in formal thanks/apologies. Compared with 너무 ('so/too'), 진짜 still leans on a truth-flavor ('I'm not kidding') rather than pure degree. It collocates with surprise and strong reactions (진짜 놀랐다, 진짜 대박, 진짜 좋다) and is frequently doubled (진짜 진짜) in speech. The English-speaker pitfall: because it sounds fun, learners drop it into formal writing, emails, or speeches where it reads as slangy — there, switch to 정말 or 매우. Also note 진짜 vs 가짜: as an adverb it is 'really,' but as a noun it is 'a real/authentic thing,' so 이거 진짜야? can mean either 'Is this for real?' or 'Is this genuine?' depending on context.

Using 진짜 in formal writing, business email, or a speech where it sounds slangy; replace with 정말 or 매우 in those registers.
Assuming 진짜 only intensifies; as a noun it means 'the genuine article' (opposite 가짜), so 진짜 명품 = 'an authentic luxury item,' not 'really luxury.'
Pronouncing or writing it 진자; the word is 진짜 with the tense ㅉ, and the spelling matters for being understood.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 잘 means "well" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 잘 (jal) means "well". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 잘 자요. ("Sleep well."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잘 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 잘 + verb describing the manner of an action
Fuses with 하다 to mean 'be good at'
잘 softens into 'not quite' when negated

usagePhrases.en: I look forward to working with you.
usagePhrases.note: Set greeting; literally 'please treat me well'

examples.en: That person sings well.
examples.note: Basic: 잘하다 = to be skilled at something

examples.en: I'm not good at exercising.
examples.note: Everyday: 잘 못하다 = 'cannot do well / be bad at'

examples.en: Sir, I'll be in your care from now on.
examples.note: Real situation: fixed humble greeting on joining a team

extendedVocab.nuance: 잘 means 'well/skillfully/properly,' and unlike English 'well' (which trails the verb: 'sleep well'), Korean 잘 sits directly BEFORE the verb: 잘 자다, 잘 먹다, 잘 하다. Its opposite pair is 못 ('cannot/poorly'), so 잘하다 vs 못하다 is the core skill axis. Watch the spacing rule, which trips everyone up: when it means 'be good at,' it fuses into one word 잘하다 (잘해요), but when it just modifies an action it stays separate 잘 자다, 잘 듣다. A near-synonym for the 'properly' sense is 제대로 ('correctly, as it should be'); 잘 is broader and warmer while 제대로 stresses 'done right, no shortcuts.' 잘 also has idiomatic softening uses: 잘 모르겠어요 isn't 'I know well-not' but a polite 'I'm not quite sure,' and 잘 부탁드립니다 ('please look after me well') is an essential set greeting. The English-speaker pitfall: do not put 잘 before an adjective — you cannot say 잘 예뻐요 for 'pretty well'; 잘 modifies verbs/actions, while degree on adjectives uses 매우/정말/너무. Also remember the negation splits: 잘 못해요 (separate) for ability, and the position of 못 right before the verb.

Placing 잘 before an adjective (예: 잘 예뻐요) to mean 'quite pretty'; 잘 only modifies verbs/actions — use 매우/정말 for adjectives.
Writing the skill meaning as two words (잘 해요) when you mean 'be good at'; that meaning is one word 잘하다 → 잘해요, while the manner meaning stays split (잘 듣다).
Copying English order and saying '자요 잘' for 'sleep well'; the adverb precedes the verb in Korean: 잘 자요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 더 means "more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "more" is 더 (deo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 더 주세요. ("Please give me more."). Watch the particle attached to 더 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 더 before a verb to request a greater amount
더 + adjective forms the comparative
Pairs with 조금 to soften the increase
Set phrase 더 이상 + negative = 'no longer'

examples.en: This bag is more expensive.
examples.note: Basic: 더 + adjective makes the comparison

examples.en: I want to eat a little more.
examples.note: Everyday: 조금 더 softens 'more' politely

examples.en: Today is much hotter than yesterday.
examples.note: Real situation: 보다 marks the standard, 훨씬 stacks before 더 for 'much more'

extendedVocab.nuance: 더 is the basic comparative marker meaning 'more,' and crucially Korean has no '-er/more...than' suffix — you simply put 더 before the adjective and (optionally) mark the standard of comparison with the particle 보다: A가 B보다 더 크다 = 'A is bigger than B.' Its direct antonym is 덜 ('less'). A common booster is 훨씬 ('by far, much'), which stacks in front: 훨씬 더 좋다 = 'much better.' Watch two set phrases: 더 이상 + negative = 'no longer / not anymore' (더 이상 못 참아 = 'I can't take it anymore'), and 더 ~ -ㄹ수록 patterns for 'the more...'. The English-speaker pitfall: learners often drop 더 entirely because they expect the adjective itself to change form ('big' → 'bigger'), but 크다 never inflects for comparison — without 더 the sentence just says 'is big,' not 'is bigger.' Another trap is the 보다 direction: 보다 attaches to the thing you compare AGAINST (the 'than' item), so '내가 너보다 커' = 'I'm taller than you,' which feels backwards to English ears. Also don't confuse spoken 더 with the homophone-ish 덜; they are opposites.

Omitting 더 and expecting the adjective to inflect like English 'bigger'; 크다 doesn't change form — you must add 더: 더 커요.
Attaching 보다 to the wrong noun; 보다 marks the standard you compare against ('than X'), so put it on X: 사과가 배보다 더 싸요 = 'apples are cheaper than pears.'
Confusing 더 (more) with 덜 (less) in fast speech; they are exact opposites, so 덜 비싸요 = 'less expensive,' the reverse of 더 비싸요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 덜 means "less" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 덜 (deol) = "less". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 덜 매워요. ("It is less spicy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 덜, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 덜 + adjective lowers the degree
덜 + 익다 means 'not fully cooked/ripe'

usagePhrases.en: I'm tired because I slept less.
usagePhrases.note: 덜 + verb reduces the amount of an action

usagePhrases.en: It barely went down, only a little less.
usagePhrases.note: Contrasts a partial decrease

examples.en: Today is less hot than yesterday.
examples.note: Basic: 덜 + adjective with 보다 for the standard

examples.en: The meat isn't cooked through yet.
examples.note: Everyday: 덜 익다 = 'underdone,' a key cooking phrase

examples.en: It was nice because it was less crowded than on weekdays.
examples.note: Real situation: 덜 lowers the verb 붐비다 with a 보다 comparison

extendedVocab.nuance: 덜 means 'less / not fully / to a smaller degree,' and it is the exact mirror image of 더 ('more'): wherever you could add 더 to raise the degree, 덜 lowers it (덜 비싸다 = 'less expensive'). Beyond pure comparison it carries a very useful 'not all the way / incompletely' sense that English splits into different words: 덜 익다 = 'underdone/unripe,' 덜 마르다 = 'not fully dry,' 덜 깨다 = 'still half-asleep.' Contrast it with the flat negation 안 ('not at all') and with 별로 ('not particularly'): 덜 좋다 still means it IS somewhat good, just less so, whereas 안 좋다 means 'not good.' Like other degree adverbs it stands before the adjective or verb (덜 자다, 덜 짜다). The English-speaker pitfall: learners try to translate 'less' with 적게 ('in small quantity') for everything, but 적게 is about countable/measurable amount of an action (소금을 적게 넣다 = 'add little salt'), while 덜 scales the degree or completeness (덜 짜게 = 'less salty'). Also do not mix up 덜 with 더 in listening — one syllable flips the meaning entirely. Note: with a negative, 덜 안 ... is unusual; 덜 already lowers, so you rarely negate it.

Using 적게 ('a small amount') where degree is meant; for 'less spicy' say 덜 맵게, not 적게 맵게 — 적게 is for quantity of an action (적게 먹다 = eat little).
Reading 덜 익다 as 'cooked less' = 'cooked a bit'; it actually means 'undercooked / not done yet,' a warning that the food isn't ready.
