extendedVocab.explanation: 가장 (gajang) means "most". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가장 좋아요. ("It is the best."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 가장 + adjective forms the superlative
Modifying an adjective inside a noun phrase

usagePhrases.en: the highest mountain in the world
usagePhrases.note: 가장 with 에서 marking the field of comparison
가장 can mark 'most/first' with adverbs too

examples.en: This mountain is the highest.
examples.note: Basic: pick one out of many with 가장

examples.ko: 저는 사계절 중에 봄을 가장 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun sagyejeol junge bomeul gajang joahaeyo.
examples.en: Of the four seasons, I like spring the most.
examples.note: Everyday: 중에 ('among') sets the group 가장 selects from

examples.en: It is the most trusted product in our company.
examples.note: Real situation: 가장 in a formal/written superlative claim

extendedVocab.nuance: 가장 marks the superlative — 'the most / -est' — singling out the top item from a group of three or more (이 중에서 가장 = 'the most among these'). It is the slightly more formal, written-leaning twin of 제일 (which comes from Sino-Korean 第一, 'number one'); the meaning is identical, but 가장 sounds a touch more refined and is preferred in writing, signage, and careful speech, while 제일 is the everyday spoken default. Both stand before the adjective (가장 크다 / 제일 크다). To name the field you compare within, Korean uses 중에(서) ('among') or 에서 ('in'): 셋 중에 가장, 세계에서 가장. The English-speaker pitfall is using a superlative for only two items: English loosely says 'the best of the two,' but Korean superlatives 가장/제일 want three-plus; for exactly two, prefer the comparative 더 ('A가 B보다 더 좋다'). A second trap is forgetting that 가장 modifies the adjective, not the noun, so 'the highest mountain' is 가장 높은 산 (가장 → 높은), never 가장 산. Also note 가장 is unrelated to the homograph 가장(假裝, 'pretense/disguise'); context and usually a following adjective disambiguate.

Attaching 가장 to the noun instead of the adjective; 'the tallest building' is 가장 높은 건물, with 가장 modifying 높은, not 가장 건물.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 제일 means "most" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "most" is 제일 (jeil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 제일 좋아요. ("It is the best."). Watch the particle attached to 제일 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Casual everyday superlative
제일 + 좋아하다 in a relative clause

제일 used like a noun: 'the number one'

examples.en: I like summer the most.
examples.note: Basic: 제일 + 좋아하다 for a favorite

examples.en: I'm the tallest in our class.
examples.note: Everyday: 에서 sets the group 제일 selects from

examples.en: Say what you will, health is what matters most.
examples.note: Real situation: idiomatic 제일이다 = 'is the top priority'

extendedVocab.nuance: 제일 means 'the most / number one' and is the casual, high-frequency spoken twin of 가장. It is Sino-Korean 第一 — literally 'order-one,' i.e. 'first/foremost' — which is why besides modifying adjectives (제일 크다) it can also stand alone like a noun meaning 'the best/top': 건강이 제일이다 = 'health comes first,' 네가 제일이야 = 'you're number one.' 가장 is its near-perfect synonym for the adverb use, the difference being register only: 제일 dominates everyday conversation while 가장 feels a bit more formal/written. Both pick the top of a group of three or more, with the field marked by 중에/에서. The English-speaker pitfall: as with 가장, don't use a superlative for just two items (use 더 instead), and don't glue 제일 onto the noun — 'the cheapest restaurant' is 제일 싼 식당, with 제일 modifying 싼. A further nuance learners miss: because 제일 can be nominal (第一 = 'the first/best'), set expressions like 제일이다 and 제일가다 ('to be foremost') exist, so 그게 제일이야 = 'that's the best option,' not literally 'that is most.' Keep 제일 for talk and texts; switch to 가장 in essays, reports, and formal announcements.

가장 is its near-perfect synonym for the adverb use, the difference being register only: 제일 dominates everyday conversation while 가장 feels a bit more formal/written. Keep 제일 for talk and texts; switch to 가장 in essays, reports, and formal announcements.
It is Sino-Korean 第一 — literally 'order-one,' i.e. 'first/foremost' — which is why it can be nominal as well as adverbial (第一 = 'the first/best').
As with 가장, don't use a superlative for just two items (use 더 instead), and don't glue 제일 onto the noun — 'the cheapest restaurant' is 제일 싼 식당, with 제일 modifying 싼.

extendedVocab.explanation: 별로 (byeollo) = "not really". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 별로 안 좋아요. ("It is not really good.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 별로, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 별로 must be answered by a negative later
별로 + 안 + adjective softens the negation
Standalone lukewarm verdict

usagePhrases.note: Pairs with the -지 않다 negative

examples.en: That movie wasn't really fun.

examples.note: Everyday: 별로 + 안 softens the cold

examples.note: Real situation: 별로이다 as a polite way to say 'underwhelming'

extendedVocab.nuance: 별로 means 'not particularly / not really,' a soft, hedged negative, and its defining grammatical rule is that it MUST be completed by a negative form somewhere in the clause — 별로 안 ~, 별로 ~지 않다, or an inherently negative word like 재미없다/모르다. So 별로 좋아요 is ungrammatical; it has to be 별로 안 좋아요. It descends from Sino-Korean 別(별, 'separate/special') + 로, roughly 'in a special way,' which in the negative frame became 'not especially.' The standalone 별로예요/별로였어요 is an extremely common, face-saving way to say something was 'meh, nothing special' without being harshly critical. Contrast it with 전혀 ('not at all'), which is total denial, versus 별로 which is partial/mild ('not so much'); and with 그다지, a more formal/literary synonym of 별로 that follows the same negative-required rule. The big English-speaker pitfall is positive use: learners say 별로 좋아요 thinking 'pretty good,' but 별로 only points downward and needs a negative — 'pretty good' would be 꽤 좋아요 or 제법 좋아요. extendedVocab.explanation: 거의 (geoui) means "almost". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 거의 다 왔어요. ("We've almost arrived."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 거의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 거의 + 다 = 'almost all the way'
거의 before a verb marking near-completion
거의 + negative = 'almost never / hardly'
거의 before a time/frequency word

examples.en: I've almost finished the homework.
examples.note: Basic: 거의 다 = 'nearly all done'

examples.en: I hardly ever watch TV.
examples.note: Everyday: 거의 + 안 = 'almost never'

examples.ko: 공사가 거의 마무리되어 다음 주에 문을 엽니다.

examples.en: Construction is nearly wrapped up, so it opens next week.
examples.note: Real situation: 거의 with a verb in an announcement register

extendedVocab.nuance: 거의 means 'almost / nearly / practically,' marking that something falls just short of 100% (거의 다 = 'almost all'). Its standout feature for learners is the flip with negatives: 거의 + 안/없다 doesn't mean 'almost not' but renders English 'hardly / scarcely / almost never' — 거의 안 자요 = 'I barely sleep,' 거의 없어요 = 'there's hardly any.' A close synonym is 대부분 ('mostly, for the most part'), but 대부분 is more about the majority portion of a group while 거의 is about proximity to a full degree or completion; and 약 / 대략 ('approximately') are for rounding numbers, whereas 거의 says 'not quite reaching.' It collocates heavily with 다 (거의 다 됐어요), with completion verbs (거의 끝나다, 거의 도착하다), and with frequency words (거의 매일/매번). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 거의 for an exact figure — 'almost exactly 3 o'clock' isn't 거의 세 시 정각; for 'about/approximately' a number, use 약/대략 or '거의 ~ 가까이.' Another trap is forgetting that 거의 안 = 'hardly,' so beginners read 거의 안 봐요 as 'almost watch' when it means 'barely watch.' Place 거의 before the verb, adverb, or quantity it scopes (거의 한 시간, 거의 다 왔다).

usagePhrases.note: 전혀 demands a negative ending

usagePhrases.en: I had no idea at all.

extendedVocab.nuance: 전혀 means 'not at all / not in the slightest,' the strongest, most absolute negative degree adverb, and like 별로 it is grammatically bound to a negative — 전혀 안 ~, 전혀 ~지 않다, 전혀 없다, 전혀 아니다. It comes from Sino-Korean 全(전, 'whole/entire'), so the image is 'wholly (not),' i.e. zero across the board. The key contrast is intensity: 전혀 = 0% (total denial) while 별로 = 'not so much' (partial), and 그다지 sits with 별로 as a milder 'not particularly'; so 전혀 안 좋아요 = 'not good at ALL' versus 별로 안 좋아요 = 'not that good.' It collocates with 모르다, 없다, 아니다, 상관없다 and reassurances (전혀 안 아파요, 전혀 문제없어요). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 전혀 in a positive sentence — you cannot say 전혀 좋아요 for 'totally good'; 전혀 only points to zero and needs a negative. Note that in casual modern speech some younger speakers jokingly attach 전혀 to a positive ('전혀 괜찮아 = totally fine'), but this is colloquial and best avoided by learners. Also keep it before the predicate, and don't confuse 전혀 with 전부 (全部, 'all/everything'), which is the positive 'entirely.'

extendedVocab.explanation: 아마 (ama) = "probably". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아마 올 거예요. ("They'll probably come.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아마, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 아마 pairs with the -ㄹ 거예요 guess ending
아마도 is a slightly softer/heavier variant
아마 with the casual conjecture -ㄹ걸요
아마 over a negated guess

examples.en: That person is probably a student.
examples.note: Basic: 아마 + 일 거예요 (noun guess)

examples.ko: 내일은 아마 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: naeireun ama biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow, I think.
examples.note: Everyday: 아마 reinforced by -ㄹ 것 같다

examples.en: Even if we leave now, we'll probably be late.
examples.note: Real situation: 아마 framing a resigned prediction

extendedVocab.nuance: 아마 means 'probably / perhaps,' expressing the speaker's reasonable guess, and its grammar is almost inseparable: it is normally completed by a conjecture ending — most often -ㄹ/을 거예요 ('will probably'), or -ㄹ 것 같다, -겠-, -ㄹ걸요. The bare statement 아마 비가 와요 sounds unfinished; you want 아마 비가 올 거예요. A near-synonym is 아마도, which is just a softer, slightly more deliberative version of 아마 (interchangeable; 아마도 can feel a touch more written or musing). Distinguish the certainty scale: 아마 is a fairly confident guess (~maybe 70-80%), 어쩌면/혹시 lean toward 'possibly, by any chance' (lower, more tentative), and 분명히/틀림없이 mean 'surely/definitely' (high certainty). The English-speaker pitfall is using 아마 with a flat present/past as if it were the English adverb that can float anywhere ('he's probably home'): in Korean the verb itself must carry the guessing form, so 'he's probably home' = 아마 집에 있을 거예요, not 아마 집에 있어요. Also avoid 아마 with established facts — 아마 물은 H2O일 거예요 sounds odd because you're hedging a certainty. Place 아마 near the front of the clause, and let the sentence-final ending do the conjecture work.

Pairing 아마 with a plain present/past tense; the predicate must take a guess ending — 아마 올 거예요, not 아마 와요, for 'will probably come.'
Using 아마 about a known fact or certainty; for 'definitely/surely' switch to 분명히/틀림없이, e.g. 분명히 맞아요, since 아마 hedges.
Confusing 아마 ('probably,' fairly confident) with 혹시/어쩌면 ('possibly, by any chance,' tentative); 혹시 시간 있어요? = 'do you by any chance have time?', a softer probe than a 아마 prediction.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 같다 means "to be the same" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 같다 (gatda) means "to be the same". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N하고 같다 ("to be the same as N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 같다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to be the same as N
usagePhrases.note: 하고 = casual 'with/as'; 와/과 is the written equivalent

usagePhrases.en: to seem like N / to be like N
usagePhrases.note: no 하고 here — this means 'resembles', a different sense
똑 intensifies 같다 to 'identical'
lit. 'hearts are the same'

examples.en: Our bags are the same.
examples.note: subject takes 이/가; the two items being equated

examples.en: We're the same age.
examples.note: the compared-to person takes 하고, the matching trait takes 가

examples.en: Your thinking is exactly like mine, so I was startled.
examples.note: real reaction; 랑 = casual 하고, 똑같다 raises the emphasis

extendedVocab.nuance: 같다 says two or more things match or are identical — 'A and B are the same'. To compare, the yardstick noun takes 하고/와·과 and the matching trait takes 이/가: 저하고 키가 같아요 ('our height is the same as mine'). Watch the sharp split from 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 means literally no difference, while 비슷하다 allows a gap — friends who 'look alike but aren't twins' are 비슷하다, not 같다. A second trap is the homophone-feeling N 같다 ('seems like N', as in 학생 같아요 'seems to be a student'), which drops 하고 and shifts meaning entirely; 같이 (together / -like) shares the root but is an adverb. English speakers also over-apply 'the same as' with 처럼 — but 처럼 means 'like/as', not 'identical', so keep 같다 for true equality.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 같다 for things that merely resemble each other — for 'similar but not identical' use 비슷하다; 같다 claims zero difference.
Dropping the particle: native Korean is 'A하고 B가 같아요', not 'A B 같아요'. The yardstick needs 하고/와, the trait needs 이/가.
Confusing 같아요 ('is the same') with N 같아요 ('seems like N') — 학생 같아요 means 'seems to be a student', not 'is the same as a student'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 다르다 is the antonym of 같다 and conjugates as a 르-irregular: the stem 다르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ and drops 으 to give 달라요 (never 다라요); past is 달랐어요. The pre-noun form 다른 is one of the most-used words in Korean and covers both 'different' and 'another' (다른 색 = 'a different/another colour'). The dangerous trap for English speakers is 틀리다, which means 'to be wrong / incorrect' — even native speakers loosely say 틀리다 for 'different' in speech, but in correct Korean 답이 틀리다 = 'the answer is wrong' while 답이 다르다 = 'the answer is different'. Mixing them can imply someone is mistaken when you only meant they differ, which can sound rude. Pair 다르다 with 하고/와 for the thing compared: 작년하고 달라요 ('it's different from last year').

Conjugating it as 다라요 — it's a 르-irregular, so the correct present form is 달라요 (and past 달랐어요).
Forgetting the comparison particle: say '이거하고 달라요', not '이거 달라요'.

Mixing them can imply someone is mistaken when you only meant they differ, which can sound rude.

extendedVocab.english: to be exactly the same / identical
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 똑같다 means "to be exactly the same / identical" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 똑같다 (ttokgatda) = "to be exactly the same / identical". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: N하고 똑같다 ("to be identical to N") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 똑같다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하고 marks the thing compared
pre-noun form, e.g. 똑같은 옷 'identical clothes'
adverb — handy for ordering or copying
맨날 'every day' adds a fed-up nuance

examples.en: It's exactly the same as this one.
examples.note: pointing while comparing; 하고 on the reference item

examples.en: The two have identical faces.
examples.note: 둘이 = 'the two of them'; said of twins/look-alikes

examples.en: Give me exactly the same as the person ahead of me.
examples.note: real café line; adverb 똑같이 directs the action

extendedVocab.nuance: 똑같다 is the emphatic cousin of 같다: the prefix-like 똑 (a mimetic 'precisely / spot-on') pushes 'the same' all the way to 'identical, no difference whatsoever'. Where 같다 can be a calm statement of equality, 똑같다 adds feeling — surprise at a resemblance, or, with words like 맨날 ('every day'), boredom that nothing changes. It dominates everyday speech far more than its formal feel suggests. The adverb 똑같이 ('identically / the same way') is genuinely useful for service situations ('make mine 똑같이'). Beware the same particle trap as 같다: the reference noun needs 하고/와, so 저거하고 똑같아요, not 저거 똑같아요. And don't reach for 똑같다 when things are only roughly alike — that gap is 비슷하다 territory; 똑같다 insists they are indistinguishable.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 똑같다 when things are merely similar — 똑같다 claims they are indistinguishable, so for 'kind of alike' use 비슷하다.
Dropping the particle: say '저거하고 똑같아요', not '저거 똑같아요' — the compared item takes 하고/와.
Forgetting the adverb form when modifying a verb: to copy an action say '똑같이 하세요', not '똑같다 하세요'.

extendedVocab.explanation: 아름답다 (areumdapda) means "to be beautiful". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 아름다운 N ("a beautiful N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 아름답다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular pre-noun form, e.g. 아름다운 풍경
adverb form, e.g. 아름답게 꾸미다 'decorate beautifully'
praises inner character, not looks
참 'truly' gives a soft, admiring tone

examples.en: The sea is beautiful.
examples.note: scenery is the prototypical subject; note ㅂ-irregular 아름다워요

examples.en: It's a beautiful song.
examples.note: pre-noun 아름다운 before the noun

examples.ko: 노을이 너무 아름다워서 한참 서 있었어요.
examples.romanization: noeuri neomu areumdawoseo hancham seo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The sunset was so beautiful I stood there a long while.
examples.note: real moment; 아서 links beauty to the resulting action

extendedVocab.nuance: 아름답다 is the 'proper', somewhat literary word for beautiful, reserved most often for scenery, nature, music, art, a person's heart, or a moving moment rather than everyday cuteness. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the final ㅂ turns to 우 before a vowel, giving 아름다워요 / 아름다운 / 아름다워서 (never 아름답어요). The key boundary for learners is 예쁘다: in casual speech, a pretty face, a cute café, or a nice dress is 예쁘다, while 아름답다 sounds more elevated and emotional — calling a snack 아름답다 sounds odd, but a mountain view is 아름답다. 예쁘다 leans 'pretty/cute', 아름답다 leans 'beautiful/sublime'. Note also 곱다 (refined, graceful beauty, often of older speech), which is gentler and more old-fashioned. Use 아름답다 to admire the grand or heartfelt, and don't force it onto small, cute, or tasty things.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it regularly as '아름답어요' — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the form is '아름다워요' (pre-noun 아름다운).
Using 아름답다 for food or small cute objects; 예쁘다 ('pretty/cute') or 맛있다 ('tasty') fits those, while 아름답다 suits scenery, art, and heartfelt beauty.
Saying 아름답은 N for the pre-noun form — the ㅂ-irregular gives 아름다운 N.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 훌륭하다 means "to be excellent / splendid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be excellent / splendid" is 훌륭하다 (hullyunghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 훌륭한 N ("an excellent N"). Watch the particle attached to 훌륭하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 훌륭한 작품 'an excellent work'
adverb, e.g. 훌륭하게 해내다 'pull it off splendidly'
common praise of a person's integrity
참 adds warm, sincere praise

examples.en: The food is truly excellent.
examples.note: praising a meal a notch above 맛있어요

examples.en: She's an excellent teacher.
examples.note: pre-noun form praising ability and character

examples.en: You've grown up so admirably for your age.
examples.note: real compliment to a young person; adverb 훌륭하게

extendedVocab.nuance: 훌륭하다 is high, somewhat formal praise for quality, ability, or moral character — 'excellent, admirable, fine, splendid'. It sits clearly above 좋다 ('good'): 좋다 is everyday and broad, while 훌륭하다 implies something genuinely impressive and worthy of respect, so it shines in reviews, classrooms, and sincere compliments about work, skill, or a person's integrity (인격이 훌륭하다). Compare it with 대단하다: 대단하다 is a hot, spoken 'wow, impressive!' reaction to an achievement, whereas 훌륭하다 is a calmer, more considered verdict on worth — a child's drawing earns 대단하다 in the moment but a master's life work earns 훌륭하다. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates regularly (훌륭해요 / 훌륭했어요) and, being descriptive, takes the pre-noun -ㄴ: 훌륭한 사람, never 훌륭하는 사람. Don't sprinkle it on trivial 'nice' situations, where it can sound grandiose.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 훌륭하다 for casual 'nice/good' situations where 좋다 is enough — it can sound overly grand and formal.
Forming the pre-noun as 훌륭하는 N — adjectives use -ㄴ/은, so it's 훌륭한 N (the -는 form is for verbs).
Treating 훌륭하다 and 대단하다 as interchangeable; 훌륭하다 is a measured judgement of worth, while 대단하다 is a spontaneous 'wow' reaction.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 대단하다 means "to be amazing / impressive" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 대단하다 (daedanhada) = "to be amazing / impressive". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 대단한 N ("an amazing N") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 대단하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 대단한 실력 'amazing skill'

usagePhrases.en: a big deal / a serious matter
usagePhrases.note: flat-tone sense = 'considerable', not praise
진짜 = casual 'really', very common in reactions

usagePhrases.en: it's not that big a deal
usagePhrases.note: modest deflection set phrase

examples.en: Wow, that's really amazing!
examples.note: spontaneous admiration; 와 sets the reaction tone

examples.en: That's an amazing skill.
examples.note: 실력 = skill/ability, a classic partner noun

examples.ko: 혼자 그걸 다 했다고요? 진짜 대단해요!
examples.romanization: honja geugeol da haetdagoyo? jinjja daedanhaeyo!
examples.en: You did all that by yourself? You're really amazing!
examples.note: real praise of effort; 다고요 shows surprised confirmation

extendedVocab.nuance: 대단하다 is the everyday go-to compliment — 'impressive, amazing, remarkable' — usually aimed at a person's achievement, effort, or ability, and it carries warm, spoken energy (often opened with 와 or 진짜). Set against 훌륭하다, 대단하다 is the hotter, more emotional in-the-moment reaction ('wow, you're amazing!'), while 훌륭하다 is a cooler verdict on worth; you'd gush 대단하다 at someone who just aced a race, but reserve 훌륭하다 for praising their character or a polished body of work. A second sense surfaces with a flat tone: 대단한 일 = 'a big/serious matter', and the modest deflection 별로 대단한 일 아니에요 means 'it's no big deal'. Watch the adverb 대단히 ('very, greatly', as in 대단히 감사합니다) — it modifies other words and is not the same as the adjective. Also, aim 대단하다 at others; using it on your own success sounds boastful.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 대단하다 about your own achievement — it sounds boastful; Koreans use it to praise others and deflect their own with 별거 아니에요.
Confusing the adjective 대단하다 with the adverb 대단히 ('very/greatly') — 대단히 감사합니다 modifies 'thanks', it doesn't mean 'amazing'.
Using 대단하다 for a measured judgement of quality where 훌륭하다 fits — 대단하다 is a spontaneous reaction, not a formal evaluation.

extendedVocab.explanation: 평범하다 (pyeongbeomhada) means "to be ordinary / average". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 평범한 N ("an ordinary N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 평범하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 평범한 회사원 'an ordinary office worker'
지극히 'extremely' is the idiomatic intensifier here
adverb 평범하게 + 살다, a common life-goal phrase
일상 'daily life' is a frequent partner noun

examples.en: I'm an ordinary student.
examples.note: modest self-description, a very natural use

examples.en: The taste is kind of ordinary.
examples.note: honest, mild review; 좀 softens it

examples.en: I just want to live an ordinary life like everyone else.
examples.note: heartfelt wish; adverb 평범하게 + 처럼 'like'

extendedVocab.nuance: 평범하다 (平凡, 平 'flat/level' + 凡 'ordinary') means 'ordinary, average, nothing special', and it is essentially neutral, not an insult — Koreans use it modestly about themselves or their routines, and 'I want a 평범한 life' is a sincere, even wistful wish. Its sharp antonym is 특별하다 ('special'), and it overlaps with 흔하다 ('common') but from a different angle: 평범하다 judges character/quality ('unremarkable, run-of-the-mill'), while 흔하다 judges frequency ('found everywhere'). So a name can be 흔하다 (lots of people have it) and a person 평범하다 (an average sort) — they aren't swappable. Tone decides the colour: said warmly it's humble; said with a sigh it edges toward 'mediocre/disappointing'. As a 하다-adjective it takes the pre-noun -ㄴ (평범한 사람, not 평범하는 사람) and the adverb 평범하게.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 평범하다 as purely negative — it usually just means 'normal/unremarkable' and is often a modest or even fond description.
Swapping it with 흔하다: 평범하다 rates how ordinary something's quality is, while 흔하다 rates how frequently it occurs — a 흔한 이름 is a common name, a 평범한 사람 is an average person.
Making the pre-noun 평범하는 사람 — adjectives use -ㄴ, so it's 평범한 사람.

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be common / commonplace" is 흔하다 (heunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 흔한 N ("a common N"). Watch the particle attached to 흔하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 흔한 이름 'a common name'
negated, a frequent way to say 'rare'
adverb, e.g. 흔히 쓰는 말 'a commonly used phrase'

usagePhrases.en: to be dirt-common / a dime a dozen
usagePhrases.note: 흔해 빠지다 adds a dismissive nuance

examples.en: That name is very common.
examples.note: talking about frequency of a name

examples.en: It's a common thing around here.
examples.note: 일 = thing/occurrence; 여기서는 'around here'

examples.ko: 이런 디자인은 흔해서 별로 안 끌려요.
examples.romanization: ireon dijaineun heunhaeseo byeollo an kkeullyeoyo.
examples.en: This kind of design is so common it doesn't appeal to me.
examples.note: real opinion; here 흔하다 carries the 'unoriginal' shade

extendedVocab.nuance: 흔하다 means something is common, plentiful, easily found, or seen everywhere — its core is frequency/availability. Its direct antonym is 드물다 ('rare, scarce'), and the negated 흔하지 않다 is a natural way to say 'uncommon'. The line to draw is against 평범하다: 흔하다 = 'occurs a lot / is everywhere' (a 흔한 성씨, a common surname), whereas 평범하다 = 'is unremarkable in quality' (a 평범한 영화, an average movie); a thing can be one without the other. Tone gives 흔하다 two flavours: neutrally it just means 'widely available' (마트에서 흔하게 팔아요), but about taste or style it can turn faintly negative — 'too common, unoriginal', as in 흔한 디자인. The adverb is 흔히 ('commonly, often'), as in 흔히 볼 수 있어요. English speakers sometimes reach for 흔하다 to describe a plain personality — but a person's ordinariness is 평범하다, not 흔하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 흔하다 (common/frequent) with the look-alike 흔들다 (to shake) — unrelated words that just resemble each other.
Using 흔하다 for a person's character; for 'an ordinary/unremarkable person' say 평범한 사람 — 흔하다 is about how often something occurs, not personality.
Saying the adverb as 흔하게 when the idiomatic choice is 흔히 (e.g. 흔히 쓰는 표현 'a commonly used expression').

Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 소중한 추억 'a precious memory'
소중히 + 하다 = 'treat as precious'
여기다 'to consider' is a natural partner

usagePhrases.note: 무엇보다 'more than anything' intensifies

examples.note: 제일 = most; emotional value, not price

extendedVocab.nuance: 소중하다 (所重, 'that which is weighty/important') describes something dear and treasured — people, time, memories, relationships, a meaningful gift — measuring worth to the heart, not price in money. Keep it apart from two neighbours: 비싸다 is about cost ('expensive'), and 귀하다 is closer but leans 'rare/precious because scarce or noble' (귀한 손님 'an honoured guest'), while 소중하다 is the emotional 'dear to me'. So a cheap toy from a late grandparent is 소중하다 even though it's not 비싸다. It carries warm, sincere feeling, which makes it a lovely word for cards, letters, and heartfelt moments (시간이 소중하다 'time is precious'; 너는 나에게 소중한 사람이야 'you're precious to me'). The adverb 소중히/소중하게 pairs with verbs like 간직하다 ('keep dear') and 여기다 ('regard'). As a 하다-adjective the pre-noun is 소중한, never 소중하는.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 소중하다 for monetary cost — for 'expensive' say 비싸다; 소중하다 is emotional worth, not a price tag.
Confusing it with 귀하다: 귀하다 leans 'rare/precious because scarce or honoured', while 소중하다 means 'dear to my heart'.
Forming the pre-noun as 소중하는 N — adjectives take -ㄴ, so it's 소중한 N (소중한 사람).

所重, 'that which is weighty/important'.

extendedVocab.explanation: 익숙하다 (iksukada) means "to be familiar / used to". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N에 익숙하다 ("to be used to N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 익숙하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the thing you're accustomed to takes 에, not 을/를
익숙해지다 = the 'becoming' verb form

usagePhrases.en: to get the hang of (by hand)
usagePhrases.note: related idiom from the 익- root, for skills

examples.en: I'm used to the work now.
examples.note: 이제 = now; 일 takes 에

examples.note: pre-noun form describing a known route

extendedVocab.nuance: 익숙하다 means 'familiar / accustomed to' — something you've done or seen enough that it now feels easy and natural. The crucial grammar point is the particle: the thing you're used to is marked with 에 (not 을/를), so 운전에 익숙해요 ('I'm used to driving'), 분위기에 익숙해요 ('used to the atmosphere'). Its antonym is 낯설다 ('unfamiliar, strange'), and to say you gradually get accustomed you switch to the 'becoming' verb 익숙해지다. Distinguish it from 친숙하다, which adds an affectionate 'close/cosy' warmth (a 친숙한 멜로디 feels endearing), whereas 익숙하다 is the neutral 'this is routine for me'. The 익- root also gives 익다 ('to ripen / be cooked', as in 고기가 익다), so don't let the shared syllable confuse the meanings. 익숙하다 is invaluable for talking about settling into a new job, city, or life.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the thing with 을/를 instead of 에 — say '한국 음식에 익숙해요', not '한국 음식을 익숙해요'; 익숙하다 takes 에.
Confusing 익숙하다 ('familiar/accustomed') with 익다 ('to ripen / be cooked') — they share 익- but mean different things (고기가 익다 = 'the meat is cooked').
Using 익숙하다 for the act of 'getting used to' something gradually — for the change of state use the verb 익숙해지다 (익숙해졌어요).

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be clear / obvious" is 분명하다 (bunmyeonghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분명한 N ("a clear / definite N"). Watch the particle attached to 분명하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 분명한 이유 'a clear reason'
adverb — even more common than the adjective in speech
expresses the speaker's certainty about a past act
태도 'attitude' is a frequent partner

examples.en: The reason is clear.
examples.note: 이유 = reason; the matter is unambiguous

examples.note: real puzzled moment; 분명히 voices the speaker's certainty

extendedVocab.nuance: 분명하다 (分明, 分 'divide' + 明 'bright/clear') means something is clear, definite, and unambiguous — used for reasons, answers, facts, intentions, and stances (입장이 분명하다 'one's position is clear'). In everyday speech the adverb 분명히 ('clearly / surely / definitely') is even more frequent, often broadcasting the speaker's own certainty: 분명히 잠갔어요 ('I definitely locked it'). The fine line is against 확실하다: 분명하다 stresses that something is objectively obvious/unmistakable, while 확실하다 stresses the speaker's subjective confidence that it's true — '증거가 분명하다' (the evidence is clear-cut) vs '나는 확실해' (I'm sure). A second, separate word is 선명하다, which is visual sharpness — a 선명한 사진 ('a vivid, crisp photo') or clear sound; you can't use 분명하다 for image clarity. Note also that the natural adverb is 분명히, not 분명하게, in most speech.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 분명하다 for visual or audio clarity — for a sharp photo or crisp sound use 선명하다; 분명하다 is for ideas, reasons, and facts being unambiguous.
Treating 분명하다 and 확실하다 as identical — 분명하다 = objectively obvious, 확실하다 = the speaker is confident it's true.
Saying the adverb as 분명하게 in casual speech — the natural, idiomatic form is 분명히 (분명히 그랬어요).

usagePhrases.note: pre-noun form, e.g. 확실한 증거 'solid evidence'
adverb, common when confirming
negated form, a soft way to express doubt

usagePhrases.en: to make sure / nail it down

examples.note: 그건 = 'as for that'; speaker is sure

extendedVocab.nuance: 확실하다 (確實, 確 'firm/sure' + 實 'real/true') expresses certainty and confidence — you're sure something is true, settled, or reliable. The adverb 확실히 ('certainly, definitely, for sure') is very common when answering or confirming (확실히 그래요 'that's definitely so'). The sharp contrast is with 분명하다: 확실하다 centres on the speaker's subjective confidence ('I'm sure of it'), while 분명하다 centres on a thing being objectively obvious/unambiguous — so 나는 확실해 ('I'm certain') but 증거가 분명해 ('the evidence is clear-cut'). It also brushes against 틀림없다 ('there's no mistake / definitely'), which is even more emphatic. Crucially, 확실하다 is for certainty, not possibility: to say 'maybe' you need 아마 ('probably') or '-ㄹ지도 몰라요' ('might'), not 확실하다. The natural adverb is 확실히 in everyday speech (확실하게 is a touch stiffer).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 확실하다 when you actually mean 'maybe / probably' — for uncertainty use 아마 or '-ㄹ지도 몰라요'; 확실하다 asserts the opposite (full certainty).
Treating 확실하다 and 분명하다 as the same — 확실하다 = the speaker's confidence, 분명하다 = something objectively obvious.
Defaulting to 확실하게 in casual speech — the idiomatic adverb is 확실히 (확실히 알겠어요).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 가능하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: drops 이/가 in shop talk, e.g. 예약 가능해요?
polite request softener, very high-frequency
set frame, e.g. 가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible'

examples.en: Is delivery possible today?
examples.note: asking at a shop; 배달 가능해요? is a fixed service phrase

examples.note: 환불 = refund; the noun stands directly before 가능하다

extendedVocab.nuance: 가능하다 (可能, 可 'can/permissible' + 能 'ability') means 'possible / doable / available', and it is wonderfully practical for daily service questions — 예약 가능해요? ('Is a reservation possible?'), 카드 가능해요? ('Can I pay by card?'). In these, a noun sits directly before it and it neatly replaces a longer '-ㄹ 수 있다' clause, sounding crisp and businesslike. The softener 가능하면 ('if possible') makes requests polite, and the fixed frame 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb means 'as ~ as possible' (가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible') — note this is different from 가능한 N ('a possible N'). Its antonym is 불가능하다. One pitfall: while 가능하다 and '-ㄹ 수 있다' both render English 'can', '-ㄹ 수 있다' attaches to a verb stem describing an action you're able to do (갈 수 있어요 'I can go'), whereas 가능하다 attaches to a noun or stands alone judging feasibility — don't merge them into 갈 가능해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 가능하다 (possible) with its 불- prefixed antonym 불가능하다 (impossible).
Mixing 가능한 N ('a possible N') with the 'as ~ as possible' meaning — for the latter the set form is 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb (가능한 한 천천히 'as slowly as possible').
Gluing 가능하다 onto a verb like '갈 가능해요' — to express ability with a verb use '-ㄹ 수 있다' (갈 수 있어요); 가능하다 follows a noun or stands alone.

examples.en: A reservation isn't possible today.
examples.note: polite refusal; the matter takes 이/가 here

examples.en: That's a bit impossible.
examples.note: 좀 softens the 'no' — a very Korean cushioning

examples.en: A refund isn't possible, but an exchange is.

extendedVocab.nuance: 불가능하다 (不可能, the prefix 不 'not/un-' on 가능 'possible') is the direct antonym of 가능하다: 불 flips it to 'cannot be done, impossible'. The 不-prefix pattern recurs across Sino-Korean adjectives (불편하다 'uncomfortable', 불확실하다 'uncertain'), so recognising 불- as a negator unlocks many words. In service settings 불가능하다 is a firm but polite way to refuse, and Koreans habitually cushion it with 좀 ('a bit') or pair it with a 'but...' offer (환불은 불가능하지만 교환은 가능해요) to soften the blow. For an everyday personal 'I can't', the '-ㄹ 수 없다' pattern (갈 수 없어요 'I can't go') is more natural than forcing 불가능하다, which leans toward declaring something infeasible in principle. As a 하다-adjective the pre-noun is 불가능한, never 불가능하는.

Mixing up 불가능하다 (impossible) with 가능하다 (possible) — the 불- prefix flips the meaning, so listen for that first syllable.
Using 불가능하다 for a casual personal 'I can't (do something)' — for that, '-ㄹ 수 없다' (못 가요 / 갈 수 없어요) is more natural; 불가능하다 declares something infeasible in principle.
Forming the pre-noun as 불가능하는 N — adjectives take -ㄴ, so it's 불가능한 N (불가능한 요구 'an impossible demand').

Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

extendedVocab.nuance: 답답하다 spans two worlds with one word: a physical airless, closed-in feeling (a small windowless room, a stuffy nose, a tight chest) and an emotional one — being penned-in frustrated when a situation won't budge or you cannot make yourself understood. The dividing line from 화나다 (angry) is direction: 화나다 explodes outward at a target, while 답답하다 is the smothered, helpless 'I can't breathe / can't fix this' pressure that turns inward; 짜증나다 (irritated) is sharper and more peevish. It is a 하다 adjective, so 답답하 + 아요 fuses to 답답해요 (never 답답하요). It loves the subjects 가슴/속/마음 (chest/stomach/heart) and the phrase 말이 안 통하다. English-speaker pitfall: do not translate 'I'm frustrated WITH you' word-for-word with an object particle — 답답하다 describes the speaker's own stifled state, so you say 답답해요, and if you must name the cause you append it with -아서/어서, not with 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating as 답답하요; 하다 adjectives fuse 하+아 into 해, giving 답답해요.
Using it to mean 'angry at someone' — 답답하다 is the stifled, helpless feeling; for outward anger use 화나다.
Attaching a person with 을/를 (사람을 답답해요 ✗); state the cause with -아서/어서 instead: 말이 안 통해서 답답해요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 배부르다 literally welds 배 (belly) + 부르다 here meaning 'swollen/filled', and names the satisfied, can't-eat-more fullness after a meal — the exact opposite of 배고프다 (hungry). Mind the boundary: 배부르다 is a finished state ('I AM full'), whereas the verb 부르다/불렀다 describes the belly filling up, and 질리다 means 'sick of / fed up with' a food rather than physically full. It is a 르-irregular adjective: when an ending starting with 아/어 attaches, the 르 drops its ㅡ and doubles the ㄹ, so 배부르 + 어요 → 배불러요 (past 배불렀어요). Socially it doubles as a polite signal that you enjoyed the meal and are content — saying 잘 먹었어요. 배불러요 graciously declines a second helping. English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm full' is a whole-body sentence in English, but Korean keeps the belly in view, so the natural line is just 배불러요, not 저는 가득해요 (a 직역 of 'full' that sounds like a filled container).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 배부러요; the 르-irregular doubles the ㄹ before 어, giving 배불러요.
Confusing it with 배고프다 (hungry) — 배부르다 is the full, satisfied state, its direct antonym.
Using 질리다 when you just mean physically full — 질리다 means 'sick of' a food, a different feeling from 배불러요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 재미없다 means "to be boring; not fun" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be boring; not fun" is 재미없다 (jaemieopsda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 재미없어요 ("It's boring / not fun"). Watch the particle attached to 재미없다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: present 요-form
하나도 + negative = not in the least
재미없게 되다 = end up dull
-는 attributive before a noun

examples.en: This game is boring.
examples.note: simple opinion; topic + 재미없어요

examples.en: I had high hopes, but the movie was boring.
examples.note: everyday: -았는데 contrast + past tense

examples.en: Playing alone is no fun, so let's play together.
examples.note: real-situation: -(으)니까 reason + suggestion

extendedVocab.nuance: 재미없다 is the fixed antonym of 재미있다 (fun/interesting), built from the noun 재미 (fun/enjoyment) + 없다 (there isn't) and written solid as one word. It judges whether an activity or media delivers enjoyment — a film, game, class, party, person's stories. Distinguish it from 심심하다, which describes YOUR own state of having nothing to do ('I'm bored'), and from 지루하다, which stresses tedious, drags-on dullness; 재미없다 is the verdict on the THING ('it's not fun'). Crucial structure point: 없다 already carries the negative, so you never stack 안 in front of it (안 재미없어요 ✗). To flip it positive you must swap the whole word to 재미있어요, not negate this one. English-speaker pitfall: learners try to say 'I'm not having fun' by negating the adjective, but Korean assigns the quality to the event, so you say 이거 재미없어요 ('this is boring'), and the spacing trap 재미 없어요 (two words) reads as raw 'there is no fun' rather than the dictionary headword.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing it as two words 재미 없어요; the standard headword is solid 재미없어요.
Stacking 안 (안 재미없어요 ✗) — 없다 is already negative; to say it IS fun, switch to 재미있어요.
Using 재미없다 for your own boredom — 'I'm bored with nothing to do' is 심심해요, which describes the person, not the thing.

Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: present 요-form; pronounced [마덥써요]

usagePhrases.en: I ate it even though it wasn't tasty
usagePhrases.note: context-dependent, 맛없게 = un-deliciously
좀 softens the criticism
-는 attributive before a noun

examples.en: This bread tastes bad.
examples.note: simple verdict on food; topic + 맛없어요

examples.en: It tastes bad because it got cold.
examples.note: everyday: 식다 (cool down) + -아서/어서

examples.ko: 맛없으면 억지로 먹지 말고 남겨도 돼요.
examples.romanization: maseopseumyeon eokjiro meokji malgo namgyeodo dwaeyo.
examples.en: If it's bad, don't force it down — you can leave it.
examples.note: real-situation: -(으)면 + permission -아도 되다

extendedVocab.nuance: 맛없다 is the straight antonym of 맛있다 (delicious), welded from the noun 맛 (taste) + 없다 (there isn't), written as one word. It is a blunt taste verdict, so soften it in company with 좀 (좀 맛없어요, 'it's a bit off') rather than declaring it flatly to a host. Watch the pronunciation: the final ㅅ of 맛 resyllabifies and tenses into the next syllable, so 맛없어요 is said [마덥써요], not letter-by-letter [맏업어요]. As with 재미없다, the 없다 already supplies the negative, so 안 맛없어요 is wrong — to flip it positive you change the whole word to 맛있어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'this is not tasty' tempts learners to negate with 안, but Korean treats 맛없다 as its own lexical antonym; also note 맛없다 means literally tasteless/bad, while 별로예요 ('it's not great / so-so') is the gentler, more common dodge Koreans use to avoid bluntly insulting someone's cooking.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pronouncing it syllable-by-syllable; the natural sound for 맛없어요 is [마덥써요] with the ㅅ linking over.
Adding 안 (안 맛없어요 ✗) — 없다 is already negative; to say it IS tasty, switch to 맛있어요.
Saying it bluntly to a cook — soften with 좀 맛없어요 or dodge with 별로예요 to stay polite.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 편하다 means "to be comfortable; convenient" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 편하다 (pyeonhada) means "to be comfortable; convenient". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 편해요 ("It's comfortable / convenient"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 편하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: present 요-form (편하 + 아요 → 편해요)
마음 = heart/mind; emotional comfort
편하게 = comfortably (adverb)
-(으)ㄴ attributive before a noun

examples.en: This chair is really comfortable.
examples.note: simple: object + 편해요 (physical comfort)

examples.en: The subway is more convenient than the bus.
examples.note: everyday: N보다 comparison + 'convenient' sense

examples.ko: 집에 오니까 마음이 편해서 잠이 잘 와요.
examples.romanization: jibe onikka maeumi pyeonhaeseo jami jal wayo.
examples.en: Now that I'm home I feel at ease, so I sleep well.
examples.note: real-situation: -(으)니까 + -아서/어서 emotional ease

extendedVocab.nuance: 편하다 carries the Sino-Korean root 便 (편, 'convenient / at ease') and stretches across three senses English splits into separate words: physical comfort (a comfy chair, loose clothes), practical convenience (handy transport, an easy method), and inner ease (a relaxed, untroubled mind, 마음이 편하다). It is the antonym of 불편하다. Mind two boundaries: 쉽다 means 'easy to DO' a task (the problem is simple), whereas 편하다 means 'comfortable/convenient' (low effort or strain) — a method can be 쉽다 yet not 편하다; and 편안하다 is the softer, more soothing 'peaceful/at rest' cousin you meet in 편안한 밤 (a restful night). As a 하다 adjective it becomes 편해요, and the adverb 편하게 powers warm invitations like 편하게 드세요 / 편하게 계세요 ('help yourself / make yourself at home'). English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 편하다 to translate 'easy' on a test — 시험이 편했어요 sounds like the exam was low-strain, not 'the questions were easy'; for that you want 쉬웠어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating as 편하요; 하다 adjectives fuse to 해요, so it is 편해요.
Using it to mean an 'easy' task — 'the test was easy' is 시험이 쉬웠어요, not 편했어요 (which means low-strain/relaxed).
Forgetting the inner-ease sense — 마음이 편해요 ('I feel at ease') is just as core as physical comfort.

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be uncomfortable; inconvenient" is 불편하다 (bulpyeonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 불편해요 ("It's uncomfortable / inconvenient"). usagePhrases.note: present 요-form (불편하 → 불편해요)

usagePhrases.en: I feel unwell / my body is impaired
usagePhrases.note: polite way to say unwell or disabled
불편하게 하다 = to inconvenience

usagePhrases.en: a point of inconvenience / a complaint
usagePhrases.note: 불편한 + 점 (point), service contexts

examples.en: These shoes are uncomfortable.
examples.note: simple: object + 불편해요 (physical)

examples.ko: 여기는 교통이 불편해서 차가 꼭 필요해요.
examples.romanization: yeogineun gyotongi bulpyeonhaeseo chaga kkok piryohaeyo.
examples.en: Transit here is inconvenient, so you really need a car.
examples.note: everyday: -아서/어서 + consequence

examples.ko: 처음 만난 사람이랑 단둘이 있으면 좀 불편해요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum mannan saramirang danduri isseumyeon jom bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: Being alone with someone I just met feels a bit awkward.
examples.note: real-situation: social-discomfort sense + 이랑/단둘이

extendedVocab.nuance: 불편하다 fronts the Sino-Korean negative prefix 不 (불, 'not') onto 便 (편, 'convenient'), literally 'not-convenient', and is the all-purpose antonym of 편하다. It covers physical discomfort (tight shoes, a hard bed), practical inconvenience (poor transport, a clunky process), social unease (feeling awkward around someone), and gently, being unwell or physically impaired (몸이 불편하다 is the courteous phrase for illness or disability). It is the polite backbone of complaints — service desks ask 불편한 점이 있으셨어요? ('was anything inconvenient?'). Boundary note: 불편하다 is the broad 'uncomfortable/inconvenient', while 어색하다 zeroes in on the awkward unfamiliarity between people who aren't close, and 아프다 is plain physical pain. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 불편해요. English-speaker pitfall: the literal calque 안 편하다 is understood but sounds like a learner workaround — the natural single lexical antonym is 불편하다; and don't use 불편하다 for sharp pain, which is 아파요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying the calque 안 편하다 — it is understood but the natural single word is 불편하다.
Conjugating as 불편하요; 하다 adjectives take 해요, giving 불편해요.
Using 불편하다 for sharp physical pain — that is 아파요; 불편하다 is discomfort/inconvenience, or a soft word for being unwell.

extendedVocab.explanation: 속상하다 (soksanghada) = "to be upset; distressed; hurt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 속상해요 ("I'm upset / heart-sore") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 속상하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: present 요-form (속상하 → 속상해요)
속상해하다 = to act/show upset, comforting someone

usagePhrases.en: I'm so upset I could die
usagePhrases.note: -아 죽겠다 = unbearably
third-person uses 속상해하다 + honorific

examples.en: I'm upset because I did badly on the test.
examples.note: simple: -아서/어서 cause

examples.en: I worked hard on it but ruined it all, so I'm gutted.
examples.note: everyday: -았는데 contrast heightens the letdown

examples.ko: 아이가 아픈데 해 줄 게 없어서 너무 속상해요.
examples.romanization: aiga apeunde hae jul ge eopseoseo neomu soksanghaeyo.
examples.en: My child is sick and there's nothing I can do, so it breaks my heart.
examples.note: real-situation: tender, helpless distress

extendedVocab.nuance: 속상하다 literally pairs 속 (one's insides / heart) with 상하다, which uses the hanja 傷 (상, 'to wound, spoil') — so the image is your insides getting bruised. It is the warm everyday word for being upset, gutted, or heart-sore over a letdown, a hurtful word, or something that goes wrong, and Koreans apply it to small daily disappointments as readily as bigger hurts. Mark the boundaries carefully: 화나다 is hot anger aimed outward, 슬프다 is plain sadness (a sad film, a loss), while 속상하다 sits in between as a tender, often self-directed 'this hurts / I'm so disappointed' ache, frequently mixed with helplessness. Grammar trap unique to feeling-adjectives: for your OWN feeling say 속상해요, but to describe someone ELSE's visible upset you must add 하 → 친구가 속상해해요 ('my friend is upset'), because Korean treats another person's inner emotion as something you observe, not assert. English-speaker pitfall: don't substitute 화나다 for every 'upset' — in English 'upset' often means hurt/disappointed, which is exactly 속상하다, whereas 화나다 means genuinely angry.

Equating it with 화나다 (angry) — 속상하다 is hurt/disappointed and inward, not outward fury.
Conjugating as 속상하요; as a 하다 adjective it becomes 속상해요.
Using plain 속상해요 for another person — describe someone else's upset with 속상해해요 (친구가 속상해해요).

extendedVocab.explanation: 간지럽다 (ganjireopda) means "to be ticklish; itchy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 간지러워요 ("It tickles / it's itchy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 간지럽다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: present 요-form; ㅂ-irregular (간지럽 → 간지러워요)

usagePhrases.en: The sole of my foot is ticklish
usagePhrases.note: body part takes 이/가
간지럽게 하다 = to tickle (casual)
-아서/어서 cause

examples.en: My throat feels ticklish.
examples.note: simple: common pre-cough sensation, body part + 이

examples.en: When you touch my armpit it tickles.
examples.note: everyday: -(으)니까 trigger + tickle

examples.ko: 새 스웨터가 목에 닿아서 간지러워 죽겠어요.
examples.romanization: sae seuweteoga moge daaseo ganjireowo jukgesseoyo.
examples.en: The new sweater touches my neck and it's unbearably itchy.
examples.note: real-situation: scratchy-fabric itch + -아 죽겠다

extendedVocab.nuance: 간지럽다 covers two related skin sensations: the squirmy tickle when someone touches a ticklish spot, and a light, fluttery itch on the skin or throat (the kind that makes you clear your throat). It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so before an 어 ending the ㅂ turns into 우 and merges: 간지럽 + 어요 → 간지러워요 (past 간지러웠어요). The key contrast is intensity and intent: 간지럽다 is the lighter, ticklish/mildly-itchy feeling, whereas 가렵다 is the stronger 'must-scratch' itch (a mosquito bite, a rash). English-speaker pitfall: English uses 'itchy' for both, but Korean splits them, so a serious itch you'd scratch hard is 가려워요, not 간지러워요. Also, mark the body part with the subject particle 이/가 (등이 간지러워요, 'my back is itchy'), never the object particle 을/를 — the back is what HAS the sensation, not something being acted on.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating as 간지럽어요; the ㅂ-irregular makes it 간지러워요.
Using it for a strong scratch-worthy itch — that is 가려워요; 간지럽다 is the lighter, ticklish feeling.
Marking the body part with 을/를 — use 이/가 (등이 간지러워요), since the body part is the subject that feels it.

분위기 = atmosphere/mood collocation

examples.note: simple: -아서/어서 cause + 좀 softener

extendedVocab.nuance: 어색하다 traces to the Sino-Korean 語塞 (어 語 'speech' + 색 塞 'blocked/stuck') — the picture of words getting jammed — and names two feelings: the stiff, uneasy awkwardness between people who aren't yet close, and the sense that something looks or feels unnatural or out of place (a forced smile, a new haircut, an odd-sounding sentence). Draw the line from 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: those are shyness/embarrassment about YOURSELF (blushing, shame), whereas 어색하다 is the awkwardness of an unfamiliar situation or relationship — no shame, just lack of ease; and 불편하다 is broader discomfort, while 어색하다 specifically flags social unfamiliarity. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 어색해요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 어색하다 for personal embarrassment ('I was so embarrassed' is 창피했어요); reserve 어색하다 for that not-yet-comfortable-together or 'this looks unnatural' feeling.

Conjugating as 어색하요; 하다 adjectives become 어색해요.
Treating it as a synonym of 불편하다 — 어색하다 is narrower: specifically the social awkwardness of not being close yet.

usagePhrases.note: present 요-form; ㅂ-irregular (반갑 → 반가워요)

extendedVocab.nuance: 반갑다 is the warm rush of gladness at meeting or seeing someone, and it powers Korea's everyday introduction 만나서 반가워요 ('nice to meet you'). It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before an 아/어 ending the ㅂ becomes 우 and merges, so 반갑 + 아요 → 반가워요 (formal 반갑습니다, past 반가웠어요). Keep it firmly about PEOPLE (or news/voices tied to people) — you are glad to encounter someone — unlike 기쁘다, which is general happiness about any good thing (passing an exam, a sunny day). A handy contrast: 기쁘다 = happy in general; 반갑다 = specifically happy to see/meet someone; 즐겁다 = enjoyable/having a good time. English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm glad' in English covers everything, but you can't say 반가워요 about an event or an achievement — 시험에 붙어서 반가워요 is wrong; that is 기뻐요. Conjugating as 반갑아요; the ㅂ-irregular gives 반가워요.
Using it for general happiness — 'I'm happy I passed' is 기뻐요, not 반가워요; 반갑다 is specifically about meeting/seeing someone.
Saying it about objects or events — 반갑다 attaches to people, voices, or welcome news, not things in general.

body part takes 이/가

usagePhrases.note: -아서/어서 + 긁다 (to scratch)

extendedVocab.nuance: 가렵다 is the everyday word for a real, scratch-it itch — on skin, scalp, a healing wound, anywhere — the sensation that makes your hand reach to scratch (긁다). Conjugating as 가렵어요; the ㅂ-irregular gives 가려워요.
Marking the body part with 을/를 — use 이/가 (등이 가려워요), since the body part is the subject that itches.
Swapping it with 간지럽다 for a hard itch — 가렵다 is the strong scratch-worthy itch; 간지럽다 is the lighter, ticklish one.

귀찮게 하다 = to bother/pester (casual)

usagePhrases.en: I can't be bothered with anything
usagePhrases.note: 다 = everything; flat-mood phrase

extendedVocab.nuance: 귀찮다 is the daily-life feeling that something is too much of a bother, not worth the effort — the 'ugh, I can't be bothered' reluctance to get up, cook, reply, or go out. It descends from a contraction of 귀하지 않다 ('not precious / not worth it'), which is why the ㅎ is nearly silent and 귀찮아요 is pronounced [귀차나요]. It pairs constantly with the -기 nominalizer to label a chore as a drag: 청소하기 귀찮아요, 나가기 귀찮아요 ('cleaning/going out is a hassle'). Draw the boundary from 피곤하다 and 짜증나다: 피곤하다 is physical tiredness (your body is worn out), 짜증나다 is irritation/annoyance at something, while 귀찮다 is specifically the can't-be-bothered, effort-averse feeling — you might feel 귀찮다 while perfectly rested. English-speaker pitfall: there's no clean one-word English match, so learners borrow 'annoying' and wrongly say 짜증나다; if the meaning is 'too much effort / I don't feel like it', the word is 귀찮다, often + a -기 chore.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pronouncing the ㅎ; 귀찮아요 is said [귀차나요].
Confusing it with 피곤하다 (physically tired) — 귀찮다 is about not wanting the effort, not bodily fatigue.
Using 짜증나다 when you mean 'too much hassle' — 짜증나다 is irritation; the can't-be-bothered feeling is 귀찮다, usually with a -기 form.

usagePhrases.en: Are you having a hard time?
usagePhrases.note: honorific; ㄹ drops before -세요

usagePhrases.en: I earned it with great effort
usagePhrases.note: 힘들게 = with difficulty (adverb)

extendedVocab.nuance: 힘들다 literally takes 힘 (strength) + 들다 ('to take/cost'), i.e. 'it costs strength', and covers anything physically OR emotionally hard, tiring, or tough — a grueling shift, single-handed childcare, a rough stretch of life. With the -기 nominalizer it labels a hard task: 공부하기 힘들어요, 참기 힘들어요 ('studying/enduring is hard'). It is a ㄹ-stem word, so the ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ/ㅅ/ㅂ: honorific 힘드세요?, attributive 힘든 일, 힘듭니다 — not 힘들세요/힘들은. The crucial contrast is with 어렵다: 어렵다 is 'difficult to understand or solve' (a hard math problem, a tricky concept), whereas 힘들다 is 'taxing — tiring or emotionally draining'. A problem can be 어렵다 without being 힘들다, and a job can be 힘들다 (exhausting) yet not 어렵다 (intellectually hard). English-speaker pitfall: English 'hard' blurs both, so learners say 어렵다 for an exhausting day — if it drains your energy or spirit, it's 힘들어요, not 어려워요.

Forgetting the emotional sense — 힘들다 also means a hard TIME in life (요즘 힘들어요), not only physical tiredness.

extendedVocab.nuance: 외롭다 is the inner ache of loneliness — feeling alone, isolated, or cut off from people you love, even in a crowd. usagePhrases.note: 적다 partners naturally with 양 (amount)
for countable things use 수 (number)

usagePhrases.en: to be not few (= quite a lot)
usagePhrases.note: litotes; a polite way to say 'a fair amount'
adverb 적게 modifies the verb

examples.en: There are few people.
examples.note: subject takes 이/가, and the verb stays an adjective: 적어요, never 적어 있어요

examples.en: I have little work these days, so I'm free.
examples.note: 적어서 (-아서) links the small amount to its result, being free

extendedVocab.nuance: 적다 means small in QUANTITY — few in number or little in amount — and never small in physical SIZE. The killer pitfall for English speakers is that 'small' covers both, so they reach for 작다 (small size) when they mean 적다 (small amount); the two even sound close. Rule of thumb: if you could put a number on it (사람, 돈, 시간, 양), use 적다; if you could measure it with a ruler (가방, 방, 손), use 작다. Its opposite is 많다 (many/much), not 크다. Don't confuse the adjective 적다 with the adverb 조금/적게 either: 'There's little money' is 돈이 적어요 (adjective describing the money), while 'eat a little' is 조금/적게 먹어요 (adverb describing how you eat). A natural near-synonym is 모자라다 (to fall short/be insufficient), but 모자라다 implies 'not enough for the need,' whereas 적다 is just a neutral 'small amount.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가방이 적어요 for 'the bag is small' — that describes a small QUANTITY of bags; for a small-SIZE bag it must be 가방이 작아요.
Using 적다 as if it were a verb: 돈이 적어 있어요 is wrong. 적다 is a descriptive adjective, so it's simply 돈이 적어요.
Confusing the adjective with the adverb: for 'eat less' don't say 적어 먹어요; the adverb form is 적게 먹어요 or 조금 먹어요.

extendedVocab.explanation: 느리다 (neurida) = "to be slow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 속도가 느리다 ("the speed is slow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 느리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 느리다 is literally about 속도 (speed)

usagePhrases.en: to be slow on one's feet
usagePhrases.note: idiom for a slow walker/runner
adverb 느리게 describes the action's pace

usagePhrases.en: to be slow to act / sluggish
usagePhrases.note: describes a slow-moving manner

examples.en: The internet is slow.
examples.note: everyday complaint; 느리다 → 느려요 in the 해요-form

examples.en: This bus is so slow it's frustrating.
examples.note: 느려서 (-아서) ties the slowness to the feeling it causes

extendedVocab.nuance: 느리다 describes LOW SPEED — a slow bus, slow internet, a slow walker — and its opposite is 빠르다 (fast). The single biggest trap for English speakers is mixing it up with 늦다, because English 'slow' and 'late' both feel like 'not fast'; but 느리다 is about RATE OF MOTION while 늦다 is about being LATE IN TIME relative to a deadline. The internet being 느리다 (slow) has nothing to do with you being 늦다 (late) for the meeting. There is a second near-synonym worth knowing: 이르다 means 'early (in time),' the time-opposite of 늦다, so the two pairs are 느리다↔빠르다 (speed) and 이르다↔늦다 (timing) — keep the axes separate. 느리다 collocates with 속도 (speed), 발 (feet, = slow-footed), and 행동 (movement/action). It is a plain, neutral word usable in any register, and as an adjective it cannot take 있다: say 버스가 느려요, never 버스가 느려 있어요.

Using 느리다 to mean 'I'm late': 회사에 느렸어요 is wrong. Being late for something is 늦다 → 회사에 늦었어요.
Swapping the time-word and speed-word: 'the train is early' is 기차가 일러요 (이르다), not 기차가 느려요 — 느리다 only covers slow speed.
Treating 느리다 like a verb: 차가 느려 있어요 is incorrect; it's a descriptive adjective, so 차가 느려요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 낮다 means "to be low" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 낮다 (natda) means "to be low". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기온이 낮다 ("the temperature is low"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 낮다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the standard collocation for weather
낮다 covers low numbers/levels, not just height
낮다 also means low in pitch
낮다 + -아지다 = a change to a lower state

examples.en: This chair is low.
examples.note: 낮다 → 낮아요; describes height off the ground

examples.en: The temperature is low today, so I wore a padded coat.
examples.note: 낮아서 (-아서) links the low temperature to the resulting action

examples.en: Interest rates are low these days, so it's a good time to take out a loan.
examples.note: real-situation: 낮다 is the natural word for low rates/levels in news and finance talk

extendedVocab.nuance: 낮다 means LOW on a scale — low in height off the ground, low temperature, low price, low level, or low pitch — and its opposite throughout is 높다 (high). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 낮다 for a SHORT PERSON, because English says 'low/short' loosely; but a person's shortness is 키가 작다 (small in stature), never 키가 낮다. Reserve 낮다 for things measured against a level or scale, and use 작다 for the size of a person or object. Note also that 낮다 (low) is a different word from the noun 낮 'daytime' (as in 낮에 = during the day) — same syllable, unrelated meaning. A subtle pairing point: 낮다 vs 짧다 — a low table is 낮은 탁자 (its top sits low), but a short string is 짧은 줄 (little length); 낮다 is vertical position, 짧다 is length. As an adjective it cannot take 있다: 천장이 낮아요, not 낮아 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 그 사람은 키가 낮아요 for 'that person is short' — a person's height uses 작다: 키가 작아요.
Confusing the adjective 낮다 (low) with the noun 낮 (daytime): '낮에 만나요' means 'let's meet during the day,' nothing to do with 낮다.
Forgetting the ㅈ batchim carries over: the 해요-form is 낮아요 (pronounced 'na-ja-yo'), and the past is 낮았어요, not 낮어요.

usagePhrases.note: the most basic, literal use
얕다 also works figuratively for thin knowledge
얕은 잠 = light, easily-broken sleep
adverb 얕게 describes the depth of the action

examples.en: This water is shallow.
examples.note: 얕다 → 얕아요; the ㅌ batchim links to 얕아요 ('ya-ta-yo')

examples.ko: 여기는 바다가 얕아서 아이들이 놀기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: yeogineun badaga yataseo aideuri nolgi joayo.
examples.en: The sea is shallow here, so it's good for kids to play.
examples.note: 얕아서 (-아서) connects the shallowness to why it's safe

examples.ko: 그 사람은 아는 게 얕아서 깊이 있는 대화가 어려워요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun aneun ge yataseo gipi inneun daehwaga eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: His knowledge is shallow, so a deep conversation is hard.
examples.note: real-situation: 얕다 used figuratively for shallow/thin understanding, contrasted with 깊이 (depth)

extendedVocab.nuance: 얕다 means SHALLOW — little depth from top to bottom — and its exact opposite is 깊다 (deep). It works both literally (얕은 물 shallow water, 얕은 접시 a shallow dish) and figuratively (얕은 지식 shallow knowledge, 얕은 잠 light sleep). The pitfall for English speakers is hearing 'shallow' and reaching for a color or thinness word: 얕다 is about DEPTH, not about pale color (that's 연하다/옅다) and not about a thin flat object (that's 얇다). Keep three look/sound-alike pairs apart: 얕다 (shallow depth) vs 옅다 (faint/pale, of color or fog) vs 얇다 (thin, of a flat object). Note the spelling — the batchim is ㅌ, so it conjugates 얕아요/얕았어요, and the stem 얕- is unrelated to 얇- despite looking similar. As a descriptive adjective it never takes 있다: 강이 얕아요, not 얕아 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 얕다 with 옅다: pale or faint color/fog is 색이 옅다 / 안개가 옅다, while 얕다 is only about depth.
Mixing 얕다 (shallow depth) with 얇다 (thin, flat): a thin book is 얇은 책, not 얕은 책.
Spelling the batchim wrong — it's 얕다 with ㅌ, conjugating to 얕아요; writing 얄아요 or 얕어요 is incorrect.

extendedVocab.explanation: 깊다 (gipda) = "to be deep". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 물이 깊다 ("the water is deep") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 깊다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the core literal meaning

usagePhrases.en: to sleep deeply / be a heavy sleeper
usagePhrases.note: 깊은 잠 = deep, sound sleep
깊다 stretches to emotional depth
the derived noun-and-adverb form of 깊다

examples.en: This river is deep.
examples.note: 깊다 → 깊어요 (ㅍ batchim, 'gi-peo-yo'); takes 어 because the stem vowel is ㅣ

examples.en: The water is deep, so please be careful.
examples.note: 깊으니까 (-으니까) gives a reason that leads to a warning

examples.en: I had a deep talk with a friend after a long time.
examples.note: real-situation: 깊은 이야기 = a heart-to-heart; 깊다 carries emotional, not just physical, depth

extendedVocab.nuance: 깊다 means DEEP — far from top to bottom (깊은 물 deep water, 깊은 구덩이 a deep hole) — and its opposite is 얕다 (shallow). Beyond the physical, it stretches naturally to deep sleep (잠이 깊다), deep thought (깊은 생각), and close relationships and feelings (정이 깊다), which English also calls 'deep,' so this metaphor transfers well. The English-speaker pitfall is using 깊다 for HEIGHT: a tall building or person is NOT 깊다 — height upward is 높다 (high) or 키가 크다 (tall of a person). 깊다 measures downward/inward depth, 높다 measures upward height; don't let English 'deep voice' mislead you either — a low/deep voice is 목소리가 낮다 (low pitch), not 깊다. Watch the spelling: the batchim is ㅍ, giving 깊어요/깊었어요 (never 깁어요), and the very common derived form 깊이 serves as both the noun 'depth' and the adverb 'deeply.' As an adjective it does not take 있다: 강이 깊어요, not 깊어 있어요.

Saying 목소리가 깊어요 for 'a deep voice' — low vocal pitch is 목소리가 낮아요; 깊다 is for depth, not pitch.
Spelling slip: the 해요-form is 깊어요 (ㅍ batchim), not 깁어요; the past is 깊었어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 굵다 means "to be thick (in diameter); to be coarse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 굵다 (gulkda) means "to be thick (in diameter); to be coarse". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 면이 굵다 ("the noodles are thick"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 굵다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 굵다 = wide in diameter, for long round things
bold strokes are 굵은 글씨

usagePhrases.en: to have a deep, full voice
usagePhrases.note: a thick, resonant voice (a man's low boom)
adverb 굵게; common in cooking instructions

examples.en: These noodles are thick.
examples.note: 굵다 → 굵어요; the ㄺ batchim reads 'gulg-eo-yo'

examples.en: I cut the vegetables thick and put them in the soup.
examples.note: 굵게 (adverb) tells you how to cut; common recipe phrasing

examples.en: The raindrops were so fat today that an umbrella was useless.
examples.note: real-situation: 비가/빗방울이 굵다 is the idiomatic way to say the rain came down in big, heavy drops

extendedVocab.nuance: 굵다 means THICK in the sense of WIDE DIAMETER — thick noodles, a thick rope, thick fingers, a fat tree trunk, bold writing, and even a deep booming voice. Its opposite is 가늘다 (thin/slender in diameter). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is that English 'thick' covers two different Korean ideas: 굵다 is for the cross-section of a long, round, or solid thing, whereas 두껍다 is for the thickness of a FLAT thing (a thick book, a thick blanket, thick paper). So a thick rope is 굵은 밧줄 but a thick book is 두꺼운 책 — never 굵은 책. A natural extension is 비가 굵다 / 빗방울이 굵다 to describe big, fat raindrops (heavy rain). Pronunciation is a hurdle: the ㄺ cluster surfaces as a hard g before a vowel, so 굵어요 is 'gulg-eo-yo' and 굵게 is 'guk-ge.' As a descriptive adjective it cannot take 있다: 줄이 굵어요, not 굵어 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 굵다 for a flat object's thickness — a thick book or blanket is 두껍다 (두꺼운 책), not 굵다.
Calling a deep male voice 큰 목소리 (that means loud) when you mean rich/deep — a deep, full voice is 목소리가 굵다.
Mispronouncing the ㄺ cluster — 굵어요 is 'gulg-eo-yo' (the g is pronounced before the vowel), not 'gu-eo-yo.'

usagePhrases.note: 가늘다 = slim in diameter

usagePhrases.en: to have a thin, faint voice
usagePhrases.note: a small, reedy voice
adverb 가늘게; standard cooking phrase

examples.en: This string is thin.
examples.note: 가늘다 → 가늘어요 in the 해요-form (ㄹ stays before a vowel)

examples.en: I sliced the green onion thin and put it on the noodles.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가늘다 means SLENDER / THIN IN DIAMETER — thin fingers, a thin thread, a thin wire, a faint reedy voice — and its opposite is 굵다 (thick in diameter). Use 가늘다 for the cross-section of a long or round thing, but use 얇다 for a FLAT thin thing (thin paper, a thin slice of bread, a thin book). The mirror-image pitfall of 굵다 applies: English 'thin' splits into two Korean words (가늘다 for round cross-section, 얇다 for flat objects). Don't carry the one English word across both.

extendedVocab.english: to be light (in color); to be tender/weak (in strength)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 연하다 means "to be light (in color); to be tender/weak (in strength)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 연하다 (yeonhada) = "to be light (in color); to be tender/weak (in strength)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 색이 연하다 ("the color is light/pale") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 연한 분홍색 = pale pink
weak/diluted in strength, opposite of 진하다
연한 고기 = soft, tender meat
연하게 + 타다 (mix/brew) = brew it light

examples.en: The color is light (pale).
examples.note: 연하다 → 연해요 (하다-adjective); describes a pale shade

examples.en: I drink my coffee weak.
examples.note: 연하게 (adverb) modifies how you drink it; cafe-ready phrase

examples.ko: 이 집 갈비는 고기가 연해서 어른들이 좋아하세요.
examples.romanization: i jip galbineun gogiga yeonhaeseo eoreundeuri joahaseyo.
examples.en: The galbi here is so tender that the older folks love it.
examples.note: real-situation: 연하다 = tender, the praise word for soft meat, with 연해서 (-아서) giving the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 연하다 comes from the hanja 軟 'soft/pliant' and fans out into three everyday senses: light/pale in COLOR (연한 색 a pale color), weak/diluted in STRENGTH (연한 커피 weak coffee, 연한 차 weak tea), and tender in TEXTURE (연한 고기 tender meat). Across color and strength its opposite is 진하다 (dark/deep/strong: 진한 커피 strong coffee, 진한 색 a deep color). The main English-speaker pitfall is using 연하다 for a WEAK PERSON: a frail or physically weak person/body is 약하다 (몸이 약하다), not 연하다 — 연하다 weakens drinks and softens meat, but it does not describe a person's constitution. A second trap is confusing it with 얇다 (physically thin) and 옅다 (faint): pale coffee is 연한/옅은, but a thin sheet is 얇은; keep 'weak/pale/tender' (연하다) apart from 'thin/flat' (얇다). It is a polite, neutral word and shines in cafes and restaurants: '연하게 해 주세요' = please make it weak.

Using 연하다 for a frail person — physical weakness of a body/person is 약하다 (몸이 약해요), not 연하다.
Mixing 연하다 (pale/weak/tender) with 얇다 (thin and flat): a thin blanket is 얇은 이불, not 연한 이불.
Asking for strong coffee with the wrong opposite — the opposite of 연한 커피 is 진한 커피 (strong), not 굵은/큰 커피.
