extendedVocab.english: to be clear; to be clean/sunny
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 맑다 means "to be clear; to be clean/sunny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 맑다 (malkda) means "to be clear; to be clean/sunny". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 하늘이 맑다 ("the sky is clear/sunny"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 맑다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the everyday weather collocation
see-through, clean water
맑은 공기 = crisp, clean air
맑다 also describes a clear, alert mind

examples.en: The sky is clear today.
examples.note: 맑다 → 맑아요; ㄺ reads 'malg-a-yo'; the staple weather sentence

examples.ko: 계곡 물이 맑아서 바닥이 다 보여요.
examples.romanization: gyegong muri malgaseo badagi da boyeoyo.
examples.en: The valley water is so clear you can see all the way to the bottom.
examples.note: 맑아서 (-아서) connects the clearness to the visible result

examples.ko: 산에 오니까 공기가 맑아서 기분이 좋아요.
examples.romanization: sane onikka gonggiga malgaseo gibuni joayo.
examples.en: Now that I've come to the mountains, the air is fresh and I feel great.
examples.note: real-situation: 공기가 맑다 = fresh clean air, paired with -으니까 (now that)

extendedVocab.nuance: 맑다 means CLEAR or CLEAN in the sense of pure and transparent — clear see-through water (맑은 물), a cloudless sky (맑은 하늘 = sunny), fresh unpolluted air (맑은 공기), a clear ringing sound or a clear alert mind (정신이 맑다). Its opposite is 흐리다 (cloudy/murky). The key English-speaker pitfall is using 맑다 for a tidy ROOM: English 'clean' covers both purity and tidiness, but a clean, tidy room is 깨끗하다 (방이 깨끗하다), not 맑다. Reserve 맑다 for natural clearness/transparency (water, sky, air, sound) and use 깨끗하다 for cleanliness/neatness of objects and spaces. As a weather word it pairs with 날씨 and 하늘 and is the standard term in forecasts: 내일은 맑겠습니다 (it will be clear/sunny tomorrow). Pronunciation: the ㄺ surfaces as g before a vowel, so 맑아요 is 'malg-a-yo' and 맑게 is 'mak-ge.' As a descriptive adjective it never takes 있다: 물이 맑아요, not 맑아 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 맑다 for a tidy room — cleanliness/neatness of a space is 깨끗하다 (방이 깨끗해요), not 맑아요.
Saying 맑은 날씨예요 is fine, but for 'a clear/cloudless sky' remember the noun pairing 맑은 하늘; don't substitute 깨끗한 하늘.
Mispronouncing the ㄺ cluster — 맑아요 is 'malg-a-yo' (the g sounds before the vowel), not 'mal-a-yo.'

extendedVocab.english: to be cloudy; to be blurry/murky
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 흐리다 means "to be cloudy; to be blurry/murky" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be cloudy; to be blurry/murky" is 흐리다 (heurida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 날씨가 흐리다 ("the weather is cloudy/overcast"). Watch the particle attached to 흐리다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the most common everyday use
cloudy, not see-through water
out of focus / unclear image
흐리다 also fits a faint, fuzzy memory

examples.en: The weather is cloudy today.
examples.note: 흐리다 → 흐려요 (ㅣ + 어 contracts to 려); core weather word

examples.en: It rained, so the river water turned murky.
examples.note: 흐려지다 (-아지다) = became murky; shows the change of state

examples.ko: 사진이 흐려서 글씨가 잘 안 보여요.
examples.romanization: sajini heuryeoseo geulssiga jal an boyeoyo.
examples.en: The photo is blurry, so I can't read the text well.
examples.note: real-situation: 흐리다 = blurry/out of focus, with 흐려서 (-아서) giving the reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 흐리다 is the all-purpose word for 'unclear,' covering CLOUDY weather (흐린 날 an overcast day), MURKY water (흐린 물), and BLURRY/out-of-focus images or hazy memories (사진이 흐리다, 기억이 흐리다). Its opposite is 맑다 (clear), and for weather these two are the everyday pair: 맑아요 (clear/sunny) ↔ 흐려요 (cloudy). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 흐리다 to mean DIRTY: murky water that's hard to see through is 흐리다, but water or a surface that is dirty/filthy is 더럽다 — 흐리다 is about lack of CLARITY, not presence of grime. Note also a near-synonym for blurriness: 뿌옇다/희미하다 also describe a hazy, faint look, but 흐리다 is the plain default learners should master first. The conjugation trap: like other ㅣ-stems, 흐리다 contracts in the 해요-form to 흐려요 (not 흐리어요), past 흐렸어요. As a descriptive adjective it does not take 있다: 하늘이 흐려요, not 흐려 있어요.

Using 흐리다 for dirty things — filthy water or a dirty floor is 더럽다 (물이 더러워요); 흐리다 means murky/unclear, not grimy.
Writing the 해요-form as 흐리어요 — the ㅣ-stem contracts, so it's 흐려요, and the past is 흐렸어요.
Mixing the weather opposites: 'it's clear/sunny' is 맑아요, not 안 흐려요 — use the positive adjective 맑다 rather than negating 흐리다.

extendedVocab.english: to be hard; to be firm/solid
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 단단하다 means "to be hard; to be firm/solid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 단단하다 (dandanhada) = "to be hard; to be firm/solid". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 단단한 돌 ("a hard/solid rock") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 단단하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 단단하다 = firm and solid to the touch
adverb 단단하게 for a secure knot
solid, well-compacted ground
단단하다 extends to a firm, resolute mind

examples.en: This bread is hard.
examples.note: 단단하다 → 단단해요 (하다-adjective); describes firm texture

examples.en: I tied the string firmly, so it won't come undone.
examples.note: 단단하게 (adverb) = securely; ties the firmness to the result

examples.en: The potatoes are still firm because they're undercooked.
examples.note: real-situation: 단단하다 for food that hasn't softened yet, with 덜 (not fully) + reason

extendedVocab.nuance: 단단하다 means HARD, FIRM, or SOLID to the touch — a hard rock, solid ice, firm undercooked potatoes, a tightly-tied knot, well-packed ground — and it extends warmly to a person who is steady, tough-minded, and dependable (마음이 단단하다 mentally strong). Its opposite is 부드럽다 (soft) or 무르다 (mushy/yielding). The nuance English speakers miss is the difference from 딱딱하다: both translate as 'hard,' but 단단하다 has a positive ring of solid, sturdy, well-put-together firmness, while 딱딱하다 stresses STIFF, RIGID, unpleasant hardness — stale rock-hard bread is 딱딱한 빵, and a stiff, awkward atmosphere is 분위기가 딱딱하다 (you would never say 단단한 분위기). So choose 단단하다 when 'firm/solid/sturdy' is a good thing, and 딱딱하다 when 'stiff/rigid' is the point. It is a regular 하다-adjective: 단단해요 / 단단했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 단단하다 and 딱딱하다 as identical — for unpleasantly stiff, rigid hardness (stale bread, a stiff mood) use 딱딱하다; 단단하다 implies positive, solid firmness.
Using 단단하다 for a hard/difficult task — 'hard' as in difficult is 어렵다, not 단단하다; 단단하다 is only physical/mental firmness.
Limiting 단단하다 to food only — it also fits firm ground (땅이 단단하다), a tight knot, and a steady mind (마음이 단단하다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 둥글다 means "to be round" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 둥글다 (dunggeulda) means "to be round". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 둥근 얼굴 ("a round face"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 둥글다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: before a noun the ㄹ drops → 둥근 (not 둥글은)
둥글다 for the overall round form of an object

usagePhrases.en: to have an easygoing, agreeable nature
usagePhrases.note: 둥글다 also means smooth/non-prickly in personality
adverb 둥글게 = in a round arrangement

examples.en: A ball is round.
examples.note: 둥글다 → 둥글어요 in the 해요-form (ㄹ stays before a vowel)

examples.en: The full moon came up round.
examples.note: 둥글게 (adverb) describes the round shape it shows; 보름달 = full moon

examples.en: People sat around in a circle and talked.
examples.note: real-situation: 둥글게 둘러앉다 = to sit gathered in a ring; a natural set phrase

extendedVocab.nuance: 둥글다 means ROUND — having a rounded, circular, or spherical form: a round moon, a round table, a ball, a round face. Beyond shape it has a lovely figurative use for personality: 성격이 둥글다 means easygoing, agreeable, and non-confrontational (literally 'rounded,' i.e. no sharp edges). The fine line learners blur is 둥글다 vs 동그랗다: both mean 'round,' but 둥글다 is the broader, often three-dimensional 'rounded' (a globe, a face, a mound), while 동그랗다 feels SMALL, NEAT, and precisely circular (a little dot, round wide eyes: 눈이 동그래지다 = eyes go round with surprise). The grammar trap is the ㄹ-stem rule: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, so the noun-modifying form is 둥근 N (둥근 얼굴, 둥근 달), never 둥글은. In the 해요-form the ㄹ stays: 둥글어요. The related noun is 동그라미 (a drawn circle). As an adjective it does not take 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop before a noun — it's 둥근 얼굴 / 둥근 식탁, not 둥글은 얼굴.
Using 둥글다 where 동그랗다 fits better — for small, neat, perfectly round things (wide surprised eyes, a little dot) Koreans prefer 동그랗다.
Writing the 해요-form as 둥근어요 — before a vowel ending the ㄹ stays, so it's 둥글어요 (the drop only happens before ㄴ).

extendedVocab.english: to be pointy; to be sharp (in shape)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뾰족하다 means "to be pointy; to be sharp (in shape)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be pointy; to be sharp (in shape)" is 뾰족하다 (ppyojokada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 뾰족한 연필 ("a sharp(ened) pencil"). Watch the particle attached to 뾰족하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뾰족하다 = having a pointed tip
끝 (tip) is the typical subject

usagePhrases.en: a clever way out / a good solution
usagePhrases.note: idiom: 뾰족한 수가 없다 = no good solution
adverb 뾰족하게 + 깎다 (whittle/sharpen)

examples.en: The pencil is sharp (pointy).
examples.note: 뾰족하다 → 뾰족해요 (하다-adjective); about the pointed tip

examples.ko: 이 가위는 끝이 뾰족해서 조심해야 해요.
examples.romanization: i gawineun kkeuchi ppyojokaeseo josimhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: The tip of these scissors is pointy, so you have to be careful.
examples.note: 끝이 뾰족하다 = the end is pointed; 뾰족해서 (-아서) gives the reason for caution

examples.ko: 좋은 방법을 찾아봤지만 뾰족한 수가 없네요.
examples.romanization: joeun bangbeobeul chajabwatjiman ppyojokan suga eopsneyo.
examples.en: I looked for a good way, but there's no clever solution.
examples.note: real-situation: idiomatic 뾰족한 수가 없다 = no bright/sure-fire way out

extendedVocab.nuance: 뾰족하다 describes a POINTY, sharp-TIPPED SHAPE — a sharpened pencil, a pointed roof, a peaked mountain, the pointy end of scissors. The key distinction from 날카롭다 is shape vs cutting power: 뾰족하다 is about coming to a POINT, whereas 날카롭다 is about a keen, SHARP EDGE that cuts (a knife) — and 날카롭다 also extends to a sharp/cutting tone or gaze (날카로운 눈빛), which 뾰족하다 does not. So a well-sharpened knife is 칼이 날카롭다 (cuts well), while the tip being pointed is 칼끝이 뾰족하다 (shape). There is a very common idiom to memorize: 뾰족한 수가 없다 = 'there's no clever/sure solution,' a set phrase you'll hear when someone is stuck. Spelling is the trap: it is 뾰 with the double consonant ㅃ plus ㅛ — write 뾰족하다, not 뽀족하다 or 뾰쪽하다. It's a regular 하다-adjective: 뾰족해요 / 뾰족했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 뾰족하다 for a knife that cuts well — a keen cutting edge is 날카롭다; 뾰족하다 only describes a pointed shape/tip.
Spelling it 뽀족하다 — the correct form has 뾰 (ㅃ + ㅛ): 뾰족하다.
Applying 뾰족하다 to a sharp tone or sharp eyes — a cutting gaze/voice is 날카롭다 (날카로운 눈빛), not 뾰족한 눈빛.

There is a very common idiom to memorize: 뾰족한 수가 없다 = 'there's no clever/sure solution,' a set phrase you'll hear when someone is stuck. It's a regular 하다-adjective: 뾰족해요 / 뾰족했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.

The key distinction from 날카롭다 is shape vs cutting power: 뾰족하다 is about coming to a POINT, whereas 날카롭다 is about a keen, SHARP EDGE that cuts (a knife) — and 날카롭다 also extends to a sharp/cutting tone or gaze (날카로운 눈빛), which 뾰족하다 does not. So a well-sharpened knife is 칼이 날카롭다 (cuts well), while the tip being pointed is 칼끝이 뾰족하다 (shape).
Spelling is the trap: it is 뾰 with the double consonant ㅃ plus ㅛ — write 뾰족하다, not 뽀족하다 or 뾰쪽하다.

extendedVocab.english: to be flat; to be even/level
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 평평하다 means "to be flat; to be even/level" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 평평하다 (pyeongpyeonghada) = "to be flat; to be even/level". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 땅이 평평하다 ("the ground is level/flat") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 평평하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 평평하다 = an even surface, no bumps or slope
smooth, level path with no inclines

usagePhrases.en: to spread out flat / smooth out
usagePhrases.note: adverb 평평하게 + 펴다 (spread/flatten)
a level base, good for placing things

examples.en: This road is flat.
examples.note: 평평하다 → 평평해요 (하다-adjective); about a smooth, level surface

examples.en: The floor is level, so it's good for setting up a desk.
examples.note: 평평해서 (-아서) links the levelness to why it's convenient

examples.en: I looked for a flat spot to pitch the tent.
examples.note: real-situation: 평평한 곳 = a level patch of ground, exactly what you need for camping

extendedVocab.nuance: 평평하다 means FLAT and LEVEL — an even surface with no bumps, dips, or slopes: level ground, a flat road, a smooth level floor or tabletop. It is built from the repeated Sino-Korean syllable 平 'flat/level' (平平), the very same 平 in 평지 (flatland) and 평야 (a plain), so the root literally doubles down on 'level.' Two confusions to avoid. First, the look-alike 평범하다 (平凡 'ordinary/common'): it sounds and looks similar but means 'ordinary, average, nothing special' about a person or thing — never use 평평하다 for that. Second, 납작하다: that describes something SQUASHED FLAT or low-profile (a flat squashed box, a flat nose), i.e. flattened in thickness, whereas 평평하다 describes a surface being EVEN and level. So flat level ground is 평평한 땅, but a flattened/squashed shape is 납작한 상자. It is a regular 하다-adjective: 평평해요 / 평평했어요, and as an adjective it does not take 있다.

Confusing 평평하다 (flat/level) with 평범하다 (ordinary/average) — they look alike but mean completely different things; an ordinary person is 평범한 사람, not 평평한 사람.
Using 평평하다 for a squashed, low, flattened shape — that's 납작하다 (납작한 상자); 평평하다 is for an even, level surface.
Treating 평평하다 as describing height — it describes evenness, so 'low ground' is still 낮은 땅, while bumpless level ground is 평평한 땅.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 많이 means "a lot, much, many" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 많이 (mani) means "a lot, much, many". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 많이 먹어요 ("I eat a lot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 많이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Sits directly before the verb; the default way to mark a large amount
Handy when ordering food or asking a server for more
Before an adjective 많이 shifts from 'a lot' to a degree word, 'very'
너무 많이 마셨어요 = I drank too much; 너무 adds the 'over the line' feeling

examples.en: It's raining a lot today.
examples.note: 비가 오다 is the set verb for 'it rains'; 많이 measures the quantity

examples.en: I really like Korean food.
examples.note: With 좋아하다, 많이 means the feeling is strong, like 'a lot'

examples.en: Please help yourself / enjoy your meal.
examples.note: 드세요 is the honorific of 먹다; this is what a host warmly says at the table

extendedVocab.nuance: 많이 is the adverb form of the adjective 많다 ('to be many/much') and is the everyday word for 'a lot/much', sitting right in front of the verb it modifies (많이 먹어요, 많이 자요). Its near-synonym is 너무: 많이 just states a large amount neutrally, while 너무 carries an 'excessive, over the line' feeling, so 많이 매워요 is 'quite spicy' but 너무 매워요 is 'too spicy (uncomfortably)'. With feeling-verbs and adjectives 많이 stretches to mean 'very/badly', as in 많이 아파요 ('it hurts a lot'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the adjective 많다 directly before a verb — you must use the adverb 많이 (많이 먹어요, never 많다 먹어요) — and remembering that, like all Korean adverbs, it comes before the verb, not after it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using the adjective 많다 where the verb needs the adverb: before a verb it is 많이 먹어요, not 많다 먹어요. 많다 can only sit at the end as a predicate (책이 많아요).
Putting 많이 after the verb on the English word order: 먹어요 많이 sounds broken; Korean adverbs go before the verb (많이 먹어요).
Treating 많이 and 너무 as interchangeable: 너무 implies 'too much/excessive', so 너무 좋아요 ('I like it so much') and 많이 좋아요 carry slightly different feelings.

extendedVocab.english: a little, a bit, a few
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 조금 means "a little, a bit, a few" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "a little, a bit, a few" is 조금 (jogeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조금 주세요 ("Please give me a little"). Watch the particle attached to 조금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The exact opposite of 많이; requests a small amount
Before an adjective it softens the degree to 'a bit'
조금만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just a moment; 만 ('only') caps it small
A fixed time phrase meaning 'a moment ago'

examples.en: I speak a little Korean.
examples.note: The perfect modest answer for a beginner; 조금 lowers the claim

examples.en: I drank a little water.
examples.note: 조금 before the verb marks a small quantity of the object

examples.en: I'm a little tired today.
examples.note: 조금 softens 피곤하다 so you don't overstate it

extendedVocab.nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. Its closest relative is its own contracted form 좀: 조금 is the full, slightly more careful version you can write and say, while 좀 is the quick spoken reduction (조금만요 ↔ 좀만요 are the same idea). Compared with the noun-ish 약간 ('slightly', a touch more formal/written), 조금 is the warm conversational choice. It naturally collocates with quantities and gentle states — 조금 더 ('a little more'), 조금 있다가 ('in a little while') — and its softness makes it ideal for modest answers and polite requests. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 좀 in speech and not realizing it is just 조금 reduced, and over-stacking it with big-amount words: 조금 많이 is self-contradictory because 조금 only ever points to a small degree.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Not recognizing that 조금 usually contracts to 좀 in casual speech; both are correct, but learners who only study 조금 get lost when they hear 좀.
Pairing 조금 with large amounts: 조금 많이 contradicts itself; 조금 is strictly a small degree, so use 많이 or 너무 for big quantities.
Confusing 조금 with 잠깐/잠시 for time: 조금만 means a small amount, while 잠깐만 specifically means 'for a short moment' of time.

structuredNuance.t: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 좀 means "a bit, a little (casual); please" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 좀 (jom) = "a bit, a little (casual); please". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 좀 비싸요 ("It's a bit pricey") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 좀, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The short, spoken reduction of 조금
Here 좀 is a softener, not really an amount, like a gentle 'please'
Extremely common when ordering or asking for things at a shop
잠깐만요 buys a moment of time; pairs naturally with 좀 in requests

examples.en: It's a bit cold in here.
examples.note: 좀 makes the comment sound soft and offhand rather than a complaint

examples.en: Some water, please.
examples.note: Slipping in 좀 makes the request friendlier and more natural than 물 주세요

examples.en: I'm a little busy today.
examples.note: 좀 cushions a refusal so it lands gently

extendedVocab.nuance: 좀 is the contracted, spoken form of 조금 and is everywhere in daily conversation. Its key second life — the part that trips up English speakers — is as a request softener: in 물 좀 주세요 or 좀 도와주세요, 좀 is not measuring a 'little' amount at all but functioning like 'please/if you would', taking the bluntness off a command. So 물 주세요 is grammatically fine but can feel abrupt, whereas 물 좀 주세요 sounds warm and natural. Compared with the full 조금, 좀 is purely conversational and a touch more casual; in formal writing or stiff announcements you revert to 조금 or a fuller polite request form. Collocates constantly with request verbs (좀 주세요, 좀 해 주세요, 좀 보여 주세요) and with mild complaints (좀 춥다, 좀 그렇다). The pitfall is over-literal reading: don't try to translate the 'softener' 좀 as 'a little', and don't drop it from requests — Koreans add it precisely to sound polite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 좀 always means 'a little': in 좀 도와주세요 it works as a politeness softener ('please'), not a quantity. Translating it as 'help me a little' misses the tone.
Dropping 좀 from requests to be 'cleaner': bare commands like 물 주세요 can sound blunt; native speakers add 좀 (물 좀 주세요) to soften them.
Using 좀 in formal writing or speeches, where it reads as too casual; switch to 조금 or a full polite form there.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 다 means "all, everything, completely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 다 (da) means "all, everything, completely". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다 먹었어요 ("I ate it all"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Right before the verb; signals the action is complete or the whole thing covered

usagePhrases.en: Everything is fine / I'm good with all of it
usagePhrases.note: Means 'all of it' is acceptable

usagePhrases.en: I did it all / I'm done
usagePhrases.note: The natural way to report finishing a task
거의 다 왔어요 = we're almost there; 거의 ('nearly') tempers 다

examples.en: I finished all my homework.
examples.note: 다 + 했어요 says the whole thing is complete

examples.en: I ate all my food.
examples.note: What you say when your plate is empty

examples.en: All my friends came.
examples.note: Here 다 covers 'all of them', the people, not completion

extendedVocab.nuance: 다 is a small but powerful native word meaning 'all / everything / completely', placed directly before the verb. It carries two senses that context separates: completion of an action (다 했어요 = 'all done', the task is finished) and total coverage of a group (다 왔어요 = 'everyone came'). Its near-synonym is the fuller 모두; 다 is the short, ultra-frequent spoken default, while 모두 is a touch more deliberate and can also stand alone as a noun ('everyone'). A subtle bonus sense is 'about to be used up/finished' — 시간 다 됐어요 ('time's up'). The classic English-speaker pitfalls are mixing the look-alike one-syllable adverbs (다 'all' vs 또 'again' vs 더 'more'), and English word order: 다 must precede the verb (다 먹었어요), never follow it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the short adverbs by shape: 다 (all), 또 (again), and 더 (more) are all one syllable but mean different things — 다 먹었어요 ('ate it all') vs 또 먹었어요 ('ate again').
Placing 다 after the verb: it goes before, so 다 먹었어요, not 먹었어요 다.
Reading every 다 as 'completely' when it often means 'all of them (people/things)': 친구들이 다 왔어요 is about everyone, not about thoroughness.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 모두 means "all, everyone, altogether" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "all, everyone, altogether" is 모두 (modu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 모두 모였어요 ("Everyone gathered"). Watch the particle attached to 모두 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: A clearer, fuller 'all/everyone' than the terse 다
모두 합쳐서 얼마예요? = how much for everything together?
여러분 모두 환영해요 = welcome, everyone; 모두 trails the noun as 'all'
Stacking 모두 + 다 adds emphasis: 'all of it, the whole lot'

examples.en: There are four of us in my family.
examples.note: 모두 sums up a total head count, 'in all'

examples.en: Hello, everyone!
examples.note: 모두 as a noun addressing the whole group

examples.en: All my friends are Korean.
examples.note: 모두 here covers 'all of them' as an adverb

extendedVocab.nuance: 모두 means 'all / everyone / in total' and feels a notch fuller, clearer, and slightly more formal than the very short native 다. Its distinctive trait — and the reason to learn it alongside 다 — is its flexibility of part of speech: it can be a noun ('everyone': 모두 환영해요, 모두의 꿈 'everyone's dream') or an adverb ('all': 모두 모였어요), whereas 다 leans adverbial. Near-synonyms split by feel: 다 is the quick everyday choice, 모두 is the cleaner one for counting or addressing a whole group, and 전부 ('the entirety/the whole') stresses 'every last bit' and pairs well with things and totals. It collocates with gatherings, totals, and greetings (모두 모이다, 모두 합쳐서, 여러분 모두). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 모두 is only an adverb and only for people; it also stands as a noun and freely covers things and sums (모두 합쳐서).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 모두 is only an adverb: it can stand as a noun meaning 'everyone' (모두 안녕하세요, 모두의 의견 'everyone's opinion').
Restricting 모두 to people: it equally covers things and totals, as in 모두 합쳐서 ('all together in total') or 짐을 모두 챙겼어요 ('I packed all the bags').
Treating 모두 and 다 as identical in register: 다 is the casual spoken default, while 모두 sounds a touch fuller and fits writing or addressing a crowd.

structuredNuance.t: 모두 means 'all / everyone / in total' and feels a notch fuller, clearer, and slightly more formal than the very short native 다. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 함께 means "together, along with" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 함께 (hamkke) = "together, along with". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 함께 가요 ("Let's go together") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 함께, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A clear, slightly polished way to say 'together'
A common, warm invitation to share a meal
친구와 함께 = together with a friend; needs the 와/과 particle
다 함께 노래해요 = let's all sing together; 다 + 함께 = everyone, together

examples.en: Let's watch a movie together this weekend.
examples.note: 함께 before the verb means 'do it together'

examples.en: I had dinner with my family.
examples.note: The pattern is N과 함께 = 'together with N'

examples.en: Let's study together.
examples.note: A friendly suggestion to a classmate; 함께 sounds inclusive and warm

extendedVocab.nuance: 함께 means 'together / along with' and is the slightly warmer, more polished sibling of the everyday 같이. The two overlap almost completely in meaning, but they differ in feel and grammar habits: 같이 is the casual spoken default and also doubles as 'like/as' with 처럼-style nouns (눈같이 'like snow'), whereas 함께 is purely 'together', sounds a touch softer and more heartfelt, and shows up in invitations, slogans, and announcements (함께 가요, 함께 만들어요 'let's build it together'). Both commonly take the particle 와/과 (or casual 하고/랑) to name the companion: 친구와 함께, 가족과 함께. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping that particle — 'with my friend' must be 친구와 함께, not 친구 함께 — and assuming 함께 and 같이 are sharply different when they are really register twins, with 함께 just sounding a shade more polished.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 함께 and 같이 as sharply different words: they overlap closely; 함께 just sounds a bit softer and more polished, 같이 a bit more casual.
Omitting the particle 와/과 before 함께 when naming the companion: it is 친구와 함께, not 친구 함께.
Forgetting 같이 has an extra 'like/as' meaning that 함께 lacks: 별같이 빛나다 ('shine like a star') cannot use 함께.

structuredNuance.t: 함께 means 'together / along with' and is the slightly warmer, more polished sibling of the everyday 같이. It shows up in invitations, slogans, and announcements (함께 가요, 함께 만들어요 'let's build it together'). It commonly takes the particle 와/과 (or casual 하고/랑) to name the companion: 친구와 함께, 가족과 함께.

함께 and 같이 overlap almost completely in meaning, but they differ in feel and grammar habits: 같이 is the casual spoken default and also doubles as 'like/as' with 처럼-style nouns (눈같이 'like snow'), whereas 함께 is purely 'together' and sounds a touch softer and more heartfelt. extendedVocab.explanation: 그냥 (geunyang) means "just, simply, for no special reason". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그냥 집에 있어요 ("I'm just staying home"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그냥 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Means 'simply' doing something, nothing special going on

usagePhrases.en: I just feel kind of off
usagePhrases.note: A vague, soft way to avoid a full explanation
Here it means 'plain / without changes / as-is'
그냥 standing alone answers 'just because'

examples.en: I just want to rest today.
examples.note: 그냥 softens it to 'simply rest, nothing planned'

examples.en: I just asked, no special reason.
examples.note: A very common casual cushion for a question

examples.en: For coffee, just a plain americano, please.
examples.note: 그냥 = 'just the basic/default one'

extendedVocab.nuance: 그냥 means 'just / simply / for no particular reason' and is one of the most useful filler-style words in casual Korean, prized because it lets you decline to over-explain. Its sense flexes with context: 'simply, with no agenda' (그냥 집에 있어요), 'plain / as it is, unchanged' (그냥 주세요, 그냥 아메리카노), and the stand-alone 'no reason' reply (왜? 그냥). Its near-neighbor 그저 ('merely, simply') is more literary and emphatic, while 막 ('just, randomly/recklessly') is rougher and busier — so 그냥 is the gentle, neutral middle. It collocates with low-key states and soft hedges (그냥 좀 그래요, 그냥 그래요 'it's so-so', 그냥 한번 'just once for the heck of it'). The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for one fixed translation — 'just' won't always fit — and over-using it in formal or business contexts, where its vagueness can read as evasive or unpolished.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pinning 그냥 to one English word: it slides between 'just', 'plain/as-is', and 'no reason' depending on context — 그냥 주세요 ('as is') vs 그냥 물어봤어요 ('no special reason').
Over-using 그냥 in formal or business settings: it is casual and its vagueness can sound evasive; a fuller explanation fits there.
Confusing 그냥 with 그래서 ('so/therefore') because both start with 그: they are unrelated — 그냥 means 'just', 그래서 links cause and result.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 꼭 means "definitely, surely, without fail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "definitely, surely, without fail" is 꼭 (kkok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 꼭 갈게요 ("I'll definitely go"). Watch the particle attached to 꼭 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Adds a firm, sincere promise to the verb
A warm but insistent invitation
Stresses that something is genuinely essential
Standard in reminders and instructions

examples.en: I'll be sure to call tomorrow.
examples.note: 꼭 makes the promise sound committed, not casual

examples.en: Make sure to take your medicine.
examples.note: A caring reminder; 꼭 = without fail

examples.en: Let's definitely go together next time.
examples.note: Sincere, friendly suggestion

extendedVocab.nuance: 꼭 means 'definitely / for sure / without fail' and injects strong intention or a firm request into a sentence: with promises it sounds sincere and committed (꼭 갈게요), and with requests it makes them warm but insistent (꼭 오세요). Its near-synonym 반드시 carries the same 'without fail' core but is more formal, rule-like, and written (regulations and warnings favor 반드시 …해야 한다), whereas 꼭 is the warmer, more personal everyday choice; 절대 is its negative-side cousin ('absolutely not', 절대 안 돼요). 꼭 also has a secondary 'exactly/just like' sense (꼭 엄마 같아요 'just like Mom'), though learners use the 'for sure' meaning most. The English-speaker pitfall is the look-alike/sound-alike 곧 ('soon'): 꼭 갈게요 ('I'll definitely go') is a promise of certainty, while 곧 갈게요 ('I'll go soon') is about timing — keep the tense 꼭 distinct from the timing 곧.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 꼭 (for sure) with 곧 (soon): they look and sound close but differ — 꼭 갈게요 is certainty, 곧 갈게요 is timing.
Using 꼭 for casual maybes: it asserts real certainty or a firm wish, so it clashes with '아마' ('probably') — say 아마 갈 거예요 for a tentative plan.
Reaching for 꼭 in stiff regulations: rules and official warnings prefer the formal 반드시 (반드시 착용해야 합니다), while 꼭 stays personal and warm.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 바로 means "right away; exactly, right (there)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 바로 (baro) = "right away; exactly, right (there)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 바로 가요 ("I'll go right away") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 바로, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The time sense: immediately, with no delay
The location sense: points to an exact spot
바로 앞에 있어요 = it's right in front; 바로 pins the position
Confirms 'yes, precisely that one'

examples.en: I'll go right now.
examples.note: 지금 바로 = right this very moment, no waiting

examples.en: The school is right next to my house.
examples.note: 바로 옆 = directly beside

examples.en: Let's leave right away.
examples.note: 바로 before the verb signals immediacy

extendedVocab.nuance: 바로 carries two everyday senses split by context: 'right away / immediately' with actions (바로 가요, 바로 출발해요) and 'exactly / right (there)' with places and identifications (바로 여기, 바로 앞, 바로 그거예요). For the time sense, its near-synonym 곧 means 'soon / shortly' — a small gap remains — while 바로 means truly 'this instant, with zero delay', so 바로 가요 is more immediate than 곧 가요. For the location/identification sense, 바로 tightens 'next to/in front of' into 'directly, precisely' and has no single English twin; it behaves like 'right' in 'right next to'. It collocates tightly with position words (바로 옆/앞/뒤/위) and with emphatic confirmations (바로 그거, 바로 너 'you, exactly'). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 바로 only means 'immediately' and missing its 'exactly/right-there' use, plus stranding it from the word it marks — keep 바로 hugging the verb or noun (바로 앞, not 앞 바로).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 바로 only means 'immediately': it equally means 'exactly/right (there)' for places and things, as in 바로 여기 and 바로 그거예요.
Separating 바로 from the word it modifies: it must hug the verb or noun — 바로 앞, not 앞 바로; 바로 가요, not 가요 바로.
Swapping 바로 and 곧 for the time sense: 바로 가요 ('go this instant') is more immediate than 곧 가요 ('go soon'), which leaves a short gap.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빨리 means "quickly, fast, hurry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 빨리 (ppalli) means "quickly, fast, hurry". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 빨리 가요 ("Let's go quickly"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 빨리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The default word for doing an action fast
Doubled for emphasis; a famous shorthand for the Korean pace of life
Politely urging someone to hurry
더 빨리 해 주세요 = please do it faster; 더 ('more') raises the speed

examples.en: Hurry up, the bus is coming!
examples.note: Everyday urging when you're in a rush

examples.en: I ate quickly.
examples.note: 빨리 before the verb describes the speed of the action

examples.en: Get well soon.
examples.note: A caring set phrase to someone who is sick; 낫다 ('heal') is ㅅ-irregular

extendedVocab.nuance: 빨리 means 'quickly / fast', the adverb derived from the adjective 빠르다 ('to be fast'), and is among the first action adverbs a beginner needs. Doubled as 빨리빨리, it famously captures the Korean 'hurry, hurry' tempo and adds real urgency. Watch the synonym line with 일찍: 빨리 is about speed ('do it fast'), while 일찍 is about an early point in time ('early'), so 빨리 일어났어요 means 'I got up fast' but 일찍 일어났어요 means 'I got up early' — English 'quick/early' blurs this. The deeper pitfall is the adverb-vs-adjective split: from the stem 빠르- you use the adverb 빨리 before a verb (빨리 먹어요), but to describe a noun you must switch to the adjective form 빠른 (빠른 차 'a fast car') — never 빨리 차. 빠르다 is a 르-irregular, so its polite form is 빨라요. It collocates with motion and effort verbs (빨리 가다/오다/하다) and warm wishes (빨리 나으세요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up the adverb 빨리 (quickly) with the adjective 빠르다 (to be fast): before a verb use 빨리 (빨리 먹어요); as a sentence predicate use 빨라요 (차가 빨라요).
Using 빨리 to describe a noun: 'a fast car' is 빠른 차, never 빨리 차 — noun-modifying needs the adjective form 빠른.
Confusing 빨리 (fast, speed) with 일찍 (early, time): 빨리 와요 ('come quickly') is about pace, 일찍 와요 ('come early') is about the hour.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 더욱 means "even more, all the more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "even more, all the more" is 더욱 (deouk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 더욱 좋아요 ("It's even better"). Watch the particle attached to 더욱 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Fuller and warmer than the plain 더
A staple of sincere promises
Doubling to 더욱더 pushes the increase strongly
A kind, slightly formal good wish

examples.en: I'll work even harder from now on.
examples.note: A polished, sincere commitment

examples.ko: 날씨가 더우니까 물을 더욱 많이 마셔요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga deounikka mureul deoung mani masyeoyo.
examples.en: Since it's hot, drink even more water.
examples.note: 더욱 강조 = stresses 'even more so'

examples.en: After practicing, it got even better.
examples.note: 더욱 marks a further step up from before

extendedVocab.nuance: 더욱 means 'even more / all the more' and is the fuller, warmer, slightly more formal cousin of the basic comparative adverb 더 ('more'). The two share a core, but they split by register and rhythm: 더 is the plain everyday workhorse (더 주세요 'give me more'), while 더욱 adds a literary, heartfelt lift and shows up in earnest statements, speeches, and good wishes (더욱 노력할게요, 더욱 건강하세요), with the reduplicated 더욱더 cranking the emphasis higher still. A neighboring word, 한층 ('a notch more'), is similarly elevated and written. 더욱 collocates with effort, improvement, and wishes (더욱 열심히, 더욱 좋아지다, 더욱 발전하다). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 더욱 in casual chat or texting, where it sounds stiff — there you just say 더 — and assuming it is a wholly separate word from 더 rather than its more polished register-partner.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 더욱 is unrelated to 더: they share the 'more' meaning; 더욱 is just fuller and more formal, 더 is the plain everyday form.
Using 더욱 in casual texting or chit-chat: it sounds stiff and literary there — say 더 instead (더 좋아 rather than 더욱 좋아).
Forgetting 더욱 leans toward earnest, positive contexts: it fits 더욱 발전하다 / 더욱 건강하세요, but a neutral 'a bit more please' is just 더 주세요, not 더욱 주세요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 참 means "really, truly, quite" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 참 (cham) = "really, truly, quite". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 참 좋아요 ("It's really nice") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 참, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A warm, gentle 'really', softer than 너무
A sincere compliment with a kind tone
Everyday warm praise for food
참 standing alone flags a sudden 'oh, that reminds me'

examples.en: The weather is really lovely today.
examples.note: 참 lends a soft, sincere, almost admiring feeling

examples.en: Your Korean pronunciation is really good.
examples.note: A warm, genuine compliment; pairs well with 네요

examples.en: Oh, by the way, are you free tomorrow?
examples.note: 참 as a 'that just reminded me' opener

extendedVocab.nuance: 참 means 'really / truly / quite' but with a gentle, sincere, faintly admiring warmth that makes it lovely for heartfelt compliments (참 좋아요, 참 예뻐요, 참 착하다 'so kind'). Its register is the dividing line against its near-synonyms: 너무 is strong and can tip into 'too much', 정말/진짜 are emphatic 'really!', while 참 is the soft, warm, slightly old-fashioned 'really' that sounds caring rather than intense — elders use it often. A completely separate, very common use is the stand-alone interjection 참! meaning 'oh, that reminds me!' when something pops into your head mid-conversation. It collocates with gentle praise and pleasant states (참 좋다, 참 예쁘다, 참 잘했어요 'well done'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting 참 to hit hard like 너무 and being puzzled by its softness, and reading the interjection 참! as an intensifier when it actually signals a sudden memory.

Reading every 참 as an intensifier: standing alone, 참! means 'oh, that reminds me!', a discourse marker, not 'really'.
Expecting 참 to sound strong: it is a soft, warm 'really' (참 좋아요), unlike the heavier 너무 or emphatic 진짜/정말.
Confusing 참 with 잘 ('well'): 참 잘했어요 stacks both — 참 ('really') intensifies 잘 ('well') — so they are not the same word.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가득 means "fully, full (to the brim)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 가득 (gadeuk) means "fully, full (to the brim)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가득 채우다 ("to fill it full"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가득 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Describes filling a container right to the top
방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 = the room is packed with people
가득 담아 주세요 = please fill it right up
Standard at a gas station: 가득이요 = full tank

examples.en: I poured the cup full of water.
examples.note: 가득 = right up to the brim

examples.en: The mart is packed with people.
examples.note: 가득하다 = to be full/packed; 가득 + 하다

examples.en: Please fill it all the way.
examples.note: Useful at a gas station or when asking for a full serving

extendedVocab.nuance: 가득 means 'fully / full to the brim' and specifically describes a container, space, or even a feeling being filled completely — its meaning is about capacity reached, not just quantity. This is the key line against its near-synonym 많이: 많이 marks 'a large amount' in general (많이 먹어요 'eat a lot'), while 가득 says 'filled to the limit', so 컵에 물이 가득 means the cup is brimming, not merely that there is much water around. It pairs habitually with filling verbs — 채우다 ('fill'), 차다 ('become full'), 담다 ('put in'), 넣다 ('insert') — and the bound form 가득하다 means 'to be full/packed' (사람으로 가득하다). It also extends to emotion (행복이 가득하다 'full of happiness'). A handy real-life anchor is the gas station, where 가득이요 means 'fill the tank'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 가득 as a general 'a lot' with any verb; it only fits filling/packing situations, so 가득 먹어요 sounds odd where you want 많이 먹어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가득 as a general 'a lot' with any verb: it means 'filled full', so 가득 먹어요 is odd — say 많이 먹어요 for 'eat a lot'.
Treating 가득 and 많이 as identical: 많이 is plain quantity ('much'), 가득 is 'to the brim/capacity' — 물이 많아요 vs 컵에 물이 가득 차 있어요.
Forgetting 가득 wants a filling verb: it naturally needs 채우다/차다/담다/넣다 or the form 가득하다, not just any action verb.

structuredNuance.t: 가득 means 'fully / full to the brim' and specifically describes a container, space, or even a feeling being filled completely — its meaning is about capacity reached, not just quantity. It also extends to emotion (행복이 가득하다 'full of happiness'). A handy real-life anchor is the gas station, where 가득이요 means 'fill the tank'.

The key line against its near-synonym 많이: 많이 marks 'a large amount' in general (많이 먹어요 'eat a lot'), while 가득 says 'filled to the limit', so 컵에 물이 가득 means the cup is brimming, not merely that there is much water around.
The English-speaker pitfall is using 가득 as a general 'a lot' with any verb; it only fits filling/packing situations, so 가득 먹어요 sounds odd where you want 많이 먹어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 푹 means "deeply, soundly (rest/sleep); thoroughly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "deeply, soundly (rest/sleep); thoroughly" is 푹 (puk). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 푹 쉬다 ("to rest fully"). Watch the particle attached to 푹 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 푹 쉬세요 = rest up well, a caring set phrase
푹 잤어요 = I slept deeply and well
In cooking: boil slowly until soft and rich
드라마에 푹 빠졌어요 = I'm totally hooked on the drama

examples.en: Please rest up well at home today.
examples.note: A warm thing to say to someone who's tired or unwell

examples.en: I slept soundly yesterday, so I feel refreshed.
examples.note: 푹 자다 = sleep deeply; pairs with feeling 개운하다

examples.en: For a cold, resting well is best.
examples.note: Standard caring advice

extendedVocab.nuance: 푹 is a vivid native mimetic adverb (의태어) meaning doing something deeply, soundly, and thoroughly, and it lives most in the caring collocations 푹 쉬다 ('rest well') and 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly'), which beginners hear constantly as warm wishes. Unlike a general intensifier such as 많이 ('a lot') or 잘 ('well'), 푹 adds a specific texture of 'completely, comfortably, all the way down' — 푹 자다 isn't just sleeping much, it's sleeping deep and restoring. It splits into a few homes: rest/sleep (푹 쉬다/자다), slow cooking ('simmer until tender', 푹 끓이다/삶다), and the figurative 푹 빠지다 ('be totally absorbed/hooked'). It also describes sinking softly into something (소파에 푹 파묻히다). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 푹 as an all-purpose 'very'; it is not — it specifically means 'deeply/soundly/thoroughly' and only suits resting, sleeping, simmering, and being absorbed. Above all, memorize the everyday set phrase 푹 쉬세요, the natural way to tell someone to rest up.

Treating 푹 as a general 'very': it specifically means deeply/soundly/thoroughly and fits resting, sleeping, simmering, and being absorbed — not any adjective.
Forgetting the high-frequency set phrase 푹 쉬세요: this is the natural caring way to tell someone to rest, and learners often reach for a clunkier phrase instead.
Swapping 푹 for 잘 carelessly: 잘 자요 ('sleep well') is the everyday goodnight, while 푹 자다 stresses deep, sound sleep — close but 푹 adds the 'all the way down' texture.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매일 means "every day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 매일 (maeil) = "every day". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 매일 아침 ("every morning") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 매일, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 매(每) 'each' stacks before a time word: 매일 아침, 매일 밤, 매주 월요일.

usagePhrases.en: day after day, every single day
usagePhrases.note: Reduplicating it adds warmth/emphasis, common in songs and encouragement.
거의 (almost) is the natural softener when it isn't literally 100% of days.
Write it closed (매일같이, not 매일 같이) — it stresses how relentlessly often, sometimes with mild complaint.

examples.en: I study Korean every day.
examples.note: Core habit pattern; 매일 sits right before the verb phrase.

examples.en: I get up at seven every morning.
examples.note: Here the clock time takes 에 (일곱 시에), but 매일 itself never does.

examples.ko: 요즘 거의 매일 비가 와서 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum geoui maeil biga waseo himdeureoyo.
examples.en: Lately it rains almost every day, so it's tough.
examples.note: 거의 매일 + a real complaint; shows the word in a fuller, lived-in sentence.

extendedVocab.nuance: 매일 means 'every day' and is the default word for habits and routines. The 매 is Sino-Korean 每 'each/every', and 일 is 日 'day', so it literally reads 'each-day'; swap the second half for 매주 每週 'every week', 매월/매달 'every month', 매년 每年 'every year'. Crucially 매일 is an adverb of frequency, so unlike clock times it takes NO 에 — say 매일 운동해요, never 매일에. English speakers also confuse it with 하루, which is the counter 'one day / a day' (하루 종일 'all day long'); 매일 is the recurring habit, 하루 is a single day. A near rival is 날마다 'each day', which is interchangeable in meaning but feels a touch more literary/measured, while 매일 is the plain everyday choice. It almost always comes before the verb and pairs happily with 거의, 아침/밤, and the emphatic 매일같이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 매일에 공부해요 — frequency adverbs take no particle. Drop 에: 매일 공부해요. (The 에 belongs only on the clock time, e.g. 일곱 시에.)
Using 하루 where you mean a repeated habit, e.g. ✗ 하루 운동해요 for 'I exercise every day'. 하루 = one single day; the habit is 매일 운동해요.
Writing the verb 늘다-style 매일다 or treating it as a noun with 을/를. 매일 is purely an adverb — it modifies the verb directly.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 나중에 means "later" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 나중에 (najunge) means "later". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 나중에 봐요 ("see you later"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 나중에 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Standard friendly sign-off when you'll meet again at no fixed time.
Polite way to defer without committing to when; 연락하다 = to get in touch.
Frequently paired with 다시 (again) for 'I'll try again later'.
Common warning frame: 나중에 + a future consequence.

examples.en: Let's talk about that later.
examples.note: Gently deferring a topic right now; 나중에 before the verb.

examples.en: I'm busy now, so I'll call back later.
examples.note: Pairs 지금 (now) against 나중에 (later) — the contrast that defines the word.

examples.ko: 이거 지금 안 하면 나중에 후회할 거예요.
examples.romanization: igeo jigeum an hamyeon najunge huhoehal geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you don't do this now, you'll regret it later.
examples.note: Real-situation warning; shows 나중에 reaching into an indefinite future.

extendedVocab.nuance: 나중에 means 'later' at some vague, unspecified future point — possibly today, possibly next week, the time is deliberately left open. That open-endedness is exactly why it's so handy for politely putting things off (나중에 할게요 'I'll do it later'). The sharp contrast to learn is 나중에 vs 이따가: 이따가 means 'a little later but still TODAY', whereas 나중에 carries no same-day promise and can mean any future time. Don't reach for English 'after' here — 나중에 is a standalone time adverb, not the connector '-(으)ㄴ 후에/다음에' you use to say 'after doing X'. Note the fixed 에 is baked in: the word is 나중에, and bare 나중 sounds incomplete in speech. It naturally collocates with 봐요, 연락하다, 다시, and 후회하다, and its opposite pole is 먼저/지금 (first/now).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 나중에 for 'in a little while today', e.g. ✗ 나중에 점심 먹어요 meaning soon. For same-day soon use 이따가 점심 먹어요.
Dropping the 에 and saying just 나중 — the adverb is 나중에. Bare 나중 only survives in compounds like 나중 일 (a later matter).
Translating English 'after' with 나중에, e.g. ✗ 밥을 먹고 나중에 for 'after eating'. 'After doing X' is 밥을 먹은 후에 / 먹고 나서; 나중에 is just 'later' on its own.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이따가 means "in a bit (later today)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "in a bit (later today)" is 이따가 (ittaga). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이따 봐요 ("see you in a bit"). Watch the particle attached to 이따가 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 이따 is the everyday clipped form of 이따가; both are fine in speech.

usagePhrases.en: I'll call you in a bit
usagePhrases.note: Promising a call soon, still within today.
Same-day plan that's close but not right now.
봬요 (from 뵈다) lifts the register when speaking to someone you respect.

examples.en: Let's have lunch together in a bit.
examples.note: Simple same-day near-future plan; 이따가 up front.

examples.en: I'm in a meeting now, so I'll reply a bit later.
examples.note: Contrasts 지금 (now) with 이따가 (soon, today) — the heart of the word.

examples.en: Let's meet at the cafe around five later.
examples.note: Real plan: 이따가 sets 'later today' and 다섯 시쯤에 pins the rough clock time.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이따가 means 'a little later, but still today' — a short gap measured in hours, never days. The defining contrast is 이따가 vs 나중에: 나중에 is open-ended 'later' (maybe another day), while 이따가 firmly stays within the current day, so 이따가 봐요 implies you'll genuinely see them again today. It's casual, conversational, and in fast speech almost always clipped to 이따 (이따 봐요). The notorious English-speaker trap is the homophone 있다가, which sounds identical but is 있다 'to stay/be' + '-다가' and means 'after staying/being a while' (여기 좀 있다가 가요 'stay here a bit then go'); the time adverb meaning 'in a bit' is spelled 이따가 with ㅇ, not 있다가. Like other frequency/time adverbs it takes no particle, sits before the verb, and collocates with 봐요, 전화하다, 만나요, and a soft 쯤에 clock time.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이따가 for next week or 'someday', e.g. ✗ 이따가 여행 가요 for a trip days away. Beyond today use 나중에.
Spelling it 있다가 when you mean 'in a bit'. 있다가 = 'after staying'; the time word is 이따가. Same sound, different word and meaning.
Saying 이따가에 — no particle. Just 이따가, or add a real clock time like 이따가 세 시에.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 늘 means "always" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 늘 (neul) = "always". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 늘 그래요 ("it's always like that") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 늘, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Set phrase for a constant pattern; resigned or matter-of-fact.
늘 shines in warm wishes — softer and kinder than a flat 항상.
Conveys ongoing, heartfelt gratitude rather than a one-time thanks.
언제나 ('whenever it is, always') overlaps fully; pick by rhythm/feel.

examples.en: I always eat breakfast.
examples.note: Plain habit; 늘 sits right before the verb, no particle.

examples.en: That restaurant always has a lot of people.
examples.note: Describes a constant state, not a one-off.

examples.en: Thank you for your help. Please always stay healthy.
examples.note: Real closing wish — the warm register where 늘 outshines 항상.

extendedVocab.nuance: 늘 means 'always / all the time' and is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja), which gives it a softer, warmer color than its Sino-Korean twin 항상 恒常 'constant-ever'. In meaning they're interchangeable and both sit right before the verb, but 늘 feels gentle and affectionate, so it's the natural pick in heartfelt wishes like 늘 행복하세요 / 늘 건강하세요, while 항상 leans slightly more neutral or formal. A third near-synonym, 언제나, literally 'whenever-it-is' and so 'always', is also swappable. The big spelling pitfall for English speakers: 늘 (the adverb) versus 늘다 (the verb 'to increase/grow'), e.g. 실력이 늘다 'one's skill improves' — never tack a verb ending onto the adverb. And like all such adverbs it refuses particles: write 늘 웃어요, never 늘에 or 늘은. It collocates with state verbs and warm imperatives (그래요, 고마워요, 건강하세요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 늘다 or 늘어요 for the adverb. 늘다 is a separate verb 'to increase' (살이 늘다 'to gain weight'). The frequency adverb is just 늘.
Adding a particle: ✗ 늘은 / ✗ 늘에. Adverbs like 늘 attach to nothing — 늘 + verb directly.
Reaching for stiff 항상 in a tender wish. 항상 행복하세요 isn't wrong, but native speakers more often warm it to 늘 행복하세요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이제 means "now, from now on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이제 (ije) means "now, from now on". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이제 괜찮아요 ("I'm okay now"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이제 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Implies 'not before, but now' — the recovery is the point.
Marks that the moment to leave has finally arrived.
Add 부터 'starting from' for a fresh-start resolution.
Set phrase: enough of what was happening up to this point.

examples.en: I'm going home now.
examples.note: Signals the turning point — time to wrap up and leave.

examples.ko: 한국어를 일 년 배워서 이제 조금 알아요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul il nyeon baewoseo ije jogeum arayo.
examples.en: I studied Korean a year, so now I know a little.
examples.note: The 'now, unlike before' change is explicit — perfect home for 이제, not 지금.

examples.en: From now on I'll exercise every day.
examples.note: Real resolution; 이제부터 draws a line between the old me and the new.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이제 means 'now', but with a built-in sense of CHANGE from a previous state — 'not until now, but now'. That's the whole game: the sharp contrast is 이제 vs 지금. 지금 is a neutral pointer at the present moment ('right now', as on a clock: 지금 몇 시예요?), whereas 이제 frames the present against a different past, so 이제 알아요 means 'now I get it (I didn't before)'. Choose 이제 whenever something has finally turned a corner, and 지금 for a plain timestamp. Add 부터 for 이제부터 'from now on', the go-to phrase for resolutions, and note the fixed expressions 이제 그만 ('enough now') and 이제야 ('only now, at last'). English 'now' covers both Korean words, which is exactly why learners overuse 지금 where the feeling of change calls for 이제. As an adverb it takes no particle (✗ 이제에) and sits before the verb; it commonly pairs with 괜찮다, 가다, 그만, and 부터.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 이제 and 지금 as identical. 지금 = neutral 'right now' (clock time); 이제 = 'now, in contrast to before'. Say 지금 몇 시예요?, but 이제 다 나았어요 ('I'm all better now').
Saying 이제에 — no particle. Use bare 이제, or 이제부터 for 'from now on'.
Using 지금부터 when you mean a life-change resolution. 지금부터 is fine for 'starting this second', but the 'turn over a new leaf' feel is 이제부터.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매번 means "every time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "every time" is 매번 (maebeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매번 고마워요 ("thank you every time"). Watch the particle attached to 매번 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Warm appreciation for help that keeps recurring.
Describes a recurring pattern, often with a sigh.
거의 softens it when it isn't literally every single occasion.
Common complaint frame: 똑같다 'be identical' + the repetition.

examples.en: Sorry for being late every time.
examples.note: Apologizing for a repeated occasion, not a calendar day.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 갈 때마다 매번 줄을 서야 해요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun gal ttaemada maebeon jureul seoya haeyo.
examples.en: Every time I go to that restaurant, I have to line up.
examples.note: Pairs 갈 때마다 ('each time I go') with 매번 — both stress the recurring occasion.

examples.en: You always help me — honestly, thank you every time.
examples.note: Real thanks; 매번 ties the gratitude to each separate instance of help.

extendedVocab.nuance: 매번 means 'every time / each time an occasion arises', and the key is that it counts OCCASIONS, not calendar days. The 매 is Sino-Korean 每 'each/every' (same as in 매일), and 번 is 番 'a time/turn' (as in 한 번 'once', 두 번 'twice'), so it literally reads 'each-turn'. That's the dividing line from 매일 每日 'each-day': use 매일 for things tied to the daily calendar (매일 운동해요), but 매번 when something recurs every time a particular situation comes up (그 사람은 매번 늦어요 'he's late every time'). A close cousin is the suffix '-(으)ㄹ 때마다' '(each) time when', often used right alongside it for emphasis (갈 때마다 매번). Adding a particle: ✗ 매번에. None is needed — 매번 + verb directly.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 금방 means "in a moment; just now" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 금방 (geumbang) = "in a moment; just now". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 금방 올게요 ("I'll be right back") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 금방, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Future use: promising a very quick return.

usagePhrases.en: it'll be done in no time
usagePhrases.note: Reassuring someone the wait is short.
Past use: it happened a moment ago.
On the phone, 'I'll be there in a sec'.

examples.en: I'll be there in a moment.
examples.note: Simple future 'soon'; reassuring you'll arrive quickly.

examples.en: Ramyeon cooks fast, so just wait a little.
examples.note: 금방 + 되다 ('be ready') — the everyday 'ready in no time' collocation.

examples.en: The person who just called left a moment ago.
examples.note: Past 금방 = 'just now'; note 방금 nearby — both can be past, but only 금방 also reaches forward.

extendedVocab.nuance: 금방 is a two-faced time word: with a FUTURE verb it means 'in a moment / very soon' (금방 올게요 'I'll be right back'), and with a PAST verb it means 'just now / a moment ago' (금방 갔어요 'left just now'). The tense of the verb decides which reading you get, so the same word swings both ways around the present — that's the thing to internalize. The sharp contrast is 금방 vs 방금: 방금 'just now' is strictly PAST (방금 도착했어요 'I just arrived') and cannot mean 'soon', whereas 금방 covers both directions. Origin-wise 금방 is Sino-Korean 今方 'now-just', and it's thoroughly casual, everyday speech. The classic English-speaker error is forcing 방금 into a future sentence or assuming 금방 only means 'soon' and missing its 'a moment ago' use. It takes no particle, sits before the verb, and habitually pairs with 오다/가다, 되다 ('be ready'), and 끝나다.

Using 방금 for the future, e.g. ✗ 방금 갈게요 for 'I'll go soon'. 방금 is past-only; the forward-looking 'soon' is 금방 갈게요.
Assuming 금방 only means 'soon' and missing its past sense. With a past verb, 금방 왔어요 = 'I just got here a moment ago', not 'I'll come soon'.
Adding 에: ✗ 금방에. No particle — 금방 attaches straight to the verb.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 계속 means "continuously, keep ~ing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 계속 (gyesok) means "continuously, keep ~ing". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 계속하세요 ("please continue"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 계속 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 계속 + 하다 fused as a verb; common when telling someone to carry on.
Connected -아서 form for 'keep on (doing)' without a break.
An ongoing, unchanging situation.
Useful in directions: 계속 직진하세요 'keep going straight'.

examples.en: It keeps raining.
examples.note: Ongoing, unbroken action; 계속 before the verb.

examples.en: If you keep going straight here, you'll reach the subway station.
examples.note: 계속 + 직진하다 in real directions — 'continuously, without turning'.

examples.ko: 아기가 자꾸 깨서 밤새 계속 안아 줬어요.
examples.romanization: agiga jakku kkaeseo bamsae gyesok ana jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The baby kept waking up, so I held her all night long.
examples.note: Contrasts 자꾸 (over and over, intermittently) with 계속 (the whole time, unbroken).

extendedVocab.nuance: 계속 means an action or state keeps going WITHOUT a break — 'continuously / the whole time / keep ~ing'. It's Sino-Korean 繼續 'connect-continue', which is exactly the image: things joined end to end with no gap. It can fuse with 하다 into the verb 계속하다 'to continue (something)' and appears as the connector 계속해서 'on and on'. The contrast to nail is 계속 vs 자꾸: 계속 is unbroken duration (비가 계속 와요 'it rains nonstop'), while 자꾸 is 'again and again, repeatedly' with gaps between tries, and usually carries a tinge of annoyance (자꾸 전화가 와요 'calls keep coming, ugh'). So 'the baby cried the whole time' is 계속 울었어요, but 'the baby kept waking up (on and off)' leans 자꾸 깼어요. Also distinguish the durative '-고 있다' (in progress right now) — 계속 stresses unbroken continuation over a stretch. No particle, before the verb; collocates with 오다, 가다, 하다, and direction verbs like 직진하다.

Using 계속 (nonstop, unbroken) when you mean 'over and over' with mild irritation, e.g. on-and-off pestering. That intermittent, annoyed nuance is 자꾸: 자꾸 물어봐요 'they keep asking (and it's bugging me)'.
Saying 계속에 — no particle. Use bare 계속, or the verb 계속하다 / connector 계속해서.
Forgetting 계속 can take an object via 계속하다, e.g. 'continue the meeting' is 회의를 계속하다, not ✗ 회의를 계속 (adverb alone needs a following verb).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 평소 means "usually, normally" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "usually, normally" is 평소 (pyeongso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 평소에 ("usually, in normal times"). Watch the particle attached to 평소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The natural adverbial form — 평소 almost always wears 에 here.
처럼 'like' + 평소 = behaving the same as on an ordinary day.
보다 'than' makes it a comparison against your normal baseline.
Used attributively before a noun: 평소 실력대로 'as per usual form'.

examples.en: I usually go to bed early.
examples.note: Plain habit; the 에 is essential here for the 'usually' sense.

examples.en: Today there are far more people than usual.
examples.note: 평소보다 comparison; 오늘 (today) is implicitly measured against the normal baseline.

examples.en: I was nervous but presented calmly, as usual.
examples.note: Real situation; 평소처럼 means 'the same way I normally do'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 평소 is a Sino-Korean noun, 平素 'level-plain / ordinary times', meaning your normal, everyday baseline — the way things usually are when nothing special is going on. Because it's fundamentally a noun, it leans on particles: in conversation it's overwhelmingly 평소에 'usually', or comparative 평소보다 'than usual', or 평소처럼 'as usual'. Its job is to set a default against which you contrast today (평소보다 많아요 'more than usual'). The near-synonym 보통 普通 also means 'usually/ordinarily' and overlaps heavily; the subtle feel is that 평소 points to 'one's ordinary times/baseline' while 보통 states 'as a general rule', so 평소에 운동해요 and 보통 운동해요 are both fine. The English-speaker trap is treating 평소 like a bare adverb such as 항상 and dropping the particle — 'I usually...' wants 평소에, not lonely 평소. It's also not a verb, so never conjugate it; pair it with 에, 보다, 처럼, and attributive nouns (실력, 생활).

Treating 평소 as a verb or conjugating it (✗ 평소해요). It's a noun/time word; the action comes from a separate verb after 평소에.
Forcing a 평소보다 comparison without the thing compared, e.g. ✗ 평소보다요 alone. You need both sides: 평소보다 사람이 많아요 ('more people than usual').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어서 means "quickly; please go ahead" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어서 (eoseo) = "quickly; please go ahead". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어서 오세요 ("welcome (come on in)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 어서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The standard shop/host greeting — you'll hear it everywhere in Korea.
Warmly urging a guest to start their meal.
Inviting someone inside with welcoming haste.
Standalone, softened with 요 when nudging someone to proceed.

examples.en: Welcome! / Come on in.
examples.note: The all-purpose greeting in every store and restaurant.

examples.en: It's cold, so please come on in.
examples.note: 어서 + a caring reason; the urging is warm, not bossy.

examples.en: We're out of time, please hurry up.
examples.note: Even when rushing, 어서 keeps a polite tone — paired with 서두르다 'to hurry'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어서 urges someone to do something soon, but its color is WARM and welcoming rather than the brusque 'hurry up!' of English. That register is everything: it lives almost entirely with polite imperatives, above all the ubiquitous 어서 오세요 'welcome', plus 어서 드세요 / 어서 들어오세요. The sharp contrast is 어서 vs 빨리: 빨리 is plain, neutral-to-blunt 'fast/quickly' and can sound impatient or commanding (빨리 와! 'come fast!'), whereas 어서 hospitably invites and would feel odd shouted in irritation. So a host says 어서 오세요, but a stressed coach barks 빨리빨리. A close, even gentler relative is 어여/얼른 in casual speech ('quick, come on'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 어서 as a sharp command or sticking it on blunt forms — keep it with warm 세요-imperatives. It takes no particle and stands before the verb; alone it softens to 어서요.

Using 어서 as an impatient 'hurry up!', e.g. snapping ✗ 어서! at someone you're annoyed with. For blunt urgency use 빨리; 어서 is welcoming, not scolding.
Pairing it with a cold command form, e.g. ✗ 어서 가 (blunt). It belongs with polite imperatives: 어서 가세요 / 어서 오세요.
Confusing the adverb 어서 with the connector ending '-아서/어서' (because/and-then). 어서 'go ahead, quickly' is one word; 먹어서 'because (I) ate' is a verb stem + ending — totally different.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 잠깐 means "for a moment, briefly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 잠깐 (jamkkan) means "for a moment, briefly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 잠깐만요 ("just a moment, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잠깐 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Super useful for asking someone to hold on a sec; 만 'just' + 요.
Same idea among friends — 'wait a sec'.
Polite opener when you want a brief word with someone.
동안 'during' frames the short span of time.

examples.en: Please wait a moment.
examples.note: Everyday polite request; 잠깐 sets the short duration.

examples.en: Hold on a sec — I didn't bring my wallet.
examples.note: 잠깐만요 as a real-life 'wait!' interjection mid-situation.

examples.en: Let's rest here a bit before we go.
examples.note: 잠깐 + 쉬다 ('rest'); the natural way to suggest a quick breather.

extendedVocab.nuance: 잠깐 means 'for a short moment / briefly', a span felt in seconds to a few minutes — never a long stretch. It's everyday, conversational, and the derived 잠깐만요 is one of the single most useful phrases a learner can own: it's how you say 'wait a sec / excuse me, hold on' to stop someone politely. The near-twin to contrast is 잠시: 잠시 means the same 'briefly' but sounds a touch more formal and refined, so you hear 잠시 후에 ('shortly') and 잠시만 기다려 주세요 in announcements, whereas 잠깐 dominates casual speech. Both are essentially native-flavored time words taking no particle. The English-speaker pitfall is stretching 잠깐 to cover a genuinely long wait ('I waited a while' that lasted an hour isn't 잠깐) and adding 에 (✗ 잠깐에). Place it before the verb; it collocates with 기다리다, 쉬다, 시간 있다, and the attention-getting 잠깐만(요).

Adding a particle: ✗ 잠깐에. None needed — 잠깐 + verb, or 잠깐 동안 for 'for a brief while'.
Reaching for stiff 잠시 with close friends. 잠시만요 isn't wrong but can sound formal; among friends 잠깐만 is more natural.

usagePhrases.note: Polite 'hold on'; a notch more formal than 잠깐만요.
Stock announcement phrase: 잠시 후에 출발합니다.
동안 'during' marks the brief span.
Polite set phrase for stepping away briefly.

examples.en: Please wait just a moment.
examples.note: Polite and slightly formal; common at counters and on the phone.

examples.en: The train will arrive shortly.
examples.note: 잠시 후에 in its natural habitat — public announcements.

examples.en: Excuse me for a moment during the meeting.
examples.note: Formal register; 잠시 + 실례하다 to step out politely.
