extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목구멍 means "throat (the inside passage)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 목구멍 (mokgumeong) means "throat (the inside passage)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목이 아프다 ("to have a sore throat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목구멍 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the short, far more common everyday version

usagePhrases.en: for the throat to sting/be raw
usagePhrases.note: 따갑다 = to sting/prickle; that scratchy cold feeling

usagePhrases.en: to get stuck in the throat
usagePhrases.note: 걸리다 = to get caught; 가시가 목구멍에 걸렸어요
붓다 (ㅅ-irregular) = to swell; 목이 부었어요

examples.en: I caught a cold and my throat hurts.
examples.note: simple: the everyday short form 목이 아프다

examples.en: My throat was raw, so I drank warm water.
examples.note: everyday: 목구멍이 따갑다 + reason -아서

examples.ko: 생선 가시가 목구멍에 걸려서 병원에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: saengseon gasiga mokgumeonge geollyeoseo byeongwone gasseoyo.
examples.en: A fish bone got stuck in my throat, so I went to the clinic.
examples.note: real-life: 목구멍에 걸리다; precise inner-passage sense

extendedVocab.nuance: 목구멍 is the throat as the inner passage/gullet, literally 목 (neck/throat) + 구멍 (hole) — 'throat-hole.' The crucial register/synonym point is 목 vs 목구멍: 목 covers both the neck (the outside) AND the throat, and in everyday speech a sore throat is almost always the short 목이 아파요 — people rarely say 목구멍이 아파요 in casual talk. You reach for 목구멍 when you need to specify the inside cavity: something lodged in it (가시가 목구멍에 걸리다), or a raw, stinging sensation deep inside (목구멍이 따갑다). At the clinic the formal term is the Sino-Korean 인후(咽喉), as in 인후염 (pharyngitis) or 이비인후과 (ENT clinic, 'ear-nose-throat dept'). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 목구멍 every time you'd say 'throat' — default to 목 for sore throats and save 목구멍 for the literal inner passage. Spelling: keep the ㅁ — 목구멍, not 목구머. Collocations: 목구멍이 따갑다, 목구멍에 걸리다, 목이 아프다, 목이 붓다, 목이 잠기다 (to go hoarse).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Defaulting to 목구멍이 아파요 for an ordinary sore throat. Everyday Korean is 목이 아파요; 목구멍 is for the specific inner passage.
Forgetting 목 also means 'neck,' so 목 alone is ambiguous — use 목구멍 only when you must specify the inside throat.
Dropping the final consonant: writing 목구머. It's 목구멍 (with ㅁ).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뇌 means "brain" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "brain" is 뇌 (noe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 머리가 좋다 ("to be smart (lit. head is good)"). Watch the particle attached to 뇌 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be smart (lit. head is good)
usagePhrases.note: casual mental ability uses 머리, not 뇌
쓰다 = to use; can be literal or jokingly 'think hard'
informal: 머릿속이 하얘지다 nearby; blanking out
뇌(腦) + 세포(細胞); 뇌세포가 죽다 = brain cells dying, joking

examples.en: The human brain is really fascinating.
examples.note: simple: 뇌 as the literal organ + 신기하다

examples.en: While you sleep, your brain rests too.
examples.note: everyday: -는 동안 (during) + 뇌가 쉬다

examples.ko: 시험 때 너무 긴장하면 뇌가 멈추는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: siheom ttae neomu ginjanghamyeon noega meomchuneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: When I'm too nervous during an exam, it's like my brain freezes.
examples.note: real-life: informal 뇌가 멈추다 for going blank

extendedVocab.nuance: 뇌 is the brain as the physical organ — Sino-Korean 腦 ('brain') — and it's the right word for anatomy, health, and science: 뇌 수술 (brain surgery), 뇌세포 (brain cells), 뇌가 손상되다 (the brain is damaged). The key contrast for learners is 뇌 vs 머리: for everyday talk about intelligence, thinking, or memory, Koreans say 머리 (head/mind), NOT 뇌 — 'she's smart' is 머리가 좋다, you 'rack your brain' as 머리를 쓰다, and an idea pops into 머릿속 (inside the head). So reserve 뇌 for the literal organ and use 머리 for mental ability; saying 뇌가 좋다 for 'smart' sounds like a textbook mistranslation. Pronunciation pitfall: 뇌 is a single syllable, the diphthong 외 — roughly 'nö'/'nwe' (close to French eu or a quick 'nweh') — so don't split it into two beats ('no-i') or say 'noy.' Collocations (organ sense): 뇌가 쉬다, 뇌를 쓰다, 뇌 수술, 뇌세포, 뇌가 활성화되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 뇌가 좋다 for 'smart.' Casual intelligence is 머리가 좋다; 뇌 is the physical organ.
Using 뇌 for 'in my mind/head' (an idea, a memory): 뇌에 떠올랐어요. Everyday Korean is 머릿속에 떠올랐어요.
Pronouncing 뇌 as two syllables ('no-i') or 'noy.' It's one syllable with the vowel 외 (≈ 'nö/nwe').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 남자 means "man, male" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 남자 (namja) = "man, male". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 남자 ("man, male") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 남자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the plain, neutral noun for a male person
noun + 이에요/예요; 남자 ends in a vowel, so the contracted 예요
남자 used as a modifier in front of another noun, no particle needed
with a space it is a friend who happens to be male; 남자친구 written solid means boyfriend

examples.en: That person is a man.
examples.note: the simplest A는 B예요 identity sentence

examples.en: The men's restroom is on the second floor.
examples.note: 남자 glued to 화장실 acts like an adjective 'men's'

examples.en: The tall man is my older brother.
examples.note: real situation: a modifier clause 키 큰 plus subject 남자가

extendedVocab.nuance: 남자 (Sino-Korean 男子, literally 'male-person') is the flat, everyday noun for a man or male, with no warmth or rudeness built in — it simply states the category, the way 'male' does on a form. Its mirror word is 여자 (woman), and the dividing line you must keep straight is 남자 = any male in general versus 남편 (husband, 男便) = the specific man a woman is married to; an English speaker who reaches for 'my man' and says 내 남자 sounds like a song lyric, not 'my husband'. As a noun it takes 이에요/예요 and the subject marker 가 because it ends in a vowel (남자예요, 남자가), and it loves to sit in front of other nouns with no particle at all: 남자 화장실, 남자 옷, 남자 목소리. The notorious trap is spacing — 남자 친구 with a space is just a friend who is male, while 남자친구 squeezed into one word is a romantic boyfriend, so a stray space can change your whole sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 남자이에요 — because 남자 ends in the vowel ㅏ, the 이에요 contracts and the correct form is 남자예요.
Calling a husband 남자; a husband is 남편, and 남자 alone just means 'a male', so 우리 남자 for 'my husband' sounds wrong.
Writing 남자친구 (solid) when you only mean a buddy who is male — that solid form reads as 'boyfriend'; keep the space: 남자 친구.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 여자 means "woman, female" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 여자 (yeoja) means "woman, female". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 여자 ("woman, female"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 여자 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the plain, neutral noun for a female person
noun + 예요 because 여자 ends in a vowel
여자 used as a modifier before another noun
with a space, a friend who is female; 여자친구 solid means girlfriend

examples.en: That person is a woman.
examples.note: the basic identity pattern A는 B예요

examples.en: The women's clothing store is on the first floor.
examples.note: 여자 stacked in front of 옷 to mean 'women's'

examples.ko: 빨간 옷을 입은 여자가 제 친구예요.
examples.romanization: ppalgan oseul ibeun yeojaga je chinguyeyo.
examples.en: The woman in red is my friend.
examples.note: real situation: a modifier clause describing which 여자

extendedVocab.nuance: 여자 (Sino-Korean 女子, literally 'female-person') is the neutral, all-purpose noun for a woman or female and is the exact counterpart of 남자 (man); like 남자 it carries no built-in politeness or insult, it just names the category. The boundary to memorize is 여자 = any female in general versus 아내 (wife) = the specific woman a man is married to, so saying 내 여자 for 'my wife' sounds like a possessive movie line rather than 아내. Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (여자예요, 여자가), and it pairs effortlessly as a modifier: 여자 화장실, 여자 목소리, 여자 옷. Two spacing pitfalls follow the same rule as 남자: 여자 친구 with a space is a platonic friend who is female, but 여자친구 written solid is a girlfriend — and unlike English, you cannot stick 'a' or 'the' in front; the bare noun already covers both.

Using 여자 to mean 'wife'; a wife is 아내 (or 와이프 in casual speech), while 여자 alone just means 'a female'.
Saying 여자친구 (solid) for a casual female friend — that reads as 'girlfriend'; keep the space for a plain friend: 여자 친구.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어른 means "adult, grown-up" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "adult, grown-up" is 어른 (eoreun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어른 ("adult, grown-up"). Watch the particle attached to 어른 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: a fully grown person; also one's elders
noun + 이에요 after the final consonant ㄴ
subject marker 이 because 어른 ends in a consonant
plural with 들, often the seniors you must respect

examples.en: I am an adult now.
examples.note: 어른 + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ

examples.en: We use polite speech to adults/elders.
examples.note: everyday: shows the respect sense, 어른 = elder

examples.en: The grown-ups helped the child.
examples.note: real situation: 어른 contrasted directly with 아이 (child)

extendedVocab.nuance: 어른 is a native Korean word (no hanja) that covers two linked ideas: an adult as opposed to 아이 (child), and, just as importantly, one's elders — the older people a Korean is socially obliged to treat with respect. That second sense is where English speakers slip: 'adult' in English is a neutral age category, but 어른 often means 'a senior I must bow and use 존댓말 to', so 어른을 공경하다 (respect your elders) is a core phrase. Compare it with three neighbors — 성인 (成人, the legal/clinical 'adult' on documents and age ratings, e.g. 성인 영화), 노인 (an elderly person), and 아이 (child): 어른 is the warm, relational everyday word, 성인 is the bureaucratic one. It ends in the consonant ㄴ, so it takes 이에요 and 이 (어른이에요, 어른이). The adjective 어른스럽다 (to be mature, grown-up in manner) is built straight from it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 어른예요 — because 어른 ends in the consonant ㄴ, the full form 어른이에요 is required.
Treating 어른 as a pure age label like English 'adult'; on official forms and age ratings the word is 성인 (e.g. 성인 인증), while 어른 carries the 'respect your elders' nuance.
Confusing 어른 with 노인 — every 노인 is an 어른, but most 어른 are not 노인 (elderly); don't call a 30-year-old 노인.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아기 means "baby, infant" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 아기 (agi) = "baby, infant". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아기 ("baby, infant") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: a very young child; also a term of endearment
noun + 예요 because 아기 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
아기 modifying 옷 with no particle

examples.en: The baby is sleeping.
examples.note: simplest 아기 + 가 + verb

examples.en: The baby is really cute.
examples.note: everyday: pairs with the adjective 귀엽다

examples.en: Our baby is one year old now.
examples.note: real situation: 돌 = first birthday; 우리 아기 as endearment

extendedVocab.nuance: 아기 is a native, affectionate word for a baby or infant — soft and warm in a way the clinical term 아이(아이 = child, broader and older) is not. The boundary to hold: 아기 is roughly 'baby/infant' (newborn up to toddler), 아이 covers any child up through about pre-teen, and 어린이 (children) is the formal/institutional word you see on signs (어린이 보호구역 = school zone). In casual speech 아기 is very often softened to 애기, and shortened further to 애 in fast talk, though 아기 is the textbook spelling. The endearment use matters culturally: parents say 우리 아기 ('our baby') even to a grown child the way English speakers say 'my baby'. Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (아기예요, 아기가), and as a modifier it needs no particle: 아기 옷, 아기 침대, 아기 손.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 아기이에요 instead of 아기예요 — after the vowel ㅣ the copula contracts to 예요.
Treating 아기 and 아이 as interchangeable; 아기 is a baby/infant, while 아이 is a child of a much wider age range.
Assuming 애기 is wrong — it is the very common spoken form, but in writing the standard spelling is 아기.

extendedVocab.nuance: 노인 (Sino-Korean 老人, literally 'old-person') is the standard, neutral word for an elderly person in writing and statistics — 노인 복지 (elderly welfare), 노인 인구 (elderly population), 노인정 (senior center). extendedVocab.nuance: 주인 (Sino-Korean 主人, literally 'master/main-person') means the owner of a thing or the person running a place — 가게 주인 (shop owner), 식당 주인 (restaurant owner) — and by extension a 'host' or a master to a pet (강아지가 주인을 따라가요 = the dog follows its owner). Distinguish 주인 from 사장(님) (社長, the boss/CEO you address staff-side, common for any shop boss) and from 손님 (a guest/customer — the opposite role to 주인-as-host). Writing 집 주인 with a space for 'landlord'; the established word is the solid 집주인 — a space makes it read as 'the house's owner' generically.
Using 주인 where Korean expects 사장님; to a shop boss you usually say 사장님, reserving 주인 for describing who owns the place.

extendedVocab.nuance: 부부 (Sino-Korean 夫婦, literally 'husband-wife') means specifically a married couple — the husband and wife taken together as one social unit. The boundary English speakers must respect is 부부 (married) versus 커플 (a loanword from 'couple', a dating pair who may not be married at all); calling your boyfriend-and-yourself 부부 implies you are actually married. It is a dignified, neutral word that combines readily: 신혼부부 (newlyweds), 노부부 (an elderly couple), 잉꼬부부 (a lovebird couple who get along beautifully), 부부 싸움 (a marital spat). Because it ends in a vowel it takes 예요 and 가 (부부예요, 부부가). One more nuance: 부부 names the relationship/unit, not the individuals, so you don't use it to point at one person — for that you'd say 남편 (husband) or 아내 (wife).

Writing 부부이에요 instead of 부부예요 — after the vowel ㅜ the copula contracts.
Using 부부 for a dating couple; an unmarried pair is 커플, while 부부 specifically implies marriage.
Applying 부부 to one individual; 부부 is the pair as a unit — a single spouse is 남편 (husband) or 아내 (wife).

extendedVocab.nuance: 본인 (Sino-Korean 本人, literally 'origin/root-person', i.e. the actual person concerned) is a formal-leaning word meaning 'oneself' or 'the very person in question'. Its natural home is officialdom — counters, banks, forms, hospitals: 본인 확인 (identity check), 본인 서명 (sign it yourself), 본인 부담금 (the portion the patient pays). The trap for English speakers is two-fold. First, register: in friendly conversation 본인 sounds stiff and bureaucratic, so for 'myself' say 저/나 and for 'yourself' use the person's name or title — overusing 본인 with friends is like saying 'the undersigned' at a coffee shop. Second, reference: 본인 always points back to the relevant person, not necessarily the speaker, so 본인이 오세요 means 'have the person themselves come', whereas to volunteer yourself you'd say 제가 갈게요. Compare 자기 (a casual 'oneself', and also a sweetheart's 'honey') and 스스로 (an adverb, 'by oneself / of one's own accord'). Ending in ㄴ, it takes 이에요 and 이.

Using 본인 to mean 'I' in casual chat; it sounds stiff and official — say 저 or 나 among friends, and use names for 'you'.
Assuming 본인 always means the speaker; it means 'the person concerned', so 본인이 직접 means 'that very person in person', not automatically 'I'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 누군가 is a native indefinite pronoun meaning 'someone / somebody' — an unknown or unspecified person. It is built from 누구 ('who') plus the bound 가, and the single most important fact about it is that, unlike bare 누구, it is a STATEMENT word, not a question; 누군가 왔어요 is 'someone came', never 'who came?'. This is exactly the trap for English speakers, because English 'who' and the indefinite blur together — in Korean you must switch words: question → 누구 (누구예요? = who is it?), indefinite → 누군가 (someone). Although the 가 inside it looks like a subject marker, it is fused into the word, so you still add fresh particles freely: 누군가가 (someone, subject), 누군가를 (someone, object), 누군가에게/한테 (to someone). Compare its relatives 아무 ('anyone', needs 도/나) and 어떤 사람 ('a certain person'); 누군가 is the warm, vague 'somebody out there' of songs and wishes.

Using 누군가 to ask a question; for 'who?' use 누구 (누구예요? / 누가 왔어요?), since 누군가 only states 'someone'.
Thinking the built-in 가 is the subject marker and refusing to add particles; you still say 누군가가 (subj.) and 누군가를 (obj.) normally.
Confusing 누군가 with 아무; 누군가 = 'some specific-but-unknown person', while 아무(나/도) = 'any/no person' and needs 나 or 도.

extendedVocab.nuance: 아무 is a native word meaning 'any (person/thing)', but its defining feature is that it almost never stands alone — it lives only with a partner particle, and which partner you choose flips the meaning, which is the core hurdle for English speakers used to one word 'any'. With 도 plus a NEGATIVE verb it means nobody/nothing: 아무도 없어요 ('no one is here'), 아무것도 몰라요 ('I know nothing'). With 나 plus a POSITIVE verb it means 'anyone/anything at all, no preference': 아무나 와도 돼요 ('anyone may come'), 아무거나 주세요 ('give me anything'). So the polarity of the verb must match the particle: 도 ↔ negative, 나 ↔ positive. Memorize the family as fixed sets — 아무도 (nobody), 아무나 (anybody), 아무것도/아무거나 (nothing/anything), 아무 데도/아무 데나 (nowhere/anywhere), 아무 때나 (anytime). Compare 누군가 ('a certain someone'), which is positive and specific-ish, against 아무 which is sweepingly general.

Using 아무도 with a positive verb; 아무도 must pair with a negative — 아무도 없어요 / 아무도 안 와요, never 아무도 있어요.
Saying 아무 alone to mean 'anyone'; it is incomplete — you need 아무나 (anyone) or 아무도 (no one) to finish the meaning.
Mixing the particles: 'anyone CAN come' is 아무나 와도 돼요 (positive→나), not 아무도, which would force a negative and mean 'no one'.

noun + 예요 because 아저씨 ends in a vowel

extendedVocab.nuance: 아저씨 is a native word for a middle-aged or grown man, and it does double duty as a friendly way to flag down a male stranger — a shopkeeper, a taxi driver, a delivery man — much like English 'mister' or 'sir', but warmer and more casual. The cultural pitfall for English speakers is age sensitivity: because 아저씨 implies 'middle-aged', calling a man in his twenties or early thirties 아저씨 can sting, since you're effectively saying he looks past his youth; for a younger-looking man people hedge with 저기요 ('excuse me') or 선생님. Note that 아저씨 is informal — in a business or polite setting you'd upgrade to 선생님 or 사장님 rather than 아저씨.

Calling a young man 아저씨; it implies he looks middle-aged and can offend — use 저기요 or 선생님 for a younger-looking man.

extendedVocab.explanation: 이웃 (iut) means "neighbor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이웃 ("neighbor"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이웃 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a person living nearby; also neighbors collectively
noun + 이에요 after the final consonant ㅅ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
옆집 (the house next door) + 이웃; cf. 이웃 사람 (a neighbor)

examples.en: Our neighbor is very kind.
examples.note: 이웃 + 은 as topic; can be one person or 'the neighbors'

examples.en: A neighbor shared rice cakes with us.
examples.note: everyday: note the liaison — 이웃이 sounds like 이우시

examples.en: I get along well with my next-door neighbor.
examples.note: real situation: 이웃과 = 'with the neighbor', 사이가 좋다 idiom

extendedVocab.nuance: 이웃 is a native word (no hanja) for a neighbor — someone who lives close by — and it flexibly means either one specific neighbor or neighbors as a group, depending on context: 좋은 이웃 (a good neighbor), 이웃 사람 (the people next door), 이웃 나라 (a neighboring country). Two practical points for English speakers. First, pronunciation: the final ㅅ is unreleased and sounds like a ㄷ-stop when alone (이웃 ≈ '이욷'), but before a vowel-initial particle it links and softens, so 이웃이 comes out like '이우시' and 이웃을 like '이우슬' — getting this liaison right is what makes it sound natural. Second, it ends in a consonant, so it takes 이에요 and 이 (이웃이에요, 이웃이), not 예요. Culturally, the phrase 이웃사촌 ('a neighbor as close as a cousin') captures how a good 이웃 is valued, and greeting your 옆집 (next door) when you move in is a normal courtesy.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이웃예요 — after the final consonant ㅅ it must be 이웃이에요.
Pronouncing the final ㅅ as a clear English 's'; alone it is a stopped 'ㄷ' sound, and before a vowel it links — 이웃이 → '이우시'.
Forcing a plural 's'; 이웃 already serves for one neighbor or many, so 우리 이웃 can mean 'our neighbor(s)' without 들.

extendedVocab.explanation: "surroundings, area nearby" is 주변 (jubyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주변에 ("in the area, nearby"). Watch the particle attached to 주변 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks where things exist; pairs with 있다/많다
N + 주변 = the surroundings of N, no 의 needed
을 marks what you scan with your eyes
주변 also covers the people in one's circle

examples.en: There are many restaurants around the hotel.
examples.note: the everyday frame: N 주변에 + 있어요/많아요

examples.en: I took a walk around the area near the station.
examples.note: 주변을 둘러보다 = scan/look around, object particle 을

examples.ko: 여기 주변에 환전할 데가 있는지 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: yeogi jubyeone hwanjeonhal dega inneunji jom allyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you tell me if there's somewhere to exchange money nearby?
examples.note: real travel ask — note polite 주시겠어요? softens the request

extendedVocab.nuance: 주변 is Sino-Korean 周邊 ('encircling edge'), the zone wrapping around a fixed point — 'the area around X'. The near-synonym is 근처 (近處 'near place'): 근처 just means 'somewhere close by, in the vicinity', while 주변 implies the full ring of surroundings on every side, so 호텔 주변 feels like the whole neighborhood and 호텔 근처 feels like 'a spot near the hotel'. 주변 also stretches to people (주변 사람들 = those around you, your circle), which 근처 cannot do. It is neutral in register, fine in both speech and signage. The English-speaker trap is dropping the particle: 'restaurants around the hotel' tempts you to say 주변 식당 있어요, but to state existence you need 주변에 식당이 있어요 (에 = location). Also do not visually confuse it with 주말 (weekend) — same 주 but unrelated.

Saying 주변 식당이 있어요 (no 에). To say things exist in the surroundings you mark location with 에: 주변에 식당이 있어요.
Using 주변 for one nearby spot. If you mean 'a place close by', 근처 is more natural (근처에 카페 있어요?); 주변 leans toward the whole encircling area.
Reading 주변 as 주말 (weekend) because both start with 주 — they share no meaning; 주변 = surroundings, 주말 = weekend.

Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

N + 끝 = the far end/tip of N
맨 = 'the very/outermost', intensifies 끝

usagePhrases.en: all the way to the end
usagePhrases.note: 까지 = up to; 'to the very end' in space or effort

examples.en: There's a convenience store at the end of the road.
examples.note: 길 끝에 = at the road's end, location 에

examples.ko: 이 줄 맨 끝에 서시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: i jul maen kkeute seosimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can stand at the very end of this line.

extendedVocab.nuance: 끝 is the native-Korean noun for the terminal point of something — the far tip of a line, road, or hallway, and by extension the end of a period of time (방학 끝, 여행 끝). Distinguish it from 가장자리 (the outer rim/edge of a flat thing like a table or page) and from 구석 (an inside corner where two walls meet): 끝 is the end of something long or linear, not a rim or a nook. Register is neutral and everyday. Two pitfalls for English speakers: spelling and the noun/verb split. The word ends in a single ㅌ (끝), often miswritten 끋 or 끝ㅌ; before a vowel that ㅌ links, so 끝에 sounds like 'kkeu-te'. And 끝 is only the noun 'the end' — to say something 'finishes/ends' you need the verb 끝나다 (영화가 끝났어요), not the bare noun. Handy collocations: 길 끝, 맨 끝, 끝까지.

Writing 끋 or 끝ㅌ. The correct form is 끝 with one final ㅌ, and it links to a following vowel (끝에 → 'kkeu-te').
Using the noun 끝 where you need the verb. 'The movie ended' is 영화가 끝났어요 (verb 끝나다), not 영화가 끝이에요 unless you mean 'this is the final part'.
Saying 길 끝 있어요 without 에. To place something at the end, mark location: 길 끝에 편의점이 있어요.

extendedVocab.explanation: 쪽 (jjok) means "side, direction, way". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이쪽 / 저쪽 ("this way / that way"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 쪽 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: the right side / the left side
usagePhrases.note: 오른·왼 + 쪽 for left and right
으로 = toward, the direction particle
어느 + 쪽 for asking direction

examples.note: 저쪽이에요 = 'it's that way', a bare location answer

examples.note: 이쪽으로 = in this direction; 으로 with movement

extendedVocab.nuance: 쪽 is a native dependent noun meaning 'side / direction' and is the workhorse of everyday directions. It attaches to demonstratives (이쪽/그쪽/저쪽/어느 쪽) and to 오른/왼 (오른쪽, 왼쪽). The key contrast is 쪽 vs 방향 (方向): 쪽 is concrete and deictic — a side you can point at right here ('over there, this way') — while 방향 is the more abstract heading of travel ('the opposite direction', 'the right direction'); you point 이쪽 but you check 방향이 맞아요?. 쪽 can also politely mean 'your side/end' (그쪽 = 'you' softly). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: write 이쪽/저쪽/오른쪽 as ONE word (이 쪽 with a space is wrong), and use the direction particle 으로 for movement — 이쪽으로 가요 ('go this way'), not 이쪽에 가요 (에 marks a static spot, not a heading).

Writing 이 쪽 / 오른 쪽 with a space. 이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽, 왼쪽 are single words.
Saying 이쪽에 가요 for movement. Direction toward something takes 으로: 이쪽으로 가요 / 오른쪽으로 도세요.
Using 쪽 for an abstract heading like 'the wrong direction'. For that, 방향 is more natural (반대 방향), since 쪽 points at a concrete side.

adjective + 곳; a frequent modifier pattern

examples.note: 유명한 곳이에요 = 'it's a famous place', noun + 이에요

examples.en: I want to rest somewhere quiet.
examples.note: 곳에서 = at the place where you rest; action particle 에서

extendedVocab.nuance: 곳 is a native dependent noun meaning 'place/spot', and it almost always rides on a modifier — an adjective or a relative clause (조용한 곳, 가 본 곳, 이곳). The near-synonym is 데, and the dividing line is register: 곳 is the slightly more formal, written-feeling word (you see it in guidebooks, reviews, signs), while 데 is the casual, spoken word. There is also a grammar difference — 곳 can pair with demonstratives to stand a bit more independently (이곳/그곳), whereas 데 leans even harder on a preceding modifier. Compare 위치 too: 위치 (位置) is the abstract coordinates 'where something sits', but 곳 is a place you go to or are in. Pronunciation pitfall: the final ㅅ is an unreleased 't' stop, so 곳 alone sounds like 'got' with the t held; before a vowel it surfaces, so 곳에 → 'go-se'. And don't drop the particle: say 곳에서 쉬어요, not 곳 쉬어요.

Pronouncing 곳 as a fully released 'got'. The final ㅅ is a held 't' stop; it only releases before a vowel (곳에 → 'go-se').
Dropping the particle. An action 'at a place' needs 에서: 조용한 곳에서 쉬어요, not 조용한 곳 쉬어요.
Using 곳 for abstract position. If you mean 'its location/position is good', use 위치 (위치가 좋아요), not 곳.

extendedVocab.nuance: 데 is the casual, conversational dependent noun for 'place/spot', and it is grammatically bound: it can never stand alone the way 곳 sometimes can — it must follow a modifier (갈 데, 먹을 데, 조용한 데, 아픈 데). The contrast with 곳 is purely register and feel: in speech Koreans reach for 데 (갈 데 없어요), while writing, reviews, and formal signage prefer 곳 (방문할 곳). 데 also has a special sense English speakers love once they see it — 'the spot/part that…', as in 아픈 데 (the place that hurts) or 불편한 데 (the part that's uncomfortable), which 곳 does not naturally cover. The big trap is homonym confusion: this place-noun 데 is unrelated to the sentence connector -는데/-은데 ('and/but/background'), even though they look identical; 갈 데가 없어요 (noun) vs 가고 싶은데 표가 없어요 (connector). Keep a modifier in front and you'll always read it as the place-noun.

Using 데 with no modifier (데가 있어요 ✗). It must follow a modifier: 갈 데가 있어요 / 조용한 데가 있어요.
Confusing the place-noun 데 with the connector -는데. 갈 데가 없어요 (place) vs 가고 싶은데 (but…) are different grammar despite the same shape.
Forcing 데 into formal writing. A review or sign prefers 곳 (가 볼 만한 곳); 데 sounds too casual there.

extendedVocab.nuance: 자리 is the native everyday noun for a seat or a spot you occupy — a seat on a train, a table at a restaurant, a place in a line, even a 'position' in life (좋은 자리 = a good job/standing). The crucial contrast is 자리 vs 의자: 의자 (椅子) is the physical chair as an object, while 자리 is the seat/spot as a space you take or reserve — so you ask 자리 있어요? ('is there a seat/spot?'), not 의자 있어요? Register is neutral and friendly. English-speaker pitfall: with 앉다 ('sit') use the location particle 에 — 자리에 앉아요, not 자리 앉아요; and to choose a seat type use 로/으로 (창가 자리로).

Dropping 에 with 앉다. 'Sit in the seat' is 자리에 앉아요; 자리 앉아요 is missing the particle.
Using 있다 wrong for a free seat. Ask 빈자리 있어요? ('is there an empty seat?'); 자리가 비었어요? is also fine but means 'is the seat vacated?'.

extendedVocab.explanation: "corner (inside)" is 구석 (guseok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 구석에 ("in the corner"). N + 구석 = the inside corner of N
구석 + 자리, a quiet nook seat

examples.en: The bag is in the corner of the room.
examples.note: 구석에 있어요 = sits in the inside corner; location 에

examples.en: Shall we sit at the corner table?
examples.note: 구석 자리 = a tucked-away corner seat; -ㄹ까요? suggests

extendedVocab.nuance: 구석 is a native noun for an inside corner — the nook where two walls of a room or the inner edges of a box meet — and figuratively a tucked-away, out-of-the-way spot. The sharp contrast is 구석 vs 모퉁이: 모퉁이 is the OUTSIDE corner of a street or building, the bend you turn at (모퉁이를 돌다 = turn the corner), whereas 구석 is an INSIDE nook you tuck into; you can sit in a 구석 but you turn a 모퉁이. There is also the lovely reduplicated form 구석구석 ('every nook and cranny, thoroughly'). Register is neutral, slightly cozy/colloquial. Note 구석 can carry a faintly negative shade (a 'neglected back corner'), so a hotel 'corner room' marketed positively might be called 코너 instead. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 구석 for a street corner — that's 모퉁이; and keep the particle — 구석에 있어요 for location, 구석에서 for an action done there.

Using 구석 for a street corner you turn. The bend of a street/building is 모퉁이 (모퉁이를 도세요); 구석 is an inside nook.
Dropping the particle. Location takes 에 (구석에 있어요); an action done there takes 에서 (구석에서 사진을 찍었어요).
Treating 구석 as always neutral. It can imply a 'back, neglected' corner, so for a flatteringly described corner room Koreans often say 코너 instead.

examples.en: My passport is inside the bag.
examples.note: 가방 속에 = down inside the bag; location 에

extendedVocab.nuance: 속 is a native noun for the inside, interior, or depths of something — especially a filled, enclosed, or three-dimensional thing (가방 속, 물속, 숲속), and figuratively the inside of an image or a heart (사진 속, 마음속 = deep in one's heart). The essential contrast is 속 vs 안: 안 marks being within a boundary or enclosure (방 안 = inside the room, 건물 안 = inside the building), neutral and structural, while 속 stresses being embedded in the substance or down in the depths (물속 = under the water, 가방 속 = buried in the bag). So 방 안 is natural but 방 속 sounds odd; 물속 is natural but 물 안 sounds odd. 속 also has bodily/emotional senses (속이 안 좋다 = upset stomach; 속상하다 = heartsick) that 안 lacks. Register neutral. English-speaker pitfall: don't reflexively map 'inside' to whichever you learned first — use 안 for rooms/buildings/bounded areas and 속 for filled or deep spaces; and keep 에: 가방 속에 있어요.

Swapping 속 and 안 by habit. Rooms and buildings take 안 (방 안, 건물 안); filled or deep spaces take 속 (물속, 가방 속).
Forgetting the particle. Location 'inside' needs 에: 가방 속에 있어요, not 가방 속 있어요.
Saying 물 안 for being submerged. 'In the water' is 물속 (written together); 물 안 is unnatural.

extendedVocab.nuance: 바깥 is a native noun meaning the outside / the outdoors, the natural opposite of 안 (inside). Its near-synonym is 밖: the two are largely interchangeable for 'outside' (바깥에/밖에, 바깥 날씨/바깥 = 'out there'), but 바깥 feels a touch more concrete and substantial — 'the outdoors as a place' — while 밖 is the lighter, more frequent 'outside' and also forms compounds like 창밖 (outside the window) and 문밖 (outside the door). Be very careful: the string 밖에 doubles as the grammar particle '밖에' meaning 'only/nothing but' (천 원밖에 없어요 = 'I have only 1,000 won'), so when you want the location 'outside' it is safer and clearer to say 바깥에. Register is neutral; there's also a dated sense 바깥양반/바깥일 ('the husband / outside affairs'). English-speaker pitfalls: spell it with final ㅌ — 바깥 (not 바깟/바같), and that ㅌ links to vowels so 바깥에 sounds like 'ba-kka-te'; for going out use direction 으로 (바깥으로 나가요).

Confusing 바깥에 (outside, location) with the particle 밖에 ('only'). 밖에 + negative = 'only' (물밖에 없어요); for 'outside' prefer 바깥에.
Using 에 for going out. Movement outward takes 으로: 바깥으로 나가요, not 바깥에 나가요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 양쪽 is 양 (兩 'two/both', the Sino-Korean root also in 양손 'both hands', 양면 'both sides') plus the native 쪽 ('side'), literally 'both sides'. It names the two opposing sides of something — a road, a door, a choice between two options. Compare 양쪽 vs 양옆: 양쪽 is the general 'both sides', while 양옆 specifically means 'both flanks / the two sides beside' something (양옆에 앉다 = sit on either side of). Keep the particle: 양쪽에 for location.

examples.note: 위치를 보내다 = share location; -ㄹ 테니까 = 'I'll…, so…'

extendedVocab.nuance: 위치 is Sino-Korean 位置 (位 'position/rank' + 置 'to place'), literally 'where something is set' — the abstract location or position of a thing. It is the natural word in maps, GPS, apps, and reviews: 위치가 좋다 (good location), 현재 위치 (current location), 위치를 공유하다/보내다 (share/send location). The key contrast is 위치 vs 곳/데: 곳 and 데 are 'a place you go to or are in' (조용한 곳, 갈 데), whereas 위치 is the coordinate/position 'where it sits' relative to other things — you don't 'go to a 위치', you check or describe one. Compare also 장소 (場所), which is a concrete venue/site for an event (모임 장소 = meeting place); 위치 is more abstract than 장소. Register is neutral-to-formal, common in writing and signage. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 위치 to mean 'a nice place to visit' — say 곳/데; and pronounce 치 as 'chi' (위치 = 'wi-chi'), not 'wi-ti'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 위치 for 'a place to go'. A destination is 곳 or 데 (좋은 곳, 갈 데); 위치 is the abstract position of something.
Mispronouncing 치 as 'ti'. 위치 is 'wi-chi'.
Confusing 위치 with 장소. An event venue is 장소 (모임 장소); 위치 is the more abstract 'where it sits'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 방향 means "direction" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 방향 (banghyang) means "direction". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 방향이 맞다 ("the direction is right"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 방향 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 가/이 + 맞다 = 'is correct'
반대 (反對) = opposite
으로 = toward; pairs with 가다
어느 + 방향 for asking a heading

examples.en: Is this the right direction?
examples.note: 방향이 맞다 = the heading is correct; basic check

examples.en: I took a bus going the opposite direction.
examples.note: 반대 방향으로 = the opposite way; 으로 with 가다

examples.ko: 서울역은 지금 어느 방향으로 가야 하는지 잘 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: seouryeogeun jigeum eoneu banghyangeuro gaya haneunji jal moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: I'm not sure which direction I should head for Seoul Station.
examples.note: 어느 방향으로 가야 하다 = which way to head; real lost-traveler line

extendedVocab.nuance: 방향 is Sino-Korean 方向 (方 'direction/region' + 向 'to face/head toward'), the abstract heading or orientation of movement. The central contrast is 방향 vs 쪽: 쪽 is the concrete, point-at-it 'side/way' right in front of you (이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽), while 방향 is the abstract course of travel you reason about — 'the opposite direction', 'the right direction', 'which way leads there'. So you point 이쪽 ('this way, here') but you verify 방향이 맞아요? ('am I heading right?') and warn 반대 방향이에요 ('that's the wrong way'). Compare 위치 too: 위치 is where something is (static position), 방향 is which way it faces or you move. Register neutral, fine in speech and signs (e.g., 부산 방향 on a road sign = 'toward Busan'). English-speaker pitfalls: for movement use 으로 (반대 방향으로 가요), not 에 (방향에 가요 is wrong); and don't confuse 방향 with the look-alike 방학 (school vacation) — same 방, unrelated meanings.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 방향에 가요 for movement. A heading takes 으로: 반대 방향으로 가요.
Using 방향 where 쪽 fits better. To point at a concrete side say 이쪽/저쪽; 방향 is the abstract course of travel.
Confusing 방향 (direction) with 방학 (school vacation). They share 방 but mean entirely different things.

extendedVocab.explanation: "the front, directly in front" is 정면 (jeongmyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정면에 ("at the front, directly in front"). Watch the particle attached to 정면 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: at the front, directly in front
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the front-facing spot
N + 정면 = the front face of N
으로 = straight in that direction
에서 = the front as where an action happens

examples.en: There's a big door at the front of the building.
examples.note: 정면에 = on the front face; location 에

examples.en: Just go straight ahead from here.
examples.note: 정면으로 쭉 가다 = head straight on; direction 으로

examples.ko: 역 정면에서 만나는 게 제일 찾기 쉬울 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: yeok jeongmyeoneseo mannaneun ge jeil chatgi swiul geot gatayo.
examples.en: Meeting right in front of the station seems easiest to find.
examples.note: 정면에서 만나다 = meet at the front; 에서 for the meeting spot

extendedVocab.nuance: 정면 is Sino-Korean 正面 (正 'straight/correct' + 面 'face/surface'), literally 'the straight face' — the front-facing side of something or the space directly ahead of you. The key contrast is 정면 vs 앞: 앞 is the general, everyday 'front / in front of' (집 앞 = in front of the house) and is what casual speech uses; 정면 is more specific and emphatic, the face that looks straight at you or the line dead-ahead — a building's façade (건물 정면) or 'straight in front' (정면으로 가다). So everyday 'in front of me' is 제 앞, but 'the front of the building / head-on' is where 정면 shines. It also appears in 정면충돌 (head-on collision) and 정면으로 보다 (face head-on). Register neutral-to-formal. English-speaker pitfalls: don't reach for 정면 in casual 'in front of' situations — use 앞; and keep particles straight — 정면에 for a static location, 정면으로 for the straight-ahead direction, 정면에서 for an action done at the front.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 정면 for casual 'in front of me'. Everyday speech uses 앞 (제 앞, 집 앞); 정면 stresses the front face / dead-ahead.
Mixing up the particles. Location is 정면에, direction is 정면으로, action-spot is 정면에서.
Treating 정면 as just 'front side' of any object. It implies the main front-facing face (a façade or head-on line), not a random side.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the rim as a location
N + 가장자리 = the outer rim of N
를 따라 = following the rim
으로 = in the direction of the rim

examples.en: I set the cup at the edge of the table.
examples.note: 가장자리에 = on the rim; location 에

examples.en: I walked slowly along the edge of the lake.
examples.note: 가장자리를 따라 걷다 = walk along the rim

examples.ko: 컵을 가장자리에 너무 가까이 두면 떨어질 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: keobeul gajangjarie neomu gakkai dumyeon tteoreojil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: If you leave the cup too close to the edge, it might fall.
examples.note: 가장자리에 가까이 = close to the rim; -ㄹ 수도 있다 = 'might'

extendedVocab.nuance: 가장자리 is a native noun for the outer edge or rim of a flat or bounded thing — a table, a page, a lake, a field. It contrasts sharply with three neighbors: 끝 is the end/tip of something long or linear (길 끝 = the road's end), 구석 is an inside corner where two walls meet (방 구석), and 모퉁이 is the outside corner of a street you turn at (모퉁이를 돌다) — so a tabletop has a 가장자리 (rim) but a hallway has a 끝 (end) and a room has a 구석 (nook). A close synonym is 끄트머리 ('the very edge/tip', more colloquial), and 테두리 means specifically a border/frame line around something. Register is neutral, everyday. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 가장자리 for the end of a road or hallway (that's 끝), and don't confuse the noun 가장자리 (edge) with the unrelated superlative adverb 가장 ('most / -est', as in 가장 큰 = biggest) — they merely share the first two syllables. Keep the particle: 가장자리에 for location, 가장자리를 따라 for 'along'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 가장자리 for the end of a road or hallway. That linear end is 끝 (길 끝); 가장자리 is the rim of a flat/bounded thing.
Confusing 가장자리 (edge) with 가장 (most/-est). 가장 is a superlative adverb (가장 큰 = biggest), unrelated to the noun.
Dropping the particle. Location is 가장자리에; 'along the edge' is 가장자리를 따라, not bare 가장자리 따라.

extendedVocab.explanation: 물건 (mulgeon) means "thing, object, item". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 물건이 있어요 ("There is a thing / I have something"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 물건 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: There is a thing / I have something
usagePhrases.note: 물건 + 이/가 있어요
이/그/저 + 물건
물건 + 을/를 + verb

usagePhrases.en: There are a lot of things
usagePhrases.note: 물건 + 이/가 많다

examples.en: What is this thing?
examples.note: Pointing at an unknown physical object

examples.en: There are too many things in the bag.
examples.note: 에 marks the container; 물건이 많다 = lots of stuff

examples.ko: 손님, 이 물건은 환불이 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: sonnim, i mulgeoneun hwanburi an dwaeyo.
examples.en: Sir/Ma'am, this item can't be refunded.
examples.note: Shop register: 물건 = the merchandise itself

extendedVocab.nuance: 물건 is the Sino-Korean 物件 (物 'thing' + 件 'item/case'), the catch-all word for a tangible, hold-in-your-hand object when you don't know or don't need its specific name, and in a store it shifts to mean the merchandise/goods. The sharp contrast is with 것 (and its spoken form 거): 것 is a grammatical 'thing' that can stand for anything at all, even abstractions or whole situations (좋은 것 = a good thing/one), whereas 물건 is strictly a concrete physical item you could pick up — you would never call an idea, a plan, or a feeling a 물건. It is neutral in register and safe with anyone. Common collocations: 물건을 사다/팔다 (buy/sell goods), 물건이 좋다 (the goods are good quality), 물건을 고르다 (pick out an item). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 물건 every time you'd say 'thing' in English; for 'I have a lot of things to do' you need 일 (work/matter), not 물건, and to count items you say 물건 다섯 개, never '다섯 물건'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 할 물건이 많아요 for 'I have many things to do' — 물건 is only physical objects, so this must be 할 일이 많아요 (using 일 = task/matter).
Using 물건 as a counter, e.g. 한 물건 — 물건 is a noun, not a measure word, so count with 개: 물건 한 개, 물건 두 개.
Calling an abstract 'thing' like a good idea 좋은 물건 — for non-physical 'things' use 것: 좋은 것이에요 (it's a good thing).

상자 + 안에 (interior location)

adjective (큰) + 상자

examples.en: What's inside the box?
examples.note: 안에 = inside; asking about contents

examples.ko: 이 상자는 너무 무거워서 못 들겠어요.
examples.romanization: i sangjaneun neomu mugeowoseo mot deulgesseoyo.
examples.en: This box is too heavy, I can't lift it.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 들다 = lift

examples.en: I cut open the delivery box with a knife.
examples.note: 택배 = parcel; 뜯다 = rip/tear open

extendedVocab.nuance: 상자 is the Sino-Korean 箱子 (箱 'box/chest' + the noun-forming 子), the standard word for a rigid box or carton — cardboard moving boxes, gift boxes, shipping cartons. Its everyday rival is the loanword 박스 (from English 'box'); the two overlap heavily and a Korean might say 박스 하나 just as readily, but 상자 sounds a touch more proper/written while 박스 is breezier and dominates for things like a 'case' of bottled water (생수 한 박스). Contrast it with the soft containers it is NOT: 봉투 (a flat envelope or paper bag) and 봉지 (a flimsy plastic/paper sack) collapse and have no rigid walls. Count boxes with the generic 개 (상자 한 개) or, for full-box quantities, the loan counter 박스. The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 상자 for a tiny rigid case — a jewelry or glasses case is usually 케이스 or 갑, not 상자.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a plastic shopping bag a 상자 — a bag that collapses is 봉지 (plastic) or 봉투 (paper/envelope); 상자 has rigid walls.
Using 상자 for a small hard case like a ring box or pencil case — Koreans say 케이스 or 갑 (반지 케이스, 필통), reserving 상자 for larger cartons.
Opening a sealed cardboard box with 열다 only — 열다 works for a lid, but to slit packing tape you naturally say 뜯다 (tear/cut open): 상자를 뜯다.

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 종이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 종이 + 이/가 있어요
종이 + 장 (counter for flat things)

examples.en: Just give me one sheet of paper, please.
examples.note: 장 counts flat sheets; 만 = just/only

examples.ko: 여기 종이에 이름하고 전화번호를 써 주세요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 종이 is a pure native Korean word for paper, both as the material (made from 나무/pulp) and as a sheet of it. The crucial point is its counter: flat, thin things are counted with 장 (종이 한 장, 두 장) — the same 장 used for tickets (표 한 장), photos (사진 한 장), and pizza slices, so learning 종이 anchors the whole 'flat-sheet' counter family. Distinguish the raw material 종이 from finished paper products that have their own names: a 신문 (newspaper), a 책 (book), a 공책/노트 (notebook), and a filled-out 서류 (document) are all made of 종이 but are never just called 종이. Useful collocations: 종이에 쓰다/적다 (write on paper), 종이를 접다 (fold paper), 종이를 자르다/찢다 (cut/tear paper). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: defaulting to 개 instead of 장 to count sheets, and using 종이 for a form you must complete — that is 서류 (paperwork) or the document's specific name.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting sheets with 개 — say 종이 한 장 (one sheet), not 종이 한 개; flat things take the counter 장.
Calling a form or official document 종이 — the paper you fill in is 서류 (paperwork) or the named form; 종이 is the blank material.

extendedVocab.nuance: 비닐봉지 stitches together 비닐 (from English 'vinyl', here meaning thin plastic film) + 봉지 (a flimsy sack/pouch), i.e. the thin film bag you get at shops and markets. Because Korean stores charge for bags and supermarkets have largely stopped offering single-use ones, 비닐봉지 주세요 / 봉투 필요하세요? are bread-and-butter checkout lines. The big pitfall is the word 비닐 itself: it does NOT mean English 'vinyl' as in vinyl records (that's LP/레코드) or vinyl flooring siding — in Korean 비닐 just means cheap plastic sheeting/film. extendedVocab.nuance: 바구니 is a native Korean word for a basket — an open-topped container, often with handles, that you carry or fill: a market basket, a laundry basket, a fruit basket. extendedVocab.nuance: 양동이 is a bucket or pail — a deep, usually handled vessel for carrying or holding water, typical of cleaning and chores. It is one indivisible native word: do NOT split it into 양 + 동이. In real daily speech you will constantly hear the casual substitutes 통 (a generic tub/canister — 물통, 쓰레기통) and the older loanword 바께쓰 (from Japanese-via-Dutch 'bucket'), but 양동이 is the clean standard form to learn and say. The verbs that pair with water-into-bucket are 담다 (put/load in) and 받다 (catch/collect running water): 양동이에 물을 받다. Contrast it with smaller open vessels: a 그릇 is a bowl/dish for food, a 대야 is the wide shallow basin you wash your face or feet in, and a 양동이 is the tall bucket for hauling water. Pitfall: English 'a bucket of X' tempts a 의 ('of'), but Korean simply juxtaposes — 물 한 양동이 (one bucket of water), counting with the noun itself.

extendedVocab.nuance: 깡통 is a metal can or tin — a food tin, a paint can, an old biscuit tin. The verb to open it is 따다 (to pop/pull open), the very same verb used for opening a bottle or popping a drink can, which is the key collocation to lock in: 깡통을 따다, 병을 따다, 캔을 따다. Here is the register/usage split learners miss: for a beverage can specifically (soda, beer, coffee), Koreans overwhelmingly say the loanword 캔 — 콜라 캔, 맥주 한 캔, 음료수 캔 — and 캔 is also the recycling category, while 깡통 leans toward food/industrial tins and can carry a slightly humble or old-timey flavor (깡통차 = a beat-up old car). Pitfall: opening a can with 열다 sounds off — 열다 is for doors, lids, and books; a sealed can is 따다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 자물쇠 is the physical lock device itself — a padlock or hasp lock — the native-Korean counterpart that forms a matched pair with 열쇠 (key): the 자물쇠 is what you lock, the 열쇠 is what opens it. Mind the verbs, because Korean splits 'lock' across several: 잠그다 is the all-purpose verb 'to lock' (문을 잠그다 = lock the door); 채우다 is 'to fasten/put a lock on' something (자물쇠를 채우다); and to unlock you say 풀다 (undo) or 열다 (open). Pitfall: English 'lock' is both noun and verb, but in Korean the object 자물쇠 cannot be verbed — you can't '자물쇠 something'; you 자물쇠를 채우다 or simply 잠그다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 손잡이 is a transparent native compound — 손 (hand) + 잡이 (a holder/gripping part, from 잡다 'to grasp') — literally 'the hand-grab', i.e. any handle, knob, grip, or hold you take hold of: a door handle, a drawer knob, a mug's handle, a kettle grip, the strap/rail you hang onto in a bus or subway. Because it's built from 잡다, the natural partner verb is 잡다 (hold/grab) — 손잡이를 잡다 — and for a turning knob, 돌리다 (turn): 손잡이를 돌리다. It is extremely productive in compounds: 문 손잡이 (door handle), 컵 손잡이 (cup handle), 가방 손잡이 (bag handle), so you rarely need a separate word per object. Two contrasts help: 손잡이 is the grip you hold, whereas 자물쇠/도어록 is the lock mechanism, and 버튼 is a press-button — different parts of the same door. Pitfall: don't reach for 들다 ('lift the whole object') when you only mean grabbing the grip; you 잡다 a 손잡이. Also, the strap you hold standing on the subway is exactly 손잡이, not a borrowed English word.

extendedVocab.nuance: 끈 is a one-syllable native word (note the double-consonant ㄲ onset and the ㄴ batchim) covering flexible string, cord, strap, or lace — anything you tie or carry with: shoelaces (신발 끈), bag straps (가방 끈), apron ties (앞치마 끈), a drawstring (끈). It sits in the middle of a thickness scale that learners should sort out: 실 is fine sewing thread, 끈 is a string/cord/strap you bind and fasten with, and 줄 is a thicker line/rope (and 줄 also means a 'line/queue' of people). Its bread-and-butter verbs are 묶다 (tie/bind) and 풀다 (untie/loosen), with 풀리다 as the 'comes undone by itself' intransitive. Useful collocations: 끈을 매다 (tie/do up a lace), 끈을 조이다 (tighten a cord), 끈을 묶다/풀다. Pitfall: English uses 'tie' for shoelaces, but watch the active/passive split — you 끈을 묶다 (you tie it), yet when it loosens on its own you say 끈이 풀렸다 (it came untied), not 끈을 풀었다 (which means you deliberately untied it).

Confusing 끈 with 실 (fine sewing thread) or 줄 (thicker rope / a queue) — match by thickness and function: thread < string/strap < rope.
Saying 끈을 풀었어요 when a lace came undone by itself — that means you untied it on purpose; the accidental version is 끈이 풀렸어요 (passive).

extendedVocab.nuance: 바늘 is a native word for a needle — the thin, sharp implement used with 실 (thread) for sewing; 바늘과 실 (needle and thread) is a set phrase, like English. Crucially, 바늘 stretches by metaphor to two other 'needle-shaped' things English keeps separate: the hands of a clock (시계 바늘 — the 긴 바늘 minute hand, 짧은 바늘 hour hand) and a hypodermic needle (주삿바늘), so the one Korean word spans sewing needle, clock hand, and syringe. The verb you must pair correctly is 꿰다 — to pass thread through the eye — 바늘에 실을 꿰다 (thread is threaded into the needle, marked with 에). Because it's sharp, it collocates with 뾰족하다 (pointy) and 찌르다 (prick/stab): 바늘에 찔리다 (get pricked by a needle). Pitfall: don't use 묶다 (tie) for threading — you 꿰다 the thread through; and English 'thread the needle' inverts the Korean direction, where the needle takes the 에 particle (into the needle) and the thread is the object.

실 + 을 + 꿰다

examples.note: 하고 = and (casual); asking to borrow

examples.note: 엉키다 = get tangled; 자꾸 = repeatedly

examples.note: 한 가닥 = one strand; 달다 = sew/attach on

extendedVocab.nuance: 실 is the native word for thread or yarn — the fine strand used for sewing and knitting, the lifelong partner of 바늘 in the set phrase 바늘과 실. The single most useful fact is its dedicated counter: a strand of thread is counted with 가닥 (실 한 가닥, 두 가닥), the same 가닥 used for a strand of hair (머리카락 한 가닥), so 실 teaches you a counter, not just a word. Sort it firmly from its thicker cousins: 실 is fine thread/yarn, 끈 is a string/cord/strap for tying, and 줄 is a rope or line — a gradient from thinnest to thickest. Natural collocations: 실을 꿰다 (thread it through a needle), 실이 엉키다/풀리다 (the thread tangles/unravels), 실이 끊어지다 (the thread snaps), and the compound 실타래 (a skein of yarn). Two pitfalls: first, don't borrow 끈 for sewing thread — that's too thick. Second, beware the homophone trap — the syllable 실 also appears as a Sino-Korean prefix 實 'real/actual' (실시간 'real-time', 실제 'actual') and as 室 'room' (교실 'classroom'); as a free-standing noun, though, 실 means 'thread'.

Using 끈 (string/strap) where you mean sewing thread — sewing/knitting strand is 실; 끈 is thicker cord for tying.
Counting thread with 개 — a single strand takes 가닥: 실 한 가닥, not 실 한 개.
Confusing the noun 실 (thread) with the bound morphemes 實 'real' (실제, 실시간) or 室 'room' (교실) — those only exist inside other words; alone, 실 = thread.

examples.note: 채우다 = fasten; 끝까지 = to the very end

examples.romanization: syeocheu danchuga tteoreojyeoseo dasi daraya dwaeyo.
examples.en: A shirt button came off, so I have to sew it back on.
examples.note: 떨어지다 = fall off; 달다 = sew on

extendedVocab.nuance: 단추 is specifically a clothing button — the disc you fasten on a shirt, blouse, or coat. The verbs are a tidy set worth memorizing together: 채우다 (or 잠그다) to button up, 풀다 to unbutton, and 달다 to sew a button on (with 떨어지다 for one falling off). The contrast that trips up every English speaker is 단추 vs 버튼: English uses 'button' for both clothing fasteners AND press-buttons on machines, but Korean splits them — a button on a remote, elevator, keyboard, or website is 버튼 (loanword), reserved for the press kind, while 단추 is strictly the sew-on clothing kind. So you press the 버튼 on the 엘리베이터 but fasten the 단추 on your 셔츠. (There is also the idiom 첫 단추를 잘못 끼우다 — 'fasten the first button wrong' = get off on the wrong foot, where buttoning is 끼우다.) Pitfall: never say 단추 for a device button (that's 버튼), and don't use 묶다 (tie) to button — buttons are 채우다/잠그다, not tied.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a press-button on a remote, elevator, or app a 단추 — that is 버튼; 단추 is only a clothing fastener.
Buttoning up with 묶다 (tie) — use 채우다 or 잠그다 (단추를 채우다); 풀다 to unbutton.
Saying 단추를 떨어뜨렸어요 when a button simply fell off — for it dropping off by itself use the intransitive 단추가 떨어졌어요; the transitive 떨어뜨리다 means you dropped it.

extendedVocab.nuance: 우산 is Sino-Korean 雨傘, literally 雨 'rain' + 傘 'umbrella/parasol' — so the word transparently means 'rain-umbrella', which is your built-in reminder it's for rain. The verb is the deceptively busy 쓰다: to put up/use an umbrella is 우산을 쓰다, the same 쓰다 that covers wearing a hat (모자를 쓰다) and glasses (안경을 쓰다) — Korean groups 'things over your head/face' under 쓰다, distinct from 입다 (clothes on the torso/legs) and 신다 (footwear). The contrast to file away is 우산 vs 양산: both are 傘, but 우산 (雨傘) is the rain umbrella while 양산 (陽傘, 'sun-shade') is a parasol against sunlight — different words for different weather. Useful collocations: 우산을 쓰다/접다/펴다 (put up / fold / open an umbrella), 우산을 챙기다 (remember to grab an umbrella), 우산을 깜빡하다 (forget the umbrella). A folding umbrella is 접는 우산 or 3단 우산, a long one 장우산. Pitfall: English 'wear/carry an umbrella' must become 쓰다 (use over the head), never 입다, and don't reuse 우산 for a sun parasol — that's 양산.

Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.en: Let's meet at noon.

examples.note: 정오 is the word announcements and schedules use

examples.note: 부터 marks the starting point of an event

extendedVocab.nuance: 정오 is Sino-Korean 正午 ('exact' 正 + 'the horse hour' 午, the old zodiac slot for midday), so it literally pins down 12:00 in the daytime with a crisp, official feel. The everyday spoken equivalent is 낮 12시, which is what friends actually say; 정오 belongs to schedules, broadcasts, train timetables and writing. Do not confuse it with plain 낮, which is the whole bright part of the day, not the single instant — 정오 is one point, 낮 is a span. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the clock reading and tacking on 시: there is no 정오 시. Just say 정오 by itself, or switch to 낮 12시 if you want the casual register. Its mirror-image partner is 자정 (midnight, 12 a.m.).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 정오 시 — 정오 already means 12:00, so adding 시 is redundant; use 정오 alone or 낮 12시.
Confusing 정오 (noon, 12 p.m.) with 자정 (midnight, 12 a.m.) — they share the 正/正 'exact' feel but mark opposite ends of the day.
Using 정오 for the whole afternoon — it is one instant; for the daytime span say 낮.

examples.note: the set way to ask the day-of-month number

examples.en: I rested well for a few days.
examples.note: 며칠 동안 = over the span of several days

extendedVocab.nuance: 며칠 carries two everyday senses decided purely by context: the indefinite 'a few days' (며칠 동안 쉬었어요 = I rested for a few days) and the question 'what date' (오늘 며칠이에요? = what's today's date?). The single most important point for any learner — native or foreign — is the spelling: it is ALWAYS 며칠, never 몇일. Even though 'how many' is 몇 and 'day' is 일(日), the fused word lost that shape and is written 며칠 by rule, so 몇일 is simply a misspelling. Mind the boundary with two neighbours: 며칠 asks the date (a number, 17th), whereas 무슨 요일 asks the day of the week (Monday, Tuesday), and 얼마나 asks 'how long'. So if you want 'which weekday is it', do not say 며칠 — use 무슨 요일이에요? Tone and the surrounding words tell a listener instantly whether you are estimating a span or asking the calendar.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 몇일 — the standard, correct form is always 며칠, despite 몇 + 일.
Confusing 며칠 (what date / a few days) with 무슨 요일 (which day of the week) — date number vs weekday name.
Using 며칠 to ask 'how long' — that is 얼마나 (얼마나 걸려요?); 며칠 names days, not open duration.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그때 means "that time, then, back then" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그때 (geuttae) means "that time, then, back then". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그때 ("that time / then"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그때 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: a moment both speakers already know
부터 = starting from that point
까지 = up to that point
그때 + 그 + noun, e.g. 그때 그 사람

examples.en: That's when we first met.
examples.note: 처음 = for the first time

examples.en: Back then I was a student.
examples.note: 는 frames that period as the topic/contrast

examples.en: Okay, see you then.
examples.note: 그때 reused for an agreed FUTURE time

extendedVocab.nuance: 그때 is the demonstrative 그 ('that', the listener-known one) fused with 때 ('time, occasion'), so it points at a specific moment both speakers can already identify — looking back ('back then') or to a plan just arranged ('see you then'). Write it solid as 그때; the spaced 그 때 is non-standard. Mind the demonstrative trio that mirrors 이/그/저: 이때 = this moment / now in the flow of events, 그때 = that known moment, and the question 언제 = 'when?'. The key English-speaker pitfall is the 'that' default: because English freely says 'that time' for brand-new information, learners reach for 그때 even when the listener has no idea which moment is meant. But 그때 presupposes shared knowledge — if the time is new to your listener you must first establish it (give the date or event), and only then can 그때 refer back to it.

Writing it as two words 그 때 — the standard spelling is the single word 그때.
Using 그때 for a brand-new time the listener can't yet identify — 그때 needs a shared, already-known moment.
Confusing 그때 (that known time) with 이때 (this/now) or 언제 (when?) — the 이/그/저 logic still applies.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 나중 means "later, afterward (a later time)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "later, afterward (a later time)" is 나중 (najung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 나중에 ("later / afterward"). Watch the particle attached to 나중 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: almost always used with 에
a stock friendly goodbye
맨 = the very (most), so 'dead last'
rare 나중 without 에, here object of 위해

examples.en: I'll call you later.
examples.note: -ㄹ게요 = a friendly promise to do it

examples.en: Let's talk about that later.
examples.note: polite way to postpone a topic

examples.en: I'll eat dessert dead last.
examples.note: 맨 나중에 = at the very end of the sequence

extendedVocab.nuance: 나중 is the native noun for a later, unspecified time, and in practice it is almost fused with its particle: you will hear 나중에 ('later, afterward') far more than bare 나중. It is the go-to word for gently postponing things — 나중에 이야기해요 (let's talk later), 나중에 봐요 (see you later). The crucial dividing lines are with two near-synonyms. 이따가 means 'in a little while', but specifically LATER THE SAME DAY, a short wait; 나중에 is open-ended and can be days, months, or a vague someday. 다음에 means 'next time', tied to the next occasion or meeting rather than just elapsed time. So 'see you later today' leans 이따가 봐요, 'see you next time' is 다음에 봐요, and the all-purpose vague 'later' is 나중에 봐요. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the particle (bare 나중 sounds incomplete) and over-using 나중에 for the same-day 'in a bit', where 이따가 is more precise.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using bare 나중 as an adverb — say 나중에; 나중 almost always needs its 에.
Using 나중에 for 'in a little while (today)' — that short same-day wait is 이따가.
Confusing 나중에 (vague later) with 다음에 (next time/occasion) — time elapsed vs the next meeting.

extendedVocab.explanation: 스물 (seumul) = "twenty (native number)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 스물 ("twenty") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 스물, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the plain, standalone form — used when no counter follows (e.g. counting out loud)
스물 drops its final ㄹ and becomes 스무 before the counter 살
compound number: tens word 스물 + ones word 하나, said as one breath
스물 → 스무 again; 명 is the polite counter for people

examples.en: One, two… nineteen, twenty!
examples.note: standalone counting keeps the full form 스물 with no shape change

examples.en: I'm twenty years old this year.
examples.note: real age uses native numbers + 살, and 스물 becomes 스무 here

examples.en: There are twenty students in the class.
examples.note: the counter 명 still triggers 스무, never 스물 명

extendedVocab.nuance: 스물 is the native-Korean twenty (the 고유어 set 하나·둘…열·스물…), and it is the default for human age and for counting tangible people and things — Sino-Korean 이십 sounds clinical there. Like the low numbers, 스물 has a special pre-counter shape: it loses its final ㄹ to become 스무 directly before any counter (스무 살, 스무 개, 스무 명), which is the single biggest trap here. Crucially, 스물 is the LAST native ten to do this — 서른·마흔·쉰 and up never change. Standalone (counting aloud, or with 이/가) it stays 스물: '스물이 넘었어요'. English speakers also wrongly reach for 이십 when stating age; '저는 이십 살이에요' is ungrammatical, it must be 스무 살.

Saying '스물 살' or '스물 개' — before a counter the ㄹ drops, so it must be 스무 살, 스무 개.
Using Sino-Korean 이십 for age ('이십 살'); native 스무 + 살 is the only natural form for a person's age.
Keeping 스무 when no counter follows, e.g. '나이가 스무예요' — standalone it returns to 스물: '스물이에요'.

extendedVocab.explanation: 서른 (seoreun) means "thirty (native number)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서른 ("thirty"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서른 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

native number + 살 is the natural way to give an adult's age
only the ones digit shifts: 둘 → 두, so 서른두 not 서른둘
서른 + subject 이 + 되다 = reach the age of thirty

examples.en: Counting one by one: twenty-nine, thirty.
examples.note: standalone 서른 in plain counting

examples.en: My older sister is thirty.
examples.note: everyday age statement; 서른 stays whole before 살

examples.en: I turned thirty this year.
examples.note: 서른이 되다 marks crossing into a new decade of age

A key relief: unlike 하나~넷 and 스물, the tens word 서른 itself does NOT change before a counter — you say 서른 살, 서른 명 with the full form. For round '30 years old' specifically, plain 서른 살 is what Koreans actually say.

Leaving the ones digit unchanged: '서른둘 살', '서른셋 살' — it must be 서른두 살, 서른세 살.
Assuming 서른 itself shrinks like 스물 → 스무; it does not — 서른 살, never '서르 살'.

extendedVocab.explanation: "forty (native number)" is 마흔 (maheun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마흔 ("forty"). Watch the particle attached to 마흔 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: native tens word; stays whole before a counter (마흔 살)
native number + 살 = a person's age around forty
마흔 + 다섯; the ones digit 다섯 does not change before 살
마흔 + 이 + 넘다 = to be past the age of forty

examples.en: After thirty-nine comes forty.
examples.note: standalone 마흔 in counting order

examples.en: My dad is forty.
examples.note: natural spoken age; 마흔 keeps its full form

examples.en: I'm past forty.
examples.note: 마흔이 넘다 expresses 'over' an age threshold

extendedVocab.nuance: 마흔 is the native-Korean forty, the everyday word for someone's age in their forties — Koreans rarely say 사십 살 about a real person. Like 서른, the tens word stays intact before counters (마흔 살, 마흔 명); only an added ones digit changes (마흔한, 마흔두, 마흔세, 마흔네, from 하나·둘·셋·넷), while 다섯~아홉 stay the same (마흔다섯 살). Note the irregular sound of 마흔: it is spelled with ㅎ but pronounced as if [마흔], and many learners both mis-spell it '마은' and mishear it. Don't confuse it in writing with 만 (10,000); 마흔 is a native counting word for forty only, never used for prices or phone digits.

Changing the ones digit when it shouldn't: '마흔다서 살' — 다섯 stays whole, so it's 마흔다섯 살.

쉰 + 여섯; the ones digit 여섯 keeps its form

In Korean the particle or ending next to 첫째 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: native ordinal for #1; also 'first of all' when listing
the eldest child; 첫째 alone can mean 'the eldest'
first day of a trip, course, or job
the next native ordinal, used in the same series as 첫째

examples.en: I'm the eldest (first child).
examples.note: 첫째 alone names birth order in a family

examples.en: On the first day of the trip we went to the sea.
examples.note: 첫째 날 = the first day in a sequence

examples.en: First of all, health matters most.
examples.note: 첫째 opens a list, pairing with 둘째 next

extendedVocab.nuance: 첫째 is the native-Korean ordinal 'first', built from 첫 (the bound 'first' form of 하나) + the ordinal suffix -째; the rest of the family runs 둘째, 셋째, 넷째 'second/third/fourth'. It does three jobs: it names the eldest child (저는 첫째예요), it labels the first item in a sequence (첫째 날, 첫째 주 'first week'), and it works like 'firstly/first of all' to organize spoken or written points, almost always followed by 둘째. Don't confuse the ORDINAL system (첫째, 둘째 — order/rank) with the CARDINAL-plus-번/번째 way of listing (일 번, 1번째 'item no. 1'); 첫째 ranks, 일 번 labels. Also note the bound adjective 첫 'first' (첫사랑 first love, 첫날 first day, 첫인상 first impression) — same root, but 첫 attaches to a noun while 첫째 stands as the ordinal itself. A common slip is using the plain number 하나 to mean 'first'; ordering requires 첫째, never 하나.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using plain 하나 to mean 'first'; the ordinal is 첫째 (하나 is just the count 'one').
Mixing the ordinal 첫째 with the Sino-Korean label 일 번/1번 in a list — they aren't interchangeable.
Saying '첫 아이' and '첫째 아이' as if identical; both occur, but for birth-order 'the eldest' the noun is 첫째.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 영 means "zero" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "zero" is 영 (yeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 영 ("zero"). Watch the particle attached to 영 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-Korean reading of 0; the default in math, scores, and temperature
after the decimal point each digit is read one by one
영(zero) + 下 하(below); the standard weather word for minus temperatures
대(對 'against') links the two sides of a score

examples.en: Five plus zero is five.
examples.note: Simplest case: 영 as a plain math value, read exactly like the digit 0.

examples.en: This morning it was minus five degrees.
examples.note: 영하 is the everyday way to say 'sub-zero'; note it is one word, not 영 + 하.

examples.ko: 축구 경기가 영 대 영으로 끝났어요.
examples.romanization: chukgu gyeonggiga yeong dae yeongeuro kkeunnasseoyo.
examples.en: The soccer match ended zero to zero.
examples.note: Reporting a real scoreline: 대 sits between the two numbers like English 'to'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 영 is the Sino-Korean reading of the digit 0 (한자 零, 'nothing/nil'), and it is the form you reach for in mathematics, temperatures, scores, percentages, and the figures after a decimal point. Its near-rival is 공 (孔/空-style reading): both translate as 'zero', but the dividing line is sharp — 영 is for quantities and measured values (영 도 = 0 degrees, 영 점 = 0 points), whereas 공 is for zeros recited inside a string of digits like phone and room numbers (공일공). They are NOT freely swappable. It collocates tightly with 영하 (below zero), 영 점 (0.0…), and 영 대 영 (a 0-0 tie). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, do not reuse 영 when reading out '010' or '302' — a Korean would never say 영일영; second, there is no native-Korean counting word for zero at all, so when you need 'zero' you are always choosing between these two Sino readings, never a 하나-series word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading the 0 in a phone number as 영 (영일영) — strings of recited digits take 공, so 010 is 공일공.
Hunting for a 'native' zero to match 하나/둘/셋 — there is none; both 영 and 공 are Sino, and you pick by context (measured value vs. recited digit).
Saying 영하 as two stressed words or inserting a particle (영 가 하) — it is a single fixed noun 영하 meaning 'below zero'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 공 means "zero (in phone numbers)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 공 (gong) = "zero (in phone numbers)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공 ("zero (recited digit)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the 0 spoken aloud inside phone, room, and account numbers
the universal Korean mobile prefix, read digit by digit
the Seoul landline area code
공 voices the middle 0; 호 is the room/unit counter

examples.en: The front part of my number is 010.
examples.note: Simplest use: reading the standard mobile prefix one digit at a time.

examples.en: The room number is 505.
examples.note: Hotels and dorms recite room numbers digit by digit, so the middle 0 is 공.

examples.en: Seoul's area code is 02.
examples.note: Real situation: distinguishing the 02 (공이) prefix when someone asks where to dial.

extendedVocab.nuance: 공 is how Koreans voice the digit 0 when reading off a sequence of digits — phone numbers, area codes, room numbers, building codes, account and card numbers. Although the dictionary gloss is identical to 영 ('zero'), the two split cleanly by function: 공 is for digits you recite one-by-one in an identifier, while 영 is for a measured quantity (temperature, score, decimal). The dividing test: if the whole 'number' is really a label or address rather than an amount, use 공. It habitually appears in fixed strings — 공일공 (010), 공이 (02), and any 호(號) room number with a 0 inside. The English-speaker pitfall is importing the English habit of saying 'zero' or 'oh' interchangeably and then defaulting to 영: a phone number read as 영일영 sounds plainly wrong to natives. Also note 공 is invariable here — you do not pluralize or add a counter; you simply chain the digits (공-일-공) in a flat, even rhythm.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 영 for the 0 in 010 (영일영) — recited identifier digits take 공, so it must be 공일공.
Pausing or stressing 공 like a separate word — phone numbers are read in an even, flat string (공일공) with no emphasis.
Looking for a native counting word ('zero') to read a digit — Korean has none; the recited-digit zero is always 공.
