extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이십 means "twenty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이십 (isip) means "twenty". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이십 ("twenty (20)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이십 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 二十: 이(2) × 십(10), the Sino-Korean tens-builder
minutes always take Sino numbers
일(日) gives the calendar date
ratios and discounts use Sino numbers

examples.en: Count from one to twenty.
examples.note: Plainest use: 이십 as the end-point of a Sino-Korean count.

examples.en: It's 2:20 now.
examples.note: Clock split: the hour is native (두 시) but the minutes are Sino (이십 분).

examples.en: Today is June 20th, so it's payday.
examples.note: Real situation: a calendar date, where 이십 일 reads '20th' with Sino numbers.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이십 is the Sino-Korean twenty, transparently built as 二十 — 이(two) stacked on 십(ten) — and this stacking logic extends all the way up the tens. Its native counterpart is 스물/스무, and the contrast is the single biggest hurdle for beginners: Sino 이십 governs minutes, calendar dates, money, percentages, math, and any number over about a hundred, while native 스물 governs hours on a clock, ages, and most counted objects (스무 명, 스무 살). The collocations to lock in are 이십 분 (twenty past), 이십 일 (the 20th), and 이십 퍼센트. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating '20' as one word and using 이십 everywhere — but '20 o'clock' is native (스무 시 is rare; people say 여덟 시 in the evening), and '20 years old' is 스무 살, never 이십 살. A useful rule of thumb: measured/abstract quantities lean Sino, hand-counted things and the hour lean native.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이십 시 / 이 시 for the hour — clock hours are native, so 2 o'clock is 두 시, not 이십/이 시.
Saying 이십 살 for age — age uses native, so '20 years old' is 스무 살.
Forgetting the word order of compounds — 20 is 이십 (二十), but 12 is 십이 (十二); the multiplier-then-ten order is fixed.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 삼십 means "thirty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "thirty" is 삼십 (samsip). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 삼십 ("thirty (30)"). Watch the particle attached to 삼십 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the most frequent use — telling time
일(日) as a date or a day-count
초(秒) seconds also take Sino numbers

examples.en: Thirty minus ten is twenty.
examples.note: Simplest use: 삼십 as a pure arithmetic value.

examples.en: It's 7:30 now.
examples.note: Half past: native hour 일곱 시 plus Sino 삼십 분 — the everyday way to say 7:30.

examples.ko: 환불은 삼십 일 안에 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: hwanbureun samsip il ane haeya haeyo.
examples.en: Refunds must be made within thirty days.
examples.note: Real situation: a policy window, where 삼십 일 means '30 days' as a duration.

extendedVocab.nuance: 삼십 is the Sino-Korean thirty (三十, 삼 over 십), and for learners it earns its keep mainly in telling time, because '...:30' / half past comes up in nearly every spoken time. The native rival 서른 covers age (서른 살) and bare object counts, while 삼십 owns minutes, seconds, dates, durations, and money. Watch the meaning of 일(日) after it: 삼십 일 is either 'the 30th' (a date) or 'thirty days' (a span), disambiguated only by context — 삼십 일에 (on the 30th) vs. 삼십 일 동안 (for thirty days). Habitual collocations: 삼십 분 (half past), 삼십 일 (the 30th / 30 days), 삼십 초. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving off 분: '7:30' must be 일곱 시 삼십 분, and saying only 일곱 시 삼십 sounds unfinished; equally, never promote 삼십 into the hour slot (삼십 시 does not exist as a clock hour in ordinary speech).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the counter and saying 일곱 시 삼십 — you must close with 분: 일곱 시 삼십 분.
Using 삼십 for age (삼십 살) — age is native, so 'thirty years old' is 서른 살.
Reading 삼십 일 only as 'the 30th' — depending on context it is also 'thirty days', so check 동안/안에 vs. 에.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사십 means "forty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사십 (sasip) = "forty". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사십 ("forty (40)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사십, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: duration or '...:40' on the clock
stack the ones digit straight on: 사십+오
만(10,000) groups large money figures

examples.en: Forty is four tens.
examples.note: Simplest use: 사십 unpacked as 4×10, reinforcing the build.

examples.en: It takes about forty minutes from here to school.
examples.note: Everyday duration; 쯤 ('about') softens the estimate.

examples.en: The rent is 400,000 won excluding the deposit.
examples.note: Real situation: quoting rent, where 사십만 reads with the 만 grouping.

extendedVocab.nuance: 사십 is the Sino-Korean forty (四十), and like every Sino ten it is fully compositional: glue the ones digit on with no spacer, so 45 is 사십오 and 48 is 사십팔. It rules minutes, prices, percentages, and distances, while the native 마흔 is reserved for age (마흔 살) and a few hand-counts. A pronunciation note worth flagging: 사(四) is a single short syllable, and because Korean has several look-alike one-syllable numbers (사 4, 삼 3, 오 5), beginners must keep it crisp or '사십' blurs into a neighbour. Typical collocations: 사십 분, 사십만 원, 사십 퍼센트. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping money one-to-one onto Western grouping: 400,000 is not 'four hundred thousand' built on 천, but 사십만 — forty units of 만(10,000) — so you must regroup by four digits, not three. And as always, 사십 never names an age (use 마흔) or a clock hour.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사십 for age (사십 살) — age is native, so 'forty years old' is 마흔 살.
Building 400,000 on the English grouping (사백천) — Korean groups by 만, so it is 사십만 원.
Clipping 사 so it merges with 삼/오 — keep the digit distinct, since 사십(40), 삼십(30), 오십(50) differ by one syllable.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 오십 means "fifty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 오십 (osip) means "fifty". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오십 ("fifty (50)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오십 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: telling time and durations
the headline number on sale signs
ones digit attaches directly: 오십+삼

examples.en: Half is fifty percent of a hundred.
examples.note: Simplest use: 오십 in a clean ratio statement.

examples.ko: 지금 아홉 시 오십 분이라 곧 열 시예요.
examples.romanization: jigeum ahop si osip bunira got yeol siyeyo.
examples.en: It's 9:50, so it'll be ten soon.
examples.note: Everyday clock-reading; native hour 아홉 시 with Sino 오십 분.

examples.ko: 이 신발 오십 퍼센트 할인이라 바로 샀어요.
examples.romanization: i sinbal osip peosenteu harinira baro sasseoyo.
examples.en: These shoes were fifty percent off, so I bought them right away.
examples.note: Real situation: a sale, where 오십 퍼센트 할인 is the fixed 'half-price' phrase.

extendedVocab.nuance: 오십 is the Sino-Korean fifty (五十), and beyond time it is the number you meet most on shop signs, because 오십 퍼센트 할인 ('50% off') is the great rallying cry of Korean sales. It governs minutes, money, scores, and percentages; the native rival 쉰 carries age (쉰 살). Composition is regular — 오십삼 (53), 오십칠 (57) — with the ones digit fused directly on. Core collocations: 오십 분, 오십 퍼센트, 오십 원. A small sound caution: 오(五) alone is 'five', so listen for the 십 that turns it into 'fifty'; in fast speech beginners sometimes hear 오 and miss the tens. The English-speaker pitfall is, again, the slots reserved for native numbers — '50 years old' is 쉰 살, not 오십 살, and there is no 오십 시 hour on a clock. When in doubt: a measured amount or ratio is Sino (오십), a person's age is native (쉰).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오십 살 for age — age is native, so 'fifty years old' is 쉰 살.
Hearing only 오 and writing 5 when the speaker said 오십 (50) — the 십 is the load-bearing syllable.
Placing 오십 in the hour slot (오십 시) — hours are native; 오십 belongs to minutes and amounts.

duration phrasing

examples.en: One minute is sixty seconds.
examples.note: Simplest use: a basic time fact, all Sino numbers.

examples.ko: 여기까지 오는 데 육십 분 넘게 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: yeogikkaji oneun de yuksip bun neomge geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took over sixty minutes to get here.
examples.note: Everyday duration; 넘게 ('more than') leans on the count 육십.

examples.ko: 저희 할아버지는 올해 육십 세가 되셨어요.
examples.romanization: jeohui harabeojineun olhae yuksip sega doesyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My grandfather turned sixty this year.
examples.note: Real situation: formal age with the honorific 되셨어요, so 세 (not 살) takes Sino 육십.

extendedVocab.nuance: 육십 is the Sino-Korean sixty (六十). Beyond seconds and minutes, it introduces a register split English speakers often miss: age can be said two ways, and the counter decides the number system. The formal/written counter 세(歲) takes Sino numbers — 육십 세 — and shows up on documents, news, and respectful speech, while the everyday counter 살 takes the native number 예순 (예순 살). So 'sixty years old' is 육십 세 OR 예순 살, but crossing them (육십 살 / 예순 세) is wrong. Pronunciation note: 육(六) is initial-ㅇ here but links smoothly into 십, and many speakers nasalize the boundary (yuk-ssip). Habitual collocations: 육십 초, 육십 분, 육십 세. The pitfall, then, is the counter-number agreement: pick 세 with Sino (육십 세) for formality, or 살 with native (예순 살) for daily talk — never mix the two halves.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 육십 살 for casual age — 살 takes native numbers, so use 예순 살 (keep 육십 for the formal 육십 세).
Pairing 세 with a native number (예순 세) — the formal counter 세 takes Sino, giving 육십 세.
Reversing the digits as 십육 (16) when you mean 육십 (60) — multiplier-before-십 fixes the order.

extendedVocab.nuance: 칠십 is the Sino-Korean seventy (七十). It is the number of test scores (칠십 점), distances (칠십 미터), prices, and formal ages (칠십 세), and it composes regularly: 칠십이 (72), 칠십오 (75). As with 60, the age register splits by counter — formal 칠십 세 (Sino) versus everyday 일흔 살 (native 일흔). The collocation worth memorizing is 점(點) for scores, which always rides Sino numbers, so a grade is 칠십 점, never a native count. Pronunciation: 칠(七) ends in ㄹ and flows into 십, kept as two crisp syllables. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, scores feel 'countable' to English minds, tempting a native number, but 점 demands Sino (칠십 점); second, the age mismatch again — say 일흔 살 in conversation and reserve 칠십 세 for respectful or formal contexts, but never blend them into 칠십 살 or 일흔 세.

Saying 칠십 살 in casual speech — everyday age is native, so use 일흔 살 (keep 칠십 for formal 칠십 세).
Flipping to 십칠 (17) for 칠십 (70) — the tens-multiplier (칠) comes before 십.

extendedVocab.nuance: 팔십 is the Sino-Korean eighty (八十), the everyday number of battery levels, survey results, scores, and percentages, and it composes by simple stacking: 팔십육 (86), 팔십삼 (83). The collocation pattern to internalize is 퍼센트 — percentages are ratios, so they always take Sino numbers, making 팔십 퍼센트 the natural phrasing for '80% battery' or '80% agreed'. Pronunciation note: 팔(八) ends in ㄹ and links into 십, and the cluster is read smoothly (pal-ssip). The English-speaker pitfall is the temptation to treat percentages or scores as 'counted things' deserving native numbers; they are measured ratios, so Sino 팔십 is required. And, predictably, casual age is native (여든 살) while only the formal counter 세 takes Sino (팔십 세) — keep the two halves matched.

Saying 팔십 살 for everyday age — casual age is native, so use 여든 살 (formal 팔십 세 keeps Sino).
Reading 팔십 (80) as 십팔 (18) — the multiplier 팔 precedes 십 in the tens.

examples.en: On this exam you must score over ninety to pass.
examples.note: Real situation: a pass threshold, where 구십 점 is the cutoff.

extendedVocab.nuance: 구십 is the Sino-Korean ninety (九十), the final two-digit ten before the unit 백(100) takes over, and it composes to the very top of the range: 구십구 (99). It governs scores, percentages, prices, and formal ages (구십 세), with native 아흔 reserved for casual age (아흔 살). Two ordering traps make this entry worth special care. First, 구십 (90) versus 십구 (19): the multiplier 구 must precede 십 for a ten, so reversing the syllables flips the value drastically. Second, once you pass 99 you do not keep stacking tens — 100 becomes 백, not 십십, so 구십 is genuinely the ceiling of this pattern. Collocations: 구십 점, 구십 퍼센트, 구십구. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the digit order, is the same age-register rule: say 아흔 살 in everyday talk, 구십 세 in formal contexts, and never the hybrids 구십 살 or 아흔 세.

Reversing 구십 (90) and 십구 (19) — the tens-multiplier (구) comes before 십.
Continuing to stack tens past 99 (구십십) — 100 is the new unit 백, so count rolls over there.
Saying 구십 살 for casual age — everyday age is native (아흔 살); the formal counter 세 keeps Sino (구십 세).

extendedVocab.explanation: 백만 (baengman) = "one million". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 백만 ("one million (1,000,000)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 백만, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: a common monthly-salary and big-ticket price figure
이 + 백만, the ones-multiplier sits in front

examples.en: A hundred ten-thousands make a million.
examples.note: Simplest use: showing the 만-based build (100 × 10,000).

examples.romanization: i noteubugi baengman woni jogeum neomeoyo.
examples.en: This laptop is a little over a million won.
examples.note: Everyday price; 넘다 ('exceed') pairs with the figure 백만 원.

examples.ko: 콘서트 표가 일 분 만에 백만 장이 팔렸어요.
examples.romanization: konseoteu pyoga il bun mane baengman jangi pallyeosseoyo.

examples.note: Real situation: a headline-style sales figure with the counter 장 (sheets/tickets).

extendedVocab.nuance: 백만 is one million (百萬), literally 백(hundred) multiplied by 만(ten-thousand), and it exposes the deepest structural difference between Korean and English numbers: Korean groups by four digits (만 = 10,000), not three (thousand). So a million is not a free-standing 'million' word but a composite of 백 × 만, and 2,000,000 simply prefixes the multiplier as 이백만. There is no native rival here — large numbers are exclusively Sino. The everyday collocations are 백만 원 (a million won, the scale of salaries and laptops) and 백만 명/장 (a million people/tickets). The English-speaker pitfall is enormous and worth drilling: you cannot translate 'one million' digit-group by digit-group through 천(thousand). If you mentally chunk 1,000,000 as '1,000 × 1,000' you will reach for 천, but Korean parses it as '100 × 10,000' → 백만. Train yourself to insert a comma every four digits (100,0000) rather than every three, and the 만/억 units fall into place naturally.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Building a million on 천 like English thousands — Korean groups by 만, so 1,000,000 is 백만 (100 × 10,000).
Comma-grouping by threes (1,000,000) when reading aloud — regroup by fours (100,0000) so the 만 boundary is visible.
Saying 천천 or 만만 for 'ten thousand / million' — the unit words 만 and 억 are single morphemes, not doubled ones.

examples.en: Ten thousand times ten thousand is one hundred million.
examples.note: Simplest use: deriving 억 as 만 × 만 (10,000²).

examples.en: Seoul apartments usually cost several hundred million each.
examples.note: Everyday housing talk; 몇억 ('several 억') and 씩 ('apiece') are very natural here.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 복권으로 십억 원에 당첨됐대요.

examples.en: They say he won a billion won in the lottery.
examples.note: Real situation: a windfall, where 십억 (10 × 억 = 1,000,000,000) is reported second-hand with -대요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 억 is the Sino unit for a hundred million (億), and it sits one rung above 만 on the four-digit ladder: 만 → 억 → 조, where each step multiplies by 10,000 (so 억 = 만 × 만). In Korea this is not an exotic 'big number' — it is the everyday currency of real estate, since apartments and houses are quoted in 억 (보통 몇억). The usual collocation keeps a multiplier in front: 일억, 삼억, 십억, plus the money counter 원. The English-speaker pitfall is the false friend with English magnitude words: 억 is NOT 'a million' and not even cleanly 'a hundred million' in the way English chunks it — because Korean groups by four digits, 1억 = 1,0000,0000. If you try to anchor 억 to a three-digit-grouped English word you will be off by an order of magnitude. The reliable move is positional: 만 is the 5th digit, 억 is the 9th digit. Note too that 일억 normally keeps its 일 (unlike 백 or 천, which can stand alone), so 'one hundred million won' is 일억 원.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 억 with English 'million' — 억 is a hundred million (10^8); mapping it to a three-digit-grouped word loses a factor of 100.
Confusing 억 (10^8) with 만 (10^4) — they are four digits apart on the 만→억 ladder, not adjacent zeros.
Dropping the 일 in '100 million' (saying just 억 원) — unlike 백/천, 억 normally keeps its multiplier: 일억 원.

Watch the particle attached to 번 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. usagePhrases.note: 番: counter for an assigned position or ID, with Sino numbers
list items, exam questions, jersey or seat numbers
asking for a bus, room, exit, or question number

examples.en: What number is this?
examples.note: Simplest use: 몇 번 asking the assigned number of an item.

examples.ko: 저는 지하철 삼 번 출구에서 기다릴게요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jihacheol sam beon chulgueseo gidarilgeyo.
examples.en: I'll wait at subway exit number 3.
examples.note: Everyday meet-up; 삼 번 출구 names a specific exit with Sino 삼.

examples.romanization: o beon beoseureul tago du beon garatasseoyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: 번 (한자 番) is the counter for an assigned, ordered number — bus and route numbers, subway exits, exam questions, list items, jersey and seat numbers — and in this ID sense it always takes Sino-Korean numbers: 삼 번 출구, 오 번 버스, never 세 번 출구. Its tricky twin is the homograph 번 meaning 'times/occasions', which takes NATIVE numbers: 세 번 (three times), 다섯 번 (five times). The dividing line is meaning, not spelling: does 번 label a thing (use Sino) or count repetitions (use native)? A near-synonym for the labelling sense is 호(號), but 호 attaches to rooms and issue/model numbers (302호, 창간호) while 번 covers routes, exits, and questions. The English-speaker pitfall is the Sino/native split inside a single counter: learners who have just mastered '세 번 = three times' over-apply native numbers to bus and exit numbers, producing 세 번 버스 — which a Korean parses as 'the bus, three times', not 'bus number 3'. Anchor it with the contrast pair 삼 번 (No. 3) vs. 세 번 (3 times).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using native numbers for an ID (세 번 버스, 세 번 출구) — labelling 번 takes Sino, so it is 삼 번 버스 / 삼 번 출구.
Using Sino numbers for repetitions (삼 번 갔어요) — 'times' 번 takes native, so 'went three times' is 세 번 갔어요.
Swapping 번 and 호 — rooms and issues use 호 (302호), while routes, exits, and questions use 번 (삼 번).

il-cheung; the street-level floor

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이것 means "this (thing)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이것 (igeot) means "this (thing)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이것은 ("this (as topic)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이것 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 이것 + 은. Sets 'this' as what the sentence is about; contracts to 이건 when spoken.
이것 + 이. Marks 'this' as the doer/identity; in speech almost always becomes 이게.
이것 + 을. Marks 'this' as what the verb acts on; spoken form is 이걸.
이것 + 좀 softens a request when you hand over or point at a nearby object.

examples.en: This is a book.
examples.note: 이것은 names something near you; the 은 frames it as the topic.

examples.en: Where did you buy this?
examples.note: 이것을 is the object form — note the 을 marks what was bought.

examples.en: Sir/Ma'am, this is the new product.
examples.note: Polished service register; 이것이 (not 이거) suits a clerk speaking formally.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이것 is the full, written-leaning form of 'this thing,' pointing to an object physically close to the speaker (이/그/저 = here/by-you/yonder). Its everyday spoken twin is 이거; the meaning is identical, but the dividing line is register — 이것 belongs to writing, announcements, and polite service speech, while 이거 dominates casual talk. It pairs with particles to make 이것은/이것이/이것을, and a native ear expects those to shrink to 이건/이게/이걸 the moment the situation turns conversational. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for 이것 to mean 'this' before a noun — but as a determiner you need 이 (이 책 'this book'); 이것 already bakes in '것/thing,' so 이것 책 is wrong. Also never use 이것 for a person; a human is 이분/이 사람, never a 'thing.'

Saying 이것 책 for 'this book' — 이것 already means 'this thing,' so before a noun use the determiner 이: 이 책.

usagePhrases.note: 그것 + 은. Frames a thing by the listener, or one already mentioned, as the topic; spoken 그건.
그것 + 이. Marks it as subject; in speech becomes 그게.
그것 + 을. The object form; spoken 그걸.

examples.note: 그것 points to a thing nearer the listener than to you.

examples.en: Please explain that.
examples.note: Here 그것 refers back to something already mentioned, not a physical object.

examples.en: That is exactly the problem.
examples.note: Formal/written tone; 그것이 (not 그게) fits a serious or business register.

usagePhrases.note: 저것 + 은. Frames a far-off thing as the topic; spoken 저건.
저것 + 이. The subject form; in speech becomes 저게.
저것 + 을. The object form; spoken 저걸.
저것 + 봐. Casual exclamation drawing eyes to something distant.

examples.en: That over there is a mountain.
examples.note: Both of you look at something far away — only 저것 fits this distance.

examples.en: Please show me that one over there.
examples.note: 저것을 is the object form; you point across a counter at a distant item.

examples.en: That thing visible far away is Namsan Tower.
examples.note: 저것이 (subject) naming a landmark in the distance.

extendedVocab.nuance: 저것 means 'that thing over there,' reserved for what is far from BOTH the speaker and the listener — the third slot in the 이것/그것/저것 set (here / by-you / yonder). Its casual spoken form is 저거 (저게/저걸/저건). examples.note: 이거 stands in for 'this dish/thing' right in front of you.

examples.note: Sentence-initial 저기 cushions a hesitant or awkward request.

extendedVocab.nuance: 저기 is the 'place' member of the 이/그/저 family — 'over there,' far from both people — completing 여기 (here) / 거기 (there, by you) / 저기 (yonder). Beyond location it has two social jobs English keeps separate: 저기요 is the go-to polite 'excuse me' for hailing a stranger or a waiter when you don't know their name, and a sentence-opening 저기… works like 'um / you know,' softening the ground before a request or bad news. The synonym to separate is 저거 — 저기 is a SPOT, 저거 is a THING, so 저기 뭐 있어요? ('what's over there?') versus 저거 뭐예요? ('what is that object?'). One register caution: in a restaurant, 저기요 is gentler and safer than the blunter 여기요, and calling a stranger 아저씨/아주머니 can sound abrupt, so 저기요 is the diplomatic choice.

Using 저기 for a place near the listener — that spot is 거기 (여기/거기/저기 track distance).
Confusing 저기 (a place) with 저거 (a thing): 저기 있어요 'it's over there' vs 저거예요 'it's that one.'
Saying just 여기 to flag a server when 저기요 would sound more polite and natural.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무엇 means "what" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "what" is 무엇 (mueot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무엇 ("what"). Watch the particle attached to 무엇 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Question word for things, the full form of spoken 뭐.
무엇 + 을. Spoken form contracts to 뭘 or drops to 뭐.
무엇 + 이. In speech becomes 뭐가.
무엇 + 보다. Set adverbial meaning 'above all, most of all.'

examples.en: What is your name?
examples.note: 무엇입니까 is a formal/written register; speech would say 이름이 뭐예요?

examples.en: How may I help you?
examples.note: A polished service phrase; 무엇을 (object) keeps it courteous.

examples.en: Health matters more than anything.
examples.note: 무엇보다 is a fixed expression — note it's one set phrase, not free 'what + than.'

extendedVocab.nuance: 무엇 means 'what' (asking about things) and is the full, dictionary form that lives in writing, exam questions, signage, and formal speech (무엇입니까?). Its everyday spoken reduction is 뭐, with 무엇을 → 뭘 and 무엇이 → 뭐가; the meaning never changes, only the register, so the dividing line between 무엇 and 뭐 is exactly formal-vs-casual. The near neighbor to contrast is 무슨, which is NOT interchangeable: 무엇/뭐 is a standalone pronoun ('what?'), whereas 무슨 always modifies a following noun and asks 'what kind of' (무슨 책? 'what book?'). English speakers, used to one word 'what,' wrongly say 무엇 책 — but you must choose 무슨 책. Memorize the frozen idiom 무엇보다 ('above all'), where 무엇 fuses with 보다 and does not mean a literal comparison.

Saying 무엇 책 for 'what book' — 무엇 is a standalone pronoun; to modify a noun use 무슨 (무슨 책).
Using 무엇 in casual chat, where 뭐 (and 뭘/뭐가) sounds far more natural.
Treating 무엇보다 as literal 'than what'; it's a fixed phrase meaning 'more than anything.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어느 means "which" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어느 (eoneu) = "which". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어느 것 ("which one") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 어느, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 어느 + 것 (spoken 어느 거). Picks one item out of a known set.
어느 + 나라. Extremely common in 'where are you from?' questions.
어느 + 쪽. Choosing between directions or two options.

usagePhrases.en: to what extent / about how much
usagePhrases.note: 어느 + 정도. Set phrase asking degree or rough amount.

examples.en: Which one is better?
examples.note: 어느 needs a following noun (것 here) — it can't stand alone.

examples.en: What country are you from?
examples.note: 어느 나라 is the natural Korean framing of 'where from.'

examples.en: How much Korean can you speak?
examples.note: 어느 정도 asks degree — a fixed, very useful collocation.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어느 means 'which' and is a determiner: it ALWAYS sits in front of a noun and selects one option from a limited, often visible set (어느 것, 어느 나라, 어느 쪽). The synonym you must not blur is 무슨: 어느 chooses from a known, bounded group ('which of these?'), while 무슨 asks 'what kind of' from an open field (무슨 음악 좋아해요? 'what kind of music?'). So 어느 영화 leans toward 'which (of the movies we're choosing among)?' and 무슨 영화 toward 'what (kind of) movie?' The English-speaker pitfall is using 어느 like the pronoun 'which one' on its own — but it cannot stand alone; you must attach a noun, and for 'which one' specifically you say 어느 것/어느 거. Learn 어느 정도 as a unit; it idiomatically means 'to what extent / roughly how much.'

Using 어느 alone as 'which one' — it must precede a noun; say 어느 것/어느 거.
Confusing 어느 (which, from a set) with 무슨 (what kind of): 어느 나라 'which country' vs 무슨 일 'what kind of matter.'
Reading 어느 정도 word-for-word; treat it as a set phrase meaning 'to what degree / about how much.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 자기 means "oneself; honey (term of endearment)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 자기 (jagi) means "oneself; honey (term of endearment)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자기 ("oneself"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Reflexive pronoun pointing back to the sentence's subject.
자기 (+의) 일. The 의 usually drops, so people say plain 자기 일.
자기 + 가, typically inside a subordinate clause referring back to the main subject.
Affectionate address between romantic partners (자기 + 야).

examples.en: You should do your own work yourself.
examples.note: Both 자기 (one's own) and 자기가 (the doer) loop back to the subject.

examples.en: He admitted his own fault.
examples.note: 자기 = 'his own,' bound to the third-person subject 그.

examples.en: Babe, what time do you finish today?
examples.note: 자기야 is intimate couple-speak — only for a partner, never coworkers.

extendedVocab.nuance: 자기 (Sino-Korean 自己, literally 'self-self,' 自 'self' + 己 'oneself') has two everyday lives. As a reflexive pronoun it points back to the subject already named in the sentence, usually third person — 그는 자기 방에 있어요 'he is in his (own) room' — and pairs habitually with 자기 일, 자기 잘못, 자기 자신. Separately, 자기(야) is a tender way couples address each other, like English 'honey/babe.' The synonym to contrast is 자신, which also means 'oneself' but is more formal/emphatic and combines into 자기 자신 ('one's very own self') or 자신감 ('self-confidence'). The sharp English-speaker pitfall is translating reflexive 자기 as 'myself': it almost never means the speaker — it tracks the grammatical subject, so it usually lands as 'himself/herself/themselves.' And socially, never aim 자기야 at a stranger, friend, or colleague; it reads as romantic and will feel jarring.

Translating reflexive 자기 as 'myself' — it refers to the sentence's subject, normally 'himself/herself,' not the speaker.
Calling a coworker, friend, or stranger 자기(야) — it's intimate couple-language and sounds like flirting otherwise.
Forgetting that 자기 일 means 'one's OWN business'; mistaking it for a generic 'job' loses the reflexive 'own.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 남 means "another person; a stranger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "another person; a stranger" is 남 (nam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 남의 ("someone else's"). Watch the particle attached to 남 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 남 + 의. 'Belonging to another person,' as in 남의 물건 'others' belongings.'
남 + 이. 'Other people' acting as the subject.
남 + 한테. 'To someone outside your circle' (남에게 in writing).
남 + 얘기. Chatter concerning other people.

examples.en: Don't worry about other people's business.
examples.note: 남의 = 'someone else's'; a very common warning-style phrase.

examples.en: We're strangers now.
examples.note: 남 as 'outsider' — emotionally loaded, said after a falling-out.

examples.en: Don't speak carelessly to others.
examples.note: 남한테 = 'to other people'; note 한테 for a person target.

extendedVocab.nuance: 남 is a native Korean word for 'another person / others' — people OUTSIDE your own circle — and it carries a real emotional charge of 'an outsider, someone unrelated to me,' not just a neutral 'other.' It sits in a pointed contrast with 자기 (oneself) and especially 우리 (us): saying 이제 남이야 ('we're strangers now') means an intimate bond has been severed, which is far heavier than English 'we're not close anymore.' Habitual collocations include 남의 일 ('someone else's affair'), 남의 시선 ('other people's gaze/judgment'), and 남 얘기 ('gossip'). The first English-speaker pitfall is confusing 남 with 남자 ('a man') — they overlap on screen but are unrelated in meaning. The second is using 남 for your own family or close friends; by definition 남 draws the insider/outsider line, so applying it to your inner circle either is wrong or signals a painful estrangement.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 남 (another person/outsider) with 남자 (a man) — similar shape, unrelated meaning.
Calling your own family or close friends 남 — it marks outsiders, so it either misfires or implies a serious rift.
Missing the weight of 이제 남이야 ('we're strangers now'); it signals a broken relationship, not mild distance.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 우리 means "we; us; our" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 우리 (uri) = "we; us; our". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 ("we / us / our") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 우리, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: First-person plural; also stands in for 'my' with family and in-group nouns.
우리 + 가. Marks 'we' as the doer.
우리 + 집. Koreans say this even for their own household.
Humble equivalent of 우리, lowering the speaker's group toward a listener.

examples.en: Let's go together.
examples.note: 우리 here includes the listener — an invitation.

examples.en: My mom cooks well.
examples.note: 우리 엄마 is 'my mom' in English, even though it literally says 'our.'

examples.en: We will prepare it.
examples.note: Humble 저희 toward a customer/superior; use it instead of 우리 when deferring.

extendedVocab.nuance: 우리 is 'we / us / our,' but it ranges far wider than English 'our' because Korean frames family and group as shared property: 우리 집 ('my home'), 우리 엄마 ('my mom'), 우리 학교, even 우리 나라 — places English would render with 'my.' The crucial register partner is 저희, the humble form: when speaking to a customer, an elder, or anyone you defer to, you lower your own side by switching 우리 → 저희 (저희 회사, 저희가 하겠습니다). The dividing line is politeness/deference, not number. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is over-translating: 우리 엄마 almost always means 'MY mom,' not literally 'our mom,' so rendering it as 'our' sounds odd. A subtle second point: you cannot humble-shift 우리 나라 to 저희 나라 when speaking to fellow citizens, since the nation isn't 'lowered' between insiders.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 우리 엄마/우리 집 literally as 'our mom/our house' — in most contexts it just means 'my mom/my home.'
Using plain 우리 toward a customer or superior where the humble 저희 is expected (저희 회사, 저희가).
Over-applying humility as 저희 나라 to fellow Koreans; 우리 나라 is the natural form among insiders.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이쪽 means "this way; this side" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이쪽 (ijjok) means "this way; this side". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이쪽 ("this way / this side"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이쪽 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Direction or side near the speaker (이쪽/그쪽/저쪽).
이쪽 + 으로. Shows direction of movement — the guiding phrase.
이쪽 + 에. Marks a static location near the speaker.
이쪽 + 은. Polite way to present a person: '이쪽은 김 부장님이세요.'

examples.en: Come this way.
examples.note: 이쪽으로 (direction) is the standard phrase for guiding someone.

examples.en: The exit is this way.
examples.note: Giving directions; 이쪽 points along a path, not at an object.

examples.en: This is my colleague, Ms. Park Jimin.
examples.note: 이쪽은 politely introduces a person — softer than pointing with 이 사람.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이쪽 means 'this way / this side,' the direction or area near the speaker, and belongs to the directional set 이쪽 / 그쪽 / 저쪽 (this way / your way / yonder way), mirroring the 이/그/저 system. Its workhorse collocation is 이쪽으로 오세요 ('come this way') for guiding people, plus 이쪽에 앉으세요 for seating them. A refined, very Korean use English lacks: 이쪽 politely points to a PERSON when making introductions — 이쪽은 ~예요 ('this is ~') — which sounds more courteous than bluntly indicating someone with 이 사람. The synonym/confusion to separate is 이것: 쪽 is about WHICH DIRECTION or side, while 것 is a thing, so 이쪽이에요 ('it's this way') is not 이거예요 ('it's this one'). Also note 그쪽 can mean 'you/your side' as a slightly distancing way to address someone, so the set carries social nuance beyond literal direction.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 이쪽 (a direction/side) with 이것/이거 (a thing): 이쪽이에요 'it's this way' vs 이거예요 'it's this one.'
Using 이쪽 for a far-off direction — for 'that way over there' use 저쪽 (and 그쪽 for the listener's side).
Pointing out a person bluntly with 이 사람 in a polite introduction where 이쪽은 ~예요 is more courteous.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 왜 means "why" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "why" is 왜 (wae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 왜요? ("Why?"). Watch the particle attached to 왜 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: One-word polite reply asking for a reason; the 요 is what keeps it courteous.

usagePhrases.en: What's wrong? / Why are you like that?
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase for asking why someone acts or feels off; not literally 'why do you do'.
왜 sits before the negation 안, which itself sits before the verb.
Sentence-opener that gives the reason; pairs with a preceding 왜 question or statement.

examples.en: Why are you crying?
examples.note: Simplest shape: 왜 + verb, nothing between them.

examples.en: Why aren't you going to school today?
examples.note: Even with a time word and place, 왜 stays just before the verb cluster 안 가요.

examples.en: Why is this so expensive?
examples.note: 왜 ... 이렇게 = 'why so ~'; a real complaint you'd voice in a shop.

extendedVocab.nuance: 왜 is the everyday 'why', asking the reason or cause behind something, and it lands directly in front of the verb or adjective (왜 늦었어요?), or stands alone as 왜요? The closest cousin is 어째서, but where 어째서 sounds slightly puzzled, bookish, or 'how on earth come', 왜 is the neutral, all-purpose choice you'll hear constantly in spoken Korean. Tone matters enormously here: a clipped, flat 왜? to a stranger or elder reads as irritated or even confrontational ('what?!'), so attaching 요 (왜요?) or softening to 왜 그러세요? keeps you polite. It collocates naturally with 왜냐하면 (because) as the answer, and with 안/못 in negative why-questions (왜 안 해요?). The English-speaker pitfall is word order: English lets 'why' float to the end ('You're late, why?'), but Korean never parks 왜 sentence-finally, and you must not translate 'Why don't you...?' as a literal 왜 안 — that Korean form is a genuine demand for a reason, not a soft suggestion.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Placing 왜 at the very end like English 'You didn't come, why?' — Korean keeps it before the verb: 왜 안 왔어요?
Dropping 요 and saying a sharp 왜? to a stranger or senior; it sounds annoyed. Use 왜요? or 왜 그러세요?
Translating English 'Why don't you rest?' as 왜 안 쉬어요? expecting a suggestion — that asks an actual reason. A suggestion is 좀 쉬는 게 어때요?

extendedVocab.english: how much; how long; to what degree
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 얼마나 means "how much; how long; to what degree" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 얼마나 (eolmana) = "how much; how long; to what degree". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 얼마나 걸려요? ("How long does it take?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 얼마나, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Default phrase for duration; 걸리다 = to take (time).
얼마나 stacked onto the adverb 자주 to ask frequency.
얼마나 + adjective 멀다 to ask degree of distance.
얼마나 + 많이; use this for amount, never 얼마 alone.

examples.en: How big is it?
examples.note: Bare degree question: 얼마나 + adjective.

examples.en: How long does it take from here to the airport?
examples.note: 얼마나 with 걸리다 for travel time; the route is framed by 에서...까지.

examples.en: How much do you like that person?
examples.note: 얼마나 measuring the intensity of a feeling, not a price.

extendedVocab.nuance: 얼마나 asks 'to what degree / how much / how long', measuring intensity, distance, frequency, duration, or size, and it sits before the verb or adjective it scales (얼마나 예뻐요? = how pretty is it?). The trap is its lookalike 얼마: 얼마 asks a price or a bare quantity (얼마예요? = how much is it [in money]?), whereas 얼마나 adds the adverbial -나 to ask about a *degree along a scale*. Mixing them is the number-one English-speaker error, because English collapses both into 'how much'. It collocates tightly with measurement verbs and adjectives: 얼마나 걸리다 (take how long), 얼마나 멀다/크다/비싸다 (how far/big/expensive), and with other adverbs to form 얼마나 자주 (how often) and 얼마나 많이 (how much in amount). A second subtle point: when answering, the matching degree word is 이렇게/그렇게 or 너무, so 얼마나 비싸요? naturally invites 너무 비싸요. Using 얼마나 to ask a price: 'How much is this?' is 얼마예요?, not 얼마나예요?. 얼마나 is for degree, not money.
Saying 얼마 걸려요? for duration — duration needs the degree word: 얼마나 걸려요?

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어떤 means "what kind of; which" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어떤 (eotteon) means "what kind of; which". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어떤 거예요? ("Which one is it? / What kind is it?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어떤 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Which one is it? / What kind is it?
usagePhrases.note: 어떤 + 거 (casual 'thing/one'); a go-to phrase when pointing at choices.
어떤 + noun, asking about character or type, not identity.

usagePhrases.en: What kind of food do you like?
usagePhrases.note: 어떤 sits right against the noun 음식.
어떤 + 색; implies choosing among available colors.

examples.en: What color is it?
examples.note: Bare 어떤 + noun + 이에요; the simplest frame.

examples.en: What kind of movies do you usually watch on weekends?
examples.note: 어떤 asks for the *type/quality* of film, inviting a description like 'action' or 'romantic'.

examples.en: What kind of person is he, really?
examples.note: 도대체 ('on earth') intensifies a real curiosity about someone's character.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어떤 is a modifier that clamps directly onto a noun to ask 'what kind of' or 'which one (out of a set)', probing the quality, character, or choice — 어떤 사람이에요? wants a description (kind? funny? tall?). Its constant rival is 무슨: 무슨 asks plainly *which item / what is it* when you have no clue (무슨 색이에요? = just name the color), while 어떤 leans toward *qualities or selecting among known options* (어떤 색이 더 예뻐요? = which color is prettier?). Keep both apart from 어떻게 (how, an adverb modifying verbs) and the predicate 어때요? (how is it?). Origin-wise 어떤 is the adnominal form derived from 어떠하다 ('to be how/in what state'), which is exactly why it can never stand alone and always needs a noun trailing it. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping that noun: English 'Which do you like?' can end on 'which', but Korean 어떤 must be followed by 거/것 at minimum (어떤 거 좋아해요?), never left bare.

Leaving 어떤 with no noun: 어떤 좋아해요? is broken. Add a noun or 거 — 어떤 거 좋아해요?
Swapping in 어떻게: 어떻게 사람이에요? is wrong because 어떻게 modifies verbs (어떻게 가요?). For a noun use 어떤 사람이에요?
Using 어떤 to simply name an unknown (어떤 요일이에요?). For naming the day/color outright, 무슨 is more natural: 무슨 요일이에요?

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무슨 means "what; what kind of" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "what; what kind of" is 무슨 (museun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 무슨 일이에요? ("What's the matter? / What's going on?"). Watch the particle attached to 무슨 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: What's the matter? / What's going on?
usagePhrases.note: Fixed phrase; 무슨 일 literally 'what affair', used when something seems off.

usagePhrases.en: What day (of the week) is it?
usagePhrases.note: 무슨 + 요일; the standard way to ask the weekday.
무슨 + noun, just asking you to name it.
무슨 뜻 = 'what meaning'; the everyday way to ask a word's sense.

examples.en: What color is it?
examples.note: Bare frame: 무슨 + noun + 이에요, just name the color.

examples.en: What music are you listening to right now?
examples.note: 무슨 asks you to identify the item; answer with a song or genre name.

examples.en: What are you talking about all of a sudden?
examples.note: 무슨 소리 ('what sound/talk') is an idiomatic 'what do you mean?!' reaction.

extendedVocab.nuance: 무슨 sits before a noun to ask 'what / what kind of', typically when you have no information yet and just want the thing identified — 무슨 영화 봤어요? simply asks for the title or genre. The sharp contrast is with 어떤: 무슨 + noun seeks the *identity or category* (무슨 색이에요? → 'it's blue'), whereas 어떤 + noun seeks *qualities or a choice among options* (어떤 색이 좋아요? → 'the brighter one'). 무슨 has hardened into many fixed, high-frequency idioms you should memorize whole: 무슨 일이에요? (what's wrong?), 무슨 뜻이에요? (what does it mean?), 무슨 요일이에요? (what day?), and the exasperated 무슨 소리예요? / 무슨 말이에요? (what are you on about?). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, 무슨 must always be glued to a following noun (never bare like English 'What?'); second, learners reach for 어떤 in these set phrases — 어떤 일이에요? is grammatical but means 'what sort of task', not the idiomatic 'what's wrong?'.

Over-applying 무슨 to quality questions: to ask which option is better, use 어떤 — 어떤 게 더 좋아요?, not 무슨 게 더 좋아요?

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어디서 means "where (from); at what place" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어디서 (eodiseo) = "where (from); at what place". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어디서 만나요? ("Where shall we meet?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 어디서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 어디서 is the spoken contraction of 어디에서; 만나다 is an action, so 에서/서 fits.

usagePhrases.en: Where are you from? / Where did you come from?
usagePhrases.note: Source of motion; 오다 takes the 에서 'from' reading here.
Marks the place an action (사다) is carried out.
Action verb 먹다 needs the action-location 에서, contracted to 서.

examples.en: Where shall we meet up?
examples.note: Tiny frame: 어디서 + action verb; 보다 here means 'meet'.

examples.en: Where did you buy this bag?
examples.note: 어디서 marks where the buying happened; a very common compliment-opener.

examples.en: Where should we eat lunch?
examples.note: 어디서 with the suggestion ending -ㄹ까요 when proposing a spot.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어디서 is the everyday spoken shortening of 어디에서 and tags the place *where an action is performed* or the *source* something comes from (어디서 만나요?, 어디서 왔어요?). The crucial split is against 어디에/어디 + 예요: 어디에 (or bare 어디) plus 있다/가다 marks mere *existence or destination* (화장실이 어디예요? = where is the bathroom?), but the moment you have a dynamic action verb — 사다, 먹다, 만나다, 일하다 — Korean demands the 에서 location, i.e. 어디서. Because 서 already *is* 에서, the most common English-speaker pitfall is doubling the particle (어디서에서 ✗) or, conversely, using 어디서 to ask a static location: 어디서예요? is wrong for 'where is it?', which must be 어디예요?. A second pitfall is mapping English 'where' uniformly; English uses one word for 'where is', 'where to', and 'where ... at', but Korean forces you to pick 어디(예요)/어디로/어디서 by the verb's nature.

Stacking particles: 어디서에서 doubles 에서. 어디서 already contains it — just say 어디서 사요?
Putting 에서 on existence/destination verbs: 어디에서 있어요? for 'where is it?' is unnatural; use 어디에 있어요? / 어디 있어요?

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 언제부터 means "since when; from when" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 언제부터 (eonjebuteo) means "since when; from when". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 언제부터예요? ("Since when is it? / From when?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 언제부터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Since when is it? / From when?
usagePhrases.note: 언제 + 부터 (from); a bare question about a start point.
Pairs naturally with 시작하다 (to begin).
Set pairing that brackets a whole time range.

usagePhrases.en: Since when have you been learning?
usagePhrases.note: 부터 marks the onset; the past tense shows it began earlier.

examples.en: Since when have you been sick?
examples.note: Simple frame asking the onset of a state with past tense.

examples.en: When did you start studying Korean?
examples.note: 언제부터 pinning down the beginning point of an ongoing activity.

examples.en: From what time does this shop open in the morning?
examples.note: 언제부터 used for an opening time, not just a date.

extendedVocab.nuance: 언제부터 fuses the question word 언제 (when) with the particle 부터 ('from / starting at'), asking the *onset* — the moment from which something has been true (언제부터 아팠어요? = since when have you been ill?). Its built-in partner is 언제까지 (until when), and the two frame a span: 언제부터 언제까지 일해요?. The key distinction learners blur is 부터 vs 에서: both gloss as English 'from', but 부터 marks a *starting point in time or sequence*, while 에서 marks a *place of origin or action* — so 'where are you from?' is 어디서 왔어요?, never 어디부터. A further nuance: 부터 stresses where something *begins* (often implying it continues), so it answers 'since/from when', not 'by when' (that deadline sense belongs to 까지). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 'from' overlap — defaulting to 부터 for a physical source — plus forgetting that 부터 attaches straight onto 언제 with no extra particle (언제부터, not 언제에부터).

Confusing direction: 언제부터 asks the start, so it can't mean a deadline. 'By when?' is 언제까지.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 언제까지 means "until when; by when" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "until when; by when" is 언제까지 (eonjekkaji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 언제까지예요? ("Until when is it? / By when?"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Until when is it? / By when?
usagePhrases.note: 언제 + 까지 (until/by); a bare question about an end point.

usagePhrases.en: By when do I have to do it?
usagePhrases.note: Deadline reading of 까지; common about tasks.
Duration-endpoint reading; how long someone remains.
까지 marking a payment deadline.

examples.en: Until when is the vacation?
examples.note: Simplest endpoint frame: 언제까지 + 예요.

examples.en: By when do I have to submit this report?
examples.note: 언제까지 + 야 해요 for an obligation deadline at work or school.

examples.en: Until when are you going to be here?
examples.note: 언제까지 with the future -ㄹ 거예요 to ask how long someone will stay.

extendedVocab.nuance: 언제까지 joins 언제 (when) with 까지 ('until / by'), asking the *terminal point* of something — either the end of a stretch ('until when') or a cutoff deadline ('by when'): 언제까지 있어요? vs 언제까지 내야 해요?. It is the natural mirror of 언제부터, and the pair 언제부터 언제까지 maps a full range. Two senses of 까지 hide inside this one word: a *durative* 'all the way up to' (계속 ~까지 있다) and a *deadline* 'no later than' (~까지 끝내다); English 'until' only captures the first, which is why learners miss the deadline meaning. The contrast to drill is 까지 vs 부터: 까지 closes the interval, 부터 opens it, so swapping them flips your meaning entirely (시작 vs 마감). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'until' = 까지 always means continuous presence and then being puzzled by 언제까지 내요? — here 까지 is the 'by' of a due date. As with 부터, attach 까지 straight to 언제 (언제까지, not 언제에까지).

Assuming 'until' = 까지 always means continuous presence and then being puzzled by 언제까지 내요? — here 까지 is the 'by' of a due date. As with 부터, attach 까지 straight to 언제 (언제까지, not 언제에까지).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 누가 means "who (as subject)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 누가 (nuga) = "who (as subject)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 누가 왔어요? ("Who came?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 누가, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 누가 = 누구 + 가, the subject form; the asker doesn't know the doer.

usagePhrases.en: Who does it / will do it?
usagePhrases.note: 누가 as the one performing the action.
Common spoken challenge; 누가 as subject of 그러다.
Rhetorical too — can mean 'nobody knows'; 누가 stays the subject.

examples.en: Who's here? / Who came?
examples.note: Bare subject question; note 누가, never 누구가.

examples.en: Who made this cake?
examples.note: 누가 marks the doer of 만들다; the object 케이크 takes its own slot.

examples.en: Among us, who is the fastest?
examples.note: 누가 as the subject of an adjective (빠르다) in a comparison.

extendedVocab.nuance: 누가 is the *subject* form of the question word 누구 (who): it is literally 누구 + the subject particle 가, but the 구 contracts away, so the correct, fixed shape is 누가 — never the regularized 누구가. Use 누가 precisely when 'who' is the one *doing* the action or *being* the adjective (누가 전화했어요?, 누가 키가 커요?). For every other role, 누구 stays intact with its own particle: 누구예요? (who is it?), 누구를 만나요? / 누구 만나요? (whom do you meet?), 누구한테 줘요? (to whom?), 누구하고 가요? (with whom?). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'who' never changes shape for subject vs object, so learners either say the over-regular 누구가 or wrongly use 누가 as an object — but 'whom did you meet?' is 누구를 만났어요?, not 누가 만났어요? (which would mean 'who met [someone]?'). One more subtlety: 아무도 (nobody) is the negative answer partner, so 누가 왔어요? can be answered 아무도 안 왔어요.

Saying 누구가 by analogy with other nouns. The contracted subject form is irregular: it must be 누가.
Using 누가 for the object 'whom': 'Who(m) did you meet?' is 누구를 만났어요?. 누가 만났어요? means 'who met someone?'.
Adding another particle to 누가 (누가가/누가는). 누가 already carries 가; for topic/other roles, go back to 누구 (누구는, 누구를).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어디로 means "to where; where to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어디로 (eodiro) means "to where; where to". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어디로 가요? ("Where are you going (to)?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 어디로 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 어디 + 로 (toward); 로 follows a vowel, so no 으.
어디로 with the suggestion ending when proposing a destination.
Direction of sending; 보내다 takes the 로 'toward' marker.
어디 + direction particle (으)로 with 떠나다.

examples.en: Where to?
examples.note: Bare frame; the 로 makes it about direction, not just location.

examples.en: Where does this bus go?
examples.note: 어디로 asks the route/direction of movement — exactly what you'd ask a driver.

examples.en: Where are you heading off to this vacation?
examples.note: 어디로 + 떠나다 framing a travel destination you set out toward.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어디로 is 어디 plus the directional particle (으)로, asking 'to where / in which direction' something moves, and it pairs with motion verbs like 가다, 오다, 보내다, 떠나다 (어디로 가요?). Here 어디 ends in a vowel, so the particle surfaces as plain 로, not 으로 (that 으 only appears after a consonant, e.g. 집으로). The contrast set is three-way and worth fixing firmly: 어디(예요)/어디에 for *static location or existence* (어디예요? = where is it?), 어디서 for the *place an action happens* (어디서 먹어요?), and 어디로 for *direction/destination of movement* (어디로 가요?). English 'where' flattens all three, which is the core pitfall — and a subtler one is that 가다 can take either 에 (어디에 가요?, endpoint) or 로 (어디로 가요?, direction/route); 로 feels more about the *path or general heading*, 에 about the *arrival point*, so for 'which way does this bus go?' Koreans prefer 어디로. Don't use 어디로 for a still location: 어디로 있어요? is wrong; existence is 어디에 있어요?.

Confusing 어디로 with 어디서: 어디로 가요? (which way you head) vs 어디서 만나요? (the spot you meet). Movement vs action-place.
Forcing 으로 after 어디: since 어디 ends in a vowel it's just 어디로, not 어디으로.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어디에 means "where; at/to where" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "where; at/to where" is 어디에 (eodie). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어디에 있어요? ("Where is it?"). Watch the particle attached to 어디에 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 어디 + 에 with 있다 to mark where something exists.
어디 + 에 with 가다 marking the destination/endpoint.
에 marking the place to set something down (두다).
어디에 with 살다; in fast speech often just 어디 살아요?

examples.en: Where is it?
examples.note: Core frame: 어디에 + 있다 for location of a thing or person.

examples.en: Where should I put the bag?
examples.note: 어디에 marks the resting place; 둘까요 asks for instruction.

examples.en: Where are you headed right now?
examples.note: 어디에 + 가다 for a destination, softened by the 'on the way' phrasing.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어디에 is 어디 with the particle 에, which marks either where something *exists* (있다/없다: 어디에 있어요?) or the *endpoint* you go to (가다/오다/도착하다: 어디에 가요?), as well as where you place something (두다, 놓다, 걸다). In everyday speech the 에 frequently drops after 어디 — 어디 있어요?, 어디 가요? — and that reduction is completely natural, even preferred. The contrast you must internalize: 에 is for *existence and destination*, but the place where a dynamic action is *performed* takes 에서 (so 'where do you eat?' is 어디서 먹어요?, not 어디에 먹어요?). For a heading or direction you use 어디로. This 에 vs 에서 split is the classic English-speaker pitfall, since English 'at/in/to' don't line up with it: learners wrongly attach 에 to action verbs (어디에 사요? for 'where do you buy?' should be 어디서 사요?). Also note 살다 (to live) idiomatically takes 에 for residence (어디에 살아요?), even though living feels like an activity.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Putting 에 on action verbs: 'Where do you eat/buy?' needs 에서 — 어디서 먹어요?, not 어디에 먹어요?.
Over-formalizing casual speech: in conversation 어디 있어요? / 어디 가요? (dropping 에) is natural; insisting on 어디에 every time sounds stiff.
Using 어디에 for direction of travel where 어디로 fits better: for 'which way does it go?' say 어디로 가요?, not 어디에 가요?.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 어째서 means "how come; why" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 어째서 (eojjaeseo) = "how come; why". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어째서요? ("How come? / Why is that?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 어째서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Polite one-word reply; the 요 keeps the puzzled tone courteous.

usagePhrases.en: Why doesn't it work? / Why not?
usagePhrases.note: 어째서 before the negation 안; expresses genuine bafflement.
Asking the reason behind a puzzling situation.
Close to 왜 but a touch softer and more wondering.

examples.en: How come you're not coming?
examples.note: Bare frame: 어째서 + 안 + verb; reads as puzzled, not accusatory.

examples.en: How did things end up like this?
examples.note: 어째서 over a whole situation; 이렇게 되다 = 'turn out this way'.

examples.en: Why on earth do you think so?
examples.note: 어째서 probing the reasoning behind an opinion, with a reflective shade.

extendedVocab.nuance: 어째서 means 'how come / why on earth', asking a reason but carrying a shade of puzzlement, surprise, or 'I can't figure out why', and like 왜 it sits before the verb (어째서 늦었어요?). Its near-twin is 왜, and the dividing line is register and feeling: 왜 is the neutral, ultra-frequent default of daily speech, while 어째서 sounds a little more deliberate, formal, or emotionally loaded — closer to written Korean, narration, or a moment of real bewilderment, so in casual chat 왜 is usually the safer pick. Structurally 어째서 comes from 어찌하여서 ('by doing how'), which is why it feels slightly weightier than the bare 왜. It collocates with negatives and 'turned out' expressions: 어째서 안 돼요?, 어째서 이렇게 됐어요?. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 어째서 and 왜 as freely interchangeable and over-using 어째서 in light conversation (it can sound stagey or intense); the other pitfall, shared with 왜, is word order — 어째서 must precede the verb and cannot trail at sentence end like English 'how come?'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Over-using 어째서 in casual talk; it can sound dramatic or formal. Everyday 'why' is just 왜.
Placing 어째서 at the end like English 'How come?'. Korean keeps it before the verb: 어째서 안 왔어요?
Assuming 어째서 = 어떻게: 어째서 asks the reason (why), while 어떻게 asks the manner/method (how you do it). Don't substitute one for the other.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이야기 means "story, talk" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이야기 (iyagi) means "story, talk". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이야기를 하다 ("to talk, to have a conversation"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이야기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to talk, to have a conversation
usagePhrases.note: the default verb; 이야기 itself is a noun, so you almost always pair it with 하다
나누다 (to share/divide) is warmer and more two-sided than 하다 — used for heartfelt talks
always 듣다 (hear/listen), never 보다; you 'hear' a story even when reading is involved
the adjective 재미있는 sits before the noun; 이야기가 재미있다 puts it after

examples.en: I talk with my friend.
examples.note: 하고 = 'with' in casual speech; here 이야기하다 works as one verb, no 를 needed

examples.en: Yesterday I had a talk with my teacher about my career path.
examples.note: 나누다 signals a meaningful, mutual conversation, not idle chatter

examples.en: Grandma told me an old folktale.
examples.note: 옛날이야기 = a folk/old-times tale; 들려주다 = to tell (lit. let one hear), with 셨 honoring grandma

extendedVocab.nuance: 이야기 covers both a 'story' (a tale, an account) and 'talking/chatting' in the abstract, so 이야기하다 is the everyday verb for 'to talk, to converse.' The nearest neighbor is 대화(對話): 대화 is a slightly more formal, two-directional 'dialogue/conversation,' while 이야기 is the warm, native-Korean word for casual talk and also for a narrated story — a meaning 대화 never has. Note 말하다 means 'to say/speak (utter words)' and centers on the act of producing speech, whereas 이야기하다 frames a whole exchange or telling. In real speech Koreans constantly contract 이야기 to 얘기, so 얘기해요 and 이야기해요 are identical. The English-speaker pitfall: 'story' makes learners reach for 보다 ('I saw a story'), but a story is something you 듣다 (hear) or 읽다 (read), and 'talk to someone' is 누구하고 이야기하다 with 하고/랑, not the English 'talk to' mapped onto an object particle.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이야기를 봐요 for 'I hear/read a story' — a story is 듣다 (listen) or 읽다 (read), never 보다.
Treating 이야기 as a verb on its own; 'to talk' needs 하다/나누다: 이야기하다, not bare 이야기.
Using 말하다 when you mean a back-and-forth chat — 말하다 is 'to utter/say,' while a conversation is 이야기하다 or 대화하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 소식 means "news, word (from someone)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "news, word (from someone)" is 소식 (sosik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 좋은 소식 ("good news"). Watch the particle attached to 소식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the classic collocation; its opposite is 나쁜 소식 or the heavier 슬픈 소식 (sad news)
news 'arrives at your ear,' so 듣다, not 보다 — even for written word
전하다 (to convey) is the verb for relaying news to a third person

usagePhrases.en: to lose touch (lit. news is cut off)
usagePhrases.note: 끊기다 = to be severed; describes losing all contact with someone

examples.en: I have good news.
examples.note: 있다 marks existence; 소식이 있다 = 'there is news / I have news'

examples.en: I heard word about an old friend for the first time in ages.
examples.note: 소식 here means 'how they're doing,' not a headline; 오랜만에 = after a long time

examples.ko: 이사 간 뒤로 그 사람 소식이 끊겼어요.
examples.romanization: isa gan dwiro geu saram sosigi kkeunkyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I've lost touch with that person since they moved away.
examples.note: 소식이 끊기다 is the natural way to say 'we lost contact'

extendedVocab.nuance: 소식(消息) is Sino-Korean — 消 'disappear/wane' + 息 'breath/rest' — and originally meant the ebb and flow of things; today it means 'news, word, tidings,' especially personal news about how a person or situation is faring. The sharp contrast is with 뉴스: 뉴스 is the English loanword reserved for broadcast/press news (TV, newspapers, current events), whereas 소식 is the news of individuals and private matters — a friend's wedding, a relative's health. Compare also 정보(情報) 'information/data,' which is impersonal facts you look up. Natural partners are 좋은/나쁜 소식, 소식을 전하다/듣다, and the poignant 소식이 없다/끊기다 ('haven't heard from them'). The pitfall for English speakers: 'I watched the news' tempts 소식을 봤어요, but media news is 뉴스를 봤어요; reserve 소식 for word about people, and remember you 듣다 (hear) personal news rather than 보다 it.

Using 소식 for TV/press news — that is 뉴스; 소식 is personal word about someone.
Saying 소식을 봐요 ('see news') — personal news is heard: 소식을 들어요.
Confusing 소식(personal news) with 정보 (impersonal information/data) — you 'look up' 정보 but 'hear' 소식.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 거짓말 means "lie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 거짓말 (geojinmal) = "lie". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 거짓말을 하다 ("to tell a lie") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 거짓말, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 거짓말 is a noun, so 'to lie' = 거짓말하다 / 거짓말을 하다, never bare 거짓말
set idiom; 새빨간 'crimson' intensifies it to 'total, blatant lie'
-쟁이 turns it into a (mildly mocking) person-noun, like 'fibber'

usagePhrases.en: as if by magic (lit. like a lie)
usagePhrases.note: 거짓말 + 처럼; describes something so good/sudden it seems unreal

examples.en: Please don't lie.
examples.note: -지 마세요 = 'please don't'; here 거짓말하다 acts as one verb

examples.en: My little sibling told another barefaced lie.
examples.note: 새빨간 거짓말 = a flat-out lie; 또 = 'again,' hinting it's a habit

examples.en: No way! You really passed?
examples.note: among friends 거짓말! is an exclamation of happy disbelief, not an accusation

extendedVocab.nuance: 거짓말 is built transparently from native roots: 거짓 'false, untrue' + 말 'words/speech,' literally 'false words,' i.e. a lie. As a noun it needs 하다 to become the verb 거짓말하다 ('to lie'). The near-synonym to separate it from is 변명(辨明) 'excuse/justification': a 거짓말 is a deliberate falsehood, while a 변명 is a (possibly true) defense or rationalization for one's behavior. Note also 농담 'joke' is harmless fun, not deception. Collocations to know: 새빨간 거짓말 'barefaced lie,' 거짓말을 들키다 'get caught lying,' 거짓말쟁이 'liar.' A lovely register twist: among close friends, 거짓말! shouted alone means 'No way! / You're kidding!' as delighted shock. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'lie' is itself a verb, so learners say 거짓말 alone to mean 'lie' — but you must say 거짓말을 하다; and don't confuse the noun with 진짜 'real' or 사실(事實) 'fact, truth,' its true opposite.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using bare 거짓말 as a verb; 'to lie' is 거짓말을 하다 / 거짓말하다.
Mixing up 거짓말 (a deliberate lie) with 변명 (an excuse/justification, which may be true).
Forgetting the opposite is 사실/진실 (fact/truth); learners often grab 진짜 ('real'), which is an adjective-ish word, not the noun 'truth.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 농담 means "joke" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 농담 (nongdam) means "joke". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 농담을 하다 ("to make a joke, to kid"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 농담 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to make a joke, to kid
usagePhrases.note: 농담 is a noun; 'to joke' = 농담하다 / 농담을 하다
set phrase to defuse a remark and show you didn't mean it
-(으)로 marks manner: 'in a joking way,' often 농담으로 한 말 'something said in jest'
fixed idiom for a remark that's partly a real hint

examples.en: I'm joking, don't be upset.
examples.note: tacking on 농담이에요 instantly softens what you just said

examples.en: He took the joke as if I meant it seriously.
examples.note: 진담 = serious talk; the pair 농담 vs 진담 is the key contrast

examples.ko: 농담 반 진담 반으로 같이 가자고 했어요.
examples.romanization: nongdam ban jindam baneuro gachi gajago haesseoyo.
examples.en: Half joking, half serious, I suggested we go together.
examples.note: 농담 반 진담 반 hints the speaker partly means it

extendedVocab.nuance: 농담(弄談) is Sino-Korean — 弄 'to play with, tease' + 談 'talk' — literally 'playful talk,' i.e. a joke meant to amuse, not to wound. Its built-in opposite is 진담(眞談) 'earnest/serious talk' (眞 'true' + 談 'talk'), and Koreans lean on the pair constantly: 농담이야, 진담이야? 'Are you kidding or serious?' Distinguish it from 거짓말 'a lie': a 농담 is openly non-serious fun that listeners are meant to recognize, while a 거짓말 is meant to deceive. Also separate it from 장난 'a prank/mischief (often an action),' versus 농담 which is verbal wit. Natural collocations: 농담을 하다, 농담으로 한 말, 농담이 심하다 'the joke goes too far,' 농담 반 진담 반. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 농담 as a verb on its own — say 농담하다; and 'You're joking!' as an exclamation is usually 거짓말! or 진짜?, not 농담!, since 농담이에요 is what YOU say about YOUR OWN remark to signal you weren't serious.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying bare 농담 for 'to joke' — use 농담을 하다 / 농담하다.
Confusing 농담 (harmless joke meant to be seen through) with 거짓말 (a lie meant to deceive).
Mixing up 농담 (verbal wit) with 장난 (a prank or physical mischief) — 장난치다 is 'to mess around,' not 'to joke.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 연락 means "contact, getting in touch" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "contact, getting in touch" is 연락 (yeollak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 연락을 하다 ("to contact, to get in touch"). Watch the particle attached to 연락 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to contact, to get in touch
usagePhrases.note: 연락 is a noun; 'to contact' = 연락하다 / 연락을 하다

usagePhrases.en: to hear from someone (lit. contact comes)
usagePhrases.note: 오다, not 을 오다 — the contact is the subject that 'comes to' you: 연락이 오다
되다 here = 'manages to connect'; 연락이 안 돼요 = 'I can't reach them'
연락 + 처(處) 'place/point' → the point at which to reach you = phone/contact info

examples.en: I'll get in touch later.
examples.note: -ㄹ게요 = a casual promise about your own action

examples.en: I heard from my friend.
examples.note: 한테서 = 'from (a person)'; 연락이 오다 takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: I can't reach them by call or text.
examples.note: 연락이 되다/안 되다 = to (not) get through; note 도…도 'neither…nor'

extendedVocab.nuance: 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean — 連 'connect/link' + 絡 'tie, network' — literally 'to link up,' and it covers ANY channel of reaching a person: a call, a text, a message, an email. The near-synonym to contrast is 소식: 연락 is the ACT/CHANNEL of getting in touch ('drop me a line'), while 소식 is the CONTENT/word about how someone is. Compare 통화(通話) 'a phone call (specifically)' — narrower than 연락. The crucial grammar quirk for English speakers: 연락 flips between particles. When YOU reach out it's 연락을 하다 / 연락하다 (object 를), but when contact COMES to you it's 연락이 오다 and reachability is 연락이 되다 (subject 이/가) — saying 연락을 오다 is a classic error. Also, English 'contact someone' has a direct object, so learners drop the person-marking 한테/에게: it should be 친구한테 연락하다, and incoming contact is 친구한테서/에게서 연락이 오다. 연락처 (with 처) means your number/details, not the verb.

Saying 연락을 오다 for incoming contact — it must be 연락이 오다 (이/가), since the contact is what 'comes.'
Dropping the person particle: 'contact me' is 저한테 연락하세요, not 저를 연락하세요.
Confusing 연락 (the act of getting in touch) with 소식 (the news/word itself) — 연락이 없다 = 'they haven't reached out'; 소식이 없다 = 'no word on how they are.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 부탁 means "favor, request" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 부탁 (butak) = "favor, request". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부탁을 하다 ("to ask a favor") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부탁, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 부탁 is a noun; 'to make a request' = 부탁하다 / 부탁을 하다

usagePhrases.en: I have a favor to ask
usagePhrases.note: softly opens a request; 있다 marks 'there is a favor (on my side)'

usagePhrases.en: I look forward to working with you (lit. I kindly entrust this)
usagePhrases.note: humble 드리다 form; the standard polite phrase at introductions/handovers
들어주다 = to grant/heed a request; 좀 softens it

examples.en: I have one favor to ask.
examples.note: 하나 'one' makes the ask feel small and polite

examples.en: Could you take care of this for me?
examples.note: 좀 softens; 부탁해요 here = 'I'm entrusting this to you'

examples.en: I look forward to working with you from now on.
examples.note: the go-to humble greeting when joining a team or starting a project

extendedVocab.nuance: 부탁(付託) is Sino-Korean — 付 'hand over/entrust' + 託 'commit, consign' — literally 'to entrust (a matter) to someone,' i.e. to ask a favor. The near-synonym to separate is 요청(要請) 'a (formal) request/demand': 요청 is businesslike and official (a 요청서 is a request form, 협조를 요청하다 'request cooperation'), whereas 부탁 is personal and softens the asker into the lower, indebted position. Compare 부탁 with 명령 'an order/command,' its opposite in power. Register is the heart of this word: among equals 부탁해요, but upward or formally you switch to the humble verb 드리다 → 부탁드립니다 / 잘 부탁드립니다, a set phrase at introductions, handovers, and emails meaning roughly 'please look kindly on me/this.' Collocations: 부탁을 들어주다 'grant a favor,' 부탁을 거절하다 'refuse,' 어려운 부탁. The English-speaker pitfall: 'ask someone a favor' makes learners say 누구를 부탁하다, but the person takes 한테/에게 (친구한테 부탁하다), and bare 부탁 can't be the verb — you need 부탁하다 or the humble 부탁드리다 in polite settings.

Using bare 부탁 as a verb; 'to request' is 부탁을 하다 / 부탁하다 (humble: 부탁드리다).
Saying 잘 부탁해요 to a superior or in formal writing — the expected humble form is 잘 부탁드립니다.
Confusing 부탁 (a personal favor) with 요청 (a formal/official request) — you 요청하다 cooperation from an institution, but 부탁하다 a friend.
