영어 화자는 'tray'라는 한 단어 안에 쟁반과 식판을 뭉뚱그리기 쉬운데, 칸이 나뉘어 그 위에서 바로 먹으면 '식판', 그릇을 얹어 옮기기만 하면 '쟁반'으로 갈라 기억하세요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그릇뚜껑 means "bowl lid / dish cover" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그릇뚜껑 (geureutttukkeong) = "bowl lid / dish cover". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그릇뚜껑을 덮다 ("to put the lid on the bowl") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그릇뚜껑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to put the lid on the bowl
usagePhrases.note: 덮다 = to cover; the lid goes over the bowl's opening
열다 = to open; here lifting off the cover
맞다 = to fit/match; used about whether the lid is the right size

usagePhrases.en: to close the bowl with its lid
usagePhrases.note: 닫다 = to close; common for sealing leftovers

examples.en: The bowl lid doesn't fit.
examples.note: 맞다 = to fit; 안 makes it negative — a frequent kitchen complaint about mismatched lids.

examples.en: Put the lid on the leftover food (and leave it).
examples.note: -어 두다 = do and leave in that state; 덮다 is the verb for covering with a lid.

examples.en: It's hot, so open the bowl lid carefully.
examples.note: -니까 gives the reason; 열다 → 여세요 (the ㄹ drops before 세요) when opening.

extendedVocab.nuance: 그릇뚜껑은 그릇(bowl/vessel) + 뚜껑(lid)이 합쳐진 순우리말로, 그릇 위에 덮는 뚜껑을 가리켜요. 음식을 따뜻하게 보관하거나 남은 음식을 덮어 둘 때 써요. 핵심 동사 짝은 '덮다(cover)'와 '열다(open)'인데, 한국어는 뚜껑을 '덮다/열다'라고 하지 영어 'close/open'을 그대로 옮겨 '닫다'만 쓰면 어색할 때가 있어요(덮다가 더 자연스러움). 그냥 '뚜껑'이라고만 해도 대개 통하지만, 냄비뚜껑·병뚜껑처럼 무엇의 뚜껑인지 분명히 하고 싶을 때 앞에 명사를 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 해요. 가장 가까운 혼동은 '냄비뚜껑(pot lid)'으로, 둘 다 뚜껑이지만 받치는 대상이 그릇이냐 냄비냐로 갈려요. 영어 화자는 'a lid for the bowl'을 직역해 '그릇을 위한 뚜껑'이라고 하기 쉬운데, 한국어는 두 명사를 그대로 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 한다는 점을 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 뚜껑 when it's unclear which lid you mean; if a pot lid and a bowl lid are both around, specify 그릇뚜껑 vs 냄비뚜껑 by attaching the noun in front.
Translating 'a lid for the bowl' as 그릇을 위한 뚜껑 with 위한; Korean just compounds the nouns → 그릇뚜껑.
Using 닫다 ('close') for putting a lid on; Koreans more naturally say 뚜껑을 덮다 (cover with the lid) and 뚜껑을 열다 (open it).

structuredNuance.t: 그릇 위에 덮는 뚜껑을 가리켜요. 음식을 따뜻하게 보관하거나 남은 음식을 덮어 둘 때 써요. 핵심 동사 짝은 '덮다(cover)'와 '열다(open)'인데, 한국어는 뚜껑을 '덮다/열다'라고 하지 영어 'close/open'을 그대로 옮겨 '닫다'만 쓰면 어색할 때가 있어요(덮다가 더 자연스러움). 그냥 '뚜껑'이라고만 해도 대개 통하지만, 냄비뚜껑·병뚜껑처럼 무엇의 뚜껑인지 분명히 하고 싶을 때 앞에 명사를 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 해요.
가장 가까운 혼동은 '냄비뚜껑(pot lid)'으로, 둘 다 뚜껑이지만 받치는 대상이 그릇이냐 냄비냐로 갈려요.
그릇뚜껑은 그릇(bowl/vessel) + 뚜껑(lid)이 합쳐진 순우리말이에요.
영어 화자는 'a lid for the bowl'을 직역해 '그릇을 위한 뚜껑'이라고 하기 쉬운데, 한국어는 두 명사를 그대로 붙여 '그릇뚜껑'이라고 한다는 점을 기억하세요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 받침 means "saucer / coaster (stand under something)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 받침 (batchim) means "saucer / coaster (stand under something)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 받침에 놓다 ("to set on the saucer/stand"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 받침 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the stand as the surface; 놓다 = to put down
받치다 = to support from below — the verb the noun comes from
있다 expresses existence; 받침 없이 = without a stand
받침 compounds: 컵받침 (coaster), 냄비받침 (trivet) — '받침' = the thing underneath

examples.en: There's no saucer.
examples.note: 있다/없다 existence; a quick way to point out a missing stand under your cup.

examples.en: Put the hot cup on the saucer.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination; the saucer protects the table from the hot cup.

examples.en: Without a stand the cup slides around.
examples.note: -(으)면 = if/when; explains why the 받침 underneath is useful.

extendedVocab.nuance: 받침은 동사 '받치다(아래에서 받쳐 주다, to support from underneath)'에서 나온 명사로, 컵이나 그릇 '아래에' 받쳐 두는 작은 판을 두루 가리켜요. 그래서 핵심 의미는 '무엇의 아래에 두어 받쳐 주는 것'이고, 영어처럼 용도별로 saucer/coaster/trivet으로 쪼개지 않고 한 단어로 폭넓게 써요. 가장 가까운 짝은 '컵받침'인데, 받침이 일반적인 '아래 받치는 것' 전체를 뜻한다면 컵받침은 '컵 전용 받침'으로 범위가 좁아요 — 즉 컵받침은 받침의 한 종류예요. 같은 원리로 냄비받침(trivet)도 만들어져요. 영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 받침을 음식을 담아 먹는 접시로 오해하는 것인데, 받침은 먹는 그릇이 아니라 다른 것을 받쳐 두는 '바닥 판'이에요. 또 한국어 받침은 글자에서 자음이 아래에 받치는 부분(예: '강'의 ㅇ)도 가리키니, 식기 맥락인지 한글 맥락인지 문맥으로 구별하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 받침 is a plate you eat from; it's a stand placed underneath something (a cup, a pot), not a serving dish — the word literally comes from 받치다 'to support from below'.
Assuming 받침 only means a cup coaster; it's the general word for 'the thing underneath', so a trivet under a pot is 냄비받침 and a coaster under a cup is 컵받침.
Forgetting that 받침 also means the bottom consonant of a Korean syllable block; in a tableware context it's the physical stand, but learners sometimes mix the two senses.

structuredNuance.t: 컵이나 그릇 '아래에' 받쳐 두는 작은 판을 두루 가리켜요. 그래서 핵심 의미는 '무엇의 아래에 두어 받쳐 주는 것'이고, 영어처럼 용도별로 saucer/coaster/trivet으로 쪼개지 않고 한 단어로 폭넓게 써요.
가장 가까운 짝은 '컵받침'인데, 받침이 일반적인 '아래 받치는 것' 전체를 뜻한다면 컵받침은 '컵 전용 받침'으로 범위가 좁아요 — 즉 컵받침은 받침의 한 종류예요. 같은 원리로 냄비받침(trivet)도 만들어져요.
받침은 동사 '받치다(아래에서 받쳐 주다, to support from underneath)'에서 나온 명사예요. 또 한국어 받침은 글자에서 자음이 아래에 받치는 부분(예: '강'의 ㅇ)도 가리키니, 식기 맥락인지 한글 맥락인지 문맥으로 구별하세요.
영어 화자가 흔히 하는 실수는 받침을 음식을 담아 먹는 접시로 오해하는 것인데, 받침은 먹는 그릇이 아니라 다른 것을 받쳐 두는 '바닥 판'이에요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 컵받침 means "coaster (for a cup)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "coaster (for a cup)" is 컵받침 (keopbatchim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 컵받침에 놓다 ("to put on the coaster"). Watch the particle attached to 컵받침 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the coaster as the surface for the cup
깔다 = to spread/lay flat; what you do before setting the cup
받치다 = to support from below; 컵 아래에 컵받침을 받치다
counter 개; 컵받침 = 컵(cup) + 받침(stand)

examples.en: The coaster is pretty.
examples.note: Simple descriptive sentence; subject marker 이 after consonant-final 컵받침.

examples.en: Please put the cup on the coaster.
examples.note: 위에 = on top of; spells out that the cup sits above the coaster.

examples.en: I laid a coaster under the coffee cup.
examples.note: 밑에 = underneath; 깔다 → 깔았어요 is the natural verb for laying a flat coaster down.

extendedVocab.nuance: 컵받침은 컵(cup) + 받침(아래에 받치는 것)이 결합한 말로, 컵 아래에 까는 작은 받침을 뜻해요. 물방울이나 뜨거운 자국이 책상·식탁에 남지 않게 해 주는 것이 주된 쓰임이라 영어 'coaster'와 잘 맞아요. 상위 개념인 '받침'이 아래에 받치는 것 일반을 가리킨다면, 컵받침은 '컵 전용'으로 콕 집은 말이라는 점에서 갈려요. 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '냅킨'인데, 컵받침은 컵을 받쳐 자국을 막는 단단한 받침이고 냅킨은 입·손을 닦는 종이라 기능이 전혀 다르니 섞지 마세요. 격식을 갖춘 찻잔 세트의 받침 접시는 '컵받침'보다 '받침 접시'나 외래어 '소서(saucer)'라고도 하지만, 일상 카페에서는 '컵받침'이 가장 흔해요. 함께 쓰는 동사 '깔다(to lay flat)'도 익혀 두면 좋은데, 컵받침을 '깔다/놓다'라고 자연스럽게 말합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 컵받침 (a firm coaster the cup rests on) with 냅킨 (a paper napkin for your mouth/hands); their functions are completely different.
Using 컵받침 for any saucer; it specifically means a cup coaster, so a formal teacup's plate is better called 받침 접시 or 소서.
Saying 컵받침을 놓다 only and never 깔다; for laying a flat coaster down, Koreans naturally use 깔다 (깔았어요) as well as 놓다.

컵받침은 컵(cup) + 받침(아래에 받치는 것)이 결합한 말이에요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 냅킨 means "napkin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 냅킨 (naepkin) = "napkin". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 냅킨으로 닦다 ("to wipe with a napkin") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 냅킨, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 = with (tool/means); 닦다 = to wipe
a constant restaurant request; 주세요 = please give
뽑다 = to pull out; you pull napkins from the 냅킨통 (dispenser)
counter 장 for thin flat sheets — not 개

examples.en: Just one more napkin, please.
examples.note: Counter 장 for flat paper; 만 = just, 더 = more — a precise, polite ask.

examples.en: I wiped my mouth with a napkin.
examples.note: 으로 marks the napkin as the tool; the typical after-eating action.

examples.ko: 냅킨은 식탁 위 통에서 뽑아 쓰면 돼요.
examples.romanization: naepkineun siktak wi tongeseo ppoba sseumyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can just pull napkins from the holder on the table.
examples.note: -(으)면 되다 = it's fine to / you may; describes the self-serve 냅킨통 setup.

extendedVocab.nuance: 냅킨은 영어 'napkin'을 그대로 들여온 외래어로, 입이나 손을 닦는 종이(또는 천)를 가리켜요. 한국 일상에서는 거의 항상 식당 식탁 위 '냅킨통'에 든 종이 냅킨을 뽑아 쓰는 일회용을 떠올려요. 가장 중요한 구분은 '휴지'와의 차이인데, 휴지는 코를 풀거나 화장실에서 쓰는 두루마리·갑 티슈 같은 일반 화장지를 뜻하고, 냅킨은 식사 중 입·손을 닦는 용도로 식탁에 두는 것이라 쓰임과 장소가 달라요. 식당에서 코를 닦을 종이가 필요할 때 무심코 '휴지'를 달라고 하면 다른 것을 가져올 수 있으니 상황에 맞게 골라 쓰세요. 가장 흔한 문법 실수는 분류사인데, 냅킨은 얇고 납작한 종이라 '개'가 아니라 '장(sheet)'으로 세요 — 냅킨 한 장이 맞고 냅킨 한 개는 어색해요. 또 닦는 도구임을 나타낼 때는 조사 '으로(with)'를 붙여 '냅킨으로 닦다'라고 합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting napkins with 개 instead of the flat-sheet counter 장; thin paper like napkins, tickets, and paper takes 장 (냅킨 한 장, not 한 개).
Confusing 냅킨 (for wiping mouth/hands at the table) with 휴지 (general tissue/toilet paper for your nose or the bathroom); asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong paper.
Dropping the 으로 particle and saying 냅킨 닦다; to mark the napkin as the means you wipe with, use 냅킨으로 닦다.

structuredNuance.t: 입이나 손을 닦는 종이(또는 천)를 가리켜요. 한국 일상에서는 거의 항상 식당 식탁 위 '냅킨통'에 든 종이 냅킨을 뽑아 쓰는 일회용을 떠올려요. 또 닦는 도구임을 나타낼 때는 조사 '으로(with)'를 붙여 '냅킨으로 닦다'라고 합니다.

냅킨은 영어 'napkin'을 그대로 들여온 외래어예요.
가장 흔한 문법 실수는 분류사인데, 냅킨은 얇고 납작한 종이라 '개'가 아니라 '장(sheet)'으로 세요 — 냅킨 한 장이 맞고 냅킨 한 개는 어색해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이쑤시개 means "toothpick" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이쑤시개 (issusigae) means "toothpick". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이쑤시개로 이를 쑤시다 ("to pick one's teeth with a toothpick"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이쑤시개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to pick one's teeth with a toothpick
usagePhrases.note: 으로 = with; 쑤시다 = to poke/pick at (between the teeth)
있다 question to ask staff; very common after a meal

usagePhrases.en: to use it while covering with one hand
usagePhrases.note: -고 links 'cover' then 'use'; the polite manner is to shield your mouth
counter 개; small stick taken from a holder near the register

examples.en: Do you have a toothpick?
examples.note: 있다 to check availability; the natural thing to ask the cashier after eating.

examples.en: I used a toothpick after eating.
examples.note: Sequence with -고; 쓰다 (to use) → 썼어요 for a one-off past action.

examples.ko: 이쑤시개는 한 손으로 입을 가리고 쓰는 게 예의예요.
examples.romanization: issusigaeneun han soneuro ibeul garigo sseuneun ge yeuiyeyo.
examples.en: It's polite to use a toothpick while covering your mouth with one hand.
examples.note: 가리다 = to cover/shield; -는 게 예의다 frames it as the courteous etiquette.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이쑤시개는 이(teeth) + 쑤시개(쑤시다 'to poke at'의 명사형)가 합쳐진 순우리말로, 글자 그대로 '이를 쑤시는 도구'예요. 그래서 이름만 봐도 용도가 보이고, 핵심 동사 '쑤시다(틈을 후비다)'와 한 세트로 외우면 좋아요. 영어 'toothpick'과 일대일로 대응하지만, 쓰임의 문화 규칙이 달라요 — 한국에서는 보통 한 손으로 입을 가리고 조심스럽게 써야 예의 바르게 보여요. 영어 화자가 흔히 범하는 실수는 칵테일 음식이나 과일을 콕 찍어 먹는 데 쓰는 'cocktail pick(꼬치/픽)'과 혼동하는 것인데, 이쑤시개는 어디까지나 이 사이를 청소하는 용도이지 음식을 찍어 먹는 도구가 아니에요(그건 보통 '꼬치'나 '포크'를 써요). 또 '있어요?'로 물을 때 조사 없이 '이쑤시개 있어요?'라고 자연스럽게 말하고, 도구임을 강조할 때만 '이쑤시개로'처럼 으로를 붙입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Picking your teeth out in the open without shielding your mouth; in Korea the polite way is to cover with one hand (한 손으로 가리고), so doing it openly looks rude.
Using an 이쑤시개 to spear fruit or appetizers as if it were a cocktail pick; it's meant for cleaning between teeth, while food is speared with a 꼬치 (skewer/pick) or 포크 (fork).
Adding the wrong particle in 이쑤시개를 있어요; existence with 있다 takes 이/가 or no particle (이쑤시개 있어요?), and 으로 only when marking it as the tool you use.

structuredNuance.t: 글자 그대로 '이를 쑤시는 도구'예요. 그래서 이름만 봐도 용도가 보이고, 핵심 동사 '쑤시다(틈을 후비다)'와 한 세트로 외우면 좋아요. 영어 'toothpick'과 일대일로 대응하지만, 쓰임의 문화 규칙이 달라요 — 한국에서는 보통 한 손으로 입을 가리고 조심스럽게 써야 예의 바르게 보여요. 또 '있어요?'로 물을 때 조사 없이 '이쑤시개 있어요?'라고 자연스럽게 말하고, 도구임을 강조할 때만 '이쑤시개로'처럼 으로를 붙입니다.
이쑤시개는 이(teeth) + 쑤시개(쑤시다 'to poke at'의 명사형)가 합쳐진 순우리말이에요.
영어 화자가 흔히 범하는 실수는 칵테일 음식이나 과일을 콕 찍어 먹는 데 쓰는 'cocktail pick(꼬치/픽)'과 혼동하는 것인데, 이쑤시개는 어디까지나 이 사이를 청소하는 용도이지 음식을 찍어 먹는 도구가 아니에요(그건 보통 '꼬치'나 '포크'를 써요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 빨대 means "(drinking) straw" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "(drinking) straw" is 빨대 (ppaldae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 빨대로 마시다 ("to drink with/through a straw"). Watch the particle attached to 빨대 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 = with (means); 마시다 takes the drink as object, not the straw
꽂다 = to insert/stick into; what you do to a juice pouch or cup
종이(paper) + 빨대; the eco-friendly type many cafes now use
counter 개; 빨대 = from 빨다 (to suck) + 대 (rod/stick)

examples.en: I drank juice through a straw.
examples.note: 으로 marks the straw as the means; the object you drink is 주스, not the straw.

examples.en: Please stick a straw in for me.
examples.note: 꽂다 = to insert; 좀 softens the request to put the straw into the drink.

examples.ko: 요즘은 카페에서 종이 빨대를 많이 줘요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun kapeeseo jongi ppaldaereul mani jwoyo.
examples.en: These days cafes often give paper straws.
examples.note: Trend note; 종이 빨대 (paper straw) contrasts with the older 플라스틱 빨대.

extendedVocab.nuance: 빨대는 '빨다(to suck)' + '대(가느다란 막대·줄기를 뜻하는 순우리말 명사, 막대기·낚싯대의 그 '대')'가 합쳐진 말로, 음료를 빨아 마시는 가느다란 관이에요. 이름에 동사 '빨다'가 들어 있어 쓰임이 바로 드러나는 점이 외우기 쉬워요. 가장 중요한 문법 포인트는, 영어 'drink the straw'식으로 '빨대를 마시다'라고 하면 틀린다는 거예요 — 마시는 대상은 음료이고 빨대는 수단이므로 '빨대로 (주스를) 마시다'처럼 조사 '으로'를 써야 해요. 발음·철자에서 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '빨래(laundry)'인데, 빨대(straw)와 빨래(washing)는 둘 다 '빨다'에서 왔지만 뜻이 전혀 다르니 받침과 끝소리에 주의하세요. 요즘 카페에서는 환경을 위해 플라스틱 대신 '종이 빨대'를 주는 곳이 많아, '종이 빨대'라는 합성도 자주 들려요. 빨대를 컵·팩에 꽂을 때는 동사 '꽂다(to insert)'와 함께 씁니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 빨대를 마시다 ('drink the straw') by copying English; you drink the beverage, so it's 빨대로 마시다 — the straw takes 으로 as the means.
Mixing up 빨대 (straw) and 빨래 (laundry) because they sound alike and both come from 빨다; watch the ending — 대 vs 래.
Using 넣다 ('put in') for inserting a straw when the precise verb is 꽂다 (to stick/insert into), as in 빨대를 꽂다.

structuredNuance.t: 음료를 빨아 마시는 가느다란 관이에요. 이름에 동사 '빨다'가 들어 있어 쓰임이 바로 드러나는 점이 외우기 쉬워요. 요즘 카페에서는 환경을 위해 플라스틱 대신 '종이 빨대'를 주는 곳이 많아, '종이 빨대'라는 합성도 자주 들려요. 빨대를 컵·팩에 꽂을 때는 동사 '꽂다(to insert)'와 함께 씁니다.
발음·철자에서 자주 헷갈리는 짝은 '빨래(laundry)'인데, 빨대(straw)와 빨래(washing)는 둘 다 '빨다'에서 왔지만 뜻이 전혀 다르니 받침과 끝소리에 주의하세요.
빨대는 '빨다(to suck)' + '대(가느다란 막대·줄기를 뜻하는 순우리말 명사, 막대기·낚싯대의 그 '대')'가 합쳐진 말이에요.
가장 중요한 문법 포인트는, 영어 'drink the straw'식으로 '빨대를 마시다'라고 하면 틀린다는 거예요 — 마시는 대상은 음료이고 빨대는 수단이므로 '빨대로 (주스를) 마시다'처럼 조사 '으로'를 써야 해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 종이컵 means "paper cup" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 종이컵 (jongikeop) = "paper cup". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 종이컵에 따르다 ("to pour into a paper cup") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 종이컵, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to pour into a paper cup
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the cup; 따르다 (르-irregular) → 따라요

usagePhrases.en: to get water in a paper cup
usagePhrases.note: 받다 = to receive/catch (water from a dispenser) into the cup
일회용(一回用) = single-use; stresses that it's used once and tossed
counter 개; 종이(paper) + 컵(cup, from English)

examples.en: I got water in a paper cup and drank it.
examples.note: 받다 = to catch/receive water; -아 links filling then drinking.

examples.en: Please give me a paper cup.
examples.note: A quick, polite request; 하나 = one, 주세요 = please give.

examples.en: At work dinners people use a lot of paper cups.
examples.note: 때 = at the time of; practical setting where disposables get used.

extendedVocab.nuance: 종이컵은 종이(paper) + 컵(cup, 영어 외래어)이 합쳐진 말로, 한 번 쓰고 버리는 일회용 종이 컵이에요. 정수기 옆, 사무실, 행사장에서 흔히 보여요. 핵심 의미는 '일회용(一回用, single-use)'이라는 점이라, 여러 번 쓰는 '유리컵(glass)'이나 '머그컵(mug)'과 정반대 개념으로 묶여요 — 재질(종이)과 일회성이 동시에 강조되는 단어예요. 영어 화자가 그냥 'cup'을 떠올려 '컵 주세요'라고만 하면 어떤 컵인지 모호하니, 일회용 종이 컵이 필요할 때는 콕 집어 '종이컵'이라고 해야 해요. 함께 알아 둘 동사로, 정수기에서 물을 담을 때는 '따르다(pour)'보다 '받다(receive/catch)'를 더 자연스럽게 써서 '종이컵에 물을 받다'라고 합니다(물이 위에서 떨어지는 것을 받는 느낌). 또 따르다는 르불규칙이라 '따라요'로 활용되는 점도 함께 기억하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reusing a 종이컵 many times like a normal cup; by definition it's 일회용 (single-use), so for a reusable one you'd want a 유리컵 or 머그컵.
Just saying 컵 when you specifically need a disposable paper one; 컵 alone is ambiguous, so specify 종이컵.
Using 따르다 (pour) for filling a cup at a water dispenser when 받다 (to catch/receive the falling water) is the natural verb: 종이컵에 물을 받다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수저통 means "cutlery holder (for spoons and chopsticks)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 수저통 (sujeotong) means "cutlery holder (for spoons and chopsticks)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수저통에서 꺼내다 ("to take out of the cutlery holder"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수저통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to take out of the cutlery holder
usagePhrases.note: 에서 = out of (source); 꺼내다 = to take out

usagePhrases.en: the holder is on the table
usagePhrases.note: 위에 있다 = is on top of; where the holder usually sits
열다 = to open; some holders have a lid you lift

usagePhrases.en: one set of spoon and chopsticks
usagePhrases.note: counter 벌 for sets; 수저 = 숟가락(spoon) + 젓가락(chopsticks)

examples.en: I took a spoon and chopsticks out of the holder.
examples.note: 에서 marks the source; 이랑 casually links the two utensils you pull out.

examples.en: The cutlery holder is on the table.
examples.note: 위에 있다 locates it; this is where you self-serve utensils at a Korean eatery.

examples.ko: 수저는 수저통에서 직접 꺼내 쓰면 돼요.
examples.romanization: sujeoneun sujeotongeseo jikjeop kkeonae sseumyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can just take the utensils from the holder yourself.
examples.note: -(으)면 되다 = it's fine to; 직접 = personally, highlighting the self-serve custom.

extendedVocab.nuance: 수저통은 수저(숟가락+젓가락) + 통(桶, case/bin)이 결합한 말이에요. 여기서 가장 중요한 어휘 포인트는 '수저'인데, 영어로는 보통 'spoon' 하나로 옮기기 쉽지만 한국어 '수저'는 '숟가락(spoon)과 젓가락(chopsticks)을 함께 부르는 말'이라는 점이에요 — 그래서 수저통에는 숟가락과 젓가락이 같이 들어 있어요. 한국 식당에서는 보통 식탁 위나 서랍 속 수저통에 수저가 들어 있어, 종업원을 기다리지 말고 손님이 직접 꺼내 쓰는 셀프 문화가 일반적이에요. 함께 쓰는 동사로 '꺼내다(to take out)'와 출발점을 나타내는 조사 '에서(from/out of)'를 묶어 '수저통에서 꺼내다'로 외우면 좋아요. 또 수저를 셀 때는 한 벌, 두 벌처럼 분류사 '벌(set)'을 써서 숟가락과 젓가락 한 쌍을 한 벌로 센다는 점도 알아 두세요. 통(桶)이라는 한자는 김치통·반찬통처럼 '무언가를 담는 통'에 두루 쓰입니다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 수저 means only a spoon; 수저 is the cover term for spoon + chopsticks together, which is why a 수저통 holds both 숟가락 and 젓가락.
Waiting for staff to set your utensils; in Korea they're usually in the 수저통 on the table or in a drawer, so you self-serve by 수저통에서 꺼내다.
Counting a spoon-and-chopstick set with 개 instead of 벌; a matched set is 한 벌 (one set), since 수저 comes as a pair.

structuredNuance.t: 수저(숟가락+젓가락)를 담아 두는 통이에요. 여기서 가장 중요한 어휘 포인트는 '수저'인데, 영어로는 보통 'spoon' 하나로 옮기기 쉽지만 한국어 '수저'는 '숟가락(spoon)과 젓가락(chopsticks)을 함께 부르는 말'이라는 점이에요 — 그래서 수저통에는 숟가락과 젓가락이 같이 들어 있어요. 한국 식당에서는 보통 식탁 위나 서랍 속 수저통에 수저가 들어 있어, 종업원을 기다리지 말고 손님이 직접 꺼내 쓰는 셀프 문화가 일반적이에요. 함께 쓰는 동사로 '꺼내다(to take out)'와 출발점을 나타내는 조사 '에서(from/out of)'를 묶어 '수저통에서 꺼내다'로 외우면 좋아요. 또 수저를 셀 때는 한 벌, 두 벌처럼 분류사 '벌(set)'을 써서 숟가락과 젓가락 한 쌍을 한 벌로 센다는 점도 알아 두세요.
수저통은 수저(숟가락+젓가락) + 통(桶, case/bin)이 결합한 말이에요. 통(桶)이라는 한자는 김치통·반찬통처럼 '무언가를 담는 통'에 두루 쓰입니다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 도로 means "road" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "road" is 도로 (doro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 고속도로 ("highway / expressway"). Watch the particle attached to 도로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 고속 (high speed) + 도로 = the big inter-city expressway
fixed traffic phrase; 막히다 (be blocked) is intransitive, so use 가/이 not 을/를
공사 工事 = construction work; the sign you see when a lane is closed

usagePhrases.en: go by this road / take this road
usagePhrases.note: route-marking 로/으로, not 에서; tells which road you travel along

examples.en: This road is wide.
examples.note: simplest description; 넓다 (wide) takes the subject with 은/는 here

examples.en: It's rush hour, so the road is really jammed.
examples.note: everyday complaint; 막히다 stays intransitive, so 도로'가' not 도로'를'

examples.en: The GPS told me to take this road.
examples.note: real driving situation; route particle 로 + indirect command 가라고 하다

extendedVocab.nuance: 도로 道路 (道 way + 路 path) is the neutral, infrastructure word for a paved road that cars drive on — what an engineer or a traffic report means by 'road'. The sharp contrast is with 거리: 도로 stresses the vehicle surface (도로가 막히다, 도로 공사), while 거리 is a shopping/walking street you stroll down; you would never say 거리가 막히다 about car traffic. It is also broader than 골목(길) (a narrow alley) and 차도 (the car-only carriageway as opposed to 인도, the sidewalk). Register is plain and works everywhere from signs to news. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle when you mean a route: 'go by this road' is 이 도로'로' 가요 (route-marking 로/으로), not 도로'에서' 가요, because 에서 marks where an action happens, while 로 marks the path you move along.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 도로를 막혀요 — 막히다 (to be jammed/blocked) is intransitive, so the road is the subject: 도로'가' 막혀요.
Using 도로 for a lively shopping street: a street you walk and browse is 거리 (e.g. 가로수길 같은 거리), whereas 도로 sounds like an asphalt traffic artery.
Marking the route with 에서: to express 'let's take this road' say 이 도로'로' 가요, not 이 도로에서 가요 (에서 would mean an action performed on the road).

structuredNuance.t: 도로 is the neutral, infrastructure word for a paved road that cars drive on — what an engineer or a traffic report means by 'road'. Register is plain and works everywhere from signs to news.

The sharp contrast is with 거리: 도로 stresses the vehicle surface (도로가 막히다, 도로 공사), while 거리 is a shopping/walking street you stroll down; you would never say 거리가 막히다 about car traffic. It is also broader than 골목(길) (a narrow alley) and 차도 (the car-only carriageway as opposed to 인도, the sidewalk).
道路 = 道 (way) + 路 (path).
The trap is the particle when you mean a route: 'go by this road' is 이 도로'로' 가요 (route-marking 로/으로), not 도로'에서' 가요, because 에서 marks where an action happens, while 로 marks the path you move along.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주유소 means "gas station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주유소 (juyuso) = "gas station". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 주유소에 가다 ("go to the gas station") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주유소, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: destination 에 + 가다; 주유소 is a place you head to
the verb is 넣다 (put in); the object is 기름 (oil/fuel), not 주유소
셀프 (self) + 주유소; you pump it yourself, very common in Korea
기름값 = fuel price; describe the station's prices, not the station 'being cheap'

examples.en: Is there a gas station nearby?
examples.note: simple existence question; 있다 takes the subject with 가

examples.en: I filled the tank all the way up at the gas station.
examples.note: everyday refueling; 에서 marks where the action happens, 가득 = full

examples.en: It's a self-service station, so you have to pump it yourself.
examples.note: real situation; -아야 하다 (have to) + 직접 (in person/oneself)

extendedVocab.nuance: 주유소 注油所 literally stacks 注 (pour) + 油 (oil) + 所 (place) = 'a place where you pour oil', i.e. a fuel station. Because the 油 is 'oil/fuel', Koreans say 기름(을) 넣다 ('put in oil') even for gasoline — 기름 covers gasoline, diesel, everything in the tank. The natural verb is 넣다 (put in), so the object is 기름, never the station itself. As a 소(所) place-noun it behaves like other locations: 에 for going there (주유소에 가요), 에서 for the action done there (주유소에서 넣어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is importing 'gas': do not say 가스 — 가스 in Korean means cooking/LPG gas, and a fuel stop is 주유소. A second trap is making the station the grammatical object: you fill the car with 기름, so it's 기름을 넣다, not 주유소를 넣다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling it a 가스 station — 가스 means household/LPG gas in Korean; the place to refuel a car is 주유소.
Saying 주유소를 넣어요 — the thing you put in is fuel, so it must be 주유소'에서' 기름'을' 넣어요.
Saying 주유소가 싸요 to mean fuel is cheap — describe the price: 그 주유소는 기름값이 싸요 (its gas price is cheap).

structuredNuance.t: 주유소 is a fuel station. Because the 油 is 'oil/fuel', Koreans say 기름(을) 넣다 ('put in oil') even for gasoline — 기름 covers gasoline, diesel, everything in the tank. The natural verb is 넣다 (put in), so the object is 기름, never the station itself. As a 소(所) place-noun it behaves like other locations: 에 for going there (주유소에 가요), 에서 for the action done there (주유소에서 넣어요).
注油所 literally stacks 注 (pour) + 油 (oil) + 所 (place) = 'a place where you pour oil'.

The big trap is importing 'gas': do not say 가스 — 가스 in Korean means cooking/LPG gas, and a fuel stop is 주유소. A second trap is making the station the grammatical object: you fill the car with 기름, so it's 기름을 넣다, not 주유소를 넣다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 좌석 means "seat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 좌석 (jwaseok) means "seat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 창가 좌석 ("window seat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 좌석 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 창가 (window side) + 좌석; opposite is 통로 좌석 (aisle seat)
번호 番號 = number; the figure printed on your ticket
예약하다 (book in advance); 좌석 is the object with 을
등급 = class (e.g. 일반실/특실 on the KTX)

examples.en: Where is my seat?
examples.note: simple question on a train or plane; 은/는 marks 'my seat' as topic

examples.en: A window seat, please.
examples.note: everyday booking line; 으로 = 'as/in the form of', i.e. choosing among options

examples.ko: 예매한 좌석에 다른 사람이 앉아 있었어요.
examples.romanization: yemaehan jwaseoge dareun sarami anja isseosseoyo.
examples.en: Someone else was sitting in the seat I'd reserved.
examples.note: real-trip trouble; 예매하다 (book a ticket) + 에 앉다 (sit in/at)

extendedVocab.nuance: 좌석 座席 (座 a seat + 席 a mat/place) is the formal, ticketed word for a numbered seat on a bus, train, plane, or in a theater. Its everyday near-synonym is 자리, and the dividing line is register and specificity: 자리 is the casual catch-all ('a spot/place to sit', also 'a vacant spot'), while 좌석 is what appears on tickets, signboards, and reservation screens — you reserve a 좌석, but you save someone a 자리. Natural partners are 창가/통로 좌석 (window/aisle), 좌석 번호, 좌석 예약. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: first, pick the verb by the surface — you 앉다 'on/at' a seat with 에 (좌석에 앉다), not 좌석을 앉다; second, watch the spelling, since 자석 (磁石) means 'magnet' and 좌석 is the seat — the ㅗ vs ㅏ vowel is the whole difference.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 좌석 in casual chat where 자리 fits — for 'save me a spot' say 자리 좀 맡아 줘, not 좌석; 좌석 sounds like a booked transport seat.
Saying 좌석을 앉아요 — you sit at a seat: 좌석'에' 앉아요 (place particle 에).
Misspelling it 자석 — that is 磁石 'magnet'; the seat is 좌석 with the ㅗ vowel.

structuredNuance.t: 좌석 is the formal, ticketed word for a numbered seat on a bus, train, plane, or in a theater. Natural partners are 창가/통로 좌석 (window/aisle), 좌석 번호, 좌석 예약.

Its everyday near-synonym is 자리, and the dividing line is register and specificity: 자리 is the casual catch-all ('a spot/place to sit', also 'a vacant spot'), while 좌석 is what appears on tickets, signboards, and reservation screens — you reserve a 좌석, but you save someone a 자리.
座席 = 座 (a seat) + 席 (a mat/place).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목적지 means "destination" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "destination" is 목적지 (mokjeokji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 목적지에 도착하다 ("arrive at the destination"). Watch the particle attached to 목적지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: goal-marking 에 + 도착하다; 에 is required, never 를
최종 最終 (final) + 목적지; the last stop when you have transfers
입력하다 (input) into a GPS; here 목적지 is the object with 를

usagePhrases.en: all the way to the destination
usagePhrases.note: 까지 = up to/as far as; marks the end point of the route

examples.en: Where are you headed?
examples.note: simple; a taxi driver's opening question, subject marked with 가

examples.en: It takes about an hour to the destination.
examples.note: everyday travel time; 까지 (up to) + 걸리다 (take time)

examples.en: I entered the destination into the GPS.
examples.note: real driving step; here 목적지 is the object you type in, so 를

extendedVocab.nuance: 목적지 目的地 stacks 目 (eye/aim) + 的 (target) + 地 (place/ground) = 'the targeted place', the spot you are traveling toward. The instructive contrast is with 도착지 and 출발지: 목적지 highlights intention ('where I aim to go'), 도착지 is the neutral 'arrival point', and its true opposite is 출발지 (departure point) — pairing 목적지 with 출발지 is the standard map/app framing. Do not confuse 목적지 (place) with 목적 alone (目的 = a purpose/aim, abstract), nor with 목표 (a goal you strive for). It is a slightly formal travel word used by taxi drivers and navigation apps. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you arrive 'at' it with 에 — 목적지'에' 도착하다 — never 목적지를 도착하다, because 도착하다 is intransitive; but when you type it into a GPS the verb is transitive, so it flips to 목적지'를' 입력하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 목적지를 도착해요 — 도착하다 (to arrive) is intransitive and needs the goal particle: 목적지'에' 도착해요.
Confusing 목적지 (the place) with 목적 (the purpose) — 'my destination is Busan' is 목적지는 부산이에요, not 목적은 부산이에요 (that would mean 'my purpose is Busan').
Using 목적지 for a starting point — that is 출발지; 목적지 is only the place you are going to.

structuredNuance.t: 목적지 means 'the targeted place', the spot you are traveling toward. It is a slightly formal travel word used by taxi drivers and navigation apps.

The instructive contrast is with 도착지 and 출발지: 목적지 highlights intention ('where I aim to go'), 도착지 is the neutral 'arrival point', and its true opposite is 출발지 (departure point) — pairing 목적지 with 출발지 is the standard map/app framing. Do not confuse 목적지 (place) with 목적 alone (目的 = a purpose/aim, abstract), nor with 목표 (a goal you strive for).

extendedVocab.nuance: 거리 (street) is a native Korean word — note it is NOT the Sino-Korean 距離 'distance', even though the two are spelled and written identically and are told apart only by context. As 'street' it means a public way lined with shops, cafes, and pedestrians that you stroll and browse (think 명동 거리, 가로수길). The sharp contrast is with 도로 道路: 거리 centers on people and street life (거리 공연, 거리가 복잡하다), while 도로 centers on the car surface (도로가 막히다) — Koreans say 도로가 막히다 for a traffic jam but never 거리가 막히다 in that sense. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this homonym: 'the distance is far' is 거리가 멀다, but 'the street is busy' is 거리가 복잡하다 — same word, and only the predicate and situation tell you whether someone means a road you walk or a span you measure.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 거리 for a car-jammed highway — a traffic artery is 도로; 거리 evokes a walkable shopping street, so a jam is 도로가 막히다, not 거리가 막히다.
Forgetting the distance/street homonym — 거리가 멀어요 means 'the distance is far', not 'the street is far'; let context (멀다 vs 복잡하다) disambiguate.
Saying 거리를 걸어가요 vs 거리에서 — to 'walk along' the street the path can take 를 (거리를 걷다); 에서 is for an action located on the street (거리에서 공연을 보다).

extendedVocab.nuance: 승강장 乘降場 stacks 乘 (board/get on) + 降 (alight/get off) + 場 (place/field) = 'the place where you board and get off', i.e. the platform along the tracks. It is the formal term on signage and in announcements; the everyday spoken equivalent is 플랫폼 (the English loanword), and 타는 곳 ('boarding place') is the plain-Korean label posted in many stations — all three point to the same spot. Saying 승강장을 기다려요 — you don't wait for the platform; you wait for the train there: 승강장'에서' 기차'를' 기다려요.
Mixing up 승강장 with 정류장 — 승강장 is the train/subway platform inside a station, while 정류장 is a roadside bus stop.

extendedVocab.nuance: 안전벨트 is a hybrid: Sino-Korean 안전 安全 (安 peace/safe + 全 complete) = 'safety' + the loanword 벨트 (belt) — so literally a 'safety belt'. A common everyday synonym is just 벨트 ('안전벨트 매', often shortened to '벨트 매'), and on signs/laws you meet 착용 (着用 'wearing'). The make-or-break point is the verb: Korean fastens a belt with 매다 (to tie/fasten, the same verb as a necktie) and undoes it with 풀다 (to loosen) — NOT 입다/벗다, which are for clothing you put on the body. That is the central English-speaker pitfall: English 'wear/put on a seatbelt' tempts learners toward 입다, but 안전벨트를 입다 is wrong; it must be 안전벨트를 매다. Likewise 'take it off' is 풀다 (undo), not 벗다 (which is for shoes/clothes/hats).

Saying 안전벨트를 입다 — clothing verbs don't apply; a belt is fastened: 안전벨트를 '매다'.
Saying 안전벨트를 벗다 to take it off — 벗다 is for clothes/shoes; undo a belt with 안전벨트를 '풀다'.
Mixing up 매다 (fasten) with 메다 — 메다 means to sling a bag over the shoulder; the seatbelt verb is 매다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 헬멧 is a straight loanword from English 'helmet', with no hanja, used for the protective head shell worn on bikes, motorcycles, and especially 전동킥보드 (electric kickboards). A close native-ish synonym is 안전모 安全帽 (安全 safety + 帽 hat/cap), but 안전모 leans toward construction/industrial hard hats, while 헬멧 is the everyday sports/riding word — both can appear in safety rules. The decisive grammar point is the verb family for things worn on the HEAD: Korean uses 쓰다 to put on a helmet, hat, or glasses, and 벗다 to take them off. This is the key English-speaker pitfall — 'wear a helmet' invites 입다 (clothing) or even 풀다 (undo, from belts), but neither fits: it must be 헬멧을 쓰다 and 헬멧을 벗다. Note 쓰다 is a busy homonym (also 'to write', 'to use', 'to be bitter'), so context, not the verb alone, tells you it means 'wear on the head' here.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 헬멧을 입다 — 입다 is for body clothing; head gear uses 헬멧을 '쓰다'.
Saying 헬멧을 풀다 to remove it — 풀다 is for undoing belts/knots; take off head gear with 헬멧을 '벗다'.
Assuming 안전모 and 헬멧 are interchangeable — 안전모 sounds like an industrial hard hat, while a riding/cycling helmet is 헬멧.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 출발역 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 + 타다; the action of getting on happens there
the natural pair; 과/와 links the two endpoints
출발 出發 + 시각 時刻 (point in time); the time on your ticket
existence/identity question with 이/가

examples.note: simple identity sentence; 이에요 (it is)

examples.note: everyday step; 미리 (beforehand) + 에서 for the place of the action

extendedVocab.nuance: 출발역 出發驛 stacks 出 (go out) + 發 (set off/emit) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you set off from', the origin of a train trip. Its built-in opposite is 도착역 (arrival station, 到着驛), and the two are the standard pair on tickets and booking screens. Note the difference between 출발역 (the origin STATION) and 출발 (出發, the act of departing) and 출발지 (a more general 'departure point', not necessarily a rail station): for trains and subways you want 출발역. Register is plain and travel-flavored. The English-speaker pitfall is the boarding particle: you get on a train AT the station, so it's 출발역'에서' 타다 (action-location 에서), never 출발역을 타다 — 타다 takes the vehicle as its object (기차를 타다), while the station is just where that happens.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 출발역을 타요 — you board the train, not the station: 출발역'에서' 기차'를' 타요.
Confusing 출발역 with 도착역 — 출발역 is where you start/board, 도착역 is where you end/get off; don't swap them on a booking.
Using 출발 (the departure event) where you need the station — 'my departure station is Seoul Station' is 출발역이 서울역이에요, not 출발이 서울역이에요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 도착역 到着驛 stacks 到 (reach) + 着 (attach/land) + 驛 (station) = 'the station you arrive at', the endpoint of a train trip. Its mirror-image partner is 출발역 (departure station), and the pair frames every ticket. Distinguish 도착역 (the arrival STATION) from 도착 (到着, the act/fact of arriving) and from 목적지 (your overall destination, which may be reached after leaving the station): on the train itself, the stop where you alight is your 도착역. The contrast with 종착역 (終着驛, the train's final terminus) also matters — your 도착역 is where YOU get off, which may come before the line's 종착역. Confusing 도착역 with 출발역 — 도착역 is where you get off at the end; 출발역 is where you boarded.

usagePhrases.note: 사다 (buy); the ticket is the object with 를, verb is not 하다

usagePhrases.en: book a plane ticket in advance
usagePhrases.note: 예매하다 豫買 = reserve-and-buy ahead, the natural word for flights/trains
왕복 往復 (going and returning) ↔ 편도 (one way)
비싸다 (expensive) describes the fare with 가/이

examples.en: I bought a plane ticket.
examples.note: simple past of 사다; ticket as object with 를

examples.en: It's peak season, so plane tickets are way too expensive.
examples.note: everyday gripe; 성수기 (high season) + 비싸다 about the fare

examples.en: I booked a round-trip plane ticket in advance.
examples.note: real planning; 왕복 (round trip) + 예매하다 (book ahead)

extendedVocab.nuance: 비행기표 is a transparent compound: 비행기 飛行機 (飛 fly + 行 go + 機 machine = 'flying machine', airplane) + 표 票 (ticket) = 'plane ticket'. A common synonym is 항공권 航空券 (航空 aviation + 券 ticket/voucher), which is the formal/written term you see on booking sites and itineraries, whereas 비행기표 is the everyday spoken version — same thing, different register. The bare 표 means any ticket (train, movie, concert), so 비행기 is what specifies a flight. The verbs are 사다 (buy) and especially 예매하다 (book ahead), with 예약하다 (reserve) also fine. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 'do/get a ticket' does not translate — you 'buy' or 'book' it, so say 비행기표를 사다 / 예매하다, not 비행기표를 하다. A second trap is dropping 비행기 and saying only 표, which is too vague when a flight is meant.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비행기표를 해요 — you don't 'do' a ticket; you 비행기표를 '사요' (buy) or '예매해요' (book).
Using bare 표 for a flight — 표 alone could be any ticket; specify with 비행기표 (or 항공권) for a plane.
Treating 항공권 and 비행기표 as different things — they're the same; 항공권 is just the formal/written term you meet on booking sites.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 해 means "sun" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 해 (hae) means "sun". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 해가 떠요 ("the sun rises"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 해 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the motion verb 뜨다, not 오다
지다 = sink/go down, same verb as for flowers wilting
나다 = emerge, used after clouds or rain clear
switch to 햇볕 when you mean the warmth, not the disk

examples.en: The sun rises in the morning.
examples.note: 해가 떠요 is the fixed beginner phrase for sunrise; 떠요 comes from 뜨다.

examples.en: The rain stopped and the sun came out.
examples.note: 해가 나다 specifically means the sun reappears after bad weather.

examples.en: The sun is blazing today.
examples.note: 쨍쨍 is the sound-feel adverb Koreans use for a strong, glaring sun.

extendedVocab.nuance: 해 is the pure-Korean word for the sun as the physical disk in the sky, and it is also the everyday word for 'a day' (오늘 하루, 해가 바뀌다 = the year turns). Its near-synonym 태양(太陽) is the Sino-Korean, more scientific or literary word — you say 태양계 (solar system) and 태양이 빛나다 in writing, but in casual speech you almost always say 해. The dividing line: 해 = warm, daily, spoken; 태양 = grand, formal, written. 해 takes the motion verbs 뜨다 (rise) and 지다 (set), so the trap for English speakers is reaching for 오다/가다 by analogy with 'the sun comes up' — 해가 와요 is wrong; it must be 해가 떠요. A second pitfall is confusing 해 (the sun itself) with 햇빛 (sunlight you see) and 햇볕 (sun-warmth you feel on your skin): you do not 'look at the 해' to mean basking — that is 햇볕을 쬐다.

Saying 해가 와요 because English says 'the sun comes up.' Korean uses the rising verb: 해가 떠요 (from 뜨다). 오다 never describes the sun.
Using 해 when you mean the warmth or the light. 해 is the disk; the warmth is 햇볕 (햇볕이 따뜻해요) and the visible light is 햇빛 (햇빛이 눈부셔요).
Reaching for 태양 in casual conversation. 태양 sounds textbook-formal; a real Korean chatting about the weather says 해 (해 떴다, 해 진다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 햇볕 means "sunshine" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "sunshine" is 햇볕 (haetbyeot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 햇볕이 따뜻해요 ("the sunshine is warm"). Watch the particle attached to 햇볕 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 따뜻하다 pairs with the felt warmth of 햇볕
강하다 for intensity; 따갑다 if it stings the skin
쬐다 is the dedicated verb for soaking up sun/heat
들다 = light enters a room, 볕이 잘 드는 집 = a sunny house

examples.en: The sun is really warm today.
examples.note: Classic small talk; 햇볕 + 따뜻하다 is the natural warmth collocation.

examples.en: The sun stung, so I wore a hat.
examples.note: 따갑다 (prickly/stinging) fits strong 햇볕 better than just 강하다.

examples.en: This room gets good sunlight.
examples.note: Real-estate phrase: 볕이 잘 들다 = a bright, sun-filled room.

extendedVocab.nuance: 햇볕 is the sun's warmth and rays as you physically feel them on your skin — the heat, not the brightness. Its crucial near-synonym is 햇빛 (sun + 빛 light), which is the visible light you see with your eyes. The dividing line is touch vs. sight: you warm up in 햇볕 (햇볕이 따뜻하다, 햇볕을 쬐다) but you squint at 햇빛 (햇빛이 눈부시다 = the light is dazzling). 햇볕 is a compound of 해(sun) + 볕(sunlight/ray, with the ㅅ inserted as a 사이시옷), which is why the spelling ends in ㅌ — a very common spelling trap. 햇볕 takes the special verb 쬐다 (to bask/soak up), so the English-speaker pitfall is translating 'get some sun' as 햇볕을 봐요 (literally 'look at the sunshine'), which is wrong; the natural verb is 햇볕을 쬐다. Note Koreans also drop the 해 and just say 볕 (볕이 좋다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Spelling it 햇빛 when you mean warmth. Warmth on your skin is 햇볕(felt); the light you see is 햇빛(seen). They are different words, not spelling variants.
Writing the final consonant wrong: 햇볃 or 햇빛 instead of 햇볕. The correct ending is ㅌ (받침 티읕), pronounced [핻뼏].
Saying 햇볕을 봐요 for sunbathing. You don't 'see' the warmth; you absorb it: 햇볕을 쬐어요 (verb 쬐다).

structuredNuance.t: 햇볕 is the sun's warmth and rays as you physically feel them on your skin — the heat, not the brightness.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 노을 means "sunset glow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 노을 (noeul) = "sunset glow". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 노을이 지다 ("the glow spreads at sunset") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 노을, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 지다 — the same setting verb as for the sun
붉다 (deep red) is the signature color of 노을
fixed compound; 아침노을 exists but is far rarer

usagePhrases.en: the sky is dyed with the glow
usagePhrases.note: 물들다 = to be stained/dyed with color, very poetic

examples.en: The sunset glow is really pretty in the evening.
examples.note: Everyday compliment for a beautiful sky; 노을 + 예쁘다.

examples.en: The sky was dyed red with the sunset glow.
examples.note: 물들다 paints the whole sky — a step up in vividness from 지다.

examples.en: We went to the beach to watch the sunset glow.
examples.note: 노을 보러 가다 = go specifically to see the sunset, a real outing.

extendedVocab.nuance: 노을 is the red-orange glow that paints the sky at sunrise or (usually) sunset — the colored light on the clouds, not the sun itself. Do not confuse it with 일몰(日沒), which is the technical event of the sun sinking below the horizon (a forecast/almanac word), nor with 석양(夕陽), the Sino-Korean 'evening sun' that refers to the low sun itself rather than the painted sky. The dividing line: 노을 = the colors in the sky (pure-Korean, warm, everyday); 석양 = the setting sun disk (literary); 일몰 = the timed event (technical). 노을 takes 지다 (the same verb as 해가 지다), so 노을이 지다 = the glow comes out as the sun sets — an English speaker easily mis-hears this as 'the glow disappears,' but here 지다 means the sunset is happening, not fading. The pitfall is using 오다 (노을이 와요 ✗); the right verbs are 지다, 붉다, or the lovely 물들다 (to be dyed).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 노을이 와요 by analogy with 'the sunset comes.' Korean uses the setting verb: 노을이 져요 (from 지다), or describe it with 물들다/붉다.
Confusing 노을 (the colored sky) with 석양 (the low evening sun) or 일몰 (the timed sunset event). 노을 is about the colors, not the sun or the clock.
Mishearing 노을이 지다 as 'the glow is fading.' Here 지다 marks the sunset happening — the glow is at its peak, not disappearing.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 폭풍 means "storm" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 폭풍 (pokpung) means "storm". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 폭풍이 몰아치다 ("a storm rages"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 폭풍 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 몰아치다 = beat down violently, the strong verb for 폭풍
불다 because 폭풍 is fundamentally about wind
지나가다 = pass through, used once it clears
fixed idiom for tense calm before trouble

examples.en: They say a storm is coming tonight.
examples.note: -대요 reports a forecast you heard; 폭풍이 오다 is fine for 'a storm comes.'

examples.en: The storm blew and trees fell over.
examples.note: 폭풍 + 불다 (blow) shows it is wind-driven; -어서 gives the cause.

examples.en: The storm raged so the ship couldn't leave.
examples.note: 몰아치다 conveys a violent, battering storm — stronger than 불다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 폭풍(暴風) is Sino-Korean, literally 暴 'violent' + 風 'wind' — a violent windstorm, with heavy rain implied. Its near-synonyms split by what dominates: 태풍(颱風) is a named typhoon (a specific tropical cyclone with a forecast track), 비바람 is pure-Korean 'rain-and-wind' for an ordinary nasty day, and 폭풍우(暴風雨) adds 雨 'rain' to stress the downpour. The dividing line: 폭풍 = a fierce wind event (can be metaphorical), 태풍 = the meteorological typhoon, 비바람 = everyday wet-and-windy weather. Because 風 means wind, 폭풍 naturally takes 불다 (to blow) or the intensive 몰아치다 (to rage), while 오다 also works for 'a storm comes.' The English-speaker pitfall is 폭풍이 해요 — 'storm' is a noun, never a 하다 verb. Also note 폭풍 is used metaphorically (폭풍 성장 = explosive growth, 폭풍 오열 = sobbing one's heart out), a flavor English 'storm' doesn't carry the same way.

Saying 폭풍이 해요. 폭풍 is a noun; it cannot take 하다. Use 폭풍이 와요 / 불어요 / 몰아쳐요.
Confusing 폭풍 with 태풍. 태풍 is a specific named typhoon with a forecast; 폭풍 is any violent windstorm (and 폭염 is a heat wave — a totally different word).
Forgetting that 폭풍 takes wind verbs. Because 風 = wind, the natural pairings are 불다 (blow) and 몰아치다 (rage), not just generic 오다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 우박 means "hail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "hail" is 우박 (ubak). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우박이 내리다 ("hail falls"). Watch the particle attached to 우박 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 내리다 is the standard precipitation verb
쏟아지다 for a sudden heavy burst
떨어지다 stresses individual stones hitting
굵다 (thick/coarse) is the natural size word, not 크다

examples.en: Hail is suddenly falling.
examples.note: 갑자기 (suddenly) is almost a fixed partner — hail is abrupt; 내리다 is the core verb.

examples.en: Hail poured down and cracked the car window.
examples.note: 쏟아지다 captures a violent burst; -어서 links cause to result.

examples.en: Hailstones the size of fists fell.
examples.note: 주먹만 하다 (fist-sized) is how Koreans dramatize big hail; verb 떨어지다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 우박 is hail — the balls of ice that fall during a storm. Do not confuse it with three look-alike winter words: 진눈깨비 is sleet (rain mixed with wet snow), 싸락눈/싸라기눈 is tiny grain-snow (much smaller, softer, and it is snow not ice), and 서리 is frost that forms on the ground. The dividing line: 우박 = hard ice balls falling from storm clouds (any season, often summer); 진눈깨비 = mushy half-rain-half-snow; 싸락눈 = fine dry snow pellets. 우박 takes 내리다 (fall), the intensive 쏟아지다 (pour), or 떨어지다 (drop), and casual 오다 works too (우박이 와요, parallel to 비가 와요). The key collocation learners miss: hail size is 굵다/굵은 우박 (coarse), not 큰 우박. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the wind verb 불다 — hail doesn't 'blow,' it falls: 우박이 불어요 ✗, 우박이 내려요 ✓.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 우박이 불어요 with the wind verb. Hail falls, it doesn't blow: 우박이 내려요 / 와요 / 쏟아져요.
Confusing 우박 (ice balls) with 진눈깨비 (sleet, slushy rain+snow) or 싸락눈 (tiny snow pellets). 우박 is hard ice; the others are snow-based.
Saying 큰 우박 for big hail. The idiomatic size word is 굵다: 우박이 굵다 / 굵은 우박이 내리다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 보름달 means "full moon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 보름달 (boreumdal) = "full moon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 보름달이 뜨다 ("the full moon rises") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보름달, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 뜨다, the same rising verb as 해 and 달

usagePhrases.en: the full moon is brilliantly bright
usagePhrases.note: 휘영청 is the set adverb for a dazzling full moon
둥글다 for the round shape; 동그랗다 for small round things

usagePhrases.en: make a wish on the full moon
usagePhrases.note: fixed cultural collocation, esp. at 정월대보름

examples.en: The full moon rose tonight.
examples.note: 보름달이 뜨다 is the base phrase; 뜨다 covers all rising sky bodies.

examples.en: The full moon is brilliantly bright.
examples.note: 휘영청 밝다 is a near-set phrase — the poetic way to say a full moon is dazzling.

examples.en: I made a wish while looking at the full moon.
examples.note: 소원을 빌다 (make a wish) is the Chuseok/대보름 custom learners should know.

extendedVocab.nuance: 보름달 is the full moon — a pure-Korean compound of 보름 (the 15th day of the lunar month, i.e. mid-month) + 달 (moon). Its opposite is 초승달 (crescent moon), and its plain superordinate is just 달 (moon). The cultural weight matters: the full moon is tied to 추석 (Chuseok, the harvest festival) and especially 정월대보름 (the first full moon of the lunar year), when Koreans make wishes — so 보름달 carries warm festive connotations a bare 'full moon' lacks in English. It takes 뜨다 (rise) like all sky bodies, and its signature description is 휘영청 밝다 (brilliantly bright). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) reaching for 오다 — 보름달이 와요 ✗, it must be 보름달이 떠요; (2) assuming 'full' is a separate adjective — there is no 가득한 달; the fullness is baked into the single word 보름달.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 보름달이 와요. The moon rises, so use 뜨다: 보름달이 떠요. 오다 doesn't apply to moons.
Confusing 보름달 (full moon) with 초승달 (crescent). 보름(mid-month, round) vs 초승(start of the lunar month, thin sliver) are opposites.
Trying to build 'full moon' from an adjective + 달 (e.g. 가득한 달). It is one fixed word, 보름달, where 보름 already means the 15th/full phase.

structuredNuance.t: 보름달 is the full moon. extendedVocab.explanation: 초승달 (choseungdal) means "crescent moon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 초승달이 뜨다 ("the crescent moon rises"). usagePhrases.note: 뜨다, the standard rising verb
가늘다 (slender) for the thin sliver shape
눈썹 같다 is the classic shape metaphor
걸리다 = to be hung/caught, poetic for a sliver moon

examples.en: A crescent moon rose in the sky.
examples.note: Base sentence; 초승달 + 뜨다 just like any moon.

examples.en: The crescent moon is thin like an eyebrow.
examples.note: 눈썹처럼 가늘다 — the standard simile Koreans use for a slim crescent.

examples.en: A crescent moon hangs in the western sky.
examples.note: 걸려 있다 (is hanging) gives a still, picturesque image.

extendedVocab.nuance: 초승달 is the thin crescent moon seen just after the new moon — a pure-Korean compound from 초승 (the very start of the lunar month) + 달 (moon). It is the direct opposite of 보름달 (full moon). Be careful with two relatives: 그믐달 is also a crescent but the waning one seen at the END of the lunar month (just before the new moon), and the shapes face opposite ways; 반달 is the half moon, a separate phase in between. Using 크다/작다 for its shape. A crescent's defining trait is thinness — describe it with 가늘다 (가는 초승달), not size words.

extendedVocab.explanation: "starlight" is 별빛 (byeolbit). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 별빛이 반짝이다 ("the starlight twinkles"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 반짝이다 is the signature twinkle verb
쏟아지다 paints a sky overflowing with stars
아래 = beneath; a set romantic/poetic phrase
물들다 = to be steeped/dyed in the light, literary

examples.en: Starlight twinkles in the night sky.
examples.note: 별빛 + 반짝이다 is the core, must-know pairing for twinkling light.

examples.en: Out in the countryside, starlight pours down.
examples.note: 쏟아지다 conveys a dazzling, dense field of stars — far from city lights.

examples.en: We talked under the starlight.
examples.note: 별빛 아래(서) is a fixed atmospheric phrase for a romantic night scene.

extendedVocab.nuance: 별빛 is starlight — a transparent compound of 별 (star) + 빛 (light), where the ㅅ is a 사이시옷 inserted between the two nouns (so it is written 별빛, pronounced [별삗]). Distinguish it cleanly from its sibling 달빛 (moonlight) and from plain 별 (the star itself): 별 is the body you point at, 별빛 is the light it casts. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb 오다: light does not 'come' in Korean, so 별빛이 와요 ✗; light 반짝여요/비쳐요/쏟아져요. A second pitfall is using 별빛 when you simply mean stars — 'I saw the stars' is 별을 봤어요 (별), not 별빛을 봤어요; you watch 별, you bask in 별빛.

extendedVocab.explanation: 달빛 (dalbit) = "moonlight". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 달빛이 비치다 ("moonlight shines (onto something)") shows how it actually behaves. usagePhrases.note: 비치다 = to shine/be reflected onto a surface

usagePhrases.en: the moonlight is soft and mellow
usagePhrases.note: 은은하다 is the trademark adjective for gentle moonlight
환하다 (brightly lit) for a bright moonlit night
set phrase for a calm, romantic night

examples.en: The moonlight is bright tonight.
examples.note: 환하다 fits a clear, well-lit moonlit night; 달빛 + 환하다.

examples.en: Moonlight shines in through the window.
examples.note: 비치다 needs a surface/opening the light falls on — here 창문으로(through the window).

examples.en: The moonlight shines softly and mellow.
examples.note: 은은하다, the signature 'soft glow' word, distinguishes gentle moonlight from harsh light.

extendedVocab.nuance: 달빛 is moonlight — a compound of 달 (moon) + 빛 (light) with the same 사이시옷 as 별빛 (written 달빛, pronounced [달삗]). Contrast it with 별빛 (starlight) and with bare 달 (the moon disk you point at): you gaze at 달 but you are bathed in 달빛. The defining adjective is 은은하다 (soft, mellow, understated) — moonlight is gentle, so Koreans rarely call it 강하다 (strong); it is 은은하다 or 환하다. The natural verb is 비치다 (to shine onto / be cast on a surface), which is why 창문으로 달빛이 비치다 (moonlight shines through the window) is so common — 비치다 implies the light lands somewhere. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 함박눈 means "large snowflakes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 함박눈 (hambangnun) means "large snowflakes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 함박눈이 내리다 ("big snowflakes fall"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 함박눈 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 내리다, the formal precipitation verb

usagePhrases.en: snow comes down in big thick flakes
usagePhrases.note: 펑펑 is the set adverb for heavy fluffy snow
쏟아지다 for a sudden, abundant snowfall
소복이 쌓이다 = accumulate in a soft mound

examples.en: Big snowflakes are falling outside.
examples.note: 함박눈 + 오다, exactly parallel to 비가 와요/눈이 와요.

examples.en: Big fluffy snowflakes are coming down thickly.
examples.note: 펑펑 내리다 is the near-fixed phrase for heavy, fat-flake snow.

examples.en: Overnight, big snowflakes piled up in a soft mound.
examples.note: 소복이 쌓이다 describes the gentle, deep accumulation 함박눈 is loved for.

extendedVocab.nuance: 함박눈 is big, fluffy snowflakes that fall thick and slow — the picturesque snow Koreans adore. Its key contrast is 싸락눈 (or 싸라기눈), the fine dry snow pellets that fall in very cold, hard weather: 함박눈 = large soft flakes (often near 0°C, sticks and piles up beautifully); 싸락눈 = tiny gritty grains (bitter cold, doesn't stick well). Also distinguish 진눈깨비 (sleet — wet, slushy rain mixed with snow, which Koreans dislike). The name comes from 함박 (a big wooden bowl / the large 함박꽃 peony blossom), so 함박눈 literally evokes 'bowl-big / peony-big snow' — the same 함박 in 함박웃음 (a big beaming smile). It takes the snow verbs 오다 (casual) and 내리다 (standard), and its trademark adverb is 펑펑 (펑펑 내리다 = pouring down in fat flakes). English-speaker pitfalls: using the wind verb 불다 (함박눈이 불어요 ✗ → 와요/내려요 ✓), and treating 함박 as if it described size with 큰 (don't say 큰 눈; the single word 함박눈 already means 'big-flake snow').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 먹구름 means "dark rain cloud" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "dark rain cloud" is 먹구름 (meokgureum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 먹구름이 끼다 ("dark clouds gather/set in"). Watch the particle attached to 먹구름 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 끼다 is the dedicated verb for clouds/fog covering the sky
몰려오다 = surge in as a mass, for an approaching storm
짙다 (dense, deep-colored) for heavy cloud cover
드리우다 = to hang/cast over, also metaphorical for gloom

examples.en: Dark clouds gathered in the sky.
examples.note: 먹구름 + 끼다 is the core pairing; 꼈어요 is the past of 끼다.

examples.ko: 먹구름이 몰려와서 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: meokgureumi mollyeowaseo got biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: Dark clouds rolled in, so it looks like rain soon.
examples.note: 몰려오다 shows the clouds advancing as a front; -ㄹ 것 같다 makes a guess.

examples.en: Dark clouds loomed over the company's future.
examples.note: Metaphorical use: 먹구름이 드리우다 = trouble/gloom looms — a flavor English shares.

extendedVocab.nuance: 먹구름 is a dark, gray-black rain cloud — a pure-Korean compound of 먹 (ink, the black inkstick used in calligraphy) + 구름 (cloud), so literally 'ink cloud.' Contrast it with plain 구름 (any cloud, neutral) and with 뭉게구름 (big white fluffy cumulus, a fair-weather cloud): 먹구름 specifically signals rain or a storm is coming, while 뭉게구름 signals a nice day. The defining verb is 끼다 — the special verb for clouds, fog, or haze settling over the sky (구름이 끼다, 안개가 끼다), so the sky 'wears' clouds rather than having them 'come.' It also takes 몰려오다 (roll in) and 드리우다 (loom), and 먹구름 is freely metaphorical for impending bad news (앞날에 먹구름이 끼다). The main English-speaker pitfall is 먹구름이 와요 (by analogy with 비가 와요 'rain comes') — clouds don't 'come,' they gather: 먹구름이 껴요 ✓. Don't strip it to plain 구름 when you mean ominous clouds; the darkness and warning are in the 먹.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 온도 means "temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 온도 (ondo) = "temperature". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 온도가 높다 / 낮다 ("the temperature is high / low") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 온도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 높다·낮다, never 크다·작다, for temperature
올라가다·내려가다 for the reading moving
재다 = to measure (with a thermometer)
맞추다 for setting an AC, oven, or bath to a target

examples.en: The room temperature is just right.
examples.note: 딱 좋다 (just right) is the everyday comfort phrase; 온도 covers a room.

examples.en: I set the AC to 26 degrees.
examples.note: 온도를 맞추다 = set a device's temperature — a very common daily action.

examples.en: I took the patient's temperature.
examples.note: 온도를 재다 (measure temperature); for body temp 체온 is even more precise.

extendedVocab.nuance: 온도(溫度) is Sino-Korean — 溫 'warm' + 度 'degree' — the general word for temperature of air, water, a room, an oven, anything you can read on a thermometer. Its near-synonyms are narrower: 기온(氣溫, 'air-temperature') is specifically the outdoor air temperature in a weather report, and 체온(體溫, 'body-temperature') is body heat. The dividing line: use 온도 broadly (방 온도, 물 온도), but switch to 기온 for the weather forecast (오늘 기온이 영하예요) and 체온 for a fever (체온이 38도예요). Because it is measured in degrees on a scale, the correct adjectives are 높다/낮다 (high/low), and it moves with 올라가다/내려가다. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is 온도가 커요/작아요 — English says 'high/low temperature,' and Korean agrees: it must be 온도가 높아요/낮아요, never 크다/작다. A second is using 온도 for the outdoor weather when 기온 is what newscasters say.

Confusing 온도 with 체온. Your body temperature / fever is 체온 (체온을 재다); 온도 alone usually means the temperature of a room, water, or the air around you.

The dividing line: use 온도 broadly (방 온도, 물 온도), but switch to 기온 for the weather forecast (오늘 기온이 영하예요) and 체온 for a fever (체온이 38도예요).
온도(溫度) is Sino-Korean — 溫 'warm' + 度 'degree'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 영하 means "below zero" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 영하 (yeongha) means "below zero". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영하 5도 ("minus five degrees"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영하 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 영하 comes BEFORE the number
떨어지다 (plunge) is more vivid than 내려가다 for crossing zero
영하 + -의 + noun to modify
-권 (zone/range) for 'down in the minuses'

examples.en: This morning it's minus five degrees.
examples.note: Word order to memorize: 영하 + number + 도. Never 5도 영하.

examples.en: The temperature dropped below zero.
examples.note: 영하로 떨어지다 = the reading plunges past zero; 로 marks the endpoint.

examples.en: Subzero cold is coming tomorrow.
examples.note: 영하권 (the subzero zone) is how forecasters frame a cold snap.

extendedVocab.nuance: 영하(零下) is Sino-Korean — 零 'zero' + 下 'below' — meaning below 0°C. Its exact opposite is 영상(零上, 'above zero'), used for plus temperatures (영상 3도 = +3°C). The crucial structural fact, opposite to English, is word order: the marker comes BEFORE the number, so 'minus five degrees' is 영하 5도 (literally 'below-zero five degrees'), never 5도 영하. English speakers also say 'negative five' / 'minus five,' but Korean does not use 마이너스 in weather speech — it is always 영하. 영하 most often appears in winter forecasts and pairs with 떨어지다 (plunge below) and 내려가다 (drop), plus the handy forecaster word 영하권 (the subzero range). The pitfalls: (1) putting the number first (5도 영하 ✗); (2) confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero) — they look and sound similar but are opposites; (3) saying 마이너스 5도 in everyday weather talk, which sounds like a math/English calque rather than natural 영하 5도.

Putting the number before 영하, e.g. 5도 영하. Korean states the zone first: 영하 5도 (below-zero, five degrees).
Confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero). 하=below, 상=above. They are direct opposites, easy to mix up by sound.
Saying 마이너스 5도 for the weather. That's an English-style calque; natural Korean weather speech is 영하 5도.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가뭄 means "drought" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "drought" is 가뭄 (gamum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 가뭄이 들다 ("a drought sets in"). Watch the particle attached to 가뭄 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 들다, the set verb (as for sickness/famine 'setting in')
심하다 for severity/intensity
계속되다 for a prolonged dry spell
풀리다 = to be relieved/loosened, when rain finally comes

examples.en: The drought is severe this year.
examples.note: 가뭄 + 심하다, the everyday way to say a bad drought.

examples.en: A drought set in because it didn't rain.
examples.note: 가뭄이 들다 (a drought sets in) — note 들다, not 오다; -어서 gives the cause.

examples.en: A welcome rain fell and the drought broke.
examples.note: 가뭄이 풀리다 = the drought lifts; 단비(welcome rain) is its natural rescuer.

extendedVocab.nuance: 가뭄 is a drought — a pure-Korean noun for a long stretch with little or no rain. It is the direct opposite of 장마 (the summer monsoon rainy season), and learners often pair the two. The defining verb is 들다, which here means 'to set in / take hold' — the same 들다 used when an illness or a famine grips (병이 들다, 흉년이 들다) — so 가뭄이 들다 frames the drought as something that settles over the land, not something that 'arrives.' It is described with 심하다 (severe) and 계속되다 (continues), and lifts with 풀리다 (가뭄이 풀리다 = the drought breaks), often thanks to 단비 (a welcome, much-needed rain). The English-speaker pitfall is 가뭄이 와요 (by analogy with 'a drought comes' / 비가 와요) — a drought doesn't 'come,' it 들어요. Also keep 가뭄 (no rain, dryness) distinct from 장마 (too much rain): they are opposite weather problems, and mixing the verbs (가뭄이 오다 / 장마가 들다) sounds wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가뭄이 와요. A drought sets in, it doesn't come: 가뭄이 들어요 (verb 들다). Compare 비가 와요, but weather conditions like drought take 들다.
Confusing 가뭄 (drought, too little rain) with 장마 (the monsoon rainy season, too much rain). They are opposite situations.
Using the wrong verb when the rain finally comes. The drought 'breaks' is 가뭄이 풀리다 (loosen/relieve), not 가뭄이 끝나 오다 or similar.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 직업 means "job; occupation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 직업 (jigeop) = "job; occupation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 직업이 뭐예요? ("What's your job?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 직업, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The standard polite way to ask someone's occupation; note the particle is 이, not 가.
바꾸다 = swap one thing for another; use it for switching careers, not just today's task.
전문 (專門, specialty) marks a skilled profession like doctor or lawyer.
없다, not 안 있다; this is the natural way to say 'unemployed' softly.

examples.en: What is your job?
examples.note: The go-to first-meeting question; the verb is hidden inside 뭐예요.

examples.en: My job is a nurse.
examples.note: Topic 직업은 + the profession + 예요; you name the job, you don't 'do' it.

examples.en: I want to have a good occupation.
examples.note: 갖다(가지다) 'to hold/have' pairs with 직업 when talking about aspirations.

extendedVocab.nuance: 직업 (職業, 'duty-work') is the abstract category of one's profession or line of work — the answer to 'what do you do for a living,' not the daily grind itself. The dividing line you must feel: 직업 is the occupation as an identity (간호사, 교사), 직장 is the specific company you belong to, and 일/업무 is the actual work you perform. So 직업이 뭐예요? asks WHAT you are, while 무슨 일 해요? asks more casually what work you do day to day. Register is neutral-to-formal, perfect for a first meeting; among close friends 무슨 일 해? feels warmer. The classic English-speaker trap is 직업을 해요 to mean 'I work' — Korean never 'does' an occupation; you simply state it with 이에요/예요 (선생님이에요), and the particle after 직업 is 이 (직업이), since the word ends in a consonant.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 직업을 해요 for 'I work' — you cannot 'do' an occupation in Korean. Name the job instead: 저는 요리사예요 (I'm a cook).
Confusing 직업 (the profession/identity) with 직장 (the workplace/company). '회사가 멀어요' uses 직장, but '의사예요' is your 직업.
Using 가 after 직업 (직업가) — because 직업 ends in a consonant, the subject particle is 이: 직업이 뭐예요?

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 직원 means "employee; staff member" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 직원 (jigwon) means "employee; staff member". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회사 직원 ("a company employee"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 직원 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 sits in front as a noun modifier; no particle needed between them.
한테 marks the human recipient of the question; 에게 is its formal twin.
Place + 직원 names the staff of a specific business.
뽑다 literally 'to pull/pick out' is the everyday verb for hiring.

examples.en: I am a bank employee.
examples.note: Workplace + 직원 + 이에요 states your role simply.

examples.en: Please ask a staff member.
examples.note: You hear this constantly in shops; 한테 + 물어보다 = ask (a person).

examples.en: The staff at this shop are kind.
examples.note: 직원이 + adjective; Korean keeps it singular even for 'the staff' collectively.

extendedVocab.nuance: 직원 (職員, 'duty-personnel') is the plain, everyday word for anyone who works at a company, shop, bank, or office — the person on the other side of the counter helping you. The synonym contrast to nail: 직원 is generic 'staff' regardless of rank, while 사원 (社員) specifically names the entry-level rung on the corporate ladder, and 종업원 sounds older/more clerical (waitstaff, hired help). In daily life 직원 is overwhelmingly the natural choice — 직원한테 물어보세요 (ask a staff member) is a sentence you'll use weekly. Register is neutral and safe for everyone. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't call the customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the one who WORKS there, not the visitor (that's 손님); second, English says 'I asked the staff' with no particle, but Korean must mark the person with 한테/에게: 직원에게 물어봤어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the worker; the customer is a 손님. Mixing these reverses who serves whom.
Dropping the particle: 직원 물어봤어요 is wrong. You must mark the person you asked with 한테/에게 → 직원한테 물어봤어요.
Assuming 직원 means a high-ranked person. It's rank-neutral; the boss is 사장 or 상사, not just 직원.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 직장 means "workplace; one's job" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "workplace; one's job" is 직장 (jikjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 직장에 다니다 ("to be employed; to go to work regularly"). Watch the particle attached to 직장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be employed; to go to work regularly
usagePhrases.note: 다니다 'attend regularly' is the set verb; this whole phrase means 'have a job.'
직장 + 동료 (同僚, fellow worker) — your colleague at the same company.

usagePhrases.en: to look for / find a job
usagePhrases.note: 구하다 'to seek/obtain' is the natural verb for job-hunting.

usagePhrases.en: work life; life as an employee
usagePhrases.note: 생활 (生活, daily life) added to mean the whole experience of being employed.

examples.en: I have a job (I go to work).
examples.note: 직장에 다니다 = be employed; the 에 marks the place you regularly attend.

examples.en: My workplace is far from home.
examples.note: 직장이 + 멀다; here 직장 means the physical workplace.

examples.en: I'm looking for a new job.
examples.note: 새 (new) directly modifies 직장; 구하다 = seek/find.

extendedVocab.nuance: 직장 (職場, 'duty-place') literally means the 'place of one's work' and covers both the physical workplace and the broader fact of being employed. The crucial contrast: 직업 is your profession/identity (what you are — a teacher), while 직장 is the specific organization you belong to (where you work — Samsung). So 직장에 다니다, literally 'attend a workplace,' is THE idiomatic way to say 'I have a job,' built with 다니다 (to go regularly), the same verb used for 학교에 다니다 (attend school). A salaried worker is a 직장인. Register is neutral and extremely common. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb: don't say 직장에 가다 to mean 'I'm employed' — 가다 only describes today's single trip to the office, whereas 다니다 captures the ongoing state of holding a job. Also resist the literal 'I have a job' = 직장을 가지다; Koreans say 직장에 다녀요 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 직장에 가다 to mean 'I have a job.' 가다 = today's trip; the state of being employed is 직장에 다니다.
Swapping 직장 (where you work) and 직업 (what you do). '의사예요' is 직업; '병원에 다녀요' is 직장.
Saying 직장을 가지다 ('have a workplace') by translating English literally. Natural Korean is 직장에 다녀요.
