extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사원 means "staff member; rank-and-file employee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사원 (sawon) = "staff member; rank-and-file employee". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 신입 사원 ("a new employee; new hire") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 신입 (新入, newly entered) + 사원 — the fresh recruit, hired every spring.

usagePhrases.en: to join as an entry-level employee
usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the rank you enter AT; 입사하다 = enter a company.
정규 (正規, regular) contrasts with 계약직 (contract worker).
평 (平, plain/flat) stresses 'just a regular worker,' no title.

examples.en: I am a new employee.
examples.note: 신입 사원 is a fixed compound; + 이에요 states your level.

examples.en: I joined as an entry-level employee.
examples.note: 으로 marks the entering rank; 입사하다 = enter the company, past 입사했어요.

examples.en: Before being promoted to 대리, I was a 사원.
examples.note: Shows the rank ladder: 사원 → 대리; 이었어요 = was.

extendedVocab.nuance: 사원 (社員, 'company-member') is specifically the BOTTOM formal rung on the Korean corporate title ladder — the rank a fresh hire holds before climbing to 대리 → 과장 → 차장 → 부장. The contrast you must internalize: 직원 is the generic, everyday word for 'staff' at any rank, whereas 사원 is a precise rank-title used mostly in HR and on org charts. So every 사원 is a 직원, but a 부장 (department head) is a 직원 and NOT a 사원. You'll hear 신입 사원 (new recruit) everywhere during 공채 (open hiring season). Register is formal/official. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 사원 just because you mean 'an employee' in casual conversation — say 직원. And note the particle 으로 in 사원으로 입사하다 marks the rank you enter as, an 'as/in the capacity of' meaning English drops entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사원 for any worker in casual speech. For generic 'staff' say 직원; 사원 is the specific entry rank.
Thinking a manager (부장/과장) is a 사원. Those are higher ranks; 사원 is the lowest rung only.
Saying 사원에 입사하다. The rank you enter AS takes 으로: 사원으로 입사했어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 업무 means "work; task; duties" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 업무 (eommu) means "work; task; duties". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 업무를 보다 ("to attend to / handle one's work"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 업무 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to attend to / handle one's work
usagePhrases.note: 보다 'to see/handle' is the set verb for processing duties, esp. office/admin work.
업무 + 시간; the time block during which work or service is done.
많다 describes the volume of duties; 바쁘다 describes you being busy.

usagePhrases.en: to take charge of a task
usagePhrases.note: 맡다 'to be entrusted with' = be assigned a duty or responsibility.

examples.en: I have a lot of work today.
examples.note: 업무가 + 많다; describes the amount of work, not your feelings.

examples.en: Working hours are from 9 to 6.
examples.note: 업무 시간 + 부터...까지 frames the start and end of the workday.

examples.en: I've been assigned a new task.
examples.note: 맡다 + 게 되다 = ended up being entrusted with; sounds natural for new duties.

extendedVocab.nuance: 업무 (業務, 'occupation-affairs') is the formal word for the specific duties, tasks, and functions tied to a job — the work content itself, especially in office and administrative settings. The synonym contrast to feel: 일 is the broad, native, casual word for 'work/thing/matter' you'd use with friends (일이 많아 = so much to do), while 업무 is its Sino-Korean, businesslike counterpart used in emails, reports, and with superiors (업무 협조 부탁드립니다). They overlap, but 업무 carries an official, structured tone; you would not say 업무 for chores at home. The fixed verb 업무를 보다 ('handle work') mirrors 일을 보다 and 볼일을 보다 (run an errand). extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 회의실 means "meeting room; conference room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "meeting room; conference room" is 회의실 (hoeuisil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 회의실에서 ("in the meeting room"). Watch the particle attached to 회의실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the LOCATION where an action takes place (a meeting happens there).
예약하다 (豫約, reserve in advance) — the verb for booking rooms, tables, tickets.
비다 'be empty' + 어 있다 (resultant state) = currently available.
대 (大, big) prefixed; contrast 소회의실 (小, small room).

examples.en: There is a meeting in the meeting room.
examples.note: 회의실에서 + 있다; the meeting (회의) happens IN the room (회의실).

examples.en: I booked the meeting room.
examples.note: 회의실을 + 예약하다, past 예약했어요; 을 marks the room as the object reserved.

examples.en: Is the meeting room free right now?
examples.note: 비어 있다 = is (currently) empty/available — a natural way to check.

extendedVocab.nuance: 회의실 (會議室, 'meeting-room') is built transparently from 회의 (a meeting) + 실 (room) — and that 실 is a powerful building block: once you know it, you recognize 사무실 (office), 화장실 (restroom), 교실 (classroom), and 연구실 (lab/study). The key contrast learners blur is 회의 vs 회의실: 회의 is the EVENT (the meeting), 회의실 is the PLACE (the room) — 회의실에서 회의를 해요 means 'we hold a meeting in the meeting room,' two different words. A near-synonym is 미팅룸 (a borrowed English term used in some modern offices), but 회의실 is the standard, safe word. Register is neutral/workplace. The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the particle: an action OCCURS at 회의실에서 (dynamic location), not 회의실에 (static existence/destination). 회의실에 있어요 = 'it is IN the meeting room'; 회의실에서 일해요 = 'I work IN the meeting room.' Choosing 에 vs 에서 wrong is the classic beginner slip.

Confusing 회의 (the meeting event) with 회의실 (the meeting room). You attend a 회의 that takes place in a 회의실.
Using 에 for an action: 회의실에 회의해요 is wrong. Actions happen at 회의실에서; 에 is only for existence/destination.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상사 means "boss; one's superior" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 상사 (sangsa) = "boss; one's superior". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 직장 상사 ("a workplace superior") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 직장 (workplace) + 상사; specifies a boss in the work context.
보고하다 (報告, report) + 한테 marking the person you report TO.
직속 (直屬, directly attached) = the boss right above you in the chain.
지시 (指示, directive); 의 links the superior to their command.

examples.en: My boss is really kind.
examples.note: 상사는 + adjective; used when TALKING ABOUT the boss, not addressing them.

examples.en: I have to report to my boss first.
examples.note: 상사한테 + 보고하다; 한테 = to (a person); 야 하다 = have to.

examples.en: A new boss has arrived.
examples.note: Honorific 오시다→오셨어요 shows respect for the superior's action.

extendedVocab.nuance: 상사 (上司, 'upper-office/superior') is the general, descriptive term for anyone who outranks you at work, whatever their specific title. The vital register caution: 상사 is a word you use ABOUT your boss when describing them to others (우리 상사는…), almost never TO their face — addressing them directly, you must use their title + 님: 부장님, 팀장님, 과장님. Calling someone '상사님' to their face sounds odd, like addressing a teacher as 'Superior.' The opposite pole is 부하 ((部下), a subordinate), and a near-synonym 윗사람 ('person above') is softer/more general and can extend beyond work to any senior. Contrast also with 선배, who joined before you but isn't necessarily your boss. The English-speaker pitfall: English freely says 'my boss' and even addresses them by first name, but Korean hierarchy forbids both — you neither say 상사님 nor use their bare name; you use title + 님. Also mark the person you report to with 한테/에게, not just a bare noun.

Addressing your boss as '상사님' to their face. Use their title + 님 instead: 부장님, 팀장님. 상사 is for describing them to others.
Calling your boss by their first name like in English. Korean requires title + 님; using the bare name is rude across rank.
Confusing 상사 (a superior person) with 회사 (the company). They sound similar but mean boss vs. corporation.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 선배 means "senior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 선배 (seonbae) means "senior (colleague or schoolmate)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회사 선배 ("a senior at work"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 선배 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 (company) + 선배 — someone who joined before you, not necessarily your boss.
Add 님 to address a 선배 respectfully to their face.
한테 marks the source you learn FROM; 배우다 = learn.
대학 (university) + 선배 — an older schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: A senior at work helped me a lot.
examples.note: 선배가 + 도와주다 (help, with benefit); past 도와줬어요.

examples.en: Senior, please show me this.
examples.note: Direct address 선배님 + 알려 주세요 (kindly tell/show me).

examples.en: I really respect that senior.
examples.note: 선배를 + 존경하다 (respect); 를 marks the object of respect.

extendedVocab.nuance: 선배 (先輩, 'earlier-generation/fellow') means someone senior to you who entered the same school, university, company, or field BEFORE you — a relationship that structures enormous amounts of Korean social life. The sharp contrast: a 선배 is defined by entering EARLIER, while a 상사 is defined by RANK — your 선배 may or may not be your boss, and your boss may not be your 선배 if they transferred in. Also distinguish 선배 from 어른 (an elder/adult by age generally). Unlike 상사, you CAN and do address a 선배 directly, adding 님 for politeness: 선배님. A 선배 traditionally looks after their 후배 (junior), often picking up the meal tab. Register: warm but respectful, deeply tied to hierarchy. The English-speaker pitfall: English has no real equivalent and learners default to 'senior' = 'boss' — but 선배 is about timing, not authority; treating every 선배 as a 상사 (or vice versa) misreads the relationship. Mark whom you learn from with 한테/에게.

Equating 선배 with 'boss.' A 선배 joined before you but may hold no authority; a boss with power is a 상사.
Confusing 선배 (joined before you) with 후배 (joined after you). They are mirror opposites — get the direction right.
Dropping 님 when speaking TO a senior. To their face it's 선배님; bare 선배 in direct address can sound too casual.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 후배 means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "junior (colleague or schoolmate)" is 후배 (hubae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 회사 후배 ("a junior at work"). Watch the particle attached to 후배 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 + 후배 — someone who joined the company after you.
가르치다 = teach; seniors often guide their 후배.

usagePhrases.en: to treat a junior (buy for them)
usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the receiver; 사 주다 = buy (for someone's benefit).
대학 + 후배 — a younger schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: I have one junior.
examples.note: 후배가 + 한 명 (one person) + 있다; 명 is the counter for people.

examples.en: I bought my junior a coffee.
examples.note: 후배한테 + 사 주다, past 사 줬어요; the 줬 shows you did it FOR them.

examples.en: That junior is really good at their work.
examples.note: 후배는 + 일을 잘하다 (be good at work).

extendedVocab.nuance: 후배 (後輩, 'later-generation/fellow') is the mirror image of 선배: someone who entered the same school, company, or field AFTER you, regardless of their age in some cases (entry timing usually outweighs age). The contrast to keep straight is purely directional — 선배 = earlier, 후배 = later — and neither word is about workplace RANK (that's 상사 vs 부하). Within Korea's senior-junior culture, the 선배 is expected to look after the 후배: guiding them at work, answering questions, and famously treating them to meals or coffee (후배한테 밥 사 주다). Register: friendly and caring, but still hierarchy-aware. The key English-speaker pitfall is honorifics: you do NOT attach 님 to 후배 — 님 elevates seniors, so '후배님' is unnatural; you address a junior by name or with 씨. Many learners over-apply 님 to everyone out of caution, which actually misfires here. Also, don't assume a 후배 is younger or lower-ranked — they're simply LATER to the group.

Mixing up 후배 (joined after you) and 선배 (joined before you). They are exact opposites — direction matters.
Assuming 후배 means 'younger.' It marks LATER entry to the group, not necessarily a younger age.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 출장 means "business trip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 출장 (chuljang) = "business trip". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 출장을 가다 ("to go on a business trip") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 출장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to go on a business trip
usagePhrases.note: 가다 is the set verb; you GO on a 출장, you don't 'do' one.
중 (中, in the middle of) + 이다 = currently on the trip.
해외 (海外, overseas) + 출장 — a trip abroad for work.

usagePhrases.en: to return from a business trip
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks the place you come back FROM; 돌아오다 = come back.

examples.en: I'm going to Busan on a business trip tomorrow.
examples.note: Place + 으로 (toward) + 출장을 가다; 으로 marks the direction.

examples.en: The manager is away on business now.
examples.note: 출장 중 + honorific 이세요 to respect the superior.

examples.en: This business trip has a tight schedule.
examples.note: 일정 (schedule) + 빡빡하다 (tight/packed) — a real coworker's complaint.

extendedVocab.nuance: 출장 (出張, 'go-out-stretch/dispatch') means being sent away from your usual workplace to do work elsewhere — typically a trip to another city or country, often with an overnight stay. The synonym contrast that matters: 출장 is travel FOR WORK, sharply distinct from 여행 (a leisure trip) — never call a vacation a 출장. Within work travel, contrast 출장 (a farther/longer dispatch, often overnight) with 외근 (外勤, off-site work done and returned within the same day, like visiting a client across town). The set verb is 가다 (출장을 가다, go on a trip) and the status phrase is 출장 중이에요 (away on business). Register: standard workplace vocabulary. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — learners say 출장을 하다 ('do a business trip') by analogy with English 'take/do,' but Korean uses 가다 (go); and direction takes 으로 (부산으로 출장 가요), not just 에. Also don't confuse the noun-internal 장 here (dispatch) with the 장 in 직장/공장 (place).

Saying 출장을 하다. The natural verb is 가다: 출장을 가다 (go on a business trip).
Confusing 출장 (work travel) with 여행 (leisure travel). A vacation is never a 출장.
Marking the destination with 에: 부산에 출장 가요 is awkward. Use 으로 for direction → 부산으로 출장 가요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 면접 means "job interview" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 면접 (myeonjeop) means "job interview". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 면접을 보다 ("to have a job interview"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 면접 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 'to see' is the FIXED verb here, exactly like 시험을 보다 (take an exam).
합격하다 (合格, pass) + 에 marking the interview you pass; opposite is 떨어지다 (fail).
면접 + 준비 (準備, preparation) — getting ready for the interview.
1차 (1次, first round); Korean hiring often has 1차, 2차 면접 stages.

examples.en: I have a job interview tomorrow.
examples.note: 면접을 보다 → present 봐요; literally 'see an interview' = have one.

examples.en: I prepared hard for the interview.
examples.note: 면접 준비 + 하다, past 했어요; 열심히 = diligently.

examples.en: I'm so happy I passed the interview.
examples.note: 면접에 합격하다 + ~아서 (reason) + 기쁘다 (glad).

extendedVocab.nuance: 면접 (面接, 'face-contact/meet') literally means meeting face-to-face, and refers to the job interview where you sit before evaluators. The most important thing to lock in is the FIXED verb: 면접을 보다, literally 'to see an interview,' which uses the same 보다 as 시험을 보다 (take a test) — Korean treats undergoing an evaluation as 'seeing' it. The synonym contrast: 면접 is the oral, face-to-face interview, while 시험 (試驗) is a written test/exam, and 면담 (面談) is a softer counseling-style talk (e.g., with a professor), not a hiring screen. After a 면접 you hope to 합격하다 (pass) rather than 떨어지다 (fall/fail) or 불합격하다. Register: neutral, used in any job-search context. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 면접을 하다 sounds off from the candidate's side — you 면접을 보다 (take it); the company that conducts it may 면접을 진행하다. Also note you pass 면접에 (with 에), patterning like 시험에 합격하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 면접을 하다 as the candidate. The fixed verb is 면접을 보다 (just like 시험을 보다).
Confusing 면접 (oral, face-to-face interview) with 시험 (a written exam). Different formats, different prep.
Using 를 with 합격: 면접을 합격하다 is wrong. You pass INTO it with 에 → 면접에 합격하다.

The pitfall is reaching for 하다: 면접을 하다 sounds off from the candidate's side — you 면접을 보다 (take it); the company that conducts it may 면접을 진행하다. Also note you pass 면접에 (with 에), patterning like 시험에 합격하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이력서 means "resume; CV" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "resume; CV" is 이력서 (iryeokseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이력서를 쓰다 ("to write a resume"). Watch the particle attached to 이력서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

내다 'to put/hand out' = submit; 이력서를 제출하다 is its formal twin.
에 marks WHERE you write; 적다 = jot/note down onto the document.
이력서 + 사진 — the ID-style photo traditionally attached in Korea.

examples.en: I'm writing my resume.
examples.note: 이력서를 + 쓰다 + 고 있다 (ongoing) → 쓰고 있어요.

examples.en: I submitted my resume to the company.
examples.note: 회사에 (to the company) + 이력서를 내다, past 냈어요.

examples.en: I wrote my work experience on the resume in detail.
examples.note: 이력서에 + 경력 (career) + 적다, past 적었어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 연봉 means "annual salary" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 연봉 (yeonbong) = "annual salary". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연봉이 높다 ("to have a high (annual) salary") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연봉, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 높다 'be high' is the adjective for salary level — NOT 비싸다 (expensive).
올리다 'to raise' (transitive); the intransitive 'salary rises' is 연봉이 오르다.
협상 (協商, negotiation) — the talk where you settle your yearly pay.

usagePhrases.en: How much is the annual salary?
usagePhrases.note: 얼마 asks the amount; a direct (somewhat blunt) money question.

examples.en: This company's salary is high.
examples.note: 연봉이 + 높다; salary takes 높다/낮다 (high/low), not 비싸다.

examples.en: My salary went up a little this year.
examples.note: 연봉이 + 오르다 (rise, intransitive), past 올랐어요.

examples.en: I negotiated my salary when I joined.
examples.note: 입사할 때 (when joining) + 연봉 협상을 하다, past 했어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 연봉 (年俸, 'year-stipend') is your pay expressed as a YEARLY total — and crucially, this is the default unit Koreans use to discuss and compare pay (연봉 3천 = 30 million won a year), unlike the English habit of quoting an hourly or monthly figure. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 승진 means "promotion (at work)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 승진 (seungjin) means "promotion (at work)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 승진을 하다 ("to get a promotion"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 승진 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 turns the noun into the event; or just 승진하다 as one verb.

usagePhrases.en: to be promoted to department head
usagePhrases.note: Rank + 으로 (to/as) + 승진하다 marks the rank you rise TO.
빠르다 'be fast' describes the pace of climbing the ladder.
축하하다 (祝賀, congratulate); a set phrase when a coworker moves up.

examples.en: I got promoted this time.
examples.note: 승진을 하다, past 했어요; 이번에 = this time/round.

examples.en: I was promoted to section chief.
examples.note: Rank 과장 + 으로 + 승진하다, past 승진했어요.

examples.en: Congratulations on your promotion!
examples.note: Fixed congratulation; just 승진 + 축하해요, no particle needed.

extendedVocab.nuance: 승진 (昇進, 'rise-advance') means moving UP to a higher rank or title at work — climbing the corporate ladder from 사원 to 대리 to 과장 and beyond. The contrasts to keep distinct: 승진 is rising in RANK within a workplace, different from 합격 (passing an exam or interview to get IN), from 취직/취업 (landing a job in the first place), and from 이직 (changing to a different company). The verb is 승진하다, and to name the rank you rose to, use rank + 으로: 부장으로 승진했어요 (promoted to department head), where 으로 carries an 'into/as' meaning. When a colleague is promoted, the ready-made phrase is 승진 축하해요. Register: neutral, congratulatory. The English-speaker pitfall: English says 'I GOT a promotion,' tempting learners into 승진을 받다 ('receive a promotion') — but Korean treats it as something you DO/achieve: 승진을 하다 or simply 승진하다, not 받다. Also don't mark the new rank with 에 (부장에 승진 is wrong); the directional 으로 is required.

Saying 승진을 받다 ('receive a promotion') from English 'got a promotion.' Korean uses 승진을 하다 / 승진하다.
Confusing 승진 (rising in rank) with 합격 (passing an exam/interview) or 취직 (getting hired). Different stages entirely.
Marking the new rank with 에: 부장에 승진했어요 is wrong. Use 으로 → 부장으로 승진했어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 나 means "I; me (casual)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "I; me (casual)" is 나 (na). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 나 ("I / me (casual)"). Watch the particle attached to 나 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Plain first-person pronoun used down or sideways: to close friends, younger people, or family. Never up to elders.
나 + 가 fuses to 내가, never '나가.' This shape change is irregular and must be memorized.
나 + 는 marks the topic ('as for me'); shortened to 난 in fast speech and texting.
나 + 도 ('also'); the everyday way to say 'me too' among friends, e.g. 나도 갈래.

examples.en: I'm hungry.
examples.note: Pure 반말: bare 나 with no particle, the most casual register among close friends.

examples.en: Can you give this to me?
examples.note: 나 here is the recipient ('to me'); the bare pronoun stands in for 나한테 in relaxed speech.

examples.en: I'll get everything ready.
examples.note: Real-situation promise: 나 must become 내 before 가, giving the subject 내가.

extendedVocab.nuance: 나 is the plain, intimate word for 'I/me' — the counterpart of the humble 저. Choosing between them is not about meaning but about RELATIONSHIP and DIRECTION: 나 points downward or sideways (to friends, juniors, family), while 저 lowers you toward someone you respect; saying 나 to a boss or stranger sounds blunt or rude. 나 carries a warm, unguarded feel, so it dominates 반말 and shows up constantly in 나도 (me too), 나는 (as for me), 내 거 (mine). The classic English-speaker pitfall is the subject form: English keeps 'I' fixed, but Korean fuses 나 + 가 into 내가 — '나가' actually reads as the verb 'go out,' so it is not just wrong but confusing. Also resist supplying a pronoun for every English 'I'; Koreans drop it whenever context is clear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '나가' for 'I (subject)' — that string means 'go out'; the fused subject form is 내가.
Using 나 with a boss, teacher, or stranger; it sounds rude there, so switch to the humble 저.
Forcing 나 into every sentence to match English 'I' — Korean omits the pronoun once it is obvious who is speaking.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 너 means "you (casual)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 너 (neo) = "you (casual)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 너 ("you (casual)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 너, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Plain second-person pronoun, safe only with close friends and people clearly younger than you.
너 + 가 becomes written 네가, but almost everyone says 니가 out loud to avoid clashing with 내가.
너 + 는 ('as for you'); contracts to 넌 in speech, e.g. 넌 어때?
너 + 도; the casual 'you too,' as in 너도 올래? (Want to come too?).

examples.en: Where are you?
examples.note: Bare 너 in 반말; texting a close friend, no politeness ending at all.

examples.en: Do you like this too?
examples.note: 너 + 도 ('you too') checking a shared taste between friends.

examples.en: You speak first.
examples.note: Real exchange: subject form 네가 (said 니가) telling a friend to go ahead.

extendedVocab.nuance: 너 is the plain 'you,' the partner of 나, and is genuinely usable only downward or among intimates — close friends, a younger sibling, a child. The crucial difference from English is that Korean has no neutral, all-purpose 'you': to elders, strangers, coworkers, or anyone you respect, 너 sounds disrespectful or even hostile, so Koreans switch to the person's name + 씨/님, a role word (선생님, 사장님), or simply drop 'you' entirely. Note the famous subject form: 너 + 가 is written 네가 but pronounced 니가 in real life, because 네가 and 내가 (I) collapse to the same sound otherwise. The big pitfall is mapping English 'you' straight onto 너 — pointing 너 at a waiter or a senior is a real social error; default to a name or title and let context carry the rest.

Aiming 너 at an elder, stranger, or boss — it sounds rude; use their name + 씨/님 or a role title instead.
Writing '너가' for the subject; the standard written form is 네가 (commonly said 니가).
Translating every English 'you' as 너 — in polite Korean the 'you' word is usually omitted or replaced by a name.

extendedVocab.explanation: 저 (jeo) means "I; me (humble/polite)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저 ("I / me (humble)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 저 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Humble first-person pronoun; the safe default with elders, strangers, customers, and in formal settings.
저 + 가 fuses to 제가, never '저가.' Use it to volunteer or take responsibility politely.
저 + 는; the standard opener for introducing yourself: 저는 ...이에요/입니다.
humble 'we'; 저희 회사, 저희 집 politely lowers your own group toward the listener.

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: Simple self-introduction; 저 + 는 paired with the polite 요-form.

examples.en: I'll help you.
examples.note: Everyday offer at work: subject 제가 plus the humble 도와드리다 to lift the listener.

examples.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Kim Minsu.
examples.note: Real first meeting in 격식체 (formal -ㅂ니다); 저 is obligatory here.

extendedVocab.nuance: 저 is the humble 'I/me,' the polite counterpart of 나. It does not mean something different from 나 — it encodes DEFERENCE, lowering yourself to raise the listener, so it is the correct choice with elders, strangers, customers, and any formal moment, and it sits naturally with 요-form and -ㅂ니다 speech. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 당신 means "you (distant/formal)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "you (distant/formal)" is 당신 (dangsin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 당신 ("you (formal/distant)"). Watch the particle attached to 당신 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Sino-Korean 當身; a 'high' you that, said to a stranger's face, often reads as cold or confrontational.
당신 + 이 (consonant ending takes 이, not 가); appears in lyrics, vows, and between spouses.
당신 + 은; common in ads and self-help writing that address 'you, the reader.'
당신 + 을; literary and romantic, as in 당신을 사랑해요.

examples.en: I love you.
examples.note: Affectionate spousal use; in songs and marriage 당신 is warm, not cold.

examples.en: You are a precious person.
examples.note: Ad / writing voice addressing an unseen reader as 당신.

examples.en: Who are you to talk to me like that?
examples.note: Real argument: the same 당신 turns sharp and confrontational toward a stranger.

extendedVocab.nuance: 당신 is a formal 'you' from the Sino-Korean 當身 (當 'this/that', 身 'body/self'), and it is one of the most misleading words for learners. Unlike a flat English 'you,' 당신 has split lives: warm and intimate between spouses ('dear/honey'), poetic in lyrics and prayer, and reader-facing in ads or essays — yet aimed at a stranger's face in conversation it sounds cold, distancing, or like the opening of a fight (it is a staple of street arguments). So although dictionaries gloss it as 'you,' it is NOT the everyday polite 'you'; the honest truth is Korean has no neutral spoken 'you' at all. The pitfall is reaching for 당신 to a clerk, a senior, or a new acquaintance the way you'd say 'you' in English — instead use the person's name + 씨/님, a title (선생님, 사장님, 손님), or drop the word entirely. Reserve 당신 for writing, lyrics, or your own spouse.

Writing '당신가' for the subject — 당신 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이: 당신이.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 아버지 means "father" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 아버지 (abeoji) = "father". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아버지 ("father") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아버지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The standard, respectful word for one's father, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 지 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 아버지예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 아버지 + 님; used for another person's father or one's father-in-law.

examples.en: My father is an office worker.

examples.en: I respect my father.
examples.note: 아버지 as object with 를; pairs with the humble self-pronoun 저.

extendedVocab.nuance: 아버지 is the respectful, neutral word for 'father,' used in polite conversation, in writing, and whenever you speak about your dad to others. One step higher is 아버님, reserved for someone else's father or your father-in-law. Because a father is an elder, 아버지 naturally pulls honorific machinery: the subject marker 께서, the dative 께, and -(으)시- verb endings (읽으세요, 주무세요). examples.en: My mother is cooking.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 낮 means "daytime, day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "daytime, day" is 낮 (nat). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 낮 ("daytime"). Watch the particle attached to 낮 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The bright part of the day, the opposite of 밤 (night).
낮 + 에 marks the time-when; pronounced '나제' from the ㅈ liaison.
낮 + 잠 (sleep) = a daytime sleep; pairs with the verb 자다 (낮잠을 자다).
한 ('full/peak') + 낮 = the hottest, brightest middle of the day.

examples.en: It's warm during the day.
examples.note: 낮 + 에 + 는 sets a daytime topic, implying a contrast with night.

examples.en: I take a nap on weekends.
examples.note: Everyday habit: the compound 낮잠 with its set verb 자다.

examples.en: I work in the daytime and study at night.
examples.note: Real routine contrasting 낮 with its antonym 밤 across one sentence.

extendedVocab.nuance: 낮 means the daytime — the bright stretch between morning and evening — and lives as the natural antonym of 밤 (night). It is a pure native Korean noun (not Sino-Korean), and its key feature is pronunciation: the final ㅈ links onto a following vowel, so 낮에 sounds like '나제' and 낮이 like '나지'; before a consonant or pause the ㅈ neutralizes to a 't' sound ('낟'). Its near-synonym 오후 'afternoon' is narrower and Sino-Korean (the clock-time after noon), whereas 낮 is the whole bright span and feels more everyday. The headline English-speaker pitfall is a cluster of look-alikes that differ by one final consonant: 낮 (daytime), 낯 (face, as in 낯설다 'unfamiliar'), and 낫 (a sickle; also 낫다 'to be better / to recover'). They sound nearly identical in isolation, so rely on meaning and the liaison to keep them straight, and pair 낮 with 에 to say 'during the day.'

Forgetting the liaison: 낮에 is pronounced '나제,' not a clipped 'nat-e.'
Treating 낮 and 오후 as identical — 오후 is specifically 'afternoon' (post-noon), while 낮 is the whole bright daytime.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 색깔 means "color" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 색깔 (saekkkal) = "color". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 색깔 ("color") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 색깔, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday standalone word for color; feels fuller and warmer than the bare 색.
무슨 + 색깔 asks which color something is: 무슨 색깔이에요?
색깔 + 이 as subject with an adjective; 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular (예뻐요).
set collocation; 진하다 (deep) vs 연하다 (light) describe color intensity.

examples.en: What color is it?
examples.note: Simplest color question; 색깔 stands alone naturally as the subject.

examples.en: This bag has a pretty color.
examples.note: Double-subject pattern: 가방은 (topic) ... 색깔이 (subject) ... 예뻐요.

examples.en: My favorite color is blue.
examples.note: Real answer: 색깔 as topic, but a specific shade uses 색 inside 파란색.

extendedVocab.nuance: 색깔 is the everyday, standalone word for 'color,' built on the Sino-Korean root 색 (色 'color') plus a native suffix that makes it feel fuller and more conversational. Its near-synonym is just 색: the dividing line is grammatical, not meaning — 색깔 stands on its own (색깔이 예뻐요, 무슨 색깔?), while 색 is the building block that fuses to a specific shade name (파란색 blue, 빨간색 red, 노란색 yellow). A more formal, technical synonym is 색상, common in design and shopping ('color option'). The main English-speaker pitfall is over-using 색깔 by sticking it onto shade names — '파란색깔' is wrong; the named colors take 색, giving 파란색. Also, to ask 'what color,' the natural question word is 무슨 색깔, not 어떤 색깔 (which leans toward 'what kind/sort of color').

Attaching a shade directly to 색깔, e.g. '파란색깔'; named colors use 색, as in 파란색.
Asking '어떤 색깔' for 'what color' when 무슨 색깔 is the natural phrasing.
Forgetting 색깔 is for color only — for a person's complexion or facial expression use 안색 / 얼굴색, not 색깔.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 초록색 means "green" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 초록색 (choroksaek) means "green". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 초록색 ("green"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 초록색 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The standard color noun for green (草綠色); 초록 alone is also common.
color noun + noun, the basic modifier pattern (no extra particle).

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the green one, please
usagePhrases.note: instrumental 으로 ('in the form of') for choosing a color at a store.
a fresh, pale spring green; a distinct shade, not just 'light 초록.'

examples.en: I like green.
examples.note: Naming a favorite color; 초록색 + 을 좋아하다.

examples.en: Do you have a green umbrella?
examples.note: Shopping: 초록색 directly modifies 우산 with no particle.

examples.en: Now that spring has come, the leaves are green.
examples.note: Real scene: 초록색 + 이에요 describing fresh leaves.

extendedVocab.nuance: 초록색 is the standard word for 'green' — the green of leaves and grass. It is Sino-Korean: 草 'grass' + 綠 'green' + 色 'color,' literally 'grass-green color,' which is a handy memory hook. In casual speech people drop 색 and say just 초록 (초록 좋아해), and in fashion you'll also hear the English loan 그린. Its near-synonyms are real shade distinctions, not loose alternatives: 연두색 is a paler, yellowish spring green, and 청록색 is a bluish teal-green — so reserve 초록색 for ordinary mid-green. The standout English-speaker pitfall is the traffic light: a 'green light' is logically 초록불, and that's correct, but by long habit Koreans overwhelmingly call it 파란불 ('blue light'). So a green go-signal is usually 파란불 in everyday speech even though the lamp is green.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 초록색, 연두색, and 청록색 as the same — they are distinct shades (mid-green, pale green, teal).
Insisting on 초록불 for a traffic 'green light'; Koreans habitually say 파란불 (blue light) for it.
Adding an extra particle in 초록색 옷 — a color noun modifies the next noun directly, with no 의/을.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: The standard color noun for white; 하얀색 is an equally common synonym.
color noun + clothing item, a very common pairing (no particle).
흰색 + 이에요 to state a color (consonant-final 색 → 이에요).

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the white one, please
usagePhrases.note: instrumental 으로 for picking the white option at a store.

examples.en: This shirt is white.
examples.note: Simple statement of color; 흰색 + 이에요.

examples.en: I bought white sneakers.
examples.note: 흰색 directly modifies 운동화; everyday shopping past tense.

examples.ko: 흰색하고 검은색 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요?
examples.romanization: huinsaekago geomeunsaek junge mwoga deo joayo?
examples.en: Between white and black, which do you prefer?
examples.note: Real choice: 흰색 contrasted with its opposite 검은색 (black).

extendedVocab.nuance: 흰색 is the standard color noun for 'white,' built from the native adjective stem 희- (희다 'to be white') plus 색 (色 'color'). Its near-synonym 하얀색 (from 하얗다) is just as common and means the same; the nuance is feel — 흰색 is a touch more neutral and matter-of-fact, 하얀색 a touch softer and more vivid. Keep the noun separate from the adjectives that describe whiteness: name the color with 흰색 (흰색 셔츠, 흰색이에요), but describe how white something looks with 하얗다 → 하얘요 (눈이 하얘요 'the snow is white'); 하얗다 is a ㅎ-irregular, hence 하얘요, 하얀. The main English-speaker pitfalls are two near-neighbors: don't blur 흰색 (white) with 회색 (gray, 灰色), which looks and sounds similar, and don't say '하얀색이다' when you mean to describe a thing — use the adjective 하얘요 for that.

Mis-conjugating 하얗다 as '하얗어요'; it is a ㅎ-irregular, so the form is 하얘요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 술 means "alcohol, alcoholic drink" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 술 (sul) = "alcohol, alcoholic drink". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 술 ("alcohol") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 술, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: General native word for any alcoholic drink (소주, 맥주, 막걸리...).
술 + 을 with 마시다 (drink), the standard verb — not 먹다.
술 + 집 (house) = a drinking place; the everyday word for a bar.
literally 'do one glass of alcohol'; a warm invitation to drink together.

examples.en: I don't drink.
examples.note: Simple statement; 술 + 을 + the standard verb 마시다, negated with 안.

examples.en: Let's grab a drink together today.
examples.note: Set phrase 술 한잔하다 as a friendly invitation; 잔 is the glass/cup counter.

examples.en: You have to drive, so please don't drink.
examples.note: Real caution: 술은 (contrast topic) + polite prohibition -지 마세요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 술 is the general native word for any alcoholic drink — the umbrella over 소주, 맥주, 막걸리, 와인, and more. Like other liquids it takes the verb 마시다 'to drink' (술을 마시다), NOT 먹다; in very casual speech you will hear 술을 먹다 too, but 마시다 is the form to learn and use. Beyond the noun, drinking is deeply social in Korea, so 술 anchors set phrases: 술 한잔하다 'to go for a drink' (a friendly invite), 술자리 'a drinking gathering,' 술집 'a bar,' and the morning-after 술이 깨다 'to sober up.' There is also etiquette baked into the word: you pour for others, not yourself, and a junior turns slightly away when drinking before an elder. The big English-speaker pitfall is reflexively pairing 'drink' with 먹다 (which means 'eat'); in careful Korean alcohol is 마시다. Also keep 술 (alcohol) distinct from 물 (water) — they differ by a single vowel.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing 술 with 먹다 in careful speech; the standard verb is 마시다 (술을 마셔요).
Confusing 술 (alcohol) with 물 (water) — one vowel apart but very different drinks.
Counting drinks with the wrong counter — a glass of alcohol is 술 한 잔, using the cup/glass counter 잔.

NATIVE 둘 → 두 + 시, never '이 시.'
몇 + 시 asks the hour: 몇 시예요? (What time is it?).
the HOUR (시) takes native numbers, the MINUTES (분) take Sino numbers.

examples.en: What time is it now?
examples.note: Core question; 몇 시 + 예요 asks for the hour.

examples.en: Class ends at 3:30.
examples.note: Mixed systems in one clause: NATIVE 세 시 for the hour, SINO 삼십 분 for the minutes.

extendedVocab.nuance: 시 is the counter for the o'clock HOUR (from 時 'time/hour'), and it is one of the great beginner traps because Korean splits its two number systems across the clock: the HOUR uses NATIVE numbers (한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시, 다섯 시...), while the MINUTES counter 분 uses SINO-Korean numbers (일 분, 십 분, 삼십 분). So 3:30 is 세 시 삼십 분 — native for the hour, Sino for the minutes — and mixing them up ('삼 시' or '세십 분') is the classic mistake. Watch the irregular shape changes the native numbers make right before 시: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (스무 시 in 24-hour form). To say 'at' a time, attach 에: 두 시에 'at two o'clock.' Don't confuse the noun 시 'o'clock' with its homophones 시 'poem' (詩) or the city suffix 시 (市, as in 부산시) — the counter use is always preceded by a native number.

Using Sino numbers for the hour, e.g. '삼 시' for three o'clock; it must be the native 세 시.
Using native numbers for minutes — 분 takes Sino numbers, so say 삼십 분, never '서른 분' or '세십 분.'
Forgetting the pre-시 shape change: 둘 → 두 시, 셋 → 세 시, not '둘 시' / '셋 시.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 소 means "cow, ox" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cow, ox" is 소 (so). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 소가 있어요 ("There is a cow"). Watch the particle attached to 소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 소 + 가 because 소 ends in a vowel
all animals are counted with 마리, never 개
키우다 = to raise/keep an animal, takes 를
풀 = grass; everyday subject-object sentence

examples.en: There's a cow over there.
examples.note: Simple existence: 소 + 가 + 있어요.

examples.en: My grandfather raises two cows.
examples.note: Counter 마리 sits after the number, before 를.

examples.en: The cow goes 'moo'.
examples.note: Animal cries use 울다; 음매 is the Korean 'moo'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 소 is the live animal — a cow or ox grazing in a field. The crucial trap for English speakers is that the meat is a completely different word: 소고기 (소 'cow' + 고기 'meat'), so ordering '소' at a restaurant sounds like you want a whole live animal. Compare 소 with the loanword 우유 territory — milk is 우유 (牛乳, 'cow-milk'), not 소 something. 소 is one syllable ending in a vowel, so it always takes the subject marker 가 (소가), and like every animal it is counted with 마리, never 개 (which is for inanimate objects). A second pitfall: the verb for the cow's sound is 울다 'to cry', the same verb used for nearly all animal noises, so 소가 울어요 is natural even though English would never say a cow 'cries'.

Saying 소 주세요 to mean 'beef, please' — 소 is the live animal; the meat is 소고기, so say 소고기 주세요.
Counting cows with 개 (소 한 개). 개 is for objects; animals always take 마리, so say 소 한 마리.
Using 만들다 'make' for raising a cow. To keep/raise a live animal the verb is 키우다, so 소를 키워요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 쥐 means "mouse, rat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 쥐 (jwi) = "mouse, rat". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쥐가 있어요 ("There is a mouse") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쥐, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 쥐 + 가 because 쥐 ends in a vowel
animals take the counter 마리
잡다 = to catch/trap, takes 를
작다 = small; describes size

examples.en: There's a mouse in the kitchen!
examples.note: Existence at a place: 부엌에 + 쥐가.

examples.en: The cat caught the mouse.
examples.note: Past tense 잡다 → 잡았어요; 쥐 is the object.

examples.ko: 쥐 한 마리가 벽 뒤로 숨었어요.
examples.romanization: jwi han mariga byeok dwiro sumeosseoyo.
examples.en: A mouse hid behind the wall.
examples.note: 숨다 = to hide; 마리 counts the one animal.

extendedVocab.nuance: 쥐 covers both 'mouse' and 'rat' — Korean does not lexically split the small one from the big one the way English does, so context (or 큰 쥐 'big rat') carries the difference. The number-one pitfall is the computer device: a computer mouse is the loanword 마우스, never 쥐, so 쥐 클릭 would baffle a listener. Culturally 쥐 carries a negative, dirty, sneaky image (it is also the first animal of the zodiac, 쥐띠 'born in the year of the Rat'). It is one syllable ending in a vowel, so it takes 가 (쥐가), and as an animal it is counted with 마리. Note the verb pairing: you 잡다 'catch/trap' a 쥐, and a cat 잡다 it too — the same verb works for the hunter and the trap.

Calling a computer mouse 쥐. The device is the English loanword 마우스; 쥐 only means the live rodent.
Counting mice with 개 (쥐 한 개). Animals take 마리, so say 쥐 한 마리.
Trying to distinguish 'rat' with a separate base word. There is no everyday separate word — 쥐 is both; add 큰 'big' if size matters: 큰 쥐.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뱀 means "snake" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 뱀 (baem) means "snake". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 뱀이 있어요 ("There is a snake"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뱀 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 뱀 + 이 because 뱀 ends in the consonant ㅁ
animals take the counter 마리
무섭다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 무서워요
뱀 + 을 because it ends in a consonant

examples.en: Whoa, a snake!
examples.note: Plain-form exclamation 이다 → 이다! after a consonant.

examples.en: I saw a snake on the mountain.
examples.note: Object 뱀을; 한 마리 can float before the verb.

examples.en: The snake slithered through the grass.
examples.note: 지나가다 = pass through; 스르르 mimics slithering.

extendedVocab.nuance: 뱀 is a snake, and for learners it is a perfect drill word for the consonant-ending particle rule: because 뱀 ends in ㅁ, the subject marker is 이 (뱀이, never 뱀가) and the object marker is 을 (뱀을, never 뱀를). This single word trips up beginners who default to 가/를 after every noun. There is no Sino-Korean layer here — 뱀 is pure native Korean. It is counted with 마리 like all animals. Watch the adjective 무섭다 'scary': it is ㅂ-irregular, so 'snakes are scary' becomes 뱀이 무서워요 (the ㅂ turns into 워), not 무섭어요. Snakes carry an ominous, sometimes sly cultural image, and 뱀 also names the zodiac sign 뱀띠 'year of the Snake'.

Saying 뱀가 있어요 or 뱀를 봤어요. After the final consonant ㅁ you must use 이 and 을: 뱀이 있어요, 뱀을 봤어요.
Counting snakes with 개. Animals take 마리, so say 뱀 한 마리.
Conjugating 무섭다 as 무섭어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 무섭다 → 무서워요, so 뱀이 무서워요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 개구리 means "frog" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "frog" is 개구리 (gaeguri). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 개구리가 있어요 ("There is a frog"). Watch the particle attached to 개구리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 개구리 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
animals take the counter 마리
animal sounds use 울다, not 노래하다
뛰다 = to jump/leap

examples.en: The frog hops.
examples.note: 폴짝 is the mimetic word for a light hop.

examples.en: There are two frogs in the rice paddy.
examples.note: 논 = rice paddy; 마리 counts them.

examples.en: When it rains the frogs go 'ribbit'.
examples.note: 개굴개굴 is the Korean frog sound + 울다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 개구리 is a frog, a four-syllable native word that learners must keep whole — dropping the final 리 to say 개구 is a common slip. The big pitfall is the verb for its sound: Korean uses 울다 'to cry' for almost every animal noise, so a frog 'croaks' as 개구리가 울어요, never 노래하다 'sing' and never 말하다. The onomatopoeia is 개굴개굴 (the English 'ribbit'). Distinguish the life stages: a tadpole is a separate word, 올챙이, and there is even a proverb 개구리 올챙이 적 생각 못 한다 ('the frog forgets its tadpole days', i.e. people forget their humble beginnings). It ends in a vowel so it takes 가 (개구리가), and it is counted with 마리.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 개구리가 노래해요 for the sound it makes. Animal cries use 울다, so 개구리가 울어요.
Dropping a syllable and writing 개구 instead of the full 개구리.
Calling a tadpole a 'baby 개구리'. The tadpole has its own word, 올챙이.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 벌레 means "bug, insect, worm" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 벌레 (beolle) = "bug, insect, worm". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 벌레가 있어요 ("There is a bug") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 벌레, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 벌레 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
even tiny creatures take 마리
잡다 = catch; 벌레 + 를
무섭다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 무서워요

examples.en: There's a bug in the room.
examples.note: Existence at a place: 방에 + 벌레가.

examples.en: I caught the bug with a tissue and threw it out.
examples.note: 잡다 + 버리다 chained with -아서.

examples.ko: 작은 벌레 한 마리가 스멀스멀 기어가요.
examples.romanization: jageun beolle han mariga seumeolseumeol gieogayo.
examples.en: A tiny bug is creeping along.
examples.note: 기어가다 = crawl; 스멀스멀 = creepily.

extendedVocab.nuance: 벌레 is the everyday, slightly negative catch-all for a creepy-crawly — a bug, insect, or worm you would rather not see. The sharp contrast learners need is 벌레 vs 곤충: 곤충 (昆蟲, the Sino-Korean term for 'insect') is the neutral, scientific six-legged classification you meet in textbooks and museums, while 벌레 is the casual spoken word loaded with a faint 'yuck'. So a child at a science class says 곤충, but the same child screaming in the bathroom says 벌레. 벌레 also extends figuratively to a person obsessed with something (공부벌레 'study-bug', i.e. a bookworm). It ends in a vowel, taking 가 (벌레가), and even the tiniest creature is counted with 마리, never 개.

Using the textbook word 곤충 when you scream at a roach. In casual speech the natural word is 벌레; reserve 곤충 for scientific/neutral contexts.
Counting bugs with 개 (벌레 한 개). Small creatures still take 마리: 벌레 한 마리.
Assuming 벌레 means only 'worm'. It is a broad term covering bugs, insects and worms together; 'worm' alone in the ground is often 지렁이 (earthworm).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 모기 means "mosquito" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 모기 (mogi) means "mosquito". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 모기가 있어요 ("There is a mosquito"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 모기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 모기 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
small creatures take 마리

usagePhrases.en: I got bitten by a mosquito
usagePhrases.note: passive 물리다 + agent particle 에
active 물다 = to bite; 모기 + 가

examples.en: There are lots of mosquitoes in summer.
examples.note: Topic 여름에는 sets the season; 모기가 많다.

examples.en: I got a mosquito bite so it's really itchy.
examples.note: 물리다 + -어서 + 가렵다 cause chain.

examples.ko: 밤새 모기 한 마리가 윙윙거려서 못 잤어요.
examples.romanization: bamsae mogi han mariga wingwinggeoryeoseo mot jasseoyo.
examples.en: One mosquito buzzed all night so I couldn't sleep.
examples.note: 윙윙거리다 = to buzz; 마리 counts it.

extendedVocab.nuance: 모기 is a mosquito, and the must-learn point is the bite construction. English says 'a mosquito bit me' (mosquito = subject), but the natural Korean is the passive: 모기에 물렸어요 'I was bitten by a mosquito', where 물리다 is the passive of 물다 'to bite' and the biter is marked with 에, not 가. Saying 모기가 물렸어요 wrongly makes the mosquito the one bitten. If you want the mosquito as the actor you must use active 물다: 모기가 나를 물었어요. The itch that follows is 가렵다 'itchy' (an adjective), and the buzzing is 윙윙. 모기 ends in a vowel, taking 가, and is counted with 마리. It is a constant Korean summer complaint, so this passive bite phrase is extremely high-frequency.

Saying 모기가 물렸어요 to mean 'a mosquito bit me'. That literally means the mosquito got bitten. Use the passive with 에: 모기에 물렸어요.
Treating 가렵다 'itchy' like a verb. It is an adjective, so 'it itches' is 가려워요 (ㅂ-irregular), not 가렵어요.
Counting mosquitoes with 개. They take 마리: 모기 한 마리.

extendedVocab.explanation: "butterfly" is 나비 (nabi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 나비가 있어요 ("There is a butterfly"). 날다 (ㄹ-irregular) → 날아요

usagePhrases.en: the butterfly perched on the flower
usagePhrases.note: 앉다 = to perch/land; modifies 나비

examples.en: There's a spider on the ceiling.
examples.note: 천장 = ceiling; 거미 + 가 + 있어요.

examples.en: The spider spun a web in the corner.
examples.note: 거미줄 + 치다 is the natural pairing.

examples.en: A spider crept down.
examples.note: 내려오다 = come down; 스르르 = smoothly.

extendedVocab.nuance: 거미 is a spider, a native word ending in a vowel, so it takes 가 (거미가). The key collocation to learn as a chunk is the web: 거미줄 is a compound of 거미 'spider' + 줄 'line/thread', and the idiomatic verb for spinning one is 거미줄을 치다 'to set/string a web', not 만들다 'make' — using 치다 (the same verb as in 줄을 치다 'string a rope') marks you as natural. Note that, strictly, a spider is an arachnid, not a 곤충 'insect', but in everyday speech Koreans lump it in with 벌레 'bugs' anyway. It is counted with 마리. The adjective 무섭다 'scary' is ㅂ-irregular, so 거미가 무서워요, not 무섭어요.

Calling the web 거미. The spider is 거미; its web is the compound 거미줄.
Saying 거미줄을 만들어요 'make a web'. The idiomatic verb is 치다: 거미줄을 쳐요.
Counting spiders with 개. They take 마리: 거미 한 마리.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 땅 means "ground, land, earth (soil)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 땅 (ttang) means "ground, land, earth (soil)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 땅이 넓어요 ("The land is wide"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 땅 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 땅 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅇ
땅 + 에 marks the location of resting
땅 + 을 + 파다 'to dig'
real-estate sense; 땅 + 을 + 사다

examples.en: The child sat on the ground.
examples.note: 땅에 marks where they sat.

examples.en: The land here is really wide.
examples.note: 땅이 = subject; 넓다 'spacious'.

examples.en: I dug the ground and planted a small tree.
examples.note: 파다 + -아서 + 심다 'plant'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 땅 is the native word for the ground, land, or soil under our feet, and it stretches from the physical dirt you 파다 'dig' to the legal land you 사다 'buy'. The biggest English-speaker trap is 'Earth': the planet is 지구 (地球, 'earth-sphere'), never 땅, so '지구가 둥글다' (the Earth is round), not 땅. Distinguish three near-neighbors: 땅 = ground/land in general; 흙 = the soil/dirt as a substance you hold in your hand; 토지 (土地) = land as a formal real-estate/legal term. 땅 ends in the consonant ㅇ, so it takes 이 (땅이, never 땅가) and the object 을 (땅을). To sit or fall 'on' the ground, mark the spot with 에: 땅에 앉다.

Using 땅 for the planet Earth. The planet is 지구; 땅 is only ground/land/soil here below.
Saying 땅가 넓어요. After the final consonant ㅇ you must use 이: 땅이 넓어요.
Blurring 땅 and 흙. 땅 is the ground/land; 흙 is the soil substance itself — you plant a seed 흙에 (in the soil) but you fall 땅에 (onto the ground).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 불 means "fire; light (lamp)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "fire; light (lamp)" is 불 (bul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 불이 나다 ("for a fire to break out"). Watch the particle attached to 불 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: for a fire to break out
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; 불 + 이 + 나다, never 불이 시작하다

usagePhrases.en: to put out a fire / turn off a light
usagePhrases.note: 불 + 을 + 끄다 (ㅡ-irregular) → 꺼요

usagePhrases.en: to light a fire / turn on a light
usagePhrases.note: 불 + 을 + 켜다 = switch on
불 + 이; 뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 뜨거워요

examples.en: Please turn off the light.
examples.note: 끄다 → 꺼; 좀 softens the request.

examples.en: The room is dark. I'll turn on the light.
examples.note: 켜다 → 켤게요 'I'll switch it on'.

examples.en: A fire broke out in the neighbor's kitchen.
examples.note: 불이 나다 → 났어요, the fixed 'fire starts' phrase.

extendedVocab.nuance: 불 is a single native word covering two ideas English keeps apart: 'fire' (flames) and the 'light' of a lamp. So 불을 켜다 / 불을 끄다 means both 'light/extinguish a fire' and 'switch a light on/off' — context decides. The verb pair to memorize is 켜다 (on) / 끄다 (off); never use 열다 'open' / 닫다 'close' for lights, the way some learners do by analogy with English 'open the light'. For a fire breaking out, the fixed phrase is 불이 나다 'a fire occurs' (with 나다 'to come out'), not 불이 시작하다. 불 ends in ㄹ, so it takes 이 (불이, never 불가). Watch the irregulars: 끄다 is ㅡ-irregular (끄다 → 꺼요) and 뜨겁다 'hot' is ㅂ-irregular (뜨거워요). Related: 불꽃 = flame/spark, 모닥불 = campfire.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 불을 열다 / 불을 닫다 for a light. Korean uses 켜다 (on) and 끄다 (off); 열다/닫다 are only for doors and windows.
Saying 불가 났어요. After ㄹ the subject marker is 이: 불이 났어요.
Saying 불이 시작했어요 for a fire breaking out. The set phrase is 불이 나다: 불이 났어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 공기 means "air" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 공기 (gonggi) = "air". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공기가 맑다 ("the air is clear/fresh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 공기 + 가; 맑다 is the set adjective for clean air
공기 + 가; used for polluted/stuffy air
맑다 → 맑은 modifies 공기
공기 + 를 + 마시다 (lit. 'drink' air)

examples.en: The mountain air is so fresh.
examples.note: 산 공기 = mountain air; 맑다 'clear'.

examples.en: I opened the window and breathed in fresh air.
examples.note: 마시다 used for inhaling air.

examples.ko: 요즘 미세먼지 때문에 공기가 너무 나빠요.
examples.romanization: yojeum misemeonji ttaemune gonggiga neomu nappayo.
examples.en: The air is really bad these days because of fine dust.
examples.note: 미세먼지 때문에 = because of fine dust.

extendedVocab.nuance: 공기 is the air we breathe, a Sino-Korean word: 空氣 ('empty-energy/vapor'), the same 氣 'qi/energy' seen in 기분 'mood' and 날씨-adjacent 일기. Two boundaries matter. First, do not confuse 공기 'air' with 날씨 'weather' or 기후 'climate' — they are different concepts, and '오늘 공기 좋다' (good air today) is not the same as '오늘 날씨 좋다' (good weather today). Second, the natural collocation for clean air is 공기가 맑다 'the air is clear', slightly more idiomatic than 공기가 깨끗하다 'clean'; bad air is 공기가 나쁘다. Note that 공기 'to breathe' uses 마시다, literally 'to drink/inhale'. For pollution the everyday term is 미세먼지 'fine dust'. (Beware a homophone: 공기 also names a children's game of jacks and a bowl of rice — context separates them.)

Confusing 공기 'air' with 날씨 'weather'. 공기가 좋다 is about clean air; 날씨가 좋다 is about sunny/nice weather.
Saying 공기를 숨 쉬다. To breathe air the verb is 마시다 (inhale) or just 숨을 쉬다 'to breathe'; you don't pair 공기 with 숨 쉬다 directly.
Always reaching for 깨끗하다 for clean air. The more idiomatic set phrase is 공기가 맑다 'the air is clear'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 오렌지 means "orange (fruit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 오렌지 (orenji) means "orange (fruit)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 오렌지가 있어요 ("There is an orange"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오렌지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 오렌지 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
whole fruit is counted with 개, not 마리
오렌지 + 를 + 먹다
fixed compound; 주스 is also a loanword

examples.en: I eat an orange in the morning.
examples.note: 오렌지를 = object of 먹다.

examples.en: One glass of orange juice, please.
examples.note: 잔 counts glasses of liquid.

examples.en: This orange is sweet and tangy.
examples.note: 새콤달콤하다 = sweet-and-sour, classic for citrus.

extendedVocab.nuance: 오렌지 is the imported orange, written as a loanword straight from English. The essential contrast is with 귤 (gyul), the native Korean tangerine/mandarin: 귤 is the small, easy-peel, winter-staple citrus that Koreans actually eat by the boxful at home, while 오렌지 is the bigger, thicker-skinned imported fruit usually bought for juice. Calling a 귤 an 오렌지 (or vice versa) is a real giveaway. As a loanword its spelling is fixed — 오렌지, not 오린지 or 오랜지. Being inanimate fruit, it is counted with 개 (오렌지 한 개), never the animal counter 마리; a glass of its juice is counted with 잔. The taste vocabulary that pairs with it is 새콤달콤하다 'sweet and tangy' and 달다 'sweet'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 오렌지 (imported orange) with 귤 (Korean tangerine/mandarin). They are different fruits; 귤 is the small winter one eaten at home.
Counting fruit with 마리 (오렌지 한 마리). 마리 is only for animals; whole fruit takes 개: 오렌지 한 개.
Misspelling the loanword as 오린지 or 오랜지. The standard form is 오렌지.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 고추 means "chili pepper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "chili pepper" is 고추 (gochu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 고추가 맵다 ("the chili pepper is spicy"). Watch the particle attached to 고추 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 고추 + 가; 맵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 매워요
vegetables are counted with 개
고추 + 를 + 넣다 'put in'
고추 + 가루 with 사이시옷 (inserted ㅅ)

examples.en: This chili is really spicy.
examples.note: 맵다 → 매워요; 진짜 'really' is casual.

examples.en: I sliced chili and added it to the stew.
examples.note: 썰다 'slice' + 넣다; 송송 = finely.

examples.en: You need plenty of chili powder for kimchi to turn red.
examples.note: 고춧가루; 빨갛다 → 빨개요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 고추 is the chili pepper, the backbone of Korean spice, and it spawns a small family you should keep straight: ground it becomes 고춧가루 'chili powder' (note the 사이시옷 — an inserted ㅅ for the compound, so 고춧가루, not 고추가루); the fermented red paste is 고추장; a fresh green chili is 풋고추. The sharpest pitfall is 고추 vs 후추: 후추 is black pepper, a totally different seasoning, so swapping them ruins a recipe. The adjective for its heat is 맵다 'spicy', which is ㅂ-irregular (맵다 → 매워요), not 매웠다-style regular. Inanimate, it is counted with 개. Culturally 고추 is loaded — its red color symbolized a baby boy, and it is also slang for a little boy's genitals, so the word carries a knowing double meaning adults will recognize.

Writing the powder as 고추가루. The compound takes 사이시옷: the standard spelling is 고춧가루.
Confusing 고추 (chili pepper) with 후추 (black pepper). They are different seasonings.
Conjugating 맵다 as 맵어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 맵다 → 매워요, so 고추가 매워요.

extendedVocab.explanation: 극장 (geukjang) = "theater, cinema". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 극장에 가다 ("to go to the theater") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 극장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 극장 + 에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: to watch a movie at the cinema
usagePhrases.note: 극장 + 에서 marks where the action happens
극장 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅇ

usagePhrases.en: to meet in front of the theater
usagePhrases.note: 극장 앞 = place word + 에서

examples.en: I go to the cinema on weekends.
examples.note: 극장에 = where you go (destination).

examples.en: I watched a movie at the theater.
examples.note: 극장에서 = where the watching happened.

examples.en: Let's meet in front of the theater at 7.
examples.note: 극장 앞 + 에서 marks the meeting spot.

extendedVocab.nuance: 극장 is a place to watch a show — historically a live theater, today most often a movie cinema. It is Sino-Korean: 劇場 ('drama-place', 劇 'play/drama' + 場 'place/arena', the same 場 in 시장 'market' and 운동장 'sports field'). The register/usage contrast to know is 극장 vs 영화관: 영화관 (映畵館, 'movie-hall') specifically means a film cinema and sounds a touch more modern, while 극장 is the older, broader word that still covers cinemas and is universally understood — a multiplex like CGV is fine to call either. The grammar drill here is the 에 vs 에서 split: use 에 for the destination you go to (극장에 가다) but 에서 for the location where an action occurs (극장에서 영화를 보다). Because 극장 ends in ㅇ, it takes 이 (극장이, never 극장가).

Saying 극장에서 가요 for 'I go to the theater'. Movement-toward takes 에: 극장에 가요. Use 에서 only for an action done there.
Saying 극장가 커요. After the final consonant ㅇ the subject marker is 이: 극장이 커요.
Assuming 극장 means only a live-play theater. In everyday Korean it usually means the movie cinema; the live-stage nuance is context-dependent.

extendedVocab.explanation: 서점 (seojeom) means "bookstore". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서점에 가다 ("to go to the bookstore"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 서점 + 에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: to buy a book at the bookstore
usagePhrases.note: 서점 + 에서 marks where you buy
서점 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅁ
크다 → 큰 modifies 서점

examples.en: I bought a book at the bookstore.
examples.note: 권 counts books; 서점에서 = where you bought.

examples.en: There's a bookstore near the school.
examples.note: 서점이 = subject of 있다.

examples.en: Want to go to the bookstore together this weekend?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ래요? casual invitation.

extendedVocab.nuance: 서점 is a bookstore, where you buy books. It is Sino-Korean: 書店 ('book-shop', 書 'book/writing' + 店 'store', the same 店 in 편의점 'convenience store' and 음식점 'restaurant'). The contrast every beginner must lock in is 서점 vs 도서관: a 서점 is a shop where you pay and own the book, whereas 도서관 (圖書館, 'library') is where you borrow and return — confusing them produces sentences like 'I bought a book at the library'. A nearly synonymous word is 책방, a warmer, more old-fashioned native-flavored term for a (often small) bookshop. The grammar point is the same 에/에서 contrast: 서점에 가다 (go to) but 서점에서 책을 사다 (buy at). Since 서점 ends in ㅁ, it takes 이 (서점이, never 서점가); books inside are counted with 권.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 서점 (bookstore — you buy) with 도서관 (library — you borrow). They are different places.
Saying 서점가 있어요. After the final consonant ㅁ the subject marker is 이: 서점이 있어요.
Counting books with 개. Books take the bound-volume counter 권: 책 한 권.

structuredNuance.t: 서점 is a bookstore, where you buy books. The grammar point is the 에/에서 contrast: 서점에 가다 (go to) but 서점에서 책을 사다 (buy at). Since 서점 ends in ㅁ, it takes 이 (서점이, never 서점가); books inside are counted with 권.

The contrast every beginner must lock in is 서점 vs 도서관: a 서점 is a shop where you pay and own the book, whereas 도서관 (圖書館, 'library') is where you borrow and return — confusing them produces sentences like 'I bought a book at the library'. A nearly synonymous word is 책방, a warmer, more old-fashioned native-flavored term for a (often small) bookshop.
It is Sino-Korean: 書店 ('book-shop', 書 'book/writing' + 店 'store', the same 店 in 편의점 'convenience store' and 음식점 'restaurant').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 미용실 means "hair salon, beauty salon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "hair salon, beauty salon" is 미용실 (miyongsil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 미용실에 가다 ("to go to the hair salon"). Watch the particle attached to 미용실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to go to the hair salon
usagePhrases.note: 미용실 + 에 marks the destination

usagePhrases.en: to get a haircut at the salon
usagePhrases.note: 머리를 자르다 = cut one's hair
미용실 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㄹ
미용실 + 을 + 예약하다 'reserve'

examples.en: I'm going to the hair salon tomorrow.
examples.note: 미용실에 = destination.

examples.en: I got my hair cut short at the salon.
examples.note: 짧게 'short(ly)' + 자르다 → 잘랐어요.

examples.en: I booked the salon — I'm going to get a perm.
examples.note: 파마하다 'to perm'; -려고요 states intent.

extendedVocab.nuance: 미용실 is a hair/beauty salon where you cut, dye, or perm your hair. It is Sino-Korean: 美容室 ('beauty-grooming-room', 美 'beauty' + 容 'appearance/grooming' + 室 'room', the same 室 in 교실 'classroom' and 화장실 'restroom'). The contrast to know is 미용실 vs 이발소: an 이발소 (理髮所, 'barbershop') is the traditional men's barber — think the spinning pole — and now sounds old-fashioned, while 미용실 serves everyone and is the default modern word; younger speakers also say the loanword 헤어숍 or just 미용실. The key collocation is 머리를 자르다 'to cut one's hair' (literally 'cut the head'), with 자르다 → 잘랐어요 in the past. Note 머리 here means 'hair', not 'head', in this context. Since 미용실 ends in ㄹ, it takes 이 (미용실이, never 미용실가).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 미용실 (modern unisex hair salon) with 이발소 (traditional men's barbershop). 미용실 is the everyday default.
Saying 미용실가 있어요. After the final consonant ㄹ the subject marker is 이: 미용실이 있어요.
Saying 머리를 깎다 vs 자르다 incorrectly. For a normal salon haircut Koreans say 머리를 자르다; 깎다 sounds like shaving/clippers, more for very short or buzzed cuts.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 구체적이다 means "to be concrete, specific, detailed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 구체적이다 (guchejeogida) = "to be concrete, specific, detailed". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 구체적인 예 ("a concrete example") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 구체적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common pairing; 구체적인 예를 들어 주세요 = 'give a concrete example.'
구체적으로 말씀해 주세요 is how you politely ask someone to stop being vague.
Implies real dates, numbers, steps — not just a vague intention.

usagePhrases.en: to be a bit more specific
usagePhrases.note: 좀 더 구체적이었으면 좋겠어요 = 'I wish it were a bit more specific.'

examples.en: The plan isn't concrete yet.
examples.note: Predicate use: 구체적이다 → 구체적이지 않다 for the negative.

examples.ko: 면접에서는 구체적인 경험을 이야기하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseoneun guchejeogin gyeongheomeul iyagihaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: In an interview it's good to talk about specific experiences.
examples.note: 구체적인 + noun describes detailed, real content.

examples.ko: '열심히 하겠다'보다 구체적으로 어떻게 할 건지 말해 주세요.
examples.romanization: 'yeolsimhi hagetda'boda guchejeogeuro eotteoke hal geonji malhae juseyo.
examples.en: Rather than 'I'll work hard,' tell me concretely how you'll do it.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 구체적으로 demands actionable detail over slogans.

extendedVocab.nuance: 구체적이다 (具體的 — 具 'equip/possess' + 體 'body/form,' literally 'having a fleshed-out body') is the everyday word for ideas that come with real detail, examples, and numbers, and it is the exact antonym of 추상적이다. Compare it with 자세하다: 자세하다 means 'detailed/thorough' about information already given (자세한 설명 = a thorough explanation), whereas 구체적이다 is about whether something has tangible substance at all (vague plan vs concrete plan). In speech you will hear the adverb 구체적으로 far more than the bare adjective, above all in 구체적으로 말해 주세요. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers: do not drop the 적 (there is no 구체하다; it is always 구체적이다 / 구체적으로), and do not borrow English 'concrete' for physical solidity — for a hard, firm object you need 단단하다, not 구체적이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 구체하다 — the word always keeps 적: it is 구체적이다 as the adjective and 구체적으로 as the adverb. (구체화하다 exists, but that means 'to give shape to / flesh out.')
Using 구체적이다 for physical hardness because English 'concrete' is also a building material — for a solid, firm object use 단단하다; 구체적이다 is only about detail/specificity.
Writing the connective as 구체적이여서; the correct form from the 이다 stem is 구체적이어서 ('because it is concrete').

具體的 — 具 'equip/possess' + 體 'body/form,' literally 'having a fleshed-out body.'
