extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 추상적이다 means "to be abstract" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 추상적이다 (chusangjeogida) means "to be abstract". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 추상적인 개념 ("an abstract concept"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 추상적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 추상적인 개념 is the textbook collocation; e.g. 사랑, 자유 같은 추상적인 개념.
Usually a complaint: 설명이 너무 추상적이에요 = 'the explanation is too abstract.'
추상적으로만 설명하지 마세요 = 'don't explain only in the abstract.'
Vague, non-concrete phrasing that leaves the listener unsure.

examples.en: That statement is a bit abstract.
examples.note: Simple predicate: 추상적이다 → 추상적이에요 in the polite present.

examples.ko: 사랑 같은 추상적인 개념은 말로 설명하기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: sarang gateun chusangjeogin gaenyeomeun mallo seolmyeonghagi himdeureoyo.
examples.en: Abstract concepts like love are hard to put into words.
examples.note: 추상적인 + 개념 is a very frequent pairing.

examples.ko: 너무 추상적으로 말하지 말고 예를 하나 들어 주세요.
examples.romanization: neomu chusangjeogeuro malhaji malgo yereul hana deureo juseyo.
examples.en: Don't speak so abstractly — give me one example.
examples.note: Real-situation use: people push back on 추상적 talk by asking for an example.

extendedVocab.nuance: 추상적이다 (抽象的 — 抽 'draw out' + 象 'image,' i.e. an idea 'drawn out' from concrete things) describes what exists only as a concept, with no tangible detail, and is the direct opposite of 구체적이다. In conversation it usually carries a mildly negative tone: calling someone's explanation 추상적 implies it is too vague to be useful, so it works almost as a soft request for specifics. Do not confuse it with 막연하다, which means 'vague/hazy' in the sense of unclear and uncertain (막연한 불안 = a vague unease); 추상적 is specifically about being conceptual rather than concrete. The main English-speaker pitfall is the connective spelling: write 추상적이어서, never 추상적이여서, and memorize the chunk 추상적이어서 이해하기 어렵다 ('so abstract it's hard to understand').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 추상적이여서 — the 이다 stem gives 추상적이어서 ('because it is abstract'); the 여 spelling is wrong.
Confusing 추상 with 추억 ('memory') because they share 추 — they are unrelated; the noun for a memory is 추억, while 추상 means abstraction.
Treating 추상적이다 as purely negative — it is also neutral/technical, e.g. 추상적인 사고 ('abstract thinking') is a valued cognitive skill, not an insult.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 객관적이다 means "to be objective" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be objective" is 객관적이다 (gaekgwanjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 객관적으로 보면 ("objectively speaking / looking at it objectively"). Watch the particle attached to 객관적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: objectively speaking / looking at it objectively
usagePhrases.note: A set discourse opener that signals you're giving a fair, feelings-aside view.
객관적인 사실만 전하다 = 'report only the objective facts' (news register).
The natural adverb + verb pairing for fair decision-making.
Uses the noun 객관성; formal/academic register.

examples.en: That assessment is objective.
examples.note: Simple predicate use of 객관적이다.

examples.ko: 기사에는 객관적인 사실만 담겨 있어야 해요.
examples.romanization: gisaeneun gaekgwanjeogin sasilman damgyeo isseoya haeyo.
examples.en: An article should contain only objective facts.
examples.note: 객관적인 + 사실 is a high-frequency newsroom pairing.

examples.ko: 감정을 빼고 객관적으로 한번 판단해 보세요.
examples.romanization: gamjeongeul ppaego gaekgwanjeogeuro hanbeon pandanhae boseyo.
examples.en: Set emotion aside and try judging it objectively for once.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 객관적으로 is invoked precisely to counter 감정적 reactions.

extendedVocab.nuance: 객관적이다 (客觀的 — 客 'guest/outsider' + 觀 'view,' i.e. seeing as an outside observer would) means 'grounded in facts rather than personal feeling,' and is the standard antonym of 주관적이다. Keep the 客 'outsider' image: the objective view is the one a neutral third party would share. Korean speakers routinely launch an opinion with 객관적으로 보면 ('objectively speaking') to frame it as fair, so the phrase is as much a politeness/credibility move as a literal claim. Do not confuse it with 공정하다 ('fair/just'), which is about even-handed treatment and ethics, whereas 객관적 is about fact-based, feelings-free perception. The recurring pitfall for English speakers is the adverb form: it is 객관적으로 (the 적 + 으로 suffix), never 객관적게 — Sino-Korean 적 adjectives form adverbs with 으로, not the native 게.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 객관적 (objective) and 주관적 (subjective) by accident — they are exact opposites; anchor them with 客 (outside) vs 主 (self).
Forming the adverb as 객관적게 — Sino-Korean -적 words take 으로, so it must be 객관적으로.
Using 객관적이다 to mean 'fair/just' — for fair treatment use 공정하다; 객관적 is specifically fact-based and emotion-free.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주관적이다 means "to be subjective" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주관적이다 (jugwanjeogida) = "to be subjective". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 주관적인 의견 ("a subjective opinion") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주관적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: A polite hedge: 이건 제 주관적인 의견인데요 = 'this is just my subjective opinion, but…'
맛 평가는 주관적일 수밖에 없어요 = 'taste judgments are inevitably subjective.'

usagePhrases.en: to speak subjectively / from one's own view
usagePhrases.note: 주관적으로 말하면… frames a personal take.
Uses the noun 주관; this one is a compliment, not a criticism.

examples.en: That's too subjective.
examples.note: Simple predicate; often a gentle pushback on someone's claim.

examples.en: That's not a fact but a subjective opinion.
examples.note: Routinely contrasted with 사실/객관적.

examples.ko: 너무 주관적으로만 보지 말고 다른 관점도 들어 보세요.
examples.romanization: neomu jugwanjeogeuroman boji malgo dareun gwanjeomdo deureo boseyo.
examples.en: Don't view it only subjectively — hear out other perspectives too.
examples.note: Real-situation use: paired with the implied antonym 객관적으로.

extendedVocab.nuance: 주관적이다 (主觀的 — 主 'self/main' + 觀 'view,' i.e. seeing from one's own standpoint) describes something shaped by personal feeling, taste, or viewpoint, and is the opposite of 객관적이다 (anchored by 主 'self' vs 客 'outsider'). It is most useful as a soft hedge: tagging a statement 주관적인 의견 signals 'this is only my take, not a fact,' which softens assertions politely. Be careful not to use it for 'biased/prejudiced' in a strong moral sense — for prejudice you need 편견 (편견을 가지다 = 'to hold a prejudice'); 주관적 merely means personal, not bigoted. Also distinguish the noun 주관 in 주관이 뚜렷하다, which praises someone for having clear, independent views — there 주관 is a positive trait, the opposite flavor from the cautious 주관적인 의견.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 객관적이다 — remember 주(主, self) vs 객(客, guest/outside) to keep the pair straight.
Using 주관적이다 to mean 'biased/prejudiced' — that strong negative sense needs 편견(을 가지다); 주관적 only means 'personal/viewpoint-based.'
Forming the adverb as 주관적게 — it must be 주관적으로 (-적 + 으로).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 일반적이다 means "to be general, common, usual" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 일반적이다 (ilbanjeogida) means "to be general, common, usual". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일반적으로 ("generally, as a rule"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 일반적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: A top-tier discourse opener: 일반적으로 한국에서는… states a norm.
일반적인 경우에는 = 'in the usual case'; sets up a default before exceptions.
What most people assume, often before you challenge it.
그건 아주 일반적인 일이에요 = 'that's a totally ordinary thing.'

examples.en: That kind of reaction is common.
examples.note: Simple predicate: reassuring someone their response is normal.

examples.ko: 그건 아주 일반적인 반응이니까 걱정하지 마세요.
examples.romanization: geugeon aju ilbanjeogin baneunginikka geokjeonghaji maseyo.
examples.en: That's a very common reaction, so don't worry.
examples.note: 일반적인 + noun = typical/ordinary.

examples.ko: 일반적으로 한국에서는 신발을 벗고 집에 들어가요.
examples.romanization: ilbanjeogeuro hangugeseoneun sinbareul beotgo jibe deureogayo.
examples.en: Generally in Korea you take your shoes off before entering a home.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 일반적으로 introduces a cultural norm/general rule.

extendedVocab.nuance: 일반적이다 (一般的 — 一 'one' + 般 'sort/kind,' i.e. 'of one common sort') means 'typical, common, what is usually the case,' and the adverb 일반적으로 is one of the most useful words for stating a general rule in explanations and writing. Compare it with 보통: 보통 is the casual, everyday word for 'usually' and works in any conversation (보통 7시에 일어나요), whereas 일반적으로 is more formal and explanatory, the kind of phrase you use to lay down a norm or generalization. Watch the meaning shift when you drop 적: 일반 on its own means 'general public / ordinary (non-specialist)' and appears in compounds like 일반인 ('ordinary person'), 일반석 ('regular seat'), 일반실 — so keep the 적 when you mean 'common/typical.' The English speaker's pitfall is reaching for 일반적으로 in casual chat where a Korean would simply say 보통.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 일반적으로 in casual conversation where 보통 is more natural — 보통 = everyday 'usually,' 일반적으로 = formal 'generally/as a rule.'
Dropping the 적: 일반이다 / 일반 shifts to 'general public / non-specialist' (일반인, 일반석), so 'common/typical' must stay 일반적이다.
Forming the adverb as 일반적게 — Sino-Korean -적 takes 으로, giving 일반적으로.

structuredNuance.t: Means 'typical, common, what is usually the case,' and the adverb 일반적으로 is one of the most useful words for stating a general rule in explanations and writing.

Compare it with 보통: 보통 is the casual, everyday word for 'usually' and works in any conversation (보통 7시에 일어나요), whereas 일반적으로 is more formal and explanatory, the kind of phrase you use to lay down a norm or generalization.

一般的 — 一 'one' + 般 'sort/kind,' i.e. 'of one common sort.' Watch the meaning shift when you drop 적: 일반 on its own means 'general public / ordinary (non-specialist)' and appears in compounds like 일반인 ('ordinary person'), 일반석 ('regular seat'), 일반실 — so keep the 적 when you mean 'common/typical.'
The English speaker's pitfall is reaching for 일반적으로 in casual chat where a Korean would simply say 보통.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 합리적이다 means "to be rational, reasonable" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be rational, reasonable" is 합리적이다 (hamnijeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 합리적인 가격 ("a reasonable/fair price"). Watch the particle attached to 합리적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Very common in shopping: 가격이 합리적이에요 = 'the price is fair/justified.'
합리적으로 생각해 보세요 = 'think about it rationally.'
Frames a decision as logical rather than emotional or impulsive.
The antonym, built with the prefix 비-(非).

examples.en: That decision is reasonable.
examples.note: Simple predicate; a positive evaluation of a choice.

examples.ko: 이 가격이면 정말 합리적인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i gagyeogimyeon jeongmal hamnijeogin geot gatayo.
examples.en: At this price it really seems reasonable.
examples.note: 합리적인 가격 = a fair, justified price (not merely cheap).

examples.ko: 감정적으로 말고 합리적으로 한번 판단해 봅시다.
examples.romanization: gamjeongjeogeuro malgo hamnijeogeuro hanbeon pandanhae bopsida.
examples.en: Let's judge rationally rather than emotionally for once.
examples.note: Real-situation use: explicitly set against 감정적으로.

extendedVocab.nuance: 합리적이다 (合理的 — 合 'fit/accord' + 理 'reason/principle,' i.e. 'in accord with reason') spans two English ideas at once: 'logical/rational' (합리적으로 생각하다 = think logically) and 'reasonable/fair' (합리적인 가격 = a fair price). It almost always carries positive evaluation. Distinguish it from 합당하다, which means 'fitting/warranted/deserved' for a specific case (합당한 처벌 = a fitting punishment) — 합리적 is about overall logic and good sense, not case-by-case appropriateness. The key pitfall: 합리적인 가격 does NOT mean 'cheap'; it means a price that is justified for what you get, so a high price can still be 합리적. And form the opposite with the Sino prefix — 'irrational' is 비합리적이다, not 안 합리적이다 in any careful or written register.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 합리적인 가격 as 'a cheap price' — it means a fair, justified price; something expensive can still be 합리적.
Saying 안 합리적이다 for 'irrational' — the standard form uses the prefix 비-: 비합리적이다.
Confusing 합리적 with 합당하다 — 합당하다 = 'fitting/warranted' for a particular case, while 합리적 = 'logical/reasonable' in general.

合理的 — 合 'fit/accord' + 理 'reason/principle,' i.e. 'in accord with reason.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 현실적이다 means "to be realistic, practical" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 현실적이다 (hyeonsiljeogida) = "to be realistic, practical". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 현실적으로 ("realistically, in practical terms") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 현실적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 현실적으로 가능할까요? = 'is it realistically possible?'
Contrasts an attainable aim with a pie-in-the-sky 이상적인 목표.
Used when an idea is rejected for being too idealistic.
The antonym with 비-(非); 비현실적인 기대 = unrealistic expectations.

examples.en: That goal is realistic.
examples.note: Simple predicate; says an aim is actually attainable.

examples.ko: 꿈도 좋지만 좀 더 현실적인 목표를 세워 보세요.
examples.romanization: kkumdo jochiman jom deo hyeonsiljeogin mokpyoreul sewo boseyo.
examples.en: Dreams are fine, but try setting a more realistic goal.
examples.note: 현실적인 목표 = an achievable, down-to-earth goal.

examples.ko: 현실적으로 생각하면 그 계획은 시간이 너무 부족해요.
examples.romanization: hyeonsiljeogeuro saenggakamyeon geu gyehoegeun sigani neomu bujokaeyo.
examples.en: Realistically, that plan just doesn't have enough time.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 현실적으로 생각하면 pulls a discussion back to feasibility.

extendedVocab.nuance: 현실적이다 (現實的 — 現 'present/appear' + 實 'real/actual,' i.e. 'of present reality') describes something grounded in reality and actually feasible, and is the natural foil to 이상적이다 ('ideal'). Applied to a person it usually means practical and down-to-earth (그 사람은 현실적이에요), which is generally a compliment, not a put-down. Crucially, do not confuse it with 사실적이다 (寫實的, 'lifelike/realistic') — 사실적 is an art-and-description word for vividly true-to-life depiction (사실적인 묘사 = a lifelike portrayal), whereas 현실적 is about practicality and what can really be done. The adverb 현실적으로 is the go-to phrase for steering a conversation toward what is actually possible. Pitfall: don't call a practical person 현실 — 현실 alone is the noun 'reality'; the adjective must be 현실적이다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 현실적이다 (realistic/feasible) with 사실적이다 (lifelike/true-to-life) — the latter is for art and vivid description, e.g. 사실적인 그림.
Calling a down-to-earth person 현실 — 현실 is the noun 'reality'; the adjective is 현실적이다.
Forming the opposite as 안 현실적이다 — use the prefix form 비현실적이다 ('unrealistic').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이상적이다 means "to be ideal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이상적이다 (isangjeogida) means "to be ideal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이상적인 직장 ("an ideal job/workplace"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이상적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 이상적인 + noun = perfect for its purpose: 이상적인 조건, 이상적인 환경.
이상적으로는 좋지만… sets up the 'but in reality' turn.
Often gently critical: 'a nice idea, but unrealistic.'
Uses the noun 이상; describes someone aspirational (neutral-to-positive).

examples.en: That environment is truly ideal.
examples.note: Simple predicate; high praise for near-perfect conditions.

examples.ko: 집에서 가깝고 월급도 좋으니 이상적인 직장이네요.
examples.romanization: jibeseo gakkapgo wolgeupdo joeuni isangjeogin jikjangineyo.
examples.en: It's close to home and pays well, so it's an ideal job.
examples.note: 이상적인 + noun = ideal/perfect for a purpose.

examples.ko: 이상적으로는 다 같이 가면 좋지만 현실은 좀 달라요.
examples.romanization: isangjeogeuroneun da gachi gamyeon jochiman hyeonsireun jom dallayo.
examples.en: Ideally we'd all go together, but reality's a bit different.
examples.note: Real-situation use: the 이상적으로는 …, 현실은 … contrast is everywhere in speech.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이상적이다 (理想的 — 理 'reason/principle' + 想 'thought,' i.e. an idea conceived as perfect) means 'ideal, perfect in theory,' and pairs naturally as the opposite of 현실적이다. The set frame 이상적으로는 …, 현실은 … ('ideally …, but in reality …') is one of the most common rhetorical moves in everyday Korean, so learn it as a unit. Note that, depending on tone, 이상적인 생각 can tip into mild criticism ('too idealistic / not feasible'), much like English 'that's idealistic.' Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not confuse this 이상(理想, 'ideal') with the identical-sounding 이상(異常) in 이상하다 ('strange/odd') — same syllables, opposite feel, different hanja. Second, don't overuse 이상적이다 for ordinary 'good'; reserve it for something close to perfect, and use 좋다 for everyday approval.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing 이상적이다 (ideal, 理想) with 이상하다 (strange, 異常) — identical 이상 sound but different hanja and opposite feel.
Overusing 이상적이다 for plain 'good' — reserve it for near-perfect; for ordinary approval say 좋다.
Forming the opposite as 안 이상적이다 — there's no common 비이상적; instead say 현실적이지 않다 or 비현실적이다 to express the realistic counterpoint.

structuredNuance.t: Means 'ideal, perfect in theory,' and pairs naturally as the opposite of 현실적이다. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 전통적이다 means "to be traditional" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be traditional" is 전통적이다 (jeontongjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 전통적인 음식 ("traditional food"). Watch the particle attached to 전통적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 전통적인 + noun for culturally inherited things: 전통적인 결혼식, 전통적인 방식.
전통적으로 명절에는 가족이 모여요 — introduces a long-standing practice.
Often set against modern/younger-generation attitudes.
Uses the noun 전통; also 전통문화, 전통시장.

examples.en: That method is rather traditional.
examples.note: Simple predicate; can be neutral or hint at 'old-school.'

examples.ko: 설날에는 전통적인 한복을 입는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: seolnareneun jeontongjeogin hanbogeul imneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: On Lunar New Year, many people wear traditional hanbok.
examples.note: 전통적인 + noun describes culturally inherited things.

examples.ko: 전통적으로 한국에서는 어른께 먼저 인사를 드려요.
examples.romanization: jeontongjeogeuro hangugeseoneun eoreunkke meonjeo insareul deuryeoyo.
examples.en: Traditionally in Korea, you greet your elders first.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 전통적으로 + honorific 드리다 introduces a respected custom.

extendedVocab.nuance: 전통적이다 (傳統的 — 傳 'pass down' + 統 'lineage/system,' i.e. 'of a handed-down lineage') means 'in keeping with long-standing tradition,' and is the natural adjective for food, clothing, ceremonies, and values passed down over generations; the noun 전통 saturates compounds like 전통문화, 전통시장, 전통혼례. It carries a respectful, valued tone. Do not let English 'traditional = old-fashioned' bleed in: when you mean outdated or behind-the-times, use 구식이다 (구식 휴대폰 = an outdated phone), which is slightly negative, whereas 전통적이다 honors heritage. Also keep 전통(傳統, 'tradition') apart from the near-homophone 정통(正統, 'orthodox/authentic-lineage,' as in 정통 이탈리아 요리 = authentic Italian cuisine) — one syllable apart, clearly different meaning. The adverb is 전통적으로, never 전통적게.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 전통적이다 for 'old-fashioned/outdated' — that nuance is 구식이다; 전통적이다 is respectful about heritage, not a criticism.
Confusing 전통 (tradition, 傳統) with 정통 (orthodox/authentic, 正統) — similar sound, different hanja and meaning.
Forming the adverb as 전통적게 — it must be 전통적으로.

structuredNuance.t: Means 'in keeping with long-standing tradition,' the natural adjective for food, clothing, ceremonies, and values passed down over generations; the noun 전통 saturates compounds like 전통문화, 전통시장, 전통혼례. It carries a respectful, valued tone.

extendedVocab.english: to be representative, the most typical example
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 대표적이다 means "to be representative, the most typical example" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 대표적이다 (daepyojeogida) = "to be representative, the most typical example". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 대표적인 음식 ("a representative/iconic food") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 대표적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: The dominant pattern: 한국의 대표적인 음식 = Korea's signature food.
대표적으로 김치를 들 수 있어요 = 'kimchi is a prime example.'
Introduces the clearest illustration of a category.
이 작가의 대표적인 작품 = this author's defining work.

examples.en: Kimchi is a representative food of Korea.
examples.note: 대표적인 + noun = the most iconic example of a category.

examples.en: As prime examples, Busan and Jeju are popular travel spots.
examples.note: 대표적으로 opens a list with its leading members.

examples.ko: 한국의 대표적인 명절이라고 하면 보통 설날과 추석을 꼽아요.
examples.romanization: hangugui daepyojeogin myeongjeorirago hamyeon botong seolnalgwa chuseogeul kkobayo.
examples.en: Asked for Korea's representative holidays, people usually name Seollal and Chuseok.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 대표적인 + noun + 꼽다 = to single out as the top example.

extendedVocab.nuance: 대표적이다 (代表的 — 代 'on behalf of' + 表 'show/express,' i.e. 'standing in to represent') means 'serving as the most typical or famous example' of a category, and in practice you meet it almost only as 대표적인 + noun or as the list-opener 대표적으로 — the bare predicate 이건 대표적이에요 sounds incomplete and unnatural. Compare it with 유명하다 ('famous'): something can be 유명하다 simply by being widely known, but 대표적 specifically frames it as the standard-bearer that typifies a whole group (대표적인 한식 = the dish that represents Korean food as a category). The root 대표 also lives on its own meaning 'representative/leader' (회사 대표 = company head, 학급 대표 = class rep), so context tells you whether it is the noun 'representative' or this adjective sense. Pitfall: avoid using 대표적이다 as a stand-alone predicate — attach a noun.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 대표적이다 as a bare predicate (이건 대표적이에요) — it sounds incomplete; say 대표적인 음식이에요 or 대표적인 예예요.
Treating 대표적 as a synonym for 유명하다 — 유명하다 just means 'famous,' while 대표적 means 'typifying/standing for a whole category.'
Forming the adverb as 대표적게 — it must be 대표적으로 ('as a prime example').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 직접적이다 means "to be direct" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 직접적이다 (jikjeopjeogida) means "to be direct". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 직접적인 영향 ("a direct effect/influence"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 직접적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 직접적인 영향을 주다/받다 = to have/receive a direct effect.
Contrasts with 간접적인 원인 (an indirect/contributing cause).
직접적으로 말하기는 좀 그래요 = 'saying it directly is a bit awkward.'
Wording that states things head-on, sometimes too bluntly for comfort.

examples.en: That expression is too direct.
examples.note: Simple predicate; flags wording as overly blunt.

examples.en: Stress has a direct effect on health.
examples.note: 직접적인 영향/원인 are core collocations.

examples.ko: 한국에서는 거절을 직접적으로 말하지 않는 경우가 많아요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseoneun geojeoreul jikjeopjeogeuro malhaji anhneun gyeonguga manayo.
examples.en: In Korea, refusals are often not stated directly.
examples.note: Real-situation use: a cultural point — direct refusal can feel rude.

extendedVocab.nuance: 직접적이다 (直接的 — 直 'straight' + 接 'connect,' i.e. 'straight-connected, nothing in between') describes something direct, with no intermediary: 직접적인 원인 (direct cause), 직접적인 영향 (direct impact), a blunt 직접적인 표현. Its antonym is 간접적이다. The big trap for English speakers is that the bare root 직접 is a high-frequency adverb meaning 'in person / by oneself' (직접 만들다 = to make it yourself, 직접 가다 = to go in person) — that 직접 is NOT interchangeable with the adjective-derived 직접적으로, which means 'directly = bluntly/without an intermediary.' So 직접 가다 ('go in person') and 직접적으로 말하다 ('speak bluntly') are different ideas; never swap them. Register note: because Korean often favors indirectness, calling speech 직접적 can carry a faint 'too blunt' overtone. And the connective is 직접적이어서, not 직접적이여서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the adverb 직접 ('in person/oneself,' 직접 가다) with 직접적으로 ('bluntly/without intermediary') — 직접 가다 ≠ 직접적으로 가다.
Writing the connective as 직접적이여서 — the 이다 stem gives 직접적이어서.
Assuming 직접적이다 is always neutral — about speech it can imply 'too blunt'; the polite, softened option is often 간접적인 표현.

structuredNuance.t: Describes something direct, with no intermediary: 직접적인 원인 (direct cause), 직접적인 영향 (direct impact), a blunt 직접적인 표현. Its antonym is 간접적이다. Register note: because Korean often favors indirectness, calling speech 직접적 can carry a faint 'too blunt' overtone.
直接的 — 直 'straight' + 接 'connect,' i.e. 'straight-connected, nothing in between.'

The big trap for English speakers is that the bare root 직접 is a high-frequency adverb meaning 'in person / by oneself' (직접 만들다 = to make it yourself, 직접 가다 = to go in person) — that 직접 is NOT interchangeable with the adjective-derived 직접적으로, which means 'directly = bluntly/without an intermediary.' So 직접 가다 ('go in person') and 직접적으로 말하다 ('speak bluntly') are different ideas; never swap them. And the connective is 직접적이어서, not 직접적이여서.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 간접적이다 means "to be indirect" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be indirect" is 간접적이다 (ganjeopjeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 간접적으로 듣다 ("to hear (something) secondhand/indirectly"). Watch the particle attached to 간접적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 친구를 통해 간접적으로 들었어요 = 'I heard it indirectly through a friend.'
The polite alternative to a blunt 직접적인 표현.
An effect transmitted through something else, not first-hand.
A fixed compound using the root 간접; literally 'indirect smoking.'

examples.en: That approach is a bit indirect.
examples.note: Simple predicate; notes that something goes the roundabout way.

examples.ko: 그 소식은 친구를 통해 간접적으로 들었어요.
examples.romanization: geu sosigeun chingureul tonghae ganjeopjeogeuro deureosseoyo.
examples.en: I heard that news indirectly through a friend.
examples.note: 간접적으로 듣다/알다 = to learn secondhand.

examples.ko: 한국 사람들은 부탁을 거절할 때 간접적인 표현을 더 선호해요.
examples.romanization: hanguk saramdeureun butageul geojeolhal ttae ganjeopjeogin pyohyeoneul deo seonhohaeyo.
examples.en: Koreans tend to prefer indirect expressions when refusing a request.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 간접적인 표현 is the culturally softer, more polite choice.

extendedVocab.nuance: 간접적이다 (間接的 — 間 'gap/between' + 接 'connect,' i.e. 'connected through a gap/intermediary') is the exact antonym of 직접적이다 and describes anything done or learned via a go-between: 간접적으로 듣다 (hear secondhand), 간접적인 영향 (a knock-on effect), 간접적인 표현 (a softened, roundabout way of putting something). Learning the 직접/간접 pair together pays off, and the root 간접 anchors fixed compounds like 간접흡연 (secondhand smoke) and 간접 경험 (vicarious experience). Register note: in Korean culture 간접적인 표현 is often the polite, face-saving option, so 'indirect' here is frequently a positive — quite unlike the slightly evasive ring of English 'indirect.' Pitfalls: keep 간접 (indirect) and 직접 (direct) straight, and write the connective as 간접적이어서, never 간접적이여서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping 간접 (indirect, 間接) and 직접 (direct, 直接) — they are exact opposites; anchor on 間 'gap/between.'
Writing the connective as 간접적이여서 — the correct form is 간접적이어서.
Reading 간접적인 표현 as evasive/negative — in Korean it's often the polite, considerate choice, not a dodge.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 적극적이다 means "to be active, proactive, enthusiastic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 적극적이다 (jeokgeukjeogida) = "to be active, proactive, enthusiastic". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 적극적으로 참여하다 ("to participate actively") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 적극적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 적극적으로 참여해 주세요 = 'please take part actively' (events, meetings).
A common workplace/school compliment about willingness and drive.

usagePhrases.en: to step up / take the initiative
usagePhrases.note: Describes someone volunteering or pushing things forward.
The antonym; learn the pair 적극적/소극적 together.

examples.en: That person is really proactive.
examples.note: Simple predicate; a warm compliment about someone's drive.

examples.ko: 적극적인 태도 덕분에 좋은 평가를 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jeokgeukjeogin taedo deokbune joeun pyeonggareul badasseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to a proactive attitude, they got a good evaluation.
examples.note: 적극적인 태도 is a stock workplace phrase.

examples.ko: 새 직원이 회의에서 아주 적극적으로 의견을 냈어요.
examples.romanization: sae jigwoni hoeuieseo aju jeokgeukjeogeuro uigyeoneul naesseoyo.
examples.en: The new employee gave opinions very actively in the meeting.
examples.note: Real-situation use: 적극적으로 + 동사 describes eager, take-charge participation.

extendedVocab.nuance: 적극적이다 (積極的 — 積 'accumulate' + 極 'utmost,' i.e. pushing to the fullest extent) describes an energetic, take-initiative attitude and is a strong compliment in workplace and school settings (적극적인 참여, 적극적으로 나서다); its direct antonym is 소극적이다 (消極的, 'passive/timid'), and Koreans habitually use the pair to characterize personality. Distinguish it carefully from 긍정적이다 ('positive/optimistic'): 긍정적 is about outlook and mood (긍정적인 사람 = an upbeat person), while 적극적 is about action and initiative — someone can be cheerful (긍정적) yet still hang back (소극적). Two pitfalls: the opposite of 적극적이다 is 소극적이다, NOT 부정적이다 (which is the antonym of 긍정적, 'negative'); and form the adverb as 적극적으로, never 적극적게. Memorize 적극적 / 소극적 as a matched set, since they are the standard vocabulary for describing how forward someone is.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 적극적이다 (proactive/take-initiative) with 긍정적이다 (positive/optimistic) — one is about action, the other about outlook; they don't always go together.
Thinking the antonym is 부정적이다 — that's the opposite of 긍정적; the true antonym of 적극적이다 is 소극적이다 (passive).
Forming the adverb as 적극적게 — it must be 적극적으로 ('actively/proactively').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 결과 means "result, outcome" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 결과 (gyeolgwa) means "result, outcome". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 시험 결과 ("exam results"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 결과 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 결과 + noun: the result OF something; the modifier comes first, no 의 needed
the verb of 'being released' is 나오다 with 이/가, never 를
attaches to a past-tense verb stem: 노력한 결과 = as a result of having tried
sentence-initial discourse connector linking a cause sentence to its outcome

examples.en: How are your exam results?
examples.note: Simple: 결과 as a plain noun taking 이/가 — note Korean has no plural -s

examples.ko: 검사 결과가 아직 안 나와서 기다리고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geomsa gyeolgwaga ajik an nawaseo gidarigo isseoyo.
examples.en: The test results haven't come out yet, so I'm waiting.
examples.note: Everyday: the fixed collocation 결과가 나오다 for results being released

examples.ko: 일 년 동안 열심히 운동한 결과 몸무게가 십 킬로그램이나 줄었어요.
examples.romanization: il nyeon dongan yeolsimhi undonghan gyeolgwa mommugega sip killogeuraemina jureosseoyo.
examples.en: As a result of exercising hard for a year, my weight dropped by a full 10 kg.
examples.note: Real situation: -(으)ㄴ 결과 turns the whole first clause into the cause of the second

extendedVocab.nuance: 결과 (結果, literally '結 form/bear + 果 fruit', i.e. the fruit that an action bears) is the end outcome of an action or event, and it almost always pairs with 나오다 (come out) or 나타나다 (appear) rather than any verb of 'making'. Its built-in partner is 과정 (the process leading up to it) and its mirror image is 원인 (the cause behind it), so Koreans constantly say 과정도 중요하고 결과도 중요하다. Register is neutral — fine in a doctor's office (검사 결과), a classroom (시험 결과), or a news report. The big English-speaker trap is twofold: first, you do not 'get' a result with a transitive verb the way English does — the result 나오다 (comes out) on its own and takes 이/가, so 결과를 나오다 is wrong; second, do not confuse the outcome 결과 with the reason 원인/이유 — 결과 is what happened at the end, never why.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 결과를 나오다 — 나오다 ('come out') is intransitive, so the result takes 이/가: 결과가 나오다.
결과 is the outcome, not the cause; for 'the reason/cause' use 원인 (objective cause) or 이유 (personal reason), e.g. 사고의 원인, not 사고의 결과, when you mean what triggered it.
Don't force an English plural — there is no 결과들 in 'exam results'; 시험 결과 already covers singular and plural.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 원인 means "cause" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "cause" is 원인 (wonin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사고의 원인 ("the cause of the accident"). Watch the particle attached to 원인 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 원인 names the objective, usually negative, source of a problem; 의 links the two nouns
the investigative collocation; also 원인을 밝히다 = uncover/clarify the cause
X이/가 원인이 되다 = X causes/leads to; subject takes 이/가, not 을/를
habitually modified by 근본적(인) 'fundamental' when discussing deep causes

examples.en: What's the cause of a cold?
examples.note: Simple: 원인 as a plain noun with 의 joining it to 감기

examples.ko: 스트레스가 여러 질병의 원인이 될 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: seuteureseuga yeoreo jilbyeongui wonini doel su isseoyo.
examples.en: Stress can become the cause of various illnesses.
examples.note: Everyday: the X이/가 원인이 되다 pattern, where the cause is the subject

examples.ko: 화재의 정확한 원인은 경찰이 아직 조사하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: hwajaeui jeonghwakan wonineun gyeongchari ajik josahago isseoyo.
examples.en: The police are still investigating the exact cause of the fire.
examples.note: Real situation: 원인 with 조사하다/밝히다 in a serious, investigative register

extendedVocab.nuance: 원인 (原因, '原 origin + 因 reason/factor', the originating factor) is the objective, analytical cause of a result — typically a problem, accident, illness, or phenomenon — and it locks together with 결과 as the textbook 원인과 결과 (cause and effect). The crucial dividing line for English speakers is 원인 vs 이유: 이유 is the personal reason or justification a person gives ('the reason I was late'), something you 말하다/대다 (state/offer), whereas 원인 is an impersonal cause you 찾다/밝히다/조사하다 (find/uncover/investigate). So '왜 늦었어요?' is answered with an 이유, never an 원인. Register is neutral-to-formal, common in news, medicine, and engineering. Watch the particle: the cause is the subject of 되다, so it is 원인이 되다, and you say 'X가 Y의 원인이다' (X is the cause of Y), not the reverse.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 원인 for a personal reason like 'the reason I'm late' — that is 이유 (지각한 이유). 원인 sounds clinical and wrong for human motives.
Say 원인이 되다 ('becomes a cause'), not 원인을 되다 — 되다 takes 이/가 on the thing it turns into.
Don't reverse the of-relation: 'the cause of the accident' is 사고의 원인, not 원인의 사고.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목적 means "purpose, goal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 목적 (mokjeok) = "purpose, goal". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 여행 목적 ("purpose of travel") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 목적, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase on immigration/visa forms; also 방문 목적 = purpose of visit
the right verb is 이루다 (accomplish) or 달성하다, never 하다
describes an intended aim behind an action; 뚜렷한 목적이 있다 = have a clear aim
Verb-는 것이 목적이다 states what the aim is

examples.en: What's the purpose of this gathering?
examples.note: Simple: asking for the aim of an event with 의 + 목적

examples.ko: 이 프로그램의 목적은 외국인을 돕는 것이에요.
examples.romanization: i peurogeuraemui mokjeogeun oegugineul domneun geosieyo.
examples.en: The purpose of this program is to help foreigners.
examples.note: Everyday: the N의 목적은 -는 것이다 framing that defines a purpose

examples.ko: 입국 심사관이 방문 목적을 물어봐서 '관광'이라고 대답했어요.
examples.romanization: ipguk simsagwani bangmun mokjeogeul mureobwaseo 'gwangwang'irago daedapaesseoyo.
examples.en: The immigration officer asked my purpose of visit, so I answered 'tourism'.
examples.note: Real situation: 방문 목적 in the official border-control register every traveler meets

extendedVocab.nuance: 목적 (目的, '目 eye + 的 target' — the target your eye is fixed on) is the conscious aim or intention behind an action, more deliberate and goal-directed than 이유 (the reason behind it) or 원인 (the cause that produced it). Compare the near-synonym 목표: 목표 is a concrete, often measurable target you aim to hit (this month's sales 목표, a finish-line 목표), while 목적 is the underlying purpose or 'what it is for' — a company's 목적 may be 'to help people' but its 목표 is 'sell 1000 units'. Register leans formal/written: it dominates immigration forms (방문 목적), reports, and mission statements. Two pitfalls: do not pair it with 하다 (you 이루다/달성하다 a 목적, you never 목적을 하다), and do not confuse 목적 (purpose) with 목적지 (目的地, 'purpose-place' — the destination, an actual place).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 목적 (purpose, abstract) with 목적지 (destination, a physical place you travel to) — adding 지(地, 'place') changes the meaning entirely.
Use 이루다/달성하다 with 목적, not 하다: 목적을 이루다 ('achieve a purpose'), never 목적을 하다.
Don't use 목적 where 목표 fits: a numeric/concrete target ('my goal is to lose 5 kg') is 목표, while 목적 is the broader 'what it is for'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 과정 means "process, course" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 과정 (gwajeong) means "process, course". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성장 과정 ("the growth process"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 과정 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 과정 follows a noun to name a developmental process over time
Verb-는 과정에서 = while/during the process of; highlights events along the way
the dedicated verb is 거치다 (pass through stages), not 가다
also a formal program: 박사 과정 = a doctoral program

examples.en: The cooking process is fun.
examples.note: Simple: -는 과정 nominalizing 'the process of cooking'

examples.ko: 한국어를 배우는 과정에서 실수를 많이 했어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul baeuneun gwajeongeseo silsureul mani haesseoyo.
examples.en: I made a lot of mistakes in the course of learning Korean.
examples.note: Everyday: -는 과정에서 framing events that happen along the way

examples.ko: 이 신청은 서류 심사, 면접, 최종 발표까지 여러 과정을 거쳐야 해요.
examples.romanization: i sincheongeun seoryu simsa, myeonjeop, choejong balpyokkaji yeoreo gwajeongeul geochyeoya haeyo.
examples.en: This application has to go through several stages: document screening, an interview, and the final announcement.
examples.note: Real situation: 과정을 거치다 listing concrete bureaucratic stages

extendedVocab.nuance: 과정 (過程, '過 pass through + 程 a stage/measured stretch') is the unfolding process — the sequence of stages something passes through over time — and it also doubles as a formal 'course' of study (교육 과정, 박사 과정, 정규 과정). Its natural opposite is 결과 (the final outcome), which is why Koreans pair them: 결과보다 과정이 중요하다. A close relative is 절차, but 절차 is the fixed set of official procedures/steps you must follow (a legal 절차, an application 절차), while 과정 is the broader, more organic course of how things actually develop. The standout pattern is -는 과정에서 'in the course of doing', perfect for describing side-events that occur while a bigger thing happens. Pitfalls: use 거치다 (not 가다) for 'go through stages', and beware the homophone-ish 과장 (誇張 exaggeration, or 課長 a section chief) — a single jamo separates them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 과장 (exaggeration / section chief) when you mean 과정 (process) — they are different words with different hanja.
Use 거치다 with 과정 for 'go through stages' (과정을 거치다), not 가다 — 가다 means physically 'go', not 'pass through a process'.
Don't substitute 과정 for 절차 when you mean fixed official steps: an application's required steps is 신청 절차, while 과정 is the looser overall course.

The standout pattern is -는 과정에서 'in the course of doing', perfect for describing side-events that occur while a bigger thing happens.

過程, '過 pass through + 程 a stage/measured stretch'.
Use 거치다 (not 가다) for 'go through stages', and beware the homophone-ish 과장 (誇張 exaggeration, or 課長 a section chief) — a single jamo separates them.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 관계 means "relationship, relation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "relationship, relation" is 관계 (gwangye). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 인간관계 ("interpersonal relationships"). Watch the particle attached to 관계 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: very common compound (人間關係) for one's web of social ties; written as one word
관계가 좋다/나쁘다 describes the quality of a relationship; subject takes 이/가
이웃과의 관계 = relationship with neighbors; 와/과 marks the other party

usagePhrases.en: be related, have to do with
usagePhrases.note: X와/과 관계가 있다 = is connected to X; 관계없다 = irrelevant

examples.en: I have a good relationship with my friend.
examples.note: Simple: N과의 관계 + 좋다 for relationship quality

examples.ko: 그 일은 저와 아무 관계가 없어요.
examples.romanization: geu ireun jeowa amu gwangyega eopseoyo.
examples.en: That matter has nothing to do with me.
examples.note: Everyday: 관계가 없다 = unrelated, also 'none of my business'

examples.ko: 이번 사건은 그 회사의 자금 문제와 깊은 관계가 있는 것으로 보여요.
examples.romanization: ibeon sageoneun geu hoesaui jageum munjewa gipeun gwangyega inneun geoseuro boyeoyo.
examples.en: This incident appears to be deeply connected to that company's financial troubles.
examples.note: Real situation: abstract 관계가 있다 linking two facts/events in a formal report tone

extendedVocab.nuance: 관계 (關係, '關 a barrier-gate that connects + 係 to tie/link' — a binding link) spans two senses: warm personal relationships (인간관계, 친구 관계, 부부 관계) and abstract relations or connections between facts, events, or ideas. With 있다/없다 it shifts toward 'to be related / have to do with', so 관계없다 / 관계가 없다 is the everyday way to say 'irrelevant' or 'none of my business' (relevant-but-blunter than English). Mark the other party with 와/과, and note the formal genitive 와/과의 관계. A near-synonym is 사이 ('the space between' two people), which is more colloquial and intimate — 우리 사이 좋아 ('we're close') feels warmer and chattier than 우리 관계 좋아, which sounds more analytical. The classic English-speaker slips: never say 관계를 있다 (it must be 관계가 있다), and do not confuse 관계 (relationship) with the look-alike 관심 (關心, interest/attention).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 관계를 있다 — existence/relation takes 이/가: 관계가 있다.
Don't mix up 관심 (interest, 'I'm interested in K-pop' = K팝에 관심이 있다) with 관계 (relationship); they share 관 but mean different things.
For casual closeness between friends, 사이 is often more natural than 관계: 우리 사이 좋아 sounds warmer than 우리 관계 좋아.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 영향 means "influence, effect, impact" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 영향 (yeonghyang) = "influence, effect, impact". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영향을 주다 ("give influence, affect") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 영향, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: X이/가 Y에/에게 영향을 주다 = X affects Y; everyday register
X에게서/에서 영향을 받다 = to be affected by X; the receiving side
more formal than 주다; standard in writing and news
modified by 좋은/나쁜/큰 to describe the effect's quality and size

examples.en: The weather affects my mood.
examples.note: Simple: N에 영향을 주다 — the affected target takes 에, not 을/를

examples.ko: 저는 어릴 때 할머니께 많은 영향을 받았어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun eoril ttae halmeonikke maneun yeonghyangeul badasseoyo.
examples.en: I was greatly influenced by my grandmother when I was little.
examples.note: Everyday: 영향을 받다 with 께 for the respected person who influenced you

examples.ko: 이번 정책은 자영업자들에게 큰 영향을 미칠 것으로 보입니다.
examples.romanization: ibeon jeongchaegeun jayeongeopjadeurege keun yeonghyangeul michil geoseuro boimnida.
examples.en: This policy is expected to have a big impact on the self-employed.
examples.note: Real situation: formal 영향을 미치다 in news/report register

extendedVocab.nuance: 영향 (影響, '影 shadow + 響 echo' — a shadow-and-echo that one thing casts onto another) is influence or impact, and it crucially works in two opposite directions you must keep straight: the source 영향을 주다 / 미치다 (gives/exerts an effect) while the recipient 영향을 받다 (receives/is affected). 미치다 is the formal, news-and-essay verb for 'exert an effect', whereas 주다 is everyday conversation. The decisive English-speaker trap is the particle: the affected target is marked with 에 (for things — 환경에 영향을 주다) or 에게/께 (for people — 아이들에게/부모님께 영향을 주다), NOT with 을/를, because the actual object slot is already filled by 영향(을). So 'it affects the environment' is 환경에 영향을 줘요, never 환경을 영향을 줘요. Compare 효과 (效果, the resulting effect/efficacy of a measure, e.g. 약의 효과 'the medicine's effect'): 영향 is the act of influencing, 효과 is the beneficial result that comes out.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap the direction: the affecter uses 주다/미치다, the affected uses 받다. '나는 영향을 줬어요' means YOU influenced something, not that you were influenced.
Mark the target with 에 (things) or 에게/께 (people), not 을/를: 환경에 영향을 주다, never 환경을 영향을 주다.
Don't use 영향 for the beneficial 'effect' of a remedy — that is 효과 (약의 효과); 영향 is the broader, often neutral act of influencing.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상황 means "situation, circumstances" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 상황 (sanghwang) means "situation, circumstances". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 현재 상황 ("the current situation"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상황 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 상황 follows a noun/modifier naming the state of affairs
상황이 좋다/나쁘다/심각하다 describe how things stand; subject takes 이/가
frames advice or a reaction to a set of conditions
상황에 따라(서) 다르다 = it depends on the situation

examples.en: How's the situation right now?
examples.note: Simple: 상황 with 이/가 asking after the state of things

examples.ko: 이런 상황에서는 어떻게 해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: ireon sanghwangeseoneun eotteoke haeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: In a situation like this, I don't know what I should do.
examples.note: Everyday: 이런 상황에서(는) framing a reaction to circumstances

examples.ko: 회사 사정이 어려워서, 상황에 따라 채용 일정이 바뀔 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: hoesa sajeongi eoryeowoseo, sanghwange ttara chaeyong iljeongi bakkwil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: Since the company is in a tough spot, the hiring schedule may change depending on the situation.
examples.note: Real situation: the hedging phrase 상황에 따라 in a workplace context

extendedVocab.nuance: 상황 (狀況, '狀 condition/form + 況 circumstances' — the configuration of circumstances) describes the overall set of conditions surrounding a moment or event, broader than a single 경우 (a specific case or instance — 이런 경우 = 'in this one case', vs 이런 상황 = 'in this whole situation'). The reflexive phrase 상황에 따라(서) 다르다 ('it depends on the situation') is one of the most useful hedges in Korean, and 이런/그런 상황에서 sets up advice or reactions. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls: keep 상황 (the circumstances around an event) distinct from 상태 (狀態, the state/condition of a single thing or body — 건강 상태 'health condition', 배터리 상태 'battery state'); you describe a person's mood with a 상태, but the events around them with a 상황. And use 에 따라 (not 으로) for 'depending on': 상황에 따라, never 상황으로.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 상황 (the situation/circumstances around an event) with 상태 (the state or condition of a thing or body): 건강 상태, not 건강 상황.
Use 에 따라 for 'depending on the situation', not 으로: 상황에 따라(서), never 상황으로.
For one specific instance, 경우 is sharper than 상황: '이런 경우' = 'in this particular case' vs '이런 상황' = 'in this whole situation'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 조건 means "condition, requirement, terms" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "condition, requirement, terms" is 조건 (jogeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조건이 좋다 ("the terms are good"). Watch the particle attached to 조건 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: common for job/contract terms; 조건이 좋다/나쁘다 rates the deal
갖추다 = to be equipped with / fulfill; also 조건을 만족하다
조건 follows a noun naming the relevant terms (계약 조건 = contract terms)
조건에 맞는 사람 = a person who fits the requirements; 에 맞다, not 을 맞다

examples.en: This job has good terms.
examples.note: Simple: 조건이 좋다 rating an offer's terms

examples.ko: 지원하려면 몇 가지 조건을 갖춰야 해요.
examples.romanization: jiwonharyeomyeon myeot gaji jogeoneul gatchwoya haeyo.
examples.en: To apply, you have to meet a few requirements.
examples.note: Everyday: 조건을 갖추다 = fulfill the requirements

examples.ko: 월급은 마음에 드는데 근무 조건이 안 맞아서 고민이에요.
examples.romanization: wolgeubeun maeume deuneunde geunmu jogeoni an majaseo gominieyo.
examples.en: I like the salary, but the working conditions don't suit me, so I'm torn.
examples.note: Real situation: 근무 조건 weighed in a realistic job-decision context

extendedVocab.nuance: 조건 (條件, '條 an article/clause + 件 an item' — itemized clauses) means both the requirements that must be satisfied and the terms/conditions of an arrangement (jobs, contracts, deals, even relationships). With 갖추다/만족하다 it means 'fulfill requirements'; with 맞다 it means 'fit/match the conditions'; and a great everyday word is 조건이 좋다 ('the terms are good'). It is more concrete than 상황 (the overall circumstances): 조건 are the specific, often listed terms, not the general state of affairs. The number-one English-speaker trap is grammatical interference: 'if' in the sense of a conditional sentence is the verb ending -(으)면, NOT the noun 조건. You cannot say '조건 you come, ...' — say '오면 ...'. Use 조건 only as the noun 'a condition/requirement'. Also note 조건에 맞다 (fit) takes 에, while 조건을 갖추다 (possess/fulfill) takes 을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use the noun 조건 to translate the conjunction 'if' — a conditional clause is the ending -(으)면 ('if you come' = 오면), not 조건.
Say 조건에 맞다 ('fit the conditions') with 에, not 조건을 맞다.
Don't blur 조건 with 상황: 조건 are the specific terms/requirements, while 상황 is the broader surrounding circumstances.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기준 means "standard, criterion, basis" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기준 (gijun) = "standard, criterion, basis". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기준이 높다 ("the standard is high") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기준, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기준이 높다/낮다/엄격하다 describe how strict a standard is

usagePhrases.en: based on / using N as the standard
usagePhrases.note: 성적을 기준으로 = on the basis of grades; do not drop 으로
기준에 맞추다 = to align/adjust to the standard
기준 follows a noun naming what the standard is for (채용 기준 = hiring criteria)

examples.en: The standard is too high.
examples.note: Simple: 기준이 높다 describing a strict benchmark

examples.en: We lined up based on age.
examples.note: Everyday: N을/를 기준으로 = using N as the reference point

examples.ko: 이 제품은 정부의 안전 기준을 모두 통과했습니다.
examples.romanization: i jepumeun jeongbuui anjeon gijuneul modu tonggwahaetseumnida.
examples.en: This product passed all the government's safety standards.
examples.note: Real situation: 안전 기준 + 통과하다 in an official/regulatory register

extendedVocab.nuance: 기준 (基準, '基 foundation + 準 a level/measuring standard' — a foundational measuring line) is the standard or yardstick against which things are measured, judged, or sorted. The workhorse phrase N을/를 기준으로(하다) means 'taking N as the basis/reference point' and is everywhere when explaining how something is organized or decided (나이를 기준으로, 가격을 기준으로). The key contrast is 기준 vs 조건: 기준 is the measuring criterion itself (the bar you measure against), while 조건 is a requirement that must be met — a job's 채용 기준 (hiring criteria, the yardstick) differ from its 지원 조건 (application requirements you must satisfy). Register is neutral-to-formal, heavy in administration, hiring, and regulations. Pitfalls: never drop the 으로 in the set phrase (it is N을 기준으로, not N을 기준), and mind the vowel — 기준 (standard) is not 기분 (氣分, mood/feeling).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't drop 으로 in the set phrase: it is N을/를 기준으로 ('based on N'), not N을 기준.
Don't confuse 기준 (standard) with 기분 (mood/feeling) — one vowel apart but completely different words.
Don't swap 기준 and 조건: 기준 is the yardstick you measure by, 조건 is a requirement you must meet.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정도 means "degree, extent, about" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정도 (jeongdo) means "degree, extent, about". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 어느 정도 ("to some degree, roughly how much"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정도 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to some degree, roughly how much
usagePhrases.note: 어느 정도 알아요 = I know to some extent; also asks 'how much, roughly?'
그 정도면 충분해요 = that much is enough
한 시간 정도 = about an hour; attaches after a quantity
울 정도로 = to the point of crying; shows intensity

examples.en: It takes about an hour.
examples.note: Simple: N 정도 after a quantity = 'approximately'

examples.ko: 한국어를 어느 정도 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul eoneu jeongdo hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can speak Korean to some degree.
examples.note: Everyday: the set phrase 어느 정도 = 'to some extent'

examples.ko: 어제는 말도 못 할 정도로 피곤해서 일찍 잤어요.
examples.romanization: eojeneun maldo mo tal jeongdoro pigonhaeseo iljjik jasseoyo.
examples.en: Yesterday I was tired to the point I couldn't even speak, so I slept early.
examples.note: Real situation: -(으)ㄹ 정도로 conveying how extreme the state was

extendedVocab.nuance: 정도 (程度, '程 a stage/measure + 度 a degree' — a measured degree) expresses degree or extent, and after a number it means 'about/approximately', overlapping with 쯤 but slightly broader: 쯤 attaches tightly to points in time/space (세 시쯤 'around 3'), while 정도 also covers amounts and intensity (열 명 정도 'about ten people', 그 정도 'that much'). The set phrases 어느 정도 ('to some extent') and 그 정도 ('that much') are essential intermediate vocabulary, and the grammar -(으)ㄹ 정도로 ('to the extent/point that') is the go-to way to dramatize how strong something is (죽을 정도로 'to death'). Register is fully neutral. The main English-speaker trap is redundancy: because 정도 already means 'about', do not also add 약 ('approximately') — 약 한 시간 정도 doubles up; pick one, normally 한 시간 정도. Also keep 정도 (degree/extent) apart from the look-alike 제도 (制度, a system/institution).

Don't double up on 'about': 정도 already means 'approximately', so drop the extra 약 — say 한 시간 정도, not 약 한 시간 정도.
Don't confuse 정도 (degree, extent) with 제도 (system, institution) — similar shape, unrelated meanings.
After a number 정도 means 'about'; don't read 세 시 정도 as 'the degree of 3 o'clock' — it just means 'around 3'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 변화 means "change" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "change" is 변화 (byeonhwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 변화가 생기다 ("a change occurs"). Watch the particle attached to 변화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the natural intransitive way to say a change arises; subject takes 이/가
분위기에 변화를 주다 = add a change to the mood/atmosphere
modified by 급격한/큰/작은 to describe scale and speed
the thing you adapt to takes 에: 변화에 적응하다

examples.en: These days the weather changes a lot.
examples.note: Simple: 변화가 심하다 = the change is severe/big

examples.ko: 기분 전환하려고 머리 스타일에 변화를 줬어요.
examples.romanization: gibun jeonhwanharyeogo meori seutaire byeonhwareul jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I changed up my hairstyle for a change of mood.
examples.note: Everyday: 변화를 주다 = deliberately introduce a change for variety

examples.ko: 새로운 환경의 변화에 적응하는 데 거의 반년이 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: saeroun hwangyeongui byeonhwae jeogeunghaneun de geoui bannyeoni geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took nearly half a year to adapt to the changes of the new environment.
examples.note: Real situation: 변화에 적응하다 over a realistic adjustment period

extendedVocab.nuance: 변화 (變化, '變 to alter + 化 to transform' — alteration-and-transformation) is the noun 'change', used for shifts in states, trends, weather, society, technology, or one's life, and it is more abstract and global than the plain verb 변하다/바뀌다 (a specific thing changes). Distinguish 변화를 주다 ('introduce/make a change', usually for freshness or variety) from 변화가 생기다 ('a change occurs' on its own), and mark what you adapt to with 에 (변화에 적응하다). The subtle English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 변화하다 as the verb for everyday change: 변화하다 exists but sounds formal/scientific ('the climate is changing' 기후가 변화하다), so for ordinary 'something changed' use 변하다 or 바뀌다 (전화번호가 바뀌었어요 'my number changed'), and reserve 변화 for the noun. Compare 발전 (發展, development/progress — change specifically in a better, advancing direction), which carries positive growth that neutral 변화 does not.

Say 변화를 주다 ('make/introduce a change') in the 'add variety' sense, not 변화를 하다.
Don't use neutral 변화 when you mean improvement: positive, advancing change is 발전 (회사가 발전했어요), while 변화 is direction-neutral.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 의미 means "meaning, significance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 의미 (uimi) = "meaning, significance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 의미가 있다 ("be meaningful / have a meaning") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 의미, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 의미 있는 일 = a meaningful thing; covers both 'significant' and 'has a meaning'
the everyday way to say something has no point
축하하는 의미에서 = in the spirit of celebrating
결과에 의미를 두다 = to attach significance to the result

examples.en: What does this word mean?
examples.note: Simple: asking a word's meaning — though casual speech often prefers 뜻

examples.en: I prepared a small gift as a token of thanks.
examples.note: Everyday: -는 의미에서 = 'in the sense/spirit of'

examples.ko: 혼자 떠난 여행은 저에게 특별한 의미가 있었어요.
examples.romanization: honja tteonan yeohaengeun jeoege teukbyeolhan uimiga isseosseoyo.
examples.en: The trip I took alone had a special significance for me.
examples.note: Real situation: 의미가 있다 in the deeper 'significance/value' sense

extendedVocab.nuance: 의미 (意味, '意 intention/thought + 味 flavor' — the flavor of an intention) covers both the literal 'meaning' of a word and the deeper 'significance/value' of an experience, so 의미가 있다 elegantly straddles 'has a meaning' and 'is meaningful'. Its near-synonym 뜻 overlaps heavily but skews toward literal word-meaning and is the more colloquial choice: when asking 'what does this mean?' in everyday speech Koreans usually say 무슨 뜻이에요?, saving 의미 for writing or for talking about significance (큰 의미가 있다). The pattern -는 의미에서 ('in the sense/spirit of doing') is a handy intermediate connector for spelling out the intention behind an action. Register is neutral; 뜻 just feels a notch warmer and more spoken. Pitfalls: say 의미가 있다, never 의미를 있다; and don't assume 의미 and 뜻 are always interchangeable — 뜻 also means 'one's will/intention' (그 뜻을 따르다 'follow that wish'), a sense 의미 lacks.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For 'what does this word mean?' both work, but casual speech prefers 뜻: 무슨 뜻이에요? sounds more natural than 무슨 의미예요? in conversation.
Don't say 의미를 있다 — it is 의미가 있다.
Don't treat 뜻 and 의미 as perfect twins: 뜻 also means one's will/intention (부모님의 뜻 'parents' wishes'), a meaning 의미 does not carry.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 역할 means "role, part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 역할 (yeokal) means "role, part". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 역할을 하다 ("play a role"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 역할 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 중요한 역할을 하다 = to play an important role; also for the function of a thing
맡다 = to be put in charge of a role/part; stresses being assigned
modified by 중요한/큰/핵심적인 to rate its weight
splitting up who does what within a team

examples.en: Each person has their own role.
examples.note: Simple: 역할이 있다 = to have a role; 각자 = each person

examples.en: Teachers play an important role for students.
examples.note: Everyday: 역할을 하다 = play/serve a role

examples.ko: 이번 연극에서 저는 주인공 역할을 맡게 되었어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeongeugeseo jeoneun juingong yeokareul matge doeeosseoyo.
examples.en: In this play I ended up taking on the lead role.
examples.note: Real situation: 역할을 맡다 for being cast/assigned a part

extendedVocab.nuance: 역할 (役割, '役 a duty/service + 割 a portion' — the portion of duty allotted to you) is the role or part a person, factor, or even an object plays, covering family members (가족 안에서의 역할), team assignments, and the function of things or causes. 역할을 하다 means 'to play/serve a role', while 역할을 맡다 emphasizes being assigned or taking the part on (맡다 = be put in charge). Pronunciation is a real trap: 역할 is pronounced [여칼], with the final ㄱ aspirating the following ㅎ, so learners who say [역할] sound off; and the single most common native misspelling is 역활 — even Koreans get it wrong, but the standard form is 역할. A near-synonym is 기능 (機能, function), but 기능 is the mechanical/technical function of a system or device (이 버튼의 기능 'this button's function'), while 역할 implies a part played within a larger whole, often by a person. Use 맡다 (not 잡다) for taking on a role.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't write 역활 — even many natives slip, but the correct spelling is 역할 (pronounced [여칼]).
Use 맡다 for taking on a role (역할을 맡다), not 잡다 — 잡다 means physically 'grab/catch'.
Don't swap 역할 and 기능: a device's technical 'function' is 기능 (이 앱의 기능), while 역할 is a part played within a larger whole, usually by a person.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기회 means "chance; opportunity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "chance; opportunity" is 기회 (gihoe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기회가 있어요 ("there is a chance"). Watch the particle attached to 기회 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: existence takes 가, never 를: 기회가 있다
잡다 (grab) is the default verb, not 하다
좋은 modifies the noun directly, no 의
set phrase for a soft, open-ended offer

examples.en: Is there a chance?
examples.note: simplest existence frame with 가 있다

examples.ko: 저는 외국에서 일할 기회를 잡고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun oegugeseo ilhal gihoereul japgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to seize a chance to work abroad.
examples.note: a verb + ㄹ 기회 = 'a chance to do X'

examples.ko: 좋은 기회였는데 그때 안 잡아서 지금도 아쉬워요.
examples.romanization: joeun gihoeyeonneunde geuttae an jabaseo jigeumdo aswiwoyo.
examples.en: It was a good opportunity, but I didn't take it then, so I still regret it.
examples.note: real-talk: 기회를 잡다/놓치다 in past reflection

extendedVocab.nuance: 기회 (機會, 機 'opportune moment/device' + 會 'meeting') is a window of opportunity that may not come twice, so it carries a faint pressure to act. The key contrast is 기회 vs 기능: 기회 is a chance to do something, while 기능 is a 'function/feature.' Koreans treat 기회 as something you physically handle — 기회를 잡다 (seize), 기회를 놓치다 (miss), 기회를 주다/얻다 (give/get) — so the partner verb is concrete, never 기회를 하다. With existence it is 기회가 있다/없다, and 기회가 되면 is a gentle, non-committal 'if the chance comes up.' The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 기회를 하다 by mapping 'take a chance' word-for-word, and don't mark existence with 를 (기회를 있다 ✗ → 기회가 있다 ✓). Register is neutral, fine in both polite speech and writing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기회를 하다 by translating 'take a chance' literally — the verb is 기회를 잡다 (seize) or 기회를 얻다 (get)
Marking existence with 를: 기회를 있다 ✗. Existence always takes 가: 기회가 있다 ✓
Treating 기회 like 기능 (function/feature); they share 기 but mean different things

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 태도 means "attitude" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 태도 (taedo) = "attitude". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 태도가 좋아요 ("the attitude is good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 태도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: describing state takes 가, not 를
바꾸다 (change) takes the object 를
에 대한 = 'toward/about', a fixed frame
신랄한 평가; can sound like a complaint

examples.en: Your attitude is good.
examples.note: simple praise; state-adjective with 가

examples.ko: 그분은 일에 대한 태도가 정말 진지해요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun ire daehan taedoga jeongmal jinjihaeyo.
examples.en: That person's attitude toward work is really serious.
examples.note: 에 대한 태도 = the standard 'attitude toward X' frame

examples.ko: 실수한 뒤에 태도를 싹 바꿔서 다들 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: silsuhan dwie taedoreul ssak bakkwoseo dadeul nollasseoyo.
examples.en: After the mistake he completely changed his attitude, so everyone was surprised.
examples.note: real-situation: 태도를 바꾸다 + adverb 싹 (cleanly/completely)

extendedVocab.nuance: 태도 (態度, 態 'state/manner' + 度 'degree') is the disposition someone reveals through behavior — their stance toward work, people, or a situation. Contrast it sharply with 자세: 자세 can be a literal body posture ('sit up straight' = 자세를 바로 하다) and a metaphorical mindset, but 태도 stays in the mental/behavioral lane and never means physical posture. Habitual collocations are 일에 대한 태도, 태도가 좋다/나쁘다, 태도를 바꾸다, 진지한/적극적인 태도. Note the social weight: 태도가 나쁘다 about a person is a real criticism, so use it carefully with superiors. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'have a good attitude' tempts 태도를 좋다 ✗ — but 좋다 is descriptive, so it must be 태도가 좋다 ✓ (를 only with action verbs like 바꾸다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 태도를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 describes a state, so the particle is 가: 태도가 좋다 ✓
Using 태도 for physical posture — that is 자세 (자세를 바로 하다 'straighten your posture')
Dropping the frame in 'attitude toward X' — Korean needs 에 대한 태도, e.g. 공부에 대한 태도

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 내용 means "content; contents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 내용 (naeyong) means "content; contents". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 내용이 어려워요 ("the content is hard"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 내용 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: descriptive adjective takes 이, not 을
이해하다 (understand) takes object 을
정리하다 = organize/sum up neatly
확인하다 = verify; common in work email

examples.en: The content is hard.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 이

examples.en: I summarized the meeting content briefly and sent it.
examples.note: 내용을 정리하다 — staple office collocation

examples.ko: 문자 내용이랑 실제 약속 시간이 달라서 다시 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: munja naeyongirang silje yaksok sigani dallaseo dasi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: The text's content and the actual appointment time differed, so I checked again.
examples.note: real-situation: 내용 = the substance/wording inside a message

extendedVocab.nuance: 내용 (內容, 內 'inside' + 容 'contain') is the substance or gist inside something — a book, message, lecture, contract — as opposed to its outer form. The sharp contrast is 내용 (what it says) vs 형식 (the form/format): a report can have weak 내용 but proper 형식. Don't confuse it with a physical container either; the box itself is 상자/봉투, while 내용물 specifically means the physical 'contents' (items) inside a package. Typical partners: 내용을 이해하다/정리하다/확인하다, 내용이 어렵다/풍부하다, 회의 내용, 문자 내용. The English-speaker pitfall is particle choice driven by the adjective: 'the content is hard' becomes 내용이 어렵다 ✓, not 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 를/을 attaches only to action verbs like 이해하다, never to descriptive 어렵다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 이: 내용이 어렵다 ✓
Using 내용 for the physical box/wrapper — that is 상자/봉투; physical contents inside are 내용물
Confusing 내용 (substance) with 형식 (form/format) when contrasting what a text says vs how it looks

The sharp contrast is 내용 (what it says) vs 형식 (the form/format): a report can have weak 내용 but proper 형식. Don't confuse it with a physical container either; the box itself is 상자/봉투, while 내용물 specifically means the physical 'contents' (items) inside a package.
內容 = 內 'inside' + 容 'contain' — what is contained within.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 종류 means "kind; type" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

usagePhrases.note: quantity adjective takes 가, not 를
needs 의 before the noun it classifies
여러 (several) attaches directly
같은 종류의 X = 'the same type of X'

examples.en: There are many kinds.
examples.note: simplest frame; 많다 takes 가

examples.en: What kind of music do you like?
examples.note: 어떤 종류의 + noun — the 의 is required

examples.ko: 같은 종류의 제품인데 매장마다 가격이 달라요.

examples.note: real-situation: 같은 종류의 for classifying, not counting

extendedVocab.nuance: 종류 (種類, 種 'seed/kind' + 類 'category') is the type or category something belongs to, so 종류가 많다 means 'there are many varieties.' Using 종류 as a number-counter — to count, use 가지 (세 가지 'three kinds/ways')

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수준 means "level; standard" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 수준 (sujun) = "level; standard". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수준이 높아요 ("the level is high") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

낮다 = low; pair of 높다
noun + 수준 compounds with no particle
높이다 (raise, causative) takes object 을

examples.en: The level is high.
examples.note: state-adjective 높다 with 이

examples.en: My Korean level is still intermediate.
examples.note: noun + 수준: 한국어 수준, no 의 needed

examples.ko: 꾸준히 연습해서 실력 수준을 한 단계 높이고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: kkujunhi yeonseupaeseo sillyeok sujuneul han dangye nopigo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to raise my skill level up one notch by practicing steadily.
examples.note: real-situation: 수준 (overall level) + 단계 (a discrete step)

extendedVocab.nuance: 수준 (水準) literally composes 水 'water' + 準 'level' — picture a carpenter's water level, hence an abstract gauge of where ability or quality sits. It measures how HIGH/LOW something is: 수준이 높다/낮다, 수준을 높이다, 생활 수준, 한국어 수준. The sharp contrast is 수준 vs 단계: 수준 is a continuous level on a scale ('the class is high-level'), while 단계 is a discrete step/stage in a sequence ('move to the next stage' = 다음 단계로). You raise your 수준 but advance through 단계. Note a social caution: saying someone's 수준이 낮다 sounds dismissive about their class/quality, so it can land as an insult. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle — 'the level is high' is 수준이 높다 ✓, not 수준을 높다 ✗; 을 appears only with the action verb 높이다 (raise).

Saying 수준을 높다 ✗ — 높다 is descriptive, so use 이: 수준이 높다 ✓ (을 only with 높이다 'raise')
Confusing 수준 (a level on a scale) with 단계 (a discrete step/stage in a sequence)
Casually saying someone's 수준이 낮다 — it can sound like an insult about their quality or class

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상태 means "state; condition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
