Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: descriptive 좋다 takes 가
나쁘다 (bad), ㅂ-irregular → 나빠요
noun + 상태 compound, no particle
확인하다 (verify) takes object 를

examples.en: The condition is good.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 가

examples.ko: 요즘 잠을 못 자서 건강 상태가 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jameul mot jaseo geongang sangtaega an joayo.
examples.en: I haven't slept well lately, so my health condition isn't good.
examples.note: 건강 상태 + 안 좋다 (negated state)

examples.ko: 중고차라서 사기 전에 상태를 꼼꼼히 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: junggocharaseo sagi jeone sangtaereul kkomkkomhi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Since it's a used car, I checked its condition carefully before buying.
examples.note: real-situation: 상태를 확인하다 about a physical object

extendedVocab.nuance: 상태 (狀態, 狀 'shape/form' + 態 'condition') is the present condition of one specific thing — a person's health, an object, a system — captured at a moment. The sharp contrast is 상태 vs 상황: 상태 zooms in on the CONDITION of a single entity (건강 상태 'health condition'), while 상황 is the broader CIRCUMSTANCE/situation surrounding events (교통 상황 'traffic situation', 지금 상황이 복잡해요). Habitual partners: 상태가 좋다/나쁘다, 상태를 확인하다, 건강/배터리/도로 상태, ~한 상태 ('in a … state'). A handy grammar use: 술에 취한 상태로 = 'in a drunken state.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the condition is good' is 상태가 좋다 ✓ (좋다 descriptive), never 상태를 좋다 ✗; and don't reach for 상황 when you mean one thing's condition.

Saying 상태를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 describes a state, so the particle is 가: 상태가 좋다 ✓
Using 상황 (broad situation) when you mean the condition of one specific thing → 상태
Forgetting the compound has no particle: it is 건강 상태, not 건강의 상태 in everyday speech

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 보이다 (be seen) takes subject 이
a verb + 는 모습 = 'the image of doing'
modifier attaches directly, no 의
떠오르다 = surface/come to mind

examples.en: I can see the figure.
examples.note: 보이다 'be visible' takes 이, intransitive

examples.ko: 오랜만에 친구의 밝은 모습을 봐서 기뻤어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane chinguui balgeun moseubeul bwaseo gippeosseoyo.
examples.en: I was glad to see my friend looking cheerful after so long.
examples.note: 모습을 보다 — here you actively look (보다, takes 를)

examples.ko: 열심히 일하는 부모님의 모습이 아직도 눈에 선해요.
examples.romanization: yeolsimhi ilhaneun bumonimui moseubi ajikdo nune seonhaeyo.
examples.en: The image of my hardworking parents is still vivid in my mind's eye.
examples.note: real-situation: ~하는 모습 + 눈에 선하다 (vividly remembered)

extendedVocab.nuance: 모습 is a native Korean word (고유어, not Sino-Korean) for the visible figure, look, or scene of a person or thing — and crucially the whole impression of how someone appears or behaves, e.g. 일하는 모습 'the sight of someone working.' The sharp contrast is 모습 vs 얼굴: 얼굴 is just the face, whereas 모습 takes in the entire silhouette, manner, and even a remembered image. It also differs from 외모, which is narrowly 'physical looks/attractiveness'; 모습 is more about the captured sight or impression, often with emotional warmth. Watch the transitivity pair: with 보이다 (be visible) use 모습이 보이다 (intransitive, 이); with 보다 (look at) use 모습을 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing these — 모습을 보이다 ✗ for 'something is visible'; that should be 모습이 보이다 ✓ (모습을 보이다 instead means 'to show a certain side of oneself').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 모습을 보이다 to mean 'is visible' — use 모습이 보이다 ✓ (이 + intransitive 보이다)
Using 모습 only for the face — that is 얼굴; 모습 covers the whole figure and manner
Confusing 모습 with 외모 (physical looks/attractiveness) when you mean a captured sight or impression

usagePhrases.note: descriptive 좋다 takes 가
띄우다 (lift) takes object 를
바꾸다 = change the vibe
어색하다 describes a tense vibe

examples.en: The atmosphere is nice.
examples.note: simplest vibe sentence with 가

extendedVocab.nuance: 분위기 (雰圍氣, 雰 'mist/vapor' + 圍 'surround' + 氣 'air/energy') is literally 'the air that surrounds you' — the collective mood of a place, gathering, or moment. The sharp contrast is 분위기 vs 기분: 분위기 is the SHARED vibe in the room (회식 분위기가 좋다), while 기분 is one person's INNER feeling (제 기분이 좋다 'I'm in a good mood'). extendedVocab.nuance: 범위 (範圍, 範 'pattern/model' + 圍 'enclose') is the bounded extent something covers — an exam syllabus, a budget, a topic. examples.en: There is a limit.
examples.note: existence frame with 가 있다

examples.ko: 혼자서 할 수 있는 일에는 한계가 있어요.
examples.romanization: honjaseo hal su inneun ireneun hangyega isseoyo.
examples.en: There's a limit to what I can do alone.
examples.note: ~에는 한계가 있다 = 'there's a limit to ~'

examples.ko: 야근이 계속되니까 이제 체력의 한계를 느껴요.
examples.romanization: yageuni gyesokdoenikka ije cheryeogui hangyereul neukkyeoyo.
examples.en: Since the overtime keeps going, I now feel the limit of my stamina.
examples.note: real-situation: 체력의 한계를 느끼다 — reaching one's ceiling

extendedVocab.nuance: 한계 (限界, 限 'restrict' + 界 'boundary') is the outer ceiling beyond which something can't go — ability, stamina, patience. 한계를 느끼다 means 'to feel you've hit your limit,' and 한계를 넘다/극복하다 means to push past or overcome it. The sharp contrast is 한계 (the LIMIT you cannot exceed) vs 끝 (the plain END point of a thing): a road has an 끝, but human endurance has a 한계 — 끝 is concrete/sequential, 한계 is the abstract maximum. It also differs from 범위 (the SPAN covered, not the ceiling). Habitual partners: 한계가 있다, 한계를 느끼다/넘다/극복하다, 체력의/인내의 한계. The English-speaker pitfall is the existence particle: 'there is a limit' is 한계가 있다 ✓, not 한계를 있다 ✗ — existence always takes 가/이, never 를/을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한계를 있다 ✗ — existence takes 가: 한계가 있다 ✓
Confusing 한계 (the abstract ceiling/limit) with 끝 (the concrete end point of something)
Using 한계 for the span something covers — that breadth is 범위, while 한계 is the outer boundary

extendedVocab.english: moreover; on top of that; what's more
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 더구나 means "moreover; on top of that; what's more" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 더구나 (deoguna) = "moreover; on top of that; what's more". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 더구나 비까지 왔어요 ("and on top of that it even rained") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 더구나, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: and on top of that it even rained
usagePhrases.note: The particle 까지 ('even') loves to sit on the added item, underlining that it's one burden too many
Frequently follows a -은/는데 clause that has already laid out the first reason

usagePhrases.en: especially at a time like now
usagePhrases.note: Stresses that the surrounding circumstances make the added fact land even harder

usagePhrases.en: and on top of it I'm sick too
usagePhrases.note: The 도 on the new clause signals 'this as well,' the natural partner of 더구나

examples.en: It's raining. On top of that, the wind is blowing too.
examples.note: Simple two-sentence stack; note 도 on the second, added point

examples.ko: 그 식당은 비싸요. 더구나 맛도 별로였어요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun bissayo. deoguna matdo byeolloyeosseoyo.
examples.en: That restaurant is expensive. What's more, the food wasn't even good.
examples.note: Everyday complaint that piles a second negative onto the first

examples.ko: 초보자에게는 어려운 책인데, 더구나 분량까지 많아서 다 못 읽었어요.
examples.romanization: chobojaegeneun eoryeoun chaeginde, deoguna bullyangkkaji manaseo da mot ilgeosseoyo.
examples.en: It's a hard book for beginners, and on top of that it's so long that I couldn't finish it.
examples.note: Real situation: 까지 marks the final straw that produced the outcome

extendedVocab.nuance: 더구나 piles an extra fact on top of what you just said, and that extra fact almost always tips the situation further in one direction — usually worse ('and to make matters worse'). Its closest rivals are 게다가 and 더욱이: all three mean 'on top of that,' but 게다가 is the neutral everyday default that happily adds good or bad news, 더욱이 is the most bookish, and 더구나 sits between them, leaning emotional and feeling like the speaker is fed up. It habitually teams up with 도/까지 on the new clause (비도, 사람까지) and trails after a -는데 set-up. It is purely an adverb that opens or links a clause — never a noun. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 더구나 to tack a cheerful, neutral item onto a list ('I bought apples, and moreover bananas'); there 그리고 or 게다가 is right, because 더구나 quietly promises that the addition raises the stakes.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 더구나 to add a positive or purely neutral item ('샀어요, 더구나 바나나도'): it implies the addition intensifies (usually worsens) the situation, so a flat list needs 그리고/게다가 instead.
Treating it as a noun or object ('더구나가 있어요'): it is an adverb that opens or links a clause, so it can never take 이/가 or 을/를.
Forgetting the 도/까지 partner: '비 왔어요. 더구나 추웠어요' feels bare — Koreans naturally say '더구나 춥기까지 했어요' so the 'one more thing' flavor is carried by the particle.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 특히 means "especially; in particular" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 특히 (teuki) means "especially; in particular". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 특히 N을/를 좋아해요 ("I especially like N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 특히 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Singles out one favorite member from a larger set you just named
Sits directly in front of an adjective to boost that one quality
The set phrase 그중에서도 ('even among those') often leads into 특히 to narrow down
특히나 is a slightly stronger, more colloquial variant of 특히

examples.ko: 저는 과일을 좋아하는데, 특히 딸기를 제일 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun gwaireul joahaneunde, teuki ttalgireul jeil joahaeyo.
examples.en: I like fruit, and I especially like strawberries the most.
examples.note: Simple: state the category, then 특히 zooms to one item

examples.ko: 이번 시험은 특히 듣기 부분이 어려웠어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon siheomeun teuki deutgi bubuni eoryeowosseoyo.
examples.en: This time the exam was especially hard in the listening section.
examples.note: Everyday: 특히 highlights which part stood out from the rest

examples.ko: 주말에는 사람이 많은데, 특히 일요일 오후가 제일 붐벼요.
examples.romanization: jumareneun sarami maneunde, teuki iryoil ohuga jeil bumbyeoyo.
examples.en: It's crowded on weekends, and Sunday afternoons in particular are the most packed.
examples.note: Real situation: narrows a general statement down to the worst case

extendedVocab.nuance: 특히 (Sino-Korean 特, 'special/distinct') points at one member of a group and says 'this one stands out from the rest' — exactly English 'especially' or 'in particular.' The word it constantly gets confused with is its sibling 특별히 (特別, 'special-distinct'): 특히 selects the most notable item from a set, while 특별히 says something was done in a special, deliberate way ('특별히 준비했어요' = I went out of my way to prepare it). Picture 특히 as a spotlight that picks one face out of a crowd, and 특별히 as the extra effort behind a gesture. 특히 naturally rides after a general statement and then pinpoints the exception, and it loves the lead-in 그중에서도. The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 특히 to mean 'I did it specially' — that intent meaning belongs to 특별히, not 특히.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 특히 (singling out one from a group) with 특별히 (doing something in a special/deliberate way): '특히 준비했어요' wrongly says 'I prepared it, of all things,' when you mean '특별히 준비했어요' (I made special preparations).
Parking 특히 far from the item it highlights so the listener can't tell what is being singled out: keep it right next to that word — 특히 듣기가, not 특히 ... 듣기가 ... 어려웠어요 with words in between.
Trying to negate with 특히 ('not especially'): the idiomatic 'not particularly' uses 특별히 + 부정 (특별히 어렵지 않아요), so don't say '특히 어렵지 않아요.'

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주로 means "mainly; mostly; usually" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "mainly; mostly; usually" is 주로 (juro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주로 V해요 ("I mainly do V"). Watch the particle attached to 주로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: States your dominant habit while leaving room for exceptions
Marks the place where something typically happens
Identifies the chief object, target, or ingredient
Often follows a time frame to describe what usually fills it

examples.en: On weekends I mostly rest at home.
examples.note: Simple: 주로 describes the typical, default pattern

examples.en: Mostly students come to this cafe.
examples.note: Everyday: marks the dominant kind of customer, not 'only'

examples.ko: 점심은 주로 회사 근처에서 간단히 먹는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: jeomsimeun juro hoesa geuncheoeseo gandanhi meongneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: I usually eat lunch simply near the office.
examples.note: Real situation: 주로 + -는 편이다 softens it to 'as a rule, tend to'

extendedVocab.nuance: 주로 (Sino-Korean 主, 'main/principal') means 'mainly/mostly' and names the dominant case among several options, leaving the door open for exceptions. It overlaps with 보통 ('usually') and 대부분 ('for the most part'), but the dividing line is what each emphasizes: 보통 is about frequency over time, 대부분 is about proportion/quantity, and 주로 is about which option is the principal one ('주로 버스로 다녀요' = the bus is my main mode, though not the only one). It is the natural word for describing habits, typical locations, and the main type of thing involved. Crucially it is strictly an adverb here, not the noun 주류 ('the mainstream') that shares the 主 root. The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'mostly' slide into 'always': 주로 signals a strong tendency, so if you truly mean 100%, you need 항상 or 늘 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 주로 to mean 'absolutely always': it names a tendency, so for a no-exceptions claim use 항상/늘 — '저는 항상 집에서 쉬어요' is total, '주로' is just usual.
Confusing the adverb 주로 with the noun 주류 ('mainstream/alcoholic beverages'): here it can only modify a verb or adjective, never take a particle like 주로가.
Reaching for 주로 to talk about pure frequency ('I mostly go three times a week'): for counting how often, 보통 fits better, while 주로 is for which option dominates.

structuredNuance.t: 주로 means 'mainly/mostly' and names the dominant case among several options, leaving the door open for exceptions. It is the natural word for describing habits, typical locations, and the main type of thing involved.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비교적 means "relatively; comparatively" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 비교적 (bigyojeok) = "relatively; comparatively". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 비교적 쉬워요 ("it's relatively easy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 비교적, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Sits in front of an adjective to soften the claim against an unstated standard
Can name the yardstick explicitly with -에 비해

usagePhrases.en: it's on the relatively small side
usagePhrases.note: Often pairs with -은/는 편이다 to hedge an amount or degree
Modifies time words too: 'fairly recently, as these things go'

examples.en: This neighborhood is relatively quiet.
examples.note: Simple: hedges the claim against other areas you have in mind

examples.ko: 오늘은 비교적 일이 적어서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun bigyojeok iri jeogeoseo iljjik toegeunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Today there was comparatively little work, so I left early.
examples.note: Everyday: implies 'less than usual,' an implicit comparison to normal days

examples.ko: 한국어 발음은 영어에 비해 비교적 규칙적이라서 배우기 쉬워요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo bareumeun yeongeoe bihae bigyojeok gyuchikjeogiraseo baeugi swiwoyo.
examples.en: Korean pronunciation is relatively regular compared to English, so it's easy to learn.
examples.note: Real situation: -에 비해 makes the standard explicit

extendedVocab.nuance: 비교적 (Sino-Korean 比較的, literally '比較 comparison' + the 的 '-ish/in-the-manner-of' suffix) means 'relatively/comparatively' and tells the listener that the quality holds only against some standard, not in absolute terms. That hedge makes you sound careful and measured. Set it against 꽤 and 좀: 꽤 means 'quite/considerably' as a plain intensifier with no comparison built in, 좀 just means 'a bit,' while 비교적 specifically invokes a yardstick ('relative to other options'). Unlike 별로, it carries no negative bias — 비교적 can be relatively good or relatively bad. Because of the 的 suffix it stays adverbial and never conjugates: you cannot say 비교적이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that — turning 'relative' into a predicate; in Korean 비교적 only modifies (비교적 쉬워요), and there should always be at least an implied point of comparison behind it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Conjugating it as a predicate ('이 일은 비교적이에요'): the 的 makes 비교적 adverb-only, so it must modify something — 비교적 쉬워요, 비교적 빨라요.
Using it where there is genuinely nothing to compare against: 비교적 needs a baseline (even unspoken), so for a flat statement with no yardstick, plain 좀/꽤 is better.
Treating 비교적 as a strong intensifier like 'very': it actually tones a claim down to 'relatively,' so '비교적 어려워요' means moderately hard, not extremely hard — for 'very' use 아주/정말.

structuredNuance.t: 비교적 means 'relatively/comparatively' and tells the listener that the quality holds only against some standard, not in absolute terms. That hedge makes you sound careful and measured.

extendedVocab.english: on the whole; generally; for the most part
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 대체로 means "on the whole; generally; for the most part" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 대체로 (daechero) means "on the whole; generally; for the most part". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 대체로 만족해요 ("I'm generally satisfied"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 대체로 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Extremely common in reviews and overall evaluations
Gives a big-picture verdict that tolerates minor exceptions
Smooths over small differences to state the overall impression
Often sets up a 'mostly good, with one caveat' structure

examples.en: The food at this restaurant is generally good.
examples.note: Simple: an overall verdict, not a claim about every dish

examples.ko: 호텔은 대체로 깨끗했지만 와이파이가 좀 느렸어요.
examples.romanization: hotereun daechero kkaekkeutaetjiman waipaiga jom neuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: The hotel was on the whole clean, though the Wi-Fi was a bit slow.
examples.note: Everyday: -지만 carves out the one exception to the general impression

examples.ko: 설문 결과를 보면 사람들은 대체로 새 정책에 찬성하는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: seolmun gyeolgwareul bomyeon saramdeureun daechero sae jeongchaege chanseonghaneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: Looking at the survey, people seem to generally support the new policy.
examples.note: Real situation: summarizes a broad trend across many responses

extendedVocab.nuance: 대체로 (Sino-Korean 大體, 'the 大 large 體 body/substance' → the main gist) delivers an overall, big-picture judgment — 'on the whole' — while quietly admitting that small exceptions exist. It is the natural word for summaries and evaluations and sounds a touch analytical. Compare it with 주로 and 보통: 주로 picks the single dominant case ('주로 학생이 와요' = mainly students), whereas 대체로 averages over the whole situation to state a general tendency ('대체로 만족스러워요' = satisfied overall, weighing everything). It often pairs with -지만 to add the one caveat. Do not confuse 대체로 with the look-alike 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth') used in exasperated questions like '대체 왜?' — same first syllable, unrelated meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is using 대체로 about a single concrete event ('today's lunch was generally good'); it describes overall tendencies across a set, so for one instance you would just say 맛있었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 대체로 for one single, concrete instance ('오늘 점심은 대체로 맛있었어요'): it sums up an overall tendency across many cases, so for a single event just say 맛있었어요.
Confusing it with 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth/in the world') in questions: '대체 왜 그래요?' is exasperation, while 대체로 is 'on the whole' — same syllable, opposite job.
Swapping 대체로 and 주로 freely: 주로 names the dominant option, 대체로 gives an averaged overall verdict, so 'mainly students come' is 주로, while 'the service was good overall' is 대체로.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 일반적으로 means "generally; in general; typically" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "generally; in general; typically" is 일반적으로 (ilbanjeogeuro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일반적으로 A/V ("generally, A/V"). Watch the particle attached to 일반적으로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: States what is usually true as a rule or principle
A set lead-in that opens a broad generalization
The adjective form 일반적이다 modifies nouns directly
Frequently sets up a norm to be contrasted with exceptions

examples.en: Generally, the weather is warm in spring.
examples.note: Simple: states a rule-of-thumb truth

examples.en: Generally, symptoms like these get better within a few days.
examples.note: Everyday: gives a typical expectation, the explanatory register of a doctor or article

examples.ko: 일반적으로 말하면, 경험이 많을수록 일이 수월해져요.
examples.romanization: ilbanjeogeuro malhamyeon, gyeongheomi maneulsurok iri suwolhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: Generally speaking, the more experience you have, the easier the work becomes.
examples.note: Real situation: 말하면 frames a broad principle before stating it

extendedVocab.nuance: 일반적으로 (Sino-Korean 一般, 'one-kind' → ordinary/common, + 的 + the adverbial -으로) introduces a general rule or what is typically the case — 'in general,' 'typically.' It is noticeably more formal and explanatory than the everyday 보통, which is why it dominates writing, explanations, and academic-leaning speech, whereas 보통 fits casual chat ('보통 7시에 일어나요'). Think of 일반적으로 as the voice of a textbook or an expert stating a norm. Its built-in counterpart is 예외적으로 ('as an exception'), and the two often frame a rule-versus-exception contrast. The form matters: the adverbial -으로 is obligatory, so you cannot drop it and use bare 일반적 as an adverb (that stem only lives inside 일반적인 N or 일반적이다). The English-speaker pitfall is using this formal word for personal habits ('I generally wake at seven'); for your own routines 주로/보통 sound far more natural than 일반적으로.

Using formal 일반적으로 for personal habits ('저는 일반적으로 7시에 일어나요'): for your own routine 보통/주로 are natural, and 일반적으로 sounds like you're stating a societal law about yourself.
Forgetting it sets up a norm vs. exception: pairing it with a one-off surprise is odd, since 일반적으로 invites the implicit 'but sometimes 예외적으로…' frame.

usagePhrases.note: Marks a deliberate, out-of-the-ordinary effort
Common collocation: deliberately paying extra attention

usagePhrases.en: there's nothing in particular I want to V
usagePhrases.note: 특별히 + negative is the idiomatic 'not really / nothing special'
특별히 = in a special way; 특히 = singled out from a group

examples.ko: 오늘은 손님이 와서 특별히 음식을 많이 준비했어요.
examples.romanization: oneureun sonnimi waseo teukbyeolhi eumsigeul mani junbihaesseoyo.
examples.en: We have guests today, so I specially prepared a lot of food.
examples.note: Simple: emphasizes deliberate, beyond-the-usual effort

examples.ko: 특별히 가고 싶은 곳은 없어요. 아무 데나 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: teukbyeolhi gago sipeun goseun eopseoyo. amu dena gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: There's no place I particularly want to go. Anywhere is fine.
examples.note: Everyday: the very common 특별히 + 없다 'nothing in particular' pattern

examples.ko: 선생님이 저를 특별히 챙겨 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi jeoreul teukbyeolhi chaenggyeo jusyeoseo jeongmal gamsahaesseoyo.
examples.en: The teacher looked after me especially well, so I was really grateful.
examples.note: Real situation: marks special, individualized treatment toward one person

extendedVocab.nuance: 특별히 (Sino-Korean 特別, 'special-distinct') means doing or feeling something in a special, deliberate, out-of-the-ordinary way, and in negative sentences it softens into 'not particularly.' Its constant point of confusion is 특히 ('especially'): 특별히 is about the special manner or intent behind an action ('특별히 만들었어요' = I made it specially, with effort), while 특히 just selects the standout item from a set ('과일 중에 특히 딸기' = strawberries above the other fruits). A useful mental split: 특별히 answers 'in what way?' (specially), 특히 answers 'which one?' (that one). 특별히 strongly favors negative frames — 특별히 ~없어요/않아요 is the everyday way to say 'nothing in particular / not really.' The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: using 특별히 when you mean 'among these, especially X' (that's 특히), and forgetting that the most natural 'not especially' is precisely 특별히 + a negative, not 특히 + a negative.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 특별히 where you mean 'among these, especially X' ('과일 중에 특별히 딸기'): selecting one from a group is 특히 — 특별히 would imply the strawberry was treated in some special way.
Forgetting that 'not particularly / nothing in particular' is idiomatically 특별히 + negative: say '특별히 어렵지 않아요' / '특별히 없어요,' not 특히 어렵지 않아요.
Reading 특별히 as plain 'very': it means 'in a special/deliberate way,' so '특별히 비싸요' implies an unusual, pointed expensiveness, not a generic 'very expensive' (that's 아주 비싸요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 무엇보다 means "above all; more than anything" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 무엇보다 (mueotboda) means "above all; more than anything". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무엇보다 중요해요 ("it's important above all"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 무엇보다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: The signature collocation — flags the single most important point
Adding -도 to 무엇보다 strengthens the 'above absolutely all' feel
A common lead-in that announces your key point
Stresses priority in both order and importance

examples.en: Health is more important than anything.
examples.note: Simple: the textbook 무엇보다 + 중요하다 pairing

examples.ko: 여러 이유가 있지만, 무엇보다 가족과 가까워서 이 동네를 골랐어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo iyuga itjiman, mueotboda gajokgwa gakkawoseo i dongnereul gollasseoyo.
examples.en: There are several reasons, but above all I chose this neighborhood to be near family.
examples.note: Everyday: highlights the decisive reason among many

examples.ko: 새 직장은 무엇보다도 분위기가 좋아서 정말 마음에 들어요.
examples.romanization: sae jikjangeun mueotbodado bunwigiga joaseo jeongmal maeume deureoyo.
examples.en: More than anything, I really like my new workplace because the atmosphere is good.
examples.note: Real situation: 무엇보다도 points to the top factor in a personal judgment

extendedVocab.nuance: 무엇보다 (literally 무엇 'what' + 보다 'than') is a fixed expression — 'than anything,' i.e. 'above all / more than anything' — that elevates one point over everything else, not just over one rival. It is the go-to way to mark your top priority or the most decisive factor when several are in play, and it pairs especially naturally with 중요하다. Adding -도 gives 무엇보다도, slightly more emphatic. Compare it with 특히 ('especially'), which merely spotlights a notable member of a group without ranking it first; 무엇보다 actively crowns one thing #1. It works in both speech and writing and feels warm and emphatic. The English-speaker pitfall is taking 보다 literally as a two-item comparison ('better than what?') and trying to name a single rival noun after it — 무엇보다 is frozen as 'above all,' comparing one point against the entire field, so don't parse it as 'than what' or expect a specific 'than X' object.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 무엇보다 as a two-noun comparison and inserting a rival ('커피보다 무엇보다'): it is fixed as 'above all,' ranking one point over the whole field, not against one named thing.
Reading it literally as 'than what': 무엇 here doesn't ask a question — 무엇보다 functions as a set discourse phrase meaning 'above all / most of all.'
Confusing it with 특히: 특히 just spotlights a standout from a group, while 무엇보다 ranks one thing as the single most important, so 'health is #1' needs 무엇보다, not 특히.

extendedVocab.english: never; by no means (with a negative)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 결코 means "never; by no means (with a negative)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "never; by no means (with a negative)" is 결코 (gyeolko). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 결코 V지 않다 ("never V; by no means V"). Watch the particle attached to 결코 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: never V; by no means V
usagePhrases.note: Must be completed by a negative predicate — the core pattern
Very common with adjective + -지 않다 for emphatic denial
Pairs with 아니다 to firmly reject an identity or quality
결코 is more written/formal; 절대로 is the spoken everyday twin

examples.ko: 저는 그 약속을 결코 잊지 않을 거예요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu yaksogeul gyeolko itji aneul geoyeyo.
examples.en: I will never forget that promise.
examples.note: Simple: 결코 demands the negative 잊지 않다 to land

examples.en: This was by no means an easy decision.
examples.note: Everyday: pairs with 아니다 to emphatically deny a quality

examples.ko: 그분은 결코 그런 말을 할 사람이 아니에요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun gyeolko geureon mareul hal sarami anieyo.
examples.en: He is by no means the kind of person who would say that.
examples.note: Real situation: firmly defends someone by rejecting a possibility

extendedVocab.nuance: 결코 is an emphatic negative adverb — 'never / by no means / not in the slightest' — and its defining rule is that it MUST co-occur with a negative ending such as -지 않다, 아니다, or 없다. It cannot stand alone or sit with a plain affirmative verb; the sentence feels broken without the negation. Its everyday partner is 절대(로): the two are close in meaning, but 결코 is more formal, written, and declaration-like (oaths, firm statements, editorials), while 절대로 is what you actually say out loud in conversation. 전혀 ('not at all') also negates but answers 'to what degree' (전혀 안 매워요), whereas 결코 conveys resolute 'never under any circumstances.' The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto English 'never,' which can stand in a positive-looking sentence ('I never go') — Korean 결코 cannot float free; you must supply the negative predicate, so 'I will never go' becomes '결코 가지 않을 거예요,' never '결코 갈 거예요.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing 결코 with an affirmative predicate ('결코 갈 거예요'): it structurally requires a negative — -지 않다 / 아니다 / 없다 — so the correct form is '결코 가지 않을 거예요.'
Using formal 결코 in light, casual chat where 절대(로) or 전혀 fits: '결코' in a relaxed conversation sounds stiff or theatrical; spoken Korean prefers '절대 안 그래' / '전혀 안 매워요.'
Assuming 결코 alone already means 'no' like English 'never' can: it only colors a clause that is itself negated, so it can't carry the negation by itself.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마침내 means "finally; at last; in the end" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 마침내 (machimnae) = "finally; at last; in the end". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 마침내 V했어요 ("finally, V happened") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 마침내, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Caps a long, drawn-out process with its awaited result

usagePhrases.en: after a long N, at last
usagePhrases.note: Often follows '오랜 ~ 끝에' (after long effort/waiting)
Common with achievement verbs to mark a hard-won success
마침내 is more literary/weighty; 드디어 is more spoken and excited

examples.en: The long-awaited news finally arrived.
examples.note: Simple: 마침내 frames the result as the end of a long wait

examples.ko: 몇 년 동안 준비한 끝에 마침내 시험에 합격했어요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon dongan junbihan kkeute machimnae siheome hapgyeokaesseoyo.
examples.en: After preparing for years, I finally passed the exam.
examples.note: Everyday: '~ 끝에' supplies the long effort that 마침내 caps

examples.ko: 여러 번 실패했지만 마침내 원하던 결과를 얻었어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo beon silpaehaetjiman machimnae wonhadeon gyeolgwareul eodeosseoyo.
examples.en: I failed several times, but in the end I got the result I wanted.
examples.note: Real situation: closes a struggle with the hard-won outcome

extendedVocab.nuance: 마침내 (native Korean) means 'finally / at last' and frames an outcome as the culmination of a long process, sustained effort, or anxious wait — it carries the weight of something hard-won. Its everyday twin is 드디어: both mean 'finally,' but 드디어 is warmer, more spoken, and bursts with the speaker's excitement ('드디어 끝났다!'), while 마침내 is more literary, composed, and narrative — the word a novel or news report uses to crown a climax. A third cousin, 결국 ('in the end / after all'), can mark a neutral or even disappointing conclusion, whereas 마침내 implies the end was awaited and welcome. It loves the set-up '오랜 노력 끝에.' Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't use 마침내 for trivial 'and then finally' sequencing (just listing steps) — it promises a significant, awaited result — and don't confuse it with the look-alike 마침 ('as it happens / just in time'), e.g. '마침 너를 만났네,' which is about lucky coincidence, not culmination.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 마침내 for trivial step-sequencing ('먼저 씻고, 마침내 잤어요'): it implies a meaningful, long-awaited result, so plain sequencing wants 그다음에/마지막으로 instead.
Confusing 마침내 ('at last, after a long process') with 마침 ('as it happens / just in time'): '마침 시간이 있었어요' means 'I happened to have time,' a coincidence, not a culmination.
Substituting 마침내 wherever English says 'in the end' even for letdowns: a disappointing or merely neutral conclusion is 결국 ('결국 안 됐어요'), since 마침내 leans toward a welcome, hard-won outcome.

extendedVocab.english: on the contrary; conversely; the other way around
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 반대로 means "on the contrary; conversely; the other way around" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 반대로 (bandaero) means "on the contrary; conversely; the other way around". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is A. 반대로 B. ("A. Conversely, B."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반대로 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Links two opposite situations across sentences

usagePhrases.en: to do it the other way around
usagePhrases.note: Concrete physical sense: reversed manner or direction
오히려 strengthens it into 'no — the reverse, against expectation'
The 과/와 marks the specific reference point being reversed

examples.ko: 형은 활발한데, 반대로 동생은 아주 조용해요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeun hwalbalhande, bandaero dongsaengeun aju joyonghaeyo.
examples.en: The older brother is outgoing; conversely, the younger one is very quiet.
examples.note: Simple: contrasts two people directly

examples.ko: 쉬울 거라고 생각했는데 반대로 정말 어려웠어요.
examples.romanization: swiul georago saenggakaenneunde bandaero jeongmal eoryeowosseoyo.
examples.en: I thought it would be easy, but on the contrary it was really hard.
examples.note: Everyday: reverses the speaker's expectation

examples.ko: 설명서와 반대로 조립해서 다시 해야 했어요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongseowa bandaero joripaeseo dasi haeya haesseoyo.
examples.en: I assembled it the opposite way from the manual, so I had to redo it.
examples.note: Real situation: 'in the reverse manner,' with 과/와 naming the reference

extendedVocab.nuance: 반대로 (Sino-Korean 反對, '反 anti/reverse + 對 face/oppose' → opposition) means 'the opposite way,' covering both 'on the contrary' (contrasting facts or expectations) and 'the other way around' (reversed manner or direction). Compare it with the connector 반면(에) ('whereas/on the other hand'): 반면(에) calmly sets two differing facts side by side ('도시는 편리한 반면 복잡해요'), while 반대로 points to an actual, literal opposite — a flipped action, a reversed direction, or an outcome contrary to what was expected. So 'the manual said left, I went right' is 반대로, but 'the city is convenient, whereas the countryside is quiet' is more naturally 반면에. When you reverse a specific reference, keep the 과/와: 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 반대로 as a neutral 'on the other hand' clause-linker where 반면(에) belongs — 반대로 specifically signals a true opposite, not merely a different angle.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 반대로 as a neutral 'on the other hand' where two facts merely differ ('도시는 편리하고 반대로 시골은 조용해요'): a calm side-by-side contrast prefers 반면(에); 반대로 implies a true reversal.
Dropping the particle in 'N과/와 반대로' ('설명서 반대로'): when reversing a specific reference, the 과/와 is needed — 설명서와 반대로, 예상과 반대로.
Confusing it with 거꾸로: 거꾸로 is physically upside-down/backwards ('티셔츠를 거꾸로 입었어요'), while 반대로 is the broader 'opposite/conversely,' so 'wore it inside-out' is 거꾸로, not 반대로.

Compare it with the connector 반면(에) ('whereas/on the other hand'): 반면(에) calmly sets two differing facts side by side ('도시는 편리한 반면 복잡해요'), while 반대로 points to an actual, literal opposite — a flipped action, a reversed direction, or an outcome contrary to what was expected. Sino-Korean 反對, '反 anti/reverse + 對 face/oppose' → opposition.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 오로지 means "only; solely; entirely" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "only; solely; entirely" is 오로지 (oroji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 오로지 N만 ("only N (and nothing else)"). Watch the particle attached to 오로지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Habitually closes with -만 to seal the exclusivity

usagePhrases.en: solely for the sake of N
usagePhrases.note: Stresses a single dedicated purpose
Pairs with -ㄹ 뿐이다 for 'merely/only'
오로지 conveys single-minded, wholehearted devotion

examples.ko: 그동안 오로지 가족만 생각하며 일해 왔어요.
examples.romanization: geudongan oroji gajongman saenggakamyeo ilhae wasseoyo.
examples.en: All this time I've worked thinking only of my family.
examples.note: Simple: the -만 partner seals 'only family, nothing else'

examples.ko: 이 결과는 오로지 본인의 노력 덕분이에요.
examples.romanization: i gyeolgwaneun oroji boninui noryeok deokbunieyo.
examples.en: This result is entirely thanks to your own effort.
examples.note: Everyday: attributes a cause to one factor alone

examples.ko: 그 선수는 오로지 우승만을 목표로 몇 년을 훈련했어요.
examples.romanization: geu seonsuneun oroji useungmaneul mokpyoro myeon nyeoneul hullyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: That athlete trained for years aiming solely at the championship.
examples.note: Real situation: 오로지 + 만을 marks one exclusive, all-consuming goal

extendedVocab.nuance: 오로지 (native Korean) means 'only / solely / entirely' and emphasizes single-minded exclusivity — one purpose, one person, one cause, with everything else shut out. Its near-synonym is 오직, and both mean 'only,' but the dividing line is emotional temperature: 오직 is plainer and more matter-of-fact, while 오로지 carries a warmer, almost devotional weight, suggesting wholehearted dedication ('오로지 너만을 위해'). It naturally leans on -만 or -뿐 to complete the 'and nothing else' meaning. Crucially, 오로지 is about exclusive focus, not about small quantities — it is NOT the 'only/just X items' of counting. The English-speaker pitfall flows from that: English 'only' covers both devotion ('I think only of you') and scarcity ('only three left'), but Korean splits them — use 오로지/오직 for exclusive focus and 단지/겨우 for 'merely/only (so few),' so 'only three remain' is '겨우 세 개 남았어요,' never 오로지 세 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 오로지 for small quantities ('오로지 세 명 왔어요'): scarcity 'only/just' is 단지/겨우, so say '겨우 세 명 왔어요' — 오로지 is exclusive focus, not a low count.
Dropping the supporting -만/-뿐 ('오로지 가족 생각했어요'): the 'only' sense needs the partner particle — '오로지 가족만 생각했어요' completes it.
Treating 오로지 and 오직 as identical in tone: 오직 is neutral and crisp, while 오로지 adds wholehearted, devotional warmth, so an emotional dedication line ('오로지 너를 위해') loses force if flattened to 오직.

extendedVocab.english: in a word; in short; to put it simply
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 한마디로 means "in a word; in short; to put it simply" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 한마디로 (hanmadiro) = "in a word; in short; to put it simply". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 한마디로 N이다 ("in a word, it's N") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 한마디로, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Sums the whole thing up with a single blunt label

usagePhrases.en: to put it in one word
usagePhrases.note: The fuller set form that explicitly announces a summary
Variant lead-in, slightly more 'let me be frank'
한마디로 is punchier, more spoken and opinionated

examples.en: That movie was, in a word, a waste of time.
examples.note: Simple: compresses a whole judgment into one phrase

examples.en: To put it simply, we just weren't prepared enough.
examples.note: Everyday: 말하면 leads into a blunt one-line summary

examples.ko: 새 제도는 복잡해 보여도 한마디로 누구에게나 공평한 제도예요.
examples.romanization: sae jedoneun bokjapae boyeodo hanmadiro nuguegena gongpyeonghan jedoyeyo.
examples.en: The new system may look complex, but in short it's one that's fair to everyone.
examples.note: Real situation: cuts through detail to deliver the bottom line

extendedVocab.nuance: 한마디로 (native Korean: 한 'one' + 마디 'a word/segment of speech' + -로 'by/in') means 'in a word / in short' and signals that you are about to condense everything into one blunt summary or label. It is conversational and usually evaluative — you reach for it right before dropping your bottom line, often a verdict ('한마디로 별로예요'). Compare it with the more neutral, businesslike 요약하면 ('to summarize'): 요약하면 sounds like minutes of a meeting, while 한마디로 sounds like a friend cutting to the chase with an opinion. Its fuller forms 한마디로 말하면 / 한마디로 말해서 are equally common. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't follow 한마디로 with a long, multi-clause explanation — it literally promises ONE short takeaway, so keep what comes after crisp — and don't parse it word-for-word as 'with one word said'; it is a frozen discourse marker meaning 'in short / to sum up,' so the listener expects a punchy summary, not a literal single vocabulary word.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Reading it literally as 'with one word' and then giving a literal single noun only: 한마디로 is a set marker for 'in short,' and the summary can be a short clause, not strictly one vocabulary word.
Using punchy, opinionated 한마디로 in a formal neutral report where 요약하면/정리하면 fits: 한마디로 carries an evaluative, conversational tone that can sound too blunt in dry writing.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사업 means "business; enterprise; venture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사업 (saeop) means "business; enterprise; venture". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사업을 하다 ("to run a business"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사업 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 사업하다 is also one verb; once you add the object marker 을 you must split it: 사업을 하다
시작하다 = to begin; 사업을 차리다 (to set up a business) is a more colloquial alternative
잘되다 is one word and intransitive; the opposite is 사업이 안되다 (business is doing badly)
계획 = plan; 사업 모델, 사업 분야, 사업 자금 also use 사업 as a bare modifier (no 의)

examples.en: I want to run a small business.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 사업을 하다 split by 을; 작은 modifies 사업

examples.ko: 요즘 경기가 안 좋아서 사업이 잘 안돼요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gyeonggiga an joaseo saeobi jal andwaeyo.
examples.en: Business isn't going well these days because the economy is bad.
examples.note: 안돼요 = isn't going well; -아서 gives the reason and can't take a past tense before it

examples.ko: 그분은 맨손으로 시작해서 사업으로 크게 성공한 분이에요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun maensoneuro sijakaeseo saeobeuro keuge seonggonghan bunieyo.
examples.en: He started from nothing and made it big in business.
examples.note: 사업으로 = through/in business; 맨손으로 = with bare hands, a real-life success-story phrase

extendedVocab.nuance: 사업 (事業, literally 'affair-work') is business as an active undertaking — running a company, launching a commercial project, or being self-employed. The key boundary is against 산업 (産業, industry as a whole sector): 사업 is what one person or firm concretely does, while 산업 is the field that many businesses belong to (자동차 산업 = the auto industry, but 자동차 사업 = a particular auto-related business venture). It is also broader than the English word — a government or non-profit project is a 사업 too (복지 사업 = welfare project), so don't restrict it to 'for-profit'. Register is neutral; everyone from a small shop owner to a CEO uses it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 사업하다 as a fixed block: the moment an object marker appears you must break it apart (사업을 하다, 사업을 시작하다), never 사업하다를. Also resist translating 'do business with someone' word-for-word — Koreans say 거래하다 (to trade/deal) for that, not 사업을 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 사업 (a venture you actively run) with 산업 (an industry sector): say 자동차 산업이 발전했다 for the sector, but 그는 자동차 사업을 한다 for one person's business.
사업하다 is one verb, but adding the object marker forces a split: 사업을 하다, never 사업하다를.
'Do business with a partner' is not 그 사람과 사업을 하다 — Koreans say 그 사람과 거래하다 (to deal/trade with) for an ongoing commercial relationship.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 산업 means "industry (sector of the economy)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "industry (sector of the economy)" is 산업 (saneop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 자동차 산업 ("the automobile industry"). Watch the particle attached to 산업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 산업 follows the field as a bare modifier: 반도체 산업, 관광 산업, 게임 산업
발전하다 = to develop/advance; 산업이 성장하다 (to grow) is an equally common partner
구조 = structure; describes how an economy's sectors are organized and is heavy news/policy vocabulary
첨단 = cutting-edge; the natural contrast is 전통 산업 (traditional industry) or 사양 산업 (declining industry)

examples.en: Korea's semiconductor industry is well developed.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 발달해 있다 = is in a developed state; V-아/어 있다 marks a resulting condition

examples.ko: 인공지능 관련 산업이 빠르게 성장하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: ingongjineung gwallyeon saneobi ppareuge seongjanghago isseoyo.
examples.en: AI-related industries are growing fast.
examples.note: 관련 = related (attached directly, no 의); -고 있다 here marks an ongoing change/trend

examples.ko: 이 지역은 한때 조선 산업으로 먹고살았지만 지금은 관광에 의존해요.
examples.romanization: i jiyeogeun hanttae joseon saneobeuro meokgosaratjiman jigeumeun gwangwange uijonhaeyo.
examples.en: This region once lived off the shipbuilding industry but now depends on tourism.
examples.note: (으)로 먹고살다 = to make a living off; 의존하다 = to depend on — a real regional-economy sentence

extendedVocab.nuance: 산업 (産業, 'produce-work') is an industry as an entire economic sector — manufacturing, tourism, IT — never a single company. Use it for macro-level talk: news, government reports, and any discussion of how the economy is structured. The sharp dividing line is against 사업 (事業, business venture): many 사업체 (businesses) together make up one 산업. So 산업을 시작하다 is wrong for 'start a business' — a person cannot launch a whole sector; they start a 사업. A related near-synonym is 업종 (業種, line of business / business category), but 업종 is narrower and is used to classify an individual shop ('what 업종 is your store?'), whereas 산업 is the broad sector above it. Register is formal-to-neutral; you will rarely hear 산업 in casual chat about your own job, but constantly in writing. The English-speaker pitfall is letting the romanization blur it with 사업 — the 산(ㄴ받침) vs 사 distinction is the entire meaning, and the two are not interchangeable.

산업 is a sector, so 산업을 시작하다 cannot mean 'start a business' — use 사업을 시작하다; a person starts a venture, not a whole industry.
Don't let the similar sound merge 산업 (industry) and 사업 (business): the ㄴ batchim in 산 carries the entire meaning difference.
To say what field a small shop is in, Koreans usually ask 업종이 뭐예요? (what's the line of business?), not 산업이 뭐예요? — 산업 is too macro for one store.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 경력 means "career experience; work history" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 경력 (gyeongnyeok) = "career experience; work history". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 경력이 있다 ("to have (professional) experience") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 경력, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 경력이 없다; this is a track record, not a one-off experience
쌓다 = to pile up/accumulate — the idiomatic verb; 경력을 만들다 sounds wrong
number + 년 directly after 경력 states length; 경력 단절 = a career gap/break
-직 = position/post; the contrast term in hiring is 신입 (new-graduate hire)

examples.en: I don't really have much (work) experience.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 경력이 없다; 별로 + negative = not really/much

examples.ko: 마케팅 분야에서 경력을 더 쌓고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: maketing bunyaeseo gyeongnyeogeul deo ssako sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to build up more experience in the marketing field.
examples.note: 분야에서 = in the field of; 쌓다 is the fixed verb for accumulating a career

examples.ko: 경력이 화려해도 인성이 안 좋으면 뽑지 않아요.
examples.romanization: gyeongnyeogi hwaryeohaedo inseongi an joeumyeon ppopji anayo.
examples.en: Even with a dazzling résumé, we don't hire someone with poor character.
examples.note: 경력이 화려하다 = to have an impressive career; -아도 = even if — a real hiring-panel remark

extendedVocab.nuance: 경력 (經歷, 'pass-through + experience', i.e. things you have lived/worked through) means accumulated professional experience or work history — exactly what fills the career section of a résumé. The critical contrast is with 경험 (經驗): 경험 is experience of any kind, including a fun trip, a first kiss, or eating something new, whereas 경력 is specifically a documented work/professional track record. A backpacking trip is a great 경험 but is not 경력; three years at a company is both. Because it is a record, 경력 is counted in years with 년 (경력 3년), not with 번 (times) or 개 (items). High-frequency offshoots dominate Korean hiring: 경력직 (experienced hire) versus 신입 (new graduate), and 경력 단절 (a career break, often used for women returning to work). Register is neutral and shows up on every job posting. The English-speaker pitfall is using 경력 wherever English says 'experience' — for the broad sense ('It was a great experience'), you need 경험, and swapping them sounds odd to a Korean ear.

Don't use 경력 for general life experience: 'It was a good experience' is 좋은 경험이었어요, not 좋은 경력이었어요 — 경력 is only a professional track record.

To build a career, use 경력을 쌓다 (accumulate); 경력을 만들다 (make a career) is unnatural in Korean.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 채용 means "recruitment; hiring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 채용 (chaeyong) means "recruitment; hiring". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 직원을 채용하다 ("to hire an employee"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 채용 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 채용하다 is what the company does; the agent is the employer, not the applicant
공고 = public notice; the place openings are announced (채용 공고를 보다 = to see a job ad)
신입 = entry-level; the partner term is 경력 채용 (experienced-hire recruitment)
과정 = process; 채용이 되다 = to get hired (passive); 채용을 취소하다 = to cancel a hire

examples.ko: 그 회사는 올해 신입을 많이 채용해요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesaneun olhae sinibeul mani chaeyonghaeyo.
examples.en: That company is hiring a lot of new graduates this year.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 신입을 채용하다 — the company is the subject

examples.en: I saw the job posting and submitted my application.
examples.note: -고 = and then; 지원서를 내다 = to hand in an application — note the applicant 지원한다, not 채용한다

examples.ko: 요즘은 수시 채용이 늘어서 공채 시즌이 거의 사라졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun susi chaeyongi neureoseo gongchae sijeuni geoui sarajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Open-ended hiring has grown lately, so the mass-recruitment season has nearly vanished.
examples.note: 수시 채용 = rolling/as-needed hiring vs 공채 (公採, scheduled mass recruitment) — current job-market vocabulary

extendedVocab.nuance: 채용 (採用, 'pick/gather + use', i.e. to select and put to use) is the formal, institutional word for recruitment and hiring that companies use — it dominates 채용 공고 (job postings) and 채용 과정 (the hiring process). The register contrast is against the everyday verb 뽑다 (to pick/select): a friend might casually say 회사에서 사람 뽑는대 (I hear the company is taking people on), but the official notice says 채용. The directional pitfall trips up English speakers constantly: the employer 채용한다 (hires/recruits), while the applicant 지원한다 (applies) — these are not interchangeable, so '저는 그 회사에 채용했어요' to mean 'I applied' is wrong; you 지원했어요 and were then 채용됐어요 (got hired). Note also that 입사하다 (to enter a company, already in vocab) is the later step of actually joining after the offer. Spelling matters: the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ), not 체. Worth knowing the modern split: 공채 (scheduled mass hiring) versus 수시 채용 (rolling hiring), a frequent news topic.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
채용하다 is what the employer does; the applicant 지원하다 (applies). 'I applied to the company' is 그 회사에 지원했어요, never 그 회사에 채용했어요.
Don't write 채용 as 체용 — the first syllable is 채 (ㅐ).
Getting hired is the passive 채용되다 (저는 채용됐어요), not the active 채용하다, which would mean you did the hiring.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수입 means "income; revenue (also: imports)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "income; revenue (also: imports)" is 수입 (suip). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 수입이 많다 ("to have a high income"). Watch the particle attached to 수입 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 수입이 적다; describes how much money comes in
줄다 = to decrease (intransitive); 수입이 늘다 = income increases
한 달 = one month; 고정 수입 = fixed/steady income, 부수입 = side income
지출 (already in vocab) = outgo; this is the standard budgeting pair (in vs out)

examples.ko: 저는 한 달 수입이 많지 않아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun han dal suibi manchi anayo.
examples.en: My monthly income isn't very high.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 수입이 많다/적다; 많지 않다 = not much

examples.ko: 프리랜서는 매달 수입이 일정하지 않아서 불안해요.
examples.romanization: peuriraenseoneun maedal suibi iljeonghaji anaseo buranhaeyo.
examples.en: A freelancer's income isn't steady month to month, so it's stressful.
examples.note: 일정하다 = to be steady/fixed; -지 않아서 chains the negative reason

examples.ko: 수입보다 지출이 많으면 적자가 나니까 가계부를 써 보세요.
examples.romanization: suipboda jichuri maneumyeon jeokjaga nanikka gagyebureul sseo boseyo.
examples.en: If spending exceeds income you run a deficit, so try keeping a budget book.
examples.note: 적자가 나다 = to go into the red; N보다 = than — a practical money-management line

extendedVocab.nuance: 수입 for personal money means income or revenue — the money coming in — and lives in opposition to 지출 (spending going out). Crucially it is a homograph hiding two different hanja: 收入 ('gather + enter') is income, while 輸入 ('transport + enter') is imports, the opposite of 수출 (輸出, exports). Spoken aloud they are identical, so only context tells you whether 수입 means a paycheck or a shipment of foreign goods; in an economics lecture both senses can appear in one paragraph. The near-synonym for the income sense is 소득 (所得, already in vocab): 소득 is the more formal/statistical word (소득세 = income tax, 소득 수준 = income level), whereas 수입 feels closer to everyday earnings, especially 한 달 수입 (monthly take). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'income' maps only to one fixed word and then panicking when 수입 shows up meaning 'imports' — train yourself to read the surrounding sentence. Also note 수입 is a noun describing a state (수입이 많다), so you don't conjugate it like a verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
수입 is a homograph: it means both 'income' (收入) and 'imports' (輸入). Context decides — don't assume the paycheck meaning when the sentence is about trade.
Don't confuse 수입 (income/imports, 入 = enter) with 수출 (exports, 出 = exit); they are economic opposites.
For formal or statistical 'income' (income tax, income bracket) Koreans prefer 소득 (소득세, 소득 수준), not 수입.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 손해 means "loss; damage (financial)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 손해 (sonhae) = "loss; damage (financial)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 손해를 보다 ("to suffer/incur a loss") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 손해, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 here means 'to incur', not 'to see' — the single most important collocation to memorize
입다 = to suffer (slightly more formal); 손해를 끼치다 = to cause a loss to someone else
크다/적다 size the loss; 손해가 막심하다 = the loss is severe (set phrase)
배상 = indemnity; 손해 배상을 청구하다 = to claim damages — legal/business register

examples.en: If we do it that way, I lose out.
examples.note: Beginner frame: noun-as-predicate 손해(이)다 = to be a loss/disadvantage to someone

examples.ko: 지금 팔면 손해를 볼 것 같아서 조금 더 기다리려고요.
examples.romanization: jigeum palmyeon sonhaereul bol geot gataseo jogeum deo gidariryeogoyo.
examples.en: I think I'll take a loss if I sell now, so I'll wait a bit longer.
examples.note: 손해를 보다 = to incur a loss; -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 = it seems — note 보다 is NOT 'see' here

examples.ko: 환불을 안 해 주면 결국 소비자만 손해를 보는 거잖아요.
examples.romanization: hwanbureul an hae jumyeon gyeolguk sobijaman sonhaereul boneun geojanayo.
examples.en: If they won't refund it, in the end it's only the consumer who loses out, right?
examples.note: 결국 = in the end; -잖아요 = appeals to shared knowledge — a real complaint-line

extendedVocab.nuance: 손해 (損害, 'damage + harm') is a loss or disadvantage, almost always financial or in terms of coming out worse off — the direct opposite of 이익/이득 (profit/gain). Its make-or-break collocation is 손해를 보다, where 보다 does NOT mean 'to see' but 'to incur/take', so 손해를 보다 = 'to take a loss'; English speakers often mis-hear this and either mistranslate it or wrongly substitute 손해를 하다, which is simply not Korean. The boundary against 피해 (被害, harm/damage suffered) matters: 손해 leans toward monetary or deal-based disadvantage (a bad sale, an unfair trade), while 피해 covers broader harm including physical or disaster damage (태풍 피해 = typhoon damage, 피해자 = victim). For a machine breaking, use 고장 (malfunction), not 손해. Register is neutral and it even works conversationally as a predicate noun: 나만 손해야 (I'm the only one who loses out). The pitfall to drill is the verb pairing — 손해를 보다 / 입다, never 손해를 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 손해를 보다 (보다 = incur, not see) or 손해를 입다 for 'to suffer a loss'; 손해를 하다 is not Korean.
손해 is monetary/disadvantage loss; for broad harm — physical, disaster, victim — use 피해 (태풍 피해, 피해자), and for a device breaking use 고장.
손해 is the opposite of 이익 (profit), so don't mix it up with 손님 (guest/customer), which only looks similar.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 가치 means "value; worth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 가치 (gachi) means "value; worth". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 가치가 있다 ("to be worthwhile / have value"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가치 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 가치가 없다 (worthless); covers both economic and abstract worth
오르다/떨어지다 for value going up/down (property, stocks, currency, a collectible)
예: 볼 가치가 있다 (worth seeing), 도전해 볼 가치가 있다 (worth trying)
-관 (觀) = view; 가치관이 다르다 = to have different values — a very common relationship phrase

examples.en: This really has value / is worthwhile.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 가치가 있다 as a simple predicate of worth

examples.ko: 그 그림은 시간이 지날수록 가치가 올라갔어요.
examples.romanization: geu geurimeun sigani jinalsurok gachiga ollagasseoyo.
examples.en: That painting rose in value as time went by.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ수록 = the more...; 가치가 오르다/올라가다 for appreciating value

examples.ko: 저는 일을 고를 때 연봉보다 그 일의 가치를 더 중요하게 봐요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun ireul goreul ttae yeonbongboda geu irui gachireul deo jungyohage bwayo.
examples.en: When I pick a job, I weigh the meaning of the work over the salary.
examples.note: 고를 때 = when choosing; 중요하게 보다 = to regard as important — a real values-based statement

extendedVocab.nuance: 가치 (價値, 'price + value') means value or worth, spanning both economic value (가치가 오르다 = rises in value, of property or stocks) and abstract worth (인생의 가치 = the value of life, 일의 가치 = the worth of one's work). The most useful pattern built on it is V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 ('worth doing': 볼 가치가 있다 = worth seeing), and the derived 가치관 (one's value system/worldview) is extremely high-frequency, especially 가치관이 다르다 when people clash. The dividing line is against the concrete-amount words 가격 (價格, the listed price/price tag) and 값 (the cost/amount you actually pay): 가치 is how much something is truly worth, which may diverge sharply from its 가격 — a cheap gift can have huge 가치 but a low 가격. Register is neutral-to-elevated. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 가치 into the 'worth doing' slot with the wrong verb (가치가 하다 is wrong; it's 가치가 있다), and mixing it up with 가격 when you mean the sticker price rather than intrinsic worth.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 가치 (intrinsic worth/value) with 가격 (the listed price): a discounted item has a low 가격 but can still hold high 가치.
For 'worth doing' use V-(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 (볼 가치가 있다), never 가치가 하다.
To say people have clashing values, the idiom is 가치관이 다르다 (different value systems), not 가치가 다르다.

Register is neutral-to-elevated.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 품질 means "quality (of a product)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "quality (of a product)" is 품질 (pumjil). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 품질이 좋다 ("to be of good quality"). Watch the particle attached to 품질 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the negatives are 품질이 나쁘다 and 품질이 떨어지다 (quality drops/is poor)
높이다 = to raise (transitive); 품질을 관리하다 = to manage/control quality
관리 = management; a standard business term, often abbreviated 품질 관리부 (QC department)
고- (高) / 저- (低) prefixes attach directly to 품질

examples.en: This clothing is good quality.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 품질이 좋다 — 품질 is the subject, 좋다 the descriptive verb

examples.ko: 가격은 조금 비싸지만 품질이 정말 좋아서 만족해요.
examples.romanization: gagyeogeun jogeum bissajiman pumjiri jeongmal joaseo manjokaeyo.
examples.en: It's a bit pricey, but the quality is so good that I'm satisfied.
examples.note: -지만 = but; -아서 chains the reason 'because the quality is good'

examples.ko: 요즘 소비자들은 가격보다 품질을 더 꼼꼼하게 따져요.
examples.romanization: yojeum sobijadeureun gagyeokboda pumjireul deo kkomkkomhage ttajyeoyo.
examples.en: These days consumers scrutinize quality more carefully than price.
examples.note: 따지다 (already in vocab) = to scrutinize; 꼼꼼하게 = meticulously — a market-trend sentence

extendedVocab.nuance: 품질 (品質, 'goods + substance/quality') refers specifically to the quality of goods or products — how well-made and reliable something is. It is THE word in commerce and reviews: 품질 관리 (quality control), 품질 보증 (quality guarantee), 품질이 떨어지다 (quality slips). The sharp restriction English speakers must learn is that 품질 only modifies products/goods, not abstract or experiential things: 'quality of life' is 삶의 질, 'quality of sleep' is 수면의 질, 'quality time' is not 품질 시간 — for all of those you drop the 품 and use bare 질 (質, quality/nature). So 품(品) literally pins it to merchandise. The near-synonym to keep separate is 성능 (性能, performance/specs of a device): a phone can have great 성능 (fast chip) but poor 품질 (cheap, breaks easily) — capability versus build quality. Register is neutral. The pitfall: 품질 is a noun naming a state, so you describe it with 좋다/나쁘다 (품질이 좋다), and you never say 품질을 잘하다, which treats it like an action.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 품질 only for products. 'Quality of life' is 삶의 질, not 삶의 품질 — for abstract quality drop 품 and use bare 질.
품질이 좋다/나쁘다 describes the state; 품질을 잘하다 is wrong because 품질 is a noun, not an action you perform.
Don't equate 품질 (build quality) with 성능 (performance/specs): a gadget can have high 성능 but low 품질.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 생산 means "production; manufacturing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 생산 (saengsan) = "production; manufacturing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 제품을 생산하다 ("to produce products") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생산, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 생산하다 = to make/manufacture; the factory or firm is the agent
늘다/줄다 (intransitive) for output rising/falling; 생산을 늘리다 = to increase output (transitive)
대량 = large quantity; the contrast is 소량 생산 (small-batch) and 다품종 소량 생산 (high-mix low-volume)
라인, 과정 attach to 생산 as compounds; 생산성 = productivity

examples.en: This factory produces cars.
examples.note: Beginner frame: A를 생산하다; 공장 (factory) as the natural subject

examples.ko: 원자재 가격이 올라서 생산 비용이 늘었어요.
examples.romanization: wonjajae gagyeogi ollaseo saengsan biyongi neureosseoyo.
examples.en: Production costs rose because raw-material prices went up.
examples.note: 원자재 = raw materials; 비용 (already in vocab) = cost — 생산 as a compound modifier

examples.ko: 수요가 갑자기 늘면 생산을 그만큼 늘려야 하는데 공장이 못 따라가요.
examples.romanization: suyoga gapjagi neulmyeon saengsaneul geumankeum neullyeoya haneunde gongjangi mot ttaragayo.
examples.en: If demand suddenly jumps you have to raise output to match, but the factory can't keep up.
examples.note: 수요 = demand; 생산을 늘리다 (transitive); 따라가다 = to keep pace — a real supply-chain bind

extendedVocab.nuance: 생산 (生産, 'give birth/bring forth + produce') means production or manufacturing — the making of goods. It is the supply side of the economy and pairs naturally with 소비 (消費, consumption) as a set: 생산과 소비. The agent is a 생산자 (producer), the mirror of 소비자 (consumer). Keep three look-alike Sino-Korean economy words apart: 생산 (making things/output) vs 산업 (産業, the industry sector that does the making) vs 사업 (事業, a specific business venture) — they share syllables but mean output, sector, and enterprise respectively. The most common grammar pitfall is the transitivity pair English flattens into one verb 'increase': 생산이 늘다 is intransitive ('production increases', no object), but to actively raise output you need the transitive 생산을 늘리다 ('increase production'); using 생산을 늘다 is ungrammatical. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in business and news. Note 대량 생산 (mass production) as a fixed term and 생산성 (productivity) as a high-value derivative.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
생산 is making/output; don't stretch it to mean 'industry' (use 산업) or 'business venture' (use 사업), even though all three share syllables.
Match transitivity: 생산이 늘다 (production rises, intransitive) vs 생산을 늘리다 (raise production, transitive). 생산을 늘다 is ungrammatical.
The person who produces is 생산자, not 생산가 — the agent suffix here is -자 (者), paralleling 소비자 (consumer).

structuredNuance.t: 생산 means production or manufacturing — the making of goods. It is the supply side of the economy and pairs naturally with 소비 (consumption) as a set: 생산과 소비. The agent is a 생산자 (producer), the mirror of 소비자 (consumer). Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in business and news. Note 대량 생산 (mass production) as a fixed term and 생산성 (productivity) as a high-value derivative.

生産 means 'give birth/bring forth + produce'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 소비 means "consumption; spending" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 소비 (sobi) means "consumption; spending". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 돈을 소비하다 ("to spend money"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 소비 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 소비하다 also takes 에너지를/자원을 소비하다 (consume energy/resources)
늘다/줄다 (intransitive) for spending rising or falling; 소비를 줄이다 = to cut spending (transitive)
-자 (者) = person; the mirror of 생산자 (producer); 소비자 보호 = consumer protection
과- (過) = excessive; the positive contrast is 합리적 소비 (sensible consumption)

examples.en: I'm cutting back on spending these days.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 소비를 줄이다 (transitive); -고 있다 for an ongoing effort

examples.en: When the economy worsens, people reduce their spending.
examples.note: 나빠지다 = to get worse; 줄이다 = to reduce — the cause–effect of a downturn

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 세대는 가치 소비를 중요하게 생각해서 비싸도 의미 있는 걸 사요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun sedaeneun gachi sobireul jungyohage saenggakaeseo bissado uimi inneun geol sayo.
examples.en: Young people today value 'ethical/meaningful consumption', so they buy meaningful things even if pricey.
examples.note: 가치 소비 = value-driven consumption; -아도 = even if — a current consumer-culture trend

extendedVocab.nuance: 소비 (消費, 'dissolve/use up + spend') means consumption or spending — using up money, goods, or resources — and is the demand-side counterpart to 생산 (production), giving the staple pair 생산과 소비. Its standout derivative 소비자 (consumer) is one of the most useful economy words you can own (소비자 보호 = consumer protection). Two boundaries matter. First, against 지출 (支出, expenditure, already in vocab): 지출 is an accounting outflow — a line item in a budget — while 소비 is the broader economic act of consuming, including consuming non-money resources. Second, and the key value judgment, against 낭비 (浪費, waste): 소비 is neutral and often necessary (you must consume food and electricity), whereas 낭비 is always negative — money or resources thrown away pointlessly. So calling ordinary, reasonable spending 낭비 is an insult the speaker may not intend. Register is neutral. The grammar pitfall mirrors 생산: use the transitive 소비를 줄이다 to 'reduce spending', not the intransitive 소비를 줄다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
소비 (consumption) is neutral and can be necessary; 낭비 (waste) is always negative. Don't label normal spending 낭비 unless you mean it was wasteful.
Match transitivity: 소비를 줄이다 (cut spending, transitive) vs 소비가 줄다 (spending falls, intransitive). 소비를 줄다 is wrong.
소비 is the broad act of consuming; an individual budget outflow/expense entry is 지출 — don't use 소비 where the accounting term 지출 is meant.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 예산 means "budget" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "budget" is 예산 (yesan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예산을 짜다 ("to draw up a budget"). Watch the particle attached to 예산 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 짜다 = to put together/plan; the most natural verb (it's a structured plan you assemble)
부족하다 = to be short; the opposite is 예산이 남다 (budget left over)
세우다 = to set up; 예산을 초과하다 = to exceed the budget
안에서 = inside; the contrast is 예산을 넘다/초과하다 (to go over budget)

examples.en: I'm a bit short on budget for this trip.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 예산이 부족하다; 좀 softens it

examples.ko: 회사에서 내년 마케팅 예산을 줄이기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo naenyeon maketing yesaneul jurigiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The company decided to cut next year's marketing budget.
examples.note: -기로 하다 = to decide to; 예산을 줄이다 = to reduce the budget

examples.ko: 예산을 미리 짜 두면 충동구매를 줄일 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yesaneul miri jja dumyeon chungdonggumaereul juril su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you set a budget in advance, you can curb impulse buying.
examples.note: -아/어 두다 = do in advance and leave it; 충동구매 = impulse purchase — a practical money tip

extendedVocab.nuance: 예산 (豫算, 'beforehand + calculate', i.e. money figured out in advance) is a budget — a planned amount of money set aside for a project, household, or organization before it is spent. The idiomatic verb is 예산을 짜다 ('to weave/assemble a budget'), reflecting that a budget is a structured plan you build; 예산을 세우다 (to set up) also works, but 예산을 만들다 (to make) sounds flat and unnatural. The defining contrast is the plan-versus-actual distinction English blurs under 'budget': 예산 is the forward-looking plan, whereas 지출 (expenditure, already in vocab) and 비용 (the cost incurred) are what actually leaves your pocket, and 가계부 is the record of what was spent. So you 예산을 짜다 first, then track your 지출 against it. Register is neutral and identical in households, companies, and government (국가 예산 = the national budget). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 to 'make a budget' and confusing the planned 예산 with already-spent 지출/비용 — keep 'plan' (예산) and 'spent' (지출) firmly apart.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 예산을 짜다 or 예산을 세우다 for 'make a budget'; 예산을 만들다 sounds unnatural to Koreans.
예산 is the planned amount looking forward, not money already spent — that is 지출 (expenditure) or 비용 (cost).
To go over budget say 예산을 초과하다/넘다, not 예산을 지나다 (which means physically pass by).
