extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 토론 means "debate; structured discussion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "debate; structured discussion" is 토론 (toron). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 토론을 하다 ("to hold a debate / discuss"). Watch the particle attached to 토론 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 is the standard verb, and 토론하다 also works as one word; the topic attaches with ~에 대해.
벌어지다 ('unfold, break out') is natural for a lively, spontaneous debate, more dynamic than 하다.
찬반 ('for and against', 贊反) is the set modifier for a structured two-sided debate, common in school.
주제 ('topic', 主題) forms a common compound for the set issue under discussion.

examples.ko: 우리 반은 오늘 짧은 토론을 했어요.
examples.romanization: uri baneun oneul jjalbeun toroneul haesseoyo.
examples.en: Our class did a short debate today.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 토론을 하다 is the core frame; 짧은 토론 shows it can be brief and classroom-scale.

examples.ko: 이 주제는 찬반 토론을 하기에 아주 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i jujeneun chanban toroneul hagie aju joayo.
examples.en: This topic is great for a pro-and-con debate.
examples.note: Everyday: 찬반 토론 = the set phrase; ~하기에 좋다 = 'good for ~ing' attaches the activity to a judgment.

examples.ko: 토론에서는 상대방의 의견도 끝까지 들어야 해요.
examples.romanization: toroneseoneun sangdaebangui uigyeondo kkeutkkaji deureoya haeyo.
examples.en: In a debate you have to listen to the other side's opinion to the end.
examples.note: Real-situation: teaches register — 토론 demands 상대방 ('the other party', a polite formal word) and 끝까지 ('to the very end').

extendedVocab.nuance: 토론 (討論, 討 'examine/discuss' + 論 'argue, treatise') is an organized, rule-based discussion where people exchange and defend opinions on a set topic — classroom debates, panel discussions, formal meetings. Place it on a spectrum between two near-synonyms: it is more structured and goal-oriented than 대화 (relaxed everyday conversation), yet calmer and more cooperative than 논쟁 (a heated dispute where sides clash). The dividing line from 논쟁 is intent: a good 토론 stays respectful and aims to weigh views, even when people disagree, whereas 논쟁 carries friction. Natural collocations are 토론을 벌이다/하다, 찬반 토론, 토론 주제. The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 'debate/discuss' for any back-and-forth: a casual chat with friends is 대화 or 이야기, never 토론 — reserve 토론 for a deliberate, topic-driven exchange.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 토론 (a structured, civil debate) with 논쟁 (a heated argument); 토론 aims to exchange and examine views, 논쟁 implies open conflict and emotion.
Using 토론 for a casual chat with friends — that everyday back-and-forth is 대화 or 이야기, and calling it 토론 sounds oddly stiff and formal.
Pairing the topic with the wrong particle — say 환경 문제에 대해 토론하다 ('debate about ~'), not 환경 문제를 토론하다 in careful speech.

structuredNuance.t: An organized, rule-based discussion where people exchange and defend opinions on a set topic — classroom debates, panel discussions, formal meetings. Natural collocations are 토론을 벌이다/하다, 찬반 토론, 토론 주제.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 논쟁 means "argument; controversy; dispute" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 논쟁 (nonjaeng) = "argument; controversy; dispute". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 논쟁을 벌이다 ("to engage in / wage an argument") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 논쟁, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to engage in / wage an argument
usagePhrases.note: 벌이다 ('start, wage') is the idiomatic verb for an active, ongoing dispute between sides.
일어나다 ('arise') is natural when a dispute breaks out on its own from some trigger.
뜨겁다 ('hot') is the set temperature metaphor; 뜨거운 논쟁 = a fierce, passionate dispute.

usagePhrases.en: to be open to dispute / debatable
usagePhrases.note: 여지 ('room', 餘地) in a fixed phrase: literally 'there is room for argument', i.e. it's arguable.

examples.ko: 그 말 한마디가 작은 논쟁을 일으켰어요.
examples.romanization: geu mal hanmadiga jageun nonjaengeul ireukyeosseoyo.
examples.en: That one remark caused a small argument.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 논쟁을 일으키다 ('cause an argument'); 말 한마디 = 'a single remark'.

examples.ko: 인터넷에서 그 문제를 두고 뜨거운 논쟁이 벌어졌어요.
examples.romanization: inteoneseseo geu munjereul dugo tteugeoun nonjaengi beoreojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A heated argument broke out online over that issue.
examples.note: Everyday-online: ~을/를 두고 = 'over (an issue)'; 벌어지다 = 'break out'; 뜨거운 논쟁 is the set phrase.

examples.ko: 이건 논쟁의 여지가 없는 명백한 사실이에요.
examples.romanization: igeon nonjaengui yeojiga eopsneun myeongbaekan sasirieyo.
examples.en: This is an obvious fact that leaves no room for dispute.
examples.note: Real-situation: the negative idiom 논쟁의 여지가 없다 ('no room for argument'); 명백하다 ('obvious') reinforces it.

extendedVocab.nuance: 논쟁 (論爭, 論 'argue/discourse' + 爭 'contend, fight for') is a heated argument or public controversy in which sides clash, often emotionally or over high-stakes issues — note the 爭 'contend' character that 토론 lacks, which is exactly where the friction lives. The nearest near-synonym is 토론, and the dividing line is conflict: 토론 is an orderly, cooperative exchange of views, while 논쟁 is adversarial and charged, with people pushing to win. It is also broader and more public/intellectual than a personal quarrel (싸움 or 다툼). Habitual collocations: 논쟁을 벌이다, 논쟁이 일어나다, 뜨거운 논쟁, 논쟁의 여지가 있다/없다, and the adjective 논쟁적이다 ('controversial'). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 논쟁 for a personal fight between friends — that is 싸움/다툼; 논쟁 belongs to issues and ideas, typically in public or written contexts, not bickering.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 논쟁 and 토론 as interchangeable — 논쟁 carries conflict, emotion, and a will to win, while 토론 is a calm, structured exchange of views.
Using 논쟁 for a personal fight between friends; that is usually 싸움 or 다툼, whereas 논쟁 is more public, issue-based, or intellectual.
Saying 논쟁을 하다 when describing an unfolding clash — the more vivid, idiomatic choice is 논쟁을 벌이다 (wage) or 논쟁이 벌어지다 (break out).

論爭: 論 'argue/discourse' + 爭 'contend, fight for'. Note the 爭 'contend' character that 토론 lacks, which is exactly where the friction lives.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 설득 means "persuasion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 설득 (seoldeuk) means "persuasion". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 설득을 하다 ("to persuade"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 설득 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 form; 설득하다 is the common one-word verb, and it takes the PERSON as object: 친구를 설득하다.
성공하다 ('succeed') and 실패하다 ('fail') pair naturally, framing persuasion as an attempt with an outcome.
설득 + 력 (力 'power'); 설득력이 있다/없다 = to be / not be persuasive, an extremely common judgment.
당하다 makes the passive: you ended up convinced by someone, sometimes against initial resistance.

examples.en: I persuaded my younger sibling and we went together.
examples.note: Graded-simple: note 동생을 (person as direct object); ~해서 chains 'persuaded, so (then)'.

examples.en: That person's argument is persuasive.
examples.note: Everyday: 설득력이 있다 = 'to have persuasive power', a key intermediate phrase you'll hear constantly.

examples.ko: 아무리 설득해도 그는 끝내 마음을 바꾸지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: amuri seoldeukaedo geuneun kkeunnae maeumeul bakkuji anasseoyo.
examples.en: No matter how much I tried to persuade him, in the end he didn't change his mind.
examples.note: Real-situation: 아무리 ~해도 = 'no matter how much ~'; 마음을 바꾸다 = 'change one's mind'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 설득 (說得, 說 'speak/explain' + 得 'obtain, gain') is the act of persuading someone to accept your view or do something — literally 'gaining them by speaking', i.e. winning agreement through reasoning rather than force. The crucial near-synonym contrast is with 강요 (強要 'coercion'): 설득 wins willing agreement, while 강요 imposes against the person's will, so they are ethically opposite. The derived noun 설득력 ('persuasiveness') is everyday vocabulary — Koreans judge arguments by whether 설득력이 있다 or 없다. The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the particle on the object: 설득하다 takes the PERSON directly with 을/를 (친구를 설득했어요), unlike the English frame 'persuade someone OF something', so learners wrongly produce 친구에게 설득했어요. Use 설득에 성공하다/실패하다 to talk about the result.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 설득 (persuading by reason, winning willing agreement) with 강요 (forcing/coercion against someone's will) — they are opposite in respect for the other's choice.
Marking the object with 에게 — say 친구를 설득했어요 (person as direct object), never 친구에게 설득했어요, because 설득하다 governs the person with 을/를.
Translating English 'I have no power to persuade' loosely — the Korean noun is 설득력 (없다), so say 설득력이 없어요, not a word-by-word rendering.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 협상 means "negotiation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "negotiation" is 협상 (hyeopsang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 협상을 하다 ("to negotiate"). Watch the particle attached to 협상 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 form; 협상하다 also works as a single verb; the counterpart attaches with ~와/과.
결렬되다 ('break down', 決裂) is the standard news verb for talks that collapse.

usagePhrases.en: negotiations are concluded / reach a deal
usagePhrases.note: 타결되다 ('be settled', 妥結) is the fixed counterpart for a successful outcome.
협상 테이블에 앉다 = 'sit at the negotiating table', a common idiom for entering talks.

examples.en: We negotiated briefly over the price.
examples.note: Graded-simple: ~을/를 두고 협상하다 = 'negotiate over ~'; 잠깐 keeps it small-scale.

examples.en: The wage negotiations ultimately broke down.
examples.note: Everyday-news: 임금 협상 = 'wage negotiations'; 결렬되다 = 'fall through', the set failure verb.

examples.ko: 양측은 며칠간의 협상 끝에 합의에 이르렀어요.
examples.romanization: yangcheugeun myeochilganui hyeopsang kkeute habuie ireureosseoyo.
examples.en: After several days of negotiation, both sides reached an agreement.
examples.note: Real-situation: 협상 끝에 = 'after negotiation'; 합의에 이르다 = 'reach an agreement', formal register.

extendedVocab.nuance: 협상 (協商, 協 'cooperate/jointly' + 商 'discuss, deliberate, trade') is formal negotiation between parties with differing interests — business deals, labor talks, diplomacy — literally 'jointly deliberating' toward a mutually acceptable compromise. The everyday near-synonym to contrast is 흥정: 흥정 is informal haggling over a single price at a market or with a vendor, whereas 협상 is structured, institutional, and higher-stakes. News reports fix its outcome with the paired verbs 타결되다 (reach a deal, 妥結) versus 결렬되다 (break down, 決裂) — memorize them as opposites. Other set collocations: 협상 테이블에 앉다, 협상을 벌이다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 협상 for casual bargaining ('I negotiated the price down at the market'), which should be 흥정했어요; also keep 타결 and 결렬 straight, since swapping them inverts whether the deal succeeded or collapsed.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 협상 for casual price haggling at a market — that is 흥정, while 협상 is formal, often institutional negotiation with stakes.
Mixing up 타결 (a successful settlement) and 결렬 (a breakdown); they are opposite outcomes, so 협상이 타결됐어요 and 협상이 결렬됐어요 mean reverse things.
Marking the other party with 에게 — the counterpart in negotiation attaches with ~와/과 (회사와 협상하다), not 에게.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 연설 means "speech; public address" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 연설 (yeonseol) = "speech; public address". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연설을 하다 ("to give a speech") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연설, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 is the standard verb; 연설하다 also works; the audience attaches with ~앞에서 ('before').
연설 + 문 (文 'writing'); the written script an address is read from or prepared as.
취임 ('taking office', 就任) + 연설; a common fixed compound, also 축사 for congratulatory addresses.
감동적이다 ('moving', 感動的) is the natural modifier for a memorable, emotionally powerful address.

examples.ko: 반장이 친구들 앞에서 짧은 연설을 했어요.
examples.romanization: banjangi chingudeul apeseo jjalbeun yeonseoreul haesseoyo.
examples.en: The class president gave a short speech in front of the others.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 앞에서 = 'in front of'; shows 연설 needs an audience, even a small one.

examples.en: His graduation speech was truly moving.
examples.note: Everyday: 졸업식 연설 = 'graduation speech'; 감동적이다 = the set adjective for a stirring address.

examples.en: The president's inauguration speech was broadcast live nationwide.
examples.note: Real-situation: 취임 연설 = fixed compound; 생중계되다 = 'be broadcast live', formal news register.

extendedVocab.nuance: 연설 (演說, 演 'perform/expound' + 說 'speak') is a formal spoken address delivered to an audience — by a politician, a graduate, a public figure — almost always prepared in advance, the literal sense being 'to expound by speaking'. Two near-synonyms mark its borders: it differs from 발표 (a presentation of information, results, or a project, where the point is content/data) and from 강의 (a lecture meant to teach). The dividing line is purpose: 연설 aims to address and often inspire a gathered audience, not to instruct or report. Habitual collocations: 연설을 하다, 취임 연설, 감동적인 연설, 연설문. The English-speaker pitfall is stretching 연설 to any 'speech': a few informal words or a toast at a small gathering is 인사말 ('a few words of greeting') or 건배사 (a toast), and a project briefing is 발표 — reserve 연설 for the prepared, formal public address.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 연설 (a prepared public address) with 발표 (a presentation of a project, results, or information) — the goals differ: inspire/address versus inform/report.
Using 연설 for an informal toast or a few words at a small gathering — for that say 인사말 ('a few words') or 건배사 (a toast).
Saying 연설을 말하다 by translating 'give a speech' loosely — the verb is 연설을 하다 (or 연설하다); 말하다 doesn't collocate here.

structuredNuance.t: A formal spoken address delivered to an audience — by a politician, a graduate, a public figure — almost always prepared in advance. Its purpose is to address and often inspire a gathered audience, not to instruct or report. Habitual collocations: 연설을 하다, 취임 연설, 감동적인 연설, 연설문.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 강의 means "lecture; (university) course" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 강의 (gangui) means "lecture; (university) course". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 강의를 듣다 ("to take / attend a lecture"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 강의 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 듣다 ('listen') is the idiomatic verb — you 'hear' a lecture or course; never 받다 or 배우다.
From the teacher's side; 강의하다 also works as one verb (교수님이 강의하다).
온라인 강의 became extremely common; the older slang clip is 인강 (인터넷 강의).
강의 + 실 (室 'room'); the physical room where a university lecture is held.

examples.en: I'm taking a history course this semester.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 강의를 듣다 = the idiomatic 'take a course'; note 듣다, literally 'listen'.

examples.ko: 그 교수님의 강의는 항상 인기가 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu gyosunimui ganguineun hangsang ingiga manayo.
examples.en: That professor's lectures are always very popular.
examples.note: Everyday: 인기가 많다 = 'be popular'; 교수님 carries the honorific ~님 for a professor.

examples.ko: 요즘은 집에서 온라인 강의를 들을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jibeseo ollain ganguireul deureul su isseoyo.
examples.en: These days you can take online lectures from home.
examples.note: Real-situation: 온라인 강의 = set compound; ~을 수 있다 = 'can', highlighting the convenience.

extendedVocab.nuance: 강의 (講義, 講 'expound/teach' + 義 'meaning, principle') means a lecture or an academic course, especially at university level, where a teacher expounds material to students — the hanja literally 'expounding the principles'. The key near-synonym is 수업: 수업 is the general word for a class at ANY level (elementary, middle school, a tutoring session), while 강의 leans academic and university, with a content-delivery, one-direction feel. The signature collocation is the verb 강의를 듣다 ('listen to a lecture') for attending or taking a course — this is the heart of the English-speaker pitfall, because learners reach for 받다 ('receive') or 배우다 ('learn') on the model of 'take/receive a course'; both are wrong, the only natural verb is 듣다. Other collocations: 강의를 하다 (teach side), 온라인 강의, 강의실.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 강의를 받다 or 강의를 배우다 for 'take a lecture' — the only correct verb is 강의를 듣다, literally 'listen to a lecture'.
Using 강의 for an elementary or middle-school class; 강의 leans academic/university, while 수업 is the neutral word for any class at any level.
Confusing 강의 (a course/lecture series) with 강연, which is a one-off public talk/lecture by a guest speaker — a semester course is 강의, a single invited talk is 강연.

structuredNuance.t: A lecture or an academic course, especially at university level, where a teacher expounds material to students. The signature collocation is the verb 강의를 듣다 ('listen to a lecture') for attending or taking a course. Other collocations: 강의를 하다 (teach side), 온라인 강의, 강의실.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 인터뷰 means "interview" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "interview" is 인터뷰 (inteobyu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 인터뷰를 하다 ("to do / conduct an interview"). Watch the particle attached to 인터뷰 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 form; used for BOTH the interviewer and the interviewee side, so context decides who.

usagePhrases.en: to agree to / give an interview
usagePhrases.note: 응하다 ('comply, respond to', 應) is the formal verb for accepting a request to be interviewed.
인터뷰 + 기사 (記事 'article'); a written press piece based on an interview.
방송 ('broadcast') marks the medium, distinguishing it from a print or job interview.

examples.en: That actor gave an interview on the broadcast.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 인터뷰를 하다 works for the interviewee here; 방송에서 = 'on air'.

examples.en: A reporter conducted interviews with citizens in the street.
examples.note: Everyday-press: 인터뷰를 진행하다 = 'conduct an interview'; ~와 = 'with (the interviewee)'.

examples.ko: 내일 회사 면접이 있어서 너무 떨려요.
examples.romanization: naeil hoesa myeonjeobi isseoseo neomu tteollyeoyo.
examples.en: I have a job interview at the company tomorrow, so I'm really nervous.
examples.note: Real-situation: deliberately uses 면접 (not 인터뷰) — a hiring interview is standardly 면접 in Korea.

extendedVocab.nuance: 인터뷰 is a loanword (from English 'interview') covering media and research interviews — a reporter questioning someone, or the Q&A of gathering a story or opinion. The essential near-synonym contrast for learners is with 면접 (面接, 'face-meeting'): a JOB/admissions interview is standardly 면접, while 인터뷰 leans toward press, broadcast, celebrity, or research questioning. You will hear 면접 인터뷰 too, but for hiring, default to 면접. Natural collocations: 인터뷰를 하다, 인터뷰에 응하다, 인터뷰를 진행하다, 인터뷰 기사. The two big English-speaker pitfalls: first, defaulting to 인터뷰 for a job interview (say 면접); second, the verb for 'be interviewed' — English makes it passive ('I was interviewed'), but Korean says 인터뷰를 하다 (the interviewee also 한다) or the formal 인터뷰에 응하다, never 인터뷰를 받다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Defaulting to 인터뷰 for a job interview — the standard word in Korea is 면접, so say 면접을 보다 ('have/sit a job interview').
Saying 인터뷰를 받다 for 'be interviewed' on the model of English passive — Koreans say 인터뷰를 하다 or, formally, 인터뷰에 응하다.
Using 인터뷰를 보다 the way you'd say 면접을 보다 — 면접 takes 보다, but a press 인터뷰 takes 하다/진행하다, not 보다.

The essential contrast is with 면접 (面接, 'face-meeting'): a JOB/admissions interview is standardly 면접, while 인터뷰 leans toward press, broadcast, celebrity, or research questioning. You will hear 면접 인터뷰 too, but for hiring, default to 면접.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 방송 means "broadcast; (a TV/radio) program" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 방송 (bangsong) = "broadcast; (a TV/radio) program". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방송에 나오다 ("to appear on a broadcast / be on TV") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방송, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to appear on a broadcast / be on TV
usagePhrases.note: 나오다 ('come out') = appear on air from the viewer's side; 방송에 나가다 ('go out') = air, from the producer's side.
생 ('raw, live') + 방송; a real-time broadcast, contrasted with 녹화 방송 (pre-recorded).
방송 + 국 (局 'bureau/station'); the company or organization that broadcasts, e.g. KBS, MBC.

usagePhrases.en: to make it onto a broadcast
usagePhrases.note: 타다 ('ride') idiomatically = to get aired and gain attention, often used when a place suddenly goes viral on TV.

examples.en: That singer is on a broadcast today.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 방송에 나오다 = 'appear on TV', the most basic frame; ~에 = the air/program.

examples.ko: 이 프로그램은 매주 금요일 저녁에 생방송으로 진행돼요.
examples.romanization: i peurogeuraemeun maeju geumyoil jeonyeoge saengbangsongeuro jinhaengdwaeyo.
examples.en: This program airs live every Friday evening.
examples.note: Everyday: 생방송으로 = 'live (as a live broadcast)'; ~으로 진행되다 = 'be run/aired as'.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 방송을 탄 뒤로 손님이 줄을 서요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun bangsongeul tan dwiro sonnimi jureul seoyo.
examples.en: Ever since that restaurant got on TV, customers line up.
examples.note: Real-situation: the idiom 방송을 타다 ('ride the broadcast' = get aired and go viral); 줄을 서다 = 'line up'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 방송 (放送, 放 'release/send out' + 送 'send') covers both the act of broadcasting and a specific TV or radio program — the hanja image is 'sending out (a signal)'. There isn't one tidy synonym to contrast; instead, learn its internal map: 생방송 (live, 生) versus 녹화 방송 (pre-recorded, 錄畫), and the directional pair 방송에 나오다 (appear, viewer's view) versus 방송에 나가다 (go on air, producer's view). The vivid idiom 방송을 타다 ('ride the broadcast') means something got aired and drew attention. The English-speaker pitfall is conflating 방송 with neighboring words: 채널 is the 'channel', 프로그램 is a specific 'program/show', and 방송 is the airing/broadcast itself — so for a named show, 프로그램 is clearer than 방송. Also note 방송 frequently appears as a verb 방송하다 ('to broadcast').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 방송 (a broadcast / the airing) with 채널 ('channel') or 프로그램 ('a specific show') — 방송 is the broadcasting/airing itself, not the slot or the title.
Mixing up 방송에 나오다 (appear on air, said by a viewer) and 방송에 나가다 (go on air, said from the production side) — the direction of 나오다 vs 나가다 flips the perspective.
Forgetting the contrast 생방송 (live) vs 녹화 방송 (pre-recorded) and calling a taped show 생방송 — 생 specifically marks real-time airing.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 여론 means "public opinion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 여론 (yeoron) means "public opinion". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 여론이 나빠지다 ("public opinion turns negative"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 여론 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 나빠지다 / 악화되다 ('worsen', 惡化) describe collective sentiment souring; 여론 is the subject with 이/가.
여론 + 조사 (調査 'survey'); written as one compound, the standard term for a public poll.
형성하다 ('form', 形成) is the formal verb, often with media as the agent that shapes opinion.
여론 paired with 관심 ('interest') for what the public collectively cares about.

examples.en: After that incident, public opinion turned negative.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 여론이 나빠지다 = 'opinion sours'; 이후로 = 'after, ever since'.

examples.ko: 최근 여론조사에서 그 정책에 대한 반대가 높게 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: choegeun yeoronjosaeseo geu jeongchaege daehan bandaega nopge nawasseoyo.
examples.en: In a recent poll, opposition to that policy came out high.
examples.note: Everyday-news: 여론조사 = the compound 'opinion poll'; 높게 나오다 = 'come out high'.

examples.ko: 언론은 여론을 형성하는 데 큰 역할을 해요.
examples.romanization: eolloneun yeoroneul hyeongseonghaneun de keun yeokareul haeyo.
examples.en: The press plays a big role in shaping public opinion.
examples.note: Real-situation: 여론을 형성하다 = 'shape opinion'; ~는 데 역할을 하다 = 'play a role in ~ing', formal civic register.

extendedVocab.nuance: 여론 (輿論, 輿 'public/the multitude, the carriage of the people' + 論 'discourse, opinion') is public opinion — the collective views and mood of society on an issue, especially as measured by polls or reflected in media. The sharp near-synonym contrast is with 의견 ('opinion', 意見): 의견 is one individual's view (제 의견은...), while 여론 is always the aggregate sentiment of the public — you cannot have a personal 여론. Because it is a collective abstract noun, it takes characteristic verbs: 여론이 나빠지다, 여론이 들끓다 ('boil over'), 여론이 형성되다. Set collocations: 여론조사, 여론을 형성하다, 여론의 관심. The English-speaker pitfall is using 여론 for a single person's opinion ('in my opinion'), which must be 제 의견에는 / 제 생각에는, never 여론; also write 여론조사 as one compound, not loosely as 여론 조사.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 여론 for one person's view — that is 의견 or 생각; 여론 is always the collective public mood and can't be personal ('my public opinion' is wrong).
Writing 여론 조사 as two loose words inconsistently — the standard fixed term is the compound 여론조사.
Pairing 여론 with 말하다 ('여론을 말하다') — opinion of the public is shaped/measured: 여론이 형성되다, 여론조사를 하다, not 'spoken'.

extendedVocab.english: the press; the media (as an institution)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 언론 means "the press; the media (as an institution)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "the press; the media (as an institution)" is 언론 (eollon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 언론에 보도되다 ("to be reported in the press"). Watch the particle attached to 언론 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be reported in the press
usagePhrases.note: 보도되다 ('be reported', 報道) is the standard passive paired with 언론; the press is the medium with ~에.
자유 ('freedom', 自由) in a fixed civic phrase about the press's rights and independence.
언론 + 사 (社 'company'); a newspaper or broadcaster as a business entity.
언론 + 보도 (報道 'report'); how the media collectively covered an event.

examples.en: That incident was reported widely in the press.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 언론에 보도되다 = the core passive; 크게 = 'in a big way, widely'.

examples.en: Freedom of the press is an important pillar of democracy.
examples.note: Everyday-civic: 언론의 자유 = the fixed phrase; 기둥 = 'pillar', a common metaphor for a foundation.

examples.ko: 여러 언론사가 같은 사건을 다르게 보도했어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo eollonsaga gateun sageoneul dareuge bodohaesseoyo.
examples.en: Several news organizations reported the same event differently.
examples.note: Real-situation: 언론사 = 'news organization (as a company)'; 보도하다 = 'report (news)', active form.

extendedVocab.nuance: 언론 (言論, 言 'speech/words' + 論 'discourse') refers to the press or news media as a social institution — newspapers, broadcasters, and journalists collectively, together with their public role of informing society; the hanja literally evokes 'public speech/discourse'. Contrast three near terms learners blur: 언론 is the institution, 뉴스 is the news content you watch/read, and 신문 is one specific newspaper. There is also 미디어 (loanword 'media'), but in formal civic discussion of the press's role and rights, 언론 is the standard, weightier term (언론의 자유, never 미디어의 자유 in serious usage). Habitual collocations: 언론에 보도되다, 언론의 자유, 언론사, 언론 보도. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping 언론 with 뉴스 or 미디어 — 'I saw it on the press' should map to 뉴스/언론 보도, and the institution that holds 'freedom of the press' is specifically 언론.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 언론 (the press as an institution) with 뉴스 (the news content) or 신문 (one specific newspaper) — 언론 is the collective social institution, not the content or a single outlet.
Using 미디어 interchangeably in formal civic contexts — for the press's public role and rights, the standard term is 언론 (언론의 자유), not 미디어의 자유.
Saying 언론을 보다 for 'watch the news' — you watch 뉴스 (뉴스를 보다); 언론 is the abstract institution, not something you sit and watch.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 게시판 means "bulletin board; (online) message board" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 게시판 (gesipan) = "bulletin board; (online) message board". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 게시판에 글을 올리다 ("to post on the board") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 게시판, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 글을 올리다 ('put up a post') is the standard verb; 글 ('a written post') is the thing you upload, with ~에 for the board.
자유 ('free', 自由) + 게시판; the open, anything-goes section of a community site.

usagePhrases.en: a notice appears on the board
usagePhrases.note: 뜨다 ('come up, pop up') is natural for a post or notice showing up on screen.
질문 ('question', 質問) + 게시판; the section where users post questions for others to answer.

examples.en: I posted one photo on the board.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 올리다 = 'upload/put up'; 한 장 uses the counter 장 for flat things like photos.

examples.ko: 궁금한 점이 있으면 자유게시판에 글을 남기세요.
examples.romanization: gunggeumhan jeomi isseumyeon jayugesipane geureul namgiseyo.
examples.en: If you have questions, leave a post on the open board.
examples.note: Everyday: 글을 남기다 = 'leave a post' (alt. of 올리다); 궁금한 점 = 'something you're curious about'.

examples.ko: 그 글이 게시판에서 큰 화제가 되었어요.
examples.romanization: geu geuri gesipaneseo keun hwajega doeeosseoyo.
examples.en: That post became a big topic of discussion on the board.
examples.note: Real-situation: 화제가 되다 = 'become a hot topic'; ~에서 marks the board as the location of buzz.

extendedVocab.nuance: 게시판 (揭示板, 揭示 'to post up, display' + 板 'board/plank') is a bulletin board — both the physical kind (a notice board on a wall) and the online kind (a forum or message board on a website); the hanja literally means 'display board'. Online, the key system of collocations is: you 글을 올리다 ('upload a post') or 글을 남기다 ('leave a post') on a 게시판, and others respond underneath with 댓글 ('comments', 답글 for a direct reply). The near concept to keep distinct is 댓글 — the 게시판 is the structured space where original posts (글) live, while 댓글 are the replies attached to a post; don't confuse the container with the comments. It also contrasts with live 채팅 (chat), which is real-time. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 게시판에 쓰다 ('write on the board') alone for posting — the idiomatic phrasing needs the object 글: 게시판에 글을 올리다/남기다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 게시판 (the board where original posts live) with 댓글 (the comments left under a post) — the board holds 글, and 댓글 are the replies.
Saying 게시판에 쓰다 by itself for posting online — the idiomatic phrasing is 게시판에 글을 올리다 or 글을 남기다, with 글 as the object.
Using 글을 내리다 carelessly for 'delete' — 글을 내리다 means take a post down/unpublish it; to erase it you 글을 삭제하다.

揭示板: 揭示 'to post up, display' + 板 'board/plank' — the hanja literally means 'display board'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기사 means "(news) article; report" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기사 (gisa) means "(news) article; report". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기사를 쓰다 ("to write an article"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쓰다 is the standard verb from the journalist's side; 기자가 기사를 쓰다 ('a reporter writes an article').

usagePhrases.en: an article comes out / is published
usagePhrases.note: 나다 ('come out') is idiomatic for an article appearing in print or online.
신문 ('newspaper', 新聞) + 기사; the most common compound for a print article.
검색하다 ('search', 檢索) for finding articles online, e.g. by keyword or date.

examples.en: I read one article in today's newspaper.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 신문에서 = 'in the newspaper'; 하나 counts the article casually.

examples.ko: 그 사건에 대한 기사가 모든 신문에 났어요.
examples.romanization: geu sageone daehan gisaga modeun sinmune nasseoyo.
examples.en: An article about that incident came out in every newspaper.
examples.note: Everyday: ~에 대한 기사 = 'an article about ~'; 기사가 나다 = 'an article comes out', the set verb.

examples.ko: 요즘은 종이 신문보다 온라인 기사를 더 많이 봐요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jongi sinmunboda ollain gisareul deo mani bwayo.
examples.en: These days I read online articles more than paper newspapers.
examples.note: Real-situation: 온라인 기사 = 'online article'; ~보다 더 많이 = 'more than ~', a comparison frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 기사 (記事, 記 'record/write down' + 事 'matter, event') means a news article or report — a single written piece of journalism in a newspaper, magazine, or online; the hanja literally means 'a written record of an event'. Distinguish it carefully from neighbors: 언론 is the press as an institution, 보도 (報道) is the ACT of reporting, and 기사 is the concrete written unit of content that results. A crucial English-speaker pitfall is the homonym trap: 기사 is also a completely separate word meaning 'driver' (司機/운전기사) — and historically 'knight' (騎士) — so 택시 기사 is 'taxi driver', not 'taxi article'; only context tells which 기사 is meant. Natural collocations: 기사를 쓰다, 기사가 나다, 신문 기사, 기사를 검색하다. Don't reach for 기사 when you mean the abstract media institution — that is 언론.

Confusing the two senses of 기사 — 'news article' (記事) versus 'driver' (운전기사); 택시 기사 is a taxi driver, so rely on context to disambiguate.
Using 기사 for the abstract media institution — that is 언론, while 기사 is one specific written article.
Saying 기사를 만들다 ('make an article') by translating loosely — a reporter 기사를 쓰다 (writes it); 만들다 doesn't collocate with a news article.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 책임 means "responsibility" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "responsibility" is 책임 (chaegim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 책임이 있다 ("to be responsible / to bear responsibility"). Watch the particle attached to 책임 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to be responsible / to bear responsibility
usagePhrases.note: the core stative pattern; the duty rests on you (책임이 없다 = it's not on you)
fixed phrase with 지다 (to carry on the back); this is how you say you'll own the outcome
add 감(感, feeling) to name the inner trait; describes a person, not the duty itself
add 자(者, person) for the responsible party, e.g. the manager handling an issue

examples.en: That's my responsibility.
examples.note: simplest form: 책임 + 이에요 to flatly claim a duty as yours

examples.en: Parents have a responsibility toward their children.
examples.note: N에 대한 책임 marks who or what the responsibility is for

examples.ko: 이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임을 지겠습니다.
examples.romanization: i ireun jega matasseunikka kkeutkkaji chaegimeul jigetseumnida.
examples.en: Since I took on this work, I will take responsibility for it to the end.
examples.note: formal 합니다 form with 책임을 지다; common at work when committing to a task

extendedVocab.nuance: 책임 (責任, 責 'demand/blame' + 任 'duty entrusted') is the abstract weight of being answerable for an outcome, and it lives almost entirely through verbs: 책임을 지다 (shoulder it) and 책임이 있다 (it falls on you). The dividing line you must learn is 책임 vs 의무: 책임 is accountability AFTER the fact (who answers if it goes wrong), while 의무 is a duty you are required to perform regardless of result. Also distinguish the bare noun 책임 from 책임감, which is the inner sense of duty a person feels, so describe an obligation with 책임 but a person's character with 책임감. The classic English-speaker trap is treating 책임 like the verb 'to be responsible' and saying 책임하다; Korean has no such verb, so you must reach for 책임을 지다 or 책임이 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 책임하다 — 책임 is a noun, not a verb stem; the action is 책임을 지다 (take it) or the state is 책임이 있다.
Do not swap 책임 with 의무: 책임 is being answerable for an outcome (blame/credit), while 의무 is a duty you are required to perform.
Avoid 책임을 가지다 (a 직역 of 'have responsibility'); the natural collocation is 책임이 있다 with the subject particle 이, not 가지다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 의무 means "duty, obligation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 의무 (uimu) = "duty, obligation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 의무가 있다 ("to have an obligation / to be obligated") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 의무, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to have an obligation / to be obligated
usagePhrases.note: the standard pattern; pairs with -아/어야 한다 ideas of 'must'
fixed phrase with 다하다 (to do fully); sounds formal and earnest
N의 의무 names a specific civic duty; one of the constitutional 4대 의무
의무 + 적 + 으로 makes the adverb for things you must do, not by choice

examples.en: Education is a duty of citizens.
examples.note: simplest N은/는 N의 의무 frame stating a flat civic duty

examples.en: I only fulfilled my duty.
examples.note: modest reply when thanked; 의무를 다하다 + -았을 뿐이다 (nothing more)

examples.en: You have to take this training as a requirement.
examples.note: 의무적으로 stresses it is mandatory; pairs naturally with -아/어야 하다

extendedVocab.nuance: 의무 (義務, 義 'righteousness/what is right' + 務 'task') is a duty imposed from OUTSIDE, by law, rule, or role, that you are required to carry out, and it is the natural opposite of 권리 (rights) — the pair 권리와 의무 is almost a set phrase. The boundary against 책임 is the key one for learners: 의무 is the binding requirement to act (you MUST), while 책임 is being answerable once something is done or goes wrong. It feels distinctly more formal and rule-bound than 책임, so you'll meet 의무 in civic contexts like taxes (납세), military service (국방), and compulsory education. The English-speaker pitfall is using 의무 for a casual favor: because English 'I'm obligated to' can be loose, learners overreach, but 의무 implies a genuinely binding requirement, so a friendly request is never an 의무.

Do not use 의무 for a casual favor or social nicety; it implies a legally or institutionally binding requirement, not a friendly request.
Do not confuse 의무 with 책임: 의무 is the required duty to act, while 책임 is accountability for the outcome.
Avoid saying 의무하다; 의무 is a noun, so use 의무가 있다 or 의무를 다하다 to express the action.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 권리 means "right (entitlement)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 권리 (gwolli) means "right (entitlement)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 권리가 있다 ("to have a right"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 권리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: the core pattern; states an entitlement you are owed (권리가 없다 = you have no claim)
주장하다 (to claim/insist); used when standing up for what you are owed
기본(基本) + 권리 for fundamental rights; 기본권 is the compressed legal term
보호하다 (to protect); appears in formal, legal, and consumer contexts

examples.en: I have a right to know too.
examples.note: simple V-(으)ㄹ 권리가 있다; everyday way to assert an entitlement

examples.ko: 소비자는 자신의 권리를 잘 알아야 해요.
examples.romanization: sobijaneun jasinui gwollireul jal araya haeyo.
examples.en: Consumers should know their rights well.
examples.note: common in consumer education; 권리 as the noun object of 알다

examples.en: Obligations always follow rights.
examples.note: 권리 and 의무 paired as opposites; 권리에는 ... 따르다 is a stock saying

extendedVocab.nuance: 권리 (權利, 權 'authority/power' + 利 'benefit') is a right in the sense of a justly-owed entitlement you may claim, and it is the structural partner of 의무 (duty) — they are introduced together as 권리와 의무. The synonym line to watch is 권리 vs 권한: 권리 is what an individual is OWED (a citizen's right to vote), whereas 권한(權限) is delegated AUTHORITY to act within limits (a manager's authority to approve), so don't say a boss has 권리 to sign off — that's 권한. A pronunciation note: 권리 surfaces as [궐리] because ㄴ assimilates to ㄹ next to 리. The big English-speaker pitfall is the false friend with direction: 권리 never means 'right' as in right-versus-left — that is 오른쪽 — so 'turn right' is 오른쪽으로, never 권리.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 권리 (a right/entitlement) with 오른쪽 (the right-hand side/direction) — English 'right' covers both, Korean does not.
Do not say 권리하다; express it with verbs like 권리를 주장하다 or the state 권리가 있다.
Do not mix up 권리 (what you're owed) with 권한 (authority delegated to act); a manager's sign-off power is 권한, not 권리.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 의지 means "will, willpower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "will, willpower" is 의지 (uiji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 의지가 강하다 ("to have a strong will"). Watch the particle attached to 의지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the most common description; 강하다 (strong) vs 약하다 (weak)
used to admit you give in easily, e.g. on a diet or quitting smoking
add 력(力, power) to emphasize will as raw strength against temptation

usagePhrases.en: to have the will to do something
usagePhrases.note: V-(으)ㄹ 의지가 있다 shows the determination to actually act

examples.en: I have weak willpower.
examples.note: simplest 의지가 약하다; a common half-joking confession before a diet

examples.ko: 그 사람은 의지가 강해서 끝까지 포기하지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun uijiga ganghaeseo kkeutkkaji pogihaji anasseoyo.
examples.en: That person has a strong will, so they didn't give up to the end.
examples.note: explaining a result with 의지가 강하다 + -아/어서

examples.ko: 저는 한국어를 끝까지 배울 의지가 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hangugeoreul kkeutkkaji baeul uijiga isseoyo.
examples.en: I have the will to learn Korean to the end.
examples.note: V-(으)ㄹ 의지가 있다 expressing firm personal determination

extendedVocab.nuance: 의지 (意志, 意 'intention' + 志 'aspiration/resolve') is willpower — the inner resolve to push through difficulty — and it is overwhelmingly described as 강하다 (strong) or 약하다 (weak). The contrast to draw is 의지 vs 의욕(意慾): 의지 is the steady RESOLVE to endure and not quit (의지가 강하다), while 의욕 is the eager DRIVE or motivation to start (의욕이 넘치다, brimming with enthusiasm), so a person can have 의욕 to begin yet lack the 의지 to finish. Because it implies effort against temptation or hardship, 의지 is wrong for a light wish — wanting a snack is never 의지. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the homophone trap: the noun 의지 (will) looks identical to the verb stem in 의지하다, but 의지하다 means 'to lean on / rely on someone' — a completely different idea — so 친구에게 의지하다 is 'lean on a friend,' not 'will a friend.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse the noun 의지 (willpower) with the verb 의지하다 (to lean on / depend on someone) — same spelling, unrelated meaning.
Do not use 의지 for a light wish like wanting a snack; reserve it for serious determination against hardship.
Do not blur 의지 (resolve to endure) with 의욕 (eager drive to start); you can have 의욕 but no 의지 to follow through.

extendedVocab.explanation: 정신 (jeongsin) = "spirit, mind, consciousness". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 정신이 없다 ("to be frazzled / too busy to think straight") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to be frazzled / too busy to think straight
usagePhrases.note: very common idiom; means overwhelmed/swamped, not literally mindless

usagePhrases.en: to pull oneself together / come to one's senses
usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase; snap back to focus or regain composure after a shock
정신 + 적(的): 정신적 스트레스 (mental stress), as opposed to 육체적 (physical)
adverb; doing something so busily you lose all track of time

examples.en: These days I'm swamped.
examples.note: the everyday meaning of 정신이 없다: overwhelmed, not insane

examples.en: Don't panic and pull yourself together.
examples.note: 정신(을) 차리다 said to someone flustered or in shock; 을 often dropped in speech

examples.ko: 몸도 중요하지만 정신 건강도 챙겨야 해요.
examples.romanization: momdo jungyohajiman jeongsin geongangdo chaenggyeoya haeyo.
examples.en: The body matters, but you also have to take care of mental health.
examples.note: 정신 건강 (mental health) explicitly contrasted with 몸 (body)

extendedVocab.nuance: 정신 (精神, 精 'refined essence/vital energy' + 神 'spirit') spans spirit, mind, and mental clarity, and in daily speech it lives mostly inside idioms you should memorize as whole chunks: 정신이 없다 means too busy or flustered to focus, and 정신을 차리다 means to regain composure. The synonym boundary that trips learners is 정신 vs 마음: 정신 leans toward mental FOCUS, alertness, and consciousness (the cognitive faculty), while 마음 is the heart — feelings, intentions, and emotional warmth — so 마음이 아프다 is 'heartbroken' but 정신이 아프다 is not idiomatic. It also contrasts with 몸 (body) in 정신 건강 (mental health). The English-speaker pitfall is reading 정신이 없다 literally as 'has no mind/is mindless'; it actually means frazzled or swamped, so never translate these idioms word by word.

정신이 없다 does NOT mean 'having no mind' or 'being stupid'; it means being frazzled, swamped, or too busy to think straight.
Do not confuse 정신 with 마음: 정신 is mental focus/consciousness, while 마음 is the heart, feelings, and intentions.
Avoid 정신을 잡다 as a 직역 of 'grab your mind'; the correct collocation is 정신을 차리다 (차리다, to set/ready).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상상 means "imagination" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 상상 (sangsang) means "imagination". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상상하다 ("to imagine"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상상 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 상상 + 하다 makes the transitive verb; picture a scene in your mind
the high-frequency idiom; 상상이 되다 = it's imaginable, 안 되다 = it isn't
add 력(力, power) for the faculty of imagination, often praised in children
fixed phrase: 상상 + 이상(以上, above) + 으로, meaning far more than expected

examples.en: I couldn't have even imagined it.
examples.note: compact 상상도 못 하다 for total surprise; 도 adds 'even'

examples.ko: 그 영화가 얼마나 무서웠는지 상상이 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: geu yeonghwaga eolmana museowonneunji sangsangi an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You can't imagine how scary that movie was.
examples.note: 상상이 안 되다 is the natural way to say 'unimaginable'

examples.en: The result was better than I imagined.
examples.note: 상상 이상으로 stresses exceeding all expectation

extendedVocab.nuance: 상상 (想像, 想 'think/conceive' + 像 'image') is imagination — forming pictures or hypothetical scenarios in the mind — and it becomes a verb as 상상하다. The synonym line is 상상 vs 생각: 상상 specifically conjures something UNREAL, hypothetical, or not-yet-experienced (picturing life on Mars), while 생각 is ordinary thinking, opinion, or recollection, so 'I think it's true' is 생각, never 상상. The single most useful everyday chunk is 상상이 안 되다 (I can't even picture it), used for things too extreme or surprising to grasp; for a person's creative capacity use 상상력. The English-speaker pitfall is the negative form: learners model 'I can't imagine' on English and produce 상상이 없다, but Korean treats it as the process failing, so it must be 상상이 안 되다 (it won't come into image), not 없다.

Do not confuse 상상 (picturing something unreal/hypothetical) with 생각 (ordinary thought or opinion); 'I think so' is 그렇게 생각해요, not 상상해요.
Avoid 상상이 없다 for 'I can't imagine it'; the idiomatic form is 상상이 안 되다.
Do not say 상상을 하다 for the simple verb when 상상하다 is cleaner; reserve the spaced form for emphasis like 즐거운 상상을 하다.

usagePhrases.note: 판단 + 하다; to weigh a situation and form a conclusion

usagePhrases.en: to make a judgment / reach a decision
usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase with 내리다 (to hand down); sounds deliberate and weighty
add 력(力, power) for the ability to judge well: 판단력이 뛰어나다
올바르다 (to be upright/right) + 판단; common in advice and reflection

examples.en: It's hard to judge.
examples.note: simplest 판단하다 + -기 어렵다 when you can't yet form a conclusion

examples.ko: 성급하게 판단하지 말고 끝까지 들어 보세요.
examples.romanization: seonggeupage pandanhaji malgo kkeutkkaji deureo boseyo.
examples.en: Don't judge hastily; hear it out to the end.
examples.note: common advice; 성급하게 판단하다 (to judge rashly) as the thing to avoid

examples.en: You have to make the final judgment yourself.
examples.note: 판단을 내리다 for arriving at a weighty decision

extendedVocab.nuance: 판단 (判斷, 判 'discern/divide' + 斷 'cut/decide') is the mental act of weighing a situation and forming a reasoned conclusion — the assessment step that comes BEFORE acting. The boundary learners must hold is 판단 vs 결정: 판단 emphasizes the REASONING and evaluation ('is this safe?'), while 결정(決定) is the final CHOICE that follows ('then I'll go'), so a doctor makes a 판단 about your condition and you make the 결정 to have surgery. It collocates with 내리다 as 판단을 내리다 (hand down a judgment), and 판단력 names the skill of judging well. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing 판단 for ordinary 'decide': everyday choices like picking a restaurant are 결정하다 or 정하다, while 판단 carries a heavier, analytical, almost evaluative tone — and note the verb is 판단하다, never 판단이 하다 or 판단을 하다 in neutral use.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 판단 (the reasoning/assessment) with 결정 (the final choice itself); 판단 weighs, 결정 settles.
Do not say 판단이 하다; the verb is 판단하다, or use the phrase 판단을 내리다.
Avoid using 판단 for trivial everyday picks (lunch, a movie); those are 결정하다 or 정하다 — 판단 implies serious evaluation.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목표 means "goal, target" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 목표 (mokpyo) = "goal, target". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 목표를 세우다 ("to set a goal") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 목표, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase with 세우다 (to set up/erect); how you establish an aim
이루다 (to accomplish); reaching what you aimed for (also 달성하다)
정하다 (to fix/settle); pinning down exactly what you'll aim for

usagePhrases.en: to aim for / set as a goal
usagePhrases.note: N을/를 목표로 하다 marks the target you work toward

examples.en: My goal is to pass.
examples.note: simplest 제 목표는 N(이)에요 frame for stating an aim

examples.ko: 작은 목표부터 하나씩 이루어 나가고 있어요.
examples.romanization: jageun mokpyobuteo hanassik irueo nagago isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm achieving them one by one, starting from small goals.
examples.note: 목표를 이루다 + -아 나가다 for steady ongoing progress

examples.en: I'm studying with the goal of passing TOPIK level 3.
examples.note: N을/를 목표로 marks the concrete target you aim for

extendedVocab.nuance: 목표 (目標, 目 'eye' + 標 'mark/sign' — literally the mark the eye fixes on) is a concrete, measurable goal or target you aim at, and it travels with a tight verb family: 세우다 or 정하다 to set it, 이루다 or 달성하다 to achieve it. The synonym line is 목표 vs 꿈: 목표 is specific and outcome-focused (pass TOPIK 3, save 1,000,000 won, run 5km), while 꿈 is broader, emotional, and aspirational (become a doctor, a better world), so use 목표 for things you can tick off and 꿈 for the life vision behind them. Note also 목표 vs 목적(目的): 목표 is the concrete TARGET, 목적 is the underlying PURPOSE/reason. The English-speaker pitfall is forming a verb directly: 'to goal' tempts learners into 목표하다, which is unnatural in writing — say 목표를 세우다 or 목표로 하다 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 목표하다 in writing; prefer 목표를 세우다 (set) or 목표로 하다 (aim for).
Do not confuse 목표 (a concrete, achievable target) with 꿈 (a larger, emotional dream/aspiration).
Do not blur 목표 (the target you hit) with 목적 (the purpose/reason behind it); 'the goal is 3급' is 목표, 'the purpose of studying' is 목적.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 인상 means "impression" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 인상 (insang) means "impression". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 첫인상 ("first impression"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 인상 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 첫 (first) + 인상; the impression you make on first meeting
describes how someone comes across in looks or manner (인상이 나쁘다 = off-putting)
인상(이) 깊다 = it left a deep impression; 깊다 literally 'deep'
좋은 인상을 주다 = to make a good impression on someone

examples.en: You give such a nice impression.
examples.note: 인상이 좋다 as a warm compliment about someone's manner; honorific -으시-

examples.en: First impressions are really important in interviews.
examples.note: 첫인상 in a practical, high-stakes context

examples.en: That movie's ending was very memorable.
examples.note: 인상(이) 깊다 for something that stuck with you

extendedVocab.nuance: 인상 (印象, 印 'stamp/imprint' + 象 'image' — literally an image stamped on the mind) is the impression a person or thing leaves on you, and it surfaces mostly in 첫인상 (first impression), 인상이 좋다 (comes across well), and 인상(이) 깊다 (memorable). The synonym line is 인상 vs 느낌: 인상 is the overall IMPRESSION someone gives others (often judged from appearance and manner: 인상이 좋다), while 느낌 is the subjective FEELING/vibe YOU personally get ('I got a weird feeling'), so 첫인상 is what you project, 느낌 is what you sense. The big English-speaker pitfall is the homophone with economics: 인상 also means a price/wage HIKE (가격 인상, 인상되다), a totally separate word, so 'a deep impression' is 인상이 깊다 but '가격이 인상되다' is 'the price was raised' — context disambiguates, and 인상 깊다 must never be read literally as 'a deep face.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse the mind-sense 인상 (impression) with the economic 인상 (a price/wage increase, e.g. 가격 인상); they are homophones with unrelated meanings.
인상(이) 깊다 means 'memorable / left a deep impression'; do not read it literally as 'a deep face' or physiognomy.
Do not swap 인상 with 느낌: 인상 is the impression you give others, while 느낌 is the personal feeling/vibe you receive.

印象: 印 'stamp/imprint' + 象 'image' — literally an image stamped on the mind.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 양심 means "conscience" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "conscience" is 양심 (yangsim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 양심이 있다 ("to have a conscience"). Watch the particle attached to 양심 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: says someone has moral sense; the negative 양심이 없다 is a harsh insult

usagePhrases.en: to feel a pang of conscience / guilty
usagePhrases.note: fixed idiom with 찔리다 (to be pricked/stabbed); a guilty twinge inside
양심 + 적(的): 양심적인 사람 = a person who acts on conscience

usagePhrases.en: to keep one's conscience / stay honest
usagePhrases.note: 지키다 (to keep/guard); to act rightly even when no one is watching

examples.en: My conscience bothers me.
examples.note: bare 양심에 찔리다; the everyday way to admit you feel guilty

examples.en: That person works conscientiously.
examples.note: 양심적으로 (adverb) for acting with honest integrity

examples.ko: 아무도 안 봐도 양심을 지키는 게 중요해요.
examples.romanization: amudo an bwado yangsimeul jikineun ge jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: Even if no one is watching, keeping your conscience matters.
examples.note: 양심을 지키다 for staying honest unobserved

extendedVocab.nuance: 양심 (良心, 良 'good' + 心 'heart/mind' — literally 'the good heart') is the conscience, your inner sense of right and wrong, and it surfaces in the idiom 양심에 찔리다 (to feel a twinge of guilt) and the adjective 양심적 (conscientious). The synonym line is 양심 vs 의식(意識): 양심 is the MORAL faculty that judges right from wrong and produces guilt, while 의식 is AWARENESS/consciousness in the cognitive or social sense (의식을 잃다 'lose consciousness'; 환경 의식 'environmental awareness'), so a guilty pang is 양심, not 의식. The crucial register caution — the English-speaker pitfall here — is that 양심이 없다 ('to have no conscience') is NOT a neutral remark like English 'unscrupulous'; it is a strong moral insult meaning shameless or brazen (often heard as 양심 없다!), so deploy it carefully and never casually about a colleague.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 양심 (the moral conscience judging right vs wrong) with 의식 (awareness/consciousness, e.g. losing consciousness or social awareness).
Be careful with 양심이 없다 — it is a strong insult implying someone is shameless or brazen, not a neutral observation.
Avoid saying 양심을 느끼다 ('feel conscience') as a 직역; the idiom for feeling guilty is 양심에 찔리다 (the conscience is pricked).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기억 means "memory, recollection" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기억 (gieok) = "memory, recollection". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기억하다 ("to remember (actively hold in mind)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기억, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 기억 + 하다; the transitive verb for deliberately remembering
fixed phrase with 나다 (to arise); the memory surfaces on its own
the everyday way to say it slipped your mind (not a refusal)

usagePhrases.en: to stay in one's memory / be memorable
usagePhrases.note: 남다 (to remain); something you won't forget

examples.en: I can't remember.
examples.note: the default, natural way to say something slipped your mind

examples.ko: 그날 일을 아직도 똑똑히 기억하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: geunal ireul ajikdo ttokttoki gieokago isseoyo.
examples.en: I still clearly remember what happened that day.
examples.note: active 기억하다 + -고 있다 = deliberately holding it in mind, unlike the passive 기억이 나다

examples.ko: 어릴 때 살던 동네가 아직도 기억에 남아 있어요.
examples.romanization: eoril ttae saldeon dongnega ajikdo gieoge nama isseoyo.
examples.en: The neighborhood I lived in as a child still stays in my memory.
examples.note: 기억에 남다 (+ -아 있다) for a lasting, vivid memory

extendedVocab.nuance: 기억 (記憶, 記 'record/write down' + 憶 'recall/think of') is memory or recollection, and the key intermediate skill is choosing the idiom over the bare verb. The contrast learners must internalize is 기억하다 vs 기억이 나다: 기억하다 is ACTIVE, deliberate holding-in-mind ('be sure to remember this', 꼭 기억하세요), while 기억이 나다 is the memory PASSIVELY surfacing on its own ('oh, it just came back to me'), so 'I can't recall' is the spontaneous 기억이 안 나다, not the deliberate-sounding 기억하지 않다. 기억에 남다 describes something that stays with you. There is also a synonym boundary against 추억(追憶): 추억 is specifically FOND, nostalgic memory of the past (good old days), so warm childhood memories can be 추억, but a phone number you forgot is only 기억. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'don't remember' to 기억하지 않다, which wrongly implies a willful choice not to remember.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For 'can't remember,' use 기억이 안 나다, not the stiff 기억하지 않다 — the latter implies a deliberate refusal to remember.
Do not confuse 기억 (general memory/recall) with 추억 (fond, nostalgic memories of the past); a forgotten password is 기억, cherished childhood days are 추억.
Do not say 기억을 잊다 redundantly; use 잊다/잊어버리다 for 'forget' and reserve 기억 for the recall side (기억이 나다 / 기억에 남다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 성실하다 means "sincere, diligent, conscientious" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 성실하다 (seongsilhada) means "sincere, diligent, conscientious". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성실한 사람 ("a diligent, dependable person"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 성실하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Top-tier compliment for a worker or student; pairs with the noun directly via the -ㄴ form
성실하게 = adverb form; the habitual partner is 일하다 or 공부하다, framing steady effort
태도 (attitude) is praised more than raw talent in Korean work culture
성실히 = slightly more formal -히 adverb; 임하다 (to undertake) is written/formal register

examples.en: That friend is truly diligent and dependable.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 성실하다 + 요-ending; note the stem 하 becomes 해요

examples.ko: 저는 무슨 일이든 성실하게 하려고 노력해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun museun irideun seongsilhage haryeogo noryeokaeyo.
examples.en: I try to do everything diligently, whatever the task.
examples.note: Everyday self-PR line for interviews; 무슨 일이든 = whatever the task; adverb 성실하게 modifies 하다

examples.en: We gave a scholarship to the student who attended faithfully.
examples.note: Real situation: 출석하다 = attend; here 성실 covers showing up consistently over a term

extendedVocab.nuance: 성실하다 (誠實하다, from 誠 'sincerity' + 實 'substance/truth') is one of the most valued character words in Korean work and school culture: it means earnest, diligent, and reliable in carrying out duties — the steady person who shows up and follows through. Because it praises consistent effort rather than results, it is the single safest strength to claim in an interview ('저는 성실합니다'). The key near-synonym to separate is 정직하다 (honest): 성실 is about diligence and faithfulness to your work, while 정직 is about not lying — a lazy person can still be 정직, and a liar can technically be 성실. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not double the 하 (the 요-form is 성실해요, never 성실하해요), and do not reach for 성실하다 when you mean 'sincere' in the sense of heartfelt feelings — that emotional sincerity is 진실하다 or 진심이다; 성실 is sincerity expressed as hard work.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 성실하해요: the stem already ends in 하다, so it conjugates 성실해요 / 성실한 — only one 해
Using it for 'honest' (doesn't lie): that overlapping-but-different idea is 정직하다; 성실 is about diligence/reliability
Using it for heartfelt 'sincere' (a sincere apology): that emotional sincerity is 진심으로/진실하다, not 성실하다

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정직하다 means "honest, truthful, upright" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "honest, truthful, upright" is 정직하다 (jeongjikada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정직한 사람 ("an honest, upright person"). Watch the particle attached to 정직하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Moral praise; implies they don't lie or cheat, a deeper claim than mere friendliness
정직하게 = adverb; very often paired with owning up to a mistake or telling an uncomfortable truth
Set phrase about leading an upright, above-board life — a moral self-image
Proverb-style saying taught in school; 정직이 takes the subject particle 이

examples.en: That person is very honest.
examples.note: Plain frame; 정직하다 → 정직해요, a flat moral judgment about character

examples.ko: 실수했을 때 정직하게 말하는 게 제일 중요해요.
examples.romanization: silsuhaesseul ttae jeongjikage malhaneun ge jeil jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: When you make a mistake, being honest about it is the most important thing.
examples.note: Everyday work advice; 실수 = mistake; 정직하게 말하다 = come clean rather than cover up

examples.ko: 그 가게는 30년 동안 정직하게 장사해서 단골이 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu gageneun 30nyeon dongan jeongjikage jangsahaeseo dangori manayo.
examples.en: That shop has done business honestly for 30 years, so it has many regulars.
examples.note: Real situation: 정직 applied to a business — no overcharging or cheating; 단골 = regular customer

extendedVocab.nuance: 정직하다 (正直하다, 正 'correct/upright' + 直 'straight') means honest and truthful in the moral sense: not lying, not cheating, dealing straight with people. The near-synonym you must distinguish is 솔직하다 (率直, frank/candid): 솔직하다 is about openly saying what you really think or feel ('솔직히 말하면…' = to be frank…), whereas 정직하다 is about not deceiving anyone — a moral judgment, not a communication style. You praise a child, a clerk, or a business as 정직하다; you call someone 솔직하다 when they bluntly share an opinion. Register: 정직하다 is a weighty ethical compliment, while 솔직하다 is everyday and can even be a mild warning ('너무 솔직해' = a bit too blunt). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping both English 'honest' senses onto one word — in 'Honestly, I think…' English 'honestly' means 솔직히, not 정직히. Also, 정직해 보이다 means 'seems honest/trustworthy,' not 'looks smart.'

겸손하게 = adverb form; act without boasting or putting yourself above others

examples.en: That person is truly humble.
examples.note: Basic frame; honorific noun 그분 + 겸손해요 — a respectful compliment

examples.ko: 그 선배는 실력이 뛰어난데도 항상 겸손해요.
examples.romanization: geu seonbaeneun sillyeogi ttwieonandedo hangsang gyeomsonhaeyo.
examples.en: That senior is outstanding yet always humble.
examples.note: Everyday praise; -(으)ㄴ데도 = even though; 실력 = skill — the more skilled, the more impressive the humility

examples.ko: 칭찬을 들으면 한국 사람들은 겸손하게 '아니에요'라고 해요.
examples.romanization: chingchaneul deureumyeon hanguk saramdeureun gyeomsonhage 'anieyo'rago haeyo.
examples.en: When praised, Koreans humbly say 'no, not at all.'
examples.note: Real cultural situation: deflecting a compliment is expected politeness, not real disagreement

Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Compliment for someone who thinks before acting or speaking
신중하게 = adverb; the textbook partners are 결정하다 (decide) and 선택하다 (choose)
Often advised before a big, irreversible choice
Formal set phrase (기하다 = 'aim for'); common in announcements and official notices

examples.en: That person makes decisions carefully.
examples.note: Simple frame pairing the adverb 신중하게 with its core partner 결정하다

examples.ko: 큰돈이 들어가는 일이라 신중하게 결정해야 해요.
examples.romanization: keundoni deureoganeun irira sinjunghage gyeoljeonghaeya haeyo.
examples.en: It involves a lot of money, so we have to decide carefully.
examples.note: Everyday practical use for contracts or real estate; 큰돈 = a large sum; -아/어야 하다 = have to

examples.en: Think it over carefully before you decide to change jobs.
examples.note: Real situation: -고 나서 = after doing; 이직 = changing jobs — a weighty life choice

extendedVocab.nuance: 신중하다 (愼重하다, 愼 'careful/prudent' + 重 'weighty/grave') means prudent and careful specifically about decisions and words — weighing things seriously before you act or speak, rather than rushing. Its negative twin is 우유부단하다 (indecisive): 신중하다 weighs wisely and then chooses, while 우유부단 just can't choose. Register: fully positive and usable formally (신중을 기하다 in notices). Saying 신중하해요: the 하다 stem yields 신중해요 / 신중한

extendedVocab.explanation: "generous, tolerant, big-hearted (forgiving)" is 너그럽다 (neogeureopda). usagePhrases.note: ㅂ-irregular in the modifier: 너그럽다 → 너그러운 (the ㅂ becomes 우)

usagePhrases.en: let it slide, go easy on someone
usagePhrases.note: 너그럽게 봐주다 = forgive/overlook generously; a fixed, very common pairing
마음이 + 너그럽다 = generous in spirit; 마음 (heart/mind) is the typical subject
너그러이 = literary -이 adverb form; 용서하다 = forgive — elevated register

examples.en: Our manager is big-hearted and easygoing.
examples.note: Basic frame showing the ㅂ-irregular 요-form: 너그럽다 → 너그러워요 (not 너그럽어요)

examples.ko: 부장님이 너그러워서 작은 실수는 그냥 넘어가 주세요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimi neogeureowoseo jageun silsuneun geunyang neomeoga juseyo.
examples.en: The manager is big-hearted, so they let small mistakes slide.
examples.note: Everyday: 너그러워서 (ㅂ-irregular + -아서); 넘어가 주다 = let it pass for someone's sake

examples.en: Since it's my first time, could you go easy on me?
examples.note: Real situation: a polite newcomer's request; honorific -시- + 봐주다 softens the ask

extendedVocab.nuance: 너그럽다 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) describing a generous, tolerant, forgiving spirit — a broad-minded person who doesn't nitpick and readily overlooks faults. Its core is emotional generosity and patience with people, not giving money. The synonym boundary matters: for being lenient/tolerant it overlaps with 관대하다 (寬大, formal, often used of authorities being lenient — 관대한 처벌 = a lenient punishment), but generosity with money or food leans on 후하다 (후하게 주다 = give generously) or 인심이 좋다. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 냉정하다 means "coolheaded, level-headed; cold, detached" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 냉정하다 (naengjeonghada) = "coolheaded, level-headed; cold, detached". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 냉정하게 판단하다 ("judge coolly/objectively") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 냉정하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Positive sense: 냉정하게 = without letting emotion sway you; the praise-worthy reading
Negative sense — chilly and unfeeling — when applied to how someone treats others
Toward a person this sounds harsh; the same word that praised judgment now stings
Set phrase; 냉정 as a noun = composure; 되찾다 = recover/get back

examples.en: That person is a bit cold/detached.
examples.note: Simple frame; here the people-directed reading dominates — chilly rather than warm

examples.ko: 감정에 휘둘리지 말고 냉정하게 판단해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gamjeonge hwidulliji malgo naengjeonghage pandanhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: Don't get swept up in emotion; you have to judge coolly.
examples.note: Everyday: the admiring 'level-headed' sense; 휘둘리다 = be swayed; 냉정하게 판단하다 is a compliment

examples.ko: 헤어지자는 말을 너무 냉정하게 해서 상처받았어요.
examples.romanization: heeojijaneun mareul neomu naengjeonghage haeseo sangcheobadasseoyo.
examples.en: They said 'let's break up' so coldly that it hurt.
examples.note: Real situation: the chilly, hurtful sense; 헤어지다 = break up; same adverb, opposite feeling

extendedVocab.nuance: 냉정하다 (冷靜하다, 冷 'cold' + 靜 'quiet/calm') is two-faced and context decides everything. Admiringly it means 'coolheaded / objective' — judging without being swayed by emotion, a real strength under pressure (냉정한 판단, 냉정하게 분석하다). Critically it means 'cold / detached' — treating a person with chilly distance (냉정하게 대하다, 냉정한 말투), which hurts. The same sentence frame can flip: 냉정한 판단 praises, 냉정한 사람 usually faults. Two synonyms sharpen the picture: 침착하다 is purely positive composure (no cold undertone at all), so for a job interview you say 침착하다, not 냉정하다, about yourself; and 차갑다 is the native word that leans almost entirely on the cold-hearted reading and never carries the 'objective judgment' praise. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 냉정하다 is always negative like 'cold-blooded' — calling your own decision-making 냉정하다 is actually a compliment, while calling a friend 냉정하다 is a complaint. Stem note: 냉정해요, not 냉정하해요.

침착하게 = adverb; the classic partner is 대처하다 (handle a situation)
침착함 = the -ㅁ noun form; 잃다 = lose — staying steady when others panic

examples.en: That person is always composed.
examples.note: Basic frame; 침착하다 → 침착해요, describing a steady temperament

examples.en: I was nervous in the interview but answered composedly.
examples.note: Everyday self-description; 긴장되다 = get nervous — an excellent interview strength to claim

examples.ko: 불이 났는데도 그 사람은 침착하게 사람들을 대피시켰어요.
examples.romanization: buri nanneundedo geu sarameun chimchakage saramdeureul daepisikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Even though a fire broke out, that person calmly evacuated everyone.
examples.note: Real crisis: -(으)ㄴ데도 = even though; 대피시키다 = evacuate others — composure under real pressure

examples.romanization: hoeuieseo neomu sogeukjeogeuro itji malgo uigyeoneul naeseyo.
examples.en: Don't be too passive in meetings; speak up with your opinions.
examples.note: Everyday workplace nudge; 의견을 내다 = offer an opinion; 소극적으로 있다 = hang back

examples.ko: 처음엔 소극적이었는데 지금은 많이 적극적으로 변했어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen sogeukjeogieonneunde jigeumeun mani jeokgeukjeogeuro byeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I was passive at first, but now I've become much more proactive.
examples.note: Real growth story: contrast with 적극적; 소극적이었는데 = past + -는데; 변하다 = change

extendedVocab.nuance: 소극적이다 (消極的이다, 消 'extinguish/dwindle' + 極 'pole/extreme' + 的 '-ish/-ive') means passive, reticent, and unassertive — hanging back, not volunteering, doing only the minimum. The hanja literally evokes energy 'dwindling toward zero,' the mirror image of 적극적 (積極的, 積 'accumulate' = energy building up). It is the standard negative counterpart of 적극적이다 and is usually framed as something to work on. The near-synonym to separate is 내성적이다 (introverted): an introvert recharges alone but can still be 적극적 and decisive at work, whereas 소극적 is specifically about not engaging or taking initiative — a behavior, not an energy source. So 'I'm introverted but proactive' is 내성적이지만 적극적이에요, a perfectly normal self-description. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation: because it ends in 이다, it is 소극적이에요 / 소극적인 / 소극적으로 — never the 하다-style 소극적해요. Mapping introvert directly onto 소극적 is the second trap; they are not the same.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 소극적해요: it ends in the copula 이다, so it is 소극적이에요 / 소극적인 / 소극적으로
Treating it as a synonym for 내성적이다 (introverted): 소극적 is lack of initiative/engagement, not inward energy
Forming the adverb as 소극적하게: -적 words take 으로, giving 소극적으로
