extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이기적이다 means "selfish, self-centered" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이기적이다 (igijeogida) = "selfish, self-centered". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이기적인 사람 ("a selfish person") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이기적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Clear criticism: only thinks of themselves; opposite is 이타적인 사람
이기적으로 = adverb form (-적 + 으로), describing self-serving behavior
생각 = thought/idea; faulting the motive behind an action
Direct banmal accusation, typically thrown in an argument

examples.en: That person is really selfish.
examples.note: Basic frame; the copula 이다 gives 이기적이에요 (not 이기적해요) — a real criticism

examples.ko: 룸메이트가 너무 이기적이라서 같이 살기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: rummeiteuga neomu igijeogiraseo gachi salgi himdeureoyo.
examples.en: My roommate is so selfish that living together is hard.
examples.note: Everyday housing complaint; -(이)라서 = because; 같이 살다 = live together

examples.ko: 가끔은 이기적으로 자기를 챙기는 것도 필요해요.
examples.romanization: gakkeumeun igijeogeuro jagireul chaenggineun geotdo piryohaeyo.
examples.en: Sometimes you need to selfishly take care of yourself, too.
examples.note: Real modern usage: softer self-care framing; 챙기다 = look after; said about oneself it can be半-positive

extendedVocab.nuance: 이기적이다 (利己的이다, 利 'benefit' + 己 'self' + 的 '-ish' — literally 'benefit-self-ish') means selfish or self-centered: putting your own interests first at others' expense. It is a genuine criticism, not a light tease, and its clean antonym is 이타적이다 (利他的, 利 'benefit' + 他 'others' = altruistic). A useful nearby contrast is 자기중심적이다 (self-centered, seeing everything from one's own viewpoint), which is slightly more analytical/clinical, while 이기적 is the blunt everyday blame word. In recent casual speech you will hear 이기적 used half-positively about yourself in a self-care sense (이기적으로 나를 챙기다 = put myself first for once), but aimed at someone else it stays firmly negative. The English-speaker pitfall is softening it to mean merely 'independent' or 'self-reliant' — English 'self-sufficient/independent' is 독립적이다, and using 이기적 there wrongly accuses someone of ignoring others. The second pitfall is the copula conjugation: 이기적이에요 / 이기적인 / 이기적으로, never 이기적해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이기적해요: it ends in 이다, so it is 이기적이에요 / 이기적인 / 이기적으로
Softening it to mean 'independent/self-reliant': that is 독립적이다; 이기적 carries real blame for ignoring others
Forming the adverb as 이기적하게: -적 words take 으로 → 이기적으로

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정중하다 means "courteous, polite, respectful (in manner)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정중하다 (jeongjunghada) means "courteous, polite, respectful (in manner)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정중하게 부탁하다 ("ask politely/respectfully"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정중하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 정중하게 = adverb; signals formal courtesy, a notch above casual 친절
Valued in service and business settings toward customers or clients
Softening a refusal with formal courtesy so it doesn't offend
정중히 = formal -히 adverb; 사과드리다 = humbly apologize — standard in written apologies

examples.en: That person is always courteous.
examples.note: Basic frame; 정중하다 → 정중해요, describing dignified, respectful manners

examples.en: I appreciated the offer but declined politely.
examples.note: Everyday: 제안 = proposal; 정중하게 거절 = a graceful, face-saving no

examples.ko: 고객에게는 이메일을 정중한 표현으로 써야 해요.
examples.romanization: gogaegegeneun imeireul jeongjunghan pyohyeoneuro sseoya haeyo.
examples.en: You must write emails to clients using courteous expressions.
examples.note: Real business situation: 표현 = expression; 정중한 표현 = formal, respectful wording

extendedVocab.nuance: 정중하다 (鄭重하다; the 重 carries 'weighty/grave,' so the word evokes treating someone with weighty respect) means courteous and respectful in a formal, dignified way — proper manners and respectful language. The near-synonym you must separate is 친절하다 (kind/friendly), and the dividing line is warmth vs. form: 친절하다 is personal warmth and helpfulness (a 친절한 점원 smiles and helps you happily), while 정중하다 is formal respect shown through correct manners and language (a 정중한 점원 is impeccably proper, not necessarily warm). For a careful apology, a polite refusal, or staff toward an important guest, you reach for 정중하다, where 친절하다 would feel too casual-warm. Also distinguish 겸손하다 (inner humility about oneself) from 정중하다 (outward courtesy toward others) — different directions. Register: 정중하다 is itself a formal-leaning word, at home in business Korean and written apologies (정중히 사과드립니다). The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing all 'polite' into one word: friendly-polite is 친절하다, formally-courteous is 정중하다. Stem note: 정중해요, not 정중하해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 친절하다 (warm, friendly kindness): 정중하다 is formal respect/courtesy shown through manners
Saying 정중하해요: the 하다 stem gives 정중해요 / 정중한 / 정중하게
Confusing it with 겸손하다: 겸손 is humility about yourself, 정중 is courtesy directed at others

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사교적이다 means "sociable, outgoing (good with people)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "sociable, outgoing (good with people)" is 사교적이다 (sagyojeogida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사교적인 사람 ("a sociable, people-friendly person"). Watch the particle attached to 사교적이다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Compliment: gets along easily with everyone; uses -ㄴ form before a noun
성격 = personality; one of the most common partner nouns
사교적으로 = adverb (-적 + 으로); -아/어 보이다 = seem/appear
어울리다 = blend in; the plain-Korean paraphrase of what 사교적 means

examples.en: That friend is really sociable.
examples.note: Basic frame; the copula 이다 gives 사교적이에요 (not 사교적해요)

examples.en: I'm not really all that sociable.
examples.note: Everyday modest hedge; -(으)ㄴ 편이다 = tend to be on the ... side

examples.ko: 사교적인 동료 덕분에 회식 분위기가 좋았어요.
examples.romanization: sagyojeogin dongnyo deokbune hoesik bunwigiga joasseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to a sociable coworker, the company dinner had a great vibe.
examples.note: Real situation: 덕분에 = thanks to; 회식 = work dinner; 분위기 = atmosphere

extendedVocab.nuance: 사교적이다 (社交的이다, 社 'society/group' + 交 'mingle/associate' + 的 '-ish' — literally 'social-mingling-ish') means sociable and good with people: comfortable mingling, making conversation, and forming connections, often noted in networking or group settings. It is almost always positive. The near-synonym to separate is 외향적이다 (外向的, extroverted): 외향적 is the inner-energy trait — drawing energy from being around others — whereas 사교적 specifically highlights social skill and getting along smoothly with people. The two often coincide but are not identical: someone can be 외향적 (high-energy, loud) yet not especially 사교적 (not actually skilled or graceful with people), and a calm person can be quietly 사교적. So in a self-introduction, 사교적이에요 claims 'I work well with people,' while 외향적이에요 claims 'I'm energized by people.' The English-speaker pitfall is treating 사교적 as a one-to-one match for 'extroverted' and the conjugation: it ends in 이다, giving 사교적이에요 / 사교적인 / 사교적으로, never 사교적해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사교적해요: it ends in the copula 이다, so it is 사교적이에요 / 사교적인 / 사교적으로
Treating it as identical to 외향적이다: 사교적 stresses skill with people, 외향적 is the inner extrovert energy
Forming the adverb as 사교적하게: -적 words take 으로 → 사교적으로

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 우유부단하다 means "indecisive, wishy-washy, unable to make up one's mind" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 우유부단하다 (uyubudanhada) = "indecisive, wishy-washy, unable to make up one's mind". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우유부단한 사람 ("an indecisive person") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 우유부단하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Mild criticism; can't pick or commit to a choice
Four-character word (優柔不斷) used as a 하다-adjective; 성격이 = in personality
Explains the trait through its effect; 결정을 못 하다 = can't make the call
굴다 = behave (in a certain way); describes dithering as it happens

examples.en: I'm a bit indecisive.
examples.note: Simplest frame; the 하다 stem gives 우유부단해요 — a common gentle self-label

examples.ko: 저는 우유부단해서 메뉴 고르는 데도 한참 걸려요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun uyubudanhaeseo menyu goreuneun dedo hancham geollyeoyo.
examples.en: I'm so indecisive that even picking off a menu takes me ages.
examples.note: Everyday relatable use; -아/어서 = so/because; 한참 = a long while

examples.en: When a leader is indecisive, the whole team struggles.
examples.note: Real workplace observation; -(으)면 = when/if; -아/어지다 = become/get

extendedVocab.nuance: 우유부단하다 is a four-character Sino-Korean word (優柔不斷, 優 'gentle/yielding' + 柔 'soft' + 不 'not' + 斷 'cut/decide' — literally 'soft-and-yielding, cannot cut/decide') meaning indecisive and wishy-washy: chronically unable to make up your mind or commit to a choice. The image of 斷 'cutting' is exactly the English 'can't make the cut/call.' The crucial near-synonym to separate is 신중하다 (prudent): 신중하다 weighs options wisely and then decides, a compliment, whereas 우유부단하다 just can't decide at all, a flaw — the same hesitation seen as wisdom (신중) versus paralysis (우유부단). It is a common, mildly self-deprecating word people use about themselves when they agonize over small choices. The English-speaker pitfall is grammatical: despite being a long noun-like idiom, it behaves as a normal 하다-adjective, so it is 우유부단해요 / 우유부단한, never 우유부단이에요 (do not treat the 단 ending as a noun + 이다). The second pitfall is mixing it up with 신중하다 and accidentally praising indecision, or vice versa.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 우유부단이에요: it is a 하다-adjective, so it conjugates 우유부단해요 / 우유부단한 / 우유부단해서
Mixing it up with 신중하다 (wise, prudent caution): 우유부단 is failure to decide, not admirable deliberation
Reading 부단 as a separate noun and inflecting it — the whole 優柔不斷 is one fixed idiom taking 하다

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정확하다 means "to be accurate, exact, correct" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정확하다 (jeonghwakada) means "to be accurate, exact, correct". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정확한 ("accurate (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정확하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier form drops 다 and adds -ㄴ: 정확한 정보 'accurate information', 정확한 시간 'the exact time'.
Polite present. As a 하다 adjective it contracts 하 + 여요 to 해요, never '정확하요'.
Both adverbs are correct; 정확히 is the more idiomatic, slightly more written choice.
Long negative, softer than 틀리다; 정확하지 않아요 gently flags 'that's not quite right'.

examples.en: The clock is accurate.
examples.note: Plain predicate use; 하다 adjective → 해요, the most basic pattern.

examples.en: Thank you for keeping exactly to the time.
examples.note: Adverb 정확히 + 지키다 is the fixed way to praise punctuality.

examples.en: If my memory is correct, the meeting was definitely at 3.
examples.note: Real-situation hedge: -다면 'supposing that' softens a confident claim.

extendedVocab.nuance: 정확하다 means matching the truth or a standard with zero error — accurate numbers, correct facts, precise timing or aim. Its hanja 正確 literally combines 正 'correct/upright' and 確 'firm/sure', so the feel is 'firmly correct'. The nearest synonym is 맞다 'be right', but 맞다 just says an answer is acceptable, while 정확하다 stresses exactness and is more formal — a guess can be 맞다 yet not 정확하다. It habitually pairs with 정보, 시간, 발음, 위치, 수치 and the adverb 정확히 지키다/맞히다. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates 정확해요, 정확한 N, 정확히/정확하게. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating it like a verb and saying '정확하다 정보' — Korean needs the modifier 정확한 정보 — and confusing it with 확실하다, which is about your certainty, not the fact's correctness.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '정확하다 정보' to mean 'accurate information' — 정확하다 is a predicate; before a noun you must use the modifier 정확한 정보.
Using 정확하다 when you mean you feel sure: '확실해요' (I'm certain) ≠ '정확해요' (it is correct). 정확하다 describes the fact, 확실하다 describes your confidence.
Forming the polite present as '정확하요' — 하다 adjectives contract to 해요, so it must be 정확해요.

As a 하다 adjective it conjugates 정확해요 (predicate), 정확한 N (modifier), 정확히/정확하게 (adverb).

The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating it like a verb and saying '정확하다 정보' — Korean needs the modifier 정확한 정보 — and confusing it with 확실하다, which is about your certainty, not the fact's correctness.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 자세하다 means "to be detailed, in detail" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be detailed, in detail" is 자세하다 (jasehada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 자세한 ("detailed (+ noun)"). Watch the particle attached to 자세하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 자세한 설명 'a detailed explanation', 자세한 내용 'detailed content'.
The go-to adverb: 자세히 설명하다 'explain in detail', 자세히 보다 'look closely'.
Polite present; correct but rarer than the adverb 자세히 in everyday talk.
Set request phrase in conversation, email and Q&A.

examples.en: This book's explanations are detailed.
examples.note: Plain predicate: 자세하다 → 자세해요.

examples.ko: 이 부분을 좀 더 자세히 설명해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: i bubuneul jom deo jasehi seolmyeonghae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you explain this part in a bit more detail?
examples.note: Polite request; 자세히 + 설명하다 is a fixed collocation.

examples.en: Read the contract closely before you sign.
examples.note: Real-situation: here 자세히 shifts to 'thoroughly, closely', not just 'in detail'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 자세하다 describes something packed with specific detail, and its adverb 자세히 doubles as 'closely / thoroughly' when you read, look or listen. The hanja 仔細 pairs 仔 'careful' with 細 'fine/minute', giving the sense of 'finely careful'. Compare it with 구체적이다 'concrete/specific': 자세하다 means there is a lot of detail (length, thoroughness), while 구체적이다 means the content is concrete rather than vague — a long answer can be 자세하지만 추상적 (detailed yet abstract). It collocates with 설명, 내용, 일정, 정보 and the request 좀 더 자세히. In speech you hear the adverb 자세히 far more than the bare adjective. The pitfall for English speakers is mapping it to 'careful' in the sense of caution — that is 조심하다 — and writing 자세하게 everywhere when set phrases prefer 자세히.

Using 자세하다 for 'careful/cautious' (watch out, be careful) — that meaning is 조심하다. 자세하다 only means 'detailed / closely, thoroughly'.
Defaulting to 자세하게 in fixed phrases — both adverbs exist, but '자세히 설명해 주세요' and '자세히 보다' are far more idiomatic than 자세하게.
Confusing it with 구체적이다: 'be detailed' (lots of detail) ≠ 'be concrete/specific'. A reply can be 자세하지만 모호할 수 있어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 적절하다 means "to be appropriate, suitable, apt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 적절하다 (jeokjeolhada) = "to be appropriate, suitable, apt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 적절한 ("appropriate (+ noun)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 적절하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 적절한 표현 'an apt expression', 적절한 대응 'an appropriate response'.
Polite present; common in feedback, reviews and evaluations.
Adverb: 적절하게 사용하다 'use appropriately', 적절하게 대처하다 'respond aptly'.
적절하지 않은 표현 'an inappropriate expression'; softer than 틀리다.

examples.en: That expression is appropriate.
examples.note: Plain predicate; 적절하다 → 적절해요.

examples.en: We're looking for an appropriate solution to the problem.
examples.note: 적절한 + noun in a formal written register.

examples.ko: 그 상황에서는 그 말이 적절하지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: geu sanghwangeseoneun geu mari jeokjeolhaji anasseoyo.
examples.en: In that situation, those words weren't appropriate.
examples.note: Real-situation past negative: 적절하지 않았어요 judges social fit after the fact.

extendedVocab.nuance: 적절하다 means well-suited to the situation, context or purpose — the 'right' choice given the circumstances. Its hanja 適切 joins 適 'fit/suitable' and 切 'apt/keen', so it literally reads 'aptly fitting'. The crucial near-synonym is 적당하다: 적절하다 is about contextual/social aptness (the right word, the right response) and sounds proper and judgment-oriented, whereas 적당하다 is about a moderate, just-right amount or degree and is more casual. They are not freely swappable — '적당한 표현' sounds careless where '적절한 표현' is expected. It collocates with 표현, 대응, 조치, 해결책 and the adverb 적절하게 대처하다. It is more formal than 맞다 and frequent in work and writing. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 적당하다 (just-right amount) when judging suitability, and writing '적절하다 표현' instead of the modifier 적절한 표현.

Swapping 적절하다 and 적당하다: 적절하다 = 'fitting/apt for the context'; 적당하다 = 'a moderate, just-right amount/degree' and is more casual. '적당한 표현' weakens the meaning.
Writing '적절하다 해결책' before a noun — use the modifier 적절한 해결책.
Using 적절하다 in casual quantity contexts (e.g., temperature, portion) where Koreans say 적당하다: a comfortable amount is 적당해요, not 적절해요.

extendedVocab.english: to be moderate, just right, adequate
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 적당하다 means "to be moderate, just right, adequate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 적당하다 (jeokdanghada) means "to be moderate, just right, adequate". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 적당한 ("moderate / just-right (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 적당하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 적당한 운동 'moderate exercise', 적당한 크기 'a suitable size'.
Polite present; very common in everyday speech about amount or degree.
Adverb: 적당히 하다 'do it in moderation / don't overdo it'.

usagePhrases.en: give it a rest / don't overdo it
usagePhrases.note: Casual idiom (반말) telling someone to stop going too far.

examples.en: The soup's seasoning is just right.
examples.note: Plain predicate of taste/amount; 적당하다 → 적당해요.

examples.ko: 이 정도 가격이면 적당한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i jeongdo gagyeogimyeon jeokdanghan geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think this price is about right.
examples.note: 적당한 것 같다 'seems just right' softens a judgment in conversation.

examples.en: On weekends I rest a bit and work a bit, in good balance.
examples.note: Real-situation: repeated 적당히 conveys easygoing balance, not measured amounts.

extendedVocab.nuance: 적당하다 expresses a comfortable middle — not too much, not too little, neither extreme. The hanja 適當 combines 適 'fit' with 當 'proper/right', so it reads 'fittingly proper', but in everyday use the feel is quantity- and degree-focused and notably more casual than its cousin 적절하다, which judges contextual aptness. The big watch-point is the adverb 적당히: depending on tone it swings from positive 'in moderation' (적당히 드세요 'don't overeat') to a slack 'just enough to get by, half-heartedly' (적당히 했어 'I did it sloppily'). It pairs with 크기, 가격, 온도, 양, 운동 and the scolding 적당히 좀 해. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 적당히 as always positive — context and tone decide — and over-using formal 적절하다 for casual 'just-right' amounts where Koreans naturally say 적당해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 적당히 as automatically positive: '적당히 했어' often means 'I did it roughly/half-heartedly'. Check the tone before assuming praise.
Using 적당하다 in a formal evaluation where 적절하다 fits better — for an apt expression or proper response, 적절하다 sounds correct, 적당하다 sounds offhand.
Writing '적당하다 크기' before a noun — use the modifier 적당한 크기.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 충분하다 means "to be enough, sufficient, ample" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be enough, sufficient, ample" is 충분하다 (chungbunhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 충분한 ("enough / sufficient (+ noun)"). Watch the particle attached to 충분하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 충분한 시간 'enough time', 충분한 준비 'sufficient preparation'.
Polite present; a very common reassurance ('that's plenty').
Adverb that often means 'fully/totally': 충분히 가능해요 'it's totally doable'.
Softer than 부족하다 for gently saying 'that's not quite enough'.

examples.en: There's enough time.
examples.note: Plain predicate; mark the resource with 이/가: 시간이 충분하다.

examples.ko: 이 정도면 두 명이 먹기에 충분해요.
examples.romanization: i jeongdomyeon du myeongi meokgie chungbunhaeyo.
examples.en: This much is enough for two people to eat.
examples.note: Pattern -기에 충분하다 'enough to ~' states a threshold.

examples.en: I fully understand how you feel.
examples.note: Real-situation: 충분히 here intensifies to 'fully, well enough', not literal quantity.

extendedVocab.nuance: 충분하다 means a quantity, time or degree reaches or exceeds what is needed. Its hanja 充分 joins 充 'fill' and 分 'portion', literally 'a filled portion', so the image is 'the share is filled up'. It is the natural opposite of 부족하다. The near-synonym 풍부하다 means 'abundant/rich' and stresses plentifulness beyond the need, whereas 충분하다 only asserts that the need is met — water can be 충분하다 without being 풍부하다. The adverb 충분히 is hugely useful and often means 'fully/plenty' rather than bare 'enough' (충분히 가능해요 'totally possible'). It collocates with 시간, 준비, 잠, 돈 and the frame -기에 충분하다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 충분 like a noun and saying '충분 있어요' — it is an adjective, so use 충분해요 or 충분한 N — and under-using 충분히 as an intensifier where it naturally means 'more than enough'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '충분 있어요' to mean 'there's enough' — 충분하다 is an adjective; use 충분해요 or 충분한 N (e.g., 시간이 충분해요).
Confusing 충분하다 with 풍부하다: 충분하다 = 'enough for the need'; 풍부하다 = 'abundant/rich'. Resources can be 충분하지만 풍부하지는 않다.
Translating 충분히 only as 'enough' — in 충분히 이해해요 / 충분히 가능해요 it means 'fully / totally', an intensifier.

extendedVocab.english: to be lacking, insufficient, short of
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 부족하다 means "to be lacking, insufficient, short of" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 부족하다 (bujokada) = "to be lacking, insufficient, short of". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부족한 ("lacking / insufficient (+ noun)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 부족하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 부족한 부분 'the lacking part', 부족한 점 'shortcomings'.
Polite present; an everyday way to flag a shortage.
잠이 부족하다 'be short on sleep', 경험이 부족하다 'lack experience'.
Set humble phrase: 부족하지만 잘 부탁드립니다 'I'm lacking, but please bear with me'.

examples.en: I'm a bit short on money.
examples.note: Plain predicate; the short item takes 이/가: 돈이 부족하다.

examples.en: I've been short on sleep lately, so I'm exhausted.
examples.note: 잠이 부족하다 is a fixed collocation; -아서 gives the reason.

examples.en: I have many shortcomings, but I'll work hard.
examples.note: Real-situation: humble self-description, a stock first-day/interview line.

extendedVocab.nuance: 부족하다 is the direct opposite of 충분하다 and marks the thing in short supply with 이/가 (잠이 부족하다, 돈이 부족하다). Its hanja 不足 literally means 不 'not' + 足 'sufficient', i.e. 'not enough'. Beyond literal shortages, Koreans use it as a humble, polite way to downplay their own ability or work (부족하지만 열심히 하겠습니다) — this modest 부족하다 is extremely common and expected in interviews, greetings and toasts. The near-synonym 모자라다 carries the same 'fall short' meaning but is more colloquial and, applied to a person, can rudely mean 'dim-witted', so 부족하다 is the safe, neutral choice. It collocates with 잠, 경험, 시간, 돈, 점. The English-speaker pitfall is marking the missing item with 을/를 ('시간을 부족해요') instead of 이/가, and reaching for 모자라다 about people without sensing its insulting edge.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the short item with 을/를: say 시간이 부족해요, not '시간을 부족해요'. The lacking thing is the subject (이/가).
Swapping in 모자라다 about a person — it can mean 'dim-witted' and sound insulting; 부족하다 is the neutral, polite choice.
Treating humble 부족하지만 as literal self-criticism — it is a set modesty formula, not a real confession of incompetence.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 풍부하다 means "to be abundant, rich, plentiful" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 풍부하다 (pungbuhada) means "to be abundant, rich, plentiful". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 풍부한 ("abundant / rich (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 풍부하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 풍부한 경험 'rich experience', 풍부한 자원 'abundant resources'.
Polite present, often as praise for plentifulness.
비타민이 풍부하다 'be rich in vitamins', 경험이 풍부하다 'be very experienced'.
Adverb: 영양이 풍부하게 들어 있다 'richly packed with nutrients'.

examples.en: This fruit is rich in vitamins.
examples.note: 비타민이 풍부하다 is a stock health phrase; rich thing takes 이/가.

examples.en: She's very experienced, so I trust her.
examples.note: 경험이 풍부하다 = 'has rich experience'; -아서 gives the reason.

examples.en: She's an actor with rich emotional range.
examples.note: Real-situation descriptive praise: 풍부한 + noun in a reviewing register.

extendedVocab.nuance: 풍부하다 emphasizes plentiful abundance — generously more than enough, full and rich. Its hanja 豐富 doubles up 豐 'abundant' and 富 'wealthy', so it literally piles 'abundant' on 'rich'. The key contrast is with 충분하다: 충분하다 only says the need is met ('enough'), while 풍부하다 highlights that there is a great deal of something, almost always as a positive quality — experience, resources, nutrients, emotion, knowledge. It marks the abundant thing with 이/가 (자원이 풍부하다) and collocates with 경험, 자원, 비타민/영양, 감정 표현, and the adverb 풍부하게 들어 있다. It leans slightly formal or descriptive. The English-speaker pitfall is marking the abundant thing with 을/를 ('자원을 풍부하다'), and overextending the English 'rich/full' to a person's body — for 'plump' Korean uses 통통하다, never 풍부하다.

Using 풍부하다 for a plump body shape (mapping English 'full-figured') — Korean uses 통통하다; 풍부하다 is for experience, resources, nutrients, emotion.
Blurring it with 충분하다: 풍부하다 = 'abundant, a lot' (positive), 충분하다 = merely 'enough for the need'. They are not interchangeable.

extendedVocab.explanation: "to be unique, distinctive, one-of-a-kind" is 독특하다 (dokteukada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 독특한 ("unique / distinctive (+ noun)"). Watch the particle attached to 독특하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 독특한 디자인 'a unique design', 독특한 맛 'a distinctive taste'.
Polite present; usually positive for food, design, style.
Adverb: 독특하게 꾸미다 'decorate in a distinctive way'.
About a person it can hint at 'eccentric'; tone decides praise vs. caution.

examples.en: This cafe has a distinctive atmosphere.
examples.note: Plain predicate; 분위기가 독특하다 'unique vibe' is a stock phrase.

examples.ko: 향이 독특해서 호불호가 갈릴 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: hyangi dokteukaeseo hobulhoga gallil geot gatayo.
examples.en: The scent is distinctive, so opinions will probably be split.
examples.note: 독특해서 + 호불호가 갈리다 'tastes will divide' is a natural pairing.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 생각이 좀 독특한 편이에요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun saenggagi jom dokteukan pyeonieyo.
examples.en: That person's thinking is a bit unusual.
examples.note: Real-situation: about a person 독특하다 leans toward 'quirky' — softened by 좀 and -ㄴ 편이다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 독특하다 describes something noticeably different from the ordinary — distinctive, original, one-of-a-kind. Its hanja 獨特 joins 獨 'alone/sole' and 特 'special', literally 'singularly special'. For food, design, scent or style it is usually positive ('characterful, unlike anything else'). The near-synonym 특별하다 means 'special/significant' — 독특하다 says 'unlike others (distinctive)', 특별하다 says 'precious or out of the ordinary', so a gift can be 특별하지만 독특하지는 않다. Crucially, applied to a person's personality or ideas, 독특하다 tilts toward 'quirky/eccentric', so tone and context decide whether it flatters or gently warns. It collocates with 디자인, 맛, 향, 분위기, 스타일. The English-speaker pitfall is equating 'unique' with 'special' and calling someone 독특하다 as a compliment, when it can read as a polite way of saying 'odd'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 독특하다 and 특별하다 as the same: 독특하다 = 'distinctive, unlike others'; 특별하다 = 'special, significant'. Unique is not always special.
Calling a person 독특하다 expecting it to flatter — about personality it often softens 'odd/eccentric'. Use it knowingly.
Writing '독특하다 디자인' before a noun — use the modifier 독특한 디자인.

extendedVocab.english: to be effective, produce good results
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 효과적이다 means "to be effective, produce good results" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 효과적이다 (hyogwajeogida) = "to be effective, produce good results". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 효과적인 ("effective (+ noun)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 효과적이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: ~적이다 adjectives take 적인 before a noun: 효과적인 방법 'an effective method'.
Polite present of ~적이다; keep the 이 (효과적이에요, not 효과적어요).
Adverb form ~적으로: 효과적으로 활용하다 'use effectively'.
효과적이지 않은 방법 'an ineffective method'.

examples.en: This method is effective.
examples.note: Plain predicate of ~적이다; note 효과적이에요 keeps the 이.

examples.ko: 시간을 효과적으로 쓰는 법을 배우고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: siganeul hyogwajeogeuro sseuneun beobeul baeugo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to learn how to use time effectively.
examples.note: Adverb 효과적으로 (~적으로) modifies 쓰다.

examples.en: The ad was effective, so sales went up.
examples.note: Real-situation: ~적이다 + -아/어서 contracts to 효과적이어서.

extendedVocab.nuance: 효과적이다 means something actually works and produces the intended result — effective. Its hanja 效果 joins 效 'effect/efficacy' and 果 'result/fruit', plus the suffix 的 'of the nature of', so it reads 'of an effect-producing nature'. The decisive contrast is with 효율적이다 'efficient': 효과적이다 asks 'does it work / does it achieve the goal?', while 효율적이다 asks 'is the result worth the time, effort or cost?'. A campaign can be 효과적이지만 효율적이지 않다 — it hits the target but burns too much budget. Being a ~적이다 adjective, it follows fixed forms: 효과적인 N (modifier), 효과적이에요 (predicate), 효과적으로 (adverb). It collocates with 방법, 전략, 광고, 학습. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 이 and saying '효과적다/효과적어요', and blending the three patterns — using 효과적이다 where a noun needs 효과적인 or an adverb needs 효과적으로.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the 이: it is 효과적이다 / 효과적이에요, never '효과적다' or '효과적어요'. The 이 is part of the ~적이다 frame.
Mixing the three forms: before a noun use 효과적인, as an adverb use 효과적으로, as a predicate use 효과적이에요. Swapping them is a very common error.
Treating it as a synonym of 효율적이다: 효과적이다 = 'it works (achieves the goal)', 효율적이다 = 'good output for the input'. They answer different questions.

extendedVocab.english: to be efficient (good output for the input)
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 효율적이다 means "to be efficient (good output for the input)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 효율적이다 (hyoyuljeogida) means "to be efficient (good output for the input)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 효율적인 ("efficient (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 효율적이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 효율적인 동선 'an efficient route/flow', 효율적인 일 처리 'efficient handling of work'.
Polite present of ~적이다; keep the 이 (효율적이에요).
Adverb ~적으로: 시간을 효율적으로 관리하다 'manage time efficiently'.
Prefix 비- negates it: 비효율적인 방식 'an inefficient way'.

examples.en: This way is more efficient.
examples.note: Plain predicate of ~적이다; 효율적이에요 keeps the 이.

examples.ko: 이렇게 하면 일을 더 효율적으로 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ireoke hamyeon ireul deo hyoyuljeogeuro hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you do it this way, you can work more efficiently.
examples.note: Adverb 효율적으로 + 하다, a staple workplace phrase.

examples.en: I bought an appliance that uses energy efficiently.
examples.note: Real-situation: 효율적으로 쓰다 frames cost-saving use.

extendedVocab.nuance: 효율적이다 is about getting the most result with the least time, effort or resources — efficiency. Its hanja 效率 joins 效 'effect' and 率 'rate/ratio', so it literally means 'effect-rate', i.e. the ratio of output to input. The defining contrast is with 효과적이다 'effective': 효과적이다 asks 'does it work?', 효율적이다 asks 'is it worth the input?'. Something can be effective but wasteful, or efficient yet ineffective, so the two are not interchangeable. As a ~적이다 adjective it follows 효율적인 N, 효율적이에요, 효율적으로, and negates with the prefix 비- → 비효율적이다. It collocates with 시간 관리, 동선, 에너지, 일 처리, 업무. The English-speaker pitfall is using it as a loose synonym for 효과적이다, dropping the 이 ('효율적다'), and forgetting that 'inefficient' is the prefixed 비효율적이다 rather than a long negation.

Using it as a synonym for 효과적이다: efficiency (cost/input) and effectiveness (result) are different ideas — keep 효율적 vs 효과적 distinct.
Dropping the 이 or mixing forms: 효율적인 N, 효율적이에요, 효율적으로; never '효율적다'.
Saying '효율적이지 않다' when the natural word is the prefixed 비효율적이다 — Koreans usually say 비효율적이에요 for 'it's inefficient'.

extendedVocab.english: to be clear, distinct, vivid, marked
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뚜렷하다 means "to be clear, distinct, vivid, marked" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "to be clear, distinct, vivid, marked" is 뚜렷하다 (tturyeotada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 뚜렷한 ("clear / distinct (+ noun)"). Watch the particle attached to 뚜렷하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 뚜렷한 목표 'a clear goal', 뚜렷한 차이 'a distinct difference'.
Polite present; native (non-Sino) adjective.
Both adverbs exist; 뚜렷하게 is more common in speech, 뚜렷이 a touch more written.
Near 모호하다/흐릿하다 when an impression is vague or blurred.

examples.en: The photo is sharp/clear.
examples.note: Plain predicate; here 뚜렷하다 = visibly distinct, not blurry.

examples.en: The difference between the two products is very marked.
examples.note: 차이가 뚜렷하다 'a sharp difference'; distinct thing takes 이/가.

examples.en: He's a person with clear-cut opinions.
examples.note: Real-situation: 의견이 뚜렷하다 = 'has firm, well-defined views'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 뚜렷하다 means something stands out clearly and is well-defined — distinct four seasons, a sharp difference, a firm opinion, a vivid memory. Unlike most words here it is native Korean, not Sino-Korean, and the feel is visual and sensory: 'sharply outlined, vivid'. Its near-synonyms are 분명하다 and 명확하다, but those lean toward 'logically certain / unambiguous in reasoning', whereas 뚜렷하다 leans toward 'visibly distinct, sensory-clear' — a memory or a season is 뚜렷하다, while a conclusion is 분명하다. It marks the distinct thing with 이/가 (차이가 뚜렷하다) and collocates with 목표, 차이, 의견, 사계절, 기억. It is the natural opposite of 모호하다 and 흐릿하다. The English-speaker pitfall is marking the distinct thing with 을/를, and stretching 'clear' to mean 'certain it's true' — for that certainty use 확실하다 or 분명하다, not 뚜렷하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the distinct thing with 을/를: say 차이가 뚜렷하다, not '차이를 뚜렷하다'. The distinct thing is the subject.
Using 뚜렷하다 to mean 'certain that something is true' — for conviction use 확실하다 or 분명하다. 뚜렷하다 is about visible/sensory distinctness.
Forcing 뚜렷하다 onto abstract logical clarity (rules, definitions) where 명확하다 fits better — 뚜렷하다 suits seasons, differences, memories, opinions.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 명확하다 means "to be clear, explicit, unambiguous" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 명확하다 (myeonghwakada) = "to be clear, explicit, unambiguous". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 명확한 ("clear / explicit (+ noun)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 명확하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 명확한 기준 'clear criteria', 명확한 답변 'a clear answer'.
Polite present; common in work and academic contexts.
명확하게 밝히다 'state explicitly'; 명확히 is slightly more formal.
명확하지 않은 부분 'the part that isn't clear'.

examples.en: The criteria are clear.
examples.note: Plain predicate; 기준이 명확하다 = 'well-defined standards'.

examples.ko: 규정을 좀 더 명확하게 설명해 주세요.
examples.romanization: gyujeongeul jom deo myeonghwakage seolmyeonghae juseyo.
examples.en: Please explain the rules a bit more explicitly.
examples.note: 명확하게 설명하다 = 'spell out, leave no ambiguity'.

examples.ko: 책임 소재가 명확하지 않아서 문제가 생겼어요.
examples.romanization: chaegim sojaega myeonghwakaji anaseo munjega saenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It wasn't clear who was responsible, so a problem arose.
examples.note: Real-situation: 명확하지 않다 = 'ambiguous'; the long negative flags missing clarity.

extendedVocab.nuance: 명확하다 means clearly defined and free of ambiguity — explicit criteria, unambiguous answers, well-defined responsibilities. Its hanja 明確 joins 明 'bright/clear' and 確 'firm/sure', literally 'brightly certain'. The near-synonyms are 분명하다 and 뚜렷하다: 명확하다 is the most formal/written and stresses conceptual, definitional clarity (rules, criteria, logic), 분명하다 is everyday 'obvious/evidently so', and 뚜렷하다 is sensory 'visibly distinct'. So criteria are 명확하다, a sunset's colors are 뚜렷하다, and 'it's obviously true' is 분명하다. Note too the contrast with 정확하다: 명확하다 = unambiguous/clearly stated, 정확하다 = factually correct — an instruction can be 명확하지만 부정확할 수 있다. It collocates with 기준, 답변, 입장, 목표 and the adverb 명확하게 밝히다. The English-speaker pitfall is conflating clarity (명확) with correctness (정확).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 명확하다 (clear/unambiguous) with 정확하다 (accurate/correct): a statement can be clearly worded yet factually wrong. Clarity ≠ correctness.
Writing '명확하다 기준' before a noun — use the modifier 명확한 기준; the adverb is 명확하게/명확히.
Using 명확하다 for sensory vividness (a sharp photo, vivid memory) where 뚜렷하다 fits — 명확하다 suits criteria, logic and definitions.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 모호하다 means "to be vague, ambiguous, unclear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 모호하다 (mohohada) means "to be vague, ambiguous, unclear". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 모호한 ("vague / ambiguous (+ noun)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 모호하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Modifier: 모호한 태도 'an ambiguous attitude', 모호한 표현 'a vague expression'.
Polite present; often tinged with mild frustration.
Adverb: 모호하게 대답하다 'answer noncommittally'.
Emphatic compound (애매 + 모호); very common in speech.

examples.en: The answer is vague.
examples.note: Plain predicate; 대답이 모호하다 = 'a noncommittal reply'.

examples.en: If the criteria are vague, each person reads them differently.
examples.note: 기준이 모호하다 = 'unclear standards'; -면 sets up the consequence.

examples.ko: 그는 태도가 모호해서 속을 알 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: geuneun taedoga mohohaeseo sogeul al su eopseoyo.
examples.en: His attitude is so noncommittal that I can't read his real feelings.
examples.note: Real-situation: 태도가 모호하다 + -아서 conveys frustration at vagueness.

extendedVocab.nuance: 모호하다 is the opposite of 명확하다/뚜렷하다 — blurry, open to several readings, impossible to pin down. Its hanja 模糊 pairs 模 'pattern/indistinct' with 糊 'paste/blurred', literally 'pasted-over and indistinct'. It applies to language, criteria, attitudes and boundaries, and usually carries a mildly negative tone of frustration that something isn't clear. The everyday near-synonym is 애매하다 'iffy / hard to decide', which is more colloquial; 모호하다 sounds a touch more formal and written, and the two fuse into the very common emphatic 애매모호하다. Crucially, distinguish it from 헷갈리다 'to get confused/mixed up': 모호하다 describes the thing being vague, while 헷갈리다 describes the person's confusion — a vague rule (모호하다) makes you 헷갈리다. It collocates with 태도, 표현, 기준, 입장, 경계. The English-speaker pitfall is using 모호하다 for the listener's confusion, where Korean needs 헷갈리다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 모호하다 with 헷갈리다: 모호하다 = the thing is vague; 헷갈리다 = the person is confused/mixed up. Say '설명이 모호해서 제가 헷갈려요'.
Reaching for 모호하다 in very casual 'iffy/unclear' moments — Koreans more often say 애매하다 in speech; 모호하다 sounds slightly formal/written.
Writing '모호하다 태도' before a noun — use the modifier 모호한 태도; the adverb is 모호하게.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사회 means "society" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "society" is 사회 (sahoe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 현대 사회 ("modern society"). Watch the particle attached to 사회 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 현대 attaches directly with no 의; this is the single most common frame 사회 appears in.
Compound noun used constantly in news and essays; note no spacing change, just 사회 + 문제.

usagePhrases.en: working life / getting along in the adult world
usagePhrases.note: Written as one word; means workplace and adult social duties, NOT 'social life' in the party sense.

usagePhrases.en: to go out into society (e.g., after graduating)
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination; idiom for entering the workforce and adult world.

examples.en: There are many problems in our society.
examples.note: Simple frame: 사회 takes 에 + 는 for 'in (our) society', the location-of-existence particle.

examples.en: Once you graduate from university, you really start your working life.
examples.note: Here 사회생활 = professional/adult life — the everyday meaning a learner must internalize.

examples.ko: 인터넷이 우리 사회를 크게 바꿔 놓았어요.
examples.romanization: inteonesi uri sahoereul keuge bakkwo noasseoyo.
examples.en: The internet has greatly changed our society.
examples.note: 바꿔 놓다 = 'changed it (and it stays that way)'; the lingering-result auxiliary, natural with 사회.

extendedVocab.nuance: 사회 (社會, 社 'community/shrine-group' + 會 'gathering') means 'society' as the whole body of people living together, and as a noun-modifier it stacks directly: 현대 사회, 사회 문제, 사회 복지. The trap for English speakers is 사회생활: it does NOT mean 'social life / hanging out', but working life and managing adult/workplace relationships, so 사회생활을 잘하다 praises someone for handling colleagues and obligations well. Contrast 사회 with 모임 — a 모임 is one concrete small gathering (study group, dinner club), while 사회 is the abstract collective; never use 사회 for 'a get-together'. The particle to learn is 에 for location-of-existence (사회에 문제가 있다), not 에서, when you simply say something exists in society.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 사회생활 as 'social life / partying'. It almost always means working life and getting along at work, so '제 사회생활이 바빠요' implies a busy professional/adult life, not a busy party schedule.
Using 사회 for a small social gathering ('let's have a 사회 this weekend'). 사회 is the abstract collective; for a get-together use 모임 (모임이 있어요).

structuredNuance.t: 사회 means 'society' as the whole body of people living together, the abstract collective. As a noun-modifier it stacks directly with no 의: 현대 사회, 사회 문제, 사회 복지.
Contrast 사회 with 모임: a 모임 is one concrete small gathering (study group, dinner club), while 사회 is the abstract collective. Never use 사회 for 'a get-together'.
社會, 社 'community/shrine-group' + 會 'gathering'.

Also, the particle for location-of-existence is 에 (사회에 문제가 있다), not 에서, when you simply say something exists in society.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 전통 means "tradition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 전통 (jeontong) = "tradition". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전통 문화 ("traditional culture") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전통, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 전통 modifies the next noun attributively with no 의: 전통 문화, 전통 음식, 전통 시장.
지키다 ('protect, keep') is the default verb; you guard a tradition the way you guard a promise.
Adjective form: 전통적인 + noun (전통적인 결혼식 = a traditional wedding).
오랜 ('longtime') is the fixed modifier for time-depth here, never 긴 ('long' in length).

examples.en: This food is our traditional food.
examples.note: Simplest use: 전통 sits straight in front of 음식 with no particle between them.

examples.ko: 이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
examples.romanization: i maeureun oraedoen jeontongeul geudaero ieo gago isseoyo.
examples.en: This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
examples.note: 이어 가다 = 'carry on / continue (and keep going)'; the habitual collocation with 전통.

examples.ko: 저는 전통적인 음악보다 현대 음악을 더 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jeontongjeogin eumakboda hyeondae eumageul deo joahaeyo.
examples.en: I like modern music more than traditional music.
examples.note: Real preference talk: 전통적인 (adjective) modifies 음악, paired against 현대 in a A보다 B 더 frame.

extendedVocab.nuance: 전통 (傳統, 傳 'hand down/pass on' + 統 'lineage/unbroken line') is a custom, value, or practice passed down across generations, and the hanja literally pictures an unbroken line being handed on — which is why it carries a respectful, valued tone. Contrast it sharply with 습관 (習慣, 'habit'): 전통 is shared and inherited by a group, while 습관 is one individual's repeated personal routine (제 습관, never 제 전통). For the descriptive 'it is traditional', you must switch to the adjective 전통적이다 → 전통적인 + noun; 전통 alone is the abstract noun. The classic 직역 trap is time-length: English 'a long tradition' tempts 긴 전통, but Korean fixes this as 오랜 전통, because 오랜 expresses depth in time while 긴 means physically long.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 긴 전통 for 'a long tradition'. 긴 describes physical length; for time-depth Korean uses the fixed form 오랜 전통.
Confusing 전통 with 습관. 전통 is a group's inherited custom; 습관 is one person's repeated routine — '아침에 운동하는 건 제 습관이에요', not 제 전통.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 현대 means "modern times; the present age" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 현대 (hyeondae) means "modern times; the present age". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 현대 사회 ("modern society"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 현대 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 현대 modifies a noun directly: 현대 사회, 현대 미술, 현대 의학 — all without 의.
Adjective form for look-and-feel: 현대적인 디자인 = a modern-style design.
현대 + 인 (person) = the people of the present age; very common in essays and editorials.

usagePhrases.en: in the modern era; coming into modern times
usagePhrases.note: Set sentence-opener equivalent to 'in modern times…'.

examples.en: This is modern art.
examples.note: Bare frame: 현대 attaches straight to 미술 as a noun-modifier, no particle in between.

examples.en: People today live constantly chased by time.
examples.note: 현대인 = 'modern people'; 시간에 쫓기다 = 'be chased by time', a stock collocation.

examples.ko: 이 건물은 전통과 현대가 잘 어우러져 있어요.
examples.romanization: i geonmureun jeontonggwa hyeondaega jal eoureojyeo isseoyo.
examples.en: This building blends tradition and modernity well.
examples.note: 전통과 현대 is the habitual old-vs-new pairing; 어우러지다 = 'blend in harmony'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 현대 (現代, 現 'present/appear' + 代 'age/generation') means the modern or contemporary age and works mainly as a noun-modifier (현대 사회, 현대 미술) rather than standing alone in a sentence. Two contrasts matter. First, time-words: 현대 is a whole era, while 최근/요즘 mean 'recently/these days' — so 'I bought it recently' is 최근에 샀어요, never 현대에 샀어요. Second, register/form: to call a thing 'modern in style' you must use the adjective 현대적이다 → 현대적인 디자인; 현대 디자인 sounds like a fixed genre label, not a description of feel. 현대 is the natural counterweight to 전통 whenever you set up an old-versus-new comparison.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 현대 to mean 'recently'. 현대 is a whole era; for 'recently/these days' say 최근 or 요즘 — '요즘 바빠요', not '현대에 바빠요'.
Dropping the adjective form: 'modern-style design' is 현대적인 디자인. Bare 현대 디자인 reads as a genre name, not a description of how something looks.

structuredNuance.t: 현대 means the modern or contemporary age and works mainly as a noun-modifier (현대 사회, 현대 미술) rather than standing alone in a sentence. It is the natural counterweight to 전통 whenever you set up an old-versus-new comparison.
Time-words: 현대 is a whole era, while 최근/요즘 mean 'recently/these days' — so 'I bought it recently' is 최근에 샀어요, never 현대에 샀어요.
現代, 現 'present/appear' + 代 'age/generation'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 국가 means "nation; state; country" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "nation; state; country" is 국가 (gukga). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 민주 국가 ("a democratic nation"). Watch the particle attached to 국가 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 국가 is the political-entity word for a country; 나라 is the everyday word for the same idea.
국가 modifies official nouns directly: 국가 정책, 국가 기관, 국가 대표.
Formal tone; heard about public service, soldiers, sacrifice.
국가적 + noun (국가적 행사 = a national-scale event); the 차원 phrase 국가적인 차원에서 is common.

examples.en: Korea is a democratic nation.
examples.note: Simple definition frame; 국가 functions as the predicate noun with 예요.

examples.ko: 이번 행사는 국가적인 차원에서 준비되고 있어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon haengsaneun gukgajeogin chawoneseo junbidoego isseoyo.
examples.en: This event is being prepared on a national level.
examples.note: 국가적인 차원에서 = 'at a national level', a formal set collocation worth memorizing.

examples.ko: 여러 국가가 이 문제를 함께 논의했어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo gukgaga i munjereul hamkke nonuihaesseoyo.
examples.en: Several nations discussed this issue together.
examples.note: 여러 국가 = 'several nations'; 논의하다 = 'discuss (formally)', matching the institutional register.

extendedVocab.nuance: 국가 (國家, 國 'country' + 家 'house/family' — literally the 'country-household', the state seen as one great family/estate) is the formal, institutional word for a country as a political and legal entity, at home in news, law, and academic writing. The sharp boundary every learner needs is 국가 vs 나라: they share the same dictionary gloss 'country', but 나라 is the warm everyday word and 국가 is the official one — so 우리 나라 is the natural 'our country', while 우리 국가 sounds stiff and almost wrong in conversation. Choose 국가 only when the focus is the state as an institution (government, policy, sovereignty); pair it with formal modifiers like 민주, 국가적, and the phrase 국가적인 차원에서. Do not confuse 국가 'state/nation' with the identically-pronounced 국가 (國歌) 'national anthem'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 우리 국가 in casual conversation. The natural everyday phrase is 우리 나라; 국가 here sounds bureaucratic and unnatural.
Treating 국가 and 나라 as fully interchangeable. 국가 is formal/institutional (국가 정책, 민주 국가); 나라 is the everyday word (나라가 좋아요).

structuredNuance.t: 국가 is the formal, institutional word for a country as a political and legal entity, at home in news, law, and academic writing. Choose 국가 only when the focus is the state as an institution (government, policy, sovereignty); pair it with formal modifiers like 민주, 국가적, and the phrase 국가적인 차원에서.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정부 means "government" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정부 (jeongbu) = "government". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 정부 정책 ("government policy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 정부, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Extremely common in news; 정부 modifies the noun directly with no 의.
발표하다 is the standard verb for official statements by the 정부.
The standard administrative split between national and regional authority.
Heard constantly about funding, benefits, and aid (정부 지원을 받다 = receive government support).

examples.en: The government announced a new policy.
examples.note: Core news frame: 정부 + 발표하다, the textbook subject-verb pairing.

examples.ko: 많은 사람들이 정부의 결정에 반대하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: maneun saramdeuri jeongbuui gyeoljeonge bandaehago isseoyo.
examples.en: Many people are opposing the government's decision.
examples.note: 정부의 결정 uses 의 to link two nouns; 반대하다 takes 에 (결정에 반대하다).

examples.ko: 정부에서 소상공인을 위한 지원을 늘리기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbueseo sosanggongineul wihan jiwoneul neulligiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The government decided to increase support for small business owners.
examples.note: 정부에서: organizations as subjects often take 에서, which sounds slightly more institutional than 가.

extendedVocab.nuance: 정부 (政府, 政 'governing/administration' + 府 'office/seat of authority' — literally the 'office of governance') is the government as the concrete administrative body that runs the state. The contrast to lock in is 정부 vs 정치: 정부 is the institution/body, while 정치 (politics) is the activity and field — '정부가 발표했어요' (the body announced) but '정치에 관심 없어요' (not interested in the field). A grammar point unique to organizational subjects: Korean lets you mark 정부 as the actor with 에서 as well as 가 — both 정부에서 발표했어요 and 정부가 발표했어요 are correct, with 에서 feeling a touch more formal/institutional. Pair 정부 with official verbs: 발표하다, 결정하다, 지원하다, 추진하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 정부 with 정치. 정부 is the governing body (정부가 결정하다); 정치 is the field/activity (정치를 하다, 정치에 관심이 있다).
Assuming organizational subjects only take 가. With bodies like 정부, the 에서 form is equally natural: 정부에서 발표했어요 ≈ 정부가 발표했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 정부 is the government as the concrete administrative body that runs the state. Pair 정부 with official verbs: 발표하다, 결정하다, 지원하다, 추진하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정치 means "politics" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정치 (jeongchi) means "politics". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정치에 관심이 있다 ("to be interested in politics"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정치 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 관심이 있다/없다 takes 에 on the topic: 정치에 관심이 있다 — never 정치를 관심.
정치 + 인 (person) = a person in politics; 정치가 is a near-equivalent.
Adjective form: 정치적인 문제 = a political issue (often with a sensitive/calculated undertone).

usagePhrases.en: to go into / be active in politics
usagePhrases.note: 하다 here means working in the political arena, e.g. running for office.

examples.en: I'm not interested in politics.
examples.note: Bedrock pattern: interest in a topic is X에 관심이 있다/없다, so 정치 takes 에 here.

examples.ko: 요즘 정치 뉴스를 보면 답답할 때가 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeongchi nyuseureul bomyeon dapdapal ttaega manayo.
examples.en: These days, watching political news often feels frustrating.
examples.note: 정치 뉴스 = 'political news'; 답답하다 = 'stifling/frustrating', a very Korean emotion word.

examples.ko: 그 문제는 너무 정치적이라서 이야기하기 조심스러워요.
examples.romanization: geu munjeneun neomu jeongchijeogiraseo iyagihagi josimseureowoyo.
examples.en: That issue is too political, so I'm careful about discussing it.
examples.note: 정치적이라서 = adjective + 라서 ('because it is…'); shows the cautious tone Koreans attach to 정치.

extendedVocab.nuance: 정치 (政治, 政 'governing' + 治 'rule/manage' — literally 'governing and ordering [a state]') is the abstract field and activity of politics. Hold three related words apart: 정치 is the field, 정부 (government) is the concrete body, and 정치인 is an individual politician — so 'a politician' is 정치인/정치가, never the literal 정치 사람. The adjective 정치적이다 labels something 'political', usually with an undertone of being calculated, partisan, or socially sensitive. The particle pitfall is interest: 'interested in politics' is 정치에 관심이 있다 (topic marked with 에), not 정치를 관심이 있다. Culturally, 정치 is treated as a touchy subject, so 정치적인 이야기 is something many Koreans deliberately avoid in polite company.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 정치 and 정부. 정치 is the activity/field (정치에 관심이 있다); 정부 is the institution (정부가 발표하다).
Saying 정치 사람 for 'politician'. The correct word is 정치인 (or 정치가); 정치 사람 is not idiomatic Korean.

structuredNuance.t: 정치 is the abstract field and activity of politics. The adjective 정치적이다 labels something 'political', usually with an undertone of being calculated, partisan, or socially sensitive. Culturally, 정치 is treated as a touchy subject, so 정치적인 이야기 is something many Koreans deliberately avoid in polite company.

政治, 政 'governing' + 治 'rule/manage' — literally 'governing and ordering [a state]'.
The particle pitfall is interest: 'interested in politics' is 정치에 관심이 있다 (topic marked with 에), not 정치를 관심이 있다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 경제 means "economy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "economy" is 경제 (gyeongje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 경제가 어렵다 ("the economy is bad / struggling"). Watch the particle attached to 경제 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 어렵다 (lit. 'difficult') is the idiomatic way to say the economy is in a slump, not 나쁘다.
Standard compound (성장 = growth); 경제 성장률 = the economic growth rate.
Two senses: 'economical (cheap)' and 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden).
경제 takes scope modifiers directly: 세계 경제, 한국 경제, 지역 경제.

examples.en: The economy is tough these days.
examples.note: Plain version of the key idiom: 경제가 어렵다 = 'the economy is struggling', using 어렵다 not 나쁘다.

examples.ko: 정부는 경제 성장을 위해 여러 정책을 내놓았어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbuneun gyeongje seongjangeul wihae yeoreo jeongchaegeul naenoasseoyo.
examples.en: The government put forward various policies for economic growth.
examples.note: 경제 성장을 위해 = 'for economic growth'; 내놓다 = 'put forward (a plan/policy)'.

examples.en: Using public transportation is much more economical.
examples.note: Here 경제적이다 = 'economical / cost-saving' — the everyday wallet-friendly sense, not 'economic'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 경제 (經濟, 經 'manage/govern' + 濟 'aid/relieve' — from 經世濟民 'govern the world and relieve the people') means 'the economy' as a system. The biggest learner trap is the adjective 경제적이다, which splits into TWO everyday meanings: (1) 'economical', i.e. money-saving (버스가 더 경제적이에요), and (2) 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden) — context decides which. Equally important is the slump idiom: to say the economy is doing badly, Korean uses 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다, NOT a literal 경제가 나쁘다, because 어렵다 ('hard, strained') is the conventional collocation. Keep 경제 (the system/field) distinct from 경영 (經營, business management of a company); they look similar but 경영 is running a firm.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 'the economy is bad' word-for-word as 경제가 나쁘다. Natural Korean is 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다.
Forgetting that 경제적이다 can mean 'economical (saves money)', so '이게 더 경제적이에요' means 'this is cheaper/more cost-effective', not 'this is more economic'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 제도 means "system; institution (a set of rules/structures)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 제도 (jedo) = "system; institution (a set of rules/structures)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교육 제도 ("the education system") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 제도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 제도 = an organized social system of rules; pairs with 교육, 의료, 복지, 연금.
바꾸다 ('change') and 고치다 ('fix/reform') are the common verbs with 제도.
제도적인 문제 = a systemic problem (the structure's fault, not one person's).
도입하다 ('introduce, adopt') is the formal verb for bringing a 제도 in.

examples.en: Korea has a good healthcare system.
examples.note: Simple frame: 의료 제도 sits as the subject; 제도 names the whole system, not a single rule.

examples.en: The company newly introduced a work-from-home system.
examples.note: 제도 + 도입하다, the textbook collocation for adopting a formal system.

examples.ko: 이건 한 사람의 잘못이 아니라 제도적인 문제예요.
examples.romanization: igeon han saramui jalmosi anira jedojeogin munjeyeyo.
examples.en: This isn't one person's fault but a systemic problem.
examples.note: 제도적인 문제 = 'systemic/structural problem'; the adjective shifts blame from a person to the structure.

extendedVocab.nuance: 제도 (制度, 制 'regulate/establish' + 度 'measure/standard' — an 'established standard', i.e. a set framework) is an organized system of rules or an institution in the abstract: an education system, welfare system, or company-wide policy framework. Draw two lines. Against 규칙 ('rules'): 제도 is large-scale and structural (교육 제도, the whole system), while 규칙 is the concrete everyday rules you follow (게임 규칙, 교통 규칙). Against 기관 (機關, an organization/agency as a body or building): 제도 is the intangible framework, whereas 기관 is the actual institution you can walk into (정부 기관, 교육 기관). The adjective 제도적이다 is the handy tool for saying a problem is 'systemic' rather than one individual's fault.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 제도 with 규칙. 제도 is a large institutional framework (복지 제도); 규칙 is everyday rules (회사 규칙, 게임 규칙).
Using 제도 for a physical institution or building. For the organization/agency you enter, use 기관 (교육 기관) or the specific place name, not 제도.

structuredNuance.t: 제도 is an organized system of rules or an institution in the abstract: an education system, welfare system, or company-wide policy framework. The adjective 제도적이다 is the handy tool for saying a problem is 'systemic' rather than one individual's fault.

制度, 制 'regulate/establish' + 度 'measure/standard' — an 'established standard', i.e. a set framework.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 법률 means "law (formal/legal term)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 법률 (beomnyul) means "law (formal/legal term)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 법률을 지키다 ("to obey the law"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 법률 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 지키다 ('keep, observe') is the standard verb; the opposite is 법을 어기다 ('break the law').
법률 modifies formal nouns: 법률 상담, 법률 문제, 법률 전문가.
법률적인 책임 = legal responsibility (as opposed to moral responsibility).
제정하다 ('legislate, enact') is the formal verb; heavy news/legal register.

examples.en: A new law goes into effect starting next month.
examples.note: 법률 + 시행되다 ('take effect/be enforced'), the formal collocation for laws coming into force.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 법률 전문가의 도움이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: i munjeneun beomnyul jeonmungaui doumi piryohaeyo.
examples.en: This issue needs help from a legal expert.
examples.note: 법률 전문가 = 'legal expert'; the 의 links 전문가 to the help that is needed.

examples.en: All citizens are equal before the law.
examples.note: 법률 앞에서 평등하다 = 'equal before the law', a formal set expression you will see in civics texts.

extendedVocab.nuance: 법률 (法律, 法 'law/method' + 律 'statute/rule' — two 'law' characters doubled for the formal sense, i.e. enacted statutes) is the written, official term for 'law' as legislation and the legal system, at home in documents, news, and academic prose. The crucial register split is 법률 vs 법: in everyday speech Koreans shorten it to 법 (법을 어기다 = break the law, 법대로 하다 = do it by the book), so 법률을 어기다 sounds stiff in casual chat — reserve 법률 for official contexts or for laws as a body of legislation. Keep it apart from 법원 (法院, the court — the institution that applies the law) and 변호사 (a lawyer): 법률 is the rules themselves, not the people or place that handle them.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 법률 in casual speech. When chatting, say 법을 어기다 / 법을 지키다; 법률을 어기다 sounds overly formal and bookish.
Confusing 법률 with 법원. 법률 is the law itself (the statute); 법원 is the court, the institution that applies and interprets it.

structuredNuance.t: 법률 is the written, official term for 'law' as legislation and the legal system, at home in documents, news, and academic prose.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 권력 means "power (political/authority)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "power (political/authority)" is 권력 (gwollyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 권력을 잡다 ("to seize / take power"). Watch the particle attached to 권력 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 잡다 ('grab') is the idiomatic verb for gaining political power, not 받다 or 하다.
남용하다 ('misuse, abuse') is a frequent, important pairing in news and politics.
권력 + 자 (person) = someone who holds authority; often carries a critical tone.
다툼 ('fight, struggle') captures open conflict over authority within a group.

examples.en: That person has power (authority).
examples.note: Simplest frame: 권력이 있다 = 'has power' in the authority sense; existence marked with 이.

examples.ko: 그 정치인은 권력을 남용해서 결국 자리에서 물러났어요.
examples.romanization: geu jeongchiineun gwollyeogeul namyonghaeseo gyeolguk jarieseo mulleonasseoyo.
examples.en: That politician abused his power and eventually stepped down.
examples.note: 권력을 남용하다 + 자리에서 물러나다 ('step down from one's post'), natural news-style phrasing.

examples.en: Looking at history, power is not eternal.
examples.note: 권력은 영원하지 않다 = 'power is not eternal', a reflective set sentence with topic-marking 은.

extendedVocab.nuance: 권력 (權力, 權 'authority/right' + 力 'force/might' — 'the force of authority') means political power: the authority to control people, decisions, and resources, and it carries a weighty, frequently negative tone (권력 남용 = abuse of power, 권력 다툼 = power struggle). The boundary learners must respect is 권력 vs 힘 (also 'power'): 힘 is general strength — physical (힘이 세다), emotional (힘을 내다 'cheer up'), or everyday influence — whereas 권력 is reserved for institutional/political authority. So 'he is strong' is 힘이 세요, never 권력이 세요. The verb pitfall is collocation: power is something you 잡다 (seize), 가지다 (have), or 행사하다 (exercise) — there is no 권력을 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 권력 for physical strength or everyday 'power'. For those use 힘 — '힘이 세요' (strong), 힘을 내다 (cheer up); 권력 is only political/institutional authority.
Saying 권력을 하다. Power is something you 잡다 (seize), 가지다 (have), or 행사하다 (exercise), so 권력을 잡다 — not 권력을 하다.

extendedVocab.english: the people; citizens of a nation
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 국민 means "the people; citizens of a nation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 국민 (gungmin) = "the people; citizens of a nation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 국민의 권리 ("the rights of the people") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 국민, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 국민 pairs with 권리 ('rights') and 의무 ('duties') in civic contexts.
전 ('whole') + 국민 = everyone in the country (전 국민이 = all citizens [as subject]).
Fixed compound written as one word; a direct vote by all citizens.
뽑다 ('choose, pick, elect') is the natural verb in election contexts.

examples.en: The people elect the president.
examples.note: Simple civic frame: 국민이 (subject) + 뽑다; 뽑다 is the everyday verb for 'elect/choose'.

examples.ko: 이 정책은 전 국민에게 영향을 줘요.
examples.romanization: i jeongchaegeun jeon gungminege yeonghyangeul jwoyo.
examples.en: This policy affects all citizens.
examples.note: 전 국민에게 uses 에게 for the people affected; 영향을 주다 = 'have an effect on'.

examples.ko: 국가는 국민의 안전과 행복을 위해 일해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gukganeun gungminui anjeongwa haengbogeul wihae ilhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: The state should work for the safety and happiness of its citizens.
examples.note: 국가 + 국민, the classic civic pairing; 의 links 국민 to 안전과 행복.

extendedVocab.nuance: 국민 (國民, 國 'nation' + 民 'people' — 'the people of the nation') means the people as citizens of a particular country: a civic, collective term bound up with rights (권리), duties (의무), and the state. Distinguish it from two neighbors. Against 사람들 ('people' in general): 국민 is people specifically as a national citizenry, so '거리에 사람들이 많아요' (lots of people on the street) could never be 국민. Against 시민 (市民, 'citizens'): 시민 leans toward city residents or civil society (시민 단체 = civic groups, 서울 시민 = Seoul residents), while 국민 frames people in relation to the nation and government. Use 국민 whenever the context is national identity, elections, law, or the state's relationship to its population.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 국민 to mean 'people' in a general, casual sense. For an unspecified crowd use 사람들 — '사람들이 많아요', not '국민이 많아요'.
Confusing 국민 with 시민. 국민 = citizens of a nation (national level); 시민 = city residents / civil society (서울 시민, 시민 단체).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 환경 means "environment; surroundings" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 환경 (hwangyeong) means "environment; surroundings". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 환경을 보호하다 ("to protect the environment"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 환경 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 보호하다 (保護, 'guard and protect') is the fixed eco verb, never 지키다 alone here.
Headline compound; chains with 오염(pollution)·기후(climate)·쓰레기(trash).
Shows the non-nature sense: the conditions around you at work.

usagePhrases.en: to be good for the environment
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the thing affected; 환경이 좋다 instead means the place itself is nice.

examples.en: I'm very interested in the environment.
examples.note: Simple 관심이 많다 = to have much interest; 에 marks the topic of interest.

examples.ko: 일회용품을 줄이면 환경을 보호할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ilhoeyongpumeul jurimyeon hwangyeongeul bohohal su isseoyo.
examples.en: If we cut down on disposables, we can protect the environment.
examples.note: 환경을 보호하다 — the textbook collocation; 줄이다 = to reduce.

examples.ko: 이 회사는 근무 환경이 좋아서 직원들이 오래 다녀요.
examples.romanization: i hoesaneun geunmu hwangyeongi joaseo jigwondeuri orae danyeoyo.
examples.en: This company has a good work environment, so employees stay a long time.
examples.note: Real-situation use of 환경 for workplace conditions, paired with 다니다 (to attend/commute to).

extendedVocab.nuance: 환경 is Sino-Korean 環境 ('ring/encircle' 環 + 'boundary' 境), literally the boundary that rings you — hence it covers BOTH the natural environment (nature, pollution, climate) and the human conditions around a person: 근무 환경 (work environment), 가정 환경 (home background). The near-synonym 주변(周邊) means the physical 'surroundings/vicinity' you can point at, while 환경 is the abstract set of conditions that shape you, so a noisy 주변 creates a bad 환경. Register is neutral and works in essays, news, and speech alike; it collocates with 보호하다 (protect), 오염되다 (be polluted), and 파괴하다 (destroy). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: say 환경이 좋다 ('the environment is good') or 환경에 좋다 ('good FOR the environment'), never 환경을 좋다 — 좋다 is an adjective and can't take 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 환경 only for nature — it equally means general conditions/surroundings, as in 근무 환경 or 주변 환경; restricting it loses half its range.
Saying 환경을 좋다 — 좋다 is a descriptive adjective, so use 환경이 좋다 (the environment is good) or 환경에 좋다 (good for the environment).
Swapping in 주변 for the abstract sense — 주변 is the visible vicinity, while the set of life conditions is 환경 (가정 환경, not 가정 주변).
