extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 지식 means "knowledge" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "knowledge" is 지식 (jisik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 지식을 쌓다 ("to build up knowledge"). Watch the particle attached to 지식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 쌓다 ('to stack') is the native verb; 만들다 (make) is wrong for knowledge.
전문(專門) = specialty; standard on résumés and job posts.
풍부하다(豊富) = abundant; a compliment about a well-read person.
What you already know that helps you grasp a new topic.

examples.en: My knowledge of history is lacking.
examples.note: Simple 부족하다 = to be insufficient; note 지식 takes the topic directly (역사 지식).

examples.ko: 책을 많이 읽으면 다양한 지식을 쌓을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: chaegeul mani ilgeumyeon dayanghan jisigeul ssaeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you read a lot, you can build up varied knowledge.
examples.note: 지식을 쌓다 in an everyday motivational frame; 다양한 = varied.

examples.ko: 이 일을 하려면 어느 정도 전문 지식이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: i ireul haryeomyeon eoneu jeongdo jeonmun jisigi piryohaeyo.
examples.en: To do this job you need a certain level of specialized knowledge.
examples.note: Real-situation work talk; 어느 정도 = to some degree, 전문 지식이 필요하다 a set phrase.

extendedVocab.nuance: 지식 is Sino-Korean 知識 ('to know' 知 + 'recognize/perceive' 識), i.e. accumulated facts and information gained from study or experience. The sharp contrast is with 지혜(智慧) 'wisdom' — the good judgment to USE knowledge well: a scholar may have great 지식 but little 지혜. It also differs from 정보(情報) 'information', which is raw data/news you receive, whereas 지식 is what you've internalized and can apply. Register is neutral-to-formal and fits essays, interviews, and class. The habitual verb is 지식을 쌓다 (picture stacking bricks), and people 풍부하다 in it. English-speaker pitfall: 'knowledge' feels uncountable in English, but Korean freely says 다양한 지식 / 많은 지식, and you never 'make' knowledge (지식을 만들다 ✗) — you accumulate it (쌓다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 지식을 만들다 — knowledge is stacked up over time (지식을 쌓다), never 'made' like an object.
Confusing 지식 (facts/information you've learned) with 지혜 (wisdom, the judgment to apply it) — '경험에서 지혜를 얻다' vs '책에서 지식을 얻다'.
Blurring 지식 with 정보 — 정보 is incoming raw data (e.g. 정보를 검색하다), while 지식 is the internalized understanding.

structuredNuance.t: Accumulated facts and information gained from study or experience. Register is neutral-to-formal and fits essays, interviews, and class. The habitual verb is 지식을 쌓다 (picture stacking bricks), and people 풍부하다 in it.

The sharp contrast is with 지혜(智慧) 'wisdom' — the good judgment to USE knowledge well: a scholar may have great 지식 but little 지혜. It also differs from 정보(情報) 'information', which is raw data/news you receive, whereas 지식 is what you've internalized and can apply.
Sino-Korean 知識 ('to know' 知 + 'recognize/perceive' 識).
'Knowledge' feels uncountable in English, but Korean freely says 다양한 지식 / 많은 지식, and you never 'make' knowledge (지식을 만들다 ✗) — you accumulate it (쌓다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교육 means "education" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 교육 (gyoyuk) = "education". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교육을 받다 ("to receive an education") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 교육, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) is the learner's-side verb — you take education in.
Add 하다 and it's the teacher's-side verb meaning to teach/train.
공(公) = public; contrasts directly with 사교육 (private tutoring).
Common compound when comparing schools or regions.

examples.en: I want to receive a good education.
examples.note: Simple 교육을 받다 from the learner's side — note 받다, not 하다.

examples.ko: 회사에서 신입 사원을 대상으로 교육을 진행했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo sinip sawoneul daesangeuro gyoyugeul jinhaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: The company carried out training for new employees.
examples.note: Everyday workplace sense; -을 대상으로 = targeting, 진행하다 = to conduct.

examples.ko: 한국 부모들은 자녀 교육에 정말 많은 관심을 가져요.
examples.romanization: hanguk bumodeureun janyeo gyoyuge jeongmal maneun gwansimeul gajyeoyo.
examples.en: Korean parents take a great deal of interest in their children's education.
examples.note: Real social topic; 자녀 = one's children (formal), 관심을 가지다 = to take interest.

extendedVocab.nuance: 교육 is Sino-Korean 敎育 ('teach' 敎 + 'raise/nurture' 育) — literally to teach-and-rear, so it spans schooling, parenting, and on-the-job training, not just classrooms. The crucial direction split is in the verb: the learner says 교육을 받다 ('receive education'), while the provider says 교육하다 or 교육(을) 시키다 ('cause to be educated'). Near-synonym 훈련(訓練) 'training' is narrower and physical/repetitive (군사 훈련 military training, 직업 훈련 vocational training), whereas 교육 includes intellectual and moral formation. In Korea the 공교육(public) vs 사교육(private cram-school) divide is a constant social theme. English-speaker pitfall: don't say 교육을 하다 when you mean 'to study' — that means you're the one teaching; a student always uses 교육을 받다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교육을 하다 to mean 'I study/get educated' — 하다 puts you in the teacher's seat; learners use 교육을 받다.
Limiting 교육 to schools — it also covers corporate 교육 (training sessions), parental 교육, and safety briefings (안전 교육).
Using 교육 where 훈련 fits better — repetitive skill drilling (운전 훈련, 군사 훈련) is 훈련, while 교육 is broader teaching.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 종교 means "religion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 종교 (jonggyo) means "religion". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 종교를 믿다 ("to believe in / practice a religion"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 종교 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: to believe in / practice a religion
usagePhrases.note: 믿다 (believe) is the set verb — literally 'to believe a religion'.
Neutral existence frame; the basis of the polite question 종교가 있으세요?
자유(自由) = freedom; appears in civic and constitutional contexts.
Attending services, volunteering, study groups, etc.

examples.en: I don't have a religion.
examples.note: Simple, fully natural answer; 있다/없다 is how Korean frames 'having' a faith.

examples.en: Do you happen to follow any religion?
examples.note: Polite real-life question; 혹시 softens it and 믿는 modifies 종교 ('the religion you believe').

examples.ko: 한국에서는 다양한 종교가 평화롭게 공존하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeseoneun dayanghan jonggyoga pyeonghwaropge gongjonhago isseoyo.
examples.en: In Korea various religions coexist peacefully.
examples.note: Discussion register; 공존하다(共存) = to coexist, 평화롭게 = peacefully.

extendedVocab.nuance: 종교 is Sino-Korean 宗敎 ('ancestral/principal' 宗 + 'teaching' 敎), 'the principal teaching', the general term for religion as a belief system; a religious person is a 종교인. The key contrast is with 신앙(信仰) 'faith/devotion' — 종교 is the institution or category (불교, 기독교 are 종교), while 신앙 is the personal inner belief one holds, so an atheist studies 종교 academically but has no 신앙. Don't confuse 종교 with a specific 교회 (church building / Protestant church) or 절 (Buddhist temple). The verb pair 종교를 믿다 literally 'believe a religion' covers both holding and practicing it. Register is neutral; faith is treated as fairly private, so 종교가 있으세요? is acceptable but not pressed. English-speaker pitfall: never say 종교를 하다 ('do a religion') — you 믿다 (believe) it, or simply 종교가 있다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 종교를 하다 — you 믿다 (believe/practice) a religion or 종교가 있다; you never 'do' a religion.
Confusing 종교 (religion in general) with 교회 (a church / Protestant congregation) or 절 (Buddhist temple) — those are specific places/branches.
Equating 종교 with 신앙 — 종교 is the system/category, while 신앙 is the personal inner faith ('깊은 신앙', not '깊은 종교').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 예술 means "art; the arts" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "art; the arts" is 예술 (yesul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예술 작품 ("work of art"). Watch the particle attached to 예술 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 작품(作品) = piece/work; the standard pairing for any art form.
-가(家) makes the practitioner; covers musicians, painters, dancers alike.
전통(傳統) = tradition; e.g. 판소리, 탈춤, crafts.
-적(的) builds the adjective form: 예술적인 감각 (artistic sense).

examples.en: I like art.
examples.note: Simple statement; 예술 here means the arts broadly, not just paintings.

examples.ko: 이 미술관에서 다양한 예술 작품을 감상할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i misulgwaneseo dayanghan yesul jakpumeul gamsanghal su isseoyo.
examples.en: At this gallery you can appreciate various works of art.
examples.note: Everyday outing frame; 감상하다(鑑賞) = to appreciate art, the right verb (not 보다).

examples.en: I think cooking is also a form of art.
examples.note: Opinion register; 하나의 = 'one (kind of)', a natural way to call something an art.

extendedVocab.nuance: 예술 is Sino-Korean 藝術 ('skill/craft' 藝 + 'technique/art' 術), the arts as a whole — 미술(visual art), 음악(music), 무용(dance), 문학(literature), 연극(theatre) all live under it. The sharp contrast is with 미술(美術) 'fine/visual art', which is the narrower branch of painting, drawing and sculpture; a concert is 예술 but not 미술. Don't confuse it with 기술(技術) 'technology/skill', which shares 術 but means practical know-how. Register is neutral and slightly elevated, common in reviews and culture talk; it collocates with 작품 (work), 감상하다 (appreciate), and 표현 (expression). For the adjective, use 예술적(이다) 'artistic', as in 예술적인 표현. English-speaker pitfall: don't make the adjective with 스럽다 — 예술스럽다 ✗; the correct form is 예술적이다 / 예술적인.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예술 only for paintings — that narrower visual sense is 미술; 예술 spans music, dance, literature and more.
Saying 예술스럽다 for 'artistic' — the natural adjective is 예술적이다 / 예술적인 (예술적인 감각).
Mixing 예술 with 기술 — both carry 術, but 기술 is practical technology/skill, while 예술 is the creative arts.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 문학 means "literature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 문학 (munhak) = "literature". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문학 작품 ("literary work") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 문학, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 작품(作品) = work; the standard pairing for novels, poems, plays.
Put the nation or era before 문학 to specify the body of work.
고전(古典) = classic; contrasts with 현대 문학 (modern literature).
전공하다(專攻) = to major in; standard academic phrasing.

examples.en: I like literature.
examples.note: Simple; here 문학 names the whole field, the academic word for the love of reading-as-art.

examples.ko: 이 소설은 한국 현대 문학의 대표 작품이에요.
examples.romanization: i soseoreun hangu kyeondae munhagui daepyo jakpumieyo.
examples.en: This novel is a representative work of modern Korean literature.
examples.note: Everyday review frame; 대표 작품 = representative/landmark work, 현대 = modern.

examples.ko: 문학을 통해 그 시대 사람들의 삶을 엿볼 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: munhageul tonghae geu sidae saramdeurui salmeul yeotbol su isseoyo.
examples.en: Through literature you can glimpse the lives of people of that era.
examples.note: Reflective register; -을 통해 = through, 엿보다 = to catch a glimpse of.

extendedVocab.nuance: 문학 is Sino-Korean 文學 ('writing/letters' 文 + 'learning' 學), 'the study of letters' — literature as the art built from language: 소설(novels), 시(poetry), 희곡(drama), 수필(essays). It is one branch under 예술 and is the academic, field-level word, NOT a casual one: to talk about reading for fun, Koreans just say 소설 (novel) or 책 (book), and a single title is a 작품, never '하나의 문학'. The notorious near-miss is 문화(文化) 'culture' — one syllable apart (學 vs 化) but entirely different; '한국 문학' is Korean literature, '한국 문화' is Korean culture. Register is formal/intellectual, fitting essays and university talk. English-speaker pitfall: English 'literature' can loosely mean 'the readings/brochures', but Korean 문학 is strictly the artistic body of writing — product leaflets are 자료/책자, not 문학.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 문학 (literature) with 문화 (culture) — they differ by one syllable (學 vs 化) but mean completely different things.
Using 문학 for a single novel — one book is 소설 or 작품; 문학 is the entire field of imaginative writing.
Calling everyday reading material 문학 — pamphlets or info sheets are 자료/책자, while 문학 is writing-as-art.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 언어 means "language" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 언어 (eoneo) means "language". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 언어를 배우다 ("to learn a language"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 언어 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 배우다 (learn) is the natural verb; works for any tongue in the abstract.
외국(外國 foreign) + 어; 어(語) is the bound 'language' suffix.
능력(能力) = ability; very common on résumés and in linguistics.
모국(母國 homeland) + 어 = the language you grew up speaking.

examples.en: I want to learn a new language.
examples.note: Simple goal sentence; 언어 = language as a general concept, 배우다 the right verb.

examples.ko: 언어는 그 나라의 문화를 이해하는 열쇠예요.
examples.romanization: eoneoneun geu naraui munhwareul ihaehaneun yeolsoeyeyo.
examples.en: Language is the key to understanding a country's culture.
examples.note: Everyday metaphor; 열쇠 = key (figurative), -는 = topic marker on the subject.

examples.ko: 그분은 언어 능력이 뛰어나서 통역사로 일해요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun eoneo neungnyeogi ttwieonaseo tongyeoksaro ilhaeyo.
examples.en: She has excellent language ability, so she works as an interpreter.
examples.note: Real-situation; 통역사 = interpreter, 뛰어나다 = to be outstanding, -로 marks the job role.

extendedVocab.nuance: 언어 is Sino-Korean 言語 ('speech' 言 + 'words/talk' 語), language as the abstract human faculty or any language as a phenomenon. The structural point: a SPECIFIC named language takes the bound suffix 어(語) — 한국어 Korean, 영어 English, 일본어 Japanese — so you STUDY 한국어 but DISCUSS 언어 in general. The casual native near-synonym is 말, which is warmer and also means 'speech/words/remark' (말을 잘하다 = to speak well), whereas 언어 is the technical/written term used in linguistics, policy, and essays. English-speaker pitfall: never glue 언어 onto a country name — '한국언어' ✗ is not a word; the language is 한국어 (country + 어). Also, when you mean everyday 'words' or 'what someone said', use 말, not 언어 (그 말은 상처였어요 = those words hurt).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한국언어 — a named language uses the bound suffix 어: 한국어, 영어, 중국어, never country + 언어.
Using 언어 for casual 'words/talk' — that everyday sense is 말 (말이 많다, 좋은 말), while 언어 is the abstract/technical term.
Forgetting 언어 is the general concept — you can't 'speak 언어'; you speak a specific 한국어/영어, and discuss 언어 as a topic.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 인구 means "population" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "population" is 인구 (ingu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 인구가 많다 ("to have a large population"). Watch the particle attached to 인구 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Describe size with 많다/적다 (many/few), never 크다 (big).
늘다/줄다 for increase/decrease; 늘어나다 is the fuller variant.
감소(減少) = decrease; a flagship social-issue compound.
고령(高齡) = advanced age; pairs in 고령 인구 증가 (rise in the elderly).

examples.en: Seoul has a large population.
examples.note: Simple; the core lesson — size of 인구 is 많다, not 크다.

examples.ko: 요즘 한국은 인구 감소 문제가 심각해요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hangugeun ingu gamso munjega simgakaeyo.
examples.en: These days population decline is a serious problem in Korea.
examples.note: Everyday news frame; 심각하다(深刻) = to be serious/grave, 인구 감소 a set compound.

examples.ko: 이 지역은 젊은 인구가 점점 줄고 있어요.
examples.romanization: i jiyeogeun jeolmeun inguga jeomjeom julgo isseoyo.
examples.en: The young population in this area is gradually shrinking.
examples.note: Real-situation; 점점 = gradually, 줄다 = to decrease, -고 있다 shows ongoing trend.

extendedVocab.nuance: 인구 is Sino-Korean 人口 ('person' 人 + 'mouth' 口) — literally a head-count by 'mouths to feed', the number of people in a place. The decisive collocation rule: its quantity is 많다(many)/적다(few) and its change is 늘다(increase)/줄다(decrease); Korean does NOT use 크다/작다 (big/small), which belong to physical size. Don't confuse 인구 with the look-alike 인기(人氣) 'popularity' (인기가 많다 = popular) or with 식구(食口) 'family members / household mouths', which is the small home unit, not a region's count. Register is neutral-to-formal, dominating demographics and news; today 인구 감소 (decline) and 고령화 (aging) are perennial themes. English-speaker pitfall: 'a big population' tempts 인구가 크다 — wrong; say 인구가 많다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 인구가 크다 — population is counted, so use 인구가 많다/적다 (many/few), not 크다/작다 (big/small).
Confusing 인구 (population) with 인기 (popularity) — they look alike but 인기가 많다 means 'is popular', unrelated to headcount.
Mixing 인구 with 식구 — 식구 is the members of one household ('우리 식구는 네 명'), while 인구 is a region's total people.

Register is neutral-to-formal, dominating demographics and news; today 인구 감소 (decline) and 고령화 (aging) are perennial themes.
Don't confuse 인구 with the look-alike 인기(人氣) 'popularity' (인기가 많다 = popular) or with 식구(食口) 'family members / household mouths', which is the small home unit, not a region's count.
Sino-Korean 人口 ('person' 人 + 'mouth' 口) — literally a head-count by 'mouths to feed'.
'A big population' tempts 인구가 크다 — wrong; say 인구가 많다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 지역 means "region; area; local district" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 지역 (jiyeok) = "region; area; local district". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이 지역 ("this area/region") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 지역, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Common demonstrative + 지역, for any defined locale.
주민(住民) = residents; the set pairing in civic talk.
사회(社會) = society; 지역 사회 = the local community as a whole.
수도권(首都圈) = the greater-Seoul metropolitan zone.

examples.en: This area is quiet.
examples.note: Simple description; 지역 as a neutral 'area' you can point to on a map.

examples.en: Dialects and food differ a little from region to region.
examples.note: Everyday observation; 지역마다 = every region, 사투리 = dialect, 조금씩 = bit by bit.

examples.ko: 지역 주민들이 환경 보호 활동에 적극적으로 참여했어요.
examples.romanization: jiyeok jumindeuri hwangyeong boho hwaldonge jeokgeukjeogeuro chamyeohaesseoyo.
examples.en: Local residents actively took part in environmental protection activities.
examples.note: Civic-news register; 적극적으로 = actively, 참여하다 = to participate, -에 marks the activity.

extendedVocab.nuance: 지역 is Sino-Korean 地域 ('land/earth' 地 + 'boundary/territory' 域), a bounded geographic area, and by extension the 지역 사회 (local community). Two contrasts matter. Against 지방(地方) 'the provinces': 지역 is any neutral region (수도권 지역 included), whereas 지방 specifically means everywhere OUTSIDE Seoul (지방에 살다 = to live in the provinces), often with a center-vs-rest nuance. Against 동네: 지역 is formal/administrative (지역 경제, 지역 주민), while 동네 is your warm, familiar block where neighbors know you. Register is neutral-formal, common in news and policy. English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm from the countryside/regions' becomes 지방, not 지역; and your cozy neighborhood is 동네, so '우리 동네' (my neighborhood) sounds natural where '우리 지역' would feel like a press release.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 지역 (any neutral region/area) with 지방 — 지방 specifically means the provinces outside the capital ('지방 출신' = from outside Seoul).
Using 지역 for your cozy neighborhood — that warmer, personal sense is 동네 (우리 동네 빵집).
Saying 지역이 크다 for community closeness — for a tight-knit local society use 지역 사회, and describe size of land with 넓다 (wide), not just 크다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 발명 means "invention" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 발명 (balmyeong) means "invention". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 발명하다 ("to invent"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 발명 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Add 하다 for the act: 전화를 발명하다 (to invent the telephone).
품(品) = item; the physical thing that was invented.
-가(家) makes the person who invents; 에디슨은 발명가예요.
위대하다(偉大) = great; standard praise for a landmark creation.

examples.en: The telephone is a great invention.
examples.note: Simple; 발명 as the noun for a created thing, framed with 위대한 (great).

examples.en: Edison is famous for inventing the light bulb.
examples.note: Everyday fact frame; -(으)ㄴ 것으로 유명하다 = to be famous for having done.

examples.ko: 그 학생은 재미있는 발명품을 만들어서 상을 받았어요.
examples.romanization: geu haksaengeun jaemiinneun balmyeongpumeul mandeureoseo sangeul badasseoyo.
examples.en: That student made an interesting invention and won a prize.
examples.note: Real-situation; 발명품 (the invented item) is what you 만들다, then 상을 받다 = win a prize.

extendedVocab.nuance: 발명 is Sino-Korean 發明 ('emit/bring forth' 發 + 'bright/clear' 明), 'to bring something into the light' — creating a device or method that did not exist before, with 발명품 being the resulting product. The essential contrast is with 발견(發見) 'discovery' ('emit' 發 + 'see' 見): you 발명하다 a telephone (made new) but 발견하다 a planet or a law of nature (already there, newly found). Register is neutral, common in history, science and patents; it collocates with 발명가 (inventor), 발명품 (the product), and 특허 (patent). English-speaker pitfall: keep act vs object straight — the abstract act/concept is 발명/발명하다, but the physical gadget you hold is a 발명품, so '재미있는 발명을 만들다' is odd; say '재미있는 발명품을 만들다'. Also don't reach for 발견 (discover) when nothing pre-existed.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 발명 (invention — creating something new) with 발견 (discovery — finding what already existed) — you 발명하다 a machine but 발견하다 a fossil.
Saying 발명을 만들다 for a physical item — the made object is 발명품, so 발명품을 만들다; 발명하다 alone is the act.
Using 발견 for human-made things — a new app or recipe is 발명/개발, not 발견.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 발견 means "discovery" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "discovery" is 발견 (balgyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 발견하다 ("to discover; to find out"). Watch the particle attached to 발견 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Add 하다 for the act of coming across or realizing something.
새로운 = new; the staple pairing in science writing.
우연하다(偶然) = by chance; 우연히 발견하다 (find by chance).
Passive 되다 when the discoverer is unknown or unstated.

examples.en: Scientists discovered a new planet.
examples.note: Simple active sentence; 발견하다 with a clear agent (scientists) and object (planet).

examples.ko: 그 그림은 한 농부에 의해 우연히 발견되었어요.
examples.romanization: geu geurimeun han nongbue uihae uyeonhi balgyeondoeeosseoyo.
examples.en: That painting was discovered by chance by a farmer.
examples.note: Everyday passive; -에 의해 = by (agent), and 발견되다 backgrounds the finder.

examples.ko: 여행하면서 나 자신에 대한 새로운 점을 발견했어요.
examples.romanization: yeohaenghamyeonseo na jasine daehan saeroun jeomeul balgyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: While traveling, I discovered something new about myself.
examples.note: Figurative real-situation; 발견하다 = to realize, -에 대해 = about, 새로운 점 = a new aspect.

extendedVocab.nuance: 발견 is Sino-Korean 發見 ('emit/bring forth' 發 + 'see' 見) — to bring into sight something that already existed but was unknown: a planet, an old manuscript, even a fresh truth about yourself. The pivotal contrast is with 발명(發明) 'invention', which CREATES the never-before-existing (telephone, light bulb), whereas 발견 only uncovers what was there. The verb 발견하다 stretches figuratively to 'realize/notice' (새로운 면을 발견하다 = to discover a new side of someone). Register is neutral, frequent in science, news and reflection; it collocates with 새로운 (new), 우연히 (by chance), and the passive 발견되다. English-speaker pitfall: when no agent is named, English keeps active voice ('they found...'), but Korean prefers the passive 발견되다 (유물이 발견되었다 = artifacts were discovered); and don't use 발견 for human creations — those are 발명.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 발견 (discovery — finding what already existed) with 발명 (invention — creating the new) — a comet is 발견되다, a smartphone is 발명되다.
Forgetting the passive 발견되다 — when you don't name who found it, Korean uses 발견되다 (화석이 발견되었어요), not active 'found'.
Using 발견하다 for inventing something — bringing a brand-new product into being is 발명하다/개발하다, not 발견하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기술 means "technology; skill; technique" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기술 (gisul) = "technology; skill; technique". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기술이 발달하다 ("technology develops/advances") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기술, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 발달하다(發達) is the idiomatic verb for tech progress, not 자라다.
Fixed pairing in news, policy and R&D talk.
Shows the hands-on sense: a practical, learnable craft.
최신(最新) = newest; standard product/marketing phrasing.

examples.en: These days technology develops quickly.
examples.note: Simple; the core collocation 기술이 발달하다 with 빠르게 (quickly).

examples.ko: 그는 요리 기술이 뛰어나서 유명한 식당에서 일해요.
examples.romanization: geuneun yori gisuri ttwieonaseo yumyeonghan sikdangeseo ilhaeyo.
examples.en: He has outstanding cooking skills, so he works at a famous restaurant.
examples.note: Everyday personal-skill sense; here 기술 = hands-on technique, not high-tech.

examples.ko: 새로운 기술 덕분에 많은 일이 자동화되고 있어요.
examples.romanization: saeroun gisul deokbune maneun iri jadonghwadoego isseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to new technology, many tasks are being automated.
examples.note: Real-situation; -덕분에 = thanks to, 자동화 = automation, -고 있다 ongoing change.

extendedVocab.nuance: 기술 is Sino-Korean 技術 ('skill/ability' 技 + 'technique/art' 術), and it straddles two senses context disambiguates: macro-level technology (과학 기술, IT 기술, 최신 기술) and an individual's practical skill or technique (요리 기술, 운전 기술). Contrast with 예술(藝術), which shares 術 but is the creative arts, and with 능력(能力) 'ability/capacity', which is innate or general capability rather than a trained, specific technique — a person has 능력 broadly but acquires a concrete 기술. Register is neutral. The collocations split by sense: technology 발달하다 (advances) or 발전하다, while a person 기술을 배우다/익히다 (learns/masters). English-speaker pitfall: 'technique improved' tempts 기술이 발전되다 for a person, but for an individual's skill say 기술이 늘다 (skill grows); reserve 발달/발전 for technology at large.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 기술 only for high-tech — it equally means a hands-on personal craft (요리 기술, 운전 기술).
Saying 기술이 발전되다 for a person's skill — for someone getting better use 기술이 늘다; reserve 발달하다/발전하다 for technology broadly.
Mixing 기술 with 능력 — 능력 is general capacity/ability, while 기술 is a specific learned technique ('운전 능력' is your overall driving capacity, '운전 기술' the concrete maneuvering skill).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 연구 means "research; study (academic)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 연구 (yeongu) means "research; study (academic)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 연구하다 ("to research; to study deeply"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연구 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Add 하다 for sustained academic/scientific investigation.
결과(結果) = result; the standard outcome pairing.
진행하다(進行) = to carry out/proceed with a study.
원(員) = staff member; the person who does the research.

examples.en: I research the Korean language.
examples.note: Simple; 연구하다 frames deep, systematic study — heavier than '공부해요'.

examples.ko: 이번 연구 결과가 학계에서 큰 주목을 받았어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeongu gyeolgwaga hakgyeeseo keun jumogeul badasseoyo.
examples.en: These research findings drew great attention in academia.
examples.note: Everyday academic frame; 학계 = academic world, 주목을 받다 = to draw attention.

examples.ko: 대학원에서 한국어 교육에 대해 연구하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: daehagwoneseo hangugeo gyoyuge daehae yeonguhago isseoyo.
examples.en: I'm researching Korean language education in graduate school.
examples.note: Real-situation; -에 대해 = about/on, 대학원 = grad school, -고 있다 ongoing project.

extendedVocab.nuance: 연구 is Sino-Korean 硏究 ('grind/hone' 硏 + 'investigate to the end' 究) — to grind away at a question until you reach its depths, i.e. systematic academic or scientific research aimed at producing NEW knowledge. The decisive contrast is with 공부(工夫) 'studying': you 공부 a textbook to absorb what's already known (for an exam), but you 연구 a problem to discover what isn't yet known — a grad student 공부하다 coursework yet 연구하다 a thesis. Near-synonym 조사(調査) is narrower 'survey/investigation' (설문 조사 = questionnaire survey, 경찰 조사 = police inquiry), a fact-finding step rather than the whole scholarly enterprise. Register is formal/academic, clustering with 연구실 (lab), 연구원 (researcher), 연구 결과 (findings). English-speaker pitfall: don't use 연구 for everyday schoolwork ('I studied for the test' = 공부했어요, not 연구했어요), and findings 'come out' — 연구 결과가 나오다 — rather than being 'made'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 연구 for ordinary studying — daily school study or exam prep is 공부; 연구 is investigative, new-knowledge research.
Saying 연구를 만들다 for results — findings emerge, so 연구 결과가 나오다 (results come out) or 결과를 얻다 (obtain results).
Confusing 연구 with 조사 — 조사 is a focused survey/inquiry (설문 조사, 시장 조사), while 연구 is the broader, deeper scholarly study.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 문화 means "culture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "culture" is 문화 (munhwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한국 문화 ("Korean culture"). Watch the particle attached to 문화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: country name + 문화, no particle between them — it reads as one compound noun
문화 + 차이; this is the standard phrase for the gap between two cultures, e.g. 문화 차이 때문에 (because of cultural difference)
문화 + 를 + 경험하다; 경험하다 (to experience firsthand) is the habitual partner verb, stronger than just 보다
전통 + 문화; often written as one word 전통문화, contrasted with 대중문화 (pop culture)

examples.en: I like Korean culture.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 문화 as a plain object with 를. Notice 한국 문화 sits together with no particle inside it.

examples.en: Culture differs a little from country to country.
examples.note: 나라마다 = 'every country / from country to country'; 문화가 달라요 is the everyday way to say cultures differ — 다르다, not 틀리다.

examples.ko: 외국에서 살면 처음에는 문화 차이 때문에 힘들 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: oegugeseo salmyeon cheoeumeneun munhwa chai ttaemune himdeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: When you live abroad, at first it can be hard because of cultural differences.
examples.note: Real-situation register: 문화 차이 때문에 (because of cultural difference) is the exact phrase Koreans reach for to explain culture shock politely.

extendedVocab.nuance: 문화 means 'culture' in the broad sense — the customs, arts, food, and shared ways of life of a group. It is Sino-Korean, 文化 ('writing/civilization' 文 + 'become/transform' 化), literally 'becoming civilized', so it leans toward the refined, collective sense of culture rather than one person's habits. The nearest trap-word is 문학 文學 (literature): the two look and sound almost identical, but 학 'study' vs 화 'transform' completely changes the meaning, so an English speaker who half-hears the word can easily swap them. 문화 also is NOT used for bacterial 'culture' (that is 배양) or for being a 'cultured/refined person' (that is 교양 있다). It loves to form compounds — 대중문화 (pop culture), 문화재 (cultural heritage), 문화생활 (cultural life/leisure) — and the habitual verb is 경험하다 (to experience), as in 다른 문화를 경험하다. The everyday phrase 문화 차이 (cultural difference) is how Koreans tactfully explain awkward moments. Register is neutral, fine in both casual chat and formal writing.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 문화 (culture, 文化) with 문학 (literature, 文學). They differ by one syllable (화 vs 학); saying 한국 문학에 관심이 있어요 means 'interested in Korean literature', not culture. Listen for 화 'transform' vs 학 'study'.
Using 틀리다 to say cultures 'are different': 나라마다 문화가 틀려요 literally means each culture is 'wrong'. The correct verb is 다르다 → 문화가 달라요. 틀리다 = incorrect; 다르다 = different.
Adding a particle inside the compound: writing 한국의 문화 sounds stiff and over-literal in speech. Natural spoken Korean drops it — 한국 문화 — treating the two nouns as one unit.

structuredNuance.t: 문화 means 'culture' in the broad sense — the customs, arts, food, and shared ways of life of a group. It leans toward the refined, collective sense of culture rather than one person's habits. It loves to form compounds — 대중문화 (pop culture), 문화재 (cultural heritage), 문화생활 (cultural life/leisure) — and the habitual verb is 경험하다 (to experience), as in 다른 문화를 경험하다. The everyday phrase 문화 차이 (cultural difference) is how Koreans tactfully explain awkward moments. Register is neutral, fine in both casual chat and formal writing.
It is Sino-Korean, 文化 ('writing/civilization' 文 + 'become/transform' 化), literally 'becoming civilized', which is why it leans toward the refined, collective sense.

The nearest trap-word is 문학 文學 (literature): the two look and sound almost identical, but 학 'study' vs 화 'transform' completely changes the meaning, so an English speaker who half-hears the word can easily swap them. 문화 is also NOT used for bacterial 'culture' (that is 배양) or for being a 'cultured/refined person' (that is 교양 있다).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 감동 means "deep emotion; being moved/touched" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 감동 (gamdong) = "deep emotion; being moved/touched". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 감동을 받다 ("to be moved/touched") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 감동, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 감동 + 을 받다; the standard way to say YOU were moved — literally 'to receive emotion'. This is the most common form.
감동 + 을 주다; literally 'to give emotion' — used when a film, person, or story moves others
감동 + 적이다 makes the adjective; modifier form 감동적인 영화 (a moving film)
casual/slang; 감동 먹었어 = 'I was so touched' among friends — never in formal writing

examples.en: That movie was really moving.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 감동이다 used directly as 'was moving'. Casual-polite 요-speech, the most natural quick reaction.

examples.en: I read grandma's letter and was moved.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 감동을 받다 = the experiencer was touched. Note 을 받다 ('receive'), not 했다 — this is how Korean frames being moved.

examples.ko: 선수의 마지막 인사가 모든 사람에게 큰 감동을 줬어요.
examples.romanization: seonsuui majimak insaga modeun saramege keun gamdongeul jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The athlete's final farewell gave everyone deep emotion.
examples.note: Real-situation: 감동을 주다 (give emotion) flips the viewpoint to the SOURCE. 큰 감동 (great emotion) is the natural collocation, not 많은 감동.

extendedVocab.nuance: 감동 is the warm, welling-up feeling of being moved or touched — the lump-in-the-throat reaction to a kind gesture, a film, or a reunion. It is Sino-Korean, 感動 ('feel' 感 + 'move/stir' 動), literally 'the heart being moved', which is exactly the English metaphor 'to be moved', so the image transfers nicely. The key learner difficulty is the verb frames: Korean splits 'being moved' (감동을 받다, 'receive emotion') from 'moving others' (감동을 주다, 'give emotion'), and the standalone verb 감동하다/감동받다 means YOU felt it — never 'to move a physical object' (that is 옮기다 or 움직이다). Compare the near-synonym 인상 印象 (impression): 인상 깊다 ('it left a deep impression') is more neutral and cognitive, while 감동 is purely emotional and positive. Compare also 감격 (overwhelming emotion, often tears) which is stronger and rarer. Natural collocations: 감동을 받다/주다, 큰 감동 (not 많은 감동), 감동적인 N. Tone is sincere and a touch earnest; the slang 감동 먹다 is friendly but casual only.

Treating 감동하다 like English 'to move (an object)': 책상을 감동했어요 is wrong — for moving things use 옮기다 (relocate) or 움직이다 (budge). 감동하다 only means a person was emotionally moved.
Saying 많은 감동 for 'a lot of emotion'. Korean counts this feeling by size, not amount, so the natural phrase is 큰 감동 (great/deep emotion). 많은 감동 sounds off.
Mixing up who feels it: using 감동을 줬어요 when you mean YOU were touched. 주다 = give (you moved others); to say you yourself were moved, use 감동을 받았어요 or 감동했어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 다양하다 means "to be various; diverse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 다양하다 (dayanghada) means "to be various; diverse". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다양해요 ("it's diverse/varied"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다양하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb → drop 하다, the 여 fuses to 해, giving 다양해요 (polite present). The 요-form anchor for this word.
modifier form 다양한 + noun; 다양한 종류, 다양한 의견 are common partners
종류가 + 다양하다; the thing that varies takes 가/이 — 색깔이 다양하다, 의견이 다양하다
adverb form 다양하게; 다양하게 즐기다 (enjoy in various ways), 다양하게 준비하다

examples.en: The menu is diverse.
examples.note: Simplest frame: [N]이/가 다양해요. As a 하다-adjective, 다양 + 해요; the subject (what varies) takes 가.

examples.en: Everyone thinks differently, so it's interesting.
examples.note: Everyday frame with 다양해서 (because it's varied). Shows the 해서 reason form and the collocation 생각이 다양하다.

examples.ko: 이번 축제에서는 다양한 나라의 음식을 맛볼 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon chukjeeseoneun dayanghan naraui eumsigeul matbol su isseoyo.
examples.en: At this festival you can taste food from various countries.
examples.note: Real-situation: 다양한 + N as a modifier in a full sentence. 다양한 나라의 음식 = 'food from many different countries' — note the variety nuance, not mere counting.

extendedVocab.nuance: 다양하다 means 'to be various / diverse', stressing a wide RANGE of different kinds, not just a big number. It is a 하다-adjective from Sino-Korean 多樣 ('many' 多 + 'shape/kind' 樣), literally 'many shapes', which captures its core sense of qualitative variety. Because it is a descriptive adjective, the present polite form follows 하다-conjugation — 다양 + 해요 — and the noun-modifying form is 다양한 N (never 다양하는 N, the present-participle ending reserved for action verbs). The near-synonym trap is 여러 (several) and the number-word 많다 (to be many): 여러 나라 and 많은 나라 simply count 'several / many countries', while 다양한 나라 highlights that they are DIFFERENT in kind. So '메뉴가 많아요' = there are lots of menu items; '메뉴가 다양해요' = the items are varied in type — a real distinction English 'a variety of' blurs. The thing that varies takes 이/가 (종류가 다양하다, 의견이 다양하다), and the adverb 다양하게 pairs with verbs (다양하게 준비하다). Register is neutral, equally at home in casual speech and formal writing.

Using the verb-style modifier 다양하는 N. 다양하다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 다양한 (다양한 메뉴). 다양하는 is ungrammatical here because -는 marks ongoing action verbs, not descriptive adjectives.
Swapping 다양하다 for 많다 when you mean 'many'. 친구가 다양해요 sounds odd (your friends are 'of varied types'); to say you have many friends use 친구가 많아요. Reserve 다양하다 for difference in kind.
Marking the varied thing with 을/를: 메뉴를 다양해요 is wrong. Adjectives take a subject, not an object — the varying thing gets 이/가: 메뉴가 다양해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 과거 means "the past" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "the past" is 과거 (gwageo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 과거에 ("in the past"). Watch the particle attached to 과거 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: time adverbial; 과거에는 sets up an explicit contrast with 지금/현재
collocation with 돌아보다 (reflect); also 과거를 회상하다
pairs with 먼/가까운 to mark how far back the time is

usagePhrases.en: ask about / dredge up someone's past
usagePhrases.note: 과거를 묻지 마세요 = don't ask about my past

examples.en: In the past, this whole place was rice fields.
examples.note: 과거에(는) frames a then-vs-now contrast

examples.ko: 이제 과거는 잊고 앞으로 나아가려고 해요.
examples.romanization: ije gwageoneun itgo apeuro naagaryeogo haeyo.
examples.en: Now I'll forget the past and move forward.
examples.note: 과거 as 'bygones' you leave behind, paired with 앞으로

examples.ko: 그 사람의 과거에 대해서는 저도 잘 몰라요.
examples.romanization: geu saramui gwageoe daehaeseoneun jeodo jal mollayo.
examples.en: Even I don't really know about that person's past.
examples.note: 과거 = someone's personal history; -에 대해서 = about

extendedVocab.nuance: 과거 is Sino-Korean (過去, 過 'pass' + 去 'go away', literally 'what has gone by'), the past as an abstract span that sits in a tidy set with 현재 (present) and 미래 (future); it also means a person's personal history and, in grammar, the past tense (과거형). The key dividing line is with 예전 and 옛날: those are the warm, conversational words for 'a while back / the old days,' whereas 과거 is cooler, more analytical and at home in writing, news and reflection (과거를 돌아보다). The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 과거 to translate 'last time' or 'a while ago' in casual chat — that slot belongs to 저번/예전, and 과거 there sounds oddly philosophical. Also remember 과거 is a noun, never a verb: 'in the past it was…' is 과거에는 ~였어요, not 과거했어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 과거에 만났어요 for 'we met a while ago' sounds too grand/abstract — for casual 'last time/before' use 예전에 or 저번에 instead.
과거 is a noun, not a verb; 'in the past it was a school' is 과거에는 학교였어요, never 과거했어요 (no such verb).
Dropping the topic particle in a contrast (과거에 vs 과거에는) loses the 'used to, but now…' nuance; add 는 when you mean to contrast with the present.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 현재 means "the present, currently" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 현재 (hyeonjae) = "the present, currently". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 현재 ("currently, at present") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 현재, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: stands alone as a sentence-initial adverb with no particle
현재까지의 결과 = the results so far
set phrase in news, reports and announcements

usagePhrases.en: as of now / based on the present
usagePhrases.note: 현재 기준으로 = taking this moment as the reference point

examples.en: I'm currently living in Seoul.
examples.note: 현재 used adverbially, with NO 에 attached

examples.ko: 현재까지 신청한 사람이 백 명이 넘어요.
examples.romanization: hyeonjaekkaji sincheonghan sarami baeng myeongi neomeoyo.
examples.en: So far, over a hundred people have applied.
examples.note: 현재까지 = counting up to this moment

examples.en: The present matters more than the past or future.
examples.note: 현재 as a noun contrasted with 과거 and 미래

extendedVocab.nuance: 현재 is Sino-Korean (現在, 現 'appear/manifest' + 在 'exist', literally 'what now exists'), serving both as the noun 'the present' and as an adverb 'currently / at present.' Its nearest rival is 지금, and the line between them is register, not meaning: 지금 is the everyday spoken word, while 현재 is its formal, written twin that fills reports, news tickers and official notices (현재 상황, 현재까지). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 현재 like an English noun and bolting 에 onto it: you say 현재 살고 있어요, never 현재에 살고 있어요 — as an adverb it stands bare. A second trap is overusing 현재 in friendly conversation, where it can sound stiff and bureaucratic; switch to 지금 the moment the tone relaxes.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
현재 used adverbially takes no particle: say 현재 살고 있어요, not 현재에 살고 있어요 (unlike English 'at present', the 에 is wrong).
Using 현재 in casual chat ('현재 뭐 해?') sounds like a news anchor; the natural spoken word is 지금 (지금 뭐 해?).
Don't confuse 현재 (present) with 현실 (現實, reality); 현실 is 'real life / actuality', a different concept even though both start with 현.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 미래 means "the future" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 미래 (mirae) means "the future". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 미래에 ("in the future"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 미래 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: broad time adverbial for things yet to come
pairs with 밝은/어두운 to color one's outlook
natural with 준비하다/계획하다/대비하다
미래 지향적인 사고 = forward-looking thinking

examples.en: In the future, cars might fly through the sky.
examples.note: 미래에(는) for broad predictions; -지도 몰라요 = might

examples.ko: 아이들의 밝은 미래를 위해 열심히 일해요.
examples.romanization: aideurui balgeun miraereul wihae yeolsimhi ilhaeyo.
examples.en: I work hard for the children's bright future.
examples.note: 밝은 미래 collocation; -를 위해 = for the sake of

examples.ko: 먼 미래보다 가까운 미래를 먼저 계획하세요.
examples.romanization: meon miraeboda gakkaun miraereul meonjeo gyehoekaseyo.
examples.en: Plan for the near future before the distant one.
examples.note: 가까운/먼 미래 contrast

extendedVocab.nuance: 미래 is Sino-Korean (未來, 未 'not yet' + 來 'come', literally 'what has not yet come'), the future as a broad abstract concept that completes the trio with 과거 and 현재; it loves adjectives like 밝은/어두운 and verbs like 준비하다 and 계획하다. The sharp contrast to learn is 미래 vs 앞으로/나중에: 미래 is the panoramic, somewhat formal 'the future' you'd put in an essay or a speech, while 앞으로 ('from now on') and 나중에 ('later') handle concrete, near-term plans in real conversation. So the English-speaker pitfall is saying 미래에 ~할 거예요 for a personal intention like 'in the future I'll exercise more' — a Korean naturally says 앞으로 ~할 거예요; 미래에 there sounds grandiose. Likewise 'later today / soon' is 나중에/이따가, never 미래.

For a personal resolution ('in the future I'll study harder') say 앞으로 ~할 거예요, not 미래에 ~ — 미래에 sounds like a grand essay statement, not a plan.
'Later today / soon' is 나중에 or 이따가, not 미래; 미래 is the broad far-off future, not the near term.
미래 is a noun, so 'a bright future' is 밝은 미래 (adjective + noun); don't try to make it a verb like 미래하다 (not a word).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 순간 means "moment, instant" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "moment, instant" is 순간 (sungan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그 순간 ("at that moment"). Watch the particle attached to 순간 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: points back to a specific instant just mentioned
보는 순간 = the instant one sees; always present 는
adverb for a split-second, reflexive reaction
pairs with 결정적인/마지막 for a crucial instant

examples.en: At that moment my mind went blank.
examples.note: 그 순간 = at that very instant

examples.en: The instant I opened the door, I was startled.
examples.note: -는 순간 stays present even for a past event

examples.ko: 행복한 순간들은 늘 빨리 지나가는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: haengbokan sungandeureun neul ppalli jinaganeun geot gatayo.
examples.en: Happy moments always seem to pass by quickly.
examples.note: 순간 as a countable noun + 들; pairs with 지나가다

extendedVocab.nuance: 순간 is Sino-Korean (瞬間, 瞬 'blink of an eye' + 間 'interval', literally 'the space of a blink'), so it is a razor-thin instant — far shorter than 동안 (a stretch you endure) or 시기 (a phase). Its most powerful use is the pattern Verb-는 순간 ('the very moment that…'), the go-to for dramatic timing, and 순간적으로 for a reflexive, in-a-flash action. The synonym to keep apart is 잠깐/잠시: those mean 'for a little while' (a short duration), whereas 순간 is a single point with no duration — so 'please wait a moment' is 잠깐만요, never 순간만요. The other classic English-speaker trap is conjugating that pattern into the past: even for a past event you keep the present 는, as in 문을 여는 순간 놀랐어요, not 연 순간.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'Wait a moment, please' is 잠깐만요 or 잠시만요, not 순간만요 — 순간 is a zero-duration instant, while 잠깐/잠시 is a short span.
The pattern -는 순간 keeps the present 는 even for past events: 문을 여는 순간 놀랐어요, NOT 문을 연 순간 놀랐어요.
순간 is a noun; for 'momentarily / in a flash' as a manner adverb you need 순간적으로, not bare 순간.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시기 means "period, time (season of)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 시기 (sigi) = "period, time (season of)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이 시기 ("this period/phase") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: a particular stretch of time defined by what's happening
시기 follows a noun naming the phase
pairs with 적절한/적당한 for an opportune moment
놓치다 = to let the opportune timing slip by

examples.en: Now is the best time to move.
examples.note: 시기 = an opportune phase for doing something

examples.en: During the job-hunting period, there's a lot of stress.
examples.note: -는 시기에(는) = during the phase of

examples.en: I hurried so as not to miss the good timing.
examples.note: 시기를 놓치다 collocation; -지 않으려고 = so as not to

extendedVocab.nuance: 시기 is Sino-Korean (時期, 時 'time' + 期 'term/period'), a phase of time defined by what is happening within it — broader than a 순간 but narrower than 시대 (an era like 조선 시대). It carries a strong flavor of 'the right timing' for an action, hence 적절한 시기 and 시기를 놓치다. The crucial contrast is 시기 vs 기간 (期間, a measured duration with a clear start and end): 시험 기간 ('the 3-day exam period' you can count) versus 성장 시기 ('the growing phase,' a qualitative stage) — English 'period' covers both, which is exactly why learners mix them up. A pure homophone hazard: 시기 also exists as a separate word meaning 'envy/jealousy' (猜忌), so context, not sound, tells them apart. Use 기간 when you can put a number of days on it; use 시기 for a named phase or the opportune moment.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For a countable, bounded span ('a 7-day trial period') use 기간, not 시기; 시기 is a qualitative phase or the right moment, not a measured duration.
Don't pick 시기 to translate 'era / age' like 'the Joseon era' — that's 시대 (조선 시대); 시기 is a smaller phase within a life or process.
Beware the homophone: 시기 can also mean 'jealousy' (시기하다 = to envy); make sure context makes clear you mean the time-period 시기.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 당시 means "at that time, back then" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 당시 (dangsi) means "at that time, back then". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그 당시 ("at that time, in those days"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 당시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: at that time, in those days
usagePhrases.note: the most common form; a past time already in context
sets up a then-vs-now contrast
사고 당시 = at the time of the accident
set phrase in accounts, reports and testimony

examples.ko: 그 당시에는 휴대폰이 없어서 정말 불편했어요.
examples.romanization: geu dangsieneun hyudaeponi eopseoseo jeongmal bulpyeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Back then there were no cell phones, so it was really inconvenient.
examples.note: 그 당시에(는) = in those days, contrasting with now

examples.en: At the time of the accident, I was at home.
examples.note: N 당시 attaches straight to the event noun

examples.en: At that time, I was still a university student.
examples.note: 당시 placed before the clause it frames

extendedVocab.nuance: 당시 is Sino-Korean (當時, 當 'the very / corresponding' + 時 'time', literally 'that very time'), and it always points back to a specific past time already fixed in context, so it lives in forms like 그 당시 and N 당시 (사고 당시, 졸업 당시). The sharp contrast to master is 당시 vs 그때: both mean 'at that time,' but 그때 is the neutral, everyday spoken word, while 당시 is its formal cousin that belongs in narration, news reports and written testimony — say 그때 to a friend, 당시 in an essay. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: first, 당시 is anchored to the past only, so you can never use it for 'now' or the future; second, learners try to use it bare as a free-standing adverb, but it normally rides on 그 or an event noun (그 당시에는, 사고 당시), not floating alone like English 'at the time.'
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
당시 refers only to a past time fixed in context; you cannot use it for 'now' or the future (no 미래 당시).
In casual conversation 그때 sounds far more natural than 당시; 당시 can feel like written news copy among friends.
Don't use 당시 bare to mean 'at the time' out of nowhere; it needs an anchor — 그 당시 or an event noun like 사고 당시.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 동시 means "simultaneity, the same time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "simultaneity, the same time" is 동시 (dongsi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 동시에 ("at the same time, simultaneously"). Watch the particle attached to 동시 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the core adverbial; almost always carries 에
two actions together, or a dual quality
거의 softens to 'nearly at the same instant'
compound noun; 동시 + 통역

examples.ko: 두 사람이 동시에 같은 말을 했어요.
examples.romanization: du sarami dongsie gateun mareul haesseoyo.
examples.en: The two of them said the same thing at the same time.
examples.note: 동시에 = simultaneously

examples.en: He is a singer and at the same time an actor.
examples.note: N인 동시에 = is X and also Y

examples.ko: 문이 닫히는 동시에 비가 쏟아지기 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: muni datineun dongsie biga ssodajigi sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: The instant the door closed, rain started pouring down.
examples.note: -는 동시에 = simultaneously with the action

extendedVocab.nuance: 동시 is Sino-Korean (同時, 同 'same' + 時 'time', literally 'same time') and almost never stands alone — it lives as 동시에 ('simultaneously') or in the patterns -는 동시에 (with a verb: two actions at once) and N인 동시에 (with a noun: 'is X and also Y', two qualities at once, as in 가수인 동시에 배우). The contrast to nail is 동시에 vs 한꺼번에: 동시에 means precisely 'at the same instant' (two events lined up in time), while 한꺼번에 means 'all in one go / in a single batch' (quantity bundled together), so 'I paid it all at once' is 한꺼번에 냈어요, not 동시에 냈어요. The main English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using bare 동시 where you need 동시에 — the 에 is almost obligatory; and (2) reaching for 동시에 when you really mean 'all together in one batch,' which is 한꺼번에.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
동시 is rarely used bare; for 'at the same time' say 동시에 (with 에), not just 동시.
'I bought them all at once' = 한꺼번에 샀어요 (one batch), not 동시에 샀어요 (which means at the same instant); don't swap them.
With a noun you need the copula form: '(is) a singer and also an actor' is 가수인 동시에, not 가수 동시에.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 평생 means "(one's) whole life, a lifetime" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 평생 (pyeongsaeng) = "(one's) whole life, a lifetime". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 평생 ("for one's whole life") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 평생, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: used adverbially with no particle
동안 makes the duration explicit
compound: a workplace one keeps for life

usagePhrases.en: never forget for one's whole life
usagePhrases.note: emphatic 평생 + negative verb

examples.en: Grandmother lived in this village her whole life.
examples.note: 평생 used adverbially = 'all her life'; -셨- honorific

examples.en: I'll never forget this kindness as long as I live.
examples.note: 평생 + negative = 'never in my life'

examples.ko: 평생 한 번 있을까 말까 한 기회예요.
examples.romanization: pyeongsaeng han beon isseulkka malkka han gihoeyeyo.
examples.en: It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.
examples.note: 평생 한 번 stressing rarity across a whole life

extendedVocab.nuance: 평생 is Sino-Korean (平生, 平 'level/ordinary' + 生 'life', literally 'the ordinary course of a life', i.e. one's entire lifespan) and is used mostly as an adverb ('for my whole life') with no particle, or as 평생 동안. It carries real emotional weight, which is why it powers heartfelt promises (평생 사랑할게요) and statements of rarity (평생 한 번). The synonym to contrast is 일생 (一生): 일생 is the bookish, biographical 'a lifetime' you meet in a written life-story, while 평생 is the warm, spoken word that feels personal and felt rather than clinical. The English-speaker pitfall is over-stacking the meaning: 평생 already contains 'whole,' so 평생 전체 is redundant — just say 평생 or 평생 동안. Also note 평생 typically modifies a verb directly (평생 살다, 평생 기억하다), so don't force an extra particle onto it as if it were an object.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
평생 already means 'whole life,' so 평생 전체 is redundant; use plain 평생 or 평생 동안 to stress the span.
평생 is normally adverbial (평생 살았어요); don't add an object particle as in 평생을 살았어요 unless you deliberately want a literary, emphatic tone.
Mind the spelling: it's 평생, not 평셍 or 평성 — the vowel is ㅐ→생 with ㅇ batchim.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 순서 means "order, sequence, turn" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 순서 (sunseo) means "order, sequence, turn". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 순서대로 ("in order, in sequence"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 순서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 순서대로 하다 = do things in the proper order

usagePhrases.en: keep the order, wait one's turn
usagePhrases.note: common at lines and queues
바뀌다 = to be reversed/rearranged
다음 순서는 누구예요? = whose turn is next?

examples.en: You may go in in numerical order.
examples.note: 순서대로 = following the sequence; -면 됩니다 = it's fine to

examples.en: Please line up and wait your turn.
examples.note: 순서를 지키다 = observe the proper order

examples.en: The presentation order suddenly changed.
examples.note: 순서가 바뀌다 collocation

extendedVocab.nuance: 순서 is Sino-Korean (順序, 順 'follow/comply' + 序 'sequence/order', literally 'the sequence one follows'), meaning the order or arrangement in which things are lined up or done, and by extension a person's 'turn.' Two set phrases are essential: 순서대로 ('in order') and 순서를 지키다 ('keep the order / wait your turn'). The synonym to contrast is 차례 (次例/次序): 차례 leans toward an individual's turn in a rotation ('it's my turn now' is most idiomatically 이제 제 차례예요), while 순서 emphasizes the overall sequence or arrangement of the whole set. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'do it in order' is 순서대로 하다, with the special 대로 ('according to'); 순서로 하다 sounds incomplete and learners habitually drop the 대로. Also note 순서 (sequence) is distinct from 차이 (difference) and 차례 (turn) even though all feel related in English.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'In order' is 순서대로 (with 대로 = 'according to'); plain 순서로 sounds incomplete — don't omit the 대로.
For 'it's my turn now,' 이제 제 차례예요 is more idiomatic than 제 순서예요; 차례 highlights the turn, 순서 the whole sequence.
순서 is a noun; 'put them in order' uses a verb like 순서대로 놓다/정리하다, not a non-existent 순서하다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시초 means "the beginning, the start (origin)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "the beginning, the start (origin)" is 시초 (sicho). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like N의 시초 ("the origin/beginning of N"). Watch the particle attached to 시초 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 이 축제의 시초 = the origin of this festival
X이/가 시초가 되다 = X marks the beginning
emphasizes a single originating point
거슬러 올라가다 = go back upstream to the source

examples.ko: 이 작은 가게가 그 회사의 시초였어요.
examples.romanization: i jageun gagega geu hoesaui sichoyeosseoyo.
examples.en: This small shop was the beginning of that company.
examples.note: N의 시초였다 = was the origin of N

examples.ko: 사소한 말다툼이 큰 싸움의 시초가 됐어요.
examples.romanization: sasohan maldatumi keun ssaumui sichoga dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: A trivial argument became the start of a big fight.
examples.note: 시초가 되다 = to mark the beginning of

examples.ko: 그 발견이 현대 의학의 시초라고 해요.
examples.romanization: geu balgyeoni hyeondae uihagui sichorago haeyo.
examples.en: That discovery is said to be the start of modern medicine.
examples.note: 시초 for a historical starting point; -라고 해요 = it's said

extendedVocab.nuance: 시초 is Sino-Korean (始初, both 始 and 初 mean 'beginning' — a doubled 'begin-begin' that stresses the very first origin point), the source from which something all started. It is decidedly formal and 'origin/historical' in flavor, unlike the everyday 처음 ('first time / at first') or 시작 ('the start of an activity'). The contrast to fix: 시작 is the act of starting and is used constantly in speech (수업을 시작하다 = start class), whereas 시초 names the originating point of something larger — a company, a custom, a conflict — and appears as N의 시초 or 시초가 되다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 시초 for casual 'at first / in the beginning' — that is 처음(에), not 시초. And because 시초 is a noun naming an origin, there is no verb 시초하다; to start an action you must use 시작하다.

For casual 'at first / in the beginning' say 처음(에), not 시초; 시초 is the formal originating point of something larger.
There is no verb 시초하다; to 'start' an action use 시작하다 (수업을 시작하다), and reserve 시초 for naming an origin.
Don't confuse 시초 (origin) with 시작 (the start/launch of an activity); you launch a class with 시작, you trace a custom's roots with 시초.

usagePhrases.note: 막바지에 이르다 = to reach the final stage
막바지 + noun for last-stage tasks
접어들다 = to move into a stage/phase

usagePhrases.en: summer is in its final days
usagePhrases.note: N이/가 막바지다 = N is winding down

examples.en: The construction has now entered its final stage.
examples.note: 막바지에 접어들다 = enter the home stretch

examples.en: Exam prep is in its final stretch, so I'm really busy.
examples.note: N이/가 막바지다 = is in its last phase; -라서 = so/because

examples.en: This year too has reached its final days before we knew it.
examples.note: 막바지에 이르다 collocation; 어느덧 = before one realizes

extendedVocab.nuance: 막바지 is native Korean (from 막 'the very last / the end' + 바지, a phase-marking element), meaning the very last stretch of something that has been underway for a while — a season, a project, a year — exactly 'the home stretch' or 'final phase,' usually with a feel of intensity or winding down just before the end. The contrast to master is 막바지 vs 마지막: 마지막 simply means 'the last (one/item)' of a set (마지막 페이지 = the last page), with no sense of process, whereas 막바지 is the final ongoing phase of something that takes time. A close colloquial cousin is 막판 (a more casual 'the last round / final stretch'). The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 막바지 for 'the last one/item' (that is 마지막), and pair it with the right verbs — 막바지에 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 ('reach/enter the home stretch'), not 막바지에 가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't use 막바지 for 'the last item/one' — that's 마지막 (마지막 줄 = the last line); 막바지 is the final ongoing phase of a process.
Pair 막바지 with 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 for 'reach the home stretch,' not 가다 (막바지에 가다 is unnatural).
막바지 implies something has been going on for a while; don't apply it to a brand-new task that just started — there's no 'final phase' yet.

extendedVocab.english: in the meantime, during that time
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그사이 means "in the meantime, during that time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그사이 (geusai) means "in the meantime, during that time". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그사이에 ("in the meantime, meanwhile"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그사이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: often with 에; marks the interval between two points

usagePhrases.en: change a lot in the meantime
usagePhrases.note: highlights change over the interval

usagePhrases.en: did something happen in the meantime?
usagePhrases.note: asking about events during the gap

usagePhrases.en: can't endure even that short interval
usagePhrases.note: 그사이를 못 참고 = unable to wait even that briefly

examples.ko: 잠깐 나갔다 왔는데 그사이에 비가 왔나 봐요.
examples.romanization: jamkkan nagatda wanneunde geusaie biga wanna bwayo.
examples.en: I just stepped out and back, and it seems it rained in the meantime.
examples.note: 그사이에 = during that short interval; -나 봐요 = it seems

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만났는데 그사이 아이가 많이 컸네요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane mannanneunde geusai aiga mani keonneyo.
examples.en: It's been a while since I saw them, and the child has grown so much in the meantime.
examples.note: 그사이 stressing change over the gap

examples.ko: 제가 자리를 비운 그사이에 무슨 일 있었어요?
examples.romanization: jega jarireul biun geusaie museun il isseosseoyo?
examples.en: Did something happen while I was away?
examples.note: 그사이에 = in the gap when one was absent

extendedVocab.nuance: 그사이 (그 'that' + 사이 'gap/interval'; also written spaced as 그 사이) means 'in the meantime / during that interval' — the gap between two moments, typically while someone was away or time quietly slipped past, and it very often appears as 그사이에 alongside a remark about unexpected change. The contrast to lock in is 그사이 vs 그동안: 그동안 covers a longer, continuous stretch ('all this while, over the whole period' — 그동안 잘 지냈어요?), whereas 그사이 zooms in on a shorter in-between gap, often surprisingly eventful for its brevity. The main English-speaker pitfalls: (1) reaching for 그동안 when you mean a brief 'while I was gone' gap (use 그사이) or vice versa; and (2) spelling worry — both 그사이 (one word) and 그 사이 (spaced) are accepted, so just stay consistent within your text rather than agonizing over it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't swap 그사이 (a short in-between gap) for 그동안 (the whole continuous stretch up to now); '그동안 잘 지냈어요?' asks about the long period, not a brief gap.
그사이 marks an interval between two points, so it needs that two-point framing; using it for an open-ended 'these days' (요즘) is wrong.
Both 그사이 and 그 사이 are accepted spellings; pick one and stay consistent rather than mixing them in the same piece of writing.

extendedVocab.english: (the old) days, one's time/era of life
extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시절 means "(the old) days, one's time/era of life" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "(the old) days, one's time/era of life" is 시절 (sijeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 학창 시절 ("one's school days"). Watch the particle attached to 시절 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the most common collocation, full of nostalgia
어린 시절의 추억 = childhood memories
refers fondly to a remembered period
pairs with 좋은/힘든 to color the remembered period

examples.en: I sometimes miss my school days so much.
examples.note: 학창 시절 = one's school years; 그립다 = to miss/long for

examples.en: In my childhood, I grew up in the countryside.
examples.note: 어린 시절에(는) = during one's young days

examples.en: In those days everyone was poor but happy.
examples.note: 그 시절 evoking a nostalgic era; -지만 = but

extendedVocab.nuance: 시절 is Sino-Korean (時節, 時 'time' + 節 'season/segment', literally a 'season of time'), and it names a remembered stage of one's life almost always tinged with nostalgia — 학창 시절 (school days), 어린 시절 (childhood), 그 시절 (those days). The contrast to feel is 시절 vs 시기 and 때: 시기 is a neutral, analytical phase (성장 시기 = the growth period) and 때 is a plain 'time when…,' whereas 시절 is warm, personal and backward-looking, glowing with fondness. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 시절 looks back — you cannot use it for a future or coolly neutral period, so 'a difficult time ahead' is not 어려운 시절 in the future sense; and (2) 시절 almost always rides on a descriptor (학창/어린/그/좋은), so using it bare to mean just 'time' sounds unfinished — you need that modifier to evoke the remembered stage.

Don't confuse 시절 (a remembered life-stage) with 계절 (季節, the four seasons); they share 節 but 계절 means spring/summer/autumn/winter.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사실 means "fact, truth" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사실 (sasil) = "fact, truth". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사실은 제가 한국 사람이 아니에요. ("Actually, I am not Korean.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사실, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 사실은 at the very front softens an honest reveal, like English 'actually'
사실 + 이에요 asserts something is objectively true
사실대로 = 'as it really is'; the suffix -대로 means 'in accordance with'

usagePhrases.en: I want to know the truth.
usagePhrases.note: 사실 as the object of a verb takes 을

examples.ko: 사실 저는 매운 음식을 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: sasil jeoneun maeun eumsigeul mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: Actually, I cannot eat spicy food.
examples.note: Bare 사실 (no 은) at sentence start = a casual 'to be honest' before a confession

examples.en: This story is not true.
examples.note: 사실이 아니다 is the set phrase for 'is not true / is false'

examples.ko: 사실은 오늘 그 얘기를 하려고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: sasireun oneul geu yaegireul haryeogo wasseoyo.
examples.en: The truth is, I came today to talk about that.
examples.note: 사실은 + a -려고 왔어요 clause reveals a hidden real reason behind an action

extendedVocab.nuance: 사실 (事實, 事 'matter' + 實 'real/true') literally means 'the real state of a matter', so it covers both the noun 'fact' and the adverb 'actually/in fact'. Compare it with 진실: 사실 is a neutral, verifiable fact ('it rained yesterday'), while 진실 is the deeper moral 'truth' you uncover behind lies, so a courtroom seeks 진실, but a weather report states a 사실. Also distinguish 진짜, which is the casual spoken 'really/for real' and an intensifier ('진짜 맛있어!'), whereas 사실 introduces information. The phrase 사실은 / 사실 at the head of a sentence is enormously common in conversation as a gentle 'to tell the truth' before a correction or confession. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 사실 to mean 'really' as an intensity word — '진짜 추워요' (it's really cold) is natural, but '사실 추워요' shifts the meaning to 'actually, it's cold (contrary to what you thought)'. Keep 사실 for facts and reveals, not for emphasis.

Using 사실 as an intensifier like English 'really' (e.g. saying 사실 맛있어요 hoping for 'it's really tasty'). That actually means 'in fact it's tasty (surprisingly)'. For pure emphasis use 진짜 or 정말: 정말 맛있어요.
Saying 사실 아니에요 to mean 'that's not true'. The natural set phrase needs the subject particle: 사실이 아니에요. Dropping 이 sounds broken.
Confusing 사실 with 진실 and using 사실 for a profound, hidden truth. A detective uncovers the 진실; a footnote states a 사실.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 비밀 means "secret" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 비밀 (bimil) means "secret". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이것은 비밀이에요. ("This is a secret."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 비밀 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 비밀 + 이에요 labels information as private
비밀을 지키다 = 'protect/guard a secret', the standard collocation
비밀이 없다 with the subject particle states you hide nothing
비밀로 하다 = 'treat it as secret'; -로 marks the resulting state

examples.en: I told my friend a secret.
examples.note: 한테 marks the human recipient you told it to

examples.en: That is a secret just between us.
examples.note: 우리만의 = 'ours only'; -만의 stacks 'only' + possessive

examples.en: This is a secret only you and I know.
examples.note: Casual 반말 register with friends; 너랑 나만 = 'only you and me'

extendedVocab.nuance: 비밀 (祕密, 祕 'hidden/mysterious' + 密 'dense/close') paints a secret as something kept tightly closed in. The verb it lives with is 지키다 ('to guard/keep'), giving 비밀을 지키다 — note that English 'keep a secret' tempts learners to reach for 가지다 ('to have/hold'), but 비밀을 가지다 sounds wrong; you 지키다 (guard) a secret, or 비밀로 하다 (make it secret). Contrast 비밀 with 비결: both share 비(祕), but 비결 (祕訣) is a 'secret know-how / the trick to success' (성공의 비결 = the secret to success), not confidential information. So a chef's 비결 is their technique, while their 비밀 might be that they hate cooking. The word is register-neutral and used freely from children's games to government affairs. Pitfall to avoid: 비밀 is a noun only — there is no verb 비밀하다. To say 'keep something secret' you must add a verb: 비밀로 하다 or 비밀을 지키다.
