Treating 비밀 as a verb: 비밀해요 does not exist. Use 비밀로 해요 (make it secret) or 비밀을 지켜요 (keep the secret).
Saying 비밀을 가지다 by translating 'have/keep a secret' literally. Korean guards a secret: 비밀을 지키다. To say you simply possess secrets, use 비밀이 있다 / 없다.
Mixing up 비밀 (confidential info) and 비결 (the secret trick/know-how). 'The secret to long life' is 장수의 비결, not 장수의 비밀.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 규칙 means "rule" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "rule" is 규칙 (gyuchik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 규칙은 아주 중요해요. ("Rules are very important."). Watch the particle attached to 규칙 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 규칙은 sets 'rules' as the topic being discussed
규칙을 지키다 = 'observe/abide by rules', the core collocation
규칙이 많다 describes a place full of rules
규칙을 만들다 = 'create a rule'

examples.en: I follow the school rules well.
examples.note: 규칙 takes a noun modifier directly: 학교 규칙 = school rules

examples.en: Each company has different rules.
examples.note: -마다 = 'each/every'; pairs naturally with 다르다

examples.en: If you break the rule, you have to pay a fine.
examples.note: 규칙을 어기다 = 'break a rule', the antonym of 지키다

extendedVocab.nuance: 규칙 (規則, 規 'compass/standard' + 則 'rule') evokes a measured standard you align to, and its life-partner verbs are 지키다 ('keep/observe') and its opposite 어기다 ('break/violate'). The sharp contrast learners need is 규칙 vs 법: 규칙 is a rule set by a group, school, or game (게임 규칙, 교통 규칙), enforceable socially, while 법 (法) is the law of the land, enforced by the state with courts and penalties. Breaking a 규칙 gets you scolded; breaking a 법 gets you arrested. Also distinguish 규칙 from 규정 (規定), which are formal written 'regulations/provisions' in an official document — a workplace handbook lists 규정, but a casual house rule is a 규칙. Collocations: 규칙을 정하다 (set rules), 규칙대로 하다 (do it by the rules). Pitfall: English 'follow the rules' often becomes 규칙을 따라가다 by literal translation, but the idiomatic verb is 지키다 — 규칙을 지키다. Save 따르다/따라가다 for following a person or path.

Using 규칙을 따라가다 for 'follow the rules' by direct translation. The natural verb is 지키다: 규칙을 지키다. 따라가다 means physically following someone.
Confusing 규칙 (a group/game rule) with 법 (state law). Traffic etiquette taught at school is 교통 규칙; the criminal code is 법.
Saying 규칙을 부수다 ('smash a rule') for 'break a rule'. To violate a rule, use 어기다: 규칙을 어기다. 부수다 is for breaking physical objects.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 습관 means "habit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 습관 (seupgwan) = "habit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이것은 좋은 습관이에요. ("This is a good habit.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 습관, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 좋은/나쁜 + 습관 describes the quality of a habit

usagePhrases.en: I want to fix a bad habit.
usagePhrases.note: 습관을 고치다 = 'correct/break a habit'; 고치다 = repair
습관이 되다 = 'turn into a habit', now automatic

usagePhrases.en: I have a habit of going to bed early.
usagePhrases.note: verb + -는 + 습관이 있다 = 'have the habit of ~ing'

examples.en: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
examples.note: -는 습관이 있다 is the frame for stating any routine

examples.en: I changed my coffee-drinking habit.
examples.note: 습관을 바꾸다 = 'change a habit' (swap it), milder than 고치다

examples.en: I can't break my nail-biting habit.
examples.note: Here a small bad tic is a 버릇, not 습관 — note the register difference

extendedVocab.nuance: 습관 (習慣, 習 'to practice/learn' + 慣 'to grow accustomed') frames a habit as something drilled in until it feels natural, and it leans slightly formal and neutral. The key contrast is 습관 vs 버릇: 습관 is a broad, often deliberate routine (early rising, daily exercise, good study habits), while 버릇 is colloquial and usually a quirky or annoying unconscious tic — nail-biting, leg-shaking, a child's bad manners. Crucially, scolding a child you say 버릇없다 ('has no manners / is rude'), never 습관없다. Both pair with 고치다 ('fix') for breaking them and 들이다/생기다 for forming them (습관을 들이다 = cultivate a habit; 습관이 생기다 = a habit forms). To say you have one, use 습관이 있다. extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 성격 means "personality" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 성격 (seonggyeok) means "personality". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제 성격은 조용해요. ("My personality is quiet."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 성격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 성격은 + adjective describes a fixed trait
성격이 좋다 = 'is good-natured/easygoing', a common compliment
성격이 비슷하다 compares two people's natures
밝다 ('bright') applied to 성격 = cheerful and warm

examples.en: My friend has a very lively personality.
examples.note: 활발하다 ('active, lively') is a stock 성격 adjective

examples.en: Because our personalities differ, we sometimes argue.
examples.note: -아서/어서 links the trait to its consequence

examples.en: I'm impatient by nature.
examples.note: 성격이 급하다 = a fixed temperament; contrast with the mood word 기분

extendedVocab.nuance: 성격 (性格, 性 'nature/disposition' + 格 'character/frame') is a person's enduring inborn character — the stable temperament you are born with and keep for life. Contrast it carefully with 기분, which is a passing mood that changes hourly: '오늘 기분이 좋아요' = I'm in a good mood today (temporary), whereas '성격이 좋아요' = he's a good-natured person (permanent). Mixing these is the single most common error: never use 성격 for how you feel right now. The phrase 성격이 좋다 is a warm social compliment meaning kind, tolerant, easy to get along with — broader than English 'good personality'. Note also 성격이 급하다 ('impatient/hot-tempered nature') is an idiomatic fixed expression. Common partner adjectives: 밝다 (cheerful), 활발하다 (lively), 조용하다 (quiet), 까다롭다 (fussy/picky), 무뚝뚝하다 (blunt). Pitfall beyond the 기분 trap: 'I have a ~ personality' is most naturally 성격이 + adjective (성격이 밝아요), not the heavier 저는 ~한 성격을 가지고 있어요 calque, though 급한 성격이에요 is fine.

Confusing 성격 with 성질. 성질 also means temperament but skews negative/temper-flare ('성질을 내다' = lose one's temper). To neutrally describe character, use 성격.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 능력 means "ability" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "ability" is 능력 (neungnyeok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그분은 능력이 있어요. ("That person is capable."). Watch the particle attached to 능력 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 능력이 있다 = 'has ability', i.e. is competent

usagePhrases.en: I want to build up my ability.
usagePhrases.note: 능력을 키우다 = 'grow/develop ability' over time
능력이 부족하다 = a humble admission of falling short
noun + 능력 names a specific competence: 언어 능력 = language ability

examples.en: That person's work ability is outstanding.
examples.note: -는 능력 = 'the ability to ~'; 뛰어나다 = excel

examples.en: I'm building up my Korean ability.
examples.note: Ongoing -고 있다 with the develop verb 키우다

examples.en: Effort matters more than ability.
examples.note: 능력보다 = 'compared to ability'; -보다 marks the standard

extendedVocab.nuance: 능력 (能力, 能 'can/be able' + 力 'power/force') is literally 'the power to be able' — innate or acquired capability to actually get things done, broader and more practical than book knowledge. Its verbs are 있다/없다 (have/lack), 키우다 ('raise/develop'), and 기르다 (cultivate). Contrast 능력 with 실력: 실력 is demonstrated skill/proficiency in a specific domain that you trained for (그 선수는 실력이 좋다 = that player is genuinely skilled), while 능력 is overall capacity, including raw potential and the power to handle responsibility. A new hire may have 능력 (capability/potential) but not yet 실력 (proven skill). Also distinguish 가능성 ('possibility'), which is the abstract noun 가능 + 성 — a chance that something happens, not a person's power. Pitfall: English 'I'm able to ~ / I can ~' should not be forced through 능력. To say 'I can swim', use the verb pattern 수영할 수 있어요, not 수영 능력이 있어요 (which sounds like a formal assessment). Reserve 능력 for describing overall competence, not everyday 'can do'.

Using 능력 to express everyday 'I can ~'. '저는 능력이 운전해요' is wrong. Use -ㄹ 수 있다: 운전할 수 있어요. 능력 describes capacity, not a single action.
Confusing 능력 with 가능 / 가능성. 'There's a possibility of rain' is 비가 올 가능성이 있어요, never 능력. 능력 belongs to people's competence.
Mixing 능력 and 실력. To praise proven, trained skill say 실력이 좋다; 능력이 좋다 emphasizes overall capability and potential.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 실수 means "mistake" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 실수 (silsu) = "mistake". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 실수했어요. ("I made a mistake.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 실수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 실수하다 = 'to slip up'; the noun + 하다 acts as one verb
실수 + 예요 to own up to an error

usagePhrases.en: I make a lot of mistakes.
usagePhrases.note: 실수가 많다 describes a tendency, not one event
실수를 하다 split out, with the negative command -지 마세요

examples.en: I made a mistake at work today.
examples.note: Everyday accidental slip; 실수를 하다 with location 에서

examples.en: It's a small mistake, so it's fine.
examples.note: -니까 gives the reason for reassurance

examples.ko: 깜빡하고 이름을 잘못 썼어요. 제 실수예요.
examples.romanization: kkamppakago ireumeul jalmot sseosseoyo. je silsuyeyo.
examples.en: I spaced out and wrote the name wrong. My mistake.
examples.note: Real apology context — 실수 fits an honest, blameless slip

extendedVocab.nuance: 실수 (失手, 失 'to lose' + 手 'hand') literally means 'to lose control of one's hand' — a slip, a careless unintended error, with no moral blame attached. This is the crucial contrast with 잘못 (잘 'well' + 못 'cannot'), which means a 'wrong/fault' that carries responsibility or wrongdoing: 실수 is 'oops, I tripped on the word', while 잘못 implies 'I did something wrong and it's my fault'. When you bump someone you say 실수예요 ('sorry, my slip'); when you genuinely wronged them you admit 제 잘못이에요. Also distinguish 실패 ('failure'), which is not achieving a goal, versus 실수, a momentary error along the way — you can make a 실수 and still succeed. The verb is 하다 (실수하다), and a frequent collocation is 실수로 ('by accident/mistake': 실수로 전화했어요 = I called by mistake). Pitfall: English speakers say 실수를 만들다 ('make a mistake') by translating 'make' literally — Korean does not 만들다 (build) a mistake, it 하다 (does) one: 실수를 하다 / 실수하다.

Saying 실수를 만들다 for 'make a mistake', copying English 'make'. The verb is 하다: 실수했어요 or 실수를 했어요.
Using 실수 when you mean genuine fault or wrongdoing. A blameless slip is 실수; an actual wrong you're responsible for is 잘못 — 제 잘못이에요 for a real apology.
Confusing 실수 with 실패. Forgetting one line is a 실수 (a slip); not passing the whole exam is 실패 (a failure). They are not interchangeable.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 성공 means "success" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 성공 (seonggong) means "success". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성공했어요. ("I succeeded."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 성공 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 성공하다 = 'to succeed'; noun + 하다 forms the verb
성공이 + adjective treats success as the topic
성공하다 + -고 싶다 to state an aspiration
성공하다 takes 에 for the field you succeed IN, not 을

examples.en: After long effort, I finally succeeded.
examples.note: -끝에 = 'at the end of ~'; pairs with effort then success

examples.en: To succeed, you must keep trying.
examples.note: -려면 = 'if you want to ~'; sets up advice

examples.en: I'm so happy I passed the exam.
examples.note: For passing a test Koreans say 합격, not 성공 — note the boundary

extendedVocab.nuance: 성공 (成功, 成 'to accomplish' + 功 'achievement/merit') means achieving a goal or making it big in life, and its verb is 하다 (성공하다), the natural antonym of 실패하다 ('to fail'). A grammar point English speakers stumble on: 성공하다 governs the particle 에 (or 에서) for the domain — 사업에 성공하다 ('succeed in business'), 시험에 성공하다 is odd; you say 시험에 합격하다 instead. This is the sharp contrast: 합격 (合格) is specifically 'passing' an exam, audition, or qualification screening, while 성공 is broad life or project success. Passing the bar exam is 합격; building a thriving company is 성공. Both differ from 성취 (成就), the more literary 'accomplishment/attainment' of a personal achievement. Common collocations: 크게 성공하다 (make it big), 성공을 거두다 (achieve success, formal/written). Pitfall: do not pair 성공하다 with the object particle 을/를 for the thing you succeed at — it's 에 (시험에 합격, 사업에 성공). And use 합격, not 성공, the moment you mean passing a test.

Saying 시험을 성공했어요 for 'I passed the exam'. Use 합격: 시험에 합격했어요. 성공 is for broad goals/business, not test results.
Marking the domain with 을/를: 사업을 성공했어요 is wrong. 성공하다 takes 에: 사업에 성공했어요.
Treating 성공 as the opposite of 실수. Its true antonym is 실패 (failure). A 실수 is a small slip, not the opposite of success.

extendedVocab.explanation: "failure" is 실패 (silpae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 실패했어요. ("I failed."). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 실패하다 = 'to fail (at a goal)'; noun + 하다
실패는 as topic, softening the concept
실패를 두려워하다 = 'fear failure'; 두려워하다 takes 를
실패하다 takes 에 for the area you failed in

examples.en: At first I failed, but I challenged it again.
examples.note: -지만 = 'but'; 도전하다 (take on) fits the resilience tone

examples.en: I learned a lot from failure.
examples.note: 실패에서 = 'from failure'; 에서 marks the source

examples.en: It's okay to fail, so give it a try.
examples.note: -아도 괜찮다 ('even if ~, it's fine') is gentle encouragement

extendedVocab.nuance: 실패 (失敗, 失 'to lose' + 敗 'defeat') literally 'to lose and be defeated' — the failure to reach a goal, the clean antonym of 성공 (성공 ↔ 실패). Like 성공하다, the verb 실패하다 governs the particle 에 for the domain: 사업에 실패하다 ('fail in business'), 시험에 실패했어요 is possible but Koreans far more often say 시험에 떨어졌어요 ('I fell off the exam' = flunked) for not passing. That is the contrast to master: 실패 is broad, often big-picture failure, while 떨어지다 is the everyday idiom for failing a test or audition (the opposite of 합격). The big distinction for learners is 실패 vs 실수: 실수 (失手) is a small careless slip you make in passing, whereas 실패 is the larger non-achievement of an outcome — you can commit many 실수 and still avoid 실패. And for flunking a test, prefer 떨어지다 over 실패.

usagePhrases.note: 노력이 + adjective frames effort as the topic

usagePhrases.en: I make an effort every day.
usagePhrases.note: 노력하다 = 'to make an effort/try hard'; noun + 하다

usagePhrases.en: I put in a lot of effort.
usagePhrases.note: 노력을 하다 split out, with 많이 = 'a lot'

usagePhrases.en: If you try hard, you can do well.
usagePhrases.note: 노력하다 + -면 conditional offering encouragement

examples.en: I'm making an effort to learn Korean.
examples.note: -려고 = 'in order to'; the goal you exert effort toward

examples.en: Without effort, there is no success either.
examples.note: 없이는 = 'without ~ (emphatic)'; a common motivational pairing

examples.en: Let's try a little harder.
examples.note: 반말 자기 격려 / friends; 노력해 보다 = 'try making an effort'

extendedVocab.nuance: 노력 (努力, 努 'to strive/exert' + 力 'power/strength') is literally 'to put forth strength' — sustained, earnest effort toward a goal, a warm and admired virtue in Korean culture where 노력하는 사람 ('a person who tries hard') is high praise. Its verb is 하다 (노력하다), and the most natural way to say 'try to do X' is verb-려고 노력하다 (배우려고 노력하다 = make an effort to learn). Contrast 노력 with 애 (애쓰다 = 'to take pains/struggle to do something'): 애쓰다 highlights the toil and is used to thank someone — 애쓰셨어요 ('you worked hard / thanks for your trouble') — while 노력 is the neutral noun for effort itself. Do not confuse 노력 with 노동 (勞動), which is physical 'labor/work' as in a job or workforce. Also distinguish 수고 (受苦), the 'trouble/hard work' you acknowledge in others: 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work'). Pitfall: 노력하다 is intransitive toward a goal — to say 'try TO do something' use the -려고 노력하다 frame, not a direct object; '한국어를 노력해요' is incomplete — say 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요 or 한국어 공부를 열심히 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 노력 (effort/striving) with 노동 (manual labor). 'Hard work pays off' is 노력은 배신하지 않아요; a labor union is 노동조합 — never swap them.
Saying 한국어를 노력해요 to mean 'I try at Korean'. 노력하다 needs a goal clause: 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요.
Using 노력하세요 to thank someone for their hard work. To acknowledge effort, say 수고하셨어요 or 애쓰셨어요; 노력하세요 means 'go try hard (a command)'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 차이 means "difference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 차이 (chai) means "difference". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 차이가 커요. ("The difference is big."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 차이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 차이가 크다 = 'the gap is large'; 차이 pairs with size adjectives
차이가 있다 = 'there is a difference (between)'

usagePhrases.en: I can't really tell the difference.
usagePhrases.note: 차이를 모르다 with -겠- softening to 'I'm not sure'
noun + 차이: 나이 차이 = age difference/gap

examples.en: Korean and Japanese have differences.
examples.note: A와 B는 차이가 있다 is the frame for comparing two things

examples.en: The price difference is too big.
examples.note: 가격 차이 (price gap); 크다 expresses the magnitude

examples.en: The two look similar, but they do differ.
examples.note: 차이가 나다 = 'a difference arises/shows'; 나다 = to occur

extendedVocab.nuance: 차이 (差異, 差 'to differ' + 異 'different/unlike') is the noun 'difference/gap' between two or more things, and it lives with two verbs: 있다 ('there is a difference') and 나다 ('a difference arises/shows') — 차이가 있다 and 차이가 나다 are both natural, the latter stressing that a gap becomes apparent. It also pairs with size adjectives: 차이가 크다/적다 (big/small difference). The contrast to learn is the noun 차이 vs the verb 다르다 ('to be different'): 차이 names the gap as a thing ('there is a difference'), while 다르다 is how you actually say two things 'are different' — '한국어는 일본어와 달라요' (Korean is different from Japanese). English speakers often try to turn 차이 into the predicate ('they are difference'), but you need either 차이가 있다 (noun) or 다르다 (adjective-verb). Also distinguish 차이 (the gap itself) from 차이점 (the specific point/respect in which they differ): 두 제품의 차이점을 알려 주세요 = tell me the specific differences. Pitfall: do not say 차이해요 — 차이 has no verb form; use 차이가 나다/있다 or switch to 다르다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Trying to use 차이 as a verb/predicate: 두 개가 차이해요 is wrong. Say 차이가 있어요 / 차이가 나요, or use the adjective 달라요.
Marking what differs FROM with the wrong particle when using 다르다. 'A is different from B' uses 와/과: A는 B와 달라요, not B를 달라요.
Confusing 차이 (the gap) with 차이점 (the specific differing points). 'List the differences' = 차이점을 알려 주세요; '차이가 크다' is about overall magnitude.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 전부 means "all, everything" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "all, everything" is 전부 (jeonbu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이게 전부예요? ("Is this everything?"). Watch the particle attached to 전부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Asking if nothing remains
전부 paired with 다 doubles the emphasis
전부 here works as an adverb 'completely'
전부 = 'entirely', taking the whole blame

examples.en: I'll give you all the snacks.
examples.note: Casual 반말; 전부 as the object 'the whole lot'

examples.en: All the guests left.
examples.note: 전부 covers every single person in the group

examples.en: I'll double-check whether all the documents have been reviewed.
examples.note: Formal workplace register; 전부 = the entire set, nothing skipped

extendedVocab.nuance: 전부 is the Sino-Korean noun 全部 ('whole' 全 + 'part' 部, literally 'the whole of every part'), meaning the complete quantity with absolutely nothing left out. The nearest rival is the native word 다: 다 is a pure adverb ('all' / 'completely') and never takes a particle, while 전부 is a noun that can be a subject (전부가), an object (전부를), or stand adverbially — and the two are so close that Koreans habitually stack them as 전부 다 for extra force. Watch the dividing line with 모두: 모두 leans toward 'everyone, every person' and is a touch more formal, whereas 전부 leans toward 'the whole amount/thing'. 전부 is neutral and works in both casual speech and formal writing. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the English 'all the' that glues onto a noun: you don't say 전부 책 — you say 책 전부 or 모든 책, because 전부 follows the noun (or stands alone) rather than premodifying it like 모든.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 전부 책 ('all books') by copying English 'all the books': 전부 cannot premodify like English 'all'. Use 책 전부 ('the books, all of them') or 모든 책.
Using 전부 when you mean 대부분 ('most'). 전부 leaves out nothing; if a few are excluded, you must say 대부분.
Forcing a particle where 전부 is acting as an adverb, e.g. 전부를 먹었어요 when you just mean 'I ate it all' — 전부 다 먹었어요 is the natural choice.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 절반 means "half" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 절반 (jeolban) = "half". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사과를 절반 먹었어요. ("I ate half the apple.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 절반, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 절반 = exactly one of two equal parts
절반 attached to a whole via possessive 의
절반 as a topic-marked subject
절반으로 = 'into halves', the division endpoint

examples.en: I'll split the candy in half for you.
examples.note: Casual; 절반 as the shared portion

examples.en: Half of the students passed the exam.
examples.note: 절반이 = half of a group as subject

examples.en: More than half of the budget goes to labor costs.
examples.note: Formal; 절반 이상 = 'more than half'

extendedVocab.nuance: 절반 is Sino-Korean 折半 ('break/fold' 折 + 'half' 半 = literally 'fold something in two'), so it carries the feel of cleanly dividing a whole into two equal portions. Its everyday twin is the one-syllable 반, which is the plain Sino-Korean reading of that same 半: 반 is shorter, more casual, and used constantly (반만 주세요, 반반), whereas the two-character 절반 sounds more deliberate and precise, favored when you're stressing the exactness of the split or writing a report. Note 반 also forms set time expressions (한 시 반 'half past one') and compound words (반값 'half price') where 절반 cannot substitute. Register is neutral; both are fine in polite speech. The English-speaker pitfall is the 'into halves' construction: to say 'cut it in half' you need the goal particle 으로 — 절반으로 자르다 — not a bare noun; learners often drop 으로 and produce the incomplete 절반 잘라요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 절반 잘랐어요 for 'I cut it in half' without the goal particle. Use 절반으로 잘랐어요 — 으로 marks the resulting state.
Using 절반 for a vague 'about half / roughly half'. 절반 is exactly one half; for a rough amount say 반쯤 or 절반쯤.
Swapping 절반 into fixed 반 expressions, e.g. 한 시 절반 for 'half past one'. The set form is 한 시 반.

structuredNuance.t: 절반 carries the feel of cleanly dividing a whole into two equal portions. Register is neutral; it is fine in polite speech, and the two-character form sounds deliberate and precise, favored when stressing the exactness of the split or writing a report.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 일부 means "part, a portion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 일부 (ilbu) means "part, a portion". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일부 사람만 왔어요. ("Only some people came."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 일부 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 일부 directly premodifying a noun, unlike 전부

usagePhrases.en: I paid part of the money.
usagePhrases.note: 일부 linked to the whole by 의
일부 + 뿐 = 'merely a portion'
일부 as a topic-marked subject

examples.en: Just take some of this.
examples.note: Casual; 일부만 = 'only a portion'

examples.en: Some of the members opposed the meeting.
examples.note: 일부가 = a subset acting as subject

examples.en: What was reported is only a fraction of the facts.
examples.note: Formal; 일부에 불과하다 = 'is nothing but a part'

extendedVocab.nuance: 일부 is Sino-Korean 一部 ('one' 一 + 'part' 部 = 'one portion'), naming a limited slice of a larger whole. It sits on a spectrum: 일부 (a part) < 절반 (half) < 대부분 (most) < 전부 (all), and its sharpest contrast is with 전부 — 일부 deliberately implies the rest is excluded. Unlike 전부, 일부 CAN stand right before a noun (일부 사람 'some people'), which makes it behave a bit like English 'some'. Distinguish it from 약간: 약간 is about a small degree/amount of something (a little salt), while 일부 is a countable sub-section of a defined whole (some of the members). Register is neutral and slightly bookish; it's everywhere in news and reports. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 일부 to translate 'a few' when you really mean a small number of discrete things — for 'a few people' Koreans more often say 몇몇 사람 or 몇 명; 일부 frames them as 'a faction/portion of the whole' rather than just 'a small number'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 일부 when you mean 전부 ('the whole thing'). 일부 always signals a remainder is left out.
Translating 'a few friends' as 일부 친구 in casual talk. More natural is 몇몇 친구 or 친구 몇 명; 일부 sounds like 'a faction of (a known group of) friends'.
Dropping the 의 that links 일부 to its whole, e.g. 돈 일부를 for 'part of the money' — say 돈의 일부를.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 대부분 means "most, the majority" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "most, the majority" is 대부분 (daebubun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 대부분 집에 있어요. ("Most people are at home."). Watch the particle attached to 대부분 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 대부분 used adverbially = 'mostly'

usagePhrases.en: Most of the students are Korean.
usagePhrases.note: 대부분이 = subject 'the majority'

usagePhrases.en: Most of the shops are closed.
usagePhrases.note: 대부분의 + noun = 'most (of the)'

usagePhrases.en: I use most of my time studying.
usagePhrases.note: 대부분을 = object 'the greater part'

examples.en: On weekends I mostly rest at home.
examples.note: Casual; 대부분 as adverb 'usually/mostly'

examples.en: Most of the attendees were in favor.
examples.note: 대부분이 marking the majority as subject

examples.ko: 설문에 응답한 사람의 대부분이 긍정적으로 평가했습니다.
examples.romanization: seolmune eungdapan saramui daebubuni geungjeongjeogeuro pyeonggahaetseumnida.
examples.en: Most of the survey respondents rated it positively.
examples.note: Formal report register; 대부분이 with a quantified group

extendedVocab.nuance: 대부분 is Sino-Korean 大部分 ('big' 大 + 'part' 部 + 'portion' 分 = 'the large part'), meaning almost all but stopping just short of everything — a small remainder is always implied. On the quantity ladder it sits between 일부 (a portion) and 전부 (the whole), and its key contrast is exactly with 전부: claim 대부분 and you leave a little room, claim 전부 and you leave none. It doubles as an adverb meaning 'mostly/usually' (주말엔 대부분 쉬어요), which 전부 cannot do. Compare 거의 다 ('almost all'), which is a near-synonym but feels more spoken and approximate, while 대부분 is comfortable in both speech and formal writing. As a noun it links to its whole with 의 (학생의 대부분) or premodifies with 대부분의 (대부분의 학생). The English-speaker pitfall is omitting 의 and writing 대부분 학생 by analogy with 'most students' — the natural patterns are 대부분의 학생 or 학생의 대부분.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 대부분 as 전부. A small part is still excluded, so don't use it for a true 100%.
Saying 대부분 학생 for 'most students' without 의. Use 대부분의 학생 (premodifier) or 학생의 대부분 (noun + of).
Forgetting that adverbial 대부분 means 'usually/mostly', and overusing it for countable nouns where 대부분의 + noun reads better.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 약간 means "a little, a bit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 약간 (yakgan) = "a little, a bit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 약간 매워요. ("It is a little spicy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 약간, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 약간 as a degree adverb before an adjective
약간 = a small amount of an uncountable thing
약간의 + noun, the bookish noun use
약간 softening the strength of the state

examples.en: The soup is a bit salty.
examples.note: Casual; 약간 dialing a quality down a notch

examples.en: Please add just a little sugar to my coffee.
examples.note: 약간만 = 'only a little', polite request

examples.en: Sales rose slightly this quarter.
examples.note: Formal; 약간 = 'slightly' with a change verb

extendedVocab.nuance: 약간 is Sino-Korean 若干 (here meaning 'some small amount / a few'), used both as a degree adverb ('a little, slightly') and, with 의, as a noun ('a small quantity of'). Its closest rivals are 조금 and 좀: 조금 is the everyday native word for 'a little' and is interchangeable in many spots, while 좀 is the contracted, very colloquial form that also functions as a softener in requests (좀 도와주세요). 약간 sounds a shade more measured and is the default when describing a slight degree of a quality (약간 맵다, 약간 다르다) or a small change in formal/written contexts (약간 증가하다). Note it covers small DEGREE and small AMOUNT, unlike 일부, which is a sub-portion of a countable whole. The English-speaker pitfall is putting 약간 after the verb or treating it like a quantity noun on its own: it normally comes right before the adjective/verb it scales (약간 추워요), and when it modifies a noun you need 약간의 (약간의 돈), not a bare 약간 돈.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 약간 for a large quantity. It always means 'a little/slightly'; for a big amount use 많이 or 상당히.
Writing 약간 돈 for 'a little money'. To modify a noun use 약간의 돈, or rephrase as 돈을 약간 (with a verb).

In Korean the particle or ending next to 여러 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 여러 must sit directly before the noun
여러 + counter 번 = 'several times'
여러 가지 = 'various kinds of'
여러 stressing variety, not just number

examples.en: Several friends came over.
examples.note: Casual; 여러 명 = 'several people' with a counter

examples.note: 여러 + plural noun as subject

examples.note: Formal; 여러 emphasizing multiple distinct parties

extendedVocab.nuance: 여러 is a native determiner (관형사) meaning 'several / various / a number of', and its defining trait is that it ONLY ever stands in front of a noun — it can never be a subject, object, or stand alone, and it never takes a particle (no 여러가, no 여러를). Its nearest neighbors are 몇 and 여러 가지: 몇 means 'a few / how many' and asks or implies a small uncertain count (몇 명?), while 여러 asserts 'quite a few, more than two or three' and often adds a flavor of 'various, of different sorts'. For countable people/things you pair it with a counter (여러 명, 여러 번, 여러 개); for 'various kinds' you say 여러 가지. Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall is trying to use 여러 the way you'd use the noun 'several' in 'several came' — Korean cannot say 여러가 왔어요; you must supply a noun, e.g. 여러 사람이 왔어요 or 여러 명이 왔어요.

Using 여러 alone as a subject/object, e.g. 여러가 왔어요. 여러 must modify a noun: 여러 사람이 왔어요.
Attaching a particle to 여러 (여러를, 여러가). It's a determiner and takes none; particles go on the noun after it.
Confusing 여러 with 몇: 여러 번 = 'several (many) times' asserts a fair number, while 몇 번 = 'a few / how many times' is small or questioning.

수량 = the counted number of items
수량 stated with a number + counter

examples.note: Casual; 수량 = how many pieces

extendedVocab.nuance: 수량 is Sino-Korean 數量 ('number' 數 + 'amount' 量 = 'numbered amount'), and it specifically means a COUNTABLE number of discrete items — it lives in shopping, ordering, inventory, and shipping contexts. Compare 양 (量) alone, which means 'amount' in a broader, often uncountable sense (물의 양 'the amount of water', 일의 양 'the amount of work'); you would not say 물의 수량. Compare also 개수 (個數), which narrowly means 'the number of pieces' and is even more strictly about a count, while 수량 can feel a touch more formal/commercial. Because 수량 is about number, it pairs with 많다/적다 ('many/few'), not 크다/작다 ('big/small'). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping the English 'amount' (which English uses for both countable and uncountable) onto 수량 across the board — for liquids, time, work, or emotion you need 양, and for water specifically 물의 수량 sounds wrong; say 물의 양.

Using 수량 for uncountable things (water, time, work, feelings). Those take 양: 물의 양, 일의 양 — not 수량.
Pairing 수량 with 크다/작다. Since it's a count, use 수량이 많다/적다 ('the quantity is large/small').
Confusing 수량 with 수: bare 수 means 'number' abstractly (학생 수 'number of students'), while 수량 implies a counted stock or order amount.

extendedVocab.nuance: 단위 is Sino-Korean 單位 ('single' 單 + 'position/rank' 位 = 'a single standard place'), meaning a unit of measurement (meter, kilogram, won) and, by extension, the basic block by which something is counted or grouped (가족 단위 'by household', 학년 단위 'by grade'). Its crucial contrast is with 수량: 단위 is the YARDSTICK (kg, m), while 수량 is the COUNT you get when you measure (열 개, 5킬로그램). Don't confuse it either with 단계 ('stage/step', 段階), which sounds similar but means a phase in a process. A very productive pattern is 단위로 ('in/by units of') — 천 원 단위로, 시간 단위로 ('by the hour'). Register is neutral to formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 단위 for the counted amount itself: English 'a unit of three' tempts learners to say 단위 for the quantity, but the number is 수량/개수 and 단위 only names the measuring standard or grouping.

Confusing 단위 (the measuring standard, e.g. kg) with 수량 (the counted amount, e.g. 5 of them).
Mixing up 단위 with 단계 ('stage/step'). They look alike but 단계 is about phases in a process, not measurement.
Dropping the 로 in the 'by units of' pattern, e.g. 천 원 단위 팔아요 — say 천 원 단위로 팔아요.

두께 = the front-to-back dimension
두께 stated with a value
두께 paired with 두껍다

examples.ko: 이 이불 두께 좀 봐, 엄청 두꺼워.
examples.romanization: i ibul dukke jom bwa, eomcheong dukkeowo.

examples.note: 두께 explaining a real consequence

examples.note: Formal; 두께 with a precise measurement

extendedVocab.nuance: 두께 is a native noun built from the adjective 두껍다 ('thick') plus the nominalizing suffix -이/-께, and it names the front-to-back dimension of a flat or layered object — paper, a wall, fabric, glass, a steak. Its matched adjectives are 두껍다 ('thick') and 얇다 ('thin'), and a frequent trap is reaching for the wrong 'thick': 두껍다 is for flat/layered things (두꺼운 책), while 굵다 ('thick/stout') is for long round things like rope, fingers, or tree trunks — so a thick rope is 굵은 줄, never 두꺼운 줄. Keep 두께 separate from the other -이 measurement nouns: 길이 (length), 높이 (height), 넓이 (area), 깊이 (depth). Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'thick' covers both flat things and round things, so learners over-apply 두께/두껍다 to ropes, wires, and noodles, where Koreans switch to 굵기/굵다.

Using 두께 for height. 두께 is the thin front-to-back dimension; vertical extent is 높이.
Saying 두꺼운 줄 for a 'thick rope'. Round, long things take 굵다: 굵은 줄, and their measure is 굵기, not 두께.
Pairing 두께 with the wrong scale word — describe it with 두껍다/얇다, e.g. 두께가 얇다, not 두께가 작다.

무게 stated with a value

extendedVocab.nuance: 무게 is a native noun from the adjective 무겁다 ('heavy') plus the -에/-게 nominalizer, meaning how heavy something is. Its matched adjectives are 무겁다 ('heavy') and 가볍다 ('light'), and the standard verb for measuring it is 재다 (무게를 재다 'to weigh'). Beyond the physical sense, 무게 also carries the figurative meaning of 'gravity, importance, dignity' — 말의 무게 'the weight of one's words', 무게를 잡다 'to put on a serious air'. Keep it distinct from 수량 (how MANY) and from 양 (how much in a general/uncountable sense): a box's 무게 is its heaviness, its 수량 is how many boxes there are. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: English 'weigh' is one word, but Korean splits it — 무게를 재다 means 'to measure the weight (of something)', whereas the intransitive 'it weighs 5 kg' is 5킬로그램이 나가다 (무게가 나가다), so learners wrongly say 무게를 재다 when they mean 'it weighs ~'.

Confusing 무게 (weight) with 수량 (the count of items) — a heavy box vs. how many boxes there are.

extendedVocab.nuance: 길이 is a native noun from the adjective 길다 ('long') plus the -이 nominalizer, naming the end-to-end (usually horizontal) extent of something. Its matched adjectives are 길다 ('long') and 짧다 ('short'), and you measure it with 재다 (길이를 재다). It belongs to a tidy family of -이 measurement nouns you should keep straight: 길이 (length, side to side), 높이 (height, bottom to top), 깊이 (depth, surface to bottom), 넓이 (area), and the odd one out 두께/굵기 for thickness. The sharp contrast is 길이 vs 높이: a desk's 길이 is how long it is across, its 높이 is how tall it stands — confuse them and a Korean will picture the wrong dimension. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is using 길이 for vertical 'how tall', because English loosely says 'the length of the pole' even when standing upright; in Korean a standing object's vertical measure is 높이, and 길이 implies the laid-flat, lengthwise dimension.

Using 길이 for vertical height. 길이 is the lengthwise (horizontal) dimension; 'how tall' is 높이.
Pairing 길이 with the wrong adjective, e.g. 길이가 크다. Use 길이가 길다/짧다 ('long/short').
Mixing up the -이 family: 깊이 (depth) and 넓이 (area) are not interchangeable with 길이 — match the dimension to the word.

examples.note: Formal; 높이 with an impressive figure

extendedVocab.nuance: 높이 is a native noun from the adjective 높다 ('high/tall') plus the -이 nominalizer, naming the bottom-to-top (vertical) extent of something — a building, a mountain, a shelf, a jump. Its matched adjectives are 높다 ('high') and 낮다 ('low'), and you measure it with 재다 (높이를 재다). A key distinction: for a PERSON's height you don't use 높이 — you use 키 (키가 크다 'is tall'), so 사람의 높이 is wrong and 키 is required. Within the -이 measurement family, the constant trap is 높이 vs 길이: 높이 is how tall something stands upright, 길이 is how long it is laid out lengthwise. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't apply 높이 to people (that's 키), and don't pair it with 크다/작다 — even though English says 'big height', Korean says 높이가 높다/낮다. English 'high/tall' collapsing into one word is exactly what trips learners between 키, 높이, and (for length) 길이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 높이 for a person's height. People take 키: 키가 크다/작다, not 높이가 높다.
Confusing 높이 (vertical) with 길이 (horizontal length) — a building's 높이 vs a bridge's 길이.
Describing 높이 with 크다/작다. Use 높이가 높다/낮다 ('high/low').

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 피부 means "skin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "skin" is 피부 (pibu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 피부가 좋아요 ("your skin is nice"). Watch the particle attached to 피부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the default compliment; 좋다 here means clear and healthy, not merely 'good'
건조하다 (乾燥) is the set adjective for dry skin, never 마르다
a borrowed phrase Koreans use for acne and irritation as a noun
note the particle 에 (to/for the skin), the standard frame for skincare claims

examples.en: Your skin is really nice.
examples.note: a stock compliment; mark the topic with 가, the thing praised

examples.ko: 겨울에는 피부가 너무 건조해서 로션을 발라요.
examples.romanization: gyeoureneun pibuga neomu geonjohaeseo rosyeoneul ballayo.
examples.en: In winter my skin gets so dry that I put on lotion.
examples.note: 건조해서 (because dry) links cause to action with -아서

examples.ko: 햇볕에 오래 있었더니 피부가 따갑고 빨개졌어요.
examples.romanization: haetbyeote orae isseotdeoni pibuga ttagapgo ppalgaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After being in the sun a long time my skin stings and turned red.
examples.note: 빨개지다 = 빨갛다 + 지다, 'become red'; the ㅎ-irregular drops in 빨개

extendedVocab.nuance: 피부 is the skin as a surface and a beauty concern, so it overwhelmingly turns up in compliments (피부가 좋다 = clear, glowing) and skincare talk (피부에 좋다, 피부 트러블, 피부가 건조하다). The near-synonym 살 also means 'skin/flesh' but refers to the soft fleshy meat under the surface and to body fat (살이 찌다 = gain weight), so 손등 살이 텄어요 is the chapped flesh while 피부 관리 is the cosmetic surface — never swap them. 피부 is Sino-Korean, 皮膚 'hide-skin', which is why it sounds slightly clinical yet is perfectly everyday. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for 마르다 ('dry up, become thin') for dry skin; skin takes the adjective 건조하다 instead, and 'I have sensitive skin' is 피부가 예민해요/민감해요, not a 직역 with 'sensitive' as a noun.

Saying 피부가 말라요 for dry skin. 마르다 is for laundry drying or a person becoming thin; skin uses the adjective 건조하다, so say 피부가 건조해요.
Translating 'skin and bones' or 'get under my skin' literally. Those English idioms don't exist in Korean; describe the meaning instead (e.g. 너무 말랐어요 for very thin).
Using 살 when you mean the cosmetic surface. 얼굴 살이 좋아요 sounds like 'nice facial flesh/cheeks'; for clear complexion say 얼굴 피부가 좋아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 뼈 means "bone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 뼈 (ppyeo) = "bone". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 뼈가 부러졌어요 ("my bone broke") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 뼈, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 부러지다 is the verb reserved for snapping long rigid things like bones and branches
튼튼하다 = sturdy/robust; the go-to word for healthy bones, not 강하다
note 에 (for the bones); the frame used in food and calcium ads
an idiom for being extremely thin or worn out

examples.en: The puppy likes bones.
examples.note: a simple object sentence; 뼈를 takes the object particle

examples.en: I fell and broke the bone in my arm.
examples.note: 부러지다 is intransitive — the bone breaks 'by itself', so use 가

examples.ko: 나이가 들면 뼈가 약해져서 칼슘을 챙겨 먹어야 해요.
examples.romanization: naiga deulmyeon ppyeoga yakaejyeoseo kalsyumeul chaenggyeo meogeoya haeyo.
examples.en: As you age your bones weaken, so you should take calcium.
examples.note: 약해지다 'become weak' + 챙겨 먹다 'make sure to eat'

extendedVocab.nuance: 뼈 is the hard bone inside the body and, by extension, a bone in meat or fish. The crucial collocation is 뼈가 부러지다 'a bone breaks': Korean fusses over WHICH break-verb you use — 부러지다 is for snapping rigid long things (bones, pencils, branches), 깨지다 is for shattering brittle things (glass, plates, a skull as 두개골), and 금이 가다 is a hairline crack/fracture. So a clean break is 부러지다, but a fracture a doctor sees on an X-ray is often 뼈에 금이 갔어요. Native, non-Sino word, so it feels plain and bodily; the formal medical counterpart is 골(骨), seen in compounds like 골절 'fracture' and 골다공증 'osteoporosis'. English speakers misfire by saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 (sounds like the bone shattered into pieces) for an ordinary break — use 부러졌어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 for a normal broken bone. 깨지다 implies shattering brittle objects; a snapped bone is 부러졌어요. Reserve 금이 갔어요 for a hairline fracture.
Using 강하다 for strong bones. 강하다 fits force or personality; healthy sturdy bones take 튼튼하다, so say 뼈가 튼튼해요.
Forgetting 부러지다 is intransitive and adding 를. Don't say 뼈를 부러뜨렸어요 unless you mean someone actively broke it; for 'my bone broke' say 뼈가 부러졌어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 근육 means "muscle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 근육 (geunyuk) means "muscle". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 근육이 뭉쳤어요 ("my muscle is knotted up"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 근육 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 뭉치다 'to clump/lump together' is the set verb for a stiff, knotted muscle
생기다 'come into being'; the natural way to say muscle has appeared
풀다 'to release/undo'; used for stretching out tension, opposite of 뭉치다
근육통 (筋肉痛) is the noun for the soreness after a workout

examples.en: That person has a lot of muscle.
examples.note: describing build; 많다 'be many/much' takes 가 on the thing

examples.ko: 어제 운동을 무리해서 오늘 온몸 근육이 아파요.
examples.romanization: eoje undongeul murihaeseo oneul onmom geunyugi apayo.
examples.en: I overdid the workout yesterday so today my muscles ache all over.
examples.note: 무리하다 'to overdo it' + 온몸 'whole body'

examples.ko: 오래 앉아 있었더니 어깨 근육이 뭉쳐서 좀 풀어 줬어요.
examples.romanization: orae anja isseotdeoni eokkae geunyugi mungchyeoseo jom pureo jwosseoyo.
examples.en: After sitting a long time my shoulder muscles knotted up, so I worked them loose.
examples.note: 뭉치다 ↔ 풀다 pairing; 줬어요 here adds a gentle 'did for it' nuance

extendedVocab.nuance: 근육 is muscle tissue, the body part you build at the gym and the thing that gets sore or knotted. It is Sino-Korean, 筋肉 'sinew-flesh', which is why the soreness noun is 근육통 (筋肉痛, lit. muscle-pain). The signature collocation is 근육이 뭉치다 'the muscle clumps up' — 뭉치다 literally means to lump together (rice 뭉치다 into a ball), and a stiff knotted muscle is pictured the same way; its natural opposite is 근육을 풀다 'release the muscle' by stretching. Don't confuse 근육 (the tissue) with 힘 (strength/power, the force it produces): 힘이 세다 = strong, but 근육이 많다 = muscular. The English-speaker pitfall is describing a knot as 딱딱하다 'hard' — that just states a texture; the idiomatic medical-feeling phrase Koreans actually say is 근육이 뭉쳤어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 근육이 딱딱해요 for a knotted muscle. 딱딱하다 only states it feels hard; the natural phrase for a tense knot is 근육이 뭉쳤어요.
Mixing up 근육 and 힘. 근육이 세요 is wrong; for 'I'm strong' say 힘이 세요, and reserve 근육이 많아요 for being muscular.
Saying 근육을 키워요 expecting it to mean a quick 'flex'. 키우다 means to grow/raise muscle over time (training); to flex a muscle right now is 힘을 줘요 or 알통을 만들어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 심장 means "heart (organ)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "heart (organ)" is 심장 (simjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 심장이 뛰어요 ("my heart is beating"). Watch the particle attached to 심장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 뛰다 'to run/leap' doubles as 'to beat' for the heart
두근거리다 is the onomatopoeic verb for a fast, fluttering heartbeat
약하다 'be weak'; a standard medical description
심장마비 (心臟痲痺) lit. 'heart paralysis', the medical term

examples.en: People have one heart.
examples.note: a simple fact sentence; 하나 'one' + 예요

examples.ko: 갑자기 뒤에서 불러서 심장이 멎는 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi dwieseo bulleoseo simjangi meonneun jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: Someone suddenly called from behind and I thought my heart would stop.
examples.note: 멎다 'to stop/cease'; -는 줄 알았다 'I thought it would'

examples.ko: 계단을 뛰어 올라왔더니 심장이 터질 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: gyedaneul ttwieo ollawatdeoni simjangi teojil geot gatayo.
examples.en: I ran up the stairs and now my heart feels like it'll burst.
examples.note: 터지다 'to burst'; vivid but everyday exaggeration for racing

extendedVocab.nuance: 심장 is the physical heart organ — the muscle that beats — and it is Sino-Korean, 心臟 'heart-organ'. The key boundary for English speakers: in Korean the SEAT OF EMOTION is not 심장. Love, sincerity and feelings live in 마음 (the mind-heart, 마음이 아프다 = heartbroken) or 가슴 (the chest, 가슴이 뛰다/벅차다 for excitement and emotion). 심장 stays literal and medical: it 뛰다 (beats), 두근거리다 (pounds with adrenaline or fear), or 멎다/터지다 in vivid shock. Note 심장 vs 가슴: a doctor checks your 심장, but you clutch your 가슴 (chest) in feeling. The classic 직역 trap is writing 'my heart aches (emotionally)' as 심장이 아파요 — that sounds like cardiac pain; for emotional hurt say 마음이 아파요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 심장 for emotions. 심장이 아파요 implies a literal cardiac problem; for heartbreak or sadness say 마음이 아파요.
Confusing 심장 with 가슴. To say your chest feels tight or fluttery with emotion, Koreans say 가슴이 답답해요 / 가슴이 뛰어요, not 심장이.
Translating 'from the bottom of my heart' as 심장. The idiom is 진심으로 or 마음 깊은 곳에서, never with 심장.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 혈액 means "blood" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 혈액 (hyeoraek) = "blood". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 혈액 검사 ("blood test") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 혈액, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 검사 (檢査) 'examination'; this compound is the standard hospital term
혈액형 (血液型) lit. 'blood-type'; the everyday word even in casual chat
뽑다 'to pull out/draw'; the verb for drawing blood or pulling teeth
순환 (循環) 'circulation'; common in health talk, e.g. 혈액 순환이 잘 돼요

examples.en: My blood type is A.
examples.note: the one casual spot 혈액 appears daily; 혈액형 + 이에요

examples.en: They drew blood at my health checkup.
examples.note: 건강 검진 'health screening'; 뽑다 for the draw

examples.ko: 손발이 찬 건 혈액 순환이 잘 안 돼서 그래요.
examples.romanization: sonbari chan geon hyeoraek sunhwani jal an dwaeseo geuraeyo.
examples.en: Cold hands and feet happen because circulation isn't good.
examples.note: 혈액 순환이 안 되다 'circulation doesn't work well'

extendedVocab.nuance: 혈액 is the formal, clinical word for blood — Sino-Korean 血液 'blood-fluid' — so it lives in hospital and health vocabulary: 혈액 검사 (blood test), 혈액형 (blood type), 혈액 순환 (circulation), 혈액 기증 (blood donation). Its everyday counterpart is the native word 피, which is what you say for blood you actually SEE: a bleeding cut is 피가 나요, never 혈액이 나요. So the dividing line is register and visibility — 피 = the red liquid in daily life, 혈액 = the technical substance in medical contexts. The one exception where the Sino word wins in casual speech is 혈액형 'blood type', which almost everyone says over 피의 형. The English-speaker pitfall is using 혈액 for ordinary bleeding (sounds like a lab report) — for a nosebleed or a scrape, say 피.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 혈액이 나요 for a bleeding cut. That sounds like a clinical report; visible bleeding is 피가 나요.
Over-formalizing casual blood-type talk. While 혈액형 is correct, don't say 혈액 for the blood in 'I'm bleeding' — switch to 피.
Mixing up the verbs. You don't 마시다 or 흘리다 혈액 in normal speech; blood is 뽑다 (drawn) or 검사하다 (tested), while you 흘리다 피 (shed blood).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 침 means "saliva; spit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 침 (chim) means "saliva; spit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 침을 뱉어요 ("I spit"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 침 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 뱉다 'to spit out'; the set verb, used literally and in 'spit it out (confess)'
삼키다 'to swallow'; also used for swallowing words/anger
고이다 'to pool/collect'; what your mouth does at a tasty smell
침이 마르다 'mouth goes dry'; idiom for praising someone endlessly

examples.en: The baby is drooling.
examples.note: 흘리다 'to let flow'; simple everyday drooling

examples.en: You mustn't spit on the street.
examples.note: manners; -으면 안 되다 'must not'

examples.ko: 맛있는 냄새를 맡으니까 입에 침이 고여요.
examples.romanization: masinneun naemsaereul mateunikka ibe chimi goyeoyo.
examples.en: Smelling the delicious food makes my mouth water.
examples.note: Korean's exact equivalent of 'mouth waters' = 침이 고이다

extendedVocab.nuance: 침 is the saliva in your mouth, and it pairs with a precise set of verbs: 침을 뱉다 (spit out), 침을 삼키다 (swallow), 침을 흘리다 (drool), and 침이 고이다 (pool — the 'mouth waters' image). Beware the homonyms: this same syllable 침 also means an acupuncture needle (침을 맞다 = get acupuncture), a (clock/compass) needle/hand, and 'sting'(벌침 = bee sting) — context fully disambiguates, but it surprises learners. Two vivid idioms ride on it: 침이 마르도록 칭찬하다 'praise until your mouth runs dry' and 군침이 돌다 'mouth waters with craving'. The pitfall is the verb: English 'water' (as in mouth-watering) tempts a 직역 with 물, but Korean says 침이 고이다 (saliva pools), and 'I'm drooling' is 침을 흘려요, not anything with 물.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the homonyms. 침을 맞다 means 'get acupuncture', not 'get hit with spit'; saliva-침 takes 뱉다/삼키다/흘리다.
Translating 'mouth waters' with 물. The fixed phrase is 입에 침이 고이다 (or 군침이 돌다); never 입에 물이 나요.
Wrong verb for drooling. 침이 나와요 is understandable but flat; natural Korean is 침을 흘려요 for drooling.

structuredNuance.t: 침 is the saliva in your mouth, and it pairs with a precise set of verbs: 침을 뱉다 (spit out), 침을 삼키다 (swallow), 침을 흘리다 (drool), and 침이 고이다 (pool — the 'mouth waters' image). Two vivid idioms ride on it: 침이 마르도록 칭찬하다 'praise until your mouth runs dry' and 군침이 돌다 'mouth waters with craving'.

Beware the homonyms: this same syllable 침 also means an acupuncture needle (침을 맞다 = get acupuncture), a (clock/compass) needle/hand, and 'sting' (벌침 = bee sting) — context fully disambiguates, but it surprises learners.
The pitfall is the verb: English 'water' (as in mouth-watering) tempts a 직역 with 물, but Korean says 침이 고이다 (saliva pools), and 'I'm drooling' is 침을 흘려요, not anything with 물.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 땀 means "sweat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "sweat" is 땀 (ttam). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 땀을 흘려요 ("I sweat / I work hard"). Watch the particle attached to 땀 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 흘리다 'to shed'; literal sweating AND the idiom for hard effort
나다 'to come out/occur'; the most everyday way to say you're sweating
닦다 'to wipe/clean'; with a towel or sleeve
식은땀 lit. 'cooled sweat'; the sweat of fear, nausea, or close calls

examples.en: It's hot so I'm sweating.
examples.note: the basic frame; 땀이 나다 with 가 on the spontaneous event

examples.en: After exercising I wiped off the sweat with a towel.
examples.note: -고 나서 'after doing'; 닦다 takes 를

examples.en: Right before the presentation I broke out in a cold sweat.
examples.note: 식은땀이 나다 = the fear/nerves version of sweating

extendedVocab.nuance: 땀 is sweat, a native word, and the verb choice carries the meaning. 땀이 나다 (sweat occurs) is the neutral everyday 'I'm sweating', while 땀을 흘리다 (shed sweat) both describes heavy sweating AND works as a metaphor for hard work — 땀 흘려 일하다 'to work by the sweat of one's brow', and 노력의 땀 'the sweat of effort'. A key compound is 식은땀 'cold sweat', the clammy sweat of fear, illness, or a near-miss (식은땀이 나다/흐르다). Contrast 땀 with 눈물 (tears) and 침 (saliva): all three are bodily fluids that idiomatically 나다, but only 땀 carries the 'effort/labor' connotation. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'sweat' as a verb and saying 땀을 해요 — Korean has no 'to sweat' verb; you either 흘리다 the sweat or it 나다 on its own.

Saying 땀을 해요 for 'I sweat'. There's no verb 'to sweat'; say 땀이 나요 (it comes) or 땀을 흘려요 (I shed it).
Missing the idiom. 땀을 흘리다 can mean hard work, so 땀 흘려 번 돈 means 'money earned through hard work', not literally sweaty money.
Using plain 땀 for the fear-sweat. The clammy nervous kind is specifically 식은땀, e.g. 식은땀이 났어요, not just 땀이 났어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 눈물 means "tears" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 눈물 (nunmul) = "tears". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 눈물이 나요 ("tears come / I start to cry") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 눈물, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: tears come / I start to cry
usagePhrases.note: 나다 'to come out'; the most natural way to say tears well up
흘리다 'to let flow'; slightly more vivid/literary than 나다
describing a person, not a quantity of liquid
참다 'to endure/hold in'; fighting off crying

examples.en: I'm tearing up because I watched a sad movie.
examples.note: cause + 눈물이 나다; the spontaneous event takes 가

examples.en: I yawned and tears welled up in my eyes.
examples.note: 눈물이 핑 돌다 = tears suddenly well up; 핑 is the swirl mimetic

examples.ko: 울고 싶었지만 사람들 앞이라 눈물을 꾹 참았어요.
examples.romanization: ulgo sipeotjiman saramdeul apira nunmureul kkuk chamasseoyo.
examples.en: I wanted to cry but I held the tears back hard in front of people.
examples.note: 꾹 참다 'endure firmly'; 눈물을 참다 takes the object 를

extendedVocab.nuance: 눈물 is tears, a transparent native compound 눈(eye)+물(water). Its default verb is 눈물이 나다 'tears come' — note that 'I cry' is often expressed this way (눈물이 나요 ≈ 'I'm tearing up') rather than only with the verb 울다 'to cry/weep'. 눈물을 흘리다 'shed tears' is a touch more vivid, and 눈물을 참다 means to hold them back. Watch the idiom 눈물이 많다: it does NOT mean you produce a lot of liquid — it means you're a soft-hearted person who cries easily; its opposite 눈물이 없다 means stoic. Vivid set phrases: 눈물이 핑 돌다 (tears suddenly well), 눈물이 그렁그렁하다 (eyes brimming). The pitfall is the 직역 눈물을 울어요 — you can't 'cry tears' in Korean; tears 나다 (come) or you 흘리다 (shed) them, while 울다 stands alone as 'to cry'.

Saying 눈물을 울어요. 울다 already means 'to cry' and takes no object; say 눈물이 나요 (tears come) or just 울어요.
Literalizing 눈물이 많아요 as 'lots of tear liquid'. It describes a tender person who cries easily, like English 'a crybaby/soft-hearted'.
Wrong particle on the spontaneous event. 'Tears came' is 눈물이 났어요 (가), not 눈물을 났어요; the object 를 only fits 흘리다/참다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 숨 means "breath" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 숨 (sum) means "breath". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 숨을 쉬어요 ("I breathe"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 숨 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 쉬다 — the SAME verb as 'to rest'; 숨을 쉬다 = 'breathe'
차다 'to fill up'; the set phrase for being winded
참다 'to hold in/endure'; also used for holding back emotion

usagePhrases.en: I take a deep breath in
usagePhrases.note: 들이쉬다 'breathe in' vs 내쉬다 'breathe out', built on 쉬다

examples.en: Try breathing slowly.
examples.note: clinic instruction; -아 보세요 'try doing'

examples.en: I ran up the stairs and now I'm out of breath.
examples.note: 숨이 차다 — winded; the event takes 가

examples.en: I held my breath for 30 seconds underwater.
examples.note: 숨을 참다 takes the object 를; 동안 'for (a duration)'

extendedVocab.nuance: 숨 is a breath / one's breathing, a native word, and its core verb is 숨을 쉬다 'to breathe' — note that 쉬다 is also the verb 'to rest', a neat overlap (breathing is the body resting). Directional variants build on it: 들이쉬다 (breathe in), 내쉬다 (breathe out), 한숨을 쉬다 (sigh). To say you're winded, Korean uses 숨이 차다 'breath fills up' (the event takes 가), and to hold your breath is 숨을 참다. Compare 숨 with the Sino-Korean 호흡 (呼吸 'exhale-inhale'), which is the technical 'respiration' used in yoga, medicine, and 인공호흡 (CPR) — 숨 is the plain everyday word. Vivid idioms: 숨이 막히다 'be suffocated/overwhelmed', 숨을 거두다 'to pass away (lit. gather one's breath)'. The pitfall is saying 숨을 해요 — there's no 'to breath' verb; you 쉬다 (do/rest) the breath.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 숨을 해요 for 'I breathe'. The verb is 쉬다, so say 숨을 쉬어요 — and note 쉬다 also means 'rest'.
Using 숨 in a yoga/medical setting where 호흡 fits. 'Focus on your breathing' in class is usually 호흡에 집중하세요.
Wrong particle for being winded. 'I'm out of breath' is 숨이 차요 (가); don't say 숨을 차요. Use 를 only with 참다 (hold).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수염 means "beard; mustache" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "beard; mustache" is 수염 (suyeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 수염을 길러요 ("I'm growing a beard"). Watch the particle attached to 수염 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 기르다 'to grow/raise'; the verb for growing hair, beards, pets
깎다 'to shave/pare'; same verb as shaving and sharpening a pencil
나다 'to grow/sprout'; how facial/body hair appears
콧(nose)수염 vs 턱(chin)수염 specify which when it matters

examples.en: Cats have whiskers.
examples.note: 수염 also = animal whiskers; simple 있다 sentence

examples.en: Dad shaves every morning.
examples.note: daily routine; 깎다 takes 를

examples.ko: 한동안 면도를 안 했더니 수염이 덥수룩하게 났어요.
examples.romanization: handongan myeondoreul an haetdeoni suyeomi deopsurukage nasseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't shave for a while so a scruffy beard grew in.
examples.note: 덥수룩하다 'be bushy/scruffy'; 수염이 나다 for it coming in

extendedVocab.nuance: 수염 covers all facial hair — beard and mustache together — and also animal whiskers (고양이 수염), so context tells you which; to be specific Koreans add a body part: 콧수염 (mustache, nose-beard), 턱수염 (chin beard), 구레나룻 (sideburns). It's Sino-Korean, 鬚髥. The verbs are the heart of it: you 기르다 (grow) a beard over time, it 나다 (sprouts) on its own, and you 깎다 (shave) it off — 깎다 is the same verb as shaving hair short and sharpening a pencil, picturing paring something down. Note the everyday near-synonym 면도(面刀)하다 'to shave' (lit. 'face-blade'): 면도하다 is the act of shaving, while 수염을 깎다 names the beard as object. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 자르다 'to cut' — you cut hair with scissors (머리를 자르다), but a beard is pared/shaved with 깎다, not 잘라요.

Saying 수염을 잘라요 for shaving. 자르다 is cutting with scissors (good for hair length); shaving a beard is 수염을 깎아요 or 면도해요.
Forcing 수염 to mean only 'beard'. It also means a mustache and animal whiskers; specify 콧수염/턱수염 if the distinction matters.
Using 자라다 transitively for growing a beard. 자라다 'to grow' is intransitive (수염이 자라요 = it grows); to deliberately grow one say 수염을 길러요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주름 means "wrinkle" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주름 (jureum) = "wrinkle". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 주름이 생겼어요 ("wrinkles have formed") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주름, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 'to form/appear'; the set verb for wrinkles coming with age
자글자글 is the mimetic word for lots of tiny crinkly wrinkles
펴다 'to unfold/straighten'; for skin or ironing cloth
눈가 'eye area'; the most-mentioned wrinkle spot

examples.en: Grandma has many wrinkles.
examples.note: appearance; 많다 takes 가 on 주름

examples.ko: 웃을 때 눈가에 주름이 살짝 생겨요.
examples.romanization: useul ttae nungae jureumi saljjak saenggyeoyo.
examples.en: When I smile, slight wrinkles form around my eyes.
examples.note: 눈가에 'at the eye area' + 살짝 'slightly'

examples.en: I ironed out the wrinkles in the shirt.
examples.note: same 주름 for cloth creases; 펴다 removes them

extendedVocab.nuance: 주름 means a wrinkle on skin AND a fold/crease in fabric or paper — same word for both. It's a native word, and its defining verb is 주름이 생기다 'wrinkles form' (생기다 = come into being), the standard way to talk about aging skin; you smooth them with 주름을 펴다 (unfold/straighten, also used for ironing). Common spots: 눈가 주름 (crow's feet), 이마 주름 (forehead lines), 팔자 주름 (nasolabial folds, named for the 八 shape). A vivid mimetic, 자글자글하다, describes finely crinkled skin. Don't confuse 주름 (a line/fold in a surface) with 흉터 (a scar from a wound) or 점 (a mole) — different skin features entirely. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'wrinkles appear' tempts 주름이 나다 (the 나다 you'd use for pimples or sweat), but wrinkles specifically 생기다 — say 주름이 생겼어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 주름이 나요 for wrinkles. The verb 나다 fits pimples/sweat; wrinkles use 생기다, so say 주름이 생겼어요.
Treating 주름 as skin-only. The same word means cloth creases — 주름이 가다/지다, and 주름치마 is a pleated skirt.
Confusing 주름 with 흉터. A line from aging is 주름; a mark left by a cut or burn is 흉터 (scar).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 점 means "mole; spot" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 점 (jeom) means "mole; spot". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 점을 빼요 ("I remove the mole"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 빼다 'to take out/remove'; the set verb for laser mole removal
있다 'to exist'; describing where a mole sits

usagePhrases.en: I draw on a beauty spot
usagePhrases.note: 찍다 'to dot/stamp'; making a point, also photos and dipping sauce
검은 'black/dark'; the common color descriptor

examples.en: I have one mole on my face.
examples.note: appearance; 하나 'one' counts it

examples.ko: 눈 밑에 있는 점을 병원에서 뺐어요.
examples.romanization: nun mite inneun jeomeul byeongwoneseo ppaesseoyo.
examples.en: I had the mole under my eye removed at a clinic.
examples.note: 점을 빼다; 눈 밑 'under the eye'

examples.en: The teacher made a dot on the board.
examples.note: same 점 = 'dot/point'; 찍다 for marking it

extendedVocab.nuance: 점 is a mole on the skin, and the very same word means a dot, point, spot, period (punctuation), and even a 'point' as in a score or aspect (좋은 점 = a good point). It's Sino-Korean, 點. For a skin mole the defining collocation is 점을 빼다 'remove the mole' — 빼다 means to take/pull out (also used for 'lose weight', 살을 빼다), reflecting how a mole is extracted by laser. Don't use 지우다 'to erase' (that's for writing, stains, or files) — you 빼다 a mole, not 지워요. Useful relatives: 주근깨 (freckles), 기미 (age/sun spots, melasma). Beware the homonym range: 점심 (點心, lunch) literally 'dot the heart', 점수 (點數, score), 점 보다 (have one's fortune told). The English-speaker pitfall is calling a mole a 'spot' and erasing it — Korean removes (빼다) the 점.

Saying 점을 지워요 to remove a mole. 지우다 is for erasing writing/stains/data; a mole is 점을 빼요 (taken out, often by laser).
Assuming 점 only means 'mole'. It also means a dot, a (score) point, and an aspect — e.g. 좋은 점 'a good point', 점수 'score'.
Using 자르다 for mole removal. You don't 'cut' a mole off in normal speech; the clinic verb is 빼다 (or 제거하다 in formal medical contexts).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 속옷 means "underwear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "underwear" is 속옷 (sogot). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 속옷을 갈아입어요. ("I change my underwear."). Watch the particle attached to 속옷 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: the verb 갈아입다 'change clothes' is the natural partner, not just 입다
underwear is counted with 벌, the counter for clothing sets
면(綿) names the fabric; 면 + garment is a fixed modifier pattern
차림 means 'state of being dressed in', describing what someone has on

examples.en: I change my underwear every day.
examples.note: 갈아입다 (change-into) is the habitual verb; plain 입다 sounds like a first-time action

examples.en: My underwear got all wet.
examples.note: 이/가 marks 속옷 as the thing that got into the wet state — 다 = 'completely'

examples.ko: 새 속옷을 사야 하는데 어디 가지요?
examples.romanization: sae sogoseul saya haneunde eodi gajiyo?
examples.en: I need to buy new underwear, but where should I go?
examples.note: real shopping moment: -는데 sets up the problem, -지요? asks for advice

extendedVocab.nuance: 속옷 is the umbrella word for anything worn directly against the body under your outer clothes — it transparently breaks down as 속 'inside, inner part' + 옷 'clothes', so literally 'inner clothes'. It covers both men's and women's items and is the neutral term you'd use shopping or at home; in clinical or marketing contexts you may also meet the Sino-Korean 내의(內衣, 'inner-garment') for thermal underwear specifically. The crucial trap for English speakers is the verb: although you 'wear' underwear in English, the everyday Korean verb is 갈아입다 ('change into') because underwear is something you swap daily, and the counter is 벌 (one 속옷 한 벌), never 개. Do not confuse 속옷 with 잠옷 (pajamas) or 수영복 (swimsuit) — those are worn over the body for a purpose, while 속옷 stays hidden underneath.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 속옷을 신어요 — 신다 is only for things you put on your feet (socks, shoes). Underwear bottoms still take 입다/갈아입다, so say 속옷을 입어요/갈아입어요.
Counting with 개: 속옷 두 개 sounds like two random objects. Use the clothing counter 벌 → 속옷 두 벌 ('two sets of underwear').
Treating 속옷 and 내복 as identical. 내복/내의 specifically means warm thermal long-johns for winter; plain 속옷 is the general everyday term.

extendedVocab.explanation: 잠옷 (jamot) = "pajamas". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 잠옷으로 갈아입어요. ("I change into pajamas.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 잠옷, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the result you change into; 갈아입다 is the natural verb at bedtime
바람으로 = 'wearing only ~', stressing you're underdressed to go out
커플 + item is a popular set-phrase for matching outfits
-은 채로 = 'in the unchanged state of', i.e. without taking it off

examples.en: At night I wear pajamas.
examples.note: 은 on 밤에 contrasts night with the daytime; 입다 is fine for the habitual statement

examples.en: The pajamas are so comfy I don't want to take them off.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; 벗다 'take off' is the opposite of 입다

examples.en: I ran to the convenience store in my pajamas.
examples.note: 잠옷 차림으로 = 'dressed only in pajamas', a very Korean way to say you went out underdressed

extendedVocab.nuance: 잠옷 literally stacks 잠 'sleep' (the noun from 자다 'to sleep') + 옷 'clothes', so 'sleep-clothes' — clothes whose whole job is to be comfortable in bed. It overlaps with the borrowed 파자마 (pajamas) and the broader 실내복 ('indoor wear', 室內服), but 잠옷 specifically frames the garment around sleeping, while 실내복 is any loungewear you'd relax in awake. Register is fully neutral and casual. The English-speaker pitfall is cultural rather than grammatical: in Korea wearing 잠옷 outside the home reads as notably sloppy, so the phrases 잠옷 바람으로 / 잠옷 차림으로 ('in just your pj's') carry a faintly embarrassed nuance. Grammatically remember the opposite of 입다 ('put on') is 벗다 ('take off'), and use the clothing counter 벌, not 개.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 to count: 잠옷 두 개 is wrong for a garment. Say 잠옷 한 벌 / 두 벌 with the clothing counter 벌.
Saying 잠옷을 신어요 — 신다 is reserved for footwear. Pajamas take 입다 (top and bottom together): 잠옷을 입어요.
Assuming 잠옷 = any home clothes. If you mean general loungewear you stay awake in, 실내복 or 편한 옷 is more accurate; 잠옷 implies you're going to bed.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정장 means "suit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정장 (jeongjang) means "suit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정장을 차려입어요. ("I dress up in a suit."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I dress up in a suit.
usagePhrases.note: 차려입다 ('dress up smartly') is the verb that matches formal wear
a jacket-and-trousers set is counted as 한 벌, since 벌 means a full matching set
차림 = 'the way one is dressed', so 정장 차림 = dressed formally
맞춤 (from 맞추다 'to have made to fit') marks a custom-ordered suit

examples.en: I wore a suit today.
examples.note: basic statement; 을 marks the object, 입다 the verb

examples.en: Since it's a job interview, I dressed up in a suit.
examples.note: -이라서 'because it is' gives the reason; 차려입다 stresses dressing up properly

examples.ko: 검은색 정장에 흰 셔츠가 제일 무난해요.
examples.romanization: geomeunsaek jeongjange huin syeocheuga jeil munanhaeyo.
examples.en: A black suit with a white shirt is the safest choice.
examples.note: A에 B = 'B paired with A'; 무난하다 'safe/unobjectionable' is the go-to word for fail-proof outfits

extendedVocab.nuance: 정장 is Sino-Korean 正裝, literally 正 'proper, correct' + 裝 'attire' — 'correct/proper dress', i.e. the formal outfit appropriate for serious occasions (interviews, weddings, funerals, important meetings). It overlaps with 양복(洋服, 'Western clothes'), but there is a real dividing line: 양복 names the Western-style tailored garment as a thing (and skews masculine and slightly old-fashioned), whereas 정장 names the formal register of the outfit and applies equally to men's and women's formal wear. The opposite is 캐주얼 or 평상복 ('everyday clothes'). The English-speaker pitfall is counting and the verb: a suit is one matched set, so 정장 한 벌 (not 한 개), and the natural verb is 입다 or, for the 'dress up' feel, 차려입다 — never 신다, which is only for footwear.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting with 개: 정장 한 개 is wrong. A suit is a set → 정장 한 벌.
Using 정장 and 양복 interchangeably for women. 양복 sounds like a man's Western suit; for a woman's formal outfit say 정장.
Saying 정장을 신어요 — 신다 is for shoes/socks only. A suit takes 입다 or 차려입다: 정장을 입어요.
