extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 청바지 means "jeans" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "jeans" is 청바지 (cheongbaji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 청바지를 입어요. ("I wear jeans."). Watch the particle attached to 청바지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: trousers take 입다 (put on the legs), with 를 as the object marker
borrowed style adjectives like 스키니 sit directly in front of 청바지
딱 맞다 'fit exactly' is the set phrase for a perfect fit
A에 B lists a paired outfit, 'B worn with A'

examples.en: On weekends I wear jeans.
examples.note: 은 on 주말에 contrasts the weekend with workdays; casual register

examples.ko: 청바지가 좀 끼어서 한 치수 큰 걸 샀어요.
examples.romanization: cheongbajiga jom kkieoseo han chisu keun geol sasseoyo.
examples.en: The jeans were a bit tight, so I bought one size up.
examples.note: 끼다 'be tight/snug' is the natural fit complaint; -아서 gives the reason

examples.en: These jeans don't shrink even when washed.
examples.note: -아도 'even if'; 줄어들다 'shrink' is the verb for fabric shrinking

extendedVocab.nuance: 청바지 = 청(靑) 'blue/indigo' + 바지 'trousers', literally 'blue trousers' — the 청 element is what specifically marks denim, since plain 바지 just means 'pants' of any kind. It's the standard, completely neutral word for jeans across all ages and is far more common in speech than the English loan 진/데님 (데님 normally refers to the fabric, not the finished garment). Casual register, never formal. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, jeans are grammatically singular in Korean — 청바지 한 벌 / 한 개, never a plural form — so you don't 'wear a pair'; second, the verb is 입다 ('put on the lower body'), and a tight or loose fit is described with 끼다 ('snug/tight') or 헐렁하다 ('loose'), not the English 'tight'. Pair it naturally with 티셔츠 or 운동화 for the default casual look.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating jeans as plural like English. There is no plural; say 청바지 한 벌 ('one pair of jeans'), and 'these jeans' is just 이 청바지.
Saying 청바지를 신어요 — 신다 is for footwear. Trousers take 입다: 청바지를 입어요.
Calling jeans 데님. 데님 is the fabric (denim); the garment is 청바지. 'A denim jacket' would be 청재킷, not 데님.

extendedVocab.explanation: 티셔츠 (tisyeocheu) = "t-shirt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 티셔츠를 입어요. ("I wear a t-shirt.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 티셔츠, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: tops take 입다; 를 marks the object
반팔 'half-sleeve' specifies sleeve length, vs 긴팔 'long-sleeve'
thin flat tops are often counted with 장, the counter for flat sheet-like things
A에 B names the classic paired casual outfit

examples.en: In summer I often wear t-shirts.
examples.note: 은 contrasts summer with other seasons; 자주 'often' marks the habit

examples.en: The t-shirt shrank, so I gave it to my younger sibling.
examples.note: 줄어들다 'shrink'; -아서 reason; 주다 'give' takes the recipient with 에게/한테 (here dropped casually)

examples.en: The neckline of this t-shirt has stretched out.
examples.note: 목 here = the collar/neckline; 늘어나다 'stretch out' is the opposite of 줄어들다

extendedVocab.nuance: 티셔츠 is a direct loanword from English 'T-shirt' (named for its T shape), and it specifically means a pull-over knit top — most often short-sleeved cotton. The key contrast English speakers miss is 티셔츠 vs 셔츠: in Korean 셔츠 by itself implies a button-up collared shirt (a dress shirt / 와이셔츠), so a casual tee must keep the 티 to stay distinct. Sleeve length is built right into the noun phrase: 반팔 티셔츠 (half-sleeve) vs 긴팔 티셔츠 (long-sleeve). Register is casual and neutral. The pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다, never 신다; (2) thin tees are frequently counted with 장 ('흰 티 한 장' = one plain white tee), though 벌 also works for an outfit; and (3) Koreans clip it to 티 in speech (흰 티, 검은 티), so don't be thrown when the 셔츠 disappears.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 셔츠 for a casual tee. 셔츠 alone suggests a button-up dress shirt; keep 티셔츠 (or 티) for a pull-over t-shirt.
Saying 티셔츠를 신어요 — 신다 is footwear only. A top takes 입다: 티셔츠를 입어요.
Forcing English plural 'two t-shirts' as a plural noun. Say 티셔츠 두 장 / 두 벌 — Korean marks number with a counter, not a plural ending.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 스웨터 means "sweater" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 스웨터 (seuweteo) means "sweater". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 스웨터를 입어요. ("I wear a sweater."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 스웨터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: knit tops take 입다; 를 marks the object
목폴라 'turtleneck' specifies the collar type before the noun
보풀이 일어나다 'form lint balls/pills' is the set phrase for knitwear pilling
손빨래(하다) 'hand-wash' — the care verb knitwear usually needs

examples.en: It got cold, so I took out a sweater.
examples.note: -아서 reason; 꺼내다 'take out' (of storage) fits seasonal clothes

examples.en: I layer a shirt under the sweater.
examples.note: 받쳐 입다 'wear underneath as a layer' is the exact verb for layering

examples.en: This sweater is warm but a bit itchy/prickly.
examples.note: -는데 contrasts the two qualities; 따갑다 'prickly' is what wool feels like on skin

extendedVocab.nuance: 스웨터 is a loanword from English 'sweater' and names a warm knitted pullover top for cold weather. It sits in a tight cluster of near-synonyms you should separate: 니트 (from 'knit') is the broad fashion word for any knitted top and is currently more trendy in clothing shops; 가디건 (cardigan) is the open-front, button-up knit you wear like a jacket; 스웨터 leans toward the closed pull-over you slip over your head. So a buttoned knit is 가디건, not 스웨터. Register is neutral/casual. Pitfalls for English speakers: (1) the verb is 입다, and layering under it is 받쳐 입다; (2) describe wool's feel with 따갑다 ('prickly') or warmth with 따뜻하다, not a borrowed word; (3) count with 벌, and remember knit care vocabulary like 보풀 (pilling) and 손빨래 (hand-wash) that comes up constantly when shopping for one.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an open button-front knit a 스웨터. That garment is a 가디건; 스웨터 is the closed pull-over type.
Using 개 to count: 스웨터 한 개. A garment takes the set counter 벌 → 스웨터 한 벌.
Saying it's 'warm' as 더워요. 덥다 is for hot weather/feeling hot; a cozy warm sweater is 따뜻하다 → 스웨터가 따뜻해요.

structuredNuance.t: Names a warm knitted pullover top for cold weather; 스웨터 leans toward the closed pull-over you slip over your head. Register is neutral/casual.

Watch the particle attached to 원피스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: a one-piece garment takes 입다; 를 marks the object
무늬 'pattern' attaches to a noun: 꽃무늬 'flower pattern'
어울리다 'suit/match' is the standard compliment verb for clothes
season + garment is a fixed modifier pattern

examples.en: Today I wore a dress.
examples.note: 은 on 오늘 highlights today as different from usual; simple past with 입다

examples.ko: 이 원피스 너무 예쁜데 좀 비싸요.
examples.romanization: i wonpiseu neomu yeppeunde jom bissayo.
examples.en: This dress is so pretty, but it's a bit pricey.
examples.note: -는데 sets up the 'but'; 예쁘다 is the ㅡ-irregular adjective for 'pretty'

examples.en: I'm going to buy a dress to wear to the wedding.
examples.note: 입을 (future-modifier) + noun = 'a dress to wear'; -려고요 states the intention

extendedVocab.nuance: 원피스 is a loanword from English 'one-piece', and that literal sense is the whole point: it's a dress where top and skirt are a single connected garment, as opposed to a 투피스 ('two-piece', a matching top-and-skirt set). The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 원피스 vs 드레스: everyday casual or work dresses are 원피스, while 드레스 in Korean is reserved for a formal gown — a wedding dress (웨딩드레스) or evening gown — so calling your sundress a 드레스 sounds like you're going to a gala. The word is essentially female-coded. Register is neutral. Pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다; (2) compliment the fit with 어울리다 ('it suits you'), the single most useful clothes-shopping verb; (3) count with 벌, and (4) never split a 원피스 into separates — that's literally a 투피스.

Calling a casual dress a 드레스. 드레스 means a formal gown (wedding/evening); an everyday dress is 원피스.
Saying 원피스가 예뻐요 to mean 'it looks good on you'. 예쁘다 describes the dress itself; to say it suits the person use 어울리다 → 원피스가 잘 어울려요.
Using 개 to count: 원피스 한 개. Use the clothing counter 벌 → 원피스 한 벌.

examples.en: When it's hot, I wear shorts.
examples.note: -(으)면 'if/when'; 덥다 ㅂ-irregular → 더우면

examples.en: The shorts are long, reaching down to the knee.
examples.note: -아서 result; 까지 'up to'; 무릎 'knee' is the reference length for shorts

examples.ko: 회사에는 반바지를 입고 가면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeneun banbajireul ipgo gamyeon an dwaeyo.

extendedVocab.nuance: 반바지 = 반(半) 'half' + 바지 'trousers' — literally 'half-pants', i.e. trousers cut short, ending around or above the knee, in direct contrast with 긴바지 ('long pants'). It's the standard neutral word for shorts in everyday speech, used for both casual summer wear and athletic shorts. The 반 here is the same Sino-Korean 'half' you meet in 반(half-hour) and 반값(half-price), so the morphology is worth banking. Register is casual; like 청바지 it would read as too informal for an office, which is exactly why dress-code sentences (회사에 반바지는 좀…) come up. Pitfalls for English speakers: (1) shorts are grammatically singular — 반바지 한 벌, never plural and never 'a pair'; (2) the verb is 입다, not 신다; and (3) describe the airy feel with 시원하다 ('cool/breezy'), not 추워요 ('cold'), which would imply the weather, not the comfort.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating shorts as plural like English. No plural form exists; say 반바지 한 벌 and 'these shorts' = 이 반바지.
Saying 반바지를 신어요 — 신다 is footwear only. Shorts take 입다: 반바지를 입어요.
Using 짧은바지 as the normal word. While understandable, the everyday term is the single word 반바지; 긴바지 is its natural opposite.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 벨트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 매다 'tie/fasten' (or 하다) is the verb for putting on a belt — never 입다
풀다 'undo/loosen' is the natural opposite of 매다
가죽 'leather' as a material modifier sits before the noun
구멍 'hole'; 벨트를 한 칸 줄이다 'take the belt in one notch' is the related phrase

examples.en: I put a belt on my pants.
examples.note: 에 marks where the belt goes; 매다 is the correct verb

examples.ko: 살이 빠져서 벨트를 한 칸 더 조였어요.
examples.romanization: sari ppajyeoseo belteureul han kan deo joyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I lost weight, so I tightened my belt one more notch.

examples.en: This belt goes well even with a suit.
examples.note: 에도 'even with'; 어울리다 for matching accessories to an outfit

extendedVocab.nuance: 벨트 is a loanword from English 'belt' — the strap worn around the waist to hold up trousers or as an accent, very often leather (가죽). A more traditional native synonym exists, 허리띠 (허리 'waist' + 띠 'band/sash'), which sounds plainer and a touch old-fashioned; in fashion and shopping contexts 벨트 dominates. The single most important point for English speakers is the verb. You do NOT 입다 a belt; you 매다 ('tie/fasten') or, very commonly, 하다 (벨트를 하다 'put a belt on'), and you take it off with 풀다 ('undo'). This 매다/하다 pattern is the same one used for 넥타이 and 스카프 — accessories you fasten rather than slip your body into. Tightening or loosening is counted in 칸 (notches): 벨트를 한 칸 조이다/풀다. Count belts with 개 (벨트 한 개), since they're individual objects, not garment sets.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 벨트를 입어요. 입다 is only for clothes you put your body through. A belt is fastened: 벨트를 매요 / 벨트를 해요.
Using 벗다 to take it off. 벗다 is for taking off worn clothing; for a belt you 풀다 ('undo') → 벨트를 풀어요.
Counting with 벌: 벨트 한 벌. 벌 is for clothing sets; a belt is one object → 벨트 한 개.

usagePhrases.note: 매다 'tie/knot' (or 하다) is the verb for a tie — never 입다

usagePhrases.en: I loosen / take off the tie.
usagePhrases.note: 풀다 'undo' is the natural opposite of 매다
무늬 'pattern' → 줄무늬 'stripe pattern' modifies the noun
고쳐 매다 'fix and re-tie' = adjust a crooked knot

examples.en: I put on a tie when I go to work.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 'when'; 매다 is the correct verb for tying it

examples.en: The tie has gone a little crooked.

examples.ko: 면접 때문에 넥타이를 새로 하나 샀어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 넥타이 is a loanword from English 'necktie' — the long strip of cloth knotted at the neck of a dress shirt, standard in business and formal wear and largely male-associated. Korean has no everyday native equivalent, so 넥타이 (often clipped to 타이 in fashion contexts) is simply the word. The decisive thing for English speakers is again the verb: a tie is fastened, so you 매다 ('tie/knot') it or use the catch-all 하다 (넥타이를 하다), and you undo it with 풀다 — using 입다 here is a classic beginner error, because 입다 is strictly for garments you put your torso or legs into. This is the same 매다/하다/풀다 family as 벨트 and 스카프. Adjusting a crooked knot is 고쳐 매다 or describing it as 비뚤어지다 ('go askew'). Count ties with 개 (넥타이 한 개), not the clothing-set counter 벌.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 넥타이를 입어요. A tie isn't put on the body like clothing; it's tied: 넥타이를 매요 / 넥타이를 해요.
Using 벗다 to remove it. Take a tie off with 풀다 ('undo') → 넥타이를 풀어요, the mirror image of 매다.
Counting with 벌. 넥타이 한 벌 is wrong; a single tie is 넥타이 한 개.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 목걸이 means "necklace" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 목걸이 (mokgeori) = "necklace". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 목걸이를 해요. ("I put on a necklace.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 목걸이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 is the everyday verb for wearing accessories — not 입다
걸다 'hang' fits literally, since a necklace hangs from the neck
진주 'pearl' names the material before the noun
어울리다 'suit/match' for jewelry paired with an outfit

examples.en: Today I put on a necklace.
examples.note: 은 on 오늘 marks the contrast with usual; 하다 → 했어요 is the natural past

examples.en: I got a necklace from a friend for my birthday.
examples.note: 한테서 'from (a person)'; 받다 'receive' — necklaces are a common gift

examples.en: The necklace chain snapped.
examples.note: 줄 'chain/string'; 끊어지다 'snap/break (of a line)' is the exact verb for a chain breaking

extendedVocab.nuance: 목걸이 is, unusually for this list, a pure native Korean word, transparently built from 목 'neck' + 걸이, a noun from 걸다 'to hang' — so literally 'a neck-hanger', the thing you hang around your neck. That etymology is also a memory hook for the verb: you can 걸다 ('hang') a necklace, though the most common everyday verb for putting on any accessory is simply 하다 (목걸이를 하다). The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 입다 ('wear'), which only works for clothing you put your body into; jewelry takes 하다/걸다, removed with 풀다 or 빼다. Register is neutral. Watch the family of related neck/ear words that share 걸이 or a body part: 귀걸이 (ear-ring, 귀 'ear' + 걸이) and 팔찌 (bracelet) all take 하다, not 입다. Count with 개 (목걸이 한 개), and note that the cord is the 줄, which can 끊어지다 ('snap').
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 목걸이를 입어요. Jewelry is never 입다; say 목걸이를 해요 (most natural) or 목걸이를 걸어요.
Using 벗다 to take it off. 벗다 is for clothes; remove a necklace with 풀다 or 빼다 → 목걸이를 빼요.
Counting with 벌: 목걸이 한 벌. An accessory is an object → 목걸이 한 개.

extendedVocab.explanation: 반지 (banji) means "ring". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 반지를 껴요. ("I put on a ring."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 끼다 'insert (onto a finger)' is the dedicated verb for rings — not 입다 or even 하다
빼다 'pull out/remove' is the natural opposite of 끼다
커플 + item names matching rings worn by a couple

usagePhrases.en: The ring fits the finger perfectly.
usagePhrases.note: 딱 맞다 'fit exactly' for ring sizing

examples.en: I wear a ring on my ring finger.
examples.note: 약지 'ring finger'; 에 marks where; 끼다 is the verb

examples.ko: 반지가 너무 꽉 껴서 안 빠져요.
examples.romanization: banjiga neomu kkwak kkyeoseo an ppajyeoyo.
examples.en: The ring is so tight it won't come off.
examples.note: 꽉 끼다 'fit too tightly'; -아서 reason; 빠지다 'come off/slip out'

examples.en: I gave a ring when I proposed.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 때 'when'; 주다 'give'; rings carry the engagement meaning here too

extendedVocab.nuance: 반지 is the everyday word for a finger ring, a piece of jewelry worn for decoration or as an engagement/couple symbol (커플 반지, 결혼 반지). The verb is the headline for English speakers, and it's special: rings take 끼다 ('to insert/slip onto'), because you slide your finger through them — not 입다 (clothing), not even the general accessory verb 하다 that 목걸이 and 벨트 use. So 반지를 껴요 ('I put on a ring'), removed with 빼다 ('pull out'); a too-tight ring 꽉 끼다 and won't 빠지다 ('come off'). This 끼다 also governs other finger/face items you thread or slot on — 장갑을 끼다 (gloves), 안경을 끼다 (glasses) — so learning it here pays off broadly. Register is neutral. Count rings with 개 (반지 한 개), and place them with 에 on a finger: 손가락에/약지에 반지를 끼다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 반지를 입어요 or 반지를 해요. A ring uses its own verb 끼다 → 반지를 껴요; 하다 sounds off for rings specifically.
Using 벗다 to remove it. 벗다 is for clothing; pull a ring off with 빼다 → 반지를 빼요.
Saying 반지가 작아요 to mean it's too tight to wear. For the snug fit say 반지가 꽉 껴요 ('the ring fits too tightly'); 작다 just describes the ring's size in the abstract.

extendedVocab.explanation: "joy" is 기쁨 (gippeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기쁨이 커요 ("The joy is big"). Watch the particle attached to 기쁨 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 기쁨 ends in a vowel, so the subject marker is 이, not 가
the fixed verb for emotions is 느끼다 'feel', not 가지다 'have'
Koreans 'divide' (나누다) a feeling rather than 'share' it the English way
큰 'big' is the natural adjective for 기쁨, not 높은 'high'

examples.en: I'm really glad
examples.note: the everyday way to express the feeling is the adjective 기쁘다, not the noun 기쁨

examples.en: I felt great joy at the news that I passed
examples.note: 에 marks the trigger of the emotion, like 'at' the news

examples.ko: 아이의 웃음이 부모에게는 가장 큰 기쁨이에요
examples.romanization: aiui useumi bumoegeneun gajang keun gippeumieyo

extendedVocab.nuance: 기쁨 is the noun 'joy/gladness', the nominalized form of the adjective 기쁘다 (기쁘 + ㅁ). It names a bright, often momentary delight sparked by a specific good event — passing an exam, a reunion, good news. The near-synonym to separate is 행복 (幸福), 'happiness': 행복 is a broad, lasting state of life ('a happy marriage'), while 기쁨 is the sharp spike of gladness at one happy thing. So you feel 기쁨 about your friend's wedding but wish them lifelong 행복. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the noun in speech: to say 'I'm happy/glad' a Korean almost always uses the adjective 기뻐요, and saves the noun 기쁨 for when it is the subject or object of a sentence (기쁨을 느끼다, 기쁨이 크다). Note too that the verb is 느끼다 'feel', never 가지다 'have'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기쁨이에요 to mean 'I'm glad'. 기쁨 is a noun ('joy'), so that literally says 'It is joy'. To report your own feeling use the adjective: 기뻐요.
Using 행복 and 기쁨 interchangeably. 행복 is a lasting state of well-being; 기쁨 is the burst of gladness at one event. 'I felt 행복 that I passed' sounds odd — use 기쁨 for the moment of good news.
Pairing it with the wrong verb: 기쁨을 가지다 ('have joy') is unnatural. The set verb is 기쁨을 느끼다 'feel joy', or simply 기쁘다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 슬픔 means "sadness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 슬픔 (seulpeum) = "sadness". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 슬픔이 밀려와요 ("Sadness washes over me") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 슬픔, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 슬픔 + 이; 밀려오다 'surge in' is the vivid collocation for waves of feeling
느끼다 'feel' is the fixed verb, not 있다 'have/exist'
슬픔 collocates with 깊은 'deep', mirroring English
에 잠기다 'be submerged in' is an idiom for being lost in an emotion

examples.en: I'm so sad
examples.note: to say you feel sad, use the adjective 슬프다, not the noun

examples.en: I felt great sadness because my pet passed away
examples.note: -아서/어서 gives the cause; 떠나다 'leave' is a gentle euphemism for death

examples.en: That film left a quiet sadness
examples.note: 잔잔한 'calm, gentle' + 슬픔 captures a lingering, bittersweet mood

extendedVocab.nuance: 슬픔 is the noun 'sadness/sorrow', built from the adjective 슬프다 (슬프 + ㅁ). It is a heavy, quiet grief that wells up inside — from loss, parting, or disappointment — and it lingers, unlike a flash of irritation. Compare it with 우울 (憂鬱), 'depression/gloom': 우울 is a duller, more clinical low mood with no single cause ('I feel 우울 today for no reason'), whereas 슬픔 is sorrow you can usually point to a reason for. It also differs from 아쉬움, the mild 'too bad / wish it were otherwise' regret. The classic English-speaker mistake is using the noun where the adjective belongs: 'I am sad' is 슬퍼요 (adjective), never 슬픔이에요, which would mean 'It is sadness'. Reserve the noun 슬픔 for subject/object roles (슬픔을 느끼다, 슬픔이 깊다).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 슬픔이에요 for 'I'm sad'. That means 'It is sadness'. Your own feeling takes the adjective: 슬퍼요.
Confusing 슬픔 with 우울. 슬픔 is sorrow with a cause (a loss, a goodbye); 우울 is a cause-less heavy/depressed mood. Don't say 슬픔 for a vague gloomy day.
Using 있다 instead of 느끼다: 슬픔이 있어요 sounds like inventory-taking. Say 슬픔을 느껴요 'I feel sadness' or simply 슬퍼요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 분노 means "anger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 분노 (bunno) means "anger". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 분노가 치밀다 ("anger surges up"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 분노 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 분노 + 가; 치밀다 'boil/well up' is the set verb for rising rage
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb for the emotion
참다 'endure/suppress' is the habitual partner for restraining 분노
분노 + 의 + noun links the feeling to what shows it

examples.en: I'm so angry
examples.note: in daily speech the everyday phrase is 화가 나다, not the heavy noun 분노

examples.en: I felt anger at the unfair ruling
examples.note: 에 marks the trigger; 분노 suits weighty, public injustices

examples.en: The citizens' anger burst out into the streets
examples.note: this grave, news-style register is exactly where 분노 belongs

extendedVocab.nuance: 분노 is the Sino-Korean noun for 'anger/wrath', 분노 憤怒 — 憤 'indignation' + 怒 'rage' — so by its very characters it is righteous, intense fury, not petty annoyance. The crucial contrast for learners is the everyday word 화 (火, literally 'fire'): in conversation Koreans say 화가 나다 'anger arises' or 화를 내다 'show anger' for ordinary irritation, while 분노 is reserved for grave, often moral or collective rage — social injustice, betrayal, public outrage — and shows up in news, speeches, and writing far more than in casual chat. Saying 분노했어요 over a late bus sounds comically overblown; 짜증 났어요 'I got annoyed' or 화가 났어요 fits. The pitfall: English 'angry' is one word covering all intensities, so learners overuse 분노. Match the register — keep 분노 for the heavy stuff and use 화/짜증 for daily friction.

Using 분노 for everyday irritation. 분노 is grave wrath (often moral/public). For 'I'm annoyed/angry' in daily life, say 화가 났어요 or 짜증 났어요.
Treating 분노 like an adjective: 분노해요 to mean 'I'm angry' is stiff. Either use the verb 분노하다 only for serious outrage, or switch to 화가 나요.
Mismatched verb: 분노를 하다 is wrong. Use 분노를 느끼다 'feel anger', 분노가 치밀다 'anger surges', or 분노하다 as one verb.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 두려움 means "fear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "fear" is 두려움 (duryeoum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 두려움이 밀려와요 ("Fear washes over me"). Watch the particle attached to 두려움 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 두려움 + 이; 밀려오다 conveys fear creeping or surging in
느끼다 'feel' is the standard verb for this inner emotion
이겨내다 'win out over' is the inspiring partner verb
noun + 없이 'without' is the set adverbial phrase

examples.en: I'm scared to sleep alone
examples.note: for plain 'I'm scared' use the adjective 무섭다, not the noun 두려움

examples.en: I felt fear before a new challenge
examples.note: 앞에서 'in front of' frames what you face; 두려움 fits abstract dread

examples.ko: 실패에 대한 두려움이 그를 멈추게 했어요
examples.romanization: silpaee daehan duryeoumi geureul meomchuge haesseoyo
examples.en: Fear of failure made him stop
examples.note: N에 대한 두려움 'fear of/about N' is the standard frame for what is feared

extendedVocab.nuance: 두려움 is the noun 'fear/dread', from the adjective 두렵다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 두렵 + 음 → 두려움). It names a deep, often anticipatory inner fear — of the future, failure, the unknown — more reflective and lasting than a sudden jolt. Separate two relatives: 무서움/무섭다 is concrete, gut-level scared ('a scary movie', 'the dog is scary'), the word you actually say in conversation, whereas 두려움 is heavier, more abstract and literary, and is the one paired with big life anxieties. A third, 공포 (恐怖), is sheer terror/horror, the genre word for horror films and panic. So a spider triggers 무서움, an uncertain future triggers 두려움, a horror movie deals in 공포. Saying 두려움이에요 for 'I'm scared'. That means 'It is fear'. Use the adjective 무서워요 (everyday) or 두려워요 (weightier).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 외로움 means "loneliness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 외로움 (oeroum) = "loneliness". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 외로움을 타다 ("to be prone to loneliness") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 외로움, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 외로움을 타다 'catch/feel loneliness' is the idiomatic set phrase, like catching a chill
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb
외로움 pairs with 깊은 'deep', as in English
달래다 'comfort/soothe' is the tender partner verb

examples.en: I'm a bit lonely these days
examples.note: for 'I feel lonely' use the adjective 외롭다, not the noun

examples.en: I feel loneliness living away from home
examples.note: 에서 marks the situation that produces the feeling

examples.ko: 사람들 속에서도 외로움을 느낄 때가 있어요
examples.romanization: saramdeul sogeseodo oeroumeul neukkil ttaega isseoyo
examples.en: There are times I feel lonely even amid people
examples.note: 속에서도 'even within' captures the ache of loneliness in a crowd

extendedVocab.nuance: 외로움 is the noun 'loneliness', from the adjective 외롭다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 외롭 + 음 → 외로움). It is the empty, aching emotional sense of being cut off from others — a feeling you can have even surrounded by people. The sharp contrast learners need is 혼자 'alone' (just the physical fact of being by oneself, no feeling implied) versus 외로움 (the emotion). You can be 혼자 and perfectly content, or in a crowd and full of 외로움. A subtler neighbor is 고독 (孤獨), 'solitude': 고독 is weightier, often chosen or even noble — the solitude of an artist — while 외로움 is the plain, sad pang of missing connection. A very Korean collocation is 외로움을 타다, literally 'to ride/catch loneliness', meaning someone gets lonely easily. Pitfall: don't equate 외로움 with 혼자 — being alone and feeling lonely are different words, and 'I'm lonely' is the adjective 외로워요, not 외로움이에요.

Equating 외로움 with 혼자. 혼자 means 'alone' (a fact); 외로움 is the painful feeling. '혼자 있어요' just says you're by yourself, with no sadness implied.
Saying 외로움이에요 for 'I'm lonely'. That says 'It is loneliness'. Use the adjective 외로워요 (note the ㅂ-irregular).
Missing the idiom 외로움을 타다 ('to get lonely easily') and instead overusing 외로움이 많다, which sounds less natural for a personality trait.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 그리움 means "longing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 그리움 (geurium) means "longing". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그리움이 사무치다 ("longing pierces deep"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그리움 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 그리움 + 이; 사무치다 'pierce to the bone' is the literary set verb
느끼다 'feel' is the everyday verb
에 젖다 'be soaked in' is the poetic idiom for being filled with the feeling
그리움 + 의 + noun marks who/what is missed

examples.en: I miss my mom
examples.note: to say 'I miss ___' Koreans use 보고 싶다 'want to see', not the noun 그리움

examples.en: Longing for my hometown washes over me
examples.note: N에 대한 그리움 'longing for N' is the standard frame

examples.ko: 오래된 편지가 그 시절의 그리움을 불러일으켜요
examples.romanization: oraedoen pyeonjiga geu sijeorui geuriumeul bulleoireukyeoyo
examples.en: An old letter stirs up longing for those days
examples.note: 불러일으키다 'stir up/evoke' pairs with deep nostalgic feelings

extendedVocab.nuance: 그리움 is the noun 'longing/yearning', from the verb 그리워하다 / adjective 그립다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 그립 + 음 → 그리움). It is a warm, bittersweet ache for someone or somewhere absent — a person far away, a lost time, your hometown — blending sweetness with quiet sorrow, close to English 'nostalgia' when aimed at the past. The key contrast is the everyday verb 보고 싶다, literally 'want to see', which is how Koreans actually say 'I miss you/it' in conversation; 그리움 is the noun naming that emotion and lands more poetic and reflective, common in songs and writing. Don't confuse it with 후회 'regret' (wishing you'd acted differently) — 그리움 carries no fault, only tender missing. The pitfall for English speakers: 'I miss you' is not 당신의 그리움 or 그리움이에요; it is 보고 싶어요. Save the noun 그리움 for when the feeling itself is the subject or object (그리움이 밀려오다, 그리움을 느끼다), and remember the ㅂ-irregular: 그립다 → 그리워요, 그리움.

Translating 'I miss you' as 그리움이에요. That means 'It is longing'. The natural sentence is 보고 싶어요 ('I want to see you').
Confusing 그리움 with 후회 'regret'. 그리움 is tender missing with no blame; 후회 is wishing you had done otherwise. Don't use 그리움 when you mean you regret something.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular: the adjective is 그립다 → 그리워요, and the noun 그리움 — not '그립음'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 즐거움 means "enjoyment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "enjoyment" is 즐거움 (jeulgeoum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 즐거움이 가득하다 ("to be full of enjoyment"). Watch the particle attached to 즐거움 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 즐거움 + 이; 가득하다 'be full' collocates with abundant feeling
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb
누리다 'enjoy, partake of' is the elevated partner verb for pleasures one gets to have
소소한 'small, modest' + 즐거움 is a very common warm collocation

examples.en: I really had fun today
examples.note: for 'it was fun / I had fun' use the adjective 즐겁다, not the noun

examples.en: I felt great enjoyment on the trip
examples.note: 에서 marks the activity that gives the pleasure

examples.ko: 요리는 저에게 소소한 즐거움 중 하나예요
examples.romanization: yorineun jeoege sosohan jeulgeoum jung hanayeyo
examples.en: Cooking is one of my small everyday joys
examples.note: 중 하나 'one among' frames it as a recurring source of pleasure

extendedVocab.nuance: 즐거움 is the noun 'enjoyment/fun', from the adjective 즐겁다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 즐겁 + 음 → 즐거움). It is the lively, active pleasure you get from doing something you like — a trip, a hobby, good company — more outward and activity-driven than the inner glow of 기쁨 'joy'. Draw the line clearly: 기쁨 spikes at a good event (you passed!), while 즐거움 flows from an enjoyable experience (the party was fun). The everyday word is the adjective 재미있다 'be fun/interesting', used for movies, games, and stories; 즐겁다/즐거움 is a touch warmer and more about your own good time than about the thing being amusing. A lovely set phrase is 소소한 즐거움 'small everyday pleasures'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'fun' is an adjective in English, so learners say 즐거움이에요 meaning 'it's fun' — but that's the noun ('It is enjoyment'); say 즐거워요 or 재미있어요. Mind the ㅂ-irregular: 즐겁다 → 즐거워요, 즐거움.

Saying 즐거움이에요 for 'it's fun'. That means 'It is enjoyment'. Use the adjective 즐거워요 (your good time) or 재미있어요 (the thing is fun).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 부끄러움 means "shyness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 부끄러움 (bukkeureoum) = "shyness". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 부끄러움을 타다 ("to be shy by nature") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 부끄러움을 타다 'catch shyness' is the idiom for being a shy person
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb
부끄러움이 많다 'have much shyness' describes a bashful personality
도 없이 'without even' intensifies the absence of embarrassment

examples.en: I was so embarrassed when presenting
examples.note: for 'I felt shy/embarrassed' use the adjective 부끄럽다

examples.en: I felt shy at being praised
examples.note: -고 links the cause; blushing-shyness, not moral shame

examples.ko: 그는 부끄러움이 많아서 처음엔 말이 없어요
examples.romanization: geuneun bukkeureoumi manaseo cheoeumen mari eopseoyo
examples.en: He is very shy, so he's quiet at first
examples.note: 부끄러움이 많다 describes a bashful temperament

extendedVocab.nuance: 부끄러움 is the noun 'shyness/embarrassment', from the adjective 부끄럽다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽 + 음 → 부끄러움). It spans two warm, social shades: bashful shyness (blushing when praised or on stage) and light embarrassment (a small social slip). Crucially, contrast it with 창피함/창피하다, which is sharper, more 'mortified / lost face' embarrassment — tripping in public, an awkward gaffe you cringe at — and with 수치심 (羞恥心), a heavy, dignity-wounding shame tied to disgrace. So a blush at a compliment is 부끄러움, spilling coffee on yourself in front of everyone leans 창피함, and a scandal that destroys your honor is 수치심. A native collocation is 부끄러움을 타다 'to be the shy type', parallel to 외로움을 타다. Saying 부끄러움이에요 for 'I'm embarrassed'. That means 'It is shyness'. Use 부끄러워요, the adjective.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 용기 means "courage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 용기 (yonggi) means "courage". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 용기가 필요해요 ("Courage is needed"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 용기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 용기 ends in a vowel → 가; 필요하다 'be needed' is the set partner
용기를 내다 'put out courage' is the fixed idiom — not 만들다 'make' or 가지다 'have'
잃다 'lose' is the opposing partner verb
북돋우다 'spur on' is the verb for giving others courage

examples.en: Be brave / Take heart
examples.note: 용기를 내다 is THE everyday phrase for 'work up the nerve'

examples.en: I worked up the courage to confess
examples.note: Verb-ㄹ/을 용기 'the courage to do' modifies 용기 with what you dared

examples.en: Your support gave me courage
examples.note: 용기를 얻다 'gain courage' pairs naturally with encouragement from others

extendedVocab.nuance: 용기 is the Sino-Korean noun 'courage/bravery', 용기 勇氣 — 勇 'brave' + 氣 'spirit/energy' — literally 'brave spirit'. Contrast 용기 with 자신감 (自信感) 'confidence/self-assurance': 자신감 is belief in your own ability ('confidence in your English'), built from skill, while 용기 is the nerve to act despite fear, regardless of skill. You also 얻다 'gain' or 잃다 'lose' 용기. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — saying 용기를 가지다 instead of the idiomatic 용기를 내다 — and conflating 'courage' with 'confidence' (자신감), which are distinct in Korean.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 희망 means "hope" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "hope" is 희망 (huimang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 희망이 있어요 ("There is hope"). Watch the particle attached to 희망 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 희망 + 이; 있다/없다 'there is/isn't' is the core partner
unlike most feelings, 희망 naturally takes 가지다 'have', plus 품다 'cherish'
잃다 'lose' is the standard opposite collocation
희망 + 의 + noun forms set phrases like 희망의 끈 'a thread of hope'

examples.en: There's still hope
examples.note: 있다 'exist' is the everyday verb; 아직 'still' is a frequent companion

examples.en: I hold hope for the future
examples.note: N에 대한 희망 'hope for/about N' is the standard frame for what is hoped for

examples.en: Don't let go of that small thread of hope
examples.note: 희망의 끈 'thread of hope' + 놓다 'let go' is a set encouraging idiom

It is a bright, forward-looking expectation that good things will come, weightier and more enduring than a casual wish, and it gives comfort and strength in hard times. Separate it from two relatives. 소원 (所願) is a specific 'wish' you make — the one wish on a shooting star or a birthday candle — concrete and singular, whereas 희망 is broader, an outlook on the future. 기대 (期待) is 'expectation/anticipation', leaning toward something you fairly confidently await ('I have high 기대 for the movie'), while 희망 keeps the sense of hoping for an uncertain but desired outcome. The English-speaker pitfall is using 희망 for a small, immediate wish where 소원 or the grammar pattern -았으면 좋겠다 'I wish that…' is natural, e.g. for 'I hope it doesn't rain' Koreans say 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요, not a sentence built on 희망.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 추억 means "memory" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 추억 (chueok) = "memory". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 추억이 떠오르다 ("a memory comes to mind") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 추억, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 추억 + 이; 떠오르다 'float up' is the set verb for memories surfacing
추억을 만들다 'make memories' is the exact, very common collocation
에 잠기다 'be submerged in' is the idiom for reminiscing
추억 + 의 + noun marks a spot tied to fond recollection

examples.en: I have many good memories
examples.note: 추억 collocates with 좋은 'good' and 많다 'be many'

examples.en: We made many memories traveling together
examples.note: 추억을 만들다 'make memories' — the natural verb is 만들다, never 하다

examples.ko: 이 노래를 들으면 학창 시절 추억에 잠겨요
examples.romanization: i noraereul deureumyeon hakchang sijeol chueoge jamgyeoyo
examples.en: When I hear this song I sink into memories of my school days
examples.note: 추억에 잠기다 captures dwelling in fond nostalgia

extendedVocab.nuance: 추억 is the Sino-Korean noun for a 'cherished memory', 추억 追憶 — 追 'pursue, trace back' + 憶 'recollect' — so literally 'tracing back a recollection', a warm act of looking fondly on the past. The vital contrast is with 기억 (記憶), 'memory' in the neutral, factual sense: 기억 is your mental record of any information — a phone number, where you parked, what someone said — and can be good or bad, while 추억 is specifically a treasured, emotionally warm past experience you reminisce about. So you 기억하다 'remember' a fact, but you 추억을 만들다 'make memories' on a trip and look back on 좋은 추억 'good memories' from childhood. A signature collocation is 추억을 만들다 'make memories', built with 만들다, not 하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 추억 for ordinary remembering — 'Do you remember his name?' must use 기억 (그 사람 이름 기억나요?), because 추억 implies sentiment and a whole experience, not mere recall.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 추억 for plain factual memory. 'Do you remember the password?' needs 기억 (기억나요?), not 추억, which means a fond, sentimental past experience.
Saying 추억을 하다 for 'make memories'. The fixed verb is 만들다: 추억을 만들다. To reminisce, use 추억에 잠기다 or 추억을 떠올리다.
Calling a bad event a 추억. 추억 carries warmth; an unpleasant thing you recall is just a 기억 (안 좋은 기억) or 일.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 감정 means "emotion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 감정 (gamjeong) means "emotion". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 감정이 상하다 ("to get one's feelings hurt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 감정 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 감정이 상하다 'feelings spoil' is the fixed idiom for being hurt/offended
표현하다 'express' is the natural partner verb
숨기다 'hide/conceal' is the common opposite collocation
감정 + 의 + noun links the feeling to its shift

examples.en: My feelings got hurt
examples.note: 감정이 상하다 is THE set phrase for feeling hurt or offended

examples.ko: 저는 감정 표현을 잘 안 해요
examples.romanization: jeoneun gamjeong pyohyeoneul jal an haeyo
examples.en: I don't really express my emotions
examples.note: 감정 표현 'emotional expression' is a common compound noun

examples.en: There are times feeling runs ahead of reason
examples.note: 감정 vs 이성 'reason' is the classic paired contrast

extendedVocab.nuance: 감정 is the Sino-Korean cover term for 'emotion/feeling', 감정 感情 — 感 'feel, sense' + 情 'feeling, affection' — the umbrella under which 기쁨, 슬픔, 분노 and the rest all sit, broader than any single mood. Two contrasts matter. Against 기분 (氣分), 'mood/how you feel right now': 기분 is the transient, surface state of the moment — 기분이 좋아요 'I'm in a good mood', 기분 나빠 'that bugs me' — and it is what you use in everyday chat, whereas 감정 is the deeper, more general category of human emotion and sounds more analytical. Against 이성 (理性), 'reason/rationality': 감정 vs 이성 is the standard 'heart vs head' pairing in Korean. The signature idiom is 감정이 상하다, literally 'the feelings spoil', meaning to get hurt or offended — a phrase learners must know. The English-speaker pitfall: for everyday 'I feel good/bad' do not say 감정이 좋아요; the natural sentence is 기분이 좋아요. Reserve 감정 for talking about emotions in general, expressing/hiding them (감정을 표현하다/숨기다), or being hurt (감정이 상하다).

Missing the idiom 감정이 상하다 ('to get hurt/offended') and instead saying 감정이 아프다 ('emotion hurts'), which is unnatural for offense.
Treating 감정 as one specific feeling. 감정 is the umbrella term; to name an actual feeling, use 기쁨, 슬픔, 화 etc. '복잡한 감정' (mixed emotions) is fine, but a single feeling is better named directly.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 식사 means "meal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "meal" is 식사 (siksa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식사를 해요 ("I have a meal"). Watch the particle attached to 식사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 식사하다 is the verb; 를 marks the meal as object
subject 가 — the meal itself is delayed
honorific -시- greeting to elders
준비하다 = prepare; sets the table/cooks

examples.en: Let's eat together.
examples.note: casual invite; 식사하다 fuses noun + 하다

examples.en: Today's meal was really delicious.
examples.note: compliment to the cook; past tense

examples.en: Director, have you eaten yet?
examples.note: standard polite greeting up the hierarchy

extendedVocab.nuance: 식사 食事 (literally 'eat-affair') is the dignified, Sino-Korean word for a meal, while 밥 is the plain native word that also literally means cooked rice. The dividing line is register, not meaning: with friends or children you say 밥 먹었어? but to a boss, an elder, or a customer you switch to 식사하셨어요?, which sounds respectful and adult. 식사 pairs naturally with 하다 (식사하다), 준비하다, 대접하다 (treat someone to a meal). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the verb 식사를 먹다; Korean treats 식사 as an activity, so you either say 식사하다 or, more plainly, 밥을 먹다 — never 식사를 먹다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 식사를 먹어요. 식사 already implies eating, so it takes 하다: 식사해요, or use 밥을 먹어요 instead.
Greeting a close friend with 식사하셨어요? — it sounds stiffly formal; with peers say 밥 먹었어?
Treating 식사 as countable like 'three meals'. Koreans count meals with 끼: 하루 세 끼 (three meals a day), not 세 식사.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 소금 means "salt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 소금 (sogeum) = "salt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 소금을 넣어요 ("I add salt") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 소금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = put in; 을 marks the salt
subject 이 — the food is over-salted
조금 = a little, softens the amount
좀 + 주세요 = soft polite request

examples.en: I add a little salt to the soup.
examples.note: cooking action with 에 (into the soup)

examples.en: This food is a bit salty.
examples.note: describe taste with 짜다, not 소금이 많다

examples.en: If it's bland, add more salt.
examples.note: conditional -으면; 더 = more

extendedVocab.nuance: 소금 is plain native-Korean table salt, the baseline seasoning whose taste is 짜다 (salty). Don't confuse the substance with the flavor: the food is described as 짜요 (salty) or 싱거워요 (bland/under-seasoned), while 소금 is the thing you add to fix bland food. Its constant opposite in the kitchen is 설탕 (sugar), and the two look and pour alike, which is exactly the running joke when a cook grabs the wrong jar. 소금 collocates with 넣다, 뿌리다 (sprinkle), 치다 (toss salt on), and 간을 하다 (season to taste). The English-speaker trap is the particle on requests: say 소금 좀 주세요, not 소금을 주세요 with full force — the bare 소금 + 좀 sounds far more natural and polite at a table.

Confusing 소금 (salt) with 설탕 (sugar) — they sit side by side; taste-check before adding.
Using 소금을 주세요 stiffly. At the table, 소금 좀 주세요 is the warm, idiomatic request.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 설탕 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = put in; 을 marks the sugar
but for taste prefer the adjective 달다

usagePhrases.en: I add a lot of sugar
usagePhrases.note: 많이 = a lot, adverb before the verb
없이 = without (no particle after it)

examples.en: I add sugar to the coffee.
examples.note: 에 marks the drink it goes into

examples.ko: 저는 단 거 별로 안 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun dan geo byeollo an joahaeyo.
examples.en: I don't really like sweet things.
examples.note: express preference with 단 거, not 설탕

examples.en: This bread is too sweet.
examples.note: describe taste with 달다, not 설탕이 많다

extendedVocab.nuance: 설탕 雪糖 (literally 'snow-sugar', for its white crystals) is refined white sugar; the taste it gives is 달다 (sweet). As with salt, separate the substance from the flavor — food is 달아요 (sweet), and 설탕 is what makes it so. Korean savory cooking quietly uses a spoon of 설탕 to round off salty-spicy sauces, so 설탕 is a normal pantry item, not just for dessert. Its kitchen partner-opposite is 소금, and it collocates with 넣다, 뿌리다, and 타다 (dissolve sugar into a drink). A frequent English-speaker pitfall: to say a dish 'is sweet' use 달아요, not 설탕이 많아요, which oddly reports the ingredient amount rather than the taste.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 이 빵은 설탕이 많아요 for 'this bread is sweet'. Say 달아요 — describe the taste, not the dose.
Mixing up 설탕 (sugar) with 소금 (salt); both are white powders, so confirm before adding.
Forgetting 없이 takes no particle: it's 설탕 없이, never 설탕을 없이.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the sauce
subject 이 + adjective 짜다

usagePhrases.en: I dip it in soy sauce

붓다 (ㅅ-irregular) → 부어요

examples.note: 찍어 먹다 = dip-and-eat, one motion

examples.note: describe with 짜다

extendedVocab.nuance: 간장 (the 간 here is the native root meaning 'saltiness/seasoning', not a hanja for liver) is dark fermented soy sauce that delivers a deep savory saltiness plain 소금 can't reach. Two real types matter in a Korean kitchen: 국간장 (light, for seasoning soups) versus 진간장/양조간장 (darker, for stir-fries and braises and as a dip), so 'soy sauce' is really a small family. It collocates with 찍다 (dip), 넣다, 붓다, 조리다 (braise in soy sauce), and 졸이다. The English-speaker pitfall is the dipping particle: you dip food INTO sauce with 에 — 간장에 찍다 — not 간장을 찍다; and note 붓다 is ㅅ-irregular, dropping the ㅅ to give 부어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 간장을 찍어요 for dipping. The sauce is the destination: 간장에 찍어 먹어요.
Calling 간장 sweet. Its defining taste is salty/savory — 짜다 — though braises add sugar.
Conjugating 붓다 as 붓어요. It is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요 (pour).

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 고추장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the paste
맵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 매워요

usagePhrases.en: I mix it with chili paste
usagePhrases.note: 비비다 = mix; 에 marks what you mix into
바르다 (르-irregular) → 발라요

examples.en: I add chili paste to bibimbap.
examples.note: 에 marks the dish it goes into

examples.en: This chili paste is really spicy.
examples.note: 매워요 from ㅂ-irregular 맵다

examples.en: I mix rice with chili paste and eat it.
examples.note: 비벼 먹다 = mix-and-eat

extendedVocab.nuance: 고추장 (고추 'chili pepper' + 장 醬 'fermented paste') is thick red fermented chili paste — spicy 맵다 but with an underlying sweetness and fermented depth, so it isn't just 'hot'. Keep it apart from its jar-mate 된장 (brown soybean paste, savory not spicy) and from 고춧가루 (dry chili powder); all three live in Korean cooking but do different jobs. 고추장 collocates with 비비다 (mix into rice), 넣다, 풀다 (dissolve into stew), and 찍다 (dip lettuce/cucumber). Two conjugation traps hide here: the partner verbs 맵다 (→ 매워요, ㅂ-irregular) and 바르다 (→ 발라요, 르-irregular) both shift stems, and you mix rice 고추장에 비벼요 with 에, not 고추장을.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 고추장 and 된장 as the same paste. 고추장 is red and spicy; 된장 is brown, salty-savory soybean paste.
Saying 맵어요. 맵다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 매워요.
Confusing 고추장 (the paste) with 고춧가루 (dry chili powder) — different texture and use.

extendedVocab.explanation: 된장 (doenjang) means "soybean paste". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 된장을 풀어요 ("I dissolve soybean paste"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 된장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 풀다 = dissolve/loosen into liquid
subject 이 + 짜다
으로 = with/using (instrument)
넣다 = add

examples.en: Mom makes stew with soybean paste.
examples.note: 으로 marks 된장 as the means

examples.en: This soybean paste is a bit salty.
examples.note: taste check with 짜다

examples.en: I dissolve soybean paste into the broth.
examples.note: 풀다 = stir paste until it spreads

extendedVocab.nuance: 된장 (된 'thick/stiff' + 장 醬 'fermented paste') is brown fermented soybean paste with a deep, salty, almost cheesy umami; it is the backbone of 된장찌개, perhaps the most everyday Korean stew. The key verb is 풀다 (literally 'loosen'): because the paste is dense, you don't just drop it in, you stir it until it dissolves through the broth — 된장을 물에 풀다. Don't mix it up with red 고추장 (spicy chili paste) or with Japanese-style miso, which is milder and sweeter. 된장 collocates with 풀다, 끓이다, 넣다, and 으로/로 (cook WITH it). The English-speaker pitfall is the instrument particle: 된장으로 끓이다 (because 된장 ends in a consonant it takes 으로, not 로).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 된장 (brown, savory) with 고추장 (red, spicy). Different color, different taste.
Saying 된장을 넣다 and stopping. For stew you 풀다 — stir it until it dissolves through the broth.
Using 된장로. After a final consonant the instrument particle is 으로: 된장으로 끓여요.

Watch the particle attached to 식초 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 넣다 = add; 를 marks the vinegar
시다 → 시어요 (sour)
조금 = a little
섞다 = mix together

examples.en: I add a little vinegar to the cold noodles.
examples.note: 에 marks the dish

examples.en: This vinegar is too sour.
examples.note: describe with 시다

examples.ko: 식초 한 숟가락 넣으면 더 새콤해요.
examples.romanization: sikcho han sutgarang neoeumyeon deo saekomhaeyo.
examples.en: Add one spoon of vinegar and it gets tangier.
examples.note: 새콤하다 = pleasantly tangy

extendedVocab.nuance: 식초 食醋 (literally 'food-vinegar') is sour vinegar used to give food a fresh, sharp tang. Its core taste word is 시다 (sour), but Koreans often prefer the softer, appetizing 새콤하다 ('pleasantly tangy'), which carries a positive nuance that plain 시다 lacks — vinegar in cold noodles or pickles is 새콤해요, not merely 셔요. It collocates with 넣다, 섞다, 치다 (splash vinegar on), and the flavor pair 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour). The English-speaker pitfall is conjugating 시다: the 요-form is 시어요/셔요, not 'sieyo' as a literal vowel-by-vowel reading might suggest, and learners often default to 'sour' = 시다 when describing dressed dishes, where 새콤하다 sounds far more natural and tasty.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Expecting 식초 to be sweet. Its defining taste is sour — 시다.
Describing dressed cold noodles only as 셔요. The tastier, idiomatic word is 새콤해요 (pleasantly tangy).
Forgetting 식초 ends in a vowel, so the object particle is 를: 식초를 넣어요, not 식초을.

extendedVocab.explanation: 후추 (huchu) = "pepper (black pepper)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 후추를 뿌려요 ("I sprinkle pepper") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 후추, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 뿌리다 = sprinkle/scatter; 를 marks pepper
맵다 → 매워요
조금 = a little
좀 + 주세요 polite request

examples.en: I sprinkle pepper on the meat.
examples.note: 에 marks the surface; 뿌리다 = scatter on top

examples.note: 후추 맛 = pepper flavor

examples.en: Pass me the pepper, please.
examples.note: at the table; bare noun + 좀

extendedVocab.nuance: 후추 (originally from 호초 胡椒, 'foreign/barbarian pepper', reflecting that black pepper came via the Silk Road) is ground black pepper that gives a sharp, warm, slightly numbing pungency. The crucial contrast is 후추 (black pepper) versus 고추 (chili pepper) and 고춧가루 (chili powder): they sound alike to beginners but are botanically unrelated and taste different — 후추 is woody and aromatic, 고추 is fiery red heat. 후추 collocates with 뿌리다 (its signature verb — you sprinkle it on at the end), 넣다, 갈다 (grind), and 후추 맛/향 (pepper taste/aroma). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly the 후추/고추 mix-up, plus reaching for 넣다 when the natural finishing verb is 뿌리다, scattering it over the top.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 후추 (black pepper) with 고추 (chili pepper). One is a brown ground spice, the other a red hot vegetable.
Saying 후추를 넣어요 for a final sprinkle. The idiomatic verb is 뿌리다 — 후추를 뿌려요.
Using 후추을. 후추 ends in a vowel, so the particle is 를: 후추를.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 양념 means "seasoning; marinade" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 양념 (yangnyeom) means "seasoning; marinade". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 양념을 만들어요 ("I make the seasoning"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 양념 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 만들다 = make; 을 marks the seasoning mix
맵다 → 매워요

usagePhrases.en: I marinate it in the seasoning
usagePhrases.note: 재우다 = let marinate; 에 marks the bath
넣다 = add

examples.en: Mom makes the marinade for the meat.
examples.note: 고기 양념 = seasoning for meat

examples.en: This seasoning is a bit spicy.
examples.note: describe with 맵다

examples.en: I marinate the chicken in the seasoning.
examples.note: 재우다 = leave to soak up flavor

extendedVocab.nuance: 양념 is the native-Korean word for a whole blend of seasonings — soy sauce, garlic, sesame oil, sugar, chili — mixed to flavor a dish, NOT a single spice. This is the key contrast: one spice is a 향신료 or just its name (소금, 후추), but the prepared mixture you rub or pour on is 양념. The word also signals a style: 양념치킨 is chicken coated in sweet-spicy 양념 sauce, opposite 후라이드 (plain fried). 양념 collocates with 만들다 (make), 무치다 (toss/dress vegetables in it), 재우다 (marinate), 바르다 (brush on), and the verb 양념하다 (to season). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 양념 = one spice; if you only added salt, that's not really 양념 — 양념 implies a composed blend, and you marinate IN it with 에 (양념에 재우다).

Thinking 양념 means a single spice. It's a blended seasoning/marinade; one spice is its own name (소금, 후추).
Saying 양념을 재워요. You marinate the food IN seasoning: 닭고기를 양념에 재워요.
Forgetting the verb form 양념하다 (to season), distinct from just naming the noun 양념.

extendedVocab.explanation: "broth; soup liquid" is 국물 (gungmul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국물을 마셔요 ("I drink the broth"). Watch the particle attached to 국물 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 마시다 = drink; 을 marks the liquid
뜨겁다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 뜨거워요
시원하다 here = soothing, not cold
더 = more

examples.en: I drank up all the ramyeon broth.
examples.note: 다 = all the way; 마시다 for liquid

examples.en: This broth is really soothing.
examples.note: hot soup that feels good going down

examples.note: -니까 = because; warning

extendedVocab.nuance: 국물 (국 'soup' + 물 'water') is the liquid part of a soup or stew, as opposed to the 건더기 (the solid pieces) — that pair is the contrast to know. Its most famous quirk is the word 시원하다: applied to a steaming hot broth, 시원해요 does NOT mean cold — it means the hot liquid feels refreshing, clearing, soothing, the way a hot bath or a sip of hot soup makes you exhale 'ahh'. 국물 collocates with 마시다 (drink — you drink broth, you don't 먹다 it), 우러나다 (flavor steeps out), 진하다 (rich/concentrated), and 시원하다/뜨겁다. The headline English-speaker pitfall is hearing 시원한 국물 and translating 'cold broth' — for liquid you actually drink, use 마시다, and read 시원하다 as 'soothing'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 시원한 국물 as 'cold broth'. For hot soup it means refreshing/soothing as it goes down.
Saying 국물을 먹어요. Broth is a liquid you 마시다 (drink): 국물을 마셔요.
Conjugating 뜨겁다 as 뜨겁어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 뜨거워요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 참기름 (참 'true/genuine' + 기름 'oil') is fragrant toasted sesame oil, prized for finishing dishes — added at the very end for aroma, not used for high-heat frying. Watch the particle attached to 거실 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 거실 + 이 because the word ends in a consonant; subject of a description

usagePhrases.en: There is a TV in the living room.
usagePhrases.note: static existence uses 에, not 에서

usagePhrases.en: I rest in the living room.
usagePhrases.note: an action happens here, so 에서 replaces 에
거실 as a direct object takes 을

examples.en: This is the living room.
examples.note: simplest 이다 sentence introducing a room to a guest

examples.en: The family gathers in the living room and watches TV.
examples.note: everyday: 거실 collocates with 모이다 (gather) and 텔레비전을 보다

examples.ko: 손님이 오면 거실로 안내해서 소파에 앉으시게 해요.
examples.romanization: sonnimi omyeon geosillo annaehaeseo sopae anjeusige haeyo.
examples.en: When guests come, I show them to the living room and seat them on the sofa.
examples.note: real situation: direction 로 (to the living room) + honorific 앉으시다

extendedVocab.nuance: 거실 is the shared 'living/common' room of a Korean home — the social hub where the family relaxes together and where guests are received, almost always centred on a 소파 and a TV. It is Sino-Korean: 居室, literally 居 'to dwell/reside' + 室 'room', so the feel is 'the room you live in (together)'. Contrast it with 응접실 (應接室, a formal parlour for receiving visitors), which sounds old-fashioned and upper-class today, and with 방, the generic word for any closed 'room/bedroom'; 거실 specifically names the open central area. Register is fully neutral — children and adults alike say 거실. The big English-speaker pitfall is location particles: because a TV simply sits there you say 거실에 텔레비전이 있어요 (에 = existence), but because you *do* something there you switch to 거실에서 쉬어요 (에서 = action). Mixing these up (거실에서 텔레비전이 있어요) is the single most common error.

Saying 거실에서 소파가 있어요 to mean 'there is a sofa in the living room'. Existence/location of a thing takes 에 (거실에 소파가 있어요); 에서 only marks the place where an action occurs.
Calling the living room 방. 방 means a closed private room (often a bedroom); the open central area is specifically 거실. Use 거실, not 방, for the family room.
Treating 거실 as 'house' and saying 거실에 가요 for 'I'm going home'. To go home you say 집에 가요; 거실 is just one room inside the 집.

usagePhrases.note: existence of furniture uses 에
sleeping is an action, so 에서
침실 as object takes 을

examples.note: simple 이다 sentence labelling a room

examples.note: real situation: topic-marked 에서는 + 발소리를 죽이다 idiom

extendedVocab.nuance: 침실 is the private 'sleeping room', Sino-Korean 寢室 from 寢 'to sleep/lie down' + 室 'room' — so literally 'sleep-room', which makes its core meaning easy to remember. It names the room by its function (sleeping), whereas the everyday word 방 is the neutral term for any room and is what Koreans most often say in casual speech ('내 방' = my room) even when they mean their bedroom; 침실 sounds slightly more formal or descriptive, the word you'd see on a floor plan or in a real-estate ad (안방 = the main/master bedroom). usagePhrases.note: existence of objects uses 에

usagePhrases.note: drying is an action → 에서

examples.note: simple description with 가

extendedVocab.nuance: 베란다 is a loanword (from English 'veranda'), so there is no hanja — and that loan path creates the main pitfall: in Korean apartments 베란다 actually refers to what English calls a *balcony/utility deck*, the enclosed strip off the living room where families keep 화분 (potted plants), dry 빨래 (laundry) and 고추 (chillies), and store overflow. Technically architects distinguish 발코니 (balcony) from 베란다 and from 테라스 (terrace, a ground-level open deck), but in ordinary speech most Koreans just say 베란다 for that apartment space. Contrast it with 마당, the open *yard/ground* of a detached house — 베란다 hangs off an upper-floor flat, 마당 is earth you stand on. Register is fully neutral. Watch the particles: plants simply sit there (베란다에 화분이 있어요, 에) but laundry is actively dried there (베란다에서 빨래를 말려요, 에서); and because it ends in a vowel the subject marker is 가, not 이.

usagePhrases.note: shoes exist there → 에

usagePhrases.note: taking off is an action → 에서

extendedVocab.nuance: 현관 is the indoor 'entry hall' of a home — the small sunken or tiled area just inside the door where you step out of your shoes before going up into the living space. It is Sino-Korean 玄關, literally 玄 'dark/profound' + 關 'barrier/gate', a term originally from Zen architecture meaning the threshold into a dwelling. The all-important cultural point: Koreans always remove shoes at the 현관 (현관에서 신발을 벗어요), so this word carries the whole shoes-off custom. Distinguish it sharply from 대문, the *outer gate* opening from the street into the yard: 대문 is outside on the property line, 현관 is the door/hall of the building itself — an apartment has a 현관 but no 대문. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'entrance' as one undifferentiated word and so reaching for 입구 (the entrance *to* a public place like a station or shop); for the entry of a *home* you must use 현관, and remember existence is 에 (신발이 현관에 있어요) but the act of removing shoes is 에서.

usagePhrases.note: thing hanging there → 에

extendedVocab.nuance: 벽 is a *vertical* dividing surface — the side of a room, the partition between flats, or a freestanding masonry wall — and it is the surface things get hung *on*. Using 벽 for a garden's boundary wall. The outer enclosing wall of a yard is 담 or 담장; 벽 is a structural/room wall.
Conjugating 하얗다 as 하얗아요. It is ㅎ-irregular: 벽이 하얘요 (drop ㅎ, contract to 얘).

sitting down onto the floor surface → 에

extendedVocab.nuance: 바닥 is the *floor* you stand, sit and (with 온돌 under-floor heating) even sleep on — a native-Korean word with no hanja. Its core sense is broader than English 'floor': 바닥 means the *bottom surface* of anything, so it also covers the bed/bottom of a pan, a river or the sea (강 바닥, 바다 바닥), and figuratively 'rock bottom' (가격이 바닥이다 = the price has hit bottom). For the part of a building you must not confuse it with 마루 (a wooden-floored area/hall) or with 층, which means a *storey/level* of a building — '2층' is the second floor *as a level*, but the surface you walk on is 바닥. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 층 when you mean the physical surface, and remember sitting *down onto* the floor uses 에 (바닥에 앉아요). Saying 바닥에서 가방이 있어요. The bag's presence takes 에 (바닥에 가방이 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action.
Conjugating 차갑다 as 차갑아요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 바닥이 차가워요 (ㅂ → 워).

usagePhrases.note: 천장 + 이 as subject of a quality

usagePhrases.en: There is a light on the ceiling.
usagePhrases.note: fixture mounted there → 에
the dripping happens/originates there → 에서

usagePhrases.en: I look up at the ceiling.
usagePhrases.note: 천장 as object takes 을

examples.en: This room has a high ceiling.
examples.note: simple description; 천장 collocates with 높다/낮다

examples.note: everyday: 천장에 달리다 (hung from the ceiling) modifying 등

examples.note: real situation: 물이 새다 (leak) + 얼룩이 생기다 (a stain forms)

extendedVocab.nuance: 천장 is the *inside* upper surface of a room — what you see when you lie down and look up, with the 등 (light) fixed to it. It is Sino-Korean 天障, literally 天 'sky' + 障 'barrier/screen', i.e. the 'sky-screen' overhead, a nice image for the indoor counterpart of the sky. The essential contrast is 천장 vs 지붕: 천장 is *inside* (ceiling), 지붕 is *outside* (roof). English collapses both into 'roof/ceiling' loosely, which is the main trap — indoors, always 천장. 천장 pairs with 높다/낮다 (high/low), 등이 달리다 (a light is hung), and 물이 새다/얼룩이 생기다 for leak damage. Register is neutral and descriptive. The particle pitfall is the familiar one: the light *is mounted* there (천장에 등이 있어요, 에) but water *drips* there (천장에서 물이 떨어져요, 에서, because dripping is the action/source). Memory hook: 천(天, sky) is up high → ceiling; 지붕 starts with 지 like 지구(earth)'s outer shell.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 지붕 for the indoor ceiling. The inside surface with the light is 천장; 지붕 is the outdoor roof only.
Saying 천장에서 등이 있어요. A mounted light's existence takes 에 (천장에 등이 있어요); reserve 에서 for the dripping/leaking action.
Pronouncing/writing it 천정. The standard form is 천장 (天障); 천정 is a common but non-standard variant — use 천장.

usagePhrases.en: There is a tree in the yard.
usagePhrases.note: the tree exists there → 에
playing is an action → 에서
마당 as object takes 을; 쓸다 (sweep)

examples.note: simple existence sentence; topic 집에는 + 마당이 있다

examples.note: everyday: 마당에서 + 뛰어놀다, comitative 랑

examples.note: real situation: 평상을 깔다 + 구워 먹다, a vivid Korean summer scene

extendedVocab.nuance: 마당 is the open *ground/yard* belonging to a detached house — bare earth or paving where the family dries crops, sweeps leaves, sets out a 평상, or grills meat in summer. It is a native-Korean word (no hanja) and carries a warm, traditional, single-house feel; an apartment dweller does *not* have a 마당, so the word itself implies a 단독주택 (detached home). Distinguish it sharply from 정원 (庭園), a cultivated ornamental *garden* with planned flowers and lawn — 마당 is plain working ground, 정원 is decorative; and from 베란다, the small deck off an apartment. Figuratively 마당 can even mean an 'occasion/situation' (이 마당에 = 'at this point/in this situation'), though beginners can set that aside. 마당 collocates with 넓다 (spacious), 쓸다 (sweep), 놀다 (play), 나무/꽃이 있다. Register is neutral and homely. Pitfall: don't use 마당 for an apartment's outdoor space (that's 베란다), and keep 에 for existence (마당에 나무가 있어요) versus 에서 for actions (마당에서 놀아요).

Using 마당 for an apartment's outdoor deck. 마당 is the ground of a detached house; an apartment's outdoor strip is 베란다.
Treating 마당 and 정원 as identical. 마당 is plain open yard/ground; 정원 is a planned ornamental garden. Pick by whether it's working ground or decorative planting.
Saying 마당에서 나무가 있어요. A tree's existence takes 에 (마당에 나무가 있어요); 에서 only marks where an action like 놀다 happens.

extendedVocab.nuance: 울타리 is a light, often see-through *fence/hedge* — wooden slats, wire, or a row of shrubs — that gently marks where a yard or field ends. It is native Korean (no hanja). Its core collocation is 울타리를 치다 ('put up a fence'), and figuratively it means a protective boundary ('가족이라는 울타리' = the shelter of family). Distinguish it sharply by *solidity and material*: a 울타리 is open and low, whereas 담 / 담장 is a *solid masonry wall* (brick or concrete) enclosing a property — English 'fence/wall' blurs these, but a thing you can see through is 울타리, a thing you cannot is 담. Don't confuse it with 벽 either: 벽 is a *building's* wall (a room side or partition), while 울타리 stands outdoors around open ground. Register is neutral, slightly rural/homely. The particle pitfall: leaning against or blooming on the fence uses 에 (울타리에 기대요), and because the word ends in a vowel its subject marker is 가, never 이.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 울타리 with 담. 담/담장 is a solid masonry boundary wall; 울타리 is a light open fence or hedge. Choose by whether you can see through it.
Using 울타리 for a room's wall. The wall of a building/room is 벽; 울타리 is an outdoor boundary around a yard.

extendedVocab.nuance: 대문 is the main *outer gate* of a house — the large door in the boundary wall through which you pass from the street into the 마당. It is Sino-Korean 大門, literally 大 'big' + 門 'gate/door' = 'big gate', which fits its sense as the principal entrance to the property. The crucial contrast is 대문 vs 현관: 대문 is *outside* on the property line (street → yard), while 현관 is the *building's* own entry hall where you take your shoes off (yard → inside); a detached house has both, but an apartment has only a 현관 and no 대문. Also distinguish the generic 문 ('door/gate' of anything) — 대문 specifically names the big front gate. 대문 collocates with 열다/닫다 (open/close), 잠그다 (lock), 두드리다 (knock), and 대문 앞 (in front of the gate). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfall: don't call the apartment building's entry door a 대문 (that's the 현관/공동현관), and keep 에 for what sits on the gate (대문에 자물쇠가 있어요) versus 에서 for actions like waiting (대문에서 기다려요).

Confusing 대문 with 현관. 대문 is the outer street gate into the yard; 현관 is the building's entry hall where shoes come off. Apartments have a 현관 but no 대문.
Using 대문 for an apartment building's entrance. That shared door is the 공동현관/현관, not 대문 — 대문 belongs to detached houses with a yard.
Saying 대문에서 자물쇠가 있어요. A lock's presence takes 에 (대문에 자물쇠가 있어요); 에서 marks the place of an action such as 기다리다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 회사원 means "office worker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 회사원 (hoesawon) means "office worker". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저는 회사원이에요. ("I am an office worker."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 회사원 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 이에요 after a final consonant (원)
subject 이 after consonant
평범하다 = ordinary, a very common pairing

usagePhrases.en: I want to become an office worker.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: I'm an office worker.
examples.note: the default polite way to state your job

examples.en: My older brother is an office worker at a bank.
examples.note: 에서 marks the workplace where the action happens

examples.ko: 회사원들은 보통 아침 아홉 시까지 출근해요.
examples.romanization: hoesawondeureun botong achim ahop sikkaji chulgeunhaeyo.
examples.en: Office workers usually clock in by nine in the morning.
examples.note: 출근하다 'go to work' is the verb that lives with 회사원

extendedVocab.nuance: 회사원 is 會社員 ('company-member'), literally a member of a company, and it is the neutral catch-all a salaried employee of a private firm gives when asked 무슨 일 하세요? Contrast it with 직장인, which means 'a working person' in general (anyone with a paid job, including teachers or nurses): every 회사원 is a 직장인, but not every 직장인 is a 회사원. Also separate it from 사업가, the owner who runs the business — a 회사원 is employed by someone else. The pitfall for English speakers is twofold: 회사원 ends in a consonant so the copula is 회사원이에요, never 'office worker'-style 회사원예요; and don't translate 'I work at a company' as a job title — to name the job you simply say 회사원이에요 rather than literally rendering the English sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 회사원예요 — wrong, because 원 ends in a consonant you must use 이에요: 회사원이에요.
Using 회사원 for a self-employed shop owner — that person is 자영업자 or 사장님; 회사원 is specifically a salaried employee of someone else's company.
Calling any working adult 회사원 — a nurse or teacher is a 직장인 but not a 회사원; 회사원 implies a typical office/company job.
