extendedVocab.explanation: "civil servant" is 공무원 (gongmuwon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 공무원이에요. ("I am a civil servant."). Watch the particle attached to 공무원 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 이에요 after the consonant ending 원
subject 이 after consonant
공무원 시험 is a fixed compound; 시험을 보다 = sit an exam

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a civil servant.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 pairs with 이/가

examples.en: I'm a civil servant.
examples.note: stated plainly, like any job

examples.en: My older sister is a civil servant working at city hall.
examples.note: 시청 'city hall' is a typical 공무원 workplace

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 사람들이 공무원 시험을 많이 준비해요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun saramdeuri gongmuwon siheomeul mani junbihaeyo.
examples.en: These days many young people study for the civil-service exam.
examples.note: 준비하다 'prepare for' is the verb that collocates with 시험

extendedVocab.nuance: 공무원 is 公務員 ('public-affairs-member'), one who handles 공무, the affairs of the state, so it covers anyone employed by the government — a ward office clerk, a public-school teacher, a tax officer. The key contrast is with 회사원: a 회사원 works for a private 회사, while a 공무원 works for the 나라 (state) and has 정년 (guaranteed tenure to retirement). Don't confuse it with 정치인 (a politician, who is elected) — a 공무원 is hired through the 공무원 시험 and is meant to be politically neutral. For learners the pitfalls are the copula (consonant ending → 공무원이에요, not 공무원예요) and the cultural weight: in Korea 공무원 is prized for 안정성 (stability), so saying 공무원이 되고 싶어요 carries a strong 'I want a secure life' overtone that the bare English 'civil servant' doesn't convey.

Saying 공무원예요 — wrong; 원 ends in a consonant, so it must be 공무원이에요.
Equating 공무원 with 정치인 — a 공무원 is an appointed/hired official, whereas a 정치인 is an elected politician; mixing them sounds confused.
Assuming 공무원 means only office desk staff — public-school teachers and firefighters are also 공무원, so the word is broader than English 'civil servant' feels.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주부 means "homemaker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주부 (jubu) = "homemaker". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 저는 주부예요. ("I am a homemaker.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 주부, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 부
subject 가 after a vowel
전업 'sole occupation' stresses it is full-time work
집안일 'household chores' is the typical object

examples.en: My mom is a homemaker.
examples.note: the most natural everyday sentence with 주부

examples.en: I'm a full-time homemaker raising children.
examples.note: 키우다 'raise (a child)' collocates with 주부

examples.en: These days homemakers also earn money with a side job.
examples.note: 부업 'side work' shows 주부 is treated as real labor

extendedVocab.nuance: 주부 is 主婦 ('head-wife'), the person who is the 主 (head, manager) of household affairs; historically it implies a married woman running the home. The sharp modern contrast is 전업주부 (full-time homemaker, no outside job) versus 맞벌이 (a dual-income couple where both work) — and note the rising 주부 covers men too, though many will specify 전업주부 or use 살림하다 'to keep house' for the activity. Don't confuse 주부 (the person) with 가사 / 집안일 (the housework itself). The English-speaker pitfalls: 부 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 주부예요, never 주부이에요; and 'housewife' in English can sound dated, but 주부 in Korean is a perfectly neutral, respectable job answer — pair it warmly, e.g. 부지런한 주부 'a diligent homemaker'.

Saying 주부이에요 — wrong; 부 ends in a vowel, so use 주부예요.
Using 주부 to mean the chores — the chores are 집안일/가사; 주부 is the person who does them.
Assuming 주부 is always female or always married — modern usage allows men, and 전업주부 just marks that homemaking is the person's full-time role.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 사업가 means "businessperson" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 사업가 (saeopga) means "businessperson". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저는 사업가예요. ("I am a businessperson."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사업가 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
subject 가 after a vowel
성공하다 'succeed' is the classic modifier

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a businessperson.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 pairs with 이/가

examples.en: My uncle is a businessperson.
examples.note: stating someone's occupation plainly

examples.en: He's a businessperson who founded a small company.
examples.note: 세우다 'establish (a company)' collocates with 사업가

examples.ko: 성공한 사업가가 되려면 위험을 감수해야 해요.
examples.romanization: seonggonghan saeopgaga doeryeomyeon wiheomeul gamsuhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: To become a successful businessperson you have to take risks.
examples.note: 위험을 감수하다 'bear risk' captures the core of 사업가

extendedVocab.nuance: 사업가 is 事業家 ('enterprise-expert'), where 가(家) is the suffix for a person skilled in a field (as in 작가, 화가, 음악가); it pictures someone who builds and runs an 사업 (a business venture) and shoulders its risk. Contrast three near words: 사업가 = the entrepreneur/operator with vision and risk; 사장(님) = the literal 'company president/boss' title you address people by; and 자영업자 = a small self-employed shop owner. So a corner-store owner is rarely called a 사업가 — that word sounds bigger, more ambitious. Don't mix 사업가 (the person) with 사업 (the business itself: 사업을 하다 'run a business'). Pitfalls: 가 ends in a vowel so it's 사업가예요, never 사업가이에요; and don't borrow English 'I do business' literally as a title — to name the job say 사업가예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사업가이에요 — wrong; 가 ends in a vowel, so it must be 사업가예요.
Confusing 사업가 (the owner/person) with 사업 (the business activity) — you run a 사업, you are a 사업가.
Calling a tiny shop owner a 사업가 — that everyday person is usually 자영업자 or 사장님; 사업가 implies a larger, risk-taking venture.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 디자이너 means "designer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "designer" is 디자이너 (dijaineo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 디자이너예요. ("I am a designer."). Watch the particle attached to 디자이너 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 너
멋있다 'stylish/cool' fits the creative field
the field word goes in front: 옷/웹/그래픽 디자이너

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a designer.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm a designer.
examples.note: the bare job statement

examples.en: My friend is a designer who makes clothes.
examples.note: the -는 clause 옷을 만드는 specifies the kind of designer

examples.ko: 그 디자이너가 이번 시즌 신상품을 디자인했어요.
examples.romanization: geu dijaineoga ibeon sijeun sinsangpumeul dijainhaesseoyo.
examples.en: That designer designed this season's new products.
examples.note: 디자인하다 'to design' is the matching verb

extendedVocab.nuance: 디자이너 is a direct loanword from English 'designer', written in 외래어 (foreign-loan) spelling, used for anyone who designs — clothes, graphics, web pages, products. Because the bare word is broad, Koreans almost always front a field: 옷 디자이너 (fashion), 웹 디자이너 (web), 그래픽 디자이너 (graphic). Be careful not to confuse 디자이너 with 디자인 (the design itself: 디자인이 예쁘다 'the design is pretty') — one is the person, one is the output. A nearby word is 설계자, but that leans toward technical/architectural 'designer-engineer', so for fashion or visual work stick with 디자이너. Pitfalls for English speakers: 너 ends in a vowel, so it's 디자이너예요, never 디자이너이에요; and the matching verb is 디자인하다, so 'I design clothes' is 옷을 디자인해요, not a literal word-by-word transfer of the English.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 디자이너이에요 — wrong; 너 ends in a vowel, so use 디자이너예요.
Confusing 디자이너 (the person) with 디자인 (the design) — you do 디자인, you are a 디자이너.
Leaving the field off when it matters — 디자이너 alone is vague; specify 옷 디자이너, 웹 디자이너, etc., as Koreans naturally do.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 프로그래머 means "programmer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 프로그래머 (peurogeuraemeo) = "programmer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 저는 프로그래머예요. ("I am a programmer.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 프로그래머, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 예요 after the vowel ending 머
subject 가 after a vowel
실력 있다 'have skill' is the natural praise

usagePhrases.en: I want to become a programmer.
usagePhrases.note: 되다 takes 이/가

examples.en: I'm a programmer.
examples.note: the plain job answer

examples.en: My younger sibling is a programmer who makes games.
examples.note: 만들다 'make' describes what they build

examples.en: The programmer writes code late into the night.
examples.note: 코드를 짜다 'write/assemble code' is the insider collocation

extendedVocab.nuance: 프로그래머 is the loanword 'programmer', the person who writes computer 프로그램 (programs). The most useful contrast is with 개발자 ('developer', 開發者 'one who develops'): in real Korean tech workplaces 개발자 is now the more common, broader title (covering design, building, and shipping software), while 프로그래머 highlights specifically the coding act and can sound slightly narrower or more old-school. Both are fine to say. Don't confuse 프로그래머 (the person) with 프로그램 (the program) — you make a 프로그램, you are a 프로그래머. The natural verb for the work is 코드를 짜다 or 개발하다, not a literal calque of English 'to program'. Pitfall: 머 ends in a vowel, so it must be 프로그래머예요, never 프로그래머이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 프로그래머이에요 — wrong; 머 ends in a vowel, so use 프로그래머예요.
Confusing 프로그래머 (the person) with 프로그램 (the software) — you build a 프로그램, you are a 프로그래머.
Assuming 프로그래머 is the only modern title — in Korean tech 개발자 'developer' is now more common and often preferred.

extendedVocab.nuance: 교수 is 敎授 ('teach-confer'), a university professor who both teaches and researches — note this is higher and narrower than 선생님, the general word for any teacher (and the polite word for a schoolteacher). The huge register point: in real use you almost always attach 님 → 교수님, and you conjugate verbs about them with honorific -시- (가르치세요, 오셨어요). Pitfall: 수 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 교수예요, never 교수이에요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 통역사 is 通譯士 ('through-translate-specialist'), where 士(사) is the dignified suffix for a licensed/qualified professional (also in 변호사 lawyer, 회계사 accountant). It means specifically an interpreter of spoken language in real time. The essential contrast is 번역사 (翻譯士), who translates written text: spoken = 통역, written = 번역, and the people and verbs differ (통역하다 vs 번역하다). extendedVocab.nuance: 사거리 is literally 四거리 — the Sino-Korean 四 (four) glued to native 거리 (street), so it names a point where four roads cross, the single most useful landmark for directions. English speakers wrongly say 사거리에 가요 for 'turn at the intersection' — 가다 with 에 only means 'go (to) the intersection' as a destination; to describe an action performed there (turn, meet, wait) you must switch to 에서. extendedVocab.nuance: 골목 is a small, narrow back-lane between buildings — think the winding side streets of an old neighborhood, often lined with tiny homes and hidden eateries; the longer 골목길 stresses it as a walkable path. Contrast it sharply with 길, the general word for any road or way: every 골목 is a 길, but you call something a 골목 precisely when it is narrow, branching off a bigger street. It is a native Korean word (no hanja), warm and homey in feeling — 골목 carries nostalgia, which is why 골목 상권 (alley shopping district) and 골목길 are beloved. English speakers misuse 길 for a tiny side street; if a car can barely pass, Koreans feel it as a 골목, not a 길. Avoid the direct-translation trap of 'small road' = 작은 길; the natural phrase is 좁은 골목.

Using 길 for a tight back lane — Koreans reserve 골목 for narrow branching lanes; 길 sounds too wide.
Saying 작은 길 as a literal 'small road' — the natural collocation is 좁은 골목 (narrow alley).
Putting 에 on an action: 골목에 놀아요 is wrong; playing needs 골목에서 놀아요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 광장 is 廣場 — 廣 (wide) + 場 (place/ground), literally 'wide ground', so it names a large paved public square where crowds gather for rallies, festivals, or rest, like 광화문 광장. Do not confuse it with 공원 (park): a 공원 is green, with trees, grass and benches for leisure, while a 광장 is an open hard-surfaced civic space built for people to assemble. Because 광장 historically hosts demonstrations and ceremonies, it carries a civic, public-life connotation that 공원 lacks. English speakers reach for 공원 when they mean a city square — if it is paved and made for crowds, it is a 광장. Also resist 'big park' = 큰 공원 for a plaza; the right word is simply 광장.

extendedVocab.nuance: 다리 is a native Korean word and a famous homonym: the very same 다리 means 'leg', and context alone tells them apart — 다리가 아프다 is 'my leg hurts', while 다리를 건너다 is 'cross the bridge'. As a structure it lets you pass over a river, road, or valley and is a top landmark in directions. Distinguish it from 육교, which is specifically a pedestrian overpass/footbridge across a road, and 고가도로, an elevated car roadway; plain 다리 is the everyday cover term, especially the great river bridges (한강 다리). The verb that pairs with it is 건너다 (to cross), taking the object particle 를. English speakers sometimes say 다리를 가다 — but you 'cross' a bridge (다리를 건너다), you do not simply 'go' it.

Saying 다리를 가요 for 'cross the bridge' — the verb is 건너다: 다리를 건너요.
Forgetting that 다리 also means 'leg' — listen to context; 다리가 아프다 is about your leg, not a bridge.
Using 다리 for a footbridge over a road — that specific one is 육교 (pedestrian overpass).

extendedVocab.nuance: 터널 is a direct loanword from English 'tunnel' (written in Hangul), naming a passage bored through a mountain or under ground so cars and trains can pass. There is a pure-Korean-style equivalent 굴, but 굴 leans toward a natural cave or burrow, whereas 터널 is the engineered road/rail structure — so a subway runs through a 터널, while a bear sleeps in a 굴. The verbs that pair with it are 지나다 / 통과하다 (pass through, with 를) and 들어가다 / 나오다 (enter / exit, with 에). English speakers sometimes overuse 다리 for 'a way through a mountain', but a bridge goes over and a 터널 goes through. Resist also the literal 'go in the tunnel' = 터널에 가다; you 'enter' it: 터널에 들어가다.

Using 다리 for a passage through a mountain — over a gap is 다리, through a mountain is 터널.
Saying 굴 for a highway tunnel — 굴 suggests a natural cave; the engineered road one is 터널.
Saying 터널에 가다 — to go through, use 터널을 지나다 or to enter, 터널에 들어가다.

를 + 내려가다 for descending

examples.en: Go up the stairs slowly.
examples.note: 올라가다 takes 를; 천천히 = slowly

extendedVocab.nuance: 계단 is 階段 — 階 (step/rank) + 段 (level/section), literally 'stepped levels', the fixed set of steps between floors. Distinguish it from 층계 (a more bookish synonym for a flight of steps) and especially from 계단 vs the moving 에스컬레이터: a 계단 is stationary and you climb it under your own power. The natural verbs are 올라가다 (go up) and 내려가다 (go down), each taking 를 because the staircase is the path traversed; to say you choose stairs as your method, use 계단으로 (by the stairs). The classic English-speaker error is 계단을 타다 (ride the stairs) — you ride a vehicle or an escalator, but ordinary stairs you 올라가다/내려가다, not 타다. Also 계단 is the steps; one single step is a 계단 한 칸.

Marking the means with 를: 계단을 가요 for 'take the stairs' should be 계단으로 가요.
Confusing 계단 with 층 (floor) — 층 is a building level; 계단 is the steps connecting levels.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 엘리베이터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: 고장 나다 = break down, common notice

extendedVocab.nuance: 엘리베이터 is the English loanword 'elevator' in Hangul, the small moving cabin that carries people between floors. A common synonym you will see on signage is 승강기 (昇降機, 'rise-descend machine'), the formal/legal term in building notices, while 엘리베이터 is the everyday spoken word. Crucially it is treated like a ride: the verb is 타다 (to board/ride), taking 를 — the very same 타다 used for buses and taxis — and you 내리다 (get off) with 에서. English speakers wrongly map their 'get in/out' onto 들어가다/나가다, but Korean frames it as boarding: say 엘리베이터를 타다, not 엘리베이터에 들어가다. Do not mix it up with 에스컬레이터 (escalator), which is the open moving staircase; the 엘리베이터 is the enclosed box.

Mixing up 엘리베이터 (the enclosed box) with 에스컬레이터 (the moving stairs).
Using 가다 for boarding: 엘리베이터를 가요 is wrong; the verb is 타다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 에스컬레이터 is the loanword 'escalator' in Hangul — the moving staircase you stand on in subway stations and department stores. The dividing line from 엘리베이터 is movement type: an 에스컬레이터 is an open, continuously moving set of steps you stand on, while an 엘리베이터 is an enclosed cabin that lifts you; English keeps them apart too, but their similar Korean spellings make learners blur them, so anchor 에스컬레이터 = 'stairs that move'. extendedVocab.nuance: 입구 is 入口 — 入 (enter) + 口 (mouth/opening), literally the 'mouth you enter through', i.e. the way into a building or area. Its exact opposite is 출구 (出口, 'exit-mouth'), and the two share the 口 'opening' character, so learning them as a 入/出 pair makes both stick. Contrast 입구 with 정문 (正門, 'main gate'), the principal front gate of a campus or large building — a place can have one grand 정문 plus several smaller 입구. For meeting people, the action verb 만나다 takes 에서 (입구에서 만나요), while merely stating something is located there uses 에. English speakers often confuse 입구 and 출구 because both end in 구; remember 입 = in, 출 = out. Avoid the literal 'in-door' = 안 문; the real word is 입구.

examples.en: Where is the exit?
examples.note: the mirror question to 입구가 어디예요?

examples.ko: 저는 칠 번 출구 앞에서 기다릴게요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun chil beon chulgu apeseo gidarilgeyo.
examples.en: I'll wait in front of exit 7.
examples.note: 출구 앞 = in front of the exit; -ㄹ게요 = I will

extendedVocab.nuance: 출구 is 出口 — 出 (go out) + 口 (opening), literally the 'exit-mouth', the way you leave a building or station; in the subway each is numbered (몇 번 출구), so 'meet at exit 7' is everyday Korean. It is the exact opposite of 입구 (入口, entrance), and the shared 口 'opening' character ties the 出/入 pair together. Distinguish 출구 from 비상구 (非常口, 'emergency exit'), the marked fire-escape door — a normal way out is a 출구, the emergency one is a 비상구. To leave through it you say 출구로 나가다, where 으로 marks the exit as your route. English speakers blur 출구 and 입구 because both end in 구; fix the memory with 출 = out, 입 = in. And note exits are counted with the native-Sino number + 번 (삼 번 출구), not with English ordinals.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 출구 (exit, 出) with 입구 (entrance, 入) — both end in 口, but 출 = out, 입 = in.
Saying 출구를 나가요 — to mark the route out, use 출구로 나가요.
Using 출구 for a fire escape — the emergency one is specifically 비상구.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 복도 means "hallway" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "hallway" is 복도 (bokdo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 긴 복도 ("long hallway"). Watch the particle attached to 복도 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 길다 fits a corridor stretching past many rooms
에서 marks where; 뛰지 마세요 is the school sign
끝 = far end, where the last room sits
를 + 지나다, pass along it

examples.en: The classroom is at the end of the hallway.
examples.note: 복도 끝 = the far end; 에 marks where it is located

examples.en: Don't run in the hallway.
examples.note: 에서 marks where; -지 마세요 = please don't

examples.en: The hallway is quiet.
examples.note: 조용하다 = quiet, a typical descriptor

extendedVocab.nuance: 복도 is 複道 — the indoor corridor or passage inside a building that links rooms, offices, and classrooms; picture a school or office hallway. The key boundary is indoor vs outdoor: a 복도 is always inside a building, whereas a 골목 is a narrow lane outside between buildings — so you wait for a friend 복도에서 inside the school, but explore a 골목 out in the neighborhood. Do not stretch 복도 to mean a road; it is strictly an interior walkway. Natural verbs are 지나다 (pass along, 를) and the activity-marking 에서 for things done there (복도에서 기다리다, 복도에서 뛰다). English speakers sometimes reach for 골목 for an inside passage — keep it straight: outside lane = 골목, inside corridor = 복도. Also 복도 is the passage itself, while the entrance hall of a home is rather 현관.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 골목 for an indoor passage — outside it's a 골목, but inside a building it's a 복도.
Marking an activity with 에: 복도에 기다려요 should be 복도에서 기다려요.
Calling a building's entry hall 복도 — the front entry of a home is 현관, not 복도.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 옥상 means "rooftop" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 옥상 (oksang) = "rooftop". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 건물 옥상 ("building rooftop") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 옥상, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: the flat top you can actually stand on
에 + 올라가다 marks the destination up top
에서 because resting is an action done there

usagePhrases.en: see the night view from the rooftop
usagePhrases.note: 야경을 보다 = take in the night scenery

examples.en: Let's go up to the rooftop.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination; 올라가다 = ascend

examples.en: I hang the laundry on the rooftop.
examples.note: 빨래를 널다 = hang washing, a classic 옥상 activity

examples.en: The night view from the rooftop is gorgeous.
examples.note: 에서 marks the vantage point you view from

extendedVocab.nuance: 옥상 is 屋上 — 屋 (house/building) + 上 (on top), literally 'on top of the building', meaning the flat, accessible roof terrace where people dry laundry, grow plants, or take in the view. The sharp contrast is with 지붕, the sloped roof of a house that simply covers it and that you do not walk on: a Korean apartment block has an 옥상 you can climb to, a traditional 한옥 has a tiled 지붕 you cannot stand on. Because 옥상 is a usable open space, it pairs with 올라가다 (go up to, with 에) and activity 에서 (옥상에서 쉬다, 빨래를 널다, 야경을 보다). English 'roof' lumps both together, so learners overuse 지붕 — but if you can stand on it, it is an 옥상; if it is the sloping cover, it is a 지붕. Note also 옥상 is the open top of a building, distinct from 다락 (an attic room under the roof).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a flat usable rooftop 지붕 — 지붕 is the sloped cover you can't stand on; the open terrace is 옥상.
Marking resting with 에: 옥상에 쉬어요 should be 옥상에서 쉬어요 (an action happens there).
Confusing 옥상 (open rooftop) with 다락 — 다락 is the attic space tucked under the roof.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 점수 means "score" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 점수 (jeomsu) means "score". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 점수가 좋아요 ("the score is good"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 점수 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: with 좋다 use the subject particle 가, not 를: 점수가 좋다, never 점수를 좋다
when an action verb like 받다 acts on it, the object particle 를 returns
나오다 is intransitive, so the score is the subject (가), not the object
Koreans pair a score with 높다/낮다 (high/low), never 크다/작다 (big/small)

examples.en: The score is good.
examples.note: The simplest frame: just the noun plus 가 and an adjective, the everyday way to comment on a result.

examples.en: I got my Korean test score back.
examples.note: 받다 takes 를 because you actively receive the number that was handed to you.

examples.ko: 선생님, 제 점수가 왜 이렇게 낮아요?
examples.romanization: seonsaengnim, je jeomsuga wae ireoke najayo?
examples.en: Teacher, why is my score so low?
examples.note: A real classroom complaint: 낮다 (low) is the natural opposite of 높다, never 작다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 점수 is the numeric points you earn on a test, quiz, or game — the raw figure itself, written 95점 with the counter 점. The hanja is 點數, literally 'dot-number', from 點 (point/dot) plus 數 (number), so it is intrinsically a counted quantity. Do not confuse it with its near-synonym 성적 (成績): 성적 is your broader academic standing or report-card record (overall grades, ranking, a transcript), while 점수 is one concrete number on one item — you can have a good 점수 on a single quiz yet a poor overall 성적. The natural verbs are 점수가 나오다 (the score comes out / is released) and 점수를 받다 (to receive a score); for high or low you must say 점수가 높다/낮다, NOT 크다/작다. The English-speaker trap is the particle: with the descriptive 좋다/높다 the score is the subject and takes 가 (점수가 좋다), so saying 점수를 좋다 by copying English 'I scored a good score' is ungrammatical.

Saying 점수가 커요 by translating 'a big score'. Korean rates a score on a high/low axis, so the correct form is 점수가 높아요 (the score is high).
Using 성적 and 점수 interchangeably. 성적 is your overall record; for the single number on one test you want 점수, e.g. 시험 점수가 좋아요, not 시험 성적이 좋아요 unless you mean the whole grade.
Marking the score with 를 before 좋다: 점수를 좋아요 is wrong because 좋다 is an adjective taking a subject. Say 점수가 좋아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교과서 means "textbook" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "textbook" is 교과서 (gyogwaseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 교과서를 펴요 ("open the textbook"). Watch the particle attached to 교과서 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 펴다 (spread open) is the standard classroom verb for opening a book to a page, not 열다
나오다 with 에 is how Koreans say content 'comes up' in a book
로 marks the textbook as the tool/means you study by
a subject name directly modifies 교과서 with no particle between them

examples.en: Please open your textbook.
examples.note: The exact phrase a teacher says: 펴다 plus the polite command -세요.

examples.en: The answers are all right there in the textbook.
examples.note: 에 marks the book as the location where the answers appear (나와 있다).

examples.ko: 저는 인터넷 강의보다 교과서로 공부하는 게 편해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun inteonet ganguiboda gyogwaseoro gongbuhaneun ge pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: I find studying with the textbook easier than online lectures.
examples.note: 로 frames the textbook as the means, contrasted with 강의 via 보다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 교과서 is the official course book for a specific school subject — the authorized text a class is taught from, often government-approved (국정/검정 교과서). The hanja 敎科書 breaks down as 敎 (teach) + 科 (subject/branch) + 書 (book), literally 'teaching-subject book', which is exactly its job. Keep three near-words apart: a 공책 (空冊, 'empty book') is a blank notebook you write in; a 참고서 (參考書) is a supplementary study/reference guide; and a plain 책 is any book at all — only 교과서 is the core subject text used in lessons. The natural verb is 교과서를 펴다 (open it to a page) rather than 열다 (which suits a door or lid), and you study 교과서로 (by means of the textbook). The English-speaker pitfall is calling any school book a 책 or mixing it with 공책: if you say 교과서에 써요 meaning you write in it, a Korean pictures defacing the printed text — you write 공책에, in your notebook, not in the 교과서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 열다 to open a textbook, as in 교과서를 열어요. 열다 is for doors and lids; to open a book to a page Koreans say 교과서를 펴요.
Confusing 교과서 with 공책. 공책 is a blank notebook for writing; the printed subject book is 교과서. Say 공책에 써요 for writing, 교과서를 봐요 for reading.
Treating 교과서 as any book. A novel or comic is just 책; reserve 교과서 for the official text of a school subject.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 필통 means "pencil case" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 필통 (piltong) = "pencil case". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 필통에 넣어요 ("put it in the pencil case") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 필통, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: put it in the pencil case
usagePhrases.note: 넣다 (put in) naturally pairs with 에 to mark where something goes
existence/possession uses 있다 with the subject particle 이
unlike a book, a case has a lid, so 열다 (open) is correct here
filled pencil cases are typically described with 귀엽다 (cute) by students

examples.en: The pencil case is on the desk.
examples.note: A simple location statement: 위에 (on top) plus 있어요 for where it sits.

examples.en: I put the pencil into the pencil case.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination of 넣다; the pencil (object) takes 를.

examples.ko: 새 필통을 샀는데 연필이랑 지우개가 안 들어가요.
examples.romanization: sae piltongeul sanneunde yeonpirirang jiugaega an deureogayo.
examples.en: I bought a new pencil case but the pencil and eraser don't fit.
examples.note: A real-life grumble: 들어가다 (to fit inside) with the negative 안.

extendedVocab.nuance: 필통 is the small case or box that holds your writing implements — pens, pencils, eraser. The word is Sino-Korean 筆筒, from 筆 (writing brush/pen) + 筒 (tube/cylinder), originally a 'brush-tube', a holder for calligraphy brushes that now means any pencil case. Do not confuse the container with its contents: 연필 (鉛筆, 'lead-brush') is the pencil itself, 볼펜 a ballpoint, and 지우개 the eraser — the 필통 is merely the case they live in. Because a case has a lid you 필통을 열다 (open it) and you 연필을 필통에 넣다 (put a pencil in), so the location particle 에 marks where things go. The English-speaker pitfall is naming the part for the whole: a beginner may point at a pencil and say 필통, but 필통 is strictly the case — if you mean the pencil, say 연필. Also avoid the verb 입다/신다 here; you do not 'wear' a 필통, you 열다 it or 가지고 다니다 (carry it around).

Calling the pencil itself 필통. 필통 is only the case; the pencil is 연필. Point at the pencil and say 연필, point at the box and say 필통.
Using 열다 for a textbook by analogy after learning 필통을 열다. The lid case opens (필통을 열다), but a book opens to a page with 펴다 (교과서를 펴다).
Saying 필통에 연필이 있다 when you mean to put it in, then using 있다 instead of 넣다. 있다 states it is already there; the action of inserting is 넣다 (필통에 넣어요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 책가방 means "school bag" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 책가방 (chaekgabang) means "school bag". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 책가방을 메요 ("carry the school bag (on the back)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 책가방 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: carry the school bag (on the back)
usagePhrases.note: 메다 is the dedicated verb for shouldering a backpack, not 들다 or 입다

usagePhrases.en: put it in the school bag
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the bag as the place something goes into with 넣다
책가방 is habitually described as 무겁다 (heavy) because of the books inside
싸다 (to pack/wrap) is how Koreans say they get their bag ready

examples.en: The school bag is heavy.
examples.note: The basic complaint frame: subject plus the adjective 무겁다.

examples.en: I put the textbook into my school bag.
examples.note: 에 marks where the textbook goes; 넣다 is the action of putting in.

examples.en: Every morning I put my bag on my back and head to school.
examples.note: 메고 (shouldering, and then…) chains the bag onto the going; -고 links the two actions.

extendedVocab.nuance: 책가방 is the bag a student carries books and supplies in — in practice a backpack worn on both shoulders. It is a compound of 책 (冊, book, Sino-Korean) + 가방 (bag, a native-feeling loanword), literally 'book-bag'. The crucial point is the verb: a backpack worn on the back/shoulder takes 메다 (책가방을 메다), whereas a handbag or briefcase carried in the hand takes 들다 (가방을 들다) — choosing the wrong one sounds off, like saying you 'hold' a backpack in your fist. You also 책가방을 싸다 (pack it) the night before and 책가방에 넣다 (put things in). Its near-words: a generic 가방 is any bag, a 백팩 is the English loan 'backpack', and a 핸드백 is a woman's handbag — 책가방 specifically frames it by its school-book purpose. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 입다 (wear) or 들다 (hold) because English says 'wear a backpack' or 'carry a bag'; in Korean a backpack is neither worn like clothes nor held like a purse — it is 메다, shouldered.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 책가방을 입어요 by translating 'wear a backpack'. 입다 is for clothing; a backpack is shouldered, so say 책가방을 메요.
Using 들다 for a backpack. 들다 means to carry in the hand (a handbag, a suitcase). For a bag on your back use 메다: 책가방을 메고 가요.
Marking the bag with 에서 when putting things in. Insertion is a destination, so use 에: 책가방에 넣어요, not 책가방에서 넣어요.

Its near-words: a generic 가방 is any bag, a 백팩 is the English loan 'backpack', and a 핸드백 is a woman's handbag — 책가방 specifically frames it by its school-book purpose.

The pitfall is reaching for 입다 (wear) or 들다 (hold) because English says 'wear a backpack' or 'carry a bag'; in Korean a backpack is neither worn like clothes nor held like a purse — it is 메다, shouldered.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 운동장 means "playground" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "playground" is 운동장 (undongjang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 운동장에서 놀아요 ("play at the playground"). Watch the particle attached to 운동장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 활동(놀다) happens AT a place, so the action particle 에서 is required
모이다 marks the field as the end point of movement, so 에
a 운동장 is rated by area with 넓다 (spacious), not 크다

usagePhrases.en: run a lap around the field
usagePhrases.note: 돌다 with 을 treats the track as the path you traverse

examples.en: The playground is spacious.
examples.note: A first sentence: subject 가 plus 넓다, the standard way to size up an area.

examples.en: The students play soccer on the field.
examples.note: 에서 because 축구를 하다 (the activity) happens there; the place hosts an action.

examples.ko: 체육 시간에 운동장에 나가서 줄을 섰어요.
examples.romanization: cheyuk sigane undongjange nagaseo jureul seosseoyo.
examples.en: In PE class we went out to the field and lined up.
examples.note: 에 marks the destination of 나가다 (go out to); then 줄을 서다 (line up) follows.

extendedVocab.nuance: 운동장 is the open sports field or grounds of a school where pupils exercise, run, and play — typically a large dirt or turf area with a track, the heart of Korean school PE and 체육대회 (sports day). The make-or-break grammar is 에서 vs 에: use 에서 for what you DO there (운동장에서 뛰다/놀다/축구하다), because 에서 marks the location of an action, but use 에 only for motion toward it (운동장에 가다/나가다/모이다). Its near-word 놀이터 is the little playground with swings and a slide for small children, whereas 운동장 is the big school athletic field — do not mix them. Size is 넓다 (spacious), not 크다. The English-speaker pitfall is using a single 'at' particle for everything: English 'play at the playground' and 'go to the playground' both feel like one preposition, but Korean splits them — 운동장에서 놀다 (play, action) yet 운동장에 가다 (go, destination), and putting 에 where an activity happens (운동장에 놀아요) is a classic error.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교문 means "school gate" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 교문 (gyomun) = "school gate". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교문 앞에서 만나요 ("meet in front of the gate") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 교문, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: meet in front of the gate
usagePhrases.note: 교문 앞 (gate-front) is the usual meeting spot; 에서 marks where you meet
지나다 (pass) takes 을, treating the gate as the point you go past
닫히다 (be closed) is the verb for a gate shutting at curfew time
앞 (front) attaches to 교문 to pinpoint the area before it

examples.en: The school gate is big.
examples.note: Plain description: 교문 as subject with 크다, fine for a physical structure's size.

examples.en: I met my friend in front of the school gate.
examples.note: 에서 marks the spot of the meeting; 교문 앞 is the conventional rendezvous point.

examples.ko: 지각해서 교문이 닫히기 전에 뛰어 들어갔어요.
examples.romanization: jigakaeseo gyomuni datigi jeone ttwieo deureogasseoyo.
examples.en: I was running late, so I dashed in before the gate closed.
examples.note: 닫히기 전에 (before it closes) plus 뛰어 들어가다 (run in) — the real drama of a tardy student.

extendedVocab.nuance: 교문 is the main gate at the entrance of a school — the formal threshold students pass through each day, often guarded and shut after the bell. Note that 門 in Korea names large gates and named structures (광화문 Gwanghwamun, 동대문 Dongdaemun), so 교문 carries that weightier 'gateway' feel, not a flimsy door. The natural collocations are 교문 앞에서 만나다 (meet in front of the gate — the default student meetup) and 교문을 지나다 (pass through it), and a gate 닫히다 (closes) at curfew. Unlike a sports field judged by 넓다, a gate's size is 크다. The English-speaker pitfall is over-generalizing 'gate/door' to plain 문 — 문을 지나다 sounds like passing some random door; for the school's entrance gate you want 교문을 지나다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교복 means "school uniform" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 교복 (gyobok) means "school uniform". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교복을 입어요 ("wear the uniform"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교복 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 입다 is the verb for putting on upper-body/whole clothing, which a uniform is
어울리다 (to suit) with 가 is how Koreans compliment how clothes look on someone
맞추다 means to have clothes custom-made to your size, common for new uniforms
교복 is typically bought new (새) at the start of a school year

examples.en: The uniform is pretty.
examples.note: Simple appraisal: subject 가 plus 예쁘다, the everyday way to praise its looks.

examples.ko: 저는 매일 교복을 입고 학교에 가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maeil gyobogeul ipgo hakgyoe gayo.
examples.en: I wear my uniform to school every day.
examples.note: 입고 (wearing, and then…) links dressing to going via -고; 를 marks the uniform.

examples.ko: 교복 치마가 너무 짧아서 좀 불편해요.
examples.romanization: gyobok chimaga neomu jjalbaseo jom bulpyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The uniform skirt is so short it's a bit uncomfortable.
examples.note: A real student remark: 치마 (skirt) as a part of the 교복, with 짧다 (short).

extendedVocab.nuance: 교복 is the prescribed uniform students wear at a Korean middle or high school — a recognizable set (blazer, shirt, skirt or trousers, often a name tag) that signals which school you attend. The hanja 校服 is 校 (school) + 服 (clothes/garment), literally 'school-clothes'. The 服 element appears in many clothing words — 한복 (Korean dress), 양복 (a Western suit), 교복 — so it reliably means 'attire'. Crucially the verb is 입다 (입다 covers shirts, jackets, dresses, and uniforms — anything worn on the torso or as a full outfit), NOT 신다 (which is only for footwear) and NOT 쓰다 (for hats/glasses): you 교복을 입다. Other natural phrases are 교복을 맞추다 (have it tailored) and 교복이 어울리다 (it suits you). Its near-word 사복 (私服, 'private clothes') means your own casual clothes worn on non-uniform days — a 사복 데이 is a free-dress day. The English-speaker pitfall is treating Korean 'wear' as one word the way English does: English 'wear' covers shoes, hats, and shirts alike, but Korean splits them by body zone, so saying 교복을 신다 (using the shoe verb) is a telltale beginner slip — it must be 교복을 입다.

Saying 교복을 신어요 by using the single English 'wear'. 신다 is only for footwear; clothing worn on the body uses 입다, so the uniform is 교복을 입어요.
Using 쓰다 for the uniform after learning 모자를 쓰다 (wear a hat). 쓰다 is for things on the head; the uniform garment is 입다.
Confusing 교복 with 사복. 사복 is your own casual clothes; the school's required outfit is 교복. On a free-dress day you wear 사복, not 교복.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 급식 means "school meal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "school meal" is 급식 (geupsik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 급식을 먹어요 ("eat the school meal"). Watch the particle attached to 급식 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 (eat) takes 를; 급식 is treated as the food you consume
맛있다 (tasty) with 가 is the universal verdict students pass on the food
급식 directly modifies 시간 to name the scheduled meal slot

usagePhrases.en: the meal is served / comes out
usagePhrases.note: 나오다 describes today's menu 'coming out' on the tray

examples.en: Today's school meal is tasty.
examples.note: The classic lunchroom line: 오늘 (today) plus subject 가 and 맛있다.

examples.en: The students go to the cafeteria to eat lunch.
examples.note: 먹으러 (in order to eat) shows purpose with -(으)러; 를 marks 급식.

examples.ko: 오늘 급식에 제가 제일 좋아하는 닭갈비가 나왔어요!
examples.romanization: oneul geupsige jega jeil joahaneun dalkgalbiga nawasseoyo!
examples.en: My favorite dak-galbi came out in today's school lunch!
examples.note: An excited report: 급식에 ... 나오다 (appear in the meal); 에 marks the meal as where the dish shows up.

extendedVocab.nuance: 급식 is the meal supplied institutionally — the school (or workplace) lunch served en masse and eaten together, usually on a divided tray (식판). The hanja 給食 is 給 (give/supply) + 食 (food/meal), literally 'supplied food', which captures that it is provided to a group rather than ordered individually. This is the dividing line from its near-words: 식사 (食事) is the formal/general word for 'a meal' (any meal, politely), 밥 is the casual everyday word for 'a meal' or 'rice', and 점심 names specifically 'lunch' by time of day — but only 급식 carries the sense of a meal institutionally provided to students/staff. The English-speaker pitfall is using 급식 for any lunch — if you ate lunch at a café you say 점심을 먹었어요 or 밥을 먹었어요, not 급식을 먹었어요, because 급식 specifically means the provided school/work meal.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수업료 means "tuition fee" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 수업료 (sueomnyo) = "tuition fee". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수업료를 내요 ("pay the tuition") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수업료, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: fees are 내다 (pay/hand over to an institution), never 사다 (buy)
price is judged with 비싸다/싸다 (expensive/cheap), with 가 marking the subject
오르다 (rise) is the verb for prices increasing; note the 르 irregular (올라요)
한 달 (one month) modifies 수업료 to specify the period being paid for

examples.en: The tuition is expensive.
examples.note: A plain price judgment: subject 가 with 비싸다, the core way to call something pricey.

examples.en: I pay the academy tuition every month.
examples.note: 매달 (every month) sets the frequency; 내다 takes 를 for the fee you hand over.

examples.ko: 올해 등록금이랑 수업료가 또 올라서 부담이 커요.
examples.romanization: olhae deungnokgeumirang sueomnyoga tto ollaseo budami keoyo.
examples.en: With registration and tuition fees rising again this year, the burden is heavy.
examples.note: A real worry: 오르다 (rise) plus 부담이 크다 (the burden is big), 등록금 vs 수업료 distinguished.

extendedVocab.nuance: 수업료 is the fee charged for taking lessons — the money you pay an academy (학원), school, or course for instruction. The hanja 授業料 is 授 (give/confer) + 業 (work/study) — together 授業 means 'a lesson/class', the act of teaching being given — plus 料 (fee/charge), so literally 'lesson-fee'. The element 料 marks fees throughout Korean: 입장료 (admission), 수수료 (commission), 사용료 (usage fee), 수업료 (tuition). Distinguish it from the near-word 등록금 (登錄金, 'registration money'), the lump enrollment fee for a university semester — at a 대학교 you usually pay 등록금, while at a 학원 you pay 수업료 each month; many learners blur them. The essential verb is 내다 (수업료를 내다, to pay/remit a fee), and prices 오르다 (rise) or are 비싸다 (expensive). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사다 (buy) because English can 'pay for' a class as if purchasing it — but in Korean you do not 'buy' a fee; you 내다 (pay/hand over) it: 수업료를 사다 is wrong, 수업료를 내다 is right.

Saying 수업료를 사요 by analogy with 'buying a class'. A fee is paid, not bought; the verb is 내다: 수업료를 내요.

Describing the fee with 커요 for 'high'. A price is 비싸다 (expensive), not 크다: 수업료가 비싸요. Reserve 크다 for physical size.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 장학금 means "scholarship" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 장학금 (janghakgeum) means "scholarship". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 장학금을 받아요 ("receive a scholarship"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 장학금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) takes 를; a scholarship is awarded to you
신청하다 (to apply/request) is the verb for putting in an application
나오다 describes the award money being granted/disbursed
타다 colloquially means to be awarded a prize or scholarship

examples.en: I got a scholarship.
examples.note: The proud one-liner: 받다 plus past -았어요, 를 marking the award.

examples.ko: 성적이 좋아서 이번 학기에 장학금을 신청했어요.
examples.romanization: seongjeogi joaseo ibeon hakgie janghakgeumeul sincheonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: My grades were good, so I applied for a scholarship this term.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason (good grades); 신청하다 is the act of applying.

examples.ko: 전액 장학금을 타서 등록금 걱정이 없어졌어요.
examples.romanization: jeonaek janghakgeumeul taseo deungnokgeum geokjeongi eopseojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I won a full scholarship, so my tuition worries are gone.
examples.note: 전액 (full amount) modifies it; 타다 (win) plus the relief of 걱정이 없어지다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 장학금 is the award money granted to a student to support their studies — for merit (성적 장학금), need, or special talent — money you do not repay, unlike a loan. Distinguish it sharply from 학자금 (學資金, 'study-capital'), which is the broader pool of money for education and often appears in 학자금 대출 (a student loan you must repay): a 장학금 is given to you, whereas 학자금 대출 is borrowed. Also unlike a plain 돈 (money) or 용돈 (allowance), 장학금 specifically denotes an academic award. The natural verbs are 장학금을 받다 (formally receive) and the colloquial 장학금을 타다 (win/get one), plus 장학금을 신청하다 (apply) and 장학금이 나오다 (it comes through). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it just 돈 — saying 학교에서 돈을 받았어요 to mean a scholarship loses the meaning; the award is 장학금, and confusing it with the repayable 학자금 대출 reverses who gives money to whom.

Confusing 장학금 with 학자금 (대출). A 장학금 is granted and not repaid; 학자금 대출 is a student loan you must pay back. They are opposite directions of obligation.
Using 사다 or 벌다 for getting a scholarship. You neither buy nor earn-by-working a scholarship; you 받다 (receive) or 타다 (win) it: 장학금을 받아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 동아리 means "club" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "club" is 동아리 (dongari). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 동아리에 들어가요 ("join a club"). Watch the particle attached to 동아리 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 들어가다 (enter/go into) with 에 is the set phrase for joining a club
활동하다 (to be active/take part) happens at the club, so 에서
가입하다 (to enroll/become a member) is the more formal 'join'
the activity name (사진) modifies 동아리 directly to name the club's focus

examples.en: I joined a music club.
examples.note: 에 marks the club as what you entered (들어가다); past tense -았어요.

examples.en: Our club meets every Friday.
examples.note: 에서 because 모이다 (the activity of gathering) takes place there; 매주 sets the rhythm.

examples.en: Thanks to club activities I got close with the older students.
examples.note: 덕분에 (thanks to) plus 친해지다 (grow close) — the real social payoff of joining.

extendedVocab.nuance: 동아리 is a student club or society — a voluntary group bound by a shared hobby or interest (band, film, basketball, debate) that meets regularly, central to Korean school and university life. Unlike most school vocabulary here, it is a NATIVE Korean word, not Sino-Korean, which is why it has no hanja and a soft, homegrown feel. Distinguish it from its near-words: 동호회 (同好會) is the equivalent club for adults/the general public (a hiking 동호회, a tennis 동호회), 모임 is any informal gathering or get-together (a dinner 모임), and 클럽 the English loan tends to mean a nightclub or a formal organization — only 동아리 specifically names the student-interest club. The set verb is 동아리에 들어가다 (literally 'go into the club' = join) or the formal 가입하다, and you 동아리에서 활동하다 (are active in it), with 에서 marking the place of activity. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: using 모임 (a one-off gathering) for what is really an ongoing 동아리, and reaching for 참가하다/join with a wrong particle — Korean says 동아리에 들어가다 (에, destination of entering), not 동아리를 들어가다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 모임 for a school club. 모임 is a casual one-time gathering (a meal, a meetup); an ongoing student interest group is a 동아리. Say 동아리에 들어갔어요, not 모임에 들어갔어요, for joining a club.
Marking the club with 를 when joining: 동아리를 들어가요 is wrong. 들어가다 here takes the destination particle 에: 동아리에 들어가요.
Confusing 동아리 with 동호회. 동아리 is for students at school/university; 동호회 is the same kind of club for adults in society. A working adult joins a 동호회, a student a 동아리.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기숙사 means "dormitory" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기숙사 (gisuksa) = "dormitory". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기숙사에 살아요 ("live in the dormitory") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기숙사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 살다 (live/reside) takes 에 to mark the dwelling place
지내다 (to stay/get by) is an action over time, so the place takes 에서
들어가다 with 에 means to move in / take up residence there
기숙사 modifies 생활 (life) to name the experience of living in one

examples.en: I live in the dormitory.
examples.note: The basic residence statement: 살다 with the location particle 에.

examples.en: I'm staying in the dorm with a roommate.
examples.note: 에서 because 지내다 (the ongoing activity of living) happens there; 룸메이트랑 (with a roommate).

examples.ko: 기숙사는 밤 11시에 통금이라서 일찍 들어가야 해요.
examples.romanization: gisuksaneun bam 11sie tonggeumiraseo iljjik deureogaya haeyo.
examples.en: The dorm has an 11 p.m. curfew, so I have to go in early.
examples.note: A real rule of dorm life: 통금 (curfew) plus -아야 하다 (have to); 들어가다 for going in.

extendedVocab.nuance: 기숙사 is a dormitory — a residential building where students or workers live communally near their school or job, typically with shared rooms, rules, and a curfew (통금). The hanja 寄宿舍 is 寄 (lodge/entrust) + 宿 (stay overnight/lodge) + 舍 (house/building), literally a 'lodging house', a place you stay away from home. The 宿 element recurs in lodging words — 숙박 (宿泊, lodging), 합숙 (合宿, a training-camp stay), 숙소 (宿所, the place you stay) — all sharing 宿 'lodge / stay overnight'. Distinguish it from its near-words: 자취방 / 자취 is living alone off-campus in a rented room (자취하다, to live on one's own), 하숙 (下宿) is boarding with a family who provides meals, and 원룸 is a studio flat — only 기숙사 means the institution-run communal dorm. The dual-particle logic matters: use 에 for the state of residing (기숙사에 살다) and motion in (기숙사에 들어가다), but 에서 for activities done there (기숙사에서 공부하다/지내다). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it 집 (home) — your 기숙사 is where you stay, but 집 evokes your family home; a student says 기숙사에 가요 to go back to the dorm, while 집에 가요 means going to their actual home, often a different place entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the dorm 집. 집 is your (family) home; the communal student residence is 기숙사. 'I'm going back to the dorm' is 기숙사에 가요, distinct from 집에 가요 (going to your real home).
Confusing 기숙사 with 자취/하숙. 기숙사 is an institution-run dormitory; 자취 is living alone in a rented place; 하숙 is boarding with a family who feeds you. Pick the one that fits the living arrangement.
Using 에서 for simply residing: 기숙사에서 살아요 is off. The state of living takes 에 (기숙사에 살아요); save 에서 for actions done there (기숙사에서 지내요/공부해요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 상점 means "store" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 상점 (sangjeom) means "store". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상점에서 옷을 사요. ("I buy clothes at the store."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I buy clothes at the store.
usagePhrases.note: place + 에서 marks where an action happens
상점 + 운영하다 is the set phrase for operating a shop
주인 attaches with no particle to mean the shopkeeper
동네 (local area) is the most common modifier

examples.en: There are many stores.
examples.note: simple 이/가 subject statement; 많다 = to be many

examples.en: Let's meet in front of the store.
examples.note: 앞에서 (in front of + at) names a meeting spot

examples.ko: 그 상점은 물건이 좋아서 손님이 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu sangjeomeun mulgeoni joaseo sonnimi manayo.
examples.en: That store has good goods, so it has many customers.
examples.note: real situation: -아서 links cause (good goods) to result (many customers)

extendedVocab.nuance: 상점 is the broad, slightly bookish word for a retail shop, built from the hanja 商店 (商 'commerce' + 店 'shop'), so it literally reads 'commerce-shop.' Its everyday rival is 가게, which is the warm, native-feeling word people actually say out loud ('동네 가게', the corner shop); 상점 sounds a notch more formal and is what you see on signs, in textbooks, and in writing. Compare also 매장, which is a brand's sales floor inside a bigger building. The English-speaker pitfall: do not stretch 상점 to cover a restaurant or a café — those are 식당 and 카페, never 상점. And because English says 'at the store,' learners reach for 에, but the location of an action takes 에서 (상점에서 사요), while 에 marks a destination or static existence (상점에 가요 / 상점에 있어요).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '상점에 옷을 사요' for 'I buy clothes at the store.' Buying is an action performed there, so it needs the action-location particle: 상점에서 옷을 사요. 에 would only fit a verb of going or existing.
Calling a restaurant a 상점. 상점 sells goods, not meals; a place you eat at is 식당 (or 음식점), and a coffee place is 카페.
Treating 상점 and 가게 as interchangeable in casual speech. They overlap in meaning, but in spoken Korean 가게 is far more natural ('가게 가서 우유 사 와'), while 상점 can sound stiff.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매장 means "retail outlet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "retail outlet" is 매장 (maejang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매장을 둘러봐요. ("I look around the outlet."). Watch the particle attached to 매장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 둘러보다 (look around) takes 매장 as its object with 을
직원 attaches directly to mean the floor employee
오프라인 distinguishes a real shop from an online one
들르다 (stop by) pairs with 에, the destination particle

examples.en: The outlet is spacious.
examples.note: simple description; 넓다 = to be wide/spacious

examples.en: I try on clothes at the outlet.
examples.note: 입어 보다 = 'try wearing'; 에서 marks where you do it

examples.ko: 이 브랜드는 백화점 안에 매장이 있어요.
examples.romanization: i beuraendeuneun baekwajeom ane maejangi isseoyo.
examples.en: This brand has an outlet inside the department store.
examples.note: real situation: 안에 (inside) shows a 매장 nested in a bigger building

extendedVocab.nuance: 매장 comes from the hanja 賣場 (賣 'to sell' + 場 'place/floor'), literally 'selling-floor,' and that image is the key: it is the sales space of a brand or company, very often a counter or section housed inside a department store, mall, or large building. The near-synonym 가게 is a standalone little shop someone owns; 매장 is corporate and branch-like — Nike has 매장, your aunt has a 가게. 상점 is the generic textbook word, while 매장 specifically foregrounds the selling area itself. The English-speaker pitfall: 'outlet' in English can mean a discount store, but Korean 매장 has no discount sense at all — a discount mall is 아울렛 (a separate loanword). Also do not call a website a 매장; an online shop is 온라인 쇼핑몰 or just 쇼핑몰.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 매장 for an internet shop because English 'outlet' feels online-friendly. 매장 is a physical selling floor; an online store is 온라인 쇼핑몰 / 인터넷 쇼핑몰.
Assuming 매장 means a bargain/discount store like an English 'outlet.' A Korean discount mall is the loanword 아울렛; plain 매장 carries no cheap-price meaning.
Saying '매장에서 가요' for 'I go to the outlet.' Going is movement toward a destination, so use 에: 매장에 가요. Reserve 에서 for actions done inside it (매장에서 봐요).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 영업시간 means "business hours" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 영업시간 (yeongeopsigan) = "business hours". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영업시간을 확인해요. ("I check the business hours.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 영업시간, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 확인하다 (check) takes 영업시간 as object with 을
외 (outside of) marks times the shop is closed
끝나다 (to end) pairs with 이; the day's service is over
안내 (guidance/notice) is the posted sign of opening times

examples.en: The business hours are long.
examples.note: simple description with 이 + 길다 (to be long)

examples.en: Weekend business hours differ from weekdays.
examples.note: everyday: 와/과 다르다 = 'differs from'; note 과 after 평일

examples.en: What are your business hours here?
examples.note: real situation: 어떻게 되세요? is the polite set phrase to ask a shop's hours

extendedVocab.nuance: 영업시간 is the stretch of time a business is open for service, from 영업 (營業, 'operate a business': 營 'manage' + 業 'enterprise') plus 시간 (時間, 'time-interval': 時 'hour' + 間 'gap'). So the whole word reads 'business-operating time-interval.' Distinguish it from plain 시간, which is just 'time/hours' in general; 영업시간 is specifically the open-for-customers window, and its opposite edge is marked by 영업 종료 ('closing') or 영업 시작 ('opening'). A related sign word is 휴무일, the regular day off when there are no 영업시간 at all. The English-speaker pitfall: to ask the hours, English logic tempts a literal '영업시간이 뭐예요?', but Koreans say 영업시간이 어떻게 되세요? (or 몇 시까지 해요?). Also note 영업시간 is the period; the act of being open is 영업하다 ('to be open for business'), so 'Are you open now?' is 지금 영업해요?, not 지금 영업시간이에요?.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Asking '영업시간이 뭐예요?' for 'What are your hours?' It is grammatical but unnatural; the idiomatic question is 영업시간이 어떻게 되세요? or simply 몇 시까지 해요?.
Using plain 시간 when you mean opening hours, e.g. '이 가게 시간이 어때요?' — that just asks about time vaguely. Specify 영업시간 to mean when the shop is open.
Saying '지금 영업시간이에요?' to ask if a shop is currently open. Use the verb: 지금 영업해요? ('Are you open now?'). 영업시간 names the window, not the live open/closed state.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 정가 means "list price" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 정가 (jeongga) means "list price". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 정가로 사다 ("to buy at list price"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정가 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 정가 + 로 means 'at the full price', no discount
의 links 정가 to 절반 (half) for '50% off' phrasing
정가 + 표 (table/tag) is the posted sheet of fixed prices
적혀 있다 = 'is written (and stays so)' on the tag

examples.en: The list price is expensive.
examples.note: simple 이/가 statement; 비싸다 = to be expensive

examples.en: I bought it cheaper than the list price.
examples.note: everyday: 보다 = 'than'; 싸게 (cheaply) is the adverb form of 싸다

examples.ko: 이 책은 정가가 만 오천 원인데 할인해서 만 원에 샀어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegeun jeonggaga man ocheon woninde harinhaeseo man wone sasseoyo.
examples.en: This book's list price is 15,000 won, but with a discount I bought it for 10,000.
examples.note: real situation: -는데 sets up contrast between 정가 and the price actually paid (에)

extendedVocab.nuance: 정가 is the official, fixed, manufacturer-or-seller-set price printed on a product before any markdown — from the hanja 定價 (定 'to fix/decide' + 價 'price'), literally 'decided price.' Its sharp opposite within shopping is 할인가, the 'discount price,' and you will constantly hear them paired: '정가 30,000원 → 할인가 21,000원.' Do not confuse it with 가격, which is the neutral, general word for 'price' of anything; 정가 specifically claims 'this is the standard, undiscounted figure.' Related is 정찰제, a 'fixed-price system' where haggling isn't allowed. The English-speaker pitfall: 'list price' makes learners want to say 정가 is what you pay, but in Korea the figure on the receipt is often the 할인가 or 판매가 (selling price), not the 정가. Also remember to pay 'at' a price uses 로/으로 (정가로 샀어요), not 에서.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 정가 as the price you actually pay. 정가 is the pre-discount sticker figure; what you hand over may be the 할인가 (discount price) or 판매가 (selling price).
Swapping 정가 for the all-purpose 가격. 가격 just means 'price' in general; choose 정가 only when you specifically mean the fixed, official, undiscounted price.
Saying '정가에서 샀어요' for 'I bought it at list price.' The price you transact at takes 로/으로: 정가로 샀어요. 에서 would wrongly mark a location.

usagePhrases.en: to pay with a gift certificate
usagePhrases.note: 으로 marks the means of payment; 결제하다 = to settle payment
문화 (culture) + 상품권 is the popular book/media voucher brand type

usagePhrases.en: to give a gift certificate as a present
usagePhrases.note: 선물하다 (to gift) takes 상품권 as its object with 을
권 here is the counter-suffix for the bill's face value

examples.en: I have a gift certificate.
examples.note: simple existence with 이 + 있다

examples.en: I paid with the gift certificate.
examples.note: everyday: 으로 = 'by means of'; 계산하다 = to pay/check out

examples.ko: 백화점 상품권은 현금처럼 쓸 수 있어서 선물로 인기가 많아요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 상품권 is a prepaid voucher you spend like cash at shops, from the hanja 商品券 (商品 'merchandise/goods' + 券 'ticket, certificate'), literally 'goods-ticket.' That final 권 (券) is the same 'ticket/coupon' morpheme in 입장권 (admission ticket) and 할인권 (discount coupon), so recognizing it unlocks a whole family of words. Distinguish 상품권 from 쿠폰, a coupon that knocks a percentage or amount off — a 상품권 carries real stored money you redeem, whereas a 쿠폰 just discounts. Culturally, gifting 상품권 (especially 백화점 상품권 and 문화상품권) is extremely common and not seen as impersonal. The English-speaker pitfall: don't confuse it with 영수증 (receipt) or 보증서 (warranty card); only 상품권 holds spendable value. And to pay with one, use 으로 (상품권으로 샀어요), the instrument particle — not 로 after a consonant-final noun mistakenly, since 상품권 ends in ㄴ and correctly takes 으로.

Writing '상품권로 샀어요.' Because 상품권 ends in the consonant ㄴ, the instrumental particle is 으로: 상품권으로 샀어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 교환 means "exchange" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 교환 (gyohwan) = "exchange". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교환하다 ("to exchange") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 교환, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 교환 + 하다 turns the noun into the verb 'to swap an item'
가능하다 (be possible) pairs with 이; the standard shop phrasing
로 marks what you swap into (the target size)
및 (and, formal) is the set sign wording at counters

examples.en: Can I exchange it?
examples.note: simple: 되다 here means 'is allowed/possible'

examples.ko: 이 옷을 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i oseul keun geollo gyohwanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to exchange this for a bigger one.
examples.note: everyday: 걸로 (= 것으로) marks the replacement; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: You can exchange it only if you have the receipt.
examples.note: real situation: -아야 (only if) states the condition for 교환

extendedVocab.nuance: 교환 means swapping a purchased item for a different size, color, or model of the same kind of product, from the hanja 交換 (交 'to cross/mutual' + 換 'to change'), literally 'mutually change.' The crucial shopping contrast is with 반품, a 'return' that gives your money back: 교환 keeps the transaction (you walk out with goods), 반품 undoes it (you walk out with a refund). Counters typically post '교환·반품 안내' together. Note 교환 is also used more broadly than shopping — 의견 교환 (exchanging opinions), 정보 교환 (exchanging information) — so the word isn't shop-only, but here it's the item-swap sense. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'exchange money' tempts a literal 돈을 교환하다, but currency exchange is 환전 (a different word). To swap into the replacement item, use 로/으로 (큰 사이즈로 교환), and remember the verb is 교환하다, so 'I want to exchange' is 교환하고 싶어요, not 교환을 싶어요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 교환 (swap for another item) with 반품 (return for a refund). If you want your money back, that's 반품; 교환 means you leave with replacement goods.
Saying 돈을 교환하다 for changing currency. Money exchange is 환전(하다); 교환 is for swapping purchased items or, figuratively, opinions/information.
Marking the replacement with the wrong particle: '큰 사이즈에 교환해요.' Use 로/으로 for what you swap into — 큰 사이즈로 교환해요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 반품 means "return" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 반품 (banpum) means "return". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 반품하다 ("to return (an item)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 반품 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 반품 + 하다 forms the verb 'to send goods back'
가능하다 pairs with 이; the policy-statement phrasing
신청 (application) + 반품 is the online button to start a return

usagePhrases.en: return due to a change of mind
usagePhrases.note: 단순 변심 ('simple change of heart') is the fixed policy term

examples.en: Can I return it?
examples.note: simple: 되다 = 'is allowed', the quick counter question

examples.en: I'd like to return these shoes and get a refund.
examples.note: everyday: -고 chains 반품하다 and 환불받다 (receive a refund)

examples.ko: 택을 떼면 반품이 안 되니까 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: taegeul ttemyeon banpumi an doenikka josimhaseyo.
examples.en: If you remove the tag, a return isn't possible, so be careful.
examples.note: real situation: -니까 gives the reason warning before acting

extendedVocab.nuance: 반품 is sending a purchased item back to the seller, normally to undo the sale and get a refund, from the hanja 返品 (返 'to send back/return' + 品 'goods'), literally 'return the goods.' The sharp pair is 교환 (swap for another item, transaction kept) versus 반품 (give it back, transaction reversed) — Korean shops list them side by side as '교환·반품.' Closely linked is 환불 (還拂, 'refund'): you do a 반품 in order to receive a 환불, so they often appear together (반품하고 환불받다). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'return to the store' can make learners think of going back to a place, but 반품 is about returning the goods, not yourself returning somewhere — physically going back is 돌아가다, while handing the item back is 반품하다. Also, 반품하다 already contains 하다, so don't add an extra verb: 'I returned it' is 반품했어요, not 반품을 했어요 in the sense of doing something else.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 반품 (return for refund) and 교환 (swap for a different item). If you want money back, say 반품; 교환 leaves you with replacement goods.
Using 반품 for 'returning to a place.' 반품 means sending goods back; physically going back somewhere is 돌아가다. 'I'm going back to the store' is 가게에 다시 가요, not 가게에 반품해요.
Confusing 반품 with 환불. 반품 is the act of sending the item back; 환불 is getting the money. The sequence is 반품한 뒤에 환불받아요 — you return it, then you're refunded.

structuredNuance.t: 반품 is sending a purchased item back to the seller, normally to undo the sale and get a refund.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 품절 means "sold out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "sold out" is 품절 (pumjeol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 품절되다 ("to be/become sold out"). Watch the particle attached to 품절 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 품절 + 되다 makes the passive 'to sell out' (no human agent)
품절 modifies 상품 (product) directly, like an adjective
일시 ('temporarily') softens it — restock expected
임박 ('imminent') is the urgency tag on shopping sites

examples.en: This is sold out.
examples.note: simple 이에요 statement after a consonant-final noun

examples.en: That color is already sold out.
examples.note: everyday: 품절되다 + 벌써 ('already') stresses how fast it went

examples.en: I wanted to buy it, but it was sold out, so I couldn't.
examples.note: real situation: -이라서 ('because it is') gives the reason for 못 사다

extendedVocab.nuance: 품절 describes a product that is completely sold out and currently unavailable, from the hanja 品切 (品 'goods' + 切 'cut off/run out'), literally 'goods cut off.' The natural opposites/relatives are 재고 ('stock on hand') and 입고 ('arrival of new stock'); a thing is 품절 precisely when the 재고 hits zero, and it returns when 재입고 (restock) happens. Distinguish 품절 from 매진 (賣盡, 'sold out'), which carries the same idea but is used for tickets and seats (콘서트 매진, a sold-out concert) rather than store merchandise — say 품절 for products, 매진 for tickets. The English-speaker pitfall: 품절 is a noun/state, and Koreans most often state it as 품절이에요 or with the verb 품절되다 (품절됐어요), so avoid forcing the English passive into something like 품절돼졌어요. Also, to say a specific variant is gone, name it as the subject: 이 사이즈는 품절이에요 ('this size is sold out'), not 품절이 이 사이즈예요.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 품절 for tickets or seats. Sold-out tickets/concerts/seats are 매진 (매진됐어요); reserve 품절 for store products and merchandise.
Over-conjugating into '품절돼졌어요.' The natural forms are the noun statement 품절이에요 or the verb 품절됐어요. 되다 already supplies the passive sense.
Confusing 품절 (sold out, none left) with 재고 (stock available). 재고가 없어요 ('there's no stock') and 품절이에요 overlap, but 재고가 있어요 is the in-stock opposite of 품절.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 재고 means "stock" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 재고 (jaego) = "stock". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 재고가 있다 ("to have stock / be in stock") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 재고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to have stock / be in stock
usagePhrases.note: 있다 with 이 is the core 'we have it' phrase
확인하다 takes 재고 as object with 를; the staff's action
떨어지다 ('fall/run out') idiomatically means stock is depleted
정리 ('sorting out') + 세일 names an inventory-clearing sale

examples.en: It's in stock.
examples.note: simple existence: 이 + 있다 = 'there is stock'

examples.en: Is this size still in stock?
examples.note: everyday: 남아 있다 ('remain') is how shoppers ask if any is left

examples.en: There's no stock in the warehouse, so we have to order it.
examples.note: real situation: -아서 gives the reason; -아야 하다 = 'have to'

extendedVocab.nuance: 재고 is the quantity of goods a shop currently has on hand to sell, from the hanja 在庫 (在 'to exist/be present' + 庫 'storehouse'), literally 'present in the warehouse.' It is the direct counterpart of 품절: while stock 재고 remains, you can buy; when 재고 runs out, the item becomes 품절. Don't confuse 재고 with 창고 (倉庫, the physical 'warehouse' building) — they share the 庫 'storehouse' character, but 재고 is the inventory inside, 창고 is the room itself. A common collocation is the idiom 재고가 떨어지다 ('stock runs out,' literally 'falls'), the same 떨어지다 used for running out of supplies generally. The English-speaker pitfall: English says 'in stock,' tempting 재고에, but Korean uses existence — 재고가 있어요 ('there is stock') for in stock and 재고가 없어요 for out of stock. To ask a clerk, the idiomatic line is 이거 재고 있어요? rather than a literal translation of 'Do you have this in stock?'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '재고에 있어요' to mean 'it's in stock.' Stock is expressed by existence: 재고가 있어요 (in stock) / 재고가 없어요 (out of stock). 에 would wrongly mark a location.
Confusing 재고 (the inventory) with 창고 (the warehouse building). 'There's no stock' is 재고가 없어요; 'it's in the warehouse' is 창고에 있어요.
Treating 재고 and 품절 as the same word. 재고가 없어요 (no stock) leads to 품절이에요 (sold out). When 재고가 있어요, the item is still buyable — the opposite of 품절.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 계산서 means "bill" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 계산서 (gyesanseo) means "bill". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 계산서를 주세요. ("Please give me the bill.").
