Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 를 + 주세요 is the polite 'please give me' request
나오다 ('come out') is how a bill is said to be issued
확인하다 takes 계산서 as object; you verify the amounts
좀 softens the request; 보여 주다 = 'show'

examples.en: The bill, please.
examples.note: simple: drop the particle in casual speech for a quick ask

examples.en: The bill seems a bit off.
examples.note: everyday: 좀 ('a bit') + 이상하다 (be strange) flags a possible error

examples.en: When I looked at the bill, the drink was rung up twice.
examples.note: real situation: -니까 ('upon doing') leads into the discovery

extendedVocab.nuance: 계산서 is the itemized statement of what you owe, from 계산 (計算, 'calculation/reckoning': 計 'to count' + 算 'to compute') plus the suffix 서 (書, 'written document'), so it reads 'a written reckoning.' That 서 (書) 'document' morpheme also forms 신청서 (application form) and 보증서 (warranty), a handy pattern to learn. The key contrast is with 영수증 (領收證, 'receipt'): a 계산서 is the request for payment showing the itemized total before/at paying, while 영수증 is the proof you already paid — at a restaurant you get the 계산서 to settle, then the 영수증 afterward. Note 계산서 also has a formal tax sense (세금계산서, 'tax invoice') in business. The English-speaker pitfall: 'bill' in English also means paper money, but Korean 계산서 never means a banknote — a bill/note of money is 지폐. And to ask for the check politely, Koreans say 계산서 주세요 or simply 계산할게요 ('I'll pay'), not a literal 'check, please.'

Using 계산서 for paper money because English 'bill' is ambiguous. A banknote is 지폐 (or 돈); 계산서 is only the itemized statement of charges.
Confusing 계산서 (the bill/invoice you pay from) with 영수증 (the receipt proving you paid). Ask for 계산서 before paying; keep the 영수증 after.
Forcing a literal 'check please' as something like '체크 주세요.' At a restaurant, say 계산서 주세요 or 계산할게요 to ask for and settle the bill.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 봉지 means "bag" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "bag" is 봉지 (bongji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 봉지에 담다 ("to put into a bag"). Watch the particle attached to 봉지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination; 담다 = to put/pack into a container
비닐 (vinyl) + 봉지 is the everyday convenience-store bag
하나 (one) + 주세요; you often pay extra for it
봉지 doubles as a counter: 'a packet of'

examples.en: A bag, please.
examples.note: simple request; particle dropped in casual speech

examples.en: You have to pay for a plastic bag.
examples.note: everyday: -아야 하다 ('have to') reflects Korea's paid-bag rule

examples.ko: 산 물건을 봉지에 담아서 들고 갔어요.
examples.romanization: san mulgeoneul bongjie damaseo deulgo gasseoyo.
examples.en: I packed what I bought into a bag and carried it out.
examples.note: real situation: 담아서 ('pack and then') chains into 들고 가다 (carry along)

extendedVocab.nuance: 봉지 is a thin plastic or paper bag for carrying purchases, and it doubles as a counter for packeted goods (과자 한 봉지, 'a bag of chips'). The most common compound is 비닐봉지 ('vinyl/plastic bag'). Crucially, distinguish 봉지 from 가방: a 가방 is a durable bag you own and reuse — a handbag, backpack, or suitcase — whereas a 봉지 is the flimsy throwaway sack the cashier gives you; calling your backpack a 봉지 sounds odd. Also nearby is 봉투, which is more for envelopes and sturdier paper/shopping bags (종이봉투), with some overlap. Culturally, Korean shops charge for 비닐봉지 by law, so 봉지 드릴까요? ('Shall I give you a bag?') usually implies a small fee. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'bag' covers everything, so learners over-apply 봉지; reserve it for disposable shopping sacks, and use 가방 for personal bags. To pack items 'into' it, use 에 with 담다 (봉지에 담다), the destination particle, not 에서.

Calling a backpack, purse, or suitcase a 봉지. Those reusable personal bags are 가방; 봉지 is the disposable shopping sack the store hands you.
Saying '봉지에서 담아요' for 'I put it in the bag.' 담다 packs into a destination, so use 에: 봉지에 담아요. 에서 marks where an action happens, not where things go in.
Forgetting 봉지 works as a counter and saying '과자 한 개' when you mean a packet. A packaged bag of snacks is 과자 한 봉지; 한 개 would suggest a single piece.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 거스름돈 means "change" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 거스름돈 (geoseureumdon) = "change". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 거스름돈을 받다 ("to receive change") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 거스름돈, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 takes 거스름돈 as object with 을; you get it back
주다 hands the change to the customer; the everyday verb pairing
됐어요 ('it's fine') politely declines the change
잔돈 is the shorter near-synonym, also meaning loose coins

examples.en: Please give me my change.
examples.note: simple request; particle dropped casually

examples.en: The change is short.
examples.note: everyday: 모자라다 ('be insufficient') flags a shortfall

examples.ko: 만 원을 냈는데 거스름돈을 안 줬어요.
examples.romanization: man woneul naenneunde geoseureumdoneul an jwosseoyo.
examples.en: I paid with 10,000 won, but they didn't give me the change.
examples.note: real situation: -는데 contrasts paying with not receiving change

extendedVocab.nuance: 거스름돈 is the money handed back when you pay more than the exact price — pure native Korean, from the verb 거스르다 ('to give change back; to go against the flow') plus 돈 ('money'), so it pictures money 'flowing back' to you. Its close synonym is 잔돈, but the two differ: 거스름돈 is specifically the change returned from a payment, while 잔돈 more broadly means small coins/loose change you carry (잔돈 있어요? = 'Do you have small change?'). From a customer's side it pairs with 받다 (거스름돈을 받다, 'receive change'); from the cashier's side it pairs with 주다 (거스름돈을 줬어요, 'gave the change') — note you say 거스름돈을 주다, not the redundant 거스름돈을 거슬러 주다, since the noun and the verb 거슬러 주다 both come from 거스르다 and stacking them doubles the meaning. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'change' is overloaded, and learners confuse this money sense with 바꾸다 ('to change/alter') or 환전 (currency exchange) — 거스름돈 has nothing to do with those. Also beware 용돈, which sounds vaguely similar but means 'pocket money/allowance,' a completely different word. To say 'keep the change,' don't translate literally; Koreans say 거스름돈은 됐어요 or 그냥 가지세요.

Confusing 거스름돈 (change from a payment) with the verb 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') or 환전 (currency exchange). 거스름돈 is only the cash returned after overpaying.
Mixing up 거스름돈 with 용돈. They sound a little alike, but 용돈 is 'pocket money/allowance,' while 거스름돈 is the change a cashier gives back.
Translating 'keep the change' word-for-word. The natural phrasings are 거스름돈은 됐어요 or 그냥 가지세요 — a literal version sounds unnatural.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 노트북 means "laptop" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 노트북 (noteubuk) means "laptop". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노트북으로 일해요. ("I work on a laptop."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노트북 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Tool/means takes -으로 after a consonant: 노트북 ends in ㄱ, so 노트북으로, never 노트북로.
The on/off pair is 켜다/끄다; for booting you also hear 부팅하다, but 켜다 is the everyday word.
가볍다 (light) vs 무겁다 (heavy) is the standard weight pair buyers care about; 가벼워요 is the ㅂ-irregular polite form.
충전(充電) 'fill electricity'; you charge the 배터리, and when it dies you say 배터리가 다 됐어요.

examples.en: This laptop is light.
examples.note: Simple description; 가볍다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so polite form is 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.

examples.en: I watch movies on my laptop too.
examples.note: 도 'also' attaches to the object to add it to other uses; note the means particle 으로 on the device.

examples.en: The company gave me a laptop.
examples.note: Computers and machines are counted with the counter 대, so 한 대 = one (machine).

extendedVocab.nuance: 노트북 is the default Korean word for a laptop computer — it comes from English 'notebook' (short for 노트북 컴퓨터), so a beginner's instinct that it means a paper notebook is the classic 직역 trap: a paper notebook is 공책 or just 노트, and only the computer is 노트북. The near-synonym 컴퓨터 is the umbrella term for any computer, while 노트북 specifically marks the portable/foldable kind; a desktop is 데스크톱 or 데스크탑. 랩탑 exists as a transliteration but sounds foreign and is rarely spoken — Koreans say 노트북. Register is fully neutral, fine in any setting. Habitual collocations: 노트북을 켜다/끄다 (turn on/off), 노트북으로 일하다/공부하다 (work/study on it), 노트북이 느리다/빠르다, 가볍다/무겁다, and 노트북을 충전하다 (charge it). The pitfall for English speakers is the particle: 'on a laptop' is 노트북으로 (means), not 노트북에 — 노트북에 would mean physically 'onto/in the laptop' (e.g. saving a file).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 랩탑 because it matches English 'laptop'. It is understood but sounds unnatural — Koreans overwhelmingly say 노트북.
Using 노트북 for a paper notebook. A spiral paper notebook is 공책 or 노트; 노트북 is only the computer. 'I wrote in my 노트북' would sound like you typed into a laptop.
Writing 노트북에서 영화를 봐요 for 'I watch movies on a laptop'. The device as a means takes 으로 (노트북으로 영화를 봐요); 에서 marks a location, so it implies the movie is somewhere inside the device.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 마우스 means "mouse" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "mouse" is 마우스 (mauseu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마우스로 클릭하다 ("to click with a mouse"). Watch the particle attached to 마우스 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 마우스 ends in a vowel (ㅡ→스), and the rule still gives 마우스로; 클릭하다 borrows 'click' + 하다.
고장 나다 = 'a breakdown occurs', the natural way to say a device stopped working; spaced 고장 나다.
움직이다 is the everyday verb for moving an object slightly; 마우스를 움직여요 in polite speech.
무선(無線) 'no-wire'; the opposite wired is 유선(有線), so 유선 마우스 vs 무선 마우스.

examples.en: The mouse isn't working.
examples.note: 안 되다 'doesn't work/function' is how you report a device problem in casual speech.

examples.en: I even draw pictures with the mouse.
examples.note: 도 adds drawing as an extra use; 그리다 (draw) → 그려요.

examples.en: I bought a new mouse.
examples.note: Small countable items use 하나 (one) naturally; 새 (new) goes directly before the noun.

extendedVocab.nuance: 마우스 is purely the computer pointing device — it is a transliteration of English 'mouse' and, crucially, never means the animal. The live animal is 쥐 (which covers both mice and rats; Korean does not split them the way English does), so the English habit of one word for both is exactly the pitfall: '쥐가 고장 났어요' would be absurd, and '마우스가 집에 있어요' sounds like hardware, not a pet. Register is neutral and technical-everyday. Natural collocations: 마우스로 클릭하다 (click), 마우스를 움직이다 (move it), 마우스가 고장 나다 / 안 되다 (it breaks / doesn't work), and the wired/wireless split 유선 마우스 vs 무선 마우스. The means particle is again 으로 — 마우스로 클릭하다, not 마우스에 클릭하다 (English 'click ON' tempts 에/에서, but Korean treats the mouse as the instrument, so 으로).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 마우스 for the animal. The rodent is 쥐; 마우스 only ever means the computer device.
Saying 마우스에 클릭해요 by analogy with 'click ON the mouse'. You click WITH the mouse, so it's the instrument: 마우스로 클릭해요. 클릭하다 itself takes the screen target with 을/를 or just the place you click.
Expecting a separate word for a small mouse vs a big rat in everyday talk — Korean uses 쥐 for both, so don't search for a 마우스/쥐 size distinction the way English has mouse/rat.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 모니터 means "monitor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 모니터 (moniteo) = "monitor". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 모니터로 영화를 보다 ("to watch a movie on a monitor") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 모니터, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to watch a movie on a monitor
usagePhrases.note: Means particle 으로 marks the screen you view it through; 보다 (watch) → 봐요.
Size pair 크다 (big) / 작다 (small); 화면(畫面) 'screen' is the display surface, so 화면이 크다 is also common.
연결(連結) 'link-tie'; you 연결하다 (connect) a monitor to a 노트북 with a 케이블.
Borrowed 듀얼 'dual'; two screens side by side, very common phrasing in offices: 모니터 두 대.

examples.en: The monitor is too bright.
examples.note: 너무 'too (much)' before an adjective; 밝다 (bright) → 밝아요.

examples.en: I view photos large on the monitor.
examples.note: 크게 is the adverb form of 크다 'big' → 'largely/in big size'.

examples.ko: 큰 모니터를 한 대 사고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: keun moniteoreul han dae sago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to buy a big monitor.
examples.note: Screens are machines, so counter 대; -고 싶다 expresses the speaker's own desire.

extendedVocab.nuance: 모니터 is specifically a computer display screen, distinct from a 텔레비전/TV which is a broadcast set you watch programs on — the dividing line is function, not shape: even an identical-looking panel is a 모니터 if it shows your computer and a 텔레비전 if it receives channels. From English 'monitor', it stays neutral in register. Note the related word 화면 (畫面, 'picture-surface') means the screen/display *content or surface* itself, so '화면이 꺼졌어요' = the display went dark, while '모니터를 샀어요' = I bought the physical unit. Habitual collocations: 모니터를 켜다/끄다, 모니터로 ~를 보다, 모니터를 연결하다 (connect), 모니터가 크다/작다/밝다/어둡다, and 듀얼 모니터 / 모니터 두 대. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a TV a 모니터 (and vice versa), plus reaching for 에서 — you watch 모니터로 (through it as a means), and 모니터에 means onto the monitor (e.g. 모니터에 먼지가 있어요, dust on the monitor).

Calling a television a 모니터. A TV that receives channels is 텔레비전 (or TV); 모니터 is the computer screen only.
Mixing up 모니터 and 화면. 모니터 is the physical device; 화면 is the screen surface/picture. '화면이 안 나와요' = no picture is showing, which is about the display, not the box.
Saying 모니터에서 영화를 봐요 for watching via the monitor. Use 모니터로 (by means of the monitor); 에서 marks a location and sounds like the movie lives inside the device.

In Korean the particle or ending next to 프린터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. usagePhrases.note: The machine is 프린터; the action is 인쇄(印刷)하다 'print'. 프린트하다 (from 'print') also exists colloquially.
고장 나다 for a malfunction; office printers famously 자주 고장 나요 (break down often).

usagePhrases.en: the printer is out of paper
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the container/location here — paper is inside the printer, so 프린터에, not 프린터로.
흑백(黑白) 'black-white'; color is 컬러, so 컬러 프린터 vs 흑백 프린터.

examples.en: I print photos with the printer.
examples.note: 뽑다 'pull out/print out' is the casual verb for getting a printout; means particle 으로.

examples.en: There is a printer at the office.
examples.note: Existence 있다 with location 에; machines counted with 대.

examples.en: The printer ran out of paper.
examples.note: 다 떨어지다 'be all used up'; 에 marks where the paper is (inside the printer).

extendedVocab.nuance: 프린터 is the physical printing machine (from English 'printer'), and the key contrast learners must internalize is device vs action: the act of printing is 인쇄하다 (印刷하다, Sino-Korean 'print') or casually 프린트하다 / 뽑다, while a printed handout itself is 프린트 (a 프린트, a printout). So '프린터를 했어요' is wrong — you 인쇄를 했어요 (did the printing) using the 프린터. Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 프린터로 인쇄하다/뽑다, 프린터가 고장 나다, 프린터에 종이가 없다/떨어지다, 프린터로 ~를 출력하다 (출력 出力, the more technical 'output/print'), and 컬러/흑백 프린터. Two particle traps: the means is 프린터로 (print *with* it), but supplies live *in* it, so paper and ink take 에 — 프린터에 종이가 없어요, 프린터에 잉크가 떨어졌어요. English 'print it on the printer' wrongly suggests 에 for the action.

Saying 프린터를 해요 for 'I print'. 프린터 is the machine, not the act. The action is 인쇄(를) 하다 or 프린트하다 / 뽑다; the machine is just the tool: 프린터로 인쇄해요.
Confusing 프린터 (machine) with 프린트 (a printout/handout). 'Give me the 프린트' = the printed sheet; 'turn on the 프린터' = the device.
Using 프린터로 종이가 없어요 for 'out of paper'. The paper is inside the machine, so use 에: 프린터에 종이가 없어요. Reserve 으로 for the printing action itself.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 스피커 means "speaker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "speaker" is 스피커 (seupikeo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 스피커로 음악을 듣다 ("to listen to music on a speaker"). Watch the particle attached to 스피커 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to listen to music on a speaker
usagePhrases.note: Means 으로; 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular → 들어요 (the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel).
소리 'sound', 크다 'big/loud'; for sound, 크다/작다 = loud/quiet, so 소리가 커요.
켜다/끄다 on/off; a Bluetooth speaker you 블루투스로 연결하다 (connect via Bluetooth) first.
블루투스 'Bluetooth'; wireless portable ones are everywhere, phrased 블루투스 스피커.

examples.en: The speaker is too loud.
examples.note: Sound volume uses 크다 (loud) / 작다 (quiet), not 시끄럽다 here; 시끄럽다 is 'noisy/annoying'.

examples.en: I play songs on the speaker.
examples.note: 틀다 'turn on/play (audio/video)' is the natural verb for playing music; means particle 으로.

examples.en: I bought a new speaker.
examples.note: 하나 for one small item; 새 directly before the noun for 'new'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 스피커 (from English 'speaker') means the audio output device that plays sound — and the trap is that, unlike English, it does NOT mean a person speaking. A speaker at an event/lecture is 발표자 (發表者, 'presenter') or 연사 (演士), and a native speaker of a language is 원어민; calling a presenter a 스피커 is a 직역 mistake. Register is neutral, technical-everyday. Useful contrast: 스피커 outputs sound out loud, whereas 이어폰/헤드폰 send it privately to your ears. Habitual collocations: 스피커로 음악을 듣다/틀다, 스피커를 켜다/끄다, 스피커 소리가 크다/작다, 스피커를 (블루투스로) 연결하다, and 블루투스 스피커. For volume use 소리가 크다/작다 (loud/quiet), and note 음량/볼륨 (volume) is the level you 높이다/낮추다 (raise/lower). The particle pitfall: play music 스피커로 (means), not 스피커에서.

Using 스피커 for a person who speaks. A presenter is 발표자/연사; a native speaker is 원어민. 스피커 is only the sound device.
Saying 스피커가 시끄러워요 to mean 'the speaker is loud'. 시끄럽다 means 'noisy/bothersome'. For plain loudness say 소리가 커요; use 시끄럽다 only when the sound is annoying.
Saying 스피커에서 음악을 들어요 for listening via the speaker. The device is the means: 스피커로 음악을 들어요. 에서 marks a place and sounds odd here.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 이어폰 means "earphones" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 이어폰 (ieopon) = "earphones". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이어폰으로 음악을 듣다 ("to listen to music with earphones") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이어폰, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to listen to music with earphones
usagePhrases.note: Means 으로 after consonant ㄴ; 이어폰으로. Listening is 듣다 → 들어요 (ㄷ-irregular).
끼다 'insert/wear (snug things)' is the verb for in-ear buds; 끼다/빼다 = put in / take out.
줄 'cord/wire'; 엉키다 'get tangled'. Wired buds are 유선 이어폰.
무선(無線) 'wireless'; the true-wireless buds (like AirPods) are 무선 이어폰 or 블루투스 이어폰.

examples.en: I put in earphones and listen to music.
examples.note: -고 links two actions in sequence; 끼다 is the right verb for in-ear buds (not 쓰다/입다).

examples.en: On the subway I use earphones.
examples.note: Here 쓰다 'use' is fine for the general act of using; 에서는 = at (location) + topic 는.

examples.en: The earphone cord keeps tangling.
examples.note: 자꾸 'repeatedly/keep ~ing' captures the recurring annoyance; 엉키다 → 엉켜요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이어폰 (from 'earphone') are small in-ear listening devices, and the sharp contrast is with 헤드폰 — the bigger over-the-ear cans: don't call headphones 이어폰. Within earbuds, wired ones are 유선 이어폰 and the true-wireless type (AirPods-style) are 무선 이어폰 / 블루투스 이어폰, though many people just say 에어팟 generically. Register is neutral. The verb pitfall is choosing how to 'wear' them: in-ear buds take 끼다 (insert snugly) — 이어폰을 끼다 — while over-ear 헤드폰 take 쓰다 (wear on the head); 입다 (wear clothes) is wrong for both. Habitual collocations: 이어폰을 끼다/빼다, 이어폰으로 음악을/영어를 듣다, 이어폰 줄이 엉키다, and 무선/유선 이어폰. Particle note: listen 이어폰으로 (means), and the cord 줄 takes 이/가 as the subject that tangles (줄이 엉켜요), not 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling over-ear headphones 이어폰. Big over-the-head ones are 헤드폰; 이어폰 are the small in-ear kind.
Saying 이어폰을 입다 or 이어폰을 신다 for putting them in. In-ear buds take 끼다 (이어폰을 끼다). 입다 is for clothing and 신다 is for footwear.
Using 이어폰에서 음악을 들어요. The earphones are the means, so 이어폰으로 음악을 들어요. Reserve 에서 for a location, not a device you listen through.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 데이터 means "data" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 데이터 (deiteo) means "data". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 데이터로 영상을 보다 ("to watch videos using data"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 데이터 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Means 으로; mobile data as the means of connecting. 데이터로 = on (mobile) data.
부족(不足)하다 'be insufficient'; near month-end people say 데이터가 부족해요.

usagePhrases.en: to use up all the data
usagePhrases.note: 다 'all' + 쓰다 'use'; 데이터를 다 썼어요 = the allowance is gone.
무제한(無制限) 'no-limit'; a 데이터 무제한 요금제 is an unlimited-data plan.

examples.en: I'm low on data this month.
examples.note: 이번 달 'this month' sets the time frame; 부족하다 'be insufficient/short'.

examples.en: I use data because there's no wifi.
examples.note: -아서/어서 gives reason; 없어서 'because there isn't', then the result clause.

examples.ko: 데이터를 다 써서 영상이 안 나와요.
examples.romanization: deiteoreul da sseoseo yeongsangi an nawayo.
examples.en: I used up my data, so videos won't play.
examples.note: Chained -아서/어서 for cause; 안 나오다 'won't come out/play' for media not loading.

extendedVocab.nuance: 데이터 (from English 'data') in everyday Korean almost always means your mobile-phone data allowance, not abstract research information — that everyday narrowing is the pitfall: a scientist's 'the data shows...' is 자료 (資料, 'reference material') or 데이터 in technical writing, but '데이터가 없어요' to a normal person means your phone's data ran out, not 'there is no information.' The near-synonym is 정보 (情報, 'information'), which is the content/knowledge itself, distinct from the data allowance you buy. Register is neutral and very common when newcomers set up a phone. Habitual collocations: 데이터를 쓰다/다 쓰다, 데이터가 부족하다/남다 (be short / be left over), 데이터로 영상을 보다, 데이터를 켜다/끄다 (toggle mobile data), and 데이터 무제한 (unlimited). Particle pitfall: connect 데이터로 (by means of data), not 데이터에서. Also, 'a lot of data' is 데이터가 많다, and 'out of data' is 데이터가 떨어지다/다 되다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 데이터 with 정보 in daily talk. To a normal person 데이터 = your phone's data allowance; abstract information is 정보, and research data is 자료.
Saying 데이터에서 영상을 봐요 for watching on mobile data. Data is the means: 데이터로 영상을 봐요. 에서 marks a location and is wrong here.
Using 데이터가 없어요 to mean 'there is no information'. To most listeners that means your mobile data is used up. For 'no information' say 정보가 없어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 요금제 means "phone plan" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "phone plan" is 요금제 (yogeumje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 새 요금제로 바꾸다 ("to switch to a new plan"). Watch the particle attached to 요금제 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to switch to a new plan
usagePhrases.note: 바꾸다 'change/switch'; the target plan takes 으로 (요금제로 바꾸다) = 'change INTO a plan'.
고르다 'pick' is a 르-irregular → 골라요; you compare and 고르다 a 요금제.
비싸다 (expensive) / 싸다 (cheap) is the price pair; 비싸요/싸요 in polite speech.
A 요금제 named by its feature; 무제한(無制限) 'no-limit', a very common plan type.

examples.en: I want to switch to a cheaper plan.
examples.note: Target of 바꾸다 takes 으로; -고 싶다 for the speaker's wish.

examples.en: This plan has a lot of data.
examples.note: Topic 는 introduces the plan, then comments on its data; 많다 'be a lot' → 많아요.

examples.en: Could you recommend a plan?
examples.note: 좀 softens the request; -아/어 주세요 'please do for me'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 요금제 (料金制, literally '料金 fee/charge + 制 system' = 'fee system/plan') is a mobile-phone service pricing plan — the package of data, calls, and texts you sign up for — and it is one of the first words a newcomer needs when getting a phone. The crucial contrast is 요금제 (the plan/scheme) vs 요금 (料金, the fee/charge itself): 요금제를 바꿨어요 = I changed my PLAN, but 요금이 많이 나왔어요 = the CHARGE came out high (my bill was big). Confusing them is the main pitfall. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 요금제를 바꾸다/고르다/선택하다, 요금제가 비싸다/싸다, 요금제를 추천하다, and feature names like 데이터 무제한 요금제, 알뜰 요금제 (budget/MVNO plan). Particle note: when switching, the new plan is the destination with 으로 — 새 요금제로 바꾸다, not 요금제를 바꾸다 alone when you mean 'switch TO'. The 알뜰폰 (budget carrier) world is where newcomers often hunt for a cheap 요금제.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 요금제 with 요금. 요금제 = the plan/scheme; 요금 = the actual fee/bill. '요금이 나왔어요' = the charge came; '요금제를 바꿨어요' = I changed plans.
Saying 요금제에 바꿨어요 for 'switched to a plan'. The new plan is the destination, marked 으로: 새 요금제로 바꿨어요. 바꾸다 pairs the old thing (을/를) with the new (으로).
Treating 요금제 as a generic 'price'. It specifically means a telecom service plan, not the price of goods (that's 가격 or 값).

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 문자 means "text message" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 문자 (munja) = "text message". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문자로 연락하다 ("to contact by text") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 문자, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 연락(連絡)하다 'get in touch'; 문자로 = by text. After a vowel the means particle is plain 로, and 문자 ends in the vowel ㅏ, so 문자로, never 문자으로.
오다 'come' is the natural verb for an incoming message; 문자가 왔어요 = a text arrived.
보내다 'send'; the send/receive pair is 보내다 / 받다, and incoming ones 오다.
확인(確認)하다 'confirm/check'; you 확인하다 a message you received.

examples.en: A text came in.
examples.note: Incoming messages use 오다 (come), not 받다, in this announcing sense: 문자가 왔어요.

examples.en: A text came from the bank.
examples.note: 에서 marks the source 'from' (an organization); the bank as origin of the text.

examples.en: Please send the address by text.
examples.note: Means 문자로 'by text'; -아/어 주세요 for a polite request.

extendedVocab.nuance: 문자 (文字, 'written character/letter') in daily speech is the everyday word for an SMS text message — short for 문자 메시지. The pitfall is its double life: literally 문자 means written characters/letters (e.g. 한글은 한국의 문자예요, 'Hangul is Korea's writing system'), so context decides. Crucially, 문자 is NOT a paper letter in the mail — that is 편지 (便紙). extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 영상통화 means "video call" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 영상통화 (yeongsangtonghwa) means "video call". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영상통화로 이야기하다 ("to talk over video call"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영상통화 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Means 으로; 영상통화로 = by/over video call. 이야기하다 'talk/chat'.
통화 is a 하다-noun, so the action is 영상통화를 하다 'do a video call', i.e. make one.
끊기다 'be cut off (passive)'; a bad connection 끊겨요. Contrast 끊다 'hang up (on purpose)'.
연결(連結) 'connection'; 안 되다 'fails to work' — a frequent complaint with weak signal.

examples.en: I video-call with my family.
examples.note: 이랑 'with' (casual) marks the other party; the action is 영상통화를 하다.

examples.en: We talk while seeing each other's faces on video call.
examples.note: -면서 'while (doing both)'; the appeal of video is 얼굴을 보다 (see the face).

examples.en: I video-called my parents on the weekend.
examples.note: Time 에 (주말에) + companion 이랑; past 했어요.

extendedVocab.nuance: 영상통화 (映像通話, '映像 video-image + 通話 phone-call' = literally 'video phone call') is a phone call with live video — invaluable for newcomers keeping in touch with family abroad. The sharp contrast is with plain 통화 (通話), a voice-only call: 그냥 통화 = a normal voice call, but 영상통화 = with video, so dropping 영상 changes the meaning. Don't say just 통화 when you specifically mean seeing each other's faces. The near-synonym 화상통화 exists (more formal/business, e.g. video conferencing leans 화상 회의), while 영상통화 is the everyday personal term, and people also say 페이스타임/영통 casually. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 영상통화를 하다, 영상통화로 이야기하다/얼굴을 보다, 영상통화가 끊기다, and 영상통화 연결이 안 되다. Particle/verb traps: it is a 하다-noun, so 'make a video call' = 영상통화를 하다 (not 영상통화하다 in writing, though spoken); the other party takes 이랑/하고/와/과 ('with'); 'over video call' is 영상통화로.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 배경화면 means "wallpaper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "wallpaper" is 배경화면 (baegyeonghwamyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다 ("to make a photo into wallpaper"). Watch the particle attached to 배경화면 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: to make a photo into wallpaper
usagePhrases.note: Means/material 으로 'with/from (a photo)'; 만들다 'make' → 만들어요.
바꾸다 'change/swap'; the most common action — 배경화면을 자주 바꿔요.
설정(設定)하다 'set/configure'; 으로 marks the role 'as' — 사진을 배경화면으로 설정하다.
Related: 잠금(lock)+화면(screen). The lock screen is 잠금화면, the home/background is 배경화면.

examples.en: The wallpaper is pretty.
examples.note: 예쁘다 (pretty) is a ㅡ-irregular → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before 어).

examples.en: I changed my wallpaper to a dog photo.
examples.note: Material 으로 'with (a dog photo)'; past 바꿨어요.

examples.en: I set this photo as my wallpaper.
examples.note: Role 으로 'as'; 설정하다 is the menu-style verb for 'set/apply'.

extendedVocab.nuance: 배경화면 (背景畫面, '背景 background + 畫面 screen-picture' = 'background screen image') is the wallpaper/background image on a phone or computer — and the pitfall is the English word 'wallpaper': this is purely the digital screen background, never the paper you put on a real room wall. Room wallpaper is 벽지 (壁紙, 'wall-paper'), so '방 배경화면을 발랐어요' would be nonsense — you 벽지를 바르다 (paste wallpaper) on a wall. Within screens, contrast 배경화면 (the home/background image) with 잠금화면 (lock screen) and 바탕화면 (the desktop on a computer); they overlap but name different surfaces. The component 화면 (畫面) means 'screen/display', the same 화면 as in 모니터 화면. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 배경화면을 바꾸다/설정하다, 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다, 배경화면이 예쁘다/어둡다, and the pair 배경화면/잠금화면. Particle note: the photo you use is the material/role with 으로 — 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다, 배경화면으로 설정하다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 배경화면 for real room wallpaper. The digital screen background is 배경화면; physical wall covering is 벽지 (you 벽지를 바르다, paste it).
Saying 배경화면에 사진을 만들어요. The photo is the material you make it FROM, so use 으로: 사진으로 배경화면을 만들어요 / 설정해요.
Conflating 배경화면 with 잠금화면. 배경화면 is the home/background image; 잠금화면 is the lock screen you see before unlocking. They are set separately on a phone.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 평일 means "weekday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 평일 (pyeongil) = "weekday". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 평일에 ("on a weekday") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 평일, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에 for 'on'; 평일에 갔어요 = went on a weekday
No particle: 평일 sticks directly to the next noun to modify it
Common slot for off-peak hours, doctor visits, quiet cafes
After-work time; 평일 저녁에 운동해요 = I work out on weeknights

examples.en: On weekdays I go to school.
examples.note: Topic 은 makes a 'weekdays, as for them' contrast with weekends

examples.en: On weekdays there are fewer people.
examples.note: 에는 = 에(on) + 는(contrast), the natural way to set the scene

examples.en: It's hard to make time on a weekday.
examples.note: Real-life 직장인 complaint: 시간(을) 내다 = to make/spare time

extendedVocab.nuance: 평일 is Sino-Korean 平日 (平 'flat/ordinary' + 日 'day'), literally an 'ordinary day' — Monday through Friday, the regular working days, set against 주말 (weekend) and 휴일 (holiday/day off). The dividing line vs 주중 (週中, 'inside the week'): 평일 simply names the ordinary days as a category, while 주중 frames those same days as the span 'during the week' and pairs naturally with 주말 as a matched contrast (주중에는 바쁘고 주말에는 쉬어요). 평일 is neutral and used by everyone in any register, from a weather report to a friend's text. It habitually appears as 평일 + time-of-day (평일 아침/낮/저녁) and with 에/에는. The English-speaker pitfall: 'weekday' in English can mean 'any single working day' OR the whole work portion of the week, but in Korean 평일 leans toward the category of ordinary days, so for a duration like 'during the week I'm busy' Koreans more often say 주중에는 바빠요; also don't write the near-homophone 휴일 (rest day) by mistake.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 평일날 to mean 'on a weekday' is redundant — 일(日) already means 'day', so 날 doubles it; just say 평일에.
Writing 주말 (weekend) when you mean 평일 — they are exact opposites, so 평일에 일해요 (work on weekdays) vs 주말에 쉬어요 (rest on weekends).
Forgetting 에 in time phrases: not 평일 갔어요 but 평일에 갔어요, because a point-in-time noun needs the locative-time particle 에.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 주중 means "midweek" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 주중 (jujung) means "midweek". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주중에 ("during the week"). Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에; the default frame for 'on weekdays as a span'

usagePhrases.en: during the week (as opposed to weekends)
usagePhrases.note: 에는 sets up the 주중 vs 주말 contrast
No particle before the noun it modifies
내내 = 'the whole time'; 주중 내내 바빴어요 = busy the whole week

examples.en: I work during the week.
examples.note: 에는 frames the span and implies 'but on weekends I don't'

examples.en: I have no time during the week.
examples.note: 있다/없다 take 이/가 on the thing possessed: 시간이 없어요

examples.en: I work on weekdays and rest on weekends.
examples.note: Real rhythm-of-life sentence pairing 주중 with 주말

extendedVocab.nuance: 주중 is Sino-Korean 週中 (週 'week' + 中 'middle/inside'), literally 'inside the week' — the Monday-to-Friday stretch viewed as a span of time. It overlaps heavily with 평일 (平日), but the dividing line is framing: 평일 names the ordinary days as a category, whereas 주중 emphasizes the duration 'during the week' and is the natural partner of 주말 (週末, 'week-end') in a balanced contrast — Koreans reflexively say 주중에는 ... 주말에는 .... The English-speaker pitfall: 'midweek' in English often means specifically Tuesday–Thursday, but 주중 covers the whole working span, so don't narrow it to just the middle days; and because 주중 is a time-span noun it still needs 에 (주중에 바빠요), unlike a bare adverb.

Treating 주중 as 'Wednesday-ish only' the way English 'midweek' can — 주중 means the whole Mon–Fri span, so 주중에 바빠요 = busy all week, not just the middle.
Writing 주말 (weekend) when you mean 주중 — one letter (중 vs 말) flips the meaning to the opposite half of the week.
Dropping 에: not 주중 시간이 없어요 (ambiguous) but 주중에 시간이 없어요, since the time span needs the 에 particle to mean 'during'.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 매주 means "every week" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "every week" is 매주 (maeju). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매주 월요일 ("every Monday"). Watch the particle attached to 매주 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: Add a specific day right after: 매주 월요일에 회의해요
Pair with a frequency count; 매주 한 번 청소해요
마다 intensifies 'each and every'; optional but common
꼬박꼬박 = without ever skipping; stresses regularity

examples.en: I exercise every week.
examples.note: 매주 sits right before the verb like an adverb — no particle

examples.en: I go to the library every week.
examples.note: 에 attaches to the place 도서관, not to 매주

examples.en: I take a Korean class every week.
examples.note: 수업을 듣다 = to take/attend a class (literally 'listen to')

extendedVocab.nuance: 매주 is Sino-Korean 每週 (每 'each/every' + 週 'week'), literally 'each week' — every week without exception. The 每 prefix is the same building block in 매일 (every day), 매달/매월 (every month), 매년 (every year), so learning it once unlocks the whole set. Unlike a time-point noun, 매주 behaves as a frequency adverb and normally takes NO particle, sitting just before the verb (매주 만나요), though you can add 마다 for emphasis (매주마다). It collocates with a following day (매주 금요일), with counts (매주 두 번), and with 꼬박꼬박/규칙적으로 for 'regularly'. The English-speaker pitfall: learners copy the 'on weekdays → 평일에' habit and wrongly stick 에 onto 매주 (✗매주에); 매주 is already adverbial, so 매주 가요 is complete. Also distinguish 매주 (every week, recurring) from 이번 주 (this week, one specific week) — different concept entirely.

Confusing 매주 (every week) with 일주일 (one week / a week long) — 매주 운동해요 = exercise weekly, but 일주일 동안 = for one week.
Saying ✗매주일 as one fused word; the word is 매주, and a day is added separately as 매주 + 월요일/화요일.

extendedVocab.nuance: 매년 is Sino-Korean 每年 (每 'every' + 年 'year'), literally 'each year' — every year without exception, the time-axis sibling of 매일/매주/매달. It functions as a frequency adverb and takes NO particle (매년 가요). Its near-synonym 해마다 (해 = native 'year' + 마다 'each') means exactly the same and is slightly warmer/more spoken; both are correct, so 매년 여행해요 = 해마다 여행해요. 매년 collocates with seasons (매년 봄/겨울), recurring events (매년 생일/명절/시험), and 초/말 (year's start/end). The English-speaker pitfall: pronunciation — 매년 is [매년], NOT [메년]; the vowel ㅐ should not collapse to ㅔ in careful speech. Also keep 매년 (every year, recurring) distinct from 작년 (last year) and 내년 (next year), which are single specific years, and from 일 년 (one year's duration: 일 년 동안 = for one year).

Adding 에: ✗매년에 가요 → ✓매년 가요, because 매- frequency words are adverbs that reject 에.
Confusing 매년 (every year) with 일 년 (one year long) — 매년 만나요 = meet yearly, but 일 년 동안 = for one whole year.
Sloppy vowel: pronouncing it [메년]; the first syllable is 매 [mæ], so keep the ㅐ distinct from ㅔ.

Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 만 = 'only'; 오 분만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just five minutes
정도 = 'about/approximately' for a soft estimate

usagePhrases.en: in ten minutes / ten minutes later
usagePhrases.note: 후에 = 'after'; counts forward from now
동안 = 'during/for' a duration of minutes

examples.en: Ten minutes are left.
examples.note: 분 always uses Sino numbers: 십 분, never ✗열 분

examples.en: It takes ten minutes from here.
examples.note: (시간이) 걸리다 = to take (time); the go-to duration verb

examples.en: Let's meet at 3:30.
examples.note: Mixed clock: native 세 시 (3 o'clock) + Sino 삼십 분 (30 min)

extendedVocab.nuance: 분 is the time unit 'minute', written with the hanja 分 (to divide/a part) — a minute being a division of the hour. The crucial rule: 분 ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·사·오·...), so it's 오 분, 삼십 분, never the native 하나·둘·셋. This creates Korea's famous mixed clock, where the HOUR uses native numbers + 시 (한 시, 두 시) but the MINUTE uses Sino numbers + 분 (십 분, 삼십 분): 한 시 십 분 = 1:10. Note 분 also means 'a respected person' (한 분 = one person, honorific) and is the honorific counter for people — same syllable, totally different word, disambiguated by context. The English-speaker pitfall: applying the native numbers used for 시 to 분 as well (✗한 분 for one minute — that actually means 'one person, honorific'); the correct 'one minute' is 일 분. Collocates with 후/전 (after/before), 동안 (for), 정도 (about), 만 (only), and 걸리다 (to take).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using native numbers: ✗열 분, ✗다섯 분 → ✓십 분, ✓오 분, because 분 (minute) demands Sino-Korean numbers.
Carrying the hour pattern into minutes: 한 시 (1 o'clock, native) is right, but 'one minute' is 일 분, not ✗한 분 (which means 'one honored person').
Forgetting the mixed system in a full time: 1:30 is 한 시 삼십 분 — native hour + Sino minute — not all-native or all-Sino.

usagePhrases.note: 만 = 'only'; 십 초만 기다려요
동안 = 'for' a span; 삼십 초 동안 흔드세요 = shake for 30 sec
후에 = 'after'; 삼 초 후에 출발해요

examples.en: Count ten seconds.
examples.note: 초 takes Sino numbers: 십 초, never ✗열 초

examples.en: Ramyeon takes 3 minutes 30 seconds.
examples.note: 초 pairs with 분 for precise durations: 삼 분 삼십 초

examples.en: Answer within ten seconds.
examples.note: (시간) 안에 = 'within' a time limit — quiz/game register

extendedVocab.nuance: 초 is the time unit 'second', from the hanja 秒 (a tiny fraction of time). Like 분 (minute), it ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·...), so it's 십 초, 삼십 초, never native 열·서른. It most often appears alongside 분 to give a precise duration (삼 분 삼십 초 = 3:30 of cooking time, lap times, countdowns) and with 동안 (for), 안에 (within), 후/전 (after/before). Beware: the syllable 초 is a homonym jungle — 초 also means 'candle' (촛불 = candlelight), 'vinegar' (식초), and 'the beginning of' a period (월초 = early month, 초반 = early stage); only context tells them apart. The English-speaker pitfall: again, do not import native numbers (✗열 초); and don't confuse the duration 초 (second) with 첫/처음 (first/at first) — 'the first second' is 첫 일 초, while 처음 means 'at first' in a sequence. For everyday speech Koreans round to 분 and rarely specify 초 except in cooking, sports, or countdowns.

Using native numbers: ✗열 초, ✗스무 초 → ✓십 초, ✓이십 초, since 초 (second) requires Sino-Korean numbers.
Mixing up the homonyms: 초 here is 'second (time)'; 'candle' is also 초 but appears as 촛불/생일 초, and 'vinegar' is 식초 — context decides.
Saying ✗일 초 for 'at first' — that means 'one second'; 'at first/first of all' is 처음(에) or 우선, a different word.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 시각 means "point in time" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 시각 (sigak) means "point in time". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 출발 시각 ("departure time"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 시각 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed compound on schedules: 출발 시각을 확인해요
도착 시각이 늦었어요 = the arrival time was late
정확하다 → 정확한; 정확한 시각을 알려 주세요
Formal clock-reading, e.g. on a station display or news

examples.en: I look up the train time.
examples.note: 알아보다 = to look into/check; travel-schedule register

examples.en: The meeting time has changed.
examples.note: 바뀌다 = to change (intransitive); subject takes 이

examples.en: Boarding time is 3 p.m.
examples.note: Airport/announcement tone — 시각 fits formal -습니다 speech

extendedVocab.nuance: 시각 is Sino-Korean 時刻 (時 'time' + 刻 'a carved mark/notch') — literally a 'carved mark of time', i.e. one precise point on the clock, like a departure, arrival, or boarding moment. The all-important contrast is with its near-twin 시간 時間 (時 'time' + 間 'interval/space'): 시각 = a single instant ('at what moment'), whereas 시간 = a span/duration OR the general notion of 'time/hours' ('how long'). So 출발 시각 = the departure moment (e.g. 3:00), but 비행 시간 = the flight duration (e.g. 2 hours). 시각 carries a formal, schedule-board, announcement flavor — you meet it on tickets, timetables, and in news ('현재 시각'), but in casual chat people just say 시간 even for a point in time (몇 시에 만나? rather than 몇 시각에). The English-speaker pitfall: 'time' in English covers both, so learners reach for the familiar 시간 everywhere and never use 시각, or worse, swap them — saying ✗시각이 없어요 for 'I have no time' (that should be 시간이 없어요, a duration). Use 시각 only when you mean a pinpoint moment, usually formal.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying ✗시각이 없어요 for 'I have no time' — that needs 시간 (duration): 시간이 없어요. 시각 is a single clock point, which you can't 'lack'.
Using 시각 in casual speech for 'what time' — Koreans say 몇 시에 만나요?, not ✗몇 시각에; reserve 시각 for formal schedules.
Confusing 시각 (point in time) with the homonym 시각(視覺, 'eyesight/visual sense') — same sound, different hanja; context (clock vs senses) tells them apart.

extendedVocab.explanation: "period" is 기간 (gigan). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 시험 기간 ("exam period"). usagePhrases.note: 시험 기간이 길어요 = the exam period is long

examples.note: Official-notice tone; 접수 = receiving applications

examples.en: I learned a lot in a short period.
examples.note: 짧다 → 짧은; 기간 takes 에 to mean 'within that span'

extendedVocab.nuance: 기간 is Sino-Korean 期間 (期 'a fixed term/appointed time' + 間 'interval') — a defined stretch of time with a clear START and END, such as an exam season, a vacation, a contract term, or a sale window. Contrast it sharply with 시간 時間: 시간 is generic 'time/hours/duration' you measure (세 시간 = three hours), while 기간 is a bounded named span you don't usually count in hours (시험 기간 = the exam period, not '×N hours'). Also distinguish 동안, which is the grammatical word for 'during/for' and attaches to spans (방학 동안), whereas 기간 is the noun naming the span itself (often combined: 방학 기간 동안). 기간 collocates with administrative life — 접수/신청 기간 (application period), 계약/임대 기간 (contract/lease term), 유효 기간 (validity period/expiry), 공사 기간 — and takes 에 ('within') or 동안 ('throughout'). The English-speaker pitfall: translating every 'time' as 시간 and saying ✗시험 시간이 길어요 to mean 'the exam season is long' — that actually reads as 'the exam's duration (one sitting) is long'; the season is 시험 기간.

Saying ✗기간이 걸려요 for 'it takes time' — taking time is 시간이 걸려요; 기간 names a fixed span and doesn't go with 걸리다.
Confusing 'how long is the period' (기간) with 'how much time' (시간): 유효 기간이 언제까지예요? (until when is it valid) vs 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? (how long does it take).

usagePhrases.note: 최근에 이사했어요 = I moved recently — 에 needed for the time point
As a modifier, 최근 attaches directly: 최근 뉴스를 봤어요
까지 = 'up to'; 최근까지 일했어요 = worked until lately

examples.en: I've been reading a lot of books lately.
examples.note: 최근에 + present = an ongoing recent habit

examples.en: I met a friend recently.
examples.note: With past tense, 최근에 marks a recent completed event

examples.ko: 최근 몇 년 동안 많이 변했어요.
examples.romanization: choegeun myeon nyeon dongan mani byeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: It has changed a lot over the past few years.
examples.note: 최근 + 몇 년 동안 = 'over the recent few years', written/formal feel

extendedVocab.nuance: 최근 is Sino-Korean 最近 (最 'most' + 近 'near') — literally 'most near (in time)', i.e. the recent stretch right up to now. Its near-synonym 요즘 (native, 'these days') overlaps but differs in register and shape: 최근 is more written/formal and works both as a noun-modifier (최근 동향 = recent trends) and, with 에, as a time adverb (최근에 = recently); 요즘 is purely casual-spoken and adverbial (요즘 바빠요), never a noun-modifier (✗요즘 뉴스 sounds off; 최근 뉴스 is right). A subtle nuance gap: 최근 can point to a recent completed event (최근에 갔어요 = I went recently), while 요즘 leans toward the ongoing present situation (요즘 가요 ≈ I go these days). 최근 collocates with 에, 까지, 들어, and number spans (최근 3년/몇 달). The English-speaker pitfall: 'recently' is a bare adverb in English, so learners drop the particle and say ✗최근 갔어요; as a time-point noun 최근 needs 최근에 갔어요. Conversely, when modifying a noun, you DON'T add 에 (최근 소식, not ✗최근에 소식).

Dropping 에 as a time adverb: ✗최근 이사했어요 → ✓최근에 이사했어요, because the recent time point takes the 에 particle.
Using 요즘 as a noun-modifier: ✗요즘 뉴스 → ✓최근 뉴스; 요즘 is adverb-only, while 최근 can sit before a noun.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 요즘 means "these days" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 요즘 (yojeum) means "these days". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 요즘 어때요? ("How are things these days?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 요즘 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: Stock friendly opener — no particle on 요즘
들어 = 'coming into'; 요즘 들어 자주 피곤해요 = tired often lately
요즘 같은 시대에 = 'in an age like today's'
요즘 유행이에요 = it's trendy these days (spoken)

examples.en: Are you busy these days?
examples.note: 요즘 needs no particle; it works straight as an adverb

examples.en: I haven't been sleeping well lately.
examples.note: 못 자다 = can't sleep; 요즘 frames an ongoing present state

examples.en: What have you been up to these days?
examples.note: 지내다 = to get along/spend one's days — warm small-talk Korean

extendedVocab.nuance: 요즘 is a native Korean word (a contraction of 요사이 → 요즈음 → 요즘) meaning 'around now, these days, lately'. It is one of the single most common small-talk openers in Korean, the natural lead-in to 'how have you been?' Its near-synonym 최근(에) (最近, Sino 'most near') means roughly the same time but differs in register and grammar: 요즘 is warm, casual, spoken, strictly adverbial (요즘 바빠요) and CANNOT modify a noun (✗요즘 소식 → use 최근 소식); 최근 is more formal/written and can both modify nouns and, with 에, act as an adverb. Crucially 요즘 takes NO particle — it stands alone before the clause (요즘 어때요?). It pairs with 들어 ('요즘 들어' = of late), with present-tense verbs for ongoing situations, and with 같은 ('요즘 같은' = like nowadays). The English-speaker pitfall: treating 요즘 like a past-time word and saying ✗요즘 갔어요 ('I went these days'?) — 요즘 describes the ongoing present, so use present tense (요즘 가요 / 요즘 다녀요); for a finished recent event switch to 최근에 갔어요.

Adding a particle: ✗요즘에 바빠요 → ✓요즘 바빠요, because 요즘 is already adverbial and rejects 에.
Pairing 요즘 with a one-off past event: ✗요즘 친구를 만났어요 (sounds like a habit) → for a single recent meeting say 최근에 친구를 만났어요.
Using 요즘 to modify a noun: ✗요즘 뉴스 → ✓요즘 나오는 뉴스 or simply 최근 뉴스; 요즘 can't directly precede a noun.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 예전 means "the past" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "the past" is 예전 (yejeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예전에 ("in the past / back then"). Watch the particle attached to 예전 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 예전에 여기 살았어요 = I used to live here
부터 = 'from/since'; 예전부터 알았어요 = I've known since long ago
보다 = 'than'; 예전보다 좋아졌어요 = better than before
예전 모습 그대로예요 = just like you used to be

examples.en: In the past I had lots of time.
examples.note: 에는 (에+는) adds 'as for back then', contrasting with now

examples.en: I met an old friend again.
examples.note: 예전 modifies 친구 directly — an old/former friend

examples.en: We don't see each other as often as we used to.
examples.note: 예전만큼 = 'as much as before'; nostalgic, real-life tone

extendedVocab.nuance: 예전 means 'the (fairly distant) past, the old days, a while back' and carries a gently nostalgic flavor, the feeling of looking back on how things used to be. Its near-synonyms map onto a distance scale: 옛날 (옛날, native 'olden times') is the most remote — fairy-tale 'once upon a time' (옛날 옛적에) or 'the old days' long gone; 예전 is past but within a person's own lived memory ('back when I was younger'); 최근 (最近) is the recent past close to now. So you'd say 예전에 여기 살았어요 (I used to live here, a few years back) but 옛날 사람들 for 'people of old'. 예전 works both as a time adverb with 에 (예전에) and as a noun-modifier (예전 사진 = old photos), and it loves 부터 (since), 보다/만큼 (than/as much as), and 그대로 (just as it was). The English-speaker pitfall: using 예전 for 'a moment ago / just now' — that's 아까 or 방금, not 예전; 예전 implies a meaningful gap of time, often months or years, viewed with hindsight, not 'earlier today'.

Using 예전 for the very near past: ✗예전에 전화했어요 for 'I called a moment ago' → use 아까/방금 전화했어요; 예전 implies a long-ago time.
Dropping 에 as an adverb: ✗예전 살았어요 → ✓예전에 살았어요, since the past time point needs the 에 particle.
Treating 예전 and 옛날 as identical — 옛날 is the remote 'once upon a time / olden days', while 예전 is the nearer, personally-remembered past.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 기온 means "temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 기온 (gion) = "temperature". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기온이 높아요 ("the temperature is high") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기온, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: air temperature takes 높다/낮다, never 크다
fixed phrase: 기온은 떨어지다/오르다, not 내려가다 in forecasts
일교차 means the daily high-low gap
영하 = below zero, 영상 = above zero

examples.en: The temperature is high today.
examples.note: simplest 이/가 + 높다 frame

examples.en: When night comes the temperature drops a lot.
examples.note: time clause + the set verb 떨어지다

examples.ko: 일교차가 커서 아침저녁으로 기온이 많이 달라요.
examples.romanization: ilgyochaga keoseo achimjeonyeogeuro gioni mani dallayo.
examples.en: The daily temperature range is big, so the temperature differs a lot morning and evening.
examples.note: real forecast register with 일교차

extendedVocab.nuance: 기온 is the air temperature expressed as a number of degrees (氣溫, 기 'air/atmosphere' + 온 'warmth'), so it is the measurable reading the forecaster gives, whereas 날씨 is the whole overall feel of the weather (sunny, humid, windy) and 온도 is the neutral word for the temperature of any object or liquid like 물 온도 water temperature or 체온 body temperature. Use 기온 only for outdoor air. It pairs with 높다 high and 낮다 low, and with the motion verbs 오르다 rise and 떨어지다 fall; the big English-speaker trap is reaching for 크다/작다 (big/small) the way English lets you say a 'big' difference, but a temperature itself is 높다/낮다, and only the gap 일교차 or 차이 can be 크다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기온이 커요 to mean a high temperature; size words do not apply, say 기온이 높아요.
Using 온도 for the weather outside (온도가 높아요 about the sky); for outdoor air use 기온, and reserve 온도 for objects or water.
Saying 기온이 내려가요 by translating 'go down'; the idiomatic verb for the reading is 기온이 떨어지다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 일기예보 means "weather forecast" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 일기예보 (ilgiyebo) means "weather forecast". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일기예보를 보다 ("to check the forecast"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 일기예보 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: forecasts are watched/read with 보다, not 듣다 by default
맞다 = turn out correct; opposite 틀리다
quote source with 에서 + 고 하다
주간 weekly, 오늘/내일 일기예보 for the day

examples.en: I check the weather forecast every morning.
examples.note: habit with 마다 + 보다

examples.en: The forecast was right, so I grabbed an umbrella.
examples.note: 맞다 as result + practical action

examples.en: The forecast said it would snow tomorrow.
examples.note: reported speech with 에서 ... 고 하다

extendedVocab.nuance: 일기예보 is the official weather forecast you get from the news or an app (日氣豫報, literally 일기 'the day's air = weather' + 예보 'fore-report'), so it names the prediction itself, not the weather. Contrast it with plain 날씨, which is the actual weather happening now: you say 날씨가 좋아요 for today's nice weather but 일기예보가 좋아요 only when the predicted outlook is good. Koreans habitually 일기예보를 보다 (watch/read it) and judge it as 맞다 right or 틀리다 wrong, and they quote it with 일기예보에서 ~고 했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a verb ('to forecast') — it is a noun, so attach a verb like 보다 or 확인하다, and use 에서 (the source particle) rather than 에 when reporting what it announced.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 듣다 by default (일기예보를 들었어요) because English says 'hear the forecast'; the unmarked verb is 보다 since people watch or read it.
Saying 일기예보를 했어요 as if it were a verb; it is a noun, so say 일기예보를 봤어요/확인했어요.
Marking the source with 에 (일기예보에 ~고 했어요); the quoting source particle is 에서: 일기예보에서 비가 온다고 했어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 장마 means "rainy season" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "rainy season" is 장마 (jangma). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 장마가 시작되다 ("the rainy season begins"). Watch the particle attached to 장마 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: set inchoative 시작되다 / opposite 끝나다, 물러가다
철 = season; 장마철에 = during the rainy season
전선 = the weather front that brings it
마른장마 = a dry spell with little rain

examples.en: The rainy season begins in summer.
examples.note: season + inchoative 시작되다

examples.en: During the rainy season laundry does not dry well.
examples.note: 철 period + a real everyday consequence

examples.en: This year the rainy season is long, so I am worried about mold.
examples.note: real-life worry: humidity and mold

extendedVocab.nuance: 장마 is Korea's long early-summer monsoon, the roughly three-to-four-week stretch around late June and July when a stationary rain front parks over the peninsula and brings steady, humid rain day after day. It is a whole climatic period, not a single rainfall, so it contrasts sharply with 비 (one instance of rain) and with 소나기 (a sudden short downpour): you can have 비 during 장마, but 장마 names the season. The word is treated as native Korean (it is not a hanja compound), and it lives in fixed phrases — 장마가 시작되다/끝나다 and the compound 장마철 'rainy-season time'. The pitfall for English speakers is calling any rainy day 장마; reserve it for the seasonal monsoon, and note that 장마 takes 시작되다/끝나다 rather than the falling verbs 오다/내리다 that plain rain uses.

Calling a single rainy day 장마 (오늘 장마예요 for one wet afternoon); 장마 is the multi-week season — for one rain say 비가 와요.
Saying 장마가 와요 / 장마가 내려요 by analogy with rain; the season 시작되다 begins and 끝나다 ends, while only 비 오다/내리다.
Dropping 철 when you mean 'during the rainy season'; say 장마철에 rather than just 장마에 for the time frame.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 태풍 means "typhoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 태풍 (taepung) = "typhoon". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 태풍이 오다 ("a typhoon comes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 태풍, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 태풍 moves, so it uses 오다/지나가다/북상하다
지나가다 = pass by, leaving calm after
영향권 = the affected zone forecasters mention
strength is 강하다/세다, named 태풍 + name

examples.en: A typhoon is coming tomorrow.
examples.note: basic motion verb 오다

examples.en: Because the typhoon came, all the flights were canceled.
examples.note: cause + a real consequence (결항)

examples.en: As the typhoon moves north it is gradually getting stronger.
examples.note: news register: 북상하다 + 세지다

extendedVocab.nuance: 태풍 is a typhoon, the large tropical storm system that strikes Korea mainly in late summer and early autumn (颱風, literally 태 'typhoon' + 풍 'wind'). Even though the second character means wind, 태풍 is conceived as a moving body of weather, so it travels with 오다 come, 지나가다 pass, and the news verb 북상하다 move north — it does not 'blow.' That is the key contrast with plain 바람 wind, which 불다 blows: you must not say 태풍이 불어요. Distinguish it too from 폭풍 (a general violent storm, including at sea) and 돌풍 (a sudden gust); 태풍 specifically names the seasonal tropical cyclone, each one given an official name. Strength is described with 강하다/세다. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'the wind blows' onto 태풍 and producing 태풍이 불어요 — say instead 태풍이 와요 / 태풍이 지나가요.

Saying 태풍이 불어요 because in English 'the wind blows'; a typhoon is a moving system, so 태풍이 와요/지나가요, while only 바람 불다.
Confusing 태풍 with 바람; ordinary wind is 바람, and 태풍 is the named seasonal storm — 바람이 불어요 vs 태풍이 와요.
Using 폭풍 loosely for any typhoon; 폭풍 is a generic violent storm, whereas 태풍 is specifically the tropical cyclone the forecast names.

extendedVocab.nuance: 그늘 is shade — the cool, dimmer area where an object blocks the sun, and it is the natural opposite of 햇빛/햇볕, prized as a refuge on a hot day (그늘이 시원하다 'the shade is cool'). Translating 'I get hot easily' as 더위를 먹어요; that idiom means heatstroke. 'I'm sensitive to heat' is 더위를 타요.
Swapping 더위 and 기온; a high reading is 기온이 높다, while 더위 is the felt heat — 더위가 심하다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 첫눈 is the first snowfall of the season (첫 'first' + 눈 'snow'), and in Korea it is wrapped in romantic feeling: there is a widespread sentiment that meeting or confessing love on the day of 첫눈 brings good luck, so the word carries warmth a plain 눈 does not. extendedVocab.nuance: 장화 is tall waterproof boots — rain boots or rubber wellies — worn to keep feet dry on wet days (長靴, literally 장 'long' + 화 'shoe/boot,' i.e. 'long boots' reaching up the calf). Because the hanja names height, 장화 implies the tall shaft, distinguishing it from ordinary low 신발/구두 shoes and from 부츠, the borrowed word for fashion boots: 장화 is specifically the practical, often rubber, rain-and-mud boot (고무장화). Like all footwear it takes the verb 신다 to put on and 벗다 to take off, and pairs by the 켤레 (a pair). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 입다 'to wear' the way English uses one verb for all clothing — boots, like shoes and socks, demand 신다 (장화를 신다), never 입다; reserve 입다 for body garments like coats and shirts.

extendedVocab.nuance: 하나 is the native-Korean (고유어) word for "one," the counting system Koreans use for tangible things, people, age, and the clock hour — as opposed to its Sino-Korean twin 일, which rules dates, money, minutes, and phone numbers. The single biggest fact to internalize: when 하나 sits directly in front of a counter (개, 명, 시, 살, 마리), it loses its last syllable and becomes 한 — 한 개, 한 명, 한 시 — while the full 하나 only stands alone (as in counting "하나, 둘" or taking a particle, 하나만). English speakers reliably trip here by saying 하나 개 or, worse, importing the Sino number and saying 일 개; both sound clearly wrong to a Korean ear. There is no hanja because it is purely native, so do not look for one.

Saying 하나 개 — before any counter the form must contract to 한, so it is 한 개. The full 하나 is only used standalone or with a particle.
Using the Sino 일 for the hour or for objects (일 시, 일 개). The clock hour and counting things are native territory, so it must be 한 시, 한 개.
Writing it solid as 한개 — Korean keeps a space between the number-word and the counter: 한 개.

extendedVocab.nuance: 일 is the Sino-Korean (漢字語) number "one," from the hanja 一 (a single horizontal stroke). English speakers, used to a single set of numbers, constantly blur the line — saying 일 시 for one o'clock or 하나 분 for one minute. A handy memory hook: anything that already feels like a 'code' or a 'measurement' (clock minutes, addresses, prices) is Sino 일.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이 is the Sino-Korean number "two," from the hanja 二 (two horizontal strokes). It runs dates, money, minutes, floors, math, and counts in the hundreds and up — versus native 둘/두, which counts physical things, people, and the clock hour. 만 is the Sino-Korean number, from the hanja 萬.
The classic mistake is calculating 'a million' as 천천 (thousand-thousand) — it does not exist; a million is 백만.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 신청 means "application" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "application" is 신청 (sincheong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신청을 하다 ("to apply / submit an application"). Watch the particle attached to 신청 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 신청 + 하다 is the verb form
으로 marks the method/channel
받다 = the office receives them
noun-noun compound for the open window

examples.en: I apply for a card here.
examples.note: Simple frame: 신청하다 turns the noun into 'to apply for' + object 를.

examples.en: I applied for a bankbook online.
examples.note: Everyday errand: method 으로 + object + 신청하다 in past tense.

examples.en: Applications are accepted until next Friday.
examples.note: Real counter notice: 신청 as the thing the office 받다 (accepts) within a deadline 까지.

extendedVocab.nuance: 신청 is a Sino-Korean noun (申請, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') meaning a formal application or request you put in to an office, bank, or service — you are asking an authority to grant or process something. It overwhelmingly takes 하다 to become the verb 신청하다 ('to apply for'), and 신청서 is the physical form you fill in. Compare it carefully with 지원 (支援/志願): 신청 is the neutral 'put in a request' (카드를 신청하다 = apply for a card), while 지원 is 'apply to/for' a job or school where you are a candidate being selected (회사에 지원하다 = apply to a company). Also distinguish 접수, which is the office's act of RECEIVING and logging your 신청. Register is neutral-to-formal, standard in any official or banking setting. The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 지원 for everyday errands (it sounds like job-hunting) and forgetting that 신청 needs 하다 to act as a verb — 신청 by itself is only the noun, so 'I apply' is 신청해요, not bare 신청.

Using 지원 for everyday requests like 'apply for a card' — 지원하다 implies competing for a job/school; for services and paperwork use 신청하다 (카드를 신청해요).
Saying bare 신청 to mean 'I apply' — 신청 is a noun; you must add 하다 (신청해요) or 을/를 하다 (신청을 해요).
Confusing 신청 (your request) with 접수 (the office logging it) — you 신청하다, then the counter 접수하다; they are two sides of one transaction.

extendedVocab.explanation: 신청서 (sincheongseo) = "application form". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 신청서를 작성하다 ("to fill out an application form") shows how it actually behaves. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: to fill out an application form
usagePhrases.note: 작성하다 = write up/complete a document
제출하다 = hand in officially
양식 = the blank format/layout
에 marks where you sign on it

examples.en: Please fill out this application form.
examples.note: Simple frame: 신청서 as object of 쓰다 (write/fill in) with polite request.

examples.en: I write my name and phone number on the application form.
examples.note: Everyday: 에 marks the form as the surface you write 적다 the details onto.

examples.ko: 신청서를 작성하신 후에 1번 창구에 제출해 주세요.
examples.romanization: sincheongseoreul jakseonghasin hue 1beon changgue jechulhae juseyo.
examples.en: After completing the application form, please submit it at window 1.
examples.note: Real counter instruction: formal 작성하다 + 제출하다 with the sequence 후에.

extendedVocab.nuance: 신청서 is a Sino-Korean compound (申請書, 신청 'application' + 書 'document/writing') — the actual paper or digital FORM you complete to make a 신청. The 書 suffix is the same 'written document' element in 서류, 계약서 (contract), and 보고서 (report), so recognizing it helps you read official office vocabulary. Distinguish 신청서 (the specific application form) from the broader 서류 (any documents/paperwork) and from 양식 (the blank template/format itself): you grab the 양식, write on it, and it becomes your 신청서, which is one piece of 서류. The verbs that pair with it are formal: 작성하다 (fill out/complete) and 제출하다 (submit), rather than casual 쓰다/내다 — though 쓰다 and 내다 are fine in speech. Register is neutral-formal, standard at counters. The English-speaker pitfall is calling every document a 신청서: it is specifically an APPLICATION form, so a contract is 계약서 and general paperwork is 서류 — and remember the form-filling verb is 작성하다, not 만들다 (make).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling all paperwork 신청서 — it is specifically the application form; use 서류 for documents in general and 계약서 for a contract.
Saying 신청서를 만들다 ('make the form') for filling it in — the correct verb is 작성하다 (complete/fill out) or casual 쓰다.
Confusing 신청서 with 양식 — 양식 is the blank template/format; once you write your details on it, it becomes your 신청서.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 서류 means "documents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 서류 (seoryu) means "documents". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 서류를 준비하다 ("to prepare the documents"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 서류 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 준비하다 = get them ready beforehand
제출하다 = hand them in
necessary papers for a procedure
the office's paper-based examination

examples.en: I need more documents.
examples.note: Simple frame: 서류 as subject of 필요하다 (to be needed).

examples.en: I gather the documents before going to the bank.
examples.note: Everyday errand: 챙기다 (gather/pack) the papers ahead of the 전에 clause.

examples.ko: 여권 사본 같은 필요한 서류를 모두 제출하셔야 합니다.
examples.romanization: yeogwon sabon gateun piryohan seoryureul modu jechulhasyeoya hamnida.
examples.en: You must submit all the required documents, such as a passport copy.
examples.note: Real procedure: 필요한 서류 (required documents) as object of formal obligation 제출하셔야 합니다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 서류 is a Sino-Korean noun (書類, 書 'writing/document' + 類 'kind/category') meaning official documents or paperwork as a category — the bundle of forms, copies, and certificates a procedure demands. It is a collective, somewhat abstract term: 서류를 준비하다 = get your paperwork in order, covering many individual papers at once. Contrast it with 문서 (文書), which is 'a document' as a discrete file or record (often electronic or archival, e.g. an internal 문서), while 서류 evokes the practical stack you submit for an application. A single sheet is 종이 (paper) and one specific form is e.g. 신청서; 서류 is the umbrella. Natural collocations are 서류를 준비하다/챙기다/제출하다/접수하다 and 서류 심사 (document review). Register is neutral, ubiquitous at banks, immigration, and government offices. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 서류 as countable like 'a document' — Korean uses it as a mass/collective noun, so you rarely say 한 서류; for one item name the specific form (신청서 한 장) or use 문서 for a discrete record.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting it like English 'a document' (한 서류) — 서류 is collective/mass; for one sheet say 신청서 한 장 or 서류 한 부 (one set).
Swapping 서류 and 문서 freely — 서류 is the practical paperwork you submit; 문서 is a discrete document/file, often archival or electronic.
Using 종이 for official papers — 종이 is the physical material 'paper'; the forms and certificates you submit are 서류.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 신분증 means "ID card" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "ID card" is 신분증 (sinbunjeung). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신분증을 제시하다 ("to present one's ID"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 제시하다 = show it for inspection
확인하다 = the staff verifies it
사본 = photocopy/duplicate
지참하다 = carry it with you (formal)

examples.en: Do you have your ID?
examples.note: Simple frame: the everyday counter question, 있다 + honorific 으세요.

examples.en: You need an ID when opening a bankbook.
examples.note: Everyday: 신분증 as subject of 필요하다 inside a 때 (when) clause.

examples.ko: 본인 확인을 위해 신분증을 제시해 주시기 바랍니다.
examples.romanization: bonin hwagineul wihae sinbunjeungeul jesihae jusigi baramnida.
examples.en: Please present your ID for identity verification.
examples.note: Real formal notice: 제시하다 with 위해 (for the purpose of) 본인 확인 (identity check).

extendedVocab.nuance: 신분증 is a Sino-Korean compound (身分證, 身分 'social status/identity' + 證 'certificate/proof') — any official photo ID that proves who you are: a 주민등록증 (national ID), 운전면허증 (driver's license), or 여권 (passport) all count as a 신분증. The 證 'proof' suffix recurs in 학생증 (student ID), 자격증 (certificate), and 영수증 (receipt), so it flags 'certifying document'. Note the difference from 신분 alone, which is the abstract 'identity/social standing' (신분을 밝히다 = reveal one's identity), while 신분증 is the physical card. At banks and offices the set verbs are formal: 제시하다 (present) and 지참하다 (bring), with staff doing 확인하다 (verify); in speech 보여 주다 (show) and 가져오다 (bring) are natural. Register is neutral, indispensable for any errand. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 아이디 (a loanword that in Korean means a login USERNAME, not a physical ID) when you mean the card — for a photo identity card always use 신분증, and never confuse it with 카드 alone (which suggests a bank/credit card).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 아이디 for a physical ID card — in Korean 아이디 means a login username; the photo identity card is 신분증.
Using 신분 instead of 신분증 — 신분 is abstract 'identity/status'; the card you hand over is 신분증 (add 證 = the proof document).
Calling it just 카드 — 카드 alone suggests a bank/credit card; specify 신분증 for an identity document.

usagePhrases.note: 만들다 = the standard verb for opening one
개설하다 = formally establish (an account)
정리 = bringing entries up to date
noun-noun: the account one's pay goes into

examples.en: I want to open a bankbook.
examples.note: Simple frame: 통장 as object of 만들다 with desire 고 싶다.

examples.en: How much money is in the account?
examples.note: Everyday: 통장에 (in the bankbook) as location of 돈 with 있다.

examples.ko: 새 통장을 개설하려면 신분증과 도장이 필요합니다.
examples.romanization: sae tongjangeul gaeseolharyeomyeon sinbunjeunggwa dojangi piryohamnida.
examples.en: To open a new bankbook, you need an ID and a seal.
examples.note: Real bank procedure: formal 개설하다 + intention 려면 listing required items with 과.

extendedVocab.nuance: 통장 is a Sino-Korean noun (通帳, 通 'pass through/circulate' + 帳 'ledger/book') — the physical passbook that records deposits and withdrawals, and by extension the everyday word Koreans use for a bank account itself (통장을 만들다 = open an account). Here is the key contrast learners must master: 통장 is the tangible book / the account in casual speech, while 계좌 (計座) is the technical ACCOUNT NUMBER and the formal term used for transfers (계좌이체 = wire transfer, 계좌번호 = account number). So you 'open a 통장' but you 'transfer to a 계좌'. The verb for opening is colloquial 만들다 or formal 개설하다 (establish). Natural collocations: 월급 통장 (salary account), 통장 정리 (update the passbook), 통장 사본 (a copy of the passbook). Register is neutral, fully everyday. The English-speaker pitfall is using 계좌 where 통장 is natural and vice versa: to open the book say 통장을 만들다, but when giving someone your details for a transfer, you give your 계좌번호, not your 통장번호.
