Using 계좌 for the physical book/casual 'account' — you 통장을 만들다 (open a bankbook); 계좌 is the formal account/number used for transfers.
Saying 통장번호 for the number you give for a transfer — that is 계좌번호; 통장 is the book itself.
Using 열다 ('open' a door) to mean 'open an account' — the verb is 만들다 (make) or formal 개설하다 (establish).

usagePhrases.note: 개설하다 = formally establish an account
알려 주다 = tell/inform someone of it
money moved account-to-account
로 marks the destination account

examples.en: Please tell me your account number.
examples.note: Simple frame: 계좌번호 as object of 알려 주다 with polite request.

examples.en: I sent 100,000 won to my friend's account.
examples.note: Everyday: 계좌로 (to the account) as destination of 보내다 (send).

examples.en: Your salary is automatically transferred to the registered account.
examples.note: Real notice: 계좌로 as destination of passive 이체되다 (be transferred), with 등록된 (registered).

extendedVocab.nuance: 계좌 is a Sino-Korean noun (計座, 計 'count/reckon' + 座 'seat/position') meaning a bank account in the technical, financial sense — the entity identified by a 계좌번호 (account number) that money moves into and out of. It is the formal counterpart to 통장 (the physical passbook / casual word for account): banks, transfer screens, and official forms all say 계좌 — 계좌이체 (account transfer), 가상계좌 (virtual account), 계좌 개설 (account opening). The distinction is functional: you 통장을 만들다 (open the book) but you 입금하다 / 이체하다 to a 계좌, and you give your 계좌번호 for someone to pay you. The verb is 개설하다 (formal, 'establish') rather than 만들다 in official contexts. Register is neutral-formal, the standard term in any financial transaction. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing 계좌 and 통장: when transferring money or quoting the number, always use 계좌(번호); reserve 통장 for the passbook or casual 'I opened an account'. Also do not confuse 계좌 with 계산 (計算, calculation/paying a bill) — close-looking 한자 but different words.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Saying 계좌를 만들다 in formal contexts — banks say 계좌를 개설하다 (establish); 만들다 pairs more with 통장.
Confusing 계좌 (account) with 계산 (paying/calculating a bill) — similar 한자 but 계산하다 means to settle a bill, not to bank.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 입금 means "deposit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "deposit" is 입금 (ipgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 입금을 하다 ("to make a deposit"). Watch the particle attached to 입금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 입금 + 하다 = put money in
에 marks the receiving account
확인되다 = it is verified as received
내역 = itemized record of incoming money

examples.en: I deposited 50,000 won into the account.
examples.note: Simple frame: 입금하다 with amount + 계좌에 as destination 에.

examples.en: When you deposit money, a text message comes.
examples.note: Everyday: 입금하다 in a 면 (when/if) clause; deposit triggers an alert.

examples.ko: 입금이 확인되는 대로 상품을 보내 드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: ipgeumi hwagindoeneun daero sangpumeul bonae deurigetseumnida.
examples.en: We will ship the item as soon as the deposit is confirmed.
examples.note: Real transaction: passive 입금이 확인되다 with 는 대로 (as soon as) in formal commerce.

extendedVocab.nuance: 입금 is a Sino-Korean noun (入金, 入 'enter' + 金 'money') meaning the act of money coming IN — depositing funds into an account, or money being received. It takes 하다 (입금하다 = to deposit/pay in) and pairs with 에 for the destination: 계좌에 입금하다. Its exact opposite is 출금 (出金, money going out / withdrawal), and the 入/出 pair is worth memorizing together, like 입구/출구 (entrance/exit). Distinguish 입금 from 송금 (送金, 'remitting/sending money', emphasizing the transfer ACROSS to another party) and from 이체 (移替, the account-to-account 'transfer' operation): when you pay a seller, you 입금하다 (the money enters their account) or 송금하다 (you send it); the bank's mechanism is 이체. Natural collocations: 입금 확인 (deposit confirmation), 입금 내역, 무통장 입금 (bankless/cash deposit). Register is neutral, everyday in shopping and banking. The English-speaker pitfall is using 저금 (saving up) or 예금 (a savings deposit/balance) for the act of paying in — those describe SAVING money, while 입금 is the transactional act of putting funds into an account right now.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 입금 (depositing/money in) with 출금 (withdrawing/money out) — they are 入/出 opposites; double-check which direction the money moves.
Using 저금 or 예금 for 'pay this in' — 저금/예금 mean saving money; the act of depositing into an account is 입금하다.
Forgetting the destination particle — it is 계좌에 입금하다 (에 = into); using 로 here sounds off for the receiving account.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 출금 means "withdrawal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 출금 (chulgeum) = "withdrawal". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 출금을 하다 ("to make a withdrawal") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 출금, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 출금 + 하다 = take money out
에서 marks the source account
한도 = the maximum allowed
money drawn out automatically

examples.en: I withdrew some cash.
examples.note: Simple frame: 출금하다 with object 현금 (cash) in past tense.

examples.en: I'm going to withdraw 100,000 won from the account.
examples.note: Everyday: 출금하다 with source 에서 + amount and intention 려고 하다.

examples.ko: 하루 출금 한도는 백만 원으로 제한됩니다.
examples.romanization: haru chulgeum handoneun baengman woneuro jehandoemnida.
examples.en: The daily withdrawal limit is capped at one million won.
examples.note: Real bank rule: 출금 한도 as subject with 으로 제한되다 (be limited to).

extendedVocab.nuance: 출금 is a Sino-Korean noun (出金, 出 'exit/go out' + 金 'money') meaning the act of money going OUT — withdrawing funds from an account. It takes 하다 (출금하다 = to withdraw) and, crucially, pairs with 에서 (the source) rather than 에: 계좌에서 출금하다 = withdraw FROM the account. It is the direct opposite of 입금 (入金, depositing), and learners should drill the 入/出 contrast plus the particle switch (입금은 '에', 출금은 '에서'). Near terms: 인출 (引出) is a more formal synonym for cash withdrawal seen on ATM screens and forms, while 출금 is the everyday word; 이체 (transfer) moves money to another account rather than taking it out as cash. Natural collocations: 출금 한도 (withdrawal limit), 자동 출금 (auto-debit), 출금 수수료 (withdrawal fee). Register is neutral, standard at ATMs and banks. The English-speaker pitfall is using 에 instead of 에서 with 출금 (the money LEAVES, so it is the source 에서), and confusing 출금 with 입금 — because the 한자 differ by only one character, mixing them up can send money the wrong way.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 에 instead of 에서 — withdrawal is FROM a source, so it is 계좌에서 출금하다 (에서), not 계좌에 출금하다.
Swapping 출금 (money out) and 입금 (money in) — the 한자 differ by one character (出 vs 入); confirm the direction before acting.
Assuming 출금 always means cash — at an ATM yes, but on forms the formal synonym is 인출; a transfer to another account is 이체, not 출금.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 수수료 means "fee, commission" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 수수료 (susuryo) means "fee, commission". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수수료가 들다 ("a fee is incurred"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수수료 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 들다 = (cost/fee) is required
내다 = pay out the charge
붙다 = a charge attaches to the transaction
noun-noun: the charge for sending money

examples.en: Is there a fee?
examples.note: Simple frame: the everyday counter question, 수수료 + 있다.

examples.en: If you send to another bank, a fee is added.
examples.note: Everyday: 수수료가 붙다 (a fee attaches) inside a 면 condition about cross-bank transfers.

examples.ko: 타행 이체 시 건당 오백 원의 수수료가 부과됩니다.
examples.romanization: tahaeng iche si geondang obaek wonui susuryoga bugwadoemnida.
examples.en: A fee of 500 won per transaction is charged for transfers to other banks.
examples.note: Real bank notice: 수수료가 부과되다 (be levied) with 건당 (per case) and 시 (upon/when).

extendedVocab.nuance: 수수료 is a Sino-Korean noun (手數料, 手數 'effort/handling' + 料 'charge/fee') meaning a service fee or commission — the charge a bank, agency, or service takes for handling a transaction (transfer fees, ATM fees, brokerage commission). The 料 'fee' suffix recurs in 요금 (utility/usage charge), 입장료 (entrance fee), 수업료 (tuition), so it flags 'a charge for ~'. Distinguish 수수료 from those siblings: 요금 is a usage charge for a service you consume (전기 요금 = electricity bill, 통화 요금 = call charges), 세금 (稅金) is a tax to the government, and 비용 (費用) is general 'cost/expense' — while 수수료 specifically is the HANDLING fee skimmed for processing your transaction. Natural verbs: 수수료가 들다/붙다/부과되다 (a fee is incurred/added/levied) and 수수료를 내다 (pay it). Register is neutral-formal, standard wherever transactions carry charges. The English-speaker pitfall is using 요금 or 비용 for a transaction commission — for the per-transaction handling charge at a bank or service, the precise word is 수수료, and remember it 'attaches' with 붙다 rather than being 'made'.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 요금 for a bank commission — 요금 is a usage charge (전기 요금); the per-transaction handling fee is 수수료.
Calling it 세금 — 세금 is a government tax; a service's processing charge is 수수료, not a tax.
Saying 수수료를 만들다 — fees are not 'made'; they 들다/붙다/부과되다 (are incurred/added/levied), and you 내다 (pay) them.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 등록 means "registration" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "registration" is 등록 (deungnok). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 등록을 하다 ("to register"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 등록 + 하다 = enter oneself/something on a register
되다 = the registration goes through
the open window to register
being enrolled automatically

examples.en: I register my name here.
examples.note: Simple frame: 등록하다 with object 이름 in present tense.

examples.ko: 외국인 등록을 하러 출입국 사무소에 가요.
examples.romanization: oegugin deungnogeul hareo churipguk samusoe gayo.
examples.en: I'm going to the immigration office to do my alien registration.
examples.note: Everyday: 외국인 등록 (alien registration) as object of 하다 with purpose 러.

examples.ko: 수강 신청 후 등록금을 납부해야 등록이 완료됩니다.
examples.romanization: sugang sincheong hu deungnokgeumeul napbuhaeya deungnogi wallyodoemnida.
examples.en: Registration is complete only after you pay tuition following course sign-up.
examples.note: Real procedure: passive 등록이 완료되다 (registration is completed) tied to 납부 (payment) condition.

extendedVocab.nuance: 등록 is a Sino-Korean noun (登錄, 登 'record/ascend' + 錄 'register/record') meaning officially entering a person or thing onto a register or roll — enrolling, registering, recording in a system. It takes 하다 (등록하다 = to register) or 되다 (등록되다 = to be registered), and appears in 외국인 등록증 (alien registration card), 주민등록 (resident registration), 등록금 (registration/tuition fee), 등록 번호 (registration number). The contrast learners need is with 신청 and 접수: 신청 is REQUESTING something, 접수 is the office RECEIVING your request, and 등록 is the result of being formally ENTERED onto the official record — often you 신청 first, the desk 접수, and finally you are 등록 in the system. Compare also 가입 (加入, 'joining/subscribing' to a membership, service, or insurance — 보험 가입, 회원 가입), which is about becoming a MEMBER, whereas 등록 is about being recorded in a registry. Register is neutral-formal. The English-speaker pitfall is using 등록 for joining a club or signing up for a service (that is 가입) and using 가입 for recording an official entry (that is 등록) — and remembering 등록 needs 하다/되다 to function as a verb.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 등록 for joining a membership or service — that is 가입 (회원 가입); 등록 is being entered on an official register.
Confusing 등록 with 신청 — you 신청하다 (request) something first; 등록 is the resulting formal entry in the records.
Saying bare 등록 as a verb — add 하다 (등록해요) or 되다 (등록됐어요); 등록 alone is only the noun.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 접수 means "reception, filing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 접수 (jeopsu) = "reception, filing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 접수를 하다 ("to file/submit (and have it logged)") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 접수, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 접수 + 하다 = lodge your application at the desk
되다 = the office has logged it
the counter that takes submissions
the number assigned when filed

examples.en: File it here. / Register here.
examples.note: Simple frame: 접수하다 with honorific request at an intake desk.

examples.en: I filed the documents in the morning.
examples.note: Everyday: 접수하다 with object 서류 in past tense — handed in and logged.

examples.ko: 접수가 완료되면 접수 번호를 문자로 보내 드립니다.
examples.romanization: jeopsuga wallyodoemyeon jeopsu beonhoreul munjaro bonae deurimnida.
examples.en: Once your filing is complete, we send the reference number by text.
examples.note: Real procedure: passive 접수가 완료되다 with the assigned 접수 번호 being sent.

extendedVocab.nuance: 접수 is a Sino-Korean noun (接受, 接 'receive/connect' + 受 'accept') meaning the RECEIVING and logging of an application or document by an office — both the act of an institution taking your submission in, and (loosely) your act of handing it in at the 접수 창구 (intake window). It takes 하다 and 되다: from your side 서류를 접수하다 can mean 'submit/file', while 접수가 되다 / 접수되다 means 'it has been received/registered by them'. The crucial trio for learners: 신청 (you REQUEST) → 접수 (the office RECEIVES/logs it) → 처리 (處理, they PROCESS it). So 접수 sits in the middle, the moment your paperwork is officially accepted and assigned a 접수 번호. Distinguish it from 제출 (提出, the physical act of 'submitting/handing over' a document) — 제출 is the handing in, 접수 is the institution accepting and registering it. Register is neutral-formal, standard at hospitals, offices, and event desks (병원 접수 = hospital reception/check-in). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 접수 as plain 'submit' (that is 제출) and missing its 'be accepted/logged' meaning — 접수가 됐어요 means your application is now officially in the system, not merely handed over.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 접수 as just 'submit' — 제출 is handing the document over; 접수 is the office RECEIVING and logging it (접수되다 = it's now registered).
Confusing 접수 (intake/logging) with 등록 (being entered on the register) — 접수 comes first at the desk; 등록 is the later formal record.
Reading 병원 접수 as 'hospital application' — here 접수 is the reception/check-in desk where you register your visit.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 발급 means "issuance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 발급 (balgeup) means "issuance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 발급을 받다 ("to be issued (something)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 발급 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 발급 + 받다 = receive an issued document
하다 = the office issues it
the charge to have it issued
재 + 발급 = issuing a replacement

examples.en: I got a passport issued.
examples.note: Simple frame: 발급받다 (receive issuance) with object 여권 in past tense.

examples.ko: 증명서는 무인 발급기에서 뽑을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeungmyeongseoneun muin balgeupgieseo ppobeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can get the certificate from an automated issuing machine.
examples.note: Everyday: 발급 in the compound 발급기 (issuing kiosk) with 뽑다 (print/pull) + ability.

examples.en: If you have lost your card, you must apply for a reissue.
examples.note: Real procedure: 재발급 as object of 신청하다 under a 다면 (if) condition, formal obligation.

extendedVocab.nuance: 발급 is a Sino-Korean noun (發給, 發 'issue/send out' + 給 'give/supply') meaning the official ISSUING of a document, card, or certificate by an authority — passports, ID cards, certificates, bank cards are all 발급. Crucially, it splits by direction: the OFFICE 발급하다 (issues), but YOU 발급받다 (receive the issuance) — so for your own errand the natural verb is 발급받다, not 발급하다 (which would mean you are the issuer). This 받다 pattern mirrors other 'receive an action' verbs. 재발급 (reissue) is the common compound when something is lost. Distinguish 발급 from 신청 and 등록: you 신청 (request) a document, the office 발급 (issues) it, after which you might be 등록 (recorded) somewhere. Compare also 교부 (交付), a more bureaucratic synonym for 'issue/hand over' seen in legal/government text, versus everyday 발급. Register is neutral-formal, standard at banks and government counters. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 발급하다 about getting your OWN document — that wrongly casts you as the issuing authority; to say 'I got X issued', use 발급받다.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 발급하다 for getting your own document — that means YOU issue it; to receive one, use 발급받다 (여권을 발급받았어요).
Confusing 발급 (issuing a document) with 신청 (requesting it) — you 신청하다 first, then the office 발급하다; they are different steps.
Forgetting the 재 in 재발급 for replacements — a lost card needs 재발급 (reissue), not a fresh 발급, on the form.

Register is neutral-formal, standard at banks and government counters.

usagePhrases.note: 의견 + 을 with 말하다, the default verb for voicing a view
의견 + 이 with 다르다, the set way to say 'we disagree'
의견 + 을 with 듣다, asking for input
의견 stands as a count noun you can put 다른 'other' in front of

examples.en: My opinion is a little different.
examples.note: Simple frame: 의견은 + adjective states where you stand on something.

examples.ko: 이 문제에 대해 여러분의 의견을 듣고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i munjee daehae yeoreobunui uigyeoneul deutgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to hear your opinions on this issue.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~에 대해 (about) + 의견을 듣다, common in class or meetings.

examples.ko: 회의에서 제 의견을 솔직하게 말했지만 받아들여지지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuieseo je uigyeoneul soljikage malhaetjiman badadeuryeojiji anasseoyo.
examples.en: I gave my opinion frankly in the meeting, but it wasn't accepted.
examples.note: Real situation: voicing 의견 at work, with the realistic outcome that it may be rejected.

extendedVocab.nuance: 의견 is Sino-Korean (意見, 意 'mind/intention' + 見 'view/seeing'), literally 'how your mind sees something' — a considered position or judgment you can defend, usually about a topic, plan, or issue. The crucial contrast is with 생각: 생각 is the broad word for any 'thought' that crosses your mind, while 의견 is specifically a stance offered for discussion or evaluation, so a meeting asks for 의견 (positions), not just 생각 (musings). It is register-neutral and very common in school and workplace settings; the polite request 의견을 여쭤봐도 될까요? raises it a notch. Natural collocations: 의견을 말하다/내다/제시하다 (state/put forward), 의견이 다르다/같다 (disagree/agree), 의견을 모으다 (gather opinions), 반대 의견 (an opposing view). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 의견 every time you'd say 'I think' — 'I think it's good' is 좋은 것 같아요 or 좋다고 생각해요, NOT 좋은 의견이에요; 의견 is the opinion itself as a thing, not the act of thinking. Also don't say 의견하다 — there is no such verb; you 의견을 말하다.

Saying 의견하다 to mean 'to opine' — 의견 is a noun with no verb form; use 의견을 말하다 / 의견을 내다.
Using 의견 where English 'I think...' just hedges — 'I think it'll rain' is 비가 올 것 같아요, not an 의견; 의견 is a stance offered for discussion.

생각 + 이 with 들다, a thought arises in you
생각 + 을 with 하다, the everyday 'to think things over'
생각 + 이다 evaluates a suggestion as good

examples.en: That's a good idea!
examples.note: Simple frame: 생각 + 이에요 to praise a suggestion someone just made.

examples.en: Yesterday's events suddenly came to mind.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 생각나다 (one written verb) = 'to remember / cross one's mind' on its own.

examples.ko: 며칠 동안 곰곰이 생각해 봤는데, 그냥 포기하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: myeochil dongan gomgomi saenggakae bwanneunde, geunyang pogihaneun ge naeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: I thought it over carefully for a few days, and I feel it's better to just give up.
examples.note: Real situation: 생각해 보다 (think it over) leading to a tentative conclusion with ~것 같다.

extendedVocab.nuance: 생각 is the native Korean catch-all noun for a 'thought', 'idea', or 'opinion' — anything that happens in the mind: memories, intentions, plans, beliefs, judgments. It also overlaps with 마음 ('heart/mind' as feeling/will), but 생각 is the cognitive 'thinking' side while 마음 is the emotional/volitional side — 생각이 바뀌다 = I changed my mind (reasoning), 마음이 바뀌다 = my heart changed (feelings). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb pattern: 'I think that it's true' is 사실이라고 생각해요 with the quotative ~라고, not 사실 생각해요; and 'I remember' is most naturally 생각나요, not a literal translation. In Korean the particle or ending next to 이유 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

이유 + 를 with 묻다, to inquire why
이유 + 없이 forms the adverb 'for no reason'
이유 + 로 with 무슨, asking the grounds 'on what reason'

examples.en: There's no special reason.
examples.note: Simple frame: 이유 + 없다 to brush off a 'why' question politely.

examples.en: Please explain the reason you're late.
examples.note: Everyday frame: [modifier]~(으)ㄴ + 이유 packs the reason into a noun phrase.

examples.ko: 회사를 그만둔 이유는 여러 가지가 있지만, 가장 큰 이유는 건강이었어요.
examples.romanization: hoesareul geumandun iyuneun yeoreo gajiga itjiman, gajang keun iyuneun geongangieosseoyo.
examples.en: There are several reasons I quit the company, but the biggest reason was my health.
examples.note: Real situation: layering reasons (여러 가지 이유 / 가장 큰 이유) when explaining a big decision.

extendedVocab.nuance: 이유 is Sino-Korean (理由, 理 'principle/logic' + 由 'cause/origin'), the 'reason' or grounds behind something — the answer to 'why?'. Its sharpest contrast is with 원인 (原因, 'cause'): 이유 is the justification or motive a person gives ('the reason I'm late'), often subjective and explainable, while 원인 is the objective, often impersonal cause of a result ('the cause of the fire', 화재의 원인). So you ask a friend 무슨 이유로 늦었어? but an investigator looks for the 원인 of an accident. Also distinguish 까닭, a more native, slightly literary synonym of 이유. Register-neutral and extremely common. Core collocations: 이유가 있다/없다, 이유를 묻다/대다/설명하다, 이유 없이 (for no reason), 그런 이유로 (for that reason), ~는 이유는 (the reason that ~ is). The English-speaker pitfall: don't bolt 이유 onto a 'because' clause redundantly — Korean already has 왜냐하면 ... 때문이에요 / ~기 때문에 to say 'because', so '왜냐하면 그 이유는...' is clunky; pick one. Also, 'the reason is because...' should be ~는 이유는 ... 때문이에요, where the sentence ends in 때문이다, not a second 이유.

Saying 원인 for a personal motive — the reason you skipped class is 이유, while 원인 is an objective cause (사고의 원인 = the cause of the accident).
Doubling up 'because': '왜냐하면 그 이유는 비가 와서요' is redundant; say 왜냐하면 비가 왔기 때문이에요, or simply 비가 와서요.
Forgetting 때문이다 closes a 'the reason is...' sentence: 늦은 이유는 차가 막혔기 때문이에요, not 늦은 이유는 차가 막혔어요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 관심 means "interest, attention" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "interest, attention" is 관심 (gwansim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 관심이 있다 ("to be interested"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 관심 + 이 with 있다, the standard 'I'm interested'
관심 + 을 with 가지다, to develop interest
~에 marks the target; 관심이 많다 = lots of interest
관심 + 을 with 끌다, to draw interest

examples.en: I'm very interested in Korean music.
examples.note: Simple frame: ~에 관심이 많다/있다 names the topic you're into with ~에.

examples.ko: 요즘 사람들이 환경 문제에 관심을 가지기 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum saramdeuri hwangyeong munjee gwansimeul gajigi sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: People have started taking an interest in environmental issues lately.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 관심을 가지다 = to take/develop an interest, with 시작하다 for 'start to'.

examples.ko: 처음엔 그냥 관심이었는데, 이제는 진지하게 공부하고 싶어졌어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen geunyang gwansimieonneunde, ijeneun jinjihage gongbuhago sipeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: At first it was just curiosity, but now I've come to want to study it seriously.
examples.note: Real situation: 관심 as a starting spark that grows into a serious commitment.

extendedVocab.nuance: 관심 is Sino-Korean (關心, 關 'to be connected/concerned' + 心 'heart/mind'), literally 'the heart being connected to something' — interest, concern, or attention directed at a topic, activity, or person. Two contrasts matter. Against 흥미 (興味): 흥미 is the felt 'fun/excitement' kind of interest, a momentary enjoyment (흥미로운 영화 = an interesting/fun movie), whereas 관심 is a steadier, often deliberate concern you choose to 'have' or 'give' (관심을 가지다). Against 호기심 (好奇心, curiosity): 호기심 is the itch to find out, while 관심 is broader attention or care. Note 관심 also means romantic/personal attention — 관심 있어? can imply 'do you like me?' in the right context. Register-neutral, very high frequency. Collocations: ~에 관심이 있다/없다/많다, 관심을 가지다/두다/끌다/받다, 관심 분야 (field of interest), 무관심 (indifference). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the thing you're interested in takes ~에 (or ~에 대해), so it's 음악에 관심이 있어요, NOT 음악을 관심이 있어요 or 음악 관심 있어요. Also 'I'm interested' is a state with 있다 (관심이 있다), not 관심하다 — there is no verb 관심하다.

Saying 관심하다 — there's no such verb; use 관심이 있다 (state) or 관심을 가지다 (take interest).
Swapping 관심 and 흥미 — a fun, momentary 'that's interesting!' is 흥미롭다, while 관심 is steady concern/attention you give to a topic or person.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 복잡하다 means "to be complicated" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 복잡하다 (bokjapada) = "to be complicated". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 복잡해요 ("it is complicated") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 복잡하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 contracts to 해요, never 복잡하요
modifier form 복잡한 + noun

usagePhrases.en: to have a lot on one's mind
usagePhrases.note: 머리가 복잡하다, an idiom for a cluttered, stressed mind
복잡하다 also covers crowded, tangled places

examples.en: This problem is too complicated.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 복잡해요 to call something hard to untangle.

examples.en: Because it was the weekend, downtown was crowded with people.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 복잡하다 = 'crowded/congested' for places, with ~로 'with (people)'.

examples.ko: 설명을 들을수록 더 복잡해져서, 결국 포기하고 싶어졌어요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongeul deureulsurok deo bokjapaejyeoseo, gyeolguk pogihago sipeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The more I listened to the explanation, the more complicated it got, so in the end I felt like giving up.
examples.note: Real situation: 복잡해지다 (become complicated) showing a situation worsening as it's explained.

extendedVocab.nuance: 복잡하다 is a Sino-Korean 하다-adjective (複雜 + 하다, 複 'multiple/layered' + 雜 'mixed/miscellaneous'), literally 'many things mixed together', so it spans three English ideas at once: (1) complicated/intricate (복잡한 문제 = a complex problem), (2) crowded/congested (길이 복잡하다 = the road is jammed), and (3) mentally cluttered/troubled (머리가 복잡하다 = my head is a mess). Its opposite is 간단하다 (simple). Contrast it with 어렵다: 어렵다 is 'difficult' (hard to do or understand, possibly even if simple in structure), while 복잡하다 stresses having too many tangled parts — a problem can be 복잡하지만 어렵지 않다 (complicated but not hard). As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 복잡해 → 복잡해요 (never 복잡하요), modifier 복잡한, adverb 복잡하게, and 'become complicated' is 복잡해지다. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 복잡하다 for a task that is merely 'hard' — use 어렵다 for difficulty; and for a crowded café, Koreans naturally say 사람이 많다 or 복잡하다, but never the literal 'busy'. Also avoid 복잡하고 있다 — it's a state (복잡해요), not an ongoing action.

examples.note: Everyday frame: flavor compounds 단맛(sweet)/매운맛(spicy)/짠맛(salty) + ~보다 to compare.

examples.ko: 오랫동안 끓였더니 국물에서 깊은 맛이 나기 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: oraetdongan kkeuryeotdeoni gungmureseo gipeun masi nagi sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: After simmering it a long time, a deep flavor began to come out of the broth.
examples.note: Real situation: 맛이 나다 (a flavor comes out) plus 깊은 맛 (deep, rich flavor) in cooking.

extendedVocab.nuance: 맛 is the native Korean noun for taste or flavor — both the literal taste on the tongue and, by extension, the 'flavor/charm' of an experience (사는 맛 = the joy of living; 그 영화는 보는 맛이 있다 = that movie is fun to watch). Its most important behavior is fusion: 맛 + 있다 → 맛있다 (delicious) and 맛 + 없다 → 맛없다 (not tasty) are written as single words and are the everyday way to praise or pan food. Contrast 맛 with 향 (香, scent/aroma, from the nose, e.g. 커피 향) and with 식감 (食感, texture/mouthfeel) — Koreans separate flavor (맛), smell (향), and texture (식감). The five basic tastes form compounds: 단맛, 짠맛, 신맛(sour), 쓴맛(bitter), 매운맛(spicy/hot). Register-neutral, extremely high frequency. Collocations: 맛이 있다/없다, 맛을 보다 (taste it), 맛이 나다 (a taste comes out), 맛이 진하다/연하다 (strong/mild), 입맛 (appetite/palate). The English-speaker pitfall: 'this is tasty' is 맛있어요 (one word), not 맛이 좋아요 in casual speech (though 맛이 좋다 exists, it sounds more written/evaluative); and don't say 맛이 나빠요 for 'it tastes bad' — say 맛없어요. To ask 'what does it taste like?', use 무슨 맛이에요? or 맛이 어때요?, not a literal 'how is the taste'.

Saying 맛이 나빠요 for 'it tastes bad' — natural Korean is 맛없어요; 나쁘다 is for general 'bad', not flavor.
Confusing 맛 (taste) with 향 (smell) or 식감 (texture) — 'it smells good' is 향이 좋아요, not 맛이 좋아요.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 방법 means "method, way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "method, way" is 방법 (bangbeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 방법이 있다 ("there is a way/method"). Watch the particle attached to 방법 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 방법 + 이 with 있다, a way exists
방법 + 을 with 찾다, to look for a solution
adjective + 방법, naming a good approach
방법 + 없다, 'no other choice/method'

examples.en: There's no other way.
examples.note: Simple frame: 방법이 없다 = there's no method/option, a common resigned phrase.

examples.ko: 이 단어를 외우는 좋은 방법이 있어요?
examples.romanization: i daneoreul oeuneun joeun bangbeobi isseoyo?
examples.en: Is there a good way to memorize this word?
examples.note: Everyday frame: [verb]~는 + 방법 = 'a way to do X', the go-to question for tips.

examples.ko: 여러 방법을 다 시도해 봤지만, 결국 가장 단순한 방법이 제일 효과적이었어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo bangbeobeul da sidohae bwatjiman, gyeolguk gajang dansunhan bangbeobi jeil hyogwajeogieosseoyo.
examples.en: I tried all sorts of methods, but in the end the simplest method was the most effective.
examples.note: Real situation: surveying 여러 방법 (various methods) and concluding which worked best.

extendedVocab.nuance: 방법 is Sino-Korean (方法, 方 'direction/manner' + 法 'rule/method'), the 'way', 'method', or 'means' of doing something — the procedure or approach to reach a goal. Compare it with 방식 (方式, 'style/mode/manner'): 방법 is the concrete how-to ('a method to fix it'), while 방식 is the overall style or fashion in which something is done (생활 방식 = lifestyle, 사고방식 = way of thinking) — you wouldn't say 사고방법. Also distinguish 수단 (手段, 'means/instrument', often the tool or even an unscrupulous means: 교통수단 = means of transport, 수단과 방법을 가리지 않다 = by any means necessary). Register-neutral, very common. Core collocations: 방법이 있다/없다, 방법을 찾다/알다/모르다/바꾸다, [동사]~는 방법 (a way to do ~), 해결 방법 (solution), 사용 방법 (how to use). The English-speaker pitfall is the 'a way to do X' frame: it's [verb in ~는 form] + 방법, e.g. 'a way to study' is 공부하는 방법, NOT 공부 방법 in spoken contexts (though 공부 방법 as a fixed noun-noun compound is fine for 'study method'). Don't say 방법으로 어떻게 when you just mean 어떻게 ('how') — 방법 is the noun 'method', not the question word 'how'.

Using 방법 where the question word 어떻게 ('how') is needed — 'How do I do this?' is 이거 어떻게 해요?, not 이거 무슨 방법으로 해요? unless you truly want to ask which method.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 장점 means "strength, merit, advantage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 장점 (jangjeom) = "strength, merit, advantage". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장점이 있다 ("to have a merit/strength") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장점, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.note: 장점 + 이 with 있다, an advantage exists
장점 + 이 with 많다, lots of good points
가장 큰 + 장점, ranking the top merit

usagePhrases.en: to make the most of a strength
usagePhrases.note: 장점 + 을 with 살리다, to leverage an advantage

examples.en: This method has many advantages.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 장점이 많다/있다 to list what's good about something.

examples.ko: 온라인 수업의 장점은 시간을 아낄 수 있다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: ollain sueobui jangjeomeun siganeul akkil su itdaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: The advantage of online classes is that you can save time.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~의 장점은 ...라는 것이다, the set 'the advantage of X is that ~' pattern.

examples.ko: 면접에서 자신의 장점과 단점을 솔직하게 말하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseo jasinui jangjeomgwa danjeomeul soljikage malhaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: In an interview, it's good to honestly state your own strengths and weaknesses.
examples.note: Real situation: 장점과 단점 paired in the classic interview question about yourself.

extendedVocab.nuance: 장점 is Sino-Korean (長點, 長 'long/superior' + 點 'point'), literally a 'strong point' — a merit, advantage, or strength of a thing, plan, or person. It is almost always used in deliberate contrast with its antonym 단점 (短點, 'short point' = weakness/drawback); the pair 장점과 단점 is a fixed collocation, like English 'pros and cons'. Compare 장점 with 강점 (強點, 'strong point/forte'): 강점 emphasizes a competitive strength relative to others (우리 회사의 강점 = our company's competitive edge), while 장점 is the neutral 'good point' of anything. Also note 좋은 점 (a more colloquial 'the good thing about it'). Register-neutral and common in reviews, interviews, and comparisons. Collocations: 장점이 있다/많다, 장점을 살리다 (leverage), 장점을 살펴보다 (examine the merits), 큰 장점, 최대 장점 (greatest advantage). The English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'advantage' as 이득 or 이점 indiscriminately — 이득 (利得) is material 'gain/profit', and 이점 (利點) is 'an advantageous point/benefit' often in a strategic sense; for the everyday 'good point of X', 장점 is the natural choice. Also, when describing a person's virtue, 장점 (good trait) differs from 매력 (charm/appeal) — a reliable friend has a 장점, a charismatic one has 매력.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing the wrong antonym: the opposite of 장점 is 단점 (장점과 단점 = pros and cons), not 약점 (which is 'a vulnerability/weak spot', e.g. in a fight or argument).
Using 이득 for 'advantage' of a method — 이득 is monetary gain; the merit/strength of a plan is its 장점.
Saying 장점이 좋다 — that's redundant ('the good point is good'); just say 장점이 있다/많다, or 좋은 점이 있다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 단점 means "weakness, drawback, shortcoming" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 단점 (danjeom) means "weakness, drawback, shortcoming". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 단점이 있다 ("to have a drawback"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 단점 + 이 with 있다, a weak point exists
단점 + 을 with 고치다, to improve a flaw
가장 큰 + 단점, ranking the worst weakness

usagePhrases.en: to make up for a weakness
usagePhrases.note: 단점 + 을 with 보완하다, to compensate for a flaw

examples.en: This phone has almost no drawbacks.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 단점이 없다/있다 to evaluate the downsides of a product.

examples.ko: 제 단점은 가끔 너무 솔직하다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je danjeomeun gakkeum neomu soljikadaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My weakness is that I'm sometimes too honest.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~의 단점은 ...라는 것이다, the 'my weakness is that ~' interview pattern.

examples.ko: 이 방법의 단점은 시간이 오래 걸린다는 점인데, 그래도 가장 안전해요.
examples.romanization: i bangbeobui danjeomeun sigani orae geollindaneun jeominde, geuraedo gajang anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The drawback of this method is that it takes a long time, but it's still the safest.
examples.note: Real situation: conceding a 단점 (~다는 점) while still recommending the option.

extendedVocab.nuance: 단점 is Sino-Korean (短點, 短 'short/lacking' + 點 'point'), literally a 'short point' — a weakness, drawback, flaw, or shortcoming of a thing, plan, or person. It is the fixed antonym of 장점 (長點, merit), and the pair 장점과 단점 functions exactly like English 'pros and cons / strengths and weaknesses'. The key contrast to master is 단점 vs 약점 (弱點, 'weak point/vulnerability'): 단점 is a general flaw or downside that's just part of something (이 차의 단점 = this car's drawback, e.g. poor mileage), while 약점 is an exploitable vulnerability or sensitive spot — a rival attacks your 약점, a coach targets the opponent's 약점, and a personal sore subject is a 약점, not a 단점. Also compare 결점 (缺點, a 'defect/fault', slightly stronger, hints at something missing) and 흠 (a native word for a 'flaw/blemish'). Register-neutral. Collocations: 단점이 있다/없다, 단점을 고치다/보완하다 (fix/compensate), 단점을 인정하다 (admit a flaw), 큰 단점. The English-speaker pitfall: in self-introductions, 'my weakness' should be 단점 (a manageable shortcoming), not 약점 — calling it your 약점 sounds like you're confessing an exploitable vulnerability. And don't say 단점이 나쁘다 ('the drawback is bad') — that's redundant; just 단점이 있다.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 차이 means "difference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: "difference" is 차이 (chai). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 차이가 있다 ("there is a difference"). Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.note: 차이 + 이 with 있다, a difference exists
차이 + 이 with 나다, a difference appears between things
차이 + 이 with 크다, a large gap
~와 marks the thing compared against; 차이가 있다

examples.en: The two photos have almost no difference.
examples.note: Simple frame: A는/두 N은 + 차이가 없다/있다 to say things are (not) different.

examples.ko: 이 두 단어는 의미에 큰 차이가 있어요.
examples.romanization: i du daneoneun uimie keun chaiga isseoyo.
examples.en: These two words have a big difference in meaning.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~에 차이가 있다 (a difference IN ~), here 의미에 (in meaning).

examples.ko: 가격은 비슷한데 품질에서 차이가 많이 나서, 결국 더 비싼 걸 샀어요.
examples.romanization: gagyeogeun biseutande pumjireseo chaiga mani naseo, gyeolguk deo bissan geol sasseoyo.
examples.en: The prices are similar, but there's a big difference in quality, so in the end I bought the more expensive one.
examples.note: Real situation: 차이가 나다 in 품질에서 (in quality) driving a purchase decision.

extendedVocab.nuance: 차이 is Sino-Korean (差異, 差 'discrepancy/gap' + 異 'different'), the 'difference', 'gap', or 'disparity' between two or more things. It pairs with two key verbs: 차이가 있다 (a difference exists, more static) and 차이가 나다 (a difference shows up/emerges, more dynamic, often for a noticeable gap, e.g. 실력 차이가 나다 = a clear skill gap). The thing you compare with takes ~와/과 (A는 B와 차이가 있다), and the dimension of difference takes ~에(서) (의미에 차이가 있다 = a difference in meaning). Contrast 차이 with 다르다, the adjective 'to be different': 다르다 describes that two things are not the same (A와 B는 달라요), while 차이 is the noun naming the gap itself (A와 B는 차이가 있어요) — Koreans often use 다르다 for a qualitative 'different' and 차이 for a measurable/quantifiable gap (나이 차이 = age gap, 온도 차이 = temperature difference). Don't confuse 차이 with 차별 (差別, 'discrimination'), which is unfair treatment based on a difference. Register-neutral, very common. Collocations: 차이가 있다/없다/나다/크다, 차이를 느끼다 (feel a difference), 큰 차이, 별 차이 없다 (no real difference), 나이 차이/시차 (time difference). The English-speaker pitfall: 'A is different from B' is most naturally A는 B와 달라요 (using 다르다 + 와), not A는 B에서 차이예요; reach for the noun 차이 when you mean 'the difference between/in', and the verb 다르다 when you simply mean 'differs'.

Marking the compared item with 을/를: it's A는 B와 차이가 있어요 (differ FROM B with ~와), not B를 차이가 있어요.
Confusing 차이 (a neutral difference/gap) with 차별 (discrimination) — 남녀 차이 = differences between men and women; 남녀 차별 = gender discrimination.

adjective + 태도, describing one's manner

examples.en: That person has a really good attitude.
examples.note: Simple frame: 태도가 좋다/나쁘다 to judge someone's manner or disposition.

examples.ko: 선생님은 항상 학생들에게 친절한 태도로 말해요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimeun hangsang haksaengdeurege chinjeolhan taedoro malhaeyo.
examples.en: The teacher always speaks to students with a kind attitude.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~한 태도로 (with a ~ attitude) describes the manner of an action.

examples.ko: 실력도 중요하지만, 일을 대하는 성실한 태도가 더 중요하다고 생각해요.
examples.romanization: sillyeokdo jungyohajiman, ireul daehaneun seongsilhan taedoga deo jungyohadago saenggakaeyo.
examples.en: Skill matters too, but I think a sincere attitude toward work is more important.
examples.note: Real situation: weighing 태도 (work attitude) against 실력 (skill) in a values statement.

extendedVocab.nuance: 태도 is Sino-Korean (態度, 態 'form/manner/bearing' + 度 'degree/measure'), a person's 'attitude', 'manner', 'bearing', or 'stance' — both the outward way they carry and conduct themselves (공손한 태도 = a polite manner) and their inner posture toward something (인생을 대하는 태도 = one's attitude toward life). Contrast it with 자세 (姿勢): 자세 literally means physical 'posture/pose' (바른 자세로 앉다 = sit with good posture) but is also used figuratively for a committed 'attitude/stance', often a praiseworthy, proactive one (배우려는 자세 = a willing-to-learn attitude) — so 자세 leans toward earnest mindset, while 태도 is the broader, more neutral 'manner' that can be good OR bad (태도가 나쁘다 is normal; 자세가 나쁘다 usually means literal bad posture). Also distinguish 입장 (立場, 'position/standpoint' on an issue) and 성격 (性格, 'personality', a stable trait vs. a situational 태도). Register-neutral, common in evaluations of behavior, work, and manners. Collocations: 태도가 좋다/나쁘다, 태도를 바꾸다/취하다 (change/take an attitude), ~에 대한 태도 (attitude toward ~), 근무 태도 (work attitude), 강경한 태도 (a hard-line stance). The English-speaker pitfall: 'attitude' in English can imply a personality trait or even sass, but Korean 태도 is more about manner/conduct in a given context; for a fixed personality trait use 성격, and don't say 태도하다 — there is no such verb; you 태도를 취하다/보이다 (take/show an attitude).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 태도하다 — 태도 is a noun with no verb form; use 태도를 보이다/취하다 (show/take an attitude) or describe with ~한 태도로.
Confusing 태도 (manner/conduct, can be good or bad) with 성격 (personality, a stable trait): 'he has a kind personality' is 성격이 착해요, while 태도가 좋다 judges his behavior in a situation.
Mixing up 태도 and 자세 — 자세 is literal posture (자세를 바르게 하다) or an earnest mindset (적극적인 자세); for a generic, possibly negative 'attitude', use 태도.

extendedVocab.shortExplanation: 느낌 means "feeling, impression, vibe" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
extendedVocab.explanation: 느낌 (neukkim) means "feeling, impression, vibe". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 느낌이 좋다 ("to have a good feeling/vibe"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 느낌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.note: 느낌 + 이 with 좋다, something feels right
느낌 + 이 with 들다, an impression arises
느낌 + 이 with 오다, intuition kicks in
modifier + 느낌, 'a feeling of being ~'

examples.en: This café has a good vibe.
examples.note: Simple frame: 느낌이 좋다 to say a place/person gives a pleasant impression.

examples.en: I get the feeling something is wrong.
examples.note: Everyday frame: [modifier]~ㄴ + 느낌이 들다 = 'I get a ~ feeling/sense that ~'.

examples.ko: 설명을 들어도 완전히 이해한 느낌이 안 와서, 한 번 더 물어봤어요.
examples.romanization: seolmyeongeul deureodo wanjeonhi ihaehan neukkimi an waseo, han beon deo mureobwasseoyo.
examples.en: Even after hearing the explanation, I didn't get the feeling I fully understood, so I asked once more.
examples.note: Real situation: 느낌이 안 오다 (it doesn't click) prompting a follow-up question.

extendedVocab.nuance: 느낌 is the native Korean noun from the verb 느끼다 ('to feel'), meaning a 'feeling', 'impression', 'sense', or 'vibe' — the subjective sensation or intuition something gives you, whether physical (차가운 느낌 = a cold feeling) or atmospheric (느낌이 좋은 사람 = someone who gives off a good vibe). The crucial contrast is with 기분 (氣分): 기분 is your own emotional 'mood/spirits' caused by events (기분이 좋다 = I'm in a good mood, 기분 나빠 = I'm upset), whereas 느낌 is the impression/sense you get OF something external (그 사람 느낌이 좋다 = that person gives a good impression — about them, not your mood). Also distinguish 감정 (感情, 'emotion' as a category: love, anger) and 감각 (感覺, 'sense/sensation', the faculty). Register-neutral and hugely frequent in casual speech, where 느낌 also works as a vague 'kind of, sort of, like' filler (약간 매운 느낌? = kind of spicy?). Collocations: 느낌이 좋다/이상하다, 느낌이 들다 (a feeling arises), 느낌이 오다 (it clicks/I get a hunch), 첫 느낌 (first impression), ~는 느낌 (a feeling of ~ing). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 느낌 for your own mood — 'I feel good/happy today' is 오늘 기분이 좋아요, NOT 느낌이 좋아요 (which describes an external thing's vibe). And 'I feel that ~' is naturally ~ㄴ 느낌이 들어요 with 들다, not 느낌해요 (no such verb).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 느낌 for your own mood: 'I'm in a good mood' is 기분이 좋아요, while 느낌이 좋아요 means 'it/he gives a good vibe' (an external impression).
Saying 느낌하다 — there's no verb; the natural patterns are 느낌이 들다 / 느낌이 오다, or the source verb 느끼다 ('느꼈어요').
Forgetting the ~ㄴ/는 modifier: 'a warm feeling' is 따뜻한 느낌, and 'I get the feeling it's true' is 사실인 느낌이 들어요, not 사실 느낌.

expressions.shortExplanation: 안녕하세요 is a practical expression meaning "Hello. / Hi.".
expressions.explanation: "Hello. / Hi." — that is 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 안녕하세요 ("hello (polite)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: the default greeting to almost anyone you meet
반말, to a close friend, a child, or someone clearly younger
격식체; soldiers, announcers, staff to customers, formal speeches
natural extension when greeting someone you know

examples.en: A: Hello! / B: Yes, hello.
examples.note: the bare greeting returned with the same words — no extra 'how are you?' needed

examples.en: Hello, nice to meet you (first time).
examples.note: everyday: chaining the greeting into a first introduction

examples.en: (walking into a shop) Hello~ is the owner in?
examples.note: real situation: 안녕하세요 doubles as 'excuse me' to get attention in a shop

expressions.nuance: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose 존댓말 greeting for strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers — basically any adult you are not on 반말 terms with. The root 안녕(安寧) means 'peace/well-being', so the phrase literally asks 'are you at peace?', but modern Koreans hear it simply as 'hello'; it works morning, noon, and night since Korean has no separate 'good morning/afternoon/evening' equivalents. The register ladder runs: 안녕 (반말, close friends / children / clear juniors) → 안녕하세요 (standard polite) → 안녕하십니까 (격식체, formal broadcasts and service settings). A key social rule: saying 안녕 to a teacher, boss, or older stranger signals either extreme intimacy or disrespect — always default to 안녕하세요 until 반말 is mutually established. The classic English-speaker trap is splitting greetings by time of day or tacking on 어떻게 지내세요? every time — in Korean, 안녕하세요 alone is the complete, natural hello, and opening with a wellbeing question to a stranger sounds oddly probing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안녕 to a teacher, boss, or older stranger — that is 반말 and sounds rude/childish; use 안녕하세요 with anyone you owe respect.
Searching for a 'good morning / good evening' equivalent — Korean uses one 안녕하세요 all day; time-of-day greetings are not standard.
Writing or saying 안녕하새요 — the verb ending is 세요 (하 + 세요), never 새요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'are you at peace?' (안녕安寧 + 하세요). In practice, Koreans hear it simply as 'hello' — the question about well-being has been bleached away through daily use.

Use 안녕하세요 as your default with any adult you are not on 반말 terms with: strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers. It works morning, noon, and night — Korean has no 'good morning / good evening' split. Do NOT say 안녕 to a senior or stranger; that is 반말 and reads as rude.
안녕 (반말, friends/kids/juniors) → 안녕하세요 (standard polite) → 안녕하십니까 (격식체, formal speeches, service staff). Chain into 안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다 for a first meeting, or 안녕하세요, 잘 지내셨어요? for a warm reconnection.

안녕하세요 is a neutral all-day greeting. 안녕하십니까 is stiffer and used in one-directional formal contexts (news anchors, soldiers, staff). 여보세요 is only for phone calls — never use it face-to-face as a hello.

English speakers split greetings by time of day (good morning / afternoon) and routinely add 'how are you?' — Korean does neither. 안녕하세요 alone is complete. Adding 어떻게 지내세요? to a new acquaintance sounds overly intimate.

expressions.shortExplanation: 감사합니다 is a practical expression meaning "Thank you.".
expressions.explanation: 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) = "Thank you.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 감사합니다 ("thank you (formal-polite)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: the all-purpose 존댓말 thanks to anyone
반말, to a close friend or someone younger
격식, public, written, or to a customer
natural extension adding warmth

examples.en: Thank you.
examples.note: the bare safe thanks you can say to anyone in any situation

examples.en: Thank you for helping me.
examples.note: attach ~아/어 주셔서 before 감사합니다 to thank for a specific action

examples.ko: A: 바쁘신데 시간 내 주셔서 정말 감사합니다. / B: 별말씀을요, 당연히 해야죠.
examples.romanization: A: bappeusinde sigan nae jusyeoseo jeongmal gamsahamnida. / B: byeolmalsseumeuryo, dangyeonhi haeyajyo.
examples.en: A: Thank you so much for making time despite being so busy. / B: Not at all, of course I would.
examples.note: full polite exchange after someone goes out of their way; note the humble reply 별말씀을요

expressions.nuance: 감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' safe with literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝), giving it a slightly formal, composed feel compared to the warmer native alternative 고맙습니다. The formality ladder runs: 고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gentle polite) → 감사합니다 (standard polite) → 대단히 감사합니다 / 감사드립니다 (격식, speeches, written). The nearest alternative is 고맙습니다, which is pure native Korean and sounds a touch warmer and more personal; both are equally polite, and the choice is mostly about tone rather than rank. The classic English-speaker error is stacking a noun directly: you cannot say '도움 감사합니다' as if words simply pile up — to thank for an action you must attach ~아/어 주셔서 (도와주셔서 감사합니다). Another mistake is using 고마워 with strangers or anyone older, which sounds presumptuous and rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고마워 to a stranger, clerk, or anyone older — that is 반말 and sounds rude; default to 감사합니다 or at least 고마워요.
Trying to thank for an action by just naming it ('도와 감사합니다') — Korean needs ~아/어 주셔서: 도와주셔서 감사합니다.
Writing 감사 합니다 with a space — 감사합니다 is one word; the space is wrong.

structuredNuance.t: 감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' safe with literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝), giving it a slightly formal, composed feel compared to the native alternative 고맙습니다.

Formality ladder: 고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gentle polite) → 감사합니다 (standard polite) → 대단히 감사합니다 / 감사드립니다 (격식, speeches, written). 감사드립니다 uses the humble auxiliary 드리다 and is the most deferential spoken form.
Nearest alternative is 고맙습니다 — pure native Korean, equally polite, and a touch warmer. The dividing line is tone and origin, not rank. Use 고맙습니다 when you want sincerity over formality.
To thank for a specific action, insert ~아/어 주셔서: 도와주셔서 감사합니다, 기다려 주셔서 감사합니다. To amplify, add 정말/너무/대단히 before 감사합니다.

English speakers try to thank for a noun by stacking it directly ('도움 감사합니다') — Korean needs the favor connector ~아/어 주셔서. Also, overusing 고마워 with strangers or seniors is a common register mistake; it is 반말 and sounds rude to anyone you are not already close with.

expressions.shortExplanation: 죄송합니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'm sorry. / I apologize.".
expressions.explanation: 죄송합니다 (joesonghamnida) means "I'm sorry. / I apologize.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 죄송합니다 ("I'm sorry (formal-polite)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: the safe 존댓말 apology to anyone, esp. seniors/strangers
반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer
격식, serious fault, customer/public setting
natural extension adding sincerity

examples.en: I'm sorry.
examples.note: the bare polite apology, safe with anyone you don't know well

examples.en: I'm sorry I'm late.
examples.note: reason + 아/어서 + 죄송합니다; the standard structure for apologizing for a cause

examples.ko: A: 제 실수로 불편을 드렸습니다. 정말 죄송합니다. / B: 아니에요, 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: A: je silsuro bulpyeoneul deuryeotseumnida. jeongmal joesonghamnida. / B: anieyo, gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: A: I caused inconvenience because of my mistake. I'm truly sorry. / B: No, it's all right.
examples.note: formal exchange owning the fault clearly; notice how 불편을 드리다 (cause inconvenience upward) pairs naturally

expressions.nuance: 죄송합니다 is the higher-deference 'I'm sorry', from Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I have committed a fault and am fearful before you'. That deferential weight makes it the correct apology toward strangers, seniors, customers, and your boss — situations where showing you lower yourself is required. The formality ladder: 미안해 (반말, peers/friends) → 미안해요 (gentle polite) → 죄송해요 / 죄송합니다 (polite, upward-safe) → 대단히 죄송합니다 / 죄송스럽습니다 (격식, serious fault). The dividing line versus 미안하다 is deference: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is always safe upward; 미안하다 is more horizontal and personal, and sounds too casual to a boss. Three concrete English-speaker mistakes: (1) attaching the reason wrong — use X-아/어서 죄송합니다 (늦어서 죄송합니다), not '늦은 것 죄송'; (2) using 미안해 to a boss or stranger; (3) confusing it with 실례합니다, which is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not an apology for fault.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 미안해 to a boss, teacher, or stranger — that is 반말; use 죄송합니다 (or at least 미안해요) for a real apology upward.
Forming the reason wrong, e.g. '늦은 거 죄송' — use the ~아/어서 connector: 늦어서 죄송합니다.
Swapping in 실례합니다 to apologize for a real mistake — 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor intrusion, not an apology for fault.

structuredNuance.t: From Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I have committed a fault and am fearful/ashamed before you'. The real function is a deferential apology that lowers the speaker — stronger and more formal than 미안합니다.
Formality: 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gentle polite) → 죄송해요 / 죄송합니다 (polite, upward-safe) → 대단히 죄송합니다 / 죄송스럽습니다 (격식). Use 죄송합니다 as your default to strangers, seniors, and customers.

Key dividing line versus 미안하다: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is always safe upward; 미안하다 is more horizontal/personal. Using 미안해요 to a boss sounds under-deferential; using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds oddly stiff.
Add the reason with ~아/어서: 늦어서 죄송합니다, 잘못해서 죄송합니다. Intensify: 정말 / 대단히 죄송합니다. Very formal written form: 심심(深深)한 사과를 드립니다.

Three traps: (1) attach reason with ~아/어서, not a noun — '늦은 것 죄송' is wrong; say 늦어서 죄송합니다. (2) Never use 미안해 to a boss or stranger — it's 반말. (3) Do not swap in 실례합니다 for a real fault — 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not an apology.

expressions.english: It's okay. / That's all right. / No, thank you.
expressions.shortExplanation: 괜찮아요 is a practical expression meaning "It's okay. / That's all right. / No, thank you.".
expressions.explanation: 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) = "It's okay. / That's all right. / No, thank you.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 괜찮아요 ("it's okay / I'm fine"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

반말, to a friend or someone younger/closer

examples.romanization: han jan deo deurilkkayo? — aniyo, gwaenchanayo. jal masyeotseumnida.

examples.ko: 많이 다치셨어요? — 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 걱정 마세요.
examples.romanization: mani dachisyeosseoyo? — anieyo, gwaenchanayo. geokjeong maseyo.
examples.en: Are you badly hurt? — No, I'm all right. Don't worry.
examples.note: 괜찮아요 reassuring someone about your own physical state

expressions.nuance: 괜찮아요 does triple duty: 'it's okay / don't worry about it' (accepting an apology or reassuring), 'I'm fine' (about your own state or health), and crucially 'no, thank you' (politely declining an offer). The word traces back to 괜찮다, a contracted form of 관계없다 (關係없다) — literally 'there is no relationship/connection (to worry about)', i.e. 'it doesn't matter'. That origin explains why all three uses share the idea that the matter has no hold over you. The decline meaning trips English speakers most, because English 'okay' or 'fine' to an offer usually signals acceptance — but 괜찮아요 to a Korean host's offer means you are turning it DOWN. To accept, you must clearly say 네, 주세요 / 네, 부탁드립니다. Register: 괜찮아 (반말) → 괜찮아요 (polite) → 괜찮습니다 (firmer/격식). The nearest relatives are 됐어요 (also 'I'm good/no need', but sharper and can sound curt or dismissive) and 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing', used mainly to deflect apologies). 괜찮아요 is the softest and most versatile of the three.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering an offer of food/drink with 괜찮아요 expecting MORE — it means 'no, I'm fine'; to accept, say 네, 주세요.
Using 괜찮아 with a stranger or senior — that is 반말; say 괜찮아요/괜찮습니다.
Confusing 괜찮아요 with 됐어요 in tone — 됐어요 can sound blunt/annoyed; 괜찮아요 stays gentle.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮다 is a contracted form of 관계없다 (關係없다), literally 'there is no relationship/connection (to worry about)'. From this 'it doesn't matter' root, the word branches into three real uses: accepting apologies, stating you are fine, and declining offers. All three share the idea that the matter has no hold over you.
괜찮아 (반말, friends/juniors) → 괜찮아요 (polite, most common) → 괜찮습니다 (firmer/격식). Keep 괜찮아 for people you are close with; use 괜찮아요 or 괜찮습니다 with strangers and seniors.

Nearest relatives: 됐어요 (also 'no need / I'm done', but can sound curt or even annoyed); 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing', for deflecting apologies). 괜찮아요 is the softest and most versatile of the three. Choose 됐어요 only when you want finality, not just reassurance.
To soften a decline: 아, 괜찮아요 / 정말 괜찮아요. To reassure: 걱정 마세요, 괜찮아요. To check on someone: 괜찮으세요? (question, honorific form). Never say 괜찮어 — the stem is 괜찮다, so polite is 괜찮아요 (아-ending, not 어).

When a host offers food or a refill and you say 괜찮아요, you are turning it DOWN, not accepting. To accept, say 네, 주세요. Also, 됐어요 (an alternative decline) can sound blunt or even annoyed — 괜찮아요 is always gentler for refusals.

expressions.nuance: 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor social intrusion — getting a stranger's attention, asking a question, passing by, or entering a space. From Sino-Korean 실례(失禮), literally 'I am committing a breach of etiquette'. It is NOT an apology for a real fault (that requires 죄송합니다) and NOT 'pardon? / say again?' (that is 네? / 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?). Register: 실례합니다 is standard polite; the 격식 form is 실례하겠습니다 / 실례합니다만; clipped 실례 sounds odd in formal contexts and is only murmured casually. The nearest alternatives are 저기요 and 잠시만요/잠깐만요: 저기요 hails a server or stranger casually and is more common in eateries; 잠시만요 means 'one moment / let me through' but can also ask someone to wait. 실례합니다 is the more polished opener before a question or when entering a space. English speakers often misuse it as an all-purpose 'sorry' or as 'pardon?' — neither is correct. In casual restaurants Koreans typically call 저기요, not 실례합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례합니다 as 'sorry' for a real mistake — for fault use 죄송합니다; 실례합니다 is only for a small intrusion.
Saying 실례합니다 to mean 'pardon? / say again?' — to ask for a repeat use 네? or 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Hailing a waiter with 실례합니다 every time — Koreans more often call 저기요 or 여기요 in casual eateries.

structuredNuance.t: From 실례(失禮), literally 'I am committing a breach of etiquette'. The real use is a polite preface to a minor intrusion — getting attention, asking a question, or passing by. It is not an apology for a real fault.
실례합니다 is standard polite; 실례하겠습니다 / 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식 (entering a room, stepping away from a meeting). Clipped 실례 sounds awkward in formal settings. You almost never use it in 반말.

Alternatives: 저기요 hails a server or stranger casually and is the default in eateries; 잠시만요/잠깐만요 means 'one moment / let me through' but can also ask someone to wait. 실례합니다 is the more formal, polished opener before a question.
Soften with 저: 저, 실례합니다. Add a clause: 실례지만 (when prefacing an intrusive question). Formal step-away: 잠시 실례하겠습니다. Never say 실례해요 — the verb stem needs either 합니다 or 하겠습니다, not 해요, in this set phrase.

English speakers use 실례합니다 as an all-purpose 'sorry' or 'pardon?' — both are wrong. For fault: 죄송합니다. For 'say again?': 네? / 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요? Also, using 실례합니다 to hail a waiter at a casual restaurant sounds overly formal — use 저기요 there.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기요 is a practical expression meaning "Excuse me! (calling the server)".
expressions.explanation: 여기요 (yeogiyo) = "Excuse me! (calling the server)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기요 ("Excuse me! / Over here!"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the default call to get a server's attention from your seat, pitched up at the end
Adds 좀 to soften the summons when the room is noisy or staff look run off their feet

usagePhrases.en: Could you look over here, please?
usagePhrases.note: Fuller and gentler — good when you've waved once and been missed
Swap in 사장님 / 이모님 in a small family-run place to sound warm, not just transactional

examples.en: Excuse me!
examples.note: The single word, pitched up at the end, is a complete and normal way to call a server — no full sentence needed

examples.en: Excuse me, we'd like to order.
examples.note: Chain it straight into your request so the server arrives already knowing why you called

examples.ko: A: 여기요, 물 좀 더 주시겠어요? / B: 네, 금방 갖다드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiyo, mul jom deo jusigesseoyo? / B: ne, geumbang gatdadeurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Excuse me, could we get some more water? / B: Sure, I'll bring it right over.
examples.note: 여기요 opens, a polite -주시겠어요 request follows, and staff close with 갖다드리다 ('bring it for you')

expressions.nuance: 여기요 is literally 여기 ('here') + 요 (the politeness particle), so word-for-word it is 'over here, please' — you summon a server by calling out the PLACE rather than the person, which is exactly how Korean service-calling works and why it's fine to say before anyone has looked your way. It is polite-neutral: any customer can say it to any server, but it is NOT honorific, so to an elderly owner you'd warm it up to 사장님 / 이모님 or soften to 여기 좀 봐 주세요. The nearest rival is 저기요, a hair more tentative because 저기 ('over there') feels less pointed than 여기; Koreans swap them freely indoors, but 저기요 also works to stop a stranger on the street, whereas 여기요 is almost purely for service settings where you're already seated. The trap for English speakers is reaching for 실례합니다 as 'excuse me' — but 실례합니다 apologizes or asks to squeeze past, so calling a waiter that way sounds oddly stiff and over-apologetic. Raising your hand or even calling out across a busy room while saying 여기요 is completely normal and not rude in Korea; many casual places even have a call button (호출벨) you press instead.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 실례합니다 to call a waiter.

실례합니다 means 'pardon me (for the intrusion)' and is used to apologize or pass by, not to summon staff. It makes a simple service call sound stiff and oddly apologetic, as if you've done something wrong. To get a server's attention, say 여기요 or 저기요.
Adding 씨 or a name and saying 여기요 씨.

여기요 flags the situation, not a person, so there's no name for 씨 to attach to and the result is ungrammatical. If you want warmth in a small shop, address the person directly with 사장님 or 이모님, not 여기요 씨.
Dropping to bare 여기 with an unfamiliar server.
Bare 여기 is 반말 and can land as abrupt or bossy to a stranger doing their job. Keep the 요 — 여기요 — unless the server is clearly a friend or it's an extremely casual stall where everyone is on 반말 anyway.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word 여기 ('here') + 요 = 'over here, please', but as a set call it just means 'excuse me, server!'. The logic is that you flag the location, not the person — so it works even before you make eye contact, unlike English 'excuse me' which usually waits for a glance. That's why you can shout it across a room and still sound normal.

Polite-neutral and made for service settings: a customer to any waiter, fine in any eatery from a pojangmacha to a mid-range restaurant. It is NOT honorific, so to an older owner soften it with 사장님 / 이모님 or 여기 좀 봐 주세요. Raising a hand or calling across the room is expected here, not rude — and many casual spots have a 호출벨 (call button) on the table instead.

Nearest is 저기요, slightly softer because 저기 ('over there') is less pointed than 여기. Indoors they're interchangeable, but 저기요 also stops a stranger outside, while 여기요 stays in seated service. In a fancy restaurant with dedicated table service, many people skip both and just catch the server's eye or raise a hand — calling out can feel a touch loud there.

Softer/warmer ladder: 여기요 → 여기 좀요 → 여기 좀 봐 주세요 → 사장님, 여기요. Drop to bare 여기 only as 반말 with a server you actually know. You normally chain it with your request — 여기요, 주문할게요 / 여기요, 물 좀요 / 여기요, 계산할게요 — rather than leaving it hanging in the air.

Don't translate 'excuse me' as 실례합니다 here — that's for apologizing or passing by, and aimed at a waiter it sounds weirdly formal and apologetic. Also don't attach a name particle (여기요 씨); 여기요 addresses the situation, not a person, so 씨 has nothing to grab onto. And don't whisper it timidly — under-projecting just gets you missed in a busy room.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll have this one, please".
expressions.explanation: 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo) means "I'll have this one, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 주세요 ("This one, please"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

이걸로 = 'with this (choice)' — picking among options, very common at cafés
Add 하나 / 둘 / 세 개 to nail down the quantity
Chain 이거랑 이거 to point to two items in a row

examples.en: This one, please.
examples.note: Said while pointing at the menu or a photo of the dish — the bare point-and-order

examples.ko: 저기요, 이거 하나랑 콜라 하나 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, igeo hanarang kolla hana juseyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, one of these and one cola, please.

examples.ko: A: 이걸로 드릴까요? / B: 네, 이걸로 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: igeollo deurilkkayo? / B: ne, igeollo juseyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I get you this one? / B: Yes, I'll go with this one.

expressions.nuance: 이거 주세요 is 이거 (the spoken contraction of 이것, 'this thing') + 주세요 ('please give'), the point-and-order workhorse for any item you can indicate. Crucially 이거 ('this, near me') sits in a three-way set — 그거 ('that, near you'), 저거 ('that, away from both') — so you pick by where the thing actually is on the menu or table, and the wrong one leaves the server guessing. A subtle but important variant is 이걸로 주세요 (이거 + -로, 'with/by this'): use 이걸로 when you are CHOOSING among options ('I'll go with this'), and plain 이거 when you simply want the object itself; menus and cafés hear 이걸로 constantly. The English-speaker mistake is forcing the object particle in speech and saying 이것을 주세요 — natives contract to 이거 and usually drop the particle, so the full form sounds bookish at a table. Another is pointing 이거 at a person; 이거 is for things only, so you'd never indicate someone and say 이거 — that's rude. Add 하나/둘/세 개 for quantity (이거 둘 주세요), and note the close cousin 이거 뭐예요? only ASKS what something is, it doesn't order it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이것을 주세요 in conversation.

The full 이것을 is bookish and the particle 을 is normally dropped in speech; spoken Korean contracts to 이거 주세요. The written form sounds stiff and overly careful at a casual table, like reading aloud from a textbook.
Using 이거 when the item is near the server or far away.

이거 is only for what's near YOU. If you're pointing at something across the room it's 저거; if it's near the listener it's 그거. The wrong demonstrative leaves the server guessing which dish you actually mean.
Confusing 이거 주세요 with 이거 뭐예요.
주세요 orders the item; 뭐예요 only asks what it is. If you want to buy it, say 이거 주세요 — 이거 뭐예요 ('what is this?') will just get you an explanation of the dish, not the dish itself on your table.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'this thing, please give', i.e. 'I'll have this one.' There's no idiom hiding here — the work is done by the demonstrative. 이것 (written/formal) contracts to 이거 in speech, and the object particle 을 normally drops, so the natural spoken form is the short 이거 주세요, with the full 이것을 reserved for writing.

Polite (해요체) and standard customer-to-staff in any shop, stall, café, or restaurant where you can point. Drop to 이거 줘 with a friend or at a super-casual stall. It's a service request, not something you'd say to a peer about their own belongings — for that you'd use a different, more deferential frame entirely.

이거 주세요 (you want the object) vs 이걸로 주세요 (you're choosing among options — 'this one, then'). And mind the 이/그/저 trio: 이거 = near you, 그거 = near the listener, 저거 = far from both. Picking the wrong one points the server at the wrong dish. Against 이거 뭐예요?, that only asks 'what is this?', it never places the order.
Quantity: 이거 하나 / 둘 / 세 개 주세요. Listing: 이거랑 이거 주세요 / 이거 두 개랑 저거 하나요. Choosing: 이걸로 주세요 / 이걸로 할게요. Politeness floor: 이거 줘 (반말) → 이거 주세요. Pair it with a named item too: 이거 하나랑 콜라 하나 주세요.

Don't say 이것을 주세요 at a table — the full particle is bookish and stiff; speech wants 이거 주세요. And never point 이거 at a person (it's for things only); for a person you'd use a name, 저분, or 이쪽, not 이거. Also don't confuse it with the question 이거 뭐예요?, which only gets you an explanation, not the dish.

expressions.shortExplanation: 계산해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Check, please".
expressions.explanation: 계산해 주세요 (gyesanhae juseyo) = "Check, please". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 계산해 주세요 ("Check, please / I'd like to pay"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Check, please / I'd like to pay
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asks staff to ring up the bill
The version YOU say announcing your own action at the counter
Natural follow-on once you're at the register
What you ask AFTER paying — not the request to pay

examples.en: Check, please.
examples.note: Said at the counter or to the server when you're ready to pay

examples.en: Excuse me, we'd like to pay. How much is it?
examples.note: Pair with 얼마예요 to ask the total in the same breath

examples.ko: A: 다 드셨어요? / B: 네, 잘 먹었습니다. 계산할게요. / A: 32,000원입니다.
examples.romanization: A: da deusyeosseoyo? / B: ne, jal meogeotseumnida. gyesanhalgeyo. / A: 32,000wonimnida.
examples.en: A: All finished? / B: Yes, it was great. I'll pay now. / A: That's 32,000 won.
