expressions.nuance: 계산해 주세요 is 계산 ('calculation/reckoning', Sino-Korean 計算) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'), literally 'please do the reckoning' — the standard 'check, please.' Korean names the ACT of totting up the bill rather than a paper 'check', so nothing physical gets handed over; you're asking for the action. In Korea you usually pay at the front counter (계산대) on the way out, not at the table, so this is often said while standing to leave or handed to whoever's at the register — waiting for a check to arrive at your seat will leave you sitting indefinitely. The near-twin 계산할게요 ('I'll pay') is the version YOU say announcing your own action at the counter, while 계산해 주세요 asks staff to ring it up; both are common and natural. A casual stand-in is 얼마예요? ('how much?'), which doubles as 'let me pay' at the register. The English-speaker error is asking for 'the bill/check' as a physical object — 영수증 주세요 means 'give me the RECEIPT', which you get AFTER paying, not the request to pay; to settle up, say 계산해 주세요. Don't confuse 계산 ('the bill') with 영수증 ('receipt') or with the similar-sounding 계좌 ('bank account').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 영수증 주세요 to ask for the check.

영수증 is the receipt you receive AFTER paying, so this asks for proof of a completed payment — it won't prompt staff to total your bill. To request the bill / to pay, say 계산해 주세요; the receipt comes later if you want it.
Expecting the bill to be brought to your table.

Korean restaurants usually have you pay at the front counter (계산대), not at your seat, so waiting for a check to be delivered can leave you sitting indefinitely. Say 계산해 주세요 as you head to the register.
Confusing 계산 with 계좌.

계산 is 'calculation / the bill'; 계좌 is a 'bank account'. They sound close but 계좌 has nothing to do with paying at a restaurant — 계좌 주세요 would bizarrely ask the cashier for an account number instead of letting you pay.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please do the reckoning/calculation' (계산 'calculation' + 해 주다 'do for me'). It means 'the check, please / I'd like to pay.' Korean names the ACT of totting up the bill rather than the paper 'check', which is why there's no slip handed over — you're asking for the action of calculating and settling, not a document.

Polite (해요체), staff-facing, and usually said at the 계산대 (front counter) as you leave — Korean restaurants rarely bring a check to the table, so you go to the register rather than wait. Drop to 계산해 줘 with a friend treating; say 계산할게요 when announcing your own move at the counter.

계산해 주세요 (you ask staff to ring it up) vs 계산할게요 (you announce you're paying yourself). 얼마예요? doubles as 'let me pay' at the register. And keep 계산 ('the bill') apart from 영수증 ('receipt', handed AFTER) and 계좌 ('bank account', totally unrelated despite the similar sound).

Politeness ladder: 계산해 줘 (반말) → 계산해 주세요 → 계산 좀 부탁드려요 (extra polite). Self-announce: 계산할게요. Natural pairings at the register: 카드 돼요?, 얼마예요?, 따로 계산해 주세요 (split), 현금영수증 해 주세요 (cash receipt), 영수증 주세요 (after).

Don't ask for the 'check/bill' as an object via 영수증 주세요 — that's the RECEIPT, issued after you pay, so it won't make staff ring you up. To settle the bill, say 계산해 주세요. And don't expect a check delivered to your table; head to the counter, where payment usually happens in Korea.

expressions.english: To go, please / Pack it up
expressions.shortExplanation: 포장해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "To go, please / Pack it up".
expressions.explanation: 포장해 주세요 (pojanghae juseyo) means "To go, please / Pack it up". Say it as one set phrase — for example 포장해 주세요. ("Please pack it to go."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Customer choosing takeout; 포장 = packing/wrapping to take away
반말; with a friend only
Clipped one-word answer to the dine-in-or-takeout question

usagePhrases.en: Can I get this to go?
usagePhrases.note: Extension: ask first whether takeout is possible for this particular item

examples.ko: A: 드시고 가세요? / B: 아니요, 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: deusigo gaseyo? / B: aniyo, pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Eating in? / B: No, to go please.
examples.note: The natural takeout answer to the dine-in-or-to-go question; 포장해 주세요 tells staff to pack it, not just that you're leaving

examples.ko: 라떼 한 잔 포장해 주세요. 캐리어도 주시고요.
examples.romanization: ratte han jan pojanghae juseyo. kaerieodo jusigoyo.
examples.en: One latte to go, please. A carrier too.
examples.note: 캐리어 = the cardboard or plastic drink carrier; 주시고요 chains a second request after the main one — natural at a busy counter

examples.ko: 남은 거 포장해 주세요. 집에서 먹을게요.
examples.romanization: nameun geo pojanghae juseyo. jibeseo meogeulgeyo.
examples.en: Please pack up the leftovers. I'll eat them at home.
examples.note: 남은 거 = 'the leftovers'; 포장하다 works for restaurant doggy-bags too — the same phrase covers café takeout and restaurant leftovers

expressions.nuance: 포장해 주세요 is the all-purpose 'to go' or 'pack it up' request — for a café drink ordered fresh, a bakery item, or restaurant leftovers. 포장 (包裝) literally means 'wrapping/packaging.' Plain polite -요 for all staff; the even shorter clipped form 포장이요 works as a quick answer to a binary dine-in question; 반말 포장해 줘 is friends-only. The near alternative is 가져갈게요 ('I'll take it away') — the dividing line is who does the action: 포장해 주세요 asks staff to actively pack the item, while 가져갈게요 simply announces you're taking it; in practice both achieve takeout but 포장해 주세요 is more specific. Another alternative is 싸 주세요 ('wrap it up') — homey and natural for restaurant leftovers but slightly informal for a fresh café order. The English-speaker mistake is defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood at chains but 포장 is the fully native word, and 테이크아웃 컵 refers specifically to the cup type, not the whole transaction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood but the natural, fully Korean word is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Confusing 포장해 주세요 with dine-in — 포장해 주세요 is the takeout request; to eat in say 먹고 갈게요 or 여기서 먹을게요.
Using 포장 when you mean gift wrapping — in a café 포장 means 'pack to go'; for gift wrap specify 선물 포장해 주세요 so staff know the difference.

structuredNuance.t: 포장해(pack/wrap — verb 포장하다 + connective) + 주세요(please do for me). Literally 'please do the packaging for me' — really 'to go, please' or 'pack it up.' It covers both fresh café orders and restaurant doggy-bags.

Use at cafés when answering for-here-or-to-go, at bakeries, at restaurants to box leftovers. Plain -요 polite; clipped 포장이요 is even quicker; 반말 포장해 줘 with friends. Works for drinks, pastries, and restaurant food alike.

가져갈게요 ('I'll take it away') states your action but does not ask staff to pack anything — both mean takeout but 포장해 주세요 is the explicit pack-it-up request. 싸 주세요 ('wrap it') is homey/informal, natural for restaurant leftovers but slightly casual for a café. 테이크아웃 해 주세요 is understood at chains but 포장 is the fully native word.

포장 (包裝): 包 = wrap/envelop + 裝 = pack/outfit. Literally 'wrapping and packing.' The same 包 appears in 포함 (包含, inclusion) and 포기 has different characters. 포장도로 (paved road) uses 鋪裝, different 포 — do not confuse them.

Saying 테이크아웃 해 주세요 is understood but marks the loanword answer; the natural Korean is 포장해 주세요. Do not confuse 포장 (to-go packaging) with 선물 포장 (gift wrapping) — if you want gift wrap, specify: 선물 포장해 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is it?".
expressions.explanation: "How much is it?" — that is 얼마예요? (eolmayeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 얼마예요? ("How much is it?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: The standard polite price question to any shop staff
반말; to a friend or a very familiar person
Softer, slightly more polite and indirect variant
Extension: point with 이거 ('this one') at the specific item

examples.en: A: How much is it? / B: It's 4,500 won.
examples.note: Staff answer with 원입니다; the bare question works anywhere — no subject needed because the item is understood from context

examples.en: How much is this bread? There's no price tag.
examples.note: -네요 expresses a fresh observation ('I notice there's no tag'); 이 빵 names the item you're asking about

examples.en: How much all together? Do you take card?
examples.note: 다 해서 = 'all in, total'; a natural two-question checkout combo — ask total then payment method

expressions.nuance: 얼마예요? is one of the first and most essential phrases for any Korean learner — the everyday polite 'how much?' for any purchase. 얼마 = 'how much / how many (price-related)' + 예요 the polite copula. Plain -요 covers every store, market, and taxi; 반말 얼마야? is for friends. Softer is 얼마인가요? (indirect, slightly more formal). For a total: 다 해서 얼마예요? The dividing line between 얼마예요? and 얼마인가요? is degree of indirectness — same meaning. The top English-speaker spelling mistake is writing 얼마에요 — after the vowel-final word 얼마, the polite copula must be 예요, not 에요 (얼마에요 is a common but wrong romanization habit). A semantic trap: 얼마 있어요? means 'how much (money) do you have?' — not 'how much does it cost'; always use 얼마예요? for price. Korean prices use 만 (10,000) and 천 (1,000) units, so train your ear: 사천오백 = 4,500, 일만 이천 = 12,000.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 얼마에요 — after vowel-final 얼마 the polite copula is 예요, not 에요: correct form is 얼마예요.
Saying 얼마 있어요? to ask a price — that asks how much money someone has; the cost question is 얼마예요?.
Expecting digit-by-digit prices — Koreans use 만/천/백 units (사천오백 원 = 4,500 won); train your ear for these chunked number units.

structuredNuance.t: 얼마(how much/many — price) + 예요(polite copula 'is'). Literally 'How much is it?' — exactly what it says. The subject (the item) is dropped because it is understood; this short question works at any counter with no additional context.

Appropriate everywhere: cafés, markets, taxis, clothing stores, pharmacies. -요 polite for strangers and staff; 반말 얼마야? only with close friends. Pointing at the item while asking (이거 얼마예요?) avoids any ambiguity.

얼마인가요? is the indirect, slightly more formal version — same meaning but sounds less blunt. 가격이 어떻게 돼요? ('what is the price?') is a wordy alternative heard at fancier shops. For the total: 다 해서 얼마예요? is the standard checkout phrase.
얼마예요? → 이거 얼마예요? (point at item) → 다 해서 얼마예요? (total) → 할인되나요? (any discount?). 반말: 얼마야? Formal: 얼마인가요?
Writing 얼마에요 is the top spelling mistake — after the vowel-final 얼마 the copula is 예요, not 에요. Also do not say 얼마 있어요? for a price — that asks how much money you possess; the price question is 얼마예요?.

expressions.shortExplanation: 카드 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I pay by card?".
expressions.explanation: 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?) means "Can I pay by card?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 카드 돼요? ("Does card work?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — quick, natural way to ask if cards are accepted
반말 — to a friend, e.g. checking a shared cab
More formal — 결제/가능 is fuller and more polite

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay if I pay by card?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension — 카드로 names the method explicitly

examples.en: Can I pay by card?
examples.note: The complete two-word check — 카드 돼요? is a full, polite sentence; nothing more is needed

examples.ko: A: 현금이 없는데 카드 돼요? / B: 네, 카드 되세요.
examples.romanization: A: hyeongeumi eopsneunde kadeu dwaeyo? / B: ne, kadeu doeseyo.
examples.en: A: I don't have cash — does card work? / B: Yes, card is fine.
examples.note: Explaining why you're asking removes any awkwardness; the driver's 되세요 is the honorific-elevated response form

examples.en: Can I pay by card? Or could I even do a bank transfer?
examples.note: Real situation offering a backup: 계좌이체 (bank transfer) is increasingly used via KakaoBank/Toss for taxi fares

expressions.nuance: This asks whether the cab accepts card payment, customer-to-driver, in casual 존댓말. The verb is 되다 ('to work / to be possible'), not 할 수 있다 — 카드 돼요? literally means 'does card work (here)?', which is exactly how Koreans ask if something is accepted or feasible. The fuller polite form is 카드 결제 가능할까요?; 반말 is 카드 돼?. The most explicit alternative is 카드로 계산해도 돼요? ('may I settle up by card?'), but in the speed of a taxi exit the clipped 카드 돼요? is what you'll hear and use. Note: while all Korean taxis are legally required to accept cards, in practice some older drivers or certain cabs may have faulty readers — so this question remains relevant. The English-speaker's trap is mapping 'can I' onto 할 수 있다 and producing 카드 할 수 있어요?, which sounds like asking about your own ability to do card-related actions, not whether the service accepts it. Also watch spelling: the correct form is 돼요 (되+어요 contracted), not 되요, which is one of the most common native-speaker typos.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 카드 할 수 있어요? — that asks about your ability; acceptance/possibility uses 되다, so 카드 돼요?.
Using 에 with card: it's the method, so use 로 — 카드로 돼요? or 카드로 해도 돼요?, never 카드에.
Spelling/pronouncing it 되요 — the correct form is 돼요 (되+어요); 되요 is a common native typo to avoid.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 돼요? literally = 'does card become/work?'. 되다 in this usage means 'to be feasible / to be accepted'. The phrase skips the subject (카드로 결제가) and the verb complement (가능해요?) entirely — context (a taxi, end of ride) makes it unambiguous. This radical compression is normal in spoken Korean.

Customer-to-driver, ideally before you board or at the end of the ride. 존댓말 카드 돼요? is exactly right. For formal or written contexts use 카드 결제 가능한지 확인하고 싶습니다. 반말 카드 돼? only with a friend in a shared ride.

카드 돼요? vs 카드 받아요? — 받아요 ('do you receive') is understandable but less native; 돼요? is what Koreans actually say. vs 카드로 계산해도 돼요? — same meaning but longer and more explicit, suited when you want to be very clear or if the driver seems uncertain.
카드로 해도 돼요? (explicit method); 카드 결제 가능할까요? (formal); 카드 돼요, 현금도 돼요? (asking both at once); 삼성페이/카카오페이 돼요? (asking about mobile pay apps).

Saying 카드 할 수 있어요? — this asks about your own ability, not the service's acceptance. The idiom uses 되다: 카드 돼요?. Also, the most common spelling error even among native speakers: 되요 is wrong; always write 돼요 (되+어요 contracted).

expressions.shortExplanation: 길을 잃었어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm lost.".
expressions.explanation: 길을 잃었어요 (gireul ireosseoyo) = "I'm lost.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 길을 잃었어요 ("I'm lost (lit. I lost the road)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'm lost (lit. I lost the road)
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a passerby, shop staff, or anyone who can help
반말 to a friend or family on the phone
-어버리다 stresses the loss is total and you feel helpless

usagePhrases.en: It's my first time here, so I don't really know the way
usagePhrases.note: Softer framing that explains why you're lost without sounding panicked

examples.ko: 저… 실례지만 길을 잃었어요. 혹시 도와주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: jeo… sillyejiman gireul ireosseoyo. hoksi dowajusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: Um… excuse me, I'm lost. Is there any chance you could help?
examples.note: Polite opener to a stranger; 실례지만 ('excuse me for bothering you') is the ideal softener before admitting you're lost

examples.ko: A: 왜 이렇게 늦어? / B: 미안, 길을 잃었어. 지금 찾아가고 있어.
examples.romanization: A: wae ireoke neujeo? / B: mian, gireul ireosseo. jigeum chajagago isseo.
examples.en: A: Why are you so late? / B: Sorry, I got lost. I'm finding my way now.
examples.note: 반말 A/B exchange; 찾아가다 = 'to make one's way to a place'

examples.ko: 지하철역에서 나왔는데 길을 잃었어요. 이 주소 어떻게 가요?
examples.romanization: jihacheoryeogeseo nawanneunde gireul ireosseoyo. i juso eotteoke gayo?
examples.en: I came out of the subway station and got lost. How do I get to this address?
examples.note: Real situation: show the address on your phone while asking; 어떻게 가요? = 'how do I get there?'

expressions.nuance: 길을 잃었어요 literally says 'I lost the road' — 길 (road/way) is the object, so it takes the object marker 을, and 잃다 (to lose) is conjugated in the past because the loss has already happened. This particle is crucial: it is 길을 잃다, never 길이 잃다 or 길에 잃다. Adding the completive suffix -어버리다 (길을 잃어버렸어요) intensifies the sense of hopelessness, as if you've truly wandered into nowhere and can't recover on your own. The nearest alternative, 여기가 어디예요? ('where is this?'), only asks your location — it doesn't explain your predicament or invite extended help; fluent speakers often combine both in one breath: 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어디예요? The follow-up questions — 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요? ('is there a subway station nearby?') or 이 주소 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to this address?') — are what unlock practical help. English speakers often say 나는 잃어버렸어요 (no object — 'I lost something' with nothing named) or mark 길 with the wrong particle, such as 길이, because in English 'I' is the subject; in Korean, 길 (the road) is the grammatical object of 잃다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나는 잃어버렸어요 with no object.
잃어버리다 needs an object. To mean 'I'm lost', say what was lost — the way: 길을 잃었어요.
Using the wrong particle: 길이 잃었어요 or 길에 잃었어요.
잃다 takes the object marker. It must be 길을 잃었어요.
Saying 길을 잊었어요.
잊다 is 'to forget'; 잃다 is 'to lose'. Being lost is 길을 잃었어요, not 잊었어요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I lost the road' (길을 잃다). Korean frames being lost as having lost your path — 길 is the object with 을, not the subject. The past tense 잃었어요 reflects that the losing already happened, which is how Korean describes a current state that resulted from a past action.

존댓말 잃었어요 is for any stranger or helper. 반말 잃었어 is for friends or family on the phone. Soften the approach to a stranger with 저기요 (excuse me) or 실례지만 before launching into 길을 잃었어요 — Korean conversation openers matter, even in distress.

여기가 어디예요? only asks where you are — a single factual question. 길을 잃었어요 describes your whole situation and signals you need sustained help. Experienced Korean speakers often pair both: 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어디예요? for the most complete plea.
길을 잃었어 (반말) → 길을 잃었어요 (존댓말) → 길을 잃어버렸어요 (completive, more helpless). The -어버리다 version is the most emotionally expressive and is common in speech.

Saying 나는 잃어버렸어요 with no object leaves Koreans wondering what you lost. You must keep 길을 as the object. Also, 잊었어요 (from 잊다 'to forget') is a different word entirely — 'I forgot the road' is not 'I got lost'.

examples.ko: A: 한국어를 잘 못해서요. 좀 천천히 말해 주실 수 있어요? / B: 아, 그러세요! 이렇게요.
examples.romanization: A: hangugeoreul jal motaeseoyo. jom cheoncheonhi malhae jusil su isseoyo? / B: a, geureoseyo! ireokeyo.
examples.en: A: My Korean isn't great — could you speak a bit slowly? / B: Oh, of course! Like this?
examples.note: identifying yourself as a learner almost always triggers warmth and patience — most Koreans will happily slow down and even adjust their vocabulary

examples.ko: 죄송하지만 조금만 더 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요? 잘 못 알아들어서요.
examples.romanization: joesonghajiman jogeumman deo cheoncheonhi malsseumhae jusigesseoyo? jal mot aradeureoseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, could you speak just a bit more slowly? I didn't quite catch it.
examples.note: '잘 못 알아듣다' (can't quite catch/hear) is the most natural reason to give — 조금만 더 (just a little more) signals you're almost there, not completely lost

expressions.nuance: 천천히 is the natural word for 'at a slow/leisurely pace' — it covers walking, eating, and speaking alike. The benefactive 주세요 turns it from a statement into 'please do it for me'. To a friend, 천천히 말해 줘; to a stranger or superior, 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요? (말씀하다 = the honorific verb for speaking). Adding 조금/조금만 ('a little/just a little') makes it sound less demanding, as though you're almost keeping up. The classic Korean-language learner trap is using 느리게 말해 주세요 — 느리다 means slow in the sense of low-speed or sluggish (a slow car, slow internet), and 느리게 말하다 suggests dragging out words awkwardly rather than pacing naturally. Mentioning you're still learning Korean ('한국어 공부 중이라서요') typically generates extra warmth and patience from native speakers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '느리게 말해 주세요'.
느리다 means low-speed/sluggish and sounds off for speech pace. The natural word is 천천히: '천천히 말해 주세요.'
Dropping 주세요: '천천히 말해요'.
Without the benefactive it sounds flat or like a statement. Keep '말해 주세요' so it's a request done for you.
Using plain 말해 to a stranger or elder.
That's curt/반말. Raise it: '천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?' with the honorific 말씀하다.

structuredNuance.t: 천천히 말해 주세요 = 'slowly + speak + give-to-me (please)'. 천천히 covers all activities done at a relaxed pace — walking, eating, speaking. The benefactive 주세요 makes it 'please do this FOR me', not a description or command.

Whenever someone speaks too fast to follow — on the phone, at a counter, in conversation, in class. Say it early, not after twenty seconds of nodding. 말해 주세요 (존댓말) for anyone; 말씀해 주시겠어요? (격식) for an elder, a teacher, or formal phone service. Including a self-disclosure ('한국어가 서툴러서요') almost always improves the response.

천천히 말해 주세요 vs. 느리게 말해 주세요: 느리다 = low-speed/sluggish (cars, internet, people being slow at tasks) — applied to speech it sounds odd or slightly insulting, as if you're calling them sluggish. Use 천천히, always. vs. 다시 한번 말해 주세요: for repeating what was said, not for changing speaking pace.
천천히 말해 줘 (반말) → 천천히 말해 주세요 (기본 존댓말) → 조금만 더 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요? (격식). Pairing with '잘 못 알아들어서요' or '한국어를 잘 못해서요' makes any form more effective.

느리게 말해 주세요 is the classic wrong choice — 느리다 means sluggish/slow-in-speed, not 'at a relaxed conversational pace'. Use 천천히. Also, dropping 주세요 and saying just '천천히 말해요' sounds like a flat observation or a command rather than a polite benefactive request.

usagePhrases.note: polite; honest admission of uncertainty — works with anyone

examples.note: expressing uncertainty about a choice, then proposing collaborative review — shows it can open a discussion

expressions.nuance: 잘 모르겠어요 is the natural, polite 'I'm not sure / I honestly don't know', used with anyone. Two things make it different from the bare 몰라요: first, 잘 ('well / properly') softens and naturalizes the admission — 'I don't really know well' is gentler than a flat 'I don't know'; second, the -겠- modal adds a layer of hedging or conjecture ('I guess I don't know'), making 모르겠어요 more polite and tentative than 몰라요. Together, 잘 모르겠어요 is the default softened 'I'm uncertain'. Casual is 잘 모르겠어; formal is 잘 모르겠습니다. The nearest alternative is 글쎄요 — the line: 잘 모르겠어요 genuinely reports lack of knowledge or certainty, while 글쎄요 is attitudinal hedging. Important: for not knowing a person (acquaintance), use 잘 몰라요 (present, factual), not 모르겠어요 — the -겠- marks inference or uncertainty, not factual ignorance of people.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering with a flat 몰라요 — it can sound blunt/cold; soften to 잘 모르겠어요.
Using 잘 모르겠어요 for 'I don't know a person' — for that use (잘) 몰라요; 모르겠어요 is about uncertainty/can't-tell.
Dropping 잘 in polite refusals of help — 잘 모르겠어요 is gentler than 모르겠어요 alone.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 잘(well/properly) 모르겠어요(I don't seem to know) → 실제 뜻: 'I'm not really sure'. 두 가지 완화 장치: 잘 (부드럽게 만들기) + -겠- (추측/유보 표시). 이 둘 덕분에 bare 몰라요보다 훨씬 공손하다.
존댓말: 잘 모르겠어요 (누구에게나 자연스럽다). 반말: 잘 모르겠어. 격식: 잘 모르겠습니다. 특히 손님, 상사, 선생님에게 모른다고 할 때 bare 몰라요 대신 잘 모르겠어요나 잘 모르겠습니다를 써야 예의 바르다.

잘 모르겠어요 vs 글쎄요: 잘 모르겠어요 = honest report of lacking knowledge or certainty; 글쎄요 = noncommittal hedging (might know but is unsure whether to commit). 잘 모르겠어요 vs 몰라요: 몰라요 is blunter and can sound cold to strangers or superiors; 잘 모르겠어요 is softer.
기본: 잘 모르겠어요. 강조: 솔직히 잘 모르겠어요 ('honestly I'm not sure'). 해결책 추가: 잘 모르겠어요, 알아볼게요 ('not sure, let me find out'). 과거: 그때는 잘 몰랐어요 ('I didn't know at the time' — past uses 몰랐다).

1) Bare 몰라요 as a reply — it can sound blunt or cold, especially to someone you should be polite to; always soften to 잘 모르겠어요. 2) 잘 모르겠어요 for 'I don't know a person' — for not knowing a person use 잘 몰라요 (factual present); 모르겠어요 implies inference. 3) Dropping 잘 in polite contexts — 모르겠어요 alone is shorter but less warm; keep 잘 with strangers or seniors.

examples.romanization: A: eoseo oseyo. / B: yeyakaesseoyo. bakjiyeongieyo.

examples.ko: 이틀 전에 전화로 예약했는데, 확인 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: iteul jeone jeonhwaro yeyakaenneunde, hwagin jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: I booked by phone two days ago — could you check, please?

expressions.nuance: 예약했어요 means 'I already made a reservation' — the past tense of 예약하다 signals that the booking exists, so staff know not to treat you as a walk-in. Register is neutral-polite 존댓말; raise it to 예약했습니다 at formal desks, or drop to 예약했어 with friends. The trailing 예약했는데요 ('I booked...') is softer because it leaves a gap the clerk fills, while 예약했어요 is a complete assertion. The important vocabulary contrast: hotels, restaurants, and trains use 예약, while arranging to meet a person (an appointment) uses 약속 — confusing the two is the classic mistake. Do not say the English-loan 'reservation 있어요'; the Korean noun is 예약. And never swap future 예약할게요 ('I'll book now') for this past-tense expression when you mean the booking already exists.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약속했어요 to mean 'I have a reservation' — 약속 is a promise/appointment between people, not a room booking. Use 예약했어요 for hotels, restaurants, tickets.
예약했어요.
Using present 예약해요 when you mean it's already done. Korean needs the past -했어요 to show the booking exists. 예약했어요.
예약했어요.
Saying 예약할게요 at the desk thinking it confirms your booking — that means 'I'll book now'. To state an existing booking, use the past 예약했어요.
예약했어요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I reserved (it, already)' — the past tense -했어요 is load-bearing: it tells the clerk that the booking exists. Saying the present 예약해요 or the future 예약할게요 instead completely changes what you are communicating.

Neutral-polite (존댓말). Use at any service counter — hotel, restaurant, clinic, airline — where a booking was made ahead of time. 예약했습니다 is the 격식 upgrade for business trips or formal settings. 예약했어 is 반말 for friends only.

예약했는데요 contains the same past-tense assertion but trails off so the clerk takes the next action (looking it up). 예약 있어요 ('I have a booking', noun + 있다) is also natural but slightly less assertive than the verb form. Use 예약했어요 as a confident opener, 예약했는데요 when you want them to search first.

Name: [이름]으로 예약했어요 — 으로 marks whose name the reservation is under, not the destination. Channel: 온라인으로 예약했어요 / 전화로 예약했어요 / 앱으로 예약했어요 — naming how you booked often speeds up the lookup. Party size: 두 명으로 예약했어요 — 으로 again, here meaning 'for two'. At a restaurant, 4인으로 예약했어요 and 2인 2실로 예약했어요 (two rooms for two) are common patterns. All use the same structure: [detail]으로 예약했어요.

The biggest trap is 약속했어요 — 약속 is a promise or social appointment between people, not a service booking. Hotel/restaurant/ticket reservations always use 예약. A second trap: using the present or future form when the booking already exists. It must be past tense: 예약했어요.

expressions.explanation: 아파요 (apayo) means "I'm sick. / It hurts.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 아파요 ("I'm sick / It hurts"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

반말 to a friend or family member

Name the body part + 가/이 (subject marker) + 아파요 — the standard template for all body-part pain

examples.en: I'm feeling a bit sick. Where is the pharmacy?
examples.note: Bare statement paired with the natural follow-up; 좀 softens the admission and 약국이 어디예요? is the first practical step for mild illness

examples.ko: A: 왜 그래? / B: 어제부터 머리가 너무 아파. 열도 있는 것 같아.
examples.romanization: A: wae geurae? / B: eojebuteo meoriga neomu apa. yeoldo inneun geot gata.
examples.en: A: What's wrong? / B: My head has been really hurting since yesterday. I think I have a fever too.
examples.note: 반말 A/B; 어제부터 = 'since yesterday'; 열이 있다 = 'to have a fever' — the full clinical picture in two sentences

examples.ko: 배가 너무 아파요. 토할 것 같아요. 병원에 가야 할까요?
examples.romanization: baega neomu apayo. tohal geot gatayo. byeongwone gaya halkkayo?
examples.en: My stomach really hurts. I feel like throwing up. Should I go to a doctor?
examples.note: Real scene; 토할 것 같다 = 'feel like vomiting'; 병원에 가야 할까요? = 'should I go to the hospital?' — a full self-triage question

expressions.nuance: 아파요 is the polite conjugation of 아프다, a single Korean adjective that covers both 'to be in pain' and 'to be sick/ill' — one word handles what English splits between 'hurt' and 'sick'. To name the body part that hurts, that part becomes the grammatical subject with 가/이: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 무릎이 아파요. Note the irregular conjugation: 아프다 has a ㅡ-irregular stem; 아프 + 아요 → the ㅡ drops → 아파요, not 아프아요. The dividing line from 다쳤어요 is cause and type: 아프다 = pain or illness from any source (infection, stomachache, headache, muscle soreness); 다치다 = physical injury from an external accident (a fall, a cut, a collision). Both can describe the same body part at the same time: 넘어져서 무릎을 다쳤어요. 무릎이 아파요 ('I fell and hurt my knee; my knee hurts'). The follow-up toolkit: 병원에 가야 해요 ('I need to go to a clinic'), 약국이 어디예요? ('where's the pharmacy?'), 진통제 주세요 ('please give me painkillers'). English speakers say 배를 아파요 (object marker 를 on the body part) — but 아프다 is an adjective and the painful body part is its subject: 배가 아파요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the body part with 을/를: 배를 아파요.
The hurting part is the subject of 아프다: 배가 아파요.
Writing 아프요 instead of 아파요.
아프다 is a ㅡ-irregular: 아프 + 아요 → 아파요.
Using 아파요 for an accident injury.
For a wound from a fall or cut, use 다쳤어요; 아파요 is general pain/illness.

structuredNuance.t: 아파요 = polite form of 아프다, literally 'am painful/sick'. It covers both 'it hurts' and 'I'm sick' — Korean does not split these meanings. The body part that hurts is the subject with 가/이 (배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요), not the object.

존댓말 아파요 to any stranger, medical staff, or pharmacist. 반말 아파 to friends and family. 격식 아픕니다 on medical forms or formal reports. At a 119 call or emergency, describe the body part and severity: 가슴이 너무 아파요 ('my chest hurts a lot') tells the dispatcher it may be cardiac.

아프다 (pain or illness from any cause: cold, stomachache, injury pain) vs 다치다 (physical injury from an accident). A headache is 머리가 아파요. A bruise from a fall is 다쳤어요. The pain FROM a bruise is 아파요. You need both words; one describes the injury event, the other describes the sensation.
아프다 → 아파요 (존댓말) → 아파 (반말) → 아픕니다 (격식). With body parts: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 다리가 아파요. The ㅡ drops in conjugation: 아프 + 아요 → 아파요.

The most common error is 배를 아파요 — treating the body part as an object with 를. But 아프다 is an adjective (descriptive verb) and the aching part is its subject: 배가 아파요. Also, 아프요 (skipping the irregular contraction) is wrong — the correct form is 아파요.

expressions.nuance: ㅋㅋ is the texted shape of the snicker 크크/큭큭 (ㅋ is the consonant for the 'k' giggle), and among Korean 20-30s it is the default 'I'm-relaxed-and-friendly' marker — even more than a real laugh, it signals you're at ease, so chats feel cold without it. Length is meaning: ㅋㅋ is a polite chuckle, ㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋ is genuine laughter, and you stretch the string to match how funny something is (it helps that ㅋ sits under one key, so spamming it is effortless). Its near-rival ㅎㅎ is the softer cousin (a smile, not a laugh), so swapping them shifts tone — ㅋㅋ is funny, ㅎㅎ is gentle/warm. The sharp English-speaker pitfall is the lone ㅋ: in English a solo 'lol' is harmless, but a single ㅋ (or ㅋ.. / ㅋ?) can read as cold, sarcastic, even passive-aggressive — the texting equivalent of a flat 'ha,' so never go below ㅋㅋ. And keep all of it out of messages to a boss, professor, or stranger, where laughter letters look unserious; there you write plain-polite sentences with no ㅋ at all.

Literally just a written laugh sound (the consonant ㅋ repeated). ㅎㅎ is the nearest relative: ㅋㅋ = amused/laughing, ㅎㅎ = smiling/softening (warm, gentle). expressions.nuance: ㅎㅎ comes from the soft breathy chuckle 흐흐/하하 (ㅎ is the 'h' breath), and its real job in Korean chat is not 'this is funny' but 'I'm being warm and gentle.' That is the sharp line vs its rival ㅋㅋ: ㅋㅋ = amused/laughing, ㅎㅎ = smiling/softening. Because it reads as polite rather than rowdy, Koreans sprinkle it onto otherwise bare replies (넵 ㅎㅎ, 알겠습니다 ㅎㅎ) so they don't land as curt — and it slips into friendly-coworker messages where ㅋㅋ would feel too loose. A subtler trap is the lone ㅎ: just like a single ㅋ, one bare ㅎ or 'ㅎ...' can read as a tight, awkward, even cynical smile, so keep it to at least ㅎㅎ. And in a strictly formal note to a boss or stranger, still drop it; 'warmer than ㅋㅋ' does not mean 'formal-safe.'

expressions.nuance: ㅇㅇ is the texted form of 응 (eung, casual 'yeah'), doubled to 응응, so it carries pure banmal — the informal register you'd use with people you speak 반말 to out loud. That register IS the meaning: it broadcasts 'we're equals/close.' Its near-neighbor is the polite 네/넵, and the gap between them is exactly the politeness gap, which is why the English-speaker pitfall is severe: English 'yeah' is fine to almost anyone, but firing ㅇㅇ at a boss, professor, or older stranger skips every layer of politeness and reads as blunt, even disrespectful — like grunting 'uh-huh' at a superior. The safe upgrade ladder for seniors is 네 (polite) → 넵 (cheerful-polite) → 네네 (warm). Don't confuse ㅇㅇ (yes/agreement, from 응응) with ㅇㅋ (okay/got it, from 오케이): you ANSWER a yes/no question with ㅇㅇ, but you CONFIRM an instruction with ㅇㅋ. And length carries warmth — a bare ㅇㅇ to a friend who's clearly excited can read as flat, even reluctant, so match their energy with ㅇㅇㅇㅇ or 응응!!; worse, a single curt ㅇ alone can feel like an annoyed 'k.'

expressions.nuance: ㄴㄴ comes from the doubled English-borrowed 노노 ('no-no'), and the doubling is what makes it playful and soft rather than a hard rejection — it lands like 'nah' or 'nope,' not a stern 'No.' Its polite counterparts are 아니요 / 아니에요 (and very formal 아닙니다), and the whole point of ㄴㄴ is that it lives only in the casual zone with friends and peers. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold. First, register: 'nope' feels harmless in English to anyone, but ㄴㄴ to a boss or older stranger is too flip and can read as dismissive, so soften to 아니요/아닙니다 there. Second, watch the bluntness of a bare ㄴㄴ even among friends — Koreans usually cushion a refusal with a reason (ㄴㄴ 나 내일 출근이라…) because a naked 'no' can feel abrupt, and English speakers tend to under-cushion. Pair ㄴㄴ with a quick reason or a ㅠ and it stays warm. Note too that the doubling is softening, not intensifying: for a strong 'absolutely not' you say 절대 아니야, not just more ㄴ. And ㄴㄴ refuses or corrects — to decline an OFFER especially kindly, ㄴㄴ 괜찮아 reads warmer than a bare ㄴㄴ.

Literally 'no-no' (two negations). But the repetition does NOT mean a stronger or double no — it's a softener that makes a single refusal sound casual and unfussy. Real meaning: a relaxed 'nope,' not an emphatic 'no no!'

Casual only: friends and peers. Too flip for anyone senior — to a boss, professor, or older stranger it reads as dismissive. Polite replacements: 아니요 / 아니에요 (polite), 아닙니다 (formal). In a work chat, decline with 아니요 plus a reason, never ㄴㄴ.

ㄴㄴ vs 아니요/아닙니다 is purely the politeness gap — same 'no,' different register. For an emphatic refusal, ㄴㄴ is the wrong tool entirely: use 절대 아니야 (banmal) or 절대 아닙니다 (formal). To decline an offer kindly, 아니야 괜찮아 / 괜찮아요 reads softer than a bare ㄴㄴ.
ㄴ (curt) → ㄴㄴ (default nah) → ㄴㄴㄴ (playful 'nope nope'). Cushioned forms are the natural ones: ㄴㄴ 괜찮아, ㄴㄴ 나 ~라서, ㄴㄴㅠ. Polite escalations replace it wholesale: 아니요 → 아닙니다 → 절대 아닙니다.

Twofold. (1) Register: 'nope' is harmless to anyone in English, but ㄴㄴ up the hierarchy reads as dismissive — soften to 아니요/아닙니다. (2) Bluntness: a bare ㄴㄴ even to friends can feel abrupt; Koreans add a reason (ㄴㄴ 나 ~라서). Don't read the doubling as emphatic — for 'absolutely not' say 절대 아니야.

expressions.nuance: ㄱㄱ is the texted form of 고고, Korea's reading of English 'go-go,' and it spread from gaming ('go go!' to launch a match) into all of casual life: heading out, ordering food, starting a task, kicking off a plan. It's energetic and breezy — closer to 'let's GO / let's do this' than a neutral 'okay.' The nearest sober alternatives are 가자 (let's go) and the work-safe 바로 진행하겠습니다 (I'll proceed right away). The big English-speaker pitfall is misreading the letters: ㄱㄱ is 고고 (go-go = let's go), NOT 'good good' — and especially NOT gaming's English 'gg = good game' (which Koreans write out as 'gg' or say 잘 쳤어, never ㄱㄱ); a learner who sees the letters and thinks 'good game / good job' will read the message backwards. Second pitfall is register/hype mismatch: that gamer energy is fun with friends but reads as flippant to a boss, so don't ㄱㄱ a superior's task request — write 바로 시작하겠습니다 instead. Third, it's a call to ACT, not a plain 'yes': use it for proposals to do something, not to answer a factual yes/no (that's ㅇㅇ). It loves to ride after ㅇㅋ or ㅇㅇ to seal a decision.

expressions.nuance: ㅈㅅ is the initials of 죄송 (Sino-Korean 罪悚, literally 'sin + dread/fear' — i.e. 'I feel the weight of having done wrong'), the same word inside the full apology 죄송합니다/죄송해요. Shrinking that heavy word to two consonants is exactly what makes it casual: it deflates the seriousness into a light 'my bad,' fit only for trivial slips among friends — a late text, the wrong cup, a small bump. Its register-mates are 미안 (banmal sorry, also casual) and the proper 죄송합니다 (formal). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is thinking 'sorry is sorry' and using ㅈㅅ for anything real or to anyone senior: because the abbreviation strips out all gravity, sending ㅈㅅ to a boss, professor, or older person — or for an actual mistake — reads as careless and even insulting, like mumbling 'my bad' for breaking something important. For those, type the full 죄송합니다 (very formal) or 죄송해요 (polite). Note 미안 vs 죄송: 미안 is for equals/juniors, 죄송 outranks it in politeness, so even the full 미안해 wouldn't suit a boss. And the FORM itself signals SIZE — a two-letter ㅈㅅ inherently says 'this is small,' so it's wrong for anything that genuinely matters; for a real-but-casual apology, type at least 미안해/정말 미안해, not ㅈㅅ.

expressions.nuance: ㅊㅋ is the initials of 축하 (Sino-Korean 祝賀, 'celebrate + congratulate'), the noun inside 축하해 (banmal), 축하해요 (polite), and 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble-formal, with 드리다 'to give up to someone'). As an abbreviation it's bright and offhand — perfect for friends celebrating jobs, birthdays, moves, exams, or a new relationship. The English-speaker pitfall is the one that bites every abbreviation here: 'congrats' feels universally friendly in English, but ㅊㅋ to someone you respect (a boss, professor, older relative) can read as too breezy for a real milestone — the curt letters undercut the sincerity. For them, write it out and go UP a level with the humble form 축하드려요/축하드립니다, which literally offers the congratulations up to them. A subtler pitfall: don't attach ㅊㅋ to genuinely heavy life events even spelled-as-slang (a wedding, a 60th birthday, a new baby) — those want full, warm sentences, not abbreviations. And note the politeness climb isn't just 해요: superiors expect 드리다, the humble 'give upward,' which a plain 축하해요 doesn't supply — for a boss's promotion, 승진 축하드립니다 lands right where 축하해요 sounds flat.

Literally just the two initials of 축하 ('congratulation'). Real meaning is a quick, cheerful 'congrats!' — but the very shortness encodes 'this is a light, casual cheer.' For a sincere, weighty congratulation the abbreviation can't carry the warmth; the spelled-out humble form does.

Casual, friends and peers, for everyday good news. Too breezy for someone you respect — to a boss, professor, or older relative the curt letters undercut sincerity. Write it out, and for seniors climb to the HUMBLE form 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 (offers the congratulations upward), not just 축하해요.

The ladder is one word at four heights: ㅊㅋ (slang) → 축하해 (banmal) → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble-formal). The jump that matters for seniors is to 드리다 — 축하해요 is merely polite, while 축하드립니다 humbly gives the congratulations up to them.
ㅊㅋ → ㅊㅋㅊㅋ (warmer) → 헐 ㅊㅋㅊㅋㅋ (excited). Slot after the occasion: 생일 ㅊㅋ, 졸업 ㅊㅋ, 합격 ㅊㅋ. Combo: ㅊㅋㅊㅋ 부럽다 (congrats + 'jealous,' a friendly compliment). Upward: 승진 축하드려요 / 진심으로 축하드립니다.

'Congrats' is universally friendly in English, but ㅊㅋ to someone you respect reads as too breezy for a real milestone. Worse, even spelled-out slang is thin for heavy events (weddings, elders' big birthdays, a new baby) — those need full warm sentences. Fix: 축하드립니다 for seniors; whole sentences for big occasions.

expressions.nuance: ㅠㅠ is pure visual: the Korean vowel letter ㅠ is reused as a picture of two eyes with tears streaming down (its twin ㅜㅜ is the same face with eyes scrunched), so it's read with the EYES, not pronounced — there's no spoken 'yuyu.' It's one of the most common feeling-markers in Korean chat, and crucially its range runs from genuine sadness all the way to playful, exaggerated 'aw man / waaah' whining; more letters = more drama, often tongue-in-cheek. The English-speaker pitfalls are mostly mechanical and tonal. Mechanically: Koreans attach it with NO space, fused to the last word (취소됐어ㅠㅠ), where English would float an emoji after a space — a gap (휴무래 ㅠㅠ) reads slightly off. Tonally: because it's text and a little cute, English speakers sometimes drop it into semi-professional messages thinking it's neutral like 🙁 — but in a formal or work note it reads as childish and unprofessional, so leave it for friends and dating partners; to a boss, put the feeling in words (아쉽네요/속상하네요) instead. And don't read every ㅠㅠ as real tears; very often it's just light 'ugh, bummer.' Its blends ㅋㅋㅠㅠ / ㅎㅠ even mix laughing-while-crying ('I'm dying').

ㅜㅜ is the same teary face, eyes scrunched (fully interchangeable). Mixed forms blend emotions: ㅋㅋㅠㅠ / ㅎㅠ = laughing-while-crying ('I'm dying'). For a plain neutral sad tone in polite text you wouldn't use any of these — you'd write 아쉬워요 / 속상해요.

expressions.nuance: ㄹㅇ is the consonant skeleton of 리얼, Korea's borrowing of English 'real,' and it works two ways: as a reply it's emphatic agreement ('for real / no joke / facts'), and dropped inside a sentence it's an intensifier meaning 'genuinely/seriously' (이거 ㄹㅇ 웃겨 = 'this is genuinely funny'). It's very current 20-30s slang, at home in friend chats and comments, and frequently fused with ㅋㅋ as ㄹㅇㅋㅋ. Its native-Korean cousins are 진짜 and 정말 ('really/truly'), which carry the same meaning but sound a notch less slangy — and those are what you'd upgrade to in polite contexts (진짜요/정말요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't decode ㄹㅇ as 'right now' or any English-acronym guess — it's strictly '리얼/real (for real).' Second, ㄹㅇ overlaps heavily with the agreement word ㅇㅈ (인정, 'agreed'), but they aren't identical: ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's TRUE,' while ㅇㅈ concedes 'I ADMIT/agree' — close enough to stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but ㄹㅇ also works as a standalone intensifier where ㅇㅈ can't. And keep it casual: this is young-person slang, so with seniors say 진짜요/정말요, not ㄹㅇ. Note too that position rewrites the meaning — bare ㄹㅇ is 'true,' ㄹㅇ? is 'seriously?!', and mid-sentence ㄹㅇ is just 'really' — so the same two letters do three different jobs.

structuredNuance.t: ㄹㅇ is the consonant skeleton of 리얼 (Korea's borrowing of 'real'). It works two ways: as a reply, emphatic agreement ('for real / no joke / facts'); inside a sentence, an intensifier meaning 'genuinely/seriously' (이거 ㄹㅇ 웃겨 = 'genuinely funny'). Very current 20-30s slang.

Literally 'real' (리얼) reduced to two consonants. Real meaning splits by position: standalone it's 'for real / that's true,' a strong yes; with ? it's 'seriously?!'; mid-sentence it's just 'really/genuinely.' Same letters, three jobs — position tells you which.

Casual, young, friend chats and online comments. Not for work or formal messages — it's distinctly slangy and reads as too loose to a senior. Polite upgrades that mean the same thing: 진짜요 / 정말요 ('really'), 맞아요 ('that's right') for the agreement sense.

Native cousins 진짜/정말 mean the same but sound less slangy (and are the polite path: 진짜요/정말요). vs ㅇㅈ (인정): ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's TRUE,' ㅇㅈ concedes 'I ADMIT/agree.' They stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ), but only ㄹㅇ works as a plain mid-sentence intensifier.
ㄹㅇ (default) → ㄹㅇㅋㅋ (agree + laugh) → ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ (double emphasis) → ㄹㅇ? (surprised). As intensifier: 이거 ㄹㅇ 맛있음, ㄹㅇ 대박. Spelled out: 리얼? / 리얼루 (playful). Polite swap: 진짜요 / 정말요.

(1) Don't decode ㄹㅇ as 'right now' or any English acronym — it's 리얼/real. (2) Don't treat it as identical to ㅇㅈ — ㄹㅇ is a truth-claim/intensifier, ㅇㅈ is agreement/admission; they pair but aren't swappable everywhere. (3) Keep it out of formal chats — use 진짜요/정말요 with seniors.

expressions.nuance: ㅂㅂ is the consonant frame of 바이바이, Korea's reading of English 'bye-bye,' so it's a borrowed-word goodbye that feels breezy and a touch cute — fine for closing a casual chat with friends, peers, or a dating partner. Its register-mates run from the neutral 잘 가 / 또 봐 (banmal 'see ya') up to the polite parting set 들어가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 / 안녕히 가세요. The English-speaker pitfall is closing UP with it: in English 'bye!' ends a message to almost anyone, but ㅂㅂ to a boss, professor, or stranger reads as too informal to sign off a polite exchange — there you want a proper closing like 들어가세요 (go in well / take care) or, in a work context, 수고하셨습니다 (thank you for your hard work). A finer point most learners miss: Korean goodbyes split by who is leaving — 안녕히 가세요 to the person LEAVING, 안녕히 계세요 to the person STAYING — a distinction English's single 'bye' erases. ㅂㅂ sidesteps that only because it's casual; the moment you go polite, you must pick the right one. And note ㅂㅂ is just a sign-off, not a promise to meet — for a real next plan say 또 봐 / 담에 봐. One more trap: don't read the doubled letters as 'see you LATER (a set plan)'; the borrowed 바이바이 only ends the chat — it commits to nothing.

structuredNuance.t: ㅂㅂ is the consonant frame of 바이바이, Korea's reading of English 'bye-bye' — a breezy, slightly cute goodbye to end a chat. It closes a conversation casually; it does not by itself promise a next meeting.

Literally 'bye-bye' (a borrowed English word). Real use: a quick chat sign-off among friends, nothing more — it carries no warmth-of-promise and no politeness. The cuteness comes from the doubled borrowed sound, not from any added meaning.

Casual only: friends, peers, dating partners. Too informal to close a polite exchange — to a boss, professor, or stranger, end with a proper closing instead: 들어가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 / 안녕히 가세요, or in a work chat 수고하셨습니다 ('thank you for your hard work').

Banmal siblings: 잘 가 / 또 봐 ('see ya'). Polite set splits by who moves — 안녕히 가세요 to the one LEAVING, 안녕히 계세요 to the one STAYING — a split English 'bye' erases. ㅂㅂ dodges it only by being casual; once polite, you must pick the right one. For 'see you again,' 또 봐/담에 봐, not ㅂㅂ.
ㅂㅂ → ㅂㅂ! (cheerful) → ㅂㅂ2 ('bye-bye'). With wrap-up lead-ins: 그럼 ㅂㅂ, 나 갈게 ㅂㅂ. Caring combos: ㅂㅂ 조심히 가, ㅂㅂ 잘 자. Spelled out: 바이 / 바이바이. Polite replacements: 들어가세요 / 수고하셨습니다.

Closing UP with it. English 'bye!' ends a message to anyone; ㅂㅂ to a senior is too informal — use 들어가세요 / 수고하셨습니다. And don't read ㅂㅂ as 'see you (a definite plan)' — it's only a sign-off; confirm a next meeting with 또 봐 / 담에 봐 or by spelling the plan out.

expressions.nuance: ㅇㅈ is the consonant frame of 인정 (Sino-Korean 認定, 'recognize + fix/settle'), literally 'to acknowledge/admit something as so' — and as slang it became young Koreans' punchy way to say 'agreed, that's facts.' Its polite equivalents are 맞아요 ('that's right'), 동의해요 ('I agree'), and very formal 동의합니다, which are what you'd use with seniors. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the literal core is 'acknowledge/admit,' so beyond cheerful agreement it can carry a faint flavor of conceding a point ('okay, I'll grant you that') — and the bare-noun 인정 even works as a real verb (그 실수는 인정 = 'I admit that mistake'); reading it as only upbeat 'yes!' misses that edge. Second, don't blur it with ㄹㅇ: ㅇㅈ = 'I agree/admit (인정),' a stance toward what you said; ㄹㅇ = 'for real/genuinely (리얼),' a claim about truth that can also intensify a sentence. They pair (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but aren't swappable everywhere. As always, keep ㅇㅈ casual — to a boss write 맞습니다 / 동의합니다. And mind the function: ㅇㅈ endorses an OPINION/take, so it fits 'good song / weekdays are better' — it is not a plain factual 'yeah' to a yes/no (that's ㅇㅇ).

Literal root 인정 = 'acknowledge / admit / recognize as settled.' The slang sense is upbeat 'agreed!' — but the literal core leaves a faint shade of CONCEDING ('okay, I'll grant you that'). The bare noun even works as a verb: 그 실수는 인정 = 'I admit that mistake.' It's not purely cheerful.

Casual, young, friends and peers. Not for formal writing or seniors. Polite equivalents to use upward: 맞아요 / 맞습니다 ('that's right'), 동의해요 / 동의합니다 ('I agree'). In a work chat agree with 동의합니다, never ㅇㅈ.

Don't blur with ㄹㅇ: ㅇㅈ (인정) = 'I agree/admit it,' a stance toward what was said; ㄹㅇ (리얼) = 'for real/genuinely,' a truth-claim that can also intensify mid-sentence. They stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but aren't interchangeable — only ㄹㅇ works as a plain intensifier. And vs ㅇㅇ: ㅇㅈ endorses an opinion, ㅇㅇ just says 'yeah' to a yes/no. Polite path: 맞아요 / 동의해요.
ㅇㅈ → ㅇㅈㅇㅈ (strong) → ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ (double). The set-phrase game ㅇㅈ? ㅇㅇㅈ (call-and-response 'right?'/'yeah agreed'). Spelled out: 인정 (also a standalone verb, 인정한다). Polite swap: 맞습니다 / 동의합니다.

(1) Hearing it as purely upbeat 'yes!' and missing the 'I'll admit/concede' shade from its root 인정 — it can mark grudging agreement. (2) Treating it as identical to ㄹㅇ — they're different (agreement vs truth-claim) and only ㄹㅇ intensifies. (3) Using it upward — write 동의합니다/맞습니다 to seniors.

expressions.nuance: ㄱㅊ is the initials of 괜찮아 ('it's okay'), and it inherits that word's famously wide three-way range: (1) reassuring — 'it's fine, don't worry'; (2) self-report — 'I'm okay'; and (3) soft declining — 'I'm good' (i.e. 'no thanks'). Its polite forms are 괜찮아요 / 괜찮습니다, which is what seniors get. The standout English-speaker pitfall is sense (3): when someone offers you food or a drink and you reply 괜찮아요/ㄱㅊ, a Korean hears 'no thanks, I'm fine WITHOUT it' — a polite refusal — whereas English speakers, hearing 'it's okay,' often think they just ACCEPTED. So 'ㄱㅊ' to '커피 마실래?' means you're declining, not saying yes; if you actually want it, say 응 줘 / 네 주세요. The second pitfall is the usual register one: ㄱㅊ is friends-only, so don't reassure a boss with it — write 괜찮습니다. The near-synonyms for the decline sense are worth knowing: 됐어 is the blunter cousin ('no, that's enough,' can sound curt or annoyed), so ㄱㅊ/괜찮아 is the gentler way to turn something down. And the ? matters: ㄱㅊ states 'I'm fine,' but ㄱㅊ? flips it to 'are YOU okay?' It naturally follows apologies like ㅈㅅ/미안 to brush them off kindly.

structuredNuance.t: ㄱㅊ is the initials of 괜찮아 ('it's okay'), inheriting that word's wide three-way range: (1) reassuring — 'it's fine, don't worry'; (2) self-report — 'I'm okay'; (3) soft declining — 'I'm good / no thanks.' It naturally follows apologies (ㅈㅅ/미안) to brush them off kindly.

Literally just 'okay / fine' (괜찮아 abbreviated). But the real meaning depends entirely on context: as a reply to an apology it reassures, about yourself it's a status report, and — the tricky one — as a reply to an OFFER it's a polite REFUSAL ('I'm fine without it'), not acceptance.

Casual, friends and peers. Don't reassure or decline UP with it — to a boss or elder write 괜찮아요 (polite) / 괜찮습니다 (formal). The function (reassure / decline / self-report) stays the same at every level; only the form changes.

For the DECLINE sense, 아니야 괜찮아 / 됐어 are close kin — but 됐어 is blunter and can sound annoyed ('no, that's enough'), so ㄱㅊ/괜찮아 is the gentler turn-down. Crucially, ㄱㅊ is NOT how you accept: if you want the thing offered, say 응 줘 / 네 주세요, never ㄱㅊ. Polite forms: 괜찮아요 / 괜찮습니다.
ㄱㅊ → ㄱㅊㄱㅊ (warmly waving off) → 나 ㄱㅊ (I'm fine) → ㄱㅊ? (are YOU okay?). After apologies: ㅈㅅ → ㄱㅊㄱㅊ. Spelled out: 괜찮아 → 괜찮아요 → 괜찮습니다. The ? alone flips speaker from self to other.

Sense (3): replying ㄱㅊ/괜찮아요 to an offer means 'no thanks' to a Korean, but English speakers hear 'it's okay' and think they ACCEPTED. So ㄱㅊ to '커피 마실래?' DECLINES it — say 응 줘/네 주세요 to accept. Second: it's friends-only; reassure a boss with 괜찮습니다, not ㄱㅊ.

반말-leaning, gentler everyday lead-in

usagePhrases.note: 격식, very polite preface to a question

usagePhrases.en: excuse me, but might you happen to…
usagePhrases.note: natural extension; 혹시 softens a personal question

examples.en: Excuse me, but who are you?
examples.note: softening a direct identity question with 실례지만 — without it, 누구세요? sounds blunt

examples.en: Pardon me, but how old are you?
examples.note: prefacing a sensitive personal question; Korean culture expects this cushion

examples.ko: A: 실례지만 길 좀 여쭤봐도 될까요? / B: 네, 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: A: sillyejiman gil jom yeojjwobwado doelkkayo? / B: ne, malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: A: Excuse me, but may I ask for directions? / B: Yes, go ahead.
examples.note: a courteous full request-exchange to a stranger; note 여쭤보다 (ask, humble form)

expressions.nuance: 실례지만 is the polite 'excuse me, but…' you put BEFORE a question that might intrude — asking a stranger's name, age, relationship status, or for directions. It is 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but', meaning 'it's a bit forward of me, but…'. This buffer is not optional small talk — it is culturally expected when your question crosses into personal territory, especially with someone you don't know. Register: 실례지만 is standard polite; 실례하지만 and 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식; a softer, more casual variant is 실례인데. The nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans more apologetic and frames asking a favor; the dividing line is that 실례지만 frames a social intrusion ('this question is a bit forward'), while 죄송하지만 frames an imposition ('I'm imposing on you'). Critical grammar rule English speakers miss: 실례지만 must attach to a following clause — it CANNOT end a sentence by itself like English 'excuse me'. To stand alone, say 실례합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례지만 alone like English 'excuse me' — it needs a following clause (실례지만, 누구세요?); to stand alone use 실례합니다.
Asking personal questions (age, name, marital status) with no cushion — Korean expects 실례지만/혹시 in front to soften.
Swapping it freely with 죄송하지만 — 실례지만 frames an intrusive question; 죄송하지만 leans toward asking a favor.

structuredNuance.t: 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but' = 'it's a bit forward of me, but…'. The real function is a social cushion that pre-apologizes for an intrusive question, signaling you are aware you might be crossing a line.

실례지만 is standard polite; 실례하지만 / 실례합니다만 are more 격식; 실례인데 is softer and slightly casual. Use any of these before personal questions to a stranger. Never drop the cushion — asking personal questions cold sounds blunt in Korean.

Nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans apologetic and frames an imposition. The dividing line: 실례지만 = 'this question is a bit forward'; 죄송하지만 = 'I'm imposing on you / asking too much'. They can often swap, but 실례지만 is more about the question's intrusiveness.
Add 혹시 for extra softness: 실례지만 혹시 어디서 일하세요? Use 실례지만 말씀 좀 여쭙겠습니다 as a formal complete opener. In writing, 실례합니다만 is common.

English speakers drop the cushion entirely, firing 나이가 어떻게 되세요? cold — which sounds blunt and rude in Korean. Also, 실례지만 cannot end a sentence alone like English 'excuse me'; it must attach to a following clause. Use 실례합니다 to stand alone.

expressions.english: The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)
expressions.shortExplanation: 다름이 아니라 is a practical expression meaning "The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)".
expressions.explanation: "The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)" — that is 다름이 아니라 (dareumi anira). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다름이 아니라, 부탁이 하나 있어서요. ("The thing is, I have a favor to ask."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: The thing is, I have a favor to ask.
usagePhrases.note: Easing into a request; trailing -서요 leaves it softly open

usagePhrases.ko: 다름이 아니라 잠깐 드릴 말씀이 있어서요.
usagePhrases.romanization: dareumi anira jamkkan deuril malsseumi isseoseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Actually, there's something I wanted to tell you.
usagePhrases.note: 드릴 말씀 = humble 'something to say to you'

usagePhrases.ko: 다름이 아니라, 다음 주 일정 때문에 연락드렸어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: dareumi anira, daeum ju iljeong ttaemune yeollakdeuryeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: I'm reaching out about next week's schedule, actually.
usagePhrases.note: Stating the purpose of a call/email

usagePhrases.ko: 다름이 아니고 돈 좀 빌릴 수 있을까 해서.
usagePhrases.romanization: dareumi anigo don jom billil su isseulkka haeseo.
usagePhrases.en: So, the thing is, I was wondering if I could borrow some money.
usagePhrases.note: 다름이 아니고 = looser spoken variant

examples.en: The thing is — do you have a minute?
examples.note: Short build-up to a simple ask; the listener knows a real request is coming

examples.ko: A: 여보세요? 누구세요? / B: 저 민준이에요. 다름이 아니라 이번 주말에 시간 있으세요?
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo? nuguseyo? / B: jeo minjunieyo. dareumi anira ibeon jumare sigan isseuseyo?
examples.en: A: Hello? Who is this? / B: It's Minjun. The thing is, are you free this weekend?
examples.note: Phone call where 다름이 아니라 signals the speaker is now getting to the actual reason for calling

examples.ko: 과장님, 다름이 아니라 연차 하루만 쓸 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: gwajangnim, dareumi anira yeoncha haruman sseul su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: Manager, the thing is, could I take just one day of leave?
examples.note: Real workplace request to a senior, fully polite — 다름이 아니라 softens the directness of asking a superior

expressions.nuance: Polite set phrase literally meaning 'it's nothing other (than this)' — from 다르다 ('to differ') → 다름 ('difference') + 이 아니라 ('it's not that') — signaling 'I'm now about to get to the real reason.' It creates a small moment of suspense that primes the listener for a request or announcement, which is why it's so common before favors, phone call purposes, and workplace asks. The near-synonyms 저기요 and 저 ('um, hey') just flag the start of a turn, whereas 다름이 아니라 specifically promises 'here comes my actual point,' making it heavier and more formal. 다름이 아니고 is the slightly looser conversational variant. Because it is a lead-in, it cannot end the sentence — the real content must follow immediately. Pitch it at 존댓말 contexts: phone calls, emails, and talking to seniors. Among close friends it can feel unnecessarily stiff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's a lead-in, not a full sentence — 다름이 아니라. on its own says nothing. Always attach your actual point: 다름이 아니라, 부탁이 하나 있어요.
Spelling: 다름이 (not 다림이). It comes from 다르다 (to differ), so the noun is 다름. 다림이 wrongly suggests 다리미 'an iron'.
Don't drop the connective and say 다름 아니라 in careful writing; standard is 다름이 아니라 with the subject 이.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'it's nothing different (from this)' — 다름 ('difference') + 이 아니라 ('it's not that'). In practice it means 'I'm now getting to the real reason I approached/called you,' priming the listener for a request or announcement.

Polite 존댓말, especially suited to phone calls, emails, and speaking to seniors at work or in service contexts. Among close friends it can feel unnecessarily stiff; replace with 있잖아 or 사실은 for casual speech.

vs 저기요 / 저: those just open a conversational turn ('um, hey'), whereas 다름이 아니라 specifically signals 'what follows is the whole point of this conversation,' so it carries more weight and formality. vs 사실은: 사실은 ('the truth is') reveals a contrast with what might be assumed; 다름이 아니라 simply frames the purpose of contact.
다름이 아니고 = slightly looser spoken variant, same meaning. The trailing sentence often ends in -서요 (e.g. 부탁이 있어서요) to keep the turn open and soft rather than closing it with a blunt demand.

It is a lead-in, NOT a complete sentence — never say 다름이 아니라. alone without your actual point. Spelling trap: it's 다름이 (noun from 다르다 'to differ'), never 다림이, which suggests 다리미 ('a clothes iron') and is simply wrong.

expressions.english: Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)
expressions.shortExplanation: 죄송한데요 is a practical expression meaning "Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)".
expressions.explanation: 죄송한데요 (joesonghandeyo) = "Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 죄송한데요, 이거 환불 가능할까요? ("Sorry, but is this refundable?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite complaint/request at a store

usagePhrases.ko: 죄송한데 조금만 조용히 해 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: joesonghande jogeumman joyonghi hae jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Sorry, but could you keep it down a little?
usagePhrases.note: 죄송한데 (no 요) = slightly shorter, still polite

usagePhrases.ko: 죄송한데요, 지금은 좀 어려울 것 같아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: joesonghandeyo, jigeumeun jom eoryeoul geot gatayo.
usagePhrases.en: I'm sorry, but it'd be hard right now.
usagePhrases.note: Softening a refusal with 좀 + 것 같아요

usagePhrases.en: Excuse me, could you let me through?
usagePhrases.note: More apologetic in tone than 실례지만

examples.en: Sorry, could I get some water?
examples.note: Simple polite request to restaurant staff — 죄송한데요 keeps the tone warm even before 'could you'

examples.ko: A: 주문하시겠어요? / B: 죄송한데요, 주문한 거랑 다른 게 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: jumunhasigesseoyo? / B: joesonghandeyo, jumunhan georang dareun ge nawasseoyo.
examples.en: A: Are you ready to order? / B: Sorry, but this isn't what I ordered.
examples.note: Two-person restaurant exchange: 죄송한데요 opens the complaint without sounding accusatory

examples.ko: 죄송한데요, 제가 지금 통화가 좀 어려워서요.
examples.romanization: joesonghandeyo, jega jigeum tonghwaga jom eoryeowoseoyo.
examples.en: I'm sorry, but I can't really talk right now.
examples.note: Trailing -서요 leaves the refusal gently unfinished, making it softer than a full sentence

expressions.nuance: Polite 존댓말 cushion built on 죄송 (罪悚: 罪 'sin/guilt' + 悚 'fear/trepidation') — originally a very strong apology implying guilt and awe — plus the ending -ㄴ데요 ('…, and so / …but'), turning it into a universal friction-reducer before a request, complaint, or soft refusal. Because it leads with an apology, it feels more deferential than 실례지만 (courteous but not guilty) — you'd say 죄송한데요 when complaining about your food or softly refusing a request, but 실례지만 when asking a stranger for directions. Koreans reach for this phrase constantly because leading with 죄송 keeps social friction very low. 죄송한데 (dropping -요) is the same phrase in slightly less formal speech. A critical distinction: this is a SOFTENING LEAD-IN, not a genuine apology for a real wrongdoing — if you actually hurt someone, you need a sincere 정말 죄송합니다, not this prefix.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't spell it 죄성한데요 — the word is 죄송 (罪悚). Listen for the ㅗ: 죄송.
It's a softener, not a real apology. If you genuinely wronged someone, 죄송한데요 sounds too light — use a full 정말 죄송합니다.
Avoid stacking it with a blunt demand: 죄송한데요, 빨리 해요 clashes. Keep the request equally polite: 죄송한데요, 조금만 빨리 해 주실 수 있을까요?

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '(I feel) guilty/fearful, but…' (罪悚 + -ㄴ데요). Real meaning: a universal friction-reducer placed before any request, complaint, or soft refusal. The apology-first structure keeps social harmony — Koreans use it constantly for exactly this reason.

Polite 존댓말. Works for requests to staff, complaints at stores, declining invitations, or asking a stranger to move. 죄송한데 (no -요) is slightly less formal but still polite. Do NOT use with close friends — just say 있잖아 or start directly.

vs 실례지만: 실례지만 is courteous-but-not-apologetic, good for asking strangers for information. 죄송한데요 leads with guilt and fits complaints and refusals too. vs 미안한데요: 미안한데요 is the casual-polite version for semi-formal situations; 죄송한데요 is the more formal, deferential choice.
죄송한데 (no 요) = slightly less formal. 정말 죄송한데요 = adds genuine weight ('I'm really sorry, but…'). For a full apology without a trailing request: 정말 죄송합니다.

Don't spell it 죄성한데요 — the word is 죄송 (罪悚); the second syllable ends in ㅇ. This is a SOFTENER, not a real apology for wrongdoing — using it alone after a serious mistake sounds too light. If you've genuinely wronged someone, use 정말 죄송합니다.

expressions.english: Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그러게요 is a practical expression meaning "Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.".
expressions.explanation: 그러게요 (geureogeyo) means "Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러게요 ("right? / I know"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, agreeing with someone you respect

usagePhrases.en: yeah, right / tell me about it
usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, to a friend
fuller polite form, stronger agreement
casual emphatic, half-resigned agreement

examples.ko: A: 오늘 진짜 덥다 / B: 그러게.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jinjja deopda / B: geureoge.
examples.en: A: It's really hot today / B: Right?
examples.note: the bare agreement — echoing a shared feeling; you feel it too, so 그러게 is exactly right here

examples.ko: A: 요즘 왜 이렇게 시간이 빨라요 / B: 그러게요, 벌써 6월이에요.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum wae ireoke sigani ppallayo / B: geureogeyo, beolsseo 6worieyo.
examples.en: A: Why does time fly these days / B: I know, right — it's June already.
examples.note: everyday: polite agreement with a mutual observation; the 벌써 6월이에요 follow-up adds your own evidence of the shared feeling

examples.ko: A: 그때 그거 샀어야 했는데 / B: 그러게 말이에요. 지금은 품절이래요.
examples.romanization: A: geuttae geugeo sasseoya haenneunde / B: geureoge marieyo. jigeumeun pumjeoriraeyo.
examples.en: A: We should've bought it back then / B: Exactly. It's sold out now apparently.
examples.note: real situation: 그러게 말이에요 agreeing with a shared regret — the emphatic form feels more heartfelt than bare 그러게요

expressions.nuance: 그러게(요) means 'right? / exactly / I know, I feel the same' — you agree with something the other person said, often with a faint helpless, resigned, or rueful tinge. It's built from 그러다 'to be/do like that' + the sentence-final 게/게요. Casual 그러게, polite 그러게요, emphatic 그러게 말이에요 'exactly, you said it.' The critical dividing line is against 그렇구나 / 그렇군요: 그러게(요) responds to a SHARED feeling or opinion you already hold ('I know, right'), while 그렇구나 / 그렇군요 reacts to NEW information you just learned ('oh, I see / I didn't know that'). Both respond to something the other person just said, but the agreement type is opposite. Saying 그러게요 to new facts implies you already knew and can sound dismissive. To a superior 그러게요 is acceptable but 맞아요 / 그러네요 can feel a touch more attentive and engaged. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그러게요 as a response to new information — e.g., someone tells you their hometown for the first time and you say 그러게요, which would mean 'I know' and imply you already knew. The second pitfall is misreading its tone as disagreement; it is agreement, just with a resigned or rueful undertone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew; for news you just learned use 그렇군요 / 그렇구나.
Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; keep the polite 그러게요 (or 그러게 말이에요) with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Reading 그러게요 as disagreement or doubt — it actually means 'right, I feel the same,' a soft, often resigned agreement.

structuredNuance.t: 그러게(요) means 'right? / I know / exactly' — you agree with something the other person just said, often with a faint resigned or rueful undertone ('yeah, I know, what can you do'). It is agreement, not disagreement.

그러게 (casual banmal to friends) → 그러게요 (polite, to seniors/coworkers) → 그러게 말이에요 (emphatic full agreement) → 그러게 말이야 (casual emphatic, half-resigned). With a superior, 맞아요 or 그러네요 can feel slightly more attentive.

그러게(요) = 'I know, right' — confirms shared feeling/opinion you already held. 그렇구나 / 그렇군요 = 'oh, I see' — reacts to NEW information you just learned. 맞아요 = 'that's right / correct' — cleaner factual agreement, less rueful. Swap 그러게요 for 그렇군요 with new info or you sound like you already knew.

Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew and sounds dismissive. Misreading 그러게요 as doubt or disagreement — it is definitely agreement. Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — banmal; use 그러게요 or 그러게 말이에요.

expressions.english: It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)
expressions.shortExplanation: 어쩔 수 없죠 is a practical expression meaning "It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)".
expressions.explanation: "It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)" — that is 어쩔 수 없죠 (eojjeol su eopjyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 비가 오니까 어쩔 수 없죠. ("Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped.
usagePhrases.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason the situation is fixed

usagePhrases.en: Can't be helped — let's go next time.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩔 수 없지 = casual

usagePhrases.en: If it's sold out, oh well, nothing to do.
usagePhrases.note: Trailing 뭐 adds a resigned shrug

usagePhrases.en: I had no choice but to take a taxi.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩔 수 없이 = the adverb 'unavoidably'

examples.ko: A: 오늘 문 닫았네요. / B: 어쩔 수 없죠.
examples.romanization: A: oneul mun dadanneyo. / B: eojjeol su eopsjyo.
examples.en: A: They're closed today. B: Oh well, can't be helped.
examples.note: Quick, calm resignation — no blame, no distress, just acceptance

examples.ko: A: 기차표가 다 매진이에요. / B: 그래요? 어쩔 수 없죠, 버스 타죠 뭐.
examples.romanization: A: gichapyoga da maejinieyo. / B: geuraeyo? eojjeol su eopsjyo, beoseu tajyo mwo.
examples.en: A: The train tickets are all sold out. B: Oh well — let's just take the bus then.
examples.note: Graceful acceptance followed immediately by a practical fallback — the -죠 on 버스 타죠 recruits agreement

examples.ko: 몸이 안 좋으면 쉬어야죠, 어쩔 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: momi an joeumyeon swieoyajyo, eojjeol su eopseoyo.
examples.en: If you're not well you have to rest — there's no other way.
examples.note: 어쩔 수 없어요 = flatter, plainer final statement; used when the concession has already been discussed

expressions.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for gracefully accepting something outside your control — a verbal shrug built from 어찌하다 ('to do how/what') contracted to 어쩌다 → 어쩔 수 없다 ('there's no way to do anything about it'). The -죠 softens the inevitability with 'right? / don't you agree?' — making the resignation feel communal rather than bitter. The closest near-synonym is 할 수 없죠, nearly interchangeable in most situations. The sharper contrast is with 포기하다 ('to give up'): 어쩔 수 없죠 is passive ACCEPTANCE of a situation that was never in your hands, while 포기하다 is an ACTIVE choice to stop something you could have continued. Tone is everything: said calmly it reads as mature and easygoing; said with a sharp sigh or flat affect, it tips into passive-aggressive 'fine, whatever.' The adverb variant 어쩔 수 없이 is a separate form that modifies verbs ('I unavoidably went') and cannot substitute for the standalone phrase.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't use it about things within your control. Saying 어쩔 수 없죠 about a choice you could make sounds like a dodge — it claims the situation is genuinely out of your hands.
Don't confuse the two forms: 어쩔 수 없죠 (a standalone 'it can't be helped') vs 어쩔 수 없이 (the adverb 'unavoidably' before a verb, e.g. 어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).
Watch the spelling/sound: it's 어쩔 (double ㅉ), not 어절. And 없죠 is pronounced 'eopjyo', a contraction of 없지요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'there is no way to do anything about it' (어쩌다 + -ㄹ 수 없다). Real meaning: a verbal shrug — calm, communal acceptance of something beyond your control. The -죠 ending invites the listener to agree, making the resignation feel shared.
Casual-polite 존댓말 (어쩔 수 없죠 / 없어요). Among friends: 어쩔 수 없지 / 어쩔 수 없어. Fits informal and semi-formal spoken situations. Tone matters: calm = easygoing; flat/sharp = passive-aggressive.

vs 할 수 없죠: nearly interchangeable; both mean 'nothing can be done.' vs 포기하다: 포기하다 is an active CHOICE to quit something you could have pursued; 어쩔 수 없죠 is passive acceptance of a situation that was never in your hands — so use 어쩔 수 없죠 for sold-out tickets, but 포기했어요 for a project you gave up on.

어쩔 수 없죠 (casual-polite) → 어쩔 수 없지 (casual) → 어쩔 수 없어요 (plainer polite statement). Trailing 뭐 (어쩔 수 없죠, 뭐) adds a resigned shrug. The adverb form 어쩔 수 없이 ('unavoidably') modifies verbs and cannot replace the standalone phrase.

Don't use it about situations you actually control — it claims helplessness, so applying it to a choice you could make sounds evasive. Don't swap the two forms: 어쩔 수 없죠 stands alone as an acceptance; 어쩔 수 없이 is an adverb that must precede a verb (어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).

expressions.english: Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)
expressions.shortExplanation: 무슨 말씀을요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)".
expressions.explanation: 무슨 말씀을요 (museun malsseumeuryo) = "Oh, not at all / Don't mention it / Please, you're too kind (humbly deflecting thanks or praise)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 무슨 말씀을요, 당연히 도와드려야죠. ("Not at all, of course I should help."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Not at all, of course I should help.
usagePhrases.note: Deflecting thanks for a favor; 도와드리다 = humble 'help'

usagePhrases.en: Please, I'm the one who's grateful.
usagePhrases.note: 무슨 말씀을 (no 요) = slightly shorter, still polite

usagePhrases.en: Oh come on, don't say that.
usagePhrases.note: 에이 + the phrase brushes off excessive praise

usagePhrases.en: What do you mean — you're not late at all.
usagePhrases.note: 무슨 말씀이세요 = 'what are you saying?' to gently contradict

examples.en: A: Thank you. B: Oh, not at all.
examples.note: Shortest polite deflection — the brief reply conveys 'your thanks are unnecessary'

examples.ko: A: 음식 솜씨가 정말 좋으시네요. / B: 무슨 말씀을요, 별거 아니에요.
examples.romanization: A: eumsik somssiga jeongmal joeusineyo. / B: museun malsseumeuryo, byeolgeo anieyo.
examples.en: A: You're such a great cook. B: Oh, you're too kind — it's nothing really.
examples.note: Deflecting a compliment and adding a modest follow-up; the two moves must be consistent

examples.ko: A: 폐 끼쳐서 죄송해요. / B: 무슨 말씀을요, 괜찮아요. 또 오세요.
examples.romanization: A: pye kkichyeoseo joesonghaeyo. / B: museun malsseumeuryo, gwaenchanayo. tto oseyo.
examples.en: A: Sorry for being a bother. B: Not at all, it's fine — please come again.
examples.note: Host reassuring a guest who apologized; 또 오세요 turns the deflection into a warm invitation

expressions.nuance: A polite, animated deflection of thanks or praise, literally 'what words (are you even saying)!' — built on the honorific 말씀 (the respectful elevated form of 말, 'speech/words') so the phrase shows deference to the person praising you. The full underlying structure is 무슨 말씀을 (하세요/하십니까) 'What are you saying?' with the verb dropped for rhetorical brevity. The near-synonym is a flat 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing'), but 무슨 말씀을요 is warmer, more animated, and more deferential — it actively protests on the other person's behalf, making it ideal when speaking to elders, customers, seniors, or anyone you're being especially courteous to. 아니에요 is the neutral everyday choice. After deflecting, the phrase must be followed by something modest (별거 아니에요, 당연한 거죠); deflecting and then accepting the compliment in the same breath is contradictory. Pitfall: you must use 말씀 (honorific), not plain 말 — 무슨 말을요 is awkward and under-polite here.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Use 말씀 (the honorific), not 말. 무슨 말을요 sounds under-polite and slightly wrong; the fixed phrase is 무슨 말씀을요.
Don't deflect and then accept. Saying 무슨 말씀을요 and then 네, 제가 좀 잘하죠 contradicts the humility — follow with modesty like 별거 아니에요.
Don't read it as a literal question demanding an answer. It's a rhetorical deflection, so the other person isn't expected to explain 'what they said.'

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'What words [are you saying]!' (무슨 말씀을 하세요? with verb dropped). Real meaning: 'Your thanks or praise is unnecessary — please don't.' The rhetorical force comes from pretending the thanks itself is so unwarranted it's hard to hear. Uses honorific 말씀 throughout.

Polite 존댓말; best used with elders, seniors, customers, or anyone you're being especially courteous to. 무슨 말씀을 (no 요) is slightly shorter but still polite. Do NOT substitute plain 말 — 무슨 말을요 is under-polite and sounds awkward.
