structuredNuance.t: Literally 'the steam leaks out' — picture a hot 만두 going limp as its steam escapes — and it means built-up excitement or a good mood suddenly goes flat. You say it when something spoils the anticipation: a cancellation, a spoiler, a buzzkill comment. Partners: 팍 (suddenly/totally), 미리 말하다 (spoil in advance), 반응이 없다 (no reaction).

Register is casual, used freely among friends (아, 김새) and in texts. In a formal or work setting you'd choose plainer wording like 흥미가 떨어졌어요 ('I lost interest') rather than the playful 김새다. It vents mild disappointment, not anger — a deflated 'aw, never mind' feeling.

Its near-synonym expression is 김(이) 빠지다 ('the steam drains out'), essentially interchangeable. Don't confuse it with 흥이 깨지다 ('the festive mood is broken'), which specifically describes a lively, party-like 흥 being shattered, whereas 김이 새다 is the broader, quieter deflation of any built-up anticipation. 분위기 깨다 ('break the mood') is the agent-side version of killing it.

The contracted 김새다 is the everyday form; 김 빠지다 is its twin. Intensify with 김이 팍 새다 ('totally deflate'), and add finality with 김이 새 버리다 ('end up fizzling'). The exclamation 김새! ('what a buzzkill!') is common in speech. All stay casual.

A homonym trap: the 김 here is steam/vapor, NOT 김 the edible seaweed (laver) — there is no food in this idiom. And it describes deflated feeling, not a literal leak, so never use it for actual gas or air escaping (that's plain 새다, e.g. 가스가 새다).

expressions.english: to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')
expressions.shortExplanation: 속이 타다 is a practical expression meaning "to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')".
expressions.explanation: "to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')" — that is 속이 타다 (sogi tada). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 속이 타다 ("to be eaten up with worry"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: to be eaten up with worry
usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 속 (insides) takes 이, verb 타다 ('burn'). 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타 = sick with worry over no reply.

usagePhrases.en: to fret / to make someone worry
usagePhrases.note: Causative 태우다 — either you fret, or you cause others worry; 부모 속을 태우다 = worry one's parents.

usagePhrases.en: for worry to gnaw deeper and deeper
usagePhrases.note: Intensified 타들어 가다 = the burning spreads inward; stronger and more drawn-out, the worst phase of dread.
Close synonym idiom with 애 (one's innards/heart): 애가 타 죽겠어 = I'm dying of anxiety.

examples.en: I can't reach them and I'm worried sick.
examples.note: Simple frame; 안 되다 (can't get through) triggers the worry — the unreachable-person scenario is the classic trigger.

examples.en: I'm on edge waiting for the results.
examples.note: Everyday: -느라 names the anxious waiting as the cause; polite 요 form fits sharing real distress with someone.

examples.ko: A: 왜 이렇게 안절부절못해? / B: 애가 시험 보러 갔는데 연락이 없어서 속이 타 죽겠어.
examples.romanization: A: wae ireoke anjeolbujeolmotae? / B: aega siheom boreo ganneunde yeollagi eopseoseo sogi ta jukgesseo.
examples.en: A: Why are you so on edge? / B: My kid went to take an exam and hasn't called, so I'm worried sick.
examples.note: A/B turn: 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of worry') is the hyperbolic peak you reach when waiting helplessly on someone.

expressions.nuance: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry'): 걱정하다 is the everyday mental act of worrying, while 속이 타다 is the physical, churning agony of it, the way English 'worried SICK' outweighs 'worried.' Register is casual-to-polite and the feeling is genuine distress, so it's apt when you truly can't sit still, not for minor concerns. A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards/heart-strings), nearly identical in force, while 발을 동동 구르다 ('stamp one's feet') adds the restless, can't-stay-put body language. The key grammar is the 이/을 voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the burning anxiety (it happens to you), whereas the causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone else worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다 = a child makes the parents worry). Intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish (for a stomach ailment use 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다) — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying and who is causing the worry.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't take it literally as heartburn or indigestion. 속이 타다 is emotional anxiety, not a stomach ailment (that would be 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다).
Keep the 이/을 voice distinction: 속'이' 타다 = you feel anxious; 속'을' 태우다 = you cause worry (often to others). Swapping them flips who is at fault.
It's stronger than 걱정하다. Don't downgrade it to mere 'worry' in feel — 속이 타다 is 'worried sick,' the churning, can't-sit-still kind.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. Intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety').

Register is casual-to-polite, and the feeling is genuine distress — apt when you truly can't sit still (a child unreachable, results pending), not for trivial concerns. Saying it tells the listener your worry is serious and physical, so don't apply it to small everyday hassles, where 걱정돼요 fits better.

It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry') — the churning agony, like 'worried SICK' vs 'worried.' A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards), nearly identical in force; 발을 동동 구르다 ('stamp one's feet') adds the restless body language of helpless waiting.
The key voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the anxiety (happens to you); causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다). Stronger: 속이 타들어 가다; hyperbolic: 속이 타 죽겠어.

Don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish (for a stomach ailment use 속이 안 좋다 / 속이 쓰리다) — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying (속이 타다) and who is causing the worry (속을 태우다).

expressions.english: to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')
expressions.shortExplanation: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is a practical expression meaning "to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')".
expressions.explanation: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (bal didil teumi eopda) = "to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 ("to be jam-packed (no room to step)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: to be jam-packed (no room to step)
usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; mind the spacing: 발 디딜 (to step) + 틈이 없다 ('no gap'). 가게가 발 디딜 틈이 없어 = the shop is mobbed.

usagePhrases.en: to have not even room to step
usagePhrases.note: Swapping 이→도 ('even') heightens the crowding to extreme — not a sliver of space left.
The verb core; 디디다 = to plant your foot down, here modifying 틈 as the attributive 발 디딜.
Sino-Korean near-synonym EXPRESSION (人山人海, 'people-mountain-people-sea'); punchier and more dramatic, common in news.

examples.en: The shop is jam-packed.
examples.note: Simple frame; subject + 발 디딜 틈이 없어 — the plainest way to say a place is mobbed.

examples.ko: 출근 시간 지하철은 발 디딜 틈도 없어요.
examples.romanization: chulgeun sigan jihacheoreun bal didil teumdo eopseoyo.
examples.en: The subway at rush hour has no room to even stand.
examples.note: Everyday: 틈도 없다 intensifies the rush-hour crush; polite 요 form works in description or report.

examples.ko: A: 주말에 그 카페 갈까? / B: 거기 주말엔 발 디딜 틈도 없어, 평일에 가자.
examples.romanization: A: jumare geu kape galkka? / B: geogi jumaren bal didil teumdo eopseo, pyeongire gaja.
examples.en: A: Want to go to that cafe on the weekend? / B: It's totally packed there on weekends — let's go on a weekday.
examples.note: A/B turn: 발 디딜 틈도 없어, 평일에 가자 is the real-life way to steer plans away from a crowded spot.

expressions.nuance: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals — anywhere overflowing with a crowd — usually with a slightly overwhelmed tone; register is casual-to-polite and works fine in conversation and writing alike. Its Sino-Korean near-synonym expression is 인산인해 (人山人海, literally 'people-mountain, people-sea'), a punchier four-character idiom for an enormous throng often seen in news and dramatic description; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational, everyday way to say it, while 미어터지다 ('to be bursting at the seams') is an even more colloquial sibling. The single most important thing to get right is spacing and the verb: it is 발 디딜 틈이 없다, where 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다, 'to set a foot down') modifies 틈 ('gap') — beginners wrongly fuse it as 발디딜. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, so don't use it for a room cluttered with objects — for that you'd better say 어질러져 있다 (it's a mess). Natural partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing/verb error: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (발 디딜 = 'to step,' from 발을 디디다), not the fused 발디딜. Keep the space and the verb 디디다.
It's specifically about crowds of PEOPLE, not a room cluttered with objects. For a messy, cluttered space use 어질러져 있다, not this crowd idiom.
Don't drop 틈: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 needs 틈 ('gap'). 발 디딜 데가 없다 exists but shifts nuance toward 'nowhere to step/stand,' so keep 틈이 없다 for the 'jam-packed' meaning.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals. Partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).

Used with a slightly overwhelmed tone to describe a crush of people. Register is casual-to-polite and fits both speech and writing — you can warn a friend (거기 발 디딜 틈도 없어) or describe a festival in a polite report. It is hyperbole, so reserve it for genuinely heavy crowds, not a moderately busy room.

Its Sino-Korean near-synonym expression is 인산인해 (人山人海, 'people-mountain, people-sea'), punchier and more dramatic, common in news; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational version. An even more colloquial sibling is 미어터지다 ('bursting at the seams'); 북적북적하다 is the milder 'bustling' for moderate crowds.
Word-for-word 'no gap to step' = utterly packed. Heighten it with 발 디딜 틈'도' 없다 ('not even room to step') or the adverbial 발 디딜 틈도 없이. Keep the spacing 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다) — never fuse to 발디딜.

Scope trap: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, not a room cluttered with objects — for clutter say 어질러져 있다 ('it's a mess'). And don't fuse the spelling: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다, with 발 디딜 (verb 디디다) kept separate, not 발디딜.

expressions.english: Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그렇구나 is a practical expression meaning "Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.".
expressions.explanation: 그렇구나 (geureokuna) means "Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그렇구나 ("oh, I see"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, to a friend — the bare two-syllable 'got it' you breathe out
polite -요 version, keeps respect — use this with anyone you'd use 요 with (coworker, staff, stranger)
with 아 as a natural lead-in breath that softens it and marks the realization landing
past form, reacting to a past event they told you — also carries quiet sympathy ('oh, you went through that')

examples.en: Oh, I see.
examples.note: the bare reaction — just absorbing a new fact, no follow-up needed; 아 marks it clicking right now

examples.ko: A: 나 사실 부산 출신이야 / B: 아, 그렇구나. 어쩐지 사투리가.
examples.romanization: A: na sasil busan chulsiniya / B: a, geureokuna. eojjeonji saturiga.
examples.en: A: I'm actually from Busan / B: Oh, I see. No wonder the accent.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 그렇구나 receives the new fact, then pairs naturally with 어쩐지 when a clue suddenly clicks

examples.ko: A: 그 가게 월요일에 쉬어요 / B: 그렇군요. 알려주셔서 감사해요.
examples.romanization: A: geu gage woryoire swieoyo / B: geureokunyo. allyeojusyeoseo gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: A: That shop is closed on Mondays / B: I see. Thanks for letting me know.
examples.note: register lift: the polite 그렇군요 to a stranger who helped you — bare 그렇구나 here would sound too familiar

expressions.nuance: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. Literally it is 그렇다 'to be so' + the discovery ending -구나/-군요, which Korean reserves for something you have JUST taken in, so it always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization rather than neutral acknowledgment. The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. For a past event shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened,' which also lets you show quiet sympathy. The English-speaker pitfall is register: 'I see' feels neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is banmal; with anyone you keep -요 with it must be 그렇군요, and to a senior even 그러시군요. A second trap is using it as filler — overusing 그렇구나 to every line can read as only half-listening, so reserve it for genuine new info.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그렇구나 to a boss, teacher, or elder — the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar; use 그렇군요 (polite) or 그러시군요 (honorific) instead.
Answering surprising NEW info with 그러게요 instead of 그렇군요 — 그러게(요) means 'right, same here' about a shared feeling, so it implies you already knew; for genuinely new facts use 그렇구나/그렇군요.
Using present 그렇구나 for something that already happened — if a friend tells you about a past event, the natural reaction is the past form 그랬구나, not 그렇구나.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. It always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization, not neutral acknowledgment. Reacting to a past event, shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened,' which can also carry quiet sympathy.

Word by word it is 그렇다 'to be so' + the realization ending -구나, so it literally lands as 'ah, it IS so!' The real force is reactive discovery: 'oh, I didn't know that until just now.' It is not a statement of fact — it is the sound of new info settling in, which is why a flat present-tense statement can't replace it.

The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. Against 아 그래(요)?: that questions/checks the fact ('oh really?'), while 그렇구나 already accepts it and needs no answer.

Bare 그렇구나 is banmal — friends, juniors, kids only. With anyone you'd use 요 with (coworker, store staff, a stranger), use 그렇군요; to a clear senior or in deference, 그러시군요. The variant ladder is 그렇구나 → 그렇군요 → 그러시군요, each step adding respect; mismatching the step is the most common social slip.

'I see' feels register-neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar. A second trap: sprinkling 그렇구나 on every line reads as half-listening — reserve it for genuinely new info, and for a past event use 그랬구나, not present 그렇구나.

expressions.english: True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.
expressions.shortExplanation: 하긴 is a practical expression meaning "True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.".
expressions.explanation: "True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point." — that is 하긴 (hagin). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 하긴 ("true, fair enough"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: conceding a point after a beat of reconsidering — almost always opens the reply
agreeing once you reconsider — the most common full form, lands the concession
-네 marks realizing they have a point just now, the fresh 'oh' moment
casual, half-resigned agreement, slightly trailing off into a shrug

examples.en: Fair enough, that part's true.
examples.note: the bare concession — granting one specific point while you reconsider it on the spot

examples.ko: A: 지금 가도 차 막혀서 똑같아 / B: 하긴, 그냥 천천히 가자.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum gado cha makyeoseo ttokgata / B: hagin, geunyang cheoncheonhi gaja.
examples.en: A: Even if we leave now traffic's the same / B: Fair enough, let's just go slow.
examples.note: A/B exchange: conceding their logic and then changing the plan with a friend

examples.ko: A: 비 오는데 배달이 낫지 않아? / B: 하긴 그러네, 그냥 시키자.
examples.romanization: A: bi oneunde baedari natji ana? / B: hagin geureone, geunyang sikija.
examples.en: A: It's raining, isn't delivery better? / B: Huh, you're right, let's just order.
examples.note: the turn of mind: 하긴 그러네 marks the exact moment you switch your view to theirs

expressions.nuance: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It is the frozen, idiomatic shortening of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + the topic-contrast -기는), and as a reaction it almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. The contrast to keep clear is with 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair'; that reconsideration nuance is the whole point. It also differs from a flat 맞아 'you're right,' which is plain agreement with no 'hmm, on reflection' beat. Register-wise it is firmly banmal-flavored — everywhere among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock — but in formal or business speech it sounds too offhand; there you say 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not a strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant. Stronger/softer variants: 하긴 그래 (settled) vs 하긴 뭐 (half-resigned shrug).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 하긴 as full, firm agreement — it is a mild 'fair enough, you have a point,' not a strong yes; for committed agreement say 맞아 / 맞아요 or 그러게.
Using 하긴 in a formal meeting or with a superior — it sounds too offhand and casual; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요.
Spelling or saying it as the full 하기는 in conversation — as a reaction it is the frozen short form 하긴; 하기는 in speech sounds stiff and unnatural.

structuredNuance.t: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. That 'I hadn't thought of it like that' reconsideration is the whole flavor.

Under the hood it is the frozen short form of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + contrast -기는), literally something like 'as for doing/it being so…'. But nobody hears the literal parts: as a reaction it just means 'true, fair enough, on second thought you're right.'

Against 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair.' Against flat 맞아: 맞아 is plain agreement with no reconsidering beat, while 하긴 specifically marks a fresh concession after a pause. Against 하긴 한데, which concedes BUT then objects — 하긴 alone simply yields the point.

Firmly banmal-flavored — natural among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock. In a formal meeting or to a superior it sounds too offhand; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. Softer/stronger variants: 하긴 그래 (settled), 하긴 뭐 (half-resigned shrug).

Treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant. Also don't expand it to 하기는 in speech as a reaction — the frozen 하긴 is what's natural.

expressions.english: No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.
expressions.shortExplanation: 어쩐지 is a practical expression meaning "No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.".
expressions.explanation: 어쩐지 (eojjeonji) = "No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어쩐지 ("no wonder"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: reacting the moment an explanation lands and a small mystery resolves
with -더라 recalling the oddness you'd already noticed earlier
you'd already sensed something was up before the reveal — 했어 = 'I'd been thinking'

usagePhrases.en: that's why it seemed that way
usagePhrases.note: casual full-sentence reaction tying the reason to what you observed

examples.en: No wonder.
examples.note: the bare one-word reaction when it all suddenly fits together — no answer expected

examples.ko: A: 나 어제 밤새웠어 / B: 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.
examples.romanization: A: na eoje bamsaewosseo / B: eojjeonji pigonhae boideora.
examples.en: A: I pulled an all-nighter / B: No wonder you looked tired.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 어쩐지 + -더라 ties the explanation to what you'd already observed

examples.ko: A: 그 사람 사실 사장님 아들이래 / B: 어쩐지. 다들 조심하더라.
examples.romanization: A: geu saram sasil sajangnim adeurirae / B: eojjeonji. dadeul josimhadeora.
examples.en: A: He's actually the boss's son / B: No wonder. Everyone was careful around him.
examples.note: the long puzzle clicks: a standing mystery finally gets its reason

expressions.nuance: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It is rooted in 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so under the hood it carries 'so THAT'S why,' and it loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed. The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': they share the 어쩌- stem and beginners blur them, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of the reason'). A softer near-synonym is 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why,' which is more explicit and complete; 어쩐지 keeps it punchy and can stand alone. It works in casual and softly polite speech alike — just surround it with 요-level verbs for politeness (어쩐지 …하더라고요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is a satisfied 'ah, no wonder.' A second trap: leaving the verb in plain present (어쩐지 피곤해) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' nuance — the natural shape adds -더라/-더라고요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 어쩐지 (no wonder, causal) with 어쨌든 (anyway, regardless) — they share the 어쩌- root but are opposites: 어쩐지 embraces the reason, 어쨌든 sets it aside.
Treating 어쩐지 as a question like 왜 ('why?') — it is a reaction meaning 'ah, that explains it,' so it expects no answer.
Forgetting the -더라 that usually follows — saying just 어쩐지 피곤해 (present) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' feel; the natural form is 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.

structuredNuance.t: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed.

Built from 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so literally it is 'somehow / for some reason.' In reaction use that flips to the satisfied 'so THAT'S why' — the reason that was missing has just been supplied, and you're confirming, not asking.

The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': same 어쩌- stem, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of it'). Softer twin 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why' is more explicit and complete; 어쩐지 stays punchy and can stand alone.

The word itself is register-neutral and works casual or polite — politeness comes from the verbs around it (어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라 to a friend, 어쩐지 …하더라고요 to someone you keep 요 with). On its own as a one-word 어쩐지, it's a light, everyday reaction fine with almost anyone.

Reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is 'ah, no wonder.' Second trap: a flat present (어쩐지 피곤해) loses the 'I'd noticed it before' feel — the natural shape adds -더라/-더라고요 to replay the earlier observation.

expressions.english: Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그나저나 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.".
expressions.explanation: 그나저나 (geunajeona) means "Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그나저나 ("anyway, by the way"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: dropping one thread for a new one you actually want to raise
leading warmly into the new topic — 말이야 softens the pivot
casual combo with 근데, doubling the 'shifting gears' feel
pivoting straight into a new question — a very common shape

examples.en: Anyway, what should we eat for dinner?
examples.note: the bare pivot to a fresh topic — drops whatever came before

examples.ko: A: 그래, 그것도 맞아 / B: 그나저나 너 이사 준비는 잘 돼 가?
examples.romanization: A: geurae, geugeotdo maja / B: geunajeona neo isa junbineun jal dwae ga?
examples.en: A: Yeah, that's true too / B: By the way, is your moving prep going okay?
examples.note: A/B exchange: closing one point, then raising what you actually care about

examples.ko: A: 그 얘긴 됐고 / B: 그나저나 주말에 시간 돼?
examples.romanization: A: geu yaegin dwaetgo / B: geunajeona jumare sigan dwae?
examples.en: A: Enough about that / B: Anyway, are you free this weekend?
examples.note: deliberate drop: abandoning a topic to set up a plan

expressions.nuance: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It comes from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way,' so it literally shrugs off the previous talk to pivot. The contrast you must keep sharp is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one — answer 'so what's the conclusion?' with 그나저나 and you've changed the subject instead of finishing. It also differs from 그건 그렇고 'that aside,' which is the slightly more composed, can-be-polite way to do the same pivot. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?). It is fine in everyday polite talk, but in formal writing or business email it is too chatty; there you use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라. English speakers map all of 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so they reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — that is the trap. A second trap: it is one word, 그나저나, not 그 나 저 나.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그나저나 to wrap up and conclude the current topic — that is 아무튼/어쨌든's job; 그나저나 switches to a brand-new topic, so it derails a conclusion.
Putting 그나저나 in formal writing or a business email — it is conversational and too chatty there; use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라.
Confusing it with 그러나 'however' because they look alike — 그러나 contrasts ideas within one topic, while 그나저나 leaves the topic entirely.

structuredNuance.t: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?).

It is worn down from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way / whichever way,' so literally it brushes 'this or that' aside. The real use is purely functional: it signals 'leaving all that — new topic now,' regardless of where the previous talk was heading.

The sharp contrast is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one. Closest twin is 그건 그렇고 'that aside,' which does the same pivot but is a touch more composed and can sit in polite/semi-formal talk.

Conversational and warm — fine in everyday polite talk and great between friends. In formal writing or a business email it is too chatty; there use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라 to change subject. Combine casually as 근데 그나저나 with friends for an even breezier pivot.

English maps 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so learners reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — but that's 아무튼/어쨌든. Also it is one word, 그나저나, and it is NOT 그러나 'however' (which contrasts ideas within one topic).

expressions.english: Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.
expressions.shortExplanation: 아무튼 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.".
expressions.explanation: "Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point." — that is 아무튼 (amuteun). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 아무튼 ("anyway, in any case"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: wrapping up a tangent and driving to the point
closing a thought casually, letting the detail go
cutting past the explanation to land the warm message
slightly stronger 'regardless,' a firmer wrap-up

examples.en: Anyway, the point is I can't go.
examples.note: the bare wrap-up to a conclusion — 결론은 underlines that you're landing the point

examples.ko: A: 설명하자면 길어 / B: 아, 그래? / A: 아무튼 도와줘서 진짜 고마워.
examples.romanization: A: seolmyeonghajamyeon gireo / B: a, geurae? / A: amuteun dowajwoseo jinjja gomawo.
examples.en: A: It's a long story / B: Oh yeah? / A: Anyway, thanks so much for the help.
examples.note: A/B exchange: brushing past details to land the real message

examples.ko: A: 그래서 어떻게 됐는데? / B: 아무튼 잘 끝났어.
examples.romanization: A: geuraeseo eotteoke dwaenneunde? / B: amuteun jal kkeunnasseo.
examples.en: A: So how did it turn out? / B: Anyway, it ended fine.
examples.note: glossing over the messy middle and giving the upshot

expressions.nuance: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It is built from 아무 'any' + the -튼/-든 'whichever' ending, so it literally says 'whatever the case, here's the point.' Two contrasts matter. First, against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one — they are not interchangeable even though both translate as 'anyway.' Second, against its closest twin 어쨌든: the two are near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.' It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.' The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'anyway' to cover both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners. A second pitfall: leaning on 아무튼 to cut off someone mid-explanation can sound impatient, so save it for genuinely 'enough detail, here's the upshot.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 아무튼 to switch to a new topic — that is 그나저나; 아무튼 wraps up the current topic and drives to its point.
Assuming 아무튼 and 어쨌든 are always identical — they overlap heavily, but 어쨌든 leans more on 'regardless of the case,' often after weighing reasons, while 아무튼 is the plain 'anyhow, moving on.'
Stretching 아무튼 to mean 'either way both options are fine' — for genuinely weighing two outcomes, 어쨌든 fits better; 아무튼 just signals 'enough detail, here's the point.'

structuredNuance.t: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.'

It is 아무 'any' + the -든/-튼 'whichever' ending, so literally 'whichever way it is.' The real job is to signal 'setting all that aside, the point is…' — it drives toward a conclusion, not away from the topic, which is what separates it from 그나저나.

Against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one. Against its closest twin 어쨌든: near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.'

Neutral and flexible — comfortable from casual chat (아무튼 그래) to polite speech, and acceptable in light writing. 아무튼 간에 bumps it toward a firmer 'regardless.' For very formal writing, 어쨌든 or 여하튼 can feel a touch more composed.

Using one English 'anyway' for both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners. Also, cutting someone off with 아무튼 mid-explanation can read as impatient, so reserve it for a genuine 'enough detail, here's the point.'

expressions.english: Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.
expressions.shortExplanation: 어쨌든 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.".
expressions.explanation: 어쨌든 (eojjaetdeun) = "Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어쨌든 ("anyway, either way"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: setting the rest aside and proceeding to the outcome
stronger 'no matter what,' a firmer dismissal of the reason
interchangeable variant, handy for tone variety
leading to the outcome that stands regardless

examples.en: Either way, it's fine.
examples.note: the bare 'regardless, that settles it' — closes off further debate

examples.ko: A: 그게 내 잘못은 아니잖아 / B: 이유야 어쨌든, 늦은 건 늦은 거야.
examples.romanization: A: geuge nae jalmoseun anijana / B: iyuya eojjaetdeun, neujeun geon neujeun geoya.
examples.en: A: That's not my fault, though / B: Whatever the reason, late is late.
examples.note: A/B exchange: acknowledging a reason but dismissing it as not changing the outcome

examples.ko: A: 환불은 어렵다고 하던데 / B: 어쨌든 한번 문의는 해 봐.
examples.romanization: A: hwanbureun eoryeopdago hadeonde / B: eojjaetdeun hanbeon munuineun hae bwa.
examples.en: A: They said a refund is hard / B: Either way, try asking once.
examples.note: pushing forward in spite of the obstacle

expressions.nuance: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so it literally carries 'however things turned out.' Its near-twin is 아무튼, and in most sentences they swap freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason' — it often follows a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든) — while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart, too, from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a new one rather than concluding it. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant. Two English-speaker traps: spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌 with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ); and overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection can sound dismissive, so use it when you genuinely mean 'that aside, let's proceed.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 어쨋든 — the correct spelling is 어쨌든 (the middle syllable is 쨌, with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ); 어쨋든 is a very common but wrong typo.
Treating 어쨌든 and 그나저나 as the same 'anyway' — 어쨌든 concludes/sets aside the current point, while 그나저나 switches to a new topic entirely.
Overusing 어쨌든 to brush off every counterpoint — repeated, it sounds dismissive; reserve it for genuinely 'regardless, let's move on,' not for ignoring valid objections.

structuredNuance.t: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. It works in casual and polite speech alike, and 어쨌거나 is a fully interchangeable variant.

It is 어찌하- 'however it be' + past 었 + the -든 'whichever' ending, so literally 'however it turned out.' Functionally it concedes the point ('whatever the case may be') and pivots to the outcome that stands regardless — a concession plus a push forward.

Near-twin 아무튼 usually swaps freely; the fine line is that 어쨌든 leans harder on 'no matter what the situation/reason,' often after a reason you are setting aside (이유야 어쨌든), while 아무튼 is the plainer 'anyhow, here's the point.' Keep it apart from 그나저나, which abandons the topic for a NEW one rather than concluding it.

Neutral — fine casual or polite, and 어쨌든 간에 adds a firmer 'no matter what.' Slightly more composed than 아무튼 in writing, so it sits comfortably in semi-formal speech and reports; 어쨌거나 is a free variant for tone variety.

Spelling — it is 어쨌든, never 어쨋든 (the middle syllable is 쨌 with a double ㅆ batchim, not 쨋 with a single ㅅ). And overuse — leaning on 어쨌든 to wave away every objection sounds dismissive; reserve it for genuine 'that aside, let's proceed.'

expressions.english: That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그렇긴 한데 is a practical expression meaning "That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.".
expressions.explanation: 그렇긴 한데 (geureokin hande) means "That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그렇긴 한데 ("that's true, but…"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: partial agreement before a reservation — the cushion goes first
conceding casually with -지, lightest concession on the ladder
trailing off into hesitation, objection left soft and unstated
polite agreement before the but — for a senior or coworker

examples.en: That's true, but…
examples.note: the bare concede-then-hedge, trailing off so the objection stays gentle

examples.ko: A: 거기 싸고 좋잖아 / B: 그렇긴 한데 너무 멀어.
examples.romanization: A: geogi ssago jochana / B: geureokin hande neomu meoreo.
examples.en: A: It's cheap and nice there / B: True, but it's too far.
examples.note: A/B exchange: granting the point, then the real objection after -ㄴ데

examples.ko: A: 운동 좀 해야 돼 / B: 그렇긴 해요. 시간이 없어서요.
examples.romanization: A: undong jom haeya dwae / B: geureokin haeyo. sigani eopseoseoyo.
examples.en: A: You should work out / B: That's true. It's just I have no time.
examples.note: polite half-agreement softening a 'but' with a senior or coworker

expressions.nuance: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴 (그렇다 'be so' + the contrast-marking -긴), then -ㄴ데 swings the door open for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. The contrast to internalize is against a flat 아니 'no' or 그건 아니지 'that's not it': those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps the other person's dignity by agreeing partway first — Korean conversation strongly prefers this cushioned route. It also differs from plain 그런데/근데 'but,' which simply contrasts; the -긴 here adds a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that plain 그런데 lacks. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), it is never 그렇 긴; and skipping the concession and jumping straight to the objection, which in Korean lands as blunt and a little cold. Softer/stronger range: 그렇긴 하지 (light concede) → 그렇긴 한데 (full concede + clear but) → 그렇긴 한데 좀… (concede, then trail off to keep it soft).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 그렇 긴 한데 — 긴 attaches to the stem 그렇, so it is written 그렇긴 한데 (and 한데 is a separate chunk).
Dropping the concession and objecting head-on — Korean strongly prefers the cushion of 그렇긴 한데 before a 'but'; a flat 아니 or 그건 아니지 sounds blunt and cold.
Forgetting to make it polite when needed — to a senior, plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal; use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and then state your reservation.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴, then -ㄴ데 opens the door for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue.

Literally 'it IS so (그렇긴), but/and (한데)…'. The -긴 (from -기는) contrasts and concedes, so the real force is 'I'll give you that much, however…' — a built-in cushion, not a plain contrast. The listener hears the agreement first and the pushback as softened.

Against flat 아니 / 그건 아니지: those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps face by agreeing partway first — Korean strongly prefers this cushioned route. Against plain 그런데/근데 'but': 근데 just contrasts; the -긴 adds a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that 근데 lacks.

Plain 그렇긴 한데 is banmal — to a senior or in polite talk use 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요, then state the reservation. Softer/stronger ladder: 그렇긴 하지 (light) → 그렇긴 한데 (clear but) → 그렇긴 한데 좀… (concede then trail off).
Spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), never 그렇 긴 (and 한데 is its own chunk). And skipping the concession to jump straight to the objection — in Korean that lands as blunt and a little cold.

expressions.english: Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그럼요 is a practical expression meaning "Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.".
expressions.explanation: "Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech." — that is 그럼요 (geureomyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그럼요 ("of course"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: warm, emphatic polite yes — radiates welcome, not mere consent
casual version to a friend (NOT the connective 그럼 'then')
doubling up for extra warmth and reassurance
granting permission graciously

examples.en: Of course.
examples.note: the bare warm 'absolutely, yes' — full agreement, no hesitation

examples.ko: A: 자리 좀 맡아 주실 수 있어요? / B: 그럼요, 앉으세요.
examples.romanization: A: jari jom mata jusil su isseoyo? / B: geureomyo, anjeuseyo.
examples.en: A: Could you save my seat? / B: Of course, have a seat.
examples.note: A/B exchange: agreeing warmly to a small request from a stranger or acquaintance

examples.ko: A: 이거 정말 가져가도 돼요? / B: 그럼요, 편하게 드세요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo jeongmal gajyeogado dwaeyo? / B: geureomyo, pyeonhage deuseyo.
examples.en: A: Can I really take this? / B: Of course, help yourself.
examples.note: reassuring a hesitant guest generously

expressions.nuance: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 plus the polite -요, so it literally affirms 'it certainly IS so.' Its near-synonym is 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously,' and the two often stack (그럼요, 당연하죠) for extra warmth; the subtle difference is that 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is a homograph clash: the SAME letters 그럼 also serve as the transition word 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자 'then let's go'). With the -요 attached, 그럼요 is almost always the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is the bare 그럼 plus a clause. Mixing them up makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…', which is confusing. A second pitfall: 그럼요 is emphatic and warm, so using it for a flat, lukewarm 'yes' overshoots — for a neutral factual yes use 네/예. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Confusing 그럼요 (of course) with the transition 그럼 (then / in that case) — 그럼요 with -요 is an emphatic 'yes, of course,' while bare 그럼 + a clause means 'then…'; answering a question with the connective sense sounds off.
Saying plain 그럼 to a customer, senior, or stranger when you mean 'of course' — that is casual; the polite warm form is 그럼요.
Using 그럼요 to mean a neutral, lukewarm 'yes' — it is emphatic and warm ('absolutely!'); for a flat, factual yes use 네 / 예 instead.

structuredNuance.t: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.
It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 + polite -요, so literally 'it IS so.' The real force is an emphatic, friendly 'of course! absolutely!' — affirmation with warmth, the opposite of a grudging yes.

Near-synonym 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously' often stacks with it (그럼요, 당연하죠); 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. Against a flat 네/예: those are neutral 'yes'; 그럼요 adds emphasis and warmth ('of course!').

그럼요 is the polite warm form — right for customers, seniors, strangers, hosting a guest. Plain 그럼 is the banmal version for friends. To a customer or elder, dropping to bare 그럼 for 'of course' sounds too casual; keep 그럼요.

Homograph clash: the same letters 그럼 also mean 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자). With -요, 그럼요 is the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is bare 그럼 + a clause. Mixing them makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…'. Also, 그럼요 is emphatic — for a flat factual yes use 네/예.

expressions.english: Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'
expressions.shortExplanation: 그러게 is a practical expression meaning "Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'".
expressions.explanation: 그러게 (geureoge) = "Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그러게 ("right? I know"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: casual sympathetic agreement to a shared feeling
polite -요 version for someone you keep 요 with
stronger 'totally, I feel it' — ramps the agreement up
emphatic 'see, I told you' — pairs with 내 말이

examples.en: Right, exactly.
examples.note: the bare strong 'totally, I feel the same' — full fellow-feeling

examples.ko: A: 날씨 진짜 춥다 / B: 그러게, 갑자기 겨울 됐어.
examples.romanization: A: nalssi jinjja chupda / B: geureoge, gapjagi gyeoul dwaesseo.
examples.en: A: It's so cold / B: I know, it suddenly turned winter.
examples.note: A/B exchange: warmly echoing a friend's complaint you already share

examples.ko: A: 진작 예약할걸 / B: 그러게, 자리가 없네.
examples.romanization: A: jinjak yeyakalgeol / B: geureoge, jariga eopsne.
examples.en: A: We should've booked sooner / B: Right, there are no seats.
examples.note: shared regret with a soft 'told you' undertone

expressions.nuance: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' It comes from 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending and works as a fellow-feeling echo. The contrast to fix is against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share ('yeah, I know, right?'), while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact you didn't know ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and you sound like cold weather is breaking news. A second near-synonym is 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying,' which is even more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이). Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up. The English-speaker pitfall is mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.' A second trap: because it can carry 'told you,' aiming it at a senior's mistake or complaint can sound smug, so keep it for shared feelings, not 'I-told-you-so' at someone above you.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing 그러게 as the question 'why did you (do that)?' — it is an agreeing reaction meaning 'right, I know,' not an interrogative.
Using 그러게 to react to brand-new information — 그러게 echoes a feeling you ALREADY share; for news you just learned, use 그렇구나 / 그렇군요.
Saying plain 그러게 to a senior — it is banmal; with someone you keep -요 with, use 그러게요.

structuredNuance.t: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up.

It is 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending — literally close to 'so it be / be that way.' The real force is fellow-feeling: 'right, I know, exactly — I felt the same.' It's an agreement noise, not a description, so don't parse it word-for-word.

Against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share, while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and cold weather sounds like breaking news. Near-synonym 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying' is more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이).

Plain 그러게 is banmal — friends and peers; with someone you keep 요 with use 그러게요. Because it can carry 'told you so,' it's best for shared feelings; aimed at a senior's complaint or mistake it can sound smug, so be careful upward.

Mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.' Second trap: its faint 'I-told-you-so' edge means it can read as smug if aimed at someone above you; reserve it for genuine shared feeling.

expressions.english: Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그러길래 is a practical expression meaning "Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.".
expressions.explanation: 그러길래 (geureogillae) means "Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러길래 ("since you said so"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: reacting to their words or actions as YOUR reason — the cause is them
naming who prompted you — the trigger is the other person
with 하도 for 'so insistently,' adding 'they wouldn't stop'
justifying your reaction — '(you prompted me) so I did, obviously'

examples.en: I did it because you said so.
examples.note: the bare 'you prompted me, so I acted' — note the cause is YOU, not me

examples.ko: 네가 먹고 싶다 그러길래 사 왔어.
examples.romanization: nega meokgo sipda geureogillae sa wasseo.
examples.en: You said you wanted some, so I bought it.
examples.note: your action explained by their words — quotative 다 + 그러길래

examples.ko: A: 왜 먼저 갔어? / B: 다들 바쁘다 그러길래.
examples.romanization: A: wae meonjeo gasseo? / B: dadeul bappeuda geureogillae.
examples.en: A: Why'd you leave first? / B: Everyone said they were busy, so…
examples.note: A/B exchange: the reason trails off, the result left implied

expressions.nuance: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the connective -길래, and the defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself: that is exactly what separates it from plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that can take any subject. So 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained, neutral cause) is fine, but to say 'YOU kept saying it's good, so I tried it' you need 하도 맛있다고 그러길래 시켜 봤어 — the cause sits with them. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…). A close cousin is -기에, which means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form. The English-speaker pitfall: learners use 그러길래 for their own internal reason (because I was tired, because I wanted to) — for that you must use 그래서, since -길래 demands an external trigger from someone else. A second trap: when reporting speech, keep the quotative 다(고) — it is X-다고/-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…'); dropping the 다 garbles the 'because they said' sense.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러길래 (or -길래) for your OWN reason — it must react to someone else's words or actions; for your own internal reason ('because I was tired') use 그래서, e.g. 피곤해서, not 피곤하길래.
Writing -길래 in a formal essay or report — there the more literary -기에 is expected; -길래 is the casual spoken form.
Forgetting the quotative 다(고) when reporting speech — it is X-다고/-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…'); dropping it (X 그러길래 with no 다) garbles the 'because they said' meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. The defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…).

It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the reason connective -길래, so literally 'because (you/they) were doing/saying so.' Real use: 'since you said/did that, that's why I…' — your action framed as a direct response to their cue, with the spotlight on their prompt.

Against plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that takes any subject: 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained) is fine, but -길래 must point the cause at the OTHER party. Close cousin -기에 means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form.

Spoken and casual — natural in everyday talk, often trailing off (그러길래…). For an essay or report, the more literary -기에 is expected instead. It's neutral in politeness: you can attach polite endings to the result clause (사 왔어요).

Using 그러길래/-길래 for your OWN reason — it needs an external trigger from someone else; for 'because I was tired' use 그래서 (피곤해서), not 피곤하길래. Second: keep the quotative 다(고) when reporting speech — X-다 그러길래 ('they SAID X, so…').

expressions.english: I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그런가 봐요 is a practical expression meaning "I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.".
expressions.explanation: "I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing." — that is 그런가 봐요 (geureonga bwayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그런가 봐요 ("I guess so, seems so"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: soft polite inference from a clue you can see or hear
casual to a friend, same tentative hunch
negative version — 'seems like it's not the case'
hedging gently when unsure — stacks two softeners

examples.en: I guess so.
examples.note: the bare soft guess from a hunch, no firm claim being made

examples.ko: 불이 꺼져 있네요. 오늘 쉬는 날인가 봐요.
examples.romanization: buri kkeojyeo inneyo. oneul swineun naringa bwayo.
examples.en: The lights are off. I guess they're closed today.
examples.note: inferring from a visible clue — the evidence (불이 꺼져 있네요) comes first

examples.ko: A: 비 오려나 / B: 하늘 보니까 그런가 봐.
examples.romanization: A: bi oryeona / B: haneul bonikka geureonga bwa.
examples.en: A: Is it going to rain / B: Looking at the sky, I guess so.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 보니까 + 그런가 봐 grounds the guess in evidence

expressions.nuance: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright. The engine is the ending -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 'it looks like / I guess,' which marks a guess drawn from external evidence, so 그런가 봐요 = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' The contrast that matters is against -겠- and against 것 같다. -겠다 (그렇겠어요) is a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays more tentative; 그런 것 같아요 is very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the signs suggest so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.' Two English-speaker pitfalls: spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with 봐요 written separately as the auxiliary (not 그런가봐요); and don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd unless you mean it half-jokingly. Note the 봐 here is the verb 보다 in its inference sense, not 'look at it' — it is what makes this a hunch, not a command.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 그런가봐요 — the standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written as a separate word.
Using -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you infer about others/the world, not yourself; for your own state say 그런 것 같아요 or just state it, not 그런가 봐요.
Swapping it for confident -겠어요 when you only have a hunch — 그런가 봐요 is tentative (evidence-based guess); 그렇겠어요 sounds like a firmer 'it must be so.'

structuredNuance.t: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright, so it = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.'

Literally 'I look-and-see whether it is so' — the 봐(요) is 보다 in its inference sense, not the literal 'look at.' That's why the real meaning is a tentative, evidence-based 'I guess so,' not a statement and not a command to look.

Against -겠다 (그렇겠어요): a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays tentative. Against 그런 것 같아요: very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the outward signs suggest so.'

그런가 봐요 is the polite form; 그런가 봐 is casual to friends. Tone is gentle and non-committal, which makes it useful for not sounding too sure — good with seniors when you'd rather hedge than assert. Stack 그런가 봐요, 잘 모르겠어요 to hedge further.

Spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written separately (not 그런가봐요). And don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings/actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd; say 그런 것 같아요 or state it plainly.

expressions.english: Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.
expressions.shortExplanation: 듣고 보니 is a practical expression meaning "Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.".
expressions.explanation: 듣고 보니 (deutgo boni) = "Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 듣고 보니 ("now that you mention it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: reconsidering after listening — your view shifts on the spot
agreeing after a beat of reconsidering — 그렇네 marks the penny dropping
with -까 leading into a fuller clause that follows
after a second listen, re-judging with fresh ears

examples.en: Now that you say it, yeah.
examples.note: the bare 'on hearing it, you're right' — the mind changes on the spot

examples.ko: A: 이 색이 너한테 더 어울려 / B: 듣고 보니 네 말이 맞는 것 같아.
examples.romanization: A: i saegi neohante deo eoullyeo / B: deutgo boni ne mari manneun geot gata.
examples.en: A: This color suits you better / B: Now that you mention it, I think you're right.
examples.note: A/B exchange: coming around to their view after listening

examples.ko: 듣고 보니까 그 식당 좀 비싸긴 했어.
examples.romanization: deutgo bonikka geu sikdang jom bissagin haesseo.
examples.en: Come to think of it, that restaurant was kind of pricey.
examples.note: recalling and re-judging once the topic comes up

expressions.nuance: 듣고 보니 literally stacks 듣다 'to hear' + -고 보니 'having done and then found,' so it means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. The -고 보니 frame is a 'do X, then discover' construction (cf. 가 보니 'on going, I found,' 자고 보니 'after sleeping, I realized'), which is why it signals a fresh after-the-fact realization rather than a prior opinion. The contrast to keep is against 그러게: 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 듣고 보니 means 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it — and now I do,' so it foregrounds a CHANGE of mind. It also differs from 알고 보니 'as it turns out,' which reveals a hidden FACT rather than a shift in your opinion. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause. The English-speaker pitfall is reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not just chronology. A second trap: 보니 here is 'I found/realized,' not the purpose '-(으)려고 to hear,' so don't read it as 'in order to hear.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 듣고 보니 as merely 'after listening' (time order) — in conversation it specifically signals 'now that you mention it, I've reconsidered and tend to agree.'
Using 듣고 보니 when you already held that view — it marks a CHANGE of mind prompted by what you just heard; if you already agreed, use 그러게 or 내 말이.
Confusing the -고 보니 'discover after doing' frame with -고 (으)려고 'intending to' — 듣고 보니 means 'on hearing, I found,' not 'in order to hear.'

structuredNuance.t: 듣고 보니 means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause.

It stacks 듣다 'hear' + -고 보니 'having done, then found' (cf. 가 보니 'on going I found'). So literally 'having heard, I find…'; the real force is 'on hearing it, I've reconsidered — and now I agree.' It marks a fresh realization, not a prior view.

Against 그러게 ('right, I already felt the same'): 듣고 보니 foregrounds a CHANGE of mind — 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it.' Against 알고 보니 'as it turns out': that reveals a hidden FACT, while 듣고 보니 reports a shift in YOUR opinion after listening.

Register-neutral — works casual (듣고 보니 그러네) or polite (듣고 보니 맞는 것 같아요), and it's a graceful way to concede to a senior because it credits their point. Use -까 (듣고 보니까) when a longer clause follows; 다시 듣고 보니 for a second listen.

Reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not mere chronology. Second: 보니 is 'I found/realized,' not purpose -(으)려고 'to hear,' so it does NOT mean 'in order to hear.'

expressions.english: Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그러게 말이에요 is a practical expression meaning "Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)".
expressions.explanation: 그러게 말이에요 (geureoge marieyo) means "Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요. ("Tell me about it — I was thinking the exact same thing."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

-ㅂ니다 form, polite to a senior or at work

examples.ko: A: 요즘 물가가 너무 올랐어요. B: 그러게 말이에요.

expressions.nuance: Whole-hearted, sympathetic agreement that means far more than a flat 네 or 맞아요 — it carries the extra charge 'and I've felt exactly that myself.' The phrase is built from 그러게 ('right, isn't it') plus 말이에요 (literally 'it is [my] words'), making it the heavier, more emphatic cousin of plain 그러게요: where 그러게요 is a quick nod, 그러게 말이에요 is a shared sigh that says 'you took the words out of my mouth.' Contrast it with 맞아요, which simply confirms a fact ('that's correct'); 그러게 말이에요 instead bonds you emotionally over a shared feeling — usually a complaint or a 'what can you do' resignation, but also a mutual positive surprise. Register: casual-polite 해요체 is the default; drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends and go up to 그러게 말입니다 with a boss or in formal settings. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for it to accept a compliment about yourself ('You're so good!' → 그러게 말이에요 sounds like you're agreeing you're great) — it only mirrors the other person's observation about something you both perceive from the outside.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

English speakers use it to accept praise ('You did great!' → 그러게 말이에요), which sounds like smug self-agreement. It's only for echoing a remark about something you both see, not about yourself — for praise say 감사합니다 instead.
It only confirms what was just said, so don't follow it with a counter-argument. To agree-then-disagree you need 그건 그런데… ('that's true, but…'), not 그러게 말이에요.
Don't shorten it to just 말이에요 hoping to keep the meaning — without 그러게 it just means 'I'm telling you / it's true,' losing the empathetic-agreement function.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'right, it is [my] words' (그러게 + 말이에요). The real meaning is 'you took the words out of my mouth' — a charged, emotionally resonant echo that signals you've been feeling the same thing all along. It goes well beyond a simple factual confirmation like 맞아요.

Best after shared complaints, mutual frustrations, or joint positive surprises — any situation where both of you have observed the same thing from the outside. Casual-polite 해요체 suits friends, coworkers, and acquaintances. Drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends (반말); shift to 그러게 말입니다 with a senior colleague or boss (격식체). Safe with strangers at a polite register.

그러게요 is a quick, light nod ('yeah, right'); 그러게 말이에요 is the same emotion amplified into a shared sigh. 맞아요 confirms a fact ('that's correct') without the bonding warmth. 그렇군요 is the cool, detached 'I see,' used when processing new information rather than resonating with it.

그러게 말이야 (반말, friends) → 그러게 말이에요 (해요체, default) → 그러게 말입니다 (격식체, seniors). 그러게나 말이에요 adds a slightly heavier, more resigned sigh. You can extend: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요 piles on your own confirmation.

Don't use it to accept a compliment directed AT yourself ('You're so talented!' → 그러게 말이에요 sounds like smug self-agreement). It only mirrors an observation you both see from the outside. For praise, say 감사합니다 or 과찬이세요. Also: it's not interchangeable with a counter-argument — you can't agree then disagree with it; for that, use 그건 그런데… ('that's true, but…').

expressions.english: No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그게 아니라 is a practical expression meaning "No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)".
expressions.explanation: "No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)" — that is 그게 아니라 (geuge anira). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그게 아니라, 제 말은 좀 다른 뜻이었어요. ("No, that's not it — what I meant was a bit different."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 그게 아니라, 제 말은 좀 다른 뜻이었어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geuge anira, je mareun jom dareun tteusieosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: No, that's not it — what I meant was a bit different.
usagePhrases.note: Clarifying after being misunderstood

usagePhrases.ko: 아니 그게 아니라, 시간이 없어서 그래.
usagePhrases.romanization: ani geuge anira, sigani eopseoseo geurae.
usagePhrases.en: No no, it's not that — it's because I don't have time.
usagePhrases.note: 그게 아니라 = casual; correcting a wrong assumption with the real reason

usagePhrases.ko: 그런 게 아니라 그냥 좀 피곤해서요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureon ge anira geunyang jom pigonhaeseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: It's not like that, I'm just a bit tired.
usagePhrases.note: 그런 게 아니라 = 'it's not that KIND of thing' — denies a category, not just one claim

usagePhrases.en: That's not it — let me explain again.
usagePhrases.note: 그게 아니고 = looser spoken variant; softer, less urgent

examples.ko: A: 이거 싫어요? B: 그게 아니라 배가 불러서요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo sireoyo? B: geuge anira baega bulleoseoyo.
examples.en: A: You don't like this? B: It's not that — I'm just full.
examples.note: Short two-clause correction: denial + real reason in one breath

examples.ko: A: 저 싫어서 안 오시는 거예요? B: 아, 그게 아니라 오늘 진짜 바빠서 그래요.
examples.romanization: A: jeo sireoseo an osineun geoyeyo? B: a, geuge anira oneul jinjja bappaseo geuraeyo.
examples.en: A: Are you not coming because you don't like me? B: Oh, that's not it — it's just that I'm really busy today.
examples.note: Heading off a hurt feeling before it settles; 아, 그게 아니라 is a common spoken cluster

examples.ko: A: 환불해 달라는 거죠? B: 그게 아니라 사실은 교환을 하고 싶어서 말씀드린 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: hwanbulhae dallaneun geojyo? B: geuge anira sasireun gyohwaneul hago sipeoseo malsseumdeurin geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: So you want a refund? B: No — actually I brought it up because I'd like an exchange.
examples.note: Real service-desk correction: polite, clear, complete — the true intent follows right after

expressions.nuance: An everyday repair phrase you fire off the instant someone misreads your words or your motive. Literally '그게 (that) + 아니라 (it is not, and so…)': 아니라 is the connective form of 아니다 ('to not be'), so the phrase is grammatically incomplete on purpose — it leans forward, pulling the correct version along behind it. Leading with 그게 아니라 softens a correction the way English 'no, what I mean is…' does: you're fixing a misunderstanding, not winning an argument, so it protects the other person's face. 그게 아니라요 (with 요 added to the phrase itself) adds extra politeness when you're in formal or cautious mode. Distinguish it carefully from 그게 아니면 (sounds nearly identical but means 'if not that, then…' — offers an alternative rather than denying) and from 그런 게 아니라 ('it's not that kind of thing' — rejects a whole category). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a standalone 'No.' and stopping; Korean listeners expect the real explanation to follow immediately, or the phrase sounds unfinished and slightly rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
English speakers use it as a complete reply ('That's not it.') and stop. Korean needs the real meaning attached: 그게 아니라 + your actual point. On its own it leaves the listener waiting.
Confusing 그게 아니라 (denying: 'it's not that') with 그게 아니면 (offering an alternative: 'if not that, then…'). One corrects, the other proposes a plan B — swapping them derails the conversation.
Saying 그것이 아니라 in casual speech sounds stiff and bookish; the natural spoken contraction is 그게 아니라. Reserve the full 그것이 for formal writing.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'that — it is not, and…' (그게 = 그것이 contracted; 아니라 = connective of 아니다). It's grammatically a dangling clause that REQUIRES the true statement to follow. In use it means 'No, you've misread me — here's what I actually meant.'

Use it the instant you feel misread — a wrong inference about your motive, a misheard request, or a badly landed joke. Works at every speech level: 그게 아니라 + 요 (그게 아니라요) is a standalone polite softener; 그게 아니라 (without 요) is casual-neutral; 그게 아니야 is pure 반말 with close friends. Safe with any interlocutor — it's explicitly face-saving. Avoid a harsh or loud delivery, which can make it sound like scolding.

그게 아니면 sounds almost identical but means 'if not that, then…' — it proposes a plan B rather than correcting. 그런 게 아니라 rejects a whole assumed category ('it's not that kind of situation') rather than one specific claim. 아니에요 is a plain flat denial with no built-in segue to your real meaning.

그게 아니라 (neutral) → 그게 아니라요 (extra-polite standalone) → 그게 아니라고요 (emphatic repeat, 'No — I said it's NOT that!') → 그런 게 아니라 (category denial) → 그게 아니고 (softer variant, 'it's not that and…'). In writing or formal speech: 그것이 아니라 (uncontracted, stiff).

Treating it as a complete sentence and stopping: 'That's not it.' In Korean, 그게 아니라 is a dangling clause — the real explanation MUST follow immediately, or you sound like you've cut yourself off and left the listener confused. Also: don't reach for 그것이 아니라 in spoken, casual conversation — it sounds overly formal and bookish.

expressions.english: Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그러고 보니 is a practical expression meaning "Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)".
expressions.explanation: 그러고 보니 (geureogo boni) = "Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그러고 보니 오늘 점심을 안 먹었네요. ("Come to think of it, I haven't eaten lunch today."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 그러고 보니 오늘 점심을 안 먹었네요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureogo boni oneul jeomsimeul an meogeonneyo.
usagePhrases.en: Come to think of it, I haven't eaten lunch today.
usagePhrases.note: Solo realization as you speak — nothing triggered it except the flow of thought

usagePhrases.en: Now that I look — did you get a haircut?
usagePhrases.note: 그러고 보니까 = -까 makes it more pointed, like 'wait, actually now that I think about it...'

usagePhrases.en: Now that you mention it, it's already December.
usagePhrases.note: Noticing the passage of time sparked by what someone just said

usagePhrases.en: Now that I hear it, you're right.
usagePhrases.note: Related: 듣고 보니 = 'now that I've heard it through' — specifically prompted by listening

examples.en: Come to think of it, I didn't bring an umbrella.
examples.note: Simple solo realization, one clause — the most common minimal pattern

examples.ko: A: 민수 씨 요즘 안 보이네요. B: 그러고 보니 진짜 한참 못 봤네요.
examples.romanization: A: minsu ssi yojeum an boineyo. B: geureogo boni jinjja hancham mot bwanneyo.
examples.en: A: I haven't seen Minsu lately. B: Now that you mention it, it really has been a while.
examples.note: Other person's remark sparks the realization — 그러고 보니 signals it's fresh, triggered by what B just heard

examples.ko: 그러고 보니 우리 처음 만난 지 벌써 일 년이나 됐네요, 시간 참 빠르다.
examples.romanization: geureogo boni uri cheoeum mannan ji beolsseo il nyeonina dwaenneyo, sigan cham ppareuda.
examples.en: Now that I think about it, it's already been a whole year since we first met — time really flies.
examples.note: Real reflection spun into a fuller thought; -네요 + 시간 참 빠르다 is a natural follow-through

expressions.nuance: A connector for the exact moment a thought clicks into place mid-conversation. It breaks down as 그러고 ('having done/been so,' from 그러다) + 보니 ('upon looking/seeing,' from the -고 보니 pattern meaning 'do and then notice'), so literally 'looking at it that way, I now notice….' The realization is always FRESH — sparked by what someone just said or by something you just glimpsed; you can't use it for something you already knew. Compare three near-synonyms: 그러고 보니 is the broadest 'huh, now that I consider it'; 알고 보니 ('as it turns out') reveals a hidden truth that was previously unknown to both parties; 듣고 보니 ('now that I've heard it') is specifically triggered by what the other person said; and 생각해 보니 ('on reflection') implies deliberate thinking rather than a sudden click. Register is neutral — the form itself stays identical, only the ending verb changes (네요 for polite surprise, 네 for casual). Two critical pitfalls for English speakers: first, it marks new awareness — using it for known facts sounds odd; second, 그러고 is NOT 그리고 ('and') — one vowel separates them but the meaning is entirely different.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
