Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it for something you already knew. 그러고 보니 specifically flags a fresh realization; for known facts use 사실은 ('actually') or just state it plainly.
Writing or saying 그리고 보니 instead of 그러고 보니. 그리고 means 'and'; 그러고 (from 그러다, 'to do so') is the correct base. The mix-up is the single most common slip here.
Jamming it into a single word (그러고보니). Standard spacing keeps 그러고 보니 as two words; the 보니 part is a separate verb.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'having done/been so (그러고) + upon seeing/noticing (보니)' — the -고 보니 pattern in Korean signals 'I did X, and THEN I noticed Y.' The real meaning is: 'I just connected the dots — here's something I've freshly realized.' The whole point is that the insight is new.

Use it at the moment a realization lands mid-conversation — your own thought or triggered by what someone just said. Extremely common in casual and casual-polite speech (반말 and 해요체 equally). Not used in formal written or presentation Korean; the form itself is invariant — only the following verb changes for register. Fine with anyone from close friends to polite acquaintances.

알고 보니 ('as it turns out') reveals a hidden truth now confirmed; 듣고 보니 ('now that I've heard it') specifically needs the other person's words as a trigger; 생각해 보니 ('on reflection') sounds more deliberate, implying you've actively thought it over. 그러고 보니 is the lightest and broadest — any fresh click, no deliberate effort required.

그러고 보니 (standard) → 그러고 보니까 (more emphatic/pointed) → 그러고 보면 ('if you think about it that way,' hypothetical) → 듣고 보니 (when the trigger is specifically something you heard) → 알고 보니 (when a hidden truth has now emerged).

Two traps: (1) Using it for facts you already knew — it specifically flags a NEW awareness; for known information just state it directly or use 사실은 ('actually'). (2) Writing or saying 그리고 보니 — 그리고 means 'and'; 그러고 comes from 그러다 ('to do so'). One vowel difference, entirely different meaning. Standard orthography also keeps it two words: 그러고 보니 (not 그러고보니).

expressions.english: Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그래서 그런지 is a practical expression meaning "Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)".
expressions.explanation: 그래서 그런지 (geuraeseo geureonji) means "Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요. ("I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요.
usagePhrases.romanization: eoje jameul mot jasseoyo. geuraeseo geureonji haru jongil pigonhaneyo.
usagePhrases.en: I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day.
usagePhrases.note: Classic two-sentence pattern: state the cause, then express the hedged result

usagePhrases.en: Maybe because it's the weekend, there are so many people.
usagePhrases.note: N(이)라 그런지 = 'perhaps because it's N' — noun-attached variant

usagePhrases.en: Perhaps because it's raining, the streets are quiet.
usagePhrases.note: V/A-아서/어서 그런지 = 'maybe because ~' — attaches directly to a verb/adjective

usagePhrases.ko: 요즘 운동을 해서 그런지 컨디션이 좋아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: yojeum undongeul haeseo geureonji keondisyeoni joayo.
usagePhrases.en: Maybe it's because I've been exercising — I feel great lately.
usagePhrases.note: Crediting a positive habit for a good result; the hedge signals you're not 100% sure

examples.en: Maybe because I'm tired, I keep yawning.
examples.note: One cause, one observed symptom — the minimal, everyday pattern

examples.ko: A: 오늘따라 가게가 한가하네요. B: 평일이라 그런지 손님이 별로 없어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneulttara gagega hangahaneyo. B: pyeongirira geureonji sonnimi byeollo eopseoyo.
examples.en: A: The shop's unusually quiet today. B: Maybe because it's a weekday, there aren't many customers.
examples.note: Noun-attached 이라 그런지 in dialogue — speculating about a cause you can't confirm

examples.ko: 새 안경을 바꿔서 그런지 눈이 좀 피곤하고 머리도 살짝 아프네요.
examples.romanization: sae angyeongeul bakkwoseo geureonji nuni jom pigonhago meorido saljjak apeuneyo.
examples.en: Maybe because I changed to new glasses, my eyes feel tired and my head aches a little too.
examples.note: Tentative self-diagnosis stacking two noticed symptoms — note 살짝 ('slightly') matches the hedging tone

expressions.nuance: A soft, speculative cause-marker meaning 'I suspect this is the reason, though I'm not certain.' The hedge is baked into the -ㄴ지 ending (from 그렇다, 'to be so'): 그런지 literally asks-to-itself 'whether it's so,' keeping the speaker from overcommitting. So 그래서 그런지 = 'so, [maybe] because of that…' and points back to a cause already stated, while the extended patterns -아서/어서 그런지 and -(이)라 그런지 attach the guess directly onto a cause clause. The sharpest contrast to master is against bare 그래서 ('so, therefore'), which states a cause you're SURE of: 비가 와서 길이 막혀요 ('traffic is jammed because it's raining' — definite) vs 비가 와서 그런지 길이 막히네요 ('maybe because it's raining, traffic seems jammed' — tentative). Using plain 그래서 when you're only guessing sounds overconfident; using 그래서 그런지 when the link is obvious can sound oddly wishy-washy. Because it introduces an OBSERVED result, English speakers sometimes try to bolt a request onto it (그래서 그런지 + 도와주세요) — that is grammatically and functionally wrong.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그래서 그런지 for a cause you're certain of. It always carries a 'maybe' hedge; for a definite cause-effect, drop to plain 그래서 (e.g. 비가 와서 길이 막혀요).
Attaching a request or command after it ('그래서 그런지 좀 도와주세요'). It links a cause to an OBSERVED result, so it must end in a statement of what you noticed, not an imperative.
Mishandling the connector on a noun: it's 주말이라 그런지 (N+이라), not 주말이어서 그런지 in casual speech. With 이다, the natural form is N(이)라 그런지.

structuredNuance.t: 그런지 = '(I wonder) whether it's so' — the -ㄴ지 ending is a self-directed question that bakes uncertainty into the clause. So 그래서 그런지 literally means 'so, whether it's because of that…' and the real English sense is 'maybe that's why / perhaps that's the reason' — always hedged, never definite.

Use it when you notice a result and want to name a likely — but unconfirmed — cause. Extremely common in casual and casual-polite conversation, both spoken and texted. The pattern is neutral in register: 그래서 그런지 (standalone), -아서 그런지 (verb), -(이)라 그런지 (noun) all ride any speech level. Not typical in formal reports or academic writing, where you'd use 아마도 … 때문인 것으로 보인다 instead.

그래서 ('so, therefore') states a cause you're certain of — the result is definite. 그래서 그런지 adds a hedge — the result is observed but the causal link is your best guess. 덕분에 ('thanks to') credits a positive cause with gratitude and no uncertainty. 탓에 ('because of,' blame) attributes a negative result with certainty to a cause.

V/A-아서/어서 그런지 (cause = verb/adjective clause) → N(이)라 그런지 (cause = noun) → 그래서 그런지 (cause just stated in previous sentence). All share the same 그런지 hedge. The negative: 그래서 그런 건 아닌지 ('maybe it's NOT because of that') escalates the speculation.

Two traps: (1) Using plain 그래서 when you're only guessing — it sounds overconfident if the link is uncertain; add 그런지 to signal the hedge. (2) Trying to follow 그래서 그런지 with a request or command — it's a cause-to-observed-result connector, so only a statement of what you noticed can follow, never an imperative. And for nouns, use N(이)라 그런지, not 이어서 그런지, which is unnatural in everyday speech.

expressions.english: Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그건 그렇고 is a practical expression meaning "Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)".
expressions.explanation: "Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)" — that is 그건 그렇고 (geugeon geureoko). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그건 그렇고, 점심 뭐 먹을까요? ("Anyway, what should we eat for lunch?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Anyway, what should we eat for lunch?
usagePhrases.note: Pivoting cleanly from a closed topic to a new one

usagePhrases.ko: 그건 그렇고 너 요즘 회사는 어때?
usagePhrases.romanization: geugeon geureoko neo yojeum hoesaneun eottae?
usagePhrases.en: By the way, how's work these days?
usagePhrases.note: Casual subject change with a friend; signals 'I've set the previous thing aside'

usagePhrases.ko: 그건 그렇다 치고, 다음 얘기 해요.
usagePhrases.romanization: geugeon geureota chigo, daeum yaegi haeyo.
usagePhrases.en: Setting that aside, let's move on.
usagePhrases.note: 그건 그렇다 치고 = 'even granting that, anyway' — stronger, implies more deliberate shelving
그나저나 = close synonym; almost interchangeable but feels slightly more colloquial

examples.en: Anyway, did you eat?
examples.note: Quickest possible pivot to a new question — one topic closed, one opened

examples.ko: A: 그 드라마 결말이 좀 아쉬웠어요. B: 그러게요. 그건 그렇고, 주말에 시간 돼요?
examples.romanization: A: geu deurama gyeolmari jom aswiwosseoyo. B: geureogeyo. geugeon geureoko, jumare sigan dwaeyo?
examples.en: A: That drama's ending was a bit disappointing. B: Right. Anyway, are you free this weekend?
examples.note: Acknowledge the previous point, then steer toward unrelated business — the two-step pivot

examples.ko: 회의 보고는 잘 끝났어요. 그건 그렇고, 아까 말씀하신 그 책 제목이 뭐였죠?
examples.romanization: hoeui bogoneun jal kkeunnasseoyo. geugeon geureoko, akka malsseumhasin geu chaek jemogi mwoyeotjyo?
examples.en: The meeting report wrapped up fine. By the way, what was the title of that book you mentioned earlier?
examples.note: Real situation: parking a work topic to reopen an earlier unrelated thread

expressions.nuance: A friendly topic-switcher that literally says 'that — that's so, and…' (그건 = 그것은 contracted; 그렇고 = 그렇다 'to be so' + connective -고). It gently certifies the current topic as settled before swinging to a new one — you're acknowledging, not dropping, which is why it never sounds abrupt or rude. Compare three close neighbors: 그건 그렇고 closes a topic to open any new, unrelated one; 그나저나 ('anyway, be that as it may') is nearly interchangeable and equally common; but 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it's come up') does the OPPOSITE — it segues to a RELATED point, riding the current topic rather than leaving it. So the decision is: is your next remark connected to what's being discussed? Then use 말이 나왔으니까. Are you leaving the topic entirely? Use 그건 그렇고. Register is casual-polite, natural in both speech and written chat. Two English-speaker pitfalls: 'by the way' in English can preface a jab or a sudden challenge, but 그건 그렇고 only steers topics — never pushes back. And the spelling: 그렇고 keeps the ㅎ from 그렇다 (do NOT write 그러고, which comes from the different verb 그러다).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it to disagree or push back, the way English 'by the way…' sometimes does. 그건 그렇고 only changes the topic; to object you'd say 그건 아니고 ('that's not it') or 그렇긴 한데 ('that may be, but…').
Spelling 그렇고 as 그러고. 그렇고 comes from 그렇다 ('to be so') and keeps the ㅎ; 그러고 comes from 그러다 ('to do so') and means something else. Different verb, different meaning.
Using it to introduce a closely RELATED follow-up. If the new remark grows out of the same topic, the natural choice is 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it came up'); 그건 그렇고 implies you're leaving the topic behind.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'that thing (그건 = 그것은) — it is so, and… (그렇고).' The real effect: a polite certification that the previous topic is accepted and closed, followed by an opening for something new. Not a dismissal — an acknowledgment, then a pivot.

Use when you want to leave a topic behind cleanly without the previous speaker feeling ignored — you've 'filed' their point before moving on. Casual-polite (해요체) in default use; works equally in 반말 between friends (그건 그렇고 너 밥은 먹었어?). Very common in spoken Korean and texted conversation. Polite formal registers tend to use 그 점은 그렇고 or 그 부분은 그렇다 치고 in meetings.

그나저나 is an almost interchangeable swap — slightly more colloquial, the same casual register, same function. 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it's come up') is the OPPOSITE: it leans INTO the current topic rather than switching away. 아무튼/어쨌든 ('anyway, in any case') can also switch topics but has a stronger 'regardless' flavor that can dismiss rather than acknowledge.
그건 그렇고 (standard) → 그건 그렇다 치고 (stronger: 'even granting that') → 그나저나 (near-synonym, slightly more colloquial) → 뭐 그건 그렇고 (softened with 뭐 for an even more casual pivot).

Two traps: (1) Using it to disagree or push back — English 'by the way' can preface a challenge, but 그건 그렇고 never does; for objection use 그건 아니고 or 그렇긴 한데. (2) Spelling 그렇고 as 그러고 — 그렇고 comes from 그렇다 (keeps the ㅎ); 그러고 comes from the different verb 그러다 and means something else entirely.

expressions.english: Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)
expressions.shortExplanation: 말이 나왔으니까 is a practical expression meaning "Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)".
expressions.explanation: 말이 나왔으니까 (mari nawasseunikka) = "Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요. ("Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: mari nawasseunikka haneun marinde, jeodo geuge jom bulpyeonhaesseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too.
usagePhrases.note: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 = a set lead-in that signals an honest opinion is coming, softened by being 'invited' by the topic

usagePhrases.en: Since we're already on it, let's decide now.
usagePhrases.note: 말 나온 김에 = shorter, casual variant stressing convenient timing: 'while we're at it'

usagePhrases.ko: 여행 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 다음에 같이 갈래요?
usagePhrases.romanization: yeohaeng mari nawasseunikka marinde, daeume gachi gallaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Speaking of travel — want to go together next time?
usagePhrases.note: Topic-surfacing pattern: name the topic + 말이 나왔으니까 + request

usagePhrases.en: Since money came up, I'll be honest.
usagePhrases.note: 얘기가 나왔으니까 = 'since the talk (얘기) has come up' — 얘기 variant is equally natural

examples.en: Since it's come up, let me ask just one more thing.
examples.note: Short segue into a single follow-up question — the follow-up must be genuinely related

examples.ko: A: 회식은 다음 주 금요일이에요. B: 아, 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 저는 그날 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: hoesigeun daeum ju geumyoirieyo. B: a, mari nawasseunikka marinde, jeoneun geunal jom neujeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: The team dinner is next Friday. B: Oh, since it's come up — I'll probably be a bit late that day.
examples.note: Adding relevant information while the topic is still live; 아, 말이 나왔으니까 말인데 is a very natural spoken cluster

examples.ko: 이사 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 혹시 그 동네에 괜찮은 집 있으면 좀 소개해 줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: isa mari nawasseunikka marinde, hoksi geu dongnee gwaenchaneun jip isseumyeon jom sogaehae jul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Speaking of moving — if you happen to know a decent place in that neighborhood, could you put me onto it?
examples.note: Real situation: riding the current topic into a polite, related request — notice 혹시 and -아 줄 수 있어요? soften the ask

expressions.nuance: A spoken segue that piggybacks on a topic SOMEONE JUST RAISED so your follow-up feels naturally invited rather than out of nowhere. It parses as 말이 ('the topic/word,' subject) + 나왔으니까 (나오다 'to come out,' past form 나왔다 + -(으)니까 'since/because'), literally 'since the subject has come out [just now].' The past tense is essential — the topic has ALREADY surfaced. The fuller idiom 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it's come up, this is what I want to say…') cushions a candid remark or a small request by framing it as triggered by the conversation, not by your own agenda. Two sharp contrasts: against 그건 그렇고, which switches AWAY to an unrelated topic — 말이 나왔으니까 leans INTO the current one; against 말 나온 김에 (using -(으)ㄴ 김에 'while we're at it'), which stresses opportune timing ('let's decide NOW while the subject is live') rather than the candid-addition flavor. English-speaker pitfall: 'speaking of which' in English can drift far from the original topic, but 말이 나왔으니까 requires a genuinely related thread that just surfaced. And like all these lead-ins, it's grammatically incomplete — the real remark must follow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it to jump to an unrelated topic, the way English 'speaking of which' can drift. 말이 나왔으니까 requires the point to be genuinely tied to what just came up; for an unrelated switch use 그건 그렇고.
Leaving it dangling as if it were a full sentence. It's a lead-in — you must follow it with the actual remark or request (often via …말인데, …할게요, …물어볼게요).
Mis-conjugating 나오다: it's 나왔으니까 (past + 으니까), not 나오니까. The topic has ALREADY come up, so the past tense is what makes the 'now that it's surfaced' meaning work.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'since the topic (말이) has come out (나왔으니까).' The past tense 나왔 is load-bearing: the topic has ALREADY surfaced in the conversation just now. Real meaning: 'I'm adding something related while the door is open — you opened this topic, not me, so my addition feels invited.' It frames your remark as a natural, non-pushy extension.

Use it when the other person has JUST mentioned a topic you have a related comment or question on — you ride their wave rather than changing the subject. Casual-polite 해요체 in default use. Short variant 말 나온 김에 (spoken, casual) is common with friends. The fuller 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 softens a candid remark or request especially well in semi-formal settings like team chats or with acquaintances. Not typical in formal writing or presentations.

그건 그렇고 ('anyway, by the way') does the OPPOSITE — it switches AWAY from the current topic to something unrelated; 말이 나왔으니까 stays ON the current topic. 말 나온 김에 shares the same base but stresses TIMING: 'let's do it now while the subject is live,' rather than 'I have something related to add.' 주제가 나온 김에 is a more formal variant with the same logic.
말이 나왔으니까 (standard) → 말이 나왔으니까 말인데 (softer, candid-remark version) → 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 (fullest version, most cushioned) → 말 나온 김에 (casual, timing-focused) → 얘기가 나왔으니까 (얘기 variant).

English 'speaking of which' can drift loosely from the original topic — Korean 말이 나왔으니까 demands the new point be genuinely tied to what JUST came up. For an unrelated topic switch, use 그건 그렇고. Also: it's incomplete on its own — the follow-up remark must come immediately (often via 말인데, 물어볼게요, 솔직히 말하면). And mis-conjugating: it's 나왔으니까 (past 나왔다 + 으니까), not 나오니까 — the past tense is what makes 'since it's surfaced' work.

expressions.english: Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)
expressions.shortExplanation: 다행이네요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)".
expressions.explanation: 다행이네요 (dahaengineyo) means "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다 잘 끝났다니 다행이네요. ("I'm glad to hear it all worked out."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'm glad to hear it all worked out.
usagePhrases.note: Reacting with relief to good news you've just heard; -다니 = 'the fact that…'
다행이다 = casual; 정말 ('really') adds weight and sincerity

usagePhrases.en: It could've been worse / Silver lining.
usagePhrases.note: 불행 중 다행 = fixed idiom: '(something) fortunate amid (greater) misfortune'
V/A-아서/어서 다행이다 = 'lucky that ~' — attaches the relieving clause directly

examples.ko: A: 시험 통과했어요. B: 아, 다행이네요.
examples.romanization: A: siheom tonggwahaesseoyo. B: a, dahaengineyo.
examples.en: A: I passed the exam. B: Oh, what a relief.
examples.note: Bare relief reaction — the -네요 ending signals spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth

examples.ko: A: 검사 결과 괜찮대요. B: 아, 다행이네요. 저도 걱정 많이 했어요.
examples.romanization: A: geomsa gyeolgwa gwaenchantaeyo. B: a, dahaengineyo. jeodo geokjeong mani haesseoyo.
examples.en: A: The test results are fine. B: Oh, what a relief. I was really worried too.
examples.note: Relief on someone else's behalf + sharing your own worry — shows genuine care

examples.ko: 가방에 있을 줄은 몰랐어요. 진짜 잃어버린 줄 알고 한참 찾았는데, 있어서 정말 다행이에요.
examples.romanization: gabange isseul jureun mollasseoyo. jinjja ireobeorin jul algo hancham chajanneunde, isseoseo jeongmal dahaengieyo.
examples.en: I had no idea it was in my bag. I really thought I'd lost it and searched for ages — I'm so relieved it turned up.
examples.note: Real situation: the longer build-up ('I thought… I searched…') makes the 정말 다행이에요 payoff feel earned and natural

expressions.nuance: A warm, sincere reaction of relief at a bad outcome that has been avoided. The core noun 다행 is Sino-Korean 多幸 — literally 'much (多) good fortune (幸)' — so the phrase means 'how fortunate' rather than just 'good.' When aimed at someone else's news it reads as caring ('I'm genuinely relieved FOR you'); about your own situation it's a heartfelt 'phew.' The -네요 ending (해요체) adds spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth — a beat more emotional than the flatter 다행이에요. The attached pattern -아서/어서 다행이에요 lets you name exactly what you're relieved about: 늦지 않아서 다행이에요 ('good thing we weren't late'), 없어서 다행이에요 ('lucky there wasn't any'). Two sharp neighbors: 잘됐네요 ('that turned out well / good for you') celebrates a positive OUTCOME, while 다행이에요 specifically exhales relief that something bad was AVOIDED; and 축하해요 ('congratulations') marks an earned achievement, not a near-miss someone survived. Casual form: 다행이다 (반말). Critical English-speaker spelling trap: 다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다) vs 다행히 (adverb 'fortunately') — only the noun form can end a sentence as a reaction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 다행히네요 or ending a reaction with 다행히. 다행히 is the adverb 'fortunately' and modifies a verb; the relief reaction is 다행이에요/다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다).
Using it as congratulations for an achievement. 다행이에요 is relief that something bad was avoided; for an earned success say 축하해요, and for a happy outcome say 잘됐네요.
Saying 다행이네요 about a trivial non-event where nothing was ever at risk. The word implies there WAS a worry or danger that has now passed — without that tension it sounds odd.

structuredNuance.t: 다행 is Sino-Korean 多幸: 'much (多) good fortune (幸).' So 다행이네요 literally says 'it is much good fortune' — but the real meaning is an exhale of relief that something bad was narrowly avoided. It carries emotional warmth, not just a factual assessment.

Use it specifically when there WAS a real worry or danger that has now passed — good medical news, a found lost item, an escaped accident, a passed exam. Without that prior tension the word sounds hollow. Casual: 다행이다 (반말, close friends). Casual-polite: 다행이에요 / 다행이네요 (해요체, default). The -네요 form is more spontaneous and warm; 다행이에요 is slightly more composed. Safe with any interlocutor.

잘됐네요 ('that turned out well') celebrates a positive result; 다행이에요 exhales relief that a bad result was avoided — the underlying emotion is different. 축하해요 ('congratulations') marks an achievement earned through effort. 다행히 is the ADVERB form ('fortunately…') and modifies a verb in the middle of a sentence — it cannot end a sentence as a reaction.

다행이다 (반말) → 다행이에요 (polite, composed) → 다행이네요 (polite, spontaneous warmth) → 정말 다행이에요 (emphasis) → 진짜 다행이다 (casual emphasis) → V-아서/어서 다행이에요 (specifying what you're relieved about) → 불행 중 다행이에요 (fixed idiom: 'silver lining').

Two traps: (1) Spelling: 다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다 conjugated) vs 다행히 (adverb 'fortunately') — only 다행이에요/네요 ends a sentence as a standalone reaction; 다행히 must modify a verb. (2) Using it as congratulations for an achievement — 다행이에요 is relief that something bad was avoided, not praise for effort. For achievements, use 축하해요 or 잘했어요.

expressions.english: Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)
expressions.shortExplanation: 큰일 났다 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)".
expressions.explanation: "Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)" — that is 큰일 났다 (keunil natda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어. ("Oh no, I left my wallet at home."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어.
usagePhrases.romanization: keunil natda, jigabeul jibe dugo wasseo.
usagePhrases.en: Oh no, I left my wallet at home.
usagePhrases.note: Realizing a concrete problem mid-action; fully casual 반말

usagePhrases.en: What do I do, this is a disaster.
usagePhrases.note: 큰일 났어요 = polite; pairs naturally with 어떡해요 ('what do I do')

usagePhrases.en: At this rate something bad's going to happen.
usagePhrases.note: 큰일 나다 (future/conditional) = 'trouble will/might occur' — warning or prediction

usagePhrases.en: That was a close call — could've been a disaster.
usagePhrases.note: 큰일 날 뻔하다 = 'nearly went terribly wrong' — past near-miss

examples.en: Oh no, I'm late!
examples.note: Two-word alarm blurted in the heat of the moment — the simplest pattern

examples.ko: A: 기차 막차 끊겼대요. B: 헐, 큰일 났네요.
examples.romanization: A: gicha makcha kkeunkyeotdaeyo. B: heol, keunil nanneyo.
examples.en: A: They say the last train's gone. B: Oh no, we're in trouble.
examples.note: Reacting to bad news together; 헐 + 큰일 났네요 is a very natural pair

examples.ko: 발표 자료를 USB에 안 넣어 왔어, 이거 진짜 큰일 났다, 어떡하지?
examples.romanization: balpyo jaryoreul USBe an neoeo wasseo, igeo jinjja keunil natda, eotteokaji?
examples.en: I didn't load the presentation onto the USB — this is seriously bad, what do I do?
examples.note: Real situation: genuine panic; 이거 진짜 큰일 났다 + 어떡하지 is a go-to spoken cluster when things go wrong

expressions.nuance: A high-alarm reaction that literally says 'a big thing (큰일) has happened (났다)': 큰일 is 큰 ('big') + 일 ('matter/affair'), and 났다 is the past of 나다 ('to occur, break out'). Fired off the moment you realize something concrete has gone wrong or is about to. Tone covers the full range from genuine panic (발표 자료를 깜빡했을 때) to a half-joking 'uh-oh' (작은 실수에 과장할 때). Tense is critical: 큰일 났다/났어 (past) = trouble has ALREADY landed; 큰일 나겠다 (future/predictive) warns of trouble looming; 큰일 날 뻔했다 is a past near-miss ('almost went wrong'). Contrast with the gentler 어쩌나 ('oh dear, what to do'), which is soft, sympathetic worry usually for SOMEONE ELSE's predicament — 큰일 났다 is an urgent alarm about a concrete problem, typically your own. Register: 큰일 났다/났어 (casual), 큰일 났어요 (polite); it pairs naturally with 어떡해 ('what do I do'). One spelling fact: in this fixed expression 큰일 is treated as one compound noun — don't split it to 큰 일 in text, which reads as a 'big task/job' rather than the idiom.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 큰 일 in this fixed expression. Here 큰일 ('serious trouble') is treated as one word; written apart, 큰 일 reads literally as 'a big task' and loses the idiom.

Using the past 큰일 났다 for trouble that hasn't happened yet. For looming danger use the future/conditional: 이러다 큰일 나겠다 ('something bad's going to happen at this rate') or 큰일 날 뻔했다 ('almost went wrong').

Deploying it for minor annoyances (a small typo, a tiny delay). It implies a genuinely serious problem; overusing it for trifles makes you sound melodramatic. For small hiccups, 어떡하지 or 아 이런 fits better.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'a big affair (큰일) has broken out (났다).' Real meaning: an urgent, alarmed reaction to a concrete problem that has just materialized or been realized. The 'broke out' framing (나다 = to occur, emerge) implies the trouble arrived suddenly — not a gradual worry but an acute alert.

Use it when a concrete, specific problem has just come to light or you've just realized a mistake — left wallet behind, missed a deadline, last train gone. Tone ranges from genuine alarm to exaggerated comic 'uh-oh.' Casual: 큰일 났다 / 났어 (반말). Polite: 큰일 났어요. Pairs beautifully with 어떡해(요) ('what do I do'). Don't use it at truly trivial inconveniences — even comedically, the baseline implies a real or plausible problem.

어쩌나 ('oh dear') is softer, warmer, and usually aimed at SOMEONE ELSE's difficulty — sympathy, not alarm. 어떡해 ('what do I do') is equally alarmed but focuses on the need for a solution; 큰일 났다 focuses on the gravity of the problem itself. 아, 망했다 ('ah, I'm done for / ruined') is more self-deprecating and final-sounding.

큰일 났다/났어 (past, trouble landed) → 큰일 났어요 (polite) → 이러다 큰일 나겠다 (future: 'at this rate trouble will come') → 큰일 날 뻔했다 (past near-miss: 'almost went wrong') → 진짜 큰일 났다 (emphatic). Often paired: 큰일 났어, 어떡하지?

Two traps: (1) Spacing: in this fixed expression 큰일 is one compound noun ('serious trouble'); written as 큰 일 (two words) it reads as 'a big job/task' — the idiom dissolves. (2) Tense: don't use the past 났다 for trouble that hasn't happened yet — use 나겠다 (predictive) or 날 뻔했다 (near-miss). The past form means the bad thing has ALREADY occurred.

expressions.english: Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)
expressions.shortExplanation: 어쩌나 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)".
expressions.explanation: 어쩌나 (eojjeona) = "Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 아이고, 어쩌나. ("Oh dear, what to do."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 아이고 + 어쩌나 = classic pair; the 아이고 amplifies the sympathetic sigh

usagePhrases.en: Oh no, what now — the tickets are all sold out.
usagePhrases.note: 이를 어쩌나 = 'what to do about this' — the 이를 adds a lamenting 'alas'

usagePhrases.en: I was worried, but it sorted itself out.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩌나 했는데 = 'I was thinking (anxiously) 어쩌나, but…' — embeds the word in reported thought

usagePhrases.en: You have to go alone? Oh dear.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩌니 = slightly softer/more old-fashioned color; same sympathetic murmur

examples.en: Oh no, and it's raining.
examples.note: Minimal sympathetic murmur — one breath, no follow-up needed

examples.ko: A: 감기가 안 낫네요. B: 어쩌나, 병원은 가 보셨어요?
examples.romanization: A: gamgiga an nanneyo. B: eojjeona, byeongwoneun ga bosyeosseoyo?
examples.en: A: My cold won't go away. B: Oh no — have you seen a doctor?
examples.note: Sympathy for another's trouble + a caring follow-up question; the -나 ending signals it's a felt response, not a real question

examples.ko: 면접에 늦으면 어쩌나 싶어서 새벽부터 조마조마했어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobe neujeumyeon eojjeona sipeoseo saebyeokbuteo jomajomahaesseoyo.
examples.en: I was on edge since dawn, fretting over what I'd do if I were late to the interview.
examples.note: Real situation: 어쩌나 싶다 = 'I kept anxiously thinking 어쩌나' — embedded inner worry, past tense

expressions.nuance: A soft exclamation of concern, worry, or tenderness — 'oh dear, what's to be done.' It contracts from 어찌하나 ('how shall [I/we] do it'): 어찌 ('how') + 하다 ('do') + the musing -나 ending, a self-directed question you murmur aloud rather than actually ask. That self-directed quality is why it lands as a feeling — an empathetic sigh — not a genuine request for instructions. It can stand alone as a reaction or nest inside a clause: …면 어쩌나 싶다 ('worrying that…') / 어쩌나 했는데 ('I was anxiously thinking, but…'). The crucial contrast is with 큰일 났다: 큰일 났다 is a loud, urgent alarm about your own concrete problem, whereas 어쩌나 is gentler and warmer, typically aimed at SOMEONE ELSE's predicament — concern, not panic. Near-synonyms carry different angles: 어쩌지 leans toward your OWN dilemma ('what should I do about this?'), 어쩌니 is a slightly softer, old-fashioned sister form, and 이를 어쩌나 adds a lament flavor ('alas, what to do about this'). English-speaker pitfall: because it LOOKS and ends like a question, learners answer it or deploy it to solicit advice. It is not a genuine question — for real advice-seeking, use 어떻게 하죠? or 어떡하면 좋을까요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating standalone 어쩌나 as a real question and waiting for / giving an answer. It's an expression of feeling, not a request for advice. To actually ask, use 어떻게 하죠? or 어떡하면 좋아요?
Aiming it at someone as criticism ('어쩌나' with a blaming tone). It conveys sympathy and worry, never reproach — pointing it accusingly at a person misreads the warmth built into it.
Confusing 어쩌나 (soft worry, often for others) with 어쩌지 (your own 'what should I do'). They overlap, but 어쩌지 fits self-directed indecision better, while 어쩌나 suits sighing over another's trouble.

structuredNuance.t: Contracted from 어찌하나 — 어찌 ('how') + 하다 ('do/handle') + the musing -나 ending ('I wonder…'). Literally 'how shall [one] handle this, I wonder?' But the real meaning is an empathetic sigh of concern, not a request for a plan. The self-directed -나 is what makes it feel like a murmur rather than a real question.

Best aimed at ANOTHER person's difficulty or bad news — a sick friend, bad exam result, a missed opportunity. Signals you care without forcing a solution. It can also express your own quiet inner worry when embedded: 면 어쩌나 싶어서 걱정했어요. Register is casual and slightly warm-old-fashioned; it's equally at home in 반말 and 해요체 speech. Not used in formal professional contexts — too emotionally soft. Close synonyms: 아이고 (adds exclamatory weight), 이를 어쩌나 (adds lament).

큰일 났다 is a loud alarm about your OWN concrete problem (urgent, specific); 어쩌나 is a gentle sigh, typically over someone ELSE's predicament (concern, not panic). 어쩌지 targets your own dilemma ('what should I personally do?'). 어쩌니 is the same tone but slightly softer and more old-fashioned in flavor. 어떡해 ('what do I do') is more panicked and urgent than all of them.

어쩌나 (standard sigh) → 이를 어쩌나 (stronger lament: 'alas, what to do about this') → 어쩌니 (softer, old-fashioned sister) → 어쩌나 했는데 (reported inner anxiety, 'I was anxiously thinking…') → -면 어쩌나 싶다 (embedded worry: 'worried that if…').

Because it ends with -나 and looks like a question, English speakers answer it as if it were a request for advice, or they use it to actually ask for help. It is an empathetic murmur, not a genuine question. For real advice-seeking, use 어떻게 하죠? ('what should we/I do?') or 어떡하면 좋을까요? ('what would be the best way to handle this?'). Also: pointing it at someone in an accusatory tone ('어쩌나?!' as blame) misreads its inherent sympathy — it conveys concern, never reproach.

expressions.english: That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그럴 수도 있죠 is a practical expression meaning "That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)".
expressions.explanation: 그럴 수도 있죠 (geureol sudo itjyo) means "That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 뭐, 그럴 수도 있죠. ("Well, that can happen, I suppose."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Well, that can happen, I suppose.
usagePhrases.note: Accepting something gracefully — 뭐 softens it further into a relaxed shrug

usagePhrases.en: That can happen — everyone makes mistakes.
usagePhrases.note: 그럴 수도 있지 = 반말, casual reassurance; adding the reason 누구나 실수하잖아 makes it warmer
Conditioned with -으면: 'IF [reason], then that's forgivable'

usagePhrases.en: I suppose that could be the case.
usagePhrases.note: 그럴 수도 있겠네요 = one step more tentative: 'I imagine that could happen' — conceding a point as plausible

examples.ko: A: 제가 길을 잘못 들었어요. B: 그럴 수도 있죠.
examples.romanization: A: jega gireul jalmot deureosseoyo. B: geureol sudo itjyo.
examples.en: A: I took the wrong road. B: That happens.
examples.note: Short, easygoing absolution — zero blame, maximum generosity

examples.ko: A: 그 사람이 오해했나 봐요. B: 그럴 수도 있죠, 설명이 좀 부족했으니까요.
examples.romanization: A: geu sarami ohaehaenna bwayo. B: geureol sudo itjyo, seolmyeongi jom bujokaesseunikkayo.
examples.en: A: I think they misunderstood. B: That's possible — the explanation was a bit lacking.
examples.note: Conceding a reasonable point and then adding a reason; validates without endorsing

examples.ko: A: 제가 깜빡하고 답장을 못 했어요, 죄송해요. B: 괜찮아요, 그럴 수도 있죠, 바쁘셨을 텐데요 뭐.
examples.romanization: A: jega kkamppakago dapjangeul mo taesseoyo, joesonghaeyo. B: gwaenchanayo, geureol sudo itjyo, bappeusyeosseul tendeyo mwo.
examples.en: A: I forgot to reply, I'm sorry. B: It's fine, that happens — you must've been busy.
examples.note: Real situation: warmly waving off a small slip; 뭐 at the end softens further into a comfortable, light shrug

expressions.nuance: An easygoing, generous phrase meaning 'that falls within the range of normal — no big deal.' It's built from 그렇다 ('to be so') → 그럴 (prospective modifier, 'such a thing happening') + 수도 있다 ('there's even the possibility'), with 수 being the bound noun for 'possibility/ability.' The -죠 ending (from -지요) fishes for soft mutual agreement — 'right?' — which is what makes it feel understanding rather than merely declarative. Its core job is to forgive a minor mistake, validate a feeling, or grant that a possibility is reasonable. The warm counterpoint is 말도 안 돼요 ('no way / that makes no sense'), and the near-opposite twin is 그럴 리가 없죠 ('there's no way that's true') — identical rhythm, flipped meaning. Learn the one-word swap: 수 ('possibility') → 리 ('reason/likelihood that') turns acceptance into disbelief. Casual form: 그럴 수도 있지. The English-speaker pitfall: because it means 'understandable / no harm done,' deploying it in response to something genuinely serious or a real grievance reads as flippant and dismissive — as if you're shrugging off something that actually matters.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Using it to brush off something serious. 그럴 수도 있죠 means 'that's understandable / no big deal,' so applied to a real problem or a hurt feeling it sounds flippant. For weighty matters, acknowledge properly rather than minimizing.
Confusing 그럴 수도 있죠 (accepting: 'it's possible / that happens') with 그럴 리가 없죠 (denying: 'no way that's true'). The 수 vs 리 swap reverses the meaning entirely.
Spacing 그럴 수도 as 그럴수도. 수 is a bound noun and stays a separate word: 그럴 수도 있죠. Writing it joined is a common orthography slip.

structuredNuance.t: 수 is the bound noun 'possibility/ability'; 수도 있다 = 'there is even the possibility of it being so.' So literally: 'there could even be such a case.' The real effect is warmly generous absolution — 'that's within the normal range of human experience, so no judgment.'

Best for small mistakes, understandable lapses, or plausible possibilities you want to grant without fully endorsing. Forgiving a forgotten reply, validating a misread, accepting someone's tentative theory. Casual-polite 해요체 default. Casual: 그럴 수도 있지 (반말). One notch more tentative: 그럴 수도 있겠네요. Not for serious transgressions or major failures — it will sound like you're minimizing a real problem.

그럴 리가 없죠 ('there's no way that's true') is the near-opposite — identical rhythm but 수 → 리 flips from acceptance to denial. 괜찮아요 ('it's fine') is warmer and more complete forgiveness; 그럴 수도 있죠 accepts the possibility without fully absolving. 어쩔 수 없죠 ('can't be helped') accepts something as inevitable rather than understandable.
그럴 수도 있죠 (standard) → 그럴 수도 있지 (반말) → 그럴 수도 있겠네요 (tentative, 'I suppose') → 뭐 그럴 수도 있죠 (extra relaxed shrug) → 바쁘면 그럴 수도 있죠 (conditioned: 'if X, then understandable').

Two traps: (1) Using it to shrug off something serious — 'understandable / no big deal' reads as dismissive when the situation calls for real acknowledgment. (2) Confusing 그럴 수도 있죠 (accepts: 'it's possible / that happens') with 그럴 리가 없죠 (denies: 'no way that's true'). Swapping 수 and 리 completely reverses the meaning. Also: spacing — 그럴 수도 (수 is a separate bound noun), not 그럴수도.

expressions.english: I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그러는 게 좋겠어요 is a practical expression meaning "I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)".
expressions.explanation: "I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)" — that is 그러는 게 좋겠어요 (geureoneun ge jokesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요. ("Yes, I think that'd be best."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Yes, I think that'd be best.
usagePhrases.note: Short endorsement of a course ALREADY raised in the conversation — 그러다 = 'to do so' stands in for the mentioned action

usagePhrases.en: If you're tired, you'd better rest a bit.
usagePhrases.note: V-는 게 좋겠다 = 'had better ~'; casual 반말; the -겠- bakes in polite tentativeness

usagePhrases.en: It'd be best to book in advance.
usagePhrases.note: Recommending a sensible step proactively; V-는 게 좋겠어요 with the actual verb named

usagePhrases.en: I don't think you should do that.
usagePhrases.note: Negative form: 그러지 않는 게 좋겠어요 = gentle 'better not' / 'I'd advise against it'

examples.en: That would be best.
examples.note: Bare endorsement of an idea on the table — simplest, most minimal form

examples.ko: A: 의사한테 한번 물어볼까요? B: 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: uisahante hanbeon mureobolkkayo? B: ne, geureoneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Should I ask the doctor? B: Yes, that'd be the way to go.
examples.note: Backing a wise action someone just proposed — 그러는 게 echoes their suggestion

examples.ko: 내일 아침 일찍 출발해야 하니까, 오늘은 일찍 자는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: naeil achim iljjik chulbalhaeya hanikka, oneureun iljjik janeun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: Since we have to leave early tomorrow morning, you'd better get to sleep early tonight.
examples.note: Real situation: caring, reasoned advice; the -니까 reason clause anchors the recommendation and makes it feel considerate rather than bossy

expressions.nuance: A polite, gentle recommendation. The engine is V-는 게 좋겠다: 는 게 (from 는 것이, 'the act of doing') + 좋겠다 ('would be good'), literally 'it'd be good if [you/we] did ~,' i.e. English 'had better' or 'I think you should.' The -겠- is a supposition softener — it downgrades the bare fact (좋다, 'is good') into a tentative 'would probably be good,' so you advise without bossing. 그러는 게 좋겠어요 specifically endorses a course ALREADY raised in the conversation — 그러다 ('to do so') stands in for the action just mentioned — making it useful as 'yes, that sounds like the way to go.' Two contrasts matter: first, against the blunt command V-(으)세요 ('please do it') — 예약하세요 orders, 예약하는 게 좋겠어요 advises; second, against V-는 게 어때요? ('how about doing ~?'), which OFFERS an option and leaves the decision open, whereas -는 게 좋겠어요 expresses your considered RECOMMENDATION. Casual form: 그러는 게 좋겠어. The English-speaker pitfall: 'you'd better' in English can carry a threat of consequences, but Korean -는 게 좋겠어요 is always gentle and caring. Hear it as advice, not a warning.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it where a firm instruction is needed. -는 게 좋겠어요 is advice, not a command; for a clear directive (to a subordinate, on a sign, in instructions) use V-(으)세요.
Hearing 'you'd better' as a threat. In English 'you'd better…' can warn of consequences, but Korean V-는 게 좋겠어요 is gentle, considerate advice. Don't add a menacing tone that isn't there.
Spacing 그러는 게 as 그러는게. 게 is the contraction of 것이 ('the thing,' subject) and remains a separate word: 그러는 게 좋겠어요.

structuredNuance.t: V-는 게 좋겠다: '는 게' = 'the act of doing V' + '좋겠다' = 'would be good (I suppose).' The -겠- softens 좋다 from a fact into a tentative opinion. Real meaning: 'I think it'd be the best course of action' — advice, not command.

Use it to recommend an action to a peer, friend, or anyone you advise rather than command — a worried friend, a colleague considering options, a student choosing next steps. 그러는 게 좋겠어요 specifically echoes the other person's already-proposed action ('yes, do that'). Casual: 그러는 게 좋겠어 (반말). More formal: 그러시는 게 좋겠어요 (with subject honorific 시). Avoid using it downward to a subordinate who needs a clear directive — use V-(으)세요 for that.

V-(으)세요 is a polite command ('please do it') — more directive and appropriate for clear instructions. V-는 게 어때요? is a suggestion that invites the listener's judgment ('how about doing ~?') — more open-ended. V-는 게 좋겠어요 sits between them: a recommendation that expresses your considered opinion while leaving the decision to the other person.
그러는 게 좋겠어 (반말) → 그러는 게 좋겠어요 (casual-polite) → 그러시는 게 좋겠어요 (with -시- honorific, more deferential) → 그러지 않는 게 좋겠어요 (negative: 'better not') → V-는 편이 좋겠어요 (softer: 'it's probably better to…').

Two traps: (1) Hearing 'you'd better' as a warning or threat — English 'you'd better' can imply consequences, but Korean -는 게 좋겠어요 is always gentle and caring advice with no menace. (2) Spacing: 그러는 게 (게 = 것이 contracted, a separate word) — don't write 그러는게. The gap is mandatory in standard Korean spelling.

expressions.english: Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')
expressions.shortExplanation: 마음대로 하세요 is a practical expression meaning "Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')".
expressions.explanation: 마음대로 하세요 (maeumdaero haseyo) = "Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 편하실 대로 마음대로 하세요. ("Please do whatever's comfortable for you."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Please do whatever's comfortable for you.
usagePhrases.note: Warm version — genuinely leaving the choice to them; 편하실 대로 ('as you find comfortable') strengthens the generous reading
마음대로 해 = 반말; tone decides entirely whether it's kind or curt

usagePhrases.en: Help yourself, eat as much as you like.
usagePhrases.note: 마음껏 = 'to your heart's content' — shares the 마음 root but NEVER carries the cold edge; always warm encouragement

usagePhrases.en: Then do whatever you want, see if I care.
usagePhrases.note: -든가 makes it pointedly cold and dismissive; this form signals you've given up

examples.ko: A: 여기 앉아도 돼요? B: 네, 마음대로 하세요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi anjado dwaeyo? B: ne, maeumdaero haseyo.
examples.en: A: Can I sit here? B: Sure, go right ahead.
examples.note: Short, friendly permission — warm tone, clearly not cold

examples.ko: 메뉴는 마음대로 고르세요, 오늘은 제가 살게요.
examples.romanization: menyuneun maeumdaero goreuseyo, oneureun jega salgeyo.
examples.en: Order whatever you like — it's on me today.
examples.note: Warm: generously handing the choice over; 살게요 ('I'll pay') confirms the generous intent

examples.ko: A: 그냥 제 방식대로 할게요. B: …그래요, 마음대로 하세요.
examples.romanization: A: geunyang je bangsikdaero halgeyo. B: …geuraeyo, maeumdaero haseyo.
examples.en: A: I'll just do it my way. B: …Fine, suit yourself.
examples.note: Real situation: the pause (…) and flat delivery cue the cold, resigned, passive-aggressive reading — same words, opposite feeling

expressions.nuance: Literally 'act according to your heart' — from 마음 ('mind/heart') + -대로 ('in accordance with') + 하세요 ('please do'). The critical point is that tone is the entire message: said warmly with an open gesture it's genuine generosity ('go right ahead, no need to ask'); said flatly or with a sigh it flips into a frosty 'fine, do what you want, I give up' — the same words, opposite feeling, much like English 'suit yourself.' The -든가 variant (마음대로 하든가, 'do whatever, see if I care') pulls even further cold. The friendly cousin 마음껏 ('to your heart's content': 마음껏 드세요) shares the 마음 root but never carries the cold edge — so when you only mean warm encouragement, 마음껏 is the unambiguously safer pick. Casual: 마음대로 해 / 맘대로 해 (with 맘 as a casual contraction for 마음). Two pitfalls: first, because the icy reading triggers so easily, be careful with seniors or during any tension — it can land as dismissive even if you meant it warmly; second, 마음대로 is one word (no space before -대로), and 맘대로 is acceptable in casual speech but too informal for polite or written contexts.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Using it casually with a senior or in a tense moment without minding tone. The cold 'fine, whatever' reading triggers easily, so to a superior it can sound dismissive — soften with 편하실 대로 하세요 ('do as suits you') when you mean it warmly.
Spacing it as 마음 대로. -대로 is a particle attached to the noun, so it's one word: 마음대로. And 맘대로 (the 맘 contraction) is fine in casual speech but too informal for formal or written use.

Assuming it always sounds generous. Unlike 마음껏 ('to your heart's content,' always warm), 마음대로 하세요 can read as passive-aggressive depending on delivery — if you only mean encouragement, 마음껏 or 편하신 대로 is safer.

structuredNuance.t: 마음 ('heart/mind') + -대로 ('in accordance with') + 하세요 ('please do'): literally 'please act according to your heart.' The real meaning is ENTIRELY dependent on delivery — generous and warm (open permission) OR cold and resigned (passive-aggressive 'fine, whatever'). The words themselves are neutral; the tone is everything.

Warm reading: inviting someone to choose freely (menu, seat, schedule). Cold reading: after a disagreement where you've given up pushing back. Polite form: 마음대로 하세요 (해요체). Casual: 마음대로 해 / 맘대로 해 (반말). Sharply cold: 마음대로 하든가 (-든가 form). Extremely risky to use with seniors or in tense moments — even the polite form can read as dismissive if delivery is flat. In genuinely warm contexts, soften to 편하신 대로 하세요 or 마음껏 하세요.

마음껏 ('to your heart's content') shares the 마음 root and is ALWAYS warm — no cold reading possible (마음껏 드세요 = 'please eat as much as you like'). 편하신 대로 하세요 ('do as is comfortable for you') is similarly unambiguously warm. 알아서 하세요 ('figure it out yourself') is more dismissive-neutral, closer to the cold edge of 마음대로 하세요.

마음대로 하세요 (polite, ambiguous tone) → 마음대로 해 (반말) → 맘대로 해 (casual contraction, 반말) → 마음대로 하든가 (cold: 'do whatever, I don't care') → 마음껏 하세요 (unambiguously warm: 'do as much as you like') → 편하신 대로 하세요 (safely warm, formal).

Two traps: (1) Assuming it always sounds generous — unlike 마음껏, 마음대로 하세요 can flip cold depending on delivery, so be cautious with seniors or in tense moments; when you mean warmth, 마음껏 or 편하신 대로 is safer. (2) Spacing and register: 마음대로 is one word (no space before -대로); 맘대로 (contraction) is fine in casual text but too informal for polite or written contexts.

expressions.english: for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')
expressions.shortExplanation: 발등에 불 떨어지다 is a practical expression meaning "for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')".
expressions.explanation: 발등에 불 떨어지다 (baldeunge bul tteoreojida) means "for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새 했어. ("It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 떨어지다 is past here as 떨어져서 ('because it fell')

usagePhrases.ko: 마감이 코앞이라 이제 발등에 불 떨어졌어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: magami koapira ije baldeunge bul tteoreojyeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: The deadline's right there, so now it's crunch time.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; pairs naturally with 코앞 ('right in front')

usagePhrases.en: I only get moving once it's down to the wire.
usagePhrases.note: -아야 = 'only when/once'; describes a procrastinator habit

usagePhrases.ko: 발등에 불이 떨어졌는데 아직도 시작을 안 했어?
usagePhrases.romanization: baldeunge buri tteoreojyeonneunde ajikdo sijageul an haesseo?
usagePhrases.en: It's crunch time and you still haven't started?
usagePhrases.note: Subject 이/가 often added: 불이 떨어지다

examples.ko: A: 야, 발등에 불 떨어졌다, 마감이 내일이잖아! / B: 아, 진짜? 부랴부랴 해야겠다.
examples.romanization: A: ya, baldeunge bul tteoreojyeotda, magami naeirijana! / B: a, jinjja? buryaburya haeyagetda.
examples.en: A: Hey, it's crunch time — the deadline is tomorrow! / B: Oh, for real? Gotta rush.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 부랴부랴 ('in a frantic rush') is the natural partner adverb

examples.ko: 발등에 불 떨어지고 나서야 짐을 부랴부랴 쌌어요.
examples.romanization: baldeunge bul tteoreojigo naseoya jimeul buryaburya ssasseoyo.
examples.en: Only when it became urgent did I hurriedly pack.
examples.note: -고 나서야 = 'only after (something happened)'; classic procrastinator structure

examples.ko: 다들 발등에 불 떨어진 듯이 회의실로 뛰어갔어.
examples.romanization: dadeul baldeunge bul tteoreojin deusi hoeuisillo ttwieogasseo.
examples.en: Everyone ran to the meeting room like it was an emergency.
examples.note: Group panic; -ㄴ 듯이 = 'as if'; describes the sudden scramble

expressions.nuance: Literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot (발등)' — when a live ember lands on your instep you jump instantly, so this paints a crisis that has suddenly arrived and demands you drop everything this second. The near-synonym 코앞이다 ('right in front of your nose') only states that a deadline is close in time; 발등에 불 떨어지다 adds the involuntary, panicked scramble of having to act right now, which is why it so naturally pairs with 부랴부랴 ('frantically') and 밤새다 ('pull an all-nighter'). It carries a wry, self-aware, procrastinator's tone — Koreans use 발등에 불 떨어져야 움직인다 ('I only move once the fire hits my foot') as an almost affectionate admission of leaving things to the last minute. The scale from casual to polite is very wide: 발등에 불 떨어졌어 (casual) through 발등에 불 떨어진 상황입니다 (formal briefing). The English-speaker pitfall: do not read 떨어지다 as 'runs out' — here it means the fire 'fell/dropped' onto you, so the crisis has arrived, not vanished; and 발등 is specifically the instep/top of the foot, not just 발 ('foot').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't read it literally as a burn injury — it is about sudden urgency, not pain, so 'My foot got burned' is a complete mis-hearing.
It's 발등 (the top/instep of the foot), not 발 ('foot') — drop 등 and the vivid image of an ember landing on the exposed instep is lost.
Keep 떨어지다 in the right direction: it means the fire FELL (the crisis is here), so don't confuse it with the meaning 'to run out / be used up.'

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'fire (불) falls (떨어지다) onto the instep of the foot (발등)' — like a hot ember landing on your foot, you jump instantly. In use it means a crisis or deadline has arrived so suddenly and pressingly that you must act this very second with no buffer left.

Fits any situation where something once distant is now breathing down your neck — work deadlines, paperwork, exams, event preparations. Casual (발등에 불 떨어졌어) to polite (발등에 불 떨어진 상황이에요) to formal written context. Safe to use with friends, colleagues, and bosses. Often tinged with self-deprecating humor about procrastinating.

코앞이다 ('right in front of one's nose') states that a deadline is close in time but without the bodily panic. 발등에 불 떨어지다 adds the involuntary scramble — things are urgent AND you must move right now. 급하다 ('to be urgent') is the plain adjective; this idiom dramatizes the same idea with vivid imagery.

Particles shift freely: 불이 떨어지다 (subject 이) or 불 떨어지다 (topic/zero). Common extensions: 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새다 ('pull an all-nighter because it got urgent'), 발등에 불 떨어져야 움직이다 ('only move once the fire hits') for habitual procrastination.

Do not read 떨어지다 as 'run out' — here it means the fire 'fell/dropped' (crisis arrived), not 'ran out' (crisis ended). Also, 발등 is specifically the instep/top of the foot; dropping 등 removes the vivid image. Finally, this is not about injury — it is pure urgency metaphor.

expressions.english: to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')
expressions.shortExplanation: 코앞이다 is a practical expression meaning "to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')".
expressions.explanation: "to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')" — that is 코앞이다 (koapida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 시험이 코앞이야, 큰일 났어. ("The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; time sense, looming pressure

usagePhrases.en: The deadline's right on top of us, so it's hectic.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; -이라 = 'since it is'; very common with 마감

usagePhrases.en: The convenience store is right there but I'm too lazy to go.
usagePhrases.note: Distance sense — 'a stone's throw'

usagePhrases.en: It was right under my nose and I still couldn't find it.
usagePhrases.note: 코앞에 두다 = 'to have right in front of you'

examples.ko: A: 이사 날짜 언제야? / B: 코앞이야, 이번 주 토요일.
examples.romanization: A: isa naljja eonjeya? / B: koapiya, ibeon ju toyoil.
examples.en: A: When's the moving date? / B: Super soon — this Saturday.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 이사 날짜 ('moving date') with time sense

examples.ko: 설날이 코앞인데 기차표를 아직 못 구했어.
examples.romanization: seolnari koapinde gichapyoreul ajing mot guhaesseo.
examples.en: Lunar New Year is around the corner and I still can't get a train ticket.
examples.note: Seasonal urgency; 구하다 = 'to secure/get'

examples.en: The office is right by my place — five minutes on foot.
examples.note: Distance sense: X 코앞이다 = 'right by X'

expressions.nuance: Literally 'right in front of the nose' (코 'nose' + 앞 'front'), 코앞이다 frames something as extremely near — either in TIME (an event or deadline almost upon you) or in DISTANCE (a place a few steps away). The dividing line from the neutral near-synonym 가깝다 ('to be close') is vividness and immediacy: 가깝다 is a measurable, unemotional word ('the station is near'), while 코앞이다 dramatizes 'practically touching your face,' loading on urgency for time and a 'no excuse not to go' feeling for distance. When time is the axis it typically pairs with pressure: 마감이 코앞이라 정신없어요. The compound 코앞 is written as one word, not 코 앞. Register is casual-to-polite and the expression is extremely common in everyday speech. The English-speaker pitfall: 'right under my nose' in English usually means 'I missed something obvious,' but plain Korean 코앞이다 just means 'very near' — the 'missed the obvious' shade only appears when context (e.g. 코앞에 두고도 못 찾다) supplies it explicitly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Write 코앞 as one word, not 코 앞 — it's a fixed compound noun.
Context decides whether it means 'soon' (time) or 'nearby' (distance); don't assume only the time reading, or you'll misread 집 코앞 ('right by the house').
Don't auto-map it to the English idiom 'right under my nose' (= 'missed something obvious'); plain 코앞이다 just means 'very close.'

structuredNuance.t: 코앞 = 코 ('nose') + 앞 ('front'), literally 'right in front of the nose.' In use it means something is extremely near — either in time (an imminent event or deadline) or in physical distance (a place just a few steps away). It dramatizes closeness with the vivid image of something nearly touching your face.

Used constantly in casual and polite speech alike. TIME sense: 마감/시험/이사 날짜가 코앞이다 — an event is almost here and you feel the pressure. DISTANCE sense: 편의점/회사가 코앞이다 — a place is so close it would be silly not to go. Safe with anyone; no formality issues.

가깝다 ('to be close') is the neutral, measurable word — 'the station is near.' 코앞이다 dramatizes the same idea: 'practically touching your face,' making it feel more pressing for time and more obvious-convenience for distance. 임박하다 is the formal written equivalent for time-proximity.
코앞에 두다 ('to have/leave something right in front of you'), 코앞에서 놓치다 ('to miss something right there'). Spatial formula: [place] 코앞에 [place 2] 있다 ('place 2 is right in front of place 1').

'Right under my nose' in English usually means 'I missed something obvious,' but Korean 코앞 plainly means 'very near.' The 'missed the obvious' shade only appears when context (e.g. 코앞에 두고도 못 찾다) explicitly supplies it. Also write it as one word: 코앞, not 코 앞.

expressions.english: to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')
expressions.shortExplanation: 등골이 오싹하다 is a practical expression meaning "to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')".
expressions.explanation: 등골이 오싹하다 (deunggori ossakada) = "to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그 얘기 듣고 등골이 오싹했어. ("I got chills down my spine hearing that."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I got chills down my spine hearing that.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; fear/creepiness, past tense 오싹했어

usagePhrases.ko: 밤에 혼자 그 길 걸으니까 등골이 오싹하더라고요.
usagePhrases.romanization: bame honja geu gil georeunikka deunggori ossakadeoragoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Walking that road alone at night gave me the shivers.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; -더라고요 reports a felt experience

usagePhrases.ko: 사고 영상 보니까 등골이 다 오싹해.
usagePhrases.romanization: sago yeongsang bonikka deunggori da ossakae.
usagePhrases.en: Watching the accident footage sent a total chill down my spine.
usagePhrases.note: 다 here = 'completely,' intensifying the shiver

usagePhrases.en: Just thinking about it sends a chill down my back.
usagePhrases.note: 등골이 서늘하다 = close variant ('spine goes cool')

examples.ko: A: 그 귀신 나오는 장면에서 어땠어? / B: 등골이 오싹해서 눈도 못 뜨겠더라.
examples.romanization: A: geu gwisin naoneun jangmyeoneseo eottaesseo? / B: deunggori ossakaeseo nundo mot tteugetdeora.
examples.en: A: How did you feel at the ghost scene? / B: I had chills down my spine and could barely open my eyes.
examples.note: A/B exchange; horror-movie startle, 눈도 못 뜨겠더라 = 'could barely keep my eyes open'

examples.ko: 하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했다고 생각하니 등골이 오싹해.
examples.romanization: hamateomyeon keunil nal ppeonhaetdago saenggakani deunggori ossakae.
examples.en: Thinking I almost got into real trouble gives me the chills.
examples.note: 하마터면 ~ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost (nearly) happened'; dread over a close call

examples.ko: 그 사람 눈빛이 너무 차가워서 등골이 오싹했어요.
examples.romanization: geu saram nunbichi neomu chagawoseo deunggori ossakaesseoyo.
examples.en: His gaze was so cold it sent a shiver down my spine.
examples.note: Real-situation: an unsettling person, not weather cold; shows non-horror usage

expressions.nuance: 등골 is the spine or its marrow, and 오싹하다 is that sudden, involuntary cold-shudder, so together they capture the physical chill running down your back from fear, eeriness, or the retrospective dread of realizing you barely dodged disaster. It describes the bodily sensation rather than naming the emotion — which is why it is more vivid than just saying 무섭다 ('it's scary'). The near-synonym 등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool') conveys a quieter, more lingering unease — a slow dread — while 등골이 오싹하다 is the sharp, sudden goose-bump spike from a sudden noise, revelation, or image. Use it for horror, ghost stories, near-miss anecdotes, and cold-eyed strangers. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: this is fear-chills, NOT being physically cold from the weather (use 춥다 for that); the body-part partner 등골 collocates with 오싹하다 and 서늘하다 — 등골이 춥다 is unnatural; and note the romanization: 오싹 is the mimetic of a sudden shiver, so it also appears standalone as 오싹! when someone flinches.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about fear/dread chills, not feeling physically cold from the weather — for cold air you want 춥다, not 등골이 오싹하다.
Pair 등골 with 오싹하다 or 서늘하다 — don't swap in 춥다 ('cold'); '등골이 춥다' is not idiomatic.
Don't replace it with bare 무섭다 ('scary') when you mean the physical shiver — 무섭다 names the feeling, 등골이 오싹하다 conveys the spine reaction.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 등골 ('spine/spinal marrow') + 오싹하다 ('to go cold and shivery in an instant'). 실제 뜻: the involuntary spine-chill you feel from fear, eeriness, or the retroactive dread of a near-miss — emphasizing the physical bodily reaction rather than the emotion itself.

Fits horror movies, ghost stories, a frightening news story, a creepy stranger's gaze, or realizing you barely avoided danger. Casual to polite; fine among friends and in storytelling contexts. Not used in formal writing — switch to 공포를 느끼다 in serious/formal prose.

등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool') is the close variant — quieter, more lingering dread. 오싹하다 is the sharper spike from a sudden noise, image, or revelation. 무섭다 ('to be scared') names the emotion but gives no bodily sensation; 등골이 오싹하다 paints the physical shiver.
등골이 서늘하다 (slower chill/dread), 소름이 돋다 ('goosebumps rise' — same fear zone but on the skin surface), 오싹! as a standalone mimetic for a shiver. Intensifier: 등골이 다 오싹해 ('completely chilled').

This is fear-chills, not cold weather — for cold air use 춥다. The body-part partner 등골 collocates with 오싹하다 and 서늘하다, not 춥다 ('등골이 춥다' is unnatural). Also, 오싹하다 captures sudden fright; don't use it for general anxiety or unease — prefer 불안하다 for that.

expressions.english: to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)
expressions.shortExplanation: 입에 침이 마르다 is a practical expression meaning "to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)".
expressions.explanation: 입에 침이 마르다 (ibe chimi mareuda) means "to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라. ("Mom couldn't stop singing your praises."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라.
usagePhrases.romanization: eommaga neo chingchaneul ibe chimi mareuge hadeora.
usagePhrases.en: Mom couldn't stop singing your praises.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; usual frame 입에 침이 마르게 + 칭찬하다

usagePhrases.ko: 사장님이 그 직원을 입에 침이 마르도록 칭찬하셨어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: sajangnimi geu jigwoneul ibe chimi mareudorok chingchanhasyeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: The boss praised that employee to no end.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; 마르도록 ('to the point of drying') is a common form

usagePhrases.ko: 다들 그 식당을 입에 침이 마르게 추천해.
usagePhrases.romanization: dadeul geu sikdangeul ibe chimi mareuge chucheonhae.
usagePhrases.note: Extends to enthusiastic recommendations (추천하다)

usagePhrases.ko: 입에 침이 마르게 자랑하던데 진짜 좋은가 봐.
usagePhrases.romanization: ibe chimi mareuge jaranghadeonde jinjja joeunga bwa.
usagePhrases.en: They bragged about it endlessly, so it must be really good.
usagePhrases.note: With 자랑하다 = relentless bragging

examples.ko: A: 선생님이 오늘 뭐라고 하셨어? / B: 네 그림을 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하셨어.
examples.romanization: A: seonsaengnimi oneul mworago hasyeosseo? / B: ne geurimeul ibe chimi mareuge chingchanhasyeosseo.
examples.en: A: What did the teacher say today? / B: She praised your drawing to the skies, nonstop.
examples.note: A/B exchange; lavish praise reported naturally

examples.ko: 친구가 그 카페를 입에 침이 마르도록 얘기해서 가 봤어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga geu kapereul ibe chimi mareudorok yaegihaeseo ga bwasseoyo.
examples.en: My friend raved about that cafe so much that I finally went.
examples.note: Praise leading to action; -아서 ('so') links cause to result

examples.ko: 할머니는 손주 얘기만 나오면 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하세요.
examples.romanization: halmeonineun sonju yaegiman naomyeon ibe chimi mareuge chingchanhaseyo.
examples.en: Grandma gushes nonstop whenever her grandkids come up.
examples.note: Real-situation habitual gushing; -세요 honorific for grandma; -만 나오면 = 'whenever ~ comes up'

expressions.nuance: Literally 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — talk up someone or something for so long that your mouth runs dry, conveying lavish, tireless, unstoppable praise. The dividing line from plain 칭찬하다 ('to praise') is intensity and duration: a single 'good job' is 칭찬하다, whereas 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다 means gushing on and on without end. Crucially, this idiom almost never stands alone — it is an adverbial modifier that clamps onto a verb, nearly always 칭찬하다 ('praise'), 자랑하다 ('brag'), or 추천하다 ('recommend'), in the fixed adverbial forms 입에 침이 마르게 or 입에 침이 마르도록. The tone is warm, affectionate, and admiring — it is almost never used sarcastically. Register is casual-to-polite, appropriate from family to workplace storytelling. The English-speaker pitfalls: 이 idiom has nothing to do with literal thirst or dehydration ('dry mouth' as a medical symptom); thirst is 목이 마르다 ('my throat/neck is dry'), not 입에 침이 마르다, and mixing them causes real confusion.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It means praising endlessly, not literally being thirsty or having a dry mouth — for real thirst use 목이 마르다 ('my throat is dry').
Don't drop the verb — it's used as 입에 침이 마르게/마르도록 + (칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다), not as a standalone statement.
Don't conjugate it as a finished action ('입에 침이 말랐다' to describe one compliment); it lives in the adverbial -게/-도록 form modifying the praising verb.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 입 ('mouth') + 침 ('saliva') + 마르다 ('to dry up'), literally 'the saliva in one's mouth dries from talking so much.' 실제 뜻: to praise, brag about, or recommend something or someone lavishly and without stopping — the mouth works overtime until it runs dry.

Fits warm storytelling: a parent bragging about a child, a friend raving about a restaurant, a boss publicly lauding an employee. Tone is affectionate and admiring, never sarcastic. Casual to polite. Fine in family and work contexts. Not formal-written (use 극찬하다 'to lavish praise' in formal prose).

칭찬하다 ('to praise') is a single act — one compliment qualifies. 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다 is relentless, sustained gushing. 극찬하다 ('to lavish praise') is the formal/written equivalent. 자화자찬하다 ('to praise oneself') is boasting, but this idiom covers praising others too.
Two adverbial forms are both natural: 입에 침이 마르게 (plainer, more common) and 입에 침이 마르도록 (slightly more literary/emphatic, 'to the point of drying'). Always followed by a verb: ~게/~도록 + 칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다.

Nothing to do with literal thirst or dry-mouth symptoms — for real thirst use 목이 마르다 ('my throat is dry'). Also, this idiom needs a partner verb: never drop 칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다 and let it stand alone, or it loses its meaning. Don't conjugate it as a completed action to describe one compliment — it lives in the adverbial -게/-도록 form.

expressions.english: to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')
expressions.shortExplanation: 손발이 맞다 is a practical expression meaning "to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')".
expressions.explanation: "to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')" — that is 손발이 맞다 (sonbari matda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 우리 둘은 손발이 잘 맞아. ("The two of us work together really well."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: The two of us work together really well.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 잘 ('well') is the usual partner adverb

usagePhrases.ko: 새 팀이랑 손발이 맞아서 일이 수월해요.
usagePhrases.romanization: sae timirang sonbari majaseo iri suwolhaeyo.
usagePhrases.en: I'm in sync with the new team, so work goes smoothly.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; ~이랑 손발이 맞다 = 'in sync WITH ~'

usagePhrases.ko: 손발이 안 맞아서 자꾸 실수가 나.
usagePhrases.romanization: sonbari an majaseo jakku silsuga na.
usagePhrases.en: We're out of sync, so mistakes keep happening.
usagePhrases.note: 손발이 안 맞다 = the opposite

usagePhrases.ko: 오래 같이 일하니까 손발이 척척 맞네.
usagePhrases.romanization: orae gachi ilhanikka sonbari cheokcheong manne.
usagePhrases.en: We've worked together so long we're perfectly in sync.
usagePhrases.note: 척척 = 'smoothly, snappily,' an intensifying mimetic

examples.ko: A: 오늘 행사 어땠어요? / B: 팀이랑 손발이 딱 맞아서 무사히 끝냈어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul haengsa eottaesseoyo? / B: timirang sonbari ttang majaseo musahi kkeunnaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: How did the event go? / B: We were perfectly in sync as a team so it finished without a hitch.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 딱 맞다 = 'match exactly'; 무사히 = 'without incident'

examples.ko: 주방이랑 홀이 손발이 맞아야 장사가 잘돼요.
examples.romanization: jubangirang hori sonbari majaya jangsaga jaldwaeyo.
examples.en: The kitchen and the floor have to be in sync for business to run well.
examples.note: Restaurant teamwork; -아야 = 'only if/when'

examples.ko: 처음엔 손발이 안 맞았는데 이제 호흡이 잘 맞아요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen sonbari an majanneunde ije hoheubi jal majayo.
examples.en: At first we were out of sync, but now we work in great harmony.
examples.note: Real-situation arc; 호흡이 맞다 introduced as the close synonym for contrast

expressions.nuance: Literally 'hands and feet match,' it describes two or more people whose actions line up like a well-rehearsed team — the right rhythm where each anticipates what the other will do next. It is about working chemistry: coordinated task-timing, mutual anticipation, smooth handoffs. The dividing line from the near-synonym 호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') is subtle: both mean 'in sync,' but 손발이 맞다 stresses coordinated physical or operational action (who does what, when), while 호흡이 맞다 emphasizes an intuitive shared tempo or feel, and is especially common for performance partners or sports. Crucially, 손발이 맞다 is about professional/cooperative chemistry, NOT romantic compatibility or personality — for those use 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다. Register is casual-to-polite, ubiquitous at work, in sport, and whenever teamwork is the topic. The English-speaker pitfall: 'we match' or 'we get along' tempts learners to use it for personal affinity, but its domain is strictly shared action; and it is always mutual — mark the partner with ~와/과 or ~이랑.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Use it for teamwork/coordination, not for romantic or personality compatibility — that's 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다.
It needs two or more people — you can't be 손발이 맞다 by yourself; the partner is marked with ~와/과 or ~이랑 ('in sync WITH ~').
Don't confuse it with 호흡이 맞다 carelessly: 손발 stresses coordinated actions/tasks, 호흡 stresses intuitive shared rhythm.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 손 ('hands') + 발 ('feet') + 맞다 ('to match/fit'), literally 'hands and feet match.' 실제 뜻: two or more people work together in perfectly coordinated rhythm — each anticipates the other, tasks mesh without collision, teamwork flows.

Use it for work teams, restaurant kitchen-floor coordination, sports duos, project partners, any cooperative setting. Casual to polite. Safe between friends, coworkers, and in business contexts. Never in formal written reports — use 협업이 원활하다 ('cooperation proceeds smoothly') there.

호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') leans toward intuitive shared tempo — especially natural in performance or sport. 손발이 맞다 is more operational: who does what, timing of tasks. Both are positive; the choice is how you frame the sync. 잘 어울리다 / 궁합이 맞다 is for personality or romantic fit — not 손발이 맞다.
손발이 잘 맞다 (positive, 'work well together'), 손발이 안 맞다 (negative, 'out of sync'), 손발이 딱 맞다 ('match exactly, perfectly'). Intensifier mimetic 척척: 손발이 척척 맞다 ('work in perfect, snappy sync').

'We match' or 'we get along' tempts learners to use 손발이 맞다 for romantic or personality compatibility, but that belongs to 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다. 손발이 맞다 is strictly about coordinated action. It is inherently mutual — you cannot be 손발이 맞다 alone; mark the partner with ~와/과 or ~이랑.

expressions.english: to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')
expressions.shortExplanation: 발 벗고 나서다 is a practical expression meaning "to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')".
expressions.explanation: 발 벗고 나서다 (bal beotgo naseoda) = "to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 네가 발 벗고 나서 줘서 진짜 고마워. ("Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 네가 발 벗고 나서 줘서 진짜 고마워.
usagePhrases.romanization: nega bal beotgo naseo jwoseo jinjja gomawo.
usagePhrases.en: Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; -아 주다 ('do it for me') adds the favor nuance

usagePhrases.en: The neighbors went out of their way to help.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; -아서 chains 'stepped up AND helped'

usagePhrases.ko: 회사가 발 벗고 나서서 문제를 해결했어.
