usagePhrases.romanization: hoesaga bal beotgo naseoseo munjereul haegyeolhaesseo.
usagePhrases.en: The company actively stepped in and solved the problem.
usagePhrases.note: Subject can be an organization taking initiative

usagePhrases.ko: 친구 일이라면 발 벗고 나서는 사람이야.
usagePhrases.romanization: chingu iriramyeon bal beotgo naseoneun saramiya.
usagePhrases.en: He's the type to drop everything to help a friend.
usagePhrases.note: ~라면 ('when it comes to ~'); describes a generous character

examples.ko: A: 아무도 안 도와줘서 걱정이야. / B: 내가 발 벗고 나설게, 같이 하자.
examples.romanization: A: amudo an dowajwoseo geokjeongiya. / B: naega bal beotgo naseolge, gachi haja.
examples.en: A: Nobody's helping and I'm worried. / B: I'll roll up my sleeves and step in — let's do this together.
examples.note: A/B exchange; B volunteers wholeheartedly; -ㄹ게 = commitment

examples.ko: 선배가 발 벗고 나서서 취업을 도와줬어요.
examples.romanization: seonbaega bal beotgo naseoseo chwieobeul dowajwosseoyo.
examples.en: A senior went all in to help me find a job.
examples.note: Going above and beyond; shows the senior-junior helping dynamic common in Korean workplaces

examples.ko: 그 문제는 아무도 발 벗고 나서지 않아서 오래 방치됐어요.
examples.romanization: geu munjeneun amudo bal beotgo naseoji anaseo orae bangchidwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Nobody stepped up for that issue, so it was left alone for ages.
examples.note: Real-situation negative — no one took initiative; 방치되다 = 'be left neglected'; shows the negative form

expressions.nuance: Literally 'to take off your shoes and step forward' — in old Korea shoes were valuable, so kicking them off to wade barefoot into a muddy task signalled 'I'm completely committed, no holding back.' The key distinction from plain 돕다 ('to help') is initiative and wholehearted energy: 돕다 can be passive or asked-for, but 발 벗고 나서다 highlights someone who volunteers of their own accord, going well out of their way. Compare 앞장서다 ('to take the lead, go in front'), which stresses being out front leading a group, while 발 벗고 나서다 stresses self-giving willingness regardless of rank or role. The tone is warm and approving — it is almost always a compliment for the helper. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: write it as three orthographic words, 발 벗고 나서다 (not 발벗고 나서다), and because the idiom implies voluntary, eager involvement, avoid it for reluctant or coerced help — use 마지못해 돕다 ('reluctantly help') for that.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mind the spacing: 발 벗고 나서다, not 발벗고 나서다 — 발 and 벗고 are separate words.
It implies wholehearted, voluntary effort to help — don't use it for reluctant or forced help; for that, plain 도와주다 (with 마지못해 'reluctantly') fits better.
Don't reduce it to 앞장서다 ('take the lead'): leading a group is one thing, but 발 벗고 나서다 highlights self-giving willingness, not necessarily being out front.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 발 ('foot/shoes') + 벗다 ('to take off') + 나서다 ('to step forward'), literally 'to take off one's shoes and step forward.' 실제 뜻: to voluntarily throw oneself into helping, with complete commitment and eagerness — going well out of one's way for another person.
Rooted in old Korean life: shoes (짚신/미투리) were valuable and not worn into muddy or dirty work. Kicking them off to wade in barefoot was a signal of 'I am all in, nothing held back.'

Use when praising someone who stepped up voluntarily and energetically for another person: a senior helping a junior find work, neighbors helping with disaster relief, a friend dropping everything for you. Almost always a compliment for the helper. Casual to polite; fine across all relationships. Not for the helper themselves to say — too self-congratulatory; let others use it about you.

돕다 ('to help') is neutral and covers any aid, asked or unasked. 발 벗고 나서다 specifies volunteer eagerness, going out of one's way. 앞장서다 ('to take the lead, go in front') means leading a group — the position matters. 발 벗고 나서다 emphasizes self-giving willingness regardless of position.

Write it as three separate words: 발 벗고 나서다 — not 발벗고 나서다. Because it implies voluntary, wholehearted effort, do not use it for reluctant or forced help (use 마지못해 돕다 instead). And don't reduce it to 앞장서다 ('lead') — leading a group is different from the self-sacrificing willingness this idiom highlights.

expressions.english: to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')
expressions.shortExplanation: 어깨가 무겁다 is a practical expression meaning "to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')".
expressions.explanation: 어깨가 무겁다 (eokkaega mugeopda) means "to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 책임이 커서 어깨가 무거워. ("The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 책임 ('responsibility') is the core partner noun

usagePhrases.en: I've taken on an important task, so I feel the responsibility.
usagePhrases.note: Polite/formal -습니다; staple of work speeches and new-role announcements

usagePhrases.en: As the breadwinner, I carry a heavy load.
usagePhrases.note: ~로서 ('in the role of'); family responsibility framing

usagePhrases.ko: 기대가 큰 만큼 어깨가 더 무거워.
usagePhrases.romanization: gidaega keun mankeum eokkaega deo mugeowo.
usagePhrases.en: The bigger the expectations, the heavier the burden.
usagePhrases.note: ~만큼 ('to the extent that') links expectation to pressure

examples.ko: A: 팀장 맡았다면서요? / B: 네, 어깨가 무거워요. 열심히 해야죠.
examples.romanization: A: timjang matatdamyeonseoyo? / B: ne, eokkaega mugeowoyo. yeolsimhi haeyajyo.
examples.en: A: I heard you took on the team lead role? / B: Yes, I feel the weight of it. I'll have to work hard.
examples.note: A/B exchange; classic new-role acceptance speech formula

examples.ko: 다들 나만 믿는다고 하니까 어깨가 무거워.
examples.romanization: dadeul naman minneundago hanikka eokkaega mugeowo.
examples.en: Everyone says they're counting on me, so I feel the weight of responsibility.
examples.note: Pressure from others' trust; common before a big presentation or performance

examples.ko: 큰 프로젝트를 혼자 맡아서 어깨가 너무 무거워요.
examples.romanization: keun peurojekteureul honja mataseo eokkaega neomu mugeowoyo.
examples.en: I'm handling a big project alone, so the burden feels heavy.
examples.note: Real-situation: overloaded and under pressure; 혼자 ('alone') adds the isolation that deepens the weight

expressions.nuance: Literally 'shoulders are heavy,' this idiom expresses the psychological weight of responsibility or others' expectations pressing down on you — the dignified seriousness of a duty you have accepted. The dividing line from the near-synonym 부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened or pressured') is tone and dignity: 부담스럽다 can be mild and social (an expensive gift is 부담스럽다 because it obliges reciprocation), covering any degree of social discomfort, whereas 어깨가 무겁다 is a humble, almost noble admission that an important charge rests squarely on you — the expected phrase in acceptance speeches, new-role announcements, and earnest talks about duty. Its relief counterpart is 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders get lighter'). Core partner nouns are 책임 ('responsibility') and 기대 ('expectation'); core partner verb is 맡다 ('to take on'). Register covers casual through formal. The English-speaker pitfalls: this is emotional/responsibility weight, NOT literal shoulder pain (use 어깨가 결리다 or 아프다 for physical aches); and do not confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which expresses dejection or discouragement rather than the weight of duty.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about emotional/responsibility burden, not literal shoulder pain or stiffness — physical aches are 어깨가 결리다 / 어깨가 아프다.
Don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected, not weighed down by duty.
Don't swap in 부담스럽다 when you want the dignified 'weight of duty' nuance; 부담스럽다 can sound merely uncomfortable or about an over-generous favor.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 어깨 ('shoulders') + 무겁다 ('to be heavy'), literally 'shoulders are heavy.' 실제 뜻: to feel the psychological weight of responsibility, duty, or others' expectations — the dignified acknowledgement that something important rests on you.

The go-to phrase in new-role acceptance speeches, promotions, project kick-offs, and earnest self-reflection about duty. Casual (어깨가 무거워) to formal written (어깨가 무겁습니다). Safe across all registers and social levels. Also used about others: 어깨가 무거운 자리 ('a post carrying heavy responsibility').

부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened/pressured') is broader and milder: a too-generous gift is 부담스럽다. 어깨가 무겁다 is the dignified, heavy-duty version — specifically about the weight of an important role or expectation, not social awkwardness. 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop') means dejection, not responsibility.

Relief counterpart: 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders become lighter'). Stronger: 어깨가 짓눌리다 ('shoulders are crushed'). Collocate: 어깨가 무거운 자리 ('a position of heavy responsibility'). -아지다 form: 어깨가 무거워졌어요 ('the weight has grown').

This is emotional/responsibility weight, NOT physical shoulder pain — stiff or sore shoulders are 어깨가 결리다 / 어깨가 아프다. Don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop' = feeling dejected/down), which is a different emotion entirely. Also, 부담스럽다 cannot fully substitute here when you want the dignified 'weight of duty' nuance.

expressions.english: to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')
expressions.shortExplanation: 얼굴이 두껍다 is a practical expression meaning "to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')".
expressions.explanation: "to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')" — that is 얼굴이 두껍다 (eolguri dukkeopda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 걔 진짜 얼굴 두껍다, 또 부탁하네. ("He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 걔 진짜 얼굴 두껍다, 또 부탁하네.
usagePhrases.romanization: gyae jinjja eolgul dukkeopda, tto butakane.
usagePhrases.en: He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again.
usagePhrases.note: Casual, mildly critical; 을/를 often dropped: 얼굴 두껍다

usagePhrases.en: Asking for that takes a lot of nerve.
usagePhrases.note: Polite but pointed; -시- here is sarcastically deferential

usagePhrases.ko: 나도 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야 하나 봐.
usagePhrases.romanization: nado jom eolgul dukkeowojyeoya hana bwa.
usagePhrases.en: Maybe I need to grow a thicker skin.
usagePhrases.note: Self-talk; -아지다 = 'become'; positive 'less self-conscious' sense

usagePhrases.en: He's so brazen he doesn't even feel sorry.
usagePhrases.note: 낯짝/낯이 두껍다 = blunter, harsher variants

examples.ko: A: 저 사람 또 왔어? 지난번에 그러고도? / B: 그러니까, 진짜 얼굴 두껍다.
examples.romanization: A: jeo saram tto wasseo? jinanbeone geureogodo? / B: geureonikka, jinjja eolgul dukkeopda.
examples.en: A: That person came back? After what happened last time? / B: I know, seriously — what nerve.
examples.note: A/B exchange; shared incredulity at someone's brazenness

examples.ko: 그렇게 민폐 끼치고도 태연한 거 보면 얼굴 두껍다.
examples.romanization: geureoke minpye kkichigodo taeyeonhan geo bomyeon eolgul dukkeopda.
examples.en: Causing all that trouble and staying calm — what nerve.
examples.note: 민폐(를) 끼치다 = 'to be a nuisance to others'; classic shamelessness scenario

examples.ko: 면접 땐 얼굴이 좀 두꺼워야 떨지 않아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop ttaen eolguri jom dukkeowoya tteolji anayo.
examples.en: For interviews you need a bit of thick skin so you don't get nervous.
examples.note: Real-situation positive flip: not easily flustered; shows the encouraging 'don't be shy' usage

expressions.nuance: Literally 'the face is thick,' it labels someone shameless or brazen — a person who feels no embarrassment where a normal person would. English has the parallel image 'thick-skinned,' but beware the register gap: English 'thick-skinned' is typically a compliment ('unbothered by criticism'), whereas Korean 얼굴이 두껍다 is most often mildly negative or teasing ('no shame'). It only flips positive in contexts like job interviews or public speaking — 얼굴 좀 두꺼워야 해 ('you need to be a bit bolder/less shy'). The dividing line from the near-synonym 뻔뻔하다 ('brazen, impudent') is register and sharpness: 뻔뻔하다 is the plain adjective and can sound flatly accusatory; 얼굴이 두껍다 is the idiomatic, often lighter or jokier phrasing between familiar people. Blunter, rougher variants: 낯이 두껍다, 낯짝이 두껍다; the noun for the trait is 철면피 (鐵面皮, 'iron-face skin'). Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfall: it has nothing to do with literal facial skin thickness; and tone-awareness is essential — it can sting as an insult, so never say it bluntly to a superior.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Nothing to do with literal skin thickness on the face — it's about shamelessness, so a dermatology reading is wrong.
Tone matters: it can sound insulting, so don't say it bluntly to a superior or anyone you must stay polite with.
Don't assume it maps to the English compliment 'thick-skinned' (= unbothered by criticism); the default Korean sense is the negative 'shameless.'

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 얼굴 ('face') + 두껍다 ('to be thick'), literally 'the face is thick.' 실제 뜻: shameless, brazen — lacking the embarrassment a situation calls for. Carries the idea that a thick face acts as armor against shame. Default tone is mildly negative or teasing; occasionally positive ('bold, not easily flustered').

Casual to polite; most common among friends commenting on someone audacious. In workplace chat it can sting, so use carefully with seniors or strangers. Fine as self-deprecating humor: '나 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야겠어' ('I need to grow a thicker skin'). Avoid in formal or official speech — use 뻔뻔하다 in writing.

뻔뻔하다 ('brazen/impudent') is the plain adjective form and can sound directly accusatory. 얼굴이 두껍다 is idiomatic and often carries a joking or sighing tone. 낯짝이 두껍다 / 낯이 두껍다 are rougher, harsher synonyms. The Sino-Korean noun 철면피 (鐵面皮) means 'one who is completely shameless' — a more formal label.

Blunter variants: 낯이 두껍다, 낯짝이 두껍다 (harsher register). Noun form: 철면피 ('iron face'). Becoming/growing: 얼굴이 두꺼워지다 ('to become thicker-faced,' i.e. bolder or more brazen). Opposite: 얼굴이 얇다 (not common but exists: 'easily embarrassed').

English 'thick-skinned' is usually a compliment (unbothered by criticism); Korean 얼굴이 두껍다 is most often the negative 'shameless.' Nothing to do with literal facial skin. Tone matters: it can land as an insult, so never say it bluntly to a superior or in formal contexts. Map it carefully — it is not the same as 대담하다 ('to be bold') or 자신감이 있다 ('to be confident').

expressions.english: to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')
expressions.shortExplanation: 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is a practical expression meaning "to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')".
expressions.explanation: 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (nunko tteul sae eopda) = "to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 요즘 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠. ("I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 요즘 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠.
usagePhrases.romanization: yojeum nunko tteul sae eopsi bappa.
usagePhrases.en: I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; almost always with 바쁘다, joined by -이 (눈코 뜰 새 없이)

usagePhrases.ko: 연말이라 눈코 뜰 새 없이 지내고 있어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: yeonmarira nunko tteul sae eopsi jinaego isseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: It's year-end, so I'm run off my feet.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; -고 있다 ('have been') for an ongoing hectic stretch

usagePhrases.ko: 애 둘 키우느라 눈코 뜰 새가 없어.
usagePhrases.romanization: ae dul kiuneura nunko tteul saega eopseo.
usagePhrases.en: Raising two kids leaves me no time to breathe.
usagePhrases.note: 새가 없다 form with subject 이/가

usagePhrases.ko: 오픈 시간엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 손님이 밀려와.
usagePhrases.romanization: opeun siganen nunko tteul sae eopsi sonnimi millyeowa.
usagePhrases.en: At opening time customers pour in nonstop.
usagePhrases.note: 밀려오다 = 'to flood in'; workplace rush scene

examples.ko: A: 요즘 어때? / B: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 밥도 제대로 못 먹어.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum eottae? / B: nunko tteul sae eopsi bappaseo bapdo jedaero mon meogeo.
examples.en: A: How are things lately? / B: I'm so slammed I can barely eat properly.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 밥도 제대로 못 먹다 = 'can't even eat a proper meal,' a natural stacking phrase

examples.ko: 행사 준비로 일주일 내내 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일했어.
examples.romanization: haengsa junbiro iljuil naenae nunko tteul sae eopsi ilhaesseo.
examples.en: I worked flat out all week preparing for the event.
examples.note: 일주일 내내 = 'all week long'; sustained, not one-off busyness

examples.ko: 식당이 점심엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 정신이 하나도 없어요.
examples.romanization: sikdangi jeomsimen nunko tteul sae eopsi bappaseo jeongsini hanado eopseoyo.
examples.en: The restaurant is so slammed at lunch I can't think straight.
examples.note: Real-situation: 정신이 없다 ('frazzled') stacks naturally; peak-hour restaurant rush

expressions.nuance: Literally 'no gap (새 = 사이, 'interval') to even open your eyes and nose,' it is a vivid hyperbole for being so frantically busy that you cannot spare a single second to breathe or collect yourself. The dividing line from plain 바쁘다 ('to be busy') is extreme intensity: 바쁘다 covers any degree of busyness, while 눈코 뜰 새 없다 sits at the absolute top — you can't even blink. It functions almost entirely as the set adverbial chunk 눈코 뜰 새 없이 + 바쁘다/일하다/지내다, which is why many textbooks treat 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다 as a fixed phrase. The alternative form 눈코 뜰 새가 없다 takes the subject 이/가. Note 새 here is the noun 사이/간격 ('gap, interval'), not the bird 새 ('bird') — that homophone trips beginners into a baffling literal image. Register is casual-to-polite, extremely common for any hectic stretch at work or home. The English-speaker pitfall: keep the exact spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one compound word; 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open'); and don't deploy it for a calm 'I have no time' — there must be breathless, overwhelming busyness for this extreme hyperbole to fit.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Keep the spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one word; 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open') — not 눈 코 뜰새 없다.
It's an intensity phrase usually attached to 바쁘다 — don't use it for a neutral 'I have no time'; it requires real, breathless busyness.
새 here means 'gap/interval' (사이), not 새 ('bird') — don't let the homophone mislead your reading.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 눈코 ('eyes and nose') + 뜰 새 ('a gap/moment to open') + 없다 ('there is none'). The image: so rushed you cannot even take a moment to open your eyes and nose — no time for even the most basic awareness. 실제 뜻: at the absolute peak of busyness, utterly overwhelmed.

Used for sustained, peak busy periods — year-end at work, restaurant rush hour, exam prep week, childcare overload. Casual to polite; safe with friends, coworkers, and bosses. Conveys vivid, almost humorous self-awareness about being swamped. Not for written formal reports — use 업무가 과중하다 ('workload is excessive') there.

바쁘다 ('to be busy') is the neutral, any-degree word. 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is extreme-hyperbole: you can't blink. 정신없이 바쁘다 ('frantically busy') is a close competitor but less idiom-vivid. 몸이 열 개라도 모자라다 ('even if I had ten bodies it wouldn't be enough') focuses on understaffing; 눈코 뜰 새 없다 focuses on sheer time pressure.
Adverbial form: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 + verb (most common). Subject form: 눈코 뜰 새가 없다. Common completions: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다, 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일하다, 눈코 뜰 새 없이 지내다. Intensifier: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁜 하루.

새 here is 사이/간격 ('gap/interval'), not 새 ('bird') — the homophone is a common source of confusion. Keep the correct spacing: 눈코 is one word, then 뜰 새 없다. Don't use it for a casual 'I don't have time' — it requires genuine, breathless busyness to justify the hyperbole.

expressions.english: to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')
expressions.shortExplanation: 바가지를 쓰다 is a practical expression meaning "to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')".
expressions.explanation: 바가지를 쓰다 (bagajireul sseuda) means "to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 관광지에서 완전 바가지 썼어. ("I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 를 often dropped (바가지 쓰다); buyer overpays

usagePhrases.ko: 택시 타다가 바가지 쓴 것 같아요.
usagePhrases.romanization: taeksi tadaga bagaji sseun geot gatayo.
usagePhrases.en: I think I got overcharged in the taxi.
usagePhrases.note: Polite; -ㄴ 것 같다 ('seems that') softens a suspicion

usagePhrases.ko: 여기 비싸니까 바가지 쓰지 않게 가격 먼저 물어봐.
usagePhrases.romanization: yeogi bissanikka bagaji sseuji anke gagyeong meonjeo mureobwa.
usagePhrases.en: It's pricey here, so ask the price first to avoid getting fleeced.
usagePhrases.note: -지 않게 ('so as not to'); practical advice

usagePhrases.en: The owner ripped the foreigner off.
usagePhrases.note: 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER does the overcharging

examples.ko: A: 그 시장 어땠어? / B: 흥정 안 했더니 완전 바가지 썼어.
examples.romanization: A: geu sijang eottaesseo? / B: heungjeong an haetdeoni wanjeon bagaji sseosseo.
examples.en: A: How was that market? / B: I didn't haggle and totally got fleeced.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 흥정 ('haggling') as the prevention; -더니 shows cause-and-effect regret

examples.en: I bought it without knowing the going rate and got overcharged.
examples.note: 시세 = 'market/going price'; -다가 marks the slip-up that led to the loss

examples.ko: 축제 음식이 평소의 두 배라 바가지 쓴 기분이었어요.
examples.romanization: chukje eumsigi pyeongsoui du baera bagaji sseun gibunieosseoyo.
examples.en: The festival food was double the usual price — felt like a total ripoff.
examples.note: Real-situation: inflated event pricing; 평소의 두 배 = 'double the usual price'; 기분이었다 ('felt like') adds subjectivity

expressions.nuance: Literally 'to wear (쓰다) a gourd dipper (바가지)' — in folk imagery an overloaded debt was said to be dumped on your head like a basinful of water, so 바가지를 쓰다 means being charged far above the fair market price, being gouged. It thrives in talk of tourist traps, open-air markets, unlicensed taxis, and festival stalls. The dividing line from plain 비싸다 ('expensive') is fairness: 비싸다 just means the price is high (possibly justified), whereas 바가지(를) 쓰다 implies you were charged ABOVE the fair going rate, unfairly. The crucial grammar pair you must learn: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = YOU, the buyer, got overcharged (쓰다 = to wear/put on — the gourd lands on your head); 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER dumps the gourd on someone (씌우다, causative 'to make wear'). Register is casual-to-polite, and 바가지 is also used as a standalone noun: '이건 바가지야' ('this is a ripoff'). The English-speaker pitfalls: reversing 쓰다 ('I got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('they ripped someone off') is a very common mistake; and do not use it for poor product quality — overcharge is strictly about price, not product.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't reverse the verbs: 쓰다 = you got ripped off; 씌우다 = the seller (or someone) ripped another person off.
It refers to being overcharged, not to a bad-quality product — for poor quality use 별로다 / 안 좋다.
Don't substitute plain 비싸다 ('expensive'): high price alone isn't 바가지; the nuance is being gouged ABOVE the fair rate.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 바가지 ('gourd dipper/basin') + 쓰다 ('to put on/wear'), literally 'to have a gourd placed on one's head.' 실제 뜻: to be charged far above the fair market price — to get gouged. The folk image is an overloaded debt or price being dumped on the buyer like a basinful of water.

Fits tourist areas, open markets, unlicensed taxis, festival stalls, unfamiliar repair shops — anywhere pricing is opaque or exploitative. Casual to polite. Fine to say to friends ('완전 바가지 썼어!') or in polite narrative ('바가지 쓴 것 같아요'). Also used as a preventive warning: 바가지 쓰지 않으려면 흥정해.

비싸다 ('expensive') is neutral — a Michelin-starred restaurant is 비싸다 but not 바가지. 바가지(를) 쓰다 means the price is specifically above fair market value in an exploitative way. 뜯기다 ('to get fleeced/taken') is a blunter synonym. The noun 바가지 alone as 이건 바가지야 means 'this is a ripoff.'

Buyer side: 바가지(를) 쓰다. Seller side: 바가지(를) 씌우다 ('to fleece/gouge someone'). Noun alone: 바가지 ('a ripoff'), 바가지요금 ('overcharge/gouge price'). Prevention phrase: 바가지 쓰지 않게 흥정하다 ('haggle to avoid getting ripped off').

Reversing 쓰다 ('got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('ripped someone off') is a very common error — keep the directionality: 쓰다 = the gourd lands ON YOU; 씌우다 = someone places the gourd ON ANOTHER. 바가지는 strictly about price, not product quality (use 별로다 / 안 좋다 for poor quality). And 비싸다 alone does not mean 바가지.

expressions.english: you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')
expressions.shortExplanation: 국물도 없다 is a practical expression meaning "you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')".
expressions.explanation: "you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')" — that is 국물도 없다 (gungmuldo eopda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 한 번만 더 늦으면 국물도 없어. ("Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 한 번만 더 늦으면 국물도 없어.
usagePhrases.romanization: han beonman deo neujeumyeon gungmuldo eopseo.
usagePhrases.en: Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me.
usagePhrases.note: Casual warning/threat; -으면 ('if') sets the condition

usagePhrases.ko: 약속 안 지키면 국물도 없을 줄 알아.
usagePhrases.romanization: yaksok an jikimyeon gungmuldo eopseul jul ara.
usagePhrases.en: If you break the promise, don't expect anything good.
usagePhrases.note: Half-joking threat; -을 줄 알아 = 'you'd better know / be warned'

usagePhrases.en: Even though I helped this time, I got nothing out of it.
usagePhrases.note: -아도 ('even if'); complaining about zero payoff

usagePhrases.ko: 그렇게 해 봤자 너한테 국물도 없어.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureoke hae bwatja neohante gungmuldo eopseo.
usagePhrases.en: Even if you do that, there's nothing in it for you.
usagePhrases.note: -아 봤자 ('no matter how much you ~'); framing a pointless effort

examples.ko: A: 저한테 뭔가 좀 돌아오나요? / B: 이번엔 국물도 없어, 그냥 해.
examples.romanization: A: jeohante mwonga jom doraonayo? / B: ibeonen gungmuldo eopseo, geunyang hae.
examples.en: A: Is there anything in it for me? / B: Nothing this time — just do it.
examples.note: A/B exchange; casual, blunt refusal of any payoff

examples.ko: 밤새 도왔는데 고맙단 말도 없고, 정말 국물도 없네.
examples.romanization: bamsae dowanneunde gomapdan maldo eopsgo, jeongmal gungmuldo eopsne.
examples.en: I helped all night and didn't even get a thanks — nothing to show for it.
examples.note: Zero reward after significant effort; resigned -네 ending

examples.ko: 사장님이 또 실수하면 국물도 없다고 하셨어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi tto silsuhamyeon gungmuldo eopsdago hasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The boss said if it happens again there'll be no mercy.
examples.note: Workplace warning relayed with -다고 하다; shows it is reportable in polite speech

expressions.nuance: Literally 'there isn't even broth (국물)' — picture a shared pot of stew scraped so clean that not a single drop of soup remains for you, so 국물도 없다 means there is absolutely nothing to be gained: no share, no benefit, no leftover mercy. Its most common use is as a half-joking but pointed warning from someone with the upper hand: 한 번만 더 그러면 국물도 없어 ('do that once more and you'll get nothing from me'). A second use is grumbling that effort yielded zero reward ('도와줬는데 국물도 없더라'). The dividing line from the threat-phrase 가만 안 두다 ('I won't let it slide') is what is threatened: 가만 안 두다 threatens active punishment, whereas 국물도 없다 threatens total withholding of any goodwill or payoff — the carrot disappears rather than a stick appearing. Register is firmly casual and the phrasing can sting, so it suits friends, family, or clearly informal settings — never in professional or deferential speech. The English-speaker pitfalls: 국물 here is NOT literal soup — it means 'leftover benefit/share'; and the implied subject is 'you' or 'there will be none for you,' so the sentence is essentially shorthand for 너한테 돌아오는 것이 국물도 없다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Nothing to do with actual soup — 국물 here means 'leftover benefit/payoff/share,' not broth you can drink.
The threatening tone is informal and can sound harsh; don't use it in polite or professional contexts where you must stay deferential.
It threatens WITHHOLDING any reward or mercy, not active punishment — for 'I'll make you pay' use 가만 안 두다, not 국물도 없다.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 국물 ('broth/soup') + 도 없다 ('not even … exists'), literally 'there isn't even broth left.' 실제 뜻: there is absolutely nothing to be gained — no benefit, no share, no payoff, no mercy. The image is a shared pot scraped completely clean; you get not a drop.

Two main settings: (1) Half-joking warning from someone with leverage — 한 번만 더 그러면 국물도 없어 — among friends, family, or a parent to a child. (2) Grumbling that an effort went unrewarded — 도와줬는데 국물도 없더라. Firmly casual; never polite or professional speech. If you must convey the same idea at work, say 혜택이 전혀 없습니다 ('there are no benefits whatsoever').

가만 안 두다 ('I won't let it slide') threatens active punishment — a stick. 국물도 없다 threatens withholding any goodwill — the carrot vanishes. 得도 없다 (formal written) and 건질 게 없다 ('nothing to salvage') are near-synonyms in the 'no payoff' sense but lack the pointed warning edge.

Condition + threat: -으면 국물도 없어 ('if ~, you'll get nothing'). Even-if frame: -아도/-아 봤자 국물도 없어. Softer: 뭔가 돌아오는 게 없다 ('nothing comes back to you'). Standalone noun: 국물 = 'a share, a cut': 국물 좀 줘 ('give me a cut/share').

국물 here is NOT literal soup — it is figurative 'leftover benefit/payoff/share.' Don't picture food. Because the tone is so informal and can sting, never use it in polite or professional contexts. Also note the implied 'for you': the full thought is 너한테 돌아오는 국물도 없다, so it is personal and pointed, not just a statement about scarcity.

expressions.english: to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')
expressions.shortExplanation: 찬물을 끼얹다 is a practical expression meaning "to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')".
expressions.explanation: 찬물을 끼얹다 (chanmureul kkieonda) = "to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 분위기 좋았는데 걔가 찬물을 끼얹었어. ("The mood was great but he threw cold water on it."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: The mood was great but he threw cold water on it.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 분위기 ('mood/vibe') is the classic object being ruined

usagePhrases.ko: 좋은 소식에 찬물을 끼얹고 싶진 않지만요.
usagePhrases.romanization: joeun sosige chanmureul kkieonjgo sipjin anchimanyo.
usagePhrases.en: I don't mean to rain on the good news, but…
usagePhrases.note: Polite hedge before delivering bad news; -지만 = 'but'

usagePhrases.ko: 다들 신났는데 그 말 한마디가 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: dadeul sinnanneunde geu mal hanmadiga chanmureul kkieonjeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Everyone was excited, but that one comment killed it.
usagePhrases.note: 말 한마디 = 'a single remark' as the subject; one-word buzzkill

usagePhrases.ko: 계획에 자꾸 찬물 끼얹지 말고 좀 응원해 줘.
usagePhrases.romanization: gyehoege jakku chanmul kkieonjji malgo jom eungwonhae jwo.
usagePhrases.en: Stop pouring cold water on the plan and cheer me on.
usagePhrases.note: -지 말다 ('don't'); 을 dropped colloquially

examples.ko: A: 다들 여행 가자고 신났었는데. / B: 근데 민준이가 찬물을 끼얹어서 분위기가 식었어.
examples.romanization: A: dadeul yeohaeng gajago sinnasseonneunde. / B: geunde minjuniga chanmureul kkieonjeoseo bunwigiga sigeosseo.
examples.en: A: Everyone was hyped about the trip. / B: But Minjun threw cold water on it and the vibe died.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 분위기가 식다 = 'the mood cooled/died' pairs naturally

examples.ko: 회의 분위기가 살아나려는데 부장님이 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui bunwigiga saranaryeoneunde bujangnimi chanmureul kkieonjeosseoyo.
examples.en: The meeting was warming up, but the manager threw cold water on it.
examples.note: -려는데 = 'just as it was about to'; workplace momentum killed by a senior comment

examples.ko: 축하 자리에 굳이 찬물을 끼얹는 말을 할 필요는 없잖아.
examples.romanization: chuka jarie guji chanmureul kkieonjneun mareul hal piryoneun eopsjana.
examples.en: There's no need to say something that ruins a celebration.
examples.note: Real-situation: 굳이 ('needlessly/without cause') + advice to be tactful; shows the disapproving framing

expressions.nuance: Literally 'to pour cold water over (something hot),' it means to suddenly and actively kill an upbeat mood, rising excitement, or building momentum — typically with a negative remark or unwelcome news, like dousing a warm fire. The key dividing line from the near-synonym 김(을) 빼다 / 김새다 ('to let the steam out / deflate') is agency: 김새다 describes excitement that fizzles on its own with no clear culprit, whereas 찬물을 끼얹다 firmly points the finger at an active party who chose to throw the buzzkill. For the expression to land correctly, there must be heat to douse — enthusiasm, a rising vibe, a plan people were excited about — so do not apply it to neutral situations. Partners: 분위기에 ('to the mood'), 좋은 소식에 ('to good news'), 계획에 ('to a plan'). Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: the verb 끼얹다 is frequently misspelled — it carries the ㄶ batchim (끼얹-, romanized kki-eon-da), so avoid 끼언다 or 끼엊다; and the phrase requires a target atmosphere to ruin, so never use it where there was no positive mood to begin with.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling: it's 찬물을 끼얹다 (끼얹- has the ㄶ batchim, read 'kki-eon'), not 끼언다 or 끼엊다.
It implies actively spoiling a POSITIVE mood, so don't use it for just any bad news; there must be enthusiasm or momentum to ruin.
Don't blur it with 김새다 ('to fizzle'): 김새다 is the excitement deflating on its own, while 찬물을 끼얹다 points the finger at a deliberate buzzkill.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 찬물 ('cold water') + 끼얹다 ('to pour/splash over'), literally 'to pour cold water over.' 실제 뜻: to actively kill an upbeat mood, rising excitement, or building momentum — like suddenly dousing a warm fire with cold water. The key: something must be 'hot' (excited, positive) before the cold water lands.

Used when a single remark, news item, or person kills an enthusiastic atmosphere: a fun plan deflated, a meeting momentum broken, a celebration disrupted. Casual to polite. Fine with friends and in workplace storytelling. The expression carries mild reproach for the buzzkill — use it to describe, not to lecture someone in their face (try 분위기 파악 좀 해 'read the room' for that).

김새다 / 김이 빠지다 ('steam escapes / deflates'): the excitement fizzles without a clear culprit — it just happens. 찬물을 끼얹다 points to a specific active agent who threw the buzzkill. 분위기를 망치다 ('to ruin the atmosphere') is a broader, plainer phrasing; 찬물을 끼얹다 is the vivid idiomatic version.
Subject flexibility: 그 말이/그 사람이 찬물을 끼얹다. Target marked with 에: 분위기에/계획에/축하 자리에 찬물을 끼얹다. Object 을 frequently dropped colloquially: 찬물 끼얹다. Noun phrase: 찬물을 끼얹는 말 ('a buzzkill remark').

끼얹다 carries the ㄶ batchim (pronounce kki-eon-da) — commonly misspelled as 끼언다 or 끼엊다. The expression requires a target positive mood to ruin; don't apply it to neutral situations. Don't blur it with 김새다 ('to fizzle on its own') — 찬물을 끼얹다 points the finger at an active buzzkill, not natural deflation.

expressions.english: Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?
expressions.shortExplanation: 통화 괜찮으세요? is a practical expression meaning "Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?".
expressions.explanation: 통화 괜찮으세요? (tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo?) means "Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 통화 괜찮으세요? ("Is now a good time to talk?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Is now a good time to talk?
usagePhrases.note: the standard polite opener AFTER you placed the call and they picked up

usagePhrases.en: Are you free to talk right now?
usagePhrases.note: 지금 = right now; pins the timing so they know you mean this moment

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a minute to talk?
usagePhrases.note: 잠깐 (briefly) shrinks the ask and makes it easy to say yes
반말 해체; only with close friends/younger people

examples.ko: A: 여보세요, 김 과장님? 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? / B: 네, 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo, gim gwajangnim? jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo? / B: ne, malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: A: Hello, Manager Kim? Is now a good time to talk? / B: Yes, go ahead.
examples.note: model call opener — 여보세요 first, then the check; B's 말씀하세요 signals the green light

examples.en: Sorry to bother you when you're busy. Do you have a minute?
examples.note: lead with 죄송해요 before the request to soften any imposition

examples.ko: 야, 통화 괜찮아? 할 말 있어.
examples.romanization: ya, tonghwa gwaenchana? hal mal isseo.
examples.en: Hey, can you talk? I've got something to say.
examples.note: 반말 between close friends; -세요 disappears entirely in this register

expressions.nuance: This is the reflexive courtesy line the CALLER says the instant the other person answers — you confirm they can actually talk before diving in, the way an English speaker says 'Is this a good time?' The literal structure is 통화 ('a phone conversation') + 괜찮으세요? ('is it okay for you?'), so you're asking whether a call is okay for THEM. 통화(通話) is Sino-Korean, 通 'pass/connect' + 話 'speech,' meaning a connected voice conversation — it is strictly phone or voice-call territory; for face-to-face talking use 얘기 or 대화. The honorific 괜찮으세요? must stay with any boss, elder, or client. Key 변형형: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 지금 to pin the moment), 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 잠깐 to minimize the ask), and bare 괜찮아? in 반말. A near-synonym is 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'), but that works in any context (in person, over text), while 통화 괜찮으세요? anchors you specifically to this live call. The big English-speaker directional trap: only the CALLER asks this — the person who PICKED UP does not confirm permission; they simply respond 네, 말씀하세요 or 잠깐만요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking it when YOU received the call. The caller initiates this check; if you answered, you just say 네, 여보세요? — the dialer is the one who confirms it's a good time.
Using 괜찮아? with a boss or client. It is 반말 and sounds too familiar with anyone you'd 존댓말 — the honorific 괜찮으세요? (괜찮- + 으시- + 어요) is the safe default.
Saying 통화 to mean an in-person chat. 통화 is strictly a phone call; a face-to-face conversation is 대화 or just 얘기 — '얘기 좀 괜찮아요?' for talking in person.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '통화(call) + 괜찮으세요?(is it okay for you)?' — asking whether a connected conversation is acceptable RIGHT NOW. The caller says it; the receiver does not. It is the Korean equivalent of 'Is this a good time?'

Said the moment the other person picks up, before any content. -세요 (존댓말) is mandatory with bosses, elders, clients, and anyone you'd 존댓말. Flip to 괜찮아? only with close friends or younger people you speak to in 반말.

지금 시간 괜찮으세요? is the closest rival — it asks 'do you have time?' and works in any medium (in person, text, call). 통화 괜찮으세요? is phone-exclusive; it explicitly names the call as the thing you're asking permission for.
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 지금 to pin the moment) → 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요? (adds 잠깐 to minimize the ask) → 통화 괜찮으세요? (baseline) → 통화 괜찮아? (반말). The honorific ending -세요 on 괜찮다 is formed as 괜찮- + -으시- + -어요 → 괜찮으세요.

Direction error: English speakers sometimes say it after ANSWERING a call ('Hello, is now a good time?'). Only the dialer asks this; the receiver simply responds. A second trap: using 괜찮아? with a senior colleague — always 괜찮으세요? with any 존댓말 relationship.

expressions.english: Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment
expressions.shortExplanation: 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment".
expressions.explanation: "Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment" — that is 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 (kkeunchi malgo gidaryeo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 ("Please don't hang up and hold on"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please don't hang up and hold on
usagePhrases.note: full polite form said to a caller you've put on hold

usagePhrases.en: Please stay on the line for a moment
usagePhrases.note: 끊지 마시고 inserts honorific -시-; the extra-polite call-center grade
shorter and brisk; 잠깐만요 = 'just a sec'
반말 to a friend; note 주세요 is gone

examples.ko: A: 담당자 연결 부탁드려요. / B: 네, 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요. 바로 연결해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: damdangja yeongyeol butakdeuryeoyo. / B: ne, kkeunchi malgo gidaryeo juseyo. baro yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Could you connect me to the right person? / B: Of course, please hold — I'll put you right through.
examples.note: full service exchange: caller's request, agent's hold phrase, then transfer promise

examples.ko: 담당자 확인해 드릴게요. 끊지 마시고 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
examples.romanization: damdangja hwaginhae deurilgeyo. kkeunchi masigo jamsiman gidaryeo juseyo.
examples.en: I'll check with the person in charge. Please stay on the line a moment.
examples.note: call-center grade; 마시고 carries the honorific -시-; 잠시만 adds urgency

examples.en: I'll ask Mom. Don't hang up, hold on.
examples.note: casual household hand-off; no 주세요, plain 기다려

expressions.nuance: This phrase is what the person holding the receiver says when they must step away briefly but want you to remain on the line — the Korean equivalent of 'please hold.' Two clauses are bolted together: 끊지 말고 ('don't hang up and instead') warns you off ending the call, while 기다려 주세요 ('please wait for me') uses the favor verb 주다 to frame the wait as a kindness you're granting. 끊다 literally means 'to cut or sever,' which is exactly how Korean conceptualizes hanging up — you cut the call. Without 주세요, bare 기다려 sounds like a command; bare 끊지 마 sounds curt to a customer. The critical confusion to avoid is 끊다 (end a call) vs 끄다 (power off a device): a phone call is 끊어, but a TV, light, or powered device is 꺼. A near-synonym hold phrase is 잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment'), which only asks you to wait; 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 adds the explicit 'don't hang up,' making it the right choice when there's any risk the caller gives up and disconnects.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 끊다 with 끄다. A phone call is hung up: 전화 끊어; a device is turned off: 불 꺼 / 휴대폰 꺼. Saying 전화 꺼 means 'turn the phone OFF,' a different action.
Dropping 주세요 with a customer. 끊지 말고 기다려 to a stranger sounds like an order; the favor verb 기다려 주세요 makes it a polite request.
Writing 끊지 as 끈지. The verb is 끊다 (with the ㄶ cluster); 끈 means 'a string,' so 끈지 말고 is a spelling slip.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'don't cut (끊지 말고) + please wait for me (기다려 주세요).' Said by whoever is on the line when they need to step away briefly. The two clauses together equal the English 'please hold.' The favor verb 주다 softens the wait into a polite request, not a command.

Used in service contexts (call centers, offices) and at home. Keep 주세요 with any stranger or customer. 끊지 마시고 기다려 주세요 (with -시-) is the extra-polite call-center standard. Drop to 끊지 말고 기다려 only with intimates.

잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment') only asks you to wait and says nothing about hanging up. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 explicitly warns 'don't hang up' — use it whenever the hold is long enough that the caller might give up.
끊지 마시고 잠시만 기다려 주세요 (extra-polite, -시-) → 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요 (standard) → 끊지 말고 잠깐만요 (quick/brisk) → 끊지 말고 기다려 (반말). The honorific -시- in 마시고 marks the formal tier.

Confusing 끊다 (end a call) with 끄다 (power off): '전화 끊어' = hang up the phone; '불 꺼' = turn off the light; '전화 꺼' = power off the phone itself. These are different actions. Also: dropping 주세요 with a customer turns a request into an order.

expressions.english: Shall I take a message (for them)?
expressions.shortExplanation: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? is a practical expression meaning "Shall I take a message (for them)?".
expressions.explanation: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? (memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?) = "Shall I take a message (for them)?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 메모 남겨 드릴까요? ("Would you like me to leave a message?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Would you like me to leave a message?
usagePhrases.note: humble offer to write down a message for the absent person

usagePhrases.en: Is there anything you'd like me to pass on?
usagePhrases.note: alternative; 전하다 = 'convey,' 말씀 = honorific 'words'

usagePhrases.en: Would you like to leave a message?
usagePhrases.note: -시겠어요 puts the choice politely on the caller

usagePhrases.en: Want me to leave them a message?
usagePhrases.note: 반말 version, e.g. at home

examples.ko: A: 김 부장님 좀 바꿔 주세요. / B: 자리에 안 계신데요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: A: gim bujangnim jom bakkwo juseyo. / B: jarie an gyesindeyo. memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: A: Could I speak to Manager Kim? / B: He's not at his desk right now — shall I take a message?
examples.note: realistic call exchange: request → absence explanation → message offer; B uses 안 계신데요 to honor Kim

examples.en: They're in a meeting — would you like to leave a message?
examples.note: -신데 = honorific soft lead-in providing the reason before the offer

examples.ko: 형 지금 없는데, 메모 남겨 줄까?
examples.romanization: hyeong jigeum eopsneunde, memo namgyeo julkka?
examples.en: Bro's not here — want me to pass on a message?
examples.note: casual at home; 줄까 instead of 드릴까요; 형 = older brother

expressions.nuance: Said by whoever answers when the person the caller wants is unavailable, offering to write the caller's message down for the absent party. The engine is 드리다, the humble verb meaning 'to give / do for' a person you respect, so 남겨 드릴까요? politely volunteers to take a note as a favor to you — compare 남겨 줄까? (with plain 주다), the casual home version. 메모 here is borrowed from English 'memo' but in Korean refers specifically to a short handwritten or jotted note, not a formal corporate circular. A near-synonym phrase is 전하실 말씀 있으세요? ('is there anything to convey?'), which is slightly more formal and avoids the English loanword 메모 entirely, making it the safer choice in ultra-formal or governmental settings. The verb 남기다 ('leave behind') trips learners conjugating it: 남기- + -어 contracts neatly to 남겨, not 남기어 or 남겨다. Register is the central pitfall: offering 남겨 줄까요? to a business caller uses plain 주다 where humble 드리다 is expected, because you are doing the favor for both the caller AND the absent colleague.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 남겨 줄까요? to a customer. The situation calls for the humble 드리다: 남겨 드릴까요?. Plain 주다 (줄까요) is fine at home but under-polite at a reception desk.
Writing 남기다 as 남끼다. The stem is 남기- (남겨 = 남기 + 어). 남끼다 is not a word.
Treating 메모 like an English 'memo' (a formal circular). On the phone 메모 = a quick message/note; the office document is 공지 or 회람, not 메모.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '남겨(leave) + 드릴까요?(shall I do for you?)' — a humble offer to take a note for the absent person. The humble 드리다 (not plain 주다) signals you are performing the favor upward, towards the caller and the absent person simultaneously.

Said at a reception desk, in an office, or over the phone when the wanted person is away. With customers or seniors, 드릴까요 is mandatory. At home or with close peers, 줄까? is fine. 전하실 말씀 있으세요? is the ultra-formal alternative for official or governmental contexts.

메시지 남기시겠어요? ('would you like to leave a message?') puts the initiative on the CALLER — they choose to leave it. 메모 남겨 드릴까요? puts the initiative on YOU — you volunteer to take it. 전하실 말씀 있으세요? avoids the loanword 메모 and is more formal.
남기다 → 남겨 → 남겨 드릴까요? (humble offer) / 남겨 줄까? (반말). The contraction 남기어 → 남겨 is regular for -이어 verbs.

Offering 남겨 줄까요? to a customer swaps humble 드리다 for plain 주다, which undercuts the politeness needed in a service setting. Also: treating 메모 as a 'corporate memo' — in Korean everyday speech, 메모 is just a quick note or jot, not a formal document.

expressions.shortExplanation: 연결해 드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll connect you (transfer your call)".
expressions.explanation: 연결해 드릴게요 (yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo) means "I'll connect you (transfer your call)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 연결해 드릴게요 ("I'll put you through"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: agent transferring your call to another line — humble -아 드릴게요

usagePhrases.en: I'll connect you to the right department
usagePhrases.note: 담당 부서 = 'department in charge'; -로 marks the destination
formal -겠습니다 grade heard in call centers
반말, e.g. patching a friend through

examples.ko: A: 고객센터 어디로 연결해 줘요? / B: 기술 지원팀으로 연결해 드릴게요. 잠시만요.
examples.romanization: A: gogaeksenteo eodiro yeongyeolhae jwoyo? / B: gisul jiwontimeuro yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo. jamsimanyo.
examples.en: A: Which department should I go to? / B: I'll connect you to tech support. One moment.
examples.note: A/B transfer request and response; -팀으로 marks the target

examples.ko: 제가 처리할 수 없는 건이라, 담당자에게 연결해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jega cheorihal su eopsneun geonira, damdangjaege yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: I can't handle this, so I'll transfer you to the right person.
examples.note: -이라 gives the reason for escalating the call

examples.ko: 아, 그건 누나가 알아. 연결해 줄게.
examples.romanization: a, geugeon nunaga ara. yeongyeolhae julge.
examples.en: Oh, my sister knows that. I'll put her on.
examples.note: casual hand-off at home; plain 줄게, not 드릴게요

expressions.nuance: This is the agent's phrase for transferring a caller to another extension or department — you are routing the CALL through the system to a new endpoint. 연결(連結) is Sino-Korean: 連 'join' + 結 'tie,' literally 'join-and-bind,' which captures a technical connection between two telephone lines. The humble -아 드리다 frames the routing as a favor done for the caller, which is why formal centers escalate to 연결해 드리겠습니다. The most important near-synonym contrast is 연결 vs 바꾸다: 연결해 드릴게요 means routing the call through a phone system to a new line or department (you may not even see the person), while 바꿔 드릴게요 means handing the same physical handset to a person who is standing right there — two completely different mechanical acts. A second critical contrast is 연결 vs 연락: 연결 = connect two parties right now; 연락 = reach out to someone later. Saying 나중에 연결드릴게요 to mean 'I'll contact you later' is a wiring error. Key 변형형: 연결해 드릴게요 (standard) → 연결해 드리겠습니다 (extra-formal) → 연결해 줄게 (반말). The redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 is a common over-expansion; 연결하다 already means 'connect,' so 시키다 adds nothing and sounds off to native ears.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 연결시켜 드릴게요. The causative 시키다 is redundant here; 연결하다 already means to connect a call, so the natural form is 연결해 드릴게요.
Confusing 연결 with 연락. 연결 = link two parties right now (transfer); 연락 = contact someone (later). '담당자에게 연락해 주세요' means have them CALL you, not transfer you.
Using 연결해 드릴게요 to hand a phone to a family member. That household hand-off is 바꿔 드릴게요; 연결 implies a technical transfer to another line.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '연결해(connect) + 드릴게요(I'll do for you).' The agent promises to route the call through a phone system to a new line or department. The humble 드리다 marks the routing as a service favor. Formal centers use 연결해 드리겠습니다 for an extra tier of formality.
Standard polite in any service or business call. -아 드릴게요 is the baseline. Escalate to 드리겠습니다 for call-center announcements or VIP callers. At home or with peers, 연결해 줄게 is natural.

연결해 드릴게요 routes the call through a phone SYSTEM to another line. 바꿔 드릴게요 hands the SAME handset to a person nearby — a physical swap, not a system transfer. Don't use 연결 for a home hand-off; that sounds comically corporate.

연결해 드릴게요 (standard polite) → 연결해 드리겠습니다 (extra-formal, call-center) → 연결해 줄게 (반말). Adding 바로 before the verb (바로 연결해 드릴게요) signals immediacy. Avoid the redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 — 연결하다 already means 'connect.'
Two traps: (1) Redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 — 연결하다 already means 'connect,' so 시키다 is unnecessary and sounds unnatural. (2) Swapping 연결 for 연락: '나중에 연결드릴게요' is wrong — later contact is 연락, not 연결.

expressions.english: They're not available / not in (missed call)
expressions.shortExplanation: 부재중이에요 is a practical expression meaning "They're not available / not in (missed call)".
expressions.explanation: "They're not available / not in (missed call)" — that is 부재중이에요 (bujaejung-ieyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 부재중이에요 ("They're not in / unavailable"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: plain polite statement that someone is away
fixed compound noun — the label your phone screen shows
honorific -세요 when the absent person outranks you
formal -입니다, voicemail/announcement style

examples.ko: A: 박 부장님 계세요? / B: 죄송하지만 지금 부재중이세요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: A: bak bujangnim gyeseyo? / B: joesonghajiman jigeum bujaejungiseyo. memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: A: Is Manager Park available? / B: I'm sorry, she's out right now. Shall I take a message?
examples.note: classic office exchange; B uses 부재중이세요 to honor Park, then offers next step

examples.ko: 부재중 전화가 세 통이나 와 있네.
examples.romanization: bujaejung jeonhwaga se tongina wa inne.
examples.en: Whoa, I've got three missed calls.
examples.note: 통 = counter for calls; -이나 conveys 'as many as three'

examples.ko: 담당자가 부재중입니다. 잠시 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: damdangjaga bujaejungimnida. jamsi hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: The agent is unavailable. We will contact you again shortly.
examples.note: formal -입니다 and -겠습니다; the voice-announcement register

expressions.nuance: A semi-formal word meaning 'absent from one's seat,' used both to explain someone can't come to the phone and, as the fixed compound 부재중 전화, to label a missed call on your screen. The 한자 roots mark the register: 부재(不在) — 不 'not' + 在 'present/exist' — means 'not present,' while 중(中) means 'in the midst of,' so 부재중 is 'in a state of being absent.' That makes it distinctly more official than everyday 없어요 ('isn't here') or 나갔어요 ('stepped out'), which feel too casual for an office phone. The key synonym contrast: 부재중 means physically AWAY from the phone or desk, while 통화 중 means they ARE at the phone but already speaking to someone else — use the wrong one and you misdirect the caller. Key 변형형: 부재중이에요 (neutral polite) → 부재중이세요 (honorific, about a respected person) → 부재중입니다 (formal announcement) → 부재중 전화 (fixed compound noun for a missed call). Using 부재중 with a close friend who just stepped out would sound oddly stiff; in that case say 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Pronouncing/spelling it 부제중. It is 부재중 — the 한자 is 在 (재 'present'), not 제. 부제 means a 'subtitle,' a totally different word.
Using it for a friend who just stepped out. 부재중 is office/formal; casually say 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요.
Confusing 부재중 (away from the phone) with 통화 중 (on another call). They describe opposite reasons someone can't take your call.

structuredNuance.t: 부재중 = 不在中, 'in a state of being absent from one's post.' In practice it means: the person is away from their desk or phone right now. As a compound noun, 부재중 전화 is the standard label for a missed call on every Korean smartphone.

Office and phone contexts: 부재중이세요 raises the absent person; 부재중이에요 is neutral. Formal announcements use 부재중입니다. With a friend or in casual speech, 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요 is more natural — 부재중 sounds stiff in casual situations.
부재중 (away from the phone entirely) vs 통화 중 (at the phone but already on a call). They explain opposite problems. 자리 없어요 / 나갔어요 are the casual near-synonyms for 'stepped out.'

부재중이에요 (neutral polite) → 부재중이세요 (honorific, about someone you respect) → 부재중입니다 (formal announcement register) → 부재중 전화 (compound noun = missed call). The honorific tier is determined entirely by who the absent person is, not who is calling.

Spelling trap: 부재중 is often misspelled as 부제중. The 한자 is 在 (재), meaning 'present,' not 제. 부제 is a totally different word meaning 'subtitle.' Also: using 부재중이에요 in casual conversation sounds oddly formal — stick to 나갔어요 with friends.

expressions.english: I'll get in touch with you later
expressions.shortExplanation: 나중에 연락드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll get in touch with you later".
expressions.explanation: 나중에 연락드릴게요 (najung-e yeollak-deurilgeyo) = "I'll get in touch with you later". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 나중에 연락드릴게요 ("I'll contact you later"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: humble promise to reach back out; -드릴게요 raises the listener

usagePhrases.en: I'll reach out in a bit
usagePhrases.note: 이따가 = later TODAY (not 나중에, which can be open-ended)

usagePhrases.en: I will get back to you
usagePhrases.note: formal -겠습니다; business close
반말; plain 연락하다 + -ㄹ게

examples.ko: A: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? / B: 지금 좀 바빠서요. 나중에 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo? / B: jigeum jom bappaseoyo. najunge yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Is now a good time to talk? / B: I'm a bit busy right now. I'll contact you later.
examples.note: natural back-and-forth ending a call gracefully; -아서요 trails off to soften

examples.en: I'll check and get back to you later.
examples.note: -고 chains 'check first, then contact'

examples.ko: 나 지금 운전 중이야. 나중에 연락할게.
examples.romanization: na jigeum unjeon jungiya. najunge yeollakalge.
examples.en: I'm driving right now. I'll call you later.
examples.note: casual; 운전 중 = mid-driving; plain 연락할게, no 드리다

expressions.nuance: The polite way to wrap up or postpone a conversation by promising to reach out again — it gracefully ends a call or defers a decision. 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean: 連 'connect' + 絡 'tie/wrap,' literally 'connecting threads,' and it covers ANY form of contact — call, text, or message — so don't read it as 'phone call only.' The humble 드리다 raises the listener, making -드릴게요 the respectful form; with peers or juniors it relaxes to 연락할게요 / 연락할게. Key 변형형: 나중에 연락드릴게요 (standard) → 이따가 연락드릴게요 (same-day tighter commitment) → 제가 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (formal business) → 나중에 연락할게 (반말). Three contrasts English speakers need: first, 연락 (get in touch later) vs 연결 (transfer a call right now) — never interchangeable; saying 나중에 연결드릴게요 is a clear wiring error. Second, timing words: 나중에 means 'later' with no deadline (could be tomorrow or next week), while 이따가 means 'a bit later TODAY' — promising 이따가 sets a tighter implicit commitment. Third, register: 드리다 honors the listener, so using 연락드릴게요 toward someone clearly junior to you can sound over-deferential; plain 연락할게요 is more natural then.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 연락 as 'phone call' only. 연락 = contact by any channel (call OR text). '연락 주세요' means 'get in touch,' not specifically 'phone me.'
Swapping in 연결 for 연락. 나중에 연결드릴게요 is wrong — 연결 is connecting a call now; later contact is 연락.
Using 드릴게요 to someone clearly below you in status. The humble 드리다 raises the listener; with a junior, plain 연락할게요 sounds more natural than over-deferential 연락드릴게요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '나중에(later) + 연락(contact) + 드릴게요(I'll do for you).' A humble promise to reach back out by ANY channel — call, text, or message — at a future time. Used to close a call gracefully or defer an answer.

Said when ending a call because you're busy, need to check something, or simply can't talk now. -드릴게요 is the respectful form for seniors and clients. With peers or juniors, 연락할게요 / 연락할게 is natural and avoids sounding over-deferential.

연락 (get in touch later) vs 연결 (connect / transfer a call right now): never swap them. 나중에 (unspecified future) vs 이따가 (later today): 이따가 implies a tighter same-day commitment. Both pairs carry real social weight.
나중에 연락드릴게요 (standard) → 이따가 연락드릴게요 (tighter, same-day) → 제가 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (formal business) → 나중에 연락할게요 (neutral, no 드리다) → 나중에 연락할게 (반말). The humble 드리다 is the only element that shifts with register.

Two traps: (1) Using 드릴게요 with a junior — it over-honors them; use plain 연락할게요 instead. (2) Swapping 연락 for 연결: '나중에 연결드릴게요' sounds like 'I'll transfer your call later,' which makes no sense — later contact is 연락, not 연결.

expressions.english: I'll put them on / pass you over (to another person)
expressions.shortExplanation: 바꿔 드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll put them on / pass you over (to another person)".
expressions.explanation: 바꿔 드릴게요 (bakkwo deurilgeyo) means "I'll put them on / pass you over (to another person)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 바꿔 드릴게요 ("I'll put them on the line"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'll put them on the line
usagePhrases.note: humble; handing the SAME phone to the person you want

usagePhrases.en: One moment, I'll pass you over
usagePhrases.note: 잠시만요 buys the beat while you fetch them

usagePhrases.en: I'll put the person in charge on
usagePhrases.note: formal -겠습니다 service grade
반말 / at home; plain 주다

examples.ko: A: 아버지 계세요? / B: 네, 잠시만요. 바꿔 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: abeoji gyeseyo? / B: ne, jamsimanyo. bakkwo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Is your father there? / B: Yes, one moment. I'll put him on.
examples.note: typical home call hand-off; B confirms presence, then offers to pass the phone

examples.ko: 제가 잘 몰라서요. 아는 사람으로 바꿔 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jega jal mollaseoyo. aneun sarameuro bakkwo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: I'm not sure, so I'll put on someone who knows.
examples.note: -으로 marks who you're swapping TO; reason given first with -아서요

examples.en: Looking for Mom? Hold on, I'll put her on.
examples.note: casual at home; 줄게 not 드릴게요

expressions.nuance: Used when the person who answered hands the physical receiver (or the call) to the person the caller actually wants. The verb is 바꾸다, literally 'to change or swap,' which on the phone idiomatically means swapping who is speaking — you are not changing any object; you are exchanging voices on the line. The humble -아 드리다 makes it a service favor; 바꿔 줄게 is the peer/home version with plain 주다. The single most critical contrast is 바꾸다 vs 연결하다: 바꿔 드릴게요 is for physically handing the same device to a person standing right there (a colleague, a family member), while 연결해 드릴게요 is a system-level transfer to a different line or extension that you cannot simply hand-deliver. Using 연결 at home to hand mom the phone sounds comically corporate; using 바꾸다 for a multi-department transfer in an office sounds naively low-tech. The irregular conjugation trips learners: the stem is 바꾸-, and 바꾸- + -어 contracts cleanly to 바꿔, not 바껴 (which would falsely imply a stem 바끼-).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 연결해 드릴게요 to hand the phone to a family member. At home it's 바꿔 드릴게요; 연결 implies a technical transfer to another line, not passing the same handset.
Writing 바꿔 as 바껴. The stem is 바꾸- (바꾸 + 어 = 바꿔). 바껴 wrongly assumes a stem 바끼-, which does not exist.
Confusing 바꾸다 (swap/change) with 바라다 (hope) or 비꾸다 (no such word). On the phone, 'put someone on' is strictly 바꾸다 → 바꿔.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '바꿔(swap) + 드릴게요(I'll do for you).' Handing the phone to the person you want — swapping who speaks, not transferring through a system. The 바꾸다 in phone context always means this person-to-person voice exchange.
Home and office. Keep 드릴게요 (humble 드리다) with customers, seniors, or anyone you'd 존댓말. 바꿔 드리겠습니다 is the formal call-center equivalent. At home with peers, 바꿔 줄게 is natural.

바꿔 드릴게요 = hand the SAME phone to a person physically nearby (home or small office). 연결해 드릴게요 = route the call through a phone SYSTEM to a different line or department. They are different mechanical acts; swapping them sounds wrong in both directions.
바꾸다 → 바꿔 (바꾸 + 어) → 바꿔 드릴게요 (humble) / 바꿔 드리겠습니다 (formal) / 바꿔 줄게 (반말). Stronger form: 잠시만요, 바로 바꿔 드릴게요 (right away).

Conjugation error: the stem is 바꾸-, so 바꾸 + 어 = 바꿔, NOT 바껴. 바껴 implies a non-existent stem 바끼-. Also: using 연결해 드릴게요 when you mean 바꿔 드릴게요 — they are not synonyms; one is a physical hand-off, the other a system transfer.

expressions.shortExplanation: 전화 잘못 거셨어요 is a practical expression meaning "You've got the wrong number".
expressions.explanation: "You've got the wrong number" — that is 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (jeonhwa jalmot geosyeosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 전화 잘못 거셨어요 ("You've dialed the wrong number"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite, said TO the caller; 거셨어요 = honorific past of 걸다

usagePhrases.en: I think you have the wrong number
usagePhrases.note: -것 같다 hedges so you don't sound blunt

usagePhrases.en: There's no one by that name here
usagePhrases.note: the usual follow-up; -는데요 trails off softly
반말 — typically the CALLER admitting it

examples.ko: A: 거기 서울 치과 아닌가요? / B: 아닌데요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같은데요.
examples.romanization: A: geogi seoul chigwa aningayo? / B: anindeyo. jeonhwa jalmot geosin geot gateundeyo.
examples.en: A: Isn't this Seoul Dental? / B: No, it isn't. I think you may have the wrong number.
examples.note: A/B exchange; B uses the softened -신 것 같은데요 to avoid sounding blunt while correcting the caller

examples.ko: 죄송하지만 전화 잘못 거셨어요. 그런 분 안 계세요.
examples.romanization: joesonghajiman jeonhwa jalmot geosyeosseoyo. geureon bun an gyeseyo.
examples.en: Sorry, but you've got the wrong number — no one by that name here.
examples.note: 죄송하지만 cushions the correction; 그런 분 안 계세요 = honorific 'no such person is here'

examples.ko: 어? 미안, 내가 전화 잘못 걸었어.
examples.romanization: eo? mian, naega jeonhwa jalmot georeosseo.
examples.en: Huh? Sorry, I dialed the wrong number.
examples.note: the caller owning the mistake; 내가 + 걸었어 — subject shifts to I, no honorific needed

expressions.nuance: What you say when a stranger has reached you by mistake. The verb is 걸다, the standard Korean verb for placing a call (전화를 걸다, literally 'hook up / hang a call'), and here it appears as the honorific past 거셨어요, so you are politely informing the CALLER that they dialed wrong — note you still raise them with -시- even while delivering bad news. When the CALLER realizes the mistake and apologizes, they own it as 제가 잘못 걸었어요 ('I misdialed'), so subject determines verb form: 거셨어요 (you did) vs 걸었어요 (I did). To soften an awkward correction, Koreans add a hedge: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('it seems you may have the wrong number') is far gentler than the bare statement. The headline English-speaker trap is the irregular conjugation: 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb — before honorific -시-, the ㄹ drops, giving 거시- → 거셨어요, not the over-regularized 걸으셨어요. A second near-synonym follow-up line is 여기 그런 분 안 계세요 ('there is no such person here'), which provides the evidence behind the wrong-number claim.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 전화 잘못 걸으셨어요. 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular: the ㄹ drops before -시-, giving 거셨어요. 걸으셨어요 over-regularizes the stem.
Using 거셨어요 about yourself. When YOU misdial, the subject is 제가, so say 제가 잘못 걸었어요 — keep the honorific -시- only for the other person.
Mixing 걸다 (place a call) with 받다 (answer a call). You 전화를 걸다 to dial and 전화를 받다 to pick up; 'wrong number' is about 걸다, the dialing.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '전화(call) + 잘못(wrongly) + 거셨어요(you placed).' Notifies a caller they've reached the wrong number. Despite correcting them, the honorific -시- remains because Korean politeness is independent of the message content. Softened version: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('it seems you may have the wrong number').

Said by the person who received the mistaken call. Standard polite -세요 / -셨어요 with any stranger. The caller admitting the error uses plain past 잘못 걸었어요 (polite) or 잘못 걸었어 (반말). 죄송하지만 as a lead-in is a natural cushion before correcting.

여기 그런 분 안 계세요 ('there's no such person here') is the natural follow-up line rather than a synonym — it gives the concrete evidence for the wrong-number claim. 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 is the hedged, softer alternative to the direct 잘못 거셨어요.
걸다 → 거셨어요 (you, honorific past) / 걸었어요 (I, plain past) / 거신 것 같은데요 (hedged). Caller admitting it: 제가 잘못 걸었어요. The ㄹ-drop before -시- is the key irregular to master.
Over-regularizing the ㄹ-irregular: 걸다 drops the ㄹ before -시-, so the honorific past is 거셨어요, NOT 걸으셨어요. 걸으셨어요 is a beginner error that sounds like you are conjugating 걷다 (to walk) instead.

expressions.english: Please call back in a little while
expressions.shortExplanation: 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please call back in a little while".
expressions.explanation: 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 (jamsi hue dasi georeo juseyo) = "Please call back in a little while". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 ("Please call again shortly"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: asks the caller to retry later rather than wait on hold

usagePhrases.en: Call back in a bit, please
usagePhrases.note: 조금 이따 = casual 'in a little bit'
-아 주시겠어요 = extra-polite request form
반말; bare 걸어, no 주세요

examples.ko: A: 지금 연결이 어렵나요? / B: 회의 중이라서요. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum yeongyeori eoryeomnayo? / B: hoeui jungiraseoyo. jamsi hue dasi georeo juseyo.
examples.en: A: Is it hard to connect right now? / B: I'm in a meeting. Please call back in a little while.
examples.note: A/B exchange; B gives reason with -이라서요 then makes the callback request

examples.ko: 통화량이 많습니다. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
examples.romanization: tonghwaryangi manhseumnida. jamsi hue dasi georeo juseyo.
examples.en: Call volume is high. Please call again shortly.
examples.note: the exact wording of an automated busy-line announcement — recognizing this saves frustration

examples.ko: 나 밥 먹고 있어. 이따 다시 걸어.
examples.romanization: na bam meokgo isseo. itta dasi georeo.
examples.en: I'm eating. Call me back later.
examples.note: casual; -고 있어 = in the middle of; 이따 pins it to today

expressions.nuance: A polite request for the caller to try again soon instead of holding the line. It breaks into 잠시 후에 ('after a short while': 잠시 from 한자 暫時 'brief time,' + 후 後 'after' + -에 locative) and 다시 걸어 주세요 ('please dial again'), where 걸다 is the verb for placing a call and 주세요 frames the redial as a favor you are requesting. This phrase is verbatim the wording of Korean automated busy-line recordings, so recognizing it in the wild is as useful as producing it yourself. Key 변형형: 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 (standard) → 잠시 후 다시 걸어 주시겠어요? (extra-polite) → 이따 다시 걸어 주세요 (casual/same-day) → 이따 다시 걸어 (반말). Two English-speaker voice traps: first, 'call back' is the ACTIVE verb 걸다 → 걸어 주세요, NOT the passive 걸리다 (걸려 주세요 is wrong because 걸리다 means 'be caught/take time'); second, don't confuse 잠시 후에 ('after a moment' — telling someone to ACT later) with 잠시만요 ('hold on just a sec' — telling someone to STAY put now); they give opposite instructions.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다시 걸려 주세요. The active verb is 걸다 (걸어 주세요 = 'please dial'). 걸리다 is passive ('be caught / take time'), so 걸려 주세요 is wrong here.
Confusing 잠시 후에 with 잠시만요. 잠시 후에 = 'after a short while' (go retry later); 잠시만요 = 'hold on a second' (stay put now). Opposite instructions.
Treating 잠시 후 and 잠깐 as fully interchangeable in formal speech. 잠시 후(에) is the standard announcement register; 잠깐만 is more casual and odd in an automated message.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '잠시 후에(after a short while) + 다시(again) + 걸어 주세요(please dial).' Sends the caller away to retry rather than holding. This is the exact wording of Korean automated busy-line announcements — recognizing it in the wild matters as much as saying it yourself.

Said when you cannot take the call now — in a meeting, on another call, in a noisy place. Standard polite 주세요 suits any situation. 주시겠어요? softens it further for a VIP or formal context. 이따 다시 걸어 is the casual peer/반말 version.

잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 = call back after a moment (future action). 잠시만요 = wait/stay on the line for a second (present freeze). They give opposite directions to the caller — one sends them away, the other holds them in place. 이따 다시 전화 주세요 is the colloquial near-synonym.

잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요 (standard polite) → 잠시 후 다시 걸어 주시겠어요? (extra-polite) → 이따 다시 걸어 주세요 (casual, same-day) → 이따 다시 걸어 (반말). The active stem 걸- (걸어 주세요) must not be confused with passive 걸리- (걸려요 = 'it takes time').

잠시(暫時): 暫 'brief/for now' + 時 'time' = 'a brief time.' 후(後) = 'after/behind.' Together 잠시 후에 = 'after a brief period.' The 한자 origin explains why this phrase sounds formal and fits automated announcements.

Voice confusion: 'call back' is ACTIVE 걸다 → 걸어 주세요; the passive form is 걸리다 (걸려 주세요 = 'please be caught/take time'), which makes no sense as a callback request. Also: 잠시 후에 ≠ 잠시만요 — one dismisses, the other freezes. Using the wrong one creates confusion about what the caller should do.

expressions.english: The signal is weak / poor reception
expressions.shortExplanation: 신호가 약해요 is a practical expression meaning "The signal is weak / poor reception".
expressions.explanation: 신호가 약해요 (sinho-ga yakaeyo) means "The signal is weak / poor reception". Say it as one set phrase — for example 신호가 약해요 ("The signal is weak"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: states the reception problem; 신호 takes -가 as subject

usagePhrases.en: It's because reception is weak here
usagePhrases.note: -아서요 trails off, giving the reason a call dropped

usagePhrases.en: I can't get a good signal
usagePhrases.note: 잡히다 = the signal is 'caught'/picked up; very natural alt
반말; particle 가 dropped

examples.ko: A: 여보세요? 목소리가 자꾸 끊겨요. / B: 여기 신호가 약해서요. 이따 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo? moksoriga jakku kkeunkyeoyo. / B: yeogi sinhoga yakaeseoyo. itta dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: A: Hello? Your voice keeps cutting out. / B: The signal's weak here. I'll call you back in a bit.
examples.note: A/B troubleshoot exchange; A names the symptom, B gives the cause and proposes the fix

examples.ko: 지하라서 신호가 약해요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: jiharaseo sinhoga yakaeyo. kkeunko dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: I'm underground so the signal's weak. Let me hang up and call back.
examples.note: -라서 reason; 끊고 다시 = hang up then redial — the natural fix sequence

examples.en: I'm in the mountains, signal's weak. Let's talk later.
examples.note: casual; -자 = let's; 통화하자 = let's talk by phone; 이따 = later today

expressions.nuance: The natural way to explain why a call sounds garbled or keeps dropping: the cellular 신호 is 약하다 ('weak'). 신호(信號) is Sino-Korean: 信 'trust/sign' + 號 'mark/number,' literally a 'signal mark,' covering signals broadly — traffic lights are also 신호등 ('signal lamp') — so context tells you it means cell reception here. The key near-synonym is 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 ('the signal isn't being picked up well'), which uses the passive 잡히다 ('be caught') and is equally natural; in Korea people alternate freely between the two. Key 변형형: 신호가 약해요 (standard) → 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 (passive alternative, equally common) → 여기 신호가 약해서요 (reason-trailing form) → 신호 약해 (반말). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, reaching for the loanword 사인 — in Korean, 사인 means a 'signature' or a gestured 'sign,' not cell reception; phone signal is 신호. Second, the adjective choice: signal strength pairs with 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다 (small/big) — saying 신호가 작아요 sounds wrong the way 'the signal is small' does in English. Pair the signal complaint with 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well') to explain to the other person WHY you keep saying 뭐라고요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 사인 for 'signal.' Cell reception is 신호; 사인 in Korean means a signature or a hand sign, so '사인이 약해요' is wrong.
Saying 신호가 작아요/커요. Strength pairs with 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다 (small/big). '신호가 세요' = 'the signal is strong.'
Confusing 신호 with 신호등. Bare 신호 on the phone = reception/signal; 신호등 specifically is a traffic light. Don't add 등 when talking about a call.

structuredNuance.t: 신호 = cell signal/reception; 약해요 = is weak. Together: 'the reception is poor.' Pair it with 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well') to link the cause (weak signal) to the effect (garbled audio). Used whenever a call sounds broken, drops, or gets patchy.

Said mid-call to explain audio problems. Polite 약해요 suits any phone situation. Casual 신호 약해 (particle dropped, plain stem) is natural with friends. 신호가 약해서요 with a trailing -아서요 works as a soft apology-reason.
