examples.note: -ㄹ지 embeds the unknown future fact inside 모르겠어요, showing the EMBEDDED QUESTION structure essential for real speech.

expressions.nuance: 모르다 is the antonym of 알다 'to know', and the -겠- before the polite -어요 ending softens the assertion into 'I can't seem to tell / I'm not certain' rather than a blunt fact. This makes 모르겠어요 notably more humble and polite than 몰라요 — which, without -겠-, can sound curt or even dismissive, like 'I don't know and that's that'. Use 모르겠어요 with customers, teachers, seniors, or anyone you're being careful with; 몰라요 is fine between close friends. Adding 잘 (잘 모르겠어요) counterintuitively intensifies the not-knowing — it does NOT mean 'I know well'; in negative verbs, 잘 boosts the negative, meaning 'I really have no idea'. The -ㄴ지/-ㄹ지 construction embeds questions inside 모르겠어요: 어디인지 모르겠어요, 맞는지 모르겠어요, 언제 오실지 모르겠어요 — this pattern is essential for natural speech. Compare 안 알아요: Korean does not negate 알다 with 안; the dedicated negative is 모르다, making 안 알아요 wrong for 'I don't know'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 잘 모르겠어요 as 'I know it well'.
잘 here intensifies the negative verb, so it means 'I really don't know', the opposite of what 잘 ('well') suggests in English.
Defaulting to 몰라요 with strangers or superiors.
몰라요 sounds blunt, even cold; the -겠- in 모르겠어요 adds politeness and humility, which is safer in service or formal settings.
Saying 안 알아요 for 'I don't know'.
Korean does not negate 알다 with 안; the dedicated antonym verb is 모르다. Use 몰라요 / 모르겠어요, never 안 알아요.

structuredNuance.t: 모르다 = 'to not know' + -겠- = epistemic softener + -어요 = polite ending. The -겠- is NOT future tense here; it hedges the claim. Literal: 'I (seemingly) don't know.' Real meaning: 'I'm not sure / I can't quite tell' — more tentative and humble than plain 몰라요.

모르겠어요 = polite, for service contexts, seniors, teachers, strangers. 모르겠습니다 = formal 합쇼체, office/official settings. 모르겠어 = casual, friends and peers. 몰라요 = neutral but blunter; fine between friends but can sound curt to superiors.

몰라요 = flat fact, can sound dismissive. 모르겠어요 = hedged, polite, open to reconsidering. 기억이 안 나요 = 'I can't recall' (memory issue, not ignorance). 잘 모르겠어요 = 'I really have no idea' (stronger negative, not 'I know well').
Embedded questions: [clause]-ㄴ지/-ㄹ지 + 모르겠어요 (어디인지, 언제 오실지, 맞는지). Add 아직 for 'not yet': 아직 모르겠어요. Strengthen with 정말: 정말 모르겠어요. Full formal: 모르겠습니다.

잘 모르겠어요 looks like 'I know (잘) well' — but 잘 before a negative verb intensifies the negative: it means 'I truly have no idea'. Also, never say 안 알아요 for 'I don't know': 알다 is negated only by the separate verb 모르다, not by 안 + 알다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 잠깐만요 is a practical expression meaning "Hold on a sec".
expressions.explanation: "Hold on a sec" — that is 잠깐만요 (jamkkanmanyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잠깐만요 ("Hold on a sec"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Asking for a brief pause
Slightly more formal twin
Full polite request form
Squeezing past in a crowd

examples.en: Hold on a sec!
examples.note: Rapid stop-signal when someone is about to walk away or do something — the clipped form works as an interjectional grab of attention.

examples.ko: A: 이제 출발할까요? / B: 잠깐만요, 전화 좀 받을게요.
examples.romanization: A: ije chulbalhalkkayo? / B: jamkkanmanyo, jeonhwa jom badeulgeyo.
examples.en: A: Shall we head off? / B: One second — let me grab this call.
examples.note: -ㄹ게요 announces B's own next action; B is not asking permission, just signaling a tiny delay.

examples.en: Excuse me, let me get past.
examples.note: Subway/crowd context: used exactly like English 'excuse me, coming through' — the wait-request doubles as an attention-getter for physical space.

expressions.nuance: 잠깐 means 'a brief moment', 만 is the limiter particle 'only/just', and 요 makes it polite — so 잠깐만요 is literally 'just a brief moment, please', covering both 'hold on a sec' (asking to wait) and 'excuse me' (getting attention or space), the way English 'one second' or 'excuse me' pulls double duty. The near-twin 잠시만요 uses 잠시, the more literary synonym for 'a moment'; 잠시만요 leans slightly more formal and is preferred in service announcements or with older strangers, while 잠깐만요 is everyday conversational. Neither is rude, but 잠깐만요 without the 요 — bare 잠깐만 — drops into 반말 and can sound abrupt to strangers. Compare with 기다려요 ('wait'), which is a direct command; 잠깐만요 is gentler because 만 limits the imposition to 'only a tiny moment'. The full 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 is grammatically complete but sounds over-elaborate in quick spoken exchanges where the clipped form is natural.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping the 요 with strangers: just 잠깐만.
잠깐만 alone is 반말 and can sound abrupt or even rude to someone you don't know; keep the polite 요 — 잠깐만요.
Confusing it with 잠깐 as a noun meaning 'briefly'.
잠깐 by itself is the adverb/noun 'for a moment' (그는 잠깐 왔어요); 잠깐만요 is the fixed interjection 'hold on'. They aren't interchangeable in a sentence.
Using 잠깐만요 to make someone wait a long time.
It promises only a tiny pause (만 = just); for a real wait, say 조금만 기다려 주세요 or give a time, or it feels misleading.

structuredNuance.t: 잠깐 = 'a brief moment' + 만 = limiter 'only/just' + 요 = politeness. Literal: 'only a brief moment, please.' Real uses: (1) 'hold on / wait a sec', (2) 'excuse me, coming through / may I have your attention' — same word, two jobs depending on whether you're asking for time or physical space.

잠깐만요 = polite everyday speech, anyone you're not on casual terms with. 잠시만요 = slightly more formal, service contexts, elders, announcements. 잠깐만 (no 요) = 반말, close friends or juniors only. Never bare 잠깐만 to strangers.

잠시만요 = same meaning, marginally more formal. 기다려요 = blunt command 'wait'; 잠깐만요 is gentler because it frames the request as tiny (만). 실례합니다 = formal 'excuse me' for interrupting someone; 잠깐만요 is faster and more casual for the same purpose.
Scale up to full request: 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 (please wait a moment). Expand with reason: 잠깐만요, 메모 좀 할게요 ('hold on, let me take a note'). Casual short: 잠깐만!
English speakers over-formalize: they say 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 for every situation, but fast Korean conversation just uses 잠깐만요. Separately, they drop 요 with strangers — bare 잠깐만 is 반말 and sounds abrupt.
chips: 잠깐만요 is the natural fast form

expressions.shortExplanation: 천만에요 is a practical expression meaning "You're welcome.".
expressions.explanation: "You're welcome." — that is 천만에요 (cheonmaneyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 천만에요 ("you're welcome"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite reply to thanks; slightly formal/old-fashioned
반말, brushing off a friend's thanks
격식, very humble downward-deflection
the natural everyday reply people actually use

examples.en: A: Thank you. / B: You're welcome.
examples.note: the textbook A/B reply, correct but slightly formal-sounding in daily life

examples.en: Thank you. — You're welcome; I'm glad it helped.
examples.note: softening 천만에요 with a follow-up clause so it doesn't sound stiff

examples.ko: 덕분에 잘 끝냈어요. — 천만에요, 별것도 아닌데요.
examples.romanization: deokbune jal kkeunnaesseoyo. — cheonmaneyo, byeolgeotdo anindeyo.
examples.en: Thanks to you it went well. — You're welcome, it was really nothing.
examples.note: pairing with 별것 아니에요 for a humble, natural close

expressions.nuance: 천만에요 is the textbook 'you're welcome' reply to 감사합니다, but in real daily life it sounds a little formal or even old-fashioned to younger Koreans, so people more often say 아니에요, 별말씀을요, or 별거 아니에요 to wave off thanks. The literal phrase means '(that's) ten thousand and more (words of thanks)' — i.e. 'far from it, not at all'. The formality ladder: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 / 별거 아니에요 (everyday polite) → 천만에요 (polite, slight vintage feel) → 천만의 말씀입니다 (격식, very humble). The dividing line versus 별말씀을요 is tone: 별말씀을요 is humble and flows naturally upward when a senior thanks you, while 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook and can sound a touch awkward. The key English-speaker mistake is treating 천만에요 like the constant, reflexive 'you're welcome' of English — Koreans often reply to thanks with a smile, 네, or 아니에요, and over-firing 천만에요 sounds stilted and overly formal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 천만에요 reflexively after every thanks like English 'you're welcome' — it sounds stiff; 아니에요 or 별말씀을요 is more natural.
Saying 천만에요 to a close friend — too formal; use 뭘 or 아니야 in 반말.
Misspelling it 천만애요 — it is 천만에요 (에, not 애).

structuredNuance.t: 천만에요 literally means 'ten thousand and more (words)' — i.e. '(there are) ten million [thanks to give back]; not at all.' The real function is deflecting thanks politely. The archaic feel comes from 천만(千萬) 'ten million', an idiom of rhetorical excess meaning 'far from it'.
Formality ladder: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 / 별거 아니에요 (everyday polite) → 천만에요 (polite, slightly vintage) → 천만의 말씀입니다 (격식, very humble). Use 아니에요 in most everyday situations — it's warmer and less dated.

The dividing line versus 별말씀을요: 별말씀을요 is humble and flows naturally upward (when a senior or customer thanks you), while 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook and can sound slightly stiff. In daily life, 아니에요 or 별말씀을요 sounds more genuine.

Soften by adding a follow-up clause: 천만에요, 도움이 됐다니 다행이에요. To intensify or write formally: 천만의 말씀입니다. To wave off thanks in 반말: 뭘, 뭘 그런 걸. Never say 천만이에요 — the fixed form is 천만에요, not a copula construction.

English speakers fire 천만에요 reflexively after every thanks, like 'you're welcome' — it sounds stilted. Koreans often reply with 네 + a nod, or 아니에요 in daily life. Reserve 천만에요 for slightly formal moments.

expressions.english: Don't mention it. / Not at all.
expressions.shortExplanation: 별말씀을요 is a practical expression meaning "Don't mention it. / Not at all.".
expressions.explanation: 별말씀을요 (byeolmalsseumeuryo) = "Don't mention it. / Not at all.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 별말씀을요 ("don't mention it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: humble polite reply, often upward to a senior/customer
반말-ish casual shortening among close people

usagePhrases.en: you're too kind to say so (formal)
usagePhrases.note: 격식, very humble deflection of praise/thanks
natural extension softening with 아니에요

examples.ko: A: 정말 도움이 많이 됐습니다. / B: 별말씀을요.
examples.romanization: A: jeongmal doumi mani dwaetseumnida. / B: byeolmalsseumeuryo.
examples.en: A: You were a real help. / B: Don't mention it.
examples.note: humble deflection when someone above you thanks you

examples.en: You were a huge help. — Please, don't mention it.
examples.note: deflecting a senior's thanks modestly in the workplace

examples.ko: 바쁘신데 직접 와 주셔서 감사합니다. — 별말씀을요, 당연히 와야죠.
examples.romanization: bappeusinde jikjeop wa jusyeoseo gamsahamnida. — byeolmalsseumeuryo, dangyeonhi wayajyo.
examples.en: Thank you for coming in person despite being busy. — Not at all, of course I'd come.
examples.note: pairing with 당연히 ~죠 to sound gracious and unforced

expressions.nuance: 별말씀을요 is a humble, polite way to wave off thanks or praise — literally '(what) unusual words (you say)' — meaning 'you needn't say such a thing; it was nothing'. It is the go-to when someone above you (a customer, a senior, an elder) thanks you and you want to sound genuinely modest, not just polite. The 말씀 is the honorific word for 'words/speech', so the phrase already raises the SPEAKER — making it naturally respectful upward. The formality ladder: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 (everyday polite) → 별말씀을요 (humble-polite, upward) → 별말씀을 다 하십니다 (격식). The dividing line versus 천만에요 is that 천만에요 is neutral-textbook, while 별말씀을요 leans 'I'm too humble to accept this praise' and works especially well toward seniors and customers. English speakers often mis-segment it as '별 말씀 이요' with spaces — it is a single set phrase 별말씀을요, where 을요 is the object marker + softening particle. Also, do not use it to a close friend — it is too formal; say 뭘 or 아니야.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 별말씀을요 with a close friend — it is humble/formal; in 반말 just say 뭘 or 아니야.
Breaking it into 별 말씀 with a space or writing 별말씀이요 — the set phrase is 별말씀을요.
Thinking it only answers thanks — it also gracefully deflects praise ('you flatter me').

structuredNuance.t: Literally '(what) unusual/extra words (you say)' — i.e. 'you needn't say such a thing; it was nothing'. The 말씀 is the honorific for 'words/speech', which already makes the phrase deferential by design.
Formality: 뭘 / 아니야 (반말) → 아니에요 (everyday) → 별말씀을요 (humble-polite, flows upward) → 별말씀을 다 하십니다 (격식). Best used when a senior or customer thanks you; sounds too formal to a close friend.

The dividing line versus 천만에요 is humility and direction: 별말씀을요 leans 'I'm too humble to accept this thanks' and flows naturally upward; 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook and slightly vintage. 별말씀을요 is the safer choice when a superior or customer thanks you.

Extend with a follow-up: 별말씀을요, 당연히 해야죠 / 별말씀을요, 저도 배운 게 많았습니다. To soften, prepend 아니에요: 아니에요, 별말씀을요. Very formal written or spoken escalation: 별말씀을 다 하십니다. In 반말 among friends the phrase shrinks to 별말을 — but that sounds odd in formal contexts.

English speakers mis-segment it as '별 말씀 이요' with spaces — it is the set phrase 별말씀을요. Also, using it with a close friend sounds overly formal; say 뭘 or 아니야 instead. Do not confuse 을요 here with the topic marker — it is object + softening particle.

expressions.shortExplanation: 다음에 또 오세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please come again".
expressions.explanation: "Please come again" — that is 다음에 또 오세요 (daeume tto oseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다음에 또 오세요 ("Please come again"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Shop/restaurant staff farewell
Shorter, friendly version
Mutual goodbye, 뵙다 = humbly meet

usagePhrases.en: Get home safe and come again
usagePhrases.note: Warm layered send-off

examples.en: Goodbye! Come again!
examples.note: Cheery shout as a customer leaves — staff may overlap both phrases for a warmer send-off.

examples.ko: A: 잘 먹었습니다. / B: 맛있게 드셨어요? 다음에 또 오세요.
examples.romanization: A: jal meogeotseumnida. / B: masitge deusyeosseoyo? daeume tto oseyo.
examples.en: A: That was a great meal. / B: Did you enjoy it? Please come again.
examples.note: Classic restaurant farewell exchange: A's gratitude triggers B's invite — only the host staying behind issues the 오세요.

examples.ko: 감사합니다! 다음에 또 오세요, 조심히 가세요.
examples.romanization: gamsahamnida! daeume tto oseyo, josimhi gaseyo.
examples.en: Thank you! Please come again — take care going home.
examples.note: Cashier layering both the come-back invite and a safe-home wish in one warm send-off.

expressions.nuance: 다음에 ('next time') + 또 ('again') + 오세요 (honorific imperative of 오다 'to come') = 'please come again next time' — the standard warm send-off from staff or hosts to departing guests. The direction of the verb is crucial: the host uses 오다 (come toward me) because from their perspective the customer returns toward them; 가다 (go away from me) would be a directional error. The word 또 ('again, also') does the 'come back' work; 다시 ('again, redo') sounds like you're asking for a repeat of something that went wrong, so 다시 오세요 can inadvertently imply the visit wasn't good enough. One-way flow: this is the host's line, not the guest's — a customer should not say 다음에 또 오세요 to the shop; instead, reply with 잘 먹었습니다 or 감사합니다. Casual short form: 또 오세요 alone is friendly and common; 다음에 또 오세요 adds the 'next time' warmth. Mutual farewell between friends uses 다음에 봐요 ('see you next time') or 다음에 또 봐 (반말), not 오세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다음에 또 가세요 to invite someone back.
From the host's view the customer comes toward them, so the verb is 오다 → 오세요. 가세요 ('go') reverses the direction and sounds wrong.
A customer repeating 또 오세요 to the staff.
This is the host's line; customers reply with 네, 감사합니다 or 잘 먹었습니다, not by inviting the staff to 'come again'.
Swapping 또 for 다시 as 다음에 다시 오세요.
다시 nudges toward 'redo/once more'; for 'come another time' natives say 또. 다시 오세요 can hint you did something wrong the first time.

structuredNuance.t: 다음에 = next time + 또 = again + 오세요 = honorific imperative of 오다 'to come'. Literal: 'please come again next time.' Real: the host's warm standing invitation to return — social glue that ends a commercial or hosting interaction on a warm note.

Said exclusively by the person staying (shop, restaurant, host) to the person leaving (customer, guest). Never said by the guest to the host. Register: 오세요 = polite standard; if the customer is a VIP senior, 또 방문해 주세요 ('please visit again') is even more formal. Casual short: 또 오세요.

다음에 봐요 = mutual casual farewell between equals ('see you next time'). 다음에 또 오세요 = host-to-guest, directional. 다시 오세요 = sounds like the visit needs to be redone (avoid). 또 오세요 = friendly shorter version of the same phrase.
Shorter: 또 오세요. Layered: 조심히 가시고 또 오세요. Formal: 다음에도 방문해 주세요. 반말 (to a young regular): 또 와요 / 또 와.

Guests sometimes mirror 다음에 또 오세요 back to the staff — this is the host's line only. Guests reply with 잘 먹었습니다 / 감사합니다. Second trap: 다시 오세요 feels like a logical 'come again' but implies a redo, not a warm repeat visit.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "Here it is".
expressions.explanation: 여기 있어요 (yeogi isseoyo) = "Here it is". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기 있어요 ("Here it is / here you go"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Here it is / here you go
usagePhrases.note: Handing something over
More formal 합쇼체 service form
Calling a server's attention
With a handing gesture

examples.en: Here you go.
examples.note: Said while physically extending something — the action and the phrase happen simultaneously; no additional words needed.

examples.ko: A: 영수증 드려요? / B: 괜찮아요, 됐어요. 거스름돈 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: yeongsujeung deuryeoyo? / B: gwaenchanayo, dwaesseoyo. geoseureumdon yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Would you like a receipt? / B: No thank you — here's your change.
examples.note: Cashier exchange: B pairs 괜찮아요 ('it's fine/no need') with the handover phrase; 거스름돈 = change.

examples.en: Here's the Americano you ordered.
examples.note: Server placing a drink: the item name precedes 여기 있어요, pinpointing which drink is being presented, common in cafes.

expressions.nuance: 여기 있어요 = 여기 ('here, this place') + 있어요, the polite form of 있다 'to exist / to be located' — literally 'it is here', used the moment you physically hand or present something, like English 'here you go / here it is'. 있다 is the existence-and-location verb (opposite of 없다); do not substitute 이다 'to be (identifying)', so 'here it is' is 여기 있어요, never 여기 이에요. A critical distinction: the clipped 여기요 is the standard call for a server in a restaurant ('excuse me, over here!') — the same root word but a completely different function, distinguished by whether you are holding something out (여기 있어요) or signaling for attention (여기요). The negative is 여기 없어요 ('it's not here'), using 없다, not 안 있어요. The formal version 여기 있습니다 is used in polished service settings. In fast daily exchange, Koreans may also just say 여기요 while extending an item to a familiar person, but this risks ambiguity with the server-call; adding 있어요 removes all ambiguity.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using bare 여기요 to mean 'here you go' when handing something over.
여기요 alone is the call for a server ('excuse me!'). To present an item, say the full 여기 있어요, or the listener hears 'waiter, over here'.
Saying 여기 이에요 instead of 여기 있어요.
Location/existence uses 있다 (있어요), not the identifying copula 이다 (이에요). 여기 이에요 is ungrammatical for 'it's here'.
Negating with 여기 안 있어요 for 'it's not here'.
있다 has its own antonym 없다; 'it's not here' is 여기 없어요, not 안 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 = 'here (this place)' + 있어요 = polite 있다 'to exist/be located'. Literal: 'it exists here.' Real: 'here you go / here it is' — accompanies the physical act of handing something over. The existence verb 있다 points to the item's location, not its identity.

여기 있어요 = standard polite handover (service, shopping, daily life). 여기 있습니다 = formal service register, polished staff. Casual 여기 있어 = 반말 only, close friends. 여기요 = completely different function — calling a server.

여기요 = call for a server ('excuse me/over here'), NOT a handover phrase. 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you') = announces the giving action, while 여기 있어요 = presents the item as already in hand. 여기 있어요 is presentation; 드릴게요 is announcement.
Formal: 여기 있습니다. With item name: [거스름돈/영수증/주문하신 음식] + 여기 있어요. With invitation to take: 여기 있어요, 받으세요. Casual: 여기 있어 (반말).

English speakers use bare 여기요 trying to say 'here you go' when handing something — but 여기요 calls a server. Add 있어요 when presenting an item. Also, 여기 없어요 (not here) uses 없다, never 안 있어요 — 있다 negates only with its own antonym.

examples.ko: A: 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? 비행기 시간이 좀 빠듯해서요. / B: 지금 막히면 40분, 안 막히면 25분이요.
examples.romanization: A: gonghangkkaji eolmana geollyeoyo? bihaenggi sigani jom ppadeutaeseoyo. / B: jigeum makimyeon 40bun, an makimyeon 25buniyo.
examples.en: A: How long to the airport? My flight time is a bit tight. / B: With traffic maybe 40 mins, without 25.
examples.note: Explaining your time pressure prompts the driver to give a more useful range estimate

examples.ko: 이 시간에 강남까지 얼마나 걸려요? 차 많이 막혀요?
examples.romanization: i sigane gangnamkkaji eolmana geollyeoyo? cha mani makyeoyo?
examples.en: How long to Gangnam at this hour? Is there a lot of traffic?
examples.note: Real situation: 이 시간에 ('at this hour') signals you're worried about rush-hour — the follow-up question is natural

expressions.nuance: This asks the taxi driver how long the ride will take, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말. The verb 걸리다 means 'to take (time/effort)' — it is the dedicated Korean verb for duration and has no English cognate, so it must be learned as a fixed collocation: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? or just 얼마나 걸려요?. Make it more tentative and polite with 얼마나 걸릴까요? (inviting the driver's estimate); 반말 is 얼마나 걸려?. Pin the destination with the particle 까지: 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요?. The dividing line to watch carefully: 얼마예요? (얼마 alone) asks about MONEY (price), while 얼마나 걸려요? asks about TIME (duration) — the presence of 나 and 걸리다 is what fixes this as a time question. The English-speaker's most common error is reaching for 길다 (physical length) and asking 얼마나 길어요? — this literally asks 'how long (in size) is it?' and makes no sense for a trip duration. Another trap is 시간이 얼마나 있어요?, which turns the question around and asks 'how much time do you have?', a completely different and confusing meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 얼마나 길어요? — 길다 is physical length; for time taken you must use 걸리다, so 얼마나 걸려요?.
Confusing it with price: 얼마예요? asks the cost, not the time; keep 걸려요 strictly for duration.
Marking the destination with 에 (공항에 얼마나 걸려요) — duration to a place uses 까지, so 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요?.

structuredNuance.t: 얼마나 걸려요? = literally 'how much does it hang/take?'. 걸리다 originally means 'to hang/be suspended', but in time expressions it is a fixed idiom meaning 'to take (time)'. There is no structural transparency here — English speakers must simply memorize 걸리다 as the time-duration verb.

Customer-to-driver in 존댓말 at the start of the ride. Add 공항까지, 강남까지 etc. to pin the endpoint. Soften with 얼마나 걸릴까요? when you want to invite an estimate rather than demand a number. 반말 얼마나 걸려? to a friend.

얼마예요? = asks price (money). 얼마나 걸려요? = asks duration (time). They are easy to confuse because 얼마 appears in both — the presence of 나 and 걸리다 signals time. 시간이 얼마나 있어요? = 'how much time do you have?' — a completely different question directed at the other person's schedule, not your trip.
공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? (with destination); 얼마나 걸릴까요? (softer estimate request); 얼마나 걸릴 것 같아요? (asking the driver's guess); 보통 얼마나 걸려요? (asking the usual/average time).

Saying 얼마나 길어요? — 길다 is physical length ('how long is this rope?'), not duration. Time duration always uses 걸리다. Another error: using 에 instead of 까지 for the destination (공항에 얼마나 걸려요?) — idiomatic Korean pairs 까지 with 걸리다 for 'how long to [place]'.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What is this?".
expressions.explanation: "What is this?" — that is 이거 뭐예요? (igeo mwoyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 뭐예요? ("What is this?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Pointing at an item, casual-polite
이게 = 이것이, with subject particle
저거 for something farther off
Asking the purpose/function

examples.en: What is this?
examples.note: Bare pointing question — natural while holding or tapping an unfamiliar item; the whole meaning is in gesture + phrase.

examples.ko: A: 이거 뭐예요? 매워요? / B: 이건 떡볶이인데요, 좀 매워요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo mwoyeyo? maewoyo? / B: igeon tteokbokkiindeyo, jom maewoyo.
examples.en: A: What's this? Is it spicy? / B: This is tteokbokki — it's a bit spicy.
examples.note: Food stall A/B: B uses 이건 (이것은, topic marker) to gently introduce the answer; 인데요 softens the information delivery.

examples.ko: 이 버튼 뭐예요? 누르면 어떻게 돼요?
examples.romanization: i beoteun mwoyeyo? nureumyeon eotteoke dwaeyo?
examples.en: What's this button? What happens if I press it?
examples.note: 이 + noun directly (no 것/거), then a natural follow-up: -면 어떻게 돼요? = 'what happens if I…' — shows 이거 뭐예요 as an opener to a fuller inquiry.

expressions.nuance: 이거 뭐예요? = 이거 (casual contraction of 이것 'this thing') + 뭐 (colloquial contraction of 무엇 'what') + 예요 (polite copula) — the everyday 'what is this?' spoken while pointing. Three contraction layers are standard in speech: 이것 → 이거, 이것이 → 이게 (with subject particle), 무엇이에요 → 뭐예요. 이거 뭐예요? and 이게 뭐예요? mean the same thing; the latter adds the subject particle for a marginally more deliberate delivery. Distance vocabulary: 이거 (near speaker) / 그거 (near listener) / 저거 (far from both) — match the word to where the object actually is. A crucial social rule: 뭐 (what) is for THINGS; asking about PEOPLE with 뭐예요 ('what are you?') is rude and grammatically wrong — 누구예요? ('who is this/are you?') is required. For function rather than identity, add 뭐 하는 거예요? or 어디에 써요? ('what's it used for?'). The copula fuses: write 뭐예요, not 뭐 이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 이거 뭐예요? about a person.
뭐 (what) is for things only; asking 'who is this?' takes 누구 → 이분 누구세요? Using 뭐예요 for a person is grammatically wrong and sounds rude.
Writing 이것이에요 / 무엇이에요 in casual speech.
Spoken Korean contracts these to 이게 / 뭐예요. The full forms are correct but sound stiff and written; natives say 이거 뭐예요?
Mixing up the distance words 이거/그거/저거.
이거 = near me, 그거 = near you, 저거 = away from both. Pointing at a far object but saying 이거 confuses the listener about which thing you mean.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 = this thing (spoken form of 이것) + 뭐 = what (spoken form of 무엇) + 예요 = polite copula. Literal: 'this thing — what is it?' Real: 'what is this?' — identity question about a nearby object, usually accompanied by pointing.

이거 뭐예요? = polite everyday speech, fine with shopkeepers, staff, strangers. 이게 뭐예요? = same meaning, slightly more careful pronunciation. 이거 뭐야? = casual 반말, close friends only. 이것이 무엇입니까? = very formal, almost written — not said in conversation.
이거 뭐예요? = what IS it (identity). 이거 뭐 하는 거예요? = what does it DO (function). 이게 누구 거예요? = whose IS it (ownership). For PEOPLE: never 뭐예요? — always 누구예요? or 이분이 누구세요?
Distance variants: 이거/그거/저거 + 뭐예요? With noun: 이 [음식/버튼/단어] 뭐예요? Follow-up question: 어디에 써요? / 어떻게 써요? Casual: 이거 뭐야?
Using 뭐예요? for a person ('what are you?') is rude and wrong — use 누구예요? or 이분 누구세요?. Also, writing or saying 뭐 이에요 as two words is unnatural — the copula fuses: 뭐예요, one unit.

expressions.shortExplanation: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 is a practical expression meaning "I will use the restroom".
expressions.explanation: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 (hwajangsil jom sseulgeyo) = "I will use the restroom". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 ("I'll use the restroom"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite heads-up about your own move
Asking the location
Asking permission, -아도 돼요?
다녀오다 = go and come back

examples.en: I'll just pop to the restroom.
examples.note: 다녀오다 = go and come back — implies you'll return promptly; more complete than 쓸게요 alone and very natural before a meeting or meal.

examples.ko: A: 저기요, 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? / B: 네, 들어가세요.
examples.romanization: A: jeogiyo, hwajangsil jom sseodo dwaeyo? / B: ne, deureogaseyo.
examples.en: A: Excuse me, may I use the restroom? / B: Sure, go right in.
examples.note: Cafe/shop permission exchange: A uses the -아도 돼요? form to genuinely ask; B's 들어가세요 = 'please go in', confirming it's fine.

examples.ko: 밥 먹기 전에 화장실 좀 쓸게요.
examples.romanization: bam meokgi jeone hwajangsil jom sseulgeyo.
examples.en: I'll just use the restroom before we eat.
examples.note: -기 전에 = before doing [something]; the phrase signals a brief departure and implicit return, softened by 좀.

expressions.nuance: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 = 화장실 (化粧室, literally 'makeup/grooming room', the standard polite term for toilet/restroom) + 좀 (lubricating softener, worn-down 조금 'a little') + 쓸게요, the -ㄹ게요 form of 쓰다 'to use'. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the defining feature: it announces your own intention as a polite heads-up ('I'm going to do this — just letting you know'), not a request for permission. This contrasts sharply with -아도 돼요? 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? ('may I use the restroom?'), which genuinely asks permission. Use the -ㄹ게요 form at a friend's apartment or in a meeting room where it's obviously OK; use the -아도 돼요? form in a shop or someone's home where you are not certain. 좀 is purely a politeness softener here — 화장실 쓸게요 without it is grammatical but slightly blunt; 화장실 좀 쓸게요 is warmer. 화장실 is the standard neutral term; 변소 is crude and dated. A common natural alternative: 화장실 좀 다녀올게요 (using 다녀오다 'go and come back') emphasizes you'll return.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 쓸게요 when you actually need permission.
-ㄹ게요 announces your own plan, not a request. In someone's home or a shop, ask 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? with the permission ending -아도 돼요.
Treating 좀 as the literal 'a little'.
Here 좀 is a politeness softener that smooths the request, not a quantity. 화장실 좀 쓸게요 doesn't mean 'use the restroom a little'.
Calling the room 변소 or asking 화장실 있어요? to find it.
변소 is crude/dated; the neutral polite word is 화장실. To locate it, ask 화장실 어디예요?, not just 'is there a restroom?'

structuredNuance.t: 화장실(化粧室) = 'grooming room' (standard polite term for restroom) + 좀 = softener + 쓸게요 = -ㄹ게요 form of 쓰다 'use'. Literal: 'I intend to use the restroom (a little).' Real: polite self-announcement — 'just letting you know I'm stepping out to use the restroom', NOT a request for permission.

Announcement (화장실 좀 쓸게요 / 다녀올게요) = at a friend's home, office, classroom, any place where permission is assumed. Permission ask (화장실 좀 써도 돼요?) = at a shop, stranger's home, formal venue. Casual: 화장실 좀 쓸게 (반말, drop 요). Very formal: 화장실 좀 다녀오겠습니다.

화장실 좀 쓸게요 = announce intent, you expect it's fine. 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? = genuinely request permission. 화장실 좀 다녀올게요 = 'I'll pop to the restroom and be right back' (implies return). 화장실 어디예요? = asking location, not announcing or asking permission.
With return: 화장실 좀 다녀올게요. With timing: 밥 먹기 전에 / 시작 전에 화장실 좀 쓸게요. Formal: 잠시 화장실 다녀오겠습니다. 반말: 화장실 좀 쓸게 / 다녀올게.

Using the announcing -ㄹ게요 form when permission is actually needed — in a shop or stranger's home, switch to 써도 돼요?. Also, treating 좀 as a literal quantity ('use the restroom a little') — it is a social softener, not a measure.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여보세요 is a practical expression meaning "Hello (on the phone)".
expressions.explanation: 여보세요 (yeoboseyo) means "Hello (on the phone)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여보세요? ("Hello?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Rising intonation when you pick up an unknown call; the tone alone signals you're waiting for the caller to speak
여보세요 opens the voice channel, then 안녕하세요 is the actual social greeting — both are normally said in quick succession
Re-used mid-call to check a silent line; the attention-getting origin makes it natural as a line-test signal

usagePhrases.en: Hello, is that the Korean restaurant?
usagePhrases.note: Confirming you reached the right place after dialling; 이죠? seeks confirmation with a soft rising tone

examples.ko: A: 여보세요? / B: 네, 여보세요. 어떻게 도와드릴까요?
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo? / B: ne, yeoboseyo. eotteoke dowadeurilkkayo?
examples.en: A: Hello? / B: Yes, hello. How can I help you?
examples.note: Classic call-centre exchange showing 여보세요 as both the caller's opener and the agent's polite response; the agent pairs it with a service phrase

examples.en: Hello, is this Kim Minsu's phone?
examples.note: Number-check right after the opener — notice 맞으세요? ('is this correct?') rather than the blunt '누구세요?'

examples.en: Hello? Hello? It keeps cutting out.
examples.note: Repeated on a dropping line; the doubling is natural Korean stress, not impatience

expressions.nuance: 여보세요 is Korean's dedicated telephone 'hello' and almost never appears face to face — the rare exception is snapping a daydreamer to attention, where it works like English 'hello? anybody home?' The phrase evolved from 여기 보세요 ('look/attend over here'), a call for attention, which also explains why it works mid-call when a line goes suspiciously quiet. Crucially, it is NOT a wellbeing greeting: 안녕하세요 asks 'are you at peace?' and is the true in-person or opening-the-conversation greeting; 여보세요 merely opens the voice channel. Register is neutral-polite thanks to the -세요 ending, appropriate for strangers, customer service, and elders alike, but never truncated to 여보 — that independent word has drifted to mean 'honey/darling' between spouses. The English-speaker trap is treating it like a general 'hi', using it to greet someone face to face or at the start of a KakaoTalk voice note; keep it firmly in the phone or attention-getting lane.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it only belongs on the phone or to snap a distracted person back; for meeting people say 안녕하세요.
Shortening it to 여보 to sound casual — 여보 alone means 'dear/honey' between spouses, so to a stranger it's bizarre; always keep the full 여보세요.
Treating it as a complete greeting and saying nothing else on a polite call — after 여보세요 you still add 안녕하세요 or state who you are, because 여보세요 only opens the channel.

structuredNuance.t: 여보세요 evolved from 여기 보세요 ('look/attend here') — a literal call for attention. Its real function today is simply opening a telephone voice channel; it carries no social warmth the way 안녕하세요 does. Think of it as 'channel open' not 'nice to meet you'.

Use it the moment you answer or place a call — with strangers, customer service, elders, or close friends alike. The -세요 ending keeps it comfortably polite across all relationships. On a bad line it doubles naturally (여보세요? 여보세요?) without sounding rude. Face to face it works only for theatrical effect ('hello? are you listening?').

안녕하세요 is the in-person social greeting ('are you at peace?'); 여보세요 is only a call-opener. They are not interchangeable: starting a phone call with 안녕하세요 alone sounds like you skipped the channel-open step, and saying 여보세요 to someone standing next to you sounds like a joke.
여보세요 has no formal upgrade; you can lower it to 여보 only with your spouse. To sound more natural on a business call, pair it immediately with 저는 OO입니다 or 안녕하세요.

English speakers often use 여보세요 as a general 'hi' when meeting someone, or drop it into a KakaoTalk voice note opener. Both are wrong. Also: shortening to 여보 with a stranger signals 'darling' — keep the full form.

expressions.shortExplanation: 누구세요? is a practical expression meaning "Who is it? (at the door/intercom)".
expressions.explanation: "Who is it? (at the door/intercom)" — that is 누구세요? (nuguseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 누구세요? ("Who is it?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — answering the door or intercom to an unknown caller
반말 — to family, or when you expect a friend

usagePhrases.en: May I ask what brings you?
usagePhrases.note: 격식/정중 — softer; asks purpose rather than bluntly demanding identity
The typical answer you'll hear back through the door or intercom

examples.en: A: (Ding-dong) Who is it? / B: Delivery.
examples.note: The standard intercom exchange when the bell rings; 택배입니다 = 'It's a parcel/courier' — no need for full sentences on the intercom

examples.en: Who is it? What do you need from us?
examples.note: Adding 무슨 일이세요? ('what is your business?') asks for their purpose politely; natural when you're cautious about an unexpected visitor

examples.ko: 밤늦게 모르는 사람이 벨을 눌러서 문 안 열고 누구세요? 하고 물었어요.
examples.romanization: bamneutge moreuneun sarami bereul nulleoseo mun an yeolgo nuguseyo? hago mureosseoyo.
examples.en: A stranger rang late at night, so without opening I asked 'who is it?' through the door.
examples.note: Real safety habit: 문 안 열고 ('without opening') + 누구세요? is the standard cautious protocol — you ask before you open, especially late at night

expressions.nuance: 누구세요? is the phrase you call through a closed door or the 인터폰 (intercom) when someone rings. 누구 = 'who', 세요 is the honorific present of 이다/되다 used for 'who are you?' — polite enough for any adult stranger. The two-way register split: 존댓말 누구세요? for unknowns and adults; 반말 누구야? for family or when you already know it's a close friend. The near-synonym 어떻게 오셨어요? ('what brings you?') softens the question by asking purpose rather than demanding identity, and is more appropriate once the door is slightly open or when you're fairly sure the person is legitimate. The critical English-speaker trap is answering a doorbell with 여보세요? — that phrase is strictly telephone hello; it sounds wrong at a physical door. Another trap: using 당신 누구예요? sounds confrontational and aggressive to a stranger (당신 as a second person is distancing and challenging in Korean); drop the subject entirely and say just 누구세요?. Korean home safety practice: always ask 누구세요? before opening the door, especially to unannounced visitors.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering the door with 여보세요? — that's the phone 'hello'; at a door or intercom say 누구세요?.
Adding 당신 (당신 누구예요?) — 당신 to a stranger sounds confrontational; the bare 누구세요? is correct.
Using 누구예요? flat — at the door the honorific 누구세요? is safer/politer to an unknown adult than plain 누구예요?.

structuredNuance.t: 누구세요? = 'who are you?' (polite). The real use is specifically at a door, intercom, or through a closed barrier — asking identity before deciding whether to open. This is a safety function as much as a social one.

존댓말 누구세요? to any unknown adult at the door or intercom. 반말 누구야? to family members or when you're certain it's a friend. Most polite/indirect: 어떻게 오셨어요? ('what brings you?') — used when opening the door to someone who appears legitimate. Do not use 당신 누구예요? — the pronoun 당신 sounds challenging to a stranger.

누구세요? = direct identity question (who?), fine for an unknown buzz. 어떻게 오셨어요? = purpose question (what brings you?), softer and better face-to-face. 여보세요? = telephone hello ONLY — never use at a physical door. The choice signals how guarded or welcoming you are.
누구야? (반말) → 누구세요? → 어떻게 오셨어요? (가장 정중). Extensions: 누구세요? 무슨 일이세요? (who + what business?). If they don't answer: 잠깐만요 ('just a moment') while you check the CCTV.
Saying 여보세요? at the door — 여보세요 is the telephone greeting only; it sounds bizarre at a physical door. Also: 당신 누구예요? sounds confrontational; the subject-less 누구세요? is natural and polite.

expressions.shortExplanation: 통화 괜찮아요? is a practical expression meaning "Can you talk now?".
expressions.explanation: 통화 괜찮아요? (tonghwa gwaenchanayo?) = "Can you talk now?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 지금 통화 괜찮아요? ("Is now okay to talk?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 지금 ('now') pins the question to this exact moment — the most common opening line after 여보세요
잠깐 signals you plan to be brief — a considerate way to set expectations before you start

usagePhrases.en: Is it all right to talk?
usagePhrases.note: 괜찮으세요 lifts the register to deferential — use with clients, customers, or elders

usagePhrases.en: Would later be okay to talk?
usagePhrases.note: Offering a callback if this moment is inconvenient — note it switches from a present check to a future offer

examples.ko: A: 여보세요, 지금 통화 괜찮아요? / B: 잠깐만요, 회의 중이라서요. 이따가 다시 걸어도 될까요?
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo, jigeum tonghwa gwaenchanayo? / B: jamkkanmanyo, hoeui jungiraseoyo. ittaga dasi georeodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: A: Hello, is now a good time to talk? / B: One sec — I'm in a meeting. Can I call you back later?
examples.note: Classic real-world exchange: one person checks timing, the other declines politely and suggests a callback — very natural and complete

examples.en: Are you busy by any chance? Got a moment to talk?
examples.note: 혹시 softens the question further — useful when you're unsure about the other person's schedule

examples.ko: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 업무 관련해서 여쭤볼 게 있어서요.
examples.romanization: jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo? eommu gwallyeonhaeseo yeojjwobol ge isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Is now convenient to talk? I have a work-related question.
examples.note: Upgrading to 괜찮으세요 for a professional context and giving a reason up front — reduces the chance they decline

expressions.nuance: 통화 괜찮아요? is the standard Korean 'is now a good time to talk?' and it hinges on a word distinction English smooths over: 통화 (通話) is the actual connected voice conversation, while 전화 (電話) is the phone device or the act of calling. Asking 전화 괜찮아요? would mean 'is the phone okay?' — odd — because you want to ask about the act of conversing, not the hardware. 괜찮아요 ('it's fine / no problem') here means 'is it convenient'. The closest near-synonym 시간 괜찮아요? ('do you have time?') is broader — it works for in-person meetings too — whereas 통화 괜찮아요? is specifically 'can we talk right now on this line'. Register: the 요-ending is polite-casual, right for friends and colleagues; bump to 통화 괜찮으세요? for clients or elders, or add a reason (업무 관련이라서요) to pre-justify the call. English speakers often try 말할 수 있어요? ('can you speak?'), which tests physical ability rather than availability — awkward and clinical; the natural frame is always the convenience check.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 말할 수 있어요? for 'can you talk?' — that tests physical speaking ability; the natural phone courtesy check is 통화 괜찮아요?
Swapping in 전화 to get 전화 괜찮아요? — 전화 (電話) is the device or the act of phoning; the ongoing voice conversation is 통화 (通話), so always use 통화 for this question.
Dropping the courtesy check entirely and launching straight into your business — Koreans almost always open with 통화 괜찮아요? to respect the other person's time, especially on an unplanned call.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'is the phone-call okay?' — but the real meaning is 'is this a convenient moment for you to talk?' 괜찮아요 shifts from its base meaning 'fine/no problem' to a convenience check the moment it is combined with a situational noun like 통화.

Say it right after 여보세요 — it is the polite opener for every unplanned call. The 요-form is standard with friends, coworkers, and acquaintances. For clients or seniors, use 통화 괜찮으세요? or the fuller 지금 잠깐 통화 가능하세요? Tip: adding 잠깐 ('briefly') signals you won't take long and reduces the chance they decline.

시간 괜찮아요? ('do you have time?') is broader — it applies to both calls and in-person meetings. 통화 괜찮아요? is specifically for right now on the phone. Neither should be replaced with 전화 괜찮아요? — that asks about the device/act of calling, not the conversation itself.
지금 통화 괜찮아요? (casual-polite) → 통화 괜찮으세요? (deferential) → 지금 잠깐 통화 가능하세요? (more formal) → 통화 가능한 시간 알려 주시겠어요? (most formal, asking them to name a time).

Translating 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요? asks about physical ability and sounds clinical — the Korean way is the convenience check 통화 괜찮아요? Also, swapping in 전화 is wrong: 전화 괜찮아요? asks if the phone itself is okay, not if the moment is convenient.

expressions.shortExplanation: 잘 안 들려요 is a practical expression meaning "I cannot hear you well".
expressions.explanation: 잘 안 들려요 (jal an deullyeoyo) means "I cannot hear you well". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘 안 들려요. ("I can't hear you well."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 잘 = 'well'; 안 = negation; 들리다 = passive 'to be audible' — the sound isn't reaching the ear
소리가 as the grammatical subject makes clear it's the sound that's failing, not your listening effort

usagePhrases.en: It's choppy so I can't hear.
usagePhrases.note: 뚝뚝 끊기다 = the onomatopoeic phrase for a breaking-up line — very natural and native-sounding

usagePhrases.ko: 조금만 크게 말씀해 주세요, 잘 안 들려요.
usagePhrases.romanization: jogeumman keuge malsseumhae juseyo, jal an deullyeoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Could you speak a bit louder? I can't hear well.
usagePhrases.note: 크게 말씀해 주세요 = polite request for more volume; note 말씀 as the honorific form of 말

examples.ko: A: 여보세요? 잘 안 들려요. / B: 저도요. 지금 신호가 약한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo? jal an deullyeoyo. / B: jeodoyo. jigeum sinhoga yakan geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: Hello? I can't hear you well. / B: Same here. I think the signal is weak right now.
examples.note: Both sides confirming a bad line — 저도요 ('me too') and 신호가 약하다 are the most natural collocations for this situation

examples.ko: 목소리가 잘 안 들려요. 좀 크게 말해 줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: moksoriga jal an deullyeoyo. jom keuge malhae jul su isseoyo?
examples.en: I can't hear your voice well. Can you speak up a bit?
examples.note: 목소리가 as the subject clarifies the problem is volume, not connection — good when the line is clear but the person speaks softly

examples.ko: 지금 지하철 안이라서 잘 안 들려요. 이따 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: jigeum jihacheol aniraseo jal an deullyeoyo. itta dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: I'm on the subway so I can't hear well. I'll call back later.
examples.note: Explaining the cause and offering a callback — 지하철 안 (inside a subway car) is one of the most common real-life reasons

expressions.nuance: 잘 안 들려요 rests on a grammatical distinction that trips up every English speaker: 들리다 is the INTRANSITIVE/potential 'to be audible, to be heard' — the sound reaching the ear passively — while 듣다 is the ACTIVE 'to listen'. So a bad line is 안 들려요 ('[your voice] isn't getting through to me'), never 안 들어요, which means 'I am not listening' — implying you're deliberately ignoring them, rude on a call. The vowel contraction is: 들리+어요 → 들려요. Add 잘 ('well') and 안 (negation) for 잘 안 들려요 = 'isn't audibly reaching me well'. For tense: 잘 안 들려요 is ongoing ('I can't hear you'), whereas 잘 안 들렸어요 is past ('I didn't catch that'). Natural subjects to put in front are 소리가 ('the sound'), 목소리가 ('your voice'), or 신호가 약하다 ('the signal is weak'). Register: keep the 요 ending with strangers; dropping to 안 들려 with someone you should address politely is disrespectful.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 들어요 instead of 안 들려요 — 안 들어요 means 'I'm not listening' (active, rude); the passive potential form 들리다 → 안 들려요 is the only correct choice for a bad connection.
Marking yourself as subject: 저는 안 들려요 sounds awkward — the SOUND is what fails, so either put 소리가 as subject or use the bare 잘 안 들려요.
Clipping to 안 들려 with someone you should be polite to — keep the 요 ending: 잘 안 들려요.

structuredNuance.t: 'Well not audible-is' — the literal stack of 잘 + 안 + 들리다. The real meaning is 'the sound isn't reaching me clearly'; the SUBJECT is the sound (소리가), not the listener. This passive framing is crucial: the problem is the transmission, not your attention.

Say it the instant the line degrades — with friends, strangers, or clients alike. The 요-form works everywhere. In an office call to a senior, you can be more deferential: 말씀이 잘 안 들려서요, 조금만 크게 말씀해 주시겠어요? If you're the one speaking softly, the other party will tell you 잘 안 들려요 as a signal to raise your voice.

안 들려요 = '[sound] isn't audible' (the passive form, correct for a bad line). 안 들어요 = 'I'm not listening' (active, implies deliberate inattention — rude). This single vowel difference changes the entire meaning and social register. Never use 안 들어요 for a bad connection.
Present: 잘 안 들려요. Past: 잘 안 들렸어요. With subject: 소리가 잘 안 들려요. Onomatopoeic: 뚝뚝 끊겨서 잘 안 들려요. Volume request follow-up: 조금만 크게 말씀해 주세요.
Never use 안 들어요 for a bad line — that is the active form and means 'I'm not listening', implying you're ignoring the caller. The passive 들리다 → 안 들려요 is the ONLY correct form for 'can't hear you'.

expressions.shortExplanation: 다시 걸게요 is a practical expression meaning "I will call you back".
expressions.explanation: "I will call you back" — that is 다시 걸게요 (dasi geolgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다시 걸게요. ("I'll call back."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 걸다 = to place a call (literally 'hook'); 다시 = again — the most concise form

usagePhrases.en: I'll call back in a bit.
usagePhrases.note: 이따 = 'a little later today' — signals it won't be long before you redial

usagePhrases.en: I'll be the one to call back.
usagePhrases.note: 제가 stresses that YOU will redial — often used to tell the other person not to bother calling again

usagePhrases.en: Let me hang up and call again.
usagePhrases.note: 끊고 links two actions — the fix for a glitchy connection where a fresh call often restores quality

examples.ko: A: 지금 통화 괜찮아요? / B: 미안해요, 지금 회의 중이라서요. 이따 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: A: jigeum tonghwa gwaenchanayo? / B: mianhaeyo, jigeum hoeui jungiraseoyo. itta dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: A: Can you talk now? / B: Sorry, I'm in a meeting right now. I'll call back later.
examples.note: Realistic turn-based exchange: someone checks timing, the other person declines politely and promises a callback with 다시 걸게요

examples.ko: 소리가 자꾸 끊겨요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
examples.romanization: soriga jakku kkeunkyeoyo. kkeunko dasi geolgeyo.
examples.en: It keeps cutting out. I'll hang up and redial.
examples.note: 끊고 daisy-chains the two actions and is the natural Korean fix for choppy audio — 자꾸 ('keeps doing') emphasises the repeated breaks

examples.en: I'll call back 30 minutes after the meeting.
examples.note: Giving a concrete time is the considerate move — it sets an expectation so the other person doesn't wonder when to expect you

expressions.nuance: 다시 걸게요 rests on two points English speakers often miss. First, the verb: Korean 'to place a phone call' is 전화를 걸다 — 걸다 literally 'to hang/hook', a relic of the hook-and-cradle phone era — so you 'hook' a call, and 다시 걸다 = 'hook/call again'. Never use 부르다 ('to call out a name / summon'), which cannot mean telephoning. Second, the ending -ㄹ게요 (걸+게요) is a first-person PROMISE or INTENTION that implies your action is done for the other person's sake: 다시 걸게요 = 'I'll redial, you can count on me'. This is warmer than the neutral future 다시 걸 거예요 ('I will call again' — a mere prediction). Because -ㄹ게요 is first-person only, you cannot say 그 사람이 다시 걸게요 to mean 'he will call'; use 걸 거예요 or 건대요 for third parties. The natural opposite — when THEY should call you — is 다시 걸어 주세요. For clients or formal situations, step up to 다시 연락드리겠습니다 ('I will contact you again', humble and deferential).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 부르다 for phoning (다시 불러요) — 부르다 is calling out a name or summoning; a phone call is 전화를 걸다, so 'call back' is 다시 걸게요.
Saying 다시 걸게요 when you want the OTHER person to redial — -ㄹ게요 commits the first-person speaker; if they should call, say 다시 걸어 주세요.
Confusing 다시 걸게요 with the flat prediction 다시 걸 거예요 — the -ㄹ게요 ending makes it a personal promise to the listener, not just a neutral forecast.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'again hook-will' — 걸다 (to hook/place a call) + 다시 (again). The real meaning is a personal promise to redial, with a connotation of doing so for the listener's benefit. The word 걸다 comes from hooking an old telephone cradle, but today it simply means 'place a call'.

Use on any unplanned call when you need to bow out and ring back — with friends, colleagues, or acquaintances. For a client or senior, upgrade to 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (humble deferential). Pair with 이따 / 나중에 / 끊고 or a specific time to make the promise concrete.

structuredNuance.e: VS 다시 걸 거예요 / 다시 걸어 주세요
structuredNuance.t: 다시 걸 거예요 is a plain future prediction (no personal commitment). 다시 걸게요 is a first-person promise that implies care for the listener — it feels warmer and more reassuring. 다시 걸어 주세요 flips the direction: you are asking THEM to call back.
Casual promise: 다시 걸게. Polite promise: 다시 걸게요. Formal/deferential: 다시 연락드리겠습니다. Requesting callback: 다시 걸어 주세요. Time-specific: 이따 5시에 다시 걸게요.
Using 부르다 for phoning (다시 불러요) is wrong — 부르다 means calling someone's name or summoning them. Also: saying 다시 걸게요 when the OTHER person should redial — -ㄹ게요 promises YOUR action, not someone else's.

expressions.shortExplanation: 문자 보낼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I will send a text".
expressions.explanation: 문자 보낼게요 (munja bonaelgeyo) = "I will send a text". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 문자 보낼게요. ("I'll text you."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 문자(를) 보내다 = to send a text message — 를 is often dropped in casual speech

usagePhrases.en: I'll send the address by text.
usagePhrases.note: 문자로 = 'via text / by text'; 로 marks the means of sending — don't omit this particle
이따 sets a soon-ish future time — the most common timing adverb with this phrase

usagePhrases.en: I'll check first and then text you.
usagePhrases.note: Promising a follow-up after doing something — -하고 chains the check with the send

examples.ko: A: 장소가 어디예요? / B: 지금 전화하기 어렵네요. 문자 보낼게요.
examples.romanization: A: jangsoga eodiyeyo? / B: jigeum jeonhwahagi eoryeomneyo. munja bonaelgeyo.
examples.en: A: Where's the venue? / B: It's hard to talk right now. I'll text you.
examples.note: Real exchange showing text as the fallback channel when a call isn't possible — very common in everyday Korean life

examples.ko: 시간하고 장소는 문자로 보낼게요. 확인해 두세요.
examples.romanization: siganhago jangsoneun munjaro bonaelgeyo. hwaginhae duseyo.
examples.en: I'll text you the time and place. Keep an eye out.
examples.note: 문자로 marks the sending channel; 확인해 두세요 = 'check and remember it' — a natural pair when sending important details

examples.en: If you don't pick up, I'll text you.
examples.note: Backup-plan promise using -으시면 ('if you') — shows the two channels working together, as Koreans routinely use both

expressions.nuance: 문자 보낼게요 = 'I'll send a text (SMS)'. 문자 is Sino-Korean 文字 ('written characters'), short for 문자 메시지. The important lexical landscape for a Korean learner: 문자 (formal 'SMS text'), 문자 메시지 (full form), 카톡 (KakaoTalk message — what younger Koreans actually use most often), and 메시지 (generic English loanword). In real life 카톡 보낼게요 is extremely common because most personal communication in Korea runs through KakaoTalk, whereas 문자 tends to appear in business, automated verification codes, or when you don't have someone's KakaoTalk. The verb 보내다 ('to send') pairs with the channel particle 로: 문자로 보내다 = 'send BY text'. The ending -ㄹ게요 again signals a first-person promise to the listener, warmer than the bare future -ㄹ 거예요. A subtlety: 보내 줄게요 (adding 주다) adds the nuance of 'I'll send it as a favor for you', slightly more considerate — fine to use but not required. Never mix up 문자 (text) with 전화 (call) in what you promise to send.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 문자 (a text message) with 전화 (a phone call) and saying 전화 보낼게요 — you send (보내다) a 문자 but place (걸다) a 전화; the verb and noun must match.
Omitting the channel particle 로 when it matters — 문자로 보내다 means 'send by text', while 문자 보내다 without 로 is fine informally but may be ambiguous if other channels are being discussed.
Forgetting -ㄹ게요 is first-person — you can't say 그 사람이 문자 보낼게요; for third-party actions use 보낼 거예요 or 보낸대요.

structuredNuance.t: 'Written-characters send-will-I' — literally promising to transmit written characters. The real meaning is a commitment to follow up via SMS text message rather than by voice. The 文字 etymology underscores that 문자 is about written script, not a voice channel.

Common on any call when you want to send information (addresses, times, links) that should be written down. The -ㄹ게요 ending is polite-casual — fine for friends, classmates, and colleagues. For clients or formal situations, say 문자 드리겠습니다 or 메시지 보내 드리겠습니다.

문자 = specifically SMS. 카톡 보낼게요 = the default for most personal Korean communication today (KakaoTalk). 메시지 보낼게요 = generic. Never say 전화 보낼게요 — 전화 (call) is placed with 걸다, not sent with 보내다. Mixing these verbs with the wrong nouns is a telltale learner error.
Plain promise: 문자 보낼게요. Favor form: 문자 보내 줄게요. As-a-service/deferential: 문자 드리겠습니다. KakaoTalk variant: 카톡 보낼게요. Channel-marked: 문자로 보낼게요.

Mixing up 문자 (text) with 전화 (call) and saying 전화 보낼게요 is wrong — you send (보내다) a 문자 but place (걸다) a 전화. Also, omitting 로 when naming the channel (say 문자로 보낼게요, not just 문자 보낼게요, if specifying the channel matters in context).

expressions.shortExplanation: 메모 남겨 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please leave a message".
expressions.explanation: 메모 남겨 주세요 (memo namgyeo juseyo) means "Please leave a message". Say it as one set phrase — for example 메모 남겨 주세요. ("Please leave a message."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 남기다 = to leave (something) behind; -어 주세요 = polite favor request

usagePhrases.en: Please leave your name and contact number.
usagePhrases.note: Standard office intake: 성함 (honorific 'name') + 연락처 ('contact details') — both objects of 남기다

usagePhrases.en: Please leave it after the beep.
usagePhrases.note: 삐 소리 = the beep tone; 후에 = after — the classic voicemail prompt wording

usagePhrases.en: Please leave a brief message about your business.
usagePhrases.note: 용건 = the purpose/matter; 간단히 = briefly — a common voicemail phrase encouraging callers to be concise

examples.ko: A: 이 대리님 계십니까? / B: 지금 자리 비우셨어요. 메모 남겨 주시면 전달해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: i daerinim gyesimnikka? / B: jigeum jari biusyeosseoyo. memo namgyeo jusimyeon jeondalhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Is Deputy Manager Lee in? / B: He's stepped away. If you leave a message I'll pass it along.
examples.note: Typical office reception exchange: checking availability and offering to relay a message — 전달해 드릴게요 is the key follow-up phrase

examples.ko: 삐 소리 후에 성함과 메모 남겨 주세요. 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: ppi sori hue seonghamgwa memo namgyeo juseyo. yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: After the beep, please leave your name and a message. I'll get back to you.
examples.note: Complete voicemail greeting format: beep cue → name + message request → callback promise

examples.ko: 연결이 안 되는 것 같아요. 혹시 메모라도 남겨 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: yeongyeori an doeneun geot gatayo. hoksi memorado namgyeo deurilkkayo?
examples.en: It seems we can't reach them. Shall I at least leave a message for you?
examples.note: 메모라도 = 'even just a message' (라도 signals doing the lesser option); the 드릴까요 offers the service from a service-provider perspective

expressions.nuance: 메모 남겨 주세요 = 'please leave a message/note'. 메모 is the English loanword 'memo', used for a brief written or spoken message left for someone who wasn't available. The verb 남기다 'to leave (something) behind' is the crucial choice: English uses a single word 'leave' for both leaving a place (떠나다) and leaving an object behind (남기다), so learners reach for 떠나다 — never correct here. 남기다 is transitive: it takes a direct object (메모를, 이름을, 연락처를), and the politeness is carried by -어 주세요 ('please do X for me/as a favor'). Stripping that down to just 남겨 sounds like a curt command. Close synonyms: 메시지 남겨 주세요 is interchangeable (메시지 = English-derived 'message', slightly more modern), and 전할 말씀 있으세요? ('do you have something you'd like relayed?') is what a secretary proactively asks rather than instructing the caller. In the fine-grained register of Korean office calls: 메모를 남기다 = to leave a written note, while 음성 메시지를 남기다 = to leave a voice message — the modifier distinguishes the two. Collocations: 성함 / 연락처 / 용건을 남기다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reaching for 떠나다 because English says 'leave' — 떠나다 is leaving a PLACE; leaving a note or message behind is 남기다, so it's 메모 남겨 주세요.
Dropping 주세요 and saying just 메모 남겨 — that's a blunt command; the -어 주세요 construction is what makes it a polite favor request.
Calling the message 편지 — 편지 is a postal letter; a phone message is 메모 or 메시지.

structuredNuance.t: 'Memo leave please' — 남기다 means 'make something remain behind (for someone)'. The real meaning is asking the caller to deposit a note or spoken message so the unavailable person can respond later. The intent is ensuring no communication is lost.

Used by receptionists, recorded voicemails, or secretaries when the intended person is unavailable. The -어 주세요 ending is polite-standard and appropriate in any professional or semi-formal phone setting. For customers or important callers, soften further: 메모 남겨 주시면 감사하겠습니다 or offer 전할 말씀 있으세요?

structuredNuance.e: VS 메시지 남겨 주세요 / 전할 말씀 있으세요?
structuredNuance.t: 메모 남겨 주세요 and 메시지 남겨 주세요 are interchangeable; 메시지 is slightly more modern/informal. 전할 말씀 있으세요? is what you proactively ask (pushing agency to the caller) rather than instructing them to leave something.
Plain instruction: 메모 남겨 주세요. Modern variant: 메시지 남겨 주세요. Voicemail prompt: 삐 소리 후에 성함과 메모 남겨 주세요. Deferential offer: 전할 말씀 있으세요? Voice-message specific: 음성 메시지 남겨 주세요.

English 'leave a message' uses one verb for both leaving a place and leaving an object. In Korean these are different verbs: 떠나다 = leave a place, 남기다 = leave something behind for someone. Using 떠나다 here (메시지를 떠나세요) is nonsensical — 남기다 is the only correct choice.

expressions.shortExplanation: 끊지 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please do not hang up".
expressions.explanation: "Please do not hang up" — that is 끊지 마세요 (kkeunchi maseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 끊지 마세요. ("Please don't hang up."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 끊다 = to cut/sever (the line); -지 마세요 = polite negative command 'please don't ~'

usagePhrases.en: One sec, please don't hang up.
usagePhrases.note: 잠깐만요 is the verbal gesture that freezes the moment — followed by 끊지 마세요 to keep the other person on the line
아직 = 'not yet' — signals more is coming and asks them to hold on a little longer

usagePhrases.ko: 바로 바꿔 드릴 테니 끊지 마세요.
usagePhrases.romanization: baro bakkwo deuril teni kkeunchi maseyo.
usagePhrases.en: I'll transfer you right away, so don't hang up.
usagePhrases.note: -ㄹ 테니 links a promised action to the request — natural in reception or call-centre speech

examples.ko: A: 잠깐만요! 끊지 마세요. 담당자 확인해 볼게요. / B: 네, 알겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: jamkkanmanyo! kkeunchi maseyo. damdangja hwaginhae bolgeyo. / B: ne, algesseoyo.
examples.en: A: One moment! Don't hang up. Let me check with the person in charge. / B: Okay, understood.
examples.note: Classic call-centre hold request: the agent asks the caller to wait; the caller's 네, 알겠어요 confirms they'll stay on

examples.en: Don't hang up, I'll put you through in a sec.
examples.note: Collocating with 바꿔 드릴게요 — the standard pair for transferring a call

examples.ko: 아직 할 얘기가 있어요. 끊지 마세요.
examples.romanization: aji kal yaegiga isseoyo. kkeunchi maseyo.
examples.en: I still have something to say. Don't hang up.
examples.note: Used in a personal call when the other person is about to end it too soon — 아직 (not yet) sets up the reason

expressions.nuance: 끊지 마세요 = 'please don't hang up'. The verb 끊다 means 'to cut or sever', which is exactly how Koreans conceptualise ending a phone call — you 'cut' the connection, the natural opposite of 걸다 ('hook' a call). This cut metaphor extends: 담배를 끊다 ('quit smoking'), 연락을 끊다 ('cut off contact'), 말을 끊다 ('interrupt someone's speech'). Context makes it clear which 끊다 is in play. The grammar core is -지 말다 → -지 마세요 ('please don't V'): attach -지 마세요 directly to the dictionary stem (끊 + 지 마세요). The error English speakers make is using 안 instead: 안 끊어요 simply describes your own action ('I'm not hanging up') — it has NO power to instruct the other person to stop. Prohibitions need -지 마세요. Politeness levels: 끊지 마 (반말, close friends only), 끊지 마세요 (standard polite), 끊지 마십시오 (formal announcements). The phrase collocates most naturally with 잠깐만요 and 바꿔 드릴게요, the two phrases most often said right before asking someone to hold.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 끊어요 to mean 'don't hang up' — that only states your own current action; a prohibition directed at another person needs -지 마세요, i.e. 끊지 마세요.
Using 끄다 instead of 끊다 — 끄다 is 'to turn off (a device or light)'; ending a call is 끊다 ('to cut the line'), so 'don't hang up' is 끊지 마세요, not 끄지 마세요.
Clipping to 끊지 마 with someone you owe politeness — the 세요 is needed for anyone other than a close friend.

structuredNuance.t: 'Cut-don't please' — 끊다 literally means to cut or sever. On a phone call it means severing the connection (hanging up). The metaphor is vivid: you hooked (걸다) the call and now you're severing (끊다) it. 끊지 마세요 asks the other person not to sever that connection.

Mostly heard in call-centre or office settings when you need the caller to wait for a transfer, or in personal calls when you need a moment. The 마세요 ending is polite and works universally. In formal recorded announcements: 끊지 마십시오. With close friends: 끊지 마. Always pair with a reason or action: 잠깐만요, 확인할게요, 바꿔 드릴게요.

잠깐 기다리세요 ('please wait a moment') and 끊지 마세요 ('please don't hang up') often appear together. The difference: 기다리세요 focuses on the waiting; 끊지 마세요 specifically warns against ending the call. In practice both appear back to back: 잠깐 기다리세요, 끊지 마세요.
끊지 마 (반말, friends only) → 끊지 마세요 (standard polite) → 끊지 마십시오 (formal/announcement). Related uses of 끊다 beyond phone calls: 담배를 끊다 (quit smoking), 연락을 끊다 (cut off contact), 말을 끊다 (interrupt).

Saying 안 끊어요 to mean 'don't hang up' only describes your own present action ('I'm not hanging up') — it cannot command someone else. Prohibitions in Korean require -지 마세요, not 안. Also: 끄지 마세요 is wrong here (끄다 = turn off a device); ending a call is 끊다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 잠깐 기다리세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please wait a moment".
expressions.explanation: 잠깐 기다리세요 (jamkkan gidariseyo) = "Please wait a moment". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잠깐 기다리세요. ("Please wait a moment."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 잠깐 = briefly (spoken); 기다리다 = to wait; -세요 = polite request
잠깐만 (with 만 'only/just') feels a shade shorter and more urgent — 'just this one brief moment'
-어 주세요 adds a favor framing — sounds warmer and more considerate; preferred for customers
여기서 marks the location the person should stay — used in person when directing someone to a waiting spot

examples.ko: A: 박 부장님 좀 바꿔 주시겠어요? / B: 잠깐 기다려 주세요. 지금 바로 연결해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: bak bujangnim jom bakkwo jusigesseoyo? / B: jamkkan gidaryeo juseyo. jigeum baro yeongyeolhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Could you put Manager Park on? / B: Please hold a moment. I'll connect you right now.
examples.note: Call-transfer sequence: request → hold instruction + callback promise; 기다려 주세요 here instead of 기다리세요 because the caller is a customer who deserves the favor framing

examples.en: Just a moment please. Let me find some notepaper.
examples.note: 잠깐만 signals you'll be extremely quick; explaining WHY you're pausing (메모지 찾을게요) is courteous Korean phone etiquette

examples.ko: 네, 잠깐만요. 담당자 바로 바꿔 드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: ne, jamkkanmanyo. damdangja baro bakkwo deurigetseumnida.
examples.en: Yes, just one moment. I'll put the person in charge on right away.
examples.note: 잠깐만요 as a standalone exclamation to freeze the moment, then the promise — a very natural call-centre or office formula

expressions.nuance: 잠깐 기다리세요 = 'please wait a moment' — 잠깐 is the everyday spoken adverb for a brief pause, while its near-twin 잠시 carries the same meaning but skews slightly more formal or written (잠시만 기다려 주십시오 is the announcement register heard at service counters). The verb 기다리다 'to wait' is entirely regular here. The crucial register distinction is between 잠깐 기다리세요 (a polite command, -세요) and 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (-어 주세요 = please do it as a favor for me): the 주세요 version is warmer and is strongly preferred in customer-facing situations. A complementary phrase 잠깐만요 ('just a second!') is often thrown out first as a verbal gesture to freeze the conversation, then followed by 기다리세요 or 기다려 주세요. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'hold on' as 잡으세요 (잡다 = physically grab) — that phrase is not used for phone holding; always 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요. Don't confuse 기다리다 ('wait') with 기대하다 ('expect / look forward to') — similar syllables, completely different meanings.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'hold on' as 잡으세요 — 잡다 means to physically grab; 'please wait/hold' on a phone call is 잠깐 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요.
Confusing 기다리다 (wait) with 기대하다 (expect/look forward to) — they share an opening syllable but are completely different; 'please wait' is only 기다리세요.
Using the bare command 잠깐 기다려 with a customer or elder — for respectful contexts always add -세요 or use the fuller 잠깐 기다려 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'briefly wait-please' — 잠깐 (briefly) + 기다리다 (to wait) + -세요 (polite command). The real function is asking someone to pause in place while you do something — finding a person to transfer to, checking information, or fetching a note. The brevity adverb 잠깐 implicitly promises you won't take long.

The -세요 form is polite and works in most settings. In customer service, service counters, or when the other person is your social superior, prefer 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (favor framing) or the fully formal 잠시만 기다려 주십시오. With close friends: 잠깐 기다려 or 잠깐만. The standalone 잠깐만요 is used as a conversational freeze before the full instruction.

잠깐 = everyday spoken 'a short while'. 잠시 = same meaning, slightly more formal or written; heard in service announcements and formal speech. They are nearly interchangeable, but choosing 잠깐 in a business announcement and 잠시 in casual speech both sound slightly off register.
잠깐만요 (standalone freeze) → 잠깐 기다리세요 (polite command) → 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (favor, warmer) → 잠시만 기다려 주십시오 (formal/announcement). Each step up adds deference.

Translating 'hold on' as 잡으세요 is wrong — 잡다 means to physically grip something; for phone-hold always use 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요. Also, confusing 기다리다 (wait) with 기대하다 (expect/look forward to): they share syllables but mean completely different things.

expressions.shortExplanation: 연락해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please contact me".
expressions.explanation: 연락해 주세요 (yeollakhae juseyo) means "Please contact me". Say it as one set phrase — for example 연락해 주세요. ("Please get in touch."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 연락하다 = to make contact (by any channel — call, text, email, messenger)

usagePhrases.en: Please contact me when you arrive.
usagePhrases.note: -(으)면 sets the trigger condition — 'once X happens, do Y'

usagePhrases.en: Please be sure to reach out.
usagePhrases.note: 꼭 = 'without fail, definitely' — adds urgency to the request

usagePhrases.en: Please contact me whenever's convenient for you.
usagePhrases.note: 편하실 때 ('when it is comfortable/convenient for you') is deferential and leaves timing entirely to the other person

examples.ko: A: 그럼 오늘 결정 나면 연락해 주세요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다. 바로 연락 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: geureom oneul gyeoljeong namyeon yeollakae juseyo. / B: ne, algetseumnida. baro yeollak deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Then please contact me once you decide today. / B: Yes, understood. I'll reach out right away.
examples.note: Business exchange: A requests contact on a condition; B promises it with the humble 연락 드릴게요 — shows both sides of the phrase in a real professional context

examples.en: If any problem comes up, reach out any time.
examples.note: 언제든지 ('any time') combined with the condition -면 makes this a standing open invitation — very common at the end of a service call

examples.ko: 결정하시면 저한테 연락해 주세요. 다른 분한테 말씀하시면 제가 못 받을 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: gyeoljeonghasimyeon jeohante yeollakae juseyo. dareun bunhante malsseumhasimyeon jega mot badeul sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: Once you've decided, please contact me directly. If you tell someone else I might not receive it.
examples.note: 저한테 marks 'to me' as the specific destination — the contrast 저한테 vs 다른 분한테 teaches the 한테 particle direction naturally

expressions.nuance: 연락해 주세요 = 'please contact me'. 연락 is Sino-Korean 連絡 (連 link + 絡 tie/entwine), literally 'making a link' — and critically, it is channel-agnostic: it covers phone calls, texts, emails, KakaoTalk, or any other means of reaching someone. Use 연락하다 when you don't care how they reach you; reach for 전화하다 only if you specifically want a voice call. Structurally, 연락해 주세요 = 연락해 (연락하다 contracted) + 주세요 (favor request). The destination particle is 한테/에게, not 를: 저한테 연락해 주세요 ('contact me'); saying 저를 연락하다 is ungrammatical. A very common shortened form is 연락 주세요 (dropping 하), which natives use constantly with no change in meaning. For formal or client-facing contexts, step up to 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 or the humble 연락드리겠습니다 (when YOU are the one promising to reach out). Don't conflate 연락 with 약속 ('a promised appointment'): 연락 is merely reaching out; 약속 commits to an actual meeting time.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 를: 저를 연락해 주세요 is wrong — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게 as the direction, so it's 저한테 연락해 주세요.
Using 전화해 주세요 when you mean any channel — 전화하다 is specifically a voice call; for 'reach out however you like', 연락해 주세요 is the correct phrase.
Forgetting it's a 하다-verb: the polite present is 연락해요 (not 연락하어요), the request is 연락해 주세요, and the humble promise is 연락드리겠습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 'Link-make please-do-for-me' — 連絡 (연락) literally means 'making a link/tie'. The real meaning is any act of reaching out — a call, text, email, or message — to let someone know something. Its channel-agnostic breadth is the defining feature.
chips: 連絡 (연락) = link/tie → contact by any channel

structuredNuance.t: The -아/어 주세요 form is polite and standard for peers, colleagues, and most situations. For clients, customers, or seniors, upgrade: 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (deferential) or 연락 부탁드립니다 (formal). The short form 연락 주세요 is extremely common in casual and semi-formal speech.
전화해 주세요 specifically requests a voice call. 연락해 주세요 covers any channel — it's the general request. Never replace 연락하다 with 약속하다: 약속 commits to a meeting or promise, while 연락 is just 'get in touch'.
연락해 주세요 → 연락 주세요 (colloquial clip) → 연락 부탁드립니다 (formal) → 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (very deferential). When YOU promise to contact: 연락할게요 or 연락드리겠습니다 (humble).

Marking the person with 를: 저를 연락해 주세요 is ungrammatical — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게 as the direction marker. Also, using 전화해 주세요 when you mean any channel — 전화하다 is specifically a phone call; for open-channel contact always use 연락하다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 바꿔 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please put them on".
expressions.explanation: "Please put them on" — that is 바꿔 주세요 (bakkwo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 김민수 씨 바꿔 주세요. ("Please put Kim Minsu on."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: [name] 바꿔 주세요 = ask for that specific person — the standard way to request someone on a call

usagePhrases.en: Could you put the person in charge on?
usagePhrases.note: 좀 ('a bit') softens the request — essential politeness when you don't know the person's name

usagePhrases.en: If the manager's there, please put him on.
usagePhrases.note: 계시면 = 'if (he/she) is in' — the honorific conditional; saves face if the person turns out to be away
내선 번호 = extension number; 바꿔 주세요 works equally for persons and extension numbers

examples.ko: A: 여보세요, 영업부 이 과장님 바꿔 주세요. / B: 잠깐만요, 연결해 드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: yeoboseyo, yeongeopbu i gwajangnim bakkwo juseyo. / B: jamkkanmanyo, yeongyeolhae deurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Hello, please put Deputy Manager Lee from the sales department on. / B: One moment, I'll connect you.
examples.note: Complete office call formula: department + name + title + 바꿔 주세요, followed by the receptionist's hold-and-transfer response
