examples.note: Asking the teller to verify an incoming transfer; -는지 = 'whether'

examples.ko: A: 방금 보냈는데 입금됐어요? / B: 잠깐요. 네, 방금 들어왔어요.
examples.romanization: A: banggeum bonaenneunde ipgeumdwaesseoyo? / B: jamkkanyo. ne, banggeum deureowasseoyo.
examples.en: A: I just sent it — did it come in? / B: One moment. Yes, it just came in.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 보냈다 (sent — sender's side) vs 들어왔어요 ('came in' — receiver's side); 들어오다 is the vivid casual alternative to 입금되다

examples.ko: 월급이 아직 입금 안 됐는데 언제 들어와요?
examples.romanization: wolgeubi ajik ipgeum an dwaenneunde eonje deureowayo?
examples.en: My salary hasn't come in yet — when will it arrive?
examples.note: 들어오다 ('to come in') is the casual spoken verb for money landing in an account

expressions.nuance: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is 입금 (入金, 'money in = deposit') + 되다 (passive 'be done') + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the word for money ARRIVING in an account — the receiving side of any transfer. It pairs naturally with 송금/이체 (the sending side): the sender says 이체했어요 ('I sent it'), the receiver checks 입금됐어요? ('did it come in?'). A warmer, common alternative is 들어오다 ('to come in'): 돈 들어왔어요? and 월급 들어왔어요? are everyday spoken forms. The grammar point: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit money) — 'did it arrive?' is passive 입금됐어요?, while 'I'll deposit it' is active 입금할게요. The -는지 structure makes an indirect question embedded in 확인해 주세요 and attaches to the verb stem (됐는지), not as a separate word. Casually: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 입금되다 and 입금하다.
입금되다 = 'be deposited / come in' (passive, money arrives): 입금됐어요?. 입금하다 = 'to deposit' (active, you put money in): 입금할게요. Use the passive for 'did it arrive'.
Confusing 입금 (in) with 출금 (out).
입금 (入金) is money coming IN; 출금 (出金) is money going OUT. 입금됐어요? asks if a deposit arrived; for a withdrawal you'd say 출금.
Saying 입금했는지 확인해 주세요 to check arrival.
That asks whether someone DEPOSITED (active). To check if money CAME IN, use the passive: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 입금 (入金, 'money in') + 되다 (passive) + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the receiving side of a transfer. -는지 creates an embedded indirect question: it attaches to the verb stem (입금됐는지), not as a separate clause. Casual: 입금됐어? / 돈 들어왔어?

입금됐어요? (formal 'was it deposited?') vs 돈 들어왔어요? (casual 'did the money come in?'). Key grammar contrast: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit). Use the passive to ask if money arrived; use the active when you're the one depositing.
입금 is 入金 — 入 'enter/in' + 金 'money'. Paired with 출금 (出金, 'money out = withdrawal'): 入 and 出 are the directional opposites that run through all banking vocabulary.
입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is polite 존댓말 to a teller or someone you paid. Checking your own account informally: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어? With salary: 월급 들어왔어? is what everyone says payday morning.

The passive/active confusion: 입금됐어요? (passive — did it arrive?) vs 입금했어요? (active — did you deposit it?). To ask if money has ARRIVED for you, use the passive 됐어요? If you accidentally use the active, you're asking if the other person did a manual deposit action, which is a different question.

expressions.shortExplanation: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please freeze/cancel my card".
expressions.explanation: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 (kadeu jeongjisikyeo juseyo) means "Please freeze/cancel my card". Say it as one set phrase — for example 카드 정지시켜 주세요 ("Please freeze/block my card"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-urgent; 정지 (停止) = 'suspension/halt'; used when you notice the card missing

usagePhrases.en: I want to report my card lost
usagePhrases.note: 분실 신고 = 'loss report'; the formal procedure for a permanently lost/stolen card
막다 ('to block/plug') — urgent spoken version people blurt at the call center
재발급 = 'reissue' — the step you take after blocking to get a new card

examples.en: Please freeze my card.
examples.note: Said urgently at the bank when you can't find your card or suspect fraudulent use

examples.ko: A: 카드를 잃어버린 것 같아요. 정지시켜 주세요. / B: 네, 바로 정지하겠습니다. 재발급도 원하세요?
examples.romanization: A: kadeureul ireobeorin geot gatayo. jeongjisikyeo juseyo. / B: ne, baro jeongjihagetseumnida. jaebalgeupdo wonhaseyo?
examples.en: A: I think I lost my card. Please freeze it. / B: Of course, I'll suspend it right away. Would you also like a replacement?
examples.note: Full urgent exchange: 정지 → B offers 재발급; B uses -하겠습니다 (bank staff's formal register)

examples.ko: 일단 카드 막아 주시고, 재발급도 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ildan kadeu maga jusigo, jaebalgeupdo hae juseyo.
examples.en: First please block the card, then reissue it too.
examples.note: 일단 ('first of all') prioritizes the freeze before the replacement — natural two-step request

expressions.nuance: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'suspension/halt') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. This is high-stakes vocabulary — get it right. 정지(시키다) means to SUSPEND/freeze the card (potentially reversible); for a lost or stolen card you'll also 분실 신고하다 ('file a loss report'), which permanently blocks it so you then 재발급 ('reissue') a new one. The spoken urgent verb is 막다 ('to block/stop up') — 카드 막아 주세요 is what a panicked person blurts at the call center. The grammar point: 정지하다 (intransitive, 'the card stops') vs 정지시키다 (causative, 'cause it to be stopped') — when asking the bank to freeze YOUR card, 정지시켜 주세요 is the cleaner choice. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'cancel' as 취소하다 — 취소하다 cancels a transaction or reservation, NOT a card; a card is 정지/해지/분실 신고, never 취소. Also distinguish 정지 (temporary freeze, reversible) vs 해지 (permanent termination of the card/account). Always 존댓말 to staff in this situation.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 카드 취소해 주세요 to block a card.
취소하다 cancels a transaction/order/reservation, not a card. To block a card say 카드 정지시켜 주세요, or for a lost card 분실 신고하려고요.
Using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다.
정지하다 can sound like the card itself stops. To request the bank CAUSE it to be suspended, the causative 정지시키다 is clearer: 카드 정지시켜 주세요.
Confusing 정지 (suspend) with 해지 (terminate).
정지 is a (possibly temporary) freeze; 해지 permanently terminates the card/account. If you only lost it and want a new one, you 정지/분실 신고 + 재발급, not 해지.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'stop/suspend') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. 정지 = temporary freeze (can be reversed); 분실 신고 = permanent block for lost/stolen cards; 재발급 = reissue a new card after blocking. The causative 시키다 is important: you're asking the bank to CAUSE the suspension.

카드 정지시키다 (formal, reversible suspend) vs 분실 신고하다 (formal procedure, permanently blocks for loss) vs 카드 막다 (spoken urgent 'block it'). Critical: 정지 (freeze, reversible) ≠ 해지 (terminate the card permanently). And: 취소하다 = cancel a transaction/reservation, NOT a card.
정지 is 停止 — 停 'stop/halt' + 止 'cease'. 분실 is 紛失 'loss/misplacement'. 재발급 is 再發給 're-issue/re-supply'.

Always 존댓말 — this is an urgent call-center or counter interaction. There is no casual version you'd realistically need; even with bank app chat support you use polite forms. Staff will respond in formal 합쇼체: 바로 정지하겠습니다.

Two traps: (1) using 취소하다 for 'cancel a card' — 취소 cancels a transaction/order, not a card; say 정지/해지/분실 신고. (2) using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다 — 정지하다 can sound like 'the card stops on its own' (intransitive); the causative 시키다 makes your request clear: 'please MAKE it stop'.

expressions.english: My card didn't work / got declined
expressions.shortExplanation: 카드가 안 됐어요 is a practical expression meaning "My card didn't work / got declined".
expressions.explanation: "My card didn't work / got declined" — that is 카드가 안 됐어요 (kadeuga an dwaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 카드가 안 됐어요 ("My card didn't go through"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the general catch-all 'it didn't work' at a register — covers any failure
결제 ('payment/settlement') is the precise noun at checkout; used when the card itself is fine but payment fails
거절되다 ('be rejected') — more explicit and formal, often mirrors error messages
한도 초과 = the exact on-screen error message you'll see for overspending

examples.en: My card didn't work.
examples.note: Said to the cashier when the terminal rejects the card; the all-purpose opening line

examples.ko: A: 결제가 계속 안 돼서요. 다시 한번 해 봐도 될까요? / B: 네, 카드 다시 대 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: gyeoljega gyesok an dwaeseoyo. dasi hanbeon hae bwado doelkkayo? / B: ne, kadeu dasi dae juseyo.
examples.en: A: The payment keeps failing. Could we try one more time? / B: Sure, please tap the card again.
examples.note: A/B exchange at a cashier: 결제가 안 되다 is the precise payment-failure framing; B asks to tap again (대다 = tap/present a card)

examples.ko: 카드 정지돼서 그런지 결제가 자꾸 거절돼요.
examples.romanization: kadeu jeongjidwaeseo geureonji gyeoljega jakku geojeoldwaeyo.
examples.en: Maybe because my card's frozen, payments keep getting declined.
examples.note: 정지돼서 그런지 ('maybe because it's frozen') — 그런지 expresses a tentative reason; 거절되다 is the more explicit 'declined'

expressions.nuance: 카드가 안 됐어요 is 카드 + 가 (subject particle) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('to work/function') in past polite. 되다 is the workhorse verb for 'something functions/goes through', so 안 되다 ('doesn't work') is the first thing to say whenever a card fails — it covers a declined card, a frozen card, a dead chip, or a bad terminal. For more precision at checkout the noun is 결제 ('payment/settlement'): 결제가 안 돼요 ('the payment won't go through'). For an explicit 'declined', 거절되다 mirrors the error message. A common real cause is 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded'). Grammar trap: it must be 카드가 안 됐어요 (subject particle 가, past 됐), not 카드를 안 했어요 (object particle 를 means 'I didn't do the card' — nonsense). The English-speaker trap is translating 'work' as 일하다 ('to labor') — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and confusing; a device 'working' is 되다, never 일하다. Also: 카드가 틀렸어요 ('the card is incorrect', like a wrong answer) is wrong for a declined card; use 안 됐어요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'work' as 일하다.
일하다 means 'to do labor/have a job'. A card/machine functioning is 되다: 카드가 안 됐어요. 카드가 일 안 해요 is incorrect.
Saying 카드를 안 했어요.
With 를 it means 'I didn't do the card'. The card is the SUBJECT of failing, so use 가: 카드가 안 됐어요.
Using 틀리다 for a declined card.
틀리다 = 'to be wrong/incorrect (an answer)'. A card that won't process is 안 되다 / 거절되다, not 틀리다. Say 카드가 안 됐어요.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 + 가 (subject) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('work/function'): 되다 is the Korean verb for 'something functions/goes through'. 안 되다 is the catch-all when a card fails for any reason. The past form 됐 → 안 됐어요 = 'didn't go through'. For an ongoing failure use the present: 카드가 안 돼요.

카드가 안 됐어요 (general 'didn't work', broadest) vs 결제가 안 돼요 ('payment fails', precise at a checkout) vs 거절됐어요 ('was declined', mirrors official error message). 한도 초과 = 'limit exceeded' (the specific cause if you've overspent).
Past (just happened): 카드가 안 됐어요. Present (still failing): 카드가 안 돼요. Guessing cause: 한도 초과인 것 같아요 ('I think it's over the limit'). Urgent re-try: 다시 한번 해 볼게요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.

Used with cashiers, tellers, or bank staff — always 존댓말. 되다/안 되다 is the appropriate register level: direct but polite. In casual chat with a friend you'd just say 카드 안 돼 or 카드 긁혔어? ('did the card go through?'). 긁히다 ('to be swiped') is the casual verb for a card transaction.

Two traps: (1) 일하다 for 'work' — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and funny; a device/process working is 되다. (2) 틀리다 for a declined card — 틀리다 means 'to be incorrect (an answer)'; a non-functioning card is 안 되다 / 거절되다. Also: subject particle 가 (not object 를) is required.

expressions.shortExplanation: 환전하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to exchange money".
expressions.explanation: 환전하고 싶어요 (hwanjeonhago sipeoyo) = "I'd like to exchange money". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 환전하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to exchange currency"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 환전 (換錢) is the standard word for currency exchange at a bank or 환전소
Specifying the target currency with 로/으로 — direction particle for the result
-는데요 softens and opens the conversation with the teller
환율 ('exchange rate') is the partner word you'll always ask about before committing

examples.en: I'd like to exchange money.
examples.note: Said at a bank counter or 환전소 (dedicated exchange booth)

examples.ko: A: 원화를 달러로 환전하고 싶어요. / B: 오늘 환율이 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: A: wonhwareul dalleoro hwanjeonhago sipeoyo. / B: oneul hwanyuri eolmayeyo?
examples.en: A: I'd like to exchange won into dollars. / B: What's today's exchange rate?
examples.note: A/B exchange: A states currencies with A를 B로 pattern; B asks the rate before quoting

examples.ko: 환율이 오늘 안 좋아서 조금만 환전할게요.
examples.romanization: hwanyuri oneul an joaseo jogeumman hwanjeonhalgeyo.
examples.en: The rate's bad today, so I'll only exchange a little.
examples.note: 환율이 안 좋다 ('the rate is unfavorable') — the natural everyday collocation for judging whether to exchange

expressions.nuance: 환전하고 싶어요 is 환전 (換錢, 'exchange-money = currency exchange') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Currency exchange is done at a bank or a 환전소 (dedicated booth, often better rates). The essential partner word is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') — ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? and judge with 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 ('the rate is good/bad'). To name currencies, use 로/으로 for the target: 달러로 환전하다 ('exchange INTO dollars'), 원화로 바꾸다. A plainer synonym is 바꾸다 ('change/swap') — 달러로 바꾸고 싶어요 is natural and slightly more colloquial. The critical confusion to avoid: 환전 (換錢, 'exchange money') vs 환불 (還拂, 'refund') — they look and sound similar but 환불 means getting your money back for a returned purchase; never say 환전 at a store return counter. Another trap: 교환하다 ('exchange goods, swap sizes') is for trading items, not currency. Also keep 환율 (the rate) distinct from 수수료 (the fee charged for the exchange), which is a separate cost worth asking about. To staff use 존댓말 throughout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 환전 (exchange money) with 환불 (refund).
환전 (換錢) = swap currency; 환불 (還拂) = refund a purchase. At a store you ask 환불, at a bank 환전. They're not interchangeable.
Using 교환하다 for currency.
교환하다 is exchanging GOODS (swap a size/item). Currency is 환전하다 or 바꾸다. 돈을 교환하다 sounds like bartering objects, not changing money.
Marking the target currency with 에.
The currency you change INTO takes 로/으로: 달러로 환전하다. 달러에 환전하다 is wrong. Source uses 을/를: 원화를 달러로.

structuredNuance.t: 환전 (換錢, 'exchange-money') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. To specify what you exchange and into what, use A를 B로: 원화를 달러로 환전하다. The target currency takes 로/으로 (direction). Partner word: 환율 (exchange rate) — 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 to judge timing.

환전하다 (formal, standard) vs 바꾸다 (casual, 'change/swap'). Critical contrasts: 환전 (currency exchange) ≠ 환불 (refund for returned goods) ≠ 교환 (swapping goods/sizes). Use 환전 only for money-for-money conversion.
환전 is 換錢 — 換 'swap/exchange' + 錢 'money'. 환율 is 換率 — same 換 + 率 'rate/ratio'. 환불 is 還拂 — 還 'return' + 拂 'pay out': different 한자, different meaning.

Used at a bank or 환전소 — always 존댓말. With a currency exchange app or comparison website, you still use the same formal term 환전. Casual equivalent: 달러로 바꾸고 싶은데요. Asking about the rate first is culturally expected — exchange booths assume you'll ask before deciding.

Two traps: (1) confusing 환전 with 환불 — similar sound, opposite meanings; 환불 = refund, 환전 = currency swap. (2) marking the target currency with 에 — the direction particle is 로/으로: 달러로 환전하다, not 달러에 환전하다. Source uses 을/를: 원화를 달러로.

expressions.shortExplanation: 환율 어떻게 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the exchange rate?".
expressions.explanation: 환율 어떻게 돼요? (hwanyul eotteoke dwaeyo?) means "What's the exchange rate?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 환율 어떻게 돼요? ("What's the exchange rate?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the idiomatic way to ask for a rate or numeric figure
얼마예요 ('how much') when you want the number directly and the currency is specified

usagePhrases.en: Do I get a preferential rate?
usagePhrases.note: 환율 우대 = a preferred/discount rate banks offer to app users or regulars

usagePhrases.en: Is the rate good right now?
usagePhrases.note: Asking whether it's a favorable time to exchange — 좋다/안 좋다 is the natural judgment phrase

examples.en: What's the exchange rate?
examples.note: Asked at the bank or exchange booth before deciding how much to convert

examples.ko: A: 오늘 달러 환율 얼마예요? / B: 지금 1,350원이에요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul dalleo hwanyul eolmayeyo? / B: jigeum 1,350wonieyo.
examples.en: A: What's the dollar rate today? / B: Right now it's 1,350 won.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 얼마예요? asks for the number; B gives the rate as 원 per 1 dollar — the standard Korean quote format

examples.ko: 환율 우대 받으면 수수료가 좀 줄어요?
examples.romanization: hwanyul udae badeumyeon susuryoga jom jureoyo?
examples.en: If I get a preferential rate, does the fee drop a bit?
examples.note: 환율 우대 ('rate preference') often bundles with a reduced 수수료 — worth asking together

expressions.nuance: 환율 어떻게 돼요? is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') + 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it come to be?'), the idiomatic Korean way to ask for a numeric figure or status. The construction 어떻게 돼요? is broadly useful — Koreans use it for rates, prices, totals, even your name (이름이 어떻게 되세요?) — and sounds more natural and polite than blunt 얼마예요? for abstract figures, though both work for 환율. A money-saving phrase: 환율 우대 ('preferential exchange rate') — banks and their apps give 우대 (優待, 'preferential treatment') to regulars or digital users, so asking 환율 우대 돼요? can get you a better deal. Don't confuse 환율 (the rate, a number) with 환전 (the act of exchanging). The English-speaker trap is calquing 'what is the exchange rate?' as 환율이 뭐예요? — but 뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?', so it sounds like you're asking the meaning of the term; use 어떻게 돼요? or 얼마예요? for the numeric value. Casual form with a friend: 환율 어떻게 돼?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 환율이 뭐예요? for the number.
뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?'. For a numeric rate use 환율 어떻게 돼요? or 환율 얼마예요?. 뭐예요? sounds like asking the meaning of the term.
Confusing 환율 with 환전.
환율 (換率) is the RATE (a number); 환전 (換錢) is the ACT of exchanging. You ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? then say 환전할게요 to do it.
Not knowing 우대 and missing a better rate.
환율 우대 ('preferential rate') is a real discount banks offer. Asking 환율 우대 돼요? can save money; without the word you may pay the full rate.

structuredNuance.t: 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') + 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it work out?'). 어떻게 돼요? is the idiomatic question for 'what is the value/status of X?' — also used for prices, totals, names. Both 어떻게 돼요? and 얼마예요? work for rates; the former is slightly softer and more natural. Casual: 환율 어떻게 돼?
환율 어떻게 돼요? (polite, for a figure/status) vs 환율 얼마예요? (direct, 'how much?'). Key vocabulary pair: 환율 (the rate, a number) vs 환전 (the act of exchanging). Don't confuse the rate with the transaction.
환율 is 換率 — 換 'swap/exchange' + 率 'rate/ratio'. 우대 in 환율 우대 is 優待 — 優 'preferential/excellent' + 待 'treatment': a better rate for valued customers.

Used at a bank, exchange booth, or app — always 존댓말 with staff. With friends discussing their recent trip: 환율 어떻게 됐어? is casual. Culturally, asking the rate before committing to an exchange is expected and shows savvy; follow up with 환율 우대 돼요? to potentially get a better deal.

Asking 환율이 뭐예요? — 뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?', sounding like you want an explanation of the term 'exchange rate'. For the numeric value, use 어떻게 돼요? or 얼마예요?. This is one of the most common awkward-phrasing errors at exchange booths.

expressions.english: Please change this into smaller bills/coins
expressions.shortExplanation: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please change this into smaller bills/coins".
expressions.explanation: "Please change this into smaller bills/coins" — that is 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 (jandoneuro bakkwo juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 ("Please break this into change"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 잔돈 = 'small change/small bills'; the standard request to break a large bill
Specify the denomination with 짜리 ('worth ~'); the most natural way to name a bill type

usagePhrases.ko: 동전으로 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: dongjeoneuro jom bakkwo jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you change this into coins?
usagePhrases.note: 동전 = 'coins' specifically; -주실 수 있어요 is extra polite for a slightly unusual request

usagePhrases.en: Please give me 10,000 won in change
usagePhrases.note: When you want only PART of an amount as small bills — 만 ('just/only') limits it

examples.en: Please break this into change.
examples.note: Handing a 50,000-won note over the counter and asking for smaller bills

examples.ko: A: 오만 원권을 만 원짜리로 바꿔 주세요. / B: 네, 오만 원 맞으시죠? 잠깐만요.
examples.romanization: A: oman wongwoneul man wonjjariro bakkwo juseyo. / B: ne, oman won majeusijyo? jamkkanmanyo.
examples.en: A: Please change this 50,000-won note into 10,000-won bills. / B: Right, that's 50,000 won? One moment.
examples.note: Full exchange: 권 = large-denomination note; 짜리 = denomination you want; B confirms amount

examples.ko: 동전이 필요한데 천 원만 동전으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: dongjeoni piryohande cheon wonman dongjeoneuro bakkwo jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I need coins — could you change just 1,000 won into coins?
examples.note: Asking specifically for 동전 (coins) for a vending machine or coin locker; limiting amount with 만

expressions.nuance: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 is 잔돈 ('small change/change') + -으로 ('into') + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + 주세요. 잔돈 covers both small-denomination bills and coins, and is also the word for the change you get back after paying — though 거스름돈 is the more precise term for 'change returned by a cashier'. To specify the denomination you want, use -짜리 ('a thing worth ~'): 천 원짜리 ('a 1,000-won bill'), 만 원짜리 ('a 10,000-won bill'). For coins specifically say 동전. The verb 바꾸다 ('to swap/change') is the same one used casually for currency exchange — context tells the listener you mean breaking a bill. The particle trap: it's 잔돈으로 바꾸다 (target marked with 으로 = 'change INTO small bills'), not 잔돈을 바꾸다 (which would mean 'change the small bills themselves'). Confusing 잔돈 (physical small cash) with 잔액 (account balance figure) is a real learner mix-up despite both having 잔 (殘, 'remaining'). Casual: 잔돈으로 바꿔 줘.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the target with 을 instead of 으로.
You change money INTO small bills: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 (으로 = 'into'). 잔돈을 바꾸다 would mean 'change the small money itself'.
Confusing 잔돈 with 잔액.
잔돈 = physical small change/bills; 잔액 = your account balance (a number). Both have 잔, but ask 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 for cash, 잔액 확인 for the balance.
Using -원 instead of -원짜리 for a denomination.
To name a bill type, use 짜리 ('worth'): 천 원짜리 ('a 1,000-won note'). Bare 천 원 is just the amount; 천 원짜리로 specifies the bill you want.

structuredNuance.t: 잔돈 ('small change') + -으로 ('into', direction particle) + 바꾸다 ('to swap/change') + 주세요. -으로 marks the target form (what you want it changed INTO). To name the denomination: -짜리 (천 원짜리 = 1,000-won bill). For coins: 동전. Casual: 잔돈으로 바꿔 줘.

잔돈 ('small bills and coins, change') vs 거스름돈 ('change returned by a cashier') — 잔돈 is the broader term; 거스름돈 specifically means the change a seller gives back. Also: 잔돈 (physical small cash) ≠ 잔액 (account balance figure) — both use 잔 (殘) but are completely different.
Generic: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요. Named denomination: 천 원짜리로 바꿔 주세요. Coins only: 동전으로 바꿔 주세요. Partial: 만 원만 잔돈으로 주세요. If the cashier forgets your change: 거스름돈요 ('my change, please').

Used with bank tellers, cashiers, or convenience store staff — polite 존댓말 is standard. Breaking a bill is a routine, unawkward request in Korea. With a friend you'd ask 잔돈으로 바꿔 줄 수 있어? Denomination names use native Korean numbers + 원짜리 (천 원짜리, 오천 원짜리).

The particle: it's 잔돈으로 바꾸다 ('change INTO small bills', target takes 으로), not 잔돈을 바꾸다 ('change the small bills', which means something different). Also: confusing 잔돈 (cash in hand) with 잔액 (balance in account) — both share 잔 (殘) but refer to entirely different things.

expressions.shortExplanation: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you update my bankbook?".
expressions.explanation: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요 (tongjang jeongni jom hae juseyo) = "Could you update my bankbook?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요 ("Could you update my bankbook?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 통장 정리 = printing recent transactions into the physical passbook

usagePhrases.en: Please print out my transaction history
usagePhrases.note: 거래 내역 = 'transaction record'; 뽑다 ('to print/pull') — for a paper statement

usagePhrases.en: I'm here to update my passbook
usagePhrases.note: Stating your purpose at the counter or the self-service 통장정리기 machine

usagePhrases.ko: 입출금 내역 좀 볼 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: ipchulgeum naeyeok jom bol su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can I see my deposit/withdrawal history?
usagePhrases.note: 입출금 내역 = the full deposit-and-withdrawal list; 볼 수 있어요? for viewing on screen

examples.en: Could you update my bankbook, please?
examples.note: Handing the passbook to a teller, or walking up to the self-service 통장정리기 machine

examples.ko: A: 통장 정리하려고 하는데 기계 어디 있어요? / B: 저 안쪽에 통장정리기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: tongjang jeongniharyeogo haneunde gigye eodi isseoyo? / B: jeo anjjoge tongjangjeongnigi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: I want to update my passbook — where's the machine? / B: The passbook machine is further inside.
examples.note: A/B at the branch: 통장정리기 is the self-service machine; B directs you in

examples.ko: 지난달 거래 내역 좀 뽑아 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: jinandal georae naeyeok jom ppoba jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you print last month's transaction history?
examples.note: 거래 내역 ('transaction history') is the right term for a paper statement of past activity; 뽑다 = 'print/pull out'

expressions.nuance: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요 is 통장 ('bankbook/passbook') + 정리 (整理, 'tidying/sorting') + 좀 + 해 주세요. 통장 정리 is a distinctly Korean banking ritual — feeding your physical passbook into a 통장정리기 (self-service machine) or handing it to a teller to PRINT the latest transactions into it. Here 정리 means 'putting the records in order', NOT its common meaning of 'cleaning up/throwing away'. This distinction matters: if someone hears 정리 and thinks 'dispose of', 통장 정리해 주세요 might sound like 'close my account' — but it does NOT. To close an account, you'd say 통장 해지 / 계좌 해지 ('terminate'). For a broader printed statement, ask for 거래 내역 (transaction history) or 입출금 내역 (deposit/withdrawal history), which you 뽑다 ('print/pull') or 출력하다. Korea still uses physical passbooks, making this a common real-world request. Another key distinction: 통장 (the physical passbook) vs 계좌 (the account, a number in the banking system) — you do 정리 on the 통장, but funds and balances live in the 계좌. Casually: 통장 정리 좀 해 줘 with a teller you know, but 존댓말 is the norm.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 정리 as 'close/clear out' the account.
통장 정리 means PRINTING recent transactions into the passbook, not closing it. To close an account, say 통장 해지 / 계좌 해지. 정리 ≠ termination.
Confusing 통장 with 계좌.
통장 is the physical passbook; 계좌 is the account (number/funds). You 통장 정리 (update the book), but transfers and balances refer to the 계좌.
Saying 통장 내역 for a printed statement.
The standard term is 거래 내역 or 입출금 내역 ('transaction/deposit-withdrawal history'). 통장 정리 updates the book; 거래 내역 뽑다 prints a statement.

structuredNuance.t: 통장 ('bankbook') + 정리 (整理, 'put in order') + 좀 + 해 주세요. 정리 here = printing recent transactions into the passbook, NOT 'tidying/disposing'. It's a specific action: you feed the book into the 통장정리기 machine or hand it to a teller to print the entries.

통장 정리 (print entries into the passbook) vs 거래 내역 뽑다 (print a separate paper statement). Critical contrast: 통장 정리 ≠ 통장 해지 (terminating/closing the account). Don't let 정리 ('tidy up') make you think the account is being closed.
정리 is 整理 — 整 'put in order/tidy' + 理 'manage/reason'. 해지 is 解止 — 解 'dissolve' + 止 'stop': actual termination of the account.

Always 존댓말 at a bank branch. This phrase is routine and polite. Many branches now have self-service 통장정리기 machines — you just feed the book in. If you need an older-style teller update, this phrase is exactly what to say at the counter.

Reading 정리 as 'tidy up/dispose of' and worrying 통장 정리 means closing the account — it doesn't. 정리 here means updating the record. To CLOSE an account say 계좌 해지. Also: assuming Korean banking is entirely digital — physical passbooks (통장) are still in regular use and 통장 정리 is a real, common request.

expressions.english: I'd like to set up an automatic payment/transfer
expressions.shortExplanation: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to set up an automatic payment/transfer".
expressions.explanation: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 (jadongiche sincheonghago sipeoyo) means "I'd like to set up an automatic payment/transfer". Say it as one set phrase — for example 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to set up auto-transfer"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to set up auto-transfer
usagePhrases.note: Polite; 자동이체 = recurring automatic account debit; 신청하다 = apply/sign up for
걸어 놓다 ('to set/hook up and leave') — the natural spoken phrase for arranging auto-debit

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to change the auto-debit date
usagePhrases.note: Adjusting which day of the month the recurring payment is pulled

usagePhrases.en: I want to cancel the auto-transfer
usagePhrases.note: 해지하다 ('to terminate') a standing recurring instruction — not 취소, which is for one-off transactions

examples.en: I'd like to set up an automatic transfer.
examples.note: Said to a teller to arrange recurring rent or utility payments

examples.ko: A: 월세 자동이체 걸어 놓으면 매달 빠져나가요? / B: 네, 지정한 날짜에 자동으로 빠져나가요.
examples.romanization: A: wolse jadongiche georeo noeumyeon maedal ppajyeonagayo? / B: ne, jijeonghan naljjae jadongeuro ppajyeonagayo.
examples.en: A: If I set up auto-pay for rent, does it come out monthly? / B: Yes, it comes out automatically on the designated date.
examples.note: Full A/B exchange: 걸어 놓다 for 'set it up'; 빠져나가다 ('slip out') is the vivid native verb for money being pulled from an account

examples.ko: 통신비는 자동이체로 해 놨는데 날짜 좀 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: tongsinbineun jadongichero hae nwanneunde naljja jom bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: I've got my phone bill on auto-pay — please change the date.
examples.note: 자동이체로 해 놓다 ('have it set to auto') — the -아/어 놓다 pattern for a state you've left in place

expressions.nuance: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 is 자동 (自動, 'automatic') + 이체 ('transfer') + 신청하다 ('to apply for / sign up') + -고 싶어요. 자동이체 is the recurring auto-debit set up for rent (월세), utilities (공과금), phone bills (통신비), and subscriptions — essential for life in Korea, where most regular bills are pulled automatically from your bank account. Formally you 신청하다 ('apply for') the arrangement at a bank; colloquially people say 자동이체 걸어 놓다 / 해 놓다 ('set it up and leave it running'), using the -아/어 놓다 pattern for a maintained state. The vivid verb for money being auto-deducted is 빠져나가다 ('to slip out/be drawn out'): 돈이 빠져나가요. To stop it, you 해지하다 ('terminate'), not 취소하다 — 취소 is for one-off transactions, 해지 is for standing instructions. Key contrast: 자동이체 (recurring account-to-account debit) vs 자동 결제 (card-based auto-charge for subscriptions) — they overlap but 이체 is account debit, 결제 is card charge. Also: 신청 (you apply) vs 접수 (the bank receives/registers your application) — you 신청, the bank 접수. Always 존댓말 with staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 자동이체 with 자동 결제.
자동이체 is recurring account-to-account debit (rent, utilities); 자동 결제 is card-based auto-charge (subscriptions). Ask for 자동이체 for bank debits, 자동 결제 for card subscriptions.
Using 취소하다 to stop a standing auto-transfer.
취소하다 cancels a one-off transaction. To END a recurring instruction, use 해지하다: 자동이체 해지하려고요. 취소 is for a single payment, not the whole arrangement.
Saying 신청 when you mean to ask the bank's confirmation.
신청하다 = YOU apply/sign up. The bank's side of receiving it is 접수. Say 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 to request setup; the bank then 접수 (processes) it.

structuredNuance.t: 자동 (自動, 'automatic') + 이체 ('transfer') + 신청하다 ('to apply for') + -고 싶어요. 자동이체 = recurring auto-debit from a bank account (rent, utilities, phone bill). Colloquial setup verb: 걸어 놓다 / 해 놓다 ('set it up and leave it'). Money leaving: 빠져나가다 ('slip out').

자동이체 (recurring account debit, 이체 = bank transfer) vs 자동 결제 (card-based auto-charge for subscriptions, 결제 = payment). For bank debits (rent, utilities): 자동이체. For subscription cards (Netflix, etc.): 자동 결제. Also: 신청 (you apply) vs 접수 (bank receives it).
자동 is 自動 — 自 'self' + 動 'move': moves by itself. 신청 is 申請 — 申 'state/declare' + 請 'request'. 해지 is 解止 — 解 'dissolve' + 止 'stop': permanently terminating a standing arrangement.

Always 존댓말 at a bank counter or call center. In app menus you tap 자동이체 신청/해지 as labels. With a friend: 자동이체 해 놨어? is casual. The -아/어 놓다 pattern (걸어 놓다, 해 놓다) is very natural in spoken Korean and marks a persistent state.

Using 취소하다 to stop a recurring auto-transfer — 취소 cancels a one-off transaction or order; to end a standing auto-debit arrangement use 해지하다: 자동이체 해지하려고요. Also confusing 자동이체 (bank account debit) with 자동 결제 (card charge) — different systems, different cancellation processes.

expressions.shortExplanation: 근처에 ATM 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there an ATM nearby?".
expressions.explanation: "Is there an ATM nearby?" — that is 근처에 ATM 있어요? (geuncheoe ATM isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 근처에 ATM 있어요? ("Is there an ATM nearby?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking a passerby or staff where to find a machine
현금인출기 ('cash withdrawal machine') is the full native Korean term for ATM
Checking your specific card is accepted at this particular machine

usagePhrases.en: Is there an ATM in the convenience store?
usagePhrases.note: Convenience-store ATMs (편의점) are ubiquitous but almost always charge a 수수료

examples.en: Is there an ATM nearby, by any chance?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') softens asking a stranger on the street — essential polite opener

examples.ko: A: 현금인출기 어디 있어요? 돈 좀 뽑으려고요. / B: 저 편의점 안에 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: hyeongeuminchulgi eodi isseoyo? don jom ppobeuryeogoyo. / B: jeo pyeonuijeom ane isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Where's the ATM? I need to take out some cash. / B: It's inside that convenience store.
examples.note: A/B on the street: pair the location question with the purpose (돈 뽑으려고요); B points you to the 편의점

examples.ko: 이 ATM 다른 은행 카드도 돼요?
examples.romanization: i ATM dareun eunhaeng kadeudo dwaeyo?
examples.en: Does this ATM take other banks' cards too?
examples.note: 다른 은행 카드 ('other bank's card') — cross-bank use usually adds a fee; ask before inserting

expressions.nuance: 근처에 ATM 있어요? is 근처 ('vicinity/nearby') + 에 (location particle for existence) + ATM + 있어요? ('is there?'). Koreans say the English initialism ATM (pronounced 에이티엠) naturally, but the native term is 현금인출기 (現金引出機, 'cash withdrawal machine') or 자동화기기 (the bank's signage term for an all-in-one deposit/withdraw kiosk) — all three are understood. The particle is the crunch point: a place where something EXISTS takes 에 (근처에 있어요?), while a place where an ACTION happens takes 에서 (ATM에서 돈을 뽑다, 'withdraw AT the ATM'). Using 에서 for 'is there an ATM' is the most common particle error here. Practically, ATMs are in bank lobbies (24-hour 365코너), convenience stores (편의점), and subway stations — but convenience-store and other-bank machines almost always charge a 수수료, and some bank ATMs restrict free service after hours. Always worth also asking 이 카드 여기서 돼요? to confirm your card works, and 외국 카드 돼요? for overseas cards. The English-speaker trap beyond particles: assuming all ATMs accept all cards — ask 다른 은행 카드도 돼요? or look for a 'Global ATM' sign for foreign cards. Casual form: 근처에 ATM 있어?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에서 instead of 에 for existence.
Existence (있다/없다) takes 에: 근처에 ATM 있어요?. 에서 marks where an action occurs (ATM에서 뽑다, 'withdraw at the ATM'). For 'is there an ATM', use 에.
Assuming every ATM takes your (or a foreign) card.
Other-bank and convenience-store ATMs often charge fees, and not all accept foreign cards. Ask 이 카드 여기서 돼요? or 다른 은행 카드도 돼요?, and look for a Global ATM for overseas cards.
Saying 인출기 alone and expecting clarity.
The full word is 현금인출기 (cash withdrawal machine) or just ATM. Bare 인출기 is understood but incomplete; 현금인출기 or 에이티엠 is what people actually say.

structuredNuance.t: 근처 ('nearby') + 에 (existence-location particle) + ATM + 있어요? ('is there?'). The particle is everything: 있다/없다 (existence) always takes 에, not 에서. 근처에 ATM 있어요? = 'Does an ATM exist near here?' Casual: 근처에 ATM 있어?

ATM (에이티엠, common loanword) = 현금인출기 (native full term) = 자동화기기 (bank signage term). All three are understood; 에이티엠 is the one people actually say on the street. Key particle contrast: 근처에 ATM 있어요? (존재, 에) vs ATM에서 돈을 뽑다 (행동 장소, 에서).
현금인출기 is 現金引出機 — 現金 'cash' + 引出 'draw out' + 機 'machine'. 자동화기기 is 自動化機器 — automated machine, the official bank term for the multi-function kiosk.

Used with strangers on the street (혹시 softens it) or in a shop/building. Add 혹시 when asking someone you don't know — it signals 'sorry to bother you' and is essential street courtesy. With a friend just say 근처에 ATM 있어? No 반말 with strangers.

Two traps: (1) 에 vs 에서 — existence takes 에 (근처에 있어요?), action location takes 에서 (ATM에서 뽑다). (2) Assuming all ATMs take all cards — other-bank and foreign-card support varies; ask 이 카드 여기서 돼요? / 외국 카드 돼요? before inserting.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please raise my transfer limit".
expressions.explanation: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 (iche hando jom ollyeo juseyo) = "Please raise my transfer limit". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 ("Please raise my transfer limit"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 한도 (限度) = 'permitted cap/ceiling', 올리다 ('to raise/increase')
1회 ('per occurrence/per transaction') vs 1일 ('per day') — different caps, both matter

usagePhrases.ko: 한도 초과라고 떠서 송금이 안 돼요
usagePhrases.romanization: hando chogwarago tteoseo songgeumi an dwaeyo
usagePhrases.en: It says 'limit exceeded' so I can't send
usagePhrases.note: 한도 초과 = the exact on-screen error that blocks a transfer above your cap

usagePhrases.ko: 출금 한도도 같이 올릴 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: chulgeum handodo gachi ollil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can I raise the withdrawal limit too?
usagePhrases.note: 출금 한도 (withdrawal cap) is separate from the transfer cap — ask about both

examples.en: Please raise my transfer limit.
examples.note: Said to a teller when you need to send an amount larger than your current cap allows

examples.ko: A: 한도 초과라고 떠서 이체가 안 돼요. 한도 올려 주세요. / B: 보안카드나 OTP 가져오셨어요?
examples.romanization: A: hando chogwarago tteoseo ichega an dwaeyo. hando ollyeo juseyo. / B: boankadeuna OTP gajyeoosyeosseoyo?
examples.en: A: It says limit exceeded so I can't transfer. Please raise the limit. / B: Did you bring your security card or OTP?
examples.note: A/B at the counter: 한도 초과 as the triggering error; B asks for identity verification (보안카드/OTP) — required to raise limits

examples.en: You're saying I can't raise the limit without a security card?
examples.note: Quote the teller's statement back as an indirect question — 못 올린다고요? checks you understood correctly

expressions.nuance: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 is 이체 ('transfer') + 한도 (限度, 'permitted ceiling/quota') + 좀 + 올리다 ('to raise') + 주세요. Korea sets surprisingly low default transfer limits — especially for new or foreigner accounts — split into 1회 한도 (per-transaction) and 1일 한도 (daily total), plus separate 출금 한도 (withdrawal cap) and 이체 한도 (transfer cap). New residents and foreigners constantly hit these, making 한도 올려 주세요 one of the most practically necessary phrases, usually requiring re-verification with a 보안카드 (security card) or OTP device. Natural verb pair: 올리다 ('raise') / 내리다 ('lower'). The blocking error is 한도 초과 ('exceeded the cap'). English-speaker trap: 한도 (permitted maximum/quota) vs 한계 (limit of ability or endurance, e.g. 체력의 한계 'physical limits') — you say 이체 한도, never 이체 한계. Another trap: 올리다 is the correct verb for raising a numeric cap; 늘리다 ('to increase/expand in size') is also acceptable but 올리다/높이다 ('raise/make higher') is more idiomatic for limits. Don't confuse 한도 (the permitted cap) with 잔액 (your actual balance) — a low 한도 can block a transfer even when your 잔액 is ample. Always 존댓말 to staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 한계 instead of 한도 for an account cap.
한도 (限度) is a permitted maximum/quota (이체 한도). 한계 is a limit of ability/endurance (체력의 한계). For a transfer or withdrawal cap, always 한도.
Confusing 한도 (cap) with 잔액 (balance).
한도 is the MAX you're allowed to move; 잔액 is how much money you actually have. You can be blocked by a low 한도 even with a high 잔액. They're different problems.
Saying 한도 크게 해 주세요.
The idiomatic verb for a cap is 올리다/높이다 ('raise'): 한도 좀 올려 주세요. 크게 하다 ('make it big') sounds off for a numeric limit.

structuredNuance.t: 이체 ('transfer') + 한도 (限度, 'permitted ceiling') + 좀 + 올리다 ('raise') + 주세요. 한도 is the cap on how much you can move at once or per day. Korea defaults to low caps for new accounts — foreigners especially hit these. The error you'll see: 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded').

한도 (permitted maximum/quota) vs 한계 (boundary of ability/endurance: 체력의 한계). For a bank transfer cap, always 한도. Verb: 올리다/높이다 ('raise a cap') — standard. Also: 한도 (cap) ≠ 잔액 (actual balance) — you can have money but be blocked by a low 한도.
한도 is 限度 — 限 'limit/restrict' + 度 'degree/extent'. 초과 (in 한도 초과) is 超過 — 超 'exceed' + 過 'pass by/over'. Together: 'exceeded the permitted degree'.

Always 존댓말 at a bank counter or call center. Raising limits requires in-person verification with ID + 보안카드 or OTP. If at a call center, they'll walk you through the same verification. Keep 올려 주세요 as the core request; you can add urgency with 급하게 보내야 해서요 ('I urgently need to send it').

Using 한계 for a bank cap — 한계 = limit of endurance/ability (e.g. 'I've hit my limits'), not a numeric banking quota. Always use 한도 for transfer and withdrawal caps. Also: 크게 하다 ('make it big') for a numeric limit sounds wrong — the idiomatic verb is 올리다/높이다 ('raise it').

expressions.shortExplanation: 구경 좀 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm just looking, thanks".
expressions.explanation: 구경 좀 할게요 (gugyeong jom halgeyo) means "I'm just looking, thanks". Say it as one set phrase — for example 구경 좀 할게요 ("I'm just looking"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard line when a beauty-shop clerk offers help
Common variant; 둘러보다 = 'look around'
반말, only with a friend, not to staff

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to look on my own
usagePhrases.note: Gently signals you don't need to be followed

examples.ko: A: 뭐 찾으세요? / B: 아, 그냥 구경 좀 할게요.
examples.romanization: A: mwo chajeuseyo? / B: a, geunyang gugyeong jom halgeyo.
examples.en: A: Can I help you find something? / B: Oh, I'm just looking, thanks.
examples.note: The most natural two-line exchange the moment a clerk approaches

examples.ko: 네, 그냥 구경 좀 할게요. 필요하면 부를게요.
examples.romanization: ne, geunyang gugyeong jom halgeyo. piryohamyeon bureulgeyo.
examples.en: Yeah, just looking — I'll call you if I need help.
examples.note: 부를게요 ('I'll call you') politely releases them and leaves the door open

examples.ko: 아직 안 정했어요. 혼자 좀 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: ajik an jeonghaesseoyo. honja jom dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: I haven't decided yet — I'll just browse on my own.
examples.note: Use when a clerk keeps hovering; 혼자 ('alone') is a gentle extra signal

expressions.nuance: 구경 좀 할게요 is 구경 ('looking around / sightseeing') + 좀 (softener) + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 'I'm going to…' volitional ending), so literally 'I'll do a little looking.' It is the polite, friendly way to tell an Olive Young or department-store beauty clerk you don't want help yet — said with a small smile, it releases social pressure without rudeness. The near-twin 그냥 둘러볼게요 is interchangeable; 구경 leans toward window-shopping while 둘러보다 emphasises walking around. For variants: add 그냥 ('just') to soften further — 그냥 구경 좀 할게요 — or replace with 혼자 좀 볼게요 to signal you want space. The English-speaker trap is rendering 'just looking' as 안 사요 ('I'm not buying'), which sounds defensive as if accusing the clerk; 구경 좀 할게요 is warm and leaves the door open. Always keep the polite -ㄹ게요 ending with staff; dropping to 구경 좀 할게 (반말) to a stranger is abrupt.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 사요 to mean 'just looking'.
안 사요 means 'I'm not buying' and sounds blunt or defensive to a clerk. The friendly, face-saving line is 구경 좀 할게요 — it doesn't shut them down, just postpones help.
Dropping 요 and saying 구경 좀 할게 to staff.
That's 반말 and sounds abrupt to a stranger. Keep the polite ending: 구경 좀 할게요.
Using 보다 alone as 좀 볼게요 expecting it to be clear.
좀 볼게요 ('I'll take a look') can sound like you want to look at one specific item the clerk is holding. For browsing the store, say 구경 좀 할게요 or 둘러볼게요.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: '(I'll) do a little sightseeing.' Real meaning: 'I'm just browsing — no help needed yet.' The 구경 ('sightseeing') root makes it light and non-committal, implying casual interest rather than rejection of the clerk.

Use the moment a clerk in any beauty shop (Olive Young, brand counter, department store) asks 뭐 찾으세요? or 도와드릴까요?. This is 존댓말 and polite enough for any staff. Never drop to 구경 좀 할게 (반말) with strangers — save that for browsing with a friend.

그냥 둘러볼게요 ('I'll just browse around') is the closest twin — both are natural; 구경 frames it as 'looking around like a visitor', 둘러보다 frames it as 'walking and scanning.' 그냥만 볼게요 is also heard but slightly more blunt. All three are polite; choose any.

Softer: 그냥 구경 좀 할게요 (adding 그냥 'just'). Stronger: 혼자 좀 볼게요 ('I'd like to look alone') signals actively wanting space. To add a follow-up: 구경 좀 하다가 필요하면 부를게요 ('I'll look around and call you if I need anything').

Translating 'just looking' as 안 사요 ('I'm not buying') sounds cold and defensive, as if accusing the clerk of pressuring you. 구경 좀 할게요 keeps the warmth and leaves the interaction open. Also avoid 저 그냥요 ('just… me') which is incomplete and odd.

expressions.english: Can I try this on (apply a sample)?
expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I try this on (apply a sample)?".
expressions.explanation: "Can I try this on (apply a sample)?" — that is 이거 발라봐도 돼요? (igeo ballabwado dwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 발라봐도 돼요? ("Can I try applying this?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking to test a sample on your skin
테스트하다 (loanword) for any tester product
반말, with a friend, not staff

usagePhrases.en: Can I try it on the back of my hand?
usagePhrases.note: 손등 ('back of the hand') = where you swatch makeup

examples.ko: A: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? / B: 네, 여기 테스터 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo ballabwado dwaeyo? / B: ne, yeogi teseuteo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Can I try this on? / B: Yes, we have a tester right here.
examples.note: The standard two-turn exchange at a cosmetics counter

examples.ko: 립스틱 색 보려고요. 손등에 발라봐도 돼요?
examples.romanization: ripseutik saek boryeogoyo. sondeunge ballabwado dwaeyo?
examples.en: I want to see the lipstick color — can I swatch it on my hand?
examples.note: 손등 is the normal swatch spot; naming it sounds experienced

examples.en: Can I try this sunscreen to see if it's sticky?
examples.note: 끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky') states exactly what you're checking

expressions.nuance: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? breaks down as 이거 ('this') + 발라보다 (바르다 'to apply/spread on skin' + -아 보다 'try doing') + -도 돼요? ('is it okay to…?'), meaning 'is it okay if I try applying this?' The -아 보다 form signals a trial attempt, so the phrase captures both the action and its tentative feel perfectly. 바르다 is the specific verb for spreading skincare or makeup onto skin (cream, sunscreen, lip balm, tinted moisturiser); it is distinct from 칠하다 ('to paint/coat', used for walls or nail polish) — using 칠하다 for face cream sounds odd, like painting yourself. The 손등 (back of the hand) is the culturally standard swatch location, so specifying it sounds like a regular. Variants: 테스터 있어요? ('Is there a tester?') asks the same thing more simply. In 반말 with a friend: 발라봐도 돼?. The English-speaker error is asking 이거 해 봐도 돼요? ('can I try doing this?') — 해 보다 is too generic for skin application; use 발라보다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 칠하다 for applying cream or sunscreen.
칠하다 means 'to paint/coat' (walls, a fence). Skincare and makeup go on with 바르다. Say 발라봐도 돼요?, not 칠해 봐도 돼요?.
Saying 이거 해 봐도 돼요? to test a sample.
해 보다 ('try doing') is too vague for putting product on skin. The specific verb is 발라보다: 이거 발라봐도 돼요?
Marking the body part with 을/를: 손등을 발라봐도 돼요?
You apply product TO a surface, so the particle is 에: 손등에 발라봐도 돼요? (손등을 would mean you're applying the hand itself).

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 'Is it okay to try applying this?' The compound 발라보다 = 바르다 ('spread on skin') + -아 보다 ('try doing'), so it captures both the action and the trial nature in one verb. The real meaning: 'May I swatch or test this product on my skin?'
Said in any beauty shop when you spot a tester or sealed product and want to try it on skin. This is 존댓말 and fits all staff interactions. With a friend in 반말: 발라봐도 돼?. Do NOT use 반말 with store staff.

테스터 있어요? asks 'is there a tester?' (existence question), while 발라봐도 돼요? asks permission to apply (action question). 이거 써봐도 돼요? ('can I try using this?') is vaguer — 쓰다 can mean use in any sense; 발라보다 is precise for skin application.

Add a body part: 손등에 발라봐도 돼요? (hand back), 팔에 발라봐도 돼요? (arm). To explain why: 색 보려고요, 발라봐도 돼요? ('I want to check the color'). Stronger: 잠깐 발라봐도 될까요? ('may I just apply it briefly?') — -ㄹ까요? is slightly more tentative than -도 돼요?.

The error is using 이거 해 봐도 돼요? — 해 보다 ('try doing') is too vague for putting product on skin. The precise verb is 발라보다. Also watch the particle for the body part: apply TO a surface uses 에 (손등에 발라요), not 을/를 — 손등을 발라봐도 돼요? makes it sound like you're applying the hand itself.

expressions.shortExplanation: 샘플 좀 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could I get some samples?".
expressions.explanation: 샘플 좀 주세요 (saempeul jom juseyo) = "Could I get some samples?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 샘플 좀 주세요 ("Could I get some samples?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday ask at any beauty counter

usagePhrases.en: Could I get a few more samples?
usagePhrases.note: Add 더 ('more') when they give you one or two

usagePhrases.en: Could you throw in some samples?
usagePhrases.note: 챙기다 ('to gather/pack for someone') sounds natural and warm
Slightly more tentative; asks if it's possible at all

examples.ko: 이거 살게요. 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: igeo salgeyo. saempeul jom chaenggyeo juseyo.
examples.en: I'll take this — could you throw in some samples?
examples.note: Buying then asking is the natural order; 챙겨 주세요 sounds warmly personal

examples.ko: A: 샘플 좀 주세요. / B: 네, 어떤 제품 써 보고 싶으세요?
examples.romanization: A: saempeul jom juseyo. / B: ne, eotteon jepum sseo bogo sipeuseyo?
examples.en: A: Could I get some samples? / B: Sure, which products would you like to try?
examples.note: Staff often ask which type you'd like — be ready to name them

examples.ko: 혹시 이 크림 샘플 있으면 좀 주세요. 먼저 써보고 싶어서요.
examples.romanization: hoksi i keurim saempeul isseumyeon jom juseyo. meonjeo sseobogo sipeoseoyo.
examples.en: If you have a sample of this cream, could I get one? I want to try it first.
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') + a polite reason makes the ask feel natural

expressions.nuance: 샘플 좀 주세요 is 샘플 (loanword 'sample') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). Sample culture in Korea is enormous — beauty staff routinely tuck free sachets into your bag especially after a purchase, so this is a routine, expected request. The warmest-sounding version uses 챙기다 ('to thoughtfully gather and pack for someone'): 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요 feels more personal and less transactional than plain 주세요. You must know the three related words: 샘플 (free take-home sachet), 테스터 (open in-store display you swatch but don't take), and 증정품/사은품 (gift-with-purchase freebie, often full-size). Asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong answer. Variants: 더 주세요 adds 'more'; 받을 수 있어요? is slightly more tentative. The English-speaker error is adding 무료 as in 무료 샘플 주세요 — 샘플 already implies free, and adding 무료 can sound slightly grabby. Another pitfall: don't ask before buying as if entitled — Koreans usually buy first, then ask, and 좀 keeps the tone gracious.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 샘플 with 테스터.
샘플 is the free take-home sachet; 테스터 is the open in-store display you swatch but can't take. To take some home, ask for 샘플, not 테스터.
Adding 무료 as in 무료 샘플 주세요.
샘플 already implies it's free; tacking on 무료 ('free') sounds a bit grabby. Just say 샘플 좀 주세요.
Saying 샘플 줘 to staff.
줘 is 반말 and too casual for a clerk. Use 주세요 (or warmer 챙겨 주세요): 샘플 좀 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 'Please give me some samples.' The 좀 is crucial — it softens from a demand to a gentle request. The real social meaning is a collaborative, warm ask that fits Korean beauty culture where sampling is expected and welcomed.

Typically said at checkout after buying something — that's the cultural norm. You CAN ask before buying but add 먼저 써보고 싶어서요 ('I want to try it first') to explain. 존댓말 always with staff. With a close friend browsing together: 샘플 좀 달라고 해봐 ('ask them for samples').

샘플 (free sachet to take home) vs. 테스터 (open display to swatch in-store, cannot take) vs. 증정품/사은품 (gift-with-purchase, often full-size). Asking for a 테스터 when you want samples to take home, or vice versa, will confuse staff.
Basic: 샘플 좀 주세요. Warmer: 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요. Tentative: 샘플 받을 수 있어요? Add 'more': 샘플 좀 더 주세요. Specific product: 이 크림 샘플 좀 주세요.
Adding 무료 ('free') sounds redundant and slightly pushy since 샘플 already implies free. Just say 샘플 좀 주세요. Also don't say 샘플 줘 to staff — 줘 is 반말 and abrupt; use 주세요 or the warmer 챙겨 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 저 피부가 건성이에요 is a practical expression meaning "My skin is dry".
expressions.explanation: 저 피부가 건성이에요 (jeo pibuga geonseongieyo) means "My skin is dry". Say it as one set phrase — for example 저 피부가 건성이에요 ("My skin is dry"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; telling staff your skin type
지성 = oily; swap in for your type
복합성 = combination (oily T-zone, dry cheeks)
민감성 ('sensitive') + 라서요 to explain a need

examples.ko: A: 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요? / B: 저 건성이에요. 보습 잘 되는 거 찾아요.
examples.romanization: A: pibu taibi eotteoke doeseyo? / B: jeo geonseongieyo. boseup jal doeneun geo chajayo.
examples.en: A: What's your skin type? / B: Dry. I'm looking for something moisturizing.
examples.note: The exact clerk question and ideal answer in two lines

examples.en: I have dry skin, so I'm looking for something moisturizing.
examples.note: 건성이라 ('since I'm dry') + the product need in one natural sentence

examples.ko: 여름엔 지성인데 겨울엔 건성이에요. 복합성인가 봐요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen jiseonginde gyeouren geonseongieyo. bokapseonginga bwayo.
examples.en: I'm oily in summer but dry in winter — I guess I'm combination.
examples.note: Describing how your skin shifts by season; an extremely common Korean experience

expressions.nuance: 저 피부가 건성이에요 is 저 ('I', humble) + 피부 ('skin') + 가 (subject particle) + 건성 ('dry-type', Sino-Korean 乾性) + 이에요 (polite copula). Korean names skin types with the -성 ('-type/-natured') suffix: 건성 (dry), 지성 (oily), 복합성 (combination), 민감성 (sensitive), 중성 (normal). These are the exact labels beauty staff use when they ask 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요?. A critical distinction: 건성 is the skin-type NOUN ('dry-type'), while 건조하다 is the ADJECTIVE 'to feel dry right now' — so your constitutional type is 건성이에요, but if your skin feels parched today you'd say 피부가 건조해요. Saying 저 건조성이에요 is wrong; the type word is 건성. The most natural shortcut in-shop is 저 건성이에요 (dropping 피부가), which sounds natural and brisk. The English-speaker error is translating 'dry skin' literally as 마른 피부 — 마르다 means 'thin/skinny (body)' or 'dried out (laundry)', never a skin type. Always keep 피부가 with the subject particle 가.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 마른 피부 for 'dry skin'.
마르다 means 'thin (body)' or 'dried (laundry)'. The skin-type word is 건성. Say 저 건성이에요 or 피부가 건성이에요, never 마른 피부.
Confusing the type noun 건성 with the adjective 건조하다.
건성 = your skin TYPE ('dry-type'); 건조하다 = a condition ('feels dry now'). Type: 건성이에요. Condition: 피부가 건조해요. Don't say 건조성.
Using 을/를 on 피부.
피부 is the subject here, so use 가: 피부가 건성이에요. 피부를 건성이에요 is ungrammatical.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'My skin is dry-type.' 건성 (乾性) is not an adjective but a noun — 'dry-nature/type'. You're classifying your skin into a Sino-Korean typology, not just describing a sensation. The real-world use is telling staff your type so they can filter recommendations.
Said whenever a clerk or dermatologist asks your skin type. The full form 저 피부가 건성이에요 is polite 존댓말. In quick shop conversation, 저 건성이에요 (dropping 피부가) is equally natural. Never use 반말 with staff.

건성이에요 (type noun, permanent classification) vs. 피부가 건조해요 (adjective, 'feels dry right now'). Don't say 건조성이에요 — that's a non-word mixing type suffix -성 onto the adjective stem 건조. The -성 type set is: 건성·지성·복합성·민감성·중성.
Shortened: 저 건성이에요. With reason: 저 건성이라 보습 제품 찾아요 ('because I'm dry, I'm looking for moisturizing products'). Conditional: 민감성이라서요 adds a reason why you need something gentle.

Translating 'dry skin' as 마른 피부 is the top error — 마르다 means 'thin/lean (body)' or 'dry (laundry)', never a skin-type. Also: using 을/를 on 피부 is ungrammatical here; it's the subject so it takes 가: 피부가 건성이에요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? is a practical expression meaning "What type/skin is this for?".
expressions.explanation: "What type/skin is this for?" — that is 이거 무슨 타입이에요? (igeo museun taibieyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 무슨 타입이에요? ("What skin type is this for?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: What skin type is this for?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking which skin a product suits
-용 ('for use by') checks a specific type fast
맞다 ('to fit/suit') asks about compatibility

usagePhrases.en: Can oily skin use this too?
usagePhrases.note: 도 ('also') asks if your type is included

examples.ko: A: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? / B: 건성·복합성 피부에 맞는 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo museun taibieyo? / B: geonseong·bokapseong pibue manneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: What skin type is this for? / B: It's for dry and combination skin.
examples.note: The open question and a typical staff answer

examples.en: I'm oily — is this for oily skin?
examples.note: State your type then check with -용 for a quick yes/no

examples.ko: 이 토너 민감성 피부에 써도 괜찮아요?
examples.romanization: i toneo mingamseong pibue sseodo gwaenchanayo?
examples.en: Is this toner okay for sensitive skin?
examples.note: 괜찮아요 ('is it okay') softens a safety-compatibility question

expressions.nuance: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? is 이거 ('this') + 무슨 ('what kind of') + 타입 (loanword 'type') + 이에요?, asking which skin type a product targets. In practice the most efficient real-shop phrasing uses the suffix -용 ('for the use of'): 건성용 ('for dry skin'), 지성용 ('for oily'), 민감성용 ('for sensitive') — so 이거 건성용이에요? gets a yes/no instantly. The dividing line: 무슨 타입이에요? is open-ended, while -용이에요? pins down your specific type. For the interrogative pair 무슨 vs. 어떤: 무슨 asks 'what category?' (identity), 어떤 asks 'what is it like?' (quality), and while both work here, 무슨 타입 is the fixed collocation. An even more contextual phrasing is 이거 어떤 피부에 맞아요? — 맞다 ('to fit/suit') frames it as compatibility. The English-speaker error is asking 이거 뭐에 써요? ('what do you use this for?'), which asks the product's purpose (face vs. body, morning vs. night), not skin type. To ask about skin type, say 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 이거 뭐에 써요? to mean 'what skin type'.
That asks the product's purpose (face? body?), not skin type. For skin type, ask 이거 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?
Saying 건성을 위한 거예요? instead of 건성용.
건성을 위한 거 is grammatical but clunky. Koreans use the compact suffix -용: 이거 건성용이에요?
Mixing 무슨 and 어떤 wrongly with 타입.
The fixed collocation is 무슨 타입. 어떤 타입 is understandable but less idiomatic for asking the category; default to 무슨 타입이에요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'This — what type is it?' The real meaning is 'which skin type does this product target?' 타입 here is specifically skin type from the standard 건성/지성/복합성/민감성/중성 set — not any general 'type.'

Said while holding a product at a beauty shelf or counter. 존댓말 with staff at all times. This phrasing is neutral and suits any formality level; with friends browsing together you could say 이거 무슨 타입이야? (반말).
무슨 타입이에요? is open-ended. -용이에요? (e.g., 건성용이에요?) is a closed yes/no. 어떤 피부에 맞아요? ('what skin does it suit?') focuses on compatibility. For speed, -용 wins; for open discovery, 무슨 타입이에요? is natural.
Shortened: 지성용이에요? Expanded: 모든 피부 타입에 써도 돼요? ('is it okay for all skin types?'). With context: 저 민감성인데 이거 써도 돼요? ('I'm sensitive — can I use this?')
이거 뭐에 써요? asks the product's PURPOSE ('what do you use it for?') — face? body? makeup removal? — not skin type. For skin type always say 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?.

expressions.english: Do you have something really moisturizing?
expressions.shortExplanation: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have something really moisturizing?".
expressions.explanation: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? (boseup jal doeneun geo isseoyo?) = "Do you have something really moisturizing?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? ("Do you have something moisturizing?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for a hydrating product
촉촉하다 ('moist, dewy') — the sensory feel you want
보습력 ('moisturizing power') + 추천
속건조 = 'inner dryness' under an oily surface

examples.ko: A: 어떤 거 찾으세요? / B: 겨울이라 너무 당겨요. 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: A: eotteon geo chajeuseyo? / B: gyeourira neomu danggyeoyo. boseup jal doeneun geo isseoyo?
examples.en: A: What are you looking for? / B: My skin feels so tight in winter — do you have something really moisturizing?
examples.note: 당기다 ('feel tight/taut') is the classic dry-skin complaint; this is the natural two-turn exchange

examples.ko: 저 지성인데 속건조가 심해요. 촉촉하면서 안 무거운 거 추천해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeo jiseonginde sokgeonjoga simhaeyo. chokchokamyeonseo an mugeoun geo chucheonhae juseyo.
examples.en: I'm oily but really dehydrated underneath — something hydrating but not heavy, please.
examples.note: The classic oily-but-dehydrated combination request

examples.ko: 보습력 좋은 거로 추천해 주세요. 크림 말고 세럼도 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: boseumnyeok joeun georo chucheonhae juseyo. keurim malgo sereomdo gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: Recommend something with good moisture retention — a serum is fine too, not just a cream.
examples.note: 보습력 + opening up the format shows you know skincare categories

expressions.nuance: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? is 보습 ('moisture retention', Sino-Korean 保濕) + 잘 되는 ('that works well at it') + 거 ('thing') + 있어요? ('do you have?'). 보습 is THE key beauty noun for hydration and moisturizing; the product quality is 보습력 ('moisturizing power'), and the sensory result is 촉촉하다 ('dewy, moist'). A critical real-life concept is 속건조 ('inner dryness') — skin that's oily on the surface but parched underneath, extremely common in Korea and something you can name to get precisely the right lightweight product. The dryness sensation is 당기다 ('to feel tight/taut'): 당겨요 = 'my skin feels taut.' The variant 촉촉한 거 있어요? focuses on the desired sensory outcome rather than the product function. The English-speaker trap is using 수분 and 보습 interchangeably: 수분 is 'water/moisture (the substance)', 보습 is 'retention of that moisture' — you can say 수분 크림 ('moisture cream') for a product name, but to ask generally for moisturizing, 보습 잘 되는 거 is the natural phrasing. Never use 젖은 거 ('wet/soggy thing') for 'moist/dewy' — that sounds unpleasant.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 젖은 거 for 'moist/dewy'.
젖다 means 'wet, soggy' (like wet hair). Dewy skin is 촉촉하다. Ask for 촉촉한 거, not 젖은 거.
Confusing the sensation 당기다 with 당기다 'to crave'.
피부가 당기다 = 'skin feels tight (dry)'; 입맛이 당기다 = 'to have an appetite'. For dry skin, 피부가 당겨요 means it feels taut — use it to describe dryness.
Asking 물 많은 거 있어요? for hydration.
물 많은 거 ('something with lots of water') sounds odd for skincare. Use 보습 잘 되는 거 or 수분 크림 / 촉촉한 거.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is there something that does moisture-retention well?' 보습 (保濕) = 'protect/retain moisture.' Real meaning: 'Do you have a strongly hydrating product?' The 잘 되는 frame ('works well at it') is a natural Korean way to ask for a product with a specific effective quality.

Said to a beauty shop clerk when your skin is dry, tight, or you're entering a dry season. 존댓말 for all staff. The whole …는 거 있어요? template ('do you have something that…?') is the all-purpose shop request frame and sounds natural at any counter.

보습 잘 되는 거 (function focus: 'retains moisture well') vs. 촉촉한 거 (sensory focus: 'feels dewy/moist'). You'd use 보습 when talking to a knowledgeable clerk; 촉촉하다 is more emotional and descriptive. 보습력 좋은 거로 추천해 주세요 asks for a specific recommendation.
보습 is Sino-Korean 保濕: 보 (保) = 'protect/keep', 습 (濕) = 'moisture/dampness'. 보습력 adds 력 (力) = 'power/strength', so 'moisturizing power.'

수분 ('water/moisture the substance') and 보습 ('retention of moisture') are different: 수분 크림 is a product category name, but asking generally for moisturizing uses 보습 잘 되는 거. Also: 젖은 거 ('wet/soggy thing') for 'moist skin feel' sounds unpleasant — the right word is 촉촉하다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 자외선 차단제 어디 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Where's the sunscreen?".
expressions.explanation: 자외선 차단제 어디 있어요? (jaoeseon chadanje eodi isseoyo?) means "Where's the sunscreen?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 자외선 차단제 어디 있어요? ("Where's the sunscreen?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite, full formal term for sunscreen
선크림 (loanword) is what people actually say day-to-day
선블록 = another casual loanword variant

usagePhrases.en: Not the cream — do you have a sun stick?
usagePhrases.note: 선스틱 ('sun stick') for the twist-up format

examples.ko: A: 어디 있어요? / B: 선크림이요? 저쪽 자외선 차단제 코너에 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: eodi isseoyo? / B: seonkeurimiyo? jeojjok jaoeseon chadanje koneoe isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Where is it? / B: Sunscreen? It's over at the UV-protection corner.
examples.note: Typical clerk redirect; note both 선크림 and 자외선 차단제 used in one exchange

examples.ko: 얼굴에 바르는 선크림 찾는데 어디 있어요?
examples.romanization: eolgure bareuneun seonkeurim channeunde eodi isseoyo?
examples.en: I'm looking for facial sunscreen — where is it?
examples.note: 얼굴에 바르는 ('the kind for the face') narrows the search away from body sunscreen

examples.ko: 에스피에프 높은 선크림 있어요? 바닷가 가서요.
examples.romanization: eseupiepeu nopeun seonkeurim isseoyo? badatga gaseoyo.
examples.en: Do you have high-SPF sunscreen? I'm going to the beach.
examples.note: SPF (에스피에프) + reason makes the request concrete and helps staff pick the right product

expressions.nuance: 자외선 차단제 어디 있어요? is 자외선 ('ultraviolet rays', Sino-Korean 紫外線) + 차단제 ('blocking agent': 차단 'block' + 제 'agent') + 어디 있어요? ('where is it?'). 자외선 차단제 is the full, formal, on-the-label term, but in daily speech everyone says 선크림 — staff understand either, and 선크림 sounds relaxed and natural. Formats have distinct names you need: 선크림 (cream), 선스틱 (twist-up stick), 선쿠션 (cushion-compact), 선스프레이 (spray). The distinction 자외선 차단 ('UV blocking' — the function) vs. 자외선 차단제 ('the product') matters: drop the 제 and you've named the feature, not the item — keep 차단제 or just say 선크림. Regarding SPF: Koreans read the abbreviation as 에스피에프 (Korean letter-names) plus the Sino-Korean number: SPF 50 = 에스피에프 오십. Saying the English 'es-pee-ef fifty' may not be understood. Default 존댓말; 어디 있어요? is the polite location question.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 햇빛 크림 ('sunlight cream') for sunscreen.
There's no such word. It's 선크림 or formally 자외선 차단제. 햇빛 크림 won't be understood as a product.
Dropping 제 and saying 자외선 차단 있어요?
자외선 차단 names the function ('UV blocking'), not the product. To buy the item, say 자외선 차단제 or, more naturally, 선크림 있어요?
Pronouncing SPF as English letters.
Koreans read it 에스피에프 plus the Sino number: SPF 50 = 에스피에프 오십. Saying 'es-pee-eff fifty' in English may not land; use 에스피에프 오십.

structuredNuance.t: 자외선 차단제 = 'ultraviolet-ray blocking agent' (literal). Real meaning and daily use: 선크림. Staff expect either, but 선크림 is what virtually everyone actually says when shopping.
Said in any cosmetics shop, pharmacy (약국), or convenience store sunscreen section. 존댓말 with staff. With friends: 선크림 어딨어? (반말). The formal 자외선 차단제 is more for labels, packaging, or formal writing.
자외선 차단제 (formal, on-label) = 선크림 (daily loanword, most common) = 선블록 (less common loanword variant). 차단제 (the product) vs. 차단 (the function/feature) — keep the 제 when asking for the product itself.
자외선 is Sino-Korean 紫外線 ('purple-outside rays' = ultraviolet); 차단 (遮斷) = 'to block/cut off'; 제 (劑) = 'agent/preparation'. Together: 'UV-ray-blocking agent.'
SPF is read as 에스피에프 not English initials — saying 'es-pee-ef' may not land. SPF 50 = 에스피에프 오십. Also: 햇빛 크림 ('sunlight cream') is not a word in Korean skincare — always say 선크림 or 자외선 차단제.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 안 무거워요? is a practical expression meaning "Isn't this heavy/greasy (on the skin)?".
expressions.explanation: "Isn't this heavy/greasy (on the skin)?" — that is 이거 안 무거워요? (igeo an mugeowoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 안 무거워요? ("Isn't this heavy on the skin?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Isn't this heavy on the skin?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; checking if a cream feels heavy
끈적이다 ('to be tacky/sticky') — a key texture worry

usagePhrases.en: How does it feel going on?
usagePhrases.note: 발리다 (passive of 바르다) asks about the application texture

usagePhrases.en: Is it on the lighter/fresher side?
usagePhrases.note: 산뜻하다 ('fresh, light') = the opposite of heavy

examples.ko: A: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? / B: 네. 이거 안 무거워요? / A: 생각보다 산뜻해요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo ballabwado dwaeyo? / B: ne. igeo an mugeowoyo? / A: saenggakboda santteutaeyo.
examples.en: A: Can I try this? / B: Sure. Isn't it heavy? / A: It's lighter than I expected.
examples.note: A real three-turn testing conversation around texture

examples.ko: 여름엔 무거운 게 싫어요. 이거 안 끈적여요?
examples.romanization: yeoreumen mugeoun ge sireoyo. igeo an kkeunjeogyeoyo?
examples.en: I don't like heavy stuff in summer — isn't this sticky?
examples.note: 끈적이다 is the top summer texture complaint for sunscreen and cream

examples.ko: 촉촉한데 산뜻하면 좋겠어요. 이거 발리는 느낌 어때요?
examples.romanization: chokchokande santteutamyeon jokesseoyo. igeo ballineun neukkim eottaeyo?
examples.en: I want hydrating but light — how does this feel going on?
examples.note: 발림성 ('application feel') is what you're really asking about here

expressions.nuance: 이거 안 무거워요? is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 무겁다 ('to be heavy') in polite question form — the 안 …요? structure voices a worry and invites reassurance. In skincare 무겁다 is a texture adjective meaning thick and occlusive, sitting heavily on the skin — not physical weight. Its opposites are 가볍다 ('light') and 산뜻하다 ('fresh, light, airy'). The other key texture worry is 끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky'), especially for sunscreen and summer products. Koreans also discuss 발림성 ('spreadability / how a product applies', from the passive 발리다 of 바르다) and 흡수 ('absorption': 잘 흡수돼요 = 'absorbs well'). The variant 산뜻한 편이에요? ('is it on the light/fresh side?') inverts the worry into a positive ask — useful for getting an encouraging answer. The English-speaker errors: (1) translating 'heavy' as 무게 있어요? — that asks about physical weight, not texture; (2) conflating 무겁다 (texture) with 기름지다/번들거리다 ('greasy/shiny' — an oily look), which is a different complaint. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 무게 있어요? for a 'heavy' feel.
무게 means physical weight. The skincare feel is the adjective 무겁다: 이거 안 무거워요? (Does it feel heavy/thick on the skin?)
Using 무겁다 to mean 'greasy'.
무겁다 is a thick, dense feel; greasy shine is 번들거리다 or 기름지다. If you mean shiny/oily, ask 번들거리지 않아요?
Saying 끈적해요 instead of 끈적여요/끈적거려요.
The natural verb forms are 끈적이다 → 끈적여요 or 끈적거리다 → 끈적거려요. 끈적해요 is non-standard; say 안 끈적여요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Isn't this heavy?' In skincare context 무겁다 has nothing to do with physical weight — it describes a thick, occlusive texture that sits densely on the skin. The real question is: 'Is this product too dense or clingy for everyday use?'

Said while testing or inspecting a cream, lotion, or sunscreen — especially richer formulas or winter products. The 안 …요? frame is a natural polite way to voice worry and prompt reassurance. 존댓말 with staff; 안 무거워? in 반말 with a friend.
안 무거워요? (texture is heavy/dense) vs. 안 끈적여요? (texture is sticky/tacky) vs. 번들거리지 않아요? (finish is shiny/greasy). These are three different texture concerns; be precise about which one you mean.
Inverted positive: 산뜻한 편이에요? ('is it on the lighter side?'). More explicit: 바르고 나서 답답한 느낌 없어요? ('no stuffy/suffocating feel after applying?'). Absorption ask: 잘 흡수돼요? ('does it absorb well?').

무게 있어요? asks about literal physical weight — wrong for texture. Use the adjective 무겁다 in question form: 안 무거워요?. Also don't use 무겁다 to mean 'greasy' (oily shine) — that's 번들거리다 / 기름지다; 무겁다 is about density and coverage, not shine.

expressions.shortExplanation: 테스터 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there a tester?".
expressions.explanation: 테스터 있어요? (teseuteo isseoyo?) = "Is there a tester?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 테스터 있어요? ("Is there a tester?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for an in-store display tester

usagePhrases.en: Is there one I can try on?
usagePhrases.note: Descriptive fallback if 테스터 isn't understood
When you can't find the open display
For makeup; asks to view/swatch the shade

examples.ko: A: 테스터 있어요? / B: 네, 여기 있어요. 손등에 발라보세요.
examples.romanization: A: teseuteo isseoyo? / B: ne, yeogi isseoyo. sondeunge ballaboseyo.
examples.en: A: Is there a tester? / B: Yes, here it is — try it on the back of your hand.
examples.note: The most natural two-turn tester exchange at any counter

examples.ko: 이 쿠션 테스터 있어요? 색 좀 보고 싶어서요.
examples.romanization: i kusyeon teseuteo isseoyo? saek jom bogo sipeoseoyo.
examples.en: Is there a tester for this cushion? I want to check the shade.
examples.note: 색 보다 ('check the color') is the specific makeup reason

examples.ko: 테스터 없으면 손등에라도 발라볼 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: teseuteo eopseumyeon sondeungerado ballabol su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: If there's no tester, could I at least try it on my hand?
examples.note: 에라도 ('even just on…') is a polite fallback when there's no display

expressions.nuance: 테스터 있어요? is the loanword 테스터 ('tester') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking for the open in-store display unit you can swatch without buying. This sits in a three-way vocabulary set every beauty shopper must know: 테스터 (in-store try unit, cannot take home), 샘플 (free take-home sachet), and 증정품/사은품 (gift-with-purchase freebie). Confusing these leads to misunderstandings — asking 샘플 있어요? at a lipstick display may get you a sachet to take home, not permission to swatch the shade. Korean beauty stores, especially Olive Young and brand counters, routinely have testers out, making this a routine ask. If the word 테스터 draws a blank, the descriptive fallback 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요? ('is there something I can try on?') always works. For makeup color specifically, 색 좀 볼 수 있을까요? ('could I check the color?') is natural. The over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까? sounds stiff and bookish — stick to 테스터 있어요?. Default 존댓말.
