commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 샘플 있어요? when you want to swatch in-store.
샘플 is the take-home freebie. The in-store try unit is 테스터. To test a shade now, ask 테스터 있어요? or 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요?
Confusing 테스터 with 증정품/사은품.
테스터 = in-store try unit; 증정품/사은품 = a gift with purchase. They're different things; ask for 테스터 to test, not 증정품.
Over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까?
That's stiff and bookish. The everyday word is the loanword 테스터: 테스터 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is there a tester?' The loanword 테스터 (English 'tester') is used directly. Real meaning: 'Is there an open display unit I can swatch/try on my skin right now, without buying?'

Said at any beauty counter when you want to try a product before buying — most commonly for lipstick, foundation, or skincare texture. 존댓말 with staff always. The simple 있어요? question is perfectly polite; you don't need a more complex framing.

테스터 (try in-store, cannot take) ≠ 샘플 (take-home free sachet) ≠ 증정품/사은품 (gift with purchase). These are three distinct things. Confuse 테스터 with 샘플 and you'll either get the wrong answer or leave empty-handed.
Fallback description: 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요? Location: 테스터 어디 있어요? Color check: 색 좀 볼 수 있을까요? Polite fallback when no tester: 손등에라도 발라봐도 돼요?

Saying 샘플 있어요? when you want to swatch in-store will get you the take-home freebie, not a tester to try now. Also avoid the over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까? — it sounds like a written form, not a shop interaction.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 트러블 안 나요? is a practical expression meaning "Won't this break me out?".
expressions.explanation: 이거 트러블 안 나요? (igeo teureobeul an nayo?) means "Won't this break me out?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 트러블 안 나요? ("Won't this break me out?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking if a product causes breakouts

usagePhrases.en: I break out easily — is this okay?
usagePhrases.note: 여드름 ('acne/pimples') for actual acne
자극 ('irritation') is the key worry for reactive skin
뒤집어지다 (vivid slang) = skin reacting badly

examples.ko: A: 이거 트러블 안 나요? / B: 네, 저자극 성분이라 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo teureobeul an nayo? / B: ne, jeojageuk seongbunira gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: A: Won't this break me out? / B: It's low-irritant ingredients, so you should be fine.
examples.note: The worry-and-reassurance exchange you'll often get at a counter

examples.ko: 저 피부 예민한데 이거 트러블 안 나요?
examples.romanization: jeo pibu yeminhande igeo teureobeul an nayo?
examples.en: My skin's sensitive — won't this break me out?
examples.note: 예민하다 ('sensitive/touchy') describes reactive skin that flares easily

examples.ko: 새 제품 쓰면 잘 뒤집어져서요. 자극 없는 거 맞아요?
examples.romanization: sae jepum sseumyeon jal dwijibeojyeoseoyo. jageuk eopsneun geo majayo?
examples.en: New products often make me break out — this is non-irritating, right?
examples.note: 뒤집어지다 as context, then confirming 자극 없는 거 맞아요?

expressions.nuance: 이거 트러블 안 나요? is 이거 ('this') + 트러블 (Konglish 'trouble' = a skin breakout or flare-up) + 안 나요? ('doesn't it come out/appear?'). The verb 나다 ('to come out/appear') is the correct partner for both 트러블 and 여드름: 트러블이 나다 ('to have a breakout'), 여드름이 나다 ('to get a pimple'). 트러블 in beauty context strictly means a skin flare or breakout — it has nothing to do with 'trouble' in general; for a general problem use 문제. It is broader than 여드름 (specifically acne/pimples): 트러블 covers redness, small bumps, any flare. The other key worry word is 자극 ('irritation/stimulation'): 자극 없어요? = 'is it non-irritating?', 자극적이에요? = 'is it harsh?' Also vivid: 뒤집어지다 ('to flip over') is slang for skin going haywire, fine for a beauty shop but soften to 트러블이 났어요 at a clinic. The English-speaker error is translating 'break out' as 부서지다 or 깨지다 ('to shatter/break apart') — wrong verb; use 나다 with 트러블/여드름. Another trap: 자극하다 ('to stimulate/provoke someone') is wrong for 'irritating product'; say 자극적이에요? or 자극 있어요?. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'break out' as 부서지다 or 깨지다.
Those mean 'shatter/break apart' for objects. Skin breaks out with 나다: 트러블이 나다 / 여드름이 나다. Ask 이거 트러블 안 나요?
Using 트러블 for general 'trouble/problem'.
In skincare 트러블 specifically means a skin breakout/flare. For a general problem use 문제. Here 트러블 = breakout only.
Saying 자극해요? to ask if it's irritating.
자극하다 means 'to stimulate/provoke (someone)'. For a harsh product ask 자극 있어요? / 자극적이에요?, or 자극 없어요? for non-irritating.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Doesn't trouble come out with this?' 트러블 is Konglish repurposed: in English 'trouble' is abstract; in Korean beauty 트러블 strictly = a skin breakout, bump, or flare. Real meaning: 'Will this product make my skin break out?'

Said before buying any new product, especially cream, foundation, or sunscreen when you have reactive skin. 존댓말 with staff. In 반말 with a friend: 이거 트러블 안 나? At a dermatology clinic, use 트러블이 났어요 or describe symptoms clinically (붉어지고 가려워요) rather than slang.

트러블 나다 (any breakout/flare, broad) vs. 여드름 나다 (acne/pimple specifically). 자극 없어요? checks irritation before use; 트러블 안 나요? checks breakout outcome. Use 자극 for ingredients, 트러블 for the resulting skin reaction.
More casual: 뒤집어지지 않을까요? With reason: 저 예민한 편이라 트러블 자주 나서요 ('I'm a bit sensitive and break out often'). Specific: 이 성분들 자극 없어요? ('are these ingredients non-irritating?')

'Break out' translates to 나다 with the skin word — 트러블이 나다, 여드름이 나다. Never use 부서지다 or 깨지다 ('shatter/break apart') — those are for objects. Also 자극하다 means 'to stimulate/provoke a person,' not 'to irritate skin'; use 자극적이에요? or 자극 없어요? for products.

expressions.english: My makeup doesn't come off well
expressions.shortExplanation: 화장 잘 안 지워져요 is a practical expression meaning "My makeup doesn't come off well".
expressions.explanation: "My makeup doesn't come off well" — that is 화장 잘 안 지워져요 (hwajang jal an jiwojyeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 화장 잘 안 지워져요 ("My makeup doesn't come off well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: My makeup doesn't come off well
usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing a removal problem
클렌징 ('cleansing/cleanser') for makeup removal

usagePhrases.en: Do I need to remove this with cleansing oil?
usagePhrases.note: 클렌징오일 for heavy or waterproof makeup
화장 지우는 거 = 'the makeup-removing thing'

examples.ko: A: 화장이 잘 안 지워지는데 어떻게 해야 해요? / B: 클렌징오일 먼저 쓰고 폼으로 이중 세안하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: hwajangi jal an jiwojineunde eotteoke haeya haeyo? / B: keullenjingoil meonjeo sseugo pomeuro ijung seanhamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: My makeup won't come off properly — what should I do? / B: Use cleansing oil first, then do double-cleansing with foam.
examples.note: The key advice exchange; introduces 이중 세안 (double cleansing)

examples.ko: 눈 화장이 잘 안 지워져요. 립앤아이 리무버 있어요?
examples.romanization: nun hwajangi jal an jiwojyeoyo. ribaenai rimubeo isseoyo?
examples.en: Eye makeup won't come off — do you have a lip & eye remover?
examples.note: 립앤아이 리무버 is the specific product for stubborn eye and lip makeup

examples.ko: 선크림이 안 지워지는 느낌이라 클렌징오일 쓰려고요.
examples.romanization: seonkeurimi an jiwojineun neukkimira keullenjingoil sseuryeogoyo.
examples.en: My sunscreen feels like it won't wash off, so I'll use cleansing oil.
examples.note: 안 지워지는 느낌 ('the feeling it won't come off') is a natural compound expression

expressions.nuance: 화장 잘 안 지워져요 is 화장 ('makeup') + 잘 ('well') + 안 ('not') + 지워져요 (passive of 지우다, 'to erase/remove'). The voice distinction is crucial: 지우다 is active ('I remove makeup', 화장을 지우다), while 지워지다 is passive ('makeup comes off', 화장이 지워지다). To say it doesn't come off, you use the passive 안 지워져요; mixing voices — 화장이 안 지워요 (active verb with subject marker) — is a grammar error. The whole area of makeup removal is called 클렌징, and products divide into 클렌징오일 (oil, best for waterproof/heavy makeup), 클렌징워터 (micellar water), 클렌징폼 (foam, for general face wash), and 리무버 (point remover, especially 립앤아이 리무버). The standard Korean skincare method is 이중 세안 ('double cleansing') — oil first to dissolve makeup, then foam to cleanse the skin. The English-speaker errors: (1) 화장을 벗다 ('take off', like clothes) — 벗다 is for clothes/shoes only, never makeup; use 지우다; (2) calling everything 비누 ('soap') — makeup removal uses 클렌징 products, not 비누. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 화장을 벗다 for removing makeup.
벗다 ('take off') is for clothes/shoes. Makeup is removed with 지우다: 화장을 지우다. Never 화장을 벗다.
Mixing active/passive: 화장이 안 지워요.
With the subject 화장이, you need the passive: 화장이 안 지워져요 ('it doesn't come off'). Active would be 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove it').
Calling all cleansers 비누 (soap).
Makeup removers are 클렌징 products (클렌징오일/워터/폼) or 리무버, not 비누. For removal, ask about 클렌징 or 리무버, not 비누.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Makeup well-not-comes-off.' The passive form 지워지다 (not the active 지우다) is key — you're saying the makeup fails to come off by itself/with effort, not that you can't actively remove it. Real meaning: 'No matter what I do, my makeup won't wash off properly.'

Said to a beauty staff member when asking for a makeup remover recommendation, or to a friend describing your skincare woes. 존댓말 with staff. The active alternative 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove my makeup') puts the fault on yourself, whereas the passive 안 지워져요 puts it on the product — both are natural, but the passive is more common.
화장 잘 안 지워져요 (passive, makeup won't come off) vs. 화장을 못 지워요 (active, I can't remove it). Both are natural. 클렌징이 안 돼요 ('cleansing isn't working') is a broader form covering skin not feeling clean too.

Active: 화장을 지우다 ('to remove makeup'). Passive: 화장이 지워지다 ('makeup comes off'). Negative passive: 화장이 안 지워져요 ('makeup won't come off'). Active negative: 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove the makeup'). Never mix: 화장이 안 지워요 is wrong.

'Take off makeup' as 화장을 벗다 is a direct-translation error — 벗다 is only for clothing and shoes. Makeup is always removed with 지우다. Also: calling all cleansing products 비누 ('soap') is odd; the category is 클렌징 (클렌징오일/폼/워터/리무버).

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 향 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Does this have a fragrance?".
expressions.explanation: 이거 향 있어요? (igeo hyang isseoyo?) = "Does this have a fragrance?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 향 있어요? ("Does this have a scent?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; checking if a product is scented
무향 ('no scent') for a quick yes/no
강하다 ('strong') to gauge scent intensity

usagePhrases.en: Do you have an unscented one?
usagePhrases.note: 향 안 나는 거 = 'the kind with no smell'

examples.ko: A: 이거 향 있어요? / B: 은은하게 나는 편이에요. 강하지 않아요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo hyang isseoyo? / B: euneunhage naneun pyeonieyo. ganghaji anayo.
examples.en: A: Does this have a fragrance? / B: It's lightly scented — not strong.
examples.note: The natural check-and-reassurance exchange about scent intensity

examples.ko: 향에 좀 민감해서요. 무향인 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: hyange jom mingamhaeseoyo. muhyangin geo isseoyo?
examples.en: I'm a bit sensitive to fragrance — do you have a fragrance-free one?
examples.note: 향에 민감하다 + 무향인 거 is the most natural way to ask for scent-free skincare

examples.ko: 향 너무 강한 건 부담스러워요. 은은한 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: hyang neomu ganghan geon budamseureowoyo. euneunhan geo isseoyo?
examples.en: Strong scents are a bit much for me — anything subtle?
examples.note: 은은하다 ('faint, subtle, delicate') is exactly the scent quality you want to name

expressions.nuance: 이거 향 있어요? is 이거 ('this') + 향 ('scent/fragrance', Sino-Korean 香) + 있어요? ('is there?'). 향 is the everyday neutral word for a product's smell; the verb 'to give off a scent' is 향이 나다 (향 나요 = 'it's scented', 향 안 나요 = 'no scent'). To ask about fragrance-free products: 무향 (無香 'no scent') is the label and the word to use. Useful scent descriptors: 은은하다 ('faint, subtle'), 강하다 ('strong'), 인공적이다 ('artificial'), 자연스럽다 ('natural'). For those with sensitive skin, 향에 민감하다 ('sensitive to fragrance') gives context. Two label terms: 무향 ('no scent added') vs. 무향료 ('no fragrance ingredient'); in conversation 무향 covers both. The English-speaker error is using 냄새 — a neutral-to-negative word meaning 'odor' — for a product's fragrance: 이거 냄새 나요? sounds like 'does this stink?', mildly insulting the product. Always use 향 for pleasant or neutral product scent, and reserve 냄새 for unpleasant odors. Particle note: 향이 있어요 / 향 있어요 (both natural), never 향을 있어요. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 이거 냄새 나요? to mean 'is it scented?'.
냄새 leans negative ('odor/stink'). For a product's fragrance use 향: 이거 향 있어요? / 향 나요? 냄새 나요? implies it smells bad.
Saying 향 없어 instead of 무향.
To ask for a fragrance-free product, the clean term is 무향: 무향인 거 있어요? 향 없어 (반말) is also too casual for staff.
Using 향기 vs 향 wrongly in a question.
향기 ('a (nice) fragrance/aroma') is more poetic. For the plain functional question, 향 is standard: 향 있어요?, 향 강해요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is there a scent in this?' 향 (香) is a neutral-to-pleasant fragrance word. Real meaning: 'Does this product contain/give off a scent?' — often asked by people with fragrance sensitivity or those buying for sensitive skin.

Said while picking up a product at a beauty counter, pharmacy, or online consultation when you can't smell it. 존댓말 with staff. 향 있어? in 반말 with a friend is natural. Those with sensitive skin or allergies often frame the context: 향에 민감해서요 ('because I'm sensitive to fragrance').

향 (neutral/pleasant product scent) vs. 냄새 (neutral-to-negative 'odor', often unpleasant). 향기 is more poetic/literary ('a lovely fragrance'). For functional skincare questions, 향 is standard. 무향 ('fragrance-free') vs. 무향료 ('no fragrance ingredient added') are label distinctions; in conversation 무향 covers both.
향 is Sino-Korean 香 ('scent/fragrance'). 무향 is 無香 ('no scent'). 향기 (香氣) adds 기 (氣) = 'air/spirit/energy', giving a more elevated, pleasantly-airy sense.

냄새 leans negative ('odor/stink'). 이거 냄새 나요? sounds like 'does this smell bad?' Use 향 for product fragrance: 이거 향 있어요? / 향 나요?. Also don't say 향 없어 as a polite request to staff — 없어 is 반말; say 무향인 거 있어요?.

expressions.english: What's the expiry date on this?
expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the expiry date on this?".
expressions.explanation: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? (igeo yutonggihan eonjekkajiyeyo?) means "What's the expiry date on this?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? ("What's the expiry date on this?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: What's the expiry date on this?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking how long it's good for

usagePhrases.en: How long does it last once opened?
usagePhrases.note: 개봉 후 ('after opening') = the PAO period
Gently checking it's not near expiry

usagePhrases.en: It's not past its use-by, right?
usagePhrases.note: 사용기한 ('use-by date') for the firmer term

examples.ko: A: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? / B: 내년 3월까지예요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo yutonggihan eonjekkajiyeyo? / B: naenyeon 3wolkkajiyeyo.
examples.en: A: What's the expiry date on this? / B: It's good until next March.
examples.note: The natural question-and-answer format for an expiry inquiry

examples.en: Do I need to use it within 6 months of opening?
examples.note: Asking about the post-opening period (PAO) — essential for serums and vitamin C products

examples.ko: 할인하는 거 보니까 혹시 유통기한 임박이에요?
examples.romanization: harinhaneun geo bonikka hoksi yutonggihan imbagieyo?
examples.en: Since it's on sale — is it maybe close to expiring?
examples.note: 임박 ('imminent/approaching') is the exact word for near-expiry discounted stock

expressions.nuance: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? is 이거 ('this') + 유통기한 ('sell-by/distribution period', Sino-Korean 流通期限) + 언제까지 ('until when') + 예요?. Korean cosmetics carry two key date labels: 유통기한 (the sell-by or best-before date, what you ask about before buying) and 사용기한 ('use-by date', how long once opened — also expressed as 개봉 후 사용기간 or the PAO mark, e.g. '12M'). The word for near-expiry stock is 임박 ('imminent'), commonly seen as 유통기한 임박 상품 ('near-expiry product') on discounted items. If a product is already expired, you say 유통기한이 지났어요 ('the expiry date has passed'), using 지나다 ('to pass'). The English-speaker trap is using 만료되다 for cosmetic expiry — that's for contracts and memberships, not physical products; use 지나다. Another error: the correct temporal frame for a deadline is 언제까지예요? ('until when?'), not 언제예요? ('when is it?'), which sounds like asking a single moment in time. Keep 예요 fused: 언제까지예요, not 언제까지 예요. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 만료되다 for product expiry.
만료되다 is for contracts/memberships expiring. For cosmetics/food say 유통기한 / 사용기한, and 지나다 for 'expired': 유통기한 지났어요?
Asking 유통기한 언제예요? instead of 언제까지예요?
A deadline takes 까지 ('until'): 언제까지예요? 언제예요? asks for a single moment and sounds off for a 'good-until' date.
Confusing 유통기한 with 개봉 후 사용기간.
유통기한 = sell-by (unopened); 개봉 후 사용기간 (PAO, e.g. 12M) = how long after opening. For 'how long once I open it', ask 개봉 후에 얼마나 써요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'This — the distribution time-limit — until when is it?' 유통기한 (流通期限) = the sell-by/best-before date on an unopened product. Real meaning: 'How long is this product fresh/safe to use before I even open it?'

Said at checkout or while examining a product, especially discounted items or older stock. This is 존댓말 and completely normal — Korean staff expect this question. Particularly important for vitamin C serums and active products that degrade quickly.

유통기한 (sell-by, while sealed) vs. 사용기한/개봉 후 사용기간 (use-by after opening, the PAO period). These are different questions: 유통기한 언제까지예요? before you buy; 개봉 후에 얼마나 써요? once you have it. Also 유통기한이 지났어요 ('it's expired') vs. 유통기한이 임박했어요 ('it's near expiry').
유통기한 is Sino-Korean 流通期限: 유통 (流通) = 'distribution/circulation', 기한 (期限) = 'time limit/deadline'. Literally 'distribution-time limit.'

만료되다 is for contracts/memberships expiring — not cosmetics. For product expiry say 유통기한/사용기한 + 지나다 ('to pass'). Also 언제까지예요? (deadline frame: 'until when?') is correct, not 언제예요? which asks for a single point in time.

expressions.english: My skin really broke out / freaked out
expressions.shortExplanation: 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 is a practical expression meaning "My skin really broke out / freaked out".
expressions.explanation: "My skin really broke out / freaked out" — that is 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 (pibuga neomu dwijibeojyeosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 ("My skin really broke out"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing a bad flare-up (슬랭 뒤집어지다)
More neutral; 트러블이 나다 + 심하게
여드름 for actual acne; 잔뜩 ('a whole lot')
예민해지다 = 'became sensitive/touchy'

examples.ko: A: 피부 왜 이래? / B: 새 크림 썼더니 피부가 다 뒤집어졌어.
examples.romanization: A: pibu wae irae? / B: sae keurim sseotdeoni pibuga da dwijibeojyeosseo.
examples.en: A: What's going on with your skin? / B: I used a new cream and my skin just freaked out.
examples.note: A candid friend-to-friend exchange using 반말 — shows the colloquial register

examples.ko: 새 제품 썼더니 피부가 다 뒤집어졌어요. 진정되는 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: sae jepum sseotdeoni pibuga da dwijibeojyeosseoyo. jinjeongdoeneun geo isseoyo?
examples.en: I used a new product and my skin freaked out — anything calming?
examples.note: 진정 ('calming/soothing') is the natural follow-up ask after a flare

examples.ko: 환절기라 그런지 트러블이 심하게 나고 화끈거려요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgira geureonji teureobeuri simhage nago hwakkeungeoryeoyo.
examples.en: Maybe it's the changing season — I'm breaking out badly and it stings.
examples.note: 화끈거리다 ('to burn/sting') + 환절기 ('season change') is a classic Korean skin concern

expressions.nuance: 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 is 피부 ('skin') + 가 + 너무 ('so much/too') + 뒤집어졌어요 (past of 뒤집어지다, literally 'to be turned upside down') — vivid, widely used colloquial slang for skin reacting badly, breaking out, or going haywire after a product. It is more dramatic and emotional than the neutral 트러블이 났어요 ('I broke out') and much more vivid than the clinical 여드름이 났어요. When skin is in this state, you ask for 진정 ('calming/soothing') products — 진정되는 거 ('something that calms'), 진정 에센스, 진정 크림 — since 진정 is the beauty word for soothing irritated or inflamed skin. Sensation vocabulary: 화끈거리다 ('to burn/sting'), 가렵다 ('to itch'), 붉어지다/빨개지다 ('to redden'). A very common trigger Koreans cite is 환절기 ('change of seasons'). Register note: 뒤집어지다 is informal and expressive — fine in a shop or with friends in either 존댓말 or 반말, but at a dermatology clinic lean on the neutral 트러블이 났어요 or describe symptoms directly. Particle: 피부가, never 피부를. 너무 in colloquial speech means 'really/so' (not just 'excessively').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 뒤집어지다 literally as 'turn upside down'.
In skincare it's slang for skin reacting badly / breaking out. 피부가 뒤집어졌어요 = 'my skin freaked out', not anything physically flipping.
Asking for 진정시키는 거 wrongly as 진정 약.
For soothing skincare say 진정되는 거 / 진정 제품 ('calming product'). 진정 약 ('sedative') is medicine for nerves, not skin.
Using 너무 to mean simply 'very' in writing.
너무 means 'too/excessively' but colloquially also 'so'. It's fine in speech (너무 뒤집어졌어요); just know it carries an 'excessive' nuance, stronger than plain 아주.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'My skin was completely turned upside down.' 뒤집어지다 = 'to flip over/invert' — vivid physical imagery applied to skin going haywire. Real meaning: 'My skin broke out badly / reacted horribly to a product.'

Informal but widely used — fine in a beauty shop (존댓말), with friends (반말: 피부가 완전 뒤집어졌어), or online posts. At a dermatology clinic, soften to 트러블이 심하게 났어요 or describe symptoms: 붉어지고 가려워요. Do NOT say this in formal medical or professional writing.
뒤집어지다 (vivid slang, strong reaction, any cause) > 트러블이 나다 (neutral, broad breakout) > 여드름이 나다 (clinical, acne specifically). Choose by register: clinic → 여드름/트러블, shop/friend → 뒤집어지다.
Intensified: 피부가 완전 뒤집어졌어요 ('my skin completely broke out'). Causal: 새 제품 쓰고 나서 뒤집어졌어요. Follow-up ask: 진정되는 거 있어요? / 진정 크림 추천해 주세요.
Don't take 뒤집어지다 literally as 'turned upside down' — it's pure skin-break-out slang. And never translate 'broke out' as 부서지다/깨지다 ('shatter'). The natural options are 뒤집어지다 (slang), 트러블이 나다, 여드름이 나다.

expressions.english: Can I get a refund on this?
expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 환불돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refund on this?".
expressions.explanation: 이거 환불돼요? (igeo hwanbuldwaeyo?) means "Can I get a refund on this?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 환불돼요? ("Can I get a refund on this?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Can I get a refund on this?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking if a refund is possible
반말, to a friendly small-shop owner

usagePhrases.en: Is a refund possible for this?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, slightly more polite with -나요
가능하다 ('to be possible'), a common interchangeable form

examples.en: Can I get a refund on this?
examples.note: Your opening move — check feasibility before making any demand; holding the item as you ask.

examples.en: I have the receipt — can I get a refund on this?
examples.note: Lead with 영수증 있는데 to signal you're prepared; 있는데 sets up a contrast ('I have it, so…').

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 이거 한 번도 안 썼는데 환불돼요?
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: igeo han beondo an sseonneunde hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: A: How can I help you? / B: I never used this — can I get a refund?
examples.note: A is the typical staff opener; B answers with the reason + question, the natural real-world two-turn sequence.

expressions.nuance: 이거 환불돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불 ('refund', Sino-Korean 還拂) + 되다 ('to be done/possible') in polite question form — 'is a refund possible for this?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility, which is exactly right as your opening move: you ask IF a refund is possible before you ask them to actually carry it out. Once they confirm it can be done, you follow with the request 환불해 주세요. Distinguish three near-synonyms by scope: 이거 환불돼요? is about one item right now; 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks about the store's general policy; 환불해 주세요 is the actual request to do it. Also keep clear the meaning trio: 환불 (money back) vs 교환 (different item) vs 반품 (physically returning the goods). The English-speaker error is over-translating 'can I' as a permission/ability question: 제가 환불할 수 있어요? sounds like YOU are asking whether you have the ability to issue a refund — backwards. The passive feasibility form 되다 is idiomatic: 환불돼요?. Another trap is the particle: 이거를 환불돼요? is wrong because 되다 here is intransitive — no object particle on 이거.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제가 환불할 수 있어요? to ask for a refund.
That asks about your own ability to issue a refund and sounds backwards. Use the passive feasibility form: 이거 환불돼요? ('can this be refunded?').
Confusing 환불 with 교환 or 반품.
환불 = money back; 교환 = swap for another item; 반품 = returning the goods. If you want your money, ask 환불돼요?, not 교환돼요?.
Adding an object particle: 이거를 환불돼요?.
되다 ('to be possible') is intransitive here, so there's no object particle. Say 이거 환불돼요? — bare 이거.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 환불(還拂) + 되다 → 'is a refund doable/possible for this?'. 되다 is intransitive feasibility, not a transitive action. This is a feasibility check, not a request — the request comes after: 환불해 주세요.

Your very first line at the counter before stating your reason. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — safe with all staff. In a tiny market 환불돼? (반말) is possible with a familiar owner. Do not use this in writing; in a customer-service chat, 환불 가능한가요? is more formal.
환불돼요? (this item, right now) vs 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (the store's general policy) vs 환불해 주세요 (actual request). Also: 환불 (money back) ≠ 교환 (swap item) ≠ 반품 (send it back).
환불돼요? → 환불 되나요? (softer) → 환불 가능해요? (near-synonym) → 환불 가능한가요? (formal/written). Lead-in: 한 번도 안 썼는데 환불돼요? ('never used it — refundable?').

'Can I' → 제가 환불할 수 있어요? implies YOUR ability to issue a refund — backwards. Use the passive feasibility form 되다: 환불돼요?. Also: 이거를 환불돼요? is wrong — 되다 is intransitive here, so no object particle on 이거.

expressions.hangul: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요?
expressions.romanization: pibugwaeseo badeun georang gachi sseodo dwaeyo?
expressions.english: Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?
expressions.shortExplanation: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?".
expressions.explanation: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? (pibugwaeseo badeun georang gachi sseodo dwaeyo?) means "Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? ("Can I use it with my derm products?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요?
usagePhrases.romanization: pibugwaeseo badeun georang gachi sseodo dwaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can I use it with my derm products?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; checking compatibility with dermatology items

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay to use together?
usagePhrases.note: Shorter; 같이 쓰다 ('use together') + 괜찮다
Asking the layering 순서 ('order/sequence')

usagePhrases.en: Can I apply it with retinol?
usagePhrases.note: 레티놀 ('retinol') = a common 'don't mix carelessly' ingredient

examples.ko: A: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? / B: 어떤 성분인지 알면 더 잘 알려드릴 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: pibugwaeseo badeun georang gachi sseodo dwaeyo? / B: eotteon seongbuninji almyeon deo jal allyeodeuril su isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist? / B: If you know the ingredients, I can give you better advice.
examples.note: Staff may ask about the prescription ingredient — be ready to name it if you know

examples.ko: 피부과에서 처방받은 연고 쓰는데 이거 같이 발라도 돼요?
examples.romanization: pibugwaeseo cheobangbadeun yeongo sseuneunde igeo gachi ballado dwaeyo?
examples.en: I use a prescribed ointment from the derm — can I apply this with it?
examples.note: 처방받다 ('to be prescribed') + 연고 ('ointment') are the exact words for prescription items

examples.ko: 레티놀 쓰는 중인데 이 비타민C랑 같이 쓰면 자극되지 않을까요?
examples.romanization: retinol sseuneun junginde i bitaminCrang gachi sseumyeon jageukdoeji aneulkkayo?
examples.en: I'm on retinol — won't using it with this vitamin C be irritating?
examples.note: Naming the active ingredients shows ingredient-layer awareness and gets a precise answer

expressions.nuance: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? is 피부과 ('dermatology clinic', Sino-Korean 皮膚科) + 에서 ('from/at') + 받은 거 ('the thing I got') + 랑 ('with') + 같이 ('together') + 써도 돼요? ('is it okay to use?'). This is a real-life advanced layering question. Key vocabulary: 피부과 (the clinic — note 과 '-department/field', as in 내과 'internal medicine', 안과 'ophthalmology'), 처방받다 ('to be prescribed'), 연고 ('ointment'), and the active ingredients people worry about — 레티놀 (retinol), 비타민C (vitamin C), AHA/BHA. The standard skincare layering 순서 in Korea is toner → essence/serum → targeted treatments → cream → sunscreen (morning). The particle structure: the thing you're mixing WITH takes 랑/이랑 (casual) or 와/과 (formal), so 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 means 'together with what I got from the clinic.' The English-speaker errors: (1) omitting 랑/이랑 after 받은 거 — 같이 alone doesn't mark 'with X'; (2) calling the clinic 피부과 의사 when you mean the place — 피부과 = clinic, 피부과 의사/선생님 = the doctor; (3) 함께 사용해도 됩니까? is too formal for a shop. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 랑/이랑 and saying 피부과 거 같이 써도 돼요?
'With X' needs the particle 랑/이랑 (casual) or 와/과 (formal): 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? 같이 alone isn't enough to mark 'with what'.
Calling the clinic 피부과 의사 when you mean the place.
피부과 = the dermatology clinic/department; 피부과 의사/선생님 = the doctor (person). To say 'got it at the clinic', 피부과에서 받은 거 is right.
Using 함께 사용해도 됩니까? in a casual shop.
That's stiff and formal. In an everyday beauty shop say 같이 써도 돼요? It carries the same meaning, naturally.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Is it okay to use together with what I got from the dermatology clinic?' The real-world question is about ingredient compatibility: will these two products react badly, cancel each other out, or cause irritation when layered together?

Said at a beauty shop when you're on a dermatologist-prescribed routine and want to add an OTC product. 존댓말 with staff. If asking a staff member who isn't a pharmacist or derm, be aware they may not know ingredients deeply — you may also want to check with the prescribing doctor.

같이 써도 괜찮아요? ('is it okay to use together?') is a shorter, vaguer version. 레티놀이랑 같이 발라도 돼요? names the specific ingredient — more precise and more likely to get a useful answer. 순서가 어떻게 돼요? ('what's the layering order?') follows up once compatibility is confirmed.
Simpler: 같이 써도 돼요? Specific ingredient: 레티놀이랑 같이 써도 돼요? Layering order follow-up: 이거 먼저 발라야 돼요 아니면 나중에요? ('should I apply this first or after?')
Omitting 랑/이랑: 같이 alone is 'together' (an adverb), not 'with X' — you need 받은 거랑 같이 to mark what you're mixing with. Also 피부과 = the clinic (place), not the doctor — 피부과 의사/선생님 is the person.

expressions.hangul: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요
expressions.romanization: je pibutone manneun kusyeon chaja juseyo
expressions.english: Help me find a cushion that matches my skin tone
expressions.shortExplanation: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Help me find a cushion that matches my skin tone".
expressions.explanation: "Help me find a cushion that matches my skin tone" — that is 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 (je pibutone manneun kusyeon chaja juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 ("Find me a cushion for my skin tone"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: je pibutone manneun kusyeon chaja juseyo
usagePhrases.en: Find me a cushion for my skin tone
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking staff to shade-match a cushion/foundation
21호/23호 = the standard Korean shade numbers
쿨톤/웜톤 = the personal-color undertone question
커버력 ('coverage power') for fuller coverage

examples.ko: A: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요. / B: 피부톤 보니까 21호 쿨톤이 맞을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: je pibutone manneun kusyeon chaja juseyo. / B: pibuton bonikka 21ho kultoni majeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: Help me find a cushion for my skin tone. / B: Looking at your skin, I think a 21 cool-tone would suit you.
examples.note: The ideal staff shade-match interaction — they assess and recommend

examples.ko: 저 21호 쓰는데 좀 밝은 것 같아요. 21.5호 있어요?
examples.romanization: jeo 21ho sseuneunde jom balgeun geot gatayo. 21.5ho isseoyo?
examples.en: I use 21, but it seems a bit light — is there a 21.5?
examples.note: Half-shades like 21.5호 exist between the main numbers in many Korean lines

examples.ko: 저 웜톤이라 핑크 베이스는 떠요. 옐로 베이스로 보여 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeo womtonira pingkeu beiseuneun tteoyo. yello beiseuro boyeo juseyo.
examples.en: I'm warm-toned, so pink-base looks ashy on me — show me a yellow-base one.
examples.note: 뜨다 ('to float/look ashy') is the precise idiom for a wrong-undertone shade sitting off on the skin

expressions.nuance: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 is 제 ('my', humble) + 피부톤 ('skin tone') + 에 맞는 ('that matches/suits') + 쿠션 ('cushion compact foundation') + 찾아 주세요 ('please find for me'). Korean base makeup runs on a shade-number system: 13호 (very fair), 21호 (light/fair), 21.5호 (half-step), 23호 (medium), 25호 (deeper) — staff will ask 몇 호 쓰세요? ('what number do you use?'). Undertone vocabulary is 쿨톤 (cool-toned) vs. 웜톤 (warm-toned), part of the huge 퍼스널 컬러 trend; base types are 핑크 베이스 vs. 옐로 베이스. The crucial idiom: 뜨다 ('to float') means a foundation looks ashy, too light, or wrong-undertone on skin (피부에서 떠요 = 'it floats off the skin / looks masky'). 커버력 ('coverage') is the key quality word. The English-speaker error is saying 'shade' as 그림자 ('shadow') — a literal-translation disaster; the right words are 호 (the number) or 색상/톤. Don't say 매치하다 for 'match'; use 에 맞다 ('to suit/fit'). Note 쿠션 here means the cushion-compact makeup format, not a sofa cushion. Default 존댓말; 찾아 주세요 hands the task to staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그림자 ('shadow') for a makeup 'shade'.
그림자 is a literal shadow. A foundation shade is a number 호 (21호, 23호) or 색상/톤. Ask 몇 호가 맞아요? not anything with 그림자.
Using Sino vs. native numbers wrongly with 호.
Shade numbers use Sino-Korean: 21호 = 이십일 호, 23호 = 이십삼 호. Say 이십일 호, not native 스물한. The counter 호 takes Sino numbers.
Translating 'it doesn't match / looks off' as 안 어울려요 only.
안 어울려요 ('doesn't suit') is general. For a foundation that sits wrong/looks ashy, the precise idiom is 떠요 ('it floats'): 피부에서 떠요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Please find for me a cushion that matches my skin tone.' 맞다 here means 'to fit/suit' — not just visual match but also undertone and finish compatibility. Real meaning: 'I need you to shade-match a cushion foundation to my skin.'

Said at a brand counter or inside Olive Young/Sephora Korea when you need help picking a shade. 존댓말 always with staff. If you already know your number, start with 저 21호예요 — saves time. If you don't know, say 제 피부톤에 맞는 거 추천해 주세요 and let staff assess.

제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 (open shade-match request) vs. 저 21호예요? 23호예요? (narrowing between specific options) vs. 이거 제 피부톤이랑 맞아요? (checking one product). 뜨다 ('floats/looks ashy') is the key complaint word when a shade is wrong.
More specific: 웜톤에 맞는 쿠션 있어요? Requesting a quality: 커버력 좋은 걸로 찾아 주세요. Asking about finish: 매트한 거로 추천해 주세요 ('recommend a matte one') vs. 광 나는 거 ('a dewy/glow one').

Saying 그림자 ('shadow') for a makeup 'shade' is a complete translation error — it means a literal shadow. A foundation shade is 호 (number) or 색상/톤. Also: 뜨다 ('floats') is the specific idiom for a wrong shade — not 안 어울려요 ('doesn't suit'), which is too general.

expressions.shortExplanation: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 is a practical expression meaning "My skin keeps flaking / peeling".
expressions.explanation: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 (gakjiri jakku ireonayo) = "My skin keeps flaking / peeling". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 ("My skin keeps flaking"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing dry flaking (각질 일어나다)
각질 제거 ('dead-skin removal') = exfoliation
각질 정리 ('tidying dead skin') for a gentle ask
갈라지다 ('to crack/split') for severe dryness

examples.ko: A: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요. / B: 주 1~2회 각질 제거제 쓰시고 충분히 보습하시면 나아질 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: gakjiri jakku ireonayo. / B: ju 1~2hoe gakjil jegeoje sseusigo chungbunhi boseupasimyeon naajil geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: My skin keeps flaking. / B: Use an exfoliant once or twice a week and moisturize well — that should help.
examples.note: The natural complaint-and-advice exchange on dry skin flaking

examples.ko: 화장하면 각질이 다 일어나서 들떠요. 어떻게 해야 돼요?
examples.romanization: hwajanghamyeon gakjiri da ireonaseo deultteoyo. eotteoke haeya dwaeyo?
examples.en: When I do makeup, the flakes lift and it cakes — what should I do?
examples.note: 들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') is the specific makeup-over-flakes complaint

examples.ko: 각질 제거하고 싶은데 너무 자극적이지 않은 거 있어요? 저 민감성이라서요.
examples.romanization: gakjil jegeohago sipeunde neomu jageukjeogiji aneun geo isseoyo? jeo mingamseongiraseoyo.
examples.en: I want to exfoliate but nothing too harsh — I have sensitive skin.
examples.note: Asking for gentle exfoliation given sensitivity; 자극적 ('harsh/irritating') is the key qualifier

expressions.nuance: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 is 각질 ('dead skin cells / flaky skin', Sino-Korean 角質) + 이 + 자꾸 ('repeatedly, keeps happening') + 일어나요 (from 일어나다, here meaning 'to lift up / flake'). 각질 is THE word for dead-skin flakiness; it pairs with fixed verbs: 각질이 일어나다 ('skin flakes/peels up'), 각질 제거 ('exfoliation'), 각질 정리 (a gentler 'tidying/smoothing'). Exfoliating products include 필링 (peeling pad/gel), 스크럽 (scrub), 각질 제거제 (exfoliant). The related makeup problem is 들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') — when foundation sits on top of flakes and looks patchy; don't confuse this with 뜨다 ('to look ashy', a shade problem). For severe dryness: 갈라지다 ('to crack/split') and 트다 ('to chap', especially 입술이 트다 'chapped lips'). 자꾸 conveys the frustrating, recurring nature — it's what makes this phrase feel real rather than clinical. The English-speaker error is using 벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off', like sunburned skin) for ongoing dry flaking — 벗겨지다 fits a sunburn or a peel mask result; everyday dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Another trap: 죽은 피부 ('dead skin') sounds morbid and medical — the cosmetic word is 각질. Particle: 각질이 일어나다 (subject marker 이/가). Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죽은 피부 for 'dead skin'.
죽은 피부 ('dead skin') sounds morbid/medical. The cosmetic term for flaky dead-skin cells is 각질: 각질이 일어나요, 각질 제거.
Using 벗겨지다 for everyday dry flaking.
벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off') fits sunburn sloughing or a peel-mask result. Ongoing dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Say 각질이 일어나요.
Confusing 들뜨다 (makeup cakes) with 뜨다 (wrong shade).
들뜨다 = foundation lifts/cakes over flakes; 뜨다 = a shade looks ashy/floats. For flaking-related caking, use 들떠요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally: 'Dead-skin-cells keep rising up.' 각질 (角質) = 'horny/keratinous substance' (the clinical Sino-Korean term). 일어나다 usually means 'to get up/rise' but also 'to lift up', giving the vivid image of flakes lifting off the skin surface. Real meaning: 'My skin keeps peeling and flaking — I can't get rid of it.'

Said to a beauty clerk or in a skincare consultation when describing a persistent dryness problem. 존댓말 with staff. The word 자꾸 ('keeps doing it') signals the problem is recurring, not just today — important context for getting the right product recommendation.

각질이 일어나다 (dry flaking, ongoing) vs. 벗겨지다 (peeling off in sheets, like sunburn) vs. 갈라지다 (cracking, severe dryness). 들뜨다 (foundation cakes over flakes) is the makeup-specific consequence. 트다 (chapping) is for lips and hands specifically.
각질 is Sino-Korean 角質 ('horny/keratinous substance') — the cosmetic term for dead-skin flakiness. 각질 제거 adds 제거 (除去) = 'removal': exfoliation.

벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off') fits sunburn sloughing or a peel mask; it's too dramatic for everyday dry flaking. Use 각질이 일어나다. Also: 죽은 피부 ('dead skin' literal translation) sounds morbid; the cosmetic term is 각질 only.

expressions.english: Hello, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team
expressions.shortExplanation: 안녕하세요, ○○팀 ○○○입니다 is a practical expression meaning "Hello, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team".
expressions.explanation: 안녕하세요, ○○팀 ○○○입니다 (annyeonghaseyo, ○○tim ○○○imnida) means "Hello, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team". Say it as one set phrase — for example 안녕하세요, 마케팅팀 김민수입니다 ("Hello, this is Kim Minsu from the Marketing team"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Hello, this is Kim Minsu from the Marketing team
usagePhrases.note: The standard opening line of almost every work email

usagePhrases.en: Hello, this is ○○○, the person in charge of ○○
usagePhrases.note: When the reader may not know you; states your role

usagePhrases.en: This is Assistant Manager ○○○ from ○○ Company
usagePhrases.note: To an external party; lead with company + title

usagePhrases.en: Good day, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team
usagePhrases.note: More formal 하십니까 for very senior or official mail

examples.en: Hello, this is Kim Minsu from the Sales team.
examples.note: Minimum viable opening: greeting + team + name + 입니다

examples.ko: 안녕하세요, 영업팀 김민수입니다. 어제 통화드린 건으로 메일 드립니다.
examples.romanization: annyeonghaseyo, yeongeoptim gimminsuimnida. eoje tonghwadeurin geoneuro meil deurimnida.
examples.en: Hello, this is Kim Minsu from Sales. I'm writing about the matter we discussed by phone yesterday.
examples.note: Greeting then immediately state WHY you're writing — the professional pattern

examples.ko: A: 안녕하세요, ABC회사 영업팀 김민수 대리입니다. 견적 관련해서 연락드렸습니다. / B: 네, 안녕하세요. 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: A: annyeonghaseyo, ABChoesa yeongeoptim gimminsu daeriimnida. gyeonjeok gwallyeonhaeseo yeollakdeuryeotseumnida. / B: ne, annyeonghaseyo. malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: A: Hello, this is Assistant Manager Kim Minsu from ABC Company's Sales team. I'm contacting you about a quote. / B: Yes, hello. Please go ahead.
examples.note: External first-contact exchange: company + team + name + title + reason; the reader's 말씀하세요 confirms the opening worked

expressions.nuance: Korean work emails almost always open with 안녕하세요 + your identity in the pattern [team/company] + [name] + [optional title] + 입니다. Skipping this feels abrupt and rude in Korean office culture, where establishing who you are before the request is a non-negotiable social script. The verb 입니다 means 'I am ~', and you state your own name plainly — never with honorific 님 attached to yourself (김민수님입니다 is wrong; 님 honors others). Title order differs from English: Korean says 김민수 대리 (name THEN rank), not 대리 김민수. The more formal variant 안녕하십니까 (합쇼체) is used for very senior recipients, official announcements, or letters; everyday inter-office mail uses 안녕하세요. The classic English-speaker trap is translating 'My name is' as 제 이름은 ~예요, which sounds like a textbook drill rather than a professional self-introduction; the natural business form is simply [name]입니다. Also avoid opening with 저는 ~ every time — Korean drops the 'I' once context is clear, so 김민수입니다 alone is cleaner.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 제 이름은 김민수예요 in a work email.
That's a casual/textbook self-intro. Professional email states identity as 김민수입니다 (or 팀 + 이름 + 입니다), not '내 이름은 ~예요'.
Attaching 님 to your own name: 김민수님입니다.
님 is an honorific for OTHERS. Referring to yourself you drop it: 김민수입니다. Using 님 on yourself sounds self-elevating and wrong.
Ordering title before name: 대리 김민수입니다.
Korean puts rank AFTER the name: 김민수 대리입니다. The English order 'Assistant Manager Kim' reversed sounds off.

structuredNuance.t: Korean work emails open with 안녕하세요 + [team/company] + [name] + [optional title] + 입니다. This is non-negotiable: jumping straight to the request feels abrupt and rude in Korean office culture, where establishing identity first is a social script. 입니다 means 'I am ~' — you state your own name plainly without attaching 님 to yourself.

안녕하세요 + 입니다 is the everyday polite (합쇼체) level safe for all internal and external email. Upgrade to 안녕하십니까 (one notch more formal) for very senior recipients, official letters, or company-wide announcements. Never use 안녕 (반말) in any professional email regardless of how well you know the colleague.
chips: 안녕 — 반말, never in work email

structuredNuance.t: 안녕하십니까 vs. 안녕하세요: both are 존댓말 but 하십니까 is one notch more formal/official (합쇼체), expected in announcements, to C-suite, or in print. For a normal intra-team or client email, 하세요 is the default. Switching to 하십니까 unnecessarily can feel stiff or bureaucratic.

Minimal: 안녕하세요, 김민수입니다. / With team: 안녕하세요, 마케팅팀 김민수입니다. / With title: 안녕하세요, 마케팅팀 김민수 대리입니다. / External full: 안녕하세요, ABC회사 마케팅팀 김민수 대리입니다. Add layers based on how well the reader knows you — more layers for strangers or external contacts.

Do not write 제 이름은 김민수예요 — that is a textbook casual self-intro, not business email. Do not attach 님 to your own name (김민수님입니다 is self-elevating and wrong). Do not put title before name (대리 김민수 is the English order; Korean is 김민수 대리). And do not add 저는 every sentence — Korean omits the subject once established.

expressions.english: Please take note / for your reference
expressions.shortExplanation: 참고 부탁드립니다 is a practical expression meaning "Please take note / for your reference".
expressions.explanation: "Please take note / for your reference" — that is 참고 부탁드립니다 (chamgo butakdeurimnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 참고 부탁드립니다 ("Please take note of this"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; asks the reader to keep it in mind
Slightly more formal/official written tone

usagePhrases.en: Just for your reference (no action needed)
usagePhrases.note: Signals it's FYI only, nothing to do
Curt note-style ending, internal memos/superiors to juniors

examples.en: Please take note of the content below.
examples.note: Points the reader to information you have included — no action expected

examples.en: The schedule has changed from last time, so please take note.
examples.note: Used to flag a change the reader should simply be aware of

examples.ko: A: 이 데이터는 최신 기준입니다. 참고 부탁드립니다. / B: 네, 확인했습니다. 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: A: i deiteoneun choesin gijunimnida. chamgo butakdeurimnida. / B: ne, hwaginhaetseumnida. gamsahamnida.
examples.en: A: This data is based on the latest figures. Please take note. / B: Understood, I've seen it. Thank you.
examples.note: Short A/B exchange showing 참고 as a pure FYI hand-off with a polite acknowledgment reply

expressions.nuance: 참고 부탁드립니다 is 참고 ('reference/consultation', Sino-Korean 參考) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly request'), meaning 'please keep this in mind / for your reference'. It is a soft, information-sharing closer: you are not demanding action, just asking the reader to be AWARE of something. The crucial contrast with 참조 (參照): in email, 참조 is the CC field (참조: 박과장님) — it names who is copied — whereas 참고 means 'for your information'. English speakers confuse these because both translate loosely as 'reference'; writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note this' reads as 'please CC this'. A second contrast: 참고하세요 (plain imperative) is fine to juniors or peers but can sound directive to a superior; 참고 부탁드립니다 with humble 부탁드리다 is safer upward. 참고 is a 하다-noun, so to make it a verb you need 참고하다 — never 참고 주세요 (you cannot 'give' a reference). The softer 참고하시기 바랍니다 or 참고만 해 주세요 (FYI-only, no action) are useful variants.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 참고 with 참조.
참조 is the email CC line ('참조: ~님'); 참고 means 'for your reference'. Writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note' sounds like 'please CC'. Use 참고 for FYI.
Saying 참고 주세요.
참고 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. The verb is 참고하다, so it's 참고해 주세요 or 참고 부탁드립니다, never 참고 주세요.
Using bare 참고하세요 to a senior.
The plain imperative can feel directive upward. To a superior, soften to 참고 부탁드립니다 or 참고하시기 바랍니다.

structuredNuance.t: 참고 부탁드립니다 means 'please keep this in mind / for your reference'. It is a soft information-sharing closer — you are not demanding an action, just asking the reader to be AWARE. The humble 부탁드리다 frame keeps the register appropriate for any level of seniority.

Safe to send upward (to bosses, clients) because 부탁드리다 is humble. Downward or to peers you can use the plainer 참고하세요 or the note-style 참고 바람. In announcements or notices, 참고하시기 바랍니다 is the more official written form.

참고 부탁드립니다 (FYI, no action needed) vs. 확인 부탁드립니다 (please check/confirm something) vs. 검토 부탁드립니다 (please examine and judge critically). The three form a spectrum from lightest (참고) to heaviest ask (검토). Also: 참조 (參照) = the CC field — writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note' is wrong.

참고 부탁드립니다 → 참고하시기 바랍니다 (more formal/official) → 참고만 해 주세요 (FYI-only, explicitly no action) → 참고 바람 (curt memo note, downward only). To soften further: 참고로 알려 드립니다 ('I'm letting you know for reference').

Do not confuse 참고 (參考, FYI) with 참조 (參照, the CC field). Do not say 참고 주세요 — 참고 is a 하다-noun; you cannot 'give' it. The verb is 참고하다, so the request form is 참고해 주세요 or 참고 부탁드립니다. Also avoid 체크 — Konglish; use 참고 for FYI and 확인 for confirmation.

expressions.shortExplanation: 첨부했습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I've attached it (please find attached)".
expressions.explanation: 첨부했습니다 (cheombuhaetseumnida) = "I've attached it (please find attached)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 첨부했습니다 ("I have attached it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; states the file is attached
Adds 드리다 to sound a touch more courteous
Pairs the attachment with a request to open it
Crisp present-tense form, common in quick mail

examples.en: I've attached the materials you requested.
examples.note: Links the attachment directly to what they asked for

examples.en: I'm attaching the quote, so please review it.
examples.note: 첨부 + follow-up 확인 부탁드립니다 — the most common two-line pattern

examples.ko: A: 수정된 보고서 다시 보내 주실 수 있나요? / B: 네, 수정본 첨부드립니다. 이전 파일은 삭제해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: sujeongdoen bogoseo dasi bonae jusil su innayo? / B: ne, sujeongbon cheombudeurimnida. ijeon paireun sakjehae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Could you resend the revised report? / B: Yes, I'm attaching the revised version. Please delete the previous file.
examples.note: Real A/B exchange: resending a corrected file with a deletion request

expressions.nuance: 첨부했습니다 is 첨부 ('attachment', Sino-Korean 添附) + 하다 in formal past: 'I have attached'. It is the standard line for 'please find attached'. The everyday options are 첨부했습니다 (I attached), 첨부합니다 (I'm attaching), and the warmer 첨부해 드립니다 / 첨부드립니다, where 드리다 ('to do for someone, humbly') signals you are doing the reader a service — common and polite upward. The key contrast: 첨부 (添附) is electronically attaching a FILE to an email, while 동봉 (同封) is physically enclosing something in a paper envelope — do not write 동봉했습니다 for an emailed PDF. A frequent English-speaker pitfall is the over-literal 'please find attached' rendered as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요 ('please go look for the attached thing'), which sounds like the file is missing; simply state 첨부했습니다. Watch the particle: it is 파일을 첨부했습니다 (object 을/를), not 파일에 첨부. And 첨부 is a 하다-noun: to ask THEM to attach something, use the verb: 첨부해 주세요, never 첨부 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'please find attached' as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요.
찾다 ('to look for') makes it sound like the file is missing. Just state 첨부했습니다 or 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다.
Using 동봉 for an email file.
동봉 (同封) is enclosing something in a physical envelope. For an emailed file use 첨부 (添附): 파일을 첨부했습니다.
Saying 첨부 주세요 when asking someone to attach.
첨부 is a 하다-noun; it can't be 'given'. Use the verb: 첨부해 주세요 ('please attach it').

structuredNuance.t: 첨부했습니다 means 'I have attached' — the standard line for 'please find attached'. The everyday options are 첨부했습니다 (past), 첨부합니다 (present), and the warmer 첨부해 드립니다 / 첨부드립니다, where 드리다 signals you are doing the reader a service. All three are correct; choice depends on how much courtesy you want to show.

Use 첨부했습니다 or 첨부합니다 in standard business email to any level. Upgrade to 첨부해 드립니다 or 첨부드립니다 for clients or senior recipients. 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다 is often added as a follow-up line to nudge the reader to actually open it.

첨부 (添附, electronic attachment) vs. 동봉 (同封, physically enclosed in a paper envelope). Do not use 동봉했습니다 in an email — it signals a letter with enclosures. Also: 첨부하다 (to attach) vs. 파일을 보내다 (to send a file, more casual).
첨부했습니다 → 첨부해 드립니다 (more courteous) → 첨부드립니다 (compact humble form) → 파일 첨부합니다 (quick present-tense). To ask the reader to check: 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다. To resend: 다시 첨부드립니다 / 재첨부드립니다.

Do not write 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요 ('please go look for the attached thing') — it sounds like the file is lost. Do not use 동봉했습니다 for an email PDF. Watch the particle: 파일'을' 첨부했습니다 (object marker), not 파일'에' 첨부. And never say 첨부 주세요 — 첨부 is a 하다-noun; to request attachment use 첨부해 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 확인 부탁드립니다 is a practical expression meaning "Please check / kindly confirm".
expressions.explanation: 확인 부탁드립니다 (hwagin butakdeurimnida) means "Please check / kindly confirm". Say it as one set phrase — for example 확인 부탁드립니다 ("Please check / confirm"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: The default polite-formal request to review something
Softer, slightly less stiff than 드립니다
More formal/official written register
Adds an explicit reply step after checking

examples.ko: 아래 금액에 이상 없는지 확인 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: arae geumaege isang eopsneunji hwagin butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: Please confirm the amounts below are correct.
examples.note: Verify a specific figure — the most common use

examples.en: Please confirm whether the schedule works for you.
examples.note: 확인 used to confirm availability, not just read content

examples.ko: A: 내일 오전 10시에 회의실 예약했습니다. 확인 부탁드립니다. / B: 확인했습니다. 참석하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: naeil ojeon 10sie hoeuisil yeyakaetseumnida. hwagin butakdeurimnida. / B: hwaginhaetseumnida. chamseokagetseumnida.
examples.en: A: I've booked the meeting room for 10 a.m. tomorrow. Please confirm. / B: Confirmed. I'll attend.
examples.note: A/B exchange: confirmation request and acknowledgment — the most natural email pair

expressions.nuance: 확인 부탁드립니다 is 확인 ('confirmation/checking', Sino-Korean 確認) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly ask'), the single most common closing request in Korean work email. 확인 covers both 'verify it is correct' and 'acknowledge you have seen it', so it is wonderfully versatile. The politeness lives in 부탁드리다 (humble 'to request'), making this safe upward to bosses and clients. The near-synonym contrast: 검토 (檢討) means a deeper REVIEW — reading critically, forming a judgment — while 확인 is a lighter 'check/confirm'. Asking a senior to 확인 a number is fine; if you want their considered opinion, use 검토 부탁드립니다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the loanword 체크 (체크 부탁드립니다) — understandable but casual Konglish; professional mail uses 확인. Another trap is the plain imperative 확인하세요, which can sound curt or bossy upward; 확인 부탁드립니다 frames the same request as a humble ask. 확인 is a 하다-noun; if you want the full verb form, it is 확인해 주세요, never 확인 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 체크 부탁드립니다.
체크 is casual Konglish. Professional Korean email uses 확인: 확인 부탁드립니다.
Sending bare 확인하세요 to a boss or client.
The plain imperative can sound like an order. Soften with the humble request frame: 확인 부탁드립니다 or 확인해 주시기 바랍니다.
Using 확인 when you need a considered review.
확인 is a light 'check/confirm'. If you want them to critically examine and give feedback, ask 검토 부탁드립니다 instead.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 부탁드립니다 is the single most common closing request in Korean work email — 'please check/confirm this'. 확인 covers both 'verify it is correct' and 'acknowledge you have seen it'. The humble 부탁드리다 makes it safe to send upward to any boss or client.

Safe at all levels because of 부탁드리다. Downward, you can use the slightly brisker 확인해 주세요. For official notices or formal documents, 확인해 주시기 바랍니다 is the most elevated written form. Never use the bare 확인하세요 upward — it sounds like an order.

확인 (light check/confirm) vs. 검토 (深 review with judgment) vs. 참고 (FYI, no action). Choosing wrong signals a mismatch: 확인 for a strategy doc undersells what you need; 검토 for just looking at a number is overstated.
확인 부탁드립니다 → 확인 부탁드려요 (softer) → 확인해 주시기 바랍니다 (official) → 확인 후 회신 부탁드립니다 (check then reply) → 확인 후 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (most courteous conditional).

Do not write 체크 부탁드립니다 — 체크 is casual Konglish. Do not send bare 확인하세요 to a boss — it sounds like an order. Do not write 확인 주세요 — 확인 is a 하다-noun; the correct verb form is 확인해 주세요. And do not use 확인 when you actually need considered feedback — use 검토 instead.

expressions.shortExplanation: 회신 부탁드립니다 is a practical expression meaning "Please reply / awaiting your response".
expressions.explanation: "Please reply / awaiting your response" — that is 회신 부탁드립니다 (hoesin butakdeurimnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 회신 부탁드립니다 ("Please reply"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; asks for a written response
답장 is the everyday word for a reply/letter back

usagePhrases.en: I'd be grateful for your reply
usagePhrases.note: Softer, extra-courteous closing
Attaches a deadline to the reply request

examples.en: Please reply after reviewing.
examples.note: Asks them to review first, then respond — the standard two-step

examples.en: I know you're busy, but please reply by Friday.
examples.note: 바쁘시겠지만 softens a deadline request so it does not feel pushy

examples.ko: A: 참석 가능하신지 회신 주시면 일정 잡겠습니다. / B: 네, 참석 가능합니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.

expressions.nuance: 회신 부탁드립니다 is 회신 ('reply/response', Sino-Korean 回信) + 부탁드립니다, asking the reader to write back — the formal email staple for 'please respond'. 회신 is the crisp, businesslike word slightly more formal than the everyday 답장 ('a letter/message back'); both are correct, but 회신 dominates in professional mail and 답장 feels a touch more personal or casual. The contrast to watch: 회신 (the act of replying, general) vs. 답변 (答辯, the ANSWER itself to a specific question). If you posed a concrete question and want that answer, 답변 부탁드립니다 fits; for a general 'please get back to me', use 회신. The English-speaker pitfall is over-literal 'reply to me' as 저에게 회신해 주세요 — 저에게 ('to me') is redundant and heavy; 회신 부탁드립니다 already implies the direction. Another trap is treating 'respond' as 반응 (反應, a physical or emotional reaction) — 반응 부탁드립니다 sounds like asking for a like or reaction, not an email reply.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 반응 부탁드립니다 for 'please respond'.
반응 is a reaction/response in a physical sense. For an email reply use 회신 부탁드립니다 or 답장 부탁드립니다.
Adding unnecessary 저에게: 저에게 회신해 주세요.
회신 부탁드립니다 already implies 'to me'. The explicit 저에게 is heavy and redundant in business mail; drop it.
Mixing up 회신 and 답변.
회신 = a reply/getting back to you; 답변 = an answer to a specific question. If you asked something concrete, 답변 부탁드립니다; for general 'reply', 회신 부탁드립니다.

structuredNuance.t: 회신 부탁드립니다 asks the reader to write back — the formal email staple for 'please respond'. 회신 is the crisp, businesslike word for a reply, slightly more formal than everyday 답장. The humble 부탁드리다 makes it safe upward and to clients.

회신 부탁드립니다 is the standard upward/outward form. For extra courtesy — especially to clients or senior executives — upgrade to 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다. With a deadline, add the date: ○일까지 회신 부탁드립니다. Soften deadline requests with 바쁘시겠지만 so they do not read as demands.

회신 (a reply, getting back to you, general) vs. 답변 (答辯, the answer to a specific question you asked). Pose a direct question → 답변 부탁드립니다. Want them to just get back to you → 회신 부탁드립니다. Using 답변 where 회신 fits is not wrong but overly formal.
회신 부탁드립니다 → 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (conditional, gentler) → ○일까지 회신 부탁드립니다 (deadline) → 검토 후 회신 부탁드립니다 (review then reply). The everyday synonym 답장 부탁드립니다 is fine in internal or less formal mail.

Do not add 저에게 ('to me') — 회신 부탁드립니다 already implies the direction; the extra pronoun sounds heavy. Do not use 반응 부탁드립니다 — 반응 (反應) is a physical or emotional reaction, not an email reply. Do not translate 'please get back to me' as 저한테 돌아와 주세요 — 돌아오다 is physical return.

expressions.shortExplanation: 검토 부탁드립니다 is a practical expression meaning "Please review (and give feedback)".
expressions.explanation: 검토 부탁드립니다 (geomto butakdeurimnida) = "Please review (and give feedback)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 검토 부탁드립니다 ("Please review this"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; asks for a careful look + opinion

usagePhrases.en: Could you give it a look?
usagePhrases.note: Lighter spoken-ish variant to a peer

usagePhrases.en: Please review and share your feedback
usagePhrases.note: Explicitly asks for comments after review

examples.en: Please review the proposal.
examples.note: Sends a document for the reader to examine critically

examples.ko: 초안이라 부족한 부분이 많은데 검토 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: choanira bujokan bubuni maneunde geomto butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: It's a draft with many rough spots, so please review it.
examples.note: 초안 ('draft') framing explicitly invites correction — humble and real

examples.ko: A: 1차 기획안 공유드립니다. 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다. / B: 읽어 보고 오후에 피드백 드릴게요.

expressions.nuance: 검토 부탁드립니다 is 검토 ('review/examination', Sino-Korean 檢討) + 부탁드립니다, asking the reader to read something critically and weigh in. Unlike the lighter 확인 ('just check/confirm'), 검토 implies real scrutiny — reading a proposal, catching problems, forming an opinion — so it is sent to someone whose judgment you want, often a senior, and implicitly invites feedback or approval. That is the key contrast English speakers blur: 확인 부탁드립니다 = 'please confirm/glance', 검토 부탁드립니다 = 'please examine and judge'. Asking a boss to merely 확인 a strategy doc undersells what you need; 검토 is right. The register is humble (부탁드리다), fully appropriate upward. The English-speaker pitfall is the loanword 리뷰 (리뷰 부탁드립니다) — acceptable in casual startup culture but reads as Konglish in formal mail; use 검토. Another trap: confusing 검토 with 검사 (檢査, an INSPECTION or test — medical or quality) — 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like requesting a lab test. 검토 is a 하다-noun: 검토하다, so 검토해 주세요 or 검토 부탁드립니다, never 검토 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 확인 when you need real review.
확인 is a light check/confirm. For a critical read with feedback or approval, ask 검토 부탁드립니다, not 확인 부탁드립니다.
Writing 리뷰 부탁드립니다.
리뷰 is casual Konglish. Formal Korean business mail uses 검토 부탁드립니다.
Confusing 검토 with 검사.
검토 = reviewing/examining (a document, plan); 검사 = inspection/testing (quality, medical). 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like requesting a test, not a document review.

structuredNuance.t: 검토 부탁드립니다 asks the reader to read something critically and weigh in. 검토 implies real scrutiny — reading a proposal, catching problems, forming an opinion — not a light glance. It is sent to someone whose judgment you want, often a senior, and implicitly invites feedback or approval.

Humble 부탁드리다 makes it appropriate upward to bosses and clients. For maximum courtesy, upgrade to 검토해 주시면 감사하겠습니다. To peers, 한번 검토해 봐 주세요 is lighter and more conversational. For a document with a revision cycle, add: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
chips: 한번 검토해 봐 주세요 — peer level

structuredNuance.t: 확인 부탁드립니다 (light check/confirm) vs. 검토 부탁드립니다 (critical review with judgment) vs. 검사 부탁드립니다 (inspection/testing — wrong for documents). Using 확인 where 검토 is needed signals you just want acknowledgment, not analysis.
검토 부탁드립니다 → 검토해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (conditional, most polite) → 검토 후 의견 부탁드립니다 (explicitly asks for comments) → 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 (full revision cycle phrase).

Do not use 리뷰 부탁드립니다 — 리뷰 is casual Konglish; formal mail uses 검토. Do not confuse 검토 with 검사 (檢査, inspection/testing) — 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like requesting a medical or quality test. Do not say 검토 주세요 — 검토 is a 하다-noun; the verb form is 검토해 주세요.

expressions.english: I'd be grateful if you could check and reply
expressions.shortExplanation: 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'd be grateful if you could check and reply".
expressions.explanation: 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (hwagin hu hoesin jusimyeon gamsahagetseumnida) means "I'd be grateful if you could check and reply". Say it as one set phrase — for example 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 ("I'd appreciate it if you'd check and reply"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'd appreciate it if you'd check and reply
usagePhrases.note: Very polite, common professional closer
Slightly more direct request form

usagePhrases.en: I'd be grateful if you'd check and contact me
usagePhrases.note: 연락 ('get in touch') instead of 회신

usagePhrases.en: Once you reply, I'll proceed right away
usagePhrases.note: Ties the reply to your next action

examples.ko: 견적서 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: gyeonjeokseo hwagin hu hoesin jusimyeon gamsahagetseumnida.
examples.en: I'd appreciate it if you'd review the quote and get back to me.
examples.note: Common closing on a proposal or quote email

examples.ko: 내용 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다. 미리 감사드립니다.
examples.romanization: naeyong hwagin hu hoesin jusimyeon gamsahagetseumnida. miri gamsadeurimnida.
examples.en: I'd be grateful for your check and reply. Thank you in advance.
examples.note: Advance thanks 미리 감사드립니다 adds a final courtesy layer

examples.ko: A: 바쁘시겠지만 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다. / B: 확인 후 내일 오전 중으로 회신드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: bappeusigetjiman hwagin hu hoesin jusimyeon gamsahagetseumnida. / B: hwagin hu naeil ojeon jungeuro hoesindeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: I know you're busy, but I'd be grateful for your check and reply. / B: I'll check and reply by tomorrow morning.
examples.note: A/B: the full polite-closer pattern and a professional reply committing a timeframe

expressions.nuance: 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 stacks 확인 ('check') + 후 ('after') + 회신 ('reply') + 주시면 ('if you would give/do') + 감사하겠습니다 ('I would be grateful'). The -(으)면 감사하겠습니다 frame is the gold-standard polite request in Korean business writing: it phrases your need as a conditional favor and thanks them in advance. This is gentler than a direct 부탁드립니다 and fits situations where maximum deference helps — clients, senior executives, first-contact emails. The contrast: 회신 부탁드립니다 is direct-polite ('please reply'), while 주시면 감사하겠습니다 is indirect-polite ('I'd be thankful if…') — the latter is a notch more formal and deferential. The English-speaker pitfall is mistranslating 'I would be grateful' as 저는 감사할 것입니다 (a flat future 'I will thank') — Korean uses the -겠- conjecture/intention form 감사하겠습니다, paired with the conditional 주시면. Dropping 주시면 (회신 감사하겠습니다) breaks the logic: it reads 'I'll be thankful for the reply' prematurely, as if they have already replied. Keep the 주시면 … 감사하겠습니다 pair intact.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 저는 감사할 것입니다 for 'I would be grateful'.
Korean uses 감사하겠습니다 (the -겠- form) for 'I would be grateful', tied to a conditional 주시면. The literal future 감사할 것입니다 sounds wrong here.
Dropping 주시면: 확인 후 회신 감사하겠습니다.
Without the conditional 주시면 ('if you would'), the sentence loses its logic. Keep the pair: 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
Stacking it with a blunt 빨리: 빨리 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
빨리 ('quickly') sounds pushy in a humble closer. If you need speed, use 가능한 한 빨리 or 바쁘시겠지만, not bare 빨리.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 is a polished, deferential closer meaning 'I'd appreciate it if you'd check and reply.' The -(으)면 감사하겠습니다 frame phrases your need as a conditional favor and thanks them in advance — the gold standard for maximum courtesy in Korean business writing.

Use this with clients, senior executives, or in first-contact emails where maximum deference is warranted. For standard internal mail, 확인 후 회신 부탁드립니다 is slightly more direct and equally acceptable. Combine with 바쁘시겠지만 at the start to cushion a deadline or urgency.
회신 부탁드립니다 (direct-polite) vs. 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (indirect-polite, conditional) vs. 회신 주시기 바랍니다 (formal/official written tone). The 주시면 감사하겠습니다 structure is the warmest and most deferential of the three.
확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 → 검토 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (with heavier review) → 확인하시고 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (연락 variant) → 회신 주시면 바로 진행하겠습니다 (ties reply to action). Append 미리 감사드립니다 for a final thanks.

Do not write 저는 감사할 것입니다 — use the -겠- form: 감사하겠습니다. Do not drop 주시면: 회신 감사하겠습니다 loses the conditional and sounds like premature thanks. Do not add 빨리 to soften urgency — 빨리 is pushy; use 가능한 한 빨리 or 바쁘시겠지만 + a deadline.

expressions.english: I think we'll need to coordinate the schedule
expressions.shortExplanation: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I think we'll need to coordinate the schedule".
expressions.explanation: "I think we'll need to coordinate the schedule" — that is 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 (iljeong joyuri piryohal geot gatseumnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 ("I think we need to coordinate schedules"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I think we need to coordinate schedules
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; raises a scheduling issue gently
More direct request to align timing

usagePhrases.ko: 일정을 한번 맞춰 봐야 할 것 같아요

usagePhrases.note: Softer spoken-ish variant with 맞추다

usagePhrases.en: If you share your availability, I'll coordinate
usagePhrases.note: Offers to do the coordinating yourself

examples.ko: 담당자분들 시간이 달라서 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다. 가능한 시간 알려 주세요.

examples.note: Explains the reason then asks for free slots

examples.ko: 회의 일정 관련해서 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다. 아래 시간 중 가능한 것 선택 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: hoeui iljeong gwallyeonhaeseo joyuri piryohal geot gatseumnida. arae sigan jung ganeunghan geot seontaek butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: I think we'll need to coordinate regarding the meeting time. Please choose a slot from the options below.
examples.note: Raises the need then immediately offers options — efficient business email pattern

examples.ko: A: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다. 다음 주 언제가 편하세요? / B: 화요일 오후나 목요일 오전이 괜찮습니다.
examples.romanization: A: iljeong joyuri piryohal geot gatseumnida. daeum ju eonjega pyeonhaseyo? / B: hwayoil ohuna mogyoil ojeoni gwaenchanhseumnida.
examples.en: A: I think we'll need to coordinate schedules. When is convenient next week? / B: Tuesday afternoon or Thursday morning works for me.
examples.note: A/B exchange: scheduling negotiation — the most natural use case for 조율

expressions.nuance: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 is 일정 ('schedule', Sino-Korean 日程) + 조율 ('tuning/coordination', Sino-Korean 調律, originally 'tuning an instrument') + 이 필요하다 ('is needed') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('seems/I think'). 조율 is the precise business word for negotiating and aligning times or terms among multiple parties — richer than just 'scheduling'. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 ('it seems / I think') is doing important politeness work: Korean business culture prefers hedged, indirect phrasing. A flat 필요합니다 sounds blunt and presumptuous; 필요할 것 같습니다 ('I think it will be needed') is softer and collaborative. The contrast: 조율 (coordinating among parties, give-and-take) vs. 조정 (調整, adjusting or modifying a plan more unilaterally by one party) — for 'let's find a time that works for everyone', 조율 is natural. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'coordinate' as 협력하다 ('to cooperate', general teamwork) — that misses the time-alignment meaning entirely. Another trap: the particle — 일정 조율'이' 필요하다 (subject marker 이/가 on what is needed), not 일정 조율을 필요하다. The loanword 스케줄 is fine casually but 일정 is the professional term.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing flat 일정 조율이 필요합니다 to a client.
The bare assertion can feel blunt. Korean business prefers the hedged 필요할 것 같습니다 ('I think we'll need to'), which sounds more collaborative.
Using 협력 for 'coordinate the schedule'.
협력 ('cooperation') is about working together generally, not aligning times. For matching schedules, the word is 조율 (or 맞추다): 일정 조율.
Wrong particle: 일정 조율을 필요합니다.
필요하다 takes the subject marker 이/가 on what is needed: 일정 조율이 필요합니다, not 일정 조율을 필요합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 means 'I think we'll need to coordinate the schedule'. 조율 (調律) is the precise business word for negotiating and aligning times among multiple parties, not just setting one person's calendar. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 hedge is essential politeness, softening 'we will need to' into 'I think we might need to'.

Polite-formal; safe upward and outward. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 hedge fits all business contexts. To peers in a direct message, 일정 맞춰 봐야 할 것 같아요 is a softer spoken-style variant. The bare imperative 일정 조율해 주세요 ('please coordinate') is fine only downward.
chips: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 — formal email
일정 맞춰 봐야 할 것 같아요 — casual/spoken
가능한 시간 알려 주시면 조율하겠습니다 — offer to coordinate yourself

structuredNuance.t: 조율 (調律, negotiating/aligning among multiple parties, give-and-take) vs. 조정 (調整, adjusting a plan more unilaterally) vs. 일정을 맞추다 (casual 'to align/match schedules'). For multi-party scheduling negotiation, 조율 is the professional choice.
일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 → 일정 조율 부탁드립니다 (direct request) → 가능한 시간 알려 주시면 일정 조율하겠습니다 (offer to handle it) → 일정 조율 후 다시 안내드리겠습니다 (promise to follow up after coordinating internally).

Do not translate 'coordinate' as 협력하다 (that is general teamwork cooperation). Do not write the flat 일정 조율이 필요합니다 to a client — the hedge 것 같습니다 is expected. Do not use the loanword 스케줄 in formal mail — use 일정. Watch the particle: 일정 조율'이' 필요하다 (subject marker 이/가), not 조율'을' 필요하다.

expressions.english: When would be a good time for you?
expressions.shortExplanation: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? is a practical expression meaning "When would be a good time for you?".
expressions.explanation: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? (eonje sigan gwaenchaneuseyo?) = "When would be a good time for you?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? ("When are you free?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asks the other person's availability
편하다 ('comfortable/convenient') variant — slightly warmer

usagePhrases.en: May I ask what time would work for you?
usagePhrases.note: More formal/tentative with 혹시 + -ㄹ까요
Proposing a specific day to narrow it down

examples.ko: 미팅 잡으려고 하는데 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: miting jabeuryeogo haneunde eonje sigan gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: I'd like to set up a meeting — when are you free?
examples.note: States the purpose first, then asks availability — the natural business order

examples.ko: 혹시 다음 주에 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? 오전, 오후 중 편하신 때 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: hoksi daeum jue eonje sigan gwaenchaneuseyo? ojeon, ohu jung pyeonhasin ttae allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Are you free sometime next week? Please let me know whether morning or afternoon works.
examples.note: 혹시 softens the question; offering two time windows narrows the back-and-forth

examples.ko: A: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? 이 건으로 잠깐 통화드리고 싶어서요. / B: 내일 오후 두 시 이후면 괜찮습니다.
examples.romanization: A: eonje sigan gwaenchaneuseyo? i geoneuro jamkkan tonghwadeurigo sipeoseoyo. / B: naeil ohu du si ihumyeon gwaenchanhseumnida.
examples.en: A: When are you free? I'd like a quick call about this matter. / B: After 2 p.m. tomorrow works for me.
examples.note: Real A/B exchange: stating the reason for the call, then the other person proposing a specific slot

expressions.nuance: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? is 언제 ('when') + 시간 ('time') + 괜찮으세요 (honorific '괜찮다', 'is it okay for you?'). It is the polite, natural way to ask someone's availability when arranging a meeting — literally 'when is your time okay?'. The honorific -으세요 on 괜찮다 directs the respect to the listener, so this is safe upward and to clients. A close variant is 언제가 편하세요? ('when is convenient?'), using 편하다 — slightly warmer and more considerate, stressing their comfort rather than just their schedule. The contrast: asking about THEIR availability (괜찮으세요 / 편하세요, honorific) vs. stating YOUR own availability (저는 ~ 괜찮아요 / 가능합니다) — keep the honorific form only for the other person. The English-speaker pitfall is the word 자유롭다 for 'free': 언제 자유로워요? means 'when are you free (as in liberated)?', not available — the correct words are 시간 괜찮다 / 시간 되다 / 한가하다. Another trap is dropping the honorific to a senior: 언제 시간 괜찮아? is 반말 and inappropriate in any work context.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 언제 자유로워요? for 'when are you free?'.
