자유롭다 is 'free' as in liberty/freedom, not availability. Use 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? or 언제 시간 되세요?
Putting honorific on your own availability.
Honor the other person: 언제 괜찮으세요? For your own time, plain 저는 ~ 괜찮아요/가능합니다. Don't say 저는 괜찮으세요.
Dropping honorific to a senior: 언제 시간 괜찮아?
괜찮아 is 반말. To a boss or client use 괜찮으세요? or 편하세요?, never the casual 괜찮아.

structuredNuance.t: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? literally means 'when is your time okay?' — the natural polite way to ask someone's availability for a meeting. The honorific -으세요 on 괜찮다 shows respect to the listener and makes the question safe for bosses, clients, and any senior person.

Safe upward and outward with the honorific -으세요. For maximum formality with executives, upgrade to 혹시 가능하신 시간이 언제일까요? The variant 언제가 편하세요? is slightly warmer, stressing their comfort. Never use 반말 괜찮아? in a work context, even with a close colleague in writing.

언제 시간 괜찮으세요? (open question, any time) vs. ○요일 어떠세요? (proposing a specific day) vs. 시간 되세요? ('does the time work?', equally common). The proposing form ○요일 어떠세요? is more efficient once you already know rough availability.
언제 시간 괜찮으세요? → 언제가 편하세요? → 혹시 가능하신 시간이 언제일까요? → ○요일 어떠세요? (propose a day). To narrow further: 오전/오후 중에 언제가 편하세요? ('morning or afternoon?'). Your own time: 저는 월요일 오후 이후 언제든 가능합니다.

Do not use 언제 자유로워요? — 자유롭다 means 'free as in liberty/freedom', not available. Use 시간 괜찮다 / 시간 되다 / 한가하다 for availability. Do not drop the honorific to a senior: 언제 괜찮아? is 반말. Do not apply the honorific -으세요 to your own time: only the other person's time gets the honorific.

expressions.english: I'd like to set up a meeting
expressions.shortExplanation: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to set up a meeting".
expressions.explanation: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 (hoeui iljeongeul japgo sipseumnida) means "I'd like to set up a meeting". Say it as one set phrase — for example 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 ("I'd like to schedule a meeting"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to schedule a meeting
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; proposes setting a meeting

usagePhrases.ko: 미팅 한번 잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다
usagePhrases.romanization: miting hanbeon jabeumyeon joeul geot gatseumnida
usagePhrases.en: It'd be good to set up a meeting
usagePhrases.note: Softer, suggestion-framed with 것 같다 hedge

usagePhrases.en: May I set up a meeting?
usagePhrases.note: Asks permission, extra courteous upward

usagePhrases.en: I'll set the schedule and share it
usagePhrases.note: When YOU will arrange and circulate it

examples.ko: 이 건으로 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다. 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: i geoneuro hoeui iljeongeul japgo sipseumnida. eonje sigan gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: I'd like to set up a meeting about this matter. When are you free?
examples.note: States the topic + immediately asks for availability — the most natural opening

examples.ko: 관련해서 한번 모여서 논의하면 좋을 것 같아 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다.
examples.romanization: gwallyeonhaeseo hanbeon moyeoseo nonuihamyeon joeul geot gata hoeui iljeongeul japgo sipseumnida.
examples.en: I think it'd help to gather and discuss, so I'd like to schedule a meeting.
examples.note: Gives the reason before proposing — softer and more justified

examples.ko: A: 가능하신 시간 몇 개 주시면 그에 맞춰 회의 일정을 잡겠습니다. / B: 화요일 오전이나 목요일 오후 괜찮습니다.
examples.romanization: A: ganeunghasin sigan myeot gae jusimyeon geue matchwo hoeui iljeongeul japgetseumnida. / B: hwayoil ojeonina mogyoil ohu gwaenchanhseumnida.
examples.en: A: If you give me a few possible times, I'll set the meeting to match. / B: Tuesday morning or Thursday afternoon works.
examples.note: A/B: invites slots and promises to finalize — the polite way to hand scheduling to the other party

expressions.nuance: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 is 회의 ('meeting', Sino-Korean 會議) + 일정 ('schedule') + 을 잡다 ('to set/fix') + -고 싶습니다 ('I would like to'). The verb 잡다 ('to catch/grab') is the idiomatic word for fixing or setting an appointment in Korean — 일정을 잡다, 약속을 잡다, 미팅을 잡다 — and English speakers rarely guess it. The -고 싶습니다 ('I'd like to') keeps it as a polite proposal rather than a command. The contrast: 회의 (a formal meeting, often internal, decision-making) vs. 미팅 (the loanword, often an external or more relaxed business meet-up) — both are common, but 회의 sounds more official/internal and 미팅 more flexible. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'set up' as 설치하다 ('to install') or 준비하다 ('to prepare') — 회의를 설치하다 is wrong (that is for installing equipment), and while 회의를 준비하다 ('prepare a meeting') is possible, the standard scheduling verb is 잡다. Watch the particle — 일정'을' 잡다 (object 을/를), not 일정에 잡다. Also -고 싶습니다 marks YOUR desire; to ask if they would like to meet, say 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 회의를 설치하고 싶습니다.
설치하다 is 'to install (equipment/software)'. To schedule a meeting, the verb is 잡다: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다.
Wrong particle: 일정에 잡고 싶습니다.
잡다 takes the object marker: 일정을 잡다. The particle is 을/를, not 에.
Attaching 싶다 to the other person.
-고 싶다 expresses YOUR desire. To ask if they'd like to meet, use 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?, not '~고 싶으세요' phrased about them awkwardly.

structuredNuance.t: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 means 'I'd like to schedule a meeting'. The key idiom is 잡다 ('to catch/grab') as the standard verb for fixing an appointment — 일정을 잡다, 약속을 잡다. The -고 싶습니다 frames it as a polite desire/proposal rather than a command.

Polite-formal (합쇼체), safe upward and to clients. For extra deference, use the softer suggestion frame 미팅 한번 잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다. To ask permission from a very senior person: 회의 일정 잡아도 될까요? Never use 반말 잡자 in any professional email context.
chips: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 — standard proposal
잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다 — softer suggestion
회의 일정 잡아도 될까요? — asks permission

structuredNuance.t: 회의 (formal/internal) vs. 미팅 (external/casual, loanword). The verb 잡다 ('to set') vs. 준비하다 ('to prepare') vs. 설치하다 ('to install', wrong for meetings). Also: 회의를 열다 ('to hold/open a meeting') describes the meeting itself, while 일정을 잡다 is the scheduling step.
회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 → 미팅 한번 잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다 (softer) → 회의 일정 잡아도 될까요? (permission) → 일정 잡아서 공유드리겠습니다 (when you handle it). Paired naturally with: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? immediately after.

Do not say 회의를 설치하고 싶습니다 — 설치하다 is 'to install equipment'. The scheduling verb is 잡다. Watch the particle: 일정'을' 잡다 (object marker), not 일정'에' 잡다. Do not use -고 싶습니다 about the other person; for their desire use 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?.

expressions.shortExplanation: 일정이 변경되었습니다 is a practical expression meaning "The schedule has changed".
expressions.explanation: "The schedule has changed" — that is 일정이 변경되었습니다 (iljeongi byeongyeongdoeeotseumnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 일정이 변경되었습니다 ("The schedule has been changed"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; announces a change neutrally

usagePhrases.en: I'm informing you the schedule has changed
usagePhrases.note: Adds the 'I'm letting you know' framing

usagePhrases.en: We've unavoidably had to change the schedule
usagePhrases.note: 부득이하게 ('unavoidably') softens/apologizes

usagePhrases.en: Would it be possible to change the schedule?
usagePhrases.note: Asking, not announcing — requests a change

examples.ko: 내부 사정으로 회의 일정이 변경되었습니다. 변경된 시간 확인 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: naebu sajeongeuro hoeui iljeongi byeongyeongdoeeotseumnida. byeongyeongdoen sigan hwagin butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: Due to internal circumstances, the meeting schedule has changed. Please check the updated time.
examples.note: States reason, announces change, requests confirmation — the full professional pattern

examples.ko: 부득이하게 발표 일정이 다음 주로 변경되었습니다. 양해 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: budeugihage balpyo iljeongi daeum juro byeongyeongdoeeotseumnida. yanghae butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: The presentation has unavoidably been moved to next week. Thank you for your understanding.
examples.note: 부득이하게 softens the announcement; 양해 부탁드립니다 completes the apology frame

examples.ko: A: 죄송하지만 일정이 변경되었습니다. 금요일 오후 두 시로 옮겨도 될까요? / B: 네, 괜찮습니다. 확인했습니다.
examples.romanization: A: joesonghajiman iljeongi byeongyeongdoeeotseumnida. geumyoil ohu du siro olmgyeodo doelkkayo? / B: ne, gwaenchanhseumnida. hwaginhaetseumnida.
examples.en: A: I'm sorry, but the schedule has changed. Would it be okay to move it to Friday at 2 p.m.? / B: Yes, that's fine. Noted.
examples.note: A/B: announcing a change with an apology and proposing the new time; recipient's polite confirmation

expressions.nuance: 일정이 변경되었습니다 is 일정 ('schedule') + 이 (subject marker) + 변경되다 ('to be changed', Sino-Korean 變更 + passive 되다) in formal past. The passive 변경되었습니다 ('has been changed') is deliberate: it states the change as a neutral fact without pointing a finger at who caused it, which Korean business culture favors for delivering inconvenient news. If you say 일정을 변경했습니다 (active, 'I changed the schedule'), you take direct ownership — sometimes appropriate but the passive is safer. The contrast: 변경 (變更, formally changing/altering a plan) vs. 바꾸다 (the plain native 'to change/swap', casual) — in business email you write 변경되었습니다, not the casual 바꿨어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and voice: 일정'이' 변경되었습니다 needs the subject marker 이/가 with the passive; the object marker 을/를 goes with the active voice (일정'을' 변경했습니다). Mixing them — 일정을 변경되었습니다 — is a classic grammar error. Always pair a schedule change with 양해 부탁드립니다 ('please understand') for courtesy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing voice/particle: 일정을 변경되었습니다.
Passive 변경되다 takes the subject marker: 일정'이' 변경되었습니다. The object marker 을/를 goes with active 일정'을' 변경했습니다.
Using casual 일정 바꿨어요 in formal mail.
바꾸다 is the plain/casual 'to change'. Professional email uses 변경: 일정이 변경되었습니다.
Announcing a change you caused with passive but no apology.
If you changed it and it inconveniences others, soften with 부득이하게 변경하게 되었습니다 and add 양해 부탁드립니다, rather than a cold passive alone.

structuredNuance.t: 일정이 변경되었습니다 announces 'the schedule has been changed'. The passive 변경되었습니다 is deliberate — it states a fact without assigning blame, which Korean business culture favors for inconvenient news. The active 일정을 변경했습니다 ('I changed it') takes direct ownership and is used when full transparency is needed.

Formal passive (변경되었습니다) for client- or senior-facing announcements. For a warmer, more apologetic tone add 부득이하게 at the start. Always follow with 양해 부탁드립니다 when the change inconveniences others. Casual internal note to peers: 일정이 바뀌었어요 is acceptable.

변경되다 (formal passive, Sino-Korean) vs. 바뀌다 (native-Korean passive, slightly more colloquial) vs. 바꾸다 (active, casual 'to change'). For professional email: 변경. For casual internal messages: 바뀌다 is fine. 바꾸다 (active) is only appropriate when owning the decision directly.
일정이 변경되었습니다 → 일정이 변경되어 안내드립니다 (adds 'I'm notifying you') → 부득이하게 일정을 변경하게 되었습니다 (apologetic active) → 일정 변경 가능할까요? (requesting a change, not announcing one). Always pair with 양해 부탁드립니다 or 죄송합니다.

Watch the particle + voice pair: passive 변경되다 takes subject marker 이/가 (일정'이' 변경되었습니다); active 변경하다 takes object marker 을/를 (일정'을' 변경했습니다). Mixing them (일정을 변경되었습니다) is a classic grammar error. Also do not write the casual 바꿨어요 in a client email.

expressions.shortExplanation: 보고드리겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I will report to you".
expressions.explanation: 보고드리겠습니다 (bogodeurigetseumnida) = "I will report to you". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 보고드리겠습니다 ("I will report (to you)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Humble-formal; you report up to a superior
Present form, heading a report email/message
Common with 진행 상황 ('progress/status')

usagePhrases.en: I'll report as soon as results are in
usagePhrases.note: Promises a follow-up report

examples.ko: 오늘까지 진행된 내용 보고드립니다. 검토 부탁드립니다.
examples.romanization: oneulkkaji jinhaengdoen naeyong bogodeurimnida. geomto butakdeurimnida.
examples.en: I'm reporting what has progressed so far today. Please review.
examples.note: Report heading + a review request — the standard upward reporting pattern

examples.ko: 말씀하신 건 확인해서 내일 오전 중으로 보고드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: malsseumhasin geon hwaginhaeseo naeil ojeon jungeuro bogodeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: I'll check the matter you mentioned and report by tomorrow morning.
examples.note: Acknowledges a superior's request and commits to a specific report time

examples.ko: A: 진행 상황 어떻게 됩니까? / B: 현재 50% 완료되었습니다. 마무리되는 대로 바로 보고드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: jinhaeng sanghwang eotteoke doemnikka? / B: hyeonjae 50% wallyodoeeotseumnida. mamuridoeneun daero baro bogodeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: How is the progress? / B: It is currently 50% complete. I will report to you as soon as it is finished.
examples.note: A/B: superior asking for status and a subordinate responding with humble 보고드리겠습니다

expressions.nuance: 보고드리겠습니다 is 보고 ('report', Sino-Korean 報告) + 드리다 (the HUMBLE form of 주다 'to give', used when the recipient is senior) + -겠습니다 ('I will'). The 드리다 is the heart of it: it lowers YOU relative to the person you are reporting to, so 보고드리다 inherently means reporting UPWARD to a boss, client, or senior — you would never use it to a junior. The contrast: 보고드리다 (humble, upward) vs. plain 보고하다 (neutral 'to report', describing the act or used horizontally) vs. 알리다 ('to inform/notify', more horizontal). The English-speaker pitfall is using 보고하다 flatly to a boss (보고합니다 / 보고할게요) — not wrong, but the humble 보고드립니다 / 보고드리겠습니다 is the expected register upward in hierarchical Korean offices, and missing 드리다 can feel under-polite. Another trap: 보고 is a 하다/드리다-noun, so you say 보고드리다 or 보고하다, written as one word — never 보고를 드리다 split apart. Also note that 보고 (報告, report) differs entirely from the connective 보고 in 보고 싶다 ('want to see') — same romanization, different origin.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using plain 보고합니다 to a senior.
To a boss/client the humble form 보고드립니다 / 보고드리겠습니다 (with 드리다) is expected. Plain 보고합니다 can feel under-polite upward.
Saying 보고드리겠습니다 to a junior.
드리다 lowers you toward a SENIOR. To a subordinate you wouldn't humble yourself; use 보고하다 or, depending on direction, just 알려 줄게요.
Confusing 보고 (報告) with 보고 (보다).
報告 = a report; 보고 in 보고 싶다 is the connective of 보다 ('see'). 보고드리겠습니다 means 'I'll report', not 'I want to see'.

structuredNuance.t: 보고드리겠습니다 means 'I will report (to you)'. The 드리다 is the core: it is the humble form of 주다, lowering yourself toward the senior recipient. This makes 보고드리다 an inherently upward-directed verb — you report to your boss, not to a subordinate.

Use 보고드리겠습니다 / 보고드립니다 upward — to bosses, seniors, clients. The present 보고드립니다 heads a report message or starts a verbal update. The future 보고드리겠습니다 commits to a follow-up. To describe reporting neutrally (e.g., in a policy document), use 보고하다. To a subordinate, simply say 알려 줄게요 or 전달할게요.

보고드리다 (humble, upward) vs. 보고하다 (neutral 'report') vs. 알리다 ('to inform', more horizontal) vs. 전달하다 ('to relay/pass on', lateral or downward). 보고드리다 is strictly upward; using it to a junior sounds odd.
보고드리겠습니다 (future) → 보고드립니다 (present heading) → 진행 상황 보고드리겠습니다 (with topic) → 결과 나오면 바로 보고드리겠습니다 (immediate follow-up promise) → 확인 후 보고드리겠습니다 (after checking). All use the same 드리다 humble core.

Do not use the plain 보고합니다 upward if 보고드립니다 is expected — it can feel slightly under-polite in hierarchical offices. Do not split 보고를 드리다 apart — 보고드리다 is written as one verb. Do not confuse 보고 (報告, report) with the connective 보고 from 보다 (as in 보고 싶다, 'want to see').

expressions.english: I'll check and get back to you
expressions.shortExplanation: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "I'll check and get back to you".
expressions.explanation: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (hwagin hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida) means "I'll check and get back to you". Say it as one set phrase — for example 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 ("I'll check and contact you again"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'll check and contact you again
usagePhrases.note: Humble-formal; promises a follow-up

usagePhrases.en: I'll look into it and get back to you
usagePhrases.note: 알아보다 ('look into') for things you must research

usagePhrases.en: I'll contact you as soon as it's confirmed
usagePhrases.note: -는 대로 ('as soon as') for prompt follow-up
Signals you must check with your team first

examples.ko: 지금 바로 답변드리기 어려워서, 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: jigeum baro dapbyeondeurigi eoryeowoseo, hwagin hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: It's hard to answer right now, so I'll check and contact you again.
examples.note: Polite way to defer an immediate answer without being evasive

examples.ko: 재고 상황 확인 후 오늘 중으로 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: jaego sanghwang hwagin hu oneul jungeuro dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: I'll check the stock and get back to you within today.
examples.note: Adds a specific time commitment — makes the promise concrete and trustworthy

examples.ko: A: 이 건 언제쯤 처리될까요? / B: 담당자에게 확인 후 내일까지 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: i geon eonjejjeum cheoridoelkkayo? / B: damdangjaege hwagin hu naeilkkaji dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: When do you think this matter will be handled? / B: I'll check with the person in charge and get back to you by tomorrow.
examples.note: A/B: client asking for a timeline; staff deflecting politely and committing to a follow-up date

expressions.nuance: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 is 확인 ('check') + 후 ('after') + 다시 ('again') + 연락 ('contact', Sino-Korean 連絡) + 드리다 (humble 'give/do for a senior') + -겠습니다 ('I will'). It is the courteous, professional way to say 'let me look into this and get back to you' — invaluable when you cannot answer on the spot. The humble 연락드리다 (vs. plain 연락하다) lowers you toward the client or senior, which is the expected register outward and upward. The contrast: 연락드리다 ('I'll contact you', humble, you reaching out first) vs. 회신드리다 ('I'll reply', responding specifically to their message) — both work, but 연락 is broader ('get in touch') while 회신 is 'a reply to your email'. The English-speaker pitfall is the calque 'get back to you' rendered as 돌아오겠습니다 ('I will physically return') — that sounds like coming back to a location, not following up; the idiom is 다시 연락드리겠습니다. Another trap is dropping 드리다 to a client (다시 연락하겠습니다) — understandable but less polite; 연락드리겠습니다 is the safe default. A bare 다시 연락드리겠습니다 with no timeframe can feel vague — add 오늘 중으로 / 내일까지 / 확인되는 대로 to make the promise concrete.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다시 돌아오겠습니다 for 'I'll get back to you'.
돌아오다 is 'to physically return/come back'. To follow up, say 다시 연락드리겠습니다, not 돌아오겠습니다.
Dropping 드리다 to a client: 다시 연락하겠습니다.
To a client/senior the humble 연락드리겠습니다 is expected. Plain 연락하겠습니다 is fine internally but less courteous outward.
Promising follow-up with no timeframe.
다시 연락드리겠습니다 alone can feel vague. Add a window — 확인되는 대로 / 오늘 중으로 다시 연락드리겠습니다 — so the reader knows when to expect you.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 means 'I'll check and get back to you' — the courteous way to defer an immediate answer. The humble 드리다 lowers you toward the client or senior, signaling this is a service-minded promise, not just a statement of intent.

The humble 연락드리다 is essential upward and outward. Downward or to peers, plain 연락하겠습니다 / 연락할게요 is fine. Always add a timeframe (오늘 중으로, 내일까지, 확인되는 대로) so the promise does not feel vague. If the delay might be longer, explain why briefly.
chips: 확인되는 대로 연락드리겠습니다 — 'as soon as confirmed'

structuredNuance.t: 연락드리다 ('I'll contact you', humble, you initiate) vs. 회신드리다 ('I'll reply', responding to their message) vs. 알아보고 드리겠습니다 ('I'll look into it and let you know', 알아보다 stresses research). Use 알아보다 when you need to gather information before reporting back.
확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 → 알아보고 연락드리겠습니다 (looking into something) → 확인되는 대로 연락드리겠습니다 (as soon as confirmed) → 내부적으로 확인 후 회신드리겠습니다 (internal check + formal reply). Add 오늘 중으로 / 내일까지 for a concrete commitment.

Do not say 다시 돌아오겠습니다 — 돌아오다 is 'to physically return'. The follow-up idiom is 다시 연락드리겠습니다. Do not drop 드리다 to a client — 연락드리겠습니다 not 연락하겠습니다. Do not leave the promise without a timeframe — 다시 연락드리겠습니다 alone sounds vague; add 오늘 중으로 or 확인되는 대로.

expressions.english: May I ask how the matter I requested is going?
expressions.shortExplanation: 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? is a practical expression meaning "May I ask how the matter I requested is going?".
expressions.explanation: "May I ask how the matter I requested is going?" — that is 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? (hwagin butakdeurin geon eotteoke doeeosseulkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? ("How is the matter I asked about going?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: How is the matter I asked about going?
usagePhrases.note: Polite follow-up/nudge on a pending item

usagePhrases.en: May I ask about the progress?
usagePhrases.note: 여쭤보다 (humble 'ask') for a gentle check-in

usagePhrases.en: Would a reply on my previous email be possible?
usagePhrases.note: References the earlier mail directly

usagePhrases.en: I know you're busy, but I'm asking once more
usagePhrases.note: Softener-led nudge for a slow reply

examples.ko: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요?
examples.romanization: bappeusin wajunge joesonghajiman, hwagin butakdeurin geon eotteoke doeeosseulkkayo?
examples.en: Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but how is the matter I asked about going?
examples.note: Face-saving softener before the nudge — essential when following up with a senior

examples.ko: 저번에 보내드린 견적 관련해서 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? 일정이 있어 여쭤봅니다.
examples.romanization: jeobeone bonaedeurin gyeonjeok gwallyeonhaeseo hwagin butakdeurin geon eotteoke doeeosseulkkayo? iljeongi isseo yeojjwobomnida.
examples.en: Regarding the quote I sent before, how is the matter going? I'm asking because there's a deadline.
examples.note: Ties the nudge to a specific earlier document and gives a reason (deadline) — more persuasive than a bare follow-up

examples.ko: A: 지난주에 검토 부탁드린 기획안 어떻게 되었을까요? / B: 아, 죄송합니다. 내일 오전까지 피드백 드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: jinanjue geomto butakdeurin gihoegan eotteoke doeeosseulkkayo? / B: a, joesonghamnida. naeil ojeonkkaji pideubaek deurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: How is the proposal I asked you to review last week going? / B: Oh, I'm sorry. I'll give you feedback by tomorrow morning.
examples.note: Real A/B exchange: gentle nudge and the recipient's apology + commitment — shows the softened form working as intended

expressions.nuance: 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? is 확인 부탁드린 ('that I asked you to check', relative clause) + 건 (contraction of 것은, 'the matter') + 어떻게 ('how') + 되었을까요 ('I wonder how it has come along', the speculative -을까요 form). This is the diplomatic way to CHASE a pending request without sounding pushy — the soft -을까요 ('I wonder if…') and the indirect 어떻게 되었- ('how has it gone') let you nudge while preserving the reader's face, which is essential in hierarchical Korean offices. Face-preservation (체면) is the social reason this indirect form exists; a blunt status demand is rude upward. The contrast: 왜 아직 확인 안 하셨어요? ('why haven't you checked yet?') is accusatory; 어떻게 되었을까요? frames the same query as innocent curiosity. Also 됐어요? (flat 'is it done?') is too direct upward. The English-speaker pitfall is the impatient calque 'any update?' as bare 업데이트 있어요? — Konglish and curt; Korean wraps the nudge in indirectness. Always lead with a face-saving softener (바쁘시겠지만, 죄송하지만) before the question when nudging a senior.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Chasing with 왜 아직 확인 안 하셨어요?
That accuses the reader of failing to act. Use the face-saving 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? to nudge gently.
Writing bare 업데이트 있어요? for 'any update?'.
Konglish and curt. Korean phrases a status nudge indirectly: 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? or 어떻게 되었을까요?
Skipping a softener before nudging a senior.
Going straight to the question can sound impatient. Lead with 바쁘시겠지만 or 죄송하지만 to cushion the follow-up.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? is the diplomatic way to follow up on a pending request without sounding pushy. The speculative -을까요 ('I wonder if…') and the indirect 어떻게 되었- ('how has it come along') preserve the reader's face — a core value in Korean hierarchical culture.

Used upward or to clients when nudging a delayed response. Always lead with a softener: 바쁘시겠지만 / 죄송하지만. For an even gentler approach, use 혹시 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? (the humble ask-permission form). Never use bare 됐어요? or 왜 안 하셨어요? upward.
chips: 혹시 여쭤봐도 될까요? — asking permission to ask

structuredNuance.t: 어떻게 되었을까요? (speculative, gentle, face-preserving) vs. 됐어요? (flat 'done?', too direct upward) vs. 왜 아직 안 하셨어요? (accusatory, never use upward). In written email, 혹시 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? with humble 여쭤보다 is also excellent.
확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? → 혹시 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? → 지난번 메일 관련 회신 가능하실까요? → 바쁘시겠지만 다시 한번 여쭤봅니다. All carry the same indirect-nudge function with varying levels of formality.

Do not write bare 업데이트 있어요? — Konglish and curt. Korean wraps the nudge in indirectness. Do not skip the softener (바쁘시겠지만 / 죄송하지만) before following up with a senior. Do not use 됐어요? or 왜 아직 확인 안 하셨어요? — these are too direct and can damage the relationship.

expressions.english: If you review and share feedback, I'll incorporate it
expressions.shortExplanation: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 is a practical expression meaning "If you review and share feedback, I'll incorporate it".
expressions.explanation: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 (geomto hu uigyeon jusimyeon banyeonghagetseumnida) = "If you review and share feedback, I'll incorporate it". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 ("I'll incorporate your feedback after you review"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'll incorporate your feedback after you review
usagePhrases.note: Polite; invites comments and promises to apply them

usagePhrases.en: I'll revise if you give comments
usagePhrases.note: 코멘트 ('comments') variant, common in practice

usagePhrases.en: I'll apply the feedback and re-share
usagePhrases.note: When you'll send an updated version back

usagePhrases.ko: 수정할 부분 알려 주시면 바로 반영하겠습니다
usagePhrases.romanization: sujeonghal bubun allyeo jusimyeon baro banyeonghagetseumnida
usagePhrases.en: Tell me what to fix and I'll apply it right away
usagePhrases.note: Asks for specific edit points

examples.ko: 초안입니다. 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: choanimnida. geomto hu uigyeon jusimyeon banyeonghagetseumnida.
examples.en: This is a draft. I'll incorporate your feedback after you review.
examples.note: Classic draft-submission line — sends the document and opens the revision loop

examples.ko: 부족한 부분 있으면 편하게 말씀해 주세요. 바로 반영하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: bujokan bubun isseumyeon pyeonhage malsseumhae juseyo. baro banyeonghagetseumnida.
examples.en: If there are weak spots, feel free to let me know. I'll incorporate it right away.
examples.note: Humble invitation: the 편하게 ('freely/comfortably') signals you welcome criticism

examples.ko: A: 1차 기획안 공유드립니다. 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영해서 2차 안 준비하겠습니다. / B: 읽어 보고 오늘 오후에 피드백 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: 1cha gihoegan gongyudeurimnida. geomto hu uigyeon jusimyeon banyeonghaeseo 2cha an junbihagetseumnida. / B: ilgeo bogo oneul ohue pideubaek deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Sharing the first draft. After review, I'll incorporate feedback into a second version. / B: I'll read it and give feedback this afternoon.
examples.note: A/B: full revision cycle stated by the sender; senior commits a feedback time — the ideal exchange for a draft submission

expressions.nuance: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 is 검토 ('review') + 후 ('after') + 의견 ('opinion/feedback', Sino-Korean 意見) + 주시면 ('if you would give') + 반영하겠습니다 ('I will reflect/incorporate', Sino-Korean 反映). The standout word is 반영하다 — literally 'to reflect (as in a mirror)', it is the precise business verb for incorporating feedback into a document, and English speakers almost never produce it naturally. The -주시면 … 반영하겠습니다 frame ('if you give … I'll incorporate') is collaborative and positions you as receptive. The contrast: 반영하다 ('incorporate/apply feedback into the work') vs. 수정하다 (修正, 'to revise/correct' the document itself) vs. 적용하다 (適用, 'to apply' a rule or setting). For taking someone's comments and working them into a document, 반영 is the exact choice — it captures both receiving and embedding the input. The English-speaker pitfall is 포함하다 ('to include'): 의견을 포함하겠습니다 sounds like attaching their opinion verbatim rather than acting on it. Also: in business you ask for 의견 ('considered feedback'), not the casual 생각 ('thought'). 반영 is a 하다-noun; the collocation is 의견을 반영하다 (object 을/를).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 의견을 포함하겠습니다 for 'incorporate feedback'.
포함하다 is 'to include/contain'. To actually work feedback into the document, the verb is 반영하다: 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
Asking for 생각 instead of 의견.
생각 ('thought') is casual. In business you request 의견 ('considered opinion/feedback'): 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
Confusing 반영 with 수정.
반영하다 = incorporate (their feedback into the work); 수정하다 = revise/correct (the document). They pair — you 반영 the 의견 by 수정하는 것 — but use 반영 for 'apply the feedback'.

structuredNuance.t: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 means 'after you review, if you give feedback I'll incorporate it'. The key word is 반영하다 — literally 'to reflect (as in a mirror)', the precise business verb for working feedback into a document. It captures both receiving input and embedding it in the work.

Polite-formal (합쇼체), used when submitting a draft to a senior or client. The -주시면 … 반영하겠습니다 conditional is courteous and collaborative. For extra humility, add 부족한 부분이 많지만 ('though there are many shortcomings') before the line. To peers, the lighter 코멘트 주시면 수정할게요 is fine.
chips: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 — formal draft submission
피드백 반영해서 다시 공유드리겠습니다 — after revision

structuredNuance.t: 반영하다 (incorporate feedback into the work) vs. 수정하다 (revise/correct the document itself) vs. 적용하다 (apply a rule/setting). The three often work together — you 반영 the 의견 by 수정하는 것 — but 반영 specifically frames the act of taking external input and weaving it in.
검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 → 코멘트 주시면 수정하겠습니다 (loanword variant) → 피드백 반영해서 다시 공유드리겠습니다 (after revision, re-sharing) → 수정할 부분 알려 주시면 바로 반영하겠습니다 (asking for specific edit points).

Do not say 의견을 포함하겠습니다 — 포함하다 ('to include/contain') sounds like attaching their opinion as an appendix, not acting on it. The verb is 반영하다. Do not ask for 생각 instead of 의견 — 생각 is casual; business uses 의견. The particle is 의견'을' 반영하다 (object marker 을/를).

expressions.english: I'm sorry to bother you when you're so busy, but…
expressions.shortExplanation: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 is a practical expression meaning "I'm sorry to bother you when you're so busy, but…".
expressions.explanation: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 (bappeusin wajunge joesonghajiman) means "I'm sorry to bother you when you're so busy, but…". Say it as one set phrase — for example 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 ("Sorry to trouble you while you're busy, but"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Sorry to trouble you while you're busy, but
usagePhrases.note: Polite softener before a request to a senior

usagePhrases.en: I know you must be busy, but
usagePhrases.note: Shorter, very common request-cushion

usagePhrases.en: I know it's a hassle, but
usagePhrases.note: Apologizes for the inconvenience of the ask

usagePhrases.en: Sorry to be a bother, but
usagePhrases.note: Warmer/more personal apology variant

examples.ko: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 잠깐 확인 부탁드려도 될까요?
examples.romanization: bappeusin wajunge joesonghajiman, jamkkan hwagin butakdeuryeodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Sorry to bother you while you're busy, but could I ask you to check quickly?
examples.note: Softener + small request — the most common business usage

examples.ko: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 이 건만 먼저 처리해 주실 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: bappeusin wajunge joesonghajiman, i geonman meonjeo cheorihae jusil su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: Sorry to trouble you, but could you handle just this one thing first?
examples.note: Softener before asking for priority — acknowledges you are asking for something extra

examples.ko: A: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 내일 회의 자료 오늘까지 회신 가능하실까요? / B: 네, 오늘 오후까지 보내드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: bappeusin wajunge joesonghajiman, naeil hoeui jaryo oneulkkaji hoesin ganeunghasilkkayo? / B: ne, oneul ohukkaji bonaedeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: A: I'm sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you reply with tomorrow's materials by today? / B: Yes, I'll send it by this afternoon.
examples.note: Real A/B: softener cushions a tight-deadline request; the senior's reply shows the formula worked — they committed rather than pushing back

expressions.nuance: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 is 바쁘신 (honorific 'busy') + 와중에 ('in the midst of', Sino-Korean 渦中 'whirlpool/turmoil') + 죄송하지만 ('I'm sorry, but'). It is a face-saving CUSHION placed before asking a senior or client for something — Korean business etiquette strongly favors acknowledging the other person's burden before adding to it. The honorific 바쁘'신' is essential: you honor THEIR busyness. The contrast: 와중에 specifically implies a hectic, turbulent stretch, slightly more vivid than the plain 바쁘시겠지만 ('you must be busy, but'); 와중에 is a touch more deferential. Do not confuse 와중 with 도중 (途中, 'on the way/midway in a process') — 와중 connotes commotion while 도중 is simply 'during/en route'. The English-speaker pitfall is omitting the cushion entirely and leading straight with the request — even if the request itself is polite, the lack of a softener sounds abrupt and demanding in Korean. Another pitfall is over-apologizing by stacking multiple softeners (죄송하지만 + 미안하지만 + 실례지만); pick one. Register note: 죄송하지만 (formal) outranks 미안하지만 (casual) upward — always use 죄송하지만 in business email.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Leading straight with the request, no cushion.
In Korean business, asking a senior bluntly feels demanding even if polite. Open with 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 or 바쁘시겠지만 to soften.
Dropping the honorific: 바쁜 와중에.
You honor the reader's busyness: 바쁘'신' 와중에. Plain 바쁜 omits the respect due to a senior/client.
Confusing 와중 with 도중.
와중 (渦中) implies a hectic/turbulent stretch; 도중 (途中) just means 'midway/on the way'. For 'while you're busy', it's 바쁘신 와중에.

structuredNuance.t: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 is a face-saving CUSHION placed before a request to a senior or client. It acknowledges their burden before adding to it — a non-negotiable step in Korean business etiquette. The honorific 바쁘'신' is essential: you honor their busyness, not your own.

Used in formal business email upward or to clients. 죄송하지만 (formal) is correct here; 미안하지만 (casual) is for friends. The shorter 바쁘시겠지만 is fine in email and even spoken requests. For extreme deference — a very senior executive — combine: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 번거로우시겠지만.
chips: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 — full, most deferential

structuredNuance.t: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 (cushion before a request to a senior, acknowledges their busy state) vs. 양해 부탁드립니다 (requests tolerance for an inconvenience you caused) vs. 번거로우시겠지만 (apologizes for the hassle of the ask itself). These serve related but different social functions — don't swap them.
바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 → 바쁘시겠지만 (shorter) → 번거로우시겠지만 (apologizes for the bother) → 귀찮게 해 드려 죄송하지만 (personal apology variant). All work as pre-request cushions; use one at a time, never stack all at once.

Do not skip the cushion — even a polite request to a senior without a softener can read as demanding in Korean. Do not stack multiple apologies (죄송하지만 + 미안하지만 together); pick one. Do not use 미안하지만 in formal email — 죄송하지만 is the business-level form. Do not confuse 와중 (turmoil/commotion) with 도중 (en route/midway).

expressions.shortExplanation: 양해 부탁드립니다 is a practical expression meaning "Thank you for your understanding".
expressions.explanation: "Thank you for your understanding" — that is 양해 부탁드립니다 (yanghae butakdeurimnida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 양해 부탁드립니다 ("Please understand / thank you for understanding"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please understand / thank you for understanding
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; asks forbearance for an inconvenience
Softer, slightly less stiff than 드립니다

usagePhrases.en: I'd be grateful for your understanding
usagePhrases.note: Extra-courteous conditional form

usagePhrases.en: We ask for your kind understanding
usagePhrases.note: 널리 ('broadly') for notices/announcements

examples.en: Sorry for the late reply. Thank you for your understanding.
examples.note: Pairs an apology with a request to understand — the standard two-step for any inconvenience

examples.ko: 내부 사정으로 일정이 변경된 점 양해 부탁드리며, 추후 다시 안내드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: naebu sajeongeuro iljeongi byeongyeongdoen jeom yanghae butakdeurimyeo, chuhu dasi annaedeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: Please understand the schedule change due to internal circumstances; I'll inform you again later.
examples.note: Business pattern: reason + 양해 부탁드리며 + promise to follow up

examples.ko: A: 처리가 이렇게 오래 걸리나요? / B: 죄송합니다, 내부 검토가 필요해서요. 양해 부탁드립니다. 내일 오전까지 처리하겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: cheoriga ireoke orae geollinayo? / B: joesonghamnida, naebu geomtoga piryohaeseoyo. yanghae butakdeurimnida. naeil ojeonkkaji cheorihagetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Does it really take this long? / B: I'm sorry, internal review is required. Please bear with us. I'll handle it by tomorrow morning.
examples.note: A/B: client expressing frustration; staff apologizing, explaining briefly, asking understanding, and committing to a deadline

expressions.nuance: 양해 부탁드립니다 is 양해 ('understanding/forbearance', Sino-Korean 諒解) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly ask'). It asks someone to TOLERATE an inconvenience you have caused — a delay, a change, a limitation. It is the courteous companion to an apology: 죄송합니다 (sorry) followed by 양해 부탁드립니다 (please bear with us). The key contrast English speakers miss: 양해 vs. 이해 (理解). 이해 is 'comprehension' — grasping a concept or instructions; 양해 is 'forbearance/tolerance' for something that went sideways. Saying 이해 부탁드립니다 wrongly asks 'please comprehend this', as if the reader might not understand your meaning, when you actually mean 'please tolerate this hiccup'. Another contrast: 양해 부탁드립니다 (asking forbearance for an inconvenience you caused) vs. 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 (a cushion before making a new request) — different social functions. The English-speaker pitfall is the literal 'thank you for your understanding' as 이해해 주셔서 감사합니다 — grammatical but subtly wrong because 이해 is about comprehension; the set business phrase is 양해 부탁드립니다. 양해 is a 하다-noun: verb is 양해하다, so 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다, never 양해 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이해 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please understand (bear with us)'.
이해 is 'comprehension' (grasping meaning). For tolerating an inconvenience, use 양해: 양해 부탁드립니다.
Saying 양해 주세요.
양해 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. Use the verb: 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다.
Using 양해 with no apology or reason.
양해 asks forbearance for something. Pair it with a brief apology/reason — 늦어 죄송합니다, 양해 부탁드립니다 — or it sounds like asking a favor out of nowhere.

structuredNuance.t: 양해 부탁드립니다 asks someone to TOLERATE an inconvenience you have caused. It is the courteous companion to an apology: 죄송합니다 + 양해 부탁드립니다 is the standard two-step for any delay, change, or limitation in Korean business communication.

Polite-formal (합쇼체), used upward and outward. Always pair with an explanation or apology — 양해 부탁드립니다 alone without context sounds like asking a favor out of nowhere. For announcements or notices, 널리 양해 부탁드립니다 adds the formal broadcast feel.

양해 (諒解, forbearance for an inconvenience) vs. 이해 (理解, comprehension of meaning/concept) vs. 용서 (容恕, forgiveness for a fault — stronger). Use 양해 when something is inconvenient; use 이해 when checking if instructions are clear; never use 용서 unless the mistake is serious.
양해 부탁드립니다 → 양해 부탁드려요 (softer) → 양해해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (conditional, most courteous) → 널리 양해 부탁드립니다 (broadcast). Always precede with the reason: 일정이 늦어진 점 / 변경된 점 + 양해 부탁드립니다.

Do not use 이해 부탁드립니다 — 이해 is comprehension, not tolerance for an inconvenience. Do not say 이해해 주셔서 감사합니다 as 'thank you for your understanding' — it means 'thanks for comprehending', subtly off. Do not say 양해 주세요 — 양해 is a 하다-noun; use 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다.

expressions.english: Please CC them (add to the CC line)
expressions.shortExplanation: 참조에 넣어 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please CC them (add to the CC line)".
expressions.explanation: 참조에 넣어 주세요 (chamjoe neoeo juseyo) = "Please CC them (add to the CC line)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 참조에 넣어 주세요 ("Please add them to CC"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asks to copy someone on the email
More polite/formal with -주시겠어요
Stating that you copied someone

usagePhrases.en: Please CC me from now on too
usagePhrases.note: Asking to be kept in the loop going forward

examples.ko: 박 과장님도 참조에 넣어 주세요. 이 건은 공유가 필요합니다.
examples.romanization: bak gwajangnimdo chamjoe neoeo juseyo. i geoneun gongyuga piryohamnida.
examples.en: Please CC Manager Park as well. This matter needs to be shared.
examples.note: Asks to copy a specific person and gives a brief reason

examples.ko: 이 건은 팀장님도 아셔야 해서 참조에 넣었습니다.
examples.romanization: i geoneun timjangnimdo asyeoya haeseo chamjoe neoeotseumnida.
examples.en: The team lead should know about this, so I CC'd them.
examples.note: Explains WHY you copied someone — prevents the team lead from wondering why they received it

examples.ko: A: 다음 메일부터는 저도 참조에 넣어 주시겠어요? 진행 상황 파악이 필요해서요. / B: 네, 앞으로 참조에 넣겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: daeum meilbuteoneun jeodo chamjoe neoeo jusigesseoyo? jinhaeng sanghwang paagi piryohaeseoyo. / B: ne, apeuro chamjoe neoketseumnida.
examples.en: A: Could you CC me from the next email? I need to keep track of the progress. / B: Yes, I'll CC you going forward.
examples.note: A/B: requesting to be added to the CC loop and the sender agreeing — the most practical daily use

expressions.nuance: 참조에 넣어 주세요 is 참조 ('CC/reference', Sino-Korean 參照) + 에 ('into') + 넣다 ('to put in') + 주세요 ('please'). In Korean email, 참조 (參照) is literally the CC field, and 참조에 넣다 ('put into CC') is the everyday office phrase for keeping someone in the loop. This is the critical contrast that trips English speakers: 참조 (參照, the CC line) vs. 참고 (參考, 'for your reference/FYI'). They look and sound nearly identical and both loosely translate as 'reference' in English, but 참조 = the CC recipients in an email header, while 참고 = 'please take note of this information'. Saying 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — you do not 'put someone into FYI'. The other field terms to know: 받는 사람 (To), 참조 (CC), 숨은 참조 (BCC). The English-speaker pitfall is the loanword 씨씨에 넣어 주세요 — understood in casual chat but not standard business Korean; use 참조. The particle: 참조'에' 넣다 (location 'into the CC field'), not 참조를 넣다. To say you already copied someone: 참조에 넣었습니다 or 참조로 넣었습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 참조 with 참고.
참조 (參照) is the CC line; 참고 (參考) is 'for your reference/FYI'. 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — to CC someone, say 참조에 넣어 주세요.
Writing 씨씨에 넣어 주세요.
씨씨 (CC) is casual/Konglish. Standard business Korean uses 참조: 참조에 넣어 주세요.
Wrong particle: 참조를 넣어 주세요 (meaning to CC a person).
You put the person INTO the CC field: 참조'에' 넣어 주세요. The location particle 에 marks where they go.

structuredNuance.t: 참조에 넣어 주세요 means 'please add [them] to the CC line'. 참조 (參照) is literally the CC field in Korean email, and 참조에 넣다 ('put into CC') is the standard business phrase. The other email field terms: 받는 사람 (To), 참조 (CC), 숨은 참조 (BCC).
참조에 넣어 주세요 is the everyday polite form. For a senior or client, upgrade to 참조에 넣어 주시겠어요? (more deferential). To state you CC'd someone: 참조에 넣었습니다. To request ongoing CC: 다음부터는 저도 참조 부탁드립니다.
chips: 참조로 넣었습니다 — stating you CC'd someone

structuredNuance.t: 참조 (參照, the CC line — a person is added to it) vs. 참고 (參考, FYI — information to note). These are the two most commonly confused terms in Korean email. A third: 숨은 참조 (BCC — blind carbon copy). Never use 참고에 넣어 주세요 — you do not 'put someone into FYI'.
참조에 넣어 주세요 → 참조에 넣어 주시겠어요? (more polite) → 참조로 넣었습니다 (stating you CC'd) → 다음부터는 저도 참조 부탁드립니다 (asking to be kept in loop) → 숨은 참조로 넣어 주세요 (BCC variant).

Do not confuse 참조 (CC line) with 참고 (FYI). 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong. Do not use the loanword 씨씨에 넣어 주세요 in formal email — use 참조. Watch the particle: 참조'에' 넣다 (location, into the field), not 참조를 넣다 when placing a person in the CC field.

expressions.shortExplanation: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll have it hot, please".
expressions.explanation: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요 (ttatteutan geollo juseyo) means "I'll have it hot, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. ("I'll take the hot one, please."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'll take the hot one, please.
usagePhrases.note: Customer to barista; standard polite when picking hot over iced
반말 to a friend behind the counter or a very casual setting; rarely said to staff
거로 and 걸로 are both fine; 걸로 (걸=거+ㄹ) is the everyday spoken form
Natural extension: name the drink instead of just 'the hot one'

examples.ko: A: 따뜻한 거 드릴까요, 아이스요? / B: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: ttatteutan geo deurilkkayo, aiseuyo? / B: ttatteutan geollo juseyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I make it hot, or iced? / B: Hot, please.
examples.note: 걸로 directly answers a binary hot/iced question — the particle -(으)로 signals 'I'm choosing this option'

examples.ko: 라떼 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. 시럽은 빼고요.
examples.romanization: ratte ttatteutan geollo juseyo. sireobeun ppaegoyo.
examples.en: A hot latte, please. No syrup.
examples.note: Adding a tweak right after the order: 빼고요 = 'leave it out'; -고요 softens any tacked-on request at a café counter

examples.ko: 밖이 너무 추워서요, 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. 큰 사이즈로요.
examples.romanization: bakki neomu chuwoseoyo, ttatteutan geollo juseyo. keun saijeuroyo.
examples.en: It's freezing outside, so a hot one please. Large size.
examples.note: Real spoken flow: optional reason ending in -서요 → temperature choice → size tweak, all politely chained

expressions.nuance: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요 is the standard answer when a barista asks 따뜻한 거요 아이스요? (hot or iced?) or when you order a hot drink unprompted. The particle -(으)로 attaches to the thing you're selecting and means 'I'll go with the ~'; 걸로 is simply 거(것) + 로 in spoken contraction, so '따뜻한 걸로' = 'the warm one.' Register is plain polite -요, which is correct for all café and store staff — never drop to 반말 (따뜻한 거 줘) with someone you don't know personally. The closest loanword alternative is 핫으로 주세요, understood by most younger baristas but 따뜻한 걸로 is the natural native default and carries no ambiguity. The critical English-speaker error is confusing 따뜻한 with 뜨거운: 뜨거운 describes something dangerously, painfully hot (a 뜨거운 냄비 = scorching pot), while 따뜻한 means pleasantly warm — using 뜨거운 걸로 at a café is technically intelligible but sounds as if you want to scald yourself.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 뜨거운 걸로 주세요 for a hot drink — 뜨거운 means scaldingly hot (burns); warm-temperature drinks are 따뜻한, so use 따뜻한 걸로.
Dropping 로 and saying 따뜻한 거 주세요 — understandable but the 걸로 form ('the ~ one') is what signals you're choosing between options; omitting -로 is grammatically loose.
Using English 'hot one please' word order as 하나 따뜻한 주세요 — Korean puts the modifier before the noun: 따뜻한 거 / 따뜻한 걸로, not a numeral first.

structuredNuance.t: Word-by-word: 따뜻한(warm) + 걸(것을, the thing) + 로(choice particle, 'going with') + 주세요(give me). The whole phrase compresses to 'please give me the warm one' — the -(으)로 particle is what signals a selection between options, making this the natural counter-answer to a hot/iced binary question.

Use at any café or convenience store to specify a hot drink, whether the staff asked or you're ordering unprompted. Always -요 polite with staff; 반말 form 따뜻한 거 줘 is only for a friend staffing a pop-up or someone you know well — never with a stranger behind a counter.

핫으로 주세요 (loanword 'hot') is popular at chains and understood everywhere, but 따뜻한 걸로 is the safe, age-neutral native choice. 따뜻하게 해 주세요 ('please make it warm') is an occasional alternative but sounds like a temperature tweak mid-drink, not an ordering phrase.
따뜻한 걸로 → 따뜻한 거로 (both correct; 걸로 is more fluent in speech) → 따뜻한 [음료명] 한 잔 주세요 (name the specific drink) → 아주 따뜻하게 해 주세요 (ask for extra-hot). Chain size and extras after: 따뜻한 걸로 주세요, 큰 사이즈로요.

The classic mistake is using 뜨거운 instead of 따뜻한. 뜨거운 = scaldingly hot (you'd yell 뜨거워! if you burned yourself). Warm drinks are 따뜻한. Asking for 뜨거운 걸로 at a café is understood but marks you as unnatural — and sounds like you want to damage your tongue.

expressions.shortExplanation: 아이스로 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Iced, please".
expressions.explanation: "Iced, please" — that is 아이스로 주세요 (aiseuro juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 아이스로 주세요. ("Iced, please."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Customer to barista; the universal way to ask for a cold drink
반말 among friends; not used toward staff
Native equivalent; slightly more formal/older-sounding than 아이스로
Extension: 'iced americano' is so common it's clipped to 아아 in texting slang

examples.ko: A: 따뜻한 거요, 아이스요? / B: 아이스로 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: ttatteutan geoyo, aiseuyo? / B: aiseuro juseyo.
examples.en: A: Hot or iced? / B: Iced, please.
examples.note: 아이스 is a fixed loanword for cold drinks; -로 marks your choice — don't skip the particle

examples.ko: 여름엔 무조건 아이스로 주세요. 얼음 많이요.
examples.romanization: yeoreumen mujogeon aiseuro juseyo. eoreum maniyo.
examples.en: In summer, always make it iced. Lots of ice.
examples.note: 얼음 많이요 = 'extra ice'; a standalone noun + 요 turns into a polite addition without a full verb

examples.ko: A: 뭐로 드릴까요? / B: 저는 아이스로 주시고, 친구는 따뜻한 걸로 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: mworo deurilkkayo? / B: jeoneun aiseuro jusigo, chinguneun ttatteutan geollo juseyo.
examples.en: A: What can I get you? / B: Iced for me, and hot for my friend.
examples.note: Two orders in one breath; 주시고 links the first request to the second smoothly — natural at a busy counter

expressions.nuance: 아이스로 주세요 is how you order any cold drink at a Korean café — 아이스 is the English word 'ice' borrowed as an adjective and is far more commonly heard than the native 차가운 거. The particle -로 marks your selection ('I'm going with iced'). The pairing opponent is 따뜻한 걸로. The practical difference between 아이스로 and 차가운 걸로: 아이스로 is the default café lingo, while 차가운 걸로 sounds a touch older or is used in a convenience store for bottled drinks. Register is plain polite -요 for all staff; 반말 아이스로 줘 is friends-only. The English-speaker pitfall is ordering 얼음 주세요 ('give me ice') thinking that means 'iced drink' — it literally requests a cup of ice cubes; the temperature selection is 아이스로, and 얼음 is used only to adjust ice quantity (얼음 많이요 / 얼음 빼고요).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 얼음으로 주세요 to mean 'iced' — that asks for ice as the item itself; the cold-drink selection is 아이스로 주세요.
Pronouncing 아이스 English-style and not adding the particle — Korean needs -로: 아이스로 (with -로) to mark it as your selection between two options.
Mixing 아이스 차가운 걸로 주세요 — redundant; pick one form: 아이스로 or 차가운 걸로, not both together.

structuredNuance.t: 아이스 (loanword 'ice') + 로 (selection particle 'going with') + 주세요 (give me). The phrase means 'please give me the iced version' — it's a temperature-selection formula, not literally 'give me ice.'

Directed at café baristas and convenience store staff when choosing cold over hot. Always -요 polite toward staff; 반말 아이스로 줘 only with a friend. Works for any cold drink, from iced coffee to bubble tea.

차가운 걸로 주세요 is the fully native equivalent; 아이스로 is today's everyday café default. 콜드로 주세요 is rarer and slightly awkward. The dividing line between 아이스로 and 차가운 걸로 is register and context: 아이스로 is casual café speech; 차가운 걸로 sounds slightly formal or suits bottled drinks.
아이스로 → 아이스 [음료명] 주세요 (name the drink) → 아이스 아메리카노 = 아아 (texting abbreviation). Ice quantity: 얼음 많이요 / 얼음 적게요 / 얼음 빼고요 (no ice).
Ordering 얼음 주세요 to mean 'iced' is a classic mistake — that literally requests a cup of ice cubes. The cold-drink choice is 아이스로 주세요. 얼음 is useful only for adjusting the ice amount afterward.

expressions.shortExplanation: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? is a practical expression meaning "What size would you like?".
expressions.explanation: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? (saijeu eotteoke deurilkkayo?) = "What size would you like?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? ("What size would you like?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Staff to customer; the polite offer formula -ㄹ까요? with humble 드리다
반말 version; only a friend working the counter would say this

usagePhrases.en: Which size would you like to go with?
usagePhrases.note: A slightly more formal staff phrasing using -하시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: As for size, which one shall I get you?
usagePhrases.note: Extension with topic 는, common when listing options before asking

examples.ko: A: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? / B: 작은 거로 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: saijeu eotteoke deurilkkayo? / B: jageun georo juseyo.
examples.en: A: What size? / B: A small, please.
examples.note: Answer with 작은/큰 거로; 드릴까요 is the staff side, 주세요 is your side — match the register: staff uses 드리다, you use 주다

examples.ko: A: 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? / B: 제일 큰 걸로요.
examples.romanization: A: saijeu eotteoke deurilkkayo? / B: jeil keun geolloyo.
examples.en: A: What size? / B: The biggest one.
examples.note: 제일 큰 = 'the biggest'; a bare [size + 걸로요] is the most natural short answer, no full verb needed

examples.ko: A: 따뜻한 라떼요. / B: 네, 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? 레귤러랑 라지 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: ttatteutal latteyo. / B: ne, saijeu eotteoke deurilkkayo? regyulleorang naji isseoyo.
examples.en: A: A hot latte. / B: Sure, what size would you like? We have regular and large.
examples.note: Staff commonly follow the size question by naming available options — listen for the offered sizes before answering

expressions.nuance: This is a staff-to-customer line, so a learner mostly needs to recognize it fast and reply confidently. 어떻게 드릴까요? literally means 'how shall I give it to you?' — 드리다 is the humble form of 주다 ('give'), and -ㄹ까요? offers a service; together they are the polite service-formula heard in cafés, restaurants, and convenience stores everywhere. You reply with a size + 걸로: 작은 걸로요 / 큰 걸로요, or chain-store English sizes 톨/그란데/벤티. A slightly more formal staff variant is 어떤 사이즈로 하시겠어요? — same meaning, a notch stiffer. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 드릴까요 and mentally translating every word: just catch 사이즈 and respond with your size choice. A second trap is answering '미디엄' — many Korean cafés do not use a medium tier; they offer 작은/큰 or the Starbucks trio, so always listen for the options they name before deciding.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Freezing because 드릴까요 sounds unfamiliar — it is just polite 'shall I give you'; catch the word 사이즈 and answer with your size choice.
Answering with bare 작은 사이즈 and no particle — the natural form is 작은 걸로(요) or 작은 거로(요), the -(으)로 particle marking your selection.
Saying 미디엄 expecting a medium — many cafés offer only 작은/큰 or 톨/그란데/벤티; always pick from the sizes the staff name.

structuredNuance.t: 사이즈 (size) + 어떻게 (how) + 드릴까요 (shall I give you — humble). Literally: 'How shall I give the size to you?' — really: 'What size would you like?' It is a polite service question, not a philosophical one about method.

Staff address you in 존댓말 using the humble verb 드리다 — you are the honored customer. Your reply stays in plain polite -요: 작은 걸로요 / 큰 걸로요. Never try to match their humility level — that would be grammatically odd.
어떤 사이즈로 하시겠어요? is the more formal alternative. 어떻게 드릴까요? is warmer and conversational; 하시겠어요? sounds like a written menu or a formal restaurant. Both ask the same thing.
Your answer options: 작은 걸로요 (small) / 큰 걸로요 (large) / 레귤러로요 / 라지로요 / 톨로요 / 벤티로요. To specify further: 제일 작은 걸로요 (the smallest) / 중간 걸로요 (medium, if offered).

Two traps: (1) Freezing because 드릴까요 sounds complex — only the word 사이즈 matters; reply with a size. (2) Answering 미디엄 — many Korean cafés have no medium; they offer two sizes or the Starbucks trio, so always wait to hear the options first.

expressions.shortExplanation: 적립해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please add my points".
expressions.explanation: 적립해 주세요 (jeongnipae juseyo) means "Please add my points". Say it as one set phrase — for example 적립해 주세요. ("Please add the points."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Customer asking staff to log loyalty/stamp points to their account
반말; only with a friend, never with cashier staff
Softer, more deferential variant using 부탁드리다 (I humbly request)

usagePhrases.en: Can I earn points here too?
usagePhrases.note: Extension: asking first whether the store runs a points program at all

examples.ko: A: 적립해 드릴까요? / B: 네, 적립해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: jeongnipae deurilkkayo? / B: ne, jeongnipae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I add your points? / B: Yes, please.
examples.note: Staff proactively offer with 드릴까요; you confirm with 주세요 — the most common exchange at any chain store

examples.en: Add my points, please. By phone number.
examples.note: 전화번호로요 = 'by (my) phone number'; most Korean stores track points via your mobile number, not a physical card

examples.ko: 계산하기 전에 적립 먼저 해 주세요. 010-1234-5678이요.
examples.romanization: gyesanhagi jeone jeongnim meonjeo hae juseyo. 010-1234-5678iyo.
examples.en: Before you ring it up, please add my points first. It's 010-1234-5678.
examples.note: Real flow: say 먼저 (first) before payment is charged, then read your number — timing matters because some systems can't add points after payment

expressions.nuance: 적립 (積立) means 'accumulating/saving up,' and 적립해 주세요 asks the cashier to credit loyalty points or stamps to your account — via phone number, an app barcode, or a membership card. This is customer-to-staff, plain polite -요; 반말 (적립해 줘) is friends-only. Say it before payment, because most POS systems cannot retroactively add points. The nearest alternatives are 적립 부탁드려요 (more deferential, very polite) and the ultra-casual 적립이요 while showing your barcode — all mean the same thing, divided only by politeness level. A frequent English-speaker mistake is 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather points') — Koreans do not phrase it that way; the correct verb is 적립하다. Also critical: 적립 is earning points; spending them is entirely different — you would say 포인트로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요 to redeem.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather points') — not the natural phrasing; the correct verb for accruing loyalty points is 적립하다: 적립해 주세요.
Confusing earning with spending — 적립 is earning points; to redeem them say 포인트로 결제할게요 / 포인트 쓸게요.
Forgetting to provide your identifier — staff need your 전화번호, app barcode, or membership card; have it ready as you say 적립해 주세요, or add 전화번호로요 immediately after.

structuredNuance.t: 적립해(accumulate/save up + verb ending) + 주세요(please give/do for me). Literally 'please do the accumulation for me' — really 'please add loyalty points to my account.' 적립하다 is the specific verb for accruing points or savings; you cannot substitute 모으다 or 쌓다 at the counter.

Say this at checkout in any store that runs a loyalty program — coffee chains, convenience stores, pharmacies, bookstores. Say it before payment. Plain polite -요 for all staff; 반말 only with friends. If you forgot, you can try 혹시 아까 적립 됐어요? ('was it added just now?') but there is no guarantee.

적립 부탁드려요 is the most deferential form (appropriate when speaking to an elder or in a high-end shop). 적립이요 (bare noun + polite marker) is quick and very casual but acceptable at chains. The line: 적립해 주세요 → polite everyday; 부탁드려요 → deferential; 적립이요 → casual shorthand.

적립 (積立): 積 = accumulate/pile up + 立 = stand/establish. The compound means 'building up a store of something' — hence the loyalty-points meaning. Same 積 appears in 축적하다 (accumulate) and 적금 (installment savings account).

Do not say 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather my points') — unnatural; the verb must be 적립하다. Also do not confuse earning (적립) with spending: to redeem points say 포인트로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요. Using 적립해 주세요 when you mean to pay with points confuses the staff.

expressions.shortExplanation: 봉투 드릴까요? is a practical expression meaning "Would you like a bag?".
expressions.explanation: "Would you like a bag?" — that is 봉투 드릴까요? (bongtu deurilkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 봉투 드릴까요? ("Shall I give you a bag?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Shall I give you a bag?
usagePhrases.note: Cashier to customer; -ㄹ까요? is the polite service offer
반말; friend-to-friend, not store staff
Equally common staff version using 필요하다 (to need)

usagePhrases.en: Shall I give you a bag separately?
usagePhrases.note: Extension: 따로 = 'separately/on the side,' since bags are usually charged

examples.ko: A: 봉투 드릴까요? / B: 네, 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: bongtu deurilkkayo? / B: ne, juseyo.
examples.en: A: Would you like a bag? / B: Yes, please.
examples.note: Say 네 주세요 to accept, 아니요 괜찮아요 to decline — do not say 괜찮아요 alone thinking it means 'yes'

examples.ko: A: 봉투 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: bongtu deurilkkayo? / B: aniyo, geunyang juseyo.
examples.en: A: Need a bag? / B: No, just hand it over as-is.
examples.note: 그냥 주세요 = 'just give it to me (without a bag)'; a concise, polite way to decline

examples.ko: A: 봉투 드릴까요? 50원이에요. / B: 네, 하나 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: bongtu deurilkkayo? 50wonieyo. / B: ne, hana juseyo.
examples.en: A: Want a bag? It's 50 won. / B: Yes, one please.
examples.note: Korean stores charge a small fee for bags by law; staff often state the price — expect it and answer 네, 하나 주세요

expressions.nuance: Since Korea mandates charges for single-use plastic bags, the cashier almost always asks 봉투 드릴까요? or 봉투 필요하세요? and will add a small fee (typically 20–50원). This phrase is staff-to-customer 존댓말 (드리다 humble 'give' + offer -ㄹ까요?); your job is just to answer. Accept with 네, 주세요 or 네, 하나 주세요; decline with 아니요, 괜찮아요 or 그냥 주세요. The near-synonym is 봉지 드릴까요? — 봉투 and 봉지 both mean 'bag' and are interchangeable in this context; the only difference is slight regional/speaker preference. The critical English-speaker trap is responding 괜찮아요 meaning 'okay yes I want one' — in Korean 괜찮아요 here means 'it's fine/no thanks,' so you would end up refusing the bag you actually wanted; say 네, 주세요 to accept.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering 괜찮아요 to mean 'yes, sure' — in Korean this declines the offer ('I'm fine without it'); to accept a bag say 네, 주세요.
Thinking bags are free — Korean stores charge for 봉투 by law; a small fee is added and the staff usually state the amount.
Treating 봉투 and 봉지 as different items — both mean 'shopping bag' in this context and are interchangeable; either form in the question gets the same answer.

structuredNuance.t: 봉투(bag) + 드릴까요(shall I give you — humble offer). Literally 'Shall I humbly give you a bag?' — really 'Would you like a bag?' It is a standard service offer, not a yes/no question about your feelings; answer with a direct 네 주세요 or 아니요 괜찮아요.

Heard at every checkout in Korea — supermarkets, convenience stores, bakeries, clothing stores. Bags are paid items. Staff use humble 드리다 toward you; you answer in plain -요. No need to match their formality level.
봉지 드릴까요? is fully interchangeable — 봉투 and 봉지 both mean a carry bag in this context. 봉투 필요하세요? is another common staff phrase ('Do you need a bag?') that calls for the same answer.
Accept: 네, 주세요 / 하나 주세요 / 큰 걸로 주세요 (large bag). Decline: 아니요, 괜찮아요 / 그냥 주세요 / 가방 있어요 (I have my own bag). If you need two: 두 개 주세요.
Answering 괜찮아요 meaning 'yes/sure' is the classic trap. In Korean 괜찮아요 ('it's fine/okay') in response to an offer means 'no thanks' — you will refuse the bag you wanted. To accept, always say 네, 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 봉투 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me a bag".
expressions.explanation: 봉투 주세요 (bongtu juseyo) = "Please give me a bag". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 봉투 주세요 ("Please give me a bag"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request at checkout
반말 to a friend
Softer, more polite request
Declining a bag, eco-minded

examples.en: Please give me a bag.
examples.note: Bare request as items are being rung up — necessary since bags are not automatically given

examples.en: A bag, please. A paper one.
examples.note: Specifying type; 종이봉투 = paper bag; 비닐봉투 = plastic bag — both cost extra in most shops

examples.ko: A: 봉투 하나 주세요. 얼마예요? / B: 비닐이요, 이십 원이에요. / A: 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: bongtu hana juseyo. eolmayeyo? / B: biniriyo, isip wonieyo. / A: juseyo.
examples.en: A: One bag please. How much? / B: Plastic, twenty won. / A: I'll take it.
examples.note: Realistic cashier exchange; 비닐봉투 = plastic bag with a small fee — shows the normal checkout script

expressions.nuance: 봉투 주세요 asks the cashier for a shopping bag at checkout; 봉투 means 'bag/envelope' and in a retail context always refers to a carry bag; 주세요 is 'please give me'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 봉투 줘; softer 봉투 하나 주시겠어요?. A critical Korean reality: since 2019 plastic bags (비닐봉투) are no longer free in most retail stores — the cashier may ask 봉투 드릴까요? ('shall I give you a bag?') and there will be a small charge. Paper bags (종이봉투) are also often sold separately. The eco-decline is 봉투 필요 없어요 ('no bag needed'). Do not confuse 봉투 (a checkout carry bag) with 가방 (a handbag, backpack, or travel bag you own) — saying 가방 주세요 would mean 'give me a handbag'. English speakers also reach for the loanword 백 (bag), but 백 in Korean implies a fashion bag; the checkout word is 봉투. And 주세요 already means 'give me', so 저에게 is redundant.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 봉투 with 가방.
봉투 = a shopping/carry bag or envelope; 가방 = a handbag/backpack you own. Ask 봉투 주세요 for a checkout bag.
Using the loanword 백 for a shopping bag.
백 suggests a fashion bag. The word for a carry bag at checkout is 봉투: 봉투 주세요.
Assuming bags are free.
Korean shops charge for 비닐봉투 (plastic). You may be asked 봉투 드릴까요? — expect a small fee.

structuredNuance.t: 봉투 = 'bag/envelope' (in retail = carry bag) + 주세요 = 'please give me'. Literally 'please give me a bag.' 봉투 in a shop context always means a checkout carry bag, not a handbag or envelope.

해요체 — say to the cashier right before or as they begin bagging your items. Since 2019 most Korean retailers charge for plastic bags; expect a small fee. Soften to 봉투 하나 주시겠어요? for extra politeness. Declining: 봉투 필요 없어요.

가방 주세요 would mean 'give me a handbag' — completely wrong at checkout. 백 (loanword 'bag') sounds like a fashion bag. 쇼핑백 is a loanword that works but is less natural than 봉투 at a cashier. 봉투 is the only natural choice.
종이봉투 주세요 (paper bag please), 큰 봉투로 주세요 (a big bag please), 봉투 두 개 주세요 (two bags please), 봉투 필요 없어요 (no bag needed). Specify material or size with the adjective before 봉투.
Saying 백 주세요 for a shopping bag — 백 = fashion bag. Confusing 봉투 (carry bag) with 가방 (personal bag/purse). Adding 저에게 — 주세요 already means 'give me'.

expressions.english: Shall I heat it up for you?
expressions.shortExplanation: 데워 드릴까요? is a practical expression meaning "Shall I heat it up for you?".
expressions.explanation: 데워 드릴까요? (dewo deurilkkayo?) means "Shall I heat it up for you?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 데워 드릴까요? ("Shall I heat it up?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Convenience-store or café staff offering to microwave your food
반말; a friend offering, never staff

usagePhrases.en: Shall I heat it for you?
usagePhrases.note: Shorter spoken staff variant; 드려요? alone is a quick offer
Extension: naming the specific item (도시락 / 삼각김밥 / 만두 etc.)

examples.ko: A: 데워 드릴까요? / B: 네, 데워 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: dewo deurilkkayo? / B: ne, dewo juseyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I heat it up? / B: Yes, please.
examples.note: Staff offer with 드릴까요; you accept with 데워 주세요 — match verb: 데우다, not 끓이다 or 요리하다

examples.ko: A: 데워 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: dewo deurilkkayo? / B: aniyo, geunyang juseyo.
examples.en: A: Want it heated? / B: No, as it is, thanks.
examples.note: 그냥 주세요 declines heating and takes it at room temperature — the softest refusal

examples.ko: 이 도시락 데워 주세요. 한 2분 정도요.
examples.romanization: i dosirak dewo juseyo. han 2bun jeongdoyo.
examples.en: Please heat this lunchbox. About two minutes or so.
examples.note: 한 ~ 정도요 = 'about ~'; you can suggest the microwave time — staff will usually decide themselves but appreciate the cue

expressions.nuance: At 편의점 (convenience stores) and some cafés, staff offer 데워 드릴까요? for ready-to-eat microwavable items — 도시락 lunchboxes, 삼각김밥 rice triangles, 컵라면 additions, 붕어빵-style pastries. 데우다 specifically means 'to warm up/reheat (food)' — it is the right verb for reheating in a microwave or warmer, distinct from 끓이다 (boil a liquid) or 굽다 (grill/bake). This phrase is staff 존댓말; you accept with 데워 주세요 or decline with 그냥 주세요 / 아니요, 괜찮아요. The near alternative is 따뜻하게 해 드릴까요? ('shall I make it warm for you?'), used loosely the same way; the dividing line is that 데우다 is specifically about reheating a pre-cooked food item, whereas 따뜻하게 하다 is vaguer. The English-speaker mistake is responding 뜨겁게 해 주세요 ('make it scalding hot') or 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — both are wrong registers; the only natural answer for reheating is 데워 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — that asks for fresh cooking from raw ingredients; reheating ready food is 데워 주세요.
Saying 끓여 주세요 ('boil it') for a lunchbox — 끓이다 is for liquids; microwaving solid food is 데우다.
Declining with a blunt 아니요 only — soften it to 아니요, 그냥 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요 to avoid sounding rude.

structuredNuance.t: 데워 (reheat — verb stem of 데우다 + connective -아/어) + 드릴까요 (shall I give/do for you — humble offer). Literally 'Shall I humbly reheat it for you?' — really 'Shall I heat this up?' It is a convenience-store service offer for microwavable ready food.

Heard mainly at 편의점 (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven, Emart24) when you pick up a 도시락, 삼각김밥, 만두, or any microwavable item. Staff use 존댓말 (드리다); you answer in plain -요. It is always a friendly low-pressure offer — declining with 그냥 주세요 is perfectly normal.
따뜻하게 해 드릴까요? is the looser alternative; 데워 드릴까요? is the more precise phrasing specific to reheating food (not warming a drink). 끓여 드릴까요? would mean boiling a liquid — not used for lunchboxes.
Accept: 데워 주세요 / 네, 부탁드려요. Decline: 그냥 주세요 / 아니요, 괜찮아요. Request specific time: 2분만 해 주세요 (just 2 minutes). Ask yourself: 전자레인지 어디 있어요? (if you want to use the store microwave yourself).

Do not say 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — that implies raw ingredients; ready food is simply 데워 주세요. Also do not say 뜨겁게 해 주세요 for reheating — that means 'make it dangerously hot'; the correct, natural word for warming food is 데우다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 드시고 가세요? 가져가세요? is a practical expression meaning "For here or to go?".
expressions.explanation: "For here or to go?" — that is 드시고 가세요? 가져가세요? (deusigo gaseyo? gajyeogaseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 드시고 가세요, 가져가세요? ("For here or to go?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Café staff to customer; 드시고 가다 = eat/drink here, 가져가다 = take away
반말; only between friends, not said by staff
More formal/standard register; 포장 = packed to go
Extension: asks only about the dine-in half, expecting a yes/no

examples.ko: A: 드시고 가세요, 가져가세요? / B: 가져갈게요.
examples.romanization: A: deusigo gaseyo, gajyeogaseyo? / B: gajyeogalgeyo.
examples.en: A: For here or to go? / B: To go.
examples.note: 가져갈게요 is the cleanest takeout answer; 포장이요 or 포장해 주세요 also work — choose any

examples.ko: A: 드시고 가세요? / B: 네, 여기서 먹고 갈게요.
examples.romanization: A: deusigo gaseyo? / B: ne, yeogiseo meokgo galgeyo.
examples.en: A: Eating in? / B: Yes, I'll have it here.
examples.note: Dine-in answer: 여기서 먹고 갈게요; note you use plain 먹다 about yourself, not the honorific 드시다 the staff used

examples.ko: A: 드시고 가세요, 가져가세요? / B: 포장해 주세요. 따로 담아 주시고요.
examples.romanization: A: deusigo gaseyo, gajyeogaseyo? / B: pojanghae juseyo. ttaro dama jusigoyo.
examples.en: A: For here or to go? / B: To go please. And could you pack them separately?
examples.note: 따로 담아 주시고요 = 'pack them in separate containers'; -고요 adds a second request naturally after the main one

expressions.nuance: This is the café's dine-in-versus-takeout question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다/마시다, so 드시고 가세요? = 'will you eat/drink here and go?'; 가져가세요? = 'will you take it away?' The question matters practically: Korean law requires cafés to serve dine-in orders in reusable mugs/glasses, while takeout uses disposables — so your answer changes the cup you receive. Staff use 존댓말 with the honorific 드시다; you answer in plain polite -요 using your own 먹다/마시다: 먹고 갈게요 (dine in) or 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요 (takeout). The more formal phrasing is 매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요?. The English-speaker error is replying 테이크아웃 — understood but unnatural; say 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. Another trap is reversing the honorific: don't say 드시고 갈게요 about yourself — reserve 드시다 for talking about others; use 먹고/마시고 for yourself.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering with English 테이크아웃 or just 고 — say 포장이요 / 가져갈게요 / 포장해 주세요 instead.
Saying 드시고 갈게요 about yourself — 드시다 is the honorific for talking about others; use 먹고 갈게요 / 마시고 갈게요 for yourself.
Assuming dine-in and takeout cups are the same — Korean law requires real mugs for dine-in; your answer changes the cup you receive.

structuredNuance.t: 드시고 가세요 = 'will you eat (honorific) and go?' + 가져가세요 = 'will you take (it) away?' Together they form the binary for-here-or-to-go question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다/마시다, used by staff to honor the customer — do not use 드시다 about yourself in your answer.

Heard at every café and many bakeries in Korea. Your answer changes the cup and packaging. Staff always use 존댓말 and honorific 드시다; you reply with plain polite -요 using 먹다 or 마시다 about yourself. Never say 드시고 갈게요 about yourself.

매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요? is the same question in slightly more formal dress, heard at restaurants. 여기서 드실 거예요? asks the dine-in half only. All call for the same answers: 먹고 갈게요 (stay) / 포장이요, 가져갈게요, 포장해 주세요 (go).
Dine-in answers: 먹고 갈게요 / 여기서 마실게요 / 네, 드시고 갈게요 (wrong — don't use 드시다 about yourself; say 먹고 갈게요). Takeout answers: 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요.

Saying 테이크아웃 is understood but marked as a loanword answer; the natural answers are 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. The grammar trap: staff say 드시고 가세요? using the honorific; do NOT reply 드시고 갈게요 — 드시다 is only for talking about other people. Use 먹고 갈게요 about yourself.

expressions.shortExplanation: 일회용 컵에 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "In a disposable cup, please".
expressions.explanation: 일회용 컵에 주세요 (ilhoeyong keobe juseyo) = "In a disposable cup, please". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 일회용 컵에 주세요. ("In a disposable cup, please."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Customer asking for a to-go paper/plastic cup even while staying in

usagePhrases.en: Put it in a paper cup.
usagePhrases.note: 반말; friends only, not for staff
Common loanword variant; same meaning and widely understood

usagePhrases.en: Please put it in a disposable cup.
usagePhrases.note: Extension with 담다 ('to fill/pour into'), a touch more precise and polite

examples.ko: A: 머그잔에 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 일회용 컵에 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: meogeujane deurilkkayo? / B: aniyo, ilhoeyong keobe juseyo.
examples.en: A: In a mug? / B: No, a disposable cup please.
examples.note: Used to override the default dine-in mug — the explicit contrast 머그잔 vs 일회용 컵 makes your preference unmistakable

examples.ko: 여기서 마실 건데 일회용 컵에 주세요. 곧 나가야 해서요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseo masil geonde ilhoeyong keobe juseyo. gon nagaya haeseoyo.
examples.en: I'll drink here but in a disposable cup, please. I have to leave soon.
examples.note: -ㄹ 건데 = 'I'm going to ~ but'; giving a reason (곧 나가야 해서) makes the unusual request more natural and reduces any awkwardness

examples.ko: 일회용 컵에 주시고, 캐리어도 하나 주세요.
examples.romanization: ilhoeyong keobe jusigo, kaerieodo hana juseyo.
examples.en: A disposable cup, please, and a cup carrier too.
examples.note: 캐리어 = drink carrier tray; 주시고 chains the second request after the first smoothly

expressions.nuance: 일회용 (一回用) means 'single-use', and 일회용 컵 is a disposable paper or plastic cup. You need this phrase in Korea because cafés are legally required to serve dine-in customers in real mugs or glasses — if you want a to-go cup even while sitting, you must ask explicitly. Customer-to-staff plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only.
