The everyday alternative is 테이크아웃 컵에 주세요 — fully interchangeable and understood at all chains; 종이컵에 주세요 is more specific if it is definitely a paper cup. The particle -에 is critical: it marks destination or container ('into the ~') — not -로 (which would change meaning). The English-speaker mistake is either saying 일회용 잔 (잔 is glassware: wine glass, mug) or omitting the particle and saying just 일회용 컵 주세요, which sounds like you want the cup handed to you empty rather than your drink poured into it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 일회용 잔 — 잔 implies glass or ceramic ware; disposable cups take the word 컵: 일회용 컵에 주세요.
Assuming dine-in automatically means a paper cup — Korean cafés give real mugs for here by law; you must request 일회용 컵 explicitly.
Using 플라스틱 컵에 주세요 woodenly — understood but stiff; 일회용 컵에 주세요 or 테이크아웃 컵에 주세요 sounds natural and confident.

structuredNuance.t: 일회용(single-use) + 컵(cup) + 에(into/destination particle) + 주세요(please give me). Literally 'please give me [the drink] into a disposable cup.' The particle -에 marks where the drink goes — it is not 일회용 컵을 주세요 (which would ask for an empty cup).

Used when dining in at a café but wanting a to-go cup — because you're leaving soon, or just prefer it. Since Korean law defaults to mugs/glasses for dine-in, you must actively request this. Plain -요 polite to staff; 반말 only with friends.
테이크아웃 컵에 주세요 is interchangeable. 종이컵에 주세요 specifies paper specifically. 플라스틱 컵에 주세요 is technically correct but stilted — 일회용 컵 or 테이크아웃 컵 sounds more natural.
일회용 (一回用): 一 = one + 回 = time/round + 用 = use. 'Single-use' — the same 用 appears in 사용 (使用, use) and 용도 (用途, intended use). Do not confuse 일회용 (one-use) with 일회 (一回, one round/time) alone.
Saying 일회용 잔 is wrong — 잔 refers to glassware and ceramicware (와인 잔, 머그잔); disposables use 컵. Also do not say 플라스틱 컵 directly — understood but stiff. The correct choice is 일회용 컵 or 테이크아웃 컵.

expressions.english: Please put it in my tumbler
expressions.shortExplanation: 텀블러에 담아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please put it in my tumbler".
expressions.explanation: 텀블러에 담아 주세요 (teombeulleoe dama juseyo) means "Please put it in my tumbler". Say it as one set phrase — for example 텀블러에 담아 주세요. ("Please fill my tumbler."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Customer handing a personal cup to the barista; 담다 = to fill/pour into
반말; friend context only
Looser spoken variant; 해 주세요 stands in for 담아 주세요 colloquially

usagePhrases.en: I brought a tumbler — please fill this one.
usagePhrases.note: Extension: announce you have a tumbler first, then point and ask; lets staff apply the discount

examples.ko: A: 텀블러에 담아 주세요. / B: 네, 할인 들어가세요.
examples.romanization: A: teombeulleoe dama juseyo. / B: ne, harin deureogaseyo.
examples.en: A: In my tumbler, please. / B: Sure, your discount will be applied.
examples.note: Bringing a personal cup usually earns a 텀블러 할인 (around 300–500원 discount) at most chains — announce it early

examples.ko: 이 텀블러 깨끗해요. 여기에 담아 주세요.
examples.romanization: i teombeulleo kkaekkeutaeyo. yeogie dama juseyo.
examples.en: This tumbler is clean. Please fill it here.
examples.note: Reassuring the barista it is clean is polite and practical; 여기에 (여기 + destination -에) = 'in here/into this'

examples.ko: 아이스 아메리카노 텀블러에 담아 주세요. 얼음 따로 주시고요.
examples.romanization: aiseu amerikano teombeulleoe dama juseyo. eoreum ttaro jusigoyo.
examples.en: An iced americano in my tumbler, please. And the ice separately.
examples.note: 얼음 따로 = ice on the side (useful when your tumbler cannot hold both drink and full ice); 주시고요 chains the second request

expressions.nuance: 텀블러 (tumbler) is a reusable personal cup, and 텀블러에 담아 주세요 hands it to the barista with a request to fill it. 담다 ('to pour/fill into a container') is the precise verb here — it emphasizes putting liquid into the vessel, making it more natural than the generic 넣어 주세요. The destination particle -에 marks where the drink goes (텀블러에 = 'into the tumbler'); using -로 instead (텀블러로 주세요) shifts meaning to 'give me a tumbler as the item,' which is wrong. Bringing a tumbler typically earns a discount (텀블러 할인) at Korean café chains, so announce it early. The loose spoken alternative is 텀블러에 해 주세요. A refill situation calls for 채워 주세요 ('fill it up'), but for a fresh drink 담아 주세요 is the correct natural form.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 텀블러로 주세요 — -로 marks the item being given ('give me a tumbler'); to fill your cup use the destination particle -에: 텀블러에 담아 주세요.
Using 넣어 주세요 ('insert it') — 넣다 is for placing solid objects; pouring a drink into a cup is 담다.
Forgetting to announce the tumbler before ordering — say 텀블러 가져왔어요 first so the barista can apply the discount and prepare the right size.

structuredNuance.t: 텀블러에 (into the tumbler — -에 marks destination) + 담아 (fill/pour in — verb 담다 + connective) + 주세요 (please). Literally 'please fill/pour into my tumbler.' The verb 담다 specifically conveys pouring a liquid into a container — it is more precise than 넣다 (to insert/put in, for solid objects).

Hand over your tumbler as you order and say this phrase. Works at all café chains and independent cafés. Earns a discount (텀블러 할인) at most chains. Plain -요 polite for all staff; 반말 with friends. Announce it before the barista starts making the drink.

텀블러에 해 주세요 is the lazy but acceptable spoken shorthand. 채워 주세요 ('fill it up') suits a refill but sounds odd for a fresh drink. 넣어 주세요 ('put it in') is for solid objects — wrong for a liquid poured into a cup; use 담다 for drinks.
Basic: 텀블러에 담아 주세요. With announcement: 텀블러 가져왔어요, 여기에 담아 주세요. Refill: 텀블러 채워 주세요 (fill it up again). Confirming discount: 텀블러 할인 되나요?

Using -로 instead of -에 is the main particle mistake: 텀블러로 주세요 means 'give me a tumbler (as the product),' not 'pour into my tumbler.' For any container you are filling, the destination particle is -에. Also, 넣어 주세요 sounds like putting a solid object in; the right verb for pouring a drink is 담다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 카드로 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll pay by card".
expressions.explanation: 카드로 할게요 (kadeuro halgeyo) = "I'll pay by card". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 카드로 할게요. ("I'll pay by card."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Customer stating payment method; -ㄹ게요 = 'I'll (do)' — declares the speaker's decision
반말; close friends only
More formal -겠습니다; in a corporate or very formal setting
Extension with 계산하다 ('to settle/pay'), fully natural and interchangeable

examples.ko: A: 현금이세요, 카드세요? / B: 카드로 할게요.
examples.romanization: A: hyeongeumiseyo, kadeuseyo? / B: kadeuro halgeyo.
examples.en: A: Cash or card? / B: Card, please.
examples.note: -로 marks the method (instrument); -ㄹ게요 is the speaker's own decision — do not say 카드로 할 거예요 (that would describe a plan, not commit here)

examples.en: By card, please. Lump-sum payment.
examples.note: 일시불 = single full payment (vs 할부 = installments); for everyday purchases always answer 일시불로요 unless splitting

examples.ko: A: 카드로 할게요. 여기 찍으면 돼요? / B: 네, 여기에 태그해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: kadeuro halgeyo. yeogi jjigeumyeon dwaeyo? / B: ne, yeogie taegeuhae juseyo.
examples.en: A: I'll pay by card. Do I tap here? / B: Yes, tap here please.
examples.note: 찍다 / 태그하다 = tap/tap for contactless; asking where the reader is is practical in smaller shops without clear signage

expressions.nuance: 카드로 할게요 tells the cashier you are paying by card; -로 marks the means or instrument ('by way of card') and -ㄹ게요 announces a decision you are committing to right now. Plain polite -요 for all stores; formal -하겠습니다 in rare stiff contexts; 반말 with close friends. After you say it, staff may ask 일시불이세요, 할부세요? (one lump payment or installments?) — for any everyday purchase answer 일시불로요. The near alternative is 카드로 계산할게요 (identical meaning, slightly more explicit) or 카드 될까요? (asking whether card is accepted — a question, not a statement). The dividing line: 할게요 commits to paying by card; 될까요? merely inquires. The English-speaker mistake is 카드로 지불할게요 — 지불하다 is the correct Sino-Korean verb for 'to pay' but it is bookish and stiff in conversation; spoken Korean uses 하다 or 계산하다. The wrong particle is also common: payment method takes -로 (instrument), not -를 or -에.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 지불하다 (카드로 지불할게요) — grammatically correct but stiff and written; say 카드로 할게요 or 카드로 계산할게요 in conversation.
Wrong particle: 카드를 할게요 or 카드에 할게요 — payment method takes the instrument particle -로: 카드로.
Freezing when asked 일시불이세요, 할부세요? — for everyday purchases just say 일시불로요 (one full payment); only ask for 할부 if you want monthly installments.

structuredNuance.t: 카드(card) + 로(instrument particle, 'by means of') + 할게요(I'll do it — volitional -ㄹ게요). Literally 'I'll do it by card' — really 'I'll pay by card.' The -ㄹ게요 ending signals a self-directed decision being announced to the listener, not a plan or a question.

Said at any checkout when you want to pay by card, either when staff ask or proactively. Plain -요 for all stores; formal -하겠습니다 in a business/formal setting; 반말 with close friends. Be ready to answer 일시불이세요, 할부세요? immediately after.

카드로 계산할게요 is fully interchangeable and slightly more explicit. 카드 될까요? asks if card is accepted (a question). 카드로 하겠습니다 is the formal version. The line: 할게요/계산할게요 = committing to card; 될까요? = asking permission.
카드로 할게요 → 카드로 계산할게요 → 카드로 하겠습니다 (formal). Installment: 할부로 해 주세요 / 3개월 할부로요. Lump-sum: 일시불로요. Inquiry: 카드 돼요? / 카드 되나요?

카드로 지불할게요 is grammatically fine but sounds written and stiff — spoken Korean says 카드로 할게요 or 카드로 계산할게요. Wrong-particle error: 카드를 할게요 or 카드에 할게요 are both wrong; payment method takes -로 (instrument particle).

expressions.english: Please give me a cash receipt
expressions.shortExplanation: 현금영수증 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me a cash receipt".
expressions.explanation: 현금영수증 해 주세요 (hyeongeumyeongsujeung hae juseyo) means "Please give me a cash receipt". Say it as one set phrase — for example 현금영수증 해 주세요. ("A cash receipt, please."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Customer paying cash and requesting a tax-linked receipt for year-end deduction
반말; friend context only
More formal/precise with 발급하다 ('to issue officially')

usagePhrases.en: A cash receipt to my phone number, please.
usagePhrases.note: Extension: specify that your number should be used as the identifier

examples.ko: A: 현금영수증 해 드릴까요? / B: 네, 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: hyeongeumyeongsujeung hae deurilkkayo? / B: ne, hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I issue a cash receipt? / B: Yes, please.
examples.note: Staff proactively offer; you confirm with 해 주세요 — have your phone number ready immediately

examples.en: I'll pay cash. And a cash receipt, please. It's 010-1234-5678.
examples.note: Real flow: state cash payment → request receipt → read your number, all in one smooth turn

examples.en: Please register the receipt for income deduction.
examples.note: 소득공제용 (personal income deduction) vs 지출증빙용 (business expense proof) — most individuals say 소득공제로요

expressions.nuance: 현금영수증 (現金領收證) is a uniquely Korean institution: a cash receipt registered to your phone number or resident registration number so that it counts toward your annual income tax deduction. Unlike a regular 영수증 (printed slip), this one is electronically submitted to the National Tax Service automatically. 해 주세요 ('please do/issue it') is the everyday request; 발급해 주세요 is the formal verb. Plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only. Staff may follow with 소득공제용이세요, 지출증빙용이세요? — for personal use say 소득공제로요; for a business expense 지출증빙으로요. The critical near-synonym comparison: 영수증 주세요 just asks for the printed paper receipt with no tax link. The English-speaker mistake is asking only for 영수증 and missing the tax benefit altogether, or trying to request it on a card payment — 현금영수증 applies exclusively to 현금 (cash); cards automatically record their own transactions.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking for plain 영수증 expecting the tax benefit — that only gets you a printed slip; the tax-registered version is 현금영수증 해 주세요.
Requesting it on a card payment — 현금영수증 is for 현금 (cash) only; card payments are automatically recorded separately.
Forgetting to give your phone number — the receipt registers to your 휴대폰 번호, so read it out immediately after the request: 010-XXXX-XXXX이요.

structuredNuance.t: 현금(cash) + 영수증(receipt) + 해 주세요(please do/issue). Literally 'please do the cash receipt' — really 'please register this cash purchase for my tax deduction.' It is not just a paper receipt; it links to your ID for year-end tax benefits.

Say this whenever you pay cash at any store. Must be done at the time of payment — you cannot add it retroactively in most systems. Plain -요 polite to staff. Have your 휴대폰 번호 (mobile number) ready; some stores accept your resident registration number instead.

영수증 주세요 is a plain printed receipt — no tax link. 현금영수증 해 주세요 is the tax-registered receipt. 현금영수증 발급해 주세요 is the formal version. The key dividing line: 영수증 is just proof of purchase; 현금영수증 is linked to the national tax system.
현금영수증 (現金領收證): 現金 = cash + 領收 = receive/collect + 證 = certificate/proof. The 領收證 part is the same 영수증 (receipt). Same 現金 appears in 현금 인출기 (ATM, cash withdrawal machine).

Asking for just 영수증 misses the tax benefit — you only get a paper slip, not the tax-registered receipt. Also do not request 현금영수증 after paying by card — it only applies to cash payments; cards automatically register their own transactions.

expressions.shortExplanation: 빨대 어디 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Where are the straws?".
expressions.explanation: "Where are the straws?" — that is 빨대 어디 있어요? (ppaldae eodi isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 빨대 어디 있어요? ("Where are the straws?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Customer asking staff or looking around for the self-serve straw station
반말; to a friend
Softer, more polite/indirect variant with -나요?
Extension: skip location-finding and just ask staff to hand you one

examples.ko: A: 빨대 어디 있어요? / B: 저쪽 셀프바에 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: ppaldae eodi isseoyo? / B: jeojjok selpeubae isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Where are the straws? / B: Over at the self-serve bar.
examples.note: 셀프바 (self-serve bar) is where most Korean cafés keep straws, lids, napkins, sugar, and water; 저쪽 = 'over there'

examples.en: Where are the straws? I can't find them.
examples.note: 안 보여서요 = 'because I can't see them' — a natural soft reason added with -서요 to soften the request and explain why you're asking

examples.en: Where are the straws and napkins?
examples.note: 랑 links two items naturally in speech; 냅킨 (napkin) or 휴지 are usually at the same 셀프바 as straws

expressions.nuance: Most Korean cafés organize a 셀프바 (self-serve station) with straws, lids, sugar, creamers, napkins, and water, so 빨대 어디 있어요? is the practical question when you cannot locate it. 빨대 means 'straw' (literally 'sucking stick,' from the verb 빨다 'to suck'). 어디 있어요? = 'where is it?' using the existence/location verb 있다. Plain polite -요 to staff; 반말 어디 있어? with friends. If you prefer not to go find it yourself, substitute 빨대 좀 주세요 (please hand me one) — the dividing line is self-serve vs staff-fetched. Note paper straws (종이 빨대) are now standard at many Korean cafés due to environmental regulations. The English-speaker mistake is the verb choice: 빨대 어디예요? uses the copula 이다 to ask 'where is it (as a place)?' — grammatically this sounds like asking where the straw is as a location/address. Object location uses 있다: 빨대 어디 있어요? Another slip is calling it a 스트로 — the native word 빨대 is what Koreans say.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 빨대 어디예요? — for object location use 있어요? (existence verb): 빨대 어디 있어요?; 어디예요? asks where a place is, not where an object is.
Calling it 스트로 — the everyday Korean word is 빨대; 스트로 sounds unnatural and foreign.
Expecting staff to bring it unasked — straws are self-serve at the 셀프바 in most Korean cafés; either locate the station or explicitly say 빨대 좀 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 빨대(straw) + 어디(where) + 있어요(is/exists — location verb). Literally 'Where does the straw exist?' — naturally 'Where are the straws?' The verb 있다 (to exist/be at) is essential for locating objects; do not use 이다 (to be/equal) as 어디예요?.

Directed at any café staff or used while looking around. Most straws are at the 셀프바 — a quick point from staff is the usual answer. Plain -요 polite; 반말 어디 있어? with friends. To avoid the location search entirely: 빨대 좀 주세요.
빨대 좀 주세요 ('please hand me a straw') skips finding it yourself — the dividing line is whether you fetch it or staff bring it. 빨대 어디에 있나요? is the softened indirect form, slightly more formal.
빨대 어디 있어요? → 빨대 어디에 있나요? (softer) → 종이 빨대 있어요? (paper straws available?) → 빨대 좀 주세요 (just give me one). Add an item: 빨대랑 냅킨 어디 있어요?

빨대 어디예요? uses 이다 (copula), which sounds like asking the straw's location as an address — awkward for an object. For locating things use 있다: 빨대 어디 있어요?. Also avoid 스트로 — the everyday Korean word is 빨대.

expressions.shortExplanation: 자리 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Are there any seats?".
expressions.explanation: 자리 있어요? (jari isseoyo?) = "Are there any seats?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 자리 있어요? ("Are there seats available?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Customer asking staff or checking a specific spot at a café or restaurant
반말; to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Are there seats, by any chance?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more polite/indirect with -나요?

usagePhrases.en: Is there a table for two?
usagePhrases.note: Extension: state party size with 명 to get a more useful answer

examples.ko: A: 자리 있어요? / B: 네, 2층에 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: jari isseoyo? / B: ne, 2cheunge isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Any seats? / B: Yes, there are some upstairs on the 2nd floor.
examples.note: Korean cafés often direct you to a floor rather than personally seating you — listen for 층 (floor) cues and go yourself

examples.ko: 혹시 자리 있어요? 콘센트 있는 자리면 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: hoksi jari isseoyo? konsenteu inneun jarimyeon jokesseoyo.
examples.en: Any seats by any chance? Preferably a spot with a power outlet.
examples.note: 혹시 softens the ask and implies 'I'm not sure but hoping'; 콘센트 있는 자리 = seat with an electrical outlet, important for café work

examples.en: Any seats right now? There are two of us.
examples.note: -인데요 adds context (party size of two) and invites the staff to respond with the most useful information, not just yes/no

expressions.nuance: 자리 있어요? asks whether a seat or spot is free — at a busy café, at a restaurant entrance, or directly to a person whose nearby seat appears empty. 자리 = 'seat, spot, place'. Plain polite -요; 반말 자리 있어? with friends; softened 자리 있나요?. Add 혹시 before the question to sound less demanding, or state party size (두 명 자리 있어요?) for a more useful reply from staff. The near alternative is 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') — the dividing line is scope: 자리 있어요? asks about general availability anywhere in the venue, while 앉아도 돼요? asks permission for one specific seat you're standing next to. For written or formal contexts (reserved seating, cinema) the more formal word 좌석 is used; in a café the natural word is always 자리. Also note 자리를 잡다 ('to claim/save a seat') is a separate phrase — 자리 있어요? only asks about availability.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자리예요? for availability — use the existence verb 있어요?: 자리 있어요?; 자리예요? would sound like 'is this a seat?'
Using 좌석 in a casual café — 좌석 is the formal/written term (cinema, reserved seating); in everyday café speech the word is 자리.
Asking 자리 있어요? when you mean a specific empty seat right next to you — for that, ask 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') instead.

structuredNuance.t: 자리(seat/spot) + 있어요?(is there/are there — existence verb). Literally 'Is there a seat/spot?' — really 'Are there any seats available?' The existence verb 있다 is critical for availability questions about objects and places.

Use at café entrances, to staff at restaurants, or to a stranger sitting near an empty adjacent seat. Plain -요 polite; 반말 with friends; 혹시 자리 있나요? for extra softness. Korean cafés often do not seat you — they answer and expect you to walk over.

여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') is specific to one seat you're pointing at, while 자리 있어요? asks about any available seat in the whole venue. 좌석 있어요? is the formal/written version (theater, ticketed seating) — in a café it sounds too stiff; use 자리.
자리 있어요? → 혹시 자리 있어요? (softer) → 두/세 명 자리 있어요? (party size) → 콘센트 있는 자리 있어요? (outlet seat) → 창가 자리 있어요? (window seat). Formal: 자리 있나요?

자리예요? uses the copula 이다 and asks 'what is this, a seat?' — nonsensical for availability. Availability questions use the existence verb 있다: 자리 있어요?. Also do not use 좌석 in a casual café — 좌석 is formal/written (cinema, plane seat numbers); 자리 is the everyday word.

expressions.shortExplanation: 어디가 아프세요? is a practical expression meaning "Where does it hurt?".
expressions.explanation: "Where does it hurt?" — that is 어디가 아프세요? (eodiga apeuseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 어디가 아프세요? ("Where does it hurt?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Doctor/nurse to patient; honorific 세요, the standard opener
반말; a parent to a child or between close friends
Softer, more formal clinic phrasing; 불편하다 = be uncomfortable

usagePhrases.en: Where does it hurt the most?
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension narrowing down the worst spot

examples.ko: A: 어디가 아프세요? / B: 목이 아파요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga apeuseyo? / B: mogi apayo.
examples.en: A: Where does it hurt? / B: My throat hurts.
examples.note: The bare A/B exchange at the moment you sit down at the clinic — the classic opener and its expected reply format

examples.en: Where does it hurt? Since when has it been like this?
examples.note: Doctor naturally chains the history-taking follow-up 언제부터 right after; practice these two lines together

examples.ko: 환자분, 어디가 아프세요? 천천히 말씀해 보세요.
examples.romanization: hwanjabun, eodiga apeuseyo? cheoncheonhi malsseumhae boseyo.
examples.en: Where does it hurt, sir/ma'am? Take your time and tell me.
examples.note: Full clinic line showing the address form 환자분 ('patient') and the gentle invitation to describe symptoms

expressions.nuance: 어디가 아프세요? is the doctor's or nurse's standard polite question to a patient: 어디가 'where (as subject)' + 아프다 'to hurt/be sick' + honorific -세요. The patient never says this to the doctor; the patient answers with a body-part subject — 목이 아파요, 배가 아파요. The critical grammar axis: 아프다 is a descriptive verb (adjective-verb), so the hurting place is the SUBJECT and takes the subject particle 가 — never 어디를 아프세요? (object particle 를 is wrong because nothing is being done to a target). Softer alternatives shift register: 어디가 아파? is 반말 for a parent with a child, 어디가 불편하세요? is a gentler front-desk variant that sounds more considerate. Note 아프다 covers both 'it hurts' and 'I am sick', so this one question opens virtually every clinic visit. English learners often calque 'what's wrong?' as 뭐가 틀렸어요? — 틀리다 means 'incorrect', not 'ill'; use 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요? instead.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어디를 아프세요? with the object particle 를.
아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the painful spot is the grammatical subject and takes 가/이. The correct form is 어디가 아프세요?
A patient using 어디가 아프세요? to the doctor.
This is the caregiver's question to the patient. As the patient you state the location yourself: 머리가 아파요 / 배가 아파요.
Translating 'what's wrong?' as 뭐가 틀렸어요?.
틀리다 means 'be wrong/incorrect' (as in an answer), not 'be ill'. For symptoms say 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요?

structuredNuance.t: The doctor's or nurse's standard polite opening to a patient, using 어디가 'where (subject)' + 아프다 'to hurt/be sick' + honorific -세요. The patient does NOT say this to the doctor — the patient answers with a body-part subject: 목이 아파요, 배가 아파요. 아프다 covers both 'it hurts' and 'I am sick', so this single question opens almost every clinic visit.

어디가 아프세요? is clinic/존댓말 — only medical staff or caregivers ask it. 어디가 아파? is 반말 used by a parent to a child or between close friends. 어디가 불편하세요? is a gentler, slightly more formal variant heard at receptions and from nurses doing intake.

어디가 아프세요? focuses on physical pain (아프다 = hurt). 어디가 불편하세요? focuses on discomfort or general malaise (불편하다 = be uncomfortable), so it can also cover non-painful issues like dizziness or fatigue. The latter is gentler and more commonly used at receptions and front desks.
어디가 아프세요? → 어디가 제일 아프세요? (narrowing down the worst spot) → 어디가 불편하세요? (softer) → 어디 좀 보여 주세요 ('let me take a look').

Two traps: (1) wrong particle — learners say 어디를 아프세요? but 아프다 is descriptive, so the hurting place is the subject (가), not the object (를). (2) wrong phrase — 'what's wrong?' calqued as 뭐가 틀렸어요? — 틀리다 means 'incorrect (like an answer)', not 'unwell'. Use 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요?.

expressions.shortExplanation: 열이 나요 is a practical expression meaning "He has a fever".
expressions.explanation: "He has a fever" — that is 열이 나요 (yeori nayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 열이 나요 ("He has a fever"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the core symptom report
반말, to your partner (열나 / 열 나)
Milder, with 있다 ('there is') for a low fever
Giving the number; 오르다 = 'to rise'

examples.en: He's had a fever since morning.
examples.note: 아침부터 ('since morning') marks onset for the teacher or doctor

examples.ko: A: 아이 열이 어느 정도예요? / B: 어젯밤부터 38.5도였는데 해열제 먹였더니 좀 내렸어요.
examples.romanization: A: ai yeori eoneu jeongdoyeyo? / B: eojetbambuteo 38.5doyeonneunde haeyeolje meogyeotdeoni jom naeryeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: How high is the fever? / B: It was 38.5 since last night, but it came down after fever medicine.
examples.note: Doctor or teacher asking; 내리다 ('to come down') for a dropping fever

examples.ko: 열이 안 떨어지면 어린이집에서 바로 연락 주세요. 데리러 갈게요.
examples.romanization: yeori an tteoreojimyeon eorinijibeseo baro yeollak juseyo. derireo galgeyo.
examples.en: If the fever won't go down, please call me right away from daycare — I'll come get him.
examples.note: 떨어지다 ('to drop') for fever going down; 연락 주세요 = 'please contact me'

expressions.nuance: 열이 나요 means '(he) has a fever' — 열 (熱, 'heat/fever') + 이 (subject particle) + 나요 (from 나다 'to come out/occur/break out'). The verb choice is everything: in Korean the fever 'comes out' (나다), not something you 'have' (가지다). This same 나다 pattern applies to many bodily events: 땀이 나다 ('sweat breaks out'), 콧물이 나다 ('runny nose'), 두드러기가 나다 ('hives break out'). For a mild lingering temperature you can say 열이 있어요 ('there is fever'), but for the dynamic event of having/running a fever, 열이 나다 is the standard. Key fever vocabulary: 열이 오르다 ('fever rises'), 열이 떨어지다/내리다 ('fever drops/comes down'), 열을 재다 ('take the temperature'), 해열제 ('fever reducer'). The particle is non-negotiable: it's 열'이' 나요 (이 marks 열 as the subject), never 열을 나요. Say this in 존댓말 to a daycare teacher or pediatrician; 반말 to your partner: 열나.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 열을 가지고 있어요 ('I have a fever').
Direct calque of English 'have'. Korean says the fever occurs: 열이 나요. 가지다 ('possess') never applies to symptoms.
Using the wrong particle: 열을 나요.
나다 here takes the subject particle: 열'이' 나요 ('fever occurs'). 열을 is ungrammatical with 나다.
Saying 뜨거워요 to report a fever.
뜨겁다 = 'hot to the touch' (objects/skin). To report the medical symptom, say 열이 나요. 뜨거워요 describes how the forehead feels, not 'he has a fever'.

structuredNuance.t: 열이 나요 = 'fever comes out/occurs'. The verb 나다 ('to occur/break out') is idiomatic for bodily events: fever, sweat, hives, a runny nose all 나다. This is NOT a direct translation of 'have a fever' — Korean doesn't say the person 'has' it, but rather the fever 'occurs'.
존댓말 (열이 나요) to daycare teacher or doctor. 반말 (열나 / 열 나) to your partner. For a slight fever: 열이 좀 있어요 (softer). For a high one: 열이 많이 나요, 38도까지 올랐어요. At the clinic you add the number: 38.5도 열이 있어요.

열이 나요 (fever is occurring — dynamic) vs 열이 있어요 (there is a fever — static, for a mild/lingering one). 뜨거워요 ('it's hot to the touch') describes the forehead tactilely but is NOT a medical report. For a dropping fever: 열이 떨어졌어요 / 내렸어요.
열이 나요 → 열이 많이 나요 ('high fever') → 열이 오르고 있어요 ('fever rising') → 열이 떨어졌어요 ('fever came down') → 해열제 먹였어요 ('gave fever reducer'). Temperature: 38도 열이 있어요.

Two traps: (1) 열을 가지고 있어요 — calque of 'have a fever'. Korean says the fever 'comes out': 열이 나요. 가지다 never fits symptoms. (2) Wrong particle: 열'이' 나요, not 열'을' 나요. 나다 here takes the subject particle because 열 (fever) is the thing that occurs, not the object of an action.
열 is Sino-Korean 熱 ('heat'). The same character appears in 고열 (高熱 'high fever'), 해열 (解熱 'reducing fever'), and 체온 (體溫 'body temperature').

expressions.shortExplanation: 머리가 아파요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a headache".
expressions.explanation: 머리가 아파요 (meoriga apayo) means "I have a headache". Say it as one set phrase — for example 머리가 아파요 ("I have a headache"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; telling a doctor or pharmacist
반말; to a friend or family
Formal 합쇼체; stiffer register
Vivid extension for a severe headache; 깨지다 = shatter/split

examples.ko: A: 어디가 아프세요? / B: 머리가 아파요. 어제 저녁부터요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga apeuseyo? / B: meoriga apayo. eoje jeonyeokbuteoyo.
examples.en: A: Where does it hurt? / B: I have a headache. Since last night.
examples.note: The textbook A/B clinic exchange — note the patient adds the duration naturally

examples.en: My head's been throbbing since this morning.
examples.note: Everyday use showing the mimetic adverb 지끈지끈 = the rhythmic, throbbing-ache sensation that is common with headaches

examples.en: My head hurt so much I left work early.
examples.note: Fuller real-life consequence; 조퇴하다 = leave work or school early due to illness

expressions.nuance: 머리가 아파요 is the everyday Korean 'I have a headache': body-part + subject particle 가 + 아파요. The subject particle 가 is mandatory because 아프다 is a descriptive verb — the head is 'the thing that is hurting', its grammatical subject, never 머리를. This frame builds all symptom sentences: 배가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 이가 아파요. Register shifts by ending only — 머리가 아파 (반말), 아파요 (존댓말), 아픕니다 (격식). One practical ambiguity: 머리 can mean 'head' (the body part) or 'hair' — in a pain context 아파요 removes all doubt. English speakers often reach for the Sino-Korean noun 두통 and produce 두통이 있어요 — that is grammatically correct and sounds more clinical (두통 = 頭痛), but in everyday speech 머리가 아파요 is far more natural; 두통 surfaces in pharmacy requests like 두통약 주세요 (give me headache medicine). Vivid intensity variants: 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요 (throbbing), 머리가 깨질 것 같아요 (splitting), 머리가 띵해요 (dull, foggy).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 머리를 아파요 with 를.
아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the body part is the subject and takes 가/이: 머리가 아파요, not 머리를 아파요.
Saying 나는 머리 아파요 dropping the particle in formal speech.
Casual speech can drop 가, but to a doctor keep it: 머리가 아파요 sounds complete and clear, while bare 머리 아파 is 반말-flavored.
Using 두통해요 as a verb.
두통 is a noun; you can't verb it with 하다. Say 두통이 있어요 or, more naturally, 머리가 아파요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'my head is sick/hurting'. 실제 뜻: 'I have a headache'. The body-part + 가/이 + 아파요 frame is the universal symptom pattern — plug in any body part: 목이, 배가, 이가, 등이.
머리가 아파요 to a doctor, pharmacist, or colleague (존댓말). 머리가 아파 to friends and family (반말). 머리가 아픕니다 in a very formal context. Using 반말 to a doctor is socially inappropriate regardless of age.

머리가 아파요 = everyday speech, immediate and natural. 두통이 있어요 = Sino-Korean clinical term (두통 = 頭痛), sounds like reading a chart. Use 머리가 아파요 to a doctor verbally; 두통 appears on packaging (두통약). 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요 adds the throbbing quality.
머리가 아파요 → 머리가 많이 아파요 → 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요 (throbbing) → 머리가 깨질 것 같아요 (splitting) → 머리가 띵해요 (dull/foggy).

Two traps: (1) wrong particle — 머리를 아파요 is wrong; use subject particle 가. (2) wrong word — over-using the formal 두통이 있어요 because 'headache' is a noun in English; in spoken Korean 머리가 아파요 is far more natural.

expressions.shortExplanation: 배가 아파요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a stomachache".
expressions.explanation: "I have a stomachache" — that is 배가 아파요 (baega apayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 배가 아파요 ("My stomach hurts"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; reporting to a doctor
반말; to family or a friend
Formal register
Extension; 콕콕 쑤시다 = sharp, stabbing pains at a point

examples.ko: A: 배가 아파요. / B: 설사도 하세요?
examples.romanization: A: baega apayo. / B: seolsado haseyo?
examples.en: A: My stomach hurts. / B: Do you also have diarrhea?
examples.note: Bare clinic A/B — note how doctors probe for 설사 (diarrhea) or 구역질 (nausea) right after this opener

examples.ko: 어제 회를 먹고 나서 배가 계속 아파요.
examples.romanization: eoje hoereul meokgo naseo baega gyesok apayo.
examples.en: My stomach has been hurting ever since I ate raw fish yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday cause-and-effect; 회 = raw fish / sashimi; the doctor needs this causal information

examples.ko: 아침부터 배가 살살 아프더니 점심 때부터 콕콕 쑤셔요.
examples.romanization: achimbuteo baega salsal apeudeoni jeomsim ttaebuteo kokkok ssusyeoyo.
examples.en: It started as a mild ache in the morning and since lunch it's been sharp and stabbing.
examples.note: Fuller progression of pain intensity showing two mimetics: 살살 아프다 (gently aching) → 콕콕 쑤시다 (stabbing)

expressions.nuance: 배가 아파요 covers stomachache, bellyache, and cramps — 배 is the whole belly/abdomen, not the stomach organ alone. The grammar is the same as all 아프다 symptoms: subject particle 가, never 배를. To pinpoint, add 윗배 (upper abdomen) or 아랫배 (lower abdomen). One important cultural note: 배가 아프다 has an idiomatic second meaning of 'to be envious' — 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 ('when a cousin buys land, your belly hurts') is a classic proverb about envy. At a clinic the medical meaning is obvious, but if a friend says 야, 배 아프다 upon hearing good news, they mean jealousy, not illness. The English-speaker error is reaching for 위가 아파요 (胃, the stomach organ) for a general bellyache — 위가 아파요 is narrower and more clinical; for ordinary abdominal pain always use 배가 아파요. Doctors may ask about 메스껍다 (nausea), 설사 (diarrhea), or 복통 (腹痛, the clinical noun) as follow-up.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 배를 아파요 with the object particle.
아프다 is descriptive, so 배 is the subject: 배가 아파요, not 배를.
Using 위가 아파요 for a general bellyache.
위 is specifically the stomach organ and sounds clinical. For ordinary belly/abdominal pain say 배가 아파요.
Reading every 배가 아파요 as physical pain.
It can idiomatically mean 'I'm jealous'. At a clinic it's literal, but among friends 배 아파 may tease 'I'm so envious', so let context decide.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'my belly is sick'. 실제 뜻: covers any stomachache, bellyache, or abdominal cramps — 배 is the whole belly, not the stomach organ. Add 윗배 (upper) or 아랫배 (lower) to narrow it. Same grammar as all 아프다 symptoms: body-part + 가 + 아파요.

배가 아파요 to a doctor (존댓말). 배가 아파 to a friend or child (반말). 배가 아픕니다 in a formal context. Important: if you say 배 아파 among friends after someone shares good news, it can be read as 'I'm jealous' (see below) — tone and context disambiguate.
배가 아파요 (general, everyday) vs 위가 아파요 (stomach organ, clinical; 위 = 胃) vs 복통이 있어요 (腹痛, medical chart language). For spoken reporting at a clinic, 배가 아파요 is always the right starting point.

배가 아프다 idiomatically means 'to be jealous/envious' — 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 is the proverb. If a friend says 배 아프다 after hearing your good news, they are teasing about envy, not reporting illness. At a clinic the physical meaning is unambiguous.

Two traps: (1) using 위가 아파요 for a generic bellyache — 위 is the stomach organ specifically and sounds clinical; stick with 배가 아파요. (2) wrong particle 배를 아파요 — 아프다 is descriptive, 배 is the subject: 배가 아파요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 감기에 걸렸어요 is a practical expression meaning "I caught a cold".
expressions.explanation: 감기에 걸렸어요 (gamgie geollyeosseoyo) = "I caught a cold". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 감기에 걸렸어요 ("I caught a cold"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; to a doctor or coworker
반말; to a friend, particle 에 often dropped

usagePhrases.en: I have come down with a cold
usagePhrases.note: Formal register

usagePhrases.en: I feel a cold coming on
usagePhrases.note: Extension for the early, mild stage before it fully hits

examples.ko: A: 오늘 왜 못 왔어요? / B: 감기에 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul wae mot wasseoyo? / B: gamgie geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: Why couldn't you come today? / B: I caught a cold.
examples.note: Everyday A/B excuse — note 걸렸어요 (past) expresses the resulting present state 'I have a cold now'

examples.en: I caught a cold from the kids.
examples.note: Everyday contagion context; 옮다 = catch/be infected from someone — useful collocation

examples.ko: 독감인 줄 알았는데 검사해 보니까 그냥 감기에 걸린 거였어요.
examples.romanization: dokgamin jul aranneunde geomsahae bonikka geunyang gamgie geollin geoyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I thought it was the flu, but after the test it turned out to be just a cold.
examples.note: Fuller situation contrasting 독감 (flu) with 감기 (cold) — a key vocabulary distinction at the clinic

expressions.nuance: 감기에 걸렸어요 means 'I caught a cold': 감기 (cold) + particle 에 + 걸리다 (to get caught/snagged) in the past tense. The particle is always 에, not 를 — you get 'caught IN' the cold like something hooking you; 감기에 걸리다 is a fixed collocation and 감기를 걸리다 is ungrammatical. Tense is a key axis: 걸렸어요 (past) conveys the resulting state 'I have a cold right now', because you got caught and are still caught. 감기에 걸려요 (present) would sound like a general tendency ('I catch colds easily') — not what you want when sick. The critical vocabulary divide: 감기 is a common cold, 독감 (毒感) is influenza — a more serious illness with a distinct test; calling the flu 감기 at a clinic seriously downplays it. For the very first hints say 감기 기운이 있어요 ('there's a hint/energy of a cold'). 옮다 ('to be infected from someone') pairs naturally: 감기를 옮았어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 감기를 걸렸어요 with 를.
걸리다 here takes 에: 감기에 걸리다 is a fixed pairing. The object particle 를 is ungrammatical.
Using present 감기에 걸려요 to mean 'I have a cold now'.
걸리다 is the moment of catching it, so the past 걸렸어요 expresses the resulting state 'I have a cold'. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.
Calling the flu 감기.
감기 is a common cold; the flu is 독감. Mixing them up downplays a serious illness to a doctor.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'got snagged in a cold'. 실제 뜻: 'I caught / have a cold'. The metaphor is of being hooked or trapped — 걸리다 is used similarly for other ailments: 독감에 걸렸어요, 폐렴에 걸렸어요. The fixed particle is 에 (걸리다 always takes 에 for the thing you catch).

감기에 걸렸어요 to a doctor, pharmacist, or colleague (존댓말). 감기 걸렸어 to a friend or family (반말, 에 often dropped). 감기에 걸렸습니다 in a formal absence report or official context. Don't say 감기에 걸릴게요 — that would mean 'I intend to catch a cold'!

감기에 걸렸어요 (common cold, 감기) vs 독감에 걸렸어요 (flu, 독감 = 毒感). The difference is medical: 감기 is a mild respiratory illness, 독감 is influenza requiring antiviral treatment. Mixing them up to a doctor misleads them. For the onset stage: 감기 기운이 있어요 ('there is a hint of a cold coming on').
감기에 걸렸어요 → 독감에 걸렸어요 → 감기 기운이 있어요 → 감기가 다 나았어요 ('the cold is all gone') → 감기를 옮겼어요 ('I passed the cold to someone').

Two traps: (1) wrong particle — 감기를 걸렸어요 is ungrammatical; 걸리다 always takes 에. (2) wrong tense — 감기에 걸려요 sounds like a general tendency; use past 걸렸어요 when you have a cold now. (3) vocabulary confusion — never use 감기 for the flu; flu is 독감.

expressions.shortExplanation: 기침이 나요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a cough".
expressions.explanation: 기침이 나요 (gichimi nayo) means "I have a cough". Say it as one set phrase — for example 기침이 나요 ("I have a cough"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; reporting a symptom to a doctor or pharmacist
반말; to a friend or family
Formal register
Extension stressing it's persistent; ~질 않다 = just won't (stop)

examples.ko: A: 기침이 나요. / B: 가래도 있어요?
examples.romanization: A: gichimi nayo. / B: garaedo isseoyo?
examples.en: A: I have a cough. / B: Any phlegm too?
examples.note: Classic clinic A/B — 가래 (phlegm) is the immediate follow-up question; learn these paired terms together

examples.ko: 밤에 누우면 기침이 더 심해지고 잠을 못 자요.
examples.romanization: bame nuumyeon gichimi deo simhaejigo jameul mot jayo.
examples.en: The cough gets worse when I lie down at night and I can't sleep.
examples.note: Everyday detail showing timing and consequence; 심해지다 = get more severe

examples.ko: 기침이 2주째 안 멈춰서 결국 병원에 갔더니 폐렴이었어요.
examples.romanization: gichimi 2jujjae an meomchwoseo gyeolguk byeongwone gatdeoni pyeryeomieosseoyo.
examples.en: I'd been coughing for two weeks without stopping, so I finally went to the doctor and it was pneumonia.
examples.note: Fuller real-life consequence; 2주째 = going on two weeks, 폐렴 = pneumonia — signals when to see a doctor

expressions.nuance: 기침이 나요 reports a cough using the same 나다 ('to come out/arise') + subject particle 이 pattern as 열이 나요 and 콧물이 나요 — bodily phenomena 'arise' in Korean. You can also say 기침을 해요 ('I cough', cough + 하다), but these have a subtle difference: 기침이 나요 = 'a cough is happening to me (a symptom I have)', while 기침을 해요 = 'I am coughing (an action I'm doing)'. Both are fine at a clinic. The English-speaker traps are consistent across this file: (1) possession calque 기침을 가지고 있어요 is wrong — use 나다; (2) wrong particle — 기침을 나요 treats 나다 as transitive, but it is intransitive: always 기침이 나요. Pair-words the doctor asks next: 가래 (phlegm you cough up), 콧물 (runny nose), 호흡 곤란 (breathing difficulty). Common partner phrase from the pharmacy: 기침에 좋은 약 있어요? ('Do you have medicine good for coughs?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 기침을 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a cough'.
This calques English 'have'. Korean says 기침이 나요 or 기침을 해요.
Saying 기침을 나요 with 를 plus 나다.
나다 is intransitive, so 기침 is the subject: 기침이 나요. (If you want 를, the verb must be 하다: 기침을 해요.)
Confusing 기침 with 가래.
기침 is the cough; 가래 is the phlegm/mucus you cough up. The doctor asks 가래도 나요? as a separate question.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'cough comes out'. 실제 뜻: 'I have a cough / I'm coughing'. Bodily phenomena 'arise' in Korean — 기침이 나다, 콧물이 나다, 열이 나다 all share this pattern. Keep subject particle 이 (not 를): 기침이 나요.
기침이 나요 to a doctor or pharmacist (존댓말). 기침이 나 to a friend (반말). 기침이 납니다 in a formal context. It's equally natural to say to a coworker as an explanation for stepping out: 기침이 나서 잠깐 나갔다 왔어요.

기침이 나요 = 'a cough is happening (to me)' — symptom framing. 기침을 해요 = 'I am coughing' — action framing. For reporting to a doctor either works. 기침이 멈추질 않아요 adds urgency: 'it won't stop'. 마른기침이 나요 = 'I have a dry cough' (마르다 = dry).
기침이 나요 → 기침이 심해요 (the cough is bad) → 기침이 멈추질 않아요 (won't stop) → 마른기침이 나요 (dry cough) → 기침이 나아졌어요 (getting better).
Two traps: (1) 기침을 가지고 있어요 — calquing 'have a cough' with 가지다 (possess); use 기침이 나요. (2) 기침을 나요 — 나다 is intransitive, so 기침 is the subject (이), not the object (를).

expressions.shortExplanation: 콧물이 나요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a runny nose".
expressions.explanation: "I have a runny nose" — that is 콧물이 나요 (konmuri nayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 콧물이 나요 ("My nose is running"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; reporting a symptom to a doctor or pharmacist
반말; particle 이 often dropped with friends
Formal register
Contrast extension for the opposite problem — a blocked nose

examples.ko: A: 콧물이 나요. / B: 코도 막혔어요?
examples.romanization: A: konmuri nayo. / B: kodo makyeosseoyo?
examples.en: A: My nose is running. / B: Is it stuffy too?
examples.note: Classic A/B — 콧물 (runny) and 코 막힘 (stuffy) are the two paired questions doctors always ask together

examples.ko: 재채기를 계속 하면서 콧물이 줄줄 나요.
examples.romanization: jaechaegireul gyeso kamyeonseo konmuri juljul nayo.
examples.en: I keep sneezing and snot is running down freely.
examples.note: Everyday combo; 재채기 = a sneeze; 줄줄 나다 = to run/drip continuously — the mimetic 줄줄 adds vividness

examples.ko: 환절기만 되면 콧물이 나고 눈이 빨개지고 가렵더라고요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgiman doemyeon konmuri nago nuni ppalgaejigo garyeopdeoragoyo.
examples.en: Every change of season my nose runs, my eyes go red and itch.
examples.note: Fuller allergy picture; 환절기 = turn-of-season period — key word for seasonal allergy context

expressions.nuance: 콧물이 나요 means 'my nose is running' — 콧물 is literally 'nose-water' (코 nose + 물 water, with the linking consonant ㅅ inserted to give 콧물), and it 'arises' using nasal particle 이 + 나다. The key contrast pair a doctor will always ask: 콧물이 나요? (runny, wet) versus 코가 막혔어요? (blocked, stuffy) — opposite problems requiring different treatments, so never confuse them. In casual speech the particle drops (콧물 나), but with medical staff say the full 콧물이 나요. The English-speaker structural trap is treating 'runny nose' as an adjective phrase and not knowing how to say it; Korean makes 콧물 (the mucus) the subject that 'comes out', so the logic is 'nose-water comes out'. Related terms to know: 재채기 (sneeze), 가래 (phlegm), 비염 (鼻炎, rhinitis — the clinical term if chronic). For allergic rhinitis a doctor may say 알레르기성 비염이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 콧물을 나요 with 를.
나다 is intransitive; 콧물 is its subject, so 콧물이 나요, never 콧물을 나요.
Confusing 콧물이 나요 with 코가 막혔어요.
콧물이 나요 = a runny (wet) nose; 코가 막혔어요 = a blocked (stuffy) nose. They are opposite symptoms.
Writing 코물 instead of 콧물.
The compound 코 + 물 inserts a ㅅ받침: it is spelled 콧물 and pronounced [콘물]. 코물 is a spelling error.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'nose-water comes out'. 실제 뜻: 'I have a runny nose'. Korean makes 콧물 (the mucus itself) the subject of 나다 (to come out) — same 나다 pattern as 열이 나다, 기침이 나다. Subject particle 이, never 콧물을 나요.
콧물 = 코 (nose) + linking ㅅ + 물 (water) — a pure native Korean compound. Pronounced [콘물] due to nasalization. The clinical term is 비염 (鼻炎, 'nose inflammation') for chronic runny nose / rhinitis.
콧물이 나요 to a doctor or pharmacist (존댓말). 콧물 나 to friends and family (반말, particle dropped). 콧물이 납니다 in a formal context. To a doctor, always add how long: 콧물이 3일째 나요 ('runny for three days now').

콧물이 나요 (runny/wet nose) vs 코가 막혔어요 (blocked/stuffy nose) — opposite symptoms, different treatments. A doctor always asks both. 비염이 있어요 is the clinical self-diagnosis for chronic rhinitis. 코를 풀다 = to blow your nose (an action, not a symptom report).

English speakers try to translate 'runny nose' as an adjective phrase and get stuck. Korean treats the mucus as the subject: 콧물이 나요. Also: 콧물을 나요 is wrong (나다 is intransitive, 콧물 is the subject). And spelling: it is 콧물 not 코물 — the ㅅ is essential.

expressions.english: I feel like I'm going to throw up
expressions.shortExplanation: 토할 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "I feel like I'm going to throw up".
expressions.explanation: 토할 것 같아요 (tohal geot gatayo) = "I feel like I'm going to throw up". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 토할 것 같아요 ("I feel like throwing up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; warning a doctor or nurse urgently
반말; to a friend or family
Formal register
Milder extension; 메스껍다 = nauseous, queasy — less urgent

examples.ko: A: 토할 것 같아요! / B: 잠깐, 봉투 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: tohal geot gatayo! / B: jamkkan, bongtu yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: I think I'm going to throw up! / B: Wait — here's a bag.
examples.note: Urgent A/B exchange at a clinic or hospital ward; the urgency of 을 것 같다 is clear in the response

examples.ko: 차만 타면 멀미가 나서 토할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: chaman tamyeon meolmiga naseo tohal geot gatayo.
examples.en: I get carsick the moment I'm in a car and feel like throwing up.
examples.note: Everyday motion-sickness context; 멀미가 나다 = get motion sickness — a frequent cause

examples.ko: 어지럽고 속이 울렁거려서 진짜 토할 것 같아요. 잠깐 앉아도 될까요?
examples.romanization: eojireopgo sogi ulleonggeoryeoseo jinjja tohal geot gatayo. jamkkan anjado doelkkayo?
examples.en: I'm dizzy and my stomach is churning, I really feel like I'll throw up. May I sit down for a moment?
examples.note: Fuller state with two accompanying symptoms; 울렁거리다 = stomach churning/heaving — natural co-report with 어지러워요

expressions.nuance: 토할 것 같아요 = 토하다 'to vomit' + -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 'it feels like / seems like it will happen' — the 을 것 같다 construction is crucial: it expresses an imminent, pending sensation, not a fact or a completed act. This is exactly why it's the right phrase to warn a nurse before it happens. Intensity scale: 속이 안 좋아요 (my stomach is off — mildest) → 메스꺼워요 / 울렁거려요 (queasy, churning) → 토할 것 같아요 (I'm about to throw up — most urgent). The completed act is 토했어요 (I threw up / I vomited). Casual/colloquial alternatives 게워요 or 올라올 것 같아요 are understood but avoid them with strangers — 토하다 is the neutral medical verb. The English-speaker grammar trap is loose 같아요: don't say 토해요 같아요 — 같다 must attach to the -(으)ㄹ 것 form (토할 것 같아요). Another error: using 던지다 from the English 'throw up' — 던지다 means to physically throw an object.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 토해요 같아요 to mean 'I feel like throwing up'.
같다 must attach to the 을 것 form: 토할 것 같아요. You can't bolt 같아요 onto a finished verb.
Using 토할 것 같아요 only after you've already vomited.
The 을 것 같다 frame is for an impending feeling. If it already happened, say 토했어요.
Saying 던지다 because a dictionary glosses 'throw up' as 'throw'.
던지다 means physically throw an object. 'Throw up' (vomit) is 토하다 — a completely different verb.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'it seems like I will vomit'. 실제 뜻: 'I feel like I'm about to throw up'. The -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 frame is key — it expresses an impending sensation, not a fact or completed act. Completed act: 토했어요. Impending sensation: 토할 것 같아요.

토할 것 같아요 to a doctor, nurse, or anyone nearby in a medical context (존댓말, urgent). 토할 것 같아 to friends (반말). At a clinic this phrase signals immediate action needed — nurses recognize it. The softer 메스꺼워요 is for a general 'I feel queasy' to the pharmacist.

Intensity scale: 속이 안 좋아요 (stomach's off, mildest) → 메스꺼워요 / 구역질이 나요 (nauseous, queasy) → 울렁거려요 (stomach churning) → 토할 것 같아요 (about to throw up, most urgent). Use the right level — 토할 것 같아요 triggers immediate nursing action.
토할 것 같아요 → 속이 메스꺼워요 (queasy) → 구역질이 나요 (nauseous) → 토했어요 (did throw up) → 속이 안 좋아요 (stomach's off, mildest).
Two traps: (1) 같아요 detached from 을 것 — 토해요 같아요 is wrong; 같다 must bind to -(으)ㄹ 것: 토할 것 같아요. (2) 던지다 from 'throw up' — 던지다 = to toss an object; vomiting is 토하다 with no shared meaning.

expressions.shortExplanation: 어지러워요 is a practical expression meaning "I feel dizzy".
expressions.explanation: 어지러워요 (eojireowoyo) means "I feel dizzy". Say it as one set phrase — for example 어지러워요 ("I feel dizzy"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; reporting to a doctor or anyone nearby
반말; to a friend or family
Formal register; note the ㅂ-irregular in action
Vivid colloquial extension; 핑 돌다 = go light-headed in a spinning sensation

examples.ko: A: 어지러워요. / B: 일단 여기 앉으세요.
examples.romanization: A: eojireowoyo. / B: ildan yeogi anjeuseyo.
examples.en: A: I feel dizzy. / B: First, please sit down here.
examples.note: Immediate A/B in a clinic — the listener's response (sit down) shows this phrase triggers action

examples.ko: 갑자기 일어나면 어지러워요. 혈압이 낮은 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi ireonamyeon eojireowoyo. hyeorabi najeun geot gatayo.
examples.en: I get dizzy when I suddenly stand up. I think my blood pressure might be low.
examples.note: Everyday trigger; 갑자기 = suddenly, 혈압이 낮다 = low blood pressure — a common cause to mention

examples.ko: 며칠째 어지럽고 속이 메스꺼워서 일도 못 하겠어요.
examples.romanization: myeochiljjae eojireopgo sogi meseukkeowoseo ildo mo tagesseoyo.
examples.en: I've been dizzy and nauseous for days and can't even work.
examples.note: Fuller picture pairing 어지러워요 with 메스꺼워요 — these two co-occur; 며칠째 = for several days running

expressions.nuance: 어지러워요 means 'I feel dizzy/light-headed'. The base adjective-verb is 어지럽다, which is a ㅂ-irregular: the final ㅂ changes to 우/워 before vowel endings, so 어지럽다 → 어지러워요 (NOT 어지럽어요). This is one of the most commonly misspelled medical words. As a descriptive verb of state, 어지러워요 stands alone — no body-part subject is needed (unlike 머리가 아파요). The near-synonym 현기증이 나요 ('I have vertigo / dizziness', 현기증 = 眩氣症) is more clinical and noun-based (the symptom 'arises' with 나다); the divide is: everyday conversational 어지러워요 vs. chart/report 현기증이 나요. When dizzy from spinning, Koreans add 핑 돌아요 for the wheeling sensation. English speakers trip on two things: (1) the ㅂ-irregular (writing 어지럽어요), and (2) reaching for 미쳐요 ('going crazy') from 'my head is spinning' — 미치다 means losing one's mind, nothing to do with physical faintness.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어지럽어요 by regularizing the verb.
어지럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the ㅂ becomes 워 before 어요, giving 어지러워요, not 어지럽어요.
Saying 머리가 어지러워요.
어지럽다 already describes your whole head/state, so a body-part subject is redundant. Just say 어지러워요.
Using 미쳐요 for 'my head is spinning'.
미치다 = go crazy/insane. Dizziness is 어지러워요 or 현기증이 나요; 미쳐요 has nothing to do with feeling faint.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '(things are) scattered/muddled'. 실제 뜻: 'I feel dizzy / light-headed'. As a descriptive verb-adjective it stands alone — no body-part subject needed. Covers both the dizzy-from-standing sensation and general vertigo.
어지럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 워 before 어요/은/을. Forms: 어지럽다 (dictionary) → 어지러워요 (present) → 어지러웠어요 (past) → 어지러운 (attributive). Never 어지럽어요.

어지러워요 to a doctor or anyone nearby (존댓말). 어지러워 to a friend (반말). Say it any time you feel faint — it signals the listener to help you sit. If it's chronic, add a duration: 며칠째 어지러워요. If severe, add 쓰러질 것 같아요 ('I feel like I'll collapse').

어지러워요 (everyday spoken, immediate) vs 현기증이 나요 (clinical noun-based, 현기증 = 眩氣症, fits a chart or formal report) vs 핑 돌아요 (colloquial, spinning/whirling feeling). Use 어지러워요 to describe your state; use 현기증이 나요 if a form asks you to fill in symptoms.
Two traps: (1) regularizing the ㅂ-irregular — 어지럽어요 is wrong; the ㅂ becomes 워: 어지러워요. (2) using 미쳐요 for 'my head is spinning' — 미치다 = go crazy/insane, nothing to do with feeling faint.

expressions.shortExplanation: 처방전 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me the prescription".
expressions.explanation: "Please give me the prescription" — that is 처방전 주세요 (cheobangjeon juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 처방전 주세요 ("Please give me the prescription"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; patient to doctor/clinic staff
반말; only in very close relationships, unusual in a clinic setting

usagePhrases.en: Could you please give me the prescription?
usagePhrases.note: More polite request; 주시겠어요 = would you be so kind as to give
Extension for lost or re-issued slips; 발급하다 = to issue a document

examples.ko: A: 처방전 주세요. / B: 여기 있습니다.
examples.romanization: A: cheobangjeon juseyo. / B: yeogi itseumnida.
examples.en: A: The prescription, please. / B: Here you are.
examples.note: The textbook A/B exchange at the clinic desk; note 여기 있습니다 is the staff's natural reply

examples.en: I need to go to the pharmacy — please give me the prescription.
examples.note: Everyday reason; shows the Korean split system: 병원 writes the 처방전, 약국 fills it

examples.ko: 전에 받은 처방전을 잃어버렸는데, 다시 발급해 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: jeone badeun cheobangjeoneul ireobeoryeonneunde, dasi balgeupae jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I lost the prescription I got before — could you possibly reissue it?
examples.note: Fuller situation; 잃어버리다 = to lose something; 발급 = issuance — a real situation for re-visits

expressions.nuance: 처방전 주세요 asks for the prescription slip: 처방전 (處方箋, 'prescription document') + 주세요 'please give me'. Korea uses a split dispensing system: the doctor (at the 병원/의원) writes the 처방전, and you take it separately to a 약국 (pharmacy) to receive the actual medicine. So saying 처방전 주세요 is specifically addressed to the doctor or clinic staff — never the pharmacist. At the pharmacy you HAND the slip over, then say 약 지어 주세요 to have it filled. The vocabulary distinctions matter: 처방전 (the slip/document) vs 처방 (the act of prescribing) vs 약 (the medicine itself). For politeness, 좀 주시겠어요? is softer than 주세요; 주실 수 있어요? is even more indirect. English speakers often bypass this system and ask for 약 at the clinic, not realizing the receipt of a slip is the intermediate step. Saying 처방전 주세요 to the pharmacist is a common foreigner mistake — at the 약국 you hand them the slip, you don't receive it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 처방전 (the slip) with 약 (the medicine).
처방전 is the paper prescription from the doctor; 약 is the medicine from the pharmacy. Ask the clinic for 처방전, the pharmacy for 약.
Asking the pharmacist 처방전 주세요.
You HAND the 처방전 to the pharmacist, you don't receive it there. At the 약국 say 약 지어 주세요 or hand over the slip.
Saying 처방 주세요 instead of 처방전.
처방 is the act of prescribing; the physical slip is 처방전. Drop the 전 and it sounds incomplete.

structuredNuance.t: Asks the clinic for the prescription document: 처방전 (the slip) + 주세요 (please give). The Korean medical system is split — the doctor writes the 처방전 at the 병원, and you take it to a separate 약국 to fill. This phrase belongs at the 병원/의원 step only.

처방전 주세요 to clinic staff (존댓말, direct but polite). 처방전 좀 주시겠어요? = softer and more polite. 처방전 다시 발급해 주세요 = for lost/re-issued slips. Never use 반말 with clinic staff regardless of how you feel — the institutional setting always calls for 존댓말.

처방전 주세요 (get the slip from the doctor's office) vs 약 지어 주세요 (ask the pharmacist to fill it) vs 약 주세요 (ask for a ready-made OTC product). Mixing these up signals you don't know how the system works: you never 'receive' a 처방전 at the pharmacy.
처방전 = 處方箋 — 處方 (dispose/prescribe + way/method) + 箋 (slip of paper/document). A Sino-Korean compound. 처방 alone means the act of prescribing; adding 전 (箋) specifies the paper document.

Two traps: (1) asking for 약 at the clinic — the 병원 gives you the 처방전, not the pills; go to the 약국 for 약. (2) saying 처방전 주세요 to the pharmacist — at the 약국 you hand them the slip, you don't ask to receive one.

expressions.english: Could you fill this prescription / make up the medicine?
expressions.shortExplanation: 약 좀 지어 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you fill this prescription / make up the medicine?".
expressions.explanation: 약 좀 지어 주세요 (yak jom jieo juseyo) = "Could you fill this prescription / make up the medicine?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 약 좀 지어 주세요 ("Please make up the medicine for me"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Please make up the medicine for me
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; patient to pharmacist; 좀 softens the request
반말; rare in a pharmacy, used jokingly with a close friend who is a pharmacist

usagePhrases.en: Could you make up the medicine, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite request form with 주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: Please fill this exactly as prescribed
usagePhrases.note: Extension handing over the slip; 처방전대로 = according to / as per the prescription

examples.ko: A: 약 좀 지어 주세요. / B: 처방전 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: yak jom jieo juseyo. / B: cheobangjeon jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: Could you fill this? / B: May I have the prescription?
examples.note: The standard A/B exchange at the pharmacy counter — this is essentially scripted

examples.ko: 감기 증상이 있는데, 처방전 없이 살 수 있는 감기약 좀 지어 주세요.
examples.romanization: gamgi jeungsangi inneunde, cheobangjeon eopsi sal su inneun gamgiyak jom jieo juseyo.
examples.en: I have cold symptoms — could you make up some cold medicine I can buy without a prescription?
examples.note: Everyday OTC request; 처방전 없이 = without a prescription; shows that 지어 주세요 works for OTC compounding too

examples.ko: 아이가 먹을 거라서 가루약으로 약 좀 지어 주세요.
examples.romanization: aiga meogeul georaseo garuyageuro yak jom jieo juseyo.
examples.en: It's for my child, so please make it up as powder medicine.
examples.note: Fuller request; 가루약 = powdered medicine (easier for children); shows that 짓다 encompasses mixing/compounding to specification

expressions.nuance: 약 좀 지어 주세요 is what you say at the pharmacy counter: 약 'medicine' + 짓다 'to make/compose' + 주세요 'please (for me)'. The verb 짓다 is a rich cultural axis — it is the same verb as 밥을 짓다 (cook rice) and 집을 짓다 (build a house), reflecting the traditional pharmacy where the 한의사 or 약사 literally measured and compounded doses for you. 짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before vowel endings — 짓다 → 지어 (NOT 짓어). So it's always 약 지어 주세요, never 약 짓어 주세요. The softener 좀 transforms a bare command into a polite request — drop it and 약 지어 주세요 starts to sound curt. The dividing line from 약 주세요 ('hand me the medicine') is that 지어 주세요 implies preparation/compounding from a prescription or for described symptoms, while 주세요 is for a ready-made product off the shelf. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'fill a prescription' with 채우다 ('fill a container') — completely wrong; 약을 짓다 is the fixed idiom.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짓어 주세요 instead of 지어 주세요.
짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ drops before 어, giving 지어. So it's 약 지어 주세요.
Using 채우다 to translate 'fill a prescription'.
채우다 means fill a physical container. 'Make up medicine' is 약을 짓다 — 약 지어 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and saying just 약 지어.
Without 좀 and with 반말 it sounds like a brusque order. To a pharmacist use 약 좀 지어 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'please compose/build the medicine for me'. 실제 뜻: 'please fill/make up the medicine'. The verb 짓다 carries the sense of assembling from components — same word as cooking rice (밥을 짓다) or building a house (집을 짓다), reflecting traditional pharmacy compounding.

짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before vowel endings. 짓다 → 지어 (not 짓어) → 지어 주세요 (please make up). Other forms: 지었어요 (made/filled), 지을게요 (I'll make up). The error 약 짓어 주세요 is one of the most common pharmacy mistakes.

약 좀 지어 주세요 (prepare/compound medicine to order) vs 약 주세요 (hand me a ready product, e.g. a box of aspirin) vs 약 추천해 주세요 (recommend a medicine). Use 지어 주세요 when you have a prescription or are describing symptoms and want the pharmacist to select and prepare your medications.

The verb 짓다 is pure native Korean, no 한자. Its richness comes from covering three domains: building (집을 짓다), cooking (밥을 짓다), and compounding medicine (약을 짓다) — all acts of assembling components into a purposeful whole.
Two traps: (1) calquing 'fill a prescription' as 채우다 ('fill a container') — completely wrong; use 약을 짓다. (2) ㅅ-irregular error: 약 짓어 주세요 is wrong; the ㅅ drops: 약 지어 주세요.

expressions.english: Take it three times a day
expressions.shortExplanation: 하루 세 번 드세요 is a practical expression meaning "Take it three times a day".
expressions.explanation: 하루 세 번 드세요 (haru se beon deuseyo) means "Take it three times a day". Say it as one set phrase — for example 하루 세 번 드세요 ("Take it three times a day"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Take it three times a day
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; pharmacist or doctor to patient

usagePhrases.en: Take it three times a day
usagePhrases.note: 반말; a parent instructing a child
Formal/clinical; 복용하다 = to administer / take (medicine)

usagePhrases.ko: 하루 세 번, 한 알씩 드세요
usagePhrases.romanization: haru se beon, han alssik deuseyo
usagePhrases.en: Take one tablet three times a day
usagePhrases.note: Extension adding dose; 한 알씩 = one tablet each time; 알 = tablet/pill counter

examples.ko: A: 하루 세 번 드세요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다. 언제 먹으면 돼요?
examples.romanization: A: haru se beon deuseyo. / B: ne, algetseumnida. eonje meogeumyeon dwaeyo?
examples.en: A: Take it three times a day. / B: Okay. When should I take it?
examples.note: A/B at the pharmacy counter — the patient's follow-up question about timing is natural here

examples.ko: 이 약은 하루 세 번, 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
examples.romanization: i yageun haru se beon, siku samsip bune deuseyo.
examples.en: Take this three times a day, thirty minutes after meals.
examples.note: Everyday full dosing instruction combining frequency (세 번) and timing (식후 삼십 분) — learn them together

examples.ko: 항생제는 증상이 없어져도 하루 세 번 끝까지 다 드세요.
examples.romanization: hangsaengjeneun jeungsangi eopseojyeodo haru se beon kkeutkkaji da deuseyo.
examples.en: Even if your symptoms disappear, take the antibiotics three times a day to the very end.
examples.note: Fuller clinically important advice; 항생제 = antibiotics; 끝까지 = all the way through — critical compliance instruction

expressions.nuance: 하루 세 번 드세요 is the dosing instruction heard at every pharmacy: 하루 'per day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 먹다. The number system axis is critical: 번 (times/occurrences) takes NATIVE Korean numerals, not Sino-Korean — 한 번, 두 번, 세 번, 네 번, not 일 번, 이 번, 삼 번. English speakers routinely say 삼 번 by analogy with other counting, but 번 always demands native numbers. Word order is also reversed from English: Korean says 하루 세 번 (day-first), not 세 번 하루. The verb for the patient is 드세요 (honorific, to a patient/elder) or the clinical 복용하세요; the plain 먹어 is 반말 for a child. Essential dosing vocabulary to pair: 식전 (before meals), 식후 (after meals), 식간 (between meals), 취침 전 (before bed), 한 알씩 (one tablet at a time). If you don't understand the dosing, ask: 하루에 몇 번 먹어요? ('How many times a day do I take it?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 삼 번 instead of 세 번 for 'three times'.
The counter 번 requires native Korean numerals: 한/두/세/네 번. 'Three times' is 세 번, not Sino-Korean 삼 번.
Putting it in English order: 세 번 하루.
Korean states the larger time unit first: 하루 세 번 ('a day, three times'), not 세 번 하루.
Using 먹으세요 vs 드세요 incorrectly to an elder patient.
To a patient the honorific 드세요 (or 복용하세요) is the norm; 먹어 is 반말 for a child. Plain 먹으세요 is acceptable but 드세요 is more polite.

structuredNuance.t: The universal pharmacy dosing instruction: 하루 'per day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요 honorific imperative. The patient's honorific verb is 드세요 (or 복용하세요 in clinical writing); the caregiver's 반말 to a child is 먹어. Pair with 식전/식후 for complete instructions.
하루 세 번 드세요 = standard pharmacy/clinic 존댓말. 하루 세 번 복용하세요 = written on labels and in clinical notes. 하루 세 번 먹어 = a parent to a child (반말). Don't use 먹으세요 to an elderly patient — 드세요 is more respectful.

번 (times/occurrences) always takes NATIVE Korean numerals: 한 번 (once), 두 번 (twice), 세 번 (3×), 네 번 (4×). Sino-Korean 삼 번 is wrong here. Contrast: 분 (minutes) and other time durations take Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min) — so the number system flips depending on the counter.

하루 세 번 드세요 (frequency only) vs 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 (timing only) — these are combined in full instructions: 하루 세 번, 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. Also: 하루 한 알씩 드세요 (one tablet per day) vs 하루 세 번 드세요 (three times per day — each use).
Two traps: (1) 삼 번 for 'three times' — 번 takes native 세 번, not Sino 삼 번. (2) reversed word order — say 하루 세 번 (day then times), not 세 번 하루.

expressions.english: Take it thirty minutes after meals
expressions.shortExplanation: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 is a practical expression meaning "Take it thirty minutes after meals".
expressions.explanation: "Take it thirty minutes after meals" — that is 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 (siku samsip bune deuseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 ("Take it 30 minutes after eating"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; standard pharmacist instruction

usagePhrases.ko: 밥 먹고 삼십 분 뒤에 먹어
usagePhrases.romanization: bam meokgo samsip bun dwie meogeo
usagePhrases.en: Eat, then take it 30 minutes later
usagePhrases.note: 반말; plainer everyday wording to a child or friend
Formal/clinical with 복용하다; found on written labels
Contrast extension; 식전 = before eating; often both are needed for different medicines

examples.ko: A: 이 약은 어떻게 먹어요? / B: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
examples.romanization: A: i yageun eotteoke meogeoyo? / B: siku samsip bune deuseyo.
examples.en: A: How do I take this medicine? / B: Take it thirty minutes after meals.
examples.note: The A/B exchange that replaces reading the label; 어떻게 먹어요? = how do I take it?

examples.ko: 속 쓰릴 수 있으니까 꼭 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
examples.romanization: sok sseuril su isseunikka kkok siku samsip bune deuseyo.
examples.en: It can irritate your stomach, so be sure to take it thirty minutes after eating.
examples.note: Everyday reasoning explaining WHY the timing matters; 속 쓰리다 = have a burning/acidic stomach

examples.ko: 이 약은 식전, 저 약은 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. 헷갈리지 마세요.
examples.romanization: i yageun sikjeon, jeo yageun siku samsip bune deuseyo. hetgalliji maseyo.
examples.en: Take this one before meals and that one thirty minutes after meals. Don't mix them up.
examples.note: Fuller two-medicine instruction; 헷갈리다 = get confused — a very real danger at home with multiple drugs

expressions.nuance: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 — 식후 (食後, 'after-meal') + 삼십 분 (30 minutes) + 에 (at/on) + 드세요(take) — is printed on almost every Korean prescription bag (약봉투). The number system here is the opposite of 번: time durations with minutes use SINO-Korean numbers, so '30 minutes' is 삼십 분, not native 서른 분. The particle 에 marks a specific point in time (시간점) and must not be dropped — 식후 삼십 분 드세요 without 에 sounds incomplete. Learn the full set of timing labels found on bags: 식전 (食前, before meals), 식후 (食後, after meals), 식간 (食間, between meals, rare), 취침 전 (before bed). The medical reality: 식후 drugs taken on an empty stomach can cause 속 쓰림 (gastric burning), so the distinction from 식전 is clinically important, not just vocabulary. English speakers mix number systems (세십 분 = native+Sino hybrid) and drop 에; both errors corrupt the instruction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using native numbers for the minutes (서른 분).
Clock/duration minutes use Sino-Korean numerals: 삼십 분, not native 서른 분.
Dropping the time particle 에: 식후 삼십 분 드세요.
The point in time needs 에: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. Without it the timing relation is unclear.
Confusing 식전 and 식후.
식전 = before meals, 식후 = after meals. They are opposites, and the wrong one can upset your stomach.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'at 30 minutes after-meal, take'. 실제 뜻: 'take it 30 minutes after eating'. The phrase combines a Sino-Korean compound (식후 = 食後) + Sino numeral (삼십 = 30) + time-point particle 에 + honorific imperative 드세요.
분 (minutes) takes SINO-Korean numerals: 십 분, 이십 분, 삼십 분, 사십오 분. This is the opposite of 번 (times), which takes native Korean. Never 서른 분 (native 30 + 분).

식후 삼십 분에 드세요 = pharmacist to patient (존댓말). On prescription bags and labels: 식후 30분 (abbreviated). In clinical notes: 식후 삼십 분 복용. For a child (반말): 밥 먹고 삼십 분 뒤에 먹어. Always confirm which label applies to each pill — taking a 식후 drug on an empty stomach can cause stomach damage.

식전 (食前, before meals) vs 식후 (食後, after meals) vs 식간 (食間, between meals) vs 취침 전 (before bed). These are the four standard timing labels on Korean prescription bags. 식전 and 식후 are medically opposite — many drug interactions depend on this distinction.

Two traps: (1) mixing number systems — 세십 분 (native+Sino) or 서른 분 (native minutes) are both wrong; use Sino 삼십 분. (2) dropping the time-particle 에 — 식후 삼십 분에 drseyo without 에 sounds like an incomplete instruction.

expressions.shortExplanation: 진통제 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have painkillers?".
expressions.explanation: 진통제 있어요? (jintongje isseoyo?) = "Do you have painkillers?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 진통제 있어요? ("Do you have painkillers?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; customer to pharmacist asking about stock
반말; asking a friend who might have some in their bag

usagePhrases.en: Would you happen to have painkillers?
usagePhrases.note: Softer polite form; 있나요? = is there / do you have (slightly more tentative)
Extension moving from asking about availability to actually requesting them

examples.ko: A: 진통제 있어요? / B: 네, 어떤 통증이세요?
examples.romanization: A: jintongje isseoyo? / B: ne, eotteon tongjeungiseyo?
examples.en: A: Do you have painkillers? / B: Yes — what kind of pain is it?
examples.note: Real pharmacy A/B — the pharmacist asks the type of pain to recommend the right product

examples.ko: 생리통이 너무 심한데 진통제 있어요? 아까부터 계속 아파요.
examples.romanization: saengnitongi neomu simhande jintongje isseoyo? akkabuteo gyesok apayo.
examples.en: My period cramps are really bad — do you have painkillers? It's been hurting for a while.
examples.note: Everyday context; 생리통 = menstrual cramps — one of the most common OTC pain reasons

examples.ko: 타이레놀 같은 진통제 있어요? 두통이 심해서요.
examples.romanization: tairenol gateun jintongje isseoyo? dutongi simhaeseoyo.
examples.en: Do you have a painkiller like Tylenol? I have a bad headache.
examples.note: Fuller request naming a reference brand; 같은 = like/such as — useful when you don't know the Korean product name

expressions.nuance: 진통제 있어요? asks a pharmacist whether they stock painkillers — 진통제 (鎭痛劑, 'pain-suppressing agent') + 있어요? ('is there? / do you have?'). 있어요? is the natural Korean way to ask about product availability in any shop; it's far more natural than the beginner calque 가지고 있어요? ('do you personally hold?'), which sounds like you're asking whether the pharmacist has it in their pocket. Painkillers like ibuprofen and acetaminophen are sold over the counter (일반의약품) without a prescription at Korean pharmacies, so this question is practically very useful. Good vocabulary to build from the same pattern: 소화제 있어요? (digestive aid?), 해열제 있어요? (fever reducer?), 파스 있어요? (pain-relief patch?). The pharmacist will typically ask 어떤 통증이세요? ('what kind of pain?') to suggest the right product — have the answer ready: 두통 (headache), 생리통 (period pain), 근육통 (muscle ache), 치통 (toothache).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 진통제 가지고 있어요? for shop stock.
가지고 있다 = personally possess. To ask whether a store stocks something, use 있어요?: 진통제 있어요?
Saying 아픔약 for 'painkiller'.
There is no 아픔약. The word is 진통제, or by symptom e.g. 두통약 (headache medicine).
Confusing 진통제 with 해열제.
진통제 relieves pain; 해열제 reduces fever. They overlap in some products but ask for the right one.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Are there painkillers?' 실제 뜻: 'Do you have painkillers (in stock)?' In Korean, availability at a shop is expressed with 있어요? — the subject is the product itself. This pattern works for any pharmacy request: 소화제 있어요?, 해열제 있어요?, 파스 있어요?.
진통제 있어요? to a pharmacist (존댓말). 진통제 있어? to a friend (반말). 진통제 있나요? slightly softer and more tentative. The pharmacist will follow up with 어떤 통증이세요? — prepare to name the pain type: 두통, 생리통, 근육통, 치통.

진통제 = 鎭痛劑 — 鎭 (suppress/calm) + 痛 (pain) + 劑 (medicinal agent). This naming pattern applies widely: 해열제 (解熱劑, fever reducer), 소화제 (消化劑, digestive aid), 소염제 (消炎劑, anti-inflammatory). Recognizing 劑 = medical agent helps you decode any drug name.

진통제 있어요? (general painkillers, open question) vs 두통약 있어요? (headache medicine, narrower) vs 타이레놀 있어요? (brand-specific). Moving from general to specific helps the pharmacist recommend faster. 진통제 주세요 = moving from asking to requesting — use once you see they have stock.

Two traps: (1) 가지고 있어요? — sounds like 'do you personally possess one on your person'; for shop stock use 있어요?. (2) 아픔약 — there is no such word; the correct term is 진통제, or by symptom type (두통약, 생리통약).

expressions.english: If it's really bad, go see a doctor
expressions.shortExplanation: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 is a practical expression meaning "If it's really bad, go see a doctor".
expressions.explanation: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 (mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo) means "If it's really bad, go see a doctor". Say it as one set phrase — for example 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 ("If it gets bad, go to the doctor"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: If it gets bad, go to the doctor
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; pharmacist advising a customer at the end of a visit

usagePhrases.en: If it's bad, go to the doctor
usagePhrases.note: 반말; a friend or older family member giving concern

usagePhrases.ko: 많이 안 좋으시면 병원에 가 보세요
usagePhrases.romanization: mani an joeusimyeon byeongwone ga boseyo
