usagePhrases.en: If you feel worse, please try seeing a doctor
usagePhrases.note: More polite; subject honorific 좋으시면 + 가 보세요 = gentler advisory

usagePhrases.en: If there's no improvement, go to the doctor
usagePhrases.note: Extension using a clinical-sounding alternative; 차도가 없다 = show no improvement

examples.ko: A: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요. / B: 네, 그럴게요. 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: A: mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo. / B: ne, geureolgeyo. gamsahamnida.
examples.en: A: If it's bad, go see a doctor. / B: Okay, I will. Thank you.
examples.note: The standard farewell A/B at the pharmacy; 그럴게요 = I'll do that — a natural acknowledgment

examples.ko: 이 약 드시고도 이틀 지나도록 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요.
examples.romanization: i yak deusigodo iteul jinadorong mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo.
examples.en: If you're still not better after two days on this medicine, go see a doctor.
examples.note: Everyday pharmacist follow-up specifying a clear time threshold: two days is the typical benchmark

examples.ko: 열도 있고 기침도 심하면 그냥 집에 계시지 마시고 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요.
examples.romanization: yeoldo itgo gichimdo simhamyeon geunyang jibe gyesiji masigo mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo.
examples.en: If you have a fever and a bad cough, don't just stay home — if it gets bad, go see a doctor.
examples.note: Fuller advice combining warning signs; 집에 계시지 마시고 = don't just stay at home — addresses the Korean tendency to avoid the clinic

expressions.nuance: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 is the kindly send-off a pharmacist uses: 많이 'a lot/really' + 안 좋으면 'if (it's) not good' (conditional ~으면 on 좋다) + 병원 가세요 'go to the hospital/clinic'. Two cultural axes matter. First, 병원 in Korea refers to any medical facility — from a tiny neighborhood clinic (동네의원, 의원) to a large hospital — so 병원 가세요 simply means 'go see a doctor', not 'get hospitalized' (which is 입원하다). This genuinely confuses English speakers who picture ER visits. Second, 안 좋다 ('not good') is the standard idiomatic Korean for 'feeling unwell' — it's softer and more natural than 나쁘다 ('bad') about how a person feels; 몸이 안 좋다 is a set phrase for being under the weather. To be more polite, upgrade with subject honorific: 많이 안 좋으시면 가 보세요 (가 보세요 = 'try going', gentler than the direct 가세요). For the conditional, ~으면 must attach to the verb 좋다 (안 좋으면); 만약 is optional emphasis and not a replacement.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing 병원 가세요 as 'go get hospitalized'.
병원 covers clinics too; it simply means 'see a doctor'. For admission you'd say 입원하다.
Saying 만약 안 좋다 병원 가세요 without the conditional ending.
'If' needs the ~으면 ending on the verb: 안 좋으면. 만약 is optional emphasis, not a replacement for 으면.
Using 나쁘면 instead of 안 좋으면 about how you feel.
For health, the idiomatic 'if you feel worse' is 안 좋으면. 나쁘다 about a person can sound like 'bad-natured'; 몸이 안 좋다 is the set phrase for feeling unwell.

structuredNuance.t: The pharmacist's kindly farewell advice: 많이 'really' + 안 좋으면 'if not well' + 병원 가세요 'go see a doctor'. The conditional ~으면 must attach to 좋다 (안 좋으면). This is a fixed, caring send-off, not a command.

많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 = pharmacist/friend to patient (존댓말). 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가 = friend to friend (반말). More polite: 많이 안 좋으시면 병원에 가 보세요 (subject honorific 좋으시면 + softer 가 보세요). Use 가 보세요 when the person hasn't decided yet; 가세요 is more direct.

안 좋으면 (if not good/well) vs 나빠지면 (if it gets worse/worsens). 안 좋다 is the idiomatic phrase for feeling unwell; 나쁘다 about a person can sound like a character judgment ('bad person'). For health, always use 몸이 안 좋다 / 안 좋으면. 차도가 없으면 ('if there is no improvement') is a more clinical variant.

병원 in Korea covers any medical facility from a neighborhood clinic (의원 / 동네 병원) to a large teaching hospital. 병원 가세요 = 'see a doctor' not 'get hospitalized'. Actual hospitalization is 입원하다. English speakers map 병원 onto 'hospital' and picture a serious ER visit — in Korea it routinely means a five-minute walk to a local clinic.
Two traps: (1) 병원 = hospital admission — wrong; 병원 = any clinic, just 'see a doctor'. (2) omitting ~으면 from the conditional: 만약 안 좋다 병원 가세요 — 만약 alone is not a conditional; the verb needs ~으면: 안 좋으면.

expressions.english: I'm aching all over / I'm run down
expressions.shortExplanation: 몸살이 났어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm aching all over / I'm run down".
expressions.explanation: "I'm aching all over / I'm run down" — that is 몸살이 났어요 (momsari nasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 몸살이 났어요 ("I ache all over / I'm run down"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I ache all over / I'm run down
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; describing the flu-like body-ache exhaustion state to a doctor
반말; particle 이 often dropped with friends

usagePhrases.en: I have body aches and exhaustion
usagePhrases.note: Formal register

usagePhrases.en: I feel run-down, like body aches coming on
usagePhrases.note: Extension for the early warning stage before full onset; 기운 = energy/signs

examples.ko: A: 몸살이 났어요. / B: 많이 힘드시겠어요. 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: A: momsari nasseoyo. / B: mani himdeusigesseoyo. puk swiseyo.
examples.en: A: I ache all over. / B: That must be really hard. Get plenty of rest.
examples.note: A/B showing the empathetic response 힘드시겠어요 + 푹 쉬세요 — learn these replies together

examples.ko: 이번 주에 무리하게 일했더니 몸살이 났어요. 온몸이 쑤시고 기운이 없어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon jue murihage ilhaetdeoni momsari nasseoyo. onmomi ssusigo giuni eopseoyo.
examples.en: I pushed too hard at work this week and now I'm aching all over — my whole body throbs and I have no energy.
examples.note: Everyday cause-and-effect; 무리하다 = overexert oneself; 온몸이 쑤시다 = whole body aches; 기운이 없다 = feel drained

examples.ko: 감기는 나은 것 같은데 아직도 몸살 기운이 있어서 움직이기가 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: gamgineun naeun geot gateunde ajikdo momsal giuni isseoseo umjigigiga himdeureoyo.
examples.en: The cold seems to be better but there are still signs of body aches, and it's hard to move.
examples.note: Fuller picture; 몸살 기운이 있다 = the early/residual body-ache signs; 움직이기가 힘들다 = hard to move around

expressions.nuance: 몸살이 났어요 has no clean English equivalent: 몸살 describes the run-down, aching-all-over, feverish-exhaustion state from overwork or a cold — not one symptom but a cluster of body aches, fatigue, and malaise that Koreans treat as a single identifiable experience. The verb is 나다 ('arise') in past tense — 몸살이 났어요 = 'the body-ache has arisen and I have it now', parallel to 감기에 걸렸어요. Subject particle 이 (몸살이), never 몸살을 했어요. Key distinction: 몸살 (body aches + exhaustion) vs 감기 (respiratory cold) — they frequently co-occur as 감기몸살, but 몸살 by itself is specifically the muscle-aching, drained feeling, commonly triggered by 무리하다 (overexertion). Present tense 몸살이 나요 sounds like a general tendency ('I tend to get body aches'); use past 났어요 for the current state. English speakers usually describe this piecemeal ('I'm tired and my whole body hurts') — 몸살이 났어요 captures it in one natural phrase.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 몸살 as the same as 감기.
감기 is a respiratory cold; 몸살 is the body-ache/exhaustion state. They co-occur (감기몸살) but aren't identical.
Saying 몸살을 했어요 with 를 + 하다.
The collocation is 몸살이 나다: 몸살이 났어요. It 'arises', it isn't 'done'.
Using present 몸살이 나요 for a current case.
Like 감기에 걸렸어요, the past 몸살이 났어요 expresses the present state of having it. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'body-ache arose'. 실제 뜻: 'I am aching all over / run down (from overwork or illness)'. 몸살 covers the whole cluster — muscle aches, fatigue, malaise — with no single English word. The past tense 났어요 expresses the current resulting state, like 감기에 걸렸어요.

몸살이 났어요 to a doctor or sympathetic colleague (존댓말). 몸살 났어 to a close friend (반말). 몸살이 났습니다 in a formal absence report. The typical cause to mention: 무리해서 (from overexerting), 일을 너무 많이 해서 (from working too much), 감기 때문에 (because of a cold).

몸살이 났어요 (body-ache/exhaustion cluster, often from overwork) vs 감기에 걸렸어요 (common cold, respiratory focus) vs 감기몸살이 났어요 (both combined). 온몸이 쑤셔요 ('my whole body aches') describes the sensation in more detail but lacks the exhaustion-fatigue component of 몸살.
몸살이 났어요 → 감기몸살이 났어요 (cold + body aches) → 몸살 기운이 있어요 (early signs) → 몸살이 다 나았어요 (all recovered).

Two traps: (1) no English equivalent — learners describe it piecemeal ('I'm tired and my body hurts'); 몸살이 났어요 does this in one phrase. (2) wrong verb — 몸살을 했어요 is wrong; the collocation is 몸살이 나다, and the past 났어요 expresses the present state.

expressions.english: Do I need to get a shot?
expressions.shortExplanation: 주사 맞아야 해요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I need to get a shot?".
expressions.explanation: 주사 맞아야 해요? (jusa majaya haeyo?) = "Do I need to get a shot?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 주사 맞아야 해요? ("Do I have to get a shot?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Do I have to get a shot?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; patient asking the doctor or nurse

usagePhrases.en: Do I have to get a shot?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; a child asking a parent, or a friend
Formal register; 합니까 = formal question ending

usagePhrases.ko: 주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요?
usagePhrases.romanization: jusa an matgo yangman meogeumyeon an dwaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can't I just take pills instead of a shot?
usagePhrases.note: Extension negotiating the alternative; very natural to a doctor

examples.ko: A: 주사 맞아야 해요? / B: 아니요, 약만 드시면 될 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: jusa majaya haeyo? / B: aniyo, yangman deusimyeon doel geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: Do I need a shot? / B: No, I think you just need to take the medicine.

examples.ko: 독감 예방 주사 맞아야 해요? 해마다 맞아야 하나요?
examples.romanization: dokgam yebang jusa majaya haeyo? haemada majaya hanayo?
examples.en: Should I get the flu vaccine? Do I need to get it every year?

examples.ko: 열이 사흘째 안 떨어지는데 주사 맞아야 해요? 솔직히 주사는 좀 무서워서요.
examples.romanization: yeori saheuljjae an tteoreojineunde jusa majaya haeyo? soljiki jusaneun jom museowoseoyo.
examples.en: My fever hasn't broken for three days — do I need a shot? Honestly I'm a bit scared of needles.
examples.note: Fuller, authentic patient exchange; 사흘째 = going on three days; 무섭다 = scared — the hesitation is very real

expressions.nuance: 주사 맞아야 해요? asks whether you need an injection, and the verb choice is the essential learning point: you 'get hit by' a shot — 주사를 맞다 — using 맞다 ('to be struck/get hit'). NOT 주사를 받다 (받다 = receive a handed object) and NOT 주사를 하다 (하다 = do; this is what the nurse does TO you, from the nurse's perspective). This is one of the most universal English-speaker errors in Korean medical language. The ~아야 하다 frame means 'have to/must': 맞아야 해요? = 'do I have to get (hit/struck)'? In casual speech 해요 swaps to 돼요 (맞아야 돼요?) — both are fine and natural. The Sino-Korean word 주사 (注射) covers both the injection and the needle/syringe. Two practical extensions: 예방 주사 맞다 (get vaccinated), and 수액 맞다 (get an IV drip) — 맞다 governs all of them. Pair with 약만 먹으면 돼요? when you want to avoid needles.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주사를 받아야 해요 with 받다.
받다 = receive a handed object. An injection uses 맞다 ('be struck'): 주사 맞아야 해요?
Saying 주사를 해야 해요 as the patient.
주사를 하다 is what the medical staff does (administers). As the one getting it, you say 주사를 맞다.
Confusing 맞다 'be hit' here with 맞다 'be correct'.
Same spelling, but 주사를 맞다 specifically means 'get an injection'. Context (주사) makes it the shot meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'do I have to be hit by a shot?' 실제 뜻: 'do I need to get an injection?' The surprising verb is 맞다 ('to be struck/hit') — you are the passive recipient of the needle. The ~아야 하다 frame = 'must/have to'. In casual speech 해요 → 돼요: 맞아야 돼요?

주사 맞아야 해요? to a doctor or nurse (존댓말). 주사 맞아야 돼? to a parent or friend (반말). 주사 맞아야 합니까? in a formal context. A useful follow-up to signal fear or preference: 주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요? ('Can I just take pills instead?').

주사를 맞다 (get an injection — patient) vs 주사를 놓다 (give an injection — nurse/doctor) vs 주사를 맞히다 (cause someone to get a shot — e.g. parent talking about a child). This matched-pair structure (맞다/놓다/맞히다) is unique to injection vocabulary.

주사 = 注射 — 注 (pour in) + 射 (shoot/inject). A Sino-Korean medical term. 맞다 is pure native Korean meaning 'to be hit' — the pairing of a Chinese medical noun with a native verb for being struck reflects how Korean absorbed medical vocabulary.
Two traps: (1) 주사를 받다 — 받다 = receive a handed object; needles aren't handed to you, they are inserted; use 맞다. (2) 주사를 하다 — 하다 is from the nurse's perspective (administering); as the patient, say 맞다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 괜찮아요? is a practical expression meaning "Are you okay?".
expressions.explanation: 괜찮아요? (gwaenchanayo?) means "Are you okay?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 괜찮아요? ("Are you okay?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the first thing you ask someone who's hurt or upset
반말, to a friend or someone younger/close
Honorific 으세요, to an elder, a customer, or a stranger
Follow-up when they may be physically injured

examples.ko: A: 괜찮아요? / B: 네, 괜찮아요. 잠깐 놀랐을 뿐이에요.
examples.romanization: A: gwaenchanayo? / B: ne, gwaenchanayo. jamkkan nollasseul ppunieyo.
examples.en: A: Are you okay? / B: Yes, I'm fine. I was just startled for a moment.
examples.note: Rising intonation on 괜찮아요? is the question; the exact same words with falling intonation in B's reply mean 'I'm fine' — tone does all the work

examples.en: That must have been a shock — are you okay?
examples.note: 놀랐죠 acknowledges the fright before checking on them; pair recognition of the feeling with the welfare check

examples.ko: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보여요. 무슨 일 있어요? 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: eolguri an joa boyeoyo. museun il isseoyo? gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: You don't look well. Is something wrong? Are you all right?
examples.note: Pairing 괜찮으세요? with 무슨 일 있어요? opens the door gently — use 으세요 any time you'd use honorifics (elder, stranger, boss, customer)

expressions.nuance: 직역: 괜찮다 = 'to be fine/acceptable' + 아요? = polite question marker, so literally 'is it fine?' used as welfare-check 'are you okay?'. The real force is checking the person's state after a stumble, bad news, a fright, or an upset — it is the all-purpose first-response comfort question. Register is the critical skill: 괜찮아? (반말, friend/younger), 괜찮아요? (polite-neutral, peer, most situations), 괜찮으세요? (honorific -으세요, elder/boss/stranger). The nearest near-synonym is 어디 아픈 데 없어요? ('are you hurt anywhere?'), which narrows to physical injury; 괜찮아요? covers physical AND emotional. The biggest English-speaker trap is adding 당신 ('you') — 당신 괜찮아요? sounds cold or even confrontational; Korean drops the subject entirely and lets context fill it. Also never use 너 괜찮아요? (mixing 반말 pronoun with polite ending) — if you add any pronoun at all to a polite form, use 선생님, a name, or omit it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 당신 괜찮아요? to someone's face.
당신 ('you') sounds distant or even confrontational when spoken directly. Korean drops the subject: just 괜찮아요? The 'you' is understood.
Using 괜찮아요? (rising) and 괜찮아요 (falling) interchangeably.
Rising intonation asks 'are you okay?'; falling intonation states 'I'm fine / it's all right'. Same words, opposite roles — control your tone.
Asking an elder 괜찮아? without the honorific.
괜찮아? is 반말 and too casual for an elder, customer, or stranger. Use 괜찮으세요? to show respect when checking on them.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮다 literally means 'to be fine/acceptable' — as a rising-tone question it becomes the all-purpose welfare check 'are you okay?', covering physical injury, emotional upset, shock, or looking unwell. The same words with falling intonation shift to the reassuring reply 'I'm fine / it's all right / no thank you'. Intonation is the only signal.

Use any time someone stumbles, cries, looks pale, gets bad news, or seems off. Register ladder: 괜찮아? (반말 — friend or someone younger/very close) → 괜찮아요? (polite-neutral — peer, acquaintance, most everyday situations) → 괜찮으세요? (honorific — elder, boss, customer, stranger). The honorific -으세요 is obligatory when you'd normally use 존댓말.

어디 다친 데 없어요? ('are you hurt anywhere?') is the closest near-synonym but narrows to physical injury. 괜찮아요? is broader — it covers emotional upset, shock, and general distress as well. Use 어디 다친 데 없어요? as a follow-up when physical harm is possible.

Stack with 많이 놀랐죠? for 'that must have been a shock — are you okay?'. Chain 괜찮아요? with 무슨 일 있어요? to gently invite them to share. When offering reassurance, the same words with falling tone become the reply: 괜찮아요 = 'I'm fine'.

Adding 당신 ('you') — 당신 괜찮아요? — sounds cold or confrontational; Koreans drop the subject and let context supply it. Also do NOT mix pronouns and endings: 너 괜찮아요? pairs 반말 너 with a polite ending — awkward and inconsistent. With an elder, a plain 괜찮아? (no honorific) can come across as rude.

expressions.shortExplanation: 힘내 is a practical expression meaning "Cheer up / Hang in there".
expressions.explanation: "Cheer up / Hang in there" — that is 힘내 (himnae). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 힘내 ("Hang in there / You got this"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Hang in there / You got this
usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Polite; to a peer or someone you're not super close with
Honorific; to an elder, a coworker, or a customer

usagePhrases.en: Stay strong, it'll all work out
usagePhrases.note: Pairing it with reassurance about the future

examples.ko: A: 시험이 너무 걱정돼. / B: 힘내! 잘 할 수 있어.
examples.romanization: A: siheomi neomu geokjeongdwae. / B: himnae! jal hal su isseo.
examples.en: A: I'm so worried about the exam. / B: Hang in there! You can do it.
examples.note: 힘내 is future-facing encouragement — said before or during a challenge, not as a response to fresh grief

examples.en: Things are rough lately, huh? Hang in there.
examples.note: 힘들지 acknowledges the struggle before the encouragement; validate first, then encourage

examples.ko: 많이 지치셨죠. 그래도 힘내세요. 제가 응원할게요.
examples.romanization: mani jichisyeotjyo. geuraedo himnaeseyo. jega eungwonhalgeyo.
examples.en: You must be worn out. Still, please hang in there — I'm rooting for you.
examples.note: 응원할게요 ('I'll cheer you on') backs the encouragement with concrete support; note 힘내세요 for someone you respect

expressions.nuance: 직역: 힘 ('strength/energy') + 내다 ('to put out/summon') — imperative 'put out your strength'. The real use is encouragement aimed at FUTURE effort — pushing through an exam, a rough patch, a job hunt, a hard week. It is not sympathy for what has already happened. The key near-synonym contrast is 화이팅 (an energetic pep-rally cheer, often for sports or go-get-em moments) vs. 힘내 (warmer, more tender support for someone who is genuinely hurting or depleted). A huge English-speaker trap is using 힘내세요 at a funeral or for a death — it can sound like 'snap out of it', because the person is not facing a hurdle to overcome, they are grieving; use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요 instead. Register ladder: 힘내 (반말) → 힘내요 (polite) → 힘내세요 (honorific). Another confusion to avoid: 힘내 ('summon strength', imperative) vs. 힘들어 ('it's tough', a state) — they share 힘 but mean opposite things.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내세요 to someone who is grieving a death.
For a challenge ahead, 힘내 fits; for a death it can sound like 'cheer up', which is jarring. At a funeral say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요.
Confusing 힘내 with 힘들어.
힘내 = 'summon your strength' (encouragement to them); 힘들어 = 'it's hard / I'm struggling' (a state). Don't tell a tired friend 힘들어 when you mean 힘내.
Treating 화이팅 and 힘내 as identical.
화이팅 is energetic pep ('go go go!'); 힘내 carries gentle, caring support for someone who's down. To comfort a struggling friend, 힘내 lands warmer than 화이팅.

structuredNuance.t: 힘 ('strength/energy') + 내다 ('to summon/put out') → literally 'put out your strength'. The real meaning is warm encouragement to keep going — aimed at future effort, not past suffering. It tells someone to push forward through an exam, a rough patch, or a hard season.

Use before an exam, during a job hunt, mid-way through a tough project, or when a friend is drained but still going. Do NOT use at a funeral or for irreversible loss — it reads as 'snap out of it'. Register: 힘내 (반말 — friend/younger) → 힘내요 (polite — peer) → 힘내세요 (honorific — elder/coworker/customer).

화이팅 is upbeat pep-rally energy ('go go go!') — sports, pre-game, celebrations. 힘내 is softer, more personal warmth for someone who is genuinely hurting or depleted. For a struggling friend, 힘내 lands warmer than 화이팅. Neither is appropriate at a funeral; use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 there.

Pair with a concrete promise: 힘내요, 제가 응원할게요 ('hang in there, I'm rooting for you'). Add a future reassurance: 힘내요, 다 잘될 거예요 ('stay strong, it'll all work out'). For a friend who needs both validation and a lift: 많이 힘들지? 힘내.

Using 힘내세요 at a funeral or for a death sounds like 'cheer up / snap out of it' — jarring and hurtful. For loss say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요. Also do not confuse 힘내 ('summon strength', a command to them) with 힘들어 ('it's tough', describing a state) — they share 힘 but point in opposite directions.

expressions.shortExplanation: 괜찮아질 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "It'll be okay".
expressions.explanation: 괜찮아질 거예요 (gwaenchanajil geoyeyo) = "It'll be okay". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 괜찮아질 거예요 ("It'll get better / be okay"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reassuring a peer or someone you respect
반말; comforting a close friend
Add 다 ('all') to widen the reassurance
곧 ('soon') when you want to promise it won't last

examples.ko: A: 이 상황이 너무 힘들어. / B: 괜찮아질 거야. 시간이 지나면 달라져.
examples.romanization: A: i sanghwangi neomu himdeureo. / B: gwaenchanajil geoya. sigani jinamyeon dallajyeo.
examples.en: A: This situation is so hard. / B: It'll be okay. Things will change with time.
examples.note: 괜찮아질 거야 for a friend; note the -아질 change verb rather than just -을 거야 — emphasizing the process of getting better

examples.en: Even if it's hard now, it'll be okay soon.
examples.note: Contrast 지금은 힘들어도 ('though hard now') with the hopeful future — acknowledge the current pain before reassuring

examples.ko: 시간이 좀 걸리겠지만, 다 괜찮아질 거예요. 너무 걱정 마요.
examples.romanization: sigani jom geolligetjiman, da gwaenchanajil geoyeyo. neomu geokjeong mayo.
examples.en: It may take some time, but everything will be okay. Don't worry too much.
examples.note: Add 너무 걱정 마요 to round out the comfort; 다 괜찮아질 거예요 is the widest, most all-encompassing form

expressions.nuance: 직역: 괜찮아지다 = 괜찮다 ('to be okay') + -아지다 (the becoming/change suffix), so 'to become okay'; -ㄹ 거예요 = future 'will' — literally 'it will become okay'. The crucial difference from the simpler 괜찮을 거예요 ('it will be okay') is the -아지- change verb: 괜찮아질 거예요 specifically promises IMPROVEMENT from the current bad state, while 괜찮을 거예요 just predicts a future state without necessarily implying movement from now. Use this for illness, breakups, work crises, anything time can heal. Do NOT use for a death or irreversible loss — 'it'll get better' rings hollow for grief; say 마음이 아프네요 instead. Register: 괜찮아질 거야 (반말) → 괜찮아질 거예요 (polite). The classic English-speaker conjugation error is inserting 하: 괜찮해질 거예요 is wrong — 괜찮다 has no 하. Pair with 너무 걱정 마요 for a complete, warm comfort.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 괜찮할 거예요 or 괜찮해질 거예요.
괜찮다 has no 하/해 in it. The future is 괜찮을 거예요; the 'get better' form is 괜찮아질 거예요. Never insert 하.
Using 괜찮을 거예요 when you mean 'it'll improve'.
괜찮을 거예요 = 'it'll be okay'; 괜찮아질 거예요 = 'it'll BECOME okay (from now)'. For 'things will get better', keep the change verb 괜찮아지다.
Saying 괜찮아질 거예요 about a death.
For irreversible loss this can sound dismissive. Reserve it for things time can heal; for a death, offer 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요 instead.

structuredNuance.t: 괜찮아지다 = 괜찮다 ('to be okay') + -아지다 (become/change suffix) + -ㄹ 거예요 (future 'will') — literally 'it will become okay'. The real meaning is forward-looking reassurance: things will improve FROM their current state. The -아지- is what signals change, not merely prediction.

Use for illness, a breakup, a work crisis, a ruined plan — anything time can genuinely heal. Do NOT use for a death or irreversible loss (sounds dismissive). Register: 괜찮아질 거야 (반말 — close friend) → 괜찮아질 거예요 (polite — peer or respectful). Soften with 너무 걱정 마요 as a closer.

괜찮을 거예요 ('it will be okay') is common and fine, but doesn't carry the CHANGE meaning — it predicts a future state. 괜찮아질 거예요 specifically says 'it will get BETTER from now', which is more comforting when someone is currently struggling. For 'things will improve', keep the change verb 괜찮아지다.

Widen with 다 ('all'): 다 괜찮아질 거예요 ('everything will be okay'). Add urgency or hope with 곧 ('soon'): 곧 괜찮아질 거예요. Frame with 지금은 힘들어도 ('even if it's hard now') before the reassurance for a more empathetic structure.

The most common error is inserting 하: 괜찮해질 거예요 is wrong — 괜찮다 has no 하 in it. Also, using 괜찮아질 거예요 for a death or permanent loss sounds dismissive ('it'll get better'); reserve it for situations that genuinely can improve over time.

expressions.shortExplanation: 걱정하지 마 is a practical expression meaning "Don't worry".
expressions.explanation: 걱정하지 마 (geokjeonghaji ma) means "Don't worry". Say it as one set phrase — for example 걱정하지 마 ("Don't worry"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Polite; to a peer or acquaintance
Honorific; to an elder, customer, or boss
Add 너무 to soften an outright 'don't'

examples.ko: A: 결과가 어떻게 될지 너무 걱정돼. / B: 걱정하지 마. 최선을 다했잖아.
examples.romanization: A: gyeolgwaga eotteoke doelji neomu geokjeongdwae. / B: geokjeonghaji ma. choeseoneul dahaetjana.
examples.en: A: I'm so worried about the outcome. / B: Don't worry. You did your best.
examples.note: 걱정하지 마 is the warm command; back it up with a reason — 최선을 다했잖아 ('you did your best, remember') makes it convincing

examples.en: I'll help you, so don't worry.
examples.note: Pair 도와줄게 ('I'll help') with 걱정하지 마 — always more convincing with a concrete offer of support

examples.ko: 잘 해결될 테니까 너무 걱정하지 마세요. 제가 옆에 있잖아요.
examples.romanization: jal haegyeoldoel tenikka neomu geokjeonghaji maseyo. jega yeope itjanayo.
examples.en: It'll work out, so please don't worry too much. I'm right here with you.
examples.note: 옆에 있잖아요 ('I'm beside you, you know') makes the reassurance personal; note 마세요 for honorific register

expressions.nuance: 직역: 걱정하다 ('to worry') + -지 마 (negative imperative 'don't') — literally 'don't do worrying'. The real function is calming someone who is anxious or fretting; it works for exam stress, relationship worries, or general anxiety. The crucial conjugation point is that -지 마 is the COMMAND form ('don't do X'), while -지 않아 is a STATEMENT ('I/you don't do X') — 걱정하지 않아 means 'I don't worry' (declarative), not 'don't worry'. The near-synonym 걱정 마요 (dropping 하) is conversational shorthand fine for friends but sounds abrupt with elders — always keep the full 걱정하지 마세요 for respectful speech. Adding 너무 ('too much') is a small but powerful softener: a bare 걱정하지 마세요 can sound like an order, but 너무 걱정하지 마세요 says 'don't worry EXCESSIVELY' — kinder and more realistic. Register: 걱정하지 마 (반말) → 걱정하지 마요 (polite) → 걱정하지 마세요 / 너무 걱정하지 마세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 걱정하지 않아 to mean 'don't worry'.
걱정하지 않아 is a statement ('I don't worry'), not a command. The imperative is 걱정하지 마(요/세요). Use -지 마, not -지 않아, to tell someone not to do something.
Confusing 걱정하지 마 with 걱정돼.
걱정하지 마 tells the other person not to worry; 걱정돼 means 'I'm worried (about you/it)'. Don't say 걱정돼 when you mean to reassure them.
Using a curt 걱정 마! with an elder.
걱정 마 (dropping 하) is friendly-casual, fine for friends but too blunt for an elder or boss. Say 너무 걱정하지 마세요 to stay respectful and gentle.

structuredNuance.t: 걱정하다 ('to worry') + -지 마 (negative imperative 'don't') — literally 'don't do worrying'. The real function is calming someone anxious, stressed, or fretting. The -지 마 form is the only proper imperative; -지 않아 is declarative, not a command.

Use when someone is anxious about an exam, a medical result, a relationship, or any future uncertainty. Register: 걱정하지 마 (반말 — friend/younger) → 걱정하지 마요 (polite — peer) → 걱정하지 마세요 / 너무 걱정하지 마세요 (honorific — elder/boss/customer). Add 너무 ('too much') to soften the command.

걱정하지 마 ('don't worry' — to the other person) vs. 걱정돼 ('I'm worried' — describing your own feeling, from 걱정되다). Same root 걱정, opposite direction. Do not say 걱정돼 when you mean to reassure them — that reports your anxiety, not theirs.

Make it more convincing by adding a reason or support: 내가 도와줄게, 걱정하지 마 ('I'll help, don't worry'). For an elder: 너무 걱정하지 마세요 + 잘 해결될 거예요 ('don't worry too much, it'll work out'). Short form: 걱정 마 (to a friend, very casual — dropping 하).

The command 'don't worry' requires -지 마, NOT -지 않아. 걱정하지 않아 is a statement ('I/you don't worry'), not an instruction. Another trap: using the shortened 걱정 마 (dropping 하) with an elder — it sounds blunt. Always use 걱정하지 마세요 for anyone you'd address with honorifics.

expressions.shortExplanation: 무슨 일 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is something wrong?".
expressions.explanation: "Is something wrong?" — that is 무슨 일 있어요? (museun il isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 무슨 일 있어요? ("Is something wrong? / What happened?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; opening when someone looks upset
반말; to a close friend
Honorific; to an elder, customer, or boss
혹시 ('perhaps') makes the question gentler, less prying

examples.ko: A: (looking worried) ... / B: 혹시 무슨 일 있어요?
examples.romanization: A: (looking worried) ... / B: hoksi museun il isseoyo?
examples.en: A: (looking worried) ... / B: Is something maybe wrong?
examples.note: 혹시 softens the question to 'by any chance' — use it when you're not sure something is wrong; it feels caring rather than prying

examples.ko: 표정이 안 좋네요. 무슨 일 있어요?
examples.romanization: pyojeongi an jonneyo. museun il isseoyo?
examples.en: You look down. Is something wrong?
examples.note: 표정이 안 좋다 ('your expression is not good') observes the signal before the gentle probe; pairing a specific observation makes the question warmer

examples.ko: 혹시 무슨 일 있으세요? 제가 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: hoksi museun il isseuseyo? jega doul il isseumyeon malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: Is something the matter? If there's anything I can do, please tell me.
examples.note: Offer help with 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요 to show you mean it; 있으세요 for honorific — 있다 → 있으세요 with -으세요

expressions.nuance: 직역: 무슨 ('what kind of') + 일 ('matter/event') + 있어요 ('is there') — literally 'is there some matter?'. The real use is a gentle probe when someone looks troubled and you want to invite them to open up, without forcing it. Note that 일 here means 'a happening/issue', not 'work' (same word, different context). The key near-synonym split: 무슨 일 있어요? checks WHETHER something is wrong (probing); 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a problem is (assuming something's already up). The golden softener is 혹시 ('perhaps, by any chance'): 혹시 무슨 일 있어요? feels caring and tactful, not intrusive. Register: 있어? (반말) → 있어요? (polite) → 있으세요? (honorific, where 있다 becomes 있으세요). The particle pitfall: 있다 ('to exist') takes a subject or nothing — never the object marker 을. So it is 무슨 일(이) 있어요?, never 무슨 일을 있어요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 무슨 일을 있어요?
있다 ('to exist') never takes the object marker 을. It's 무슨 일(이) 있어요? — subject marker or nothing, because the matter EXISTS, it isn't an object you act on.
Mixing up 무슨 일 있어요? and 무슨 일이에요?
무슨 일 있어요? checks IF something's wrong; 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a known matter is. Use 있어요? to gently probe when you're not sure anything happened.
Asking an elder 무슨 일 있어? without honorifics.
있어? is 반말. For an elder, customer, or boss, lift it to 무슨 일 있으세요?, where 있다 becomes the honorific 있으세요.

structuredNuance.t: 무슨 ('what kind of') + 일 ('matter/event') + 있어요 ('is there') — literally 'is there some matter?'. The real function is a gentle invitation to open up when you've noticed someone looks troubled. 일 here is 'a happening/issue', not 'work'.

Use when someone looks upset, quiet, or off — you notice but don't want to pry. Add 혹시 ('perhaps, by any chance') for maximum tact: 혹시 무슨 일 있어요? Register: 무슨 일 있어? (반말 — friend) → 있어요? (polite) → 있으세요? (honorific — elder/boss/customer).

무슨 일 있어요? checks IF something is wrong (probing). 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a known problem is (assuming something's already up). Use 있어요? to gently test whether anything happened; switch to 일이에요? once you know something did.
Lead with an observation: 표정이 안 좋네요, 무슨 일 있어요? ('you look down — is something wrong?'). Follow up with an offer: 제가 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요. Softest form: 혹시 무슨 일 있으세요?
chips: 표정이 안 좋네요. 무슨 일 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 있다 ('to exist') never takes the object marker 을. It's 무슨 일(이) 있어요? — subject marker 이 or nothing, never 일을 있어요. Another trap is translating 'what's wrong WITH you' literally and sounding accusatory — 무슨 일 있어요? is warm and open; don't add 너 (you) to a stranger.

expressions.english: Oh no, what do we do
expressions.shortExplanation: 어떡해요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh no, what do we do".
expressions.explanation: 어떡해요 (eotteokaeyo) = "Oh no, what do we do". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어떡해요 ("Oh no / what'll you do"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a sympathetic reaction to someone's bad news
반말; to a close friend, often half-gasped

usagePhrases.en: Oh dear, what should we do
usagePhrases.note: Polite -죠, drawing the listener in

usagePhrases.en: Oh, what a thing / good heavens
usagePhrases.note: A warmer, slightly older-flavored variant

examples.ko: A: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요. / B: 어머, 어떡해요!
examples.romanization: A: jigabeul ireobeoryeosseoyo. / B: eomeo, eotteokaeyo!
examples.en: A: I lost my wallet. / B: Oh my, that's awful!
examples.note: 어머 + 어떡해요 is the instinctive reaction to bad news — it signals shared dismay, not a request for a plan; do not wait for instructions after hearing it

examples.en: You failed the interview? Oh no.
examples.note: Echo their problem, then 어떡해요 to share the dismay — the whole expression means 'oh no, what a shame' in this context

examples.ko: 저런, 그렇게 됐다니 정말 어떡해요. 많이 놀라셨겠어요.
examples.romanization: jeoreon, geureoke dwaetdani jeongmal eotteokaeyo. mani nollasyeotgesseoyo.
examples.en: Oh dear, to think it turned out that way — what a thing. You must have been so shaken.
examples.note: Chain with 놀라셨겠어요 ('you must have been shaken') to deepen the sympathy; 저런 is the natural lead-in

expressions.nuance: 직역: 어떡해요 is a contraction of 어떻게 해요 ('how do (we/you) do?'), but as a set exclamation it has bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — pure sympathetic reaction to bad news, not an actual request for a plan. The most important spelling split in Korean emotional vocabulary: 어떡해 (standalone exclamation, contracted, takes NO following verb) vs. 어떻게 (the adverb 'how', must pair with a verb — 어떻게 해요, 어떻게 가요). Writing 어떡해 가요 is a common error; it's 어떻게 가요. Register: 어떡해 (반말) → 어떡해요 (polite). For an elder you'd often shift to 이를 어째요 or 저런 or 얼마나 놀라셨어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 어떡해요 literally as 'how should I do it?' and either waiting for instructions or answering it — in sympathy it's simply 'oh no'. Reserve it for genuine bad news, not a trivial mishap (there, use 아이고 or 어머).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 어떡해 when you mean 어떻게 ('how').
어떻게 is the question word and pairs with a verb (어떻게 해요). 어떡해 is the standalone exclamation ('oh no') and takes no following verb. 어떡해 가요 is wrong; say 어떻게 가요.
Treating 어떡해요 as a literal request for a plan.
In sympathy it means 'oh no / what a shame', not 'tell me how'. Don't wait for or expect instructions — it's an expression of shared dismay.
Using 어떡해요 for trivial mishaps.
It carries genuine concern. For a tiny slip (spilled coffee) say 아이고 or 어머; reserve 어떡해요 for real bad news so it doesn't sound melodramatic.

structuredNuance.t: 어떡해요 contracts from 어떻게 해요 ('how do we do?'), but as a set exclamation it has fully bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — pure sympathetic reaction. It signals 'I feel for you, this is awful', not a literal request for a plan of action.

Use as an immediate reaction when someone shares genuine bad news — a lost item, a failed exam, an accident, bad luck. Register: 어떡해 (반말 — friend) → 어떡해요 (polite). For an elder, 이를 어째요 or pairing with 얼마나 놀라셨겠어요 ('you must have been so shocked') is more natural.

이를 어째요 is a warmer, slightly more formal/older-generation variant with the same 'oh dear, what a thing' meaning. 어머 or 아이고 are lighter exclamations for smaller mishaps. 어떡해요 carries genuine concern — reserve it for real bad news, not a spilled coffee.

The key variant to know is 어떡하죠 (polite -죠, 'what are we to do?') — pulls the listener in to shared concern. Lead with 어머 or 저런 for a natural flow: 어머, 어떡해요. Follow up with 많이 놀라셨겠어요 to deepen sympathy.

The critical spelling trap: 어떡해 (exclamation, standalone) vs. 어떻게 (adverb 'how', must pair with a verb). You CANNOT say 어떡해 가요 — it's 어떻게 가요. Also do not take 어떡해요 literally as a question expecting a plan — in this sympathy context it means 'oh no'. Avoid using it for trivial mishaps; it implies real dismay.

expressions.english: You worked hard / Thanks for your effort
expressions.shortExplanation: 고생했어요 is a practical expression meaning "You worked hard / Thanks for your effort".
expressions.explanation: 고생했어요 (gosaenghaesseoyo) means "You worked hard / Thanks for your effort". Say it as one set phrase — for example 고생했어요 ("You've worked hard / Thanks for the effort"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: You've worked hard / Thanks for the effort
usagePhrases.note: Polite; to a peer or someone junior after hard work
반말; to a close friend or someone younger

usagePhrases.en: Thank you for your hard work
usagePhrases.note: Honorific; to an elder, senior, or someone you respect

usagePhrases.en: You've been through so much / worked so hard
usagePhrases.note: Add 많다 to stress just how much effort it took

examples.ko: A: 드디어 끝났어요. / B: 고생하셨어요. 정말 수고 많으셨어요.
examples.romanization: A: deudieo kkeunnasseoyo. / B: gosaenghasyeosseoyo. jeongmal sugo maneusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: It's finally done. / B: Thank you for your hard work. You really put in so much effort.
examples.note: 고생하셨어요 for a senior (note -시-); this is the end-of-project acknowledgment — never use 고생했어요 without -시- toward a boss or elder

examples.ko: 먼 길 오느라 고생하셨어요. 좀 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: meon gil oneura gosaenghasyeosseoyo. jom swiseyo.
examples.en: Thank you for coming all this way — you must be tired. Please rest.
examples.note: 오느라 ('in the course of coming') ties the effort to a specific act; follow with 쉬세요 as natural comfort

examples.ko: 힘든 일 겪으시느라 고생 많으셨어요. 이제 좀 나아지셨어요?
examples.romanization: himdeun il gyeokkeusineura gosaeng maneusyeosseoyo. ije jom naajisyeosseoyo?
examples.en: You've been through so much — are you feeling a bit better now?
examples.note: 겪으시느라 ('in going through it') turns it into sympathy for endured hardship; 고생 많으셨어요 is the deepest form

expressions.nuance: 직역: 고생 ('hardship/toil', Sino-Korean 苦生) + 했어요 (past tense of 하다) — literally 'you did hardship'. Despite the seemingly negative 苦 ('suffering'), this is a warm acknowledgment and compliment, equivalent to 'you worked so hard, thank you for your effort'. It does double duty: it thanks someone for difficult work AND sympathizes with someone who's been through a hard time. Register is critical: to a senior, elder, or anyone you respect you MUST include the honorific -시-: 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨어요. A plain 고생했어요 to your boss is like patting them on the head — disrespectful. The key near-synonym split: 수고했어요 ('good work, thanks') is lighter and travels DOWNWARD (to staff, a clerk, a delivery worker); 고생하셨어요 implies harder, more draining toil and is safer upward. Saying 수고하세요 to a senior can feel condescending — use 고생하셨어요 to honor their effort properly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고생했어요 (no -시-) to your boss or an elder.
To a superior you must honorify: 고생하셨어요. Plain 고생했어요 to someone senior sounds like praising a junior — add -시- to show respect.
Using 수고하세요 to an elder or boss.
수고하다 is lighter and often directed downward (to staff). To a senior it can feel condescending; 고생하셨어요 or 고생 많으셨어요 conveys respect for their effort better.
Reading 고생 as purely negative and avoiding the phrase.
Though 고생 means 'hardship', 고생했어요 is a warm thank-you/compliment for someone's effort. Don't shy away from it; it's exactly what Koreans say to honor hard work.

structuredNuance.t: 고생 ('hardship/toil', 苦生) + 했어요 (past 하다) — literally 'you did hardship'. Despite the seemingly dark character 苦 ('suffering'), this is a warm compliment: 'you worked so hard, thank you'. It covers both work effort (thanks for the effort) and endured hardship (you've been through so much).

Use at the end of a long day, project, event, or difficult period. CRITICAL: to anyone senior or older, add -시-: 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨어요. Using 고생했어요 without -시- to your boss sounds like you're patting a junior on the back. Register: 고생했어 (반말 — friend/younger) → 고생했어요 (peer/junior) → 고생하셨어요 / 고생 많으셨어요 (elder/senior).

수고했어요 ('good work / thanks for the effort') is lighter and typically travels DOWNWARD — you say it to staff, a delivery person, a service worker. 고생하셨어요 implies harder, more draining toil and is appropriate upward or laterally. Critically, 수고하세요 to an elder or boss can feel condescending; 고생하셨어요 is the safer respectful choice.

Deepen with 많다: 고생 많으셨어요 ('you went through so much hardship'). Tie to a specific act with -느라: 먼 길 오시느라 고생하셨어요 ('thank you for coming all this way'). Natural follow-up: 오늘은 푹 쉬세요 ('please rest well today').

The direct-translation trap is reading 고생 ('hardship/suffering') as negative and shying away from the phrase — it's actually a warm, respectful acknowledgment, not a complaint. The bigger error is dropping -시- with a superior: always 고생하셨어요 to an elder or boss, never 고생했어요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 푹 쉬어요 is a practical expression meaning "Get some good rest".
expressions.explanation: "Get some good rest" — that is 푹 쉬어요 (puk swieoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 푹 쉬어요 ("Rest up well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; to a peer who's tired or unwell
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Honorific; to an elder, boss, or customer

usagePhrases.en: Take good care of yourself (recover well)
usagePhrases.note: Specifically when someone is sick or recovering

examples.ko: A: 오늘 정말 힘들었어요. / B: 고생하셨어요. 오늘은 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul jeongmal himdeureosseoyo. / B: gosaenghasyeosseoyo. oneureun puk swiseyo.
examples.en: A: Today was really exhausting. / B: You worked so hard. Please rest well tonight.
examples.note: Pair 고생하셨어요 + 푹 쉬세요 — acknowledging the effort then sending them to rest is the natural two-step comfort sequence

examples.en: Rest up well so your cold gets better fast.
examples.note: Tie the rest to recovery with 나으려면 ('to get better'); note 나으려면 from 낫다 (ㅅ-irregular)

examples.ko: 많이 힘드셨을 텐데 오늘은 아무 생각 말고 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: mani himdeusyeosseul tende oneureun amu saenggang malgo puk swiseyo.
examples.en: It must have been so hard — today, don't think about anything, just rest well.
examples.note: 아무 생각 말고 ('without thinking of anything') deepens the care; 푹 쉬세요 is the gracious close

expressions.nuance: 직역: 푹 ('deeply/soundly/thoroughly', a mimetic adverb) + 쉬다 ('to rest') — literally 'rest deeply/soundly'. 푹 is the key flavor word: same as in 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly') and 푹 삶다 ('boil thoroughly'). It upgrades a plain 쉬어요 ('rest') to 'really rest, recharge fully'. The natural near-synonym is 몸조리 잘하세요 ('take good care of your body / recover well'), which is specifically for someone SICK or post-surgery/postpartum — when illness is the issue, 몸조리 쏙 is more precise. 푹 쉬세요 is for general fatigue, stress, or as a caring goodbye. Register: 푹 쉬어 (반말) → 푹 쉬어요 (polite) → 푹 쉬세요 (honorific). The natural pairing: after 고생하셨어요, add 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. Do NOT use it mid-task when the person cannot actually stop — the implication is that they now have time to rest. The English-speaker pitfall is the formal 직역 'take a rest' → 휴식을 취하세요, which is stiff HR-memo Korean, not warm spoken comfort.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 휴식을 취하세요 to comfort someone.
That's stiff, written-style Korean (like an HR memo). In warm spoken comfort, say 푹 쉬세요 — natural and caring, not bureaucratic.
Writing 폭 쉬어요 instead of 푹 쉬어요.
The adverb is 푹 ('soundly, deeply'), not 폭. 폭 means something else (width/explosion sounds). For 'rest well' it's 푹 쉬어요.
Using 푹 쉬세요 for someone who's sick when 몸조리 fits better.
푹 쉬세요 is general fatigue/stress. For illness or recovery specifically, 몸조리 잘하세요 ('recover well, take care of your body') is the precise, caring phrase.

structuredNuance.t: 푹 ('deeply/soundly/thoroughly', mimetic adverb) + 쉬다 ('to rest') — literally 'rest deeply'. 푹 is the intensity marker: same sound-symbol as in 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly'). It transforms a plain 'rest' into 'really recharge, rest fully'. The real function is a caring farewell or comfort after hard work or illness.

Use as a caring close when someone is exhausted, sick, or grieving. Natural sequence: 고생하셨어요 → 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. Do NOT say it mid-task when the person cannot stop — it implies they now have free time to rest. Register: 푹 쉬어 (반말 — friend) → 푹 쉬어요 (polite — peer) → 푹 쉬세요 (honorific — elder/boss).

몸조리 잘하세요 ('recover well, take care of your body') is the near-synonym for someone who is ill or recovering from surgery/postpartum. 푹 쉬세요 is broader: general fatigue, stress, emotional exhaustion. When someone has a cold or just left the hospital, reach for 몸조리 잘하세요 first.
Pair with acknowledgment: 고생하셨어요, 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. For illness, combine: 얼른 나으세요, 푹 쉬어요. Deepen care: 아무 생각 말고 푹 쉬세요 ('rest without thinking about anything'). Do not confuse 푹 with 폭 — different words.

The direct-translation 'take a rest' → 휴식을 취하세요 is stiff, written-register Korean (like a memo). In warm spoken comfort, say 푹 쉬세요. Also, do not write 폭 쉬어요 — the adverb is 푹 (soft u-sound), not 폭 (a different word meaning width or explosion sound).

expressions.shortExplanation: 영수증 여기 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "Here's the receipt".
expressions.explanation: 영수증 여기 있어요 (yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo) = "Here's the receipt". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 영수증 여기 있어요 ("Here's the receipt"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; handing over your receipt at the counter
반말, to a friend helping you return something
Formal 합쇼체, stiffer or to a manager
Saying you have it before you hand it over

examples.en: Here's the receipt.
examples.note: The most basic form — said as you place the receipt on the counter; no extra words needed.

examples.en: I'd like a refund. Here's the receipt.
examples.note: State your purpose first, then offer proof — this sequence signals you came prepared.

examples.ko: A: 혹시 영수증 있으세요? / B: 네, 영수증 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: hoksi yeongsujeung isseuseyo? / B: ne, yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Do you happen to have the receipt? / B: Yes, here's the receipt.
examples.note: Classic staff-customer exchange; B's reply is the natural beat after A's polite 있으세요? request.

expressions.nuance: 영수증 여기 있어요 is 영수증 ('receipt', Sino-Korean 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it is here / here it is'). 여기 있어요 is the natural Korean phrase for 'here you go / here it is' when presenting an object — it literally says 'it exists here', and the offering sense comes from context and gesture. Keep the receipt, because almost every Korean store requires 영수증 for a refund or exchange; without it you may only get 교환 (store exchange) or be refused entirely. The nearest near-synonym is 영수증 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you'), which actively announces you're handing it over and feels slightly more deferential; 여기 있어요 simply presents it — both are natural, but 여기 있어요 is the everyday default. Stronger/softer variants: 영수증 여기 있습니다 (formal), 여기 있어 (반말). The English-speaker trap is translating 'here you go' word-for-word as 여기 가요, which means 'here I go / I'm going here' — the correct presenting phrase is 여기 있어요 (존재동사 있다, not 가다). A second common confusion: 영수증 (receipt, proof of payment already made) vs 계산서 (the bill/statement, often before paying) — for a return you need 영수증.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기 가요 for 'here you go'.
여기 가요 means 'I'm going here / here I go', not 'here it is'. To present an object, say 여기 있어요 — the existence verb 있다, not the motion verb 가다.
Confusing 영수증 with 계산서.
영수증 is the receipt (proof you paid); 계산서 is the bill/itemized statement before paying. For a refund or exchange the staff want the 영수증.
Attempting a return with no receipt and expecting a full refund.
Most Korean stores require 영수증 for a cash refund; without it you may get only 교환 (exchange) or store credit. Keep and present it: 영수증 여기 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 ('receipt', 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it exists here'). The presenting force — 'here you go' — comes from context and gesture, not from a separate giving verb. It is the standard counter phrase when handing staff any document.

Used at any retail or service counter: refund desks, pharmacy pick-ups, parcel offices. Speech-level is 해요체 (polite-neutral). Upgrade to 여기 있습니다 (합쇼체) with a manager; drop to 여기 있어 (반말) with a friend helping you. Safe for strangers and staff.

영수증 드릴게요 ('I'll give you the receipt') actively announces the handover and is a touch more deferential; 여기 있어요 just presents it. Both are fine — 여기 있어요 is the unmarked everyday default. Distinguish 영수증 (paid receipt) from 계산서 (itemized bill, often before payment); for returns you need 영수증.
여기 있어요 → 여기 있습니다 (stiffer/formal) → 여기 있어 (반말). Add lead-in: 영수증 가지고 왔어요 ('I brought the receipt') to say you have it before presenting it.

'Here you go' → 여기 가요 is the classic trap. 가요 means 'I go/am going'; the presenting verb is 있어요 (existence). A second trap: using 계산서 instead of 영수증 for a return — 계산서 is the bill, not proof of payment.

expressions.shortExplanation: 환불해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me a refund".
expressions.explanation: "Please give me a refund" — that is 환불해 주세요 (hwanbulhae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 환불해 주세요 ("Please give me a refund"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard request to be refunded
반말, to a friend or very casual seller

usagePhrases.en: Could you give me a refund, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to request a refund
usagePhrases.note: Softer, deferential with 부탁드리다 ('to request a favor')

examples.en: Please give me a refund.
examples.note: Said once you've confirmed a refund is possible and shown the receipt — this is your actual request.

examples.en: The size doesn't fit — please refund it.
examples.note: Give the reason with -아서요 first, then the request; this soft reason-first structure is natural Korean complaint phrasing.

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 이거 카드로 결제했는데 환불해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: igeo kadeuro gyeoljehaenneunde hwanbulhae juseyo.
examples.en: A: How would you like to proceed? / B: I paid for this by card — please refund it.
examples.note: B mentions payment method so staff refund to the right channel (card, not cash); the A/B format mirrors a real service-desk exchange.

expressions.nuance: 환불해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me', from 해 주다, the favor-verb pattern). The 해 주다 is what turns it into a courteous request for the staff's help rather than a flat command: bare 환불하세요 would be an order ('you refund!'), which sounds bossy and rude. Use this AFTER you've confirmed a refund is possible with 환불돼요?; if you jump straight to 환불해 주세요 without the preamble, it can seem aggressive. 환불 is a 하다-noun — it needs the verb 하다, so you cannot say 환불 주세요 ('please give a refund') as though 환불 is a physical object you can hand over. To de-escalate when staff resist, soften to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요. Korean law requires card purchases to be refunded back to the same card (카드 취소), not in cash — always mention 카드로 결제했어요 so staff process it correctly. The English-speaker error is the missing favor verb (환불하세요, too blunt) or the ungrammatical 환불 주세요. Another pitfall is register mismatch: 환불 부탁드립니다 in a casual market stall sounds oddly stiff, while plain 환불 in a department store sounds rude — default to 환불해 주세요 and calibrate.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불하세요 to the staff.
Bare 환불하세요 is an imperative ('you, refund!') and sounds commanding. The polite favor form is 환불해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Saying 환불 주세요 without 하다.
환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given' directly. It needs 하다 + the favor 주다: 환불해 주세요, not 환불 주세요.
Demanding cash back for a card purchase.
By card you're refunded to the same card, not in cash (카드 결제는 카드로 환불). Say 카드로 결제했어요, 환불해 주세요, and expect the card to be credited.

structuredNuance.t: 환불(還拂) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Literally 'please do the refund for me' — the favor-verb 주다 signals a polite request for the other person's help, not a command. Use AFTER confirming 환불돼요? — this is the execution step.

Stage two at the counter — after feasibility is confirmed. 해요체 (polite-neutral) with all staff. Upgrade to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요 if the clerk is reluctant or you're at a formal department-store service desk. Do not use bare 환불하세요 — it is imperative and rude to staff.

환불해 주세요 (general request, any stage) vs 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 (specifically 'please execute/process it now', once agreed). 환불 부탁드려요 is softer and more face-saving when staff are reluctant. 환불 주세요 is wrong — 환불 is not a physical object you can give.
환불해 주세요 → 환불해 주시겠어요? → 환불 부탁드려요 → 환불 부탁드립니다 (most formal). Casual: 환불해 줘 (반말). Add reason: 사이즈가 안 맞아서 환불해 주세요.

Two errors: (1) 환불하세요 — the bare imperative is a command, not a request; add 주세요. (2) 환불 주세요 — 환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given'; it needs 하다: 환불해 주세요. Also: card refunds go back to the card (카드 취소), not in cash — state your payment method.

expressions.shortExplanation: 교환하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to exchange this".
expressions.explanation: 교환하고 싶어요 (gyohwanhago sipeoyo) = "I'd like to exchange this". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 교환하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to exchange this"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; stating you want to swap the item
반말, to a friend or casual seller
교환하려고요 ('intending to exchange'), softer announcement
Asking first whether an exchange is possible

examples.en: I'd like to exchange this.
examples.note: Stated while presenting the item; combines purpose with politeness — no need to explain yet.

examples.ko: 사이즈가 작아서 한 치수 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga jagaseo han chisu keun geollo gyohwanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: It's too small, so I'd like to exchange it for one size up.
examples.note: 한 치수 큰 걸로 ('for one size up') specifies exactly what you want; -아서 gives the reason without sounding accusatory.

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 색깔이 마음에 안 들어서 교환하고 싶은데요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: saekkkari maeume an deureoseo gyohwanhago sipeundeyo.
examples.en: A: How can I help? / B: I don't like the colour, so I'd like an exchange.
examples.note: B uses the soft -ㄴ데요 ender, which is warmer than a flat statement and naturally invites the staff to respond.

expressions.nuance: 교환하고 싶어요 is 교환 ('exchange', Sino-Korean 交換) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'), 'I want to exchange (this)'. Unlike ordering food — where 먹고 싶어요 can sound bluntly desire-focused — for returns and exchanges 하고 싶어요 is perfectly polite, because you're stating your purpose to staff who'll then guide you. Many Korean learners soften this further to 교환하고 싶은데요… (trailing -ㄴ데요) to invite the staff's response. The crucial distinction: 교환돼요? checks IF an exchange is possible; 교환하고 싶어요 declares that you WANT one — always check first if unsure. Know the three-way split: 교환 (swap for another item) vs 환불 (money back) vs 반품 (physically sending back the goods). When naming the replacement, use -로/-으로: 큰 사이즈로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. The English-speaker error is confusing 교환 with 변경 ('change/alter', used for reservations, plans, or settings) — you 교환 a product but 변경 a booking. Forgetting -로/-으로 on the replacement target makes the request vague: 큰 거 교환 is incomplete; 큰 걸로 교환 is correct.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 변경하고 싶어요 to swap a product.
변경 is for changing plans, reservations, or settings; a physical product swap is 교환. Say 교환하고 싶어요, not 변경하고 싶어요.
Forgetting -로/-으로 on the replacement.
To name what you're swapping for, use -로: 큰 걸로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. Without it (큰 거 교환) the target item is unclear.
Saying 교환하고 싶어요 when you actually want money back.
교환 gets you a different item, not cash. If you want your money, say 환불해 주세요, not 교환하고 싶어요.

structuredNuance.t: 교환(交換) + 하고 싶어요 → 'I want to do an exchange'. The -고 싶어요 desire form is entirely natural here; staff read it as a polite statement of purpose, not a brash want. Softening option: 교환하고 싶은데요… (trailing -ㄴ데요).
Said at the counter when you want a different item, not a refund. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Can say it to any staff member. If you haven't yet confirmed an exchange is allowed, open with 교환돼요? first.
교환하고 싶어요 (want an exchange) vs 교환돼요? (is it possible?) vs 환불해 주세요 (want money back) vs 반품하고 싶어요 (want to physically return the goods). 교환 ≠ 변경 — 변경 is for reservations/plans/settings, not products.
교환하고 싶어요 → 교환하고 싶은데요… → 교환하려고요 ('I'm here to exchange'). Add target with -로: 큰 사이즈로 교환하고 싶어요 / 다른 색으로 교환해 주세요.
두 함정: (1) 교환 vs 변경 — products use 교환, reservations/plans use 변경. (2) Missing -로/-으로 on the target: 큰 거 교환 is vague; 큰 걸로 교환 ('exchange for a big one') is the correct form marking what you swap INTO.

expressions.english: Please swap it for a different one
expressions.shortExplanation: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please swap it for a different one".
expressions.explanation: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 (dareun geollo bakkwo juseyo) means "Please swap it for a different one". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 ("Please swap it for a different one"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Please swap it for a different one
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking to exchange for another item

usagePhrases.en: Swap it for a different one
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or casual stall

usagePhrases.en: Could you swap it for a different one?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: Please swap it for a different color
usagePhrases.note: 다른 색으로 ('for a different color') when only the color is off

examples.en: Please swap this for a different one.
examples.note: The everyday counter request when the item itself is fine but you want a clean replacement.

examples.ko: 이거 흠집 있어서 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: igeo heumjip isseoseo dareun geollo bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: This has a scratch — please swap it for a different one.
examples.note: 흠집 있다 ('has a scratch') names the defect; -아서 links reason to request without hostility.

examples.ko: A: 뭐가 문제예요? / B: 여기 실밥 풀렸어요. 같은 걸로 새 거 있으면 바꿔 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: mwoga munjeyeyo? / B: yeogi silbap pullyeosseoyo. gateun geollo sae geo isseumyeon bakkwo juseyo.
examples.en: A: What's the problem? / B: The stitching came loose here. If you have a new one of the same, please swap it.
examples.note: B points to the exact flaw (실밥 풀리다 = stitching unraveled), then qualifies with 새 거 있으면, making the request realistic.

expressions.nuance: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is 다른 ('different/other') + 걸로 (걸 = 거 'thing' + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please change it for me'). 바꾸다 is the native Korean verb 'to change/swap', warmer and more everyday than the Sino-Korean 교환하다 — both work at a counter, but 바꿔 주세요 is what most people say naturally. The -로 on 다른 걸로 is essential: it marks the target you're swapping INTO ('for a different one'); drop it and 다른 거 바꿔 주세요 sounds incomplete. The dividing line from 환불해 주세요 is outcome: 바꿔 주세요 gets you a replacement item; 환불해 주세요 gets you your money back. Specify what's wrong or what you want (다른 색으로, 큰 사이즈로, 새 걸로) so staff know whether it's a defect swap or a preference swap. The English-speaker error is saying 다른 거 주세요 ('give me a different one') without the exchange framing — that sounds like you're starting a fresh purchase, not swapping the item you hold. Another pitfall: 바꾸다 works for physical items; don't use it for changing a reservation (use 변경하다) or changing money (use 환전하다).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -로 and saying 다른 거 바꿔 주세요.
The -로 marks what you swap INTO; without it the sentence dangles. Say 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Saying 다른 거 주세요 to mean 'exchange this'.
That sounds like asking for a different item as a new request, not swapping the one you hold. For an exchange, use 바꿔 주세요: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Using 바꿔 주세요 when you want money back.
바꾸다 swaps one item for another; it doesn't return money. If you want a refund, say 환불해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 다른 ('different') + 걸로 (thing + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please swap for me'). 바꾸다 is native Korean for 'swap/change'; -로 marks the target. Without -로, the sentence is incomplete.

Used when you want a physical replacement, not a refund. Natural at any retail counter. 해요체 (polite-neutral). With a manager or when being persistent, upgrade to 다른 걸로 바꿔 주시겠어요?. Dropping to 바꿔 줘 (반말) is only for close friends or an unusually casual seller.

바꿔 주세요 (swap item, native verb, warm) vs 교환해 주세요 (exchange, Sino-Korean, slightly more formal) — both get you a replacement. Neither returns money: for money back, say 환불해 주세요. 다른 거 주세요 (just 'give me a different one') has no exchange framing and sounds like a new purchase.
다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 → 큰 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요 → 새 걸로 바꿔 주세요 → 같은 거 새 걸로 바꿔 주세요. The -로 slot accepts any target: 다른 색으로, 다른 사이즈로.
Saying 다른 거 주세요 sounds like a new purchase, not an exchange. The swap framing requires 바꿔: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요. Also: 바꾸다 is for physical items; reservations use 변경하다, currency exchange uses 환전하다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 불량인데요 is a practical expression meaning "This one's defective".
expressions.explanation: "This one's defective" — that is 이거 불량인데요 (igeo bullyangindeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 불량인데요 ("This one's defective"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; flagging a faulty product gently
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Flat statement, a touch more direct

usagePhrases.en: I think it's a defective item
usagePhrases.note: Softer, hedged with -것 같아요 ('seems')

examples.en: This one's defective.
examples.note: Said while showing the faulty item to staff; the trailing -ㄴ데요 invites their response rather than accusing.

examples.ko: 새로 샀는데 이거 불량인데요. 작동이 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: saero sanneunde igeo bullyangindeyo. jakdongi an dwaeyo.
examples.en: I just bought it, but it's defective — it doesn't work.
examples.note: 작동이 안 되다 ('doesn't operate') names the specific malfunction; saying 새로 샀는데 heads off any suggestion you broke it through use.

examples.ko: A: 어디가 문제예요? / B: 박스 열자마자 봤는데 이거 불량인데요. 사진 찍어 뒀어요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga munjeyeyo? / B: bakseu yeoljamaja bwanneunde igeo bullyangindeyo. sajin jjigeo dwosseoyo.
examples.en: A: What's the problem? / B: I noticed it the moment I opened the box — this is defective. I took photos.
examples.note: B's 박스 열자마자 ('the instant I opened the box') makes a strong case that the defect is pre-existing, not user-caused; 사진 찍어 뒀어요 offers proof.

expressions.nuance: 이거 불량인데요 is 이거 ('this') + 불량 ('defect/defective', Sino-Korean 不良) + 인데요 (copula 이다 + soft ender -ㄴ데요). 불량 means the product is functionally faulty from the maker — a manufacturing defect — and 불량품 is the noun form 'a defective item'. The -ㄴ데요 ender is the politeness engine: it raises the problem as 'here's the situation…' and invites the staff to respond, so it's far gentler than a flat 이거 불량이에요, which can sound like an accusation. The dividing line from 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) is function vs condition: 불량 implies it doesn't work right (functional fault), while 하자 is a visible blemish — a scratch, crack, or tear. For electronics that won't turn on, 불량 fits; for a visible blemish on packaging, 하자 있어요 is more precise. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'broken' and saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new item — 고장 implies it broke down after some use, whereas a product faulty out of the box is 불량. Note: 불량 is also slang for a 'delinquent person' (불량 학생), but with a product it unambiguously means defective.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new faulty item.
고장 means it broke down (usually after use). A product faulty from the start is 불량: 이거 불량인데요 / 불량품이에요.
Dropping -ㄴ데요 and stating flat 이거 불량이에요.
The bare statement can sound accusatory. The soft ender raises it gently: 이거 불량인데요 lets staff respond without feeling blamed.
Confusing 불량 (faulty function) with 하자 (blemish/flaw).
불량 = doesn't work right; 하자 = a flaw like a scratch or crack. For a non-working item say 불량, for a visible blemish say 하자 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 불량(不良) + 인데요 → 'this is [a case of] poor quality / defective — here's the situation'. 불량 = a manufacturing fault (functional). The -ㄴ데요 ender softens the claim into a situation-framer that invites the staff's response, rather than a blunt accusation.

Used when a brand-new item doesn't function correctly. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — appropriate with all staff. Softer option: 불량품인 것 같아요 (hedge with 것 같다). Point at the defect as you speak to make it concrete. Avoid being in 반말 with staff even if frustrated.

불량 (functional fault, from factory) vs 하자 (blemish/flaw in condition: scratch, crack, tear) vs 고장 (breakdown after some use). For a never-worked item: 불량. For a visible mark: 하자 있어요. For a phone that stopped working after a week: 고장 났어요.
이거 불량인데요 (soft) → 이거 불량이에요 (direct) → 불량품인 것 같아요 (hedged) → 불량품이에요 (noun form). Escalate: 불량품이라서 교환해 주세요 / 환불해 주세요.

'Broken' → 고장났어요 is wrong for a brand-new faulty item. 고장 = broke down after use; 불량 = defective from the start. Also: 불량 is also slang for a delinquent person, but in a product context it always means defective.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기 하자 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "There's a flaw here".
expressions.explanation: 여기 하자 있어요 (yeogi haja isseoyo) = "There's a flaw here". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기 하자 있어요 ("There's a flaw here"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; pointing out a blemish on the product
반말, to a friend or casual seller
흠집 ('scratch') for a surface mark specifically

usagePhrases.en: It seems to have a bit of a flaw
usagePhrases.note: Softer, hedged with -것 같다 ('seems')

examples.en: There's a flaw here.
examples.note: Said while pointing directly at the blemish — the 여기 + gesture combination makes the complaint concrete and hard to dismiss.

examples.ko: 여기 보세요, 하자 있어요. 박음질이 터졌어요.
examples.romanization: yeogi boseyo, haja isseoyo. bageumjiri teojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Look here — there's a flaw. The stitching's come apart.
examples.note: 박음질이 터지다 ('the stitching burst') names the exact defect; 보세요 invites the staff to verify rather than just trust your word.

examples.ko: A: 언제 발견하셨어요? / B: 살 때는 몰랐는데 집에서 보니까 여기 하자 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: eonje balgyeonhasyeosseoyo? / B: sal ttaeneun mollanneunde jibeseo bonikka yeogi haja isseoyo.
examples.en: A: When did you notice? / B: I didn't see it when buying, but at home I noticed a flaw here.
examples.note: B's 집에서 보니까 explains why it wasn't caught in-store, making the late complaint more credible.

expressions.nuance: 여기 하자 있어요 is 여기 ('here') + 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) + 있어요 ('there is'). 하자 is the precise term for a defect in condition — a scratch, crack, tear, stain, or other blemish — as opposed to 불량, which leans toward a functional fault (it doesn't work). Pointing with 여기 ('here') as you say it makes the complaint concrete and helps staff see exactly what you mean. For an everyday surface mark, the native 흠집 ('scratch/nick') is even more specific: 여기 흠집 났어요. The dividing line: 하자 있어요 is calm and somewhat formal (it's the word used in warranties and consumer-protection law), 흠집 났어요 is plainer and very visual, while 불량이에요 says the thing fails to function. The English-speaker error is using 'have' literally and saying 이거 하자를 가지고 있어요 — Korean expresses 'there is a flaw' with the existence verb 있다, not 가지다; say 하자 있어요. Another pitfall is the particle: 하자 있어요 (or 하자가 있어요), never 하자를 있어요 — 있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Pair it with a defect word (터지다 'burst', 깨지다 'cracked', 찢어지다 'torn') to be unambiguous.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 하자를 가지고 있어요.
Korean uses the existence verb for 'there is a flaw': 하자 있어요, not the 'possess' verb 가지다. 가지고 있어요 sounds like a translation of English 'have'.
Using 하자를 있어요 with the object particle.
있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Say 하자 있어요 or 하자가 있어요, never 하자를 있어요.
Using 하자 for something that simply doesn't work.
하자 is a blemish/flaw in condition. If the item won't function at all, that's 불량 or 고장 — say 작동이 안 돼요 or 불량이에요.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 하자(瑕疵, 'flaw/blemish') + 있어요 ('there is'). The existence verb 있다 is what 'there is a flaw' maps to in Korean — not 가지다 ('have/possess'). Pointing as you speak makes the complaint specific and hard to argue with.

Used at a counter or on the phone when reporting a visible defect: scratch, crack, tear, stain. 해요체 (polite-neutral). 하자 is also the term used in consumer-protection policies, so staff recognize it immediately. For a casual market, 여기 흠집 났어요 (native word) is equally natural.

하자 있어요 (formal, in policies/law, blemish in condition) vs 흠집 났어요 (native, 'got scratched', very visual) vs 불량이에요 (functional fault — won't work). Don't use 하자 for things that simply don't function: that's 불량 or 고장.
여기 하자 있어요 → 여기 하자가 있어요 (subject particle added, same meaning) → 하자가 좀 있는 것 같은데요 (hedged). Add specifics: 여기 깨져 있어요 (cracked), 여기 찢어져 있어요 (torn), 여기 흠집 났어요 (scratched).
Two errors: (1) 하자를 가지고 있어요 ('it possesses a flaw') — use the existence verb: 하자 있어요. (2) Particle error: 하자를 있어요 is wrong; 있다 takes the subject particle 이/가, not the object particle 을/를.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 고장 났어요 is a practical expression meaning "This is broken".
expressions.explanation: 이거 고장 났어요 (igeo gojang nasseoyo) means "This is broken". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 고장 났어요 ("This is broken / It broke down"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: This is broken / It broke down
usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting that something stopped working
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Softer, hedged with -것 같아요 ('seems')

usagePhrases.en: It doesn't work / won't turn on
usagePhrases.note: Describing the symptom instead of naming 'broken'

examples.en: This is broken.
examples.note: Said while showing the device that won't work; clear, matter-of-fact, no blame implied.

examples.ko: 산 지 일주일밖에 안 됐는데 고장 났어요.
examples.romanization: san ji iljuilbakke an dwaenneunde gojang nasseoyo.
examples.en: It's only been a week since I bought it, and it broke.
examples.note: 산 지 일주일밖에 안 됐다 emphasizes how recently it was bought, implying the fault isn't from extended use.

examples.ko: A: 어디가 안 되세요? / B: 전원이 안 켜져요. 이거 고장 난 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga an doeseyo? / B: jeonwoni an kyeojyeoyo. igeo gojang nan geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: What seems to be the problem? / B: It won't power on. I think it's broken.
examples.note: B describes the symptom (전원이 안 켜지다 'won't power on') before naming 고장, which helps staff diagnose before asserting a defect.

expressions.nuance: 이거 고장 났어요 is 이거 ('this') + 고장 ('breakdown/malfunction', Sino-Korean 故障) + 났어요 (past of 나다, here 'to occur/arise'). The fixed collocation is 고장이 나다 — literally 'a breakdown occurs' — so 'it's broken' comes out as 고장 났어요, NOT 고장했어요 (고장 is not a 하다-verb) or 고장됐어요. This phrasing is for machines, devices, and appliances that stop working. The dividing line from 불량 is timing/cause: 고장 means it broke down, usually after some use, while 불량 means it was faulty from the factory; a phone that worked for a week and then died can use either depending on emphasis, but a never-worked item leans 불량. Don't apply 고장 to non-mechanical 'broken': a cracked screen is 깨졌어요; a torn bag is 찢어졌어요; a snapped cable is 끊어졌어요; a broken zipper is 지퍼가 고장 났어요 or 지퍼가 안 잠겨요. The English-speaker error is the wrong verb pairing: 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요 are not standard; the correct pairing is 고장 + 나다. Another pitfall is using 고장 for a torn or shattered item — those use different Korean verbs.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요.
고장 pairs with the verb 나다: the correct form is 고장 났어요 ('a breakdown occurred'). 고장하다/고장되다 are not standard.
Using 고장 for non-machines.
고장 is for devices/machinery. A snapped pencil is 부러졌어요, shattered glass is 깨졌어요, a torn bag is 찢어졌어요 — not 고장 났어요.
Confusing 고장 (broke down) with 불량 (faulty from the start).
If it worked then failed, 고장 났어요; if it never worked out of the box, 불량이에요. Pick based on whether it ever functioned.

structuredNuance.t: 고장(故障) + 났어요 ('occurred/arose') → 'a breakdown occurred'. 고장 is a noun; it collocates with 나다, not 하다 or 되다. Think of it as 'a malfunction happened' rather than 'it did a breakdown'.

For machines, electronics, appliances — things that stop functioning. Not for physical breakage (snapping, shattering). 해요체 (polite-neutral). When unsure, describe the symptom instead: 작동이 안 돼요 / 전원이 안 켜져요.
고장 났어요 (machine broke down after use) vs 불량이에요 (faulty from the factory) vs 작동이 안 돼요 (symptom description: doesn't operate). For physical damage: 깨졌어요 (shattered), 찢어졌어요 (torn), 부러졌어요 (snapped).
이거 고장 났어요 → 고장 난 것 같아요 (hedged) → 고장이 난 건 아닌데 작동이 안 돼요 (softer: 'not sure it's broken but it won't work'). Also: 고장 수리 맡기다 ('send for repair'), A/S 신청하다 ('apply for after-sales service').
고장했어요 and 고장됐어요 are both wrong — 고장 pairs with 나다. Say 고장 났어요. Also: 고장 is only for machines; for a torn/shattered/snapped item use the correct breakage verb (깨지다, 찢어지다, 부러지다).

expressions.shortExplanation: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the refund policy?".
expressions.explanation: "What's the refund policy?" — that is 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? ("What's the refund policy?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking how returns work here
반말, to a friend who works there

usagePhrases.en: How does the refund policy work?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, slightly more polite with -나요
환불 정책 ('refund policy'), a near-synonym of 규정

examples.en: What's the refund policy?
examples.note: Asked before buying — the smartest time, since you'll know your options before any problem arises.

examples.ko: 혹시 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? 며칠 안에 가능한가요?
examples.romanization: hoksi hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? myeochil ane ganeunghangayo?
examples.en: What's the refund policy — how many days do I have?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the inquiry; 며칠 안에 가능한가요? drills down to the time limit immediately.

examples.ko: A: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / B: 7일 이내에 영수증 지참하시면 가능해요.
examples.romanization: A: hwanbul gyujeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? / B: 7il inaee yeongsujeung jichamhasimyeon ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: A: What's the refund policy? / B: Within 7 days with the receipt, it's possible.
examples.note: B's reply is the typical staff formula — 이내에 ('within'), 영수증 지참 ('with receipt in hand'); learning this means you'll understand the answer too.

expressions.nuance: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is 환불 ('refund') + 규정 ('regulation/policy', Sino-Korean 規定) + 이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it go / what is it?'). The set frame …이/가 어떻게 돼요? is the natural Korean way to ask 'what is X / how does X work' for policies, fees, schedules, and personal details — it's softer and more conversational than a blunt 뭐예요?. This question asks the store to explain its full return rules: time limits, receipt requirements, sale-item exclusions.
