The dividing line from 환불돼요? is scope: 환불돼요? is about one specific item right now; 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks for the store's general policy. 규정 and 정책 are interchangeable here, with 규정 sounding slightly more like 'the official rules'. The English-speaker error is translating 'what is the policy' as 환불 규정이 뭐예요? — grammatically possible but blunt and survey-like; natives prefer the 어떻게 돼요? frame. The particle trap: 규정이 어떻게 돼요 (subject particle 이), never 규정을 어떻게 돼요. Mastering 어떻게 돼요? unlocks many polite info questions: 가격이 어떻게 돼요? (price), 영업시간이 어떻게 돼요? (hours).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 환불 규정이 뭐예요?.
Grammatically fine but abrupt and survey-like. The natural, polite frame is 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?.
Using the object particle: 환불 규정을 어떻게 돼요?.
되다 takes the subject particle here: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?. 규정을 is wrong with 되다.
Confusing the general policy with one item.
환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks the overall rules. To ask about the specific thing in your hand, say 이거 환불돼요?.

structuredNuance.t: 환불 + 규정(規定, 'regulation/policy') + 이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it become?'). 어떻게 돼요? is a versatile information frame meaning 'what/how is X' — softer than 뭐예요?, more open-ended than a yes/no. It asks staff to explain the full policy.

Ask before buying (ideally) or before the return attempt. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — correct with all staff. In writing/email, 환불 규정이 어떻게 되나요? or 환불 정책을 안내해 주시겠어요? is more formal. Don't use 반말 with staff.
환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (general policy, open) vs 이거 환불돼요? (this one specific item, closed yes/no) vs 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (the time-limit sub-question). 규정 ≈ 정책 in this context — both natural.
어떻게 돼요? transfers across topics: 교환 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / 반품 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / 가격이 어떻게 돼요?. For a specific follow-up: 며칠 이내예요? ('within how many days?').
환불 규정이 뭐예요? is grammatically fine but sounds abrupt — use 어떻게 돼요?. Particle error: 규정을 어떻게 돼요? is wrong; 되다 takes the subject particle: 규정이 어떻게 돼요?.

expressions.english: By how many days do I have to get a refund?
expressions.shortExplanation: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "By how many days do I have to get a refund?".
expressions.explanation: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo?) = "By how many days do I have to get a refund?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? ("Within how many days do I have to refund it?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Within how many days do I have to refund it?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking the return deadline

usagePhrases.en: How many days do I have to refund?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: How many days is the refund window?
usagePhrases.note: 환불 기간 ('refund period'), asking the window directly

usagePhrases.en: Until when is a refund possible?
usagePhrases.note: 언제까지 ('by when'), asking the cutoff date

examples.en: By how many days do I have to get this refunded?
examples.note: The smart follow-up to ask at the moment of buying so you know your exact deadline before any problem arises.

examples.ko: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? 일주일 지나면 안 돼요?
examples.romanization: myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo? iljuil jinamyeon an dwaeyo?
examples.en: How many days do I have? Is it no good after a week?
examples.note: 일주일 지나면 ('if a week passes') probes the boundary; this two-beat structure is natural in real negotiation.

examples.ko: A: 선물할 건데요, 혹시 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? / B: 14일 이내에 영수증 있으시면 가능해요.
examples.romanization: A: seonmulhal geondeyo, hoksi myeochil ane hwanbulhaeya dwaeyo? / B: 14il inaee yeongsujeung isseusimyeon ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm buying this as a gift — within how many days must it be refunded? / B: Within 14 days, with the receipt.
examples.note: A's 선물할 건데요 explains why the window matters; B's reply gives the standard Korean policy formula — 14일 이내, 영수증.

expressions.nuance: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? is 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불하다 ('to refund') + -아야 되다 ('have to / must'). The core grammar -아/어야 되다 expresses obligation or a deadline: 'within how many days must the refund be done?'. 안에 ('within') takes a time noun directly: 일주일 안에, 14일 안에, 한 달 안에. Korean stores typically allow returns within 7 or 14 days (7일/14일 이내), so knowing this is genuinely practical. The dividing line from 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? ('how long is the refund period?') is angle: 며칠 안에 …해야 돼요? frames it as your obligation/deadline, while 환불 기간 asks for the policy window as a plain fact — both yield the same answer. Two spelling traps for English speakers: 며칠 ('how many days', one word) is often misspelled 몇 일 even by native speakers; the correct spelling is 며칠 — write it as one word. Second: 안에 ('within') and 안 ('not') look similar but are entirely different — 며칠 안에 = 'within how many days'; 안 would negate a verb. The obligation ending is 돼요 (from 되다), not 해요, so 환불해야 돼요?, not 환불해야 해요? (though -아야 하다 is also used in formal contexts).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 몇 일 안에.
The question word for 'how many days' is written 며칠, one word — not 몇 일. So it's 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?.
Confusing 안에 ('within') with 안 ('not').
안에 sets a time/space frame ('within'); 안 negates a verb. 며칠 안에 = 'within how many days'; 며칠 안 환불해요 would be nonsense.
Saying 환불해야 해요? with the wrong helper.
The obligation pattern here is -아야 되다: 환불해야 돼요? Both 돼요 and 해요 exist for -아야, but for this set deadline question 환불해야 돼요? is the natural choice.

structuredNuance.t: 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불해야 ('must refund') + 돼요? → 'within how many days must the refund happen?'. Frames it as your obligation/deadline — subtly implying you want to comply, which is politer than demanding to know if you can still get one.

Ask at point of purchase, not when you already have a problem. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Gifts and online orders especially warrant this question. If you've missed the window, it's better to ask 지금도 환불 가능한가요? ('is a refund still possible?') rather than this form.

며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (deadline as obligation) vs 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? (window as fact) vs 언제까지 환불 가능해요? (cutoff date). All three ask for the same information from different angles — 며칠 안에 is the most natural spoken form.
-아야 되다 transfers: 교환해야 돼요? (exchange deadline), 반품해야 돼요? (return deadline). Also: 며칠 이내예요? ('within how many days?', shorter). The time noun slot: 며칠 / 일주일 / 14일 / 한 달.

두 함정: (1) 며칠 spelling — the correct form is 며칠, NOT 몇 일; even many native speakers misspell this. (2) 안에 vs 안 — 안에 = 'within' (a time/space frame); 안 = 'not' (negation). They look similar but are unrelated.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to return this".
expressions.explanation: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 (igeo banpumhago sipeoyo) means "I'd like to return this". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 반품하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to return this"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; sending an item back (esp. online orders)
반말, to a friend or casual seller
반품하려고요 ('intending to return it'), softer announcement
반품 신청 ('return application'), the online/app step

examples.en: I'd like to return this.
examples.note: In a physical store, stating your purpose clearly at the start; staff will then guide you through the process.

examples.ko: 온라인에서 샀는데 반품하고 싶어요. 어떻게 해요?
examples.romanization: ollaineseo sanneunde banpumhago sipeoyo. eotteoke haeyo?
examples.en: I bought it online — I'd like to return it. How do I do that?
examples.note: 온라인에서 샀다 ('bought online') is key context since the process (app, courier) differs from in-store.

examples.ko: A: 네, 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 마음에 안 들어서 반품하고 싶은데, 택배비는 누가 내요?
examples.romanization: A: ne, eotteoke osyeosseoyo? / B: maeume an deureoseo banpumhago sipeunde, taekbaebineun nuga naeyo?
examples.en: A: How can I help you? / B: I don't like it and want to return it — who pays the shipping?
examples.note: B immediately asks the critical online-return question: 택배비 누가 내요? ('who pays shipping?'). The answer depends on 단순 변심 (buyer pays) vs 불량 (seller pays).

expressions.nuance: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 is 이거 ('this') + 반품 ('returning goods', Sino-Korean 返品) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is specifically the act of sending the product back — the physical/logistical return — which then results in a 환불 (refund) or sometimes 교환 (exchange). This word dominates online shopping, where you 반품 신청 ('file a return request') through an app and arrange for a courier pickup. The three-way distinction: 반품 = give the goods back physically; 환불 = get your money back; 교환 = swap for another item. They're related but not interchangeable: saying 환불하고 싶어요 when the agent needs to arrange a courier pickup can confuse things. For online 단순 변심 ('simple change of mind') returns you pay return shipping 택배비; for 불량 ('defect') returns the seller typically pays — always ask 택배비는 누가 내요?. Don't confuse 반품 with 반납 ('returning something borrowed or rented', like a library book or a rental car) — you 반품 a purchase but 반납 a rental. For in-store, 반품 works, but people often just say 환불해 주세요 directly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 환불 when you mean sending the item back.
환불 is the money refund; the act of returning the goods is 반품. For online orders especially, say 반품하고 싶어요, then sort out the 환불.
Confusing 반품 (return a purchase) with 반납 (return a rental/borrowed item).
반품 is for goods you bought; 반납 is for things you borrowed or rented (books, equipment). Don't say 반납하고 싶어요 for a store purchase.
Forgetting to ask about 택배비 (shipping) on online returns.
For 단순 변심 ('change of mind') the buyer usually pays return shipping; for 불량 ('defect') the seller does. Ask 택배비는 누가 내요? when you say 반품하고 싶어요.

structuredNuance.t: 반품(返品) = 'returning goods' + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is the logistics of sending the product back — it's the first step; 환불 (money) or 교환 (replacement) is the result. Dominant in online commerce; in-store people often skip to 환불해 주세요.

Use when the item actually needs to go back — especially for online orders where a courier must be arranged. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Online: 반품 신청하다 (apply through the app). In-store: 반품하고 싶어요 or 환불해 주세요. Always ask 택배비 누가 내요? for online returns.
반품하고 싶어요 (send the item back, logistics) vs 환불해 주세요 (get money back) vs 교환하고 싶어요 (swap for different item). 반품 ≠ 반납 — 반납 is for borrowed/rented items (도서관 책 반납, 렌터카 반납).
반품하고 싶어요 → 반품하려고요 (softer announcement) → 반품 신청할게요 ('I'll file a return request', online). Lead-in: 단순 변심인데 반품하고 싶어요 / 불량인데 반품하고 싶어요 (state reason, as it affects shipping cost).

'Return' maps to both 반품 and 환불 in English — but they are different steps in Korean. 반품 is the physical return; 환불 is the money. Mixing them can cause confusion. Also: 반납 (return a rental/borrowed item) ≠ 반품 (return a purchase). For 단순 변심 online returns, you (the buyer) pay 택배비.

expressions.english: Can I get a refund even without the receipt?
expressions.shortExplanation: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refund even without the receipt?".
expressions.explanation: "Can I get a refund even without the receipt?" — that is 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? (yeongsujeung eopsido hwanbuldwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? ("Can I refund it even without the receipt?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Can I refund it even without the receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; checking the no-receipt case
반말, to a friendly seller

usagePhrases.en: Is there no refund without a receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Phrased as 'won't it work without one?'

usagePhrases.en: Do I absolutely need the receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Asking directly if the receipt is mandatory

examples.en: Can I get a refund even without the receipt?
examples.note: When you've lost or thrown away the receipt; the -도 ('even') acknowledges you know it's normally required.

examples.en: I lost the receipt — can I still get a refund?
examples.note: 영수증을 잃어버리다 ('lost the receipt') explains the situation upfront, making the follow-up question less awkward.

examples.ko: A: 영수증 있으세요? / B: 카드로 샀는데 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? 카드 내역 있잖아요.
examples.romanization: A: yeongsujeung isseuseyo? / B: kadeuro sanneunde yeongsujeung eopsido hwanbuldwaeyo? kadeu naeyeok itjanayo.
examples.en: A: Do you have the receipt? / B: I paid by card — can I refund without the receipt? There's a card record.
examples.note: B pivots to 카드 내역 (card transaction record) as an alternative to the receipt — this often works and is a genuinely useful tactic.

expressions.nuance: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? is 영수증 ('receipt') + 없이 ('without', the adverb derived from 없다) + -도 ('even/also') + 환불돼요? ('is a refund possible?'). The key element is 없이도 — 없이 means 'without', and -도 adds 'even', so together it asks 'is a refund possible EVEN without the receipt?'. The -도 is crucial: it implicitly acknowledges you know the receipt is normally required, which is more face-saving and polite than just asking as if the rule doesn't exist. Because Korean stores usually require 영수증, knowing alternatives is practically important: a card purchase (카드 결제) leaves a 카드 내역 (card transaction record) that can often substitute. The dividing line from 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요? is framing: 없이도 …돼요? hopefully asks 'can it still be done?', while 없으면 …안 돼요? pessimistically asks 'is it impossible without one?' — both are polite, 없이도 sounds more constructive. The English-speaker error is forming 'without' with a clunky negative clause like 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? — the clean adverb is 없이. Dropping -도 (영수증 없이 환불돼요?) is fine but slightly loses the 'even/acknowledging the norm' nuance.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? for 'without the receipt'.
That's clumsy. The clean way to say 'without' is the adverb 없이: 영수증 없이(도) 환불돼요?.
Confusing 없이 (without) with 없으면 (if there isn't).
없이 = 'without' (adverb); 없으면 = 'if there's none' (conditional). Both work but differ: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? vs. 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요?.
Forgetting you paid by card.
A card purchase leaves a 카드 내역 that can stand in for the receipt. Mention 카드로 샀어요 — it often unlocks a refund even 영수증 없이.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 + 없이 ('without', adverb of 없다) + 도 ('even') + 환불돼요? → 'even without the receipt, is a refund possible?'. The -도 politely signals you know the receipt is normally required — you're asking about the exception, not ignoring the rule.

When you've lost the receipt or it was a gift. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Strengthen your case by mentioning your payment method: 카드로 샀어요, 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? — card records often substitute. Don't use 반말 with staff.
없이도 …돼요? (constructive: 'can it still be done?') vs 없으면 …안 돼요? (pessimistic: 'is it impossible?') vs 영수증 꼭 있어야 돼요? ('is the receipt absolutely required?'). All three are polite; choose based on tone.
없이도 환불돼요? → 없이도 교환돼요? → 없이도 반품돼요?. Add alternatives: 카드 내역으로 가능해요? ('is the card record enough?'), 앱 구매 내역으로 가능해요? ('can the app purchase history work?').

없이 (adverb: 'without') is the clean form — don't substitute 안 가지고 ('without bringing'). Dropping -도 gives 영수증 없이 환불돼요? which is fine but loses the face-saving 'even though I know it's needed' nuance that -도 carries.

expressions.english: I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)
expressions.shortExplanation: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)".
expressions.explanation: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (geunyang hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo) = "I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 ("I'd just like a refund"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declining exchange, wanting money back
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: A refund, not an exchange, please
usagePhrases.note: 교환 말고 ('not an exchange') makes the contrast explicit

usagePhrases.en: Could I possibly get a refund?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, tentative with -ㄹ 수 있을까요

examples.en: I'd just like a refund.
examples.note: Said when staff offer an exchange but you want money back; 그냥 keeps the refusal gentle.

examples.en: Never mind the exchange — I'd just like a refund.
examples.note: 교환은 됐다 ('I'm done with the exchange [idea]') politely closes off the staff's alternative offer;됐다 here means 'no thanks, that's enough' not 'it worked'.

examples.ko: A: 교환해 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 환불받고 싶어요. 교환 말고요.
examples.romanization: A: gyohwanhae deurilkkayo? / B: aniyo, geunyang hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo. gyohwan malgoyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I arrange an exchange? / B: No, I'd just like a refund. Not an exchange.
examples.note: B uses 그냥 + 교환 말고요 together — the double-emphasis politely but unmistakably insists on money, not a replacement.

expressions.nuance: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 is 그냥 ('just/simply') + 환불받다 ('to receive a refund', 환불 + 받다 'receive') + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). The 그냥 does crucial social work: it signals 'just / never mind the alternatives', which is how you politely decline a pushy exchange offer without sounding aggressive. Korean staff often steer you toward 교환 (exchange) or store credit first, and 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 gently but firmly insists on money back. Note the giver/receiver verb distinction: 환불받다 (receive a refund, customer's perspective) vs 환불해 주다 / 환불하다 (issue a refund, staff's action); as the customer wanting your money returned, 환불받고 싶어요 is the natural form — 환불해 주고 싶어요 ('I want to give a refund') reverses the roles. The dividing line from bare 환불해 주세요 is softness: adding 그냥 frames it as 'I'd simply prefer a refund', de-escalating — useful when staff push back. For maximum clarity, combine: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요. The English-speaker error is omitting 그냥 and repeating a flat 환불해 주세요 under pressure, which can sound confrontational.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불해 주고 싶어요 to mean 'I want a refund'.
환불해 주다 is to GIVE a refund (the staff's action). As the customer receiving money, say 환불받고 싶어요.
Dropping 그냥 when declining an exchange.
Without 그냥, repeating 환불해 주세요 can sound blunt under pressure. 그냥 softens it to 'I'd simply prefer a refund' while staying firm.
Assuming a refund is automatic over an exchange.
Staff often push 교환 or store credit first. Be explicit: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 ('not an exchange — just a refund').

structuredNuance.t: 그냥 ('just, simply') + 환불받다 ('receive a refund') + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). 그냥 is the softener that says 'I'm not being difficult — I simply want my money back'. It de-escalates a potentially tense pushback.
Used when staff offer 교환 (exchange) or 적립금 (store credit) but you want cash/card credit back. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Appropriate with any staff. Combine with 교환 말고 for emphasis: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.

그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (soft, declining alternatives) vs 환불해 주세요 (direct request, no implicit decline of alternatives) vs 교환 말고 환불해 주세요 (explicit contrast). 환불받다 (customer receives) ≠ 환불해 주다 (staff gives) — don't swap the verb.
그냥 환불받고 싶어요 → 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 → 적립금 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (declining store credit). Softer: 그냥 환불받을 수 있을까요?

두 함정: (1) 환불해 주고 싶어요 reverses the roles — 해 주다 = 'give', so you'd be saying 'I want to give a refund'. Say 환불받고 싶어요 (receive). (2) Dropping 그냥 when declining an exchange makes 환불해 주세요 sound blunt under pressure; 그냥 keeps it gentle.

expressions.shortExplanation: 안 쓴 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "It's unused".
expressions.explanation: 안 쓴 거예요 (an sseun geoyeyo) means "It's unused". Say it as one set phrase — for example 안 쓴 거예요 ("It's unused"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; assuring staff the item wasn't used
반말, to a friend or casual seller
한 번도 ('not even once') for stronger emphasis

usagePhrases.en: I didn't even open the packaging
usagePhrases.note: 포장 안 뜯다 ('didn't tear the wrapping'), the strongest proof

examples.en: This is unused.
examples.note: Reassuring staff during a return so they accept it; the adnominal construction describes the item's condition, not just your past action.

examples.ko: 택도 안 뗐고 안 쓴 거예요.
examples.romanization: taekdo an ttetgo an sseun geoyeyo.
examples.en: The tag's still on and it's unused.
examples.note: 택 안 떼다 ('tag not removed') is physical, verifiable proof; stacking it with 안 쓴 거예요 makes a much stronger case.

examples.ko: A: 왜 반품하시려고요? / B: 선물 받았는데 저한테 안 맞아서요. 안 쓴 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: wae banpumhasiryeogoyo? / B: seonmul badanneunde jeohante an majaseoyo. an sseun geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: Why do you want to return it? / B: I received it as a gift but it doesn't suit me. It's unused.
examples.note: B's 선물 받았다 explains the absence of a receipt; 안 쓴 거예요 confirms the item's condition, which together is the best case for a gift return.

expressions.nuance: 안 쓴 거예요 is 안 ('not') + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'to use') + 거예요 ('it is the thing that…'), literally 'it's a not-used thing' → 'it's unused'. 쓰다 here means 'to use' (쓰다 is polysemous: also 'to write', 'to wear glasses/hat', 'to be bitter' — context disambiguates; with a product it clearly means 'use'). This phrase matters because Korean return policies hinge on condition: 미개봉 (unopened packaging), 미사용 (unused), 택 그대로 (tag intact) all strengthen your claim. The dividing line: 안 쓴 거예요 is the everyday spoken form of the formal 미사용 (未使用) printed in policies; 포장 안 뜯었어요 ('packaging not opened') and 택 안 뗐어요 ('tag not removed') are even more concrete and persuasive. The English-speaker error is reaching for the perfect tense and saying 안 사용했어요 — that's fine as 'I didn't use it', but to DESCRIBE the item as unused, the adnominal form 안 쓴 거예요 is more native. The critical verb-confusion trap: 쓰다 'use' vs 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 means 'something I didn't buy' (the opposite of helpful). Also, the past adnominal of 쓰다 is simply 쓴 (not 쓰은), so 안 쓴 거예요, never 안 쓰은 거예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 쓰은 거예요.
The past adnominal of 쓰다 is 쓴, not 쓰은. Say 안 쓴 거예요.
Confusing 쓰다 'use' with 사다 'buy'.
안 쓴 거 = unused; 안 산 거 = not bought. To say the item is unused, it's 안 쓴 거예요, not 안 산 거예요.
Thinking 'unused' alone guarantees a return.
Stores also check 택 (tag), 포장 (packaging), and time limits. Reinforce with 택도 안 뗐어요 / 포장도 안 뜯었어요 alongside 안 쓴 거예요.

structuredNuance.t: 안 + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'use') + 거예요 ('it's the thing that…') → 'it's an unused thing'. The adnominal form describes the ITEM's condition, not just your past action — more natural than the plain-past 안 썼어요 in this context.

Essential to say during any return to confirm the item's condition. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Back it up with physical evidence: 택도 안 뗐어요 (tag on), 포장도 안 뜯었어요 (packaging sealed). Staff will often check before accepting.
안 쓴 거예요 (spoken, describes item) vs 미사용 제품이에요 (formal, label language) vs 한 번도 안 썼어요 (emphasizes how often: 'not even once'). Stack for impact: 포장도 안 뜯었고 안 쓴 거예요 ('packaging intact and unused').
안 쓴 거예요 → 한 번도 안 썼어요 → 포장도 안 뜯었어요 → 택도 안 뗐어요. Formal: 미사용 상태예요. The past adnominal is 쓴 (not 쓰은): 안 쓴 거예요.
두 함정: (1) 쓰다 'use' vs 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 = 'something I didn't buy', not 'unused'. (2) Adnominal form: 쓰다 → 쓴 (not 쓰은). Say 안 쓴 거예요, never 안 쓰은 거예요.

expressions.english: I bought it not long ago
expressions.shortExplanation: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is a practical expression meaning "I bought it not long ago".
expressions.explanation: "I bought it not long ago" — that is 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 (san ji eolma an dwaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ("I bought it not long ago"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I bought it not long ago
usagePhrases.note: Polite; stressing the purchase was recent
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: It's only been a few days
usagePhrases.note: 며칠 ('a few days') pins it down more
Naming the exact day, the most concrete version

examples.ko: 이거 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: igeo san ji eolma an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I bought this not long ago.
examples.note: Establishing you're within the return window — the first thing staff mentally calculate when you walk in.

examples.ko: 산 지 얼마 안 됐는데 벌써 고장 났어요.
examples.romanization: san ji eolma an dwaenneunde beolsseo gojang nasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought it recently and it's already broken.
examples.note: 벌써 ('already') highlights how premature the failure is, implying it's a quality issue, not normal wear.

examples.ko: A: 언제 구매하셨어요? / B: 산 지 일주일도 안 됐어요. 영수증도 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: eonje gumaehasyeosseoyo? / B: san ji iljuildo an dwaesseoyo. yeongsujeungdo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: When did you buy it? / B: It hasn't even been a week. I have the receipt too.
examples.note: B answers the staff's standard question precisely (일주일도 안 됐어요 = 'not even a week') and proactively adds 영수증도 있어요 — the two things staff always need.

expressions.nuance: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 산 (past adnominal of 사다 'to buy') + 지 (bound noun marking elapsed time SINCE an action) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much has become' → 'not long has passed'). The construction -ㄴ 지 + time + 되다 is the standard Korean way to say 'it's been [time] since I did X': 산 지 일주일 됐어요 = 'it's been a week since I bought it'. 얼마 안 됐어요 means 'not much time has passed', i.e. 'it was recent'. This is crucial to establish because refund/exchange eligibility depends on the purchase date, and staff will ask 언제 사셨어요? ('when did you buy it?'). The dividing line from 어제 샀어요 ('I bought it yesterday') is precision: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is vaguer ('recently'), while naming the day is more concrete and convincing if you're close to the deadline. Two traps: the 지 marking elapsed time is written with a SPACE (산 지), unlike the connective -는지 ('whether', written attached: 샀는지); confusing them changes the meaning. Also: don't say 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 — time passing uses 되다, not 하다. And it must be the past adnominal 산 (not 사는 지, present), because the buying is complete.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 산지 (no space) or confusing it with -는지.
The elapsed-time 지 is a separate bound noun, spaced: 산 지. The connective -는지 ('whether') is different: 샀는지 몰라요 means 'I don't know whether I bought it'.
Saying 산 지 얼마 안 했어요.
Time passing uses 되다, not 하다: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not long has passed'). 안 했어요 is wrong here.
Using the wrong tense: 사는 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
The purchase is finished, so use the past adnominal 산: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요, not 사는 지.

structuredNuance.t: 산 (past adnominal of 사다) + 지 (elapsed-time noun) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has become') → 'not long has passed since I bought it'. The -ㄴ 지 되다 construction is the standard 'it's been X time since' frame. Staff use this to assess whether you're in the return window.

Say this the moment you approach the counter — it's the first data point staff need. 해요체 (polite-neutral). If you know the exact date, name it (어제 산 거예요, 이틀 전에 샀어요) for a more convincing case. Pair with 영수증 여기 있어요 for maximum impact.
산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 (vague 'recently') vs 산 지 며칠 안 됐어요 ('only a few days') vs 어제 산 거예요 (exact day, most concrete). More precise is more persuasive when you're near the deadline.
-ㄴ 지 되다 with time: 산 지 일주일 됐어요 / 산 지 이틀 됐어요 / 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요. Stress: 산 지 일주일도 안 됐어요 ('not even a week'). The -도 adds 'not even', intensifying the recency claim.
두 함정: (1) 산지 (no space) vs 산 지 (space required — this 지 is a separate bound noun). 산지 merged is wrong. (2) 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 is wrong — elapsed-time uses 되다, not 하다: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요.

expressions.english: It was already like this when I got it
expressions.shortExplanation: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 is a practical expression meaning "It was already like this when I got it".
expressions.explanation: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 (badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo) = "It was already like this when I got it". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 ("It was like this from when I got it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: It was like this from when I got it
usagePhrases.note: Polite; insisting the fault wasn't your doing

usagePhrases.en: It was like this when I got it
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: It was like this from the start
usagePhrases.note: 처음부터 ('from the beginning'), a simpler version

usagePhrases.en: I'm not the one who did it
usagePhrases.note: Stating directly that it wasn't your fault

examples.en: It was already like this when I got it.
examples.note: Defending against the implicit assumption you caused the damage — 받았을 때부터 pins the fault to before you ever touched it.

examples.ko: 저 안 떨어뜨렸어요. 받았을 때부터 이랬어요. 사진도 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeo an tteoreotteuryeosseoyo. badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo. sajindo isseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't drop it — it was like this when I got it. I have photos too.
examples.note: 안 떨어뜨렸다 ('didn't drop it') heads off the most common counter-accusation; 사진도 있어요 offers the decisive evidence.

examples.ko: A: 이거 고객님이 사용하시다가 그러신 거 아닌가요? / B: 아니요, 박스 열자마자 봤는데 받았을 때부터 이랬어요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo gogaengnimi sayonghasidaga geureosin geo aningayo? / B: aniyo, bakseu yeoljamaja bwanneunde badasseul ttaebuteo iraesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Isn't this damage from how you used it? / B: No — I noticed it the moment I opened the box. It was like this when I got it.
examples.note: This is the most realistic dispute scenario: A's 사용하시다가 그러신 거 아닌가요? is the staff deflection; B counters with 박스 열자마자 ('the instant I opened the box'), the strongest possible claim of pre-existing fault.

expressions.nuance: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 is 받다 ('to receive/get') + -았을 때 ('at the time when [past action completed]') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 (contracted past of 이렇다 'to be like this'). It means 'it was already like this from the very moment I received it'. This is the line you use when staff suspect you caused the damage and you need to insist the fault is pre-existing (not 사용자 과실, 'user's fault'). Proving it's pre-existing is what secures a free refund or exchange, as opposed to a repair cost being charged to you. 이랬어요 is the contracted spoken past of 이렇다 (이러했어요 → 이랬어요); attempting 이렇었어요 is wrong. The dividing line from 처음부터 이랬어요 ('it was like this from the beginning') is specificity: 받았을 때부터 pins it to the exact moment of receipt — especially powerful for online orders where there's a delivery record — while 처음부터 is a looser 'from the start'. The English-speaker error is tense mismatch: 받을 때 이래요 (present tense on both verbs) misses that both the receiving and the state are past. Another pitfall is the confrontational route of saying 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault') — stating facts (받았을 때부터 이랬어요) is calmer, harder to argue with, and more persuasive.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 받을 때 이래요 (present tense).
Both the receiving and the condition are in the past: 받았을 때 ('when I received it') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). Present tense misses that it was already faulty.
Trying to say 이랬어요 as 이렇었어요.
이렇다 contracts in the past to 이랬어요 (from 이러했어요), not 이렇었어요. Use 이랬어요.
Leading with 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault').
That's confrontational. Stating the fact — 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 — makes the same point more calmly and is harder to argue with, especially with 사진 (photos).

structuredNuance.t: 받았을 때 ('at the time I received it') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). 'From the very moment I got it, it was in this state.' 부터 anchors the fault before you, ruling out user damage — that's the legal/practical force of this phrase.

Used when staff challenge whether you caused the damage. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Point at the defect as you speak. Strengthen with 사진도 있어요 (unboxing photos) or 박스 열자마자 봤어요 ('I saw it the moment I opened the box'). Never drop to 반말 with staff, even under frustration.

받았을 때부터 이랬어요 (pinned to moment of receipt — strong for online delivery) vs 처음부터 이랬어요 ('from the beginning' — vaguer, works for any purchase) vs 제가 그런 거 아니에요 ('I didn't do it' — direct but confrontational). Factual > accusatory.

이랬어요 (contracted form, natural) — don't say 이렇었어요. Add evidence: 박스 열자마자 이랬어요 / 사진 찍어 뒀어요 ('I took photos'). For online orders: 배송받자마자 확인했는데 이랬어요 ('I checked as soon as it arrived and it was like this').

두 함정: (1) Tense — both the receiving and the state are past: 받았을 때 + 이랬어요, NOT 받을 때 이래요 (present). (2) 이랬어요 is the correct contracted past; 이렇었어요 is wrong. Also: 제 잘못 아니에요 is confrontational — stating facts is more persuasive.

expressions.shortExplanation: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please process the refund".
expressions.explanation: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 (hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo) means "Please process the refund". Say it as one set phrase — for example 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 ("Please process the refund"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking staff to carry out the refund
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: Could you process the refund, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요

usagePhrases.en: I'd appreciate it if you'd process the refund
usagePhrases.note: Very polite/formal, useful in writing or to a manager

examples.en: Please process the refund.
examples.note: Once the reason is accepted and the details are confirmed — this is the final execution step, asking them to push it through.

examples.ko: 확인되셨으면 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: hwagindoesyeosseumyeon hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: If you've confirmed everything, please process the refund.
examples.note: 확인되셨으면 ('if/once you've checked') acknowledges the staff's verification step and moves the conversation forward.

examples.ko: A: 네, 환불 가능하세요. 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 카드 취소로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: ne, hwanbul ganeunghaseyo. eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: kadeu chwisoro hwanbul cheori jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Yes, a refund is possible. How would you like to proceed? / B: Please process it as a card cancellation.
examples.note: B specifies 카드 취소 (card cancellation) — the correct channel for card purchases — ensuring the staff process it to the right account.

expressions.nuance: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 처리 ('processing/handling', Sino-Korean 處理) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Adding 처리 makes it about completing the administrative action — running the card cancellation, logging the return in the system — rather than just the concept of a refund. This is the natural register at a service desk where the refund is a procedure. The 좀 cushions the request and is almost always present in spoken Korean requests. The dividing line from bare 환불해 주세요 is stage: 환불해 주세요 works at any point ('please refund me'), while 환불 처리를 해 주세요 specifically says 'please execute the refund now' — you use it once the reason is accepted. 처리 is productive and transfers: 교환 처리 (process the exchange), 취소 처리 (process the cancellation), A/S 처리 (handle after-sales service). The particle: it's 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요 — 처리 is the object of 하다 — not 환불 처리가 해 주세요. The English-speaker error is treating 처리 as optional formality and either over-formalizing in a tiny shop (where 환불해 주세요 is warmer) or being too casual at a department-store counter (where 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 fits better). Always state the refund method (카드 취소 / 현금).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불 처리가 해 주세요.
처리 is the object of 하다, so it takes 를 (often dropped), not 가: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요.
Over-formalizing in a tiny shop.
At a small market stall, 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 can sound stiff. A warm 환불해 주세요 fits better; save 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 for service desks and counters.
Not stating the refund method.
Refunds go back by the original method (카드 결제 → 카드 취소). Say 카드 취소로 / 현금으로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 so it's done correctly.

structuredNuance.t: 환불 + 처리(處理, 'processing/handling') + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The addition of 처리 shifts the request from the concept of a refund to the execution of a procedure. Use it once everything is agreed — this is the 'now do it' step.

At a service desk or customer center once the refund eligibility is confirmed. 해요체 (polite-neutral). For a tiny market stall, 환불해 주세요 is warmer. For a department-store service desk or writing to customer service: 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 / 환불 처리해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.

환불 처리 해 주세요 (execute the refund now, procedural) vs 환불해 주세요 (general request, any stage). 처리 is productive: 교환 처리 (exchange), 취소 처리 (cancellation), 반품 처리 (return). Mention method: 카드 취소로 처리해 주세요 / 현금으로 처리해 주세요.
환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 → 환불 처리 좀 해 주시겠어요? → 환불 처리 부탁드려요 → 환불 처리해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (most formal/written). Add method: 카드 취소로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.

두 함정: (1) 환불 처리가 해 주세요 is wrong — 처리 is the object: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요. (2) Over-formalizing: in a casual market 처리 sounds stiff; save it for service desks. Also: always state the refund method (카드 취소 / 현금) so it's processed correctly.

expressions.english: So you're saying this can't be refunded?
expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? is a practical expression meaning "So you're saying this can't be refunded?".
expressions.explanation: "So you're saying this can't be refunded?" — that is 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? (igeo hwanburi an doendagoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? ("So this can't be refunded?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; pushing back / confirming a refusal
반말, to a friend or casual seller

usagePhrases.en: Do you mean it can't be refunded?
usagePhrases.note: Very polite, honorific 말씀 + 이세요
Asking directly for the reason

examples.en: Sorry? This can't be refunded?
examples.note: 네? (rising intonation: 'sorry?') + the echo signals genuine surprise; it politely forces the staff to re-explain rather than simply accepting the refusal.

examples.en: Even though it's defective, it can't be refunded?
examples.note: 불량인데도 ('even though it's defective') names the concrete reason why the refusal seems unreasonable; this kind of pushback often prompts a manager referral.

examples.ko: A: 세일 상품은 환불이 안 됩니다. / B: 그럼 교환은 되는데 환불이 안 된다고요?
examples.romanization: A: seil sangpumeun hwanburi an doemnida. / B: geureom gyohwaneun doeneunde hwanburi an doendagoyo?
examples.en: A: Sale items cannot be refunded. / B: So an exchange is fine but no refund?
examples.note: B doesn't argue with the policy directly but clarifies the exact scope of the refusal — this is a smart pivot that often reveals an exchange option you hadn't been offered.

expressions.nuance: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불이 안 되다 ('a refund isn't possible') + -다고요? (a quotative ending that echoes back the other person's statement with rising intonation). The -다고요? is the core of this phrase: it repeats what was just said to confirm or gently challenge it — 'you're telling me…?' — and is the polite, non-aggressive way to push back when a store refuses. The rising intonation signals surprise/disbelief without accusation, which often prompts staff to re-explain or escalate to a manager. The dividing line from 왜 안 돼요? ('why not?') is tone: 안 된다고요? mirrors their own words and sounds like incredulous confirmation rather than a demand, keeping the exchange civil while making clear you're not satisfied. To go fully polite (e.g. to a manager), use 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? ('are you saying it can't be refunded?', with honorific 말씀). The English-speaker error is dropping the quotative and saying 환불 안 돼요? again — that just re-asks the yes/no question and loses the 'wait, are you telling me that…' pushback force. The final 요 is non-negotiable: 환불 안 된다고? without 요 is 반말 and sounds confrontational or rude to staff. Particle: 환불이 안 돼요 (subject 이/가), never 환불을.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Re-asking 환불 안 돼요? instead of echoing.
That just repeats the plain question. To push back / confirm a refusal, use the quotative echo: 환불이 안 된다고요? ('you're saying it can't be refunded?').
Dropping the 요: 환불 안 된다고?.
Without the final 요, -다고 is 반말 and sounds curt or confrontational to staff. Keep it polite: 환불이 안 된다고요?.
Using 환불을 안 돼요.
되다 takes the subject particle: 환불이 안 돼요 / 환불이 안 된다고요?. 환불을 is wrong with 되다.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 환불이 안 된다 ('a refund is not possible') + -고요? (quotative echo, rising). Literally: 'you're saying a refund is not possible for this?' The -다고요? is a polite echo-back frame, not a new question — it signals surprise and invites re-explanation or escalation.

When staff refuse a refund and you want to push back without escalating. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — the 요 is essential. Upgrade to 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? (honorific 말씀) when addressing a manager. Never drop to 반말 with staff even under frustration.

-다고요? (echo-back, polite disbelief/confirmation) vs 왜 안 돼요? (direct demand for reason) vs 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? (fully honorific version). -다고요? is the most tactically useful: it keeps tone calm while clearly not accepting the refusal.
-다고요? is versatile: 교환도 안 된다고요? / 영수증 있어도 안 된다고요?. Escalate: 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? → 담당자분을 불러 주시겠어요? ('could you get the person in charge?'). Always include 요 with staff.

두 함정: (1) Re-asking 환불 안 돼요? just restates the question — it loses the 'wait, are you telling me that…' pushback force of -다고요?. (2) Dropping 요: 환불 안 된다고? (no 요) is 반말 and rude to staff. Always keep 요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 잘하시네요 is a practical expression meaning "You're really good at this!".
expressions.explanation: 잘하시네요 (jalhasineyo) means "You're really good at this!". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘하시네요 ("you're good at it (admiring)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: honorific -시-, to someone you respect
banmal, to a friend
-는데요 adds a surprised, leaning-in tone
진짜 boosts the admiration

examples.en: A: (showing a painting) / B: Wow, you're really talented!
examples.note: the bare admiring reaction to a skill on display right now

examples.ko: 요리 한 입 먹고 "어머, 요리 잘하시네요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: yori han im meokgo "eomeo, yori jalhasineyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: After one bite I said, 'Oh my, you're a wonderful cook.'
examples.note: complimenting a host's cooking mid-experience — the -시- signals upward respect

examples.ko: 한국어로 인사하니까 직원분이 "한국말 진짜 잘하시네요" 하고 놀랐어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoro insahanikka jigwonbuni "hangungmal jinjja jalhasineyo" hago nollasseoyo.
examples.en: When I greeted in Korean the staff was surprised: 'Your Korean is really good.'
examples.note: the go-to compliment Koreans give learners; respond modestly with 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요 — not 감사합니다 alone

expressions.nuance: 잘하시네요 is the present-tense 'you're good at this' said WHILE observing or experiencing someone's skill — 잘하다 'to be good at doing' + honorific -시- + the noticing ending -네요 ('oh, I notice'). Unlike 잘했어요, which judges a finished result, 잘하시네요 praises ABILITY in the moment. Because -시- and -네요 are baked in, it safely aims upward or sideways — toward an elder, a stranger, a host. The English-speaker pitfall is double: dropping the -시- (so 잘하네 alone to an elder is too casual), and treating the ubiquitous 한국말 잘하시네요 as a literal assessment of fluency — it is really a warm social icebreaker, and agreeing proudly with 네, 잘해요 sounds arrogant; the right reply is modest deflection such as 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요. Register: 잘하네 (banmal) ↔ 잘하네요 (polite) ↔ 잘하시네요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering 한국말 잘하시네요 with 네, 감사합니다 and a proud face — Korean modesty expects 아니에요 / 아직 멀었어요; agreeing sounds boastful.
Saying 잘하네 to someone older — the bare -네 is banmal; toward a senior you need the honorific 잘하시네요.
Using 잘했어요 when you mean present skill — 잘했어요 judges a finished act, while admiring live ability is 잘하시네요.

structuredNuance.t: 잘하다 = 'to do well' + -시- (honorific) + -네요 ('I notice'). Literally 'I notice you do it well (respectfully).' In use, it is a present-tense admiration of live skill — 'you're really good at this' — aimed at what you are watching or tasting right now.

Say it while watching or experiencing a skill: a host's cooking, a colleague's calligraphy, a learner's pronunciation. With -시- it is safe toward elders and strangers. To a close friend, trim to 잘하네. The famous 한국말 잘하시네요 to a foreign speaker is social warmth, not a grammar report.

The dividing line from 잘했어요: 잘했어요 judges a past completed act ('you did well'), while 잘하시네요 notices present ability ('you're good at this'). Against 대단하시네요: 잘하시네요 credits a specific skill; 대단하시네요 expresses broad awe at a person's achievement or character.
Register: 잘하네 (banmal) → 잘하네요 (polite) → 잘하시네요 (honorific). Intensify with 진짜/정말: 진짜 잘하시네요. The variant -는데요 ending (잘하시는데요) adds a surprised, leaning-in admiration.

Two traps: (1) using 잘하네 to an elder (too casual — add -시-); (2) responding to 한국말 잘하시네요 with 네, 감사합니다 and a proud nod — Korean modesty convention expects 아니에요 or 아직 멀었어요; accepting the compliment openly reads as boastful.

expressions.shortExplanation: 예뻐요 is a practical expression meaning "It's pretty / You're lovely.".
expressions.explanation: 예뻐요 (yeppeoyo) = "It's pretty / You're lovely.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 예뻐요 ("it's pretty / you're pretty"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -으시-, to an older woman
exclamatory -다, admiring something out loud

examples.ko: A: (새 옷 입고) 어때요? / B: 우와, 너무 예뻐요!
examples.romanization: A: (sae ot ipgo) eottaeyo? / B: uwa, neomu yeppeoyo!
examples.en: A: (in new clothes) How does it look? / B: Wow, it's so pretty!
examples.note: the bare compliment on someone's outfit or appearance

examples.ko: 꽃다발 받고 "꽃이 너무 예쁘다" 하면서 좋아했어요.
examples.romanization: kkotdabal batgo "kkochi neomu yeppeuda" hamyeonseo joahaesseoyo.
examples.en: Getting the bouquet I said happily, 'The flowers are so pretty.'
examples.note: everyday: 예쁘다 covers objects — flowers, rooms, handwriting — not just people

examples.ko: 아기 사진 보고 "어머, 정말 예뻐요" 했더니 엄마가 좋아했어요.
examples.romanization: agi sajin bogo "eomeo, jeongmal yeppeoyo" haetdeoni eommaga joahaesseoyo.
examples.en: After seeing the baby photo I said, 'Oh, so adorable,' and the mom was delighted.
examples.note: real situation: 예쁘다 for cute babies is a safe, warm compliment to a parent — much safer than complimenting a stranger's own face

expressions.nuance: 예뻐요 means 'pretty / lovely / adorable' and applies to people, clothes, flowers, babies, handwriting — anything visually pleasing or cute. The base 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular: drop 으 and add 어요 → 예뻐요 (never 예쁘어요). The three-way split learners miss: 예쁘다 = pretty/lovely, 귀엽다 = cutely endearing (puppies, a giggling toddler), 멋있다 = cool/impressive — a strong, handsome man is 멋있어요, not 예뻐요, as the latter implies a more feminine, delicate beauty. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation (writing 예쁘어요) and aiming compliments at strangers: in Korean, commenting on a stranger's face unprompted can feel forward, so 예뻐요 lands most warmly on friends, children, and objects; complimenting an outfit is less invasive than a face. Register: 예뻐 (banmal) ↔ 예뻐요 (polite) ↔ 예쁘세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating it 예쁘어요 — 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular, so 으 drops before 어요: the correct form is 예뻐요.
Calling a cool, manly guy 예뻐요 — it implies pretty/feminine; use 멋있어요 for cool or handsome men.
Complimenting a stranger's face with 예뻐요 out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim it at friends, kids, or objects, or compliment an outfit instead.

structuredNuance.t: 예쁘다 literally means 'pretty / beautiful (in a gentle, lovely way).' In use, it covers any visually pleasing thing: a person's face, a dress, a flower arrangement, neat handwriting. The prettiness it describes leans feminine and delicate rather than bold or impressive.

Freely used for objects, clothes, flowers, and children. For people, it is warmest between friends or toward younger people. Complimenting a stranger's face directly can feel forward; complimenting their outfit (그 옷 예뻐요) is less intrusive. For elders, soften with 예쁘세요.

Three-way split: 예쁘다 (pretty/lovely, people/things), 귀엽다 (cute/endearing, puppies, toddlers, something charming), 멋있다 (cool/impressive, bold actions, stylish men). A strong man is 멋있어요, not 예뻐요; a puppy is 귀여워요, not 예뻐요 — though 예쁘다 can stretch to puppies colloquially.
Irregular conjugation: 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (not 예쁘어요), 예뻐, 예쁘세요. Intensify with 너무/진짜/정말: 너무 예뻐요, 진짜 예뻐. Exclamatory: 진짜 예쁘다 (said to yourself).

Two traps: (1) conjugating it 예쁘어요 — the 으-irregular drops 으, giving 예뻐요; (2) complimenting a stranger's face out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim 예뻐요 at friends, kids, or objects, or comment on an outfit rather than physical features.

expressions.shortExplanation: 대단하세요 is a practical expression meaning "You're amazing / That's really impressive.".
expressions.explanation: 대단하세요 (daedanhaseyo) means "You're amazing / That's really impressive.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 대단하세요 ("you're amazing (respectful)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: honorific -세요, to someone you admire
banmal, to a friend
-시네요 adds fresh admiration upon noticing
정말 deepens the awe

examples.ko: A: 마라톤 완주했어요! / B: 와, 대단하세요!
examples.romanization: A: maraton wanjuhaesseoyo! / B: wa, daedanhaseyo!
examples.en: A: I finished the marathon! / B: Wow, that's amazing!
examples.note: the bare awe-reaction to an impressive achievement

examples.ko: 혼자 아이 셋 키운다는 말에 "진짜 대단하세요" 하고 감탄했어요.
examples.romanization: honja ai set kiundaneun mare "jinjja daedanhaseyo" hago gamtanhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Hearing she raises three kids alone I said, 'You're truly remarkable.'
examples.note: everyday: admiring someone's endurance or effort over a long period

examples.ko: 사장님이 맨손으로 회사를 일으킨 얘기를 듣고 "정말 대단하십니다" 했어요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimi maensoneuro hoesareul ireukin yaegireul deutgo "jeongmal daedanhasimnida" haesseoyo.
examples.en: Hearing the CEO built the company from nothing I said, 'That is truly remarkable, sir.'
examples.note: real situation: the formal -십니다 form for a respected senior; 대단하다 fits whole-life achievements

expressions.nuance: 대단하세요 expresses genuine AWE at someone's achievement, effort, or character — 대단하다 'to be remarkable' + honorific -세요. It is heartfelt admiration for something impressively hard ('I could never do that'), which is why its default form already points upward with -세요. The dividing line from 잘하시네요 is scale: 잘하시네요 praises a specific SKILL ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses being overwhelmed by the WHOLE accomplishment or person ('that's incredible'). The English-speaker pitfall is the bare 대단해 toward an elder — natural between friends, but to a senior it sounds flippant; use 대단하세요 or formal 대단하십니다. A subtler trap: 대단하다 can flip to sarcasm with a flat tone ('oh, wonderful...'), so deliver it with clear warmth. Register: 대단해 (banmal) ↔ 대단해요 (polite) ↔ 대단하세요 / 대단하십니다 (honorific/formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 대단해 to an elder or boss — the bare banmal can sound flippant; admire a senior with 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다.
Using 대단하세요 for a minor everyday compliment — it carries real awe, so reserve it for genuinely impressive feats, not 'nice shoes'.
Delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, wonderful'); say it with clear warmth so it lands as praise.

structuredNuance.t: 대단하다 literally means 'to be great/remarkable' (not from a 한자 compound most learners recognize). In use, it conveys genuine awe — 'I'm blown away by what you did or who you are.' The honorific -세요 is the default because the expression naturally points at someone admirable.

Use it for genuinely impressive feats — raising three children alone, building a company from scratch, finishing a marathon at 70. It aims naturally upward or sideways. Toward an elder or boss use 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다. The banmal 대단해 is warm between friends but sounds flippant to a senior.

대단하세요 vs 잘하시네요: 잘하시네요 praises a skill ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses awe at a whole accomplishment ('incredible'). Against 존경스러워요 ('I respect/admire you'): 존경스럽다 is more formal reverence toward a person's overall stature; 대단하다 reacts to a specific feat.
Register: 대단해 (banmal) → 대단해요 (polite) → 대단하세요 (honorific) → 대단하십니다 (formal). Noticing variant: 대단하시네요. Intensified: 정말/진짜 대단하세요.

Two traps: (1) saying bare 대단해 to an elder — use 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다; (2) delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, how wonderful...'), so lean into warm delivery. Also: reserve it for genuinely impressive things; using it for minor tasks (nice soup!) dilutes it.

expressions.english: Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!
expressions.shortExplanation: 화이팅 is a practical expression meaning "Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!".
expressions.explanation: "Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!" — that is 화이팅 (hwaiting). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 화이팅 ("go for it / you got this"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: go for it / you got this
usagePhrases.note: casual cheer, any close relationship
the officially correct Korean spelling, same word and meaning
polite -하세요 toward someone you respect
rallying a group together before a shared challenge

examples.ko: A: 나 이제 면접 보러 가! / B: 화이팅!
examples.romanization: A: na ije myeonjeop boreo ga! / B: hwaiting!
examples.en: A: I'm off to my interview! / B: Go get 'em!
examples.note: the bare one-word cheer just before a challenge — often with a raised fist gesture

examples.ko: 시험 앞둔 친구한테 "내일 시험 화이팅!" 하고 메시지 보냈어요.
examples.romanization: siheom apdun chinguhante "naeil siheom hwaiting!" hago mesiji bonaesseoyo.
examples.en: I texted my friend, 'Good luck on tomorrow's exam!'
examples.note: everyday: the standard pre-exam text; you can add 너 할 수 있어 for extra encouragement

examples.ko: 마라톤 나가는 선배께 "선배님, 화이팅 하세요!" 하고 응원했어요.
examples.romanization: maraton naganeun seonbaekke "seonbaenim, hwaiting haseyo!" hago eungwonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Since my senior was running a marathon I cheered, 'Go for it, sunbae!'
examples.note: real situation: add 하세요 to make the cheer politely address someone older — bare 화이팅 alone to a much older person is too light

expressions.nuance: 화이팅 (borrowed from English 'fighting') is Korea's universal pre-effort cheer — 'go for it, you've got this, I believe in you' — shouted before exams, interviews, games, or any challenge, often with a raised fist. By itself it is casual and friendly; toward someone you respect, attach a verb: 화이팅 하세요. The dividing line is against 힘내세요: 화이팅 pumps up ENERGY before an effort that has not started yet ('push!'), while 힘내세요 comforts someone who is already in the middle of a struggle ('hang in there'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: never read it as 'let's fight' — it was borrowed purely as encouragement; and the bare 화이팅 in a formal or very hierarchical setting feels too light, so use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다. Spelling note: 파이팅 is the officially standardized form, but 화이팅 is what most Koreans actually write.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight / I'll fight you' — it is borrowed to mean encouragement ('go for it'), never literal fighting.
Shouting bare 화이팅 at a senior in a formal setting — soften it to 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다.
Assuming 파이팅 is wrong — it is actually the standardized spelling; both are accepted, with 화이팅 more common in casual writing.

structuredNuance.t: 화이팅 looks like the English word 'fighting' but it was borrowed purely as an encouragement cheer — 'go for it / push hard / I believe in you.' There is no aggression implied. Think of it as Korea's 'allez' or 'vamos': pure forward energy.

Ideal before any challenge: an exam, a job interview, a first day at work, a sports match, a presentation. Between friends and peers, bare 화이팅 is perfect. To a senior or in a formal setting, attach a verb: 화이팅 하세요. There is no honorific form of the cheer-noun itself — politeness rides on the attached verb.

화이팅 vs 힘내세요: 화이팅 fires before the effort starts ('go!'), while 힘내세요 comforts someone already struggling ('hang in there'). Against 잘될 거예요: that reassures about the outcome ('it'll be fine'), while 화이팅 charges up the person's energy.

Both spellings are accepted: 화이팅 (common casual writing) and 파이팅 (official standard). Polite form: 화이팅 하세요. Group cheer: 우리 화이팅! Combo: 화이팅, 잘할 수 있어! Written online as 핫팅 or 팅 (very informal shorthand).

Two traps: (1) reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight' or 'I'll fight you' — it is borrowed encouragement, not aggression; (2) shouting bare 화이팅 at a much older person or in a formal setting — it feels too light; use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다 instead.

expressions.english: It'll work out / Things will be fine.
expressions.shortExplanation: 잘될 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "It'll work out / Things will be fine.".
expressions.explanation: 잘될 거예요 (jaldoel geoyeyo) means "It'll work out / Things will be fine.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘될 거예요 ("it'll work out fine"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, reassuring a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -시-, reassuring an elder
다 'all' makes the comfort broader and warmer

examples.ko: A: 합격할 수 있을까요? / B: 물론이죠, 잘될 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: hapgyeokal su isseulkkayo? / B: mullonijyo, jaldoel geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: Do you think I'll pass? / B: Of course — it'll work out.
examples.note: the bare reassurance about an uncertain outcome — 물론이죠 adds confidence

examples.ko: 걱정하는 친구한테 "너무 걱정 마, 다 잘될 거야" 했어요.
examples.romanization: geokjeonghaneun chinguhante "neomu geokjeong ma, da jaldoel geoya" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my worried friend I said, 'Don't worry too much, everything will work out.'
examples.note: everyday: pairs naturally with 너무 걱정 마 — one phrase addresses the worry, the other addresses the outcome

examples.ko: 수술을 앞두신 분께 "분명히 잘되실 거예요. 제가 응원할게요" 하고 위로했어요.
examples.romanization: susureul apdusin bunkke "bunmyeonghi jaldoesil geoyeyo. jega eungwonhalgeyo" hago wirohaesseoyo.
examples.en: To someone facing surgery I said, 'It will surely go well. I'm rooting for you.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 잘되실 거예요 for a senior + 응원할게요 for deeper comfort

expressions.nuance: 잘될 거예요 ('it will go well', 잘되다 'to turn out well' + future -ㄹ 거예요) reassures an anxious person about a FUTURE OUTCOME — a test result, a job application, a surgery, a new relationship. It calms worry about how things will turn out, which is its clear dividing line from 힘내세요 (strength for the present struggle) and 화이팅 (energy for the effort itself). The three smooth stacking: 너무 걱정 마세요 → 잘될 거예요 → 응원할게요. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: 잘되다 is intransitive 'turn out well', so 잘될 거예요 ≠ 잘할 거예요 ('will perform well' — active doer). Also the spelling: it is 거예요, never 꺼에요 or 거에요. To an elder, add honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요. Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) ↔ 잘될 거예요 (polite) ↔ 잘되실 거예요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘할 거예요 to comfort someone — that means 'will perform well' (active doer); the reassurance about how things turn out is 잘될 거예요 (intransitive).
Spelling the ending 잘될 꺼에요 / 거에요 — the standard future form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.
Using bare 잘될 거야 to an elder — add the honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요.

structuredNuance.t: 잘되다 = 'to turn out well' (intransitive — things go well by themselves). 잘될 거예요 = 'it will turn out well.' In use, it is the 'don't worry, it'll be fine' reassurance about an outcome the listener is anxious about — not a promise about their performance, but about how things will unfold.

Use it when someone is anxious about a result or outcome: an exam result, a job interview, a medical procedure, starting over. It looks FORWARD to how things will resolve. To a peer or younger person: 잘될 거예요. To an elder: 잘되실 거예요 (with honorific -시-). Banmal to close friends: 잘될 거야.

잘될 거예요 (outcome: 'it'll turn out fine') vs 힘내세요 (strength for the current struggle: 'hang in there') vs 화이팅 (energy pump-up for the effort: 'go for it'). These three layer beautifully: 힘내세요, 화이팅, 잘될 거예요 — covering the present, the push, and the outcome.
Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) → 잘될 거예요 (polite) → 잘되실 거예요 (honorific). Warmer: 다 잘될 거예요, 분명히 잘될 거예요. Stacks with: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요.

Two traps: (1) confusing 잘될 거예요 (things will turn out well — intransitive) with 잘할 거예요 (you/I will perform well — active doer); the verbs are different; (2) misspelling the future as 꺼에요 or 거에요 — the standard written form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 너무 걱정 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Don't worry too much.".
expressions.explanation: "Don't worry too much." — that is 너무 걱정 마세요 (neomu geokjeong maseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 너무 걱정 마세요 ("don't worry too much"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite -세요, to a peer or someone you respect
banmal, to a close friend
the uncontracted form — identical meaning, slightly softer and more careful
reassurance plus a concrete offer — far more comforting than the phrase alone

examples.ko: A: 일이 잘못될까 봐 불안해요 / B: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: iri jalmotdoelkka bwa buranhaeyo / B: neomu geokjeong maseyo, jaldoel geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm anxious it'll go wrong / B: Don't worry too much — it'll work out.
examples.note: the bare reassurance; stacking with 잘될 거예요 is the natural complete comfort phrase

examples.ko: 시험 걱정하는 동생에게 "너무 걱정 마, 충분히 준비했잖아" 했어요.
examples.romanization: siheom geokjeonghaneun dongsaengege "neomu geokjeong ma, chungbunhi junbihaetjana" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my anxious younger sibling I said, 'Don't worry — you've prepared enough, haven't you?'
examples.note: everyday: comfort in banmal, grounded with a reminder of their effort

examples.ko: 환자 보호자분께 "너무 걱정 마세요. 최선을 다하겠습니다" 하고 안심시켰어요.
examples.romanization: hwanja bohojabunkke "neomu geokjeong maseyo. choeseoneul dahagetseumnida" hago ansimsikyeosseoyo.
examples.en: To the patient's guardian I said, 'Please don't worry. We will do our very best,' as reassurance.
examples.note: real situation: professional reassurance, softened with 너무, followed by a commitment — the formula in medical or care settings

expressions.nuance: 너무 걱정 마세요 means 'don't worry too much' — 너무 'too (much)' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't.' The 너무 is essential: without it, bare 걱정 마세요 is correct but can sound slightly blunt ('stop worrying'), while 너무 softens it to 'don't worry SO much', acknowledging the concern is understandable. Grammatically, 마세요 is the polite prohibitive of 말다, not 안 + verb; the common English-learner error 안 걱정하세요 is wrong. The dividing line from 잘될 거예요 is direction: 걱정 마세요 addresses the WORRY itself ('ease up on the fretting'), while 잘될 거예요 addresses the OUTCOME ('it'll be fine') — they pair beautifully and almost always appear together. Register: 걱정 마 (banmal) ↔ 걱정 마세요 (polite) ↔ 걱정 마십시오 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Forming the negative as 안 걱정하세요 — a prohibition uses 말다: 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요, never 안 + verb here.
Saying bare 걱정 마 to an elder or boss — use 걱정 마세요 or 걱정 마십시오.
Confusing 걱정 마세요 (address the worry) with 잘될 거예요 (address the outcome) — natural comfort uses both together.

structuredNuance.t: 너무 'too much' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't' = 'please don't worry too much.' The 너무 is a softener — it acknowledges the person's concern is understandable, it just asks them not to worry EXCESSIVELY. Without 너무, the phrase is fine but a touch more direct.

Use it when someone is clearly anxious about an outcome, situation, or decision. Polite -세요 works for peers and can be used toward seniors who are worried. Banmal 걱정 마 is warm for friends. In professional settings (medical, legal, service), 걱정 마세요 + a commitment (제가 도와드릴게요 / 최선을 다하겠습니다) is a complete, reassuring phrase.

걱정 마세요 (target: the worry — 'ease up') vs 잘될 거예요 (target: the outcome — 'it'll be fine'). Natural pair: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요. Against 괜찮아요 ('it's okay / don't worry'): 괜찮아요 is shorter and more all-purpose; 걱정 마세요 specifically addresses an anxious person's ongoing worry.
Prohibitive forms: 걱정 마 (banmal) → 걱정 마세요 (polite) → 걱정 마십시오 (formal). Full uncontracted: 걱정하지 마세요. With 너무: 너무 걱정 마세요. Softer still: 너무 걱정하지 않으셔도 돼요.

Two traps: (1) building the prohibition with 안: 안 걱정하세요 is wrong; use 말다 → 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요; (2) using bare 걱정 마 with an elder or in a serious context — 걱정 마세요 is the right polite form, and for real formality, 걱정 마십시오.

expressions.shortExplanation: 자랑스러워요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm proud (of you).".
expressions.explanation: 자랑스러워요 (jarangseureowoyo) = "I'm proud (of you).". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 자랑스러워요 ("I'm proud of you"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend or child
격식 -습니다, a speech, award ceremony, or formal note
네가 identifies the person you're proud of — natural in banmal

examples.ko: A: 저 전국 1등 했어요! / B: 우와, 정말 자랑스러워요!
examples.romanization: A: jeo jeonguk 1deung haesseoyo! / B: uwa, jeongmal jarangseureowoyo!
examples.en: A: I came in first in the whole country! / B: Wow, I'm so proud of you!
examples.note: the bare expression of pride at a remarkable achievement

examples.ko: 졸업식 날 딸에게 "우리 딸, 진짜 자랑스러워" 했어요.
examples.romanization: joreopsing nal ttarege "uri ttal, jinjja jarangseureowo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: On graduation day I told my daughter, 'I'm so proud of you, my girl.'
examples.note: everyday: a parent's pride in banmal toward a child — the most natural direction for this expression

examples.ko: 후배가 큰 상을 받았을 때 "네가 우리 팀의 자랑이야. 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
examples.romanization: hubaega keun sangeul badasseul ttae "nega uri timui jarangiya. jeongmal jarangseureowo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: When the junior won a major award I said, 'You're our team's pride. I'm truly proud of you.'
examples.note: real situation: pairs with 자랑이야 ('you're our pride/glory') for a fuller compliment; senior → junior direction

expressions.nuance: 자랑스러워요 ('to feel proud', from 자랑 'pride/boasting' + -스럽다 'to feel like') expresses pride in someone's achievement or in who they are. The DIRECTION rule is crucial and uniquely Korean: pride flows DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a senior to a junior, or between peers. Telling a teacher, boss, or elder 자랑스러워요 sounds odd and presumptuous, as if you are positioned above them evaluating their worth; toward a respected senior, 존경스러워요 ('I admire/respect you') or 대단하세요 is far more natural. The dividing line: 자랑스럽다 (pride, looking down or across) vs 존경스럽다 (respect, looking up). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this cultural gap — English 'I'm proud of you' is freely said to anyone, including a teacher, so learners aim 자랑스러워요 at their Korean tutor and it lands awkwardly. Note the ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요. Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) ↔ 자랑스러워요 (polite) ↔ 자랑스럽습니다 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자랑스러워요 to a teacher, boss, or elder — pride implies a higher position; toward a senior use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요.
Conjugating it 자랑스럽어요 — 자랑스럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스러워요.
Confusing 자랑스럽다 (proud of someone) with 자랑하다 (to boast/show off) — 자랑하지 마 means 'don't brag', a different sense of 자랑.

structuredNuance.t: 자랑 means 'something one boasts about with pride.' -스럽다 means 'to feel like, to be full of.' So 자랑스럽다 = 'feels like something to be proud of / makes me feel proud.' In practice, it says 'I'm proud of you' — the speaker's internal feeling of pride at someone else's achievement.

Crucially flows DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a teacher to a student, a senior to a junior, or between close peers. Do NOT say it upward to a teacher or boss — it implies you are positioned above them. To an elder you admire, use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요 instead.

자랑스럽다 (pride, pointing downward/sideways) vs 존경스럽다 (respect/admiration, pointing upward). Confusingly similar: 자랑스럽다 (I feel proud OF someone) vs 자랑하다 (to brag/show off — 자랑하지 마 = 'don't brag', a negative sense of 자랑).
ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요 (not 자랑스럽어요). Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) → 자랑스러워요 (polite) → 자랑스럽습니다 (formal). Intensify: 정말/진짜 자랑스러워요, 네가 자랑스러워.

The English-speaker pitfall is the direction rule — English 'I'm proud of you' is used freely toward anyone including a teacher or boss. In Korean, 자랑스러워요 upward at a senior sounds presumptuous ('I'm proud of you' implies you are grading them from above). Say 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요 instead.

expressions.english: That looks nice / It's good to see.
expressions.shortExplanation: 보기 좋아요 is a practical expression meaning "That looks nice / It's good to see.".
expressions.explanation: 보기 좋아요 (bogi joayo) means "That looks nice / It's good to see.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 보기 좋아요 ("it looks nice / good to see"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: it looks nice / good to see
usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: you look great / it's lovely to see (respectful)
usagePhrases.note: honorific -으시-, noticing tone, to an elder
-네요 adds a warm, observational noticing tone

examples.ko: A: (커플 사진을 보여주며) / B: 와, 두 분 정말 보기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: (keopeul sajineul boyeojumyeo) / B: wa, du bun jeongmal bogi joayo.
examples.en: A: (showing a couple photo) / B: Wow, you two really look great together.
examples.note: the warm approval of a wholesome scene — not just prettiness, but a good-to-witness sight

examples.ko: 살 빠진 친구한테 "얼굴도 좋아 보이고 보기 좋다" 했어요.
examples.romanization: sal ppajin chinguhante "eolguldo joa boigo bogi jota" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend who lost weight I said, 'Your face looks well, and you look good.'
examples.note: everyday: 보기 좋다 approves a healthier, happier appearance — wholesome rather than merely pretty

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만난 두 분이 사이좋게 계셔서 "두 분 보기 좋으시네요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane mannan du buni saijoke gyesyeoseo "du bun bogi joeusineyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: Seeing the two of them getting along so warmly, I said, 'It's truly lovely to see you two together.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 보기 좋으시네요 toward elders, expressing warm approval of their relationship or wellbeing

expressions.nuance: 보기 좋아요 (보다 'to see' + -기 nominalizer + 좋다 'good' = 'good to look at') is the warm 'that looks nice / it's heartwarming to see' you say about a pleasing or wholesome sight — a happy couple, someone glowing with health, people getting along beautifully, a tidy home. It often carries APPROVAL of a wholesome scene rather than just visual prettiness, which is its dividing line from 예뻐요 (purely visual prettiness) and 멋있어요 (cool/impressive): 보기 좋다 = 'this is a beautiful thing to witness.' The English-speaker pitfall is the fixed structure: learners try 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기, but the correct nominalized form is 보기 좋다. Also, 보기 좋아요 ('nice to see') differs from 좋아 보여요 ('looks good / appears to be in good condition') — the word order is reversed and the meaning shifts. Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) ↔ 보기 좋아요 (polite) ↔ 보기 좋으세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다: 보기 좋아요.
Mixing it up with 좋아 보여요 — 보기 좋아요 = 'nice to see', while 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good/well' (condition); related but not identical.
Using bare 보기 좋아 toward an elder you're complimenting — use the honorific 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋으시네요.

structuredNuance.t: 보기 = 'the act of seeing' (보다 'see' + -기 nominalizer); 좋아요 = 'is good.' Literal: 'the seeing of it is good' = 'it's good to look at.' In use, it is the warm 'looks nice / heartwarming to see' — applies to wholesome scenes, not just visual beauty.

Use it when a scene or person gives you a warm, positive feeling: a happy couple, someone looking healthy, two friends getting along, a nicely arranged space. It is warmer and more approving than just 예뻐요. To an elder, use 보기 좋으시네요. Between friends, bare 보기 좋아 feels natural and genuine.

보기 좋아요 vs 예뻐요: 예뻐요 says the thing itself is pretty; 보기 좋아요 says it is good/wholesome to witness. Against 좋아 보여요: 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good (in condition/health)' — reversed word order, different meaning. Against 멋있어요: 멋있어요 = cool/impressive; 보기 좋아요 = heartwarming/wholesome to see.
Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) → 보기 좋아요 (polite) → 보기 좋으세요 (honorific). Noticing tone: 보기 좋네요, 보기 좋으시네요. For two people: 두 분 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋아요.

Two traps: (1) restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다, with 보기 (nominalizer) first; (2) confusing it with 좋아 보여요 — the reversed word order shifts the meaning from 'nice to see' to 'looks to be in good condition'; they are related but not interchangeable.

expressions.english: I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)
expressions.shortExplanation: 부러워요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)".
expressions.explanation: "I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)" — that is 부러워요 (bureowoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 부러워요 ("I'm so envious"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday warm way to say you wish you had what someone has
반말, said freely to a friend
Half-to-yourself exclamation; the most natural spoken form, even around elders
완전 ('totally') boosts the warmth — common in chat messages

examples.ko: A: 다음 주에 제주도 가요! / B: 와, 진짜요? 부러워요!
examples.romanization: A: daeum jue jejudo gayo! / B: wa, jinjjayo? bureowoyo!
examples.en: A: I'm going to Jeju next week! / B: Wow, really? I'm so jealous!
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the natural warm reaction to good news; 진짜요? adds genuine surprise

examples.ko: A: 집이 회사랑 걸어서 5분이에요. / B: 아… 너무 부럽다.
examples.romanization: A: jibi hoesarang georeoseo 5bunieyo. / B: a… neomu bureopda.
examples.en: A: My place is five minutes' walk from work. / B: Ahh… I'm so jealous.
examples.note: 반말 mutter 부럽다 as pure wistful reaction — the most natural everyday form

examples.ko: 휴가 간다고요? 진짜 부러워요. 저는 방학이 없어서요.
examples.romanization: hyuga gandagoyo? jinjja bureowoyo. jeoneun banghagi eopseoseoyo.
examples.en: You're going on vacation? I'm really jealous — I don't get time off.
examples.note: Adding your own situation (저는 방학이 없어서요) makes the envy sound sincere, not bitter

expressions.nuance: 부러워요 comes from the adjective 부럽다 ('to be envious'), and it captures the GOOD, warm kind of envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Koreans say it constantly as a friendly compliment on good news: a trip, a new phone, a five-minute commute. It is never hostile. Keep it far from 질투 / 질투하다 ('jealousy'), which is the dark, possessive jealousy of a romantic rival or someone who resents your success — saying 질투나요 to a friend's vacation news sounds creepy or bitter, so 부러워요 is the safe everyday choice. For register: 부러워요 is polite, 부러워 is 반말, and 부럽다 is the bare adjective exclamation Koreans mutter even around elders — because the plain-form exclamatory 다 functions like thinking aloud rather than 반말 aimed at someone. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle and direction: you do NOT say 당신을 부러워요 ('I envy YOU' with an object) — mark what is envied with 이/가 (가방이 부러워요 'I envy your bag', 네가 부러워 'I envy you/your situation'), or simply say 부러워요 about the whole thing. A look-alike trap: 부럽다 ('envious') vs. 부끄럽다 ('shy/embarrassed') — they share 부 but are opposite-feeling words.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 질투나요 to react to a friend's good news.
질투 is dark, possessive jealousy (a love rival, resentment). Friendly 'lucky you' envy is 부러워요. 질투나요 to a friend's vacation sounds hostile, not warm.
Marking the person as an object: 너를 부러워.
부럽다 takes the envied thing/situation with 이/가, not a person with 을/를. Say 네가 부러워 ('I envy you/your situation') or just 부러워.
Translating 'I'm jealous OF your car' as 차에 부러워요.
Don't use 에. The envied thing takes 이/가: 차가 부러워요, or simply 부러워요 about the whole thing.

structuredNuance.t: 직역 would be 'I am envious.' But in practice 부러워요 functions as a warm COMPLIMENT — 'lucky you, I wish that were me' — not a statement of bitterness. The feeling is openly shared and affectionate, not hidden or hostile.

Use freely to friends, family, coworkers of similar rank, even casual strangers, whenever you hear good news — a trip, a deal, a short commute. It is the natural warm reaction. 부러워요 is polite-casual; 부러워 is 반말; 부럽다 works as an exclamation even around seniors. Avoid it only when the context is competitive or you're already tense with someone (there 질투 might apply).

vs. 질투(나다): 질투 is dark, possessive jealousy — the resentment of a love rival. Saying 질투나요 to a friend's good news sounds hostile. vs. 부끄럽다: looks similar (부) but means 'shy/embarrassed' — completely different. 부러워요 = warm envy; 부끄러워요 = I'm embarrassed. Keep them separate.

완전 부러워요 ('totally jealous'), 진짜 부러워요 ('really jealous'), 부럽네요 (soft polite observation, '~must say I envy you'), 부러우면 지는 거예요 (joke: 'if you're jealous, you lose'). Name the envied thing with 이/가: 네 휴가가 부러워요.

Do NOT mark the person with 을/를: 너를 부러워요 is wrong. The envied thing/situation takes 이/가: 네가 부러워, 그 가방이 부러워요. Also don't confuse 부럽다 ('envious') with 부끄럽다 ('embarrassed') — they sound alike but mean opposite things.

expressions.english: I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.
