expressions.shortExplanation: 응원할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.".
expressions.explanation: 응원할게요 (eungwonhalgeyo) = "I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 응원할게요 ("I'll cheer you on"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
격식 -겠습니다, a formal pledge of support

usagePhrases.en: I'll always be rooting for you
usagePhrases.note: 항상 makes it a lasting, ongoing promise — not just for this one event

examples.ko: A: 저 이번에 도전해 보려고요! / B: 응원할게요, 잘할 수 있어요!
examples.romanization: A: jeo ibeone dojeonhae boryeogoyo! / B: eungwonhalgeyo, jalhal su isseoyo!
examples.en: A: I'm going to give it a try this time! / B: I'm rooting for you — you can do it!
examples.note: the bare pledge of personal support, combined with belief in them

examples.ko: 시험 앞둔 친구에게 "내가 응원할게, 분명 잘될 거야" 했어요.
examples.romanization: siheom apdun chinguege "naega eungwonhalge, bunmyeong jaldoel geoya" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend before the exam I said, 'I'm rooting for you — it'll definitely work out.'
examples.note: everyday: banmal support pledge, paired with reassurance — 응원할게 feels like a personal promise

examples.ko: 퇴사하고 창업한다는 선배께 "새로운 도전 진심으로 응원하겠습니다" 하고 인사드렸어요.
examples.romanization: toesahago changeopandaneun seonbaekke "saeroun dojeon jinsimeuro eungwonhagetseumnida" hago insadeuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: To the senior starting a business after leaving I said, 'I sincerely support your new challenge.'
examples.note: real situation: formal 응원하겠습니다 for a serious life step by a senior — the -겠- signals earnest commitment

expressions.nuance: 응원할게요 (應援, 응원 'support/cheering' + -ㄹ게요 'I will, for you') is a personal pledge — 'I'll cheer you on / I'm in your corner' — that promises ongoing backing for someone's effort or challenge. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the key: it is a speaker's promissory 'I commit to this, for your sake', not just a flat prediction, which is the dividing line from 응원할 거예요 ('I will cheer', a neutral future statement). It is also warmer and more committed than 화이팅: 화이팅 is a quick shout in the moment, while 응원할게요 promises you personally will keep backing them over time. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: learners write 응원할께요 (wrong — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요, though pronounced tensely as 께). Register: 응원할게 (banmal) ↔ 응원할게요 (polite) ↔ 응원하겠습니다 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요: 응원할게요 (pronounced with a tense 께 sound but written 게).
Using 응원할 거예요 instead — that is a flat prediction 'I will cheer'; the warm promise to the listener is 응원할게요.
Treating it as identical to 화이팅 — 화이팅 is an in-the-moment shout, while 응원할게요 pledges ongoing, personal support.

structuredNuance.t: 응원 (應援) = 'support, cheering, backing.' -ㄹ게요 = promissory future: 'I will (for you).' So 응원할게요 = 'I commit to rooting for you.' In use, it is a warm personal pledge — 'I've got your back, I'll keep cheering you on' — more than just saying 'good luck.'

Use it when someone is taking on a challenge, starting something new, or needs sustained encouragement: a job change, a hard exam season, a creative project, a difficult relationship. It implies ongoing support, not just a one-time cheer. To peers and younger people: 응원할게요. To a senior or in formal settings: 응원하겠습니다.

응원할게요 (personal ongoing pledge: 'I'll keep rooting for you') vs 화이팅 (immediate in-the-moment cheer: 'go!'). Against 잘될 거예요 (outcome reassurance: 'it'll work out'): these three layer naturally — 화이팅, 응원할게요, 잘될 거예요 — to cover the push, the backing, and the outcome.
Register: 응원할게 (banmal) → 응원할게요 (polite) → 응원하겠습니다 (formal). Durational: 항상 응원할게요, 끝까지 응원할게요. Intensified: 진심으로 응원할게요.

Two traps: (1) spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요 (written 게, though it sounds tense like 께); (2) substituting 응원할 거예요 — that is a flat prediction ('I will cheer') with no warmth or commitment to the listener; 할게요 carries the personal, promissory weight.

expressions.english: It suits you / It looks good on you.
expressions.shortExplanation: 잘 어울려요 is a practical expression meaning "It suits you / It looks good on you.".
expressions.explanation: 잘 어울려요 (jal eoullyeoyo) means "It suits you / It looks good on you.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잘 어울려요 ("it suits you well"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -으시-, to an elder
너무 boosts the compliment — the natural intensifier for this expression

examples.ko: A: (새 안경 쓰고) 어때요? / B: 진짜 잘 어울려요, 완전 잘 맞는 것 같아요!
examples.romanization: A: (sae angyeong sseugo) eottaeyo? / B: jinjja jal eoullyeoyo, wanjeon jal manneun geot gatayo!
examples.en: A: (in new glasses) How is it? / B: It really suits you — looks like it was made for you!
examples.note: the go-to reaction to a new look; 완전 잘 맞는 것 같아요 adds extra warmth

examples.ko: 원피스 입은 친구에게 "그 원피스 색깔이 너랑 진짜 잘 어울려" 했어요.
examples.romanization: wonpiseu ibeun chinguege "geu wonpiseu saekkkari neorang jinjja jal eoullyeo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend in a dress I said, 'That dress color really suits you.'
examples.note: everyday: name the specific item/color + 너랑 잘 어울려 — the natural collocation pattern

examples.ko: 머리 자른 부장님께 "새로 하신 머리 스타일 잘 어울리세요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: meori jareun bujangnimkke "saero hasin meori seutail jal eoulliseyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To the manager with a new haircut I said, 'That new hairstyle suits you well, sir.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 잘 어울리세요 toward a senior's new look — head straight to this form with anyone older

expressions.nuance: 잘 어울려요 (잘 'well' + 어울리다 'to match/go together') is the everyday 'it suits you / it looks good on you' for clothes, glasses, a new haircut, a makeup style, or a color — and the single most natural thing to say when someone shows off a new look. The key dividing line from 예뻐요/멋있어요: 예뻐요 judges the THING itself ('that outfit is pretty'), while 잘 어울려요 says it MATCHES THE PERSON ('that outfit fits you'), which flatters the wearer directly and is why Koreans reach for it constantly as a compliment. The English-speaker pitfall is the grammar: 어울리다 is INTRANSITIVE, so you never attach an object particle; and the natural partner is the particle 랑/이랑/하고 ('goes WITH' the person) — 그 색이 너랑 잘 어울려, not 너를. Also: drop 잘 and bare 어울려요 sounds neutral 'it matches', not a compliment. Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) ↔ 잘 어울려요 (polite) ↔ 잘 어울리세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing 'goes with' you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요.
Dropping 잘 and saying bare 어울려요 — the compliment keeps 잘 ('suits you well'); without it, it sounds like a flat 'it matches'.
Saying 예뻐요 when you mean it flatters the person — 예뻐요 praises the item itself, while 잘 어울려요 says it suits the wearer.
Using bare 잘 어울려 to an elder — raise it to the honorific 잘 어울리세요 when complimenting a senior's outfit or hair.

structuredNuance.t: 잘 = 'well'; 어울리다 = 'to match, go together harmoniously.' 잘 어울려요 literally 'goes together well' — in practice it means 'it suits you / it looks great on you.' The compliment is about the FIT between person and item, not the item in isolation.

Use it when someone tries on or shows off a new outfit, glasses, hairstyle, hair color, or makeup. It is the warmest, most direct compliment on a new look. To peers and younger people: 잘 어울려요. To an elder: 잘 어울리세요. You can also use it for two people who look good together: 두 분 잘 어울리세요.

잘 어울려요 (suits the person — the fit between person and item) vs 예뻐요 (the item itself is pretty, not about the wearer) vs 멋있어요 (it's cool/impressive, not about fit). 어울리다 vs 맞다: 잘 어울려요 is about harmonious matching (style, color); 잘 맞아요 is about physical fit (size).
Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) → 잘 어울려요 (polite) → 잘 어울리세요 (honorific). Intensified: 너무/진짜 잘 어울려요, 완전 잘 어울려. For two people: 두 사람 잘 어울려요.

Two traps: (1) adding an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing goes WITH you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요; (2) dropping 잘 (bare 어울려요 sounds neutral 'it matches' — the warm compliment keeps 잘 'suits you WELL').

expressions.shortExplanation: 남자친구 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have a boyfriend?".
expressions.explanation: "Do you have a boyfriend?" — that is 남자친구 있어요? (namjachingu isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 남자친구 있어요? ("Do you have a boyfriend?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the standard way to ask if someone's taken
반말 + the clipped 남친; among friends or once you're close
Same frame, swap to 여자친구 / 여친
Softer, less direct — 'someone you're meeting' rather than a labeled partner

examples.en: Do you maybe have a boyfriend?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') cushions what would otherwise be a blunt personal question — always add it with strangers

examples.ko: 실례지만 남자친구 있으세요? 소개해 주고 싶은 사람이 있어서요.
examples.romanization: sillyejiman namjachingu isseuseyo? sogaehae jugo sipeun sarami isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry to ask, but do you have a boyfriend? I've got someone I'd like to introduce you to.
examples.note: Honorific 있으세요 + giving a reason makes blind-intro territory feel polite and harmless, not creepy

examples.ko: A: 남자친구 있어요? B: 아니요, 솔로예요. 왜요?
examples.romanization: A: namjachingu isseoyo? B: aniyo, solloyeyo. waeyo?
examples.en: A: Do you have a boyfriend? B: No, I'm single. Why do you ask?
examples.note: The natural A/B exchange; 솔로 (solo, single) is the common self-label, and 왜요 ('why?') is the expected curious reply

expressions.nuance: 남자친구 있어요? is 남자친구 ('boyfriend') + 있다 ('to exist/have') — the everyday way to find out whether someone is romantically taken. Korean uses 있다, never 가지다 ('possess'): 남자친구를 가지고 있어요? sounds like you own a person and will earn puzzled looks. The clipped forms 남친/여친 are ubiquitous in casual speech and texting but sound too breezy in a first polite conversation, so use the full form. The gentler near-synonym 만나는 사람 있어요? ('are you seeing someone?') sidesteps the committed-relationship label and feels less presumptuous — smart when you're hinting at your own interest. Raise the ending to 있으세요? for older or higher-status people. The biggest English-speaker trap is the particle: never 남자친구를 있어요? because 있다 is not a transitive verb — it takes 이/가 or nothing in speech, never 을/를. Even asking the bare question of a near-stranger without cushioning it with 혹시 can feel nosy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 남자친구를 있어요? with the object particle.
있다 ('to have/exist') is not a transitive verb; it takes 이/가 or nothing, not 을/를. Say 남자친구 있어요? (or 남자친구가 있어요?).
Translating 'have a boyfriend' as 남자친구를 가지고 있어요?
가지다 ('to possess') is for objects; using it for a person sounds like ownership. Korean 'has' people and relationships with 있다: 남자친구 있어요?
Confusing 남자친구 with 남자 사람 친구.
남자친구 by default means a romantic boyfriend. A male friend (just a friend) is 남사친 (남자 사람 친구). Saying 남자친구 about a buddy implies you're dating.

structuredNuance.t: 남자친구 ('boyfriend') + 있다 ('to exist/have') — literally 'does a boyfriend exist (for you)?'. Korean frames possession of people with 있다, not 가지다 ('possess objects'). The everyday reading is simply 'are you taken / do you have a boyfriend?'

Safe and natural in polite conversation (존댓말) among peers, but add 혹시 with a near-stranger and give a reason (소개해 주고 싶어서요) to soften it. Use 있으세요? with someone older. The clipped 남친 있어? (반말) is only for close friends. Never ask a coworker or much older acquaintance without a clear reason — it can feel intrusive.

만나는 사람 있어요? ('are you seeing someone?') avoids labeling the relationship and feels less loaded — better when you don't know whether they're attached or you're feeling out the situation. 남자친구 있어요? implies you expect a potential boyfriend label, while 만나는 사람 is a neutral 'is there anyone?'
남자친구 있어요? (neutral polite) → 혹시 남자친구 있으세요? (deferential softened) → 남친 있어? (반말, friends) → 만나는 사람 있어요? (non-labeling softer). The clipped 남친/여친 in texting is standard among friends.

Two particle traps: (1) 남자친구를 있어요? — 있다 is not transitive, it never takes 을/를; use 남자친구 있어요? or 남자친구가 있어요?. (2) 남자친구를 가지고 있어요? — 가지다 ('to hold/possess') is for objects, not people. Both errors mark you as a very early learner.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "What's your type?".
expressions.explanation: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? (isanghyeongi eotteoke dwaeyo?) = "What's your type?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? ("What's your ideal type?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the go-to get-to-know-you question asking what someone finds attractive
반말, among friends gossiping about crushes

usagePhrases.en: What kind of person do you like?
usagePhrases.note: Plainer version, less jargon than 이상형, and slightly more casual

usagePhrases.en: What's your ideal type, may I ask?
usagePhrases.note: Honorific 되세요 for someone older or on a first meeting

examples.ko: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? 저는 유머 있는 사람이요.
examples.romanization: isanghyeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? jeoneun yumeo inneun saramiyo.
examples.en: What's your type? Mine's someone with a sense of humor.
examples.note: Answer with 속성 + 사람 + 이요; 유머 있는 사람 is a natural answer pattern

examples.en: You're totally my type.
examples.note: The compliment form; 완전 ('totally') + 제 이상형 + 이에요 — smooth and direct

examples.ko: A: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? B: 음... 눈이 크고 다정한 사람이요.
examples.romanization: A: isanghyeongi eotteoke dwaeyo? B: eum... nuni keugo dajeonghan saramiyo.
examples.en: A: What's your type? B: Hmm... someone with big eyes and a warm personality.
examples.note: Typical A/B exchange; listing two traits with 고 ('and') is the natural format

expressions.nuance: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요? is 이상형 (理想型, 'ideal type') + 이/가 + 어떻게 돼요 ('how is it?') — the standard question for 'what kind of person are you into romantically?'. The chunk 어떻게 돼요? is the polite, idiomatic Korean frame for asking about personal specifics (name, age, type, job); it's softer than blunt 뭐예요? ('what is it?'), which sounds like reading a form. Don't swap in 이상형이 뭐예요? unless you're already being casual. The contrast: 이상형 is specifically about your romantic ideal and carries a flirty charge, whereas 어떤 사람 좋아해요? ('what kind of person do you like?') is milder and could be asked platonically. 제 이상형이에요 is the compliment — natural and warm; compare with the slangy 타입 (loanword 'type') which younger Koreans use but sounds less standard. Origin note: 이상형 is Sino-Korean 理想型. Particle trap: the expression headword takes 이/가 as subject — 이상형이 어떻게 돼요; don't drop the 이 or mis-attach 을.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'you're my type' literally as 당신은 제 타입이에요.
당신 sounds stiff/confrontational in real speech, and 타입 is slangy. Natural Korean is 완전 제 이상형이에요, dropping the pronoun.
Using 뭐예요 and asking 이상형이 뭐예요? to someone you just met.
It's grammatical but blunt. The polite, idiomatic frame for personal questions is 어떻게 돼요?: 이상형이 어떻게 돼요?
Reading 어떻게 돼요 as 'how does it become'.
As a set phrase it just asks 'what is it / how is it'. 이상형이 어떻게 돼요 means 'what's your type', not 'how does your ideal type become'.

structuredNuance.t: 이상형 ('ideal type', 理想型) + 이 + 어떻게 돼요 (lit. 'how does it turn out?'). The chunk 어떻게 돼요 is a fixed, softened frame Koreans use for personal info questions — think of it as 'and what would that be?'. The whole phrase means 'what kind of person are you into?'

A natural icebreaker over drinks or on a blind date (소개팅); it signals romantic interest without being too forward. Use -어떻게 돼요? with peers; -어떻게 되세요? with someone older. Asking in a work meeting or to a much senior person would be odd unless you're setting up a 소개팅 for them.

이상형이 어떻게 돼요? (specific romantic ideal, slightly loaded) vs. 어떤 사람 좋아해요? (neutral 'what kind of person do you like?', can be platonic). To compliment someone, 제 이상형이에요 is natural and direct; the loanword 제 타입이에요 is also used colloquially but sounds younger/slangy.
이상형이 어떻게 돼요? (polite) → 이상형이 뭐야? (반말) → 이상형이 어떻게 되세요? (deferential). The compliment form: 제 이상형이에요 / 완전 제 이상형이에요.

Replacing 어떻게 돼요 with 뭐예요?: 이상형이 뭐예요? is grammatical but blunt, like demanding an answer. The polite idiomatic frame is 어떻게 돼요. Also don't say 당신은 제 타입이에요 — 당신 sounds confrontational; drop the pronoun and say 완전 제 이상형이에요.

expressions.english: I fell for you at first sight
expressions.shortExplanation: 첫눈에 반했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I fell for you at first sight".
expressions.explanation: 첫눈에 반했어요 (cheonnune banhaesseoyo) means "I fell for you at first sight". Say it as one set phrase — for example 첫눈에 반했어요 ("I fell for you at first sight"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I fell for you at first sight
usagePhrases.note: Polite; a sweet confession of instant attraction

usagePhrases.en: I fell for you at first sight
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a partner or crush you're already comfortable with

usagePhrases.en: I was smitten at one glance
usagePhrases.note: 한눈에 ('in one look') — a near-identical variant, slightly more poetic
완전 ('totally') for emphasis without the 'first sight' framing — can be said later too

examples.ko: 사실 처음 봤을 때 첫눈에 반했어요.
examples.romanization: sasil cheoeum bwasseul ttae cheonnune banhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Actually, the first time I saw you, I fell for you instantly.
examples.note: 처음 봤을 때 ('the first time I saw you') makes the timeline explicit; 사실 softens it as a confession

examples.ko: 그 사람한테 완전 반해서 잠도 안 와요.
examples.romanization: geu saramhante wanjeon banhaeseo jamdo an wayo.
examples.en: I'm so smitten with them I can't even sleep.
examples.note: 반하다 + 한테 marks the target; 잠도 안 와 ('can't even sleep') — intensity collocate

examples.ko: A: 언제부터 좋았어? B: 솔직히 첫눈에 반했어.
examples.romanization: A: eonjebuteo joasseo? B: soljiki cheonnune banhaesseo.
examples.en: A: When did you start liking me? B: Honestly, I fell for you at first sight.
examples.note: Natural A/B where 첫눈에 반했어 is the punchline confession answer

expressions.nuance: 첫눈에 반하다 is 첫눈에 (첫 'first' + 눈 'eye/look' + 에 'at') + 반하다 ('to fall for / be smitten') — the set phrase for instant infatuation, love at first sight. The core verb 반하다 means to be captivated; its target takes 에게/한테 ('by/to'), never 을/를. The form is almost always past — 반했어요, because 반하다 describes a state already entered, so 반했어요 means 'I've fallen for you (and remain so)'. Saying 반해요 in present sounds unfinished or odd. The crucial contrast: 반하다 (the sudden spark, surface attraction) is not yet 좋아하다 ('to like', more intentional) or 사랑하다 ('to love', deep and earned). 첫눈에 / 한눈에 are interchangeable ('first sight' vs. 'one glance'). Careful not to confuse 반하다 ('be smitten') with unrelated homophones, or with 반갑다 ('glad to meet you') — totally different verbs. Register: 반했어요 (polite) makes a beautiful confession line; 반했어 in 반말 with someone close.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 반했어.
반하다 takes 에게/한테 ('to/by'): 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for you'). The one you're smitten by is not a direct object.
Using present 반해요 for the feeling.
반하다 describes a state already entered, so it's normally past: 반했어요 ('I've fallen for you'). Present 반해요 sounds unfinished.
Swapping in 사랑해요 for instant attraction.
사랑하다 is deep, serious love. The sudden crush/smitten feeling is 반하다. 'I fell for you at first sight' is 첫눈에 반했어요, not 첫눈에 사랑했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 첫눈에 = 'at first eye/glance' (첫 first + 눈 eye + 에 at); 반하다 = 'to be captivated, fall for'. Together: 'I was captivated at the first glance' = 'I fell for you at first sight'. It is a fixed idiom — don't decode it piece by piece.

Said as a romantic confession to a crush, a new partner, or retrospectively to a long-term partner ('remember when I fell for you instantly?'). 반했어요 (polite) is a lovely confession line safe even early on; 반했어 is intimate 반말 for someone close. Not used in professional or formal settings.

반하다 (the sudden smitten spark — can be surface-level charm) vs. 좋아하다 ('to like', more deliberate feeling) vs. 사랑하다 ('to love', deep and serious). 첫눈에 반하다 is the spark moment; don't substitute 사랑하다 for this feeling — 첫눈에 사랑했어요 sounds strange. 첫눈에 vs. 한눈에: both mean 'at first sight / at one glance' and are interchangeable.

반하다 → 반했어요 (polite past, most common) / 반했어 (반말 past) / 반해서 (cause: 'because I fell for you...') / 완전 반했어요 (intensified). The present 반해요 is rare; the past is the default because 반하다 marks a state already entered.
Particle error: 반하다 takes 에게/한테 for the target, NOT 을/를 — 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for you'), never 너를 반했어. Also don't confuse 반하다 ('be smitten') with 반갑다 ('glad to meet someone') — completely unrelated.

expressions.shortExplanation: 우리 썸 타는 거야? is a practical expression meaning "Are we, like, a thing?".
expressions.explanation: "Are we, like, a thing?" — that is 우리 썸 타는 거야? (uri sseom taneun geoya?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 우리 썸 타는 거야? ("Are we kind of a thing?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Are we kind of a thing?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; the playful question between two people in the gray zone — half-joking, half-sincere

usagePhrases.en: Are we sort of seeing each other?
usagePhrases.note: Polite version if you're still on 존댓말 with each other
Describing the relationship status to a third party

usagePhrases.en: Are you and them a thing?
usagePhrases.note: Asking a friend about their gray-zone someone; 걔 = 'that person'

examples.ko: 요즘 누구 썸 타는 사람 있어?
examples.romanization: yojeum nugu sseom taneun saram isseo?
examples.en: Are you talking to anyone these days?
examples.note: Friend gossip; 썸 타는 사람 = 'someone you're in the gray zone with' — the standard way to probe

examples.en: We were just in that talking stage and it fizzled out without ever becoming official.
examples.note: 썸만 타다 ('only ever 썸, never went official') + 흐지부지되다 ('fizzle out')

examples.ko: A: 우리 썸 타는 거야? B: 글쎄... 뭐가 되고 싶은데.
examples.romanization: A: uri sseom taneun geoya? B: geulsse... mwoga doego sipeunde.
examples.en: A: So, are we a thing? B: Well... I want us to be something.
examples.note: The classic gray-zone confrontation; 뭐가 되고 싶다 = 'I want us to become something'

expressions.nuance: 썸 타다 is 썸 (from English 'something') + 타다 (lit. 'to ride') — the wildly popular slang for the ambiguous pre-dating stage where two people are clearly interested, flirting, and texting, but no one has confessed or made things official. There is no clean English equivalent; 'talking' or 'situationship' comes close. The verb is locked as 타다 ('ride', the same 타다 as buses): 썸을 타다 is correct, 썸 하다 is not — memorize 썸(을) 타다 as one unit. The crucial line: 썸 타다 is BEFORE official dating, 사귀다 is AFTER the 고백 (confession) and agreement — calling an official couple 썸 타는 사이 implies it's still ambiguous, which could offend. This is casual/young register — never in formal contexts or with older people who may not recognize the term. Pitfall: don't back-translate 'something' as 뭔가; the slang noun is the loanword 썸 itself.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 썸 하다 instead of 썸 타다.
The fixed verb is 타다 ('to ride'): 썸을 타다. 썸 하다 is not how Koreans say it. Memorize the collocation 썸 타다.
Using 썸 타다 for an official couple.
썸 is the stage BEFORE dating. Once you've confessed and agreed, you're 사귀다 ('dating'). Calling a committed couple 썸 implies it's still unofficial.
Translating 'something' word-for-word as 뭔가 타다.
The slang comes from English 'something' but is borrowed as the noun 썸. It's 썸 타다, not 뭔가 타다 or any literal rendering.

structuredNuance.t: 썸 = loanword from English 'something'; 타다 = 'to ride'. Literally 'to ride something'. The actual meaning is the pre-dating ambiguous stage: mutual interest is clear but no one has confessed or committed. Think 'we're in the grey zone' or 'we're talking'.

Said between the two people in the gray zone to half-jokingly name what's happening, or by a third party asking about someone's romantic status. Pure casual/반말 register — you'd never say this to a boss or older relative. Older Koreans may not know the term; it skews under-40.

썸 타다 (pre-official, ambiguous) vs. 사귀다 (officially dating, both parties have agreed). 썸 타다 PRECEDES 사귀다 — asking 우리 사귀어? when you mean 썸 jumps the gun and can make things awkward. 연애하다 ('to date / have a relationship') also implies an established relationship, not the gray zone.

썸(을) 타다 (verb) → 썸 타는 사이 ('a 썸-stage relationship') → 썸남 (썸 stage guy, 썸 + 남자) / 썸녀 (썸 stage girl) → 썸타다가 사귀다 ('go from 썸 to official'). The noun 썸 alone is used freely: 썸인 것 같아 ('I think we're in the 썸 zone').

The verb is fixed as 타다: 썸 하다 is wrong, 썸 타다 is correct. Also never literally render 'something' as 뭔가 (뭔가 타다 is nonsense). And don't use 썸 for an official couple — it implies the relationship is still ambiguous.

expressions.english: Will you go out with me?
expressions.shortExplanation: 우리 사귈래요? is a practical expression meaning "Will you go out with me?".
expressions.explanation: 우리 사귈래요? (uri sagwillaeyo?) = "Will you go out with me?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 우리 사귈래요? ("Want to go out (with me)?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; the classic ask to make it official, safe on 존댓말
반말, once you're close or both young

usagePhrases.en: Let's date / let's be a couple
usagePhrases.note: A statement-style ask, gentle and warm — almost a declaration
Earnest, even humble; 주세요 makes it a heartfelt request

examples.en: I like you. Want to go out?
examples.note: The classic one-two: 고백 (좋아해) immediately followed by the ask — standard structure

examples.en: Today is day one for us.
examples.note: Said the moment someone says yes; Korean couples count from 1일 (day one) and celebrate milestones religiously

examples.ko: A: 저랑 사귀어 주실래요? B: 네, 저도 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: jeorang sagwieo jusillaeyo? B: ne, jeodo joayo.
examples.en: A: Would you please go out with me? B: Yes, I feel the same.
examples.note: Slightly deferential ask with -주실래요? — genuine earnestness in a polite register; B's 저도 좋아요 = 'I like you too'

expressions.nuance: 사귀다 means 'to date / be in a committed relationship', and 우리 사귈래요? is the ritual question that converts 썸 into official couplehood. The ending -ㄹ래요? asks for the listener's willingness ('do you want to?'), exactly the soft, inviting register you want — not a command. The key contrast: 사귀다 (official, labeled, 'boyfriend/girlfriend') vs. 만나다 ('to meet/see' — can mean casual going-out or just meeting up without the committed label). Confessing with 사귀다 is the moment a couple becomes 'official'. After a yes, couples announce 오늘부터 1일 ('day one starts today') and count anniversaries. English-speaker traps: (1) the spelling — 사귀다 → 사귀어요, past 사귀었어요 (NOT 사겨요, an extremely common mistake). (2) The particle: 사귀다 takes the comitative 랑/와 ('with') — 나랑 사귈래? — never the object 을/를. Register note: -ㄹ래요? is warm and friendly; move to 사귈래? only once you're already using 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing/saying 사겨요 instead of 사귀어요.
사귀다 keeps the 위: present polite is 사귀어요. 사겨요 is a frequent misspelling. Conjugate it as 사귀어요, 사귀었어요.
Using 만나다 to mean 'be my official partner'.
만나다 ('to meet/see') is vaguer and can mean casual dating or just meeting up. To ask for a committed relationship, use 사귀다: 우리 사귈래요?
Attaching 을/를: 너를 사귈래?
사귀다 takes the comitative 랑/와 ('with'), not the object 을/를. Say 나랑 사귈래? ('go out WITH me?'), not 너를 사귈래?

structuredNuance.t: 우리 ('we/us') + 사귀다 ('to make friends, to socialize with → to date in romantic sense') + -ㄹ래요? ('want to?'). Literal reading: 'Do we want to go together?'. Actual meaning: 'Will you be my boyfriend/girlfriend?' — the formal-commitment ask.

Said after a period of 썸 (pre-dating ambiguity) or after a 고백 (confession of feelings) to officially become a couple. Use -ㄹ래요? with someone you're on 존댓말 with; drop to 사귈래? in 반말. This is a serious, sincere question — don't throw it around casually or it loses meaning.

사귀다 (committed relationship, 'boyfriend/girlfriend') vs. 만나다 ('to date casually / to meet up' — vaguer). Asking 우리 만나는 거야? can mean 'are we an item?' but 만나다 alone implies less commitment. 사귀다 is the clear, official step.
사귈래요? (polite ask) → 사귈래? (반말) → 사귀자 (반말 'let's date') → 사귀어 주실래요? (humble earnest) → 사귀었어요 (past: 'we dated') → 사귀고 있어요 (currently dating). Spelling: always 사귀-, never 사겨-.

Spelling/conjugation: 사귀다 → 사귀어요 (NOT 사겨요). Particle: it's 나랑 사귈래? ('go out WITH me?') using 랑/와, never 너를 사귈래? with the object marker. The comitative 랑/와 is essential — 사귀다 is about being-with, not doing-to.

expressions.shortExplanation: 고백할 거예요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm going to confess (my feelings)".
expressions.explanation: 고백할 거예요 (gobaekal geoyeyo) means "I'm going to confess (my feelings)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 고백할 거예요 ("I'm going to confess my feelings"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I'm going to confess my feelings
usagePhrases.note: Polite; telling a friend your plan before you do it
반말, to a friend you're confiding in
Past tense — you already did it and are reporting
The receiving side; 받다 ('to receive') flips the direction completely

examples.en: I worked up the courage and confessed, but got rejected.
examples.note: 용기 내다 ('gather courage') is the natural lead-in; 차이다 ('get rejected/dumped') is the feared outcome

examples.en: Someone confessed to me yesterday — what do I do?
examples.note: 고백받다 = you are the one confessed to; completely different from 고백하다

examples.ko: A: 나 오늘 고백할 거야. B: 진짜? 잘 될 거야!
examples.romanization: A: na oneul gobaekal geoya. B: jinjja? jal doel geoya!
examples.en: A: I'm going to confess today. B: Really? It'll go well!
examples.note: The pep-talk A/B exchange; B's 잘 될 거야 ('it'll work out') is the standard encouragement

expressions.nuance: 고백하다 is 고백 (告白, 'white confession' → declaring something openly) + 하다, and in a dating context it specifically means declaring your romantic feelings — the pivotal event that makes 썸 official and precedes 사귀다. This is NOT the English 'confess' in the guilty-admission sense; a romantic 고백 is hopeful and nervous, not shameful. For admitting a fault, Koreans use 자백하다 or 털어놓다 — don't mix them up. Direction is critical: 고백하다 = YOU confess TO someone; 고백받다 = someone confesses TO YOU. The target of your confession takes 에게/한테 ('to'), never 을/를: 그 사람한테 고백했어요. After a 고백 the outcome is either a yes (→ 사귀다) or rejection (차이다). 고백 is the noun, so it needs a verb: 고백하다 (to confess), 고백받다 (to receive a confession) — you can't say 고백 주세요. Register is flexible: 고백 is everyday vocabulary, equally natural in 존댓말 or 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 고백하다 to mean 'admit I did something wrong'.
Romantic 고백 = declaring feelings, not owning up to a fault. For confessing a mistake, use 자백하다 or 솔직히 말하다 / 털어놓다.
Mixing up 고백하다 and 고백받다.
고백하다 = YOU confess to them; 고백받다 = THEY confess to you. 'I got confessed to' is 고백받았어요, not 고백했어요.
Marking the person with 을/를: 그 사람을 고백했어요.
The confession target takes 에게/한테 ('to'): 그 사람한테 고백했어요. The person you confess to is not a direct object.

structuredNuance.t: 고백 (告白) literally means 'white/open declaration'. In a dating context, 고백하다 = 'to declare romantic feelings openly to someone'. It is the formal-yet-emotional step of stating your feelings and inviting a relationship — not a guilty admission.

Typically done after a period of 썸 (ambiguous closeness), often in a one-on-one setting. Koreans often plan the moment carefully — 언제 고백하지? ('when should I confess?') is a real anxiety. Said to the person you like (+ 한테/에게), or reported to friends after the fact. Register is flexible.

고백하다 (romantic declaration) vs. 자백하다 (confess a crime/misdeed, in court or to someone you wronged) vs. 털어놓다 (open up/unburden, more emotional). Don't reach for 자백 when you mean a romantic confession — the connotations are guilt-crime, not love.
고백하다 → 고백할 거야/거예요 (plan) → 고백했어/했어요 (past, reported) → 고백받았어요 (was confessed to) → 고백 성공/실패 ('confession succeeded/failed'). The noun 고백 alone works in compound phrases: 고백하러 가다 ('go to confess').

Romantic 고백 is NOT guilty admission. For owning up to a fault, say 자백하다 or 솔직히 말하다. Also watch direction: 고백하다 (I confess) ≠ 고백받다 (I receive a confession). And the target takes 한테/에게, never 을/를: 그 사람한테 고백했어요.

expressions.english: I'd like to ask you out (on a date)
expressions.shortExplanation: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to ask you out (on a date)".
expressions.explanation: "I'd like to ask you out (on a date)" — that is 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 (deiteu sincheonghago sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to ask you out"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to ask you out
usagePhrases.note: Polite; expressing the wish to ask for a date — earnest and slightly formal
반말, declaring your intention to a friend or to the crush directly

usagePhrases.en: Want to go on a date?
usagePhrases.note: The direct invite itself — skips the 신청 and just asks
The soft indirect opener that typically leads into asking someone out

examples.en: I actually wanted to ask you out.
examples.note: 사실 ('actually/honestly') makes it a slightly hesitant but sweet reveal; -었어요 past = 'I'd been wanting to'

examples.en: Want to go on a date this weekend?
examples.note: 데이트하다 + -ㄹ래요 for the actual invitation; 이번 주말에 is the natural time anchor

examples.ko: A: 주말에 시간 있어요? B: 네, 왜요? A: 같이 밥 먹으러 갈래요?
examples.romanization: A: jumare sigan isseoyo? B: ne, waeyo? A: gachi bam meogeureo gallaeyo?
examples.en: A: Are you free this weekend? B: Yes, why? A: Want to grab a meal together?
examples.note: The real-world indirect ask; Koreans rarely say '데이트하자' out of nowhere to a near-stranger — they ease in like this

expressions.nuance: 데이트 is the loanword 'date', and there are two key verb patterns: 데이트하다 ('to go on a date', the activity) and 데이트 신청하다 ('to ask someone out', lit. 'to submit a date application', 신청 申請 = applying/requesting). Using 신청하다 frames the ask as a formal request — the same verb you use to register for a class or apply for a scholarship, which makes it endearing in Korean. Contrast: 데이트하다 (the act of going on the date itself) vs. 사귀다 (being in a committed relationship) — you can 데이트 with someone before you're officially together. Koreans often avoid announcing '데이트하자' bluntly to someone they barely know; instead they float 주말에 시간 있어요? ('free this weekend?') and work up to it. Pitfall: saying 데이트를 물어보다 ('ask about a date') for 'ask out' is wrong — the idiom is 데이트 신청하다. 데이트 is a noun and needs a verb: 데이트하다 or 데이트 신청하다; you can't conjugate the noun alone. Register: 데이트 itself is casual-neutral; keep the sentence ending polite with someone new.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 데이트를 물어보고 싶어요 for 'I want to ask you out'.
물어보다 means 'ask a question'. To ask someone ON a date, the set phrase is 데이트 신청하다: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요.
Treating the loanword 데이트 as a verb on its own.
데이트 is a noun; the verb needs 하다: 데이트하다. 'Let's go on a date' is 데이트하자/데이트할래요 — you can't conjugate the noun directly (no 데이트자 / 데이트요 to mean 'let's date').
Assuming 데이트 means you're officially a couple.
데이트 is the activity of going out; you can date casually before being official. The committed-couple status is 사귀다, a separate step.

structuredNuance.t: 데이트 (loanword 'date') + 신청하다 (申請: 'to apply for / submit a request'). Literally 'to apply for a date'. The real meaning: 'to ask someone out on a date'. The 신청 framing — borrowed from formal application vocabulary — gives the phrase a slightly earnest, respectful tone.

Used after some 썸 or at least a few friendly encounters — not the first words to a stranger. Say 데이트 신청하고 싶어요 (polite) to someone you're on 존댓말 with; 데이트 신청할게 (반말) to a friend or once you're close. Koreans typically ease in with 시간 있어요? first rather than blurting the 데이트 ask.

데이트하다 (going on a date, the experience) vs. 사귀다 (being a couple, the ongoing status). You can go on a 데이트 with someone you're not yet officially dating. 데이트 신청하다 = inviting them to that experience; 사귀다 = the committed step that may come after.
데이트 신청하고 싶어요 (polite wish) → 데이트 신청할게요 (I'll ask you out) → 우리 데이트할래요? (direct invite) → 데이트하자 (반말 'let's date'). Indirect opener: 주말에 시간 있어요? → 같이 뭔가 할까요?

데이트를 물어보다 ('ask about a date') does NOT mean 'ask someone out' — use 데이트 신청하다. Also 데이트 is a noun; don't try to conjugate it directly (no 데이트요 / 데이트자 as verbs). And 데이트 ≠ 사귀다 — going on a date doesn't mean you're an official couple.

expressions.english: Let's keep in touch / Text me
expressions.shortExplanation: 연락해요 is a practical expression meaning "Let's keep in touch / Text me".
expressions.explanation: 연락해요 (yeollakaeyo) = "Let's keep in touch / Text me". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 연락해요 ("Let's stay in touch / text me"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Let's stay in touch / text me
usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; said when parting, hoping to talk again — warm but non-committal
반말, to a friend or someone you're close with
Promising YOU will reach out first — -ㄹ게요 commits your own action
Asking THEM to reach out; 주다 puts the action on the other person

examples.en: Get home safe and text me.
examples.note: 조심히 들어가다 ('get home safely') + 연락해요 is the warm standard farewell in early dating

examples.en: Why didn't you text? I was waiting for you.
examples.note: 연락 안 하다 ('not contact') is the root of 연락 없음 anxiety; 기다렸잖아 ('I was waiting, you know') is a gentle complaint

examples.ko: A: 나중에 연락할게요. B: 네, 기다릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: najunge yeollakalgeyo. B: ne, gidarilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I'll be in touch later. B: Okay, I'll wait.
examples.note: Direction contrast in one exchange: A promises their own action (-ㄹ게요); B accepts with 기다리다

expressions.nuance: 연락하다 is 연락 (連絡, 'contact/communication') + 하다 — the all-purpose verb for reaching out via any channel: calling, texting, messaging. In the dating world, it carries outsized weight: 연락 잘 하는 사람 ('someone who texts back reliably') is a highly prized quality, and 연락이 뜸해지다 ('contact grows sparse') is often the first sign a relationship is cooling. The critical distinctions are in verb form and direction: 연락할게요 = 'I'LL contact you' (-ㄹ게 promises your OWN action); 연락해요 = 'let's stay in touch / you contact me' (imperative/suggestion); 연락 주세요 = 'please reach out to me' (you put the action on them with 주다). Mixing these sends opposite messages. Particle trap: the target takes 에게/한테, not 을/를 — 나한테 연락해 ('contact ME'), never 나를 연락해. Also note you can say 연락해 주세요 (verb + 주다 favor) or 연락 주세요 (noun + 주다), but NOT 연락하 주세요 (broken split).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 연락할게 when you mean 'you text me'.
연락할게(요) promises YOUR own action ('I'll reach out'). To ask them to contact you, say 연락해(요) or 연락 줘(요)/연락 주세요.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 연락해.
The contact target takes 한테/에게 ('to'): 나한테 연락해 ('contact me'). 연락하다 doesn't take a direct-object person.
Translating 'keep in touch' literally with unrelated idioms.
There's no body-part idiom; the verb is simply 연락하다. 'Let's keep in touch' = 연락해요 / 연락하고 지내요.

structuredNuance.t: 연락 (連絡: 'contact/communication') + 하다. Literally 'do contact'. Used for any channel — call, text, KakaoTalk message. In dating it is loaded: frequent mutual 연락 is the lifeblood of a budding relationship.

Said at the end of a date or a first meeting to express you want to continue the interaction. 연락해요 (polite) is safe with someone new; 연락해 (반말) for friends. The direction the action flows — toward you or them — is set entirely by the verb form, so choose carefully.

연락할게요 ('I'll contact you' — you initiate) vs. 연락해요 / 연락해 ('contact me / let's be in touch' — they initiate or mutual) vs. 연락 주세요 ('please reach out to me' — clearly requesting they act). Mixing them reverses who is supposed to text first.

연락해요 (let's be in touch, polite) → 연락해 (반말) → 연락할게요 (I'll reach out) → 연락 주세요 (please reach out to me) → 연락해 주세요 (please reach out to me, verb form) → 연락하고 지내요 ('let's stay in contact and get along').

Particle: the person you contact takes 한테/에게, not 을/를 — 나한테 연락해, never 나를 연락해. Don't literally translate 'keep in touch' as anything involving hands (손 잡고 있어 etc.) — the Korean is simply 연락하다. And 연락하 주세요 is broken; use 연락해 주세요 or 연락 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 보고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I miss you".
expressions.explanation: 보고 싶어요 (bogo sipeoyo) means "I miss you". Say it as one set phrase — for example 보고 싶어요 ("I miss you / I want to see you"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I miss you / I want to see you
usagePhrases.note: Polite; tender, said to someone you care about romantically or as a close friend
반말, to a partner or very close friend — intimate

usagePhrases.en: I missed you / I've been missing you
usagePhrases.note: Past: best said at the moment of reunion, 'I was missing you'
많이 ('a lot') adds genuine warmth and longing — lovely for long-distance moments

examples.en: I missed you all day today.
examples.note: 하루 종일 ('all day long') intensifies the longing; past tense is the most natural form

examples.en: Being far apart makes me miss you even more.
examples.note: Long-distance context; 더 ('even more') + the gentle surprise/realization ending -네요

examples.ko: A: 나 도착했어. B: 잘 왔어, 보고 싶었어!
examples.romanization: A: na dochakaesseo. B: jal wasseo, bogo sipeosseo!
examples.en: A: I arrived. B: Welcome, I missed you!
examples.note: The reunion exchange; B's 보고 싶었어 lands warm the instant the person appears

expressions.nuance: 보고 싶다 is literally 보다 ('to see') + -고 싶다 ('want to'), so it means BOTH 'I want to see you' and 'I miss you' — Korean fuses the two ideas because missing someone IS wanting to see them. It is the standard romantic and close-friendship 'I miss you', warmer and lighter than any clinical translation. The key contrast: don't use 그립다 / 그리워하다 ('to long for, to miss deeply') for everyday 'I miss you' to a partner you'll see soon — 그립다 is a heavy, often nostalgic longing for something distant, lost, or past (a hometown, a late grandparent, childhood), so 당신이 그리워요 to a partner you're meeting tomorrow sounds dramatic or song-lyric. Also distinguish 보고 싶다 (emotional 'miss you' — about the person) from 만나고 싶다 ('I want to meet up' — more about logistics). Particle trap: the person you miss takes SUBJECT marking — 네가/당신이 보고 싶어 (lit. 'YOU are want-to-see'), not the object 너를 보고 싶어 which learners reach for instinctively.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그리워요 / 그립다 for someone you'll see soon.
그립다 is a heavy, nostalgic longing (for the lost or distant). Everyday 'I miss you' to a partner is 보고 싶어요. 그리워요 sounds melodramatic for a quick reunion.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 보고 싶어.
With -고 싶다 the desired object takes 이/가 (or 을/를 is debated, but for people the natural choice is 가): 네가 보고 싶어. Many learners over-apply 를.
Treating 보고 싶다 as only 'want to see', missing the 'miss you' sense.
Context makes it emotional: to a loved one, 보고 싶어요 means 'I miss you', not a neutral 'I'd like to see you'. Read it as the warm idiom.

structuredNuance.t: 보다 ('to see') + -고 싶다 ('want to'). Literally 'I want to see'. In emotional context to a loved one, this IS 'I miss you' — Korean collapses the two feelings because missing = wanting to see. Context makes the warm reading automatic.

Said to a romantic partner, a close friend, or family member. 보고 싶어요 (polite) works even with someone you're not yet deeply intimate with; 보고 싶어 (반말) is the tender form between partners. Most naturally in past tense 보고 싶었어요 when you reunite, or in ongoing statements ('I keep missing you').

그립다 / 그리워하다 = deep nostalgic longing for something distant, lost, or past (hometown, late relative, a past era). 보고 싶다 = everyday 'miss you' to a person you care about and will see again. Using 그리워요 to a partner you're seeing tomorrow sounds melodramatic. 만나고 싶다 leans toward logistics ('want to meet up'), while 보고 싶다 is purely the emotional 'I miss you'.

보고 싶어요 (polite) → 보고 싶어 (반말) → 보고 싶었어요 (past, at reunion) → 많이 보고 싶었어 (intensified) → 너무 보고 싶어서 못 참겠어 ('I miss you so much I can't stand it'). 빨리 보고 싶어 ('I want to see you soon') is the impatient variant.

Particle error: the person you miss takes 이/가 (subject), not 을/를 (object) — 네가 보고 싶어 ('YOU are want-to-see'), never 너를 보고 싶어. This feels backwards to English speakers. Also don't reach for 그립다 for an everyday 'I miss you' — reserve it for heavy nostalgic longing.

expressions.shortExplanation: 자기야 is a practical expression meaning "Honey / babe".
expressions.explanation: "Honey / babe" — that is 자기야 (jagiya). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 자기야 ("Honey / babe"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; the go-to pet name between Korean couples, replacing the partner's name
The same word used as a subject or reference — '자기 오늘 어때?' ('how are you today, babe?')
A woman addressing an older boyfriend; romantic when directed at a partner
The married-couple equivalent — sweet but strictly for spouses; never for a dating partner

examples.en: Babe, what are you doing?
examples.note: The everyday couple opener replacing the name; 뭐 해? is the casual 'what are you up to?'

examples.en: Babe~ buy me this.
examples.note: Drawn-out 자기야~ + a request signals 애교 (cute wheedling behavior); the tilde shows the drawn-out vowel

examples.ko: A: 자기야, 오늘 너무 보고 싶었어. B: 나도 자기 보고 싶었어.
examples.romanization: A: jagiya, oneul neomu bogo sipeosseo. B: nado jagi bogo sipeosseo.
examples.en: A: Babe, I missed you so much today. B: I missed you too, babe.
examples.note: Couple exchange; B uses 자기 (without 야) as a softer reference — both forms natural

expressions.nuance: 자기 (自己, lit. 'oneself') is repurposed as a romantic pet name; 자기야 adds the vocative particle 야 (used after vowel-ending words). As a couple term, it entirely replaces the partner's name in address — you stop calling your boyfriend 민준 and start calling him 자기야. It is exclusively couple language in 반말 register and would be bizarre said to anyone else. The stage and gender contrast is critical: 자기야 is gender-neutral and works at the dating stage; a woman often calls an older boyfriend 오빠 ('older brother') — affectionate and common; 여보 / 당신 are for MARRIED couples only. Using 여보 with a new partner is either a joke ('let's play house') or an odd misfire. Note: 자기 does mean 'oneself' grammatically (자기 자신 'oneself'), but between lovers the pet-name reading is unmistakable by context. English-speaker trap: don't try to use 당신 ('you/dear') as a neutral second-person pronoun in couple talk — 당신 to a stranger is aggressive; to a partner in everyday speech it's either formal-lyrical or married-register, not what couples actually say.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling a new girlfriend/boyfriend 여보.
여보 is the MARRIED couples' term ('dear'). For dating, the pet name is 자기야. 여보 to a new partner sounds like playing house.
Using 당신 as a casual 'you' to your partner.
당신 to a stranger is aggressive; to a partner it's married/lyrical register. In everyday couple talk use 자기 or their name, not 당신.
Reading 자기 only as the reflexive 'oneself'.
자기 does mean 'oneself' grammatically, but as a vocative to a lover it's 'babe/honey': 자기야. Context flips the meaning.

structuredNuance.t: 자기 (自己) literally means 'oneself, self' in grammar. Between couples, the same word is completely repurposed as 'babe/honey'. 자기야 adds the vocative 야 (used after vowel-ending words). Context makes it unmistakably the pet name.

Strictly for your romantic partner, in 반말. Calling anyone other than your partner 자기야 is jarring. Start using it once you're officially a couple (사귀다). Women often alternate 자기야 with 오빠 for an older boyfriend; men use 자기야 universally regardless of the partner's age relative to theirs.

자기야 (dating couples, gender-neutral) vs. 오빠 (woman to older boyfriend — affectionate but gendered) vs. 여보/당신 (married couples only). Don't use 여보 for a dating partner — it sounds like you're roleplaying being married. 여보 said in jest is funny; said seriously it confuses.

자기야 (vocative call) → 자기 (mid-sentence reference: '자기는 뭐 먹을 거야?') → 자기야~ (with drawn-out vowel for 애교) → 우리 자기 ('my babe', emphatic). Some couples switch to names or 오빠/자기 interchangeably once comfortable.

Don't read 자기 as the reflexive 'oneself' in couple context — between partners it's purely 'babe'. Don't use 당신 as a casual 'you' for your partner — 당신 is confrontational to strangers and lyrical/married-register to a partner; use 자기 or their name in everyday couple talk.

expressions.english: Do you like me, or your friend(s) more?
expressions.shortExplanation: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? is a practical expression meaning "Do you like me, or your friend(s) more?".
expressions.explanation: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? (naega joa? chinguga joa?) = "Do you like me, or your friend(s) more?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? ("Me, or your friends — who do you like more?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Me, or your friends — who do you like more?
usagePhrases.note: 반말; a half-pouting, playful jealous question in a couple or close friendship
Polite, gentler version of fishing for reassurance

usagePhrases.ko: 나랑 친구 중에 누가 더 좋아?
usagePhrases.romanization: narang chingu junge nuga deo joa?
usagePhrases.en: Between me and your friend, who do you like more?
usagePhrases.note: Spelled-out 'between X and Y, who' version — slightly more direct
The expected reassuring comeback; 당연히 ('of course') + 너

examples.en: Do you like me more, or your games?
examples.note: Swap 친구 for any rival (게임, 축구, etc.) to tease about divided attention — a widely used playful structure

examples.ko: 에이, 그걸 말이라고 해? 당연히 너지.
examples.romanization: ei, geugeol marirago hae? dangyeonhi neoji.
examples.en: Come on, you even have to ask? You, obviously.
examples.note: The reassuring comeback: 그걸 말이라고 해 ('is that even a question?') + 당연히 너 — textbook couple banter

examples.ko: A: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? B: 아, 진짜! ...당연히 자기지.
examples.romanization: A: naega joa? chinguga joa? B: a, jinjja! ...dangyeonhi jagiji.
examples.en: A: Me or your friends? B: Ugh, seriously! ...You, obviously, babe.
examples.note: Real couple exchange; B's mock-exasperation then warm 자기 makes it cute

expressions.nuance: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? is the playful 'who do you like more, me or ___?' question a partner asks to fish for reassurance — equal parts 애교 (cute behavior) and 질투 (jealousy). It fits any rivalry slot: 내가 좋아? 게임이 좋아? / 내가 좋아? 축구가 좋아? — the structure is X가 좋아? Y가 좋아?. The verb is 좋다 ('to be good/likable'), an ADJECTIVE in Korean, so the liked thing takes the subject marker 이/가 — 내가 좋아? literally 'am I good (to you)?' = 'do you prefer me?'. This is the single biggest grammar trap: English speakers reach for 좋아하다 ('to like', a transitive verb) + 을/를, producing 나를 좋아해? — grammatical and understandable, but the comparison frame uses 좋다 + 이/가, not 좋아하다 + 를. The 'I' pronoun shifts: 나 → 내가 with the subject marker. Register is 반말; this is intimate couple-talk, never a question for coworkers or strangers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 좋아하다 + 를 in the comparison: 나를 좋아해, 친구를 좋아해?
The teasing frame uses the adjective 좋다 with 가: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? Using 좋아해 here breaks the idiom (though it's understandable).
Marking 'me' with 를: 내를 좋아?
좋다 is an adjective; what's liked takes 이/가, and 'I' becomes 내가. So it's 내가 좋아?, never 내를.
Saying it in 존댓말 to a non-partner.
This is intimate, teasing couple-talk. Asking a coworker or stranger 내가 좋아, 친구가 좋아? is bizarre. Keep it for someone you're dating.

structuredNuance.t: 내가 ('I/me' + 이/가 subject) + 좋아? ('am I good to you?'). 좋다 is an adjective meaning 'to be good/likable'; what is liked takes 이/가, not 을/를. The literal meaning 'am I good? is your friend good?' translates into 'do you prefer me or your friend?' — the comparison frame is built into the repeated 좋아.

Quintessential couple banter in 반말, usually said when a partner feels the other is spending too much time with friends, gaming, or anything that isn't them. Works as a gentle jealous tease, not a serious accusation. Only between romantic partners or very close friends; asking a coworker 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? would be bizarre.
좋다 + 가 (adjective frame, 내가 좋아?) vs. 좋아하다 + 를 (verb frame, 나를 좋아해?). Both mean 'do you like me?', but the comparison pattern uses 좋다: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아?. 더 좋다 ('like more') is the comparative: 내가 더 좋아?
내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? → 내가 좋아? 게임이 좋아? → 내가 더 좋아? (simpler comparative) → 내가 더 좋아요? (polite). The reassuring answer pattern: 당연히 너지 / 당연히 자기지.

좋다 is an adjective; what's liked takes 이/가, and 'I' becomes 내가 — so 내가 좋아? (correct) vs. 나를 좋아해? (uses the verb 좋아하다, grammatical but breaks the comparison-frame idiom). Never 내를 (impossible: 나 + 를 would be me as direct object, and 'I' contracted is 내, not 내를).

expressions.shortExplanation: 질투 나요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm jealous".
expressions.explanation: 질투 나요 (jiltu nayo) means "I'm jealous". Say it as one set phrase — for example 질투 나요 ("I'm jealous"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; admitting jealousy, often with a half-playful smile in a relationship
반말, to a partner or close friend you can be honest with
Telling someone to stop acting jealous; 질투하다 = the active behavior
Owning it openly and a bit cutely; -는 거야 = 'it's that I'm doing'

examples.en: If I'm honest, I'm jealous.
examples.note: 솔직히 말하면 ('if I'm honest') is the natural lead-in for admitting feelings you'd normally hide

examples.en: I got jealous when you laughed with someone else.
examples.note: Naming the specific trigger: 다른 사람이랑 웃다 ('laughing with another person') + 질투 나다 past

examples.ko: A: 왜 그래? B: 질투하는 거 아니야! ...조금 질투 나긴 해.
examples.romanization: A: wae geurae? B: jiltuhaneun geo aniya! ...jogeum jiltu nagin hae.
examples.en: A: What's wrong? B: I'm not jealous! ...Okay, maybe a little.
examples.note: Classic deny-then-admit pattern; 질투 나긴 해 = 'I am, to some extent, jealous' — the 긴 qualifies

expressions.nuance: 질투 나다 is 질투 (嫉妬, 'jealousy') + 나다 ('to arise/come out') — jealousy framed as a feeling that wells up in you rather than something you actively do. The same 나다 appears in 화나다 ('get angry'), 짜증 나다 ('get annoyed'), 겁나다 ('be scared') — Korean systematically treats emotions as arising events. The key contrast: 질투 나다 (feeling wells up) vs. 질투하다 (the behavior, what you do with that feeling or how you act it out). 'I feel jealous' = 질투 나(요); 'stop being jealous' = 질투하지 마 (active verb, commanding behavior). There is also 부럽다 ('to envy', wanting what someone has with no romantic sting): your friend's new phone makes you 부럽다, not 질투. English blurs 'jealous' and 'envious'; Korean separates them sharply. The particle trap: 질투(가) 나다 takes the feeling as grammatical subject — never force a 'I jealous YOU' structure like 너를 질투해. Register: 질투 나요 is fine and even endearing with a partner when said semi-playfully; in serious accusation it escalates.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 부럽다 when you mean romantic jealousy.
부럽다 is envy (wanting what someone has, no romance). Feeling jealous about a partner is 질투 나다. 'I'm jealous (of who you're with)' = 질투 나, not 부러워.
Saying 질투해요 to describe your own feeling.
질투하다 leans toward the behavior/accusation ('to act jealous'). To say you FEEL jealous, the natural phrase is 질투 나요 (the feeling arises).
Forcing an English structure like 너를 질투해 for 'I'm jealous of you'.
질투(가) 나다 takes the feeling as subject: 질투 나. To say you got jealous over a situation, name the trigger + 질투 났어, e.g. 다른 사람이랑 있어서 질투 났어 ('I got jealous because you were with someone else').

structuredNuance.t: 질투 ('jealousy', 嫉妬) + 나다 ('to arise/come out'). Literally 'jealousy arises [in me]'. This framing treats emotions as events that visit you — the same pattern as 화나다 ('anger comes out') and 짜증 나다 ('annoyance arises'). The real meaning: 'I feel jealous'.

Said to a romantic partner when they interact with someone in a way that stirs possessive feelings. 질투 나요 (polite) is safe even in early dating; 질투 나 (반말) is more intimate. Said semi-playfully it's cute and endearing; said as a serious confrontation it changes the dynamic significantly.

질투 나다 (feeling arises — 'I feel jealous') vs. 질투하다 (acting jealous — 'to be jealous, to act on it'): 나는 질투 나 = 'I feel jealous inside'; 질투하지 마 = 'stop acting jealous'. Also: 부럽다 ('I envy you/them' — coveting what someone has, zero romantic possessiveness). Korean separates 질투 (romantic/possessive jealousy) and 부럽다 (envy over someone's advantage).
질투 나요 (polite present) → 질투 나 (반말) → 질투 났어 (past: jealousy arose) → 질투하지 마 (stop it) → 질투 나는 거야? (are you jealous?). Intensified: 진짜 질투 나 / 너무 질투 나.

English blurs 'jealous' and 'envious'; Korean splits them (질투 vs. 부럽다). Particle trap: 질투(가) 나다 takes the emotion as subject — don't say 너를 질투해 ('I jealous you') — instead name the trigger: 네가 그 사람이랑 있어서 질투 났어 ('I got jealous because you were with that person').

expressions.shortExplanation: 바람피우지 마 is a practical expression meaning "Don't cheat (on me)".
expressions.explanation: "Don't cheat (on me)" — that is 바람피우지 마 (barampiuji ma). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 바람피우지 마 ("Don't cheat"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; said to a partner, either as a half-joking caution or in deadly seriousness
Polite-formal version; the topic is heavy so the -요 softens the confrontation
The accusing question, past tense; 설마 바람피운 거야? ('don't tell me you cheated?') is also common

usagePhrases.en: Apparently they cheated / are having an affair
usagePhrases.note: Gossip form; 바람나다 = the affair happened, 대 = 'I heard/apparently'

examples.en: Don't tell me you cheated?
examples.note: 설마 ('surely not' / 'don't tell me') signals shocked suspicion — the accusation is still being denied mentally

examples.en: They broke up — apparently one of them cheated.
examples.note: 바람나다 in gossip: 바람나다 = the affair surfaced; 헤어지다 = broke up

examples.ko: A: 바람피우지 마. B: 무슨 말이야, 내가 왜?
examples.romanization: A: barampiuji ma. B: museun mariya, naega wae?
examples.en: A: Don't cheat on me. B: What are you talking about, why would I?
examples.note: The cautionary warning and the defensive reply; -지 마 is 반말 command, B's 내가 왜 is the protest

expressions.nuance: 바람피우다 is a fixed idiom for cheating / having an affair: 바람 ('wind') + 피우다 ('to cause/give off') — 'to kick up wind', meaning to stray or be unfaithful. It is the standard, everyday word for romantic infidelity. Two related but distinct forms confuse learners: 바람피우다 (active verb, 'to cheat' — what the cheater intentionally does: 바람피우지 마) vs. 바람나다 (inchoative, 'an affair occurred / got swept into one' — describes the event or situation: 바람났대 'I heard they had an affair'). Command/accusation form is always 바람피우다; the gossip/news form uses 바람나다. 속이다 ('to deceive/lie') is general deception — romantic infidelity specifically is 바람피우다, so 속이다 sounds too mild or generic. Particle: if you name the affair partner, use 랑/하고 ('with') — 다른 사람이랑 바람피우다; you don't mark anyone with 를 in this structure. Register: 바람피우지 마 is 반말 and heavy; even joking about it carries real emotional weight.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 바람 literally as 'wind' and getting lost.
바람피우다 is a fixed idiom for cheating; 바람 here is not weather. Learn the whole phrase as 'to cheat', don't decode it word-by-word.
Confusing 바람피우다 and 바람나다.
바람피우다 = the active 'to cheat' (what one does); 바람나다 = 'an affair occurred / got swept into one' (the event). Command form is 바람피우지 마.
Using 속이다 for cheating on a partner.
속이다 is general 'to deceive/lie'. Romantic infidelity is specifically 바람피우다. 'He cheated' = 바람피웠어, not 속였어 (which just means 'lied').

structuredNuance.t: 바람 ('wind') + 피우다 ('to give off, produce'). Literally 'to kick up wind'. This is a fixed idiom for romantic infidelity — do not decode it word by word. The actual meaning is 'to cheat on a partner / have an affair'.

Said to a partner as a half-joking preemptive warning ('just don't cheat!') or as a serious confrontation. Always between people in a romantic relationship — not a topic for strangers or casual acquaintances. 바람피우지 마 is 반말 command; use 바람피우지 마세요 if you want to soften the confrontation with politeness.

바람피우다 (active 'to cheat', what one intentionally does) vs. 바람나다 (inchoative 'an affair occurred / was swept into one' — describes the event/state). Use 바람피우지 마 for the command; use 바람났대 for gossip/reporting. Also 속이다 ('to deceive/lie') is generic; romantic infidelity specifically is 바람피우다.
바람피우다 → 바람피우지 마 (command) → 바람피웠어? (past accusation) → 바람피운 것 같아 ('seems like they cheated'). 바람나다 → 바람났어 (past, stated) → 바람났대 (reported hearsay).

The literal trap: 바람 means 'wind' but the idiom has nothing to do with weather — never translate it piece by piece. The verb trap: using 속이다 ('to lie/deceive') for cheating — 속이다 is too generic; 바람피우다 is the specific romance-infidelity word.

expressions.shortExplanation: 우리 잘 어울려요 is a practical expression meaning "We go well together".
expressions.explanation: 우리 잘 어울려요 (uri jal eoullyeoyo) = "We go well together". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 우리 잘 어울려요 ("We suit each other well"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; saying a couple looks/fits good together — lovely early-dating or compliment line
반말, to your partner — warm and affirming

usagePhrases.en: You two really suit each other
usagePhrases.note: Said about a couple by an onlooker; 진짜 ('really') — a compliment from the outside looking in

usagePhrases.en: You're a match made in heaven
usagePhrases.note: Stronger praise; 천생연분 = destined pair — for a couple that clearly fits perfectly

examples.ko: 우리 진짜 잘 어울리는 것 같아.
examples.romanization: uri jinjja jal eoullineun geot gata.
examples.en: I think we really go well together.
examples.note: -는 것 같다 ('I think/seems like') sweetly softens what might sound overconfident — it's a modest hedge

examples.ko: 이 옷 색이 너한테 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: i ot saegi neohante jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: This outfit's color really suits you.
examples.note: 어울리다 for clothes suiting a person — same verb, shows the word's dual use for couples AND style

examples.ko: A: 우리 잘 어울리지? B: 응, 완전 잘 어울려!
examples.romanization: A: uri jal eoulliji? B: eung, wanjeon jal eoullyeo!
examples.en: A: We go well together, right? B: Yes, totally!
examples.note: Fishing for reassurance and the enthusiastic confirmation — natural couple micro-conversation

expressions.nuance: 어울리다 means 'to match / suit / go well together', and 우리 잘 어울려요 conveys that a couple is a good fit — looks good together, has chemistry. The same verb covers clothing ('this color suits you') and interpersonal compatibility, so it spans both the visual ('you look great together') and the relational ('we click'). The crucial contrast: 어울리다 (compatibility/fit) vs. 사귀다 (official relationship status) — saying 잘 어울려요 doesn't mean you're an official couple, only that you'd be a good one. For destiny-level praise, escalate to 천생연분 ('heaven-made match') or 잘 맞다 ('we click'). The difference between 어울리다 and 맞다: 잘 어울리다 leans toward the visual and social fit ('you look right together, you complement each other'), while 잘 맞다 ('to click') is about personality alignment and compatibility from the inside. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 어울리다 is intransitive — 'it suits you' is 너한테 잘 어울려 (한테/에게 for the target), never 너를 어울려. (2) Don't mangle the stem — it is 어울리다, conjugating 어울려요; not 어울다 or 어우르다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 를: 너를 잘 어울려.
어울리다 is intransitive; the one something suits takes 한테/에게: 너한테 잘 어울려 ('it suits you'). For a couple, just use a plural subject: 우리 잘 어울려.
Thinking 잘 어울려 means 'we're officially dating'.
어울리다 = compatible / go well together (fit), not relationship status. To say you're a couple, that's 사귀다. You can suit each other without being official.
Confusing 어울리다 with 어울다/어우르다.
The verb is 어울리다 ('to match/suit'). 'It suits you' = 잘 어울려요. Don't mangle the stem; conjugate 어울리다 → 어울려요.

structuredNuance.t: 어울리다 = 'to go together harmoniously, to match, to suit'. 우리 잘 어울려요 = 'we (잘 well) go together'. The literal meaning is already the real meaning, but the word covers both the visual (this outfit suits you) and the relational (we are a good match as a couple).

Said to a partner or about a couple (by a third party). 우리 잘 어울려요 (polite) is a warm, early-dating affirmation; 우리 잘 어울려 (반말) is the intimate version. 두 사람 잘 어울려요 is the compliment a matchmaker, friend, or family member gives when seeing a couple together.

어울리다 (visual + social fit: 'go together, look right') vs. 잘 맞다 ('click', personality compatibility from within). A couple can 잘 어울리다 without 잘 맞다 (look perfect but have friction) or vice versa. 천생연분 ('destined pair', heaven-made match) is the superlative for both.

우리 잘 어울려요 → 우리 잘 어울려 → 잘 어울리는 커플 ('a well-matched couple') → 너한테 잘 어울려 (clothes suit you) → 천생연분이에요 (you're a perfect match). The compliment 잘 어울린다 (dictionary form -ㄴ다) is the casual declarative used observationally.

(1) 어울리다 is intransitive — use 한테/에게 for who something suits (너한테 잘 어울려), never 너를 어울려. (2) Stem confusion: the verb is 어울리다 → 어울려요; don't substitute 어울다 or 어우르다 (different or non-existent). (3) Don't confuse 잘 어울리다 ('good fit, look right together') with 잘 맞다 ('click in personality').

expressions.shortExplanation: 밀당하지 마 is a practical expression meaning "Stop playing hard to get".
expressions.explanation: 밀당하지 마 (mildanghaji ma) means "Stop playing hard to get". Say it as one set phrase — for example 밀당하지 마 ("Stop playing hot and cold / stop the push-pull"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Stop playing hot and cold / stop the push-pull
usagePhrases.note: 반말; calling out someone's calculated hot-and-cold behavior

usagePhrases.en: Please don't play hard to get
usagePhrases.note: Polite version of the same plea — softens a potentially confrontational topic

usagePhrases.en: Are you playing hard to get?
usagePhrases.note: Asking half-amused or half-frustrated if this is a deliberate tactic

usagePhrases.en: You're really good at the push-pull game
usagePhrases.note: A teasing remark about someone's skill at it; 잘하다 ('good at')

examples.en: Just be honest with me, stop playing games.
examples.note: 솔직하게 ('honestly') is directly contrasted with the game-playing — be real instead

examples.ko: 답장 일부러 늦게 해? 밀당하는 거야?
examples.romanization: dapjang ilbureo neutge hae? mildanghaneun geoya?
examples.en: Are you texting back late on purpose? Is this push-pull?
examples.note: 일부러 ('on purpose') names the calculated tactic behind delayed replies

examples.ko: A: 밀당도 적당히 해야지. B: 나 밀당 같은 거 안 해!
examples.romanization: A: mildangdo jeokdanghi haeyaji. B: na mildang gateun geo an hae!
examples.en: A: You should keep the push-pull in moderation. B: I don't play those games!
examples.note: 적당히 해야지 ('do it in moderation') + the defensive denial — typical back-and-forth

expressions.nuance: 밀당 is a slangy contraction of 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'), from 밀다 ('push') + 당기다 ('pull') — the calculated pre-dating game of alternating interest and coolness to keep the other person hooked. 밀당하다 = to play this game. It covers deliberate mixed signals: texting enthusiastically then going quiet, seeming available then suddenly busy. Very current Korean slang, dominant among young adults (roughly under 40); older Koreans may not use the term. The important contrast is 밀당 (ongoing strategic push-pull pattern) vs. 튕기다 ('to bounce / play coy', specifically feigning reluctance or disinterest at a single moment to seem less eager — like declining the first ask-out to appear hard-to-get). 밀당 is a repeated pattern; 튕기다 is a one-time coy refusal. English-speaker pitfall: there is no word-by-word route — 게임 하다 literally means playing a videogame; the dating game is 밀당하다. And it's a 하다-compound: 밀당하다, 밀당하지 마, never 밀당 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'play games' as 게임 하다.
게임 하다 means playing a (video)game. The dating push-pull is 밀당하다. 'Stop playing games (with my feelings)' = 밀당하지 마, not 게임 하지 마.
Using 밀당 in formal or professional settings.
밀당 is casual slang for romance/relationships. It sounds out of place in formal speech or non-dating contexts. Keep it to friends and partners.
Confusing 밀당 (ongoing strategy) with 튕기다 (feigning reluctance once).
밀당하다 is the continuous hot-and-cold game; 튕기다 is acting coy/refusing at a moment to seem less eager. Related but not identical — pick by whether it's a one-time coyness or a pattern.

structuredNuance.t: 밀당 = contraction of 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'), from 밀다 (push) + 당기다 (pull). Literally 'pushing and pulling'. The real meaning: the calculated dating tactic of hot-and-cold behavior — showing interest then pulling back, to keep someone invested.

Used in casual conversation between people in the 썸 or early-dating stage when one person perceives the other's behavior as strategically inconsistent. Pure informal/반말 register — said to a crush, partner, or a friend describing someone else's behavior. Don't use in formal speech or around older people unfamiliar with the slang.

밀당하다 (ongoing push-pull strategy, a repeated pattern) vs. 튕기다 ('play coy / bounce', a single moment of feigning reluctance — e.g. turning down a first ask-out to seem less eager). 밀당 is the continuous game; 튕기다 is one strategic refusal. Related but not the same.
밀당 (noun) → 밀당하다 (verb) → 밀당하지 마 (stop it, command) → 밀당하는 거야? (are you doing this?) → 밀당 고수 ('push-pull expert'). Related compound: 썸과 밀당 ('the 썸 stage and the push-pull game').
게임 하다 = playing a (video)game, NOT playing romantic games. The dating game is 밀당하다. Also 밀당 is a 하다-noun: 밀당하다, 밀당하지 마 — never 밀당 주세요 or 밀당 줘.

expressions.english: We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark
expressions.shortExplanation: 권태기가 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark".
expressions.explanation: "We've hit a rough patch / lost the spark" — that is 권태기가 왔어요 (gwontaegiga wasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 권태기가 왔어요 ("We've hit a slump in our relationship"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: We've hit a slump in our relationship
usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing a stale phase in an established relationship — confiding to anyone
반말, confiding to a close friend

usagePhrases.en: I think we're in a slump
usagePhrases.note: Tentative -ㄴ/ㄹ 것 같다 ('seems like') — not yet sure, testing the idea

usagePhrases.en: We got through the rough patch
usagePhrases.note: 극복하다 ('to overcome') — came out the other side, now stronger

examples.ko: 요즘 권태기 온 것 같아. 예전 같지 않아.
examples.romanization: yojeum gwontaegi on geot gata. yejeon gatji ana.
examples.en: I think the slump has hit lately. It doesn't feel like before.
examples.note: -ㄴ 것 같아 (tentative 'seems like') + 예전 같지 않다 ('not like before') — two natural ways to voice the feeling

examples.en: Dating for 3 years, the slump eventually set in.
examples.note: -더라고요 reports a realized, experienced truth — 'I noticed that...' — very natural in this frame

examples.ko: A: 요즘 권태기야? B: 글쎄... 권태기 극복하고 싶어.
examples.romanization: A: yojeum gwontaegiya? B: geulsse... gwontaegi geukbokago sipeo.
examples.en: A: Are we in a slump these days? B: I don't know... I want to work through it.
examples.note: Naming the phase and immediately pivoting to 극복 ('overcoming') — the hopeful couple response

expressions.nuance: 권태기 (倦怠期, 'weariness period') is the relationship slump — the stage in a long-term couple when excitement fades and daily life feels routine, like 'the honeymoon's over' or 'we've lost the spark'. The fixed collocation is 권태기가 오다 ('the slump arrives/comes') — Korean frames emotional phases as visitors that come to you, the same structure as 사춘기가 오다 ('puberty hits') and 감기가 오다 ('a cold comes'). This framing is important: learners wrongly try 권태기를 하다 or 가지다 (to have/do it as an object), but it 'arrives'. The contrast: 권태기 (a phase within an ongoing relationship, with the possibility of 극복 'overcoming') is entirely different from 헤어지다 (actually breaking up). Saying 권태기 왔어 does NOT mean the couple is over. Also 권태기 implies a relationship of some duration — you wouldn't use it for a two-week fling; for something that fizzled fast, say 흐지부지됐어 instead. Register: 권태기 is everyday vocabulary, equally natural in polite speech or 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 권태기를 해요 / 권태기를 가지고 있어요.
권태기 collocates with 오다 ('to come'): 권태기가 왔어요. You don't 'do' or 'possess' it as an object. The slump 'arrives'.
Thinking 권태기 means you broke up.
권태기 is a stale/bored phase WITHIN a relationship, often overcome (권태기 극복). Breaking up is 헤어지다. 권태기 왔어 means the spark faded, not that it's over.
Using 권태기 for a brand-new fling.
권태기 presupposes a longer relationship that's gone stale. For a short thing losing steam, you'd say it fizzled (흐지부지됐어), not 권태기.

structuredNuance.t: 권태기 (倦怠期) = 倦 (weary) + 怠 (sluggish/idle) + 期 (period). Literally 'the period of weariness'. In relationship terms: the phase where excitement fades and things feel routine. 오다 ('come') treats it as a visiting phase — 'the slump arrived'.

Used to describe a stale phase in an established relationship — implies the couple has been together long enough to have developed routine. Said to a close friend you're confiding in, or between partners acknowledging the phase. Not a term for a new relationship or casual fling.

권태기 (boredom/stale phase within a relationship — can be overcome) vs. 헤어지다 (breaking up, the relationship ends). 권태기 came = still together but struggling; 헤어졌어 = it's over. Also 흐지부지되다 ('fizzle out', for short things that never built momentum) is for new/casual things losing steam, not for an established relationship.
권태기가 오다 (arrive) → 권태기인 것 같다 (seems like we're in it) → 권태기를 극복하다 (overcome the slump) → 권태기가 풀리다 ('the slump loosens/resolves'). Intensified: 심한 권태기 ('a severe slump').

(1) Verb error: 권태기가 오다 (it 'comes') — never 권태기를 하다 or 가지다. (2) Don't assume 권태기 means they broke up — it's a phase within the relationship. (3) Don't use 권태기 for a brand-new or short relationship; the word implies established history.

expressions.shortExplanation: 우리 헤어져요 is a practical expression meaning "Let's break up".
expressions.explanation: 우리 헤어져요 (uri heeojyeoyo) = "Let's break up". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 우리 헤어져요 ("Let's break up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the breakup line said gently but with finality — heavy even with -요
반말, to a partner; 헤어지자 ('let's') is the slightly softer 반말 version
A softer phrasing — 'stop meeting' rather than the blunt 헤어지다; somewhat kinder
Reporting the breakup to a third party, past tense — what you tell friends

examples.en: I'm sorry. Let's break up.
examples.note: -자 ('let's') is 반말; 미안해 cushions the blow — the standard Korean breakup structure leads with an apology

examples.en: I think it'd be better for us to stop seeing each other.
examples.note: -는 게 좋겠어요 ('I think it'd be better to') — a gentle, indirect breakup phrasing Koreans use to soften the blow

examples.ko: A: 우리 헤어지자. B: 왜? 무슨 일이야?
examples.romanization: A: uri heeojija. B: wae? museun iriya?
examples.en: A: Let's break up. B: Why? What's going on?
examples.note: The shocked B response — 왜? 무슨 일이야? is the natural reply when a partner suddenly says this

expressions.nuance: 헤어지다 means 'to break up / part ways', and 우리 헤어져요 is the direct breakup line. Crucially, 헤어지다 is reciprocal and intransitive — both people part, so the partner is marked with 와/랑/하고 ('with'), NOT 을/를: 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요 ('I broke up WITH my boyfriend'). The single most common learner error is 남자친구를 헤어졌어요 with the object particle — you part WITH someone, you don't 'break up someone'. Note 헤어지다 also means simply 'to part ways' in a neutral, non-romantic sense (after meeting a friend: 여기서 헤어져요 'let's say goodbye here'), so context determines the weight. For a gentler breakup, Koreans reach for 그만 만나다 ('stop seeing each other') rather than the blunt 헤어지다. Don't confuse 헤어지다 (mutual parting) with 차다 (one person dumps the other) and 차이다 (to get dumped). Register: even the polite 헤어져요 is a heavy line; the word itself signals the end.
