commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the partner with 을/를: 남자친구를 헤어졌어요.
헤어지다 is reciprocal ('part WITH'): the partner takes 랑/와/하고. Say 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요. You don't break someone up as a direct object.
Confusing 헤어지다 with 차다/차이다.
헤어지다 = mutually parted. 차다 = 'to dump (someone)'; 차이다 = 'to get dumped'. 'I got dumped' is 차였어요, not 헤어졌어요 (which is neutral 'we broke up').
Using only the blunt 헤어져 when you want to soften it.
헤어지자 is direct. To be gentler, Koreans say 우리 그만 만나자 / 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어 ('let's stop seeing each other'), which lands softer.

structuredNuance.t: 헤어지다 = 'to come apart, to part ways'. In dating context, 우리 헤어져요 = 'let's break up'. The verb is reciprocal (both people part), not one-directional. The same word is used neutrally after any meeting ('let's say goodbye here'), so context carries the romantic weight.

Said to a partner to end a romantic relationship. 우리 헤어져요 (polite) is the slightly gentler form; 우리 헤어지자 (반말, 'let's') is the standard direct form between couples. Koreans typically lead with 미안해 ('I'm sorry') before the actual line. This is never a casual or public conversation.

헤어지다 (mutual parting, neutral as to who ended it) vs. 차다 ('to dump', one-directional — the dumper's act) vs. 차이다 ('to get dumped' — the dumpee's experience). For softer phrasing: 그만 만나다 / 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어. 헤어지자 is blunter; 그만 만나자 sounds slightly kinder.
우리 헤어져요 (polite) → 우리 헤어지자 (반말 suggestion 'let's') → 우리 그만 만나요 (softer) → 헤어졌어요 (past, reporting) → 헤어지고 싶어요 ('I want to break up'). The comitative: 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요.
헤어지다 is intransitive and reciprocal — the partner takes 랑/와/하고 ('with'), NOT 을/를. 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요 is correct; 남자친구를 헤어졌어요 is the #1 learner error. You part WITH someone, you don't 'break up someone'.

expressions.english: I want to get back together
expressions.shortExplanation: 재회하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I want to get back together".
expressions.explanation: 재회하고 싶어요 (jaehoehago sipeoyo) means "I want to get back together". Say it as one set phrase — for example 재회하고 싶어요 ("I want to get back together"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I want to get back together
usagePhrases.note: Polite-formal; earnest and slightly literary — wanting to reunite with an ex

usagePhrases.en: I want to see you / be together again
usagePhrases.note: 반말, warmer and plainer than the formal 재회 — what you'd actually whisper to an ex
A tender, hopeful invitation to restart; 다시 시작하다 ('start again') feels fresh and forward-looking

usagePhrases.en: I got back together with my ex-boyfriend
usagePhrases.note: Reporting it to a friend; 전 남자친구 ('ex-boyfriend') + 랑

examples.en: We broke up, but I still want to get back together.
examples.note: 헤어졌지만 ('though we split') sets up the longing; 아직도 ('still') intensifies the lingering feeling

examples.ko: 우리 다시 만날 수 있을까? 한 번만 더 해보자.
examples.romanization: uri dasi mannal su isseulkka? han beonman deo haeboja.
examples.en: Can we get back together? Let's try just one more time.
examples.note: 다시 만나다 + 한 번만 더 ('just once more') — the emotionally raw appeal; -ㄹ 수 있을까 adds uncertain hope

examples.ko: A: 재회해도 똑같을까 봐 무서워요. B: 이번엔 다를 거야.
examples.romanization: A: jaehoehaedo ttokgateulkka bwa museowoyo. B: ibeonen dareul geoya.
examples.en: A: I'm scared it'll be the same even if we reunite. B: This time will be different.
examples.note: -ㄹ까 봐 ('afraid that') voices the core reunion fear; B's 이번엔 다를 거야 is the classic reassurance

expressions.nuance: 재회하다 (再會 + 하다) means 'to reunite / get back together' after an actual breakup. It is the formal-ish or literary word for rekindling; in everyday speech Koreans almost always say the simpler 다시 만나다 ('meet again') — 전 남친이랑 다시 만나요 is what someone tells a friend, while 재회하고 싶어요 is more earnest/formal, like something from a drama monologue. Don't confuse 재회 ('reunite after a breakup') with 화해하다 ('to make up / reconcile after a fight while still together') — 화해 is for in-relationship disputes, 재회 is for after 헤어지다. Also 다시 만나다 carries ambiguity in context: with an ex it naturally reads as romantic reunion, but without context it can simply mean 'let's meet again sometime' — context resolves it. Particle: the ex takes 랑/와 ('with'), not 를 — 전 여자친구랑 재회했어요. 재회 is a 하다-noun: 재회하다, 재회하고 싶다, never 재회 주세요 or 재회를 원해요 (unnatural). Register: 재회하고 싶어요 (polite-earnest); 다시 만나고 싶어 (intimate 반말, what you'd actually say).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the ex with 을/를: 전 남자친구를 재회했어요.
재회/만나다 take 랑/와 ('with'): 전 남자친구랑 재회했어요. The reunion partner is not a direct object.
Confusing 재회 (get back together) with 화해 (reconcile after a fight).
화해하다 = make up while still together after an argument. 재회하다 = reunite after an actual breakup. Use 재회 only if you'd split up.
Overusing formal 재회 in casual conversation.
재회 sounds literary. In everyday speech Koreans say 다시 만나다: 전 남친이랑 다시 만나기로 했어 ('decided to get back with my ex'). Save 재회하다 for earnest/formal moments.

structuredNuance.t: 재회 (再會) = 再 (again) + 會 (meet/gather). Literally 're-meet'. 재회하다 = 'to reunite'. In a dating context this specifically means getting back together with an ex after a breakup — not just seeing someone again socially.

Said after a real breakup when feelings linger and you want to try again. 재회하고 싶어요 is more earnest/formal — works in a sincere face-to-face moment with the ex or when reporting to someone. 다시 만나고 싶어 is the warmer 반말 you'd say directly to an ex late at night over the phone.

재회하다 (reunite after a breakup — formal, literary) vs. 다시 만나다 (everyday 'get back together' OR just 'see each other again' — context-dependent) vs. 화해하다 ('reconcile after a fight while still together' — NOT after a breakup). Use 화해 for in-relationship conflict; 재회 only after 헤어지다.
재회하다 → 재회하고 싶어요 (I want to reunite) → 재회했어요 (we got back together) → 전 남자친구랑 재회했어 (reported). Casual equivalent: 다시 만나고 싶어 → 다시 시작하자 ('let's start over').
(1) Partner takes 랑/와, not 를: 전 남자친구랑 재회했어요. (2) 재회 is a 하다-noun — 재회하다 / 재회하고 싶다, never 재회 주세요. (3) Overusing formal 재회 in casual conversation — 다시 만나다 sounds far more natural in real speech.

expressions.shortExplanation: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 is a practical expression meaning "No really, I'm fine".
expressions.explanation: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 (anieyo, gwaenchanayo) = "No really, I'm fine". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 ("No really, it's fine"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a firmer, warmer double 'no thanks'
반말, refusing a friend
Formal 합쇼체, to staff or in business
Add 진짜 ('really') to insist when they keep offering

examples.en: No really, I'm fine.
examples.note: Said while gently pushing back when someone insists

examples.ko: 이거 가져가세요. — 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 마음만 받을게요.
examples.romanization: igeo gajyeogaseyo. — anieyo, gwaenchanayo. maeumman badeulgeyo.
examples.en: Take this. — No really, I'm fine. I appreciate the thought.
examples.note: 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll just take the thought') softens the refusal

examples.ko: 제가 도와드릴게요. — 아, 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 혼자 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jega dowadeurilgeyo. — a, anieyo, gwaenchanayo. honja hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: Let me help you. — Oh no, it's fine. I can do it alone.
examples.note: Declining offered help while reassuring them

expressions.nuance: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 stacks 아니에요 ('it's not so / no') in front of 괜찮아요 to make a refusal that is both clear and warm — the 아니에요 firmly turns down the offer while 괜찮아요 reassures 'I'm okay, don't worry about me.' Koreans typically offer two or three times out of politeness, so you often need this stronger version when one 괜찮아요 isn't taken. Register: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 is polite; 아니야, 괜찮아 with friends; 아닙니다, 괜찮습니다 formally. The key learner point is that 아니에요 (the soft 'it's not / no') is the natural refusal particle here, NOT 아니요 — though both exist, 아니에요 flows better before 괜찮아요 and sounds gentler. A trap: do NOT decline a gift or kindness with a cold single 싫어요 ('I don't like/want it'), which is for genuine dislike and sounds harsh; 싫어요 to a host's food can be offensive. Another English-speaker error is over-insisting in a Western way ('no, no, I really couldn't') with literal translations; the natural Korean cushions are 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll accept just the thought') or 부담스러워요 ('it makes me feel indebted').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Refusing food or a gift with 싫어요.
싫어요 means 'I dislike/don't want it' and sounds harsh or ungrateful about someone's kindness. Use 아니에요, 괜찮아요 to decline warmly.
Confusing 아니에요 with 아니요 and overusing the curt form.
아니요 is a plain 'no'; 아니에요 ('it's not so') is the softer refusal that pairs naturally here: 아니에요, 괜찮아요. Lead with 아니에요 to sound gentle.
Giving up after one 괜찮아요 and accepting because they offered again.
Re-offering is Korean politeness, not pressure. If you truly don't want it, repeat 아니에요, 괜찮아요 or 진짜 괜찮아요 — repetition is expected, not rude.

structuredNuance.t: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 stacks 아니에요 ('it's not so / no') in front of 괜찮아요 to make a refusal that is both clear and warm — the 아니에요 firmly turns down the offer while 괜찮아요 reassures 'I'm okay, don't worry about me.' Koreans typically offer two or three times out of politeness, so you often need this stronger version when one 괜찮아요 isn't taken.

Do NOT decline a gift or kindness with a cold single 싫어요 ('I don't like/want it'), which is for genuine dislike and sounds harsh; 싫어요 to a host's food can be offensive. The natural Korean cushions instead are 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll accept just the thought') or 부담스러워요 ('it makes me feel indebted').
Register: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 is polite; 아니야, 괜찮아 with friends; 아닙니다, 괜찮습니다 formally.

The key learner point is that 아니에요 (the soft 'it's not / no') is the natural refusal particle here, NOT 아니요 — though both exist, 아니에요 flows better before 괜찮아요 and sounds gentler. Another error is over-insisting in a Western way ('no, no, I really couldn't') with literal translations.

expressions.english: Right now isn't great for me
expressions.shortExplanation: 지금은 좀 그래요 is a practical expression meaning "Right now isn't great for me".
expressions.explanation: 지금은 좀 그래요 (jigeumeun jom geuraeyo) means "Right now isn't great for me". Say it as one set phrase — for example 지금은 좀 그래요 ("Now isn't a great time"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; vague soft refusal without giving a reason
반말, to a friend
Formal, to a senior or in business
Swap 지금은 for 그건 to call a specific thing awkward

examples.en: Now isn't really a good time.
examples.note: Declining an invite or request without spelling out why

examples.ko: 오늘 같이 술 한잔 어때요? — 아, 오늘은 좀 그래요. 다음에요.
examples.romanization: oneul gachi sul hanjan eottaeyo? — a, oneureun jom geuraeyo. daeumeyo.
examples.en: How about a drink today? — Ah, today's not great for me. Another time.
examples.note: Softly declining tonight while leaving the door open with 다음에요

examples.ko: 이 가격에 어떠세요? — 음… 그건 좀 그런데요.
examples.romanization: i gagyeoge eotteoseyo? — eum… geugeon jom geureondeyo.
examples.en: How about this price? — Hmm… that's a bit much.
examples.note: Using 그건 좀 그런데요 to push back on an offer without flat rejection

expressions.nuance: 좀 그래요 is one of the most Korean phrases there is: literally '(it's) a bit like that', it deliberately leaves the negative UNSAID. 그렇다 ('to be so/like that') stands in for an awkward, uncomfortable, or undesirable quality the speaker won't name, and 좀 ('a bit') softens it further — so the whole thing means 'it's kind of… not ideal' without you ever having to say why. This indirectness is the point: it declines or expresses reluctance while saving everyone's face. Register: polite 좀 그래요, casual 좀 그래, formal 좀 그렇습니다 / 좀 그런데요. The dividing line from 안 돼요 ('it's not possible / no') is bluntness — 안 돼요 is a hard no, while 좀 그래요 is a soft, deniable 'eh, not really.' The huge English-speaker trap is treating 그래요 as 'yes, that's right' (its other meaning, as agreement) — but 좀 그래요 with a hesitant tone is the OPPOSITE: a polite refusal. Another error is demanding or expecting a reason; Korean culture accepts 좀 그래요 as a complete, reason-free decline, and pressing 'why?' (왜요?) can feel pushy. Deliver it with a slight trailing tone and maybe 좀 그런데요 to invite the other person to back off gracefully.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing 좀 그래요 as 'yes, that's right'.
Plain 그래요 can mean 'that's so/okay', but 좀 그래요 with a hesitant tone is a soft refusal meaning 'it's kind of not great'. Read the 좀 and the tone.
Demanding a reason after someone says 좀 그래요.
It's intentionally vague to save face. Pressing 왜요? ('why?') feels pushy. Accept it as a polite 'no', or offer an alternative like 다음에요.
Using 좀 그래요 for a hard, non-negotiable no.
It signals mild reluctance, not a firm refusal. If you absolutely cannot, say 안 돼요 or 어려울 것 같아요; 좀 그래요 may sound like you could still be persuaded.

expressions.shortExplanation: 다음에 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll do it next time".
expressions.explanation: "I'll do it next time" — that is 다음에 할게요 (daeume halgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다음에 할게요 ("I'll do it next time"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declines now but promises later
반말, to a friend
Formal 합쇼체, to a senior or at work
Short form; just 'next time' as a gentle pass

examples.en: I'll do it next time.
examples.note: Politely passing on something offered now

examples.ko: 같이 점심 어때요? — 오늘은 약속이 있어서, 다음에 할게요.
examples.romanization: gachi jeomsim eottaeyo? — oneureun yaksogi isseoseo, daeume halgeyo.
examples.en: Lunch together? — I have plans today, so let's do it next time.
examples.note: Give a light reason, then defer with 다음에 할게요

examples.ko: 멤버십 가입하시겠어요? — 아, 다음에 할게요. 오늘은 그냥 살게요.
examples.romanization: membeosip gaipasigesseoyo? — a, daeume halgeyo. oneureun geunyang salgeyo.
examples.en: Would you like to sign up for membership? — Ah, maybe next time. I'll just buy it today.
examples.note: Declining a sales pitch politely while still making the purchase

expressions.nuance: 다음에 할게요 is 다음에 ('next time') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 promise/intention form of 하다 'to do'), meaning 'I'll do it next time' — a soft refusal that declines the present offer while leaving the relationship warm by implying you'll come back to it. The -ㄹ게요 ending is key: it frames the deferral as YOUR own intention/promise, which feels considerate. Often it's just politeness, not a real commitment — both sides understand 다음에 ('next time') may never come, like the English 'maybe some other time.' Register: 다음에 할게요 polite, 다음에 할게 casual, 다음에 하겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from 안 할게요 ('I won't do it') is that 안 할게요 closes the door, while 다음에 할게요 keeps it ajar — much softer for declining invitations, sign-ups, or offers. The English-speaker trap is using 다음에 합시다 ('let's do it next time') when YOU are the one declining: 합시다 ('let's') is a suggestion/command to the group and can sound like you're scheduling them, whereas 할게요 humbly states your own choice. Another error is over-promising — Koreans read 다음에 할게요 as a polite brush-off, so don't be hurt if a 다음에 plan never materializes, and don't feel you broke a promise if yours doesn't either.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 다음에 합시다 when you're the one declining.
-합시다 ('let's') suggests/orders the group and can sound presumptuous. To politely defer your own participation, say 다음에 할게요 (your intention), not 합시다.
Taking or making 다음에 as a firm appointment.
다음에 할게요 is often a gentle brush-off, like 'some other time'. Don't treat it as a scheduled commitment, and don't feel guilty if it doesn't happen.
Confusing 할게요 with 하고 싶어요.
하고 싶어요 means 'I want to do it'. To politely defer doing it now, say 다음에 할게요. Saying 다음에 하고 싶어요 sounds like expressing a wish, not declining the present offer.

expressions.shortExplanation: 다음에 갈게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll go next time".
expressions.explanation: 다음에 갈게요 (daeume galgeyo) = "I'll go next time". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다음에 갈게요 ("I'll go next time"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declines an outing but stays friendly
반말, to a friend inviting you out
Formal, to a senior or boss
다음 기회에 ('next opportunity') sounds a touch warmer/sincerer

examples.en: I'll go next time.
examples.note: Turning down an invitation to go somewhere together

examples.ko: 회식 오실 거죠? — 오늘은 몸이 안 좋아서, 다음에 갈게요.
examples.romanization: hoesik osil geojyo? — oneureun momi an joaseo, daeume galgeyo.
examples.en: You're coming to the work dinner, right? — I'm not feeling well today, so I'll go next time.
examples.note: Declining a 회식 (company dinner) with a health reason

examples.ko: 노래방 갈래요? — 저는 먼저 갈게요. 다음에 같이 가요.
examples.romanization: noraebang gallaeyo? — jeoneun meonjeo galgeyo. daeume gachi gayo.
examples.en: Wanna go to noraebang? — I'll head off first. Let's go together next time.
examples.note: Bowing out now while proposing a real future plan with 다음에 같이 가요

expressions.nuance: 다음에 갈게요 is 다음에 ('next time') + 갈게요 (-ㄹ게요 form of 가다 'to go'), the standard soft way to decline an invitation to go somewhere — a meal, a 회식 (work dinner), a 노래방 trip — while signalling goodwill ('I'll join next time'). Like 다음에 할게요, it is often a courteous brush-off rather than a firm plan, especially for the near-obligatory Korean 회식 culture where bowing out gracefully matters. Register: 갈게요 polite, 갈게 casual, 가겠습니다 formal. A warmer, more sincere upgrade is 다음 기회에 꼭 갈게요 ('I'll definitely go next chance'), where 꼭 ('for sure') signals you really mean it. The dividing line from 안 갈게요 ('I won't go') is openness — 안 갈게요 flatly refuses, which can feel cold for a group invite, while 다음에 갈게요 declines without rejecting the relationship. The English-speaker trap is pairing it with the wrong particle on the place: Korean marks the destination with -에 (회식에 갈게요), and learners often misuse -에서 (which is for the location of an action, not the destination). Another error is treating a refused 회식 lightly in a strict workplace; even with 다음에 갈게요, add a real reason (몸이 안 좋아서, 선약이 있어서) to soften it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the destination with -에서 instead of -에.
Destination of 가다 takes -에: 회식에 갈게요. -에서 marks where an action happens, so 회식에서 갈게요 is wrong for 'go to the dinner'.
Declining a 회식 with a bare 안 갈게요 and no reason.
In many Korean workplaces a flat refusal sounds cold. Soften with a reason plus 다음에 갈게요: 오늘은 선약이 있어서 다음에 갈게요.
Promising 다음에 꼭 갈게요 you don't mean.
꼭 ('definitely') raises the commitment. If it's really just a polite pass, plain 다음에 갈게요 is enough; over-promising with 꼭 can create expectations.

expressions.english: Today won't work for me, I think
expressions.shortExplanation: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "Today won't work for me, I think".
expressions.explanation: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 (oneureun an doel geot gatayo) means "Today won't work for me, I think". Say it as one set phrase — for example 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 ("Today probably won't work"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; softened 'no' using '~것 같다' (it seems)
반말, to a friend
Formal, swapping in 어렵다 for the workplace
힘들다 ('to be hard') variant, very common spoken hedge

examples.en: I don't think today will work.
examples.note: Turning down a same-day plan gently

examples.ko: 이따 잠깐 볼 수 있어요? — 죄송한데 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: itta jamkkan bol su isseoyo? — joesonghande oneureun an doel geot gatayo.
examples.en: Can we meet briefly later? — Sorry, but today probably won't work.
examples.note: 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') + the hedge makes a courteous refusal

examples.ko: 내일까지 끝낼 수 있을까요? — 음, 솔직히 내일까지는 힘들 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: naeilkkaji kkeunnael su isseulkkayo? — eum, soljiki naeilkkajineun himdeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: Could you finish it by tomorrow? — Hmm, honestly by tomorrow seems tough.
examples.note: Hedging on a deadline you can't meet without a flat 'no'

expressions.nuance: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 wraps a refusal in the hedge -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems / I think'), turning a flat 안 돼요 ('it's not possible') into the much gentler 'I don't think it'll work.' That -것 같다 is the single most important softening tool in Korean: by framing the 'no' as your tentative impression rather than a hard fact, you avoid sounding blunt or final. 오늘은 ('as for today', with the topic particle 은 implying contrast) hints 'maybe another day', which softens further. Register: 안 될 것 같아요 polite, 안 될 것 같아 casual, 어려울/안 될 것 같습니다 formal. Common swap-ins are 어렵다 ('to be difficult') and 힘들다 ('to be hard/tough') — 어려울 것 같아요 and 힘들 것 같아요 are slightly more graceful than the plain 안 되다. The English-speaker trap is dropping the hedge and saying a bald 오늘 안 돼요, which is grammatically fine but socially harder; Koreans almost always cushion refusals with 것 같다. Another error is mixing the form up as 안 될 거 같아요 vs the textbook 안 될 것 같아요 — both are heard (거 is the casual contraction of 것), so don't be thrown. Adding 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') at the front is the natural, polite opener for declining.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Declining with a bald 오늘 안 돼요 and no hedge.
It's correct but blunt. Soften with -것 같다: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요. The hedge frames it as your impression, not a hard refusal, which is far more polite.
Building the form wrong, e.g. 안 돼 것 같아요.
The pattern is verb-stem + -ㄹ/을 것 같다. From 안 되다 you get 안 될 것 같아요 (future-leaning) — not 안 돼 것 같아요. Keep the -ㄹ 것 같다 frame.
Forgetting 오늘은 leaves no 'maybe later' nuance.
The topic 은 in 오늘은 implies contrast ('today specifically'), hinting another day is fine. Dropping it (오늘 안 될 것 같아요) is okay but loses that soft, door-open feeling.

expressions.shortExplanation: 생각해 볼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll think about it".
expressions.explanation: "I'll think about it" — that is 생각해 볼게요 (saenggakae bolgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 생각해 볼게요 ("I'll think about it"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; non-committal, often a soft no
반말, to a friend
Formal 합쇼체, business or to a senior

usagePhrases.en: Let me think a bit more
usagePhrases.note: Add 좀 더 ('a bit more') to ask for time / hedge harder

examples.en: I'll think about it.
examples.note: Non-committal reply to an offer or a sales pitch

examples.ko: 이 제품 어떠세요? — 음, 생각해 볼게요. 좀 둘러보고 올게요.
examples.romanization: i jepum eotteoseyo? — eum, saenggakae bolgeyo. jom dulleobogo olgeyo.
examples.en: How about this product? — Hmm, I'll think about it. Let me look around.
examples.note: Politely escaping a pushy salesperson

examples.ko: 주말에 등산 같이 갈래요? — 오, 좋은데… 생각해 볼게요. 일정 보고 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jumare deungsan gachi gallaeyo? — o, joeunde… saenggakae bolgeyo. iljeong bogo yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: Want to hike this weekend? — Oh, sounds good… I'll think about it. I'll check my schedule and let you know.
examples.note: Buying time on an invite while leaving it genuinely open

expressions.nuance: 생각해 볼게요 is 생각하다 ('to think') + -아/어 보다 ('to try doing') + -ㄹ게요 (intention), literally 'I'll try thinking about it' — i.e. 'I'll consider it.' The -어 보다 ('give it a try') makes it tentative, and like in English, 'I'll think about it' is frequently a polite, face-saving NO, especially toward salespeople and pushy invitations. But it can also be a genuine 'let me check' — context and tone decide. Register: 생각해 볼게요 polite, 생각해 볼게 casual, 생각해 보겠습니다 formal/business. The dividing line from 안 살게요 / 안 할게요 ('I won't buy/do it') is that those are clear refusals, while 생각해 볼게요 declines softly and defers, avoiding an awkward direct 'no.' The English-speaker trap is treating it as a firm commitment to genuinely deliberate and then feeling obligated — in Korean service contexts it's understood as a graceful exit. Another error is omitting the -어 보다 and saying 생각할게요, which sounds more like 'I will think (definitely)' and is heavier; the natural hedge keeps 보다. To buy time more explicitly, add 좀 더 ('a bit more') or follow with 둘러보고 올게요 ('I'll look around and come back'), the classic line for leaving a shop without buying.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 보다 and saying 생각할게요.
생각할게요 sounds like a firmer 'I will think (about it)'. The natural non-committal hedge keeps -어 보다: 생각해 볼게요 ('I'll try to think it over').
Reading it as a firm promise to deliberate.
Toward salespeople and many invites it's a polite 'no'. Don't feel bound to actually decide, and don't expect a definite yes when someone says it to you.
Confusing 생각해 볼게요 with 생각이 나요.
생각이 나요 means 'it comes to mind / I remember'. To say 'I'll consider it', use 생각해 볼게요. They share 생각 but mean different things.

But it can also be a genuine 'let me check' — context and tone decide. The dividing line from 안 살게요 / 안 할게요 ('I won't buy/do it') is that those are clear refusals, while 생각해 볼게요 declines softly and defers, avoiding an awkward direct 'no.'
생각해 볼게요 is 생각하다 ('to think') + -아/어 보다 ('to try doing') + -ㄹ게요 (intention).
Register: 생각해 볼게요 polite, 생각해 볼게 casual, 생각해 보겠습니다 formal/business.

expressions.english: It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable
expressions.shortExplanation: 좀 부담스러워요 is a practical expression meaning "It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable".
expressions.explanation: 좀 부담스러워요 (jom budamseureowoyo) = "It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 좀 부담스러워요 ("It's a bit much for me"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: It's a bit much for me
usagePhrases.note: Polite; declining because it feels like too big a favor/gift
반말, to a friend
Formal, in business or to a senior
Flip side: what you say to relieve someone else's pressure

examples.en: It feels like a bit much.
examples.note: Declining an over-generous gift or gesture

examples.ko: 이거 받으세요. — 아유, 이렇게까지… 좀 부담스러워요.
examples.romanization: igeo badeuseyo. — ayu, ireokekkaji… jom budamseureowoyo.
examples.en: Please take this. — Oh, you didn't have to… this is a bit much.
examples.note: 이렇게까지 ('to go this far') + 부담스러워요 to refuse an extravagant gift

examples.ko: 제가 다 계산할게요. — 아니에요, 그러면 제가 너무 부담스러워요. 더치페이해요.
examples.romanization: jega da gyesanhalgeyo. — anieyo, geureomyeon jega neomu budamseureowoyo. deochipeihaeyo.
examples.en: I'll pay for everything. — No, then I'd feel too indebted. Let's split it.
examples.note: Declining to be treated, proposing 더치페이 (Dutch pay) instead

expressions.nuance: 부담스럽다 means 'to feel burdened / pressured / indebted' — it describes the uncomfortable feeling of receiving something so generous that you feel you owe the giver. 좀 부담스러워요 ('it's a bit much for me') is the polite way to decline an over-the-top gift, an offer to pay, or a favor that feels too big, precisely BECAUSE Korean relationships track reciprocity (정 and obligation). Saying it signals 'your kindness is so great it makes me uneasy' — a culturally fluent, face-saving refusal. Register: 부담스러워요 polite, 부담스러워 casual, 부담스럽습니다 formal. The flip side is 부담 갖지 마세요 ('don't feel obligated'), what the GIVER says to put you at ease — knowing both lets you navigate the back-and-forth. The dividing line from 싫어요 ('I dislike it') is crucial: 싫어요 rejects the THING, which is rude about a gift, while 부담스러워요 praises the gesture as too generous — it declines while honoring the giver. The English-speaker trap is mistranslating 부담 as merely 'pressure/stress' and missing the indebtedness nuance, or using 스트레스 받아요 ('I'm stressed'), which is about general stress, not the specific 'this is too much kindness' feeling. Pair it with 마음만 받을게요 ('I'll accept just the thought') for the most graceful refusal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Declining a gift with 싫어요 instead of 부담스러워요.
싫어요 rejects the item and sounds ungrateful. 부담스러워요 declines by honoring the gesture as too generous — the polite, relationship-safe choice.
Translating 부담스럽다 as plain 'stressful' and using 스트레스 받아요.
스트레스 받아요 is general stress. 부담스럽다 specifically means feeling indebted by someone's kindness. Use 부담스러워요 to decline over-generosity.
Saying 부담돼요 instead of 부담스러워요.
The adjective for the feeling is 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요. 부담이 되다 ('to become a burden') is also valid but conjugated 부담이 돼요; don't blend them into the non-standard 부담돼요 in this slot.

expressions.shortExplanation: 마음만 받을게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll just accept the thought".
expressions.explanation: 마음만 받을게요 (maeumman badeulgeyo) means "I'll just accept the thought". Say it as one set phrase — for example 마음만 받을게요 ("I'll accept just the thought"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; graciously refuses a gift while honoring the giver
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I shall accept your kind thought
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, very gracious

usagePhrases.en: Just the thought is more than enough
usagePhrases.note: Warmer expansion stressing gratitude

examples.en: I'll just accept the thought.
examples.note: Refusing a gift kindly without seeming ungrateful

examples.ko: 이거 작은 거예요, 받으세요. — 아유, 마음만 받을게요. 정말 감사해요.
examples.romanization: igeo jageun geoyeyo, badeuseyo. — ayu, maeumman badeulgeyo. jeongmal gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: It's just a small thing, please take it. — Oh, I'll just accept the thought. Thank you so much.
examples.note: The standard warm refusal of a gift, capped with thanks

examples.ko: 용돈 좀 드릴게요. — 아니에요, 어머니. 마음만 받을게요. 저 충분해요.
examples.romanization: yongdon jom deurilgeyo. — anieyo, eomeoni. maeumman badeulgeyo. jeo chungbunhaeyo.
examples.en: Let me give you some pocket money. — No, mother. I'll just accept the thought. I have enough.
examples.note: Declining money from an elder while honoring their care

expressions.nuance: 마음만 받을게요 is 마음 ('heart/thought/intention') + 만 ('only') + 받을게요 ('I'll receive', -ㄹ게요 form of 받다), literally 'I'll receive only the heart' — i.e. 'I appreciate the gesture, but I can't take the gift itself.' It is the most graceful, culturally fluent way to refuse a present, money, or a favor: you accept the GIVER'S kindness (마음) while declining the object, so no one loses face. The particle 만 ('only') is the whole engine — it narrows acceptance to the intention. Register: 받을게요 polite, 받을게 casual, 받겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from a flat 안 받을게요 ('I won't take it') is warmth — 안 받을게요 can sound like rejecting the person, while 마음만 받을게요 explicitly cherishes their thought. The English-speaker trap is having no direct equivalent and resorting to literal 'it's the thought that counts' translations that don't exist idiomatically; just memorize 마음만 받을게요 as a set phrase. Another error is misreading 마음 as only 'mind/heart' in the emotional sense — here it means the giver's caring intention. Pair it with 부담스러워요 ('it's too much') and 감사해요 for a complete, gracious refusal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Refusing a gift with a flat 안 받을게요.
안 받을게요 ('I won't take it') can feel like rejecting the person. 마음만 받을게요 accepts their kindness while declining the object — warmer and face-saving.
Dropping 만 and saying 마음 받을게요.
The 만 ('only') is essential: it means you take ONLY the thought, not the gift. Without it, 마음 받을게요 loses the whole 'just the gesture' meaning.
Trying to translate 'it's the thought that counts' literally.
Korean has no word-for-word version; the set phrase is 마음만 받을게요. Don't construct 생각이 중요해요 — memorize this idiom for refusing gifts.

expressions.shortExplanation: 선약이 있어서요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a prior engagement".
expressions.explanation: "I have a prior engagement" — that is 선약이 있어서요 (seonyagi isseoseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 선약이 있어서요 ("I have prior plans, so…"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a respectable reason to decline, trailing off
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I have a prior engagement, so it'll be difficult
usagePhrases.note: Formal, completing the sentence for the workplace
약속 ('appointment') is the everyday-word equivalent

examples.en: I have prior plans, so…
examples.note: Declining an invite by citing an existing commitment

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 시간 돼요? — 아, 죄송해요. 오늘은 선약이 있어서요.
examples.romanization: oneul jeonyeoge sigan dwaeyo? — a, joesonghaeyo. oneureun seonyagi isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Free this evening? — Ah, I'm sorry. I already have plans today.
examples.note: The polite trailing -서요 lets you decline without a blunt full stop

examples.ko: 회식 참석 가능하세요? — 죄송합니다. 그날은 선약이 있어서 참석이 어려울 것 같습니다.
examples.romanization: hoesik chamseok ganeunghaseyo? — joesonghamnida. geunareun seonyagi isseoseo chamseogi eoryeoul geot gatseumnida.
examples.en: Can you attend the work dinner? — I'm sorry. I have a prior engagement that day, so attending will be difficult.
examples.note: Formal workplace refusal stacking 선약 + 어려울 것 같다

expressions.nuance: 선약이 있어서요 is 선약 (Sino-Korean 先約, 'a prior appointment') + 이 있어서 ('because there is') + 요, used to decline by naming an existing commitment — a socially solid, blame-free reason. The magic is the trailing -서요 ('because…, so…'): it leaves the sentence unfinished, letting the listener infer 'so I can't make it' without you having to say the hard 'no' out loud — a hallmark of polite Korean refusals. 선약 is slightly more formal/elegant than the everyday 약속 ('appointment/promise'); both work, but 선약 specifically stresses it was arranged FIRST, which strengthens the excuse. Register: 선약이 있어서요 polite, 선약 있어서 casual, 선약이 있어서 어렵겠습니다 formal. The English-speaker trap is the false friend with 약속: 약속 means both 'appointment' and 'promise', so beginners may say 약속이 있어요 fine, but then mistranslate 'I promise' situations; in declining, stick to 선약/약속 있어서요 for 'I have other plans.' Another error is ending too abruptly with 선약이 있어요 (full stop), which is correct but loses the soft, deferential trail; the -서요 ending is what makes it gentle. Open with 죄송한데 / 죄송해요 to cushion it further.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Ending bluntly with 선약이 있어요 (full stop).
It's correct but final-sounding. The softer refusal trails with -서요: 선약이 있어서요. The unfinished clause lets the listener gracefully infer the 'no'.
Confusing 약속 as only 'promise'.
약속 means both 'appointment' and 'promise'. For declining, 약속/선약 있어서요 means 'I have other plans'. Don't avoid it thinking it only means a vow.
Saying 선약을 있어서요 with the object particle.
있다 ('to exist/have') takes the subject particle 이/가, not 을/를: 선약이 있어서요, never 선약을 있어서요.

expressions.english: If it's okay with you, maybe next time
expressions.shortExplanation: 괜찮으시면 다음에 is a practical expression meaning "If it's okay with you, maybe next time".
expressions.explanation: 괜찮으시면 다음에 (gwaenchaneusimyeon daeume) = "If it's okay with you, maybe next time". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 괜찮으시면 다음에 ("If you don't mind, next time"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: If you don't mind, next time
usagePhrases.note: Polite; defers using honorific 시 to respect the other person
반말/plain, to a friend or peer

usagePhrases.en: If you're okay with it, I'll do it next chance
usagePhrases.note: Formal full sentence for work

usagePhrases.en: If you happen to be okay with it
usagePhrases.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') makes it extra tentative

examples.en: If it's okay with you, let's do it next time.
examples.note: Deferring respectfully to someone senior

examples.ko: 오늘 한잔 어떠세요? — 아, 부장님, 괜찮으시면 다음에 모실게요. 오늘은 몸이 좀…
examples.romanization: oneul hanjan eotteoseyo? — a, bujangnim, gwaenchaneusimyeon daeume mosilgeyo. oneureun momi jom…
examples.en: How about a drink today? — Ah, sir, if you don't mind, I'll treat you next time. Today I'm a bit…
examples.note: Declining a senior's invite with 모시다 (humble 'serve/accompany')

examples.ko: 지금 회의 가능할까요? — 죄송한데, 괜찮으시면 30분 뒤에 해도 될까요?
examples.romanization: jigeum hoeui ganeunghalkkayo? — joesonghande, gwaenchaneusimyeon 30bun dwie haedo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Could we meet now? — Sorry, but if it's okay with you, could we do it in 30 minutes?
examples.note: Using the frame to politely push a request, not just refuse

expressions.nuance: 괜찮으시면 다음에 is 괜찮다 ('to be okay') + the honorific infix -시- + the conditional -면 ('if'), so 괜찮으시면 = 'if YOU (respectfully) are okay with it', followed by 다음에 ('next time'). It declines or postpones while explicitly handing the decision to the other person's comfort — the honorific 시 elevates THEM, making this ideal for declining a senior, boss, or anyone you must respect. The conditional 'if you're okay' frame is deeply polite because it asks permission to defer rather than just announcing it. Register: 괜찮으시면 (honorific, to superiors), 괜찮으면 (plain, to peers/friends). The crucial learner point is the honorific 시: you put 시 on the OTHER person's state (괜찮으시면), never on your own actions humbly — mixing this up (e.g. honoring yourself) is a classic register error. The English-speaker trap is dropping 시 with a senior and saying 괜찮으면, which is too flat/casual upward, or conversely over-stacking honorifics awkwardly. Pair it with humble verbs toward seniors: 모실게요 ('I'll accompany/treat you', humble) or 하겠습니다. Add 혹시 ('by any chance') up front for maximum tentativeness. This frame also works to soften REQUESTS, not just refusals ('if you're okay with it, could we…?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using plain 괜찮으면 toward a boss or elder.
Upward, you should honor their state with 시: 괜찮으시면. 괜찮으면 is for peers/friends and sounds too flat when deferring to a senior.
Putting 시 on your own humble action.
Honorific 시 elevates the OTHER person (괜찮으시면 = 'if you're okay'). For your own action, stay humble: 다음에 할게요 / 모실게요 — don't honor yourself.
Reading it as only a refusal.
괜찮으시면 + clause is a general polite softener. It can defer ('if okay, next time') OR soften a request ('if okay, could we…?'). Use it both ways.

This frame also works to soften REQUESTS, not just refusals ('if you're okay with it, could we…?').

expressions.english: That'll probably be a bit difficult
expressions.shortExplanation: 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "That'll probably be a bit difficult".
expressions.explanation: 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 (geugeon jom eoryeoul geot gatayo) means "That'll probably be a bit difficult". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 ("That'll be a bit hard, I think"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: That'll be a bit hard, I think
usagePhrases.note: Polite; firm-but-soft 'no' to a request
반말, to a friend
Formal 합쇼체, business refusal

usagePhrases.ko: 그건 제가 좀 곤란할 것 같아요
usagePhrases.romanization: geugeon jega jom gollanhal geot gatayo
usagePhrases.en: That would put me in a tough spot
usagePhrases.note: 곤란하다 ('to be in a bind') variant for an awkward ask

examples.en: That'll be a bit difficult, I think.
examples.note: Declining a specific request without a flat 'no'

examples.ko: 주말에도 좀 나와 줄 수 있어요? — 아… 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요. 주말엔 가족이랑 약속이 있어서요.
examples.romanization: jumaredo jom nawa jul su isseoyo? — a… geugeon jom eoryeoul geot gatayo. jumaren gajogirang yaksogi isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Could you come in on weekends too? — Ah… that'll be a bit difficult. I have family plans on weekends.
examples.note: Refusing extra work with a hedge plus a reason

examples.ko: 가격 좀 더 깎아 주실 수 있어요? — 죄송한데 그건 좀 어려울 것 같습니다. 이미 많이 빼 드린 거예요.
examples.romanization: gagyeok jom deo kkakka jusil su isseoyo? — joesonghande geugeon jom eoryeoul geot gatseumnida. imi mani ppae deurin geoyeyo.
examples.en: Could you discount it a bit more? — Sorry, but that'll be difficult. I've already taken a lot off.
examples.note: A seller declining a further discount politely but firmly

expressions.nuance: 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 combines 그건 ('that (thing), as for it') + 좀 ('a bit') + 어렵다 ('to be difficult') + the hedge -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems') into the go-to polite-but-firm refusal of a specific request. Here 어렵다 ('difficult') is a euphemism for 'impossible / no' — Koreans rarely say a blunt 안 돼요 ('can't') to a request when they can say 'that would be difficult', which softens the rejection while still being clearly negative. The -것 같다 hedge and the cushioning 좀 add deniability and politeness. Register: 어려울 것 같아요 polite, 어려울 것 같아 casual, 어려울 것 같습니다 formal. The dividing line from 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 (the time-based 'today won't work') is scope — 그건 ('that') targets the specific request/condition itself, making it the right tool to refuse a demand, a discount ask, an extra task. The English-speaker trap is taking 어렵다 literally as 'difficult but possible with effort' and then pushing harder ('but could you try?'); in refusal context it means 'no', so pressing is impolite. Another error is omitting the hedge for a bald 그건 어려워요, which is harsher; keep 좀 + 것 같다. A near-synonym is 곤란하다 ('to be in an awkward bind'), used when the ask would personally embarrass or trouble you.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Taking 어렵다 as 'hard but doable' and pushing harder.
In a refusal, 어려울 것 같아요 is a polite 'no'. Pressing 'but could you try?' ignores the soft rejection and feels rude. Treat it as a decline.
Dropping the hedge: 그건 어려워요.
Bald 어려워요 is harsher. The natural soft refusal keeps the cushion: 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 — 좀 plus -것 같다 makes it gentle and face-saving.
Confusing 어렵다 (difficult) with 어둡다 (dark) or 두렵다 (afraid).
They look similar but only 어렵다 means 'difficult'. For a refusal say 어려울 것 같아요; 어두울/두려울 것 같아요 mean entirely different things.

structuredNuance.t: 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 is the go-to polite-but-firm refusal of a specific request. Here 어렵다 ('difficult') is a euphemism for 'impossible / no' — Koreans rarely say a blunt 안 돼요 ('can't') to a request when they can say 'that would be difficult', which softens the rejection while still being clearly negative. The -것 같다 hedge and the cushioning 좀 add deniability and politeness.

The dividing line from 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요 (the time-based 'today won't work') is scope — 그건 ('that') targets the specific request/condition itself, making it the right tool to refuse a demand, a discount ask, an extra task. A near-synonym is 곤란하다 ('to be in an awkward bind'), used when the ask would personally embarrass or trouble you.
그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요 combines 그건 ('that (thing), as for it') + 좀 ('a bit') + 어렵다 ('to be difficult') + the hedge -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems').

expressions.shortExplanation: 어렵겠는데요 is a practical expression meaning "That'd be tough, I'm afraid".
expressions.explanation: "That'd be tough, I'm afraid" — that is 어렵겠는데요 (eoryeopgenneundeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 어렵겠는데요 ("That'd be tough, I'm afraid…"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; soft refusal with conjecture 겠 + trailing 는데요
반말, to a friend
Formal 합쇼체, clean business 'no'
Add 좀 to soften the refusal even more

examples.en: That'd be tough, I'm afraid.
examples.note: Reacting to a request you can't grant, trailing off

examples.ko: 내일까지 가능할까요? — 음, 내일까지는 좀 어렵겠는데요. 모레는 어떠세요?
examples.romanization: naeilkkaji ganeunghalkkayo? — eum, naeilkkajineun jom eoryeopgenneundeyo. moreneun eotteoseyo?
examples.en: Possible by tomorrow? — Hmm, by tomorrow would be tough. How about the day after?
examples.note: Decline the deadline, then counter-propose with 모레는 어떠세요

examples.ko: 환불 가능한가요? — 아, 영수증이 없으시면 환불은 좀 어렵겠는데요.
examples.romanization: hwanbul ganeunghangayo? — a, yeongsujeungi eopseusimyeon hwanbureun jom eoryeopgenneundeyo.
examples.en: Can I get a refund? — Ah, without a receipt a refund would be difficult.
examples.note: A staff member softly refusing a refund using 어렵겠는데요

expressions.nuance: 어렵겠는데요 packs three softeners onto 어렵다 ('to be difficult'): the conjecture/volition marker -겠- ('would/probably be'), and the trailing connective -는데요 ('…, but / you see…'). The result is a beautifully indirect refusal: 'it would be difficult, you see…' — the -겠- makes it a soft prediction rather than a flat fact, and -는데요 leaves the sentence dangling, inviting the listener to read 'so, no' and to respond. This is the polished register staff and professionals use to decline requests (refunds, deadlines, exceptions) without an offensive 안 돼요. Register: 어렵겠는데요 polite, 어렵겠는데 casual, 어렵겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from 어려워요 (plain 'it's difficult') is the layered hedging — 어렵겠는데요 is markedly softer and more deferential, ideal upward or to customers. The English-speaker trap is hearing the trailing -는데요 as an incomplete, confused sentence and waiting for more; in Korean the dangling ending IS the polite point — it's complete as a soft refusal. Another error is misusing -겠- as simple future ('I will') rather than its conjecture sense here ('would/likely'). Crucially, recognize 어렵겠는데요 from the OTHER side too: when a clerk says it to you, it means 'no, sorry' — don't keep pushing. A natural follow-up is to counter-offer (모레는 어떠세요? 'how about the day after?').

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

From the other side it's a courteous 'no'. Continuing to press is impolite. Accept it, or politely propose an alternative (모레는 어떠세요?).

expressions.english: Let me think it over and get back to you
expressions.shortExplanation: 생각 좀 해 보고 연락드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "Let me think it over and get back to you".
expressions.explanation: 생각 좀 해 보고 연락드릴게요 (saenggak jom hae bogo yeollakdeurilgeyo) = "Let me think it over and get back to you". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 생각 좀 해 보고 연락드릴게요 ("Let me think it over and contact you"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Let me think it over and contact you
usagePhrases.note: Polite; buys time with humble 연락드리다

usagePhrases.en: Let me think and I'll call you
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I'll consider it and get back to you
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, business

usagePhrases.en: Let me look into it and get back to you
usagePhrases.note: 알아보다 ('look into') variant when you need to check, not just think

examples.en: Let me think it over and get back to you.
examples.note: Deferring a decision without committing either way

examples.ko: 계약하시겠어요? — 큰 결정이라서, 생각 좀 해 보고 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: gyeyakasigesseoyo? — keun gyeoljeongiraseo, saenggak jom hae bogo yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: Will you sign the contract? — It's a big decision, so let me think it over and get back to you.
examples.note: 큰 결정이라서 ('since it's a big decision') justifies taking time

examples.ko: 저희 모임에 들어오실래요? — 아, 감사해요. 생각 좀 해 보고 연락드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jeohui moime deureoosillaeyo? — a, gamsahaeyo. saenggak jom hae bogo yeollakdeurilgeyo.
examples.en: Want to join our group? — Oh, thank you. Let me think about it and I'll let you know.
examples.note: Politely non-committal to an invitation, with thanks

expressions.nuance: 생각 좀 해 보고 연락드릴게요 chains 생각 좀 해 보다 ('try thinking about it') + -고 ('and then') + 연락드리다 ('to contact', humble) + -ㄹ게요. It declines to commit NOW while promising a future reply — the professional, face-saving way to defer a decision on a contract, a job, an invitation, or a sale. The standout feature is 연락드리다: 드리다 is the humble form of 주다 ('to give'), so 연락드리다 = 'to give (you) contact' humbly, the polite/business default for 'I'll get back to you' to someone you respect or a customer. Like 'I'll think about it', it can be a genuine 'let me decide' OR a graceful soft no. Register: 연락드릴게요 polite/humble, 연락할게 casual, 연락드리겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from a bare 생각해 볼게요 ('I'll think about it') is that adding 연락드릴게요 commits you to closing the loop with a reply, which sounds more responsible and is expected in business. The English-speaker trap is using plain 연락할게요 toward a client or senior, missing the humble 드리다 that politeness demands upward; 연락드릴게요 is the correct deferential form. Another error is saying 연락 줄게요 to a superior — 주다 ('give') is too flat upward; humble it to 드리다. Swap in 알아보고 ('after looking into it') when you need to check facts rather than merely think.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using plain 연락할게요 to a client or senior.
Upward and in business, humble 드리다 is expected: 연락드릴게요. Plain 연락할게요 is fine among peers but sounds under-polite to a superior or customer.

주다 ('give') is too flat upward. The humble form is 드리다: 연락드릴게요. Reserve 연락 줄게 for friends/peers.

Unlike a vague 생각해 볼게요, this explicitly pledges a reply. If you won't actually contact them, a softer hedge is better; otherwise you may seem to flake on a commitment.

expressions.english: I really appreciate the thought, but…
expressions.shortExplanation: 마음은 정말 감사한데요 is a practical expression meaning "I really appreciate the thought, but…".
expressions.explanation: 마음은 정말 감사한데요 (maeumeun jeongmal gamsahandeyo) means "I really appreciate the thought, but…". Say it as one set phrase — for example 마음은 정말 감사한데요 ("I truly appreciate the thought, but…"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I truly appreciate the thought, but…
usagePhrases.note: Polite; cushions a refusal with gratitude first
반말, to a friend (고맙다 instead of 감사하다)
Formal 합쇼체 with the literary 만 ('however')

usagePhrases.en: I'm grateful for that thought, but…
usagePhrases.note: Point 그 마음 at a specific kind gesture

examples.en: I really appreciate the thought, but…
examples.note: Opening a refusal by honoring the offer first

examples.ko: 제가 소개팅 시켜 줄까요? — 아, 마음은 정말 감사한데요, 지금은 그럴 생각이 없어서요.
examples.romanization: jega sogaeting sikyeo julkkayo? — a, maeumeun jeongmal gamsahandeyo, jigeumeun geureol saenggagi eopseoseoyo.
examples.en: Want me to set you up on a blind date? — Oh, I really appreciate the thought, but I'm not looking right now.
examples.note: Declining matchmaking while thanking them sincerely

examples.ko: 저희 회사로 오시는 게 어때요? — 마음은 정말 감사한데요, 지금 회사에 좀 더 있어 보려고요.
examples.romanization: jeohui hoesaro osineun ge eottaeyo? — maeumeun jeongmal gamsahandeyo, jigeum hoesae jom deo isseo boryeogoyo.
examples.en: Why not come work for us? — I really appreciate the offer, but I'm going to stay at my current company a bit longer.
examples.note: Turning down a job offer graciously

expressions.nuance: 마음은 정말 감사한데요 is 마음 ('thought/intention') + 은 (contrast topic) + 정말 ('truly') + 감사하다 ('to be grateful') + the trailing -ㄴ데요 ('…, but you see'). It is the textbook 'thank you, BUT…' refusal-opener: you first honor the giver's intention (마음), then the contrast particle 은 and the dangling -ㄴ데요 set up the gentle 'however' that lets you decline what follows. Leading with gratitude is essential Korean politeness — refusing kindness cold is face-threatening, so you cushion it with sincere thanks first. Register: 감사한데요 polite, 고마운데 casual (note 고맙다 for friends vs 감사하다 for formality), 감사합니다만 formal. The contrast topic 은 on 마음 is doing quiet work: it implies 'the THOUGHT I'm grateful for, but the offer itself…', neatly separating appreciation from acceptance. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'thank you but no' too bluntly (감사하지만 안 돼요), which can sound like the thanks is perfunctory; the natural pattern trails off with -ㄴ데요 and a soft reason, never a hard 안 돼요. Another error is mixing up 감사하다 (formal 'thank') and 고맙다 (warmer/casual) for the register. Follow with a gentle reason ending in -서요 (지금은 생각이 없어서요) to complete the graceful decline.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying a blunt 감사하지만 안 돼요.
It can sound like the thanks is just a formality before a hard 'no'. The natural cushion trails off: 마음은 정말 감사한데요, … with a soft reason, not a flat 안 돼요.

Dropping the contrast 은 on 마음.
마음은 (with 은) separates 'the thought I'm grateful for' from the offer you're declining. Without it the 'but' setup weakens; keep 마음은 … -ㄴ데요.

expressions.english: Sorry, but it puts me in a tough spot
expressions.shortExplanation: 죄송한데 제가 좀 곤란해서요 is a practical expression meaning "Sorry, but it puts me in a tough spot".
expressions.explanation: "Sorry, but it puts me in a tough spot" — that is 죄송한데 제가 좀 곤란해서요 (joesonghande jega jom gollanhaeseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 죄송한데 제가 좀 곤란해서요 ("Sorry, but it's awkward for me…"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Sorry, but it's awkward for me…
usagePhrases.note: Polite; apologize + 'I'm in a bind' refusal

usagePhrases.en: Sorry, but it's awkward for me
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend (미안하다 + 나)

usagePhrases.en: I'm sorry, but I'm in a difficult position
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체

usagePhrases.en: Doing that would be awkward for me…
usagePhrases.note: Spell out the action with -기엔 ('to do that…')

examples.en: Sorry, but it puts me in a tough spot.
examples.note: Declining an awkward favor that would compromise you

examples.ko: 돈 좀 빌려줄 수 있어? — 미안한데, 나 지금 좀 곤란해. 나도 빠듯해서.
examples.romanization: don jom billyeojul su isseo? — mianhande, na jigeum jom gollanhae. nado ppadeutaeseo.
examples.en: Could you lend me some money? — Sorry, but I'm in a tight spot right now. I'm stretched too.
examples.note: Refusing a loan to a friend with a relatable reason

examples.ko: 이번 일 좀 눈감아 주시면 안 될까요? — 죄송한데 그건 제가 좀 곤란해서요. 규정이라서요.
examples.romanization: ibeon il jom nungama jusimyeon an doelkkayo? — joesonghande geugeon jega jom gollanhaeseoyo. gyujeongiraseoyo.
examples.en: Could you look the other way this once? — Sorry, but that puts me in a difficult position. It's the rules.
examples.note: Declining an improper request, citing 규정 (regulations)

expressions.nuance: 죄송한데 제가 좀 곤란해서요 opens with 죄송한데 ('I'm sorry, but…') and refuses via 곤란하다 ('to be in an awkward/difficult bind'), with the trailing -서요 ('because…, so'). 곤란하다 is the precise word for 'this request would personally put me in a difficult or compromising position' — perfect for declining favors you can't or shouldn't grant (lending money, breaking a rule, an imposition) because it frames the problem as YOUR predicament, not the asker's fault, which protects their face. Leading with 죄송한데 (apology) is standard for refusing a direct request. Register: 곤란해서요 polite, 곤란해 casual (with 미안한데 + 나), 곤란합니다 formal. The dividing line from 어렵다 ('difficult') is feeling: 어렵다 is neutral 'hard/not feasible', while 곤란하다 carries 'it would embarrass or trouble ME personally' — use 곤란하다 when the ask is awkward or improper. The English-speaker trap is translating 곤란하다 as just 'difficult' and using 어려워요, losing the 'puts me on the spot' nuance; also, 곤란하다 describes a SITUATION/person's predicament, so you say 제가 곤란해요 ('I'm in a bind'), not 곤란을 해요. Another error is omitting 죄송한데 before refusing a favor, which can feel abrupt. The -서요 trail again softens the ending into a polite, unfinished 'so…'.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Refusing a direct favor with no apology opener.
For declining a personal request, lead with 죄송한데 / 미안한데 to soften. Jumping straight to 곤란해서요 without the apology can feel curt.

examples.en: Hmm, I'm not sure…
examples.note: Buying a beat when you don't want to commit or agree

examples.ko: 이거 사는 게 좋을까요? — 글쎄요, 저는 잘 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: igeo saneun ge joeulkkayo? — geulsseyo, jeoneun jal moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: Should I buy this? — Hmm, I'm not really sure.
examples.note: Declining to give a firm opinion or push someone either way

examples.ko: 주말에 시간 되세요? — 글쎄요, 한번 봐야 알 것 같아요. 확실하진 않아요.
examples.romanization: jumare sigan doeseyo? — geulsseyo, hanbeon bwaya al geot gatayo. hwaksilhajin anayo.
examples.en: Are you free this weekend? — Hmm, I'd have to check. I'm not certain.
examples.note: Hedging an invite without committing or flatly refusing

expressions.nuance: 글쎄요 is the classic Korean verbal hedge — a non-committal 'hmm, well, I'm not sure' that lets you avoid both 'yes' and 'no.' It buys time, signals reluctance or uncertainty, and very often functions as a soft pre-refusal or a polite way to withhold agreement without contradicting the other person. The 요 makes it polite; 글쎄 alone is 반말 and can also mean 'we'll see' or even an insistent 'I told you…' depending on tone. Register: 글쎄요 polite, 글쎄 casual. The dividing line from 모르겠어요 ('I don't know') is intent: 모르겠어요 states genuine lack of knowledge, while 글쎄요 is a strategic hedge — you may well have an opinion but are choosing not to commit, so it's softer and more diplomatic for declining or dodging. The English-speaker trap is hearing 글쎄요 as a real 'I don't know' and re-explaining or pressing for an answer; in many cases it politely means 'eh, probably not' or 'I'd rather not say', and pushing is impolite. Another error is overusing it as a filler the way English uses 'well' — too many 글쎄요s can read as evasive or wishy-washy. Pair it with 잘 모르겠는데요 ('I'm not really sure') or 생각해 봐야겠어요 ('I'd have to think') to extend the hedge gracefully. Crucially, recognize it from the other side: when a Korean answers your request with 글쎄요, treat it as a likely soft 'no', not an invitation to argue your case.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Taking 글쎄요 as a literal 'I don't know' and pressing harder.
It's often a strategic hedge meaning 'eh, probably not' or 'I'd rather not commit'. Re-explaining or pushing for a yes ignores the soft refusal and feels pushy.
Confusing 글쎄요 with 모르겠어요.
모르겠어요 = genuine 'I don't know (the fact)'. 글쎄요 = a diplomatic 'well, I'm not sure / we'll see' used to dodge or soft-decline. They aren't interchangeable.
Overusing 글쎄요 as an English-style filler 'well'.
Sprinkling it on every sentence reads as evasive or noncommittal. Use it deliberately when you actually want to hedge, then follow with a reason or a defer.

expressions.shortExplanation: 아니요, 됐어요 is a practical expression meaning "No, that's alright / never mind".
expressions.explanation: 아니요, 됐어요 (aniyo, dwaesseoyo) means "No, that's alright / never mind". Say it as one set phrase — for example 아니요, 됐어요 ("No, I'm good / that's enough"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; a firmer 'no thanks', waving something off
반말, to a friend; can sound curt or annoyed
Cushion 됐어요 with 괜찮아요 to keep it gentle
이거면 됐어요 = 'this is all I need', declining extras

examples.en: No, I'm good, thanks.
examples.note: Firmly but politely waving off a repeated offer

examples.ko: 봉투 드릴까요? — 아니요, 됐어요. 그냥 주세요.
examples.romanization: bongtu deurilkkayo? — aniyo, dwaesseoyo. geunyang juseyo.
examples.en: Shall I give you a bag? — No, I'm good. Just hand it to me as is.
examples.note: Declining a bag more firmly than 괜찮아요 when they insist

examples.ko: 더 시켜 드릴까요? — 아유, 됐어요 됐어요. 이미 너무 많아요.
examples.romanization: deo sikyeo deurilkkayo? — ayu, dwaesseoyo dwaesseoyo. imi neomu manayo.
examples.en: Shall I order you more? — Oh, no no, that's plenty. It's already way too much.
examples.note: Repeating 됐어요 to firmly stop someone over-ordering for you

expressions.nuance: 됐어요 comes from 되다 ('to be done/enough') in the past — literally 'it's become (enough)' — and as a refusal it means 'that's enough / I'm good / never mind, don't bother.' It is a FIRMER, more final 'no thanks' than 괜찮아요: you use it to wave something off decisively, often after a first soft refusal didn't land, or to stop someone from doing more for you. Tone is everything: said warmly it's a friendly 'I'm all set', but said flatly or sharply — especially bare 됐어 in 반말 — it can sound curt, dismissive, or even annoyed ('forget it / drop it'), so it carries risk upward. Register: 됐어요 polite-casual, 됐습니다 formal, 됐어 casual/blunt. The dividing line from 괜찮아요 is firmness and finality: 괜찮아요 gently declines and invites no friction, while 됐어요 closes the matter and can imply mild impatience if overdone — so default to 괜찮아요 with strangers/seniors and reserve 됐어요 for when you need to be more definite. The English-speaker trap is using 됐어요 too readily as a neutral 'no thanks' and accidentally sounding short with a server or elder; soften it with 아니요 or 괜찮아요 in front (아니요, 됐어요 / 괜찮아요, 됐어요). Another error is confusing the refusal 됐어요 with the affirmative 됐어요/됐다 meaning 'it worked! / it's done!' (e.g. 와, 됐어! 'yes, it worked!') — same word, opposite feel, separated only by context and tone. Avoid the curt bare 됐어 toward anyone you must respect.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using bare 됐어 toward a server, elder, or boss.
Bare 됐어 is blunt 반말 and easily sounds annoyed ('forget it'). Upward, soften to 아니요, 괜찮아요, or at least 됐어요 / 됐습니다 with a friendly tone.
Treating 됐어요 as identical to 괜찮아요.
됐어요 is firmer and more final, and can imply mild impatience. For a gentle, frictionless 'no thanks', prefer 괜찮아요; save 됐어요 for when you need to be definite.
Confusing the refusal 됐어요 with the 'it worked!' 됐어요.
되다 also means 'to succeed/be done': 됐어! can mean 'it worked!'. Context and tone separate them; as a refusal it means 'that's enough', not 'success'.

structuredNuance.t: 됐어요 as a refusal means 'that's enough / I'm good / never mind, don't bother.' It is a FIRMER, more final 'no thanks' than 괜찮아요: you use it to wave something off decisively, often after a first soft refusal didn't land, or to stop someone from doing more for you. Tone is everything: said warmly it's a friendly 'I'm all set', but said flatly or sharply — especially bare 됐어 in 반말 — it can sound curt, dismissive, or even annoyed ('forget it / drop it'), so it carries risk upward. Avoid the curt bare 됐어 toward anyone you must respect.

The dividing line from 괜찮아요 is firmness and finality: 괜찮아요 gently declines and invites no friction, while 됐어요 closes the matter and can imply mild impatience if overdone — so default to 괜찮아요 with strangers/seniors and reserve 됐어요 for when you need to be more definite.

Register: 됐어요 polite-casual, 됐습니다 formal, 됐어 casual/blunt.

The trap is using 됐어요 too readily as a neutral 'no thanks' and accidentally sounding short with a server or elder; soften it with 아니요 or 괜찮아요 in front (아니요, 됐어요 / 괜찮아요, 됐어요). Another error is confusing the refusal 됐어요 with the affirmative 됐어요/됐다 meaning 'it worked! / it's done!' (e.g. 와, 됐어! 'yes, it worked!') — same word, opposite feel, separated only by context and tone.

expressions.english: May I ask you for directions?
expressions.shortExplanation: 길 좀 여쭤볼게요 is a practical expression meaning "May I ask you for directions?".
expressions.explanation: "May I ask you for directions?" — that is 길 좀 여쭤볼게요 (gil jom yeojjwobolgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. ("May I ask you for directions?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: May I ask you for directions?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 opener to any adult stranger on the street; 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다 — it lowers the speaker and honors the listener

usagePhrases.en: Let me ask you for directions.
usagePhrases.note: 반말 to a friend or someone clearly younger; plain 물어보다 instead of humble 여쭤보다 — never use the humble form when speaking casually

usagePhrases.en: May I trouble you with a question?
usagePhrases.note: 격식 — very formal; 겠습니다 ending lifts the level further, suited to an elder, a government clerk, or a serious setting

usagePhrases.en: Excuse me, may I ask you for directions?
usagePhrases.note: Softest and most natural street version; 저기요 grabs attention first and 봐도 될까요 ('would it be okay to ask') is extra courteous

examples.ko: 저기요, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 서울역이 어느 쪽이에요?
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, gil jom yeojjwobolgeyo. seouryeogi eoneu jjogieyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, may I ask for directions? Which way is Seoul Station?
examples.note: Lead with 저기요 to signal a stranger before launching into your question; chaining the actual question directly is the most efficient real-life pattern

examples.ko: A: 죄송한데요, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 이 근처에 약국이 있나요? / B: 네, 저 골목으로 들어가시면 바로 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: joesonghandeyo, gil jom yeojjwobolgeyo. i geuncheoe yakgugi innayo? / B: ne, jeo golmogeuro deureogasimyeon baro isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Sorry, may I ask directions? Is there a pharmacy near here? / B: Yes, go into that alley and it's right there.
examples.note: Shows the complete opener-plus-question structure; B's natural answer is a direction with a landmark

examples.ko: 실례합니다, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 제가 이 동네가 처음이라서요. 종로 쪽은 어디예요?
examples.romanization: sillyehamnida, gil jom yeojjwobolgeyo. jega i dongnega cheoeumiraseoyo. jongno jjogeun eodiyeyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, may I ask for directions? I'm new to this neighborhood. Where's Jongno?
examples.note: Adding 처음이라서요 ('I'm new here') softens the interruption and invites the listener to be more patient and detailed

expressions.nuance: This is the courteous opener a stranger uses before asking directions on the street. 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다 — it lowers the speaker and elevates the listener, which is exactly right when you're asking a favor of someone you don't know: polite without being stiff. With a friend or someone much younger, drop to the plain 물어볼게, and in a very formal setting with an elder say 여쭤보겠습니다. The nearest alternative phrase is 저기요, 말씀 좀 묻겠습니다, but 묻다 is neutral while 여쭤보다 actively honors the person; that humility is the real dividing line. Variants: 여쭤볼게요 (standard polite) → 여쭤봐도 될까요? (extra courteous, seeking permission) → 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식). The classic English-speaker mistake is launching straight into 'Where is...?' with no opener, which feels abrupt or rude; Koreans almost always cushion the question with an opener first.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 물어볼게요 to a stranger thinking it's polite — 물어보다 is merely neutral; the humble 여쭤보다 is what makes asking a favor sound respectful to an adult you don't know.
Skipping the opener and going straight to 시청 어디예요? — without 저기요 or 죄송한데요 first, it reads as a command, not a request; always cushion before the question.
Using 여쭤보다 about yourself answering ('제가 여쭤봐 드릴게요' meaning 'I'll tell you') — 여쭤보다 only flows upward (YOU ask UP); it cannot mean 'I'll inform you'.

structuredNuance.t: The courteous opener a stranger uses before asking directions on the street. 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다 — it lowers the speaker and elevates the listener, which is exactly right when asking a favor of someone you don't know: polite without being stiff. Use it with any adult stranger or someone socially above you; switch to plain 물어보다 with friends or juniors.

Nearest alternative: 저기요, 말씀 좀 묻겠습니다. The dividing line is humility — 묻다 is a neutral 'ask', but 여쭤보다 actively honors the listener by lowering the speaker. 묻겠습니다 is also fine but more formal and blunt; 여쭤볼게요 is warmer and more natural for a street request.

Softness scale: 물어볼게 (반말, friend) → 여쭤볼게요 (polite, stranger) → 여쭤봐도 될까요? (courteous, seeking permission) → 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식, elder/formal). The 봐도 될까요 form is especially safe when you're stopping someone who looks busy.

The classic English-speaker mistake is skipping the opener and launching straight into 시청 어디예요? — without 저기요 or 죄송한데요 first, it sounds like a demand. A second trap: trying to use 여쭤보다 when YOU are answering someone's question ('I'll 여쭤보 you the answer') — 여쭤보다 only works when you are asking UP toward the other person, never when giving information.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기 어떻게 가요? is a practical expression meaning "How do I get here?".
expressions.explanation: 여기 어떻게 가요? (yeogi eotteoke gayo?) = "How do I get here?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기 어떻게 가요? ("How do I get here?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a passerby or station staff; point at a map, phone screen, or written address when you say 여기 so the destination is clear
반말 to a friend; identical structure, just drop the 요 — the most natural form between close people

usagePhrases.en: How am I supposed to get here?
usagePhrases.note: Slightly more anxious/careful tone; 가야 돼요 = 'what do I need to do to go there', useful when the route seems complicated

usagePhrases.en: What do I do to get here?
usagePhrases.note: Natural alternative framing; 가려면 ('in order to go') puts the purpose first, common when talking to a ticket window or information desk

examples.en: How do I get here?
examples.note: Said while holding up your phone map to the listener — 여기 refers to the spot on the screen, not where you're standing

examples.ko: A: 이 주소 여기 어떻게 가요? 걸어갈 수 있어요? / B: 좀 멀어요. 지하철 타시는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: A: i juso yeogi eotteoke gayo? georeogal su isseoyo? / B: jom meoreoyo. jihacheol tasineun ge naayo.
examples.en: A: How do I get to this address? Can I walk? / B: It's a bit far. You'd be better off taking the subway.
examples.note: Showing the address makes 여기 concrete; B's natural answer gives advice about the best mode

examples.ko: 여기 어떻게 가요? 지하철로 가는 게 나아요, 버스가 나아요? 아니면 택시가 나아요?
examples.romanization: yeogi eotteoke gayo? jihacheollo ganeun ge naayo, beoseuga naayo? animyeon taeksiga naayo?
examples.en: How do I get here? Is subway better, bus, or taxi?
examples.note: Listing the options you're considering invites a specific recommendation and makes the conversation more useful

expressions.nuance: This is the all-purpose 'how do I get there' you say while pointing at a destination on your phone map, a screenshot, or a written address. The key insight: 여기 ('here') works because you're showing the destination visually — it refers to the spot on your screen, not where you're physically standing. This trips up English speakers who instinctively want 거기 ('there'). Politeness lives entirely in the ending: 가요? is the everyday polite for strangers, 가? is 반말 for friends, and 가야 돼요? sounds more deferential and worried. The closest alternative phrase is 여기 어떻게 찾아가요? ('how do I find my way there'), which carries the nuance of tracking down a hard-to-find spot; plain 어떻게 가요? just asks the route. The big English-speaker mistake is translating 'How can I go?' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which asks whether it is POSSIBLE or PERMITTED — for directions, use 어떻게 가요? (how by what route).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 거기 어떻게 가요? while pointing at a map — when the destination is right in front of you on the screen, Koreans say 여기 because it is visually present; 거기 implies a place neither of you can see.
Using 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? for 'how can I get there' — 갈 수 있어요 asks if it is physically possible or permitted; for the route use plain 어떻게 가요?.
Dropping 어떻게 and asking 여기 가요? alone — that sounds like 'are you going here?'; you need 어떻게 to turn it into a route question.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Here how do (you) go?' The real function is 'What's the route to this place?' said while showing the destination to the listener. 여기 ('here') refers to the spot on your screen or map, not your current location — the destination becomes 'here' because it is right in front of both of you.

여기 어떻게 찾아가요? adds the nuance of hunting down a hidden or confusing address ('how do I find my way there'), implying extra difficulty. Plain 어떻게 가요? just asks the route. 여기 가려면 어떻게 해요? restructures as 'what should I do to get there', natural at information desks.
Politeness is the ending alone: 가요? (polite, stranger) → 가? (반말, friend) → 가야 돼요? (polite + anxious). Combine with 버스로 or 지하철로 to specify the mode: 지하철로 어떻게 가요?

Two traps: (1) Using 거기 어떻게 가요? when you're pointing at a map — the destination in your hand is 여기 to the speaker, not 거기. (2) Translating 'How can I go?' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? — 갈 수 있어요 tests ability or permission; for route information, always use 어떻게 가요?.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기서 멀어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is it far from here?".
expressions.explanation: 여기서 멀어요? (yeogiseo meoreoyo?) means "Is it far from here?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여기서 멀어요? ("Is it far from here?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a stranger; 여기서 = 여기에서 ('from here'), marking the departure point of the distance measurement — this 에서 cannot be dropped
반말 to a friend; drop the 요; the meaning and structure are identical

usagePhrases.en: Is it really far from here?
usagePhrases.note: 많이 ('a lot') signals you're worried about a long walk or ride; slightly more pressing than the bare 멀어요?
The hopeful flip side; use this when you're hoping for a short walk rather than bracing for bad news

examples.en: Is it far from here?
examples.note: The bare check you drop in right after someone names your destination — tone implies you're ready to hear the worst

examples.ko: A: 남대문시장 여기서 멀어요? / B: 아뇨, 걸어서 한 십 분이면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: namdaemunsijang yeogiseo meoreoyo? / B: anyo, georeoseo han sip bunimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Is Namdaemun Market far from here? / B: No, about ten minutes on foot.
examples.note: B's natural answer gives both the verdict (아뇨) and the time estimate — the most common real-world exchange

examples.ko: 여기서 멀어요? 멀면 택시 탈게요. 다리가 좀 아파서요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseo meoreoyo? meolmyeon taeksi talgeyo. dariga jom apaseoyo.
examples.en: Is it far from here? If it's far I'll take a taxi — my legs are a bit sore.
examples.note: Explaining your plan (멀면 택시 탈게요) and reason (다리가 아파서) helps the listener calibrate their definition of 'far'

expressions.nuance: You say this to a stranger or staff member right after they tell you where something is, so you can decide whether to walk or take transport. 여기서 is the contracted 여기에서 marking the starting point ('from here') — the 에서 is non-negotiable because distance is measured FROM a point, not AT it. Politeness is the ending only. The natural opposite 가까워요? is not just a synonym for 'not far' — it carries a hopeful tone ('please tell me it's nearby'), while 멀어요? braces for inconvenience; that emotional lean is the true dividing line between the two. For extra emphasis of worry, insert 많이: 여기서 많이 멀어요? English speakers often construct 'Is it far?' as 그것은 멀어요? with an explicit subject, but Korean drops it entirely — the bare 여기서 멀어요? is what people say, and a textbook-style subject sounds foreign.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 여기에 멀어요? instead of 여기서 멀어요? — distance 'from' a departure point requires 에서 (contracted to 서); 에 marks a destination, not an origin.
Adding an explicit subject like 그 장소는 멀어요? — Korean drops the subject here; the bare 여기서 멀어요? is natural and complete, and adding a subject sounds foreign.
Confusing 멀어요 (far) with 모르겠어요 (I don't know) in fast speech — 멀다 conjugates cleanly to 멀어요; never say 멀라요 or 모르겠어요 when asking distance.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'From here is it far?' The real function is asking whether walking is realistic — you say this the moment someone tells you a location, to decide on foot vs. transit. 여기서 (= 여기에서) marks the departure point of the measurement; without 서/에서 the grammar breaks.

가까워요? is the hopeful version: you use it when you expect or hope the place is nearby, and want confirmation. 멀어요? is the cautious version: you ask it bracing for bad news. Both ask distance, but the emotional stance differs. 많이 멀어요? intensifies the worry further.
멀어요? (polite) → 멀어? (반말) → 많이 멀어요? (worried/emphasized). You can also add a mode: 걸어서 멀어요? ('far on foot?') or 지하철로 멀어요? ('far by subway?').

English speakers often add an explicit subject: 그것은 멀어요? or 그 장소는 멀어요? — grammatically possible but sounds like a textbook. Native speech drops it entirely: bare 여기서 멀어요? is complete. A second slip is 여기에 멀어요? — distance FROM a starting point requires 에서, not the destination particle 에.

expressions.english: Can I get there on foot?
expressions.shortExplanation: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get there on foot?".
expressions.explanation: "Can I get there on foot?" — that is 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? (georeoseo gal su isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? ("Can I get there on foot?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Can I get there on foot?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a passerby or staff; 걸어서 = 'by walking' (걷다 + 어서, means/manner connector), 갈 수 있어요 = 'is it possible to go' — together: 'is it an option to walk there'
반말 to a friend; same structure, drop 요

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay to walk there?
usagePhrases.note: Shorter and very common; 도 돼요 ('is it fine/allowed') leans toward advisability rather than raw possibility — 'would it be reasonable to walk?'

usagePhrases.en: Is it walkable / worth the walk?
usagePhrases.note: 갈 만하다 ('worth going') frames the question as a value judgment, not just feasibility; use when you want a qualitative assessment

examples.en: Can I get there on foot?
examples.note: The bare question when you'd rather not take transit and need a quick feasibility check

examples.ko: A: 경복궁까지 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? / B: 네, 한 20분 걸려요. 충분히 걸어갈 만해요.
