examples.romanization: A: gyeongbokgungkkaji georeoseo gal su isseoyo? / B: ne, han 20bun geollyeoyo. chungbunhi georeogal manhaeyo.
examples.en: A: Can I walk all the way to Gyeongbokgung? / B: Yes, it takes about 20 minutes. It's definitely walkable.
examples.note: 까지 ('all the way to') marks the destination; B naturally uses 갈 만해요 to confirm it's reasonable

examples.ko: 여기서 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? 아니면 버스 타야 돼요? 짐이 좀 있어서요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseo georeoseo gal su isseoyo? animyeon beoseu taya dwaeyo? jimi jom isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Can I walk from here? Or do I have to take a bus? I have some luggage.
examples.note: Giving a reason (짐이 있어서 = 'I have bags') helps the listener adjust their advice — the most natural street exchange

expressions.nuance: Said to a passerby or staff when deciding whether to walk instead of taking transit. 걸어서 is formed from 걷다 (walk) + 어서, the manner connector meaning 'by means of' or 'while doing', so 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? literally asks 'is going by walking possible?' The three close variants have different focuses: 갈 수 있어요? (can I / is it possible), 걸어가도 돼요? (is it okay, advisable), 갈 만해요? (is it worth the walk, a quality judgment). Politeness is the ending alone. The English-speaker trap is saying 걸을 수 있어요?, which asks whether your legs work or whether you are physically capable of the act of walking — you need the directional compound 걸어서 가다 ('walk THERE') to ask about the route. A second mistake: 걸어서 갈게요 is a statement of intent ('I'll walk'), not a question; keep the question form 갈 수 있어요? to ask for the answer.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 걸을 수 있어요? — that asks if you are physically capable of walking (are your legs okay); for 'can I walk THERE' you need the motion compound 걸어서 갈 수 있어요?.
Using 걸어서 갈게요 (a statement of intent 'I'll walk') when you mean to ask — to ask feasibility, keep the question form 갈 수 있어요?.
Forgetting 서 and saying 걸어 갈 수 있어요? — the natural manner form is 걸어서 (걷다+어서); dropping 서 sounds clipped and unnatural.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'By walking can (one) go?' Real meaning: 'Is walking there a viable option?' 걸어서 is the manner connector form of 걷다 (걷다 + 어서), meaning 'by the means of walking'. This structure — verb-stem + 어서 — is essential; 걸어 alone or 걷고 would be unnatural here.

갈 수 있어요? = feasibility (can I physically/logistically go). 걸어가도 돼요? = advisability (is it okay, sensible). 갈 만해요? = worth it (is the walk reasonable / pleasant). All ask about walking but from different angles — pick by what you really want to know.
Softness/intent scale: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? (polite question) → 걸어서 갈 수 있어? (반말) → 걸어가도 돼요? (advisability) → 걸어서 갈 만해요? (worth it). Statement of intent: 걸어서 갈게요 ('I'll walk there').

Biggest trap: 걸을 수 있어요? means 'are you/am I physically capable of walking' (as in, are my legs functional?) — NOT 'can I walk there'. You need the directional compound 걸어서 가다. A second trap: forgetting the 서 connector and writing 걸어 갈 수 있어요? — the natural form always has 걸어서.

expressions.english: Which exit number do I go out?
expressions.shortExplanation: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? is a practical expression meaning "Which exit number do I go out?".
expressions.explanation: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? (myeot beon chulguro nagayo?) means "Which exit number do I go out?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 몇 번 출구로 나가요? ("Which exit do I take?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to station staff or any rider; 몇 번 = 'what number', 출구 = 'exit', 로 marks the direction 'out through'; combine all three
반말 to a friend; drop the 요

usagePhrases.en: Which exit do I have to take?
usagePhrases.note: 나가야 돼요 ('have to go out') is a touch more urgent or careful, used when you're not sure you'll find it
The shortest form when you need only the number — drop the verb entirely

examples.en: Which exit do I go out?
examples.note: The bare question to a station worker — pointing at nothing, relying on them to know the destination from context

examples.ko: 롯데백화점 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요? 3번이요?
examples.romanization: rotdebaekwajeom garyeomyeon myeot beon chulguro nagayo? 3beoniyo?
examples.en: Which exit for Lotte Department Store? Is it number 3?
examples.note: 가려면 ties the exit to your destination; guessing (3번이요?) invites quick confirmation or correction

examples.ko: A: 시청역인데요, 몇 번 출구로 나가야 시청이 바로 나와요? / B: 5번 출구로 나가시면 바로 앞이에요.
examples.romanization: A: sicheongyeogindeyo, myeot beon chulguro nagaya sicheongi baro nawayo? / B: 5beon chulguro nagasimyeon baro apieyo.
examples.en: A: I'm at City Hall Station — which exit comes out right at City Hall? / B: Take exit 5 and it's right in front.
examples.note: 바로 나와요 ('comes out right there') asks which exit delivers you closest; B's natural answer with 바로 앞이에요 is what staff say

expressions.nuance: Korean subway exits are numbered (1번 출구, 2번 출구, 3번 출구…), so this is the precise question to ask station staff or a fellow rider when you need the right street exit. The particle 로 marks direction — 출구로 나가다 means 'exit through/via a numbered door' — and swapping it for 에서 (출구에서 나가요?) changes the meaning and sounds wrong. Politeness is only the ending. Close alternative: 몇 번 출구예요? when you only need the number label rather than the action of exiting; the dividing line is that 나가요? asks the process of exiting while 출구예요? just asks for the identifier. A common variant heard from local Seoulites is 몇 번 출구로 나오면 돼요? ('which exit do I come out of?'), which is equally natural. The English-speaker mistake is translating 'which exit' as 어느 출구 — but because Seoul exits are numbered, Koreans ask 몇 번 ('what number'), not 어느 ('which of a few unspecified choices').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 어느 출구로 나가요? — exits are numbered, so Koreans ask 몇 번 출구 ('what number exit'); 어느 fits unnumbered selections.
Using 출구에서 나가요? — exiting through a door takes the direction particle 로 (출구로); 에서 marks the location you act within, not the door you pass through.
Saying 몇 출구 without 번 — the counter 번 is required when asking about numbered items: 몇 번 출구, not 몇 출구.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'By what number exit do I go out?' The real function: 'Which numbered subway exit do I use?' Seoul's subway system uses numbered exits (1번 출구, 2번, 3번…) so every local knows the system — you ask by number, not by direction.

몇 번 출구예요? asks only for the label/number. 몇 번 출구로 나가요? asks the action of exiting through it. 몇 번 출구로 나오면 돼요? ('which exit should I come out of?') is equally natural and very common. Pick 나가요? for a clear action question, 출구예요? when you're in a hurry.
Polite: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? → 몇 번 출구로 나가야 돼요? (more careful) → 몇 번 출구예요? (quickest). 반말: 몇 번 출구로 나가?. Add destination: [장소] 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요?

English speakers say 어느 출구로 나가요? by analogy with 'which exit' — but Korean subway exits are numbered, so 몇 번 ('what number') is the natural question word. 어느 works for an unnumbered choice between things; 몇 번 fits a numbered system. Also: never use 출구에서 나가요? — the direction particle is 로, not 에서.

expressions.english: Does this go to City Hall?
expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 시청 가요? is a practical expression meaning "Does this go to City Hall?".
expressions.explanation: "Does this go to City Hall?" — that is 이거 시청 가요? (igeo sicheong gayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 시청 가요? ("Does this (bus/train) go to City Hall?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Does this (bus/train) go to City Hall?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; 이거 ('this one') points at the specific vehicle in front of you — the most natural boarding check to a driver or fellow passenger

usagePhrases.en: Does this go to City Hall?
usagePhrases.note: 반말 to a friend boarding together

usagePhrases.en: Does this bus go to City Hall?
usagePhrases.note: 이 버스 is more specific than 이거 when there are multiple vehicles and you want to be unambiguous about which one

usagePhrases.en: Does this head toward City Hall?
usagePhrases.note: 쪽으로 ('in the direction of') asks about general heading rather than exact stop — useful when you only need to go roughly that way

examples.en: Driver, does this go to City Hall?
examples.note: 기사님 is the respectful address term for a bus or taxi driver — always use it when speaking to the driver; it keeps the exchange polite at the door

examples.en: Does this go to City Hall? I'm trying to get off at City Hall.
examples.note: 내리려고요 ('I'm intending to get off there') explains your purpose and helps the driver confirm if this is the right service

examples.ko: A: 이거 시청 가요? / B: 네, 가요. 세 정류장 더 가면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo sicheong gayo? / B: ne, gayo. se jeongnyujang deo gamyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Does this go to City Hall? / B: Yes, it does. Three more stops.
examples.note: B's natural answer gives both confirmation and the count of remaining stops — the most useful reply a rider gets

expressions.nuance: This is the quick boarding check you fire at a bus driver or fellow passenger as you step on or approach. 이거 ('this one') points at the exact vehicle you're about to board or are standing on — efficient and natural. You can drop the destination particle 에 (no need to say 시청에 가요?) because casual transit speech compresses it. Always address the driver as 기사님 ('driver') to keep the tone polite. The near alternative 이거 시청 쪽으로 가요? asks for general direction rather than 'does it actually stop there' — useful when you only need to head that way; the dividing line is exact destination vs. general direction. English speakers sometimes over-formalize as 이것은 시청에 갑니까? — grammatically correct but textbook-stiff and far too slow for a doorway; real riders use the clipped 이거 시청 가요?. A crucial wrong form: 이거 시청 와요? uses 오다 ('come'), but from the rider's perspective the bus 가다 ('goes') there.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이거 시청 와요? — from your viewpoint as a passenger the bus 'goes' (가다) to City Hall, not 'comes'; use 가요.
Over-formalizing as 이것은 시청에 갑니까? — correct but textbook-stiff and too slow for a doorway; real riders say 이거 시청 가요?.
Forgetting 기사님 and just barking the question at the driver — addressing them as 기사님 first keeps the interaction polite and is standard practice.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'This one — City Hall — does it go?' The real function: a rapid boarding check asking whether this specific vehicle stops at your destination. 이거 is a very casual pronoun pointing at the vehicle; it works precisely because both speakers can see it.

이거 시청 쪽으로 가요? asks general direction ('does it head toward City Hall?') — fine when you just need to be in that area. 이거 시청 가요? asks whether it actually stops there. The first is safer if you're unsure of the exact stop; the second is sharper if you need the right stop.

존댓말 이거 시청 가요? is right for drivers (always add 기사님 first) and adult strangers. 반말 이거 시청 가? for friends. The Sino-Korean formal 이 버스가 시청에 정차하나요? is correct but sounds like a survey, not a quick boarding question.

Two traps: (1) 이거 시청 와요? — from the passenger's side the bus 가다 (goes) to the destination, not 오다 (comes); reverse the direction. (2) 이것은 시청에 갑니까? — grammatically fine but stiff and way too slow for a bus door; the clipped 이거 시청 가요? is the real form.

expressions.shortExplanation: 어디서 갈아타요? is a practical expression meaning "Where do I transfer?".
expressions.explanation: 어디서 갈아타요? (eodiseo garatayo?) = "Where do I transfer?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어디서 갈아타요? ("Where do I transfer?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to station staff or any knowledgeable rider; 갈아타다 = 'change vehicles', 어디서 = 'at which location' — the transfer happens AT a station, so 에서 is required
반말 to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Where do I have to transfer?
usagePhrases.note: 갈아타야 돼요 ('have to change') conveys mild urgency — use when you're worried about missing the stop

usagePhrases.en: Which line do I transfer to?
usagePhrases.note: When you need the line number rather than the station name; 호선 = 'subway line', 으로 marks the direction of transfer

examples.en: Where do I transfer?
examples.note: The bare question once you know your journey isn't direct — let the listener fill in the station name

examples.en: Where do I transfer to get to Gangnam? Sindorim?
examples.note: 가려면 ties the transfer to your final destination; guessing (신도림이요?) gets a faster yes/no response

examples.ko: A: 이 지하철 타고 가다가 어디서 갈아타야 돼요? / B: 고속터미널역에서 3호선으로 갈아타시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: i jihacheol tago gadaga eodiseo garataya dwaeyo? / B: gosokteomineoryeogeseo 3hoseoneuro garatasimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: Riding this subway, where do I need to transfer? / B: Transfer to Line 3 at Express Terminal Station.
examples.note: 가다가 ('while going, then') marks a mid-journey switch; B's natural answer gives both station AND line number

expressions.nuance: You ask this of station staff or a knowledgeable rider when your route requires a transfer. 갈아타다 is a single compound verb meaning 'change vehicles' — composed of 갈다 ('replace/change') + 타다 ('ride') — and it is far more natural than trying to say 버스를 바꿔서 타요 (which sounds like swapping a ticket). The station where you transfer is the place the action occurs, so it takes 에서 (contracted to 서 in 어디서): 어디서 갈아타요? Use 에서 throughout. The related question 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? asks which LINE to switch to (note 으로, direction toward the line), versus 어디서 갈아타요? which asks the station where you switch — pick by what information you're missing. The English-speaker pitfall is building 'transfer' from two English ideas: 어디서 버스를 바꿔서 타요? sounds like you're exchanging one bus for another; the single idiomatic verb 갈아타다 is always the right choice.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어디에 갈아타요? — transferring is an action done AT a station, so it takes 에서 (어디서); 어디에 marks a destination you go to, not where you perform an action.
Translating 'change buses' literally as 버스를 바꿔서 타요 — the idiomatic single compound verb is 갈아타다; 바꾸다 sounds like swapping physical objects.
Using 에 for the new line — you transfer TO a line with 으로: 2호선으로 갈아타요, not 2호선에 갈아타요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'At where do I change-and-ride?' 갈아타다 is a single compound: 갈다 (replace/swap) + 타다 (ride). The transfer is an action performed AT a station, so the location takes 에서: 어디서 (= 어디에서). This 에서 is non-negotiable; 어디에 갈아타요? is wrong.

어디서 갈아타요? asks the station (where). 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? asks the line (which line). Often you need both — 어디서 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? is a natural combined question. The 으로 in 호선으로 marks the new line as the destination of the transfer.
어디서 갈아타요? (polite) → 어디서 갈아타야 돼요? (urgent/careful) → 어디서 갈아타? (반말). Combine: 어디서 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? adds the line question in one breath.

The temptation is to build 'change buses' as two verbs: 버스를 바꿔서 타요 — sounds like you're swapping a ticket for another physical item. The correct single verb 갈아타다 is what all Koreans use. Also: do NOT say 어디에 갈아타요? — 에 marks a destination, not the location of an action; the action particle is 에서.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기서 내려요 is a practical expression meaning "I get off here.".
expressions.explanation: 여기서 내려요 (yeogiseo naeryeoyo) means "I get off here.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여기서 내려요. ("I'm getting off here."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; both a statement and an implicit 'please step aside'; 내리다 = 'get off/down from a vehicle'; 여기서 (여기에서) marks the spot — 에서 is required, not 에

usagePhrases.en: I'm getting off here. / Get off here.
usagePhrases.note: 반말; can be either a personal statement or telling a friend where they should alight
내릴게요 ('I'll get off') is a soft heads-up using the 게요 ending — the most considerate form for a packed bus because it warns others ahead of time

usagePhrases.en: Is this where we get off?
usagePhrases.note: Same words with a rising tone become a question; checking with a companion or another passenger whether this is your shared stop

examples.en: Excuse me, I'll be getting off here. Let me through.
examples.note: 잠시만요 (just a moment) + 내릴게요 + 지나갈게요 ('let me pass') is the full polite package on a crowded bus — three phrases, one move

examples.ko: A: 다음에서 내려요? / B: 아니요, 여기서 내려요. 지금이에요.
examples.romanization: A: daeumeseo naeryeoyo? / B: aniyo, yeogiseo naeryeoyo. jigeumieyo.
examples.en: A: Are we getting off at the next stop? / B: No, we get off here — this is it.
examples.note: Contrasting 다음 (next) with 여기 (here) and adding 지금이에요 ('it's now') creates real urgency — the most natural panicked exchange

examples.ko: 기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요. 저 여기서 내려요.
examples.romanization: gisanim, yeogiseo sewo juseyo. jeo yeogiseo naeryeoyo.
examples.en: Driver, please stop here. I'm getting off here.
examples.note: Pairing 세워 주세요 (stop the vehicle) with 내려요 (I'll alight) is the safest combo when asking a taxi or bus driver to halt — shows the difference between the two phrases

expressions.nuance: 내려요 covers both 'I'm getting off here' (a personal announcement) and, on a packed bus, a polite signal that people should step aside. 여기서 (= 여기에서) marks the location of the alighting — 내리다 takes 에서 for the spot, never the destination particle 에. Register shapes the nuance: 내릴게요 (using the 게 'I'll do it' ending) is the gentlest, framing it as a consideration for others; 내려요 is a neutral polite statement; 내려 is casual. The neighbor phrase 세워 주세요 ('please stop the vehicle') is what you say to a driver to COMMAND the stop; 내려요 only announces your own action. These two often appear together: 기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요 — 저 내려요. The English-speaker error is saying 여기서 나가요 for 'get out' — 나가다 is for exiting a building or room; leaving a vehicle is always 내리다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기서 나가요 to mean 'I get off here' — 나가다 is exiting a room or building on foot; leaving a vehicle is always 내리다.
Using 여기에 내려요 — the spot where you alight takes 에서 (여기서), not the destination particle 에.
Telling a taxi driver only 여기서 내려요 to make them stop — that announces your action but doesn't command the driver; add 여기서 세워 주세요 to explicitly ask for a halt.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'From here I get down.' 내리다 is the correct verb for alighting from any vehicle — bus, subway, taxi. The point of alighting takes 에서 (여기서); using 에 (여기에) is wrong. In a crowded vehicle 여기서 내릴게요 also serves as a social signal meaning 'please make room for me'.

세워 주세요 ('please stop the vehicle') commands the driver to halt. 여기서 내려요 announces your own action of alighting. You often need both: 기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요 — 저 여기서 내려요. Using 내려요 alone to a taxi driver without 세워 주세요 means they might not know to stop.

Softness scale: 내릴게요 (heads-up, softest) → 내려요 (polite statement) → 내려 (반말). For action-oriented urgency: 지금 내려요! ('I'm getting off NOW!'). Question form (rising tone): 여기서 내려요? = 'is this where we get off?'

여기서 나가요 is wrong for 'get off a vehicle' — 나가다 means exiting a room, building, or enclosed space on foot; 내리다 is specifically for descending from / leaving a vehicle. A second trap: 여기에 내려요 with 에 instead of 에서 — the spot of alighting requires 에서.

expressions.shortExplanation: 다음 역이 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the next station?".
expressions.explanation: 다음 역이 어디예요? (daeum yeogi eodiyeyo?) means "What's the next station?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다음 역이 어디예요? ("What's the next station?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the name of the upcoming subway stop
Use 정류장 for buses instead of 역
이번 역 = the stop arriving right now, vs 다음 = the one after it

usagePhrases.en: Is the next one City Hall, right?
usagePhrases.note: Confirming the next stop by name — 맞아요? invites agreement

examples.en: What's the next station?
examples.note: Ask a fellow passenger when you can't read the announcement board — simple and always understood.

examples.en: Excuse me, what's the next bus stop?
examples.note: On a bus, swap 역 for 정류장 — using 역 on a bus sounds incorrect and may confuse the person you ask.

examples.ko: A: 이번 역이 강남역이에요? / B: 네, 이번이 강남이에요.
examples.romanization: A: ibeon yeogi gangnamyeogieyo? / B: ne, ibeoni gangnamieyo.
examples.en: A: Is this station Gangnam? / B: Yes, this one is Gangnam.
examples.note: 이번 역 = the stop pulling in NOW; 다음 역 = the one after. Mixing them up makes you get off one stop too early or too late.

expressions.nuance: 다음 역이 어디예요? is 다음 ('next') + 역 ('station') + 이 어디예요? ('is where/what?'). A common confusion: 이번 역 is the station arriving AT THIS MOMENT (the subway announcement says 이번 역은… 'this stop is…'), while 다음 역 is the station AFTER THAT — one stop further down the line. Mixing these two makes you get off one stop early or late. The other essential vocab swap is 역 vs 정류장: 역 (驛) is a subway or train station, while a bus stop is a 정류장 (停留場) — you would never call a bus stop a 역. Particle note: you are asking 'the next station is where/what?', so 역 is the grammatical subject and takes 이 (subject marker), not 을 (object marker): 다음 역이 어디예요?, not 다음 역을 어디예요?. 어디예요 literally means 'where is it?' but in this context it naturally means 'which station is it?'. Polite -요 is correct with any nearby stranger or station agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 이번 역 (arriving now) with 다음 역 (the one after).
이번 역 is the stop you are currently pulling into; 다음 역 is the next one after that. Announcements use 이번 역은…. Ask 이번 역이 어디예요? for the current stop, 다음 역이 어디예요? for the following one.
Calling a bus stop a 역.
역 is a subway or rail station. A bus stop is a 정류장. On a bus, ask 다음 정류장이 어디예요? — saying 다음 역 on a bus sounds like you're asking about a train station.
Using 을/를: 다음 역을 어디예요?
어디예요 takes a subject, not an object: 다음 역이 어디예요? You are asking 'the next station is where?', so mark 역 with the subject particle 이, not the object marker 을.

structuredNuance.t: 다음 역이 어디예요? = 'the next station — which is it?' 어디예요 ('where is it?') here means 'which station is it?' — Koreans use 어디 both for physical location and for 'which one' when asking about named places.
Ask to any nearby passenger or look at the digital station display. Polite -요 is appropriate with strangers. On a bus, swap 역 for 정류장; never say 역 for a bus stop.

이번 역 = the station you are currently arriving at (used in announcements). 다음 역 = the one after that. Using the wrong one means getting off at the wrong stop. For buses, 역 (subway station) → 정류장 (bus stop). 종점 = the final terminus, distinct from any regular stop.
다음 역 ('next subway station') / 다음 정류장 ('next bus stop') / 이번 역 ('current stop') / 마지막 역 ('last station of the journey'). The pattern [이번 / 다음 / 마지막] + 역/정류장 covers all your positional questions.

Two traps: (1) confusing 이번 역 (arriving now) and 다음 역 (the stop after) — this is the most common error leading to missed stops; and (2) using the object marker 을 instead of subject marker 이: 다음 역이 어디예요?, NOT 다음 역을 어디예요?.

expressions.shortExplanation: 지하철이 빨라요 is a practical expression meaning "The subway is faster.".
expressions.explanation: 지하철이 빨라요 (jihacheori ppallayo) = "The subway is faster.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 지하철이 빨라요. ("The subway is faster."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; practical advice given to someone deciding between transit options; 빠르다 is 르-irregular → 빨라요 (not 빠르어요)
반말 to a friend — the everyday casual form
더 ('more') makes the comparison explicit — use when the alternative has just been mentioned so the contrast is clear

usagePhrases.en: At this hour the subway is faster.
usagePhrases.note: 이 시간엔 = '이 시간에는' ('at this time') pins the advice to current conditions, especially rush hour traffic jams

examples.ko: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. 지금 길이 많이 막혀요.
examples.romanization: beoseuboda jihacheori ppallayo. jigeum giri mani makyeoyo.
examples.en: The subway is faster than the bus — traffic's really backed up.
examples.note: 보다 ('than') sets up the explicit comparison; 막혀요 ('traffic is blocked') gives the practical reason — the most natural advisory form

examples.ko: A: 버스로 갈까요, 지하철로 갈까요? / B: 지하철이 빨라요. 이 시간엔 버스가 많이 막혀요.
examples.romanization: A: beoseuro galkkayo, jihacheollo galkkayo? / B: jihacheori ppallayo. i siganen beoseuga mani makyeoyo.
examples.en: A: Should we go by bus or by subway? / B: The subway's faster. Buses get stuck in traffic at this hour.
examples.note: B gives a recommendation + reason — the natural two-part answer; the comparison is implied by 이 시간엔

examples.ko: A: 인천공항 가는 데 지하철 타는 게 나아요? / B: 네, 시간도 빠르고 가격도 싸요.
examples.romanization: A: incheongonghang ganeun de jihacheol taneun ge naayo? / B: ne, sigando ppareugo gagyeokdo ssayo.
examples.en: A: Is it better to take the subway to Incheon Airport? / B: Yes, it's both faster and cheaper.
examples.note: 빠르다 and 싸다 paired together give two reasons — shows that 빨라요 is often just one of several practical advantages

expressions.nuance: You'll say or hear this as practical travel advice when someone is weighing transit options. 빠르다 is a 르-irregular verb: before 아/어, the stem doubles the 르 as 빠+르 → 빨라요 (not 빠르어요) — getting this conjugation right is the most common grammar point to master here. To set up the comparison explicitly, put the slower option + 보다 ('than') before the subject: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요 ('the subway is faster THAN the bus'). Register is the ending alone. The near alternative 지하철이 더 나아요 ('the subway's better overall') is broader — it can fold in cost, comfort, and reliability — whereas 빨라요 specifically means speed; choose 빨라요 when time is what matters. A common extension: 이 시간엔 ('at this hour') turns the advice situational and prevents an unhelpful blanket statement. English speakers sometimes confuse 빠르다 (fast, of speed) with 이르다 (early, of time) — 일찍 arrived is not 빨라요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating it as 빠르어요 — 빠르다 is 르-irregular and becomes 빨라요 (not 빠르어요 or 빠러요).
Wrong particle placement: 지하철은 버스가 빨라요 is garbled — put 보다 on the slower option: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요.
Using 빨라요 for 'I arrived early' (clock time) — speed and earliness overlap in Korean but for 'I came early' say 일찍 왔어요; 빨라요 alone means 'it is fast'.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'The subway is fast/faster.' Practical use: an advisory recommendation about transit choice, usually in a comparison. The 이/가 particle on 지하철이 marks it as the focus of the comparison ('it is the subway that is fast').

지하철이 더 나아요 ('the subway is better') is broader — it covers speed, cost, and comfort together. 지하철이 빨라요 is specifically about speed. If you mean 'I recommend the subway for all reasons', say 나아요; if you mean 'it's strictly quicker', say 빨라요.
르 불규칙: 빠르다 → 빨라요 / 빨라 / 빨랐어요 (past). Comparison: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. Stronger: 훨씬 빨라요 ('much faster'). Situational: 이 시간엔 / 지금은 지하철이 빨라요.

Two traps: (1) 빠르어요 — 르-irregular rules change the stem; the correct form is always 빨라요. (2) 빨라요 for 'early' — 빠르다 can mean early in some contexts (빨리 came = arrived early), but for a specific clock time 'I'm early' use 일찍 왔어요 or 이르다, not 빨라요. (3) Wrong particle order: 지하철은 버스가 빨라요 is garbled; put 보다 on the slower item — 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 버스 정류장 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "Where's the bus stop?".
expressions.explanation: 버스 정류장 어디예요? (beoseu jeongnyujang eodiyeyo?) means "Where's the bus stop?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 버스 정류장 어디예요? ("Where's the bus stop?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a passerby on the street; 정류장 = 'stop' for buses; often shortened to just 정류장 어디예요? in context
반말 to a friend; 어디예요 → 어디야

usagePhrases.en: Where is there a bus stop?
usagePhrases.note: 있어요 ('is there') foregrounds existence — use when you're not sure there's one nearby and you're searching for any stop at all
Same frame, swap 정류장 → 역; useful when you're switching from bus to subway mid-journey

examples.en: Excuse me, where's the nearest bus stop?
examples.note: 가까운 ('nearest') is the most natural modifier — you almost always want the CLOSEST one; 저기요 grabs attention politely

examples.en: Where's the stop where I catch the 151 bus?
examples.note: 151번 타는 ('where you board the 151') is more specific than a generic stop question; 있어요 is used because you're searching for a specific one

examples.ko: A: 버스 정류장 어디예요? 비 올 것 같아서요. / B: 저기 편의점 앞에 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: beoseu jeongnyujang eodiyeyo? bi ol geot gataseoyo. / B: jeogi pyeonuijeom ape isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Where's the bus stop? Looks like rain. / B: It's right in front of that convenience store over there.
examples.note: A's reason (비 올 것 같아서요 = 'looks like rain') explains the urgency; B's natural answer uses a landmark (편의점 앞) — the most common real-world exchange

expressions.nuance: A plain, high-frequency question to a passerby when you need to find where buses load. The key vocabulary: 정류장 is 'bus stop'; 역 is a railway or subway station — they are not interchangeable. 버스 역 is simply wrong, and 버스 스탑 (the English loanword) is not idiomatic. In fast speech the subject particle is usually dropped: 버스 정류장 어디예요? rather than 버스 정류장이 어디예요? — and that bare form is the most natural street version. Register is just the ending. The subtle distinction between 어디예요? and 어디 있어요?: 어디예요? assumes the stop exists and asks its location; 어디 있어요? foregrounds existence and fits when you're not sure there's a stop in this neighborhood. In some contexts 버스 정류장 is shortened to just 정류장 once it's clear you're talking about a bus.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling it 버스 역 — a 역 is a rail or subway station; a bus stop is always 정류장.
Using the English-loanword 버스 스탑 — not idiomatic Korean; say 버스 정류장 or just 정류장.
Over-inserting the topic particle: 버스 정류장은 어디예요? is correct but slightly stiff; the natural street form drops the particle entirely — 버스 정류장 어디예요?.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Bus stop — where is it?' High-frequency street question. 정류장 is the only correct word for a bus stop; 역 belongs to trains and subways, and 버스 역 is ungrammatical in natural Korean. The subject particle 이 is normally dropped in street speech.

어디예요? = 'where is it?' — assumes the stop exists nearby. 어디 있어요? = 'where is there one?' — you're searching, uncertain one exists. If you've just arrived in an unfamiliar area and genuinely don't know if buses run there, use 있어요?; if you're in a normal city neighborhood, use 어디예요?.
To any adult stranger on the street: 존댓말 버스 정류장 어디예요? or 어디 있어요?. To a friend: 반말 버스 정류장 어디야?. To narrow down: add 가까운 ('nearest'), a bus number (151번 타는), or a direction (이 쪽에).

Two traps: (1) 버스 역 or 버스 스탑 — neither is standard; 버스 정류장 (or just 정류장) is always right. (2) Over-inserting the particle: 버스 정류장은 어디예요? is grammatically fine but sounds slightly formal; the bare 버스 정류장 어디예요? is what people actually say.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이 근처예요? is a practical expression meaning "Is it around here?".
expressions.explanation: 이 근처예요? (i geuncheoyeyo?) = "Is it around here?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이 근처예요? ("Is it near here?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a stranger; 이 근처 = 'this vicinity'; the 이 points to where you both stand — softer than 여기서 멀어요? because you're confirming a guess, not asking from scratch
반말 to a friend; 근처예요 → 근처야
있어요 ('does it exist') stresses existence/location — use when you want to know if there's one nearby, not just where a known one is
맞아요 ('is that right?') seeks confirmation of a guess you've already made — strongest when you think you're close but aren't sure

examples.en: Is it around here? The map shows it somewhere around here.
examples.note: 지도에는 여기쯤 나오는데요 ('the map shows it around here') gives the source of your guess and makes the question collaborative

examples.ko: 편의점 이 근처에 있어요? 약이 필요해서요.
examples.romanization: pyeonuijeom i geuncheoe isseoyo? yagi piryohaeseoyo.
examples.en: Is there a convenience store near here? I need some medicine.
examples.note: 있어요 asks existence; giving a reason (약이 필요해서요) often prompts a more helpful answer — natural request structure

examples.ko: A: 제가 찾는 호텔이 이 근처예요? 주소가 이건데요. / B: 네, 저 골목 들어가시면 바로 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: jega channeun hoteri i geuncheoyeyo? jusoga igeondeyo. / B: ne, jeo golmok deureogasimyeon baro isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Is the hotel I'm looking for around here? This is the address. / B: Yes, go into that alley and it's right there.
examples.note: Showing the address makes the question concrete; B's landmark answer (저 골목) is the natural local response

expressions.nuance: You say this to a stranger to confirm whether your destination is in the immediate area — it's a check on a guess, not a request for directions from scratch. 근처 is a noun meaning 'vicinity/nearby area', and 이 근처 ('this vicinity') points to where you both physically stand. The grammar split matters: 이 근처예요? (without 있어요) asks identity — 'is [the place] around here?'; 이 근처에 있어요? (with 있어요 and the 에 of location) asks existence — 'is there one nearby?'. The near synonym 주변 ('surroundings/area') appears in 이 주변이에요? but 근처 is slightly more colloquial and closer in feel. A common colloquial variant: 이쪽이에요? ('is it this way/in this direction?') is even more casual and directional. The English-speaker error is using the adverb 가까이 as a noun — 이 가까이예요? is ungrammatical; the noun for the nearby area is 근처.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이 가까이예요? — 가까이 is an adverb ('nearby' modifying a verb, e.g. 가까이 있어요), not a noun; the noun for the nearby area is 근처.
Dropping 에 when asking existence: 이 근처 있어요? should be 이 근처에 있어요? — the 에 marking the location of existence is required.
Confusing 근처 (vicinity, nearby area) with 근래 (recently, recent times) — only 근처 means 'the area nearby'; 근래 is purely time-related.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Is it this vicinity?' 근처 is a noun meaning 'vicinity/nearby area'. 이 근처 ('this vicinity here') is a deixis pointing to where you both stand. This is a guess-confirming question — you already think you're close and want validation, not full directions from scratch.

이 근처예요? = is [a specific known place] in this area? (identity). 이 근처에 있어요? = is there one (of a type) in this area? (existence). 이 주변이에요? uses 주변 ('surroundings'), nearly synonymous but slightly more formal and broader. 이쪽이에요? = 'is it this way?' — even more casual and directional.
이 근처예요? (standard) → 이 근처 맞아요? (confirming your strong guess) → 이 근처에 있어요? (existence). 반말: 이 근처야? / 이 근처 맞아?. Add a subject: [장소]가 이 근처예요?

가까이 is an adverb ('nearby', modifies verbs: 가까이 있어요), NOT a noun. Saying 이 가까이예요? is ungrammatical — for 'the nearby area' the noun is 근처. Second trap: dropping 에 when asking existence — 이 근처 있어요? needs to be 이 근처에 있어요?; the 에 marking location of existence is required.

expressions.shortExplanation: 쭉 가세요 is a practical expression meaning "Go straight.".
expressions.explanation: 쭉 가세요 (jjuk gaseyo) means "Go straight.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 쭉 가세요. ("Go straight ahead."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 command; mostly something you HEAR from a local directing you; 쭉 = vivid native adverb meaning 'straight on, continuously without stopping'
반말; directing a friend or someone younger
직진 ('straight-advance', Sino-Korean) is the formal/written register — road signs, driving-test language, formal instructions; warmer 쭉 is for spoken directions
가다가 + 도세요 is the most natural way to chain 'keep going and then turn'; 으로 is required for the direction of the turn

examples.ko: 쭉 가세요. 오른쪽에 큰 건물이 보이면 거기예요.
examples.romanization: jjuk gaseyo. oreunjjoge keun geonmuri boimyeon geogiyeyo.
examples.en: Go straight. When you see a big building on the right, that's it.
examples.note: A landmark cue (큰 건물이 보이면) is the most natural second half of a direction — Koreans almost always add a visual landmark to 쭉 가세요

examples.ko: 이 길로 쭉 가다가 사거리에서 왼쪽으로 도세요.
examples.romanization: i gillo jjuk gadaga sageorieseo oenjjogeuro doseyo.
examples.en: Go straight along this road, then turn left at the intersection.
examples.note: 가다가 ('while going, then') chains the straight section to the turn; 사거리 ('four-way intersection') + 으로 도세요 is the natural next direction step

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 가요? / B: 쭉 가시다가 편의점 지나면 바로 오른쪽이에요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke gayo? / B: jjuk gasidaga pyeonuijeom jinamyeon baro oreunjjogieyo.
examples.en: A: How do I get there? / B: Go straight, pass the convenience store, and it's immediately on the right.
examples.note: B uses a convenience store (편의점) as the landmark — one of the most common Korean direction landmarks; 바로 오른쪽 ('immediately on the right') pins the turn

expressions.nuance: 쭉 가세요 is mainly something you HEAR when a local gives you directions, but you'll also say it when directing someone. 쭉 is a vivid native Korean adverb meaning 'straight on, continuously, all the way without detouring' — warmer and more conversational than the Sino-Korean 직진 (literally '直進' straight-advance), which sounds like a driving exam or road sign term. That formality gap is the key dividing line: use 쭉 when speaking to people, 직진 in formal or written contexts. To chain two direction steps, use 가다가 ('go, and then'): 쭉 가다가 사거리에서 오른쪽으로 도세요. Turns always use 으로 (direction), not 에. The English-speaker trap is translating 'go straight' as 똑바로 가세요 — 똑바로 is also 'straight' but carries the extra meaning 'properly/upright', so it can come across as a mild scolding ('walk properly!'); 쭉 is the safe, neutral word. Also avoid marking a turn with 에: 오른쪽에 도세요 is wrong, it must be 오른쪽으로 도세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 똑바로 가세요 for 'go straight ahead' — 똑바로 can mean 'properly/upright' in Korean and may sound like a mild reprimand; for 'straight on' use 쭉 or 직진하세요.
Marking a turn with 에: 오른쪽에 도세요 is wrong; you turn 'toward' a direction with 으로 — 오른쪽으로 도세요.
Treating 쭉 as formal — it's a casual, spoken adverb; for written or formal directions (signs, official instructions) use 직진하세요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Go straight (continuously).' 쭉 is a native adverb conveying uninterrupted forward motion — 'all the way, without turning or stopping'. It is almost always followed by a landmark or a second direction step in real conversations.

직진하세요 uses the Sino-Korean 직진 (直進) and belongs to formal or written contexts — driving tests, road signs, formal notices. In face-to-face spoken directions, 쭉 가세요 is warmer and more natural. 똑바로 가세요 technically means 'go straight' but 똑바로 also means 'properly/upright', risking a scolding tone — avoid it for directions.
Forms: 쭉 가세요 (polite command) → 쭉 가 (반말) → 직진하세요 (격식). Chaining: 쭉 가다가 + [turn/landmark]. Turns: always 으로 도세요 (오른쪽으로 도세요 = turn right).

Two traps: (1) 똑바로 가세요 for 'go straight' — 똑바로 can mean 'properly/upright' and may sound like a mild scolding rather than a direction; use 쭉 for neutral 'straight ahead'. (2) 오른쪽에 도세요 — turns take the direction particle 으로 (오른쪽으로), not the location particle 에.

expressions.english: Could you call me a taxi, please?
expressions.shortExplanation: 택시 좀 불러 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you call me a taxi, please?".
expressions.explanation: 택시 좀 불러 주세요 (taeksi jom bulleo juseyo) means "Could you call me a taxi, please?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 택시 좀 불러 주세요. ("Please call me a taxi."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — to a hotel/restaurant staff member
반말 — to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Could you call a taxi for me?
usagePhrases.note: More formal — 한 대 ('one [vehicle]') + 시겠어요 is polished
Natural extension — 잡다 = flag one down on the street

examples.en: Please call a taxi for me.
examples.note: The bare request to a front-desk clerk — 좀 is essential; without it the request sounds abrupt

examples.ko: 죄송한데 택시 좀 불러 주세요. 비가 와서 잡기가 힘들어서요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande taeksi jom bulleo juseyo. biga waseo japgiga himdeureoseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry to trouble you, but could you call me a taxi? It's raining and I can't hail one.
examples.note: 죄송한데 + reason is the natural Korean way to open a favor-request; explaining why you can't do it yourself is considerate

examples.ko: A: 체크아웃하는데 공항 가는 택시 좀 불러 주시겠어요? / B: 네, 잠깐만요. 예약해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: chekeuautaneunde gonghang ganeun taeksi jom bulleo jusigesseoyo? / B: ne, jamkkanmanyo. yeyakae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I'm checking out — could you call a taxi to the airport? / B: Sure, just a moment. I'll arrange one for you.
examples.note: Real situation at hotel checkout — 예약해 드릴게요 ('I'll book/arrange it for you') is the staff's natural response

expressions.nuance: You say this to a third party — hotel front desk, restaurant host, building security — asking them to phone for a taxi on your behalf, customer-to-staff, in 존댓말 with 좀. 부르다 means 'to call/summon' and is the correct verb when you ask someone to arrange transportation: 택시를 부르다 = 'to summon/call a taxi'. More formal is 한 대 ('one vehicle') + 불러 주시겠어요?; 반말 is 불러 줘. The critical distinction against 잡아 주세요: 부르다 involves calling or app-booking a cab to come to you, while 잡다 ('to catch/grab') means physically flagging down a passing taxi on the street — the dividing line is method. In modern Korea 부르다 increasingly implies calling via app (카카오택시, etc.), while 잡다 is for the roadside scenario. An English speaker's first instinct is to map 'call' onto 전화하다 ('to telephone') and say 택시한테 전화해 주세요, but this wrongly suggests phoning the taxi cab directly; you summon a taxi service with 부르다. Omitting 좀 makes the request noticeably abrupt to a staff member.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 택시한테 전화해 주세요 — you summon a cab with 부르다, not 전화하다; say 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
Confusing 부르다 and 잡다 — 부르다 is call/summon (by phone/app), 잡다 is hail on the street; pick by method.
Dropping 좀 — without the softener 택시 불러 주세요 sounds abrupt; add 좀: 택시 좀 불러 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 택시 좀 불러 주세요 = 'please call/summon a taxi a little for me'. 부르다 spans 'to call out, to summon, to order [a service]'. Here the meaning is to arrange for a taxi to come — by phone or app — not to shout at one. 좀 softens the request.

Customer-to-service-staff (hotel, restaurant, office building) — 존댓말 with 좀 always. More formal: 택시 한 대 불러 주시겠어요?. Lead with 죄송한데 if asking someone to go out of their way. 반말 불러 줘 only to a friend doing you a favor.

부르다 (call/summon via phone or app) vs 잡다 (hail on the road). When it's raining or late and no taxis are visible, you want 불러 주세요 (arranged pickup). When a staff member is standing at a roadside and you want them to flag one, 잡아 주세요 fits. In daily practice 부르다 increasingly dominates as app-based rides grow.
택시 한 대 불러 주시겠어요? (more formal, explicit count); 카카오택시 불러 주실 수 있어요? (app-specific); 택시 좀 잡아 주세요 (hail version); 택시 예약해 주실 수 있어요? (asking for a pre-booked cab).

Saying 택시한테 전화해 주세요 — 전화하다 ('to telephone') targets a person, not a service; you use 부르다 to summon a taxi. Also, confusing 부르다 (summon) with 잡다 (hail) — pick based on whether it involves a phone/app or flagging on the street.

expressions.shortExplanation: 건배! is a practical expression meaning "Cheers!".
expressions.explanation: 건배! (geonbae!) = "Cheers!". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 건배! ("Cheers!"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: The standard toast as everyone raises glasses
More casual/cute; the onomatopoeia of glasses clinking
Formal toast, often led by the boss after a short speech
'One shot' — drink the whole glass in one go (English loan)

examples.en: Okay, everyone, cheers!
examples.note: 자 ('alright') gathers attention right before the toast; the whole table echoes 건배! together

examples.ko:
A: 오늘 고생하셨습니다. 자, 건배!
B: 건배!
examples.romanization: A: oneul gosaenghasyeotseumnida. ja, geonbae! B: geonbae!
examples.en:
A: You all worked hard today — cheers!
B: Cheers!
examples.note: A short line of appreciation from the senior precedes the toast; everyone echoes

examples.en: The team leader proposed a toast.
examples.note: 건배 제의(를) 하다 = 'to propose a toast'; only the most senior person at the table usually does this

expressions.nuance: 건배 is Sino-Korean 乾杯 (literally 'dry the cup'), the all-purpose 'cheers' you say while clinking glasses at the start of drinking. In a 회식 (company dinner) the most senior person says a few words and then leads it, and everyone echoes 건배! in unison. The casual cousin is 짠 (the clink sound), natural among friends or younger coworkers; the formal cousin is 위하여! ('for the sake of ~'), shouted after a stated reason: 우리 팀의 발전을 위하여! ('to our team's growth'). Crucially, 건배 does NOT obligate you to empty the glass — it just means 'cheers'. 원샷 ('one shot') is the separate phrase ordering everyone to down it in one gulp; mixing them up can pressure people to chug when you only meant to toast. The English-speaker pitfall is often the posture, not the word: with a senior present you hold your glass slightly LOWER than theirs when clinking and often turn your head slightly away while drinking — saying 건배 perfectly but clinking above the boss's glass reads as rude. 건배 is a set expression; do not attach particles or split it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 원샷! when you just mean 'cheers'.
원샷 orders everyone to empty the glass in one gulp. If you only mean to toast, say 건배!; save 원샷 for when you actually intend to down it.
Clinking your glass above a senior's glass.
The word 건배 is fine, but with elders/bosses you lower your glass below theirs when clinking. Holding yours higher looks disrespectful regardless of the words.
Writing it as 건배에 or 건배를 in the toast.
As a shouted toast it stands alone: 건배! You don't attach particles. 건배를 제의하다 only appears in the longer phrase 'to propose a toast'.

structuredNuance.t: 건배 is Sino-Korean 乾杯, literally 'dry the cup'. The real meaning is simply 'cheers' — a toast said while clinking glasses. It does NOT tell anyone to empty their glass; it is purely a social flourish to mark the start of drinking.

건배 is neutral-register and suits 반말 through 존댓말 tables alike because it is a shouted-together word, not addressed to one person. At a 회식 the senior leads; among friends anyone can call it. 짠 is the warmer, cuter version between close peers; 위하여 is the formal, speech-paired version at official dinners.

건배 (general cheers) vs 짠 (onomatopoeia clink, very casual) vs 위하여 (formal toast following a stated reason) vs 원샷 (orders everyone to down the entire glass). Confusing 건배 with 원샷 is the most common error — 건배 is about clinking, 원샷 is about emptying.
건배 is Sino-Korean 乾杯 ('dry cup'), the same character set as Japanese 乾杯 (kanpai) and Chinese 干杯 (gānbēi). The shared root helps intermediate learners remember it.

The trap is the clinking posture: hold your glass below a senior's when touching glasses, and turn your head slightly away while drinking — saying 건배 correctly but holding your glass higher than the boss's reads as disrespectful. Also, 건배 is a standalone exclamation; do not attach particles (건배를, 건배에) in the toast itself.

expressions.shortExplanation: 한 잔 더 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "One more glass, please".
expressions.explanation: 한 잔 더 주세요 (han jan deo juseyo) means "One more glass, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 한 잔 더 주세요 ("One more glass, please"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the server or your neighbor to pour
반말, to a close coworker or friend

usagePhrases.en: Let me pour you one more
usagePhrases.note: Offering to fill SOMEONE ELSE'S glass (honorific)
Setting a limit: 딱 ~만 = 'only exactly'

examples.ko: 여기 소주 한 잔 더 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi soju han jan deo juseyo.
examples.en: One more glass of soju here, please.
examples.note: Naming the drink (소주) makes the order clear to staff; at a 포차 you can also say 한 병 더 (one more bottle)

examples.ko:
A: 잔 비었네요. 한 잔 더 드릴까요?
B: 네, 한 잔 더 주세요. 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: A: jan bieonneyo. han jan deo deurilkkayo? B: ne, han jan deo juseyo. gamsahamnida.
examples.en:
A: Your glass is empty — can I pour you another?
B: Yes, one more please — thank you.
examples.note: The full A/B exchange at a typical 회식: A notices the empty glass, B accepts politely

examples.ko: 저 한 잔만 더 하고 일어날게요.
examples.romanization: jeo han janman deo hago ireonalgeyo.
examples.en: I'll have just one more and then head out.
examples.note: 일어나다 ('to get up/leave') politely signals you'll leave soon; 딱 한 잔만 더 makes the limit even firmer

expressions.nuance: 한 잔 더 is 한 ('one', native number) + 잔 (counter for cups/glasses) + 더 ('more'), the core phrase for another round. Crucially the counter 잔 takes NATIVE numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — saying 이 잔 더 instead of 두 잔 더 is a constant learner slip. Watch the direction of the favor verb: 주세요 ('please give') asks someone to pour FOR YOU, while 받으세요 ('please receive') is what you say while pouring for THEM — mixing these completely reverses who is serving whom. The near-synonym 한 잔 더 할게요 uses 하다 ('to do/have a drink') to announce you'll have another yourself, vs. 주세요 which requests it from someone else. Korean pouring culture means you generally don't refill your OWN glass at the table — you pour for others and wait for them to pour for you — so loudly asking 한 잔 더 주세요 while topping up only yourself can look slightly off. Better to offer 한 잔 더 받으세요 to your neighbor first. With a senior pouring for you, receive with two hands and a slight bow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using Sino-Korean numbers with 잔: 이 잔 더.
잔 takes native numbers. 'Two more glasses' is 두 잔 더, not 이 잔 더. One is 한 잔, two 두 잔, three 세 잔.
Saying 받으세요 when you want them to pour for you.
받으세요 ('please receive') is for when YOU pour into their glass. To ask them to pour for you, say 한 잔 더 주세요 (주다 = give).
Pouring your own glass and announcing 한 잔 더.
Korean drinking custom is to fill others' glasses, not your own. Offer 받으세요 to a neighbor or let someone pour for you, rather than topping up yourself.

structuredNuance.t: 한 잔 더 = one(native) + glass(counter) + more. The phrase is literal and transparent, but the cultural meaning is the request within a shared-pouring system: you are asking someone else to pour for you, not grabbing the bottle yourself.

주세요 is polite-neutral and safe for servers, coworkers, or seniors. Drop to 줘 with friends. To offer rather than ask, flip to 받으세요 (polite) or 받아 (casual). Use 주세요 to staff and 받으세요 / 따라 드릴게요 for the person sitting next to you.

한 잔 더 주세요 (ask someone to pour for you) vs 한 잔 더 받으세요 (offer to pour for them) vs 한 잔 더 할게요 (announce you'll have one more yourself). These three are easy to mix up; the verb direction tells you whose glass is being filled.
Scale up: 두 잔 더 주세요 (two more), 한 병 더 주세요 (one more bottle). Scale down: 조금만 더 주세요 (just a little more). Limit: 딱 한 잔만 더 할게요 (exactly one more and that's it).

Two traps: (1) using Sino-Korean numbers with 잔 — 이 잔 대신 두 잔, 삼 잔 대신 세 잔; (2) flipping 주다 and 받다 — 받으세요 is what you say to THEM while pouring into their glass, not what you say when you want a refill yourself.

expressions.english: Let me pour you a drink
expressions.shortExplanation: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "Let me pour you a drink".
expressions.explanation: "Let me pour you a drink" — that is 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 (jega han jan ttara deurilgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 ("Let me pour you a glass"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Let me pour you a glass
usagePhrases.note: Polite-humble; offering to pour for a senior
반말, to a friend or close junior

usagePhrases.en: Allow me to pour you one (formal)
usagePhrases.note: Very deferential, to a boss/elder at a formal table
Short prompt as you tilt the bottle toward their glass

examples.ko: 부장님, 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim, jega han jan ttara deurilgeyo.
examples.en: Director, let me pour you a glass.
examples.note: Address the senior by title first, then offer; this is the model 회식 junior-to-senior move

examples.ko:
A: 잔 비셨네요.
B: 아, 제가 따라 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jan bisyeonneyo. B: a, jega ttara deurilgeyo.
examples.en:
A: Your glass is empty.
B: Oh, let me pour for you.
examples.note: B catches the empty glass and offers immediately — the attentive-junior show

examples.ko: 두 손으로 따라 드리는 게 예의예요.
examples.romanization: du soneuro ttara deurineun ge yeuiyeyo.
examples.en: Pouring with both hands is the polite way.
examples.note: 두 손으로 ('with both hands') is essential toward elders; right hand on bottle, left supporting the forearm

expressions.nuance: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 breaks down as 제가 ('I', humble subject) + 한 잔 ('one glass') + 따르다 ('to pour') + 드리다 (humble 'give', elevating the receiver) + -ㄹ게요 ('I'll ~'). The verb 따르다 means 'to pour' and is a 르-irregular: 따라, not 따르어. The honorific chain is the whole point: use 드리다 (humble-give) with seniors, plain 주다 (→ 따라 줄게) with peers and juniors. The most formal upgrade is 한 잔 올리겠습니다 (올리다= 'raise/offer upward'), reserved for very senior figures. Do not confuse 따르다 ('to pour') with 따르다 ('to follow') — same spelling; drinking context (bottle + glass) makes the meaning 'pour'. A key cultural note: pouring your OWN glass is avoided; you pour for the person next to you, and they pour for you. Both-hands etiquette: hold the bottle with your right hand and support your right forearm with your left; over-filling to the brim is considered less polished — 80–90% is ideal. Saying 제가 따라 드릴게요 is THE phrase that marks you as socially aware at a Korean table.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 주다 instead of 드리다 to a senior.
따라 줄게요 is too casual/flat for a boss. The humble 드리다 shows respect: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요. Use 줄게 only with friends/juniors.
Pouring with one hand to an elder.
Toward seniors, pour with both hands (right hand on the bottle, left supporting). One-handed pouring is fine only among close peers/juniors.
Conjugating 따르다 as 따르어/따르어요.
따르다 is a 르-irregular: 따라요, 따라 드릴게요 — not 따르어요. The 르 drops and -아 is added.

structuredNuance.t: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 = 'I (humble) will pour one glass (for you, humbly)'. The humble double-marker 제가 + 드리다 together signal you are serving someone of higher status. Strip those out for peers: 한 잔 따라 줄게.

Use 따라 드릴게요 with seniors (boss, elder, professor). Use 따라 줄게요 with coworkers/peers. Use 따라 줄게 in casual 반말. Upgrade to 한 잔 올리겠습니다 for very deferential formal occasions. Never pour for yourself at the table — always pour for the person beside you.

따라 드릴게요 (polite offer to pour) vs 받으세요 (short prompt said while actually tipping the bottle) vs 한 잔 올리겠습니다 (most deferential form). 받으세요 tends to accompany the action; 따라 드릴게요 announces the intention first.
따르다 is a 르-irregular: 따라요 (present polite), 따라 드릴게요 (future polite humble), 따라 줄게 (casual). The common slip is 따르어요 — wrong; it must be 따라요.

Two pitfalls: (1) using 줄게요 instead of 드릴게요 for a senior — 따라 줄게요 sounds too flat with a boss; (2) forgetting both-hands etiquette — pouring one-handed toward an elder looks careless. Also, over-filling a glass past 90% is seen as less polished.

expressions.english: Your glass is empty — here, let me pour you one
expressions.shortExplanation: 잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 is a practical expression meaning "Your glass is empty — here, let me pour you one".
expressions.explanation: 잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 (jan bieonneyo, han jan badeuseyo) = "Your glass is empty — here, let me pour you one". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 ("Your glass is empty — have one"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Your glass is empty — have one
usagePhrases.note: Polite; noticing and offering to refill a senior

usagePhrases.en: Your glass is empty — take one
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend/close junior

usagePhrases.en: Please allow me to pour you one
usagePhrases.note: More deferential -시죠 toward a boss

usagePhrases.en: Please top up my glass too
usagePhrases.note: 채우다 ('to fill'); inviting them to pour back

examples.ko: 부장님, 잔 비었네요. 한 잔 받으세요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim, jan bieonneyo. han jan badeuseyo.
examples.en: Director, your glass is empty — let me pour you one.
examples.note: Spot the empty glass and offer; the junior's job at 회식 is to monitor the senior's glass

examples.ko:
A: 어, 잔 비었네. 내가 한 잔 따라 줄게.
B: 아, 고마워. 나도 줄까?
examples.romanization: A: eo, jan bieonne. naega han jan ttara julge. B: a, gomawo. nado julkka?
examples.en:
A: Oh, your glass is empty — I'll pour you one.
B: Thanks. Want me to pour you one too?
examples.note: Peer exchange: offering and reciprocating naturally

examples.ko: 계속 비어 있길래 한 잔 채워 드렸어요.
examples.romanization: gyesok bieo itgillae han jan chaewo deuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: It was sitting empty, so I filled it up for you.
examples.note: -길래 ('since I noticed that') explains why you poured without being asked; 채우다 emphasizes filling to a level

expressions.nuance: 잔 비었네요 is 잔 ('glass') + 비다 ('to be empty') in past form 비었- + -네요 (a noticing/remarking ender), meaning 'oh, your glass is empty' — the observation that triggers a refill. You then say 한 잔 받으세요 (받다 'receive' + honorific 으세요), literally 'please receive one', the set phrase said WHILE pouring. This sequence is core 회식 etiquette: watch others' glasses, and when one empties, offer to fill it — you do NOT just refill your own. The verb direction is the main trap: 받으세요 ('please receive') goes with pouring INTO their glass; 주세요 ('please give') is when you want THEM to pour for YOU — beginners flip these and accidentally ask to be poured for instead of offering. 비다 is intransitive ('to be/become empty'), so it's 잔이 비다, not 잔을 비우다 (transitive 비우다 = 'to empty/drain', as in 잔을 비우다 = 'drink the glass dry', a more forceful 'bottoms up' implication). When the senior pours back for you in return, receive with two hands and a slight bow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주세요 when you're the one pouring for them.
받으세요 ('please receive') goes with pouring into their glass; 주세요 ('please give') asks them to pour for you. Offering a refill is 한 잔 받으세요, not 주세요.
Confusing 잔이 비다 (be empty) with 잔을 비우다 (drain it).
비다 = the glass became empty (state). 비우다 = to empty/drain it (e.g. 잔을 비우세요 = 'down your glass'). Don't say 잔을 비웠네요 to mean 'it's empty'.
Stating 'your glass is empty' without offering.
In Korean drinking culture it's an implicit offer to refill. Pair it: 잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 — just noting it and doing nothing can seem inattentive.

structuredNuance.t: 잔 비었네요 = 'The glass has become empty (I notice)'. 한 잔 받으세요 = 'Please receive one glass'. Together they form a paired observation-plus-offer, the most natural way to refill someone's glass at a Korean table. The remark by itself without the offer sounds incomplete.

잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 is polite-neutral and the standard move junior-to-senior. With peers/friends: 잔 비었다, 받아. To be more deferential to the boss: 한 잔 받으시죠. This sequence happens THROUGHOUT the meal; attentiveness to empty glasses is a social skill.

비다 (intransitive, 'become empty' — state) vs 비우다 (transitive, 'to empty/drain' — action). 잔 비었네요 = the glass IS empty; 잔 비우세요 = drain/finish your glass (more pressure). 받으세요 (you pour into their glass) vs 주세요 (ask them to pour into yours) — never flip these.
More deferential: 한 잔 받으시죠 (-시죠 = polite suggestion). Add 제가: 제가 한 잔 드릴게요. Casual: 한 잔 받아. If they decline: 괜찮으세요? 조금만요?

The classic error is saying 주세요 ('give me') when you mean to OFFER a pour. 받으세요 is what you say to THEM as you tilt the bottle toward their glass; 주세요 is what you say when you want THEM to fill YOUR glass. Also, don't just note the empty glass and do nothing — in Korean drinking culture the observation is implicitly an offer.

expressions.shortExplanation: 술이 약해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm a lightweight (can't drink much)".
expressions.explanation: 술이 약해요 (suri yakaeyo) means "I'm a lightweight (can't drink much)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 술이 약해요 ("I have a low tolerance"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; explaining you can't drink much
반말, to friends/close coworkers
-는 편이다 softens it to 'tend to be on the weak side'

usagePhrases.en: You can hold your liquor (high tolerance)
usagePhrases.note: The opposite: 세다 ('strong'), said of a strong drinker

examples.en: I have a low tolerance, so I'll only drink a little.
examples.note: 약해서 ('because weak') gives a polite reason to go slow without fully refusing

examples.ko:
A: 한 잔 더 하세요!
B: 저 원래 술이 약해서요. 조금만요.
examples.romanization: A: han jan deo haseyo! B: jeo wollae suri yakaeseoyo. jogeummanyo.
examples.en:
A: Have one more!
B: I'm naturally a lightweight, so just a little.
examples.note: A typical 회식 exchange: the offer, and the polite limit-set in response

examples.ko: 제가 술이 약한 편이라 한 잔이면 얼굴 빨개져요.
examples.romanization: jega suri yakan pyeonira han janimyeon eolgul ppalgaejyeoyo.
examples.en: I'm rather a lightweight, so one glass turns my face red.
examples.note: 얼굴(이) 빨개지다 ('face turns red') is a concrete, relatable tell that English speakers can picture

expressions.nuance: 술이 약해요 is 술 ('alcohol') + 이 (subject marker) + 약하다 ('to be weak'), meaning 'my alcohol tolerance is weak'. It is the polite, face-saving phrase to announce a low limit before anyone over-pours. The opposite is 술이 세다 (세다 = 'strong'), used for heavy drinkers. The PARTICLE is the classic grammar trap: it must be 술이 약하다 (subject 이), because 약하다 is a descriptive adjective, not a transitive verb — saying 술을 약해요 with the object particle 을 is ungrammatical. The near-synonym 술이 잘 안 받아요 ('alcohol doesn't agree with me') focuses on your body's reaction, while 약하다 focuses on your tolerance level; both are natural. Do not confuse this with 술을 못 마셔요 ('I can't drink at all'): 약하다 means low tolerance — you WILL have some — while 못 마시다 is total inability. Critically, 술이 약해요 is not a hard refusal; in a 회식 it is a polite negotiating move that lets you sip slowly while still participating. Pair it with 조금만 마실게요 ('I'll just have a little') to signal continued social presence.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 술을 약해요 with the object particle.
약하다 is a descriptive adjective; its subject takes 이/가. Correct: 술이 약해요. 술을 약해요 is ungrammatical.
Confusing 술이 약해요 with 술을 못 마셔요.
약하다 = low tolerance (you can drink a little); 못 마시다 = can't drink at all. If you'll still sip, use 술이 약해요, not 못 마셔요.
Translating 'weak to alcohol' as 술에 약해요 by default.
The idiomatic, most natural form is the subject construction 술이 약해요. Lead with that rather than 술에 약해요.

structuredNuance.t: 술이 약해요 = 'alcohol is weak (for me)'. The literal structure names alcohol as the subject, which feels backwards in English ('I am weak to alcohol'), but the Korean idiom always uses 술이 (subject) not 저는 술에 (topic+to). The real meaning is 'I have a low tolerance' — a polite, social qualifier before someone pours too generously.

Use this early in a 회식 or when being poured for — ideally before the glass is full. With seniors: 저는 술이 약해서 조금만 마실게요 (full polite sentence). With peers/friends: 나 술 약해. This is not a refusal; it signals you'll participate but at a smaller pace.

술이 약해요 (low tolerance, will sip) vs 술을 못 마셔요 (total inability) vs 술이 잘 안 받아요 (doesn't agree with my body, focuses on physical reaction). The dividing line: 약하다 = you'll drink a little; 못 마시다 = you won't drink at all.
Soften with 편이다: 술이 좀 약한 편이에요 ('I tend to be a bit of a lightweight'). Strengthen: 술이 완전 약해요 ('I really can't hold it'). Opposite: 술이 세다 / 술이 강하다 ('high tolerance').

Two traps: (1) the particle — 술을 약해요 is ungrammatical; 약하다 is an adjective needing a subject (이/가), not an object (을/를). (2) Treating this as a hard refusal — it isn't. Saying 술이 약해요 still implies you'll have some; if you cannot drink at all, say 술을 못 마셔요 instead.

expressions.shortExplanation: 저는 술 못 마셔요 is a practical expression meaning "I can't drink (alcohol)".
expressions.explanation: "I can't drink (alcohol)" — that is 저는 술 못 마셔요 (jeoneun sul mon masyeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 저는 술 못 마셔요 ("I can't drink alcohol"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; firm but courteous refusal
반말, with friends
전혀 ('not at all') + 술(을) 하다 makes it absolute
안 ('don't') = choice, vs. 못 = inability

examples.ko: 죄송한데 저는 술을 못 마셔요. 사이다 마실게요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande jeoneun sureul mon masyeoyo. saida masilgeyo.
examples.en: Sorry, I can't drink — I'll have cider instead.
examples.note: Offer a soft alternative (사이다 = lemon-lime soda) to stay social and show you're still participating in the mood

examples.ko: 체질상 술을 못 마셔요. 건강상 이유예요.
examples.romanization: chejilsang sureul mon masyeoyo. geongangsang iyuyeyo.
examples.en: I can't drink for constitutional reasons — it's a health thing.
examples.note: 체질상 ('due to my constitution/body type') is the gold-standard unarguable reason that shuts down pressure politely

examples.ko:
A: 한 잔만 하세요.
B: 저 진짜 술 못 마셔서요. 사이다로 건배할게요!
examples.romanization: A: han janman haseyo. B: jeo jinjja sul mon masyeoseoyo. saidaro geonbaehalgeyo!
examples.en:
A: Just have one glass.
B: I really can't drink — I'll toast with cider!
examples.note: B deflects the push with 못 마시다 + offers a soft-drink toast so the mood doesn't break

expressions.nuance: 저는 술 못 마셔요 is 술 ('alcohol') + 못 ('cannot') + 마시다 ('to drink') — stating inability, not choice. The crucial 못 vs. 안 contrast: 못 마셔요 = UNABLE (body, allergy, medication, constitution), while 안 마셔요 = CHOOSING not to (today, or in general). Using 안 to a pushy senior can sound like deliberate refusal ('I won't'), whereas 못 ('I can't') is physiological and harder to argue with, saving both parties' face. 못 마시다 is a total inability — a step beyond 술이 약해요 (low tolerance, will still sip). A particle note: in natural speech 술 못 마셔요 (particle dropped) is common; the fuller 술을 못 마셔요 is also fine. The English-speaker pitfall is expecting one flat 'no' to end pressure. Korean 회식 culture has historically pushed drinks, so reinforce 못 마셔요 with an unarguable reason (운전해야 해서 'I have to drive'; 약 먹고 있어서 'I'm on medication'; 체질상) and offer to toast with a soft drink. A firm 못 마셔요 + reason + cider toast is far more effective than repeating 'no'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 안 마셔요 when you mean you physically can't.
안 = choosing not to (can sound like refusing); 못 = unable. To a senior, 못 마셔요 ('I can't') is safer and harder to push back on than 안 마셔요.
Saying just '노' or a bare 'no' to refuse a drink.
A blunt refusal can offend in 회식 culture. Give a reason and an alternative: 술 못 마셔서 사이다 마실게요. Soften the no.
Confusing 못 마셔요 with 안 좋아해요.
안 좋아해요 ('I don't like it') invites persuasion ('just try it!'). 못 마셔요 ('I can't') states inability and ends the negotiation more cleanly.

structuredNuance.t: 저는 술 못 마셔요 = 'I cannot drink alcohol (am unable to)'. The word 못 marks inability, not unwillingness. The real social function is not just information but a face-saving exit from the pour cycle — saying 못 마셔요 protects your host too, because they did not cause you discomfort.

저는 술 못 마셔요 is polite-neutral. With seniors add 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') and a reason first. Among friends: 나 술 못 마셔. The firmer formal version: 저는 음주를 못 합니다. Always follow with an alternative drink (사이다, 콜라, 물) to show you'll join the mood.

못 마셔요 (unable — physiological) vs 안 마셔요 (choosing not to — can sound like 'I won't') vs 술이 약해요 (low tolerance, will still sip). With a senior, 못 마셔요 is always safer than 안 마셔요 because inability is unarguable; choice invites persuasion.

Add emphasis: 체질상 술을 전혀 못 마셔요 ('constitutionally cannot drink at all'). Softer variant: 술은 잘 못 해요 ('I'm really not good with alcohol'). Keep the 못 in all forms — never swap to 안 when inability is the point.

The trap is choosing 안 마셔요 when you mean 못 마셔요. 안 = choice (invites 'just one sip!'); 못 = inability (hard to argue with). Also, a bare refusal without a reason or a soft-drink alternative can feel socially abrupt in Korean group settings — always soften with 죄송한데, give a reason, and offer to join with 사이다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 조금만 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Just a little, please".
expressions.explanation: 조금만 주세요 (jogeumman juseyo) = "Just a little, please". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 조금만 주세요 ("Just a little, please"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for a small pour
반말, to a friend pouring
반 잔 ('half a glass') is a concrete small amount
Said mid-pour to halt the bottle at the current level

examples.en: I'm a lightweight, so just a little, please.
examples.note: Lead with the reason (술이 약해서) so the pour-er understands before they fill the glass

examples.ko:
A: 얼마나 드릴까요?
B: 조금만요, 거기까지만요!
examples.romanization: A: eolmana deurilkkayo? B: jogeummanyo, geogikkajimanyo!
examples.en:
A: How much should I pour?
B: Just a little — stop right there!
examples.note: B signals both a small amount and a live stop mid-pour; 거기까지만요 is said DURING the pour

examples.en: I have to drive, so I'll take just half a glass.
examples.note: 운전 ('driving') is an accepted and respected reason to cap intake; 반 잔 gives a concrete, unambiguous amount

expressions.nuance: 조금만 주세요 is 조금 ('a little') + 만 ('only') + 주세요 ('please give') — 'only a little, please'. The particle 만 ('only/just') is doing the limiting work; without it, 좀 주세요 is merely a polite request for a pour ('please give', no quantity limit). Many learners say 좀 주세요 thinking it means 'a little' but it actually means 'please give (politely)' — the quantity is unspecified. The most effective live phrase at the table is 거기까지만요 ('just to there'), said mid-pour to stop the bottle at whatever level is in the glass — Koreans use this constantly. For a concrete cap, 반 잔만 주세요 ('just half a glass') leaves nothing ambiguous. The English-speaker pitfall is timing: these words need to come WHILE the person is pouring, not after. Staying silent until the glass is full and then complaining is the non-native move. Gesture matters too: you can slightly bow or tilt the glass toward the pourer to signal 'good, stop'. Abruptly covering the glass with your hand toward a senior can feel rude; a verbal 조금만 주세요 with a slight bow is the graceful version.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 좀 주세요 to mean 'a little'.
좀 is a politeness softener, not a quantity; it means 'please give'. For a small amount use 조금만 주세요 (만 = 'only/just').
Staying silent during the pour, then saying it's too much.
Speak up mid-pour: 조금만요 or 거기까지만요 ('just to there'). Korean pouring is interactive; you signal the amount as it's poured.
Covering the glass with your hand toward a senior.
Abruptly capping a senior's pour can read as rude. Instead say 조금만 주세요 and tilt the glass slightly; a verbal limit is more polite.

structuredNuance.t: 조금만 주세요 = 'give (me) only a little'. The word 만 ('only') is the quantity limiter, not the politeness marker 좀. Without 만 — 좀 주세요 — you get 'please pour (politely)' with no amount limit. That single particle 만 is what makes this a request for less, not just a polite request.

Say this as the bottle tilts toward your glass, not after. Polite with seniors: 조금만 주세요 or 거기까지만요 with a slight bow. Casual with friends: 조금만 줘 or 거기서 멈춰. The mid-pour stop phrase 거기까지만요 is essential regardless of register.

조금만 주세요 (small amount, polite) vs 반 잔만 주세요 (half a glass, more specific) vs 거기까지만요 (live stop mid-pour, very practical) vs 됐어요 ('that's enough / no more', used after a full-glass pour). 됐어요 declines further; 조금만 shapes the current pour.
Scale the limit: 조금만 (a little) → 반 잔만 (half a glass) → 한 모금만 (just a sip). Live stop: 거기까지만요 / 거기면 충분해요. Accept but limit: 딱 조금만 주세요 (딱 = exactly, reinforces the cap).

Three traps: (1) saying 좀 주세요 thinking it means 'a little' — it doesn't; add 만 for quantity. (2) Saying it AFTER the glass is full — speak up MID-pour. (3) Slapping a hand over the glass toward a senior — use words and a slight tilt of the glass instead.

expressions.shortExplanation: 저 술 깼어요 is a practical expression meaning "I've sobered up".
expressions.explanation: 저 술 깼어요 (jeo sul kkaesseoyo) means "I've sobered up". Say it as one set phrase — for example 저 술 깼어요 ("I've sobered up"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the buzz/drunkenness has worn off
반말, with friends

usagePhrases.en: I need to sober up a bit
usagePhrases.note: -아야겠다 = 'I'd better ~'; you intend to sober up

usagePhrases.en: I can't shake the alcohol / still drunk
usagePhrases.note: 안 깨다 = it won't wear off (e.g. next morning)

examples.en: Getting some fresh air sobered me up.
examples.note: 바람(을) 쐬다 ('get some air outside') is the standard first step to sober up — the go-to before deciding to drive

examples.ko:
A: 아직 좀 취한 것 같아요.
B: 해장국 먹으면 술이 좀 깰 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: ajik jom chwihan geot gatayo. B: haejanggung meogeumyeon suri jom kkael geoyeyo.
examples.en:
A: I think I'm still a bit drunk.
B: Hangover soup will help you sober up.
examples.note: 해장국 (haejang-guk) is the classic next-day remedy; B reassures A with practical advice

examples.ko: 아직 술이 안 깬 것 같아요. 운전 안 할게요.
examples.romanization: ajik suri an kkaen geot gatayo. unjeon an halgeyo.
examples.en: I don't think I'm sober yet — I won't drive.
examples.note: 안 깬 것 같다 ('seems not sober yet') is the responsible self-assessment before DUI risk; the sentence models good judgment

expressions.nuance: 술 깨다 is 술 ('alcohol') + 깨다 ('to wake from / break out of a state') — to come out of drunkenness, i.e. 'sober up'. The PARTICLE trap: 깨다 is intransitive here — the state changes on its own — so it is 술이 깨다 / 술(이) 깼어요, NOT 술을 깨다 (술을 would make 깨다 transitive, which is wrong here; 술을 깨다 is not a natural form). To express deliberate effort, use purpose framing: 술 좀 깨야겠어요 ('I'd better sober up') or 술 깨려고 바람 쐬러 나갔어요 ('went out for air to sober up'). Watch 깨다's homographs: it also means 'to break (a dish)' and 'to hatch (an egg)' — context with 술 fixes the 'sober up' meaning. Don't confuse with 깨우다 (transitive 'wake someone up'): 술 깼어요 = I sobered up (happens to me); 깨우다 = you wake another person. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 정신 차리다 ('snap out of it / regain focus') — that phrase is about mental alertness, not metabolizing alcohol; for the physical wearing-off of a buzz, use 술 깨다. Key collocations: 술이 깼다 (sobered), 술이 안 깬다 (still drunk), 술 깨는 데 좋다 ('good for sobering up', said of 해장국/꿀물).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 술을 깼어요 with the object particle.
깨다 ('to sober up') is intransitive; the alcohol/state is the subject: 술이 깼어요. 술을 깼어요 is wrong.
Using 정신 차리다 to mean 'sober up'.
정신(을) 차리다 means 'snap out of it / get focused', about alertness. For the alcohol physically wearing off, use 술(이) 깨다.
Confusing 깨다 (sober up) with 깨우다 (wake someone).
술 깼어요 = I sobered up (happened to me). 깨우다 is transitive 'to wake another person'. Don't say 술 깨웠어요 for yourself sobering up.

structuredNuance.t: 술 깼어요 = 'the alcohol has broken/woken' (intransitive). The literal image is the drunken state cracking open and passing. In real use it means 'I've sobered up' — the buzz is gone, the alcohol has metabolized. It does NOT mean you woke up (일어났어요) or snapped to attention (정신 차렸어요).

Use this to report your state: 술 깼어요 (I'm sober now). To say you plan to sober up: 술 좀 깨야겠어요. To describe still being drunk: 술이 안 깨요. Register: 깼어요 (polite), 깼어 (casual). Comes up before deciding to drive, call a 대리운전, or before a next-day commitment.

술 깨다 (sober up, intransitive, alcohol wears off) vs 정신 차리다 (regain focus/alertness, NOT about alcohol) vs 깨우다 (transitive, wake someone else up). The alcohol-sobriety meaning is uniquely 깨다 with 술 as subject or dropped-particle companion.
State: 술이 깼어요 / 술 깼어요. Still drunk: 술이 안 깨요. Intention: 술 좀 깨야겠어요 / 깨려고요. Cause: -면 깰 거예요 ('if X, you'll sober up').

Two traps: (1) 술을 깼어요 with the object particle — wrong; 깨다 here is intransitive, so the subject particle (이/가) or no particle is correct. (2) Using 정신 차렸어요 to mean 'I sobered up' — that phrase is about alertness/composure, not blood-alcohol. Always use 술 깼어요 for the physical sobriety.

expressions.english: What snacks should we order (to go with drinks)?
expressions.shortExplanation: 안주 뭐 시킬까요? is a practical expression meaning "What snacks should we order (to go with drinks)?".
expressions.explanation: "What snacks should we order (to go with drinks)?" — that is 안주 뭐 시킬까요? (anju mwo sikilkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 안주 뭐 시킬까요? ("What anju should we order?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
