examples.note: 퇴근 시간 ('leaving-work time') = evening rush hour; 출근 시간 ('going-to-work time') = morning rush

examples.ko: A: 사고 났나 봐요, 길이 너무 막혀요. / B: 다른 길로 가 볼게요.
examples.romanization: A: sago nanna bwayo, giri neomu makyeoyo. / B: dareun gillo ga bolgeyo.
examples.en: A: Looks like there was an accident — traffic's terrible. / B: I'll try another route.
examples.note: 사고 나다 ('an accident happens') with -나 봐요 for a guess; 다른 길로 ('via another road') is the natural response

expressions.nuance: 길이 막혀요 is 길 ('road/way') + 이 (subject) + 막히다 ('to be blocked/clogged') in polite present, 'the road is jammed.' 막히다 is the intransitive/passive of 막다 ('to block') — the road IS blocked by traffic — so the subject is the road or the cars: 길이 막히다 or 차가 막히다, both completely standard. The natural opposite is 뚫리다 ('to be unclogged, flowing freely'): 길이 뻥 뚫렸어요, where 뻥 is an expressive adverb meaning 'wide open.' The English-speaker trap is calquing 'there is traffic' as 교통이 많아요 or 트래픽이 있어요 — 교통 (交通) means 'transportation' as a system, not a jam, so 교통이 많아요 sounds odd; use 막히다. The other trap is using transitive 막다: 길을 막아요 means YOU are blocking the road. For the noun 'traffic jam' Koreans say 교통 체증 or 차 막힘, but the practical verb sentence is always 막히다. Register: 막혀요 is polite-neutral; drop 요 to a friend. Tenses: 막혀요 (currently jammed), 막혔어요 (was/got jammed), 막힐 거예요 (will be jammed — useful when asking about rush hour).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 길을 막아요 ('I block the road').
막다 is transitive ('to block something'); the road being jammed is intransitive 막히다. Say 길이 막혀요. 길을 막아요 means you are physically obstructing it.
Saying 교통이 많아요 for heavy traffic.
교통 means 'transportation/traffic' as a system, not a jam. 'Traffic is heavy' is 길이/차가 막혀요. 교통이 많아요 sounds unnatural.
Using 막혀요 for a clogged drain only.
막히다 covers both a jammed road and a blocked pipe/nose. In a driving context 길이 막혀요 clearly means a traffic jam — context, not a different verb, distinguishes them.

structuredNuance.t: 길 ('road') + 이 (subject) + 막히다 (intransitive 'to be blocked') in polite present — 'the road is jammed.' 막히다 is the intransitive/passive of 막다 ('to block'): the road is blocked BY traffic. Both 길이 막히다 and 차가 막히다 are standard. Opposite: 뻥 뚫리다 ('to open wide', 뻥 = expressive 'all the way open').

Used when explaining lateness (길이 막혀서 늦었어요), warning a driver (막힐 것 같아요 — 'it'll probably be jammed'), or chatting about a commute. Polite 막혀요 for most contexts; 막혀 (반말) to close friends. -네요 (차가 많이 막히네요) adds mild surprise.

막히다 (intransitive, road/cars are jammed) vs 막다 (transitive, someone blocks something): 길을 막아요 means YOU are blocking it. The noun form is 교통 체증 ('traffic jam', formal) or 차 막힘 (casual). Don't use 교통이 많아요 — 교통 (交通) is the traffic system, not a jam.
막혀요 (now jammed) → 막혔어요 (was jammed) → 막힐 거예요 (will be jammed) → 너무 막혀서 못 가겠어요 ('so jammed I can't go').
Two traps: (1) 길을 막아요 (transitive) means YOU block the road, not that the road is jammed — use 길이 막혀요 (intransitive). (2) 교통이 많아요 / 트래픽이 있어요 — unnatural translations; Koreans say the road/cars 막히다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you set the GPS?".
expressions.explanation: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 (naebi jom jjigeo juseyo) = "Could you set the GPS?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 ("Please set the GPS"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking a passenger to punch the destination into the navigation screen
반말, to a friend in the passenger seat while you keep your eyes on the road

usagePhrases.en: Please enter the address in the GPS
usagePhrases.note: Fuller version spelling out 주소 ('address') — useful when you're about to dictate the address
Just powering it on (켜다 = 'to turn on') — said when the screen is off

examples.ko: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요. 주소 불러 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: naebi jom jjigeo juseyo. juso bulleo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: Set the GPS, please — I'll read out the address.
examples.note: 불러 드리다 ('read aloud for you') as you dictate; this two-step is the natural flow

examples.ko: A: 내비 찍어 봤어요? 몇 분 걸려요? / B: 한 35분 걸린대요.
examples.romanization: A: naebi jjigeo bwasseoyo? myeot bun geollyeoyo? / B: han 35bun geollindaeyo.
examples.en: A: Did you set the nav? How long does it say? / B: It says about 35 minutes.
examples.note: 찍어 보다 ('try setting it') then ask the ETA — 걸린대요 ('it says it takes') uses reported speech

examples.en: Just follow the nav — it says right turn soon.
examples.note: 내비대로 ('according to the nav', -대로 = 'as per') + 우회전 ('right turn'); -이래요 is reported speech from the nav

expressions.nuance: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 is 내비 (clipped from 내비게이션 'navigation', i.e. car GPS) + 좀 (softener, makes the request gentler) + 찍다 ('to punch in / tap / mark a point') + 주세요 ('please, as a favor'), 'please punch the destination into the GPS.' The key word is 찍다: its core sense is 'to stamp/press/tap,' and Koreans use it for tapping entries on screens — 주소를 찍다 ('punch in the address'), 목적지를 찍다 ('tap in the destination'), 점을 찍다 ('mark a point on a map'). English speakers reach for 입력하다 ('to input', technically correct but stiff/office-style) or invent 내비 해 주세요 (vague, not natural). The address particle is 내비에 ('into the nav', destination-of-content): 내비에 주소(를) 찍어 주세요. Useful partners: 켜다 ('turn on'), 끄다 ('turn off'), 내비대로 ('according to the nav'). Register: 찍어 주세요 to a passenger or anyone polite; 찍어 줘 to a friend. Beware: 찍다 also means 'to take a photo/stamp,' so context matters — near a GPS screen, it clearly means 'enter/tap.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 내비 입력해 주세요 in casual speech.
입력하다 ('to input') is technically correct but sounds stiff/technical. Everyday Korean uses 찍다: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요.
Wrong particle: 내비를 찍어 주세요 for the destination.
You punch the address INTO the nav: 내비에 (주소를) 찍어 주세요. 내비를 찍다 sounds like you're physically tapping the device body, not entering a destination.
Inventing 내비 해 주세요.
내비 ('navigation') isn't used with 하다 as a verb here. To set it, use 찍다 ('punch in') or 켜다 ('turn on'): 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 / 내비 켜 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 내비 (clipped from 내비게이션 'navigation/GPS') + 좀 (softener) + 찍다 ('to tap/punch in') + 주세요 — 'please punch the destination into the GPS.' 찍다's core is 'to press/stamp'; on a screen it means 'tap in, enter'. Particle: 내비에 ('into the nav') for the address destination — 내비에 주소 찍어 주세요.

Said to a passenger while you're driving and can't safely operate the screen. 좀 makes it a soft favor request. To a friend: 내비 좀 찍어 줘. Without 좀 it sounds more direct: 내비 찍어 주세요. The full form 내비게이션 is fine but 내비 is universal and preferred in speech.

찍다 ('tap in', casual/natural) vs 입력하다 ('to input', stiff/formal). Don't use 내비 해 주세요 — 하다 is too vague here; you need 찍다 ('tap in the destination') or 켜다 ('turn it on'). 내비대로 가다 ('go according to the nav') is the partner phrase once the destination is set.
내비 좀 찍어 주세요 → 내비에 주소(를) 찍어 주세요 → 목적지 찍어 주세요. Others: 내비 켜 주세요 (turn it on) / 내비 꺼 주세요 (turn it off) / 내비대로 가면 돼요 (just follow the nav).

Two traps: (1) 찍다 is not obvious — English speakers try 입력하다 (too formal) or 내비 해 주세요 (too vague); learn 찍다 as the natural GPS-entry verb. (2) Wrong particle: 내비를 찍어 주세요 sounds like tapping the device itself; you want 내비에 (주소를) 찍어 주세요 — into the nav.

expressions.shortExplanation: 막차 끊겼어요 is a practical expression meaning "The last bus/train is gone".
expressions.explanation: 막차 끊겼어요 (makcha kkeunkyeosseoyo) means "The last bus/train is gone". Say it as one set phrase — for example 막차 끊겼어요 ("The last bus/train's gone"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; explaining that transit has stopped for the night — the line is no longer running
반말, to a friend — often realizing too late that service has ended
Asking ahead of time so you don't miss it — the preventive question

usagePhrases.en: Guess I'll have to take a taxi
usagePhrases.note: The consequence — falling back on 택시 after missing the 막차; natural follow-up

examples.en: The last train's already gone.
examples.note: 벌써 ('already') adds a sense that it left sooner than hoped or expected

examples.ko: A: 지하철 막차 끊겼어요. 택시 타야겠어요. / B: 카카오택시 불러 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jihacheol makcha kkeunkyeosseoyo. taeksi tayagesseoyo. / B: kakaotaeksi bulleo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: The last subway is gone. I'll have to grab a taxi. / B: Let me call a Kakao Taxi for you.
examples.note: 지하철 ('subway') + pivot to 택시; 카카오택시 불르다 ('call Kakao Taxi') is what most people do after midnight

examples.ko: 막차 몇 시예요? 놓치면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: makcha myeot siyeyo? notchimyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: What time's the last one? I can't miss it.
examples.note: 놓치다 ('to miss') — the verb for missing a bus, train, or opportunity; -면 안 돼요 for 'must not'

expressions.nuance: 막차 끊겼어요 is 막차 ('the last bus/train of the day', 막 'final/last' + 車 'vehicle') + 끊기다 ('to be cut off / stop running') in polite past, 'the last ride has stopped for the night.' The idiom is 끊기다 — the passive of 끊다 ('to cut') — used idiomatically for a service ending: 막차가 끊기다 literally 'the last vehicle gets cut,' meaning it's no longer running. This is one of the most practically important transport phrases in Korea, since subways stop around midnight and you must either catch the 막차 or take a taxi. Contrast 막차 (last departure) with 첫차 ('the first bus/train of the day', 첫 'first'). To say you missed it: 막차 놓쳤어요 (놓치다 = 'to miss/let slip'). The English-speaker trap is saying 막차 떠났어요 ('the last bus departed'), calquing 'the last bus left' — understandable but not the idiomatic Korean; 끊기다 ('service is cut') is about the LINE stopping, not one vehicle leaving. Also, the fixed compound is 막차 (not 마지막차) — 마지막 차 is understandable but 막차 is the natural word. Don't confuse 끊기다 ('be cut off, of service or a call') with transitive 끊다 ('to cut/hang up/quit'): 막차 끊었어요 would wrongly imply someone cut the service.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 막차 떠났어요 for 'last train's gone'.
Koreans idiomatically use 끊기다 ('service is cut off') for transit ending: 막차 끊겼어요. 떠났어요 ('it departed') is understandable but not the lived-in phrase.
Saying 마지막차 instead of 막차.
The fixed word for the night's final bus/train is 막차 (and 첫차 for the first). 마지막 차 is understandable but 막차 is the natural compound Koreans actually say.
Using 끊다 instead of 끊기다.
끊다 is transitive ('to cut/hang up/quit'). The last train STOPPING on its own is passive 끊기다: 막차 끊겼어요. 막차 끊었어요 would mean someone deliberately cut the service.

structuredNuance.t: 막차 ('last bus/train of the day', 막 'final' + 車 'vehicle') + 끊기다 (passive 'to be cut off') in polite past — the service is cut, the night's last ride is no longer running. 끊기다 is the passive of 끊다 ('to cut'); the LINE stops, not just one vehicle. Korea's subways typically stop near midnight, making this phrase genuinely urgent.

Said late at night when realizing transit has stopped. Polite 끊겼어요 to anyone; 끊겼어 (반말) to friends. Often followed by a plan: 택시 타야겠어요 or 카카오택시 불러야겠어요. Preventive question: 막차 몇 시예요? — ask this before leaving the venue, not after.

막차 끊겼어요 ('service is cut') vs 막차 놓쳤어요 ('I missed the last one' — 놓치다 'to miss/let slip') vs 막차 떠났어요 ('the last one departed' — possible but not idiomatic). Contrast 막차 (last) with 첫차 ('first bus/train', 첫 'first'). 끊기다 (passive, service stops) vs 끊다 (transitive, someone cuts it).
막차 끊겼어요 → 막차 놓쳤어요 → 이미 막차 지났어요 ('the last one has already passed'). Question: 막차 몇 시예요? / 막차 아직 있어요? ('is there still a last train?').

Two traps: (1) 막차 떠났어요 — calquing 'the last bus left'; 끊기다 is the idiomatic verb meaning the LINE is cut/done, not just one bus left. (2) 막차 끊었어요 (transitive 끊다) — wrongly implies someone cut the service; use passive 끊기다.

expressions.hangul: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요
expressions.romanization: myeonheo ttan ji eolma an dwaesseoyo
expressions.english: I just got my license recently
expressions.shortExplanation: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is a practical expression meaning "I just got my license recently".
expressions.explanation: "I just got my license recently" — that is 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 (myeonheo ttan ji eolma an dwaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ("I just got my license"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요
usagePhrases.romanization: myeonheo ttan ji eolma an dwaesseoyo
usagePhrases.note: Polite; warning passengers or other drivers that you are a new driver — a natural pre-emptive disclosure

usagePhrases.ko: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어
usagePhrases.romanization: myeonheo ttan ji eolma an dwaesseo
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to friends when explaining your cautious or slow driving
초보운전 ('beginner driver') — the sticker label new drivers in Korea put on their car
The basic factual statement — you hold a 운전면허; used when asked, not for self-deprecation

examples.ko: 저 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요. 천천히 갈게요.
examples.romanization: jeo myeonheo ttan ji eolma an dwaesseoyo. cheoncheonhi galgeyo.
examples.en: I just got my license, so I'll drive slowly.
examples.note: Set expectations honestly, then 천천히 가다 ('drive slowly') as the natural follow-through

examples.ko: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 돼서 고속도로는 무서워요.
examples.romanization: myeonheo ttan ji eolma an dwaeseo gosokdoroneun museowoyo.
examples.en: I just got licensed, so highways scare me.
examples.note: 고속도로 ('expressway/highway') is the intimidating part for new drivers; -어서 gives the reason

examples.ko: A: 면허 딴 지 한 달밖에 안 됐어요. 아직 초보예요. / B: 괜찮아요, 천천히 가도 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: myeonheo ttan ji han dalbakke an dwaesseoyo. ajik choboyeyo. / B: gwaenchanayo, cheoncheonhi gado dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: It's only been a month since I got my license. Still a beginner. / B: That's fine, you can take it slow.
examples.note: 밖에 + 안 됐다 ('only … has passed') stresses how new it is; 천천히 가도 돼요 ('it's OK to go slowly') is the reassuring reply

expressions.nuance: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 면허 ('license', 免許; full form 운전면허 = driver's license) + 따다 ('to obtain/earn', the verb for GETTING a certificate) + -ㄴ 지 ('since [doing]') + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has passed'), i.e. 'it hasn't been long since I got my license.' Two idioms to master: (1) 면허를 따다 — you 따다 ('pluck/earn') a license by passing a test, NOT 받다 ('receive') or 가지다 ('have'); 따다 captures the achievement of passing. (2) -은 지 + 얼마 안 됐다 is the fixed frame for 'I recently started X' — this 지 is the time-elapsed noun (always written with a space, attached to a past-style -ㄴ/은 form), completely different from the conjunctive ending -ㄹ지 ('whether'). The culturally vital partner phrase is 초보운전 ('beginner driver'), the label new Korean drivers attach to their car as a courtesy sticker so other drivers give them more patience. The English-speaker trap is the elapsed-time construction — using 동안 ('during') instead of -은 지 for 'since I got it.' To a friend, 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어. Don't confuse 면허 ('driving license/permit') with 자격증 (a professional skills certificate) — driving is specifically 운전면허.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 면허 받았어요 instead of 면허 땄어요.
A license is obtained with 따다 ('to earn/win', as in passing a test): 면허(를) 땄어요. 받다 ('receive') sounds like it was simply handed to you without effort.
Using 동안 instead of -은 지 for elapsed time.
'It hasn't been long since I got it' uses -은 지 ... 됐어요: 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요. 동안 ('during/for') is for an ongoing duration — 한 달 동안 ('for a month') — not time-since-an-event.
Confusing the time 지 with the ending -ㄹ지.

딴 지 ('since getting it') is the spaced time-noun 지 after a past form. -ㄹ지 ('whether') is a verb ending, e.g. 갈지 (whether to go). They look alike in text but serve entirely different grammatical roles.

structuredNuance.t: 면허 ('license', 免許) + 따다 ('to earn/get by passing a test') + -ㄴ 지 ('since doing') + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has passed') — 'it hasn't been long since I earned my license.' 따다 captures passing the test; 받다/가지다 do not. -은 지 + 됐어요 is the fixed elapsed-time frame.

A natural disclosure to passengers or when chatting with other drivers to explain cautious driving. Polite 됐어요 to most people; 됐어 (반말) to friends. Cultural note: many Korean new drivers put a 초보운전 sticker on their car — this phrase is the spoken equivalent.

저 초보운전이에요 ('I'm a beginner driver') is a direct label. 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is more specific and conversational, giving the actual time frame. Don't confuse 면허 ('driver's license') with 자격증 (a professional skills certificate) — the driving-specific term is 운전면허.
면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 → 면허 딴 지 한 달밖에 안 됐어요 ('only a month') → 면허 딴 지 일 년도 안 됐어요. Also: 처음 혼자 운전하는 거예요 ('first time driving alone').
chips: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요

structuredNuance.t: Two traps: (1) 면허 받았어요 — a license is earned by passing; use 따다, not 받다. (2) Using 동안 ('during') for elapsed time — the correct structure is -은 지 + 됐어요 ('it has been [time] since…'), not 동안 ('during/for a period'). Also, the time-elapsed 지 (written with a space) is NOT the same as the conjunctive ending -ㄹ지 ('whether').

expressions.shortExplanation: 과속하지 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Don't speed".
expressions.explanation: 과속하지 마세요 (gwasokaji maseyo) = "Don't speed". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 과속하지 마세요 ("Please don't speed"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite imperative; warning a driver to stay within the speed limit
반말, to a close friend driving — a direct but casual warning
Gentler — nudging for a slower pace without explicitly naming speeding as a violation
Indirect cue — naming the camera lets the driver decide; 단속 카메라 = enforcement camera

examples.en: Don't speed — it's dangerous.
examples.note: Pair with 위험하다 ('to be dangerous') to give the reason, not just the rule

examples.en: This is a school zone. Don't speed.
examples.note: 어린이 보호구역 ('child protection zone') — fines are doubled and police actively patrol here

examples.ko: A: 앞에 과속 카메라 있어요, 속도 줄이세요. / B: 아, 몰랐어요. 고마워요.
examples.romanization: A: ape gwasok kamera isseoyo, sokdo juriseyo. / B: a, mollasseoyo. gomawoyo.
examples.en: A: Speed camera ahead — slow down. / B: Ah, didn't see it. Thanks.
examples.note: 속도 줄이다 ('reduce speed') is the actionable instruction; 과속 카메라 = speed enforcement camera

expressions.nuance: 과속하지 마세요 is 과속 ('speeding', 過 'excess' + 速 'speed') + 하다 (making it the verb 과속하다 'to speed') + -지 마세요 (the polite prohibitive, from 말다 'to stop/refrain'), 'please don't speed.' The grammar pattern -지 마세요 is the standard polite 'don't do X' in Korean — a top learner error is negating with 안: 과속 안 하세요 means 'you don't speed' (a description/statement), not the command 'don't speed.' For prohibitions, -지 마세요 is the form to use. Korea enforces speed limits hard: 단속 카메라 / 과속 카메라 (speed cameras) are common on expressways and urban roads, 어린이 보호구역 (school zones, 시속 30km) carry doubled fines, and 벌금/과태료 are steep. A softer alternative to 과속하지 마세요 is 천천히 가세요 ('drive slowly') or 속도 줄이세요 ('reduce speed'), which nudge rather than prohibit. The English-speaker trap is also calquing 'don't drive fast' as 빨리 운전하지 마세요 — understandable but 과속하다 is the precise, sign-matching term. Don't confuse 과속 (過速 'excessive speed') with 가속 (加速 'acceleration') — one letter apart, opposite intent. To a friend, 과속하지 마.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 과속 안 하세요 to mean 'don't speed'.
안 + verb negates a statement ('you don't speed'). A command 'don't do X' is -지 마세요: 과속하지 마세요. This is the core prohibition pattern and applies to all verbs.
Mixing up 과속 and 가속.
과속 ('excessive speed/speeding') is the violation; 가속 ('acceleration') is neutrally speeding up. 가속하지 마세요 would oddly mean 'don't accelerate'. Use 과속 for the speeding warning.
Saying 빨리 운전하지 마세요.
It's understandable but the exact, enforcement-aware term is 과속하다. 과속하지 마세요 matches the signs, cameras, and tickets you'll actually encounter; it sounds like you know the law.

structuredNuance.t: 과속 ('speeding', 過速 'excess speed') + 하다 (verb) + -지 마세요 (polite prohibitive, from 말다 'to refrain') — 'please don't speed.' -지 마세요 is the standard polite 'don't do X' pattern. Korea enforces speed limits heavily: 단속 카메라 / 과속 카메라, doubled fines in 어린이 보호구역 (school zones, speed limit 시속 30km).

Said by a passenger warning a driver, or as a general instruction. Polite 마세요 to any driver. 마 (반말) to close friends. Softer nudges: 천천히 가세요 (gentle), 속도 좀 줄여 주세요 (polite favor). 과속하지 마세요 is direct — use it when there is real risk or enforcement nearby.

과속하지 마세요 (direct prohibition) vs 천천히 가세요 (gentle nudge) vs 속도 줄이세요 (action instruction). Don't confuse 과속 (過速 'excessive speed = speeding') with 가속 (加速 'acceleration') — gasoghada means 'to speed up' neutrally; 과속하다 means 'to exceed the limit.'
과속하지 마세요 → 제발 과속하지 마세요 ('please, please don't speed') → 속도 좀 줄여 주세요. Informational: 여기 단속 카메라 있어요 / 어린이 보호구역이에요.

Two traps: (1) 과속 안 하세요 — this is a statement ('you don't speed'), not a command; use -지 마세요 for a prohibition. (2) 빨리 운전하지 마세요 — understandable but 과속하다 is the precise term matching road signs, fines, and cameras.

expressions.shortExplanation: 주차비 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is parking?".
expressions.explanation: 주차비 얼마예요? (juchabi eolmayeyo?) means "How much is parking?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 주차비 얼마예요? ("How much is parking?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking the parking fee at a lot, booth, or building — the basic cost check
반말, to a friend who might know the lot or has parked there before
More formal; 주차 요금 ('parking charge') with 어떻게 돼요 — used when calling ahead or on a booking form
Asking the per-unit rate when the lot is metered — 에 here means 'per'

examples.en: How much is parking here?
examples.note: Asked at the booth or to staff before committing to park; 여기 ('here') specifies this particular lot

examples.en: How much is parking? Is there a discount if I eat here?
examples.note: 할인되다 ('to be discounted') — many Korean lots validate free hours or give discounts for customers

examples.ko: A: 주차비 얼마예요? / B: 30분에 천 원이에요, 초과되면 10분에 오백 원이고요.
examples.romanization: A: juchabi eolmayeyo? / B: 30bune cheon wonieyo, chogwadoemyeon 10bune obaek wonigoyo.
examples.en: A: How much is parking? / B: It's 1,000 won per 30 min, then 500 won per 10 min after that.
examples.note: 초과되다 ('to exceed the included time') is the key word — know it to understand the rate structure

expressions.nuance: 주차비 얼마예요? is 주차비 ('parking fee', 주차 + 費 'cost/fee') + 얼마예요 ('how much is it?'), the basic question for a paid lot. The suffix -비 (費) is a productive Sino-Korean fee-marker you'll meet throughout driving: 주차비 (parking), 주유비 / 기름값 (fuel cost), but note 통행료 (toll) uses -료, not -비 — a detail worth fixing. A slightly more formal variant is 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? (요금 = 'charge/rate'); 얼마예요? is the warm everyday choice. Practically, the smart follow-up after learning the fee is 혹시 할인돼요? or 무료예요? — many Korean lots offer customer validation (영수증 validation, 식당 stamp) or free hours for building users. For per-time rates, use the pattern 30분에 얼마예요? (에 = 'per' for rate). The English-speaker trap is using 가격 ('price', for goods you buy) for a service fee — a parking CHARGE is 주차비 or 요금, not 주차 가격; 가격 sounds like a price tag on a product. Another trap: 비 in 주차비 is the fee suffix, not the word for rain (비) — same hangul, different word. With a friend, 주차비 얼마야?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주차 가격 얼마예요?
가격 is the price of goods. A service charge like parking is 주차비 or 주차 요금. 주차 가격 sounds like you're asking the 'price' of parking as if it were a product for sale.
Confusing 통행료 with 주차비.
Both are driving costs, but 통행료 is a road TOLL (uses 료) and 주차비 is a PARKING fee (uses 비). Ask 통행료 얼마예요? at a tollgate, 주차비 얼마예요? at a lot.
Not asking about validation/free time.
Many Korean lots are free or discounted for customers. After 주차비 얼마예요?, ask 무료예요? or 할인돼요? — and specifically 영수증 가져오면 할인돼요? ('discount if I bring a receipt?') at restaurants.

structuredNuance.t: 주차비 ('parking fee', 주차 + 費 'cost/fee') + 얼마예요 ('how much is it?') — a direct cost question. -비 (費) is the fee suffix: 주차비 (parking), 주유비 (fuel), 입장비 (entry). Note 통행료 (toll) uses 료, not 비 — these are different Sino-Korean charge words. For per-time rates: 30분에 얼마예요? (에 = 'per').

Asked at a lot booth, via intercom, or to building staff before parking. Polite 예요 to staff or strangers. To a friend who's been there: 주차비 얼마야? More formal 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? for calling ahead. Smart follow-up: 혹시 할인돼요? or 무료예요?

주차비 얼마예요? (simple cost check) vs 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? (asks for the full rate structure). Distinguish 주차비 (parking fee) from 통행료 (highway toll, uses 료) and 주유비/기름값 (fuel cost). Don't confuse 주차비 (cost) with 주차장 (the lot itself).
주차비 얼마예요? → 주차비 무료예요? → 혹시 할인돼요? → 30분에 얼마예요? → 영수증 가져오면 할인돼요?

The trap is using 가격 ('price', for goods) for a service fee — a parking CHARGE is 주차비 or 요금, not 주차 가격; 가격 is the tag on something you buy. Also: 비 in 주차비 is the Sino-Korean fee suffix (費), not the word for 'rain' (비) — same hangul, different word.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기 주차하면 안 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can't I park here?".
expressions.explanation: "Can't I park here?" — that is 여기 주차하면 안 돼요? (yeogi juchahamyeon an dwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 여기 주차하면 안 돼요? ("Is it not OK to park here?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Is it not OK to park here?
usagePhrases.note: Polite question; checking whether parking is forbidden — the negative phrasing implies you suspect it might not be allowed
The positive version — asking permission directly; more neutral than the negative form
반말statement telling a friend the spot is off-limits
Stating the rule matter-of-factly — 주차 금지 ('parking prohibited') is the sign language

examples.en: Is it OK to park here?
examples.note: The everyday way to ask permission before leaving your car — use BEFORE parking, not after

examples.en: You can't park here — they'll tow it.
examples.note: 견인되다 ('to be towed', passive) is the consequence; 견인 is a real risk in Korean cities

examples.ko: A: 잠깐 세우는 것도 안 돼요? / B: 네, 여기 주차 금지예요. 앞에 세우세요.
examples.romanization: A: jamkkan seuneun geotdo an dwaeyo? / B: ne, yeogi jucha geumjiyeyo. ape seuseyo.
examples.en: A: Not even for a moment? / B: No, it's a no-parking zone. Pull up ahead.
examples.note: 주차 금지 ('no parking') applies even to brief stops at many designated spots; 앞에 세우세요 gives an alternative

expressions.nuance: 여기 주차하면 안 돼요? is 여기 ('here') + 주차하다 ('to park') + -면 안 돼요 ('it's not OK if'), literally 'is it not OK if I park here?' — a polite check on whether parking is forbidden, with the negative phrasing implying you suspect it might not be. This is the entry point to the most important 되다 grammar pair in Korean: -아/어도 돼요? ('may I? is it OK to?', asking PERMISSION) vs -(으)면 안 돼요 ('it's not allowed / you mustn't', a PROHIBITION). So 주차해도 돼요? = 'can I park?'; 주차하면 안 돼요 = 'you can't park.' Mixing these is the single biggest 돼요 error for learners. In Korea illegal parking is actively enforced: 불법 주차 (illegal parking), 견인 (towing, very common in Seoul), 주차 금지 (no-parking zones), and 과태료 (fines). Note that 안 돼요 comes from 되다, so it's spelled 돼요, never 되요. Also note 주차하다 can take 에 for the spot: 여기에 주차해도 돼요?, though 여기 alone is fine in speech. To a friend, 여기 주차하면 안 돼. Don't confuse 안 돼요 ('not allowed', from 되다) with 안 해요 ('don't do', from 하다).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing -도 돼요? (permission) with -면 안 돼요 (prohibition).
주차해도 돼요? = 'may I park?'; 주차하면 안 돼요 = 'you mustn't park.' Use the right frame: to ask permission, -도 돼요?; to state a ban, -면 안 돼요.
Saying 주차 허락돼요?
허락 ('formal permission/consent') is too heavy for parking. Use the everyday 주차해도 돼요? ('is it OK to park?') instead.
Writing 안 돼요 as 안 되요.
From 되다, the correct contracted form is 돼요 (되어요 → 돼요). 되요 is a common misspelling. So it's 주차하면 안 돼요.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 주차하다 ('to park') + -면 안 돼요 ('it's not OK if') — 'is it not OK to park here?' The negative framing implies you already suspect it might be forbidden. 안 돼요 comes from 되다, so it's spelled 돼요 (= 되어요), NEVER 되요.

Ask staff, a guard, or any nearby person before leaving your car in an uncertain spot. Polite with 안 돼요?; 반말 안 돼 to friends. The positive permission form 주차해도 돼요? is equally natural and slightly more neutral. In Korea, towing (견인) is common in cities, so asking before parking is genuinely important.

Critical pair: -아/어도 돼요? (asking permission, 'may I?') vs -(으)면 안 돼요 (prohibition, 'it's not allowed'). 주차해도 돼요? = 'can I park?' / 주차하면 안 돼요 = 'you can't park.' These are not interchangeable — confusing them reverses the meaning entirely. Also don't say 허락돼요? — too formal for parking; use the -도 돼요/-면 안 돼요 patterns.
여기 주차해도 돼요? (positive ask) → 주차하면 안 돼요 (statement of prohibition) → 주차 금지예요 (the rule) → 주차하면 견인돼요 (the consequence).
The biggest -돼요 error: confusing -도 돼요? (permission) with -면 안 돼요 (prohibition). They are opposite patterns. Also: 안 돼요 is spelled with 돼, not 되 — write 주차하면 안 돼요, not 안 되요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 접촉사고 났어요 is a practical expression meaning "I had a fender-bender".
expressions.explanation: 접촉사고 났어요 (jeopchoksago nasseoyo) = "I had a fender-bender". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 접촉사고 났어요 ("I had a minor collision"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting a small fender-bender to a passenger, friend, or insurance — the go-to phrase for a light contact accident
반말, to a close friend — often texted right after a minor bump
The general version — 사고 ('accident') of any severity; use this if you're not sure or it's more serious

usagePhrases.en: I need to call the insurance company
usagePhrases.note: The next immediate step — calling your 보험 회사 to the scene is standard in Korea

examples.en: I had a fender-bender while parking.
examples.note: -다가 ('while in the middle of') shows the accident occurred during the action of parking — not before or after

examples.ko: 접촉사고 났어요. 많이 안 다쳤어요, 차만 살짝 긁혔어요.
examples.romanization: jeopchoksago nasseoyo. mani an dachyeosseoyo, chaman saljjak geulkyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Had a small collision. No one's seriously hurt — just a scratch on the car.
examples.note: 긁히다 ('to get scratched', passive) for minor paint or body damage; 살짝 ('slightly/lightly') scales it down

examples.ko: A: 접촉사고 났는데 어떻게 해야 돼요? 보험 부를까요? / B: 네, 일단 사진 찍고 보험 부르세요.
examples.romanization: A: jeopchoksago nanneunde eotteoke haeya dwaeyo? boheom bureulkkayo? / B: ne, ildan sajin jjikgo boheom bureuseyo.
examples.en: A: I had a fender-bender — what should I do? Should I call insurance? / B: Yes, first take photos and then call insurance.
examples.note: 보험 부르다 ('call insurance to the scene') + 사진 찍다 ('take photos') are the standard first two steps

expressions.nuance: 접촉사고 났어요 is 접촉사고 ('contact accident/fender-bender', 접촉 'contact' 接觸 + 사고 'accident' 事故) + 나다 ('to occur/happen') in polite past, 'a fender-bender occurred.' The core idiom is 사고(가) 나다 — accidents 나다 ('occur/happen/break out'), an intransitive spontaneous event verb — so you do NOT say 사고를 했어요 ('I did an accident') or 사고를 가졌어요 ('I had an accident'), both calques from English 'have an accident.' Events like accidents, fires, and emergencies all use 나다: 불이 나다 ('a fire breaks out'), 문제가 나다. 접촉사고 specifically means a light scrape or contact — contrast it with 추돌 ('rear-end collision') and 충돌 ('crash/head-on') for more serious accidents. Culturally, after a fender-bender in Korea the standard sequence is: (1) 사진 찍다 ('take photos of the damage'), (2) 보험 부르다 ('call your insurance company to the scene'), (3) 교통경찰 부르다 if there's an injury. Saying 충돌했어요 for a tiny bump is too strong. To a friend, 접촉사고 났어. Don't confuse 사고 ('accident') with 사거리 ('intersection') — similar sound but unrelated.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 사고를 했어요 or 사고 가졌어요.
Accidents 나다 ('occur'), not 하다/가지다. The correct frame is 사고(가) 났어요 / 접촉사고 났어요. English 'have an accident' doesn't translate literally into Korean.
Using 충돌했어요 for a tiny scrape.
충돌 ('crash/collision') is strong and implies serious impact. A minor bump is 접촉사고 ('contact accident'). Save 충돌했어요 for a real crash; say 접촉사고 났어요 for a fender-bender.
Calling only the police, not insurance.
In Korea you typically 보험 부르다 ('call your insurance to the scene') for fender-benders, often before calling police. Saying 접촉사고 났어요 and asking 보험 부를까요? is the normal next move.

structuredNuance.t: 접촉사고 ('contact accident/fender-bender', 接觸事故) + 나다 ('to occur/happen', intransitive spontaneous-event verb) in polite past. 사고가 나다 is the fixed idiom — accidents 나다 like fires (불이 나다) and problems; they are events that OCCUR, not things you DO or HAVE. Do NOT use 하다 or 가지다.

Reported to passengers, friends, or insurance right after a minor collision. Polite 났어요 to most people; 났어 to close friends (often via text). The professional register when calling insurance: 접촉사고가 발생했어요 ('a contact accident has occurred', 발생하다 = 'to arise'). But in everyday speech, 났어요 is universal.

접촉사고 (light contact/scrape) vs 추돌 ('rear-end collision', more serious) vs 충돌 ('crash', severe) vs 사고 (any accident, general). Use 접촉사고 for the smallest category. Don't confuse 사고 ('accident') with 사거리 ('intersection') — they rhyme but are unrelated.
접촉사고 났어요 → 사고 났어요 (general) → 사고가 발생했어요 (formal/professional). Post-accident steps: 사진 찍으세요 → 보험 부르세요 → 경찰 부르세요 (if injury).

Two traps: (1) 사고를 했어요 / 사고를 가졌어요 — calquing 'have an accident'; accidents 나다 (occur), not 하다/가지다. (2) 충돌했어요 for a tiny scrape — 충돌 is a serious crash; save it for real impact. Use 접촉사고 났어요 for a fender-bender.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기서 좌회전해요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I turn left here?".
expressions.explanation: 여기서 좌회전해요? (yeogiseo jwahoejeonhaeyo?) means "Do I turn left here?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 여기서 좌회전해요? ("Do I turn left here?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; checking the turn with a passenger or checking what the GPS said
반말, to a friend navigating — quick confirmation mid-drive

usagePhrases.en: Is it a right turn here?
usagePhrases.note: The right-turn version — 우회전 ('right turn'); double-check before committing

usagePhrases.en: Turn left at the next intersection
usagePhrases.note: Giving the instruction to a driver; 사거리 ('intersection') as a clear landmark

examples.en: Do I turn left here?
examples.note: Asked at a junction when you're unsure — the uncertainty turns the statement into a rising-intonation question

examples.en: Do I turn left here, or go straight?
examples.note: 직진하다 ('to go straight', 直進) as the clear alternative; 아니면 ('or') for a binary choice

examples.ko: A: 여기서 좌회전하면 안 돼요, 비보호예요. 신호 받고 가세요. / B: 아, 몰랐어요. 고마워요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiseo jwahoejeonhamyeon an dwaeyo, bibohoyeyo. sinho batgo gaseyo. / B: a, mollasseoyo. gomawoyo.
examples.en: A: You can't just turn left here — it's an unprotected turn. Wait for the green arrow. / B: Ah, I didn't know. Thanks.
examples.note: 비보호 (좌회전) = 'unprotected left turn' — turn only when safe or on a dedicated arrow signal; foreigners get fined misjudging these

expressions.nuance: 여기서 좌회전해요? is 여기서 ('here', 여기 + 에서 contracted to 서 'at this point') + 좌회전하다 ('to turn left', 左 'left' + 回轉 'rotation') + 해요? (polite question), 'do I turn left here?' The four essential driving directions are Sino-Korean: 좌회전 (left turn), 우회전 (right turn), 직진 (straight, 直進), and 유턴 (U-turn, English loan). These are exactly the words your GPS (내비) says and the road signs show — memorize them as a set. The particle is 에서 (spoken as 서) because the turn is an action performed AT that location, not a destination you arrive at: 여기서 좌회전해요. Using 에 instead — 여기에 좌회전해요 — is a learner error. In Korea, a critical cultural vocabulary item is 비보호 좌회전 ('unprotected left turn'): you must either have a dedicated green-arrow signal or turn only when oncoming lanes are completely clear; foreigners misread this constantly and get fines. The English-speaker trap beyond the particle is using plain 돌다 ('to turn/spin') as 왼쪽으로 돌아요? — understandable informally but 좌회전하다 is the precise, sign-matching verb. To a friend, 여기서 좌회전해?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에 instead of 에서/서 for the turn location.
A turn is an action performed AT a place, so use 에서 (spoken 서): 여기서 좌회전해요? 여기에 좌회전 is wrong — 에 marks a destination, not where an action happens.
Saying 왼쪽으로 돌아요? for a driving turn.
돌다 ('to spin/turn around') is loose and imprecise for driving. The exact driving verb is 좌회전하다, matching road signs and your nav: 여기서 좌회전해요?
Confusing 좌회전 (left) with 우회전 (right).
좌 = left (左), 우 = right (右). Swapping them reverses your route. Lock in 좌회전/우회전/직진/유턴 as the four driving directions as a set.

structuredNuance.t: 여기서 ('here', from 에서 'at this point') + 좌회전하다 ('to turn left', 左回轉) + 해요? — 'do I turn left here?' The particle 에서/서 marks where the action happens (NOT 에, which marks a destination). The four driving directions to know: 좌회전 / 우회전 / 직진 / 유턴 — the same words your GPS speaks.

Asked mid-drive to a passenger or checked against the GPS. Polite 해요? to any passenger. 반말 해? to a friend navigating. When giving the instruction to a driver: 여기서 좌회전하세요 (polite imperative) or 좌회전이에요 (factual announcement).

좌회전 (left) vs 우회전 (right) vs 직진 (straight) vs 유턴 (U-turn) — the four GPS/sign terms. Key cultural item: 비보호 좌회전 = 'unprotected left turn', where you turn only when clear or on a dedicated arrow — missing this causes fines. 왼쪽으로 돌아요? is informal but 좌회전하다 matches signs and nav.
여기서 좌회전해요? → 여기서 좌회전이에요? → 다음 사거리에서 좌회전하세요. Opposite: 여기서 우회전해요? / 직진해요?

Two traps: (1) Using 에 instead of 에서/서 for the turn location — a turn is an action AT a point (에서), not a destination (에): say 여기서 좌회전해요? (2) Saying 왼쪽으로 돌아요? — informal and imprecise; 좌회전하다 is the driving-specific verb matching road signs and your nav.

expressions.shortExplanation: 하이패스로 가세요 is a practical expression meaning "Take the Hi-Pass lane".
expressions.explanation: "Take the Hi-Pass lane" — that is 하이패스로 가세요 (haipaeseuro gaseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 하이패스로 가세요 ("Take the Hi-Pass lane"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; directing a driver to the electronic-toll lane on an expressway
반말, to a friend driving — a quick directional cue as you approach the tollgate

usagePhrases.en: No Hi-Pass? Take the regular lane
usagePhrases.note: 일반 차로 ('regular/general lane') where you pay cash or card at a staffed or card-only booth
통행료 ('toll fee', 通行料) + 내다 ('to pay') — explaining the payment point at a manned booth

examples.en: Got Hi-Pass? Then take the Hi-Pass lane.
examples.note: First check for the device (있어요?), then direct them — this is the complete two-step exchange

examples.en: Take the Hi-Pass lane — you don't have to stop.
examples.note: 안 멈춰도 되다 ('don't need to stop') captures the whole point of Hi-Pass; the gate opens automatically

examples.ko: A: 하이패스 단말기 없어서 일반 차로로 가야 돼요. 통행료 현금으로 내도 돼요? / B: 네, 아니면 카드로도 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: haipaeseu danmalgi eopseoseo ilban charoro gaya dwaeyo. tonghaengnyo hyeongeumeuro naedo dwaeyo? / B: ne, animyeon kadeurodo dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: No Hi-Pass unit, so I have to use the regular lane. Can I pay the toll in cash? / B: Yes, or card works too.
examples.note: 단말기 ('the transponder unit') + 통행료 by 현금 ('cash') or 카드 ('card'); both are accepted at 일반 차로 booths

expressions.nuance: 하이패스로 가세요 is 하이패스 ('Hi-Pass', Korea's electronic toll-collection brand/system) + 로 ('via/by way of', the means-and-route particle) + 가세요 ('please go'), 'go through the Hi-Pass lane.' Hi-Pass is a prepaid RFID transponder (단말기 'unit') with a chip card that lets you pass tollgates at low speed without stopping; without it you use a 일반 차로 ('regular lane') and pay 통행료 (通行料 'toll', note 료 not 비) by cash or card. The particle 로/으로 marks the route or means — a high-frequency pattern: 이쪽으로 가세요 ('go this way'), 카드로 내다 ('pay by card'). A top learner error is using 에 or 에서 — 하이패스로 가다 means 'go VIA the Hi-Pass lane', which is correct; 하이패스에 가다 would sound like going TO a place called Hi-Pass. Practically, if your Hi-Pass card runs out of balance it beeps and the gate may not open, potentially causing a rear-end situation — top it up at a 편의점 or 주유소. The English-speaker trap is treating 하이패스 as just a card; in Korean 하이패스 names the entire lane and system, so 하이패스로 가세요 is the natural instruction. To a friend, 하이패스로 가. Distinguish 통행료 (highway toll) from 주차비 (parking fee) and 주유비 (fuel cost).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에/에서 instead of 로 for the lane.
To go VIA the Hi-Pass lane you mark the route with 로/으로: 하이패스로 가세요. 하이패스에 가세요 sounds like going TO a place called Hi-Pass, not passing through that lane.
Thinking 하이패스 is only a card.
In Korean 하이패스 names the whole electronic-toll lane/system, not just the card. So 하이패스로 가세요 ('take the Hi-Pass lane') is the natural instruction.
Confusing 통행료 (toll) with 주차비/주유비.
통행료 (uses 료) is the highway toll; 주차비 is parking, 주유비/기름값 is fuel. At a tollgate you 통행료(를) 내다 ('pay the toll'), not 주차비.

structuredNuance.t: 하이패스 (Korea's electronic-toll system/lane) + 로 ('via/by way of', means-and-route particle) + 가세요 ('please go') — 'go through the Hi-Pass lane.' 하이패스 uses a RFID transponder (단말기) + chip card; gate opens automatically at low speed. Without one, use 일반 차로 and pay 통행료 (통行料, note 료 not 비) by cash or card.

Said as you approach an expressway tollgate — either to direct a driver or to tell a friend which lane to use. Polite 가세요; 반말 가 to friends. The opposite instruction: 하이패스 없으면 일반 차로로 가세요. The particle 로 is the key: it marks route/means, a pattern reusable in many situations (이쪽으로, 카드로, 버스로).

하이패스 차로 (Hi-Pass lane) vs 일반 차로 (regular pay lane). 통행료 (highway toll, uses 료) vs 주차비 (parking fee, uses 비) vs 주유비/기름값 (fuel cost) — all driving costs, different words. Don't confuse 차로 ('traffic lane') with 통행료.
하이패스로 가세요 → 하이패스 차로로 가세요 (fuller) → 하이패스 없으면 일반 차로로 가세요. Related: 하이패스 잔액 확인하세요 ('check your Hi-Pass balance'), 하이패스 충전해야 돼요 ('need to top up the Hi-Pass').

Two traps: (1) Using 에/에서 instead of 로 — 하이패스에 가세요 sounds like going TO a place called Hi-Pass; you want 하이패스로 ('via the Hi-Pass lane'). (2) Thinking 하이패스 is just a card — in Korean it names the whole lane/system, so 하이패스로 가세요 ('take the Hi-Pass route') is natural and complete.

expressions.shortExplanation: 도와주세요! is a practical expression meaning "Help me, please!".
expressions.explanation: 도와주세요! (dowajuseyo!) = "Help me, please!". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 도와주세요! ("Please help me!"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Standard polite call for help to anyone, strangers included
반말, shouted to a close friend or family member
Softer, more formal request when there's no immediate danger
누가 (someone) added when calling out to a crowd

examples.en: Help! Help me!
examples.note: Shouted twice in rapid succession — the bare repeated cry that draws attention fast in a crowd

examples.ko: A: 가방을 못 들겠어요. 좀 도와주세요. / B: 네, 잠깐만요!
examples.romanization: A: gabangeul mot deulgesseoyo. jom dowajuseyo. / B: ne, jamkkanmanyo!
examples.en: A: I can't lift this bag. Please help me. / B: Sure, just a moment!
examples.note: Everyday non-emergency use; 좀 softens the request to 'a little help'

examples.en: My grandmother collapsed! Somebody please help!
examples.note: Real crisis; 누가 scans the crowd, and 쓰러지셨어요 uses honorific because the person is an elder

expressions.nuance: 도와주세요 is built from the irregular verb 돕다 (to help) + -아/어 주세요 (please do for me), so the stem changes: 돕- → 도와, giving 도와주세요, literally 'please do the helping for me'. In a true emergency you shout it bare and loud; for ordinary favors you soften with 좀 ('just a little') or upgrade to 도와주시겠어요? to sound polite rather than panicked. The 반말 form 도와줘 is strictly for close friends or younger family — shouting it at a stranger reads as rude even under stress. The nearest life-or-death alternative is 살려 주세요 ('please keep me alive'), but that crosses the line into mortal peril; for anything from a stuck zipper to a medical scare, 도와주세요 covers it. English speakers often say just '도움!' (the noun 'help/aid'), which isn't a cry for assistance, or bark bare 도와, which sounds like a blunt command — always keep 주세요 to stay both intelligible and polite.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 도움 to mean 'Help!'
도움 is the noun 'help/aid', not a cry. To call for help you need the verb plus 주세요: 도와주세요.
Shouting 도와 to a stranger.
Bare 도와 is a blunt 반말 command that sounds rude under stress. Add 주세요 (도와주세요) for anyone you don't know.
Building it as 도와 주세요 with the wrong stem, e.g. 돕아주세요.
돕다 is irregular: the ㅂ changes to 와, giving 도와주세요, not 돕아주세요. The correct form is 도와주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please do the helping for me' — built from 돕다 (to help, irregular ㅂ stem) + 아/어 주세요. The ㅂ changes to 와: 돕- → 도와. The real meaning is an all-purpose cry for help, covering emergencies and everyday favors alike.

존댓말 형태 도와주세요 is safe with anyone — strangers, staff, elders. In genuine danger you shout it bare. For a small everyday request, 좀 도와주세요 or 도와주시겠어요? sounds less panicked. Reserve 반말 도와줘 strictly for close friends or younger family, never a stranger.

살려 주세요 ('please save my life') is the step beyond: use it only when your life is genuinely at risk — drowning, an attacker. For everything from a heavy box to a medical incident, 도와주세요 covers it. 도움을 주시겠어요? is a polite formal phrasing but rarely shouted in crisis.
도와줘 (반말) → 도와주세요 (존댓말) → 좀 도와주세요 (softened) → 도와주시겠어요? (formal request) → 누가 좀 도와주세요! (appeal to a crowd). All share the same 도와- stem.

English speakers shout '도움!' (the noun 'help/aid') — that's not a verb cry. Others drop 주세요 and bark '도와' at a stranger, which sounds like a blunt order. And some mistakenly say '돕아주세요' — wrong: 돕다's ㅂ changes to 와, so it must be 도와주세요.

expressions.english: Save me! / Help, I'm in danger!
expressions.shortExplanation: 살려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Save me! / Help, I'm in danger!".
expressions.explanation: 살려 주세요 (sallyeo juseyo) means "Save me! / Help, I'm in danger!". Say it as one set phrase — for example 살려 주세요 ("Please save me"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 cry used only in life-threatening danger
반말, screamed to anyone when there's no time for politeness
Fixed set phrase shouted to a crowd; literally 'save a person'

usagePhrases.en: Please, I'm begging you, save me
usagePhrases.note: 제발 ('I beg you') added to plead for mercy or to an attacker

examples.en: Save me! Help!
examples.note: Repeated bare scream when you genuinely fear for your life — the raw sound of mortal terror

examples.ko: A: 물에 빠졌어요! 살려 주세요! / B: 거기 있어요! 지금 가요!
examples.romanization: A: mure ppajyeosseoyo! sallyeo juseyo! / B: geogi isseoyo! jigeum gayo!
examples.en: A: I'm drowning! Save me! / B: Stay there! I'm coming now!
examples.note: A/B exchange in a water emergency; 빠지다 = 'to fall/sink into'

examples.ko: 불이 났는데 못 나가요. 사람 살려!
examples.romanization: buri nanneunde mon nagayo. saram sallyeo!
examples.en: There's a fire and I can't get out. Somebody help!
examples.note: Trapped-in-fire scenario; 사람 살려 is the reflexive crowd-alert, shorter and rawer than 살려 주세요

expressions.nuance: 살려 주세요 is built from 살리다 (to keep alive, causative of 살다 'to live') + 아/어 주세요, so it literally begs 'please keep me alive' — a step of mortal urgency beyond 도와주세요. You use it only when your life is genuinely at risk: drowning, a physical attack, a fire with no exit. The critical line: 도와주세요 covers any need for help, including danger; 살려 주세요 signals that without intervention you will die or be seriously harmed. Under that level of terror, register collapses — strangers may hear 살려 줘 or the fixed crowd-shout 사람 살려 ('save a person!'), which Koreans produce almost reflexively. 제발 살려 주세요 pleads desperately and is also used when begging an attacker to stop. English speakers most commonly mistranslate 'save me' as 저장해 주세요 (save a file), or reach for 구해 주세요, which is correct but sounds less viscerally desperate than the idiomatic 살려 주세요 / 사람 살려.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 저장해 주세요 for 'save me'.
저장하다 means to save data/a file. To save a life you need 살리다: 살려 주세요.
Using 살려 주세요 for minor trouble like a heavy box.
It signals mortal danger and will alarm people. For ordinary help say 도와주세요.
Writing 살여 주세요 or 살려주새요.
The stem is 살리- → 살려, and the ending is 주세요 (not 주새요). Correct: 살려 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please keep me alive' — 살리다 is the causative of 살다 ('to live'), so the request is: cause me to continue living. The real meaning is an absolute emergency plea used only when you believe your life is at immediate risk.

존댓말 살려 주세요 is appropriate even to a stranger in mortal danger. Under extreme fear, 살려 줘 (반말) and the fixed 사람 살려! (ageless crowd cry) both occur naturally. 제발 살려 주세요 is the begging form used toward an attacker. You would never use this for minor trouble — it will alarm everyone within earshot.

도와주세요 vs 살려 주세요: the difference is whether you might die. A heavy suitcase or a medical scare → 도와주세요. Drowning, a mugger, a locked burning room → 살려 주세요. 구해 주세요 also means 'rescue me' and is correct, but 살려 주세요 is more viscerally urgent and idiomatic.
살려 줘 (반말) → 살려 주세요 (존댓말) → 제발 살려 주세요 (desperate pleading) → 사람 살려! (fixed crowd-alarm). 사람 살려 has no politeness level — it's a reflexive shout.

The fatal mistake is 저장해 주세요 — that's 'please save (a file/data)'. To save a life use 살리다: 살려 주세요. 구해 주세요 is also correct but less instinctive to Koreans in a panic. Never use 살려 주세요 for non-life-threatening help — it causes immediate alarm.

expressions.shortExplanation: 불이야! is a practical expression meaning "Fire!".
expressions.explanation: "Fire!" — that is 불이야! (buriya!). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 불이야! ("Fire!"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: The set alarm shout; shouted to everyone regardless of age or formality
존댓말 report to people around you; 나다 = 'to break out'
Fuller, clearer 존댓말 form — best when phoning 119 or reporting calmly
저기 (over there) added to point to the location

examples.en: Fire! Fire! Everyone get out!
examples.note: Bare alarm cry paired with 다 나가요 ('everyone leave') — the natural combination that empties a building

examples.ko: A: 불났어요! 빨리 나가세요! / B: 어디요? / A: 저기 주방이요!
examples.romanization: A: bulnasseoyo! ppalli nagaseyo! / B: eodiyo? / A: jeogi jubangiyo!
examples.en: A: There's a fire! Get out quickly! / B: Where? / A: Over there, the kitchen!
examples.note: Real A/B exchange showing how to direct people; 주방 = kitchen

examples.ko: 주방에서 불이 났어요. 119에 신고해 주세요! 다들 밖으로 나가세요!
examples.romanization: jubangeseo buri nasseoyo. 119e singohae juseyo! dadeul bakkeuro nagaseyo!
examples.en: A fire has started in the kitchen. Call 119! Everyone go outside!
examples.note: Calm full-sentence report to bystanders; 신고하다 = 'report (to authorities)'

expressions.nuance: 불이야! is the fixed Korean alarm cry equivalent to English 'Fire!' — 불 (fire) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after a consonant). It is grammatically 반말, but the convention is that anyone shouts this to anyone in a fire emergency because politeness is irrelevant when lives are at risk. Contrast the alarm with the report: 불이야! is what you shout to get people moving; 불이 났어요 or 불났어요 is the calmer explanation you give to a 119 dispatcher or a bystander you're briefing. The verb 나다 ('to break out/occur') is the natural partner: 불이 나다, just as 사고가 나다 — in Korean, fires and accidents 'break out', not 'happen'. English speakers most often say bare '불' (just the noun 'fire/flame') which won't read as an alarm, or try '불 알람!' mixing in English, or attach the post-vowel 야 to get '불야' — but 불 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), so the exclamatory ending must be 이야: 불이야!.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Shouting just 불 to mean 'Fire!'
불 alone is the noun 'fire/light' and sounds incomplete as an alarm. Use the set cry 불이야! or 불났어요!
Saying 불 알람! for 'Fire!'
That mixes English 'alarm' and is not idiomatic. Koreans shout 불이야!
Writing 부리야 or 불이얌.
It's 불 + 이야 = 불이야!. Keep the ㄹ on 불 and the plain 이야 ending.

structuredNuance.t: 불 (fire) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after consonant) literally means 'It's fire!' The real function is a mass alarm shout that overrides politeness. Everyone — children, elders, staff — uses this same form in a fire.

불이야! is a register-free alarm — the only situation where 반말 to strangers is fully expected. To report or explain, switch to 불났어요 (casual 존댓말) or 불이 났어요 (fuller 존댓말). When phoning 119, the clear 불이 났어요 with address and floor is what dispatchers need.

불이야! = alarm cry to make people move. 불이 났어요 = factual report to describe what is happening. 119에 신고해 주세요 = direct bystanders to call the emergency line. All three serve different moments in the same emergency.
불이야! (bare alarm) → 불났어요! (존댓말 report) → 불이 났어요! (fuller report) → 주방에서 불이 났어요 (location added). Always pair the alarm with 나가세요 ('get out') to direct people.

Saying bare 불 does not work as an alarm — 불 is just the noun 'fire/flame/light'. Saying 불야! also fails because 불 ends in ㄹ (a consonant), so the exclamatory ending must be 이야: 불이야!. Mixing in English as '불 알람!' is also not Korean.

expressions.shortExplanation: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 is a practical expression meaning "I lost my wallet.".
expressions.explanation: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 (jigabeul ireobeoryeosseoyo) means "I lost my wallet.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 ("I lost my wallet"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to staff, police, or any passerby who might help
반말 to a friend or family on the phone
분실하다: the formal/written word used at a lost-and-found counter or police desk

usagePhrases.en: I think my wallet was stolen
usagePhrases.note: 도둑맞다 when you suspect deliberate theft, not just accidentally dropping it

examples.en: I lost my wallet. Have you seen it by any chance?
examples.note: Bare report to a café or shop staff; 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the question and signals you don't assume blame

examples.ko: A: 어디 있었어? / B: 택시에 지갑 두고 내렸어. 잃어버렸어.
examples.romanization: A: eodi isseosseo? / B: taeksie jigap dugo naeryeosseo. ireobeoryeosseo.
examples.en: A: Where were you? / B: I left my wallet in the taxi and got off. I lost it.
examples.note: 반말 A/B; 두고 내리다 = 'to leave behind and get off a vehicle'

examples.ko: 저 여기 카페에서 지갑을 잃어버렸어요. 분실물 센터가 있나요?
examples.romanization: jeo yeogi kapeeseo jigabeul ireobeoryeosseoyo. bunsilmul senteoga innayo?
examples.en: I lost my wallet here at the café. Is there a lost-and-found?
examples.note: Real situation: asking about the 분실물 센터 (lost-property desk) is the next practical step

expressions.nuance: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 = 지갑 (wallet) + 을 (object marker) + 잃어버리다, where the completive suffix -어버리다 adds the nuance that the loss is total and the speaker feels genuine regret — which is why Koreans almost always use 잃어버리다 rather than bare 잃다 when talking about a missing personal belonging. At a police desk or lost-property counter, the formal equivalent 분실하다 is expected: 지갑을 분실했어요. The critical distinction: 잃어버리다 implies you accidentally misplaced or dropped the wallet (your fault or bad luck), while 도둑맞다 or 도난당하다 means someone stole it — police need to know which, because the report form and the investigation differ. If you were pickpocketed, say 지갑을 소매치기당했어요 or 도난당했어요. English speakers often say just 잃었어요 (sounds abruptly clipped), drop the object marker, or say 지갑이 잃어버렸어요 with the subject particle — but the wallet is the object of losing, so 지갑을 is mandatory.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 지갑이 잃어버렸어요.
The wallet is the object of 잃어버리다, so use 을: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.
Saying 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 when it was clearly stolen.
잃어버리다 implies you misplaced it. If stolen, say 지갑을 도둑맞았어요 or 도난당했어요.
Confusing 지갑 with 가방.
지갑 is a wallet/purse; 가방 is a bag. Name the right item: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I lost-and-it's-gone my wallet' — the suffix -어버리다 marks the action as complete and regretted, which is why it almost always replaces bare 잃다 when talking about a personal belonging. The real meaning is both a factual report and an expression of distress.

존댓말 잃어버렸어요 for any stranger or official. 반말 잃어버렸어 for friends/family. At a formal counter (police desk, lost-and-found, airline desk) use the Sino-Korean 분실하다: 지갑을 분실했어요. This is the register cue that you understand the procedure.

잃어버리다 = accidentally misplaced (you don't know where it went). 도둑맞다 = stolen by someone (implies a criminal). 도난당하다 = same as 도둑맞다 but more formal/written. Police and insurance forms require you to specify which — a mistake here changes the entire paperwork.
지갑을 잃었어요 (clipped, less natural) → 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 (standard, with regret) → 지갑을 분실했어요 (formal) → 지갑을 도둑맞았어요 (stolen). Pair with 분실물 신고 (lost-property report) or 분실물 센터 (lost-and-found).

Dropping the object marker (지갑 잃어버렸어요) is fine in fast speech but can sound unclear when reporting to an official. The bigger error is 지갑이 잃어버렸어요 with the subject particle — the wallet is the object being lost, so 지갑을 is required.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여권을 잃어버렸어요 is a practical expression meaning "I lost my passport.".
expressions.explanation: "I lost my passport." — that is 여권을 잃어버렸어요 (yeogwoneul ireobeoryeosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 여권을 잃어버렸어요 ("I lost my passport"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to police, embassy staff, or hotel concierge
반말 to a friend or family member you're calling for advice
분실하다 at a police station, embassy desk, or formal written report

usagePhrases.en: I need to get my passport reissued
usagePhrases.note: 재발급 받다: the natural follow-up phrase you'll need at the embassy

examples.en: I lost my passport. What should I do?
examples.note: Bare report plus 어떻게 해야 돼요? ('what should I do?') — the most useful opener because it invites guidance from staff or the police

examples.ko: A: 언제 마지막으로 봤어요? / B: 호텔 체크아웃 때 봤는데 그 이후로 없어요.
examples.romanization: A: eonje majimageuro bwasseoyo? / B: hotel chekeuaut ttae bwanneunde geu ihuro eopseoyo.
examples.en: A: When did you last see it? / B: I had it at hotel checkout but haven't seen it since.
examples.note: A/B exchange with a police officer; 체크아웃 때 = 'at checkout time'

examples.ko: 여권을 잃어버려서 대사관에 가야 하는데, 경찰 신고부터 해야 하나요?
examples.romanization: yeogwoneul ireobeoryeoseo daesagwane gaya haneunde, gyeongchal singobuteo haeya hanayo?
examples.en: I lost my passport so I need to go to the embassy — should I report to the police first?
examples.note: Real situation; 신고부터 해야 하나요 = 'should I report first?' — asking about the procedure correctly

expressions.nuance: 여권을 잃어버렸어요 = 여권 (passport, Sino-Korean: 旅券, lit. 'travel document') + 을 + 잃어버리다. Losing a passport abroad is a chain of bureaucracy — hotel, police, then your embassy — so you'll say this phrase multiple times, always in 존댓말, and switch to the formal 여권을 분실했어요 at official desks where the word 분실 (loss/misplacement) triggers the right paperwork. Police will ask whether it was lost (잃어버리다) or stolen (도둑맞다 / 도난당하다), because a stolen passport triggers an Interpol notice while a lost one triggers a reissue (재발급) process — the difference matters legally. The next phrase you need is 여권 재발급 신청을 하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to apply for passport reissuance') or simply 여권 재발급 받아야 해요. English speakers confuse 여권 with 여건 (conditions/circumstances) because the two words sound similar, and they often drop the object marker 을 in a formal report — keep it for clarity.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여건을 잃어버렸어요.
여건 means 'circumstances/conditions'. A passport is 여권: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
Dropping the object marker: 여권 잃어버렸어요 in a formal report.
In casual speech 을 can drop, but for a clear official report keep it: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
Using 잃어버렸어요 when it was stolen.
If stolen, the police need 여권을 도둑맞았어요 / 도난당했어요, which triggers a different report.

structuredNuance.t: 여권 (旅券, 'travel document') + 을 + 잃어버리다. The Sino-Korean 여권 is the only standard word for passport. The -어버리다 suffix signals the loss is total and regretted — exactly the emotional reality when your passport is gone abroad.

존댓말 잃어버렸어요 to hotel staff, police, fellow tourists. Switch to 분실했어요 at a police desk or embassy — that word signals you understand the formal procedure. Never use 반말 잃어버렸어 to officials. At the embassy ask for 여권 분실 신고서 (passport loss report form).

잃어버리다 = misplaced/lost accidentally. 도난당하다 = stolen. The Korean police form requires you to choose one — a passport stolen by a pickpocket needs 도난당했어요, which triggers a criminal report and an alert to immigration authorities. Don't use 잃어버렸어요 if it was taken from you.
여권을 잃어버렸어요 → 여권을 분실했어요 (formal) → 여권 재발급 받아야 해요 (next step) → 여권 분실 신고서를 작성하고 싶어요 (I'd like to fill out a loss report).

여권 and 여건 (conditions/circumstances) sound very similar — a slip here will completely confuse your listener. Listen carefully: 여-권 (旅券) vs 여-건 (與件). Also, dropping the object marker in a formal report (여권 잃어버렸어요) sounds casual; keep 여권을 for clarity.

expressions.shortExplanation: 경찰을 불러 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please call the police.".
expressions.explanation: 경찰을 불러 주세요 (gyeongchareul bulleo juseyo) = "Please call the police.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 경찰을 불러 주세요 ("Please call the police"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 request to a bystander or shop staff
반말 to a friend in a sudden crisis; 좀 softens the urgency slightly

usagePhrases.en: Could you please call the police?
usagePhrases.note: More formal and polite — when you have a moment to be composed
112 is Korea's police number; 신고하다 = 'to report a crime to authorities'

examples.ko: 경찰을 불러 주세요! 저 사람이 제 가방을 훔쳤어요!
examples.romanization: gyeongchareul bulleo juseyo! jeo sarami je gabangeul humchyeosseoyo!
examples.en: Please call the police! That person stole my bag!
examples.note: Bare urgent request; 훔치다 = 'to steal' — cleaner and more precise than just 가져가다

examples.ko: A: 무슨 일이에요? / B: 싸움이 났어요. 빨리 경찰 좀 불러 주세요!
examples.romanization: A: museun irieyo? / B: ssaumi nasseoyo. ppalli gyeongchal jom bulleo juseyo!
examples.en: A: What's happening? / B: There's a fight. Please quickly call the police!
examples.note: A/B exchange showing how the phrase fits into a real frantic moment; 싸움이 나다 = 'a fight breaks out'

examples.ko: 사고가 났어요. 다친 사람이 있어요. 경찰이랑 구급차 좀 불러 주세요!
examples.romanization: sagoga nasseoyo. dachin sarami isseoyo. gyeongcharirang gugeupcha jom bulleo juseyo!
examples.en: There's been an accident. Someone is hurt. Please call the police and an ambulance!
examples.note: Real scene combining both services; 경찰이랑 구급차 = 'police and ambulance'

expressions.nuance: 경찰을 불러 주세요 = 경찰 (police) + 을 + 부르다 (to call/summon) + 주세요. The verb choice is important: 부르다 means to summon someone to your location — it's the same verb you use to call a taxi (택시를 부르다) or beckon a person over. This is different from 전화하다 (to make a phone call to), which you'd use for 112에 전화해 주세요. The real-world distinction between the two: 부르다 = bring the police here; 112에 전화하다 or 신고하다 = contact the police by phone or formally report the incident. Korea's police line is 112 (not 911, which doesn't exist in Korea); fire and ambulance is 119. Mixing up 112 and 119 in an emergency wastes critical seconds. English speakers often say 경찰에게 전화해 주세요 ('please phone the police'), which is grammatically fine but less natural as a shout than the summon verb 불러 주세요. Another pitfall: 경찰을 불어 주세요 — that's from 불다 ('to blow'), not 부르다 ('to call/summon').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling 119 for police.
119 is fire and ambulance. Police is 112: 112에 신고해 주세요.
Using 경찰을 전화해 주세요.
전화하다 never takes 을/를. To phone the institution use 에 (경찰에 전화해 주세요 / 112에 전화); to summon them here, use 부르다: 경찰을 불러 주세요.
Saying 경찰을 불어 주세요.
The verb is 부르다 → 불러, not 불어 (which is 불다 'to blow'). Correct: 경찰을 불러 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please call/summon the police (here)'. The verb 부르다 means to summon to your location — the same word used for calling a taxi. The real meaning is: get law enforcement to arrive at this spot right now.

존댓말 경찰을 불러 주세요 to any bystander, staff, or passerby. 반말 경찰 불러 줘 to a friend. The polished 경찰 좀 불러 주시겠어요? is for calmer moments — a dispute, not an assault. In the heat of the moment, bare 경찰 불러 주세요! is correct and fully natural.

경찰을 불러 주세요 = summon the police to come here (focus on their presence). 112에 신고해 주세요 = formally report the incident by calling 112 (focus on filing a report). In a theft or fight, both are useful: shout 경찰 불러 주세요! first, then 112에 신고하다 afterward.
경찰 불러 줘 (반말) → 경찰을 불러 주세요 (존댓말) → 경찰 좀 불러 주시겠어요? (formal polite) → 112에 신고해 주세요 (phone report). Korea: 112 = police, 119 = fire + ambulance.
경찰을 전화해 주세요 is wrong — 전화하다 never takes 을/를 before the institution you're calling; you need 에 (경찰에 전화해 주세요). Also, 경찰을 불어 주세요 is wrong — 불다 means 'to blow'; the summon verb is 부르다 → 불러.

expressions.shortExplanation: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please call an ambulance.".
expressions.explanation: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 (gugeupcha jom bulleo juseyo) means "Please call an ambulance.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 ("Please call an ambulance"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 request to bystanders; 좀 softens the urgency into a natural appeal
반말 to a friend in a sudden emergency

usagePhrases.en: Could you please call an ambulance?
usagePhrases.note: Polite formal version — slightly less urgent in tone
119 dispatches both ambulances and fire trucks in Korea; 전화하다 = 'to phone'

examples.ko: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요! 사람이 쓰러졌어요!
examples.romanization: gugeupcha jom bulleo juseyo! sarami sseureojyeosseoyo!
examples.en: Please call an ambulance! Someone collapsed!
examples.note: Bare urgent cry; 쓰러지다 = 'to collapse' — the most important context word to know

examples.ko: A: 할아버지가 가슴이 아프대요. 어떻게 해요? / B: 빨리 119에 전화해! 구급차 불러!
examples.romanization: A: harabeojiga gaseumi apeudaeyo. eotteoke haeyo? / B: ppalli 119e jeonhwahae! gugeupcha bulleo!
examples.en: A: Grandpa says his chest hurts. What do we do? / B: Quickly call 119! Call an ambulance!
examples.note: 반말 A/B family crisis exchange; 가슴이 아프다 = 'chest hurts' — always potentially serious

examples.ko: 여기 사람이 의식이 없어요. 빨리 구급차 좀 불러 주세요! 저는 CPR 할게요!
examples.romanization: yeogi sarami uisigi eopseoyo. ppalli gugeupcha jom bulleo juseyo! jeoneun CPR halgeyo!
examples.en: Someone here is unconscious. Please quickly call an ambulance! I'll do CPR!
examples.note: Real scene; 의식이 없다 = 'is unconscious'; 'CPR 할게요' signals you're taking action while others call

expressions.nuance: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = 구급차 (救急車, lit. 'emergency-relief vehicle') + 좀 + 부르다 + 주세요. 구급 (救急) means 'emergency relief/first aid' and 차 means 'vehicle' — so 구급차 is literally an emergency-relief car. As with the police, you summon an ambulance with 부르다 (to call/summon to this location), not 전화하다 (to phone). The 좀 is not really 'a little' here; in spoken Korean 좀 added to a request smooths out the urgency so it doesn't sound like a bark — it's a pragmatic softener that native speakers use even in genuine crises. In practice, 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 and 119에 전화해 주세요 are near-synonyms in emergency situations; the second is more specific about the action (dial the number). Korea's emergency number is 119 for fire and ambulance — not 911 as in the US, and not 112 which is police. English speakers sometimes say 앰뷸런스 (the loanword), which Koreans understand but it sounds foreign and may slow comprehension with a frightened bystander; native 구급차 is clearer and faster to process.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dialing 911 or 112 for an ambulance.
In Korea, ambulance and fire are 119. Police is 112. Say 119에 전화해 주세요.
Using 구급차를 전화해 주세요.
To summon it, use 부르다: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요. To phone the number, say 119에 전화해 주세요.
Confusing 구급차 (ambulance) with 구급상자 (first-aid kit).
구급상자 is a first-aid box. You need the vehicle: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 구급차 = 救急車, literally 'emergency-relief vehicle' (구급 = emergency relief + 차 = vehicle). The real meaning of the full phrase is: summon an ambulance to arrive here immediately. 좀 is a pragmatic softener, not literal 'a little'.

존댓말 불러 주세요 to any bystander or stranger. 반말 불러 줘 to a friend in panic. The softener 좀 stays in both registers — it makes the request sound human rather than a command. For phoning 119 yourself, say 여기 구급차가 필요해요 ('we need an ambulance here') to the dispatcher.

구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = summon the vehicle here (action-focused). 119에 전화해 주세요 = call the emergency line (phone-focused). 응급실이 어디예요? = find the ER room (travel-focused, if the person can move). In the worst cases, you shout the first two and leave the third for later.
구급차 좀 불러 줘 (반말) → 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 (존댓말) → 119에 전화해 주세요 (dial the number). 응급 처치 (emergency treatment) and 응급실 (ER) are the related terms you'll need next.

앰뷸런스 is understood but slows comprehension. Use 구급차. A critical number mistake: Korea is 119 for ambulance/fire, NOT 911 (US) or 999 (UK). 112 is police only. Getting the number wrong in an emergency can cost minutes.

expressions.shortExplanation: 119에 전화해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please call 119.".
expressions.explanation: "Please call 119." — that is 119에 전화해 주세요 (119e jeonhwahae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 119에 전화해 주세요 ("Please call 119"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a bystander; 119 = fire + ambulance dispatch center
반말 to a friend in an emergency
신고하다 stresses that you are officially reporting an emergency, slightly more formal

usagePhrases.en: Quick, get 119 on the line — call an ambulance!
usagePhrases.note: 빨리 (quickly) + 좀 emphasizes both speed and urgency

examples.en: Quickly call 119! There's a fire!
examples.note: Bare urgent command to a bystander; pairs 119에 전화 with 불이 났어요 naturally

examples.ko: A: 사람이 쓰러졌어요! / B: 제가 119에 전화할게요! 움직이지 마세요!
examples.romanization: A: sarami sseureojyeosseoyo! / B: jega 119e jeonhwahalgeyo! umjigiji maseyo!
examples.en: A: Someone collapsed! / B: I'll call 119! Don't move them!
examples.note: A/B showing task distribution in a crisis; 움직이지 마세요 = 'don't move (the person)'

examples.ko: 사람이 차에 치였어요. 119에 신고하고 움직이지 마세요! 제가 신고할게요!
examples.romanization: sarami chae chiyeosseoyo. 119e singohago umjigiji maseyo! jega singohalgeyo!
examples.en: A person got hit by a car. Call 119 and don't move them! I'll report it!
examples.note: Real scene; 치이다 = 'to get hit by a vehicle'; 신고할게요 = 'I will report it' — taking ownership is natural in Korean emergency response

expressions.nuance: 119에 전화해 주세요 = 119 + 에 (destination particle 'to') + 전화하다 (to phone) + 주세요. The particle 에 is not optional here: 전화하다 marks the number you call with 에 ('phone TO a number'), never 를 or 에서. Korea's 119 is a combined fire-and-ambulance dispatch line — not the police (112), and not 911 or 999, which do not exist in Korea. Knowing this single number can be the most important piece of Korean in a medical or fire emergency. The distinction between 전화하다 and 신고하다 is subtle: 전화해 주세요 = 'phone the number' (action-focused); 신고해 주세요 = 'formally report the emergency' (report-focused, sounds slightly more official). In the field both are used interchangeably. The digits 119 are read in Korean as 일일구 (il-il-gu), not as English 'one one nine'. English speakers also reach for 911 out of habit, and some use the wrong particle (119를 전화해 주세요 or 119에서 전화해 주세요 — both wrong).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 119를 전화해 주세요.
전화하다 marks the destination with 에: 119에 전화해 주세요.
Calling 911 instead of 119.
Korea uses 119 for fire/ambulance and 112 for police. There is no 911.
Reading 119 as English 'one one nine'.
Read the digits in Korean: 일일구 (il-il-gu).

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please phone to 119'. The particle 에 marks the destination of a phone call — you call TO a number. The real meaning is: contact Korea's combined fire-and-ambulance emergency line right now.

존댓말 전화해 주세요 to a bystander or stranger. 반말 전화해 줘 to a friend. The more formal 신고해 주세요 is also correct and slightly more official-sounding. If you call 119 yourself, say 여기 불이 났어요 or 여기 사람이 쓰러졌어요 plus your location immediately — dispatchers are trained for this.

119에 전화해 주세요 = dial the number (action). 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = get an ambulance to arrive here (result). 119에 신고해 주세요 = officially report the emergency (formality). All three are correct in emergencies; 119에 전화해 주세요 is the most concise and universally understood.
119에 전화해 줘 (반말) → 119에 전화해 주세요 (존댓말) → 119에 신고해 주세요 (formal report). Always read 119 as 일일구 in Korean. 112 = police only.

Three compounding errors: (1) dialing 911 instead of 119 — there is no 911 in Korea; (2) wrong particle — 119를 전화해 주세요 is wrong; use 119에; (3) reading the digits as English 'one one nine' — Korean dispatchers expect 일일구.

expressions.shortExplanation: 응급실이 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "Where is the emergency room?".
expressions.explanation: 응급실이 어디예요? (eunggeupsiri eodiyeyo?) = "Where is the emergency room?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 응급실이 어디예요? ("Where is the emergency room?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to staff, a taxi driver, or a passerby; subject marker 이 after consonant-final 응급실
반말 to a friend who knows the area
어디 있어요? is an equally polite variant, slightly more explicit
가장 가까운 ('nearest') added when speed matters and you're not at a hospital yet

examples.ko: 저기요, 응급실이 어디예요? 빨리 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, eunggeupsiri eodiyeyo? ppalli gaya haeyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the emergency room? I need to go quickly.
examples.note: Bare question with urgency cue; 빨리 가야 해요 communicates the seriousness to whoever you ask

examples.ko: A: 지금 어디야? / B: 병원 안인데 응급실 어디야? / A: 1층이야, 빨리 와!
examples.romanization: A: jigeum eodiya? / B: byeongwon aninde eunggeupsil eodiya? / A: 1cheungiya, ppalli wa!
examples.en: A: Where are you now? / B: I'm inside the hospital — where's the ER? / A: First floor, come quick!
examples.note: 반말 A/B exchange between friends rushing to hospital; 1층 = first floor

examples.ko: 애가 열이 너무 높아요. 가장 가까운 응급실이 어디예요? 밤에도 문 여나요?
examples.romanization: aega yeori neomu nopayo. gajang gakkaun eunggeupsiri eodiyeyo? bamedo mun yeonayo?
examples.en: My child's fever is very high. Where's the nearest emergency room? Is it open at night too?
examples.note: Real scene; 문 열다 = 'to be open'; asking about night hours is critical for emergency visits

expressions.nuance: 응급실이 어디예요? = 응급실 (emergency room, Sino-Korean: 應急室, lit. 'emergency office-room') + 이 (subject marker after consonant) + 어디예요 ('where is it?'). Korean asks 'where is the ER?' by making 응급실 the subject of the question — not the object — which is why you must use the subject marker 이 and cannot say 응급실을 or 응급실를. For a true life-threatening emergency, calling 119 and letting them dispatch is usually faster than finding the ER yourself; ask 응급실이 어디예요? when you're already mobile and the patient can be transported by yourself or a taxi. The distinctions that save confusion: 응급실 = the hospital's ER for walk-in emergencies; 병원 = hospital or clinic in general; 약국 = pharmacy for minor ailments. To ask a taxi driver, just say 응급실이요! and the hospital name if you know it. English speakers sometimes say 어디 있어요? without the subject marker (fine in casual speech), or confuse 응급실 with 응급 (just the adjective prefix), or pronounce it 응급식 — but it ends in ㄹ: 응급실 (eung-geup-sil).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 응급실을 어디예요?
어디예요 takes the subject marker, not the object: 응급실이 어디예요?
Confusing 응급실 with 병원 or 약국.
응급실 = ER, 병원 = hospital/clinic, 약국 = pharmacy. Name the one you need.
Pronouncing 응급실 as 응급식.
It ends in ㄹ: 응급실 (eung-geup-sil). 응급식 is not a word.

structuredNuance.t: 응급실 (應急室) literally means 'emergency response room'. 이 is the subject marker after the consonant ㄹ. 어디예요 = 'where is (it)?'. The question makes 응급실 the subject: 'where is the emergency room (as a place that exists)?'

존댓말 어디예요 to any stranger, staff, or taxi driver. 반말 어디야 to friends. Add 가장 가까운 ('nearest') when you need to find one urgently and are not at a hospital. To a taxi driver, 응급실 빨리요! ('ER, quickly!') plus the hospital name is the most urgent form.
