응급실 = the ER (for serious emergencies and walk-in crises). 병원/의원 = clinic or hospital for regular medical care. 약국 = pharmacy (for minor issues, no prescription needed for many things). 119를 부르다 = call 119 and be dispatched (faster than finding the ER yourself in a real crisis).
응급실 어디야 (반말) → 응급실이 어디예요? (존댓말) → 응급실이 어디 있어요? (어디 있어요 variant) → 가장 가까운 응급실이 어디예요? (nearest). Also useful: 야간 응급실 있어요? ('is there a night ER?').

응급실을 어디예요? is wrong — 어디예요 takes the subject particle, not the object. Also: 응급 (the Sino-Korean prefix meaning 'emergency') is not a standalone noun for ER; you need the full 응급실. And the pronunciation ends in -실 (sil), not -식 (sik).

expressions.shortExplanation: 다쳤어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm hurt. / I got injured.".
expressions.explanation: 다쳤어요 (dachyeosseoyo) means "I'm hurt. / I got injured.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다쳤어요 ("I'm hurt / I got injured"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to any stranger, 119 dispatcher, or medical staff
반말 to a friend or family member
격식 -습니다 when reporting to officials, police, or 119
다친 사람 ('a hurt/injured person') when reporting about someone else, not yourself

examples.en: I'm hurt. I hurt my knee.
examples.note: Bare report naming the body part; 무릎을 다치다 = 'to injure one's knee' — the body part takes 을/를

examples.ko: A: 괜찮아요? / B: 아니요, 넘어져서 발목을 다쳤어요. 걷기가 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: A: gwaenchanayo? / B: aniyo, neomeojyeoseo balmogeul dachyeosseoyo. geotgiga himdeureoyo.
examples.en: A: Are you okay? / B: No, I fell and hurt my ankle. It's hard to walk.
examples.note: A/B exchange; 넘어지다 = 'to fall down'; 발목 = ankle; 걷기가 힘들다 = 'hard to walk'

examples.ko: 계단에서 굴러서 머리를 다쳤어요. 의식은 있는데 많이 아파요.
examples.romanization: gyedaneseo gulleoseo meorireul dachyeosseoyo. uisigeun inneunde mani apayo.
examples.en: I rolled down the stairs and hurt my head. I'm conscious but in a lot of pain.
examples.note: Real scene; 의식은 있다 = 'is conscious'; helps a 119 dispatcher assess severity immediately

expressions.nuance: 다쳤어요 is the past tense of 다치다 ('to get injured'), and Korean naturally frames an injury in the past tense because the injury event has already occurred — saying present 다쳐요 would mean 'I am in the process of injuring myself right now', which makes no sense. The body part that was injured takes the object marker 을/를: 무릎을 다쳤어요, 발목을 다쳤어요, 손을 다쳤어요. The critical distinction from 아파요 is cause and type: 다치다 describes an accidental physical injury (a fall, a cut, a collision), while 아프다 describes pain or illness from any source, including sickness. A broken bone from falling is 다쳤어요; stomach pain from food poisoning is 아파요. Note that even if an injury is very painful, you use 다쳤어요 to name the injury and 아파요 to describe the pain — both often appear in the same sentence: 무릎을 다쳤어요. 너무 아파요. English speakers often say present-tense 다쳐요 (wrong), use 아프다 for a wound (imprecise), or mark the body part with 이/가 instead of 을/를 (grammatical error).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다쳐요 (present) for an injury that just happened.
Korean uses the past for a completed injury: 다쳤어요.
Using 아파요 to report a wound.
아프다 is general pain/illness. For an injury from an accident, say 다쳤어요.
Marking the body part with 이/가: 무릎이 다쳤어요.
다치다 takes the object marker on the body part: 무릎을 다쳤어요.

structuredNuance.t: 다쳤어요 is the past tense of 다치다 ('to get injured'). Korean uses the past for an injury because the damaging event has already happened — the injury is a completed result, not an ongoing action. The real meaning is 'I have sustained a physical injury (from an accident)'.

존댓말 다쳤어요 to strangers, doctors, and 119. 반말 다쳤어 to friends. The formal 다쳤습니다 is used when reporting to police or in official statements. Adding the body part with 을/를 (무릎을 다쳤어요) is essential for medical staff to assess severity.

다치다 = physical injury from an external accident (fall, cut, collision). 아프다 = general pain or illness from any cause (sickness, cramps, headache, plus injury pain). A wound is 다쳤어요; the pain from that wound is 아파요. The two can coexist: 다쳤는데 아파요 ('I got injured and it hurts').
다쳤어 (반말) → 다쳤어요 (존댓말) → 다쳤습니다 (격식). With body part: 무릎을 다쳤어요, 손을 다쳤어요. For someone else: 다친 사람이 있어요 ('there's an injured person').

Using present-tense 다쳐요 for an injury that just happened sounds like 'I injure myself' (habitual/general) — always use the past 다쳤어요. Using 이/가 on the body part (무릎이 다쳤어요) is also wrong — 다치다 takes 을/를 on the body part.

expressions.shortExplanation: 도둑이야! is a practical expression meaning "Thief! / Stop, thief!".
expressions.explanation: "Thief! / Stop, thief!" — that is 도둑이야! (dodugiya!). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 도둑이야! ("Thief!"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: The fixed crowd-alarm shout; register-free, used by anyone in theft shock

usagePhrases.en: It's a thief! / There's a thief!
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말-flavored form when reporting more calmly to staff or security
저 사람 (that person over there) added to point out the culprit to others
소매치기: specifically for pickpocketing in a crowded place — more precise than 도둑

examples.en: Thief! Please catch him!
examples.note: Bare alarm immediately followed by 잡아 주세요 ('please catch him') — the two shouts that always go together

examples.ko: A: 제 핸드폰이 없어요! / B: 저 사람이 가져갔어요! 도둑이야! 잡아요!
examples.romanization: A: je haendeuponi eopseoyo! / B: jeo sarami gajyeogasseoyo! dodugiya! jabayo!
examples.en: A: My phone is gone! / B: That person took it! Thief! Catch them!
examples.note: A/B exchange showing how bystanders respond; 가져가다 = 'took/carried off'

examples.ko: 지하철에서 누가 제 지갑을 빼 갔어요. 소매치기야! 112에 신고해 주세요!
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo nuga je jigabeul ppae gasseoyo. somaechigiya! 112e singohae juseyo!
examples.en: Someone slipped my wallet out on the subway. Pickpocket! Please call 112!
examples.note: Real scene; 빼 가다 = 'to slip something out and leave'; 112 = police for crime reports

expressions.nuance: 도둑이야! is built from 도둑 (thief/burglar) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after a consonant), literally 'it's a thief!' — and like 불이야! it functions as a register-free alarm that any Korean shouts in the moment of shock, regardless of who is listening, because there's no time for politeness. The key structural rule: because 도둑 ends in a consonant (ㄱ), you must use 이야, not plain 야 (which follows a vowel). To report calmly to staff or write a statement, you switch to 도둑이에요 or 저 사람 도둑이에요. The lexical distinction: 도둑 is any thief or burglar; 소매치기 is specifically a pickpocket — the person who silently slips items from bags, pockets, or coats in crowded places. In a subway or market theft, 소매치기야! is the more accurate and useful alarm. After shouting, the natural sequence is 잡아 주세요! ('please catch them!') and calling 112 (police). English speakers try to shout bare 도둑 (incomplete as an alarm) or say 도적 (a more archaic literary word for 'bandit'), or attach the wrong exclamatory ending 야 instead of 이야.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Shouting just 도둑.
As an alarm it's incomplete. The set cry is 도둑이야! (or polite 도둑이에요).
Using 도둑야 instead of 도둑이야.
After a consonant the ending is 이야: 도둑이야!. 야 follows a vowel.
Saying 도둑 for a pickpocket on the subway.
A pickpocket is 소매치기. Shout 소매치기야! when someone slips something out of your bag.

structuredNuance.t: 도둑 (thief) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after consonant) = 'It's a thief!' The real function is a crowd alarm — the same register-free emergency shout as 불이야!. Anybody shouts this to everybody, overriding normal politeness entirely.

도둑이야! is register-free in the moment of shock. Once the immediate chaos passes, switch to 도둑이에요 or 저 사람 도둑이에요 for a composed report to staff or police. For a written statement or police report, describe the incident: 지갑을 소매치기당했어요 or 가방을 도둑맞았어요.

도둑 = a thief or burglar (general term). 소매치기 = specifically a pickpocket (silent theft of items from pockets/bags in crowds). 강도 = a robber who uses force or threat. Use the right word: 소매치기야! in a subway, 강도야! if someone threatened you with force.
도둑이야! (alarm) → 도둑이에요! (composed report) → 저 사람 도둑이에요 (pointing out the culprit) → 소매치기야! (pickpocket alarm). Always follow with 잡아 주세요! and call 112.

Bare 도둑! sounds incomplete as an alarm — the 이야 ending is what turns it into a shout. Saying 도둑야! is wrong because 도둑 ends in a consonant (ㄱ): the ending must be 이야, not 야. 도적 is literary/historical Korean, not a street cry.

expressions.english: Where is this? / Where am I?
expressions.shortExplanation: 여기가 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "Where is this? / Where am I?".
expressions.explanation: 여기가 어디예요? (yeogiga eodiyeyo?) = "Where is this? / Where am I?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기가 어디예요? ("Where is this place?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 to a passerby when you don't know where you are
반말 to a friend you're calling or texting
어디인가요 — a touch softer and more formal, like asking a shop owner or elder

usagePhrases.en: Where exactly am I right now?
usagePhrases.note: Longer form that spells out the first-person perspective — used when genuinely disoriented

examples.en: Excuse me, where is this place? It's my first time here.
examples.note: Pair with the explanatory -서요 ending which gives a reason naturally; 처음 와봐서요 = 'because it's my first visit'

examples.ko: A: 어디야? 왜 안 와? / B: 택시에서 내렸는데 여기가 어디야? 길을 잃었어.
examples.romanization: A: eodiya? wae an wa? / B: taeksieseo naeryeonneunde yeogiga eodiya? gireul ireosseo.
examples.en: A: Where are you? Why aren't you here? / B: I got out of the taxi but where is this? I got lost.
examples.note: 반말 A/B; combines 여기가 어디야? with 길을 잃었어 — the two companion phrases natives use together

examples.ko: 휴대폰 배터리가 나갔어요. 여기가 어디예요? 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요?
examples.romanization: hyudaepon baeteoriga nagasseoyo. yeogiga eodiyeyo? i geuncheoe jihacheoryeok isseoyo?
examples.en: My phone died. Where am I? Is there a subway station nearby?
examples.note: Real scene; 배터리가 나가다 = 'battery dies'; combining location question with the follow-up need

expressions.nuance: 여기가 어디예요? = 여기 (here/this place) + 가 (subject marker after vowel) + 어디예요 ('where is it?'), literally 'where is here?' — which is exactly how Korean frames 'where am I?'. The subject particle is 가 (not 이) because 여기 ends in a vowel. This is a location-centered question: Korean grammar focuses on the place rather than the person, unlike English 'where am I?' which centers the self. Because of this, the English-speaker instinct to say 나는 어디예요? ('where am I as a person?') sounds bizarre in Korean — as if asking what category of thing 나 (I) belongs to. The natural companion to this phrase is 길을 잃었어요 — saying both gives a more complete picture and invites practical help rather than just a map pointer. The useful follow-ups are 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요? ('is there a subway station nearby?') or 이 주소 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to this address?'). To ask about a remote location, use 거기가 어디예요? (거기 = there); 여기 is strictly 'here'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나는 어디예요? for 'Where am I?'
Korean asks about the place: 여기가 어디예요?, literally 'where is here?'
Using 여기를 어디예요?
어디예요 takes the subject marker: 여기가 어디예요?
Confusing 여기 (here) and 거기 (there).
Ask about where you are with 여기; 거기/저기 point elsewhere.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 (here) + 가 (subject marker) + 어디예요 ('where is it?') = literally 'where is here?' Korean frames the PLACE as the subject, not the person. Saying 나는 어디예요? ('where am I?') sounds like asking what type of thing 나 is — not natural. The correct form centers the location: 여기가 어디예요?

존댓말 여기가 어디예요? to any stranger, passerby, or shop owner. 반말 여기가 어디야? on the phone to a friend. Open the conversation with 저기요 ('excuse me') to a stranger before asking. 지금 제가 어디에 있는 거예요? is the most explicit and thorough version for when you're truly disoriented.

여기가 어디예요? = single factual question about your current location. 길을 잃었어요 = full explanation of being lost that invites extended help. Native speakers often chain both: 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어디예요? — losing the road is the cause, not knowing where you are is the result.
여기가 어디야? (반말) → 여기가 어디예요? (존댓말) → 여기가 어디인가요? (polite formal) → 지금 제가 어디에 있는 거예요? (explicit, disoriented). Often followed by 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요? or 이 주소 어떻게 가요?

나는 어디예요? is the direct calque of 'where am I?' — but Korean centers the place, not the person. Use 여기가 어디예요? Also, the particle must be 가 (not 를): 여기를 어디예요? is wrong because 어디예요 needs the subject, not an object.

expressions.shortExplanation: 한국어를 잘 못해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm not good at Korean.".
expressions.explanation: 한국어를 잘 못해요 (hangugeoreul jal motaeyo) means "I'm not good at Korean.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 한국어를 잘 못해요 ("I'm not good at Korean"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말, the standard polite way to flag your limited Korean to any stranger
반말 to a friend or peer your age

usagePhrases.en: I do not speak Korean well
usagePhrases.note: 격식 -습니다; 한국말 is the slightly more colloquial word for the language
The essential follow-up request — always pair this with 잘 못해요 when asking someone to accommodate you

examples.en: I'm sorry, I'm not good at Korean.
examples.note: The most natural opener; 죄송해요 cushions the admission and invites the other person's patience

examples.ko: A: 주문하시겠어요? / B: 저 한국어를 잘 못해요. 혹시 영어 되세요? / A: 조금요!
examples.romanization: A: jumunhasigesseoyo? / B: jeo hangugeoreul jal motaeyo. hoksi yeongeo doeseyo? / A: jogeumyo!
examples.en: A: Are you ready to order? / B: I'm not good at Korean. Do you happen to speak English? / A: A little!
examples.note: Real A/B restaurant exchange; 혹시 영어 되세요? is a natural, gentle way to ask

examples.ko: 한국어를 잘 못해요. 죄송한데 조금만 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul jal motaeyo. joesonghande jogeumman cheoncheonhi malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: I'm not good at Korean. Sorry, but could you speak just a bit more slowly?
examples.note: Real scene; 조금만 ('just a little') + 천천히 + 말씀해 주시겠어요 is the full polite request to slow down

expressions.nuance: 한국어를 잘 못해요 = 한국어 (Korean language) + 를 (object marker) + 잘 (well) + 못하다 (to be unable to do well). The key interpretive point: 잘 못하다 means 'can't do it well' (ability is limited), while 안 하다 means 'I don't do it' (by choice). Using 안 하다 — 한국어를 안 해요 — implies you are refusing or unwilling, which is not what you mean. The 잘 softens the claim from 'I can't speak Korean at all' (한국어 못해요) to 'I'm not good at it', which is more accurate and humble. 한국어 is the neutral/formal word for the language, while 한국말 is more colloquial and warm; both are correct. The classic follow-up toolkit: 천천히 말씀해 주세요 ('please speak slowly'), 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요? ('could you say that again?'), and 영어 하시는 분 계세요? ('is there anyone who speaks English?'). English speakers most often get the particle wrong (한국어가 잘 못해요 — the language is the object, not the subject) or write 잘못해요 as one word, which means 'to do something wrong/make a mistake' — a completely different word.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 한국어를 안 해요.
안 하다 = 'choose not to do'. To say you lack ability, use 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Using the subject particle: 한국어가 잘 못해요.
The language is the object of 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Splitting 못해요 wrongly or writing 잘못해요.
Here 못 means 'cannot' (잘 못해요 = can't do well). 잘못하다 as one word means 'to do wrong / make a mistake' — a different meaning.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'cannot do Korean well' — 잘 (well) + 못하다 (cannot do). The real meaning is 'my Korean ability is limited', which is a polite, humble admission rather than a flat refusal. 잘 is the crucial modifier that makes this sound honest rather than helpless.

존댓말 잘 못해요 for any stranger, service staff, official, or elder. 반말 잘 못해 for friends. 격식 잘 못합니다 for more formal settings. Always pair this phrase with the follow-up request: 천천히 말씀해 주세요 or 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?

한국어를 잘 못해요 ('not very good') vs 한국어를 못해요 ('can't speak Korean at all') — the 잘 makes it softer and more accurate. 한국어를 안 해요 ('I don't do Korean') sounds like a choice or refusal and is the wrong phrase. 한국어를 배우고 있어요 ('I'm learning Korean') is the positive alternative.
한국어 잘 못해 (반말) → 한국어를 잘 못해요 (존댓말) → 한국어를 잘 못합니다 (격식) → 한국어가 서툴러요 (lit. 'clumsy at Korean', softer alternative). Follow with 천천히 말씀해 주세요 or 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?

Two critical errors: (1) 잘못해요 written as one word means 'to do something wrong / make a mistake' — completely different. Always write 잘 못해요 with a space. (2) 한국어가 잘 못해요 uses the wrong particle — Korean is the object of 못하다, so 한국어를 is required.

expressions.english: Is there anyone who speaks English?
expressions.shortExplanation: 영어 하시는 분 계세요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there anyone who speaks English?".
expressions.explanation: "Is there anyone who speaks English?" — that is 영어 하시는 분 계세요? (yeongeo hasineun bun gyeseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 영어 하시는 분 계세요? ("Is there anyone who speaks English?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Is there anyone who speaks English?
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 with double honorific — 분 (honorific for person) + 계세요 (honorific for 있다) — correct when addressing a group of strangers
반말 to friends; plain 하는 사람 + 있어 — casual, fine among equals

usagePhrases.ko: 영어 하실 수 있는 분 계신가요?
usagePhrases.romanization: yeongeo hasil su inneun bun gyesingayo?
usagePhrases.en: Is there someone who can speak English?
usagePhrases.note: More formally polite — 하실 수 있는 + 계신가요 — at a service counter or in a formal setting
Direct question to one specific person; 할 줄 알다 = 'to know how to do'

examples.en: Is there by any chance anyone who speaks English?
examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') is the essential softener — it signals you don't assume anyone will help and makes the request feel less demanding

examples.ko: A: 여기 영어 하시는 분 계세요? / B: 네, 제가 조금 할 수 있어요. 뭐가 필요하세요?
examples.romanization: A: yeogi yeongeo hasineun bun gyeseyo? / B: ne, jega jogeum hal su isseoyo. mwoga piryohaseyo?
examples.en: A: Is there anyone here who speaks English? / B: Yes, I can speak a little. What do you need?
examples.note: A/B exchange; B's response 조금 할 수 있어요 ('I can speak a little') is the most common reply

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 영어 하시는 분 계세요? 제가 한국어를 잘 못해서요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande, yeongeo hasineun bun gyeseyo? jega hangugeoreul jal motaeseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, is there anyone who speaks English? It's because my Korean isn't very good.
examples.note: Real scene; -서요 trailing explanation ('because…') is natural and polite; pairs directly with 한국어를 잘 못해요

expressions.nuance: 영어 하시는 분 계세요? deploys two layers of honorific simultaneously: 분 (the honorific word for 'person', vs plain 사람) and 계세요 (the honorific existence verb, vs plain 있어요). Both are necessary when you're addressing a room full of strangers or asking staff — Koreans notice if you undercut the register by saying 사람 있어요? to an elder or manager. The verb for using a language in Korean is 하다 (to do/speak), not 말하다 or 말해요: you say 영어 하다, 영어 하시다, 영어 할 줄 알다. The dividing line between 계세요? and 할 줄 아세요?: 계세요? scans a group ('is there someone who…?'); 할 줄 아세요? is a direct question to one identified person in front of you. The softener 혹시 ('by any chance') before the question is nearly obligatory in polite speech — without it, the question can feel like a demand. English speakers often say 영어 말해요? (calquing 'speak English' with 말하다) or use plain 사람 있어요? to an official context, both of which under-register the respect the situation calls for.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 사람 있어요? to elders or staff.
To a roomful of strangers the honorific 분 + 계세요 is more courteous: 영어 하시는 분 계세요?
Saying 영어 말해요? for 'speak English'.
Korean uses 하다 for languages: 영어 하시는 분, or 영어 할 줄 아세요? for one person.
Using 있으세요? wrongly here.
For 'is there a person', the honorific existence verb is 계세요 (people exist with 계시다): 영어 하시는 분 계세요?

structuredNuance.t: 영어 (English) + 하시는 (honorific relative clause 'who speaks') + 분 (honorific 'person') + 계세요 (honorific 'is there?'). Literally 'is there a person (honorific) who speaks English (honorific)?'. The double honorific is not redundant — both are socially required when addressing a group of strangers.

Use the double-honorific form 하시는 분 계세요? with any group of strangers, at service counters, hospitals, or hotels. Reduce to 하는 사람 있어? only with peers or friends. Always add 혹시 at the start to soften. If a specific person is in front of you, switch to the direct 영어 할 줄 아세요?

영어 하시는 분 계세요? = scans a group for any English speaker. 영어 할 줄 아세요? = asks one specific person. 영어 되세요? = casual-polite shorthand ('does English work for you?'), common in service contexts like restaurants. All three are correct in different frames.
영어 하는 사람 있어? (반말) → 영어 하시는 분 계세요? (존댓말 group) → 영어 하실 수 있는 분 계신가요? (formal polite) → 영어 할 줄 아세요? (direct to one person) → 혹시 영어 되세요? (service-context shorthand).

영어 말해요? calques 'speak English' with 말하다, but Korean uses 하다 for languages. 영어 말하시는 분 계세요? is intelligible but unnatural. Also, 사람 있어요? to a manager or elder is under-polite — always use 분 + 계세요 with strangers in a service context.

expressions.shortExplanation: 사고가 났어요 is a practical expression meaning "There's been an accident.".
expressions.explanation: 사고가 났어요 (sagoga nasseoyo) = "There's been an accident.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 사고가 났어요 ("There's been an accident"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 reporting any accident to 119, bystanders, or police
반말 to a friend or family member
격식 -습니다 when reporting formally to police, insurance, or in a written statement
교통사고 (traffic accident) specifies a vehicle crash — the word dispatchers need to send the right unit

examples.en: There's been an accident! Someone is hurt!
examples.note: Bare report paired with 사람이 다쳤어요 — the two pieces of information a dispatcher needs first

examples.ko: A: 여기 교통사고가 났어요. / B: 지금 어디예요? / A: 강남대로 3번 출구 앞이요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi gyotongsagoga nasseoyo. / B: jigeum eodiyeyo? / A: gangnamdaero 3beon chulgu apiyo.
examples.en: A: There's been a car accident here. / B: Where are you now? / A: In front of exit 3 on Gangnam-daero.
examples.note: A/B exchange with a 119 dispatcher; giving the exact location immediately is critical

examples.ko: 고속도로에서 사고가 났어요. 차가 두 대 부딪혔어요. 다친 사람이 있어요. 119 좀 불러 주세요!
examples.romanization: gosokdoroeseo sagoga nasseoyo. chaga du dae budityeosseoyo. dachin sarami isseoyo. 119 jom bulleo juseyo!
examples.en: There's been an accident on the highway. Two cars collided. Someone is hurt. Please call 119!
examples.note: Real scene; 부딪히다 = 'to collide'; 두 대 = 'two (vehicles)'; full three-sentence report is the 119 template

expressions.nuance: 사고가 났어요 = 사고 (accident, Sino-Korean: 事故) + 가 (subject marker) + 나다 ('to break out/occur') in the past tense. Korean uses the verb 나다 for events that 'break out' — the same verb as 불이 나다 ('a fire breaks out') and 문제가 나다 ('a problem arises'). The grammatical key: the accident is the subject of 나다 (사고가 났어요), so the subject marker 가 is required — you cannot say 사고를 났어요 (that would need 사고를 일으켰어요 = 'caused an accident'). The specificity: 사고 = any accident; 교통사고 = specifically a traffic/vehicle accident; 산업재해 = workplace accident. For a 119 call, lead with 교통사고가 났어요 or 사람이 쓰러졌어요 so dispatchers immediately route correctly. If you were the victim, use 사고를 당했어요 ('I was in an accident', literally 'I received an accident') — this centers the victim's experience, unlike 사고가 났어요 which is a neutral third-person report. English speakers say 사고를 만들었어요 ('I made an accident') — accidents aren't 'made' in Korean; they 'break out' with 나다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 사고를 만들었어요 for 'there was an accident'.
Accidents 'occur' with 나다, not 'are made'. Say 사고가 났어요.
Using 사고를 났어요.
With 나다 the accident is the subject: 사고가 났어요. (Use 사고를 당했어요 if you want 'I had an accident'.)
Saying just 사고 to a dispatcher.
Specify what kind for the right response: 교통사고가 났어요 for a car crash.

structuredNuance.t: 사고 (事故, accident) + 가 (subject marker) + 나다 ('to break out/occur'). Literally 'an accident broke out'. Korean uses 나다 for uncontrolled events that erupt — fires, accidents, problems. The accident is the grammatical subject, not an object; 나다 is intransitive here.

존댓말 났어요 for 119 calls, bystanders, and initial reports. 반말 났어 to family or friends. 격식 났습니다 for official statements, insurance reports, or police interviews. When phoning 119, follow immediately with 위치 ('location') — dispatchers always ask 어디예요? first.

사고가 났어요 = neutral report: an accident occurred (no blame assigned, no victim identified). 사고를 당했어요 = victim-centered: I was involved in/affected by an accident. 사고를 냈어요 = 'I caused an accident' (you are at fault). These three carry completely different legal weight — use the right one.
사고 났어 (반말) → 사고가 났어요 (존댓말) → 사고가 났습니다 (격식) → 교통사고가 났어요 (specific: vehicle) → 사고를 당했어요 (victim frame) → 사고를 냈어요 (I caused it).

사고를 만들었어요 ('made an accident') is wrong — accidents 나다 ('break out'), not 만들다 ('make/create'). Also: 사고를 났어요 is wrong; 나다 requires the subject marker: 사고가 났어요. And 사고를 냈어요 (transitive causative) means you CAUSED it — don't use this unless you are admitting fault.

expressions.shortExplanation: 짜증나요 is a practical expression meaning "It's so annoying / I'm irritated".
expressions.explanation: 짜증나요 (jjajeungnayo) = "It's so annoying / I'm irritated". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 짜증나요 ("It's annoying / I'm irritated"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; about a situation, NOT usually said directly at the person causing it
반말, to a close friend or muttered to yourself when frustrated

usagePhrases.en: It's driving me crazy with irritation
usagePhrases.note: -아 죽겠어요 ('to death') maxes out the frustration for comic effect
네요 turns it into a shared grumble rather than a complaint aimed at someone

examples.ko: A: 와이파이 또 끊겼어? / B: 응, 아 진짜 짜증나.
examples.romanization: A: waipai tto kkeunkyeosseo? / B: eung, a jinjja jjajeungna.
examples.en: A: Did the WiFi cut out again? / B: Yeah, ugh, this is so annoying.
examples.note: A/B exchange; the friends vent together about a situation — not a person

examples.en: The bus isn't coming again. So annoying.
examples.note: Venting about a frustrating situation; natural because the irritation targets the bus, not a person

examples.ko: 계속 같은 거 물어봐서 좀 짜증났어요.
examples.romanization: gyesok gateun geo mureobwaseo jom jjajeungnasseoyo.
examples.en: They kept asking the same thing, so I got a bit irritated.
examples.note: Past tense 짜증났어요 reports the irritation after the fact; 좀 softens it into a grumble rather than an accusation

expressions.nuance: 짜증나요 is from 짜증(이) 나다 ('irritation arises') — a verb built on the noun 짜증 ('irritation, annoyance'). It is the everyday word for the prickly, fed-up feeling when small things go wrong: the bus is late, the wifi drops, someone nags you for the fifth time. The word is honest and extremely common, but it is BLUNT, even slightly crude, so the safe zone is venting about a SITUATION to a friend, or muttering to yourself. Saying 짜증나요 straight to a person's face — especially a senior, a coworker, or staff — is confrontational, like snapping 'you're pissing me off.' For a controlled, polite complaint, soften with 좀 짜증나네요 or step up to 불편해요 ('it's uncomfortable/inconvenient') in formal contexts. The phrase people confuse it with is 화나요 ('I'm angry'): 화나다 is real, bigger outward anger, while 짜증나다 is petty irritation — using 화나요 for a late bus overstates it, and using 짜증나요 for a serious betrayal understates it. The grammar trap: 짜증(이) 나다 is intransitive, so you say 짜증나요 (irritation arises in you), never 짜증해요 (no such verb). Mark the cause with 때문에: 너 때문에 짜증나 ('I'm annoyed because of you') — still 반말-only and pointed.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짜증나요 directly to staff or a senior.
It's blunt and confrontational, like 'you're annoying me.' For a polite complaint use 좀 불편해요 or describe the problem; save 짜증나 for friends/yourself.
Saying 짜증해요.
There is no verb 짜증하다. It's 짜증(이) 나다 — the irritation 'arises': 짜증나요. The 나다 part is essential.
Using 화나요 for minor annoyances.
화나다 is genuine anger; for a late bus or slow wifi it's overkill. The right word for petty irritation is 짜증나요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '짜증(irritation) 나다(arises)' — irritation wells up inside you. The real meaning is a caught-in-traffic, low-boil prickling irritation, not rage. It is situational and fleeting, not a judgment of character.

Use to vent about a situation to close friends or yourself — a late bus, a slow server, repeated interruptions. DO NOT say it to the face of a stranger, a senior, or someone serving you. That registers as 'you're annoying me' and causes a scene. With seniors, use 좀 불편하네요 or describe the problem calmly.

vs. 화나요: 화나다 is real, bigger anger directed at someone — using it for a late bus is overkill. vs. 불편해요: the polite alternative for formal complaints ('I'm a bit uncomfortable with this'). vs. 답답해요: the stuck, suffocating frustration (can't get through, not just annoyed). 짜증나다 = petty prickle; 화나다 = real anger; 답답하다 = boxed-in helplessness.
짜증 나 죽겠어요 (maxed-out, comic), 좀 짜증나네요 (softened shared grumble), 짜증났어요 (past tense report), 짜증 나게 하다 (causative — 'make someone irritated'). The irritation source takes 때문에: 너 때문에 짜증나.

짜증하다 does not exist — it's 짜증(이) 나다. Also do NOT say it directly to a person's face in a non-close relationship; this is a venting word for situations and close friends. Saying 화나요 for every 'upset' feeling misses the lighter, pricklier 짜증 register entirely.

expressions.shortExplanation: 설레요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm fluttering with excitement (sweet anticipation)".
expressions.explanation: 설레요 (seolleyo) means "I'm fluttering with excitement (sweet anticipation)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 설레요 ("My heart's fluttering / I'm so giddy"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: My heart's fluttering / I'm so giddy
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the sweet, hopeful, butterflies-in-the-stomach excitement
반말, to a close friend
Plain-form exclamation muttered to yourself; very natural

usagePhrases.en: I'm so giddy / I can barely stand it
usagePhrases.note: 너무 ('so/too') amps the flutter into an almost-overwhelming sweetness

examples.ko: A: 내일 첫 데이트잖아요! / B: 알아요, 어떡하지… 너무 설레요.
examples.romanization: A: naeil cheot deiteujanayo! / B: arayo, eotteokaji… neomu seolleyo.
examples.en: A: Tomorrow's your first date! / B: I know, oh man… I'm so nervous-excited.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the sweet romantic flutter; -잖아요 = 'you know, right?' and 어떡하지 expresses flustered delight

examples.en: It's a new semester, so I'm excited but also a little nervous.
examples.note: Pairing 설레다 (pleasant flutter) with 떨리다 (nervous trembling) shows the real mix most people feel

examples.en: The first snow fell. Somehow my heart's fluttering.
examples.note: 설레다 for a seasonal moment, not romance — shows how broadly Koreans use this word

expressions.nuance: 설레요 comes from 설레다 ('to flutter, to feel one's heart race with sweet anticipation'). This is the warm, hopeful, butterflies-in-the-stomach excitement — before a trip, a date, a reunion, the first snow. It is gentle, inward, and romantic-leaning, and Koreans use it constantly in everyday life and all over song lyrics and dramas. The crucial contrast is with 떨리다 ('to tremble / be nervous'): 떨리다 is the JITTERY nerves before an exam or a speech (can be bad nerves), while 설레다 is the PLEASANT flutter you actively welcome — they overlap (a first date is often both), but if you say 설레요 before a scary job interview it sounds strange, because 설레다 implies you're looking forward to it rather than dreading it. A cooler near-word is 기대돼요 ('I'm looking forward to it') — that is more mental and measured, while 설레다 is the physical, heart-fluttering sensation. Register: 설레요 is polite; 설레 is 반말; 설렌다 is the natural self-exclamation. The English-speaker pitfall is spelling and conjugation: the stem is 설레-, so present is 설레요 and past is 설렸어요 — NOT 설레여요 (a very common wrong form) and NOT 설래요 (equally common misspelling). Also it's intransitive: 마음이 설레요 ('my heart flutters'), you do not do 설레 to an object.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing or saying 설레여요 / 설래요.
The stem is 설레-, so present is 설레요 and past is 설렸어요. 설레여요 and 설래요 are common but wrong; lock in 설레요.
Using 설레요 before something you dread (exam, scary interview).
설레다 implies happy anticipation. For nervous jitters use 떨려요 ('I'm nervous'). Mixing is fine only when you're genuinely excited too.
Treating it as 'excited' in the loud/hyped sense.
설레다 is a soft inner flutter, not pumped-up hype. For 'pumped/thrilled' loudness, 신나요 fits better; 설레다 is gentle anticipation.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 설레다 = 'to flutter.' The real meaning is a sweet, whole-body flutter of anticipation — something you actively welcome, not a neutral tremble. Koreans use it for romantic feelings, seasons changing, travel, and any warm hopeful moment.

Use freely with anyone — friends, family, even in polite conversation, because the feeling is positive and warm. 설레요 (polite), 설레 (반말), 설렌다 (self-exclamation). It fits any happy anticipation: trips, romance, gifts, new seasons. Don't use it for something you dread — that signals a misread of the situation.

vs. 떨리다: 'to tremble/be nervous' — can be good OR bad nerves. 설레다 is always the happy flutter. A first date might be both (설레고 떨려요). vs. 기대돼요: 'I'm looking forward to it' — cooler, more mental. 설레다 is the physical heart-race. vs. 신나요: pumped/hyped energy. 설레다 is quieter and more inward.
너무 설레요, 설레서 잠이 안 와요 ('I'm so giddy I can't sleep'), 마음이 설레요 (명시적 subject), 설레는 마음으로 ('with a fluttering heart' — common in messages/cards). Past: 설렜어요.

Two traps: (1) misspelling — it's 설레요 / 설렸어요, NOT 설래요 or 설레여요; the stem is 설레-, a clean ㅔ-ending verb. (2) using 설레요 before something you dread — 설레다 implies you welcome it, so it sounds incongruous before a scary interview.

expressions.shortExplanation: 민망해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm so embarrassed / awkward".
expressions.explanation: "I'm so embarrassed / awkward" — that is 민망해요 (minmanghaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 민망해요 ("It's so embarrassing / I feel awkward"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: It's so embarrassing / I feel awkward
usagePhrases.note: Polite; mild social embarrassment, lighter than mortification
반말, to a close friend after a small social slip
네요 shares the awkwardness softly, inviting a smile
-아 죽겠어요 maxes it for comic effect — for truly cringe moments

examples.en: Ugh, how embarrassing.
examples.note: Muttered after a small social slip-up — dropped something in public, said the wrong name

examples.ko: A: 발표하다가 말이 막혔어요. 어떡해요. / B: 아이고, 민망했겠다. 다들 이해해요.
examples.romanization: A: balpyohadaga mari makyeosseoyo. eotteokaeyo. / B: aigo, minmanghaetgetda. dadeul ihaehaeyo.
examples.en: A: I froze up mid-presentation. What do I do. / B: Oh no, that must've been so awkward. Everyone gets it.
examples.note: A/B exchange using past 민망했겠다 ('you must have felt awkward') to empathize

examples.ko: 칭찬을 너무 많이 받으니까 좀 민망하네요.
examples.romanization: chingchaneul neomu mani badeunikka jom minmanghaneyo.
examples.en: Getting so much praise makes me a bit bashful.
examples.note: 민망하다 for the squirmy feeling of over-the-top praise — not just a slip-up

expressions.nuance: 민망해요 (from 민망하다) is the squirmy, shrink-in-place embarrassment you feel after a small social misstep — you fell in public, got caught in a white lie, received too much praise, or an awkward silence dragged on. It is the 'oh no, this is so awkward, I want to disappear' feeling. Crucially, it is light and social — not deep shame or genuine mortification. The three-way contrast matters: 민망하다 = light awkward embarrassment; 부끄럽다 = shy/bashful blushing, also used for moral shame in formal writing; 창피하다 = mortified, 'I've lost face, I really screwed up publicly.' Many learners grab one word and overuse it — matching the strength is essential. If you froze during a presentation, 민망해요 or 창피해요 fits; if you're blushing at a compliment, 부끄러워요 or 민망해요; if you did something publicly shameful, 창피해요. Register: 민망해요 polite, 민망해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) defaulting to 부끄러워요 for every 'embarrassed' — a public trip or awkward moment is 민망해요, not the shy 부끄러워요; (2) confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다 ('sorry for an apology') — they sound similar to beginners but mean entirely different things. Also it's an adjective for your state: 민망해요, never 민망당했어요 or 민망나요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다.
They sound similar but 미안하다 = 'sorry (apology)', 민망하다 = 'awkward/embarrassed'. 'I feel awkward' is 민망해요, not 미안해요.
Using 부끄러워요 for an awkward public slip-up.
부끄럽다 leans 'shy/bashful.' A public fall or cringe moment is better 민망해요 (awkward) or 창피해요 (mortified). Pick the strength that fits.
Overshooting with 창피해요 for a tiny awkwardness.
창피하다 is strong 'humiliated/lost face.' For a small, harmless awkward moment, 민망해요 is the right, lighter word.

structuredNuance.t: 민망하다 has no clean etymology hook for learners, but the feeling is clear: the squirmy, 'I want to shrink' social embarrassment after a minor misstep or too much attention. It is NOT shame about your character — it's social awkwardness.

민망해요 is polite-casual and appropriate in most registers. You can say it to a coworker ('아, 민망하네요') without it sounding unprofessional. It's softer and more relatable than 창피해요 in everyday speech. 민망해 is 반말; 민망하네요 is the most conversational polite form.

민망하다 = light awkward embarrassment (slip, pause, too much praise). 부끄럽다 = shy/blushing (modest shyness; formal moral shame). 창피하다 = mortified, lost face (real public screw-up). The strength order: 민망 < 창피 < 수치스럽다 (deep shame). Pick the level that fits the situation.
좀 민망하네요 (softened, shared), 민망해 죽겠어요 (comic max), 민망했겠다 (empathy past: 'you must have felt so awkward'), 민망한 상황 ('an awkward situation').

Two traps: (1) confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다 ('sorry for an apology') — they sound similar but mean opposite things: 민망해요 = 'I feel awkward,' 미안해요 = 'I'm sorry'; (2) reaching for 부끄러워요 for every 'embarrassed' — 부끄럽다 is shy/bashful, while 민망하다 fits awkward public slips better.

expressions.english: I feel proud and full (warm satisfaction)
expressions.shortExplanation: 뿌듯해요 is a practical expression meaning "I feel proud and full (warm satisfaction)".
expressions.explanation: 뿌듯해요 (ppudeutaeyo) = "I feel proud and full (warm satisfaction)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 뿌듯해요 ("I feel so proud / fulfilled"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the warm glow of quiet accomplishment — humble and relatable
반말, shared with a friend after doing something well
Self-exclamation after completing something; often with a deep breath

usagePhrases.en: I'm really proud / that really fills me
usagePhrases.note: 진짜 deepens the warm satisfaction without sounding boastful

examples.ko: A: 드디어 3킬로 뺐어요! / B: 와, 진짜 뿌듯하겠다!
examples.romanization: A: deudieo 3killo ppaesseoyo! / B: wa, jinjja ppudeutagetda!
examples.en: A: I finally lost three kilos! / B: Wow, you must feel so proud!
examples.note: A/B exchange: 뿌듯하겠다 ('you must feel fulfilled') as a warm reaction to someone's achievement

examples.ko: 애가 상 받는 거 보니까 너무 뿌듯했어요.
examples.romanization: aega sang banneun geo bonikka neomu ppudeutaesseoyo.
examples.en: Seeing my kid get an award, I felt so proud.
examples.note: 뿌듯하다 for warm pride watching someone you love succeed — not just your own effort

examples.ko: 한 달 동안 운동했더니 살이 빠져서 뿌듯해요.
examples.romanization: han dal dongan undonghaetdeoni sari ppajyeoseo ppudeutaeyo.
examples.en: After a month of exercise I lost weight, so I feel really fulfilled.
examples.note: Pride in your own sustained effort paying off; -았더니 shows the result of that effort

expressions.nuance: 뿌듯해요 (from 뿌듯하다) is the warm, chest-swelling, quietly full satisfaction you feel when you (or someone you love) accomplished something — you finished a hard task, your kid did well, your effort paid off. The image is your chest swelling with happy fullness; it is INWARD and humble-feeling, which is why Koreans use it freely about themselves without sounding arrogant. The key contrast is with 자랑스럽다 ('to be proud of'): 자랑스럽다 is more outward, declarative pride you express ABOUT someone or something (아들이 자랑스러워요 'I'm proud of my son') — often directed at or about others. 뿌듯하다 describes the felt inner glow, usually for your own effort or a heartwarming moment you witnessed. Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 about yourself can sound boastful; saying 뿌듯해요 sounds modest and relatable — that is the crucial social difference. Don't confuse it with 만족하다 ('to be satisfied'), which is cooler, more evaluative, and less warm. Register: 뿌듯해요 polite, 뿌듯해 반말. Don't attach an object (뿌듯하다 is a state adjective): mark the cause with -아서/-니까 (끝내서 뿌듯해요).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 for personal satisfaction.
자랑스럽다 is outward, declarative pride and can sound boastful about yourself. The humble inner glow is 뿌듯해요.
Attaching an object: 시험을 뿌듯해요.
뿌듯하다 describes your state, not a target. Mark the cause: 시험 끝나서 뿌듯해요 ('I feel fulfilled because the exam's over').
Swapping in 만족해요 for the warm feeling.
만족하다 is cool, evaluative 'satisfied (it met the standard).' The warm, chest-swelling pride is 뿌듯해요. They're not interchangeable.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '뿌듯하다' means a full, swollen-feeling state — like your chest is pleasantly full. The real meaning is quiet, humble inner pride or satisfaction, not the public declaration 'I'm proud.' It is a feeling you have inside, not a performance for others.

Use freely with friends, family, coworkers — it never sounds arrogant because it describes a felt inner state, not a boast. You can say it after a personal achievement, a child's success, or a collective win. 뿌듯해요 is polite; 뿌듯해 is 반말. Even bosses/elders can hear it without it feeling off.

vs. 자랑스럽다: outward, declarative pride directed at someone/something — 아들이 자랑스러워요. Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 can sound boastful. 뿌듯해요 is the humble alternative for personal satisfaction. vs. 만족해요: cool, evaluative satisfaction ('it met the standard'). The warm, chest-filling feeling is 뿌듯해요.
진짜 뿌듯해요 (deeper satisfaction), 너무 뿌듯해요 ('so fulfilled'), 뿌듯하겠다 ('you must feel proud' — empathy form), 뿌듯했어요 (past tense, reporting after the fact). Cause takes -아서/-니까: 끝내서 뿌듯해요.

The pitfall is using 자랑스러워요 for personal warm-fuzzy satisfaction — that word signals outward pride and can sound boastful about yourself. When YOU feel the inner glow, say 뿌듯해요. Also don't attach an object: it's an adjective for your state, so mark the cause: 시험 끝나서 뿌듯해요, not 시험을 뿌듯해요.

expressions.english: I feel stifled / frustrated / boxed in
expressions.shortExplanation: 답답해요 is a practical expression meaning "I feel stifled / frustrated / boxed in".
expressions.explanation: 답답해요 (dapdapaeyo) means "I feel stifled / frustrated / boxed in". Say it as one set phrase — for example 답답해요 ("I feel stifled / frustrated"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the closed-in, can't-breathe-or-get-through feeling — physical OR emotional
반말, to a friend when you need to vent the boxed-in feeling

usagePhrases.en: It's driving me up the wall (with stifled frustration)
usagePhrases.note: -아 죽겠어요 maxes the stifled frustration — strong but commonly used among friends
Stronger idiom: '속(my insides) 터지다(burst)' — for the truly helpless, explosive pent-up feeling

examples.en: The room is really small, so it feels a bit stifling.
examples.note: Literal physical sense: cramped, stuffy, closed-in — not emotional at all

examples.ko: A: 어디가 힘들어요? / B: 말이 안 통해서 너무 답답해요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga himdeureoyo? / B: mari an tonghaeseo neomu dapdapaeyo.
examples.en: A: What's been hard? / B: We can't communicate at all, so it's so frustrating.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the emotional sense: blocked, can't get through to someone

examples.ko: 엄마가 제 말은 안 듣고 자기 말만 해서 답답해 죽겠어요.
examples.romanization: eommaga je mareun an deutgo jagi malman haeseo dapdapae jukgesseoyo.
examples.en: Mom won't listen to me and only talks, so it's driving me crazy.
examples.note: The classic stuck, can't-make-them-understand frustration; -만 ('only') sharpens the one-sided feel

expressions.nuance: 답답해요 (from 답답하다) is a uniquely Korean feeling word that covers a whole family of 'closed-in' sensations: physically stuffy/cramped (a tiny room, tight clothes, a congested chest when sick), AND emotionally stifled/frustrated when you can't get through — communication is blocked, a slow person won't understand, you're stuck and powerless. The unifying image is 'blocked, can't breathe, can't get out.' This feeling is crucially different from 짜증나다 ('irritated') and 화나다 ('angry'): 짜증나다 is prickly annoyance at small things; 화나다 is outward anger directed at someone; but 답답하다 is the INWARD, helpless, suffocating frustration of being stuck — often with no one clear to blame. There is no single English word for it, which is exactly why English speakers default to 화나요 ('angry') when a Korean would say 답답해요 ('stifled/stuck'). A stronger sibling idiom is 속(이) 터지다 ('my insides burst') for extreme 답답함. Register: 답답해요 polite, 답답해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-때문에; the stifling thing can also be the grammatical subject: 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest feels tight').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 화나요 for the stuck, can't-get-through feeling.
화나다 is outward anger at someone. The helpless, boxed-in 'I can't make this work/get through' feeling is 답답해요. They're different emotions.
Forcing one English word and missing the physical sense.
답답하다 also means physically stuffy/cramped (room, chest, clothes): 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest feels tight'). It's not only emotional.
Saying 답답나요 like 짜증나요.
답답하다 is an adjective: 답답해요, not 답답나요. Only 짜증 takes 나다. Keep 답답해요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 답답하다 = 'to be stuffy/blocked.' The real meaning spans physical (a cramped room, a congested chest) AND emotional (blocked communication, stuck with no exit). The thread is the same blocked, can't-breathe sensation in both domains — that's what makes it uniquely Korean.

Use 답답해요 freely with close friends and family when venting about a situation — a room, a relationship, a slow process. 답답해 is 반말. With superiors or in formal situations, soften: 좀 힘드네요 or describe the problem neutrally. Never direct it at a person's face in a formal setting.

vs. 짜증나요: petty irritation at a specific thing, more outward. vs. 화나요: real anger directed at someone — more explosive. vs. 속상해요: heartsore upset about a loss or loved one's pain. 답답해요 = inward, helpless, boxed-in stifling. There is no English word — that's why English speakers misfire.
답답해 죽겠어요 (maxed-out frustration), 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest is tight'), 속 터져요 (idiom: 'my insides are bursting'), 답답한 마음 ('a stifled/frustrated heart'). Cause takes -아서/-때문에.

(1) Defaulting to 화나요 for the stuck, can't-get-through feeling — 화나다 is anger, 답답하다 is stifled helplessness; different emotions. (2) Missing the PHYSICAL dimension — 가슴이 답답해요 is 'my chest feels tight (stuffy/congested),' not metaphorical. (3) Saying 답답나요 by analogy with 짜증나요 — it's 답답해요 (adjective), never 답답나요.

expressions.english: I feel a little hurt / let down (by someone close)
expressions.shortExplanation: 서운해요 is a practical expression meaning "I feel a little hurt / let down (by someone close)".
expressions.explanation: "I feel a little hurt / let down (by someone close)" — that is 서운해요 (seounhaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 서운해요 ("I feel a bit hurt / let down"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I feel a bit hurt / let down
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the quiet, wistful disappointment when someone close didn't show up for you
반말, to a close friend or family member — tender, not aggressive
네요 voices it gently and opens the door for the other person to respond

usagePhrases.en: Why are you being so cold? It hurts me.
usagePhrases.note: Direct but still tender; pushing back on distance without starting a fight

examples.ko: A: 생일인 거 몰랐어요. / B: 아, 그래도 좀 서운했어요.
examples.romanization: A: saengirin geo mollasseoyo. / B: a, geuraedo jom seounhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: I didn't know it was your birthday. / B: Ah, still... I was a little hurt.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 서운하다 as gentle, non-aggressive hurt — the B doesn't escalate, just gently admits the sting

examples.en: You went without me? That kind of stings.
examples.note: 반말 grumble of being left out — playful-wistful, not angry

examples.en: You're leaving already? I'm sad to see you go. Do stay longer.
examples.note: 서운하다 at parting — warm, regretful, not upset; -지 wishes they'd stay

expressions.nuance: 서운해요 (from 서운하다) is one of the most important feeling words in Korean relationships and has no clean English equivalent. It is the soft, wistful hurt/disappointment you feel when someone CLOSE — a friend, family member, partner — does less than you hoped: they forgot to call, left you out, didn't notice your effort, or are leaving sooner than you'd like. The feeling is gentle and tinged with affection: you say it BECAUSE you care about them, not to attack. The contrast to nail is 섭섭하다 (a near-synonym, almost interchangeable, maybe a touch more 'sad to part') versus 화나다 ('angry') and 실망하다 ('disappointed in someone's character/standards'). Say 화났어요 and you've declared a fight; say 실망했어요 and you've judged their character harshly; say 서운했어요 and you've gently shown that their distance hurt because you're close. This is the phrase that repairs relationships without breaking them. Register: 서운해요 polite, 서운해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-니까: 연락 안 해서 서운했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is enormous: with no equivalent word, learners reach for 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded' — too strong, implies deep damage) or 실망했어요 (too judgmental) when the warm, fixable feeling is 서운해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 화났어요 when you mean 서운했어요.
화나다 is anger and signals conflict. 서운하다 is gentle, affectionate hurt that someone close let you down. To repair rather than fight, say 서운했어요.
Reaching for 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded').
That's too strong for a small letdown — it implies deep damage. For 'you kind of hurt my feelings,' the soft word is 서운했어요.
Translating it as cold 'disappointed' with 실망했어요.
실망하다 judges someone's character/standards harshly. 서운하다 is warm and relational ('I wish you'd cared more'). Don't swap them; the tone is opposite.

structuredNuance.t: 서운하다 has no clean literal origin for learners, but the feeling is precise: the soft, wistful sting when someone close didn't show up for you as much as you hoped. It is tinged with affection — you feel it BECAUSE you care. It is not anger, not cold disappointment, not wounded pride.

ONLY between close people — friends, family, partners. To a stranger or in formal settings it would be out of place and odd. 서운해요 is polite-intimate; 서운해 is 반말. Never use it with strangers, bosses (unless very close), or in professional complaints — those need neutral language.

vs. 섭섭하다: near-synonym, almost interchangeable; slightly more 'sad to part' in feeling. vs. 화나다: anger, signals conflict. vs. 실망하다: disappointed in someone's character/standards — harsh judgment. vs. 상처받다: 'I was wounded/damaged' — too strong for a small letdown. 서운하다 is the gentle, relational one.
서운하네요 (soft observation), 서운했어요 (past: 'I was hurt'), 서운하게 ('in a way that hurts': 서운하게 왜 그래), 많이 서운하시겠어요 ('you must be so hurt' — honorific empathy). Cause with -아서/-니까.

No English word exists, so learners misfire: 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded') is too strong for a small letdown; 실망했어요 ('I was disappointed') is too judgmental. The warm, fixable, relational hurt is 서운해요. Also don't confuse with 억울하다 ('I feel wronged/treated unjustly') — that involves perceived unfairness, not relationship closeness.

expressions.english: I feel relieved and unburdened (a weight lifted)
expressions.shortExplanation: 후련해요 is a practical expression meaning "I feel relieved and unburdened (a weight lifted)".
expressions.explanation: 후련해요 (huryeonhaeyo) = "I feel relieved and unburdened (a weight lifted)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 후련해요 ("I feel so relieved / unburdened"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the clean, cleared-out relief after a burden finally lifts
반말, to a close friend after something heavy is over

usagePhrases.en: What a total load off my chest
usagePhrases.note: 속이 ('insides') + 다 ('completely') names the bodily release — very vivid
Compound of 시원하다 (refreshed) + 섭섭하다 (a little sad) — for when the relief is tinged with something to let go of

examples.ko: A: 드디어 논문 제출했어요! / B: 진짜요? 후련하겠다!
examples.romanization: A: deudieo nonmun jechulhaesseoyo! / B: jinjjayo? huryeonhagetda!
examples.en: A: I finally submitted my thesis! / B: Really? You must feel so relieved!
examples.note: A/B exchange: 후련하겠다 ('you must feel unburdened') is the natural empathy response to someone finishing something big

examples.ko: 할 말 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련해요.
examples.romanization: hal mal da hago nanikka sogi huryeonhaeyo.
examples.en: After saying everything I needed to, I feel a weight off my chest.
examples.note: 후련함 from finally getting something off your chest; -고 나니까 = 'now that I've...'

examples.ko: 오래 미루던 일을 끝내서 후련하면서도 좀 시원섭섭해요.
examples.romanization: orae mirudeon ireul kkeunnaeseo huryeonhamyeonseodo jom siwonseopseopaeyo.
examples.en: Finishing the thing I'd put off so long, I feel relieved but also a little bittersweet.
examples.note: Pairs 후련하다 with 시원섭섭하다 for the nuanced bittersweet version

expressions.nuance: 후련해요 (from 후련하다) is the clean, lightened, cleared-out RELIEF you feel right after a heavy burden lifts — exams end, you finally say what was bottled up, a long worry resolves, you have a good cry. The image is your chest and insides (속) opening up and breathing freely; it is the natural opposite of 답답하다 ('stifled'). Often paired with 속이: 속이 후련해요 ('what a load off'). The word to distinguish it from is 시원하다, which overlaps a lot ('refreshing/relieving') but literally means 'cool/refreshing' and covers cold drinks, cool weather, and even a hot bath that 'hits the spot' — 후련하다 is specifically the EMOTIONAL/psychological unburdening, while 시원하다 is broader and more physical. Another nearby word is 안심하다 ('to be reassured that a worry is OK' — relief from anxiety about an outcome), vs. 후련하다's relief from a carried weight. And 다행이에요 ('thank goodness it turned out OK') comments on the situation, not the bodily feeling. The bittersweet cousin 시원섭섭하다 (relieved but sad to let go) is essential for endings. Register: 후련해요 polite, 후련해 반말. Mark the cause with -아서/-고 나니까.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 다행이에요 for the unburdened feeling.
다행이에요 = 'thank goodness it turned out OK' (a comment on the situation). The felt 'weight lifted off my chest' is 후련해요. Different relief.
Defaulting to 시원해요 for emotional relief.
시원하다 is broad 'cool/refreshing' (drinks, weather, soup). For the specifically emotional unburdening, 후련해요 is sharper and more correct.
Confusing it with 안심해요.
안심하다 = relief from worry/anxiety ('I'm reassured it's fine'). 후련하다 = relief from a weight/burden lifting. Match the source of relief.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 후련하다 = 'to be clear/unburdened.' The real meaning is a PHYSICAL sensation of your chest/insides opening up after a weight lifts — not just a mental 'that's good news.' This bodily unburdening is what distinguishes it from 다행이에요 or 안심하다.

Use after finishing something long and heavy: exams, a hard project, a difficult conversation, a cry. 후련해요 is polite-casual; 후련해 is 반말. Fine with anyone — friends, family, coworkers. The vivid 속이 다 후련해요 is warmly colloquial; for huge, long-pent relief, 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요 is the vivid idiom.

vs. 다행이에요: comments on a situation turning out OK ('thank goodness'). vs. 안심하다: relief that a specific worry is resolved ('I'm reassured'). vs. 시원하다: broadly cool/refreshing (physical). 후련하다 = the felt bodily unburdening of a carried weight. These are not interchangeable.
속이 다 후련하다 (full release), 후련했어요 (past), 후련하겠다 ('you must feel relieved' — empathy), 시원섭섭하다 (bittersweet relief). Idiom for huge relief: 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요 ('like a ten-year knot finally untied').

The pitfall is using 다행이에요 ('thank goodness') for this bodily unburdening — they're different kinds of relief: 다행이에요 = 'the situation turned out OK,' 후련하다 = 'I physically feel the weight gone.' Also don't swap in 시원해요 for emotional relief — 시원하다 is broader and physical.

expressions.shortExplanation: 부럽다 진짜 is a practical expression meaning "Man, I'm seriously jealous (mutter)".
expressions.explanation: 부럽다 진짜 (bureopda jinjja) means "Man, I'm seriously jealous (mutter)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 부럽다 진짜 ("Ugh, so jealous, for real"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Half-to-yourself mutter; warm envy that escapes as an exhaled exclamation
아 ('ahh') vents the wistful envy even more — very natural spoken Korean
Polite -네요 said aloud to the person; shares the observation gently
Playful set phrase to tease yourself or lighten jealousy in a group

examples.ko: A: 나 이번에 유럽 여행 갔다 왔어! / B: 와… 부럽다 진짜. 나도 가고 싶다.
examples.romanization: A: na ibeone yureop yeohaeng gatda wasseo! / B: wa… bureopda jinjja. nado gago sipda.
examples.en: A: I just got back from a trip to Europe! / B: Wow… I'm seriously jealous. I want to go too.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the most natural conversational mutter; the warmth comes from the shared wish (-고 싶다)

examples.en: Seeing how close you two are makes me envious.
examples.note: Polite 부럽네요 said directly to the person — a soft compliment on their relationship

examples.ko: 나도 그런 거 갖고 싶다. 부럽다 진짜.
examples.romanization: nado geureon geo gatgo sipda. bureopda jinjja.
examples.en: I want one of those too. Man, I'm jealous.
examples.note: Pairing with -고 싶다 ('I want...') to make the wishful side explicit

expressions.nuance: 부럽다 진짜 is the spoken, exclamatory form of 부럽다 ('to be envious') — Koreans constantly drop the polite ending and just exhale 부럽다 (often with 진짜 'for real' or 아 'ahh') as a warm, wistful 'lucky you / I wish that were me.' It is the SAME friendly envy as 부러워요 but in its most natural muttered shape. You can say the bare 부럽다 even around elders without it being rude, because the exclamatory adjective-다 form functions like thinking out loud rather than 반말 directed AT someone. To say it politely straight to the person, use 부럽네요 ('I must say, I envy you'). The contrast to keep in mind is the dark 질투(나다) ('possessive jealousy') — 부럽다 is never hostile. There's also the famous playful phrase 부러우면 지는 거다 ('if you're envious, you've already lost') used to tease yourself for being jealous. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, learners over-formalize and only ever use 부러워요, so they miss the much more natural spoken 부럽다 and sound stiff; second, they confuse the plain-form exclamation 부럽다 (fine to mutter even around elders) with using full 반말 verbs or commands at an elder (not fine). Also mark what you envy with 이/가 if you name it: 네가 부럽다, not 너를 부럽다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking the bare 부럽다 is rude to elders.
Exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud, not 반말 aimed at someone. Muttering 부럽다 near an elder is fine; to address them say 부럽네요.
Always saying 부러워요 and never the natural 부럽다.
Koreans constantly exclaim 부럽다 / 부럽다 진짜. Only using the textbook 부러워요 sounds stiff. Learn the muttered form too.
Adding 을/를 to what you envy.
It's 네가 부럽다 / 그게 부럽다 with 이/가, not 너를 부럽다. The envied thing/situation takes the subject marker.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '나는 부럽다' = 'I am envious.' The real meaning: a warm, involuntary exhale of friendly envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Absolutely not hostile or bitter; it functions like a compliment.

부럽다 진짜 is 반말/informal and is used freely among close peers. As a bare exclamation (without 진짜), 부럽다 can also be muttered around elders without being rude — because exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud. To address someone politely, use 부럽네요. Never appropriate in formal written or professional communication.

vs. 부러워요: the textbook polite form — grammatically complete but in fast speech sounds a touch formal. vs. 질투나요: dark, possessive jealousy — completely wrong register for friendly envy. vs. 부럽네요: polite observation form, gentle enough to say to the person directly. 부럽다 진짜 is the most natural spoken mutter.
아 진짜 부럽다, 완전 부럽다, 부럽네요 (polite version), 부러우면 지는 거예요 (joke). To name the envied thing: 네가 부럽다 / 그게 부럽다 (이/가, never 을/를).

Two traps: (1) only using formal 부러워요 and sounding stiff — Koreans in real speech constantly say 부럽다; (2) thinking 부럽다 is rude to elders — exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud, which is acceptable even near seniors. Mark the envied thing with 이/가, not 을/를.

expressions.hangul: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요
expressions.romanization: jjajeung jom an nage hae juseyo
expressions.english: Please don't make this so frustrating / annoying
expressions.shortExplanation: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please don't make this so frustrating / annoying".
expressions.explanation: "Please don't make this so frustrating / annoying" — that is 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요 (jjajeung jom an nage hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요 ("Please don't make this so annoying"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.ko: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: jjajeung jom an nage hae juseyo
usagePhrases.en: Please don't make this so annoying
usagePhrases.note: Polite-ish but pointed; use only when genuinely fed up — not casual small talk
반말, to a close friend who's intentionally winding you up

usagePhrases.en: You're really getting on my nerves
usagePhrases.note: 사람 ('a person') stands for 'me'; a muttered aside — sharp even among friends
Cleaner, less crude way to ask someone to stop — safer in most situations

examples.ko: A: 자꾸 끼어들지 마세요. / B: 미안요. / A: 짜증 나게 하지 말아요, 진짜.
examples.romanization: A: jakku kkieodeulji maseyo. / B: mianyo. / A: jjajeung nage haji marayo, jinjja.
examples.en: A: Stop cutting in, please. / B: Sorry. / A: Don't make this annoying, seriously.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing how this escalates — the second line only lands after a first warning

examples.ko: 아, 진짜 사람 짜증 나게 하네.
examples.romanization: a, jinjja saram jjajeung nage hane.
examples.en: Ugh, you're really getting on my nerves.
examples.note: Muttered 사람 짜증 나게 하다 about someone exasperating — blunt and clearly about them

examples.en: Are you doing it on purpose? So annoying.
examples.note: Trailing 짜증 나게 as a sharp aside — the accusation that it might be deliberate makes it sting more

expressions.nuance: This entry teaches the CAUSATIVE pattern — 짜증 나게 하다 ('to make someone annoyed/irritated'), built from 짜증(이) 나다 plus -게 하다 ('make it so that...'). It's how you point at the SOURCE of irritation instead of just venting your own state. Be warned: it's confrontational. 짜증 나게 하지 마(세요) ('stop annoying me') and 사람 짜증 나게 하네 ('you're getting on my nerves') are reserved for people you're close to or when you're genuinely fed up — never to staff, seniors, or in polite company, where you'd say 좀 그만해 주세요 ('please stop') or describe the problem calmly. The milder alternative is 신경 쓰이다 / 신경 쓰게 하다 ('to bother / weigh on the mind'), which carries more distraction/worry and less open 'you're pissing me off.' The English-speaker grammar pitfall is structural: learners try 너 나를 짜증해 (wrong on two counts) — 짜증(이) 나다 is intransitive, and to cause someone to feel it you need the causative -게 하다: 짜증 나게 하다. So 'you're annoying me' is 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해, NOT 너 짜증나. Note: 사람 here is not a specific person — idiomatically 사람 짜증 나게 하다 means 'you're irritating me.' Default to softer phrasing unless you truly mean to push back hard.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 너 짜증나 to mean 'you're annoying me'.
너 짜증나 means 'YOU feel annoyed.' To say someone annoys YOU, use the causative: 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해. Direction matters.
Using it with staff or seniors.
짜증 나게 하다 is blunt and confrontational. With staff/seniors say 좀 그만해 주세요 or calmly state the issue. Reserve this for close, genuinely-fed-up moments.
Writing 짜증나게해 as one chunk wrongly.
It's 짜증(이) 나다 + -게 하다 → 짜증 나게 하다. Spacing/structure: the 나다 + 게 하다 causative is what carries 'make someone annoyed.'

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 짜증 나게 하다 = 'to make (something/someone) cause irritation to arise.' The real meaning: 'you are the SOURCE of my annoyance, stop it.' This is not a neutral observation — it is a direct confrontation, pointing the finger at a person's behavior.

Only appropriate with close friends/family when genuinely fed up. Do NOT use with staff, seniors, strangers, coworkers above you, or in any formal setting — it will cause a conflict or seem rude/childish. Use 좀 그만해 주세요 or neutrally describe the issue in all other contexts.

vs. 신경 쓰게 하다: milder 'you're on my mind / distracting me' — more worried than annoyed. vs. 귀찮게 하다: 'to bother/hassle me (laziness frame)' — different annoyance type. vs. 화나게 하다: 'to make me angry' — even stronger, implies real anger. 짜증 나게 하다 is in the irritation register, not full anger.
짜증 나게 하지 마 (반말 prohibition), 사람 짜증 나게 하네 (muttered blunt complaint), 짜증 나게 왜 그래 ('why are you being so annoying?'), 좀 그만해 주세요 (polite neutral alternative).

(1) Saying 너 짜증나 to mean 'you're annoying me' — that actually means 'YOU feel irritated.' To say someone annoys YOU, use the causative: 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해. (2) Structural error: 짜증(이) 나다 is intransitive; 나를 짜증해 is doubly wrong (wrong verb + no such word). The causative -게 하다 is essential.

expressions.shortExplanation: 마음이 설레요 is a practical expression meaning "My heart is fluttering".
expressions.explanation: 마음이 설레요 (maeumi seolleyo) = "My heart is fluttering". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 마음이 설레요 ("My heart is fluttering"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; explicitly names the heart as grammatical subject — the most natural full form
두근거리다 ('to pound/throb') for the physical heartbeat — stronger and can be excitement OR fear
Set phrase for cards, messages, and warm sign-offs: 'with an eager heart, I...'
The nervous-jitters cousin — for contrast; can be bad nerves, not sweet anticipation

examples.ko: A: 그 사람 좋아해요? / B: 응, 그 사람만 보면 마음이 설레.
examples.romanization: A: geu saram joahaeyo? / B: eung, geu saramman bomyeon maeumi seolle.
examples.en: A: Do you like them? / B: Yeah, my heart flutters every time I just see them.
examples.note: A/B exchange: -만 보면 = 'every time I just see...' — the most natural romantic flutter sentence

examples.ko: 내일 콘서트라 벌써 가슴이 두근거리고 마음이 설레요.
examples.romanization: naeil konseoteura beolsseo gaseumi dugeungeorigo maeumi seolleyo.
examples.en: The concert's tomorrow, so my heart's already pounding and fluttering.
examples.note: Pairing 두근거리다 (pounding) with 설레다 (fluttering) to show the compound excitement

examples.en: I'll wait for your reply with an eager heart.
examples.note: 설레는 마음으로 as a warm, slightly literary sign-off in a message or letter

expressions.nuance: 마음이 설레요 makes explicit what 설레다 implies — that it's the HEART (마음, the heart/mind) that flutters. This teaches the natural Korean subject pattern: body/heart words often take 이/가 as the grammatical subject of feeling verbs (마음이 설레요, 가슴이 두근거려요, 가슴이 답답해요), which is structurally very different from English 'I feel...' Mastering this pattern fixes a whole class of grammatical errors. The flutter words to keep straight: 설레다 = sweet, welcome anticipatory flutter; 두근거리다 / 두근두근하다 = the heart physically POUNDING (can be excitement OR fear/nerves); 떨리다 = trembling/nervous jitters (often bad nerves). For a happy crush, 마음이 설레요 and 가슴이 두근거려요 overlap beautifully; but if you only say 두근거려요 it's ambiguous (could be fear), while 설레요 specifies the happy kind. The lovely set phrase 설레는 마음으로 ('with an eager/fluttering heart') is standard in warm messages and cards. Register: 설레요 polite. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) saying 나는 설레요 and forgetting that Korean prefers 마음이/가슴이 as the subject for heart-feelings; (2) the perennial misspelling 설레여요/설래요 — always 설레요 / 설렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나는 설레요 and skipping the heart subject.
Korean heart-feelings often take 마음이/가슴이 as subject: 마음이 설레요. It's a different structure from English 'I feel...'. Learn the body-as-subject pattern.
Using 두근거려요 assuming it's always happy.
두근거리다 is the heart POUNDING — could be excitement or fear. For specifically sweet anticipation, 설레요 makes the happy meaning clear.
Misspelling as 설래요 / 설레여요.
Stem is 설레-: present 설레요, past 설렸어요. 설래요 and 설레여요 are common errors. Lock in 설레요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '마음(heart/mind) + 이(subject) + 설레요(flutters)' = 'the heart flutters.' This is NOT a metaphor in Korean — the heart literally flutters as the grammatical subject. Mastering this body-as-subject structure (마음이, 가슴이, 마음이) is a key step beyond intermediate Korean.

Use freely in any warm context — romance, travel excitement, a first snow, a concert. 마음이 설레요 is polite; 마음이 설레 is 반말. The set phrase 설레는 마음으로 is slightly literary and fits cards or messages. With close friends, 설레 alone is the natural short form.

vs. 두근거리다: physical heart pounding — can be excitement or fear, ambiguous. 설레다 always means the happy flutter. vs. 떨리다: nervous trembling, often bad nerves. vs. 기대돼요: 'I'm looking forward to it' — mental anticipation, cooler and less physical. 마음이 설레요 = heart physically flutters with sweet anticipation.
마음이 설레요 (full polite), 설레 (반말 short), 설렸어요 (past: 'my heart was fluttering'), 설레는 마음으로 (set phrase for messages), 두근두근해요 (onomatopoeia pounding form).

(1) Saying 나는 설레요 and missing that Korean puts 마음이/가슴이 as subject for heart-feelings — learn the body-subject pattern. (2) Misspelling: 설레여요 and 설래요 are very common errors; the stem is 설레-, so it's always 설레요 / 설렸어요. Lock these in.

expressions.shortExplanation: 왠지 설레네요 is a practical expression meaning "Somehow my heart's fluttering".
expressions.explanation: 왠지 설레네요 (waenji seolleneyo) means "Somehow my heart's fluttering". Say it as one set phrase — for example 왠지 설레네요 ("Somehow I feel giddy"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 왠지 ('for some reason I can't pin down') + soft -네요 of shared realization
반말, to a friend — the most natural casual spoken form
뭔가 ('somehow/something') variant — slightly vaguer, still warm

usagePhrases.en: I'm giddy for no good reason (and I know it)
usagePhrases.note: 괜히 ('for no good reason, pointlessly') — self-aware flutter, slightly self-deprecating

examples.en: Maybe because the first snow fell — somehow I feel giddy.
examples.note: 왠지 + 네요 musing about a vague happy flutter; -어서 그런가 = 'maybe because...'

examples.ko: A: 오늘 왠지 설레지 않아요? / B: 맞아요, 저도 그래요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul waenji seolleji anayo? / B: majayo, jeodo geuraeyo.
examples.en: A: Don't you feel giddy today, somehow? / B: Right, me too.
examples.note: A/B exchange using -지 않아요? to invite agreement — perfect for the shared atmospheric flutter

examples.en: I start a new job tomorrow, so I'm giddy for no real reason.
examples.note: 괜히 admits the flutter is hard to logically justify — self-aware and charming

expressions.nuance: 왠지 설레네요 layers two very natural Korean pieces onto 설레다: 왠지 ('somehow, for some reason I can't name') and the soft sentence-ending -네요 (mild realization/observation, inviting the listener to share the feeling). The result is the cozy, atmospheric 'ooh, somehow this gives me butterflies' you say about first snow, a song, a season changing, a small good omen — not romance specifically. Mastering 왠지 / 괜히 / 뭔가 here is the real lesson: they're vibe-softeners Koreans sprinkle constantly: 왠지 ('for some reason'), 괜히 ('for no good reason/pointlessly,' often self-deprecating), 뭔가 ('something/somehow'). And -네요 vs. -요: 설레요 states the flutter flatly; 설레네요 adds 'oh, I notice I'm fluttering' and invites the listener into it — warmer and more conversational. Register: 설레네요 polite; 설레 반말; 설레네 is 반말 informal. The English-speaker pitfall is primarily spelling: 왠지 ('somehow,' from 왜인지 = 'why-ever') is constantly confused with and miswritten as 웬지 — remember only 왠지 is correct for 'somehow'; 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. Also: don't translate 왠지 as a literal 'why' — it's an atmospheric 'vibe' word, not a question.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 웬지 instead of 왠지.
'Somehow' is 왠지 (from 왜인지). 웬지 is wrong; 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. For the giddy-for-some-reason feeling: 왠지 설레네요.
Translating 왠지 as literal 'why'.
왠지 is a vibe word meaning 'somehow/for some reason I can't pin down,' not a question 'why.' It softens the statement and makes it atmospheric, it doesn't ask anything.
Dropping 요 from 설레네 with non-intimates.
-네 alone is 반말. Politely it's 설레네요. The -네요 adds 'oh, I notice...' warmth while staying polite.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 왠지 = 'for some reason' (from 왜인지 'why-ever'), 설레다 = 'flutters,' -네요 = observational ending. The real meaning: a soft, cozy, atmospheric observation of a feeling you can't fully explain — 'somehow I have butterflies and I'm sharing that with you.'

Use in warm, casual conversation about seasonal moments, music, new starts, gentle excitement — not romantic confessions (for that 마음이 설레요 is more direct). 왠지 설레네요 is polite-conversational; 왠지 설레 is 반말. The -네요 ending makes it feel like shared musing rather than a declaration.

왠지 = 'for some reason' (can't name why). 괜히 = 'for no good reason, pointlessly' (often with a self-deprecating awareness). 뭔가 = 'somehow / something' (the vaguest). All soften 설레요 but with different shades. 설레요 alone is a clear declaration; 왠지/괜히/뭔가 + 설레요 admits the feeling is a bit mysterious or unwarranted.
왠지 설레 (반말), 괜히 설레요 (self-aware flutter), 뭔가 설레요 (vaguer), 왠지 설레서 잠이 안 와요 ('I'm too giddy to sleep, somehow'). Polite: 설레네요; 반말: 설레; formal: avoid — instead say 기대가 됩니다.

(1) Spelling trap: 왠지 is correct ('somehow' = 왜인지); 웬지 is wrong. 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. (2) Don't translate 왠지 as a literal 'why' — it's a vibe softener, not a question. (3) Dropping 요 from 설레네: -네 alone is 반말; polite is -네요. The -네요 ending also adds warmth by inviting shared feeling.

expressions.english: I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)
expressions.shortExplanation: 속상해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)".
expressions.explanation: "I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)" — that is 속상해요 (soksanghaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 속상해요 ("I'm upset / it pains me"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; heartsore distress over something that went wrong or someone who's hurting
반말, to a close friend or family when venting heartsore feelings
-아 죽겠어요 maxes the heartache — usually comic unless the situation is truly serious
Honorific empathy form — how you comfort someone with this word

examples.en: My favorite cup broke, so I'm upset.
examples.note: 속상하다 for a small personal loss; 아끼던 = 'that I had treasured'

examples.ko: A: 시험 망쳤어요. / B: 많이 속상하겠다. 이번 한 번이야, 다음에 잘하면 돼.
examples.romanization: A: siheom mangchyeosseoyo. / B: mani soksanghagetda. ibeon han beoniya, daeume jalhamyeon dwae.
examples.en: A: I bombed the exam. / B: You must be so upset. It's just this once — you'll do well next time.
examples.note: A/B exchange: 속상하겠다 as natural empathy; B comforts with 이번 한 번이야

examples.ko: 애가 아픈데 해 줄 게 없어서 너무 속상해요.
examples.romanization: aega apeunde hae jul ge eopseoseo neomu soksanghaeyo.
examples.en: My child is sick and there's nothing I can do — it breaks my heart.
examples.note: 속상하다 for the helpless, tender heartache of a loved one's pain — not anger, just love-pain

expressions.nuance: 속상해요 (from 속상하다, literally 속 'insides' + 상하다 'to be spoiled/hurt') is the heartsore, distressed UPSET you feel when something goes wrong and it pains your insides — a treasured object breaks, your child is hurting, your effort failed, someone you love is in trouble. It is warmer and more tender than anger: the 'aw, this makes my heart sink' feeling, often with a note of helplessness.
