At Chuseok the equivalent cultural-food question is 송편 드셨어요? ('did you have songpyeon?'). Both are warm, culturally loaded food-as-greeting patterns. 떡국 vs 떡볶이 are entirely different foods — do not confuse them.
떡국 드셨어요? → 떡국 먹었어? (반말) → 떡국 한 그릇 드세요 (offering). Natural follow-up: 한 살 더 드셨네요 (polite) / 한 살 더 먹었네 (casual). Counter: 한 그릇 = one bowl, 두 그릇 = two bowls.

Two traps: (1) Answering literally — saying just 'yes, I had soup' without engaging with the 한 살 더 먹다 age-joke loses all the cultural warmth; play along. (2) Register clash: mixing 드셨어요? with a 반말 follow-up (한 살 더 먹었네) when speaking to an elder sounds jarring. Keep the register consistent throughout.

expressions.shortExplanation: 명절 잘 보내세요 is a practical expression meaning "Have a good holiday".
expressions.explanation: 명절 잘 보내세요 (myeongjeol jal bonaeseyo) means "Have a good holiday". Say it as one set phrase — for example 명절 잘 보내세요 ("Have a good holiday"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite default; said before 설날/추석 to almost anyone
반말, to friends
연휴 ('consecutive days off') focuses on the holiday break itself
Swap in the specific holiday name when you know which one

examples.ko: A: 명절 잘 보내세요! / B: 감사합니다, 과장님도 명절 잘 보내세요.
examples.romanization: A: myeongjeol jal bonaeseyo! / B: gamsahamnida, gwajangnimdo myeongjeol jal bonaeseyo.
examples.en: A: Have a good holiday! / B: Thank you, you too, manager.
examples.note: The workplace farewell before the holiday — always mirror it back politely

examples.en: Have a good holiday in advance!
examples.note: 미리 ('in advance') is added when you say it a day or two before the holiday

examples.ko: 연휴 동안 푹 쉬세요. 명절 잘 보내세요.
examples.romanization: yeonhyu dongan puk swiseyo. myeongjeol jal bonaeseyo.
examples.en: Rest well during the break. Have a good holiday.
examples.note: 푹 쉬세요 ('rest well') is a kind add-on for the holiday break

expressions.nuance: 명절 is the word for a traditional Korean holiday — specifically the big two, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (Chuseok/harvest festival) — and 잘 보내세요 means 'spend (it) well', from 보내다 ('to spend/pass time'). So 명절 잘 보내세요 is the standard 'have a good holiday' said to coworkers, neighbors, and shopkeepers in the days BEFORE the holiday. The crucial contrast is 명절 vs 연휴: 명절 names the cultural holiday with its rituals (제사, 차례, 성묘), while 연휴 just means the consecutive days off — say 연휴 잘 보내세요 when you mean 'enjoy the long weekend' generically (works for any holiday block including modern ones). Adding 미리 ('in advance') is very common because people scatter to their hometowns right before the holiday. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: learners reach for 가지세요 ('have/possess') as a 직역 of English 'have a good holiday', but Korean uses 보내다 ('spend/pass'); 명절 가지세요 is wrong. A second pitfall is timing — 잘 보내세요 is for BEFORE the holiday; afterward you switch to the past 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 명절 가지세요 ('have a holiday').
Korean uses 보내다 ('spend/pass time'), not 가지다 ('possess'). The set phrase is 명절 잘 보내세요. 가지세요 is a direct-translation error.
Confusing 명절 with 연휴.
명절 is the cultural holiday (설날/추석); 연휴 is just the string of days off. For a generic long weekend say 연휴 잘 보내세요; for the traditional holiday, 명절.
Saying 잘 보내세요 after the holiday is over.
보내세요 (future) wishes a good holiday ahead. After it's done, switch to past: 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'spend the holiday well'. 보내다 means 'to pass/spend time', so the phrase literally invites the listener to spend the holiday period pleasurably. The word 명절 specifically names a traditional Korean holiday (설날, 추석), not any generic day off.

Said in the days leading up to 설날 or 추석 to coworkers, neighbors, shopkeepers — basically anyone you interact with. Polite 보내세요 is the default; 보내 for close friends. Add the specific holiday name (설날 잘 보내세요 / 추석 잘 보내세요) when you want to be more specific.

명절 잘 보내세요 (cultural holiday with rituals) vs 연휴 잘 보내세요 (just the days-off block). Use 명절 when the cultural/family dimension matters; use 연휴 for any long weekend including modern public holidays that aren't traditional.
명절 잘 보내세요 → 미리 명절 잘 보내세요 (in advance) → 명절 잘 보내셨어요? (past, after the holiday). Companions: 푹 쉬세요 ('rest well'), 고향 잘 다녀오세요 ('travel safely to your hometown').

Two traps: (1) Wrong verb — learners try 명절 가지세요 (직역 of 'have a holiday') but 가지다 means 'possess'; use 보내다. (2) Timing mismatch — 보내세요 (future) is for before the holiday; after it ends use the past form 명절 잘 보내셨어요? Saying 보내세요 after the holiday has passed sounds strange.

expressions.shortExplanation: 차례 지내요 is a practical expression meaning "We hold the ancestral rite".
expressions.explanation: "We hold the ancestral rite" — that is 차례 지내요 (charye jinaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 차례 지내요 ("We hold the ancestral rite"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; describing the holiday-morning ceremony
반말, asking a friend if their family does it
Add -러 가다 for 'going in order to'
제사 = the death-anniversary rite; 차례 is the holiday version

examples.ko: A: 설날에 차례 지내세요? / B: 저희 집은 기독교라 대신 추도 예배를 드려요.
examples.romanization: A: seolnare charye jinaeseyo? / B: jeohui jibeun gidokgyora daesin chudo yebaereul deuryeoyo.
examples.en: A: Do you hold charye on Seollal? / B: Our family is Christian, so we have a memorial service instead.
examples.note: Shows it's natural to ask — not all families observe 차례

examples.ko: 내일 아침 일찍 차례 지내고 성묘 가요.
examples.romanization: naeil achim iljjik charye jinaego seongmyo gayo.
examples.en: Tomorrow we do charye early then visit the graves.
examples.note: 차례 (home rite) often pairs with 성묘 ('visiting ancestors' graves')

examples.ko: 요즘은 차례 간소하게 지내는 집도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun charye gansohage jinaeneun jipdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many families keep charye simple.
examples.note: 간소하게 ('simply') reflects the modern trend of scaling it down

expressions.nuance: 차례 (茶禮) is the ancestral memorial rite families perform on the morning of 설날 and 추석 — food is set on a table for the ancestors and the family bows together. The crucial collocation is the verb: you 지내다 a rite, never 하다. 지내다 here means 'to observe/hold (a ceremony)', and it is the required verb for both 차례 지내다 and 제사 지내다; using 차례 해요 marks you instantly as a learner. The key contrast is 차례 vs 제사: 차례 is the simpler rite tied to the two big HOLIDAYS (always in the morning, shorter food setup), while 제사 is the memorial held on the ANNIVERSARY of a specific ancestor's death (traditionally late at night). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the verb, is assuming every Korean family holds 차례 — increasingly families simplify (간소화) or skip it entirely, and many Christian families hold a 추도 예배 (memorial worship) instead. It's polite to ask 차례 지내세요? rather than assume. Pair words: 성묘 (visiting graves) and 벌초 (clearing weeds from the grave before Chuseok), which often follow 차례.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 차례 해요 instead of 차례 지내요.
Rituals take the verb 지내다, not 하다. It's 차례(를) 지내다, 제사(를) 지내다. 차례 해요 sounds wrong to natives.
Confusing 차례 with 제사.
차례 is the rite on the holidays (설날/추석), held in the morning. 제사 is the rite on an ancestor's death anniversary, traditionally at night. They're not interchangeable.
Assuming everyone holds 차례.
Many families simplify or skip it, and Christian families often hold a 추도 예배 instead. Ask 차례 지내세요? rather than assuming.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'we hold 차례 (茶禮)'. 차례 is an ancestral rite — food is laid out for the ancestors and the family bows. The phrase describes a ritual event, not a casual activity, so 지내다 ('observe/hold a ceremony') is the required verb.

Used on 설날 and 추석 mornings. The rite is family-internal; when talking about it to others, polite 지내요 is standard. It's natural to ask friends whether their family holds it — 차례 지내세요? — since practice varies. Christian families often don't observe it.

차례 (holiday rite: 설날/추석, morning, family-holiday-focused) vs 제사 (death-anniversary rite, traditionally late at night, for one specific ancestor's passing date). Don't use them interchangeably — the timing, occasion, and food setup differ.
차례 지내다 → 차례 지내러 가다 (going to attend) → 차례 간소하게 지내다 (simplify the rite) → 차례 안 지내다 (not observing it). Related: 성묘 가다 (grave visit), 벌초하다 (cut grave weeds).

The biggest trap is using 하다 instead of 지내다: 차례 해요 sounds wrong to every native speaker. Memorial and ancestral rites require 지내다. Beyond the verb, assuming all Koreans do 차례 can be socially awkward — ask rather than state, since many modern families simplify or skip it.

expressions.english: We make songpyeon (shape the rice cakes)
expressions.shortExplanation: 송편 빚어요 is a practical expression meaning "We make songpyeon (shape the rice cakes)".
expressions.explanation: 송편 빚어요 (songpyeon bijeoyo) = "We make songpyeon (shape the rice cakes)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 송편 빚어요 ("We make songpyeon"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; 빚다 is the verb for shaping rice cakes by hand
반말 suggestion, to family/friends
같이 ('together') — it's a family group activity
Same verb 빚다 for dumplings, common at 설날

examples.ko: A: 오늘 추석 준비하세요? / B: 네, 가족들이랑 같이 송편 빚고 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul chuseok junbihaseyo? / B: ne, gajokdeurirang gachi songpyeon bitgo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Preparing for Chuseok today? / B: Yes, I'm making songpyeon with the family.
examples.note: Shows 같이 빚다 as a group activity — a real holiday scenario

examples.ko: 송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸 낳는대요.
examples.romanization: songpyeon yeppeuge bijeumyeon yeppeun ttal nanneundaeyo.
examples.en: They say if you shape pretty songpyeon you'll have a pretty daughter.
examples.note: A famous old saying that comes up every Chuseok — a gentle tease while shaping

examples.ko: 저는 송편 빚는 거 잘 못해서 모양이 엉망이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun songpyeon binneun geo jal motaeseo moyangi eongmangieyo.
examples.en: I'm bad at shaping songpyeon, so mine look a mess.
examples.note: 엉망이에요 ('a mess') — a relatable thing to say while helping

expressions.nuance: 송편 are the small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut that Koreans make for 추석 (Chuseok). The verb is the specific 빚다 — used for things you shape with your hands from dough or clay: you 빚다 송편, 빚다 만두 (dumplings), and even 빚다 (brew) traditional liquor. You do NOT use 만들다 ('make') for the ritual shaping; 송편 빚어요 captures the hands-together, generational bonding aspect. 빚다 is a regular consonant-stem verb: 빚다 → 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는 — learners often trip on the stem-final ㅈ. Culturally, making 송편 together the evening before Chuseok is a bonding activity across generations, hence the famous saying 송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는다 ('shape pretty songpyeon and you'll have a pretty daughter'). The nearest synonym situation: 만들다 (make generally) is understood but loses the hand-shaping, ritual warmth. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 만들다 for everything; the second pitfall is mixing up Chuseok food 송편 with the New Year food 떡국 — each holiday has its signature dish. Note 빚 (same sound) also means 'debt' — an entirely different word.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 송편 만들어요 in the ritual context.
Native speakers use the hand-shaping verb 빚다 for songpyeon and dumplings: 송편 빚어요. 만들다 ('make') is understood but less idiomatic here.
Mangling the conjugation (빚다 → 빚다요/빚는다요).
빚다 conjugates 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는. Attach endings to the 빚 stem (빚-어요), not the dictionary form; 빚어요 is the polite present.
Mixing up holiday foods: 송편 at New Year.
송편 is the 추석 (Chuseok) food; 떡국 is the 설날 (New Year) food. Pair the right rice cake with the right holiday.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'we 빚다 songpyeon'. 빚다 means to shape/mold by hand — the verb implies a deliberate, hands-on craft process. It carries a connotation of care and artisanship that 만들다 ('make') does not, which is why 빚다 is the idiomatic choice for these rice cakes.

Said at home the evening before 추석, as a family activity. Casual register is common since it's a domestic setting: 빚어요 (polite), 빚자 (let's, 반말), 같이 빚어요 (together). You can also describe it to outsiders: 추석 준비로 송편 빚고 있어요 ('making songpyeon in prep for Chuseok').

송편 빚어요 (hand-shape with ritual warmth) vs 송편 만들어요 (make, neutral). Both are understood, but 빚다 is the native choice. Compare: 만두 빚어요 (same verb for dumplings, set phrase). Do not confuse 송편 (Chuseok) with 떡국 (Seollal/New Year) — different holidays, different foods.
송편 빚다 → 같이 빚다 (make together) → 예쁘게 빚다 (shape nicely) → 빚는 거 잘 못하다 ('bad at shaping'). Conjugation reminder: 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는 (attach to 빚- stem).

Two traps: (1) Defaulting to 만들다 — while understood, it loses the cultural warmth; 빚다 is what natives say. (2) Holiday food confusion —송편 is 추석 (Chuseok), 떡국 is 설날 (New Year). Saying 설날에 송편 빚어요 pairs the wrong food with the wrong holiday and will confuse Koreans.

expressions.shortExplanation: 한복 입어요 is a practical expression meaning "We wear hanbok".
expressions.explanation: 한복 입어요 (hanbok ibeoyo) means "We wear hanbok". Say it as one set phrase — for example 한복 입어요 ("We wear hanbok"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; 입다 is the verb for wearing clothes on the body
반말, to a friend
입고 가다 ('go while wearing') for showing up dressed in it
한 벌 = the counter for a set/suit of clothes

examples.en: On Seollal we wear hanbok and do the New Year bow.
examples.note: 한복 + 세배 — the classic New Year morning image

examples.ko: A: 돌잔치에 한복 입고 가요? / B: 아, 저는 그냥 정장 입고 갈 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: doljanchie hanbok ipgo gayo? / B: a, jeoneun geunyang jeongjang ipgo gal geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: Are you going to the first-birthday party in hanbok? / B: Oh, I'll probably just wear a suit.
examples.note: A realistic exchange — shows hanbok is now optional even at celebrations

examples.en: We dressed the baby in hanbok and took photos.
examples.note: 입히다 ('dress someone') — the causative, since you put it ON the baby

expressions.nuance: 한복 (韓服) is traditional Korean dress, worn for 설날, 추석, weddings, 돌잔치 (first-birthday parties), and palace photo tours. The verb is 입다 ('to wear/put on the torso/body') — Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 for clothes/garments, 쓰다 for hats/glasses, 신다 for shoes/socks, 끼다 for rings/gloves, 차다 for watches/accessories. A 직역 of English 'wear' with one verb is a classic error; for 한복 it is always 입다. The important causative is 입히다 ('to dress someone'): you 입다 your own 한복 but 입히다 a child's hanbok (한복 입혔어요), which learners routinely miss. Wearing hanbok on holidays used to be near-universal but is now optional — many families wear regular clothes, and renting (빌리다) a 한복 for palace photos is now very popular with tourists and young Koreans alike. The English-speaker pitfall beyond the wear-verb split is the counter: a hanbok outfit is counted with 벌 (한 벌 = one set/outfit), not 개. Do not confuse 한복 (Korean dress) with 한식 (Korean food).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 입다 for hats/shoes too.
Korean splits 'wear': 옷은 입다, 모자는 쓰다, 신발은 신다. You 입다 a 한복 but 쓰다 a hat and 신다 shoes. Don't use one verb for all.
Saying 한복 입어요 when you mean dressing a child.
To put clothes ON someone else, use the causative 입히다: 애기한테 한복 입혔어요. 입다 is for dressing yourself.
Counting hanbok with 개: 한복 한 개.
Clothing sets take the counter 벌: 한복 한 벌. 개 is for generic objects and sounds wrong for an outfit.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'we wear (put on) hanbok (韓服 = Korean traditional dress)'. 입다 specifically covers clothing worn on the torso/body. The phrase describes putting on the full traditional outfit for a celebration or holiday, often the New Year bow (세배) or a major life-event party.

Worn on 설날, 추석, weddings, 돌잔치, and at traditional venues (궁궐). Wearing it is now optional for most — don't assume guests will appear in 한복. Renting a 한복 set (빌리다) for palace photo tours is mainstream and perfectly normal.

입다 (clothes on body) vs 쓰다 (hat/glasses) vs 신다 (shoes) vs 끼다 (ring/glove) vs 차다 (watch). All translate English 'wear' but each covers a specific body region — you cannot use 입다 for shoes, and 신다 for a hanbok gown would be comically wrong.
한복 입다 → 한복 입히다 (dress someone else) → 한복 입고 가다 (go wearing it) → 한복 빌리다 (rent hanbok). Counter: 한 벌 (one set/outfit), 두 벌 (two sets).

Two traps: (1) Using one 'wear' verb for everything — 입다 is only for garments on the body; confusing this leads to 모자를 입어요 (wrong) or 신발을 입어요 (wrong). (2) Counter error — 한복 한 개 is wrong; clothing sets use the counter 벌: 한복 한 벌.

expressions.shortExplanation: 용돈 드려요 is a practical expression meaning "I give (an elder) spending money".
expressions.explanation: "I give (an elder) spending money" — that is 용돈 드려요 (yongdon deuryeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 용돈 드려요 ("I give them pocket money"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-humble; 드리다 because you give it UP to a parent/elder
When giving DOWN to a child — 주다 (plain give)
세뱃돈 = the cash kids get for their New Year bow

usagePhrases.en: I made sure to slip them some money
usagePhrases.note: 챙기다 ('see to/take care of') — warmer, 'I looked after them'

examples.en: On holidays I give my parents some money.
examples.note: Adults giving money to parents — note 께 + 드리다 (honorific direction)

examples.ko: A: 조카들한테 세뱃돈 얼마나 줬어요? / B: 한 명에 오만 원씩 줬어요.
examples.romanization: A: jokadeulhante sebaetdon eolmana jwosseoyo? / B: han myeonge oman wonssik jwosseoyo.
examples.en: A: How much New Year money did you give your nieces and nephews? / B: I gave 50,000 won to each.
examples.note: Giving DOWN to children uses 한테 + 주다; 에 + 씩 means 'per person'

examples.en: Grandma gave the grandkids their New Year money.
examples.note: 주시다 (honorific of 주다) because Grandma is the respected giver

expressions.nuance: On holidays money flows two directions in Korea, and the verb is dictated by the DIRECTION OF RESPECT. 용돈 is 'spending money/allowance'; 세뱃돈 is specifically the cash children receive after giving their 세배 (New Year bow). When YOU give money UP to a parent or elder, use the humble 드리다: 부모님께 용돈 드려요. When you give DOWN to a child or junior, use plain 주다: 조카한테 세뱃돈 줘요. Swapping these is the number-one English-speaker pitfall — 부모님한테 용돈 줘요 is doubly disrespectful (wrong verb AND wrong particle: 한테 is casual, elders take 께). The second contrast is 용돈 (general allowance, any time, including parents) vs 세뱃돈 (only at New Year, tied to the bow, only for children) — adults giving parents holiday money is 용돈, never 세뱃돈. Culturally, adult children giving parents 용돈 at 설날/추석 is a strong filial expectation; the verb 챙기다 ('to see to / not neglect') adds warmth (용돈 챙겨 드렸어요 = 'I made sure to take care of them with money'). Traditional practice: give fresh bills in a clean white envelope.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 부모님한테 용돈 줘요.
To a parent/elder, give-up is humble 드리다 and the particle is honorific 께: 부모님께 용돈 드려요. 한테 줘요 is doubly too casual.
Calling the parents' holiday money 세뱃돈.
세뱃돈 is the cash KIDS get for their 세배. Money adults give their parents is 용돈, not 세뱃돈. Match the word to the direction.
Using 드리다 when giving to a child.
드리다 is humble (giving UP). To a child you give DOWN, so use plain 주다: 조카한테 세뱃돈 줬어요. 드리다 to a kid is wrong.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I give 용돈 (pocket money/allowance)'. 드리다 ('give humbly to a superior') signals respect upward; 주다 ('give') is the neutral form used downward. The verb is not interchangeable — using the wrong one changes the entire social meaning.

Said at 설날/추석 and at parent-honoring occasions. 드리다 + 께 forms a respectful set when giving to elders; 주다 + 한테 is the casual set for giving to children. Giving parents holiday 용돈 is a strong social expectation — the verb 챙기다 ('see to it') adds warmth.

용돈 (general spending money, any time, including to parents) vs 세뱃돈 (New Year cash, tied to the 세배 bow, only for children — never use 세뱃돈 for money given to parents). The word tells you both the occasion and the generational direction.
용돈 드리다 → 용돈 챙겨 드리다 (thoughtfully take care of / not forget) → 용돈 좀 드렸어요 (gave a little money). For children: 세뱃돈 주다 → 세뱃돈 챙겨 주다 (make sure they get their money).

The number-one trap is 부모님한테 용돈 줘요 — two errors at once: 한테 is casual (elders take 께), and 주다 is plain (elders require humble 드리다). Always pair 께 + 드리다 for upward giving. A second trap: calling any holiday money gift 세뱃돈 — that word is only for children receiving money after the bow.

expressions.english: How much should I give as a wedding gift?
expressions.shortExplanation: 축의금 얼마 해요? is a practical expression meaning "How much should I give as a wedding gift?".
expressions.explanation: 축의금 얼마 해요? (chuguigeum eolma haeyo?) = "How much should I give as a wedding gift?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 축의금 얼마 해요? ("How much do you give as wedding money?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: How much do you give as wedding money?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the going rate, 하다 = 'do/put in' an amount

usagePhrases.en: How much are you putting in?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, asking a friend
면 돼요 ('would it be okay to') — asking what's appropriate

usagePhrases.en: How much for the gift money?
usagePhrases.note: 부조 = the older general term for congratulatory/condolence money

examples.ko: A: 친한 친구 결혼식인데 축의금 얼마 해요? / B: 친한 친구면 10만 원 이상 해야죠.
examples.romanization: A: chinhan chingu gyeolhonsiginde chuguigeum eolma haeyo? / B: chinhan chingumyeon 10man won isang haeyajyo.
examples.en: A: It's a close friend's wedding — how much should I give? / B: If it's a close friend, you should do at least 100,000 won.
examples.note: The most natural question-and-advice exchange — closeness is the key variable

examples.en: These days people usually give around 100,000 won.
examples.note: 정도 ('about') — the typical figure for a normal relationship

examples.ko: 밥 먹고 가면 좀 더 내는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: bam meokgo gamyeon jom deo naeneun ge joayo.
examples.en: If you stay for the meal, it's better to give a bit more.
examples.note: A real rule of thumb: attending the buffet means giving more

expressions.nuance: 축의금 (祝儀金) is the cash you put in an envelope at a Korean wedding — you almost never bring a wrapped present; you give MONEY at a reception desk. The idiomatic verb is 하다 ('to do', here 'to put in/contribute an amount'): 축의금 얼마 해요? = 'how much do you do as wedding money?'. You can also say 내다 ('to pay/submit') — 축의금 내다 — but 하다 is the most natural when asking the going rate. The amount is socially calibrated: ~5만 원 for an acquaintance, ~10만 원 for a normal friend/colleague, more if you're close or eat at the reception (a real rule: 밥값, 'the meal cost', factors in). An English-speaker pitfall is bringing a physical gift instead of cash — that can be awkward at the reception desk. A second pitfall: Koreans give 'auspicious' figures (3, 5, 7, 10만; avoid 4 because 四 sounds like 死 'death'). The biggest vocabulary trap: do NOT confuse 축의금 (weddings, happy events) with 부의금/조의금 (funerals, condolences) — giving the wrong envelope wording is a grave social error. General umbrella term for both: 부조(금).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Bringing a wrapped gift instead of cash.
Korean weddings expect 축의금 (money in an envelope) at the reception desk, not presents. A physical gift can be awkward; give cash.
Giving an amount with 4 in it (4만, 14만).
4 (四) sounds like 死 ('death') and is avoided for celebrations. Stick to auspicious figures like 3, 5, 7, or 10만 원.
Confusing 축의금 with 부의금.
축의금 is congratulatory money (weddings, happy events); 부의금/조의금 is condolence money (funerals). The envelopes and wording differ — never mix them up.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'how much do you 하다 for the wedding money?'. 하다 here means 'to contribute/put in an amount' — a Korean-specific idiom for deciding the gift amount. The whole social act (envelope + cash + amount) is called 축의금 (祝儀金 = congratulatory ceremony money).

Asked among friends or colleagues before a wedding. 얼마 해요? (polite), 얼마 내? (반말). The amount varies by relationship closeness: ~5만 원 (acquaintance), ~10만 원 (normal friend/colleague), more if you attend the meal or are very close. At the reception desk you sign the guestbook (방명록) and hand the envelope.
축의금 (祝儀金, congratulatory — weddings and happy events) vs 부의금/조의금 (弔意金, condolence — funerals). The envelopes, wording, and occasions are opposite; never mix them up. General umbrella term: 부조(금).
축의금 하다 → 축의금 내다 → 부조 하다. The 면 돼요 form (얼마 내면 돼요?) is softer and more deferential. To describe giving it: 축의금 냈어요 ('I gave wedding money').

Two traps: (1) Bringing a physical gift — Korean weddings expect cash in an envelope, not wrapped presents; a gift box at the reception desk is awkward. (2) Using unlucky amounts — avoid any figure with 4 (四 ~ 死); stick to auspicious amounts (3, 5, 7, 10만 원). A third trap: the vocabulary confusion 축의금/부의금 — the wrong word for the wrong ceremony is a serious gaffe.

expressions.shortExplanation: 결혼 축하해요 is a practical expression meaning "Congratulations on your wedding".
expressions.explanation: 결혼 축하해요 (gyeolhon chukahaeyo) means "Congratulations on your wedding". Say it as one set phrase — for example 결혼 축하해요 ("Congratulations on your wedding"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite default; to the couple or their family
반말, to a close friend
축하드리다 (humble) — more respectful, to elders or formally

usagePhrases.en: I wish you a happy life together
usagePhrases.note: The warm follow-up wish for the newlyweds

examples.en: Congratulations on your wedding! You look beautiful.
examples.note: Said to the bride/groom at the hall, with a sincere compliment

examples.en: I sincerely congratulate you both on your marriage.
examples.note: 진심으로 ('sincerely') + 축하드립니다 for a formal, heartfelt toast or written message

examples.ko: A: 결혼 축하드려요. 신혼여행 어디로 가세요? / B: 감사합니다! 몰디브로 가요.
examples.romanization: A: gyeolhon chukadeuryeoyo. sinhonyeohaeng eodiro gaseyo? / B: gamsahamnida! moldibeuro gayo.
examples.en: A: Congrats on the wedding. Where are you honeymooning? / B: Thank you! We're going to the Maldives.
examples.note: 신혼여행 ('honeymoon') — a natural friendly follow-up; note humble 축하드려요 to the couple

expressions.nuance: 결혼 축하해요 ('congratulations on your marriage') is the core wedding congratulation. 축하하다 (祝賀) is 'to congratulate', and the politeness ladder matters at a formal event like a wedding: 축하해 (반말, friends only) → 축하해요 (polite, standard) → 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble, to elders, the couple's parents, or in a speech). The humble 드리다 form is genuinely common at weddings because you are often congratulating people older than you — the parents at the entrance door. The nearest near-synonym is 결혼 축하드려요: the 드리다 form does NOT change the meaning, only the respect level. The particle pitfall: learners insert 을 (결혼을 축하해요), but the natural set phrase drops it — 결혼 축하해요 (noun directly + 축하하다). Another direct-translation trap: 'congratulations on your wedding' suggests 결혼식 축하해요 ('congrats on the ceremony'), but Koreans congratulate the 결혼 (the marriage), not the event. Warm Korean add-on: 행복하게 잘 살아요 ('live happily together'). Critical rule: 축하하다 is ONLY for joyful occasions — never at a funeral.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Inserting 을: 결혼을 축하해요.
The natural phrase attaches the noun directly: 결혼 축하해요. The 을 isn't wrong grammar but sounds stiff/textbook; drop it for the idiomatic feel.
Using 축하해 with the couple's parents.
축하해 is 반말. To elders (the parents at the wedding) use the humble 축하드려요/축하드립니다, which is standard at formal events.
Saying 축하해요 at a funeral by reflex.
축하하다 is only for joyful occasions. At a funeral it's offensive — use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ('may the deceased rest in peace') instead.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'congratulate-하다 (the) marriage'. 축하하다 (祝賀) is a pure 'to congratulate/celebrate', and the object is 결혼 (the state of getting married), not 결혼식 (the ceremony event). The distinction matters — you congratulate the life change, not the party itself.

Said at a 결혼식 (wedding) to the couple, their family, or written in cards. To the couple's parents and any elder guest, use humble 축하드려요/드립니다; to peers use 축하해요; to very close friends 축하해 (반말). Never use 축하 at a funeral — it is strictly for joyful events.

결혼 축하해요 (any well-wisher) vs 결혼 축하드려요 (humble, to an elder couple or parents). Add-on 행복하게 잘 살아요 ('live happily together') is distinctly Korean and very warm — it wishes the marriage itself well, not just the day.
축하해 → 축하해요 → 축하드려요 → 진심으로 축하드립니다. Pair with: 두 분 결혼 (both of you, formal), 행복하게 잘 살아요 (follow-up wish), 신혼여행 잘 다녀오세요 (safe travels on the honeymoon).

Two traps: (1) Inserting 을: 결혼을 축하해요 is slightly stiff/textbook — drop the particle for natural speech: 결혼 축하해요. (2) Object confusion: 'wedding' suggests 결혼식, but Korean targets the marriage (결혼), not the ceremony event. A third trap: saying 축하해요 to the grieving family at a funeral — 축하하다 is only for happiness.

expressions.english: When are you getting married? (lit. when will you feed us noodles?)
expressions.shortExplanation: 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? is a practical expression meaning "When are you getting married? (lit. when will you feed us noodles?)".
expressions.explanation: "When are you getting married? (lit. when will you feed us noodles?)" — that is 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? (guksu eonje meogyeo jwoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? ("When's the wedding? (feed us noodles)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Playful-polite teasing of a dating couple

usagePhrases.en: When are you gonna get married?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, teasing a close friend

usagePhrases.ko: 언제 국수 먹게 해 줄 거예요?
usagePhrases.romanization: eonje guksu meokge hae jul geoyeyo?
usagePhrases.en: When do we get to eat your wedding noodles?
usagePhrases.note: Variant with 먹게 해 주다 ('let us eat')

usagePhrases.en: When do we get the wedding noodles?
usagePhrases.note: Said by the friend group, asking collectively

examples.ko: A: 둘이 사귄 지 오래됐는데 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? / B: 아이, 아직 멀었어요!
examples.romanization: A: duri sagwin ji oraedwaenneunde guksu eonje meogyeo jwoyo? / B: ai, ajing meoreosseoyo!
examples.en: A: You two have been dating a long time — when's the wedding? / B: Oh, that's still far off!
examples.note: The classic tease and deflection — the B line 멀었어요 ('still far away') is a very natural reply

examples.en: It's about time you got married!
examples.note: 때 됐지 ('it's about time') — friendly pressure among close friends

examples.en: When might we get to eat the wedding noodles?
examples.note: A gentler, more roundabout version of the same joke — suitable even with semi-formal politeness

expressions.nuance: This is an idiom you must not take literally. 잔치국수 (banquet noodles) were traditionally served at wedding feasts, so '국수 먹다' ('to eat noodles') became slang for 'to attend someone's wedding', and 국수 먹여 주다 ('to feed us noodles') means 'to get married'. So 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? = 'when are you two getting married?' — a teasing, affectionate comment directed at a long-term couple. The causative chain is key: 먹다 ('eat') → 먹이다/먹여 주다 ('feed someone') — the couple FEEDS (hosts) the noodles and the friends EAT them; getting this backwards breaks the idiom. Register: even the 요 form is inherently playful here; with close friends it's 반말 (먹여 줄 거야?). Social caution: this implies pressure to marry, so use it only with people close enough to joke; saying it to an acquaintance or someone sensitive about being single can feel intrusive. The English-speaker pitfall is total: a 직역 ('when will you feed us noodles?') is baffling in English, and answering about real noodles misses the joke entirely. Compare 잔치 ('feast') — a 돌잔치 is a first-birthday feast, same root.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Taking it literally as an offer of food.
국수 먹여 주다 is idiom for 'get married' (from wedding banquet noodles). Don't answer about real noodles — it means 'when's the wedding?'
Saying it to acquaintances or the marriage-sensitive.
It's a tease that implies 'hurry up and marry'. Use only with people close enough to joke; to others it can feel like pressure.
Mangling the causative: 국수 언제 먹어 줘요?
The couple FEEDS the noodles, so it's the causative 먹여 주다 ('feed someone'), not 먹어 ('eat'). 먹여 줘요? = 'when will you feed (treat) us?'

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'when will you feed us noodles?'. Real meaning: 'when are you two getting married?' — because 잔치국수 (banquet noodles) were the traditional wedding feast food, so eating noodles = attending a wedding, and feeding noodles = hosting one. Without knowing this cultural link the sentence makes no sense.

Teasing of a dating couple, typically said by their close friends or family. The 요 form is still playful; full 반말 (먹여 줄 거야?) for very close friends. Social caution: this implies marriage pressure — only say it to people close enough to take the joke. Never to acquaintances or the marriage-sensitive.

국수 언제 먹여 줘요? (when are you getting married?) vs 결혼은 언제 해요? (direct, polite: when are you getting married?). The 국수 version is indirect and teasing; the 결혼 version is direct and more neutral. The noodle idiom is warmer among close friends.
국수 먹여 주다 → 먹여 줄 거야? (반말) → 국수 먹게 해 주다 (variant form) → 우리 언제 국수 먹어요? (group asking). Escalation: 먹여 줄 때 됐지! ('it's time already!') adds stronger teasing pressure.

The pitfall is complete: a 직역 leaves you baffled about noodles and you miss the marriage joke entirely — worse, you might try to answer about actual food. Memorize it as a fixed idiom. A grammar trap: the causative must be 먹여 주다 ('feed someone'), not 먹어 주다 ('eat [for someone]') — the couple feeds, the friends eat.

expressions.english: My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)
expressions.shortExplanation: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is a practical expression meaning "My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)".
expressions.explanation: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida) = "My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ("May the deceased rest in peace"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: May the deceased rest in peace
usagePhrases.note: Formal set phrase; the standard thing said/written at a funeral

usagePhrases.en: May the departed rest in peace
usagePhrases.note: Slightly shorter; still formal and correct

usagePhrases.en: I'm at a loss for words
usagePhrases.note: Said directly to the bereaved family, expressing helpless sorrow
A gentler, spoken comfort to a grieving friend (less formal)

examples.en: My deepest condolences.
examples.note: The phrase you say while bowing at the 빈소, or write on the condolence envelope and funeral wreath — nearly always used as a complete utterance

examples.ko: A: 갑작스러운 비보에 정말 놀랐어요. / B: 정말요. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
examples.romanization: A: gapjakseureoun biboe jeongmal nollasseoyo. / B: jeongmaryo. samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida.
examples.en: A: I was truly shocked by the sudden sad news. / B: Indeed. My deepest condolences.
examples.note: Natural exchange between two people who both knew the deceased — 비보 ('sad news') opens the condolence naturally

examples.ko: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다. 얼마나 힘드세요.
examples.romanization: samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida. eolmana himdeuseyo.
examples.en: My condolences. This must be so hard for you.
examples.note: After the formal phrase, switch to 얼마나 힘드세요 to comfort the living family — the two serve different purposes

expressions.nuance: This is the Korean funeral phrase, and it is almost entirely fixed — memorize it as one unit. Breaking it down: 삼가 ('respectfully/humbly'), 고인 (故人 = 'the deceased'), 명복 (冥福 = 'happiness/blessing in the afterlife'), 빌다 ('to pray/wish') → 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's blessing in the next life'. You say it and write it on the plain white condolence envelope and on funeral wreaths (근조화환) at a 빈소/장례식장. The phrase is for the DECEASED — it is not addressed to the grieving person as a greeting. To the bereaved family you offer 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 ('I don't know what to say') or 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be for you'). The single biggest English-speaker error is saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 as 'I'm sorry (for your loss)' — those mean 'I apologize for a fault' and are completely wrong here. Korean condolence is the 명복을 빕니다 formula. A second pitfall: saying anything cheerful (축하, upbeat 힘내세요 before acknowledging grief). The phrase has no 반말 version; register stays formal throughout. Do not smile; tone is everything.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 to mean 'sorry for your loss'.
Those mean 'I apologize (for a fault)'. Korean condolence isn't an apology — say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다, or to the family 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
Saying 축하해요 or anything upbeat by reflex.
축하하다 ('congratulate') is for happy events; at a funeral it's deeply offensive. Keep to the solemn 명복을 빕니다 formula.
Directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living as a hello.
That phrase prays for the DECEASED. To comfort the grieving person, say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 힘내세요; reserve 명복을 빕니다 for the deceased.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's 명복 (冥福 = happiness/blessing in the afterlife)'. 삼가 adds the humble, solemn tone. The phrase directs good wishes toward the soul of the deceased, not toward the living mourner — that distinction is essential.

고인 (故人) = 'the late/deceased person'; 명복 (冥福) = 'blessing in the underworld/afterlife' (冥 = dark/underworld, 福 = blessing); 빌다 = 'to pray/wish'. The Sino-Korean layer makes it formal and irreplaceable with everyday words.

Used exclusively at funerals (장례식장/빈소) — said aloud while bowing, written on condolence envelopes, and inscribed on funeral wreaths. Always formal; no 반말 version exists. The phrase goes toward the DECEASED; to the grieving person you say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
chips: 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 (to the bereaved)

structuredNuance.t: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (for the deceased, always formal) vs 얼마나 힘드세요 (directed at the living mourner, empathetic) vs 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 (loss for words, for the bereaved). These serve different recipients — do not conflate them.

The critical trap: translating English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 — both mean apologizing for a fault, not condolence. Korean condolence has no apology structure; use 명복을 빕니다. A second trap: using 축하해요 or any cheerful phrase by social reflex. A third: directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living mourner as a greeting — it is only for the deceased.

expressions.shortExplanation: 조의금 받으세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please accept the condolence money".
expressions.explanation: 조의금 받으세요 (jouigeum badeuseyo) means "Please accept the condolence money". Say it as one set phrase — for example 조의금 받으세요 ("Please accept the condolence money"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: What you might murmur handing the envelope; often given silently

usagePhrases.en: How much for the condolence money?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the appropriate amount (부의 = the older term)

usagePhrases.en: I just passed on the condolence money and left
usagePhrases.note: 전하다 ('convey/deliver') — when you couldn't stay

usagePhrases.en: I'll go pay my respects (with money)
usagePhrases.note: 부조하다 — the general verb for giving event money

examples.en: Condolence money goes in a plain white envelope.
examples.note: 흰 봉투 ('white envelope') — the required plain envelope for funerals; never use a decorative one

examples.ko: A: 장례식에 직접 못 갔는데 어떻게 하죠? / B: 조의금만 전달해도 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: A: jangnyesige jikjeom mot ganneunde eotteoke hajyo? / B: jouigeumman jeondalhaedo gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: A: I couldn't attend the funeral — what should I do? / B: It's okay to just send condolence money.
examples.note: A practical A/B: sending money without attending is socially acceptable

examples.ko: 부의금은 보통 5만 원에서 10만 원 정도 해요.
examples.romanization: buuigeumeun botong 5man woneseo 10man won jeongdo haeyo.
examples.en: Condolence money is usually around 50,000 to 100,000 won.
examples.note: The typical range, same avoidance of the number 4 as with wedding money

expressions.nuance: 조의금 (弔意金) / 부의금 (賻儀金) is the cash given at a funeral, the solemn counterpart to the wedding 축의금. The verbs: you 내다 ('submit/pay') or 하다 it (조의금 하다, 부조 하다), and if you cannot stay long you 전하다 ('convey/deliver') it. The make-or-break rule for English speakers is the ENVELOPE and its wording: funeral money requires a PLAIN WHITE envelope (흰 봉투) with sober Chinese-character wording — 부의 (賻儀) or 근조 (謹弔). Using a decorative or colorful envelope, or any congratulatory wording (祝), is a grave offense. The cardinal error is carrying over a wedding 축의금 mindset — the verb logic is similar, but tone, envelope, and wording are entirely opposite. Distinguishing the vocabulary: 조의(금) / 부의(금) name the money itself; 근조 is the wording on wreaths and banners ('humbly mourning'). Amounts mirror weddings (~5–10만 원), same avoidance of the number 4. Procedure: sign the 부의록 (condolence guestbook), hand the white envelope quietly, then bow to the portrait. Over-talking is a pitfall — handing the envelope is often done in near silence, and no cheerful speech is needed.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using a colored/decorative envelope or 祝 wording.
Funeral money requires a PLAIN WHITE envelope with sober wording (부의/근조). Festive envelopes or 祝('congratulate') are a serious gaffe — that's for weddings.
Calling it 축의금.
축의금 is congratulatory (weddings). Funeral money is 조의금/부의금. The words AND the envelopes are opposite; don't transfer the wedding term.
Giving an amount containing 4.
As with weddings, avoid 4 (四 ~ 死 'death'), which is doubly inappropriate at a funeral. Use figures like 5, 7, or 10만 원.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'please receive (accept) the condolence money'. 조의금 (弔意金) = 'money expressing condolence'. The phrase is murmured while handing the white envelope at a 빈소 — it is performative, completing the ritual act of offering rather than starting a conversation.

Used at a 장례식장 (funeral home) or 빈소 (funeral parlour). Give the money quietly at the reception desk: sign the 부의록, hand the plain white envelope, say the phrase (or stay silent) and bow. If you cannot attend, you can 전하다 ('convey/send') the money through someone else — this is acceptable.

조의금 / 부의금 (money label) vs 근조 (written mourning expression, used on wreaths/banners). Compare: 축의금 (wedding money, opposite occasion) — same cash-in-envelope logic but entirely different occasion, envelope style, and wording. Never mix the two up.
조의금 내다 → 조의금 전하다 (send/convey) → 부조 하다 (general: pay respects with money). Asking the rate: 조의금 얼마 해요? / 부의금 얼마 내요?

The cardinal trap is treating condolence money like wedding money — the envelopes are opposite (plain white for funerals vs any for weddings), and the occasion wording reverses completely (근조 / 부의 instead of 祝). A second trap is over-talking: hand the envelope quietly with a bow; a long upbeat speech at a funeral is inappropriate.

expressions.english: You must be heartbroken (I'm so sorry for your loss)
expressions.shortExplanation: 상심이 크시겠어요 is a practical expression meaning "You must be heartbroken (I'm so sorry for your loss)".
expressions.explanation: "You must be heartbroken (I'm so sorry for your loss)" — that is 상심이 크시겠어요 (sangsimi keusigesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 상심이 크시겠어요 ("Your grief must be great"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-honorific; said gently to the bereaved family

usagePhrases.en: How great your sorrow must be
usagePhrases.note: Warmer, more exclamatory version to the mourner

usagePhrases.en: I don't know what words of comfort to offer...
usagePhrases.note: Trailing off — the very Korean way to show you're lost for words
부디 ('please, earnestly') + 힘내세요, a soft encouragement

examples.en: You must be heartbroken. Please stay strong.
examples.note: The standard two-part comfort: acknowledge grief first, then gently encourage

examples.ko: A: 갑자기 이런 일이... / B: 상심이 크시겠어요. 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요.
examples.romanization: A: gapjagi ireon iri... / B: sangsimi keusigesseoyo. mwora deuril malsseumi eopsneyo.
examples.en: A: For this to happen so suddenly... / B: Your grief must be immense. I don't know what to say.
examples.note: A natural A/B at a 빈소 — A trails off in shock, B responds with empathy and a lost-for-words follow-up

examples.ko: 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요. 상심이 크시겠어요.
examples.romanization: mwora deuril malsseumi eopsneyo. sangsimi keusigesseoyo.
examples.en: I'm at a loss for words. You must be heartbroken.
examples.note: Pairs with 드릴 말씀이 없다 ('no words to offer'), the classic combo at a Korean funeral

expressions.nuance: While 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is addressed about the DECEASED, 상심이 크시겠어요 is what you say TO the grieving family member — and that distinction is exactly what English speakers miss. 상심 (傷心) is 'heartbreak/grief', 크다 ('to be great') in the honorific empathetic form 크시겠어요 ('must be immense for you') → 'your grief must be immense'. The -겠- here is the inferential/empathetic 'must be' (reading the other person's emotion from the outside), and the honorific -시- shows respect to the mourner; both are essential — 상심이 크겠어요 (no -시-) sounds cold. The nearest near-synonym is 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be for you'), which is softer and more like 'I see how hard this is'; 상심이 크시겠어요 is slightly more literary. The cardinal pitfall is translating English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다/미안해요 — those apologize for wrongdoing. Korean condolence comfort is indirect and often unfinished: trailing off (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) is genuinely more natural and heartfelt than a polished complete sentence. Pair 힘내세요 ('stay strong') AFTER acknowledging the grief — leading with it alone sounds dismissive.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죄송합니다/미안해요 to mean 'sorry for your loss'.
Those apologize for a fault. To comfort the bereaved, say 상심이 크시겠어요 or 얼마나 힘드세요 — empathy, not apology.
Dropping the honorific -시-: 상심이 크겠어요.
To the grieving family you need -시-: 상심이 크시겠어요. Without it the sympathy sounds detached and under-respectful.
Trying to say something upbeat or 'fix it'.
Korean condolence is restrained and indirect. Trailing off (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) is more appropriate than a cheerful or solution-oriented remark.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'your 상심 (傷心 = heartbreak/grief) must be great'. The phrase uses the empathetic -겠- form ('must be') plus honorific -시- to gently infer the mourner's feeling and show you see their pain. It addresses the LIVING bereaved person, not the deceased.

Said face-to-face to a grieving family member at a funeral or condolence visit, after bowing and exchanging the standard phrase about the deceased. Keep voice low and tone subdued. There is no 반말 version of this comfort — even to a close friend who is grieving, maintain respectful tone.
chips: 뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지... (trailing off)

structuredNuance.t: 상심이 크시겠어요 ('your grief must be immense', more literary) vs 얼마나 힘드세요 ('how hard this must be', softer, broader) vs 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 ('I am at a loss for words', the ultimate indirect comfort). All three go to the living mourner, never to pray for the deceased.
상심이 크시겠어요 → 얼마나 상심이 크세요 (warmer, more exclamatory) → (paired with) 부디 힘내세요. The trailing-off variants (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) are genuinely the most culturally natural Korean comfort moves.

Two traps: (1) 죄송합니다/미안해요 as 'I'm sorry' — those are apologies for faults, not condolence; they are wrong here. (2) Being too articulate or solution-y ('they're in a better place') — Korean funeral register is restrained sorrow, not problem-solving. Trailing off or short empathy phrases are more appropriate than polished complete sentences.

expressions.english: I'd like to invite you to the first-birthday party
expressions.shortExplanation: 돌잔치 초대할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to invite you to the first-birthday party".
expressions.explanation: 돌잔치 초대할게요 (doljanchi chodaehalgeyo) = "I'd like to invite you to the first-birthday party". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 돌잔치 초대할게요 ("I'll invite you to the doljanchi"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I'll invite you to the doljanchi
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the parents inviting guests to the 1st-birthday feast

usagePhrases.en: I'll invite you to the first birthday
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to close friends

usagePhrases.en: Please come to the first-birthday party
usagePhrases.note: Direct invitation with 와 주세요 ('please come')

usagePhrases.en: We've decided to hold a doljanchi
usagePhrases.note: Announcing the plan; 하다 here is fine for 잔치

examples.ko: A: 다음 달에 아기 돌잔치 해요. 초대할게요. / B: 어머, 정말요? 꼭 갈게요!
examples.romanization: A: daeum dare agi doljanchi haeyo. chodaehalgeyo. / B: eomeo, jeongmaryo? kkok galgeyo!
examples.en: A: Next month is our baby's first birthday party. I'll invite you. / B: Oh, really? I'll definitely come!
examples.note: The natural invitation and enthusiastic acceptance — 꼭 갈게요 is the warm reply

examples.ko: 돌잔치 와 주실 수 있어요? 돌 반지 안 가져오셔도 돼요.
examples.romanization: doljanchi wa jusil su isseoyo? dol banji an gajyeoosyeodo dwaeyo.
examples.en: Can you come to the first birthday? You don't need to bring a gold ring.
examples.note: 돌 반지 ('first-birthday gold ring') — a traditional gift; hosts politely wave it off, but guests often still bring money

examples.en: We had the doljanchi this weekend, so it was hectic.
examples.note: 정신없다 ('hectic/frazzled') — relatable host talk after the event

expressions.nuance: 돌잔치 is the celebration of a baby's first birthday (돌 = first birthday + 잔치 = feast/party), a major family event in Korea — historically significant because surviving the first year was once far from certain. 초대하다 (招待) is 'to invite', and 초대할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 intention form) is the host warmly announcing 'I'll invite you / consider yourself on the list.' The highlight ritual is the 돌잡이, where the baby is presented with objects (money, pencil, thread, stethoscope, etc.) and whichever one is grabbed supposedly forecasts the child's future. Gift-wise, the traditional present is a 돌 반지 (a small gold ring) or cash in an envelope (similar logic to 축의금). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) verb confusion — a 잔치 takes 하다 (돌잔치 하다), which feels inconsistent with memorial rites like 차례 지내다, but for a joyful 잔치/파티 you DO use 하다; 돌잔치 지내다 is wrong. (2) Invite verb — 부르다 ('call/summon') for guests sounds blunt; 초대하다 is the courteous choice. (3) The host disclaimer 돌 반지 안 가져오셔도 돼요 is courtesy — guests typically still bring cash or a small gift. Compare 환갑잔치/칠순잔치 (60th/70th birthday celebrations) — same 잔치 root, for elders.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 돌잔치 지내요.
지내다 is for ancestral rites (차례/제사). A celebratory party takes 하다: 돌잔치 해요. Save 지내다 for memorial rituals.
Using 부르다 instead of 초대하다 for guests.
부르다 ('call') sounds blunt for inviting people to an event. The courteous verb is 초대하다: 돌잔치에 초대할게요.
Bringing nothing because the host said 'no gift'.
Hosts politely wave off the 돌 반지, but guests typically still give money or a small gold gift. The disclaimer is courtesy, not a literal 'bring nothing'.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I will invite you to the 돌잔치 (first-birthday feast)'. 돌 = the first birthday; 잔치 = feast/party; 초대하다 = to invite (courteously). The -ㄹ게요 signals the speaker's intention/promise: 'I'll make sure to invite you', conveying warmth and inclusion.

Said by new parents to friends, relatives, and colleagues when they're organizing the first-birthday party. 초대할게요 (polite intention) for most adults; 초대할게 (반말) for close friends. The event itself uses 하다: 돌잔치 해요. To describe attending: 돌잔치에 가요.

초대하다 (invite, courteous) vs 부르다 (call/summon, blunt for inviting guests). 돌잔치 하다 (hold the party) vs 차례 지내다 (hold a ritual rite) — the verb differs by occasion: 하다 for celebrations, 지내다 for memorial rites. Compare 환갑잔치 (60th birthday feast) — same 잔치 structure.
초대할게요 → 와 주세요 (please come) → 돌잔치 하기로 했어요 (announcing the plan). Post-event: 돌잔치 잘 됐어요 ('the party went well'). The 돌잡이 ritual is the centerpiece — baby grabs an object, everyone predicts the future.

Three traps: (1) Wrong verb for the event — 돌잔치 지내다 is wrong; use 돌잔치 하다. (2) Wrong invite verb — 부르다 sounds blunt; use 초대하다. (3) Taking the host's 'no gift needed' disclaimer at face value — it's polite deflection; guests typically still bring cash or a small gold gift.

expressions.english: It's already been a year (said at a first birthday/memorial)
expressions.shortExplanation: 벌써 일 년이네요 is a practical expression meaning "It's already been a year (said at a first birthday/memorial)".
expressions.explanation: 벌써 일 년이네요 (beolsseo il nyeonineyo) means "It's already been a year (said at a first birthday/memorial)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 벌써 일 년이네요 ("It's already been a year"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; marveling at how fast the year went, at a 돌잔치

usagePhrases.en: Has it already been a year?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: The baby's grown so much already
usagePhrases.note: Cooing over the child's growth at the party
The all-purpose companion remark

examples.ko: A: 우리 아기 돌잔치예요! / B: 어머, 벌써 일 년이네요. 정말 빨리 컸다!
examples.romanization: A: uri agi doljanchiyeyo! / B: eomeo, beolsseo il nyeonineyo. jeongmal ppalli keotda!
examples.en: A: It's our baby's first birthday party! / B: Wow, it's already been a year. They've grown so fast!
examples.note: The most natural 돌잔치 exchange — -네요 captures the on-the-spot wonder

examples.ko: 엊그제 태어난 것 같은데 벌써 일 년이네요.
examples.romanization: eotgeuje taeeonan geot gateunde beolsseo il nyeonineyo.
examples.en: Feels like she was just born, but it's already been a year.
examples.note: 엊그제 같다 ('feels like just the other day') — the natural partnering sentiment

examples.ko: 벌써 일 년이네요. 그동안 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요.
examples.romanization: beolsseo il nyeonineyo. geudongan kiuneura gosaeng maneusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Already a year. You've worked so hard raising her.
examples.note: 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard') — praising the parents' effort is very Korean

expressions.nuance: 벌써 일 년이네요 ('it's already been a year') is a warm, reflective remark perfect for a 돌잔치 (first birthday) — and, in a somber key, for a one-year memorial (일주기). 벌써 means 'already (sooner than expected)', 일 년 is 'one year', and -네요 is the soft exclamatory ending for noticing/realizing something on the spot ('oh, it's already been a year!'). The -네요 is the heart of it: it conveys mild surprise and shared feeling — exactly the register for marveling at how fast a baby's first year flew. The nearest contrast is 벌써 vs 이미: both translate as 'already', but 벌써 carries the emotional 'wow, so soon!' resonance ideal here, while 이미 is flatter and factual ('already done/completed'), so 이미 일 년이네요 loses the warmth. The counting trap: 일 년 uses Sino-Korean 일, and 년 always takes Sino-Korean numbers (일 년, 이 년, 삼 년) — 한 년 (native-Korean number) is wrong. Tone-matching is important: at a happy 돌잔치 this is delighted; the exact same words at a one-year memorial become quietly wistful — read the room. Companion line: 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard raising the child') is very natural added praise for the parents.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 이미 instead of 벌써.
이미 is flat/factual 'already'; 벌써 carries 'wow, so soon!' emotion. For the warm surprise at a first birthday, say 벌써 일 년이네요, not 이미.
Saying 한 년 instead of 일 년.
The counter 년 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년. 한 년 (native number) is incorrect. One year is 일 년.
Dropping -네요 for flat 일 년이에요.
-네요 adds the on-the-spot 'oh, it's already a year!' feeling that fits the moment. Plain 일 년이에요 just states a fact and sounds cold.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'it's already one year, isn't it (-네요)'. The literal reading IS the meaning here — but the emotional weight is in 벌써 ('already, sooner than expected') and -네요 (on-the-spot realization/mild wonder). Together they produce warm, shared amazement at how fast time passed.

Said at a 돌잔치 to the parents, or at a one-year memorial. The polite -네요 form is standard for both contexts. With close friends, drop to 반말: 벌써 일 년이야?. Tone-matching matters: delight at a party, quiet wistfulness at a memorial — the words are the same, but delivery differs completely.

벌써 (already, emotional 'so soon!') vs 이미 (already, neutral/factual). For this warm, marveling moment use 벌써; 이미 일 년이네요 sounds like a flat report. Also: 엊그제 같다 ('feels like just the other day') is a natural companion — the two phrases pair beautifully.
벌써 일 년이네요 → 벌써 이 년이네요 / 삼 년이네요 (two/three years). Add-on praise: 그동안 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard raising them all this time'). Companion: 시간 진짜 빠르네요 ('time really flies').

Two traps: (1) Number error — 년 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년. Saying 한 년 (native-Korean numeral) is wrong for the year counter. (2) Dropping -네요 — saying 일 년이에요 is a flat statement of fact with none of the warm on-the-spot amazement; -네요 is what makes the phrase feel alive and socially natural.

expressions.english: We go to visit the ancestors' graves
expressions.shortExplanation: 성묘 가요 is a practical expression meaning "We go to visit the ancestors' graves".
expressions.explanation: "We go to visit the ancestors' graves" — that is 성묘 가요 (seongmyo gayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 성묘 가요 ("We go grave-visiting"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the holiday trip to tend ancestors' graves

usagePhrases.en: Are you going to the graves?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: We went and visited the graves
usagePhrases.note: 갔다 오다 ('went and came back') — reporting it's done

usagePhrases.en: We're going to clear the grave weeds
usagePhrases.note: 벌초 = cutting the weeds on the grave before Chuseok

examples.ko: A: 추석에 뭐 해요? / B: 가족이랑 성묘 가요. 할아버지 산소에 절 드리러요.
examples.romanization: A: chuseoge mwo haeyo? / B: gajogirang seongmyo gayo. harabeoji sansoe jeol deurireoyo.
examples.en: A: What are you doing for Chuseok? / B: We're going grave-visiting with the family — to bow at Grandfather's grave.
examples.note: The most natural holiday small-talk exchange — 산소 (honorific grave) and 절 드리다

examples.en: We went and bowed at Grandfather's grave.
examples.note: 산소 ('grave', honorific) + 절하다 ('to bow') — the key actions at the grave

examples.ko: 요즘은 벌초 대행 서비스 부르는 집도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun beolcho daehaeng seobiseu bureuneun jipdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many families hire a grave-weeding service.
examples.note: 벌초 대행 ('weeding-by-proxy') — a real modern convenience that shows changing practices

expressions.nuance: 성묘 (省墓) is visiting and tending an ancestor's grave, a core part of both 추석 and 설날 — families travel to the gravesite, clean it, set out a little food and drink, and bow (절하다). The verb for the trip is simply 가다: 성묘(를) 가요. To report the trip is done, use 갔다 오다 ('go and come back'): 성묘 갔다 왔어요. A related but distinct word is 벌초 (伐草), specifically cutting the weeds and grass on the grave mound, done shortly before Chuseok — so 성묘 (the respectful visit) and 벌초 (the maintenance work) are different activities. Many busy families now hire a 벌초 대행 service. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) grave vocabulary — use 산소 (honorific term for an ancestor's grave) when speaking of your own family's grave, not the blunt general word 무덤, which feels cold for your own ancestor. (2) The bow at the grave is 절, NOT 세배 — 세배 is only the living New Year bow to elders; confusing them in context is a clear error. (3) Don't 직역 'visit' as 방문하다 — 방문하다 is for visiting people or places socially; for graves the fixed expression is 성묘 가다. Note that Korean burial increasingly uses cremation (화장) with 납골당 (charnel houses), so 성묘 may mean visiting a 납골당 rather than a hillside grave mound.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling your ancestor's grave 무덤.
무덤 is a generic/blunt 'grave'. For your own ancestor use the respectful 산소 or 묘: 할아버지 산소에 성묘 가요.
Saying 세배 for the bow at the grave.
세배 is only the living New Year bow to elders. The bow at a grave (or any ritual bow) is just 절: 산소에서 절했어요.
Using 방문하다 for visiting the grave.
방문하다 is for social visits to people/places. The fixed expression is 성묘 가다 ('go grave-visiting'); 산소를 방문하다 sounds off.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I/we go 성묘 (省墓 = visit the grave)'. 성묘 is a Sino-Korean compound: 省 (visit/inspect) + 墓 (grave). The phrase captures the full act of the holiday trip — travel to the gravesite, tidy it, offer food/drink, bow, and leave.

A routine holiday topic during 추석 and 설날 conversations. Plain polite 가요 (성묘 가요) is standard. At the grave, refer to your ancestor's resting place as 산소 (honorific) or 묘, not the generic 무덤. The bow is 절 (not 세배).

성묘 (the respectful visit to pay respects, bow, offer food) vs 벌초 (the practical work of cutting weeds/grass on the grave). They often happen together but are separate activities. Also: 산소 (honorific ancestor's grave) vs 무덤 (generic grave, blunt for a family context).
성묘 가다 → 성묘 갔다 오다 (go and come back) → 성묘 갔다 왔어요 (past, reported). Before the visit: 벌초하러 가다 (go to clear weeds). At the grave: 산소에 절하다 ('bow at the grave'), 술/음식을 올리다 ('offer food/drink').

Three traps: (1) 무덤 instead of 산소 for your own ancestor — 산소 is the respectful, natural choice; 무덤 sounds detached and blunt. (2) 세배 instead of 절 for the grave bow — 세배 is exclusively the living New Year bow to elders; grave bows are 절. (3) 방문하다 instead of 성묘 가다 — 방문하다 is for social visits to living people or places, not for grave visits.

expressions.english: I go down to my hometown for the holiday
expressions.shortExplanation: 명절에 고향 내려가요 is a practical expression meaning "I go down to my hometown for the holiday".
expressions.explanation: 명절에 고향 내려가요 (myeongjeore gohyang naeryeogayo) = "I go down to my hometown for the holiday". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 명절에 고향 내려가요 ("I go down to my hometown for the holiday"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I go down to my hometown for the holiday
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; the classic holiday travel home

usagePhrases.en: You heading to your hometown for the holiday?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I'm not going home this holiday
usagePhrases.note: The common 'staying put' version

usagePhrases.en: The trip home will be jammed
usagePhrases.note: 귀성길 = the holiday journey home (notorious traffic)

examples.ko: A: 명절에 고향 내려가요? / B: 네, 부산이 고향이라서 KTX 타고 내려가요.
examples.romanization: A: myeongjeore gohyang naeryeogayo? / B: ne, busani gohyangiraseo KTX tago naeryeogayo.
examples.en: A: Are you going down to your hometown for the holiday? / B: Yes, my hometown is Busan, so I take the KTX.
examples.note: The most common holiday small-talk A/B — the answer mentions the hometown and mode of transport

examples.ko: 설날에 고향 내려가는데 차 막혀서 다섯 시간 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: seolnare gohyang naeryeoganeunde cha makyeoseo daseot sigan geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Going home for Seollal, traffic made it a 5-hour drive.
examples.note: 차 막히다 ('traffic jams') — the universal holiday-travel complaint;귀성 전쟁 ('going-home war')

examples.ko: 이번엔 고향 안 내려가고 그냥 집에서 쉬려고요.
examples.romanization: ibeonen gohyang an naeryeogago geunyang jibeseo swiryeogoyo.
examples.en: This time I'm not going home, just resting at home.
examples.note: A natural way to say you're skipping the trip this year

expressions.nuance: During 설날 and 추석 most Koreans travel to their family hometown, and the fixed verb is 내려가다 ('to go down') — because Seoul is perceived as 'up' and the provinces as 'down' (a Seoul-centric mental map). You 내려가다 to your 고향 ('hometown') and 올라오다 ('come up') back to Seoul after. The up/down orientation applies even if your hometown is north, east, or west of Seoul — it is about cultural perception, not geography, and this is the key thing English speakers miss when they try 고향에 가요 (fine, but not idiomatic). The holiday exodus is called 귀성 (歸省), and the brutal traffic is 귀성길 ('the road home') / 귀성 전쟁 ('the going-home war') — knowing these makes you sound local. The direction verb matters depending on your position: from Seoul you say 내려가다 ('go down there'); someone already at the hometown says the Seoulite 내려온다 ('comes down here'). The particle 에 is technically correct (고향에 내려가요) but is often dropped in natural speech (고향 내려가요). Don't confuse 고향 ('where you're from / parents' hometown') with 집 ('house/home in the city').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고향에 올라가요 to mean going home to the provinces.
From Seoul you go DOWN to the provinces: 내려가요. 올라가요 ('go up') is for heading toward Seoul. The up/down is Seoul-centric, not compass-based.
Mixing 내려가다 and 내려오다.
Use 내려가다 ('go down there') when you're in Seoul heading to the hometown. 내려오다 ('come down here') is from the hometown's viewpoint. Direction depends on where you are.
Translating 'hometown' as 집.
집 is your house/home; 고향 is the region you're from / your parents' place. For the holiday journey it's 고향 내려가요, not 집에 내려가요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'I go down to my hometown for the holiday'. The literal reading is the meaning, but 내려가다 ('go down') encodes a Seoul-centric worldview — Seoul is perceived as 'up', the provinces 'down'. Using 올라가다 ('go up') for the provinces would be backwards.

A universal holiday conversation topic. Polite 내려가요 (standard for colleagues, acquaintances); 내려가? (반말, friends). The counter-phrase for staying: 고향 안 내려가요. Asking about traffic is natural: 귀성길 많이 막혔어요? ('Was the road home very jammed?')

고향에 가요 ('I go to my hometown', neutral/correct but flat) vs 고향 내려가요 (idiomatic, Seoul-centric, what natives actually say). 고향 ('hometown/region of origin') vs 집 ('house in the city') — for the holiday journey the word is 고향, not 집.
명절에 고향 내려가다 → 고향 안 내려가다 (not going) → 고향 갔다 오다 (went and came back). Return to Seoul: 올라오다 / 올라왔어요 ('came back up'). Traffic talk: 귀성길 막히다 ('road home jammed'), 귀성 전쟁 ('going-home war').

Two traps: (1) Direction reversal — 고향에 올라가요 ('I go UP to my hometown in the provinces') is backwards; the provinces are always 'down'. Saying 올라가요 to mean heading out of Seoul signals you don't know the Seoul-centric map. (2) 집 vs 고향 — 집 is your city apartment; 고향 is the ancestral hometown you travel to for the holidays. 집에 내려가요 makes no sense for this.

expressions.english: Your parcel's here / A delivery came
expressions.shortExplanation: 택배 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "Your parcel's here / A delivery came".
expressions.explanation: 택배 왔어요 (taekbae wasseoyo) means "Your parcel's here / A delivery came". Say it as one set phrase — for example 택배 왔어요. ("Your parcel's here."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — courier or family member announcing a delivery to you
반말 — to a friend, roommate, or younger family member
격식 — an app/SMS notification or a building intercom announcement

usagePhrases.en: There's a delivery — can you come get it?
usagePhrases.note: Courier at the door checking if you can receive it now

examples.ko: A: 택배 왔어요. / B: 네, 잠깐만요.
examples.romanization: A: taekbae wasseoyo. / B: ne, jamkkanmanyo.
examples.en: A: Your parcel's here. / B: Yes, one moment.
examples.note: The bare doorstep announcement and the natural response; 잠깐만요 buys a few seconds to get to the door

examples.ko: 어, 택배 왔나 봐. 누가 좀 받아 줘.
examples.romanization: eo, taekbae wanna bwa. nuga jom bada jwo.
examples.en: Oh, looks like a delivery came. Someone grab it.
examples.note: 왔나 봐 = 'looks like it came' — guessing from the doorbell sound, not direct sight

examples.ko: 택배 왔는데 지금 집에 아무도 없어서요. 경비실에 맡겨 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: taekbae wanneunde jigeum jibe amudo eopseoseoyo. gyeongbisire matgyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A parcel came but nobody's home right now. Could you leave it at the security office?
examples.note: Real situation: redirecting a courier when you can't open the door; 경비실 = building security booth

expressions.nuance: 택배 왔어요 is the everyday phrase for 'a package arrived', said by a 택배 기사님 (courier) at your door, by a family member who heard the bell, or by an app push notification. Literally it means 'the taxi-delivery came' — 택배 (宅配) refers both to the parcel and the courier service that brings it door-to-door. Register follows the relationship: 존댓말 왔어요 to anyone you don't know well, including the courier; 반말 왔어 inside the family or to a close friend. Automated building notices use the fuller 도착했습니다. The nearest alternative is 배송 왔어요, but 배송 is the abstract shipping-process word stores use (배송 시작, 배송 완료) — it's not natural for the physical box at your door. Critically, do not confuse 택배 with 배달: 배달 is hot-food delivery (치킨, 피자), a completely different service and verb set. The English-speaker trap is trying to name the person — 'the delivery guy is here' — as 배달원이 있어요, which sounds robotic; Koreans simply announce the object: 택배 왔어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 배달 왔어요 for a parcel — 배달 is food delivery (치킨, 피자); a courier box is 택배, so the bell-ring announcement is 택배 왔어요.
Calling the courier 택배맨 or 배달원 to their face — the polite term is 택배 기사님 (driver-sir); 기사님 shows respect.
Using 배송 for the box itself (배송 왔어요 sounds off) — 배송 is the shipping process; the arrived parcel is 택배.

structuredNuance.t: Literally '택배 came' — 택배 (宅配, door-to-door delivery) is both the parcel and the service. The phrase announces 'a courier package has arrived', used by the courier at your door, a family member who heard the bell, or an app push notification.

존댓말 왔어요 to the courier or any adult you don't know well; 반말 왔어 inside the family or to a close friend; automated notices and official SMS use 도착했습니다. Never say it to a boss to mean 'your parcel arrived' without 주문하신 택배 왔습니다 — a bare 택배 왔어요 to a superior can sound too casual.
배송 왔어요 sounds unnatural for a box at the door — 배송 is a shop's process word (배송 시작/완료). 배달 왔어요 is specifically hot-food delivery (치킨, 피자); using 배달 for a courier parcel is a major category error.
택배 왔어 (반말) → 택배 왔어요 (존댓말) → 택배 도착했습니다 (격식). To redirect: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 / 경비실에 맡겨 주세요.

English speakers try to name the person — '배달원이 있어요' ('the delivery person is here') — which sounds robotic. Also, calling any delivery 배달 왔어요 is wrong if it's a parcel: 배달 = food, 택배 = courier parcel.

expressions.english: Please leave it at the door
expressions.shortExplanation: 문 앞에 놔 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please leave it at the door".
expressions.explanation: "Please leave it at the door" — that is 문 앞에 놔 주세요 (mun ape nwa juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 문 앞에 놔 주세요. ("Please leave it at the door."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please leave it at the door.
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — to a courier; standard contactless-delivery request

usagePhrases.en: Just leave it by the door.
usagePhrases.note: 반말 — to a friend or family member dropping something off

usagePhrases.en: You can just leave it at the door, thank you.
usagePhrases.note: 격식/정중 — fuller, very polite written or spoken request

usagePhrases.en: You can just leave it at the door and go.
usagePhrases.note: Natural extension telling the courier they needn't wait

examples.ko: A: 문 앞에 놔 주세요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다.
examples.romanization: A: mun ape nwa juseyo. / B: ne, algetseumnida.
examples.en: A: Please leave it at the door. / B: Sure, got it.
examples.note: The core contactless request and the courier's standard reply; most delivery apps have a 요청사항 box where you type exactly this

examples.ko: 지금 손이 안 비어서요. 그냥 문 앞에 놔 주세요.
examples.romanization: jigeum soni an bieoseoyo. geunyang mun ape nwa juseyo.
examples.en: My hands are full right now — just leave it at the door, please.
examples.note: 그냥 = 'just', softens it and signals the courier doesn't need to wait for you to answer

examples.ko: 벨 누르지 마시고 문 앞에 놔 주세요. 아기가 자고 있어서요.
examples.romanization: bel nureuji masigo mun ape nwa juseyo. agiga jago isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Please don't ring the bell, just leave it at the door — the baby's sleeping.
examples.note: Real note typed in a delivery-app 배송 요청사항 box; adding the reason makes the request feel natural, not demanding

expressions.nuance: This is the contactless-delivery line you say to a courier or type into a delivery app's 요청사항 (request) field. 놔 주세요 is the contracted spoken form of 놓아 주세요 ('please place/put it') — 놔 in speech, 놓아 in careful writing; both are correct. To a stranger-courier use 존댓말 (놔 주세요); to family or a friend 놔 줘. Adding 그냥 ('just') before it softens the request and implies no need to hand it over personally. The near-synonym 두고 가세요 ('leave it and go') adds the nuance that they needn't wait; 놔 주세요 focuses purely on the spot. The classic English-speaker slip is translating 'at the front door' as 앞문에 — 앞문 means the actual door panel (literally 'front door'), whereas 문 앞 means 'the space in front of the door', the location you want. Word order matters: 문 앞 ≠ 앞문.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 앞문에 놔 주세요 — 앞문 = the front door panel itself; the spot 'in front of the door' is 문 앞에. Particle/word-order matters.
Using 놓으세요 as a bare command — to a service person, soften with 주세요 (놔 주세요) so it's a request, not an order.
Writing 나 주세요 for 놔 주세요 — it's 놓다 → 놔, with ㅎ; spelling it 나 changes the verb entirely.

structuredNuance.t: 놔 주세요 = contracted form of 놓아 주세요, 'please place it (for me)'. 문 앞 = 'in front of the door' (location). The phrase means: put the parcel in the space just outside my door, no need to hand it to me.
Exists in three tiers: 놔 줘 (반말 to family/friends) → 놔 주세요 (존댓말, standard to couriers) → 놓아 주시면 됩니다 (격식, formal written). Typed into the app's 배송 요청사항 box, 존댓말 is expected even though it's text.

두고 가세요 adds the cue 'and you can leave' — the courier needn't wait. 놔 주세요 focuses only on placement. For building-wide contactless, 경비실에 맡겨 주세요 (leave it at the security booth) is the alternative when you're away.
놔 줘 → 놔 주세요 → 놓아 주시면 됩니다. Extensions: 벨 누르지 마시고 문 앞에 놔 주세요 (don't ring), 그냥 문 앞에 두고 가셔도 돼요 (feel free to leave).
앞문에 놔 주세요 ≠ 'leave it at the front door' — 앞문 is the door panel itself; the location 'in front of the door' is 문 앞에. Also: 나 주세요 is unrelated (the verb 나다); it must be spelled 놔 주세요 (from 놓다).

expressions.shortExplanation: 너무 시끄러워요 is a practical expression meaning "It's too loud / too noisy".
expressions.explanation: 너무 시끄러워요 (neomu sikkeureowoyo) = "It's too loud / too noisy". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 너무 시끄러워요. ("It's too noisy."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — complaint to a neighbor, staff, or stranger
반말 — to a friend, family, or roommate
격식 — written complaint to 관리실 or a formal report

usagePhrases.en: It's that the upstairs unit is so loud…
usagePhrases.note: Trailing -서요 softens it into a polite lead-in to a request

examples.ko: A: 너무 시끄러워요. / B: 죄송합니다, 조심할게요.
examples.romanization: A: neomu sikkeureowoyo. / B: joesonghamnida, josimhalgeyo.
examples.en: A: It's too loud. / B: Sorry, we'll be more careful.
examples.note: The bare complaint and the apology you hope to hear back; 조심할게요 = 'I'll be careful' is the standard contrite reply

examples.ko: 밤늦게 음악 소리가 너무 시끄러워요. 좀 줄여 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: bamneutge eumak soriga neomu sikkeureowoyo. jom juryeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: The music is way too loud late at night. Could you turn it down a bit?
examples.note: Pairs the description (시끄러워요) with a request (줄여 주시겠어요) — the natural two-step structure for a noise complaint

examples.ko: 안녕하세요, 아래층인데요. 밤마다 너무 시끄러워서 잠을 못 자겠어요.
examples.romanization: annyeonghaseyo, araecheungindeyo. bammada neomu sikkeureowoseo jameul mot jagesseoyo.
examples.en: Hi, I'm from the unit below — it's so loud every night I can't sleep.
examples.note: Real doorstep opener: 아래층인데요 identifies you first, which softens the complaint significantly before the real grievance

expressions.nuance: 시끄러워요 is an adjective-based complaint meaning 'it is (too) loud/noisy' — you're describing a state, not accusing someone. 너무 ('too/extremely') intensifies it. Use this to flag noise to a neighbor at the door, to café staff, or in a building complaint. With a stranger keep 존댓말 (시끄러워요); to a friend 시끄러워; a written or formal report upgrades to the noun phrase 소음이 심합니다 ('the noise is severe'). The key difference from 조용히 해 주세요 is direction: 시끄러워요 states the problem, 조용히 해 주세요 requests the fix — Koreans typically lead with the problem and follow with the request. Never open a neighbor complaint with a bare 시끄러워요! without first saying 안녕하세요, 아래층인데요 ('Hi, I'm from downstairs') — unannounced bluntness sounds like a fight, not a polite heads-up.
