Using plain 도와줄 수 있어요? to a senior — add the honorific -시-: 도와주실 수 있을까요?
Defaulting to the bare imperative 도와주세요 for a big favor — it's direct; the tentative 도와주실 수 있을까요? is more courteous.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'A bit (좀), help-give me (도와주다), would [you] honorably be able to (수 있을까요)?' 실제: 'Could you help me out a bit?' — every softening layer is intentional; together they make the request easy to decline without embarrassment.

도와주실 수 있을까요? (honorific + tentative) for seniors and anyone you need to address politely. 도와줄 수 있어? (반말) for peers. 도와주실 수 있으신가요? (격식, double honorific) for very formal situations or high superiors. Never omit 좀 — it's the main politeness softener.

도와주세요 = direct imperative 'help me' — fine for quick, easy requests. 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? = face-saving tentative request — better for larger favors that take the other person's time. 혹시 도움이 필요하시면 말씀해 주세요 = 'Let me know if you need help' — offering help rather than requesting it.
혹시 [task] 좀 도와주실 수 있을까요? adds 혹시 for extra tentativeness. Add context: [reason] + 도와주실 수 있을까요? — a reason acknowledges the imposition. After: 감사합니다 / 덕분에 잘 됐어요 ('Thanks to you it worked out well').

도와줄 수 있어요? to a senior — plain stem instead of honorific -시- sounds flat. Dropping 좀 — the request immediately sounds blunt and entitled. 도와주세요 for a big favor — that's the imperative; use the tentative -을까요? frame instead.

expressions.shortExplanation: 좋아요 눌렀어요 is a practical expression meaning "I hit 'like'".
expressions.explanation: 좋아요 눌렀어요 (joayo nulleosseoyo) = "I hit 'like'". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 좋아요 눌렀어요 ("I hit 'like'"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; reporting you liked someone's post
반말, telling a friend
Asking viewers/followers to like (e.g. a creator's request)
Very casual slang; 박다 ('to ram') = liked enthusiastically

examples.en: I just hit like.
examples.note: Reporting a simple completed action with 방금 ('just now')

examples.ko: A: 제 사진 봤어요? / B: 네, 좋아요 눌렀어요!
examples.romanization: A: je sajin bwasseoyo? / B: ne, joayo nulleosseoyo!
examples.en: A: Did you see my photo? / B: Yes, I liked it!
examples.note: Classic two-person exchange; 눌렀어요 confirms the tap was done

examples.en: Please subscribe and hit like!
examples.note: The set creator-request phrase; 구독 ('subscribe') pairs with 좋아요

expressions.nuance: 직역하면 '좋아요'는 '(it) is good' 또는 '(I) like it'이라는 완성된 문장이지만, 모든 한국 플랫폼(인스타그램, 유튜브, 카카오스토리, 네이버)에서 하트나 엄지 버튼을 가리키는 고정 명사로도 쓰여요. 따라서 좋아요 눌렀어요 = '(나는) 좋아요(버튼)를 눌렀다'는 뜻이에요. 버튼을 누르는 것이라 동사는 반드시 누르다를 써야 하고, 하다나 치다는 틀려요. 친한 친구한테는 좋아요 박았어요처럼 박다(세게 꽂다)를 써서 '엄청 좋아요를 눌렀다'는 뉘앙스를 줄 수 있어요. 가장 중요한 함정: 좋아요(버튼 누르기) vs 좋아해요(감정, 좋아하다의 현재형) — 당신 게시물에 좋아요 눌렀어요는 버튼 클릭이고, 당신을 좋아해요는 낭만적 감정 표현이라 완전히 달라요. 비공개 계정에는 좋아요를 누를 수 없으니 상황도 체크해야 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 좋아요 했어요 ('I did a like').
Korean treats the like as a button you PRESS, so the verb is 누르다, not 하다. Correct: 좋아요 눌렀어요.
Saying 좋아했어요 to mean 'I liked your post'.
좋아했어요 is past-tense of the FEELING 좋아하다 ('I used to like it'). For the button action say 좋아요 눌렀어요.
Saying 좋아요 쳤어요 by analogy with 'hit like'.
치다 ('to hit/strike') is wrong for a button. Koreans 누르다 (press) a button: 좋아요 눌렀어요, or casually 좋아요 박았어요.

structuredNuance.t: '좋아요' literally means 'it is good / I like it' (좋다 + polite 요), a complete polite sentence. But on every Korean platform it doubles as the FIXED NOUN for the like button itself — the heart or thumb. So 좋아요 눌렀어요 = 'I pressed [the] 좋아요 [button]'. The action verb is 누르다 ('to press a button'), never 하다 or 치다.

Used in any SNS context: telling a friend you liked their post, asking followers to tap the button, or reacting to content. With strangers or content creators, keep the polite -았어요 form (좋아요 눌렀어요). Among close friends drop to 반말: 좋아요 눌렀어. Young people use the slang 좋아요 박았어요 (박다 = 'to ram in') for enthusiastic likes — fine with peers, odd with a brand account.

좋아요 눌렀어요 (button action) vs 좋아해요 (the FEELING, 좋아하다 present tense). '당신을 좋아해요' means 'I have feelings for you' — romantic — while '좋아요 눌렀어요' is just the tap. 좋아했어요 (past of 좋아하다) means 'I used to have that feeling', nothing to do with the button.

English speakers directly translate 'I liked it' as 좋아했어요, which is past tense of the FEELING 좋아하다 and has no connection to the like button. For the button action the only natural phrase is 좋아요 눌렀어요. Also, 좋아요 했어요 ('I did a like') is wrong — the verb is 누르다, not 하다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 팔로우할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll follow you".
expressions.explanation: 팔로우할게요 (pallouhalgeyo) means "I'll follow you". Say it as one set phrase — for example 팔로우할게요 ("I'll follow you"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; announcing you'll follow their account
반말, to a friend
맞팔 = mutual follow; common request between users
Asking someone to follow your account

examples.en: Tell me your account, I'll follow you.
examples.note: Chain 계정 알려 주세요 ('tell me your account') then the action

examples.ko: A: 저 팔로우했어요. / B: 아, 맞팔 가능해요?
examples.romanization: A: jeo pallouhaesseoyo. / B: a, matpal ganeunghaeyo?
examples.en: A: I followed you. / B: Oh, can we follow each other?
examples.note: Typical exchange after discovering someone; 맞팔 가능해요 = follow-back request

examples.en: I passed a thousand followers!
examples.note: 팔로워 ('follower') is the person; note it differs from the act 팔로우

expressions.nuance: 팔로우는 영어 'follow'의 한국어 표기로, SNS에서 '팔로우(하다)'는 팔로우 행위 자체, '팔로워'는 나를 팔로우하는 사람을 뜻해요. 즉 직역하면 '나 팔로우할게요'는 '나 너를 팔로우(follow) 할(will do) 게요(polite volition)'예요. 핵심 구분: 팔로우 ≠ 팔로워 — 팔로우할게요(동사), 팔로워가 많아요(명사). 맞팔(맞+팔로우)은 서로 팔로우하는 것으로 한국 SNS의 인사 문화예요. 반대어는 언팔(언팔하다 = unfollow)이고, 더 강한 조치는 차단이에요. -ㄹ게요는 '내가 그렇게 할게'라는 의지·예고를 뜻해요. 친구한테는 팔로우할게라고 해도 돼요. 따라가다('물리적으로 뒤따르다')를 SNS에 쓰면 스토킹처럼 들리니 절대 쓰지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 팔로워할게요 to mean 'I'll follow you'.
팔로워 is the NOUN for the person (a follower). The verb is 팔로우하다: 팔로우할게요.
Using 따라가다 for following on SNS.
따라가다 means physically tailing a person and sounds stalkerish. The platform sense is 팔로우하다: 팔로우할게요.
Saying 팔로우가 많아요 to mean 'I have many followers'.
The people are 팔로워. 'I have many followers' = 팔로워가 많아요. 팔로우 is the act, not the people.

structuredNuance.t: 팔로우할게요 = '팔로우(follow) + 할게요(I will do it, polite volition)' — a straightforward loan-verb. The critical split: 팔로우(하다) is the ACT of following, while 팔로워 is the PERSON who follows you. 팔로우할게요 = 'I'll follow you (the act)'; 팔로워가 많아요 = 'I have many followers (the people)'.

Said when you discover someone's account online and want to connect, or after a mutual introduction. -ㄹ게요 is polite first-person volition ('I'll do it, heads-up'). With friends use 팔로우할게. For a mutual follow-back, the fixed request is 맞팔해요 or 맞팔 가능해요?. The opposite of following is 언팔 (unfollow, 언팔했어요) and the harsher 차단 (block).

팔로우할게요 (I will follow = one-directional) vs 맞팔해요 (let's follow EACH OTHER = bilateral). The loanword 팔로워 is the noun for the person; never say 팔로워할게요 — that treats the noun as a verb. Don't use 따라가다 ('physically follow/tail') for SNS — it sounds like stalking.

The two big traps: (1) Using 팔로워 as a verb ('I'll 팔로워 you') — 팔로워 is only the noun for the follower-person, the verb is 팔로우하다. (2) Using 따라가다 ('to physically walk behind someone') for SNS following — it sounds like stalking; the platform sense is 팔로우하다 only.

expressions.shortExplanation: 디엠 보낼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll send you a DM".
expressions.explanation: "I'll send you a DM" — that is 디엠 보낼게요 (diem bonaelgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 디엠 보낼게요 ("I'll send you a DM"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; you'll message them privately
반말, to a friend
Asking them to message you privately
Specifying the channel with -으로 ('via')

examples.en: I'll DM you the details.
examples.note: 자세한 건 ('as for the details') routes private info to DM

examples.ko: A: 문의 있는데요. / B: 디엠 주세요, 바로 답해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: munui inneundeyo. / B: diem juseyo, baro dapae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I have an inquiry. / B: DM me — I'll reply right away.
examples.note: Typical seller-to-buyer exchange routing contact to private channel

examples.en: For group-buy inquiries, DM me.
examples.note: Sellers route questions to DM; 디엠 주세요 = 'DM me'

expressions.nuance: 디엠은 'DM(Direct Message)'의 한국어 음차로 '디-엠'이라 읽어요. 직역하면 '다이렉트 메시지를 보내겠습니다'이지만 실제로는 인스타그램·X 등에서 1:1 비공개 채팅을 시작하는 행동을 가리켜요. 보내다('전달하다')와 주다('주세요 형태로 상대에게 요청')가 자연스러운 동사예요. 채널을 표시할 때는 수단 조사 -으로(디엠으로)를 써야 해요. 디엠은 1:1 비공개인 반면, 댓글은 공개 댓글이에요. 카카오톡을 쓸 때는 카톡 보낼게요라고 해야 자연스러워요. 디엠 하다(디엠했어요)처럼 하다를 붙일 수도 있지만, 보내다/주다가 더 표준적이에요. 보내다(send) vs 받다(receive)를 혼동하면 방향이 반대가 되니 주의하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 디엠 말할게요 ('I'll say a DM').
A message is sent, not 'said'. Use 보내다: 디엠 보낼게요, or 디엠 주세요 to ask them.
Confusing 디엠 (private) with 댓글 (public comment).
디엠 is a private direct message; 댓글 is a public comment under a post. For something private, say 디엠으로 보내 주세요, not 댓글로.
Saying 디엠 보냈어요 when you mean you received one.
보내다 is to send; 받다 is to receive. 'I got a DM' = 디엠 받았어요, not 보냈어요.

structuredNuance.t: 디엠 is the phonetic Korean spelling of the initials 'DM' (Direct Message), read 'dee-em'. 디엠 보낼게요 literally means 'I will send a DM' — the DM is the noun object and 보내다 ('to send') is the verb. The key point: it signals a PRIVATE one-to-one message on Instagram or X, as opposed to a public 댓글 (comment).

Used when someone needs private info (price, address, personal detail) that shouldn't be public. On sales posts you'll see 디엠 주세요 or 디엠으로 문의 주세요. -ㄹ게요 is polite ('I'll do it, heads-up'); with friends use 디엠 보낼게. When using KakaoTalk, say 카톡 보낼게요 instead — using 디엠 for KakaoTalk sounds off.

디엠 (private, one-to-one on SNS) vs 댓글 (public comment under a post) vs 문자/메시지 (SMS text). For KakaoTalk specifically, 카톡 보낼게요 is the natural phrase; 디엠 is reserved for Instagram/X. Also: 보내다 (send, you give it out) vs 받다 (receive, it comes to you) — 디엠 받았어요 = 'I GOT a DM', the opposite direction from 디엠 보냈어요.

The main pitfalls: (1) Writing 'DM' in Latin letters in Korean speech/text — always romanize as 디엠. (2) Saying 디엠 말할게요 ('I'll say a DM') — a message is sent (보내다), not 'said'. (3) Confusing 보내다 (send) with 받다 (receive) and saying 디엠 보냈어요 when you mean you got one — that should be 디엠 받았어요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 댓글 달아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please leave a comment".
expressions.explanation: 댓글 달아 주세요 (daetgeul dara juseyo) = "Please leave a comment". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 댓글 달아 주세요 ("Please leave a comment"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; inviting people to comment
반말, to a friend
남기다 ('to leave behind') variant, slightly more formal

usagePhrases.en: Let me know in the comments
usagePhrases.note: Routing replies to the comment section with -로

examples.ko: 궁금한 거 있으면 댓글 달아 주세요.
examples.romanization: gunggeumhan geo isseumyeon daetgeul dara juseyo.
examples.en: If you have questions, leave a comment.
examples.note: -으면 ('if') invites comments conditionally

examples.ko: A: 여기 맛있어요? / B: 네! 댓글로 후기 남겨 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi masisseoyo? / B: ne! daetgeullo hugi namgyeo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Is it tasty there? / B: Yes! I'll leave a review in the comments.
examples.note: 댓글로 routes the reply to the comment section; 후기 = review

examples.en: Please post kind comments, not hateful ones.
examples.note: Contrast 악플 ('hate comment') with 선플 ('kind comment')

expressions.nuance: 댓글은 게시물이나 영상 아래 달리는 공개 댓글이에요. 핵심 동사는 달다로, '걸다/붙이다'처럼 무언가를 게시물에 '매달다'는 뉘앙스예요(직역: 'to hang/attach'). 댓글 달아 주세요는 '댓글을 달아주세요'의 압축형이에요. 남기다('두고 가다')도 비슷하지만 약간 더 격식 있어요. 대댓글이나 답글은 댓글에 달리는 답변이에요. 문화적으로 중요한 단어: 악플(악성 댓글, hate comment) vs 선플(선한 댓글, kind comment). 댓글 쓰다('쓰다'로 글을 쓰다)는 어색하진 않지만 원어민은 달다/남기다를 훨씬 많이 써요. 디엠은 비공개이고 댓글은 공개라는 점이 핵심 차이예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 댓글 써 주세요 by translating 'write a comment'.
Korean ATTACHES a comment: 댓글 달다. Say 댓글 달아 주세요 or 댓글 남겨 주세요; 쓰다 fits a full post, not a comment.
Using 코멘트 instead of 댓글.
The everyday word is the native-style 댓글. 코멘트 sounds like jargon. Say 댓글 달아 주세요.
Confusing 댓글 (comment) with 답글 (reply).
A 댓글 is a top-level comment; a 답글 (or 대댓글) is the reply to one. 'I replied to your comment' = 답글 달았어요.

structuredNuance.t: 댓글 달아 주세요 = '댓글 (a comment) + 달아 주세요 (please hang/attach it for me)'. 달다 literally means 'to hang/attach something' — a comment is conceptualized as something you ATTACH to a post, not just write. This is why natives say 달다 or 남기다 ('leave behind'), not 쓰다 ('write'), for comments specifically.

Used by creators inviting interaction, sellers soliciting feedback, or anyone wanting a reply. 달아 주세요 is the standard polite request; friends get 달아 줘. 댓글로 알려 주세요 ('let me know in the comments') routes the answer publicly. Note: -로 here is the channel particle ('through/via comments'), so you could say 디엠으로 알려 주세요 for a private reply instead.

댓글 달아 주세요 (public comment under a post) vs 디엠 주세요 (private message to you) vs 후기 남겨 주세요 (leave a review/rating). Also: 댓글 (top-level comment) vs 답글/대댓글 (reply to a comment). Don't say 코멘트 — the native word 댓글 is standard. 악플 (hate comment) vs 선플 (kind comment) are culture-specific terms you'll see constantly.

The main English-speaker mistake is using 쓰다 ('to write'): 댓글 써 주세요 is understandable but not idiomatic. Natives strongly prefer 달다/남기다 for comments. Also, don't say 코멘트 — that sounds like borrowed jargon; the everyday word is 댓글. And confusing 댓글 (comment) with 답글 (reply to a comment) will make your sentence mean the wrong thing.

expressions.shortExplanation: 링크 보내 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please send me the link".
expressions.explanation: 링크 보내 주세요 (ringkeu bonae juseyo) means "Please send me the link". Say it as one set phrase — for example 링크 보내 주세요 ("Please send me the link"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking for a URL
반말, to a friend
걸다 ('to hang') = paste a clickable link somewhere
Telling someone to click through; 타고 들어가다 ('enter via')

examples.en: Send me the link to that video.
examples.note: Name the thing (그 영상) then ask for its 링크

examples.ko: A: 어디서 살 수 있어요? / B: 프로필에 링크 걸어 놨어요, 타고 들어가세요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiseo sal su isseoyo? / B: peuropire ringkeu georeo nwasseoyo, tago deureogaseyo.
examples.en: A: Where can I buy it? / B: I've posted the link in my profile — click through it.
examples.note: Seller's typical answer; 링크 걸어 놨어요 = a standing link is already posted there

examples.en: If you click the link, you can sign up right away.
examples.note: 클릭하다 ('to click') + 신청되다 ('gets applied')

expressions.nuance: 링크는 'link'의 음차로 클릭 가능한 URL을 뜻해요. 상황에 따라 동사가 달라지는 게 핵심이에요: 누군가에게 보낼 때는 보내다(링크 보내 주세요), 공개 장소(프로필, 댓글)에 올릴 때는 걸다(링크 걸다 — 직역: 걸어두다/매달다), 클릭해서 들어갈 때는 클릭하다 또는 링크 타고 들어가다('링크를 타고 이동하다')예요. 보내다 vs 걸다의 차이: 보내다는 상대방에게 전달, 걸다는 공개 장소에 게시해 두는 것이에요. 링크 vs 주소: 주소는 URL 텍스트 그 자체, 링크는 클릭 가능한 연결이지만 일상 대화에서는 혼용돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 링크 줘 보내 (wrong word order).
Korean puts the verb last: 링크 보내 줘 (casual) / 링크 보내 주세요 (polite). The object comes before the verb.
Using 보내다 when you mean post a clickable link publicly.
보내다 sends it to a person. To embed a live link in a bio/comment, use 걸다: 링크 걸어 주세요.
Confusing 링크 with 좋아요 (because both involve buttons).
링크 is a URL you click through; 좋아요 is the like button. 'Send the link' = 링크 보내 주세요, unrelated to liking.

structuredNuance.t: 링크 보내 주세요 = '링크(link/URL) + 보내 주세요(please send it to me)'. Straightforward, but the verb changes by action: 보내다 ('send to a person'), 걸다 ('hang/post a clickable link in a public spot'), 클릭하다 / 타고 들어가다 ('click through'). Using the wrong verb for the situation sounds unnatural.

보내 주세요 is the everyday polite request when chatting one-to-one. When someone posts a link in their bio or comment section, 걸다 is the idiom: 링크 걸어 놨어요 ('I've hung the link there'). To tell someone to navigate through it: 링크 타고 들어가세요. Friends hear 링크 보내 줘. Register is generally casual-to-polite for these SNS contexts.

링크 보내 주세요 (send TO a person privately) vs 링크 걸어 주세요 (post it publicly for anyone to see). 링크 vs 주소: 주소 is the raw URL text; 링크 implies a clickable connection — but in casual speech, 링크/주소 보내 주세요 both work. Don't use 붙여넣다 ('paste') to mean publicly posting a link — that's the clipboard action; 걸다 is posting a live link.

Two traps: (1) Word order — learners say 링크 줘 보내 instead of 링크 보내 줘; in Korean the main verb comes at the end: 링크 보내 줘/주세요. (2) Using 붙이다 ('to stick/paste') for 'paste the link' in the public sense — 붙여넣다 is fine for a clipboard paste, but to make a live link visible to others say 걸다. Also, 링크 열다 ('open the link') exists but 링크 타고 들어가세요 sounds far more native for 'click through'.

expressions.shortExplanation: 사진 업로드했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I uploaded a photo".
expressions.explanation: "I uploaded a photo" — that is 사진 업로드했어요 (sajin eomnodeuhaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 사진 업로드했어요 ("I uploaded a photo"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; standard report of posting media
More natural native verb 올리다 ('to raise/post')
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay if I post the photo?
usagePhrases.note: Asking permission before posting someone's pic

examples.en: I just posted my travel photos.
examples.note: 올리다 is the everyday word natives reach for first

examples.ko: A: 어제 찍은 사진 어디 있어요? / B: 인스타에 올렸어요, 태그해 드렸어요.
examples.romanization: A: eoje jjigeun sajin eodi isseoyo? / B: inseutae ollyeosseoyo, taegeuhae deuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: A: Where are the photos from yesterday? / B: I posted them on Instagram and tagged you.
examples.note: 올리다 for posting; 태그하다 for mentioning someone

examples.en: The file's too big so it won't upload.
examples.note: 업로드가 안 되다 ('uploading doesn't work') for a failure

expressions.nuance: 사진 업로드했어요와 사진 올렸어요는 같은 행동이지만 느낌이 달라요. 올리다는 직역하면 '위로 올리다'인데, SNS에 게시하는 것을 '올린다'고 표현해요. 업로드(하다)는 영어 'upload'의 음차로 버튼이나 파일 전송에서 더 기술적인 느낌이에요. 일상 대화에서는 올리다가 훨씬 자연스러워요. 업로드 ≠ 다운로드: 업로드는 올리는 것(게시), 다운로드/내려받다는 내 기기로 저장하는 것이에요. 올리다 vs 보내다: 올리다는 공개 게시, 보내다는 1:1 개인 전송. 게시하다는 올리다/업로드보다 공문서 느낌이라 인스타 셀카에는 쓰기 어색해요. 올리다 불규칙 활용: 올려요/올렸어요 (올리어요가 아님)를 잊지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 업로드 for every casual SNS post.
It sounds techie. For posting a photo to SNS, the natural verb is 올리다: 사진 올렸어요. Save 업로드 for file transfers.
Saying 업로드 when you mean download.
업로드 = send up (post). Saving to your device is 다운로드/내려받다. Don't swap the direction.
Saying 사진 올리어요 (wrong conjugation).
올리다 conjugates to 올려요/올렸어요, not 올리어요. Present: 사진 올려요; past: 사진 올렸어요.

structuredNuance.t: 올리다 literally means 'to raise/put up' — you lift the photo up onto the platform. 업로드하다 is the loanword 'upload'. Both mean the same SNS action, but 올리다 sounds warm and colloquial, while 업로드 sounds technical (like file transfers). For casual Instagram chat, 사진 올렸어요 is the default; 업로드 is better reserved for talking about file size issues or button failures (업로드가 안 돼요).

올렸어요 is the go-to polite past; friends get 올렸어. Before posting a group photo, ask permission: 사진 올려도 돼요? ('Is it okay to post this?'). The irregular conjugation 올리다 → 올려요/올렸어요 (not 올리어요) trips learners. 게시하다 ('to publish/post') exists but reads like officialese — save it for notice boards, not selfies.

올리다 (post publicly) vs 보내다 (send privately one-to-one) vs 다운로드/내려받다 (download — opposite direction, saving TO your device). Don't say 업로드 when you mean you saved a photo to your phone — that's 내려받다. And 게시하다 is formal/official; too stiff for everyday SNS posts.

The two pitfalls: (1) Over-using 업로드 for every casual SNS post — 사진 올렸어요 is what natives say; save 업로드 for technical file-transfer contexts. (2) Wrong conjugation 사진 올리어요 — 올리다 contracts to 올려요/올렸어요. Another trap: saying 업로드 when you mean downloading — they're opposite directions.

expressions.shortExplanation: 스토리 올렸어요 is a practical expression meaning "I posted a story".
expressions.explanation: 스토리 올렸어요 (seutori ollyeosseoyo) = "I posted a story". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 스토리 올렸어요 ("I posted a story"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; about Instagram/KakaoStory stories
반말, to a friend
Checking if they saw it (stories disappear in 24h)

usagePhrases.en: I'll put it on my story
usagePhrases.note: Specifying the destination with -에

examples.en: I posted a story earlier — did you see it?
examples.note: -는데 softly links your post to the question

examples.ko: A: 이 사진 스토리에 올려도 돼요? / B: 네, 괜찮아요.
examples.romanization: A: i sajin seutorie ollyeodo dwaeyo? / B: ne, gwaenchanayo.
examples.en: A: Can I post this photo to my story? / B: Yes, that's fine.
examples.note: Always ask permission before posting someone in your story; 올려도 돼요? = polite ask

examples.en: I'll screenshot the story and send it.
examples.note: 캡처하다 ('to capture/screenshot') for saving a story

expressions.nuance: 스토리는 인스타그램 등의 24시간 후 사라지는 게시물 포맷이에요. 동사는 올리다('올리다/게시하다')이고, 게시 위치를 나타낼 때는 장소 조사 -에를 써요: 스토리에 올릴게요. 스토리와 피드의 차이가 핵심이에요: 스토리는 24시간 임시 게시물(상단에 표시), 피드/게시물은 영구 게시물(프로필 그리드에 남음). 스토리 보존 방법은 캡처하다('캡처')이에요. -에 vs -를: '스토리에 올리다'는 올바른 방향(목적지), '스토리를 올리다'는 스토리 자체를 목적어로 하는 것이라 맥락에 따라 달라요. 이야기(narrative/tale)와 스토리(SNS 포맷)는 전혀 달라요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 스토리를 올렸어요 with the wrong particle for the destination.
When naming where it goes, use -에: 스토리에 올렸어요 ('posted it to my story'). You put media ONTO the story.
Using 이야기 instead of 스토리 for the app feature.
이야기 means a narrative/tale. The disappearing SNS post is the loanword 스토리: 스토리 올렸어요.
Calling a permanent grid post a 스토리.
스토리 vanishes in 24h. A permanent post is 게시물/피드: 게시물 올렸어요 or 피드에 올렸어요.

structuredNuance.t: 스토리 올렸어요 = '스토리(story format) + 올렸어요(I put it up)'. 스토리 is the borrowed word for the 24-hour disappearing post format on Instagram. The verb is 올리다, same as for any SNS post. Critical: this 스토리 (SNS feature) is completely different from 이야기 ('a narrative/tale') — don't interchange them.

Said between friends or followers after sharing a temporary story. Because stories vanish after 24 hours, 봤어요? ('did you see it?') and 캡처하다 ('to screenshot it') are natural follow-ups. The destination particle is -에: 스토리에 올릴게요 ('I'll put it ON my story'). Polite: 올렸어요; 반말: 올렸어. Before posting someone else's photo, always ask 올려도 돼요? to avoid social friction.

스토리 (temporary 24h post, top of the app) vs 피드/게시물 (permanent post on your grid) vs 릴스 (short video Reels) vs 라이브 (live stream). If you mean the permanent grid post, say 게시물 올렸어요 or 피드에 올렸어요, not 스토리. And this 스토리 is the app feature — 이야기 올렸어요 would mean 'I posted a written tale', which sounds odd.

The particle trap: learners say 스토리를 올렸어요 when specifying where the media goes, but to mark DESTINATION you need -에: 스토리에 올렸어요 / 스토리에 올릴게요. Also confusing 스토리 (SNS format) with 이야기 (narrative) — saying 이야기 올렸어요 implies a written story, not the app feature.

expressions.shortExplanation: 태그하지 마세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please don't tag me".
expressions.explanation: 태그하지 마세요 (taegeuhaji maseyo) means "Please don't tag me". Say it as one set phrase — for example 태그하지 마세요 ("Please don't tag me"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking not to be tagged
반말, to a friend
The opposite: asking to be tagged
풀다 ('to undo/release') = remove an existing tag

examples.en: Don't tag photos with my face in them.
examples.note: Set a boundary: 얼굴 나온 ('with my face showing')

examples.ko: A: 이 사진 태그해도 돼요? / B: 아니요, 태그하지 마세요.
examples.romanization: A: i sajin taegeuhaedo dwaeyo? / B: aniyo, taegeuhaji maseyo.
examples.en: A: Can I tag you in this photo? / B: No, please don't tag me.
examples.note: Direct exchange establishing consent before tagging

examples.ko: 이미 올린 거면 태그 풀어 주세요.
examples.romanization: imi ollin geomyeon taegeu pureo juseyo.
examples.en: If it's already posted, please untag me.
examples.note: 태그 풀다 ('release the tag') = remove a tag after the fact

expressions.nuance: 태그(하다)는 영어 'tag'의 음차로, 사진이나 게시물에 특정 계정을 연결해 알림을 보내는 행동이에요. 태그하지 마세요 = '-지 마세요(부드러운 금지 요청)'를 사용한 정중한 거절이에요. 이미 달린 태그를 없애려면 태그 풀다('풀다' = 묶인 것을 풀다, release)를 써요. 반대로 태그를 요청할 때는 태그해 주세요예요. 태그 vs 해시태그: 사람 태그는 계정을 연결하는 것이고, 해시태그(#키워드)는 카테고리 태그예요. 태그 vs 언급/멘션: 멘션은 댓글이나 글에서 @으로 텍스트로 부르는 것이고, 태그는 미디어에 계정을 연결하는 것이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 태그하세요 to mean 'don't tag me'.
안 + verb negates a statement, not a command. A polite prohibition uses -지 마세요: 태그하지 마세요.
Saying 태그 지워 주세요 to remove a tag.
지우다 ('erase') fits deleting text. To remove a tag the idiom is 태그 풀다: 태그 풀어 주세요.
Confusing 사람 태그 (tagging a person) with 해시태그 (hashtag).
Tagging a person links their account; a 해시태그 is a #keyword. 'Don't tag me' = (사람) 태그하지 마세요.

structuredNuance.t: 태그하지 마세요 = '태그(하다)(to tag) + -지 마세요(please don't)'. 태그하다 links someone's account to a photo/post so it appears on their profile and notifies them. The negative request formula is -지 마세요 for polite prohibitions and -지 마 for 반말. To remove an existing tag the idiom is 태그 풀다 ('release/untie the tag'), not 태그 지우다 ('erase').

Used when someone posts a photo of you without permission, or as a pre-emptive boundary. It's appropriate to say to anyone — friend or acquaintance — since tagging involves someone's public image. -지 마세요 is the standard polite prohibition; 반말: 태그하지 마. The friendly opposite: 태그해 주세요 ('please tag me'). For removing an already-posted tag: 태그 풀어 주세요.

태그하다 (link an account to media) vs 언급하다/멘션하다 (@ mention someone in text) vs 해시태그 달다 (add a #keyword). The key dividing line: 태그 links a person's account to a photo so it shows in their tagged photos; 언급 is a text ping in a comment or caption. Also: 태그 풀다 (untag, remove the link) vs 태그 지우다 (sounds like deleting text — wrong idiom).

Two pitfalls: (1) Forming the prohibition as 안 태그하세요 — 안 + verb negates a statement, not a command; polite prohibitions use -지 마세요. (2) Saying 태그 안 돼요 ('tagging doesn't work') when you mean 'don't tag me' — 안 돼요 states impossibility or rules, while 태그하지 마세요 is a personal request to someone.

expressions.shortExplanation: 계정 비공개예요 is a practical expression meaning "My account is private".
expressions.explanation: "My account is private" — that is 계정 비공개예요 (gyejeong bigonggaeyeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 계정 비공개예요 ("My account is private"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; stating your account's visibility
반말, to a friend
공개 ('public') is the opposite of 비공개
계정 ('account') as a countable noun with 개

examples.ko: 제 계정 비공개라서 팔로우 승인해야 돼요.
examples.romanization: je gyejeong bigonggaeraseo pallou seunginhaeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: My account's private, so I have to approve follows.
examples.note: -라서 ('because') links privacy to needing 승인 ('approval')

examples.ko: A: 팔로우하려는데 계정을 못 찾겠어요. / B: 비공개예요, 요청 보내 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: pallouharyeoneunde gyejeongeul mot chatgesseoyo. / B: bigonggaeyeyo, yocheong bonae juseyo.
examples.en: A: I'm trying to follow you but can't find the account. / B: It's private — please send a follow request.
examples.note: Explains why an account is hard to find; 요청 = follow request

examples.en: I think my account got hacked.
examples.note: 해킹당하다 ('to get hacked') is a key safety phrase

expressions.nuance: 계정(計定)은 플랫폼상의 로그인 ID 전체를 뜻하고, 비공개(非公開)는 '공개하지 않음'으로 팔로우 승인 없이는 콘텐츠를 볼 수 없는 상태예요. 반대는 공개(公開). 비공개로 설정할 때는 '-로 하다/해 놓다' 구문을 써요: 비공개로 해 놨어요. 개인 계정 ≠ 비공개 계정: '개인'은 개인용(업무용의 반대), '비공개'는 프라이버시 설정이에요. 계정 vs 프로필 vs 아이디: 계정은 로그인 정보 전체, 프로필은 남들이 보는 페이지, 아이디는 @태그 이름이에요. 해킹당하다(수동태)와 해킹하다(능동태)를 꼭 구분해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 개인 계정 to mean 'private (hidden) account'.
개인 = 'personal' (vs work). Privacy setting is 비공개: 계정 비공개예요. 개인 계정 just means a personal-use account.
Using 어카운트 instead of 계정.
The standard word is 계정. 어카운트 sounds like raw English. Say 계정 비공개예요.
Saying 계정 해킹했어요 when YOUR account was hacked.
해킹하다 = you did the hacking. If you're the victim, use the passive 해킹당하다: 계정 해킹당했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 계정 비공개예요 = '계정(account) + 비공개(non-public/private) + 예요(it is)'. 비공개 is the Sino-Korean 非公開 ('not publicly opened') — it specifically refers to the privacy setting where followers must be approved, not to 'personal' vs 'work'. The opposite is 공개(公開, 'openly available'). To set it: 비공개로 해 놨어요 ('I've set it to private').

Explains why someone can't see your posts or needs to send a follow request. Polite: 비공개예요; 반말: 비공개야. Korean SNS culture has 본계정 (main account) vs 부계정/부계 ('secondary / finsta' account), so 계정 is freely counted with 개: 계정 두 개 있어요. To change the setting: 비공개로/공개로 바꿨어요. The safety phrase for hacking: 해킹당했어요 (passive — happened to you).

계정 (the whole account) vs 프로필 ('profile' — the displayed page/bio) vs 아이디 (your @username handle, from 'ID'). 아이디 is the @name for login; 프로필 is what others see; 계정 is the full account entity. Critical: 개인 계정 ('personal account', opposite of 업무용/work account) ≠ 비공개 계정 ('private account' by setting). Don't use the loanword 어카운트 — 계정 is the natural word.

The biggest trap: 개인 계정 does NOT mean 'private (hidden) account'. 개인 means 'personal' (as opposed to a work account). Privacy settings are 비공개/공개. Saying 개인 계정이에요 when you mean your account is set to private will confuse native speakers. Also: use 계정 not 어카운트, and use 해킹당했어요 (passive) not 해킹했어요 (active) when YOUR account was the victim.

expressions.shortExplanation: 프로필 사진 바꿨어요 is a practical expression meaning "I changed my profile picture".
expressions.explanation: 프로필 사진 바꿨어요 (peuropil sajin bakkwosseoyo) = "I changed my profile picture". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 프로필 사진 바꿨어요 ("I changed my profile picture"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; reporting a profile update
프사 = ultra-common abbreviation of 프로필 사진
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I changed my status message too
usagePhrases.note: 상태 메시지 (상메) = KakaoTalk status line

examples.ko: A: 프사 바꿨네요? / B: 네, 어때요?
examples.romanization: A: peusa bakkwonneyo? / B: ne, eottaeyo?
examples.en: A: Oh, you changed your pfp? / B: Yes, what do you think?
examples.note: 프사 바꿨네요 is how friends notice and comment on a profile update; -네요 = warm observation

examples.en: I changed my KakaoTalk profile pic.
examples.note: 카톡 ('KakaoTalk') often precedes 프사

examples.en: I added a link to my profile too.
examples.note: 프로필 (the page) holds your 프사, bio, and links

expressions.nuance: 프로필 사진(프사)은 계정에 표시되는 본인 사진이에요. 거의 모든 한국인이 프사라는 줄임말을 써요 — 이 표현을 모르면 대화를 이해하기 어려울 정도예요. 동사는 바꾸다('교체하다'): 프사 바꿨어요. 카카오톡의 상태 메시지는 상메라는 줄임말로 불려요. 가장 중요한 문법: 바꾸다(타동사 '내가 바꿨다') vs 바뀌다(자동사 '저절로 바뀌었다'). 본인이 바꾼 것이니 바꿨어요(타동사)를 써야 해요. 사진을 칭찬할 때는 잘 나왔어요('잘 나왔다' = 잘 찍혔다/예쁘게 나왔다)를 쓰고, 좋아요(좋아하다)는 안 어울려요. 프사(특정 사진) vs 프로필(전체 프로필 페이지) vs 배경 사진(커버 사진)의 차이도 알아두세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 프사 바뀌었어요 when you changed it yourself.
바뀌다 = it changed on its own (intransitive). You did it, so use transitive 바꾸다: 프사 바꿨어요.
Saying 프로필 그림 for a profile photo.
그림 is a drawing/painting. A photo is 사진: 프로필 사진/프사. 프로필 그림 implies an illustration.
Using the stiff 변경했습니다 in casual chat.
That's system/officialese. In conversation say 프사 바꿨어요. Reserve 변경하다 for formal notices.

structuredNuance.t: 프로필 사진 바꿨어요 = '프로필 사진(profile picture) + 바꿨어요(I changed it)'. In real speech almost everyone shortens 프로필 사진 to 프사 — one of the most common Korean SNS abbreviations. The verb is 바꾸다 ('to change/swap something'), a transitive verb meaning YOU did it. 상태 메시지 ('status message') shortens to 상메.

Said after updating a profile pic on KakaoTalk, Instagram, etc. — often prompts friends to notice and comment. Polite: 프사 바꿨어요; 반말: 프사 바꿨어. The compliment formula for a good photo is 잘 나왔어요 ('it came out well'), literally 'it emerged well' — the standard idiom for a flattering photo, not 좋아요 (which just means you like it). Avoid the stiff 프로필 사진을 변경했습니다 in chat — that sounds like a system notification.

프사 (specifically the profile photo) vs 프로필 (the whole profile page — bio, links, and photo) vs 배경 사진 ('the background/cover photo'). Don't say 프사 when you mean the cover image. Also: the stiff 변경했습니다 is officialese (like a system alert); in conversation say 바꿨어요. And 그림 ('a drawing/painting') ≠ 사진 ('photo') — 프로필 그림 would imply an illustration, not a photograph.

The critical grammar trap: 바뀌다 (intransitive, 'it changed on its own') vs 바꾸다 (transitive, 'I changed it'). Since YOU updated the photo, use the transitive: 프사 바꿨어요. Saying 프사 바뀌었어요 sounds like the photo changed by itself, like a glitch. Also, 그림 means a drawing/painting, not a photo — always use 사진 for a photograph.

expressions.shortExplanation: 디엠 확인 좀 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please check your DMs".
expressions.explanation: 디엠 확인 좀 해 주세요 (diem hwagin jom hae juseyo) means "Please check your DMs". Say it as one set phrase — for example 디엠 확인 좀 해 주세요 ("Please check your DMs"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; nudging someone to read your message
반말, to a friend
Asking if they've read it
읽씹 = read-but-no-reply; playful complaint

examples.ko: 아까 디엠 보냈는데 확인 좀 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: akka diem bonaenneunde hwagin jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: I sent a DM earlier — please check it.
examples.note: -는데 sets up the context before the request

examples.ko: A: 답이 없어서요, 디엠 확인했어요? / B: 아, 미안해요, 못 봤어요.
examples.romanization: A: dabi eopseoseoyo, diem hwaginhaesseoyo? / B: a, mianhaeyo, mot bwasseoyo.
examples.en: A: I haven't heard back — did you check my DM? / B: Oh, sorry, I didn't see it.
examples.note: Real nudge-and-apology exchange; 못 봤어요 = I didn't see it

examples.en: I got left on read — so mean.
examples.note: 읽씹 당하다 ('to be read-ignored'), the passive complaint

expressions.nuance: 확인하다('확인하다')는 '체크하다/보다'는 뜻인데, 메시지를 '확인하다'는 단순히 읽는 것을 넘어 '인지했음을 확인하다'는 의미예요. 좀은 여기서 양을 나타내는 게 아니라 '좀'처럼 부드럽게 요청하는 역할이에요(물 좀 주세요처럼). 한국 메시지 문화에서 꼭 알아야 할 단어: 읽씹(읽+씹다) = 읽고 씹는다/무시한다('left on read'), 안읽씹 = 아예 읽지도 않는다('left on delivered'). 카카오톡 메시지 옆의 숫자 1은 상대가 아직 안 읽었다는 표시예요. 확인하다(읽기/체크) vs 답하다/답장하다(답변) — 읽씹 사태의 핵심이 바로 이 차이예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 디엠 읽어 주세요 to mean 'please check my DM'.
읽다 is literal reading. The idiom for checking a message is 확인하다: 디엠 확인 좀 해 주세요.
Treating 좀 as 'a little'.
Here 좀 is a politeness softener, not a quantity. 확인 좀 해 주세요 = 'please kindly check', not 'check a little'.
Using joking 읽씹 with a superior.
읽씹 ('left on read') is casual/playful. To a boss it's rude; just say 확인 부탁드려요 ('please kindly check') formally.

structuredNuance.t: 디엠 확인 좀 해 주세요 = '디엠(DM) + 확인(check/confirm) + 좀(softener) + 해 주세요(please do for me)'. 확인하다 is the verb for checking/confirming you've seen a message — it's stronger than just 읽다 ('to read'). The 좀 is a request-softener, like 'kindly', not a quantity ('a little').

Used when you've sent a DM and haven't heard back — a polite nudge to prompt a reply. Polite: 확인 좀 해 주세요; 반말: 확인 좀 해 줘. Korean messaging culture has two colorful non-reply words: 읽씹 (read but ignored, 'left on read') and 안읽씹 (not even opened). 읽씹/안읽씹 are casual/joking — fine between friends, but accusing a boss of 읽씹 is rude; use formal 확인 부탁드려요 instead.

확인하다 (check — have you seen it?) vs 답하다/답장하다 (reply — write back). Reading a message and replying are distinct acts, which is exactly why 읽씹 ('read and ghosted') exists as a concept. Also: 확인하다 vs 체크하다 — 체크 leans toward ticking a box; 확인 is the natural verb for 'see a message'. For formal messages: 확인 부탁드립니다 is the respectful form to a superior.

Two pitfalls: (1) Using 디엠 읽어 주세요 for 'please check my DM' — 읽다 is literal reading; the natural idiom for 'see/check it' is 확인하다. (2) Misreading 좀 as 'a little' — here it is a softening particle for polite requests, not a quantity indicator.

expressions.english: I'll screenshot it and send it
expressions.shortExplanation: 스크린샷 찍어서 보낼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll screenshot it and send it".
expressions.explanation: "I'll screenshot it and send it" — that is 스크린샷 찍어서 보낼게요 (seukeurinsyat jjigeoseo bonaelgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 스크린샷 찍어서 보낼게요 ("I'll screenshot it and send it"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I'll screenshot it and send it
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; capture then share

usagePhrases.en: I'll capture it and send it
usagePhrases.note: 캡처(하다) is the shorter, very common variant
스샷 = casual abbreviation; 반말

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay to screenshot this?
usagePhrases.note: Asking permission before capturing

examples.en: I'll screenshot the chat and send it.
examples.note: 대화 내용 ('the conversation') is a common thing to capture

examples.ko: A: 그 공지 못 봤어요. / B: 스샷 찍어서 보낼게요, 잠깐만요.
examples.romanization: A: geu gongji mot bwasseoyo. / B: seusyat jjigeoseo bonaelgeyo, jamkkanmanyo.
examples.en: A: I missed that notice. / B: I'll screenshot it and send it — just a moment.
examples.note: Typical two-person exchange; 잠깐만요 = just a moment while I do it

examples.en: Can I screenshot this? I want to save it.
examples.note: Ask 캡처해도 돼요? when capturing someone's content

expressions.nuance: 스크린샷(스샷)과 캡처(하다) 두 표현 모두 일상적으로 써요. 스크린샷은 'screenshot'의 음차이고, 캡처는 'capture'에서 왔어요. 사진을 찍는 것과 동사 찍다를 공유하기 때문에 스크린샷 찍다라고 해요. 캡처해서 보낼게요에서 -아서는 두 행동을 '결과적으로 연결'하는데, '캡처한 그것을 보낸다'는 뉘앙스예요. 캡처하고 보낼게요는 단순히 두 행동을 나열하지만, -아서는 순서와 인과 관계를 더 잘 나타내요. 중요한 문화 맥락: 한국에서 스크린샷은 증거(증거)로 자주 쓰이고, '캡처해 놨어요'는 약한 의미의 경고가 될 수 있어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 사진 찍어서 보낼게요 for a screenshot.
사진 찍다 = photograph with the camera. To capture the screen, say 캡처해서 / 스크린샷 찍어서 보낼게요.
Saying 캡처하고 보낼게요 when you mean 'capture it and send that'.
-고 just lists two actions. -아서 ties them (the send uses the capture): 캡처해서 보낼게요.
Confusing 캡처 (screen grab) with 저장 (save file).
캡처/스크린샷 grabs what's on screen; 저장하다 saves a file you already have. 'Screenshot it' = 캡처해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 스크린샷 찍어서 보낼게요 = '스크린샷(screenshot) + 찍어서(take it and —, sequential -아서) + 보낼게요(I'll send it)'. The -아서 connector is crucial: it ties the two actions so that 'sending' uses the RESULT of 'taking the screenshot' — more native than the list connector -고. 캡처(하다) ('capture') is an equally common and often preferred synonym.

Said when someone missed a post, message, or announcement and you offer to share a saved image. -ㄹ게요 is polite 'I'll do it'; friends get 스샷 보내 줘. Always ask 캡처해도 돼요? before capturing someone else's private content. Culturally, screenshots serve as 증거 ('evidence') in Korea — 캡처해 놨어요 ('I've got a screenshot') can carry an implicit warning.

스크린샷 찍다 / 캡처하다 (capture the screen) vs 사진 찍다 (take a photo with the camera) vs 저장하다 (save a file you already have). The dividing line: 캡처/스크린샷 grabs what's currently visible on the screen; 사진 찍다 uses the camera hardware; 저장 saves data to storage. Using 사진 찍다 for a screenshot implies you photographed the physical screen with another camera.

Two traps: (1) Saying 사진 찍어서 보낼게요 for a screenshot — 사진 찍다 implies using the camera; say 캡처해서 / 스크린샷 찍어서. (2) Confusing -아서 (캡처해서 보낼게요 — the send uses the capture's result) with -고 (캡처하고 보낼게요 — lists two separate actions). Use -아서 when the second action directly uses the output of the first.

expressions.shortExplanation: 본인 인증 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please complete identity verification".
expressions.explanation: 본인 인증 해 주세요 (bonin injeung hae juseyo) = "Please complete identity verification". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 본인 인증 해 주세요 ("Please verify your identity"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; what a site/service asks
Reporting you completed it
휴대폰 인증 = the phone-number method
인증번호 = the OTP code you receive

examples.en: To sign up, you have to verify your identity.
examples.note: 가입하다 ('to sign up') triggers 본인 인증

examples.ko: A: 인증번호 안 와요. / B: 문자로 6자리 왔을 거예요, 확인해 보세요.
examples.romanization: A: injeungbeonho an wayo. / B: munjaro 6jari wasseul geoyeyo, hwaginhae boseyo.
examples.en: A: The verification code isn't coming. / B: It should have arrived as a 6-digit text — check your messages.
examples.note: Troubleshooting exchange for the common OTP issue; 문자로 = via SMS

examples.en: Did the code come by text?
examples.note: 문자로 ('by SMS') is how 인증번호 usually arrives

expressions.nuance: 인증(認證)은 한국 온라인 생활에서 빠질 수 없는 단어예요. '본인 인증'은 거의 모든 서비스에서 요구하는 휴대폰 본인 확인 절차예요. 핵심 어휘: 본인 인증(본인 확인), 인증번호(OTP 코드, 문자로 받음), 입력하다(번호를 넣다). 동사는 하다: 인증하다/인증 해 주세요. 하지만 인증에는 두 가지 전혀 다른 의미가 있어요: (1) 공식적인 신원 확인 (본인 인증), (2) SNS에서 '직접 갔음을 증명하는 사진' (인증샷 올리다). 이 두 가지를 혼동하면 안 돼요. 인증번호 vs 비밀번호: 인증번호는 OTP(일회용), 비밀번호는 설정된 고정 패스워드예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 인증번호 with 비밀번호.
인증번호 = the one-time code sent to verify you; 비밀번호 = your standing password. 'Enter the code' = 인증번호 입력하세요.
Reading 인증 only as 'certification'.
인증 also means identity verification (본인 인증) AND a proof-shot on SNS (인증샷). Context decides; don't fix it to one gloss.
Saying 인증 만들어 주세요 to mean 'verify me'.
You don't 'make' a verification. The verb is 하다: 본인 인증 해 주세요, or 인증번호 입력하세요 for the code.

structuredNuance.t: 본인 인증 해 주세요 = '본인(本人, the person themselves) + 인증(認證, verification/authentication) + 해 주세요(please do)'. It literally means 'please verify that you are yourself'. Almost every Korean online service requires this via SMS — you receive a 6-digit 인증번호 (OTP) and 입력하다 ('enter') it. Crucially, 인증 has a SECOND everyday meaning: on SNS, 인증샷 ('proof shot') means posting a photo to show you really went somewhere or did something.

You'll encounter this phrase on every Korean app sign-up screen. The process: enter your phone number → receive 인증번호 via SMS → 입력하다. 해 주세요 is polite (from the service to you); to report you completed it: 인증 했어요. The informal SNS sense 인증샷 ('proof shot') appears when someone posts evidence they visited a place or completed a challenge — totally different context from identity verification.

인증 (verify/prove — identity check OR SNS proof) vs 가입 ('signing up/joining' — the whole process) vs 로그인 ('log in' — after signing up). Verification is one step inside signing up. Critical: 인증번호 ('verification code', one-time OTP) vs 비밀번호 ('password', your standing secret) — both contain 번호 but are completely different things. Mixing them at a login screen is a very common learner error.

Three pitfalls: (1) Reading 인증 only as 'certification' (its dictionary gloss) and missing its 'identity verification' and 'SNS proof-shot' senses. (2) Confusing 인증번호 (OTP) with 비밀번호 (password) — both have 번호. (3) Saying 인증 만들어 주세요 — you don't 'make' a verification; the verb is 하다: 인증 해 주세요.

expressions.english: I want to grow my followers
expressions.shortExplanation: 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I want to grow my followers".
expressions.explanation: 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요 (pallowo neulligo sipeoyo) means "I want to grow my followers". Say it as one set phrase — for example 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요 ("I want to grow my followers"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: I want to grow my followers
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; talking about building an audience
반말, to a friend
Intransitive 늘다 ('to increase on its own')
맞팔 ('mutual follow') as a method

examples.en: You have to post steadily to gain followers.
examples.note: 꾸준히 ('steadily') + the condition -아야 ('only if')

examples.ko: A: 팔로워 얼마나 돼요? / B: 아직 적어요, 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: A: pallowo eolmana dwaeyo? / B: ajik jeogeoyo, pallowo neulligo sipeoyo.
examples.en: A: How many followers do you have? / B: Still not many — I want to grow my followers.
examples.note: Natural conversation about follower count; 얼마나 돼요 = how many does it come to

examples.en: If you don't follow back, I'll unfollow.
examples.note: 언팔하다 ('to unfollow'), the consequence

expressions.nuance: 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요는 SNS 크리에이터 관점의 표현이에요. 핵심 문법: 늘리다(타동사, '내가 증가시키다') vs 늘다/늘어나다(자동사, '저절로 증가하다'). 즉 내가 적극적으로 늘리고 싶으면 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어요(늘리다), 자연적으로 늘어났으면 팔로워가 늘었어요(늘다)예요. 이 타동사/자동사 구분은 한국어에서 매우 중요해요. -고 싶다는 내 욕구(1인칭)에만 붙이고, 제3자의 욕구는 -고 싶어하다로 표현해요: 그 사람은 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어해요. 크리에이터 생태계 어휘: 맞팔(상호 팔로우), 언팔(언팔하다), 알고리즘, 떡상(급상승 슬랭).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 팔로워가 늘리고 싶어요 (wrong particle + wrong verb pairing).
Your action takes the transitive 늘리다 with object -를: 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어요. 팔로워가 늘다 means they grew on their own.
Using 늘다 when you mean you actively grow them.
늘다/늘어나다 = increase by itself ('팔로워가 늘었어요'). To actively grow them, use transitive 늘리다.
Using -고 싶어요 about someone else's desire.
-고 싶다 is for your OWN wish. For a third person, use -고 싶어하다: 그 사람은 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어해요.

structuredNuance.t: 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요 = '팔로워(followers) + 늘리고(increase — transitive -리-) + 싶어요(I want to)'. 팔로워 is the countable noun for follower-people. The transitive verb 늘리다 ('to make something increase') is exactly right here: YOU are the agent causing the increase. If followers grew on their own, use the intransitive 늘다: 팔로워가 늘었어요.

The transitive/intransitive split is the essential grammar here: 늘리다 = 'I make them grow' (팔로워를 늘리고 싶어요); 늘다/늘어나다 = 'they grow on their own' (팔로워가 늘었어요). Also: -고 싶다 is FIRST-PERSON desire only. For a third person's wish: 늘리고 싶어해요 (그 사람은 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어해요). Don't confuse 늘리다 ('increase') with 줄이다 ('reduce') — they are opposite directions.

팔로워 늘리다 (actively grow your followers, you are the agent) vs 팔로워가 늘다 (followers increase on their own — a passive outcome). Related creator ecosystem: 맞팔 ('mutual follow' as a growth tactic), 언팔 ('unfollow'), 알고리즘 ('the algorithm'), 떡상 (slang 'to blow up/skyrocket'). Count followers with 명 (명 = person counter): 팔로워 만 명.

The main pitfalls: (1) Wrong particle — 팔로워가 늘리고 싶어요 uses 가 (subject), implying the followers want to grow themselves; use object 를: 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어요. (2) Using -고 싶어요 about someone else — it's only for your own desire; for others say -고 싶어하다. (3) Wrong counter — followers are people, so use 명 not 개: 팔로워 만 명이에요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 악플 신고했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I reported the hate comment".
expressions.explanation: "I reported the hate comment" — that is 악플 신고했어요 (akpeul singohaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 악플 신고했어요 ("I reported the hate comment"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; reporting abusive content
반말, to a friend
Pairing 신고 ('report') with 차단 ('block')
스팸으로 ('as spam') gives the reason

examples.en: They kept posting hate, so I reported them.
examples.note: -길래 ('since/because') gives the trigger for acting

examples.ko: A: 악플 많이 달려요? / B: 네, 신고하고 바로 차단했어요.
examples.romanization: A: akpeul mani dallyeoyo? / B: ne, singohago baro chadanhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Do you get a lot of hate comments? / B: Yes — I reported them and blocked them right away.
examples.note: Typical creator complaint; the standard two-step: 신고 then 차단

examples.en: It was false info so I hit the report button.
examples.note: 신고 버튼 ('report button') + 누르다 ('to press')

expressions.nuance: 신고(申告)는 규칙 위반이나 악성 콘텐츠를 플랫폼(또는 당국)에 신고하는 행위예요. 악플 신고했어요 = '악플(악성 댓글)을 신고했다'. 신고 대상은 -을/를로, 신고 사유는 -으로로 표현해요: 악플을 스팸으로 신고했어요. 중요한 구분: 신고하다(플랫폼에 고발) vs 차단하다(내 쪽에서 차단) vs 고소하다(법적 소송). 한국에서는 악플로 실제로 명예훼손 소송이 제기되기도 해서 고소가 단순한 과장이 아니에요. 신청하다(신청)는 '지원하다/신청하다'는 뜻으로 완전히 달라요. 보고하다(보고)는 직장 상사에게 하는 업무 보고이지, 콘텐츠 신고가 아니에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 신고하다 with 신청하다.
신청 = apply/sign up; 신고 = report a violation. To flag a hate comment: 악플 신고했어요, not 신청했어요.
Using 보고하다 to mean report content.
보고하다 is a work report to a superior. Flagging abuse to a platform is 신고하다: 신고 버튼 눌렀어요.
Treating 신고 (report) and 차단 (block) as the same.
신고 flags it to the platform; 차단 walls the user off on your side. You often do both: 신고하고 차단했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 악플 신고했어요 = '악플(악성 댓글, hate comment) + 신고했어요(I reported/filed)'. 신고(申告) means filing a formal report to a platform or authority about rule-breaking content. The particles: -을/를 for the thing reported (악플을), -으로 for the category (스팸으로, 허위 정보로). The verb is 하다 (신고하다) and pairs naturally with 차단하다 ('to block') as a two-step action.

Used when flagging hateful, spam, or false-information content on any platform. The standard two-step for serious abuse: 신고하고 차단했어요 ('I reported and blocked'). Register: -했어요 polite; friends get 신고했어. Note: 악플 (악성 댓글, hate comment) vs 선플 (선한 댓글, kind comment) is a cultural axis in Korean SNS — you'll see 악플 금지 ('no hate comments') widely. In Korea, serious 악플 can lead to 고소 (defamation lawsuit), so the word 신고 carries real weight.

신고하다 (report TO the platform/authorities — flags it for review) vs 차단하다 (block — a private wall on your side, no report) vs 고소하다 ('to sue/press legal charges' — an actual legal step). These are escalating steps: block < report < sue. Also: 언팔 (unfollow — softest, just stop seeing them) vs 차단 (block — they can't contact or see you) vs 신고 (notify the platform).

Two false friends that English speakers mix up: (1) 신고하다 vs 신청하다 — 신청 means 'to apply/sign up for something'; 신고 means 'to report a violation'. They sound similar but mean opposite things. (2) 보고하다 vs 신고하다 — 보고하다 is a workplace status report to a superior, not content flagging; always use 신고하다 for platform abuse reports.

expressions.shortExplanation: 디엠으로 문의 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please inquire via DM".
expressions.explanation: 디엠으로 문의 주세요 (diemeuro munui juseyo) = "Please inquire via DM". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 디엠으로 문의 주세요 ("Please inquire via DM"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; sellers routing questions to DM
Fuller verb form 문의하다
자세한 ('detailed') scopes which questions go to DM
Steering away from public 댓글 to private 디엠

examples.en: For price inquiries, please DM me.
examples.note: 가격 문의 ('price inquiry') is the most common DM ask

examples.ko: A: 재고 있어요? / B: 디엠으로 문의 주세요, 바로 확인해 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jaego isseoyo? / B: diemeuro munui juseyo, baro hwaginhae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Do you have stock? / B: Please DM me — I'll check right away.
examples.note: Classic small-seller exchange routing stock questions to private channel

examples.ko: 재고 문의 주셔서 감사해요, 디엠 확인해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jaego munui jusyeoseo gamsahaeyo, diem hwaginhae juseyo.
examples.en: Thanks for asking about stock — please check your DM.
examples.note: 재고 ('inventory') + the follow-up 디엠 확인

expressions.nuance: 디엠으로 문의 주세요는 한국 SNS 판매자나 인플루언서 게시물 하단에서 흔히 볼 수 있는 표현이에요. 문의(問議)는 '공식 문의/질문'이고, -으로는 수단 조사('~로/를 통해')예요. 직역하면 '디엠 채널을 통해 문의를 주세요'예요. 문의 주세요는 문의(를) 주세요처럼 문의를 '주다'로 표현한 구어체 형태이고, 더 완전한 표현은 문의해 주세요예요. 핵심 구분: 문의하다(비즈니스적 '질문') vs 물어보다(일상적 '물어보다'). 판매 게시물에는 문의가 맞고, 친구한테는 물어보다가 자연스러워요. 문의(질문) vs 신청(지원) vs 주문(주문)도 구분해야 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 디엠에 문의 주세요 (wrong particle).
-에 marks a static location. For 'via/through a channel' use -으로: 디엠으로 문의 주세요. Same with 카톡으로, 문자로.
Using casual 물어보다 under a sales post.
물어보다 ('to ask') is everyday-casual. The businesslike term is 문의하다: 디엠으로 문의해 주세요.
Confusing 문의 (inquiry) with 주문 (order).
문의 is asking a question; 주문 is placing an order. 'DM me to ask' = 디엠으로 문의 주세요; to order is 주문할게요.

structuredNuance.t: 디엠으로 문의 주세요 = '디엠(DM) + -으로(via/through, channel particle) + 문의(inquiry) + 주세요(please give/send)'. The particle -으로 marks the CHANNEL used, not a location — it means 'through the medium of DM'. 문의 주세요 treats 문의 as a noun you 'give'; the fuller verb form is 문의해 주세요. Either is correct and natural.

The go-to phrase under Korean sales posts, group-buy announcements, or creator profiles. It routes private questions (price 가격, stock 재고, group-buy 공구 participation) OUT of the public 댓글 section INTO the private 디엠 channel — hence the common variant 댓글 말고 디엠으로요. Register: inherently semi-formal (seller-to-customer). The seller might post 문의 받습니다 ('I take inquiries') instead.

문의하다 ('to inquire', business-register) vs 물어보다 ('to ask', everyday casual). Under a sales post 문의 is appropriate; with a friend you'd just 물어보다. Also: 문의 (just asking a question) vs 신청 (applying/signing up) vs 주문 (placing an order) — these are different steps in a purchase process. The channel particle: 디엠으로 (via DM) vs 카톡으로 (via KakaoTalk) vs 문자로 (via SMS) — all use -으로.

The key particle mistake: learners say 디엠에 문의 주세요 — -에 marks a static LOCATION, but for 'via/through a channel' you need the means particle -으로: 디엠으로. The same applies to all communication channels: 카톡으로, 전화로, 문자로. Saying -에 here sounds like you're directing someone to stand IN the DM, not communicate through it.

expressions.shortExplanation: 공유했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I shared it".
expressions.explanation: 공유했어요 (gongyuhaesseoyo) means "I shared it". Say it as one set phrase — for example 공유했어요 ("I shared it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; you reposted/forwarded content
반말, to a friend
Asking people to spread your post

usagePhrases.en: I shared it to my story
usagePhrases.note: Reposting to your story with destination -에

examples.en: I liked this post so I shared it.
examples.note: -아서 ('because') links the reason to the share

examples.ko: A: 이 영상 봤어요? / B: 네, 좋아서 공유했어요, 친구들도 봐야 해요.
examples.romanization: A: i yeongsang bwasseoyo? / B: ne, joaseo gongyuhaesseoyo, chingudeuldo bwaya haeyo.
examples.en: A: Did you see this video? / B: Yes, I liked it so I shared it — my friends need to see it too.
examples.note: 공유했어요 explains the reason and the outcome; -아서 chains them naturally

examples.ko: 많이 공유해 주세요, 널리 알려야 해요.
examples.romanization: mani gongyuhae juseyo, neolli allyeoya haeyo.
examples.en: Please share it widely — we need to spread the word.
examples.note: 널리 알리다 ('spread far') is why you ask for shares

expressions.nuance: 공유(共有)하다는 'share' 버튼을 눌러 콘텐츠를 다시 배포하는 행위예요. 직역하면 '함께 가지다/공동으로 소유하다'인데, SNS에서는 '리포스트/전달'을 의미해요. 목적지를 나타낼 때는 -에(스토리에 공유했어요), 받는 사람은 -한테/에게(친구한테 공유했어요)로 구분해요. 중요한 오류: 친구를 공유했어요는 '친구를 나눠 가졌다'는 이상한 뜻이 돼요. 받는 사람에게는 -한테를 써야 해요. 공유하다 vs 보내다: 공유는 여럿이 볼 수 있게 퍼뜨리는 것, 보내다는 1:1 비공개 전송이에요. 공유하다 vs 퍼가다: 퍼가다는 구식 블로그 시대 표현이에요. 음식 나눠 먹을 때는 나눠 먹다를 써야 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 친구를 공유했어요 to mean 'I shared it with a friend'.
Object -를 makes it sound like you shared the friend. Use -한테/에게 for the recipient: 친구한테 공유했어요.
Using 공유하다 for sharing food.
공유하다 is for content/information/co-owning. Sharing food is 나눠 먹다 ('divide and eat'). 'Let's share' (food) = 나눠 먹어요.
Confusing 공유 (share/repost) with 좋아요 (like).
공유 actively redistributes a post; 좋아요 just reacts to it. 'I shared it' = 공유했어요, not 좋아요 눌렀어요.

structuredNuance.t: 공유(共有)하다 literally means 'to hold in common / co-own', from the Sino-Korean 共有. On SNS it means hitting the Share button to redistribute content — Instagram repost, KakaoTalk forward, YouTube share. The destination takes -에 (스토리에 공유했어요 = 'shared TO my story') and a recipient takes -한테/에게 (친구한테 공유했어요 = 'shared WITH a friend').

Said when you forward content to a friend or repost to your story, or when asking followers to spread your post (공유 좀 해 주세요). Polite: 공유했어요; 반말: 공유했어. The channel or destination is marked with -에 or -한테. 공유 also covers the real-world sense 'share/co-own' (방을 공유하다 = 'share a room'), so context tells which meaning applies. SNS context is always clear from what comes before the verb.

공유하다 (share/redistribute to many, SNS button) vs 보내다 (send privately one-to-one) vs 퍼가다 ('grab and repost' on your own page — older blog-era usage, now sounds dated or implies lifting content). For modern SNS, 공유하다 is default. Don't use 공유하다 for sharing food — that's 나눠 먹다 ('divide and eat'). And don't confuse 공유 (share/repost) with 좋아요 (like) — sharing redistributes, liking just reacts.

Two traps: (1) Wrong recipient particle — 친구를 공유했어요 with object -를 sounds like you shared the FRIEND as an object. Use -한테/에게 for the person you sent it to: 친구한테 공유했어요. (2) Over-applying 공유하다 to food sharing — Koreans say 나눠 먹다 for sharing food, not 공유하다. Using 공유하다 for 'let's share this dish' sounds odd.

expressions.shortExplanation: 차단했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I blocked them".
expressions.explanation: "I blocked them" — that is 차단했어요 (chadanhaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 차단했어요 ("I blocked them"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; you blocked a user/number
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I went ahead and blocked them
usagePhrases.note: -아 버리다 adds 'just did it, done with it'
차단 풀다 ('release the block') = undo a block

examples.en: They kept bothering me so I blocked them.
examples.note: 귀찮게 하다 ('to pester') + the reason ending -아서

examples.ko: A: 그 사람이 왜 답 안 해요? / B: 아마 차단당했을 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: geu sarami wae dap an haeyo? / B: ama chadandanghaesseul geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: Why isn't that person replying? / B: You were probably blocked.
examples.note: 차단당하다 (passive — it happened to you); 아마 + -을 거예요 for a guess

examples.en: It was a spam number so I blocked it right away.
examples.note: 차단 works for phone numbers too, not just SNS

expressions.nuance: 차단(遮斷)하다는 'block' 버튼을 눌러 상대방을 완전히 차단하는 것이에요. SNS, 카카오톡, 전화번호 모두에 쓸 수 있어요. 차단했어요 = 내가 차단한 것, 차단당했어요 = 내가 차단을 당한 것(수동태). 이 능동/수동 구분이 핵심이에요! 차단 풀다('풀다' = 묶인 것을 풀다)는 언블록이에요. -아 버리다는 '미련 없이 해치웠다'는 감정적 뉘앙스를 더해요. 중요한 단계: 언팔(구독 취소) < 차단(완전 차단) < 신고(플랫폼에 신고). 뮤트/숨기기는 피드에서만 안 보이는 것이고 상대는 여전히 나에게 접근 가능해요. 블록하다 대신 차단하다를 써야 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 차단했어요 when YOU got blocked.
차단하다 = you did the blocking. If it happened to you, use the passive 차단당하다: 차단당했어요 ('I was blocked').
Using 블록하다 instead of 차단하다.
The native, standard word is 차단. 블록 sounds like raw English. Say 차단했어요.
Confusing 차단 (block) with 언팔 (unfollow).
언팔 just stops you seeing them; 차단 cuts them off entirely (they can't see or reach you). To fully cut contact, say 차단했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 차단(遮斷)하다 = 'to cut off/block' (Sino-Korean 遮斷, 'to obstruct and sever'). 차단했어요 means you hit the block button so the person can no longer contact you, see your content, or find your account. To undo it: 차단 풀다 ('release/untie the block'). The emotional color -아 버리다 in 차단해 버렸어요 adds 'I just did it decisively — good riddance'.

The active/passive split is essential: 차단하다 = YOU block someone (차단했어요); 차단당하다 / 차단되다 = you GET blocked, it happened to you (차단당했어요 = 'I was blocked'). Saying 차단했어요 when you were the one blocked is the opposite meaning. Also: 차단 풀다 ('unblock') vs 차단 받다 is not the natural passive — use 차단당하다.

Escalating severity: 언팔 (unfollow — just stop seeing their posts, they can still message you) < 뮤트/숨기기 (mute — their posts hidden in your feed, but you're still connected) < 차단 (block — total cut-off, they vanish from your world) < 신고 (report to platform). Saying 차단했어요 when you only muted someone significantly overstates the action. Don't use the loanword 블록하다 — 차단하다 is the natural Korean word.

Two pitfalls: (1) Active/passive confusion — saying 차단했어요 when YOU were blocked (should be 차단당했어요). Direction of the block matters. (2) Using 블록하다 — Koreans don't use this loanword; the standard verb is 차단하다. Also: confusing 차단 (total block) with 뮤트/숨기기 (mute — softer, hidden feed only); they are not the same and overstating it is a social misstep.

expressions.shortExplanation: 제 생각에는 is a practical expression meaning "In my opinion / I think...".
expressions.explanation: 제 생각에는 (je saenggageneun) = "In my opinion / I think...". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 제 생각에는 ("in my opinion"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; opens your view to anyone
반말; to a friend or younger person

usagePhrases.en: the way I see it / from my perspective
usagePhrases.note: slightly more formal variant — emphasizes the angle, not just the thought

usagePhrases.ko: 제 생각에는 좀 다른 것 같아요
usagePhrases.romanization: je saenggageneun jom dareun geot gatayo
usagePhrases.en: I think it's a bit different
usagePhrases.note: natural extension that softens disagreement while staying polite

examples.ko: 제 생각에는 이 방법이 더 빠를 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: je saenggageneun i bangbeobi deo ppareul geot gatayo.
examples.en: In my opinion, this method might be faster.
examples.note: basic use: the opener leads into a hedged recommendation with -ㄹ 것 같다

examples.ko: A: 어떤 색이 더 잘 어울려요? / B: 제 생각에는 파란색이 훨씬 자연스럽게 보여요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteon saegi deo jal eoullyeoyo? / B: je saenggageneun paransaegi hwolssin jayeonseureopge boyeoyo.
examples.en: A: Which color suits me better? / B: In my opinion, the blue looks much more natural.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B uses 제 생각에는 to give a personal aesthetic judgment without sounding pushy

examples.ko: 제 생각에는 이 방법도 좋지만, 비용 면에서 좀 더 따져봐야 할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: je saenggageneun i bangbeopdo jochiman, biyong myeoneseo jom deo ttajyeobwaya hal geot gatayo.
examples.en: In my opinion this approach is fine too, but I think we need to look more carefully at costs.
examples.note: fuller discussion turn: agrees in part, then raises a concern — shows the phrase opens a nuanced view, not just simple agreement

expressions.nuance: 제 생각에는 is the standard polite opener that signals 'this is just my view, not a command or fact'. 제 is the humble form of 나 ('my'), and 에는 sets up a frame — literally 'as for within my thinking'. It works with anyone: strangers, seniors, classmates, colleagues, customers. To go casual with a close friend, swap to 내 생각에는; for a more considered, slightly formal feel use 제 생각으로는 (the -으로는 particle stresses the viewpoint angle). The nearest alternative is 제가 보기에는 — the dividing line is thinking vs observing: 제 생각에는 comes from your internal reasoning, while 제가 보기에는 is based on what you see or sense from evidence. The classic English-speaker mistake is calquing 'in my opinion' literally as 제 의견에는, which is bookish and rare in spoken Korean. A second trap: dropping the particle entirely (제 생각 좋아요) — without 에는 or 엔 the opener is ungrammatical.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제 의견에는 as a literal translation of 'in my opinion' — it sounds bookish; natural speech uses 제 생각에는.
Using 제 생각에는 with a friend — it's polite register; with friends drop to 반말: 내 생각에는.
Omitting the particle (제 생각 좋아요) — you need 제 생각에는 / 제 생각엔; the bare noun can't open the clause this way.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '제(my/humble) 생각(thought) 에는(as for within)' → 실제 뜻: 'in my opinion / I think...'. It frames what follows as personal view, not fact — a politeness device as much as a meaning marker. Works with anyone in polite speech.
적절한 격식: 존댓말 (제 생각에는), 반말 (내 생각에는). 격식체: 제 생각으로는 (meetings, written). 친구에게 제 생각에는 쓰면 지나치게 격식적으로 들린다 — 내 생각에는이 훨씬 자연스럽다.

제가 보기에는 is the nearest neighbor. 제 생각에는 = internal reasoning ('I figure/think'); 제가 보기에는 = observation-based judgment ('from what I see'). A second near-synonym is 제 입장에서는 ('from my position/standpoint'), which stresses situational perspective over pure opinion.
더 세게: 솔직히 제 생각에는 ('honestly, in my opinion'). 더 부드럽게: 제 생각에는 그런 것 같아요 (adds -것 같아요 hedge). 과거 상황: 제 생각에는 그게 맞는 것 같았는데요 ('I thought at the time that was right').

1) 제 의견에는 — a literal calque that sounds stiff and bookish; spoken Korean uses 제 생각에는. 2) 생각에 (dropping 는) — weakens the topic frame; keep 에는 or at minimum 에는 → 엔 in fast speech. 3) Using 제 생각에는 with a close friend — drop to 내 생각에는 so you don't sound overly formal.

expressions.english: The way I see it / From what I can tell...
expressions.shortExplanation: 제가 보기에는 is a practical expression meaning "The way I see it / From what I can tell...".
expressions.explanation: 제가 보기에는 (jega bogieneun) means "The way I see it / From what I can tell...". Say it as one set phrase — for example 제가 보기에는 ("the way I see it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; offering a judgment from observation
반말; to a friend
same meaning, more conversational; very common in spoken Korean

usagePhrases.ko: 제가 보기에는 별문제 없을 것 같아요
usagePhrases.romanization: jega bogieneun byeolmunje eopseul geot gatayo
usagePhrases.en: from what I can see, I don't think there'll be a problem
usagePhrases.note: full reassuring judgment based on what you've observed

examples.en: From what I can see, it looks fine.
examples.note: bare judgment, softened by -는데요 which invites the listener's take

examples.ko: A: 이 지원자 어떻게 보세요? / B: 제가 보기에는 경험이 부족한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: i jiwonja eotteoke boseyo? / B: jega bogieneun gyeongheomi bujokan geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: What do you make of this applicant? / B: The way I see it, they seem a bit short on experience.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B gives an observation-based assessment in a professional context where 보기에는 is very natural

examples.ko: 제가 보기에는 가격은 비슷한데 품질 면에서는 이쪽이 확실히 낫네요.
examples.romanization: jega bogieneun gagyeogeun biseutande pumjil myeoneseoneun ijjogi hwaksilhi nanneyo.
examples.en: The way I see it, the price is similar but this one is clearly better in terms of quality.
examples.note: fuller real opinion weighing two options from visible evidence

expressions.nuance: 제가 보기에는 means 'judging from what I observe/see', used when you give an assessment rooted in visible evidence or your read of a situation — polite, works with anyone. The grammar is 보다 ('to see') + -기 (nominalizer) + 에는, literally 'as for in my seeing'. The casual form is 내가 보기에는; the contracted 제가 보기엔 is extremely common in natural speech. The nearest neighbor is 제 생각에는 — the dividing line is evidence vs reasoning: 제가 보기에는 says 'based on observable signs' (appearance, behavior, data), while 제 생각에는 expresses your internal reasoning or opinion independent of direct observation. For pure feelings ('I feel nervous') neither works — state the feeling directly. English speakers often say 제가 봤을 때 ('when I looked', a specific past moment) when they mean the general present-tense judgment 제가 보기에는; keep it present and nominalized.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing it with 제가 봤을 때 ('when I saw it', a specific past moment) — for a general read use the present 제가 보기에는.
Saying 제 보기에는 without 가 — the subject marker is needed: 제가 보기에는.
Using it for pure feelings ('I feel sad') — 보기에는 is for judgments/assessments, not emotions; for feelings use 제 생각에는 or just state the feeling.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '제가(I) 보기(the act of seeing) 에는(as for)' → 실제 뜻: 'from what I can see / the way I see it'. It grounds the judgment in observation — if you just went from gut feeling alone, 제 생각에는 fits better.
적절한 격식: 존댓말 (제가 보기에는), 반말 (내가 보기에는). 격식: 제가 보기에는/제가 보기엔 모두 polite setting에서 자연스럽다. 직장 선배나 처음 만난 사람에게도 쓸 수 있다. 친구에게는 내가 보기에는 또는 줄여서 내가 보기엔.

제 생각에는 vs 제가 보기에는: 생각에는 = inner reasoning; 보기에는 = outward observation. A third near-synonym is 제 느낌에는 ('from my sense/feel'), which is even more subjective and emotional — use it for gut feelings rather than visible evidence.
기본: 제가 보기에는. 단축: 제가 보기엔 (very common in speech). 반말: 내가 보기에는 / 내가 보기엔. 강조: 솔직히 제가 보기에는... 완화: 제가 보기엔 좀 그런 것 같아요 (adds -것 같아요 to soften further).

1) 제가 봤을 때 (past 'when I looked') vs 제가 보기에는 (general present judgment) — don't use the past form for a general assessment. 2) Dropping 가: 제 보기에는 is ungrammatical — the subject marker 가 is obligatory. 3) Using it for emotions: '제가 보기에는 무서워요' is odd; for feelings, just say 무서워요 or 제 생각에는 무서운 것 같아요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 맞아요 is a practical expression meaning "That's right / You're right.".
expressions.explanation: "That's right / You're right." — that is 맞아요 (majayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 맞아요 ("that's right"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite agreement/factual confirmation; works with anyone
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
격식체; announcements, customer service, work presentations
doubled for enthusiastic agreement; very common in conversation as a back-channel signal

examples.ko: A: 이 길로 가면 돼요? / B: 네, 맞아요.
examples.romanization: A: i gillo gamyeon dwaeyo? / B: ne, majayo.
examples.en: A: Do we go this way? / B: Yes, that's right.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B confirms a factual claim; the most common single-word confirmation in everyday Korean

examples.ko: 맞아요, 저도 어제 그 기사 봤어요. 진짜 충격적이더라고요.
examples.romanization: majayo, jeodo eoje geu gisa bwasseoyo. jinjja chunggyeokjeogideoragoyo.
examples.en: Right, I saw that article yesterday too. It was really shocking.
examples.note: agreeing and chaining your own experience; -더라고요 reports what you personally discovered

examples.ko: 아, 맞아요! 그 카페 주말엔 오후 다섯 시에 문 닫더라고요. 저도 그냥 돌아왔었어요.
examples.romanization: a, majayo! geu kape jumaren ohu daseot sie mun datdeoragoyo. jeodo geunyang dorawasseosseoyo.
examples.en: Oh, that's right! That cafe closes at 5 PM on weekends. I turned back empty-handed too.
examples.note: recalling a fact with -더라고요 and sharing a personal story that confirms the point

expressions.nuance: 맞아요 comes from 맞다, which originally means 'to fit / to be correct', and it confirms that what the other person said is factually accurate — the Korean equivalent of 'right, exactly'. It's polite and works with anyone; casual is 맞아; formal is 맞습니다. The nearest alternative is 그렇죠 / 그래요 — the dividing line is precision: 맞아요 judges a specific statement as correct or accurate (like a fact check), while 그렇죠 is a warmer, more empathetic 'yeah, that's how it is' that builds conversational rapport rather than verifying truth. The biggest English-speaker trap is treating 맞아요 as 'okay / sure' for agreeing to requests — for 'okay, I'll do it' you need 알겠어요 or 좋아요. A second trap is answering negative questions: if someone asks 안 더워요? ('isn't it hot?'), a flat 맞아요 is confusing; Koreans typically answer the embedded proposition. Grammatically, 맞다 is intransitive here — 맞아요 stands alone as a complete reply; do not combine it with 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 맞아요 to mean 'okay, I'll do that' — for agreeing to a request say 알겠어요 or 좋아요; 맞아요 only confirms correctness.
Writing 맞어요 — the conjugation of 맞다 is 맞아요 (ㅏ stem), not 맞어요.
Saying 맞아요를 해요 or adding 하다 — 맞다 already is the verb; 맞아요 is a complete reply.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 맞다 = 'to fit/be correct' → 실제 뜻: 'that's right / you're correct'. 맞아요 is a factual confirmation: it says the thing the other person stated is accurate. It does NOT simply express enthusiasm or assent to a request.

존댓말: 맞아요 (anyone — friend's parent, teacher, customer, coworker). 반말: 맞아 (close friend, younger person). 격식: 맞습니다 (business presentation, customer service reply, formal announcement). 가장 자연스러운 상황: 누군가가 사실을 말하거나 방향/정보를 확인할 때.

맞아요 vs 그렇죠: 맞아요 = 'that statement is correct' (factual); 그렇죠 = 'yeah, that's the way it is' (empathetic/rapport-building). In casual chat, 그렇죠 often sounds warmer; use 맞아요 when you're actually verifying accuracy.
단독: 맞아요 / 맞아. 강조: 맞아요, 맞아요 (doubled = emphatic). 격식: 맞습니다. 과거 확인: 맞았어요 ('that was right'). 관형어: 맞는 말이에요 ('that's the right/correct thing to say').

1) Using 맞아요 to mean 'okay, I'll do it' — for consent to a request say 알겠어요 or 좋아요. 2) Conjugating it 맞어요 — the stem vowel is ㅏ, so it must be 맞아요, not 맞어요. 3) Answering a negative question (안 ~요?) with 맞아요 — this is ambiguous; restate the proposition clearly.

expressions.shortExplanation: 그렇죠 is a practical expression meaning "That's right, isn't it / Exactly.".
expressions.explanation: 그렇죠 (geureochyo) = "That's right, isn't it / Exactly.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그렇죠 ("right? / exactly"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; seeking or giving warm, shared agreement
반말; to a friend — same meaning, same warmth
격식체; formal confirmation in presentations or service settings
rising tone to invite the listener to agree with YOUR statement; a tag-question equivalent

examples.ko: 요즘 진짜 피곤하죠? — 그렇죠, 요즘 일이 너무 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jinjja pigonhajyo? — geureochyo, yojeum iri neomu manayo.
examples.en: It's really exhausting lately, right? — Exactly, there's just too much work.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B uses 그렇죠 to echo the feeling and validate it, building rapport

examples.ko: 그렇죠. 그래서 제가 미리 확인해 뒀어요.
examples.romanization: geureochyo. geuraeseo jega miri hwaginhae dwosseoyo.
examples.en: Right, exactly — that's why I checked ahead of time.
examples.note: falling tone: agreeing with what was just said, then showing you acted on that shared understanding

examples.ko: 그렇죠, 사실 저도 처음엔 좀 망설였는데 막상 해보니까 괜찮더라고요.
examples.romanization: geureochyo, sasil jeodo cheoeumen jom mangseoryeonneunde maksang haebonikka gwaenchanteoragoyo.
examples.en: Right, honestly I hesitated at first too, but once I actually tried it, it was fine.
examples.note: agreeing, adding personal context, then sharing a nuancing discovery

expressions.nuance: 그렇죠 comes from 그렇다 ('to be so') + the ending 죠, which is a contraction of 지요. The -지요 ending uniquely seeks mutual confirmation or shared understanding — it says 'you'd agree, right?' — making 그렇죠 feel warm and socially connective rather than merely factual. This is the key distinction from 맞아요: 맞아요 verifies a fact as correct; 그렇죠 says 'yeah, we're on the same page / that's how life is'. Casual is 그렇지; formal is 그렇습니다. With a rising tone (그렇죠?) it becomes a tag question inviting the listener to confirm your view. A common near-synonym is 그래요 — 그렇죠 is slightly more emphatic and warmer, nudging for agreement; 그래요 is a neutral 'yes, that's right'. English speakers often miss this warmth and reach for the more transactional 맞아요 everywhere; in small talk and emotional sharing, 그렇죠 is the more natural choice. Watch the spelling: the stem is 그렇다, so keep the ㅎ — it's 그렇죠, not 그러죠.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 그러죠 — the stem is 그렇다, so it keeps ㅎ: 그렇죠.
Using 그렇죠 to correct a factual claim — for 'that's the correct answer' use 맞아요; 그렇죠 is empathetic agreement.
Treating the ending 죠 as casual — 죠/지요 is polite (it contains 요); the casual version is 그렇지 without 요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그렇다(to be so) + 죠(지요 contracted) → 실제 뜻: 'that's how it is, right?' The -죠 ending is the key: it creates mutual ground, not just factual confirmation — it says 'we both know this is true'. That warmth sets it apart from bare 그래요.
존댓말: 그렇죠. 반말: 그렇지. 격식: 그렇습니다. 상황: 소소한 일상 대화, 상대방의 말에 공감할 때, 자기 말에 상대의 동의를 구할 때 (그렇죠? 질문형). 상사나 고객에게도 자연스럽다.

맞아요 vs 그렇죠: 맞아요 = 'that statement is factually correct'; 그렇죠 = 'yeah, that's how things are / we're aligned'. 그래요 vs 그렇죠: 그래요 is neutral agreement; 그렇죠 is warmer and more emphatic, actively pulling the other person into shared understanding.
평서: 그렇죠 (falling tone = 'exactly'). 의문: 그렇죠? (rising tone = 'isn't it?'). 반말: 그렇지 / 그렇지? 격식: 그렇습니다. 강조: 맞죠, 그렇죠? (stacking for extra emphasis).

1) 맞아요 everywhere — 그렇죠 is warmer and more natural in small talk and emotional sharing. 2) Spelling 그러죠 — the stem keeps ㅎ: 그렇죠. 3) Treating 죠 as casual — 죠/지요 is polite (contains 요 level); casual is 그렇지.

expressions.shortExplanation: 동의해요 is a practical expression meaning "I agree.".
expressions.explanation: 동의해요 (donguihaeyo) means "I agree.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 동의해요 ("I agree"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; slightly formal, natural in discussions, meetings, or reacting to an opinion
반말; to a friend or peer in a relaxed setting
격식체; presentations, debates, official decisions — the expected form in business Korean

usagePhrases.en: I agree with that opinion too
usagePhrases.note: extension naming what you agree with; note the particle 에

examples.ko: 네, 저도 동의해요. 그게 훨씬 합리적인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: ne, jeodo donguihaeyo. geuge hwolssin hamnijeogin geot gatayo.
examples.en: Yes, I agree. That seems much more reasonable.
examples.note: polite agreement followed by a reason — the reason softens and substantiates the agreement

examples.ko: A: 이번 계획을 좀 더 구체화해야 할 것 같아요. / B: 동의해요. 일정표를 먼저 잡는 게 좋겠어요.
