examples.romanization: A: ibeon gyehoegeul jom deo guchehwahaeya hal geot gatayo. / B: donguihaeyo. iljeongpyoreul meonjeo jamneun ge jokesseoyo.
examples.en: A: I think we need to flesh out this plan a bit more. / B: I agree. We should lock down a schedule first.
examples.note: A/B meeting exchange: B uses 동의해요 then adds a concrete next step — natural in Korean work discussions

examples.ko: 전반적으로는 동의하는데, 예산 부분만 좀 더 검토가 필요할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jeonbanjeogeuroneun donguihaneunde, yesan bubunman jom deo geomtoga piryohal geot gatayo.
examples.en: I agree overall, but I think the budget section needs a bit more review.
examples.note: agrees in principle, then politely raises a reservation — the -는데 (but) pivot is key

expressions.nuance: 동의해요 comes from 동의[同意], the Sino-Korean word for 'agreement of intent/purpose', plus 해요. It is the slightly formal, discussion-register way to say 'I agree' — comfortable with anyone in meetings, class, or when reacting to a proposal or argument. For casual friend chat it can feel stiff; 맞아 or 나도 그렇게 생각해 are more natural there. Casual is 동의해; formal is 동의합니다 (standard in business settings). The nearest everyday alternative is 저도 그렇게 생각해요 — the dividing line: 동의해요 signals 'I endorse this position', closer to a formal agreement vote; 저도 그렇게 생각해요 is a warmer 'I feel the same way'. A related word is 동감이에요 ('I share the feeling') — 동감 is emotional resonance; 동의 is intellectual assent. The most common English-speaker error is the particle: you agree WITH something using 에 (그 의견에 동의해요), not 을/를 — English 'agree with' misleads learners into using the object marker.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그 의견을 동의해요 — 동의하다 takes 에, not 을/를: 그 의견에 동의해요.
Using 동의해요 in casual friend chat — it sounds formal; friends say 맞아 or 나도 그렇게 생각해.
Confusing 동의 with 동감 — 동감이에요 ('I feel the same') stresses shared feeling; 동의해요 stresses agreeing with a stated position.

structuredNuance.t: 直譯: 동의[同意](same intention/agreement) + 해요 → 실제 뜻: 'I endorse this position / I agree'. It is more deliberate and formal than a casual 맞아 — you're aligning yourself with a stated stance or argument, not just nodding.
존댓말: 동의해요 (meetings, class, semi-formal discussion). 반말: 동의해 (peers, friends — but can still feel a bit bookish). 격식: 동의합니다 (business presentations, formal votes). 친구들끼리: 맞아 / 나도 그렇게 생각해가 더 자연스럽다.

동의해요 vs 저도 그렇게 생각해요: 동의해요 = 'I endorse the position' (intellectual, slightly formal); 저도 그렇게 생각해요 = 'I feel/think the same' (warmer, conversational). 동의해요 vs 동감이에요: 동의 = intellectual agreement with a statement; 동감 = emotional resonance/shared feeling.
기본: 동의해요. 강조: 완전히 동의해요 ('I completely agree'). 격식: 동의합니다. 부분 동의: 어느 정도는 동의해요 ('I agree to some extent'). 부정: 동의하지 않아요 / 동의 못 해요.

1) 그 의견을 동의해요 (wrong particle) — 동의하다 takes 에: 그 의견에 동의해요. English 'agree with' misleads into 을/를. 2) Using 동의해요 in casual friend chat — too bookish; friends say 맞아 or 나도 그렇게 생각해. 3) Confusing 동의 with 동감 — 동감이에요 stresses shared feeling; 동의해요 stresses endorsing a position.

expressions.shortExplanation: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 is a practical expression meaning "I think so too.".
expressions.explanation: "I think so too." — that is 저도 그렇게 생각해요 (jeodo geureoke saenggakaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 저도 그렇게 생각해요 ("I think so too"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; the warm everyday way to echo someone's opinion
반말; to a close friend or peer
격식체; work meetings, formal discussions
polished near-synonym; slightly more literary but common in written and semi-formal speech

examples.ko: A: 이 식당 분위기가 참 좋죠? / B: 저도 그렇게 생각해요. 또 오고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: A: i sikdang bunwigiga cham jochyo? / B: jeodo geureoke saenggakaeyo. tto ogo sipeoyo.
examples.en: A: This restaurant has a great vibe, right? / B: I think so too. I want to come back.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B echoes the feeling and adds their own desire — the most natural way to agree about atmosphere or impressions

examples.ko: 맞아요, 저도 그렇게 생각해요. 지금 바로 결정하기엔 이른 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: majayo, jeodo geureoke saenggakaeyo. jigeum baro gyeoljeonghagien ireun geot gatayo.
examples.en: Right, I think so too. I think it's a bit early to decide right now.
examples.note: agreeing with a caution and restating the shared hesitation

examples.ko: 사실 저도 그렇게 생각했어요. 근데 막상 써 보니까 생각보다 훨씬 편하더라고요.
examples.romanization: sasil jeodo geureoke saenggakaesseoyo. geunde maksang sseo bonikka saenggakboda hwolssin pyeonhadeoragoyo.
examples.en: Honestly I thought so too. But when I actually used it, it was way more convenient than I expected.
examples.note: past tense form: agreeing about a former view, then pivoting to a surprising discovery — shows the phrase works in narrative

expressions.nuance: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 ('I too think like that') is the warm, conversational default for agreeing with someone's opinion — used with anyone in polite speech, and a natural filler for building rapport. Each part carries weight: 저도 = 'I too / me too'; 그렇게 = 'like that / in that way'; 생각해요 = 'think'. Casual is 나도 그렇게 생각해; formal is 저도 그렇게 생각합니다. The nearest alternatives are 동의해요 (more formal, argument-based) and 저도 같은 생각이에요 (a touch more polished, common in semi-formal writing). The most frequent English-speaker mistake is dropping 그렇게 — 저도 생각해요 means only 'I think too' without the 'like that', leaving the sentence incomplete. A second issue: 저도 already encodes 'too/also', so adding 또 or 역시 on top creates redundancy. This phrase is versatile for both facts and feelings, making it the go-to opinionating phrase in everyday Korean.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 그렇게 (저도 생각해요) — that means only 'I think too' and is incomplete; you need 저도 그렇게 생각해요.
Using polite 저도 그렇게 생각해요 in casual chat — with friends drop to 반말: 나도 그렇게 생각해.
Adding a redundant 또 ('also') — 저도 already means 'me too'; 저도 또 그렇게 생각해요 is doubled.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 저도(I too) 그렇게(like that) 생각해요(think) → 실제 뜻: 'I think so too'. 그렇게 is load-bearing — it refers back to what the other person just said. Drop it and the sentence breaks.
존댓말: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 (누구에게나). 반말: 나도 그렇게 생각해 (친구, 동생). 격식: 저도 그렇게 생각합니다 (회의, 발표). 가장 자연스러운 맥락: 상대가 의견을 말한 뒤 공감을 표현할 때.

저도 그렇게 생각해요 vs 동의해요: 생각해요 = warm, conversational, opinion-based; 동의해요 = formal, intellectual, endorsing a position. 저도 그렇게 생각해요 vs 저도 같은 생각이에요: 같은 생각이에요 is slightly more polished and common in writing, but means the same thing.
약한 동의: 저도 그런 것 같아요 ('I think so too' — hedged). 강한 동의: 저도 정말 그렇게 생각해요 / 완전히 같은 생각이에요. 과거: 저도 그렇게 생각했어요 (I thought so too). 의문: 혹시 저도 그렇게 생각하는 게 맞나요? (seeking validation).

1) 저도 생각해요 (dropping 그렇게) — incomplete; means only 'I think too' without referent. 그렇게 is required. 2) 저도 또 그렇게 생각해요 — redundant; 저도 already means 'too'. 3) Using polite 저도 form in casual chat — with friends swap to 반말: 나도 그렇게 생각해.

expressions.english: That doesn't seem right / I don't think that's okay.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "That doesn't seem right / I don't think that's okay.".
expressions.explanation: "That doesn't seem right / I don't think that's okay." — that is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 (geugeon jom anin geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 ("that's not really okay, I think"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: that's not really okay, I think
usagePhrases.note: polite; the standard indirect way to voice disagreement or disapproval without a blunt 'no'
반말; to a close friend — still softened with 것 같아, not a harsh 아니야
격식체; work or formal setting — the most measured way to object

usagePhrases.en: that's not really okay, is it?
usagePhrases.note: extension seeking the listener's agreement on your objection — a tag-question form that shares responsibility

examples.ko: 음, 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요. 다른 방법을 찾아봐요.
examples.romanization: eum, geugeon jom anin geot gatayo. dareun bangbeobeul chajabwayo.
examples.en: Hmm, I don't think that's okay. Let's look for another way.
examples.note: softly rejecting an idea and suggesting an alternative — the combination is very Korean

examples.ko: A: 그냥 몰래 처리해 버릴까요? / B: 그렇게 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요. 투명하게 하는 게 낫겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: geunyang mollae cheorihae beorilkkayo? / B: geureoke haneun geon jom anin geot gatayo. tumyeonghage haneun ge natgesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Should we just handle it secretly? / B: I don't think doing it that way is right. It'd be better to be transparent.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B objects to unethical conduct using the indirect form — direct 틀렸어요 would be too confrontational

examples.ko: 취지는 이해하는데, 그렇게까지 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: chwijineun ihaehaneunde, geureokekkaji haneun geon jom anin geot gatayo.
examples.en: I get the intention, but I don't think going that far is right.
examples.note: acknowledging a valid purpose, then drawing a line at excessive methods — a very natural disagreement structure

expressions.nuance: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is the polite, face-saving way to object in Korean — 'that seems a bit wrong/inappropriate to me'. Three elements work together: 아니다 ('to not be so') provides the judgment; -ㄴ 것 같다 ('it seems') turns it into personal opinion rather than a verdict; and 좀 ('a bit') cushions the blow. Remove any of these and the phrase gets harsher. The casual form 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아 keeps the same hedges; the formal 그건 좀 아닌 것 같습니다 is for work. The nearest alternative is 저는 반대예요 — the dividing line: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is situational, indirect disapproval (a soft 'that's not right'); 저는 반대예요 is a clear on-the-record stance ('I oppose this'). The classic English-speaker mistake is being too direct — saying 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') or 안 돼요 for disagreement, which sounds confrontational and rude in Korean. Always keep 좀 and 것 같아요 to stay polite. Grammar note: it's 아닌 (adjective form from 아니다), not 안 인.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Disagreeing with 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') — too blunt/confrontational; soften to 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
Dropping 좀 and 것 같아요 (그건 아니에요) — that's much harsher; the hedges are what make it polite.
Writing 안인 것 같아요 — the correct form from 아니다 is 아닌 것 같아요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그건(that) 좀(a bit) 아닌(not-so) 것 같아요(seems) → 실제 뜻: 'I don't think that's right/okay'. The literal meaning is face-saving by design — 'seems a bit off' rather than 'that's wrong'.
존댓말: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 (누구에게나). 반말: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아. 격식: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같습니다. 상황: 누군가의 제안이나 행동이 부적절하거나 과도하다고 느낄 때, 상대를 직접 비판하지 않고 간접적으로 이의를 제기할 때.

그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 vs 저는 반대예요: 아닌 것 같아요 = indirect, situational ('that seems off'); 반대예요 = explicit on-record objection ('I'm against it'). 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 vs 그건 좀 그래요: 그건 좀 그래요 is even softer/vaguer ('that's a bit...hmm') — maximum indirectness.
세 가지 완화 장치: 좀('a bit') + 아닌(adjective 'not-right') + 것 같아요('seems'). 모두 제거하면 그건 아니에요 — 훨씬 강하고 직접적이다. 확장: 그렇게까지 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 ('going that far seems a bit off').

1) 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') — too blunt and confrontational; soften to 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요. 2) 그건 안 돼요 ('that can't be done/not allowed') — this is a hard prohibition, much stronger than polite disagreement. 3) Writing 안 인 것 같아요 — wrong; the form from 아니다 is 아닌 것 같아요.

expressions.english: It's not great / I don't really like it.
expressions.shortExplanation: 별로예요 is a practical expression meaning "It's not great / I don't really like it.".
expressions.explanation: 별로예요 (byeolloyeyo) means "It's not great / I don't really like it.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 별로예요 ("it's not that good / meh"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; mildly negative opinion — the standard way to say you're unimpressed without being rude
반말; to a friend — the most common casual negative verdict

usagePhrases.en: I don't think it's that great
usagePhrases.note: softer, hedged variant; 것 같아요 adds a layer of uncertainty, making it gentler than a bare 별로예요
past tense extension — used after actually trying something (food, movie, experience)

examples.ko: 그 영화 어땠어요? — 솔직히 좀 별로였어요.
examples.romanization: geu yeonghwa eottaesseoyo? — soljiki jom byeolloyeosseoyo.
examples.en: How was that movie? — Honestly, it wasn't that great.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B gives a mildly negative verdict in past tense after having seen it — 별로였어요 is the natural post-experience form

examples.en: The food was okay, but the service was kind of disappointing.
examples.note: splitting a verdict — one part positive, one part 별로 — a very common review structure

examples.ko: 음... 별로예요. 제 스타일이 아닌 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: eum... byeolloyeyo. je seutairi anin geot gatayo.
examples.en: Hmm... it's not great. I don't think it's my style.
examples.note: giving a mildly negative aesthetic verdict and offering a polite reason — 제 스타일이 아닌 것 같아요 softens the critique

expressions.nuance: 별로예요 is the everyday 'meh / not that great', a mildly negative opinion used with anyone in polite speech. 별로 originally means 'particularly / especially', and in its classic use it pairs with a negative verb: 별로 안 좋아요 ('not particularly good'), 별로 없어요 ('not particularly many'). In spoken Korean, 별로예요 has evolved to stand alone as 'it's not that great / I don't really like it' — the negative is implied. The casual form is 별로야; the hedged 별로인 것 같아요 is gentler. The nearest alternative is 그저 그래요 — the dividing line: 별로예요 leans clearly negative ('it's not good for me'), while 그저 그래요 is neutral 'so-so / average'. The top English-speaker mistakes: (1) spelling — it's 별로예요, never 별로에요 (after a pure-noun slot, the copula -이에요 contracts to 예요); (2) saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 needs a negative; the correct form is 별로 안 좋아요 or stand-alone 별로예요; (3) treating 별로예요 as very strongly 'bad' — it's mild disapproval; for genuine dislike use 너무 별로예요 or 안 좋아요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 별로에요 — the correct copula spelling here is 별로예요.
Saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 needs a negative; use 별로 안 좋아요 or 별로예요.
Treating 별로예요 as strongly 'bad' — it's mild ('not great'); for strong dislike use 너무 별로예요 or 안 좋아요.

structuredNuance.t: 直譯: 별로(particularly/especially) + 예요(is/am/are) → 실제 뜻: 'it's not particularly good = it's meh'. 별로 comes from 별달리 ('particularly differently') and inherently implies 'not much' when used as a predicate standalone.
존댓말: 별로예요 / 별로인 것 같아요. 반말: 별로야. 격식: 별로 마음에 들지 않습니다 (more circumspect). 상황: 음식, 영화, 디자인, 서비스 등 어떤 것에 대한 평가를 물어봤을 때. 사람에 대해 직접 쓰면 무례할 수 있다 — 상대 앞에서 '그 사람 별로예요'는 피하자.

별로예요 vs 그저 그래요: 별로예요 = clearly negative ('I don't like it'); 그저 그래요 = neutral 'so-so / average'. 별로예요 vs 안 좋아요: 안 좋아요 is more direct and a bit stronger ('it's not good'). 별로 너무 싫어요: for strong dislike.
현재: 별로예요. 과거(경험 후): 별로였어요. 완화: 별로인 것 같아요. 강조: 진짜 별로예요 / 너무 별로예요. 결합: 별로 안 좋아요 (original structure — 별로 + negation + adjective).

1) Spelling 별로에요 — after the standalone 별로, the copula contracts to 예요: 별로예요. 2) 별로 좋아요 ('particularly good') — completely reverses the meaning; 별로 needs a negative: 별로 안 좋아요. 3) Treating 별로예요 as strongly 'bad' — it's mild; for strong dislike say 정말 별로예요 or 싫어요.

expressions.english: I think so / It seems that way.
expressions.shortExplanation: 그런 것 같아요 is a practical expression meaning "I think so / It seems that way.".
expressions.explanation: "I think so / It seems that way." — that is 그런 것 같아요 (geureon geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그런 것 같아요 ("I think so / seems so"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; softened confirmation — the standard hedge for opinions and assessments
반말; to a friend — same hedged quality
격식체; work settings, reporting, formal discussion
extension adding 아마 ('probably/maybe') for even more hedging when you're uncertain

examples.ko: 오늘 비 올까요? — 그런 것 같아요. 아침부터 하늘이 어두웠거든요.
examples.romanization: oneul bi olkkayo? — geureon geot gatayo. achimbuteo haneuri eoduwotgeodeunyo.
examples.en: Will it rain today? — Seems like it. The sky has been dark since morning.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B infers from visible evidence and adds the reason with -거든요 — how 그런 것 같아요 works with observable cues

examples.ko: 다들 그 의견에 찬성하는 것 같아요. 분위기를 보니 그런 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: dadeul geu uigyeone chanseonghaneun geot gatayo. bunwigireul boni geureon geot gatayo.
examples.en: Everyone seems to be for that idea. From the mood, it seems so.
examples.note: reading a group situation and hedging the conclusion — the repeated 것 같아요 is natural in Korean

examples.ko: A: 이 방법이 더 효율적인 것 같죠? / B: 네, 그런 것 같아요. 시간이 많이 절약되는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: A: i bangbeobi deo hyoyuljeogin geot gatjyo? / B: ne, geureon geot gatayo. sigani mani jeoryakdoeneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: A: This method seems more efficient, right? / B: Yes, it does seem that way. Seems like it saves a lot of time.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B confirms softly and adds an observation — notice both people use 것 같다, which is very natural in Korean conversation

expressions.nuance: 그런 것 같아요 ('it seems to be that way / so') is the hedged 'I think so', used constantly in Korean because -ㄴ/는 것 같다 is the core politeness device for expressing opinions tentatively rather than asserting flatly. Casual is 그런 것 같아; formal is 그런 것 같습니다. The nearest confident alternatives are 맞아요 and 그렇죠 — the dividing line: 그런 것 같아요 hedges ('seems so, I'm not fully certain'), while 맞아요/그렇죠 express confidence. Even when quite sure, Koreans often reach for 것 같아요 to avoid sounding pushy or presumptuous — this is a cultural politeness norm, not just uncertainty. The English-speaker tendency is to over-assert with 그래요/맞아요 where 그런 것 같아요 sounds more natural and modest. The reverse error is using 것 같다 for your own clear, immediate feelings when directness is actually expected (a doctor asking 'does it hurt?' — 아픈 것 같아요 can sound odd; 아파요 is more natural). Spacing: 그런 것 (two words), not 그런것.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Over-asserting with 맞아요/그래요 when unsure — 그런 것 같아요 is the natural hedge for 'I think so'.
Writing 그런것 같아요 — 것 is a bound noun and is spaced: 그런 것 같아요.
Confusing 그런 것 같다 (seems so) with 그렇다 (is so) — the 것 같다 version is tentative on purpose.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그런(such/that kind of) 것(thing) 같아요(seems) → 실제 뜻: 'it seems to be so / I think so'. The -ㄴ 것 같다 construction is the Korean opinion hedge: it frames your statement as a perception or tentative inference, not a certainty.
존댓말: 그런 것 같아요. 반말: 그런 것 같아. 격식: 그런 것 같습니다. 이 표현은 의견, 인상, 추론 등 모든 상황에서 자연스럽다. 그러나 '아파요?' 같은 직접적인 신체 반응 질문에는 직접 대답(아파요)이 더 자연스러울 수 있다.

그런 것 같아요 vs 맞아요/그렇죠: 것 같아요 = hedged ('seems so'); 맞아요/그렇죠 = confident ('right / exactly'). 그런 것 같아요 vs 그런 것 같습니다: same hedge, higher formality. 아마 그런 것 같아요 vs 그런 것 같아요: 아마 adds probability ('probably seems so').
완화: 아마 그런 것 같아요 (with 아마 = 'probably'). 강화: 확실히 그런 것 같아요 ('it definitely seems so'). 관련: ~ㄴ/는 것 같아요 패턴으로 어떤 형용사/동사와도 결합 가능 — 어려운 것 같아요, 갈 것 같아요 등.

1) Over-asserting with 맞아요/그래요 when unsure — 그런 것 같아요 is the natural modest hedge. 2) Writing 그런것 같아요 — 것 is a bound noun and MUST be spaced: 그런 것 같아요. 3) Overusing 것 같다 for strong personal feelings — for direct sensations (pain, hunger), stating directly (아파요, 배고파요) is more natural than hedging with 것 같다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 저는 반대예요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm against it / I disagree.".
expressions.explanation: 저는 반대예요 (jeoneun bandaeyeyo) means "I'm against it / I disagree.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 저는 반대예요 ("I'm against it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: polite; clear on-the-record opposition — use when you need your stance to be known
반말; to a close friend or peer
격식체; business meetings, votes, formal decisions
extension naming what you oppose — note the particle 에, not 을/를

examples.ko: 미안하지만 저는 반대예요. 리스크가 너무 클 것 같아서요.
examples.romanization: mianhajiman jeoneun bandaeyeyo. riseukeuga neomu keul geot gataseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, but I'm against it. I think the risk would be too high.
examples.note: polite opposition softened with 미안하지만 and a reason (-어서요) — the recommended structure

examples.ko: 다들 찬성하시는 것 같은데, 저는 솔직히 반대예요. 이유를 말씀드려도 될까요?
examples.romanization: dadeul chanseonghasineun geot gateunde, jeoneun soljiki bandaeyeyo. iyureul malsseumdeuryeodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Everyone seems to be in favor, but honestly I'm against it. May I explain my reasons?
examples.note: voicing a minority objection in a group, then asking permission to elaborate — shows how to use 반대예요 without seeming stubborn

examples.ko: A: 이 안건 찬반 의견 주세요. / B: 저는 반대입니다. 예산 대비 효과가 불확실하기 때문입니다.
examples.romanization: A: i angeon chanban uigyeon juseyo. / B: jeoneun bandaeimnida. yesan daebi hyogwaga bulhwaksilhagi ttaemunimnida.
examples.en: A: Please share your opinions on this agenda item. / B: I'm opposed. The return on the budget is uncertain.
examples.note: formal meeting exchange: B uses 반대합니다 and gives a business reason — the expected register in a work setting

expressions.nuance: 저는 반대예요 is the explicit, on-the-record 'I'm against it', used when you want your opposition known — typical in meetings, planning sessions, or group decisions. 반대[反對] means 'opposition' (literally 'against / facing the other way'); its antonym is 찬성[贊成] ('approval / being for'). Casual is 나는 반대야; formal is 저는 반대합니다, which is standard in business Korean. The nearest alternative is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 — the dividing line: 저는 반대예요 is explicit and committed (you're registering a position), while 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is indirect and situational (a gentle 'that seems off'). Because clear opposition can feel blunt in Korean social settings, it's conventional to soften: lead with 미안하지만 ('sorry, but') or follow with a reason ending in -아서요/-어서요. The particle rule: you oppose something using 에 (그 의견에 반대예요), not 을/를 — the English phrase 'oppose something' misleads learners into the object marker. Also distinguish 반대 from 반대로 ('on the contrary / in reverse'), which is an adverb about direction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그 의견을 반대예요 — 반대(하다) takes 에: 그 의견에 반대예요.
Opposing bluntly with no cushion — add 미안하지만 or a reason (-아서요) so it doesn't sound combative.
Confusing 반대 with 반대로 — 반대로 means 'on the contrary/in reverse'; for 'I'm against it' it's 저는 반대예요.

structuredNuance.t: 反對(한자): 반(against) + 대(facing) = 'opposing'. 저는 반대예요 = 'I stand in opposition'. This is a committed stance, not a vague feeling of discomfort — it registers you as being against a proposal.
존댓말: 저는 반대예요 (누구에게나). 반말: 나는 반대야 (친구). 격식: 저는 반대합니다 (회의, 공식 발표). 가장 자연스러운 상황: 회의에서 의견 표명, 팀 결정, 투표. 부드럽게 하려면 미안하지만을 앞에 붙이거나 이유를 뒤에 덧붙인다.

저는 반대예요 vs 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요: 반대예요 = explicit registered opposition (you're staking a position); 아닌 것 같아요 = gentle indirect disapproval. 반대예요 vs 저는 동의 안 해요: 동의 안 해요 = 'I don't agree' (less formal, based on 동의); 반대예요 is the cleaner native expression.
완화: 미안하지만 저는 반대예요 + 이유. 격식: 저는 반대합니다. 부분 반대: 일부에는 동의하지만 이 부분은 반대예요. 반의어: 저는 찬성이에요 / 찬성합니다.

1) 그 의견을 반대예요 (wrong particle) — 반대하다 takes 에: 그 의견에 반대예요. 2) No cushioning — direct opposition can feel abrupt; add 미안하지만 or a reason. 3) Confusing 반대 with 반대로 — 반대로 means 'on the contrary / in reverse' (an adverb about direction), not 'I oppose'.

expressions.shortExplanation: 좋은 생각이에요 is a practical expression meaning "That's a good idea.".
expressions.explanation: "That's a good idea." — that is 좋은 생각이에요 (joeun saenggagieyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 좋은 생각이에요 ("that's a good idea"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; warmly endorsing someone's suggestion — the most natural compliment for an idea
반말; to a close friend — same warmth, lower register
격식/경어; toward a senior or customer — the -시- honorific marks deference
extension with -네요: adds mild surprise or fresh realization — 'oh, that IS a good idea'

examples.ko: 같이 점심 먹을까요? — 좋은 생각이에요! 어디로 갈까요?
examples.romanization: gachi jeomsim meogeulkkayo? — joeun saenggagieyo! eodiro galkkayo?
examples.en: Shall we have lunch together? — Great idea! Where should we go?
examples.note: A/B exchange: B enthusiastically endorses and immediately moves forward — shows how the phrase opens collaborative planning

examples.ko: 회의를 오전으로 옮기자고요? 좋은 생각이에요. 그 시간대가 더 집중이 잘 될 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: hoeuireul ojeoneuro olmgijagoyo? joeun saenggagieyo. geu sigandaega deo jipjungi jal doel geot gatayo.
examples.en: Move the meeting to the morning? Good idea. I think we can focus better at that time.
examples.note: endorsing and backing it with a reason — 이에요 + reason is a natural work-chat response pattern

examples.ko: A: 미리 예약해 두면 어때요? / B: 오, 좋은 생각이에요! 나중에 줄 서는 거 싫거든요.
examples.romanization: A: miri yeyakae dumyeon eottaeyo? / B: o, joeun saenggagieyo! najunge jul seoneun geo silkeodeunyo.
examples.en: A: What if we make a reservation in advance? / B: Oh, that's a great idea! I hate waiting in line later.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B reacts with -네요 energy (mild pleased surprise) via 좋은 생각이에요 + personal reason

expressions.nuance: 좋은 생각이에요 ('that's a good thought/idea') is the warm, natural way to praise a suggestion in Korean — used with anyone in polite speech. The components: 좋은 (adjective modifier from 좋다 'good') + 생각 ('thought/idea') + 이에요 (copula). Adding -네요 (좋은 생각이네요) adds a tone of pleasant discovery — 'oh, that IS a good idea'. Casual is 좋은 생각이야; the honorific 좋은 생각이십니다 is used with seniors or customers. The nearest alternative is 좋아요 — the dividing line: 좋은 생각이에요 specifically compliments the idea as clever or sensible; 좋아요 is general assent ('sounds good, fine, okay') without the compliment. For accepting a request you don't particularly need to praise, 좋아요 works; for genuinely endorsing someone's creative suggestion, 좋은 생각이에요 is warmer. English speakers sometimes say 좋은 아이디어예요 (using the loanword 아이디어), which is perfectly common in Korea, but 좋은 생각이에요 is the more natively Korean phrasing. Watch the copula: after 생각 (consonant ending), the copula is 이에요, not 에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 좋은 생각에요 — after 생각 (ends in a consonant) the copula is 이에요: 좋은 생각이에요.
Saying 좋는 생각 — 좋다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 좋은, not 좋는.
Reducing it to bare 좋아요 when you mean to praise the idea — 좋아요 is general assent; 좋은 생각이에요 compliments the idea itself.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 좋은(good) 생각(thought/idea) 이에요(is) → 실제 뜻: 'that's a good idea'. It actively praises the quality of the idea — not just 'okay' but 'that is genuinely good thinking'.
존댓말: 좋은 생각이에요 (누구에게나). 반말: 좋은 생각이야. 경어: 좋은 생각이십니다 (선생님, 상사, 손님). 상황: 누군가의 제안이나 아이디어에 반응할 때. 일상적인 계획(식사, 여행, 일정)부터 직장 회의까지 모두 자연스럽다.

좋은 생각이에요 vs 좋아요: 생각이에요 = compliments the idea specifically ('that's a smart suggestion'); 좋아요 = general assent ('sounds fine / okay'). 좋은 생각이에요 vs 좋은 아이디어예요: 아이디어 is the loanword variant — equally common in modern Korean, slightly more casual or youthful.
기본: 좋은 생각이에요. 발견/감탄: 좋은 생각이네요 (with -네요 for fresh realization). 반말: 좋은 생각이야. 경어: 좋은 생각이십니다. 강조: 정말 좋은 생각이에요 / 아주 좋은 생각인 것 같아요.

1) 좋은 생각에요 — after 생각 (consonant-ending noun) the copula is 이에요: 좋은 생각이에요. 2) 좋는 생각 — 좋다 is an adjective; the correct modifier is 좋은, not 좋는. 3) Defaulting to 좋아요 when you want to compliment the idea — 좋아요 is general assent; 좋은 생각이에요 is the warmer, idea-praising phrase.

expressions.english: What I mean is... / My point is...
expressions.shortExplanation: 제 말은 is a practical expression meaning "What I mean is... / My point is...".
expressions.explanation: 제 말은 (je mareun) = "What I mean is... / My point is...". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 제 말은 ("what I mean is..."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: polite; used to clarify, restate, or rescue your point — especially after being misunderstood
반말; same function, lower register — to a friend or peer
격식/경어; toward a senior, customer, or in formal writing — raises the politeness of your own speech

usagePhrases.en: what I mean is, it's not that
usagePhrases.note: the most common extension: correcting a misunderstanding head-on before restating the real point

examples.ko: 아니, 제 말은 그게 아니라, 미리 준비하자는 거예요.
examples.romanization: ani, je mareun geuge anira, miri junbihajaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: No, what I mean is, it's not that — I'm saying we should prepare in advance.
examples.note: the most typical use: 제 말은 그게 아니라 + the corrected intent — rescuing a misunderstood point

examples.ko: A: 저 그렇게까지 하라는 말이에요? / B: 아니요, 제 말은 방향만 잡아 두자는 거예요.
examples.romanization: A: jeo geureokekkaji haraneun marieyo? / B: aniyo, je mareun banghyangman jaba dujaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: A: Are you saying I should go that far? / B: No, what I mean is, let's just set the direction.
examples.note: A/B exchange: B uses 제 말은 to narrow the misunderstood scope — very natural in Korean work discussions

examples.ko: 제 말은, 지금 당장 결정할 필요는 없다는 거예요. 시간이 좀 있잖아요.
examples.romanization: je mareun, jigeum dangjang gyeoljeonghal piryoneun eopsdaneun geoyeyo. sigani jom itjanayo.
examples.en: What I'm saying is, there's no need to decide right now. We have some time.
examples.note: clarifying a misread urgency without a conflict — shows 제 말은 without 그게 아니라 when no direct correction is needed

expressions.nuance: 제 말은 ('as for my words / what I'm saying is') is the go-to repair phrase in Korean — you use it to reframe, clarify, or rescue your intended meaning when you've been misunderstood or when your point hasn't landed. 제 = humble 'my'; 말 = 'words / speech'; 은 = topic particle ('as for'). The casual form is 내 말은; 제 말씀은 raises deference and is used toward seniors or customers. The most natural extension is 제 말은 그게 아니라 ('my point isn't that — it's...'), which corrects a misreading before restating. The nearest alternative is 그러니까 ('so / what I'm saying is') — the dividing line: 그러니까 reframes or continues your reasoning as a logical next step; 제 말은 explicitly re-centers on YOUR intended meaning after a misunderstanding. English speakers reach for 제가 의미하는 건 ('what I mean is' translated literally), which is unnatural in spoken Korean. Another mistake: dropping the topic particle 은 (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은 for the frame to work.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calquing 'I mean' as 제가 의미하는 건 — unnatural; say 제 말은.
Using 내 말은 with someone you must be polite to — switch to 제 말은 (or 제 말씀은).
Dropping the topic particle (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은: 제 말은 그게 아니라.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 제(my/humble) 말(words/speech) 은(as for) → 실제 뜻: 'as for what I'm saying / what I mean is'. It is a repair opener — it signals 'let me re-anchor what I actually intended'. Most powerful before 그게 아니라 ('it's not that').
존댓말: 제 말은 (누구에게나). 반말: 내 말은 (친구, 동생). 경어/격식: 제 말씀은 (선생님, 상사, 손님). 상황: 상대가 자신의 말을 잘못 이해했을 때, 요점을 다시 강조할 때, 오해를 바로잡을 때.

제 말은 vs 그러니까: 그러니까 = 'so / in other words' (continues/reframes reasoning); 제 말은 = 're-centers on MY intended meaning' (usually after misunderstanding). 제 말은 그게 아니라 vs 그게 아니에요: 그게 아니에요 is a blunt correction; 제 말은 그게 아니라 is gentler and explains rather than just denies.
기본: 제 말은 + [내용]. 수정형: 제 말은 그게 아니라 + [진짜 의도]. 반말: 내 말은 그게 아니라... 경어: 제 말씀은 그게 아니라... 강조: 제 말은 결국 이거예요 ('my point comes down to this').

1) 제가 의미하는 건 — a literal calque of 'what I mean is'; unnatural in spoken Korean; use 제 말은. 2) 내 말은 with someone you must be polite to — switch to 제 말은 or 제 말씀은. 3) Dropping the topic particle (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은: 제 말은 그게 아니라.

expressions.english: I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)
expressions.shortExplanation: 강아지 키워요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)".
expressions.explanation: 강아지 키워요 (gangaji kiwoyo) means "I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 강아지 키워요 ("I have a dog"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday way to say you own/raise a pet
반말, with friends
Progressive; stresses you currently have one
Swap 강아지 → 고양이 for a cat

examples.ko: A: 혹시 반려동물 키워요? / B: 네, 강아지 키워요. 말티즈예요.
examples.romanization: A: hoksi ballyeodongmul kiwoyo? / B: ne, gangaji kiwoyo. maltijeuyeyo.
examples.en: A: Do you have a pet? / B: Yes, I have a dog. It's a Maltese.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 키워요 as the natural response to a pet ownership question; breed names are used freely in Korean

examples.en: I have two cats at home.
examples.note: Count pets with 마리: 한 마리, 두 마리 — never 두 개

examples.en: I've had my dog for 3 years.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 지 ... 됐어요 = 'it's been ... since I started'; set phrase for elapsed time

expressions.nuance: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up', and it is THE verb Koreans use for having a pet — you 'raise' a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant, so it carries warmth and active care. 강아지 키워요 is the polite-neutral form (존댓말), natural with anyone from a neighbor to a vet; with friends drop to 강아지 키워. The nearest near-synonym is 반려동물 있어요 ('I have a companion animal'), which is more formal/documentary and less the casual bonding opener 키워요 is. Variants: 키우고 있어요 (progressive, stressing ongoing care), 키워 본 적 있어요? (have you ever raised one?). The big English-speaker trap is translating 'I have a dog' as 강아지 있어요 — grammatically fine but means 'a dog is present here', not 'I own and care for one'; for pet ownership, 키워요 is mandatory. A second trap: 강아지 가지고 있어요 (using 가지다 'possess') treats the animal like an held object, which feels cold. Note 강아지 technically means 'puppy' but Koreans use it affectionately for any dog; the blunter neutral word 개 is used in compounds (개 짖는 소리) but sounds abrupt solo.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 강아지 있어요 to mean 'I have a dog'.
있어요 means 'exists / is here', so it reports a dog's presence, not that you own and care for one. For having a pet, say 강아지 키워요.
Saying 강아지 가지고 있어요.
가지다 ('to possess/hold') treats the animal like an object. A pet is 'raised', so use 키우다: 강아지 키워요.
Counting pets with 개 (the general counter).
Animals take the counter 마리: 강아지 두 마리. 개 is the counter for inanimate items (and also the word 'dog'), so 강아지 두 개 sounds wrong.

structuredNuance.t: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up' — you raise a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant. 강아지 키워요 implies active, caring ownership; it is THE verb for having a pet, not just reporting that an animal exists nearby. 강아지 technically means 'puppy' but Koreans call any dog 강아지 affectionately; the neutral 개 sounds blunt used alone.

강아지 키워요 is polite-neutral 존댓말, comfortable with anyone — a neighbor, a vet, a new acquaintance. Drop to 강아지 키워 in 반말 with close friends. It's a natural small-talk opener that invites follow-up questions about breed and name.

강아지 있어요 means 'a dog is present (here)' — it reports existence, not caretaking ownership. 반려동물 있어요 is more formal and documentary. For the warm, relationship-based sense of 'I own and care for a pet', 키워요 is the only natural choice.
키우고 있어요 (progressive: 'I am currently raising'), 키운 지 N년 됐어요 ('it's been N years since I started'), 키워 본 적 있어요? ('have you ever raised one?'). Count animals with native numbers + 마리: 한 마리, 두 마리.

Trap 1: 강아지 있어요 for 'I have a dog' — this says the animal is present, not that you own it. Trap 2: 강아지 가지고 있어요 using 가지다 'possess' — treats a living animal like a held object, which sounds cold and strange. Always use 키우다 for pet ownership.

expressions.shortExplanation: 산책 가자 is a practical expression meaning "Let's go for a walk".
expressions.explanation: "Let's go for a walk" — that is 산책 가자 (sanchaek gaja). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 산책 가자 ("Let's go for a walk"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; what you say to your dog or a close friend
Polite, to a person (e.g. a partner)

usagePhrases.en: Let's go (out) to take a walk
usagePhrases.note: -하러 가다 spells out the purpose
산책시키다 = to walk a pet (causative)

examples.ko: A: 우리 강아지 산책 안 시키면 어떡해? / B: 알아, 지금 산책 가자!
examples.romanization: A: uri gangaji sanchaek an sikimyeon eotteokae? / B: ara, jigeum sanchaek gaja!
examples.en: A: What do we do if we don't walk the dog? / B: I know, let's go for a walk now!
examples.note: A/B showing 산책 가자 as a casual, cheerful decision to head out; dogs learn the word 산책 fast

examples.ko: 비 와서 오늘은 산책 못 가.
examples.romanization: bi waseo oneureun sanchaeng mot ga.
examples.en: It's raining, so no walk today.
examples.note: 못 가 = 'can't go' (due to circumstance), softer than 안 가 ('won't go')

examples.en: I'll go walk the dog and be back.
examples.note: 산책시키다 = make the pet take a walk (causative); you make IT walk, you're not walking yourself

expressions.nuance: 산책 is 'a leisurely walk / stroll' (Sino-Korean 散策), and 산책 가다 = 'go for a walk' is the daily ritual every Korean dog owner knows. The crucial split English speakers miss is between 산책하다 / 산책 가다 (YOU go for a walk) and 산책시키다 (causative: you WALK THE DOG — make it take its walk). So you say 산책 가자 to your dog meaning 'let's both go', but report to others 강아지 산책시켜요 meaning 'I walk the dog (for it)'. Saying 강아지를 산책해요 is wrong — 산책하다 is intransitive and can't take a direct object; you need 산책시키다 to put the dog as object. To your dog, 반말 is totally normal; 산책 가자 or just 산책! is what owners shout. The nearest near-synonym invitation is 나가자 ('let's go out'), but 산책 가자 specifies the purpose is a walk. Note 산책 is for relaxed walking only — brisk exercise-walking is 걷기 운동, and a mountain hike is 등산, a completely different word; calling a mountain trip 산책 sounds odd. With a person (not your pet), use polite 산책 가요 unless you're close.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 강아지를 산책해요 to mean 'I walk the dog'.
산책하다 is intransitive — only the walker can 'do' a walk. To walk a pet, use the causative 산책시키다: 강아지 산책시켜요.
Using 존댓말 to your own dog.
Koreans speak 반말 to pets. 산책 가요 to your dog sounds unnatural; say 산책 가자.
Calling a mountain hike 산책.
산책 is a gentle stroll. Hiking a mountain is 등산. 산에 산책 가요 sounds off — say 등산 가요.

structuredNuance.t: 산책 (散策) means a leisurely stroll — not exercise-walking (걷기 운동) or hiking (등산). 산책 가자 means 'let's go take a stroll', an invitation that includes both speaker and listener. When said to a dog, it's a warm summons to go out together.
To your dog or a close friend: 반말 산책 가자. To a partner, coworker, or someone you've just met: polite 산책 가요. Koreans speak 반말 to pets routinely — 산책 가요 to a dog sounds unnaturally formal.

나가자 ('let's go out') is vaguer. 산책 가자 specifies the activity is a stroll. 산책시키다 vs 산책 가다: if you're walking the dog as its exercise routine (you're the agent making it walk), use the causative 산책시키다. If you're inviting it to come along, say 산책 가자.
산책하러 가자 (-하러 가다 = 'go to do'): stresses going OUT for the purpose. 산책 다녀올게요 ('I'll go for a walk and come back'): the return is implied. 산책 어때요? ('how about a walk?'): softened suggestion.
Trap 1: 강아지를 산책해요 for 'I walk the dog' — 산책하다 is intransitive; use the causative 산책시키다. Trap 2: calling a mountain hike 산책 — that is 등산. Trap 3: using 존댓말 산책 가요 to your own dog — pets get 반말.
산책 is 散策, a Sino-Korean word meaning leisurely walking/strolling.

expressions.english: What kind of food do you feed (your pet)?
expressions.shortExplanation: 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? is a practical expression meaning "What kind of food do you feed (your pet)?".
expressions.explanation: 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? (saryo eotteon geo meogyeoyo?) = "What kind of food do you feed (your pet)?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? ("What food do you feed it?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: What food do you feed it?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking another owner or a vet
반말, to a friend
Asking staff at a pet shop
-(으)려고요 = 'I intend to'

examples.ko: A: 강아지 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? / B: 저는 오리 고기 사료 먹이고 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: gangaji saryo eotteon geo meogyeoyo? / B: jeoneun ori gogi saryo meogigo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: What food do you feed your dog? / B: I'm feeding duck-meat kibble.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the full feed-question-and-answer pattern; 어떤 거 invites a category/brand answer

examples.en: My cat only eats this food.
examples.note: From the pet's side use 먹다 ('eats'), not 먹이다; the cat is subject here

examples.ko: 수의사 선생님, 사료 어떤 거 먹이는 게 좋아요?
examples.romanization: suuisa seonsaengnim, saryo eotteon geo meogineun ge joayo?
examples.en: Doctor, what food is best to feed?
examples.note: 먹이는 게 좋아요 = 'it is good to feed (it)' — asking the vet for advice

expressions.nuance: 사료 is the specific word for animal feed or pet kibble (Sino-Korean 飼料) — do NOT call it 음식 or 밥 when referring to commercial pet food, though owners affectionately say 밥 먹자 ('let's eat') to the pet itself. The verb pair is the key trap: 먹다 = '(the pet) eats', while 먹이다 = '(I) feed / make eat' (causative). So 'I feed the dog kibble' is 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요, and 'the dog eats kibble' is 강아지가 사료를 먹어요. The nearest near-synonym question is 사료 뭐 먹여? (반말, same meaning), while 뭐 먹어요? ('what does it eat?') shifts to the pet's perspective with 먹다. The pet takes the recipient particle 한테 or formal 에게 — 강아지한테 먹여요; the phrasing 강아지를 먹여요 alone can sound like 'feeding ON the dog'. This phrase is polite-neutral, fitting for another owner, a 펫숍 clerk, or a vet. Note 어떤 거 ('which kind') invites a category/brand answer; 뭐 is more open. Don't confuse 사료 (staple kibble/feed) with 간식 ('treats/snacks') — asking about 사료 is about the daily diet.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling pet food 음식 or 밥 in a serious question.
Commercial pet food is 사료. 음식 is human food; use 사료 when asking a vet or shop: 사료 어떤 거 먹여요?
Saying 강아지가 사료 먹여요 to mean 'I feed the dog'.
먹이다 (feed) needs the feeder as subject and the pet as 한테: (제가) 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. 강아지가 ... 먹여요 mixes up who eats and who feeds.
Marking the pet with 를 alone: 강아지를 먹여요.
The fed animal takes 한테/에게 for the recipient: 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. 강아지를 먹여요 sounds like feeding on the dog.

structuredNuance.t: 사료 (飼料) is the specific term for commercial animal feed/kibble — not 음식 (human food) nor casual 밥. 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? literally asks 'what kind of feed do you feed it?' and is the standard way to inquire about another pet's diet.

사료 어떤 거 먹여요? is polite-neutral 존댓말, perfect with a stranger owner, a pet-shop clerk, or a vet. With a close friend: 사료 뭐 먹여? (반말). In a vet context you might say 사료 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend a food').

사료 어떤 거 먹여요? (what do you feed it?) vs. 사료 뭐 먹어요? (what does it eat?): the first focuses on the owner as feeder (먹이다 causative); the second focuses on the pet as eater (먹다). The former is more proactive ownership talk; the latter sounds like asking about the pet's preferences. Also: 사료 (daily diet) vs. 간식 (treats/snacks) — don't confuse them.
사료 바꿔 봤어요? ('have you tried switching food?'), 사료 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend a food'), 사료 성분 확인해 봤어요? ('have you checked the ingredients?').
사료 is 飼料, the Sino-Korean word for animal feed or fodder.

Trap 1: confusing 먹다 (pet eats) and 먹이다 (owner feeds) — use 먹이다 when YOU are the one providing the food. Trap 2: marking the pet with 를 as a direct object (강아지를 먹여요) without the food — it sounds like you're feeding ON the dog; add 한테: 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. Trap 3: calling kibble 음식 — that is human food.

expressions.english: I'll fill up your water bowl
expressions.shortExplanation: 물그릇 채워 줄게 is a practical expression meaning "I'll fill up your water bowl".
expressions.explanation: 물그릇 채워 줄게 (mulgeureut chaewo julge) means "I'll fill up your water bowl". Say it as one set phrase — for example 물그릇 채워 줄게 ("I'll fill the water bowl"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 반말, talking to your pet / casually
갈아 주다 = swap for fresh water

usagePhrases.en: I should wash the food bowl
usagePhrases.note: 밥그릇 = food bowl; -아야겠다 = 'I'd better'
Noticing the bowl is empty

examples.ko: A: 왜 이렇게 보채? / B: 아, 물그릇 비었네. 채워 줄게.
examples.romanization: A: wae ireoke bochae? / B: a, mulgeureut bieonne. chaewo julge.
examples.en: A: Why are you so fussy? / B: Oh, the water bowl is empty. I'll fill it.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 채워 줄게 as a caring response to a pet's behavior; 비다 = to be empty

examples.ko: 고양이 물은 매일 갈아 줘야 돼요.
examples.romanization: goyangi mureun maeil gara jwoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: You should change a cat's water every day.
examples.note: 갈아 주다 = replace with fresh water, not just top up — hygiene distinction

examples.ko: 밥 줬으니까 이제 물그릇만 채우면 돼.
examples.romanization: bap jwosseunikka ije mulgeureunman chaeumyeon dwae.
examples.en: I fed it, so now I just need to fill the water bowl.
examples.note: ...면 돼 = 'all I need to do is ...'; lists two care tasks

expressions.nuance: 물그릇 = 'water bowl' (물 'water' + 그릇 'bowl'), and 밥그릇 = 'food bowl' — Koreans use these compound words naturally for pet dishes. The verb choices carry real distinctions: 채우다 = 'to fill up' (add water to an existing amount), 갈다 = 'to change / replace' (dump and refill with fresh), 비우다 = 'to empty'. In daily pet care, 갈아 주다 is the hygiene-conscious verb because cats especially need fresh water; just 채우다 implies you topped up old water. The -아/어 줄게 form ('I'll do it for you / as a favor') and -아/어 줄게 / -아/어 줘 ('do it for me') express care-giving, which is the natural register owners use toward pets in 반말. The nearest near-synonym action would be 물 넣어 줘 ('put water in'), which is understandable but less idiomatically pet-specific than 채우다/갈아 주다. Don't confuse 그릇 ('bowl, round vessel') with 접시 ('flat plate') — pets use 그릇, not 접시. Speaking to a person helping you: 물 좀 채워 주세요 (polite). The -줄게 ending is self-directed ('I'll do it'), so you say it to your pet; 갈아 줘 or 채워 줘 is what you ask of a family member helping.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 물 채워 줘 when you mean 'give fresh water'.
채우다 just adds water to what's there. To replace stale water with clean, say 물 갈아 줘 ('change the water').
Using 접시 for the water dish.
접시 is a flat plate. A pet's bowl is 그릇: 물그릇, 밥그릇.
Over-formal 채워 드릴게요 toward your pet.
Honorifics like 드리다 are for elevating people. To a pet, 반말 is normal: 물그릇 채워 줄게.

structuredNuance.t: 물그릇 채워 줄게 literally means 'I'll fill up the water bowl for you' — 채우다 = to fill, 줄게 = I'll do it (as a favor/for you). It's directed at the pet in 반말 and expresses the caring daily routine of checking and refilling water.

반말 with the affectionate -줄게 (-아/어 줄게) is the natural register when talking to your pet. To a family member helping: 물 좀 채워 줘 (반말) or 물 좀 채워 주세요 (polite). 줄게 is self-directed; 줘/주세요 is a request to someone else.

채우다 vs. 갈아 주다: 채우다 = add more water (top up), 갈아 주다 = dump the old and replace with fresh. For daily care, 갈아 주다 is the hygiene-minded choice. 물 넣어 줘 ('put water in') works but is more generic. Never 접시 for a pet bowl — use 그릇.
물 갈아 줄게 ('I'll change your water'), 밥그릇 씻어야겠다 ('I'd better wash the food bowl'), 물 다 마셨네 ('it drank all the water, huh').

Trap 1: reaching for generic 만들다 or 넣다 — the idiomatic care-verbs are 채우다 and 갈아 주다. Trap 2: using 접시 (a flat plate) for a pet bowl — pets use 그릇: 물그릇, 밥그릇. Trap 3: over-formal 채워 드릴게요 toward a pet — 드리다 honors people, not animals; keep it 반말 with -줄게.

expressions.english: I have to pick up the poop
expressions.shortExplanation: 응가 치워야 돼요 is a practical expression meaning "I have to pick up the poop".
expressions.explanation: "I have to pick up the poop" — that is 응가 치워야 돼요 (eungga chiwoya dwaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 응가 치워야 돼요 ("I have to pick up the poop"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I have to pick up the poop
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; 응가 = cute word for poop
반말; 똥 is blunter than 응가

usagePhrases.en: Did you grab a poop bag?
usagePhrases.note: 배변봉투 = poop/waste bag
오줌 (을) 싸다 = to pee; 쌌어 = peed

examples.ko: A: 여기서 잠깐만요. / B: 왜요? / A: 강아지 응가 치워야 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiseo jamkkanmanyo. / B: waeyo? / A: gangaji eungga chiwoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: One moment here. / B: What? / A: I have to pick up the poop.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing the phrase arising naturally during a walk

examples.en: I picked up the poop with a bag and came back.
examples.note: 배변봉투로 = 'using a waste bag' (instrument 로); 똥 is more blunt than 응가 but fine among friends

examples.ko: 우리 강아지 아직 화장실 못 가려요.
examples.romanization: uri gangaji aji kwajangsil mot garyeoyo.
examples.en: My dog isn't potty-trained yet.
examples.note: 화장실 가리다 = to be house-trained / able to control toileting; lit. 'distinguish the bathroom'

expressions.nuance: 치우다 = 'to clear away / clean up / pick up', the precise verb for scooping pet waste — not 청소하다 ('clean a room/surface'), which is too broad for a single pick-up action. For the waste itself, register matters: 응가 is soft and slightly babyish ('poop / number two'), widely used by owners and parents, and appropriate in polite company; 똥 is the plain, blunter everyday word for 'poop/crap', fine in 반말; and 대변 is the clinical/formal term used with a vet. A 배변봉투 ('defecation bag') is what you must carry on walks — scooping is both social etiquette and, in many Korean municipalities, the law. The nearest near-synonym command is 똥 치워 (반말, same action), so the register difference between 응가/똥/대변 is the main dividing line. Potty-training is 화장실(을) 가리다 (lit. 'to distinguish the bathroom'), and peeing is 오줌(을) 싸다 or politely 소변 보다. The English-speaker trap is 응가 잡다 — 잡다 = 'grab/catch a moving thing', completely wrong; you 치우다 ('clear away') waste. Don't say 응가 만들다 either.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 응가 잡다 to mean 'pick up the poop'.
잡다 = grab/catch (something moving). For cleaning up waste use 치우다: 응가 치워야 돼요.
Using 청소하다 for scooping a single poop.
청소하다 = clean (a whole area). For picking up pet waste, the verb is 치우다.
Saying 똥 in a formal vet conversation.
똥 is blunt/casual. In a clinic, use 대변 (feces) and 소변 (urine): 대변 색이 이상해요.

structuredNuance.t: 응가 치워야 돼요 means 'I have to clear away the poop' — 치우다 = clear/pick up (not clean a surface), 돼요 = it's required/I have to. The phrase is casual but polite, naturally said to a companion during a dog walk.

응가 is the soft polite register; use it around strangers or in mixed company. 똥 works in 반말 among friends. In a vet's office use 대변/소변. Scooping is legally required in most Korean cities during public walks.

응가 (soft/cute) vs. 똥 (blunt/casual) vs. 대변 (clinical). 치우다 vs. 청소하다: 청소 is for cleaning an area; 치우다 is for removing a discrete item of waste. 화장실 가리다 = potty-trained; 오줌 싸다 = pee (don't confuse with 소변 보다, the polite form).
응가 치웠어요 ('I picked it up', reported), 배변봉투 꼭 챙기세요 ('be sure to bring a poop bag'), 아직 응가 못 가려요 ('it can't control bowels yet', about an untrained puppy).
Trap 1: 응가 잡다 — 잡다 = grab something moving; waste is 치우다. Trap 2: 청소하다 for scooping one poop — 청소 is area-cleaning. Trap 3: using 똥 with a vet — clinical contexts require 대변/소변.

expressions.english: Does it need to get vaccinated?
expressions.shortExplanation: 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Does it need to get vaccinated?".
expressions.explanation: 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? (yebangjeopjong majaya dwaeyo?) = "Does it need to get vaccinated?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? ("Does it need a vaccination?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the vet
Reporting it's done (접종하다)
접종 = the shot; short form

usagePhrases.en: I got it the rabies shot
usagePhrases.note: 주사 맞히다 = have (it) get a shot

examples.ko: A: 선생님, 이번에 어떤 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? / B: 종합백신이랑 광견병 맞으세요.
examples.romanization: A: seonsaengnim, ibeone eotteon yebangjeopjong majaya dwaeyo? / B: jonghapbaeksinirang gwanggyeonbyeong majeuseyo.
examples.en: A: Doctor, what vaccinations does it need this time? / B: Give it the combo vaccine and rabies shot.
examples.note: A/B vet exchange using 맞다 (pet receives shot); 종합백신 = combination/multi-vaccine

examples.en: I had it get the rabies vaccine this time.
examples.note: 맞히다 (causative) = I had/made it receive the shot; owner is the agent

examples.en: Bring the vaccination record card.
examples.note: 접종 기록 = vaccination record (the clinic gives you a card to keep)

expressions.nuance: 예방접종 = 'preventive vaccination' (예방 prevention + 접종 'inoculation'), the umbrella word for pet shots; 광견병 = rabies, a key annual vaccine. The verb structure is a classic learner minefield: 주사/접종을 맞다 = '(the patient) receives a shot' — in Korean the receiver 'gets hit' by the shot; 맞히다 is the causative = '(I) have it receive a shot'. So your dog 주사를 맞아요 ('gets the shot'), and you 주사를 맞혔어요 ('had it vaccinated'). The nearest near-synonym phrase is 주사 맞았어요 ('got the shot'), which swaps 예방접종 for 주사 but uses the same verb. English speakers wrongly import 'inject' as 주사하다 about themselves — for receiving, it's 맞다; saying 주사를 해요 or 주사를 때려요 are both wrong. This phrase is polite-neutral, perfect for the 동물병원. Note: 동물병원 ('animal hospital') is the standard word for a vet clinic — the vet is 수의사(선생님). Keep your 접종 기록 (vaccine record) safe; clinics ask for it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주사를 해요 / 주사하다 for getting a shot.
To receive an injection, Korean uses 맞다: 주사를 맞아요. 주사하다 isn't how you say 'get a shot'.
Confusing 맞다 (the pet gets it) with 맞히다 (you have it get it).
강아지가 주사를 맞아요 = the dog gets the shot. (제가) 강아지한테 주사를 맞혔어요 = I had it vaccinated. Pick by who's doing what.
Calling the vet clinic 병원 only.
병원 alone implies a human hospital. The vet is 동물병원: 동물병원 가야 돼요.

structuredNuance.t: 예방접종 (예방+접종, prevention+inoculation) literally means preventive vaccination. 맞아야 돼요? = 'does it need to receive (it)?', using 맞다 = to receive a shot, literally 'to be hit'. The question politely asks the vet about the pet's vaccination schedule.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, exactly right for the vet. In casual chat with another owner: 예방접종 했어? (반말). The vet is 수의사(선생님); the clinic is 동물병원 — never just 병원 (human hospital).
예방접종 맞아야 돼요? vs. 주사 맞아야 돼요?: 예방접종 specifies a scheduled preventive vaccine; 주사 is any injection. 맞다 (pet receives it) vs. 맞히다 (owner causes it): 강아지가 주사를 맞아요 vs. (내가) 강아지한테 주사를 맞혔어요.
접종 기록 확인해 주세요 ('please check the vaccine record'), 추가 접종 필요해요? ('does it need a booster?'), 예방접종 스케줄 알려 주세요 ('please tell me the vaccination schedule').

Trap 1: 주사를 해요 or 주사하다 for getting a shot — for receiving, it's 맞다: 주사를 맞아요. Trap 2: confusing 맞다 (pet gets it) with 맞히다 (you make it get it) — pick by who's doing what. Trap 3: 병원 alone for the vet clinic — say 동물병원.

expressions.shortExplanation: 동물병원 예약했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I made a vet appointment".
expressions.explanation: 동물병원 예약했어요 (dongmulbyeongwon yeyakaesseoyo) means "I made a vet appointment". Say it as one set phrase — for example 동물병원 예약했어요 ("I made a vet appointment"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting it's booked

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to book the clinic
usagePhrases.note: Saying it to the clinic / on the phone
진료 받다 = receive a medical exam
접수 = reception/check-in at a clinic

examples.ko: A: 오늘 강아지 좀 이상해 보여요. / B: 동물병원 예약했어요? / A: 네, 오늘 오후 예약했어요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul gangaji jom isanghae boyeoyo. / B: dongmulbyeongwon yeyakaesseoyo? / A: ne, oneul ohu yeyakaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: The dog looks a bit off today. / B: Did you make a vet appointment? / A: Yes, I booked this afternoon.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 예약하다 as the natural step after noticing a health concern

examples.en: I called to book my dog's exam.
examples.note: 진료 = medical consultation/exam; distinguishes from mere 예약 (booking)

examples.en: Tell them the name and symptoms at reception.
examples.note: 접수처 = the reception desk; 증상 = symptoms — give these on arrival, not just 예약

expressions.nuance: 예약하다 = 'to reserve / book' (an appointment, table, ticket), and 동물병원 예약 is how you book a vet visit. Korean clinics have three distinct steps English speakers often collapse: 예약 (book in advance), 접수 (check in / register on arrival at the desk), and 진료 (the actual exam/consultation from the doctor). You 예약하다 by phone or app, 접수하다 at the desk on arrival, then 진료(를) 받다 ('receive an exam'). The nearest near-synonym is 진료 예약했어요, which is slightly more specific. A critical error: 약속 means 'a promise / personal plans with someone', not a booked business appointment — say 예약, not 약속. Also, 진료 받다 uses 받다 ('to receive') — YOU receive the exam from the doctor; saying 진료해요 about yourself is wrong (진료하다 is what the doctor does). The clinic will call you 보호자분 ('guardian'), which is how Korean vets refer to pet owners — a telling sign of how seriously pet ownership is treated. This phrase is polite-neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 약속 for a clinic appointment.
약속 is a promise / plans with a person. A booked business appointment is 예약: 동물병원 예약했어요.
Saying 진료해요 to mean 'I'm getting an exam'.
진료하다 is what the doctor does (examines). The patient side is 진료(를) 받다: 진료 받으러 왔어요.
Skipping 접수 and going straight to the vet.
Korean clinics have you 접수 (check in) at the desk first. Say 접수 먼저 할게요 on arrival, then wait to be called.

structuredNuance.t: 예약하다 = 'to reserve / book' — 동물병원 예약했어요 reports that you've booked a vet visit in advance. It is the standard phrase whether you booked by phone, app, or in person.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, correct for reporting to family, another owner, or the clinic itself. On the phone to book: 강아지 진료 예약하고 싶은데요 ('I'd like to book my dog for an exam'). At arrival: 접수 먼저 할게요.

예약 (book in advance) vs. 접수 (check in on arrival) vs. 진료 (the actual exam): these are three separate steps — using only 예약 for all three confuses the staff. 약속 is a personal promise/plan with a person, not a booked service appointment — never 동물병원 약속했어요.
예약 취소할게요 ('I'll cancel the appointment'), 예약 변경하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to change the appointment'), 당일 예약 돼요? ('do you accept same-day bookings?').

Trap 1: 약속 for a vet appointment — 약속 is for personal social plans; booked services are 예약. Trap 2: 진료해요 about yourself — 진료하다 is the doctor's action; the patient side is 진료(를) 받다. Trap 3: skipping 접수 when you arrive — Koreans always check in (접수) at the desk first.

expressions.english: Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?
expressions.shortExplanation: 어디가 아파요? is a practical expression meaning "Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?".
expressions.explanation: "Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?" — that is 어디가 아파요? (eodiga apayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 어디가 아파요? ("Where does it hurt?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: What the vet asks; you describe the symptom
안 먹어요 = refuses food (a key symptom)
토하다 = to throw up; 계속 = continuously
다리를 절다 = to limp

examples.ko: A: 어디가 아파요? / B: 어제부터 밥을 안 먹고 자꾸 토해요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiga apayo? / B: eojebuteo babeul an meokgo jakku tohaeyo.
examples.en: A: What's wrong / where does it hurt? / B: Since yesterday it won't eat and keeps throwing up.
examples.note: A/B vet exchange showing the expected answer format: onset (어제부터) + specific symptoms

examples.en: The cat keeps throwing up and has no energy.
examples.note: 기운이 없다 = to be lethargic / low energy — key symptom to name; 자꾸 = repeatedly

examples.en: It seems to hurt when I touch here.
examples.note: 아파하다 = to show/express pain (for observed others); -것 같다 = 'it seems'; use 아파하다, not 아프다, for the pet

expressions.nuance: 아프다 = 'to be sick / hurt / in pain', and 어디가 아파요? ('where does it hurt?') is the vet's opening question — you'll mainly ANSWER by describing symptoms concretely. A subtle but important grammatical point: 아프다 describes YOUR OWN felt pain, but for an animal or another person whose pain you are observing from outside, Korean uses 아파하다 ('to show/exhibit pain') — so 강아지가 아파해요 ('the dog is showing signs of pain') is the careful form; casually owners say 아파요 too and it's understood. The nearest near-synonym question is 뭐가 문제예요? ('what's the problem?'), which is more general; 어디가 아파요? specifically invites a body-area or symptom answer. Key symptom vocabulary: 토하다 (vomit — NOT 뱉다 which is deliberate spitting), 설사하다 (have diarrhea), 절다 (limp), 기운이 없다 (lethargic), 안 먹다 (won't eat). English speakers often say 'sick' and stop — but Korean vets expect the onset (언제부터, 'since when') and the concrete symptom. Give time with -부터: 어제부터, 아침부터.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying only '아파요' without naming the symptom.
Vets need specifics. Add the symptom and onset: 어제부터 밥을 안 먹고 토해요.
Using 아프다 vs. 아파하다 loosely for the pet.
Strictly, you feel 아프다; an animal you observe 아파하다 (shows pain). 강아지가 아파해요 is the careful form.
Saying 뱉어요 to mean 'it vomits'.
뱉다 = spit out (deliberately). Vomiting is 토하다: 자꾸 토해요.

structuredNuance.t: 어디가 아파요? literally asks 'where is it that it hurts?' — a vet's diagnostic opener. When you hear this question, the expected answer is the onset time (언제부터) + the specific symptom(s), not just 'sick'.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, used by the vet asking you. Your answer should also be polite (존댓말) since you're talking to a professional. Use clinical terms in a vet context: 대변/소변, 구토, 설사, 식욕부진.

아프다 (I feel pain — self-referential) vs. 아파하다 (observed other shows pain). A dog 아파해요, not 아프다, when you're describing what you see. Also: 토하다 (vomit) vs. 뱉다 (deliberately spit out) — dogs 토해요, they don't 뱉어요.
증상이 어떻게 돼요? ('what are the symptoms?'), 언제부터 그랬어요? ('since when has it been like this?'), 아파하는 부위가 있어요? ('is there a specific area where it shows pain?').

Trap 1: saying only '아파요' without a symptom or onset — vets need 언제부터 + what symptom. Trap 2: 아프다 for an animal (strictly for self-reported pain): use 아파하다 for observed pain. Trap 3: 뱉어요 for vomiting — 뱉다 = spit deliberately; vomiting is 토하다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 중성화 수술 했어요 is a practical expression meaning "It's been neutered/spayed (had the surgery)".
expressions.explanation: 중성화 수술 했어요 (jungseonghwa susul haesseoyo) = "It's been neutered/spayed (had the surgery)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 중성화 수술 했어요 ("It's been neutered/spayed"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 중성화 covers both sexes
Common question between owners
안 했어요 = haven't done it
회복 중 = in recovery

examples.ko: A: 중성화 수술 했어요? / B: 네, 작년에 수술했어요. 지금은 완전히 회복됐어요.
examples.romanization: A: jungseonghwa susul haesseoyo? / B: ne, jangnyeone susulhaesseoyo. jigeumeun wanjeonhi hoebokdwaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Is it neutered/spayed? / B: Yes, it had surgery last year. It's fully recovered now.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 중성화 했어요? as a standard owner-to-owner question

examples.en: Neutering makes them a bit calmer.
examples.note: 차분해지다 = to become calm/settled; owners discuss behavioral benefits

examples.ko: 수술한 데 핥지 못하게 넥카라 씌웠어요.
examples.romanization: susulhan de haltji motage nekkara ssuiwosseoyo.
examples.en: I put a cone on so it can't lick the incision.
examples.note: 넥카라 (neck collar/Elizabethan cone) = the protective cone; 씌우다 = put it on (over the head)

expressions.nuance: 중성화 = 'neutering / spaying' (中性化, lit. 'making neutral in sex'), and critically this one word covers BOTH male neutering AND female spaying — unlike English, Korean doesn't need separate terms. 중성화 수술 했어요 is the standard polite phrase between owners and at the vet. The verb 수술(을) 하다 = 'to have/do surgery'; from the owner's side 했어요 is natural even though technically the vet performs it — Korean lets the responsible party say 했어요. The nearest near-synonym is 거세 했어요 ('castrated'), but 거세 is blunt and clinical, used only for male animals in clinical or agricultural settings; for a pet, 중성화 is always more appropriate. Saying 고쳤어요 ('I fixed it', using 고치다 = repair a broken thing) is a direct English-trap error — the procedure is not 'fixing' an object. Related care vocabulary: 넥카라 (the protective Elizabethan cone, from 'neck collar'), 회복 ('recovery'), 수술 부위 ('surgical site'), 핥다 ('to lick' — pets must be prevented from licking the wound). Keep 수술 with 하다/받다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 거세 for a pet's neutering.
거세 (castration) is blunt/clinical. The standard, gentle term for both sexes is 중성화: 중성화 수술 했어요.
Saying 고쳤어요 to mean 'got it fixed/neutered'.
고치다 = repair a broken thing. For the procedure say 중성화 수술 했어요, not 고쳤어요.
Assuming 중성화 only means male neutering.
중성화 covers spaying females too. You don't switch words by sex — 암컷도 중성화 한다 ('females are also neutered').

structuredNuance.t: 중성화 (中性化) literally means 'making neutral/neuter in sex' — it applies to both males and females, covering both English concepts 'neuter' and 'spay' with a single word. 중성화 수술 했어요 reports the procedure is done.

Polite-neutral 존댓말, standard between owners and at the vet. 중성화 했어요? is a very common get-to-know-your-pet question among dog park acquaintances — it's not considered rude. With a close friend: 중성화 했어? (반말).

중성화 covers both sexes — no need for separate 'neuter' vs. 'spay' distinctions. 거세 (castration) is the literal clinical/agricultural term for males; it feels blunt or harsh for a pet. 고치다 ('repair/fix') is wrong entirely — it's for broken objects, not living beings.
중성화 수술 받았어요 ('it received the surgery' — pet-side perspective), 회복 중이에요 ('in recovery'), 수술 부위 잘 낫고 있어요 ('the surgical site is healing well').
중성화 is 中性化, 'making neuter/neutral in sex'. The -화 (化) suffix means 'making X' or 'becoming X', as in 현대화 (modernization), 자동화 (automation).

Trap 1: 거세 — too blunt/clinical for pet talk; use 중성화. Trap 2: 고쳤어요 for 'got it fixed' — 고치다 = repair an object; the procedure is 중성화 수술 했어요. Trap 3: thinking 중성화 only means male neutering — it covers females (spaying) equally.

expressions.shortExplanation: 물어요? is a practical expression meaning "Does it bite?".
expressions.explanation: 물어요? (mureoyo?) means "Does it bite?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 물어요? ("Does it bite?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask BEFORE petting a stranger's dog
Asking permission to touch
Reassuring answer; 안 물어요
순하다 = mild-tempered

examples.ko: A: 강아지 만져도 돼요? / B: 네, 안 물어요. 순해요.
examples.romanization: A: gangaji manjyeodo dwaeyo? / B: ne, an mureoyo. sunhaeyo.
examples.en: A: May I pet your dog? / B: Yes, it doesn't bite. It's gentle.
examples.note: A/B exchange modeling the essential stranger-dog etiquette sequence

examples.en: My dog doesn't bite, it's gentle.
examples.note: 순하다 = good-natured, docile; reassures the asker fully

examples.ko: 낯선 사람 보면 좀 짖어요, 물진 않아요.
examples.romanization: natseon saram bomyeon jom jijeoyo, muljin anayo.
examples.en: It barks a bit at strangers, but it doesn't bite.
examples.note: 짖다 = to bark; distinguishes barking from biting — an important nuance for nervous strangers

expressions.nuance: 물다 = 'to bite', and 물어요? plus 만져도 돼요? ('may I pet it?') are the two essential phrases to say before touching a stranger's dog — social etiquette in Korea. The permission frame -아도 돼요? = 'is it okay if I...?' applies here for approach. The nearest near-synonym pair for the answer side is 순해요 (gentle/docile) vs. 사나워요 (fierce/aggressive) — knowing these lets you reassure OR warn. The critical sound-alike trap: 물다 (bite) sounds similar to 묻다 (ask / bury / stain) — both give 물어요 in present tense; only context (a dog) tells you apart. Also confuse learners: 짖다 = 'to bark' (noise, not necessarily dangerous), 으르렁거리다 = 'to growl' (warning sign), 물다 = 'to bite' (action) — a barking dog isn't necessarily a biting one. Don't say 물기 해요 or import 'bite' oddly; the plain present tense of 물다 is 물어요. Petting culture: always ask 만져도 돼요? first — reaching out silently can startle the dog and annoy its owner, even if the dog is friendly. This is polite-neutral.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 물다 (bite) with 짖다 (bark).
물어요? = does it bite? 짖어요 = it barks. A barking dog isn't necessarily biting — use the right verb.
Petting a stranger's dog without asking.
Always ask first: 만져도 돼요? 물어요? Reaching out silently can startle the dog and annoy the owner.
Mixing 물다 (bite) and 묻다 (ask).
Both can surface as 물어요, but from different verbs. With a dog, 물어요? = 'does it bite?' Keep the base verbs straight.

structuredNuance.t: 물어요? literally means 'does it bite?' — from 물다 'to bite', conjugated politely. It is the essential safety question before touching any dog you don't know. Paired naturally with 만져도 돼요? as a two-part permission-and-safety check.

Polite-neutral 존댓말, perfect for approaching a stranger with a dog. With friends asking about your dog informally: 물어? (반말). Petting culture: always ask before reaching out — silent approach is impolite and can startle the animal.

물다 (bite) vs. 짖다 (bark) vs. 으르렁거리다 (growl): these are three distinct behaviors. A barking dog (짖어요) is not necessarily biting. The temperament vocabulary: 순하다 (gentle/docile) vs. 사납다 (fierce/aggressive) vs. 낯을 가리다 (shy around strangers).
물 것 같아요 ('it looks like it might bite', caution), 잘 안 물어요 ('it rarely bites'), 처음에는 짖는데 금방 친해져요 ('it barks at first but warms up quickly').

Trap 1: confusing 물다 (bite) and 묻다 (ask/bury) — both give 물어요; a dog 물어요? = 'does it bite?', not 'does it ask?'. Trap 2: saying 물기 해요 — the plain verb 물다 conjugates 물어요 without any extra structure. Trap 3: confusing 짖다 (bark) with 물다 (bite) in descriptions.

expressions.english: Please put it on a leash
expressions.shortExplanation: 목줄 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please put it on a leash".
expressions.explanation: "Please put it on a leash" — that is 목줄 해 주세요 (mokjul hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 목줄 해 주세요 ("Please leash it"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request; 목줄 = leash/collar lead
채우다 = to fasten (a leash/collar)
입마개 = muzzle (required for some breeds)
짧게 잡다 = hold (the lead) short

examples.ko: A: 여기는 목줄 꼭 해 주세요. / B: 아, 죄송해요. 지금 할게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogineun mokjul kko kae juseyo. / B: a, joesonghaeyo. jigeum halgeyo.
examples.en: A: Please keep it on a leash here. / B: Oh, sorry. I'll do it now.
examples.note: A/B exchange of a gentle reminder about the leash rule — 꼭 = without fail

examples.en: Large dogs must also wear a muzzle.
examples.note: 대형견 = large-breed dog; 입마개 = muzzle; legally required in Korea for certain breeds

examples.en: In the elevator, hold it or keep the leash short.
examples.note: 안다 = to hold in arms; 짧게(요) = keep it short — elevator etiquette in apartment buildings

expressions.nuance: 목줄 = 'leash / collar-lead' (목 'neck' + 줄 'cord/line'), the standard everyday word; 가슴줄 / 하네스 = 'harness' (chest lead, for dogs prone to neck strain). 목줄 (을) 하다 or 채우다 = 'to put on / fasten a leash'. In Korea, leashing your dog in public is legally required, and certain large or aggressive breeds must also wear an 입마개 ('muzzle', 입 'mouth' + 마개 'plug/stopper'). The nearest near-synonym action is 목줄 채워 주세요 (slightly more specific: 'please fasten the leash on'), while 묶어 주세요 (tie it up) would imply tethering to a fixed object — a distinct concept. The English-speaker trap is calling a leash 끈 (generic 'string/strap') — understandable but 목줄 is the specific proper term. Don't use 묶다 for routine walking; 묶다 implies tying to a post and doesn't match leash-walking. The verb 채우다 here means 'to fasten/clip' — same verb as filling a bowl, but context tells you apart: leash = fasten, bowl = fill. This phrase is polite, exactly right for asking another owner or leaving a note in a community. Korean apartment etiquette: in elevators, many owners 안아요 (carry) small dogs or keep the 목줄 짧게 (short) as a courtesy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling a leash just 끈.
끈 is a generic strap/string. The specific word is 목줄 (leash) or 하네스/가슴줄 (harness).
Using 묶다 for leashing on a walk.
묶다 = tie up (to a post). Routine leashing is 목줄 하다 / 잡다. Say 목줄 해 주세요, not 묶어 주세요, for normal walks.
Forgetting the muzzle term 입마개.
Some large breeds legally need a muzzle: 입마개. Don't invent 입 가리개; the standard word is 입마개.

structuredNuance.t: 목줄 (목=neck + 줄=cord) = leash/collar-lead. 해 주세요 = please do (it) for (me/us), a polite request. 목줄 해 주세요 is both a courteous reminder and, in public spaces, a reference to a legal requirement. 입마개 (입=mouth + 마개=plug) = muzzle.
목줄 해 주세요 is polite 존댓말, ideal for asking a stranger owner. In apartment communities or parks, a sign might say 반드시 목줄 착용 ('leash required without exception'). With a family member: 목줄 해 줘 (반말).

목줄 하다 / 채우다 (fasten the leash, for walking) vs. 묶다 (tie to a fixed point, like a post). Use 목줄 채우다 for leashing during a walk; 묶어 두다 for tying the dog to something. 끈 (generic string) is too vague — use 목줄 specifically.
목줄 착용 의무 ('mandatory leash requirement', official signage), 목줄 채웠어요? ('did you put the leash on?', checking), 하네스로 바꿨어요 ('I switched to a harness').

Trap 1: 끈 for a leash — too generic; use 목줄 (or 하네스/가슴줄 for a harness). Trap 2: 묶어 주세요 for 'please leash it' — 묶다 = tie to a post, not leash-walk; say 목줄 해 주세요. Trap 3: forgetting 입마개 — some large breeds legally need a muzzle, not just a leash.

expressions.english: It was so cute that I adopted it
expressions.shortExplanation: 예뻐서 입양했어요 is a practical expression meaning "It was so cute that I adopted it".
expressions.explanation: 예뻐서 입양했어요 (yeppeoseo ibyanghaesseoyo) = "It was so cute that I adopted it". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 입양했어요 ("I adopted (it)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 입양 = adoption (of a pet or child)
유기견 = abandoned/stray dog

usagePhrases.en: I brought it from a shelter
usagePhrases.note: 데려오다 = bring (a living being) home
분양받다 = obtain a pet (often paid)

examples.ko: A: 어디서 데려왔어요? / B: 유기견 보호소에서 입양했어요. 처음에는 좀 무서워했어요.
examples.romanization: A: eodiseo deryeowasseoyo? / B: yugigyeon bohosoeseo ibyanghaesseoyo. cheoeumeneun jom museowohaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Where did you get it from? / B: I adopted it from a shelter. At first it was a bit scared.
examples.note: A/B exchange showing 입양하다 in context of a shelter rescue; 무서워하다 = to be scared

examples.en: I brought a dog home from a shelter.
examples.note: 데려오다 = bring home a living being — warmer and correct; 가져오다 = bring an object (wrong for animals)

examples.en: Adopting beats buying from a pet shop.
examples.note: 분양받다 (acquire from a breeder/shop) contrasted with 입양하다 (adopt a rescue)

expressions.nuance: 입양 = 'adoption' (入養), used for both adopting a child and taking in a pet — 입양했어요 is the warm, socially valued word for giving a rescue animal a home. The key contrast is 입양 (adopt from a shelter/rescue) vs. 분양 (acquire from a breeder or pet shop, usually for a fee). Animal-welfare-minded Koreans cite the slogan 사지 말고 입양하세요 ('don't buy, adopt'). The verb for bringing the animal home is 데려오다 ('to bring a person/animal along') — the verb 데리다 marks the animal as a companion being, not a thing; using 가져오다 ('bring an object') for a pet sounds cold and wrong. The nearest near-synonym phrase is 보호소에서 데려왔어요, which focuses on the action of bringing it home; 입양했어요 formally names the relationship (adoption). The English-speaker trap is using 사다 ('to buy') — while pets can be purchased, 사다 in casual pet conversation sounds blunt or mercenary; 분양받다 or 입양하다 are the natural choices. Another trap: 채택하다 = 'adopt (a plan/idea)' — completely wrong for a living being. This is polite-neutral; related terms: 보호소 (shelter), 임시보호 ('temporary fostering'), 유기 ('abandonment / being abandoned').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 가져왔어요 about bringing a pet home.
가져오다 is for objects. For a living animal use 데려오다: 보호소에서 데려왔어요.
Using 채택하다 for adopting an animal.
채택하다 = adopt a plan/idea. Adopting a pet (or child) is 입양하다: 강아지를 입양했어요.
Calling shelter adoption 분양.
분양 implies obtaining (often buying) from a breeder/shop. Taking in a rescue is 입양; the source is a 보호소.

structuredNuance.t: 입양 (入養) literally means 'entering and raising' — it is the formal but commonly used word for adopting a child or a pet from a rescue situation. 예뻐서 입양했어요 = 'I adopted it because it was so cute', explaining the personal motivation behind adoption.

Polite-neutral 존댓말. 입양하다 is used in both formal and casual speech. Animal welfare culture in Korea increasingly values 입양 over purchasing; saying 입양했어요 often prompts warm responses from fellow owners.

입양하다 (adopt from shelter/rescue, usually free or donation) vs. 분양받다 (acquire from breeder/shop, usually paid). Also: 데려오다 (bring a living being home — correct for pets) vs. 가져오다 (bring an object — wrong for animals). 채택하다 = adopt a plan/idea, not a living being.
입양 is 入養, literally 'entering and raising/nurturing', used for both child adoption and pet adoption in Korean.
