The dividing line against 화나다 is degree and direction: 짜증 나다 is low-grade, diffuse annoyance ('ugh, this again'), while 화나다 is real anger directed at someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb form: don't say 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — the correct forms are 짜증(이) 나다 (it arises) or 짜증 내다 (you express it). Another pitfall is register: even 짜증 나요 carries a raw, blunt edge, so to an elder or boss soften to 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — there's no verb 짜증하다; it's 짜증(이) 나다 (irritation arises) or 짜증 내다 (to show irritation).
Using 짜증 나요 with a boss or elder — even the -요 form is raw/blunt; soften to 좀 힘드네요 / 불편하네요 in respectful settings.
Confusing 짜증 나다 with 화나다 — 짜증 나다 is low-grade peevish annoyance, while 화나다 is genuine anger at someone; they differ in intensity.

structuredNuance.t: 짜증 나 is literally 'irritation arises' — 짜증 (noun: irritation/peevishness) + 나다 (to arise). The real meaning is the prickly, low-grade frustration of small things getting on your nerves. It's NOT deep anger — it's the 'ugh, again?!' feeling.

짜증 나 is casual banmal — for venting to friends or peers. 짜증 나요 is polite but still blunt in flavor — fine with coworkers your age but avoid with elders or bosses. With seniors, soften to 좀 힘드네요 (a bit tough), 불편하네요 (a bit uncomfortable), or 어렵네요 (it's difficult).

짜증 나다 = irritation arises (passive; something is getting on your nerves). 화나다 = anger arises at someone (stronger, directed outward). 짜증 내다 = you actively EXPRESS or show your irritation (can annoy others around you). 짜증 나다 + 화가 나다 can co-occur when something both annoys and angers.

Saying 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — there's no verb 짜증하다; it's 짜증(이) 나다 (irritation arises) or 짜증 내다 (to show irritation). Using 짜증 나요 with a boss or elder — even with -요 it's too raw; use 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요. Confusing 짜증 나다 with 화나다 — the first is low-grade diffuse annoyance, the second is real anger at someone.

expressions.english: I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.
expressions.shortExplanation: 신난다 is a practical expression meaning "I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.".
expressions.explanation: 신난다 (sinnanda) means "I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 신난다 ("yay, I'm so excited"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: casual exclamatory, to oneself or friends
casual banmal, plain form
polite -요, cheerful but informal
with 완전 to amp up the excitement

examples.ko: A: 내일 여행 가! / B: 신난다!
examples.romanization: A: naeil yeohaeng ga! / B: sinnanda!
examples.en: A: We go on the trip tomorrow! / B: Yay!
examples.note: the bare reaction — bubbling joy at something coming; exclamatory -다 form is natural here

examples.en: A: We finish early today, so I'm excited.
examples.note: everyday: casual self-expression of happy excitement; 신나 as a plain statement to a friend

examples.ko: A: 콘서트 티켓 구했어! / B: 진짜? 신난다! 빨리 가고 싶다.
examples.romanization: A: konseoteu tiket guhaesseo! / B: jinjja? sinnanda! ppalli gago sipda.
examples.en: A: I got the concert tickets! / B: Really? Yay! I can't wait to go.
examples.note: real situation: 신난다 + 빨리 가고 싶다 is a very natural chain — the excitement immediately becomes eager anticipation

expressions.nuance: 신난다 is bright, bubbling excitement — 'yay, this is so fun / I can't wait!' — the happy energy buzz before or during something enjoyable. Built from 신(이) 나다 'spirit/mood arises': plain 신나 (casual), exclamatory 신난다, polite 신나요. Because it's cheerful and casual, it's perfect among friends but too breezy for formal settings. The variant ladder: 신나 → 신난다 → 완전 신난다 (hyped). The dividing line against 기대돼요 and 재미있다: 신나다 is active, energetic excitement right now (you're bouncing); 기대되다 is calm, forward-looking anticipation ('I'm looking forward to it'); 재미있다 describes how fun an activity actually IS or WAS (not about anticipation). Road-trip vibe the night before → 신난다; quietly looking forward to seeing an old friend → 기대돼요; describing how the trip turned out → 재미있었어. The English-speaker pitfall is using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or anger) and sounds very off for innocent fun; the right word for happy excitement is 신나다. A second pitfall is expressing enthusiasm to a superior with 신난다 — it's too casual; use 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'excited' as 흥분되다 — that means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or anger); cheerful excitement is 신나다.
Saying 신난다 to a boss to show enthusiasm — it's breezy and casual; in respectful settings use 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.
Forming it as 신하다 or 신해 — there's no such verb; it's 신(이) 나다, so the forms are 신나 / 신난다 / 신나요.

structuredNuance.t: 신난다 comes from 신(이) 나다 — 신 (spirit/energy/mood) + 나다 (to arise). Literally 'the spirit arises.' As a reaction it means 'I'm buzzing with excitement / yay!' — active, energetic, happy anticipation.
신나 (casual plain) → 신난다 (casual exclamatory) → 신나요 (polite but informal-flavored). 완전 신난다 intensifies. With a superior or in a formal setting, switch to 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다 — 신난다 sounds too breezy.

신나다 = active, energetic excitement right now (you're bouncing with enthusiasm). 기대되다 = calm forward-looking anticipation ('I'm looking forward to it'). 재미있다 = describes how fun an activity IS or WAS (assessment). Trip-eve energy → 신난다; quietly anticipating → 기대돼요; recounting how fun it was → 재미있었어.

Using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or even anger) and sounds jarring for innocent fun. The right word for happy excitement is 신나다. Using 신난다 with a boss or superior — it's casual; switch to 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.

expressions.english: Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.
expressions.shortExplanation: 깜짝이야 is a practical expression meaning "Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.".
expressions.explanation: "Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly." — that is 깜짝이야 (kkamjjagiya). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 깜짝이야 ("you scared me!"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, instant startle reaction
with 아 as the natural gasp lead-in
fuller form, mild complaint
polite -어요, to someone you respect

examples.ko: (친구가 갑자기 등장) A: 야! / B: 아, 깜짝이야!
examples.romanization: (chinguga gapjagi deungjang) A: ya! / B: a, kkamjjagiya!
examples.en: (friend pops up suddenly) A: Hey! / B: Oh, you scared me!
examples.note: the bare startle — instant reflex; 아 leads in naturally before 깜짝이야

examples.ko: A: 뒤에서 갑자기 부르지 마, 깜짝이야.
examples.romanization: A: dwieseo gapjagi bureuji ma, kkamjjagiya.
examples.en: A: Don't call me from behind suddenly, you scared me.
examples.note: everyday: mild complaint after being startled — 깜짝이야 at the end explains WHY the request is being made

examples.ko: A: (문 열다 마주침) 어머! / B: 아, 깜짝 놀랐어요. 안에 계신 줄 몰랐어요.
examples.romanization: A: (mun yeolda majuchim) eomeo! / B: a, kkamjjang nollasseoyo. ane gyesin jul mollasseoyo.
examples.en: A: (opens door, bumps into someone) Oh! / B: Oh, you startled me. I didn't know you were inside.
examples.note: real situation: polite 깜짝 놀랐어요 to a senior after a mutual startle — you can't use 깜짝이야 politely, so you switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요

expressions.nuance: 깜짝이야 is the reflex 'whoa, you scared me!' that bursts out the instant something startles you — a friend appearing suddenly, a loud noise, a jump-scare. It comes from 깜짝 (the mimetic/sound-symbolic word for a sudden flinch) + 이야 (casual 이다 declaration). Because it's a raw reflex exclamation it's inherently casual; there's no polite 깜짝이에요 that sounds natural. In a respectful situation you switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요 ('I was startled') which carries the same meaning with -어요 politeness. The dividing line against 무섭다 ('I'm scared/afraid') is duration: 깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 is a momentary jolt that's over in a second, while 무섭다 is sustained fear or dread (a horror movie, a threatening person). A friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; a dark alley at night → 무서워. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 너 나를 무섭게 했어 ('you scared me' — literal translation) — that's unnatural; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Another pitfall is treating 놀라다 as transitive: you can't 'scare someone' directly with 놀라다 — the person 놀라다 (gets startled); to say you startled them use 놀라게 하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 너 나 무섭게 했어 for 'you scared me' — that's a literal, unnatural calque; natives say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 아, 깜짝이야.
Using 무섭다 for a momentary startle — 무섭다 is sustained fear/dread; a sudden jolt of surprise is 깜짝 놀라다 / 깜짝이야.
Treating 놀라다 as 'to scare (someone)' — the person 놀라다 (is startled); to startle them you say 놀라게 하다, since 놀라다 itself is intransitive.

structuredNuance.t: 깜짝이야 is built from 깜짝 — a mimetic (sound-symbolic) word for a sudden flinch or start — + 이야 (casual copula). Literally 'it's a 깜짝!' meaning 'what a shock!' As a reaction it means 'you startled me / you scared me!' — an instant, involuntary exclamation.

깜짝이야 is casual/banmal — a raw reflex that you can't really dress up. With a senior or in a formal situation, switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요 ('I was startled') to convey the same meaning politely. 아, 깜짝이야 with the lead-in 아 is the most natural everyday form.

깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 = momentary jolt of surprise (over in a second). 무섭다 = sustained fear/dread (horror movie, threatening situation). 헉 = a sharp gasp of fright, slightly more physical than 깜짝이야. Friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; dark alley → 무서워; sudden loud bang → 헉.

Saying 너 나 무섭게 했어 for 'you scared me' — that's a literal but unnatural calque; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Treating 놀라다 as transitive: 놀라다 is intransitive (the person gets startled); to say you caused it use 놀라게 하다. Using 무섭다 for a momentary startle — 무섭다 is sustained fear, not a flinch.

expressions.english: No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.
expressions.shortExplanation: 말도 안 돼 is a practical expression meaning "No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.".
expressions.explanation: 말도 안 돼 (maldo an dwae) = "No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 말도 안 돼 ("no way / that's ridiculous"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: casual banmal, strong disbelief
polite -요, to someone you respect
slight variant stressing 'doesn't make sense'
with 진짜 to intensify

examples.ko: A: 그 사람이 1등이래 / B: 말도 안 돼.
examples.romanization: A: geu sarami 1deungirae / B: maldo an dwae.
examples.en: A: They say that person came first / B: No way.
examples.note: the bare reaction — flat, strong disbelief; 말도 안 돼 rejects the claim as impossible, not just 'really?'

examples.ko: A: 집값이 두 배 올랐대 / B: 말도 안 돼. 어떻게 그래?
examples.romanization: A: jipgapsi du bae ollatdae / B: maldo an dwae. eotteoke geurae?
examples.en: A: They say housing prices doubled / B: That's ridiculous. How is that even possible?
examples.note: everyday: disbelief at outrageous news; 어떻게 그래? is a natural follow-up to extend the protest

examples.ko: A: 환불이 안 된다고 하시네요 / B: 네? 말도 안 돼요. 영수증도 있는데요.
examples.romanization: A: hwanburi an doendago hasineyo / B: ne? maldo an dwaeyo. yeongsujeungdo inneundeyo.
examples.en: A: They're saying no refunds / B: What? That's outrageous. I even have the receipt.
examples.note: real situation: polite 말도 안 돼요 protesting something unfair — with -요 it's still firm but directed appropriately at a service situation

expressions.nuance: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' → 'that makes no sense / no way / this is ridiculous' — a strong reaction of disbelief or protest at something absurd, shocking, or unfair. Built from 말(이) 도 안 되다 — 말 'words/speech,' 도 'even,' 안 되다 'doesn't work out.' Casual 말도 안 돼, polite 말도 안 돼요. The dividing line against 진짜? / 정말요? is strength: 진짜? is a light 'really?' that is open to it being true; 말도 안 돼 flatly rejects the claim as impossible or outrageous — much stronger. It also differs from 대박 ('wow, huge'): 대박 can be amazed positive or shocked; 말도 안 돼 specifically protests/rejects. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: 돼 is 되+어, never just 되; writing 말도 안 되 (without the final ㅓ vowel) is a very common error. Another pitfall is register/strength — 말도 안 돼요 to a superior can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 ('surely not') or 이해가 안 되네요 ('I don't quite understand').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 말도 안 되 — the form is 말도 안 돼 (되+어 = 돼); as a sentence-final reaction it must end in 돼, not 되.
Using 말도 안 돼(요) for mild surprise — it's strong rejection ('impossible/ridiculous'); for open-minded 'really?' use 진짜? / 정말요?.
Dropping 말도 안 돼요 on a superior in a dispute — it can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

structuredNuance.t: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' — the idea is so absurd or wrong that language itself can't accommodate it. In use: strong disbelief, rejection, or protest at something ridiculous or unfair. It is NOT just 'really?' — it actively denies the claim.

말도 안 돼 is casual banmal. 말도 안 돼요 is polite. Both are strong in tone, so with a superior or in a polite dispute you may need to soften further: 그럴 리가요 ('surely not'), 이해가 안 되네요 ('that doesn't quite make sense to me'). 말도 안 돼요 to a boss in anger can sound confrontational.

진짜? = light 'really?' — open-minded, you might believe it. 말도 안 돼 = strong rejection — you flatly disbelieve or protest it. 그럴 리가(요) = polite/softer disbelief ('it can't be / surely not') — same rejection, but gentler register, safer with seniors.

Spelling: 돼 = 되+어, NOT just 되; writing 말도 안 되 as a sentence-final reaction is a common error. Treating it like mild surprise — it's strong; for a light 'really?' use 진짜? or 정말요?. Using it confrontationally with a superior — soften to 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

expressions.english: Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.
expressions.shortExplanation: 어머 is a practical expression meaning "Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.".
expressions.explanation: "Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐." — that is 어머 (eomeo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 어머 ("oh my / oh!"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: neutral surprise, common (esp. women, all ages)
stronger, more emphatic gasp

usagePhrases.en: oh my, what do we do
usagePhrases.note: surprise sliding into worry
startled-apologetic, e.g. a small bump

examples.en: A: (drops a cup) / B: Oh!
examples.note: the bare gasp — instant surprise at a sudden event; pure reflex

examples.ko: A: 이거 선물이에요 / B: 어머, 뭘 이런 걸 다. 감사해요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo seonmurieyo / B: eomeo, mwol ireon geol da. gamsahaeyo.
examples.en: A: This is a gift for you / B: Oh my, you shouldn't have. Thank you.
examples.note: everyday: pleased-surprised reaction to a gift; 뭘 이런 걸 다 ('you didn't have to') is the perfect polite follow-up after 어머

examples.ko: A: 비 갑자기 쏟아진다 / B: 어머, 우산도 없는데 어떡해.
examples.romanization: A: bi gapjagi ssodajinda / B: eomeo, usando eopsneunde eotteokae.
examples.en: A: It's suddenly pouring / B: Oh my, and I don't have an umbrella, what do I do.
examples.note: real situation: 어머 triggers 어떡해 as surprise flows naturally into worry — this two-step chain is very common in women's speech

expressions.nuance: 어머 is a quick, soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — far more neutral and polite-safe than slangy 헐 or 대박. It is a pure interjection so it doesn't take -요; to be polite you follow it with a full polite sentence. The register difference: 어머 is gentle, refined surprise that anyone can use across ages and contexts, including in front of elders and in semi-formal moments where 헐 would sound rude. Stronger and more emphatic is 어머나; surprise that turns to worry naturally extends as 어머 어떡해. A social note: 어머 / 어머나 is used by everyone but has a stronger association with women's speech; men tend to reach for 어 / 어이쿠 / 헐 instead. The dividing line against 헐: 헐 is casual youth slang with a shock/dismay tilt, while 어머 is softer and registers as more composed and socially graceful. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment — with an older Korean or in a slightly formal context, 헐 can sound rude, so 어머 is the safe default. Another pitfall is treating 어머 as filler and saying it flatly; it carries genuine emotional color and should sound like a real gasp.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment, including with elders — 헐 is slang and can sound rude; 어머 is the neutral, polite-safe gasp.
Adding -요 as 어머요 — it's a reflexive interjection and doesn't take -요; for politeness, follow it with a full polite sentence.
Treating 어머 as meaningless filler — it carries genuine surprise/emotion, so saying it flatly with no feeling sounds odd; it should sound like a real gasp.

structuredNuance.t: 어머 is a soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — neutral and polite-safe across ages and contexts. It's a reflexive interjection (no -요 attached); politeness comes from the full sentence that follows.

어머 works in casual AND semi-formal settings — safe with elders, colleagues, or strangers where 헐 would sound rude. It doesn't take -요 directly. Social note: commonly used by women of all ages; men often prefer 어 / 어이쿠. 어머나 is stronger; 어머 어떡해 adds worry.

헐 = casual youth slang, shock/dismay tilt — only among friends and peers; sounds rude with elders. 어머 = softer, more refined surprise, cross-generational, polite-safe. 어이쿠 = similar neutral gasp, slightly more physical surprise (oops/ow/yikes), skewing male speech. All three are interjections that don't take -요.
어머 (base gasp) → 어머나 (stronger emphasis) → 어머 어떡해 (surprise + worry). In texts you might write 어머나 세상에 for dramatic emphasis. None of these take a -요 suffix directly.

Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment — with elders or in formal contexts 헐 is rude; 어머 is the neutral, graceful default. Adding -요 as 어머요 — interjections don't take -요; follow 어머 with a full polite sentence instead. Saying 어머 flatly without genuine surprise energy — it carries real emotional color and should sound like a true gasp.

expressions.english: I'm here to look at a place
expressions.shortExplanation: 집 보러 왔는데요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm here to look at a place".
expressions.explanation: 집 보러 왔는데요 (jip boreo wanneundeyo) = "I'm here to look at a place". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 집 보러 왔는데요 ("I came to look at a place"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I came to look at a place
usagePhrases.note: Polite; what you say walking into a 부동산 (real estate office)

usagePhrases.en: I'm here to see a place
usagePhrases.note: 반말, only with a friend tagging along, not to the agent

usagePhrases.en: I've come to look at places
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, a touch stiffer/more businesslike

usagePhrases.en: I came to look at a room
usagePhrases.note: Swap 방 ('room') when you want a one-room/studio (원룸)

examples.en: Hi, I'm here to look at a place.
examples.note: The standard opener the moment you step into the office; the -는데요 signals you're ready for the agent to take over

examples.ko: A: 원룸 보러 왔는데요, 지금 볼 수 있는 거 있어요? / B: 네, 몇 가지 준비해 뒀어요. 예산이 어떻게 되세요?
examples.romanization: A: wollum boreo wanneundeyo, jigeum bol su inneun geo isseoyo? / B: ne, myeot gaji junbihae dwosseoyo. yesani eotteoke doeseyo?
examples.en: A: I came to see studios — anything I can view now? / B: Yes, I've got a few ready. What's your budget?
examples.note: 원룸 specifies the type; 볼 수 있는 거 asks what's viewable today; the agent's reply shows how -는데요 hands the conversation over naturally

examples.ko: 학교 근처에 집 보러 왔는데요, 예산은 한 오백에 오십이요.
examples.romanization: hakgyo geuncheoe jip boreo wanneundeyo, yesaneun han obaege osibiyo.
examples.en: I'm here to look at places near the school; my budget's roughly 5 million deposit and 500k a month.
examples.note: 한 ('about') + 오백/오십 states 보증금/월세 in 만원 units — say this right after the opener so the agent filters listings for you

expressions.nuance: 집 보러 왔는데요 is 집 ('house/home') + 보러 (the -러 'in order to' form of 보다 'to see') + 왔- (past of 오다 'come') + -는데요, a soft sentence-ender that introduces a topic and invites the listener to respond. Literally 'I came in order to see places, and…' — the universal first line when you walk into a 부동산 (real-estate office). Here 보다 does NOT mean 'watch'; in the housing context it specifically means 'view/inspect a property', the way English says 'look at a place'. The nearest near-synonym is 집 구하러 왔는데요 ('I came to find/secure a place'), but the stage differs: 보러 signals you're ready to physically walk through rooms today, while 구하러 frames the broader search for housing. The English-speaker trap is dropping -는데요 for a flat 집 보러 왔어요, which is correct but blunter and doesn't invite the agent to take over. A worse trap is saying 집 찾으러 왔어요 — 찾다 ('to search for something lost') is wrong register for an agent-office visit; Koreans say 보러 or 구하러 here, never 찾으러. Keep 존댓말 with any agent; 반말 to a stranger doing business is jarringly rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 집 봐 주세요 to mean 'show me a place'.
봐 주세요 means 'please look at it (for me)' — as if asking the agent to inspect something on your behalf. To say you've come to view places, say 집 보러 왔는데요; to be shown one, 집 좀 보여 주세요.
Dropping -는데요 and stating a flat 집 보러 왔어요.
It's correct but abrupt as an opener. The soft ender 집 보러 왔는데요 hands the conversation to the agent and sounds like a real customer easing in.
Using 찾으러 instead of 보러/구하러.
찾다 is 'to search for' a lost or hidden thing. For house-hunting at an office, Koreans say 보러 왔어요 (to view) or 집 구하러 왔어요 (to secure a place), not 찾으러 왔어요.

structuredNuance.t: 집 + 보러 (to see, purpose form of 보다) + 왔- (came) + -는데요 (soft topic-opener). Literally 'I came in order to see places, and…'. Here 보다 does NOT mean 'watch'; it means 'view/inspect a property'. The -는데요 ending invites the agent to respond ('what's your budget? this way…') — it is not just filler.

This is the very first line when you walk through the door of any 부동산 (real-estate office). Always 존댓말 with an agent who is a professional stranger. The full formal variant 집 좀 보러 왔습니다 (합쇼체) is fine but sounds stiffer. 반말 (집 보러 왔어) is only appropriate when speaking to a friend who came with you, never to the agent.

집 구하러 왔는데요 ('I came to find/secure a place') differs in stage: 보러 means you're here to view units today; 구하러 frames the whole house-hunting mission. Both are natural, but 보러 is the standard opener when you're ready to physically walk through rooms.
Swap 집 for 방 (방 보러 왔는데요) when looking for a studio/one-room. Add your type upfront: 원룸 보러 왔는데요, 오피스텔 보러 왔는데요. For formal contexts use 집 좀 보러 왔습니다.

Two traps: (1) Saying 집 찾으러 왔어요 — 찾다 is for searching for a lost object; at a real-estate office Koreans say 보러 or 구하러, never 찾으러. (2) Dropping -는데요 to get 집 보러 왔어요 — grammatically correct but blunt; the soft -는데요 is what makes the opener sound like a real customer easing in.

expressions.english: Is it monthly rent or jeonse?
expressions.shortExplanation: 월세예요, 전세예요? is a practical expression meaning "Is it monthly rent or jeonse?".
expressions.explanation: 월세예요, 전세예요? (wolseyeyo, jeonseyeyo?) means "Is it monthly rent or jeonse?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 월세예요, 전세예요? ("Is it monthly rent or jeonse?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Is it monthly rent or jeonse?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking which rental scheme a listing is
반말, comparing options with a friend

usagePhrases.en: Would this be monthly or jeonse?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/more tentative with -인가요
반전세 = big deposit + smaller monthly, the in-between type

examples.en: Is this place monthly rent or jeonse?
examples.note: Pointing at one listing to pin down the scheme — ask this before any other money question

examples.ko: A: 전세는 부담돼서요, 월세로 보고 있어요. / B: 그러시면 보증금 천에 월 오십 정도 보여 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: jeonseneun budamdwaeseoyo, wolsero bogo isseoyo. / B: geureosimyeon bojeunggeum cheone wol osip jeongdo boyeo deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Jeonse is too much for me, so I'm looking at monthly. / B: In that case I'll show you places around 10M deposit and 500k a month.
examples.note: 부담되다 ('to be a burden') explains your preference; the agent's response shows how amounts are stated in 만원 units

examples.en: 10 million deposit and 500k a month — that's semi-jeonse, right?
examples.note: Naming the deposit/monthly split to confirm it's 반전세 — use this to show you understand the system

expressions.nuance: 월세 (月貰) and 전세 (傳貰) are the two pillars of Korean renting, so you'll ask this constantly. 월세 means you pay a deposit (보증금) plus rent every month, like renting in most countries. 전세 is uniquely Korean: you hand the landlord one enormous lump sum — often 50–80% of the home's market value — for the whole lease term, pay zero monthly rent, and get every won back at move-out; the landlord profits by investing your money. A third type, 반전세 ('half-jeonse'), sits in the middle: a larger-than-월세 deposit plus a smaller monthly fee. The key distinction learners blur is 보증금 vs. 전세금: in 월세 the deposit is a modest security 보증금; in 전세 that lump sum IS the rent mechanism (전세금/전셋돈) and is not a 'deposit' in the Western sense. The copula trap: after a vowel-ending noun, Korean contracts 이에요 to 예요, so it must be 월세예요, 전세예요 — saying 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form. Always 존댓말 with an agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 전세 means 'deposit' on top of monthly rent.
With 전세 you pay a huge lump sum and NO monthly rent, getting it all back at move-out. If there's monthly rent plus a deposit, that's 월세 (or 반전세), not 전세.
Confusing 보증금 with 전세금.
보증금 is the (usually smaller) security deposit in a 월세 contract; 전세금 is the whole lease sum in 전세. They aren't the same number or the same idea — ask 보증금 얼마예요? for 월세, 전세금 얼마예요? for 전세.
Saying 월세이에요 instead of 월세예요.
After the vowel-ending 월세, the copula contracts to 예요: 월세예요, 전세예요. 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form.

structuredNuance.t: 월세 (月貰, 'monthly rent') and 전세 (傳貰, 'jeonse') name the two dominant Korean rental schemes. The question is literally 'Is it monthly-rent, or is it jeonse?' — but it carries the full weight of asking which financial structure you're dealing with, since the two involve completely different sums and obligations.

Ask this the moment a listing catches your interest, before discussing price. 존댓말 is always required with an agent. The softer 월세인가요, 전세인가요? (with -인가요) is natural when asking tentatively about a listing you're not sure about yet.

The confusion is 보증금 vs. 전세금: in 월세, 보증금 is a modest returnable security deposit; in 전세, 전세금 is the entire rent-replacing lump sum — it is not a 'deposit' in the Western sense because there is no additional monthly rent at all. 반전세 ('half-jeonse') = large deposit + reduced monthly, the middle ground.
반전세예요? confirms the in-between type. You can also ask 어떤 방식이에요? ('what's the arrangement?') for a more open question. For clarity on semi-jeonse ask 보증금이랑 월세가 얼마씩이에요? ('how much each?').

Two traps: (1) Calling 전세금 a 'deposit' and expecting to also pay monthly — with true 전세 there is no monthly payment at all; the lump sum IS the rent. (2) Saying 월세이에요 — after a vowel-ending noun the copula contracts: 월세예요, 전세예요. 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form.

expressions.shortExplanation: 보증금 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is the deposit?".
expressions.explanation: "How much is the deposit?" — that is 보증금 얼마예요? (bojeunggeum eolmayeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 보증금 얼마예요? ("How much is the deposit?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the first money question on any 월세 listing
반말, with a friend comparing places
Softer, 'how does the deposit work out?' — very natural to agents
Negotiating: trade a lower 보증금 for higher 월세

examples.en: How much is the deposit here?
examples.note: Asked while looking at a specific unit; no particle needed before 얼마예요?

examples.ko: A: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? / B: 천에 오십이요.
examples.romanization: A: bojeunggeumi eotteoke dwaeyo? / B: cheone osibiyo.
examples.en: A: What's the deposit situation? / B: 10 million deposit, 500k a month.
examples.note: 어떻게 돼요? is the softer, more natural agent-question form; 천/오십 in 만원 units is the everyday way to state amounts

examples.ko: 보증금을 조금 올리면 월세 좀 깎아 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: bojeunggeumeul jogeum ollimyeon wolse jom kkakka jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: If I raise the deposit a bit, could you lower the monthly rent?
examples.note: The classic 보증금↑ → 월세↓ trade, asked politely with 깎다 — show you understand how the system works

expressions.nuance: 보증금 (保證金, 'security/guarantee deposit') is the up-front lump sum the landlord holds against unpaid rent or damage, returned in full when you leave. In Korean renting, 보증금 and 월세 slide against each other: a higher deposit buys a lower monthly rent and vice versa, so asking 보증금 얼마예요? is really asking where this unit sits on that scale. Amounts are spoken in 만원 (10,000-won) units — '천' means 천만 원 (10 million) and '오십' means 오십만 원 (500k); you almost never say the full digits. The agent-friendly variant 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does the deposit come out?') is softer and more conversational than the bare 얼마예요?. The dividing line from 전세금 is which contract you're in: 보증금 is part of a 월세 arrangement; 전세금 replaces monthly rent entirely — never ask 전세금 얼마예요? about a 월세 listing. Particle tip: with 얼마예요? you can drop the subject particle (보증금 얼마예요?), but with 어떻게 돼요? add 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. The English-speaker trap is treating 보증금 like 'first-and-last month's rent' — it is a single negotiable lump, often 10–20× the monthly rent, not a standard two-month figure. Stay in 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading '천' as 1,000 won instead of 천만 원.
Housing amounts are in 만원 units. 천 means 천만 원 (10 million); 오십 means 오십만 원 (500k). Hearing '보증금 천' as a literal 1,000 won will mis-set your whole budget.
Saying 보증금이 얼마예요 vs 보증금이 어떻게 돼요 with the wrong particle.
With 얼마예요? Koreans usually drop the particle (보증금 얼마예요?). With 어떻게 돼요? keep 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. Mixing them sounds off.
Treating 보증금 like Western first-and-last-month rent.
보증금 is one lump tied to the rent scheme, often many times the monthly rent, and it slides against 월세. It is not 'two months' rent up front'; ask the actual figure and the trade-off.

structuredNuance.t: 보증금 (保證金) literally means 'guarantee money' — the lump sum that guarantees the tenant's obligations. In practice it anchors the entire financial structure of the 월세 rental: the higher it is, the lower the monthly rent tends to be. Asking 보증금 얼마예요? is really asking 'where does this unit sit on the deposit-rent sliding scale?'

Ask after confirming the rental type is 월세. 존댓말 always. The variant 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? is softer and preferred in conversation with an agent; 보증금 얼마예요? is equally correct but slightly more direct. 반말 (보증금 얼마야?) only with a friend, never the agent.

보증금 (월세 security deposit) vs. 전세금 (전세 lump sum): they sound similar but belong to different contract types. Don't ask 전세금 얼마예요? about a 월세 listing. The trade-off expression: 보증금을 올리면 월세를 낮출 수 있어요 — raise one to lower the other.
보증금이 어떻게 돼요? (softer). 보증금 좀 낮출 수 있어요? (negotiate down). 보증금을 올리면 월세 깎아 주세요 (offer to raise it for a rent cut). In listings the shorthand is 보증금/월세: 500/50 means 5M deposit / 500k monthly.

Two traps: (1) Treating 보증금 as 'first-and-last month's rent' — it is a single negotiable lump, often far larger (10–20× the monthly). (2) Particle mix-up: 보증금 얼마예요? (no particle fine); but 보증금'이' 어떻게 돼요? needs 이. Mixing these up sounds off.

expressions.shortExplanation: 관리비는 따로예요? is a practical expression meaning "Is maintenance fee separate?".
expressions.explanation: 관리비는 따로예요? (gwallibineun ttaroyeyo?) = "Is maintenance fee separate?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 관리비는 따로예요? ("Is the maintenance fee separate?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; checking what's on top of rent
반말, with a friend
The flip side: asking if it's already baked in

usagePhrases.en: What does the maintenance fee cover?
usagePhrases.note: Drilling into what the 관리비 includes (water? internet?)

examples.en: Apart from rent, is there a separate maintenance fee?
examples.note: 월세 말고 ('aside from rent') frames it as a potential hidden cost — always ask this

examples.ko: A: 관리비 얼마예요? 거기에 수도세 포함이에요? / B: 오만 원이고, 수도세는 별도예요.
examples.romanization: A: gwallibi eolmayeyo? geogie sudose pohamieyo? / B: oman wonigo, sudoseneun byeoldoyeyo.
examples.en: A: How much is the maintenance fee? Does it include water? / B: 50,000 won, and water is separate.
examples.note: Always follow up with what's included; 별도 ('separate/extra') is the key word in the agent's answer

examples.en: If internet and cleaning are in the maintenance fee, that's not bad.
examples.note: Weigh the 관리비 by what's bundled — internet + cleaning included can make a higher 관리비 worthwhile

expressions.nuance: 관리비 (管理費, 'management/maintenance fee') is the monthly building charge billed ON TOP of your rent, covering cleaning of common areas, the elevator, security, hallway lighting, and possibly water (수도세), internet, or heating depending on the building. In a small 원룸 it might be 30,000–50,000 won; in a large apartment complex it can be much more. The question 관리비는 따로예요? ('is it separate?') is essential because a cheap-looking 월세 can hide a fat 관리비. Always follow up with 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? because what it bundles varies wildly. The dividing line is 따로 ('separate/on top') vs. 포함 (包含, 'included'): 관리비는 따로예요? assumes it might be extra and asks if so; 관리비 포함이에요? assumes it might be built in and asks if so — they expect opposite yes/no answers, so pick the one you mean. The English-speaker trap is assuming 관리비 is like a Western HOA fee paid only by owners — Korean renters pay it every month too. Another trap is skipping the follow-up: a '관리비 포함' listing might only include lighting, not water or internet, so the bundled items matter. The topic particle 는 on 관리비는 따로예요? sets up a contrast ('as for the maintenance fee…') and is the natural form; dropping it casually is fine. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Ignoring 관리비 because the rent looks cheap.
A low 월세 can hide a high 관리비. Always ask 관리비 얼마예요? and 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? — the real monthly cost is 월세 + 관리비.
Mixing up 따로 and 포함.
관리비는 따로예요? asks if it's a separate extra charge; 관리비 포함이에요? asks if it's already included in rent. They expect opposite answers — pick the one you mean.
Assuming renters don't pay 관리비.
Unlike a Western owners-only HOA fee, Korean renters pay 관리비 every month on top of rent. Budget for 월세 + 관리비 + utilities, not rent alone.

structuredNuance.t: 관리비 (管理費) literally means 'management fee'. 따로예요? asks 'is it separate/apart?' — together the question means 'Is the maintenance fee billed on top of the rent, or is it included?' The real point is to catch hidden costs: a low 월세 listing is often paired with a high 관리비.

Ask this immediately after learning the 월세 amount. 존댓말 with the agent always. The flip phrasing 관리비 포함이에요? (asking 'is it included?') is equally natural — pick whichever matches your assumption. 반말 (관리비 따로야?) only with a friend.

따로 ('separate/apart') vs. 포함 ('included'): these are the two poles of the answer. 관리비는 따로예요? and 관리비 포함이에요? ask the same thing from opposite angles — they cannot both be answered 'yes' simultaneously, so be clear which you're asking.
관리비 포함이에요? (included?). 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? (what's in it?). 관리비 말고 따로 내는 게 있어요? ('anything else to pay beyond 관리비?'). Always ask the follow-up to know what's actually covered.

Two traps: (1) Assuming 관리비 is like a Western owner-only HOA fee — Korean renters pay it monthly too, so budget 월세 + 관리비 + utilities. (2) Conflating 따로 and 포함 — they expect opposite answers, so using the wrong one gives you the wrong information.

expressions.shortExplanation: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "What's included (appliances/furniture)?".
expressions.explanation: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? (opsyeoneun mwoga isseoyo?) means "What's included (appliances/furniture)?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? ("What options (appliances) are included?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking what comes with the place
반말, with a friend
풀옵션 = fridge, washer, AC, bed, etc. all included
Asking about one specific 옵션 item

examples.en: What's included here?
examples.note: General check of what appliances/furniture come with the unit — ask this during every viewing

examples.ko: A: 풀옵션이에요? 세탁기랑 냉장고 다 있어요? / B: 네, 에어컨이랑 인덕션도 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: puropsyeonieyo? setakgirang naengjanggo da isseoyo? / B: ne, eeokeonirang indeoksyeondo isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Is it full-option? Are the washer and fridge both there? / B: Yes, and there's AC and an induction stove too.
examples.note: Confirm 풀옵션 then check specific items; the agent's answer shows how items are listed

examples.ko: 옵션에 침대는 없고 에어컨이랑 인덕션만 있어요.
examples.romanization: opsyeone chimdaeneun eopsgo eeokeonirang indeoksyeonman isseoyo.
examples.en: No bed in the options, just AC and an induction stove.
examples.note: Listing what IS and ISN'T included item by item — essential because 풀옵션 still sometimes means no bed

expressions.nuance: 옵션 here is the loanword 'option' used in a Korean-specific real-estate sense: the appliances and furniture that come with the rental — fridge (냉장고), washer (세탁기), air conditioner (에어컨), induction/gas stove (인덕션/가스레인지), bed (침대), desk, wardrobe, etc. 풀옵션 ('full option') means move-in ready with everything; a 'no-option' place is bare. This matters enormously because furnishing a Korean apartment yourself is costly, so 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? is one of the most practical viewing questions. The dividing line from 관리비 is category: 옵션 is the stuff physically INSIDE the unit (appliances, furniture), while 관리비 is the monthly building-management charge — don't conflate them. The English-speaker trap is using 옵션 in its English sense of 'alternatives/choices', which confuses the agent; in housing 옵션 always means built-in appliances and furniture. Particle trap: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? sets 옵션 as the topic with 은, then asks 뭐'가' 있어요 (subject particle, since 있다 is intransitive) — never say 뭐를 있어요. Even if told '풀옵션', confirm item by item because one essential item (often the bed) can still be missing. Always 존댓말 with the agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 옵션 in its general English sense ('choices').
In Korean real estate 옵션 means the included appliances/furniture, not 'alternatives'. 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? asks what the unit comes with, not what your choices are.
Trusting '풀옵션' without checking specifics.
풀옵션 varies by listing and may still lack the item you need (e.g. no bed). Confirm piece by piece: 세탁기 있어요? 침대도 있어요?
Saying 옵션은 뭐를 있어요.
있다 ('to exist') takes a subject, not an object: 옵션은 뭐'가' 있어요? The object particle 를 is wrong with 있다.

structuredNuance.t: 옵션은 ('as for the options') + 뭐가 있어요? ('what exists?'). Here 옵션 is a Korean real-estate term meaning the appliances and furniture included with the unit — NOT 'options' in the English sense of 'choices'. 풀옵션 means the unit comes fully equipped; a bare place with no 옵션 means you buy everything yourself.

Ask during any viewing, immediately after the rent/deposit questions. 존댓말 with the agent always. The shorthand 풀옵션이에요? ('is it full-option?') is the fastest way to get the big picture, followed by confirming specific items. 반말 (옵션 뭐 있어?) only with friends.

옵션 (appliances/furniture included with the unit) vs. 관리비 (monthly building management charge) — completely different categories. Don't ask 관리비에 세탁기 포함이에요? — appliances are 옵션, not 관리비. Also 풀옵션 vs. 반옵션: 반옵션 means some but not all basics are included.
풀옵션이에요? (all included?). 에어컨/세탁기/냉장고 있어요? (ask specific items). 옵션 목록 좀 알 수 있어요? (can I get a list?). After viewing: 옵션 중에 나중에 빼 갈 것도 있어요? (will any items be taken when the landlord moves out?).

Two traps: (1) Using 옵션 to mean 'choices/alternatives' — in Korean real estate it means built-in appliances/furniture, not options in the English sense. (2) Particle error: 뭐가 있어요? not 뭐를 있어요 — 있다 takes a subject (이/가), never an object (을/를).

expressions.shortExplanation: 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요? is a practical expression meaning "When can I move in?".
expressions.explanation: "When can I move in?" — that is 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요? (i jip eonje ipju ganeunghaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 언제 입주 가능해요? ("When is move-in possible?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the available move-in date
반말, casual 들어가다 ('go in') for moving in
More formal, naming 입주 가능일 ('available date')

usagePhrases.en: Can I move in right away?
usagePhrases.note: Asking if immediate move-in (즉시입주) is possible

examples.en: When can I move into this place?
examples.note: Pinning down availability on a unit you like — ask this as soon as you're interested, not after you've decided

examples.ko: A: 다음 달 초에 입주하고 싶은데 가능해요? / B: 지금 세입자가 이번 달 말에 나가서 가능해요.
examples.romanization: A: daeum dal choe ipjuhago sipeunde ganeunghaeyo? / B: jigeum seipjaga ibeon dal mare nagaseo ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: A: I'd like to move in early next month — is that possible? / B: The current tenant leaves at month's end, so yes.
examples.note: State your target date with 입주하고 싶다; the agent's answer shows the typical timing explanation

examples.ko: 지금 사람이 살고 있어서 다음 달에나 입주 가능해요.
examples.romanization: jigeum sarami salgo isseoseo daeum darena ipju ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: Someone's living here now, so move-in's only possible next month.
examples.note: 다음 달에나 ('not until next month') — the 에나 particle signals a reluctant minimum, a nuance worth learning

expressions.nuance: 입주 (入住, 'moving in / taking up residence') is the formal real-estate word for occupying a home. 입주 가능해요? asks when the unit is free for you to move in — critical in Korea because the previous tenant's move-out, the deposit hand-over, and the lease start all have to align. 즉시입주 ('immediate move-in') is a common listing tag meaning no waiting period; 바로 입주 돼요? asks for that. The near-synonym 들어가다 ('to go in') is the casual everyday form: 언제 들어갈 수 있어요? — both are natural, but 입주하다 is the proper word on contracts and with agents. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'move in' as 움직이다 ('to physically move/budge') — that verb is wrong for settling into a residence; use 입주하다 for the formal date a place becomes available, and 이사하다 / 이사 오다 for the whole act of relocating. Another trap is 가능하다's conjugation: it combines 가능 + 하다, so it becomes 가능해요, not 가능있어요 (a very common learner error). Also note 에나 in 다음 달에나: this stresses a reluctant minimum ('not before next month at the earliest'), a nuance plain 에 does not carry. Use 존댓말 with the agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'move in' as 움직이다.
움직이다 means to physically move/budge. Moving into a home is 입주하다 (formal) or 들어가다 (casual). Ask 언제 입주 가능해요? or 언제 들어갈 수 있어요?
Saying 입주 가능있어요.
가능하다 is a 하다-adjective: 가능해요, not 가능있어요. Correct: 언제 입주 가능해요? or 입주 가능한가요?
Confusing 입주 with 이사.
입주 is taking up the new residence (and its available date); 이사 is the act of relocating/moving your stuff. For when the place is free, ask 입주 가능해요?; for the moving day itself, 이사 언제 해요?

structuredNuance.t: 입주 (入住) literally means 'entering to reside'. 가능해요? = 'is it possible?'. Together: 'Is it possible to enter/take up residence?' In practice this asks the specific DATE the unit becomes available to move into, which is often constrained by the current tenant's departure or contract timing.

Ask this as soon as a unit interests you — before arranging a viewing is even better. 존댓말 always with the agent. 입주 가능일이 언제예요? is slightly more formal (naming 가능일 as a noun). 반말 (언제 들어갈 수 있어?) only with a friend helping you search.

입주하다 (formal, 'take up residence') vs. 들어가다 (casual, 'go in / move in') vs. 이사하다 ('relocate/move your belongings'). For asking when a unit is available: 입주 가능해요? 바로 입주 돼요? For asking about moving day itself: 이사 언제 해요?

바로 입주 돼요? (immediate move-in?). 즉시입주예요? (same, using the listing term). 입주 가능일이 언제예요? (more formal). 언제 들어갈 수 있어요? (casual spoken). After hearing the date: 그날 바로 이사 와도 돼요? (can I move stuff in that day?).

Three traps: (1) Using 움직이다 ('to budge/move physically') for 'move in' — wrong; use 입주하다 or 들어가다. (2) Saying 가능있어요 — 가능하다 is a 하다 adjective, conjugates to 가능해요. (3) Missing the nuance of 에나 in 다음 달에나 — it means 'not until next month at the earliest', stronger than plain 다음 달에.

expressions.english: How long is it from the station?
expressions.shortExplanation: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? is a practical expression meaning "How long is it from the station?".
expressions.explanation: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? (yeogeseo eolmana geollyeoyo?) = "How long is it from the station?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? ("How long does it take from the station?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: How long does it take from the station?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking walking distance to the subway
반말, with a friend

usagePhrases.en: How many minutes on foot from the station?
usagePhrases.note: Specifies 걸어서 ('on foot') for an exact walk time

usagePhrases.en: Is this near a station (prime location)?
usagePhrases.note: 역세권 = the desirable 'within walking distance of a station' zone

examples.en: How long is it from the station here?
examples.note: Standard location question at a viewing; follows naturally after the rent/options check

examples.ko: A: 지하철역에서 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요? / B: 한 십 분 정도 걸려요.
examples.romanization: A: jihacheoryeogeseo georeoseo eolmana geollyeoyo? / B: han sip bun jeongdo geollyeoyo.
examples.en: A: How long is the walk from the subway station? / B: About ten minutes.
examples.note: 걸어서 ('on foot') forces a walking answer; 한 ('about') + 십 분 정도 = 'roughly 10 minutes' — the hedged form agents use

examples.en: It's near the station, so it's pricey but the commute's easy.
examples.note: 역세권 justifies higher rent with 출퇴근 ('commute') convenience — if an agent stresses this, expect to pay more

expressions.nuance: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? is 역 ('station') + 에서 ('from', marking the source) + 얼마나 ('how much') + 걸리다 ('to take [time]') + 요. It asks how long the journey from the nearest subway station takes — the single most important location question for commuters in Korea, where subway proximity hugely affects both quality of life and rent. The buzzword 역세권 (驛勢圈, 'station-influence zone') signals a location within easy walking distance; it is a real selling point that pushes prices up. Crucially, 걸리다 here means 'to take time', which is a completely different verb from 걷다 ('to walk') and 걸다 ('to hang/call') — they look and sound similar, a notorious learner trap. Add 걸어서 ('on foot') to pin down a walking answer, since agents might otherwise quote bus or car times. The source particle is 에서 (역에서), not 에 (역에 marks a destination, not origin) — a particle error that mis-marks the direction of travel. Saying 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? ('how do you walk from the station?') wrongly uses 걷다 and asks about the manner of walking, not the duration. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent; you can ask the same about a bus stop: 버스 정류장에서 얼마나 걸려요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 걸리다 ('to take time') with 걷다 ('to walk').
역에서 얼마나 걸려요? asks how long it takes. 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? wrongly asks 'how do you walk?'. For walk TIME, keep 걸리다, optionally with 걸어서: 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요?
Using 역에 instead of 역에서.
에 marks a destination; 에서 marks a starting point. From the station, it's 역에서 얼마나 걸려요?. 역에 얼마나 걸려요 mis-marks the source.
Treating 역세권 as just 'near the station' with no cost effect.
역세권 is a value term: it signals desirability and higher rent. If an agent stresses 역세권, expect to pay more for the convenience.

structuredNuance.t: 역(station) + 에서(from) + 얼마나(how much/long) + 걸리다(to take time). Literally 'How much time does it take from the station?' In practice this is the key commute question: proximity to a subway station is the top location factor in Korean renting, and '역세권' (within easy walking distance) is a premium selling point.

Ask at every viewing, after the price and options questions. 존댓말 with the agent. Add 걸어서 ('on foot') when you want the walking time specifically: 역에서 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요? Omitting it leaves the agent free to quote driving or bus time. 반말 (역에서 얼마나 걸려?) only with friends.

걸리다 ('to take time') vs. 걷다 ('to walk') vs. 걸다 ('to hang/dial') — three different verbs that look similar. 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? (걸리다 = time taken) is correct. 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? (걷다) oddly asks 'how do you walk from the station?' — wrong verb for asking duration.
역에서 걸어서 몇 분이에요? (how many minutes on foot?). 여기 역세권이에요? (is it station-zone?). 버스 정류장에서 얼마나 걸려요? (from the bus stop?). 차로는 얼마나 걸려요? (by car?) — use when driving matters to you.

Two traps: (1) Particle: 역'에서' marks the starting point ('from the station'); 역'에' marks a destination — using 에 here flips the direction. (2) Verb confusion: 걸리다 (to take time) ≠ 걷다 (to walk). Saying 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? asks how you walk, not how long it takes.

expressions.shortExplanation: 햇빛 잘 들어요? is a practical expression meaning "Does it get good sunlight?".
expressions.explanation: 햇빛 잘 들어요? (haetbit jal deureoyo?) means "Does it get good sunlight?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 햇빛 잘 들어요? ("Does it get good sunlight?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking about natural light / direction
반말, with a friend
채광 = the technical word for natural-light quality
남향 (south-facing) = the most prized, sunniest orientation

examples.en: Does this room get good sunlight?
examples.note: Asked while standing in the room at a viewing — the answer often reveals orientation and floor before you even ask

examples.ko: A: 남향이에요? / B: 네, 남향이라 오후에 햇빛 잘 들어요.
examples.romanization: A: namhyangieyo? / B: ne, namhyangira ohue haetbit jal deureoyo.
examples.en: A: Does it face south? / B: Yes, it faces south so it gets good afternoon sun.
examples.note: 남향 ('south-facing') is the gold-standard answer; probe floor too — even south-facing units on low floors can be shaded

examples.ko: 반지하라 햇빛이 잘 안 들어서 좀 어두워요.
examples.romanization: banjihara haetbichi jal an deureoseo jom eoduwoyo.
examples.en: It's a semi-basement, so not much sun gets in — it's a bit dark.
examples.note: 반지하 ('semi-basement') is the biggest warning sign for poor light; 어둡다 = dark — factor this into 관리비 if heating covers a dark unit

expressions.nuance: 햇빛 잘 들어요? is 햇빛 ('sunlight') + 잘 ('well') + 들다 ('to enter/come in') + 요, literally 'does sunlight come in well?' — asking whether the unit gets good natural light. In Korea this matters enormously: good sun affects mood, mold prevention, heating bills, and resale value. The verb 들다 here means 'to enter/be admitted' (light coming in), NOT 'to hold' or 'to lift' — 햇빛이 들다 is a fixed collocation. The technical term is 채광 (採光, 'natural-light intake'); 채광 좋아요? is how professionals phrase it. Direction language is crucial: 남향 (south-facing) is the gold standard, 동향 (east) gets morning sun, 서향 (west) gets afternoon, and 북향 (north-facing) and 반지하 (semi-basement) units often have chronic darkness and damp. The English-speaker trap is the verb: '직역-ing 'gets sunlight' as 햇빛 가져요? or 햇빛 있어요? is meaningless; the natural collocation is 햇빛이 들다. Another is the particle: 햇빛이 잘 들어요? uses subject 이 (햇빛 is what comes in), never object 을. After asking about light, probe 곰팡이 안 생겨요? ('does mold not grow here?') to check for damp — dark, poorly lit units are mold risks. Always 존댓말 at viewings.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 햇빛 가져요? or 햇빛 있어요? for 'gets sunlight'.
The natural collocation is 햇빛이 들다 ('light comes in'). Ask 햇빛 잘 들어요?. 가지다 ('to have') and a bare 있다 don't fit how Korean talks about sun exposure.
Using the object particle: 햇빛을 잘 들어요.
들다 ('to come in') is intransitive here, so 햇빛 is the subject: 햇빛이 잘 들어요?. The object marker 을 is wrong.
Ignoring 남향/북향 and 반지하.
Direction and floor decide the light. 남향 (south-facing) is sunny; 북향 and 반지하 (semi-basement) are often dark. If sun matters, confirm 남향이에요? and avoid surprises.

structuredNuance.t: 햇빛('sunlight') + 잘('well') + 들다('to enter/come in'). Literally 'does sunlight come in well?' The verb 들다 here means light entering the space — a fixed collocation. This is NOT 햇빛을 받아요? ('do you receive sunlight?') or 햇빛 있어요? — Korean talks about light 'coming in' (들다), not 'being present'.

Ask while standing in the unit, ideally checking by looking at the windows and their direction. 존댓말 with the agent. 채광 좋아요? is slightly more technical and sounds knowledgeable. 반말 (햇빛 잘 들어?) only with a friend. Follow up with 남향이에요? and 곰팡이 안 생겨요? for a full picture.

햇빛 잘 들어요? (everyday) vs. 채광 좋아요? (technical/professional). Direction terms: 남향 (south, sunniest) > 동향 (east, morning sun) > 서향 (west, afternoon) > 북향 (north, least sun). 반지하 (semi-basement) means poor light regardless of direction.
채광 좋아요? (pro version). 남향이에요? (direct direction check). 햇빛이 오래 들어요? ('does sun stay long?'). 반지하예요? (is it semi-basement?). 곰팡이 안 생겨요? (probe mold — follows naturally from a light/damp concern).

Two traps: (1) Verb choice: 햇빛 가져요?/있어요? are unnatural — the correct collocation is 햇빛이 들다 ('light comes in'). (2) Particle: 햇빛'이' 잘 들어요? — 들다 (to come in) is intransitive, so 햇빛 is the subject (이/가), never the object (을). Saying 햇빛을 잘 들어요 is wrong.

expressions.english: Could you lower the rent a bit?
expressions.shortExplanation: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you lower the rent a bit?".
expressions.explanation: "Could you lower the rent a bit?" — that is 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 (wolse jom kkakka juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 ("Please lower the rent a bit"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please lower the rent a bit
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard rent-negotiation line
반말, only with a friend, never the landlord

usagePhrases.ko: 월세 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요?
usagePhrases.romanization: wolse jogeumman kkakka jusimyeon an dwaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Couldn't you take just a little off the rent?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more pleading 'wouldn't it be okay if…'

usagePhrases.en: At least waive some of the maintenance fee
usagePhrases.note: Fallback: ask to cut 관리비 if rent won't budge

examples.ko: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요. 오만 원만요.
examples.romanization: wolse jom kkakka juseyo. oman wonmanyo.
examples.en: Please lower the rent a bit — just 50,000 off.
examples.note: Name a concrete cut (오만 원만요 = 'just 50k') to make the ask specific and easier for the landlord to agree to

examples.ko: A: 계약 바로 할 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? / B: 오만 원은 빼 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: gyeyak baro hal tenikka wolse jom kkakka jusimyeon an dwaeyo? / B: oman woneun ppae deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I'll sign right away, so couldn't you lower the rent a little? / B: I can take off 50,000.
examples.note: Offering to commit immediately (계약 바로) as leverage is the most common negotiation tactic — the B response shows what acceptance looks like

examples.ko: 보증금 더 낼 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주세요.
examples.romanization: bojeunggeum deo nael tenikka wolse jom kkakka juseyo.
examples.en: I'll pay more deposit, so please lower the monthly rent.
examples.note: The 보증금↑ → 월세↓ trade stated as a bargaining chip — the landlord keeps the risk-benefit of a larger deposit

expressions.nuance: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is 월세 ('monthly rent') + 좀 (softener that turns the request polite, not 'a little' in amount) + 깎다 ('to cut/shave down a price') + 아 주세요 ('please do for me'). 깎다 is THE price-cutting verb in Korean — used at markets, restaurants, and real estate alike; it's the right word here. Rent negotiation is normal in Korea, especially on 월세 and 관리비, and landlords expect some back-and-forth. To make the ask more effective, name an exact amount (오만 원만요) and offer something in return: signing immediately (계약 바로 할게요) or raising the deposit (보증금 더 낼게요). The dividing line from 보증금 깎아 주세요 is which financial lever you're pulling — you can negotiate the deposit down OR the monthly up and the deposit up; both are valid. The English-speaker trap is using 내리다 ('to bring something down physically') instead of 깎다 — 월세 내려 주세요 is understandable but sounds like lowering an object, not cutting a price. Another trap is 할인해 주세요 ('give me a discount') — 할인 fits stores and sales promotions, not rent haggling. Bargaining hard while staying 존댓말 is expected and respected; 반말 with a landlord or agent would torpedo the deal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 월세 내려 주세요 for 'lower the rent'.
내리다 is to physically lower/bring down. For shaving money off a price, Koreans use 깎다: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요. 내리다 sounds like lowering an object.
Using 할인해 주세요 to haggle rent.
할인 (discount) fits stores and sales, not rent negotiation. For bargaining down rent, say 깎아 주세요. 할인해 주세요 sounds like asking a shop for a coupon.
Dropping 좀 and demanding 월세 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without the softener 좀 it sounds pushy. 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is polite; pair it with leverage (보증금 더 낼게요 / 계약 바로 할게요) to negotiate gracefully.

structuredNuance.t: 월세 + 좀 (softener) + 깎다 (to shave/cut a price) + 아 주세요 (please do for me). Literally 'please shave the monthly rent a bit'. 깎다 is the dedicated Korean price-cutting verb — used for any price negotiation, not just housing. The 좀 is a politeness softener, NOT a quantity limiter; you specify the actual cut separately (오만 원만요).

Use after you've decided on a unit but before signing. Always 존댓말 — this is a business negotiation. Pair the ask with leverage: 계약 바로 할게요 (I'll sign now) or 보증금 더 낼게요 (I'll raise the deposit). The softer form 월세 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? is more pleading and appropriate if the landlord seems firm.

깎다 (cut a price, the right verb) vs. 내리다 (lower physically, wrong for prices) vs. 할인하다 (discount, fits stores not rent). Negotiation levers: 월세 깎아 주세요 (lower the monthly) vs. 보증금 깎아 주세요 (lower the deposit) vs. 관리비 빼 주세요 (waive some maintenance) — choose the lever that makes sense.

월세 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? (softer, more pleading). 관리비라도 좀 빼 주세요 (fallback: at least cut the maintenance fee). 오만 원만 깎아 주세요 (name the exact cut). 보증금 더 낼 테니까 월세 깎아 주세요 (trade: raise deposit for lower rent).

Two traps: (1) Using 내리다 instead of 깎다 — 월세 내려 주세요 sounds like lowering an object; for shaving a price use 깎다. (2) Using 할인해 주세요 — 할인 is for store/sales discounts, not rent. In rent negotiation, 깎다 is the only natural verb.

expressions.hangul: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요?
expressions.romanization: yeogi jom deo bol su isseoyo?
expressions.english: Can I look around a bit more?
expressions.shortExplanation: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I look around a bit more?".
expressions.explanation: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? (yeogi jom deo bol su isseoyo?) = "Can I look around a bit more?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? ("Can I look around a bit more?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.ko: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: yeogi jom deo bol su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can I look around a bit more?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for more time to inspect the unit

usagePhrases.en: Can I look a bit more?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, with a friend who came along

usagePhrases.en: Could I take my time looking?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, asks to view at your own pace

usagePhrases.en: Please show me other places too
usagePhrases.note: Asking to see additional units beyond this one

examples.ko: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? 화장실도 보고 싶어서요.
examples.romanization: yeogi jom deo bol su isseoyo? hwajangsildo bogo sipeoseoyo.
examples.en: Can I look around a bit more? I'd like to see the bathroom too.
examples.note: Give a reason (화장실도 보고 싶다) to extend the viewing — it sounds more natural and the agent is more likely to give you time

examples.ko: A: 수압이랑 옵션 좀 천천히 볼 수 있을까요? / B: 네, 천천히 보세요.
examples.romanization: A: suabirang opsyeon jom cheoncheonhi bol su isseulkkayo? / B: ne, cheoncheonhi boseyo.
examples.en: A: Could I take my time checking the water pressure and appliances? / B: Sure, take your time.
examples.note: Name what to inspect (수압, 옵션) so the agent understands; 천천히 볼 수 있을까요? is softer than 볼 수 있어요?

examples.ko: 이 집은 좀 그렇고, 다른 집도 보여 주세요.
examples.romanization: i jibeun jom geureoko, dareun jipdo boyeo juseyo.
examples.en: This one's not quite it — please show me others too.
examples.note: 좀 그렇다 ('a bit meh/not quite right') politely declines without a harsh 싫어요 — the standard soft rejection before asking for more

expressions.nuance: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is 여기 ('here') + 좀 ('a bit', softener) + 더 ('more') + 볼 수 있어요 ('can I see?'), asking the agent for more time to inspect a unit — check closets, test 수압 ('water pressure'), look for 곰팡이 ('mold'), count the outlets. Korean viewings can feel rushed because agents juggle many clients, so this phrase buys you the time to look properly. The critical distinction is 보다 ('to see/inspect', what YOU do) vs. 보여 주다 ('to show', what the AGENT does): 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? means you want to keep looking yourself; 더 보여 주세요 means you want the agent to show you more. Don't say 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you just want to linger — that asks the agent to show you, not for you to inspect at your own pace. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'look around' as 둘러보다 — fine but slightly stiffer; 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is the more natural spoken ask. To reject a place without being rude, Koreans say 좀 그렇네요 / 좀 별로예요 rather than a blunt 싫어요. Stay in 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you want to keep looking yourself.
보여 주다 means the agent shows it to you. To keep inspecting on your own, say 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? (you see it). Use 보여 주세요 only when asking them to show something.
Confusing 'look around more' with 'show me other places'.
여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? extends this viewing; 다른 집도 보여 주세요 asks for additional units. Say the one you mean, or the agent stops at this one or skips ahead.
Bluntly saying 이 집 싫어요 to reject a place.
A flat 싫어요 sounds harsh to an agent. Koreans soften with 좀 그렇네요 / 좀 별로예요 ('it's kind of meh') before asking 다른 집도 보여 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 여기('here') + 좀('a bit') + 더('more') + 볼 수 있어요?('can I see?'). Literally 'can I see here a bit more?' — asking for extra time to inspect the unit yourself. The key verb is 보다 (you inspect), NOT 보여 주다 (agent shows you). If you want to keep looking yourself, this is the phrase; if you want the agent to show you something, say 보여 주세요.

Use mid-viewing when you feel rushed or want to check something specific (수압, 곰팡이, outlets, closets). 존댓말 with the agent always. The softer 천천히 좀 봐도 될까요? is better when you want to set your own pace entirely. 반말 (좀 더 봐도 돼?) only with a friend who came along.

볼 수 있어요? (you look more, THIS unit) vs. 다른 집도 보여 주세요 (agent shows MORE units). These are different requests — confusing them either cuts your inspection short or skips ahead to different places. Use the right one depending on whether you want more time here or want to move on.
천천히 좀 봐도 될까요? (softer, own-pace version). 좀 더 둘러봐도 돼요? (slightly more formal 둘러보다). 화장실/부엌도 볼 수 있어요? (request a specific room). 이 집은 좀 그렇고, 다른 집 보여 주세요 (politely move on).

Two traps: (1) Saying 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you want to keep inspecting yourself — 보여 주다 asks the agent to show you, not for you to linger. Use 볼 수 있어요? for your own inspection. (2) Rejecting a place with 이 집 싫어요 — too blunt; soften with 좀 그렇네요 / 좀 별로예요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이 집으로 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll take this place".
expressions.explanation: 이 집으로 할게요 (i jibeuro halgeyo) means "I'll take this place". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이 집으로 할게요 ("I'll go with this place"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; deciding on the unit you want
반말, with a friend confirming a choice

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to take this place
usagePhrases.note: Softer, stating preference before fully committing
More committal: moving straight to signing a contract

examples.ko: 여기 마음에 들어요. 이 집으로 할게요.
examples.romanization: yeogi maeume deureoyo. i jibeuro halgeyo.
examples.en: I like it here. I'll take this place.
examples.note: 마음에 들다 ('to like/be pleased with') leads naturally into the decision — note the fixed particle 에 in 마음에 들다, not 마음을

examples.ko: A: 고민해 봤는데 그냥 이 집으로 할게요. / B: 그러시면 바로 계약 진행할까요?
examples.romanization: A: gominhae bwanneunde geunyang i jibeuro halgeyo. / B: geureosimyeon baro gyeyak jinhaenghalkkayo?
examples.en: A: I thought it over and I'll just go with this place. / B: In that case, shall we proceed with the contract right away?
examples.note: 고민해 봤다 ('thought it over') shows you weighed it; the agent's response shows what comes next — the 계약 process

examples.ko: 이 집으로 할게요. 계약은 언제 할 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: i jibeuro halgeyo. gyeyageun eonje hal su isseoyo?
examples.en: I'll take this one. When can we do the contract?
examples.note: Decide, then move to scheduling 계약 — this two-step sequence is the natural flow

expressions.nuance: 이 집으로 할게요 is 이 집 ('this house') + -으로 ('with/via', marking the chosen option) + 하다 ('to do/go with') + -ㄹ게요 (announcing your own decision politely). The -으로 + 하다 construction means 'I'll go with this one among the options' — the same pattern as ordering at a restaurant (이걸로 할게요), here applied to choosing a home. The -ㄹ게요 ending courteously declares YOUR resolve ('I'll do it'); it differs from -ㄹ게요's sibling -ㄹ까요 ('shall we?'), which is a suggestion. The dividing line from 이 집 계약할게요 is finality: 이 집으로 할게요 announces your CHOICE; 계약하다 commits to the legal CONTRACT. In natural flow you say 이 집으로 할게요 first, then arrange the 계약. The particle -으로 carries the 'selecting from among options' nuance — dropping it (이 집 할게요) is understandable but loses that sense. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'I'll take it' as 가질게요 ('I'll possess it') or 잡을게요 ('I'll grab it') — both wrong; for choosing a rental you use 이 집으로 하다 (select) then 계약하다 (commit). Also: 마음에 들다 ('to like') is a fixed expression with the locative particle 에: 이 집이 마음에 들어요 — never 마음을 들어요. Stay in 존댓말 as you close.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이 집 가질게요 to mean 'I'll take it'.
가지다 ('to possess') doesn't fit choosing a rental. To pick this unit, say 이 집으로 할게요; to commit legally, 이 집 계약할게요.
Dropping -으로: 이 집 할게요.
The -으로 marks 'going with this choice'. 이 집으로 할게요 cleanly says 'I'll go with this one'; without it the 'among options' nuance is lost.
Mangling 마음에 들다 as 마음을 들어요.
It's a fixed phrase with 에: 이 집이 마음에 들어요 ('I like this place'). The object particle 을 is wrong here.

structuredNuance.t: 이 집(-으로) + 하다 + -ㄹ게요. 이 집으로 하다 literally means 'to do it as/with this house' — the -으로 housemarks the chosen option, like ordering (이걸로 할게요). -ㄹ게요 announces your own decision. The real meaning: 'I'm going with this one' among the options the agent showed you.

Use this the moment you've decided on a unit, before arranging the 계약. Always 존댓말 with the agent — this is the pivotal close of a business transaction. The softer 이 집으로 하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to go with this one') works when you're interested but not 100% committed yet. 반말 (이걸로 할게) only with friends.

이 집으로 할게요 (announces choice) → then 계약할게요 (commits to the legal contract). These are sequential steps, not synonyms. 이 집으로 하고 싶어요 is softer and less committed — use it if you still need to confirm something before deciding.
이 집으로 하고 싶어요 (softer: I'd like this one). 이 집 계약할게요 (more committal: I'll sign). 고민해 봤는데 이 집으로 할게요 (after deliberating). 여기 마음에 들어요, 이 집으로 할게요 (liking + decision).

Two traps: (1) Translating 'I'll take it' as 가질게요/잡을게요 — you don't 'possess' or 'grab' a rental; for choosing use 이 집으로 하다, for signing use 계약하다. (2) Mangling 마음에 들다: it's 마음'에' 들다 (fixed locative 에), not 마음'을' 들다. 이 집이 마음에 들어요 = I like this place.

expressions.shortExplanation: 계약은 어떻게 해요? is a practical expression meaning "How does the contract work?".
expressions.explanation: "How does the contract work?" — that is 계약은 어떻게 해요? (gyeyageun eotteoke haeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 계약은 어떻게 해요? ("How does the contract work?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the agent to walk you through it

usagePhrases.en: How do we do the contract?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, with a friend who knows the ropes

usagePhrases.en: What do I need to sign the contract?
usagePhrases.note: Asking what documents/money are required (신분증 등)

usagePhrases.en: How much is the down payment?
usagePhrases.note: 계약금 = the deposit-on-signing that locks the deal

examples.ko: 이 집으로 할게요. 계약은 어떻게 해요?
examples.romanization: i jibeuro halgeyo. gyeyageun eotteoke haeyo?
examples.en: I'll take this place. How does the contract work?
examples.note: Decide first with 이 집으로 할게요, then ask how to proceed — this is the natural two-step sequence

examples.ko: A: 계약할 때 신분증이랑 뭐 필요해요? / B: 신분증이랑 도장이랑 계약금 가져오시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: gyeyakal ttae sinbunjeungirang mwo piryohaeyo? / B: sinbunjeungirang dojangirang gyeyakgeum gajyeoosimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: What do I need to bring to sign — ID and what else? / B: Just bring your ID, seal/stamp, and the down payment.
examples.note: The agent's answer shows the three standard items: 신분증 (ID), 도장 (personal seal), 계약금 (down payment) — know all three before the signing day

examples.ko: 오늘 계약금 걸고 잔금은 입주할 때 내면 돼요.
examples.romanization: oneul gyeyakgeum geolgo jangeumeun ipjuhal ttae naemyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: Pay the down payment today, and the balance when you move in.
examples.note: 계약금 (down) now, 잔금 ('balance/remainder') at 입주 — this two-payment split is the standard pattern

expressions.nuance: 계약 (契約, 'contract') is the legal rental agreement, and 계약은 어떻게 해요? asks the agent to explain how signing works — what you bring, what you pay, and in what sequence. The key vocabulary clusters here: 계약금 (the down payment at signing, typically around 10% of the total deposit, which locks the deal and makes it binding on both sides), 잔금 ('the balance', paid at move-in), and 도장 (personal seal/stamp, often used in Korea instead of a signature). The dividing line from 보증금 is timing and role: 계약금 is a partial payment at signing that secures the contract; 보증금 is the full security deposit, of which 계약금 is the first installment. Critically, newcomers must ask about 전입신고 ('move-in registration') and 확정일자 ('fixed date stamp') — two official steps that legally protect your deposit from being lost if the landlord defaults; skipping them can leave your money unprotected. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'sign a contract' as 사인하다 — while colloquially understood, the proper term is 계약하다, and Koreans often 도장 (stamp) rather than sign. The topic particle 은 in 계약은 어떻게 해요? topicalizes 계약 ('as for the contract…') and is the natural form. Always 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 계약금 with 보증금.
계약금 is the down payment at signing that locks the deal (part of the total); 보증금 is the full security deposit. You usually pay 계약금 now and the 잔금 (balance) at move-in.
Saying only 사인할게요 for signing a contract.
사인 (autograph) is colloquial; the proper verb is 계약하다, and Koreans often use a 도장 (seal/stamp). Say 계약할게요 for committing to the lease.
Skipping 전입신고 and 확정일자.
These official move-in registration steps legally protect your deposit. Ask the agent 전입신고랑 확정일자 어떻게 해요? — neglecting them can leave your 보증금 unprotected.

structuredNuance.t: 계약(contract) + 은(topic) + 어떻게(how) + 해요?(do we do?). Literally 'how do we do the contract?' — asking the agent to explain the entire signing process: what to bring, what to pay, and the order of steps. It's the natural question after 이 집으로 할게요.

Use immediately after deciding on a unit. 존댓말 always — this is a legal transaction. Ask 계약하려면 뭐가 필요해요? if you want a checklist of requirements. 반말 (계약 어떻게 해?) only with a friend who has rented before and can explain the process to you.

계약금 vs. 보증금: 계약금 is the partial down payment at signing (locks the deal); 보증금 is the full security deposit — 계약금 is typically the first installment of the 보증금. 잔금 ('balance') = the rest, paid at move-in. These three terms form the payment sequence: 계약금 → 잔금 → done.
계약하려면 뭐가 필요해요? (what do I need?). 계약금은 얼마예요? (how much is the down payment?). 전입신고랑 확정일자는 어떻게 해요? (essential follow-up for deposit protection). 계약서 한번 읽어봐도 돼요? (can I read the contract first?).

Two traps: (1) Saying 사인할게요 for 'I'll sign' — colloquially understood but the proper verb is 계약하다; Koreans often stamp (도장) rather than sign. (2) Skipping 전입신고 and 확정일자 — these legally protect your deposit; neglecting them can leave your 보증금 unprotected if the landlord defaults.

expressions.shortExplanation: 수압은 괜찮아요? is a practical expression meaning "Is the water pressure okay?".
expressions.explanation: 수압은 괜찮아요? (suabeun gwaenchanayo?) = "Is the water pressure okay?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 수압은 괜찮아요? ("Is the water pressure okay?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; a key 'check before you sign' question
반말, with a friend at the viewing

usagePhrases.en: Does the hot water come out well?
usagePhrases.note: 온수 ('hot water') — vital in winter; 잘 나오다 = flows well

usagePhrases.en: Doesn't it get cold in winter?
usagePhrases.note: Probing insulation/heating (난방) for the cold months

examples.ko: 여기 수압은 괜찮아요? 좀 약한 거 같아서요.
examples.romanization: yeogi suabeun gwaenchanayo? jom yakan geo gataseoyo.
examples.en: Is the water pressure okay here? It seems a bit weak.
examples.note: 약하다 ('weak') voices the worry directly — this is the natural way to flag a concern while still asking politely

examples.ko: A: 온수도 잘 나오고 수압도 괜찮아요? / B: 네, 문제없어요. 도시가스라서요.
examples.romanization: A: onsudo jal naogo suapdo gwaenchanayo? / B: ne, munjeeopseoyo. dosigaseuraseoyo.
examples.en: A: Does the hot water run well and is the pressure okay too? / B: Yes, no problem — it's city gas.
examples.note: Bundle 온수 + 수압 in one ask; the agent's mention of 도시가스 (city gas) is useful for estimating your winter heating bills

examples.ko: 꼭대기 층이라 수압이 좀 약할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: kkokdaegi cheungira suabi jom yakal su isseoyo.
examples.en: It's the top floor, so the water pressure might be a bit weak.
examples.note: 꼭대기 층 ('top floor') is a red flag for weak 수압 — a fact to know before viewing high floors

expressions.nuance: 수압은 괜찮아요? is 수압 (水壓, 'water pressure') + 은 (topic) + 괜찮아요? ('is it okay?'), one of those practical questions that separates a savvy renter from a regretful one — weak pressure or cold showers are misery you only discover after moving in. Pair it with 온수 잘 나와요? ('does hot water come out well?') and 겨울에 안 추워요? ('isn't it cold in winter?') for a full practical inspection. The natural collocation for water/heat flowing is 나오다 ('to come out'): 물이 잘 나와요, 온수가 잘 나와요, 냉수가 잘 나와요. The dividing line from 난방 ('heating') is system: 수압/온수 concerns water flow through pipes, while 난방 concerns warmth — Korean homes commonly use 온돌 (under-floor radiant heating), and the fuel source (도시가스 vs. other) significantly affects your monthly bill, so ask 난방 어떻게 해요? too. Top floors (꼭대기 층) and old buildings often have weak 수압 — knowing this helps you ask before you fall in love with a unit. The English-speaker trap is the particle on 나오다: water is the SUBJECT coming out (물'이' 잘 나와요?), never the object — 나오다 is intransitive. Another is asking 물이 세요? ('is the water forceful/violent?') — the adjective 세다 can be used colloquially for strong pressure, but 수압 괜찮아요? is the cleaner and more natural form. Stay in 존댓말 at the viewing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 물을 잘 나와요? with the object particle.
나오다 ('to come out') is intransitive; the water is the subject: 물이 잘 나와요?, 온수가 잘 나와요?. The object marker 을 is wrong.
Only checking pressure and forgetting 온수 and 난방.
Weak 수압, no 온수 (hot water), or poor 난방 (heating) each ruin daily life. Ask 수압 괜찮아요?, 온수 잘 나와요?, and 겨울에 안 추워요? together.
Not asking what heating type it is.
Bills depend on it. Ask 난방 어떻게 해요? — 도시가스 (city gas) vs. other systems changes your winter costs a lot. 온돌 (floor heating) is common but cost varies by source.

structuredNuance.t: 수압(水壓, 'water pressure') + 은(topic) + 괜찮아요?(is it okay?). Literally 'Is the water pressure okay?'
