Polite-neutral and aimed at staff, fine at any counter, stall, or restaurant. Drop to 포장돼? with a friendly stall owner; soften to 포장 되나요? for a gentler tone. Often it's the answer to the staff's own 드시고 가세요, 포장이세요? — at a counter you can just reply 포장이요 and skip the question entirely.

포장돼요? (is takeout possible) vs 포장해 주세요 (do it) — feasibility vs request. 포장 (native-feeling, any food) vs 테이크아웃 (loanword, café-leaning, mostly drinks). And crucially 포장 (you carry it out yourself) vs 배달 (delivered to your door) — 배달돼요? orders a totally different service that may not even be offered in-store.

Feasibility: 포장돼요? / 포장 되나요? / 포장 가능해요?. Request: 이거 포장해 주세요 / 포장으로 주세요. Leftovers: 남은 거 싸 주세요 / 이거 포장돼요?. One-word reply to staff: 포장이요 (vs 여기서 먹을게요 for dine-in). Politeness floor: 포장돼? (반말) → 포장돼요?.

Don't translate 'to go' as 가지고 갈 수 있어요? — that asks permission to carry it off and sounds like you're worried it's not allowed. The idiomatic line is 포장돼요? (to check) or 포장해 주세요 (to request). Keep 포장 distinct from 배달 (delivery), and don't stop at 포장돼요? if you've already decided — follow with the request.

expressions.shortExplanation: 따로 계산해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Separate checks, please".
expressions.explanation: 따로 계산해 주세요 (ttaro gyesanhae juseyo) means "Separate checks, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 따로 계산해 주세요 ("Please ring us up separately"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; each person pays for their own
1/n(분의 일) for an even per-head split of one total
The opposite — one combined bill (often one person treating)

usagePhrases.en: I'll pay just for mine first
usagePhrases.note: 제 것만 to settle only your own portion ahead of the group

examples.en: Separate checks, please.
examples.note: Said at the counter when each person pays their own share

examples.ko: 저희 따로 계산해 주세요. 제 것만 먼저요.
examples.romanization: jeohui ttaro gyesanhae juseyo. je geonman meonjeoyo.
examples.en: Please ring us up separately — just mine first.
examples.note: 제 것만 ('just mine') to pay only your portion ahead of the others

examples.ko: A: 같이 계산하세요, 따로 하세요? / B: 따로 계산해 주세요. / A: 네, 그럼 한 분씩 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: gachi gyesanhaseyo, ttaro haseyo? / B: ttaro gyesanhae juseyo. / A: ne, geureom han bunssi kae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Together or separate? / B: Separately, please. / A: Okay, one at a time then.
examples.note: Answering the cashier's 같이/따로 question; staff line you up 한 분씩 ('one person at a time')

expressions.nuance: 따로 계산해 주세요 is 따로 ('separately, apart') + 계산해 주세요 ('please ring up'), used when each person in a group pays their own. The cashier will often ask 같이 계산하세요, 따로 하세요? ('together or separate?'), and this is your answer. Culturally Korea has long leaned toward one person treating (한턱 내다) or paying together (같이 계산), so splitting per item is less automatic than in the West — but 따로 계산 (separate) and 더치페이 (Dutch-pay) are now common among younger people, so it's a normal, unremarkable thing to ask for. The dividing line: 따로 계산 means each pays for what they had / their own check, while 같이 계산 (or 1/n, 'split into N') means one combined bill. The English-speaker error is saying 'split the bill' as 나눠 주세요 ('please divide it'), which is vague and can be mistaken for dividing the FOOD; the clear requests are 따로 계산해 주세요 (separate) or 1/n로 해 주세요 (even split). Keep the word order — 따로 modifies 계산, so lead with 따로 계산, since 계산 따로 sounds reshuffled. And don't assume separate is the default; if you want it, state it outright before the cashier rings up one total.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나눠 주세요 to mean 'split the bill'.

나누다 ('to divide') is vague at a register and can sound like you want the food itself portioned out. For separate checks say 따로 계산해 주세요; for an even money split say 1/n(분의 일)로 해 주세요 — those name exactly how to divide.
Assuming separate checks are the default.

Many Korean places expect a single payment, and culturally one person often treats or the group pays together. If you want to split, you must state 따로 계산해 주세요 explicitly, or the cashier will likely ring up one combined total and hand it to whoever's nearest.
Misordering as 계산 따로 해 주세요.
The natural adverb order puts 따로 right before the verb phrase it modifies: 따로 계산해 주세요. 계산 따로 is understandable but sounds reshuffled and non-native, as if the words got swapped. Lead with 따로.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'separately / please ring up' (따로 'apart' + 계산해 주다). It means 'separate checks — each of us pays our own.' 따로 directly modifies 계산, so the natural order is 따로 계산해 주세요; 계산 따로 해 주세요 sounds reshuffled and non-native, like the words landed out of sequence.

Polite (해요체), said to the cashier at the 계산대. Drop to 따로 계산해 줘 among friends. Socially, be aware Korea often defaults to one person treating or paying together, so if you want to split you should state it outright — don't assume the cashier will offer separate checks the way a Western server might.

따로 계산 (each pays for their own items) vs 1/n로 (one total split evenly per head) vs 같이 계산 (one combined bill, often one person treats). 더치페이 is the casual umbrella term for splitting. Choose by HOW you want the money divided: by what each person actually ate, or evenly across heads regardless of who ordered what.

Emphatic: 따로따로 해 주세요 (stresses every single person separately). Even split: 1/n로 해 주세요 / 1/n로 나눠서 계산할게요. Partial: 제 것만 먼저 계산할게요. Opposite: 같이 계산할게요 / 제가 다 계산할게요 (I'll treat). Politeness floor: 따로 계산해 줘 (반말) → 따로 계산해 주세요.

Don't say 나눠 주세요 for 'split the bill' — 나누다 ('divide') is vague and can sound like splitting the FOOD into portions. Be specific: 따로 계산해 주세요 (separate checks) or 1/n로 해 주세요 (even split). And don't assume separate is the default — Korea often expects one payment, so say it explicitly up front.

expressions.shortExplanation: 리필 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refill?".
expressions.explanation: 리필 돼요? (ripil dwaeyo?) means "Can I get a refill?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 리필 돼요? ("Can I get a refill?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; checks whether refills are possible AND free
Once confirmed, this asks them to actually refill it

usagePhrases.en: Could we get more side dishes?
usagePhrases.note: 반찬 refills are usually free; 좀 더 주세요 is the everyday way to ask
추가 = a paid add-on; asks the price when it's NOT a free refill

examples.en: Can I get a refill?
examples.note: Holding up an empty cup or side-dish plate so staff see what you mean

examples.en: Can we get more side dishes?
examples.note: 반찬 ('banchan') refills are often free in Korea — worth asking

examples.ko: A: 여기 콜라 리필 돼요? / B: 음료는 리필은 안 되고 추가는 돼요. / A: 그럼 하나 추가할게요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi kolla ripil dwaeyo? / B: eumnyoneul lipireun an doego chuganeun dwaeyo. / A: geureom hana chugahalgeyo.
examples.en: A: Are cola refills free here? / B: Drinks aren't refillable, but you can add one. / A: Then I'll add one.
examples.note: Staff distinguish 리필 (free top-up) from 추가 (paid add-on); you switch to 추가할게요

expressions.nuance: 리필 돼요? is the loanword 리필 ('refill') + 되다 ('to be possible') in polite question form: 'is a refill possible?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility — and crucially whether it's FREE — which matters because in Korea side dishes (반찬) are frequently refilled at no charge, while drinks may or may not be. Once you know it's possible, you ask 리필 좀 해 주세요 ('please refill it'). The dividing line against 추가 ('an additional order') is cost: 리필 implies topping up (often free, the same item), while 추가 (추가요 / 추가해 주세요) means ordering MORE as a paid add-on — mixing these can land you a surprise charge on the bill. The English-speaker error is using 'refill' as if Korean had a native verb and saying 다시 채워 주세요 ('please fill it again'), which is understandable but unidiomatic; 리필 돼요? is what people actually say. For free banchan specifically, 반찬 리필 돼요? or 반찬 좀 더 주세요 both work, and the latter sidesteps the refill question entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Assuming 리필 is always free.

리필 is often free for banchan, but drinks frequently cost extra or aren't refillable at all. Assuming it's free can mean a surprise on the bill; if unsure, ask 리필 돼요? 무료예요?, or check whether it's actually 추가 (a paid add-on).
Confusing 리필 with 추가.

리필 means topping up the same item (often free); 추가 means ordering an additional paid portion. Say 리필 돼요? to top up for free, but 추가요 / 추가할게요 when you're knowingly ordering more and expect to pay for it.
Saying 다시 채워 주세요 for a refill.

It's grammatically understandable ('fill it again') but not idiomatic, and may sound oddly literal to staff, like you're narrating the act. Koreans use the loanword: 리필 돼요? to ask, 리필 좀 해 주세요 to request.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'does a refill get done?' (English loan 리필 + 되다 'be possible/get done'). It means 'can I get a refill — and is it free?' The 되다 keeps it a FEASIBILITY question, so it asks whether refills are offered, not yet a command to pour more. The free-or-not subtext is baked in, since Korean refills aren't uniformly complimentary.

Polite-neutral and staff-facing, common in casual eateries, 분식집, and bar-style spots. Drop to 리필 돼? with a friendly server. Softer: 리필 되나요?. Often you ask it while lifting an empty cup or banchan plate so staff see exactly what you mean without a long explanation.

리필 (top up the SAME item, frequently free) vs 추가 (order MORE as a paid add-on). Cost is the dividing line. For free side dishes specifically, 반찬 좀 더 주세요 works without even invoking 리필. Asking the wrong one — 추가 when you wanted a free top-up — can mean an unexpected charge.
Feasibility: 리필 돼요? / 리필 되나요? / 리필 무료예요?. Request: 리필 좀 해 주세요. Banchan: 반찬 리필 돼요? / 반찬 좀 더 주세요. Paid add-on instead: 하나 추가할게요 / 추가하면 얼마예요?. Politeness floor: 리필 돼? (반말) → 리필 돼요?.

Don't say 다시 채워 주세요 ('fill it again') — it's understandable but not how Koreans phrase it; use the loanword 리필. And don't assume every refill is free: drinks often aren't, even where banchan is. If unsure, ask 리필 돼요? 무료예요? before assuming it's complimentary.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기 화장실 어디예요? is a practical expression meaning "Where's the restroom here?".
expressions.explanation: "Where's the restroom here?" — that is 여기 화장실 어디예요? (yeogi hwajangsil eodiyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 여기 화장실 어디예요? ("Where's the restroom here?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking staff for the toilet
Fuller form with the existence verb 있어요
A heads-up before you step away from the table — not a location question

usagePhrases.en: Is there a code for the restroom?
usagePhrases.note: Many Korean toilets need a 비밀번호 (door code)

examples.en: Where's the restroom here?
examples.note: Asked to a server when you need to go — the plain location question

examples.en: Excuse me, where's the restroom? Is it inside?
examples.note: 안에 ('inside') vs. out in the shared building corridor

examples.ko: A: 여기 화장실 어디예요? / B: 매장 밖으로 나가서 왼쪽이요. 비밀번호는 1234요. / A: 아, 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: A: yeogi hwajangsil eodiyeyo? / B: maejang bakkeuro nagaseo oenjjogiyo. bimilbeonhoneun 1234yo. / A: a, gamsahamnida.
examples.en: A: Where's the restroom here? / B: Out of the shop and to the left. The code is 1234. / A: Oh, thank you.
examples.note: Many Korean toilets are outside the unit and need a 비밀번호 (door code)

expressions.nuance: 여기 화장실 어디예요? is 여기 ('here') + 화장실 ('restroom', Sino-Korean 化粧室, lit. 'grooming room') + 어디 ('where') + 예요 (polite copula). 화장실 is the standard polite word for a toilet — never the crude, dated 변소, which sounds like 'outhouse.' The 여기 ('here') scopes the question to THIS establishment, useful because a Korean restroom may be inside, down the hall, or in a shared building corridor that needs a 비밀번호 (door code), so 'where is it' is a genuinely live question. A fuller variant is 화장실이 어디 있어요? ('where is the restroom located?'), using the existence verb 있다. The dividing line: 화장실 어디예요? asks LOCATION, while 화장실 좀 쓸게요 ('I'll use the restroom') ANNOUNCES you're going — a heads-up, not a where-question — so don't swap them. The English-speaker error is over-politely asking 'may I use the bathroom?' as 화장실 가도 돼요? to a server when you really need directions; in a public restaurant you don't need permission to go, you need the location, so ask 어디예요?. Also keep the copula fused: 어디예요, not the split 어디 이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 변소 instead of 화장실.
변소 is crude and old-fashioned, closer to 'outhouse/latrine', and sounds jarring in a clean restaurant or café. The neutral polite word for a public toilet is 화장실: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Asking 화장실 가도 돼요? when you want directions.
That asks permission ('may I go?'), not location, and in a public place there's no one whose permission you need, so it sounds off — almost childlike. To find it, ask where it is: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Saying 어디 이에요 separately.
The copula fuses onto the noun: 어디 + 예요 → 어디예요. Writing or saying 어디 이에요 as two separate pieces is unnatural; the smooth, native form is 화장실 어디예요?

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'here / grooming-room / where / is-it' — 화장실 is Sino-Korean 化粧室 ('makeup/grooming room'), a polite euphemism for the toilet, the same way English softens it to 'restroom.' The phrase plainly means 'where's the restroom here?' The 여기 ties it to this specific shop, which matters because the toilet is often NOT inside the unit.

Polite-neutral and staff-facing; fine to ask any server or owner. Drop to 화장실 어디야? with a friend. Always use 화장실, the neutral polite term — 변소 is crude and dated. In a café or bar the answer often includes a door 비밀번호, so be ready to ask for it if they don't volunteer it.

화장실 어디예요? (asks location) vs 화장실이 어디 있어요? (same, fuller, with 있다) vs 화장실 좀 쓸게요 (announces you're going — a heads-up, not a question). 화장실 가도 돼요? asks PERMISSION, which you don't need in a public place. Pick by whether you want directions or are just stepping away from the table.
Location: 여기 화장실 어디예요? / 화장실이 어디 있어요? / 화장실 어느 쪽이에요?. Heads-up: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 / 화장실 좀 갔다 올게요. Door code: 화장실 비밀번호 있어요? / 비밀번호 몇 번이에요?. Politeness floor: 화장실 어디야? (반말) → 화장실 어디예요?.

Don't ask permission with 화장실 가도 돼요? when you just need directions — in a public restaurant nobody's gatekeeping the toilet, so it sounds oddly childlike, like asking a teacher; ask 어디예요?. Also keep the copula fused as 어디예요 (not the split 어디 이에요), and avoid the crude 변소.

expressions.shortExplanation: 몇 명이요? is a practical expression meaning "For how many?".
expressions.explanation: 몇 명이요? (myeon myeongiyo?) = "For how many?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 몇 명이요? ("How many people?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: What staff ask; you answer with a number + 명
Your reply: native number + 명 + 이요
The HONORIFIC version staff use to you (분 + 세요)

usagePhrases.en: There are three of us — is there a table?
usagePhrases.note: State your number with 인데, then ask about seating

examples.en: How many? — Two.
examples.note: The host asks; you answer with the count plus 명

examples.en: There are three of us — is there a table?
examples.note: State your number, then ask for seating in one smooth move

examples.ko: A: 몇 분이세요? / B: 네 명이요. / A: 네, 이쪽으로 오세요.
examples.romanization: A: myeot buniseyo? / B: ne myeongiyo. / A: ne, ijjogeuro oseyo.
examples.en: A: How many in your party? / B: Four. / A: Sure, this way please.
examples.note: Staff use honorific 분 about you; YOU reply with plain 명, then they lead with 이쪽으로

expressions.nuance: 몇 명이요? is 몇 ('how many') + 명 (the counter for people) + 이요 (polite particle), the question staff ask at the door — 'for how many?'. As a customer you mostly ANSWER it, with 숫자 + 명 + 이요: 한 명이요, 두 명이요, 세 명이요. The counter 명 is the plain word for counting people, while 분 is its honorific; staff politely ask 몇 분이세요? (분 + the honorific copula 세요), but YOU refer to your own group with the humble/plain 명, never elevating yourselves with 분. That asymmetry — they honor you, you don't honor yourselves — is the key learner point. Native Korean numbers go with 명 (한, 두, 세, 네…), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — a frequent slip that instantly marks a beginner. The dividing line against 몇 사람? is register: 명 is the standard counter, while 사람 ('person') used as a counter sounds blunter and less polite in service. The English-speaker error is answering with Sino-Korean numbers (이 명) or honorifically calling their own party 분 — both sound off. Just say 두 명이요, and note a bare number ('둘') without 명 sounds clipped.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Counting your own party with the honorific 분.
분 honors OTHERS; for your own group you use the plain counter 명: 두 명이요. Saying 우리 두 분이요 wrongly elevates yourselves and sounds unintentionally self-important, like bowing to your own table.
Using Sino-Korean numbers with 명.
The counter 명 takes native Korean numbers — 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 — not 일 명, 이 명. So 'two people' is 두 명이요, never 이 명이요, which sounds like a beginner's miscount and stops the listener for a beat.
Answering 몇 명이요? with just a bare number.
A bare '둘' or '셋' can sound abrupt or incomplete to staff. Attach the counter and polite 요: 두 명이요. That's the natural, complete answer that mirrors the frame of the question they asked.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'how-many people?' (몇 'how many' + 명 'person-counter' + 이요 polite particle). It means 'for how many in your party?' This is mostly a line you HEAR from staff and answer; your reply mirrors the frame as 숫자 + 명 + 이요 (두 명이요), reusing their own counter back at them.

From staff it's polite-neutral (몇 명이요?) or honorific (몇 분이세요?). Your answer stays plain — 두 명이요 — because you don't honor your own group. Among friends deciding who's coming it's 몇 명이야? (반말). A bare number ('둘') sounds abrupt to staff; keep the counter 명 and the 요.

명 (plain people-counter, what you use for yourselves) vs 분 (honorific, what staff use about you) — never flip these. Against 사람 as a counter, 명 is the standard polite choice; 몇 사람? sounds blunter and more casual. So staff: 몇 분이세요?; you: 두 명이요 — the asymmetry is the whole point.
Native numbers with 명: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명, 네 명, 다섯 명 (NOT 일/이/삼 명). Your answers: 두 명이요 / 저희 세 명이요 / 두 명인데 자리 있어요?. Staff variants you'll hear: 몇 명이세요?, 몇 분이세요?, 일행이 몇 분이세요? ('how many in your group?').

Two errors: using Sino-Korean numbers with 명 (이 명 instead of 두 명), and honoring your own party with 분 (우리 두 분이요). Counters take NATIVE numbers, and 분 is only for honoring others, never yourself. Just say 두 명이요 — plain counter, native number.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 안 시켰는데요 is a practical expression meaning "We didn't order this".
expressions.explanation: 이거 안 시켰는데요 (igeo an sikyeonneundeyo) means "We didn't order this". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 안 시켰는데요 ("We didn't order this"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; flags a wrong dish gently with the soft -는데요 ender
주문하다 instead of 시키다 — a touch more formal

usagePhrases.ko: 저희가 시킨 거 아닌 것 같은데요
usagePhrases.romanization: jeohuiga sikin geo anin geot gateundeyo
usagePhrases.en: I don't think this is what we ordered
usagePhrases.note: Even softer, hedged with -것 같다 ('seems')
Name what you DID order so staff can spot the mix-up

examples.en: Oh, we didn't order this?
examples.note: Gently flagging a dish that arrived by mistake, with a soft 어 in front

examples.ko: 저기요, 이거 안 시켰는데요. 다른 테이블 거 아니에요?
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, igeo an sikyeonneundeyo. dareun teibeul geo anieyo?
examples.en: Excuse me, we didn't order this — isn't it another table's?
examples.note: Suggest the likely mix-up politely with 아니에요?

examples.ko: A: 김치찌개 나왔습니다. / B: 어, 저희는 된장찌개 시켰는데요. / A: 아, 죄송합니다. 바로 바꿔드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: gimchijjigae nawatseumnida. / B: eo, jeohuineun doenjangjjigae sikyeonneundeyo. / A: a, joesonghamnida. baro bakkwodeurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: Here's the kimchi stew. / B: Oh, we ordered the doenjang stew. / A: Sorry, I'll swap it right away.
examples.note: Name what you ordered; staff apologize and fix it with 바꿔드리다 ('swap it for you')

expressions.nuance: 이거 안 시켰는데요 is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 시켰- (past of 시키다 'to order') + -는데요, a soft sentence-ender that signals 'just so you know…' and invites the listener to respond. That -는데요 is the politeness engine: it raises the issue gently and leaves the sentence open-ended, so you're flagging a problem rather than accusing anyone — exactly the tone you want when correcting staff. 시키다 ('to order food / make someone do something') is the casual everyday verb here; the slightly more formal 주문하다 also works (이거 주문 안 했는데요). The dividing line against a blunt 이거 안 시켰어요 ('we didn't order this') is TONE — the -는데요 version is softer and less confrontational, which matters because a flat negative can land like blame. The English-speaker error is dropping -는데요 and stating that flat negative, or misjudging the 시키다 vs. 주문하다 register. Another trap: don't say 이거 틀렸어요 ('this is wrong/incorrect') — that's for wrong answers like a math problem, not a mis-delivered dish; for a mix-up, say you didn't order it, or name what you did. And watch the near-homophone 식히다 ('to cool down'), which would garble the sentence entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -는데요 and saying flat 이거 안 시켰어요.

The bare negative can sound accusatory, as if you're blaming the server for the mistake. The soft ender -는데요 raises it gently — 이거 안 시켰는데요? — so staff can fix the mix-up without feeling cornered or accused.
Saying 이거 틀렸어요 for a wrong dish.

틀리다 means 'to be incorrect', the way a math answer is wrong; a misdelivered dish isn't 'wrong' in that sense, so it sounds odd and confusing. Say 이거 안 시켰는데요, or name what you actually ordered: 저희는 OO 시켰는데요.
Confusing 시키다 with 식히다.

시키다 is 'to order'; 식히다 is 'to cool (food) down'. 이거 식혔는데요 would bizarrely mean 'I cooled this down', not 'I didn't order this'. Use 시켰- (the past of 시키다) for ordering — the two verbs sound close but mean entirely different things.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'this / not / ordered / but-you-see' (시키다 'order' + the trailing -는데요). The real meaning is a soft 'um, we didn't actually order this…'. The -는데요 leaves the sentence gently open-ended, handing the floor to staff so it feels like flagging an issue, not blaming them for it.

Polite (해요체) with the cushioning -는데요, ideal for correcting staff without friction. Drop to 이거 안 시켰는데 with a friend. 시키다 is casual-everyday; 주문하다 is a notch more formal if you want it. A small 어, … or 혹시 in front softens it even further, signaling you're puzzled rather than annoyed.

이거 안 시켰는데요 (soft, invites a fix) vs 이거 안 시켰어요 (flat, can sound accusatory). Even gentler: 저희가 시킨 거 아닌 것 같은데요 ('I don't think this is ours'). And don't reach for 이거 틀렸어요 — 틀리다 is for wrong ANSWERS, not a misdelivered dish; the dish isn't 'incorrect', it's just not yours.
Verb swap: 안 시켰는데요 / 주문 안 했는데요. Soften with a hedge: 시킨 거 아닌 것 같은데요. Redirect by naming yours: 저희는 OO 시켰는데요. Suggest the cause: 다른 테이블 거 아니에요?. Politeness floor: 이거 안 시켰는데 (반말) → 이거 안 시켰는데요.

Dropping -는데요 to a flat 이거 안 시켰어요 can read as an accusation pointed at the server. And don't say 이거 틀렸어요 for a wrong dish — 틀리다 means 'be incorrect (like a wrong answer)', which doesn't fit a delivery mix-up. Say you didn't order it, or name what you did. Beware 식히다 ('cool down'), a near-twin of 시키다.

expressions.shortExplanation: 예약했는데요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a reservation".
expressions.explanation: "I have a reservation" — that is 예약했는데요 (yeyakaenneundeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 예약했는데요 ("I have a reservation (just so you know)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I have a reservation (just so you know)
usagePhrases.note: Polite; said as you walk in to check in
반말, only telling a friend, never the staff
Formal 합쇼체, upscale salon or sounding crisp

usagePhrases.en: I didn't book — is it possible (to walk in)?
usagePhrases.note: The walk-in version when you have no booking

examples.en: Hi, I have a reservation.
examples.note: The standard check-in line said right after greeting; -는데요 softly invites them to look you up rather than just announcing a fact

examples.en: I booked for three o'clock — the name is Kim Minsu.
examples.note: Add time and name together so the receptionist can find your booking instantly

examples.ko: A: 어서 오세요. / B: 예약했는데요. 네이버로 했어요.
examples.romanization: A: eoseo oseyo. / B: yeyakaenneundeyo. neibeoro haesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Welcome! / B: I have a reservation — I booked through Naver.
examples.note: 네이버 예약 is how the vast majority of Koreans reserve salons; mentioning it helps staff locate your booking in the right system

expressions.nuance: 예약했는데요 is 예약(을) 하다 ('to make a reservation', Sino-Korean 豫約) in the past tense plus the soft ender -는데요, meaning roughly 'I booked, so… (I'm here / please check)'. That -는데요 is the politeness engine: it hands the situation over to the staff and invites them to look you up, rather than barking a flat statement. You use this in 존댓말 to salon staff the moment you arrive; with a close friend you'd drop to 예약했어, but 반말 is completely off-limits with any service worker. The nearest alternative is plain 예약했어요, which is grammatically fine but a shade more abrupt since it lacks that inviting soft ender. The classic English-speaker error is translating 'I have a reservation' with 있다: 예약이 있어요 is understandable but sounds like announcing an abstract fact rather than actively checking in — Koreans reach for the verb 하다 (예약했는데요). Another trap is the particle: it's 예약을 하다 (object), so never 예약에 했어요. In practice, most Korean salon bookings happen through Naver, so 네이버로 예약했는데요 is the single most common form you'll actually hear.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 예약이 있어요 to check in.
It's grammatical but means 'a reservation exists', which sounds detached. Koreans use the verb 하다: 예약했는데요 / 예약했어요 ('I made a booking').
Dropping -는데요 to a flat 예약했어요 and stopping there.
It works but is blunter and doesn't invite the staff to respond. -는데요 softens it and signals 'so please check me in': 예약했는데요.
Using 반말 예약했어 with the receptionist.
예약했어 is 반말, far too casual for staff you don't know. Keep 존댓말: 예약했는데요 or 예약했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 예약(을) 하다 is Sino-Korean 豫約 + 하다 ('make a reservation'). The past tense 예약했- plus soft ender -는데요 means roughly 'I booked, so…' — the -는데요 hands the moment to the staff and implicitly says 'please check me in', rather than stating a flat fact.
존댓말 to any service worker; said the instant you walk through the door. Drop to 예약했어 only with a friend you're telling — never to staff. Upscale salons may prefer the crisper 예약했습니다.
예약했어요 is the plain polite form — fine but a touch more abrupt. -는데요 softens further and invites a response, making it the more natural check-in phrase.
네이버로 예약했는데요 (booked via Naver), 카카오로 예약했는데요 (via Kakao), 세 시에 예약했는데요 (booked for 3 o'clock). Each adds the context staff need to locate your booking.

'I have a reservation' tempts learners to use 있다: 예약이 있어요 is grammatical but sounds like you're announcing a fact, not checking in. Use the verb 하다 (예약했는데요). Also watch the particle: 예약을 하다, never 예약에 했어요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 커트만 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "Just a cut, please".
expressions.explanation: 커트만 할게요 (keoteuman halgeyo) = "Just a cut, please". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 커트만 할게요 ("I'll just get a cut"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; declaring you only want a haircut, nothing else
반말, to a friend, not to the stylist

usagePhrases.en: I would like just a cut
usagePhrases.note: Formal 합쇼체, stiffer / upscale

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to get my hair cut
usagePhrases.note: Softer way to open with what you came for

examples.en: Today I'll just get a cut.
examples.note: 오늘은 ('today') frames it as a one-day choice, leaving the door open for other services another time

examples.en: No perm — just a cut, please.
examples.note: -만 ('only') paired with 안 하고 explicitly rules out add-ons the stylist might otherwise assume

examples.ko: A: 오늘 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 커트만 할게요. 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: A: oneul eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: keoteuman halgeyo. eolmayeyo?
examples.en: A: What can I do for you today? / B: Just a cut, please — how much is it?
examples.note: Pair the declaration with 얼마예요 to confirm the price before you sit down

expressions.nuance: 커트만 할게요 is 커트 (the loanword 'cut') + -만 ('only') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 form of 하다, announcing your intention politely). The particle -만 is doing the real work: it tells the stylist you want ONLY a haircut and nothing extra — no perm, no dye — which matters because salons often upsell or automatically include treatments. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the friendly customer register, polite but not stiff. Koreans write 커트 for a haircut (헤어컷 also appears on menus), and the plain verb for the action is 머리(를) 자르다 ('to cut hair') — the two are interchangeable, with 커트 sounding more salon-technical. The dividing line from 머리 자르려고요 ('I came to get a cut') is that 커트만 할게요 actively EXCLUDES other services via -만, while 자르려고요 simply states your purpose. The English-speaker trap is placing -만 in the wrong position: 커트 할게요만 is broken (만 attaches to the noun, not the sentence end), and substituting 그냥 ('just/casually') gives 그냥 커트 할게요 = 'I'll just casually get a cut' — a different nuance that doesn't exclude add-ons. Also note: for hair the loanword is 커트, not 컷 (컷 is for film editing).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Misplacing 만 as 커트 할게요만.
만 ('only') attaches to the noun, not the sentence end. Correct: 커트만 할게요.
Using 그냥 to mean 'just a cut'.
그냥 커트 할게요 means 'I'll just casually get a cut' (no strong reason). To mean 'only a cut, nothing else', use 만: 커트만 할게요.
Saying 머리 컷 주세요 like ordering an object.
A haircut isn't 'given' like a dish. Use the verb: 커트만 할게요 or 머리 좀 잘라 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 커트 ('cut', loanword) + -만 ('only') + 할게요 (polite first-person intention). The particle -만 is the key: it signals you want ONLY a haircut, actively excluding perms, dye, and other add-ons the stylist might assume.
존댓말 to the stylist; the first thing you say after sitting down or when asked what service you want. 커트만 할게요 is warm and natural — not stiff, not overly casual.
머리 자르려고요 ('I came to get a cut') just states your purpose without the exclusion force of -만. Use 커트만 if you specifically want to head off upselling.
오늘은 커트만 할게요 ('just a cut today'), 커트만 하고 싶어요 ('I only want a cut'), 커트만 해 주세요 (slightly more of a request). All use -만 on 커트.

Two traps: (1) putting -만 at the end — 커트 할게요만 is wrong; 만 attaches to the noun: 커트만. (2) Using 그냥 to mean 'just a cut': 그냥 커트 할게요 means 'I'll just casually get a cut' — it doesn't exclude add-ons the way -만 does.

expressions.english: Just tidy it up / trim it, please
expressions.shortExplanation: 다듬어 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Just tidy it up / trim it, please".
expressions.explanation: 다듬어 주세요 (dadeumeo juseyo) means "Just tidy it up / trim it, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다듬어 주세요 ("Please just trim/tidy it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; light cleanup, not a big change
반말, to a friend cutting your hair

usagePhrases.en: Could you tidy it up, please?
usagePhrases.note: More polite/formal with -주시겠어요
끝만 살짝 ('only the tips, slightly') for a tiny trim

examples.en: Keep the length — just tidy it up.
examples.note: 길이는 그대로 ('length as is') signals zero shortening; 다듬다 handles only the shape and damaged ends

examples.en: The ends are a bit damaged — please trim them.
examples.note: 상하다 ('to be damaged') gives the reason; the stylist now knows it's a maintenance trim, not a style change

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 많이 자르지 말고 그냥 다듬어 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: mani jareuji malgo geunyang dadeumeo juseyo.
examples.en: A: How would you like it done? / B: Don't cut much — just tidy it up.
examples.note: 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much') stacks before 다듬어 주세요 for extra protection against over-cutting

expressions.nuance: 다듬어 주세요 is 다듬다 ('to trim, neaten, tidy up') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form ('please do for me'). This is the single most useful salon word for someone who does NOT want a dramatic change: 다듬다 means cleaning up the shape and split ends while keeping essentially the same length and style. The crucial contrast is with 자르다 ('to cut'): 자르다 implies actually shortening and removing length, while 다듬다 implies maintenance — if you say 잘라 주세요 the stylist may take off far more than you wanted, so for 'just a trim' always reach for 다듬다. Stack intensifiers like 끝만 살짝 ('just the tips, lightly') or 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much') to make the limit unmistakable. The English-speaker trap is exactly this verb choice: 'trim' maps mentally to 자르다, producing a real haircut when you wanted maintenance. Conjugation note: 다듬다 keeps the ㅁ intact — the form is 다듬어 주세요, never 다듬아 주세요 or 다듬워 주세요. Bare 다듬으세요 is also wrong for this context: it would command the stylist to trim their own hair rather than requesting they trim yours.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘라 주세요 when you only want a trim.
자르다 ('cut') means shortening/removing length. For a light cleanup that keeps the length, use 다듬다: 다듬어 주세요.
Conjugating it as 다듬아 주세요 or 다듬워 주세요.
다듬다 is a regular verb keeping ㅁ: the form is 다듬어 주세요, not 다듬아/다듬워.
Saying 다듬으세요 to the stylist.
Bare 다듬으세요 is a command to the listener to trim (their own) hair. The favor form 다듬어 주세요 means 'please trim mine for me'.

structuredNuance.t: 다듬다 literally means 'to make neat/tidy'. In the salon it specifically means a light cleanup — trimming split ends and restoring the shape without shortening the overall length. The -아/어 주세요 form makes it a polite favor request: 'please do this for me'.
존댓말 with all salon staff. Use when your hair is growing out of shape but you don't want length removed. Stack 끝만 살짝 or 길이는 그대로 to make the scope clear.
자르다 = cut (removes length); 다듬다 = tidy up (keeps length, shapes ends). These are the critical two verbs. If you say 잘라 주세요 when you meant 다듬어 주세요, you may come out with a noticeably shorter haircut.
끝만 살짝 다듬어 주세요 (only the very tips), 다듬어 주시겠어요? (more formal), 다듬어 줘 (반말). For the opposite — an actual cut — switch to 잘라 주세요.

'Trim' mentally maps to 자르다 for English speakers, but 자르다 means cutting and shortening. Always use 다듬다 for a light maintenance trim. Also: 다듬어 not 다듬아/다듬워 (the ㅁ is preserved, not subject to ㅏ/ㅗ vowel harmony).

expressions.english: Please don't make it too short
expressions.shortExplanation: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please don't make it too short".
expressions.explanation: "Please don't make it too short" — that is 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 (neomu jjalbji anke hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 ("Please don't make it too short"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please don't make it too short
usagePhrases.note: Polite; capping how short they go
반말, to a friend cutting it
Direct 'don't cut' version with 마세요

usagePhrases.en: Please don't make it too long
usagePhrases.note: The opposite, when you want it shorter

examples.ko: 앞은 괜찮은데 옆은 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: apeun gwaenchaneunde yeopeun neomu jjalbji anke hae juseyo.
examples.en: The front's fine, but don't make the sides too short.
examples.note: Targeting one zone (옆 'sides') with the limit while leaving the rest alone

examples.ko: 저번에 너무 짧게 잘라서, 이번엔 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeobeone neomu jjalbge jallaseo, ibeonen neomu jjalbji anke hae juseyo.
examples.en: Last time it was cut too short, so this time please not too short.
examples.note: 저번에 … 잘라서 ('last time [they] cut it …, so') explains why you're being cautious this visit

examples.ko: A: 어느 정도 자를까요? / B: 귀는 덮을 정도로, 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eoneu jeongdo jareulkkayo? / B: gwineun deopeul jeongdoro, neomu jjalbji anke hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: About how much shall I take off? / B: Long enough to cover my ears — not too short.
examples.note: 귀를 덮다 ('cover the ears') gives the stylist a concrete anchor length

expressions.nuance: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 is 너무 ('too') + 짧다 ('short') turned into the -지 않게 negative adverb form + 해 주세요 ('please make it'). The structure [-지 않게 해 주세요] = 'please make it so that it is NOT ~' is a powerful, reusable frame for setting limits on any salon service. Here it allows cutting while capping the result: 'cut, but don't go so far that it's too short'. The closest alternative 너무 짧게 자르지 마세요 uses the direct prohibitive -지 마세요 ('don't do X') — equally correct, but slightly more confrontational; the -지 않게 version describes the desired state rather than forbidding the action, so it sounds gentler and is preferred by most customers. The English-speaker trap is the double-negative word order: 너무 안 짧게 misplaces the negation (안 must go before the adjective inside the conjugated form, i.e. 짧지 않게, not 안 짧게 tacked in freely), and scrambled forms like 짧지 않게 너무 also break. A second trap: hair length is 짧다 ('short'), not 작다 ('small') — never say 너무 작지 않게. And 너무 skews negative ('excessively'), fitting perfectly here; don't swap it with 많이, since 많이 짧지 않게 sounds awkward.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 너무 안 짧게 해 주세요.
The negation goes on the adjective with -지 않게: 짧지 않게. 너무 안 짧게 misplaces 안 and sounds broken.
Using 작다 instead of 짧다 for hair.
작다 means 'small in size'. Hair length is 짧다 ('short'). Say 너무 짧지 않게, not 너무 작지 않게.
Dropping 해 주세요 and saying just 너무 짧지 않게.
Without the verb it's an incomplete fragment. Finish it: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 (or … 잘라 주세요).

structuredNuance.t: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 = 'please make it in a way that is not too short'. 너무 ('excessively') + 짧지 않게 ('-지 않게' negative adverb of 짧다) + 해 주세요. The -지 않게 해 주세요 frame sets a limit by describing the unwanted result state rather than banning the action.
존댓말 to staff. Said at the start of the cut or when the stylist asks how short to go. Especially useful if you've been over-cut before or if your hair grows slowly.

너무 짧게 자르지 마세요 (prohibitive -지 마세요) is equally correct but a touch more direct. The -지 않게 form is preferred in polite customer speech because it frames the desired result rather than issuing a prohibition.
너무 길지 않게 해 주세요 ('not too long'); 너무 짧지 않게만 해 주세요 (with 만 for emphasis); 조금만 자르고 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 ('cut just a little, not too short').
Two traps: (1) misplacing 안 — the negation belongs inside the conjugation as 짧지 않게, not freely placed as 너무 안 짧게; (2) using 작다 ('small') for hair length — hair is 짧다 ('short'), never 작다.

expressions.english: Please give me bangs / keep the bangs down
expressions.shortExplanation: 앞머리 내려 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me bangs / keep the bangs down".
expressions.explanation: 앞머리 내려 주세요 (ammeori naeryeo juseyo) = "Please give me bangs / keep the bangs down". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 앞머리 내려 주세요 ("Please give me/keep bangs (down)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for front fringe forward over the forehead
반말, to a friend styling your hair
The opposite: 까다, swept off the forehead

usagePhrases.en: Please trim my bangs a bit
usagePhrases.note: Trimming the fringe specifically, not changing how it's worn

examples.ko: 앞머리 있는 게 좋아서 내려 주세요.
examples.romanization: ammeori inneun ge joaseo naeryeo juseyo.
examples.en: I like having bangs, so please keep them down.
examples.note: 있는 게 좋다 ('prefer having') states the preference; the stylist now knows the fringe should come forward

examples.ko: 앞머리 내려 주시고, 눈썹 정도 길이로 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ammeori naeryeo jusigo, nunsseop jeongdo giriro hae juseyo.
examples.en: Bangs down, please, and about eyebrow length.
examples.note: 눈썹 정도 길이 ('about eyebrow length') is the standard concrete cut-line for bangs in Korean salons

examples.ko: A: 앞머리는 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 원래 앞머리 까는데, 오늘은 한번 내려 볼까 해요.
examples.romanization: A: ammeorineun eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: wollae ammeori kkaneunde, oneureun hanbeon naeryeo bolkka haeyo.
examples.en: A: What shall we do with the bangs? / B: I usually push them back, but today I'm thinking of trying them down.
examples.note: 까다 vs. 내리다 contrast in one exchange; -아 볼까 해요 ('thinking of trying') is a natural hedge

expressions.nuance: 앞머리 내려 주세요 is 앞머리 (lit. 'front-head', the fixed Korean word for bangs/fringe) + 내리다 ('to lower, bring down') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form. 내리다 describes how you WEAR the fringe — down over the forehead. The essential opposite is 까다: 앞머리(를) 까다 means to push the fringe UP and BACK off the forehead — these two verbs produce completely different looks, so mixing them up at the salon chair is a real-world disaster. To MAKE bangs from scratch, say 앞머리 만들어 주세요; to TRIM existing bangs, say 앞머리 다듬어/잘라 주세요; to WEAR them down, 앞머리 내려 주세요. The English-speaker trap starts with vocabulary: there is no obvious Korean cognate for 'bangs', so learners describe it ('the hair in front') — just lock in 앞머리. A secondary trap is reaching for 자르다 thinking 'bangs = cut bangs', but 내리다 is purely about the wearing direction, not the cutting. Note that 머리 alone means 'head/hair' in general; the front fringe is specifically 앞머리. Keep 존댓말 with the stylist throughout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 내리다 with 까다.
앞머리 내리다 = wear bangs down over the forehead; 앞머리 까다 = push them back off the forehead. They're opposites — pick the right one.
Describing it as 앞에 있는 머리 instead of 앞머리.
Korean has a set word: 앞머리 ('bangs/fringe'). The roundabout 앞에 있는 머리 is unnatural and unclear to the stylist.
Using 자르다 when you mean to create or keep bangs.
To make bangs say 앞머리 만들어 주세요; to keep them worn down say 앞머리 내려 주세요. Plain 자르다 just means 'cut' and is ambiguous here.

structuredNuance.t: 앞머리 (lit. 'front-head', = bangs/fringe) + 내리다 ('lower/bring down') + 주세요. This isn't about cutting — it describes how the fringe is WORN: pulled forward and down over the forehead, as opposed to pushed back off it.

존댓말 to the stylist. Said during the style consultation, usually right after discussing the cut length. Works both when requesting new bangs and when telling the stylist how to finish styling the fringe you already have.
앞머리 까다 = push bangs UP/BACK (completely opposite look). 앞머리 만들어 주세요 = create bangs from scratch. 앞머리 다듬어 주세요 = trim existing bangs. Never swap 내리다 with 까다.
앞머리 내려 주시고, 눈썹 정도 길이로 해 주세요 (down + length cue). 앞머리 살짝만 내려 주세요 ('just slightly down'). 앞머리 옆으로 넘겨 주세요 ('sweep bangs to the side').

Two traps: (1) not knowing the word 앞머리 and describing 'the hair in front' instead — just learn 앞머리; (2) reaching for 자르다 ('cut') when you mean 내리다 ('wear down') — cutting and wearing direction are different requests.

expressions.english: Please make it like this photo
expressions.shortExplanation: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please make it like this photo".
expressions.explanation: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 (i sajincheoreom hae juseyo) means "Please make it like this photo". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 ("Please make it like this photo"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Please make it like this photo
usagePhrases.note: Polite; showing a reference picture to guide the entire style
반말, to a friend
Pointing or gesturing when you have no photo

usagePhrases.en: Could it turn out like this photo?
usagePhrases.note: Asking whether the look is achievable for your hair type

examples.en: Make it like this photo, please — is it possible?
examples.note: Always follow with 가능해요? — reference photos show someone else's hair, which may not suit yours

examples.ko: 이 사진처럼 하고 싶은데, 제 머리로 될까요?
examples.romanization: i sajincheoreom hago sipeunde, je meoriro doelkkayo?
examples.en: I want it like this photo — would it work with my hair?
examples.note: 제 머리로 될까요 ('would it work with my hair') asks the stylist for a realistic professional opinion

examples.ko: A: 어떤 스타일 원하세요? / B: 이 사진처럼 자연스럽게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteon seutail wonhaseyo? / B: i sajincheoreom jayeonseureopge hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: What style do you want? / B: Natural, like this photo, please.
examples.note: Adding 자연스럽게 ('naturally') guides the vibe even if the exact look can't be replicated

expressions.nuance: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is 이 사진 ('this photo') + -처럼 ('like, in the manner of') + 해 주세요 ('please do it for me'). Showing a reference photo is the single most reliable way to communicate a hairstyle across a language gap, and -처럼 is the particle that fuses directly onto the noun to express 'in the manner of': 사진처럼, never with a preceding object particle. A close alternative is 사진같이 (사진 + 같이), which is equally natural; -처럼 and 같이 are near-interchangeable here, with -처럼 feeling a touch more standard in this context. The English-speaker trap is over-engineering the sentence: 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 ('make it LOOK like this photo') is understandable but wordier than what Koreans actually say — plain 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is the natural form. A second pitfall is forgetting the realism check: the photo likely shows someone else's texture, thickness, or face shape, so Korean customers routinely add 가능해요? or 될까요? after handing over the phone. Keep 존댓말; the favor form 해 주세요 makes it a polite request, not a command.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Adding a particle before 처럼, like 사진을 처럼.
-처럼 attaches straight to the noun with no object particle: 사진처럼 해 주세요, not 사진을 처럼.
Saying 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 every time.
It's correct but wordy. Natives simply say 이 사진처럼 해 주세요; the 보이게 ('so it looks') is usually unnecessary.
Confusing 처럼 ('like/similar') with 때문에 ('because').
처럼 means 'in the manner of'. Don't swap in 때문에; 이 사진 때문에 해 주세요 would wrongly mean 'do it because of this photo'.

structuredNuance.t: 이 사진 ('this photo') + -처럼 ('like/in the manner of') + 해 주세요. The particle -처럼 attaches directly to the noun — no gap, no object particle before it. The phrase means 'please execute the style you see in this photo'.
존댓말 to the stylist. Said at the very start of the consultation while holding out your phone. Almost always followed by 가능해요? or 될까요? to reality-check the look.
사진같이 해 주세요 is equally natural; -처럼 and 같이 are near-interchangeable here. 이렇게 해 주세요 ('do it like this') works when you're pointing but have no photo.
이 사진처럼 자연스럽게 해 주세요 (natural vibe); 이 사진이랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 ('similar to this photo', allowing differences); 이 사진처럼 될까요? (feasibility check).

Two traps: (1) adding a particle before 처럼 — 사진을 처럼 or 사진의 처럼 are both wrong; -처럼 fuses straight onto the noun; (2) over-building as 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 — this is understandable but unnatural; just say 이 사진처럼 해 주세요.

expressions.english: Please keep it similar to my hair now
expressions.shortExplanation: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please keep it similar to my hair now".
expressions.explanation: "Please keep it similar to my hair now" — that is 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 (jigeum meorirang biseutage hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 ("Keep it similar to my hair now"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Keep it similar to my hair now
usagePhrases.note: Polite; same style, just maintained — the go-to for a returning client

usagePhrases.en: Keep it like it is now
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend
그대로 ('as is') signals zero style change at all
똑같이 ('identically') for a precise repeat of a previous visit

examples.ko: 크게 바꾸지 말고 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: keuge bakkuji malgo jigeum meorirang biseutage hae juseyo.
examples.en: Nothing drastic — keep it similar to my hair now.
examples.note: 크게 바꾸지 말고 ('without big changes') stacks with 비슷하게 to doubly signal you want maintenance, not reinvention

examples.ko: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게, 길이만 좀 줄여 주세요.
examples.romanization: jigeum meorirang biseutage, giriman jom juryeo juseyo.
examples.en: Similar to now, just shorten the length a bit.
examples.note: 길이만 줄이다 ('only shorten the length') is the one permitted tweak — style stays, length adjusts

examples.ko: A: 오늘 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 지난번에 해 주신 거랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: jinanbeone hae jusin georang biseutage hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: How can I do it for you today? / B: Similar to what you did last time, please.
examples.note: 해 주신 거 ('what you did for me') references a past appointment, implying trust in the stylist's previous work

expressions.nuance: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 is 지금 머리 ('my hair now') + -랑 (colloquial 'with/and', the comparison linker) + 비슷하게 (adverb of 비슷하다 'to be similar') + 해 주세요. The pattern 'A랑 비슷하게 해 주세요' = 'please make it similar to A' is broadly reusable throughout the salon. The particle -랑 is the spoken, casual form; formal writing prefers -과/와, but -랑 is the natural choice in the salon chair. The critical three-way contrast: 비슷하게 allows minor differences and is best when small adjustments are fine; 똑같이 demands a precise repeat; 그대로 signals absolutely no change at all — choose based on how tightly you want the result controlled. The English-speaker trap is mixing the comparison frames: 지금 머리처럼 비슷하게 is redundant (처럼 'like' and 비슷하게 'similarly' say the same thing) — use one or the other. Also, 비슷하다 is an adjective, not a command verb; you cannot say 비슷하세요 to the stylist. You need the adverb form 비슷하게 paired with the action verb 해 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing 처럼 and 비슷하게 as 지금 머리처럼 비슷하게.
처럼 already means 'like', so it's redundant with 비슷하게. Use one frame: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 or 지금 머리처럼 해 주세요.
Saying 지금 머리 같게 해 주세요.
같다 ('to be the same') as an adverb here sounds off. Natural is 비슷하게 ('similarly') or 똑같이 ('identically'): 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
Confusing 비슷하게 (similar) with 똑같이 (identical).
비슷하게 allows minor tweaks; 똑같이 demands an exact copy. If you want it precisely the same, say 똑같이; for 'roughly the same', say 비슷하게.

structuredNuance.t: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 = 'please make it similar to my current hair'. -랑 links the comparison reference ('current hair'); 비슷하게 is the adverb of 비슷하다 ('to be similar'). The phrase is the standard request for maintenance with minor adjustments allowed.
존댓말 to staff. Used by returning clients who already have a style they like and just want it maintained. -랑 is colloquial; fine in the salon chair. 지난번에 해 주신 거랑 비슷하게 is the returning-customer variant.

비슷하게 = similar (minor tweaks OK) / 똑같이 = identical (exact copy) / 그대로 = as-is (no change). Choose 비슷하게 when small adjustments are welcome; 똑같이 when you need a precise repeat; 그대로 when you want zero change in style.
크게 바꾸지 말고 비슷하게 해 주세요 (stacking 'no big changes'); 지금 머리랑 비슷하게, 길이만 좀 줄여 주세요 (style same, length tweaked); 지난번에 해 주신 거랑 비슷하게 (reference a past visit).
Two traps: (1) 지금 머리처럼 비슷하게 — redundant; 처럼 and 비슷하게 overlap; use one frame only; (2) 지금 머리 같게 — 같다 as an adverb this way sounds unnatural; use 비슷하게 or 똑같이 instead.

expressions.shortExplanation: 층 내 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please add some layers".
expressions.explanation: 층 내 주세요 (cheung nae juseyo) = "Please add some layers". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 층 내 주세요 ("Please put layers in"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for a layered cut for movement and lightness
반말, to a friend
많이 ('a lot') for heavy, dramatic layering
The opposite: one-length, blunt cut, no stepped layers

examples.ko: 답답해 보여서 층 좀 내 주세요.
examples.romanization: dapdapae boyeoseo cheung jom nae juseyo.
examples.en: It looks heavy, so please add some layers.
examples.note: 답답하다 here means 'heavy and stuffy-looking' (too much bulk with no movement) — a natural reason to request 층

examples.ko: 층 내 주시고, 숱도 좀 쳐 주세요.
examples.romanization: cheung nae jusigo, sutdo jom chyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Layers please, and thin it out a bit too.
examples.note: Pairing 층 내다 (layers for movement) with 숱 치다 (thinning for density) — related but distinct services

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 층 너무 많이 내지 말고 자연스럽게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: cheung neomu mani naeji malgo jayeonseureopge hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: How would you like it? / B: Don't over-layer — keep it natural.
examples.note: 층 너무 많이 내지 말고 ('without over-layering') + 자연스럽게 ('naturally') steers the stylist away from heavy steps

expressions.nuance: 층 내 주세요 is 층 ('layer', Sino-Korean 層 — the same character as a building floor) + 내다 ('to produce, bring out') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form. The essential collocation is 층(을) 내다 = 'to create a layered cut'; the verb is specifically 내다 (transitive: you bring them out), while 층이 나다 is the intransitive form ('layers appear/form'). Knowing this transitive/intransitive pair explains the opposite: 층 안 나게 해 주세요 uses 나다 ('don't let layers form'). A closely related but different service is 숱 치기 ('thinning', reducing density): 층 내다 creates stepped lengths for movement and volume, while 숱 치다 reduces bulk without necessarily changing the length steps — English speakers often conflate these as 'layering', but they are separate requests to the stylist. The loanword 레이어 exists on some salon menus, but plain 층 is what Koreans actually say in the chair. The idiom pair 내다/나다 is important: 층을 내다 (stylist makes layers) vs. 층이 나다 (layers result/appear) — get the transitivity right.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 층 만들어 주세요.
The idiomatic verb for layering is 내다, not 만들다: 층 내 주세요. 만들다 ('make') sounds off with 층.
Confusing 층 내기 (layers) with 숱 치기 (thinning).
층 내다 creates stepped lengths for movement; 숱 치다 reduces thickness/density. They're different — say what you actually want.
Pronouncing/writing it as 칭 or mixing with 청.
It's 층 (cheung, 'layer/floor'). Don't confuse it with similar-sounding syllables; the request is 층 내 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 층 (Sino-Korean 層, 'layer/floor') + 내다 ('to bring out/produce') + 주세요. The fixed collocation is 층(을) 내다 = cut layers into the hair. The result is stepped lengths that add movement and reduce visual weight. Opposite: 층 안 나게 해 주세요 (one-length, no layers).
존댓말 to the stylist. Said during the style consultation, often paired with 숱 치기 requests. 좀 softens the request: 층 좀 내 주세요 ('a bit of layering, please').

층 내다 = create stepped lengths for movement; 숱 치다 = reduce thickness/density with thinning shears. You can have one without the other. Many English speakers ask for 'layers' wanting only thinning — clarify which you actually need.
층 is Sino-Korean 層, the same word as a building floor (1층 = first floor, 2층 = second floor). In hair it means a 'stepped level' — the same structural idea.

Two traps: (1) saying 층을 만들어 주세요 — understandable but unidiomatic; the natural verb is 내다, not 만들다; (2) confusing layering (층 내다) with thinning (숱 치다) — they are different services and require different tools.

expressions.english: Please thin it out a bit
expressions.shortExplanation: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please thin it out a bit".
expressions.explanation: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 (sut jom chyeo juseyo) means "Please thin it out a bit". Say it as one set phrase — for example 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 ("Please thin it out a bit"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Please thin it out a bit
usagePhrases.note: Polite; reduce hair density/bulk with thinning shears
반말, to a friend
많이 for heavier, more aggressive thinning
When you want to keep all the volume

examples.ko: 머리숱이 너무 많아서 숱 좀 쳐 주세요.
examples.romanization: meorisuchi neomu manaseo sut jom chyeo juseyo.
examples.en: My hair's too thick, so please thin it out.
examples.note: 머리숱이 많다 ('to have dense/thick hair') is the natural way to describe having lots of hair — the reason for the request

examples.ko: 윗부분은 두고 아래쪽만 숱 쳐 주세요.
examples.romanization: witbubuneun dugo araejjongman sut chyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Leave the top, just thin out underneath.
examples.note: Zone-targeting: 아래쪽만 ('only the bottom part') keeps the crown full while reducing bulk below

examples.ko: A: 숱 많이 쳐 드릴까요? / B: 숱 너무 많이는 치지 마시고 조금만요.
examples.romanization: A: sun mani chyeo deurilkkayo? / B: sun neomu manineun chiji masigo jogeummanyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I thin it out a lot? / B: Don't thin it too much — just a little.
examples.note: 조금만 ('just a little') caps the thinning and is a good response to prevent over-thinning

expressions.nuance: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 is 숱 ('the density/amount of one's hair') + 좀 (softener) + 치다 ('to strike', here used as the set verb 'to thin out') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form. The key vocabulary is 숱 itself: 머리숱이 많다 means 'to have dense/thick hair', while 숱이 적다 means 'sparse/thin hair'. This is about DENSITY (how many hairs there are per square centimetre), not about the length or the individual strand width. The fixed collocation is 숱(을) 치다 — the stylists uses thinning shears to remove bulk without dramatically shortening the hair. Crucially, 층 내다 (layering for movement) and 숱 치다 (thinning for density) are different services; you can layer without thinning and vice versa. The English-speaker trap is conflating 'thin out' with 얇게 하다: 얇다 describes how THIN each individual strand is (strand width), not how dense the overall hair is — saying 머리 얇게 해 주세요 is a category error. The verb 치다 has many unrelated meanings (hit, play, count), so learners doubt it, but 숱 치다 is completely standard salon Korean. Also note the vowel: 숱 (su-l), not 술 (su-l for alcohol) — one consonant change makes a very different word.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 머리 얇게 해 주세요 to mean 'thin it out'.
얇다 is about the width of each strand, not density. To reduce bulk, say 숱(을) 쳐 주세요 ('thin out the volume').
Using a different verb like 숱 줄여 주세요.
The idiomatic collocation is 숱(을) 치다. 줄이다 ('reduce') is understandable but unnatural here; say 숱 좀 쳐 주세요.
Confusing 숱 with 술.
숱 = hair density; 술 = alcohol. Keep the ㅌ: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요, not 술 좀 쳐 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 숱 ('hair density/amount') + 치다 ('to thin out', set verb) + 주세요. The collocation 숱(을) 치다 means removing bulk with thinning shears — reducing HOW MANY hairs there are per area, without dramatically changing length or strand width.
존댓말 to the stylist. Used by anyone with naturally thick, heavy hair who wants it to sit lighter. 좀 softens the request politely. Stack 윗부분은 두고 / 아래쪽만 to target a specific zone.

숱 치다 = thin by reducing density; 층 내다 = thin by creating stepped lengths for movement. These are physically different techniques. Many English speakers mean 숱 치기 when they say 'layers' — check which you actually want.
숱 많이 쳐 주세요 (aggressive thinning); 숱 치지 말아 주세요 (keep the volume); 아래쪽만 숱 쳐 주세요 (zone-targeted thinning).

Two traps: (1) 머리 얇게 해 주세요 — 얇다 is about strand width, not density; use 숱(을) 치다 for bulk reduction; (2) doubting the verb 치다 because it usually means 'hit' — 숱 치다 is the fully standard, idiomatic salon phrase for thinning.

expressions.english: Please make the sides and back short
expressions.shortExplanation: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please make the sides and back short".
expressions.explanation: "Please make the sides and back short" — that is 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요 (yeopirang dwineun jjalbge hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요 ("Make the sides and back short"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Make the sides and back short
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the backbone instruction for a classic short men's cut
반말, to a friend cutting your hair
The natural pairing: 윗머리 ('top hair') kept longer

usagePhrases.en: Just clean up the sides and back
usagePhrases.note: 정리하다 ('tidy up') for a lighter maintenance cleanup, not a full cut

examples.ko: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 하고, 윗머리는 그대로 두세요.
examples.romanization: yeopirang dwineun jjalbge hago, winmeorineun geudaero duseyo.
examples.en: Sides and back short, leave the top as is.
examples.note: The standard two-instruction combo: short zones explicitly named, top left untouched with 두다 ('leave')

examples.ko: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게, 투블럭으로 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeopirang dwineun jjalbge, tubeulleogeuro hae juseyo.
examples.en: Sides and back short — give me a two-block.
examples.note: 투블럭 (the undercut/two-block style) is the default men's style name in Korean barbershops; naming it cuts the consultation time

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 옆은 귀 보이게, 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: yeopeun gwi boige, dwineun jjalbge hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: How would you like it? / B: Sides so the ears show, back short.
examples.note: 귀 보이게 ('so ears show') is the most concrete, universally understood length cue for the sides

expressions.nuance: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요 is 옆 ('side') + -이랑 (colloquial 'and', after consonant) + 뒤 ('back') + 는 (topic marker) + 짧게 (adverb 'short') + 해 주세요. This single instruction frames a typical short men's haircut by naming the zones: 옆 (sides), 뒤 (back), 윗머리 (top), 앞머리 (front/bangs). Memorising these four zone words gives you full directional control at any barbershop. The particle -이랑 after a consonant (and -랑 after a vowel) is the spoken equivalent of -과/와. The topic marker 는 on 뒤는 sets up a contrast — 'as for the sides and back…' — leaving the top implicitly as the contrasting zone. In Korean barbershops the style name 투블럭 (two-block undercut: very short sides, longer top) covers the most common variant and can replace the whole description once you know the term. The English-speaker trap is adjective form: 짧게 (adverb, used before 해 주세요) vs. 짧은 (noun-modifier — you can't say 짧은 해 주세요). Also, 옆 (side) and 앞 (front) are easy to confuse when stressed; make sure you mean 옆 (sides of the head) rather than 앞 (front).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짧은 해 주세요.
Before 해 주세요 you need the adverb 짧게, not the modifier 짧은. Correct: 짧게 해 주세요.
Mixing up 옆 (side) and 앞 (front).
옆 = the sides of the head; 앞 = the front. For a typical cut you shorten 옆이랑 뒤 (sides and back); don't accidentally say 앞.
Forgetting the topic marker, blurting 옆 뒤 짧게.
It's understandable but choppy. The natural phrasing groups them: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 옆 ('side') + -이랑 ('and') + 뒤 ('back') + 는 (topic marker) + 짧게 (adverb of 짧다 'short') + 해 주세요. Zone-based instruction: name the head sections you want short, implicitly contrasting with the top which is left longer.
존댓말 to any barber or stylist. Primarily a men's cut instruction. Pair immediately with 윗머리는 길게 / 그대로 to complete the picture. Saying 투블럭으로 해 주세요 achieves the same result with a single style name.

투블럭으로 해 주세요 = name the style directly (shorter sides, longer top with a visible line of difference). 옆이랑 뒤만 정리해 주세요 = just clean up those zones, less dramatic. 짧게 vs. 정리 signals the degree of shortening.
옆은 귀 보이게 해 주세요 (sides: ears visible); 뒤는 목선 정리해 주세요 (back: clean up the neckline); 투블럭으로 짧게 해 주세요 (two-block style, explicitly short).

Two traps: (1) 짧은 해 주세요 — wrong form; before 해 주세요 you need the adverb 짧게, not the modifier 짧은; (2) confusing 옆 (side) with 앞 (front) — these are different zones, and mixing them produces the wrong cut.

expressions.english: Please wash my hair / give me a shampoo
expressions.shortExplanation: 감겨 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please wash my hair / give me a shampoo".
expressions.explanation: 감겨 주세요 (gamgyeo juseyo) = "Please wash my hair / give me a shampoo". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 감겨 주세요 ("Please wash my hair (for me)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking staff to shampoo you — requires the causative form
반말, to a friend or family member
Fuller form with 머리 spelled out — clearer if context is ambiguous

usagePhrases.en: Is it okay if I don't wash it (myself)?
usagePhrases.note: Asking whether you need to arrive with clean hair or if they will wash it

examples.en: Please shampoo my hair before the cut.
examples.note: 커트 전에 ('before the cut') pins the timing — many salons wash first, but it's worth confirming

examples.en: I got it dyed, so please wash it clean.
examples.note: 깨끗하게 ('cleanly') after a dye signals you want a thorough rinse, not a quick splash

examples.ko: A: 물 온도 괜찮으세요? / B: 네, 감겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: mul ondo gwaenchaneuseyo? / B: ne, gamgyeo juseyo.
examples.en: A: Is the water temperature okay? / B: Yes, please go ahead and wash it.
examples.note: Standard exchange at the shampoo basin; 네 confirms the temperature, then 감겨 주세요 gives the go-ahead

expressions.nuance: 감겨 주세요 is the CAUSATIVE of 감다 ('to wash one's own hair'): 감다 → 감기다 ('to wash someone else's hair') → 감겨 주다 ('to wash someone's hair for them as a favor'). This causative shift is the central grammar point and the #1 learner trap. When YOU wash your own hair at home, the verb is 머리(를) 감다. At the salon, the staff wash YOUR hair, so the customer uses the causative 감기다 → 감겨 주세요 ('please have my hair washed / please wash my hair for me'). Saying 머리 감아 주세요 (plain 감다 + 주세요) is a common learner error that technically sounds like you're asking the stylist to wash their own hair as a favor — Koreans understand from context, but 감겨 주세요 is the correct causative. Compare: 머리 감았어요 ('I washed my hair', plain, about yourself) vs. 머리 감겨 주세요 ('please wash my hair', causative, you want the staff to do it). Also note: 감다 is specific to HAIR; for face-washing use 세수하다, for body-washing use 씻다 — don't generalise 감다 to any body-washing context.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 머리 감아 주세요 to the stylist.
감다 is washing your OWN hair. To ask staff to wash yours, use the causative 감기다: 감겨 주세요 ('wash my hair for me').
Using 씻겨 주세요 for hair.
씻다/씻기다 is for washing the body or objects. Hair specifically takes 감다/감기다: 머리 감겨 주세요.
Confusing 감다 (wash hair) with 감다 (close eyes / wind).
감다 is a homonym (also 'close the eyes', 'wind up'). In the salon it means washing hair; context and 머리 make it clear: 머리 감겨 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 감겨 주세요 is the causative of 감다: 감다 ('wash own hair') → 감기다 ('wash someone else's hair') → 감겨 주세요 ('please wash [my hair] for me'). The causative form is the grammatically correct form when you are the one being washed, not doing the washing.
존댓말 to salon staff at the shampoo basin. 감다 is specific to hair-washing; do not use it for face (세수하다) or body (씻다). 머리 감겨 주세요 is the clearer version if context is at all ambiguous.
감아 주세요 (plain stem + favor) is a common learner error — technically asks the stylist to wash their own hair as a favor. Only 감겨 주세요 (causative) is correct when asking the staff to wash yours.
머리 감겨 주세요 (with 머리 for clarity); 깨끗하게 감겨 주세요 (wash it cleanly/thoroughly); 커트 전에 감겨 주세요 (before the cut). The 반말 form is 감겨 줘.

English uses 'wash' regardless of who does it, so the 감다/감기다 distinction is invisible. This is the single most common grammar error at the salon: learners say 감아 주세요 instead of the correct causative 감겨 주세요.

expressions.english: Please blow-dry and style it too
expressions.shortExplanation: 드라이까지 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please blow-dry and style it too".
expressions.explanation: 드라이까지 해 주세요 (deuraikkaji hae juseyo) means "Please blow-dry and style it too". Say it as one set phrase — for example 드라이까지 해 주세요 ("Please blow-dry/style it too"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; include drying and styling as the finishing step
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: You don't need to blow-dry it
usagePhrases.note: Declining the dry/style — usually fine for casual visits

usagePhrases.en: Can I get just a blow-out today?
usagePhrases.note: Asking for styling only, no cut — 드라이 as a standalone service

examples.ko: 오늘 약속 있어서 드라이까지 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: oneul yaksok isseoseo deuraikkaji hae juseyo.
examples.en: I have plans today, so please style it too.
examples.note: 약속 있다 ('have plans') is the social reason Koreans give for requesting the full styled finish — the stylist understands immediately

examples.en: A cut and a blow-out too, please — how much?
examples.note: Bundle both services in one sentence and immediately check the combined price — common in Korean salons where 드라이 may cost extra

examples.ko: A: 드라이해 드릴까요? / B: 네, 안쪽으로 살짝 말리게 드라이해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: deuraihae deurilkkayo? / B: ne, anjjogeuro saljjang mallige deuraihae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Shall I blow-dry it? / B: Yes — please blow-dry it curling slightly inward.
examples.note: 안쪽으로 말리게 ('curling inward') directs the style direction; 바깥쪽으로 would be outward curling

expressions.nuance: 드라이까지 해 주세요 is 드라이 (loanword 'dry', meaning a professional blow-dry and styling) + -까지 ('even, up to and including') + 해 주세요. The particle -까지 carries the meaning 'go all the way through to the styling step as well' — it implies the cut is assumed and you want the process completed with a full finish. In Korean salons 드라이 is a professionally blown-out and styled finish, often using a round brush and a blow-dryer; it is sometimes a paid add-on on the menu, not simply towel-drying. The English-speaker trap is interpreting 드라이 as 'dry' in the basic sense: it means a full styled blow-out, so don't be surprised if it costs extra or needs to be listed on the service ticket. The particle nuance matters: -까지 ('up to / including') emphasises completion of the process, whereas -도 ('also') in 드라이도 해 주세요 simply adds it as another item — both work, but -까지 sounds more like 'finish it off properly'. Treat 드라이 as a 하다-noun: 드라이를 하다 / 드라이해 주세요. To decline, say 드라이 안 해도 돼요 — perfectly natural.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 드라이 just means 'dry it off'.
In Korean salons 드라이 means a styled blow-out (often a paid service), not merely removing water. It may be an extra menu item.
Saying 드라이 해 주세요만 with 만 at the end.
만 attaches to the noun: 드라이만 해 주세요 ('only a blow-out'). Tacked onto the sentence end it's broken.
Confusing -까지 ('including') with -부터 ('from/starting').
-까지 means 'up to/including' the blow-dry. -부터 ('from') would wrongly mean 'starting from the blow-dry'. Use 드라이까지.

structuredNuance.t: 드라이 (loanword, a professional blow-dry and styled finish) + -까지 ('up to and including') + 해 주세요. -까지 signals 'complete the service all the way through to the styling step'. In Korean salons this is a full blow-out with a brush, not just removing water.
존댓말 to staff. Said at the end of the consultation or when you want to confirm the full service. If you're just going home with no plans, 드라이 안 해도 돼요 is a fine, polite decline.

드라이도 해 주세요 ('do the blow-dry too') adds it as one more item in a list; 드라이까지 해 주세요 emphasises completing the whole process through to styling. Both are correct — -까지 is more emphatic about finishing properly.
드라이만 받을 수 있어요? (blow-out only, no cut); 안쪽으로 말리게 드라이해 주세요 (inward curl); 바깥쪽으로 드라이해 주세요 (outward/volume). 드라이 takes 하다: 드라이해 주세요.

Two traps: (1) 드라이 = 'dry' in English, so learners assume it is included automatically — in Korean salons it is often a paid add-on; always confirm with 드라이까지 해 주세요 or check the menu; (2) misplacing 만 — 드라이 해 주세요만 puts 만 at the sentence end (wrong); 만 must attach to the noun: 드라이만 해 주세요 ('only a blow-out, nothing else').

expressions.english: I'd like to get a perm
expressions.shortExplanation: 펌하고 싶은데요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to get a perm".
expressions.explanation: "I'd like to get a perm" — that is 펌하고 싶은데요 (peomhago sipeundeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 펌하고 싶은데요 ("I'd like to get a perm"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to get a perm
usagePhrases.note: Polite; opening that you want a perm — the -는데요 invites the stylist's guidance
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I came to get a perm
usagePhrases.note: States your purpose for the visit rather than just your desire
Asking the stylist to suggest the right style for your hair

examples.ko: 오늘 펌하고 싶은데요. 시간 얼마나 걸려요?
examples.romanization: oneul peomhago sipeundeyo. sigan eolmana geollyeoyo?
examples.en: I'd like a perm today — how long does it take?
examples.note: Perms take two to three hours; asking 시간 얼마나 걸려요 immediately after is essential before committing

examples.ko: 자연스러운 펌하고 싶은데, 어떤 게 좋을까요?
examples.romanization: jayeonseureoun peomhago sipeunde, eotteon ge joeulkkayo?
examples.en: I want a natural perm — which would be good?
examples.note: 자연스러운 ('natural') narrows the style, then 어떤 게 좋을까요 ('which is good?') hands the choice to the expert

examples.ko: A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 손상 안 되게 펌하고 싶은데요. 추천해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? / B: sonsang an doege peomhago sipeundeyo. chucheonhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: What can I do for you? / B: I'd like a perm without too much damage — could you recommend one?
examples.note: 손상 안 되게 ('without causing damage') + 추천해 주시겠어요? is the polished consultation opener for first-time perm customers

expressions.nuance: 펌하고 싶은데요 is 펌 (loanword 'perm', from 'permanent wave') + 하고 싶다 ('want to do') + the soft ender -는데요. The word choice matters: younger salon Korean firmly prefers 펌, while 파마 is the older colloquial form still understood but increasingly dated. The -는데요 ender softens and extends an implicit question ('I want a perm, so… what do you recommend?'), making the phrase a natural consultation opener rather than a flat statement. Contrast with 펌하려고 왔어요 ('I came to get a perm') which declares purpose; both are natural openers, but 싶은데요 signals you're open to the stylist's input, while 하려고 왔어요 sounds more decided. Because Korean perm culture has many styles — 셋팅펌 (setting perm), 열펌 (digital/hot perm), 볼륨매직 (volume magic), 스트레이트 펌 (straight perm) — the stylist will almost always ask which type; proactively saying 자연스러운 펌 or 추천 좀 해 주세요 saves a back-and-forth. The English-speaker trap is the want-construction: 하고 싶어요 alone is fine but can sound blunt as an opener; -는데요 turns it into a softer, more conversational lead-in.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 펌 주세요 like ordering a product.
A perm is a service you 'do', not 'receive' like an object. Use 펌하고 싶은데요 or 펌하려고요, not 펌 주세요.
Defaulting to 파마 thinking it's the only word.
파마 is older/colloquial; current salon Korean prefers 펌. Both are understood, but 펌하고 싶은데요 sounds more natural now.
Dropping -는데요 to a blunt 펌하고 싶어요 and stopping.
It's fine but abrupt as a conversation opener. -는데요 invites the stylist's input: 펌하고 싶은데요 (어떤 게 좋을까요?).

structuredNuance.t: 펌 (loanword 'perm') + 하고 싶다 ('want to do') + -는데요 (soft ender). The -는데요 means 'I want a perm, so…' — trailing off and inviting the stylist's response. It's a consultation opener, not a command or a simple statement.
존댓말 to the stylist. Said at the start of the appointment. Because a perm is a long, costly service, always follow up with 시간 얼마나 걸려요? and 가격이 어떻게 돼요? before the stylist starts.
펌하고 싶은데요 ('I'd like a perm, what do you think?') — open, invites advice. 펌하려고 왔는데요 ('I came to get a perm') — states purpose, slightly more decided. 파마 exists but is dated; use 펌.
자연스러운 펌하고 싶은데요 ('a natural perm'); 셋팅펌 / 열펌 / 볼륨매직 하고 싶은데요 (naming the style); 손상 안 되게 펌하고 싶은데요 ('a perm with minimal damage').

The trap is the want-construction register: 펌하고 싶어요 alone is grammatically fine but can sound blunt as an opener. Pairing with -는데요 makes it conversational and invites input — the natural Korean way to begin a consultation.

expressions.english: I'd like to dye my hair — could you suggest a color?
expressions.shortExplanation: 염색하고 싶은데 색 추천해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to dye my hair — could you suggest a color?".
expressions.explanation: 염색하고 싶은데 색 추천해 주세요 (yeomsaekago sipeunde saek chucheonhae juseyo) = "I'd like to dye my hair — could you suggest a color?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 염색하고 싶은데 색 추천해 주세요 ("I want to dye it — please suggest a color"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I want to dye it — please suggest a color
usagePhrases.note: Polite; a full consultation opener combining desire + request for advice

usagePhrases.en: I wanna dye it — what color's good?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: I just want a root touch-up
usagePhrases.note: 뿌리 염색 ('root dye') for covering regrowth only

usagePhrases.en: Do I need to bleach it (first)?
usagePhrases.note: Asking whether bleaching is required before the desired color

examples.ko: 염색하고 싶은데 너무 튀지 않는 색으로 추천해 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeomsaekago sipeunde neomu twiji anhneun saegeuro chucheonhae juseyo.
examples.en: I'd like to dye it — suggest a color that's not too flashy.
examples.note: 너무 튀지 않는 ('not too flashy') guides the palette before the stylist opens the swatch book
