examples.ko: 염색하고 싶은데, 제 피부톤에 뭐가 어울려요?
examples.romanization: yeomsaekago sipeunde, je pibutone mwoga eoullyeoyo?
examples.en: I want to dye it — what suits my skin tone?
examples.note: 피부톤에 어울리다 ('suit the skin tone') asks for a personalised recommendation, not just a popular color

examples.ko: A: 오늘 뭐 해 드릴까요? / B: 흰머리 가리게 염색하고 싶은데 추천해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul mwo hae deurilkkayo? / B: huinmeori garige yeomsaekago sipeunde chucheonhae juseyo.
examples.en: A: What would you like today? / B: I'd like to dye to cover the gray — any suggestions?
examples.note: 흰머리 가리다 ('cover gray hair') is one of the most common dyeing motivations in Korean salons

expressions.nuance: 염색하고 싶은데 색 추천해 주세요 chains 염색(을) 하다 ('to dye hair', Sino-Korean 染色 'dye-color') + 하고 싶다 ('want to') + -는데 (connector, 'and so') + 색 ('color') + 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend'). The connector -는데 bridges the wish and the request in a single, natural utterance rather than two choppy sentences. Essential vocabulary: 염색 = coloring/dyeing; 뿌리 염색 = root touch-up (just the regrowth near the scalp); 탈색 = bleaching (stripping pigment, often needed before vivid or light colors); 새치/흰머리 염색 = covering gray. The English-speaker trap is over-relying on the loanword 컬러: 컬러 appears on salon menus but the verb for the act is 염색하다, so 'I want to color my hair' is 염색하고 싶어요, not 컬러하고 싶어요. A second trap is the grammar of 추천: 추천 is a 하다-noun and cannot stand alone as a command or object of 주다 — it needs 하다: 색 추천해 주세요, never 색을 추천 주세요. Also keep 염색 (adding color) and 탈색 (removing color/bleaching) clearly distinct — many vivid or light shades require 탈색 first, which takes extra time and causes additional damage.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 컬러하고 싶어요 for 'dye my hair'.
The verb is 염색하다. 컬러 is a noun in menus, but 'I want to dye it' is 염색하고 싶어요, not 컬러하고 싶어요.
Saying 색 추천 주세요 without 하다.
추천 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. It needs 하다: 색 추천해 주세요.
Confusing 염색 (dye) with 탈색 (bleach).
염색 adds color; 탈색 strips it to lighten. For a bright shade you may need 탈색 first — ask 탈색해야 돼요?, not just 염색해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 염색(을) 하다 (Sino-Korean 染色, 'dye-color') + 하고 싶다 ('want to') + -는데 (connector) + 색 ('color') + 추천해 주세요. The -는데 links desire to request in one breath — natural Korean consultation language. The full phrase says: 'I want to dye it, and so please recommend a color'.

존댓말 to the stylist. Said at the very start of the consultation. Because color choice depends on skin tone, hair condition, and lifestyle, this opener immediately cues the stylist to ask clarifying questions before reaching for the swatch book.
염색 (dye/add color) vs. 탈색 (bleach/remove color) — these are opposite processes. Requesting a light or vivid color may prompt 탈색해야 돼요? ('do we need to bleach?'). Know which you want before you ask.
염색 is Sino-Korean 染色: 染 = 'dye/stain', 色 = 'color'. The same 染 appears in 탈색 (脫色: strip-color = bleach) and 새치 염색 (covering gray hair).
Two traps: (1) 컬러하고 싶어요 — 컬러 is a menu noun, not a verb; use 염색하고 싶어요; (2) 색 추천 주세요 — 추천 is a 하다-noun; you must say 추천해 주세요, never 추천 주세요.

expressions.english: Please dye it back to my natural color
expressions.shortExplanation: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please dye it back to my natural color".
expressions.explanation: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요 (wollae meorisaegeuro hae juseyo) means "Please dye it back to my natural color". Say it as one set phrase — for example 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요 ("Make it my original hair color"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Make it my original hair color
usagePhrases.note: Polite; returning to your natural shade after dyeing or bleaching
반말, to a friend
When you don't know your exact natural shade, naming a close natural tone
Capping brightness when you want a darker, more natural result

examples.ko: 탈색했던 거 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: talsaekaetdeon geo wollae meorisaegeuro hae juseyo.
examples.en: I had it bleached — please put it back to my natural color.
examples.note: 탈색했던 거 ('the bleached part') tells the stylist the history so they know the starting condition

examples.ko: 취업 때문에 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: chwieop ttaemune wollae meorisaegeuro hae juseyo.
examples.en: For job-hunting, please dye it back to natural.
examples.note: 취업 때문에 ('for getting a job') is one of the most common stated reasons in Korean salons — many workplaces expect dark, natural-looking hair

examples.ko: A: 어떤 색으로 해 드릴까요? / B: 원래 머리색이랑 비슷하게, 좀 어둡게 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: eotteon saegeuro hae deurilkkayo? / B: wollae meorisaegirang biseutage, jom eodupge hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: What color would you like? / B: Similar to my natural color, a bit darker please.
examples.note: 비슷하게 + 어둡게 ('similar to natural, but slightly darker') fine-tunes the shade and gives the stylist a clear target

expressions.nuance: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요 is 원래 ('original, originally', Sino-Korean 元來) + 머리색 ('hair color') + -으로 ('to/into', the result/direction particle) + 해 주세요. The critical grammar is -(으)로: this particle marks what something is changed INTO — 'make it INTO my original color'. The pattern 'X(으)로 해 주세요' = 'please make it X' is reusable for any target color: 어두운 갈색으로 해 주세요 ('make it dark brown'), 검은색으로 해 주세요 ('make it black'). After the consonant ㄱ in 색, the particle form is 색으로 (not 색로). 원래 means 'as it originally was / in its natural state'; it's extremely common in Korea where students and office workers often darken their hair back to a natural shade for 취업 (job hunting) or school rules. The English-speaker trap is the particle: learners use 원래 머리색을 해 주세요 (object particle 을) or 머리색에 해 주세요 (locative 에), but the change-into meaning needs -(으)로. Also distinguish 원래 ('originally') from 원해 ('want', from 원하다) — one letter apart but completely different.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 을/를 instead of (으)로: 원래 머리색을 해 주세요.
The 'change it INTO' meaning needs the particle -(으)로: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요. -을/를 marks an object, not a result.
Confusing 원래 ('originally') with 원해 ('want').
원래 머리색 = 'original hair color'. 원해 is from 원하다 ('to want'). Don't write 원해 머리색.
Saying 검은색으로 when you mean your natural shade.
Natural hair may be dark brown, not pure black. For your real shade say 원래 머리색으로; 검은색 ('black') forces full black, which can look unnatural.

structuredNuance.t: 원래 ('original, originally', Sino-Korean 元來) + 머리색 ('hair color') + -으로 ('into/to', change-result particle) + 해 주세요. The phrase means 'please transform the color back into my original natural shade'. -(으)로 is what makes this a change-into request, not just a description.
존댓말 to the stylist. Common at the start of a job-hunting season (취업준비), before school term, or simply when a customer is done with dyed hair. Pair with 좀 어둡게 or 자연스럽게 to add precision.

검은색으로 해 주세요 ('make it black') forces pure black, which can look unnatural on non-Asian natural hair; 원래 머리색으로 targets the personal natural shade, which is usually a very dark brown (흑갈색). These are different results.
원래 is Sino-Korean 元來: 元 = 'original/root', 來 = 'come/from'. It means 'as it originally came' — a natural fit for 'my original hair color'.
The particle trap: learners say 원래 머리색을 해 주세요 (을 = object) or 머리색에 해 주세요 (에 = locative), but the change-into meaning needs -(으)로. After the ㄱ in 색, the correct form is 색으로: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 커트 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is a haircut?".
expressions.explanation: "How much is a haircut?" — that is 커트 얼마예요? (keoteu eolmayeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 커트 얼마예요? ("How much is a cut?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; direct way to ask a service's price
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: How much would a cut be?
usagePhrases.note: Softer/more polite with -인가요, used with unfamiliar or upscale staff
-부터 ('starting from') asks for the bottom of a price range

examples.en: How much is a men's cut?
examples.note: 남자/여자 커트 are often priced differently; always specify gender to get the right quote

examples.en: A cut and dye — how much all together?
examples.note: 다 해서 ('all together') asks for the combined total of multiple services

examples.ko: A: 어서 오세요. / B: 학생 할인 돼요? 커트 얼마예요?
examples.romanization: A: eoseo oseyo. / B: haksaeng harin dwaeyo? keoteu eolmayeyo?
examples.en: A: Welcome! / B: Is there a student discount? How much is a cut?
examples.note: 학생 할인 ('student discount') is genuinely worth asking about in Korean salons — many offer one

expressions.nuance: 커트 얼마예요? is 커트 ('a haircut') + 얼마 ('how much in price') + 예요 (polite copula), the simplest and most direct way to ask a service's cost. The word 얼마 specifically asks about PRICE; it is not to be confused with 얼마나 ('how much/long', about extent or duration). This is the most common learner mix-up at the salon: 얼마예요? = 'how much does it cost?', while 얼마나 걸려요? = 'how long does it take?' — one extra syllable but completely different questions. Korean salons frequently price differently by gender (남자/여자 커트) and by hair length, so specifying 남자 커트 or 긴 머리 커트 before 얼마예요 gets you an accurate answer. Add-ons like perms and dye are always billed separately, so asking 다 해서 얼마예요? after listing services is standard practice. The English-speaker trap is the copula: 얼마 + 예요 fuses naturally (얼마예요), not the separated 얼마 이에요. Bare 커트 얼마예요? is more natural than the heavier 커트 가격이 얼마예요? ('what is the price of a haircut?') — the word 가격 is usually unnecessary.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 얼마 (price) with 얼마나 (extent/duration).
얼마예요? asks the cost; 얼마나 걸려요? asks the time. To ask price, use 얼마: 커트 얼마예요?.
Saying 얼마 이에요 separately.
The copula fuses after a vowel: 얼마 + 예요 → 얼마예요. Writing 얼마 이에요 is unnatural; say 커트 얼마예요?.
Over-building it as 커트 가격이 얼마예요?
It's correct but heavy. Natives simply say 커트 얼마예요?; the word 가격 ('price') is usually unnecessary.

structuredNuance.t: 커트 ('haircut') + 얼마 ('how much in price') + 예요 (polite copula). 얼마 is the Korean word specifically for a price/amount of money. It fuses directly with the copula: 얼마예요, not 얼마 이에요.
Polite-neutral; fine with any staff. Ask before sitting down to avoid surprises. Specify 남자/여자, 긴 머리/짧은 머리 for an accurate quote, as salons routinely price by gender and hair length.

얼마예요? = cost (price question). 얼마나 걸려요? = duration (time question). One extra syllable separates them, but they are completely different questions — never swap them. 얼마부터예요? asks for the starting price of a range.
남자 커트 얼마예요? (men's cut price); 다 해서 얼마예요? (combined total); 펌은 얼마부터예요? (perm starting price); 학생 할인 되나요? (student discount).
Two traps: (1) 얼마 vs. 얼마나 — 얼마예요 asks price; 얼마나 걸려요 asks duration; these are completely different; (2) over-building as 커트 가격이 얼마예요? — understandable but heavy; natives say 커트 얼마예요?.

expressions.hangul: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?
expressions.romanization: maeume an deuneunde dasi hae jusil su isseoyo?
expressions.english: I'm not happy with it — could you redo it?
expressions.shortExplanation: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "I'm not happy with it — could you redo it?".
expressions.explanation: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? (maeume an deuneunde dasi hae jusil su isseoyo?) means "I'm not happy with it — could you redo it?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? ("I don't like it — could you redo it?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.ko: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: maeume an deuneunde dasi hae jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: I don't like it — could you redo it?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the diplomatic, face-saving way to raise dissatisfaction and request a fix

usagePhrases.ko: 이거 마음에 안 들어, 다시 해 줄 수 있어?
usagePhrases.romanization: igeo maeume an deureo, dasi hae jul su isseo?
usagePhrases.en: I don't like this — can you redo it?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.ko: 조금만 더 다듬어 주실 수 있어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: jogeumman deo dadeumeo jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you trim it a bit more?
usagePhrases.note: Softer: requesting a small adjustment rather than a full redo

usagePhrases.ko: 여기 좀 더 짧게 해 주세요
usagePhrases.romanization: yeogi jom deo jjalbge hae juseyo
usagePhrases.en: Please make it a bit shorter here
usagePhrases.note: Pinpointing a specific area that needs fixing instead of redoing everything

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 생각했던 거랑 좀 달라서 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande, saenggakaetdeon georang jom dallaseo dasi hae jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, it's a bit different from what I pictured — could you redo it?
examples.note: 생각했던 거랑 다르다 ('different from what I imagined') is the softest, least blaming way to state the mismatch

examples.ko: 앞이 너무 짧은 거 같은데, 다시 봐 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: api neomu jjalbeun geo gateunde, dasi bwa jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: The front seems too short — could you take another look?
examples.note: 다시 봐 주다 ('look again') is even gentler than 다시 해 주다 ('redo') — useful when you want a reassessment, not necessarily a full fix

examples.ko: A: (거울 보여주며) 어떠세요? / B: 색이 생각보다 밝게 나왔는데, 조금 어둡게 다시 해 주실 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: A: (geoul boyeojumyeo) eotteoseyo? / B: saegi saenggakboda balkge nawanneunde, jogeum eodupge dasi hae jusil su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: A: (holding up mirror) How is it? / B: The color came out lighter than expected — could you redo it a bit darker?
examples.note: Responding to the mirror check: -ㄹ 수 있을까요 makes the redo request as tentative and polite as possible

expressions.nuance: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? combines 마음에 들다 (the fixed IDIOM 'to be to one's liking', lit. 'to enter the heart') negated as 마음에 안 들다 + -는데 (connector, 'and so') + 다시 ('again') + 해 주시다 (honorific favor verb) + -ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can you / are you able to?'). This is the standard diplomatic, face-saving formula for raising dissatisfaction in a Korean service setting — complaining outright would create awkwardness, so the -ㄹ 수 있어요? framing and the honorific -시- keep it soft and non-confrontational. The core idiom 마음에 들다 is the natural Korean verb for liking a result or outcome: 마음에 들어요 = 'I like it', 마음에 안 들어요 = 'I don't like it'. You cannot substitute 좋아하다 here — 이거 안 좋아해요 about a haircut sounds like a general dislike of haircuts as a concept, not dissatisfaction with this specific result. The English-speaker trap is exactly that substitution. The particle in the idiom is always 에 (locative): 마음에 들다 — never 마음을 들다 or 마음이 들다. Always lead with a softener (죄송한데 'sorry but'; or a reason like 생각했던 거랑 달라서 'it's different from what I imagined') before the redo request, matching Korean social norms around indirect negative feedback.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이거 안 좋아해요 to mean 'I don't like this haircut'.
좋아하다 is for general liking of people/activities. For not liking a result, use the idiom 마음에 안 들어요.
Getting the particle wrong: 마음을 안 들어요 or 마음이 안 들어요.
The idiom takes locative 에: 마음에 안 들어요 ('it doesn't enter my heart'). Not 을/를 or 이/가 on 마음.
Demanding a redo bluntly: 다시 하세요.
다시 하세요 is a command and sounds rude to staff. Ask as an ability question with honorific 시: 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?, and lead with 죄송한데.

structuredNuance.t: 마음에 들다 = the idiom 'to enter the heart' = 'to be to one's liking'. Negated: 마음에 안 들다 = 'not to my liking' = 'I'm not happy with it'. This idiom is the ONLY natural way to express dissatisfaction with a service result in Korean — 좋아하다 is wrong here.
존댓말 with honorific -시- (해 주시다) and the softened ability question form -ㄹ 수 있어요?. Never a direct command (다시 하세요 is rude). Always precede with 죄송한데 or a reason to save face.

마음에 안 들어요 ('I'm not satisfied with the result') vs. 이상해요 ('it looks strange/odd') — both valid complaints, but 마음에 안 들다 is the most diplomatic. 다시 봐 주실 수 있어요? ('could you take another look?') is even softer than 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? ('could you redo it?').
조금만 더 다듬어 주실 수 있어요? (small adjustment); 여기만 조금 더 해 주실 수 있어요? (one spot); 색이 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있을까요? (-ㄹ까요 for extra tentativeness).
The #1 trap: 'I don't like it' → 안 좋아해요, which is wrong for a result. Use 마음에 안 들어요. Second trap: the particle — it is always 마음에 들다 (locative 에), never 마음을 or 마음이.

expressions.english: Did you take attendance / has it been called?
expressions.shortExplanation: 출석 불렀어요? is a practical expression meaning "Did you take attendance / has it been called?".
expressions.explanation: "Did you take attendance / has it been called?" — that is 출석 불렀어요? (chulseok bulleosseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 출석 불렀어요? ("Did they call the roll?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask a classmate if attendance was already taken
반말, to a classmate you're friendly with
출석 체크 = 'attendance check', the everyday phrasing
아직 ('yet') when you're checking you didn't miss it

examples.en: Did they take attendance?
examples.note: Whispered to the person next to you as you slip in late

examples.en: I'm late — did they already call roll?
examples.note: 저 늦었는데 ('I'm late, so…') frames the urgency of the question

examples.ko: A: 선생님, 저 왔어요. 출석 좀 체크해 주세요. / B: 네, 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: A: seonsaengnim, jeo wasseoyo. chulseok jom chekeuhae juseyo. / B: ne, hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Teacher, I'm here — please mark me present. / B: Yes, got it.
examples.note: Use 체크해 주세요 to the TEACHER to be marked present; 부르다 is reading names, not recording

expressions.nuance: 출석 불렀어요? combines 출석 (出席, 'attendance') and the past of 부르다 ('to call out'), asking 'have they called the roll yet?' — exactly what a latecomer desperately needs to know. The polite -어요 form suits a classmate you don't know well; with a friend drop to 출석 불렀어?. The closest near-synonym is 출석 체크했어요? (출석 + the loan-word 체크), which is interchangeable in casual class talk. The critical direction split: 출석 불렀어요? asks a PEER whether the roll-call happened; to get the TEACHER to mark you present, say 출석 체크해 주세요 — don't say 출석 불러 주세요, because 부르다 means reading names aloud to the class, not individually noting your attendance. The English-speaker's biggest trap is 직역-ing 'take attendance' with 가지다 ('to take/hold an object'): 출석을 가져요 is nonsense in Korean. Also keep the antonym pair straight: 출석 (present) ↔ 결석 (absent).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 출석 가졌어요? for 'did you take attendance?'.
'Take attendance' is not 가지다 ('to hold/take an object'). Korean says 출석을 부르다 ('call the roll') or 출석 체크하다. Ask 출석 불렀어요? or 출석 체크했어요?
Saying 출석 불러 주세요 to mean 'mark me present'.
부르다 is reading names aloud to the class, not recording you individually. To be marked present, say 출석 (체크) 해 주세요 — 출석 불러 주세요 sounds like 'please call out the roll (to everyone).'
Confusing 출석 with 출근.
출석 is attendance at class/school; 출근 is 'going to work / clocking in.' Say 출석 for the classroom, not 출근.

structuredNuance.t: 출석 (出席 'attendance') + 불렀어요 (past of 부르다 'to call out'). Literally 'did they call attendance?' — the urgent question of a latecomer. Use polite -어요 with unfamiliar classmates; drop to 불렀어? with friends.
Peer-to-peer only. To ask a TEACHER to mark you present, switch to 출석 체크해 주세요 — 출석 불러 주세요 sounds like asking them to read names aloud to the class, which is not what you mean.
출석 체크했어요? (체크 = English 'check') is an interchangeable casual synonym. 출석 부르다 stresses the act of calling names; 출석 체크하다 stresses ticking off a list — same situation, slightly different mental image.
'Take attendance' tempts 가지다 (가져요), but Korean uses 부르다 ('call') or 체크하다. 출석을 가져요 is meaningless. Also keep 출석 (present) distinct from 결석 (absent) — they're antonyms, not synonyms.

expressions.english: I won't be coming to class today
expressions.shortExplanation: 오늘 결석할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I won't be coming to class today".
expressions.explanation: 오늘 결석할게요 (oneul gyeolseokalgeyo) = "I won't be coming to class today". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 오늘 결석할게요 ("I'll be absent today"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; telling the teacher you can't come
반말, to a classmate, not the teacher
Plainer, very common spoken alternative
수업 못 듣다 ('can't take the class') variant

examples.en: Teacher, I'll be absent today.
examples.note: A heads-up message to the teacher before class starts

examples.ko: 몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요. 죄송합니다.
examples.romanization: momi an joaseo oneul gyeolseokalgeyo. joesonghamnida.
examples.en: I'm not feeling well, so I'll miss today. Sorry.
examples.note: Give the reason first (몸이 안 좋다), then apologize — omitting either feels abrupt

examples.ko: A: 오늘 왜 안 와요? / B: 일이 생겨서 결석하게 됐어요. 다음 수업에 뵐게요.
examples.romanization: A: oneul wae an wayo? / B: iri saenggyeoseo gyeolseokage dwaesseoyo. daeum sueobe boelgeyo.
examples.en: A: Why aren't you coming today? / B: Something came up, so I ended up having to miss class. See you next session.
examples.note: 결석하게 됐어요 frames it as circumstance, not personal choice — softer and more polite

expressions.nuance: 오늘 결석할게요 is 오늘 ('today') + 결석 (缺席, 'absence') + -할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 ending that signals your own intention as a courteous notice). It is how you tell a teacher or academy you won't attend — and register matters deeply: to the teacher you keep -할게요 and almost always add a reason and 죄송합니다, because a bare announcement can feel dismissive. The blame-deflecting variant 결석하게 됐어요 ('it came to be that I'll be absent') frames absence as circumstance rather than choice, which sounds noticeably more considerate. A plainer everyday alternative is 오늘 못 가요 ('I can't come today'). Against the casual register, 수업 빠질게요 ('I'll skip class') implies a voluntary choice and is fine with friends but loose to a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 결석 as a state: 결석이에요 ('I am an absence') with the copula does not announce a planned absence — you must use the verb 결석하다. And never translate 'skip class' as 수업 점프해요, which is meaningless in Korean.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 오늘 결석이에요 to announce you'll miss class.
The copula 이에요 states a label, not an intended action. To tell the teacher, use the verb: 오늘 결석할게요 (or 못 가요).
Translating 'skip class' as 수업 점프해요 / 스킵해요.
직역 of 'skip/jump' doesn't work. Korean uses 결석하다 (formal) or 수업 빠지다 (casual): 오늘 수업 빠질게요.
Announcing the absence with no reason or apology.
A bare 결석할게요 can sound abrupt to a teacher. Add a reason and 죄송합니다: 몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요, 죄송합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 오늘 결석할게요 = 오늘 + 결석 (缺席 'absence') + -할게요 (courteous announcement of one's own intention). It is the polite way to notify a teacher you won't attend. Always add a reason + 죄송합니다 to soften it; omitting them can feel rude.

존댓말 only when speaking to a teacher. To classmates you can drop to 결석할게 or 오늘 못 가. The softer 결석하게 됐어요 ('it ended up that I'll be absent') de-emphasises personal agency and is ideal when you want to sound regretful, not cavalier.

오늘 못 가요 ('I can't come') is the plainest alternative. 수업 빠질게요 ('I'll skip') is fine between classmates but sounds casual-to-careless to a teacher, since 빠지다 can hint at a voluntary skip. 결석하다 is the neutral, correct verb in all formal contexts.
'Be absent' tempts 결석이에요 (copula), but you cannot notify the teacher that way — use the verb: 결석할게요. Never translate 'skip class' as 점프하다 / 스킵하다; Korean uses 빠지다 (casual) or 결석하다 (formal).

expressions.shortExplanation: 숙제가 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the homework?".
expressions.explanation: 숙제가 뭐예요? (sukjega mwoyeyo?) means "What's the homework?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 숙제가 뭐예요? ("What's the homework?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask the teacher or a classmate
반말, to a classmate
Checking whether any was assigned at all
Asking the page range (어디까지 = 'up to where')

examples.en: What's the homework?
examples.note: Asked at the end of class or to a classmate you meet later

examples.en: Is there homework today? If so, what is it?
examples.note: Two-step: first check existence, then ask what it is — natural spoken sequence

examples.ko: A: 저 어제 결석해서 그런데요, 숙제가 뭐였어요? / B: 교과서 45쪽 문제 풀어 오는 거요.
examples.romanization: A: jeo eoje gyeolseokaeseo geureondeyo, sukjega mwoyeosseoyo? / B: gyogwaseo 45jjong munje pureo oneun geoyo.
examples.en: A: I was absent yesterday — what was the homework? / B: Solve the problems on page 45 of the textbook. /
examples.note: Past 뭐였어요 for homework already assigned; 풀어 오다 ('solve and bring') is a typical phrasing

expressions.nuance: 숙제가 뭐예요? is 숙제 (宿題, 'homework') + 가 (subject particle) + 뭐예요 ('what is it?'). It is the basic, universally usable ask for any assigned work, directed at the teacher or a classmate. The subject particle 가 is the correct choice here — 숙제를 뭐예요 is ungrammatical. A major register distinction separates 숙제 from 과제 (課題): 숙제 is everyday short practice work (drills, written exercises), while 과제 is a bigger, more formal assignment like an essay or project — using 숙제 for a term paper sounds childish, and 과제 for tiny daily exercises sounds stiff. A very practical variant is 숙제 어디까지예요? ('how far is the homework?'), because Korean classes typically assign by page range. If you missed a class, shift to past tense: 숙제가 뭐였어요?. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle error (숙제를 voids the grammar) and treating 숙제 as a verb: 'do homework' is 숙제하다 / 숙제를 하다, not 숙제다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 숙제를 뭐예요?
With 뭐예요 ('what is…?') the noun takes the subject particle 가, not the object 를. Say 숙제가 뭐예요?, or in speech just 숙제 뭐예요?
Using 숙제 for a big essay/report.
숙제 is everyday practice work; a major paper or project is 과제. Calling a term paper 숙제 sounds childish — say 과제 for serious assignments.
Treating 숙제 like a verb (숙제다 / 숙제어요).
숙제 is a noun. 'Do homework' is 숙제하다 or 숙제를 하다. To say you finished it: 숙제 다 했어요, not 숙제했다 as a state.

structuredNuance.t: 숙제 (宿題 'homework') + 가 (subject particle) + 뭐예요 ('what is it?'). Straightforward question for any assigned work. Practical variant: 숙제 어디까지예요? ('up to where is the homework?') because Korean teachers assign by page range. Missed a class? Shift to past: 숙제가 뭐였어요?.

Works with both teachers (polite -어요) and classmates. With a close friend drop the particle and go 반말: 숙제 뭐야? The formula 오늘 숙제 있어요? first checks whether any was even assigned, then 뭐예요 asks the content — two-step approach is very natural in speech.

숙제 = daily practice work (short exercises, drills); 과제 (課題) = bigger formal assignment (essay, project, presentation). Using 숙제 for a major report sounds childish; 과제 for a tiny drill sounds stiff. Match the word to the scale.
Particle error: 숙제를 뭐예요 is ungrammatical — use subject 가 (or drop it in quick speech). Also do NOT treat 숙제 as a verb: 'do homework' is 숙제하다 / 숙제를 하다, not 숙제다 / 숙제어요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 숙제 언제까지예요? is a practical expression meaning "When is the homework due?".
expressions.explanation: "When is the homework due?" — that is 숙제 언제까지예요? (sukje eonjekkajiyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 숙제 언제까지예요? ("When is it due?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the deadline
반말, to a classmate
마감 ('deadline') for a formal assignment
Confirming a same-day deadline

examples.en: When's the homework due?
examples.note: Asked immediately after homework is assigned so you don't forget

examples.en: By when do I have to hand in this assignment?
examples.note: 내야 돼요 ('have to submit') makes the obligation explicit; 내다 is the natural verb

examples.ko: A: 숙제 언제까지야? / B: 다음 주 수요일 수업 전까지.
examples.romanization: A: sukje eonjekkajiya? / B: daeum ju suyoil sueop jeonkkaji.
examples.en: A: When's it due? / B: Before class next Wednesday.
examples.note: 까지 anchors both deadline question and answer — note the same particle in both turns

expressions.nuance: 숙제 언제까지예요? is 숙제 + 언제 ('when') + 까지 ('until/by') + 예요. The particle 까지 is doing the essential work: 언제까지 = 'by when' (a deadline to meet). Without 까지, the question 숙제 언제예요? sounds like asking when homework takes place, not when it's due — 까지 is non-negotiable. For formal assignments, 마감 ('deadline', lit. 'closing') surfaces: 과제 마감 언제예요?. The hand-in verb of choice is 내다 ('to hand in'), the natural classroom word — 제출하다 (提出) is more formal and better suited to written/official contexts. The contrast between 까지 and 동안: 까지 pins a deadline ('by Monday'), while 동안 marks a duration ('for a week') — keep them distinct. 'Due' has no single Korean equivalent; you always construct it from 까지 + the submission verb.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 숙제 언제예요? for the deadline.
언제 alone asks 'when (does it happen)?' To ask a due date, add 까지 ('by'): 숙제 언제까지예요?
Looking for one word for 'due'.
Korean has no single 'due'. Express it with 까지 + a verb: 언제까지 내야 돼요? ('by when must I hand it in?'). Don't invent 듀하다.
Overusing 제출하다 in casual class talk.
제출하다 ('to submit') is formal/written. In everyday speech, 내다 ('to hand in') is more natural: 숙제 언제까지 내요?

structuredNuance.t: 숙제 + 언제 ('when') + 까지 ('by/until') + 예요. 언제까지 = 'by when' = asking for a deadline. Korean has no single word for 'due'; you build it with 까지 + a verb like 내다 ('to hand in'). 마감 ('closing deadline') is the formal-register alternative: 과제 마감 언제예요?.

Fine to ask both teachers and classmates. 까지 must stay in the question — omitting it gives 숙제 언제예요? which sounds like asking when class happens. To a teacher, 언제까지 내야 돼요? ('by when must I hand it in?') is a natural fuller form. Among friends: 숙제 언제까지야?.

까지 = deadline endpoint ('by Monday'); 동안 = duration ('for a week') — never swap them. 내다 = hand in (casual classroom speech); 제출하다 = submit (formal, written). Use 내다 when talking to classmates, 제출하다 in written notices or formal academic contexts.
Dropping 까지 turns the deadline question into a vague 'when?' For the act of submission, 내다 is more natural in casual speech than 제출하다 — 언제까지 내야 돼요? is the sentence to memorize.

expressions.shortExplanation: 숙제 다 했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I finished the homework".
expressions.explanation: 숙제 다 했어요 (sukje da haesseoyo) = "I finished the homework". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 숙제 다 했어요 ("I finished the homework"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting to the teacher you're done
반말, to a classmate
끝내다 ('to finish/complete') for a bigger task

usagePhrases.en: I haven't done the homework yet
usagePhrases.note: The honest opposite, with 아직 + 못

examples.en: Teacher, I finished the homework.
examples.note: Said when the teacher checks who's done; 선생님 opener signals deference

examples.ko: 숙제 다 했는데 한 문제는 잘 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: sukje da haenneunde han munjeneun jal moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: I did all of it, but there's one problem I'm not sure about.
examples.note: 다 했는데 ('I did it all, but…') lets you flag a specific difficulty without seeming lazy

examples.ko: A: 숙제 다 했어? / B: 아니, 시간이 없어서 다 못 했어. 도와줄 수 있어?
examples.romanization: A: sukje da haesseo? / B: ani, sigani eopseoseo da mo taesseo. dowajul su isseo?
examples.en: A: Did you finish the homework? / B: No, I ran out of time so I couldn't finish. Can you help me?
examples.note: 다 못 했어 ('couldn't finish it all') sounds circumstantial, not careless; contrast with 안 했어 ('didn't do it')

expressions.nuance: 숙제 다 했어요 is 숙제 + 다 ('all/completely') + 했어요 (past of 하다). The word 다 is the completion marker — it converts 'I did homework' into 'I finished it all', making it far more natural than 완성했어요 ('completed', which sounds like finishing a painting or building). The 안/못 pair in the negative is the critical choice every learner must master: 안 했어요 = 'didn't do it (by choice / just didn't)', 못 했어요 = 'couldn't do it (tried but failed, ran out of time)'. To a teacher, 다 못 했어요 ('couldn't finish') is sympathetic; 안 했어요 ('didn't do it') sounds like you blew it off — choose deliberately. For a larger 과제, 끝냈어요 ('finished/wrapped up') sounds better than 했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is misplacing 다: it must precede the verb (다 했어요), not follow it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 숙제 안 했어요 when you ran out of time.
안 했어요 = 'didn't do it (chose not to).' If you tried but couldn't finish, say 못 했어요 ('couldn't'): 숙제 다 못 했어요 — it sounds far less like you blew it off.
Using 완성했어요 for finishing homework.
완성하다 ('to complete') fits a painting, building, or big creation. For homework, the natural word is 다 했어요 (or 끝냈어요 for a project).
Putting 다 after the verb: 했어요 다.
다 ('all') comes before the verb: 다 했어요. 했어요 다 is unnatural word order.

structuredNuance.t: 숙제 + 다 ('all') + 했어요 (past of 하다). 다 is the completion marker; without it you're just saying you did some homework, not that you finished. For a larger assignment 끝냈어요 ('wrapped up/completed') is more fitting than 다 했어요.

Polite -어요 to the teacher; drop to 다 했어 with friends. When reporting to the teacher in class, lead with 선생님 as a respectful opener. If you didn't finish, pick your negative carefully: 못 했어요 (couldn't — sympathetic) vs. 안 했어요 (didn't — sounds like negligence).

다 했어요 = finished everyday homework (idiomatic); 완성했어요 = completed something creative/substantial (feels like finishing a sculpture — awkward for homework); 끝냈어요 = wrapped up a project (suits 과제 better). Three completion verbs, three scales.
Misplacing 다: it must come BEFORE the verb (다 했어요), not after. Also the 안/못 trap: 안 했어요 sounds intentional even when you just ran out of time — use 못 했어요 to communicate circumstance, not defiance.

expressions.english: Could you explain it once more?
expressions.shortExplanation: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Could you explain it once more?".
expressions.explanation: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 (han beon deo seolmyeonghae juseyo) means "Could you explain it once more?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 ("Please explain once more"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask the teacher to repeat
반말, to a classmate helping you
More formal/deferential with 말씀 + 주시겠어요
Add 천천히 ('slowly') when you can't keep up

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 이 부분 한 번 더 설명해 주세요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande, i bubun han beon deo seolmyeonghae juseyo.
examples.en: Sorry — could you explain this part once more?
examples.note: 이 부분 ('this part') pinpoints exactly where you got lost; 죄송한데 softens the interruption

examples.ko: 이해가 잘 안 돼서, 천천히 한 번 더 설명해 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: ihaega jal an dwaeseo, cheoncheonhi han beon deo seolmyeonghae jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I don't quite get it — could you explain slowly once more?
examples.note: 이해가 안 돼서 ('because I don't understand') gives the reason, making the request more considerate

examples.ko: A: 설명해 드릴게요. 이해됐어요? / B: 아직 잘 모르겠어요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: A: seolmyeonghae deurilgeyo. ihaedwaesseoyo? / B: ajik jal moreugesseoyo. dasi han beon malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A: Let me explain. Did you follow? / B: I'm still not quite sure — could you say it once more?
examples.note: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요 is the more formal upgrade; note 말씀 used because A is superior

expressions.nuance: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 is 한 번 ('one time') + 더 ('more/additionally') + 설명하다 (說明, 'to explain') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The favor form 주세요 is indispensable — it frames the explanation as a gift to you and is what makes this polite; bare 설명하세요 is a command ('you, explain!') and is rude to a teacher. 한 번 더 ('one more time') vs. 다시 ('again'): 한 번 더 stresses 'one additional time', 다시 stresses 'from scratch / over again' — both work in class. For maximum deference to a respected teacher, upgrade 말하다 to the humble-honorific 말씀하다: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?. The word order trap: 'one more time' must be 한 번 더, NOT 한 더 번 or 더 한 번 — the number + counter unit must stay together. The English-speaker's other pitfall is expressing non-understanding: use 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood'), not 이해하지 않아요 (sounds like you're REFUSING to understand).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 설명하세요 to the teacher.
Bare -세요 here is a command ('explain!') and sounds bossy. Use the favor form: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 ('please explain for me').
Word order 한 더 번 / 더 한 번.
The counter pattern is number + counter, then 더: 한 번 더. 한 더 번 is wrong; 더 한 번 sounds off in this request.
Saying 이해하지 않아요 for 'I don't understand'.
That sounds like 'I refuse to understand.' Natural Korean is 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood') or 잘 모르겠어요.

structuredNuance.t: 한 번 ('one time') + 더 ('additionally') + 설명하다 (說明 'to explain') + 해 주세요 (favor form 'please do for me'). 주세요 converts an order into a polite request. Without it, 설명하세요 is a rude command to a teacher.

Can be used in class (to the teacher) or studying with a classmate. To a teacher, adding 죄송한데 ('sorry, but…') before, and optionally 이 부분 ('this part') to pinpoint what confused you, is considered more considerate than an unframed request. Maximum deference: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?.

한 번 더 = 'one additional time' (stresses counting); 다시 = 'again / from the start' (stresses repetition). Both combine with 설명해 주세요 naturally. 천천히 설명해 주세요 adds the speed dimension — use it when pace is the problem, not the content itself.

Word order: 'one more time' is 한 번 더 — never 한 더 번 (counter rule: number + 번 must stay together, then 더 follows). Also 이해하지 않아요 sounds like refusing to understand; say 이해가 안 돼요 ('it isn't getting understood').

expressions.shortExplanation: 질문 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a question".
expressions.explanation: "I have a question" — that is 질문 있어요 (jilmun isseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 질문 있어요 ("I have a question"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; flag that you want to ask
반말, to a classmate
Softer opener with -는데요, invites the teacher to respond
여쭤보다 (humble 'ask') to a teacher, very polite

examples.en: Teacher, I have a question.
examples.note: Raise your hand and lead with this; the simplest, safest opener in class

examples.ko: 질문 있는데요, 이 표현 언제 써요?
examples.romanization: jilmun inneundeyo, i pyohyeon eonje sseoyo?
examples.en: I have a question — when do you use this expression?
examples.note: 질문 있는데요 gently opens space; the teacher instinctively replies 네, 말씀하세요

examples.ko: A: 수업 끝나고 하나 여쭤봐도 돼요? / B: 그럼요, 이야기해요.
examples.romanization: A: sueop kkeunnago hana yeojjwobwado dwaeyo? / B: geureomyo, iyagihaeyo.
examples.en: A: May I ask you something after class? / B: Of course, let's talk.
examples.note: 여쭤봐도 돼요 is the humble ask used ONLY when you are the one requesting of a superior

expressions.nuance: 질문 있어요 is 질문 (質問, 'question') + 있어요 ('there is / I have'). It's the clean, correct signal that you want to ask something. The softer version 질문 있는데요 adds the trailing -는데요 ('just so you know…'), which naturally invites the teacher to say '네, 말씀하세요' ('yes, go ahead') — more conversationally natural than the blunt flag. For a teacher specifically, elevate to the humble verb 여쭤보다 (the humble equivalent of 물어보다 'to ask'): 여쭤봐도 돼요? is noticeably more polished than 물어봐도 돼요?. The verb contrast is central: 물어보다 = plain 'to ask' (peer or below), 여쭤보다 = humble 'to ask (a superior)'. Two other traps: (1) 질문 가지고 있어요 is a 직역 of 'have a question' using 가지다 ('to hold'), which sounds like physically clutching a question — Korean uses 있다; (2) 질문하다 means to actively pose a question, so 질문할게요 = 'I'll ask now', while 질문 있어요 = 'I have one to ask (flagging it)'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 질문 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a question'.
직역 of 'have' with 가지다 sounds like physically holding something. Korean uses 있다: 질문 있어요.
Using 물어봐도 돼요? to a respected teacher.
물어보다 is plain 'ask (a peer).' To a teacher, the humble 여쭤보다 is more polished: 여쭤봐도 돼요?
Confusing 질문하다 with 질문 있다.
질문하다 = the act of asking; 질문 있다 = having a question. To flag one, say 질문 있어요, not 질문해요 (which announces you're asking now).

structuredNuance.t: 질문 (質問 'question') + 있어요 ('there is'). Literally 'there is a question' = 'I have a question.' The -는데요 softener (질문 있는데요) is preferred in speech because it leaves a natural pause for the teacher to respond. 질문하다 is the ACT of asking; 질문 있다 is having one to ask — different frames.

Works for teachers (polite -어요) and classmates (반말: 질문 있어). To a senior teacher or outside of class, upgrade to 여쭤봐도 돼요? ('may I humbly ask?') — adding '수업 끝나고' ('after class') shows you don't want to interrupt. Never use 여쭤보다 downward — it is strictly for asking up.

물어보다 = plain 'to ask' (neutral/downward); 여쭤보다 = humble 'to ask (upward)'. Using 물어봐도 돼요? to a respected teacher is not wrong but sounds less polished. 질문하다 vs 질문 있다: former is the action, latter is flagging you have one.

질문 가지고 있어요 (직역 of 'have a question' with 가지다 'to hold') sounds like physically gripping a question — use 있어요. Also, 질문해요 (from 질문하다) announces you're asking RIGHT NOW, not that you have one to ask — say 질문 있어요 to flag it first.

expressions.english: Did you register for the course?
expressions.shortExplanation: 수강 신청했어요? is a practical expression meaning "Did you register for the course?".
expressions.explanation: 수강 신청했어요? (sugang sincheonghaesseoyo?) = "Did you register for the course?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 수강 신청했어요? ("Did you register for classes?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask a classmate about course registration

usagePhrases.en: Did you sign up for classes?
usagePhrases.note: 반말, to a classmate
등록 = enrollment/paying tuition, a related but different step
Asking the start date (언제부터 = 'from when')

examples.ko: 이번 학기 수강 신청 다 했어요?
examples.romanization: ibeon hakgi sugang sincheong da haesseoyo?
examples.en: Did you finish registering for all your courses this semester?
examples.note: 이번 학기 ('this semester') + 다 했어요 ('all done') — the practical everyday form

examples.ko: 그 수업 자리 없어서 수강 신청 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: geu sueop jari eopseoseo sugang sincheong mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: That class was full so I couldn't register.
examples.note: 자리 없다 ('no seats') explains the failure; 수강 신청 전쟁 ('registration war') is a real student concept

examples.ko: A: 수강 신청했어? 한국어 회화 들어? / B: 신청하려고 했는데 마감됐어.
examples.romanization: A: sugang sincheonghaesseo? hangugeo hoehwa deureo? / B: sincheongharyeogo haenneunde magamdwaesseo.
examples.en: A: Did you register? Are you taking Korean conversation? / B: I tried to, but it closed.
examples.note: 마감됐다 ('it closed') captures the click-race reality of Korean university registration

expressions.nuance: 수강 신청했어요? is 수강 신청 (受講申請, 'course registration') + 했어요. 수강 means 'taking a class' (受講) and 신청 means 'application' (申請) — so it literally means 'application to take a class', which is THE standard term for signing up for courses at a university or academy each semester. The critical distinction that trips up English speakers: 수강 신청 = choosing and signing up for courses; 등록 (登錄) = officially enrolling and paying tuition (등록금). They are SEPARATE steps in the Korean system, not interchangeable — mixing them up reveals unfamiliarity with school procedures. Korean university 수강 신청 is notoriously competitive (sites crash, seats vanish in seconds), so 수강 신청 전쟁 ('registration war') and 자리 없어서 못 했어요 are culturally familiar complaints. 신청하다 alone needs an object to be meaningful (장학금 신청 = scholarship application; 휴학 신청 = leave of absence); by itself 신청했어요? is ambiguous. Verb form: 수강 신청하다 / 수강 신청을 하다 — never the copula 수강 신청이다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 등록하다 to mean 'register for a course'.
등록 in school = enrolling/paying tuition (등록금). Picking courses is 수강 신청. Say 수강 신청했어요?, not 수업 등록했어요?
Saying 수강 신청이에요 instead of the verb.
수강 신청 is a noun that takes 하다: 수강 신청했어요 / 수강 신청을 했어요. The copula 이에요 doesn't express the action of signing up.
Treating 신청 as enough by itself.
신청 ('application') needs context/an object. For courses specifically, say 수강 신청; alone, 신청했어요? is ambiguous about what you applied for.

structuredNuance.t: 수강 신청 (受講 'taking a class' + 申請 'application') = the act of signing up for specific courses each term. It names course selection, not tuition payment. Verb: 수강 신청하다 / 수강 신청을 하다 — never the copula 이다. Common cultural context: seats fill in seconds, so 수강 신청 전쟁 ('registration war') is a shared student experience.
Peer conversation among students around registration period. Polite -어요 with unfamiliar classmates; 반말 with friends. Never say 수강 신청이에요 (copula) for the action — always 신청했어요 / 신청할게요.

수강 신청 (course sign-up) vs. 등록 (enrolling/paying tuition, 登錄) — two separate administrative steps. 수업 등록했어요? is understandable but slightly off; natives say 수강 신청했어요?. 신청하다 alone is ambiguous without an object.

English 'register' covers both 수강 신청 and 등록, so learners conflate them. Use 수강 신청 for picking courses, 등록 / 등록금 for tuition payment. They are not interchangeable in Korean administrative and daily speech.

expressions.shortExplanation: 시험 언제예요? is a practical expression meaning "When is the test?".
expressions.explanation: 시험 언제예요? (siheom eonjeyeyo?) means "When is the test?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 시험 언제예요? ("When is the exam?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask the teacher or a classmate
반말, to a classmate
범위 ('scope/range') — what to study

usagePhrases.en: When do we take the next test?
usagePhrases.note: 시험을 보다 ('to take an exam') phrasing

examples.en: Teacher, when are the midterms?
examples.note: 중간고사 ('midterm exam') is the specific academic term; 시험 언제예요? alone would also be natural

examples.ko: 다음 주에 시험 본다고 했는데 무슨 요일이에요?
examples.romanization: daeum jue siheom bondago haenneunde museun yoirieyo?
examples.en: You said we have a test next week — which day?
examples.note: 시험 본다고 했는데 ('you said we'd take a test') confirms the fact, then clarifies the day — natural follow-up question

examples.ko: A: 이번 시험 언제야? 기말이야? / B: 응, 3주 후에 기말 봐.
examples.romanization: A: ibeon siheom eonjeya? gimariya? / B: eung, 3ju hue gimal bwa.
examples.en: A: When's this test? Is it the final? / B: Yeah, we take the final in three weeks.
examples.note: 기말고사 shortened to 기말 in casual speech; 시험 보다 is the set collocation for a student taking an exam

expressions.nuance: 시험 언제예요? is 시험 (試驗, 'exam') + 언제 ('when') + 예요. Simple and correct. The most important collocation in the exam cluster: the verb a student uses for 'taking' an exam is 시험을 보다 (lit. 'to see an exam') or 시험을 치다 — never 시험을 하다 or 시험을 가지다. So 'we have a test next week' = 다음 주에 시험 봐요, 'I'm sitting the exam now' = 시험 보고 있어요. Key vocabulary orbiting 시험: 범위 ('exam scope'), 중간고사 (中間考査 'midterm'), 기말고사 (期末考査 'final exam'). The verb split: 시험을 보다 / 치다 is what a STUDENT does; 시험을 출제하다 ('to write/set the exam') is what the TEACHER does. A lurking near-homophone trap: 시험 (exam) vs. 실험 (實驗 'experiment') — they are very close in sound, completely different in meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is 시험을 하다 ('do a test') and 시험을 가지다 ('have a test') — both are unidiomatic; use 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 시험을 해요 for 'take a test'.
The verb for sitting an exam is 보다 (or 치다): 시험을 봐요. 시험을 하다 is not idiomatic for taking one.
Confusing 시험 with 실험.
시험 = exam/test; 실험 = experiment. 실험 언제예요? would ask when the lab experiment is — say 시험 for a school test.
Saying 시험 출제했어요 as a student.
출제하다 ('to set questions') is what the teacher does. A student says 시험 봤어요 ('I took the test'), not 출제했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 시험 (試驗 'exam/test') + 언제 + 예요. The key collocation: 시험을 보다 ('to take an exam', lit. 'to see') or 치다 — not 하다. 중간고사 = midterm; 기말고사 = final. Ask 범위 ('scope') right after to know what to study.

Neutral polite (-어요) works with both teachers and classmates. With close friends: 시험 언제야?. After the teacher mentions an exam, the natural follow-up pair is 시험 언제예요? then 범위가 어디예요? — two questions that go together every time an exam is announced.

시험을 보다 = student taking the exam; 시험을 치다 = same (slightly more colloquial, regional); 시험을 출제하다 = teacher writing the exam. Student and teacher use different verbs. 시험 vs. 실험: both sound similar but 실험 = lab experiment, completely different context.
'Do a test' tempts 시험을 하다, and 'have a test' tempts 시험을 가지다 — both unidiomatic. The correct verb for a student is 보다: 시험 봐요. Also watch the 시험/실험 near-homophone trap.

expressions.english: How far does the exam cover?
expressions.shortExplanation: 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? is a practical expression meaning "How far does the exam cover?".
expressions.explanation: "How far does the exam cover?" — that is 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? (siheom beomwiga eodikkajiyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? ("What's the exam range?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask which material is on the test
반말, to a classmate
Casual 'what comes up' phrasing

usagePhrases.en: Up to which lesson is the test?
usagePhrases.note: 몇 과까지 ('up to which lesson') for textbook units

examples.en: Is the exam range lessons 3 to 7, right?
examples.note: 부터…까지 ('from…to') confirms a span; 맞아요? softly checks accuracy

examples.ko: 교과서 어디까지 나와요? 프린트도 시험에 나와요?
examples.romanization: gyogwaseo eodikkaji nawayo? peurinteudo siheome nawayo?
examples.en: How far in the textbook is covered? Are the handouts on it too?
examples.note: 나오다 ('to come out/appear') is the idiomatic verb for material appearing on an exam — high frequency

examples.ko: A: 시험 범위 어디까지야? / B: 교과서 5과까지고, 선생님 프린트도 다 나와.
examples.romanization: A: siheom beomwi eodikkajiya? / B: gyogwaseo 5gwakkajigo, seonsaengnim peurinteudo da nawa.
examples.en: A: How far does the test cover? / B: Up to lesson 5 in the textbook, and all the teacher's handouts.
examples.note: 나와 (from 나오다) used in both directions; 프린트 ('printed handout') is normal classroom vocab

expressions.nuance: 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? is 시험 범위 (試驗範圍, 'exam scope') + 가 + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 예요. 범위 is the standard school word for 'what's on the test'; 어디까지 uses the location-to-limit word 어디 to ask for the endpoint. To state a full span, combine 부터 ('from') and 까지 ('to'): 3과부터 7과까지. A key collocation: 시험에 나오다 (lit. 'to come out on the exam') is how Koreans say material 'appears on / is tested on' — 시험에 뭐 나와요? is the casual peer ask and deserves to be memorized alongside the formal 범위 question. Textbook units use the counter 과 (제3과 / 3과 = lesson 3), not 레슨. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'cover' as 덮다 ('to cover with a lid') — 시험이 덮어요 is nonsense. Distinguish 범위 ('test span') from 분야 ('field/discipline'): 범위 is the exam's range, 분야 is a domain like medicine or law.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'cover' as 덮다.
덮다 means physically covering (with a lid/blanket). Exam coverage is 범위 + 까지, or use 나오다: 시험에 뭐 나와요? ('what's on the test?').
Saying 7 레슨까지 for textbook lessons.
Korean counts textbook units with 과: 7과까지 ('up to lesson 7'). 레슨 is rarely used for school chapters.
Using 분야 instead of 범위.
분야 = a field/discipline (e.g., 의학 분야 'the medical field'). The test's span is 범위. Ask 시험 범위가 어디까지예요?

structuredNuance.t: 시험 범위 (試驗 + 範圍 'scope') + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 예요. 범위 = what's on the test. 어디까지 asks the endpoint; combine with 부터 to give a span: 3과부터 7과까지 ('from lesson 3 to lesson 7'). Key idiom to memorize: 시험에 나오다 = 'to appear on / be tested on' — 시험에 뭐 나와요? is the natural casual version of this question.

Ask this immediately after the teacher announces an exam — 시험 언제예요? and 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? are the natural two-question pair. With classmates drop to 범위 어디까지야?. The phrasing 시험에 뭐 나와요? ('what comes out?') is even more casual, fine between students.

범위 = the test's span of material; 분야 (分野) = a subject field/discipline (e.g., 의학 분야 'the medical field') — not interchangeable for an exam scope. Lesson counter: 과 (3과, 7과), not 레슨 — using 7 레슨까지 sounds foreign.

직역-ing 'cover' as 덮다 ('to cover with a lid') — 시험이 덮어요 is nonsense. Korean expresses exam coverage with 범위 + 까지 or the idiom 나오다: 시험에 나와요 ('it comes out on the test'). Another trap: 분야 is not a synonym of 범위 for tests.

expressions.shortExplanation: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 is a practical expression meaning "I really need to review".
expressions.explanation: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 (bokseup jom haeyagesseoyo) = "I really need to review". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 ("I should review"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; saying you need to go over the material
반말, talking to yourself or a friend
예습 = previewing, the opposite of 복습

usagePhrases.en: I have no time to review
usagePhrases.note: Common lament about reviewing

examples.ko: 오늘 배운 거 복습 좀 해야겠어요.
examples.romanization: oneul baeun geo bokseup jom haeyagesseoyo.
examples.en: I should review what I learned today.
examples.note: 오늘 배운 거 ('what I learned today') is the natural object; 좀 softens the resolve

examples.ko: 시험 전에 복습 안 하면 다 까먹어요.
examples.romanization: siheom jeone bokseup an hamyeon da kkameogeoyo.
examples.en: If I don't review before the test, I forget everything.
examples.note: 까먹다 ('to forget', colloquial) vs. neutral 잊어버리다; motivates why 복습 matters

examples.ko: A: 어제 배운 거 이해했어? / B: 조금 헷갈려서 집에서 복습 좀 해야겠어.
examples.romanization: A: eoje baeun geo ihaehaesseo? / B: jogeum hetgallyeoseo jibeseo bokseup jom haeyagesseo.
examples.en: A: Did you understand what we learned yesterday? / B: I'm a bit confused so I should review at home.
examples.note: 헷갈리다 ('to be confused/mixed up') is the natural trigger word for deciding to review

expressions.nuance: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 is 복습 (復習, 'review of already-learned material') + 좀 (softener adding a slight hesitancy) + 해야겠어요 (-아/어야겠다 ending = 'I'd better do / I should do', expressing a self-directed resolution). The 좀 makes it conversational rather than formal. The indispensable three-way distinction among the 習 (습) words: 복습 = going over material you ALREADY learned (after class); 예습 = studying ahead BEFORE class; 연습 (練習) = drilling a skill (피아노 연습 'piano practice', 발음 연습 'pronunciation practice'). English uses 'review' loosely, so learners must pick the right Korean word. 복습 is a noun; it must combine with 하다: 복습하다 or 복습을 하다, never 복습이다. The casual spoken synonym 다시 보다 ('to look at again') can fill the same space informally but 복습하다 is the precise academic term. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'review' as 다시 보다 (fine but informal) and missing the 예습/복습/연습 split entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 복습 with 예습.
복습 = reviewing what you already learned (after class); 예습 = previewing ahead (before class). Don't say 예습 when you mean to go back over today's lesson — say 복습.
Mixing up 복습 and 연습.
연습 ('practice') is drilling a skill (연습 문제 'practice problems', 발음 연습 'pronunciation practice'). Going over lessons is 복습. They're different 習 words.
Saying 복습이에요 instead of 복습하다.
복습 is a noun and needs 하다: 복습해요 / 복습을 해요. 복습이에요 just labels something as 'review,' not the act of reviewing.

structuredNuance.t: 복습 (復習 — 復 'again' + 習 'study') = going over what you already learned. 해야겠어요 (from -아/어야겠다) = a self-directed resolution: 'I'd better do this.' 좀 softens it to a natural musing. 복습 needs 하다: 복습하다 / 복습을 하다.

Said to yourself or a classmate, not usually to a teacher. 복습 좀 해야겠다 (반말 / self-talk) is even more common than the polite form. Often comes right after a hard lesson or after being told you might forget without practice.

복습 = review after class (already studied); 예습 (豫習) = prepare before class (not yet taught); 연습 (練習) = skill drilling (not reviewing lessons). Three distinct 習 compounds — English collapses them all into 'review/practice/study.'

직역-ing 'review' as 다시 보다 is informal but acceptable; however, missing the 예습/복습/연습 split and using 복습 for pre-class preparation (that's 예습) or for skill drills (that's 연습) reveals a gap in academic vocabulary.

expressions.shortExplanation: 다음 시간에 봬요 is a practical expression meaning "See you next class".
expressions.explanation: "See you next class" — that is 다음 시간에 봬요 (daeum sigane bwaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다음 시간에 봬요 ("See you next class"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; said to the teacher leaving class
반말, to classmates
다음 주 ('next week') if class is weekly

usagePhrases.en: Thanks for the class / good work
usagePhrases.note: Said to the teacher at the end of class

examples.ko: 선생님, 오늘 감사했습니다. 다음 시간에 봬요!
examples.romanization: seonsaengnim, oneul gamsahaetseumnida. daeum sigane bwaeyo!
examples.en: Teacher, thank you for today. See you next class!
examples.note: 감사했습니다 first, then the goodbye — the natural end-of-class sequence

examples.en: You worked hard! See you next week.
examples.note: 뵙겠습니다 is the most formal 'I will see you' — adds -겠- for extra deference

examples.ko: A: 오늘 정말 재미있었어요. 다음 시간에 봬요. / B: 그래요, 다음 주에 봬요!
examples.romanization: A: oneul jeongmal jaemiisseosseoyo. daeum sigane bwaeyo. / B: geuraeyo, daeum jue bwaeyo!
examples.en: A: Today was really fun. See you next class. / B: Yes, see you next week!
examples.note: Both use 봬요 because they're talking to each other (equal or near-equal), confirming the humble form is not reserved for the teacher alone

expressions.nuance: 다음 시간에 봬요 is 다음 시간 ('next time/period', where 시간 means the class period) + 에 ('at/in') + 봬요 (contraction of 뵈어요, the humble form of 보다 'to see', used when encountering a SUPERIOR). The key: to a teacher you do NOT use plain 봐요 ('I see') — you use the humble 봬요 / 뵈어요 from the verb 뵈다/뵙다, which is 보다 elevated for meeting someone above you. The spelling 봬요 vs. 뵈요 confuses even native Koreans: the correct contracted form of 뵈어요 is 봬요. At the very end of class, the expected phrase to the teacher is 수고하셨습니다 ('you've worked hard'), a courtesy for someone who did effort/labour — however, 수고하셨습니다 from a student to a clearly senior teacher can feel slightly evaluative (as if you're grading their effort), so 감사합니다 is often safer and warmer. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 너를 봐요 ('I'll see you' with an explicit object pronoun and plain verb) — Korean drops the object, and the verb must be humble: just 다음 시간에 봬요. The extra-deferential 뵙겠습니다 adds future -겠- for maximum formality.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다음 시간에 봐요 to the teacher.
봐요 is plain 'see.' To a teacher use the humble 봬요 / 뵈어요 (from 뵈다, 'to see a superior'): 다음 시간에 봬요.
Adding an object: 선생님을 봐요.
The goodbye drops the object. Just say 다음 시간에 봬요, not 선생님을 봐요 (which sounds like reporting that you see the teacher).
Saying 수고하셨습니다 to a much-senior teacher.
From a student to a clearly senior teacher, 수고하셨습니다 can feel evaluative. 감사합니다 ('thank you') is safer; use 수고하셨습니다 with peers/juniors.

structuredNuance.t: 다음 시간 ('next class period') + 에 + 봬요 (contraction of 뵈어요, humble 'see'). Literally 'at the next period, (I humbly) see [you].' The object is dropped — you don't say 선생님을; just 다음 시간에 봬요. Spelling note: 봬요 (correct contraction of 뵈어요), NOT 뵈요.

Said at the end of class as you leave. To the teacher: 봬요 (humble) or 뵙겠습니다 (most formal). To classmates: 다음 시간에 보자 (반말) or 봬요 (polite, still fine). Pair with 감사합니다 or 수고하셨습니다 — saying goodbye alone without acknowledgment feels abrupt.

봬요 / 뵈어요 = humble 'see' (for a superior); 봐요 = plain 'see' (peers/juniors). 수고하셨습니다 = acknowledges the other person's effort (safe for peers, slightly delicate to a very senior teacher — 감사합니다 is safer). 뵙겠습니다 = most formal, adds future -겠-.

Using plain 봐요 to the teacher (understandable but less respectful). Adding an explicit object: 선생님을 봐요 sounds like a factual observation, not a farewell. The set phrase drops the object: just 다음 시간에 봬요. Also don't confuse 봬요 (humble goodbye) with 봐요 (plain see).

expressions.shortExplanation: 환불돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refund?".
expressions.explanation: "Can I get a refund?" — that is 환불돼요? (hwanbuldwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 환불돼요? ("Can I get a refund?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite question to a clerk
반말 to a friend or familiar staff
Softer, more formal with 가능하다
Directly requesting the refund

examples.en: Can I get a refund on this?
examples.note: Bare question holding the item and receipt — check policy before assuming yes

examples.ko: A: 사이즈가 안 맞아서요, 환불돼요? / B: 네, 영수증 있으세요? / A: 네, 여기요.
examples.romanization: A: saijeuga an majaseoyo, hwanbuldwaeyo? / B: ne, yeongsujeung isseuseyo? / A: ne, yeogiyo.
examples.en: A: It doesn't fit, so can I get a refund? / B: Yes, do you have the receipt? / A: Yes, here it is.
examples.note: Realistic refund desk exchange; 안 맞다 = doesn't fit — shows the typical receipt check

examples.ko: 어제 샀는데 한 번도 안 썼어요. 영수증도 있고요. 환불돼요?
examples.romanization: eoje sanneunde han beondo an sseosseoyo. yeongsujeungdo itgoyo. hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: I bought it yesterday and never used it. I have the receipt too. Can I refund it?
examples.note: Full real case building the best argument for a refund; 한 번도 안 = not even once

expressions.nuance: 환불돼요? asks a clerk whether a refund — getting money back — is possible; 환불 is Sino-Korean 還拂 (return + pay), and 되다 means 'to be possible/doable', so 'is a refund doable here?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 환불돼?; formal 환불 가능한가요?. You ask 환불돼요? to find out the policy, and 환불해 주세요 to actually demand it. The defining contrast in Korean retail is 환불 (refund — money back) vs 교환 (exchange — swap for a different item): these are handled by different counters and have different policies, and English 'return' blurs them; you must decide which you want before walking up. A very practical Korean reality: many shops require the original receipt (영수증), unused tags, and the item in original packaging — without these, even valid refund policy may be refused. Spelling trap: 돼요 not 되요 (되 + 어 = 돼).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 환불되요.
되다's polite form is 돼요 (되+어요). The correct spelling is 환불돼요?
Confusing 환불 (refund) with 교환 (exchange).
환불 = money back; 교환 = swap for another item. Say the one you mean — they are handled differently.
Using the loanword 리펀드.
Korean uses 환불, not a transliteration of 'refund'. Ask 환불돼요?

structuredNuance.t: 환불 = Sino-Korean 還拂 'return-pay' + 되다 = 'to be possible'. Literally 'is a return-of-payment possible?' 되다 is the Korean workhorse for 'can/may something happen here?', not a specific 'refund' verb.

해요체 — say to a clerk at a return/exchange counter or to the same cashier if same-day. Always bring the 영수증 (receipt) and keep original tags. 환불 가능한가요? is a notch more formal for department store customer service.

교환돼요? (can I exchange?) is the all-important alternative — 환불 = money back, 교환 = swap for another item. Never use the English loanword 리펀드; no Korean shopper uses it. After confirming refund is possible, say 환불해 주세요 to execute it.
환불 가능한가요? (more formal), 환불해 주세요 (please refund me), 환불 정책이 어떻게 돼요? (what is the refund policy?). The last is useful for online purchases.
English 'return' blurs 환불 and 교환 — decide which you want. Spelling: 돼요 not 되요. Loanword 리펀드 is never used in Korean shops.

expressions.english: Can I get a make-up class?
expressions.shortExplanation: 보강 가능해요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a make-up class?".
expressions.explanation: 보강 가능해요? (bogang ganeunghaeyo?) means "Can I get a make-up class?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 보강 가능해요? ("Is a make-up class possible?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask the academy for a make-up session
Slightly more casual with 되다

usagePhrases.en: Can I make up what I missed?
usagePhrases.note: 빠진 거 ('what I missed') + 보강하다

usagePhrases.en: If I'm absent, is there a make-up?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the policy in advance

examples.en: I was absent last week — can I get a make-up class?
examples.note: State the missed class first, then ask; giving context is polite and practical

examples.ko: 이번 주 못 와서요, 보강 신청하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon ju mot waseoyo, bogang sincheonghago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I can't come this week, so I'd like to request a make-up.
examples.note: 보강 신청하다 ('to apply for a make-up') is the full action form

examples.ko: A: 선생님, 보강은 언제 가능한지 여쭤봐도 돼요? / B: 수요일 오후에 자리 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: seonsaengnim, bogangeun eonje ganeunghanji yeojjwobwado dwaeyo? / B: suyoil ohue jari isseoyo.
examples.en: A: Teacher, may I ask when a make-up is possible? / B: There's a spot on Wednesday afternoon.
examples.note: 여쭤보다 (humble 'ask') is appropriate directed at the teacher; 자리 있다 = 'there's a spot/opening'

expressions.nuance: 보강 가능해요? is 보강 (補講, 'supplementary/make-up lecture') + 가능하다 ('to be possible') in polite question form. 보강 is the precise academy term for a class session held to compensate for one you missed (or one the teacher had to reschedule). English 'make-up class' is vague; Korean's 보강 is exact. The action forms: 보강하다 / 보강을 하다 = to hold or have a make-up; 보강 신청하다 = to apply for one; 보강을 받다 = to receive/take one. The contrast set: 보강 = compensating for a MISSED session; 복습 = self-review of material you already have; 추가 수업 = a bonus class beyond the regular schedule. Don't confuse them. An important near-synonym: 보충 수업 (補充授業) is common in school settings and nearly synonymous; academies (학원) tend to use 보강. The English-speaker's famous false-friend trap: 'makeup class' as 화장 수업 — 화장 means cosmetics makeup. The correct word is 보강, full stop. Grammatically, 가능하다 takes 이/가 or no particle — 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 화장 수업 for 'make-up class'.
False friend! 화장 = cosmetics makeup. A make-up (supplementary) class is 보강. Ask 보강 가능해요?, never 화장 수업.
Using 추가 수업 to mean making up an absence.
추가 수업 = an extra/bonus class beyond schedule. Making up a MISSED class is 보강. Say 보강 가능해요? for what you missed.
Saying 보강을 가능해요.
가능하다 takes 이/가 or no particle: 보강(이) 가능해요. 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical — drop 을 or use 보강할 수 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 보강 (補 'supplement' + 講 'lecture') = a class session that compensates for one missed. 가능하다 = 'to be possible.' Checks whether the academy offers make-ups at all. Action forms: 보강 신청하다 (apply for one), 보강을 받다 (receive one), 보강하다 (take/hold one).

Spoken or messaged to academy staff or the teacher. Polite -어요 is standard. To the teacher use 여쭤봐도 돼요? before asking. Always state the missed class date to show you're keeping track and being responsible, not just looking for extra sessions.

보강 = making up a missed session; 복습 = self-review; 추가 수업 = extra bonus class beyond the schedule. 보충 수업 is near-synonymous, more common in school (학교) settings; 보강 is the 학원 (academy) term. Grammatically: 보강(이) 가능해요 — not 보강을 가능해요.
False friend: 화장 수업 (makeup class = cosmetics class!). The correct word is 보강. Also 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical — use 보강 가능해요? or 보강이 가능해요?.

expressions.english: How far did the class get?
expressions.shortExplanation: 진도 어디까지 나갔어요? is a practical expression meaning "How far did the class get?".
expressions.explanation: "How far did the class get?" — that is 진도 어디까지 나갔어요? (jindo eodikkaji nagasseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 진도 어디까지 나갔어요? ("How far did we get?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask how far the class progressed
반말, to a classmate
Simpler 'what did you do today?'

usagePhrases.ko: 저 빠진 동안 진도 많이 나갔어요?
usagePhrases.romanization: jeo ppajin dongan jindo mani nagasseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Did the class move a lot while I was out?
usagePhrases.note: 빠진 동안 ('while I was absent') for catching up

examples.ko: 저 어제 못 와서요, 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?
examples.romanization: jeo eoje mot waseoyo, jindo eodikkaji nagasseoyo?
examples.en: I couldn't come yesterday — how far did you get?
examples.note: State the absence first; 못 와서요 ('because I couldn't come') sets the context naturally

examples.ko: 다른 반은 진도가 더 빨라요. 우리는 5과까지 나갔어요.
examples.romanization: dareun baneun jindoga deo ppallayo. urineun 5gwakkaji nagasseoyo.
examples.en: The other class moves faster. We got up to lesson 5.
examples.note: 진도가 빠르다/느리다 ('progress is fast/slow') is the idiomatic way to compare class pacing

examples.ko: A: 진도 어디까지 나갔어? / B: 4과 끝내고 5과 들어갔어.
examples.romanization: A: jindo eodikkaji nagasseo? / B: 4gwa kkeunnaego 5gwa deureogasseo.
examples.en: A: How far did the class get? / B: We finished lesson 4 and started lesson 5.
examples.note: 나가다 in the question mirrors 들어가다 ('to enter, start') in the answer — natural lesson-progress vocabulary

expressions.nuance: 진도 어디까지 나갔어요? is 진도 (進度, 'curriculum progress') + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 나갔어요 (past of 나가다 'to go out/advance'). This is the standard ask when you've missed a session and need to catch up. The crucial collocation: 진도가 나가다 (lit. 'progress goes forward/out') is how Korean expresses a class MOVING through the syllabus — 나가다 (motion verb) is the set partner for 진도, and swapping it for 가다 (진도 갔어요) sounds off. Related expressions from the same set: 진도가 빠르다 ('the class is moving fast'), 진도가 느리다 ('the class is slow'), 진도를 따라가다 ('to keep up with the class pace'). The contrast: 진도 ('how far into the syllabus') vs. 범위 ('exam scope') vs. 복습 ('self-review') — 진도 is about curriculum momentum, not testing or study. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'how far did we go' as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요?, which sounds like physical distance. Use the set phrase 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
직역-ing as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요?
That sounds like physical distance traveled. Class progress uses 진도 + 나가다: 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?
Saying 진도 갔어요 instead of 나갔어요.
The set collocation is 진도가 나가다 ('progress advances'). 진도 갔어요 sounds off; say 진도 (많이) 나갔어요.
Confusing 진도 with 범위.
진도 = how far the class has gotten through the curriculum; 범위 = what's on the exam. To catch up after an absence, ask 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?, not 범위.

structuredNuance.t: 진도 (進度 'curriculum progress') + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 나갔어요 (past of 나가다). The motion verb 나가다 ('go forward/out') is the set collocation for 진도 — it captures the idea of material ADVANCING through the syllabus. Related idioms: 진도가 빠르다 ('class is moving fast'), 진도를 따라가다 ('to keep up with the pace').

Said to a classmate after an absence. 못 와서요 ('because I couldn't come') as a lead-in is considerate. With a classmate who's your friend, drop to 진도 어디까지 나갔어?. A lighter alternative for the same situation: 오늘 어디 했어요? ('what part did you do today?') — simpler but slightly less precise.

진도 = forward curriculum progress; 범위 = exam scope; 복습 = self-review. All three circle the same classroom context but mean different things. To catch up after an absence you ask 진도; to study for an exam you ask 범위; to go over what you learned you do 복습.

직역-ing 'how far did we go' as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요? implies physical distance traveled — awkward or confusing in school contexts. The set phrase is 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?. Also 진도 갔어요 is off; the verb must be 나가다, not 가다.

expressions.english: How did the test go? / Did you do well?
expressions.shortExplanation: 시험 잘 봤어요? is a practical expression meaning "How did the test go? / Did you do well?".
expressions.explanation: 시험 잘 봤어요? (siheom jal bwasseoyo?) = "How did the test go? / Did you do well?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 시험 잘 봤어요? ("Did the test go well?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask a classmate how their exam went
반말, to a classmate
망치다 ('to ruin') — when it went badly

usagePhrases.en: When do the results come out?
usagePhrases.note: 결과 ('results') + 나오다 ('come out')

examples.ko: A: 시험 잘 봤어요? / B: 아니요, 좀 망친 것 같아요. 한 파트가 너무 어려웠어요.
examples.romanization: A: siheom jal bwasseoyo? / B: aniyo, jom mangchin geot gatayo. han pateuga neomu eoryeowosseoyo.
examples.en: A: Did the test go well? / B: Not really — I think I blew part of it. One section was really hard.
examples.note: 망친 것 같아요 ('seems like I ruined it') is more natural and modest than 나빴어요 ('it was bad')

examples.en: Did you get a good score? I got 84.
examples.note: 점수 나오다 ('a score comes out') + 점 받다 ('to get points') — two essential score collocations

examples.ko: 저는 못 봤어요. 한 문제 다 틀렸어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun mot bwasseoyo. han munje da teullyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't do well. I got a whole question wrong.
examples.note: 못 봤어요 (couldn't do well) + 틀리다 ('to be wrong') for wrong answers — not 잘못하다

expressions.nuance: 시험 잘 봤어요? is 시험 + 잘 ('well') + 봤어요 (past of 보다). It reuses the key exam collocation 시험을 보다 ('to take an exam'), now in the past to ask how the exam WENT — so literally 'did you see the exam well?', meaning 'did it go well / did you do well?'. This is the natural conversational follow-up after an exam, and it reinforces the rule: the verb for taking an exam is 보다, NOT 하다. The closest near-synonym expression is 시험 어땠어요? ('how was the test?') — more open-ended, inviting a fuller answer beyond just good/bad; 잘 봤어요? presupposes you're checking on success, while 어땠어요? is a neutral open invite. Good result: 잘 봤어요 ('I did well'), 점수 잘 나왔어요 ('I got a good score'), 90점 받았어요 ('I got 90'). Bad result: 망쳤어요 (망치다 = 'to ruin/botch' — THE everyday verb for bombing; far more idiomatic than 나빴어요 'it was bad'), 못 봤어요 ('didn't do well'). Score vocabulary: 점수 (點數, 'score'), 점 (the counter for points — 90점), 점수가 나오다 / 점수를 받다. Wrong answers: 틀리다 ('to be wrong, to err') for a mistaken answer — NOT 잘못하다 ('to behave wrongly/misbehave'). The English-speaker pitfall is 시험 잘 했어요? (하다 instead of 보다) — the verb for an exam is fixed as 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 시험 잘 했어요? for 'did you do well?'.
The verb for an exam is 보다, not 하다. The idiomatic ask is 시험 잘 봤어요? — 시험 했어요 sounds off.
Saying 시험이 나빴어요 for 'I did badly'.
직역 of 'bad' is unnatural here. Koreans say 시험 망쳤어요 ('I bombed it', from 망치다) or 시험 못 봤어요 ('didn't do well').
Using 잘못했어요 for wrong test answers.
잘못하다 = to misbehave / do wrong (an act). A wrong answer is 틀리다: 두 문제 틀렸어요 ('I got two wrong'), not 잘못했어요.

structuredNuance.t: 시험 + 잘 + 봤어요 (past of 보다). Literally 'did you see the exam well?' = 'did it go well?' Reinforces the key collocation: the student's verb for an exam is 보다, never 하다. Score vocabulary: 점수 (點數), 점 (points counter), 점수가 나오다 / 점수를 받다. Wrong answers: 틀리다, not 잘못하다.

Asked right after an exam, peer-to-peer. Polite -어요 with less familiar classmates; 시험 잘 봤어? with close friends. When answering badly, 망쳤어요 or 못 봤어요 are the natural honest forms — 나빴어요 ('it was bad') is technically correct but rarely used for exam results.

시험 어땠어요? = neutral open ask ('how was the test?') — the named near-synonym; 잘 봤어요? presupposes a success/failure frame and expects a yes/no-ish answer. 시험 결과 언제 나와요? = asking when graded results will be announced — different timeframe, don't conflate. 틀리다 = wrong answer (neutral); 잘못하다 = behave wrongly/make a moral mistake — completely different contexts.
'Do well' tempts 잘 했어요 (하다), but the set verb for exams is 보다: 시험 잘 봤어요?. 시험 잘 했어요? sounds slightly unnatural to a native ear. Also: 잘못하다 is not the word for a wrong exam answer — 틀리다 is.

expressions.english: Could you lend me your notes?
expressions.shortExplanation: 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Could you lend me your notes?".
expressions.explanation: 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? (noteu jom billyeojul su isseoyo?) means "Could you lend me your notes?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? ("Can you lend me your notes?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Can you lend me your notes?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask a classmate for their notes
반말, to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Can you show me your notes?
usagePhrases.note: 필기 ('written notes') + 보여주다 ('show')

usagePhrases.en: Can I take a photo (of it)?
usagePhrases.note: 사진 찍다 ('take a photo') of someone's notes

examples.ko: 미안한데, 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: mianhande, noteu jom billyeojul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, could you lend me your notes?
examples.note: 미안한데 ('sorry, but…') softens the favor request before it — essential for this kind of ask

examples.ko: 어제 결석해서요, 필기한 거 사진 찍어도 돼요?
examples.romanization: eoje gyeolseokaeseoyo, pilgihan geo sajin jjigeodo dwaeyo?
examples.en: I was absent yesterday — can I photo your notes?
examples.note: 사진 찍어도 돼요? is a lower-imposition alternative to borrowing; add 돌려줄게요 if you take the actual notebook
