examples.ko: A: 오늘 수업 노트 빌려줄 수 있어? 내가 오늘 늦게 와서 처음 부분을 못 썼어. / B: 그래, 오늘 안에 돌려줘.
examples.romanization: A: oneul sueom noteu billyeojul su isseo? naega oneul neutge waseo cheoeum bubuneul mot sseosseo. / B: geurae, oneul ane dollyeojwo.
examples.en: A: Can you lend me today's class notes? I came late and missed the first part. / B: Sure — return it today.
examples.note: 돌려주다 ('to return/give back') in the reply shows the lender is already thinking about getting it back — reassure proactively

expressions.nuance: 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? is 노트 (from English 'notes/notebook') + 좀 (softener) + 빌려주다 ('to lend') + ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can you?'). The borrow/lend distinction is the central vocabulary challenge: 빌리다 = 'to BORROW' (the action goes toward you — you take it), 빌려주다 = 'to LEND' (the action goes toward the other person — they give it to you). When asking a classmate to hand over their notes, you frame it as their lending: 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?'). You can also say 빌릴 수 있어요? ('can I borrow?') — both are correct, but the favor-framing 빌려주다 is slightly warmer. The related word 필기 (筆記, 'written notes / what was written down during class') is the more precise term for the actual content on the page — 필기 보여줄 수 있어요? ('can you show me your notes?'). In practice, Koreans often photograph notes rather than borrow the notebook, so 사진 찍어도 돼요? is a very common, low-imposition alternative. Add 돌려줄게요 ('I'll give it back') proactively — it reassures and is considered polite. English-speaker trap: 주다 ('give') without 빌려 implies you keep it; 빌려주다 signals a loan.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 빌리다 and 빌려주다.
빌리다 = you borrow (take); 빌려주다 = they lend (give). To ask a classmate to give you their notes, say 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?') — or 빌릴 수 있어요? ('can I borrow?'), but never use them backwards.
Saying 노트 줄 수 있어요? when you'll give it back.
주다 ('give') implies keeping it. To borrow and return, use 빌려주다 ('lend'): 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요?
Confusing 노트 (notebook/notes) with 노트북.
노트 = notes/notebook for writing; 노트북 = a laptop computer. Asking 노트북 빌려줄 수 있어요? requests a laptop, not class notes.

structuredNuance.t: 노트 + 좀 + 빌려주다 ('to lend') + ㄹ 수 있어요? The borrow/lend split: 빌리다 = I take (borrow); 빌려주다 = they give (lend). When asking a classmate, frame it from their side with 빌려줄 수 있어요? — or equivalently 빌릴 수 있어요? from your side. Favor framing (빌려주다) is slightly warmer. 필기 = the written content; 노트 = the physical notebook.

Peer-to-peer. 미안한데 or 죄송한데 as a preface is strongly expected for favors like this. In practice, photographing notes (사진 찍어도 돼요?) is common and lower-effort than borrowing the notebook — mention 돌려줄게요 if you do take the actual book.

빌리다 = borrow (take from); 빌려주다 = lend (give to) — never use them in reverse. 노트 줄 수 있어요? ('can you give me your notes?') implies keeping it, not borrowing. 필기 is the content written; 노트 is the physical object. 노트 vs. 노트북: 노트 = notes/notebook for writing; 노트북 = laptop.

Using 주다 alone (노트 줄 수 있어요?) implies permanent transfer, not a loan. You need 빌려주다 to signal you'll return it. The 빌리다/빌려주다 direction split is the core confusion — know which person the action is directed at.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is this?".
expressions.explanation: 이거 얼마예요? (igeo eolmayeyo?) = "How much is this?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 얼마예요? ("How much is this?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Pointing at one item near you, polite
반말 to a friend running a stall
Formal 합쇼체, 이것은 is the full written form
저거 = that thing over there, out of reach

examples.en: How much is this?
examples.note: Touching or pointing at the item as you ask — most minimal, most common form

examples.ko: A: 이거 얼마예요? / B: 이만 원이에요. / A: 좀 깎아 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo eolmayeyo? / B: iman wonieyo. / A: jom kkakka juseyo.
examples.en: A: How much is this? / B: Twenty thousand won. / A: Give me a discount, please.
examples.note: Full market exchange showing how price-asking leads naturally into haggling

examples.ko: 이거 얼마예요? 아, 생각보다 비싸네요. 좀 더 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: igeo eolmayeyo? a, saenggakboda bissaneyo. jom deo dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: How much is this? Oh, pricier than I thought. I'll look around a bit more.
examples.note: Polite exit after hearing the price; 생각보다 = more than expected; 둘러볼게요 = I'll browse

expressions.nuance: 이거 얼마예요? is the pointing version of the price question, used when the item is right in front of you or in your hand; 이거 is the spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing'), so it means 'this — how much?'. Compared to bare 얼마예요?, adding 이거 removes all ambiguity when several items sit side by side. The three-way distance system — 이거 (near me) / 그거 (near you) / 저거 (far from both) — is lost on English speakers who only have 'this/that', so 그거 and 저거 are constantly mixed up. Politeness is 해요체; casual 이거 얼마야?, formal 이것은 얼마입니까?. In speech, Koreans almost always use the contracted 이거, not the full 이것; and no particle is attached (not 이거가/이거를) before 얼마예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이것 얼마예요? in conversation.
이것 is the written form; spoken Korean contracts it to 이거. Natural speech is 이거 얼마예요?
Adding a particle: 이거를 얼마예요?
얼마예요 takes no object; the thing is simply named as the topic. Say 이거 얼마예요? with no 를/가.
Using 저거 for an item right in your hand.
저거 means 'that, far away'. For something you're holding use 이거. Pick the right distance word.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 = spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing') + 얼마예요? = 'is it how much?'. Whole meaning: 'this thing here — how much is it?' The 이거 pins the question to one specific visible item.
해요체 — use with any vendor or clerk while pointing at or holding an item. Casual 이거 얼마야? with a friend. 이것은 얼마입니까? in a formal showroom or on a price-query call.

Bare 얼마예요? with a gesture works too, but 이거 얼마예요? is unambiguous when multiple items are nearby. 이거 vs 그거 vs 저거: 이거 = near speaker; 그거 = near listener; 저거 = far from both. Mixing 그거 and 저거 is the #1 distance error.
그거 얼마예요? (that one near you), 저거 얼마예요? (that one over there), 이거 두 개에 얼마예요? (two of these). All swap only the demonstrative.
Saying 이것 얼마예요? in speech — in conversation Koreans almost always shorten 이것 to 이거. Adding a particle (이거를 얼마예요?) is also wrong; 얼마예요? takes no object particle.

expressions.shortExplanation: 좀 깎아 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me a discount".
expressions.explanation: 좀 깎아 주세요 (jom kkakka juseyo) means "Please give me a discount". Say it as one set phrase — for example 좀 깎아 주세요 ("Please knock the price down a bit"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: Please knock the price down a bit
usagePhrases.note: Polite haggling at a market
반말 to a friend or familiar vendor

usagePhrases.en: Couldn't you take just a little off?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more pleading polite form

usagePhrases.en: If you take some off, I'll buy right away
usagePhrases.note: Offering to close the deal as leverage

examples.en: Please give me a discount.
examples.note: Bare haggle line at a traditional market stall — say this while holding the item

examples.ko: A: 두 개 살게요. 좀 깎아 주세요. / B: 그럼 오백 원 드릴게요.
examples.romanization: A: du gae salgeyo. jom kkakka juseyo. / B: geureom obaek won deurilgeyo.
examples.en: A: I'll take two. Give me a bit off. / B: Okay, I'll take five hundred won off.
examples.note: Volume as a bargaining chip — classic market exchange showing a realistic seller response

examples.ko: 현금으로 낼게요. 만 원만 깎아 주세요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeumeuro naelgeyo. man wonman kkakka juseyo.
examples.en: I'll pay cash. Take off just 10,000 won, please.
examples.note: Cash offer as leverage; 만 원만 = just 10,000 won; 현금 = cash

expressions.nuance: 좀 깎아 주세요 is a customer's haggling request, appropriate only where bargaining is culturally normal — traditional markets (시장), street stalls, some electronics alleys — but emphatically NOT in department stores, franchises, or convenience stores, where it will just embarrass everyone. 깎다 literally means 'to shave or whittle down', so you ask the seller to 'shave a bit off the quoted price'; 좀 ('a little') is the essential softener that makes it a polite request rather than a blunt demand, and -아 주세요 means 'please do it for me'. It sits at polite 해요체; drop to 깎아 줘 only with a friend; soften up to 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? for a more pleading tone. The nearest alternative, 싸게 해 주세요, asks for a lower price in general, while 깎아 주세요 specifically acts on an already-stated number — the dividing line is that 깎다 cuts from a concrete price you just heard. English speakers reach for 디스카운트 or 할인해 주세요, but 할인 is a store-set promotion, not something customers demand by hand; the market verb is 깎다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 디스카운트 주세요 or 할인해 주세요 to haggle.
할인 is a store-set sale, not something you request face to face; the loanword sounds off. The market verb is 깎다: 좀 깎아 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and just saying 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without 좀 it sounds blunt, almost like an order. 좀 softens it into a polite request, so include it.
Trying to haggle in a department store or chain.
깎아 주세요 only works where bargaining is expected (markets, stalls). In fixed-price shops it just confuses the clerk.

structuredNuance.t: 깎다 = 'to shave/whittle down' + 주세요 = 'please do for me'. Literally 'please shave (the price) down a bit for me.' The image is of shaving a lump of price off, not applying a percentage discount.

해요체 — use at traditional markets (시장), street stalls, or electronics alleys where haggling is expected. NEVER in department stores, branded shops, or convenience stores — it falls flat and embarrasses the clerk. The vendor must have already said a price before 깎아 주세요 makes sense.

싸게 해 주세요 ('make it cheaper') is a softer, more general request not tied to a specific quoted number. 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? is more pleading and deferential. 깎아 주시면 바로 살게요 adds the incentive of an immediate purchase.
오천 원만 깎아 주세요 (take off just 5,000 won), 조금만 깎아 주세요 (just a tiny bit), 많이 깎아 주세요 (a lot off). Insert 조금만/얼마만/많이 to calibrate the ask.
Saying 디스카운트 주세요 or 할인해 주세요 at a market sounds off — 할인 is a store's own promotional pricing, not a face-to-face haggle. Dropping 좀 (saying just 깎아 주세요) sounds blunt, almost like an order.

expressions.shortExplanation: 너무 비싸요 is a practical expression meaning "It's too expensive".
expressions.explanation: "It's too expensive" — that is 너무 비싸요 (neomu bissayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 너무 비싸요 ("It's too expensive"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite reaction to a high price
반말 muttered to a companion or friend
Softer, indirect — gentler than a flat 비싸요
Surprised reaction with -네요

examples.en: It's too expensive.
examples.note: Bare reaction right after hearing the price — can double as an opener to haggling

examples.ko: A: 오만 원이에요. / B: 너무 비싸요. 좀 깎아 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: oman wonieyo. / B: neomu bissayo. jom kkakka juseyo.
examples.en: A: It's fifty thousand won. / B: That's too expensive. Give me a discount, please.
examples.note: Classic market exchange — reacting to price and immediately pivoting to haggling

examples.ko: 디자인은 마음에 드는데 너무 비싸요. 좀 더 생각해 볼게요.
examples.romanization: dijaineun maeume deuneunde neomu bissayo. jom deo saenggakae bolgeyo.
examples.en: I like the design, but it's too expensive. I'll think about it more.
examples.note: Polite exit strategy; -는데 = 'but'; 생각해 볼게요 = I'll think about it

expressions.nuance: 너무 비싸요 is a customer's direct reaction to a price that feels too high, said either to the seller (as an opener to haggling) or muttered to a friend; 비싸다 means 'to be expensive' and 너무 means 'too/excessively', so 'it's too expensive'. Said to a seller at a market it is practically the first move of negotiation. Politeness is 해요체; with friends it becomes 너무 비싸 (반말). To sound less blunt — avoiding offense to the goods or the seller — Koreans soften to 좀 비싼 것 같아요 ('it seems a bit pricey'), which adds hedging distance. The most confusing pair is 비싸다 vs 싸다 (cheap); do not confuse 싸다 ('cheap') with 사다 ('to buy') — they romanize the same but are entirely different verbs. English speakers often treat 너무 like 'very', as in 너무 좋아요 ('I love it so much'), but classically 너무 carries a negative 'excessively' edge that fits 너무 비싸요; for pure praise prefer 정말/아주. Spelling: 비싸요, never 비싸여요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 비싸다 (expensive) with 싸다 (cheap).
They are opposites. 비싸다 = expensive, 싸다 = cheap. Saying 너무 싸요 means 'it's too cheap', the reverse complaint.
Writing 너무 비싸여요.
비싸다's polite form is 비싸 + 요 = 비싸요, no extra 여. The correct form is 너무 비싸요.
Mixing up 싸다 (cheap) and 사다 (buy).
Different verbs that romanize alike. 싸다 = be cheap, 사다 = to buy. Context and spelling keep them apart.

structuredNuance.t: 너무 = 'too/excessively' + 비싸다 = 'to be expensive'. Literally 'it is excessively expensive.' The 너무 signals that the price crosses a line — it's not just pricey, it's over your limit.

해요체 — say to any seller after hearing a price. Said to a vendor it functions as the opening move of haggling; said to a friend beside you it's a shared complaint. Soften to 좀 비싼 것 같아요 if you don't want to offend. 반말 form 너무 비싸 for friends only.

좀 비싼 것 같아요 is indirect and tentative — 'it seems a bit pricey' — so you don't insult the seller's goods. 생각보다 비싸네요 ('pricier than I expected') adds surprise without being confrontational. The dividing line: 너무 비싸요 is direct and slightly negative; the others hedge.
꽤 비싸요 (quite expensive), 많이 비싸요 (very expensive), 좀 비싸네요 (a bit pricey, with -네요 expressing mild surprise). Each step down reduces directness.

English speakers use 너무 as a neutral intensifier like 'very', but in careful Korean 너무 still carries a faintly negative 'excessive' edge. Spelling: 비싸요 not 비싸여요 (비싸다 is already 비싸 + 요). Also beware: 싸다 = cheap, 사다 = buy — same romanization, opposite meanings.

expressions.shortExplanation: 입어 봐도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I try it on?".
expressions.explanation: 입어 봐도 돼요? (ibeo bwado dwaeyo?) = "Can I try it on?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 입어 봐도 돼요? ("Can I try it on?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request to a clothing clerk
반말 to a friend shopping with you

usagePhrases.en: Would it be okay to try it on?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more tentative polite form
Stating intent after getting the okay

examples.note: Bare request while holding a garment — the most common phrasing

examples.ko: 이 셔츠 입어 봐도 돼요? 탈의실 어디예요?
examples.romanization: i syeocheu ibeo bwado dwaeyo? taruisil eodiyeyo?
examples.en: Can I try this shirt on? Where's the fitting room?
examples.note: Natural follow-up; 탈의실 = fitting room — two questions in the right order

examples.ko: A: 사이즈가 애매해서요, 입어 봐도 돼요? M이랑 L 둘 다 볼게요. / B: 네, 탈의실은 저쪽이에요.

examples.en: A: The size is borderline, so can I try it on? I'll check both M and L. / B: Sure, the fitting room is over there.

expressions.nuance: 입어 봐도 돼요? is a customer asking a clothing clerk for permission to try a garment on; it is built from 입다 ('to wear') + -아/어 보다 ('try doing') + -아도 돼요? ('is it okay to?'), so literally 'is it okay if I try wearing it?'. The critical point for English speakers: Korean splits 'wear' strictly by body part — 입다 for clothes on the torso and legs (shirts, trousers, dresses), 신다 for shoes and socks, 쓰다 for hats and glasses, 끼다 for gloves and rings. Using 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes will confuse a clerk. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 입어 봐도 될까요? for extra deference; casual is 입어 봐도 돼?. The nearest alternative, 한번 봐도 돼요? ('can I take a look?'), only asks to look, not to put on — 입어 봐도 돼요? specifically requests to wear it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes.
입다 is for clothing on the body, not feet. Shoes take 신다, so for shoes ask 신어 봐도 돼요?
Saying 시도해 봐도 돼요? for 'try on'.
시도하다 means 'to attempt' (an action), not to try clothing. The fitting-room verb is 입어 보다: 입어 봐도 돼요?
Writing 입어 봐도 되요?
The polite form of 되다 here is 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요. Correct: 입어 봐도 돼요?

structuredNuance.t: 입다 (to wear) + -어 보다 (try doing) + -아도 돼요? (is it okay to?). Literally: 'is it okay if I try wearing it?' The -어 보다 component is what encodes 'try' — without it, 입어도 돼요? merely asks 'can I wear it?', not 'can I try it on for fit?'.

해요체 — say to any clothing clerk when holding a garment and wanting to test the fit. Soften to 입어 봐도 될까요? for extra politeness (e.g., a high-end boutique). Use only for clothes (입다), not for shoes (신어 봐도 돼요?) or hats (써 봐도 돼요?).
한번 봐도 돼요? ('can I take a look?') only requests visual inspection. 입어 봐도 돼요? specifically asks to put it on. After permission, follow with 탈의실 어디예요? (where is the fitting room?).
신어 봐도 돼요? (shoes), 써 봐도 돼요? (hats/glasses), 끼어 봐도 돼요? (gloves/rings), 한번 입어 볼게요 (I'll try it on). Match the verb to the body part.
Saying 시도해 봐도 돼요? (시도하다 = 'to attempt') is wrong — that verb is for tasks, not clothing. Using 입어 for shoes is the most common error. And write 돼요, not 되요 (되 + 어 = 돼).

expressions.shortExplanation: 신어 봐도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I try them on? (shoes)".
expressions.explanation: 신어 봐도 돼요? (sineo bwado dwaeyo?) means "Can I try them on? (shoes)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 신어 봐도 돼요? ("Can I try these on?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Softer, more tentative polite form

usagePhrases.note: Asking to test the next size

examples.en: Can I try these on?
examples.note: Bare request pointing at a shoe on display — the most common opening line in a shoe shop

examples.ko: 이 운동화 신어 봐도 돼요? 250 사이즈로요.
examples.romanization: i undonghwa sineo bwado dwaeyo? 250 saijeuroyo.
examples.en: Can I try these sneakers on? In size 250.
examples.note: Korean shoe sizes are in mm — 250 = 25.0 cm foot length; always state in mm

examples.ko: A: 발이 좀 넓어서요, 신어 봐도 돼요? / B: 네, 이쪽으로 앉으세요. / A: 좀 끼면 한 치수 큰 거 볼게요.
examples.romanization: A: bari jom neolbeoseoyo, sineo bwado dwaeyo? / B: ne, ijjogeuro anjeuseyo. / A: jom kkimyeon han chisu keun geo bolgeyo.
examples.en: A: My feet are a bit wide, can I try them on? / B: Yes, please sit here. / A: If they pinch I'll check a size up.
examples.note: Real fitting room exchange; 끼다 = to feel tight; 치수 = size step

expressions.nuance: 신어 봐도 돼요? is the shoe-shop counterpart of 입어 봐도 돼요?: a customer asks to try footwear on. 신다 is the verb specifically for putting on shoes, socks, and boots (things on your feet), combined with -어 보다 ('try') and -아도 돼요? ('may I?'), giving 'may I try putting them on?'. The body-part split is non-negotiable: 신다 for footwear, never 입다, and confusing them sounds bizarre to a native clerk. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 신어 봐도 될까요?; casual 신어 봐도 돼?. Korean shoe sizes are stated in millimeters (250, 255, 260, 265…), which surprises foreigners used to UK/US number sizing, so you'll always pair this phrase with a size: 250 사이즈로요. The nearest generic alternative, 한번 봐도 돼요? (just to look), only asks to examine, not to put on. Spelling: 신어 comes from 신다 + 어 — the stem vowel ㅣ takes 어, not 아.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes.
입다 is for clothes on the body. Footwear uses 신다, so the shoe-shop phrase is 신어 봐도 돼요?
Giving a US/UK shoe size like '8' or '9'.
Korean shoes are sized in millimeters (250, 255, 260...). Say a mm number, e.g., 250 사이즈로요.
Writing 신아 봐도 돼요?
신다 + 어 = 신어 (the stem vowel ㅣ takes 어, not 아). Correct: 신어 봐도 돼요?

structuredNuance.t: 신다 (to put on footwear) + -어 보다 (try doing) + -아도 돼요? (is it okay to?). Literally 'is it okay if I try putting them on?' 신다 is the body-part-specific verb for feet — shoes, socks, and boots only.
해요체 — use with any shoe shop clerk. Soften to 신어 봐도 될까요? for deference. Casual 신어 봐도 돼? with a friend. Korean shoe sizes run in mm (250, 255, 260…), so state the size as a number in millimeters.
한번 봐도 돼요? only asks to look. 입어 봐도 돼요? is for clothing on the body — using it for shoes sounds strange. The verb must match the body part.
다른 색 신어 봐도 돼요? (try another color), 한 치수 큰 거 신어 볼게요 (I'll try a size up), 더 큰 거 있어요? (do you have bigger?). All build on the same 신어 보다 core.

Saying 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes — English has one word 'wear' for everything, but Korean demands 신다 for feet. Giving a US/UK shoe size ('8' or '9') — say the mm number instead (250, 260). Spelling: 신어 봐도, not 신아 봐도 (stem ㅣ → 어).

expressions.explanation: "Do you have another color?" — that is 다른 색 있어요? (dareun saek isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다른 색 있어요? ("Do you have another color?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite question to a clerk
반말 to a friend or familiar seller
Softer, more tentative with -나요

usagePhrases.en: Do you have it in black?
usagePhrases.note: Naming the exact color you want

examples.en: Do you have this in another color?

examples.ko: 이 가방 다른 색 있어요? 흰색은 좀 부담스러워서요.
examples.romanization: i gabang dareun saek isseoyo? huinsaegeun jom budamseureowoseoyo.
examples.en: Do you have this bag in another color? White feels a bit much for me.
examples.note: Giving a reason; 부담스럽다 = feels overwhelming or too much

examples.ko: A: 이 코트 마음에 드는데 다른 색 있어요? / B: 네이비랑 베이지 있어요. / A: 베이지로 볼게요.
examples.romanization: A: i koteu maeume deuneunde dareun saek isseoyo? / B: neibirang beiji isseoyo. / A: beijiro bolgeyo.
examples.en: A: I like this coat — do you have other colors? / B: We have navy and beige. / A: I'll check the beige one.
examples.note: Full color consultation; 네이비/베이지 are common loanword color names

expressions.nuance: 다른 색 있어요? is a customer asking a clerk whether an item comes in a different color; 다른 means 'other/different', 색 is the short spoken form of 색깔 ('color'), and 있어요? is the availability question 'is there / do you have?'. Politeness is everyday 해요체; casual 다른 색 있어?, softer 다른 색깔도 있나요?. The verb of stock/availability is always 있다 ('to exist/have') — Korean has no separate 'have' verb for this, which trips beginners who hunt for one. To name a specific color you want, use COLOR + 으로/로 있어요? e.g., 검은색으로 있어요? The critical pair to watch is 다른 ('other/different') vs 다음 ('next') — 다음 색 would mean 'next color', which is nonsensical. The nearest alternative, 다른 거 있어요? ('do you have a different one?'), asks for a different item in general, while 다른 색 있어요? pins the question specifically to color.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Looking for a verb 'to have' and saying 다른 색 가져요?
Korean expresses 'have/there is' with 있다, not a possessive verb here. Ask 다른 색 있어요?
Confusing 다른 (other) with 다음 (next).
다른 색 = another color; 다음 색 = 'next color', which makes no sense in a shop. Use 다른.
Dropping 색 and asking only 다른 거 있어요?
That asks for a different item, not specifically a color. Keep 색: 다른 색 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 다른 = 'other/different' + 색 = short for 색깔 'color' + 있어요? = 'is there/do you have?'. Literally 'is there a different color?' Korean availability questions use 있다, not a separate 'have' verb.
해요체 — use with any clerk while holding the item you like but want in another shade. Casual 다른 색 있어? with a friend. To name the color you want: COLOR + 으로 있어요? (예: 검은색으로 있어요?).
다른 거 있어요? asks for a different item entirely; 다른 색 있어요? specifically asks about color. 다른 색깔도 있나요? is softer/more tentative. Watch 다른 (other) vs 다음 (next) — they are completely different words.
검은색으로 있어요? (in black?), 밝은 색 있어요? (lighter colors?), 무광으로 있어요? (matte finish?). All use the same 있어요? frame with a descriptor.
Hunting for a 'have' verb and saying 다른 색 가져요? — Korean uses 있다 for availability. Confusing 다른 (other) with 다음 (next). Dropping 색 and asking just 다른 거 있어요? loses the color meaning.

expressions.nuance: 더 큰 거 있어요? is a customer asking for a larger size or larger item; 더 means 'more', 큰 is 크다 ('big') in its noun-modifying form, 거 is the spoken 것 ('thing/one'), and 있어요? means 'do you have?', so literally 'is there a more-big one?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 더 큰 거 있어?, softer 더 큰 거 있나요?. The axis runs: 더 큰 거 ↔ 더 작은 거; you can also say 더 큰 사이즈 있어요? using the loanword 사이즈. The nearest vaguer alternative, 다른 사이즈 있어요? ('do you have another size?'), doesn't specify direction; 더 큰 거 is unambiguous about which way. The critical grammar error is 크는 거 — descriptive adjectives (형용사) use the -ㄴ/은 modifier form before nouns, not the -는 of action verbs; 큰 거 is correct, 크는 거 is wrong. Also note 거 is spoken; in formal writing it is 것.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 크는 거 instead of 큰 거.
크다 is a descriptive adjective; before a noun it takes -ㄴ: 큰 거. -는 is for action verbs, so 크는 거 is wrong.
Using 거 in formal writing.
거 is the spoken contraction of 것. In speech 더 큰 거 is natural; in writing use 더 큰 것.
Mixing up 크다 (big) and 작다 (small).
더 큰 거 = bigger; 더 작은 거 = smaller. Pick the right adjective for the direction you want.

structuredNuance.t: 더 = 'more' + 큰 = adjective modifier form of 크다 'big' + 거 = spoken 것 'one/thing' + 있어요? = 'is there?'. Literally 'is there a more-big one?' Korean stacks the comparator 더 before the adjective, not a separate comparative suffix like English '-er'.
해요체 — after trying on clothing or footwear that is too small. The same structure works for any comparison: 더 밝은 거 (brighter), 더 저렴한 거 (cheaper). Casual 더 큰 거 있어? with a friend.
다른 사이즈 있어요? is vaguer — it doesn't say which direction. 한 치수 큰 거 있어요? ('one size up') is even more precise. 더 큰 거 is the clearest general way to indicate you need bigger.
더 작은 거 있어요? (smaller), 한 치수 큰 거 있어요? (one size up), 더 큰 사이즈 있나요? (softened). Swap 큰 for any adjective: 더 긴 거, 더 가벼운 거.

Saying 크는 거 instead of 큰 거 — descriptive adjectives use -ㄴ, not -는 (which is for action verbs). Also 거 is spoken; write 것 in formal contexts. Don't omit 더: bare 큰 거 있어요? just asks 'is there a big one?' not specifically 'bigger than this'.

expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 세일해요? is a practical expression meaning "Is this on sale?".
expressions.explanation: 이거 세일해요? (igeo seilhaeyo?) means "Is this on sale?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 세일해요? ("Is this on sale?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite question to a clerk
반말 to a friend
Softer, 중 = in the middle of, with -ㄴ가요
Using 할인 instead of the loanword 세일

examples.en: Is this on sale?
examples.note: Bare question pointing at a tagged item in a clothing or department store

examples.ko: A: 이거 세일해요? / B: 네, 30% 할인이에요. / A: 잘됐다, 살게요.
examples.romanization: A: igeo seilhaeyo? / B: ne, 30% harinieyo. / A: jaldwaetda, salgeyo.
examples.en: A: Is this on sale? / B: Yes, it's 30% off. / A: Great, I'll take it.
examples.note: Complete exchange showing how the question naturally leads to a purchase decision

examples.ko: 이 코너 전부 세일해요? 아니면 이것만요?
examples.romanization: i koneo jeonbu seilhaeyo? animyeon igeonmanyo?
examples.en: Is this whole section on sale, or just this one?
examples.note: Real floor-browsing situation; 코너 = section; 이것만 = just this one

expressions.nuance: 이거 세일해요? is a customer checking whether an item is currently discounted; 세일 is the English loanword 'sale' used as a noun, and 하다 makes it a verb ('to be on sale'), so 'does this do a sale?'. This is the go-to word in department stores and franchises — the opposite context from 깎아 주세요 at a market, where pricing is negotiated in person. Politeness is 해요체; casual 세일해?; softer 세일 중인가요?. The native synonym is 할인 (割引), heard more in formal announcements, on receipts, and in corporate settings; 세일 is the breezy everyday spoken word. The dividing line: 세일 = colloquial, spoken, used by shoppers; 할인 = formal, written, used in store policy. English speakers mistakenly say 온 세일이에요? ('on sale') copying English syntax, but Korean treats 세일 as a 하다-verb. Also critical: Korean 세일 only means 'discounted'; 'available for purchase' is entirely different — 이거 파는 거예요? ('is this for sale?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 온 세일이에요? copying English 'on sale'.
Korean uses 세일 as a 하다-verb. Ask 이거 세일해요? — there is no 'on' construction.
Mixing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (available).
세일 = discounted only. To ask if something is purchasable, say 이거 파는 거예요?, not 세일.
Treating 세일 and 할인 as different deals.
They mean the same; 할인 is just more formal/written. Either 세일해요? or 할인돼요? works.

structuredNuance.t: 세일 (loanword 'sale') + 해요? (do you do?). Literally 'does this do a sale?' Korean attaches 하다 to the noun 세일 to make a verb — you don't need an extra 'on' preposition. The question checks for a discounted price, not store availability.

해요체 — use in department stores, branded franchises, and clothing chains where items are sometimes marked down. Not applicable at traditional markets where you just haggle (깎아 주세요). Casual 세일해? with a friend.

할인해요? / 할인되는 거예요? are native Sino-Korean equivalents, slightly more formal and written-register. 세일 is the everyday shopper's word; 할인 is the word on official signs and receipts. Both mean 'discounted'.
세일 중인가요? (mid-sale?), 몇 퍼센트 할인돼요? (what percent off?), 행사 중인가요? (is there a promotion?). Use 행사 for broader promotions beyond simple price cuts.
Saying 온 세일이에요? copies English 'on sale' — Korean uses 세일하다 as a verb: 세일해요?. Confusing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (purchasable) — 세일 = discounted only; availability is 이거 파는 거예요?

expressions.shortExplanation: 교환돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I exchange it?".
expressions.explanation: 교환돼요? (gyohwandwaeyo?) = "Can I exchange it?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 교환돼요? ("Can I exchange it?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite question to a clerk
반말 to a friend or familiar staff
Softer, more formal with 가능하다

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to exchange it for another
usagePhrases.note: Stating what you want to swap to

examples.en: Can I exchange this?
examples.note: Bare question holding the item — check policy before assuming yes

examples.ko: 사이즈가 작아서요, 더 큰 걸로 교환돼요?
examples.romanization: saijeuga jagaseoyo, deo keun geollo gyohwandwaeyo?
examples.en: It's small, so can I exchange it for a bigger one?
examples.note: Reason plus target size; 걸로 = 것으로 (for the one) — the 으로 particle marks what you're swapping to

examples.ko: A: 색이 화면이랑 달라서요. 다른 색으로 교환돼요? / B: 네, 영수증이랑 택 있으시면요. / A: 둘 다 있어요.
examples.romanization: A: saegi hwamyeonirang dallaseoyo. dareun saegeuro gyohwandwaeyo? / B: ne, yeongsujeungirang taek isseusimyeonyo. / A: dul da isseoyo.
examples.en: A: The color's different from the screen. Can I exchange it for another color? / B: Yes, if you have the receipt and tags. / A: I have both.
examples.note: Online-purchase exchange scene; 화면 = screen; 택 = product tag — shows typical conditions

expressions.nuance: 교환돼요? asks whether you can swap an item for a different size, color, or model without getting money back; 교환 is Sino-Korean 交換 ('mutual exchange') and 되다 = 'to be possible', so 'is an exchange doable?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 교환돼?; formal 교환 가능한가요?. The defining contrast remains 교환 (swap item, keep the transaction) vs 환불 (cancel transaction, get money back); knowing which you want before approaching the counter saves time. To specify what you're exchanging to, use TARGET + 으로/로 교환: 더 큰 걸로 교환돼요?, 다른 색으로 교환돼요? — the directional particle 으로/로 is essential and often dropped by English speakers. After confirming the policy, say 교환해 주세요 to actually execute it. Spelling: 교환돼요, not 교환되요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 교환되요.
되다's polite form is 돼요. Correct: 교환돼요?
Dropping the particle: 다른 색 교환돼요?
You swap INTO something, marked with 으로/로. Say 다른 색으로 교환돼요?
Confusing 교환 (exchange) with 환불 (refund).
교환 swaps the item; 환불 returns your money. Ask for the one you actually want.

structuredNuance.t: 교환 = Sino-Korean 交換 'mutual exchange' + 되다 = 'to be possible'. Literally 'is an exchange possible?' Unlike 환불 (money back), 교환 swaps the item while keeping the original transaction — no refund is involved.

해요체 — use at a return/exchange counter. After getting permission, say 교환해 주세요 to execute it. Bring the receipt (영수증) and keep tags attached — many shops refuse without them. 교환 가능한가요? for formal customer service calls.

환불돼요? = money back; 교환돼요? = item swap. English 'change it' tempts the verb 바꿔요? (바꾸다), which works casually (바꿀 수 있어요?) but the official store word on signs is 교환. Always pair with 으로/로 to name the target item.
다른 색으로 교환돼요? (exchange for another color), 더 큰 걸로 교환해 주세요 (exchange for a bigger one please), 교환 및 환불 가능한가요? (are exchanges and refunds possible? — formal query).
Dropping the 으로/로 particle — Korean marks the target of an exchange with 으로/로, not zero. Saying 교환되요 — correct spelling is 교환돼요. Using 바꿔요? casually instead of the store-official 교환.

expressions.shortExplanation: 영수증 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me the receipt".
expressions.explanation: 영수증 주세요 (yeongsujeung juseyo) means "Please give me the receipt". Say it as one set phrase — for example 영수증 주세요 ("Please give me the receipt"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request at the register
반말 to a friend, rare to staff

usagePhrases.en: Could you give me the receipt?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more polite request
The opposite — declining it

examples.en: Please give me the receipt.
examples.note: Bare request as you pay — the default at any checkout

examples.ko: 영수증 주세요. 혹시 교환할 수도 있어서요.
examples.romanization: yeongsujeung juseyo. hoksi gyohwanhal sudo isseoseoyo.
examples.en: Please give me the receipt. In case I might exchange it.
examples.note: Reason for keeping it; 혹시 = just in case — shows why receipts matter in Korean retail

examples.ko: A: 카드로 계산할게요. 영수증 주세요. / B: 현금영수증도 해 드릴까요? / A: 네, 010으로 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: kadeuro gyesanhalgeyo. yeongsujeung juseyo. / B: hyeongeumyeongsujeungdo hae deurilkkayo? / A: ne, 010euro hae juseyo.
examples.en: A: I'll pay by card. Please give me the receipt. / B: Shall I also do a cash receipt (tax)? / A: Yes, please register it to my 010 number.
examples.note: Full real checkout; 현금영수증 = tax-deductible cash receipt tied to your phone number

expressions.nuance: 영수증 주세요 is a customer asking the cashier for the receipt after paying; 영수증 is Sino-Korean 領收證 (receive + collect + proof), meaning 'proof of payment', and 주세요 is the polite 'please give me'. Politeness is 해요체; softer 영수증 좀 주시겠어요?. A key Korean reality: many stores ask 영수증 드릴까요? and the receipt is your only leverage for refunds or exchanges, so keeping it is important. Do not confuse 영수증 (standard purchase receipt) with 현금영수증 (a separate tax-deductible receipt registered to your phone number or tax ID — completely different and actively solicited at the counter). The phrase also pairs with 주세요 naturally with no particle needed, though 영수증을 주세요 is also correct and slightly more formal. Common pronunciation error: 영수정 — the final syllable is 증, from 證 'proof', not 정.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 영수증 with 현금영수증.
영수증 = the purchase receipt; 현금영수증 = a tax cash-receipt tied to your number. Different things; ask for the one you need.
Adding 저에게: 저에게 영수증 주세요.
주세요 already means 'give me'. Just say 영수증 주세요 — the 'to me' is built in.
Misspelling it 영수정.
The correct word is 영수증 (證, 'proof'). Get the final 증 right.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 = Sino-Korean 領收證 'proof of receiving payment' + 주세요 = 'please give me'. Literally 'please give me the proof of payment.' 주세요 already means 'give me', so no 저에게 or 에게 is needed.
해요체 — say to any cashier right after paying. The cashier may ask first: 영수증 드릴까요? Answer 네, 주세요 to get it or 아니요, 괜찮아요 to decline. Soften to 좀 주시겠어요? at a formal counter.

현금영수증 is NOT the same as 영수증 — it is a tax-deductible receipt registered to your phone number, used for year-end tax deductions. Ask for it separately: 현금영수증도 해 주세요. 영수증 버려 주세요 is the eco-decline option.
영수증 좀 주시겠어요? (softer), 영수증 있어야 교환돼요? (do I need the receipt to exchange?), 현금영수증도 해 주세요 (and a tax receipt please). In Korean retail these two receipts serve different purposes.
Mispronouncing/spelling it as 영수정 — the final syllable is 증 (證), not 정. Adding 저에게 — 주세요 already means 'give me'. Confusing 영수증 with 현금영수증, which is a separate tax registration.

expressions.shortExplanation: 그냥 둘러볼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm just looking around".
expressions.explanation: "I'm just looking around" — that is 그냥 둘러볼게요 (geunyang dulleobolgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 그냥 둘러볼게요 ("I'm just looking around"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite reply to a hovering clerk
반말 to a friend
구경 = browsing/sightseeing, very common
Shortest polite brush-off

examples.en: I'm just looking around.
examples.note: Bare reply when a clerk asks if you need help — the standard browse-and-decline phrase

examples.ko: A: 뭐 찾으세요? / B: 아, 괜찮아요. 그냥 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: A: mwo chajeuseyo? / B: a, gwaenchanayo. geunyang dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: A: Can I help you find something? / B: Oh, it's okay. I'm just browsing.
examples.note: Complete clerk-customer exchange showing the natural trigger for this phrase; 뭐 찾으세요? = 'what are you looking for?'

examples.ko: 도움 필요하시면 부를게요. 일단 그냥 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: doum piryohasimyeon bureulgeyo. ildan geunyang dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: I'll call you if I need help. For now I'm just looking.
examples.note: Shows the speaker proactively managing the clerk; 일단 = for now; 부를게요 = I'll call you — friendly and considerate

expressions.nuance: 그냥 둘러볼게요 is the customer's polite brush-off to a clerk who offers help: it signals 'no thanks, just browsing, no pressure needed'; 그냥 means 'just/for no particular reason', 둘러보다 is 'to look around/browse (a space)', and -ㄹ게요 expresses the speaker's intention ('I'll...'), making it gracious rather than dismissive. Politeness is 해요체; casual 그냥 둘러볼게. An equally common equivalent is 구경 좀 할게요 (구경 = 'looking around for pleasure/sightseeing'), which sounds slightly lighter and friendlier. The -ㄹ게요 ending is crucial: it signals personal intention from the speaker's side, which fits perfectly for declining unsolicited help; swapping to -아요 (둘러봐요) makes it a flat factual statement, losing the gracious 'I'll...' nuance. English speakers often say 그냥 보고 있어요 ('I'm just watching/looking'), which is understandable but flat; 그냥 둘러볼게요 is the idiomatically correct browsing phrase. Spelling: 둘러볼게요, not 둘러볼께요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그냥 보고 있어요 for 'just looking'.
That literally means 'I'm just watching' and feels flat. The natural browse-and-decline phrase is 그냥 둘러볼게요 or 구경 좀 할게요.
Using 둘러봐요 instead of 둘러볼게요.
둘러봐요 is a flat statement; -ㄹ게요 adds the polite 'I'll...' intention that fits declining help. Use 둘러볼게요.
Spelling it 둘러볼께요.
Although pronounced tense (께), the correct spelling of the -ㄹ게요 ending is 게: 둘러볼게요.

structuredNuance.t: 그냥 = 'just/for no particular reason' + 둘러보다 = 'to look around' + -ㄹ게요 = 'I will (for my part)'. Literally 'I'll just look around.' The -ㄹ게요 ending is what makes it a gracious intention, not a flat statement.

해요체 — say to any clerk who approaches you offering help. Triggered by 뭐 찾으세요? or 도와드릴까요?. Casual 그냥 둘러볼게 with a friend. You can soften further with 네, 좀 볼게요 (just a brief look) or extend courtesy by adding 도움 필요하면 부를게요 (I'll call if I need help).
구경 좀 할게요 is a near-twin using 구경 (leisurely looking), which sounds slightly lighter and friendlier. 그냥 보고 있어요 is flat and factual — it lacks the courteous 'intention' nuance of -ㄹ게요.
그냥 구경 좀 할게요 (I'll just browse), 잠깐 둘러볼게요 (I'll look around briefly), 나중에 필요하면 부를게요 (I'll call if I need you later). All use the same -ㄹ게요 intention frame.
Saying 그냥 보고 있어요 — natural but flat, not the idiom. Using 둘러봐요 (statement) instead of 둘러볼게요 (intention). Spelling: 둘러볼게요 not 둘러볼께요 (tense pronunciation but 게 spelling).

expressions.shortExplanation: 이걸로 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll take this one".
expressions.explanation: 이걸로 할게요 (igeollo halgeyo) = "I'll take this one". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이걸로 할게요 ("I'll take this one"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite, deciding to buy
반말 to a friend
Formal 합쇼체 at a counter
Same decision, asking to be handed it

examples.en: I'll take this one.
examples.note: Bare decision, pointing at your choice — the moment you commit to a purchase

examples.ko: A: 고민했는데 이걸로 할게요. / B: 포장해 드릴까요? / A: 아니요, 그냥 봉투만 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: gominhaenneunde igeollo halgeyo. / B: pojanghae deurilkkayo? / A: aniyo, geunyang bongtuman juseyo.
examples.en: A: I thought it over — I'll take this one. / B: Shall I wrap it? / A: No, just a bag is fine.
examples.note: Complete purchase decision → wrap/bag choice; shows realistic follow-up from the clerk

examples.ko: 둘 다 예쁜데 이걸로 할게요. 이거 하나만 주세요.
examples.romanization: dul da yeppeunde igeollo halgeyo. igeo hanaman juseyo.
examples.en: Both are pretty, but I'll take this one. Just this one, please.
examples.note: Choosing between two options; 하나만 = just one — a very realistic browsing-to-buying moment

expressions.nuance: 이걸로 할게요 is how a customer announces their final purchase decision to a clerk; 이걸로 is the spoken contraction of 이것으로 ('with/by means of this one'), and 하다 here means 'to go with / decide on', plus -ㄹ게요 'I'll...', so the whole meaning is 'I'll go with this one'. The particle 으로/로 is doing the selection work: Korean marks the chosen option with 으로/로, not with the object particle 을/를, which is why it must be 이걸로 and not 이걸 or 이것을. Politeness is 해요체; casual 이걸로 할게; formal 이걸로 하겠습니다. The near-twin 이걸로 주세요 is interchangeable at checkout: 할게요 foregrounds your decision/commitment, 주세요 foregrounds the request to hand it over. The -ㄹ게요 ending once again signals personal intention, perfectly suited to committing to a purchase. Spelling: 할게요, not 할께요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이것을 할게요 with the object particle.
Choosing an option uses 으로/로, not 을/를. The natural form is 이걸로 할게요 (이것으로).
Dropping the 로 and saying 이거 할게요.
Selection is marked with 으로/로. 이걸로 할게요 sounds complete; bare 이거 할게요 is a bit off.
Spelling it 할께요.
Despite the tense pronunciation, the -ㄹ게요 ending is spelled 게: 할게요.

structuredNuance.t: 이걸로 = 이것으로 (with/by this one) + 하다 = 'to go with/decide on' + -ㄹ게요 = 'I will...'. Literally 'I will go with this one.' 하다 here is not 'do' in the activity sense but a decision verb meaning 'to choose/settle on'.

해요체 — say to any clerk when you've made your final choice. Signals you are done browsing. -ㄹ게요 communicates personal commitment, which is exactly right for a purchase. Follow with 계산해 주세요 (please ring it up) to move to checkout.

이걸로 주세요 is interchangeable — it shifts the frame from 'I decide' to 'please hand me this'. 이거 살게요 ('I'll buy this one') is also natural but more casual and explicit about buying. The particle 으로 is non-negotiable for selection.
그걸로 할게요 (I'll go with that one), 저걸로 할게요 (that one over there), 이걸로 두 개 주세요 (two of this one please). Swap the demonstrative to point at different items.
Using the object particle: 이것을 할게요 — selection takes 으로/로, not 을/를. Dropping 로 and saying 이거 할게요 sounds slightly off. Spelling: 할게요 not 할께요.

expressions.english: I'd like a transit card, please
expressions.shortExplanation: 교통카드 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like a transit card, please".
expressions.explanation: 교통카드 주세요 (gyotongkadeu juseyo) means "I'd like a transit card, please". Say it as one set phrase — for example 교통카드 주세요 ("A transit card, please"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; said at a convenience store counter buying a T-money card
Add 하나 to specify a single card — natural when there are multiple buyers
Asking by brand name; 티머니 is the dominant card brand in Seoul

usagePhrases.en: Where do I buy a transit card?
usagePhrases.note: Ask this at a hotel or on the street if you can't find a 편의점

examples.en: A transit card, please.
examples.note: Said to a clerk at a GS25 or CU convenience store counter; hand over cash and the card will be activated for you.

examples.en: Excuse me, one T-money card, please.
examples.note: Using the brand name 티머니 is completely natural; clerks know it instantly and it is the most common card in Seoul.

examples.ko: A: 교통카드 사려고 하는데 여기서 팔아요? / B: 네, 얼마짜리로 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: A: gyotongkadeu saryeogo haneunde yeogiseo parayo? / B: ne, eolmajjariro deurilkkayo?
examples.en: A: I want to buy a transit card — do you sell them here? / B: Yes, which denomination would you like?
examples.note: 사려고 하다 ('intending to buy') politely checks availability before asking the clerk to retrieve one.

expressions.nuance: 교통카드 is 교통 (交通, 'transportation') + 카드 ('card'), the generic umbrella term for the rechargeable tap-to-ride card used on every Korean city subway and bus. In everyday speech Seoulites usually say the brand name 티머니, and 캐시비 is the other major brand common in other cities, but 교통카드 is the safe neutral term that any clerk anywhere understands. You buy one at any 편의점 (convenience store) for a small fee — the card itself costs money and that fee is not refunded. The critical cultural difference from many other transit systems is that you do NOT buy disposable single-journey paper tickets for daily travel; you load cash onto a reusable card and tap in and out. For English speakers the immediate trap is asking for a 표 ('ticket') at a convenience store — that word means a paper ticket for a one-off journey or intercity bus, and a convenience-store clerk will look confused. Also note that 카드 alone in a retail context usually means a credit or debit card, so always say the full 교통카드 to be unambiguous. Register: 주세요 is the natural polite form with any clerk; you would never use 반말 with a stranger behind a counter.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking for a 표 (ticket) to ride daily.
표 means a paper ticket used for single-journey tokens or intercity buses — not everyday city transit. For daily tapping on the subway and bus, buy a reusable 교통카드, not a 표.
Saying just 카드 주세요 at a convenience store.
Bare 카드 is ambiguous and typically means a credit/debit card in a shop context. Always say 교통카드 주세요 (or 티머니 주세요) to be clear you want a transit card.
Assuming the card is free or the purchase price is a refundable deposit.

The physical 교통카드 card itself costs money (roughly 2,500–4,000 won) and is not refunded when you're done with it. Only the cash balance you loaded is yours to spend; plan for the card cost when budgeting your first purchase.

structuredNuance.t: 교통카드 literally decomposes as '交通 card' — transportation card. The real meaning in daily life is the rechargeable contactless card (T-money / Cashbee) you tap on every subway gate and bus reader. You buy it at a 편의점 and load cash onto it; the card itself is not free.

Say this at any 편의점 (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven, Emart24) counter. 주세요 is the polite default with service workers; never use 반말 (informal) with a clerk you don't know. If you want a specific brand, substitute 티머니 주세요 or 캐시비 주세요.

표 means a paper ticket — for single-journey subway tokens (1회용 교통카드) sold at station machines, or intercity bus tickets. Asking for a 표 at a convenience store to ride the city bus/subway daily is the wrong word. Bare 카드 alone could be a credit card, so always say 교통카드 in full.

The single biggest English-speaker mistake is asking for a 표 ('ticket') expecting to ride the city subway daily. Korea uses a tap card system, not paper tickets for daily commuting. Budget for the card's purchase price (a few thousand won) on top of any initial load.

expressions.english: Please charge (load money on) my card
expressions.shortExplanation: 충전해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please charge (load money on) my card".
expressions.explanation: "Please charge (load money on) my card" — that is 충전해 주세요 (chungjeonhae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 충전해 주세요 ("Please load it / top it up"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please load it / top it up
usagePhrases.note: Polite; hand the card to a convenience-store clerk and say this
Amount comes BEFORE 충전; the most natural word order
Ask this first if you're not sure the shop does T-money charging

usagePhrases.en: How much shall I load for you?
usagePhrases.note: The clerk's standard reply; respond with an amount + 원

examples.en: Please top it up.
examples.note: Said while placing your card flat on the counter; the clerk will ask how much.

examples.en: Just 10,000 won, please.
examples.note: 만 원만 ('only 10,000 won') signals a small, exact top-up; 만 원 is the most common amount people load.

examples.ko: A: 교통카드 충전 돼요? / B: 네, 얼마 드릴까요? / A: 오천 원 충전해 주세요.
examples.romanization: A: gyotongkadeu chungjeon dwaeyo? / B: ne, eolma deurilkkayo? / A: ocheon won chungjeonhae juseyo.
examples.en: A: Can I charge a transit card here? / B: Yes, how much? / A: Load 5,000 won, please.
examples.note: Confirm the shop does it, then state the amount — the natural two-step for an unfamiliar shop.

expressions.nuance: 충전 is Sino-Korean 充電, literally 'fill electricity', but in Korea it has extended to mean loading money onto any prepaid balance — a transit card, a gift card, a phone data plan. When you hand your 교통카드 to a convenience-store clerk and say 충전해 주세요, they place it on a pad, you give them cash, and the amount is added to your card. The critical word order is AMOUNT first: 만 원 충전해 주세요 ('load 10,000 won'), NOT 충전해 주세요 만 원 — tacking the amount at the end sounds out of order. Subway stations also have self-serve 교통카드 충전기 (charging machines) that accept cash and give exact change, so you are not limited to convenience stores. The main difference from similar words: 결제 means 'settling a payment' (paying for something you owe), while 충전 means 'adding balance before you use it' — they go in opposite directions. 환불 ('refund') is getting money back. For English speakers the trap is treating 충전 as a battery-only word — it covers any kind of balance top-up in Korean. Register: 주세요 is correct with a clerk; the clerk addresses you back with the honorific 드릴까요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 충전 only means charging a phone or battery.
충전 also means loading money onto a transit card, prepaid gift card, or phone data plan. 교통카드 충전해 주세요 correctly means 'top up my transit card' — it is the standard verb.
Putting the amount after the verb: 충전해 주세요 만 원.
Korean states the amount first: 만 원 충전해 주세요. Tacking 만 원 on the end sounds awkward; lead with the number + 원.
Confusing 충전 (load money) with 결제 (pay) or 환불 (refund).
결제 is settling a payment you already owe; 환불 is getting money back. 충전 is adding balance before you use it — say 충전해 주세요, not 결제해 주세요, to top up your card.

structuredNuance.t: 충전(充電) literally means 'fill/charge electricity' but has expanded to cover loading money onto any prepaid balance. For a transit card it means 'add cash to the card so you can ride'. The clerk taps your card on a pad; you hand over cash for the amount you state.

Say this at any 편의점 or subway 충전기 (self-service machine). Always state the amount FIRST: 만 원 충전해 주세요. 주세요 is polite-neutral for clerks; the clerk's honorific response is 얼마 충전해 드릴까요? ('how much shall I load for you?').
충전 = adding balance in advance (top-up). 결제 = settling/paying a charge you incurred. 환불 = getting money back. These three verbs run in opposite directions — don't confuse them.
충전하다 (verb) → 충전해 주세요 (request), 충전할게요 (I'll top it up), 충전 됐어요? (did it load?). The self-service machine is 교통카드 충전기. 충전 잔액 = the loaded balance remaining.
Two traps: (1) thinking 충전 is only for batteries/phones — it fully covers transit-card top-ups; and (2) putting the amount after the verb (충전해 주세요 만 원) — Korean puts the amount BEFORE: 만 원 충전해 주세요.

expressions.shortExplanation: 잔액이 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much balance is left?".
expressions.explanation: 잔액이 얼마예요? (janaegi eolmayeyo?) = "How much balance is left?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 잔액이 얼마예요? ("How much balance is left?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking a clerk or checking the gate reader to know your card balance

usagePhrases.en: Could you check the balance, please?
usagePhrases.note: Asking the clerk to read it on the terminal for you
Reporting the gate beep or reader's 잔액 부족 error message
The everyday casual alternative — warmer and very common in speech

examples.en: How much balance is left?
examples.note: Ask a clerk when you're unsure how much is loaded; they tap the card on the reader and tell you.

examples.ko: 저기요, 카드 잔액 좀 확인해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, kadeu janaek jom hwaginhae juseyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, could you check my card balance?
examples.note: 확인해 주세요 ('please check') is slightly softer than 얼마예요 and signals you want them to look it up for you.

examples.ko: A: 왜 안 열려요? / B: 아, 잔액 부족이래요. 충전해야겠어요.
examples.romanization: A: wae an yeollyeoyo? / B: a, janaek bujogiraeyo. chungjeonhaeyagesseoyo.
examples.en: A: Why won't it open? / B: Oh, it says low balance. I'd better top up.
examples.note: Reacting to the gate's 잔액 부족 beep — the immediate fix is to step aside and 충전 before trying again.

expressions.nuance: 잔액 is Sino-Korean 殘額 ('remaining amount'), the standard financial noun for the balance left on a card. In the transit context it refers specifically to the cash loaded on your 교통카드. The gate reader always shows the remaining balance after each tap, and the dreaded 잔액 부족 ('insufficient balance') beep plus a red light means you cannot ride — step aside, 충전, and try again. The everyday casual alternative 얼마 남았어요? ('how much is left?') feels warmer and less formal because it avoids the Sino-Korean noun, but both are completely natural. The big particle trap for English speakers: because you are asking 'the balance IS how much?', 잔액 is the grammatical subject and takes 이 — so 잔액이 얼마예요?, NOT 잔액을 얼마예요? (the object marker 을 makes no sense here; you are not doing anything to the balance). Do not confuse 잔액 (money stored on the card) with 거스름돈 (cash change handed back) — they describe entirely different flows of money. Polite -요 is right with any clerk or agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 을/를 instead of 이/가: 잔액을 얼마예요?
얼마예요 needs a subject, not an object. The natural form is 잔액이 얼마예요? — you are asking 'the balance is how much?', so mark 잔액 with the subject particle 이.
Confusing 잔액 (card balance) with 거스름돈 (cash change).
잔액 is the money loaded on your card; 거스름돈 is the physical change handed back when you pay cash. To check your card, ask 잔액이 얼마예요? — 거스름돈 is a different transaction entirely.
Ignoring a 잔액 부족 beep and pushing through the gate again.
잔액 부족 means the card lacks sufficient funds and the gate will not open. Trying again repeatedly will not help. Step aside, find a 편의점 or 충전기, top up the card, then try the gate again.

structuredNuance.t: 잔액(殘額) literally means 'remaining amount'. For a transit card it is the cash balance you have loaded. The gate reader shows this balance after every tap; 잔액 부족 ('insufficient balance') triggers a beep and a locked gate.
Ask a 편의점 clerk (잔액 좀 확인해 주세요) or use the subway 충전기 machine to check. Polite -요 is correct with staff. The casual 얼마 남았어요? works between friends or with a familiar clerk.

잔액이 얼마예요? is precise and formal (uses the financial Sino-Korean noun). 얼마 남았어요? is warm and colloquial — same question, slightly softer register. Neither is wrong; choose by formality. 자리 없어요 ('no seats') looks similar but is unrelated — don't confuse 잔액 (card balance) with 거스름돈 (cash change).
잔액 조회 (balance inquiry, formal/written). 잔액이 얼마 있어요? (how much balance do you have?). 잔액이 부족해요 (the balance is insufficient). These all share the root 잔액.
Use the subject marker 이, not the object marker 을: 잔액이 얼마예요? You are stating 'the balance is how much?', so mark 잔액 as the subject. 잔액을 얼마예요? is ungrammatical.

expressions.shortExplanation: 몇 호선이에요? is a practical expression meaning "Which line is it?".
expressions.explanation: 몇 호선이에요? (myeo toseonieyo?) means "Which line is it?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 몇 호선이에요? ("Which line is it?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking which numbered subway line a station is on
Asking for directions to a specific line inside a station
Asking which line to board to reach your destination
Confirming which line you are currently standing at

examples.en: Which line is Gangnam Station on?
examples.note: 역 + 은 sets the topic, then ask 몇 호선이에요 — Gangnam is on Line 2 (and the Sinbundang Line).

examples.ko: 시청 가려면 몇 호선 타야 돼요?
examples.romanization: sicheong garyeomyeon myeo toseon taya dwaeyo?
examples.en: Which line do I take to get to City Hall?
examples.note: 가려면 ('in order to go to') frames the route question naturally; City Hall Station is on Lines 1 and 2.

examples.ko: A: 여기서 2호선으로 어떻게 가요? / B: 저쪽 계단으로 가시면 돼요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiseo 2hoseoneuro eotteoke gayo? / B: jeojjok gyedaneuro gasimyeon dwaeyo.
examples.en: A: How do I get to Line 2 from here? / B: Just head down those stairs over there.
examples.note: 2호선으로 ('toward/to Line 2') uses the direction particle 로, and the natural reply gives a landmark.

expressions.nuance: 호선 is the dedicated counter for numbered subway lines: 호(號) means 'number' and 선(線) means 'line'. The full phrase 몇 호선이에요? means 'what number line is it?' and is used constantly inside stations and when checking directions. The single most important grammar point is number system: line numbers ALWAYS use Sino-Korean numerals (일, 이, 삼, 사…), so Line 2 is 이 호선, NEVER 두 호선. This is the most consistent learner mistake because many other Korean counters take native numbers, but 호선 is Sino-Korean all the way. The direction particle toward a line is -으로/-로: 2호선으로 가요 ('go toward Line 2'). English speakers also reach for 라인 (from 'line') or say 라인 2 — Koreans say 호선 for numbered subway lines without exception; 라인 is not used. Named lines that are not numbered (신분당선, 경의중앙선, 공항철도, 수인분당선) do NOT use 호선 — for those, say the full line name. With strangers and station agents, maintain polite -요 form throughout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using native numbers: 두 호선 for Line 2.
Line numbers take Sino-Korean numerals: 2호선 = 이 호선, 3호선 = 삼 호선. Never 두 호선 or 세 호선 — this is the single most common subway-number mistake.
Saying 라인 instead of 호선.
Korean subway lines are 호선, not 라인. 'Line 2' is 2호선, never 라인 2. Use 호선 for any numbered line.
Forcing 호선 onto named lines like 신분당선.
Named or lettered lines (신분당선, 경의중앙선, 공항철도, 우이신설선) do not take 호선. Say the full name as-is; reserve 호선 for the numbered lines.

structuredNuance.t: 몇 호선이에요? = 'what number line is it?'. 호(號) = 'number', 선(線) = 'line'. The question asks which numbered Seoul Metro line (1–9 + others) a station sits on.

Ask this to any passerby inside the station or to a station agent. Polite -요 is the right register with strangers; you would not drop to 반말 when asking for directions. Inside the station, follow the color-coded signs — but when confused, this question cuts to the point.

호선 is only for NUMBERED lines (1호선 through 9호선 and the few others with numbers). Named lines like 신분당선, 경의중앙선, or 공항철도 have no 호선 suffix — say their full name. If someone asks 신분당선 몇 호선이에요? that's a non-question; just say 신분당선이에요.
몇 호선이에요? → 몇 호선 타요? (which line do you take?), 몇 호선에서 내려요? (which line do I get off on?), 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? (which line do I transfer to?). Same 호선 counter throughout.
Two pitfalls: (1) using 두 호선 instead of 이 호선 for Line 2 — line numbers are ALWAYS Sino-Korean; and (2) saying 라인 2 (English loanword) — Koreans say 호선, never 라인, for subway lines.

expressions.english: Does this go to City Hall Station?
expressions.shortExplanation: 이거 시청역 가요? is a practical expression meaning "Does this go to City Hall Station?".
expressions.explanation: "Does this go to City Hall Station?" — that is 이거 시청역 가요? (igeo sicheongyeok gayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이거 시청역 가요? ("Does this go to City Hall Station?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Does this go to City Hall Station?
usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; confirming a train or bus destination before boarding

usagePhrases.en: Does this bus go to Gangnam?
usagePhrases.note: Same sentence pattern applied to a bus

usagePhrases.en: Is this subway heading toward Incheon?
usagePhrases.note: 방향 ('direction') question — useful when direction matters more than a single stop

usagePhrases.en: To reach City Hall, is this the one to take?
usagePhrases.note: 타면 돼요 ('is it okay to board this?') confirms both destination and vehicle

examples.en: Does this go to City Hall Station?
examples.note: Quick check to a fellow passenger or driver right before you step on — a simple yes/no answer is all you need.

examples.en: Excuse me, does this bus go to Seoul Station?
examples.note: Say this to the bus driver as you approach the door; 저기요 gets attention politely without being pushy.

examples.ko: A: 이 지하철 강남 방향 맞아요? / B: 아니요, 반대예요. 저쪽 타세요.
examples.romanization: A: i jihacheol gangnam banghyang majayo? / B: aniyo, bandaeyeyo. jeojjok taseyo.
examples.en: A: Is this subway going the Gangnam direction? / B: No, it's the opposite. Take that side.
examples.note: 맞아요? ('right?') invites confirmation; the answer 반대예요 ('it's the opposite') tells you immediately to cross the platform.

expressions.nuance: 이거 시청역 가요? is 이거 ('this one') + the destination + 가요? ('does it go?') — the fastest possible boarding check. The 가요 is plain intransitive 'go to', and Korean spoken style routinely drops destination particles, so 시청역 가요? is fully natural without -에 or -까지. For buses you simply swap 이거 → 이 버스. The critical subway-specific issue is DIRECTION: every numbered line runs in two opposite directions on the same tracks, so even if you are on the correct 호선, you can board the wrong-direction train and ride away from your stop. That is why the 방향 ('direction') follow-up — 강남 방향이에요? — is so valuable. The verb for 'stop at' is 서다, not 가다: if you want to know whether the train halts at a station, ask 시청역 서요?, not 시청역 가요? ('go' and 'stop' are different). Keep all these questions in polite -요 form with strangers, drivers, and agents; 반말 would be rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Boarding the right line but the wrong direction.
One line runs both ways on the same tracks. Even on the correct 호선, confirm direction: ask 강남 방향이에요? or 이거 시청역 가요? before getting on, or you'll ride away from your stop.
Over-translating 'go to' as 가는 거예요? with extra particles.
The natural spoken question drops particles: 이거 시청역 가요? Adding -에 (시청역에 가요?) is grammatically fine but stiffer for a quick boarding check; the crisp form is best.
Confusing 가요? (does it go) with 서요? (does it stop).

가요 asks the destination or heading; 서요 (from 서다 'to stop') asks whether the train halts at a specific station. For 'does this stop at City Hall?' say 시청역 서요?, not 가요? — an express might 가다 in that direction without 서다 there.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 시청역 가요? = 'this one — does it go to City Hall Station?'. 이거 = this train/bus; 가요 = goes (intransitive). The destination particle is often dropped in speech. The question is designed to be answered with 네/아니요 instantly.

Ask before boarding to any nearby passenger, the bus driver, or a station agent. Polite -요 is right with all of them; 반말 (informal) would be impolite toward strangers. On the subway platform, aim it at someone waiting or a station worker.

가요? = does it go (toward) that destination? 서요? = does it stop at that station? — two different questions. A train going toward Incheon might not stop at your station if it is an express. For confirming direction without naming a stop, use 방향이에요?: 강남 방향이에요?
이거 시청역 가요? → 이 버스 시청역 가요?, 이 열차 시청역 서요?, 이거 시청 방향이에요? — all the same checking structure with different nouns or verbs swapped in.

English speakers over-build: they add -에 (시청역에 가요?) or rephrase as 가는 거예요? Both are grammatical but stiff for a quick boarding check. The natural spoken shortcut drops the particle: 시청역 가요? Also, the most common real mistake is boarding the right line but the wrong direction — always check 방향 too.

expressions.shortExplanation: 어디서 내려요? is a practical expression meaning "Where do I get off?".
expressions.explanation: 어디서 내려요? (eodiseo naeryeoyo?) = "Where do I get off?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어디서 내려요? ("Where do I get off?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; asking which stop is yours
Confirming this specific stop is the right one

usagePhrases.en: How many more stops to go?
usagePhrases.note: Asking how far is left, counted by stop number

usagePhrases.en: Please tell me when it's my stop
usagePhrases.note: Asking the driver or a fellow passenger to alert you

examples.en: To get to Namsan, where do I get off?
examples.note: 가려면 ('in order to go to') sets up the get-off question — a complete, polite request for directions.

examples.ko: A: 여기서 내리면 돼요? / B: 아니요, 다음이에요.
examples.romanization: A: yeogiseo naerimyeon dwaeyo? / B: aniyo, daeumieyo.
examples.en: A: Should I get off here? / B: No, the next one.
examples.note: 내리면 돼요 ('is it okay to get off here?') gets a direct answer; 다음이에요 ('the next one') tells you to stay on.

examples.ko: 기사님, 경복궁 가면 내릴 때 좀 알려 주세요.
examples.romanization: gisanim, gyeongbokgung gamyeon naeril ttae jom allyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Driver, when we reach Gyeongbokgung please let me know when to get off.
examples.note: 기사님 is the respectful address for a bus driver; 알려 주세요 ('please inform me') is the polite favor form of 알리다 ('to notify').

expressions.nuance: 어디서 내려요? breaks down as 어디 ('where') + 서 (location-of-action particle) + 내려요 ('get off', from 내리다). The particle 서 is non-negotiable here: because 내리다 ('to get off') is an action that HAPPENS AT a place, it takes the dynamic 에서/서, not the static location marker 에. This means 'getting off here' is 여기서 내려요, never 여기에 내려요. The verb pair to master is 타다 (board / get on) vs 내리다 (get off / alight) — they are opposites and cannot be swapped. On city buses stops are not always announced loudly or at all, so 내릴 때 알려 주세요 to the driver (기사님) or a kind neighbor is genuinely practical. To confirm a specific stop as yours: 여기서 내리면 돼요? The most colloquial variant just before your stop is 내릴게요 — 'I'm getting off!' — said aloud to get people near the door to step aside. Do not confuse 내리다 (exit a vehicle) with 떨어지다 ('to fall/drop') — only 내리다 applies to leaving transit. Keep it polite -요 with strangers and staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에 instead of 서: 어디에 내려요?
Getting off is an action at a location, so it takes 에서/서: 어디서 내려요?, 여기서 내려요. 어디에 내려요 sounds unnatural because 에 marks static existence, not the place where an action occurs.
Mixing up 타다 (get on) and 내리다 (get off).
타다 = board; 내리다 = alight. Saying 어디서 타요? asks where to BOARD, not where to exit. For getting off, always use 내리다: 어디서 내려요?
Saying 떨어져요? to mean 'get off'.
떨어지다 means 'to fall or drop'. To exit a bus or subway, the verb is 내리다: 여기서 내려요. 떨어져요 would imply you physically fall off the vehicle.

structuredNuance.t: 어디서 내려요? = 'at where do I get off?' 내리다 = to get off / alight (from a vehicle). 어디서 = 'at where' (어디 + action-location particle 서). The question locates the action of alighting.

Ask any fellow passenger or the bus driver (기사님). Polite -요 is right with all. On a crowded bus near your stop, the shorter 내릴게요 ('I'm getting off!') is more effective than a question — it announces your action and prompts people to make way.

타다 = get on / board; 내리다 = get off / alight — these are the essential pair. Saying 어디서 타요? asks where to BOARD, not where to exit. 떨어지다 means 'to fall or drop' and cannot replace 내리다 for exiting transit.
어디서 내려요? → 여기서 내리면 돼요? (is here where I get off?), 내릴 때 알려 주세요 (tell me when to get off), 내릴게요 (I'm getting off — announcing, not asking). All share the root 내리다.

The particle must be 에서/서 (action at a place), NOT 에 (static location): 여기서 내려요, not 여기에 내려요. English 'at here' maps to 에서 when an action happens there. Using 에 is the single most common grammatical slip.

expressions.english: Where do I go to transfer?
expressions.shortExplanation: 환승하려면 어디로 가요? is a practical expression meaning "Where do I go to transfer?".
expressions.explanation: "Where do I go to transfer?" — that is 환승하려면 어디로 가요? (hwanseungharyeomyeon eodiro gayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 환승하려면 어디로 가요? ("Where do I go to transfer?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Where do I go to transfer?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the direction to a transfer point inside a station
Checking whether this station offers a transfer connection

usagePhrases.en: I want to transfer to Line 2
usagePhrases.note: Stating the target line before asking or confirming directions
Asking specifically for the 환승 통로 (connecting corridor inside the station)

examples.en: Where do I go to transfer?
examples.note: Ask a station agent or fellow passenger mid-journey; the 로 particle signals you want a direction, not a static location.

examples.en: I want to transfer to Line 3 here — which way do I go?
examples.note: State the target line with -으로, then ask direction; giving the information up front helps the person answer quickly.

examples.ko: A: 버스에서 지하철로 환승하면 할인돼요? / B: 네, 30분 안에 찍으면 할인돼요.
examples.romanization: A: beoseueseo jihacheollo hwanseunghamyeon harindwaeyo? / B: ne, 30bun ane jjigeumyeon harindwaeyo.
examples.en: A: If I transfer from bus to subway, is there a discount? / B: Yes, as long as you tap within 30 minutes.
examples.note: A crucial practical exchange: the 환승 할인 ('transfer discount') depends on tapping the same card within the time window.

expressions.nuance: 환승 is Sino-Korean 換乘 ('change-ride'), the formal system word for switching between transit lines or modes. 환승하려면 어디로 가요? uses the grammar -려면 ('if/in order to intend to') + 어디로 ('toward where', with the direction particle 로) + 가요? — 'in order to transfer, which direction do I go?'. The direction particle 로/으로 is essential: you are asking which way to HEAD, so it must be 어디로 가요?, not 어디에 가요? (static destination). The biggest practical fact unique to Korea's transit system: if you tap your same 교통카드 when switching within roughly 30 minutes, you receive a 환승 할인 (transfer discount) and often pay little or nothing extra for the connection — but ONLY if you tap both in and out with the same card; paying cash or changing cards forfeits the discount entirely. The colloquial native-Korean equivalent is 갈아타다 ('change and board'); both 환승하다 and 갈아타다 are correct, with 환승 sounding slightly more official or system-level and 갈아타다 more conversational. Polite -요 for agents and strangers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Not tapping the card on transfer and losing the discount.
The 환승 할인 only applies if you tap OUT and tap IN with the same 교통카드, within the time limit (roughly 30 minutes). Paying cash or switching to a different card forfeits the free or discounted transfer.
Using 에 instead of 로 for direction: 어디에 가요?
'Where do I go (toward)?' uses the direction particle 로/으로: 어디로 가요? 어디에 가요 marks a static destination and sounds odd when you are asking which way to head inside a busy station.
Thinking only 환승하다 is correct and avoiding 갈아타다.
Both are correct. 갈아타다 ('to change and board') is very natural in colloquial speech: 2호선으로 갈아타요. Do not over-rely on the Sino-Korean 환승 everywhere; 갈아타다 is just as common in conversation.

structuredNuance.t: 환승(換乘) literally 'change-ride'. In practice it means switching subway lines at an interchange station, or moving from bus to subway (or vice versa). The -려면 structure means 'in order to / if you intend to'.

Ask a station agent or look for 환승 signs inside the station. Polite -요 with anyone you ask. 환승 is also used at bus hubs (환승 센터) where you switch between bus routes — the discount rule applies there too.

환승하다 (Sino-Korean, slightly formal/official) and 갈아타다 (native Korean, colloquial) both mean 'to transfer/change'. In everyday speech 갈아타다 is heard more: 2호선으로 갈아타세요. 환승 appears more in signage, apps, and system announcements. Both are always correct.
환승하다 → 환승해요 (transfer), 환승했어요 (I transferred), 환승 통로 (connecting corridor), 환승 할인 (transfer discount), 환승역 (interchange station). 환승 센터 = bus transfer hub.

The direction particle must be 로/으로: 어디로 가요? (which way do I go?). 어디에 가요? marks a static endpoint, not a direction — it sounds slightly off. Also, many English speakers forget to tap out on the bus before tapping in on the subway, losing the 환승 할인 automatically.

expressions.shortExplanation: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I change trains here?".
expressions.explanation: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? (yeogiseo garatamyeon dwaeyo?) = "Do I change trains here?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? ("Do I change trains here?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; confirming this is the correct station to transfer at
반말 — only use this with a close friend you are traveling with
Honorific -셔야 — how station staff or an elder addresses you

usagePhrases.en: Which line do I change to?
usagePhrases.note: Asking which specific line to switch onto — 로/으로 marks the target line

examples.en: Do I change here?
examples.note: Confirming with a passenger at the station before you step off — the -면 돼요? ending asks permission or confirmation of a correct action.

examples.en: You change to Line 4 at Sadang Station.
examples.note: Giving someone else directions: location + line-with-로 + 갈아타면 돼요 is the full informative sentence.

examples.ko: A: 잠실에서 갈아타야 해요? / B: 네, 거기서 2호선으로 갈아타세요.
examples.romanization: A: jamsireseo garataya haeyo? / B: ne, geogiseo 2hoseoneuro garataseyo.
examples.en: A: Do I transfer at Jamsil? / B: Yes, change to Line 2 there.
examples.note: 갈아타야 해요 (question) — 갈아타세요 (polite instruction back) — a real exchange with a helpful local.

expressions.nuance: 갈아타다 is a native Korean compound: 갈아 (from 갈다 'to change/replace') + 타다 ('to ride/board'), literally 'change what you ride'. It is the most commonly spoken word for transferring — more colloquial than the Sino-Korean 환승하다, and exactly what you'll hear from locals and helpful strangers. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? uses the confirmation grammar -면 돼요? ('is it okay if…?'), the standard way to check whether an action is correct. Two particles to get right: the PLACE of transfer takes 에서/서 (여기서, 사당역에서) because the action happens AT that station, and the TARGET LINE takes 로/으로 (4호선으로 갈아타요) because 로 marks the direction or destination you are switching toward. Register: 갈아타면 돼요? (polite -요) for strangers; 갈아타세요 (polite command/suggestion) is what staff give back to you; 갈아타 (반말) only with a friend. An English speaker's typical wrong turn is reaching for 바꾸다 ('to exchange an object') — 기차를 바꿔요 sounds like you want to literally exchange the physical train, which is nonsensical; the correct verb for switching which vehicle you ride is 갈아타다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 바꾸다 to mean 'change trains'.
바꾸다 is 'to exchange/replace an object'. Switching which vehicle you ride is 갈아타다: 여기서 갈아타요. 기차를 바꿔요 wrongly sounds like you are trying to swap the physical train for a different one.
Marking the place with 에 instead of 서: 여기에 갈아타요.
Transferring happens AT a station, so use the action-location particle 에서/서: 여기서 갈아타요, 사당역에서 갈아타요. Static 에 is wrong for the place of an action.
Using the wrong particle for the target line: 4호선에 갈아타요.
The line you switch TO takes the direction/target particle 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타요 ('change to Line 4'). 4호선에 갈아타요 misuses 에 as though it were a destination marker rather than a direction marker.

structuredNuance.t: 갈아타다 = 갈아 (change) + 타다 (ride) = 'to change what you ride'. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? = 'is it okay to change (vehicles) here?' — a polite request for confirmation that this station is the right transfer point.
Ask to any fellow passenger before stepping off. Polite -요 is right with strangers. Staff tell you 갈아타세요 (polite command) or 갈아타셔야 해요 (you must transfer — honorific). With a friend: 여기서 갈아타 (반말).
