contrastPairs.explanation: Same consonant ㅂ, different vowels. ㅗ sits with its tick pointing UP — the vowel shape tells you the sound moves upward/forward in the mouth. ㅜ has its tick pointing DOWN — the sound descends to a deeper 'oo'. The visual and physical direction match.

a.en: ha — open 'a', mouth opens wide

b.en: heo — 'uh', sound pulls back

contrastPairs.explanation: ㅏ and ㅓ look almost the same but the tick faces opposite directions. ㅏ faces right (toward open space) → mouth opens. ㅓ faces left (inward) → the sound retreats to the back of the mouth. This is not coincidence — King Sejong's design mapped physical articulation to visual direction.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: Pronouncing 으 (ㅡ) as 'oo' or 'u' based on romanization 'eu'
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 으 has no English equivalent — it is a central unrounded vowel. Keep your lips flat (no rounding) and the tongue in the middle of the mouth.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: The romanization 'eu' looks like the French 'eu' or English 'uh', so beginners round their lips. But 으 is made with flat, unrounded lips — the opposite of 'oo'. To train this sound: say 'ee' (이) and keep your lips in exactly that flat position, then move your tongue back. The sound you get is 으. Practice 이 then 으 back and forth.

exceptions: ㅢ (의) is technically ㅡ+ㅣ but in natural speech it often sounds like just 이 (ee) or 에 (e) depending on position: 의사 = 'uisa' (doctor) but the particle 의 usually sounds like 에
Vowel length (long vs. short) existed in classical Korean but modern Seoul Korean has largely lost it — beginners can ignore vowel length completely
Some compound vowels like ㅙ (ㅗ+ㅐ) and ㅞ (ㅜ+ㅔ) are rare and sound very similar to ㅘ and ㅝ respectively

exampleSentence.en: Hangul is easy to learn.
exampleSentence.note: Subject marker 은 attaches to 한글 — you will learn this particle in Chapter 2

exampleSentence.en: ㄱ is a consonant.
exampleSentence.note: 이에요 means 'is/am/are' — the simplest Korean copula; perfect for labeling what something is

exampleSentence.en: ㅏ is a vowel.
exampleSentence.note: 는 is the topic marker for vowel-ending words — 모음 ends in ㅁ so it uses 은, but ㅏ alone ends in a vowel, so 는 attaches

exampleSentence.en: What is this character?
exampleSentence.note: 뭐예요 = 'what is it?' — an essential question frame for asking about unfamiliar characters

exampleSentence.en: What is the sound of this character?
exampleSentence.note: 의 is a possessive particle — '글자의 소리' = 'the sound of the character'

exampleSentence.en: 한 has a final consonant.
exampleSentence.note: 있어요 (there is / to have) — the final ㄴ in 한 is the 받침; not all syllables have one

exampleSentence.en: The pronunciation is difficult.
exampleSentence.note: A natural comment to make as a beginner — acknowledges that pronunciation takes practice

exampleSentence.en: I read Hangul.
exampleSentence.note: Polite form 읽어요 — the verb stem 읽 + 어요; note the pronunciation shifts from 'ikda' to 'ilgeoyo' due to consonant assimilation

exampleSentence.en: I write my name.
exampleSentence.note: 쓰다 is ㅡ-irregular: the ㅡ drops before 아/어, giving 써요 not 쓰어요

exampleSentence.en: I listen to the sound.
exampleSentence.note: 듣다 is ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending → 들어요, not 듣어요

exampleSentence.en: I speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: 말하다 → 말해요 in polite form; 천천히 = slowly — essential classroom vocabulary

exampleSentence.en: Please repeat after me.
exampleSentence.note: 따라 하세요 is a polite command — very common in language class settings

exampleSentence.en: Please speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: One of the most useful phrases for a beginner — you will say this constantly in your first weeks of Korean

exampleSentence.en: I listen again.
exampleSentence.note: 다시 comes before the verb it modifies — Korean adverbs do not change form

exampleSentence.en: Yes, I understand.
exampleSentence.note: 알겠어요 literally means 'I will know it' (future-inference form of 알다) but functions as 'I get it now' — use it as a fixed phrase

extendedVocabulary.english: I don't know / I'm not sure

exampleSentence.en: I don't know this character.
exampleSentence.note: The counterpart to 알겠어요 — equally important to have in your first lesson vocabulary

exampleSentence.en: I practice Hangul every day.
exampleSentence.note: 매일 = every day; 연습하다 follows the 하다 verb pattern — 연습 (practice noun) + 하다 (to do)

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon (a Korean tutor) meets Minjun (a complete beginner) for their first online lesson

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 안녕하세요! 저는 지연이에요. 오늘 한글을 공부해요.
lines.romanization: Annyeonghaseyo! Jeoneun jiyeonieyo. Oneul hangeureul gongbuhaeyo.
lines.en: Hello! I'm Jiyeon. Today we study Hangul.
lines.grammarNote: 지연이에요 = 'I am Jiyeon' — the copula 이에요 attaches after a consonant-final name (지연 ends in ㄴ)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Hello. I'm Minjun. Is Hangul difficult?
lines.grammarNote: Rising intonation turns 어려워요 (it's difficult) into a yes/no question — Korean does not need a separate question word for this

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: No, it's easy! Hangul is a sound-based script.
lines.grammarNote: 글자예요 = 'it is a character/script' — 이에요 shortens to 예요 after a vowel-final word (글자 ends in ㅏ vowel)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: What is this? (pointing at ㅏ)
lines.grammarNote: 이게 = 이것이 (this thing + subject marker), contracted; 뭐예요 = 'what is it?' — the most useful question for new learners

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: It's ㅏ. It's a vowel. The sound is 'a'.
lines.grammarNote: Three short sentences in a row — Korean naturally uses short complete sentences instead of one long sentence with relative clauses

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: I see. Please say it again.
lines.grammarNote: 다시 말해 주세요 = V + 아/어 주세요 (please do for me) — the pattern-015 request form; 말하다 → 말해 + 주세요

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 좋아요. 천천히 해요. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ — 기본 모음이에요.
lines.romanization: Joayo. Cheoncheonhi haeyo. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ — gibon moeumieyo.
lines.en: Good. Let's go slowly. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ — these are the basic vowels.
lines.grammarNote: 기본 = basic/fundamental; 이에요 after the consonant-final 음 again — this copula pattern will become automatic

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 따라 할게요. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. 맞아요?
lines.romanization: Ttara halgeyo. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. Majayo?
lines.en: I'll repeat after you. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. Is that right?
lines.grammarNote: 할게요 = 'I will do' (first-person intention); 맞아요? = 'Is that correct?' — essential self-checking question for language learners

readingText.title: 민준의 첫 한글 공부 (Minjun's First Hangul Study)
readingText.body: 오늘 처음으로 한글을 공부했어요. 한글은 자음과 모음으로 만들어요. 자음이 열 개 있어요: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ. 모음도 있어요: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. 이 자음과 모음을 합치면 글자가 돼요. 예를 들어, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한이에요. 처음에는 어려웠지만 이제 조금 읽을 수 있어요. 내일 더 연습할 거예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today I studied Hangul for the first time. Hangul is made of consonants and vowels. There are ten consonants: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ. There are also vowels: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. When you combine these consonants and vowels, you get a character. For example, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한. At first it was difficult, but now I can read a little. I will practice more tomorrow.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How many basic consonants does Minjun list in the diary?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 열 개 (ten) — ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ

comprehensionQuestions.question: What example does the diary give for how a syllable block is made?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한 — a consonant (ㅎ) + a vowel (ㅏ) + a final consonant (ㄴ) combine into one spoken syllable block

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 이에요/예요 copula forms in the text. Why does each one appear, and when does the ending change from 이에요 to 예요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 한이에요 (한 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요), 글자가 돼요 (not a copula, but a change-of-state verb 되다). The rule: 이에요 attaches after a final consonant (받침), 예요 attaches after a vowel. So 한글이에요 (ㄹ final) vs. 모음이에요 (ㅁ final) vs. 한이에요 (ㄴ final) — but if the word ended in a vowel, it would be 예요.

culturalNote.title: 한글날 — The Holiday That Celebrates an Alphabet
culturalNote.body: October 9th is 한글날 (Hangul Day), a national holiday in South Korea celebrating the promulgation of Hangul in 1443 by King Sejong the Great. This makes Korean one of the only languages in the world with a holiday dedicated to its writing system. King Sejong commissioned Hangul because the existing Chinese characters (한자) were so difficult that ordinary people could not read or write — only the elite could. He designed Hangul specifically to be learned quickly by everyone. Historical records say it could be learned 'in a morning' by a wise person and 'in ten days' by a less clever person. Modern linguists consider it one of the most scientifically designed writing systems ever created. When you struggle with a new letter, remember: King Sejong designed it so that you would not have to struggle for long.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which character is the vowel ㅏ (the sound 'a' as in 'father')?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅏ has a vertical stroke with a short tick pointing RIGHT. ㅓ looks similar but the tick points LEFT (that is the 'uh/eo' sound). ㅗ is a horizontal stroke with a tick pointing UP (the 'o' sound). ㅣ is just a vertical bar with no tick (the 'ee' sound). The direction of the tick is the key distinguishing feature.

inlineExercises.prompt: The syllable block 한 is made of which components?
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean syllable blocks follow the order: (1) initial consonant at top-left, (2) vowel to the right or below, (3) optional final consonant at the bottom. So 한 = ㅎ (initial) + ㅏ (vowel, to the right because it is a tall vowel) + ㄴ (final, at the bottom). The other options have the order wrong or use the wrong vowel — ㅓ would give 헌, not 한.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which of these is the SILENT consonant placeholder used when a syllable starts with a vowel sound?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅇ in the onset (initial) position makes no sound — it is a placeholder that allows vowel-initial syllables to have a proper block shape. So 아 is written as ㅇ+ㅏ, not just ㅏ floating alone. ㅎ makes an 'h' sound, ㅅ makes an 's' sound, ㄴ makes an 'n' sound. Only ㅇ is silent at the start of a syllable (though it makes 'ng' at the end).

inlineExercises.prompt: How do you say 'Please speak slowly' in Korean?
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 = slowly, 말해 주세요 = please speak (V + 아/어 주세요 pattern). 다시 들어요 means 'listen again', 알겠어요 means 'I understand', 모르겠어요 means 'I don't know'. The V + 아/어 주세요 pattern (pattern-015) is used for polite requests for someone to perform an action for you.

inlineExercises.prompt: A student writes the romanization 'dasi duteeoyo' for 다시 들어요. What is wrong?
inlineExercises.explanation: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb: the final ㄷ of the stem changes to ㄹ before a vowel ending. So 듣 + 어요 → 들어요, NOT 듣어요. The pronunciation is 'deureoyo', not 'duteeoyo'. This is exactly why learning the actual Hangul matters — romanization based on the dictionary form 듣다 would mislead you. The written form 들어요 shows the actual pronunciation directly.

inlineExercises.prompt: Where does a TALL vowel like ㅏ, ㅓ, or ㅣ appear in a syllable block?
options: To the right of the consonant
inlineExercises.correct: To the right of the consonant
inlineExercises.explanation: Tall vowels (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ, ㅐ, ㅔ and their compounds) sit to the RIGHT of the consonant: 가 (ㄱ+ㅏ), 서 (ㅅ+ㅓ), 시 (ㅅ+ㅣ). Wide vowels (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ) sit BELOW the consonant: 고 (ㄱ+ㅗ), 수 (ㅅ+ㅜ). This layout rule is completely regular — once you know it, you can read any block.

inlineExercises.prompt: What does 알겠어요 most naturally mean in a classroom context?
inlineExercises.explanation: 알겠어요 literally contains 알다 (to know) + 겠 (future/inference marker) + 어요, but it functions as 'I got it / I understand / Okay' in conversation. It is NOT 모르겠어요 (I don't know / I'm not sure), NOT 다시 말해 주세요 (please say it again), NOT 맞아요? (is that right?). Use 알겠어요 to signal to your teacher that you have understood what they just explained.

bullets: Each Hangul syllable is a BLOCK built from: initial consonant + vowel (+ optional final consonant 받침) — read left-to-right, top-to-bottom within the block

MOUTH BLUEPRINTS: consonant shapes sketch the mouth position (ㅁ = closed lips, ㄴ = tongue at ridge, ㅇ = silent/circular). COMPASS ROSE: vowel ticks point in the direction of the mouth movement (ㅏ = right/open, ㅓ = left/back, ㅗ = up, ㅜ = down)
Romanization is a CHECKING TOOL, not Korean spelling — use it to verify your reading, then cover it and practice reading Hangul directly
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 2 introduces your first full sentences using 이다 (to be) and the topic marker 은/는 — you will use the Hangul you just learned to read and write complete Korean sentences like '저는 학생이에요' (I am a student).

chapters.title: Greetings And Self-Introduction
chapters.goal: Greet, thank, apologize, answer yes/no, and introduce your name politely.
chapters.scenario: First class, first meeting, store, or language exchange.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Hello.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Hello. I am Hana.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Nice to meet you.

chapters.guidedPractice: Replace the name in 저는 하나예요 with your own name, then add one greeting and one closing.
chapters.realLifeTask: Introduce yourself in three polite sentences.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 이름이 뭐예요? Learner answers with 저는 ___예요.
chapters.review: Can you greet, say your name, thank someone, and close the conversation politely?

beginnerGuide.title: Why greetings come before grammar
beginnerGuide.body: A beginner needs phrases that work immediately. 안녕하세요, 감사합니다, 죄송합니다, 네, and 아니요 let you participate politely before you can build long sentences.

beginnerGuide.title: Politeness first
beginnerGuide.body: Use polite everyday Korean until the other person clearly uses casual speech with you. This course treats 해요체 and polite chunks as your default safety zone.

beginnerGuide.title: Your first personal sentence
beginnerGuide.body: 저는 ___예요 is not just translation practice. It teaches 은/는 as “as for me,” which becomes the base for many later sentences.

checkpoints: I can greet and thank someone without reading English.
I can say 저는 ___예요 with my own name.
I can choose 감사합니다 when I want to sound safer or more formal.

hook.situation: You walk into your first Korean language exchange. Someone smiles at you and says '안녕하세요!' You want to reply, say your name, and make a good impression — but you freeze because you're not sure whether to say '나는 마이클이에요' or '저는 마이클이에요', and you have no idea where to start. This chapter gives you the exact phrases you need from the very first second.
objectives: Greet, thank, and apologize using the five most essential Korean phrases
Introduce yourself with 저는 ___이에요 / 예요 — the pattern every Korean conversation starts with
Understand why 은/는 is the topic marker and when to use 이에요 vs 예요
hook.whyItMatters: These phrases are not 'beginner drills' — they are the exact sentences Koreans use every day in every context. Getting 저는 ___예요 right from day one sets the foundation for the entire 은/는 system, which appears in hundreds of later sentences. And using 감사합니다 vs 고마워요 correctly shows you understand Korean social register — Koreans notice that instantly.

grammarNotes.title: 은/는 — The Topic Spotlight
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 은/는 as a SPOTLIGHT on a stage. When you attach 은/는 to a noun, you're shining the spotlight on it and saying: 'This is what we're talking about now.' Everything else in the sentence is what you say about that spotlight item. 저는 = 'as for me, the spotlight is on me.' This is subtly different from just saying 'I' — it announces the topic and often implies a quiet contrast ('as for me… others might be different').
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in consonant + 은 / Noun ending in vowel + 는

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: 저 ends in a vowel → 는. The spotlight is on '나/저' (me), and the sentence tells you what that spotlight item IS.

examples.en: The name is Minsu. / My name is Minsu.
examples.note: 이름 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 은. The topic 'name' is spotlit, then identified.

examples.en: Today I'm busy. (As for today, I'm busy.)
examples.note: 오늘 ends in 'l' (consonant) → 은. Spotlighting 'today' implies: 'other days might be fine.'

examples.en: I study Korean.
examples.note: 저는 sets 'me' as the topic — the sentence then tells you what I do.

examples.en: The teacher is kind.
examples.note: 선생님 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 은. The teacher is the spotlight — kindness is what's said about them.

a.en: I am Michael. (topic — 'as for me')

b.en: I am Michael. (subject — identifying who it is)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both translate as 'I am Michael' in English, but they work differently. 저는 sets the topic — you're introducing yourself as the focus. 제가 (이/가 subject marker) points a finger: 'The one who is Michael is me' — used when clarifying or answering 'who?' questions. At this stage, use 저는 for self-introductions.

a.en: I am a student. (general topic statement)

b.en: Today I am a student. (spotlight on 'today', implies other days might be different)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both use 은/는 correctly, but the spotlighted noun changes the meaning. 저는 = 'as for me.' 오늘은 = 'as for today' — implying today is being contrasted with other days.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers often over-translate: 'My name is Michael' → they try to say 'my name' separately. But in Korean, 저는 ___이에요 already means 'As for me, I am ___' — you don't need to add '이름' (name) at all. The structure is: topic (저는) + what it IS (___이에요). Also note: use 저 (polite 'I'), not 나 (casual 'I'), until you know the other person well.

exceptions: 저는 compresses to 전 in fast speech: 전 학생이에요 = 저는 학생이에요
When 은/는 follows particles like 도 (also/too), drop 은/는 and keep 도: say 저도 ('me too'), not 저는도
이름은 in the sense 'my name is' is common but optional — 저는 ___이에요 alone is fully natural for introductions

grammarNotes.title: N이에요 / 예요 — The Polite 'To Be'
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 이에요 / 예요 as a NAMEPLATE. In English, you put a nameplate on a desk to say 'this is John's desk.' In Korean, you attach 이에요 or 예요 to a noun to label it — 'this IS ___.' It is the polite present-tense form of 이다 (to be). The only choice you make is: does the noun end in a consonant? Use 이에요. Does it end in a vowel? Use 예요.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in consonant + 이에요 / Noun ending in vowel + 예요

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: 학생 ends in 'ng' (consonant) → 이에요. The nameplate reads 'student.'

examples.en: I am Hana.
examples.note: 하나 ends in 'a' (vowel) → 예요. The nameplate reads 'Hana.'

examples.en: This is a book.
examples.note: 책 ends in 'k' (consonant) → 이에요. Labeling 'this thing' as a book.

examples.en: I am an office worker.
examples.note: 회사원 ends in 'n' (consonant) → 이에요. Used for job introductions.

examples.en: This person is a teacher.
examples.note: 선생님 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 이에요. Third-person introduction using polite 이분.

a.en: I am a student. (consonant ending: 학생 → 이에요)

b.en: I am a doctor. (vowel ending: 의사 → 예요)

contrastPairs.explanation: The choice between 이에요 and 예요 is purely phonetic — does the noun end in a consonant or a vowel? There is no meaning difference. 학생 ends in 'ng' → 이에요. 의사 ends in 'a' → 예요. Getting this wrong is not a serious error, but getting it right sounds natural.

a.en: I am a student. (polite everyday speech)

b.en: I am a student. (formal / presentation speech)

contrastPairs.explanation: 이에요/예요 is polite and friendly — use it in class, language exchanges, and with new acquaintances. 입니다 is formal speech used in presentations, business meetings, and public announcements. Both are correct, but 이에요/예요 is more natural in daily conversation.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes apply 예요 to everything because it sounds simpler. But the rule is strict: consonant ending → must use 이에요. 학생 ends in 'ng' (받침/final consonant), so 학생예요 is wrong — it creates an awkward sound break. Check the final sound of the noun: if you feel a consonant at the end, attach 이에요.

exceptions: In very fast casual speech, 이에요 after a consonant is sometimes shortened: 학생이에요 → 학생이야 (casual) — but use 이에요 until you're comfortable
이에요 and 예요 are NOT used in negative sentences — the negative is 아니에요 (am not): 저는 학생이 아니에요
The formal equivalent is 입니다 / 이 아닙니다 — you'll hear it in speeches, announcements, and formal writing

exampleSentence.en: Hello. I am Jisu.
exampleSentence.note: 안녕하세요 is always the opener; then your name introduction follows naturally.

exampleSentence.en: Goodbye! See you again!
exampleSentence.note: Said to the person STAYING. The person leaving says 안녕히 가세요 to the one who stays.

exampleSentence.en: Thank you for helping me.
exampleSentence.note: 감사합니다 is the safer, more formal option — use it with strangers, in shops, and in any formal setting.

exampleSentence.en: It's a gift? Thank you so much!
exampleSentence.note: 고마워요 is warmer and more personal than 감사합니다 — great for friends and classmates.

exampleSentence.en: I'm sorry for being late.
exampleSentence.note: 죄송합니다 is the formal apology — use it when you've genuinely caused trouble or in professional/service situations.

exampleSentence.en: Sorry, I'm late.
exampleSentence.note: 미안해요 is the everyday polite apology — less heavy than 죄송합니다, appropriate for friends and classmates.

exampleSentence.en: Yes, I understand.
exampleSentence.note: 네 doesn't only mean 'yes' — it's also used as a listening signal ('I hear you') while someone is talking.

exampleSentence.en: No, I'm not a student.
exampleSentence.note: 아니요 is the polite 'no' — always softer when followed by a short explanation like 괜찮아요 or 몰라요.

exampleSentence.en: I'm Minjun. Nice to meet you!
exampleSentence.note: This is the standard 'nice to meet you' — said after exchanging names for the first time.

exampleSentence.en: One moment, please say that again.
exampleSentence.note: Use 잠시만요 any time you need a pause — at stores, classrooms, or when you haven't heard something clearly.

exampleSentence.en: I am Michael.
exampleSentence.note: 저 is the polite first-person pronoun — always use this until you're on casual terms with the other person.

exampleSentence.en: What is your name?
exampleSentence.note: 이름 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 이에요 when you predicate it: 제 이름은 ___이에요.

exampleSentence.en: I am a Korean language student.
exampleSentence.note: 학생 ends in 'ng' (consonant) → 이에요. One of the most-used identity nouns in self-introductions.

exampleSentence.en: Hello, teacher!
exampleSentence.note: 선생님 is both 'teacher' as a noun and the address form used directly — like calling someone 'Teacher' instead of their name.

exampleSentence.en: How do you do. / I'm meeting you for the first time.
exampleSentence.note: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is a very formal first-meeting phrase. In everyday language exchange settings, 만나서 반가워요 is more natural.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be glad / pleased to meet

exampleSentence.en: I'm so pleased to meet you.
exampleSentence.note: 반갑다 is an adjective meaning 'glad to see/meet someone.' In 해요 speech it becomes 반가워요 — an irregular adjective (ㅂ irregular: 반갑다 → 반가워요).

extendedVocabulary.english: am not / is not / are not

exampleSentence.en: I'm not a student. I'm a teacher.
exampleSentence.note: 아니에요 is the polite negative of 이에요/예요. Notice the pattern: N이/가 아니에요 — the noun takes 이/가 (subject marker), then 아니에요.

extendedDialogue.setting: A Korean language exchange meetup in Seoul. Minjun approaches a newcomer, Emma, who has just arrived.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Hello! Is this your first time here?
lines.grammarNote: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose polite greeting. 처음 오셨어요 = 'Did you come for the first time?' — 처음 (first time) + 오셨어요 (came, honorific past).

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.en: Yes, it's my first time. I'm Emma.
lines.grammarNote: 처음이에요 — 처음 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 이에요. 저는 엠마예요 — 엠마 ends in 'a' (vowel) → 예요. Two 이에요/예요 forms in one turn!

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Nice to meet you! I'm Minjun.
lines.grammarNote: 민준 ends in 'n' (consonant) → 이에요. 만나서 반가워요 is the standard 'nice to meet you' — use it immediately after learning someone's name for the first time.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.ko: 민준 씨, 만나서 반가워요. 한국어를 공부해요?
lines.romanization: Minjun ssi, mannaseo bangawoyo. Hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo?
lines.en: Minjun, nice to meet you. Do you study Korean?
lines.grammarNote: 씨 is a polite name suffix like 'Mr./Ms.' used with the first name — Minjun씨 is natural and friendly. 한국어를 공부해요 = 'Do you study Korean?' — no 은/는 here since the question is about the action.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 아니요, 저는 한국 사람이에요. 영어를 배워요.
lines.romanization: Aniyo, jeoneun hanguk saramieyo. Yeongeo-reul baeoyo.
lines.en: No, I'm Korean. I'm learning English.
lines.grammarNote: 아니요 politely denies the question, then 저는 sets the new topic with 은/는 spotlight. 한국 사람 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 이에요.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.ko: 아, 그래요? 저는 미국 사람이에요. 반갑습니다!
lines.romanization: A, geuraeyo? Jeoneun miguk saramieyo. Bangapseumnida!
lines.en: Oh, really? I'm American. Nice to meet you!
lines.grammarNote: 그래요 = 'Is that so?' — a very useful filler for showing engagement. 미국 사람 ends in 'm' → 이에요. 반갑습니다 = the formal 'nice to meet you' (입니다-style speech).

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: What's your English name?
lines.grammarNote: 이름이 뭐예요 = 'What is the name?' — 이름 takes subject marker 이 here (not topic marker 은). 뭐예요 = 'what is it?' (뭐 = what + 예요). 뭐 ends in a vowel → 예요.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.ko: 엠마예요. 한국 이름은 없어요. 언젠가 만들고 싶어요!
lines.romanization: Emmaeyeyo. Hanguk ireumeun eopsseoyo. Eonjenga mandeulgo sipeoyo!
lines.en: Emma. I don't have a Korean name. I'd like to make one someday!
lines.grammarNote: 엠마예요 — vowel ending → 예요. 한국 이름은 없어요 — 은/는 spotlight on 'Korean name' (contrasting with the English name just mentioned). 없어요 = 'doesn't exist / don't have.'

readingText.title: 첫 언어 교환 후 메시지 (Text messages after the first language exchange)
readingText.body:
민준: 오늘 언어 교환 어땠어요?
엠마: 정말 좋았어요! 저는 한국어가 어렵지만 재미있어요.
민준: 맞아요! 처음은 어려워요. 엠마 씨는 어디에서 왔어요?
엠마: 저는 미국에서 왔어요. 뉴욕이에요.
민준: 아, 그래요? 뉴욕은 멋있는 도시예요!
엠마: 네, 그렇지만 서울도 정말 좋아요. 다음 주에 또 만나요?
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Minjun: How was the language exchange today?
Emma: It was really good! Korean is difficult for me but it's fun.
Minjun: That's right! The beginning is hard. Where are you from, Emma?
Emma: I'm from America. New York.
Minjun: Oh really? New York is a cool city!
Emma: Yes, but Seoul is really nice too. Shall we meet again next week?

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Emma say about Korean in the text exchange?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She says Korean is difficult (어렵지만) but fun (재미있어요).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where is Emma from, and what specific city does she mention?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She is from America (미국에서 왔어요) and mentions New York (뉴욕이에요 — using 이에요 because 뉴욕 ends in 'k', a consonant).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all instances of 이에요/예요 in the text. For each one, explain whether the noun ends in a consonant or vowel and why that determines the form used.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 재미있어요 is an adjective form, not 이에요/예요. 뉴욕이에요 — 뉴욕 ends in 'k' (consonant) → 이에요. 도시예요 — 도시 ends in 'i' (vowel) → 예요. These demonstrate the phonetic rule: consonant final → 이에요, vowel final → 예요, with no difference in meaning.

culturalNote.title: 감사합니다 vs 고마워요 — Reading the Room
culturalNote.body: Both mean 'thank you,' but using the wrong one in the wrong setting is a social signal that Koreans pick up on immediately. 감사합니다 (formal, 입니다-style speech) is what you say to a shop assistant, a server, a stranger who helped you, your boss, or anyone you've just met — it's the safe, respectful default. 고마워요 (polite, 해요-style speech) is warmer and more personal — use it with classmates, language exchange partners, and friends you've started to get comfortable with. As a beginner, you'll never go wrong defaulting to 감사합니다. When someone uses 고마워요 with you, it's a small sign they feel at ease with you — a good thing.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 학생___ (I am a student.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in 'ng' — a final consonant (받침). The rule: consonant-final noun → 이에요. 학생예요 creates an awkward sound break and sounds unnatural. Check the final sound first: if you feel a consonant, attach 이에요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 의사___ (I am a doctor.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 의사 ends in 'a' — a vowel. The rule: vowel-final noun → 예요. 의사이에요 would add an extra syllable that sounds clunky. When the noun ends in a vowel, attach 예요 directly.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '나는 마이클예요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Two errors: (1) 나는 should be 저는 in polite speech — 나 is casual and sounds rude to someone you've just met. (2) 마이클 ends in 'l' (consonant) → must use 이에요, not 예요. Always use 저 until you're on casual terms.

inlineExercises.prompt: Someone asks you 이름이 뭐예요? How do you answer?
inlineExercises.explanation: Option 1 is wrong because 미국 is a country, not a name — this says 'I am America.' Option 3 is wrong because 이름 (name) is unnecessary in the answer — 저는 ___이에요 already communicates 'I am ___' perfectly. Option 2 is the natural, correct structure: topic (저는) + what you are (name + 이에요/예요).

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Nice to meet you. I'm a Korean language teacher.'
inlineExercises.hint: 선생님 ends in 'm' (consonant) — which form of 'to be' do you use? 만나서 반가워요 is the standard 'nice to meet you' phrase.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이름___ 민수예요. (The name is Minsu. / My name is Minsu.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 이름 ends in 'm' — a final consonant. The 은/는 rule mirrors 이에요/예요: consonant final → 은, vowel final → 는. 이름은 spotlights 'name' as the topic of the sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: You bump into someone accidentally and want to apologize. Which do you use in this situation?
inlineExercises.explanation: 감사합니다 means 'thank you' — not an apology. 만나서 반가워요 is 'nice to meet you' — also wrong context. 죄송합니다 is the correct formal apology for causing inconvenience to a stranger. In casual situations with friends, 미안해요 would also work, but 죄송합니다 is the safe formal choice in public.

bullets: 은/는 = SPOTLIGHT: attach to the topic noun to say 'as for ___' — 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel (학생은, 저는)
이에요/예요 = NAMEPLATE: polite 'to be' — 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel (학생이에요, 의사예요)
감사합니다 (formal) vs 고마워요 (warm/friendly) — same meaning, different register; default to 감사합니다 until you read the room
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 3 introduces numbers — both the Korean native system (하나, 둘, 셋) and the Sino-Korean system (일, 이, 삼). You'll need both to count things, tell time, and talk about age.

chapters.title: Noun Sentences: N이에요/예요 And 은/는
chapters.goal: Say what something is and set the topic with 은/는.
chapters.scenario: Names, jobs, places, and basic identity.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What is this?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: This is a menu.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: I am a student.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three N이에요/예요 sentences: your name, your role, and one object.
chapters.realLifeTask: Point to two things around you and say what they are.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend points to an object. Learner asks 이건 뭐예요? and repeats the answer.
chapters.review: Can you choose 이에요 vs 예요 and use 저는 naturally?

beginnerGuide.title: The first sentence engine
beginnerGuide.body: N이에요/예요 lets you say what something is. This is the noun-sentence engine for names, jobs, objects, places, and simple identity.

beginnerGuide.title: Topic marker in plain English
beginnerGuide.body: 은/는 marks what we are talking about. In 저는 학생이에요, Korean first says “as for me,” then gives the information.

beginnerGuide.title: Do not over-translate particles
beginnerGuide.body: Particles often do not become separate English words. Learn the Korean frame and the sentence job, not a one-word English translation.

checkpoints: I can choose 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.
I can ask 이건 뭐예요?
I can explain 은/는 as topic or contrast.

hook.situation: You're at a restaurant in Seoul and the waiter hands you something. You want to ask 'What is this?' and then introduce yourself to the Korean couple at the next table. You know a few Korean words — but how do you actually build a sentence that says what something IS? This chapter gives you the most powerful two-word engine in Korean.
objectives: Use 이에요 after a noun ending in a consonant and 예요 after a noun ending in a vowel
Ask 이건 뭐예요? (What is this?) and answer with N이에요/예요
Use 은/는 to set the topic of a sentence, including the contrast meaning
hook.whyItMatters: N이에요/예요 is the 'is' of Korean — it builds every sentence that identifies, names, or defines something. You will use it within the first minute of any real Korean conversation. And 은/는 is not just grammar: it is how Korean tells the listener what the sentence is about. Miss this and your Korean sounds like a word list. Master it and your sentences feel complete.

grammarNotes.title: N이에요/예요 — The 'Is' of Korean
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 이에요/예요 as a LABEL MAKER. You pick up any noun, press the button, and out comes a sticker that reads: '[noun] is.' The only choice is which sticker roll to load: the 이에요 roll (for nouns that end with a final consonant — they need the 이 connector) or the 예요 roll (for nouns ending in a vowel — they attach directly). One machine, two rolls, infinite labels.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in consonant (받침) + 이에요 / Noun ending in vowel + 예요

examples.en: This is a menu.
examples.note: 메뉴 ends in the vowel ㅜ → use 예요 (no connector needed)

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: 학생 ends in the consonant ㅇ (받침) → use 이에요 (이 acts as connector between the consonant and 에요)

examples.en: This is coffee.
examples.note: 커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ → 예요 attaches directly

examples.en: I am a teacher.
examples.note: 선생님 ends in 받침 ㅁ → 이에요; the 이 bridges the final consonant to 에요

examples.en: This is a map.
examples.note: 지도 ends in vowel ㅗ → 예요; no bridging consonant needed

a.en: This is bread.

b.en: This is coffee.

contrastPairs.explanation: 빵 ends in the final consonant ㅇ (받침) → 이에요. 커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ → 예요. Same structure, same meaning — only the connector changes based on what the noun ends in.

a.en: I am a student.

b.en: I am a doctor.

contrastPairs.explanation: 학생 ends in consonant 받침 → 이에요. 의사 ends in vowel → 예요. Always check the very last letter of the noun — not the last syllable block.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes want to use 예요 everywhere because it sounds simpler and more natural to say. But 예요 can only follow a vowel. 학생 ends in the final consonant ㅇ, so it absolutely requires 이에요. Saying 학생예요 creates a consonant clash that sounds wrong to every Korean ear — like saying 'I is a student' in English.

exceptions: 이에요 and 예요 are the polite present tense forms. The plain/intimate form is 이야/야 — you will hear 학생이야 between close friends.
The question form is identical — just add a rising intonation: 학생이에요? = Are you a student?
이에요 and 예요 cannot be used for adjectives or verbs — only for noun sentences. 'I am hungry' is NOT 배고프예요 — that requires a different ending covered in a later chapter.

grammarNotes.title: 은/는 — The Topic Marker
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 은/는 as a SPOTLIGHT on a stage. When you put 은/는 after a word, you shine the spotlight directly on it and say to the audience: 'This is what we are talking about right now.' Everything else in the sentence is what you say about that spotlit topic. The rule for which to use mirrors the label maker: 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in consonant (받침) + 은 / Noun ending in vowel + 는

examples.en: I am American. (As for me, I am American.)
examples.note: 저 ends in vowel ㅓ → 는; 는 spotlights 저 (me) as the topic of the whole sentence

examples.en: This (thing) is a book.
examples.note: 이건 is 이것 + 은 contracted → 은 marks 이것 as the topic; ends in consonant ㅅ → 은

examples.ko: 저는 서울 사람이 아니에요. 부산 사람이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun seoul sarami anieyo. busan saramieyo.
examples.en: I am not from Seoul. I am from Busan.
examples.note: 는 here carries a contrast meaning: 'As for ME (not someone else)' — 은/는 often implies 'but others may differ'

examples.en: As for your name, what is it? (What is your name?)
examples.note: 이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → 은; spotlighting 이름 (name) as the topic of the question

examples.en: Korean (as a topic) is interesting.
examples.note: 한국어 ends in vowel ㅓ → 는; the speaker is setting Korean as the topic and commenting on it

a.en: I am a student. (topic: me)

b.en: I am also a student. (also: me too)

contrastPairs.explanation: 은/는 sets the topic. 도 means 'also/too.' They are not interchangeable — 저는 introduces me as the topic of conversation; 저도 adds me to a list already mentioned.

a.en: Coffee, I like. / As for coffee, it's good.

b.en: Coffee is good. (coffee is the one that is good)

contrastPairs.explanation: 은/는 marks the topic (what we are talking about). 이/가 marks the subject (the grammatical actor). With 은/는 there is often a contrast or emphasis feel — 'coffee in particular.' With 이/가 it is a neutral statement of fact. This distinction is covered more deeply in Chapter 4.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes try to stack words in English word order: subject first, then 이에요 attached to the subject, then the noun. In Korean the topic marker 은/는 must come immediately after the topic noun, and 이에요/예요 comes at the very END of the sentence — always. Korean sentences consistently end with the verb or copula, never in the middle.

exceptions: 은/는 can replace the subject particle 이/가 or the object particle 을/를 when you want to topicalize that noun: 밥은 먹었어요 (As for rice, I ate it) — 밥 is the object but it is topicalized with 은
은/는 carries a subtle contrast: '저는 학생이에요' implies 'as for me (others may differ).' In a first introduction this contrast is mild, but be aware it exists.
이건 (이것은, contraction) and 그건 (그것은) are very common contracted topic forms — these sound more natural than the full form in speech

exampleSentence.en: I study Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 저 ends in vowel → 는; use 저 with strangers and elders, 나 with close friends

exampleSentence.en: What is your name?
exampleSentence.note: 이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → topic marker 은; 뭐예요? = What is it? (뭐 ends in vowel → 예요)

exampleSentence.en: I am a university student.
exampleSentence.note: 대학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요; 대학 (university) + 학생 (student)

exampleSentence.en: I am an English teacher.
exampleSentence.note: 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; 님 is a respectful suffix — never drop it when addressing a teacher

exampleSentence.en: My friend is a doctor.
exampleSentence.note: 의사 ends in vowel ㅏ → 예요; 제 is the possessive form of 저 (my)

exampleSentence.en: I am an office worker.
exampleSentence.note: 회사원 ends in consonant 받침 ㄴ → 이에요; 회사(company) + 원(member/worker)

exampleSentence.en: What country are you from?
exampleSentence.note: 나라 ends in vowel ㅏ → would take 예요 when used as the sentence topic; 어느 = which

exampleSentence.en: I am Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; [country] + 사람 is the standard pattern for nationality

exampleSentence.en: What is this?
exampleSentence.note: 이건 = 이것 + 은 (contracted); 이것 = this thing, 은 = topic marker; used constantly in real speech — more natural than 이것은

exampleSentence.en: What is your name?
exampleSentence.note: 뭐 ends in vowel → 예요; 뭐 is the spoken/colloquial form of 무엇 (what)

exampleSentence.en: I am not Japanese.
exampleSentence.note: 아니에요 is the negative of 이에요/예요; the noun before it takes 이/가 (subject marker): 일본 사람이 아니에요

exampleSentence.en: My name is Minsu.
exampleSentence.note: 제 is the possessive form of 저 (polite 'I'); 내 is the possessive of 나 (casual 'I') — use 제 in formal/polite situations

exampleSentence.en: What is your job?
exampleSentence.note: 직업 ends in consonant 받침 ㅂ → if the answer uses it as topic: 직업은; as subject in the question: 직업이

exampleSentence.en: This is Korean (the language).
exampleSentence.note: 한국어 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요; 한국(Korea) + 어(language); 한국말 is the more colloquial alternative

exampleSentence.en: I am an English teacher.
exampleSentence.note: 영어 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요 when used as the main predicate; 영(England/England's) + 어(language)

exampleSentence.en: I'm Minjun. Nice to meet you!
exampleSentence.note: 반갑습니다 is formal; 반가워요 is slightly less formal — both are appropriate when meeting someone for the first time

exampleSentence.en: Which country are you from?
exampleSentence.note: 어느 is a modifier — it must be followed by a noun; unlike 어디 (where), 어느 modifies a noun directly

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon, a Korean office worker, meets Minho, a new foreign colleague, in the break room on his first day

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Hello! I'm Jiyeon. Nice to meet you for the first time.
lines.grammarNote: 저는 — 저 ends in vowel → 는; 지연이에요 — 지연 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: Hello! I'm Minho. I'm glad to meet you too.
lines.grammarNote: 민호예요 — 민호 ends in vowel ㅗ → 예요; 저도 — 도 means 'also/too,' not a topic marker

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Minho, what country are you from?
lines.grammarNote: 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; the question has the same form as the statement — only intonation changes

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I'm Australian. I came from Sydney.
lines.grammarNote: 호주 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; 시드니에서 왔어요 uses 에서 (from) — covered in Chapter 6

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Oh, really? What is your job?
lines.grammarNote: 직업이 뭐예요? — 직업 takes subject marker 이 here (not topic marker 은); 뭐 ends in vowel → 예요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I'm a designer. What about you, Jiyeon?
lines.grammarNote: 디자이너예요 — 디자이너 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요; 씨는요? — 는 is the topic marker + 요 means 'and you?' — a natural way to return a question

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.romanization: Jeoneun hoesawon-ieyo. I hoesaeseo samnyeon ilhaesseoyo.
lines.en: I'm an office worker. I've worked at this company for three years.
lines.grammarNote: 회사원이에요 — 회사원 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요; 에서 for location of action covered in Chapter 6

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: This is my business card. Please take good care of me! (I look forward to working with you!)
lines.grammarNote: 이건 = 이것 + 은 (contraction); 명함이에요 — 명함 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; 잘 부탁드려요 is a key set phrase for first meetings

readingText.title: 새 친구 소개 (Introducing a New Friend)
readingText.body: 엄마, 저 오늘 새 친구 생겼어요! 이름은 지수예요. 지수는 대학생이에요. 우리 학교 학생이에요. 지수 씨는 제주도 사람이에요. 저는 서울 사람이에요. 지수 씨는 영어 선생님이 꿈이에요. 정말 좋은 사람이에요!
readingText.bodyTranslation: Mom, I made a new friend today! Her name is Jisu. Jisu is a university student. She's a student at our school. Jisu is from Jeju Island. I am from Seoul. Jisu's dream is to be an English teacher. She is a really good person!

comprehensionQuestions.question: What is the new friend's name and where is she from?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 이름은 지수예요 (Her name is Jisu). 제주도 사람이에요 (She is from Jeju Island).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What is Jisu's dream job?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 영어 선생님이 꿈이에요 (Her dream is to be an English teacher). 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 이에요/예요 forms in the text. For each one, explain why 이에요 or 예요 was chosen based on the noun it follows.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 지수예요 — 지수 ends in vowel ㅜ → 예요. 대학생이에요 — 대학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요. 학생이에요 — 학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요. 제주도 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 서울 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 꿈이에요 — 꿈 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 좋은 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

culturalNote.title: 명함 (Meongham) — Business Cards and First Meetings in Korea
culturalNote.body: When meeting someone in a Korean professional or semi-formal context, business cards (명함) are exchanged with both hands or with one hand supported by the other at the wrist — never one-handed or casually tossed. You receive the card with both hands, read it, and then place it respectfully on the table in front of you (never stuff it straight into a pocket). The exchange is usually accompanied by 잘 부탁드려요, which literally means 'I humbly ask for your care' but functions like 'I look forward to working with you.' Even social introductions follow a similar rhythm: name, hometown, and job are the first three pieces of information Koreans typically share. Knowing 저는 [name]이에요/예요 and 저는 [place] 사람이에요 will carry you through the first five minutes of almost any Korean introduction.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 학생___요. (I am a student.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in the final consonant ㅇ (받침). After a consonant, you must use 이에요 — the 이 acts as a phonetic bridge between the consonant and 에요. 예요 can only follow a vowel-ending noun, so 학생예요 is wrong.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이건 커피___요. (This is coffee.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ. After a vowel, 예요 attaches directly without any connector. If you chose 이에요, the 이 would create an awkward extra syllable — 커피이에요 — which sounds unnatural.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저___ 민준이에요. (I am Minjun.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 저 ends in the vowel ㅓ. After a vowel, the topic marker is 는. 은 is only used after a final consonant (받침). This is the same vowel/consonant rule as 이에요/예요 — one consistent rule governs both.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는 의사이에요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 의사 ends in the vowel ㅏ. After a vowel, you must use 예요, not 이에요. 의사이에요 sounds like adding an extra unnecessary syllable — 이 is only the bridge needed after a consonant. Correct: 저는 의사예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'What is your name?'
inlineExercises.hint: 이름 (name) + subject marker 이 + 뭐 (what) + 예요 (is). 뭐 ends in a vowel — which ending does that require?

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I am not Japanese.' Which sentence is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: The correct negative form is [noun] + 이/가 아니에요. 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → subject marker 이 before 아니에요. The first option wrongly combines 이에요 and 아니에요. The third option drops the required 이/가 before 아니에요, which sounds incomplete to Korean ears.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이___ 뭐예요? (What is this?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 이건 is the contracted form of 이것 + 은 (이것은 → 이건). This is how native speakers actually say it — 이것은 뭐예요? is grammatically correct but sounds stiff. 이는 is not a standard form. The contraction 이건 is what you will hear in real conversation every time.

bullets: LABEL MAKER rule: consonant-ending noun + 이에요, vowel-ending noun + 예요 — check the very last letter of the noun
SPOTLIGHT rule: 은/는 marks what you're talking about (topic); consonant → 은, vowel → 는; 이건 (이것은) is the contraction you'll use most
Negative: [noun]이/가 아니에요 — the 이/가 before 아니에요 is required and beginners often drop it
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Chapter 4 introduces 있어요 and 없어요 — how to say something exists or you have it. You'll also meet 이/가, the subject marker, and start to see how it differs from 은/는. The 있다 vs. 없다 pair unlocks dozens of daily sentences immediately.

chapters.title: Existence And Possession: 있어요/없어요 And 이/가
chapters.goal: Say what exists, what you have, and what is missing.
chapters.scenario: Reservations, time, money, bathrooms, and problems.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Do you have time?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes, I have time.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: There is no problem.

chapters.guidedPractice: Practice 시간이 있어요, 시간이 없어요, 예약이 있어요, 예약이 없어요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask if there is a bathroom or reservation, then answer yes/no.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 시간이 있어요? Learner answers with 있어요 or 없어요 and one reason.
chapters.review: Can you use 이/가 with 있어요 and 없어요?

beginnerGuide.title: Existence covers more than “there is”
beginnerGuide.body: 있어요 and 없어요 also mean “I have” and “I do not have.” 시간이 있어요 can mean “there is time” or “I have time.”

beginnerGuide.title: Why 이/가 appears here
beginnerGuide.body: The thing that exists, does not exist, hurts, or appears is usually marked with 이/가: 시간이 있어요, 문제가 없어요, 머리가 아파요.

beginnerGuide.title: Survival value
beginnerGuide.body: This chapter gives you high-frequency travel and daily phrases: 예약이 있어요, 시간이 없어요, 화장실이 있어요?

checkpoints: I can say I have time and I do not have time.
I can ask whether something exists with 있어요?
I do not use 을/를 for the thing that exists.

hook.situation: You arrive at a restaurant in Seoul. The host asks '예약이 있으세요?' (Do you have a reservation?) — you freeze. You know 있어요 means something like 'there is' or 'have', but why does 예약이 have that 이 on it? And how do you say you DON'T have one? This chapter gives you the two sentences that unlock dozens of real situations.
objectives: Use 있어요 and 없어요 to express existence ('there is / there isn't') and possession ('I have / I don't have')
Attach the subject particle 이/가 correctly to the noun that exists or is possessed
Avoid the #1 beginner error: using 을/를 (object marker) instead of 이/가 with 있어요/없어요
hook.whyItMatters: 있어요 and 없어요 are two of the most-used words in Korean. They cover 'is there a bathroom?', 'do you have time?', 'no problem', 'no money' — the building blocks of travel, small talk, and daily life. The subject particle 이/가 that comes with them is equally essential: nearly every Korean sentence uses it. Master these now and half of Chapter 5 and 6 becomes review.

grammarNotes.title: 있어요 / 없어요 — Existence and Possession
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 있어요 as a PRESENCE LAMP and 없어요 as the lamp being OFF. The noun before 이/가 is the thing you're checking: is the lamp on or off for this noun? 시간이 있어요 — is time present? Lamp ON. 시간이 없어요 — lamp OFF. One switch, two possible states, any noun you like.
grammarNotes.formation:
[Noun]이/가 있어요 → [Noun] exists / I have [Noun]
[Noun]이/가 없어요 → [Noun] doesn't exist / I don't have [Noun]

이 after a final consonant (시간이, 문제가 → wait, 문제 ends in a vowel so → 문제가)
가 after a final vowel (친구가, 예약이 → 예약 ends in ㄱ so → 예약이)

examples.en: Do you have time?
examples.note: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → subject particle 이. The question asks if the 'presence lamp' for time is on.

examples.en: I have a reservation.
examples.note: 예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → particle 이. This sentence doubles as 'there is a reservation' depending on context.

examples.en: I don't have money.
examples.note: 돈 ends in consonant ㄴ → particle 이. Lamp is OFF for money.

examples.en: There is no problem.
examples.note: 문제 ends in vowel 에 → particle 가. A very natural reassurance phrase.

examples.en: Is there a bathroom?
examples.note: 화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → particle 이. One of the most essential travel questions.

a.en: I have time. (lamp ON)

b.en: I don't have time. (lamp OFF)

contrastPairs.explanation: The noun (시간이) and particle stay exactly the same — only the verb flips between 있어요 (present) and 없어요 (absent). Swapping the verb is all you need to move from yes to no.

a.en: I have a reservation.

b.en: I don't have a reservation.

contrastPairs.explanation: Same structure, same particle 이, opposite meaning. At a hotel or restaurant you'll use both — the first when you've planned ahead, the second when you're hoping for a walk-in.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In English 'I have time' uses 'have' as a transitive verb with an object ('time'), so learners instinctively reach for the object marker 을/를. But 있어요 is NOT a transitive verb in Korean — it means 'exists' or 'is present.' The noun is the SUBJECT of existence, so it takes the subject particle 이/가. Never pair 있어요 or 없어요 with 을/를.

exceptions: 있다 can also mean 'to stay' or 'to remain' (as an action): 잠깐 있어요 — 'stay for a moment.' In that case no 이/가 is needed because there's no subject noun for existence.
In colloquial speech the subject 이/가 is often dropped when context is clear: '있어요?' (Do you have it?) with no noun is natural when the topic has already been mentioned.
제가 (not 저가) is the irregular form of 저 + 가: 제가 없어요 (I don't have it). This is the one common irregular with 가.

grammarNotes.title: 이 / 가 — The Subject Particle
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 이/가 as a SPOTLIGHT. It shines directly on one noun and says: 'This specific thing — right here — is the one that exists, hurts, appears, or matters right now.' When the spotlight hits a word, 이/가 is attached. 이 goes after a dark (consonant-ending) sound; 가 goes after a bright (vowel-ending) sound.
grammarNotes.formation:
Noun ending in consonant + 이: 시간이, 화장실이, 예약이
Noun ending in vowel + 가: 친구가, 문제가, 커피가

Special: 나 → 내가, 저 → 제가 (irregular, must be memorized)

examples.en: I have a friend. / A friend is here.
examples.note: 친구 ends in vowel 구 → particle 가. The spotlight is on 친구 — that's the thing that exists.

examples.en: My head hurts.
examples.note: 머리 ends in vowel 리 → particle 가. The spotlight is on 머리 as the thing experiencing pain.

examples.en: Who came?
examples.note: 누구 + 가 = 누가 (contracted). The spotlight asks: which person specifically appeared?

examples.en: I study Korean.
examples.note: 저 + 가 = 제가 (irregular). Spotlight on 'I' as the subject — used when introducing yourself or clarifying who does the action.

examples.en: It's raining. (Rain is coming.)
examples.note: 비 ends in vowel → 가. 비가 와요 is a set phrase — the spotlight identifies rain as the thing arriving.

a.en: As for me, I'm a student. (topic — background info)

b.en: I am the student. (subject — specific, important)

contrastPairs.explanation: 은/는 sets the topic — it's like a soft background frame. 이/가 puts a spotlight on the noun — it's highlighting or specifying. When answering '누가 학생이에요?' (Who is the student?), you must say 제가 학생이에요, not 저는.

a.en: Coffee is good. (general opinion about coffee as a topic)

b.en: I like coffee. / Coffee is the good thing. (spotlight on coffee as the object of liking)

contrastPairs.explanation: 좋아요 (to like, to be good) uses 이/가 for the thing liked: N이/가 좋아요. Using 은/는 instead shifts it to a general statement about a topic. Both are grammatically possible but carry subtly different meaning.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 저 (polite 'I') contracts with 가 to form 제가 — this is an irregular form that must be memorized. Saying 저가 is not natural Korean. Similarly, 나 + 가 = 내가 in casual speech. These two pronouns are the only common irregulars with 이/가.

exceptions: 나 → 내가 (casual I + subject), 저 → 제가 (polite I + subject) — both are contractions, not the regular rule
누구 → 누가 when asking 'who' as a subject: 누가 왔어요? (not 누구가)
이/가 is often omitted in casual speech when the subject is obvious from context — this is normal and natural, not a mistake

exampleSentence.en: Do you have time right now?
exampleSentence.note: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → 시간이. The presence lamp: is time available?

exampleSentence.en: Do you have a reservation?
exampleSentence.note: 예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → 예약이. Essential phrase at hotels and restaurants.

exampleSentence.en: I don't have money right now.
exampleSentence.note: 돈 ends in consonant ㄴ → 돈이. A survival phrase for daily life.

exampleSentence.en: There is no problem.
exampleSentence.note: 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 문제가. A very common reassurance phrase.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a bathroom here?
exampleSentence.note: 화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → 화장실이. One of the most important travel questions.

exampleSentence.en: My friend is here.
exampleSentence.note: 친구 ends in vowel 구 → 친구가. Spotlight on the friend as the one who exists/is present.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a vacant room?
exampleSentence.note: 방 ends in consonant ㅇ → 방이. Essential hotel check-in phrase.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a seat available?
exampleSentence.note: 자리 ends in vowel 리 → 자리가. Used at restaurants, cafés, cinemas.

exampleSentence.en: There is no water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 물이. Works for 'there is no water' or 'I don't have water.'

exampleSentence.en: Are you free tomorrow?
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있다 is the go-to way to ask if someone is available — more natural than direct schedule questions.

collocations: 시간이 있을 때 (when you have time)

exampleSentence.en: There is milk in the fridge.
exampleSentence.note: 있어요 checks the presence lamp: is milk in the fridge? Yes. Note 에 for the location and 이/가 for the thing that exists.

collocations: N에 있어요 (something IS at a place)

exampleSentence.en: I don't have time today.
exampleSentence.note: 없어요 is the lamp-OFF version. 오늘은 sets the time as topic with 은/는; 시간이 is the subject of non-existence.

exampleSentence.en: There are a lot of people today.
exampleSentence.note: 사람이 많아요 uses 이/가 — the spotlight is on 사람 as the thing that is plentiful. 많다 often pairs with 이/가.

exampleSentence.en: I made a restaurant reservation.
exampleSentence.note: When 예약 is used as a verb (예약하다), the restaurant is the object → 을/를. Compare: 예약이 있어요 (the reservation exists → 이/가).

extendedVocabulary.english: to hurt / be sick / be in pain

exampleSentence.en: My stomach hurts.
exampleSentence.note: 배 ends in vowel 배 → 배가. The body part that hurts takes 이/가 — this is a core pattern for describing symptoms.

exampleSentence.en: I like coffee. / Coffee is good.
exampleSentence.note: In the 'I like X' pattern, X takes 이/가, not 을/를. The spotlight (이/가) is on the thing liked, not the object of an action.

extendedDialogue.setting: Minji and Junho are checking in at a hotel in Busan

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Welcome. Do you have a reservation?
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있으세요? — 예약 ends in ㄱ → 이. 있으세요 is the honorific form of 있어요, used to a customer.

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: Yes, I have a reservation. I booked it under Minji.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있어요 — presence lamp ON for the reservation. 민지로 = 'under (the name) Minji' (로 = direction/means).

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Just a moment... I'm sorry, there is no reservation.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 없어요 — same noun + particle, opposite verb. Lamp OFF. The contrast shows how the same frame flips with 있어요/없어요.

lines.speaker: 준호
lines.en: Hey, there's a problem! I definitely made a reservation.
lines.grammarNote: 문제가 있어요 — 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 가. Notice 문제가 있어요 (there IS a problem) vs. 문제가 없어요 (no problem).

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 다시 확인할게요. 혹시 빈 방이 있어요.
lines.romanization: Dasi hwaginhalgeyo. Hoksi bin bangi isseoyo.
lines.en: Let me check again. There is a vacant room available.
lines.grammarNote: 방이 있어요 — 방 ends in consonant ㅇ → 이. 빈 방 = vacant room (빈 is an adjective modifying 방).

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: Really? Is there space?
lines.grammarNote: 자리가 있어요 — 자리 ends in vowel 리 → 가. Here 자리 means 'spot/room available' in a broader sense.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.romanization: Ne, i-cheunge bangi isseoyo. Munjega eopseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, there's a room on the 2nd floor. No problem.
lines.grammarNote: 방이 있어요 (room exists → 이/가) + 에 for location on the floor. 문제가 없어요 = classic reassurance phrase.

lines.speaker: 준호
lines.en: Thank you! And is there a bathroom?
lines.grammarNote: 화장실이 있어요? — 화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → 이. The question form of 있어요 is simply 있어요 with rising intonation.

readingText.title: 호텔 예약 문자 (Hotel Booking Text Exchange)
readingText.body:
유나: 오빠, 내일 시간이 있어요?
준서: 네, 시간이 있어요. 왜요?
유나: 부산에 같이 가요! 호텔 예약이 있어요?
준서: 아직 예약이 없어요. 지금 바로 예약할게요.
유나: 빈 방이 있어요?
준서: 네, 바다 뷰 방이 있어요. 문제가 없어요!
유나: 완전 좋아요! 돈이 있어요?
준서: 네, 돈이 있어요. 걱정하지 마세요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Yuna: Oppa, do you have time tomorrow?
Junseo: Yes, I have time. Why?
Yuna: Let's go to Busan together! Do you have a hotel reservation?
Junseo: Not yet, there's no reservation. I'll book it right now.
Yuna: Is there a vacant room?
Junseo: Yes, there's a room with an ocean view. No problem!
Yuna: That's great! Do you have money?
Junseo: Yes, I have money. Don't worry.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Does Junseo already have a hotel reservation when the conversation starts?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: No. He says 아직 예약이 없어요 (Not yet, there is no reservation). He books one during the conversation.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What kind of room does Junseo find?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바다 뷰 방 — a room with an ocean view.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 이/가 있어요 or 이/가 없어요 in the text. For each, identify the noun, explain why 이 or 가 was chosen, and state whether it expresses existence or possession.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1) 시간이 있어요 (×2) — 시간 ends in ㄴ → 이; possession (I have time). 2) 예약이 있어요 — 예약 ends in ㄱ → 이; possession (has a reservation). 3) 예약이 없어요 — same noun + particle, reversed meaning; absence. 4) 방이 있어요 — 방 ends in ㅇ → 이; existence (a room exists). 5) 문제가 없어요 — 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 가; absence (no problem). 6) 돈이 있어요 — 돈 ends in ㄴ → 이; possession (has money). Pattern: every time, the particle choice follows the consonant/vowel rule — not the meaning.

culturalNote.title: 문제가 없어요 — The Korean 'No Problem'
culturalNote.body: You'll hear 문제가 없어요 constantly in Korean service situations — at hotels, restaurants, customer service lines, and repair shops. It functions just like 'no problem' or 'all good' in English, and it always brings a sense of relief. The reverse, 문제가 있어요, is softer than it sounds: Koreans tend to say it matter-of-factly rather than dramatically. A related phrase you'll encounter is 괜찮아요 (it's okay / I'm fine), which overlaps in meaning. But when a Korean staff member says 문제가 없어요 after checking something for you, you can relax — that's their professional 'everything checks out.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 시간___ 있어요? (Do you have time?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → subject particle 이. You cannot use 을 (object marker) with 있어요 — that is the most common beginner mistake. 가 would be wrong here because 가 attaches after vowels only.

inlineExercises.prompt: 문제___ 없어요. (There is no problem.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 문제 ends in vowel 에 → subject particle 가. 이 would be wrong because 이 only follows consonant-final nouns. 를 (object marker) is never used with 없어요 — absence is not an action performed on an object.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '예약을 없어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 없어요 means 'does not exist / do not have' — the noun is the SUBJECT of non-existence, so it needs the subject particle 이/가, not the object marker 을/를. 예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → 예약이.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Is there a bathroom here?'
inlineExercises.hint: 화장실 ends in a consonant. Which particle follows a consonant-final noun? The question form of 있어요 uses rising intonation — the word order stays the same.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I like coffee.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아요 (to be good/to like) uses 이/가, not 을/를. The thing you like is the subject of being-good, so it takes the subject spotlight particle 이/가. 커피를 좋아요 is ungrammatical. 커피는 좋아요 is possible but shifts meaning to a general topic statement ('Coffee, in general, is good') rather than expressing personal preference.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배___ 아파요. (My stomach hurts.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 배 ends in vowel 배 → particle 가. The body part that hurts takes 이/가 in Korean — this is the same spotlight pattern as with 있어요/없어요. Never use 을 for a body part with 아프다.

inlineExercises.prompt: The hotel receptionist has found your reservation. Which sentence would they say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 예약이 있어요 — reservation exists → lamp ON → correct. 예약이 없어요 is the opposite (no reservation found). 예약을 있어요 is ungrammatical — 있어요 can never take 을/를.

bullets: PRESENCE LAMP: 있어요 = lamp ON (exists / have), 없어요 = lamp OFF (doesn't exist / don't have)
SPOTLIGHT particle 이/가: attaches to the noun that exists — 이 after consonant (시간이, 예약이), 가 after vowel (문제가, 친구가)
Never use 을/를 with 있어요 or 없어요 — the thing that exists is a SUBJECT, not an object
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 5 introduces daily action verbs and 을/를 (object markers) — now you'll finally get to use 을/를, but with action verbs like 먹다 and 마시다, not with 있어요/없어요.

chapters.title: Daily Actions: Present Tense And 을/를
chapters.goal: Say what you do every day and what object receives the action.
chapters.scenario: Meals, study, work, reading, writing, and daily routine.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Do you eat breakfast?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes, I eat breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: I study Korean.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three present-tense sentences with 을/를, then make one negative sentence.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say three things you do today and one thing you do not do.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 뭐 해요? Learner answers with one object sentence.
chapters.review: Can you use 먹어요, 마셔요, 공부해요, and 안 해요 naturally?

beginnerGuide.title: From words to actions
beginnerGuide.body: This chapter turns verbs into simple sentences: 밥을 먹어요, 커피를 마셔요, 한국어를 공부해요. The object marker 을/를 shows what receives the action.

beginnerGuide.title: Particle dropping comes later
beginnerGuide.body: Koreans often drop 을/를 in speech, but beginners should first understand the full frame. Once the structure is clear, natural short speech becomes easier.

beginnerGuide.title: Negatives start here
beginnerGuide.body: 안 먹어요 and 공부 안 해요 show the everyday short negative. This means “I do not do it,” not necessarily “I cannot.”

checkpoints: I can make a present-tense sentence with an object.
I can use 을 after a consonant and 를 after a vowel.
I can make a short negative with 안.

hook.situation: You want to tell a Korean friend 'I drink coffee every morning.' You know the word 커피, you know 마셔요 — but you're not sure what goes between them. Is it 커피가? 커피는? 커피를? One small particle changes the entire grammatical logic of the sentence.
objectives: Attach 을 or 를 correctly after the object in any present-tense sentence
Say what you eat, drink, study, read, and write every day
Use the short negative (안) to say what you don't do
hook.whyItMatters: 을/를 is the particle that tells listeners WHAT is being acted on. Without it your sentences sound like a list of disconnected words. Once this clicks, you can build an unlimited number of complete action sentences — and Koreans will immediately know you understand Korean sentence structure.

grammarNotes.title: 을/를 — The Object Marker
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 을/를 as an ARROW pointing from the verb back to what it hits. '밥을 먹어요' — the arrow from 먹어요 points back through 을 to 밥. Whatever the action hits, receives, or affects gets the 을/를 arrow. If there's no arrow, listeners don't know what's being eaten/studied/drunk.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun ending in a consonant + 을 / Noun ending in a vowel + 를

examples.en: I eat rice/a meal.
examples.note: 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을 is attached; the arrow points from 먹어요 to 밥

examples.en: I drink coffee.
examples.note: 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를 is attached; 마시다 (to drink) hits 커피

examples.en: I study Korean.
examples.note: 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; the studying action is directed at Korean

examples.en: I read a book.
examples.note: 책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book

examples.en: I listen to music.
examples.note: 음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music

a.en: I drink coffee. (coffee is the object being drunk)

b.en: There is coffee. / I have coffee. (coffee is the subject that exists)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same word 커피, completely different particles. 를 = coffee is what gets drunk (object). 가 = coffee is the thing that exists (subject). The particle tells you the coffee's role in the sentence.

a.en: I listen to music.

b.en: Music is good. / I like music.

contrastPairs.explanation: 을 marks music as the object being listened to — an active directed action. 이 marks music as the subject of a description. Korean 좋다 (to be good/likeable) takes a subject, not an object — so you can't say 음악을 좋아요 here.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English verbs like 'study' don't need a special particle before their object — you just say 'I study Korean.' Korean does require 을/를. Dropping it sounds like you're just naming things ('I ... Korean ... study') rather than building a proper sentence. Beginners drop 을/를 most often with study, eat, and drink because those sentences feel 'obvious' — but the particle is still required for natural Korean.

exceptions: In fast casual speech, Koreans often DROP 을/를 entirely: 뭐 먹어요? (What are you eating?) instead of 뭐를 먹어요? — learn the full form first, then natural dropping will feel intuitive
하다 verbs like 공부하다, 운동하다 can be split into noun + 를 + 하다: 공부를 해요 = 공부해요 — both are correct
뭐 (what) doesn't take 를 in questions: 뭐 먹어요? not 뭐를 먹어요? — 뭐 is an exception

grammarNotes.title: 안 V — The Short Negative (I don't / I'm not doing)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 안 as a STOP SIGN placed right in front of the verb. You're driving toward the action, and 안 stops it before it happens. 먹어요 = eating happens. 안 먹어요 = the stop sign blocks the eating. The sentence structure is identical — you just insert the stop sign.
grammarNotes.formation: 안 + Verb-아요/어요/해요 (for pure verbs) / Noun + 안 + 해요 (for noun+하다 verbs)

examples.en: I don't eat. / I'm not eating.
examples.note: Stop sign 안 placed directly before 먹어요 — the simplest pattern

examples.en: I don't drink.
examples.note: 안 blocks 마시다; works with any drink or alcohol context

examples.en: I don't study.
examples.note: With noun+하다 verbs: split the noun (공부) away and put 안 between noun and 해요 — NOT 안 공부해요

examples.en: I don't exercise.
examples.note: Same noun+하다 split rule: 운동 + 안 + 해요; 안 goes between the noun and 해요

examples.en: I don't read it.
examples.note: 안 in front of the verb stem; same stop-sign pattern

a.en: I don't eat it. (simple everyday negative)

b.en: I do not eat it. (more deliberate / slightly formal)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both mean the same thing, but 안 V feels like a quick natural statement (stop-sign dropped in), while V지 않아요 sounds more considered and is common in writing. In daily speech, 안 V is far more frequent.

a.en: I don't study.

b.en: (Unnatural — avoid this form)

contrastPairs.explanation: With noun+하다 verbs, the 안 MUST split the noun from 해요. Saying 안 공부해요 sounds unnatural to Korean ears. The rule: whenever the verb is [noun]+하다, split it: [noun] + 안 + 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts the negative before the whole verb phrase: 'I don't study.' Korean with noun+하다 verbs splits the compound: the noun comes first, then 안, then 해요. English speakers try to put 안 at the very front (mirroring 'don't'), but with noun+하다 verbs this sounds wrong. Pure verbs like 먹다, 마시다 can take 안 directly before them — but compound verbs need the split.

exceptions: 못 (cannot) is different from 안 (don't/won't): 안 먹어요 = I don't eat it (choice) / 못 먹어요 = I can't eat it (inability or restriction)
With 있다/없다, don't use 안: use 없어요 instead of 안 있어요 for 'there isn't'
모르다 (to not know) is its own negative — don't say 안 알아요 to mean 'I don't know'; say 몰라요

exampleSentence.en: I eat lunch.
exampleSentence.note: 점심 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating is directed at lunch

exampleSentence.en: I drink water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; the drinking action hits 물

exampleSentence.en: I study Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; can also split: 한국어 공부를 해요

exampleSentence.en: I read a book.
exampleSentence.note: 책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book

exampleSentence.en: I write a diary.
exampleSentence.note: 일기 ends in vowel 기 → 를; writing is directed at the diary

exampleSentence.en: I listen to music.
exampleSentence.note: 음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music

exampleSentence.en: I watch a movie.
exampleSentence.note: 영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie

exampleSentence.en: I exercise every day.
exampleSentence.note: 운동하다 has no object here — not everything needs 을/를; negative form: 운동 안 해요

exampleSentence.en: I'm not working today.
exampleSentence.note: Noun+하다 split negative: 일 + 안 + 해요 — the stop sign goes between noun and verb

exampleSentence.en: Are you eating? / Do you eat rice?
exampleSentence.note: 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을; 밥을 먹다 is the most common eating phrase in Korean

exampleSentence.en: I drink coffee in the morning.
exampleSentence.note: 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를; 아침에 = time marker 에 (learned in chapter 6)

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; 많이 = a lot, modifying the verb

exampleSentence.en: I read an interesting book.
exampleSentence.note: 책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; 재미있는 is an adjective modifying 책

exampleSentence.en: I listen to Korean music.
exampleSentence.note: 음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; 한국 directly modifies 음악 as an adjective

exampleSentence.en: I like movies.
exampleSentence.note: 영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; 좋아하다 (to like) takes an object with 을/를

exampleSentence.en: I drink coffee every day.
exampleSentence.note: 매일 is a time adverb — it doesn't need a particle; it modifies the entire sentence

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 많이 (adverb) modifies the verb directly — no particle needed on the adverb itself

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihee (지희) and her coworker Minho (민호) are chatting over lunch about their daily habits

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: Minho, do you eat breakfast every day?
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 먹어요 — 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating (먹다) is directed at breakfast

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: No, I don't eat breakfast. I'm busy.
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 안 먹어요 — the stop-sign 안 goes directly before 먹어요 (a pure verb, not noun+하다)

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 그래요? 저는 매일 밥을 먹어요. 건강이 중요해요.
lines.romanization: Geuraeyo? Jeoneun maeil babeul meogeoyo. Geongangi jungyohaeyo.
lines.en: Really? I eat rice every day. Health is important.
lines.grammarNote: 밥을 먹어요 — 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을 attaches; 건강이 = subject marker since 건강 is the subject of 중요하다

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I drink coffee. That's my breakfast.
lines.grammarNote: 커피를 마셔요 — 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를 attaches; drinking is directed at coffee

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: Haha, do you study Korean?
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 — 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; this is also valid as 한국어 공부를 해요 (split form)

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 매일 공부해요. 그런데 책을 안 읽어요. 앱으로 해요.
lines.romanization: Ne, maeil gongbuhaeyo. Geureonde chaegeul an ilgeoyo. Abeuro haeyo.
lines.en: Yes, I study every day. But I don't read books. I do it with an app.
lines.grammarNote: 책을 안 읽어요 — 책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; 안 is a stop sign before the pure verb 읽어요

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: I study while listening to music.
lines.grammarNote: 음악을 들으면서 — 음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; 들으면서 = while listening (V-면서 pattern, preview)

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 오, 저도 해 볼게요! 오늘부터 음악을 들으면서 공부해요.
lines.romanization: O, jeodo hae bolgeyo! Oneulbuteo eumageul deureuryeonseo gongbuhaeyo.
lines.en: Oh, I'll try that too! Starting today, I'll study while listening to music.
lines.grammarNote: 음악을 들으면서 again — notice 음악을 appears twice in the conversation, reinforcing that 를 is the natural particle here

readingText.title: 수빈의 하루 일과 (Subin's Daily Routine)
readingText.body: 저는 매일 아침 일찍 일어나요. 밥을 먹고 커피를 마셔요. 커피를 안 마시면 피곤해요. 출근해서 회사에서 일해요. 점심에 동료들과 같이 밥을 먹어요. 오후에는 이메일을 쓰고 보고서를 읽어요. 퇴근 후에 음악을 들어요. 그리고 한국어를 공부해요. 저는 드라마를 보면서 공부해요. 주말에는 운동 안 해요. 그냥 책을 읽어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: I wake up early every morning. I eat rice and drink coffee. If I don't drink coffee I feel tired. I commute and work at the office. At lunch I eat with my coworkers. In the afternoon I write emails and read reports. After work I listen to music. And I study Korean. I study while watching dramas. On weekends I don't exercise. I just read books.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Subin do if she doesn't drink coffee?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 피곤해요 — she feels tired (커피를 안 마시면 피곤해요)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do after work?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 음악을 들어요 (listens to music) and 한국어를 공부해요 (studies Korean)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 을/를 in the text. For each one, explain why 을 or 를 is used — not the other form.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 (ㅂ consonant ending → 을), 커피를 (이 vowel ending → 를), 커피를 (again, same reason), 이메일을 (ㄹ consonant ending → 을), 보고서를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 음악을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을), 한국어를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 드라마를 (아 vowel ending → 를), 책을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을). The rule: consonant-ending nouns take 을, vowel-ending nouns take 를.

culturalNote.title: 밥 먹었어요? — The Korean greeting that's really about food
culturalNote.body: In Korea, one of the most common informal greetings is '밥 먹었어요?' (Have you eaten?) — said instead of 'How are you?' to close friends and family. Offering food is central to Korean social bonding. Answering 'yes' (네, 먹었어요) or 'not yet' (아직요) is totally normal. Notice that in this casual greeting, the particle 을 is often dropped: '밥 먹었어요?' rather than '밥을 먹었어요?' This is the natural particle-dropping that Koreans do in fast speech — but you now know the full form with 을, which makes the shortened form easy to understand.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 아침___ 먹어요. (I eat breakfast.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을. 를 is only used after vowel-ending nouns. 이 and 가 are subject markers, not object markers — they mark who is doing the action, not what receives it.

inlineExercises.prompt: 커피___ 마셔요. (I drink coffee.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 커피 ends in vowel 이, so it takes 를. 을 is for consonant-ending nouns. 은/는 are topic markers, not object markers — they set the topic of the sentence, which is different from marking what is being drunk.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는 공부를 안 해요' vs '저는 안 공부해요' — 어느 것이 맞아요?
inlineExercises.explanation: Both suggested options have issues. 공부를 안 해요 is grammatically possible (공부를 하다 split form), but the most natural everyday negative for noun+하다 verbs is: noun + 안 + 해요, dropping 를. So 공부 안 해요 is the cleanest natural form. 안 공부해요 is wrong because the stop-sign 안 cannot go before a noun+하다 compound.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어___ 공부해요. (I study Korean.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 한국어 ends in vowel 어, so it takes 를. This is one of the most common sentences a Korean learner will ever say — 한국어를 공부해요 — so it's worth drilling until it's automatic.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I don't watch movies.'
inlineExercises.hint: 영화 ends in a vowel — which form of the object marker do you need? And 보다 is a pure verb, so where does 안 go?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I don't study' using the 안 negative?
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부 안 해요 is correct — noun + stop-sign + 해요. '안 공부해요' is wrong because 안 can't go before a noun-verb compound. '공부를 않아요' is missing the -지 needed for the long negative form (공부를 하지 않아요). '안 공부를 해요' mixes up the word order in an unnatural way.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '책을 읽어요.' What is the role of 을 in this sentence?
options: It marks 책 as the subject doing the reading.
It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
It marks 책 as a topic being discussed.
It is a verb ending attached to 책.
inlineExercises.correct: It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
inlineExercises.explanation: 을/를 is the object marker — it marks WHAT gets acted upon. 책 is what is being read. Subject markers (이/가) mark who does the action; topic markers (은/는) set what we're talking about. 을/를 is specifically for the thing that receives the verb's action.

bullets: 을/를 = ARROW from verb to object: consonant-ending noun + 을 / vowel-ending noun + 를
안 = STOP SIGN before a pure verb (안 먹어요); for noun+하다 verbs split it: noun + 안 + 해요
