Key daily verbs with their objects: 밥을 먹다, 커피를 마시다, 한국어를 공부하다, 책을 읽다, 음악을 듣다, 영화를 보다
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next: Chapter 6 introduces 에 and 에서 — the location particles that tell Koreans WHERE you go, WHERE you are, and WHERE actions happen. Combined with 을/를 from this chapter, you'll build full sentences like '도서관에서 한국어를 공부해요.'

chapters.title: Places And Time: 에 And 에서
chapters.goal: Say where you go, where you are, where actions happen, and when things happen.
chapters.scenario: School, work, home, appointments, and movement.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Where are you going?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I go to school.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: I study at school.

chapters.guidedPractice: Contrast 학교에 가요 with 학교에서 공부해요. Do not mix destination and action place.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say where you are, where you go, and where you study or work.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 어디에 가요? and 어디에서 공부해요? Learner answers both.
chapters.review: Can you choose 에 vs 에서 in simple sentences?

beginnerGuide.title: The 에 / 에서 split
beginnerGuide.body: 에 points to destination, time, or where something exists. 에서 marks where an action happens. 학교에 가요 and 학교에서 공부해요 are different for a reason.

beginnerGuide.title: Movement vs action
beginnerGuide.body: If the verb is 가다 or 오다, think destination: 에. If the verb is 공부하다, 일하다, 먹다, 기다리다, or 사다, think action place: 에서.

beginnerGuide.title: Time also uses 에
beginnerGuide.body: For clock time, use 에: 7시에 일어나요. Some time words like 오늘, 내일, 지금 usually do not need 에 at beginner level.

checkpoints: I can say where I go with 에.
I can say where I do an action with 에서.
I do not say 학교에서 가요 for destination.

hook.situation: You're texting a Korean friend to arrange where to meet. You type '카페에 만나요' — but your friend is confused. Did you mean you're going TO the café, or hanging out AT the café? In Korean, those are different sentences.
objectives: Use 에 correctly for destinations and static locations
Use 에서 correctly for places where actions happen
Avoid the #1 English-speaker mistake: mixing up 에 and 에서 with movement vs. action verbs
hook.whyItMatters: 에 and 에서 look almost identical to beginners, but Koreans hear the difference immediately. Using 에서 with 가다 (학교에서 가요) is a clear signal that you're still learning — after this chapter you won't make that mistake again.

grammarNotes.title: 에 — Destination, Time & Static Location
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 에 as a PIN DROP on a map. You're marking a point — either where you're headed, when something happens, or where something simply exists. No action is happening at that point; it's just a location or time stamp.
grammarNotes.formation: Place / Time + 에

examples.en: I go to school.
examples.note: 가다 is a movement verb → 에 marks the destination

examples.en: I'm at home.
examples.note: 있다 = static existence → 에 marks where something IS

examples.en: I wake up at seven.
examples.note: Time expressions use 에 — think of the clock as a pin drop in time

examples.en: I come to the office.
examples.note: 오다 is also a movement verb → destination takes 에

examples.en: I live in Korea.
examples.note: 살다 (to live/reside) treats a place as a pin drop → 에

a.en: I go TO school.

b.en: I study AT school.

contrastPairs.explanation: Same place (학교), different particles. 에 = the destination of movement. 에서 = where the studying action happens.

a.en: I'm at the café. (just sitting there)

b.en: I work at the café. (action happening)

contrastPairs.explanation: 있어요 is static — just existing somewhere → 에. 일해요 is an active verb → 에서.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says 'went FROM the library' with 'from', but 'went TO the library' with 'to'. In Korean, 가다/오다 ALWAYS take 에 for the destination — never 에서. 에서 with 가다 sounds like you're saying the library is where the going-action happened, which makes no sense.

exceptions: 있다 and 없다 always take 에, never 에서: 집에 있어요 ✅ / 집에서 있어요 ❌
살다 (to live) takes 에: 서울에 살아요 ✅
Time words like 오늘, 내일, 지금 usually don't need 에 at all

grammarNotes.title: 에서 — Where Actions Happen & Where Things Start
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 에서 as a STAGE. A stage is where the performance (action) takes place. If a verb describes something actively happening somewhere, that place is a stage → 에서. It also means FROM a starting point.
grammarNotes.formation: Place + 에서

examples.en: I study at school.
examples.note: 공부하다 = active action → 에서 marks the stage

examples.en: I meet a friend at the café.
examples.note: 만나다 = active action happening AT the café

examples.en: I read books at the library.
examples.note: 읽다 = active action → library is the stage

examples.en: I came from America.
examples.note: 에서 = FROM (starting point) — this is the second meaning of 에서

examples.en: I eat at the restaurant.
examples.note: 먹다 = active eating happening there → 에서

a.en: I come home. (destination)

b.en: I cook at home. (action)

contrastPairs.explanation: Coming home = movement with destination → 에. Cooking at home = action happening there → 에서.

a.en: I live in Seoul. (residence)

b.en: I work in Seoul. (action)

contrastPairs.explanation: 살다 treats Seoul as a static location → 에. 일하다 treats Seoul as an active stage → 에서.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'at the café' doesn't distinguish between static location and action location, but Korean does. Any active verb (work, eat, study, meet, wait, buy) needs 에서, not 에. When in doubt: if you're DOING something there, use 에서.

exceptions: 에서 + 나오다/떠나다 (to come out of / leave): 집에서 나왔어요 — here 에서 = from
Some verbs work with either 에 or 에서 with slightly different meaning: 앉다 (to sit) → 의자에 앉아요 (sit DOWN onto the chair) vs. 소파에서 앉아요 (sit at/on the sofa doing something)

exampleSentence.en: I study Korean at school.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — studying is an action

exampleSentence.en: I read books at the library.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — reading is an active action

exampleSentence.en: I wait for my friend at the café.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — waiting is an active state/action

exampleSentence.en: I work at the office for 8 hours.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — working is an active action

exampleSentence.en: I ate bibimbap at the restaurant.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — eating is an active action

exampleSentence.en: I want to rest at home.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — resting is an action at a location

exampleSentence.en: I exercise at the park.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — exercising is an action

exampleSentence.en: I go to school tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: 가다 = movement → destination takes 에, never 에서

exampleSentence.en: Come to my place.
exampleSentence.note: 오다 = movement → destination takes 에

extendedVocabulary.english: to be / to exist / to have

exampleSentence.en: I'm at the café right now.
exampleSentence.note: 있다 = static existence → ALWAYS takes 에, never 에서

exampleSentence.en: I study at the library.
exampleSentence.note: Active verb → location takes 에서

exampleSentence.en: I do a part-time job at a café.
exampleSentence.note: Action verb → 에서

exampleSentence.en: Where shall we meet?
exampleSentence.note: Meeting is an action → 에서

exampleSentence.en: I'll wait at the café.
exampleSentence.note: Waiting = active state → 에서

exampleSentence.en: Let's eat together at the restaurant.
exampleSentence.note: Eating is an action → 에서

exampleSentence.en: I made a restaurant reservation.
exampleSentence.note: The action of reserving doesn't need a location particle here — you reserve the OBJECT (식당을)

exampleSentence.en: I wake up at 7 every day.
exampleSentence.note: Time uses 에 — think of the clock as a pin drop in time

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihoon texts his coworker Sora to plan their lunch break

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Sora, where are you right now?
lines.grammarNote: 어디에 있어요? — 있다 is static existence, so the location takes 에, not 에서

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: I'm at the office. Why?
lines.grammarNote: 회사에 있어요 — same rule: 있다 + 에 = just existing at a place

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Let's have lunch together! Where should we eat?
lines.grammarNote: 어디에서 먹을까요? — eating is an action, so 에서 asks about the stage for that action

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.ko: 회사 근처 식당에서 먹어요. 거기 음식이 맛있어요.
lines.romanization: Hoesa geuncheo sikdangeseo meogeoyo. Geogi eumsigi massisseoyo.
lines.en: Let's eat at the restaurant near the office. The food there is good.
lines.grammarNote: 식당에서 먹어요 — 에서 marks the restaurant as the stage where eating happens

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Great! What time do we go?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 시에 — time takes 에; 가요 is movement so no location particle needed here

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: We go to the restaurant at 12.
lines.grammarNote: 12시에 (time → 에) + 식당에 가요 (destination of 가다 → 에) — two 에 in one sentence!

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 저는 지금 카페에서 일해요. 12시에 식당 앞에서 만나요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun jigeum kafeeseo ilhaeyo. Yeoltu-ssie sikdang apeseo mannayo.
lines.en: I'm working at a café right now. Let's meet in front of the restaurant at 12.
lines.grammarNote: 카페에서 일해요 (action at café → 에서) + 식당 앞에서 만나요 (meeting is an action → 에서)

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: Got it! See you at twelve then.
lines.grammarNote: 12시에 봐요 — time takes 에; no location particle since 보다 (to see) doesn't specify a stage here

readingText.title: 수진의 하루 (Sujin's Day)
readingText.body: 오늘 아침 7시에 일어났어요. 그리고 집에서 아침을 먹었어요. 9시에 학교에 갔어요. 학교에서 한국어를 공부했어요. 점심에 학교 식당에서 친구를 만났어요. 오후에 도서관에서 숙제를 했어요. 저녁 6시에 집에 왔어요. 집에서 쉬었어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: This morning I woke up at 7. Then I ate breakfast at home. At 9 I went to school. At school I studied Korean. At lunch I met a friend at the school cafeteria. In the afternoon I did homework at the library. At 6 in the evening I came home. I rested at home.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What time did Sujin wake up?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 7시에 (at 7 o'clock)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where did Sujin meet her friend?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 학교 식당에서 (at the school cafeteria)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 에서 in the text. Why does each one use 에서 and not 에?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 집에서 먹었어요 (eating is an action), 학교에서 공부했어요 (studying is an action), 식당에서 만났어요 (meeting is an action), 도서관에서 했어요 (doing homework is an action), 집에서 쉬었어요 (resting is an action at home)

culturalNote.title: 어디에서 왔어요? — The most important question you'll hear
culturalNote.body: One of the first things Koreans ask foreigners is '어디에서 왔어요?' (Where did you come from? / Where are you from?). Notice it uses 에서 — this is the FROM meaning. The answer also uses 에서: '미국에서 왔어요' (I came from America). You'll hear this question constantly. A common beginner mistake is answering '미국에 왔어요' — that sounds like you came TO America, not FROM it. 에서 = origin/from. Get this one right and Koreans will be impressed.

inlineExercises.prompt: 학교___ 가요. (I go to school.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 is a movement verb, so its destination takes 에. 학교에서 가요 would sound like the going-action happens at school, which makes no sense.

inlineExercises.prompt: 도서관___ 공부해요. (I study at the library.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부하다 is an action. The library is the STAGE where studying happens → 에서. If you used 에, it would sound like you're just existing at the library, not doing anything.

inlineExercises.prompt: 지금 집___ 있어요. (I'm at home right now.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 always takes 에, never 에서. It describes static existence — just being somewhere, not performing an action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '카페에서 갔어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 is a movement verb — its destination MUST take 에. 에서 with 가다 is one of the most common beginner errors. Whenever you see 가다 or 오다, the destination always takes 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I eat at the restaurant.'
inlineExercises.hint: 먹다 (to eat) is an action. The restaurant is the stage where eating happens. Which particle marks an action stage?

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend asks '어디에서 왔어요?' You want to say 'I came from England.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 에서 has a second meaning: FROM (a starting point). 영국에서 왔어요 = I came from England. If you said 영국에 왔어요, that means 'I came TO England' — the opposite!

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구를 카페___ 만나요. (I meet my friend at the café.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만나다 (to meet) is an action. The café is the stage where the meeting happens → 에서.

bullets: 에 = PIN DROP: destination of movement (가다/오다), time, or static location (있다/없다/살다)
에서 = STAGE: where an active verb (eat, study, work, meet, wait) happens — or FROM a starting point
The golden rule: if you're DOING something there → 에서 / if you're just GOING there or IT EXISTS there → 에
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 7 introduces 을/를 (object markers) — the particles that tell you WHAT is being acted on. Combined with 에/에서, you'll be able to build complete action sentences.

chapters.title: Food And Shopping
chapters.goal: Order items, ask price, pay, and explain simple restrictions.
chapters.scenario: Cafe, restaurant, convenience store, and market.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: What can I get you?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Water, please.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Is card payment okay?

chapters.guidedPractice: Practice N 주세요, 이것만 주세요, 이것도 주세요, 카드 돼요?, and 카드로 결제할 수 있어요?
chapters.realLifeTask: Order one thing, ask the price, and ask whether card payment is possible.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend plays staff. Learner orders, asks price, and chooses payment.
chapters.review: Can you ask for an item and use 로/으로 for payment?

beginnerGuide.title: Ordering is chunk-based
beginnerGuide.body: In a cafe or store, N 주세요 is more useful than a full English-style sentence. 물 주세요 and 이거 하나 주세요 are complete practical requests.

beginnerGuide.title: Payment language
beginnerGuide.body: 카드 돼요? is a common spoken shortcut. 카드로 결제할 수 있어요? is clearer and more textbook-complete. Both are useful, but they feel different.

beginnerGuide.title: Small particles, big meaning
beginnerGuide.body: 도 means also, 만 means only, and 로/으로 can show method such as payment or transportation. These small pieces change the shopping situation.

checkpoints: I can order one item with N 주세요.
I can ask price with 얼마예요?
I can ask about card payment using 카드 돼요? or 카드로 결제할 수 있어요?

hook.situation: You're at a Korean café. You want water, a croissant, and you want to pay by card. You manage to say '물 주세요' — but then you freeze. How do you add 'and the croissant too'? How do you ask if card payment is okay? You need three small but powerful particles: 도 (also), 만 (only), and 로/으로 (by means of).
objectives: Use 도 to add one more item to an order ('and this too, please')
Use 만 to set a limit ('only this, nothing else')
Use 로/으로 to express payment method, transport, or language ('by card', 'in Korean')
hook.whyItMatters: These three particles unlock real transactions. 도, 만, and 로/으로 are used in every café, restaurant, and convenience store interaction in Korea. Without them, every order is a single isolated item — with them, you can build natural, flexible requests that sound like a real customer, not a tourist reading a phrasebook.

grammarNotes.title: 도 vs. 만 — Adding vs. Limiting
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 도 as a SHOPPING CART and 만 as a SPOTLIGHT. 도 throws one more thing into the cart — it adds to what already exists. 만 shines a spotlight on one single item and says everything else is in the dark. Same menu, opposite choices.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun + 도 (also/too) | Noun + 만 (only/just)

examples.en: This too, please.
examples.note: 도 follows the item being added — 이것 gets tossed into the cart alongside whatever was ordered before

examples.en: Only water, please.
examples.note: 만 follows 물 — the spotlight is on water alone; no food, no other drinks

examples.en: I'll order too.
examples.note: 도 after a pronoun — the speaker is adding themselves to the group of people ordering

examples.en: There's a discount only today.
examples.note: 만 after a time word — the discount spotlight shines on today only, not tomorrow

examples.en: Do you drink coffee too?
examples.note: 도 in a question — asking whether coffee joins the list of drinks the person has

a.en: This too, please. (I want this in addition to what I already ordered.)

b.en: Only this, please. (Just this. Nothing else at all.)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same object (이것), completely different meaning. 도 = add to the order. 만 = limit the order to just this. In a convenience store, 이것도 주세요 means 'and this on top'; 이것만 주세요 means 'cancel everything else, just give me this.'

a.en: I eat too. (Other people eat, and so do I.)

b.en: Only I eat. (Nobody else eats — just me.)

contrastPairs.explanation: 도 makes you part of the group. 만 isolates you as the sole person. The verb is identical; the particle creates the entire contrast.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers try to keep 는 (the topic marker) and add 도 on top of it, but 도 replaces subject and topic particles — not joins them. Say 저도, never 저는도. The same rule applies to 만: 물만 주세요, never 물을만 주세요.

exceptions: 도 and 만 can follow location particles in special cases: 학교에서도 (at school too), 서울에서만 (only in Seoul) — here 도/만 follow 에서, not replace it
만 can attach to time expressions naturally: 한 번만 (just once), 5분만 (just five minutes)

grammarNotes.title: 로 / 으로 — Method, Means, and Direction
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 로/으로 as a CHANNEL SELECTOR. You're pointing at the channel through which the action flows: pay through the card channel, travel through the subway channel, speak through the Korean channel. Whatever you attach 로/으로 to is the channel being selected.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun + 로 (after vowel or ㄹ) | Noun + 으로 (after most consonants)

examples.en: Can I pay by card?
examples.note: 카드 ends in a vowel (드) → 로. Payment flows through the card channel.

examples.en: I go by subway.
examples.note: 지하철 ends in ㄹ → 로 (the ㄹ rule). Transit flows through the subway channel.

examples.en: I speak in Korean.
examples.note: Language use: the communication flows through the Korean-language channel. 어 ends in a vowel → 로.

examples.en: I write with a pen.
examples.note: 펜 ends in a consonant (ㄴ) → 으로. Writing flows through the pen channel.

examples.en: I'll pay in cash.
examples.note: 현금 ends in a consonant (ㅁ) → 으로. Paying flows through the cash channel.

a.en: I go to the subway. (destination: I'm heading TO the subway station.)

b.en: I go by subway. (method: I use the subway to get there.)

contrastPairs.explanation: 에 marks the destination of movement. 로/으로 marks the channel/method used. 지하철에 가요 means you're going to the subway (maybe to pick someone up); 지하철로 가요 means the subway is your transport method.

a.en: I buy it by card. (method of payment)

b.en: I buy a card. (card is the object being bought)

contrastPairs.explanation: 로/으로 = the card is the payment method. 를 = the card is what you're purchasing. Same noun, different particles, completely different shopping situation.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'pay by card' uses 'by', but learners often reach for 에 (which marks locations/times). 에 would suggest you're paying AT the card, as if the card were a place. 로/으로 is the method particle. Whenever you'd say 'by', 'with', 'using', or 'in (a language)' — that's 로/으로 territory.

exceptions: After ㄹ endings, use 로 not 으로: 서울로 가요 (not 서울으로), 지하철로 (not 지하철으로)
Direction meaning (toward): 집으로 가요 can also mean 'heading toward home' — context usually makes it clear whether it's method or direction

exampleSentence.en: Two Americanos, please.
exampleSentence.note: N + 주세요 = the single most useful ordering pattern in Korea

exampleSentence.en: How much is this?
exampleSentence.note: 이거 (this) + 얼마예요 — the go-to price question in any market, convenience store, or café

exampleSentence.en: Can I pay by card?
exampleSentence.note: 카드 ends in a vowel → 로 (not 으로)

exampleSentence.en: I'll pay in cash.
exampleSentence.note: 현금 ends in a consonant (ㅁ) → 으로

exampleSentence.en: Is it okay to pay by card?
exampleSentence.note: 결제하다 is the formal word for payment processing; 내다 or 계산하다 are more casual

exampleSentence.en: Receipt, please.
exampleSentence.note: Direct N 주세요 request — no extra particles needed

exampleSentence.en: May I order now?
exampleSentence.note: 주문하다 + 아/어도 돼요? = polite permission request; 받다 (receive) is often said by staff: 주문받겠습니다

exampleSentence.en: Menu, please.
exampleSentence.note: 메뉴 is a loanword from English; in practice many Korean cafés have menus only on boards, so this is more useful than it sounds

exampleSentence.en: One Americano, please.
exampleSentence.note: Quantities in ordering use native Korean numbers (하나, 둘, 셋), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼)

exampleSentence.en: Some water, please.
exampleSentence.note: 좀 softens the request; 좀 주세요 sounds more polite and natural than 주세요 alone

exampleSentence.en: A little more water, please.
exampleSentence.note: 더 = more quantity; often combined with 좀 for a polite, natural request for a refill

exampleSentence.en: Is card okay?
exampleSentence.note: 카드 돼요? is a spoken shortcut — grammatically incomplete but perfectly natural in shops

exampleSentence.en: This too, please.
exampleSentence.note: 이거 is the spoken form, 이것 is written/formal; both work at a café or shop counter

exampleSentence.en: To go, please.
exampleSentence.note: 포장 (packing) = takeout in Korean. 포장이요? is how staff ask if you want it to go

exampleSentence.en: What's the recommended menu item?
exampleSentence.note: 추천 없어요? or 추천 메뉴요? are very natural ways to ask a café or restaurant what's good

exampleSentence.en: Is there a student discount?
exampleSentence.note: 할인 + 돼요? is the pattern to ask about discounts; 학생 할인, 앱 할인, 포인트 할인 all work the same way

exampleSentence.en: Please make it not spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 맵게 is the adverbial form (spicily); 안 맵게 해 주세요 = make it in a not-spicy way — practical for dietary restrictions

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun and his coworker Yuna go to a café. Minjun orders for both of them.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Welcome! What can I get you?
lines.grammarNote: 뭐 드릴까요? — the polite 'what shall I offer you?' form staff use in Korean cafés; 드리다 is the honorific of 주다

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Two Americanos, please.
lines.grammarNote: N 주세요 ordering pattern; 두 잔 = two cups using native Korean number 두 + counter 잔

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Do you need anything else?
lines.grammarNote: 더 (more/else) here asks if there's anything to add — functions like 도 in a question context

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: One croissant too, please.
lines.grammarNote: 크루아상 + 도 = adding the croissant to the cart (SHOPPING CART rule); 하나 = one (native Korean number)

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.ko: 저는 케이크만 주세요. 커피는 안 마셔요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun keikuman juseyo. Keopineun an masyeoyo.
lines.en: Just cake for me, please. I don't drink coffee.
lines.grammarNote: 케이크 + 만 = spotlight on cake alone (SPOTLIGHT rule); this is 만 as a dietary/preference restriction

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Got it. How would you like to pay?
lines.grammarNote: 어떻게 (how) + 하시겠어요? is the polite 'how will you do X?' frame — staff asking the payment method opens the 로/으로 response

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: I'll pay by card. Card is okay, right?
lines.grammarNote: 카드 + 로 = the CHANNEL SELECTOR (method particle); 카드 ends in vowel 드 → 로, not 으로

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, card is fine. Do you need a receipt?
lines.grammarNote: 카드로 돼요 — 로/으로 again confirming payment method; 영수증 주세요 is the natural follow-up if you want the receipt

readingText.title: 편의점에서 (At the Convenience Store)
readingText.body: 오늘 퇴근 후에 편의점에 들렀어요. 직원한테 '이거 얼마예요?' 라고 물었어요. 삼천 원이라고 했어요. 현금이 없어서 카드로 계산했어요. 영수증도 받았어요. 친구한테 선물로 과자를 사서 이것만 담았어요. 다음에는 카드 할인도 확인해야겠어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: After work today I stopped by a convenience store. I asked the staff 'How much is this?' They said it was 3,000 won. I didn't have cash so I paid by card. I got a receipt too. I bought snacks as a gift for my friend, so I put only those in the basket. Next time I should check for card discounts too.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How did the speaker pay, and why?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 카드로 계산했어요 — they paid by card because they had no cash (현금이 없어서)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What did the speaker buy, and for whom?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 친구한테 선물로 과자를 샀어요 — they bought snacks as a gift (선물로 = using the gift channel/purpose) for a friend

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every 도 and 만 in the text. For each one, explain whether it is adding something or limiting something.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 영수증도 받았어요 — 도 adds the receipt to the list of things that happened (CART: one more item); 이것만 담았어요 — 만 limits the basket contents to only the snacks (SPOTLIGHT: nothing else); 카드 할인도 확인해야겠어요 — 도 adds checking discounts to next time's plan (CART: another thing to do)

culturalNote.title: 카드 돼요? — Why Korean shops sometimes say no
culturalNote.body: In Korea, the question '카드 돼요?' (Is card okay?) is completely natural and expected. Unlike many countries where card payment is assumed, some Korean small businesses — street food stalls, traditional markets, very small local cafés — are cash-only. The reason is often the transaction fee the business pays to the card company. When you hear '현금만 돼요' (cash only), don't be surprised. It's also common to see signs like '카드 최소 금액 3,000원' (minimum card purchase 3,000 won). Having small bills (천 원, 오천 원) on hand is still a practical tip for exploring traditional markets like Gwangjang or Namdaemun.

inlineExercises.prompt: 아메리카노 주세요. 케이크___ 주세요. (I want an Americano. Cake too, please.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 adds the cake to the order (SHOPPING CART — one more item). If you used 만, the sentence would mean 'only cake, please' — cancelling the Americano you just ordered.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 물___ 마셔요. 다른 건 필요 없어요. (I drink only water. I don't need anything else.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 is the SPOTLIGHT — it limits the sentence to water and excludes everything else. 도 would mean 'I drink water too (among other things)', which contradicts '다른 건 필요 없어요'.

inlineExercises.prompt: 카드___ 결제할 수 있어요? (Can I pay by card?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 로/으로 marks the method (CHANNEL SELECTOR). 카드에 would mean 'on the card' or 'at the card' as if the card were a location, which makes no sense. The payment flows through the card channel → 카드로.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는도 주문할게요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 replaces subject and topic particles — it does not sit after them. 저는 + 도 is a double-particle error; drop 는 and say 저도. The same principle applies to 만: never 이것을만, always 이것만.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I'll pay in cash. Receipt too, please.'
inlineExercises.hint: 현금 ends in a consonant → which form? And are you adding the receipt (CART) or limiting to only the receipt (SPOTLIGHT)?

inlineExercises.prompt: The staff asks how you want to pay. You want to ask 'Is it okay if I pay by card?' Which is the most natural?
inlineExercises.explanation: 로/으로 marks the method of payment — the card is the CHANNEL. 카드에 would mean 'at the card' (card as a location — doesn't work). 카드를 would mean 'pay the card' — as if the card itself is the thing being paid, not the payment method.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배고파요? 이거___ 드세요. 다른 건 없어요. (Are you hungry? Have just this. There's nothing else.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 is the SPOTLIGHT — the context confirms there's nothing else ('다른 건 없어요'), so 만 is correct. 도 would imply there are other options too, which contradicts the sentence.

bullets: 도 = SHOPPING CART: adds one more item or person to what already exists. Replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를 — never stacks on top of them.
만 = SPOTLIGHT: limits the sentence to exactly one thing, excluding everything else. Place it directly after the word you want to isolate.
로/으로 = CHANNEL SELECTOR: marks the method, means, or tool of an action. Use 로 after vowels or ㄹ; use 으로 after other consonants.
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 8 builds on ordering and transactions by introducing time expressions and scheduling — how to say 'at what time', 'from when to when', and 'how long'.

chapters.title: Want, Can, Cannot
chapters.goal: Talk about desire, ability, possibility, and real limitations.
chapters.scenario: Food choices, schedules, language ability, and travel limits.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What do you want to eat?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I want to drink coffee.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Can you go to a cafe today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I cannot go today.

chapters.guidedPractice: Transform 가다 into 가고 싶어요, 갈 수 있어요, 못 가요. Transform 먹다 into 먹고 싶어요, 먹을 수 있어요, 못 먹어요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say what you want to do, what you can do, and what you cannot do.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 갈 수 있어요? Learner answers with 갈 수 있어요 or 못 가요 and a reason.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 못 가해요 is wrong and say 못 가요 instead?

beginnerGuide.title: Three different meanings
beginnerGuide.body: 고 싶어요 is desire, ㄹ/을 수 있어요 is ability or possibility, and 못 + verb is inability. They are not interchangeable.

beginnerGuide.title: The 못 rule beginners need
beginnerGuide.body: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal verb: 못 가요, 못 먹어요. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요: 공부 못 해요. Do not make 못 가해요.

beginnerGuide.title: Why this chapter matters
beginnerGuide.body: This is the chapter that lets you explain limits politely: I want to go, I can go, I cannot go, I cannot eat spicy food.

checkpoints: I can say want to, can, and cannot with 가다 and 먹다.
I can explain 안 가요 vs 못 가요.
I know 못 가해요 is wrong.

hook.situation: A Korean colleague invites you for samgyeopsal tonight. You want to go, you probably can go — but you're not sure yet. In English you'd say 'I want to go,' 'I can go,' or 'I can't go.' Korean has three distinct grammar forms for these three meanings, and mixing them up sounds strange: saying 못 가고 싶어요 (a nonsensical blend) signals confusion between wanting and being able.
objectives: Use 고 싶어요 correctly to express what you want or desire to do
Use ㄹ/을 수 있어요 to say you can do something (ability or possibility)
Use 못 + verb to say you cannot do something — and know why 못 가해요 is wrong
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns are the engine of polite Korean conversation. Koreans use them constantly to navigate invitations, menus, schedules, and apologies. Without them you can only say what you DO — you can't express what you want, what you're capable of, or what you have to decline. Master all three and you can have real adult conversations about your life.

grammarNotes.title: 고 싶어요 — Expressing Desire (I want to...)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 고 싶어요 as a MAGNET. The verb stem is pulling you toward an action — something attracts you, something you haven't done yet but are drawn to do. The magnet doesn't move by itself; it expresses the pull. 싶다 literally means 'to feel drawn to' — it always attaches to the verb stem + 고, never to a noun.
grammarNotes.formation: Verb stem + 고 싶어요

examples.en: I want to drink coffee.
examples.note: 마시다 → stem 마시 + 고 싶어요. The magnet pulls you toward drinking coffee — you haven't drunk it yet.

examples.en: I want to go to Korea.
examples.note: 가다 → stem 가 + 고 싶어요. A desire about a future movement — the magnet pulls you toward Korea.

examples.en: I want to eat food that isn't spicy.
examples.note: 먹다 → stem 먹 + 고 싶어요. Practical desire at a restaurant — key real-life use of this form.

examples.en: I want to speak Korean well.
examples.note: 하다 → stem 하 + 고 싶어요. A longer-term aspiration, not just an immediate craving — 고 싶어요 covers both.

examples.en: Today I want to rest.
examples.note: 쉬다 → stem 쉬 + 고 싶어요. The stem keeps its final vowel; no consonant changes needed here.

a.en: I want to eat samgyeopsal. (desire)

b.en: I can eat samgyeopsal. (ability/possibility)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same action, very different meaning. 고 싶어요 = internal desire, a pull toward the action. 먹을 수 있어요 = capability or circumstantial possibility. A vegetarian might say 먹을 수 있어요 (physically capable) but not 먹고 싶어요 (no desire). A sick person might say 먹고 싶어요 (wants to) but not 먹을 수 있어요 (can't right now).

a.en: I want to watch a movie. (desire)

b.en: I can't watch a movie. (inability)

contrastPairs.explanation: These can both be true at the same time! You can want to do something and be unable to do it. 고 싶어요 is about your desire; 못 봐요 is about whether the action is possible. Together: 영화를 보고 싶은데 못 봐요 — I want to watch a movie but can't.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says 'I want coffee' with just a noun. Korean 싶다 attaches to a VERB, not a noun — you can't say 커피를 싶어요. You must always say what you want to DO: 마시고 싶어요 (want to drink). For nouns use 원해요 or rephrase: 커피 한 잔 주세요 (please give me a coffee) — but 고 싶어요 always needs a verb stem before it.

exceptions: 고 싶다 describes the speaker's own desire. To say 'Minho wants to go,' use 가고 싶어해요 (third person shows desire as observed behavior), not 가고 싶어요.
Past desire: 가고 싶었어요 = I wanted to go (but didn't / past feeling).
Negative desire: 가고 싶지 않아요 = I don't want to go (more direct than 못 가요, which means can't).

grammarNotes.title: ㄹ/을 수 있어요 & 못 — Ability and Inability
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Picture a DOOR. 수 있어요 is an open door — you CAN walk through; the path is clear. 못 is a locked door — the way is blocked, whether by circumstance, rule, or physical impossibility. The key difference from English: 못 is a pre-verb blocker (it goes BEFORE the verb), not a separate sentence ending.
grammarNotes.formation: Ability: Verb stem + ㄹ/을 수 있어요 (stem ends in vowel → ㄹ 수, ends in consonant → 을 수) | Inability: 못 + plain verb (present tense)

examples.en: I can go to the café today.
examples.note: 가다 → stem 가 (ends in vowel) → 갈 수 있어요. Open door: the possibility exists today.

examples.en: I can eat spicy food.
examples.note: 먹다 → stem 먹 (ends in consonant ㄱ) → 먹을 수 있어요. Stating ability: I'm capable of eating spicy food.

examples.en: I can speak a little Korean.
examples.note: 하다 → stem 하 (ends in vowel) → 할 수 있어요. Modest ability claim — very useful for newcomers.

examples.en: I can't go today.
examples.note: 못 blocks 가요 from the front. Notice: 못 가요, NOT 못 가해요 — 가다 is not a 하다-verb so no 해요 added.

examples.en: I can't drink alcohol.
examples.note: 못 + 마셔요. A real-life sentence for politely declining alcohol — essential for daily life in Korea.

a.en: I cannot go. (no possibility)

b.en: I can't go. (blocked — circumstance or rule)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both mean inability but with a slight nuance. 갈 수 없어요 = the possibility doesn't exist (like a road is closed). 못 가요 = something is blocking it — often external circumstances, schedules, or physical restrictions. In conversation, 못 가요 feels more natural and casual; 갈 수 없어요 sounds a bit more formal or definitive.

a.en: I can speak Korean. (general ability)

b.en: I can't speak Korean. (inability — 하다 verb!)

contrastPairs.explanation: 하다 verbs are special with 못: 못 해요 (not 못 하해요). The 하 merges with 못: 한국어를 못 해요. Compare 못 가요 (for 가다) — no extra 해요. This is the #1 mistake beginners make with 못.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 한국어를 못 해요. / 한국어를 못 말해요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Actually both forms exist — 못 말해요 (can't speak/say) and 못 해요 (can't do it) are both grammatically fine. The real pitfall is 못 가해요 for 가다: learners wrongly apply the 하다 pattern to regular verbs. 가다 is NOT a 하다 verb, so 못 가요 is correct, 못 가해요 is wrong. Only 하다 verbs (공부하다, 운동하다, 전화하다) use 못 해요.

exceptions: 하다 verbs with 못: 공부 못 해요, 운동 못 해요, 전화 못 해요 — the 하다 part becomes 해요, and 못 goes before the whole expression or between the noun and 해요.
ㄹ irregular in 수 있어요: 알다 → 알 수 있어요 (not 알을 수 있어요); 만들다 → 만들 수 있어요.
살다 (to live) → 살 수 있어요 (the ㄹ already ends the stem — just add 수 있어요).

exampleSentence.en: I want to eat something that isn't spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 먹고 싶어요 — desire form; essential at Korean restaurants for dietary preferences

exampleSentence.en: I want to drink coffee.
exampleSentence.note: 마시 + 고 싶어요 — the stem ends in a vowel so 고 attaches cleanly

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 내일 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: Two patterns in one sentence: 못 가요 (blocked today) vs 갈 수 있어요 (open tomorrow)

exampleSentence.en: I want to speak Korean well.
exampleSentence.note: 하 + 고 싶어요 — long-term aspiration; note that 못 for 하다 = 못 해요, NOT 못 하해요

exampleSentence.en: I can speak in Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 말하다 → stem 말하 + ㄹ 수 있어요 → 말할 수 있어요; often used to express language ability

extendedVocabulary.english: to be able to eat / can eat

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can eat spicy food.
exampleSentence.note: 먹 (consonant ending stem) + 을 수 있어요 — consonant stems take 을 수, vowel stems take ㄹ 수

exampleSentence.ko: 이 음식은 너무 매워서 못 먹어요.
exampleSentence.en: This food is too spicy so I can't eat it.
exampleSentence.note: 맵다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 매워서 (not 맵어서) — important for describing food limitations

exampleSentence.en: It's okay even if it's a little spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮아요 alone works as 'it's fine'; combined with 먹을 수 있어요 context it reassures the other person

exampleSentence.en: I know a little Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 알다 is ㄹ-irregular: 알 + 아요 = 알아요. For ability: 알 수 있어요 (stem already ends in ㄹ so no extra ㄹ added)

exampleSentence.en: Can you come to the party today?
exampleSentence.note: 오다 → stem 오 (vowel) → 올 수 있어요? A common social question — the ㄹ is added to the vowel stem

exampleSentence.en: I want to rest a bit today.
exampleSentence.note: 쉬 + 고 싶어요 — expressing the very human desire for rest; common in daily conversation

exampleSentence.en: Lately I'm busy so I can't exercise.
exampleSentence.note: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb: 못 + 해요 = 못 해요. The noun 운동 and 못 해요 can be separated: 운동 못 해요.

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘 시간이 있어요? 같이 밥 먹고 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: Do you have time today? I want to eat together.
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있어요 is the natural Korean way to say 'have time' — pairs perfectly with 고 싶어요 for invitations

exampleSentence.en: I'm too busy today so I can't go.
exampleSentence.note: 바쁘다 is ㅡ-irregular: 바빠서 (not 바쁘어서). Used constantly as a reason for 못 + verb

exampleSentence.en: What do you want to order?
exampleSentence.note: 주문하 + 고 싶어요 — essential restaurant phrase; 주문하다 is a 하다 verb

exampleSentence.ko: 아직 한국어를 다 이해할 수 없어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't understand all Korean yet.
exampleSentence.note: 이해하다 → 이해할 수 없어요 — a humble and accurate self-assessment for language learners

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 다음에 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go next time.
exampleSentence.note: 못 always goes BEFORE the verb. It's not a sentence ending — it's a pre-verb blocker. 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 못 마셔요.

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihye invites her coworker Minsu to dinner at a Korean BBQ restaurant

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 민수 씨, 오늘 저녁에 삼겹살 먹고 싶지 않아요?
lines.romanization: Minsu ssi, oneul jeonyeoge samgyeopsal meokgo sipji anhayo?
lines.en: Minsu, don't you want to eat samgyeopsal this evening?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶지 않아요? — negative form of 먹고 싶어요, used as a soft invitation. Literally 'don't you want to eat?' — gentler than a direct 먹고 싶어요?

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 네, 먹고 싶어요! 어디에서 먹을 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Ne, meokgo sipeoyo! Eodiese meogeul su isseoyo?
lines.en: Yes, I want to eat it! Where can we eat it?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶어요 (desire) + 먹을 수 있어요 (possibility) — two separate patterns in two sentences. 먹 ends in a consonant so 을 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 회사 근처에 좋은 식당이 있어요. 7시에 갈 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Hoesa geuncheoe joeun sikdangi isseoyo. Ilgop-ssie gal su isseoyo?
lines.en: There's a good restaurant near the office. Can you go at 7?
lines.grammarNote: 갈 수 있어요? — open-door question: is your door open at 7? 가다 stem 가 (vowel) → 갈 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 7시는 좀... 오늘 회의가 있어서 6시까지 못 가요.
lines.romanization: Ilgop-ssineun jom... oneul hoeuiga isseoseo yeoseot-ssikkaji mot gayo.
lines.en: 7 o'clock is a bit... I have a meeting today so I can't go until 6.
lines.grammarNote: 못 가요 — locked door: the meeting blocks him. 못 directly precedes the verb stem 가요. Note: NOT 못 가해요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.en: Then how about 8 o'clock? I can wait.
lines.grammarNote: 기다릴 수 있어요 — 기다리다 stem 기다리 (vowel) → 기다릴 수 있어요. She's reassuring him by stating her own capability to wait.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 감사해요! 그런데 저는 너무 매운 것은 못 먹어요.
lines.romanization: Gamsahaeyo! Geureonde jeoneun neomu maeun geoseun mot meogeoyo.
lines.en: Thank you! But I can't eat things that are too spicy.
lines.grammarNote: 못 먹어요 — locked door for spicy food: a dietary limitation. This is 못 + 먹어요 (plain verb form). Useful for communicating food restrictions.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 거기서 맵지 않은 것도 먹을 수 있어요.
lines.romanization: Gwaenchanhayo. Geogiseo maepji aneun geotdo meogeul su isseoyo.
lines.en: That's okay. You can also eat non-spicy things there.
lines.grammarNote: 먹을 수 있어요 — open door: the possibility exists. 먹 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을 수 있어요. She's reassuring with an ability/option statement.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.romanization: Wanjeon joayo! Yeodeol-ssie sikdang apeseo mannayo.
lines.en: Sounds perfect! Let's meet in front of the restaurant at 8.
lines.grammarNote: No grammar notes needed — 만나요 is a Chapter 6 review. Notice how want (먹고 싶어요), can (먹을 수 있어요), and can't (못 먹어요) all appeared naturally in this conversation.

readingText.title: 단체 채팅방 — 이번 주말에 뭐 할 수 있어요? (Group Chat — What can everyone do this weekend?)
readingText.body:
지은: 이번 주말에 같이 한강에 가고 싶어요. 다들 어때요?
유진: 저도 가고 싶어요! 토요일에 갈 수 있어요.
다니엘: 저는 토요일에 일이 있어서 못 가요. 일요일은 갈 수 있어요.
지은: 그럼 일요일에 가요! 자전거도 탈 수 있어요?
유진: 저는 자전거를 탈 수 있어요. 재미있겠다!
다니엘: 저는 자전거를 잘 못 타요. 천천히 가도 돼요?
지은: 물론이죠! 천천히 가고 싶은 사람도 있어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jieun: I want to go to the Han River together this weekend. What does everyone think?
Yujin: I want to go too! I can go on Saturday.
Daniel: I have work on Saturday so I can't go. I can go on Sunday.
Jieun: Then let's go on Sunday! Can you also ride bikes?
Yujin: I can ride a bike. That sounds fun!
Daniel: I can't ride a bike well. Is it okay if we go slowly?
Jieun: Of course! There are also people who want to go slowly.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why can't Daniel go on Saturday?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 일이 있어서 못 가요 — he has work, so something is blocking him (못 = locked door).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Daniel say about bike riding, and how does he express it?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 자전거를 잘 못 타요 — he can't ride a bike well. He uses 못 before 타요 (ride) to express inability. 잘 못 = 'not well' (not exactly the same as 전혀 못 = 'can't at all').

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 고 싶어요, ㄹ/을 수 있어요, and 못 in the text. For each one, identify which grammar pattern it is and explain why that specific pattern is used instead of the others.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 고 싶어요 (desire): 한강에 가고 싶어요 (Jieun wants to go — her desire), 저도 가고 싶어요 (Yujin shares the desire), 천천히 가고 싶은 사람도 있어요 (people who want to go slowly — desire modifier). | 수 있어요 (ability/possibility): 토요일에 갈 수 있어요 (Yujin: the door is open Saturday), 일요일은 갈 수 있어요 (Daniel: Sunday door is open), 자전거도 탈 수 있어요? (is the door open for biking?), 자전거를 탈 수 있어요 (Yujin: yes, open door). | 못 (inability): 토요일에 못 가요 (Daniel: work blocks Saturday — locked door), 자전거를 잘 못 타요 (Daniel: skill gap blocks him).

culturalNote.title: 못 해요 as the polite Korean refusal
culturalNote.body: In Korean social culture, saying you 'can't' do something (못 해요) is often more polite and face-saving than saying you 'don't want to' (싶지 않아요). If someone invites you somewhere you don't want to go, saying 오늘 못 가요 (I can't go today) is a softer decline than 가고 싶지 않아요 (I don't want to go), which can sound blunt or even rude. This is why Koreans sometimes use 못 해요 even when the real reason is lack of desire, not inability. When you start hearing 못 해요 in Korean conversations, know that it often carries the social function of a gentle 'no' — not necessarily a factual statement about impossibility.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 초밥을 먹___ 싶어요. (I want to eat sushi.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고 싶어요 requires 고 between the verb stem and 싶어요. The stem of 먹다 is 먹, so: 먹고 싶어요. 을 would start the ability form (먹을 수 있어요), and 는 is a topic marker — neither makes sense here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘 회의가 있어서 ___ 가요. (I can't go because I have a meeting today.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 expresses inability blocked by circumstances (the meeting). 안 가요 = 'I don't go / I won't go' (choice or habit, not inability). 고 싶지 않아요 = 'I don't want to go' (lack of desire). Only 못 captures 'I'm blocked — I can't.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '운동을 못 가해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb. The 못 inability form for 하다 verbs is 못 해요 — NOT 못 가해요 (that mixes in 가다 for no reason) and NOT 못 하해요 (that doubles the verb). The noun and 못 해요 can be split: 운동 못 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I can speak a little Korean.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 말할 수 있어요 = ability/capability (open door). Option A (말하고 싶어요) = 'I want to speak Korean' — that's desire, not ability. Option C (못 말해요) = 'I can't speak Korean' — the opposite of what you want to say. For expressing language ability, ㄹ/을 수 있어요 is the right tool.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I want to rest today, but I can't.'
inlineExercises.correct: 오늘 쉬고 싶어요. 그런데 못 쉬어요.
inlineExercises.hint: You need two patterns: 쉬다 (to rest) with 고 싶어요 for desire, and 못 + verb for inability. The two parts contrast with 그런데 (but/however).

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 매운 음식을 먹___ 수 있어요. (I can eat spicy food.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹다 has a consonant-ending stem (먹, ending in ㄱ). Consonant-ending stems take 을 수 있어요, not ㄹ 수 있어요. ㄹ 수 attaches to vowel-ending stems (가 → 갈 수, 오 → 올 수). 고 would start the desire form — not ability.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your Korean friend says '술 마시고 싶어요?' You can't drink alcohol. What's the most natural reply?
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 마셔요 is the most natural, socially smooth way to decline — it signals inability/circumstances rather than personal rejection, which is more polite in Korean culture. 마시고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to) sounds blunt. 마실 수 없어요 is grammatically fine but sounds formal/stiff in casual conversation. 못 마셔요 is the everyday go-to for dietary or health limitations.

bullets: MAGNET (고 싶어요): Verb stem + 고 싶어요 = desire, a pull toward an action. Always needs a verb — you can't attach it to a noun.
OPEN DOOR (ㄹ/을 수 있어요): Vowel stem + ㄹ 수 있어요 / Consonant stem + 을 수 있어요 = ability or possibility. The path is clear.
LOCKED DOOR (못 + verb): 못 goes BEFORE the regular verb form. For 하다 verbs: 못 해요, never 못 가해요 or 못 하해요.
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 9 introduces 아/어서 and 그래서 — connectors that let you give REASONS for your wants, abilities, and inabilities. You'll finally be able to say not just 'I can't go' but 'I can't go because I'm busy.'

chapters.title: Requests, Permission, And Prohibition
chapters.goal: Ask someone to do something, ask if something is okay, and understand rules.
chapters.scenario: Restaurants, classrooms, museums, stores, and public spaces.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Please help me.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Sure, how can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: May I take a photo?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Sorry, but please do not take photos.

chapters.guidedPractice: Practice 도와주세요, 앉아도 돼요?, 가지 마세요, and 가야 해요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask for help, ask permission, and understand one prohibition.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend plays staff. Learner asks permission before taking a photo or sitting.
chapters.review: Can you separate request, permission, obligation, and prohibition?

beginnerGuide.title: Requests and permission are different
beginnerGuide.body: V아/어 주세요 asks someone to do something. V아/어도 돼요? asks if you may do something. 사진 찍어 주세요 and 사진 찍어도 돼요? are not the same.

beginnerGuide.title: Prohibition is mostly for understanding first
beginnerGuide.body: 지 마세요 appears on signs and from staff. You can use it, but it can sound like an instruction, so beginners should learn to understand it before using it broadly.

beginnerGuide.title: Make requests softer
beginnerGuide.body: 좀 often softens ordinary requests: 좀 도와주세요, 물 좀 주세요, 잠깐 기다려 주세요.

checkpoints: I can ask for help with 도와주세요.
I can ask permission with 아/어도 돼요?
I can recognize 지 마세요 as “please do not.”

hook.situation: You're at a Korean museum and want to take a photo of an exhibit. You try to say 'May I take a photo?' but accidentally say '사진 찍어 주세요' — and the guard now thinks you're asking HIM to take your photo. The difference between asking permission and making a request is one tiny pattern.
objectives: Ask someone to do something with V아/어 주세요 (please do)
Ask for permission with V아/어도 돼요? (may I / is it okay to?)
Understand and use prohibition V지 마세요 (please do not) and obligation V아/어야 해요 (have to)
hook.whyItMatters: These four patterns cover almost every real-life rule situation: museum signs, restaurant staff, classrooms, public spaces. Miss one and you either sound rude, ask the wrong person for the wrong thing, or can't understand why someone is shaking their head at you.

grammarNotes.title: V아/어 주세요 vs V아/어도 돼요? — Asking vs Asking Permission
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 주세요 as a HANDOFF — you're handing the action to someone else: 'DO this FOR me.' Think of 도 돼요? as a TRAFFIC LIGHT — you're asking if the light is green for YOU to act: 'Can I GO?' One is outward (you do it), one is inward (I want to do it).
grammarNotes.formation: Request: Verb stem + 아/어 주세요 | Permission: Verb stem + 아/어도 돼요?

examples.en: Please take a photo (for me).
examples.note: 주세요 = HANDOFF — you are asking the other person to perform the action

examples.en: May I take a photo?
examples.note: 도 돼요? = TRAFFIC LIGHT — you are asking if you yourself are allowed to act

examples.en: Please help me.
examples.note: 주세요 fused with 도와 — asking the other person to give you the action of helping

examples.en: May I sit here?
examples.note: 앉다 (sit) + 아도 돼요? — asking permission for yourself to perform this action

examples.en: Please open the window a bit.
examples.note: 좀 softens the request; 열다 (open) + 어 주세요 = asking someone else to open it

a.en: Please give me water. (asking staff to bring it)

b.en: May I drink water? (asking if I am allowed to)

contrastPairs.explanation: In 물 주세요, the action (giving) belongs to the other person. In 물 마셔도 돼요?, the action (drinking) belongs to you — you're checking if it's allowed.

a.en: Please say it again. (I want you to repeat)

b.en: May I speak in Korean? (am I allowed to?)

contrastPairs.explanation: 주세요 requests the other person's action. 도 돼요? requests permission for your own action. The agent doing the action flips completely.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 사진 찍어 주세요? (trying to ask permission)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'Can I take a photo?' is ambiguous — it could mean ability OR permission. Korean has separate forms. 주세요 with a question intonation does NOT become a permission question; it still sounds like a request. Learners who add '?' to 주세요 sentences confuse their listeners.

exceptions: 주세요 can be softened with 좀: 좀 도와주세요 sounds gentler than 도와주세요
도 돼요? can be shortened in casual speech to 돼요? but beginners should use the full form
With a noun instead of a verb: 이거 돼요? (Is this one okay?) — simplified but understood

grammarNotes.title: V지 마세요 & V아/어야 해요 — Prohibition and Obligation
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 지 마세요 as a RED X SIGN — the kind you see on museum walls: STOP, do not do this. Think of 아/어야 해요 as a MUST-DO CHECKLIST — it is non-negotiable, you need to check this box. Red X stops you; checklist requires you.
grammarNotes.formation: Prohibition: Verb stem + 지 마세요 | Obligation: Verb stem + 아/어야 해요

examples.en: Please do not run here.
examples.note: 뛰다 (run) + 지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition you'll see in museums and schools

examples.en: Please do not worry.
examples.note: 걱정하다 (worry) + 지 마세요 — prohibition used as reassurance between people

examples.en: I have to go now.
examples.note: 가다 (go) + 아야 해요 — MUST-DO CHECKLIST: this is non-negotiable

examples.en: I have to buy a ticket.
examples.note: 사다 (buy) + 아야 해요 — obligation, something required before entering

examples.en: You have to show your admission ticket.
examples.note: 보여주다 (show) + 어야 해요 — staff stating a rule/requirement

a.en: Please do not take photos. (prohibition — don't do this)

b.en: I have to take a photo. (obligation — I must do this)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same topic (photo-taking), opposite instructions. 지 마세요 = stop an action. 아/어야 해요 = require an action. If a staff member says the first, put the camera away; if you say the second, you need proof of something.

a.en: Please don't go. (asking you not to leave)

b.en: I have to go. (I am obligated to leave)

contrastPairs.explanation: Both contain 가다 (go) but with opposite grammar endings. 지 마세요 = prohibition. 아야 해요 = obligation. Real conversation: one person says 가지 마세요 and the other replies 가야 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 가지 않아요. (trying to say 'do not go' as a command)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 가지 않아요 is a neutral statement: 'I don't go / I'm not going.' It is NOT a command or prohibition. English 'don't go' feels like a negative verb to learners, so they reach for 않아요. But Korean prohibition uses 지 마세요, a completely different ending. 않아요 = description; 마세요 = instruction.

exceptions: 지 말다 is the base form; 마세요 is the polite imperative form; 마 is the casual form used with close friends
아/어야 해요 can also be expressed as 아/어야 돼요 — both are correct and equally common
지 않아도 돼요 = do not HAVE to (not obligated) — completely different from 지 마세요 (prohibition)

exampleSentence.en: Please help me!
exampleSentence.note: 주다 (give) fused into a request — asking someone to give you the action of helping

exampleSentence.en: May I take a photo?
exampleSentence.note: 사진 as object — permission asked using 도 돼요?

exampleSentence.en: Please do not take photos here.
exampleSentence.note: 찍지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition on the action of taking photos

exampleSentence.en: May I sit here?
exampleSentence.note: 앉아도 돼요? — vowel ending stem: 앉 + 아도 돼요?

exampleSentence.en: May I go in?
exampleSentence.note: 가 + 아도 → 가도 is absorbed into 들어가도 — entering is checked with permission form

exampleSentence.en: Please open the window a bit.
exampleSentence.note: 열다 + 어 주세요 — asking someone else to perform the opening action

exampleSentence.en: Please close the door.
exampleSentence.note: 닫다 + 아 주세요 — the ㄷ stem is regular here; asking another person to close it

exampleSentence.en: Please speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: 말하다 + 여 주세요 → 말해 주세요 — classic classroom and daily-life request

exampleSentence.en: Please wait a moment.
exampleSentence.note: 기다리다 + 어 주세요 — 리 contracts to 려; asking someone to hold on

exampleSentence.en: Please do not run in the hallway.
exampleSentence.note: 뛰다 + 지 마세요 — common school/museum prohibition sign

exampleSentence.en: Please do not worry.
exampleSentence.note: 지 마세요 used not as a rule sign but as warm reassurance between people

exampleSentence.en: I have to go now. I'm late.
exampleSentence.note: 가다 + 아야 해요 — MUST-DO CHECKLIST: non-negotiable obligation

exampleSentence.en: Please help me (softened).
exampleSentence.note: 좀 before a request softens it — like 'kindly' or 'if you could'; almost always present in polite Korean requests

extendedVocabulary.english: I'm sorry but / I apologize but

exampleSentence.ko: 죄송하지만 여기서 음식을 드시면 안 돼요.
exampleSentence.en: I'm sorry but you cannot eat here.
exampleSentence.note: 죄송하지만 softens a refusal or prohibition — staff use this before giving bad news

exampleSentence.en: I have to buy a ticket.
exampleSentence.note: 표 + 아야 해요 — obligation before entry; common at tourist sites, transit, museums

exampleSentence.en: Please do not eat food here.
exampleSentence.note: Common museum/gallery prohibition — 지 마세요 as RED X SIGN

exampleSentence.en: Please do not touch the exhibits.
exampleSentence.note: 만지다 + 지 마세요 — classic museum rule you will definitely encounter

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihoon visits a traditional craft museum with his friend Sora. They encounter signs and staff along the way.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 소라 씨, 저 사진 찍어도 돼요?
lines.romanization: Sora ssi, jeo sajin jjigeodo dwaeyo?
lines.en: Sora, may I take a photo?
lines.grammarNote: 사진 찍어도 돼요? — TRAFFIC LIGHT: asking if the green light is on for Jihoon's own action of taking a photo

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: I'm not sure either. Let's ask a staff member.
lines.grammarNote: 직원한테 물어봐요 — 한테 is the spoken-language form of 에게 (to/from a person): asking 'to/at the staff member'

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Excuse me! May I take photos here?
lines.grammarNote: 저기요 = 'excuse me' to get attention; 여기서 사진 찍어도 돼요? — TRAFFIC LIGHT for a specific location 여기서

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 죄송하지만 이 구역에서는 사진 찍지 마세요. 저쪽은 괜찮아요.
lines.romanization: Joesonghajiman i guyeogeseo-neun sajin jjikji maseyo. Jeotjjogeun gwaenchana-yo.
lines.en: I'm sorry, but please do not take photos in this section. That area over there is fine.
lines.grammarNote: 찍지 마세요 — RED X SIGN: prohibition on photo-taking in this zone; 괜찮아요 = it's okay (implicit permission for the other area)

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 그리고 저 전시품 만져도 돼요?
lines.romanization: Algeseoyo. Geurigo jeo jeonsipm manjyeodo dwaeyo?
lines.en: Got it. And may I touch that exhibit?
lines.grammarNote: 만져도 돼요? — TRAFFIC LIGHT: 만지다 + 어도 돼요? asking permission to touch

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 아니요, 만지지 마세요. 그리고 음식도 안에서 드시면 안 돼요.
lines.romanization: Aniyo, manjiji maseyo. Geurigo eumsikdo aneseo deusimyeon an dwaeyo.
lines.en: No, please do not touch them. And food is also not allowed inside.
lines.grammarNote: 만지지 마세요 — another RED X SIGN; 드시면 안 돼요 = if you eat it won't be okay — a softer way to express prohibition using conditional

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 감사해요. 저기 사진 구역에서 사진 찍어 주세요!
lines.romanization: Gamsahaeyo. Jeogi sajin guyeogeseo sajin jjigeo juseyo!
lines.en: Thank you. Please take a photo of me in that photo zone!
lines.grammarNote: 사진 찍어 주세요 — HANDOFF: now asking Sora to perform the action of taking the photo for him

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.ko: 네, 찍어 드릴게요! 여기 서 주세요.
lines.romanization: Ne, jjigeo deurilgeyo! Yeogi seo juseyo.
lines.en: Sure, I'll take it for you! Please stand here.
lines.grammarNote: 찍어 드릴게요 — polite form of 찍어 줄게요 (I'll take it for you); 서 주세요 = please stand (서다 + 아 주세요) — another HANDOFF request

readingText.title: 국립 한국 문화 박물관 관람 안내 (National Korean Culture Museum Visitor Guide)
readingText.body: 박물관에 오신 것을 환영합니다. 즐거운 관람을 위해 다음 사항을 지켜 주세요. 전시실 내에서는 사진을 찍지 마세요. 전시품은 만지지 마세요. 음식이나 음료는 드시면 안 됩니다. 어린이는 보호자와 함께해야 해요. 박물관 안에서는 조용히 해 주세요. 입장 전에 가방을 검사받아야 해요. 궁금한 것이 있으면 직원한테 물어보세요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Welcome to the museum. Please observe the following for an enjoyable visit. Please do not take photos inside the exhibition hall. Please do not touch the exhibits. You may not eat food or drink beverages. Children must be accompanied by a guardian. Please be quiet inside the museum. You must have your bag inspected before entering. If you have any questions, please ask a staff member.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does the notice say you must NOT do with exhibits?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 사진을 찍지 마세요 (do not take photos) and 전시품은 만지지 마세요 (do not touch the exhibits)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What must children do according to the notice?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 보호자와 함께해야 해요 — children must be with a guardian (해야 해요 = must/have to)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all 지 마세요 and 아/어야 해요 forms in the text. For each one, say whether it is a prohibition (RED X SIGN) or an obligation (MUST-DO CHECKLIST), and explain why that form is used rather than the other.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 지 마세요 forms (RED X SIGN — stopping an action): 찍지 마세요 (don't take photos — prohibition on visitor action), 만지지 마세요 (don't touch — prohibition). 아/어야 해요 forms (MUST-DO CHECKLIST — requiring an action): 함께해야 해요 (children must be with guardian — positive obligation), 검사받아야 해요 (must have bag inspected — required step). The distinction is key: 지 마세요 blocks an action the visitor might want to do; 아/어야 해요 requires an action the visitor must perform.

culturalNote.title: 좀 — the magic softener every Korean learner needs
culturalNote.body: Koreans almost always add 좀 before a request to soften it: 도와주세요 is fine, but 좀 도와주세요 sounds more polite. 물 주세요 is acceptable, but 물 좀 주세요 is what locals actually say at restaurants. 좀 doesn't mean 'a little' here — it functions like 'if you could' or 'kindly' in English. Foreigners who skip 좀 don't sound rude exactly, but they do sound slightly abrupt or robotic. In contrast, 잠깐만요 (just a moment) and 실례합니다 (excuse me, pardon) are also essential softening phrases. Watch how staff at museums and cafés use 죄송하지만 before every prohibition — Koreans soften bad news first, then deliver the rule.

inlineExercises.prompt: 사진 찍___ 돼요? (May I take a photo?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 어도 돼요? = TRAFFIC LIGHT — asking if YOU are allowed to take a photo. 지 않아도 돼요 would mean 'you don't have to take a photo' (no obligation), and 아야 해요 would mean 'you have to take a photo' (obligation). Only 어도 돼요? asks for permission.

inlineExercises.prompt: 전시품을 만지___ 마세요. (Please do not touch the exhibits.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition. 어도 돼요 would turn this into a permission question. 아야 해요 would make it an obligation to touch, which is the opposite of what a museum sign says.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '사진 찍어 주세요?' (trying to ask permission to take a photo)
inlineExercises.explanation: 주세요 is a HANDOFF — it asks the OTHER person to take a photo. Adding '?' to 주세요 does not transform it into a permission question in Korean. To ask if YOU may take a photo, you need 어도 돼요? — the TRAFFIC LIGHT form.

inlineExercises.prompt: A museum staff member walks up and says something. Which sentence means 'Please do not run in the hallway'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 뛰지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition. 뛰어도 돼요? is a permission question (may I run?). 뛰어야 해요 is an obligation (you have to run). Only 지 마세요 delivers the prohibition instruction you see on signs.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Please help me a bit.'
inlineExercises.hint: 도와주다 = to help. Which pattern asks someone ELSE to perform an action? And which adverb softens requests?

inlineExercises.prompt: 내일까지 보고서를 제출하___ 해요. (I have to submit the report by tomorrow.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 아야 해요 = MUST-DO CHECKLIST — a non-negotiable obligation. 지 않아도 돼요 would mean 'you don't have to submit it' (opposite meaning). 지 마세요 would mean 'please do not submit it' — completely wrong here. Only 아야 해요 expresses the requirement.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '가지 마세요!' and you reply that you must go. What do you say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 가야 해요 = MUST-DO CHECKLIST — I have to go, it's an obligation. 가지 않아도 돼요 means 'I don't have to go' (no obligation), which contradicts your intention. 가지 마세요 would mean 'please don't go' — you'd be repeating your friend's prohibition back to them.

bullets: 주세요 = HANDOFF: V아/어 주세요 asks the OTHER person to perform the action for you
도 돼요? = TRAFFIC LIGHT: V아/어도 돼요? asks if YOU are allowed to perform the action
지 마세요 = RED X SIGN: V지 마세요 prohibits an action | 아/어야 해요 = MUST-DO CHECKLIST: V아/어야 해요 requires an action
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Chapter 10 builds on requests with time expressions — you'll learn to say 'I have to be there by 3', 'I've been waiting since morning', and 'I'll do it until Friday' using 까지, 부터, and 동안.

chapters.title: Travel And Classroom Help
chapters.goal: Ask where things are, use transportation, ask for repetition, and explain confusion.
chapters.scenario: Subway station, taxi, hotel, street, airport, or Korean class.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Where is the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Please say it again.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: I am not sure.

chapters.guidedPractice: Ask where something is, ask someone to repeat, and explain that you do not understand yet.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask where the bathroom or station is, then ask someone to say it again slowly.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend gives a short direction. Learner asks 다시 말해 주세요 or 천천히 말해 주세요.
chapters.review: Can you ask for location and classroom help without switching to English?

beginnerGuide.title: Travel Korean needs repair phrases
beginnerGuide.body: When communication breaks down, phrases like 다시 말해 주세요, 천천히 말해 주세요, and 잘 모르겠어요 keep the conversation alive.

beginnerGuide.title: Ask short, useful questions
beginnerGuide.body: 화장실 어디예요? and 지하철역 어디예요? are natural spoken questions. Adding 이 makes them more complete, but the shorter form is common.

beginnerGuide.title: Range and route
beginnerGuide.body: 부터/까지 helps with time and route: 여기부터 역까지, 9시부터 6시까지.

checkpoints: I can ask someone to repeat slowly.
I can ask where the bathroom or station is.
I can use 부터/까지 for from-to ranges.

hook.situation: You're lost at Seoul Station. You need the bathroom urgently, but the signs are all in Korean. You try 화장실 어디에요? — and a local points down the hall, speaks three fast sentences, and walks away. You caught the direction but not the words. What do you say next?
objectives: Ask where something is using 이/가 어디예요? and 이/가 있어요?
Use 부터/까지 to describe time ranges (9시부터 6시까지) and routes (여기부터 역까지)
Deploy repair phrases — 다시 말해 주세요, 천천히 말해 주세요, 잘 모르겠어요 — to keep conversations alive
hook.whyItMatters: Travel Korean lives or dies on two skills: finding things and recovering when you get lost in a conversation. 부터/까지 turns you from someone who can only ask about single moments ('몇 시에?') into someone who can talk about ranges ('여기서 거기까지 얼마나 걸려요?'). And the repair phrases are the difference between a Korean who keeps talking to you and one who switches to mime.

grammarNotes.title: 부터 / 까지 — From … to … (Ranges in Time and Space)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 부터/까지 as a RULER. Every ruler has a start end and a finish end. 부터 is the zero-end of the ruler — where you begin measuring. 까지 is the other end — where you stop. You can measure time (9시부터 6시까지 = 9 to 6) or space (여기부터 역까지 = from here to the station). A ruler without one end is fine — you can use just 까지 ('until 6') or just 부터 ('from 9 onward') — but using both creates the clearest picture.
grammarNotes.formation: Start-point + 부터 / End-point + 까지 (either or both, time or place)

examples.en: I work from 9 to 6.
examples.note: 두 끝 모두 사용 — both ends of the ruler used for a time range

examples.en: There's class from Monday to Friday.
examples.note: Days of the week can also be range endpoints — 부터 and 까지 work the same way

examples.en: I walk from here to the station.
examples.note: Space range: starting point (여기부터) + ending point (역까지)

examples.en: I'll study starting from now.
examples.note: Only the start end used — 부터 alone means 'starting from this point'

examples.en: How long does it take to Seoul Station?
examples.note: Only the end used — 까지 alone means 'as far as / all the way to'

a.en: Come at 3. (single point in time)

b.en: I'll be there from 3 to 5. (range)

contrastPairs.explanation: 에 pins a single moment — one tick on the clock. 부터/까지 draws a segment between two ticks. Use 에 for appointments ('meet me at 3'), use 부터/까지 for durations ('the shop is open from 10 to 9').

a.en: I go from home to school by bus.

b.en: From home to school by bus.

contrastPairs.explanation: For physical starting places, 에서 (집에서) is more natural than 부터 (집부터). 부터 works but sounds slightly unnatural for concrete departure points. 에서 = 'from' for places; 부터 = 'from' for time and abstract starting points. Both mean roughly the same here, but 에서 is preferred for locations.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I go from school' uses 'from', which tempts learners to use 부터. But 부터 marks the starting point of a RANGE — it needs a destination (까지) or a specific context. '학교부터 가요' sounds like 'starting from school, I go' with no endpoint, which feels incomplete. Use 에 for simple destinations (학교에 가요 = go to school) or 에서 to mean 'departing from' (학교에서 출발해요).

exceptions: For physical locations as starting points, 에서 is more natural: 서울에서 부산까지 (from Seoul to Busan) is preferred over 서울부터 부산까지
오늘부터 (from today) and 지금부터 (from now) are extremely common fixed phrases — memorize both
까지 also means 'even' as an emphasis marker (너까지 = even you), which is different from the range meaning

grammarNotes.title: V아/어 주세요 — The Request Frame & Repair Phrases
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of V아/어 주세요 as a FAVOR TICKET. In Korean culture, asking someone to do something for you is phrased as asking for a favor (주다 = to give). You hand someone a ticket that says what action you want as a gift: '다시 말해' (say again) + 주세요 (please give me that) = 'Please give me the favor of saying it again.' Swap the verb before 주세요 and you get any polite request.
grammarNotes.formation: Verb stem + 아/어 주세요 (아 after ㅏ/ㅗ vowels, 어 after all others; 하다 → 해 주세요)

examples.en: Please say it again.
examples.note: 말하다 → 말해 주세요 — 하다 verbs become 해 주세요; 다시 means 'again/once more'

examples.en: Please speak slowly.
examples.note: Same structure — add 천천히 (slowly) before the request to specify how

examples.en: Please write it (down).
examples.note: 쓰다 → 써 주세요 — essential when you can't hear but can read

examples.en: Please take a photo (of me).
examples.note: 찍다 → 찍어 주세요 — tourist classic; mention what to photograph before the request

examples.en: Please help me.
examples.note: 돕다 is irregular → 도와 주세요 / 도와주세요 (often written as one word) — survival phrase

a.en: Say it again. (statement / very direct)

b.en: Please say it again. (polite request)

contrastPairs.explanation: Without 주세요 the sentence is a statement or a command. Adding 주세요 reframes it as asking for a favor, which is much more natural and polite. Always use the 주세요 form when asking strangers.

a.en: Just a moment. (pause signal)

b.en: Please wait a moment. (explicit polite request)

contrastPairs.explanation: 잠깐만요 is a quick pause signal — common but blunt. 기다려 주세요 explicitly asks for the waiting action as a favor, which is softer and clearer.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes separate the adverb and add 주세요 at the very end after 요: '천천히 말해요 주세요.' But in Korean the verb form before 주세요 must be the plain stem form (말해), not the polite form (말해요). The 요 comes at the very end only once: 말해 주세요, not 말해요 주세요.

exceptions: 도와주세요 is almost always written as one word (not 도와 주세요), because 돕다 + 아/어 주세요 has become a fixed phrase
세요 (shorter form) is used with certain verbs: 앉으세요 (please sit), 오세요 (please come) — these are not V아/어 주세요 but honorific imperatives
주세요 can attach to nouns too: 물 주세요 = Please give me water (no verb stem needed when handing/giving is implied)

exampleSentence.en: Where is the bathroom?
exampleSentence.note: 이 follows consonant-ending 실 — subject particle, not topic particle

exampleSentence.en: How long does it take to the subway station?
exampleSentence.note: 까지 = as far as / to — the end-point of a distance range

exampleSentence.en: Which exit number is it?
exampleSentence.note: 몇 번 = which number — essential for subway navigation

exampleSentence.en: I'll study hard starting from today.
exampleSentence.note: 부터 attaches to the start-point — 오늘부터 means 'from today onward'

extendedVocabulary.english: to / until / as far as (end point)

exampleSentence.en: Until what time are you open?
exampleSentence.note: 까지 after a time = 'until' — perfect for asking business hours

exampleSentence.en: Please say it again.
exampleSentence.note: 다시 placed before the verb — it modifies the action (말하다)

exampleSentence.en: Please speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: 천천히 before 말해 주세요 specifies the speed — add it any time you need less pace

exampleSentence.en: I'm not quite sure.
exampleSentence.note: 잘 모르겠어요 is softer and more natural than just 몰라요 — 겠 adds an element of 'I think / I guess'

exampleSentence.en: I walk from here to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 걷다 is ㄷ-irregular: 걷 + 어 → 걸어요 (ㄷ changes to ㄹ before a vowel)

exampleSentence.en: It takes 30 minutes by bus.
exampleSentence.note: 얼마나 걸려요? (How long does it take?) is a must-know travel question — 걸리다 expresses time cost

exampleSentence.en: Please help me!
exampleSentence.note: 돕다 + 아/어 주다 → 도와주다 (ㅂ-irregular): 도와주세요 is a one-word survival phrase

exampleSentence.en: I'm looking for the subway station.
exampleSentence.note: 찾고 있어요 = currently searching (ongoing action) — useful when you're lost and need help

exampleSentence.en: It's a 10-minute walk from here to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 여기부터 = starting from here — pairs naturally with 까지 for distance ranges

extendedVocabulary.english: over there (that place in the distance)

exampleSentence.en: The bathroom is over there.
exampleSentence.note: 저기 = yonder/over there (visible but farther away). 여기 = here, 거기 = there, 저기 = over there

exampleSentence.en: Go to the left.
exampleSentence.note: 으로 = direction marker (go via/toward). 왼쪽으로 가다 = go left

exampleSentence.en: There's a convenience store on the right.
exampleSentence.note: 에 있다 = something exists in that location — combine direction + 에 있다 to describe where things are

exampleSentence.en: Yes, I understand. Thank you.
exampleSentence.note: 알겠어요 is warmer and more engaged than just 네 — it shows you actually processed what was said

extendedDialogue.setting: Jimin is a foreign learner at Seoul Station. She approaches 민준 (a station employee) looking confused.

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
lines.grammarNote: 저기요 = 'hey' / 'excuse me' to get attention. 화장실이 어디예요? — 이 is the subject particle after consonant-ending 실; 어디 = where

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Go toward exit 3. It's on the right.
lines.grammarNote: 쪽으로 = toward (that direction). 오른쪽에 있어요 = exists on the right side — 있어요 + 에 for static location

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 죄송한데, 천천히 말해 주세요. 잘 이해가 안 돼요.
lines.romanization: joesonghande, cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo. jal ihaega an dwaeyo.
lines.en: Sorry, please speak slowly. I don't understand well.
lines.grammarNote: 천천히 말해 주세요 — V아/어 주세요 request pattern; 잘 이해가 안 돼요 = 'understanding doesn't work well' — natural way to say 'I don't get it'

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 아, 네! 저기 계단 보여요? 계단에서 오른쪽으로 가세요.
lines.romanization: a, ne! jeogi gyedan boyeoyo? gyedaneseo oreunjjogeuro gaseyo.
lines.en: Ah, yes! Do you see those stairs over there? From the stairs, go right.
lines.grammarNote: 계단에서 오른쪽으로 가세요 — 에서 marks the starting point of the movement (stairs → go right from there)

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 알겠어요! 감사합니다. 혹시 지하철 2호선은 몇 번 출구예요?
lines.romanization: algesseoyo! gamsahamnida. hoksi jihacheol 2-hoseon-eun myeot beon chulguye yo?
lines.en: Got it! Thank you. Also, which exit is Subway Line 2?
lines.grammarNote: 알겠어요 = 'I understand' (genuine comprehension). 몇 번 = which number — essential number-question for subway exits

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.romanization: 2-hoseon-eun 5beon chulguye yo. yeogiseo 5beon chulgukka ji georeoseo 3bunieyo.
lines.en: Line 2 is exit 5. It's a 3-minute walk from here to exit 5.
lines.grammarNote: 여기서 5번 출구까지 — 에서 marks departure point; 까지 marks arrival point; 걸어서 = 'by walking / on foot'

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.romanization: 2-hoseon-eun myeot sibuteo myeot sikkaji unhaengha eyo?
lines.en: From what time to what time does Line 2 operate?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 시부터 몇 시까지 — RULER pattern for asking time ranges; 운행하다 = to operate/run (for transportation)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.romanization: 5si 30bunbuteo jajeongkkaji unhaengha eyo. oneulbuteo iyonghae boseyo!
lines.en: It runs from 5:30 to midnight. Start using it from today!
lines.grammarNote: 5시 30분부터 자정까지 — complete ruler range with both endpoints; 오늘부터 이용해 보세요 = 'try using it from today' — V아/어 보세요 = 'try doing'

readingText.title: 서울역에서 온 문자 (Text messages from Seoul Station)
readingText.body:
지민: 민아야, 지금 서울역에 있어. 근데 길을 잘 모르겠어.
민아: 어디 가려고?
지민: 2호선 타려고. 몇 번 출구인지 몰라.
민아: 14번 출구야. 거기서 2호선 홈까지 걸어서 5분이야.
지민: 아, 그리고 화장실도 찾고 있었는데.
민아: 화장실은 1번 출구 왼쪽에 있어. 출구에서 나오면 바로 보여.
지민: 알겠어! 참, 이 역 몇 시까지 열어?
민아: 서울역은 아침 5시부터 자정까지 열어.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jimin: Mina, I'm at Seoul Station now. But I don't really know my way around.
Mina: Where are you trying to go?
Jimin: I'm trying to take Line 2. I don't know which exit it is.
Mina: It's exit 14. From there to the Line 2 platform is a 5-minute walk.
Jimin: Oh, and I was also looking for the bathroom.
Mina: The bathroom is to the left of exit 1. Once you come out the exit, you'll see it right away.
Jimin: Got it! By the way, until what time is this station open?
Mina: Seoul Station is open from 5 AM to midnight.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Which exit should Jimin use to get to Line 2?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 14번 출구 (exit 14). From there it's a 5-minute walk to the Line 2 platform.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where is the bathroom?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1번 출구 왼쪽에 있어 — it is to the left of exit 1, visible as soon as you exit.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every use of 부터 and 까지 in the text. Why is each one used — and why does one sentence use both?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 몇 시까지 열어? — 까지 alone marks the end-point of the opening hours (asking 'until what time'). 아침 5시부터 자정까지 열어 — both 부터 and 까지 appear because Mina is giving the full range: 'from 5 AM (부터 = start) to midnight (까지 = end)'. The first question only needed the endpoint; the answer needed both endpoints of the ruler.

culturalNote.title: 역 문화 — Subway Station Culture in Korea
culturalNote.body: Seoul's subway is one of the world's most navigated systems, and Korean stations are built around the assumption that you might not know where you are. Every exit is numbered (1번 출구, 2번 출구…), and Koreans give directions by exit number — not left or right from the entrance. So when someone says '2호선은 5번 출구예요,' they expect you to find exit 5 on the station map and orient from there. Station staff (역무원) are trained to help and are very patient with foreigners — they will often walk you part of the way. Don't be shy about using 다시 말해 주세요 or 천천히 말해 주세요. Korean station staff hear these phrases from tourists every day, and asking for a repeat is far more respected than nodding and wandering off confused.

inlineExercises.prompt: 9시___ 6시___ 일해요. (I work from 9 to 6.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 부터 marks the start-point (9시부터 = from 9) and 까지 marks the end-point (6시까지 = to/until 6). 에 alone (9시에 / 6시에) would give two single time-points but not express a range. 에서 is for places where actions happen, not time expressions.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다시 말해 ___. (Please say it again.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The V아/어 주세요 pattern uses 주세요 (from 주다 = to give, as a favor). 말해요 alone is a statement ('you say it again'). 주어요 is not a polite request form — 주세요 is the standard polite imperative of 주다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '여기부터 역에서 걸어요.'
