inlineExercises.explanation: 에서 marks where an action happens (a stage), not a destination endpoint. The ending point of a range takes 까지 — '역까지' means 'all the way to the station.' 역에서 걷다 would mean 'walking at the station' (action happening there), not 'walking as far as the station.'

inlineExercises.prompt: A local just gave you fast directions. You didn't catch everything. What do you say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 말해 주세요 (Please speak slowly) is the best repair phrase when the issue is speed. 잘 모르겠어요 (I don't really know) signals confusion but doesn't ask for help. 다시 한 번 주세요 is missing the verb — it would mean 'give me one more time' (like asking for a second serving). 네, 알겠어요 would falsely signal comprehension.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'From Monday to Friday there is class.'
inlineExercises.hint: Which particle marks the start of a range? Which marks the end? What pattern says 'there is'?

inlineExercises.prompt: 죄송한데, 천천히 말해 ___ . (Sorry, please speak slowly.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 말해 주세요 = the complete V아/어 주세요 request form. 말해요 alone = a statement or direct command, which would sound rude to a stranger. 주다 is the infinitive/dictionary form — you cannot end a polite sentence with a bare infinitive.

inlineExercises.prompt: 역 사무소는 오전 9시___ 오후 6시___ 열어요. Which pair of particles fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a time range (opening hours), so you need the RULER pair: 부터 for the start (9시부터) and 까지 for the end (6시까지). 에 alone marks single moments, not ranges. 에서 is for physical locations where actions happen, not time expressions. Mixing 에서 or 에 with 까지 would be grammatically wrong here.

bullets: 부터/까지 = the RULER: draw a line between a start (부터) and end (까지) for time ranges and routes — 9시부터 6시까지, 여기부터 역까지
V아/어 주세요 = the FAVOR TICKET: swap any verb in front of 주세요 for any polite request — 말해 주세요, 써 주세요, 찍어 주세요
Repair toolkit: 다시 말해 주세요 (again), 천천히 말해 주세요 (slowly), 잘 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure) — use these freely and Koreans will respect you for it
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 11 introduces wants and plans — 싶다 (want to), -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (going to / planning to). You'll go from asking where things are to expressing what you want to do there.

chapters.title: Connecting Ideas
chapters.goal: Move beyond single sentences using because, and, if/when, and speaker promises.
chapters.scenario: Explaining reasons, making plans, and connecting daily actions.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Why can’t you go?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I am busy, so I cannot go.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Can you call later?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes, I will call later.

chapters.guidedPractice: Combine two ideas with 아서/어서, then make one promise with ㄹ/을게요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Make one sentence with a reason and one sentence with a condition.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 왜요? Learner answers with one reason sentence.
chapters.review: Can you connect two simple ideas without making a long confusing sentence?

beginnerGuide.title: Longer Korean starts with connectors
beginnerGuide.body: 아서/어서, 고, and 면 let you connect simple sentences. This is how beginner Korean stops sounding like isolated flashcards.

beginnerGuide.title: Reason, sequence, condition
beginnerGuide.body: 아서/어서 gives a reason, 고 connects actions or descriptions, and 면 gives a condition. 바빠서 못 가요, 먹고 가요, 시간이 있으면 전화해 주세요.

beginnerGuide.title: Promise form
beginnerGuide.body: ㄹ/을게요 is for the speaker’s decision or promise: 제가 할게요, 기다릴게요, 전화할게요. Do not use it to predict someone else.

checkpoints: I can connect a reason to a result with 아서/어서.
I can connect two actions with 고.
I can make a simple condition with 면.

hook.situation: You're texting a Korean colleague to explain why you can't come to dinner. You type '바빠 못 가요' — and it works, but it sounds choppy, like two separate broken sentences. Korean has elegant connectors that glue ideas together in one breath: 바빠서 못 가요. One sentence. One smooth thought.
objectives: Use 아서/어서 to connect a reason to its result in a single sentence
Use 고 to chain two actions or descriptions without repeating the subject
Use 면 to express conditions ('if/when'), and ㄹ/을게요 to make a speaker's promise
hook.whyItMatters: Native Korean sounds like a flowing chain of connected thoughts, not isolated flashcards. Once you have 아서/어서, 고, 면, and ㄹ/을게요, you stop sounding like a beginner who pauses between every idea. These four connectors appear in virtually every real Korean conversation.

grammarNotes.title: 아서/어서 — Because / So (Reason → Result)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 아서/어서 as a DOMINO PUSH. The first domino (reason) falls and knocks over the second (result). The push is one-directional — cause comes first, effect follows automatically. You can't flip the dominoes: 못 가요 바빠서 ❌ never works the way English 'can't go because I'm busy' does.
grammarNotes.formation: Verb/Adjective stem + 아서 (if last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ) / 어서 (all others) / 해서 (하다 verbs)

examples.en: I'm busy, so I can't go.
examples.note: 바쁘다 → stem 바쁘 → last vowel is ㅡ → 어서 → but 바쁘 + 어서 contracts to 바빠서 (ㅡ drops before 아/어)

examples.en: I'm sick, so I go to the hospital.
examples.note: 아프다 → stem 아프 → ㅡ drops → 아파 + 서 = 아파서; the reason (sick) pushes the result (going to hospital)

examples.en: I'm hungry, so I eat.
examples.note: 고프다 → 고파서; the hunger is the domino that topples eating

examples.en: I'm sorry for being late.
examples.note: 늦다 → stem 늦 → consonant-final + 어서 = 늦어서; reason (lateness) produces result (apology)

examples.en: It was expensive, so I didn't buy it.
examples.note: 비싸다 → stem 비싸 → 아서 attaches directly; the price was the domino that stopped the purchase

a.en: I was tired, so I went to sleep early.

b.en: I was tired, but I didn't go to sleep early.

contrastPairs.explanation: 아서/어서 means the first clause CAUSES or leads to the second. 지만 means 'but' — the second clause contradicts the first. The domino push of 아서/어서 can never contradict; 지만 always does.

a.en: I don't have time, so I can't meet.

b.en: If I don't have time, I can't meet.

contrastPairs.explanation: 아서/어서 states a real current reason (the domino is already falling). 면 sets a hypothetical condition (IF the domino falls). Use 아서/어서 for actual situations; use 면 for 'if' scenarios.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English allows 'I can't go because I'm busy' — the reason can come at the end after 'because'. Korean 아서/어서 MUST come first: reason clause + 아서/어서, THEN result clause. The domino must be placed before it can push. Putting 아서/어서 at the end is the most common English-speaker error with this pattern.

exceptions: 아서/어서 cannot be used before commands or suggestions: 바빠서 가세요 ❌ (can't say 'because you're busy, please go'). Use 니까/으니까 instead for commands: 바쁘니까 먼저 가세요 ✅
하다 verbs use 해서 (not 하아서 or 하어서): 공부해서, 일해서, 전화해서
있다/없다 use 있어서/없어서 — treat them like normal verbs here

grammarNotes.title: 고 / 면 / ㄹ을게요 — And, If/When, I Promise
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Picture a TRAIN with three cars: 고 is the COUPLING HOOK between cars — it just links them, with no reason or condition. 면 is a SWITCH TRACK — the train only goes down that path IF the switch is set. ㄹ/을게요 is the ENGINEER'S ANNOUNCEMENT — 'I, the speaker, will do this' — it can only describe the speaker's own decision, never someone else's.
grammarNotes.formation: 고: Verb/Adj stem + 고 (no vowel harmony) | 면: stem + 으면 (consonant-final) / 면 (vowel-final or ㄹ-final) | ㄹ/을게요: stem + ㄹ게요 (vowel/ㄹ-final) / 을게요 (consonant-final)

examples.en: I eat and then go.
examples.note: 고 as coupling hook: eating and going are linked sequentially. The hook has no direction — it just connects.

examples.en: This café is cheap and delicious.
examples.note: 고 linking two adjectives (descriptions), not actions — the coupling hook works for both verbs and adjectives

examples.en: If you have time, please call.
examples.note: 있다 (consonant-final ㅅ removed in this form) + 으면 = 있으면; the switch track — call only IF the condition is met

examples.en: If it's expensive, I don't buy it.
examples.note: 비싸다 ends in vowel → attach 면 directly: 비싸 + 면 = 비싸면; the switch determines buying behavior

examples.en: I'll do it. (speaker's decision)
examples.note: 하다 → stem 하 → vowel-final → 할게요; the engineer announces: I, the speaker, will handle this

a.en: I wash up and then sleep.

b.en: Because I wash up, I sleep well.

contrastPairs.explanation: 고 is a neutral coupling hook — it just sequences two actions with no causal link. 아서/어서 is the domino push — washing CAUSES the good sleep. If the second action results FROM the first, use 아서/어서. If they're just two things that happen in order, use 고.

a.en: I'll call later. (my own promise)

b.en: I'll call later. (neutral future plan)

contrastPairs.explanation: ㄹ/을게요 is exclusively the speaker's decision or promise, made in response to the current situation. ㄹ/을 거예요 is a general future statement that could describe anyone. Use ㄹ/을게요 when you're the one committing to do something.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 시간이 있으면 전화할게요. (said about someone else)
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 시간이 있으면 전화해요. / 시간이 있으면 전화할 거예요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: ㄹ/을게요 can ONLY describe the SPEAKER's own first-person decision. English 'he'll call if he has time' cannot use ㄹ/을게요. If you're talking about what someone else will do, use 거예요 or the plain verb form. Using ㄹ/을게요 for a third person is a very common mistake.

exceptions: ㄹ-final verb stems drop the ㄹ before 면: 알다 → 알면 ✅ (not 알으면 ❌), 만들다 → 만들면
고 does NOT change based on tense in the first clause: 먹고 가요 (eat then go) and 먹었고 갔어요 (ate and went) — beginners often incorrectly add past tense to the first clause unnecessarily
ㄹ/을게요 is only 1st-person: 갈게요 (I'll go) ✅ but you cannot use it for 2nd or 3rd person

exampleSentence.en: I've been so busy lately that I want to rest.
exampleSentence.note: 아서/어서 reason → result: the busyness causes the desire to rest

exampleSentence.en: My head hurt, so I went to the hospital.
exampleSentence.note: 아서/어서 domino: the pain is the cause that pushes the result (hospital visit)

exampleSentence.en: I'm tired, so I'll go to sleep early.
exampleSentence.note: 해서 (하다 verb → 해서) + ㄹ게요 (speaker's first-person decision): double connector usage

exampleSentence.en: I'm sorry for being late.
exampleSentence.note: 늦다 (consonant-final 다 → 어서): lateness is the reason for the apology

exampleSentence.en: If it's expensive, I don't buy it.
exampleSentence.note: 면 (condition/switch): buying decision depends on the price condition being met

exampleSentence.en: This restaurant is cheap and delicious.
exampleSentence.note: 고 as coupling hook between two adjectives — just linking, no causal relationship between them

exampleSentence.en: When I arrive, I'll contact you.
exampleSentence.note: 면 (when/if condition) + 할게요 (speaker's promise): the connector and promise form working together

exampleSentence.en: When I arrive, I'll send a text.
exampleSentence.note: 하다 verb + 면 (condition): 도착하 + 면 = 도착하면; paired with ㄹ게요 promise

exampleSentence.en: If you have time, let's eat together.
exampleSentence.note: 있으면 = 있다 + 으면 (consonant-final): the condition is whether time exists

exampleSentence.en: I have a reason, so I can't go.
exampleSentence.note: 있어서 (있다 + 어서): having a reason is the domino that causes not being able to go

exampleSentence.en: I have plans, so I have to leave early.
exampleSentence.note: 있어서 reason: having plans (약속) is the cause for needing to leave early

exampleSentence.en: If it's okay with you, let's go together.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮다 (consonant-final 다 after ㅎ drop → 괜찮 + 으면): switch track — only proceed together if condition of okayness is met

exampleSentence.en: I'll call later.
exampleSentence.note: 나중에 + ㄹ게요: a complete speaker's promise anchored in time; this exact phrase appears in the chapter dialogue

exampleSentence.en: I'll go first.
exampleSentence.note: 먼저 + 갈게요: classic speaker's promise/decision — the engineer announces departure first

extendedVocabulary.english: then / in that case / well then

exampleSentence.en: Well then, if we meet tomorrow, I'll talk about it.
exampleSentence.note: 그럼 as discourse opener + 면 condition + 게요 promise: three connective tools in one natural sentence

exampleSentence.en: If I can't call, I'll send a text.
exampleSentence.note: 못 하면 (못 + 하다 + 면): double negative condition — the inability to call triggers the text promise

exampleSentence.en: If we meet later, I'll explain it.
exampleSentence.note: 면 condition + 제가 설명할게요 (first-person promise): the engineer announces what they'll do when the switch is set

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun texts his friend Yuna to explain why he can't make it to their group dinner and makes promises about what he'll do instead

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.ko: 민준아, 오늘 저녁 같이 먹을 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Minjuna, oneul jeonyeok gachi meogeul su isseoyo?
lines.en: Minjun, can you eat dinner together tonight?
lines.grammarNote: ㄹ 수 있어요 (ability) — 먹다 + 을 수 있어요 because 먹 is consonant-final; sets up the situation Minjun needs to respond to with connectors

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 미안해요. 오늘 너무 바빠서 못 가요.
lines.romanization: Mianhaeyo. Oneul neomu bappaseo mot gayo.
lines.en: I'm sorry. I'm too busy today, so I can't go.
lines.grammarNote: 아서/어서 domino push: 바쁘다 → 바빠서 (ㅡ drops before 어) causes the result 못 가요. The busyness is the falling domino.

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.en: Why? Is something going on?
lines.grammarNote: 있어요 = static existence without a connector; Yuna is asking for the domino (reason)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 회사 일이 많아서 늦게까지 일해야 해요.
lines.romanization: Hoesa iri manaseo neutgekkaji ilhaeya haeyo.
lines.en: There's a lot of work, so I have to work until late.
lines.grammarNote: 많아서 (많다 → 많 + 아서, ㅏ vowel → 아서): too much work is domino 1, must-work-late is the result. Two clauses linked by one push.

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.en: Understood. Then let's eat together next time.
lines.grammarNote: 그럼 is a soft conditional ('in that case then'); suggests an alternative without a hard connector

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 고마워요! 다음 주에 시간이 있으면 제가 살게요.
lines.romanization: Gomawoyo! Daeum jue sigani isseumyeon jega salgeyo.
lines.en: Thank you! If I have time next week, I'll treat you.
lines.grammarNote: 있으면 (있다 + 으면, consonant-final 다 takes 으면): switch track condition. 살게요 = speaker's first-person promise/decision — the engineer announces treating.

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.en: Wow, really? Then I'll wait.
lines.grammarNote: 기다릴게요 = 기다리다 + ㄹ게요 (vowel-final 리 → 릴게요): Yuna's own speaker's promise to wait. ㄹ/을게요 is first-person only — Yuna can say it about herself.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 일 끝나면 바로 연락할게요. 오늘 저녁 맛있게 드세요!
lines.romanization: Il kkeutnnamyeon baro yeollakhalgeyo. Oneul jeonyeok masitge deuseyo!
lines.en: When I finish work, I'll contact you right away. Enjoy dinner tonight!
lines.grammarNote: 끝나면 (끝나다 + 면, vowel-final): condition 'when work ends'. 연락할게요: speaker's promise (하다 verb → 할게요). Two connectors in one message.

readingText.title: 지연 씨의 문자 대화 (Jiyeon's Text Exchange)
readingText.body:
지연: 오빠, 오늘 약속 괜찮아요? 저 요즘 좀 바빠서요.
수호: 아, 그래요? 많이 바빠요?
지연: 네, 이번 주에 시험이 있어서 공부해야 해요.
수호: 알겠어요. 그럼 시험 끝나면 만나요.
지연: 좋아요! 시험이 목요일이에요. 금요일에 시간 있어요?
수호: 금요일은 괜찮아요. 제가 예약할게요.
지연: 감사해요! 시험 잘 보고 연락할게요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jiyeon: Oppa, is our plan for today okay? I've been a bit busy lately.
Suho: Oh, is that so? Are you very busy?
Jiyeon: Yes, I have an exam this week so I have to study.
Suho: I see. Then let's meet when the exam is over.
Jiyeon: Sounds good! The exam is Thursday. Do you have time Friday?
Suho: Friday is fine. I'll make the reservation.
Jiyeon: Thank you! I'll finish the exam and then contact you.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why can't Jiyeon meet today?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바빠서 — she's busy, and specifically 시험이 있어서 (because she has an exam this week so she has to study)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Suho promise to do?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 예약할게요 — he promises to make the reservation (a first-person speaker's decision using ㄹ/을게요)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every connector (아서/어서, 고, 면, 게요) in the text. For each one, explain why that specific connector was chosen over the others.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바빠서요 — 아서/어서 because being busy is the stated REASON (domino) for the uncertainty about the plan. 있어서 — 아서/어서 because having an exam CAUSES the need to study. 공부해야 해요 — no connector; standalone result clause. 끝나면 — 면 because this is a CONDITION ('when/if the exam ends') not a reason. 예약할게요 — ㄹ/을게요 because Suho is making a first-person promise/decision. 연락할게요 — ㄹ/을게요 because Jiyeon is making her own first-person promise. 잘 보고 — 고 as a simple coupling hook: do well on the exam AND THEN contact (sequence, no causal push needed).

culturalNote.title: 바빠서 못 가요 — The Korean art of the soft no
culturalNote.body: Koreans rarely say a blunt '안 가요' (I'm not going) without offering a reason. The 아서/어서 connector does vital social work: it softens a refusal by giving a cause. 바빠서 못 가요 (I'm busy, so I can't go) sounds warmer and less abrupt than just 못 가요. Similarly, making a 게요 promise — 다음에 살게요 (I'll treat you next time) — is a culturally expected gesture when you decline something. It signals that the relationship matters even if you can't make it this time. Native Korean speakers are highly attuned to whether you're giving reasons and making promises, or just flatly refusing. Learning 아서/어서 and ㄹ/을게요 together gives you the social toolkit to say no in a way that Koreans appreciate.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배가 고파___ 밥을 먹었어요. (I was hungry, so I ate.)
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a cause-result relationship: hunger caused the eating. 아서/어서 (고파서) is the domino push connector. 고 would just link the two states without showing cause ('hungry and ate' — but that doesn't explain WHY). 면 is for hypothetical conditions, not real past causes.

inlineExercises.prompt: 씻___ 자요. (I wash up and then sleep.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 씻다 ends in a consonant (ㅅ). 고 is the neutral coupling hook: wash → sleep is a simple sequence, not a causal relationship. 아서 would imply washing causes sleeping (not the intended meaning). 으면 would make it conditional ('if I wash, I sleep'), which is too hypothetical for a daily routine.

inlineExercises.prompt: 시간이 있___ 전화해 주세요. (If you have time, please call.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 (consonant-final) + 으면 = 있으면. This is a condition (switch track): the call should only happen IF time exists. 어서 would state having time as a reason for calling, which works grammatically but changes the nuance to 'because you have time, please call' — less natural. 고 would link having-time and calling as sequential actions, which doesn't make logical sense here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '못 가요 바빠서.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 아서/어서 MUST come first in Korean. The reason clause with 아서/어서 always precedes the result clause — the domino must be placed before it can push. This is the opposite of English where 'because' can come at the end. Putting 바빠서 at the end is the most common error English speakers make.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'It's expensive, so I won't buy it. I'll buy a cheaper one.'
inlineExercises.correct: 비싸서 안 살게요. 더 싼 거 살게요.
inlineExercises.hint: 비싸다 → reason connector → then use the speaker's promise form for both decisions

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says she'll treat you. You want to respond 'Then I'll choose the restaurant!' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 고르다 (to choose) → stem 고르 → ㄹ-final stem takes ㄹ게요 (not 을게요): 고를게요. This is correct ㄹ/을게요 usage — the speaker is making a first-person decision. 고릴게요 (option 2) is wrong spelling. 고를 거예요 (option 3) is grammatically fine but sounds like a neutral future plan rather than an in-the-moment promise/decision in response to your friend's offer.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I'm tired, so let's rest.' Which connector is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: Being tired is the CAUSE of resting — a domino push — so 아서/어서 (해서 for 하다 verbs) is correct. 해면 (option 1) makes it a condition ('if tired, rest') rather than stating the actual reason. 하고 (option 3) just sequences the states ('tired and rest') without showing that tiredness is WHY you're resting.

bullets: 아서/어서 = DOMINO PUSH: reason clause comes FIRST, result follows. Cannot be used before commands. (바빠서 못 가요)
고 = COUPLING HOOK: neutral link between actions or descriptions, no cause needed (먹고 가요 / 싸고 맛있어요)
면 = SWITCH TRACK: hypothetical condition before the result (시간이 있으면 전화해요) | ㄹ/을게요 = ENGINEER'S ANNOUNCEMENT: first-person speaker's promise only (전화할게요)
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 12 introduces 을/ㄹ 수 있다/없다 (ability and possibility) and 아/어야 하다 (obligation) — the grammar that lets you say what you can do, what you can't, and what you must. Combined with the connectors from Chapter 11, you'll express complex situations with ease.

chapters.title: Opinions, Reasons & Guessing
chapters.goal: Give opinions, reasons, and soft guesses the way Koreans actually do.
chapters.scenario: Intermediate — build on the beginner chapters.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was this movie?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Hmm, in my opinion it was a bit boring.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Really? I found it fun, you know.

hook.situation: You just finished watching a Korean film with a friend. She asks '이 영화 어땠어요?' You want to say it was a bit slow — but you don't want to sound too blunt. You try '좀 느려요' and it sounds like you're stating a fact. Your friend raises an eyebrow. In Korean, the difference between 'it IS slow' and 'it SEEMS slow' is one short grammar ending — and natives use the softer version almost every time.
objectives: Use -는 것 같다 to express soft opinions and guesses without sounding arrogant
Use -잖아(요) to remind someone of something you both already know
Use -거든(요) to introduce new background information as a reason or explanation
hook.whyItMatters: At B1 level, the gap between textbook Korean and real conversation is mostly about hedging. Koreans rarely state opinions as bare facts — they soften them with -것 같다, link them to shared knowledge with -잖아, or introduce reasons with -거든. Learn these three endings and you'll immediately sound less like a robot and more like someone who understands Korean social nuance.

grammarNotes.title: -는 것 같다 — Soft Opinions & Impressions
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -것 같다 as a FROSTED GLASS screen in front of your statement. Without it, you're asserting a clear fact everyone can see — blunt and potentially arrogant. With it, you're viewing through frosted glass: 'this is my impression from where I'm standing, but I'm not claiming certainty.' Koreans put frosted glass in front of opinions constantly, especially in conversation.
grammarNotes.formation: Present verb stem + -는 것 같다 | Present adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 | Past verb/adj + -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 | Future + -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 | Polite: 것 같아요 | Spoken: 것 often becomes 거

examples.ko: 이 영화 좀 지루한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i yeonghwa jom jiruhan geot gatayo.
examples.en: This movie seems a bit boring.
examples.note: 지루하다 is an adjective → uses -(으)ㄴ: 지루한 것 같다. If you said 지루해요 alone it sounds like a blunt verdict; 지루한 것 같아요 invites the other person to disagree.

examples.ko: 그 사람 요즘 많이 바쁜 것 같아.
examples.romanization: geu saram yojeum mani bappeun geot gata.
examples.en: That person seems really busy lately.
examples.note: 바쁘다 is an adjective → 바쁜 것 같다. The speaker can see indirect evidence (hasn't replied to texts) but isn't stating a fact — just their impression.

examples.en: I think the delivery is going to be a bit late.
examples.note: Future tense: -을 것 같다 for 늦다 (to be late). Prediction softened into a guess.

examples.ko: 어제 비 온 것 같아요. 길이 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: eoje bi on geot gatayo. giri da jeojeosseoyo.
examples.en: It seems it rained yesterday. The roads are all wet.
examples.note: Past tense: -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 for 오다 → 온 것 같다. The speaker is reasoning from evidence (wet roads), not claiming direct knowledge.

examples.ko: 이 식당 음식이 맛있는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang eumsigi massinneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: The food at this restaurant seems good.
examples.note: 맛있다 behaves like a verb in this construction → present form: 맛있는 것 같다. Used as a first impression before actually tasting it.

a.en: That movie is boring. (direct fact)

b.en: That movie seems boring. (soft opinion)

contrastPairs.explanation: The first sentence states a blunt fact — you're declaring it boring for everyone. The second expresses your personal impression. In Korean conversation, the second form is almost always preferred for opinions about art, food, or people — stating it flat-out sounds harsh.

a.en: I think (they'll/I'll) go. (guess about the future)

b.en: It seems (they/I) went. (guess about the past)

contrastPairs.explanation: The tense modifier changes the meaning completely. -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 = future prediction; -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 = past inference from evidence. Getting this wrong produces a confusing sentence.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English learners apply the verb rule (-는 것 같다) to adjectives. But Korean adjectives use their modifier form: -은 after a consonant stem, -ㄴ after a vowel stem. 바쁘다 has a vowel stem (바쁘-) so it becomes 바쁜. This applies to all adjectives: 크다 → 큰, 좋다 → 좋은, 어렵다 → 어려운.

exceptions: 있다/없다 behave like verbs: 있는 것 같다 ✅ (not 있은 것 같다 ❌)
맛있다/재미있다 follow the same verb rule: 맛있는 것 같다, 재미있는 것 같다
In spoken Korean, 것 almost always contracts to 거: 바쁜 거 같아요 is the natural pronunciation
First-person opinions often drop the form entirely in casual speech: 나는 좀 이상한 것 같아 = '나 좀 이상한 것 같아' or even just '좀 이상한 거 같아'

grammarNotes.title: -잖아(요) vs -거든(요) — Shared vs New Information
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of these two endings as different INFORMATION STATUS tags. -잖아 is a REPLAY button: you're playing back something both of you already have in memory — 'remember this? you know this.' -거든 is an UPLOAD button: you're sending new information the listener didn't have — 'here's something you should now know.' The mistake English speakers make is using them interchangeably, but to Koreans they feel completely different.
grammarNotes.formation: -잖아(요): V/A stem + -잖아(요) | Past: -았/었잖아(요) | Noun: -(이)잖아(요) || -거든(요): V/A stem + -거든(요) | Past: -았/었거든(요) | Noun: -(이)거든(요)

examples.ko: 제 생각에는 좀 지루했어요. 전개가 너무 느리잖아요.
examples.romanization: je saenggageneun jom jiruhaesseoyo. jeongaega neomu neurijana yo.
examples.en: In my opinion it was a bit boring. The pacing is too slow, you know.
examples.note: -잖아요 here: both people just watched the film, so 'the pacing is slow' is shared observable information — the speaker is reminding the listener of what they both just experienced.

examples.en: That was on the news yesterday, you know.
examples.note: Past -았잖아요: reminding the listener of something that already happened that they should know about.

examples.ko: 저는 그 배우를 좋아해요. 연기를 정말 잘하거든요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu baewureul joahaeyo. yeongireul jeongmal jalhageodeunyo.
examples.en: I like that actor. They're just really good at acting, you see.
examples.note: -거든요 here: the speaker is giving a reason the listener may not have thought about. 'Here's my reason — new info for you.'

examples.ko: 나 오늘 못 가. 내일 시험 있거든.
examples.romanization: na oneul mot ga. naeil siheom itgeodeun.
examples.en: I can't go today. I have an exam tomorrow, you see.
examples.note: -거든 (no 요, casual): the friend likely didn't know about the exam, so this is genuinely new information as an explanation.

examples.ko: 왜 화났냐고? 네가 약속 또 깼잖아.
examples.romanization: wae hwanannyago? nega yaksok tto kkaetjana.
examples.en: Why am I angry? You broke your promise again, remember.
examples.note: -잖아: the listener KNOWS they broke the promise — this is a reminder, not new information. That's why -잖아 fits, not -거든.

a.ko: 나 오늘 못 가, 내일 시험 있잖아.
a.en: I can't go today — I have an exam tomorrow, remember.

b.ko: 나 오늘 못 가, 내일 시험 있거든.
b.en: I can't go today — I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

contrastPairs.explanation: Both sentences refuse the invitation, but the nuance differs sharply. -잖아 means 'we both know about this exam already — why are you even asking?' It assumes shared knowledge, and can sound slightly exasperated. -거든 means 'you probably didn't know, so here's my reason' — neutral and informative.

a.en: That actor is good at acting, you know. (everyone can see this)

b.en: That actor is actually really good, you see. (maybe you didn't know)

contrastPairs.explanation: -잖아요 here implies the listener should already know or agree — perhaps they just watched the film. -거든요 implies you're sharing your personal discovery with someone who may not share your view yet.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 학생이잖아요. (사실을 처음 말할 때 — When telling someone for the first time you're a student)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'you know' can introduce either shared or new information. In Korean, -잖아 strictly means the listener ALREADY knows or should know. If you're introducing yourself and saying 'I'm a student, you know' to a stranger, that's new information → -거든요. Using -잖아 to a stranger implies they should have known you were a student, which sounds strange or presumptuous.

exceptions: -잖아 with a question mark (rising intonation) becomes a gentle challenge: '이거 비싸잖아요?' = 'Isn't this expensive? (You agree, right?)'
-거든요 used alone as a full reply (e.g., '그냥 바쁘거든요') can sound slightly defensive or curt — soften with a fuller explanation in formal settings
In very casual speech, -거든 can contract to -거든(요) or even just trail off: '그게 좀... 거든'

exampleSentence.ko: 제 생각에는 이 방법이 더 좋을 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: In my opinion, I think this method is better.
exampleSentence.note: 제 생각에는 = 'in my view' — a standard phrase for introducing soft opinions in conversation

exampleSentence.en: Please share your opinion.
exampleSentence.note: More formal than 생각 — used in meetings, discussions, and written Korean

exampleSentence.en: There's a reason, you see. Let me explain.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 introduces the fact of having a reason as new information, then promises the full explanation

exampleSentence.ko: 그 강의 진짜 지루한 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: That lecture seems really boring.
exampleSentence.note: Adjective → -(으)ㄴ 것 같다: 지루한 것 같다. Bare 지루해요 would sound like a harsh verdict

exampleSentence.en: I found it fun, actually. I rather liked it.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요: introducing a contrasting opinion the other person didn't know you held — new information to explain your reaction

exampleSentence.ko: 이 소설은 전개가 느린 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: I think this novel's pacing is slow.
exampleSentence.note: 느리다 is an adjective → 느린 것 같다. 전개 is commonly used in film and book reviews

exampleSentence.en: I think the ending was a bit disappointing.
exampleSentence.note: 아쉽다 (to feel a lack, to be slightly disappointing) → 아쉬운 것 같다. Softening a criticism with -것 같다 is natural here

exampleSentence.ko: 그 배우 연기 정말 잘하거든요. 꼭 봐 보세요.
exampleSentence.en: That actor is genuinely great at acting, you see. Definitely watch it.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 here shares a personal assessment as new information, then follows up with a recommendation

exampleSentence.en: The acting seems natural.
exampleSentence.note: 자연스럽다 (to be natural) → irregular: 자연스러운 것 같다. The ㅂ irregular applies here

extendedVocabulary.english: to feel a slight lack, to be a (gentle) disappointment

exampleSentence.en: I think the end was a bit unsatisfying.
exampleSentence.note: ㅂ irregular adjective: 아쉽다 → 아쉬운 것 같다. This exact phrase is very common in Korean reviews and casual talk

exampleSentence.en: The protagonist seems a bit too perfect.
exampleSentence.note: 완벽하다 (to be perfect) → 완벽한 것 같다. Common critique in drama reviews

exampleSentence.ko: 그 인물한테 공감하기 어려운 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: I think it's hard to relate to that character.
exampleSentence.note: 공감하기 어렵다 = 'it's hard to empathize' — the -기 turns 공감하다 into a noun, then 어렵다 (hard) applies → 어려운 것 같다

exampleSentence.ko: 개인적으로는 이 영화가 좀 과대평가된 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: Personally, I think this movie is a bit overrated.
exampleSentence.note: 개인적으로 + -것 같다 is a double-hedging strategy very common in Korean — softens with both 'personally' and 'seems'

exampleSentence.en: To be honest, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 after an honest admission: the speaker is sharing the real reason/feeling the listener may not have guessed

exampleSentence.en: It seems everyone evaluates it differently.
exampleSentence.note: Verb → -는 것 같다: 평가하는 것 같다. Using this form for a general observation about people in general is very natural

extendedVocabulary.english: to expect, to look forward to

exampleSentence.en: I had high expectations, so I was a bit let down, you see.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 again here: explaining personal background (had expectations) that the listener didn't know — this is why the disappointment makes sense

exampleSentence.ko: 이 드라마 추천할 만한 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: I think this drama is worth recommending.
exampleSentence.note: 추천할 만하다 = 'worth recommending' → 추천할 만한 것 같다. The -(으)ㄹ 만한 것 같다 construction softens a recommendation

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun and Yujin are having coffee after watching a film at the cinema. They're comparing their reactions.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 유진 씨, 영화 어땠어요? 저는 좀 기대 이하였거든요.
lines.romanization: Yujin ssi, yeonghwa eottaesseoyo? Jeoneun jom gidae ihayeotgeodeunyo.
lines.en: Yujin, how was the movie? Personally, it was a bit below my expectations, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -거든요: Minjun is sharing his honest reaction as new personal information — Yujin didn't know he was disappointed

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 그래요? 저는 꽤 재미있었는데요. 전개가 좀 느린 것 같긴 했지만.
lines.romanization: Geuraeyo? Jeoneun kkwae jaemiisseonnunde yo. Jeongaega jom neurin geot gatgin haetjiman.
lines.en: Really? I found it quite fun. Though I did think the pacing was a bit slow.
lines.grammarNote: -는 것 같긴 했지만: conceding a partial criticism (slow pacing) using -것 같다 in the past; 긴 했지만 = 'though it did seem that way'

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 맞아요! 전개가 너무 느리잖아요. 2시간 동안 뭔가 일어나는 게 별로 없었어요.
lines.romanization: Majayo! Jeongaega neomu neurijana yo. Du-sigan dongan mwonga ireonaneun ge byeollo eopseosseoyo.
lines.en: Right! The pacing really is too slow, you know. Not much happens in those two hours.
lines.grammarNote: -잖아요: both viewers just experienced the film, so the slow pacing is shared observable knowledge — Minjun is nudging Yujin to agree

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 음, 그래도 배우들 연기가 굉장히 좋은 것 같았어요.
lines.romanization: Eum, geuraedo baeudeul yeongiga goengjanghi joeun geot gatassoyo.
lines.en: Hmm, but I thought the acting was really good though.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같았어요: past tense of -것 같다, expressing a personal impression during and after watching

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 그건 저도 동의해요. 특히 주인공 배우가 정말 잘하거든요.
lines.romanization: Geugeon jeodo donguihaeyo. Teuki juingong baeu ga jeongmal jalhageodeunyo.
lines.en: I agree on that. Especially the lead actor — they're genuinely great, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -거든요: Minjun adds this as a reason or supporting fact the listener may not have fully appreciated yet

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 맞아요, 연기가 자연스러운 것 같아요. 억지스럽지 않잖아요.
lines.romanization: Majayo, yeongiga jayeonseureon geot gatayo. Okjiseureopji anjana yo.
lines.en: Exactly, the acting seems natural. It's not forced, you know.
lines.grammarNote: Two different endings: 자연스러운 것 같아요 (soft impression) + 억지스럽지 않잖아요 (shared observable fact — both can see it's not forced)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 그래서 결말이 좀 더 강했으면 좋았을 것 같아요. 솔직히 좀 아쉬웠거든요.
lines.romanization: Geuraeseo gyeolmari jom deo ganghaesseumyeon joasseul geot gatayo. Soljiki jom aswieotgeodeunyo.
lines.en: That's why I think it would've been better if the ending were stronger. Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같아요 on a conditional (강했으면 좋았을 것 같다) softens what would otherwise sound like demanding criticism; -거든요 introduces the honest emotional reaction

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 개인적으로는 저는 이런 열린 결말을 좋아하거든요. 생각할 거리가 많잖아요.
lines.romanization: Gaeinjeoguro neun jeoneun ireon yeollin gyeolmareul joahageodeunyo. Saenggakhal georiga manchanayo.
lines.en: Personally, I happen to like open endings like this, you see. There's a lot to think about, you know.
lines.grammarNote: 개인적으로는 + -거든요 = double personal-framing; then -잖아요 to invite agreement on the 'lots to think about' observation

readingText.title: 영화 보고 나서 (After the Movie)
readingText.body:
유진: 민준 씨, 아까 영화 어떻게 봤어요? 저는 꽤 좋았거든요.
민준: 저는 좀 아쉬웠어요. 기대가 너무 컸던 것 같아요.
유진: 아, 그래요? 전 결말이 인상적인 것 같았는데.
민준: 저는 결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요. 그리고 스토리가 단순한 것 같기도 하고요.
유진: 음... 그래도 배우들 연기만큼은 정말 좋았잖아요.
민준: 그건 맞아요. 특히 주인공 배우가 굉장한 것 같아요. 이제 팬이 됐거든요!
유진: 저도요! 다음에 그 배우 나오는 드라마 같이 봐요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Yujin: Minjun, what did you think of the movie just now? I quite liked it, you see.
Minjun: I was a bit disappointed. I think my expectations were too high.
Yujin: Oh, really? I thought the ending was impressive.
Minjun: I thought the ending felt a bit rushed. And I thought the story was kind of simple too.
Yujin: Hmm... But the acting was really good, you know.
Minjun: That's true. Especially the lead actor seems amazing. I've become a fan, you see!
Yujin: Me too! Next time let's watch the drama that actor's in together.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does Minjun feel about the movie overall? What specific issues does he mention?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: Minjun was disappointed (아쉬웠어요). He thought his expectations were too high (기대가 너무 컸던 것 같아요), the ending felt rushed (결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요), and the story was a bit simple (스토리가 단순한 것 같기도 하고요).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What do both Minjun and Yujin agree on?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: They both agree the acting was great, especially the lead actor (배우들 연기만큼은 정말 좋았잖아요 / 주인공 배우가 굉장한 것 같아요). They both became fans of the actor (저도요!).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every -것 같다, -잖아요, and -거든요 in the text. For each one, explain why that ending was chosen and not one of the other two.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1) 기대가 너무 컸던 것 같아요 — Minjun uses -것 같다 (past: -던 것 같다) to frame his high expectations as a personal impression/self-reflection, softening self-criticism. 2) 결말이 인상적인 것 같았는데 — Yujin hedges her positive reaction as a personal impression (past -것 같다), not a fact. 3) 결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요 and 스토리가 단순한 것 같기도 하고요 — Minjun consistently uses -것 같다 to soften criticisms into impressions. 4) 배우들 연기만큼은 정말 좋았잖아요 — -잖아요 fits here because both speakers JUST WATCHED the film together — the good acting is shared, observable knowledge Yujin is reminding Minjun of. 5) 좋았거든요 (Yujin's opening) — -거든요 because Yujin is volunteering her positive reaction as NEW personal information Minjun didn't know yet. 6) 이제 팬이 됐거든요 — -거든요 because Minjun is sharing a new personal fact (becoming a fan) that Yujin didn't know.

culturalNote.title: 왜 한국인은 항상 '것 같아요'를 쓸까요? — Why Koreans always say 'it seems'
culturalNote.body: If you watch any Korean variety show or drama, you'll notice that Koreans rarely state opinions as flat facts — they're constantly hedging with -것 같아요, -것 같은데요, -것 같긴 해요. This isn't uncertainty or lack of confidence; it's a deep cultural preference for avoiding confrontational directness. Saying '이 영화 별로예요' (This movie isn't great) can come across as dismissive and final — it invites no discussion. But '이 영화가 별로인 것 같아요' opens space for the other person to disagree gracefully. This extends to professional settings too: in meetings, Koreans often frame even strong opinions as -것 같습니다 to maintain group harmony (눈치 culture). Mastering -것 같다 isn't just grammar — it's learning to speak with appropriate Korean social grace.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이 음식이 좀 짠___ 것 같아요. (I think this food is a bit salty.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 짜다 is an adjective ending in a consonant (ㅏ is the vowel but the stem is 짜-, which ends in a vowel — wait, 짜다 has a vowel stem 짜-, so it takes -ㄴ: 짠 것 같아요). Actually 짜다 → ㅏ stem, add ㄴ directly: 짠. The answer form is '짠 것 같아요.' The option '은' triggers when you add it after a consonant-final stem. '는' is for verbs, not adjectives. For adjectives like 짜다 (vowel stem), the modifier ㄴ attaches directly to give 짠.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있___ 거든요. (I can't go today. I have plans, you see.)
inlineExercises.explanation: -거든요 is correct because the speaker is giving the listener NEW information (the plans) as a reason. -잖아요 would only work if the listener already knew about the plans. '-는 것 같아요' expresses uncertainty — but the speaker KNOWS they have plans, so that would be odd.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '그 배우 유명하는 것 같아요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 유명하다 is an adjective (not a verb), so it takes the adjective modifier -ㄴ/-은, not the verb modifier -는. 유명하다 has a vowel-ending stem (유명하-), so the modifier is -ㄴ → 유명한 것 같아요. This is the most common -것 같다 mistake among English learners.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '나 왜 화났는지 알아?' You reply: '어제 네가 약속을 안 지켰___ .' Which ending fits?
options: 잖아 (you broke your promise, as you know / remember)
거든 (you broke your promise, just so you know)
는 것 같아 (you seem to have broken your promise)
inlineExercises.correct: 잖아 (you broke your promise, as you know / remember)
inlineExercises.explanation: -잖아 is correct here. The person you're talking TO is the one who broke the promise — they KNOW they did it. You're reminding them of their own action as the reason for your anger. -거든 would mean 'just so you know you broke the promise' — but they clearly already know. -는 것 같아 would express uncertainty about whether they broke it, which is too weak for this situation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I think it's going to rain tomorrow.'
inlineExercises.hint: This is a future prediction softened into a guess. Which tense modifier do you need on 오다 (to come) — present -는, past -(으)ㄴ, or future -(으)ㄹ?

inlineExercises.prompt: You're meeting a colleague for the first time and want to say 'I'm actually quite good at Korean, you see.' Which is correct?
options: 사실 저 한국어 꽤 잘하는 것 같아요.
inlineExercises.explanation: -거든요 is correct: you're sharing NEW information about yourself that the new colleague doesn't know. -잖아요 would imply they already knew you were good at Korean, which is impossible if you just met. -는 것 같아요 would sound strangely uncertain — 'I seem to be good at Korean?' That doesn't convey confidence; it sounds like you're guessing about your own skill.

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 식당 오늘 문 닫___ 것 같아요. 불이 꺼져 있어요. (That restaurant seems to be closed today. The lights are off.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 닫다 (to close/be closed) is a verb, but here we're inferring a PRESENT STATE from evidence — the speaker means 'it seems closed right now.' The present state is expressed with the adjective-like -(으)ㄴ modifier: 닫은 것 같다 (seems closed). If you used 닫는 것 같다 it would mean 'seems to be in the process of closing,' and 닫을 것 같다 would mean 'seems like it will close (in the future).' The correct reading is current state: 닫은 것 같다.

bullets: -는 것 같다 = FROSTED GLASS: softens opinions/guesses into impressions; verbs use -는, adjectives use -(으)ㄴ, past uses -(으)ㄴ, future uses -(으)ㄹ
-잖아(요) = REPLAY BUTTON: reminds listener of something they already know or should know — shared information
-거든(요) = UPLOAD BUTTON: introduces new background information or a reason the listener didn't have — use this when telling someone something for the first time
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 13 covers indirect speech — how to report what other people said (-(이)라고 하다, -다고 했어요). You'll use the hedging strategies from this chapter inside reported speech, making your Korean sound even more naturally layered.

chapters.title: Society, Culture & Reported Speech
chapters.goal: Talk about society and culture and report what others said.
chapters.scenario: Intermediate — build on the beginner chapters.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Is this an old Korean tradition?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes, they say it is a very important tradition.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Even as society changes, traditions remain.

hook.situation: You're watching a Korean news program and the anchor says '전문가들은 사회가 빠르게 변한다고 했습니다.' You know most of those words — but what is 변한다고 doing? Later your Korean friend texts you '교수님이 내일 시험 있냐고 물어봤어.' Again — what is 있냐고 doing? You're bumping into reported speech, and it's everywhere in real Korean.
objectives: Report what someone said using -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 (said that)
Report what someone asked using -(느)냐고 하다 (asked whether)
Use special honorific vocabulary — 계시다, 드리다, 잡수시다 — with the right people
hook.whyItMatters: Koreans relay other people's words constantly — in gossip, office messages, family updates, and news. If you can't use 다고 했어요 and 냐고 물어봤어요, you're stuck either quoting people with clumsy direct speech or avoiding the topic entirely. Master these two endings and you'll suddenly understand about a third of casual conversation you couldn't follow before.

grammarNotes.title: -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 — Reporting What Someone Said
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 as a TELEGRAM. When you send a telegram, you strip away the politeness, reduce the message to its bare content, and relay it: 'FRIEND / COMING TOMORROW / STOP.' Korean does exactly the same — it drops the polite -요, converts the verb to its plain news-report form, then wraps it in -다고 했어요 to say it came through someone else. The telegram style is always plain Korean — never polite -요 — before 다고.
grammarNotes.formation: Present verb (vowel stem): drop 다 → add ㄴ다고 (가다 → 간다고) | Present verb (consonant stem): drop 다 → add 는다고 (먹다 → 먹는다고) | Adjective / 있다 / 없다: just add 다고 (춥다 → 춥다고, 재미있다 → 재미있다고) | Past tense (any): -았/었다고 (갔다고, 먹었다고) | Noun: -(이)라고 (학생이라고, 친구라고)

examples.en: My friend said she's coming tomorrow.
examples.note: 오다 has a vowel stem (오-), so add ㄴ다고: 온다고. The polite 와요 form is never used before 다고.

examples.en: The team lead said the meeting will be late.
examples.note: 늦어지다 has a consonant stem (늦어지-... no, 지 ends in vowel → ㄴ다고: 늦어진다고). The team lead's own speech gets honorific 하셨어요.

examples.en: The news said the economy is difficult.
examples.note: 어렵다 is an adjective → just add 다고 (no ㄴ다고/는다고). Adjectives always take the simpler form.

examples.ko: 교수님이 그 전통이 아주 중요하다고 하셨어요.
examples.romanization: gyosunimgi geu jeontong-i aju jungyohada고 hasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The professor said that tradition is very important.
examples.note: 중요하다 is an adjective (ends in 하다 but describes a quality) → 중요하다고. The professor's action gets honorific 하셨어요.

examples.en: That person said they came from abroad.
examples.note: 오다 in past tense: 왔다고. Past tense always uses -았/었다고 regardless of whether the original verb is action or adjective.

a.en: Society changes. (direct statement)

b.en: The expert said society changes. (reported)

contrastPairs.explanation: Direct speech is polite 해요 form. Reported speech switches to the plain form: 변하다 (vowel stem 변하-) → 변한다고. You never say 변해요고 했어요 — the polite ending must be stripped before adding 다고.

a.en: The weather is cold. (direct)

b.en: The forecast said the weather is cold. (reported)

contrastPairs.explanation: 춥다 is an adjective. Adjectives always take 다고 directly — no ㄴ다고 or 는다고. If you tried 춥는다고 or 추운다고, it sounds completely wrong.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers naturally think 'she says she's coming → 와요 + 고 했어요.' But Korean reported speech strips the polite -요 ending entirely. You must use the plain dictionary-adjacent form: 오다 (vowel stem) → 온다고. Gluing 고 onto 와요 is one of the most common mistakes at this level — Koreans will understand you, but it marks you as someone who hasn't learned this pattern yet.

exceptions: Nouns use -(이)라고, not 다고: 학생이라고 했어요 (said [he] is a student). After a vowel, 이 drops: 의사라고 했어요.
Commands are reported with -(으)라고 하다: 선생님이 조용히 하라고 했어요 (The teacher said to be quiet).
The verb 하다 at the end can be said as 했어요 (past, said), 한대요 (colloquial hearsay: apparently says), or 한다고 하더라고요 (I heard that...).

grammarNotes.title: -(느)냐고 하다 — Reporting What Someone Asked
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -냐고 as a QUESTION BUBBLE being forwarded. In a messaging app, if someone sends you a question and you forward it to a third person, the bubble still has a question mark inside — that's -냐고. The key rule: if the original sentence had a question mark, use -냐고. If it had a period, use -다고. The question mark decides.
grammarNotes.formation: Any verb stem (action or adjective) + -냐고: 가냐고, 먹냐고, 바쁘냐고, 있냐고 | Past tense: -았/었냐고: 갔냐고, 먹었냐고 | Noun: -(이)냐고: 학생이냐고, 누구냐고 | Reporting verb: 물어봤어요 (asked, natural speech) or 했어요

examples.en: My friend asked if I have time on the weekend.
examples.note: 있다 is a verb → add -냐고: 있냐고. The reporting verb 물어봤어요 sounds natural; 했어요 also works.

examples.en: My mom asked whether I'd eaten.
examples.note: Past tense reported question: 먹다 → past 먹었다 → drop -다 → add -냐고: 먹었냐고. Mom gets honorific 하셨어요.

examples.ko: 면접관이 왜 한국 문화에 관심이 있냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeopgwani wae hanguk munhwae gwansimi innnyago mureobwasseoyo.
examples.en: The interviewer asked why I'm interested in Korean culture.
examples.note: Wh-questions also use -냐고. The question word 왜 (why) stays in place — -냐고 doesn't change its position.

examples.en: The professor asked whether I'd finished the assignment.
examples.note: 하다 in past: 했냐고. The professor's asking gets honorific 물어보셨어요 (물어보다 + -(으)시- + 었어요).

examples.en: She asked who that person is.
examples.note: 누구 is a pronoun — treat like a noun: 누구냐고 (누구 + 이냐고 → 누구냐고 because 누구 ends in vowel, so 이 drops).

a.en: My friend said he's going to Korea. (statement)

b.en: My friend asked if I'm going to Korea. (question)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same base verb 가다. If you're relaying a statement (period), use -다고 → 간다고. If you're relaying a question (question mark), use -냐고 → 가냐고. Mixing them up completely changes the meaning — one is news, the other is a request for information.

a.en: Mom said she's tired. (her statement about herself)

b.en: Mom asked if I'm tired. (her question directed at me)

contrastPairs.explanation: 피곤하다 is an adjective. 피곤하다고 = she stated she is tired. 피곤하냐고 = she asked whether I (or someone else) am tired. The particle switches the entire conversational role.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'asked if' sounds very close to 'said that' — both relay someone else's words. But Korean is strict: 다고 is only for statements, 냐고 is only for questions. If you use 있다고 물어봤어요, you're saying 'asked that I have time,' which doesn't make grammatical sense in Korean and will confuse native speakers. When the verb is 물어봤어요 (asked), the clause before it must always end in -냐고.

exceptions: The fuller written/formal form is -느냐고 for action verbs (가느냐고, 먹느냐고), but in everyday speech this sounds stiff — plain -냐고 is preferred.
Commands relayed as questions use -(으)라고 물어봤어요: 뭐 하라고 했어요? (What did he tell you to do?). Don't confuse this with -냐고.
물어봤어요 (tried asking) is more natural than 물었어요 (asked) in spoken Korean — the 보다 adds a conversational softness.

exampleSentence.en: I think our society is changing rapidly.
exampleSentence.note: 다고 생각해요 = 'I think that...' — reported-thought structure using the same 다고 pattern

exampleSentence.en: My friend said Korean culture is interesting.
exampleSentence.note: 재미있다 is 있다-type → add -다고 directly (adjective rule), not -(느)ㄴ다고

exampleSentence.ko: 이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
exampleSentence.note: 이어 가다 = keep carrying on; present progressive 가고 있어요 emphasizes the ongoing nature

exampleSentence.ko: 선생님이 한국 역사가 아주 깊다고 하셨어요.
exampleSentence.en: The teacher said Korean history is very deep.
exampleSentence.note: 깊다 is an adjective → 깊다고 (plain adjective form + 다고). Teacher gets 하셨어요.

exampleSentence.en: The news said the economy is getting increasingly difficult.
exampleSentence.note: 어려워지다 has vowel stem 어려워지- → ㄴ다고: 어려워진다고

exampleSentence.en: My friend said he has no interest in politics.
exampleSentence.note: 없다 → add -다고 directly (없다고). 없다 is in the same category as 있다 — add -다고, not -는다고.

exampleSentence.en: Experts warned that the environment is gradually getting worse.
exampleSentence.note: 나빠지다 (vowel stem 나빠지-) → ㄴ다고: 나빠진다고. 경고했어요 = warned.

exampleSentence.ko: 부모님이 교육이 가장 중요하다고 항상 말씀하세요.
exampleSentence.en: My parents always say that education is the most important thing.
exampleSentence.note: 중요하다 is an adjective → 중요하다고. 말씀하세요 is the honorific form of 말하다 (말씀하시다), used for parents.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be (honorific for 있다 — a person's presence)

exampleSentence.en: The boss isn't at his desk right now.
exampleSentence.note: 계시다 replaces 있다 entirely when the subject is a person you honor. You CANNOT say 사장님이 있으세요 to mean the boss is present — 계세요 is required.

extendedVocabulary.english: to give (humble — you giving to someone senior)

exampleSentence.en: I gave my parents a gift.
exampleSentence.note: 드리다 is used when YOU give to someone above you. 주다 is the neutral form. 부모님께 uses 께 (honorific 에게).

extendedVocabulary.english: to eat (very honorific for 먹다/드시다 — for very respected elders)

exampleSentence.en: Grandma, have you finished your meal?
exampleSentence.note: 잡수시다 is higher than 드시다 — reserved for grandparents and very senior people. 진지 is the honorific word for 밥 (meal/rice).

extendedVocabulary.english: to say / to tell (humble — you speaking to someone senior)

exampleSentence.en: I explained my situation to the professor.
exampleSentence.note: 말씀드리다 = humble form of 말하다. 교수님께 uses 께 (honorific 에게). Compare: 친구한테 말했어요 (told a friend, plain).

extendedVocabulary.english: to meet / to see (humble — you meeting someone senior)

exampleSentence.en: Would it be possible to see the professor tomorrow?
exampleSentence.note: 뵙다 is the humble form of 만나다/보다 when you are meeting someone you respect. 뵈다 is the spoken short form: 뵐게요, 뵈었어요 → 봬어요.

extendedVocabulary.english: to develop / to advance / to progress

exampleSentence.en: The researchers said technology is advancing rapidly.
exampleSentence.note: 발전하다 has vowel stem (발전하-) → ㄴ다고: 발전한다고. Classic example of the 다고 pattern with a 하다 verb.

exampleSentence.en: I think traditions still exist.
exampleSentence.note: 생각해요 (I think) also uses the 다고 pattern: 존재한다고 생각해요. 생각하다 is another common reporting verb alongside 하다.

extendedVocabulary.english: to participate / to take part in

exampleSentence.en: The teacher said to be sure to participate in the event.
exampleSentence.note: This is a reported command (not statement) → -(으)라고: 참여하라고 하셨어요. Compare with 다고 (statement) and 냐고 (question).

exampleSentence.en: Even as society changes rapidly, traditions remain.
exampleSentence.note: 변해도 = even though (it) changes (-(아/어)도 concessive). 남다 (to remain) contrasts with 변하다 (to change) in this classic Chapter 13 sentence.

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon tells her coworker Minho what she heard at a company meeting and what their boss said

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 민호 씨, 오늘 회의 어땠어요? 저는 못 갔어요.
lines.romanization: Minho ssi, oneul hoeui eottaesseoyo? Jeoneun mot gasseoyo.
lines.en: Minho, how was the meeting today? I couldn't go.
lines.grammarNote: 못 갔어요 — 못 negates the action (couldn't go), past tense 갔어요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 팀장님이 다음 달에 새 프로젝트를 시작한다고 하셨어요.
lines.romanization: timjangnimi daeum dare sae peurojekteureul sijakhanda고 hasyeosseoyo.
lines.en: The team lead said we're starting a new project next month.
lines.grammarNote: 시작하다 (vowel stem 시작하-) → ㄴ다고: 시작한다고. Team lead is respected → 하셨어요 (honorific).

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Really? Did anyone ask how many team members there would be?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 명이냐고 — 명 is a noun (counter), so -(이)냐고: 명이냐고. 물어봤어요 = asked.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 소연 씨가 물어봤어요. 팀장님이 다섯 명이라고 하셨어요.
lines.romanization: ne, Soyeon ssiga mureobwasseoyo. timjangnimi daseon myeongirago hasyeosseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, Soyeon asked. The team lead said it's five people.
lines.grammarNote: 다섯 명이라고 — noun + (이)라고 (not 다고). This is the noun reporting form. Team lead → 하셨어요.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 아, 그리고 교수님이 내일 면담 있냐고 물어보셨어요?
lines.romanization: a, geurigo gyosunimgi naeil myeondam innnyago mureobosyeosseoyo?
lines.en: Oh, and did the professor ask if there's a consultation meeting tomorrow?
lines.grammarNote: 있냐고 — 있다 + -냐고 (reported question). Professor → 물어보셨어요 (물어보다 + honorific -(으)시-).

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 교수님께서 프로젝트가 어떤 방향이냐고 물어보셨어요.
lines.romanization: ne, gyosunimkkeseo peurojekteu ga eotteon banghyanginnyago mureobosyeosseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, the professor asked what direction the project is going.
lines.grammarNote: 방향이냐고 — 방향 (direction) is a noun → 방향이냐고. 교수님께서 = honorific subject marker 께서 (vs. plain 이/가).

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: I'll tell the team lead that I want to participate.
lines.grammarNote: 참여하고 싶다고 — 싶다 is an adjective → add 다고 directly. 말씀드릴게요 = humble 말하다 (I speaking to someone senior).

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 좋아요! 팀장님이 지금 사무실에 계세요. 바로 말씀드려요.
lines.romanization: joayo! timjangnimi jigeum samusire gyeseyo. baro malsseumdeuryeoyo.
lines.en: Great! The team lead is in the office right now. Tell them right away.
lines.grammarNote: 계세요 = honorific 있다 (person present → 계시다, not 있으세요). 말씀드려요 = humble command (you telling someone senior).

readingText.title: 단체 카톡 (Group KakaoTalk Chat)
readingText.body:
지훈: 방금 교수님이 내일 발표가 없어진다고 하셨어. 다들 들었어?

수현: 진짜? 나는 못 들었는데. 왜 없어지냐고 물어봤어?

지훈: 응, 소연이가 물어봤는데 교수님이 다음 주로 미룬다고 하셨어.

수현: 다행이다! 그럼 우리 오늘 공부 안 해도 되겠다.

소연: 아, 근데 교수님이 대신 에세이 제출하라고 하셨어. 다음 주 월요일까지.

수현: 어머, 그건 물어봤을 때 왜 말 안 해줬어? ㅋㅋ

지훈: 죄송... 교수님이 준비가 돼야 한국 사회와 문화를 이해할 수 있다고도 하셨어.

소연: 맞아요, 교수님께서 한국 전통이 현대 사회에서 어떻게 발전하고 존재하는지 생각해 보라고도 하셨어.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jihoon: The professor just said tomorrow's presentation is cancelled. Did everyone hear?

Suhyeon: Really? I didn't hear. Did anyone ask why it's cancelled?

Jihoon: Yeah, Soyeon asked and the professor said it's being pushed to next week.

Suhyeon: What a relief! So we don't have to study today.

Soyeon: Oh, but the professor said to submit an essay instead. By next Monday.

Suhyeon: Oh no, why didn't you say that when I asked? lol

Jihoon: Sorry... The professor also said that you need to be prepared to understand Korean society and culture.

Soyeon: Right, the professor also said to think about how Korean traditions develop and exist in modern society.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What did the professor say about tomorrow's presentation?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 교수님이 내일 발표가 없어진다고 하셨어 — The professor said tomorrow's presentation is cancelled (pushed to next week).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What did Soyeon report about the essay?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 교수님이 대신 에세이 제출하라고 하셨어 — The professor said to submit an essay instead by next Monday. Note this uses -(으)라고 (reported command), not -다고 (statement).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all instances of -다고 하다, -냐고 물어보다, and -(으)라고 하다 in the text. Why does each one use the form it uses?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 다고 하셨어 (×3): 없어진다고 (발표가 없어지다 = action verb, vowel stem → ㄴ다고), 미룬다고 (미루다 = action verb, vowel stem → ㄴ다고), 이해할 수 있다고 (있다 → 있다고, adjective/있다 rule). | 냐고 물어봤어: 없어지냐고 — relaying a question (original had a question mark) → -냐고. | 라고 하셨어 (×2): 제출하라고, 생각해 보라고 — both relay commands (imperatives) → -(으)라고. The ending matches the type of sentence being relayed: period → 다고, question mark → 냐고, command → (으)라고.

culturalNote.title: The Honorific Gap — Why Koreans Switch Vocabulary Completely
culturalNote.body: Most languages add a polite prefix or suffix to show respect. Korean does that too (-(으)시-), but for the most common, everyday verbs, Korean uses entirely different words. When your grandmother is home, she isn't 있어요 — she's 계세요. When you give something to your boss, you don't 줘요 — you 드려요. When grandpa eats, he doesn't 먹어요 — he 잡수세요. This system, called 높임말 (honorific speech), has deep roots in Korea's Confucian social hierarchy. Understanding it matters not just for politeness but for comprehension: if you only know the plain forms, you'll be lost in conversations involving elders, bosses, or customers. The safest rule for beginners: when speaking TO or ABOUT someone you must honor, mentally scan your sentence for 있다, 먹다, and 주다 — those three are the most frequently tripped-over, and swapping them to 계시다, 드시다/잡수시다, and 드리다 will immediately raise your Korean to a more respectful level.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 내일 학교에 ___ 했어요. (My friend said she's going to school tomorrow.) — choose: 가요고 / 간다고 / 가다고
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 has a vowel stem (가-). Present action verb with vowel stem → add ㄴ다고: 간다고. '가요고' is the most common mistake — you can never attach 고 to the polite -요 form for reported speech. '가다고' would only work if 가다 were an adjective, but it's an action verb.

inlineExercises.prompt: 엄마가 피곤하냐고 / 피곤하다고 물어봤어요. (Mom asked whether I was tired.) — choose the correct form.
inlineExercises.explanation: 물어봤어요 means 'asked' — the clause before it must be a reported question, so use -냐고. '피곤하다고 물어봤어요' is a contradiction: 다고 reports a statement, but 물어봤어요 reports a question. Native speakers will immediately sense that something is off.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '교수님이 어디에 있으세요?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 있으세요 is acceptable for respected people's possessions or states (질문 있으세요? = Do you have a question?), but for a respected PERSON'S physical presence, 계시다 is required. 있으세요 for a person's location sounds awkward and slightly disrespectful to Korean ears — always use 계세요 when asking or saying where a respected person is.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your colleague relays this: '팀장님이 오늘 회의가 취소됐___ 하셨어요.' What ending goes in the blank?
inlineExercises.explanation: 취소됐다 is a verb in past tense — it's a statement of fact (the meeting is cancelled), not a question or a command. Statements → -다고. Past tense: 취소됐다 → 취소됐다고. '냐고' would mean the team lead asked if it was cancelled — different meaning. '(으)라고' would mean the team lead commanded someone to cancel it — again, different.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'My friend asked if I like Korean culture.'
inlineExercises.hint: 좋아하다 is an action verb (not adjective). The question is reported, so which ending do you need? Which verb means 'asked' in Korean?

inlineExercises.prompt: 할머니께 생일 선물을 ___ 요. (I gave a birthday present to my grandmother.) — choose: 줬어 / 드렸어
inlineExercises.explanation: 드리다 is the humble form of 주다 used when YOU give something to someone you respect. 줬어요 is perfectly grammatical but sounds flat and somewhat rude toward a grandmother. Koreans expect 드렸어요 in this context — using 줬어요 for a grandparent will strike them as unnatural, even if technically understood.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct Korean?
inlineExercises.explanation: '할아버지가 있으세요' combines the wrong subject marker (가 instead of 께서) with the wrong presence verb (있으세요 instead of 계세요). '할아버지께서 있어요' uses 께서 correctly but forgets to honor grandpa's presence with 계시다. The fully correct form uses 께서 (honorific subject marker) and 계세요 (honorific form of 있다 for a person's presence) together.

bullets: -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 = TELEGRAM: strip the polite -요, use plain verb form + 다고 to relay statements (verbs: 간다고, 먹는다고; adjectives: 춥다고; nouns: 학생이라고; past: 갔다고)
-(느)냐고 하다 = QUESTION BUBBLE: if the original had a question mark, use -냐고 + 물어봤어요 (가냐고, 바쁘냐고, 있냐고, 명이냐고)
Special honorific words: 있다→계시다 (person present), 주다→드리다 (you giving up), 먹다→잡수시다 (very senior eating) — memorize these swaps, they come up every day
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 14 introduces -아/어 보다 (try doing), -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 (almost did), and expressing regret — the tools for talking about attempts, near-misses, and lessons learned.

chapters.title: Work, Money & Decisions
chapters.goal: Discuss work and money, and talk about plans and worries.
chapters.scenario: Intermediate — build on the beginner chapters.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 저 이번에 새 사업을 시작하기로 했어요.
dialogue.romanization: jeo ibeone sae saeobeul sijakagiro haesseoyo.
dialogue.en: I have decided to start a new business.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 정말요? 잘 안될까 봐 걱정되진 않아요?
dialogue.romanization: jeongmaryo? jal andoelkka bwa geokjeongdoejin anayo?
dialogue.en: Really? Aren't you worried it might not go well?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: A little. But I am going to give it a try.

hook.situation: You're talking to a Korean colleague about your future plans. You want to say 'I decided to start my own business' — but you accidentally say something that sounds like you're making a promise on the spot, not announcing a settled decision. Then they ask if you're worried, and you want to express 'I'm afraid it might fail' — but you use the wrong pattern and it sounds like you're asking a question. These three patterns (기로 하다, -(으)ㄹ까 봐, -게 되다) define how Koreans talk about plans, worries, and how things unfold — and mixing them up sends completely wrong signals.
objectives: Use -기로 하다 to announce a firm decision or agreed-upon plan
Use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 to express worry or fear about an unwanted outcome
Use -게 되다 to describe how a situation came about through circumstances, not pure choice
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns appear constantly in adult Korean conversations about work, life decisions, and relationships. -기로 했어요 is how you announce plans. -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is how you express anxiety without sounding dramatic. -게 됐어요 is how Koreans modestly describe their own successes — saying 'it turned out that way' rather than 'I chose this.' Native speakers use -게 됐어요 constantly to soften good news. After this chapter you will sound like someone who actually thinks in Korean, not just translates from English.

grammarNotes.title: -기로 하다 — Committing to a Decision
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -기로 하다 as signing a CONTRACT with yourself (or someone else). The ink is already dry — the decision has been made. Compare this to -(으)ㄹ게요 (an on-the-spot promise you make to the listener, like saying 'I will' in the moment). 기로 했어요 = 'I already signed that contract.' It always points backward to a decision already locked in.
grammarNotes.formation: Verb stem + 기로 하다 → usually past: 기로 했어요 (decided to). Negative: -지 않기로 하다 (decided NOT to)

examples.ko: 저 이번에 새 사업을 시작하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jeo ibeone sae saeobeul sijakagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: I have decided to start a new business this time.
examples.note: 시작하다 → 시작하기로 했어요: the contract is signed — this is an announcement of a settled plan, not a new promise

examples.ko: 우리 다음 주에 같이 만나기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: uri daeum jue gati mannagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We agreed to meet together next week.
examples.note: 만나다 → 만나기로 했어요: a mutual agreement — both parties signed the same contract

examples.en: I decided to quit smoking starting this year.
examples.note: 끊다 → 끊기로 했어요: a personal resolution — the decision was made before this conversation

examples.en: I decided to join that company.
examples.note: 입사하다 → 입사하기로 했어요: announcing a career decision already made, not asking for the listener's input

examples.en: I decided to rest this weekend.
examples.note: 쉬다 → 쉬기로 했어요: even a small personal plan counts as a 'contract' when using 기로 하다

a.en: I decided (agreed) to come early tomorrow.

b.en: I will come early tomorrow (I promise you now).

contrastPairs.explanation: 기로 했어요 = you're reporting a decision already made, possibly with others. -(으)ㄹ게요 = you're making the promise right now, in this conversation, TO the listener. Using -(으)ㄹ게요 when you should use 기로 했어요 sounds like you hadn't decided until just that moment.

a.en: I decided to do this work. (already decided)

b.en: I will do this work. (statement about the future)

contrastPairs.explanation: 기로 했어요 implies agency — you deliberately chose. 할 거예요 is a neutral future statement with no sense of decision-making. When announcing plans to colleagues, 기로 했어요 carries more weight.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses 'I will start a business' for both a settled decision and an on-the-spot promise. Korean distinguishes them. -(으)ㄹ게요 in Korean is specifically a promise you're making to the listener right now — using it to announce a major life decision sounds odd, as if you just decided this second because of them. 기로 했어요 is what you want: 'I've already decided, and I'm telling you about it.'

exceptions: 기로 하다 can be present tense: 기로 해요 (we're agreeing right now, as a plan is being made together)
Negative: -지 않기로 했어요 (decided not to): 그 사람한테 연락하지 않기로 했어요 (I decided not to contact that person)
Stronger resolve: 기로 마음먹었어요 (I made up my mind to) — literally 'ate the decision in my heart'

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 — Worry-Driven Reason
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -(으)ㄹ까 봐 as a WORST-CASE WINDOW — you're looking through a window at the bad thing that might happen, and that fear is what drives your action. The structure is: [feared outcome]-ㄹ까 봐 + [what you did/are doing because of that fear]. It's the grammar of anxiety: 'I was afraid X would happen, so I did Y.'
grammarNotes.formation: Verb stem + -(으)ㄹ까 봐: vowel-ending stem + ㄹ까 봐 (가다 → 갈까 봐), consonant-ending stem + 을까 봐 (늦다 → 늦을까 봐). The main clause follows with the action taken.

examples.en: I'm worried it might not go well.
examples.note: 안되다 → 안될까 봐: the feared bad outcome is 'it not going well' — 걱정이에요 states the worry explicitly

examples.ko: 길 막힐까 봐 한 시간 일찍 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: gil makilkka bwa han sigan iljjig nawasseoyo.
examples.en: I left an hour early because I was worried traffic would be bad.
examples.note: 막히다 → 막힐까 봐: feared outcome (traffic jam) drove the action (leaving early) — classic -(으)ㄹ까 봐 structure

examples.en: I double-checked because I was afraid I might make a mistake.
examples.note: 실수하다 → 실수할까 봐: fear of making a mistake led to the action of double-checking

examples.en: I'm afraid the business might fail.
examples.note: 실패하다 → 실패할까 봐: the worst-case window shows the business failing — 두려워요 names the feeling

examples.ko: 그 사람이 화낼까 봐 말 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: geu sarami hwanaelkka bwa mal mot haesseoyo.
examples.en: I couldn't say anything because I was afraid that person would get angry.
examples.note: 화내다 → 화낼까 봐: fear of someone's reaction caused inaction — -(으)ㄹ까 봐 works equally well when the feared subject is another person

a.en: I took a taxi because I was worried I'd be late.

b.en: I took a taxi because I was late.

contrastPairs.explanation: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 = the thing HASN'T happened yet — it's a feared possibility. -아/어서 = the thing DID happen — it's a stated cause. Mix them up and you say you were late (fact) when you meant you were afraid of being late (worry).

a.en: I brought an umbrella because I was worried it might rain.

b.ko: 비가 올 것 같아서 우산을 가져왔어요.
b.en: I brought an umbrella because it looks like it might rain.

contrastPairs.explanation: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 emphasizes anxiety and self-protective action. -(으)ㄹ 것 같아서 is a neutral observation-based reason. Both are grammatically correct here, but -(으)ㄹ까 봐 carries more emotional weight.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English often expresses worry as two separate thoughts: 'What if it doesn't go well? I'm worried.' Korean fuses these into one grammar pattern: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 makes the feared outcome the grammatical reason for the worry. Saying 잘 안될까요? is actually asking the listener 'Do you think it won't go well?' — a completely different meaning. The worry stays inside the 봐 clause, not as a standalone question.

exceptions: Past fear: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 can also express past worry: 그때 정말 늦을까 봐 긴장했어요 (I was so tense back then, afraid I'd be late)
No subject needed: Korean often drops the subject — 질까 봐 (afraid [they/I] might lose) is perfectly natural
Standalone: 걱정했어요 alone (without -(으)ㄹ까 봐) just says you were worried; -(으)ㄹ까 봐 + 걱정했어요 specifies exactly WHAT you were worried about

exampleSentence.en: I decided to start a small business.
exampleSentence.note: 기로 했어요 — a settled decision to begin the business

exampleSentence.en: I ended up starting a new project.
exampleSentence.note: 게 됐어요 — the project arose through circumstances, not purely personal choice

exampleSentence.en: I can't even sleep because I'm afraid of failing.
exampleSentence.note: 실패하다 → 실패할까 봐: feared outcome expressed with -(으)ㄹ까 봐

exampleSentence.en: As I kept working hard, I came to succeed.
exampleSentence.note: 하다 보니까 + 게 됐어요: a natural combination — persistent effort led to the circumstantial outcome

exampleSentence.ko: 걱정이 많아서 잠을 잘 못 자요.
exampleSentence.en: I have so many worries that I can't sleep well.
exampleSentence.note: 걱정이 많다 — literally 'worries are many'; Korean treats worry as a countable thing

exampleSentence.en: I've already decided. I've made up my mind.
exampleSentence.note: 결정했어요 and 기로 했어요 both express decisions, but 기로 했어요 attaches to the specific action decided upon

exampleSentence.en: I decided to give it a try.
exampleSentence.note: 도전해 보기로 했어요 — 해 보다 (try doing) + 기로 했어요: decided to at least attempt

exampleSentence.en: I decided not to give up.
exampleSentence.note: -지 않기로 하다 = decided NOT to: the negative form of 기로 하다

exampleSentence.en: I'm worried that my income might decrease.
exampleSentence.note: 줄어들다 → 줄어들까 봐: the feared outcome is shrinking income

exampleSentence.en: I decided to invest in that business.
exampleSentence.note: 기로 했어요 — a definitive financial commitment, not an on-the-spot promise

exampleSentence.en: It looks like I'll end up retiring next year.
exampleSentence.note: 게 될 것 같아요 — future form of 게 되다: circumstances will likely lead to retirement

exampleSentence.en: I'm afraid of having to take responsibility.
exampleSentence.note: 지다 → 질까 봐: ㄹ irregular — 지다 adds ㄹ before 까 봐 since the stem ends in a vowel

extendedVocabulary.english: to come to know / find out

exampleSentence.en: I found out that fact later (it came to me).
exampleSentence.note: 알다 + 게 됐어요: knowing came about through circumstances — you didn't actively seek the info, it found you

exampleSentence.en: I decided to make a 5-year plan.
exampleSentence.note: 세우다 → 세우기로 했어요: the decision is to create the plan itself

exampleSentence.en: Don't be too afraid of failure.
exampleSentence.note: 두려워하다 expresses fear about a noun; -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is used when the feared thing is an action/event

exampleSentence.en: I decided to summon my courage.
exampleSentence.note: 용기를 내다 (to gather courage) + 기로 했어요: even emotional decisions use 기로 하다

exampleSentence.ko: 일을 하다 보니까 인맥이 생기게 됐어요.
exampleSentence.en: As I worked, I ended up building a network of connections.
exampleSentence.note: 하다 보니까 + 게 됐어요: a natural growth over time through circumstances, not planned directly

extendedDialogue.setting: Jieun and her colleague Hyunwoo talk over lunch about her decision to leave the company and start a business

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.en: I've decided to quit the company this time.
lines.grammarNote: 그만두다 → 그만두기로 했어요: the contract is signed — this is a settled decision, not an on-the-spot announcement

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.en: Really? Why? I'm totally surprised.
lines.grammarNote: No special grammar pattern here — 갑자기 (suddenly) and 놀라다 (to be surprised) express natural reaction

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.ko: 사실 오래전부터 사업을 해보고 싶었는데, 이번에 좋은 기회가 생기게 됐어요.
lines.romanization: sasil oraejeonbuteo saeobeul haebogo sipeotnneunde, ibeone joheun gihwaga saengigige dwaesseoyo.
lines.en: Actually I've wanted to try a business for a long time, and this time a good opportunity came about.
lines.grammarNote: 생기게 됐어요: the opportunity arose through circumstances — -게 됐어요 frames it as something that happened TO her, not something she forced

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 대단하네요. 수입이 줄어들까 봐 걱정되진 않아요?
lines.romanization: daedanhaneyo. suibi jureodleulkka bwa geokjeongdoejin anayo?
lines.en: That's impressive. Aren't you worried your income might decrease?
lines.grammarNote: 줄어들다 → 줄어들까 봐: feared outcome (income drop) + 걱정되다 (feel worried) — asking if she's looking through that worst-case window

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.ko: 솔직히 실패할까 봐 두려운 건 사실이에요. 그래도 해보기로 했어요.
lines.romanization: soljiki silpaehalkka bwa duryeoun geon sasirieyo. geuraedo haebogiro haesseoyo.
lines.en: Honestly, I'm afraid it might fail — that's true. But I decided to try anyway.
lines.grammarNote: 실패할까 봐 — fear of failure as a worst-case window; 해보기로 했어요 — despite the fear, the decision-contract is signed

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 용기 있네요! 처음에 저도 이 회사에 오게 됐을 때 많이 떨렸어요.
lines.romanization: yongi innneyo! cheoeuMe jeodo i hoesae oge dwaessseul ttae mani tteollyeosseoyo.
lines.en: That takes courage! When I first ended up coming to this company, I was really nervous too.
lines.grammarNote: 오게 됐을 때: past circumstantial form — 'when it came to be that I arrived here' — Hyunwoo frames his own job as something circumstances led him into, not a pure choice

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.ko: 그 말 들으니까 위로가 되네요. 잘 될지 모르지만 일단 시작하기로 마음먹었어요.
lines.romanization: geu mal deureunikka wiroga doeNeyo. jal doelji moreutjiman ildan sijakagiro maeumeogeosseoyo.
lines.en: Hearing that is reassuring. I don't know if it'll go well, but I've made up my mind to start at least.
lines.grammarNote: 시작하기로 마음먹었어요: stronger form of 기로 하다 — literally 'ate the decision in my heart' — expressing firm resolve

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 응원할게요! 궁금한 것 있으면 언제든지 물어보세요.
lines.romanization: eungwonhalkkeyo! gunggeumhan geot isseumyeon eonjedeunji mureoboseyo.
lines.en: I'll cheer you on! If you have any questions, feel free to ask anytime.
lines.grammarNote: 응원할게요: -(으)ㄹ게요 — an on-the-spot promise made TO Jieun right now, in this conversation. Note the contrast with 기로 했어요 used throughout the dialogue.

readingText.title: 새로운 시작 (A New Beginning)
readingText.body: 오늘 드디어 회사에 사직서를 냈어요. 몇 달 전부터 생각해 오던 일이지만 막상 하고 나니 실감이 안 나요. 솔직히 수입이 없어질까 봐 몇 번이나 포기할 뻔했어요. 하지만 오래전부터 내 사업을 하기로 마음먹었던 게 맞는 것 같아서, 결국 사직서를 내기로 했어요. 친구 지수는 '잘 안될까 봐 걱정되지 않냐'고 물었는데, 솔직히 걱정은 돼요. 그래도 아무것도 안 하다 보면 평생 후회할 것 같아서요. 어쩌다 보니 이렇게 큰 결정을 하게 됐는데, 지금은 오히려 홀가분한 느낌이에요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today I finally handed in my resignation at the company. It's something I'd been thinking about for months, but now that I've actually done it, it doesn't feel real. Honestly, I nearly gave up several times because I was afraid I'd lose my income. But since I'd long ago made up my mind to run my own business, I ultimately decided to hand in the resignation. My friend Jisu asked if I wasn't worried it might not go well — and honestly, I am worried. Still, I feel like if I just do nothing, I'll regret it for the rest of my life. Somehow I ended up making this big decision, and right now I actually feel strangely light.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things was the writer afraid might happen? (Find the -(으)ㄹ까 봐 phrases.)
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 수입이 없어질까 봐 (afraid of losing income) and 잘 안될까 봐 (afraid it won't go well).

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does the writer describe making this big decision — did they plan it carefully or did it happen circumstantially? Which phrase tells you this?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 어쩌다 보니 이렇게 큰 결정을 하게 됐는데 — 'Somehow I ended up making this big decision.' 하게 됐는데 (게 되다 form) frames the decision as something that came about through circumstances, even though the writer had been thinking about it for a long time.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the -기로 하다 / 기로 마음먹다 forms in the text. What decision does each one refer to, and why is 기로 하다 (rather than -(으)ㄹ게요) used in each case?
