comprehensionQuestions.answer: 내 사업을 하기로 마음먹었던 게: long-ago personal resolution to run a business — settled contract, not a live promise. 사직서를 내기로 했어요: the ultimate decision to actually resign — also already made before this diary entry. Neither is an on-the-spot promise to a listener, so -(으)ㄹ게요 would be wrong in both cases.

culturalNote.title: -게 됐어요 — The Korean Art of Modest Success
culturalNote.body: Korean culture values 겸손 (humility) highly, and -게 됐어요 is one of the key grammatical tools for expressing it. When Koreans announce good news — a new job, a promotion, passing an exam, even having a baby — they often say '하게 됐어요' (it came to be that I do this) rather than '했어요' (I did it). This is not dishonesty; it's social grace. Saying '그 회사에 취직했어요' (I got that job) can sound slightly boastful. Saying '그 회사에 취직하게 됐어요' frames your success as something you were led into by fortunate circumstances, deflecting too much personal credit. Foreign learners who skip this and just use plain verbs may unintentionally come across as self-congratulatory. Pay attention to how Koreans use 게 됐어요 in news announcements, wedding speeches, and even job interviews — it signals maturity and social awareness.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저 내년에 유학 ___기로 했어요. (I decided to study abroad next year.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The pattern is [verb stem] + 기로 했어요. 가다 → 가 + 기로 했어요 = 가기로 했어요. The blank is just the verb stem 가. '가기로 하기로 했어요' would be wrong (doubled), and '갈기로 했어요' doesn't exist as a form.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비가 ___까 봐 우산을 가져왔어요. (I brought an umbrella because I was worried it might rain.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 오다 (to come/rain) has a vowel-ending stem 오-, so we add ㄹ: 올까 봐. '오를까 봐' is wrong — 를 is an object marker, not part of this pattern. '왔을까 봐' uses the past marker and would mean 'afraid that it had already rained' — different nuance, unnatural here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 고치세요: '저 그 회사에 일하기로 할게요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Two errors: (1) 기로 할게요 mixes two patterns — 기로 하다 announces a settled decision, but -(으)ㄹ게요 is an on-the-spot promise. The correct form is 기로 했어요 (past, decision already made). (2) 회사에 일하다 should be 회사에서 일하다 — working is an action, so the workplace takes 에서, not 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I came to understand Korean because I kept studying.'
inlineExercises.correct: 계속 공부하다 보니까 한국어를 이해하게 됐어요.
inlineExercises.hint: Use 게 됐어요 — understanding came about through the circumstance of sustained study. 하다 보니까 = 'as I kept doing...'

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I'm afraid I might be late for the meeting'?
inlineExercises.explanation: Option 1 (늦을까요?) asks the listener 'Do you think I'll be late?' — a question, not a worry. Option 3 (늦어서) uses a causal connector for something that already happened — but the meeting hasn't started yet. Only option 2 correctly uses -(으)ㄹ까 봐 to express a feared future outcome as the reason for worry.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your Korean friend asks why you moved to Seoul. Which answer sounds most natural and culturally appropriate?
inlineExercises.explanation: Option 1 (제가 결정했어요) is correct but blunt — it emphasizes that YOU made the choice, which can sound slightly self-important in casual Korean conversation. Option 3 (이사하기로 했어요) implies you made a deliberate personal decision — fine, but implies strong agency. Option 2 (이사하게 됐어요) is the culturally natural answer: 'it came to be that I moved' — modest, implying life circumstances led you there, which is the preferred Korean register for explaining personal life changes.

inlineExercises.prompt: 열심히 하다 보니까 팀장이 ___됐어요. (As I worked hard, I ended up becoming team leader.)
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a positive outcome that came about through circumstance — the grammar for that is -게 됐어요. 되게 됐어요 = 'ended up becoming.' 되기로 했어요 would mean 'I decided to become team leader' — implying you chose it deliberately (unusual!). 될까 봐 (afraid of becoming) would make no sense here since becoming team leader is a good outcome.

bullets: 기로 했어요 = SIGNED CONTRACT: announcing a settled decision or mutual agreement — always points back to a decision already made
-(으)ㄹ까 봐 = WORST-CASE WINDOW: the feared bad outcome drives an action — 'I was afraid X would happen, so I did Y'
-게 됐어요 = CIRCUMSTANCES LED HERE: humble, natural way to describe how a situation came about — preferred in Korean for announcing life changes modestly
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 15 tackles personality and feelings with -ㄹ 것 같다 (seems like), -척 하다 (pretending to), and -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 (almost happened) — the grammar for describing what people appear to be and what nearly occurred.

chapters.title: Feelings, Personality & Pretending
chapters.goal: Describe deeper feelings and personality, and say what almost happened.
chapters.scenario: Intermediate — build on the beginner chapters.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: That person seems really diligent.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Right. But sometimes they are too cautious.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Personally, I find that respectable.

hook.situation: Your Korean friend tells you about a stressful day: someone at work was 'pretending not to know,' they 'almost cried' during a movie, and they're 'guessing the boss is angry.' You understand the gist but can't quite follow the grammar gluing it together. Those three reactions — faking something, narrowly avoiding something, and inferring from clues — each need their own structure in Korean.
objectives: Use -는 척하다 to say someone is pretending or faking a state or action
Use -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 to describe a close call — something that almost happened but didn't
Use -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 to make an evidence-based guess about someone else's situation
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns appear constantly in Korean storytelling and conversation. Without them, you can describe facts but not the texture of human experience — the white lies, the near-misses, and the inferences you draw about the people around you. Master all three and your Korean instantly sounds more natural and more adult.

grammarNotes.title: -는 척하다 — Pretend / Act Like
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -는 척하다 as putting on a MASK. The person is wearing a mask of something they're not — sleeping, working, not knowing. The mask can be any verb or adjective, and you just need to fit the right modifier ending to the mask before slipping it on. If the mask is an action happening now: -는 척. If the mask is a state (adjective): -은/-ㄴ 척. If you're pretending you already DID something: -(으)ㄴ 척.
grammarNotes.formation:
Action verb (present): verb stem + -는 척하다 (먹다 → 먹는 척하다)
Adjective: stem + -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (아프다 → 아픈 척하다, 바쁘다 → 바쁜 척하다)
Past action: stem + -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (듣다 → 들은 척하다, 보다 → 본 척하다)
척하다 conjugates normally: 척해요, 척했어요, 척할 거예요

examples.en: My boss came so I pretended to be working hard.
examples.note: 일하다 is an action verb → present modifier -는 + 척했어요; the pretense was ongoing in the past

examples.ko: 전 남자친구를 봤는데 못 본 척했어요.
examples.romanization: jeon namjachingureul bwanneunde mot bon cheokaesseoyo.
examples.en: I saw my ex-boyfriend but pretended not to have seen him.
examples.note: 보다 = past completed action → -(으)ㄴ modifier: 본 척 (pretending you already looked away)

examples.en: I pretended to be sick to skip the company dinner.
examples.note: 아프다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ modifier: 아픈 척; note the 으 is needed after the consonant stem

examples.romanization: gyae da almyeonseo moreuneun cheokajana yo.
examples.en: She totally knows but acts like she doesn't.
examples.note: 모르다 = action verb (not knowing = an active state of ignorance) → present -는 척; -잖아요 expresses mild exasperation

examples.ko: 전화 안 들리는 척하면 안 돼.
examples.romanization: jeonhwa an deulleuneun cheokhamyeon an dwae.
examples.en: You can't just pretend not to hear the phone.
examples.note: 들리다 = action verb → -는 척; -면 안 돼 = 'you shouldn't' — the pretense is framed as a conditional

a.en: He's pretending to sleep. (he's awake)

b.en: It seems like he's sleeping. (honest impression)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same base phrase, completely different meaning. 척하다 = deliberate faking — you KNOW it's false. -는 것 같다 = a genuine soft opinion. These are opposites in spirit: one is a performance, the other is an honest guess.

a.en: She pretended to be busy. (she wasn't)

b.en: She seemed busy. (your honest reading)

contrastPairs.explanation: Again: 척했어요 = the person was actively faking. -것 같았어요 = your sincere impression. When you describe someone else's pretense, use 척하다; when you describe your own perception, use -것 같다.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers apply the action-verb pattern to adjectives. But 아프다 is an adjective, not an action verb, so it takes the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ, not -는. The result is 아픈 척했어요. This is the most common 척하다 mistake — always check whether your word is an adjective (state) or a verb (action) before choosing the modifier.

exceptions: 체하다 is a less common but valid alternative to 척하다 with the same meaning: 모르는 체했어요 = 모르는 척했어요
Past action pretense uses -(으)ㄴ even for action verbs: 안 들은 척하다 (pretend not to have heard) — don't confuse with the adjective -(으)ㄴ, though the ending looks the same
The contracted spoken form 척하다 → often shortens to just 척 in casual speech: '자, 자는 척!' (Act like you're sleeping!)

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 — Almost Happened (Close Call)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 as a NEAR-MISS ALARM. The alarm went off — something was right on the edge of happening — but the disaster was avoided. The alarm is always in the past (뻔했어요) because the near-miss is already over. The adverb 하마터면 is the sound of the alarm: '하마터면...!' = 'I almost...!'
grammarNotes.formation:
Verb stem (vowel or ㄹ-ending): + -ㄹ 뻔하다 (넘어지다 → 넘어질 뻔하다, 울다 → 울 뻔하다)
Verb stem (consonant-ending): + -을 뻔하다 (죽다 → 죽을 뻔하다, 늦다 → 늦을 뻔하다)
Almost always past: 뻔했어요
Optional intensifier: 하마터면 + -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요
Only used with action verbs, not adjectives

examples.en: The road was slippery so I almost fell.
examples.note: 넘어지다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; -아서 gives the cause that nearly triggered the disaster

examples.ko: 하마터면 지하철에 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: hamateomyeon jihacheore gabangeul dugo naeril ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I almost left my bag on the subway!
examples.note: 하마터면 at the front = the 'alarm sound'; 내리다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요

examples.en: It was so moving I almost cried.
examples.note: 울다 has a ㄹ stem → just -ㄹ 뻔했어요 (the ㄹ in the stem counts); feeling-based near-misses are very natural with this pattern

examples.en: I didn't hear my alarm and almost got to work late.
examples.note: 지각하다 ends in 하 → 지각할 뻔했어요; 하다 verbs follow the vowel rule

examples.ko: 차가 갑자기 튀어나와서 사고 날 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: chaga gapjagi twieonawaseo sago nal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A car suddenly darted out and there was almost an accident.
examples.note: 나다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; 사고 나다 = an accident occurs — common pairing with this pattern

a.en: I almost fell. (it genuinely nearly happened)

b.en: It felt like I was going to fall. (my impression at the time)

contrastPairs.explanation: 뻔했어요 = a real near-miss, the event was on the physical edge of happening. -ㄹ 것 같았어요 = your mental impression or fear at the moment. If you're telling a story about a genuine close call, use 뻔했어요. If you're describing how something felt or looked from the outside, use -것 같았어요.

a.en: I almost cried (but didn't).

b.en: I feel like I'm going to cry (might still cry).

contrastPairs.explanation: 뻔했어요 is past and the event DIDN'T happen — the danger is over. -ㄹ 것 같아요 is present and the event may still happen. This is a key practical difference.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers try to keep it in the present. But a near-miss, by definition, is already over — so Korean always uses the past form 뻔했어요. 뻔해요 in the present tense sounds unnatural. The one very rare exception is live commentary ('He's about to fall!'), but in normal storytelling you always say 뻔했어요.

exceptions: Rarely used about ongoing or future events; almost exclusively past tense
Not used with adjectives: 피곤할 뻔했어요 (almost tired?) doesn't make sense — only with event verbs
Can be positive: 상을 받을 뻔했어요 (I almost won a prize) — though most near-misses described this way are negative (disasters avoided)

extendedVocabulary.english: deep emotion; being moved or touched

exampleSentence.ko: 그 영화 너무 감동적이어서 울 뻔했어요.
exampleSentence.en: That movie was so moving I almost cried.
exampleSentence.note: 감동적이다 = to be moving/touching; 울 뻔했어요 shows the emotional near-miss naturally

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람 표정 보니까 두려운가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: From that person's expression, it seems they're afraid.
exampleSentence.note: 두렵다 (adjective) → -(으)ㄴ가 보다 = evidence-based guess about someone's emotional state

exampleSentence.ko: 팀장님 말투가 그러는 걸 보니까 화나신 건가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: The way the team leader is talking, I'm guessing they're angry.
exampleSentence.note: -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 = inferring the emotion from observable evidence (their tone)

exampleSentence.ko: 합격했다는 소식을 듣고 만족스러워서 소리를 지를 뻔했어요.
exampleSentence.en: When I heard I passed, I was so satisfied I almost shouted.
exampleSentence.note: 만족스럽다 = to feel satisfied; 소리를 지르다 = to shout; 지를 뻔했어요 = almost-shouted close call

exampleSentence.ko: 그분이 모르는 척한 것 때문에 신뢰를 잃었어요.
exampleSentence.en: Because he pretended not to know, I lost trust in him.
exampleSentence.note: 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) combined with 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust) — common real-life pairing

exampleSentence.ko: 그분이 그렇게 성실한 걸 보니까 존경스러운가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: Seeing how diligent that person is, they must seem admirable.
exampleSentence.note: 존경스럽다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; guessing someone else's feeling of admiration from their behavior

exampleSentence.en: That person seems really diligent.
exampleSentence.note: 성실하다 is an adjective → 성실한 것 같다 (soft opinion); contrast with -나 보다 which implies outside evidence

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람이 모르는 척한 걸 보면 정직한가 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: Seeing them pretend not to know makes me wonder if they're actually honest.
exampleSentence.note: 모르는 척하다 directly contradicts 정직하다; this contrast appears naturally in character assessments

extendedVocabulary.english: to be careful; prudent; cautious in decisions

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람 말을 잘 안 하는 걸 보니까 신중한가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: They don't say much — I'm guessing they're the careful type.
exampleSentence.note: 신중하다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; inferring personality from observable behavior

extendedVocabulary.english: to be coolheaded; level-headed; cold; detached

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be emotionless, but it was actually tough.
exampleSentence.note: 감정이 없는 척하다 = pretend to be cold/unemotional; 척하다 used for performing emotional detachment

extendedVocabulary.english: tricky; demanding; picky; hard to satisfy

exampleSentence.ko: 심사 기준이 까다로운가 봐요. 다들 탈락했네요.
exampleSentence.en: I guess the judging criteria are strict — everyone got eliminated.
exampleSentence.note: 까다롭다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 (evidence-based inference from the result); ㅂ-irregular: 까다롭 + 은가 → 까다로운가

extendedVocabulary.english: 'I almost...'; by a narrow margin (near-miss adverb)

exampleSentence.en: I almost lost my wallet!
exampleSentence.note: 하마터면 always pairs with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 to emphasize the narrowness of the near-miss

extendedVocabulary.english: to pick up on; to sense; to figure out (from cues)

exampleSentence.ko: 걔가 눈치챈 것 같아서 아무것도 모르는 척했어요.
exampleSentence.en: I felt like they were picking up on it, so I pretended not to know anything.
exampleSentence.note: 눈치채다 → trigger for using 척하다: when someone might catch on, you put on the ignorance mask

extendedVocabulary.english: to hide; to conceal (feelings or information)

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be fine in an attempt to hide my feelings.
exampleSentence.note: 감추려고 (in order to hide) + 척하다 — a very natural Korean expression of masking emotions

extendedVocabulary.english: to be obvious; to show; to give away (that you're faking)

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be asleep but I guess it was obvious.
exampleSentence.note: 티가 났나 봐요 = evidence-based guess (someone's reaction revealed it); 척하다 + 나 봐요 together in one sentence

extendedVocabulary.english: to tremble; to be shaky (with nerves or emotion)

exampleSentence.en: During my presentation, my voice almost started shaking.
exampleSentence.note: 떨리다 ends in vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; common near-miss emotion verb in presentations and auditions

extendedDialogue.setting: Two coworkers, Jiyeon and Minsu, are eating lunch together and talking about a stressful morning

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 오늘 오전에 발표하다가 목소리가 떨릴 뻔했어요.
lines.romanization: oneul ojeone balpyohada ga moksoriga teollil ppeonhaesseoyo.
lines.en: This morning during my presentation, my voice almost started shaking.
lines.grammarNote: 떨리다 = vowel-stem verb → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; the near-miss is past and already resolved

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 어, 저도 봤는데 엄청 자연스러웠어요. 몰랐어요.
lines.romanization: eo, jeodo bwanneunde eomcheong jayeonseureowoosseoyo. mollasseoyo.
lines.en: Oh, I was watching and you were super natural. I couldn't tell.
lines.grammarNote: No grammar point here — a natural supportive reply that makes the 척하다 line in the next turn more impactful

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 고마워요. 사실 많이 떨렸는데 괜찮은 척했어요.
lines.romanization: gomawoyo. sasil mani teolryeonneunde gwaenchanheun cheokaesseoyo.
lines.en: Thank you. I was actually shaking a lot, but I pretended to be fine.
lines.grammarNote: 괜찮다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척하다: 괜찮은 척했어요; confirms the mask was successfully worn

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 그래요? 팀장님도 잘 모르시는 것 같던데요.
lines.romanization: geuraeyо? timjangnimdo jal moreusineun geot gatdeondeyo.
lines.en: Really? It seemed like the team leader didn't notice either.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같던데요 = a gentle evidence-based impression recalled from the past; softer than -나 봐요 here because the speaker is recounting their own observation

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 팀장님은 지금 다른 문제로 머리가 복잡한가 봐요.
lines.romanization: timjangnimeun jigeum dareun munjero meoriga bokjapanga bwayo.
lines.en: I think the team leader's head is full of other problems right now.
lines.grammarNote: 복잡하다 = adjective → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요: 복잡한가 봐요; evidence-based inference about someone else's mental state

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 맞아요. 아침에 표정이 안 좋더라고요. 스트레스 많이 받으시나 봐요.
lines.romanization: majayo. achime pyojeongi an jotdeoragoyo. seuteureseu mani badumsina bwayo.
lines.en: Right. The expression this morning wasn't great. I'm guessing they're under a lot of stress.
lines.grammarNote: 받다 = action verb → -나 봐요 (not -(으)ㄴ가); the visible evidence (bad expression) triggers the inference

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 하마터면 제가 먼저 물어볼 뻔했는데 참았어요.
lines.romanization: hamateomyeon jega meonjeo mureоbol ppeonaennneunde chamasseoyo.
lines.en: I almost asked first, but I held back.
lines.grammarNote: 하마터면 + 물어보다 (vowel stem) → -ㄹ 뻔했는데; -는데 adds a contrastive note (almost did, but then...)

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 잘하셨어요. 지금은 모르는 척하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
lines.romanization: jalhaseyosseoyo. jigeumeun moreuneun cheokhaneun ge naeul geot gatayo.
lines.en: Good call. Right now, playing dumb is probably better.
lines.grammarNote: 모르다 = action verb → 모르는 척하다; 하는 게 나을 것 같다 = 'it's probably better to...' — 척하다 appears as a noun-modifying clause here

readingText.title: 지연의 하루 일기 (Jiyeon's Day Diary)
readingText.body: 오늘은 정말 힘든 하루였다. 아침에 중요한 발표가 있었는데, 엄청 긴장해서 울 뻔했다. 발표하는 내내 떨렸지만 괜찮은 척하면서 끝까지 버텼다. 팀장님은 좀 무표정하게 앉아 계셨는데, 뭔가 불만이신가 봐서 마음이 불안했다. 나중에 동료한테 물어봤더니 요즘 윗사람한테 스트레스 받으시나 봐라고 했다. 그 말 듣고 조금 안심이 됐다. 퇴근하다가 지갑을 잃어버릴 뻔했다. 하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했는데, 다행히 가방 안쪽에 있었다. 내일은 오늘보다 나은 하루이길 바란다.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today was a really tough day. There was an important presentation in the morning, and I was so nervous I almost cried. I was shaking the whole time but I pretended to be fine and hung in there to the end. The team leader sat there with a blank expression, and I felt uneasy thinking they seemed dissatisfied with something. I asked a coworker later, and they said it looks like the team leader has been under stress from upper management lately. Hearing that made me feel a bit relieved. On the way out of the office, I almost lost my wallet. That was almost a disaster, but thankfully it was in the inside pocket of my bag. I hope tomorrow is a better day than today.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why did Jiyeon pretend to be fine during the presentation?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She was shaking and almost cried (울 뻔했다), but she put on a mask of composure (괜찮은 척하면서) and pushed through to the end.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does Jiyeon learn about the team leader's stress? What Korean pattern does she use for this inference?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She hears it from a coworker. She uses 스트레스 받으시나 봐 — the -나 봐 pattern (action verb 받다 → 받으시나 봐) because the information is secondhand evidence, not something she observed directly.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 척하다, 뻔하다, and -나/-(으)ㄴ가 보다 in the text. For each one, explain WHY that particular pattern is used there.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 척하다: 괜찮은 척하면서 — she is deliberately performing composure she does not feel (adjective 괜찮다 → -(으)ㄴ 척). 뻔하다: 울 뻔했다 — she genuinely nearly cried (ulda vowel stem → 울 뻔했다); 잃어버릴 뻔했다 — she genuinely almost lost her wallet (잃어버리다 vowel stem → -ㄹ 뻔했다); 큰일 날 뻔했는데 — almost a disaster (나다 vowel stem → -ㄹ 뻔했는데). -나/-(으)ㄴ가 보다: 불만이신가 봐서 — 불만이다 is a 이다 predicate → -인가 봐; vague-evidence inference from a blank expression. 스트레스 받으시나 봐 — 받다 is an action verb → -나 봐; secondhand inference from coworker's information.

culturalNote.title: 척하다 and the Art of Saving Face in Korean Workplaces
culturalNote.body: Korean workplace culture places enormous value on 눈치 (the ability to read the room) and not burdening others with your problems. 괜찮은 척하다 (pretending to be fine) is not considered dishonest — it is considered polite, professional, and emotionally mature. If your boss asks how you're doing on a Monday morning and you are exhausted, the socially expected answer is 괜찮아요, not a detailed complaint. Similarly, 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) is often used by seniors to give juniors the space to present without the senior's greater knowledge overshadowing the room. Understand this cultural context and you'll find 척하다 appearing everywhere in Korean dramas, office stories, and everyday conversation — it's not always deception; it's often grace.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배가 안 고___ 척했어요. 사실 엄청 배고팠어요. (Adjective: 고프다 = to be hungry)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고프다 is an adjective, so it takes the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ: 고픈 척했어요. If you chose -프는 척, that's the action-verb pattern (-는 척) applied to an adjective, which is the #1 척하다 mistake. Always check: adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척, verb → -는 척.

inlineExercises.prompt: 하마터면 지하철을 ___ 뻔했어요. (놓치다 = to miss a train)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 uses the future/potential modifier -(으)ㄹ, not the present continuous -는. 놓치다 has a consonant-ending stem → -을 뻔했어요. 놓치는 뻔했어요 would be a completely different (and ungrammatical) construction.

inlineExercises.prompt: 답장이 없는 걸 보니까 바쁘___ 봐요. (바쁘다 = to be busy — adjective)
inlineExercises.explanation: 바쁘다 is an adjective → use -(으)ㄴ가 보다. If it were an action verb (e.g., 일하다), you'd use -나 봐요. 바쁜가 봐요 = I guess they're busy (based on the no-reply evidence). 바쁘나 봐요 is colloquially used and understood, but 바쁜가 봐요 is the textbook-correct form.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '발표할 뻔해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Near-misses are finished events, so 뻔하다 must be in the past: 뻔했어요. 뻔해요 in the present would mean the near-miss is ongoing right now, which contradicts the logic of 뻔하다 — once you've ALMOST done something and DIDN'T, the moment is over.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I pretended not to hear.'
inlineExercises.hint: 듣다 is an action verb. But you are pretending you ALREADY didn't hear — this is a past action, so use the past action modifier -(으)ㄴ: 들은 척. Add 못 before it for 'pretended not to have heard.'

inlineExercises.prompt: You notice your friend has been very quiet lately and you want to say 'I'm guessing something happened.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 is a stative verb (to exist/have) → use -나 봐요 for evidence-based inference. Option 1 (척해요) means PRETENDING something happened — totally different, implying your friend is faking. Option 3 (뻔했어요) means something ALMOST happened but didn't — also wrong; you're guessing it DID happen.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'She pretended to be sick'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 아프다 is an adjective. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ in modifier position: 아프 + 은 → 아픈. Option 1 (아프는 척) wrongly uses the action-verb pattern -는. Option 3 (아팠는 척) incorrectly attaches -는 to a past tense stem — neither 아팠는 nor 척하다 work that way. The correct and only natural form is 아픈 척했어요.

bullets: MASK (-는/-(으)ㄴ 척하다): put on a fake face — verb actions take -는 척, adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 척, past actions take -(으)ㄴ 척; 척하다 = deliberate pretense, not an honest impression
NEAR-MISS ALARM (-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요): something almost happened but didn't — always past tense, add 하마터면 for drama, only with action verbs
EVIDENCE GUESS (-나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요): action verbs → -나 봐요, adjectives/이다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; used for inferring about OTHER people from visible clues, not your own obvious feelings
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Chapter 16 links complex ideas together: causation, contrast, and purpose across longer sentences. You'll combine the personality vocabulary from this chapter with connectors like -는 바람에 (because of, unexpectedly) and -(으)ㄹ수록 (the more... the more) to build the kind of nuanced statements Koreans make every day.

chapters.title: Connecting Complex Ideas
chapters.goal: Link cause, contrast, and purpose in longer, more natural sentences.
chapters.scenario: Intermediate — build on the beginner chapters.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: The plan got canceled because of the rain.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Ah, so that is why you couldn't come.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 네. 연습할수록 더 잘하게 될 거예요.
dialogue.romanization: ne. yeonseupalsurok deo jalhage doel geoyeyo.
dialogue.en: Yeah. The more you practice, the better you will get.

hook.situation: You're telling a Korean friend why you missed a meeting. You say '비가 와서 못 왔어요' — fine, but flat. A natural Korean speaker would say '비가 오는 바람에 못 왔어요' (the rain swept in and derailed my plans) or '비가 오길래 그냥 집에 있었어요' (I noticed the rain coming, so I just stayed home). Same fact. Completely different nuance. After this chapter you'll choose the RIGHT connector, not just any connector.
objectives: Use -더니 to narrate observed patterns that led to a result
Use -길래 to explain a spontaneous reaction to something you personally noticed
Use -(으)ㄹ수록 for 'the more X, the more Y' proportional relationships
hook.whyItMatters: Beginners connect ideas with 그래서 and -아서/어서 for everything. Intermediate speakers choose from a richer toolkit: -더니 signals you WITNESSED something over time, -길래 signals you REACTED on the spot, -(으)ㄹ수록 signals a proportional relationship. Using the right connector is what makes your Korean sound like a real person talking, not a grammar textbook.

grammarNotes.title: -더니 — I watched X happen, then Y followed
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -더니 as a SECURITY CAMERA REPLAY. You're reviewing footage of someone else's behavior (or the weather, or a situation), and then you narrate the outcome that followed. The camera was rolling on clause 1; clause 2 is the result that played out afterward. Only YOU had access to that footage — that's what makes -더니 feel personal and observational.
grammarNotes.formation: Verb/Adjective stem + -더니 (no vowel change: 먹다→먹더니, 춥다→춥더니). For your OWN past actions use -았/었더니 (먹었더니 = after I ate X, then Y happened).

examples.ko: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi maeil yasisgeul meokdeoni sari jjeosseoyo.
examples.en: My brother kept eating late-night snacks, and then he gained weight.
examples.note: -더니 here: the speaker personally watched the habit build up over time (camera rolling) and then reports the predictable outcome

examples.ko: 날씨가 아까는 맑더니 갑자기 비가 와요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga akkaneun makdeoni gapjagi biga wayo.
examples.en: It was clear earlier, and now it's suddenly raining.
examples.note: Weather observation → surprising change: the speaker witnessed the clear sky, contrasting it with the current rain

examples.romanization: chinguga yeolsimhi gongbuhadeoni siheomeseo ildeungeul haesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend studied hard and then got first place on the exam.
examples.note: I watched the studying (camera rolling on friend) → natural result: top score

examples.ko: 밥을 많이 먹었더니 배가 너무 불러요.
examples.romanization: babeul manhi meogeotdeoni baega neomu bulleoyo.
examples.en: I ate a lot and now my stomach is too full.
examples.note: -았더니 (past form) because it's the speaker's OWN past action leading to a present state they're experiencing

examples.en: That drama kept being boring, and it ended up getting cancelled.
examples.note: Speaker watched (or heard about) the ongoing boringness — camera on the drama's quality — and reports the cancellation as the observed outcome

a.en: My friend exercised every day, and then they lost weight.

b.en: My friend lost weight because they exercised every day.

contrastPairs.explanation: -더니 (A) means: I personally watched this pattern unfold over time, and I'm reporting the result I witnessed. -아서/어서 (B) is a neutral cause-and-effect statement with no sense of personal observation or contrast — just a logical reason. -더니 carries the feeling of 'I saw it coming'.

a.en: I ate a lot, so now I feel full. (my own action)

b.ko: 동생이 밥을 많이 먹더니 배가 불렀어요.
b.en: My sibling ate a lot and then had a full stomach. (watching someone else)

contrastPairs.explanation: -았/었더니 (A) is for your OWN past action whose result you now experience. Plain -더니 (B) is for observing SOMEONE ELSE'S ongoing behavior and noting its result.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English learners often use plain -더니 with first-person subjects, mirroring the English 'I exercised and then got healthy.' But plain -더니 is reserved for observations ABOUT OTHERS (or the weather/situations). When you are reporting what happened AFTER YOUR OWN action, you must use the past form: -았/었더니. 운동했더니 = after I exercised, (I found that) I got healthy.

exceptions: -더니 is almost always about another person or outside situation as the subject of clause 1; using it with 저는/나는 + plain stem sounds unnatural — use -았/었더니 instead
The contrast 아까는 … 더니 now … is very common for weather or mood changes you directly experienced: 아까는 기분이 좋더니 왜 화났어요? (You seemed fine earlier — why are you angry now?)
In speech, -더니 can be shortened to -데 informally: 그 친구 열심히 하데 결국 됐어요 (that friend was working hard and eventually made it)

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ수록 — The more X, the more Y
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of -(으)ㄹ수록 as a SLIDING SCALE dial. Imagine a dial on a machine: as you turn it further in one direction, another gauge goes up proportionally. The two gauges are linked — one cannot move without the other moving too. -수록 is the linguistic dial that links two proportional changes.
grammarNotes.formation: Consonant-ending stem + -을수록 (먹다→먹을수록, 작다→작을수록). Vowel-ending stem + -ㄹ수록 (가다→갈수록, 크다→클수록). ㄹ-ending stems drop ㄹ then add -ㄹ수록 (살다→살수록). Often paired with -(으)면 before it for emphasis: 보면 볼수록 (the more you look at it).

examples.en: The more I study Korean, the more fun it gets.
examples.note: Classic sliding scale: study ↑ → enjoyment ↑. 할수록 = consonant-ending 하다 stem 하 + -ㄹ수록

examples.en: The more you practice, the more your skills improve.
examples.note: -면 할수록 = emphatic form (if you practice, and the more you practice, ...) — both dials moving together

examples.en: The longer you live in Seoul, the more charming it becomes.
examples.note: 살다 (ㄹ-stem) drops ㄹ → 살수록. Time in Seoul ↑ → appreciation ↑

examples.en: The more you listen to this music, the more you like it.
examples.note: 듣다 → irregular: 들으 + -ㄹ수록 → 들을수록. Listening ↑ → liking ↑

examples.en: The cheaper the price, the happier consumers are.
examples.note: Here the scale is inverse: price ↓ → consumer happiness ↑, but the grammar structure is identical — one dial moving causes the other to move

a.en: The more you read this book, the more interesting it gets.

b.en: I read this book and it was interesting.

contrastPairs.explanation: -(으)ㄹ수록 (A) describes a proportional, ongoing relationship — as reading increases, interest increases. -아서/어서 (B) is a one-time cause-and-effect: I read it once and found it interesting. The sliding scale vs. a single event.

a.en: The more I look at it, the prettier it gets.

b.en: The more I look at it, the prettier it gets. (same meaning, slightly less emphatic)

contrastPairs.explanation: The -면 V-ㄹ수록 pattern (A) is more emphatic and frequently used in speech. Plain -(으)ㄹ수록 (B) alone is grammatically correct but sounds slightly more literary. Both mean the same proportional relationship.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English learners often express the 'the more...the more' pattern with -면 (if/when) alone: 공부하면 재미있어요 = 'When you study, it's fun' — a single conditional. But -면 alone cannot express the proportional SCALING relationship. -(으)ㄹ수록 is the only way to say 'as one thing increases, another increases proportionally'. Don't try to approximate this pattern with -면 alone.

exceptions: 갈수록 (from 가다, 'to go') is a frozen adverb meaning 'increasingly' or 'more and more': 갈수록 힘들어요 = It's getting harder and harder
When the subject of both clauses is the same (which is typical), no need to repeat it: 공부할수록 더 잘해요 (the more [I] study, the better [I] get)
The result clause (after -수록) usually contains 더 (more), 점점 (gradually more), or a comparative expression to make the proportional change explicit

exampleSentence.en: The event got cancelled because of the rain.
exampleSentence.note: 취소되다 is passive — the subject is what was cancelled, not who cancelled it

exampleSentence.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 옷이 다 젖었어요.
exampleSentence.en: My clothes got completely soaked because it suddenly started raining.
exampleSentence.note: 바람에 carries the nuance that the cause was unexpected or unwelcome, stronger than 때문에

exampleSentence.en: The more you practice, the fewer mistakes you make.
exampleSentence.note: Perfect partner for -(으)ㄹ수록: proportional improvement through practice

exampleSentence.en: The more you practice, the more your skills improve.
exampleSentence.note: 늘다 (to grow/increase) pairs naturally with 실력

exampleSentence.en: The more you use Korean, the more your skills grow.
exampleSentence.note: 늘다 is intransitive — the subject improves on its own; contrast with 늘리다 (to increase something intentionally)

exampleSentence.ko: 친구가 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 찐 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: My friend kept eating late-night snacks, and it seems they gained weight.
exampleSentence.note: Classic -더니 scenario: you observed the habit over time → you're now noting the result

exampleSentence.en: They've been stressed lately, and they've gained weight.
exampleSentence.note: 살이 찌다 is an expression — 살 (flesh/fat) + 이 (subject marker) + 찌다 (to fatten/swell)

exampleSentence.en: It was clear, and then suddenly there was thunder.
exampleSentence.note: 갑자기 intensifies the contrast in -더니 sentences — the unexpected shift

exampleSentence.en: They kept working hard, and in the end they passed.
exampleSentence.note: 결국 often appears in the result clause of -더니 sentences, marking the endpoint of the observed sequence

exampleSentence.en: The more experience accumulates, the more confidence you gain.
exampleSentence.note: 쌓이다 is the passive of 쌓다 (to stack/pile); -ㄹ수록 pairs perfectly with gradual accumulation

exampleSentence.en: Korean food has more charm the more you know about it.
exampleSentence.note: 알다 (ㄹ-stem) drops ㄹ → 알수록. 매력이 있다 = to have charm/appeal

exampleSentence.en: The ratings were low, and in the end the drama was cancelled.
exampleSentence.note: 폐지되다 is the passive of 폐지하다 (to abolish/cancel); -더니 here: you observed the low ratings → you're reporting the outcome

exampleSentence.en: The more success experiences accumulate, the higher your self-confidence rises.
exampleSentence.note: 자신 (self/oneself) + 감 (feeling/sense) — a great -(으)ㄹ수록 vocabulary word

exampleSentence.ko: 친구가 요즘 너무 피곤하더니 결국 쓰러졌어요.
exampleSentence.en: My friend seemed so exhausted lately, and they finally collapsed.
exampleSentence.note: -더니 with an adjective: the speaker observed the state of exhaustion over time → reports the result

exampleSentence.en: The more effort you put in, the greater the sense of fulfillment you feel.
exampleSentence.note: 보람 is a uniquely Korean concept for the rewarding feeling that comes from effort well spent

exampleSentence.en: Korean seemed hard at first, and now it's gotten easier.
exampleSentence.note: -더니 with an adjective: earlier observation (it WAS hard) contrasted with a current changed state (now it's easy)

extendedVocabulary.english: to get used to / become accustomed

exampleSentence.en: The more you use it, the more accustomed you become.
exampleSentence.note: 익숙하다 (familiar/accustomed) + -아/어지다 (become) = getting used to. Perfect -(으)ㄹ수록 partner

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon and her coworker Hyunwoo chat over coffee after a colleague's promotion

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 민준 씨가 요즘 매일 야근하더니 결국 팀장이 됐어요.
lines.romanization: Minjun ssiga yoeum maeil yagheunahadeoni gyeolguk timjangi dwaesseoyo.
lines.en: Minjun kept working late every night lately, and in the end he became team leader.
lines.grammarNote: -더니: Jiyeon personally watched the pattern of Minjun's overtime work (camera rolling) and now reports the natural outcome — his promotion

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 맞아요. 저도 봤어요. 열심히 하더니 잘 됐네요.
lines.romanization: Majayo. Jeodo bwasseoyo. Yeolsimhi hadeoni jal dwaenneyo.
lines.en: That's right. I saw it too. He worked hard and things worked out well.
lines.grammarNote: -더니 again: Hyunwoo confirming he also observed (watched) the same behavior pattern — shared camera footage, so to speak

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 사실 저도 더 노력해야겠다는 생각이 들었어요.
lines.romanization: Sasil jeodo deo noryeokaeyagessanneun saenggagi deureosseoyo.
lines.en: Honestly, it made me think I should try harder too.
lines.grammarNote: No -더니 here — Jiyeon is talking about her own internal reaction, not an observation about another person

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 경험이 쌓일수록 기회도 많아지는 것 같아요.
lines.romanization: Gyeongheomi ssahilsurok gihoedo manajineun geot gatayo.
lines.en: It seems like the more experience piles up, the more opportunities come.
lines.grammarNote: 쌓이다 ㄹ-vowel ending → -ㄹ수록. -(으)ㄹ수록 captures the proportional scale: experience ↑ → opportunities ↑

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 맞아요. 일할수록 더 잘 알게 되는 것도 있고요.
lines.romanization: Majayo. Ilhalsurok deo jal alge doeneun geotdo itgoyo.
lines.en: True. And the more you work, the more you come to understand.
lines.grammarNote: 일하다 (consonant-free vowel stem 하) → 할수록 (contracted). Two proportional relationships in one sentence: work ↑ → understanding ↑

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 그런데 민준 씨가 처음에는 많이 힘들어하더니 이제는 여유가 생겼어요.
lines.romanization: Geureonde Minjun ssiga cheoeumeeneun manhi himdeureohadeoni ijeeneun yeoyuga saenggyeosseoyo.
lines.en: By the way, Minjun seemed to struggle a lot at first, and now he has breathing room.
lines.grammarNote: -더니 marks the contrast: EARLIER state (observed struggling) vs. CURRENT changed state (now relaxed) — the quintessential use of -더니 for contrast

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 저도 적응할수록 여유가 생길 거라고 믿어요.
lines.romanization: Jeodo jeogeunghalsurok yeoyuga saengil georago mideoyo.
lines.en: I believe the more I adapt, the more breathing room I'll get too.
lines.grammarNote: 적응하다 → 적응할수록. First-person -(으)ㄹ수록 expressing hope/belief about one's own proportional growth

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 물론이죠. 보면 볼수록 지연 씨도 잘 하고 있는 게 보여요.
lines.romanization: Mulronijyo. Bomyeon bolsurok Jiyeon ssido jal hago inneun ge boyeoyo.
lines.en: Of course. The more I watch, the more I can see you're doing well too.
lines.grammarNote: 보면 볼수록: the emphatic -(으)면 V-(으)ㄹ수록 form — the most natural spoken pattern for 'the more X, the more Y'. 보여요 = it becomes visible/apparent

readingText.title: 성장의 기록 (A Record of Growth)
readingText.body: 처음 한국어를 시작했을 때는 발음이 너무 어렵더니 이제는 많이 익숙해졌어요. 그때는 ㄹ과 ㄴ의 차이도 못 느끼더니 지금은 자연스럽게 구별할 수 있어요. 공부할수록 더 많은 것이 보이기 시작했어요. 처음에는 드라마를 보면 한 마디도 못 알아듣더니 요즘은 대충 내용을 이해해요. 어휘가 늘수록 한국 문화도 더 깊이 느껴지는 것 같아요. 가끔 힘들 때도 있지만, 노력할수록 보람이 커지는 게 느껴져요. 한국어는 정말 보면 볼수록 매력 있는 언어예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When I first started Korean, the pronunciation was so hard, but now I've gotten very accustomed to it. Back then I couldn't even notice the difference between ㄹ and ㄴ, but now I can distinguish them naturally. The more I studied, the more things started to become visible. At first I couldn't understand a single word watching dramas, but lately I roughly understand the content. The more my vocabulary grows, the more deeply I seem to feel Korean culture too. Sometimes it's difficult, but the more I put in effort, the more I can feel the sense of fulfillment growing. Korean really is a language that gets more charming the more you look at it.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What specific listening change has the writer noticed about dramas?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 드라마를 보면 한 마디도 못 알아듣더니 요즘은 대충 내용을 이해해요 — they went from understanding zero words to roughly grasping the content

comprehensionQuestions.question: According to the writer, what grows alongside vocabulary growth?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 어휘가 늘수록 한국 문화도 더 깊이 느껴진다 — as vocabulary grows, their sense of Korean culture deepens proportionally

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all instances of -더니 and -(으)ㄹ수록 in the text. For each -더니, explain what was observed and what changed. For each -(으)ㄹ수록, identify the two proportional elements.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: -더니 instances: (1) 발음이 너무 어렵더니 — observed: pronunciation was difficult; changed: now accustomed. (2) ㄹ과 ㄴ의 차이도 못 느끼더니 — observed: couldn't distinguish sounds; changed: now distinguishes naturally. (3) 한 마디도 못 알아듣더니 — observed: understood nothing; changed: now grasps drama content. -(으)ㄹ수록 instances: (1) 공부할수록 더 많은 것이 보이기 시작했어요 — study ↑ → visibility of things ↑. (2) 어휘가 늘수록 한국 문화도 더 깊이 느껴지는 것 같아요 — vocabulary ↑ → cultural feeling ↑. (3) 노력할수록 보람이 커지는 게 느껴져요 — effort ↑ → fulfillment ↑. (4) 보면 볼수록 매력 있는 언어 — looking/exposure ↑ → charm ↑.

culturalNote.title: 보면 볼수록 — The most Korean way to express growing love for something
culturalNote.body: The phrase 보면 볼수록 (the more you look at/experience it) is a cultural formula in Korean for expressing that something deepens with time and exposure. Koreans use it constantly about food (먹을수록 맛있어 — the more you eat it, the better it tastes), people (알수록 좋은 사람이야 — the more you get to know them, the more you like them), and learning itself (한국어는 할수록 재미있어 — Korean gets more fun the more you do it). It reflects a cultural value of depth through perseverance — the appreciation that comes not at first glance, but after sustained engagement. When a Korean friend says 보면 볼수록 좋아 about something, it is one of the highest compliments possible: this thing rewards continued attention.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 매일 운동하___ 날씬해졌어요. (My friend kept exercising and then became slimmer.)
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a CAMERA REPLAY situation: you personally watched your friend exercise over time (camera rolling) and are reporting the observed result (became slimmer). -(으)ㄹ수록 would express a proportional scale (the more they exercise, the slimmer they get) — ongoing, not a reported sequence. -길래 would mean you reacted to something yourself, which doesn't fit here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어는 공부___ 더 재미있어요. (The more you study Korean, the more fun it gets.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The 'the more X, the more Y' proportional scale pattern requires -(으)ㄹ수록. 하다 has a vowel-class stem 하 → 할수록. -더니 would report an observed past change, not a proportional ongoing relationship. -해서 would give a simple cause-and-effect (I studied, so...) with no sense of proportionality.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는 열심히 운동하더니 건강해졌어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Plain -더니 is for observations about OTHERS. When the speaker describes the result of their OWN past action, the past tense form -았/었더니 is required. 운동하더니 with 저는 sounds like you somehow watched yourself from outside — unnatural. 운동했더니 = after I exercised (my own action), I found that I became healthier.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'The more experience you gain, the more confident you become.'
inlineExercises.hint: 쌓이다 has a vowel before the final ㄹ — how does -(으)ㄹ수록 attach? What word means 'confidence develops'?

inlineExercises.prompt: You saw your colleague looking exhausted every day for weeks, and then they took sick leave. Which sentence is most natural?
options: 동료가 매일 피곤해 보이더니 결국 병가를 냈어요.
inlineExercises.correct: 동료가 매일 피곤해 보이더니 결국 병가를 냈어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Option B (-더니) is correct: you personally observed your colleague looking tired over multiple days (camera rolling), then report the outcome (sick leave). Option A (-ㄹ수록) would mean 'the more tired they looked, the more sick leave they took' — a proportional scale that doesn't match the scenario. Option C (-길래) would mean the tiredness prompted YOU to take an action yourself, not describing their sick leave.

inlineExercises.prompt: 서울은 살___ 더 좋아지는 것 같아요. (The longer you live in Seoul, the more you come to like it.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 살다 is an ㄹ-stem verb. ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ and attach -(으)ㄹ수록 as -ㄹ수록: 살다 → 살 + -ㄹ수록 → 살수록. This expresses the proportional scale: time in Seoul ↑ → appreciation ↑. -더니 would report an observed change (you watched and noted a result), not a proportional relationship. -아서 is a simple cause connector.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses -(으)ㄹ수록 with the correct attachment?
inlineExercises.explanation: 읽다 ends in a consonant cluster (ㄱ final). Consonant-ending stems take -을수록: 읽 + 을수록 = 읽을수록. Option A (읽수록) skips the vowel buffer -을 needed after a consonant — this is wrong. Option C (읽어수록) confuses the polite ending 어요 with the -수록 attachment — 수록 never uses the -아/어 vowel; it attaches via -을/ㄹ.

bullets: -더니 = CAMERA REPLAY: you watched X happen (about someone else or a situation), then Y followed — use -았/었더니 for your OWN past actions
-(으)ㄹ수록 = SLIDING SCALE: as one thing increases, another increases proportionally — the -면 V-ㄹ수록 form is the most natural spoken version
Key test: if you're REPORTING a sequence you witnessed → -더니; if you're expressing a PROPORTIONAL relationship → -(으)ㄹ수록; if you REACTED ON THE SPOT to something you noticed → -길래
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: You've now connected complex ideas with nuance. The next step: passive and causative verbs — 문이 열렸어요 (the door opened) vs. 제가 문을 열었어요 (I opened the door). Understanding who acts and who is acted upon takes your Korean to a fully independent level.

grammarItems.title: Hangul syllable blocks
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Korean is written in syllable blocks. Each block usually has an initial consonant, a vowel, and sometimes a final consonant.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Study this before memorizing many words so you can read Korean from Hangul instead of depending on romanization.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Read each block left-to-right or top-to-bottom inside the square: 한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ, 글 = ㄱ + ㅡ + ㄹ.
grammarItems.contrastWith: Romanization is only a temporary pronunciation helper. It is not the real Korean spelling.

examples.en: Hangul / Korean writing
I eat.
I listen.

commonMistakes: Do not pronounce romanization as English spelling.
Do not pause between every syllable block when speaking.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean doesn't write letters in a straight line like English; instead it packs them into square syllable blocks, each holding one initial consonant, one vowel, and an optional final consonant (the 받침). Think of every block as one beat you say out loud: 한 is ㅎ+ㅏ+ㄴ, and 글 is ㄱ+ㅡ+ㄹ, so 한글 is just two beats. The vowel sits to the right of the initial (가) or underneath it (고), depending on the vowel's shape. The common beginner trap is trying to read the letters left-to-right across the whole word; always group them into blocks first, or words like 학교 become unreadable.

grammarItems.title: Topic and contrast
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to say what the sentence is about: “as for...” or “when we talk about this...”
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 은/는 when introducing yourself, setting the topic, comparing two things, or changing the topic.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 은 after a final consonant and 는 after a vowel: 학생은, 저는.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 이/가 points to the subject or new information. 은/는 sets the topic or contrast.

examples.en: As for me, I am a student.
As for today, I cannot go.
What is this?

commonMistakes: Do not translate 은/는 every time. It often just marks the topic.
Do not stack 도 after 은/는 as 저는도; say 저도.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 은/는 attaches to a noun to mark it as the topic, the thing the rest of the sentence is about, roughly like saying 'as for...' in English. Picture it as spotlighting one item and quietly comparing it to others: 저는 학생이에요 means 'as for me, I'm a student,' often hinting 'others might not be.' Use 은 after a final consonant (선생님은) and 는 after a vowel (저는). Beginners overuse it as a plain subject marker, but if you're introducing brand-new information or answering 'who did it?', you usually want 이/가 instead.

grammarItems.title: Subject and new information
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to mark the subject that exists, appears, hurts, or is being identified.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 이/가 with 있어요, 없어요, 아파요, 좋아요, and when the subject is new or important.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 이 after a final consonant and 가 after a vowel: 시간이, 친구가.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 은/는 is the topic. 이/가 points to the subject inside the sentence.

examples.en: I have time. / There is time.
A friend is coming.
My head hurts.

commonMistakes: Do not use 을/를 with 있어요 or 없어요 for the thing that exists.
Memorize common chunks first: 시간이 있어요, 문제가 없어요, 머리가 아파요.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 이/가 marks the grammatical subject, especially when something newly appears, exists, happens to you, or is the specific answer to a question. The intuition: 이/가 points a finger and says 'this one, right here,' while 은/는 steps back to set a theme. For example 비가 와요 ('rain is coming') and 누가 왔어요? — 친구가 왔어요 ('who came? a friend came') both spotlight fresh, specific information. Use 이 after a consonant (책이) and 가 after a vowel (친구가); a frequent slip is saying 저가 instead of the irregular 제가 for 'I.'

grammarItems.title: Object marker
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this after the thing that receives the action.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 을/를 with verbs like eat, drink, buy, read, write, study, watch, and take.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 을 after a final consonant and 를 after a vowel: 밥을, 커피를.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 이/가 marks the subject. 을/를 marks the object of an action.

examples.en: I eat rice / a meal.
I drink coffee.
I study Korean.

commonMistakes: Koreans often drop 을/를 in speech, but learners should understand it first.
Do not put 을/를 after places with 가요; say 학교에 가요.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 을/를 marks the direct object, the thing that directly receives the action of the verb, answering 'what?' or 'whom?' after a verb. A handy mental model: the object is whatever the verb is 'done to,' so in 물을 마셔요 ('I drink water'), 물 is being drunk. Attach 을 after a final consonant (밥을 먹어요) and 를 after a vowel (커피를 마셔요). In casual speech Koreans often drop this particle entirely (밥 먹어요), so don't panic when you don't hear it, but in writing and clear sentences it's the reliable signal of what's being acted on.

grammarItems.title: Time, destination, and existence place
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this for “to,” “at,” “in,” or “on” when the noun is a destination, time, or place where something exists.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 에 with 가요/와요 for destination, with times like 7시에, and with 있어요/없어요 for location.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 에 directly after the noun: 학교에, 집에, 7시에.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 에서 is where an action happens. 에 is the destination or existence location.

examples.en: I go to school.
I wake up at seven.
I am at home.

commonMistakes: For destination, use 에: 학교에 가요.
For the place of an action, use 에서: 학교에서 공부해요.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 에 is a quiet, all-purpose particle for time, a destination you're heading to, and the location where something simply exists. Think of it as pinning a noun to a point on a map or a clock: 학교에 가요 ('I go to school'), 세 시에 만나요 ('let's meet at three'), and 집에 있어요 ('I'm at home'). Notice it marks where something is, not where an action busily happens. The classic mistake is using 에 for the place of an action like eating or studying; for that you need 에서, so 도서관에 공부해요 is wrong and 도서관에서 공부해요 is right.

grammarItems.title: Action place and starting point
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this for the place where an action happens, or the place something starts from.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 에서 with study, work, eat, wait, buy, meet, and with came from.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 에서 after the place: 학교에서, 회사에서, 서울에서.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 에 is destination or existence place. 에서 is action place.

examples.en: I study at school.
I work at a company.
I came from Seoul.

commonMistakes: Do not say 학교에서 가요 for destination. Say 학교에 가요.
Use 에서 only when an action is happening there or something starts there.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 에서 marks the place where an action actively takes place, and it also means 'from' a starting point. The intuition: if a verb shows real activity happening somewhere, that location takes 에서, as in 카페에서 일해요 ('I work at the cafe') or 식당에서 먹어요 ('I eat at the restaurant'). For the 'from' sense, it shows origin: 한국에서 왔어요 ('I came from Korea'). The key beginner confusion is 에 versus 에서; remember that still existence (있다, 살다 sometimes) tends toward 에, while busy actions take 에서, so you sit 의자에 but study 도서관에서.

grammarItems.title: To a person
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this when a person receives an item, message, action, or question.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 에게 in neutral/written Korean, 한테 in everyday speech, and 께 for honorific speech.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach directly after the person: 친구에게, 저한테, 선생님께.
grammarItems.contrastWith: Use 에 for places. Use 에게/한테 for people or animals.

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: Who do I give it to?

examples.en: I give a gift to a friend.
Please give me the receipt.
I ask the teacher.

commonMistakes: Do not use 에게 for ordinary destinations. Say 학교에 가요, not 학교에게 가요.
Use 께 with respected people when you want honorific direction.

practiceItems.prompt: I give a gift to a friend.

grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 에게/한테 marks the person (or animal) who receives something, like a gift, a message, or an action directed at them, matching English 'to' someone. Picture an arrow flying toward a recipient: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요 ('I gave a present to my friend') or 엄마한테 전화했어요 ('I called mom'). The two are interchangeable in meaning, but 한테 sounds casual and conversational while 에게 feels a bit more formal or written. Two cautions for beginners: don't use these for places (a destination still takes 에, not 에게), and when speaking to someone you must respect, switch to the honorific form 께 instead.

grammarItems.title: Method, direction, and language
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this for by, with, toward, or in a language.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 로/으로 for transportation, payment, tools, direction, and language.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ ending. Use 으로 after most consonants: 카드로, 펜으로.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 을/를 marks the object. 로/으로 marks the method or tool.

examples.en: Can I pay by card?
I speak in Korean.
I go by subway.

commonMistakes: 카드로 사요 means buy by card, not buy a card.
Do not use 로/으로 for “with a friend”; use 친구하고 or 친구랑 for that meaning.
Do not confuse 로/으로 with destination 에.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: This particle marks the means, method, or direction of an action, and also the language something is spoken in. A handy mental model: attach it to a noun and think "by means of / toward / using" that noun. Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로 가요 = I go by bus; 집으로 = toward home) and 으로 after other consonants; for language, 한국어로 말해요 = I speak in Korean. The classic pitfall is confusing it with 에 (a fixed destination)—로/으로 stresses the route or tool, not the final spot itself.

grammarItems.title: Also / too / even
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to add one more thing to the same idea.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 도 for me too, this too, today too, and similar additions.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 도 after the word you are adding: 저도, 이것도, 오늘도.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 도 often replaces 은/는, 이/가, or 을/를 in that position.

examples.en: I am going too.
This too, please.
I study today too.

commonMistakes: Say 저도, not 저는도.
도 changes focus, so place it after the exact word you are adding.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 도 means "also," "too," or even "even," piling one more item onto what was already mentioned. Picture stacking things on a tray: whatever 도 attaches to gets added to the list. Crucially, 도 replaces the subject/topic and object particles—so you say 저도 학생이에요 (I'm a student too), never 저는도. Another example: 커피도 좋아요 = I like coffee too. The common beginner slip is keeping 은/는 or 이/가 in front of 도; just drop them and let 도 do the work.

Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

grammarItems.title: Only / just
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to limit the sentence to one thing.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 만 for only this, only water, only today, or just one thing.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 만 after the word you want to limit: 물만, 오늘만, 이것만.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 도 adds another thing. 만 limits the sentence to one thing.

examples.en: I only drink water.
I rest only today.
Only this, please.

commonMistakes: 만 changes focus. 물만 마셔요 means only water, not only drinking.
Place 만 after the word you want to limit.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 만 means "only" or "just," narrowing your statement down to one thing and excluding everything else. Think of it as drawing a tight circle around a single noun: nothing else counts. For example 물만 마셔요 = I drink only water, and 한 명만 왔어요 = only one person came. Unlike 도, 만 can sit with some particles (학교에서만 = only at school), but a frequent mistake is forcing 이/가 or 을/를 after it; usually 만 just replaces them, as in 이것만 주세요 = give me just this.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

grammarItems.title: From / until
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use these to mark the start and end of a time or place range.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 부터/까지 with schedules, opening hours, travel routes, and time ranges.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 부터 for the start and 까지 for the end: 9시부터 6시까지.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 에 marks one time or place. 부터/까지 marks a range.

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: From what time do you work?

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: I walk from here to the station.

examples.en: I work from 9 to 6.
I study from Monday to Friday.
I walk from here to the station.

commonMistakes: 까지 can mean until for time or as far as for place.
Do not use only 부터 if the ending point is important.

practiceItems.prompt: I walk from here to the station.

grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: This pair marks the start and end of a range: 부터 means "from" (a beginning point) and 까지 means "until/to" (an ending point), for both time and place. Imagine drawing a line with a starting dot and a finishing dot. A natural sentence is 아침부터 저녁까지 일해요 = I work from morning until evening. Note that for a starting *place* Korean usually prefers 에서 over 부터 (집에서 학교까지 = from home to school), so the pitfall is overusing 부터 for physical locations.

Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Want to do
endingItems.plainEnglish: Add 고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for your own wants: eating, going, resting, learning, buying, or trying something.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the dictionary form, then add 고 싶어요: 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Use N 주세요 to ask for an item. Use V고 싶어요 to talk about your desire.

examples.en: I want to drink coffee.
I want to go home.
I want to rest today.

commonMistakes: Do not use 고 싶어요 for adjectives like pretty or expensive.
For another person's wants, beginners can first quote or ask directly instead of overbuilding grammar.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: To say you want to do something, take a verb stem and add 고 싶어요. Mental model: 고 glues onto the action and 싶어요 adds the feeling of "I wish to." For example 먹다 (to eat) becomes 먹고 싶어요 = I want to eat, and 가다 becomes 가고 싶어요 = I want to go. Two pitfalls: this is for *your own* desire with action verbs, not for "I want a thing" (use 원해요 or 필요해요 for nouns), and when talking about someone else's want you switch to 고 싶어해요.

Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.

Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Can do / possible
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to say an action is possible because of skill, time, permission-like possibility, or circumstances.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for ability and practical possibility: can go, can eat, can read, can pay by card.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use ㄹ 수 있어요 after a vowel-ending stem and 을 수 있어요 after a consonant-ending stem.
endingItems.contrastWith: 못 + verb is the shorter everyday way to say cannot.

examples.en: I can go today.
I can read Hangul.
Can I pay by card?

commonMistakes: Do not use this for simple preference; use 고 싶어요 for want.
For quick speech, 카드 돼요? is a natural shortcut in stores.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending expresses ability or possibility—"can" or "it's possible to." Attach ㄹ 수 있어요 to a stem ending in a vowel and 을 수 있어요 to one ending in a consonant; literally 수 means a "way/method" that 있어요 (exists). For example 할 수 있어요 = I can do it, and 먹을 수 있어요 = I can eat it. To say you can't, flip 있어요 to 없어요 (갈 수 없어요 = I can't go); the common slip is forgetting the space before 수 or mixing up the ㄹ/을 choice.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Cannot / unable to
endingItems.plainEnglish: Put 못 before a verb to say you cannot do it because of ability, schedule, rules, health, or circumstances.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for real limits: schedule conflicts, food restrictions, language ability, health, rules, or practical impossibility.
endingItems.attachmentRule: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal polite verb. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun + 못 해요.
endingItems.contrastWith: 안 means you do not do something. 못 means you cannot do it.

examples.en: I cannot go today.
I cannot eat spicy food.
I cannot speak Korean well.

commonMistakes: Say 못 가요, not 못 가해요.
For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun + 못 해요: 공부 못 해요.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 못 goes right before a verb to say you *can't* do something because of a circumstance, lack of skill, or outside obstacle—not because you choose not to. Think of it as a wall blocking the action even though you might want to do it. For example 못 가요 = I can't go (something prevents me), and 수영 못 해요 = I can't swim. Don't confuse 못 with 안, which means you simply *don't* by choice (안 가요 = I'm not going); also note 하다 verbs split, so it's 수영 못 해요, not 못 수영해요.

endingItems.title: Have to / must
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to say an action is necessary or required.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for schedules, rules, health needs, work, school, and personal obligations.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use the 아/어 form of the verb, then add 야 해요: 가다 → 가야 해요, 먹다 → 먹어야 해요.
endingItems.contrastWith: V지 않아도 돼요 means the action is not necessary.

examples.en: I have to go early tomorrow.
I have to take medicine.
I have a test, so I have to study.

commonMistakes: Do not use this for a simple future plan; it sounds like obligation.
하다 verbs become 해야 해요.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending expresses necessity or obligation — the English "have to" or "must." Picture it as two ideas glued together: "if I do this action, then it's good/okay," so doing the thing is the only acceptable path. For example, 약을 먹어야 해요 means "I have to take my medicine," and 집에 가야 해요 means "I have to go home." A common beginner slip is forgetting the vowel harmony on the stem (가 + 아야 → 가야, not 가어야), and remember that for permission you switch to 아/어도 돼요, not this form.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: May I / is it okay to do?
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to ask whether an action is allowed or okay.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it before sitting, entering, taking photos, using a card, or doing anything where permission matters.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use the 아/어 form of the verb, then add 도 돼요?
endingItems.contrastWith: V지 마세요 tells someone not to do something.

examples.en: May I sit here?
May I take a photo?
Can I use a card?

commonMistakes: Use a question intonation when asking permission.
Do not confuse 돼요 with 되어요 spelling; 돼요 is the common form.

practiceItems.prompt: 사진 찍다 → may I take a photo?
카드 쓰다 → may I use a card?

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Use this to ask for or grant permission — "May I?" or "Is it okay if I...?" The intuition is "even if I do this action, it still turns out fine," so the 도 carries an "even" nuance and 돼요 means "it works / it's okay." You might ask 여기 앉아도 돼요? ("May I sit here?") and hear back 네, 앉아도 돼요 ("Yes, you may sit"). Beginners often confuse this with obligation: 가야 해요 means "I have to go," while 가도 돼요 means "I may go," so don't mix up 야 해요 and 도 돼요.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Please do
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to politely ask someone to do an action.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for help, opening, repeating, taking a photo, checking something, or saying something again.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use the 아/어 form of the verb, then add 주세요.
endingItems.contrastWith: N 주세요 asks for an item. V아/어 주세요 asks someone to do an action.

examples.en: Please help me.
Please say it again.
Please open the door.

commonMistakes: Do not use this for your own action; it asks someone else to act.
Add 좀 to soften many everyday requests.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is how you politely ask someone to do something for you — "please do (it)." Think of 주세요 as literally "please give me," so you are asking the listener to "give" you the favor of the action. For instance, 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 means "please wait a moment," and 천천히 말해 주세요 means "please speak slowly." Don't confuse this with 주세요 attached to a noun (물 주세요, "water please"); the 아/어 주세요 form needs a verb stem, and avoid it for prohibitions — "please don't" uses 지 마세요 instead.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Please do not
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this for polite prohibitions, warnings, signs, and careful requests.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when telling someone not to go, not to take photos, not to open something, or not to worry.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the dictionary form, then add 지 마세요.
endingItems.contrastWith: 안 V해요 says someone does not do an action. V지 마세요 tells someone not to do it.

examples.en: Please do not take photos here.
Please do not go yet.
Please do not worry.

commonMistakes: This can sound like an instruction, so use it carefully with people.
You will often read it on signs before you need to say it yourself.

practiceItems.prompt: 사진 찍다 → please do not take photos

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending tells someone politely NOT to do an action — you'll see it on signs and hear it from staff. Mentally, 지 마세요 attaches the "stop/don't" verb 말다 to any action, like putting a red circle over a picture. Common examples are 만지지 마세요 ("please don't touch") and 사진을 찍지 마세요 ("please don't take photos"). A frequent mistake is trying to negate with 안 here — you can't say 안 만지세요 for a command; prohibitions specifically use the 지 마세요 pattern, and note the stem keeps its 지 with no vowel harmony.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Because / so
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to connect a reason to a result.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for simple reasons: busy so cannot go, sick so rest, expensive so do not buy.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use 아서 after many ㅏ/ㅗ stems and 어서 after many other stems. 하다 becomes 해서.
endingItems.contrastWith: 고 simply connects ideas; 아서/어서 explains why.

examples.en: I am busy, so I cannot go.
I am sick, so I rest.
Sorry I am late.

commonMistakes: Avoid using 아서/어서 before commands in careful textbook grammar.
Keep the first clause short as a beginner.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This connector links a reason to its result — "because" or "so." Imagine the first clause naturally flowing downhill into the second: the cause comes first, then the effect, with no tense marking on the 아서/어서 part itself. For example, 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요 means "I was hungry, so I ate," and 비가 와서 집에 있었어요 means "because it rained, I stayed home." The big pitfall: never use 아서/어서 with commands or suggestions (don't say 피곤해서 쉬세요) — for those reasons you need 으니까 instead.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: And / and then
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use 고 to connect two actions or descriptions.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for sequence or listing: eat and go, study and work, cheap and good.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the first verb or adjective, then add 고.
endingItems.contrastWith: 아서/어서 gives a reason. 고 usually just connects.

examples.en: I eat and go to school.
I study and work.
This bag is cheap and good.

commonMistakes: 고 does not always mean a strict time order; context decides.
Do not make beginner sentences too long.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This connector strings actions or descriptions together — "and" or "and then." Think of 고 as a simple chain link: it can list qualities at the same time (이 방은 크고 밝아요, "this room is big and bright") or put events in sequence (밥을 먹고 학교에 갔어요, "I ate and then went to school"). The key intuition is that 고 stays plain — you don't conjugate tense on it; the final verb carries the tense for the whole sentence. Beginners sometimes reach for 고 to mean "because"; for cause-and-effect you want 아서/어서 instead.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: If / when
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use 면 to set a condition.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for time, price, health, permission, and simple advice.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the verb or adjective, then add 면.
endingItems.contrastWith: 아서/어서 gives a reason that already exists. 면 gives a condition.

examples.en: If you have time, please call.
If it is expensive, I do not buy it.
If you are sick, you should rest.

commonMistakes: Context can make 면 sound like if or when.
Keep the condition short at first.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Attach 면 (or 으면 after a consonant) to set up a condition — "if" or "when." The mental model is a doorway: "once this first situation happens, the second part follows." For example, 시간이 있으면 만나요 means "if you have time, let's meet," and 봄이 오면 꽃이 펴요 means "when spring comes, flowers bloom." Note that Korean uses one 면 for both "if" and "when," so context decides; a common slip is forgetting the 으 after a consonant stem (먹다 → 먹으면, not 먹면).
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: I will / speaker promise
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this when the speaker decides or promises what they will do.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when volunteering, responding to someone, leaving, waiting, or promising a call.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use ㄹ게요 after a vowel-ending stem and 을게요 after a consonant-ending stem.
endingItems.contrastWith: ㄹ/을 거예요 is a future plan. ㄹ/을게요 is the speaker's decision in response to the situation.

examples.en: I will do it.
I will wait here.
I will call later.

commonMistakes: Use this only for what the speaker will do.
Do not use it to predict another person's action.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending voices the speaker's own decision or promise — "I will (do it)." The crucial intuition is that it's a commitment made to the listener, often reacting to them, not a neutral forecast about the future. For example, 제가 할게요 means "I'll do it (so don't worry)," and 내일 전화할게요 means "I'll call you tomorrow (I promise)." The classic pitfall is using it for other people or for predictions — you can't say 비가 올게요 for "it will rain"; 을게요 only works with first-person "I," and for plain predictions use 을 거예요 instead.
studyOrder: Read the full example first.
Find the noun, verb stem, or adjective stem that changes.
Say the frame aloud with one substitution.
Check the common mistake before making a new sentence.

endingItems.title: Describing a noun: now vs later
endingItems.plainEnglish: Put a describing word in front of a noun. The ㄴ/은 form says how something is right now; the ㄹ/을 form says how it will or might be.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it whenever a describing word comes before a noun: 뜨거운 물 (hot water), 큰 가방 (a big bag), 매운 음식 (spicy food).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Adjective + ㄴ after a vowel (크다 → 큰), 은 after a consonant (작다 → 작은). ㅂ-irregulars become 운 (맵다 → 매운, 쉽다 → 쉬운); 있다/없다 use 는 (맛있다 → 맛있는). For the will/might sense, use ㄹ after a vowel and 을 after a consonant (뜨거울, 작을).
endingItems.contrastWith: 뜨거운 물 = water that is hot right now; 뜨거울 물 = water that will become hot. Same adjective, different time feeling.

examples.en: Please give me hot water.
It is a small room.
I like spicy food.
It is delicious coffee.

commonMistakes: Don't use the ㄹ/을 form for present description: it is 뜨거운 물 (hot now), not 뜨거울 물, when the water is hot right now.
ㅂ-irregular adjectives change to 운: 맵다 → 매운 (not 맵은), 쉽다 → 쉬운.
studyOrder: Pick the adjective and the noun it describes.
Choose the ㄴ/은 form for how it is now.
Apply the ㅂ-irregular (운) or 있다 (는) change if needed.
Use ㄹ/을 only when you mean it will or might be that way.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When a describing word sits in front of a noun, Korean changes its ending. The ㄴ/은 form describes how something is right now: 큰 가방 (a big bag), 작은 방 (a small room), 매운 음식 (spicy food). The intuition is a snapshot of the present — so 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot at this moment. Switch to the ㄹ/을 form only for something that will or might become that way later, which is why 뜨거울 물 (water that will get hot) feels different from 뜨거운 물. Watch two traps: ㅂ-irregular adjectives use 운 (맵다 → 매운, not 맵은), and 있다/없다 words use 는 (맛있다 → 맛있는).

endingItems.title: When the stem changes
endingItems.plainEnglish: Some stems reshape their last letter before a vowel ending. Learn the polite form as the anchor and the rest follows.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to understand why 맵다 becomes 매워요, 듣다 becomes 들어요, 크다 becomes 커요, and 살다 becomes 삽니다.
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel (맵다 → 매워요, 매운); ㄷ → ㄹ before a vowel (듣다 → 들어요); ㅡ drops before 아/어 (크다 → 커요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다, 사는).
endingItems.contrastWith: Regular stems just add the ending (먹다 → 먹어요). Irregular stems change the last letter first, so don't build them literally (not 맵어요, not 듣어요).

examples.en: The soup is spicy.
I listen to the radio.
(Someone) is tall.
I live in Seoul.

commonMistakes: Don't conjugate irregular stems literally: 맵다 → 매워요 (not 맵어요), 듣다 → 들어요 (not 듣어요).
The change only happens before a vowel ending; before a consonant the stem stays (듣고, 듣습니다).
studyOrder: Spot the irregular marker on the card (ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅡ/ㄹ).
Memorize the polite form as the anchor.
Apply the change only before a vowel ending.
Keep the plain stem before consonant endings.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Most Korean stems just take an ending (먹다 → 먹어요), but a few reshape their last letter before a vowel ending, and that surprises beginners. Four common ones: ㅂ becomes 우 (맵다 → 매워요, 매운), ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 → 들어요), ㅡ simply drops before 아/어 (크다 → 커요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요), and ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다, 사는). The safe strategy is to memorize the polite -아/어요 form as your anchor and build outward from it. The change only happens before a vowel ending — before a consonant the stem stays put (듣고, 듣습니다) — so never conjugate them literally as 맵어요 or 듣어요.

endingItems.title: Past Tense
endingItems.plainEnglish: Shows that an action or state already happened or is finished.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use to talk about completed past actions or past states, e.g. 어제 영화를 봤어요 (I watched a movie yesterday).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요 (가다→갔어요, 좋다→좋았어요). Otherwise add 었어요 (먹다→먹었어요, 마시다→마셨어요). 하다 verbs become 했어요 (공부하다→공부했어요). Irregular stems shift: ㄷ irregular 듣다→들었어요, ㅂ irregular 춥다→추웠어요, ㅡ drops 바쁘다→바빴어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with present V-아/어요 (지금 먹어요 = I am eating now) versus past V-았/었어요 (아까 먹었어요 = I ate earlier).

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I ate bread in the morning.
I studied Korean over the weekend.
The weather was really cold yesterday.

commonMistakes: Using 았어요 after a non ㅏ/ㅗ vowel, like saying 먹았어요 instead of the correct 먹었어요.
Saying 하았어요 instead of the contracted irregular form 했어요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ
Add 았어요 or 었어요, or use 했어요 for 하다
Apply irregular changes if the stem is irregular
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The past tense in Korean is built right onto the verb stem, and the only real choice is whether to add 았어요 or 었어요.
